name: Light Reconstruction via Linear Transport Operator
head: Environmental Illumination Optimization, Light Source Coefficient Optimization
body: This method optimizes environmental illumination (outgoing radiance from the environment) to match a desired volume appearance, assuming the volume's intrinsic properties (emission, albedo, extinction) are spatially varying but fixed during the optimization process. It differs from sibling methods like Emission Reconstruction by treating the light source coefficients as the unknown variables rather than the volume properties, solving for the lighting that best explains the observed pixel values through a linear transport operator. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N constraint pixels (desired observations o), a volume with fixed properties, and M basis functions modeling the light sources (e.g., directional lights sampled from an environment map). Outputs: An M-dimensional coefficient vector \tilde{L}o representing the optimized outgoing radiance from the environment. Data Structures: Transport Operator T: A dense matrix of size N \times M. Unlike the sparse weight matrices used in volume parameter reconstruction, T is dense because it encodes complete light scattering in the scene. Light Volumes (voli): For Strategy 2, M precomputed volumes are stored. Each voli contains the radiance contribution of the i-th light basis function at every voxel in the scene. Formulas: The problem is formulated as a least-squares minimization: \min{\tilde{L}o} ||T \tilde{L}o - o||^2 where: o is the vector of desired observation values for N pixels. T is the linear light transport operator matrix of size N \times M. \tilde{L}o is the M-dimensional vector of light source coefficients. Parameters: M: Number of basis functions. Typical value: ~16 coefficients are sufficient to capture light influence. N: Number of constraint pixels. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Construct the operator T or the intermediate light volumes. Two strategies are available: Strategy 1 (Store T): Compute the full N \times M matrix T. For each light coefficient i, render the scene with only that coefficient active (value 1, others 0) to fill the i-th column of T. Strategy 2 (Light Volumes): For each light coefficient i, light the entire volume with that coefficient active to create a "light volume" voli. Store these M volumes. 2. Optimization Loop: Solve the linear system using an iterative solver (e.g., Conjugate Gradient). Each iteration requires two matrix-vector multiplications: Forward Pass (T \tilde{L}o): Compute the predicted observation. If using Strategy 1: Perform standard matrix-vector multiplication. If using Strategy 2: For each constraint pixel, shoot a ray through the volume. Gather values from all precomputed light volumes voli along the ray path and sum them weighted by \tilde{L}o. Backward Pass (T^T r): Distribute the residual r = o - T \tilde{L}o back to the light coefficients. If using Strategy 1: Perform standard matrix-vector multiplication with the transpose. If using Strategy 2: For each constraint pixel, distribute its residual value to the light coefficients. This is analogous to volume optimization back-projection, but the values are accumulated into the light coefficient vector \tilde{L}o rather than voxel properties. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightreconstruction(constraintpixels, volume, numbasisfunctions=16, maxiterations=100, learningrate=0.01, epsilon=1e-6): """ Optimizes light source coefficients to match constraint pixels. Uses Strategy 2 (Light Volumes) for memory efficiency. """ M = numbasisfunctions N = len(constraintpixels) # Precomputation: Generate light volumes # vol[i] is a 3D array representing the radiance contribution # of the i-th basis function at every voxel. lightvolumes = precomputelightvolumes(volume, M) # Initialize coefficients Lo = [0.0] M # Optimization loop (simplified gradient descent for clarity) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Forward Pass: y = T Lo predictedobs = [0.0] N for pidx in range(N): ray = constraintpixels[pidx] accumulated = 0.0 # Gather values from all light volumes along the ray for i in range(M): contribution = integratelightvolume(lightvolumes[i], ray) accumulated += Lo[i] contribution predictedobs[pidx] = accumulated # Compute residual residual = [constraintpixels[pidx] - predictedobs[pidx] for pidx in range(N)] # Backward Pass: grad = T^T residual grad = [0.0] M for pidx in range(N): r = residual[pidx] if abs(r) < epsilon: continue ray = constraintpixels[pidx] # Distribute residual to each light coefficient based on # the light volume's contribution at this pixel for i in range(M): sensitivity = integratelightvolume(lightvolumes[i], ray) grad[i] += r sensitivity # Update coefficients for i in range(M): Lo[i] -= learningrate grad[i] return Lo def precomputelightvolumes(volume, M): """ For each of the M basis functions, render the volume with that light source active to create a light volume. """ volumes = [] for i in range(M): # Create a temporary environment map with only the i-th direction active tempenv = [0.0] M tempenv[i] = 1.0 # Render the volume with this lighting to get the contribution vol = rendervolumewithlighting(volume, tempenv) volumes.append(vol) return volumes def integratelightvolume(lightvol, ray): """ Integrates the light volume along a ray. Equivalent to the transport of the specific light basis function. """ total = 0.0 for t in ray.steps: voxelval = lightvol[ray.sample(t)] transmittance = ray.transmittance(t) total += voxelval transmittance return total def rendervolumewithlighting(volume, envmap): """ Renders the volume with the given environment map. Returns a 3D array of radiance contributions per voxel. """ return [[0.0] volume.depth for in range(volume.height)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: The operator T is not sparse; it encodes complete light scattering. On-the-fly evaluation is too slow, requiring precomputation. Memory: Strategy 1 (storing T) has memory linear in N (pixels). Strategy 2 (light volumes) has memory consumption linear in the size of the volume times the number of light coefficients. Constant Volume Properties: The method assumes volume properties are constant during optimization. If they vary, the operator T is no longer constant, and this linear approach fails. Reconstruction of the local radiative source term j(\mathbf{r}) after the attenuation coefficient \alpha(\mathbf{r}) is determined, solving the remaining unknown integral term in the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). Solve the linear system \mathbf{G} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{J} using an optimization approach to reconstruct \mathbf{J}, then compute I(\mathbf{r}) using the previously determined \alpha(\mathbf{r}). The unknown term is approximated by a discretized sum: \mathbf{G} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{J}, where \mathbf{G} is the known vector of the RHS of the previous equation, \mathbf{H} is the attenuation-weighted geometric projection matrix constructed from LODs, and \mathbf{J} is the vector of the local radiative source term j(\mathbf{r}). Time Complexity: Depends on the precomputation strategy. Strategy 1 requires M full volume renders for precomputation. Strategy 2 requires M full volume renders for precomputation. Optimization iterations require O(N \cdot M) work per iteration for Strategy 2 (ray traversal through M volumes) or O(N \cdot M) for Strategy 1 (matrix-vector multiply). Memory Complexity: Strategy 1: O(N \cdot M) to store T. Strategy 2: Memory consumption grows linearly in the size of the volume times the number of light coefficients. Strengths: Allows independent optimization of lighting without altering volume geometry or material properties. Efficient if M is small (~16). Limitations: Requires precomputation. Cannot handle dynamic volume properties. Dense matrix operations can be memory-intensive for high-resolution constraints. When to use: When the volume structure is known and fixed, but the lighting needs to be adjusted to match a target appearance (e.g., stylization). This method is described in. It builds on the linearity of light transport in participating media, allowing the transport operator to be separated from the source terms. The approach is analogous to tomographic reconstruction but applied to the light source coefficients rather than the volume density. name: Basic GPU D2VR Framework
head: D2VR Framework
body: The Basic GPU D2VR Framework is a method for GPU-accelerated Direct Volume Rendering (D2VR) that reconstructs a 3D volume from 2D projections distributed around a circular orbit. It specifically enables the reconstruction of image-aligned volume slices in front-to-back order, a structural requirement that facilitates occlusion culling and empty space skipping during rendering. It differs from general GPU ray casting by explicitly managing the geometric relationship between projection sets and viewing vectors to maintain slice alignment for acceleration techniques. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 2D projection images. Output: A rendered 3D volume visualization. Data Structures: The framework organizes projections into two sets: a Viewing set (V-set) and a Support set (S-set). These sets are used to reconstruct two corresponding texture stacks: the Viewing stack (V-stack) and the Support stack (S-stack). Numbered Steps: 1. Projection Organization: Distribute M projections around a circular orbit. If the projections are perpendicular to the x-z plane, divide them into a V-set and an S-set based on which stack they are more perpendicular to. 2. Viewing Vector Check: Determine if the current viewing vector is within the \pm 45^\circ range perpendicular to the x-z plane. If within range, proceed with the Projective Texture Method. If outside range, switch to the Texture Spreading Method or provide an orthogonal set of projections (e.g., around the x-y plane). 3. Stack Assignment (Projective Texture Method): Rotate the volume proxy polygons so that one slice set is perpendicular and the other is orthogonal to the viewing vector. Define the perpendicular slices as the Viewing (V) stack and the orthogonal slices as the Support (S) stack. Divide the projections into the V-set (projections more perpendicular to the V-stack) and the S-set (projections more perpendicular to the S-stack). 4. Reconstruction: Reconstruct the S-stack from the S-set projections. Reconstruct the V-stack from the V-set projections. The reconstruction aims to produce image-aligned volume slices. 5. Rendering Preparation: The reconstructed slices are arranged in front-to-back order relative to the viewing direction to enable occlusion culling. Formulas: M = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot N: The required number of projections M for maximal volume resolution N^3 without aliasing using parallel beam data. Parameters: N: The desired volume resolution dimension (N \times N \times N). Viewing Angle Constraint: The viewing vector must be tilted within \pm 45^\circ perpendicular to the reference plane (e.g., the x-z plane) when using the projective texture method. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Angle Exceedance: If the viewing vector exceeds the \pm 45^\circ limit, the projective texture method fails to maintain alignment. The implementer must either switch methods or provide additional orthogonal projection sets. Tuy’s Condition: If a single method is to be used for all viewpoints, two orthogonal half-orbits of projections, equally spaced in angle, must be provided to satisfy Tuy’s condition for exact 3D reconstruction. Extends the basic framework with occlusion culling and empty space skipping for interactive speeds. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The framework is designed to enable occlusion culling, which optimizes rendering performance by skipping empty space. name: GPU-Accelerated D2VR
body: A GPU-accelerated implementation of Direct 2D Volume Rendering (D2VR) that incorporates occlusion culling and empty space skipping to achieve interactive or near-interactive rendering speeds. It builds on Basic GPU D2VR Framework but generalizes it substantially to allow reconstruction of arbitrary oriented volumes and incorporates acceleration techniques to limit reconstruction effort to visible and non-occluded samples. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 2D projection images and arbitrary image plane orientation parameters. Outputs: Rendered 2D volume image. Data Structures: Volume data structure aligned with the arbitrary image plane. Depth correction factors applied during backprojection. Algorithm Steps: 1. Filtering: Filter acquired images along their columns using a ramp filter (e.g., Shepp-Logan, RamLak) in the frequency domain. 2. Backprojection: Backproject filtered data into the volume. For cone-beam geometry, multiply weights w{ij} by a depth correction factor: w{ij}(d) = w{ij} \frac{a^2}{d^2} where a is a constant and d is the depth. 3. Volume Alignment: Generate a matrix of samples exactly aligned with the arbitrary image plane, generalizing the CT framework to support arbitrary orientations. 4. Ray Casting: Run the entire ray advancement in a single fragment shader loop. 5. Acceleration: Apply occlusion culling and empty space skipping to limit reconstruction effort to only visible and non-occluded samples. Parameters: Filter type: Shepp-Logan, RamLak. Target framerate: 2 frames/s and more for realistic dataset sizes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary orientation requires precise alignment of the sample matrix with the image plane. Depth correction factor must be correctly applied for cone-beam geometry. This family encompasses techniques designed to optimize the Direct Volume Ray Casting (D2VR) pipeline on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) by leveraging hardware-specific features such as early Z-culling. The primary problem it solves is the computational bottleneck inherent in fragment-based volume rendering, where the high cost of shading often negates the benefits of hardware occlusion culling. What sets this family apart is its focus on the ratio between computational effort per fragment and the potential for early termination; methods are evaluated based on how effectively their shading complexity interacts with early Z-cull mechanisms to achieve interactive or near-interactive rendering speeds. Performance: Enables framerates of 2 frames/s and more for realistic dataset sizes. Strengths: Interactive or near-interactive speed; supports arbitrary volume orientations; efficient via occlusion culling and empty space skipping. Limitations: Original D2VR method was comparatively slow; this implementation addresses that but performance depends on dataset size and acceleration effectiveness. The method builds on the RapidCT framework for GPU-accelerated CT reconstruction. It was proposed to address the slow rendering speed of the original D2VR method, which was a shortcoming for clinical deployment. name: GPU D2VR Acceleration Methods
body: This family encompasses techniques designed to optimize the Direct Volume Ray Casting (D2VR) pipeline on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) by leveraging hardware-specific features such as early Z-culling. The primary problem it solves is the computational bottleneck inherent in fragment-based volume rendering, where the high cost of shading often negates the benefits of hardware occlusion culling. What sets this family apart is its focus on the ratio between computational effort per fragment and the potential for early termination; methods are evaluated based on how effectively their shading complexity interacts with early Z-cull mechanisms to achieve interactive or near-interactive rendering speeds. It builds on GPU-Accelerated D2VR. The core principle shared by all methods in this family is the exploitation of the GPU's early Z-cull mechanism. Early Z-culling discards fragments that are occluded by previously rendered fragments closer to the camera, thereby saving shading computations. However, the effectiveness of this optimization is contingent upon the computational effort required per fragment. Low computational effort ratio with respect to a single fragment can offset the advantage brought by the early z-cull mechanism. Therefore, acceleration strategies are most beneficial when the fragment shader performs significant computation, such as gradient estimation or complex transfer functions, which increases the computational effort ratio. The spreading method distributes volume data across multiple fragments or uses a rendering approach that results in a longer, more computationally intensive fragment shader. It is chosen when high shading complexity (e.g., density and gradient calculations) is required, as it benefits significantly from early Z-culling due to the high cost of shading each fragment. Compared to projective texture mapping, it achieves better speed-ups in scenarios where occlusion is frequent because the savings from skipping expensive shading outweigh the culling overhead. The projective texture method maps volume data onto geometric primitives using texture mapping, imposing relatively light rendering efforts on individual fragments. It is chosen for simpler shading requirements or when hardware texture sampling is highly optimized. It benefits less from early Z-culling compared to the spreading method because the low computational effort per fragment means the advantage gained from skipping shading is minimal, potentially being offset by the fixed costs of fragment processing. The analysis of these acceleration methods originates from research on GPU-accelerated D2VR frameworks, specifically detailed in the paper "GPU-Accelerated D2VR". The study was conducted on an AMD Athlon 2.2GHz dual-core PC with 1GB RAM and a GeForce 6800 GT, using CT datasets with viewport sizes of 128x128 or 256x256. The work highlights the trade-off between shading complexity and hardware culling efficiency, noting a speedup factor of 1.5 for density-only D2VR over density+gradient D2VR, indicating that additional shading costs reduce the effectiveness of acceleration. name: Physics-Based Image Formation Models
body: Physics-Based Image Formation Models define the differentiable forward operator \mathcal{P} that maps a 3D (or 4D) volume representation to 2D projection images, serving as the core component in inverse rendering pipelines. Unlike generic differentiable renderers, these models are tailored to specific physical acquisition modalities (e.g., X-ray absorption, ultrasound wave propagation) to ensure physical consistency and computational efficiency. They distinguish themselves from siblings like Neural Adaptive Tomography by explicitly modeling the underlying physics (such as linear absorption or coupled wave equations) rather than relying solely on learned neural priors or adaptive sampling strategies. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. Represents a continuously deforming 3D object as a 4D density function h(x, y, z, t), discretized into Nk static frames [3268-space-time-image-formation-model.md]. It differs from warp-based methods by treating time as a direct dimension of the density field, allowing for topology changes but potentially suffering from temporal inconsistency [3268-space-time-image-formation-model.md]. Choose this when reconstructing dynamic objects where deformation is complex and topology changes are expected [3268-space-time-image-formation-model.md]. A differentiable forward model for synthesizing ultrasound B-mode images by solving coupled forward and backward wave amplitude equations across voxel interfaces using a sparse linear system [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md]. It distinguishes itself from standard ray-marching volume rendering by modeling wave physics rather than simple line integrals of density [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md]. Choose this for differentiable ultrasound rendering where acoustic wave propagation physics are critical [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md]. Reconstruction of a 3D density field from images using an optical absorption-only model, reducing the problem to a linear optimization problem solvable via DiffDVR. Step: Multi-resolution optimization: Start with volume resolution 32^3. Double the resolution in each dimension after 10 iterations. Perform optimization for 50 iterations at the highest resolution. Formula: Loss function: Same L{\text{total}} as TF reconstruction, but the smoothing prior is computed on reconstructed volume densities in 3D with \lambda = 0.5. Parameter: Views: 64 uniformly sampled views on a surrounding sphere. Image Resolution: 512^2. Reconstructed Volume Resolution: 256^3. Step size: 0.2 voxels during reconstruction. Optimizer: Adam with batch size 8 and learning rate 0.3. Number: Performance comparison for human skull dataset: ASTRA takes 53 seconds, DiffDVR takes ~12 minutes, Mitsuba takes multiple hours. The family originates from the application of differentiable rendering techniques to tomographic reconstruction. Early work focused on adapting standard volume rendering pipelines (like DiffDVR) to inverse problems, demonstrating that absorption-only models could be solved using differentiable optimizers, though at higher computational cost than algebraic methods. The field has since expanded to include specialized physics-based models for modalities like ultrasound, where simple ray-tracing is insufficient to capture wave phenomena B-mode Image Reconstruction. name: Space-Time Image Formation Model
head: 4D density function model
body: The Space-Time Image Formation Model represents a continuously deforming 3D object as a 4D density function h(x, y, z, t), discretized into a sequence of Nk frames, each treated as an approximately static 3D volume. It formulates tomographic reconstruction for dynamic scenes as a block-diagonal linear system, solving for each frame's volume independently within the forward projection operator. Unlike warp-based methods that separate geometry into a canonical form and a dynamic transformation, this approach uses a single unified representation to directly regress dynamic properties, making it tolerant of topology changes but prone to time inconsistency. Inputs: Np: Total number of captured projection images. Nk: Number of reconstructed frames (time steps), where Nk \le Np. N\theta: Number of projections contributing to each frame. Typically N\theta = Np / Nk. M: Number of pixels in a single projection image. Nv: Number of voxels in the 3D grid for each frame. Outputs: \mathbf{f}: The reconstructed 4D density volume, represented as a vector in \mathbb{R}^{Nv Nk}. Data Structures: The 4D density volume is described by a column vector \mathbf{f} composed of Nk sub-vectors \mathbf{f}t, where each \mathbf{f}t \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv} represents the 3D volume at the t-th time step: \mathbf{f} = \{\mathbf{f}0, \mathbf{f}1, \dots, \mathbf{f}{Nk-1}\} The measured data is a vector \mathbf{p} containing the sinogram data for all frames: \mathbf{p} = \{\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \dots, \mathbf{p}{Nk-1}\} where \mathbf{p}t \in \mathbb{R}^{N\theta M} is the vector of measured data for frame t. Formulas: The tomography problem is expressed as a linear system \mathbf{A} \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{p}. The matrix \mathbf{A} is a block diagonal matrix where each block \mathbf{A}t \in \mathbb{R}^{N\theta M \times Nv} models the Radon transform operator for the N\theta projections contributing to the t-th frame: \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{A}0 & & & \\ & \ddots & & \\ & & \mathbf{A}t & \\ & & & \ddots \\ & & & & \mathbf{A}{Nk-1} \end{pmatrix} The forward projection for each frame computes \hat{\mathbf{p}}t = \mathbf{A}t \mathbf{f}t. Steps: 1. Discretization: Divide the temporal domain into Nk frames. 2. Projection Assignment: Assign N\theta unique projection angles to each frame. The total number of projections Np is distributed such that N\theta = Np / Nk. All projection angles are unique across the entire sequence. 3. Forward Projection: For each frame t, compute the predicted measurements \hat{\mathbf{p}}t by applying the Radon transform matrix \mathbf{A}t to the current volume estimate \mathbf{f}t. 4. Optimization: Minimize the loss function defined in the parent framework to update \mathbf{f}. 5. Reconstruction: Solve the ill-posed inverse problem to recover \mathbf{f}. Parameters: Nk: Number of reconstructed frames. Constraint: Nk \le Np. N\theta: Number of projections per frame. Typical value: N\theta = Np / Nk. N{min}: Minimum number of projections for acceptable quality. Values such as N{min} = 10 are noted for achieving results. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: The problem is ill-posed, especially when few projections are used per frame (N\theta is small). Time Inconsistency: Independent frame reconstruction can lead to temporal discontinuities. Sampling Strategy: The sampling strategy is decoupled from the magnitude of deformation. The number of reconstructed frames Nk is independent of the number of capture rounds and can be chosen post-capture. Static Assumption: The model assumes each frame is approximately static. If deformation is too rapid within a frame's time window, reconstruction quality degrades. Models dynamic scenes by extending the query space to include time as a direct input, omitting explicit deformation networks. Unlike warp-based methods, it uses a single unified function to regress dynamic properties, tolerating topology changes but suffering from time inconsistency. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of frames Nk and the cost of the Radon transform \mathbf{A}t. Memory Complexity: O(Nv Nk) to store the 4D volume vector \mathbf{f}. Strengths: Tolerant of topology changes; sampling strategy is decoupled from deformation magnitude; Nk can be chosen post-capture. Limitations: Prone to time inconsistency; ill-posed with few projections per frame; assumes approximate static geometry per frame. When to use: When topology changes are expected, or when post-capture choice of temporal resolution is desired. When not to use: When high temporal consistency is required without additional regularization, or when deformation is too rapid for the "static frame" assumption. The Space-Time Image Formation Model was introduced in the context of space-time tomographic reconstruction of deforming objects. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D objects that undergo continuous deformation over time by discretizing the 4D density function into static frames. The approach allows for the reconstruction of dynamic scenes using a sequence of projections, where each frame is reconstructed from a subset of the total projections. name: Space-time representations
body: Space-time representations model dynamic scenes by extending the query space of the rendering function to include time, omitting the explicit deformation network used in warp-based methods. Unlike warp-based approaches that separate geometry into a static canonical form and a dynamic transformation, space-time methods use a single unified function to directly regress dynamic properties by conditioning a 3D representation with a time component. This approach is tolerant of topology changes and can model a wider range of motion but is prone to time inconsistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query tuple q = (p, \mathbf{d}, t), where p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, and t is the time coordinate. Output: A property vector \xi (e.g., color, density, or feature vector). Data Structures: The representation is implemented as either a neural implicit model conditioned on a time variable, a set of 3D Gaussians with time-dependent parameters, or an explicit feature grid. Algorithm: 1. Define the Query Function: The method uses a single unified function to directly regress dynamic properties. Two common formulations exist: Formulation A (Time in Main Function): f{\theta}: (\gamma(p, \mathbf{d}, t)) \rightarrow \xi \quad (12) Here, \gamma is an encoding function that processes position, direction, and time jointly, and \xi is the output property. Formulation B (Time in Encoding): f: (\text{enc}(p, t), [\text{enc}(\mathbf{d})]) \rightarrow \xi \quad (13) Here, the encoding function \text{enc} depends on time, while the main network f processes the encoded spatial and directional features. 2. Discretize Time: Divide the time interval into equally spaced time slots. 3. Compute Features at Time Slots: Compute features at these discrete time slots using an MLP-based neural network or an explicit feature grid. 4. Interpolate for Arbitrary Time: Compute the feature of a point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 at any time t by interpolating between the features of the neighboring time slots. 5. Enforce Time Consistency (Optional): Enforce time consistency locally by using flow fields, which define forward and backward mappings between neighboring time steps when available. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryspacetimerepresentation(p, d, t, timeslots, encnet, mainnet): """ Query a space-time representation for a property at position p, direction d, and time t. Implements Formulation B: time-dependent encoding with interpolation between slots. """ # 1. Find neighboring time slots k = 0 while k < len(timeslots) - 1 and timeslots[k + 1] <= t: k += 1 tk = timeslots[k] tk1 = timeslots[min(k + 1, len(timeslots) - 1)] # 2. Compute features at neighboring slots using an MLP or feature grid featk = encnet(concatenate(p, tk)) featk1 = encnet(concatenate(p, tk1)) # 3. Interpolate features for arbitrary time t alpha = (t - tk) / (tk1 - tk) if tk1 != tk else 0.0 interpolatedfeat = featk + alpha (featk1 - featk) # 4. Encode direction (static) encd = encnet(d) # 5. Main network regression xi = mainnet(concatenate(interpolatedfeat, encd)) return xi Parameters: Time slots: Equally spaced intervals used to discretize the time domain for feature computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Time Inconsistency: Due to the flexibility of the representation, the model may produce inconsistent results across time, especially if the number of observations is limited. Models temporal changes by learning a temporally global 3D canonical representation and a learnable, time-dependent deformation field. Sets itself apart by explicitly separating geometry and appearance, ensuring long-term correspondence. Choose when topology is stable and long-term consistency is critical. A failed design that models temporal changes by storing a static feature matrix for each spatial point and computing features via an inner product with time-dependent basis functions. It differs by attempting to represent the entire volume as a linear combination of static basis volumes, which proved intractable due to memory and artifacts. Time Complexity: Using grid interpolation between time slots decreases the computational burden and enables faster training compared to evaluating an MLP at every time step. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Tolerant of topology changes; can model a wider range of motion than warp-based methods; omits the explicit deformation network. Limitations: Prone to time inconsistency; performance depends on the number of observations available. When to Use: When the scene undergoes topology changes or when a simpler pipeline without explicit deformation fields is preferred. When Not to Use: When long-term temporal consistency is critical, as the representation is prone to time inconsistency. Space-time representations emerged as an alternative to warp-based dynamic scene representations, aiming to simplify the modeling of dynamic scenes by directly incorporating time into the query space. The approach builds on the idea of conditioning 3D representations with time, allowing for a unified function to regress dynamic properties. Recent advances have explored both neural implicit models and explicit feature grids to implement this paradigm. Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Warp-based Dynamic Scene Representation
head: Deformation-based representations, Warp-based methods, Warping-based Dynamic Scene Representation
body: Warp-based dynamic scene representations model temporal changes by learning a temporally global 3D canonical representation and a learnable, time-dependent deformation field to warp canonical space to match observed scenes at each timestep. This approach ensures long-term correspondence, allowing for consistent novel view synthesis and smooth interpolation in the time dimension. Unlike Space-time representations, which extend the query space to include time directly, warp-based methods explicitly separate geometry and appearance into a static component and a deformation component. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point p in the deformed (observed) space, camera parameters \mathcal{C}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and time t. Output: An implicit field value \xi (e.g., density, color) at the queried location. Data Structures: Deformation Network T: A function mapping points from the deformed space to the canonical space (backward warp) or vice versa (forward warp). It is typically implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Alternatively, it can be modeled explicitly using polynomial bases, Fourier transforms, or learned basis functions. Static Representation F: A function that infers the implicit field from the canonical point p'. Steps: 1. Learn Canonical Representation: Learn a temporally global 3D representation (canonical space) that captures the static geometry and appearance of the scene. 2. Learn Deformation Field: Learn a deformation field T that maps points between the canonical space and the deformed space at specific time steps. Backward Warp: Map deformed states back to the canonical representation (p \rightarrow p'). Forward Warp: Alternatively, map from canonical space to dynamic time steps (p' \rightarrow p) to ensure smooth and continuous deformation. 3. Render: Query the static representation F at the warped canonical point p' to obtain the field value \xi. Formulas: The rendering function f is defined as the composition of the deformation network T and the static representation F: f = F \circ T Specifically, the mapping is formalized as: T: (p, \mathcal{C}0) \rightarrow p' F: p'[\mathbf{d}; \mathcal{C}] \rightarrow \xi Where: T is the deformation network mapping point p to its canonical counterpart p'. F is the static representation inferring the implicit field from p'. \mathcal{C}0 is the canonical camera configuration. \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. \mathcal{C} is the camera parameters. \xi is the output field value. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Discontinuous Mapping: Backward warps often result in discontinuous mappings because various object configurations can occupy the same spatial location at different time steps. Forward warps are preferred to mitigate this. Topology Changes: Warp-based methods struggle with topology changes, limiting their applicability primarily to object-level modeling where the object maintains a consistent structure over time. DeVRF is a warp-based method that combines an explicit voxel-based canonical 3D volumetric grid with a 4D deformation field. It sets itself apart by using a static-to-dynamic learning paradigm: it first learns the static scene representation from multi-view stills, then learns the deformation from a few-view dynamic sequence. This approach allows for much faster convergence than fully implicit networks and simplifies learning 4D voxel deformation fields with limited dynamic data. Choose it when efficient learning of non-rigid motion is required with limited dynamic views. Strengths: Ensures long-term correspondence, allowing consistent novel view synthesis and smooth interpolation in the time dimension. Limitations: Struggles with topology changes, limiting applicability to object-level modeling with consistent structure. Backward warps can cause discontinuities. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Warp-based methods were introduced as a class of space-time representations that condition the representation with a time component. They model geometry and appearance as a continuous function of both space and time. Key references include [PSB 21, PSH 21, TTG 21, LDZY24, WYF 24, YGZ 24] for warping-based methods and [GSD 23] for forward warp approaches. Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DeVRF
head: DeVRF, A method that designs a static-dynamic learning paradigm to simplify learning 4D voxel deformation fields using only a few dynamic sequences
body: DeVRF adapts NeRF-like volume rendering frameworks with explicit 3D representations to dynamic scenes by combining an explicit voxel-based canonical 3D volumetric grid with a 4D deformation field. It solves the problem of efficiently learning non-rigid motion in dynamic scenes by employing a static-to-dynamic learning paradigm: first learning the static scene representation from multi-view stills, then learning the deformation from a few-view dynamic sequence. This approach allows for much faster convergence than fully implicit networks and simplifies the learning of 4D voxel deformation fields using limited dynamic data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view static images for static initialization, a few-view dynamic video sequence for deformation learning, and camera poses for ray generation. Outputs: A canonical 3D voxel grid representing the static scene appearance and geometry, and a 4D deformation field mapping canonical space to observed space at specific times. Data Structures: 1. Canonical 3D Volumetric Grid: An explicit voxel-based grid storing features (e.g., density, color) for the static scene structure. The exact resolution and bit-packing are not specified in the sources. 2. 4D Deformation Field: A network or function that takes a 3D spatial coordinate (x, y, z) and a time coordinate t as input, and outputs a 3D displacement vector (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z). Numbered Steps: 1. Static Initialization: Learn the static scene representation from multi-view still images using an explicit 3D voxel-based canonical grid. This establishes the baseline geometry and appearance without temporal dynamics. 2. Deformation Learning: Using a few-view dynamic sequence, learn the 4D deformation field that warps the canonical space to match the observed dynamic scenes at each timestep. 3. Rendering: During rendering, sample points along rays. Apply the deformation transform (querying the 4D deformation field with the sample point's 3D coordinates and the current time t) to warp the point from canonical space to the observed space. Query the canonical voxel grid at the warped position to retrieve features (density, color). 4. Optimization: Optimize the deformation field parameters to minimize the difference between rendered images and the dynamic input sequence. Formulas: Let p = (x, y, z) be a point in canonical space and t be the time. The deformation field D computes the displacement: p' = p + D(p, t) where p' is the point in the observed space at time t. The radiance C and density \sigma are then queried from the canonical voxel grid at p': C, \sigma = \text{GridQuery}(p') [G: The exact mathematical formulation of the deformation network architecture is not given in the sources.] Parameters: Static-to-Dynamic Ratio: The method relies on a significant portion of static initialization followed by dynamic refinement. Specific ratios are not given in the sources. Dynamic Sequence Length: A few-view dynamic sequence is used. The exact number of frames is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Model training is prone to overfitting when modeling dynamic non-rigid scenes with 4D deformation fields on discrete voxels due to network parameter constraints. Time Information: Modeling time information and capturing point motion at different scales are challenges for voxel features in dynamic scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderdevrfray(rayorigin, raydirection, timet, canonicalgrid, deformationnet): """ Renders a single ray for DeVRF. """ tmin, tmax = 0.0, 100.0 # Scene bounds numsamples = 128 stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / numsamples accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 densitiessofar = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tmin + i stepsize pcanonical = [rayorigin[j] + t raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] # Apply deformation to get observed space point displacement = deformationnet(pcanonical, timet) pobserved = [pcanonical[j] + displacement[j] for j in range(3)] # [G: Standard trilinear interpolation on the canonical grid returns density and color] density, color = canonicalgrid.query(pobserved) # Standard volume rendering accumulation alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density stepsize) weight = alpha math.exp(-densitiessofar) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += weight densitiessofar += density stepsize if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor def traindevrfr(staticimages, dynamicvideo, canonicalgridinit, deformationnetinit): """ Two-stage training process. """ # Stage 1: Static Initialization for staticview in staticimages: rendered = renderdevrfray(staticview.rayorigin, staticview.raydirection, 0.0, canonicalgridinit, deformationnetinit) # Mean squared error loss loss = sum((rendered[j] - staticview.image[j])2 for j in range(3)) / 3.0 # Standard gradient descent update for canonicalgridinit # Stage 2: Dynamic Deformation Learning for frame in dynamicvideo: rendereddynamic = renderdevrfray(frame.rayorigin, frame.raydirection, frame.time, canonicalgridinit, deformationnetinit) loss = sum((rendereddynamic[j] - frame.image[j])2 for j in range(3)) / 3.0 # Standard gradient descent update for deformationnetinit Enables dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular videos without known camera poses by jointly optimizing intrinsics, extrinsics, and both static and dynamic radiance fields. It uses a two-branch architecture and motion masks. Choose when camera poses are unknown. RoDynRF A foundational method for dynamic NeRF using a time-conditioned deformation network. Choose for implicit representations with known poses. D-NeRF Time Complexity: Faster convergence than fully implicit networks due to the explicit voxel-based canonical grid and static initialization. Specific training times are not given in the sources, but the method claims significant acceleration in optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses an explicit voxel-based canonical 3D volumetric grid, which is generally more memory-efficient than fully implicit networks for high-resolution scenes, but the exact memory footprint is not given in the sources. Performance: On synthetic datasets, DeVRF-dynamic achieved a PSNR of 34.29 dB and SSIM of 0.982, with GPU memory usage of 4.4 GB and training time of 0.13 hours. On real-world datasets, it achieved a PSNR of 31.68 dB and SSIM of 0.972, with GPU memory usage of 6.6 GB and training time of 0.18 hours. Strengths: Fast convergence, simplified learning process for 4D deformation fields, high rendering quality. Limitations: Prone to overfitting on non-rigid scenes due to parameter constraints. Requires multi-view static images for initialization and a few-view dynamic sequence. When to use: When you have multi-view static images and a short dynamic sequence, and need fast convergence and high quality. When not to use: For scenes with complex non-rigid motion where overfitting is a concern, or when only monocular video is available without static initialization. DeVRF was proposed by Liu et al. in 2022. It was designed to address the challenges of applying voxel features to dynamic scenes, specifically modeling time information and capturing point motion at different scales. The method builds on the potential of voxel-based representations but introduces a static-dynamic learning paradigm to simplify the learning of 4D deformation fields. It is used in the context of dynamic scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis for dynamic scenes. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 Overview of NeRF technology and applications, https://www.jcad.cn/en/article/doi/10.3724/SP.J.1089.2023-00759, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Fixed Basis for Time Axis
head: Basis Function Volume Representation, Static Feature Matrix with Time Basis
body: A failed design for dynamic scene representation that models temporal changes by storing a static feature matrix for each spatial point and computing features at time t via an inner product with time-dependent basis functions. It differs from successful methods like HexPlane by attempting to represent the entire spatiotemporal volume as a linear combination of static basis volumes, which proved computationally intractable due to excessive memory requirements and reconstruction artifacts. Inputs: Spatial dimensions X, Y, Z. Number of time basis functions Rt. Feature dimension F. Time parameter t. Outputs: Feature vector \mathbf{V}t \in \mathbb{R}^F for a specific spatial location and time t. Data Structures: The naive representation stores a static feature matrix for every spatial point. Basis Volumes Stack (\hat{\mathbf{V}}): A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{XYZF \times Rt}. This can be viewed as a stack of Rt basis volumes \hat{\mathbf{V}}i, where each \hat{\mathbf{V}}i has shape \mathbb{R}^{XYZF}. Time Coefficients (\mathbf{f}(t)): A vector of shape \mathbb{R}^{Rt} containing the values of the basis functions at time t. Numbered Steps: 1. Define Basis Functions: Construct the vector \mathbf{f}(t) using a set of sine and cosine functions, similar to positional encoding in neural radiance fields. The standard definition is: \mathbf{f}(t) = [1, \sin(t), \cos(t), \sin(2t), \cos(2t), \sin(4t), \cos(4t), \dots] Legendre or Chebyshev polynomials were also explored as alternatives. 2. Compute Features (Naive Approach): For a spatial location (x,y,z), retrieve the feature matrix \mathbf{M}{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times Rt} from \hat{\mathbf{V}}. Compute the feature vector at time t using the inner product: \mathbf{V}t = \sum{i=1}^{Rt} \mathbf{f}(t)i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{V}}i(x,y,z) = \hat{\mathbf{V}}(x,y,z) \cdot \mathbf{f}(t) where \hat{\mathbf{V}}(x,y,z) is the slice of the basis stack at (x,y,z) with shape \mathbb{R}^{F \times Rt}. 3. Memory Optimization (Tensor Decomposition): Due to the memory cost of the naive approach, tensor decomposition is applied to factorize the volume into smaller components. The representation is factorized into matrices M{XY}, M{XZ}, M{YZ} and vectors vX, vY, vZ, each augmented with an additional dimension Rt. M{XY}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{XY \times Rt}. vX^T \in \mathbb{R}^{X \times Rt}. Similar structures are used for M{XZ}, M{YZ}, vY, vZ. 4. Compute Features (Decomposed Approach): a. Multiply \mathbf{f}(t) with the transposed decomposition matrices and vectors along the last dimension (Rt) to obtain time-specific matrices \mathbf{M} and vectors \mathbf{v}. b. Use the resulting \mathbf{M} and \mathbf{v} to calculate features following the HexPlane feature aggregation equation (Eq. 1 in). 5. Training Regularization: a. Apply a weighted L1 loss to regularize the time-decomposed components M{Tr} and v{Tr}. Higher weights are assigned to high-frequency coefficients to encourage smoothness. b. Use smoothly bandwidth annealing during training to gradually introduce high-frequency components. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computebasisvector(t, numfreqs=4): """ Computes the basis function vector f(t). Args: t: float, time parameter. numfreqs: int, number of frequency pairs (excluding DC). Returns: f: np.array of shape (2 numfreqs + 1,) """ f = [1.0] for i in range(1, numfreqs + 1): f.append(np.sin(i t)) f.append(np.cos(i t)) return np.array(f) def getfeaturesnaive(x, y, z, t, basisstack, ft): """ Naive feature retrieval from the full basis stack. Args: x, y, z: int, spatial coordinates. t: float, time. basisstack: np.array of shape (X, Y, Z, F, Rt). ft: np.array of shape (Rt,). Returns: Vt: np.array of shape (F,). """ # Retrieve feature matrix for point (x,y,z): shape (F, Rt) featurematrix = basisstack[x, y, z,:,:] # Inner product: (F, Rt) dot (Rt,) -> (F,) Vt = np.dot(featurematrix, ft) return Vt def getfeaturesdecomposed(x, y, z, t, MXY, MXZ, MYZ, vX, vY, vZ, ft, Ydim, Zdim): """ Feature retrieval using tensor decomposition. Args: x, y, z: int, spatial coordinates. t: float, time. MXY: np.array of shape (XY, Rt). MXZ: np.array of shape (XZ, Rt). MYZ: np.array of shape (YZ, Rt). vX: np.array of shape (X, Rt). vY: np.array of shape (Y, Rt). vZ: np.array of shape (Z, Rt). ft: np.array of shape (Rt,). Ydim, Zdim: int, spatial dimensions for index flattening. Returns: Vt: np.array of shape (F,). """ # Map 3D coordinates to 2D indices for matrices # Assuming row-major flattening for XY, XZ, YZ xyidx = x Ydim + y xzidx = x Zdim + z yzidx = y Zdim + z # Get time-specific components by multiplying with ft # MXYt: shape () -> scalar for this xy MXYt = np.dot(MXY[xyidx,:], ft) MXZt = np.dot(MXZ[xzidx,:], ft) MYZt = np.dot(MYZ[yzidx,:], ft) vXt = np.dot(vX[x,:], ft) vYt = np.dot(vY[y,:], ft) vZt = np.dot(vZ[z,:], ft) # Combine using HexPlane Eq. 1 logic # Note: The exact combination formula (Eq 1) is not fully detailed in the provided text, # but typically involves combining these projected features. # The sources state features are calculated "following Eq 1" of the parent HexPlane paper. # The exact aggregation formula is not provided in the notes, so it is omitted here. Vt = np.zeros(27) # Placeholder shape matching F=27 return Vt Parameters: Rt: Number of time basis functions. Typical value: 32. F: Feature dimension. Typical value: 27. Basis function frequencies: Powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, \dots) are used in the sine/cosine series. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: The naive implementation requires enormous GPU memory. For X=Y=Z=128, Rt=32, F=27, storage is ~7GB, and training memory reaches ~30GB due to back-propagation and Adam optimizer states. Performance: Extremely slow due to memory I/O bottlenecks when reading/writing large volumes. Visual Artifacts: Severe color jittering and distortions occur in the rendered output. Degenerate Input: Fails to produce satisfactory results when objects move too fast or when there are too few observations to synthesize details. The successful method that replaced this design. It uses a different feature aggregation strategy to avoid the memory and artifact issues of the fixed basis approach. An alternative sibling method that uses explicit deformation networks instead of basis functions or static feature planes. Time Complexity: Extremely high due to memory I/O bottlenecks in the naive implementation. The decomposed version reduces memory footprint but adds computational overhead for the tensor contractions. Memory Complexity: Naive: O(XYZF Rt). Example: 7GB for 128^3 volume. Decomposed: Significantly reduced by factorizing into M{XY}, M{XZ}, M{YZ}, vX, vY, vZ. Strengths: Conceptually simple; leverages traditional time-series basis function approaches. Limitations: Proven to be a "failed design" due to intractable memory usage, slow training/inference speeds, and poor visual quality (color jittering, distortions). When to use: Not recommended for production. Included primarily as a cautionary example of what not to do in dynamic scene representation. This method was explored as part of the development of HexPlane, a fast representation for dynamic scenes. The authors initially attempted to model dynamic scenes by extending the query space with time using fixed basis functions, similar to positional encoding. However, they found this approach computationally infeasible and visually inferior, leading to the development of the HexPlane architecture which uses feature planes instead of a full 3D basis stack. The design is discussed in Section 9.1 of the HexPlane paper as a "Failed Design for Dynamic Scenes". HexPlane: A Fast Representation for Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00021, fetched 2026-10-26

name: B-mode Image Reconstruction
head: Image Formation Model
body: B-mode Image Reconstruction is a differentiable forward model for synthesizing ultrasound B-mode images from volumetric data, primarily used in differentiable ultrasound rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard ray-marching volume rendering by modeling coupled forward and backward wave amplitudes across voxel interfaces using a sparse linear system, rather than simple line integrals of density. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric representation of tissue acoustic properties, specifically reflection coefficients R and transmission coefficients T. Output: A 2D B-mode image where pixel intensity corresponds to echo amplitude first differences, mapped to beam angle and depth. Data Structures: The core data structure is a sparse matrix A representing the coupled recursion relations for wave amplitudes. For a depth of N voxels, the matrix has dimensions (2N+2) \times (2N+2). The matrix is strictly banded with at most three non-zero entries per row, resulting in O(N) non-zero elements. The indices r (row) and c (column) are defined for i = 0, \dots, N-1 and r, c = 0, \dots, 2N+1. Formulas: The matrix elements A{r,c} are defined as: A{r,c} = \begin{cases} -T{i+1 \rightarrow i} & r = 2i + 1, c = 2i + 3 \\ -T{i \rightarrow i+1} & r = 2i + 2, c = 2i \\ 1 & r = 2i + 2, c = 2i + 2 \\ -R{i+1 \rightarrow i} & r = 2i + 2, c = 2i + 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where: T{i \rightarrow i+1} is the transmission coefficient from voxel i to i+1. R{i+1 \rightarrow i} is the reflection coefficient from voxel i+1 back to i. Steps: 1. Initialize Wave System: For a given beam direction, set up the linear system A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{x} contains the forward (gi) and backward (di) wave amplitudes for each voxel interface. 2. Solve for Amplitudes: Solve the sparse linear system to determine the wave amplitudes at each depth step k = 1, \dots, N. The implementation may use a dense solver for simplicity, though banded solvers are suitable due to sparsity. 3. Measure Echoes: At each depth step k, measure the returning echo amplitude d0^{(k)} at the transducer location. 4. Generate Depth Profile: Compile the sequence \{d0^{(1)}, \dots, d0^{(N)}\} to form the time-sequence of echoes for the current beam direction. 5. Compute B-mode Intensity: Calculate pixel intensities as the first differences of the echo amplitudes. 6. Fan-Shaped Acquisition: Repeat steps 1–5 for multiple ray directions originating from the virtual transducer position to create a fan-shaped acquisition pattern. 7. Map Coordinates: Assign spatial coordinates to pixels based on the beam angle and depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructbmode(coefficientsperbeam, beamangles): # coefficientsperbeam: list of lists, each inner list contains (Ri, Ti) tuples for i=0..N-1 image = [] for angleidx, angle in enumerate(beamangles): coeffs = coefficientsperbeam[angleidx] N = len(coeffs) size = 2 N + 2 A = [[0.0] size for in range(size)] for i in range(N): Ri1, Ti1 = coeffs[i + 1] if i + 1 < N else (0.0, 0.0) Ti = coeffs[i][1] if 2 i + 3 < size: A[2 i + 1][2 i + 3] = -Ti1 if 2 i >= 0: A[2 i + 2][2 i] = -Ti A[2 i + 2][2 i + 2] = 1.0 if 2 i + 3 < size: A[2 i + 2][2 i + 3] = -Ri1 b = [0.0] size b[0] = 1.0 x = solvelinearsystem(A, b) echoes = [x[2 k + 1] for k in range(1, N + 1)] intensities = [abs(echoes[k] - echoes[k - 1]) for k in range(1, len(echoes))] image.append(intensities) return image def solvelinearsystem(A, b): # Solve Ax = b using Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting n = len(b) M = [A[i][:] + [b[i]] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): maxrow = max(range(i, n), key=lambda k: abs(M[k][i])) M[i], M[maxrow] = M[maxrow], M[i] for k in range(i + 1, n): factor = M[k][i] / M[i][i] for j in range(i, n + 1): M[k][j] -= factor M[i][j] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): x[i] = (M[i][n] - sum(M[i][j] x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))) / M[i][i] return x Parameters: Voxel Depth (N): Number of voxels along the ray path. Reflection/Transmission Coefficients: Material properties defining wave interaction at interfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Solver Choice: While the matrix A is sparse with a fixed bandwidth, the source notes that a dense solver is used for simplicity. Using a dense solver increases computational cost to O(N^3) for solving, whereas a banded solver would be O(N). An optional post-processing stage that injects speckle as multiplicative noise with depth-dependent amplitude. The noise consists of a radially oriented term and a granular term. The strength and granularity of the noise intensify as the signal-to-noise ratio declines in deeper regions. An optional post-processing stage that imposes depth-related blurring by convolving the image with a Gaussian kernel. The width of the Gaussian kernel grows linearly with depth. Time Complexity: The construction of the sparse matrix A is O(N) due to its fixed bandwidth and local interactions. Solving the system depends on the solver: O(N^3) for dense solvers, O(N) for banded solvers. Memory Complexity: The matrix A requires O(N) storage for non-zero elements. Strengths: Physically accurate modeling of wave propagation and interference, enabling realistic ultrasound simulation for differentiable rendering. Limitations: Computational cost can be high if dense solvers are used for large N. The method is described in the DiffUS paper, which introduces a differentiable ultrasound rendering framework. It models wave propagation using coupled recursion relations for forward and backward wave amplitudes across voxel interfaces. DiffUS: Differentiable Ultrasound Rendering from Volumetric Imaging., https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-06329-83, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeFTY (Neural Field Thermal Tomography)
head: Neural Field Thermal Tomography, Ours
body: NeFTY is a hard-constrained neural field framework for label-free three-dimensional inverse heat conduction, recovering spatially varying thermal diffusivity fields from surface thermal observations. It solves the ill-posed inverse problem by parameterizing the diffusivity as a continuous coordinate-based neural network and enforcing the heat equation as a hard constraint via a differentiable implicit-Euler solver with harmonic-mean interface flux, avoiding the gradient decoupling and saturation pathologies of soft-constrained Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Unlike its siblings Space-Time Image Formation Model and B-mode Image Reconstruction which often rely on soft penalties or 1D pixel-wise inversions, NeFTY ensures the governing PDE holds exactly on the discretization, enabling non-vanishing gradients from surface data to the diffusivity network via the adjoint of the discrete heat operator. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of noisy surface temperature measurements \hat{T}(\cdot, ti) at observation window \Gamma{obs} and time steps ti for i=1,\dots,M. Output: The parameters \theta of a neural network representing the thermal diffusivity field \alpha\theta(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: 1. Neural Diffusivity Field: A fully connected MLP f\theta with depth L{MLP}, hidden width W{MLP}, ReLU activations, and a single skip connection re-injecting encoded coordinates at the middle layer. 2. Grid: A uniform Cartesian grid covering domain \Omega with Nx \times Ny \times Nz nodes, spacings \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, and Nt time steps of size \Delta t. 3. State Variables: Tn \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng}: Discrete temperature deviation from ambient at time step n. \mun \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng}: Adjoint variable at time step n. \alpha\theta(\mathbf{x}): Diffusivity field sampled at grid nodes. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Encoding: Normalize input coordinates \mathbf{x} \in [-1, 1]^3. Apply Fourier feature encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2DN}: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = [\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{N-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{N-1} \pi \mathbf{x})] where N is the bandwidth. 2. Frequency Annealing: Apply a cosine schedule to suppress high-frequency noise amplification during early training. Let \beta linearly increase from 0 to N over T{FA} optimization steps. Memory Complexity: Peak GPU memory is 4.3 GB, dominated by unrolled Jacobi iterations of the forward solve. The discrete adjoint method reduces peak GPU memory by three orders of magnitude compared to standard Autograd (from 18.63 GB to 21.9 MB). The backward sweep has constant memory in Nt. Strengths: Label-free, handles stiff parabolic PDEs without gradient decoupling, efficient memory usage via adjoint method, robust to high-contrast interfaces via harmonic mean. Limitations: Per-specimen optimization at higher latency than supervised feedforward inversion, attenuated quantitative recovery inside very high-contrast voids, evaluation against projected 2D and 2.5D supervision because public NDT benchmarks do not yet provide 3D volumetric ground truth. The method builds on the principles of differentiable physics and adjoint optimization, specifically tailored for the inverse heat conduction problem. name: 1D Slice Reconstruction with Piecewise Constant Model
head: 1D Piecewise Constant Slice Reconstruction, Constrained Minimization for 1D Slice Reconstruction
body: This method reconstructs a 2D slice from parallel projections by modeling the slice as a 1D piecewise constant function defined by n parameters. It solves for these parameters by minimizing a constrained quadratic criterion that compares model projections against measured data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured parallel projection data p for a specific 2D slice. Output: A vector of n parameters defining the 1D piecewise constant model of the slice. Data Structures: The model represents the 2D slice as a function constant along one axis and piecewise constant along the orthogonal axis. Model Parameters: A vector \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n containing the values for each of the n zones. Zones: The domain is partitioned into n contiguous zones. Steps: 1. Model Definition: Define the 1D piecewise constant model f(x; \theta) for the slice, where \theta contains n parameters representing the values of n zones. 2. Forward Projection: Compute the theoretical projection \hat{p}(\theta) of the model f(x; \theta) using parallel ray geometry. 3. Criterion Formulation: Construct a quadratic criterion J(\theta) measuring the difference between the measured data p and the model projection \hat{p}(\theta): J(\theta) = \| p - \hat{p}(\theta) \|^2 4. Regularization: Since the quadratic criterion J(\theta) is non-differentiable due to the piecewise constant nature of the model, apply one of three proposed regularization techniques to handle this non-differentiability. 5. Constrained Minimization: Solve for the optimal parameters \theta^ by minimizing the regularized criterion subject to constraints: \min\theta J{reg}(\theta) \quad \text{subject to constraints} 6. Noise Analysis (Optional): Compute the covariance matrix of the estimated parameter vector \theta to analyze sensitivity to noise in the input data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstruct1dslice(projectionsp, nzones, regularizationmethod): """ Reconstruct a 2D slice modeled as a 1D piecewise constant function. """ # Initialize parameters theta with nzones values theta = [0.0] nzones # Define the forward projection operator for the 1D piecewise constant model def forwardproject(theta): # Construct the 1D profile from theta profile = theta[:] # Compute parallel projections of the profile # For parallel rays, this involves integrating the model values along projection rays. # The source does not specify the exact ray geometry or integration method. return [sum(profile)] # Define the non-differentiable quadratic criterion def criterion(theta): phat = forwardproject(theta) return sum((p - phat[0])2 for p in projectionsp) # Apply regularization to handle non-differentiability # The source specifies three techniques but does not detail them. if regularizationmethod == "technique1": # Apply first regularization technique pass elif regularizationmethod == "technique2": # Apply second regularization technique pass elif regularizationmethod == "technique3": # Apply third regularization technique pass else: raise ValueError("Unknown regularization method") # Perform constrained minimization # The source does not specify the optimization algorithm used. # A standard constrained optimizer (e.g., projected gradient descent) would be applied here. thetaoptimal = theta return thetaoptimal def computecovariancematrix(thetaoptimal, projectionsp, nzones): """ Analyze sensitivity of the reconstructed parameter vector to noise. """ # Determine the covariance matrix of the parameter vector after reconstruction # This typically involves linearizing the forward model around the solution # and propagating the noise covariance from the projections. # Implementation details for covariance calculation are not specified in the source. covmatrix = [[0.0] nzones for in range(nzones)] return covmatrix Parameters: n: Number of parameters in the 1D piecewise constant model, corresponding to the number of zones. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiability: The quadratic criterion is non-differentiable due to the piecewise constant model structure. Specialized regularization techniques are required. Noise Sensitivity: The reconstruction is sensitive to noise in the input data, which can be analyzed via the covariance matrix of the parameter vector. This variant focuses on analyzing the sensitivity of the reconstructed parameter vector to noise present in the input data. It involves determining the covariance matrix of the parameter vector after reconstruction. This variant extends the 1D slice reconstruction to 3D objects by iterating the 1D reconstruction approach for all slices of the 3D object. It adds a smoothing term between adjacent slices during the iteration to enforce consistency across the volume. This variant addresses the core challenge of the method: the non-differentiability of the quadratic criterion. It proposes three specific regularization techniques to handle this issue. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: The non-differentiability of the criterion requires specialized regularization and optimization techniques. It is limited to 2D slice reconstruction in its basic form, requiring iteration for 3D. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from research on tomographic reconstruction. The work first studied the reconstruction of a planar slice using a 1D model described by zones with n parameters. The approach was part of a broader investigation into modeling objects for reconstruction, which later extended to 3D models characterized by separating surfaces and density fields. The specific techniques for regularization and noise analysis were proposed to address the challenges of non-differentiability and noise sensitivity in this constrained minimization framework. name: Noise Sensitivity Analysis via Covariance Matrix
head: Covariance-based Noise Sensitivity, Parameter Noise Analysis
body: This method analyzes the sensitivity of the reconstructed parameter vector to noise present in the input projection data by computing the covariance matrix of the parameters. It builds on 1D Slice Reconstruction with Piecewise Constant Model, where a 2D slice is modeled as a 1D piecewise constant function with n parameters, and reconstruction is achieved by minimizing a constrained quadratic criterion. While the parent method solves for the parameters, this analysis quantifies the uncertainty and stability of those solutions in the presence of measurement noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reconstructed parameter vector \mathbf{p} (of size n) obtained from the piecewise constant model, and the covariance matrix \mathbf{C} of this vector. Output: The covariance matrix \mathbf{C}, which characterizes the noise sensitivity of each parameter and their correlations. Data Structures: \mathbf{p}: A 1D array of length n, containing the estimated values of the piecewise constant parameters. \mathbf{C}: An n \times n symmetric matrix. The diagonal elements C{ii} represent the variance of the i-th parameter, and off-diagonal elements C{ij} represent the covariance between parameters i and j. Steps: 1. Reconstruction: Perform the 1D slice reconstruction to obtain the parameter vector \mathbf{p} by minimizing a constrained quadratic criterion. The criterion is non-differentiable, so regularization techniques are applied. 2. Covariance Determination: Compute the covariance matrix \mathbf{C} of the parameter vector \mathbf{p} with respect to the noise in the input data. The specific mathematical derivation of \mathbf{C} depends on the linearization of the forward projection model and the noise statistics of the input data, which are not detailed in the provided sources. 3. Sensitivity Analysis: Use \mathbf{C} to analyze the sensitivity of each parameter. The standard deviation of the i-th parameter is \sigmai = \sqrt{C{ii}}. High values indicate high sensitivity to noise. Formulas: \sigmai = \sqrt{C{ii}} where \sigmai is the standard deviation of the i-th parameter and C{ii} is the i-th diagonal element of the covariance matrix. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The non-differentiability of the quadratic criterion requires regularization. The sources do not specify how the noise statistics of the input data are modeled or incorporated into the covariance calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def noisesensitivityanalysis(p, C): """ Analyze noise sensitivity of reconstructed parameters. Args: p: list of floats, reconstructed parameter vector. C: list of lists of floats, covariance matrix of the parameters. Returns: stddevs: list of floats, standard deviations of each parameter. correlations: list of lists of floats, correlation matrix. """ n = len(p) stddevs = [0.0] n for i in range(n): stddevs[i] = math.sqrt(C[i][i]) correlations = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): denom = stddevs[i] stddevs[j] if denom < 1e-10: denom = 1e-10 correlations[i][j] = C[i][j] / denom return stddevs, correlations Recovers constant absorption (\sigma) and source (q) parameters from a sequence of intensity measurements by fitting a linear recurrence relation I{k+1} = a Ik + b. It is chosen when the data consists of a 1D sequence of intensity measurements with known step size ds. The method validates that intensity.size() >= 3 and ds > 0. It calculates sums Sx, Sy, S{xx}, S{xy} over k=0 to N-2 where N = \text{intensity.size()} - 1, with x = Ik and y = I{k+1}. The determinant D = N S{xx} - Sx^2 is computed; if |D| \le 10^{-14}, the result is invalid. The coefficients are a = (N S{xy} - Sx Sy) / D and b = (Sy - a Sx) / N. The absorption is \sigma = -\ln(a) / ds. The source term is q = b / ds if |1 - a| < 10^{-8}, otherwise q = \sigma b / (1 - a). A pitfall is that if a \notin (0, 1 + 10^{-10}), the result is invalid. RMSEs for the linear fit and a constant model are also computed. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strength: Provides a quantitative measure of parameter uncertainty based on the reconstruction model. Limitation: The non-differentiability of the underlying criterion complicates the analytical derivation of the covariance matrix. When to Use: Use when assessing the reliability of reconstructed parameters in the presence of noise. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from work on tomographic reconstruction from a small number of views. The author proposed analyzing the sensitivity of the parameter vector to noise after determining its covariance matrix, as part of a broader approach involving 1D slice reconstruction with regularization and 3D model construction. name: Regularization of Non-Differentiable Quadratic Criterion
head: Regularization for Piecewise Constant Model
body: This method addresses the non-differentiability of a quadratic criterion minimized under constraints for a 1D piecewise constant model. It applies regularization techniques to stabilize parameter estimation when the objective function lacks smoothness. It differs from conventional Model-Based Iterative Reconstruction (MBIR) by employing non-differentiable penalties and coordinate descent rather than simple L2-norm regularization and gradient descent. Inputs: Measured projection data vector y. Forward operator matrix F mapping the unknown radial field x to the projection space. Regularization weight parameter \mu2. Outputs: Reconstructed radial field vector x. Data Structures: x: Vector of size n representing the parameters of the 1D piecewise constant model. F: Matrix of size m \times n (where m is the number of projections). L2: Second-order finite-difference operator matrix of size n \times n. Steps: 1. Expand the objective function terms into quadratic forms: \|Fx - y\|2^2 = x^T F^T Fx - 2x^T F^T y + y^T y and \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 = \mu2^2 x^T L2^T L2 x. 2. Combine the expanded terms to form the full objective function \Phi(x). 3. Compute the derivative \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x} = 2F^T Fx - 2F^T y + 2\mu2^2 L2^T L2 x and set it to zero to find the minimum. 4. Rearrange into the regularized normal equation (F^T F + \mu2^2 L2^T L2) x = F^T y. 5. Define B^T = F^T F + \mu2^2 L2^T L2 and solve the linear system B^T x = F^T y using Cholesky factorization of B^T. 6. Determine the optimal regularization weight \mu2 using the L-curve method: scan \mu2 from 10^{-10} to 10^{-2} with Nk = 201 steps, solve for xk at each step, plot \log{10} \|Fxk - y\|2 versus \log{10} \|L2 xk\|2, and select the \mu2 corresponding to the corner of the curve. Formulas: The objective function \Phi(x) combines data fidelity and a smoothness penalty: \Phi(x) = \|Fx - y\|2^2 + \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 where: \|Fx - y\|2^2 is the data fidelity term. \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 is the Tikhonov regularization term. L2 is defined as: L2 = \frac{1}{\Delta r^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \Delta r is the radial step size. Parameters: \mu2: Regularization weight controlling the trade-off between data fidelity and smoothness. Typical scanning range is 10^{-10} to 10^{-2} with 201 steps for L-curve analysis. Edge cases and pitfalls: The second-order operator L2 acts globally and does not explicitly enforce the physical center-axis condition (\partial x / \partial r |{r=0} = 0) for axisymmetric fields, leading to inaccuracies near the symmetry axis. A regularization technique to mitigate noise amplification in direct and iterative inversions by adding a second-order smoothness penalty to the objective function. It stabilizes the reconstruction but fails to explicitly impose the zero-gradient condition at the center axis of axisymmetric fields. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Mitigates noise amplification observed in direct and iterative inversions. Limitations: Does not enforce the physical center-axis condition (\partial x / \partial r |{r=0} = 0), causing inaccuracies near the symmetry axis in axisymmetric tomography. The method addresses the non-differentiability of a quadratic criterion minimized under constraints for a 1D piecewise constant model. Single-parameter Tikhonov regularization was proposed as a standard approach to handle noise amplification in this context.
