name: MBIR Objective Function Minimization
head: Conventional MBIR, MBIR, MBIR Reconstruction
body: Conventional Model-Based Iterative Reconstruction (MBIR) solves the inverse problem of reconstructing a volume \mathbf{f} from measured projection data \mathbf{p} by minimizing a quadratic objective function. Unlike advanced methods that explicitly model and deblur motion or system blur, conventional MBIR does not deblur measured views and instead relies on photon weighting to handle noise and blur. It is distinguished from its parent method, Regularization of Non-Differentiable Quadratic Criterion, by its specific use of a simple L2-norm regularization term and a gradient descent solver. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data vector \mathbf{p}, forward projection operator \mathbf{R}s, regularization parameter \beta, and the number of volume voxels N. Output: Reconstructed volume vector \mathbf{f}. Data Structures: \mathbf{f}: A vector representing the volume voxels, initialized as a zero vector. \mathbf{p}: A vector of projection measurements, corresponding to the projection of a 512 \times 512 image using a forward model \mathbf{R}r with 8 times oversampling followed by 8 \times 8 bin averaging. \mathbf{R}s: The forward projection matrix/operator mapping the volume to the projection space. Objective Function: The method minimizes the following convex objective function \Psi(\mathbf{f}): \Psi(\mathbf{f}) = \frac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{R}s \mathbf{f} - \mathbf{p}\|2^2 + \frac{\beta}{2} \|\mathbf{f}\|2^2 Where: \|\cdot\|2 denotes the L2 norm (Euclidean norm). \mathbf{R}s \mathbf{f} is the estimated projection of the current volume estimate. \mathbf{p} is the measured projection data. \beta is the regularization parameter. Parameters: \beta: Set to 2 \times 10^{-2}. This value ensures the strong convexity of the cost function \Psi, which guarantees the uniqueness of the minimizer. Iteration Count: 400 iterations are used for computing the baseline reconstruction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the volume vector \mathbf{f} to the zero vector. 2. Gradient Calculation: Compute the gradient of the objective function \Psi(\mathbf{f}) with respect to \mathbf{f}. The gradient is given by: \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{f}) = \mathbf{R}s^T (\mathbf{R}s \mathbf{f} - \mathbf{p}) + \beta \mathbf{f} Where \mathbf{R}s^T is the adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator. 3. Update: Update the volume estimate using gradient descent: \mathbf{f}{new} = \mathbf{f}{old} - \alpha \nabla \Psi(\mathbf{f}{old}) Where \alpha is the step size (learning rate) [G: The step size \alpha is not explicitly defined in the sources; a standard constant or line-search strategy is implied by "simple gradient descent"]. 4. Convergence Check: Repeat steps 2 and 3 until convergence or until the maximum number of iterations (400) is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mbirminimize(p, Rs, RsT, beta, N, maxiterations=400, stepsize=1e-3): # Initialize volume to zero vector of size N f = [0.0] N for in range(maxiterations): # Forward projection: estimate projections from current volume pest = Rs(f) # Compute residual residual = [pest[i] - p[i] for i in range(len(p))] # Compute gradient: Rs^T residual + beta f grad = RsT(residual) for i in range(N): grad[i] = grad[i] + beta f[i] # Update volume # [G: stepsize is not given in sources; a standard constant or line-search is implied] for i in range(N): f[i] = f[i] - stepsize grad[i] return f Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blur: Conventional MBIR produces severely blurred images when applied to data acquired over large angular spans (e.g., 40.17^\circ) because it lacks a forward model for motion blur. Convexity: The choice of \beta is critical for ensuring strong convexity and uniqueness of the solution. MAP/Bayesian Reconstruction is a statistical inverse problem method that incorporates prior knowledge of the object to stabilize the reconstruction and improve image quality. It sets itself apart from standard least-squares or Maximum Likelihood methods by explicitly balancing the likelihood of the observed data against a prior probability distribution, allowing for constraints such as positivity, smoothness, or support. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: In the reference implementation, 400 iterations are required for baseline reconstruction. Strengths: Guarantees a unique minimizer due to strong convexity when \beta > 0. Simple to implement using standard gradient descent. Limitations: Produces blurred images for large angular spans due to the lack of motion blur modeling in the forward model. The simple L2 regularization may not preserve sharp edges as effectively as non-differentiable regularizers used in more advanced MBIR variants. Implementation: Often implemented using packages like SVMBIR, which use cache-optimized iterative coordinate descent and Markov random field regularization. Note that the specific "Conventional MBIR" described here uses gradient descent and L2 regularization, whereas SVMBIR's default may differ. Conventional MBIR is a baseline reconstruction method used in tomographic imaging, particularly in contexts involving coded exposures or sparse views. It was used as a comparison baseline in the CodEx framework for joint temporal de-blurring and tomographic reconstruction. The specific formulation with L2 regularization and gradient descent is detailed in studies on magnification-driven B-spline interpolation. name: MAP/Bayesian Reconstruction
head: MAP, Maximum A Posteriori, MAP-EM, MAP-GC
body:
MAP/Bayesian Reconstruction is a statistical inverse problem method that incorporates prior knowledge of the object to stabilize the reconstruction and improve image quality. It sets itself apart from standard least-squares or Maximum Likelihood methods by explicitly balancing the likelihood of the observed data against a prior probability distribution, allowing for constraints such as positivity, smoothness, or support. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Projection data P (or proj), system matrix R (forward projection operator), prior model parameters (e.g., regularization weight \lambda). Outputs: Reconstructed object volume f. Data Structures f: The object vector, typically discretized into voxels. Size N 	imes 1. P: The projection vector. Size M 	imes 1. R: The system matrix (or ray-tracing operator). Size M 	imes N. \lambda: Scalar regularization weight. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize: Set initial estimate f^{(0)} (e.g., zero or a standard reconstruction) and iteration counter k=0. 2. Compute Forward Projection and Residual: Calculate R f^{(k)} and the residual P - R f^{(k)}. 3. Compute Combined Gradient: Calculate the gradient of the regularized criterion 
abla J(f^{(k)}) = 
abla J1(f^{(k)}) + \lambda 
abla J2(f^{(k)}) based on the chosen prior model (e.g., quadratic smoothness). 4. Update: Update the estimate using an optimization algorithm such as Gradient Conjugate (MAP-GC) or Expectation-Maximization (MAP-EM). 5. Check Convergence: If convergence criteria are met, stop. Formulas The method is grounded in Bayes' theorem. The posterior probability p(f | P) is proportional to the product of the likelihood p(P | f) and the prior probability p(f): p(f | P) =  rac{p(P | f) p(f)}{p(P)} Since the projections P are known measurements, p(P) is constant and can be ignored for optimization. If no prior hypothesis is made, p(f) is constant, reducing the problem to Maximum Likelihood. To incorporate prior knowledge, the problem is formulated as minimizing a cost function J(f): J(f) = J1(f) + \lambda J2(f) Where: J1(f) = \| P - Rf \|^2 is the data fidelity term (typically least-squares error). J2(f) is the prior fidelity term, encoding the prior probability p(f) (e.g., smoothness or edge-preserving penalties). \lambda is the regularization parameter controlling the trade-off between data fidelity and prior information. Alternatively, from a general statistical estimation perspective, the solution minimizes a cost function c(f, g) integrated against the posterior: f{solution} = \arg \minf \int c(f, g) p(f = g | proj) dg For the MAP criterion, the cost function is defined as c(f, g) = 1 - \delta(f, g), where \delta is the Dirac distribution at point f. This simplifies the solution to: f{solution} = \arg \maxf p(f | proj). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mapreconstruction(P, R, lambdaval, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): # Initialize object estimate and iteration counter f = zeroslike(P) # Placeholder for object size N k = 0 while k < maxiter: # Compute forward projection and residual projest = R @ f residual = P - projest # Compute gradient of data fidelity term gradJ1 = -2 R.T @ residual # Compute gradient of prior fidelity term J2(f) gradJ2 = computepriorgradient(f) # Compute combined gradient gradJ = gradJ1 + lambdaval gradJ2 # Update estimate using optimizer (GC or EM) f = updatestep(f, gradJ, k) # Check convergence criteria if norm(gradJ) < tol: break k += 1 return f Parameters \lambda: The weight of the prior. It must be set empirically. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Tuning \lambda: The parameter \lambda requires empirical tuning to balance data fidelity and prior information. Convergence: Gradient Conjugate methods are faster but more prone to non-convergence issues compared to EM methods. Time Complexity: Depends on the optimizer; Gradient Conjugate is faster than Expectation-Maximization. Exact complexity values are Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the object f, projections P, and the system matrix R or its transpose R^T. Exact memory values are Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves image quality by incorporating prior knowledge; stabilizes ill-posed problems; allows for specific constraints (positivity, smoothness). Limitations: Requires empirical tuning of \lambda; prior model must be appropriate for the object; convergence can be sensitive to initialization and parameter choice. When to use: When prior information about the object is available and standard reconstruction methods yield noisy or artifact-prone results. When not to use: When no reliable prior information exists, or when computational resources are extremely limited and speed is critical over quality. MAP/Bayesian reconstruction originates from statistical signal processing and tomography. It was developed to address the limitations of deterministic and standard iterative methods which often produce noisy or artifact-ridden images, especially with limited or noisy data. The method formalizes the use of prior knowledge (e.g., positivity, smoothness) within a probabilistic framework. Key developments include the integration of MAP into iterative algorithms like EM (MAP-EM) and Gradient Conjugate (MAP-GC). It is used in tomographic applications. name: Iterative Solvers
head: Conjugate Gradient on the Normal Equations, Landweber, Landweber Iteration, Landweber Iteration Solver
body: Iterative solvers reconstruct volumetric data by minimizing the discrepancy between measured sinograms and forward-projected volume estimates through repeated updates. They are implemented as specialized algorithms (Conjugate Gradient, CGNE, Landweber) that exploit the linear structure of the Radon transform for efficient computation. They distinguish themselves from general Differentiable CT Execution Model approaches by providing optimized, mathematically grounded solvers tailored to tomographic inverse problems. Iterative solvers operate on the linear system Ax = b, where A is the forward projection operator (Radon transform), x is the volume to reconstruct, and b is the measured sinogram. The core mechanism relies on the differentiability of the forward operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. Inputs: radon: An object defining the geometry (angles, detector count, beam type) and providing forward() and backprojection() methods. sino: The measured sinogram tensor, shape (N{batch}, N{angles}, N{detectors}). guess: Initial volume estimate tensor, shape (N{batch}, D, D, D) or similar. alpha (Landweber only): Step size parameter. maxiter / iterations: Number of optimization steps. Outputs: rec: Reconstructed volume tensor, same shape as guess. Volume (x): 3D tensor (e.g., D \times D \times D) representing density/absorption coefficients. Sinogram (p): 2D or 3D tensor representing line integrals. Residual (r): Difference between measured sinogram and forward-projected volume. Landweber iteration is an iterative solver for CT reconstruction. It updates the volume estimate by moving in the direction of the back-projected residual. Step Size Estimation: The step size \alpha is estimated using power iteration on the operator A^T A, typically scaled by 0.95 to ensure stability. Update Rule: x{k+1} = xk + \alpha \mathcal{P}^T (p - \mathcal{P}(xk)) Where: xk is the volume estimate at iteration k. \mathcal{P}(xk) is the forward projection (synthetic sinogram). p is the measured sinogram. \mathcal{P}^T(\cdot) is the back-projection operator. \alpha is the step size. Pseudocode (Landweber): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def landwebersolve(radon, sino, guess, maxiter, alpha): """ Solve tomography reconstruction using Landweber iteration. Args: radon: Radon object with forward() and backprojection() methods. sino: Measured sinogram tensor. guess: Initial volume estimate tensor (zeros). maxiter: Number of iterations. alpha: Step size (estimated via power iteration, typically < 2/sigmamax^2). Returns: rec: Reconstructed volume. """ x = guess.clone() for in range(maxiter): # Forward projection: compute synthetic sinogram sinopred = radon.forward(x) # Compute residual in projection space residual = sino - sinopred # Back-projection of residual to update volume update = radon.backprojection(residual) x = x + alpha update return x CGNE solves the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b using the Conjugate Gradient method. Update Rule: The algorithm applies standard CG to the system M x = c where M = A^T A and c = A^T b. 1. Initialize x0, r0 = c - M x0, p0 = r0. 2. For k = 0, 1, \dots: \alphak = \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T M pk} x{k+1} = xk + \alphak pk r{k+1} = rk - \alphak M pk \betak = \frac{r{k+1}^T r{k+1}}{rk^T rk} p{k+1} = r{k+1} + \betak pk Where M pk = A^T (A pk) requires two projections (forward then back-projection). Pseudocode (CGNE): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cgnesolve(radon, sino, guess, maxiter): """ Solve tomography reconstruction using Conjugate Gradient on Normal Equations. Args: radon: Radon object. sino: Measured sinogram. guess: Initial volume estimate. maxiter: Maximum iterations. Returns: rec: Reconstructed volume. """ x = guess.clone() # Compute initial residual r = A^T b - A^T A x c = radon.backprojection(sino) Ax = radon.forward(x) Mx = radon.backprojection(Ax) r = c - Mx p = r.clone() # r^T r (standard dot product) rdot = sum(r r) for in range(maxiter): # Compute M p = A^T (A p) Ap = radon.forward(p) Mp = radon.backprojection(Ap) # alpha = (r^T r) / (p^T M p) pMp = sum(p Mp) alpha = rdot / pMp # x = x + alpha p x = x + alpha p # r = r - alpha M p r = r - alpha Mp rdotnew = sum(r r) # beta = (rnew^T rnew) / (r^T r) beta = rdotnew / rdot # p = r + beta p p = r + beta p rdot = rdotnew return x Step Size (\alpha): For Landweber, typically estimated as 0.95 \times \frac{2}{\sigma{max}^2} where \sigma{max} is found via power iteration. Iterations: 500 is a common default for convergence in test settings. Batch Processing: All solvers support batch processing, allowing multiple volumes to be reconstructed in parallel on GPU. Precision: Half-precision (16-bit) storage provides speedups of >125× but may introduce numerical instability; single precision is safer for convergence. Step Size Selection: If \alpha is too large in Landweber, the iteration diverges. Ill-Conditioning: CGNE may struggle with ill-conditioned systems (e.g., sparse views) without regularization. SIRT updates all voxels simultaneously using normalized residuals, improving convergence stability in limited-angle or sparse-view scenarios compared to unnormalized methods like ART. This framework decomposes the optimization into independent proximal sub-problems, enabling the handling of non-smooth regularization (e.g., Total Variation) and large-scale linear systems using primal-dual splitting or stochastic sampling. ART updates the volume estimate one angle (or ray set) at a time, avoiding explicit storage of the system matrix by iteratively applying back-projection of residuals. An iterative reconstruction method using PyTorch's automatic differentiation to minimize the mean squared error between simulated and measured projections. It initializes the volume as a tensor with requiresgrad=True, uses an Adam optimizer (default lr=1e-2), and runs for a specified number of iterations (default 50). Time Complexity: Each iteration requires one forward projection and one back-projection. CGNE requires two projections per iteration (for A^T A p). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the volume, sinogram, and intermediate vectors (residuals, search directions). Batch processing increases memory linearly with batch size. Performance: On a Tesla V100, TorchRadon's iterative solvers are >40× faster than Astra Toolbox in single precision, and >125× faster in half precision. Quality: In test settings, Landweber achieved an MSE of 1.39 \cdot 10^{-4} and CGNE achieved 4.42 \cdot 10^{-5}, outperforming FBP (2.22 \cdot 10^{-4}). Strengths: Handles sparse views and noise better than FBP; supports regularization; differentiable. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Iterative solvers are common algorithms for solving tomography reconstruction problems. In the context of differentiable volume rendering and deep learning, libraries like TorchRadon have implemented these solvers to leverage GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation, enabling their use in end-to-end trainable pipelines. The integration of these solvers allows for hybrid reconstruction methods combining physics-based models with deep learning priors. name: SIRT (Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique)
head: SIRT Reconstruction, Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Algorithm
body: SIRT is a global algebraic iterative reconstruction method that solves the discrete linear system Ax = b arising from tomographic projection data by updating the volume estimate simultaneously for all projection lines. It reduces computational cost compared to line-by-line methods (like ART) and improves convergence robustness in noisy conditions by normalizing residuals and updates using row and column sums of the system matrix. Unlike direct inversion methods which fail under noise, SIRT provides a stable solution by treating the reconstruction as a simultaneous correction across the entire dataset. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data (sinogram) y \in \mathbb{R}^M, forward projection operator A: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^M, backward projection operator A^T: \mathbb{R}^M \to \mathbb{R}^N, number of iterations K, relaxation parameter \omega, and volume dimensions N. Output: Reconstructed volume vector x \in \mathbb{R}^N. Data Structures: x: Reconstruction vector, initialized to zeros, shape N (number of voxels). y: Sinogram vector, shape M (number of rays/projections). R: Row preconditioner vector, shape M. C: Column preconditioner vector, shape N. A, A^T: Forward and backward projection operators. Preconditioner Calculation: The row preconditioner R normalizes each ray residual by its total intersected length. The column preconditioner C normalizes the backprojected update by accumulated voxel sensitivity. 1. Compute R: Rj = \frac{1}{(A \mathbf{1})j} \quad \text{for } j=1,\dots,M where \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones with shape N. Clamp R to prevent division by zero: Rj \leftarrow \min\left(Rj, \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right) where \epsilon is a small positive constant. 2. Compute C: Ci = \frac{1}{(A^T \mathbf{1})i} \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,N where \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones with shape M. Clamp C: Ci \leftarrow \min\left(Ci, \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right). Iterative Update: The generalized update rule for the unknown vector x at iteration k+1 is: x^{(k+1)} = \max\left(0, x^{(k)} + \omega \, C \odot A^T\left(R \odot (y - A x^{(k)})\right)\right) where: \omega is the relaxation parameter (step size). R and C are applied element-wise to the residual and backprojected update respectively. The \max(0, \cdot) operation enforces nonnegativity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sirt(y, A, AT, numiters, stepsize, epsilon): """ Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT). Args: y: Sinogram vector of length M A: Forward projection function, takes vector of length N, returns vector of length M AT: Backward projection function, takes vector of length M, returns vector of length N numiters: Number of iterations stepsize: Relaxation parameter omega epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero Returns: xrec: Reconstructed volume vector of length N """ M = len(y) # Infer N from the output shape of AT or pass explicitly N = len(AT(y)) # Initialize reconstruction vector to zeros xrec = [0.0] N # Compute row preconditioner R (length M) onesdomain = [1.0] N forwardones = A(onesdomain) R = [0.0] M for j in range(M): if forwardones[j] > epsilon: R[j] = 1.0 / forwardones[j] else: R[j] = 1.0 / epsilon # Compute column preconditioner C (length N) onesrange = [1.0] M backwardones = AT(onesrange) C = [0.0] N for i in range(N): if backwardones[i] > epsilon: C[i] = 1.0 / backwardones[i] else: C[i] = 1.0 / epsilon # Iterative update for k in range(numiters): # Forward projection proj = A(xrec) # Residual residual = [y[j] - proj[j] for j in range(M)] # Scale residual by R scaledresidual = [R[j] residual[j] for j in range(M)] # Backproject scaled residual backprojected = AT(scaledresidual) # Scale backprojected update by C update = [C[i] backprojected[i] for i in range(N)] # Update volume for i in range(N): xrec[i] = xrec[i] + stepsize update[i] # Enforce nonnegativity for i in range(N): if xrec[i] < 0.0: xrec[i] = 0.0 return xrec Parameters: numiters: Number of reconstruction iterations. Typical value: 100. Some studies use 1000 to ensure convergence. stepsize (\omega): Relaxation parameter or learning rate. Default value: 10^{-2}. epsilon: Small constant to clamp preconditioners. Exact numerical value is not specified in the sources. volshape: Dimensions of the output volume. Typical value: (96, 96, 96). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Preconditioners R and C must be clamped to prevent division by zero when rays or voxels have zero intersected length. Semi-convergence: Iterative approaches often exhibit semi-convergence even in noise-free conditions, leading to potential inaccuracies if not stopped at the optimal iteration. Nonnegativity: The \max(0, \cdot) operation is crucial for enforcing physical nonnegativity constraints. SART is an iterative algebraic reconstruction technique that solves the discrete linear system Af = b arising from tomographic projection data by updating the volume estimate simultaneously for all rays in a subset of projections. It improves upon single-ray methods (like ART) by normalizing the backprojection by the number of rays intersecting each voxel, which reduces streak artifacts and accelerates convergence. It is distinguished from its sibling SIRT by the order of normalization: SART normalizes the residual by the ray's total intersected length before backprojecting, whereas SIRT normalizes the backprojected update by the voxel's total intersected length. It is preferred over direct methods like FDK for limited projection scenarios and over Conjugate Gradient (CG) for sparse-view settings due to better convergence properties in matrix-free implementations. A classical Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) implementation using a custom backprojector, without autodiff. It initializes the volume to zeros and iteratively computes the forward projection, residual error, backprojection of the residual, and volume update using a step size. The step size is typically 10^{-2}. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot (M + N)) per iteration, where K is the number of iterations, M is the number of rays, and N is the number of voxels. Each iteration involves one forward projection and one backward projection. Memory Complexity: Memory scales with volume size N, sinogram size M, and preconditioners R, C. Measured Performance: In a 128x128x128 volume with 100 projections, SIRT converges in 100 iterations. In a 96x96x96 volume, it typically runs for 20–30 iterations. Scaling: Computationally expensive; one iteration of SIRT corresponds to approximately N iterations of ART, where N is the number of projections. Strengths: Robust to noise, handles incomplete data well, enforces nonnegativity. Limitations: Slow convergence compared to direct methods, requires careful tuning of the relaxation parameter. When to Use: Limited projection scenarios, sparse-view settings, noisy data. When Not to Use: When fast reconstruction is required and data is complete and noise-free. SIRT was developed as a global algebraic reconstruction technique to overcome the failure of direct inversion in noisy conditions. It is based on the work of Andersen and Kak (1984) and is widely used in tomographic applications. The method is implemented in various libraries, including tomosipo and custom implementations. It is used in medical imaging, industrial CT, and scientific tomography. name: SART (Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique)
head: Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique, Proximal SART, ProxiSART
body: SART is an iterative algebraic reconstruction technique that solves the discrete linear system Af = b arising from tomographic projection data by updating the volume estimate simultaneously for all rays in a subset of projections. It improves upon single-ray methods by normalizing the backprojection by the number of rays intersecting each voxel, which reduces streak artifacts and accelerates convergence. It is preferred over direct methods like FDK for limited projection scenarios and over Conjugate Gradient (CG) for sparse-view settings due to better convergence properties in matrix-free implementations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data b \in \mathbb{R}^m, system matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, initial volume estimate f^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^n, relaxation parameter \alpha, and number of outer iterations T. Output: Reconstructed volume f \in \mathbb{R}^n. Data Structures: f: 3D volume array of size n (voxels). b: 1D array of size m (projection rays). wi: 1D array of size m, where wi = \sumk a{ik} is the sum of weights for ray i (ray sensitivity). vj: 1D array of size n, where vj = \sum{i \in \text{rays through } j} a{ij} is the sum of weights for voxel j (voxel sensitivity). Algorithm Steps: The standard SART algorithm updates the volume by iterating through subsets of projections (often all projections or a subset S). For each subset, it performs three steps for each ray i: 1. Forward Projection: Compute the estimated projection \hat{b}i^{(t)} for all rays i in the current subset S using the current volume estimate f^{(t)}: \hat{b}i^{(t)} = \sum{k=1}^{n} a{ik} fk^{(t)} where a{ik} is the contribution of voxel k to ray i. 2. Correction: Compute the correction factor ci^{(t)} for each ray i \in S: ci^{(t)} = \frac{bi - \hat{b}i^{(t)}}{\sum{k=1}^{n} a{ik}} The denominator \sum{k} a{ik} is the total weight of the ray (sum of contributions from all voxels it passes through). This normalizes the residual by the ray's path length/weight. 3. Backprojection: Update the volume f for all voxels j=1 \dots n: fj^{(t+1)} = fj^{(t)} + \alpha \frac{\sum{i \in S} ci^{(t)} a{ij}}{\sum{i \in S} a{ij}} The denominator \sum{i \in S} a{ij} is the sum of weights of the rays in subset S that intersect voxel j. This normalizes the backprojected correction by the number of rays contributing to the voxel. Parameters: \alpha: Relaxation parameter. Typical values range from 0.1 to 0.8 depending on the dataset. In proximal Chambolle-Pock implementations, \alpha is set to 0.5. T: Number of outer iterations. S: Subset of projections. Often S is the set of all projections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeros(n): """Return a list of n zeros.""" return [0.0] n def ones(n): """Return a list of n ones.""" return [1.0] n def sartstandard(b, A, nvoxels, nrays, alpha, T, subsetindices=None): """ Standard SART reconstruction. Args: b: array of measured projections (size m) A: 2D list/matrix of size m x n (system matrix) nvoxels: number of voxels nrays: number of rays alpha: relaxation parameter T: number of iterations subsetindices: list of ray indices for the subset S. If None, use all rays. Returns: f: reconstructed volume """ # Initialize volume f^(0) = 0 f = zeros(nvoxels) # Precompute ray weights wi = sumk aik rayweights = zeros(nrays) for i in range(nrays): for k in range(nvoxels): rayweights[i] += A[i][k] if subsetindices is None: subsetindices = list(range(nrays)) for t in range(T): # Step 1: Forward projection for subset S bhat = zeros(len(subsetindices)) for idx, i in enumerate(subsetindices): bhat[idx] = 0.0 for k in range(nvoxels): bhat[idx] += A[i][k] f[k] # Step 2: Correction for subset S corrections = zeros(len(subsetindices)) for idx, i in enumerate(subsetindices): if rayweights[i] > 0: corrections[idx] = (b[i] - bhat[idx]) / rayweights[i] else: corrections[idx] = 0.0 # Step 3: Backprojection and Update # Compute voxel sensitivities for subset S: vj = sum{i in S} aij voxelsens = zeros(nvoxels) for idx, i in enumerate(subsetindices): for j in range(nvoxels): voxelsens[j] += A[i][j] # Compute backprojected correction: sum{i in S} ci aij backprojected = zeros(nvoxels) for idx, i in enumerate(subsetindices): for j in range(nvoxels): backprojected[j] += corrections[idx] A[i][j] # Update volume for j in range(nvoxels): if voxelsens[j] > 0: f[j] = f[j] + alpha (backprojected[j] / voxelsens[j]) return f Proximal SART (for Data Term in Optimization): When used as a proximal operator for the data fidelity term f(f) = \|Af - p\|2^2 within a Chambolle-Pock scheme, the problem is transformed into an under-determined linear system by introducing auxiliary variables y and z: \text{prox}{\lambdaf}(q) = \text{argmin}f \|Af - p\|2^2 + \frac{1}{2\lambda}\|f - q\|2^2 This is equivalent to solving: \min{\tilde{f}} \|\tilde{f}\|2^2 \quad \text{subject to: } \tilde{A}\tilde{f} = \tilde{p} where \tilde{f} = [y; z], \tilde{A} = [I \ \sqrt{2\lambda}A], and \tilde{p} = \sqrt{2\lambda}(p - Aq). The modified SART algorithm for this proximal operator is: 1. Initialization: Set y^{(0)} = 0, f^{(0)} = q. Scale inputs: \tilde{p} = \sqrt{2\lambda}p, \tilde{A} = \sqrt{2\lambda}A. 2. Outer Loop: Iterate t from 1 to T. 3. Inner Loop: Iterate over projections S in S1 \dots SN. 4. Update: Update y for indices j in current projection set S: yj^{(t+1)} = yj^{(t)} + \alpha cj^{(t)}. Compute predicted projection sum: \hat{b}i^{(t+1)} = \sumk a{ik} fk^{(t)} + yi^{(t)}. Compute correction factor: ci^{(t+1)} = \frac{bi - \hat{b}i^{(t+1)}}{\sumk a{ik} + 1}. Update volume f for all voxels j=1 \dots n: fj^{(t+1)} = fj^{(t)} + \alpha \frac{\sum{i \in S} ci^{(t+1)} a{ij}}{\sum{i \in S} a{ij}}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: In proximal SART implementations involving patch-based Jacobians, memory usage can be high. For a volume of size N, storage can be 82 times the volume size (81 for Jacobian + 1 for volume). For a 690 \times 668 \times 776 voxel volume, this requires 109 GB. Convergence: SART is preferred over CG because CG suffers from numerical noise in matrix-free tomography and convergence issues with large sparse systems. A GPU-accelerated implementation that treats forward/back-projection as splatting kernels, inverting the data flow to project voxels onto the detector. It is distinguished by its efficiency in parallel ray geometry (e.g., cryo-ET) and use of pre-integrated lookup tables. A method that integrates denoising into reconstruction using SART as the solver for the data fidelity term. It is chosen over CG for sparse-view settings to maintain consistency with raw projections. Time Complexity: Each iteration involves one forward projection and one backprojection. The cost is proportional to the number of voxels and rays. Memory Complexity: Modest memory requirements compared to direct methods that require storing the full system matrix A (O(mn)). SART is matrix-free, requiring only storage for the volume and projections. However, proximal variants may require additional storage for auxiliary variables and Jacobians. Measured Performance: On a machine with 24 cores and 48 GB RAM, SART with Kaiser-Bessel kernels (radius 2 voxels) and slice-by-slice optimization was used for reconstruction. For sparse-view settings, SART provides better reconstruction results than FDK and CG. Strengths: Handles limited projections better than FDK. Incorporates prior information (e.g., TV priors) easily. Modest memory usage. Limitations: Slower than FDK for full-view data. Convergence can be slow for high-accuracy requirements. When to Use: Sparse-view tomography, limited-angle tomography, or when incorporating regularization priors. When Not to Use: Full-view, high-quality data where speed is critical (use FDK). Large-scale problems where memory for auxiliary variables in proximal methods is prohibitive. SART was proposed by Andersen and Kak as an efficient iterative reconstruction method based on the Kaczmarz projection method. It updates the volume for each scan view, offering better results than FDK for limited projections. It has been widely used in computed tomography, including industrial CT and medical imaging. Recent developments include its use as a proximal operator in Chambolle-Pock schemes for robust 3D cone beam reconstruction and in space-time tomographic reconstruction of deforming objects. name: Voxel Splatting SART/SIRT
head: Voxel Splatting Implementation of SART/SIRT
body: Voxel Splatting SART/SIRT is a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) and Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) proximal operators for tomographic reconstruction. It solves the inverse problem of reconstructing a 3D volume from 2D projections by treating forward and back-projection operations as splatting kernels rather than ray-casting. It is distinguished from its sibling, Ray Casting SART/SIRT, by inverting the data flow: instead of casting rays from the detector to sample the volume, it projects each voxel onto the detector plane, accumulating contributions into ray-sum and weight images. This approach leverages pre-integrated lookup tables for weights, enabling efficient parallelization in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) where parallel ray geometry is common. The method implements the forward and back-projection operators required for the SART/SIRT iterative solver. The core principle is that the forward projection (splatting voxels to detector) and back-projection (splatting detector corrections to voxels) are transposes of each other. Inputs: Current volume estimate V (3D grid of voxel values). Measured projection images I(pi) in log space for each view angle. Relaxation parameter \alpha. Pre-computed weight lookup tables (LUTs) derived from line integrals of radially symmetric filter kernels at various distances. Outputs: Updated volume estimate V'. Correction image (intermediate result for back-projection). 1. Ray-sum Image (R): A 2D image matching the detector resolution. Stores the accumulated weighted sum of voxel contributions. 2. Weights Image (W): A 2D image matching the detector resolution. Stores the sum of weights for each pixel, used to normalize the correction term. 3. Correction Image (C): A 2D image matching the detector resolution. Stores the computed correction term for each pixel before back-projection. 4. Weight Lookup Table (LUT): A 1D or 2D array mapping geometric parameters (e.g., distance from voxel center to pixel center) to pre-integrated kernel weights. 1. Initialize: Zero out the Ray-sum Image R and Weights Image W. 2. Splat Voxels: For each voxel v in the volume V: a. Determine the kernel support (the spatial extent of the splatting kernel). b. For each pixel i in the kernel support: i. Calculate the geometric weight w{v,i} using the pre-computed LUT based on the distance between the voxel center and pixel i. ii. Update the Ray-sum Image: R[i] \leftarrow R[i] + w{v,i} \cdot V[v]. iii. Update the Weights Image: W[i] \leftarrow W[i] + w{v,i}. Note: Data races can occur if two voxels try to update the same pixels at once, either in the ray-sum image or the weights image. Atomic operations or parallel reduction are required to ensure correctness. 1. For each pixel i in the detector image: a. Retrieve the measured line integral I(pi) from the input projection data. b. Retrieve the computed ray sum R[i] and weight sum W[i]. c. Compute the correction term C[i] using the formula: C[i] = \alpha \cdot \frac{I(pi) - R[i]}{W[i]} where \alpha is the relaxation parameter. Edge Case: If W[i] = 0 (no voxels contributed to this pixel), C[i] should be set to 0 to avoid division by zero. 1. Initialize: Create a temporary buffer for the updated volume values, initialized to zero. 2. Splat Corrections: For each voxel v in the volume V: a. Identify the detector pixels covered by the voxel's kernel. b. For each pixel i in the kernel support: i. Retrieve the correction value C[i] from the Correction Image. ii. Retrieve the weight w{v,i} from the LUT (same weight used in forward projection). iii. Accumulate the contribution: V{new}[v] \leftarrow V{new}[v] + w{v,i} \cdot C[i]. Note: There are no data races in the back-projection operation because each voxel writes to a unique memory location in the volume buffer. 3. Update Volume: Replace V with V{new}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeros(shape): return [[0.0] shape[1] for in range(shape[0])] def computekernelsupport(voxelcenter, detectorshape, kernelradius): cx, cy = voxelcenter minx, maxx = int(cx - kernelradius), int(cx + kernelradius) miny, maxy = int(cy - kernelradius), int(cy + kernelradius) support = [] for y in range(max(0, miny), min(detectorshape[0], maxy + 1)): for x in range(max(0, minx), min(detectorshape[1], maxx + 1)): support.append((x, y)) return support def lookupweight(voxelcenter, pixelcenter): """Performs a table lookup for the pre-integrated kernel weight.""" # In practice, this reads from the pre-computed LUT based on geometric distance. return 1.0 # Placeholder for actual LUT read operation def voxelsplattingsartsirt(volume, projections, alpha, detectorshape, kernelradius): """ volume: 3D list (D, H, W) of voxel values projections: list of 2D lists (detector images) in log space alpha: float, relaxation parameter detectorshape: tuple (Hdet, Wdet) kernelradius: float, spatial extent of the splatting kernel """ D, H, W = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) numviews = len(projections) updatedvolume = [[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(D)] for viewidx in range(numviews): raysumimage = zeros(detectorshape) weightsimage = zeros(detectorshape) for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): voxelval = volume[d][h][w] if voxelval == 0.0: continue voxelcenter = (h, w) kernelsupport = computekernelsupport(voxelcenter, detectorshape, kernelradius) for pixel in kernelsupport: wval = lookupweight(voxelcenter, pixel) raysumimage[pixel[1]][pixel[0]] += wval voxelval weightsimage[pixel[1]][pixel[0]] += wval measuredprojection = projections[viewidx] correctionimage = zeros(detectorshape) for i in range(detectorshape[0]): for j in range(detectorshape[1]): wsum = weightsimage[i][j] if wsum > 0.0: correctionimage[i][j] = alpha (measuredprojection[i][j] - raysumimage[i][j]) / wsum else: correctionimage[i][j] = 0.0 viewcontribution = [[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(D)] for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): voxelcenter = (h, w) kernelsupport = computekernelsupport(voxelcenter, detectorshape, kernelradius) for pixel in kernelsupport: wval = lookupweight(voxelcenter, pixel) cval = correctionimage[pixel[1]][pixel[0]] viewcontribution[d][h][w] += wval cval for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): updatedvolume[d][h][w] += viewcontribution[d][h][w] return updatedvolume \alpha (Relaxation Parameter): Controls the step size of the update. Not given in the sources. Kernel Support: The spatial extent of the splatting kernel. Weight Lookup Table (LUT): Pre-computed weights based on line integrals of radially symmetric filter kernels at different distances. Data Races: In forward projection, multiple voxels may update the same detector pixel simultaneously. Division by Zero: If a detector pixel has no contributing voxels (W[i] = 0), the correction term calculation must handle this to avoid NaNs. Precision: The use of pre-integrated LUTs introduces approximation errors compared to exact ray casting, but linear interpolation yields results practically the same as ray-based methods. An alternative implementation of SART/SIRT proximal operators based on ray casting. In this variant, threads compute line integrals and correction terms for forward projection by casting rays from the detector through the volume, and update voxels based on correction images for back-projection. Forward projection involves casting a ray from each pixel, sampling the volume at equidistant points, and retrieving volume values via tri-linear interpolation. The correction term is computed as (I(pi) - \text{sample\rate} \times \sum{s=1}^S v{sk}) / \text{ray\length}, where I(pi) is the measured line integral, S is the number of samples, \text{sample\rate} is the distance between samples, v{sk} is the volume estimate at sample s, and \text{ray\length} is the ray-volume intersection length. Back-projection involves casting a ray from each voxel to the detector, retrieving a correction value via bi-linear interpolation, and updating the voxel. In this way, the forward projection and backward projection are not exact. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The voxel splatting approach is highly parallelizable on GPUs, making it suitable for large volumes in cryo-ET. The use of pre-integrated LUTs reduces the computational cost of weight calculation during runtime. Strengths: Efficient parallelization, no data races in back-projection, practical equivalence to ray-based methods with linear interpolation. Limitations: Data races in forward projection require synchronization to ensure correctness. When to Use: Suitable for cryo-ET with parallel ray geometry where high performance is needed and slight approximation errors are acceptable. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The voxel splatting implementation of SART/SIRT was developed as part of a framework for GPU-accelerated 3D tomographic reconstruction and visualization from noisy electron microscopy tilt-series. It was introduced to address the computational demands of cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), where large volumes and parallel ray geometry allow for efficient parallelization. The method builds on the concept of voxel splatting, where voxels are projected onto the detector plane using pre-integrated lookup tables for weights, which are computed by line integrals of rays traversing radially symmetric filter kernels. name: Proximal Jointly-Optimized Reconstruction and Denoising
head: Iterative Reconstruction with Integrated Denoising, Proximal Optimization Framework
body: Proximal Jointly-Optimized Reconstruction and Denoising is a GPU-accelerated iterative tomographic reconstruction method that integrates noise reduction directly into the reconstruction process. Unlike traditional pipelines that apply denoising as separate pre- or post-processing steps, this method solves an optimization problem where reconstruction and denoising are performed simultaneously, maintaining a direct consistency check between the reconstructed tomogram and the raw input projection images. It builds on SART (Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique) as the primary solver for the data fidelity term, preferred over Conjugate Gradient for sparse-view settings. The method formulates tomographic reconstruction as a joint optimization problem solved via a proximal algorithm framework. It alternates between minimizing the re-projection error (reconstruction) and decreasing noise (regularization/denoising). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Aligned tilt-series from cryogenic electron microscopy (noisy 2D projections). Output: A denoised 3D tomogram. Data Structures: Tilt-series: A set of 2D projection images corresponding to specific tilt angles. Tomogram: The 3D volume being reconstructed. Regularizer/Denoiser: A module implementing a specific denoising method (e.g., total variation, non-local means, or deep learning-based denoiser). Algorithm Steps: The algorithm iteratively updates the tomogram estimate x using a proximal splitting method. It alternates between two main steps: 1. Reconstruction Step (Data Fidelity): Minimize the re-projection error using an algebraic reconstruction technique, specifically SART or SIRT. This step ensures the reconstructed volume is consistent with the measured projection data. 2. Denoising Step (Regularization): Apply a regularization or denoising method to the current tomogram estimate to suppress noise. This step acts as a proximal operator in the optimization framework. Parameters: Reconstruction Algorithm: SART or SIRT. Regularizer/Denoiser: Any compatible denoising method. Number of Iterations: Not specified, but results are achieved in minutes. GPU Acceleration: The method is implemented for execution on GPUs to accelerate the iterative process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def proximaljointlyoptimizedreconstruction(tiltseries, angles, numiterations, reconstructionalgo, denoiser): # Initialize the tomogram to zeros x = [0.0] (nx ny nz) for i in range(numiterations): if reconstructionalgo == 'SART': x = sartupdate(x, tiltseries, angles) elif reconstructionalgo == 'SIRT': x = sirtupdate(x, tiltseries, angles) x = denoiser(x) return x def sartupdate(x, tiltseries, angles): # Standard SART update voxelupdates = [0.0] len(x) raycounts = [0.0] len(x) for projection, angle in zip(tiltseries, angles): estimated = forwardproject(x, angle) for rayidx, (measured, rayvoxels, rayweights) in enumerateprojectedrays(projection, estimated, angle): correction = (measured - estimated[rayidx]) / sum(rayweights) for vidx, weight in zip(rayvoxels, rayweights): voxelupdates[vidx] += correction weight raycounts[vidx] += 1 for vidx in range(len(x)): if raycounts[vidx] > 0: x[vidx] += voxelupdates[vidx] / raycounts[vidx] return x def sirtupdate(x, tiltseries, angles): # Standard SIRT update voxelupdates = [0.0] len(x) raycountssq = [0.0] len(x) for projection, angle in zip(tiltseries, angles): estimated = forwardproject(x, angle) for rayidx, (measured, rayvoxels, rayweights) in enumerateprojectedrays(projection, estimated, angle): residual = measured - estimated[rayidx] for vidx, weight in zip(rayvoxels, rayweights): voxelupdates[vidx] += weight residual raycountssq[vidx] += weight weight for vidx in range(len(x)): if raycountssq[vidx] > 0: x[vidx] += voxelupdates[vidx] / raycountssq[vidx] return x Note: forwardproject and enumerateprojectedrays are standard geometric ray-tracing operations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Levels: The method is specifically designed for cryo-ET where projections are very noisy due to low electron doses. Consistency Check: The method maintains a direct relationship between the original tilt-series and the reconstructed tomogram, enabling a direct consistency check, which is difficult in complex pipelines with separate denoising steps. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but the method is GPU-accelerated and achieves results in minutes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method produces much cleaner tomograms than existing approaches that use separate pre- or post-reconstruction denoising. It achieves excellent denoising results and sharp details. Strengths: Integrates denoising into reconstruction, removing the need for separate steps. Maintains direct consistency with raw input data. Flexible framework allowing multiple combinations of reconstruction algorithms and regularizers. GPU-accelerated for speed. Allows visualization of reconstruction error throughout the iterative process. Limitations: Specifically evaluated for cryo-ET; applicability to other modalities is not discussed. Requires aligned tilt-series as input. When to use: When reconstructing noisy tomograms (e.g., from cryo-ET) and wanting to avoid the complexity and potential inconsistency of separate denoising steps. When not to use: When high-speed, single-pass reconstruction is required without iterative refinement, or when the input projections are not noisy. The method was presented by J. Strnad, Z. Zhang, S. Li, I. Viola, and W. Heidrich in 2022. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D tomograms from noisy electron microscopy tilt-series, where the destructive nature of electron imaging necessitates low electron doses, resulting in low signal-to-noise ratios. Traditional pipelines apply denoising before reconstruction (on tilt-series) or after reconstruction (on tomograms), which can lead to inconsistencies or loss of information. This method was developed to provide a flexible, robust, and GPU-accelerated alternative that integrates these steps. It is implemented as an open-source framework, allowing easy extension with additional reconstruction and denoising methods. name: SIRT with subsets and constraints
head: Constrained SIRT with subsets, SIRT with subsets
body: This method enhances the Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) by partitioning projection data into subsets to manage memory usage and applying hard bounds to voxel values to enforce physical constraints. It solves the problem of reconstructing volumes from large datasets that exceed available RAM while preventing non-physical values (e.g., negative attenuation). It differs from standard SIRT by processing data in chunks rather than all at once, and from SART by retaining SIRT's simultaneous update nature within each subset iteration rather than updating voxel-by-voxel per ray. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: projections: 3D array of shape [numviews, height, width] (dtype float32). geometry: Geometry description object (types: 'simple', 'staticoffsets', 'linearoffsets'). settings: Configuration object containing subsets, sorting, bounds, updateresidual, and iterations. Outputs: volume: 3D array of reconstructed voxel values (dtype float32). Data Structures: Settings Object: subsets (int): Number of projection partitions. Default 10. sorting (str): Order of subsets. Options: 'sequential' or 'equidistant'. bounds (list): [lower, upper] clamping values for voxel intensities. updateresidual (bool): Whether to compute and store residual norms. iterations (int): Total number of reconstruction passes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a zero-initialized volume array volrec with shape matching the target reconstruction grid (typically [numviews, height, width] or derived from geometry). 2. Subset Partitioning: Divide the projections array into N subsets based on settings.subsets. If settings.sorting is 'equidistant', distribute views uniformly across angular space; if 'sequential', split the array contiguously. 3. Iteration Loop: For each iteration k from 1 to settings.iterations: a. Subset Processing: Iterate through each subset s of the partitioned projections. b. Forward/Backward Projection: Perform one SIRT update step using only the projections in subset s. This involves forward projecting the current volume estimate to generate simulated projections, computing the residual (difference between measured and simulated projections), and backprojecting the residual to update the volume. c. Normalization: Apply SIRT normalization factors (ray length and voxel sensitivity) as defined in the parent SIRT method. d. Residual Update (Optional): If settings.updateresidual is True, compute the L2 norm of the residual for the current subset and store it. 4. Constraint Application: After each full iteration (or optionally after each subset, depending on implementation specifics), apply bounds to the volume: volrec = clip(volrec, min=settings.bounds[0], max=settings.bounds[1]). 5. Termination: Return volrec after settings.iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SIRTwithsubsetsandconstraints(projections, geometry, settings): """ SIRT reconstruction with subsets and box constraints. Args: projections: numpy array of shape [numviews, height, width], dtype float32 geometry: Geometry object settings: Object with attributes: subsets: int (default 10) sorting: str ('sequential' or 'equidistant') bounds: list [lower, upper] iterations: int updateresidual: bool """ # Initialize volume # Note: Shape derivation from geometry is implementation-specific numviews, height, width = projections.shape vol = numpy.zeros((numviews, height, width), dtype='float32') # Partition projections into subsets if settings.sorting == 'equidistant': # Distribute views uniformly indices = numpy.linspace(0, numviews - 1, settings.subsets, dtype=int) # Create subsets by grouping views subsets = [] for i in range(settings.subsets): start = indices[i] end = indices[(i + 1) % settings.subsets] if start < end: subsets.append(projections[start:end]) else: subsets.append(numpy.concatenate([projections[start:], projections[:end]])) else: # sequential step = numviews // settings.subsets subsets = numpy.arraysplit(projections, settings.subsets, axis=0) rnorms = [] for iteration in range(settings.iterations): for subsetproj in subsets: # Perform one SIRT update step with the current subset # This involves: # 1. Forward project 'vol' using 'subsetproj' geometry to get simulated projections # 2. Compute residual: residual = subsetproj - simulatedprojections # 3. Backproject 'residual' to update 'vol' # 4. Apply SIRT normalization factors (ray length, voxel sensitivity) # Note: The exact normalization formulas are defined in the parent SIRT article vol = SIRTupdatestep(vol, subsetproj, geometry) # Apply bounds if specified if settings.bounds: vol = numpy.clip(vol, amin=settings.bounds[0], amax=settings.bounds[1]) # Update residual norm if requested if settings.updateresidual: # Compute L2 norm of residual for this subset # Note: Residual computation requires forward projection of current vol simulated = forwardproject(vol, geometry) residual = subsetproj - simulated norm = numpy.linalg.norm(residual) rnorms.append(norm) return vol Parameters: iterations: Number of reconstruction passes. Typical value: 20. subsets: Number of projection partitions. Default: 10. bounds: List [lower, upper] for clamping. Typical lower bound: 0 (non-negativity). sorting: String, 'equidistant' for uniform angular distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: Large datasets may exceed RAM. Using subsets splits the data to fit in memory. Precision: Use float32 for projections and volume to balance precision and memory. Boundary Conditions: Ensure geometry offsets are correctly applied to avoid artifacts at volume boundaries. Applies local box constraints derived from segmentation of a static reference scan to eliminate noise in specific voxel types (e.g., rock vs. fluid). Choose when material phases are known and global bounds are insufficient. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot N \cdot V), where K is iterations, N is subsets, and V is volume size. Each subset requires a forward and backward projection. Memory Complexity: O(V + P/N), where P is total projection data size. Subsets reduce memory from O(P) to O(P/N). Performance: Suitable for large datasets that do not fit in RAM. Convergence may be slower than full SIRT due to subset ordering, but memory efficiency is significantly improved. Strengths: Memory efficient, handles large datasets, enforces physical constraints. Limitations: Slower convergence than full SIRT, requires careful tuning of subset size and sorting. When to Use: Large CT datasets, memory-constrained environments, when physical bounds are known. When Not to Use: Small datasets where full SIRT fits in memory, when maximum convergence speed is critical. Originated from the SIRT method, enhanced with subsets and constraints to address memory and physical constraint issues in tomographic reconstruction. Implemented in the flexTOMO library. cicwi/flexTOMO, https://github.com/cicwi/flexTOMO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SIRT with Local Box Constraints
head: Constrained SIRT for Dynamic Tomography, Dynamic SIRT with static initialization and segmentation constraints, SIRT-LC
body: SIRT-LC is an iterative tomographic reconstruction algorithm designed for dynamic multiphase flow experiments, solving the problem of reconstructing high-quality volumes from data with significantly reduced exposure times and fewer projections. It sets itself apart from standard SIRT and its variant SIRT-IC by applying local box constraints derived from the segmentation of a high-quality static reference scan, which eliminates noise in specific voxel types (rock vs. fluid) that global constraints cannot address. Unlike difference-projection methods that reconstruct only changes, SIRT-LC reconstructs the full volume at each step while enforcing physical attenuation bounds specific to the material phase identified in the static scan. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data b \in \mathbb{R}^m (radiographs) for the current time step; Forward projection operator A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}; Segmentation mask M derived from a high-quality static reconstruction; Attenuation values for rock (\mu{rock}), oil (\mu{oil}), and water (\mu{water}); Global bounds \mu{min} and \mu{max}. Output: Reconstructed volume vector x \in \mathbb{R}^n representing voxel attenuation coefficients. Data Structures: Segmentation Mask (M): A vector of length n where each element Mi classifies voxel i into one of three categories: ROCK, FLUID, or AMBIGUOUS. Convex Set (C): Defined by the segmentation mask, specifying the allowed range [Li, Ui] for each voxel i. Numbered Steps: 1. Static Initialization: For the first time step (t=0), initialize the reconstruction volume x0 using the high-quality reconstruction of the static system. 2. Segmentation: Segment the static reconstruction volume by thresholding to identify rock and fluid regions: Identify rock voxels as those with attenuation values above a specific threshold. Identify fluid voxels as those with values below the threshold AND between the attenuation values of oil and water. Identify ambiguous voxels as those with attenuation values larger than water but smaller than rock. 3. Dynamic Initialization: For each subsequent time step t > 0, initialize the reconstruction volume with the final solution from the immediately preceding time step to maintain temporal continuity. 4. Define Local Constraints: Construct the convex set C based on the segmentation mask M from Step 2: For rock voxels: Fix the value to the expected constant attenuation value \mu{rock}. Thus, Li = Ui = \mu{rock}. For fluid voxels: Constrain values to the interval between oil and water attenuation values. Thus, Li = \min(\mu{oil}, \mu{water}) and Ui = \max(\mu{oil}, \mu{water}). For ambiguous voxels: Apply regular global box constraints. Thus, Li = \mu{min} and Ui = \mu{max}. 5. Iterative Update: Perform the SIRT update step and project the result onto the convex set C: x{k+1} = PC(xk + \alpha A^T R (b - A xk)) = PC(\text{SIRT}(xk)) Where: xk is the volume estimate at iteration k. A^T is the back-projection operator. R is a weighting matrix (typically identity or diagonal normalization). \alpha is the relaxation parameter (step size), replacing the C used in the source notation to avoid variable reuse with the convex set C. PC is the projection operator onto the convex set C. 6. Projection Operator (PC): For each voxel i, compute PC(v)i as: If Mi = \text{ROCK}: return \mu{rock}. If Mi = \text{FLUID}: return \text{clip}(vi, \min(\mu{oil}, \mu{water}), \max(\mu{oil}, \mu{water})). If Mi = \text{AMBIGUOUS}: return \text{clip}(vi, \mu{min}, \mu{max}). 7. Stopping Criterion: Iterate until a stopping criterion is met, such as the NCP (Normalized Cyclic Projection) criterion or a fixed number of iterations. Parameters: N{proj}: Number of projections acquired per time step. The method is designed to work with significantly fewer projections than traditionally required. \mu{min}: The smallest attenuation value in the sample (lower limit). Typically 0. \mu{max}: The largest attenuation value in the sample (upper limit). Typically 2.5 for the tested case. \alpha: Relaxation parameter for SIRT convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sirtlcreconstruction(projectionsb, forwardopA, backprojopAT, staticvolume, rockthreshold, muoil, muwater, mumin=0.0, mumax=2.5, numiterations=100, relaxationalpha=1.0, initialx=None): """ SIRT with Local Box Constraints for dynamic tomography. Args: projectionsb: Array of projection data for current time step. forwardopA: Function performing forward projection (A x). backprojopAT: Function performing back projection (A^T r). staticvolume: High-quality reconstruction of the static system. rockthreshold: Threshold value to segment rock from fluid in staticvolume. muoil: Attenuation value of oil. muwater: Attenuation value of water. mumin: Global minimum attenuation. mumax: Global maximum attenuation. numiterations: Number of SIRT iterations. relaxationalpha: SIRT relaxation parameter (step size). initialx: Volume estimate from previous time step (None for t=0). Returns: reconstructedvolume: The reconstructed volume for the current time step. """ # Step 1 & 2: Segment static volume to create local constraints isrock = staticvolume > rockthreshold fluidlower = min(muoil, muwater) fluidupper = max(muoil, muwater) isfluid = (staticvolume < rockthreshold) & \ (staticvolume >= fluidlower) & \ (staticvolume <= fluidupper) isambiguous = ~isrock & ~isfluid # Determine fixed rock value from static volume (expected constant attenuation) rockmask = isrock if np.any(rockmask): murock = np.median(staticvolume[rockmask]) else: murock = mumax # Step 3: Initialize volume if initialx is None: currentx = staticvolume.copy() else: currentx = initialx.copy() for k in range(numiterations): # Standard SIRT residual update forwardproj = forwardopA(currentx) residual = projectionsb - forwardproj update = backprojopAT(residual) currentx = currentx + relaxationalpha update # Step 4 & 5: Project onto Local Box Constraints projectedx = np.zeroslike(currentx) # Rock voxels: fixed to murock projectedx[isrock] = murock # Fluid voxels: constrained to [muoil, muwater] projectedx[isfluid] = np.clip(currentx[isfluid], fluidlower, fluidupper) # Ambiguous voxels: global box constraints projectedx[isambiguous] = np.clip(currentx[isambiguous], mumin, mumax) currentx = projectedx return currentx Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underestimation of Iterations: SIRT-LC may underestimate the number of iterations needed, leading to large regions within the fluid phase that are either overestimated or underestimated. Noise in Fluid Phases: While SIRT-LC eliminates noise compared to SIRT-IC, improper segmentation or thresholding in the static scan can lead to incorrect classification of ambiguous voxels, propagating errors. Temporal Deterioration: The \ell2-norm of the residual may vary across time steps due to the initialization linking the current step to the previous one, potentially causing slight performance degradation over long sequences if the dynamic changes are significant. A tomographic reconstruction method that uses a high-quality static data set to initialise the reconstruction of dynamic time steps, linking the current time step with the previous one. It initializes time step t=0 with the reconstruction of the static system and remaining time steps t>0 with the reconstruction of the previous time step t-1. It applies global box constraints to truncate voxel values to [\mu{min}, \mu{max}]. Unlike SIRT-LC, it does not apply local segmentation constraints, resulting in a fair bit of noise in the reconstructed fluid phases. In the best data case (N{proj}=360, \rho=0.25\%), SIRT-IC achieves an \ell2-norm of 1.34 \cdot 10^{-3}, which is slightly inferior to SIRT-LC (1.43 \cdot 10^{-3}) but superior to SIRT (1.70 \cdot 10^{-3}). A variant of SIRT that applies global box constraints to truncate voxel attenuation coefficients to the minimum and maximum values present in the sample. After the standard SIRT update step, it projects the resulting voxel values onto the convex set C = [\mu{min}, \mu{max}]^n. For the tested case, \mu{min}=0 and \mu{max}=2.5. It does not use initialization from previous time steps or local segmentation constraints. Time Complexity: Iterative, dependent on the number of projections N{proj}, the number of voxels n, and the number of iterations. Each iteration involves a forward and back projection. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume x, projection data b, and the system matrix A (or its efficient representation via the ASTRA toolbox). Measured Performance: SIRT-LC is considered the best algorithm in general across all data cases tested. In the worst data case (N{proj}=45, \rho=5.00\%), SIRT-LC achieves an \ell2-norm of 3.34 \cdot 10^{-3}, outperforming SIRT (11.49 \cdot 10^{-3}) and SIRT-BC (11.06 \cdot 10^{-3}). Strengths: Maintains high image quality with significantly fewer projections and higher noise levels than FBP/FDK. Eliminates noise in fluid phases better than SIRT-IC by using local constraints. Produces sharper peaks in the voxel value histogram, fitting the visual appearance of higher contrast. Limitations: Requires a high-quality static scan of the system before the dynamic process begins. Performance may degrade slightly across time steps due to initialization linking. When to Use: Dynamic multiphase flow experiments where exposure time and number of projections are limited, and a static reference scan is available. The method was developed to study fluid flow processes in porous media using laboratory X-ray tomography, addressing the limitations of low X-ray brilliance and prolonged exposure times. It extends the Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) by incorporating prior knowledge from a static scan. The algorithm was compared against FBP, FDK, SIRT, SIRT-BC, SIRT-IC, and difference-projection methods by Myers et al. and rSIRT-PWC by Van Eyndhoven et al.. The implementation utilizes the ASTRA toolbox for optimized C++ and CUDA code, callable via Python. Improved dynamic imaging of multiphase flow by constrained tomographic reconstruction., https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-91776-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: General Numerical Optimization Framework for Tomography
head: Regularized Inverse Problem Solver for Tomography, Regularized Optimization for Cryo-ET, Tomographic Reconstruction as Optimization, Variational Tomography Framework
body: This framework formulates tomographic reconstruction as a regularized inverse problem, minimizing a data fidelity term plus a regularization term to handle noisy, angle-limited, or sparse projection data. It sets itself apart by decoupling the optimization into independent proximal operators, allowing the flexible incorporation of complex, non-smooth regularizers and physics-based priors. The framework solves the inverse problem by minimizing an objective function composed of a data fidelity term and a regularization term. The image formation model in log space is linear, derived from the Beer-Lambert Law. The measured intensity I(pi) for a pixel pi is related to the incident intensity \hat{I}0(pi) and the attenuation cross-section (density) \sigma along the ray r{pi}(t): \hat{I}(pi) = -\log \frac{I(pi)}{\hat{I}0(pi)} = \int \sigma(r{pi}(t)) dt Discretizing the volume into N voxels and the projections into M rays yields the linear system W \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{p}, where \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^N is the unknown volume, \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^M is the set of known ray integrals (tilt-series), and W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N} is the weight matrix representing voxel contributions to ray integrals. The reconstruction is formulated as the optimization problem: \arg \min{\mathbf{v}} \frac{1}{2} \|W \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p}\|2^2 + \Gamma(\mathbf{v}) where the first term is the data fidelity (least-squares error) and the second term \Gamma(\mathbf{v}) is a non-linear regularizer. To apply proximal algorithms, the problem is rewritten in a constrained form: \arg \min{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}} F(\mathbf{v}) + G(\mathbf{z}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad K\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{z} where F(\mathbf{v}) = \frac{1}{2} \|W \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p}\|2^2 is the data fidelity term, G(\mathbf{z}) = \Gamma(\mathbf{v}) is the regularization term, and K is a linear operator related to the regularization term. The core mechanism is the decomposition of this problem into independent proximal operators: one for the linear least squares data term, and one for the non-linear regularizer. Due to the large size of W, a matrix-free iterative solver is required to control memory consumption. SART yields better results than Conjugate Gradients for solving the data term proximal operator, especially with sparse numbers of projections. The regularization proximal operator handles the non-smooth regularizer term and depends on the specific choice of g (e.g., Total Variation). This modular approach allows the framework to support 3D super-resolution, sparse view tomography, space-time reconstruction, warp-and-project deforming objects, and dynamic fluid capture. A first-order primal-dual optimization method that decouples the objective into two independent proximal sub-problems (data fidelity and regularization), allowing efficient handling of large-scale sparse systems. Choose when solving composite convex problems with non-smooth regularizers. A physics-based strategy coupling density and velocity fields through transport and incompressibility priors. Choose when reconstructing fluid flow fields from sparse multi-view video data where standard tomography fails due to few cameras. A matrix-free, grid-free iterative solver using random walks and kernel density estimation. Choose when avoiding fixed spatial discretization is required, or for interactive reconstruction where explicit matrix inversion is infeasible. Solves the linear inverse problem A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y} by optimizing over a latent variable \mathbf{z} of a generative model G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{z}) rather than directly over the image \mathbf{x}. It uses a weighted data fidelity term to account for non-uniform confidence in estimated sinogram values and a generator prior. The optimization objective is: \arg\min{\mathbf{z} \in S^m} \|A G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{z}) - \mu(\mathbf{r})\|{\sigma(\mathbf{r})}^2 + \lambda D(G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{z})) where \mathbf{z} lies on an m+1 dimensional sphere, \mu(\mathbf{r}) is the estimated sinogram, and \sigma(\mathbf{r}) represents the confidence. The framework originated from the need to reconstruct high-quality volumes from noisy and angle-limited tilt-series in cryogenic electron tomography (Cryo-ET). It was formalized as a proximal algorithm framework to handle non-smooth, constrained, and large-scale optimization problems. The approach was subsequently generalized to X-ray CT for 3D super-resolution, sparse view reconstruction, and space-time reconstruction of deforming objects. It has also been applied to dynamic fluid capture using RGB cameras.
