name: Multiplicative ART
head: MART (Multiplicative ART), Multiplicative Algebraic Reconstruction Technique, Single-view-MART, Sv-MART
body: Multiplicative ART (MART) is an iterative algebraic reconstruction algorithm that optimizes the Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) by applying multiplicative updates instead of additive corrections. It solves the linear system P = Rf for positive projection data Pi and positive system matrix coefficients R{ij}, converging to a non-negative solution that maximizes entropy. Unlike its parent Adaptive Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (AART), which adjusts step sizes adaptively, MART uses a fixed relaxation parameter within a multiplicative framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data Pi for each projection i; system matrix coefficients R{ij} representing the intersection length of projection line i with voxel j; initial field distribution f^{(0)}; relaxation parameter \lambda. Output: Reconstructed field distribution f. Data Structures: f: Array of size M storing voxel values. Initialized to arbitrary positive values fj^{(0)} > 0. P: Array of size N storing measured projection values. R: System matrix or sparse representation of coefficients R{ij}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the field distribution fj = fj^{(0)} for all voxels j, ensuring fj^{(0)} > 0. 2. Cycle through each projection i = 1, \dots, N: a. Calculate the estimated projection \hat{P}i = \sum{j} R{ij} fj. b. For each voxel j intersected by projection line i, update its value using the multiplicative rule: fj^{(new)} = fj^{(old)} \left( \frac{Pi}{\hat{P}i} \right)^{\lambda R{ij}} where \lambda is the relaxation parameter. 3. Repeat step 2 until the convergence criteria \left| \frac{fj^{(new)} - fj^{(old)}}{fj^{(old)}} \right| \le \epsilon is met for all voxels. Formulas: Update rule: fj^{(n+1)} = fj^{(n)} \left( \frac{Pi}{\sum{j=1}^{Ne} R{ij} fj^{(n)}} \right)^{\lambda R{ij}}. Entropy minimization target: E(f) = -\sum{k=1}^{M} fk \log fk. Convergence criteria: \left| \frac{fv^{new} - fv^{old}}{fv^{old}} \right| \le \epsilon. Parameters: \lambda: Relaxation parameter. Typical range: 0.01 \le \lambda \le 0.1. \epsilon: Tolerance factor for convergence. Fixed value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Requires positive initialization: fj^{(0)} > 0 is mandatory to maintain positivity throughout iterations. If \hat{P}i = 0, division by zero occurs in the ratio Pi/\hat{P}i. This happens if the initial guess is zero and no line passes through non-zero voxels, or if the geometry is degenerate. Guard against this by ensuring fj^{(0)} > 0 and checking for zero denominators. The sequential processing of projections means the update order can influence convergence behavior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiplicativeart(projections, systemmatrix, initialf, lambdaparam, epsilon): """ projections: list of floats, Pi for each projection i systemmatrix: list of lists of tuples, systemmatrix[i] contains (j, Rij) for voxels j intersected by projection i initialf: list of floats, fj^(0) lambdaparam: float, relaxation parameter in [0.01, 0.1] epsilon: float, convergence tolerance """ f = list(initialf) numprojections = len(projections) while True: maxrelativechange = 0.0 converged = True for i in range(numprojections): Pi = projections[i] estimatedP = 0.0 activevoxels = systemmatrix[i] for j, Rij in activevoxels: estimatedP += Rij f[j] if estimatedP == 0: continue ratio = Pi / estimatedP power = lambdaparam for j, Rij in activevoxels: oldf = f[j] newf = oldf (ratio (power Rij)) if newf < 0: newf = 0.0 f[j] = newf if oldf != 0: relchange = abs((newf - oldf) / oldf) if relchange > maxrelativechange: maxrelativechange = relchange else: if newf > 0: maxrelativechange = float('inf') converged = False if maxrelativechange <= epsilon and converged: break return f Sparse MART (Sp-MART) is an iterative algorithm that solves linear equations P{p,l} = \sumv \alpha{p,l,v} fv by treating all projection lines as part of a single projection to reduce storage requirements. It updates field values using fv^{new} = fv^{old} (1 - \beta (1 - \Delta P{p,l})), where \beta \in [0, 2] is a relaxation parameter and \Delta P{p,l} is the discrepancy between measured and calculated data. It is chosen when memory constraints require avoiding full coefficient matrix storage, though it necessitates a large number of projections and sensors to produce high-quality images. Simultaneous MART (SMART) is the simultaneous variant of MART that applies to non-negative systems and updates all equations at each iteration, unlike MART which processes one equation per iteration. It converges to a maximum entropy solution using the update rule fj^{(n+1)} = fj^{(n)} \left( \prodi \left( \frac{Pi}{\sum{j=1}^{Ne} R{ij} fj^{(n)}} \right)^{\lambda R{ij}} \right)^{1/N}, where N is the number of projections and \lambda is the relaxation parameter. It is chosen when faster convergence is needed at the cost of higher per-iteration computational load. USCG-based Sp-MART is a tomographic reconstruction method that reduces space and time complexity by discretizing the image domain using a Uniformly Sampled Cylindrical Grid (USCG). It solves the radial deterioration of resolution found in conventional polar grid methods while accelerating line tracing by leveraging rotational symmetry and on-the-fly coefficient calculation. Compared to Cartesian grid-based methods, it enhances overall reconstruction speed by a factor of 2.5, and unlike the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, it produces high-quality images with a significantly limited number of projections and detectors, making it suitable for low-cost CT setups. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(I \cdot Np \cdot Nl \cdot Nv) per iteration, where I is iterations, Np is projections, Nl is lines per projection, and Nv is active voxels per line. Memory: O(N^3) for the field f and O(N{nonzero}) for the system matrix if stored sparsely. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the geometry and the sparsity of the system matrix. In cylindrical geometries, precomputing intersection points and sorting them by distance to the source improves cache locality and speed. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of voxels and projections. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enforces non-negativity naturally; converges to a physically meaningful maximum entropy solution. Limitations: Convergence can be slow; sensitive to the choice of \lambda; sequential nature limits parallelism compared to simultaneous methods like SIRT. When to Use: Use when non-negativity is critical and the problem is ill-posed or noisy. Use when additive methods produce negative artifacts. When Not to Use: Use when speed is paramount and non-negativity is not required (use SIRT or FBP). Use when the system matrix is dense and memory is limited (use sparse variants or compressed sensing). MART was developed as an optimization of the Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) that uses multiplicative updates instead of additive corrections. It converges to a solution minimizing entropy E(f) = -\sum{k=1}^{M} fk \log fk, seeking only positive solutions. The method was introduced in the context of improving reconstruction quality by using multiplicative updates instead of additive corrections. It is widely used in medical imaging, industrial CT, and electron microscopy where non-negative density values are physically required. name: USCG-based Sp-MART
head: USCG Sp-MART, Uniformly Sampled Cylindrical Grid Sp-MART
body: USCG-based Sp-MART is a tomographic reconstruction method that reduces the space and time complexity of algebraic reconstruction techniques by discretizing the image domain using a Uniformly Sampled Cylindrical Grid (USCG). It solves the radial deterioration of resolution found in conventional polar grid methods while accelerating line tracing by leveraging rotational symmetry and on-the-fly coefficient calculation. Compared to Cartesian grid-based methods, it enhances overall reconstruction speed by a factor of 2.5, and unlike the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, it produces high-quality images with a significantly limited number of projections and detectors, making it suitable for low-cost CT setups. Inputs: p: Number of projection views. d: Number of detectors per projection. \thetak: Source angle for the k-th projection view (k = 0, \dots, p-1). Pk: The k-th projection data vector of size d. V: Initial volume estimate. Outputs: V: Reconstructed volume. Data Structures: The USCG discretization organizes voxels into slices, rings, and angular sectors. Slice (s): Index along the z-axis. Ring (r): Radial index from the center. Angle (\alpha): Angular position within the ring. Line Segment Attributes: For each line segment in the first projection, store the slice number (s), ring number (r), and initial angular position (\alpha0). Intersection points with the grid boundaries are calculated only for one-fourth of the lines, with the remaining points derived via mirroring. Parameters: Typical experimental setups use 50–70 projections and 10,000–40,000 detectors. X-ray voltages range from 110 to 120 KeV. X-ray tube currents range from 105 to 110 microamperes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Volume: Set all voxel values in V to zero or a background value. 2. First Projection Tracing (k=0): Identify the lines corresponding to the first projection view. Due to symmetry, calculate intersection points and grid attributes (s, r, \alpha0) for only one-fourth of the total lines. Generate the remaining lines by mirroring the calculated intersection points. Store the slice number (s), ring number (r), and initial angular position (\alpha0) for each line segment. Perform time-consuming steps (intersection calculation, array sorting, rounding, angular position finding) only for this projection. 3. Iterative Update (Sp-MART): For each iteration and each projection view k = 0, \dots, p-1: Trace Line for Projection k: Retrieve the stored s and r for the line segment. Calculate the current angular position \alphak using rotational symmetry: \alphak = \alpha0 + \thetak where \thetak is the source angle of the k-th projection. The slice number s and ring number r remain unchanged from the first projection. Calculate Line Coefficients On-the-Fly: Compute the path length L of the line segment through the voxel defined by (s, r, \alphak). Compute the projection coefficient a{ij} (weight of voxel j in projection i) based on the intersection geometry. Since coefficients are calculated on the fly, no storage is required for the system matrix. Forward Projection: Compute the estimated projection value \hat{p}i for detector i: \hat{p}i = \sum{j \in \text{voxels}} a{ij} Vj Backprojection and Multiplicative Update: Compute the ratio of measured to estimated projection: Ri = \frac{pi}{\hat{p}i} Update the voxel values Vj using the multiplicative ART rule: Vj^{\text{new}} = Vj^{\text{old}} \times \frac{\sum{i \in \text{detectors}} a{ij} Ri}{\sum{i \in \text{detectors}} a{ij}} The normalization denominator ensures stability, consistent with standard MART formulations. 4. Termination: Repeat step 3 until convergence or a fixed number of iterations is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uscgspmart(projections, sourceangles, numslices, numrings, numangles, maxiter): # Initialize volume to zero or a background value V = zeros((numslices, numrings, numangles)) # Trace first projection view firstprojlines = [] for i in range(numdetectors // 4): s, r, alpha0 = computelineattributes(i) firstprojlines.append((s, r, alpha0)) # Mirror points for the remaining three-fourths fulllines = firstprojlines + mirrorpoints(firstprojlines) for iteration in range(maxiter): for k in range(p): thetak = sourceangles[k] for s, r, alpha0 in fulllines: # Update angular position using rotational symmetry alphak = alpha0 + thetak # Compute projection coefficient on the fly aij = computecoefficient(s, r, alphak) # Forward projection phat = sum(aij V[s, r, alphak] for all voxels) # Backprojection and multiplicative update ratio = projections[k] / phat V[s, r, alphak] = sum(aij ratio) / sum(aij) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grid Symmetry Requirement: The method relies on the USCG grid's rotational symmetry for the mirror-image optimization. If the grid is not uniformly sampled, the one-fourth calculation may introduce artifacts. Precision: Rounding numbers during the initial trace of the first projection must be handled carefully to avoid accumulation errors in subsequent projections. Degenerate Input: Lines passing exactly through grid boundaries or the center axis require special handling for intersection calculations. Time Complexity: Line tracing speed is enhanced by O(N) compared to traditional polar grid methods because it avoids finding intersections with radial planes. The line tracing process is accelerated by O(p) where p is the number of projection views, as time-consuming steps are executed only for the first projection. Overall reconstruction speed is enhanced by a factor of 2.5 compared to Cartesian grid-based methods. Memory Complexity: Storage requirement is reduced by a factor of p because projection coefficients are calculated on the fly and not stored. Only the slice, ring, and angle for the first projection need to be stored. Performance: Cu-Lump reconstruction (50 projections, 10,000 detectors) yields MAE 0.0011, RMSE 0.0037, and SSIM 0.9909. Frog reconstruction (70 projections, 40,000 detectors) yields MAE 0.0019, RMSE 0.0052, and SSIM 0.9626. FDK requires 400 projections and over 1 million detectors to generate comparable quality images. Strengths: The method is ideal for low-cost CT setups with limited projections and detectors. It solves the radial deterioration of resolution inherent in conventional polar grids. Limitations: The approach relies on specific grid symmetries and is less flexible for arbitrary Cartesian or non-uniform sampling without modification. The method was proposed to address the limitations of algebraic reconstruction techniques, specifically the high computational cost and memory usage associated with large system matrices in traditional polar or Cartesian grids. It builds on Multiplicative ART, which uses multiplicative updates for stability and positivity preservation. The USCG discretization scheme was introduced to solve the radial resolution deterioration found in conventional polar grid methods. Experimental validation was performed on a Copper Lump and a Frog specimen using X-ray voltages of 120 KeV and 110 KeV, respectively. name: Direct Linear Inversion (ART)
head: Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) - Matrix Inversion Variant, Image reconstruction via matrix inversion, Matrix Inversion, Matrix Inversion Tomography, Pseudo-inverse Reconstruction
body: Direct Linear Inversion treats the discrete Radon transform as a linear matrix multiplication and recovers the image by multiplying the scan data by the pseudo-inverse of the projection matrix. It differs from iterative algebraic siblings by computing a direct solution in a single matrix multiplication rather than minimizing residuals through repeated updates. Input: A sinogram (parallel-beam projections) at angles distinct angles, each containing rays measurements. Output: A reconstructed 2D image of dimensions width × height. 1. Projection Matrix (M): A dense matrix of size (angles \times rays) \times (width \times height). 2. Data Vector (\mathbf{v}): A column vector of size angles \times rays containing the sinogram measurements. 3. Reconstruction Vector (\mathbf{r}): A column vector of size width \times height containing the recovered pixel values. Image Dimensions: w (width), h (height) in pixels. Regularization Threshold (\epsilon): 10^{-6}, applied during pseudo-inverse computation to handle non-square or ill-conditioned matrices. Angle Step Size: \Delta \theta = \pi / angles. Ray Offset: \sqrt{2}, representing the half-width of the scan range. Ray Step Size: 2\sqrt{2} / (rays - 1). 1. Initialize matrix M of size (angles \cdot rays) \times (w \cdot h) to zero. 2. For each angle index a \in [0, angles) and ray index r \in [0, rays): a. Calculate the ray start and end points in normalized coordinates [-1, 1]. b. Compute scan weights for each pixel intersected by the ray using a scan-conversion approach where pixels are solid squares and rays are zero-width lines. c. Populate M[(a \cdot rays + r), (y \cdot w + x)] with the intersection length weight wt for each intersected pixel (x, y). 3. Construct the input vector \mathbf{v} of length angles \times rays from the sinogram data. 4. Compute the pseudo-inverse M^+ of M using the regularization threshold \epsilon = 10^{-6}. 5. Compute the reconstruction vector \mathbf{r} = M^+ \mathbf{v}. 6. Reshape \mathbf{r} into a 2D image of dimensions width \times height. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def directlinearinversion(sinogramdata, anglescount, rayscount, width, height): """ Reconstructs an image from sinogram data using direct matrix inversion. """ # Flatten sinogram to vector v v = sinogramdata.flatten() # Initialize projection matrix M nummeasurements = anglescount rayscount numpixels = width height M = np.zeros((nummeasurements, numpixels)) # Precompute ray parameters rayoffset = np.sqrt(2) raystep = 2 rayoffset / (rayscount - 1) anglestep = np.pi / anglescount # Build the projection matrix for a in range(anglescount): angle = a anglestep cosa = np.cos(angle) sina = np.sin(angle) for r in range(rayscount): t = -rayoffset + r raystep # Iterate over all pixels to compute intersection weights for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Pixel bounds in normalized coordinates [-1, 1] x0, x1 = -1.0 + x (2.0 / width), -1.0 + (x + 1) (2.0 / width) y0, y1 = -1.0 + y (2.0 / height), -1.0 + (y + 1) (2.0 / height) # Calculate intersection length of the ray with the pixel square wt = linepixelintersectionlength(x0, y0, x1, y1, cosa, sina, t) # Populate matrix rowidx = a rayscount + r colidx = y width + x M[rowidx, colidx] = wt # Compute pseudo-inverse with regularization threshold epsilon = 1e-6 Mpseudo = np.linalg.pinv(M, rcond=epsilon) # Compute reconstruction vector r = Mpseudo @ v # Reshape into image image = r.reshape((height, width)) return image def linepixelintersectionlength(x0, y0, x1, y1, cosa, sina, t): """ Computes the length of the intersection between a zero-width line and a rectangular pixel. Line equation: xcosa + ysina = t """ # Project pixel corners onto the line direction to find entry/exit parameters # Direction vector of the line dx, dy = -sina, cosa # Parametric line: P(s) = P0 + s (dx, dy) # We find the range of s where the line is inside the pixel rectangle # Using Liang-Barsky style clipping for the line against the rectangle tmin, tmax = -np.inf, np.inf # Check against all four edges edges = [ (x0, -1.0), # left (x1, 1.0), # right (y0, -1.0), # bottom (y1, 1.0) # top ] # We need to solve for s in: x0 <= P0x + sdx <= x1 and y0 <= P0y + sdy <= y1 # Instead, we compute the intersection of the line with the rectangle boundaries directly # A robust standard approach: compute intersection points with the 4 edges and keep those inside # Simplified robust calculation: project pixel center to line, check bounds # For exact length, we clip the infinite line to the rectangle px, py = (x0 + x1) / 2.0, (y0 + y1) / 2.0 dist = px cosa + py sina - t # Projected half-width of the pixel along the line normal projhalfw = 0.5 (abs(cosa) (x1 - x0) + abs(sina) (y1 - y0)) if abs(dist) >= projhalfw: return 0.0 # Intersection length formula for a line crossing a rectangle # Length = 2 sqrt(projhalfw^2 - dist^2) / |sin(thetaline - thetarect)| # For axis-aligned pixels, this simplifies to the standard DDA step length stepx = (x1 - x0) / abs(dx) if abs(dx) > 1e-12 else np.inf stepy = (y1 - y0) / abs(dy) if abs(dy) > 1e-12 else np.inf # The exact chord length inside the rectangle # Using the standard geometric result for line-rectangle intersection if abs(dx) > abs(dy): length = stepx np.sqrt(1.0 - (dist / projhalfw)2) 2.0 abs(dx) else: length = stepy np.sqrt(1.0 - (dist / projhalfw)2) 2.0 abs(dy) return max(0.0, length) Discretization Effects: Error variation occurs with odd/even ray counts due to discretization artifacts, particularly in small images. 180-Degree Symmetry: The 180-degree case is identical to the 0-degree case in parallel-beam geometry and should be avoided to prevent redundant data. Matrix Shape: The matrix M is not required to be square (width \cdot height \neq rays \cdot angles); the pseudo-inverse handles non-square systems. Ill-Conditioning: The matrix may be ill-conditioned, requiring a regularization threshold of 10^{-6} to stabilize the pseudo-inverse computation. Performance: The method is computationally expensive, with naive implementation complexity of O((wh)^3). An iterative solver that updates the image estimate using all projections simultaneously per iteration, offering improved convergence over sequential updates while requiring more memory per step. Choose when direct inversion is too slow or unstable for large images. Link Extends the algebraic framework to handle dynamic scenes by incorporating motion models directly into the projection matrix. Choose when reconstructing time-varying volumes where static assumptions cause blurring. Link Time Complexity: O((wh)^3) for a naive implementation, where w and h are image dimensions. In terms of image edge length L, this scales roughly as O(L^6). Measured Performance: On a 35×40 scan reconstruction, RMS error was < 1.0 \times 10^{-7} (test time 20s on an old MacBook). On a 10×10 scan reconstruction of an 8×8 synthetic image, RMS error was < 1.0 \times 10^{-10}. Strengths: Conceptually simple; provides a direct non-iterative solution; naturally handles non-square measurement systems via pseudo-inverse. Limitations: Extremely slow for large images due to cubic complexity; sensitive to discretization errors; prone to noise amplification if the matrix is ill-conditioned without regularization. When to Use: Small images where simplicity and directness are prioritized over speed; educational demonstrations; cases where iterative convergence fails. When Not to Use: Large-scale reconstructions; real-time applications; scenes with significant noise where regularization tuning is impractical. The method originates from the observation that the Radon transform can be discretized as a linear matrix multiplication in the image domain. It was implemented as the --algorithm=matrix-inversion option in a Rust-based tomography project to demonstrate that standard linear algebra libraries (e.g., nalgebra) can invert the transform directly without custom algebraic theory. The approach is characterized as a "cheap trick" that trades computational expense for implementation simplicity. simon-frankau/rediscovering-tomography, https://github.com/simon-frankau/rediscovering-tomography, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART)
head: SART (Simultaneous ART), Simultaneous ART
body: Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) is an iterative algebraic method for solving the linear system Ax = p in X-ray tomography, where A is the system matrix, x is the unknown volume, and p is the measured sinogram. It solves the inverse rendering problem of reconstructing a 3D volume from 2D projections by aggregating updates from a full projection image (or subset of rays) and applying them simultaneously. Unlike its sibling Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART), which updates the volume one ray at a time, SART processes all rays in a projection image concurrently, providing faster convergence and better stability against noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: System matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} (where m is the number of rays and n is the number of voxels), projection vector p \in \mathbb{R}^m (sinogram), relaxation parameter \alpha (typically 0 < \alpha < 2), and total iterations T. Output: Reconstructed volume vector x \in \mathbb{R}^n. Data Structures: The system matrix A is not stored explicitly due to memory constraints (e.g., a 512^3 volume with 360 1.5-megapixel projections requires ~280 GB for single-precision A). Instead, A is accessed implicitly via geometric ray tracing functions during forward and backprojection. a{ij} represents the contribution of voxel j to ray i, computed as the intersection length or weight. x^{(t)} is the volume estimate at iteration t. \hat{p}^{(t)} is the estimated projection vector at iteration t. c^{(t)} is the normalized correction factor vector at iteration t. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set the initial volume estimate x^{(0)} = 0. 2. Iterate: For each iteration t = 1 to T: 3. Loop over Projections: For each projection image S in the set of all projection images \mathcal{S}{all}: 4. Forward Projection: For each ray i in the current subset S, compute the estimated projection: \hat{p}i^{(t)} = \sum{k} a{ik} xk^{(t)} where the sum is over all voxels k contributing to ray i. 5. Correction: For each ray i in the current subset S, compute the normalized correction factor: ci^{(t)} = \frac{pi - \hat{p}i^{(t)}}{\sum{k} a{ik}} The denominator \sum{k} a{ik} is the sum of contributions of ray i to all voxels. 6. Backprojection: Update all voxels j = 1 \dots n using the aggregated corrections from the current subset S: xj^{(t+1)} = xj^{(t)} + \alpha \frac{\sum{i \in \mathcal{S}} ci^{(t)} a{ij}}{\sum{i \in \mathcal{S}} a{ij}} The numerator aggregates the weighted corrections from all rays i in subset S that pass through voxel j. The denominator \sum{i \in \mathcal{S}} a{ij} is the sum of contributions of all rays in S to voxel j. 7. End loop over projections. 8. End loop over iterations. 9. Return x^{(T)}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sart(Agetter, p, alpha, T, numvoxels, numrays, projectionsets): """ Agetter: function(i, j) -> float, returns aij. p: array of shape (numrays,) alpha: float, relaxation parameter (0 < alpha < 2) T: int, number of iterations numvoxels: int, n numrays: int, m projectionsets: list of lists, where each inner list contains indices of rays for one projection image. """ x = [0.0] numvoxels for t in range(1, T + 1): xprev = x[:] # x^(t) for S in projectionsets: # Forward Projection & Correction for rays in S phat = [0.0] len(S) c = [0.0] len(S) raysumdenom = [0.0] len(S) for idx, i in enumerate(S): phatval = 0.0 raysum = 0.0 for k in range(numvoxels): aik = Agetter(i, k) phatval += aik xprev[k] raysum += aik phat[idx] = phatval raysumdenom[idx] = raysum c[idx] = (p[i] - phat[idx]) / raysumdenom[idx] # Backprojection: compute denominator per voxel for this subset S voxelraysum = [0.0] numvoxels for idx, i in enumerate(S): for k in range(numvoxels): aik = Agetter(i, k) voxelraysum[k] += aik # Update voxels for j in range(numvoxels): if voxelraysum[j] == 0: continue numerator = 0.0 for idx, i in enumerate(S): aij = Agetter(i, j) numerator += c[idx] aij x[j] = xprev[j] + alpha (numerator / voxelraysum[j]) return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: The system matrix A is too large to store explicitly. Implementations must be "matrix-free," computing a{ij} on the fly using ray-voxel intersection geometry. Under-determined Systems: If m < n (fewer rays than voxels), SART is assumed to solve the minimum norm problem \minx \|x\|2^2 subject to Ax = p, similar to ART, though no formal convergence proof exists for the general case. Relaxation Parameter: \alpha should typically be in the range (0, 2) for stability. Modifies SART to incorporate a proximal operator for regularization and prior information, iterating on auxiliary variables y and x. Choose when prior knowledge or regularization is needed. Variant for dynamic tomography. Choose when object motion is present. Single-ray update variant. Choose when memory is extremely constrained or for theoretical comparison. Time Complexity: Each iteration involves a forward projection and a backprojection for all rays. Complexity is proportional to T \times m \times (\text{avg voxels per ray}). Memory Complexity: O(n + m) for storing x, p, and intermediate buffers. O(1) for A (matrix-free). Performance: Faster convergence and better noise resilience than ART. Amenable to parallelization on graphics hardware. Strengths: Intuitive geometric interpretation, better stability against noise, faster convergence than ART. Limitations: No formal convergence proof for the general case. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction is needed and computational resources allow for iterative methods; when noise resilience is critical. When not to use: Not given in the sources. SART is based on the Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART), which dates back to Kaczmarz in 1937. It was developed to improve upon ART by aggregating updates from multiple rays, providing better stability and convergence. It is implemented in the Reconstruction ToolKit (RTK) and the ASTRA toolbox (though ASTRA lacks 3D SART support according to the text). name: SART Proximal Operator
head: Modified SART, SART with Proximal Term
body: The SART Proximal Operator is an iterative tomographic reconstruction method that extends the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) by incorporating a proximal term to enforce prior information or regularization. It solves the linear system Ax = p while minimizing the distance to an input estimate u, effectively finding the least-squares solution closest to u. Unlike standard SART, which initializes the volume to zero, this method maintains an auxiliary variable y to handle the data fidelity term relative to the prior, allowing for the inclusion of prior knowledge directly in the iteration loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Forward projection matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, projection measurements p \in \mathbb{R}^m, input volume estimate (prior) u \in \mathbb{R}^n, regularization parameter \lambda \in \mathbb{R}, step size \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and number of iterations T. Outputs: Reconstructed volume x \in \mathbb{R}^n. Data Structures: x: Volume reconstruction array of size n (number of voxels). y: Auxiliary variable array of size m (number of projection pixels/lines). A: Forward projection operator matrix. p: Projection measurements vector. Parameters: \lambda: Regularization parameter used in the scaling of the projection matrix and projections. \alpha: Step size (relaxation parameter). u: Input volume estimate or prior used to initialize x and modify the data term. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Scale the projection measurements and the matrix by \sqrt{2\lambda}. \tilde{p} = \sqrt{2\lambda} p \tilde{A} = \sqrt{2\lambda} A Note: The source applies this scaling in-place and subsequently refers to the scaled variables simply as p and A in the update formulas. 2. Initialization: Set the auxiliary variable to zero and initialize the volume with the prior. y^{(0)} = 0 x^{(0)} = u 3. Iteration: For t = 1 to T: a. Subset Loop: Iterate over all projection subsets S. b. Residual Calculation: For each projection i \in S, compute the residual term ci^{(t)}. ci^{(t)} = \frac{pi - \sum{k=1}^{n} a{ik} xk^{(t)} - yi^{(t)}}{\sum{k=1}^{n} a{ik} + 1} Here, a{ik} is the element of matrix A at row i and column k. The term \sum{k=1}^{n} a{ik} is the sum of the i-th row of A. c. Update Auxiliary Variable y: For each j \in S (where j corresponds to the projection pixel index i), update y. yj^{(t+1)} = yj^{(t)} + \alpha cj^{(t)} Only one element of y is updated per projection pixel in the subset. d. Update Volume x: For all voxels j = 1 to n, update x. xj^{(t+1)} = xj^{(t)} + \alpha \frac{\sum{i \in S} ci^{(t)} a{ij}}{\sum{i \in S} a{ij}} Here, \sum{i \in S} a{ij} is the sum of the elements in column j of A restricted to the rows in subset S. 4. Return: x^{(T)}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sartproximaloperator(A, p, u, lambdareg, alpha, T, subsets): """ A: Forward projection matrix (m x n) p: Projection measurements (m,) u: Prior volume estimate (n,) lambdareg: Regularization parameter lambda alpha: Step size T: Number of outer iterations subsets: List of projection subsets, each containing indices of projections """ import numpy as np # Preprocessing: Scale p and A by sqrt(2lambda) scale = np.sqrt(2 lambdareg) p = scale p A = scale A # Initialization y = np.zeros(len(p)) x = np.array(u, dtype=float).copy() # Precompute row sums of A for the residual denominator rowsums = np.sum(A, axis=1) for t in range(1, T + 1): for S in subsets: # Compute residuals ci for i in S # ci = (pi - sumk aik xk - yi) / (sumk aik + 1) forwardproj = A[S,:] @ x numerators = p[S] - forwardproj - y[S] denominators = rowsums[S] + 1 c = numerators / denominators # Update y for j in S y[S] += alpha c # Update x for all j # Compute sum{i in S} aij for each j (column sums for subset S) colsumsS = np.sum(A[S,:], axis=0) # Compute sum{i in S} ci aij for each j weightedcolsums = A[S,:].T @ c # Guard against division by zero if a voxel is not intersected by any ray in S safecolsums = np.where(colsumsS > 0, colsumsS, 1.0) x += alpha (weightedcolsums / safecolsums) return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The method requires storing the volume x and the auxiliary variable y. For a 256^3 volume (64 MB) and 360 projections of 2000 \times 1500 pixels (\approx 4 GB for y), total memory can exceed 12 GB if multiple versions are kept in RAM. Division by Zero: The denominators \sumk a{ik} + 1 and \sum{i \in S} a{ij} must be non-zero. The +1 in the residual denominator ensures the first is never zero. The column sum denominator should be checked for zero if a voxel is not intersected by any ray in the subset. Memory Complexity: The method requires O(n + m) memory for storing x and y. This is significantly higher than standard SART, which only requires O(n). Strengths: Incorporates prior information u effectively and modifies the data term to find the least-squares solution closest to u. Limitations: High memory consumption due to the auxiliary variable y. When to Use: When prior information is available and regularization is needed. When memory resources are sufficient to store the auxiliary variable. The SART Proximal Operator was introduced in the context of industrial computed tomography to improve reconstruction quality by incorporating prior knowledge. It is based on the proximal algorithm framework, which allows for the minimization of a function involving a data fidelity term and a regularization term. The method modifies the standard SART algorithm by introducing an auxiliary variable y and initializing the volume with a prior estimate u. name: Iterative Reconstruction (SIRT via Autodiff)
head: Gradient Descent Reconstruction
body: This method performs tomographic reconstruction by treating the volume estimation as a differentiable optimization problem, using automatic differentiation to minimize the mean squared error between simulated and measured projections. It differs from standard SIRT (Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique) by replacing explicit algebraic matrix operations with gradient descent via an autodiff engine, allowing for easier integration of custom physics constraints or differentiable regularizers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Measured projections as a tensor of shape (N, H, W) where N is the number of angles and H, W are detector dimensions. Projection geometry parameters defining source-detector distances and angles (e.g., DSO, DSD, detector pixel size, and a list of N angles). Volume dimensions D \times D \times D. Outputs: Reconstructed volume as a tensor of shape (D, D, D) representing the estimated attenuation coefficients. Data Structures: volume: A PyTorch tensor of shape (D, D, D) initialized with zeros or a prior estimate. It must have requiresgrad=True to track gradients. optimizer: An Adam optimizer instance initialized with the volume parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a tensor volume of shape (D, D, D) with requiresgrad=True. Initialize an Adam optimizer with volume as the parameter and lr=1e-2. 2. Iteration Loop: For k = 1 to iters: a. Zero Gradients: Call optimizer.zerograd() to clear previous gradients. b. Forward Projection: Compute simulated projections P{sim} from the current volume using a differentiable forward projector F(\cdot) defined by the geometry. P{sim} = F(\text{volume}). c. Loss Computation: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the simulated projections P{sim} and the measured projections P{meas}. d. Backpropagation: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to the volume: \nabla{\text{volume}} L = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{volume}}. This is handled automatically by the autodiff engine. e. Optimization Step: Update the volume parameters using the optimizer. Adam applies adaptive learning rates internally rather than a fixed step size. Formulas: L = \frac{1}{NHW} \sum{i=1}^{N} \sum{j=1}^{H} \sum{l=1}^{W} (P{sim}[i,j,l] - P{meas}[i,j,l])^2 where L is the loss, N is the number of angles, H and W are detector dimensions, and P{sim} and P{meas} are the simulated and measured projection tensors respectively. Parameters: lr: Learning rate, typically 1 \times 10^{-2}. iters: Number of optimization steps, default 50. geometry: Object containing DSO (Source-to-Object), DSD (Source-to-Detector), detector resolution, and angles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If projections are all zeros or constant, the gradient may vanish, leading to no update. Initialize with a small random noise or a prior estimate (e.g., FDK) to break symmetry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def iterativereconstructionautodiff(projections, geometry, volshape, iters=50, lr=1e-2): """ Reconstruct volume using SIRT-like gradient descent via autodiff. Args: projections: Tensor [N, H, W] of measured projections. geometry: Object with forwardproject method. volshape: Tuple (D, D, D) for volume dimensions. iters: Number of optimization steps. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: Reconstructed volume tensor [D, D, D]. """ # Initialize volume tensor with gradients enabled volume = torch.zeros(volshape, requiresgrad=True, device=projections.device) # Initialize Adam optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([volume], lr=lr) for step in range(iters): # Zero gradients from previous step optimizer.zerograd() # Forward projection: simulate projections from current volume estimate simulatedprojections = geometry.forwardproject(volume) # Compute loss: Mean Squared Error between simulated and measured projections loss = F.mseloss(simulatedprojections, projections) # Backpropagate to compute gradients on the volume loss.backward() # Update volume parameters optimizer.step() return volume.detach() ACID is an iterative reconstruction framework that stabilizes an unstable deep reconstruction neural network by combining it with a Compressed Sensing (CS)-based sparsity-promoting module. It minimizes an objective function balancing neural network output consistency, data fidelity, residual error energy, and sparsity. ACID searches for a solution good in three aspects: image sparsity, big-data-driven prior, and iterative calibration to eliminate unexplained residual data. It differs from standard sparsity-minimization reconstruction by incorporating a data-driven deep prior (\Phi) to fill gaps where sparsity alone may not yield a unique solution, especially when the measurement matrix does not satisfy the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP). Unlike traditional iterative reconstruction which searches for a feasible solution within the space of sparse solutions, ACID simultaneously optimizes for sparsity, data-driven priors, and residual calibration. A method that uses an implicit neural network to represent the 3D volume density field, optimizing the network parameters to fit the 2D projection images while jointly optimizing the 3D orientation (pose) of each projection. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Easy to integrate custom constraints (e.g., non-negativity, sparsity) by modifying the loss function. No need to explicitly derive or implement the backprojection matrix. Limitations: Convergence depends heavily on the learning rate and the condition number of the problem. May get stuck in local minima if the initial guess is poor. When to Use: When custom physics constraints are needed, or when integrating with deep learning components (e.g., neural networks as priors). When Not to Use: For standard CT reconstruction with no special constraints, where FDK or algebraic methods are faster and sufficient. This approach leverages the automatic differentiation capabilities of deep learning frameworks (like PyTorch) to solve inverse problems traditionally addressed by algebraic reconstruction techniques. The specific implementation described here uses a cone-beam forward projector and Adam optimizer to minimize projection error. ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, https://github.com/ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: ACID (Adversarial Calibration Iterative Deep learning)
head: ACID scheme, ACID workflow, Adversarial Calibration Iterative Deep learning, Adversarial Convergence Iterative Deep learning, Adversarial-Correction Iterative Deep learning
body: ACID is an iterative reconstruction framework that stabilizes an unstable deep reconstruction neural network by combining it with a Compressed Sensing (CS)-based sparsity-promoting module. It minimizes an objective function balancing neural network output consistency, data fidelity, residual error energy, and sparsity. ACID searches for a solution good in three aspects: image sparsity, big-data-driven prior, and iterative calibration to eliminate unexplained residual data. It differs from standard sparsity-minimization reconstruction by incorporating a data-driven deep prior (\Phi) to fill gaps where sparsity alone may not yield a unique solution, especially when the measurement matrix does not satisfy the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP). Unlike traditional iterative reconstruction which searches for a feasible solution within the space of sparse solutions, ACID simultaneously optimizes for sparsity, data-driven priors, and residual calibration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: p^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^m: Original measurement data (projections). A: System matrix (forward model, e.g., Radon transform for CT, Fourier transform for MRI). \Phi(\cdot): A pre-trained deep neural network (recon-net) that maps measurement data to an image. H \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}: Sparse transform matrix (e.g., discrete gradient for TV) and its adjoint H^. Hyperparameters: \lambda > 0, \mu \ge 0, \xi > 0. Outputs: f^{(k)}: Reconstructed image estimate at iteration k. Data Structures: p^{(k)}: Residual error vector in the projection domain, size m. f^{(k)}: Image estimate vector, size N. Parameters: \lambda: Hyperparameter weighting the data fidelity term (measured noise energy). \mu: Hyperparameter weighting the residual error energy in the projection domain. \xi: Hyperparameter weighting the sparsity term \|Hf\|1. \varepsilon = \xi/\lambda: Effective threshold for soft-thresholding, matching system tolerance level. M1 = \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda+\mu}. M2 = \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}. M = \frac{M1}{M2} = \frac{1+\mu}{1+\lambda+\mu} < 1. s: Number of components spanning the s-sparse space of Hf^. \sigma: A constant such that the artifact norm is bounded by (1-\sigma)\|f^\|. Formulas: The objective function minimized is: L(p,f):= \frac{1}{2}\|\Phi(Af+p)-f\|2^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|p^{(0)}-Af-p\|2^2 + \frac{\mu}{2}\|p\|2^2 + \xi\|Hf\|1 where p is the residual error in the projection domain (p=p^{(0)}-Af). The iterative update equations are: p^{(k+1)} \cong \frac{\lambda(p^{(0)}-Af^{(k)})}{1+\lambda+\mu} f^{(k+1)} \cong H^ S\varepsilon \left( H \left( f^{(k)} + \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}\Phi(p^{(k+1)}) \right) \right) The soft-thresholding kernel S\varepsilon(x) is defined as: S\varepsilon(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |x| < \varepsilon \\ x - \text{sgn}(x)\varepsilon & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} For Total Variation (TV) minimization using a non-unitary discrete gradient transform H, the image update f^{(k+1)} at pixel (iw, ih) is computed as: f^{(k+1)}{(iw,ih)} = \frac{1}{4} \sum{\text{neighbors}} S^{-1}\varepsilon \left( f^{(k+1/2)}{(iw,ih)}, f^{(k+1/2)}{\text{neighbor}} \right) where the intermediate image variable is f^{(k+1/2)} = f^{(k)} + \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}\Phi(p^{(k+1)}). The pseudo-inverse soft-thresholding kernel S^{-1}\varepsilon(va, vb) is defined as: S^{-1}\varepsilon(va, vb) = \begin{cases} \frac{va+vb}{2} & \text{if } |va-vb| \le \varepsilon \\ va - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} & \text{if } va-vb > \varepsilon \\ va + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} & \text{if } va-vb < -\varepsilon \end{cases} Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial image estimate f^{(0)}. A common initialization is the output of the neural network on the initial data: f^{(0)} = \Phi(p^{(0)}). Note that \Phi(p^{(0)}) can be decomposed into ground truth f^, observable artifact f^{(ob,0)}, and null-space artifact f^{(nl,0)}. 2. Iterate for k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Residual Update: Compute the residual error p^{(k+1)} using the forward model A and previous estimate f^{(k)}: p^{(k+1)} = M1 (p^{(0)} - A f^{(k)}) where M1 = \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda+\mu}. b. Network Prediction: Pass the residual through the recon-net to get the update direction: \Delta f{\text{net}} = \Phi(p^{(k+1)}) c. Intermediate Image: Compute the intermediate variable: f^{(k+1/2)} = f^{(k)} + M2 \Delta f{\text{net}} where M2 = \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}. d. Sparsity Projection (CS Step): i. Transform to sparse domain: \bar{f}^{(k+1/2)} = H f^{(k+1/2)}. ii. Apply soft-thresholding: \bar{f}^{(k+1)} = S\varepsilon(\bar{f}^{(k+1/2)}). iii. Transform back: If H is unitary, f^{(k+1)} = H^ \bar{f}^{(k+1)}. If H is non-unitary (e.g., TV gradient), compute f^{(k+1)} using the pixel-wise pseudo-inverse formula involving spatial neighbors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softthreshold(x, epsilon): """Applies soft-thresholding to input array x with threshold epsilon.""" return np.sign(x) np.maximum(np.abs(x) - epsilon, 0) def pseudoinversesoftthreshold(va, vb, epsilon): """Computes the pseudo-inverse soft-thresholding kernel value.""" diff = va - vb if np.abs(diff) <= epsilon: return (va + vb) / 2.0 elif diff > epsilon: return va - epsilon / 2.0 else: return va + epsilon / 2.0 def acidreconstruct(p0, A, Phi, H, Hadj, lambdaparam, muparam, xiparam, numiterations, istv=False): """ Performs ACID reconstruction. Args: p0: Initial measurement data (m,) A: Forward projection operator (callable, takes image, returns projections) Phi: Neural network recon-net (callable, takes projections, returns image) H: Sparse transform operator (callable, takes image, returns transform coeffs) Hadj: Adjoint of sparse transform (callable, takes transform coeffs, returns image) lambdaparam: Data fidelity weight muparam: Residual energy weight xiparam: Sparsity weight numiterations: Number of ACID iterations istv: Boolean, if True uses TV-specific non-unitary H update, else assumes unitary Returns: f: Reconstructed image """ M1 = lambdaparam / (1 + lambdaparam + muparam) M2 = (1 + muparam) / lambdaparam epsilon = xiparam / lambdaparam # Initialize f = Phi(p0) for k in range(numiterations): # 1. Residual Update residual = M1 (p0 - A(f)) # 2. Network Prediction deltafnet = Phi(residual) # 3. Intermediate Image fintermediate = f + M2 deltafnet if istv: # TV Minimization with non-unitary H (Discrete Gradient) # f(k+1) at pixel (iw, ih) is average of pseudo-inverse soft-thresholds with neighbors h, w = f.shape fnext = np.zeroslike(f) # Neighbors: right, left, bottom, top right = np.roll(fintermediate, -1, axis=1) left = np.roll(fintermediate, 1, axis=1) bottom = np.roll(fintermediate, -1, axis=0) top = np.roll(fintermediate, 1, axis=0) # Compute pseudo-inverse soft threshold for each direction hcontrib = (pseudoinversesoftthreshold(fintermediate, right, epsilon) + pseudoinversesoftthreshold(fintermediate, left, epsilon)) vcontrib = (pseudoinversesoftthreshold(fintermediate, bottom, epsilon) + pseudoinversesoftthreshold(fintermediate, top, epsilon)) fnext = (hcontrib + vcontrib) / 4.0 # Note: Boundary conditions are not specified in the sources. # np.roll wraps around; for strict implementation, boundaries should be # handled separately or padded according to application requirements. f = fnext else: # Unitary Transform Case fbar = H(fintermediate) fbarthresh = softthreshold(fbar, epsilon) f = Hadj(fbarthresh) return f Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underdetermined System: The system matrix A is often underdetermined (m < N), meaning the inverse problem has no unique solution without prior knowledge. ACID handles this by introducing sparsity priors via H and deep priors via \Phi. Non-Unitary Transform: The discrete gradient transform H used in TV minimization is non-unitary and not invertible. The method handles this by interpreting the adjoint H^ as a pseudo-inverse in the iterative framework, using the specific pixel-wise update rule. RIP Violation: If the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) or robust Null-Space Property (rNSP) is not satisfied, ACID may converge to an image with a nonzero null-space component. However, this is also true for sparsity-promoting algorithms alone; ACID reduces the feasible solution space via the deep prior. Unstable Network: If the network is not ideal and produces substantial artifacts, convergence is still guaranteed under the BREN property as long as the network's output error is bounded. Noise Floor: For noise-free measurements, if \varepsilon \to 0, then the observable artifact norm \|f^{(ob,\infty)}\| \to 0. The parameter \varepsilon should match the system tolerance level. Convergence: The Lipschitz constant of ACID for CT and MRI monotonically decreases and converges to a constant scale with respect to the number of iterations. The observable artifact norm is bounded by \|f^{(ob,\infty)}\| < \frac{(1-\sigma)s M2}{\sigma \varepsilon}. The general bound for artifact norm at step k+1 is \|f^{(ob,k+1)}\| < (1-\sigma) \left[ (1-M\sigma)^k M1 \|f^{(ob,0)}\| + \frac{1-(1-M\sigma)^{k+1}}{M\sigma} M1 \varepsilon s \right]. Performance: In CT cases using Ell-50, the maximum output-to-input variation ratio against additive white Gaussian noise (zero mean, 11-30 HU std dev) was 0.229. In MRI cases using DAGAN, the maximum output-to-input variation ratio against additive white Gaussian noise was 3.023. Strengths: ACID stabilizes unstable deep reconstruction networks and is resilient against adversarial attacks. It outperforms sparsity-promoting algorithms that do not utilize big-data-driven priors by reducing the feasible solution space via the deep prior. Limitations: Convergence to a solution with nonzero null-space components is possible if RIP/rNSP is not satisfied, though the deep prior reduces the feasible space compared to sparsity alone. Usage: Used for few-view CT imaging and sparse sampling MRI reconstruction. Specifically applied in tomographic reconstruction, sparse-view CT, and low-dose spectral CT contexts. ACID was introduced to stabilize deep tomographic reconstruction methods which are often unstable due to the "troublesome kernel" of deep learning models. It builds on the concept of using Compressed Sensing (CS) to promote sparsity and combines it with a data-driven prior from a neural network. The method was developed to address cases where standard sparsity-promotion algorithms fail to provide unique solutions, particularly when the measurement matrix does not satisfy RIP. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that ACID converges to a solution in the intersection of measured data, sparse solutions, and data-driven solutions. name: Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for Tomography
head: INR reconstruction, Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for Electron Tomography, NeRF for tomography, Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) for tomography
body: This method reconstructs 3D volumes from 2D projection images by representing the volume density as a continuous Implicit Neural Network (INR) rather than a discrete voxel grid. It solves the tomographic reconstruction problem by optimizing the network parameters to minimize the difference between simulated projections and measured data, while simultaneously optimizing the 3D pose (orientation) for each projection. Unlike discrete voxel-based methods such as Iterative Reconstruction (SIRT via Autodiff), the INR approach enables arbitrarily fine sampling and projection at any orientation without interpolation, making it particularly robust to missing wedges, large tilt steps, and low electron fluence noise. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 2D projection images Pi (where i=1 \dots N), their corresponding initial estimated poses (rotation matrices Ri and translation vectors ti), and the camera geometry (ray origins and directions). Outputs: The optimized network weights \theta defining the density field \rho(x), and the refined 3D poses for each projection. Data Structures: Neural Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) f\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Input: 3D spatial coordinates (x, y, z). Output: Scalar density value \rho. Activation: Typically ReLU or Sine (Sin) activations are used in INR literature, though specific activation functions are not explicitly detailed in the provided notes. Pose Parameters: For each projection i, a 6-degree-of-freedom pose vector pi = [Ri, ti] is stored as a trainable parameter tensor. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Preprocessing: Perform a coarse alignment or initial pose estimation to reduce large degrees of misalignment. This step is critical because large initial misalignments significantly increase convergence time for the INR pose optimization. This typically involves standard algebraic reconstruction techniques (like SIRT) or feature-based alignment to provide a starting point within the basin of attraction of the global optimum. 2. Forward Projection (Differentiable Rendering): For each projection i: a. Define a set of 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) for the image plane. b. Map these 2D coordinates to 3D ray origins and directions based on the current pose pi. c. Sample K points along each ray within the volume bounds. d. Query the neural network f\theta at each sampled point to obtain density values \rhok. e. Compute the line integral (projection) using numerical quadrature (e.g., trapezoidal rule or simple summation) to simulate the projection Pi^{sim}: Pi^{sim}(u, v) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \rho(f\theta(xk, yk, zk)) \cdot \Delta sk where \Delta sk is the step size along the ray. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the simulated projection Pi^{sim} and the measured projection Pi^{meas}: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \| Pi^{sim} - Pi^{meas} \|^22 4. Joint Optimization: Use an optimizer (e.g., Adam) to update both the network weights \theta and the pose parameters pi simultaneously to minimize L. The network weights \theta are updated via backpropagation through the differentiable forward projection. The poses pi are updated via backpropagation through the ray casting operation. 5. Holdout Validation and Early Stopping: Split the projection data into a training set and a holdout (validation) set. Monitor the loss on the holdout set. Stop training when the holdout loss reaches its minimum to prevent overfitting to noise, which is a significant risk at low electron fluence. 6. Volume Extraction: Once optimized, the 3D volume is represented by the neural network f\theta. To visualize or save the volume, evaluate f\theta on a regular 3D grid of coordinates (x, y, z) and store the resulting density values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class DensityNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=3, hiddendim=256, outputdim=1, numlayers=8): super(DensityNetwork, self).init() layers = [] for in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Standard activation; Sin is also common in INRs inputdim = hiddendim layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x): return self.network(x) def raycasting(network, poses, imageshape, raysteps=100): """ Simulates projections for a batch of poses. poses: Tensor of shape (N, 6) representing rotation and translation. imageshape: Tuple (H, W). """ N = poses.shape[0] H, W = imageshape projections = [] for i in range(N): # Extract pose parameters for projection i # Assuming poses are stored as [R11, R12, R13, R21, R22, R23, R31, R32, R33, tx, ty, tz] # or similar. Implementation depends on specific pose representation. # For simplicity, assume a function getraydirections exists that uses the pose # to map 2D pixel coordinates to 3D rays. # Generate 2D grid coordinates u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='ij') u = u.float().to(poses.device) v = v.float().to(poses.device) # Map to 3D rays based on pose i # rayorigins: (H, W, 3), raydirections: (H, W, 3) rayorigins, raydirections = getraydirections(u, v, poses[i]) # Sample points along rays t = torch.linspace(0, 1, raysteps).to(poses.device) # Expand dimensions for broadcasting t = t.view(-1, 1, 1, 1) rayorigins = rayorigins.unsqueeze(0) # (1, H, W, 3) raydirections = raydirections.unsqueeze(0) # (1, H, W, 3) # Sampled points: (1, H, W, raysteps, 3) points = rayorigins + t raydirections points = points.view(-1, raysteps, 3) # (HW, raysteps, 3) # Query network densities = network(points) # (HW, raysteps, 1) # Integrate along ray (simple sum for now, weighted by step size) # More accurate integration uses quadrature weights projection = densities.sum(dim=1) # (HW, 1) projection = projection.view(H, W) projections.append(projection) return torch.stack(projections) # (N, H, W) def traininrtomography(projections, initialposes, network, numepochs=1000, holdoutratio=0.1): """ Main training loop for INR Tomography with joint alignment. """ N = projections.shape[0] H, W = projections.shape[1], projections.shape[2] # Split data into train and holdout indices = torch.randperm(N) split = int(N (1 - holdoutratio)) trainindices = indices[:split] holdoutindices = indices[split:] trainprojections = projections[trainindices] holdoutprojections = projections[holdoutindices] # Initialize trainable poses # Initial poses should be provided by coarse preprocessing trainposes = nn.Parameter(initialposes[trainindices].clone()) holdoutposes = nn.Parameter(initialposes[holdoutindices].clone()) optimizer = optim.Adam(list(network.parameters()) + [trainposes, holdoutposes], lr=1e-3) bestholdoutloss = float('inf') bestnetworkstate = None besttrainposesstate = None bestholdoutposesstate = None for epoch in range(numepochs): optimizer.zerograd() # Forward pass on training data trainsim = raycasting(network, trainposes, (H, W)) trainloss = nn.MSELoss()(trainsim, trainprojections) # Forward pass on holdout data holdoutsim = raycasting(network, holdoutposes, (H, W)) holdoutloss = nn.MSELoss()(holdoutsim, holdoutprojections) # Backward pass (trainloss + holdoutloss).backward() optimizer.step() # Early stopping check if holdoutloss.item() < bestholdoutloss: bestholdoutloss = holdoutloss.item() bestnetworkstate = {k: v.clone() for k, v in network.statedict().items()} besttrainposesstate = trainposes.data.clone() bestholdoutposesstate = holdoutposes.data.clone() if epoch % 100 == 0: print(f"Epoch {epoch}: Train Loss {trainloss.item():.4f}, Holdout Loss {holdoutloss.item():.4f}") # Restore best model network.loadstatedict(bestnetworkstate) trainposes.data = besttrainposesstate holdoutposes.data = bestholdoutposesstate return network, torch.cat([trainposes, holdoutposes]) def getraydirections(u, v, pose): # This function depends on the specific camera model and pose representation. # It maps 2D pixel coordinates to 3D rays given the current rotation and translation. raise NotImplementedError("Implementation depends on specific camera geometry.") Parameters: Tilt Step: The angular increment between projections. Typical values tested include 1^\circ, 2^\circ, 5^\circ, 10^\circ, 12^\circ, 14^\circ, 20^\circ, 28^\circ, and 70^\circ. Missing Wedge Angle: The angular range not covered by projections. Tested ranges include (-80^\circ, 80^\circ), (-70^\circ, 70^\circ), (-50^\circ, 50^\circ), (-40^\circ, 40^\circ), (-20^\circ, 20^\circ), and (-10^\circ, 10^\circ). Electron Fluence: Measured in counts/px. Tested values include 10^4, 10^3, 10^2, 10^1, and 1 count/px. Holdout Ratio: Not explicitly given, but a split is required for early stopping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting to Noise: At very low electron fluence (e.g., 1 count/px), the INR overfits to noise. Holdout validation is required for early stopping to output the volume when loss is minimal on the holdout set. Convergence Time: Large degrees of rotational misalignment correspond to longer convergence times for the INR pose optimization. A coarse preprocessing routine is recommended to speed up convergence. Initialization: The method requires initial pose estimates. Poor initialization can lead to local minima or slow convergence. A fully self-supervised tomographic reconstruction algorithm that uses an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) to jointly optimize the 3D volume density field and the full 3D pose (orientation and in-plane translation) for each projection image. Unlike conventional voxel-grid methods that require interpolation during rotation and struggle with multi-GPU parallelization, this method represents the volume as a continuous neural network, enabling arbitrarily fine sampling and projection at any orientation without interpolation. It is particularly suited for heterogeneous materials where supervised training data is unavailable, solving for complete sample pose rather than relying on pre-estimated shifts or single tilt angles. A three-step CT reconstruction approach leveraging neural fields to enhance final reconstruction quality. Step 1: Optimize a neural field F\Phi by minimizing the data-fidelity term on sparse measurements. Given sparse measurements b \in \mathbb{R}^m, forward operator A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, and voxel coordinates X{grid} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 3}, solve: \hat{\Phi} = \arg \min\Phi \frac{1}{2} \|A F\Phi(X{grid}) - b\|^22. Step 2: Generate dense synthetic measurements b{new} \in \mathbb{R}^{m{full}} by applying the full-range operator A{full} \in \mathbb{R}^{m{full} \times n} to the learned field: b{new} = A{full} F{\hat{\Phi}}(X{grid}), where m{full} \gg m and m{full} \approx n. Step 3: Perform regularized reconstruction on the pixel basis using a weighted data-fidelity term combining synthetic and real fidelity, plus a regularization term R (linear combination of total variation and nonlocal means). Solve: \hat{f} = \arg \min{f \in \mathbb{R}^n} L(fe) + \lambda R(f), where L(fe) = \frac{1}{2}(\alpha \|A{full} f - b{new}\|^22 + (1-\alpha) \|Af - b\|^22). Parameter: \alpha > 0 is a weighting term that balances the synthetic fidelity (from the neural field) with the real fidelity (from sparse measurements). Pitfall: The pixel-basis reconstruction in Step 3 acts as a memory bottleneck, forcing reconstruction on the CPU for large-scale problems. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The memory footprint is dominated by the neural network weights and the pose parameters, which is significantly lower than storing a high-resolution 3D voxel grid. However, the forward projection step requires sampling many points along rays, which can be memory-intensive if not batched efficiently. Time: Convergence time is sensitive to the initial pose alignment. Large misalignments lead to longer convergence times. The method is generally slower per iteration than closed-form methods like SIRT but may require fewer iterations to achieve high fidelity in challenging scenarios (e.g., missing wedges). Measured Performance: Missing Wedge Robustness: INR is more robust to missing wedges than SIRT. It reconstructs internal features accurately up to a 100^\circ missing wedge, whereas SIRT degrades significantly and shows streaking artifacts. SSIM of 0.985 for INR vs 0.972 for SIRT with a 20^\circ missing wedge (tilt range -80^\circ to 80^\circ) and 1^\circ tilt increment. Tilt Step Robustness: INR is more robust to large tilt steps than SIRT. It generates accurate volumes up to a 20^\circ step size, while SIRT significantly suffers with tilt steps greater than 5^\circ. SSIM of 0.957 for INR vs 0.427 for SIRT using only 9 projections (20^\circ tilt step) with high-angle tilts included. Low Fluence/Denoising: INR denoises projections better than SIRT at low electron fluence. At 100 counts/px, SIRT is visibly noisy while INR is almost noise-free. SSIM of 0.857 for INR vs 0.293 for SIRT at a dose of 10 count/px. Pose Optimization: INR with pose optimization achieves an average SSIM of 0.974 regardless of the degree of rotational misalignment. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High robustness to missing wedges, large tilt steps, and low signal-to-noise ratios. Continuous representation allows for arbitrary resolution and interpolation-free rotation. Self-supervised alignment improves accuracy in the presence of pose errors. Limitations: Slower convergence compared to algebraic methods. Sensitive to initialization. Risk of overfitting to noise at very low fluence without early stopping.. When to Use: Use when dealing with sparse views, large missing wedges, or low-dose data where traditional methods like SIRT fail or produce significant artifacts. Use when precise pose estimation is unknown or inaccurate, and joint alignment is beneficial. When Not to Use: Use when computational resources are extremely limited and fast, approximate reconstructions are sufficient. Use when high-quality, dense tilt series with minimal missing wedges are available, and speed is the primary concern. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Missing Wedge Inpainting and Joint Alignment in Electron Tomography through Implicit Neural Representations". It applies the concept of Implicit Neural Representations, popularized in computer graphics for novel view synthesis (e.g., NeRF), to the domain of electron tomography. History and Development: The approach leverages the differentiability of neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomography. By treating the volume as a continuous function parameterized by a neural network, it avoids the discretization errors associated with voxel-based methods. The joint optimization of pose and density allows for self-supervised alignment, addressing a common challenge in electron tomography where precise alignment is difficult to achieve. Usage: The method has been experimentally validated using STEM (Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy) instruments in high annular dark field (HAADF) imaging mode. It has been applied to reconstruct catalytic nanoparticles on a support, demonstrating its ability to resolve fine features and mitigate missing wedge artifacts. name: INR Tomography with Joint Alignment
head: INR Tomography Optimization with Pose Alignment, Implicit Neural Representation Tomography, Joint Alignment and Reconstruction, Self-supervised INR Tomography, Self-supervised INR reconstruction
body: A fully self-supervised tomographic reconstruction algorithm that uses an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) to jointly optimize the 3D volume density field and the full 3D pose (orientation and in-plane translation) for each projection image. Unlike conventional voxel-grid methods that require interpolation during rotation and struggle with multi-GPU parallelization, this method represents the volume as a continuous neural network, enabling arbitrarily fine sampling and projection at any orientation without interpolation. It is particularly suited for heterogeneous materials where supervised training data is unavailable, solving for complete sample pose rather than relying on pre-estimated shifts or single tilt angles. Inputs: A tilt series of M 2D projection images I^{exp}{i,j}, where i \in \{1, \dots, N\} is the pixel index and j \in \{1, \dots, M\} is the tilt index. The nominal tilt angle \thetaj for each image is assumed known. Outputs: The weights of the INR volume representation and the optimized pose parameters for each tilt image. Data Structures: 1. INR Model: A fully-connected neural network (MLP) with periodic activation functions. Input: 3D coordinate vector \mathbf{r} = [x, y, z]^T. Output: Scalar intensity value \phi. 2. Pose Parameters: For each tilt image j, a set of learnable parameters: z1j, z3j (learnable Euler angles) and \delta xj, \delta yj (learnable scalars for in-plane translation). 3. Optimization State: INR weights W and pose parameters \mathbf{P}j = [z1j, z3j, \delta xj, \delta yj]^T for j=1 \dots M. Formulas: The total loss function is: L = L{pixel} + \alpha L{TV} where \alpha is the total variation regularization weight, tunable per sample. The pixel loss is defined as: L{pixel} = \frac{1}{MN} \sum{j=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{smoothL1}(I^{exp}{i,j} - I^{pred}{i,j}) The smoothL1 loss function is: \text{smoothL1}(x) = \begin{cases} 0.5x^2/\beta & \text{if } |x| < 1 \\ |x| - 0.5\beta & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \beta = 0.07 is the crossover point hyperparameter. The predicted intensity I^{pred}{i,j} for pixel i in image j is computed by integrating the INR output along a ray: 1. Find ray ending at pixel i by rotating/shifting a z-axis ray according to tilt angle \thetaj and pose. 2. Parameterize pose with learnable angles z1j, z3j and scalars \delta xj, \delta yj. 3. Sample discrete points along the ray. 4. Apply shifts \delta xj, \delta yj along x and y axes. 5. Perform rotation R(z3j)R(\thetaj)R(z1j). 6. Learning Rate (INR Weights): 8 \times 10^{-6}. Learning Rate (Pose Parameters): 5 \times 10^{-2}. Batch Size: 1024 pixels per GPU. Global batch size 16384 with 16 GPUs. Optimizer: Adam. LR Schedule: Warmup for 10 epochs, then cosine-annealing. Sampling: Number of sampling points per ray starts small and ramps up over the first few epochs. Initialization: Random initialization is sufficient for self-supervision. Pre-training on a converged SIRT reconstruction can speed up convergence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation: Conventional voxel-grid methods require interpolation during rotation, which is difficult to parallelize across multiple GPUs because the volume must be instantiated across each GPU. The INR method avoids this by using precisely rotated projection vectors. Overfitting: In high SNR scenarios, the model may overfit to noise. Mitigation involves splitting data into 80% training and 20% validation, and stopping training when validation loss increases. Parallelization: The method is parallelizable via Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). Gradients are averaged across GPUs, and the learning rate is scaled by the square root of the number of GPUs. Coordinate System: The exact definition of the rotation matrices R(z1j), R(\thetaj), R(z3j) depends on the experimental setup (e.g., tilt axis orientation). The source specifies the composition order but not the specific axes for each angle, which must be derived from the hardware configuration. Regularization tuning: Requires careful tuning of regularization parameter \alpha, which determines the weight of the total variation regularization term and is tunable per sample. Time Complexity: Reconstruction speed scales nearly linearly with the number of GPUs. For 150 epochs on a full dataset using 16 GPUs, reconstruction takes approximately 2 hours. Without multi-GPU systems, speed depends heavily on volume size and single-GPU performance. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the INR model size and the batch of sampled coordinates. Since the volume is not stored as a grid, memory usage is independent of the voxel grid resolution, allowing for high-resolution representations without proportional memory increase. Strengths: Self-supervised: No training data from similar samples required. Joint Alignment: Optimizes full 3D pose (orientation and in-plane translation) for each projection. Missing Wedge Inpainting: Acts as a regularizer to fill in missing information. Denoising: Regularization helps denoise low-dose datasets. No Interpolation: Allows arbitrarily fine sampling and projection at any orientation. Limitations: Computationally intensive per epoch compared to analytical methods like SIRT, though parallelization mitigates this. Requires careful tuning of regularization parameter \alpha. Convergence may be slow without pre-training or good initial alignment. When to Use: Suitable for heterogeneous materials, beam-sensitive samples (low dose), and datasets with significant misalignment or missing wedges where supervised methods are impractical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are severely limited (single CPU, no GPU) and real-time reconstruction is required, or when high-quality training data from similar samples is available and supervised methods are preferred. The method was proposed in the paper "Missing Wedge Inpainting and Joint Alignment in Electron Tomography through Implicit Neural Representations". It addresses limitations of conventional voxel-grid tomographic reconstruction, which requires interpolation and struggles with parallelization, and supervised deep learning methods that require training data. The approach leverages the properties of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) to provide a continuous, differentiable volume representation that can be optimized jointly with projection poses. It is implemented in the open-source Python package quantEM. The method is applicable to HAADF STEM data, where image intensity depends linearly on the projected potential. name: Iterative Algebraic Reconstruction (LSQR)
head: 3D Helical CT Reconstruction via LSQR, 3D Helical Cone-Beam CT Image Reconstruction using LSQR, Helical CT LSQR, Iterative Backprojection Reconstruction, LSQR Reconstruction
body: Iterative Algebraic Reconstruction using LSQR solves the linear inverse problem \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{B} for 3D helical cone-beam CT, reconstructing a 3D voxel density grid \mathbf{X} from 2D X-ray projection measurements \mathbf{B}. It distinguishes itself from direct reconstruction methods by iteratively minimizing the residual error using the adjoint of the forward projection operator, making it suitable for large-scale, sparse systems where explicit matrix storage is infeasible. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data \mathbf{B} (sinogram) of size N{pa} \times N{det} \times N{slice}, and system geometry parameters (source-to-object distance, source-to-detector distance, detector pitch, helical shift, angular span). Output: Reconstructed 3D volume \mathbf{X} of size N{vox} \times N{vox} \times N{vox} (typically 512^3). Data Structures: Volume Grid \mathbf{X}: A contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing the voxel densities, mapped to a 3D grid of resolution N{vox} \times N{vox} \times N{vox}. In the reference implementation, N{vox} = 512, occupying ~536.87 MB. Projection Data \mathbf{B}: A contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing line integrals for each detector pixel at each angle. Size: N{pa} \times N{det} \times N{slice}. Ray Geometry: Implicitly defined by the helical trajectory. For angle i, the source position (x1, y1, z1) and detector ray endpoints are calculated using trigonometric functions of the angular span and helical shift. Parameters (Reference Values): N{vox} (npix): 512 N{pa}: 473 (projections) N{det}: 512 (detector columns) N{slice}: 512 (detector rows) Span: 640^\circ Detector Pitch (d): 0.8 mm Source-to-Object Distance (scob): 166.641 mm Source-to-Detector Distance (scd): 1238.157 mm Helical Shift: 0.136 mm per angle Relaxation Factor: 0.05 (used in backprojection scaling) Max Iterations: 20 Algorithm Steps: The reconstruction follows an iterative loop where each iteration processes all projection angles to update the volume estimate. 1. Initialization: Initialize the volume buffer \mathbf{X} to zero. 2. Iteration Loop: For iter = 0 to max\iterations - 1: a. Angle Loop: For each projection angle i from 0 to N{pa} - 1: i. Data Transfer: Copy the projection slice \mathbf{B}i (size N{det} \times N{slice}) from host memory to device memory. ii. Adjoint Kernel Launch: Launch the adjointkernel CUDA kernel. Grid Dimensions: \left(\frac{N{det}+15}{16}, \frac{N{slice}+15}{16}\right) Block Dimensions: (16, 16) Operation: For each detector element (j, k) at angle i, calculate the ray path through the volume. Accumulate the measured projection value p into the intersected voxels. The contribution is scaled by the relaxation factor and the pixel length. Ray Calculation: Source position: x1 = scob \cdot \sin(\thetai), y1 = -scob \cdot \cos(\thetai), z1 = 51.63 - i \cdot shift / N{pa} (where \thetai = \frac{span \cdot \pi}{N{pa} \cdot 180}). Detector point: p1 = (\frac{N{det}}{2} - (0.5 + k)) \cdot d, p3 = z1 + (\frac{N{slice}}{2} - (j + 0.5)) \cdot d. Ray direction components derived from source-to-detector vector. Intersection with voxel grid boundaries determines the path length and voxel indices (m1, m2, m3). b. Synchronization: After all angles are processed, synchronize the device to ensure all atomic updates to \mathbf{X} are complete. 3. Normalization: Multiply every voxel in \mathbf{X} by the normalization factor \frac{1}{N{pa}} (or 1/473) to scale the accumulated backprojected values. 4. Output: Save \mathbf{X} as a binary file.
