y1 is near zero, the kernel returns immediately to avoid NaNs or infinite loops. Out-of-Bounds Access: Voxel indices m1 and m3 must be checked against 0 and N{vox} before accessing the volume array. Negative Projections: If the projection value is \le 0.0, backprojection is skipped for that ray. Atomic Contention: On GPU, concurrent writes to the same voxel from different rays require atomicAdd. The CPU reference uses a pre-computed sparse weight matrix to avoid this but is slower. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The CUDA implementation is significantly faster than the CPU reference due to parallel ray processing and atomic operations. Convergence metrics on the reference dataset show MSE dropping from 24.86 to 0.4478 in 10 iterations. Strengths: Handles large, sparse systems efficiently without storing the full projection matrix \mathbf{A}. Suitable for helical geometry where direct inversion is complex. Limitations: Requires many iterations for high fidelity. Sensitive to noise in projection data. The "LSQR" label in the source refers to the iterative framework, but the specific implementation uses a weighted backprojection with relaxation rather than the full LSQR linear algebra solver (which would require matrix-vector products A^T A x). The method is implemented in a GitHub repository providing an end-to-end system for 3D Helical Cone-Beam CT reconstruction. It combines ray-casting geometry with an iterative solver approach. The term "LSQR" is used in the project title to denote the iterative least-squares nature of the reconstruction, although the core loop implements a backprojection-based iterative update. The geometry parameters (512x512x512 volume, 473 angles, 640-degree span) are specific to a simulated helical CT dataset. name: Expectation-Maximization (EM) Update
head: EM Update, Expectation Maximization, Expectation Maximization reconstruction, Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization
body: The Expectation-Maximization (EM) Update is an iterative statistical reconstruction algorithm that finds the maximum likelihood estimate of a volume distribution from incomplete or missing projection data, specifically accounting for Poisson noise inherent in X-ray or emission tomography. Unlike algebraic methods such as ART or SIRT which minimize least-squares errors, EM maximizes the likelihood function using a multiplicative update rule that guarantees non-negativity and event conservation, but suffers from slow convergence and noise amplification. Inputs: projections: 1D or 2D array of measured projection data (sinogram). Must be non-negative (proji \ge 0). volume: Initial guess of the reconstruction volume. Must be strictly positive (volj > 0) for all voxels. geometry: Projection geometry object defining the forward projector R and backprojector R^. iterations: Integer number of EM updates. bounds (optional): Tuple [minval, maxval] for clipping the volume after each iteration. subsets (optional): Integer B for Ordered Subsets EM (OSEM) acceleration. If 1, standard EM is used. Outputs: volume: The reconstructed volume array updated after iterations steps. Data Structures: volume: Array of shape matching the initial guess, dtype float. residual: Temporary array matching projection shape, used to store the ratio of measured to estimated projections. s: 1D or 3D array matching volume shape, storing the normalization factor sj = \sumi R{ij}. Numbered Steps: 1. Validate inputs: ensure projections are non-negative and volume is strictly positive. 2. Compute normalization factor sj = \sumi R{ij} by backprojecting a unity image. 3. For each iteration k: a. Forward project the current volume estimate to get (Rf^{(k)})i. b. Compute the ratio proji / (Rf^{(k)})i, handling zero estimates to prevent division by zero. c. Backproject the ratio and divide by sj to get the multiplicative update factor. d. Update volume element-wise: fj^{(k+1)} = fj^{(k)} \times \text{factor}. e. Apply bounds clipping if specified. 4. Return the final volume. Formulas: The goal is to minimize the log-likelihood function for Poisson data: l(f) = \sumi (proji \log (Rf)i - (Rf)i) where R is the forward projection operator, f is the image vector, and proj is the measured projection data. The standard EM multiplicative update for iteration k+1 is: fj^{(k+1)} = fj^{(k)} \frac{1}{sj} \sumi R{ij} \frac{proji}{(R f^{(k)})i} where sj = \sumi R{ij} is the normalization factor (sum of the backprojected unity image). In matrix-vector notation, this is often written as: f^{(k+1)} = f^{(k)} \odot \left( R^ \left( \frac{proj}{R f^{(k)}} \right) \right) / s where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication, and division is element-wise. Parameters: iterations: Typically ~12 steps before overfitting occurs. subsets: Used in OSEM variants to decompose each iteration into B sub-iterations. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: 1. Negative Data: If projections.min() < 0, the algorithm fails; sources require logging an error and rejecting negative projections. 2. Zero Initial Guess: If volume.min() <= 0, the algorithm fails; sources require logging an error and ensuring a strictly positive initial guess. 3. Instability: The method becomes unstable after a large number of iterations. 4. Conservation: If initialized positively, all subsequent estimates remain positive. Voxels initialized to zero remain zero. The total number of events is conserved at each iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def emupdate(projections, volume, geometry, iterations, bounds=None, subsets=1): """ Perform Expectation-Maximization reconstruction. Args: projections: 1D or 2D array of measured projections. volume: Initial positive guess of the volume. geometry: Object with forwardproject and backproject methods. iterations: Number of EM steps. bounds: Optional tuple (min, max) to clip volume. subsets: Number of subsets for OSEM. 1 for standard EM. Returns: volume: Reconstructed volume. """ # Validation if np.any(projections < 0): raise ValueError("Wrong projection data. Make sure that projections have no negative values.") if np.any(volume <= 0): raise ValueError("Wrong initial guess. Make sure that initial guess for EM is positive.") # Precompute normalization factor sj = sumi Rij unityproj = np.oneslike(projections) s = geometry.backproject(unityproj) s = np.where(s > 0, s, 1.0) # Guard against division by zero in unobservable voxels for in range(iterations): # Forward project current estimate: estimated = R volume estimated = geometry.forwardproject(volume) # Compute ratio proj / estimated ratio = np.where(estimated > 0, projections / estimated, 0.0) # Backproject ratio and normalize: volume = volume (R^(ratio) / s) # Scale by subsets for OSEM acceleration scale = subsets if subsets > 1 else 1.0 volume = volume (geometry.backproject(ratio) / s) scale # Apply bounds if specified if bounds is not None: np.clip(volume, bounds[0], bounds[1], out=volume) return volume Accelerated variant of EM that decomposes each iteration into B sub-iterations using subsets of projection data, speeding up convergence but potentially leading to earlier divergence. Convergence: Slow compared to algebraic methods like SIRT or CG. Stability: Unstable after a large number of iterations; requires regularization or post-filtering (e.g., Gaussian filter) to stabilize. Properties: Guarantees non-negativity if initialized positively; conserves total number of events at each iteration. Noise Handling: Statistically optimal for Poisson noise inherent in low-count X-ray or emission tomography data. Regularization: Prone to high-frequency noise amplification; stabilization typically requires early stopping (~12 steps) or adding a penalty term B(f). The EM algorithm was introduced as a general method for finding maximum likelihood estimates in the presence of incomplete data. In tomography, it was adapted to handle Poisson noise in projection data. The Ordered Subsets EM (OSEM) variant was introduced by Hudson and Larkin in 1994 to accelerate convergence. It is widely used in medical imaging, particularly in SPECT and PET reconstruction, and in X-ray CT for low-dose scenarios. name: Ordered Subsets EM (OSEM)
head: MAP-OSEM, OSEM (Ordered Subset Expectation Maximisation), Ordered Subset Expectation Maximization (OSEM)
body: Ordered Subsets EM (OSEM) is an accelerated variant of the Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) algorithm used for tomographic reconstruction. It reduces reconstruction time by decomposing each full iteration into B sub-iterations, where each sub-iteration uses only a subset of the available projection data. Unlike standard EM, which processes all projections simultaneously, OSEM updates the image estimate sequentially for each subset, significantly speeding up convergence, though this acceleration can lead to earlier divergence, often necessitating regularization (MAP-OSEM). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial image estimate f^{(0)} (non-negative), projection data pi, system matrix elements R{ij} (probability that photon from voxel j is detected in bin i), and number of subsets M. Output: Reconstructed image f after convergence. Data Structures: fj: Value of voxel j. pi: Measured projection value for bin i. R{ij}: System matrix element. sm: Set of projection indices belonging to subset m, where m \in \{1, \dots, M\}. Parameters: M: Number of subsets. Must be a positive even integer less than or equal to the total number of projections. B: Number of subsamples per step (equivalent to M in the notation of). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize fj^{(0)} > 0 for all voxels j. 2. For iteration n = 0, 1, 2, \dots: 3. For each subset m = 1, \dots, M: 4. Compute the forward projection of the current image estimate using only projections in subset sm: \hat{p}i^{(n, m-1)} = \sum{j} R{ij} fj^{(n, m-1)} \quad \forall i \in sm 5. Compute the ratio of measured to estimated projections for the subset: \text{ratio}i = \frac{pi}{\hat{p}i^{(n, m-1)}} \quad \forall i \in sm 6. Compute the backprojection of the ratio, normalized by the sum of system matrix elements for the subset: \text{backproj}j = \sum{i \in sm} R{ij} \cdot \text{ratio}i \text{norm}j = \sum{i \in sm} R{ij} 7. Update the image estimate for the current sub-iteration: fj^{(n, m)} = fj^{(n, m-1)} \cdot \frac{\text{backproj}j}{\text{norm}j} 8. Set the starting point for the next iteration: fj^{(n+1)} = fj^{(n, M)} Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: projections: List of measured projection values pi. systemmatrix: 2D array Rij where i is projection bin and j is voxel. numsubsets: Integer M, number of subsets (positive even integer <= len(projections)). maxiterations: Integer, maximum number of full iterations. Returns: Reconstructed image array f. """ numprojections = len(projections) numvoxels = len(systemmatrix[0]) # Initialize image estimate to positive values # Common initialization is uniform positive value or backprojection of data image = [1.0] numvoxels # Define subsets sm # Source states subsets should be ordered to minimize redundancy (e.g., separated by 90 degrees). # A simple round-robin assignment is a valid implementation strategy if not specified otherwise. subsets = [[] for in range(numsubsets)] for i in range(numprojections): subsets[i % numsubsets].append(i) for n in range(maxiterations): # Current image state for the iteration currentimage = list(image) for m in range(numsubsets): subsetindices = subsets[m] # Step 4: Forward projection for subset estimatedprojections = [0.0] numprojections for i in subsetindices: projsum = 0.0 for j in range(numvoxels): projsum += systemmatrix[i][j] currentimage[j] estimatedprojections[i] = projsum # Step 5 & 6 & 7: Ratio, Backprojection, and Update # Precompute normalization factors for the subset normfactors = [0.0] numvoxels for j in range(numvoxels): normsum = 0.0 for i in subsetindices: normsum += systemmatrix[i][j] normfactors[j] = normsum # Update image newimage = [0.0] numvoxels for j in range(numvoxels): backprojsum = 0.0 for i in subsetindices: # Avoid division by zero if estimated projection is 0 if estimatedprojections[i] > 0: ratio = projections[i] / estimatedprojections[i] else: ratio = 0.0 backprojsum += systemmatrix[i][j] ratio if normfactors[j] > 0: newimage[j] = currentimage[j] (backprojsum / normfactors[j]) else: newimage[j] = currentimage[j] currentimage = newimage image = currentimage return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Divergence: The accelerated convergence of OSEM can lead to divergence problems occurring earlier than in standard MLEM. This often requires the use of regularization, resulting in MAP-OSEM. Subset Selection: Projections should be grouped and ordered to minimize redundancy within subsets (e.g., separated by large angles like 90 degrees) for optimal efficiency. Subsample Types: Hudson and Larkin distinguish between non-overlapping subsamples, nested subsamples, and the standard sample (which is equivalent to standard EM). Single Subset: If B=1 (or M=1), OSEM is identical to standard EM. Time Complexity: Each full iteration consists of M sub-iterations. Each sub-iteration processes only 1/M of the projections. Thus, one full iteration of OSEM has roughly the same computational cost as one iteration of MLEM, but converges faster in terms of iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the image, projection data, and system matrix (or access to it). No significant additional memory overhead compared to MLEM. Strengths: Significantly reduced reconstruction time compared to MLEM. Limitations: Prone to divergence earlier than MLEM due to acceleration. Requires careful selection of subsets. When to use: When faster convergence is needed and computational resources per iteration are not the primary bottleneck, or when combined with regularization (MAP-OSEM) to handle divergence. When not to use: When strict monotonic convergence is required without regularization, or when the number of projections is very small (making subset selection difficult). Origin: Introduced by Hudson and Larkin in 1994. History: Developed as an acceleration technique for the EM algorithm in tomographic reconstruction. The method decomposes each iteration into sub-iterations using subsets of projections. Usage: Widely used in medical imaging (e.g., PET, SPECT) and other tomographic applications where fast reconstruction is critical. name: Jacobi Iterative Solver for Thermal Tomography
head: Inner solver, Jacobi unrolling
body: An iterative method to solve the linear system A T{n+1} = Tn arising from the implicit Euler discretization of the heat equation, used as the inner solver for the differentiable physics simulation. It sets itself apart from direct factorization methods by trading exact algebraic inversion for a fixed number of unrolled iterations, enabling efficient gradient computation via the adjoint method. Unlike SIRT or ART, which solve tomographic projection equations directly, this method solves the forward physics step within an inverse rendering pipeline. Inputs and Outputs Input: Previous frame temperature state Tn, system matrix A(\alpha\theta) derived from diffusivity parameters \theta, number of iterations K. Output: Approximate next frame state T{n+1} \approx T^{(K)}. Data Structures T^{(\kappa)}: Temperature field vector of size Ng (grid nodes). D: Diagonal matrix of A. R: Off-diagonal remainder matrix of A, such that A = D + R. b: Right-hand side vector, set to Tn. Parameters K: Number of Jacobi iterations. Value: 50. Chosen large enough that the residual \|A T^{(K)} - b\| falls below the noise floor of camera measurements; empirically sufficient for the grid resolution and \Delta t. T^{(0)}: Initial guess. Value: Tn. Warm-started by the previous frame’s solution to accelerate convergence. Steps 1. Initialize T^{(0)} \leftarrow Tn. 2. For \kappa = 0 to K-1: a. Compute residual vector r^{(\kappa)} = b - R T^{(\kappa)}. b. Update temperature: T^{(\kappa+1)} \leftarrow D^{-1} r^{(\kappa)}. 3. Set T{n+1} \leftarrow T^{(K)}. Formula The iteration is defined as: T^{(\kappa+1)} = D^{-1} (b - R T^{(\kappa)}), \quad \kappa = 0, 1, \dots, K-1 where b:= Tn. This reduces to a 7-point stencil convolution. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jacobisolver(Tn, Adiag, Aoffdiag, K=50): """ Solves A T{n+1} = Tn using Jacobi iteration. A = D + R, where D is diagonal and R is off-diagonal. """ # Initialize with warm start Tcurr = Tn.clone() # Precompute b b = Tn for kappa in range(K): # Compute R Tcurr # R is the off-diagonal part of A. # In a stencil context, this is a convolution excluding the center term. RTcurr = convolveoffdiagonal(Tcurr, Aoffdiag) # Compute D^{-1} (b - R Tcurr) # D^{-1} is element-wise division by diagonal elements residual = b - RTcurr Tnext = residual / Adiag Tcurr = Tnext return Tcurr Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ill-conditioning: If the defect-to-bulk diffusivity ratio is > 1:1000, the linear system becomes severely ill-conditioned and the iterative solver stalls. Mitigation: Use a ratio of \sim 1:20, which saturates the surface-temperature signature against the perfect-insulator limit while keeping the condition number compatible with efficient optimization. A method to compute exact gradients of the discrete objective J{disc} with respect to parameters \theta by solving an adjoint recurrence backwards in time, avoiding the storage of the full computational graph. It sets itself apart from naive backpropagation-through-time by reducing memory complexity from O(K Ng Nt) to O(Ng), where K is the number of inner Jacobi iterations, Ng is the grid size, and Nt is the number of time steps. Time Complexity: O(K Ng) per time step, where K is the number of iterations and Ng is the grid size. Memory Complexity: The forward solve memory cost is part of the total budget. The naive backpropagation-through-time scales as O(K Ng Nt), but the adjoint method replaces this with O(Ng) at the cost of one backward solve. Performance: The iteration is expressed as a single fused kernel in standard autodiff frameworks and accelerated with torch.compile just-in-time autotuning. Strengths: Allows for differentiable physics simulation with exact gradients (up to iterative tolerance) without storing the full computational graph. Limitations: Convergence depends on diagonal dominance; ill-conditioned systems (high defect contrast) cause stalling. When to use: When differentiable thermal simulation is required and direct factorization is too expensive or non-differentiable in the desired framework. When not to use: When high defect contrast (>1:1000) is necessary and cannot be approximated by 1:20. Originated in the context of Neural Field Thermal Tomography, a differentiable physics approach to thermal imaging. The method leverages the strict diagonal dominance of the discretized heat equation to ensure convergence of the Jacobi iteration to the unique exact solution. It is used in synthetic 3D reconstruction tasks where the goal is to recover diffusivity fields from temperature measurements. name: Adjoint Recurrence and Gradient Assembly
head: Backward Pass for Thermal Tomography, Discrete Adjoint Method
body: A method to compute exact gradients of the discrete objective J{disc} with respect to parameters \theta by solving an adjoint recurrence backwards in time, avoiding the storage of the full computational graph. It sets itself apart from naive backpropagation-through-time by reducing memory complexity from O(K Ng Nt) to O(Ng), where K is the number of inner Jacobi iterations, Ng is the grid size, and Nt is the number of time steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Parameters \theta (defining thermal conductivity \alpha\theta via an MLP), initial temperature T0, time steps n=1, \dots, Nt, and observation indices \{n1, \dots, nM\} with corresponding measurements \hat{T}i. Outputs: Gradient \frac{d J{disc}}{d\theta}. Data Structures: Tn \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng}: Temperature state at time step n. \mun \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng}: Adjoint variables (Lagrange multipliers) for the state residuals. A(\alpha\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^{Ng \times Ng}: System matrix from the implicit Euler discretization. Note that A(\alpha\theta)^\top = A(\alpha\theta) due to the specific boundary conditions (lateral periodic, adiabatic through-thickness, homogeneous Robin). Formulas: 1. State Residual: Fn(Tn, T{n-1}, \alpha\theta):= A(\alpha\theta) Tn - T{n-1} = 0, \quad n = 1, \dots, Nt 2. Per-step Data Term: \elln(Tn):= \begin{cases} \|\Pi\Gamma Tn - \hat{T}i\|^2 & \text{if } n = ni \in \{n1, \dots, nM\} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. Augmented Lagrangian: \mathcal{L}(\theta; \{Tn\}, \{\mun\}) = \sum{n=1}^{Nt} \elln(Tn) + \lambda R(\alpha\theta) - \sum{n=1}^{Nt} \mun^\top Fn(Tn, T{n-1}, \alpha\theta) 4. Adjoint Recurrence: A(\alpha\theta)^\top \mun = \frac{\partial \elln}{\partial Tn} + \mu{n+1}, \quad \mu{Nt+1} = 0 5. Gradient Assembly: \frac{d J{disc}}{d\theta} = \frac{\partial (\lambda R)}{\partial \theta} + \Delta t \sum{n=1}^{Nt} \mun^\top \frac{\partial (L(\alpha\theta) Tn)}{\partial \alpha\theta} \frac{\partial \alpha\theta}{\partial \theta} Where \frac{\partial Fn}{\partial \alpha\theta} = -\Delta t \frac{\partial (L(\alpha\theta) Tn)}{\partial \alpha\theta}. Parameters: \mun: Adjoint variables, dimension \mathbb{R}^{Ng}. K: Number of Jacobi iterations. Empirically K=50 suffices for typical grid resolutions and \Delta t. Steps: 1. Forward Sweep: Compute T1, \dots, T{Nt} using the Jacobi solver defined in Jacobi Iterative Solver for Thermal Tomography. Store all Tn or manage memory for the backward pass. 2. Backward Sweep: Initialize \mu{Nt+1} = 0. For n = Nt down to 1: Compute \frac{\partial \elln}{\partial Tn}. Solve A(\alpha\theta) \mun = \frac{\partial \elln}{\partial Tn} + \mu{n+1} for \mun. (Note: A^\top = A). 3. Gradient Assembly: Compute \frac{d J{disc}}{d\theta} using the accumulated \mun and stored Tn. The term \frac{\partial \alpha\theta}{\partial \theta} is obtained by ordinary backpropagation through the MLP at each grid node. The term \frac{\partial (L(\alpha\theta) Tn)}{\partial \alpha\theta} is a sparse local stencil determined by harmonic-mean derivatives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adjointrecurrencegradientassembly(Tforward, alphatheta, theta, Nt, Ng, K, lambdareg, Rfunc, Lop, PiGamma, Thatindices, Thatvalues, deltat): """ Computes the gradient of the discrete objective with respect to theta. Args: Tforward: List of Tn for n=1..Nt, computed via Jacobi solver. alphatheta: Conductivity field computed from theta via MLP. theta: Parameters of the MLP. Nt: Number of time steps. Ng: Grid size. K: Number of Jacobi iterations (used for forward, not directly here). lambdareg: Regularization weight. Rfunc: Regularization function R(alphatheta). Lop: Diffusion operator L(alphatheta). PiGamma: Projection operator for observations. Thatindices: List of time indices ni where observations exist. Thatvalues: Corresponding observed temperatures. deltat: Time step size. Returns: gradtheta: Gradient of Jdisc with respect to theta. """ # Initialize adjoint variables munext = np.zeros(Ng) # mu{Nt+1} = 0 gradtheta = np.zeroslike(theta) # Gradient of regularization term w.r.t theta # Note: R depends on alphatheta, which depends on theta # We compute dR/dalpha dalpha/dtheta later or via autograd # Here we accumulate the physics part first physicsgradaccum = np.zeros(Ng) # Accumulate sum over n of mun^T d(LT)/dalpha dalpha/dtheta # Backward sweep for n in range(Nt, 0, -1): Tn = Tforward[n-1] # Tforward is 1-indexed in math, 0-indexed in list # 1. Compute data term gradient d(ln)/d(Tn) dlndT = np.zeros(Ng) if n in Thatindices: idx = Thatindices.index(n) That = Thatvalues[idx] # ln = ||PiGamma Tn - That||^2 # d(ln)/d(Tn) = 2 PiGamma^T (PiGamma Tn - That) residual = PiGamma @ Tn - That dlndT = 2 (PiGamma.T @ residual) # 2. Solve adjoint recurrence: A^T mun = d(ln)/d(Tn) + mu{n+1} # Since A^T = A, we solve A mun = rhs rhs = dlndT + munext # Solve linear system A mun = rhs # A is SPD. Use the same Jacobi solver or a direct solver. # For exactness, we assume A is solved exactly or to high tolerance. mun = solvelinearsystem(A=alphathetamatrix, b=rhs) # 3. Accumulate gradient contribution # Term: deltat mun^T d(L(alphatheta) Tn) / d(alphatheta) d(alphatheta)/d(theta) # d(L(alphatheta) Tn) / d(alphatheta) is a sparse local stencil. # Let's compute the vector vn = d(L(alphatheta) Tn) / d(alphatheta) # This is a tensor, but we contract with mun. # mun^T d(L Tn)/d(alpha) results in a vector w.r.t alphatheta components. # Compute d(L(alphatheta) Tn) / d(alphatheta) # L(alphatheta) involves harmonic means of alpha. # The derivative is non-zero only for neighbors. # Let's assume a helper function for this sparse stencil application. dLTndalpha = computediffusionjacobian(Lop, alphatheta, Tn) # Contract mun with this Jacobian to get gradient w.r.t alphatheta # mun is a vector, dLTndalpha is a matrix (Ng x Ng) where cols are alpha nodes # Actually, L(alpha) T is linear in T but non-linear in alpha. # The derivative w.r.t alphai is a vector. # We need sumi mun^T (d(L T)/d alphai) (d alphai / d theta) # Efficiently: compute vector galpha = sumn mun^T d(L Tn)/d alphatheta # This is a vector of size Ng (one per grid node alpha) # For each grid node j, compute mun^T (d(L Tn)/d alphaj) # This is equivalent to (d(L Tn)/d alphaj)^T mun # Let's assume computediffusionjacobian returns a matrix Jalpha where Jalpha[:, j] = d(L Tn)/d alphaj Jalpha = computediffusionjacobian(Lop, alphatheta, Tn) # Shape (Ng, Ng) # Contract mun with Jalpha # gradalphacontribution = Jalpha.T @ mun gradalphacontribution = Jalpha.T @ mun # Accumulate into physicsgradaccum physicsgradaccum += deltat gradalphacontribution # Update munext for next iteration munext = mun # Final gradient assembly # dJ/dtheta = d(lambda R)/dtheta + d(physicsgradaccum)/dalphatheta dalphatheta/dtheta # 1. Regularization gradient # d(lambda R)/dtheta = lambda dR/dalphatheta dalphatheta/dtheta # We can compute this via autograd if R is differentiable w.r.t alphatheta # Or manually if R is simple (e.g., L2 norm of alpha) # 2. Physics gradient # d(alphatheta)/dtheta is obtained by backprop through MLP # Let's assume we have a function to get d(alpha)/dtheta dalphadtheta = getmlpjacobian(theta) # Shape (Ng, len(theta)) # gradthetaphysics = dalphadtheta.T @ physicsgradaccum gradthetaphysics = dalphadtheta.T @ physicsgradaccum # 3. Regularization gradient # Assuming R(alpha) is differentiable dRdalpha = computeregularizationgradient(Rfunc, alphatheta) gradthetareg = dalphadtheta.T @ (lambdareg dRdalpha) gradtheta = gradthetaphysics + gradthetareg return gradtheta Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: The naive approach stores the entire computational graph of K unrolled Jacobi iterations at every time step, scaling as O(K Ng Nt). The adjoint method requires only one current and one trailing temperature slice plus the running gradient accumulator in memory beyond the cost of a single forward solve, scaling as O(Ng). Symmetry: The recurrence uses A^\top. The method relies on A(\alpha\theta)^\top = A(\alpha\theta), which holds for the specific boundary conditions (lateral periodic, adiabatic through-thickness, homogeneous Robin). If boundary conditions change, A^\top \neq A and the backward solve must use A^\top. Initial Conditions: If T0 is uncertain or learnable, additional terms appear in the gradient. Time Complexity: One forward solve (O(K Ng) per step, total O(K Ng Nt)) and one backward solve (O(K Ng Nt) if using Jacobi, or O(Ng) if using direct solver for the adjoint system, but typically the same iterative solver is used). Gradient assembly is O(Ng Nt) for stencil computations. Memory Complexity: O(Ng) for the adjoint method, compared to O(K Ng Nt) for naive backpropagation. Strengths: Exact gradients of the discrete objective J{disc}, avoiding approximations from discretizing the continuous adjoint. Significant memory savings. Limitations: Requires storing Tn or re-computing them (checkpointing) if memory is extremely constrained. The backward solve inherits the backward-parabolic structure, which can be sensitive to numerical errors if not handled carefully. When to use: When memory is a bottleneck for long time series (Nt large) and exact gradients are required for optimization. When not to use: If Nt is very small, the memory overhead of naive backprop might be acceptable, and the implementation complexity of the adjoint method may not be justified. Originated in the context of differentiable physics simulation for thermal tomography. The method is an application of the implicit function theorem in a sequential setting, providing exact gradients for the discrete objective rather than discretized gradients of the continuous adjoint. It builds on the Jacobi Iterative Solver for Thermal Tomography Jacobi Iterative Solver for Thermal Tomography. name: Iterative Reconstruction Methods
head: Méthodes itératives de reconstruction tomographique
body: Iterative Reconstruction (IR) methods solve the tomographic inverse problem by iteratively refining an estimate of the object to reduce the discrepancy between simulated and measured projections. Unlike direct analytical methods such as Filtered Back Projection (FBP), which can be unstable or produce artifacts under low-dose or sparse-view conditions, IR methods model the acquisition process and noise statistics to produce more accurate reconstructions. They are chosen when data is noisy, incomplete, or when system physics (e.g., focal spot blur, detector response) must be explicitly modeled, accepting higher computational cost and potential over-smoothing as trade-offs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data (sinogram) P, system geometry/forward projection operator \mathcal{R}, initial guess f^{(0)}. Output: Reconstructed volume estimate f^{(N)} after N iterations. Data Structures: f: The image/volume estimate, typically a 2D slice or 3D grid of voxel values. Initialized to a constant (e.g., zero or mean attenuation). P: The acquired projection data vector or matrix. \tilde{P}: The estimated projections, computed via forward projection of the current estimate f^{(n-1)} using operator \mathcal{R}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the initial object estimate f^{(0)} to a constant value. 2. Forward Projection: Calculate the estimated projections \tilde{P} in the same directions as the real acquisition using the current estimate f^{(n-1)}: \tilde{P} = \mathcal{R}(f^{(n-1)}) 3. Error Calculation: Compute the projection error \epsilonP by comparing estimated projections \tilde{P} to acquired projections P. The form depends on the method type: Additive methods: \epsilonP = P - \tilde{P} Multiplicative methods: \epsilonP = P / \tilde{P} 4. Back-Projection: Back-project the projection error \epsilonP to obtain the tomography error \epsilonf: \epsilonf = \mathcal{R}^T(\epsilonP) where \mathcal{R}^T is the back-projection operator. 5. Update: Update the object estimate f^{(n)} based on the tomography error \epsilonf: Additive methods: f^{(n)} = f^{(n-1)} + \epsilonf Multiplicative methods: f^{(n)} = f^{(n-1)} \times \epsilonf 6. Convergence Check: Repeat steps 2–5 until the difference between simulated and real projections is sufficiently low, or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Parameters: Regularization via Early Stopping: The process is often interrupted after a certain number of iterations to avoid reconstructing noise-dominated high frequencies, effectively acting as a low-pass filter. Pitfalls: Divergence due to Noise: While iterative methods converge toward the solution, they eventually diverge due to noise amplification. High frequencies (details and noise) are represented more in later iterations, causing the solution to move away from the true object. Over-smoothing: Iterative reconstruction can produce over-smoothed images that may appear "plastic," losing fine detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativereconstruction(P, forwardproject, backproject, numiterations, methodtype='additive'): """ Perform iterative tomographic reconstruction. Args: P: Measured projection data (sinogram). forwardproject: Function that computes R(f) for a given image f. backproject: Function that computes R^T(e) for a given error e. numiterations: Maximum number of iterations. methodtype: 'additive' or 'multiplicative'. Returns: f: Reconstructed image estimate. """ # Initialize f to a constant value (e.g., zeros) f = initializeimage(P) for n in range(1, numiterations + 1): # 1. Forward Project Pest = forwardproject(f) # 2. Calculate Projection Error if methodtype == 'additive': epsilonP = P - Pest elif methodtype == 'multiplicative': # Avoid division by zero; handle small Pest values appropriately epsilonP = P / Pest else: raise ValueError("methodtype must be 'additive' or 'multiplicative'") # 3. Back-Project Error epsilonf = backproject(epsilonP) # 4. Update Image Estimate if methodtype == 'additive': f = f + epsilonf elif methodtype == 'multiplicative': f = f epsilonf # 5. Check Convergence (Optional: based on residual norm) # if norm(P - forwardproject(f)) < threshold: # break return f def initializeimage(P): """ Initialize the image estimate to a constant value. Typically zeros or the mean of the projections. """ # Not given in the sources. Standard practice is zeros or mean. # Assuming 2D image for simplicity, size derived from P geometry. # Placeholder for actual image dimension logic. return 0.0 More primitive methods that aim to degrade image quality by reducing noise and artifacts through an iterative process. The image is repeatedly updated based on comparing the final reconstructed image with the measured projection data. These methods are noted to lead to more inaccurate results compared to more advanced techniques. An iterative reconstruction approach that iterates over a cycle of the forward and inverse Radon transform, applying constraints in each domain to converge on an optimal solution. The steps involve: 1) Iterating over a cycle of the forward Radon transform, 2) Applying constraints in the Radon domain, 3) Iterating over a cycle of the inverse Radon transform, and 4) Applying constraints in the image domain. Previously not commonly used due to large computational demands, it becomes practical when both forward and inverse steps are accelerated with a single piece of hardware. Time Complexity: Iterative methods are computationally expensive, requiring multiple forward and back-projection steps per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the image volume, projection data, and intermediate error terms. Performance: Can reduce dose or clean streaks compared to FBP. However, they increase compute time significantly. Strengths: Handles noisy or sparse data better than FBP; can incorporate system physics and noise statistics. Limitations: High computational cost; risk of over-smoothing ("plastic" look); prone to divergence if not regularized (e.g., via early stopping). When to Use: Low-dose CT, sparse-view CT, or when system modeling is critical. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring speed, or when high-frequency detail preservation is paramount and noise is low. Iterative reconstruction methods originated as a solution to the ill-posed nature of tomographic reconstruction, where direct inversion of the projection matrix is unstable and impractical. The term "Méthodes itératives de reconstruction tomographique" is commonly used in French literature. The general principle involves starting with a guess, forward-projecting, comparing to measured data, and updating, a process formalized in early tomography literature. The divergence due to noise amplification in later iterations is a general phenomenon in ill-posed inverse problems. name: Conjugate Gradient (CG)
body: Conjugate Gradient (CG) is an iterative descent method used to solve the linear system R^T R f = R^T \text{proj} arising from the minimization of the quadratic error functional J(f) = ||\text{proj} - Rf||^2 in overdetermined tomographic reconstruction problems. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Expectation-Maximization (EM) by its significantly faster convergence speed, though it lacks the inherent positivity guarantee of EM and may exhibit non-convergence issues more rapidly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data vector \text{proj}, forward projection operator R (or its action), initial estimate f^{(0)} (typically zero or a filtered backprojection result). Output: Reconstructed volume f. Data Structures: Vectors f, r, p of size N (number of voxels). Scalars \alphan, \betan. Matrix-vector products R v and R^T v are computed using the specific geometry of the tomographic setup (e.g., ray-driven or voxel-driven projection/backprojection). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize f^{(0)} = 0 (or another initial guess). 2. Compute initial residual: r0 = R^T (\text{proj} - R f^{(0)}). 3. Set initial search direction: p1 = r0. 4. For iteration n = 1, 2, \dots until convergence: a. Compute step size: \alphan = \frac{pn^T pn}{(R pn)^T (R pn)}. b. Update solution: f^{(n+1)} = f^{(n)} + \alphan pn. c. Compute new residual: rn = R^T (\text{proj} - R f^{(n)}). d. If n > 1, compute coefficient: \betan = \frac{(R r{n-1})^T (R pn)}{(R p{n-1})^T (R p{n-1})}. e. Update search direction: p{n+1} = rn - \betan pn. Conditions: \langle p{n+1}, rn \rangle = 0 and \langle p{n+1}, R^T R pn \rangle = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conjugategradient(proj, Rfwd, Rbwd, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): """ Solves R^T R f = R^T proj using Conjugate Gradient. Rfwd computes R v. Rbwd computes R^T v. """ N = len(proj) f = [0.0] N # f^(0) r = Rbwd([proj[i] - Rfwd(f)[i] for i in range(N)]) # r0 p = r[:] # p1 # Precompute Rp1 and Rr0 for the first beta calculation (n=2) Rp = Rfwd(p) Rr = Rfwd(r) for n in range(1, maxiter + 1): pTp = sum(p[i] p[i] for i in range(N)) RpTRp = sum(Rp[i] Rp[i] for i in range(N)) if RpTRp == 0: break alpha = pTp / RpTRp for i in range(N): f[i] += alpha p[i] residualvec = [proj[i] - Rfwd(f)[i] for i in range(N)] r = Rbwd(residualvec) # rn rnormsq = sum(r[i] r[i] for i in range(N)) if rnormsq < tol: break if n > 1: beta = sum(Rr[i] Rp[i] for i in range(N)) / sum(Rpprev[i] Rpprev[i] for i in range(N)) for i in range(N): p[i] = r[i] - beta p[i] else: for i in range(N): p[i] = r[i] # Prepare for next iteration Rpprev = Rp Rp = Rfwd(p) Rr = Rfwd(r) return f Parameters: maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. Not given in the sources. Typical values range from 10 to 100 for tomography, depending on convergence criteria. tol: Convergence tolerance. Not given in the sources. Typical values are 10^{-6} to 10^{-4}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Positivity: The additive correction term does not guarantee that the estimated values remain positive. This is a significant limitation for tomographic reconstruction where voxel values (e.g., density, attenuation) must be non-negative. Convergence: Non-convergence problems appear faster with CG compared to EM. Conditioning: The method assumes the system R^T R is positive definite. If the system is ill-conditioned, convergence may be slow or unstable. A variant used to solve linear equations with surface constraints without degrading system conditioning or losing positive definiteness. It projects residuals and solutions along the surface tangent plane during the conjugate gradient resolution and corrects particle positions by projecting them directly to the surface after resolution. This avoids the numerical instabilities associated with augmenting the system with Lagrange multipliers, which can degrade conditioning and destroy positive definiteness. The surface projection is performed using an iterative Newton-Raphson method. Time Complexity: Each iteration requires two matrix-vector multiplications (R p and R^T r). The total time is O(k \cdot (N{voxels} + N{rays})) where k is the number of iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N{voxels} + N{rays}) to store the volume, projections, and intermediate vectors. Performance: CG converges significantly faster than EM. Strengths: Rapid convergence for overdetermined systems. Limitations: Does not guarantee positivity. More prone to non-convergence issues than EM. Sensitive to the conditioning of R^T R. Conjugate Gradient is a classic descent method used for tomographic reconstruction. It is based on the minimization of a quadratic functional, commonly the quadratic error. The method is equivalent to the EM algorithm if a Gaussian distribution is chosen. It is widely used in tomographic reconstruction due to its speed. name: NCP Stopping Rule
head: Normalised Cumulative Periodogram Stopping Rule
body: The NCP Stopping Rule is a termination criterion for iterative tomographic reconstruction algorithms that halts the process when the reconstruction residual behaves like white noise. It distinguishes itself from fixed-iteration or simple residual-norm methods by adapting to the specific noise level in the projection data, ensuring the algorithm stops near the optimal solution without overfitting to noise. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: The current reconstruction estimate xk, the projection data b, the system matrix A, and the maximum iteration count N{max}. Outputs: A boolean flag indicating termination or the iteration index k where termination occurs. Data Structures rk \in \mathbb{R}^n: The residual vector at iteration k. \hat{r} \in \mathbb{C}^n: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the residual. \hat{p} \in \mathbb{R}^q: The periodogram vector, where q = \lceil n/2 \rceil. c \in \mathbb{R}^q: The Normalised Cumulative Periodogram (NCP) vector. c{white} \in \mathbb{R}^q: The reference line for white noise. Numbered Steps 1. Compute Residual: Calculate the residual vector rk = b - A xk. Note: In implementations using libraries like ASTRA, the residual norm may be available during the update step, but the full vector must be explicitly calculated for the NCP check. 2. Compute DFT: Calculate the Discrete Fourier Transform of the residual: \hat{r} = \text{DFT}(rk). 3. Compute Periodogram: Calculate the periodogram \hat{p} using the squared absolute values of the DFT coefficients. Only approximately half of the elements are used because the power spectrum of a real vector is symmetric around the midpoint: \hat{p}i = |\hat{r}i|^2, \quad i=1, 2, \dots, q where q = \lceil n/2 \rceil. 4. Compute NCP: Calculate the Normalised Cumulative Periodogram cj(rk) for j=1, \dots, q. The DC component (first element of \hat{p}) is excluded from the summation to ensure the curve starts at (0,0): cj(rk) = \frac{\sum{i=2}^{j+1} \hat{p}i}{\sum{i=2}^{q+1} \hat{p}i}, \quad j=1, 2, \dots, q 5. Compute Distance to White Noise: Calculate the \ell2-norm distance r{NCP} between the computed NCP c(rk) and the expected white noise line c{white}, which is a straight line ranging from (0,0) to (q,1): r{NCP}(k) = \| c(rk) - c{white} \|2 6. Check Termination: Terminate the reconstruction if two iterations on either side of the current r{NCP}(k) are larger than r{NCP}(k). This requires storing the r{NCP} values for the current and previous iterations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ncpstoppingrule(residualvector, n, maxiterations): """ Determines if the NCP stopping rule is met. Args: residualvector (list[float]): The residual rk = b - A xk. n (int): The dimension of the residual vector (number of voxels/pixels). maxiterations (int): Nmax to prevent infinite loops. Returns: bool: True if the algorithm should terminate, False otherwise. """ # Step 1: Compute DFT of the residual # DFT is a standard mathematical operation. # In practice, this is often accelerated via CUDA (e.g., CuPy). dftcoeffs = dft(residualvector) # Step 2: Determine q q = ceil(n / 2) # Step 3: Compute Periodogram phat # Only use the first q coefficients. # Exclude DC component (index 0) for NCP calculation later, # but keep it for periodogram definition if needed by specific DFT conventions. # The formula uses indices 1 to q (1-based) or 0 to q-1 (0-based). # Based on formula: pi = |rhati|^2 for i=1..q. # Assuming 1-based indexing for formula mapping to 0-based array: # phat[0] corresponds to i=1, phat[q-1] corresponds to i=q. phat = [abs(dftcoeffs[i])2 for i in range(q)] # Step 4: Compute NCP c # cj(r) for j=1..q # Formula: cj = sum(p2...p{j+1}) / sum(p2...p{q+1}) # Note: The formula indices are 1-based. # p2 is index 1 in 0-based phat. p{q+1} is index q in 0-based phat. # However, phat only has length q (indices 0 to q-1). # The denominator sum goes up to p{q+1}. # If q = ceil(n/2), and n is even, n=2q. DFT has 2q coeffs. # Symmetry means we use q coeffs. # The formula explicitly sums from i=2 to q+1. # This implies we need access to p{q+1}. # If phat is defined for i=1..q, then p{q+1} is outside this range? # Re-reading source: "q = ceil(n/2)... only approximately half... used". # Formula: cj(r) = (sum{i=2}^{j+1} pi) / (sum{i=2}^{q+1} pi). # If p is defined for i=1..q, then p{q+1} is not in phat? # Let's look at the denominator: sum{i=2}^{q+1} pi. # If q=ceil(n/2), and we have q periodogram values, the indices are 1..q. # The sum goes to q+1. This suggests the periodogram might be defined up to q+1 # or the indexing in the source text has a specific convention. # Standard NCP for real signals of length N uses N/2 points. # Let's assume the denominator is the sum of all available periodogram components # excluding the DC component (i=1). # If phat has length q, indices 0..q-1 correspond to i=1..q. # The sum in denominator is i=2 to q+1. # If the signal is real, the spectrum is symmetric. # The source says "pi = |rhati|^2, i=1,2,...,q". # And "cj(r) =... / sum{i=2}^{q+1} pi". # This implies p{q+1} exists. # Perhaps q is defined differently or the sum includes the Nyquist frequency if n is even? # If n is even, DFT has n/2 + 1 unique real coefficients (0 to n/2). # If q = n/2, then indices 1..q are 1..n/2. # The sum goes to q+1 = n/2 + 1. This matches the Nyquist bin. # So, phat should likely include the Nyquist bin if n is even. # Let's adjust q to include the Nyquist bin for even n. # If n is even, unique freqs are 0..n/2. Count = n/2 + 1. # If n is odd, unique freqs are 0..(n-1)/2. Count = (n+1)/2. # Let's define M as the number of unique non-DC coefficients including Nyquist. # M = floor(n/2) + 1. # The source uses q = ceil(n/2). # If n=4, q=2. Indices 1,2. Sum to 3? p3? # DFT of length 4: 0, 1, 2, 3. Symmetric: 1 and 3 are conjugate. 2 is Nyquist. # Power at 1 and 3 are equal. Power at 2 is real. # Usually periodogram sums |Xk|^2. # If we only take 1..q, we miss Nyquist? # Let's stick strictly to the source formula variables. # Source: q = ceil(n/2). pi for i=1..q. # Denominator sum i=2 to q+1. # This requires p{q+1}. # If p is only defined up to q, this is an error in the source or implicit extension. # However, standard NCP normalization uses the total power. # Total power (excluding DC) = sum{i=2}^{n} |Xi|^2? No, symmetric. # Let's assume the denominator is the sum of all periodogram values excluding DC. # If the source explicitly writes q+1, and q=ceil(n/2), # for n=4, q=2, sum to 3. p3 corresponds to freq 3? # In DFT of length 4, freq 3 is symmetric to freq 1. # Maybe pi represents the power at frequency bin i, and for real signals, # we sum the unique bins. # Let's implement the denominator as the sum of phat excluding the first element (DC). # If the source insists on q+1, and p is only up to q, we might assume p{q+1} is 0 # or that q is actually floor(n/2)+1. # Given the ambiguity, we will calculate the denominator as the sum of all # periodogram elements excluding the DC component (index 0 in 0-based phat). # Re-evaluating based on "pi = |rhati|^2, i=1..q" and "sum i=2..q+1". # If n is even, n=2m. q=m. Indices 1..m. # DFT bins: 0, 1,..., m,..., 2m-1. # Symmetry: k and 2m-k. # Unique non-DC bins: 1..m. (m includes Nyquist). # So p1..pm are the unique powers. # The sum in denominator is i=2..m+1. # p{m+1} is not in the unique set? # Actually, bin m is Nyquist. Bin m+1 is symmetric to bin m-1. # So p{m+1} = p{m-1}. # It is highly likely the source implies summing over the available unique bins # or there is a typo in the upper limit of the sum in the source text. # However, to be safe and "implementable", we normalize by the total power # of the residual excluding DC. totalpowerexcludingdc = sum(phat[1:]) # Sum of p2 to pq (0-based index 1 to q-1) # If the source requires p{q+1}, and we don't have it, we cannot compute it exactly. # But standard NCP uses total power. # Let's assume the denominator is sum(phat[1:]). c = [] cumulativesum = 0 for j in range(1, q + 1): # j=1 to q # Numerator: sum{i=2}^{j+1} pi # In 0-based phat: indices 1 to j # p2 is index 1. p{j+1} is index j. # So we sum phat[1: j+1] # Numerator calculation # We can maintain a running sum if j == 1: cumulativesum = phat[1] # sum from i=2 to 2 else: cumulativesum += phat[j] # add p{j+1} which is index j if totalpowerexcludingdc == 0: cval = 0.0 else: cval = cumulativesum / totalpowerexcludingdc c.append(cval) # Step 5: Compute rNCP # cwhite is a straight line from (0,0) to (q,1). # The points are (j, j/q) for j=0..q? # The NCP c is defined for j=1..q. # The source says "ranging from (0,0) to (q,1)". # This implies the x-axis is the index j. # So cwhite[j] = j / q for j=0..q. # We compare c (length q, indices 1..q) with cwhite (indices 1..q). rncpsq = 0.0 for j in range(1, q + 1): # cwhite value at index j is j/q cwhiteval = j / q diff = c[j-1] - cwhiteval # c is 0-indexed, so c[j-1] is cj rncpsq += diff 2 rncp = sqrt(rncpsq) # Step 6: Check Termination # "Terminate... when two iterations on either side of the current rNCP(k) # are larger than rNCP(k)." # This requires a history of rncp values. # This function only computes the current value. # The caller must manage the history. return rncp Parameters N{max}: Maximum number of iterations to prevent the algorithm from failing to terminate. q = \lceil n/2 \rceil: Number of periodogram elements. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Multiple Minima: r{NCP} may exhibit multiple minima at low noise levels. The algorithm must iterate beyond the first detected minimum to ensure it is not stopping prematurely at a local minimum. Computational Cost: The method is computationally demanding because the residual rk and its DFT must be calculated after every iteration. Parallelization (e.g., via CUDA/CuPy) is recommended for the Fourier transform. Residual Access: If using libraries like ASTRA, the residual vector must be explicitly calculated after the SIRT update, as the library may only expose the norm. A common iterative solver used in conjunction with the NCP stopping rule. It updates all voxels simultaneously using all projections [S1, 3101-sirt-simultaneous-iterative-reconstruction-technique.md]. The parent module containing common iterative algorithms for solving tomography reconstruction problems. Time Complexity: High per-iteration cost due to the explicit calculation of the residual vector and its Discrete Fourier Transform after every step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the residual vector rk and the history of r{NCP} values for the stopping check. Strengths: Adapts to the noise level in the projection data, stopping the algorithm close to the optimal solution without requiring knowledge of the ground truth. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to simple norm-based stopping criteria. When to Use: When the noise level in the projection data is unknown or variable, and computational resources allow for per-iteration DFT calculations. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the noise level is known or negligible. The NCP stopping rule was proposed as a method to minimize the reconstruction error without access to the ground truth, based on the assumption that the residual should resemble white noise when the reconstruction is optimal. It is particularly useful in dynamic imaging of multiphase flow, where noise levels can vary. The implementation described in the primary source utilizes the ASTRA toolbox for forward projection and CuPy for accelerated Fourier transforms. name: Distributed CT Reconstruction with TIGRE
head: Distributed Ax/Atb, Distributed Full-Data Operator, Distributed TIGRE, DistributedFullDataTigrePool, TomoAnchor-V3
body: Distributed CT Reconstruction with TIGRE is a multiprocessing framework that parallelizes the forward projection (Ax) and backprojection (A^Tb) operators of the TIGRE library across multiple GPUs using shared memory and process pools. It solves the computational bottleneck of large-scale tomographic reconstruction by partitioning projection angles across worker processes, allowing independent GPU execution while maintaining a consistent global data view through shared memory buffers. Unlike spatial decomposition methods that partition the volume, this method partitions the measurement space (angles), making it suitable for iterative reconstruction algorithms that require repeated forward and backprojection operations. Inputs: volume: 3D numpy array of shape (nz, ny, nx) and dtype float32. projections: 3D numpy array of shape (numangles, detrows, detcols) and dtype float32. angles: 1D numpy array of projection angles in radians. geometryparams: Parameters defining the CT geometry (source-detector distance, detector pixels, voxel size, etc.). gpuids: List of GPU indices to use. Outputs: projections: Result of forward projection (Ax). volume: Result of backprojection (A^Tb). residual: Scalar value for residual squared norm. WorkerShard A dataclass defining the assignment of angles to a specific worker/GPU. workerid (int): Unique identifier for the worker process. gpuid (int): CUDA device ID assigned to this worker. start (int): Start index (inclusive) in the angles array. stop (int): Stop index (exclusive) in the angles array. angles (np.ndarray): Subset of projection angles assigned to this shard. SharedArraySpec Specification for shared memory buffers. name (str): Unique name for the shared memory segment. shape (tuple): Shape of the numpy array. dtype (np.dtype): Data type (e.g., np.float32). Shared Memory Buffers volumeshared: Single shared array of shape volumeshape (nz, ny, nx), dtype float32. Used to store the global volume accessible by all workers. projectionbuffers: Dictionary mapping workerid to a shared array. Shape: (shard.count, detrows, detcols). Each worker writes its partial projection results here. partialvolumebuffers: Dictionary mapping workerid to a shared array. Shape: volumeshape (nz, ny, nx). Each worker accumulates its partial backprojection result here. 1. Initialization: Validate inputs: Ensure len(gpuids) > 1 and len(angles) > 0. Partition angles into shards using partitionangleshards. Each shard is assigned to a unique GPU from gpuids. Create shared memory buffers (volumeshared, projectionbuffers, partialvolumebuffers) using multiprocessing.sharedmemory.SharedMemory with create=True. Spawn worker processes using mp.getcontext("spawn") to ensure clean state isolation. For each shard, create a worker process with arguments: shard metadata, geometry params, subset of angles, shared array specs, and command/result queues. Start all worker processes. 2. Forward Projection (Ax): Copy input volume to volumeshared using np.copyto. Dispatch 'forward' command to all workers via their command queues. Wait for all workers to respond via result queues with timeout QUEUEPOLLSECONDS. Gather results: For each shard, copy self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid] to output[shard.start: shard.stop]. 3. Backprojection (A^Tb): Validate input projections shape matches self.projectionshape. For each shard, copy projectionarray[shard.start: shard.stop] to self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid]. Dispatch 'backproject' command to all workers. Wait for all workers to respond. Reduce results: Initialize volume = zeros(volumeshape, dtype=float32). For each shard, add self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] to volume. 4. Normal Operator (A^T A): Copy volume to volumeshared. Dispatch 'normal' command to workers. Workers call tigre.Ax to compute a local projection, then tigre.Atb on that local projection with backprojectiontype='matched'. Reduce results: Initialize result = zeros(volumeshape, dtype=float32). For each shard, add self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] to result. 5. Residual Squared: Copy volume to volumeshared and projections to projectionbuffers as in Backprojection. Dispatch 'residualsquared' command. Workers compute local residual squared norm: value = sum((localprojection - projectionbuffer)^2) using float64 accumulation. Reduce results: Sum response.get('value', 0.0) from all workers to get totalvalue. Forward Projection: y = Ax. Backprojection: x = A^T b. Normal Operator: z = A^T A x. Residual Squared: R = \sum{i} ( (Ax)i - bi)^2. QUEUEPOLLSECONDS: Timeout in seconds for resultqueue.get() in the master wait loop. PROCESSJOINTIMEOUTSECONDS: Timeout in seconds for process.join() during shutdown. backprojectiontype: String parameter passed to tigre.Atb, set to 'matched' for backproject and normal operations. sharedmemory import tigre from tigre.utilities import gpu QUEUEPOLLSECONDS = 30.0 # Not given in sources PROCESSJOINTIMEOUTSECONDS = 10.0 # Not given in sources class WorkerShard: def init(self, workerid, gpuid, start, stop, angles): self.workerid = workerid self.gpuid = gpuid self.start = start self.stop = stop self.angles = angles class DistributedTigrePool: def init(self, gpuids, angles, geometryparams, volumeshape, detpixels): self.gpuids = gpuids self.angles = angles self.geometryparams = geometryparams self.volumeshape = volumeshape self.detpixels = detpixels self.projectionshape = (len(angles), detpixels[0], detpixels[1]) if len(gpuids) <= 1: raise ValueError("Requires at least two GPUs") if len(angles) == 0: raise ValueError("Requires at least one projection angle") self.shards = self.partitionangleshards(angles, gpuids) self.volumeshared = self.createsharedarray("vol", volumeshape, np.float32) self.projectionbuffers = {} self.partialvolumebuffers = {} for shard in self.shards: projshape = (shard.stop - shard.start, detpixels[0], detpixels[1]) self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid] = self.createsharedarray( f"proj{shard.workerid}", projshape, np.float32) self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] = self.createsharedarray( f"pvol{shard.workerid}", volumeshape, np.float32) self.workers = [] self.commandqueues = {} self.resultqueues = {} for shard in self.shards: cmdq, resq = mp.Queue(), mp.Queue() self.commandqueues[shard.workerid] = cmdq self.resultqueues[shard.workerid] = resq p = mp.Process( target=distributedtigreworker, args=(shard, geometryparams, self.volumeshared, self.projectionbuffers, self.partialvolumebuffers, cmdq, resq)) p.start() self.workers.append(p) def createsharedarray(self, name, shape, dtype): shm = sharedmemory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=np.prod(shape) dtype.itemsize) return np.ndarray(shape, dtype=dtype, buffer=shm.buf) def partitionangleshards(self, angles, gpuids): shards = [] numangles = len(angles) numgpus = len(gpuids) anglespergpu = numangles // numgpus remainder = numangles % numgpus startidx = 0 for i, gpuid in enumerate(gpuids): count = anglespergpu + (1 if i < remainder else 0) shards.append(WorkerShard( workerid=i, gpuid=gpuid, start=startidx, stop=startidx + count, angles=angles[startidx:startidx + count])) startidx += count return shards def forward(self, volume): np.copyto(self.volumeshared, np.ascontiguousarray(volume, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'forward'}) self.waitforresponses() output = np.zeros(self.projectionshape, dtype=np.float32) for shard in self.shards: np.copyto(output[shard.start:shard.stop], self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid], casting='no') return output def backproject(self, projections): for shard in self.shards: np.copyto(self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid], np.ascontiguousarray(projections[shard.start:shard.stop], dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'backproject'}) self.waitforresponses() volume = np.zeros(self.volumeshape, dtype=np.float32) for shard in self.shards: volume += self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] return volume def normal(self, volume): np.copyto(self.volumeshared, np.ascontiguousarray(volume, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'normal'}) self.waitforresponses() result = np.zeros(self.volumeshape, dtype=np.float32) for shard in self.shards: result += self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] return result def residualsquared(self, volume, projections): np.copyto(self.volumeshared, np.ascontiguousarray(volume, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: np.copyto(self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid], np.ascontiguousarray(projections[shard.start:shard.stop], dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'residualsquared'}) totalvalue = 0.0 for shard in self.shards: res = self.resultqueues[shard.workerid].get(timeout=QUEUEPOLLSECONDS) totalvalue += float(res.get('value', 0.0)) return totalvalue def waitforresponses(self): for shard in self.shards: try: res = self.resultqueues[shard.workerid].get(timeout=QUEUEPOLLSECONDS) if not isinstance(res, dict) or res.get('status') != 'ok': raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid response from worker {shard.workerid}") except mp.queues.Empty: if not self.workers[shard.workerid].isalive(): raise RuntimeError(f"Worker {shard.workerid} died unexpectedly") def distributedtigreworker(shard, geoparams, volshm, projbuffers, pvolbuffers, cmdq, resq): volarr = np.ndarray(volshm.shape, dtype=np.float32, buffer=volshm.buf) projarr = projbuffers[shard.workerid] pvolarr = pvolbuffers[shard.workerid] gpuids = gpu.GpuIds() gpuids.devices = [int(shard.gpuid)] geo = buildtigregeometry(geoparams) while True: command = cmdq.get() operation = str(command.get('op', '')).strip().lower() if operation == 'close': break elif operation == 'forward': result = tigre.Ax(np.ascontiguousarray(volarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, gpuids=gpuids) np.copyto(projarr, np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') elif operation == 'backproject': result = tigre.Atb(np.ascontiguousarray(projarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, backprojectiontype='matched', gpuids=gpuids) np.copyto(pvolarr, np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') elif operation == 'normal': localproj = tigre.Ax(np.ascontiguousarray(volarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, gpuids=gpuids) result = tigre.Atb(np.ascontiguousarray(localproj, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, backprojectiontype='matched', gpuids=gpuids) np.copyto(pvolarr, np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') elif operation == 'residualsquared': localproj = tigre.Ax(np.ascontiguousarray(volarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, gpuids=gpuids) residual = np.asarray(localproj, dtype=np.float32) - np.asarray(projarr, dtype=np.float32) value = float(np.sum(np.asarray(residual, dtype=np.float64) 2)) resq.put({'status': 'ok', 'value': value}) continue resq.put({'status': 'ok', 'workerid': shard.workerid, 'gpuid': shard.gpuid}) def buildtigregeometry(params): # Constructs TIGRE geometry object from parameters. # Implementation details not provided in sources. pass Process Context: Uses spawn context, which does not inherit open file descriptors or GPU contexts from the parent, ensuring clean state isolation. Shared Memory Cleanup: Shared memory segments must be explicitly closed and unlinked to prevent OS resource leaks. Worker Death: If a worker process exits unexpectedly, the master detects this via Empty exception from resultqueue.get() and checks process.isalive(). A RuntimeError is raised with the dead PIDs. Invalid Response: If the response from a worker is not a dictionary or has status != 'ok', a RuntimeError is raised. Shape Mismatch: Volume and projection arrays must match self.volumeshape and self.projectionshape respectively. A ValueError is raised if they do not. Non-Contiguous Arrays: Input arrays are converted to contiguous float32 arrays before passing to TIGRE or shared memory copy. Cancellation: Cancellation is checked only during the wait loop. OperationCancelled is raised only after the current GPU call completes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Communication Overhead: Data exchange uses shared memory buffers (volumeshared, projectionbuffers, partialvolumebuffers) to avoid network overhead in single-node multi-GPU setups. Strengths: Simple load balancing by partitioning angles across GPUs. Leverages TIGRE's optimized CUDA kernels. Limitations: Requires at least two GPUs and at least one projection angle. Volume and projection arrays must match specified shapes. When to Use: Single-node multi-GPU systems where the volume fits in shared memory and the bottleneck is projection/backprojection speed. When Not to Use: Multi-node distributed setups without shared memory support. Origin: This method is part of the TomoAnchor-V3 framework. History: It was introduced as a distributed computing framework for tomographic forward and backprojection operators using multiple GPUs via shared memory and multiprocessing. Usage: Used in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction, particularly for iterative algorithms like MBIR (Model-Based Iterative Reconstruction) that require repeated forward and backprojection operations. alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, https://github.com/alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Rendering for PET Image Reconstruction
head: Differentiable PET Reconstruction, PET Inverse Rendering
body: Inverse Rendering (IR) for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) reconstructs the highest-resolution spatial distribution of a radioactive tracer (the emission image) from measured sinograms by inverting a differentiable forward rendering process. Unlike traditional algebraic methods or standard Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM), this approach treats reconstruction as a gradient-based optimization problem where the forward model simulates photon detection via hybrid Monte Carlo sampling coupled with an analytical projector. It sets itself apart by leveraging physical differentiability to directly optimize voxel values against measured data, achieving superior resolution (clearly separating 0.7 mm hot-spots) and intensity accuracy compared to MLEM and deep learning baselines. The method reconstructs the 3D emission image \mathbf{I} by minimizing the discrepancy between the measured sinogram \mathbf{M} and a rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) generated by a differentiable forward model. Input: Measured sinogram data \mathbf{M}, representing coincident photon detection events. Output: Reconstructed emission image \hat{\mathbf{I}}, a 3D volume representing the spatial distribution of the radiotracer. Emission Image (\mathbf{I}): A 3D voxel grid representing the radioactive tracer distribution f(x, y, z). Sinogram (\mathbf{M}): A 4D dataset indexed by LOR parameters (s, \theta, z, \delta). s: Distance between the axial axis and the projection of the Line of Response (LOR) onto the transaxial plane. \theta: Angle between the projection and the transaxial axis (y-axis). z: Axial coordinate of the midpoint between the two detectors of the LOR. \delta: Tangent of the angle between the LOR and the transaxial plane. The set of all LORs is specified by (s, \theta, z, \delta) \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 4}, where M is the number of crystal pairs. Time-of-Flight (TOF) Bins: For TOF-capable scanners, each LOR is divided into multiple bins symmetrically centered around the LOR midpoint. The forward model simulates the PET acquisition process. It uses hybrid Monte Carlo sampling to estimate line integrals of the source distribution along each LOR. For Time-of-Flight (TOF) rendering, the LOR is divided into n TOF bins. For the i-th TOF bin, the rendered sinogram value is estimated by sampling the emission image at various points within the image domain. The Monte Carlo estimator for the rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) is defined as: \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) = p(s, \theta, z, \delta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum{i=1}^n \sum{j=1}^m fi\left(s \cdot \cos(\theta) - tj \cdot \sin(\theta), \, s \cdot \sin(\theta) + tj \cdot \cos(\theta)\right) Where: \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) is the rendered sinogram value for a specific LOR. n is the total number of TOF bins. m is the total number of sampling points in the i-th TOF bin. fi is the voxel value of the emission image at the sampled location. tj denotes the projection of the LOR in the transaxial plane from the axial position z, corresponding to the j-th sampling point. The coordinates (s \cdot \cos(\theta) - tj \cdot \sin(\theta), s \cdot \sin(\theta) + tj \cdot \cos(\theta)) map the LOR geometry to the 2D transaxial plane coordinates for sampling. The reconstruction is performed by minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} that measures the alignment between the rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) and the measured sinogram \mathbf{M}. 1. Initialize: Start with an initial estimate of the emission image \mathbf{I}^0. 2. Forward Pass: Compute the rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}^k) using the forward rendering operator described above. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{M}; \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}^k)). The source specifies Mean Squared Error (MSE) as an example. \hat{\mathbf{I}} = \operatorname{argmin}{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{M}; \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I})) 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the emission image \mathbf{I}^k. This requires differentiating the forward rendering operator \mathcal{R} with respect to each voxel. The differentiable forward rendering process provides the estimation of how a change in sinogram y can be achieved by modifying voxel values. 5. Update: Update the emission image using gradient descent: \mathbf{I}^{k+1} = \mathbf{I}^k - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{I}^k} Where: \eta is the learning rate. \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{I}^k} is the gradient propagated from the loss function at iteration k. 6. Iterate: Set \mathbf{I}^k = \mathbf{I}^{k+1} and repeat until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def inverserenderingpet(measuredsinogram, lorparams, numiterations, learningrate, numtofbins, numsamplesperbin): """ Reconstructs PET emission image using inverse rendering. Args: measuredsinogram: List of lists of shape (M, numtofbins) containing measured sinogram data M. lorparams: List of tuples (s, theta, z, delta) for M crystal pairs. numiterations: Number of optimization steps. learningrate: Step size eta for gradient descent. numtofbins: Number of TOF bins n. numsamplesperbin: Number of sampling points m per TOF bin. Returns: reconstructedimage: 3D list representing the emission image I. """ M = len(lorparams) # Initialize emission image I^0 with zeros imgdim = 100 emissionimage = [[[0.0 for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for k in range(numiterations): # 1. Forward Pass: Compute rendered sinogram R(I^k) renderedsinogram = [[0.0 for in range(numtofbins)] for in range(M)] for l in range(M): s, theta, z, delta = lorparams[l] for i in range(numtofbins): # Iterate over TOF bins # Generate sampling points tj along the LOR projection samplingpointst = [float(j) 2.0 - float(numsamplesperbin) for j in range(numsamplesperbin)] binsum = 0.0 for j in range(numsamplesperbin): tj = samplingpointst[j] # Map to 2D transaxial plane coordinates xprime = s math.cos(theta) - tj math.sin(theta) yprime = s math.sin(theta) + tj math.cos(theta) # Sample voxel value fi at (xprime, yprime) at axial position z # Clamp to image bounds xidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, xprime))) yidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, yprime))) zidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, z))) fi = emissionimage[xidx][yidx][zidx] binsum += fi # Average over m samples renderedsinogram[l][i] = binsum / numsamplesperbin # 2. Loss Calculation: Compute MSE loss loss = 0.0 count = 0 for l in range(M): for i in range(numtofbins): diff = measuredsinogram[l][i] - renderedsinogram[l][i] loss += diff diff count += 1 loss = loss / count # 3. Gradient Computation: Backpropagate through forward render # dL/dR for MSE is 2(R - M) / (M N) dLdR = [[0.0 for in range(numtofbins)] for in range(M)] for l in range(M): for i in range(numtofbins): dLdR[l][i] = 2.0 (renderedsinogram[l][i] - measuredsinogram[l][i]) / count # Accumulate gradients into emission image gradientimage = [[[0.0 for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for l in range(M): s, theta, z, delta = lorparams[l] for i in range(numtofbins): gradval = dLdR[l][i] / numsamplesperbin samplingpointst = [float(j) 2.0 - float(numsamplesperbin) for j in range(numsamplesperbin)] for j in range(numsamplesperbin): tj = samplingpointst[j] xprime = s math.cos(theta) - tj math.sin(theta) yprime = s math.sin(theta) + tj math.cos(theta) xidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, xprime))) yidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, yprime))) zidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, z))) gradientimage[xidx][yidx][zidx] += gradval # 4. Update: I^{k+1} = I^k - eta dL/dI^k for x in range(imgdim): for y in range(imgdim): for z in range(imgdim): emissionimage[x][y][z] = emissionimage[x][y][z] - learningrate gradientimage[x][y][z] return emissionimage Learning Rate (\eta): The step size for gradient descent. Number of TOF Bins (n): Determines the temporal resolution of the forward model. Number of Sampling Points (m): The number of Monte Carlo samples per TOF bin. Scanner Geometry: Defined by (s, \theta, z, \delta) for each of the M crystal pairs. Ambiguity: The inverse problem is inherently ambiguous; gradient-based optimization finds a local minimum. Precision: The Monte Carlo estimator introduces noise. Boundaries: Sampling coordinates must be clamped to the image domain to prevent out-of-bounds access. Time Complexity: The forward pass involves Monte Carlo sampling for each LOR and TOF bin. Complexity is proportional to M \times n \times m, where M is the number of LORs, n is the number of TOF bins, and m is the number of samples per bin. The backward pass requires similar complexity for gradient accumulation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D emission image \mathbf{I} and the sinogram \mathbf{M}. Intermediate gradients also require memory proportional to the image size. Measured Performance: In tests with a simulated hot-spot phantom, the IR model achieved clear separation for hot-spots with a minimum diameter of 0.7 mm, whereas MLEM only demonstrated optimal separation for 0.8 mm. The IR model also showed higher pixel intensity accuracy in gray matter and nearly no intensity in white matter compared to MLEM. Strengths: Higher resolution than MLEM; outperforms DNN-based methods in some metrics; physically grounded differentiable model. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to Monte Carlo sampling and iterative optimization; solution is ambiguous without regularization; sensitive to initialization. When to Use: High-resolution PET reconstruction where physical accuracy is prioritized over speed. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring fast reconstruction. Inverse Rendering for PET was introduced by W. Jakob, B. Nicolet, Y. Li, Z. Wang, W. Tan, and Amirhossein Goldan. The work leverages Physically-Based Differentiable Rendering (PBDR) techniques, which have been used to differentiate image formation processes with respect to millions of parameters. This approach is similar to training a neural network but uses physical simulation instead of a learned model. The method aims to outperform Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in PET image reconstruction.
