name: Deep Learning and Neural Representations
body: This family addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by replacing or augmenting traditional discrete voxel grids with neural networks, leveraging their expressive power to recover 3D density fields from sparse, noisy, or limited-angle projections. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods and Iterative Solvers by optimizing continuous function parameters (network weights) rather than discrete voxel values, enabling high-resolution reconstruction from minimal data and simultaneous self-calibration of geometric parameters. See Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering for the shared differentiable forward projection, adjoint back-projection, and iterative optimization framework. This family encompasses methods that utilize deep neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction, mapping measured projection data (sinograms) directly or iteratively to a 3D volume estimate [8282-deep-learning-and-neural-architectures.md]. Unlike classical analytical methods (e.g., Filtered Back-Projection) or iterative algebraic techniques, these methods leverage the expressive power of neural architectures to regularize the ill-posed nature of the inverse Radon transform, particularly in sparse-view or noisy regimes [8282-deep-learning-and-neural-architectures.md]. They are distinguished from Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations by their explicit focus on tomographic geometry (Radon transforms) and often their ability to produce explicit voxel-based or parametric density volumes suitable for quantitative analysis, rather than just view-dependent rendering [8282-deep-learning-and-neural-architectures.md]. This family applies Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) to tomographic reconstruction, replacing discrete voxel grids with continuous functions parameterized by neural networks. It solves the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering 3D density fields from sparse, noisy, or limited-angle X-ray projections by leveraging the differentiability of the rendering pipeline. Unlike traditional discrete methods, these approaches optimize network weights directly, allowing for high-resolution reconstruction from minimal data and enabling simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters. Definition: HybridCT is a computationally efficient method for practical cloud tomography that combines deep learning and linear algebra to reconstruct cloud extinction volumes from multi-angle imaging observations. It combines a retrieval emulator with a reconstruction stage: (1) the retrieval is emulated using a deep learning U-Net architecture which is trained to map multi-angle radiance measurements into optical thickness values. (2) the reconstruction stage takes these multi-angle optical thickness values as input and uses SART (Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique) to computationally reconstruct the cloud extinction volume. Steps: 1. Emulate retrieval using a deep learning U-Net architecture trained to map multi-angle radiance measurements into optical thickness values. 2. Take the multi-angle optical thickness values as input and use SART to computationally reconstruct the cloud extinction volume. Parameters: The method is demonstrated using synthetic multi-angle images representing the viewing angle geometry of the Multi-angle Imaging Spectroradiometer (MISR) onboard the Terra spacecraft at its red channel wavelength of 670 nm. Usage: Designed for practical cloud tomography using synthetic cloud fields from Large Eddy Simulations and synthetic multi-angle radiance fields rendered using the 3D Monte Carlo radiative transfer model MYSTIC and the libRadtran library. The method is used in practical cloud tomography to reconstruct cloud extinction volumes from multi-angle imaging observations. Origin and history: Not given in the sources. lforster/hybridCT, https://github.com/lforster/hybridCT, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Deep Learning and Neural Architectures
body: This family encompasses methods that utilize deep neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction, mapping measured projection data (sinograms) directly or iteratively to a 3D volume estimate. It distinguishes itself from Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations by its explicit focus on tomographic geometry (Radon transforms) and its ability to produce explicit voxel-based or parametric density volumes suitable for quantitative analysis, rather than just view-dependent rendering. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem minimizes a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) where \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include forward projection to compute line integrals of density, backward projection to distribute detector error into the 3D volume, and an optimization loop to update volume parameters. Uses a neural network as an implicit regularizer, optimizing both network weights and a latent variable against measured sinogram data. It distinguishes itself by decoupling the latent variable update from network weight optimization, acting as a dynamic prior without external training data. Choose when external training data is unavailable. Adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting to sparse-view X-ray imaging by rectifying an integration bias inherent in standard splatting. It replaces the appearance-based kernel with a radiative Gaussian kernel parameterized by density, position, and covariance, and derives new X-ray rendering functions to ensure accurate volume retrieval. Choose when efficient differentiable rasterization and direct 3D density extraction are required. An end-to-end differentiable deep learning architecture that directly maps a noisy sinogram into a denoised 3D reconstruction, combining reconstruction and denoising steps to mitigate noise amplification caused by the ill-conditioning of the Radon transform. It differs from traditional Filtered Back-Projection by replacing fixed linear filtration with a trainable neural network, and from pure post-processing methods by learning acquisition geometry implicitly through the differentiable back-projection operator. Choose when a generalizable mapping from sinogram to volume is needed. Solves large-scale inverse problems by decomposing the non-local, space-variant integral transform into a sequence of simpler, local hierarchical steps. It avoids dense connectivity by introducing virtual intermediate data representations (partial line integrals) and explicitly constructs a homotopy-like continuum of data domains from line integrals to voxels. Choose when avoiding parameter explosion in fully connected networks is critical. Applies self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in volumetric data, addressing the local receptive field limitations of convolutions in volume rendering. It enables direct feature aggregation, super-resolution, and denoising across spatial or ray-based token sequences without relying solely on iterative tomographic inversion or per-scene optimization. Choose when capturing long-range dependencies is necessary. Definition: A generator network G(r, z) that maps a sinogram r and a latent vector z to a reconstructed image, used for optimization in the inverse problem. Layout: The input sinogram r passes through an Embedding Conv 2D layer and U-Net Blocks. The latent vector z is processed by a 'Modified Block' and integrated into the network. The architecture is analogous to the end-to-end reconstruction model but includes this latent injection mechanism. Definition: A supervised learning approach to map MRI intensities to acoustic impedance values Z(x, y, z) using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) fitted to paired data of MRI intensities and reference impedance values from literature. Parameter: Reference impedance values from literature [4,5,6,14] are used for supervised training. Pitfall: MRI intensities do not correspond directly to physical quantities such as density or acoustic impedance; they reflect a complex combination of tissue-specific properties (water content, fat concentration, relaxation times) modulated by the acquisition sequence. This makes impedance reconstruction from MRI fundamentally ill-posed. Not given in the sources. name: Deep Image Prior Reconstruction
head: DIP Reconstruction, DRP Denoising
body: Deep Image Prior Reconstruction is an iterative tomographic reconstruction method that uses a neural network as an implicit regularizer to optimize an intermediate latent variable and network weights against measured sinogram data. It distinguishes itself from supervised neural architectures by decoupling the latent variable update from the network weight optimization, allowing the network architecture itself to act as a dynamic prior without external training data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse or noisy sinogram p (measured projection data). Output: A reconstructed 3D volume estimate x. Data Structures: The method maintains the following state variables: 1. PriorModel: A neural network that maps a latent tensor to the volume space. 2. Latent Variable z: An intermediate tensor updated via the data consistency term. 3. Projector: An object implementing the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. 4. Optimizer: An Adam optimizer instance managing the gradients of the PriorModel parameters. 5. Loss: An MSE loss function. Algorithm Steps: The reconstruction proceeds in an alternating optimization loop consisting of outer epochs and inner steps. 1. Initialization: Initialize the PriorModel if not provided and move it to the device. Initialize the Adam optimizer with the PriorModel's parameters and a learning rate lr. Compute an initial estimate of the volume by applying Filtered Back Projection (FBP) to the sinogram p and detaching it from the computation graph: z = \text{FBP}(p).\text{detach}(). Set hyperparameters: number of outer epochs E, number of inner steps K, and latent update step size \beta. 2. Outer Loop (Epochs): For each epoch from 0 to E-1: Compute the current volume estimate: x = \text{PriorModel}(z). Compute the data consistency residual: \delta = \text{projector.backward}(p - \text{projector.forward}(x)). Update the latent variable: z = x + \beta \cdot \delta. 3. Inner Loop (Network Weight Optimization): For each inner step from 0 to K-1: Compute the forward projection of the current volume estimate: \hat{p} = \text{projector.forward}(\text{PriorModel}(z)). Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the predicted projections and the measured sinogram: \mathcal{L} = \text{MSE}(\hat{p}, p). Perform backpropagation to compute gradients with respect to the PriorModel parameters. Perform one Adam optimizer step to update the parameters. 4. Final Output: After completing all epochs, the final reconstruction is obtained by passing the final latent variable z through the prior network: x{\text{final}} = \text{PriorModel}(z). Parameters: E (epochs): Number of outer optimization epochs. Default: 250. K (innersteps): Number of Adam optimization steps per outer epoch. Default: 50. \beta (beta/stepsize): Step size for the latent variable update. Default: 0.25. lr: Learning rate for the Adam optimizer. Default not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The FBP initialization must be detached from the computation graph to prevent gradients from flowing through it during the latent update. Boundaries: The projector must handle rays passing outside the volume bounds correctly, typically by contributing zero to the integral. Degenerate Input: If the sinogram p is extremely sparse or noisy, the FBP initialization may be poor, potentially leading to slow convergence or local minima. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim import numpy as np def deepimagepriorreconstruction(sinogramp, projector, priormodel=None, epochs=250, innersteps=50, beta=0.25, lr=0.01): """ Reconstructs a volume from sinogram data using Deep Image Prior. Args: sinogramp: Tensor of measured projections. projector: Object with methods forward(x) and backward(residual). priormodel: Neural network mapping latent z to volume x. If None, initialized. epochs: Number of outer epochs. innersteps: Number of inner Adam steps per epoch. beta: Step size for latent variable update. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: Reconstructed volume tensor. """ # Standard U-Net initialization for volumetric prior if priormodel is None: priormodel = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(1, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(64, 1, 3, padding=1)) priormodel.train() optimizer = optim.Adam(priormodel.parameters(), lr=lr) # Standard FBP algorithm: filter sinograms and back-project into 3D volume z = fbp(sinogramp).detach() lossfn = nn.MSELoss() for in range(epochs): # Outer Loop: Update Latent Variable z x = priormodel(z) residual = sinogramp - projector.forward(x) delta = projector.backward(residual) z = x + beta delta # Inner Loop: Optimize PriorModel weights for in range(innersteps): phat = projector.forward(priormodel(z)) loss = lossfn(phat, sinogramp) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Final reconstruction output = priormodel(z) return output def fbp(sinogram): # Standard FBP: apply ramp filter in frequency domain, then back-project # sinogram shape: [numprojections, numdetectors] # Returns 3D volume tensor numproj, numdet = sinogram.shape volume = torch.zeros((1, numdet, numdet, numdet), device=sinogram.device) for i in range(numproj): # Simple back-projection for demonstration; production FBP applies ramp filter angle = i np.pi / numproj volume[0,:,:,:] += sinogram[i,:] return volume / numproj This variant, proposed by Xu et al., proposes an unsupervised neural network for image reconstruction of gradient-domain volumetric photon density estimation, specifically for volumetric photon mapping. It utilizes a variant of GradNet with an encoded shift connection and a separated auxiliary feature branch that includes volume-based auxiliary features such as transmittance and photon density. The network is designed to smooth images at a global scale while preserving high-frequency details on a small scale. It produces higher-quality results than previous works such as L1, L2, or standard GradNet. However, it cannot reconstruct images with strong noise and tends to over-blur some features. While originally developed for volumetric photon mapping, the method is noted as straightforward to extend to other tasks like beam radiance estimation. Time Complexity: The method is computationally intensive due to the alternating optimization loop. Each epoch involves one forward/backward pass for the latent update and K forward/backward passes for the network weight update. The total number of forward projections per epoch is K+1. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the PriorModel parameters, the latent variable z, and the intermediate tensors during backpropagation. Measured Performance: Specific quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are not provided in the sources for general scenes. Strengths: Unsupervised nature (no ground truth needed); effective regularization for sparse-view tomography; leverages the natural image bias of CNNs. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to iterative optimization. Poor FBP initialization can lead to slow convergence or local minima. When to use: Sparse-view or limited-angle tomography where traditional methods produce severe artifacts. When not to use: High-noise scenarios where the prior may over-smooth or fail to converge. Deep Image Prior Reconstruction was introduced as an application of the Deep Image Prior concept to tomographic reconstruction. The DIP concept demonstrates that the architecture of a convolutional neural network itself acts as a powerful prior for natural images. In the context of tomography, the method was adapted to handle the inverse problem of reconstructing 3D volumes from 2D projections. The specific implementation detailed in the sources is associated with the DiffTomo project. The variant for gradient-domain volumetric photon mapping was proposed by Xu et al., building upon earlier work on GradNet. name: R2-Gaussian
head: Rectified Radiative Gaussians
body: R2-Gaussian is a tomographic reconstruction method that adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to sparse-view X-ray imaging by rectifying an integration bias inherent in standard 3DGS splatting. It replaces the appearance-based 3DGS kernel with a radiative Gaussian kernel parameterized by density, position, and covariance, and derives new X-ray rendering functions to ensure accurate volume retrieval. Unlike siblings that use 3DGS only for data augmentation or replace rasterization with simulators, R2-Gaussian maintains efficient differentiable rasterization while enabling direct 3D density volume extraction. Inputs: Sparse-view X-ray projections (sinogram data), camera poses, and initial Gaussian parameters. Outputs: A set of optimized 3D Gaussian parameters representing the density field, and a reconstructed 3D volume. Data Structures: The core representation is a set of N 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: 1. Position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 2. Covariance: \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite) 3. Central Density: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} (isotropic attenuation coefficient) 4. Opacity/Alpha: \alphai \in [0, 1] (standard 3DGS parameter, though the radiative kernel focuses on density) Step 1: Initialization Initialize the Gaussian parameters using the analytical Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) or Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) method. This provides a coarse density estimate to bootstrap the optimization. Step 2: Forward Projection (X-ray Rasterization) For each view, render the projection by mapping 3D Gaussians to 2D Gaussians on the detector plane. 1. Local Affine Approximation: For a ray r(t) = o + td, approximate the 3D Gaussian transformation to the 2D image plane using a local affine approximation. 2. Rectification: Standard 3DGS splatting overlooks a covariance-related scaling factor when projecting a 3D Gaussian to 2D, leading to integration bias. R2-Gaussian derives new X-ray rendering functions that correct this bias. The rendered pixel value I(r) in logarithmic space is computed as the line integral of the density \sigma(r(t)): I(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t)) dt where tn, tf are the near and far bounds of the ray segment covered by the Gaussian. 3. Alpha Compositing: The 2D Gaussians are composited using standard alpha blending to produce the final projection image \hat{p}. Step 3: Loss Computation Compute the photometric loss between the measured X-ray projection p and the rendered projection \hat{p}. The raw pixel value I'(r) follows the Beer-Lambert Law: I'(r) = I0 \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t)) dt\right) Tomography transforms this to logarithmic space for linearization: I(r) = \log I0 - \log I'(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t)) dt \quad \text{} The loss \mathcal{L} is computed as a photometric loss between the rendered and measured log-intensity. Step 4: Optimization Optimize the Gaussian parameters (\mui, \Sigmai, \sigmai) using photometric losses. 1. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered projections: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}}. 2. Back-propagate through the differentiable rasterizer to obtain gradients for Gaussian parameters. 3. Voxel-based Regularization: Use a CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer to extract a 3D volume from the Gaussians during training. This allows the application of voxel-based regularizers to the extracted volume, improving reconstruction quality. Step 5: Volume Extraction After optimization, extract the final 3D density volume using the CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer. Pitfalls: Integration Bias: Using standard 3DGS splatting without rectification leads to inconsistent volumetric properties queried from different views, hampering accurate density retrieval. Affine Approximation Degradation: The local affine approximation used in splatting can degrade quantitative accuracy and complicate nonlinear geometric corrections. A tomography reconstruction setup that uses the volumetrically consistent rasterizer to recover the underlying 3D density field \sigma(x) from 2D images. It requires no changes to the alpha computation process and avoids the affine approximation used in standard 3DGS splatting, providing a more accurate forward rendering model for tomography. Speed: R2-Gaussian is significantly faster than NeRF-based solutions. On the IntraTomo dataset, it achieves 34.56 dB PSNR in 3 minutes (10k iterations) and 35.01 dB in 10 minutes (30k iterations). Comparison: It is 12x faster than the most efficient NeRF-based solution (NAF) and converges to optimal results in 15 minutes, improving PSNR by 0.6 dB compared to SOTA methods. Performance Metrics: IntraTomo: 33.19 dB, 138 min NAF: 33.99 dB, 32 min SAX-NeRF: 34.45 dB, 792 min R2-Gaussian (10k iters): 34.56 dB, 3 min R2-Gaussian (30k iters): 35.01 dB, 10 min Strengths: High efficiency, direct 3D density volume extraction, bias-free training pipeline. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the local affine approximation for splatting, which may degrade quantitative accuracy in complex geometries. R2-Gaussian was introduced in 2024 as the first 3DGS-based framework for sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. It addresses the under-explored potential of 3DGS in volumetric reconstruction tasks like X-ray CT. The method was developed to overcome the limitations of previous approaches that either treated 3DGS solely as data augmentation for traditional algorithms (e.g., FDK) or replaced efficient rasterization with CT simulators. name: End-to-End Reconstruction Model Architecture
head: Simultaneous Reconstruction and Denoising Model, End-to-end differentiable architecture, Sinogram-Based Tomography Reconstruction, g(r) model
body: This method is an end-to-end differentiable deep learning architecture that directly maps a noisy sinogram into a denoised 3D reconstruction, combining the reconstruction and denoising steps to mitigate noise amplification caused by the ill-conditioning of the Radon transform. It differs from traditional Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by replacing the fixed linear filtration with a trainable neural network, and from pure post-processing methods by learning the physics of the acquisition geometry implicitly through the differentiable back-projection operator. Unlike Deep Image Prior Reconstruction which optimizes a static network's weights per instance, this model learns a generalizable mapping from sinogram to volume via joint optimization of its parameters. The model, denoted as g(r), consists of two U-Net instances (g1 and g2) connected by the Radon back-projection operator A^T. The architecture is defined by the composition: g(r) = g2 (A^T g1 (r)) where r is the noisy sensor reading (sinogram), g1 is a U-Net that processes the sinogram, A^T is the transpose of the discrete Radon transform (back-projection), and g2 is a U-Net that processes the back-projected images to produce the final reconstruction. Input: A noisy sinogram r. Output: A denoised 3D reconstruction volume. The model comprises two U-Net architectures, g1 and g2. The specific configuration depends on the model size (XXS, XS, S, S-64, M, L, XL, XXL). U-Net Block Structure: Each U-Net is composed of down-sampling and up-sampling blocks. 1. Down-sampling Block: Consists of a strided convolution followed by a sequence of residual blocks. 2. Up-sampling Block: Takes the output of the previous block. Doubles the resolution using bilinear up-sampling. Concatenates the result with the skip connection from the corresponding down-sampling block at the same resolution. Weights the concatenated channels using channel attention. Shrinks the number of channels via a 1 \times 1 convolution. Processes the result via a sequence of residual blocks. Residual Block Channels: The number of channels in residual blocks is doubled every two strided convolutions. The first block of XXS, XS, and S models uses 32 channels. The first block of S-64, M, L, XL, and XXL models uses 64 channels. Model Sizes and Residual Blocks: The number of residual blocks per U-Net block depends on the resolution and model size. Let N{res}(size, resolution) be the number of residual blocks for a given model size and resolution: | Resolution | XXS | XS | S | M | L | XL | XXL | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 256 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 128 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 64 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 32 | - | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 16 | - | - | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 8 | - | - | - | 2 | 3 | 5 | 9 | | 16 | - | - | - | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 32 | - | - | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 64 | - | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 128 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 256 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 6 | Note: "-" indicates the resolution is not applicable or not used for that model size. Channel Counts for Back-Projection: The smallest end-to-end model (XXS for g1, S-64 for g2) uses 16 channels for the Radon back-projection input. Other end-to-end models use 32 channels. 1. Sinogram Embedding (g1 Input): The input sinogram r passes through an "Embedding Conv 2D" layer. The output passes through a U-Net Block. This sequence is repeated for multiple U-Net Blocks to form the g1 network. The specific number of blocks and their resolutions follow the U-Net architecture defined by the chosen model size (e.g., S-64). The final convolution of g1 reduces the number of channels to the back-projection channel count (16 or 32). 2. Radon Back-Projection: The multi-channel output of g1 is transformed into images using the Radon back-projection operator A^T. Each channel of the output from g1 is treated as a separate sinogram and back-projected into an image. 3. Positional Encoding: The output of A^T (shape (ch, 256, 256)) is concatenated with a 4-dimensional positional embedding (shape (4, 256, 256)) in the first layer of g2. This positional embedding is processed by a "Pos Features Conv 2D" layer to encode pixel coordinates. 4. Reconstruction and Denoising (g2): The concatenated input (back-projected images + positional features) is processed by a sequence of U-Net Blocks to form the g2 network. The architecture of g2 follows the same U-Net structure as g1, but with potentially different dimensions (e.g., S-64). Blocks with multiple inputs (e.g., skip connections) up-sample each input to the largest resolution using bilinear up-sampling, then concatenate all inputs on the channel dimension. The model is trained end-to-end by jointly optimizing the parameters of g1 and g2 to minimize an image reconstruction loss. The differentiability of the Radon back-projection operator A^T allows gradients to flow from the loss in the image space, through g2, through A^T, through g1, and back to the input sinogram r. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ResidualBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, channels): super().init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) def forward(self, x): out = self.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x))) out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out)) return self.relu(out + x) class ChannelAttention(nn.Module): def init(self, channels, reduction=16): super().init() self.fc = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(channels, channels // reduction, bias=False), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Linear(channels // reduction, channels, bias=False), nn.Sigmoid()) def forward(self, x): b, c,, = x.size() y = self.fc(x.mean(dim=[2, 3])).view(b, c, 1, 1) return x y.expandas(x) class UNetBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, inch, outch, numres, down=False): super().init() self.down = down if down: self.conv = nn.Conv2d(inch, outch, 3, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(outch) self.res = nn.Sequential([ResidualBlock(outch) for in range(numres)]) else: self.up = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) self.att = ChannelAttention(outch 2) self.shrink = nn.Conv2d(outch 2, outch, 1, bias=False) self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(outch) self.res = nn.Sequential([ResidualBlock(outch) for in range(numres)]) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) def forward(self, x, skip=None): if self.down: out = self.relu(self.bn(self.conv(x))) out = self.res(out) return out else: out = self.up(x) if skip is not None: out = torch.cat([out, skip], dim=1) out = self.att(out) out = self.relu(self.bn(self.shrink(out))) out = self.res(out) return out class RadonBackProjection(nn.Module): # Sources do not give the exact back-projection kernel implementation. # This operator performs the transpose of the discrete Radon transform. def init(self, imgsize=256): super().init() self.imgsize = imgsize def forward(self, sinogram): # Differentiable back-projection implementation omitted per source note. return sinogram class EndToEndReconstructionModel(nn.Module): def init(self, g1config, g2config, backprojchannels=32, imgsize=256): super().init() self.g1 = self.buildg1(g1config, backprojchannels) self.backproj = RadonBackProjection(imgsize) self.g2 = self.buildg2(g2config, imgsize) def buildg1(self, config, outchannels): self.g1embedding = nn.Conv2d(1, config['initchannels'], kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.g1blocks = nn.ModuleList() # Build blocks based on config resolution and channel progression for i, (inch, outch, numres, down) in enumerate(config['blocks']): self.g1blocks.append(UNetBlock(inch, outch, numres, down)) self.g1finalconv = nn.Conv2d(config['lastchannels'], outchannels, kernelsize=1) return self.g1blocks def buildg2(self, config, imgsize): self.g2posconv = nn.Conv2d(config['initchannels'] + 4, config['initchannels'], kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.g2blocks = nn.ModuleList() for i, (inch, outch, numres, down) in enumerate(config['blocks']): self.g2blocks.append(UNetBlock(inch, outch, numres, down)) return self.g2blocks def forward(self, r): # 1. g1 processing x = self.g1embedding(r) skipconnections = [] for block in self.g1blocks: if block.down: x = block(x) skipconnections.append(x) else: skip = skipconnections.pop() x = block(x, skip) x = self.g1finalconv(x) # 2. Radon Back-Projection images = self.backproj(x) # 3. Positional Embedding posembed = torch.zeros(images.shape[0], 4, images.shape[2], images.shape[3], device=images.device) x = torch.cat([images, posembed], dim=1) # 4. g2 processing x = self.g2posconv(x) skipconnections = [] for block in self.g2blocks: if block.down: x = block(x) skipconnections.append(x) else: skip = skipconnections.pop() x = block(x, skip) return x ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction is a learned post-processing method that maps noisy filtered backprojection (FBP) reconstructions directly to ground truth images, learning to suppress artifacts and noise. It differs from pure post-processing methods by using the physics of the acquisition geometry to guide the denoising and artifact suppression. Unlike Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction, it treats the input as a static noisy image rather than conditioning on the explicit Radon matrix. Time and Memory Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the U-Net architectures and the Radon back-projection operator. The number of parameters is less than existing approaches, leading to faster inference and training times. The exact complexity depends on the model size (XXS to XXL) and the resolution of the input sinogram. Measured Performance: The method produces more accurate reconstructions than existing approaches while using fewer parameters and less time. Strengths: Combines reconstruction and denoising to mitigate noise amplification from the ill-conditioning of the Radon transform. The multi-channel output of g1 allows richer information flow. End-to-end training leverages the differentiability of the back-projection operator. Limitations: Requires training data for supervised learning. The method assumes a specific acquisition geometry for the Radon transform. When to Use: Suitable for tomographic reconstruction tasks where noise reduction is critical and computational efficiency is desired. When Not to Use: Not suitable for unsupervised settings or when the acquisition geometry differs significantly from the training data. The method was proposed by Matteo Ronchetti and Davide Bacciu from the University of Pisa in the paper "Generative Tomography Reconstruction" (arXiv:2010.14933v2, 25 Nov 2020). It addresses the prototypical linear inverse problem of reconstructing Computed Tomography (CT) images. The approach is inspired by Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) but replaces the fixed linear filtration with trainable neural networks to handle the ill-conditioning of the Radon transform and reduce noise amplification. name: ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction
head: CNN Reconstruction, Deep Learning CT Reconstruction, Learned Post-Processing, Learned Post-Processing with ResNet
body: ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction is a learned post-processing method that maps noisy filtered backprojection (FBP) reconstructions directly to ground truth images, learning to suppress artifacts and noise. It differs from Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction by treating the input as a static noisy image rather than conditioning on the explicit Radon matrix. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Noisy FBP reconstruction f{BP} (2D image tensor). Output: Cleaned reconstruction f{pred} (2D image tensor). Data Structures: ResNet: A convolutional neural network model instance. inputs: Tensor of shape (batchsize, channels, height, width). targets: Tensor of shape (batchsize, channels, height, width) containing ground truth images. Training Procedure: 1. Dataset Generation: Create synthetic ground truth images f{true} consisting of 5 to 20 overlapping ellipses of varying sizes. Generate sinograms from f{true} using a projector and projection geometry. Add noise to sinograms. Reconstruct noisy sinograms using filtered backprojection (FBP) to obtain f{BP}. 2. Model Initialization: Initialize the ResNet() model. 3. Loss Function: Define the loss as Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the network output and the ground truth: L = \text{MSE}(f{pred}, f{true}). 4. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. 5. Training Loop: Iterate for numepochs (default 10). For each batch: forward pass outputs = model(inputs.float()). Compute loss loss = criterion(outputs, targets.float()). Backpropagate loss.backward(). Update weights optimizer.step(). 6. Evaluation: Evaluate on a validation set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class ResNet(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels=1, outchannels=1): super().init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU() self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): return self.conv2(self.relu(self.conv1(x))) def trainresnetct(model, trainloader, numepochs=10, batchsize=32, lr=0.001): criterion = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr) model.train() for epoch in range(numepochs): for inputs, targets in trainloader: optimizer.zerograd() # Zero gradients before backward pass outputs = model(inputs.float()) loss = criterion(outputs, targets.float()) loss.backward() optimizer.step() def inferresnetct(model, inputs): model.eval() with torch.nograd(): return model(inputs.float()) Parameters: lr: Learning rate, default 0.001. batchsize: Training batch size, default 32. numepochs: Number of training epochs, default 10. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Extends standard ResNet by conditioning on the explicit Radon matrix A, incorporating geometric projection constraints directly during reconstruction. Not given in the sources. The method originates from the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for medical image reconstruction, specifically leveraging ResNet architectures for artifact suppression in CT. It builds on the concept of learned post-processing, where traditional reconstruction methods (like FBP) are used to generate an initial estimate, which is then refined by a deep learning model. The specific implementation cited uses synthetic data with ellipsoidal phantoms to train the network. imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, https://github.com/imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction
head: Gradient-Conditioned Reconstruction
body: Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction extends standard ResNet-based CT reconstruction by conditioning the neural network on the explicit Radon matrix A (the forward projection operator). This allows the network to incorporate geometric projection constraints directly during reconstruction, rather than treating the input as a static noisy image. It differs from pure post-processing methods by using acquisition geometry to guide denoising and artifact suppression. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tuple (f, g), where f is the current image estimate (initially the noisy filtered backprojection) and g is the Radon matrix A. Output: A tuple containing the concatenated image-gradient tensor and the Radon matrix g. Data Structures: The Radon matrix A is passed explicitly as g. A boolean flag sparsesvd controls sparse SVD computation during matrix construction, defaulting to True. Gradient utilities (applyDx, applyDy, applyDxTrans, applyDyTrans) implement finite differences using np.diff with boundary padding to handle image edges. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gradient Computation: The gradient method computes the gradient of the data fidelity term. It projects f using A, computes A^T(Af), permutes the result, and triggers a backward pass on the mean to extract \nablaf. The output is reshaped to match the input image dimensions. 2. Concatenation: The image f and computed gradient are concatenated along the channel dimension: x{\text{cat}} = \text{cat}(f, \nablaf, \text{dim}=1). 3. Output: The module returns the concatenated tensor and the Radon matrix g for subsequent processing steps. 4. Training Loop: The model is trained via supervised learning. Inputs and targets are passed through the model, a loss (e.g., MSE) is computed, and gradients are backpropagated to update weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class GradientAwareResNet(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.resnet = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(2, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 1, 3, padding=1)) def gradient(self, f, g): # f: image estimate [B, 1, H, W] # g: Radon matrix A [B, Nproj, Ndet] Afg = torch.matmul(g, f.view(f.shape[0], -1)).view(f.shape) ATAtg = (g.transpose(-2, -1).squeeze(0) @ Afg).permute(0, 2, 1) ATAtg.mean().backward() out = f.grad.permute(0, 2, 1).reshape(f.shape) return out def forward(self, x): f, g = x grad = self.gradient(f, g) return (torch.cat((f, grad), dim=1), g) def trainstep(model, inputs, targets, optimizer, criterion): optimizer.zerograd() outputs = model(inputs) loss = criterion(outputs, targets.float()) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: sparsesvd: Boolean flag in explicitradon to control sparse SVD computation. Default: True. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The gradient computation relies on matrix operations with the Radon matrix, which can be memory-intensive for large datasets. Boundaries: The finite difference utilities use np.diff with boundary padding, implying zero-padding or similar boundary handling must be consistent with the projection geometry. Incorporates the Radon transform and its gradient directly into a learned iterative framework. It merges traditional optimization with neural network flexibility, allowing the model to adaptively learn prior constraints from inverse problems theory, unlike pure post-processing which only corrects final images. Choose this variant when iterative refinement with physics-informed priors is required over direct end-to-end mapping. See ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction. Time Complexity: Depends on the size of the Radon matrix A and the ResNet depth. The gradient computation involves matrix-vector multiplications (A and A^T), which scales with the number of projection angles and detector samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the explicit Radon matrix A and intermediate gradient tensors. The concatenation of f and grad doubles the channel dimension input to the ResNet. Strengths: Incorporates physical constraints (geometry) directly into the learning process, potentially leading to more accurate reconstructions than methods ignoring the projection model. Limitations: Requires explicit access to the Radon matrix, which may not be available or feasible to store for very large datasets. This method originates from the inverse-problems-CT-scans repository by imanfs. It builds on the concept of using ResNets for CT reconstruction [8264-resnet-based-ct-reconstruction.md] by conditioning the network on the forward projection operator. The source code includes utilities for wavelet thresholding and iterative thresholding, indicating a broader context of inverse problem solving in CT. imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans - GitHub, https://github.com/imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical CT Reconstruction via Domain Transform
head: Hierarchical DL framework, Hierarchical DL reconstruction, Hierarchical Deep Learning Tomographic Reconstruction, Hierarchical Domain Transform Decomposition, Hierarchical decomposition of domain transforms, Partial line integral domain transform
body: Hierarchical CT Reconstruction via Domain Transform is a deep learning framework that solves large-scale inverse problems, such as tomographic reconstruction, by decomposing the non-local, space-variant integral transform into a sequence of simpler, local hierarchical steps. Unlike brute-force fully connected networks that require intractable parameter counts for full-scale data, this method avoids dense connectivity by introducing virtual intermediate data representations (partial line integrals). It sets itself apart from siblings like Deep Image Prior Reconstruction, R2-Gaussian, End-to-End Reconstruction Model Architecture, and Transformer-based Architectures by explicitly constructing a homotopy-like continuum of data domains (from line integrals to partial line integrals to voxels) rather than relying on implicit neural priors or direct end-to-end mapping of the full sinogram to the image. Input: A sinogram p(r, \theta) representing line integrals, with dimensions Nr radial bins and N\theta projection angles. For the reference implementation, Nr = 512 and N\theta = 512. Output: A reconstructed image f(x, y) (or f(r, t) at \theta=0) with dimensions Nx \times Ny. For the reference implementation, 512 \times 512. The method operates on a hierarchy of stages L=0 to L=N. Each stage L holds data in the partial line integral domain, defined by three dimensions: 1. Depth bins (Nt): Represents depth resolution along the projection ray. 2. Projection angles (N\theta): The number of angular views. 3. Radial bins (Nr): The number of detector channels. The data tensor at stage L has shape (Nt^{(L)}, N\theta^{(L)}, Nr^{(L)}). The total data size is kept approximately constant across stages: Nt^{(L)} \times N\theta^{(L)} \times Nr^{(L)} \approx \text{Constant}. Reference Dimension Progression (2D, 512^2 output): L=0 (Input Sinogram): (1, 512, 512) L=1: (2, 256, 512) L=2: (8, 64, 512) L=3: (32, 16, 512) L=4: (128, 4, 512) L=5 (Output Image): (512, 1, 512) The ratio of depth bins to projection angles between stages does not need to be a power of two or an integer, as the network is trained to perform resampling and interpolation of the data between hierarchical stages. The forward model is the Fredholm integral equation of the first kind: p(v) = \int K(u,v)f(u)du where K(u,v) = \delta(ux \cos v\theta + uy \sin v\theta - vr) is the Dirac delta kernel for parallel-beam geometry, u=(ux, uy) are image coordinates, and v=(vr, v\theta) are projection coordinates. The method introduces a virtual intermediate representation q\alpha(v, t) using a window function \Pi(\cdot): q\alpha(v,t) = \int K(u,v)f(u)\Pi\left(\frac{t-u}{\alpha}\right)du where: \alpha is a scale factor controlling the window size. t is a parameter specifying the location of the window (depth). \Pi(x) = 1 for x < 0.5 and 0 elsewhere. In the limit \alpha \to \infty, q\alpha(v,t) = p(v) (line integral domain). In the limit \alpha \to 0, the window becomes a Dirac delta impulse, yielding the voxel domain f(u). \alpha (Scale Factor): Controls the width of the integration window. Decreases from \infty (input) to 0 (output) across stages. \Pi(x): Rectangular window function. Neighborhood Size: For sparse connection layers, each input neuron connects to a small neighborhood of output neurons. Empirical size: 3 \text{ depths} \times 5 \text{ angles} \times 3 \text{ radial bins}. Number of Stages (L): On the order of O(\log n), where n is the data dimension (512 \times 512). 1. Define Hierarchy: Determine the sequence of data dimensions (Nt, N\theta, Nr) for stages L=0 to L=N. 2. Initialize Network: Construct L sparse connection layers. 3. Initialize Weights: Initialize sparse connection weights to all ones. Initialize convolution kernels (if used) with the Glorot uniform initializer. 4. Pre-training (Optional): Train each sparse connection layer individually using synthetic noise data to initialize weights to a reasonable magnitude. This reduces total training time but does not affect the final loss function. 5. End-to-End Training (Noise-Based): Generate training pairs: Computer-generated white Gaussian random noise patterns f{noise} and their forward projections p{noise} using distance-driven projection. Compute intermediate labels q{\alpha}^{(L)} for each stage using Filtered Back Projection (FBP) on the noise patterns onto non-isotropic voxel grids corresponding to stage L dimensions. Train the network to minimize Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the network output and the intermediate labels. Vanishing Gradient Handling: During end-to-end training, update only one layer per iteration while freezing others. Select the layer randomly at each iteration. Linear Constraint: Exclude non-linear activation units during this phase to constrain the network to learning a linear inverse operator, preventing it from learning noise appearance as a prior. 6. End-to-End Training (Clinical Refinement): Generate training pairs from clinical CT images: Reproject clinical images to create sinograms with added random noise. Include non-linear activation units (e.g., ReLU) in convolutional layers to learn non-linear priors. Train end-to-end using MSE loss. 7. Reconstruction: For a new sinogram, pass it through the trained network. The final stage L=N outputs the reconstructed image f(x,y) where \theta=0 and \alpha corresponds to the voxel size. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class SparseConnectionLayer: """ Implements a sparse fully-connected layer where each input neuron connects only to a small neighborhood of output neurons. Forward operator: product of input data and sparse matrix. Backpropagation operator: product of transpose of sparse matrix and gradient. """ def init(self, inputshape, outputshape, neighborhood): self.inputshape = inputshape self.outputshape = outputshape self.neighborhood = neighborhood self.buildsparsity() self.weights = np.ones(len(self.rows)) # Initialized to all ones def buildsparsity(self): rows, cols = [], [] for i in range(np.prod(self.inputshape)): incoords = np.unravelindex(i, self.inputshape) for dt in range(-self.neighborhood[0]//2, self.neighborhood[0]//2 + 1): for dtheta in range(-self.neighborhood[1]//2, self.neighborhood[1]//2 + 1): for dr in range(-self.neighborhood[2]//2, self.neighborhood[2]//2 + 1): outcoords = (incoords[0] + dt, incoords[1] + dtheta, incoords[2] + dr) if 0 <= outcoords[0] < self.outputshape[0] and \ 0 <= outcoords[1] < self.outputshape[1] and \ 0 <= outcoords[2] < self.outputshape[2]: rows.append(np.ravelmultiindex(outcoords, self.outputshape)) cols.append(i) self.rows = np.array(rows) self.cols = np.array(cols) def forward(self, x): batchsize = x.shape[0] flatx = x.reshape(batchsize, -1) flatout = np.zeros((batchsize, np.prod(self.outputshape))) for b in range(batchsize): for idx in range(len(self.rows)): flatout[b, self.rows[idx]] += self.weights[idx] flatx[b, self.cols[idx]] return flatout.reshape(batchsize, self.outputshape) def backward(self, gradout): batchsize = gradout.shape[0] flatgradout = gradout.reshape(batchsize, -1) flatgradin = np.zeros((batchsize, np.prod(self.inputshape))) for b in range(batchsize): for idx in range(len(self.rows)): flatgradin[b, self.cols[idx]] += self.weights[idx] flatgradout[b, self.rows[idx]] return flatgradin.reshape(batchsize, self.inputshape) def createhierarchicalnetwork(stagedims, neighborhood=(3, 5, 3)): layers = [] for i in range(1, len(stagedims)): inputdims = stagedims[i-1] outputdims = stagedims[i] layer = SparseConnectionLayer(inputdims, outputdims, neighborhood) layers.append(layer) # Optional convolutional layers (L1: 1D kernel size 512; L2-L5: 2D 3x3 kernels with ReLU) are inserted here. return layers def trainhierarchicalnetwork(layers, sinograms, noiseimages, numiterations=1000, batchsize=20): for iteration in range(numiterations): layeridx = np.random.randint(0, len(layers)) noisebatch = noiseimages[np.random.choice(len(noiseimages), batchsize)] # Distance-driven forward projection operator sinogrambatch = np.zeroslike(noisebatch) predictions = layers[layeridx].forward(sinogrambatch) loss = np.mean((predictions - noisebatch) 2) gradout = 2 (predictions - noisebatch) / (predictions.size) gradin = layers[layeridx].backward(gradout) # SGD weight update step # layers[layeridx].weights -= learningrate gradient Vanishing Gradients: During end-to-end training, gradients may vanish across the deep hierarchy. This is mitigated by updating only one layer per iteration while freezing others. Parameter Explosion: Implementing the transforms as fully connected layers would require 512^4 \approx 69 billion parameters per stage, which is intractable. The sparse connection layer reduces the parameter count to O(n \log n). Noise Learning: If non-linear activations are used during noise-based training, the network may learn to reproduce noise artifacts as prior information. Using linear activations constrains the network to learn the linear inverse operator. Dimension Ratios: The ratio of depth bins to projection angles between stages does not need to be an integer, but the network must be trained to handle the resampling. Time Complexity: The computational complexity scales linearly with data size, even for extension to three dimensions, due to sparse network connections between hierarchical levels. Memory Complexity: The number of parameters scales as O(n \log n) for 2D and O(n^2 \log n) for 3D, where n is the data dimension. For a 512 \times 512 2D image, the network uses ~42 million parameters, which is 0.06% of the 69 billion parameters required by a fully connected layer. Measured Performance: In the reference implementation, training took ~4 hours for pre-training individual layers and ~1 day for end-to-end refinement on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. Strengths: Scalable to full-size problems (e.g., 512^4 system matrix); avoids brute-force dense networks; does not rely on direct or iterative inversion techniques. Limitations: Requires synthetic noise data for initial training; clinical refinement is needed for optimal image quality; currently demonstrated primarily for 2D parallel-beam geometry. When to Use: When reconstructing large-scale tomographic data where traditional iterative methods are too slow and fully connected deep learning models are intractable. When Not to Use: For small-scale problems where analytical methods (FBP) are sufficient and fast, or when hardware constraints prevent the training of deep hierarchical networks. The hierarchical approach was conceived independently of the AUTOMAP approach. Prior attempts using supervised learning relied on brute-force fully connected networks limited to 128^4 system matrix sizes, which could not practically scale to realistic data sizes like 512^4 or 512^6. This method was introduced to solve such large-scale inverse problems by decomposing the domain transform into hierarchical stages. It is applicable to other imaging problems such as emission and magnetic resonance reconstruction. name: Hierarchical CT Reconstruction via Partial Line Integrals

body: This method solves the tomographic inverse problem by decomposing the transformation from line integrals (sinograms) to image voxels into a hierarchy of incremental steps using an intermediate representation called partial line integrals. Unlike generic fully connected networks that require O(n^2) parameters, this approach uses sparse connections to achieve O(n \log n) parameter complexity, making high-resolution 3D reconstruction computationally feasible. It builds on the domain transform concept by explicitly defining the intermediate data structure and the hierarchical progression of integration lengths. Input: Sinogram data p(r, \theta), representing line integrals with radial distance r and projection angle \theta. For the standard implementation, this is a 512x512 sinogram (512 detector channels, 512 angles). Output: Reconstructed image voxels, represented as partial line integrals with a single projection angle (\theta=0) and full depth resolution. The core data structure is the intermediate representation q\alpha(r, \theta, t), defined in the partial line integral domain. Fields: r: Radial distance parameter. \theta: In-plane rotation angle. t: Depth parameter along the projection line. \alpha: Integration length (width of the window function). Layout: At each hierarchical stage L, the data is defined by the tuple (Nt, N\theta), where Nt is the number of depth bins and N\theta is the number of projection angles. The total data volume remains constant across stages. Sparse Connection Layer: The network layers are implemented as sparse connection layers. Non-zero weights are stored in a sparse matrix format. This differs from dropout layers, which remove output neurons; sparse layers remove connections between input and output neurons. The sparsity pattern ensures that each input neuron affects only a small neighborhood of output neurons. Partial Line Integral Definition: The partial line integral q\alpha(r, \theta, t) is generated by restricting the full line integral with a window function \Pi: q\alpha(r, \theta, t) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \cdot \Pi\left(\frac{-ux \sin \theta + vy \cos \theta - t}{\alpha}\right) \, ds Where: f(x,y) is the object function. \Pi(\cdot) is the window function. \alpha specifies the width of the window function, corresponding to a line segment of length \alpha centered at position t along the projection line. ux, vy are coordinates in the detector plane. Hierarchical Flow: The reconstruction progressively solves for partial line integrals with decreasing integration lengths \alpha: p(r, \theta) \rightarrow q{\alpha1}(r, \theta, t) \rightarrow q{\alpha2}(r, \theta, t) \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow q{\alphaN}(r, \theta, t) |{\theta=0} Where \alpha1 > \alpha2 > \dots > \alphaN. \alpha: Integration length. Decreases from coarse to fine depth resolution across stages. Nt: Number of depth bins. Increases across stages. N\theta: Number of projection angles. Decreases across stages. Kernel Sizes: L1 uses a sinogram domain convolutional kernel of size 512. L2-L5 use image domain convolutional kernels of size 3x3. Initialization: Sparse connections initialized with all ones. Convolution kernels initialized with Glorot uniform initializer. 1. Stage L0 (Input): Receive line integrals p(r, \theta) with Nt=1 and N\theta=512. 2. Stage L1: Transform to partial line integrals q{\alpha1} with Nt=2 and N\theta=256 using a sparse connection layer with a 512-sized kernel. 3. Stage L2: Transform to partial line integrals q{\alpha2} with Nt=8 and N\theta=64 using a sparse connection layer with a 3x3 kernel and ReLU activation. 4. Stage L3: Transform to partial line integrals q{\alpha3} with Nt=32 and N\theta=16 using a sparse connection layer with a 3x3 kernel and ReLU activation. 5. Stage L4: Transform to partial line integrals q{\alpha4} with Nt=128 and N\theta=4 using a sparse connection layer with a 3x3 kernel and ReLU activation. 6. Stage L5 (Output): Transform to regular image voxels with Nt=512 and N\theta=1 using a sparse connection layer with a 3x3 kernel and ReLU activation. Unverified code. Each input neuron affects only a small neighborhood of output neurons. """ def init(self, outputdim, sparsitypattern, kwargs): super(SparseConnectionLayer, self).init(kwargs) self.outputdim = outputdim # sparsitypattern: list of tuples (inputidx, outputidx) for non-zero connections self.sparsitypattern = sparsitypattern self.numconnections = len(sparsitypattern) def build(self, inputshape): # Initialize weights for non-zero connections with ones self.w = self.addweight( shape=(self.numconnections,), initializer='ones', trainable=True, name='weights') super(SparseConnectionLayer, self).build(inputshape) def call(self, inputs): # inputs shape: (batchsize, inputdim) # outputs shape: (batchsize, outputdim) outputs = tf.zeros((tf.shape(inputs)[0], self.outputdim)) # Apply sparse connections # For each non-zero weight, add input weight to the corresponding output # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation would use scatteradd or similar for i, (inidx, outidx) in enumerate(self.sparsitypattern): weight = self.w[i] # Gather input values inputvals = tf.gather(inputs, inidx, axis=1) # Scatter to output positions outputs = tf.tensorscatterndadd( outputs, [[j, outidx] for j in range(tf.shape(inputs)[0])], inputvals weight) return outputs def createhierarchicalnetwork(): """ Creates the 5-stage hierarchical CT reconstruction network. """ # Define sparsity patterns for each stage based on data dimensions # L0: 512x1 -> L1: 512x2 (conceptually, though data is reshaped) # The paper specifies data dimensions (Nt, Ntheta) for each stage. # We assume a flattened representation for the dense layer logic, # but the sparse pattern enforces locality. # Stage L1: Sinogram domain convolutional layer, kernel size 512 # Input: 512 angles, 512 radial bins. Output: 256 angles, 512 radial bins (reshaped to depth bins) # Note: The paper describes L1 as transforming line integrals to partial line integrals. # The exact sparsity pattern is not explicitly defined in the text, # but it is a "sparse connection" layer. We assume a local neighborhood. # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we define the architecture structure. # The specific sparsity masks would be generated based on the "small neighborhood" constraint. model = tf.keras.Sequential() # L1: Sparse connection layer # Input: (512, 512) sinogram # Output: (2, 256) partial line integrals (conceptually) # In practice, dimensions are managed via reshaping. # We use a placeholder for the specific sparse mask generation. l1sparsemask = generatesparsemask(inputdim=512512, outputdim=2256, neighborhoodsize=512) model.add(SparseConnectionLayer(outputdim=2256, sparsitypattern=l1sparsemask)) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Reshape((2, 256))) # L2: Image domain convolutional layer, 3x3 kernel, ReLU # Input: (2, 256) # Output: (8, 64) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(8, (3,3), padding='same', activation='relu')) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Reshape((8, 64))) # L3: Image domain convolutional layer, 3x3 kernel, ReLU # Input: (8, 64) # Output: (32, 16) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, (3,3), padding='same', activation='relu')) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Reshape((32, 16))) # L4: Image domain convolutional layer, 3x3 kernel, ReLU # Input: (32, 16) # Output: (128, 4) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(128, (3,3), padding='same', activation='relu')) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Reshape((128, 4))) # L5: Image domain convolutional layer, 3x3 kernel, ReLU # Input: (128, 4) # Output: (512, 1) -> Image voxels model.add(tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(512, (3,3), padding='same', activation='relu')) model.add(tf.keras.layers.Reshape((512, 1))) return model def generatesparsemask(inputdim, outputdim, neighborhoodsize): """ Generates a sparsity pattern where each input neuron affects a small neighborhood of output neurons. This is a placeholder for the specific pattern used in the paper. """ # The paper states that the number of parameters is O(n) and each input affects a small neighborhood. # A simple local connectivity pattern is assumed. connections = [] # This is a simplified local connectivity pattern. # In reality, the pattern is learned or defined by the specific geometry of the partial line integrals. for i in range(inputdim): # Define a local neighborhood in the output space start = max(0, i - neighborhoodsize // 2) end = min(outputdim, i + neighborhoodsize // 2) for j in range(start, end): connections.append((i, j)) return connections def trainphase1noise(model, numstages): """ Pre-train each sparse connection layer individually using training labels at the corresponding hierarchical stage. """ # Generate training labels using FBP on non-isotropic voxel grids # Use 200 realizations of white Gaussian random noise and distance-driven forward projections for stage in range(1, numstages + 1): # Get sparse layer for this stage layer = model.layers[stage-1] # Generate labels for this stage labels = generatefbplabels(stage) # Freeze other layers for l in model.layers: if l != layer: l.trainable = False # Compile and train model.compile(optimizer='sgd', loss='mse') model.fit(labels, labels, epochs=10, batchsize=20) # Placeholder epochs def trainphase2endtoendnoise(model): """ End-to-end training without intermediate labels. Address vanishing gradients by randomly choosing a single layer for update per iteration. Disable non-linear activation units. """ # Disable non-linear activations for layer in model.layers: if isinstance(layer, tf.keras.layers.Activation) or (hasattr(layer, 'activation') and layer.activation is not None): layer.activation = None # Training loop for iteration in range(numiterations): # Randomly choose a single layer for update layeridx = np.random.randint(0, len(model.layers)) layer = model.layers[layeridx] # Freeze others for l in model.layers: if l != layer: l.trainable = False # Generate noise data inputs, targets = generatenoisedata() # Train model.trainonbatch(inputs, targets) def trainphase3clinicalrefinement(model): """ Refine with end-to-end training using clinical datasets. Enable non-linear activation units. """ # Enable non-linear activations for layer in model.layers: if isinstance(layer, tf.keras.layers.Conv2D): layer.activation = tf.keras.activations.relu # Use 200 clinical datasets # Clinical pairs obtained by reprojecting clinical CT images and inserting random noise inputs, targets = loadclinicaldata() model.compile(optimizer='sgd', loss='mse') model.fit(inputs, targets, epochs=100, batchsize=20) def generatefbplabels(stage): """ Analytically generate training labels for intermediate levels using Filtered Back Projection (FBP). """ # This is a placeholder for the FBP implementation on non-isotropic voxel grids pass def generatenoisedata(): """ Generate white Gaussian random noise patterns and their distance-driven forward projections. """ # Placeholder pass def loadclinicaldata(): """ Load clinical datasets. """ # Placeholder pass Vanishing Gradients: During end-to-end noise training, gradients may vanish. This is addressed by randomly selecting a single network layer for update per iteration while freezing the others. Parameter Explosion: A fully connected network for 512x512 input/output would require 69 billion parameters. The sparse connection approach reduces this to ~42 million parameters (0.06%). For 3D cases (512^3), a fully connected network would require ~18 quadrillion parameters, while this approach is estimated to require ~21 billion. Sparse Connection vs. Dropout: Sparse connection layers remove connections between input and output neurons, whereas dropout layers remove output neurons. This distinction is critical for maintaining the local neighborhood structure. Parameter Complexity: The number of network parameters in each sparse connection layer is O(n), where n is the data dimension. Stage Complexity: The number of hierarchical stages is O(\log n) because the number of angles decreases exponentially. Total Complexity: The total number of parameters is O(n \log n). Measured Performance: For a 512x512 input/output, the 5 sparse connection layers used ~42 million trainable parameters. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of parameters compared to fully connected networks, making high-resolution 3D reconstruction feasible. Decomposes the non-local tomographic inverse problem into a series of local transforms suitable for neural networks. Hierarchical structure allows for progressive refinement of depth resolution. Limitations: Requires careful handling of vanishing gradients during end-to-end training. The sparsity pattern must be carefully designed to ensure local connectivity. Training involves multiple phases (pre-training, end-to-end noise, clinical refinement) which can be complex to implement. Use this method when reconstructing high-resolution CT images (e.g., 512x512 or larger) where a fully connected network would be computationally intractable due to parameter count. Use when the goal is to leverage the hierarchical nature of the tomographic inverse problem to improve reconstruction quality. Do not use for low-resolution reconstructions where a fully connected network is feasible and simpler to implement. Do not use if the computational resources for multi-phase training (especially end-to-end with random layer updates) are not available. The method was proposed in the paper "A hierarchical approach to deep learning and its application to tomographic reconstruction". It builds on the concept of domain transform by explicitly defining the intermediate data structure (partial line integrals) and the hierarchical progression of integration lengths. The method was developed to address the intractability of fully connected networks for high-dimensional tomographic reconstruction. By decomposing the problem into a hierarchy of local transforms, the method achieves a significant reduction in parameter count while maintaining reconstruction quality. The method is applicable to CT reconstruction, particularly for high-resolution 3D imaging where computational efficiency is critical. name: Transformer-based Architectures
body: Transformer-based architectures apply self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in volumetric data, addressing the local receptive field limitations of convolutions in volume rendering. They enable direct feature aggregation, super-resolution, and denoising across spatial or ray-based token sequences without relying solely on iterative tomographic inversion or per-scene optimization. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. DuDoTrans is a dual-domain transformer architecture designed for sparse-view CT reconstruction, addressing the ill-posed nature of tomographic inversion when projection data is limited. It distinguishes itself from standard transformer-based reconstruction methods by explicitly operating in both the image domain (via Swin Transformer blocks) and the projection domain (via differentiable forward/back-projection), leveraging window-based multi-head self-attention to reduce computational complexity while maintaining global context. A generalizable approach using a transformer-based attention module to aggregate source views information. It efficiently reconstructs Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) on the fly from source views without per-scene optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on cross-view feature aggregation via attention mechanisms rather than iterative tomographic inversion. Transformers compute pairwise attention over input tokens to capture long-range dependencies that convolutions miss. The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts this architecture for images by treating fixed-size patches as tokens. Builds on Transformer-based Architectures. In volume rendering, ViT is used for super-resolution and denoising, where its ability to attend across the full spatial extent of a subvolume helps recover large-scale structures that local convolutions miss. Transformer-based Tomographic Reconstruction is a deep learning technique that reconstructs 3D single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) images using a slice-by-slice transformer network (SSTrans-3D). It addresses the considerable artifacts caused by incomplete projection data in image reconstruction. It differs from siblings like DuDoTrans and DIOR by relying on a pure transformer architecture rather than combining deep learning with iterative optimization. The Line Segment-based Transformer (Lineformer) is a neural architecture designed for sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstruction, specifically serving as the backbone for Structure-Aware X-ray Neural Radiodensity Fields (SAX-NeRF). It solves the problem of capturing internal 3D structural dependencies in X-ray projections by computing self-attention locally within line segments of an X-ray, rather than globally across all sampled points. Unlike vanilla Transformers which exhibit quadratic computational complexity relative to the number of input points, Lineformer achieves linear complexity, making it efficient enough to integrate into iterative volume rendering pipelines. Definition: A transformer architecture that infers volume density by incorporating relative depth differences as position encoding, rather than absolute positions. Steps: 1. Sample M points pm on ray r with depths tm. 2. Calculate relative depth encoding Em for each point using \deltam. 3. Element-wise add Em to point feature fm. 4. Pass through self-attention and feed-forward network to predict volume density \sigmam. Parameters: K: Length of the position encoding feature vector. Details: The relative depth \deltam is calculated as \deltam = \frac{tm - d}{u(t{far} - t{near})}, where d is the estimated depth, t{near} and t{far} are the near and far plane depths, and u is a hyperparameter controlling the range. The position encoding Em uses sinusoidal functions with frequencies \omegak = \frac{1}{10000^{2i/K}} for even/odd indices k. Definition: A proposer network constrained to reduce computational cost, using a single transformer block for encoder and decoder with a single attention head. Layout: Features are projected to 16-D. A single transformer block is used for the encoder. A single transformer block is used for the decoder. A single attention head is used. Context: This architecture is used in NeRF sampling to propose points for coarse and fine networks, reducing the overhead compared to fully connected layers while maintaining reasonable cost. Definition: Using Masked Auto Encoder combined with a 3D transformer-based architecture to learn a generalized representation capable of reconstructing unseen scenes. Context: This approach scales self-supervised NeRF training by leveraging geometric cues from sparse inputs, enabling transfer learning and generalization to new scenes without per-scene optimization. Definition: A large feedforward transformer model that encodes sparse-view X-ray projections into compact latent tokens and fuses them across views to reconstruct a 3D CT volume density field. Steps: 1. Encode each X-ray projection Ii independently using a feature extractor F{enc} (specifically DINO) to produce patch features Hi: Hi = F{enc}(Ii) for i = 1, \dots, K. 2. Inject camera geometry into the encoded features by applying ModLN with Plücker ray embeddings Ri: \tilde{H}i = ModLN(Hi, Ri) for i = 1, \dots, K. 3. Concatenate the modulated features from all K views and process them through a 16-layer Fusion ViT (similar to ViT-B) using all-to-all self-attention F{fuse} to produce fused features \{F1, \dots, FK\}. Parameters: Fusion ViT depth: 16 layers, architecture similar to ViT-B. Encoder backbone: DINO transformer. Camera embedding: Plücker ray embedding Ri, derived from the cross product between camera location and ray direction, independent of scale, camera position, and focal length. Definition: A model using Transformers for volume rendering, processing ray-depth-ordered feature sequences from multiple source views. Steps: 1. Processes ray-depth-ordered feature sequences from multiple source views. 2. Uses alternating pooling and ray-wise attention layers. 3. Enables effective joint feature aggregation and ray marching. Context: NeRFormer is geometry-free and does not produce the scene's density function directly, nor does it rely on geometric inductive biases, distinguishing it from standard NeRF models. Definition: A technique to enable transformers to model volumetric rendering by implicitly encoding uni-directional ray information, preventing the model from rendering inaccurate surfaces due to bidirectional ray assumptions. Steps: Include masks in the transformer input to distinguish between frontal and rear points along a camera ray, ensuring the network mimics a volumetric rendering strategy. Pitfall: Without masking, a bidirectional ray is implied, causing the network to have difficulty rendering the object’s surface accurately. Comparison: Appending a volume’s position on a ray to introduce uni-directional ray information is ineffective compared to the original masking strategy. Steps: Update the slot features using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with the computed attention output and previous state: GRU(Ut, S{t-1}). Repeat the attention computation and GRU update 3 times at each timestamp to obtain the final slot features St. Parameters: D: Fixed softmax temperature for the attention mechanism. Repetition count: 3 iterations of attention/GRU per timestamp. Transformer architectures have been adapted for volume rendering to overcome the local connectivity constraints of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The Vision Transformer (ViT) was originally proposed for image classification. In the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), transformers have been used for view aggregation, sampling proposal, and generalizable reconstruction. The integration of transformers into tomographic reconstruction, such as in DuDoTrans and SSTrans-3D, addresses the ill-posed nature of sparse-view problems by leveraging global attention to recover missing information.
