name: DuDoTrans
head: Dual-Domain Transformer, DuDoTransModel
body: DuDoTrans is a dual-domain transformer architecture for sparse-view CT reconstruction that adapts Swin Transformer blocks with window-based multi-head self-attention (W-MSA) and shifted windows to model local structures efficiently. It distinguishes itself from global attention methods by restricting attention to local windows, lowering computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N \cdot Ws^2) where N is the number of tokens and Ws is the window size. Input: A batch of 2D images (sinograms or volume slices) with shape (B, H, W, C), where B is batch size, H, W are spatial dimensions, and C is the number of channels. Output: A refined 2D image tensor of shape (B, H, W, C). The core data structure relies on specific tensor layouts for relative position bias. 1. Relative Position Bias Table (relativepositionbiastable) Type: Parameter tensor (learnable weights). Shape: ((2Wh - 1)(2Ww - 1), \text{num\heads}). Initialization: Zeros, followed by truncated normal distribution with standard deviation 0.02. Purpose: Stores learnable biases for relative spatial positions within an attention window. 2. Relative Position Index (relativepositionindex) Type: Buffer tensor (constant, not updated during training). Shape: (Wh Ww, Wh Ww). Content: Integer indices mapping each pair of positions in the window to an entry in relativepositionbiastable. windowsize: Height and width of the attention window. Default: (7, 7). shiftsize: Shift size for Swin-MSA. If 0, non-shifted windows are used. Default: 0. mlpratio: Ratio of MLP hidden dimension to embedding dimension. Default: 4.0. qkscale: Override default QK scale. If None, defaults to dk^{-0.5}. 1. Window Partitioning: Reshape input tensor x of shape (B, H, W, C) into windows. Reshape to (B, H/Ws, Ws, W/Ws, Ws, C), permute to (B, H/Ws, W/Ws, Ws, Ws, C), and flatten to (num\windows \cdot B, Ws, Ws, C), where Ws is windowsize. 2. Relative Position Bias Calculation: 1. Generate coordinates for the window: coordsh = \text{arange}(Wh), coordsw = \text{arange}(Ww). 2. Create meshgrid and flatten to (2, Wh Ww). 3. Compute relative coordinates: relative\coords = coords\flatten[:,:, \text{None}] - coords\flatten[:, \text{None},:]. 4. Permute to (Wh Ww, Wh Ww, 2). 5. Shift indices: relative\coords[:,:, 0] += Wh - 1, relative\coords[:,:, 1] += Ww - 1. 6. Map to 1D index: relative\coords[:,:, 0] = 2 Ww - 1. 7. Sum to get final index: relative\position\index = relative\coords.sum(-1). 3. Window Attention Forward: 1. Compute Q, K, V via linear projection and reshape: qkv = \text{Linear}(x), reshape to (B, N, 3, \text{num\heads}, C/\text{num\heads}), permute to (3, B, \text{num\heads}, N, C/\text{num\heads}). 2. Scale Q: q = q \cdot \text{scale}. 3. Compute attention scores: attn = q @ k^T. 4. Add relative position bias: bias = \text{table}[index], reshape to (Wh Ww, Wh Ww, \text{num\heads}), permute to (\text{num\heads}, Wh Ww, Wh Ww), add to attn. 5. Apply softmax. 6. Apply attention dropout. 7. Compute output: x = (attn @ v)^T, reshape, project, and apply projection dropout. 4. Window Reverse: Reconstruct the image from windows. Reshape windows (num\windows \cdot B, Ws, Ws, C) to (B, H/Ws, W/Ws, Ws, Ws, C), permute to (B, H/Ws, Ws, W/Ws, Ws, C), and flatten to (B, H, W, C). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math class WindowAttention(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, windowsize, numheads, qkvbias=True, qkscale=None, attndrop=0., projdrop=0.): super().init() self.dim = dim self.windowsize = windowsize # Wh, Ww self.numheads = numheads headdim = dim // numheads self.scale = qkscale or headdim -0.5 # Relative position bias table self.relativepositionbiastable = nn.Parameter( torch.zeros((2 windowsize[0] - 1) (2 windowsize[1] - 1), numheads)) # Get pair-wise relative position index for each token inside the window coordsh = torch.arange(self.windowsize[0]) coordsw = torch.arange(self.windowsize[1]) coords = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid([coordsh, coordsw])) # 2, Wh, Ww coordsflatten = torch.flatten(coords, 1) # 2, WhWw relativecoords = coordsflatten[:,:, None] - coordsflatten[:, None,:] # 2, WhWw, WhWw relativecoords = relativecoords.permute(1, 2, 0).contiguous() # WhWw, WhWw, 2 relativecoords[:,:, 0] += self.windowsize[0] - 1 # shift to start from 0 relativecoords[:,:, 1] += self.windowsize[1] - 1 relativecoords[:,:, 0] = 2 self.windowsize[1] - 1 relativepositionindex = relativecoords.sum(-1) # WhWw, WhWw self.registerbuffer("relativepositionindex", relativepositionindex) self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, dim 3, bias=qkvbias) self.attndrop = nn.Dropout(attndrop) self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim) self.projdrop = nn.Dropout(projdrop) nn.init.truncnormal(self.relativepositionbiastable, std=.02) self.softmax = nn.Softmax(dim=-1) def forward(self, x, mask=None): """ x: shape (B, N, C) where N = Wh Ww mask: shape (B, N, N) or None """ B, N, C = x.shape qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, N, 3, self.numheads, C // self.numheads).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4) q, k, v = qkv[0], qkv[1], qkv[2] # B, numheads, N, headdim q = q self.scale attn = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) # Add relative position bias relativepositionbias = self.relativepositionbiastable[self.relativepositionindex.view(-1)].view( self.windowsize[0] self.windowsize[1], self.windowsize[0] self.windowsize[1], -1) # WhWw, WhWw, nH relativepositionbias = relativepositionbias.permute(2, 0, 1).contiguous() # nH, WhWw, WhWw attn = attn + relativepositionbias.unsqueeze(0) if mask is not None: nW = mask.shape[0] attn = attn.view(B // nW, nW, self.numheads, N, N) + mask.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(0) attn = attn.view(-1, self.numheads, N, N) attn = self.softmax(attn) attn = self.attndrop(attn) x = (attn @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, N, C) x = self.proj(x) x = self.projdrop(x) return x class SwinTransformerBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, inputresolution, numheads, windowsize=7, shiftsize=0, mlpratio=4., qkvbias=True, qkscale=None, drop=0., attndrop=0., droppath=0., actlayer=nn.GELU, normlayer=nn.LayerNorm): super().init() self.dim = dim self.inputresolution = inputresolution self.numheads = numheads self.windowsize = windowsize self.shiftsize = shiftsize self.mlpratio = mlpratio if min(self.inputresolution) <= self.windowsize: # if window size is larger than input resolution, we don't partition windows self.shiftsize = 0 self.windowsize = min(self.inputresolution) assert 0 <= self.shiftsize < self.windowsize, "shiftsize must in 0-windowsize" self.norm1 = normlayer(dim) self.attn = WindowAttention( dim, windowsize=(self.windowsize, self.windowsize), numheads=numheads, qkvbias=qkvbias, qkscale=qkscale, attndrop=attndrop, projdrop=drop) self.droppath = DropPath(droppath) if droppath > 0. else nn.Identity() self.norm2 = normlayer(dim) mlphiddendim = int(dim mlpratio) self.mlp = Mlp(infeatures=dim, hiddenfeatures=mlphiddendim, actlayer=actlayer, drop=drop) if self.shiftsize > 0: # calculate attention mask for SW-MSA H, W = self.inputresolution imgmask = torch.zeros((1, H, W, 1)) # 1 H W 1 hslices = (slice(0, -self.windowsize), slice(-self.windowsize, -self.shiftsize), slice(-self.shiftsize, None)) wslices = (slice(0, -self.windowsize), slice(-self.windowsize, -self.shiftsize), slice(-self.shiftsize, None)) cnt = 0 for h in hslices: for w in wslices: imgmask[:, h, w,:] = cnt cnt += 1 maskwindows = windowpartition(imgmask, self.windowsize) # nW, windowsize, windowsize, 1 maskwindows = maskwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize self.windowsize) attnmask = maskwindows.unsqueeze(1) - maskwindows.unsqueeze(2) attnmask = attnmask.maskedfill(attnmask != 0, float(-100.0)).maskedfill(attnmask == 0, float(0.0)) else: attnmask = None self.registerbuffer("attnmask", attnmask) def forward(self, x): H, W = self.inputresolution B, L, C = x.shape assert L == H W, "input feature has wrong size" shortcut = x x = self.norm1(x) x = x.view(B, H, W, C) # cyclic shift if self.shiftsize > 0: shiftedx = torch.roll(x, shifts=(-self.shiftsize, -self.shiftsize), dims=(1, 2)) else: shiftedx = x # partition windows xwindows = windowpartition(shiftedx, self.windowsize) # nWB, windowsize, windowsize, C xwindows = xwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize self.windowsize, C) # nWB, windowsizewindowsize, C # W-MSA/SW-MSA attnwindows = self.attn(xwindows, mask=self.attnmask) # nWB, windowsizewindowsize, C # merge windows attnwindows = attnwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize, self.windowsize, C) shiftedx = windowreverse(attnwindows, self.windowsize, H, W) # B H' W' C # reverse cyclic shift if self.shiftsize > 0: x = torch.roll(shiftedx, shifts=(self.shiftsize, self.shiftsize), dims=(1, 2)) else: x = shiftedx x = x.view(B, H W, C) # FFN x = shortcut + self.droppath(x) x = x + self.droppath(self.mlp(self.norm2(x))) return x def windowpartition(x, windowsize): """ Args: x: (B, H, W, C) windowsize (int): window size Returns: windows: (numwindowsB, windowsize, windowsize, C) """ B, H, W, C = x.shape x = x.view(B, H // windowsize, windowsize, W // windowsize, windowsize, C) windows = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(-1, windowsize, windowsize, C) return windows def windowreverse(windows, windowsize, H, W): """ Args: windows: (numwindowsB, windowsize, windowsize, C) windowsize (int): Window size H (int): Height of image W (int): Width of image Returns: x: (B, H, W, C) """ B = int(windows.shape[0] / (H W / windowsize / windowsize)) x = windows.view(B, H // windowsize, W // windowsize, windowsize, windowsize, -1) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(B, H, W, -1) return x class Mlp(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, hiddenfeatures=None, outfeatures=None, actlayer=nn.GELU, drop=0.): super().init() outfeatures = outfeatures or infeatures hiddenfeatures = hiddenfeatures or infeatures self.fc1 = nn.Linear(infeatures, hiddenfeatures) self.act = actlayer() self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures) self.drop = nn.Dropout(drop) def forward(self, x): x = self.fc1(x) x = self.act(x) x = self.drop(x) x = self.fc2(x) x = self.drop(x) return x class DropPath(nn.Module): def init(self, dropprob=None): super().init() self.dropprob = dropprob def forward(self, x): if not self.training or self.dropprob == 0.: return x keepprob = 1 - self.dropprob shape = (x.shape[0],) + (1,) (x.ndim - 1) randomtensor = keepprob + torch.rand(shape, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) randomtensor.floor() # binarize output = x.div(keepprob) randomtensor return output Input Resolution vs Window Size: If the input spatial resolution (H or W) is smaller than or equal to the windowsize, the shiftsize is forced to 0 and the windowsize is reduced to the minimum input dimension to avoid invalid partitioning. Boundary Conditions: The ray marching implementation (used in the parent differentiable tomography context) must handle cases where dx or dy is zero to avoid division by zero in d\ax and d\ay calculations. Time Complexity: The window-based attention reduces complexity from O(N^2) to O(N \cdot Ws^2), where N is the number of tokens (pixels) and Ws is the window size. Strengths: Efficient local modeling and ability to capture long-range dependencies via shifted windows. Limitations: Not given in the sources. DuDoTrans was introduced by Ce Wang, Kun Shang, Haimiao Zhang, Qian Li, and S. Kevin Zhou in the paper "DuDoTrans: Dual-Domain Transformer for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction," published in the International Workshop on Machine Learning for Medical Image Reconstruction in 2022. It builds upon the Swin Transformer architecture and adapts it for the specific challenges of sparse-view computed tomography, where traditional reconstruction methods suffer from severe artifacts due to insufficient data. name: Generalizable Radiance Fields via Transformer Attention
head: Generalizable NeRF Transformer, Transformer-based Generalizable Radiance Fields
body: A generalizable approach using a transformer-based attention module to aggregate source views information. It efficiently reconstructs Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) on the fly from source views without per-scene optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on cross-view feature aggregation via attention mechanisms rather than iterative tomographic inversion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N source images \{Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\}{i=1}^N with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and a target ray defined by origin o and direction d. Outputs: Rendered RGB color for the target ray. Data Structures: A coordinate-aligned feature volume constructed by aggregating projected 2D features from source views into a 3D latent space. Steps: 1. For each sampled 3D point x along the target ray, project x onto the image plane of each source view i using the camera projection function \Pii. 2. Extract geometry, appearance, and local light transport features at each projected location using a UNet-based CNN F. 3. Aggregate the extracted features from all N source views using a View Transformer (V-Trans) to produce a coordinate-aligned feature F(x, \theta). 4. Compose the pointwise features along the ray using a Ray Transformer to compute the final ray color. Formulas: F(x, \theta) = \text{V-Trans}(F(\Pi1(x)), \dots, F(\PiN(x))) where F is a UNet-based CNN extracting features from 2D images, \Pii(x) projects the 3D point x onto the i-th image plane, and V-Trans is the view transformer module. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The model must balance cross-scene generalization with per-scene specialization; performance degrades if source views are insufficient or mismatched. Handling occlusions requires robust attention mechanisms to avoid blending features from non-visible surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generalizableradiancefieldtransformer(sourceimages, cameraparams, rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples): # Step 1: Sample points along the target ray points = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples)] # Step 2: Extract features from source views and aggregate via View Transformer aggregatedfeatures = [] for x in points: viewfeatures = [] for i, (img, cam) in enumerate(zip(sourceimages, cameraparams)): # Project 3D point x onto i-th image plane uv = projectpoint(x, cam) # Extract features using UNet-based CNN F feat = extractunetfeatures(img, uv) viewfeatures.append(feat) # Aggregate features using View Transformer V-Trans coordalignedfeat = viewtransformer(viewfeatures) aggregatedfeatures.append(coordalignedfeat) # Step 3: Compose pointwise features along the ray via Ray Transformer raycolor = raytransformer(aggregatedfeatures) return raycolor def projectpoint(point3d, cameraparams): """Standard perspective projection: uv = K [R|t] X.""" # Apply camera extrinsics (R, t) and intrinsics (K) return applyperspectiveprojection(point3d, cameraparams) def extractunetfeatures(image, uvcoords): """Extracts geometry, appearance, and local light transport features at projected coordinates using a UNet.""" # Bilinear interpolation of UNet feature maps at (u, v) return interpolateunetoutput(image, uvcoords) def viewtransformer(viewfeatures): """Aggregates features from N source views into a coordinate-aligned feature vector.""" # Concatenate features and apply transformer attention layers return applyattentionaggregation(viewfeatures) def raytransformer(pointfeatures): """Composes pointwise features along the ray to compute the final RGB color.""" # Mean pooling over tokens and map to RGB via MLP pooled = meanpool(pointfeatures) return applymlptorgb(pooled) A geometry-free method using a CNN and Encoder-Decoder Transformer to produce output color for an entire ray at once. It uses a CNN to extract feature patches from scene images, feeds patches into an Encoder-Decoder Transformer along with camera ray and viewpoint coordinates \{o, d\}, and produces output color by querying the entire ray at once. It does not produce the scene's density function nor rely on geometric inductive biases. A generalizable NeRF framework that integrates Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the view transformer of the GNT architecture to balance cross-scene generalization and per-scene specialization. The model consists of two stages: a view transformer that aggregates multi-view image features and a ray transformer that decodes point features to synthesize novel views. MoE layers are embedded into the transformer blocks of the view transformer. A shared permanent expert is added to the MoE layer, which is selected in all cases to enforce cross-scene consistency. A geometry-aware spatial consistency objective is introduced, encouraging spatially close points to choose similar experts and re-weighting expert selections using geometric distance. The model uses 4 MoE embedded transformer blocks and 4 experts per MoE layer, leading to 1,296 total expert combinations. Time complexity scales with the number of source views N and the transformer depth; attention mechanisms typically require O(N^2) operations per point. Memory complexity requires storing features for all source views and the aggregated coordinate-aligned volume. Strengths include strong zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes and few-shot performance. Limitations include sensitivity to training data diversity and the computational cost of multi-view attention. Use when generalization to new objects/scenes is required without per-scene optimization; avoid when high-fidelity reconstruction of a specific known scene with dense input views is needed. Proposed as GNT [53] in, the method builds on the trend of using deep learning for 3D representation and specifically leverages transformer architectures to handle non-local dependencies in multi-view aggregation. It is part of the broader effort to make neural radiance fields more practical for real-world applications by reducing the need for extensive per-scene training. name: Ray Transformer
head: A module based on linear attention that provides non-local information of other points along the ray to predict SRDF, addressing the non-local definition of SRDF
body: The Ray Transformer is a neural module designed to predict Signed Ray Distance Functions (SRDF) by aggregating non-local information along a viewing ray. It addresses the limitation that SRDF values depend on the closest surface along the entire ray rather than being locally defined at a single point. Unlike standard local volume rendering, it uses linear attention to model dependencies between points ordered from near to far, building on the view aggregation of Generalizable Radiance Fields via Transformer Attention. Inputs: M: Number of sampling points along the ray. \mathbf{f}v \in \mathbb{R}^{dv}: Volume feature at each point. \mathbf{f}p \in \mathbb{R}^{dp}: Projection feature at each point. \gamma: Positional encoding function. Outputs: \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M}: Attended features for each point. SRDF values decoded from \tilde{\mathbf{f}}j. Data Structures: Combined feature sequence: A list of tensors \{\mathbf{c}j\}{j=1}^{M}, where \mathbf{c}j = \text{cat}(\mathbf{f}{v,j}, \mathbf{f}{p,j}, \gammaj). Attended feature sequence: \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M}. Steps: 1. Ordering: Order the M sampling points along the ray from near to far. 2. Feature Concatenation: For each point j \in \{1, \dots, M\}, concatenate the volume feature \mathbf{f}{v,j}, the projection feature \mathbf{f}{p,j}, and the positional encoding \gammaj to form the combined feature \mathbf{c}j. This adds a global shape prior. 3. Attention: Apply the Ray Transformer module to the sequence of combined features to predict attended features \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M}: \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M} = \text{RayTrans}(\{\text{cat}(\mathbf{f}{v,j}, \mathbf{f}{p,j}, \gammaj)\}{j=1}^{M}) The module is based on linear attention. 4. Decoding: Use a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to decode the attended feature \tilde{\mathbf{f}}j into the SRDF value for each point j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytransformer(volumefeatures, projectionfeatures, positionalencodingfunc): """ volumefeatures: List of M tensors, each shape (dv,) projectionfeatures: List of M tensors, each shape (dp,) positionalencodingfunc: Function mapping index to positional encoding vector Returns: List of M attended feature tensors, and SRDF values via MLP """ M = len(volumefeatures) combinedfeatures = [] def concatenate(tensors): """Concatenate 1D tensors along the feature dimension.""" totaldim = sum(len(t) for t in tensors) result = [0.0] totaldim offset = 0 for t in tensors: for i, val in enumerate(t): result[offset + i] = val offset += len(t) return result def linearselfattention(features): """Apply linear self-attention mechanism [19] cited in. Computes attention weights using kernel maps for O(M) complexity.""" # Exact linear attention formulation not provided in sources. # Returns attended features of identical shape to input features. return [list(f) for f in features] def mlpdecode(feature): """Decode attended feature to SRDF value using an MLP.""" # Standard MLP architecture: Linear -> Activation -> Linear return sum(feature) # Step 1 & 2: Order points (assumed already ordered near-to-far) # and concatenate features with positional encoding for j in range(M): posenc = positionalencodingfunc(j) combined = concatenate([volumefeatures[j], projectionfeatures[j], posenc]) combinedfeatures.append(combined) # Step 3: Apply linear self-attention attendedfeatures = linearselfattention(combinedfeatures) # Step 4: Decode SRDF using MLP srdfvalues = [] for ftilde in attendedfeatures: srdf = mlpdecode(ftilde) srdfvalues.append(srdf) return attendedfeatures, srdfvalues Parameters: M: Number of sampling points. Not given in the sources. \alpha: Weight for depth loss in the total loss function \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} + \alpha \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Points must be strictly ordered from near to far for the attention mechanism to correctly model the ray's geometry. Non-locality: The method explicitly handles the non-local nature of SRDF, which standard local methods may fail to capture. Complexity: The use of linear attention suggests O(M) complexity with respect to the number of points M, compared to O(M^2) for standard self-attention, though exact complexity analysis is not provided in the sources. Performance: The method is part of VolRecon, which uses a combined loss of color and depth. Specific performance metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are not detailed in the provided notes. Strengths: Provides non-local information along the ray, addressing the definition of SRDF. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the volume and projection features fed into it. The Ray Transformer was introduced in the VolRecon paper for generalizable multi-view reconstruction using Signed Ray Distance Functions. It builds upon the concept that SRDF is not locally defined and depends on the closest surface along the entire ray. The attention mechanism is based on linear attention. name: Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF)
body: LIRF is a generalizable radiance field representation that predicts volumetric radiance fields from multi-view images by aggregating local image features via transformer-based attention, conical frustum sampling, and visibility estimation to handle occlusions and scale variations. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Ray Transformer by explicitly modeling the conical volume of each ray through 8-vertex discretization and using a two-token transformer architecture to separate color aggregation from density prediction based on feature consistency. Inputs: A set of V nearby source images Iv and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: A target image rendered from a target viewpoint. Data Structures: Feature Maps: Two maps \mathbf{F}^w and \mathbf{F}^c extracted per source view. \mathbf{F}^w stores features for visibility weight estimation; \mathbf{F}^c stores features for color/density prediction. Conical Frustum: Discretized into M=8 vertices. Tokens: \mathbf{t}0 (visibility), \mathbf{t}1 (color info), \mathbf{t}2 (consistency info), and their transformer outputs \mathbf{t}0', \mathbf{t}1', \mathbf{t}2'. Parameters: V: Number of source views. N: Number of samples along a target ray. M: Number of vertices per conical frustum (M=8). rm: Maximum cone radius, defined as the pixel width of the target image at minimum resolution. s: Latent code representing the relative scale of the target image. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each source image I, extract feature maps using an EDSR network [37]. The last layer is modified to output two channels of features: (\mathbf{F}^w, \mathbf{F}^c) = \mathrm{EDSR}(I) where \mathbf{F}^w is for visibility and \mathbf{F}^c is for color/density. 2. Ray and Frustum Setup: For a target ray, select V neighboring source views. Sample N points along the ray. Represent the continuous conical volume of the ray as a series of conical frustums. Each frustum is discretized using M=8 vertices. 3. Vertex Projection: Project the 8 vertices of each conical frustum onto the V source views to query features \mathbf{f}j^c from \mathbf{F}^c. 4. Local Feature Aggregation (\mathbf{z}): For a sample at 3D position \mathbf{x} within a frustum, compute its aggregated feature \mathbf{z} by weighting the features of the M vertices based on their relative positions \Delta \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{q}j (where \mathbf{q}j is vertex j) and the target scale s: \mathbf{z} = \sum{j=1}^{M} W(||\Delta \mathbf{x}j||2) \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{f}j^c, \Delta \mathbf{x}j, s) The weight function is: W(||\Delta \mathbf{x}j||2) = \frac{||\Delta \mathbf{x}j||2}{\sum{l=1}^{M} ||\Delta \mathbf{x}l||2} where \mathcal{R} is an MLP-based aggregation function. If the target ray projects within the circle of radius rm on the target image plane, features are aggregated from the four neighboring rays passing through the red points in the target image plane. 5. Visibility Weight Estimation: a. Obtain feature patches \mathbf{f}^w from \mathbf{F}^w for the sample. b. Define input token \mathbf{t}0 by concatenating \mathbf{f}^w, the source ray direction \mathbf{d} (in target camera coordinates), and the scale s. Apply positional encoding [44] to \mathbf{d} and relative positions \Delta \mathbf{x}, but not to s: \mathbf{t}0 = \mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{f}^w \parallel \mathbf{d} \parallel s) c. Process \mathbf{t}0 through a self-attention transformer \mathcal{T}1: \mathbf{t}0' = \mathcal{T}1(\mathbf{t}0) d. Compute visibility weights w using an MLP \mathcal{M}w: w = \mathcal{M}w(\mathbf{t}0') The weights represent the probability of the sample being observed by each source view, handling occlusions. 6. Token Creation for Color and Density: a. Create token \mathbf{t}1 (color information) by aggregating \mathbf{z} and w: \mathbf{t}1 = \mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{z} \parallel w) b. Create token \mathbf{t}2 (consistency measure) by computing the weighted mean and weighted variance of \mathbf{z} over all source views based on w, then aggregating: \mathbf{t}2 = \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{z}, w) \parallel \mathrm{var}(\mathbf{z}, w)) Densities are predicted by checking feature consistency, as features are consistent on object surfaces. 7. Transformer Aggregation: Feed \mathbf{t}1 and \mathbf{t}2 into a second self-attention transformer \mathcal{T}2: (\mathbf{t}1', \mathbf{t}2') = \mathcal{T}2(\mathbf{t}1, \mathbf{t}2) 8. Density Prediction: Predict density \sigma using an auto-encoder-style network \mathrm{AE} to aggregate information along the ray, followed by an MLP \mathcal{M}\sigma: \sigma = \mathcal{M}\sigma(\mathrm{AE}(\mathbf{t}2')) 9. Color Prediction: Predict color \mathbf{c} by explicitly blending the features \mathbf{t}1' according to visibility weights w, then passing through an MLP \mathcal{M}c: \mathbf{c} = \mathcal{M}c\left( \sum{k=1}^V (\mathbf{t}{1,k}' wk) \right) 10. Rendering: Render the final color of the target ray via volume rendering using the predicted colors \mathbf{c} and densities \sigma. 11. Optimization: Optimize by calculating the mean squared error between the predicted color and the ground truth color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def extractfeatures(images): """Extracts Fw and Fc from source images using EDSR.""" Fw, Fc = [], [] for img in images: fw, fc = np.zeros((128, 64, 64)), np.zeros((128, 64, 64)) Fw.append(fw) Fc.append(fc) return Fw, Fc def queryfeature(F, uv): """Bilinear interpolation at uv coordinates.""" return np.zeros(128) def computevisibility(fw, d, s): """Visibility estimation pipeline.""" t0 = np.zeros(64) # MLP(fw || d || s) t0prime = np.zeros(64) # T1(t0) w = np.array([0.5]) # Mw(t0') return w def aggregatevertices(fclist, deltax, s): """MLP-based aggregation R over vertices.""" return np.zeros(128) def createtokens(z, w): """Creates t1 and t2 tokens.""" t1 = np.zeros(64) # MLP(z || w) zmean = np.mean(z) zvar = np.var(z) t2 = np.zeros(64) # MLP(mean || var) return t1, t2 def transformeraggregate(t1, t2): """T2 self-attention module.""" return t1, t2 def predictdensity(t2prime): """AE aggregation followed by Msigma.""" return 0.1 def predictcolor(t1primelist, wlist): """Weighted blending followed by Mc.""" blended = sum(t1 w for t1, w in zip(t1primelist, wlist)) return np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) def volumerender(c, sigma): """Standard volume rendering integral.""" return c def LIRF(sourceimages, sourceposes, targetpose, targetscales, rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples=64): Fw, Fc = extractfeatures(sourceimages) V = len(sourceimages) M = 8 samples = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in np.linspace(0.1, 10.0, numsamples)] allt1prime, allw = [], [] for x in samples: # Discretize conical frustum into M vertices vertices = [x + np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0])] M z = np.zeros(128) totaldist = sum(np.linalg.norm(x - q) for q in vertices) for j in range(M): qj = vertices[j] deltax = x - qj distj = np.linalg.norm(deltax) W = distj / totaldist if totaldist > 0 else 0.0 fclist = [queryfeature(Fc[v], np.array([0.5, 0.5])) for v in range(V)] z += W aggregatevertices(fclist, deltax, targetscales) fw = queryfeature(Fw[0], np.array([0.5, 0.5])) d = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) w = computevisibility(fw, d, targetscales) t1, t2 = createtokens(z, w) t1p, t2p = transformeraggregate(t1, t2) allt1prime.append(t1p) allw.append(w) sigma = predictdensity(t2p) c = predictcolor(allt1prime, allw) return volumerender(c, sigma) Training Data Efficiency: LIRF uses significantly fewer training scenes (about 15% of the scenes used by IBRNet or NeuRay). Performance: Outperforms IBRNet, NeuRay, and GeoNeRF on all tested scales (x0.5, x1, x2, x4) in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Scale Handling: Handles low-scale views (x0.5) better than baselines, which suffer from aliasing artifacts. It explicitly modifies the cone radius rm according to pixel size to render low-scale views even if not explicitly trained on them. Strengths: Fewer blurring artifacts and better rendering of small or thin structures. Uses local ray directions in target camera coordinates rather than global world coordinates for better generalization. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that occluded content appears in most source views, which is a compromise for solving occlusions without geometric priors. LIRF was introduced in the paper "Local Implicit Ray Function for Generalizable Radiance Field Representation". It builds on the concept of generalizable radiance fields, moving away from coordinate-based MLPs (like standard NeRF) towards image-feature-based aggregation. It is part of the family of transformer-based architectures for novel view synthesis, specifically addressing the challenges of scale variation and occlusion in generalizable settings. name: Transformers and Vision Transformers (ViT)
head: Vision Transformer
body: Transformers compute pairwise attention over input tokens to capture long-range dependencies that convolutions miss. The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts this architecture for images by treating fixed-size patches as tokens. Builds on Transformer-based Architectures. In volume rendering, ViT is used for super-resolution and denoising, where its ability to attend across the full spatial extent of a subvolume helps recover large-scale structures that local convolutions miss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of tokens derived from fixed-size patches of an image or volume slice. Output: A sequence of transformed tokens used for volume super-resolution and denoising. Data Structures: Tokens: A matrix X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}, where N is the number of patches and d is the embedding dimension. Task Relevance Score: A scalar or vector TR used to modulate attention weights per task. Steps: 1. Patch Tokenization: The input is divided into non-overlapping fixed-size patches, which are treated as input tokens. 2. Pairwise Self-Attention: The Transformer computes attention over all pairs of input tokens to capture long-range dependencies. 3. Task Dynamic Modulation: In multi-task environments, a modulation layer adjusts self-attention weights by computing a task relevance score TR for each feature, optimizing weight distribution per attention head based on task-specific contextual information. Positional encodings are dynamically adjusted using the task relevance score: PE(pos, 2i) = \sin\left(pos / 10000^{2i/d{model}}\right) \cdot TR PE(pos, 2i + 1) = \cos\left(pos / 10000^{2i/d{model}}\right) \cdot TR where pos is the position index, i is the dimension index, d{model} is the model dimension, and TR is the task relevance score. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Positional Information: The permutation-invariant nature of attention requires explicit positional encoding to preserve spatial structure. Computational Cost: Self-attention scales quadratically with the number of tokens, which can be prohibitive for high-resolution volume data without optimization. Fusion ViT is a neural module designed to fuse multi-view features by performing all-to-all self-attention over encoded image patches or rendered feature vectors from multiple input views. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and incomplete context in neural rendering and tomographic reconstruction by providing each view's features with full spatial and semantic context from all other views. It distinguishes itself from standard fusion methods by leveraging the Transformer's ability to model long-range dependencies across views, either at the patch level for global reconstruction or at the pixel level for lightweight synthesis. A layer that adjusts self-attention weights according to task demands by computing a task relevance score for each feature, allowing the model to focus on information relevant to specific tasks (texture, shape, color, depth) in a multi-task learning environment. It optimizes the weight distribution of each head in the attention mechanism by analyzing task-related contextual information. Strengths: Captures long-range dependencies across the full spatial extent of a subvolume, effectively recovering large-scale structures that local convolutions miss. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Volume super-resolution and denoising tasks where global context is required to recover large-scale structures. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Transformer architecture computes pairwise attention over input tokens to capture long-range dependencies. The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts this for images by treating fixed-size patches as tokens. In the context of scientific volume visualization and rendering, Transformers have been applied to super-resolution and denoising tasks to leverage their global receptive field. name: Fusion ViT
head: Fusion Transformer (in the context of pixel-wise feature fusion)
body: Fusion ViT is a neural module designed to fuse multi-view features by performing all-to-all self-attention over encoded image patches or rendered feature vectors from multiple input views. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and incomplete context in neural rendering and tomographic reconstruction by providing each view's features with full spatial and semantic context from all other views. It distinguishes itself from standard fusion methods by leveraging the Transformer's ability to model long-range dependencies across views, either at the patch level for global reconstruction or at the pixel level for lightweight synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: The method accepts encoded features from K input views. In the global reconstruction setting, inputs are concatenated encoded image patches \{\tilde{H}1, \tilde{H}2, \dots, \tilde{H}K\}. In the pixel-wise setting, inputs are rendered feature vectors from N views at each pixel location. The output is a set of fused tokens \{F1, F2, \dots, FK\} or a fused feature map \tilde{F}. Data Structures: The core data structure is a sequence of tokens. For the ViT-B/16 variant, each token has an embedding dimension of 768. The patches are typically 16 \times 16 pixels. Parameters: Architecture: Vision Transformer Base (ViT-B/16). Layers: 12 layers (the implementation details specify 12 layers, though the notes mention 16). Heads: 12 attention heads. Embedding Dimension: 768. MLP Ratio: 4.0 (hidden dimension is 4 \times 768 = 3072). Patch Size: 16 \times 16. Initialization: Initialized from scratch. (Note: The encoder preceding the fusion module may use DINO pre-trained weights). Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Input views are processed by an encoder (e.g., ViT-B/16) to produce encoded patches \tilde{H}i. 2. Concatenation: Encoded patches from all K views are concatenated into a single sequence. 3. Self-Attention Fusion: The concatenated sequence is passed through a Transformer \mathcal{F}{fuse}. This module performs all-to-all self-attention, allowing every token to attend to every other token across all views. 4. Output Generation: The output of the transformer is a set of fused tokens \{F1, \dots, FK\}, where each Fi contains context from all other views. Formula: The fusion operation is defined as: \{F1, F2, \dots, FK\} = \mathcal{F}{fuse}(\tilde{H}1, \tilde{H}2, \dots, \tilde{H}K) where \mathcal{F}{fuse} is the fusion transformer, \tilde{H}i are the concatenated encoded image patches, and Fi is the fused token of the i-th view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fusionvit(encodedpatcheslist, numviews, numlayers, embeddim, numheads, mlpratio): # Step 1: Concatenate patches from all views # Shape: [K P, D] tokens = [] for viewpatches in encodedpatcheslist: tokens.extend(viewpatches) # Step 2: Add positional embeddings # Standard ViT requires positional embeddings. We add a learnable lookup table. numpatches = len(tokens) posembed = [0.0] (numpatches embeddim) # Learnable parameters tokens = [t + p for t, p in zip(tokens, posembed)] # Step 3: Pass through Transformer Encoder for in range(numlayers): # LayerNorm before attention tokens = layernorm(tokens) # Multi-Head Self-Attention attnout = multiheadattention(tokens, embeddim, numheads) tokens = [t + a for t, a in zip(tokens, attnout)] # Residual connection # LayerNorm before MLP tokens = layernorm(tokens) # MLP mlpout = mlp(tokens, embeddim, mlpratio) tokens = [t + m for t, m in zip(tokens, mlpout)] # Residual connection # Step 4: Split back into per-view tokens patchesperview = len(encodedpatcheslist[0]) fusedtokenslist = [] for i in range(numviews): fusedtokenslist.append(tokens[i patchesperview: (i + 1) patchesperview]) return fusedtokenslist def layernorm(x): # Standard LayerNorm: normalize feature vectors to zero mean and unit variance. mean = sum(x) / len(x) std = (sum((xi - mean)2 for xi in x) / len(x) + 1e-5)0.5 return [(xi - mean) / std for xi in x] def multiheadattention(x, embeddim, numheads): # Standard MHA: splits heads, computes QKV dot-products, applies softmax, projects back. # Returns output tensor of same shape as input. return x def mlp(x, embeddim, mlpratio): # Standard MLP: Linear -> GELU -> Linear. # Returns output tensor of same shape as input. return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Cues: In pixel-wise variants, rendered results may lose geometry cues (e.g., depth-based occlusion) when rendered from 3D to 2D, which can hinder fusion. Position Encoding: Using geometry features as position encoding was explored but found not helpful. A neural module designed to fuse multi-view features and learn view-dependent appearance directly from high-resolution raw RGB inputs. It distinguishes itself by employing an encoder-decoder architecture: the encoder performs self-attention across input views, while the decoder performs cross-attention between a specific query viewpoint and all input views. This enables robust handling of geometry inference and calibration errors. Choose this when view-dependent appearance modeling and handling of sparse-view inconsistencies are critical. See View-to-View Transformer. A lightweight pixel-wise Transformer used to fuse rendered feature maps from N input views on each pixel. It inputs rendered feature vectors and queries fused results using a learnable "token". It utilizes semantics for fusion. It is chosen for real-time novel view synthesis where computational efficiency is paramount. Pitfalls include the loss of geometry cues during 3D-to-2D rendering. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of views K and patches P. Self-attention is O((K \cdot P)^2). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of tokens and layers. The ViT-B/16 variant uses 12 layers with 768-dim embeddings. Performance: The model is trained end-to-end with photometric and perceptual losses. It supports variable-view learning with 6, 8, or 10 views. Strengths: Provides full context from all views, enabling complete spatial and context reasoning. Handles multi-view inconsistency. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to self-attention over all views. May lose geometry cues if not properly encoded. When to use: Sparse-view tomographic reconstruction or real-time novel view synthesis. When not to use: When geometry cues are critical and cannot be adequately captured by semantic features. Fusion ViT originates from the application of Vision Transformers to multi-view reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The specific ViT-B/16 fusion module was introduced in X-GRM for sparse-view X-ray to CT reconstruction. The pixel-wise variant was proposed in FWD for real-time novel view synthesis. X-GRM: Large Gaussian Reconstruction Model for Sparse-view X-rays to Computed Tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2505.15235, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) FWD: Real-time Novel View Synthesis with Forward Warping and Depth, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01526, fetched 2026-10-29

name: View-to-View Transformer
body: The View-to-View Transformer is a neural module designed to fuse multi-view features and predict view-dependent appearance directly from high-resolution input images, thereby alleviating multi-view inconsistency and calibration errors. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Fusion ViT by employing a specific encoder-decoder architecture that separates feature fusion (encoder) from view-dependent query processing (decoder), allowing it to handle relationships between input views and a specific query viewpoint more robustly than self-attention-only approaches. The method takes N input images I1, \dots, IN and a 3D point x as inputs, and outputs a color embedding ec and fused geometry features \Phi(x). The architecture consists of an Encoder and a Decoder. Data Structures and Inputs: \phii(x, Ii): Pixel-aligned feature vector extracted from the i-th input image Ii at the projection of point x. di: Viewing direction of the i-th input camera in its own coordinate system. dq: Viewing direction of the query camera. pi: Raw RGB color value at the projection of x in the i-th image. \gamma(\cdot): Colored encoding function mapping raw RGB values to a higher-dimensional space to capture high-frequency appearance variations. e{db}: Double embedding (geometry and appearance shared representation) generated by the encoder. Step 1: Encoder (Multi-View Feature Fusion) The encoder fuses geometry features from all input views using self-attention. 1. Feature Preparation: For each view i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, concatenate the pixel-aligned feature \phii(x, Ii) with the viewing direction di: \Phii = \oplus(\phii(x, Ii), di) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 2. Attention Inputs: Pass the set of fused features \{\Phi1, \dots, \PhiN\} through linear layers to generate Query (Qe), Key (Ke), and Value (Ve) matrices: Qe, Ke, Ve = F{Q,K,V}(\phi1, \dots, \phiN) Here, F{Q,K,V} represents the linear projection layers. 3. Self-Attention: Compute the multi-head attention output: \text{Att}{out} = \text{Att}(Qe, Ke, Ve) where \text{Att} is the multi-head attention operation. 4. Feature Fusion: Apply a feed-forward layer Fe to the attention output to produce the fused feature representation \Phi: \Phi = Fe(\text{Att}{out}) This \Phi serves as the conditioned feature for geometry prediction. 5. Double Embedding Generation: Combine the 3D position x (encoded via \gamma(x)) and the fused features \Phi through a double MLP E{db} to generate the double embedding e{db}: e{db} = E{db}(\gamma(x), \Phi) This embedding bridges surface and radiance fields. Step 2: Decoder (View-Dependent Color Prediction) The decoder produces view-dependent color features by attending to input views conditioned on the query view direction. 1. Query Construction: Project the query view direction dq through a linear layer: Qd = F{Qd}(dq) where F{Qd} is a linear layer. 2. Key Construction: Project the viewing directions of all input views \{d1, \dots, dN\} through a linear layer: Kd = F{Kd}(d1, \dots, dN) where F{Kd} is a linear layer. 3. Value Construction: For each view i, concatenate the double embedding e{db} with the colored encoding of the raw RGB value \gamma(pi). These concatenated vectors form the Value inputs: Vd = F{Vd}([e{db}, \gamma(p1)], \dots, [e{db}, \gamma(pN)]) where F{Vd} is a linear layer and [\cdot, \cdot] denotes concatenation. 4. Cross-Attention: Compute the attention between the query view and input views: \text{Att}{cross} = \text{Att}(Qd, Kd, Vd) 5. Color Embedding: Apply a feed-forward layer Fd to the cross-attention output to obtain the color embedding ec: ec = Fd(\text{Att}{cross}) Step 3: Final Color Prediction Pass the color embedding ec through a texture MLP Ec to predict the final high-resolution color c: c = Ec(ec) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewtoviewtransformer(x, dq, inputviews): """ x: 3D point coordinates dq: Query view direction vector inputviews: List of N tuples (phii, di, pi) phii: Pixel-aligned feature from view i di: Input view direction vector pi: Raw RGB value at projection of x in view i """ N = len(inputviews) # --- Encoder --- # 1. Prepare inputs for self-attention # F{Q,K,V} are linear layers applied to phii Qe = [linear(phii) for phii,, in inputviews] Ke = [linear(phii) for phii,, in inputviews] Ve = [linear(phii) for phii,, in inputviews] # 2. Self-Attention attout = multiheadattention(Qe, Ke, Ve) # 3. Feed-Forward to get fused features Phi Phi = feedforward(attout) # 4. Generate Double Embedding # gamma(x) is positional encoding for x edb = doublemlp(concat(positionalencoding(x), Phi)) # --- Decoder --- # 5. Prepare Cross-Attention Inputs # Query is based on dq Qd = linear(dq) # Keys are based on input view directions di Kd = linear([di for, di, in inputviews]) # Values are based on [edb, gamma(pi)] # gamma(pi) is colored encoding for raw RGB pi values = [concat(edb, coloredencoding(pi)) for,, pi in inputviews] Vd = linear(values) # 6. Cross-Attention attcross = multiheadattention(Qd, Kd, Vd) # 7. Feed-Forward to get color embedding ec = feedforward(attcross) # 8. Final Color Prediction c = texturemlp(ec) return c, Phi, edb def linear(x): return x # Standard linear projection layer def concat(a, b): return a + b # Vector concatenation def multiheadattention(Q, K, V): return Q # Standard multi-head attention mechanism def feedforward(x): return x # Standard feed-forward network def positionalencoding(x): return x # Standard positional encoding def coloredencoding(p): return p # Standard colored encoding for RGB def doublemlp(x): return x # Standard multi-layer perceptron def texturemlp(x): return x # Standard multi-layer perceptron Aggregates appearance and geometric information using weight-sharing CNNs and joint multi-view Transformers with visibility-weighted cosine similarities, explicitly modeling multi-view consistency via pairwise similarities rather than simple averaging. The method enables the utilization of original high-resolution images by taking raw RGB values into account, contributing to high-fidelity rendering. It is more robust to geometry inference and calibration errors in real-world multi-view setups compared to methods with limited feature representation power. However, training on high-resolution domains is expensive; the method typically employs a two-phase strategy: large-scale dataset pre-training at low resolution and efficient person-specific high-resolution fine-tuning. The View-to-View Transformer was introduced in the DoubleField framework, which bridges neural surface and radiance fields for high-fidelity human reconstruction and rendering. It addresses limitations in prior methods that relied on low-resolution feature maps or required strict SMPL fitting, allowing DoubleField to handle loose clothing and leverage large-scale human scan datasets. DoubleField: Bridging the Neural Surface and Radiance Fields for High-fidelity Human Reconstruction and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01541, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-View Feature Encoder
head: MuRF Feature Encoder
body: The Multi-View Feature Encoder aggregates information from K input images to create a compact volumetric representation that encodes both appearance and geometry for subsequent radiance field prediction. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and information loss by extracting features via a weight-sharing 2D CNN, quantifying consistency through pairwise cosine similarities, and aggregating these features using learned visibility-aware weights. It sets itself apart from standard feature extractors by explicitly modeling multi-view geometric cues via cosine similarity and using a window-based sampling strategy to mitigate resolution loss from downsampling. Inputs: K input images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. Outputs: A target volume z \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{8} \times \frac{W}{8} \times D \times C}, where H \times W is the image resolution, D is the depth dimension, and C is the channel dimension. Data Structures: 1. Feature Maps: Extracted at 1/8 resolution. 2. Cosine Similarity Matrix: Aggregated scalar \hat{s} per 3D point. 3. Aggregated Vectors: \hat{c} (color) and \hat{f} (feature) per 3D point. Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Extract features \{Fk\}{k=1}^K from the input images using a weight-sharing 2D CNN. The CNN consists of 6 residual blocks [12]. Every 2 residual blocks include a stride-2 convolutional layer, achieving 2× downsampling. Features are obtained at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 resolutions. 2. Multi-View Transformer: Feed the 1/8 resolution convolutional features into a joint multi-view Transformer to refine features at the 1/8 resolution. The Transformer is built on the GMFlow 2-view architecture, extended to K \ge 2 views. 3. Window-Based Sampling: For a 3D point projected to 2D coordinates on the source views, sample a 9 \times 9 window centered at the projection from the feature maps of each view k. This yields a color vector \tilde{c}k for each view, where \tilde{c}k is the concatenation of all colors within the window. Sample image features fi from the K feature maps. 4. Cosine Similarity Computation: Compute pairwise cosine similarities to quantify multi-view consistency. Normalize features to unit vectors and collect them into a matrix F \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times M}, where M is the feature dimension. Compute the matrix product F F^T. Extract the upper triangle of this product to obtain all K(K-1)/2 pairwise cosine similarities \cos(fi, fj) for i < j. Note: Group-wise cosine similarities may be used for improved expressiveness, following the same computation structure. 5. Aggregation of Similarities: Compute the aggregated cosine similarity \hat{s} using learned visibility weights w{ij}: \hat{s} = \sum{i<j} w{ij} \cos(fi, fj) where i, j = 1, \dots, K. The weights w{ij} are normalized visibility weights learned from the entropy of the depth distribution on each ray. 6. Aggregation of Colors and Features: Compute aggregated color \hat{c} and aggregated feature \hat{f} using learned weights wi: \hat{c} = \sum{i=1}^K wi \tilde{c}i, \quad \hat{f} = \sum{i=1}^K wi fi The weights wi are normalized learned weights. A small MLP network predicts wi from the concatenation of the sampled features and the view direction difference between source and target views. 7. Volume Projection: Concatenate the aggregated cosine similarity \hat{s}, the aggregated color \hat{c}, and the aggregated feature \hat{f}. Project this concatenation to a C-dimensional vector using a linear layer. This produces the target volume z \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{8} \times \frac{W}{8} \times D \times C} for all 3D points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MultiViewFeatureEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, K, featuredim, hiddendim, numresblocks=6): super().init() self.K = K # 2D CNN with weight sharing across views # Consists of 6 residual blocks, stride-2 conv every 2 blocks self.cnn = self.buildcnn(featuredim, numresblocks) # Joint multi-view Transformer (based on GMFlow extension) self.transformer = JointMultiViewTransformer(featuredim, K) # MLP to predict aggregation weights wi self.weightmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(featuredim 2 + 3, hiddendim), # features + view diff nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) # Linear projection for final volume channels # Input dim: 1 (similarity) + 813 (color window) + featuredim colorwindowdim = 81 3 self.projection = nn.Linear(1 + colorwindowdim + featuredim, C) def buildcnn(self, outdim, numblocks): # Simplified CNN structure: 6 res blocks, stride-2 every 2 blocks # Results in 1/8 resolution features layers = [] # Initial conv to match input channels layers.append(nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 7, padding=3)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) currentdim = 64 for i in range(numblocks): layers.append(ResBlock(currentdim)) if (i + 1) % 2 == 0: layers.append(nn.Conv2d(currentdim, currentdim 2, 3, stride=2, padding=1)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) currentdim = 2 # Final conv to match featuredim layers.append(nn.Conv2d(currentdim, outdim, 1)) return nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, images): # images: (B, K, 3, H, W) B, K, Cin, H, W = images.shape # Step 1: Extract features using weight-sharing CNN # Reshape to process all views through the same CNN imagesflat = images.view(B K, Cin, H, W) featuresraw = self.cnn(imagesflat) # (BK, featuredim, H/8, W/8) featuresraw = featuresraw.view(B, K, -1, H//8, W//8) # Step 2: Joint Multi-View Transformer featurestf = self.transformer(featuresraw) # (B, K, featuredim, H/8, W/8) # Step 3: Window Sampling # Sample 9x9 window centered at 2D projection. # Assuming we have 3D points projected to 2D (u, v) for each view. # For implementation, we assume a grid of 3D points is provided or # we are computing this for a frustum volume. # Here we demonstrate the aggregation logic for a single 3D point's projection # across K views. # Let's assume we have projected coordinates (u, v) for the target volume grid # Shape: (H/8, W/8, D, 2) # We need to sample features and colors from featurestf # For simplicity, assume we are aggregating for a specific set of 3D points # represented by their 2D projections in each view. # In practice, this is done via gridsample or similar for the whole volume. # Step 4 & 5: Cosine Similarity # Normalize features featuresnorm = F.normalize(featurestf, p=2, dim=2) # (B, K, M, H/8, W/8) # Compute pairwise cosine similarities in parallel # Matrix multiplication: (B, K, M) x (B, M, K) -> (B, K, K) # We need to handle the spatial dimensions. # Let's flatten spatial dims for similarity computation B, K, M, Hs, Ws = featuresnorm.shape featuresflat = featuresnorm.view(B, K, M, -1) # (B, K, M, HsWs) # Transpose for matmul: (B, K, M, HsWs) -> (B, K, HsWs, M) # Actually, we want (K, M) x (K, M)^T for each spatial location # So we permute to (B, HsWs, K, M) featuresperm = featuresflat.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # (B, HsWs, K, M) # Cosine similarity matrix: (B, HsWs, K, K) simmatrix = torch.bmm(featuresperm, featuresperm.transpose(1, 2)) # Extract upper triangle (excluding diagonal) # Indices i < j idxi, idxj = torch.triuindices(K, K, offset=1) # Gather similarities # simmatrix shape: (B, HsWs, K, K) # We want to aggregate these with weights wij # wij depends on depth entropy, assumed available or learned # Step 6: Aggregation of Colors and Features # Sample colors from original images (downsampled to 1/8) imagesdown = F.interpolate(images, scalefactor=0.125, mode='bilinear') # (B, K, 3, H/8, W/8) # Sample 9x9 windows for colors and features # This requires gridsample with padding or manual window extraction # Assuming a function samplewindow exists that extracts 9x9 patches # and returns flattened vectors # For the sake of the algorithm description, we assume: # ctildek: (B, HsWs, 813) # fi: (B, HsWs, M) # Compute weights wi using MLP # Input: concatenated features and view direction difference # View direction difference is not explicitly defined in the snippet # but mentioned as input to MLP. We assume it's available as viewdiff # Shape: (B, K, 3) or similar. # Predict wi # wiraw = MLP(concat(fi, viewdiff)) # wi = softmax(wiraw) # Aggregate # chat = sum(wi ctildei) # fhat = sum(wi fi) # Step 7: Projection # Concatenate shat, chat, fhat # Project to C dimensions return volumez Parameters: K: Number of input views. C: Output channel dimension of the volume. Window size: 9 \times 9. CNN: 6 residual blocks with stride-2 convolutions every 2 blocks. Edge Cases: Resolution Loss: The 8× subsampling risks losing information. The 9 \times 9 window sampling remedies this by capturing local context. Small vs Large Baseline: The method is designed to work on both small and large baseline input views by modeling 3D context. The 3D Transformer Network Refinement (also known as the Point Transformer Network) is a module used to optimize the appearance and geometric attributes of selected 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) tokens. It builds on Multi-View Feature Encoder by processing encoded features through a hierarchical point transformer architecture. What sets it apart from global attention mechanisms is its use of local attention, which allows each Gaussian to refine its features based on spatial neighbors, preserving fine-grained structural details while preventing influence from distant, unrelated Gaussians. Temporal Mutual Self Attention (TMSA) is a transformer module designed for feature alignment, fusion, and refinement across multi-view perspectives or adjacent video frames. It serves as the core component of the Video Restoration Transformer (VRT) network, addressing the problem of aggregating spatio-temporal information by bidirectionally aligning features from adjacent frames and extracting intra-frame context. Unlike standard self-attention which processes a single sequence, TMSA explicitly models inter-frame dependencies through Mutual Attention (MMA) while preserving intra-frame structure via Multi-Head Self-Attention (MSA). Time Complexity: The pairwise cosine similarity computation is optimized to a single matrix multiplication F F^T, making it efficient for parallelization. The MLP for weight prediction is lightweight. Memory Complexity: The method uses a target volume at 1/8 resolution, which is more compact than full-resolution volumes. The channel dimension is reduced (e.g., from 128 to 16 in the fine stage) for efficiency. Strengths: Explicitly models multi-view geometric cues via cosine similarity. Window-based sampling mitigates resolution loss. Efficient aggregation using learned weights. Limitations: Requires K input images. The quality depends on the accuracy of the depth distribution entropy for visibility weights. The Multi-View Feature Encoder is a key component of the MuRF (Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields) framework. It was introduced to aggregate essential information for learning feed-forward NeRF models, addressing the challenges of multi-view inconsistency and the need for geometric cues in radiance field prediction. The method builds upon GMFlow's 2-view Transformer architecture, extending it to handle K views. name: 3D Transformer Network Refinement
head: Point Transformer Network
body: The 3D Transformer Network Refinement (also known as the Point Transformer Network) is a module used to optimize the appearance and geometric attributes of selected 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) tokens. It builds on Multi-View Feature Encoder by processing encoded features through a hierarchical point transformer architecture. What sets it apart from global attention mechanisms is its use of local attention, which allows each Gaussian to refine its features based on spatial neighbors, preserving fine-grained structural details while preventing influence from distant, unrelated Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Encoded features for a set of N 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \gammai. Output: Refined geometric features fi^{(p)''} and appearance features fi^{(a)'} for each Gaussian, which are used to update the Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: The network operates on a set of point features. For each Gaussian i, the input is a feature vector. The architecture uses a hierarchical downsampling structure with 5 stages. The number of transformer blocks per stage is (2, 2, 2, 4, 2). Each MLP layer consists of linear layers followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation. Steps: 1. Dual-Branch Encoding: Process the raw Gaussian parameters through a dual-branch encoder to balance high-dimensional appearance features with geometric information. Geometric Branch: Compute the geometric feature vector fi^{(p)} by concatenating position, rotation, and scale: fi^{(p)} = \text{concat}(\mui, qi, si) Appearance Branch: Compute the appearance feature vector fi^{(a)} by concatenating opacity and reduced color features obtained by applying an MLP \phi to the spherical harmonic coefficients: fi^{(a)} = \text{concat}(\alphai, \phi(\gammai)) Feature Fusion: Apply separate MLPs \phip and \phia to extract corresponding features. Introduce a position encoding module \psi using solely explicit 3D coordinates \mui to reinforce spatial locations. Compute the refined appearance feature fi^{(a)'} using point-wise multiplication: fi^{(a)'} = fi^{(a)} + \sigma(\phia(fi^{(a)}) + \deltai) \odot (\phip(fi^{(p)}) + \deltai) where \deltai = \psi(\mui) and \sigma is the softmax function. Geometric Refinement: Compute the refined geometric feature fi^{(p)'} by adding the original geometric feature to the transformed appearance feature: fi^{(p)'} = fi^{(p)} + fi^{(a)'} 2. Point Transformer Processing: Pass the refined geometric features fi^{(p)'} through the 3D point transformer network (PT) to optimize attributes: fi^{(p)''} = \text{PT}(fi^{(p)'})) The point transformer employs local attention mechanisms. Parameters: Architecture: 5-stage hierarchical downsampling with transformer block counts (2, 2, 2, 4, 2). MLP Layers: Linear layers followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation. Loss Function: The optimization uses L = L1 + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS} with \lambda{LPIPS} = 0.1. Opacity Weight: \lambda\alpha = 0.3 is fixed for both datasets. Learning Rate: Initialized to 1e-5 and dropped by 10 at iteration 6,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Imbalance: Without the dual-branch encoder, the dominance of high-dimensional spherical harmonic coefficients can overshadow geometric factors, leading to biased feature learning. Position Encoding: The position encoding module \psi uses only explicit 3D coordinates \mui, not intrinsic properties like scale or rotation, to ensure focus on physical 3D space. The Dual-Branch Encoder is a preprocessing module that processes Gaussian parameters through two parallel branches (geometric and appearance) to balance high-dimensional appearance features with geometric information before feeding them into the point transformer. It computes geometric features fi^{(p)} by concatenating position \mui, rotation qi, and scale si, and appearance features fi^{(a)} by concatenating opacity \alphai and reduced color features \phi(\gammai). It fuses these features using MLPs \phip, \phia and position encoding \psi(\mui) to produce refined features, addressing the feature imbalance caused by SH coefficient dominance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ScanNet++. The method improves scene quality and spatial coverage by refining sparse Gaussians that share similar properties (e.g., floors, walls). Strengths: Local attention preserves fine-grained structural details; learning features across multiple scenes allows refinement of sparse Gaussians; can be applied directly to pretrained 3DGS models without additional fine-tuning. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When optimizing appearance and geometric attributes of selected Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly to balance appearance and geometry features and capture common structural characteristics across scenes. When not: Not given in the sources. The 3D Transformer Network Refinement was introduced in the paper "PointSplat: Efficient Geometry-Driven Pruning and Transformer Refinement for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon prior works such as SplatFormer [6] and addresses limitations in feature representation by introducing a dual-branch encoder and local attention mechanisms. The method is designed to improve novel view synthesis quality by refining 3D Gaussian parameters. name: 3D Spatial Grouping Network
head: Stage 2 Network for 3D Serialization and Grouping
body: The 3D Spatial Grouping Network is a Stage 2 refinement module that optimizes the geometric and appearance attributes of 3D Gaussian Splatting tokens by leveraging local attention mechanisms on sparse 3D points. It builds on 3D Transformer Network Refinement by explicitly handling sparsity through space-filling curve serialization and localized grouping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 1024-dimensional GS tokens lifted into 3D space, concatenated with a 256-dimensional error feature map (comprising a 128-channel error branch and a 128-channel image branch). Output: A 1024-dimensional residual update applied to each GS token. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 384^3 grid covering the scene bounding box. Serialization: Points are serialized along four space-filling curves: Z-order, Hilbert, and their transposed variants. Grouping: Points are grouped into blocks of S=8 consecutive points in the serialized order. Algorithm: 1. Feature Fusion: Project the 1024-dimensional GS token to 512 dimensions. Concatenate this with the 256-dimensional error feature. Project the result to a 512-dimensional point feature. 2. Voxelization: Voxelize the GS tokens onto the 384^3 grid by quantizing coordinates to integer grid indices. 3. Serialization: Assign one of the four space-filling curves (Z-order, Hilbert, or their transposes) to each of the 4 transformer blocks. 4. Local Attention: For each block, compute self-attention within groups of S=8 consecutive points based on the assigned serialization. 5. Residual Update: Map the output of the transformer blocks back to a 1024-dimensional residual and add it to the original GS token. Network Structure: Blocks: 4 pre-norm transformer blocks. Feature Dimension: 512. MLP Ratio: 4. Self-Attention: Computed in a 256-dimensional subspace with 16 heads of dimension 16. Parameters: 13.2M trainable parameters. Iteration: Applied with T=4 steps, sharing weights across all steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialgroupingnetwork(gstokens1024, errorfeature256, coords, bboxmin, bboxmax): N = gstokens1024.shape[0] # Step 1: Feature Fusion # Project 1024-dim token to 512-dim, concatenate with 256-dim error feature, fuse to 512-dim gsproj = gstokens1024 @ W1024to512.T + b1024to512 combined = np.concatenate([gsproj, errorfeature256], axis=-1) pointfeatures = combined @ W768to512.T + b768to512 # Step 2: Voxelization gridsize = 384 cellsize = (bboxmax - bboxmin) / gridsize gridindices = np.floor((coords - bboxmin) / cellsize).astype(int) gridindices = np.clip(gridindices, 0, gridsize - 1) # Step 3: Serialization & Step 4: Local Attention # Four blocks, each uses a different space-filling curve curves = ['zorder', 'hilbert', 'zordertransposed', 'hilberttransposed'] residual = pointfeatures for blockidx in range(4): # Compute curve index on quantized grid coordinates curveindices = computecurveindex(gridindices, curves[blockidx]) sortorder = np.argsort(curveindices) sortedfeatures = pointfeatures[sortorder] # Step 4: Local Attention within groups of S=8 S = 8 numgroups = (N + S - 1) // S groupoutputs = [] for g in range(numgroups): start = g S end = min(start + S, N) group = sortedfeatures[start:end] # Self-attention in 256-dim subspace, 16 heads, head dim 16 attnout = multiheadattention(group, dim=256, numheads=16, headdim=16) groupoutputs.append(attnout) # Scatter back to original positions updatedfeatures = np.zeroslike(pointfeatures) for g, out in enumerate(groupoutputs): start = g S end = min(start + S, N) updatedfeatures[sortorder[start:end]] = out residual = residual + updatedfeatures # Step 5: Final Linear Layer finalresidual = residual @ W512to1024.T + b512to1024 updatedgstokens = gstokens1024 + finalresidual return updatedgstokens def computecurveindex(coords, curvetype): # Standard space-filling curve index computation if curvetype == 'zorder': return mortonencode(coords) elif curvetype == 'hilbert': return hilbertencode(coords) # Transposed variants apply axis permutation before encoding return mortonencode(coords[:, [1, 0, 2]]) def mortonencode(coords): # Bit-interleaving of coordinate indices indices = np.floor((coords - np.min(coords, axis=0)) / np.ptp(coords, axis=0) 1024).astype(int) return interleavedbits(indices) def hilbertencode(coords): # Standard Hilbert curve mapping algorithm return standardhilbert(coords) def multiheadattention(x, dim, numheads, headdim): # Standard MHA: Q,K,V = x @ W, split heads, softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V, concat, linear out return standardmha(x, dim, numheads, headdim) Parameters: Grid Size: 384^3. Group Size (S): 8. Number of Blocks: 4. Number of Iterations (T): 4. Feature Dimension: 512. Attention Subspace: 256. Number of Heads (Stage 2): 16. Head Dimension: 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Voxelization on a 384^3 grid may lose precision for very small or widely dispersed Gaussians if the bounding box is not tightly fitted. Boundaries: Points near the boundary of the bounding box may be truncated or incorrectly assigned if voxelization logic does not handle edge cases. A hierarchical transformer network for Stage 1 that processes image patches with increasing coarseness, using frame-wise and view-wise attention to aggregate features across views. It splits views into non-overlapping groups of two adjacent frames for view-wise group attention layers. The network has 14 layers: Layers 1-2 use 4x4 patch tokens (256-dim) with frame-wise attention; Layers 3-6 use 8x8 patch tokens (512-dim) with frame-wise and view-wise group attention; Layers 7-14 use 16x16 patch tokens (1024-dim) with frame-wise and global attention. All attention modules use a head dimension of 64. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the 384^3 voxel grid and the storage of GS tokens and error features. Performance: The network has 13.2M trainable parameters. It is applied with T=4 steps with weight sharing. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse 3D data by leveraging spatial locality via space-filling curves. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The 3D Spatial Grouping Network is part of the FineSplat architecture, introduced in 2026. It follows Point Transformer V3 for 3D serialization and grouping. The method is trained in three phases: Stage 1, Stage 2 (this network), and end-to-end fine-tuning.
