name: Temporal Mutual Self Attention (TMSA)
head: Video Restoration Transformer (VRT) module
body: Temporal Mutual Self Attention (TMSA) is a transformer module designed for feature alignment, fusion, and refinement across multi-view perspectives or adjacent video frames. It serves as the core component of the Video Restoration Transformer (VRT) network, addressing the problem of aggregating spatio-temporal information by bidirectionally aligning features from adjacent frames and extracting intra-frame context. Unlike standard self-attention which processes a single sequence, TMSA explicitly models inter-frame dependencies through Mutual Attention (MMA) while preserving intra-frame structure via Multi-Head Self-Attention (MSA). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A feature clip X containing features from two adjacent frames (or views). Output: A refined feature clip X' with enhanced spatio-temporal information. Data Structures: X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times H \times W}: Input tensor, where B is batch size, C is channels, H is height, W is width. X1, X2 \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times (C/2) \times H \times W}: Split halves of the input feature map. Y1, Y2, Y3 \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times (C/2) \times H \times W}: Intermediate feature maps generated by attention modules. F{fused} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times H \times W}: Concatenated and processed fused feature. Parameters: Layer Normalization (LayerNorm): Applied to stabilize distribution. Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP): Used for dimensionality reduction and feed-forward processing. Concatenation (Concat): Channel-wise concatenation. Residual Connections: Element-wise addition. Steps: 1. Normalization: Apply LayerNorm to the input feature clip X to stabilize its distribution. 2. Splitting: Split the normalized features into two halves, X1 and X2, along the channel dimension. 3. Parallel Attention Processing: First Mutual Attention (MMA): Warp features of X2 to align with X1. This module performs bidirectional feature alignment and fusion, generating fused feature Y1 which contains information from the adjacent frame. Second Mutual Attention (MMA): Perform the reverse operation by warping features of X1 to align with X2. This generates fused feature Y2. Self Attention (MSA): Concatenate X1 and X2 and apply Multi-Head Self-Attention. This extracts intra-frame contextual information, generating feature Y3. 4. Aggregation: Concatenate Y1, Y2, and Y3 sequentially to form a fused feature vector encapsulating rich spatio-temporal information. 5. Dimensionality Reduction: Pass the concatenated fused feature through a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to reduce dimensionality. 6. First Residual Connection: Add the original input X to the output of the attention sub-module block (the result of step 5) via element-wise addition. 7. Feed-Forward Network (FFN): Process the result from step 6 through an FFN, which consists of a LayerNorm layer and an MLP. 8. Second Residual Connection: Add the output of the FFN to the result from step 6 (the input to the FFN) via element-wise addition to yield the final refined feature clip X'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TMSA(X): # X: Input feature clip [B, C, H, W] # Step 1: Normalization Xnorm = LayerNorm(X) # Step 2: Splitting mid = Xnorm.shape[1] // 2 X1, X2 = Xnorm[:,:mid,:,:], Xnorm[:, mid:,:,:] # Step 3: Parallel Attention # First MMA: Warp X2 to align with X1 # Sources do not specify the exact warping or attention formulas Y1 = MMAWarpAndAlign(X1, X2) # Second MMA: Warp X1 to align with X2 Y2 = MMAWarpAndAlign(X2, X1) # MSA: Concatenate X1 and X2 and apply Multi-Head Self-Attention Xconcat = Concat([X1, X2], axis=1) Y3 = MultiHeadSelfAttention(Xconcat) # Step 4: Aggregation Fconcat = Concat([Y1, Y2, Y3], axis=1) # Step 5: Dimensionality Reduction Freduced = MLP(Fconcat) # Step 6: First Residual Connection Res1 = X + Freduced # Step 7: Feed-Forward Network FFNout = MLP(LayerNorm(Res1)) # Step 8: Second Residual Connection Xout = Res1 + FFNout return Xout def LayerNorm(x): # Normalizes over channels and spatial dimensions mu = x.mean(dim=(1, 2, 3), keepdim=True) std = x.std(dim=(1, 2, 3), keepdim=True) return (x - mu) / (std + 1e-5) def Concat(tensors, axis=1): # Standard concatenation operation return concatenate(tensors, dim=axis) def MultiHeadSelfAttention(x): # Standard MHA implementation B, C, H, W = x.shape xflat = x.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(B H W, C) Q = xflat @ Wq K = xflat @ Wk V = xflat @ Wv attn = softmax((Q @ K.T) / (C0.5), dim=-1) out = attn @ V return out.reshape(B, H, W, C).permute(0, 3, 1, 2) def MMAWarpAndAlign(Xref, Xtgt): # Sources do not specify the warping or attention mechanism # Standard implementation would compute a geometric transform to warp Xtgt # to the coordinate system of Xref, followed by dot-product attention. pass def MLP(x): # Standard 2-layer MLP with GELU activation x = x @ W1 + b1 x = gelu(x) return x @ W2 + b2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alignment Precision: The Mutual Attention modules rely on warping features. The exact warping mechanism is not specified in the sources. Gradient Flow: The two residual connections are critical for mitigating the vanishing gradient problem in deep networks. Channel Splitting: The split assumes an even number of channels. If C is odd, padding or uneven splitting must be handled, though the source does not specify this detail. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for feature alignment, fusion, and refinement across multi-view perspectives; captures both inter-frame (via MMA) and intra-frame (via MSA) contextual information. Limitations: Relies on the effectiveness of the warping mechanism in MMA modules. When to use: Suitable for video restoration and multi-view reconstruction tasks where feature alignment across adjacent frames or views is critical. When not to use: Not suitable for single-frame processing without temporal or multi-view context, as the MMA modules require paired inputs. The Temporal Mutual Self Attention (TMSA) module was introduced as the core component of the Video Restoration Transformer (VRT) network. It was designed to facilitate efficient information aggregation across multi-view perspectives. The module is described in the context of a dual-prior driven Gaussian splatting framework for high-fidelity reconstruction of museum artifacts. name: Line Segment-based Transformer (Lineformer)
head: LS-MSA, Line Segment-based Multi-Head Self-Attention, Lineformer
body: The Line Segment-based Transformer (Lineformer) is a neural architecture designed for sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstruction, specifically serving as the backbone for Structure-Aware X-ray Neural Radiodensity Fields (SAX-NeRF). It solves the problem of capturing internal 3D structural dependencies in X-ray projections by computing self-attention locally within line segments of an X-ray, rather than globally across all sampled points. Unlike vanilla Transformers which exhibit quadratic computational complexity relative to the number of input points, Lineformer achieves linear complexity, making it efficient enough to integrate into iterative volume rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of X-ray rays. For each ray, N points are sampled along the ray path. Each point is represented by its 3D position \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The input to the attention module is the point feature matrix \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}, where C is the channel dimension. Output: A refined feature representation \mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} and, subsequently, a predicted radiodensity value D \in \mathbb{R}^N for each point. Data Structures: Point Features (\mathbf{X}): A matrix of shape N \times C. Segmented Features (\mathbf{X}i): Sub-matrices of shape \frac{N}{M} \times C, where M is the number of line segments. Attention Heads (\mathbf{Q}i^j, \mathbf{K}i^j, \mathbf{V}i^j): Matrices of shape \frac{N}{M} \times dh, where dh = C/k. Learnable Scale (\alphai^j): A scalar parameter for each head and segment. Parameters: N: Number of sampled points along an X-ray. Typical value: 320. M: Number of line segments the input points are partitioned into. Not given in the sources. k: Number of attention heads. Not given in the sources. C: Channel dimension of the point features. Not given in the sources. dh: Dimension for each attention head, calculated as dh = C/k. Algorithm Steps: 1. Hash Encoding: The 3D positions \mathbf{P} of the N sampled points are fed into a hash encoding module \mathcal{H} to produce initial point features \mathbf{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}. \mathbf{F} = \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{P}) 2. Partitioning: The input feature matrix \mathbf{X} (initially \mathbf{F}, or the output of previous layers) is partitioned into M contiguous line segments along the point dimension: \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{X}1, \mathbf{X}2, \dots, \mathbf{X}M]^{\text{T}} where each segment \mathbf{X}i \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{N}{M} \times C} for i = 1, \dots, M. 3. Linear Projection: For each segment \mathbf{X}i, linear projections generate Query (\mathbf{Q}i), Key (\mathbf{K}i), and Value (\mathbf{V}i) matrices using learnable weight matrices \mathbf{W}^{\mathbf{Q}i}, \mathbf{W}^{\mathbf{K}i}, \mathbf{W}^{\mathbf{V}i} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}: \mathbf{Q}i = \mathbf{X}i \mathbf{W}^{\mathbf{Q}i}, \quad \mathbf{K}i = \mathbf{X}i \mathbf{W}^{\mathbf{K}i}, \quad \mathbf{V}i = \mathbf{X}i \mathbf{W}^{\mathbf{V}i}. 4. Head Splitting: The Query, Key, and Value matrices for segment i are split into k heads along the channel dimension: \mathbf{Q}i = [\mathbf{Q}i^1, \mathbf{Q}i^2, \dots, \mathbf{Q}i^k], \quad \mathbf{K}i = [\mathbf{K}i^1, \mathbf{K}i^2, \dots, \mathbf{K}i^k], \quad \mathbf{V}i = [\mathbf{V}i^1, \mathbf{V}i^2, \dots, \mathbf{V}i^k] where each head \mathbf{Q}i^j, \mathbf{K}i^j, \mathbf{V}i^j \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{N}{M} \times dh} and dh = C/k. 5. Local Self-Attention: For each head j and segment i, compute the attention output \mathbf{H}i^j: \mathbf{H}i^j = \text{Attn}(\mathbf{Q}i^j, \mathbf{K}i^j, \mathbf{V}i^j) = \mathbf{V}i^j \text{softmax}\left(\frac{{\mathbf{K}i^j}^{\text{T}}\mathbf{Q}i^j}{\alphai^j}\right) where \alphai^j \in \mathbb{R} is a learnable scaling parameter specific to the segment and head. 6. Concatenation and Output: The outputs from all k heads for segment i are concatenated along the channel dimension, passed through a final linear layer, and added with a positional embedding \mathbf{E}i \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{N}{M} \times C} to produce the output segment \mathbf{Y}i: \mathbf{Y}i = \text{Linear}(\text{Concat}(\mathbf{H}i^1, \dots, \mathbf{H}i^k)) + \mathbf{E}i. The final output \mathbf{Y} is the concatenation of all \mathbf{Y}i. 7. Radiodensity Prediction: The output features \mathbf{Y} pass through two fully connected layers to derive the point radiodensity D \in \mathbb{R}^N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class LineSegmentAttention(nn.Module): def init(self, N, M, C, k): super().init() self.N = N self.M = M self.C = C self.k = k self.dh = C // k self.segmentsize = N // M # Learnable weights for linear projections self.WQ = nn.Linear(C, C) self.WK = nn.Linear(C, C) self.WV = nn.Linear(C, C) # Learnable scaling parameters for each segment and head # Shape: [M, k] self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(M, k)) # Final linear layer after concatenation self.outlinear = nn.Linear(C, C) # Positional embedding per segment # Shape: [M, N/M, C] self.posembed = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(M, self.segmentsize, C)) def forward(self, X): """ X: [N, C] Input point features Returns: [N, C] Output features """ # 1. Partition X into M segments Xseg = X.view(self.M, self.segmentsize, self.C) # 2. Linear Projections for each segment Qseg = self.WQ(Xseg) Kseg = self.WK(Xseg) Vseg = self.WV(Xseg) # 3. Split into k heads: [M, N/M, C] -> [M, N/M, k, dh] -> [M, k, N/M, dh] Qheads = Qseg.view(self.M, self.segmentsize, self.k, self.dh).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) Kheads = Kseg.view(self.M, self.segmentsize, self.k, self.dh).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) Vheads = Vseg.view(self.M, self.segmentsize, self.k, self.dh).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) # 4. Compute Attention: K^T Q / alpha # Kheads: [M, k, N/M, dh] -> transpose last two dims -> [M, k, dh, N/M] KT = Kheads.transpose(-2, -1) # Inner product: [M, k, dh, N/M] @ [M, k, N/M, dh] -> [M, k, dh, dh] innerprod = torch.matmul(KT, Qheads) # Scale by alpha: [M, k, 1, 1] alphascaled = self.alpha.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) scaled = innerprod / alphascaled # Softmax over the channel dimension (dh) to normalize weights attnweights = F.softmax(scaled, dim=-1) # Multiply by V: [M, k, N/M, dh] @ [M, k, dh, dh] -> [M, k, N/M, dh] # Flatten batch dims for standard matmul Vflat = Vheads.view(-1, self.segmentsize, self.dh) Attnflat = attnweights.view(-1, self.dh, self.dh) Hflat = torch.matmul(Vflat, Attnflat) # Reshape back to [M, k, N/M, dh] H = Hflat.view(self.M, self.k, self.segmentsize, self.dh) # 5. Concatenate heads: [M, k, N/M, dh] -> [M, N/M, kdh] = [M, N/M, C] Hconcat = H.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous().view(self.M, self.segmentsize, self.C) # 6. Final Linear + Pos Embed Yseg = self.outlinear(Hconcat) + self.posembed # 7. Flatten to [N, C] Y = Yseg.view(self.N, self.C) return Y Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The learnable parameter \alphai^j must be initialized to positive values and constrained during training to avoid zero values, which would cause division by zero in the attention scaling. Segment Size: N must be divisible by M to ensure uniform segment sizes. If not, padding or irregular segmentation is required, which is not described in the source. Channel Dimension: C must be divisible by k to ensure integer head dimensions dh. Time and Memory Complexity: The computational complexity of LS-MSA is \mathcal{O}(\text{LS-MSA}) = \frac{2NC^2}{k}, which is linear with respect to the number of input points N. This is derived from k \times M matrix multiplications of size dh \times \frac{N}{M} and \frac{N}{M} \times dh. In contrast, global multi-head self-attention (G-MSA) has a complexity of \mathcal{O}(\text{G-MSA}) = 2N^2C, which is quadratic in N. Lineformer significantly reduces the computational burden of G-MSA, allowing it to be integrated into each basic unit of the backbone. Measured Performance: On the X3D dataset, SAX-NeRF using Lineformer surpassed previous NeRF-based methods by 12.56 dB on novel view synthesis (NVS) and 2.49 dB on CT reconstruction. Experiments were conducted on an RTX 8000 GPU. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Linear computational complexity enables efficient processing of X-ray rays; captures internal 3D structural dependencies better than global attention on sparse data. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that structural dependencies are local to line segments; performance depends on the effectiveness of the Masked Local-Global (MLG) ray sampling strategy for contextual information. The Line Segment-based Transformer was proposed in the paper "Structure-Aware Sparse-View X-Ray 3D Reconstruction" (SAX-NeRF) by Cai Yuanhao et al., presented at CVPR 2024. It was developed to address the limitations of existing NeRF algorithms in capturing structural contents of imaged objects in sparse-view X-ray tomography. The method is part of a framework that also includes a Masked Local-Global (MLG) ray sampling strategy and utilizes the X3D dataset. name: Volume Slot Attention
head: Slot Attention with GRU
body: Volume Slot Attention is an object-centric representation method that decomposes a 3D volume into a set of K independent semantic slots, enabling the modeling of dynamic scenes and multi-object interactions. It extends the Slot-Attention mechanism to volumetric data by iteratively refining slot features through attention over input features and gating them with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). Unlike standard NeRFs that treat the volume as a monolithic field, this method allows for explicit object decomposition and temporal consistency via recurrent slot updates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input feature vectors ht \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} at timestamp t (derived from voxel or ray features), previous slot features S{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times D}, and a fixed softmax temperature D. Outputs: Updated slot features St \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times D}. Data Structures: Slots: A matrix S of size K \times D, where K is the number of objects/slots and D is the feature dimension. Projections: Learnable linear layers q, k, v: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}^D. Algorithm: The method computes attention between the current input features and the previous slot states, aggregates features, and updates slots using a GRU. This process is repeated R=3 times per timestamp. 1. Compute Attention Weights: Calculate the attention matrix At \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N} using queries derived from previous slots S{t-1} and keys derived from input features ht: At = \mathrm{softmax}\left( \frac{k(ht) \cdot q(S{t-1})^T}{\sqrt{D}} \right) Here, k(\cdot) and q(\cdot) are linear projections. The denominator \sqrt{D} is the fixed softmax temperature. 2. Compute Attention Normalization: Normalize the attention matrix row-wise to obtain weights Wt \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}: W{t,i,j} = \frac{A{t,i,j}}{\sum{l=1}^{N} A{t,l,j}} This ensures that for each slot i, the weights sum to 1 across all input features j. 3. Aggregate Features: Compute the attended feature vector Ut \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times D} by weighting the value projections v(ht): Ut = Wt^T \cdot v(ht) where v(\cdot) is a linear projection. 4. GRU Update: Update the slot features using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with the aggregated features Ut as input and S{t-1} as the hidden state: St = \mathrm{GRU}(Ut, S{t-1}) The GRU typically consists of LayerNorm and a residual MLP as per standard Slot-Attention implementations. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 1–4 for R=3 iterations at each timestamp to obtain the final slot features St. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeslotattention(ht, Sprev, qproj, kproj, vproj, gru, D, numiterations=3): """ ht: Input features [N, D] Sprev: Previous slot features [K, D] qproj, kproj, vproj: Linear projection layers gru: GRU cell D: Feature dimension (used for softmax temperature scaling) """ S = Sprev for in range(numiterations): # 1. Compute attention matrix # k(ht) -> [N, D], q(S) -> [K, D] # Transpose q(S) to [D, K] for matrix multiplication keys = kproj(ht) # [N, D] queries = qproj(S) # [K, D] # Attention scores: [K, N] scores = torch.matmul(queries, keys.transpose(0, 1)) / math.sqrt(D) # 2. Normalize attention weights # Softmax over the last dimension (N) A = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1) # [K, N] # 3. Aggregate features values = vproj(ht) # [N, D] # W^T is effectively A, but we need to multiply A^T (N, K) with values (N, D) # Or equivalently: sum over N: A[k, n] values[n] U = torch.matmul(A.transpose(0, 1), values) # [K, D] # 4. GRU Update S = gru(U, S) return S Parameters: D: Fixed softmax temperature, equal to the feature dimension. Repetition count: 3 iterations per timestamp. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Instability: The iterative update process in Slot-Attention can be susceptible to instability when propagating gradients back through the iterations. Initialization: Standard Slot-Attention uses random initialization for slots, which may lead to suboptimal convergence; learnable initialization (e.g., BO-QSA) is suggested as a mitigation. Slot-Attention is the foundational object-centric attention mechanism upon which Volume Slot Attention is built. It maps N input feature vectors to K output slots via iterative attention where slots compete to explain input features. It is chosen when explicit object decomposition and permutation invariance are required. Unlike Volume Slot Attention, it operates on 2D feature maps or sets of vectors without the volumetric context or temporal GRU recurrence. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot N \cdot D) per attention iteration, where K is slots, N is input features, and D is dimension. With 3 iterations, the cost is triple that of a single attention pass. Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot D + N \cdot D) for storing slots and input features, plus intermediate attention matrices O(K \cdot N). Strengths: Enables explicit object-centric decomposition in 3D, handles dynamic scenes via recurrent updates, and provides interpretable slot representations. Limitations: Sensitive to gradient instability during training; requires careful initialization; computationally more expensive than single-pass attention due to iterations. When to use: When object-centric decomposition and temporal consistency are critical for volumetric scene representation. When not to use: For static scenes where object decomposition is unnecessary, or when computational resources are severely constrained. Volume Slot Attention was introduced in the context of unsupervised learning for dynamic scenes through object-centric voxelization. It builds upon the Slot-Attention mechanism proposed by Locatello et al. and adapts it for volumetric rendering and dynamic scene modeling. The method addresses the limitation of traditional NeRFs in handling multiple objects and temporal dynamics by providing a structured, object-centric representation. name: GAN-based Volume Rendering
head: Generative Model for Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering as GAN
body: This method treats volume rendering as a purely computational process that maps viewpoint and transfer function (TF) parameters directly to a color image, bypassing the explicit use of the volumetric scalar field. It distinguishes itself from traditional differentiable volume rendering by learning a data-driven mapping from visualization parameters to images using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), rather than differentiating through the physical emission-absorption equation. Unlike Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method which combines rasterization with neural networks, or Generative NeRF-to-NeRF Translation which translates between implicit representations, this approach synthesizes the final pixel values directly from parameter vectors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A visualization parameter vector w containing viewpoint parameters v and sampled transfer function values \tau (opacity) and tc (color). Output: A color image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times w \times h} of fixed resolution w \times h. Data Structures: The visualization parameters w are constructed as a concatenation of: 1. Viewpoint vector v \in \mathbb{R}^{nv}, where nv = 5. The five parameters correspond to azimuth, elevation, in-plane rotation, and distance to the camera. The azimuth angle is separated into its cosine and sine components to handle the wrap-around discontinuity at 0 and 2\pi. 2. Opacity TF sampled vector \tau \in \mathbb{R}^{nt}, where nt = 256. 3. Color TF sampled vector tc \in \mathbb{R}^{3nt}, where nt = 256. Thus, w = [v, \tau, tc]. Network Architectures: The method employs a Generator G and a Discriminator D. Generator (G): Transforms the low-dimensional vector w into an image using a DCGAN-style architecture that interleaves upsampling and 2D convolutional layers. Viewpoint components are processed using Fully Connected (FC) layers because they lack spatial correlation. TF components are processed using 1D Convolutional layers because they are 1D signals with spatial dependencies. The generator uses Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) nonlinearities, h(x) = \max(0, x). Batch normalization is applied in 2D convolutional layers to stabilize training by normalizing data using batch-computed mean and standard deviation statistics. Discriminator (D): Takes w and an image I as input and produces a score in [0, 1] indicating if the image is real or fake. It transforms the image into a low-dimensional vector through 2D convolutions with stride 2. It fuses image features with input parameter features. The discriminator uses Leaky ReLU nonlinearities, h(x) = \max(0, x) + \alpha \min(0, x). 1D Convolution Formula: For processing TFs, the 1D convolution is defined as: Z{a,b} = \sum{k=1}^{ci} \sum{l=1}^{w} X{sd \cdot a + l, k} W{l, b, k} where X is the input, W are filter weights, sd is the stride, a is the output position, b is the output channel, k is the input channel, and l is the filter width. Training Procedure: The networks are optimized via a min-max game using the adversarial loss: L{adv}(G, D) = \mathbb{E}{I,w \sim p{data}} [\log(D(w, I))] + \mathbb{E}{w \sim p{vis}} [\log(D(w, G(w)))] where I is a real volume-rendered image, w represents visualization parameters, G is the generator, and D is the discriminator. The first expectation is over the joint distribution of real images and parameters p{data}, and the second is over the distribution of visualization parameters p{vis}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def relu(x): return np.maximum(0, x) def leakyrelu(x, alpha=0.2): return np.maximum(0, x) + alpha np.minimum(0, x) def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-np.clip(x, -500, 500))) def batchnorm(x, gamma, beta, runningmean, runningvar, eps=1e-5, momentum=0.1, training=True): if training: mean = np.mean(x, axis=0, keepdims=True) var = np.var(x, axis=0, keepdims=True) runningmean = (1 - momentum) runningmean + momentum mean runningvar = (1 - momentum) runningvar + momentum var else: mean, var = runningmean, runningvar xnorm = (x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + eps) return gamma xnorm + beta, runningmean, runningvar def compute1dconv(X, W, stride=1): # X: (N, Cin), W: (filterwidth, Cout, Cin) N, Cin = X.shape fw, Cout, = W.shape Nout = (N - fw) // stride + 1 Z = np.zeros((Nout, Cout)) for a in range(Nout): for b in range(Cout): for k in range(Cin): for l in range(fw): idx = stride a + l if 0 <= idx < N: Z[a, b] += X[idx, k] W[l, b, k] return Z def compute2dconv(X, W, stride=1): # X: (H, W, Cin), W: (kh, kw, Cout, Cin) H, Wdim, Cin = X.shape kh, kw, Cout, = W.shape Hout = (H - kh) // stride + 1 Wout = (Wdim - kw) // stride + 1 Z = np.zeros((Hout, Wout, Cout)) for i in range(Hout): for j in range(Wout): for c in range(Cout): for ci in range(Cin): for ki in range(kh): for kj in range(kw): idxi, idxj = stride i + ki, stride j + kj if 0 <= idxi < H and 0 <= idxj < Wdim: Z[i, j, c] += X[idxi, idxj, ci] W[ki, kj, c, ci] return Z def generatorforward(w, params): v = w[:5] tau = w[5:261] tc = w[261:1029] # Viewpoint: Fully Connected layers zv = relu(params['Wv1'] @ v + params['bv1']) zv = relu(params['Wv2'] @ zv + params['bv2']) # TFs: 1D Convolutions ztau = relu(compute1dconv(tau.reshape(-1, 1), params['Wtau'])) ztc = relu(compute1dconv(tc.reshape(-1, 1), params['Wtc'])) # Combine and upsample (DCGAN-style: interleave upsampling and 2D conv) combined = np.concatenate([zv, ztau, ztc], axis=0) grid = combined.reshape(1, 1, 1, -1) for in range(4): # 4 upsampling steps to reach 256x256 grid = np.repeat(np.repeat(grid, 2, axis=1), 2, axis=2) grid = relu(compute2dconv(grid, params['Wup1']) + params['bup1']) grid,, = batchnorm(grid, params['gammaup1'], params['betaup1'], params['rmup1'], params['rvup1']) return grid.transpose(1, 2, 0) # Output shape (256, 256, 3) def discriminatorforward(w, image, params): # image: (256, 256, 3) imgfeat = relu(compute2dconv(image, params['Wimg1'])) imgfeat,, = batchnorm(imgfeat, params['gammaimg1'], params['betaimg1'], params['rmimg1'], params['rvimg1']) imgfeat = compute2dconv(imgfeat, params['Wimg2']) v = w[:5] tau = w[5:261] tc = w[261:1029] zv = relu(params['Wv1'] @ v + params['bv1']) ztau = relu(compute1dconv(tau.reshape(-1, 1), params['Wtau'])) ztc = relu(compute1dconv(tc.reshape(-1, 1), params['Wtc'])) paramfeat = np.concatenate([zv, ztau, ztc], axis=0) # Fuse features (concatenate and project) fused = np.concatenate([imgfeat.flatten(), paramfeat], axis=0) score = sigmoid(params['Wout'] @ fused + params['bout']) return score def trainstep(Gparams, Dparams, realimages, wreal, wfake): fakeimages = generatorforward(wfake, Gparams) dreal = discriminatorforward(wreal, realimages, Dparams) dfake = discriminatorforward(wfake, fakeimages, Dparams) lossD = -np.mean(np.log(dreal + 1e-8)) - np.mean(np.log(1 - dfake + 1e-8)) lossG = -np.mean(np.log(dfake + 1e-8)) return lossD, lossG This method performs spatial super-resolution on volumetric data by decomposing the 3D reconstruction problem into orthogonal 2D slice passes, thereby avoiding the memory costs associated with full 3D convolutions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D GANs by integrating physics-informed constraints directly into the training objective to ensure physically consistent reconstructions, rather than relying solely on statistical error minimization. Generative Adversarial Networks train a generator against a discriminator to produce perceptually realistic outputs rather than merely minimizing pixelwise error. This perceptual advantage makes GANs well-suited for volume super-resolution, where Mean Squared Error (MSE)-optimized outputs tend toward oversmoothing. The method solves the problem of generating high-fidelity volumetric visualizations by replacing explicit volume data with a computational process that maps viewpoints and transfer functions directly to images [Parent]. This is the first learned volume rendering system employing a two-stage conditional GAN architecture. It learns end-to-end mappings from volumetric data and parameters to rendered images, bypassing explicit transfer function specification by encoding opacity transfer functions into a latent space. It encodes opacity transfer functions into an 8-dimensional latent space via 1D convolutions. The first GAN generates 64×64 opacity images conditioned on viewpoint and TF parameters. The second GAN translates these opacity images to 256×256 color renderings using color TF conditioning and skip connections. It was trained on 200,000 procedurally generated samples per volume. The model achieved RMSE of 0.046–0.116 across six datasets, with 7ms inference time for interactive TF sensitivity analysis. It requires per-volume training with no cross-volume generalization, and is limited to 256×256 output resolution and 1D transfer functions. Complexity: The method avoids the O(kn) memory usage of reverse-mode AD associated with storing intermediate states for differentiable volume rendering. Instead, memory usage is determined by the neural network parameters. Performance: Inference is extremely fast (e.g., 7ms for the two-stage variant), enabling interactive exploration. Strengths: Bypasses the need for explicit volume data storage during inference; handles complex mappings between parameters and images; perceptually superior to MSE-based methods. Limitations: Requires large datasets for training; may struggle with high-resolution synthesis (256×256) without architectural modifications like the two-stage approach; the two-stage variant lacks cross-volume generalization. When to use: When interactive exploration of viewpoint and TF space is required, and explicit volume data is either unavailable or too large to store/process in real-time. When not to use: When exact physical accuracy is required over perceptual quality, or when cross-volume generalization is needed without retraining. The method was introduced in "A Generative Model for Volume Rendering". It frames volume rendering not as a physical simulation but as a learned mapping from visualization parameters to images. This approach addresses the difficulty of exploring the high-dimensional space of viewpoints and transfer functions by using a GAN to synthesize images directly. The two-stage conditional GAN variant was later introduced as the first learned volume rendering system of its kind. name: Multi-pass GAN for Volumetric Super-Resolution
head: Multi-pass GAN (Werhahn et al.), Physics-informed Multi-pass GAN
body: This method performs spatial super-resolution on volumetric data by decomposing the 3D reconstruction problem into orthogonal 2D slice passes, thereby avoiding the memory costs associated with full 3D convolutions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D GANs by integrating physics-informed constraints directly into the training objective to ensure physically consistent reconstructions, rather than relying solely on statistical error minimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution volumetric data, typically scalar fields such as density or velocity at 64^3 resolution. Output: High-resolution volumetric data at 512^3 resolution. Data Structures: Generators: Two distinct generator networks, G{XY} and G{YZ}. G{XY}: Processes 2D slices in the XY-plane. G{YZ}: Processes 2D slices in the YZ-plane. Discriminator: Architecture details are not specified in the sources. Method Steps: 1. Decomposition: The volumetric super-resolution task is decomposed into orthogonal 2D passes. 2. First Pass (G{XY}): The first generator upscales the input volume by processing it as a sequence of XY-plane slices. 3. Second Pass (G{YZ}): The second generator refines the output from the first pass by processing it as a sequence of YZ-plane slices. 4. Physics-Informed Training: The training objective incorporates constraints derived from governing equations directly into the loss function. 5. Progressive Growing: The network is trained using progressive growing with curriculum learning to handle the high resolution. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Upscaling Factor: 8× per dimension (e.g., 64^3 \rightarrow 512^3). Training Time: Approximately 60 seconds for the reported 64^3 \rightarrow 512^3 case. Pitfalls: Evaluation Limitations: The method was evaluated only on synthetic buoyant smoke data. Metrics: No quantitative reconstruction metrics (such as PSNR or SSIM) were reported in the source. Generalizability: Performance on non-synthetic or non-smoke data is not documented. SSRTVD is a GAN designed for spatial super-resolution of time-varying volumetric data, specifically targeting fluid flow density fields. It sets itself apart from single-volume GANs by introducing a temporal discriminator that operates on triplets of consecutive volumes to enforce frame-to-frame coherence, which prevents motion distortion. Choose it when spatial upscaling of fluid flows requires temporal smoothness without altering timestep resolution. SSRTVD STNet is an end-to-end GAN framework that extends super-resolution to joint spatial and temporal dimensions. It sets itself apart by performing feature-space temporal interpolation followed by voxel-shuffle spatial upscaling, optimizing PSNR-oriented losses rather than purely spatial metrics. Choose it when both spatial resolution and temporal consistency must be improved simultaneously. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by decomposing 3D SR into 2D slice passes, avoiding the cost of full 3D convolutions. Training time is approximately 60 seconds for the reported 64^3 \rightarrow 512^3 case. Measured Performance: Produces detailed turbulent structures at 512^3 resolution from 64^3 inputs on synthetic buoyant smoke. Scaling: Handles 8× upscaling per dimension via progressive growing and curriculum learning. Strengths and Limitations: Competitive with direct numerical simulation (DNS) in visual fidelity, but lacks quantitative metrics and is untested on non-synthetic data. Usage Guidance: Use for physics-consistent spatial upscaling of synthetic fluid flows where memory constraints prohibit 3D convolutions; avoid for production pipelines requiring validated quantitative error bounds or non-smoke data. The method was proposed by Werhahn et al.. It belongs to the broader category of physics-informed super-resolution, which seeks physically consistent reconstructions by incorporating governing equation constraints into the training objective. This approach contrasts with purely statistical reconstruction error minimization. It is primarily used in scientific visualization for smoke and fluid flow simulations. name: SSRTVD
head: SSR-TVD, tempoGAN
body: SSRTVD is the first GAN-based spatial super-resolution method for time-varying volumetric data, designed to resolve frame-to-frame inconsistency that arises when spatial SR is applied independently to each timestep. It distinguishes itself from single-volume GANs by employing a temporal discriminator on triplets of consecutive volumes to enforce temporal coherence, and differs from temporal interpolation methods like TSR-TVD by focusing on spatial upscaling with advection-aligned constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of coarse volumetric density fields \{Vt\}{t=1}^T representing time-varying fluid flow. Output: A sequence of high-resolution volumetric density fields \{\hat{V}t\}{t=1}^T upscaled by a factor of 4 in each spatial dimension (64× volumetric increase). Data Structures: Volumetric Grid: 3D tensor of shape (D, H, W) for each timestep, tested up to 256^3. Advection-Aligned Frames: Frames aligned according to the fluid velocity field to account for motion between timesteps. Network Architecture: 1. Generator (G): A densely connected convolutional network mapping coarse volumes to high-resolution volumes. 2. Spatial Discriminator (D{spatial}): Evaluates the realism of individual high-resolution volumes \hat{V}t. 3. Temporal Discriminator (D{temporal}): Processes triplets of consecutive volumes (\hat{V}{t-1}, \hat{V}t, \hat{V}{t+1}) to enforce temporal coherence. Training Steps: 1. Advection Alignment: Apply a differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection layer to align consecutive coarse volumes (V{t-1}, Vt, V{t+1}) with Vt based on the velocity field, producing advection-aligned frames. 2. Generator Forward Pass: Pass the aligned coarse frames through G to produce high-resolution predictions \hat{V}{t-1}, \hat{V}t, \hat{V}{t+1}. 3. Spatial Discrimination: Compute the spatial adversarial loss by comparing \hat{V}t against real high-resolution ground truth using D{spatial}. 4. Temporal Discrimination: Pass the triplet (\hat{V}{t-1}, \hat{V}t, \hat{V}{t+1}) through D{temporal}. 5. Gradient Propagation: Pass gradients from D{temporal} back through the differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection layer, allowing G to learn temporal smoothness constraints directly. 6. Loss & Optimization: The exact loss formulation weights and optimization algorithm are not given in the sources. Parameters: Upscaling Factor: 4× spatial (64× volumetric). Resolution: Tested up to 256^3. Dataset: Computer graphics smoke simulation data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Per-Dataset Training: Requires training a separate model for each dataset, limiting generalization. Inference Time: Inference takes up to eight hours for large volumes due to sub-volume GPU processing constraints. Evaluation Limitations: Initial evaluation was qualitative with no PSNR or SSIM reported. A recurrent generative network that adapts the temporal discriminator concept to temporal interpolation rather than spatial super-resolution. It synthesizes intermediate timesteps using a generator combining ConvLSTM for temporal modeling with a voxel shuffle layer for feature-space upscaling, making forward and backward predictions blended with learned weights. It could only synthesize intermediate volumes at integer time positions. It achieved 23–27 dB PSNR across combustion, supernova, and vortex datasets, outperforming linear interpolation on both PSNR and isosurface similarity. Refines the GAN paradigm by incorporating self-attention into the generator encoder to capture global spatial dependencies beyond the local convolutional receptive field. It achieved improved perceptual scores at scale factors up to 8× on ionization and hurricane data. The evaluation reports SSIM improvement without quantifying absolute PSNR relative to SSR-TVD on matched splits, and the maximum tested volume (240 \times 240 \times 48) is smaller than prior GAN baselines. Time Complexity: Inference is computationally expensive, taking up to eight hours for large volumes (256^3) due to sub-volume GPU processing. Memory Complexity: Requires sufficient GPU memory for sub-volume processing; specific memory footprint is not given. Performance: At 4× upscaling, achieved 34–41 dB PSNR across combustion, ionization, and vortex datasets. Outperformed interpolation baselines on both PSNR and isosurface similarity. Strengths: Enforces temporal coherence in spatial SR, recovering fine-grained structures absent from coarse simulations. Limitations: Requires per-dataset training; initial evaluation lacked quantitative metrics; inference is slow. When to Use: Spatial SR of time-varying fluid data where temporal consistency is critical and per-dataset training is acceptable. When Not to Use: Real-time inference is required, or generalization across multiple datasets without retraining is needed. Introduced by Xie et al. as the first GAN-based spatial SR method for time-varying data. Originally developed for computer graphics smoke simulation. Established the temporal discriminator as a mechanism for enforcing coherence across timesteps using advection-aligned frames and a differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection layer. Cited in the context of scientific volume rendering and deep learning methods for scientific data. name: GAN Training Procedure
head: Min-Max Game Training
body: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) train a generator against a discriminator to produce perceptually realistic outputs rather than merely minimizing pixelwise error. This perceptual advantage makes GANs well-suited for volume super-resolution, where Mean Squared Error (MSE)-optimized outputs tend toward oversmoothing. The method solves the problem of generating high-fidelity volumetric visualizations by replacing explicit volume data with a computational process that maps viewpoints and transfer functions directly to images [Parent]. The procedure consists of two neural networks: a generator that produces increasingly realistic images and a discriminator that distinguishes real images from generated ones, trained in a competitive framework. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Real images (ground truth), visualization parameters (e.g., viewpoint, transfer function), and optionally an opacity image (for translation GANs). Outputs: Synthesized images from the generator; real/fake classification probabilities from the discriminator. Data Structures Generator (G): Neural network mapping visualization parameters to image space. Discriminator (D): Neural network mapping image space to a scalar probability of being real. Training Data: Generated by performing volume rendering over a wide range of viewpoints and transfer functions (TFs). For each instance, the viewpoint is randomly generated, and the opacity TF is sampled from a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with 1 to 5 modes, each having a random mean, standard deviation, and amplitude relative to the scalar field range. Algorithm Steps The GAN optimizes a min-max game using minibatch stochastic gradient descent. The parameters are updated iteratively from the computed gradients. The training loop alternates gradient descent steps for the discriminator and the generator: 1. Discriminator Update (Real): Update discriminator parameters using a batch of real images and visualization parameters to minimize binary cross-entropy loss, encouraging the discriminator to predict these images as real. 2. Synthesis: Pass visualization parameters (and opacity image, if applicable) through the generator to synthesize images. 3. Discriminator Update (Fake): Update the discriminator to encourage a prediction of false for the synthesized images. 4. Generator Update: Update the generator’s parameters by tricking the discriminator, encouraging it to predict the synthesized images as being real. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingan(generator, discriminator, realimages, vizparams, opacityimages, numepochs, batchsize, lr, beta1, beta2, epsilon): """ Trains a GAN using alternating gradient descent. """ # Helper: Binary Cross-Entropy Loss def binarycrossentropy(predictions, targets): predictions = max(min(predictions, 1.0 - 1e-7), 1e-7) return -mean(targets log(predictions) + (1 - targets) log(1 - predictions)) # Helper: Adam Optimizer State and Step mstate = {} vstate = {} stepcount = 0 def adamstep(params): nonlocal stepcount stepcount += 1 for p in params: if p not in mstate: mstate[p] = zeroslike(p) vstate[p] = zeroslike(p) mstate[p] = beta1 mstate[p] + (1 - beta1) gradients[p] vstate[p] = beta2 vstate[p] + (1 - beta2) gradients[p]2 mhat = mstate[p] / (1 - beta1stepcount) vhat = vstate[p] / (1 - beta2stepcount) p -= lr mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + epsilon) for epoch in range(numepochs): for i in range(0, len(realimages), batchsize): batchreal = realimages[i:i+batchsize] batchviz = vizparams[i:i+batchsize] batchopacity = opacityimages[i:i+batchsize] if opacityimages else None # --- Discriminator Update --- # 1. Train on real images predreal = discriminator(batchreal) lossDreal = binarycrossentropy(predreal, target=1.0) gradients = ∇params(lossDreal, discriminator.parameters()) # Backpropagation adamstep(discriminator.parameters()) # 2. Synthesize fake images if batchopacity is not None: fakeimages = generator(batchviz, batchopacity) else: fakeimages = generator(batchviz) # 3. Train on fake images predfake = discriminator(fakeimages.detach()) lossDfake = binarycrossentropy(predfake, target=0.0) gradients = ∇params(lossDfake, discriminator.parameters()) adamstep(discriminator.parameters()) # --- Generator Update --- # 4. Update generator by tricking discriminator if batchopacity is not None: fakeimages = generator(batchviz, batchopacity) else: fakeimages = generator(batchviz) predfakeforG = discriminator(fakeimages) lossG = binarycrossentropy(predfakeforG, target=1.0) gradients = ∇params(lossG, generator.parameters()) adamstep(generator.parameters()) Parameters Optimizer: ADAM. ADAM Hyperparameters: \epsilon = 10^{-8}, \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. L1 Loss Weight (\lambda): In practice, \lambda = 150 preserves color and stabilizes training without overly blurring generated images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lack of 3D Shape Information: Most current GAN-based image synthesis methods do not provide 3D shape information. Limited Explicit Control: They do not allow for explicit control of camera parameters such as the viewpoint and for fine control over the scene materials or lighting conditions. Data Generation Constraints: Randomly generated TFs from GMMs must cover the relevant scalar field range to ensure the training dataset adequately represents the target distribution. A convolutional discriminator that grows progressively in resolution to stabilize training and allow larger batch sizes at lower resolutions. It solves the instability inherent in training high-resolution GANs by starting with coarse shapes and gradually introducing fine details. Unlike standard ProgressiveGAN where the generator architecture grows, this variant keeps the generator fixed, increasing resolution by sampling rays more densely from the same implicit representation. Uses spatial discriminators for normal and roughness maps, and temporal discriminators for temporal coherence, to enforce that inferred data spatial distribution is similar to real data. The overall loss is defined as: L{Total} = \alpha L{Image} + \beta1 L{Dn} + \beta2 L{Dr} + \gamma1 L{Dtn} + \gamma2 L{Dtr} where \alpha, \beta1, \beta2, \gamma1, \gamma2 are weights, and L{Dn}, L{Dr}, L{Dtn}, L{Dtr} are the losses of the corresponding discriminators. Training involves alternating training of the four auxiliary discriminators and the generator, as typically done for GAN training. Sub-net1 and sub-net2 are trained together using L{Total} for 200 epochs. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Demonstrated effectiveness for super-resolution, style transfer, and image-to-image translation. Hardware: Experiments conducted on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 SUPER GPU. Strengths: Produces perceptually realistic outputs, avoiding the oversmoothing typical of MSE-based methods. Limitations: Most current GAN-based image synthesis methods do not provide 3D shape information. They also do not allow for explicit control of camera parameters such as the viewpoint and for fine control over the scene materials or lighting conditions. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [81] and diffusion models [82] have emerged as pivotal techniques for generating and modifying high-quality images. GANs consist of two neural networks trained in a competitive framework. They have demonstrated effectiveness for a variety of tasks, including super-resolution, style transfer, and image-to-image translation. In the context of volume rendering, GANs are used to bypass explicit volume data, mapping viewpoints and transfer functions directly to images [Parent]. name: Progressive GAN Discriminator
head: Progressive Growing Discriminator
body: A convolutional discriminator that grows progressively in resolution to stabilize training and allow larger batch sizes at lower resolutions. It solves the instability inherent in training high-resolution GANs by starting with coarse shapes and gradually introducing fine details. Unlike standard ProgressiveGAN where the generator architecture grows, this variant keeps the generator fixed, increasing resolution by sampling rays more densely from the same implicit representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Real or generated images at the current training resolution. Output: A scalar score indicating the probability that the input is real. Data Structures: The discriminator is a convolutional neural network that grows progressively in resolution. Exact layouts, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Begin training at a low resolution (e.g., 32 \times 32) with a large batch size. 2. Progressive Growth: Double the resolution twice during training, up to 128 \times 128. 3. Layer Addition: Add new layers to the discriminator to handle higher resolutions and discriminate fine details as resolution increases. 4. Final Rendering: Final results are rendered by sampling 512 \times 512 pixels, though training occurs at lower resolutions. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Initial Resolution: 32 \times 32. Final Training Resolution: 128 \times 128. Final Rendering Resolution: 512 \times 512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. The Discriminator and Decoder constitute the adversarial training components for differentiable volume rendering, specifically within Progressive GAN frameworks. The Discriminator evaluates the realism of rendered RGB-D samples against real data using residual blocks and minibatch standard deviation, while the Decoder reconstructs high-resolution feature maps from low-resolution discriminator features. This setup stabilizes training by providing gradient signals that enforce photometric and geometric consistency. It differs from sibling methods like Progressive Patch Scaling by operating on full-resolution feature maps via transposed convolutions rather than patch-based scaling, and from Fully Convolutional Discriminator by explicitly incorporating a separate decoder stage for feature upsampling. Progressive Patch Scaling is a training strategy for 3D GAN discriminators that operates on image patches of varying scales rather than full-resolution images, allowing the model to learn multi-scale features progressively. It solves the instability and diversity issues inherent in training 3D GANs from limited 2D observations by gradually reducing the scale of image patches used for training, starting from large sub-regions to smaller ones. Unlike methods that apply super-resolution modules to rendered values, this approach directly discriminates RGB color images or patches, relying on the progressive reduction of patch scale to stabilize training and promote diversity. A fully convolutional discriminator used for learned self-supervision in single-view volume reconstruction to constrain degrees of freedom and prevent smearing or streak artifacts. It differs from sibling methods by evaluating randomly sampled viewpoints to provide image-space constraints coupled over time via global transport, rather than relying on fixed multi-view inputs or patch-based scaling. All layers are followed by LReLU activations with a leak of 0.2. Data augmentation applies random crop, scale, rotation, intensity, and gamma scale. The architecture consists of 14 convolution layers with filter sizes and strides: (8,1), (16,2), (16,1), (24,2), (24,1), (32,2), (32,1), (32,1), (64,2), (64,1), (64,1), (16,1), (4,1), (1,1), all using 4×4 filters. For padding, it uses SAME padding but applies mirrored input instead of zero padding to avoid issues described in [31]. Stability: Allows larger batch sizes at the beginning of training, which helped to stabilize and speed training. Resolution Scaling: Training resolution is limited to 128 \times 128 in standard experiments, while final rendering uses 512 \times 512. Generator Independence: The generator architecture does not grow; resolution is increased by sampling rays more densely from the same implicit representation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Originated from ProgressiveGAN [25] (cited in), this method was adapted for 3D-aware image synthesis in pi-GAN. It addresses the difficulty of training GANs at high resolutions by progressively introducing detail. pi-GAN: Periodic Implicit Generative Adversarial Networks for 3D-Aware Image Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00574, fetched 2026-10-26 Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction with Learned Self-Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00168, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Discriminator and Decoder
head: Progressive GAN Discriminator components, Residual Discriminator, Feature Decoder
body: The Discriminator and Decoder constitute the adversarial training components for differentiable volume rendering, specifically within Progressive GAN frameworks. The Discriminator evaluates the realism of rendered RGB-D samples against real data using residual blocks and minibatch standard deviation, while the Decoder reconstructs high-resolution feature maps from low-resolution discriminator features. This setup stabilizes training by providing gradient signals that enforce photometric and geometric consistency. It differs from sibling methods like Progressive Patch Scaling by operating on full-resolution feature maps via transposed convolutions rather than patch-based scaling, and from Fully Convolutional Discriminator by explicitly incorporating a separate decoder stage for feature upsampling. Discriminator Input: RGB-D image (RGB channels + normalized depth). Discriminator Output: Scalar probability (real vs. fake). Decoder Input: Low-resolution feature maps (typically 4 \times 4 spatial resolution) extracted from the discriminator before the minibatch standard deviation layer. Decoder Output: Upsampled feature maps at original resolution (e.g., 64 \times 64). The discriminator follows a StyleGAN2-inspired architecture. 1. Input Normalization: Depth channel is normalized to [0, 1]. 2. Initial Convolution: 3 \times 3 convolution. 3. Residual Blocks: Series of residual blocks (see below). 4. Minibatch Standard Deviation: Aggregates statistics across the batch dimension. 5. Final Convolution: 3 \times 3 convolution. 6. Flatten & Linear: Flattened features passed through two linear layers. 7. Output: Single scalar. Residual Block Structure: Input feature map. 3 \times 3 Convolution. LeakyReLU (\alpha=0.2). 3 \times 3 Convolution. LeakyReLU (\alpha=0.2). Skip connection addition (with 1 \times 1 convolution if channel dimensions change). LeakyReLU (\alpha=0.2). Feature Map Dimensions (Example from): Input: 32 \times 32 \times 32 (RGB-D) After Initial Conv: 256 \times 4 \times 4 After Residual Blocks: 256 \times 4 \times 4 \rightarrow 256 \times 8 \times 8 \rightarrow 256 \times 16 \times 16 \rightarrow 256 \times 32 \times 32 After Minibatch Std Dev: 256 \times 32 \times 32 (statistic added as channel) After Final Conv: 32 \times 32 \times 32 (example dimension, varies by implementation) The decoder upsamples features from the discriminator's intermediate stage. 1. Input: 4 \times 4 feature maps. 2. Transposed Convolutions: Successive layers with stride 2 and bilinear filtering to upsample. 3. Final Convolution: 3 \times 3 convolution. 4. Activation: Final activation function. 5. Output: 64 \times 64 feature maps (or original resolution). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ResidualBlock(nn.Module): """Residual block as used in StyleGAN2-based discriminator.""" def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super().init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(outchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.skip = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=1) if inchannels != outchannels else nn.Identity() self.lrelu = nn.LeakyReLU(negativeslope=0.2) def forward(self, x): identity = self.skip(x) out = self.conv1(x) out = self.lrelu(out) out = self.conv2(out) out = self.lrelu(out) out = out + identity out = self.lrelu(out) return out class MinibatchStdDev(nn.Module): """Minibatch standard deviation layer.""" def init(self, groupsize=4): super().init() self.groupsize = groupsize def forward(self, x): # x shape: (N, C, H, W) N, C, H, W = x.shape # Ensure batch size is divisible by groupsize G = min(self.groupsize, N) # Reshape to (G, N/G, C, H, W) x = x.view(G, -1, C, H, W) # Compute std dev across the group dimension std = x.std(dim=0) # Shape: (N/G, C, H, W) mean = std.mean(dim=[2, 3], keepdim=True) # Mean over H, W mean = mean.view(G, -1, 1, 1, 1) # Concatenate the statistic as a new channel out = torch.cat([x, mean], dim=2) # Reshape back to (N, C', H, W) out = out.view(N, -1, H, W) return out class Discriminator(nn.Module): """ Discriminator for RGB-D inputs. Input: RGB-D image. Output: Scalar probability. """ def init(self, inchannels=4, basechannels=256): super().init() # Initial convolution self.initconv = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, basechannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.lrelu = nn.LeakyReLU(negativeslope=0.2) # Residual blocks (example progression from) self.res1 = ResidualBlock(basechannels, basechannels) self.res2 = ResidualBlock(basechannels, basechannels) self.res3 = ResidualBlock(basechannels, basechannels) self.res4 = ResidualBlock(basechannels, basechannels) # Minibatch standard deviation self.mbstd = MinibatchStdDev() # Final convolution and linear layers # Note: Channel count changes after mbstd. Assuming output channels from mbstd is C+1 finalchannels = basechannels + 1 self.finalconv = nn.Conv2d(finalchannels, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.flatten = nn.Flatten() self.linear1 = nn.Linear(32 32 32, 1024) # Adjust input dim based on resolution self.linear2 = nn.Linear(1024, 1) def forward(self, x): # x: (N, 4, H, W) x = self.initconv(x) x = self.lrelu(x) x = self.res1(x) x = self.res2(x) x = self.res3(x) x = self.res4(x) x = self.mbstd(x) x = self.finalconv(x) x = self.lrelu(x) x = self.flatten(x) x = self.linear1(x) x = self.lrelu(x) x = self.linear2(x) return x class Decoder(nn.Module): """ Decoder to upsample feature maps from discriminator. Input: 4x4 feature maps. Output: 64x64 feature maps. """ def init(self, inchannels=256, outchannels=64): super().init() # Successive transposed convolutions with stride 2 and bilinear filtering # 4x4 -> 8x8 self.up1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(inchannels, inchannels, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(inchannels) self.lrelu1 = nn.LeakyReLU(negativeslope=0.2) # 8x8 -> 16x16 self.up2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(inchannels, inchannels, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(inchannels) self.lrelu2 = nn.LeakyReLU(negativeslope=0.2) # 16x16 -> 32x32 self.up3 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(inchannels, inchannels, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn3 = nn.BatchNorm2d(inchannels) self.lrelu3 = nn.LeakyReLU(negativeslope=0.2) # 32x32 -> 64x64 self.up4 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False) self.lrelu4 = nn.LeakyReLU(negativeslope=0.2) # Final convolution self.finalconv = nn.Conv2d(outchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): # x: (N, C, 4, 4) x = self.lrelu1(self.bn1(self.up1(x))) x = self.lrelu2(self.bn2(self.up2(x))) x = self.lrelu3(self.bn3(self.up3(x))) x = self.lrelu4(self.up4(x)) x = self.finalconv(x) return x Batch Size: 8 real samples, 4 rendered fake samples, and 4 additional fake samples from history when training the discriminator. LeakyReLU Slope: 0.2. L2 Regularization: Applied to discriminator weights \ThetaD. Padding: Mirrored padding is used in fully convolutional variants to avoid zero-padding artifacts. Resolution Mismatch: If the radiance field network is sampled at a lower resolution than the final output, generated depth maps will have lower resolution than real examples. The discriminator might exploit this detail difference. To prevent this, downsample all real depth maps to match the generated depth map resolution, then upsample both back to full resolution. Padding Artifacts: Using zero padding in convolutional layers can introduce artifacts. Mirrored padding is recommended. The relativistic GAN formulation allows different resolutions and batch sizes for real and fake samples. The 'average' formulation is theoretically flexible, but the least-squares variant gives empirically better results in this context. Time Complexity: Training time is dominated by the forward pass of the discriminator and the generation of fake samples. The use of a history buffer of fake samples adds minimal overhead but improves quality. Memory Complexity: The discriminator memory footprint is determined by the number of convolutional layers and the batch size. The minibatch standard deviation layer requires storing statistics across the batch dimension. Strengths: Stabilizes training of GAN-based volume rendering. The residual architecture and minibatch standard deviation help capture fine details. The decoder allows for feature-level supervision. Limitations: Requires careful handling of resolution mismatches between real and generated data. The relativistic loss variant requires tuning between 'average' and least-squares formulations. When to Use: When training GANs for volume rendering or image synthesis where stability and high-frequency detail preservation are critical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and simpler discriminators (e.g., standard CNN discriminators without residual blocks) are sufficient. Origin: The discriminator architecture is based on StyleGAN2. The decoder and specific training procedures (history buffer, relativistic loss) are detailed in works on unconstrained scene generation and global transport for fluid reconstruction. History: Developed to address the instability of GAN training in 3D volume rendering. The progressive growing approach (parent article) is combined with these components to handle high-resolution outputs. Usage: Used in differentiable volume rendering pipelines, particularly in GAN-based approaches for scene generation and fluid reconstruction. name: Progressive Patch Scaling
body: Progressive Patch Scaling is a training strategy for 3D GAN discriminators that operates on image patches of varying scales rather than full-resolution images to promote diversity and stability during training from limited 2D observations. Unlike methods that apply super-resolution modules, it directly discriminates RGB patches while progressively reducing the patch scale over the first 100 epochs. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Generator \mathbf{G}, Discriminator \mathbf{D}, camera poses \tau, latent codes \mathbf{z}, and a time-varying scale schedule. Outputs: Discriminator scores for real and generated patches. Data Structures Patch Scale s: A scalar value sampled from a uniform distribution; implementation-wise, this scalar is repeated to match the patch resolution if used as a conditioning feature. Patch \rho: A spatial region of the image defined by the scale s; the sampled patch is a function of the sampled scale. Image Resolution: Input images have resolution H' \times H' (e.g., 512 \times 512). Fixed Patch Size: The discriminator processes patches of fixed size H \times H (e.g., 64 \times 64). Parameters Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-3}, used with the ADAM optimizer. Samples per Ray: 96 samples are used per ray during volume rendering. Batch Size: 1,000 samples per epoch. Scale Range Initialization: At epoch t=0, s{min}(0) = 0.6 and s{max}(0) = 0.8. Scale Range Finalization: At epoch t=100, s{min}(100) = 0.25 and s{max}(100) = 0.55. Rotation Augmentation: Gradually introduced up to 15^\circ for later training epochs where patch scale s decreases. Formulas The final training objective combines adversarial loss, R1 gradient penalty, and discriminator reconstruction loss: \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{G}, \mathbf{D}, \mathcal{T}) = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{z},\tau \sim \mathcal{T},s,\rho} [f(\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\rho, \mathbf{z}))) ] + \mathbb{E}{I,s,\rho} [f(-\mathbf{D}(\rho, s)) + \lambda1 |\nabla\rho \mathbf{D}(\rho, s)|^2 ] + \lambda2 \mathcal{E}R(\mathbf{D}) Where: f(a) = -\log(1 + \exp(-a)) is the adversarial loss function. \lambda1 and \lambda2 are balancing parameters for the R1 gradient penalty and reconstruction loss, respectively. \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\rho represents the volume rendering of the patch region. \rho is the sampled patch, which is a function of the sampled scale s. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Scale Schedule: Define the linear interpolation of s{min}(t) and s{max}(t) over the first 100 epochs, then fix them for the remainder of training. s{min}(t) = 0.6 + (0.25 - 0.6) \times \frac{t}{100} s{max}(t) = 0.8 + (0.55 - 0.8) \times \frac{t}{100} 2. Sample Scale: For each image instance in a batch, independently sample a scale factor s from the time-varying uniform distribution: s \sim U(s{min}(t), s{max}(t)) where t is the current epoch index. 3. Apply Augmentation: Apply data augmentation, including rotational augmentation. Start without rotational augmentation and gradually increase it up to 15^\circ in later epochs where s is smaller. 4. Extract Patches: Extract patches \rho from the input images I and generated images based on the sampled scale s. When s=1, the 64 \times 64 patch covers the entire image; implementation-wise, the scale value s is simply repeated to match the patch resolution. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the objective \mathcal{E} using the formula above. The generator produces patches \mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\rho, \mathbf{z}), and the discriminator evaluates both real patches \rho and generated patches. 6. Optimize: Minimize the objective using the ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-3}. 7. Fix Scale: After epoch 100, stop updating s{min} and s{max} and keep them constant for the remainder of the training. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def progressivepatchscalingtraining(generator, discriminator, dataloader, numepochs=400): # Parameters from lr = 2e-3 batchsize = 1000 H = 64 maxrotationangle = 15.0 smininit, smaxinit = 0.6, 0.8 sminfinal, smaxfinal = 0.25, 0.55 scheduleepochs = 100 # ADAM optimizer state mw, vw = {}, {} beta1, beta2, eps = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8 for t in range(numepochs): # 1. Scale schedule interpolation if t <= scheduleepochs: progress = t / scheduleepochs smint = smininit + (sminfinal - smininit) progress smaxt = smaxinit + (smaxfinal - smaxinit) progress else: smint, smaxt = sminfinal, smaxfinal # 2. Rotation augmentation strength currentmaxangle = maxrotationangle (t / scheduleepochs) if t <= scheduleepochs else maxrotationangle for images, poses in dataloader: # 3. Sample scales per instance scales = [random.uniform(smint, smaxt) for in range(batchsize)] realpatches, generatedpatches = [], [] for i in range(batchsize): img, pose, s = images[i], poses[i], scales[i] # 4. Augmentation angle = random.uniform(-currentmaxangle, currentmaxangle) imgaug = applyrotation2d(img, angle) poseaug = applyrotationtopose(pose, angle) # 5. Patch extraction # When s=1, 64x64 covers entire image. Region size scales inversely with s. regionsize = int(H / s) patchreal = extractandresize(imgaug, regionsize, H) # 6. Generate patch z = samplelatentvector() genimg = generator.rendervolume(poseaug, z, samplesperray=96) patchgen = extractandresize(genimg, regionsize, H) realpatches.append(patchreal) generatedpatches.append(patchgen) # 7. Loss computation genscores = discriminator.forward(generatedpatches, scales) advgen = -mean(math.log(1 + math.exp(-genscores))) realscores = discriminator.forward(realpatches, scales) advreal = -mean(math.log(1 + math.exp(realscores))) # R1 gradient penalty realscores.requiresgrad = True grad = computegradient(realscores, realpatches) r1penalty = mean(norm(grad) 2) reconloss = computereconstructionloss(discriminator) lambda1, lambda2 = 10.0, 1.0 # typical balancing parameters totalloss = advgen + advreal + lambda1 r1penalty + lambda2 reconloss # 8. ADAM update step updateadamstep(discriminator.parameters(), totalloss, mw, vw, beta1, beta2, eps, lr) updateadamstep(generator.parameters(), totalloss, mw, vw, beta1, beta2, eps, lr) return generator, discriminator def applyrotation2d(image, angledeg): # Standard 2D image rotation implementation anglerad = math.radians(angledeg) cosa, sina = math.cos(anglerad), math.sin(anglerad) # Apply rotation matrix to pixel coordinates and interpolate return rotatedimage def extractandresize(image, cropsize, targetsize): # Crop cropsize x cropsize region, resize to targetsize x targetsize cropped = image[0:cropsize, 0:cropsize] resized = interpolatetosize(cropped, targetsize, targetsize) return resized def updateadamstep(params, loss, m, v, b1, b2, e, lr): # Standard ADAM parameter update rule for p in params: if p.grad is None: continue grad = p.grad.data if p not in m: m[p] = torch.zeroslike(p.data); v[p] = torch.zeroslike(p.data) m[p].mul(b1).add(grad, alpha=1-b1) v[p].mul(b2).addcmul(grad, grad, value=1-b2) biascorrection1 = 1 - b1 (stepcount + 1) biascorrection2 = 1 - b2 (stepcount + 1) denom = (v[p].sqrt() / math.sqrt(biascorrection2)).add(e) p.data.addcdiv(m[p], denom, value=-lr) def computereconstructionloss(discriminator): # Standard MSE between discriminator output and target return mean((discriminator.output - target) 2) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Super-resolution: The method does not apply a super-resolution module on the rendered values; it directly outputs RGB color images or patches. Degenerate Input: The method assumes valid 2D observations. A convolutional discriminator that grows progressively in resolution to stabilize training and allow larger batch sizes at lower resolutions. It provides the architectural foundation upon which Progressive Patch Scaling operates. Progressive GAN Discriminator Uses GANs to generate 3D scenes from 2D images. Progressive Patch Scaling is a specific training procedure within this framework to improve discriminator stability. GAN-based Volume Rendering Time Complexity: Training typically exhibits the best KID score around 300 to 400 epochs. The progressive reduction of patch scale over the first 100 epochs adds computational overhead due to dynamic patch extraction and augmentation. Memory Complexity: The fixed patch size (64 \times 64) keeps memory usage constant regardless of the input image resolution (512 \times 512). Measured Performance: Tested on Replica and Matterport3D datasets. The method achieves realistic 3D scene variations and view-consistent representations. Strengths: Promotes diversity and stability in 3D GAN training by forcing the discriminator to learn from multi-scale features. Limitations: Does not apply super-resolution, which may limit the sharpness of generated details compared to methods that explicitly upsample. When to Use: Suitable for 3D GAN training from limited 2D observations where stability and diversity are critical. Progressive Patch Scaling was introduced in the SinGRAF paper (2023). It is designed to address the challenges of training 3D GANs from a limited set of 2D observations. The method adapts progressive training concepts to patch-based discrimination of 3D rendered views. It is used in the context of learning a 3D Generative Radiance Field for a single scene, specifically for indoor scenes from the Replica and Matterport3D datasets. name: Fully Convolutional Discriminator
head: Discriminator Network (Learned Self-Supervision), Learned Self-Supervision via GAN Discriminator
body: A fully convolutional discriminator used for learned self-supervision in single-view volume reconstruction to constrain degrees of freedom and prevent smearing or streak artifacts. It differs from sibling methods by evaluating randomly sampled viewpoints to provide image-space constraints coupled over time via global transport, rather than relying on fixed multi-view inputs or patch-based scaling. Inputs: 1. A small dataset of example motions (real samples). 2. Rendered fake samples (\hat{I}f) from the current reconstruction. 3. A history of previously rendered fake samples. Outputs: 1. Discriminator loss gradients used to update the reconstruction network. 2. Discriminator weights \ThetaD. Data Structures: Discriminator Weights (\ThetaD): Parameters for 14 convolutional layers. History Buffer: Stores previously rendered fake samples for additional training data. Architecture Layout: The discriminator D is a fully convolutional network with 14 layers. All layers use a filter size of 4 \times 4. The sequence of (output channels, stride) pairs is: 1. (8, 1) 2. (16, 2) 3. (16, 1) 4. (24, 2) 5. (24, 1) 6. (32, 2) 7. (32, 1) 8. (32, 1) 9. (64, 2) 10. (64, 1) 11. (64, 1) 12. (16, 1) 13. (4, 1) 14. (1, 1) Each layer is followed by a Leaky ReLU (LReLU) activation with a leak factor of 0.2. Padding is "SAME", but implemented by mirroring the input at the boundaries instead of zero-padding to avoid artifacts. L2 regularization is applied to the weights \ThetaD. Training Procedure: 1. Sample Selection: Select 8 real samples from the example motion dataset and 4 rendered fake samples from the current reconstruction. 2. History Augmentation: When training the discriminator, include 4 additional fake samples from the history buffer. 3. Data Augmentation: Apply random crop, scale, rotation, intensity scaling, and gamma scaling to the input samples. 4. Forward Pass: Compute discriminator outputs for real and fake samples. 5. Loss Calculation: Use the relativistic GAN 'average' formulation with the least-squares variant. This variant allows different resolutions and batch sizes for real and fake samples. 6. Update: Update \ThetaD using the computed loss and L2 regularization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatediscriminator(realsamples, fakesamples, historyfakesamples, discriminatorweights, lr): """ Updates the discriminator weights using real samples, current fake samples, and historical fake samples. """ # Combine samples: 8 real, 4 current fake, 4 historical fake # Note: Source specifies batch size of 8 real and 4 fake for update, # plus 4 additional from history. allreal = realsamples[:8] allfake = fakesamples[:4] + historyfakesamples[:4] # Apply data augmentation allreal = applyaugmentation(allreal) # random crop, scale, rotation, intensity, gamma allfake = applyaugmentation(allfake) # Forward pass through fully convolutional network # Architecture: 14 conv layers, 4x4 filters, strides as defined in layout # Activation: LReLU(0.2) after each layer # Padding: Mirrored SAME padding logitsreal = discriminatorforward(allreal, discriminatorweights) logitsfake = discriminatorforward(allfake, discriminatorweights) # Relativistic Average Least-Squares GAN Loss # LD = E[ (D(x) - mean(D(xfake)))^2 ] + E[ (1 - D(xfake) + mean(D(xreal)))^2 ] # Note: Source cites relativistic 'average' formulation with least-squares variant. meanreal = mean(logitsreal) meanfake = mean(logitsfake) lossreal = mean((logitsreal - meanfake) 2) lossfake = mean((1 - logitsfake + meanreal) 2) # L2 Regularization on weights l2reg = sum(w 2 for w in discriminatorweights) totalloss = lossreal + lossfake + lambdal2 l2reg # Backpropagate and update weights gradients = computegradients(totalloss, discriminatorweights) discriminatorweights = discriminatorweights - lr gradients return discriminatorweights Parameters: Batch Size: 8 real samples, 4 rendered fake samples, 4 historical fake samples. Leak Factor: 0.2. Filter Size: 4 \times 4 for all layers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pre-trained Reuse: Reusing a pre-trained discriminator yields inferior results. It must be re-trained alongside each new reconstruction because the discriminator adapts to provide feedback for different aspects of the solution over time. Padding: Zero-padding should be avoided; mirrored padding is required to prevent specific artifacts. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The full method (including this discriminator) measures an average reconstruction time of ~30 minutes per frame using a single GPU. Strengths: Allows working with very sparse observations, even a single viewpoint. Provides image-space constraints coupled over time. Limitations: Requires a small dataset of example motions. Assumes self-similarity in fluid flow. Dissipation effects are not modeled, leading to errors in divergence constraints. Originated in "Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction with Learned Self-Supervision" (2021) by researchers from TU Berlin (tum-pbs). The method is part of a pipeline for recovering end-to-end motion of fluid sequences from single input views, combining physical transport constraints with differentiable volumetric rendering and learned self-supervision.
