name: Diffusive INR (DINR)
head: Diffusion-regularized Implicit Neural Representation, Diffusive Computed Tomography Inversion Framework
body: DINR is a sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reconstruction method that regularizes an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) using a pretrained diffusion model prior to suppress noise and artifacts in raw projection data. It addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of sparse-view CT, where insufficient projection views cause severe artifacts in traditional methods like Filtered Back Projection (FBP). Unlike standard INRs, which suffer from spectral bias toward low-frequency components and instability under sparse supervision, DINR incorporates a proximal formulation that integrates denoised diffusion outputs into the INR loss. It differs from sibling methods like DD3IP by replacing the UNet-based volume representation with an INR, enabling resolution-independent and memory-efficient posterior mean estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: S: A 3D coordinate grid (cubic lattice) defining the volumetric domain. y: Sparse-view parallel-beam CT projection data (sinogram). A: Sparse-view parallel beam projector matrix. A^ y: The analytical solution (FBP estimate) of the projection data. \thetaT: Pretrained diffusion model weights. \omega: Scaling parameter for noise injection (typically 0.002). \rho: Regularization parameter for the proximal term, chosen such that the ratio of the proximal term to the data-fidelity term is 1 \times 10^{-6} (or 1 \times 10^{-5} in some experimental setups). \eta: Stochasticity control variable in [0, 1] for DDIM sampling. \alpha{1:T}: Decreasing sequence in (0, 1]^T parameterizing the reverse diffusion process. Outputs: x0: The final reconstructed 3D volume tensor of attenuation coefficient values. Data Structures: INR Model (F\phi): A neural network (typically a multilayer perceptron) parameterized by weights \phi. It maps spatial coordinates S and the FBP estimate A^ y to attenuation coefficient values. Diffusion Model (D\theta): A pretrained denoising model (e.g., UNet) parameterized by weights \theta, conditioned on the projection data y. Projector (A): Implemented as a distance-driven parallel-beam projector (e.g., via Tomosipo/ASTRA toolbox). Formulas: 1. Forward Model: y = Ax + n, where x is the 3D tensor of attenuation coefficients, A is the projection matrix, and n is additive noise. 2. Proximal Loss (L\phi): Used to update INR weights \phi: L\phi (S, y, \hat{x}t, \rho) = \text{MSE} (AF\phi (S, A^ y), y) + \rho \text{MSE} (\hat{x}t, F\phi (S, A^ y)) where \hat{x}t is the denoised estimate from the diffusion model at step t. 3. DDIM Sampling Step: \text{DDIM}\theta (\hat{x}t, \eta):= \sqrt{\alpha{t-1}} \hat{x}t + \sqrt{1 - \alpha{t-1}} \eta \epsilon + (1 - \eta) \epsilon\theta where \epsilon is spherically interpolated Gaussian noise and \epsilon\theta is the noise removed by the denoising model D\theta. 4. Initialization of Reverse Process: xT \leftarrow \sqrt{\alphaT} A^ y + \sqrt{1 - \alphaT} \epsilon w where w is a scaling factor related to \omega. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the 3D coordinate grid S, the sparse-view parallel beam projector A, and the sparse-view CT projection y. 2. Compute the FBP estimate A^ y. 3. Initialize the INR weights \phiT by minimizing the standard MSE loss without the diffusion prior (\rho=0): \phiT \leftarrow \arg \min\phi \{L\phi (S, y, -, \rho = 0)\} where L\phi (S, y, -, \rho = 0) = \text{MSE} (AF\phi (S, A^ y), y). 4. Load the pretrained diffusion model weights as \thetaT. 5. Initialize the volume estimate xT using the formula: xT \leftarrow \sqrt{\alphaT} A^ y + \sqrt{1 - \alphaT} \epsilon w where \epsilon is Gaussian noise and w is the scaling parameter \omega. 6. Iterate the diffusion reverse process for t = T down to 1: a. Update Diffusion Model: Update the diffusion model parameters \theta{t-1} by minimizing the data consistency loss between the projected INR reconstruction and the measured projections: \theta{t-1} \leftarrow \arg \min\theta \{\text{MSE} (A D\theta (xt |y), y)\}. b. Denoise: Generate the denoised estimate \hat{x}t by applying the updated diffusion model D{\theta{t-1}} to the current latent xt conditioned on y: \hat{x}t \leftarrow D{\theta{t-1}} (xt |y). c. Update INR: Update the INR parameters \phi{t-1} by minimizing the proximal loss L\phi (S, y, \hat{x}t, \rho), which incorporates the diffusion prior estimate \hat{x}t and the regularization parameter \rho. d. Compute Next Latent: If t = 1: Compute the final output x{t-1} by evaluating the final INR F{\phi{t-1}} at the coordinate grid S with the FBP estimate A^ y: x{t-1} \leftarrow F{\phi{t-1}} (S, A^ y). If t > 1: Compute the next latent x{t-1} using the DDIM sampler with the updated diffusion model \theta{t-1}, the INR output F{\phi{t-1}} (S, A^ y), and the noise scaling factor \eta: x{t-1} \leftarrow \text{DDIM}{\theta{t-1}} (F{\phi{t-1}} (S, A^ y), \eta). 7. Return the final reconstruction x0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def Fphi(coords, fbpestimate, weights): """INR forward pass: maps coordinates and FBP estimate to attenuation values.""" # Standard MLP evaluation; weights are flattened parameters return np.tanh(np.dot(weights, np.concatenate([coords, fbpestimate]))) def Dtheta(latent, condition, weights): """Diffusion denoising model forward pass.""" return np.tanh(np.dot(weights, np.concatenate([latent, condition]))) def sgdstep(params, lossfn, lr=0.01): """Standard gradient descent update.""" loss = lossfn() grad = np.gradient(loss, params) return params - lr grad def minimizemse(modelfn, params, datafn, target, lr=0.01, epochs=100): """Minimize MSE loss between model output and target.""" for in range(epochs): pred = modelfn(datafn(), params) lossfn = lambda: np.mean((pred - target) 2) params = sgdstep(params, lossfn, lr) return params def minimizeproximalloss(modelfn, params, datafn, target, prior, rho, lr=0.01, epochs=100): """Minimize proximal loss: MSE(data) + rho MSE(prior).""" for in range(epochs): pred = modelfn(datafn(), params) dataterm = np.mean((pred - target) 2) priorterm = np.mean((prior - pred) 2) lossfn = lambda: dataterm + rho priorterm params = sgdstep(params, lossfn, lr) return params def samplegaussiannoise(shape): """Standard normal noise.""" return np.random.normal(0, 1, shape) def samplesphericalgaussiannoise(shape): """Spherically interpolated Gaussian noise.""" return samplegaussiannoise(shape) / np.linalg.norm(samplegaussiannoise(shape)) def getalphaschedule(t, T=1000): """Decreasing sequence parameterizing the reverse diffusion process.""" return 1.0 - (t / T) def DINR(S, y, A, Astary, thetaT, alphaT, omega, rho, eta, T): # 1. Initialize INR weights with standard MSE loss (rho=0) phi = minimizemse(Fphi, np.zeros(10), lambda: (S, Astary), A(Fphi(lambda: (S, Astary), np.zeros(10)))) # 2. Initialize diffusion model weights theta = thetaT # 3. Initialize volume estimate xT epsilon = samplegaussiannoise(S.shape) xt = math.sqrt(alphaT) Astary + math.sqrt(1 - alphaT) epsilon omega # 4. Iterate reverse diffusion process for t in range(T, 0, -1): # a. Update diffusion model weights theta{t-1} theta = minimizemse(Dtheta, theta, lambda: (xt, y), y) # b. Compute denoised estimate xhatt xhatt = Dtheta(xt, y, theta) # c. Update INR weights phi{t-1} phi = minimizeproximalloss(Fphi, phi, lambda: (S, Astary), A(Fphi(lambda: (S, Astary), phi)), xhatt, rho) # d. Compute next latent x{t-1} if t == 1: xnext = Fphi(S, Astary, phi) else: epsilontheta = xt - Dtheta(xt, y, theta) epsilonnext = samplesphericalgaussiannoise(S.shape) alphatminus1 = getalphaschedule(t - 1) xnext = math.sqrt(alphatminus1) xhatt + \ math.sqrt(1 - alphatminus1) eta epsilonnext + \ (1 - eta) epsilontheta xt = xnext return xt Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral Bias: Standard INRs exhibit strong spectral bias toward low-frequency components, leading to poor reconstruction of high-frequency structure under sparse supervision. DINR mitigates this by incorporating the diffusion prior. Initialization: The initialization of xT uses the FBP estimate A^ y corrupted with noise. The scaling parameter \omega controls the regularization by scaling the values of A^ y relative to the noise variance. Parameter Tuning: The parameter \rho must be chosen carefully. In experiments, it was set such that the ratio of the proximal term to the data-fidelity term was 1 \times 10^{-6} or 1 \times 10^{-5}. The parameter \omega was set to 0.002. Time Complexity: The method involves iterative optimization of both the diffusion model weights \theta and the INR weights \phi at each diffusion timestep t. This makes it computationally expensive compared to single-pass methods like FBP or standard INR training. Memory Complexity: The INR representation is memory-efficient and resolution-independent compared to voxel-based methods like DD3IP, as it only stores the neural network weights rather than a 3D grid. Performance: DINR delivers superior performance, reduces reconstruction artifacts, and achieves gains in PSNR and SSIM compared to traditional methods (FBP) and state-of-the-art sparse-view techniques (DD3IP, Siren). It performs on par with MBIR with a qGGMRF prior in sparse-view settings and outperforms it in the ultra-sparse regime. Strengths: High-quality reconstruction from sparse views, resolution-independent representation, ability to integrate learned priors with traditional inverse problem formulations. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the iterative nature of the diffusion process and the joint optimization of \theta and \phi. Requires a pretrained diffusion model. When to use: Sparse-view CT reconstruction, particularly when data is extremely limited (e.g., 5-33 views) and high-quality microstructural characterization is required. DINR was proposed in the paper "Regularizing INR with Diffusion Prior for Self-Supervised 3D Reconstruction OF Neutron Computed Tomography Data". It builds upon the DD3IP framework and the use of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) for inverse imaging problems. The method is designed for sparse-view parallel-beam neutron CT reconstruction of concrete microstructures. It addresses the limitations of standard INRs (spectral bias) and traditional methods (artifacts in sparse views) by combining the flexibility of INRs with the powerful generative prior of diffusion models. name: HiGDiff
head: Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion for Extreme CT Reconstruction
body: HiGDiff is a feed-forward hierarchical Gaussian diffusion framework for constrained Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction that decomposes the recovery process spatially and hierarchically from global structure to local detail. It addresses the problem of joint degradations—where sparse-view sampling aliasing, limited-angle directional incompleteness, and low-dose photon noise are coupled—by using separate Gaussian banks for attenuation geometry and residual boundaries, conditioned on acquisition metadata. Unlike sibling methods that use a single shared representation for all features, HiGDiff establishes an explicit functional hierarchy where a structure diffusion stage recovers global geometry and conditions a subsequent detail diffusion stage for tissue transitions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Degraded projection data (sinograms) affected by sparse views, limited angles, or low dose; acquisition metadata including view density, angular span, and dose levels. Outputs: A volumetric attenuation field represented by two banks of learnable 3D Gaussian primitives, refined by a residual module. Data Structures: 1. Foreground Capacity Field: A learnable scalar field estimating the utility of allocating Gaussian primitives to specific spatial regions. 2. Anatomical Anchors: Landmark-free features used to guide the allocation of primitives to informative regions. 3. Structure Gaussian Bank: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives representing global attenuation geometry. 4. Detail Gaussian Bank: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives representing residual boundaries and tissue transitions. 5. Gradient-Isolated Residual Module: A network module that compensates for residual errors under a fixed primitive budget. Method Steps: 1. Metadata Conditioning: The reconstruction process is conditioned on the input view density, angular span, and dose metadata to adapt to the specific degradation type (sparse, limited, low-dose, or joint). 2. Structure Diffusion: A diffusion process operates on the Structure Gaussian Bank to recover the global attenuation geometry. 3. Capacity Allocation: The Foreground Capacity Field and Anatomical Anchors are used to allocate learnable Gaussian primitives to anatomically informative regions, modulating their denoising features. 4. Detail Diffusion: The learned representation from the Structure Gaussian Bank conditions a second diffusion stage on the Detail Gaussian Bank to recover residual boundaries and tissue transitions. This instantiates multi-stage diffusion dependency directly in the space of explicit CT Gaussian parameters. 5. Rendering: The resulting Gaussian banks are rendered into attenuation fields. 6. Residual Refinement: A gradient-isolated residual module refines the rendered fields to compensate for residual errors and preserve the Gaussian reconstruction as the output backbone. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def HiGDiff(degradedprojections, metadata): """ metadata: dict containing 'viewdensity', 'angularspan', 'dose' """ # Step 1: Condition on acquisition metadata # Metadata is typically embedded and added to the diffusion timestep embeddings conditioning = embedmetadata(metadata) # Step 2: Structure Diffusion Stage # Initialize structure bank with noise or prior structurebank = initializegaussianbank() # Run diffusion to recover global attenuation geometry # Standard DDPM/DDIM sampling loop conditioned on structure prior structurebank = diffusionstepstructure(structurebank, conditioning) # Step 3: Foreground Capacity and Allocation # Estimate utility of allocating primitives capacityfield = computeforegroundcapacity(structurebank) anchors = computeanatomicalanchors(structurebank) # Allocate primitives to informative regions # This modulates the features of the primitives for the next stage allocatedfeatures = modulatefeatures(structurebank, capacityfield, anchors) # Step 4: Detail Diffusion Stage # Initialize detail bank detailbank = initializegaussianbank() # Condition detail diffusion on the learned structure representation # This establishes the explicit functional hierarchy detailconditioning = combine(structurebank, allocatedfeatures) # Run diffusion to recover residual boundaries and tissue transitions detailbank = diffusionstepdetail(detailbank, detailconditioning) # Step 5: Rendering # Render both banks into attenuation fields structurefield = rendergaussians(structurebank) detailfield = rendergaussians(detailbank) # Step 6: Residual Refinement # Refine the combined field using a gradient-isolated module # The module likely operates on the gradient space to isolate artifacts refinedfield = gradientisolatedrefinement(structurefield, detailfield) return refinedfield Parameters: Primitive Budget: Fixed number of Gaussian primitives per bank. Diffusion Steps: Number of denoising steps for structure and detail stages (Not given in the sources). Learning Rate: For training the Gaussian parameters and capacity field (Not given in the sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Joint Degradation: The method is designed to handle the coupling of sampling aliasing, directional incompleteness, and photon noise, which obscures both long-range anatomy and local tissue transitions. Primitive Budget Constraints: The gradient-isolated module is necessary to compensate for residual errors under a fixed primitive budget, preventing the loss of detail when the bank size is limited. Performance: On the LDCT-PD dataset, HiGDiff improves macro-average PSNR by 5.81 dB and SSIM by 0.113 over the strongest metric-specific baselines. It achieves the best macro-average SSIM on all three tested datasets and the best macro-average PSNR on both 3D datasets. Complexity: The method is feed-forward after training, implying inference speed is determined by the diffusion sampling steps and Gaussian rendering cost. Strengths: Explicitly handles joint degradations; separates global structure from local detail to prevent ambiguity; uses explicit Gaussian parameters for multi-stage diffusion dependency. Limitations: Requires training of two diffusion stages and a capacity field; performance depends on the accuracy of the foreground capacity field in allocating primitives. When to use: Severe constrained CT acquisition with sparse views, limited angles, or low dose, particularly when these degradations are present jointly. HiGDiff was proposed by Yang et al. in a preprint titled "Feed-Forward Hierarchical Gaussian Diffusion for Extreme CT Reconstruction". It addresses gaps in existing Gaussian CT methods, which typically use one bank for both global geometry and residual detail, leaving the functional hierarchy implicit under joint degradation. The work builds on the trend of using explicit Gaussian representations for CT and multi-stage diffusion models, but instantiates the dependency directly in the space of explicit CT Gaussian parameters rather than dense image/volume states. Code and experimental configurations are openly available at github.com/Bean-Young/HiGDiff. name: Self-Calibrating Differentiable NLOS Inverse Rendering
head: Differentiable transient rendering with self-calibration, Phasor-field NLOS inverse rendering, Self-Calibrating, Fully Differentiable NLOS Inverse Rendering
body: Self-Calibrating Differentiable NLOS Inverse Rendering is a fully-differentiable end-to-end pipeline for reconstructing hidden scenes from time-resolved non-line-of-sight (NLOS) measurements. It solves the problem of reconstruction artifacts and inversion ambiguities inherent in traditional NLOS imaging by automatically self-calibrating imaging parameters during the reconstruction process, eliminating the need for manual selection of filtering functions and parameters. Unlike volumetric back-projection methods or explicit polygonal mesh approaches, this method estimates an implicit geometric representation (surface points and normals) from volumetric intensities and refines the reconstruction by minimizing the error between simulated and measured illumination via gradient descent. The method operates in two domains: time and frequency. It begins with a phasor-field diffraction reconstruction to generate an initial volumetric intensity, extracts an implicit geometry from this volume, and then uses differentiable transient rendering to simulate the measurement, optimizing parameters to match the input data. Input: Measurement matrix H(xl, xs, t), representing time-resolved illumination captured at points xs on a visible relay wall from a laser beam emitted at point xl. Output: Volumetric intensity I{pf}, implicit geometry G (surface points and normals), and optimized imaging parameters \Theta{pf}, \ThetaG, \Theta{ls}. 1. Measurement Matrix H: A 3D array indexed by laser position xl, sensor position xs, and time t. In the frequency domain, this is transformed into phasors H(xl, xs, \Omega) via Fourier transform. 2. Volumetric Intensity I{pf}: The output of the phasor-field reconstruction, representing the estimated density of hidden objects. 3. Implicit Geometry G: A set of surface points and their associated normals, estimated from I{pf} without defining a polygonal mesh. 4. Parameters: \Theta{pf}: Parameters for the phasor-field reconstruction. \ThetaG: Parameters defining the implicit geometry. \Theta{ls}: Parameters for the differentiable transient rendering (light source and sensor models). 1. Phasor-Field Reconstruction: Transform the time-resolved measurement matrix H(xl, xs, t) into the frequency domain to obtain phasors H(xl, xs, \Omega). Apply a filtering function to the noisy phasor data. Perform NLOS imaging using a phasor-field diffraction method to compute the initial volumetric intensity I{pf} = R{pf}(P(H; \Theta{pf})). Here, P denotes the projection/processing and R{pf} the reconstruction operator. 2. Implicit Geometry Estimation: Estimate the implicit geometry G (surface points and normals) from the volumetric intensity I{pf} using a differentiable estimator D: G = D(I{pf}). This step avoids explicit surface mesh definition. 3. Differentiable Transient Rendering: Render the time-resolved illumination HR from the estimated geometry G using differentiable path-space transient rendering: HR = R(G; \ThetaG, \Theta{ls}). This simulates the light transport from the hidden scene back to the relay wall, accounting for the optimized parameters. 4. Optimization: Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between the measured illumination H and the rendered illumination HR: \mathcal{L} = \sum \| H - HR \|^2 + \Gamma where \Gamma represents regularization terms. Perform gradient descent to update the imaging parameters \Theta{pf}, \ThetaG, \Theta{ls} by minimizing \mathcal{L}. The geometry G is computed during the forward pass, while parameters are updated during the backward pass. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selfcalibratingnlosinverserendering(H): # H: Measurement matrix H(xl, xs, t) # Returns: Optimized parameters and reconstructed geometry # Step 1: Phasor-Field Reconstruction # Transform time-domain measurements to frequency domain (phasors) Hphasor = np.fft.fft(H, axis=-1) # Standard FFT over time axis # Apply filtering to phasors (source does not specify filter type) Hfiltered = applyfrequencyfilter(Hphasor) # Filter applied to noisy phasor data # Reconstruct initial volumetric intensity # Thetapf are initial parameters for phasor-field reconstruction Ipf = phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf) # Ipf = Rpf(P(H; Thetapf)) # Step 2: Estimate Implicit Geometry # Estimate surface points and normals from volumetric intensity G = estimateimplicitgeometry(Ipf) # G = D(Ipf) # Step 3 & 4: Differentiable Rendering and Optimization # Define loss function def lossfunction(thetapf, thetaG, thetals): Ipfnew = phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf) Gnew = estimateimplicitgeometry(Ipfnew) HR = differentiabletransientrendering(Gnew, thetaG, thetals) # HR = R(G; ThetaG, Thetals) L = np.sum((H - HR) 2) + regularizationterm(Gnew) # L = sum ||H - HR||^2 + Gamma return L # Initialize parameters thetapf = initializeparameters('pf') thetaG = initializeparameters('G') thetals = initializeparameters('ls') # Gradient descent optimization while not converged: L = lossfunction(thetapf, thetaG, thetals) gradients = computegradients(L, thetapf, thetaG, thetals) thetapf = update(thetapf, gradients['thetapf']) thetaG = update(thetaG, gradients['thetaG']) thetals = update(thetals, gradients['thetals']) if checkconvergence(L): break return thetapf, thetaG, thetals, estimateimplicitgeometry(phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf)) def applyfrequencyfilter(phasors): # Source mentions filtering but does not specify the function return phasors # Placeholder for unspecified filter def phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf): # Source defines Ipf = Rpf(P(H; Thetapf)) but does not give explicit formulas return np.zeroslike(Hfiltered) def estimateimplicitgeometry(Ipf): # Source defines G = D(Ipf) but does not give explicit formulas return {"points": np.zeros((0, 3)), "normals": np.zeros((0, 3))} def differentiabletransientrendering(G, thetaG, thetals): # Source defines HR = R(G; ThetaG, Thetals) but does not give explicit formulas return np.zeroslike(H) def regularizationterm(Gnew): # Gamma represents regularization terms but is not specified return 0.0 def initializeparameters(name): # Standard parameter initialization return np.random.randn(10) def computegradients(loss, params): # Standard automatic differentiation return {p: np.zeroslike(p) for p in params} def update(param, grad): # Standard gradient descent step return param - 0.01 grad def checkconvergence(loss): # Standard convergence check return loss < 1e-6 Memory Limitations: Computing derivatives of time-resolved radiometric data severely limits the number of unknown parameters that can be handled in differentiable methods. This method addresses this by coupling phasor-field reconstruction with differentiable rendering, but memory constraints remain a factor. Visibility Changes: Handling visibility changes in a differentiable manner is difficult and can lead to non-differentiable discontinuities. Noise: The method is designed to be robust in the presence of noise, providing consistent geometric estimations under varying capture conditions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Limited by the need to compute derivatives of time-resolved radiometric data, which restricts the number of unknown parameters. Strengths: Self-calibrates imaging parameters automatically via gradient descent, removing the need for manual parameter selection. Provides more geometric detail than previous surface-based methods and is robust to noise. Limitations: Bounded by memory limitations inherent in differentiable transient rendering. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction of hidden scenes is required without manual tuning of filtering parameters, and when implicit geometry representation is preferred over explicit meshes. The method was introduced by Kiseok Choi, Inchul Kim, Dongyoung Choi, Julio Marco, Diego Gutierrez, and Min H. Kim. It builds upon wave-based NLOS imaging methods that use diffractive phasor-based frameworks to formulate NLOS reconstruction as a virtual line-of-sight problem. It also integrates concepts from differentiable rendering pipelines in path space. The code is available at https://github.com/KAIST-VCLAB/nlos-inverse-rendering.git. name: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Layered 3D
head: Attenuation-based Light Field Synthesis, Layered 3D, Tomographic Image Synthesis for Multi-Layer HDR Displays, Tomographic Optimization, Tomographic reconstruction for attenuation displays
body: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Layered 3D is a method to optimally construct volumetric or layered attenuators to emit a target light field by minimizing the difference between emitted and target light fields subject to physical constraints on attenuation, using iterative tomographic reconstruction. It solves the inverse problem of determining the attenuation map \mu(x,y) that, when backlit, produces a desired 4D light field l(u,a). Unlike heuristic methods that blur target images to rear layer resolution, this method formulates the synthesis as a constrained linear least-squares optimization problem, proving that existing dual-layer architectures are near-optimal in the least-squares sense. It extends conventional parallax barriers to multiple disjoint layers, increasing spatial resolution, depth of field, and brightness for 3D displays, and enabling high dynamic range (HDR) for 2D displays. Inputs: Target light field l(u, a), parameterized on a relative two-plane system where u is the spatial coordinate on the slab bisector and a is the ray orientation slope. Display geometry: number of layers Nl, layer thickness/separation, and spatial resolution (e.g., 384x512 pixels per layer). Physical constraints: limited layer contrast (attenuation bounds). Outputs: Attenuation maps \mun(x, y) for each layer n \in \{1, \dots, Nl\}, where each map is a continuously-varying function nonzero only within the slab dimensions |x| < w/2, |y| < h/2. Light Field: Stored as a 4D array l(u, a) with spatial resolution (e.g., 384x512) and angular resolution (e.g., 7x7 views). Attenuation Map: Represented using a series expansion into a set of normalized linear basis functions rather than a discrete voxel grid to ensure smoother reconstructions and mitigate discrete ray sampling artifacts. Projection Matrix: A sparse matrix A mapping the basis function coefficients to the light field samples, stored directly in memory, limiting maximum display dimensions and layer count by available system RAM. The forward model is based on the Beer-Lambert law. For a single slab, the transmitted intensity I of a ray along path C is: I = I0 e^{-\intC \mu(\mathbf{r}) d\mathbf{r}} where I0 is incident intensity and \mu(\mathbf{r}) is the attenuation map. The logarithm of the normalized intensity \bar{l} is defined as: \bar{l} = \ln\left(\frac{I}{I0}\right) = -\intC \mu(\mathbf{r}) d\mathbf{r} This integral is the Radon transform p(u, a) of the attenuation map. Thus, the emitted light field is: l(u, a) = -p(u, a) For layered displays, the total attenuation is the sum of the attenuations of individual layers (assuming negligible scattering and reflection between layers). The inverse problem is to find \mu such that the emitted light field matches the target. This is solved as a constrained linear least-squares optimization: \min{\mathbf{x}} \| A \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{x}{min} \le \mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{x}{max} where \mathbf{x} represents the coefficients of the basis functions for the attenuation maps, A is the projection matrix (Radon transform), and \mathbf{b} is the target light field (log-intensity). The constraints \mathbf{x}{min}, \mathbf{x}{max} enforce physical limits on layer contrast (attenuation values). Light Field Resolution: 384x512 spatial pixels by 7x7 angular views. Layer Count (Nl): Five layers in the demonstrated prototype. Field of View: ±5 degrees. Basis Functions: Normalized linear basis functions. 1. Preprocessing: Convert the target light field l{target}(u, a) to log-intensity space: \mathbf{b} = \ln(l{target}). Evaluate color channels independently. 2. Matrix Construction: Construct the sparse projection matrix A that maps the chosen basis function coefficients to the light field samples. 3. Optimization: Solve the constrained linear least-squares problem using a sparse, constrained, large-scale trust region method (e.g., Coleman and Li 1996). Initialize \mathbf{x} to zero. Iterate until convergence (typically 8-14 iterations). Enforce constraints \mathbf{x}{min} \le \mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{x}{max} at each step. 4. Post-processing: Convert the optimized coefficients \mathbf{x} back to attenuation maps \mun(x, y) for each layer. 5. Rendering (Verification): Render the synthesized light field using POV-Ray as 7x7 oblique projections. Apply a depth-dependent 4D antialiasing filter by rendering each view with a limited depth of field (finite aperture camera) to approximate combined anti-aliasing and display prefiltering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Dict class SparseMatrix: def init(self, rows: int, cols: int): self.rows = rows self.cols = cols self.data: Dict[Tuple[int, int], float] = {} def set(self, i: int, j: int, val: float): self.data[(i, j)] = val def get(self, i: int, j: int) -> float: return self.data.get((i, j), 0.0) def computelineintegral(basisfunc, rayu: float, raya: float, pathlength: float, numsamples: int = 100) -> float: integral = 0.0 step = pathlength / numsamples for k in range(numsamples): t = (k + 0.5) step x = rayu + t raya integral += basisfunc(x) step return integral def reconstructfrombasis(coeffs: List[float], basisfuncs: List[callable], gridx: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [sum(c phi(x) for c, phi in zip(coeffs, basisfuncs)) for x in gridx] def solveconstrainedlsqr(A: SparseMatrix, b: List[float], xmin: float, xmax: float, maxiter: int = 14) -> List[float]: cols = A.cols x = [0.0] cols lr = 1e-3 for in range(maxiter): r = [0.0] A.rows for i in range(A.rows): for (j, val) in A.data.items(): if i == j[0]: r[i] += val x[j[1]] r[i] -= b[i] g = [0.0] cols for (i, j), val in A.data.items(): g[j] += val r[i] for k in range(cols): x[k] -= lr g[k] x[k] = max(xmin, min(xmax, x[k])) return x def tomographicsynthesis(targetlf: List[float], numlayers: int, spatialres: Tuple[int, int], angularres: Tuple[int, int], basisfuncs: List[callable], xmin: float, xmax: float) -> List[List[float]]: b = [math.log(val) for val in targetlf] rays = [] for u in range(angularres[0]): for a in range(angularres[1]): rays.append((u, a)) numrays = len(rays) numbasis = len(basisfuncs) numlayers A = SparseMatrix(numrays, numbasis) for i, (u, a) in enumerate(rays): for layer in range(numlayers): for j, phi in enumerate(basisfuncs): colidx = layer len(basisfuncs) + j integral = computelineintegral(phi, u, a, pathlength=1.0) A.set(i, colidx, integral) xopt = solveconstrainedlsqr(A, b, xmin, xmax, maxiter=14) maps = [] gridx = [i / spatialres[0] for i in range(spatialres[0])] for layer in range(numlayers): start = layer len(basisfuncs) end = start + len(basisfuncs) coeffs = xopt[start:end] mu = reconstructfrombasis(coeffs, basisfuncs, gridx) maps.append(mu) return maps Color Crosstalk: The standard implementation evaluates color channels independently, neglecting color crosstalk between layers. Incorporating crosstalk increases memory requirements and computation time significantly. Flip Animations: For uncorrelated multi-view imagery (flip animations), direct application of the optimization leads to significant crosstalk. A spatial downsampling constraint must be added to yield accurate results with enhanced contrast. Filtering Artifacts: Linear reconstruction filters applied to the logarithm of the light field do not correspond to the same filters applied to the light field directly. Memory Limits: Storing the sparse projection matrix directly in memory limits the maximum display dimensions, image resolution, and number of layers by system capacity. Matrix-free optimization can mitigate this but may increase computation time. Physical Assumptions: Scattering and reflection losses are assumed negligible. Interreflections between layers are ignored, though in practice they may not lead to visual artifacts if ambient lighting is controlled. Time Complexity: The optimization requires solving a large, sparse system of equations. It is not real-time; typical optimization takes 12 minutes for 5 layers on a 2.4 GHz Intel Core 2 workstation with 8 GB RAM. Convergence is typically achieved in 8-14 iterations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the sparse projection matrix, which depends on the number of light field samples and basis functions. Limited by system RAM. Strengths: Produces qualitatively optimal decompositions for dual-layer HDR displays, confirming existing heuristics. Extends naturally to multiple disjoint layers, increasing spatial resolution, depth of field, and brightness compared to parallax barriers. Limitations: Computationally expensive; not suitable for dynamic content without significant acceleration (e.g., GPU, precomputed inverses). Limited by physical constraints of layer contrast and separation. When to Use: Static images or pre-rendered content for multi-layer HDR or 3D attenuation displays. When Not to Use: Real-time dynamic applications without hardware acceleration; scenes with significant inter-layer scattering or reflection that cannot be neglected. Origin: Proposed by Wetzstein et al. in 2011. History: The method builds on tomographic reconstruction principles [Herman 1995] and light field parameterization [Chai et al. 2000]. It was developed to address the limitations of heuristic image synthesis methods for layered displays, such as parallax barriers and integral imaging, by providing a mathematically optimal solution in the least-squares sense. Usage: Demonstrated on hardware prototypes consisting of five printed transparency layers separated by clear acrylic sheets (0.3175 cm thick), illuminated by a backlight. Layers were printed on transparencies at 300 dots per inch using an Epson Stylus 2200 inkjet printer with six color primaries. Layered 3D: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Attenuation-based Light Field and High Dynamic Range Displays, https://vccimaging.org/Publications/Wetzstein2011TIG/Wetzstein2011TIG.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Analysis and Diagnostics
body: Analysis and Diagnostics methods evaluate the quality, stability, and information content of tomographic reconstructions without necessarily updating the volume parameters. They solve the problem of verifying reconstruction success and diagnosing artifacts by analyzing the relationship between the measured sinogram and the reconstructed volume. Unlike iterative solvers that minimize a loss function to find the best volume estimate, these methods provide diagnostic metrics (such as SNR or error volumes) or algebraic characterizations (such as null space analysis) to assess the reliability of the reconstruction process. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. Explicit Radon Transform Analysis constructs and analyzes the explicit forward projection matrix A for a given scanning geometry to diagnose the ill-posedness of tomographic reconstruction. It identifies the singular values and the null space of the operator, revealing volumetric perturbations that are invisible to the measurements. Unlike iterative solvers that approximate the inverse, this method provides a direct algebraic characterization of the information loss in sparse or limited-angle scenarios. Choose it when you need to understand the fundamental invertibility limits of a specific scanning geometry rather than optimizing a reconstruction algorithm. This method selects the optimal set of projection angles \thetai for tomographic reconstruction by minimizing the posterior entropy of the inferred 3D volume given the projections, H(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{X}). It operates on the principle that maximizing the joint entropy of the projections H(\mathcal{X}) reduces the uncertainty of the underlying data, which is achieved by minimizing the sum of pairwise mutual information (MI) terms between all projection pairs. Unlike sibling methods that focus on reconstruction speed or specific geometric approximations, this approach is information-theoretic, deriving angle configurations that maximize data diversity based on statistical assumptions about the volume and noise. Choose it when designing acquisition protocols to maximize information gain per projection. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography is a metric used to evaluate the robustness of a tomographic reconstruction method against acquisition noise. It quantifies how well a reconstruction algorithm preserves signal integrity when the input sinogram is corrupted by noise, distinguishing between noise introduced by the acquisition process and noise induced by the reconstruction algorithm itself. Unlike standard image quality metrics that compare a reconstruction to a ground truth, SNR for Tomography compares two reconstructions: one from a clean sinogram and one from a noisy sinogram. Choose it when benchmarking reconstruction algorithms for noise sensitivity rather than absolute accuracy. Error Volume Analysis is a diagnostic technique for tomographic reconstruction that visualizes the residual error between the measured projection data (tilt-series) and the synthetic projections generated from the current volume estimate. It solves the problem of verifying reconstruction success by providing a direct consistency check between the reconstructed tomogram and the raw input data. Unlike standard reconstruction metrics that provide scalar values, this method produces a 3D error volume or 2D error projections, allowing users to assess the reliability and trustworthiness of the reconstruction by inspecting spatial error distribution. Choose it when you need to localize artifacts, misalignments, or insufficient regularization in a completed reconstruction. The family of Analysis and Diagnostics methods in tomographic reconstruction emerged from the need to quantify the reliability of inverse solutions, particularly in limited-angle or sparse-view scenarios where standard reconstruction algorithms may produce ambiguous or artifact-ridden results. Early work focused on algebraic approaches, such as the analysis of the Radon transform's null space, to understand the fundamental limits of information recovery. As computational power increased, information-theoretic approaches, such as mutual information minimization for angle selection, were developed to optimize acquisition protocols. More recently, with the rise of differentiable rendering and inverse rendering, diagnostic tools like Error Volume Analysis have become integral to verifying the consistency of learned volumetric representations against raw sensor data. These methods are widely used in electron tomography, medical CT, and computational imaging to validate reconstruction pipelines and guide experimental design.

name: Explicit Radon Transform Analysis
head: Radon Matrix Analysis, Sparse-View Radon Transform Null Space Analysis
body: Explicit Radon Transform Analysis constructs and analyzes the explicit forward projection matrix A (or operator RV) for a given scanning geometry to diagnose the invertibility and stability of tomographic reconstruction. Unlike differentiable rendering which relies on gradient descent, this method explicitly exposes the linear algebra structure of the forward operator, allowing for the computation of singular values and the identification of the null space. Inputs: Scanning geometry parameters: number of angles n{angles}, maximum angle range \theta{max}, number of samples per ray n{samples}, and detector dimensions v{large}, h{large}. Volume dimensions: v{small}, h{small} (or 3D extent w). Optional: sparsesvd flag to determine if full or sparse SVD is computed. Outputs: The explicit Radon transform matrix A (size M \times N, where M is total detector pixels and N is total volume voxels). Singular values W of the matrix A. Data Structures: Matrix A: A sparse matrix where A{ij} represents the contribution of voxel j to detector pixel i. Singular Values W: A vector of length \min(M, N) representing the decay of the operator's energy. Steps: 1. Geometry Setup: Define the volume geometry (volgeom) and projection geometry (projgeom) based on input parameters n{angles}, \theta{max}, n{samples}, v{large}, h{large}. 2. Matrix Construction: Call the explicit Radon transform function explicitradon with parameters nangles, maxangle, nsamples, vsmall, hsmall, and sparsesvd=False to generate the matrix A and its singular values W. 3. Spectral Analysis: Compute the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of A to obtain W. 4. Null Space Identification: Identify the null space \mathcal{N}(RV) defined as: \mathcal{N}(RV) = \{ \delta V \mid RV(\delta V) = 0 \} where RV is the sparse-view Radon operator. Vectors in this null space represent volumetric perturbations invisible to the projections. 5. Visualization: Use imshow to visualize the matrix A to observe the sparsity pattern corresponding to the scanning geometry. Formulas: The sparse-view Radon transform is defined as the concatenation of Radon operators along K projection directions V = \{v1, \dots, vK\}: RV(V) = (R{v1}(V), \dots, R{vK}(V)) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times h \times w} where V is the attenuation field, Rv is the line-integral operator along direction v, and K is the number of views. For dense views (K \to \infty), R is injective. For sparse views (finite K, e.g., K \in \{10, 20, 25\}), RV is strongly underdetermined and \mathcal{N}(RV) is non-trivial. Parameters: nangles: Number of projection angles. Typical values: 10, 20, 25, 45. maxangle: Maximum angular range. Typical values: \pi (sparse, full rotation) or limited ranges (limited angle). nsamples: Number of samples per ray. vsmall, hsmall: Volume dimensions. vlarge, hlarge: Detector dimensions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underdetermined Systems: In sparse-view or limited-angle scenarios, the operator is strongly underdetermined with a non-trivial null space, meaning projection consistency alone cannot uniquely determine the density field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.sparse import csrmatrix from scipy.sparse.linalg import svds import matplotlib.pyplot as plt def explicitradonanalysis(nangles, maxangle, nsamples, vsmall, hsmall, vlarge, hlarge, sparsesvd=False): """ Constructs the explicit Radon matrix and analyzes its properties. """ # 1. Geometry Setup volgeom = {'voxelsize': (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), 'volumesize': (vsmall, hsmall, 1), 'origin': (0, 0, 0)} projgeom = {'detectorsize': (hlarge, vlarge), 'numpixels': (hlarge, vlarge), 'numangles': nangles, 'anglerange': maxangle, 'rayspacing': 1.0} # 2. Matrix Construction M = projgeom['numpixels'][0] projgeom['numpixels'][1] projgeom['numangles'] N = volgeom['volumesize'][0] volgeom['volumesize'][1] volgeom['volumesize'][2] rows, cols, vals = [], [], [] # Standard DDA ray-tracing loop to populate sparse matrix A for angleidx in range(nangles): angle = angleidx maxangle / nangles for dety in range(vlarge): for detx in range(hlarge): rayorigin = np.array([detx, dety, 0.0]) raydirection = np.array([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle), 0.0]) for z in range(volgeom['volumesize'][2]): for y in range(volgeom['volumesize'][1]): for x in range(volgeom['volumesize'][0]): # Compute ray-voxel intersection weight (e.g., distance inside voxel) weight = 1.0 rows.append(angleidx vlarge hlarge + dety hlarge + detx) cols.append(z hsmall vsmall + y vsmall + x) vals.append(weight) A = csrmatrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(M, N)) # 3. Spectral Analysis if sparsesvd: # Use scipy.sparse.linalg.svds for large matrices k = min(100, min(M, N)) U, S, Vt = svds(A, k=k) W = S else: U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A.toarray(), fullmatrices=False) W = S # 4. Null Space Identification nullspacethreshold = 1e-6 nullspacevectors = Vt[W < nullspacethreshold,:] # 5. Visualization plt.figure() plt.imshow(A.toarray().reshape(vlarge, hlarge nangles), cmap='hot') plt.title(f"Radon Matrix Sparsity (n={nangles}, maxangle={maxangle})") plt.xlabel("Voxel Index") plt.ylabel("Detector Pixel Index") plt.show() return A, W, nullspacevectors Analyzes the operator when K is small (e.g., 10-25 views) but the angular range is full (\pi). Sets it apart by isolating the effects of angular undersampling. Chosen when diagnosing missing angular data effects. Analyzes the operator when the angular range is restricted (e.g., \theta{max} < \pi). Sets it apart by isolating the effects of geometric constraints. Chosen when diagnosing missing geometric data effects. Compares the singular value decay for sparse angles (fixed max angle \pi, varying K) vs. limited angles (fixed K, varying max angle). Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides exact diagnostic information about the forward operator's invertibility and null space. Limitations: Does not provide a reconstruction itself, only analysis. Originating from the mathematical analysis of the Radon transform in computed tomography, this method was applied to 3D Gaussian tomography to diagnose optimization drift and null-space ambiguities in sparse-view settings. The explicit matrix construction and SVD analysis are implemented in inverse problems toolboxes like the ASTRA Toolbox. name: Optimal Projection Angle Selection via Mutual Information Minimization
head: Information theoretic projection angle selection, Information-Theoretic Angle Selection, Information-theoretic tomography angle selection, MI-based angle optimization, Mutual Information Optimization, Optimal Projection Angles
body: This method selects the optimal set of projection angles \thetai for tomographic reconstruction by minimizing the posterior entropy of the inferred 3D volume H(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{X}). It operates on the principle that maximizing the joint entropy of the observed projections H(\mathcal{X}) reduces the uncertainty about the underlying data, assuming the noise entropy H(\mathcal{X}|\mathcal{D}) is independent of angle choice. Unlike Explicit Radon Transform Analysis which relies on geometric completeness, or Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography which focuses on measurement fidelity, this approach uses information theory to quantify redundancy between views. It sets itself apart by approximating higher-order statistical dependencies as pairwise mutual information (MI), allowing for efficient numerical optimization of angle configurations. Inputs: N: The number of desired projection angles. \Sigma: The covariance matrix of the 3D data distribution (often assumed axisymmetric Gaussian \sigma^2 I for analytical simplification). \sigma0: The standard deviation of additive i.i.d. Gaussian noise in the projections. Geometry type: Parallel beam or Cone beam (determines periodicity and Fourier coefficients). Cone angle \phi (for cone beam): Defined by source-to-origin distance L and data spread \sigma, where \tan(\phi/2) = \sigma/L. Outputs: A set of optimal angles \Theta = \{\theta1, \dots, \thetaN\} that minimizes the sum of pairwise mutual information terms. Fourier Coefficients Table (A): A lookup table mapping cone angles \phi to Fourier coefficients ak for k=0,\dots,6. Structure: Array of shape (M, 7), where M is the number of discrete cone angles (e.g., 4 for \phi \in \{10^\circ, 15^\circ, 20^\circ, 25^\circ\}). Fields: a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6. Default values (for \varepsilon = 0.1): \phi=10^\circ: [0.66, -0.02, -0.46, -0.01, -0.13, 0.0, -0.01] \phi=15^\circ: [0.67, -0.05, -0.43, -0.03, -0.12, -0.01, -0.01] \phi=20^\circ: [0.69, -0.10, -0.39, -0.05, -0.10, -0.01, -0.02] \phi=25^\circ: [0.73, -0.16, -0.29, -0.07, -0.08, -0.02, -0.02]. 1. Define Pairwise Mutual Information Function: Calculate the mutual information I(\alpha{ij}) between two projections separated by angular distance \alpha{ij} = |\thetaj - \thetai|. Analytical Form (Axisymmetric Gaussian): For an axisymmetric Gaussian prior with noise ratio \varepsilon = \sigma0^2/\sigma^2: I(\alpha{ij}) = -\frac{1}{2} \ln \left( 1 - \frac{\cos^2 \alpha{ij}}{(1 + \varepsilon)^2} \right) where \alpha{ij} is in radians. General Form (Non-axisymmetric): If \Sigma is not axisymmetric, use: I(\alpha{ij}|\Sigma) = -\frac{1}{2} \ln \left( 1 - \frac{(\mathbf{b}i^T \Sigma \mathbf{b}j)^2}{(\sigma0^2 + \mathbf{b}i^T \Sigma \mathbf{b}i)(\sigma0^2 + \mathbf{b}j^T \Sigma \mathbf{b}j)} \right) where \mathbf{b}i = [1, 0]^T and \mathbf{b}j = [\cos \alpha{ij}, \sin \alpha{ij}]^T are direction vectors. Surrogate Form (Cone Beam Approximation): For cone beam geometries, the MI function is approximated using a Fourier series surrogate to capture decorrelation at \pi: I(\alpha) = -\frac{1}{2} \log \left( \sum{k=0}^{6} ak \cos(k\alpha) \right) where coefficients ak are retrieved from the Fourier Coefficients Table based on the cone angle \phi. 2. Formulate Optimization Objective: The goal is to maximize the joint entropy H(\mathcal{X}). Using the pairwise approximation: H(\mathcal{X}) \approx \sum{i=1}^N H(\mathcal{X}i) - \sum{1 \le i < j \le N} I(\mathcal{X}i; \mathcal{X}j) Since marginal entropies H(\mathcal{X}i) are constant with respect to angle selection, minimizing the total pairwise MI minimizes the posterior entropy: \min{\Theta} \sum{1 \le i < j \le N} I(\thetaj - \thetai). 3. Numerical Optimization: Optimize the angles \thetai \in [0, 2\pi) to minimize the surrogate MI sum. Odd N: The optimal angles are uniformly distributed: \thetai = \frac{2\pi i}{N}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1. Even N (Parallel Beam): Angles divide the half-circle: \thetai = \frac{\pi i}{N}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1 Note: Due to symmetry I(\pi)=I(0), angles \theta and \theta+\pi are redundant. Even N (Cone Beam): To increase angular separation and reduce MI, reflect some angles into the opposite half-circle. 4. Monte Carlo Verification (Optional): To validate the MI model for specific cone angles: 1. Sample N{mc}=100,000 points (x,y) from \mathcal{N}(0, I). 2. Apply cone beam projection transform: \tilde{r} = \left\| x + (x-s) \frac{L-x \cdot n}{(x-s) \cdot n} - Ln \right\| where s = [L\sin\theta, -L\cos\theta] and n = [-\sin\theta, \cos\theta]. 3. Add Gaussian noise \sigma0=0.1 to obtain r1, r2. 4. Compute correlation \rho and MI: I(\alpha) = -0.5 \log(1 - \rho). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def calculatepairwisemiparallel(alpha, sigma0, sigmadata): """ Calculates pairwise MI for parallel beam with axisymmetric Gaussian. alpha: angular separation in radians. sigma0: noise std dev. sigmadata: data std dev. """ epsilon = (sigma0 / sigmadata) 2 term = (np.cos(alpha) 2) / ((1 + epsilon) 2) # Guard against precision errors causing log(0) or complex results term = np.minimum(term, 1.0 - 1e-10) return -0.5 np.log(1 - term) def calculatepairwisemiconesurrogate(alpha, coeffs): """ Calculates surrogate MI for cone beam using Fourier coefficients. alpha: angular separation in radians. coeffs: list of 7 coefficients [a0,..., a6]. """ sumcos = sum(a np.cos(k alpha) for k, a in enumerate(coeffs)) # Guard against log of negative number due to approximation bounds sumcos = np.maximum(sumcos, 1e-10) return -0.5 np.log(sumcos) def optimizeangles(N, geometrytype, coneangledeg=None, coeffs=None): """ Returns optimal angles based on geometry type and N parity. """ if geometrytype == "parallel": if N % 2 != 0: # Odd N: Uniform distribution over 2pi return np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, N, endpoint=False) else: # Even N: Uniform distribution over pi (half-circle) return np.linspace(0, np.pi, N, endpoint=False) elif geometrytype == "cone": if N % 2 != 0: return np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, N, endpoint=False) else: # Even N cone beam: Source states higher angular separation is achieved # by reflecting some angles into the opposite half-circle. # Exact reflection pattern requires numerical optimization of the # surrogate MI sum, which is not specified in the source. # Return half-circle baseline as reference. return np.linspace(0, np.pi, N, endpoint=False) else: raise ValueError("geometrytype must be 'parallel' or 'cone'") def verifymiconemc(theta1, theta2, L, sigmadata, sigma0): """ Monte Carlo verification of MI for cone beam per source steps. """ Nmc = 100000 # 1. Sample points from axisymmetric Gaussian N(0, I) points = np.random.normal(0, 1, (Nmc, 2)) # 2. Apply coordinate transform for both angles # Source sets theta1=0 for reference, but general case rotates vectors s1 = np.array([L np.sin(theta1), -L np.cos(theta1)]) n1 = np.array([-np.sin(theta1), np.cos(theta1)]) s2 = np.array([L np.sin(theta2), -L np.cos(theta2)]) n2 = np.array([-np.sin(theta2), np.cos(theta2)]) # Eq 8 implementation: distance from origin to projected point on detector plane def projectpoint(p, s, n, L): diff = p - s t = (L - np.dot(p, n)) / np.dot(diff, n) proj = p + diff t - L n return np.linalg.norm(proj, axis=1) r1noisy = projectpoint(points, s1, n1, L) + np.random.normal(0, sigma0, Nmc) r2noisy = projectpoint(points, s2, n2, L) + np.random.normal(0, sigma0, Nmc) # 3. Add Gaussian noise sigma0=0.1 (hardcoded per source) # 4. Calculate correlation coefficient rho rho = np.corrcoef(r1noisy, r2noisy)[0, 1] # 5. Compute MI rhoclamped = np.clip(rho, -0.9999, 0.9999) return -0.5 np.log(1 - rhoclamped 2) Noise Level (\varepsilon): The Fourier coefficients in Table 3 are tabulated for \varepsilon = 0.1. Parallel Beam Symmetry: For parallel beams, I(\pi) = I(0). This forces all odd Fourier coefficients ak (k=1,3,\dots) to be zero. Cone Beam Decorrelation: For cone beams, I(\pi) < I(0). This necessitates non-zero odd coefficients to model the reduction in MI at \pi. Periodicity: The angular distance \alpha{ij} is symmetric (\alpha{ij} = \alpha{ji}) and periodic with 2\pi (or \pi for parallel). Precomputation: Fourier coefficients for the surrogate form are derived via Monte Carlo sampling (N=100,000 points) and tabulated once per cone angle configuration. Optimization: For odd N, complexity is O(1) (direct formula). For even N with cone beams, it requires numerical optimization of the surrogate MI sum, scaling with O(N^2) for pairwise evaluation. Memory: Minimal. Requires storing N angles and a small 7 \times M coefficient table. The method identifies 0^\circ and 90^\circ as optimal for N=2 parallel projections, consistent with minimizing MI. For cone beams, the method demonstrates that reflecting angles into the opposite half-circle for even N yields better angular separation than simple half-circle uniform distribution. Strengths: Provides a principled, information-theoretic basis for angle selection. Handles both parallel and cone beam geometries. Simple analytical solutions for odd N. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that higher-order mutual information can be approximated by pairwise terms. Assumes Gaussian priors for the analytical form. The surrogate Fourier approximation may lose accuracy for extreme cone angles or noise levels not covered in the table. This method originates from the work on "Neural rendering enables dynamic tomography". It applies information theory to the problem of selecting projection angles in tomographic reconstruction, specifically within the context of neural rendering and differentiable rendering. The approach builds on the postulate that minimizing the posterior entropy H(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{X}) is equivalent to maximizing the joint entropy of projections H(\mathcal{X}). It distinguishes itself from photographic NeRF angle selection (which separates views by 180^\circ) by recognizing that X-ray projections at \theta and \theta+\pi are not identical in cone beam geometry, leading to different optimal configurations. name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography
head: rapport signal sur bruit
body: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography is a diagnostic metric that evaluates the robustness of a tomographic reconstruction method against acquisition noise. It quantifies how well a reconstruction algorithm preserves signal integrity when the input sinogram is corrupted by noise, specifically isolating sensitivity to input perturbations rather than absolute fidelity to a ground truth. Unlike metrics such as SSIM or MSE which compare a reconstruction to an ideal target, SNR for Tomography compares two reconstructions: one derived from a clean sinogram and one derived from a noisy sinogram. This distinguishes it from sibling metrics like Explicit Radon Transform Analysis or Error Volume Analysis, which assess structural or geometric deviations. Inputs and Outputs: Input 1: A clean sinogram R\theta(\rho) representing an ideal, noise-free acquisition. Input 2: A noisy sinogram R\theta^{noise}(\rho) generated by applying an acquisition noise model to the clean sinogram. Input 3: A reconstruction algorithm \mathcal{R} (e.g., Back Projection, Fourier Reconstruction). Output: The SNR value in decibels (dB), quantifying the reconstruction's robustness. Data Structures: Sinogram: A 2D array indexed by projection angle \theta and detector position \rho. Reconstructed Image: A 2D or 3D array of pixel/voxel intensities I(p). Noise Model: Acquisition noise is modeled as additive white Gaussian noise. The noisy sinogram is generated by adding a random perturbation \epsilon to each value R\theta(\rho) of the clean sinogram: R\theta^{noise}(\rho) = R\theta(\rho) + \epsilon where \epsilon is sampled uniformly from the interval [-(A/2)R\theta(\rho), +(A/2)R\theta(\rho)]. The parameter A denotes the noise amplitude percentage; a standard evaluation value is A = 10\%. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Generate Noisy Sinogram: Apply the noise model to the clean sinogram R\theta(\rho) using the specified amplitude A. 2. Reconstruct Clean Image: Apply the reconstruction algorithm \mathcal{R} to the clean sinogram to obtain the reference reconstruction J. 3. Reconstruct Noisy Image: Apply the same algorithm \mathcal{R} to the noisy sinogram to obtain the noisy reconstruction JB. 4. Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE): Calculate the MSE between the reference image I{in} = J and the noisy image I{out} = JB: mse(I{in}, I{out}) = \frac{\sum{p=1}^{N} (I{in}(p) - I{out}(p))^2}{N} where N is the total number of pixels/voxels. 5. Calculate SNR: Compute the SNR in decibels using the ratio of the squared mean intensity of the reference image to the MSE: snr(I{in}, I{out}) = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{\bar{I}{in}^2}{mse(I{in}, I{out})} \right) where \bar{I}{in} is the mean intensity of I{in}. The source notation writes this as \log(\bar{I}{in}/mse) but explicitly states the result is expressed in decibels, implying the standard 10 \log{10} power-ratio conversion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatenoisysinogram(cleansinogram, noiselevelpercent=0.10): """ Adds uniform noise to the sinogram based on. Noise is uniform between -(A/2)R and +(A/2)R. """ A = noiselevelpercent noise = np.random.uniform(-A/2, A/2, size=cleansinogram.shape) noisysinogram = cleansinogram + (noise cleansinogram) return noisysinogram def computemse(imagein, imageout): """ Computes Mean Squared Error between two images. """ N = imagein.size mse = np.sum((imagein - imageout) 2) / N return mse def computesnrtomography(reconstructionfunc, cleansinogram, noisysinogram): """ Computes SNR for Tomography as defined in. """ J = reconstructionfunc(cleansinogram) JB = reconstructionfunc(noisysinogram) mseval = computemse(J, JB) meanIin = np.mean(J) if mseval == 0: return float('inf') snrdb = 10 np.log10((meanIin 2) / mseval) return snrdb Parameters: A: Noise amplitude percentage. Typical evaluation value: 10\%. Edge Cases: Zero MSE: If the reconstruction algorithm perfectly suppresses the added noise, mse = 0, resulting in infinite SNR. Negative Intensities: The noise model scales with R\theta(\rho), assuming positive sinogram values; negative reconstruction values can distort the mean intensity \bar{I}{in} and the SNR ratio. Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) evaluates the perceptual contrast of specific structures within the final rendered volume relative to background noise, rather than the reconstruction's robustness to acquisition noise [Parent]. It is chosen when validating denoising strategies or interpolation methods where visual distinguishability matters more than input stability [Parent]. Time Complexity: The SNR calculation itself is O(N) for N voxels/pixels. The dominant cost is the dual reconstruction of clean and noisy volumes, scaling with the chosen algorithm (e.g., O(N \cdot M) for Back Projection with M projections). Memory Complexity: Requires storing two sinograms and two reconstructed volumes, O(N). Measured Performance: Under 10% additive Gaussian noise on sinograms, Back Projection yields an SNR of 6.33 dB, while Fourier Reconstruction yields -0.44 dB. This demonstrates Back Projection's significantly higher robustness to acquisition noise compared to Fourier methods. Strengths: Directly quantifies algorithmic stability against input perturbations, independent of reconstruction-induced artifacts. Computationally lightweight post-reconstruction. Limitations: Does not measure absolute accuracy or structural fidelity to ground truth. Sensitive to the chosen noise model and amplitude. When to use: Comparing reconstruction algorithms for stability under noisy acquisition conditions. When not to use: When absolute geometric accuracy or structural similarity to a reference is required. The metric originates from French-language research on tomographic reconstruction quality and precision assessment, specifically detailed in the thesis "Précision et qualité en reconstruction tomographique: algorithmes et applications". It was developed to compare the robustness of classical reconstruction techniques, such as Back Projection and Fourier Reconstruction, against simulated acquisition noise. It is widely used in medical imaging and cryo-electron tomography diagnostics. name: Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR)
head: FWHM, Quantitative Image Analysis Metrics, Smoothness, FWHM evaluation, Quantitative quality metrics for volume rendering
body: Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) is a quantitative metric used to evaluate the quality of volume-rendered images by measuring the distinguishability of a feature of interest from its surrounding background relative to the noise level. It serves as a diagnostic tool for validating reconstruction algorithms, interpolation methods, and denoising strategies, particularly in scenarios where visual assessment is insufficient. Unlike Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography, which measures reconstruction robustness to acquisition noise by comparing clean and noisy sinograms [Parent], CNR focuses on the perceptual contrast of specific structures within the final rendered volume. The calculation of CNR requires defining Regions of Interest (ROIs) on the rendered volume and computing statistical moments of the intensity values within those regions. Two distinct formulations are documented in the literature, corresponding to different application domains (tomosynthesis vs. cryo-electron tomography). Inputs: 1. Rendered volume or image I. 2. Definition of ROIs: feature ROI(s) containing the structure of interest, and background ROI(s) containing uniform background or homogeneous areas. 3. (Optional) Number of paired regions N{pr} if using the paired formulation. Outputs: A scalar value representing the Contrast-to-Noise Ratio. The method operates on scalar intensity values extracted from the volume at specific voxel coordinates defined by the ROIs. Intensity Array: A 1D array or list of pixel/voxel values vi for each ROI. Statistics: Mean (\mu or l) and Standard Deviation (\sigma or r) of the intensity values in each ROI. 1. Render phantom or clinical data at specified angles (e.g., 0^\circ and 90^\circ). 2. Extract intensity profiles or slice data corresponding to the defined ROIs. 3. Calculate CNR using the appropriate formula based on the application domain. 4. Plot metrics against sampling distance or interpolation parameters to select optimal configuration. Two primary formulas exist. Formula 1: Standard Difference-of-Means (Tomosynthesis/General) Used in for evaluating interpolation and sampling in breast tomosynthesis. CNR = \frac{\mu{feat} - \mu{BG}}{\sigma{BG}} Where: \mu{feat}: Mean pixel value in the Region of Interest (ROI) over the feature (e.g., a 5.0 mm disk). \mu{BG}: Mean pixel value in the background ROI. \sigma{BG}: Mean of the standard deviations in the background ROIs. Note: If multiple background ROIs are used, \sigma{BG} is the average of their individual standard deviations. Formula 2: Paired Variance-Based (Cryo-ET/Denoising) Used in for evaluating denoising strategies in cryo-electron tomography. CNR = \frac{lf - lu}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N{pr}}} \sqrt{0.5(r^2f + r^2u)}} Where: N{pr}: Number of paired regions selected to compute the CNR. lf: Mean intensity in the selected regions containing features. r^2f: Variance in the selected regions containing features. lu: Mean intensity in the selected uniform (background) regions. r^2u: Variance in the selected uniform regions. ROI Selection: Critical for reproducibility. In, ROIs are drawn over a specific phantom feature (5.0 mm disk) and surrounding background. In, regions are manually labeled on different slices of the reconstructed tomogram. Number of Paired Regions (N{pr}): In, this is a user-defined parameter for the number of samples taken to estimate the metric. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatecnrstandard(featurevalues, backgroundvalueslist): """ Calculates CNR using the standard difference-of-means formula. """ if not featurevalues: return 0.0 mufeat = sum(featurevalues) / len(featurevalues) bgmeans = [] bgstds = [] for bgvals in backgroundvalueslist: if not bgvals: continue m = sum(bgvals) / len(bgvals) bgmeans.append(m) var = sum((x - m) 2 for x in bgvals) / len(bgvals) bgstds.append(math.sqrt(var)) if not bgstds: return 0.0 muBG = sum(bgmeans) / len(bgmeans) sigmaBG = sum(bgstds) / len(bgstds) if sigmaBG == 0: return 0.0 return (mufeat - muBG) / sigmaBG def calculatecnrpaired(featuremeans, featurevariances, uniformmeans, uniformvariances, npr): """ Calculates CNR using the paired variance-based formula. """ if npr == 0: return 0.0 lf = sum(featuremeans) / len(featuremeans) r2f = sum(featurevariances) / len(featurevariances) lu = sum(uniformmeans) / len(uniformmeans) r2u = sum(uniformvariances) / len(uniformvariances) numerator = lf - lu denominator = (1.0 / math.sqrt(npr)) math.sqrt(0.5 (r2f + r2u)) if denominator == 0: return 0.0 return numerator / denominator 1. Zero Noise/Uniform Background: If the background is perfectly uniform (\sigma{BG} = 0), the denominator in Formula 1 becomes zero. 2. ROI Definition Bias: The metric is highly sensitive to ROI placement. In, the background ROIs must be drawn in the surrounding area, not overlapping the feature. In, manual labeling introduces subjectivity. 3. Anisotropic Resolution: In tomosynthesis, the z-direction has coarser resolution than xy. CNR calculations should account for this, as features may spread in z, affecting \mu{feat} and \sigma{BG}. 4. Paired Region Count: In Formula 2, N{pr} must be consistent across comparisons. A small N{pr} leads to high variance in the metric estimate. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of pixels/voxels in the defined ROIs. The calculation involves simple statistical aggregations (mean, variance). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the intensity values of the ROIs, or O(1) if computed on-the-fly during rendering/analysis. Strengths: Provides an objective, numerical basis for comparing rendering configurations (e.g., interpolation methods, sampling distances). Effective for evaluating denoising performance by quantifying contrast preservation vs. noise reduction. Limitations: Does not account for human visual perception directly (unlike SSIM or VDP). In, it is noted that CNR alone is insufficient; it is often used alongside Smoothness and FWHM to provide a complete picture of image quality. When to use: When optimizing volume rendering parameters (sampling, interpolation) or evaluating denoising algorithms where quantitative comparison is needed. When not to use: When subjective visual quality is the primary concern, or when the background is not well-defined/uniform. In the context of volume rendering diagnostics, CNR has been applied to: 1. Breast Tomosynthesis (DBT): Used to validate and compare interpolation methods (Linear, Cubic, Nearest-Neighbor, Sinc with various windows) and sampling distances. Studies showed that optimized parameters (e.g., Hamming window with BF(z)=2, sampling 0.025 mm) significantly improved CNR compared to default settings. 2. Cryo-Electron Tomography (cryo-ET): Used to evaluate adaptive differentiable grids and denoising strategies. It measures how well a denoiser increases contrast between features and background. The metric is often part of a suite of quantitative image analysis metrics, including Smoothness and FWHM, to objectively evaluate volume rendering quality.
