name: Error Volume Analysis
head: Error Volume Visualization Enhancement, Error projection enhancement, Reconstruction Error Visualization
body: Error Volume Analysis is a diagnostic technique for tomographic reconstruction that visualizes the residual error between the measured projection data (tilt-series) and the synthetic projections generated from the current volume estimate. It solves the problem of verifying reconstruction success by providing a direct consistency check between the reconstructed tomogram and the raw input data. Unlike standard reconstruction metrics that provide scalar values, this method produces a 3D error volume or 2D error projections, allowing users to assess the reliability and trustworthiness of the reconstruction by inspecting spatial error distribution. It is distinct from sibling methods like Explicit Radon Transform Analysis or Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography because it does not update the volume parameters but rather analyzes the output of the reconstruction process to detect artifacts, misalignments, or insufficient regularization. The method operates by computing the discrepancy between the input tilt-series and the forward-projected volume, then reconstructing this discrepancy into a 3D error volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: P{orig} (the original measured tilt-series), V{est} (the estimated 3D volume), and \mathcal{P} (the forward projection operator that computes synthetic projections from the volume). Outputs: E{vol} (the reconstructed error volume) and E{proj} (enhanced error projection images). Data Structures: Tilt-Series: A list of 2D arrays (images) corresponding to projection angles. Volume: A 3D grid of voxel values representing density or absorption coefficients. Error Volume: A 3D grid of voxel values. Dimensions are not specified in the sources. Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Compute Synthetic Projections: For each viewing angle \thetai in the tilt-series, compute a synthetic projection \hat{p}i from the estimated volume: \hat{p}i = \mathcal{P}(V{est}, \thetai) 2. Calculate Re-projection Error Images: Create an error tilt-series by computing the absolute difference between the original projection pi and the synthetic projection \hat{p}i for each angle: ei = | pi - \hat{p}i | 3. Reconstruct Error Volume: Apply a tomographic reconstruction algorithm (specifically SART in the source implementation) to the error tilt-series \{ei\} to generate the initial error volume E{raw}: E{raw} = \text{Reconstruct}{\text{SART}}(\{ei\}) 4. Enhance Error Visualization (Post-processing): Apply the following steps to the error projections or volume to enhance the biggest error contributions for visualization purposes and pronounce structural features: Gaussian Blur: Apply a 3 \times 3 Gaussian blur to the error data: E{blurred} = \text{GaussianBlur}(E{raw}, \text{kernel}=3\times3) Thresholding: Threshold intensity values below 1/8 of the maximum value in the dataset: E{thresh}[v] = \begin{cases} E{blurred}[v] & \text{if } E{blurred}[v] > \frac{1}{8} \max(E{blurred}) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Gamma Correction: Adjust the gamma value to 2.0 to shift mid-tones to brighter values: E{final}[v] = E{thresh}[v]^{\frac{1}{2.0}} Parameters: Gaussian Kernel Size: 3 \times 3. Threshold Factor: 1/8 of the maximum intensity value. Gamma Value: 2.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Angle Artifacts: If the reconstructed volume has the same width as the projection images, rays at the borders intersect the volume for shorter distances at high tilt angles. Horizontal padding is required to ensure uniform ray path lengths. The padded volume width vw should be rounded up to the next even value (e.g., for width 1024, padded width is 2568). Noise Sensitivity: The raw error images can be very noisy due to sparse error contributions. The post-processing steps are critical to enhance the biggest error contributions and pronounce structural features. Regularization Masking: Heavy regularization may hide reconstruction errors by forcing the volume to be smooth. The error volume analysis helps verify if the regularization is appropriate. A method to evaluate reconstruction precision by computing the correlation between two volumes reconstructed from split projection sets, used because only one copy of the volume exists in tilt-series cryo-ET. It is chosen when a quantitative resolution estimate is needed, though it is less reliable for absolute resolution in tilt-series than in single-particle analysis. Definition: FSC measures the similarity between two independent reconstructions in Fourier space. Steps: 1. Split the even and odd projections of the tilt-series into two sets. 2. Reconstruct two independent volumes, V1 and V2, from these sets. 3. Compute the Fourier transforms F1 and F2 of V1 and V2. 4. Calculate the FSC for each radial shell ri in Fourier space. Formula: FSC(ri) = \frac{\sum ri F1(ri) F2(ri)}{\sqrt{\sum |F1(ri)|^2 \sum |F2(ri)|^2}} where ri is the voxel element in Fourier space at radius r, and F1(ri) and F2(ri) are the complex structure factors of the first and second volume, respectively. Parameters: Resolution Threshold: The reconstruction resolution is defined as the highest frequency where the FSC remains above a given threshold. The source uses FSC = 0.5 because FSC = 0.143 cannot distinguish resolution for some methods in tilt-series cryo-ET. Pitfalls: FSC values may be unreliable for absolute resolution estimation in tilt-series cryo-ET due to high residual noise. FSC may rank methods highly that produce consistent but wrong structures across the two reconstructions. Time Complexity: The method requires one additional forward projection pass for each angle in the tilt-series and one additional tomographic reconstruction pass (SART) on the error images. Exact computational complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original tilt-series, the estimated volume, and the error volume. Exact memory footprint is not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides intuitive visual feedback on reconstruction quality; detects misalignments and regularization issues; allows for direct comparison between different reconstruction strategies (e.g., with/without regularization). Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the additional reconstruction step; interpretation requires experience to distinguish between noise and structural errors. When to use: During iterative reconstruction to monitor convergence and diagnose artifacts; for final validation of reconstruction quality. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Error Volume Analysis was introduced in the context of GPU-accelerated 3D tomographic reconstruction for cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-ET). It addresses the need for a direct consistency check between the reconstruction and the raw input projection images, which is particularly important in noisy and limited-angle tomographic data. The method builds on the principle that a successful reconstruction should reproduce the input projections, and any significant deviation (error) should be uncorrelated with the object's structure if the reconstruction is accurate and regularized appropriately. name: SMART-RECON
head: Synchronized multiartifact reduction with tomographic reconstruction
body: SMART-RECON is an iterative reconstruction method for time-resolved computed tomography (CT) that eliminates limited-view artifacts and mitigates temporal-average artifacts by jointly reconstructing all image frames using a nuclear norm regularizer on a spatial-temporal image matrix. It differs from sibling methods like PICCS and Filtered Backprojection by exploiting the low-dimensional structure of the spatiotemporal data to recover high-fidelity images from ultranarrow angular subsectors (e.g., ~60°) that severely violate the Tuy data sufficiency condition. Inputs: Sinogram data p acquired over a short angular span (e.g., 200°–240°). Temporal window size defining the angular subsector width \Delta \theta (typically ~60°). Number of time frames N to be reconstructed. Outputs: A set of N reconstructed 2D image vectors \mathbf{x}1, \dots, \mathbf{x}N, which are assembled into a spatial-temporal image matrix \mathbf{X}. Data Structures: Spatial-Temporal Image Matrix (\mathbf{X}): A matrix where each column (or row, depending on convention) represents the flattened vector of a single time frame image. The dimensions are M \times N, where M is the number of pixels in the image and N is the number of time frames. Forward Projection Operator (\mathcal{P}): Maps the 3D volume or 2D slice to the sinogram space. In the context of 2D slice reconstruction described in the source, this projects the image vector \mathbf{x}i to the measured sinogram pi. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the spatial-temporal image matrix \mathbf{X}^{(0)} with zeros or a prior estimate. Set iteration counter k=0. 2. Forward Projection: For each time frame i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, compute the estimated sinogram \hat{p}i^{(k)} = \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}i^{(k)}). 3. Residual Calculation: Compute the residual in projection space for each frame: ri^{(k)} = pi - \hat{p}i^{(k)}. 4. Back-Projection: Distribute the residuals back to the image space to compute the gradient of the data fidelity term. The gradient for frame i is \mathbf{g}i^{(k)} = \mathcal{P}^T(ri^{(k)}). 5. Regularization (Nuclear Norm): Compute the gradient of the nuclear norm regularizer \|\mathbf{X}^{(k)}\| with respect to \mathbf{X}. Let the singular value decomposition (SVD) of \mathbf{X}^{(k)} be U \Sigma V^T. The subgradient of the nuclear norm is U V^T. 6. Update: Update the spatial-temporal image matrix using an optimization step (e.g., gradient descent or a proximal algorithm): \mathbf{X}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{X}^{(k)} + \alpha \left( \mathbf{G}^{(k)} - \lambda \nabla \|\mathbf{X}^{(k)}\| \right) where \mathbf{G}^{(k)} is the matrix of back-projected gradients, \alpha is the step size, and \lambda is the regularization weight. 7. Convergence Check: If the change in \mathbf{X} or the residual norm is below a threshold, stop. Otherwise, increment k and return to Step 2. Parameters: Angular Subsector Size: Approximately 60 degrees. Regularization Weight (\lambda): Not given in the sources. Step Size (\alpha): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tuy Condition Violation: The method is specifically designed for cases where the angular span is too narrow to satisfy the Tuy condition, leading to standard methods failing. Temporal Averaging: Using narrow windows reduces temporal averaging but increases limited-view artifacts; SMART-RECON addresses this joint problem. Time Complexity: Iterative, dependent on the number of frames N, image size M, and convergence iterations. Significantly slower than FBP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full spatial-temporal matrix \mathbf{X} (M \times N) and intermediate sinograms. Performance: In numerical simulations with a 240° short scan divided into four 60° subsectors, SMART-RECON achieved an average relative root mean square error (rRMSE) of 16% and Universal Quality Index (UQI) values of 0.96 and 0.95 for two local regions of interest. Comparison: For the same simulation data, PICCS reconstruction yielded an average rRMSE of 25% and UQIs of 0.78 and 0.81. Filtered backprojection yielded an average rRMSE of 45% and UQIs of 0.71 and 0.79. Strengths: Eliminates limited-view artifacts in ultranarrow temporal windows; maintains clear contrast differences between time frames. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to iterative nature and SVD computation for nuclear norm. SMART-RECON was introduced to address the trade-off in time-resolved CT between reducing temporal-average artifacts (requiring narrow temporal windows) and avoiding limited-view artifacts (requiring sufficient angular coverage). The method was validated using both numerical simulations with 2D image slices and in vivo human subject data from contrast-enhanced cone beam CT exams. Synchronized multiartifact reduction with tomographic reconstruction (SMART‐RECON): A statistical model based iterative image reconstruction method to eliminate limited‐view artifacts and to mitigate the temporal‐average artifacts in time‐resolved CT, https://doi.org/10.1118/1.4926430, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Light Field Tomographic Reconstruction from Focal Stack
head: Epipolar Image Reconstruction, Masked Back-projection, Partial light field tomographic reconstruction
body:
This method reconstructs a 2D epipolar image (a slice of the 4D light field) from a focal stack—a set of 2D images of the same scene captured at different focus distances by a fixed camera. It treats each photograph as a 2D projection of the light field and applies tomographic back-projection restricted to in-focus regions, estimating projection angles from a depth map derived via focus cues. Unlike spectral averaging approaches that deconvolve in the frequency domain, this method operates in the spatial domain, exploiting the regular linear structure of epipolar images to achieve high angular resolution with a limited number of projections. Inputs: A focal stack \{Ik\}{k=1}^K of K images captured by a fixed camera at different focus distances, and camera calibration parameters (focal length f0 and reference distance D{ref}). Outputs: A reconstructed 2D epipolar image LF(x, y, u, 0), representing the light field subset sufficient for refocusing and perspective shifts. Data Structures: 1. Focal Stack: Array of K images Ik of size W 	imes H. 2. Focus Map: Dense map l of size W 	imes H, where l{x,y} \in \{1, \dots, K\} indicates the index of the image Ik where pixel (x,y) is in focus. 3. Depth Map: Dense map D of size W 	imes H, where D{x,y} is the physical distance to the object at pixel (x,y). 4. Sharpness Layers: K intermediate layers Fk of size W 	imes H, storing sharpness scores. 5. Epipolar Image: Output buffer LF of size W 	imes U (where U is the angular dimension), initialized to background values. Parameters: K: Number of images in the focal stack. M: Number of gradient thresholds used in sharpness scoring. \alpham: Weighting coefficients for the m-th threshold. \deltak: Gradient threshold for image Ik, typically selected automatically by an edge detection algorithm. f0: Focal length of the lens. D{ref}: Distance to the reference object (green plane), chosen to lie at the reference focal distance. Steps: 1. Compute Sharpness Scores: For each image Ik in the focal stack, compute a sharpness score layer Fk(x,y) by summing weighted unit step functions of the image intensity gradient magnitude against increasing thresholds: Fk(x,y) = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham u(|
abla Ik(x,y)| - m\deltak) where u(\cdot) is the unit step function and 
abla Ik(x,y) is the image intensity gradient. 2. Estimate Focus Map: Compute the focus map l by minimizing the objective function E(l) using a graph cut algorithm: E(l) = \sum{X} D(X, lX) + \sum{X \sim X'} S(lX, l{X'}) where X=(x,y) is a pixel, X \sim X' denotes neighboring pixels, lX is the label (image index) assigned to pixel X, D is the data term, and S is the smoothness term. Data Term: D(X, lX) = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham (1 - F{lX}(x,y)). This cost decreases as the sharpness score of the assigned image increases. Smoothness Term: S(lX, l{X'}) =  egin{cases} 0 & 	ext{if } lX = l{X'} \ 0.5 + \log(|lX - l{X'}|) & 	ext{if } lX 
eq l{X'} \end{cases} The logarithmic cost avoids over-penalizing depth discontinuities. The minimization yields a dense focus map l where lX is the index of the sharpest image for pixel X. 3. Convert to Depth Map: Transform the discrete focus map l into a continuous depth map D using the camera calibration parameters and capture metadata. The precision of D is limited by K (the number of focal planes), but the map is dense due to the graph cut diffusion. 4. Calculate Back-projection Angles: For each pixel (x,y) in the epipolar image, estimate the back-projection angle 	heta based on the depth value D{x,y} from the depth map: 	heta = \arctan \left(  rac{1/D{ref} - 1/D{x,y}}{1/f0 - 1/D{ref}} ight) Here, 	an 	heta = u/x, relating the angular coordinate u to the spatial coordinate x. 5. Masked Back-projection: Reconstruct the epipolar image LF(x, y, u, 0) by back-projecting pixels from the focal stack images according to their estimated angles, using masks to restrict contributions to in-focus regions. Background: Back-project all pixels from every image in the focal stack entirely, as the background is assumed to be in focus for all or most images or serves as the base layer. Foreground/Objects: For non-background regions, back-project only the in-focus pixels. Determine in-focus regions by creating a binary mask for each image Ik where pixels satisfy lX = k. Ordering: Process objects in decreasing order of depth (from farthest to nearest). Overwriting: Instead of summing contributions (as in classical Radon back-projection), overwrite the values in the epipolar image buffer LF. This ensures that closer objects occlude distant ones, consistent with physical reality and the linear structure of epipolar images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The back-projection is O(N \cdot K) if naive, but can be optimized. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the focal stack (K \cdot W \cdot H), sharpness layers (K \cdot W \cdot H), focus map (W \cdot H), depth map (W \cdot H), and the output epipolar image (W \cdot U). Performance: The method achieves high angular resolution and perspective shifts despite using a single fixed camera and a small number of projections (focal stack images). It is more robust to variations in capturing conditions (number of images, depth ranges) than spectral averaging methods. Strengths: Preserves the full native spatial resolution of the conventional 2D camera, unlike plenoptic cameras which trade spatial for angular resolution. It handles limited projections effectively by exploiting the linear structure of epipolar images and using occlusion-aware overwriting. Limitations: The depth map precision is limited by the number of focal planes K. It requires accurate camera calibration and focus map estimation, which can fail in texture-poor regions without the graph cut diffusion step. It does not reconstruct the full 4D light field, only the subset LF(x, y, u, 0) sufficient for refocusing and perspective shifts. The method was proposed by as a technique to reconstruct 4D light fields from a focal stack captured by a conventional high-resolution camera. It addresses the limitations of plenoptic/microlens cameras, which sacrifice spatial resolution for angular resolution, and spectral averaging methods, which require deconvolution and are sensitive to capturing conditions. The approach is rooted in the tomographic principle that a photograph is a 2D projection of the 4D light field along a direction determined by the focus distance. It differs from classical medical tomography where projection angles are known; here, angles are estimated from a depth map derived from focus cues. The method enables applications such as digital refocusing, extended depth of field, and perspective shifts. name: Filtered Backprojection and Adjoint Methods
head: Filtered Backprojection, FBP, Adjoint Reconstruction
body: Filtered Backprojection (FBP) and Adjoint Methods solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by mapping 2D projection data back into a destination image or volume representation. Unlike unfiltered back-projection which directly scatters data and causes blurring, FBP applies a frequency-domain or spatial-domain filter to the projections before back-projection to correct for this effect. This family sets itself apart from Iterative Solvers by providing an analytical, closed-form solution rather than an iterative optimization loop. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space, and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process that updates volume parameters to reduce projection error. Back-projection is the adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P}, used to map 2D projection data or projection-space gradients back into a 3D volume representation. It solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by redistributing measured ray integrals along their corresponding geometric paths into the voxel grid. Unlike forward projection, which integrates density along rays to produce a 2D image, back-projection scatters 2D values into 3D space, effectively blurring the data if unfiltered. It is the core differentiable operator required for iterative optimization and gradient-based reconstruction, ensuring stable convergence when paired with forward projection. See Back-projection for implementation details. FastFDK is a CPU-optimized implementation of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, an analytical method for reconstructing a 3D volume from a stack of 2D cone-beam projection images. It solves the tomographic reconstruction problem by applying a specific convolution filter to weighted projections and back-projecting them into a 3D grid. It sets itself apart from its siblings by precomputing geometric weights and using a direct spatial-domain convolution filter to avoid the overhead of FFTs during the main reconstruction loop, prioritizing speed and memory locality on CPU architectures. See FastFDK for implementation details. Coupled Optimization is a differentiable volume rendering method that reconstructs fluid density and velocity fields by jointly optimizing for target image fidelity and physical transport consistency. It solves the problem of temporal incoherence in tomographic reconstruction by coupling the optimization of consecutive time steps through a transport loss, significantly reducing transport error compared to forward-only reconstruction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly incorporating the physics of advection into the gradient descent loop, whereas Back-projection and FastFDK rely on analytic or single-step algebraic solutions without iterative physical coupling. See Coupled Optimization for implementation details. A method to reconstruct an image from its tomographic scans (projections), producing a result that may be blurry-filtered compared to the original. Call reconstruct with scan data, width, and height to produce the destination image. For overscanned reconstruction, call reconstructoverscan with additional xover and yover parameters, then trim the result to the original dimensions. RMS error between source and reconstructed image is between 59.0 and 61.0 for a 35x40 ray/angle configuration, attributed to the blurry-filtered nature of the reconstruction. Reconstruction produces a blurry-filtered version of the original, resulting in higher RMS error compared to a perfect reconstruction, but better than a blank image baseline. Filtered Backprojection was implemented by the author of the source material in the context of a personal project to understand tomographic reconstruction. The method relies on the linearity of the Radon transform, allowing the filtering and integration steps to be performed in either order. The author noted that the "ramp" filter can be built algebraically rather than by numerically inverting an approximation to a filter with a singularity, which significantly reduces error. The approach is generally considered noisier than iterative statistical methods. simon-frankau/rediscovering-tomography, https://github.com/simon-frankau/rediscovering-tomography, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Back-projection
head: Adjoint Backprojection, Adjoint Projection, Cone Beam Adjoint, FDK Backprojection (CPU/PyTorch Path), Radon backprojection (parallel)
body: Back-projection is the adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P}, used to map 2D projection data (sinograms) or projection-space gradients back into a 3D volume representation. It solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by redistributing measured ray integrals along their corresponding geometric paths into the voxel grid. Unlike forward projection, which integrates density along rays to produce a 2D image, back-projection scatters 2D values into 3D space, effectively blurring the data if unfiltered. It is the core differentiable operator required for iterative optimization and gradient-based reconstruction, ensuring stable convergence when paired with forward projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sinogram/projection tensor p of shape [B, P, H, W] (spatial) or [B, P, H, W/2+1] (Fourier-space), and geometric parameters defining the ray paths (source positions, detector orientations, or ray anchors/directions). Output: A 3D volume tensor x of shape [B, D, H{rec}, W{rec}] or [B, D, H{rec}, W{rec}/2+1] (Fourier-space). Data Structures: Ray Specification: Defined by ray anchors \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^D and directions \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^D. Volume Grid: Defined by origin \mathbf{x}0, spacing \mathbf{\Delta}, and dimensions \mathbf{Q} (knotspec). Interpolation State: For GPU implementations, pending voxel values and indices are stored in registers or local memory to minimize atomic contention. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: For each projection pixel coordinate \mathbf{k}{proj} = (kr, kc), compute the corresponding 3D coordinate in the volume space. In Fourier-space methods, extend to 3D: \mathbf{k}{3D} = (kc, kr, 0). In spatial methods, compute the ray path from source to detector element. Apply inverse rotation/translation matrices to map detector coordinates to volume coordinates: \mathbf{k}{rec} = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{k}{3D}. 2. Interpolation Kernel Selection: Determine the interpolation order order \in \{0, 1, 2\}. order=0: Voxel-based (nearest neighbor). order=1: Trilinear (3D) or bilinear (2D). order=2: Higher-order box splines or tricubic (Catmull-Rom). 3. Scatter Accumulation: Distribute the projection value p into the volume. Spatial Domain: For each ray, iterate through voxels intersected by the ray. For each voxel, compute the interpolation weights based on the fractional distance of the ray within the voxel. Accumulate the weighted projection value into the voxel using atomic addition. Formula: x{\mathbf{q}} \leftarrow x{\mathbf{q}} + w \cdot p. Fourier Domain: Accumulate the projection value into the 3D Fourier volume at the transformed coordinate \mathbf{k}{rec} using 3D interpolation kernels in transpose mode. For trilinear, distribute to the 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood. For tricubic, distribute to the 4 \times 4 \times 4 neighborhood. 4. Gradient Computation (Differentiable Back-projection): To compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}, pass the residual gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} through the back-projection operator. To compute gradients w.r.t. geometry (source/detector positions), apply the chain rule through the interpolation derivatives, scattering gradients back to the camera parameters. Shift gradients are computed using phase modulation derivatives: \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf{s}} = -i2\pi\mathbf{k}{proj}P(\mathbf{k}{proj}). Pseudocode (Spatial Cone-Beam Adjoint): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayboxintersect(rayo, rayd, box): # box: [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz] # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero invd = torch.where(rayd.abs() > 1e-8, 1.0 / rayd, torch.zeroslike(rayd)) t1 = (box[0] - rayo[0]) invd[0] t2 = (box[1] - rayo[0]) invd[0] t3 = (box[2] - rayo[1]) invd[1] t4 = (box[3] - rayo[1]) invd[1] t5 = (box[4] - rayo[2]) invd[2] t6 = (box[5] - rayo[2]) invd[2] tmin = torch.maximum(torch.minimum(t1, t2), torch.maximum(torch.minimum(t3, t4), torch.minimum(t5, t6))) tmax = torch.minimum(torch.maximum(t1, t2), torch.minimum(torch.maximum(t3, t4), torch.maximum(t5, t6))) tmin = torch.clamp(tmin, min=0.0) return tmin, tmax def coneadjoint(projections, sources, detectors, box, nsamples, volumeshape, voxelsize): """ Computes the adjoint of the cone-beam forward projection. Args: projections: Tensor [B, 1, views, rows, cols] sources: Tensor [views, 3] detectors: Tensor [views, rows, cols, 3] box: Tensor [6] (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) nsamples: int volumeshape: tuple (Z, Y, X) voxelsize: float or Tensor [3] Returns: volume: Tensor [B, 1, Z, Y, X] """ batch,, views, rows, cols = projections.shape volume = torch.zeros(batch, 1, volumeshape, device=projections.device) z, y, x = volumeshape for view in range(views): src = sources[view] detplane = detectors[view] projview = projections[:, 0, view] raysd = detplane - src rayso = src.expandas(raysd) raysdnorm = raysd / (raysd.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(rayso, raysdnorm, box) valid = tmax > tmin # Step along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, nsamples, device=projections.device) tsampled = tmin.unsqueeze(-1) + tvals.unsqueeze(0) (tmax - tmin).unsqueeze(-1) points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + tsampled.unsqueeze(-1) raysdnorm.unsqueeze(1) # Convert to voxel coordinates voxelcoords = points / voxelsize ix, iy, iz = voxelcoords[..., 0], voxelcoords[..., 1], voxelcoords[..., 2] # Clamp to volume bounds for interpolation ix = torch.clamp(ix, 0, x - 1) iy = torch.clamp(iy, 0, y - 1) iz = torch.clamp(iz, 0, z - 1) # Trilinear weights dx = ix - ix.floor() dy = iy - iy.floor() dz = iz - iz.floor() w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz # Scatter weighted values to 8 neighboring voxels #... (Implementation detail omitted for brevity; see GPU kernels) pass return volume Parameters: detcount: Number of detector pixels. For exact reconstruction of pixels outside the inscribed circle in a 512x512 image, detcount = ceil(sqrt(2) 512). angles: Array of sampling angles. For parallel beam, equally spaced in 0, \pi). order: Interpolation order (0, 1, 2). nsamples: Number of samples per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Using atomicAdd for scatter accumulation is a major bottleneck on GPUs. Keeping pending voxels in registers minimizes atomics. Unfiltered Blurring: Unfiltered back-projection creates a blurred image due to low-frequency noise accumulation. Boundary Conditions: Volumes often require a 1-voxel zero-padding border to handle interpolation at edges without bounds checks. Precision: Relative error compared to reference implementations (e.g., Astra Toolbox) is 8.07 \times 10^{-4} for forward projection and 4.12 \times 10^{-5} for back-projection. Generates 2D projections from a 3D [volume by sampling central slices in Fourier space, implementing the Central Slice Theorem. It is the mathematical adjoint to back-projection. Maps projection weights to volume expansion coefficients using a single kernel launch per angle with a 1D NDRange, avoiding complex local memory tiling. Performs filtered backprojection using OpenCL global memory buffers, explicitly including the ramp filtering step in the GPU path. Accelerates backprojection by leveraging OpenCL image objects for hardware-accelerated bilinear interpolation of pre-filtered data. Computes 2D/3D back-projections exclusively in the Fourier domain using RFFT format, achieving 1–2 orders of magnitude speedup over spatial-domain libraries. Computes gradients of the projection error with respect to camera parameters by scattering gradients back to the source/detector positions. Materializes the full forward projection matrix for parallel-beam CT, enabling direct algebraic solutions and explicit adjoint verification. Time Complexity: O(Nv \cdot Nr \cdot Ns), where Nv is the number of views, Nr is the number of rays per view, and Ns is the number of samples per ray. In Fourier space, complexity is dominated by FFTs: O(N^3 \log N). Memory Complexity: O(Nv \cdot Nr) for storing projection data and O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for the volume buffer. Explicit Radon Matrix Construction requires O(Nv \cdot Nr \cdot Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz), which is prohibitive for large volumes. Performance: TorchRadon is up to 125× faster than Astra Toolbox for parallel/fan-beam projections due to GPU batch operations. Fourier-space methods show 1–2 orders of magnitude improvement over torch-fourier-slice. Strengths: Differentiable, stable for iterative optimization, efficient on GPUs. Limitations: Unfiltered BP is blurry. FDK yields worse results than iterative methods (e.g., SART) with limited projections. Atomic contention in spatial back-projection can limit throughput. Back-projection is the inverse of the Radon transform, forming the basis of analytical tomographic reconstruction methods like Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). It was historically implemented on CPUs and later optimized for GPUs using CUDA and OpenCL. Recent developments focus on making back-projection fully differentiable for integration into deep learning pipelines, enabling end-to-end optimization of volume representations and camera parameters. name: Fourier-space Projection Operations
head: torch-projectors
body: Fourier-space projection operations compute 2D and 3D forward and backward projections by operating directly in the frequency domain using PyTorch's RFFT format. Unlike spatial-domain methods that sample voxel grids, this method transforms reconstruction data to Fourier space, applies rotation and translation via phase modulation, and interpolates non-integer frequency coordinates. It distinguishes itself from spatial back-projection Back-projection and explicit matrix methods Explicit Radon Matrix Construction by offering high performance on CPU, CUDA, and Apple Silicon while supporting end-to-end differentiability for all inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Reconstruction Volume: Real-space tensor, shifted to center at index 0. Projections: Real-space tensor, shifted to center at index 0. Geometry: Rotation matrices and translation vectors. Output: Forward projection yields a sinogram; Backward projection yields a volume. Data Structures and Layout: The method uses PyTorch's Real Fast Fourier Transform (RFFT) format, adhering to FFTW conventions. Tensors remain in RFFT format throughout operations. 2D Reconstruction: Shape [B, N, N/2 + 1], where B is batch size, N is spatial size (must be even). 3D Reconstruction: Shape [B, D, H, W/2 + 1], where B is batch, D, H, W are spatial dimensions (must be even). Preprocessing (Shift): Apply fftshift to the real-space reconstruction or projection data to center the zero-frequency component at the tensor origin before FFT. 2. Translation: Apply translation shifts \mathbf{t} via phase modulation in Fourier space. Note: In back-projection, shifts are applied in the opposite direction to maintain the adjoint relationship. 5. Interpolation: Sample the rotated/shifted frequency grid at non-integer coordinates using interpolation kernels. Linear: Bilinear (2D) or Trilinear (3D) interpolation using 4 or 8 neighbors. Cubic: Separable Catmull-Rom kernels. The 1D kernel weight w(s) for coordinate offset s is: w(s) = \begin{cases} (a+2)|s|^3 - (a+3)|s|^2 + 1 & \text{if } |s| \leq 1 \\ a|s|^3 - 5a|s|^2 + 8a|s| - 4a & \text{if } 1 < |s| \leq 2 \\ 0 & \text{if } |s| > 2 \end{cases} where a = -0.5. Bicubic uses a 4 \times 4 neighborhood; tricubic uses 4 \times 4 \times 4. 6. Inverse Transform: Apply ifftshift to restore conventional centering, then compute the Inverse RFFT to return to real space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Preprocessing: Data is assumed shifted to center zero-frequency at index 0. # 2. Transform: Compute RFFT. volfreq = torch.fft.rfft(volume, dim=-1) # 3. Generate frequency coordinates for real-space dimensions spatialshape = list(volume.shape[2:]) freqcoords = generaterfftcoords(spatialshape) grid = torch.stack(freqcoords, dim=-1) # 4. Rotation: k' = R @ k gridflat = grid.reshape(-1, grid.shape[-1]) gridrotated = torch.einsum('...ij,...j->...i', rotationmatrices, gridflat) gridrotated = gridrotated.reshape(rotationmatrices.shape[:2], grid.shape[:-1]) # 5. Translation: Phase modulation e^{-2\pi i k \cdot t} kdott = torch.sum(gridrotated translationvectors[..., None, None,:], dim=-1) phase = torch.exp(-2j torch.pi kdott) volshifted = volfreq phase # 6. Interpolation: Sample at non-integer coordinates volinterp = separableinterpolate(volshifted, gridrotated, mode) # 7. Inverse Transform: ifftshift to restore conventional centering, then Inverse RFFT # volreal = torch.fft.irfft(volinterp, s=tuple(spatialshape), dim=-1) # return volreal return volinterp Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Even Dimensions: All spatial dimensions must be even. Square/Cubic: 2D reconstructions must be square; 3D must be cubic. Batch Broadcasting: Batch dimension B can be 1 or match the reconstruction batch size. Pose dimension P can be 1 for shared geometry. Shift Direction: In back-projection, translation shifts must be applied in the opposite direction to forward projection to ensure the adjoint property. TorchRadon is a PyTorch-integrated library providing high-performance, differentiable forward and backward projection operators for computed tomography. It solves the problem of computing Radon transforms and their adjoints within a deep learning pipeline, enabling gradient-based optimization for tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from non-differentiable alternatives by supporting automatic differentiation for all inputs, allowing gradients to flow through the projection and backprojection operations. Computes the Radon transform (sinogram) of a batch of multi-channel images by rotating the image and summing along one axis for each angle. It differs from TorchRadon by providing a specific implementation of the direct projection operator within the torchskradon library, focusing on explicit rotation and summation steps rather than optimized Fourier-space approximations. A differentiable simulation of the X-ray projection process, implemented by rotating the volume and summing along one axis. For each angle in the angles list, it rotates the volume around the Z-axis, sums the rotated volume along the first dimension to create a 2D projection, and stacks all 2D projections into a single tensor. Rotation is performed using affinegrid and gridsample with aligncorners=False. Performance: Outperforms torch-fourier-slice by 1–2 orders of magnitude. Optimized for CPU, Apple Silicon (MPS), and CUDA devices. Complexity: Dominated by FFTs (O(N^3 \log N) for 3D) and interpolation. Memory: Requires storage for RFFT-formatted tensors. No explicit Radon matrix storage needed. Strengths: Differentiable, high performance, supports linear and cubic interpolation. Limitations: Requires even, square/cubic dimensions. Originated in the context of transmission electron microscopy and electron tomography, where high optical resolution projections of Coulomb potentials are reconstructed into 3D atomic models. body: TorchRadon is a PyTorch-integrated library providing differentiable forward and backward projection operators for computed tomography. It solves the problem of computing Radon transforms and their adjoints within a deep learning pipeline, enabling gradient-based optimization for tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from non-differentiable alternatives by supporting automatic differentiation for all inputs, allowing gradients to flow through the projection and backprojection operations. TorchRadon implements linear projection operators that approximate the continuous Radon transform. The core operations are the forward projection (mapping an image to a sinogram) and the backward projection (mapping a sinogram to an image), corresponding to matrix-vector multiplications with A and A^T respectively. Inputs and Outputs: Forward Projection: Input is a 2D image tensor x of shape (N, C, H, W). Output is a sinogram tensor y of shape (N, C, D, \Theta). Backward Projection: Input is a sinogram tensor y. Output is an image tensor x{bp}. Data Structures: The library uses PyTorch tensors. The geometry is defined by parameters such as image size, number of angles, and detector configuration. Parameters: Parameters include angles, detcount, and interpolation method. Specific default values are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the Radon operator with specified geometry parameters. 2. Forward Projection: For each angle \theta, compute the line integrals of the image x along parallel or fan-beam rays to produce y = Ax. 3. Backward Projection: For each angle \theta, distribute the sinogram values back to the image grid to produce x{bp} = A^T y. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F import numpy as np def radonforward(image: torch.Tensor, angles: np.ndarray, detcount: int) -> torch.Tensor: N, C, H, W = image.shape numangles = len(angles) sinogram = torch.zeros(N, C, detcount, numangles, device=image.device) for i, theta in enumerate(angles): cost, sint = torch.cos(torch.tensor(theta)), torch.sin(torch.tensor(theta)) ygrid, xgrid = torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(-1, 1, detcount), torch.linspace(-1, 1, H), indexing='ij') xrot = xgrid cost - ygrid sint yrot = xgrid sint + ygrid cost sinogram[:,:,:, i] = F.gridsample(image, torch.stack([xrot, yrot], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)) return sinogram def radonbackward(sinogram: torch.Tensor, angles: np.ndarray, size: int) -> torch.Tensor: N, C, detcount, numangles = sinogram.shape imagebp = torch.zeros(N, C, size, size, device=sinogram.device) for i, theta in enumerate(angles): cost, sint = torch.cos(torch.tensor(theta)), torch.sin(torch.tensor(theta)) ygrid, xgrid = torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(-1, 1, size), torch.linspace(-1, 1, size), indexing='ij') xsin = xgrid cost + ygrid sint ysin = -xgrid sint + ygrid cost imagebp[:,:,:,:] = F.gridsample(sinogram[:,:,:, i].unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), torch.stack([xsin, ysin], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), aligncorners=True) return imagebp Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Effects: Rays passing near the edge of the image may have incomplete support for interpolation kernels, potentially causing artifacts. Precision: The library uses floating-point arithmetic, and relative errors compared to reference implementations are small but non-zero. Memory: High-resolution images and large numbers of angles increase memory consumption linearly with the sinogram size. The Radon transform maps a 2D image to its projections (sinogram) by integrating pixel intensities along parallel lines at various angles. It solves the forward acquisition model in computed tomography, converting spatial domain data into projection domain data. Unlike its inverse counterpart (e.g., Filtered Back-Projection), which reconstructs images from projections, the forward Radon transform generates the measurements required for reconstruction. It is distinguished from other projection methods by its strict parallel-beam geometry and linear integration nature. The Fan-Beam Radon Transform computes projections for a geometry where X-rays originate from a single fixed point source and are captured by a linear detector array. Unlike the Radon Transform which assumes parallel rays, this method models the divergent ray paths inherent to fan-beam acquisition, allowing for direct reconstruction or rebinning to parallel geometry. It is distinguished from parallel-beam by the diverging ray paths. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and angles. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the sinogram. Performance: High performance on NVIDIA GPUs via PyTorch. Strengths: Seamless integration with PyTorch, differentiability, support for both parallel and fan-beam geometries. Limitations: Interpolation artifacts at boundaries. TorchRadon was developed to provide a fast, differentiable implementation of Radon transforms for use in deep learning-based tomographic reconstruction. It is integrated with PyTorch, allowing for end-to-end training of reconstruction networks. Generative Tomography Reconstruction, https://core.ac.uk/works/91148923, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Fan-Beam Radon Transform

body: The Fan-Beam Radon Transform computes projections for a geometry where X-rays originate from a single fixed point source and are captured by a linear detector array. This configuration eliminates the linear source-detector translation required in parallel geometries, enabling faster angular-only scanning. Unlike the Radon Transform which assumes parallel rays, this method models the divergent ray paths inherent to fan-beam acquisition. It allows for direct reconstruction or rebinning to parallel geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image (phantom) f(x,y) of size N \times N. Parameters: angles: Array of sampling angles \beta, equally spaced in 0, 2\pi). sourcedistance (D): Distance from the X-ray source to the center of the object. Default is 512. detdistance: Distance from the detector to the center of the object. Default equals sourcedistance. detcount: Number of detector pixels. detspacing: Distance between detector pixels. Output: A sinogram representing the line integrals of the image along the fan-beam rays. Data Structures: The implementation typically uses array tensors for the image and sinogram to enable differentiability. The sinogram is a 2D array where one dimension corresponds to the angular index and the other to the detector bin index. Steps: 1. Geometry Setup: Place a single point source at a fixed position relative to a linear detector array. The source is located at distance D from the origin. 2. Angular Sampling: Define the set of angles \beta for the source position. For fan-beam, these are typically equally spaced in [0, 2\pi). 3. Forward Projection: For each angle \beta, compute the line integrals through the image. Rays are defined by the source position and the detector bins. The angle \gamma represents the angle between an arbitrary ray and the central ray passing through the origin. 4. [Backward Projection: Distribute the sinogram values back into the image space along the corresponding ray paths. Formulas: For regular spatial sampling, reconstruction in polar coordinates (r, \phi) can be performed directly using the fan-beam formula: f(r, \phi) = \frac{1}{2} \int0^{2\pi} \int{-Sm}^{Sm} R\beta(s) h\left(r \cos\left(\beta + \tan^{-1}\frac{s}{D}\right) - \phi\right) \frac{D^3}{D^2 + s^2} \frac{1}{(D + \sqrt{D^2 + s^2})^{3/2}} \, ds \, d\beta Where: R\beta(s) is the fan-beam projection at angle \beta and curvilinear coordinate s. h is the inverse Fourier transform of the ramp filter. D is the distance from the source to the origin. s is the curvilinear coordinate on the projection line, with the origin at the bin corresponding to the line integral passing through the origin. Sm is the maximum coordinate value on the projection line. \beta is the angle the source S makes with the reference y-axis. Alternatively, fan-beam data can be rebinned to parallel-beam geometry for standard filtered backprojection (see Subtopics). Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode demonstrates the forward and backward projection logic without external library dependencies. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fanbeamforwardprojection(image, angles, sourcedistance, detcount, detspacing): """Compute fan-beam sinogram from a 2D image.""" N = image.shape[0] numangles = len(angles) sinogram = [[0.0] detcount for in range(numangles)] for i, beta in enumerate(angles): sx = sourcedistance np.cos(beta) sy = sourcedistance np.sin(beta) for j in range(detcount): detoffset = (j - detcount // 2) detspacing dx = -np.sin(beta) detoffset dy = np.cos(beta) detoffset detx = sx + dx dety = sy + dy raydirx = detx - sx raydiry = dety - sy integral = 0.0 numsamples = 2 N step = (2.0 sourcedistance) / numsamples for k in range(numsamples): t = k step px = sx + t raydirx py = sy + t raydiry # Sample image intensity at (px, py) using bilinear interpolation val = bilinearsample(image, px, py) integral += val sinogram[i][j] = integral step return sinogram def fanbeambackwardprojection(sinogram, angles, sourcedistance, detcount, detspacing, imageshape): """Distribute sinogram values back into image space.""" image = [[0.0] imageshape[1] for in range(imageshape[0])] for i, beta in enumerate(angles): sx = sourcedistance np.cos(beta) sy = sourcedistance np.sin(beta) for j in range(detcount): detoffset = (j - detcount // 2) detspacing dx = -np.sin(beta) detoffset dy = np.cos(beta) detoffset detx = sx + dx dety = sy + dy raydirx = detx - sx raydiry = dety - sy value = sinogram[i][j] numsamples = 2 sourcedistance step = (2.0 sourcedistance) / numsamples for k in range(numsamples): t = k step px = sx + t raydirx py = sy + t raydiry # Accumulate value along the ray path ix, iy = int(px), int(py) if 0 <= ix < imageshape[0] and 0 <= iy < imageshape[1]: image[ix][iy] += value return image def bilinearsample(image, x, y): """Standard bilinear interpolation implementation.""" x0, y0 = int(np.floor(x)), int(np.floor(y)) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 dx, dy = x - x0, y - y0 x0 = max(0, min(x0, image.shape[0] - 1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, image.shape[0] - 1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, image.shape[1] - 1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, image.shape[1] - 1)) top = image[x0][y0] (1 - dx) + image[x1][y0] dx bottom = image[x0][y1] (1 - dx) + image[x1][y1] dx return top (1 - dy) + bottom dy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The sampling of the equivalent parallel projection in rebinning methods is not uniform, requiring interpolation. 2D Fan-beam Reconstruction is an analytic algorithm for reconstructing a 2D density field from projection data acquired with a diverging X-ray beam. It solves the inverse problem for fan-beam geometry by mapping the diverging ray paths to equivalent parallel-beam line integrals via a geometric Jacobian, then applying standard filtered backprojection. It differs from parallel-beam FBP by explicitly accounting for the source-to-detector divergence and the resulting non-uniform sampling density in the projection space. A preprocessing step that converts fan-beam projection data into parallel-beam geometry to allow the use of standard parallel-beam reconstruction algorithms (like FBP). It involves resampling the fan-beam rays onto a uniform parallel grid. Steps: 1. For each fan-beam angle index m and ray index n, calculate the equivalent parallel-beam angle \theta and curvilinear coordinate t using the source-to-origin distance D{SO} and the ray index n with angular step \alpha. 2. For each fixed parallel view index v (where 0 \le v \le V-1), interpolate the irregularly spaced values to estimate the uniformly spaced parallel projection values Pv^\Gamma(uh), where h is the detector spacing. Formulas: The equivalent parallel coordinate t is given by: t = D \sin \gamma where D is the source-to-origin distance and \gamma is the fan angle. For uniform angular sampling with step \alpha, where \beta = m\alpha and \gamma = n\alpha, the relationship is: R{m\alpha}(n\alpha) = P{(m+n)\alpha}(D \sin n\alpha) Pitfalls: The sampling of the equivalent parallel projection \sin n\alpha is not uniform, requiring interpolation to use standard parallel algorithms. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a 512 \times 512 Shepp-Logan phantom with 512 sampling angles equally spaced in 0, 2\pi), source distance 512, and detector distance 512: Relative error of forward projection compared to Astra Toolbox: 8.34 \cdot 10^{-4}. Relative error of backprojection compared to Astra Toolbox: 4.84 \cdot 10^{-5}. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly speeds up data acquisition by eliminating the linear translation step required in parallel geometries, keeping only angular [rotation. Limitations: Reconstruction is more complex than parallel geometry due to the divergent rays and non-uniform sampling in rebinning approaches. When to Use: Use when acquiring data from a system with a point source and linear detector array (e.g., 3rd or 4th generation scanners) where speed of acquisition is prioritized over the simplicity of parallel geometry. The fan-beam geometry, also known as géométrie en éventail, was developed to improve the speed of tomographic data acquisition. Unlike parallel geometry, which requires the source-detector pair to translate linearly across the object before rotating, fan-beam geometry allows for angular-only scanning. This corresponds to the 3rd and 4th generations of CT scanners. The method is implemented in libraries such as TorchRadon for differentiable rendering and reconstruction. body: 2D Fan-beam Reconstruction is an analytic algorithm for reconstructing a 2D density field from projection data acquired with a diverging X-ray beam. It solves the inverse problem for fan-beam geometry by mapping the diverging ray paths to equivalent parallel-beam line integrals via a geometric Jacobian, then applying standard filtered backprojection. It differs from parallel-beam FBP by explicitly accounting for the source-to-detector divergence and the resulting non-uniform sampling density in the projection space. Inputs: Fan-beam projection data g(s,t), where s is the angular parameter defining the ray direction and t is the distance along the central ray from the source to the point (x,y) in the object. Filter kernel h(s). Geometric parameters: Source-to-center-of-rotation distance d, source-to-detector distance D (if not normalized), and detector spacing. Outputs: Reconstructed 2D volume f(x,y). Data Structures: Projection array: 2D array indexed by (s, t). Filter kernel: 1D array or function h(s). Reconstruction grid: 2D array indexed by (x, y). Steps: 1. Weighting: Apply a geometric weighting factor w(s) to the raw projection data g(s,t) to compensate for the projective distance. The weighting term is an inverse projective distance-squared normalization. w(s) = \frac{1}{r(s)^2} Where r(s) is the distance from the source to the detector element corresponding to parameter s. In many implementations, if the detector is curved or the geometry is normalized, this simplifies to a constant or a function of the fan angle. The source text defines w(s) generally as an "inverse projective distance-squared normalization term". 2. Filtering: Convolve the weighted projection data with the filter kernel h(s) along the detector dimension t (or the equivalent parallel-beam coordinate). p(s,t) = [w(s) g(s,t)] h(s) Here, p(s,t) is the filtered projection data. The convolution is performed along the axis corresponding to the detector position or the parallel-beam offset t. 3. Backprojection: Distribute the filtered projection values p(s,t) back into the image space (x,y). For each pixel (x,y), determine the corresponding fan-beam parameters (s,t): s: The angle of the ray passing through (x,y). t: The distance from the source to (x,y) along the central ray of that fan beam. Apply the Jacobian weighting again during backprojection to account for the change in measure from the projection space to the image space. The backprojection sums the filtered projections weighted by the geometric factor. f(x,y) = \int p(s,t(x,y)) \cdot J(x,y) \, ds Where J(x,y) is the Jacobian of the transformation from fan-beam coordinates to Cartesian coordinates. The source text notes that the algorithm uses "appropriate geometry and Jacobian". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fanbeamreconstruction(projections, filterkernel, geometry): """ Reconstructs a 2D volume from fan-beam projections using Filtered Backprojection. Args: projections: 2D array [numangles, numdetectors], g(s, t) filterkernel: 1D array or function h(s) geometry: Object containing source-to-center distance d, source-to-detector distance D, detector spacing, etc. Returns: reconstructedvolume: 2D array [width, height], f(x, y) """ numangles, numdetectors = projections.shape reconstructedvolume = np.zeros((geometry.imagewidth, geometry.imageheight)) # Precompute filter in frequency domain for efficiency filterfreq = np.fft.fft(filterkernel, n=numdetectors) # Step 1 & 2: Weighting and Filtering filteredprojections = np.zeroslike(projections) for i in range(numangles): # Get projection for angle i proj = projections[i,:] # Apply geometric weighting w(s) # w(s) is inverse projective distance-squared normalization # For a flat detector at distance D from source, distance to detector element j is rj # rj = sqrt(D^2 + (j - numdetectors/2)^2 detspacing^2) # w(s) = 1 / rj^2 # Note: Source defines w(s) generally. Implementation depends on specific geometry. distances = np.sqrt(D2 + (np.arange(numdetectors) - numdetectors/2)2 geometry.detspacing2) weights = 1.0 / (distances2) weightedproj = proj weights # Convolve with filter kernel # Using FFT convolution projfft = np.fft.fft(weightedproj) filteredfft = projfft filterfreq filteredproj = np.real(np.fft.ifft(filteredfft)) filteredprojections[i,:] = filteredproj # Step 3: Backprojection for x in range(geometry.imagewidth): for y in range(geometry.imageheight): # Convert Cartesian (x,y) to fan-beam coordinates (s, t) # s is the angle of the ray from source to (x,y) # t is the distance from source to (x,y) # Assuming source is at origin for simplicity, or offset by geometry dx = x - geometry.centerx dy = y - geometry.centery t = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2) s = np.arctan2(dy, dx) # Interpolate filtered projection value at (s, t) # s corresponds to an angle index, t corresponds to a detector position # Map s to angle index angleidx = (s - geometry.startangle) / geometry.anglestep # Map t to detector index # t is distance along central ray. In fan-beam, t is often related to detector position # For a curved detector, t is constant for all rays? No, t is distance to point. # In standard fan-beam FBP, we map (x,y) to (angle, detectorindex) # detectorindex = t / detspacing (approx, depends on geometry) # More precisely, for a flat detector, the detector position u is related to t and s # u = D tan(s) # The value p(s, t) is interpolated from filteredprojections # Interpolation logic: # Find closest angle index and interpolate # Find closest detector index and interpolate # This is a simplification; exact mapping depends on geometry definition val = interpolate(filteredprojections, s, t, geometry) # Apply Jacobian weighting for backprojection # Jacobian J = t / D or similar depending on geometry # Source mentions "appropriate geometry and Jacobian" jacobian = t / D # Example Jacobian for flat detector reconstructedvolume[x, y] += val jacobian # Normalize by number of angles reconstructedvolume /= numangles return reconstructedvolume Parameters: Filter kernel h(s): Typically a ramp filter or Ram-Lak filter, often modified with a window (e.g., Shepp-Logan, Hamming) to reduce noise. Typical values depend on the desired resolution and noise trade-off. Geometric parameters: Source-to-center distance d, source-to-detector distance D. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Effects: The finite detector size and angular range can cause artifacts at the edges of the reconstructed field of view. Precision: Interpolation errors during backprojection can introduce artifacts. High-order interpolation is recommended. Degenerate Input: Missing projections or large gaps in angular coverage can lead to streak artifacts. Cone-beam Reconstruction (specifically Feldkamp-Davis-Kress or FDK) is an analytic 3D reconstruction method for circular source trajectories. It extends 2D fan-beam filtered backprojection to 3D by applying 2D weighting and filtering to the projection data gc(s,t,\beta) and then performing weighted backprojection. It produces approximate results because a single circular trajectory provides insufficient information to correctly reconstruct the entire volume, except for the central z=0-plane. The filtered projection data pc(s,t,\beta) = [w(s,t) gc(s,t,\beta)] h(s,t) is backprojected to calculate the 3D volume f(xi,yj,zk) using a pre-factor that handles the 3D weighting, such as \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{d^2}{(xi^2+yj^2+d^2)^{3/2}}. It is chosen when 3D reconstruction from a circular scan is required and speed is prioritized over accuracy for large cone angles, where Grangeat's method would be more accurate but complex. Time Complexity: O(N^2 \log N) for filtering and O(N^3) for backprojection in 3D, or O(N^2 \log N) for filtering and O(N^2) for backprojection in 2D, where N is the number of pixels/detectors. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for storing projections and the reconstructed volume. Strengths: Fast, analytic solution; well-understood; efficient for 2D and approximate 3D. Limitations: Approximate for 3D cone-beam; sensitive to noise; requires complete angular coverage for accurate 2D reconstruction. When to use: 2D fan-beam tomography; approximate 3D cone-beam reconstruction (FDK). When not to use: High-accuracy 3D cone-beam reconstruction with large cone angles (use iterative methods or Grangeat's method); sparse-view tomography (use iterative methods). The 2D fan-beam reconstruction algorithm is derived from the parallel-beam filtered backprojection method by accounting for the geometric differences in ray paths. The fan-beam transform is isomorphic to the parallel-beam case, with a direct geometric mapping between line integrals. The Feldkamp cone-beam reconstruction method, an extension of fan-beam FBP to 3D, was developed in the context of X-ray CT and volume rendering, with references to Feldkamp's and Grangeat's work. The method is discussed in the context of tomographic image reconstruction and rendering with texture-mapping hardware. name: Radon Transform
head: Projection intégrale continue, Sinogram Generation, Transformée de Radon
body: The Radon transform maps a 2D spatial function to its line integrals along parallel rays at various angles, producing a sinogram. It models the continuous tomographic forward acquisition process by integrating object contrast along straight projection paths. It is distinguished from other projection methods by its strict parallel-beam geometry and direct line-integral formulation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image I (discrete pixel grid) and a set of projection angles \theta. For batch processing, the input is a tensor of shape (N, C, H, W) where N is batch size, C channels, H height, and W width. Output: A sinogram tensor of shape (N, C, D, A) where D is the number of detector positions (radial bins) and A is the number of angles. Data Structures: Image Grid: Discrete indices (i, j) corresponding to pixel centers. The image is modeled as a sum of discrete Dirac impulses: f(x,y) = \sum{i=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum{j=-\infty}^{\infty} I(i,j) \Delta(x - j) \Delta(y - i) where \Delta(\cdot) is the discrete Dirac impulse. Projection Line: Defined by angle \theta and radial distance \rho (or t) from the origin. The line equation is \rho = x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta. Detector Positions: Linearly spaced values rs covering the image extent, typically from -1 to 1 normalized or in pixel units. Formulas: The continuous Radon transform is defined as: R\theta(\rho) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \delta(\rho - x \cos \theta - y \sin \theta) \, dx \, dy where \delta(\cdot) is the Dirac delta function. The discrete Radon transform R\theta(\rho) is the sum of pixel values I(i,j) whose centers lie on the projection line: R\theta(\rho) = \sum{i=0}^{H-1} \sum{j=0}^{W-1} I(i,j) \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{line } (\theta, \rho) \text{ intersects pixel } (i,j)) In practice, this is implemented via interpolation (e.g., bilinear) to approximate the integral along the ray. Parameters: theta: Array of projection angles in degrees. Typical default: np.linspace(0.0, 180.0, max(image.shape), endpoint=False). In skradon, default is torch.arange(180). rs: Detector positions. Default: linearly spaced from -1 to 1 with length equal to image height. circle: Boolean. If True, assumes zero intensity outside the inscribed circle, adjusting sinogram width to min(H, W). preserverange: Boolean. If True, preserves original dtype range; otherwise converts to float [0,1]. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Convert input image to float. If preserverange is False, scale values according to imgasfloat conventions (e.g., uint8 [0,255] to [0,1]). 2. Angle Setup: If theta is None, generate angles from 0 to 179 degrees. 3. Geometry Setup: If circle is True, calculate the radius r = \min(H, W) // 2 and mask pixels outside the inscribed circle to zero. 4. Projection Loop (for each angle \thetak in theta): a. Affine Transformation: Construct a 2 \times 3 affine matrix representing rotation by \thetak and translation to center the projection axis. b. Grid Generation: Create a sampling grid using affinegrid based on the affine matrix and image dimensions. aligncorners=False is standard. c. Sampling: Sample the image values at the grid coordinates using gridsample (bilinear interpolation). d. Accumulation: Sum along the vertical axis to obtain the projection profile and store it in the sinogram tensor. 5. Post-processing: If circle is True, pad the sinogram dimensions to square to handle inscribed circle geometry. 6. Output: Return the sinogram tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def radontransform(image: torch.Tensor, theta: torch.Tensor = None, circle: bool = False, preserverange: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the forward Radon transform (sinogram) of a batch of images. Args: image: Tensor of shape (N, C, H, W). theta: Tensor of angles in degrees. Default: arange(180). circle: If True, assumes zero outside inscribed circle. preserverange: If False, converts image to float [0, 1]. Returns: sinogram: Tensor of shape (N, C, D, A). """ # 1. Preprocessing if not preserverange: image = image.float() if image.dtype == torch.uint8: image = image / 255.0 elif image.max() > 1.0: image = image / image.max() else: image = image.float() N, C, H, W = image.shape device = image.device # 2. Angle Setup if theta is None: theta = torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) else: theta = theta.to(device=device, dtype=torch.float32) A = theta.shape[0] # 3. Detector Positions if circle: D = min(H, W) else: D = H # 4. Initialize Sinogram sinogram = torch.zeros((N, C, D, A), dtype=image.dtype, device=device) # 5. Loop over angles for k, angledeg in enumerate(theta): anglerad = torch.deg2rad(angledeg) cosa = torch.cos(anglerad) sina = torch.sin(anglerad) # Construct 2x3 affine matrix for rotation by -theta around center (0.5, 0.5) tx = 0.5 - 0.5 cosa - 0.5 sina ty = 0.5 + 0.5 sina - 0.5 cosa thetamat = torch.zeros((N, 2, 3), device=device) thetamat[:, 0, 0] = cosa thetamat[:, 0, 1] = sina thetamat[:, 0, 2] = tx thetamat[:, 1, 0] = -sina thetamat[:, 1, 1] = cosa thetamat[:, 1, 2] = ty # Generate sampling grid grid = F.affinegrid(thetamat, size=(N, C, H, W), aligncorners=False) # Sample image values rotatedimage = F.gridsample(image, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=False) # Sum along vertical axis (height) to get projection profile profile = torch.sum(rotatedimage, dim=2) # Shape: (N, C, W) # Map profile to detector positions if W == D: sinogram[:,:,:, k] = profile else: # Interpolate profile to D detectors profileresized = F.interpolate(profile.unsqueeze(2), size=(D), mode='linear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(2) sinogram[:,:,:, k] = profileresized # 6. Post-processing: Circle padding if circle: # Pad sinogram to square dimensions if needed pass return sinogram Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) is a direct tomographic reconstruction algorithm that recovers a 2D image from its measured projection profiles (sinogram). It solves the inverse Radon transform by applying a high-pass frequency-domain filter to the projections to correct for the inherent low-pass blurring of simple back-projection, followed by integrating the filtered data along sine-shaped paths. Unlike Fourier-based reconstruction methods which require interpolation between Cartesian and polar grids (leading to O(N^2) complexity or interpolation artifacts), FBP operates directly on the projections with a time complexity of O(N \log N) due to the use of Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT). It is the most popular algorithm for computed tomography. A variant that utilizes projections from only one quadrant (0 to 90 degrees) to reduce computational overhead, exploiting a four-fold redundancy. It computes back-projections by treating them as real and imaginary parts of a complex number and averaging individual back-projections. It is chosen when computational resources are limited, but requires the quadrature approach to avoid poor reconstruction quality. The quadrature Radon transform yields better results numerically and visually compared to the conventional Radon transform. A differentiable 3D Radon transform used to project LAC volumes into sinogram space, synthesizing CT measurements. It allows backpropagation of gradients through the projection operation to update the INR and motion field parameters. Optimization updates INR weights (\phi) and motion field coefficients (C) via gradient descent (ADAM optimizer, learning rate 0.001) to minimize the loss function by backpropagating derivatives through the differentiable Radon transform. The loss function is \min{\phi, C} \lambda1 \| R{\theta(t)}(\sigma(x, y, z, t)) - R{\theta(t)}(GT) \|1 + \lambda2 TV(C), where t \in [0, 1]. The TV Regularization Weight \lambda2 is set to 0.001; higher values create smoother warp fields but may underfit complex motion, while low values allow complex motion but are prone to noise. Time Complexity: O(A \cdot H \cdot W) for a single image, where A is the number of angles, H height, W width. The rotation and summation steps dominate. Memory Complexity: O(D \cdot A) for the sinogram storage, where D is the number of detectors. Performance: Efficient for moderate resolutions. GPU acceleration via PyTorch allows for batch processing. Strengths: Differentiable when implemented with gridsample, linear, and standard for forward projection in CT. Limitations: Sensitive to aliasing if angles are sparse; requires interpolation for non-integer pixel shifts. When to use: When generating synthetic sinograms for training or when the forward model is needed for differentiable tomography. When not to use: When only reconstruction is needed (use FBP or iterative methods). The Radon transform was introduced by Austrian mathematician Johann Radon in 1917, though some sources cite 1919. It provides the foundational link between projections and pixel values in tomographic reconstruction. The discrete implementation is widely used in medical imaging and industrial CT. The skimage implementation is based on Justin K. Romberg's code. The differentiable skradon implementation extends this to PyTorch for differentiable inverse rendering. name: Filtered Back-Projection (FBP)
head: Filter Back Projection, RamLak Reconstruction
body:
Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) is a direct tomographic reconstruction algorithm that recovers a 2D image from its measured projection profiles (sinogram). It solves the inverse Radon transform by applying a high-pass frequency-domain filter to the projections to correct for the inherent low-pass blurring of simple back-projection, followed by integrating the filtered data along sine-shaped paths. Unlike Fourier-based reconstruction methods which require interpolation between Cartesian and polar grids (leading to O(N^2) complexity or interpolation artifacts), FBP operates directly on the projections with a time complexity of O(N \log N) due to the use of Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT). It is the most popular algorithm for computed tomography. Inputs: Sinogram R: A 2D array of shape (Nho, N	heta), where Nho is the number of radial samples per projection and N	heta is the number of projection angles. Angles \Theta: An array of N	heta angles, typically spanning 0, \pi) radians. Radial sampling step dho: The distance between adjacent samples in the projection domain. Filter type: e.g., 'ramp', 'hann', 'hamming', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine'. Pixel kernel: The interpolation function used during [back-projection (e.g., Dirac, Linear, Area). Outputs: Reconstructed image I: A 2D array of shape (N, N), where N is the image grid size. Data Structures: The sinogram is stored as a contiguous 2D array. The frequency domain filter is a 1D array of length Nho. Steps: 1. Generate Frequency Filter: Compute the 1D frequency bins corresponding to the projection width. For a projection of length Nho, the frequencies 
u range from -
u{Nyquist} to 
u{Nyquist}, where 
u{Nyquist} =  rac{1}{2 dho}. Construct the base filter H(
u). The standard "Ram-Lak" filter is the ramp function |

u). The combined filter is: H{total}(
