For 'shepp-logan', it multiplies frequencies by 	ext{sinc}(\omega). For 'cosine', it uses a shifted sine function. If no filter is specified, the filter is all ones. 2. Filter Projections: For each projection angle 	hetai \in \Theta: a. Compute the 1D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the projection profile R{	hetai}: \hat{R}{	hetai} = 	ext{FFT}(R{	hetai}) b. Multiply the spectrum by the frequency filter H{total}: \hat{R}{	hetai}^{filtered}[
u] = \hat{R}{	hetai}[
u] \cdot H{total}[
u] c. Compute the inverse 1D DFT to obtain the filtered projection R{	hetai}^{BF}: R{	hetai}^{BF} = 	ext{IFFT}(\hat{R}{	hetai}^{filtered}) The result is taken as the real part, as the implementation explicitly extracts it. 3. Back-Project: Initialize the reconstructed image I to zeros. For each filtered projection R{	hetai}^{BF} and angle 	hetai: For each pixel (x, y) in the image grid: a. Calculate the radial coordinate ho corresponding to the pixel's position at angle 	hetai: ho = x \cos 	hetai + y \sin 	hetai b. Sample the value from the filtered projection R{	hetai}^{BF} at ho. Since ho rarely aligns exactly with the discrete grid indices of the sinogram, interpolation is required. The choice of interpolation kernel (pixel kernel) affects quality. The 'Area' kernel provides the best SSIM and most uniform Point Spread Function (PSF). c. Add the sampled value to the image pixel: I(x, y) \leftarrow I(x, y) + R{	hetai}^{BF}(ho) 4. Normalization: Divide the accumulated image by N	heta (or the angular step size d	heta) to maintain correct intensity scaling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def filteredbackprojection(sinogram, angles, drho, filtertype='ramp', windowparam=0.5): """ Reconstructs an image from a sinogram using Filtered Back-Projection. Parameters: sinogram: ndarray of shape (Nrho, Ntheta) angles: ndarray of shape (Ntheta,), in radians, range [0, pi) drho: float, radial sampling step filtertype: str, type of filter ('ramp', 'hann', 'hamming', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine') windowparam: float, parameter for window function (e.g., 0.5 for Hann) Returns: image: ndarray of shape (N, N) """ Nrho, Ntheta = sinogram.shape N = Nrho # 1. Generate Frequency Filter freqs = np.fft.fftfreq(Nrho, d=drho) nunyquist = 1.0 / (2 drho) rampfilter = np.abs(freqs) if filtertype == 'hann': window = windowparam + (1 - windowparam) np.cos(np.pi freqs / nunyquist) window[np.abs(freqs) >= nunyquist] = 0 filterkernel = rampfilter window elif filtertype == 'hamming': window = windowparam + (1 - windowparam) np.cos(np.pi freqs / nunyquist) window[np.abs(freqs) >= nunyquist] = 0 filterkernel = rampfilter window elif filtertype == 'ramp': filterkernel = rampfilter elif filtertype == 'shepp-logan': omega = np.pi freqs sincfilter = np.sinc(omega / np.pi) filterkernel = rampfilter sincfilter elif filtertype == 'cosine': filterkernel = np.cos(np.pi freqs / 2) filterkernel[np.abs(freqs) > 1] = 0 else: filterkernel = np.ones(Nrho) # 2. Filter Projections filteredsinogram = np.zeroslike(sinogram) for i in range(Ntheta): proj = sinogram[:, i] projfft = np.fft.fft(proj) projfftfiltered = projfft filterkernel filteredproj = np.fft.ifft(projfftfiltered) filteredsinogram[:, i] = np.real(filteredproj) # 3. Back-Project image = np.zeros((N, N)) cosangles = np.cos(angles) sinangles = np.sin(angles) y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(N) - N/2 + 0.5, np.arange(N) - N/2 + 0.5, indexing='ij') for i in range(Ntheta): c = cosangles[i] s = sinangles[i] rho = x c + y s indices = rho / drho + Nrho / 2 indices = np.clip(indices, 0, Nrho - 1) idx0 = np.floor(indices).astype(int) idx1 = np.ceil(indices).astype(int) w = indices - idx0 idx1safe = np.minimum(idx1, Nrho - 1) val0 = filteredsinogram[idx0, i] val1 = filteredsinogram[idx1safe, i] interpolatedval = val0 + w (val1 - val0) image += interpolatedval # 4. Normalization image /= Ntheta return image Parameters: N	heta: Number of projection angles. SSIM plateaus when N	heta \ge 40 for a 512^2 image. dho: Radial sampling step. SSIM increases for dho > 1 (undersampling) and becomes constant when dho \le 1 (standard/oversampling). Filter: 'ramp', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine', 'hamming', 'hann'. Window parameter a: 0.54 for Hamming, 0.5 for Hann. Pixel Kernel: 'Area' kernel provides best SSIM and PSF uniformity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation: Points on the backprojection paths do not align with measured grid locations, requiring interpolation. Low resolution (e.g., 512x512) can cause visible artifacts. Noise Amplification: The ramp filter amplifies high frequencies, which are sources of noise. Windowed filters (Hann, Hamming) are used to attenuate these very high frequencies to reduce artifacts. Undersampling: High radial resolution (Nho increase) without sufficient angular coverage (N	heta < 40) causes complete loss of contrast and luminance. Inconsistent Data: FBP can produce negative values in the presence of inconsistent data. The Discrete Inverse Radon Transform reconstructs a 2D image from its Radon transform (sinogram) by summing projection values into image pixels, assuming parallel beam geometry. It is conventionally implemented via Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which applies a frequency-domain filter to the sinogram before backprojecting to correct for the blurring inherent in simple summation. Unlike iterative methods, it provides a direct, closed-form solution but requires projections over a full hemisphere and can produce negative values in the presence of inconsistent data. Iterative Reconstruction with Basis Expansion models the attenuation map as a linear combination of non-negative basis functions to solve the inverse problem when filtered backprojection fails due to inconsistent projections or limited viewing angles. Unlike Fourier-space methods such as Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which assume ideal data consistency, this method formulates the reconstruction as a convex non-negative linear least-squares optimization problem, guaranteeing a solution that emits a target light field with consistent views. A method to generate a convolution filter for tomographic reconstruction that includes an overscan border (typically 30% extra pixels) to handle boundary conditions and ensure symmetry. It calculates overscan dimensions (w{over} = \lceil w \cdot 0.3 ceil) and calls a filter builder with these dimensions. Overscanned filters preserve the parity (even/odd nature) of dimensions compared to non-overscanned filters, ensuring pixel alignment consistency. The Ramp Filter is a frequency-domain filter applied to projection data prior to backprojection in Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). It corrects for the 1/r blurring inherent in simple backprojection by weighting frequencies proportional to their magnitude. Unlike iterative methods or discrete inverse transforms that solve for the volume directly, the Ramp Filter is a closed-form, frequency-space correction step within the FBP pipeline. The mathematical foundation of FBP. It states that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection R	heta at angle 	heta is equal to a radial slice of the 2D Fourier transform of the original image f(x,y) at the same angle 	heta. This allows reconstruction by combining 1D Fourier transforms of all projections to fill the 2D Fourier space, which is then inverted. Models and shapes CT noise from Poisson-distributed photon counting to a frequency-dependent Gaussian distribution via ramp filtering and interpolation during backprojection. The ideal ramp filter amplifies high-frequency noise. Windowed ramp filters (Hanning, Hamming, Butterworth) create a band-pass noise spectrum. Re-sampling profiles during backprojection using interpolation (e.g., linear) further shapes the noise spectrum. The re-sampling rate can be increased via zoom reconstruction. Models and shapes CT noise from Poisson-distributed photon counting to a frequency-dependent Gaussian distribution via ramp filtering and interpolation during backprojection. Generates a 1D frequency domain filter kernel for use in filtered backprojection. For 'shepp-logan', it multiplies frequencies by 	ext{sinc}(\omega). For 'cosine', it uses a shifted sine function. For 'hamming' or 'hann', it uses the respective window function. The base ramp filter array f is defined as f[0] = 0.25, f[1::2] = -1 / (\pi 	imes n)^2, where n = [1, 3,..., 	ext{size}//2] 	ext{ concatenated with } [	ext{size}//2-1,..., 1]. The filter is 2 	imes 	ext{real}(	ext{FFT}(f)). Time Complexity: O(N \log N), making it competitive with Fourier methods. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for storing the sinogram and the reconstructed image. Measured Performance: FBP rms reconstruction error on Shepp-Logan phantom with ramp filter is 0.0283. Scaling: The method is highly parallelizable because pixel contributions are independent, allowing for efficient GPU implementation. Strengths: Fast, direct closed-form solution, good conservation of contrast, and uniform PSF. Limitations: Requires projections over a full hemisphere (\pi radians). Sensitive to noise (amplified by ramp filter) and undersampling. Can produce negative values with inconsistent data. When to Use: Standard reconstruction algorithm for 2D CT slices from projection data. Filtered Back-Projection is the most popular algorithm for computed tomography. It is based on the inversion of the Radon transform. The method was introduced by Ramachandran and Lakshiminarayanan, hence the name "Ram-Lak" filter. It is widely used in tomography and is cited as one of the most used direct methods. In 3D, Feldkamp’s (FDK) algorithm is a popular extension for cone-beam CT, which acts as a 3D extension of 2D FBP in orthographic mode. name: Ramp Filter
body: The Ramp Filter is a frequency-domain filter applied to projection data prior to backprojection in Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). It corrects for the blurring inherent in simple backprojection by weighting frequencies proportional to their magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 1D projection array p of width N. Output: A filtered 1D projection array \hat{p}. Data Structures: The projection p is stored as a 1D array of floating-point values. Frequency bins are computed as a 1D array of floats. Steps: 1. Compute the frequency bins f corresponding to the projection width N. 2. Compute the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the projection p. 3. Multiply the FFT result by the absolute value of the frequency bins (the ramp filter kernel). 4. Compute the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) of the result to obtain the filtered projection \hat{p}. Formula: \hat{p} = \text{IFFT}\left( \text{FFT}(p) \cdot |f| \right) where f is the array of frequency bins. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the projection is all zeros, the output is zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rampfilter(projection): N = len(projection) freqbins = np.abs(np.arange(N) - N / 2.0) fftprojection = np.fft.fft(projection) filteredfft = fftprojection freqbins filteredprojection = np.fft.ifft(filteredfft).real return filteredprojection Applies a Fourier filter and Poisson weights to residual projection data. Choose this when residual updates require frequency-domain filtering. Definition: Applies a Fourier filter and Poisson weights to a residual projection data. Steps: 1. If fourierfilter is None, compute simple difference: forward = projections - forward. 2. Else, apply Fourier filter: forward = fourierfilter numpy.fft.fft2(projections, axes=(0, 2)). 3. Subtract filtered forward projection: forward -= (fourierfilter2) numpy.fft.fft2(forward, axes=(0, 2)). 4. Compute inverse FFT and take absolute value: forward = numpy.abs(numpy.fft.ifft2(forward, axes=(0, 2))).astype('float32'). 5. If poisson is True, apply Poisson weights: forward = numpy.exp(-projections / projections.mean()). Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per projection due to FFT. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the projection and frequency bins. Strengths: Fast, closed-form solution. When to use: Standard FBP reconstruction. The Ramp Filter is a fundamental component of Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), a standard algorithm in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. It was developed as part of the mathematical foundation of tomographic reconstruction, correcting the blurring introduced by simple backprojection. ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, https://github.com/ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cicwi/flexTOMO, https://github.com/cicwi/flexTOMO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Discrete Inverse Radon Transform
head: Inverse Radon Transform, R^-1
body: The Discrete Inverse Radon Transform reconstructs a 2D image from its Radon transform (sinogram) by summing projection values into image pixels, assuming parallel beam geometry. It is conventionally implemented via Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which applies a frequency-domain filter to the sinogram before backprojecting to correct for the blurring inherent in simple summation. Unlike iterative methods, it provides a direct, closed-form solution but requires projections over a full hemisphere and can produce negative values in the presence of inconsistent data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sinogram tensor S of shape (B, C, N\rho, N\theta), where B is batch size, C is channels, N\rho is the number of radial samples, and N\theta is the number of projection angles. A tensor of angles \theta in degrees of length N\theta. Output: A reconstructed image tensor of shape (B, C, H, W). Data Structures: Sinogram: 4D tensor. Radial axis corresponds to detector positions. Angles: 1D tensor of floats. Image Grid: 2D meshgrid of coordinates centered at (0,0). Parameters: filtername: String specifying the frequency filter. Options: 'ramp', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine', 'hamming', 'hann', or None. Default: 'ramp'. interpolation: String for backprojection interpolation. Options: 'linear', 'nearest', 'cubic'. circle: Boolean. If True, assumes the image is zero outside the inscribed circle, adjusting output size and masking. outputsize: Integer or None. If None, calculated based on imgshape and circle. Steps: 1. Validation and Type Conversion: Ensure input sinogram is 4-D. If not, raise error. Convert sinogram to floating point. If preserverange is false, scale integer types to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] as appropriate. 2. Angle Handling: If \theta is None, set \theta = \text{linspace}(0, 180, N\theta + 1)[:-1]. Verify len(theta) == N\theta. 3. Output Size and Geometry Setup: Let img\shape be the radial dimension of the sinogram (N\rho). If circle is True, convert the sinogram from circular to square geometry (padding zeros to match the diameter) and update img\shape. Determine outputsize: If circle is True, outputsize = imgshape. Else, outputsize = floor(sqrt(imgshape^2 / 2)). Calculate radius = outputsize // 2. 4. Filtering (Frequency Domain): Pad the sinogram along the radial axis (dim 2) to projectionsizepadded. projectionsizepadded = max(64, 2^ceil(log2(2 imgshape))). Pad with zeros to this size. Compute the 1D FFT along the radial axis: P = \text{FFT}(S{padded}). Construct the filter kernel F in the frequency domain: Ramp: f[0] = 0.25, f[1::2] = -1/(\pi n)^2 for odd n. Final filter is 2 \cdot \text{real}(\text{FFT}(f)). Shepp-Logan: Multiply Ramp filter by \text{sinc}(\omega) = \sin(\omega)/\omega, where \omega = \pi \cdot \text{fftfreq}. Cosine: Multiply by \text{FFTshift}(\sin(\text{linspace}(0, \pi, size+1)[:-1])). Hamming/Hann: Multiply by the respective window function shifted to center. None: Identity filter (all ones). Apply filter: P{filtered} = P \cdot F. Inverse FFT and take real part, truncating to original img\shape: S{filtered} = \text{real}(\text{IFFT}(P{filtered}))[:,:,:img\shape,:]. 5. Backprojection: Initialize reconstructed tensor of zeros with shape (B, C, output\size, output\size). Create meshgrids x{pr}, y{pr} of size output\size \times output\size, centered at 0: x{pr}, y{pr} = \text{meshgrid}(\text{arange}(output\size) - radius, \text{arange}(output\size) - radius). For each angle index i and angle \thetai (converted to radians): Extract column col = S{filtered}[:,:,:, i]. Calculate projection coordinates t for all pixels: t = y{pr} \cos(\thetai) - x{pr} \sin(\thetai). Flatten t to t{flat} and repeat for batch size. Interpolate col at t{flat} using the specified interpolation method. Mask values outside the original detector range [-img\shape/2, img\shape/2 - 1] to match standard behavior. Add interpolated values to reconstructed. 6. Finalization: If circle is True, set pixels outside the reconstruction circle (x{pr}^2 + y{pr}^2 > radius^2) to 0. Scale the result by \frac{\pi}{2 N\theta}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: sinogram (torch.Tensor): Shape (B, C, Nrho, Ntheta). theta (torch.Tensor): Projection angles in degrees, shape (Ntheta,). filtername (str): Filter type ('ramp', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine', 'hamming', 'hann', None). interpolation (str): Interpolation mode ('linear', 'nearest', 'cubic'). circle (bool): If True, assumes image is zero outside inscribed circle. Returns: torch.Tensor: Reconstructed image (B, C, H, W). """ # 1. Validation and Type Conversion if sinogram.ndim != 4: raise ValueError("Input must be 4-D (B, C, Nrho, Ntheta)") device = sinogram.device dtype = sinogram.dtype # Convert to float (simplified logic from converttofloat) if not dtype.isfloatingpoint: sinogram = sinogram.double() if dtype in [torch.uint8]: sinogram = sinogram / torch.iinfo(dtype).max elif dtype in [torch.int8, torch.int16, torch.int32, torch.int64]: sinogram = sinogram / torch.iinfo(dtype).max sinogram = torch.clamp(sinogram, min=-1.0) else: sinogram = (sinogram + 0.5) 2 / (torch.iinfo(dtype).max - torch.iinfo(dtype).min) sinogram = sinogram.double() else: sinogram = sinogram.double() # 2. Angle Handling Ntheta = sinogram.size(3) if theta is None: theta = torch.linspace(0, 180, Ntheta + 1, dtype=dtype, device=device)[:-1] else: theta = theta.detach().clone().to(device=device, dtype=dtype) if len(theta) != Ntheta: raise ValueError("Theta length must match number of projections") anglesrad = torch.deg2rad(theta) Nangles = len(theta) # 3. Output Size and Geometry imgshape = sinogram.size(2) # Nrho if circle: # sinogramcircletosquare pads/interpolates the sinogram to square geometry. # Not given in the sources. outputsize = imgshape else: outputsize = int(torch.floor(torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(imgshape)2 / 2.0)).item()) radius = outputsize // 2 # 4. Filtering # Pad for FFT projectionsizepadded = max(64, int(2 torch.ceil(torch.log2(torch.tensor(2 imgshape)))).item()) padwidth = (0, projectionsizepadded - imgshape) sinogrampadded = F.pad(sinogram, (0, 0, padwidth[0], padwidth[1]), mode="constant", value=0) # Get Filter fourierfilter = getfourierfilter(projectionsizepadded, filtername, device) # FFT, Multiply, IFFT projectionfft = torch.fft.fft(sinogrampadded, dim=2) projectionfilteredfft = projectionfft fourierfilter[None, None,:,:] sinogramfiltered = torch.real(torch.fft.ifft(projectionfilteredfft, dim=2)[:,:,:imgshape,:]) # 5. Backprojection reconstructed = torch.zeros((sinogram.size(0), sinogram.size(1), outputsize, outputsize), device=device, dtype=dtype) # Create meshgrid xpr, ypr = torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(outputsize, device=device) - radius, torch.arange(outputsize, device=device) - radius, indexing="ij") for i, angle in enumerate(anglesrad): col = sinogramfiltered[:,:,:, i] # Calculate projection coordinates t t = ypr torch.cos(angle) - xpr torch.sin(angle) # Flatten and repeat for batch tflat = t.flatten().unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) tflat = torch.repeatinterleave(tflat, sinogram.size(0), dim=0) # Interpolate colinterp = interp(tflat, imgshape, col, mode=interpolation) reconstructed += colinterp.view(sinogram.size(0), sinogram.size(1), outputsize, outputsize) # 6. Finalization if circle: outreconstructioncircle = (xpr2 + ypr2) > radius2 reconstructed[:,:, outreconstructioncircle] = 0.0 return reconstructed (torch.pi / (2 Nangles)) def getfourierfilter(size, filtername, device): """Helper to generate frequency domain filters.""" if filtername is None: return torch.ones(size, device=device) # Standard frequency array f = torch.fft.fftfreq(size, d=1.0).to(device) fshifted = torch.fft.fftshift(f) if filtername == 'ramp': # S1 specific construction n = torch.arange(1, size, 2, device=device).float() filt = torch.zeros(size, device=device) filt[0] = 0.25 filt[1::2] = -1.0 / (torch.pi n) 2 filt = 2.0 torch.real(torch.fft.fft(filt)) return filt elif filtername == 'shepp-logan': omega = torch.pi fshifted sincval = torch.oneslike(omega) nonzero = torch.abs(omega) > 1e-6 sincval[nonzero] = torch.sin(omega[nonzero]) / omega[nonzero] # Reconstruct ramp for multiplication n = torch.arange(1, size, 2, device=device).float() ramp = torch.zeros(size, device=device) ramp[0] = 0.25 ramp[1::2] = -1.0 / (torch.pi n) 2 ramp = 2.0 torch.real(torch.fft.fft(ramp)) return ramp sincval elif filtername == 'cosine': window = torch.sin(torch.linspace(0, torch.pi, size + 1, device=device)[:-1]) window = torch.fft.fftshift(window) n = torch.arange(1, size, 2, device=device).float() ramp = torch.zeros(size, device=device) ramp[0] = 0.25 ramp[1::2] = -1.0 / (torch.pi n) 2 ramp = 2.0 torch.real(torch.fft.fft(ramp)) return ramp window elif filtername in ['hamming', 'hann']: if filtername == 'hamming': window = 0.54 - 0.46 torch.cos(2 torch.pi torch.arange(size, device=device) / (size - 1)) else: # hann window = 0.5 - 0.5 torch.cos(2 torch.pi torch.arange(size, device=device) / (size - 1)) window = torch.fft.fftshift(window) n = torch.arange(1, size, 2, device=device).float() ramp = torch.zeros(size, device=device) ramp[0] = 0.25 ramp[1::2] = -1.0 / (torch.pi n) 2 ramp = 2.0 torch.real(torch.fft.fft(ramp)) return ramp window else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown filter: {filtername}") def interp(x, imgshape, data, mode='linear'): """ 1D linear interpolation with out-of-bounds masking. x: (B, 1, H, W) coordinates in detector space data: (B, C, Nrho) sinogram values """ half = imgshape / 2.0 xclamped = torch.clamp(x, -half, half - 1.0) idx0 = torch.floor(xclamped).long() idx1 = idx0 + 1 w1 = xclamped - idx0.float() w0 = 1.0 - w1 idx0exp = idx0.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, data.size(1), -1, -1) idx1exp = idx1.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, data.size(1), -1, -1) w0exp = w0.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, data.size(1), -1, -1) w1exp = w1.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, data.size(1), -1, -1) val0 = torch.gather(data, 2, idx0exp) val1 = torch.gather(data, 2, idx1exp) result = w0exp val0 + w1exp val1 mask = (x < -half) | (x > half - 1) result = torch.where(mask, torch.zeroslike(result), result) return result The specific algorithmic framework that uses the Discrete Inverse Radon Transform as its backprojection step, preceded by frequency-domain filtering. An alternative method that models the image as a linear combination of basis functions and solves for coefficients using optimization, handling inconsistent projections better than FBP. Time Complexity: The naive summation approach is O(N N\theta N\rho), which simplifies to O(N^2) if N\theta, N\rho \propto \sqrt{N}. With optimized mapping of pixels to contributing projection lines, it can reach O(N \log N). The FFT-based filtering adds O(N\rho \log N\rho) per angle. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the sinogram, the filtered sinogram, and the output image. The FFT padding increases the radial dimension slightly. Strengths: Fast, direct solution; well-understood; efficient implementation using FFTs. Limitations: Requires projections over a full hemisphere (180^\circ); sensitive to noise (high-pass filter amplifies it); can produce negative values in the reconstructed image if the input data is inconsistent or incomplete. When to use: When full angular coverage is available and speed is critical. When not to use: With limited-angle data, inconsistent projections, or when non-negativity constraints are strict. The Discrete Inverse Radon Transform is the mathematical foundation of computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. It is derived from the Fourier Slice Theorem, which states that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection at angle \theta is a slice of the 2D Fourier transform of the image at that angle. The method was formalized in the context of computerized tomography in the 1970s, with seminal work by Kak and Slaney. It is widely used in medical imaging, industrial CT, and light field synthesis. tomluetjen/torchskradon, https://github.com/tomluetjen/torchskradon, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Layered 3D: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Attenuation-based Light Field and High Dynamic Range Displays, https://vccimaging.org/Publications/Wetzstein2011TIG/Wetzstein2011TIG.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 Précision et qualité en reconstruction tomographique: algorithmes et applications, https://doi.org/10.70675/d2bc4875z6a5az46afz9289z2fe16b3a43f3, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Fourier Slice Theorem
head: Central Slice Theorem, FST, Théorème de Radon, Théorème de la Tranche Centrale
body:
The Fourier Slice Theorem (FST), also known as the Central Slice Theorem, establishes that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection of a function at angle 	heta equals the values of the 2D Fourier transform of the original function along a radial line at the same angle in frequency space. It serves as the theoretical foundation for Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) [11308-filtered-back-projection-fbp.md] by enabling analytical reconstruction via frequency-domain operations rather than direct spatial-domain algebraic inversion. Unlike iterative or algebraic discrete methods that solve linear systems directly, FST operates in the frequency domain to fill the 2D Fourier space with 1D transforms of projections. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 1D projections R	heta(ho) acquired at various angles 	heta, representing line integrals of the original 2D function f(x,y). Output: The reconstructed 2D function f(x,y). Data Structures Projections: Array of 1D signals R	heta(ho) for discrete angles 	hetai. Frequency Domain: 2D grid representing the Fourier transform of f, denoted F^{2D}. Coordinate Systems: Cartesian (x,y) for spatial domain; Polar (r, \phi) for spatial domain; Cartesian (
ux, 
uy) or Polar (
u, \psi) for frequency domain. Numbered Steps 1. Convert f to polar coordinates: x = r \cos \phi, y = r \sin \phi. Substitute into the Radon integral to obtain the polar projection form. 2. Combine the polar projection form with the 1D Fourier transform integral. Simplify using the Dirac delta property (non-zero only when ho = r \cos(\phi-	heta)) to eliminate the ho integral. 3. Reconstruct the 2D Fourier space of the original domain by combining the 1D Fourier transforms of each projection. Obtain the initial domain by applying a 2D inverse Fourier transform. Formulas Let f(x,y) be the original 2D function. The Radon transform (projection) at angle 	heta is: R	heta(ho) = \iint f(x,y) \delta(ho - x \cos 	heta - y \sin 	heta) \, dx \, dy where \delta is the Dirac delta function, ho is the distance from the origin, and 	heta is the angle of the projection normal. The 1D Fourier transform of the projection R	heta(ho) is: F	heta(
u) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} R	heta(ho) e^{-2i\pi
uho} \, dho where 
u is the spatial frequency variable. The 2D Fourier transform of f(x,y) in Cartesian coordinates is: \hat{f}(
ux, 
uy) = \iint f(x,y) e^{-2i\pi(x
ux + y
uy)} \, dx \, dy The theorem states that evaluating this 2D transform along a line passing through the origin at angle 	heta yields the 1D Fourier transform of the projection at that angle: \hat{f}(
u \cos 	heta, 
u \sin 	heta) = F	heta(
u) where 
ux = 
u \cos 	heta and 
uy = 
u \sin 	heta. In polar coordinates, the 2D Fourier transform is: F^{2D}(\psi, 
u) = \int{0}^{2\pi} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(r \cos \phi, r \sin \phi) |r| e^{-2i\pi
u r \cos(\phi-\psi)} \, dr \, d\phi where X = 
u \cos \psi and Y = 
u \sin \psi. Equating the 1D and 2D forms yields the theorem: F	heta(
u) = F^{2D}(f(r \cos \phi, r \sin \phi))|{\psi=	heta} which confirms that the 1D Fourier transform of the projection equals the radial line at angle 	heta in the 2D Fourier space. Parameters 
u: Spatial frequency variable. Maps to coordinates (
u \cos 	heta, 
u \sin 	heta) in the 2D frequency plane. 	heta: Projection angle. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Discretization: The theorem is exact in the continuous domain. In practice, a finite number of projections and discrete sampling introduce artifacts (e.g., streaking) if not handled with appropriate interpolation and filtering (such as the ramp filter in FBP). Aliasing: Insufficient sampling in the frequency domain (too few projections or low resolution) leads to aliasing artifacts in the reconstructed image. Boundary Effects: The assumption of infinite support for the Fourier transform can cause edge artifacts if the object is not zero-padded sufficiently. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def reconstructfourierslice(projections, angles, N): # Initialize 2D frequency domain grid F^{2D} F2D = np.zeros((N, N), dtype=complex) # 1. Compute 1D Fourier transform for each projection for i, theta in enumerate(angles): F1D = np.fft.fft(projections[i]) freqs = np.fft.fftfreq(len(projections[i])) # 2. Map values F{	hetai}(
u) into the 2D frequency domain grid for j, nu in enumerate(freqs): # Coordinates in 2D frequency plane # Scale by sampling interval dx if physical units are required nux = nu np.cos(theta) nuy = nu np.sin(theta) # Interpolate onto Cartesian grid (nearest-neighbor) # Note: Projections provide data along radial lines in polar frequency coordinates # Interpolation is required to map these values onto a Cartesian grid xidx = int((nux + 0.5) N) yidx = int((nuy + 0.5) N) if 0 <= xidx < N and 0 <= yidx < N: F2D[yidx, xidx] += F1D[j] # Accumulate to handle overlaps # 3. Compute 2D Inverse Fourier Transform to recover f(x,y) freconstructed = np.fft.ifft2(F2D) return np.real(freconstructed) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard FFT-based implementations scale as O(Np \cdot N \log N) for 1D transforms and O(N^2 \log N) for the 2D inverse transform. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for projections (O(Np \cdot N)) and the 2D frequency grid (O(N^2)). Strengths: Provides an analytical solution rather than solving linear systems directly in the spatial domain. Limitations: Sensitive to noise and missing data (limited angle tomography); requires interpolation for polar-to-Cartesian mapping; assumes infinite support or requires windowing to reduce artifacts. When to use: Not given in the sources. Typically used for analytical reconstruction when projections are dense and noise is manageable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Avoid when projections are sparse or severely limited in angle, as interpolation artifacts dominate. The theorem was demonstrated by the Austrian mathematician Johann Radon in 1917. It provides the essential link between projections and the pixel values of the slice to be reconstructed. Historically, 2D reconstruction methods were classified into analytical methods (continuous approach, seeking analytical inversion formulas) and algebraic methods (discrete approach, treating the problem as linear system inversion). The Fourier Slice Theorem is the cornerstone of the analytical approach, specifically Filtered Back-Projection [11308-filtered-back-projection-fbp.md]. name: Iterative Reconstruction with Basis Expansion
head: Linear Combination Basis Method, Non-negative Linear Least-Squares Optimization
body: Iterative Reconstruction with Basis Expansion models the attenuation map as a linear combination of non-negative basis functions to solve the inverse problem when filtered backprojection fails due to inconsistent projections or limited viewing angles. Unlike Fourier-space methods such as Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which assume ideal data consistency, this method formulates the reconstruction as a convex non-negative linear least-squares optimization problem, guaranteeing a solution that emits a target light field with consistent views. Inputs: Target logarithmic light field vector \bar{l}, where elements \bar{l}{ij} correspond to discrete rays (i, j). A set of Nb basis functions \bar{\phi}k(x, y) with known spatial support. Ray geometry parameters: display width w, height h, depth dr, and discrete ray indices (i, j) mapping to continuous coordinates (u, a). Outputs: Coefficient vector \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{Nb}, where \alphak \ge 0. Reconstructed attenuation map \mu(x, y). Data Structures: Projection Matrix P: A matrix of size Nr \times Nb, where Nr is the number of rays. Element P{ij}^{(k)} represents the line integral of basis function k along ray (i, j). Basis Functions: Defined on a domain [-h/2, h/2] \times [-w/2, w/2]. Can be conventional voxels or functions with compact/extended support. Formulas: The attenuation map is modeled as: \mu(x, y) = \sum{k=1}^{Nb} \alphak \bar{\phi}k(x, y) \quad (7) The forward model for the discrete logarithmic light field is: \bar{l}{ij} = - \sum{k=1}^{Nb} \alphak P{ij}^{(k)} \quad (9) The projection matrix element P{ij}^{(k)} is calculated via line integral: P{ij}^{(k)} = \int{-h/2}^{h/2} \int{-w/2}^{w/2} \bar{\phi}k(x, y) \delta(dr(x - (i\Delta u)) - (j\Delta a)y) \, dx \, dy \quad (10) The reconstruction solves the following convex optimization problem: \arg \min{\alpha} \| \bar{l} + P\alpha \|2^2, \quad \text{subject to } \alpha \ge 0 \quad (11) Parameters: Nb: Number of basis functions. Not given in the sources. Nl: Number of layers (in multi-layer variant). Not given in the sources. Layer spacing: Evenly spaced over total display thickness (e.g., 1.25 cm in prototype). Layer resolution: 171 dots per inch (149 µm pixels) in prototype. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import nnls def computeprojectionmatrix(basisfunctions, rayparams, numbasis, numrays, numa): """ Computes the projection matrix P where P[r, k] is the line integral of basis function k along ray r, flattened from indices (i, j). Args: basisfunctions: List of callable functions phik(x, y). rayparams: Dictionary containing deltau, deltaa, dr, h, w. numbasis: Number of basis functions Nb. numrays: Total number of rays Nr. numa: Number of discrete angle indices j. Returns: P: Matrix of shape (numrays, numbasis). """ deltau = rayparams['deltau'] deltaa = rayparams['deltaa'] dr = rayparams['dr'] h = rayparams['h'] w = rayparams['w'] P = np.zeros((numrays, numbasis)) # Integration grid for the line integral along y yvals = np.linspace(-w/2, w/2, 200) dy = yvals[1] - yvals[0] for r in range(numrays): i = r // numa j = r % numa # Ray line equation from delta constraint: x = ideltau + (jdeltaa / dr) y slope = (j deltaa) / dr intercept = i deltau for k in range(numbasis): # Evaluate basis function along the ray path xvals = intercept + slope yvals # Mask points outside the display height bounds [-h/2, h/2] valid = (xvals >= -h/2) & (xvals <= h/2) if np.any(valid): integrand = basisfunctionsk # Trapezoidal rule for line integral P[r, k] = np.trapz(integrand, y=yvals[valid]) else: P[r, k] = 0.0 return P def reconstructattenuation(lightfield, basisfunctions, rayparams, numbasis, numa): """ Reconstructs the attenuation coefficients alpha using non-negative least squares. Args: lightfield: Vector lbar of target logarithmic light field values. basisfunctions: List of callable basis functions. rayparams: Geometry parameters. numbasis: Number of basis functions. numa: Number of discrete angle indices j. Returns: alpha: Vector of non-negative coefficients. """ numrays = len(lightfield) # 1. Construct the projection matrix P P = computeprojectionmatrix(basisfunctions, rayparams, numbasis, numrays, numa) # 2. Solve the optimization problem: arg min || lbar + P alpha ||^2 s.t. alpha >= 0 # Equivalent to: arg min || P alpha - (-lbar) ||^2 # Using scipy's nnls which solves min ||b - Ax||^2 s.t. x >= 0 # Here A = P, b = -lbar b = -lightfield alpha, = nnls(P, b) return alpha def renderlightfield(alpha, basisfunctions, rayparams, numrays, numa): """ Renders the light field from the reconstructed coefficients. Args: alpha: Coefficients vector. basisfunctions: List of callable basis functions. rayparams: Geometry parameters. numrays: Number of rays. numa: Number of discrete angle indices j. Returns: lrendered: Rendered logarithmic light field. """ numbasis = len(alpha) P = computeprojectionmatrix(basisfunctions, rayparams, numbasis, numrays, numa) # Forward model: lbar = - P alpha lrendered = -np.dot(P, alpha) return lrendered Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The optimization relies on the linearity of the human visual system to logarithmic changes in illumination (Weber-Fechner law). Boundaries: The integration domain is bounded by the display dimensions [-h/2, h/2] \times [-w/2, w/2]. Basis functions extending outside this domain must be handled correctly in the projection matrix calculation. Degenerate Input: If the viewing angles are too limited, the system matrix P may be ill-conditioned, leading to unstable solutions. The non-negativity constraint helps regularize the solution. A tomographic method for reconstructing a volumetric density field from a small number of camera images by modeling the scene as a linear combination of basis functions with local support. It differs from Fourier-space methods like Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by using basis functions with finite support to create a sparse system matrix, which allows the solution space to be restricted by a visual hull to discard zero-valued variables. A model representing the attenuator as a finite number Nl of discrete attenuation layers (masks) separated by distances dk, where each mask controls spatially-varying transmittance. The forward model for the logarithmic light field is \bar{l}(u, a) = \sum{k=1}^{Nl} \ln tk(u + (dk/dr)a) = - \sum{k=1}^{Nl} ak(u + (dk/dr)a), where ak(\xi) = -\ln tk(\xi) is the absorbance of mask k at position \xi. This leads to a linear system similar to the single-layer case, allowing the use of the same iterative reconstruction algorithm. In the prototype, layers are evenly-spaced over a total display thickness of 1.25 cm, with a resolution of 171 dots per inch (149 µm pixels). Time Complexity: The method requires iterative optimization, which exhibits greater computational complexity than direct transform methods like FBP. The complexity depends on the number of basis functions Nb, the number of rays Nr, and the convergence rate of the optimization algorithm. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the projection matrix P, which is Nr \times Nb. If basis functions have local support, P is sparse, reducing memory requirements. Measured Performance: In the prototype, a 5.7 cm × 7.6 cm display with 1.25 cm thickness and 171 dpi resolution was used. The scene was rendered as a light field with 7×7 oblique projections. Strengths: Better accounts for inconsistent projections over limited angles compared to FBP. Guarantees consistent views in the least-squares sense. Limitations: Higher computational complexity than FBP. When to use: When projections are inconsistent or viewing angles are limited, making FBP unsuitable. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and projections are consistent. The method was introduced by Wetzstein et al. in 2011 in the paper "Layered 3D: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Attenuation-based Light Field and High Dynamic Range Displays". It builds on the work of Herman [1995] on iterative reconstruction algorithms. The approach is motivated by the need to synthesize attenuation maps for layered 3D displays, where traditional transform methods fail due to the discrete nature of the layers and limited viewing angles. The method leverages the Weber-Fechner law to justify the use of logarithmic light field values in the optimization. name: Iterative Reconstruction with Local Support Basis Functions
head: Algebraic Reconstruction with Visual Hull and Local Basis, Sparse-View Tomographic Reconstruction of Flames
body: A tomographic method for reconstructing a volumetric density field from a small number of camera images by modeling the scene as a linear combination of basis functions with local support. It differs from Fourier-space methods like Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by using basis functions with finite support to create a sparse system matrix, which allows the solution space to be restricted by a visual hull to discard zero-valued variables. Inputs: A set of N images from different camera viewpoints. Camera calibration data (intrinsics and extrinsics) for each viewpoint. A 3D voxel grid defining the spatial domain. A visual hull mask indicating regions where density is known to be zero. Outputs: A vector of coefficients \mathbf{a} representing the density field. The reconstructed 3D density field \phi. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A regular 3D grid defining the spatial domain. Basis Functions: Defined on the voxel grid. Two types are described: 1. Box Basis: Defined on a single voxel i. 2. Trilinear Basis: Arranged on the voxel grid with a one-voxel overlap in every dimension to ensure smooth blending. System Matrix S: A sparse matrix where rows correspond to pixels and columns to basis functions. Entry s{ni} is the integral of the i-th basis function along the backprojected ray of pixel p. Steps: 1. Define the Image Formation Model: Model the image intensity Ip for pixel p as the line integral of the density field \phi along the backprojected ray c: Ip = \intc \phi \, ds \quad (1) Assumptions: negligible absorption/scattering and proportional self-emission. 2. Basis Expansion: Assume \phi is a linear combination of basis functions \phii with coefficients ai: \phi(\mathbf{x}) = \sumi ai \phii(\mathbf{x}) Substitute into (1) and swap sum and integral: Ip = \sumi ai \left( \intc \phii \, ds \right) \quad (2) This forms the linear system \mathbf{p} = S\mathbf{a}, where \mathbf{p} is the vector of pixel intensities, S{pi} = \intc \phii \, ds, and \mathbf{a} is the vector of coefficients. 3. Construct Matrix S (Sparse Setup): Compute entries s{ni} by intersecting backprojected rays with basis function supports. Use voxel-aligned basis functions to reduce intersection computation from O(n^3) to O(3n) by intersecting 3n planes and performing a lookup. Box Basis: For a box basis function \phii^{Box} defined on voxel i with bounds [x{min}^j, x{max}^j], [y{min}^j, y{max}^j], [z{min}^j, z{max}^j]: \phii^{Box}(x,y,z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x{min}^j < x \leq x{max}^j \land y{min}^j < y \leq y{max}^j \land z{min}^j < z \leq z{max}^j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (3) Let x1 and x2 be the intersection points of ray cn with voxel i. The entry is the distance between these points: s{ni} = \|x2 - x1\| \quad (4) Trilinear Basis: Arranged on the voxel grid with one-voxel overlap in every dimension. The intersection of the ray with the support is a cubic polynomial, which is integrated analytically. 4. Restrict Solution Space (Visual Hull): Discard variables (coefficients ai) corresponding to basis functions entirely outside the visual hull (known to be zero). This restricts the solution space by keeping only coefficients that need to be computed. 5. Solve Linear System: Compute a least-squares solution \mathbf{a} = (S^T S)^{-1} S^T \mathbf{p}, but solve it via an iterative method due to ill-conditioning. The matrix S is often ill-conditioned with a large condition number (quotient of largest to smallest singular value), making direct inversion difficult. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reconstructdensity(pixels, cameras, voxelgrid, visualhullmask, basistype='box'): # 1. Identify active basis functions based on visual hull activeindices = [] for i, bounds in enumerate(voxelgrid.basisbounds(basistype)): if bounds.intersects(visualhullmask): activeindices.append(i) numpixels = len(pixels) numactive = len(activeindices) # 2. Construct matrix S using standard lists S = [[0.0] numactive for in range(numpixels)] for pidx, pixel in enumerate(pixels): ray = cameras[pixel.cameraid].backprojectray(pixel.u, pixel.v) for col, basisidx in enumerate(activeindices): if basistype == 'box': x1, x2 = ray.intersectvoxel(voxelgrid.basisbounds(basisidx)) # Euclidean distance ||x2 - x1|| S[pidx][col] = math.sqrt(sum((x2[j] - x1[j])2 for j in range(3))) elif basistype == 'trilinear': # Intersection is a cubic polynomial c0 + c1t + c2t^2 + c3t^3 polycoeffs = ray.intersecttrilinearsupport(voxelgrid.basisposition(basisidx)) # Analytical integral from 0 to 1: c0 + c1/2 + c2/3 + c3/4 S[pidx][col] = polycoeffs[0] + polycoeffs[1]/2 + polycoeffs[2]/3 + polycoeffs[3]/4 else: raise ValueError("Unknown basis type") # 3. Solve least squares system: a = (S^T S)^-1 S^T p # Compute S^T S and S^T p StS = [[sum(S[r][c] S[r][k] for r in range(numpixels)) for k in range(numactive)] for c in range(numactive)] StP = [sum(S[r][c] pixels[r] for r in range(numpixels)) for c in range(numactive)] # The source specifies solving via an iterative method due to ill-conditioning. # Standard iterative solver (e.g., Conjugate Gradient) implementation omitted. a = [0.0] numactive return a Time Complexity: Matrix construction is O(3n) per ray/basis pair due to voxel-aligned intersection optimization, where n is the number of planes intersected. Solving the linear system uses an iterative method due to ill-conditioning. Memory Complexity: The matrix S is sparse, requiring memory proportional to the number of non-zero entries, which is significantly less than the full matrix required by Fourier basis functions. Strengths: Allows high-quality reconstruction from a small number of camera images (sparse-view) by restricting the solution space with a visual hull. Handles perspective projection correctly. Trilinear basis functions are arranged with a one-voxel overlap in every dimension to ensure smooth blending during rendering and are well suited for graphics hardware visualization. Limitations: The system matrix S is ill-conditioned, making inversion difficult. Requires a static camera setup for dynamic flames. Assumes negligible absorption/scattering and proportional self-emission. Originated in the paper "Image-based tomographic reconstruction of flames". It was developed to address the difficulty of generating convincing computer-animated fire, which is chaotic and hard to simulate. The method adapts algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART) to tomography, differing from Radon transform methods by using local support basis functions and a visual hull constraint. It is applicable to static camera setups observing dynamic flames, enabling fast processing of multi-video sequences for time-varying models. name: Radon Transform (Direct)
head: Discrete Radon Transform, Kingston and Svalbe Discrete Radon Transform, skradon
body: Computes the Radon transform (sinogram) of a batch of multi-channel images by rotating the image and summing along one axis for each angle. It differs from TorchRadon by operating directly in the spatial domain via explicit rotation and summation, rather than relying on Fourier-space approximations. Inputs: image: A 4-D torch.Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) representing a batch of multi-channel images. theta: A 1-D torch.Tensor of angles in degrees. If None, defaults to torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32). circle: A boolean flag. If True, assumes the image is zero outside the inscribed circle and crops to a square; if False, pads the image to the diagonal size. preserverange: A boolean flag. If True, preserves the original value range by converting to double precision if necessary; if False, scales integer types to [0.0, 1.0] or [-1.0, 1.0]. Outputs: radonimage: A torch.Tensor of shape (B, C, N, M), where B is batch size, C is channels, N is the projection width (padded image size), and M is the number of angles. Formulas: For the discrete formulation by Kingston and Svalbe, the transform on a discrete image f(i, j) is defined as: R(k, \theta) = \sum{i=0}^{p-1} \sum{j=0}^{p-1} f(i, j) \delta(k - ijm + jim), where \delta(i) = 0 if i \neq 0 and 1 if i = 0. The number of bins Nm on a projection is not constant: Nm = p(|i| + j), with 0 \le i \le p and 0 \le j \le p. Steps: 1. Type Conversion: Convert image to float using converttofloat(image, preserverange). If preserverange is true, convert non-float types to double. If false, scale unsigned integers to [0.0, 1.0] and signed integers to [-1.0, 1.0]. 2. Validation: Validate input is 4-D. If theta is None, set theta = torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32). Clone theta and move it to the same device as image. 3. Preprocessing (Circle Mode): If circle is True: calculate shapemin = min(image.size()[2:]) and radius = shapemin // 2. Create a meshgrid x, y for the image coordinates. Calculate distance from center dist = ((coords - center.view(-1, 1, 1)) 2).sum(0). Identify outsidereconstructioncircle = dist > radius2. Warn if any non-zero values exist outside the circle. Calculate excess = imgshape - shapemin. Create slices to crop the image to a square: paddedimage = image[:,:, slices[0], slices[1]]. 4. Preprocessing (Padding Mode): If circle is False: calculate diagonal = torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2)) max(image.size()[2:]). Calculate padding pad = [int(torch.ceil(diagonal - s)) for s in image.size()[2:]]. Calculate new/old centers and pad widths. Apply torch.nn.functional.pad with mode 'constant' and value 0 to get paddedimage. 5. Square Assertion: Assert paddedimage is square. If paddedimage.size()[2] != paddedimage.size()[3], raise ValueError. 6. Center Calculation: If paddedimage.size()[2] is even, center = 0.5; else center = 0.0. 7. Initialization: Initialize radonimage tensor of shape (batch, channels, paddedsize, len(theta)) with zeros. 8. Rotation and Summation: Loop for i, angle in enumerate(torch.deg2rad(theta)): calculate cosa, sina = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle). Construct 3x3 rotation matrix R with translation terms -center (cosa + sina - 1) / (paddedimage.size()[2] / 2) and -center (cosa - sina - 1) / (paddedimage.size()[3] / 2). Warp image using rotated = warp(paddedimage, R). Sum along axis 2: radonimage[:,:,:, i] = rotated.sum(2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def radontransform(image, theta=None, circle=True, preserverange=True): # Step 1: Type Conversion if image.dtype == torch.float16: image = image.float() if preserverange: if image.dtype not in [torch.float32, torch.float64]: image = image.double() else: if not image.dtype.isfloatingpoint: if image.dtype == torch.bool: image = image.double() elif image.dtype == torch.uint8: imaxin = torch.iinfo(image.dtype).max image = image / imaxin image = image.double() elif image.dtype in [torch.int8, torch.int16, torch.int32, torch.int64]: imaxin = torch.iinfo(image.dtype).max image = image / imaxin image = image.double() # Step 2: Validation assert image.dim() == 4, "Input must be 4-D" if theta is None: theta = torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32, device=image.device) else: theta = theta.clone().to(image.device) # Step 3 & 4: Preprocessing if circle: shapemin = min(image.size()[2:]) radius = shapemin // 2 y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(image.size(2), device=image.device), torch.arange(image.size(3), device=image.device), indexing='ij') centercoord = shapemin / 2.0 dist = ((x - centercoord) 2 + (y - centercoord) 2) outsidereconstructioncircle = dist > radius 2 if torch.any((image != 0) & outsidereconstructioncircle): import warnings warnings.warn("Non-zero values exist outside the reconstruction circle") excess = [image.size(2) - shapemin, image.size(3) - shapemin] slices = [] for e in excess: if e.item() > 0: slices.append((int(torch.ceil(e / 2).item()), int(torch.ceil(e / 2).item() + shapemin))) else: slices.append(slice(None)) paddedimage = image[:,:, slices[0][0]:slices[0][1], slices[1][0]:slices[1][1]] else: diagonal = torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2.0, device=image.device)) max(image.size()[2:]) pad = [int(torch.ceil(diagonal - s)) for s in image.size()[2:]] newcenter = [(s + p) // 2 for s, p in zip(image.size()[2:], pad)] oldcenter = [s // 2 for s in image.size()[2:]] padbefore = [nc - oc for oc, nc in zip(oldcenter, newcenter)] padwidth = [(pb, p - pb) for pb, p in zip(padbefore, pad)] paddedimage = F.pad(image, (padwidth[1][0], padwidth[1][1], padwidth[0][0], padwidth[0][1]), mode="constant", value=0) # Step 5: Square Assertion if paddedimage.size()[2] != paddedimage.size()[3]: raise ValueError("paddedimage must be a square") # Step 6: Center Calculation if paddedimage.size()[2] % 2 == 0: center = 0.5 else: center = 0.0 # Step 7: Initialization radonimage = torch.zeros( (paddedimage.size(0), paddedimage.size(1), paddedimage.size(2), len(theta)), dtype=paddedimage.dtype, device=paddedimage.device,) # Step 8: Rotation and Summation for i, angle in enumerate(torch.deg2rad(theta)): cosa, sina = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle) R = torch.tensor([ [cosa, sina, -center (cosa + sina - 1) / (paddedimage.size(2) / 2)], [-sina, cosa, -center (cosa - sina - 1) / (paddedimage.size(3) / 2)], [0, 0, 1] ], dtype=paddedimage.dtype, device=paddedimage.device) # Standard affine warp using gridsample B, C, H, W = paddedimage.shape grid = F.affinegrid(R[:2,:].unsqueeze(0), [B, C, H, W], aligncorners=False) rotated = F.gridsample(paddedimage, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=False) radonimage[:,:,:, i] = rotated.sum(2) return radonimage Parameters: circle: bool, optional. If True, assumes image is zero outside inscribed circle and crops to square. If False, pads to diagonal size. preserverange: bool, optional. Whether to keep original value range or convert via imgasfloat conventions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If circle=True and image has non-zero values outside the reconstruction circle, a UserWarning is raised. If circle=False, the padded image must be square. If not, ValueError is raised. The Mojette transform is an exact discrete version of the Radon transform that allows the projection of discrete data onto a discrete hyperplane. Unlike the continuous Radon transform, which requires interpolation for arbitrary angles, the Mojette transform restricts projection directions to discrete angles defined by integer vectors, ensuring that line integrals pass exactly through pixel centers. This induces regular sampling on the projections and eliminates interpolation errors for a finite number of angles. It builds on Radon Transform (Direct) by replacing the continuous integral with a discrete sum constrained by integer geometry. Models a real-world scanner acquisition as a finite, discrete subset of the ideal continuous sinogram. It uses a finite number of projections N\theta, uniformly distributed between 0 and \pi, and a finite, constant number of samples per projection N\rho. The angular step is d\theta = \pi / N\theta, and the sampling step on a projection is d\rho = \max(W,H) / N\rho, where W and H are image width and height in pixels. The discrete sinogram S^ is a 2D image of size N\rho \times N\theta, where pixel (i\theta, i\rho) with 0 \le i\theta < N\theta and 0 \le i\rho < N\rho stores the value R\theta(\rho). Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Explicit control over rotation and summation; supports multi-channel images. Limitations: Requires square images after preprocessing. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Radon transform is a fundamental tool in tomography, mapping a function to its line integrals. The discrete formulation was described by Kingston and Svalbe. The direct implementation described here follows the principles outlined in "Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging" by Kak and Slaney. name: Mojette Transform
head: Discrete Radon Transform, Exact Discrete Radon Transform, Mojette Projection, Mojette Transformation
body: The Mojette transform is an exact discrete version of the Radon transform that allows the projection of discrete data onto a discrete hyperplane. Unlike the continuous Radon transform, which requires interpolation for arbitrary angles, the Mojette transform restricts projection directions to discrete angles defined by integer vectors, ensuring that line integrals pass exactly through pixel centers. This induces regular sampling on the projections and eliminates interpolation errors for a finite number of angles. It builds on Radon Transform (Direct) by replacing the continuous integral with a discrete sum constrained by integer geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A discrete 2D image f(k, l) defined on a Cartesian grid, where k, l are integer coordinates. Output: A projection bin value proj(t, \theta) for a specific discrete angle defined by integers (p, q). Data Structures: Image f: A 2D array indexed by integer coordinates (k, l). Projection direction: Defined by two integers (p, q), where p is the displacement in pixels along the x-axis (\vec{x}) and q is the displacement in pixels along the y-axis (\vec{y}). Projection coordinate t: The position along the projection axis, orthogonal to the direction (p, q). Mathematical Formulation: The continuous object f(x, y) is modeled using Dirac pixels: f(x, y) = \sum{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} \sum{l=-\infty}^{+\infty} f(k, l) \delta(x - \Deltap k) \delta(y - \Deltap l) where \delta(x) = 1 if x = 0 and 0 otherwise, and \Deltap is the pixel size. The Radon transform at angle \theta is: proj(t, \theta) = \int{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x, y) \delta(t + x \sin \theta - y \cos \theta) dx dy Substituting the Dirac model yields: proj\delta(t, \theta) = \sum{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} \sum{l=-\infty}^{+\infty} f(k, l) \delta(t + \Deltap k \sin \theta - \Deltap l \cos \theta) For the projection to be non-zero, the argument of the delta function must be zero: t + \Deltap k \sin \theta - \Deltap l \cos \theta = 0 Regular sampling is achieved only when \tan \theta = q/p for integers p, q. In this case: \cos \theta = \frac{p}{\sqrt{p^2 + q^2}}, \quad \sin \theta = \frac{q}{\sqrt{p^2 + q^2}} The condition for a pixel (k, l) to contribute to bin t becomes: t = \Deltap (l \cos \theta - k \sin \theta) = \frac{\Deltap}{\sqrt{p^2 + q^2}} (l p - k q) Let u = l p - k q. The projection bin index t is proportional to u. The value of the projection bin corresponding to u is the sum of all f(k, l) such that l p - k q = u. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define the discrete projection direction by integers (p, q). 2. Initialize a projection array with zeros. 3. Determine the valid range of indices for the projection array based on image bounds and (p, q). 4. Iterate over all pixels (k, l) in the input image. 5. Calculate the projection coordinate value u = l \cdot p - k \cdot q. 6. Map u to the appropriate bin index in the projection array. 7. Add f(k, l) to the value at that bin index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mojettetransform(image, p, q): """ Computes the Mojette projection for direction (p, q). Args: image: 2D array where image[l][k] accesses the pixel at integer coordinates (k, l). p: Displacement in pixels along the x-axis. q: Displacement in pixels along the y-axis. Returns: projection: Array of summed values indexed by u. """ height = image.shape[0] # Number of l values (y) width = image.shape[1] # Number of k values (x) # Calculate range of u = lp - kq minl, maxl = 0, height - 1 mink, maxk = 0, width - 1 minlp = minl p if p >= 0 else maxl p maxlp = maxl p if p >= 0 else minl p minkq = mink q if q >= 0 else maxk q maxkq = maxk q if q >= 0 else mink q minu = minlp - maxkq maxu = maxlp - minkq size = maxu - minu + 1 projection = [0.0] size offset = -minu for l in range(height): for k in range(width): u = l p - k q idx = u + offset projection[idx] += image[l][k] return projection Parameters: (p, q): Integer vector defining the projection direction. Typical values are coprime integers to avoid redundant sampling. \Deltap: Pixel size. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Directions: If p=0 and q=0, the direction is undefined. Boundary Conditions: The projection array size depends on the image bounds and (p, q). Pixels near the boundary contribute to bins that might be outside the central range if not handled correctly. Precision: Since the transform is exact and discrete, floating-point precision issues are minimal compared to interpolated Radon transforms, provided integer arithmetic is used for u. Defined on a p \times p table where p is a prime number. The continuous Radon transform integral is replaced by a discrete sum on lines k = ml + t \mod p for all intersection points 0 \le t \le p, for a line slope m such that 0 \le m \le p. The image space is considered toroidal, meaning projection lines "wrap around" the image. For an image f(k, l), the transform is: R(t, m) = \begin{cases} \sum{i=0}^{p-1} f(i, t) & \text{if } m=0 \\ \sum{j=0}^{p-1} f((mj + t)\mod p, j) & \text{if } 0 < m \le p \end{cases} This variant is chosen when a finite, cyclic geometry is required, such as in certain algebraic reconstruction techniques or discrete geometry applications. It differs from the standard Mojette transform by enforcing toroidal topology and prime-sized dimensions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with image size. The number of bins scales with the image dimensions and the slope (p, q). Strengths: Exact reconstruction for a finite set of angles; no interpolation errors. Limitations: Limited to discrete angles defined by integer vectors (p, q); cannot represent arbitrary continuous angles without approximation. When to use: Applications in discrete geometry, network coding, and medical image protection where exact discrete projections are required. When not: When arbitrary angle coverage is needed without discrete constraints. The Mojette transform was developed in 1995 by Jean-Pierre Guédon in the IVC (Image and Video Communication) team at the IRCCyN laboratory. It was introduced as an exact discrete version of the Radon transform to facilitate tomographic reconstruction and other applications requiring discrete projections. Applications include discrete geometry, networks, and medical image protection. Reconstruction Tomographique Mojette, https://theses.hal.science/tel-00426920v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gradient w.r.t Source/Detector Geometry
head: Cone Beam Geometry Gradient, Cone Beam Geometry Gradient CUDA Kernel, Gradient of Projection Error w.r.t Source and Detector Positions
body: Computes the gradient of the projection error (or forward projection loss) with respect to the 3D positions of the X-ray source and detector elements in a cone-beam geometry. It differs from standard back-projection by applying the chain rule through the trilinear interpolation derivatives, scattering gradients back to the camera parameters rather than the volume. It is the adjoint operation required for differentiable tomographic reconstruction where geometry is optimized. Inputs: volume: 3D volume data in a bricked layout with a 1-voxel zero border. sources: Array of source positions. detectors: Array of detector element positions. box: 12 floats defining volume centre (3), half-extent (3), inverse voxel spacing (3), and stored centre coordinate (3). grad: Packed gradient tensor for the current group. n: Number of sample points along each ray. Outputs: gradsources: Gradient w.r.t. source positions. graddetectors: Gradient w.r.t. detector positions. Data Structures: ConeRay: Struct containing ray origin (source), direction components (ex, ey, ez), length, entry/exit distances along the ray (entry, exit), entry/exit axes (entryaxis, exitaxis), and sample step parameters in stored coordinates (px, py, pz, sx, sy, sz). Layout: Defines volume dimensions (X, Y, Z) and brick tiling parameters (bricksx, row, plane). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each thread handling a ray, initialize F=0 (accumulated value), G[3]={0} (accumulated spatial gradients), M[3]={0} (accumulated weighted spatial gradients), and loaded=0xffffffff (cache invalidation flag). 2. Ray Setup: Construct the ConeRay from source and detector positions. Compute direction vector \vec{e} = \text{detector} - \text{source} and length L = \|\vec{e}\|. If L \le 0, skip. Normalize direction \vec{u} = \vec{e}/L. Clip the ray against the volume box defined by box to find entry, exit, and the axes of intersection (entryaxis, exitaxis). If the ray misses the volume, skip. Compute step size in stored coordinates: weight = (\text{exit} - \text{entry}) / n. Compute starting position in stored coordinates for the first sample midpoint. 3. Sampling Loop: Iterate k from 0 to n-1. Calculate the current sample position in stored coordinates using px, py, pz and steps sx, sy, sz. Determine the 8 neighboring voxel indices (trilinear stencil). If the stencil index has not been loaded (s.index != loaded): fetch the 8 voxel values from the volume for all channels, weight by g[c], store in v[q], and set loaded = s.index. Compute the interpolated value f and its spatial derivatives fx, fy, fz using the precomputed trilinear derivatives. Accumulate: F \leftarrow F + f; G[0] \leftarrow G[0] + fx, G[1] \leftarrow G[1] + fy, G[2] \leftarrow G[2] + fz; M[0] \leftarrow M[0] + w \cdot fx, M[1] \leftarrow M[1] + w \cdot fy, M[2] \leftarrow M[2] + w \cdot fz where w = (k + 0.5) / n. 4. Gradient Accumulation: Let E = [ex, ey, ez] be the ray direction vector. Let \taue = \text{entry} / L and \taux = \text{exit} / L be the normalized entry and exit positions. Let \delta = \taux - \taue be the normalized ray span. Let step = weight. Scale G[a] and M[a] by box[6+a]. Compute GE = \sum{a} G[a] \cdot E[a] and ME = \sum{a} M[a] \cdot E[a]. Compute \text{along} = \delta \cdot F / n and \text{ends} = L \cdot F / n. For each axis a \in \{0, 1, 2\}: H = \taue \cdot G[a] + \delta \cdot M[a]; \text{gd}[a] = \text{along} \cdot E[a] / L + \text{step} \cdot H; \text{gs}[a] = \text{step} \cdot G[a] - \text{gd}[a]. 5. Boundary Corrections: If a == \text{exit\axis}: c = (\text{ends} + \text{step} \cdot ME) / E[a]; \text{gs}[a] \leftarrow \text{gs}[a] - c \cdot (1 - \taux); \text{gd}[a] \leftarrow \text{gd}[a] - c \cdot \taux. If a == \text{entry\axis}: c = (-\text{ends} + \text{step} \cdot (GE - ME)) / E[a]; \text{gs}[a] \leftarrow \text{gs}[a] - c \cdot (1 - \taue); \text{gd}[a] \leftarrow \text{gd}[a] - c \cdot \taue. 6. Writing Results: Write \text{gd}[a] to graddetectors[3r + a] for active rays. Reduce \text{gs}[a] across the warp using warp shuffle instructions. If the thread is the first in the warp and the total gradient is non-zero, atomicAdd to gradsources[3view + a]. Python Wrapper Logic: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conegeometrygradwrapper(volume, gradflat, sources, detectors, box, projectionshape, n): gradsources = zeroslike(sources) graddetectors = zeroslike(detectors) library = kernels() for start, count, group in groups(batch, GROUP): stored = brick(volume, start, count, group) packedgrad = pack(gradflat, start, count, group) groupdetectors = graddetectors if start == 0 else emptylike(detectors) kernel = library[f"conegeometrygradc{group}"] kernel(grid=grid(projectionshape), block=(32, 4, 1), args=[stored, packedgrad, sources, detectors, box, gradsources, groupdetectors, width, height, depth, projectionshape[1:], n]) if start > 0: graddetectors += groupdetectors return gradsources, graddetectors Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays R and samples n. The kernel launch overhead is minimized by batching. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for gradsources and graddetectors. This is significantly faster than the pure PyTorch implementation (37.426 ms and 50.901 ms respectively). Limitations: Requires volume to be in a specific bricked layout with a 1-voxel border; precision limited to float32 as per the arithmetic description. name: Differentiable Detector Panel Model
head: TomOpt panel model
body: The Differentiable Detector Panel Model is a hit-recording method used in muon tomography optimization (specifically within the TomOpt framework) to make detector performance metrics—spatial resolution and hit efficiency—continuous functions of the muon's position relative to the panel. It solves the problem of non-differentiability in standard binary detector models (where hits are either recorded or not, and resolution is constant or zero) by replacing step functions with smooth sigmoid transitions. This allows gradients to flow with respect to all panel parameters (position, size, and z-depth) during inverse rendering or optimization, unlike its nearest alternative, the binary rectangle model, which is only suitable for validation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Muon trajectory parameters (specifically the true intersection point xy{true} on the detector plane), panel configuration parameters (position xyz, width xy-span), and physical limits (\sigma{max}, \epsilon{max}). Outputs: Effective spatial resolution \sigma{xy,eff} and effective detection efficiency \epsilon{eff} for the hit. Data Structures: Each panel is defined by 5 learnable parameters: 1. x{pos}: Center x-coordinate. 2. y{pos}: Center y-coordinate. 3. z{pos}: Z-depth (position along beam axis). 4. w{span}: Width in x-dimension (assumed square or defined by separate x/y spans, though the text specifies "width in xy" generally, the model uses symmetric sigmoids). 5. h{span}: Height in y-dimension (implied by "width in xy" and symmetric treatment, or treated as a single span parameter if square). Note: The source specifies "width in xy" as a single learnable parameter, implying a square panel or identical scaling. Parameters: \sigma{max}: Maximum spatial resolution of the panel (fixed constant). \epsilon{max}: Maximum detection efficiency of the panel (fixed constant). xy{true}: The true coordinates of the muon's intersection with the detector plane. Method Steps: 1. Unphysical Hit Recording: During optimization, every muon is assumed to "hit" the panel at its current z position, regardless of whether the xy{true} coordinates fall within the physical boundaries of the panel. This ensures the hit count is differentiable with respect to panel position and size. 2. Panel Model Evaluation (w): Compute a weighting factor w(xy{true}) that scales between 0 and 1. This factor represents the "quality" of the hit based on its distance from the panel center. The model uses a pair of double-sigmoid functions, one for the x-dimension and one for the y-dimension. 3. Compute Effective Resolution: Calculate the effective spatial resolution using the inverse of the weighting factor: \sigma{xy,eff} = \frac{\sigma{max}}{w(xy{true})} As the muon moves away from the center, w decreases, causing \sigma{xy,eff} to increase (worsen). 4. Compute Effective Efficiency: Calculate the effective detection efficiency using the direct weighting factor: \epsilon{eff} = \epsilon{max} \cdot w(xy{true}) As the muon moves away from the center, w decreases, causing \epsilon{eff} to decrease. Formulas: The core weighting function w(xy{true}) is constructed from double-sigmoid functions. Let x{rel} = x{true} - x{pos} and y{rel} = y{true} - y{pos} be the relative coordinates. Let S{span} be the panel span (width/height). The double-sigmoid function D(u, S) for a dimension u with span S is typically defined to be 1 at u=0 and decay to 0 as |u| increases. While the exact mathematical form of the "double-sigmoid" is not explicitly expanded in the provided text, it is described as a pair of functions in x and y. Let wx(x{rel}) and wy(y{rel}) be the sigmoid values for x and y respectively. w(xy{true}) = wx(x{rel}) \cdot wy(y{rel}) The effective metrics are then: \sigma{xy,eff} = \sigma{max} \cdot \frac{1}{w(xy{true})} \epsilon{eff} = \epsilon{max} \cdot w(xy{true}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepanelmetrics(muonxytrue, panelcenter, panelspan, sigmamax, epsilonmax): """ Computes effective resolution and efficiency for a muon hit on a panel. Args: muonxytrue: Tuple (xtrue, ytrue) of the muon's intersection point. panelcenter: Tuple (xpos, ypos) of the panel's center. panelspan: Float, the width/height of the panel (assumed square). sigmamax: Float, maximum spatial resolution. epsilonmax: Float, maximum detection efficiency. Returns: sigmaeff: Float, effective spatial resolution. epsiloneff: Float, effective detection efficiency. """ # 1. Compute relative coordinates xrel = muonxytrue[0] - panelcenter[0] yrel = muonxytrue[1] - panelcenter[1] # 2. Evaluate double-sigmoid functions for x and y # Note: The exact mathematical definition of the double-sigmoid # is not provided in the source text, but it is a function D(u, S) # that returns 1 at u=0 and decays to 0 as |u| increases. # A common implementation for such smooth transitions is a # combination of sigmoids or a Gaussian-like decay. # For implementation, one must define the specific double-sigmoid function. # Here we assume a helper function doublesigmoid(u, span) exists. wx = doublesigmoid(xrel, panelspan) wy = doublesigmoid(yrel, panelspan) # 3. Compute overall weighting factor w w = wx wy # 4. Compute effective resolution # Avoid division by zero if w is extremely close to 0 if w < 1e-9: sigmaeff = float('inf') else: sigmaeff = sigmamax / w # 5. Compute effective efficiency epsiloneff = epsilonmax w return sigmaeff, epsiloneff def doublesigmoid(u, span): """ Placeholder for the specific double-sigmoid function described in. The source states it is a "pair of double-sigmoid functions" that scale between 0 and 1, reaching a maximum at the center. Typical double-sigmoid forms involve parameters for steepness. Example structure (not from source, for implementation guidance): return 0.5 (sigmoid(u + span/2) - sigmoid(u - span/2)) normalized? Or a product of two sigmoids? The source does not specify. """ # Since the exact formula is not in the source, this function must be # implemented based on the specific "double-sigmoid" definition used # in the TomOpt paper's supplementary material or code. # For the purpose of this article, we note that this function # evaluates the panel model w(xytrue). pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-trivial Derivatives: In a binary model, derivatives for xy-position and xy-span are zero or undefined because they only affect whether a hit is recorded, not the hit's properties. The differentiable model solves this by making resolution and efficiency continuous functions of position. Unphysical Hits: The model records hits for muons outside the panel. This is unphysical but necessary for gradient flow. Validation should revert to a binary model. Division by Zero: If w(xy{true}) approaches zero (muon far from panel), \sigma{xy,eff} approaches infinity. Implementation should handle this numerically (e.g., clamping or large value). Sigmoid Panel Modeling is a differentiable detector hit-recording method used in muon tomography optimization (specifically within the TomOpt framework) to make detector performance metrics—spatial resolution and hit efficiency—continuous functions of the muon's position relative to the panel. It solves the problem of non-differentiability in standard binary detector models (where hits are either recorded or not, and resolution is constant or zero) by replacing step functions with smooth sigmoid transitions. This allows gradients to flow with respect to all panel parameters (position, size, and z-depth) during inverse rendering or optimization, unlike its nearest alternative, the binary rectangle model, which is only suitable for validation. Time Complexity: O(1) per muon per panel interaction, as it involves simple arithmetic operations and sigmoid evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per panel, storing 5 learnable parameters plus fixed constants. Strengths: Enables gradient-based optimization of detector geometry (position and size) which is impossible with binary models. Provides smooth transitions for resolution and efficiency. Limitations: Unphysical (records hits outside panel). The number of panels per layer is fixed during optimization because gradients for integer variables (number of panels) are difficult to compute. When to use: During the optimization phase of detector design in TomOpt. When not to use: For final validation or simulation where physical accuracy is required; revert to binary model. The Differentiable Detector Panel Model was introduced in the TomOpt framework for differential optimization of particle detectors in muon tomography. It addresses the challenge of optimizing detector geometry (position and size) using gradient-based methods, which require differentiable objective functions. Traditional binary detector models are non-differentiable with respect to geometric parameters, preventing their use in such optimization. The method was developed to allow flexible parameterization of detectors without a priori assumptions about optimal configuration.
