name: FastFDK
head: FDK, Feldkamp-Davis-Kress, Cone-Beam FDK, FDK Algorithm, FDK Backprojection, Feldkamp-Davis-Kress backprojection
body: FastFDK is a CPU-optimized implementation of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, an analytical method for reconstructing a 3D volume from a stack of 2D cone-beam projection images. It solves the tomographic reconstruction problem by applying a specific convolution filter to weighted projections and back-projecting them into a 3D grid. It sets itself apart from its siblings by precomputing geometric weights and using a direct spatial-domain convolution filter to avoid the overhead of FFTs during the main reconstruction loop, prioritizing speed and memory locality on CPU architectures. Inputs: A stack of mid projection images of size miw x mih, and scanner geometry parameters: pixel size mps, source-to-origin distance msd, origin-to-detector distance myd, volume dimensions mvw x mvw x mvd, voxel size mvs, and angular span mna in degrees. Outputs: A 3D volume mvol of type float with dimensions mvw x mvw x mvd. Data Structures: mvol: Output volume array, size mvw mvw mvd. mcyl: Boolean mask array, size mvw mvw. mcyl[i + mvwj] is true if the voxel (i,j) lies within the cylinder defined by the volume width. mflt: Float array, size mnf = miw / 2. Stores the odd-indexed coefficients of the convolution filter. mw0: Float array, size miw mih. Precomputed initial image weighting factors. mbuf: Float array, size miw. Temporary buffer for processing image rows during filtering. mimg: Float array, size miw mih mid. Storage for all filtered projection images. Parameters: mps: Adjusted pixel size. The constructor scales the input pixel size: mps = msd / (msd + myd). mk: Filter center value, 1 / (4 mps^2). angStep: Angle step in radians, -mna MPI / (mid 180). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Clear mvol to zero. Precompute mw0: For each pixel (i, j) in the projection image: v = (m{ih}/2 - 0.5 - j) \cdot m{ps} k1 = m{sd}^2 + v^2 u = (i + 0.5 - m{iw}/2) \cdot m{ps} m{w0}[i + m{iw} \cdot j] = \frac{m{sd}}{\sqrt{u^2 + k1}} Precompute mflt: mk = \frac{1}{4 \cdot m{ps}^2} For k from 0 to mnf - 1: j = 2k + 1 tmp = \pi \cdot m{ps} \cdot j m{flt}[k] = -\frac{1}{tmp^2} Precompute mcyl: For i, j from 0 to mvw - 1: m{cyl}[i + m{vw} \cdot j] = ((2i - m{vw})^2 + (2j - m{vw})^2) < m{vw}^2 2. Filtering: For each projection image img in the input stack: For each row j from 0 to mih - 1: Copy row img[:, j] to mbuf. Apply weighting: mbuf[i] = mw0[i + miw j] for all i. Apply convolution filter to mbuf: For each pixel i from 0 to miw - 1: v0 = m{buf}[i] \cdot mk For k from 0 to mnf - 1: l = 2k + 1 If i - l >= 0: If i + l < miw: v0 += (m{buf}[i-l] + m{buf}[i+l]) \cdot m{flt}[k] Else: v0 += m{buf}[i-l] \cdot m{flt}[k] Else If i + l < miw: v0 += m{buf}[i+l] \cdot m{flt}[k] Else: Break loop. outImg[i] = v0 Store filtered row in mimg. 3. Backprojection: Initialize ang = 0. For each filtered projection img (index n from 1 to mid): Compute trigonometric values: ca = \cos(ang), sa = \sin(ang). Compute projection scaling: k1 = m{sd} / m{ps}. For each volume row j from 0 to mvw - 1: Compute vy = (m{vw}/2 - 0.5 - j) \cdot m{vs}. For each volume column i from 0 to mvw - 1: Let l = j \cdot m{vw} + i. If !mcyl[l], continue (skip voxels outside the cylinder). Compute vx = (i + 0.5 - m{vw}/2) \cdot m{vs}. Apply volume rotation: vvx = vx \cdot ca - vy \cdot sa vvy = vy \cdot ca + vx \cdot sa Compute detector projection scaling: k2 = \frac{k1}{vvy + m{sd}} Compute detector coordinates: u = vvx \cdot k2 + \frac{m{iw}}{2} - 0.5 (Note: v coordinate is computed inside the depth loop below) Compute integer indices and remainders for u: iu = \lfloor u \rfloor If u < 0, iu = iu - 1. du = u - iu For each volume depth k from 0 to mvd - 1: Compute vz = (m{vd}/2 - 0.5 - k) \cdot m{vs}. Compute detector v coordinate: v = \frac{m{ih}}{2} - vz \cdot k2 - 0.5 Compute integer indices and remainders for v: iv = \lfloor v \rfloor If v < 0, iv = iv - 1. dv = v - iv Perform bilinear interpolation of img at (iu, iv) with remainders (du, dv): val = (v1 + du \cdot (v2 - v1)) + dv \cdot ((v3 + du \cdot (v4 - v3)) - (v1 + du \cdot (v2 - v1))) Where v1 = img[iu, iv], v2 = img[iu+1, iv], v3 = img[iu, iv+1], v4 = img[iu+1, iv+1]. Out-of-bounds pixels return 0. Compute post-projection weighting: k3 = \frac{m{sd}}{m{sd} + vvy} val = val \cdot k3^2 Accumulate into volume with averaging: m\vol[i, j, k] = m\vol[i, j, k] + \frac{val - m\vol[i, j, k]}{n} Update angle: ang += angStep. 4. Normalization: For each voxel p in mvol: If |p| < \epsilon and p \neq 0, set p = 0. Else, p = p / 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fastfdkreconstruct(images, iw, ih, id, ps, yd, sd, vw, vd, vs, na): """ images: list of 2D arrays (id, ih, iw) Returns: 3D array (vd, vw, vw) """ # 1. Initialization mps = ps sd / (sd + yd) mvol = [[[0.0 for in range(vd)] for in range(vw)] for in range(vw)] # Precompute mw0 mw0 = [[0.0 for in range(iw)] for in range(ih)] for j in range(ih): v = (ih / 2 - 0.5 - j) mps k1 = sd sd + v v for i in range(iw): u = (i + 0.5 - iw / 2) mps mw0[j][i] = sd / math.sqrt(u u + k1) # Precompute mflt mnf = iw // 2 mk = 1.0 / (4.0 mps mps) mflt = [0.0] mnf for k in range(mnf): j = 2 k + 1 tmp = math.pi mps j mflt[k] = -1.0 / (tmp tmp) # Precompute mcyl mcyl = [False] (vw vw) for i in range(vw): for j in range(vw): if ((2 i - vw) 2 + (2 j - vw) 2) < (vw vw): mcyl[i + vw j] = True # 2. Filtering filteredimages = [] for img in images: filteredimg = [[0.0 for in range(iw)] for in range(ih)] for j in range(ih): # Copy row to buffer and apply weighting buf = [img[j][i] mw0[j][i] for i in range(iw)] # Apply convolution for i in range(iw): v0 = buf[i] mk for k in range(mnf): l = 2 k + 1 if i - l >= 0: if i + l < iw: v0 += (buf[i - l] + buf[i + l]) mflt[k] else: v0 += buf[i - l] mflt[k] elif i + l < iw: v0 += buf[i + l] mflt[k] else: break filteredimg[j][i] = v0 filteredimages.append(filteredimg) # 3. Backprojection angstep = -na math.pi / (id 180) ang = 0.0 for nidx, img in enumerate(filteredimages): n = nidx + 1 ca = math.cos(ang) sa = math.sin(ang) k1 = sd / mps for j in range(vw): vy = (vw / 2 - 0.5 - j) vs for i in range(vw): l = j vw + i if not mcyl[l]: continue vx = (i + 0.5 - vw / 2) vs vvx = vx ca - vy sa vvy = vy ca + vx sa k2 = k1 / (vvy + sd) # Precompute u part uval = vvx k2 + iw / 2 - 0.5 iu = int(uval) if uval < 0: iu -= 1 du = uval - iu for k in range(vd): vz = (vd / 2 - 0.5 - k) vs vval = ih / 2 - vz k2 - 0.5 iv = int(vval) if vval < 0: iv -= 1 dv = vval - iv # Bilinear Interpolation # getPixel returns 0 if out of bounds def getpixel(img, u, v): if 0 <= u < iw and 0 <= v < ih: return img[v][u] return 0.0 v1 = getpixel(img, iu, iv) v2 = getpixel(img, iu + 1, iv) v3 = getpixel(img, iu, iv + 1) v4 = getpixel(img, iu + 1, iv + 1) val = (v1 + du (v2 - v1)) + dv ((v3 + du (v4 - v3)) - (v1 + du (v2 - v1))) k3 = sd / (sd + vvy) val = k3 k3 # Accumulate mvol[j][i][k] += (val - mvol[j][i][k]) / n ang += angstep # 4. Normalization epsilon = 1e-9 # Not given in the sources. for j in range(vw): for i in range(vw): for k in range(vd): p = mvol[j][i][k] if abs(p) < epsilon and p != 0: mvol[j][i][k] = 0.0 else: mvol[j][i][k] /= 2.0 return mvol A technique that reconstructs density values and gradients at arbitrary sample points along a ray directly from 2D projections, avoiding the intermediate step of creating a 3D rectilinear grid. It sets itself apart from grid-based Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by eliminating interpolation errors associated with voxel sampling, thereby producing higher visual quality for thin structures. It builds on FastFDK by utilizing the FBP reconstruction formula not just for grid generation, but as a direct resampling scheme for arbitrary ray positions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The algorithm is computationally much less expensive than iterative algorithms, making it suitable for clinical environments. The specific FastFDK implementation optimizes for CPU cache locality by precomputing weights and using spatial convolution instead of FFTs for the ramp filter. Strengths: Fast, analytical, single-pass reconstruction. Limitations: Introduces artifacts and noise compared to iterative methods. Assumes ideal geometry and linear attenuation. When to use: When speed is critical and data quality is sufficient for analytical reconstruction (e.g., clinical CT, high-quality sinograms). When not to use: When dealing with sparse data, significant noise, or when higher accuracy via iterative refinement is required. The Filtered Backprojection (FBP) algorithm is described as the most fundamental algorithm still widely used for high-precision CT reconstructions. FastFDK is a specific CPU-based reference implementation optimized for speed using precomputed geometric weights and spatial convolution. name: Filtered Back-Projection for Volume Rendering
head: D2VR, Projection-based Volume Rendering
body: Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) for Volume Rendering, also known as D2VR, is a technique that reconstructs density values and gradients at arbitrary sample points along a ray directly from 2D projections, avoiding the intermediate step of creating a 3D rectilinear grid. It sets itself apart from grid-based Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by eliminating interpolation errors associated with voxel sampling, thereby producing higher visual quality for thin structures. It applies the FBP reconstruction formula as a direct resampling scheme for arbitrary ray positions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K filtered 2D projection images Q{\thetai}, where i \in \{1, \dots, K\}, corresponding to projection angles \thetai. Camera parameters defining ray origins and directions. Outputs: A rendered image with color and opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: Projections: A list of 1D arrays representing the filtered projection data Q{\thetai} for each angle. The values are obtained by high-pass filtering the measured projection data. Ray State: For each pixel, a ray origin O and direction D. Sample points P along the ray are defined by P(s) = O + s \cdot D. Parameters: Number of Projections (K): The total number of available views. Step Size (\Delta s): The distance between sample points along the ray. It must be less than half the voxel size of the equivalent grid to ensure accuracy. Finite Difference Step (\Delta t): A small finite value used to approximate the limit in the gradient formula. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel of the image plane, cast a ray through the volumetric space enclosed by the filtered projections. 2. Sampling: Generate sample points Pj along the ray at intervals of \Delta s. 3. Density Reconstruction: At each resample location, reconstruct the underlying 3D density value using the discrete FBP formula: \tilde{f}(x, y) = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K Q{\thetai}(ti) where ti = x \cos \thetai + y \sin \thetai is the projected coordinate of the point onto the i-th projection plane. 4. Gradient Estimation: Compute the partial derivatives \tilde{f}x and \tilde{f}y directly from the projections using Newton's difference quotient: \tilde{f}x = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta x} (Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta x \cos \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti)) \tilde{f}y = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta y \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta y} (Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta y \sin \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti)) In practice, \Delta x and \Delta y are replaced by a small finite value \Delta t. The terms \cos \thetai and \sin \thetai scale the derivative of the projection data. 5. Shading: Perform shading by estimating gradients directly on the projections and using them as surface normals. 6. Compositing: Determine the final color and opacity of the pixel using the over-operator in front-to-back order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def renderpixel(rayorigin, raydirection, projections, angles, sstart, send, stepsize): """ Renders a single pixel using Filtered Back-Projection for Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) tuple, normalized projections: List of 1D arrays Qthetai angles: List of float angles thetai in radians sstart, send: Float bounds along the ray stepsize: Float distance between samples Returns: (color, opacity) tuple """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 numproj = len(angles) scale = math.pi / numproj deltat = 1.0 # Finite difference step approximating the limit s = sstart while s <= send: x = rayorigin[0] + s raydirection[0] y = rayorigin[1] + s raydirection[1] z = rayorigin[2] + s raydirection[2] density = 0.0 gradx = 0.0 grady = 0.0 for i in range(numproj): theta = angles[i] proj = projections[i] width = len(proj) # Project 3D point to 1D detector coordinate per source formula ti = x math.cos(theta) + y math.sin(theta) idx = int(ti) if 0 <= idx < width: density += proj[idx] # Approximate limit using finite difference tplusx = ti + deltat math.cos(theta) tplusy = ti + deltat math.sin(theta) idxx = int(tplusx) idxy = int(tplusy) if 0 <= idxx < width: gradx += (proj[idxx] - proj[idx]) / deltat math.cos(theta) if 0 <= idxy < width: grady += (proj[idxy] - proj[idx]) / deltat math.sin(theta) # Scale by pi / K density = scale gradx = scale grady = scale # Shading: compute normal from gradients # Assuming gradient vector in the projection plane corresponds to surface normal components. normal = normalize((gradx, grady, 0.0)) # Simple diffuse lighting model lightdir = normalize((0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) shading = 0.2 + 0.8 diffuse # Standard transfer function: density -> color, opacity opacitysample = 1.0 - math.exp(-density 0.1) colorsample = [shading density, shading density, shading density] # Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacitysample transmittance accumulatedcolor[0] += colorsample[0] alpha accumulatedcolor[1] += colorsample[1] alpha accumulatedcolor[2] += colorsample[2] alpha transmittance = (1.0 - opacitysample) s += stepsize return accumulatedcolor, 1.0 - transmittance A method to estimate derivatives of the volumetric density function directly from filtered projections, avoiding the computational cost and interpolation errors of grid-based finite difference methods. It applies Newton's difference quotient to the filtered projection data Q{\thetai} instead of the reconstructed density function. The partial derivative \tilde{f}x is calculated as the sum of scaled derivatives of the projection data: \lim{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta x} (Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta x \cos \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti)). This approach is superior to grid-based central differences, which require 6 additional interpolated samples for a gradient, accumulating interpolation errors, whereas FBP-based estimation uses density values as accurate as grid points, introducing no interpolation error. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot N \cdot S), where K is the number of projections, N is the number of pixels, and S is the number of samples per ray. Each sample requires iterating over all K projections. Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot W \cdot H) to store the projection images. No 3D volume grid is stored in memory. Measured Performance: Tested on Marschner & Lobb function (64 projections, 64x64 resolution) and Carp dataset (128 projections, 128x256 resolution). Strengths: Higher visual quality than grid-based DVR using the same amount of pixels on all projections as voxels on the regular grid, particularly reducing holes in thin structures. Avoids interpolation errors inherent in grid-based gradient estimation. Limitations: Computationally intensive per sample due to the summation over all projections. Requires pre-filtered projections. When to use: When high-quality rendering of thin structures is required and memory for a high-resolution 3D grid is prohibitive. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the number of projections is large, as the per-sample cost is high. The method was introduced in the paper "D2VR: High-Quality Volume Rendering of Projection-based Volumetric Data". It was developed to address the limitations of grid-based volume rendering, specifically interpolation errors and memory usage. The technique leverages the mathematical properties of Filtered Back-Projection, traditionally used for tomographic reconstruction, to perform direct volume rendering. name: Gradient Estimation via Filtered Back-Projection
head: FBP-based Gradient Estimation, Gradient from Filtered Projections
body: Gradient Estimation via Filtered Back-Projection estimates the spatial derivatives of a volumetric density function directly from filtered projection data, bypassing the intermediate step of reconstructing a 3D rectilinear grid. It differs from grid-based finite difference methods by eliminating interpolation errors associated with sampling a reconstructed volume, as it computes derivatives from the continuous projection functions themselves. Inputs: K: Number of projection angles \thetai. Q{\thetai}(t): Filtered projection data for angle \thetai, where t is the detector coordinate. (x, y): 2D spatial coordinates of the evaluation point. Outputs: \tilde{f}x: Estimated partial derivative with respect to x. \tilde{f}y: Estimated partial derivative with respect to y. Data Structures: The filtered projections Q{\thetai} are stored as 1D arrays. No 3D grid is allocated for the gradient estimation itself. Steps: 1. For each projection angle i \in \{1, \dots, K\}, calculate the projection coordinate ti corresponding to (x, y): ti = x \cos \thetai + y \sin \thetai. 2. Compute the partial derivative with respect to x (\tilde{f}x) by summing the scaled derivatives of the filtered projections using Newton's difference quotient: \tilde{f}x = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta x} \left( Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta x \cos \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti) \right). 3. Compute the partial derivative with respect to y (\tilde{f}y) analogously: \tilde{f}y = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta y \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta y} \left( Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta y \sin \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti) \right). 4. Higher-order derivatives are obtained by applying the difference quotient multiple times to the projection data Q{\thetai}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleprojection(Q, t, tmin, tmax): idx = t - tmin if idx < 0 or idx >= len(Q) - 1: return Q[0] if idx < 0 else Q[-1] i = int(idx) w = idx - i return Q[i] (1 - w) + Q[i + 1] w def estimategradientfbp(x, y, angles, filteredprojections, tbounds, delta=1e-5): K = len(angles) sumfx = 0.0 sumfy = 0.0 for i in range(K): theta = angles[i] Q = filteredprojections[i] ti = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta) tx = ti + delta cos(theta) ty = ti + delta sin(theta) qbase = sampleprojection(Q, ti, tbounds[0], tbounds[1]) qx = sampleprojection(Q, tx, tbounds[0], tbounds[1]) qy = sampleprojection(Q, ty, tbounds[0], tbounds[1]) fxterm = (qx - qbase) / delta fyterm = (qy - qbase) / delta sumfx += fxterm sumfy += fyterm fx = (pi / K) sumfx fy = (pi / K) sumfy return fx, fy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The choice of \Delta x and \Delta y trades truncation error against numerical noise. A typical value is one pixel size in the projection domain. Boundaries: If ti \pm \Delta x \cos \thetai or ti \pm \Delta y \sin \thetai falls outside the projection bounds, values are clamped to the nearest edge. Degenerate Input: If \cos \thetai = 0 or \sin \thetai = 0, the coordinate shift vanishes, making the difference quotient exactly zero. An approach that estimates gradients in projection space and reconstructs them alongside the density. Gradient components parallel to the viewing direction are scaled by \cos \theta and \sin \theta. The projection space gradient is stored in RGB color channels while filtered density values occupy the alpha channel. The pipeline is formally RN((p \otimes gp) \otimes hp), where p is projection data, gp is the gradient filter in projection space, hp is the interpolation filter, and RN is the reconstruction operator. This method produces images of lower perceived definition (sharpness) compared to Gradient-from-Sampling (GFS), particularly during upsampling, because the gradient filter is applied before upsampling, potentially discarding high-frequency information. Accuracy: Expects higher accuracy than traditional grid-based gradient estimation schemes. Grid-based central differences require six additional interpolated samples for a gradient, accumulating interpolation errors. FBP-based estimation uses density values as accurate as grid points, introducing no interpolation error. Computational Cost: Avoids the computational cost of computing a large 3D neighborhood of samples, which would require a large number of backprojections, especially for higher-order gradient estimation schemes. Memory: Avoids storing a 3D rectilinear grid for gradient computation, reducing memory footprint compared to grid-based finite difference methods. This method exploits the Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) reconstruction scheme to compute derivatives directly from projection data. It was introduced in the context of Differentiable Volume Rendering (D2VR) to improve the quality of gradient-based rendering. The approach is particularly relevant for tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering, where accurate gradients are needed for optimization or high-quality visualization without the artifacts of grid interpolation. name: FDK Backprojection Transpose (Adjoint)
head: FDK Backprojection Transpose CUDA Kernel
body: The FDK Backprojection Transpose computes the adjoint of the forward FDK backprojection, scattering voxel values from a 3D volume back to 2D projection panels using the same geometric mapping and weights. It accumulates scattered values into projection buffers using atomicAdd. Inputs: volume: 3D tensor of shape [batch, 1, depth, height, width] containing voxel values. matrices: 4D tensor of shape [batch, views, 12] containing camera extrinsics (source and detector positions/orientations). projectionshape: Tuple (views, rows, columns) defining the output projection grid dimensions. box: Bounding box of the volume (used for ray clipping). Outputs: out: 4D tensor of shape [batch, 1, views, rows, columns] initialized to zero, accumulating the scattered values. Data Structures: ViewColumn: Struct containing precomputed geometric weights and ray parameters for a specific view. Stencil: Struct containing 4 indices and 4 weights for bilinear interpolation onto the projection panel. ConeRay: Struct containing ray origin, direction, and weight. Parameters: TTFDKDEPTH: 4 (number of voxels processed per thread along the z-axis). C: Channel count (typically 1 for grayscale). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Extract dimensions: batch, depth, height, width from volume.shape; views, rows, columns from projectionshape. Detach and convert matrices to contiguous float32. Create zero-initialized output tensor out of shape [batch, 1, views, rows, columns]. Get kernel function "fdkbackprojecttransposec1". 2. Kernel Launch: Iterate over each item in batch. Execute kernel with grid volumegrid((depth, height, width)), block VOLUMEBLOCK, and arguments [volume[item, 0].contiguous(), matrices, out[item, 0], width, height, depth, views, rows, columns]. 3. Kernel Execution (Per Thread): Each thread handles a block of voxels along the z-axis: z0 = blockIdx.z TTFDKDEPTH. Thread indices (x, y) map to volume coordinates. Load TTFDKDEPTH voxel values from volume at (x, y, z0...z0+3). If all loaded values are zero, skip the view loop. 4. Scatter Loop (Per View): For each view v from 0 to views-1: Compute ViewColumn parameters from matrices. For each of the TTFDKDEPTH voxels (index j): If value[j] == 0, continue. Compute detector coordinates and inverse distance scale from the ConeRay and voxel position. For each of the 4 stencil points (bilinear interpolation corners on the detector): If s.weight[q] != 0: Perform atomicAdd(out[s.index[q]], s.weight[q] value[j]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fdkbackprojecttranspose(volume, matrices, projectionshape, box): B,, D, H, W = volume.shape V, R, C = projectionshape # Initialize 5D output tensor [batch, 1, views, rows, columns] out = [[[[[0.0] C for in range(R)] for in range(V)] for in range(1)] for in range(B)] # Detach and convert matrices to contiguous float32 mats = [m.detach().float().contiguous() if hasattr(m, 'detach') else m for m in matrices] # Kernel launch logic omitted; see steps 2-3 return out def panelstencil(column, row, columns, rows, inverse): """Computes bilinear interpolation stencil indices and weights.""" if not (-1 < column < columns and -1 < row < rows): return False, None columnfloor = math.floor(column) rowfloor = math.floor(row) c0 = int(columnfloor) r0 = int(rowfloor) dc = column - columnfloor dr = row - rowfloor scale = inverse inverse wc0 = 1.0 - dc if c0 >= 0 else 0.0 wc1 = dc if c0 + 1 < columns else 0.0 wr0 = (1.0 - dr) scale if r0 >= 0 else 0.0 wr1 = dr scale if r0 + 1 < rows else 0.0 left = max(c0, 0) right = min(c0 + 1, columns - 1) top = max(r0, 0) columns bottom = min(r0 + 1, rows - 1) columns indices = [top + left, top + right, bottom + left, bottom + right] weights = [wr0 wc0, wr0 wc1, wr1 wc0, wr1 wc1] return True, (indices, weights) def threadkernellogic(x, y, z0, volume, mats, out, W, H, D, V, R, C, box): TTFDKDEPTH = 4 values = [] for k in range(TTFDKDEPTH): z = z0 + k values.append(volume[x][y][z] if z < D else 0.0) if all(v == 0.0 for v in values): return for view in range(V): # Compute ViewColumn v from mats[view] # Compute ConeRay from source/detector positions and box for j in range(TTFDKDEPTH): if values[j] == 0.0: continue # Compute detector coordinates (column, row) and inverse distance scale # from ConeRay and voxel position (x, y, z0+j) column, row, inverse = computedetectorcoords(ray, x, y, z0 + j, box) valid, stencil = panelstencil(column, row, C, R, inverse) if valid: indices, weights = stencil for q in range(4): if weights[q] != 0.0: out[0][0][view][int(indices[q] // C)][int(indices[q] % C)] += weights[q] values[j] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Multiple threads may write to the same projection pixel simultaneously, requiring atomicAdd. Numerical Precision: float32 addition is not associative, so the order of accumulation matters for numerical consistency with the forward pass. Boundary Conditions: Stencil weights are clamped to zero if the interpolated coordinate falls outside the detector bounds [0, rows) x [0, columns). Zero Voxel Skip: If all TTFDKDEPTH voxels loaded by a thread are zero, the view loop is skipped to save computation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot V \cdot R \cdot C) for the output buffer. Performance: Limited by atomic contention on high-resolution projections or large batch sizes. Strengths: Efficiently computes the adjoint for differentiable tomography. Limitations: Atomic contention reduces throughput; non-associative floating-point addition may cause precision drift. The FDK Backprojection Transpose is part of the torchtomo library by itu-biai, implementing the adjoint of the FDK (Feldkamp-Davis-Kress) projection operator for differentiable tomographic reconstruction. It was developed to support end-to-end differentiable pipelines in medical imaging and materials science. itu-biai/torchtomo, https://github.com/itu-biai/torchtomo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Coupled Optimization
body: Coupled Optimization is a tomographic reconstruction method that reconstructs fluid density and velocity fields by jointly optimizing for target image fidelity and physical transport consistency. It solves temporal incoherence in reconstruction by coupling the optimization of consecutive time steps through transport losses, significantly reducing transport error compared to forward-only reconstruction. It builds on Filtered Backprojection and Adjoint Methods by replacing analytic back-projection with iterative gradient-based updates that enforce physical advection constraints. Inputs: A sequence of n+1 frames of input images \{I0, \dots, In\}, a rendering function R, a transport operator A, and optimizer hyperparameters. Outputs: Reconstructed density fields \{\rhot\}{t=0}^F and velocity fields \{ut\}{t=0}^{F-1} for each frame t in the sequence. Data Structures: \rhot: 3D tensor representing density at time t. ut: 3D vector field tensor representing velocity at time t. L{tar}: Target image loss (e.g., MSE between rendered and input image). LA(\rho): Advection/Transport loss for density. LA(u): Advection/Transport loss for velocity. L{div}: Divergence loss for velocity (incompressibility constraint). LD: Discriminator loss (optional). Formulas: The transport loss is defined as: LA(\rho) = |A(\rho{t-1}) - \rhot|^2 This term measures the deviation between the advected previous state and the current state. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize \rho and u via ReconstructForward. 2. Iterative Optimization: For each optimization step i from 0 to n: a. Discriminator Update (Optional): If useDiscriminator is true, call UpdateDiscriminator({ρ}). b. Temporal Loop: For each time step t from 0 to F: i. Density Update: Compute gradient \nabla\rho of L{total} = L{tar} + LA(\rho) + LD with respect to \rho. Update \rhot using Adam optimizer. Clip negative densities: \rho \leftarrow \max(\rho, 0). ii. Velocity Update: Compute gradient \nablau of L{total} = LA(\rho) + LA(u) + L{div} with respect to u. Update u using Adam optimizer. Enforce boundary condition: u{F-1} \leftarrow A(u{F-2}, u{F-2}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CoupledOptimization(frames, renderfunc, transportop, n, F, usediscriminator=False): # 1. Initialize via forward reconstruction rho, u = ReconstructForward(frames) optrho = AdamOptimizer(rho) optu = AdamOptimizer(u) optdisc = AdamOptimizer(Discriminator()) if usediscriminator else None historybuffer = [] for i in range(n + 1): for t in range(F + 1): # Density update lossrho = ComputeTargetLoss(rho[t], frames[t]) if t > 0: lossrho += ComputeTransportLoss(rho[t-1], rho[t]) if usediscriminator: lossrho += ComputeDiscriminatorLoss(rho[t]) UpdateDensity(rho[t], lossrho, optrho) # Velocity update lossu = 0.0 if t > 0: lossu += ComputeTransportLoss(rho[t-1], rho[t]) lossu += ComputeTransportLoss(u[t-1], u[t]) lossu += ComputeDivergenceLoss(u[t]) UpdateVelocity(u, lossu, optu) # Optional discriminator update if usediscriminator: UpdateDiscriminator(rho, renderfunc, historybuffer, optdisc) def UpdateDensity(rhot, loss, opt): gradrho = ComputeGradient(loss, rhot) opt.step(gradrho) rhot = [max(v, 0) for v in rhot] # Clip negative density def UpdateVelocity(u, loss, opt): gradu = ComputeGradient(loss, u) opt.step(gradu) u[F-1] = transportop(u[F-2], u[F-2]) # Boundary condition def UpdateDiscriminator(rho, renderfunc, historybuffer, optdisc): realsamples = SampleRealImages() # Ir ~ R fakesamples = [renderfunc(r) for r in rho] # I^f <- R(ρ, L, f) historybuffer.extend(fakesamples) # history <- history ◦ I^f historysamples = SampleFromBuffer(historybuffer) # I^h ~ history allsamples = realsamples + historysamples lossdisc = ComputeDiscriminatorLoss(allsamples) # LD(ρ, 1) optdisc.step(ComputeGradient(lossdisc, optdisc)) def ComputeGradient(loss, var): return torch.autograd.grad(loss, var, retaingraph=True)[0] def ComputeTargetLoss(rendered, target): return torch.mean((rendered - target) 2) def ComputeTransportLoss(prev, curr): return torch.mean((prev - curr) 2) def ComputeDivergenceLoss(u): return torch.mean(torch.abs(torch.div(u, u.shape[-1]))) # Simplified divergence proxy def ComputeDiscriminatorLoss(samples): return torch.mean(torch.log(torch.sigmoid(samples))) # Standard GAN discriminator loss Parameters: n: Number of global optimization iterations. F: Number of time steps. usediscriminator: Boolean flag to enable discriminator training. batchsize: 8 real samples and 4 rendered fake samples for discriminator training. Edge Cases: Negative Density: Densities must be non-negative; clipping is applied after every update. Temporal Boundaries: Velocity at the final frame F-1 is updated using the transport operator on previous velocity states. Index Bounds: Transport loss is only computed for t > 0 to avoid out-of-bounds access at the sequence start. A variant that activates multi-scale reconstruction during the coupled optimization phase. It improves the reconstruction of larger structures but increases transport error compared to the standard coupled version. Accuracy: Coupled Optimization (C) improves transport accuracy to approximately 25% of the error of the forward-only version. Trade-offs: Standard Coupled Optimization balances density error and transport accuracy. Multi-Scale Coupled Optimization trades increased transport error for better reconstruction of large structures. Performance: The method involves iterative gradient updates for both density and velocity, making it computationally more expensive than analytic methods. Limitations: The method is sensitive to the choice of transport operator A and the balance between L{tar} and physical losses. Coupled Optimization was introduced in the context of global transport for fluid reconstruction with learned self-supervision. It builds upon forward reconstruction methods by adding temporal coupling via transport losses. name: Motion Compensation and Dynamic Reconstruction
head: Dynamic Tomography, Motion-Aware Reconstruction
body: This family addresses the degradation of tomographic reconstruction quality caused by object motion during data acquisition, which manifests as motion blur or streak artifacts. Unlike static reconstruction methods that assume a rigid volume, these methods jointly estimate the 3D volume structure and the temporal displacement field (or motion blur kernel) from time-resolved or coded projection data. They are distinguished from siblings like Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods by explicitly modeling the kinematic state of the object, and from Differentiable CT Execution Model by incorporating specific physical motion models (displacement fields or coded exposure integrals) into the differentiable forward operator. All methods in this family extend the standard inverse rendering formulation by introducing motion parameters m into the forward projection operator \mathcal{P}. The optimization problem becomes: \min{x, m} \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x, m), p) + \lambda R(x) + \mu Rm(m) where x is the volume, m represents motion (displacement field or blur code), and Rm is a motion regularizer. The gradient with respect to the volume and motion parameters is computed via the chain rule through the differentiable forward projection \mathcal{P} and its adjoint \mathcal{P}^T. The core challenge is the coupling between x and m, often requiring staggered or alternating optimization strategies to decouple the volume update from the motion update. DynTomo is a staggered iterative method for reconstructing deforming 3D volumes from 2D projection data acquired over time, simultaneously identifying the full 2D space-time displacement field [7376-dynamic-tomographic-reconstruction-with-motion-identificatio.md]. It solves the problem of motion artifacts in tomography by alternating between algebraic volume reconstruction (DynART) and projection-based digital volume correlation (PDVC) for motion identification [7376-dynamic-tomographic-reconstruction-with-motion-identificatio.md]. Unlike standard Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) which produce blurry or split reconstructions under large displacements, DynTomo corrects for motion to yield sharp edges and accurate gray levels [7376-dynamic-tomographic-reconstruction-with-motion-identificatio.md]. It builds on Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering by incorporating a parametric displacement model into the optimization loop [7376-dynamic-tomographic-reconstruction-with-motion-identificatio.md]. CodEx is a modular framework for joint temporal de-blurring and tomographic reconstruction that inverts motion blur introduced in sparse-view fly-scanning by encoding acquisition with a known binary code and using a non-convex Bayesian reconstruction algorithm [18912-codex.md]. It differs from linear deconvolution methods by handling sparse view sampling without aliasing issues, and differs from previous iterative methods like DynTomo by not requiring dense view samples [18912-codex.md]. A technique using a template RGBα volume T(\mathbf{x}) and a warp volume W^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) to alter effective voxel resolution and model motion, where W^{-1} maps output positions to template sample locations. Compute final volume value: First evaluate the value of the inverse warp W^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), then sample the template volume T at the resulting warped point. Formally: \mathbf{V}{\text{RGB}\alpha}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{T}{\text{RGB}\alpha}(\mathbf{W}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) where \mathbf{x} is a 3D point in the output (rendering) space and the result is a 3D point in the RGBα template space. Forward warps cannot represent resolution-increasing transformations without additional memory; inverse warps map small output areas to larger template areas, allowing higher resolution details while remaining well-defined everywhere for usable gradients. The problem of motion artifacts in tomography has long been recognized, particularly in dynamic imaging scenarios such as cardiac CT or industrial fly-scanning. Traditional approaches often rely on gating or assuming rigid body motion. The integration of differentiable rendering with motion compensation allows for end-to-end learning of dynamic structures. The concept of using warping fields for dynamic volume representation was notably introduced in the context of neural rendering, where inverse warps are used to model non-rigid deformations and resolution changes. More recently, specific algorithms like DynTomo and CodEx have adapted these principles to physical tomographic reconstruction, addressing the ill-posed nature of joint volume-motion estimation through parametric basis functions and coded exposure models, respectively. Neural Volumes: Learning Dynamic Renderable Volumes from Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07751, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction with Motion Identification (DynTomo)
head: DynART, DynTomo, Dynamic ART-P-DVC, Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction with Displacement Field Identification, Dynamic Tomography, Dynamic reconstruction algorithm, PDVC
body: DynTomo is a staggered iterative method for reconstructing deforming 3D volumes from 2D projection data acquired over time, simultaneously identifying the full 2D space-time displacement field. It solves the problem of motion artifacts in tomography by alternating between algebraic volume reconstruction (DynART) and projection-based digital volume correlation (PDVC) for motion identification. Unlike standard Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) which produce blurry or split reconstructions under large displacements, DynTomo corrects for motion to yield sharp edges and accurate gray levels. It builds on Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering by incorporating a parametric displacement model into the optimization loop. Inputs: p(r, \theta, t): Acquired sinogram (projections) at detector coordinates r, angles \theta, and time steps t \in \{1, \dots, Nt\}. Nt: Number of time steps (projections). N\theta: Number of angles. N{scale}: Number of multiscale levels. \epsilon: Convergence threshold for inner loops. Basis functions: N\tau time functions \phii(t) and Ns spatial shape functions \Phij(x). Outputs: f(x): Reconstructed reference volume. u(x, t): Space-time displacement field. Data Structures: Displacement Field Parametrization: The displacement field is represented as a linear combination of basis functions: u(x, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N\tau} \sum{j=1}^{Ns} \alpha{ij} \phii(t) \Phij(x) where \alpha{ij} are the amplitude coefficients. The reference state is defined at t=0 such that u(x, 0) = 0, implying \phii(0) = 0. Spatial Basis: \Phij(x) are composed of C^4 mesh elements (4-node square elements with bilinear interpolation). In the source tests, Ns = 18 degrees of freedom. Time Basis: \phii(t) are time functions. In the source tests, N\tau = 2. Gaussian Kernel: Defined as G\lambda(r) = \frac{1}{2\pi\lambda^2} \exp\left(-\frac{|r|^2}{2\lambda^2}\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def DynTomo(p, Nt, Ntheta, Nscale, eps, Ntau, Ns, phi, Phi): # p: sinogram array [Ntheta, Nt, H, W] # phi: time basis functions [Ntau] # Phi: spatial basis functions [Ns] u = zeros(volumeshape + (Nt,)) # Displacement field u(x, t) for i in range(Nscale, -1, -1): lam = 2i # Convolve recorded projections with Gaussian kernel Glam = (1/(2pilam2)) exp(-rnorm2 / (2lam2)) pcheck = convolve(p, Glam) rho = pcheck.copy() Residual = 1 + eps # Force first loop while Residual > eps: # 1. Volume Reconstruction (DynART) f = DynART(pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps) # 2. Motion Identification (PDVC) u = PDVC(f, pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps, Ntau, Ns, phi, Phi) # 3. Scale Residual Update rhoold = rho.copy() fwarped = warp(f, u) rho = pcheck - forwardprojection(fwarped) Residual = norm(rho - rhoold) return f, u def DynART(pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps): f = zeros(volumeshape) n = 1 perm = permutation(Nt) # Permutation over acquisition times for in range(60): # NDynART iterations for tidx in range(Nt): tau = perm[tidx] # Warp volume to current time ftilde = warp(f, u[:, tau]) # Forward projection proj = forwardprojection(ftilde, theta=tau) # Residual rho = pcheck[:, tau] - proj # Backprojection dftilde = backprojection(rho, theta=tau) # Unwarp update to reference space df = warp(dftilde, -u[:, tau]) # Update volume with normalization factor Δf̃ from source f = f + df / max(dftilde) # Apply constraints (e.g., positivity) f = clip(f, 0, None) n += 1 return f def PDVC(f, pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps, Ntau, Ns, phi, Phi): u0 = u.copy() # Initialize residual fwarped = warp(f, u) rhoold = pcheck - forwardprojection(fwarped) Progress = 1 + eps while Progress > eps: fwarped = warp(f, u) rho = pcheck - forwardprojection(fwarped) Progress = norm(rho - rhoold) # Sensitivity computation H = zeros((Ntau Ns, Ntau Ns)) b = zeros(Ntau Ns) for i in range(Ntau): for j in range(Ns): # Compute projected sensitivities over all r, t chij = zeroslike(pcheck) for tidx in range(Nt): gradf = gradient(fwarped[:, tidx]) chij[:, tidx] = forwardprojection(Phi[j] gradf, theta=tidx) Sij = phi[i] chij # Sij(r, t) = phii(t) chij # Assemble Hessian and second member for k in range(Ntau): for l in range(Ns): chik = zeroslike(pcheck) for tidx in range(Nt): gradf = gradient(fwarped[:, tidx]) chik[:, tidx] = forwardprojection(Phi[l] gradf, theta=tidx) Skl = phi[k] chik H[iNs + j, kNs + l] = sum(Sij Skl) b[iNs + j] = sum(rho Sij) # Solve linear system [H]δα = b deltaalpha = solve(H, b) # Update displacement field u = u + reshape(deltaalpha, (Ntau, Ns)) outer(phi, Phi) rhoold = rho.copy() return u Parameters: Convergence Threshold \epsilon: Stops inner loops when residual or progress drops below this value. Basis Functions: N\tau time functions and Ns spatial shape functions. Reference state u(x, 0)=0 implies \phii(0)=0. Iterations: The source tests used 60 complete iterations per reconstruction cycle. Gaussian Kernel Width: Starts large (\lambda = 2^{N{scale}}), progressively reduced by a factor of two at each scale level. Pitfalls: Motion Regularization: Rapid variations in the displacement field can cause ill-conditioning. Weak regularization penalizes spatial/temporal variations; strong regularization uses smooth basis functions. Optical Flow Assumption: The base implementation assumes constant optical flow and does not model gray level variations. Sensitivity Bottleneck: Sensitivity computation requires deformed volumes over the entire time range, making it the computational bottleneck. Complexity: The bottleneck is the computation of sensitivity fields, which requires projecting deformed volumes over the entire time range for every PDVC iteration. Performance: In tests with 512×512 pixel images and 300 projections, 60 iterations took approximately 1 hour. The checkerboard test (38 degrees of freedom) took approximately 2 hours. Accuracy: Shepp-Logan test (max displacement 37 pixels, 27% strain): Displacement error standard deviation of 3.10 pixels after 60 iterations. Checkerboard test (max strain ~25%): Displacement error standard deviation < 1.2 pixel after 60 iterations. Strengths: Produces sharp edges and correct gray levels even with large displacements, unlike standard ART which produces blurry reconstructions with split parts. Limitations: Assumes constant optical flow; not robust to gray level variations without extension. Computationally expensive due to sensitivity calculation. Usage: Applicable to in situ mechanical tests, synchrotron beam-lines, and data assimilation. DynTomo was introduced in 2018 by. It is derived from Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) coupled with Projection-based Digital Volume Correlation (P-DVC). The method was designed to handle large displacements and strains in dynamic tomography, such as those found in in situ mechanical testing. It was tested on numerical phantoms (Shepp-Logan and checkerboard) with parallel projection geometry. Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction of Deforming Volumes, https://doi.org/10.3390/ma11081395, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CodEx
head: CodEx Reconstruction Parameters, CodEx partial update settings, Coded Exposure Tomography, Joint Temporal De-blurring and Tomographic Reconstruction
body: CodEx is a modular framework for joint temporal de-blurring and tomographic reconstruction that inverts motion blur introduced in sparse-view fly-scanning by encoding acquisition with a known binary code and using a non-convex Bayesian reconstruction algorithm. It differs from linear deconvolution methods by handling sparse view sampling without aliasing issues, and differs from previous iterative methods like DynTomo by not requiring dense view samples. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Coded projection measurements \bar{y} (vector of photon counts), the binary code c, the blur angle \Delta \theta, the number of micro-projections K, and the system geometry defining the forward projection operator A. Output: Reconstructed image x. Data Structures: Binary Code c: A vector [c0, c1, \dots, c{K-1}] where ck \in \{0, 1\}. Coded Sum Matrix C: A sparse matrix C \in \mathbb{R}^{M\theta Md \times N\theta Md} that performs the coded sum. Each row sums to 1. Forward Projection Operator A: A \in \mathbb{R}^{N\theta Md \times N}, where N\theta is the number of unique micro-projection angles, Md is the number of detector pixels, and N is the number of image voxels. Photon Flux \lambda0: Scalar representing the photon-flux per unit rotation angle. Formulas: The expected photon counts for a standard boxcar exposure (no coding) at angle \theta0 are: \bar{\Lambda}{boxcar} = \Lambda0 \int{\theta0}^{\theta0 + \Delta \theta} \exp \{-A\theta x\} d\theta where A\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{Md \times N} is the forward projection operator at angle \theta. Discrete approximation over K micro-projection angles: \bar{\lambda}{boxcar} = \lambda0 \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \exp \left\{ -A{\theta0 + k\frac{\Delta \theta}{K}} x \right\} where K is the number of closely spaced angles (micro-projections). Expected photon counts with coded exposure: \bar{\lambda}{\theta0} = \lambda0 \sum{k=0}^{K-1} ck \exp \left\{ -A{\theta0 + k\frac{\Delta \theta}{K}} x \right\} where c = [c0, c1, \dots, c{K-1}] is the binary code. Vectorized coded measurement model for all M\theta angles: \bar{\lambda} = \bar{c} \lambda0 C \exp \{-Ax\} where \bar{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^{M\theta Md} is the vector of expected photon counts, \bar{c} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} ck is the normalizing constant, and C is normalized such that each row sums to 1. Parameters: K: Number of micro-projection angles used to discretize the blur integration range \Delta \theta. \Delta \theta: The blur-angle, representing the range of projection angles over which the detector integrates photons during a single view acquisition. c: The binary code vector. Partial update iterations: np = 5 iterations for computing the deblurring step \tilde{F}d, and nt = 5 iterations for computing the reconstruction step \tilde{F}t. Algorithm Steps: The reconstruction uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to split the inverse problem into iterative deblurring and reconstruction sub-problems. 1. Initialization: Initialize the image estimate x, auxiliary variables z (for deblurring), and Lagrange multipliers u. 2. Iterate until convergence: a. Deblurring Step (\tilde{F}d): Update z by solving a non-linear deblurring problem that inverts the coded exposure model. This step uses np = 5 partial updates. b. Reconstruction Step (\tilde{F}t): Update x by solving a Model Based Iterative Reconstruction (MBIR) problem using the updated z. This step uses nt = 5 partial updates. c. Multiplier Update: Update the Lagrange multipliers u based on the difference between x and z. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def codexreconstruction(y, c, lambda0, C, A, K, np=5, nt=5, maxiter=100): """ y: observed photon counts (vector) c: binary code vector [c0,..., c{K-1}] lambda0: photon flux per unit angle C: coded sum sparse matrix A: forward projection operator K: number of micro-projections np: partial updates for deblurring nt: partial updates for reconstruction """ # Initialize variables x = zeros(N) # Image estimate z = zeros(Mtheta Md) # Auxiliary variable for deblurring u = zeros(Mtheta Md) # Lagrange multipliers # Precompute normalizing constant cbar = sum(c) for iter in range(maxiter): # Step 1: Deblurring Update (Ftilded) # Solve for z given x and u. This involves inverting the coded blur. # The sources specify np partial updates for this step. # The deblurring problem is non-linear due to the Poisson statistics and coded model. # We approximate the inverse of the coded blur operator. # Initialize z for partial updates zcurrent = z for p in range(np): # Compute expected measurements for current x # exp(-Ax) is the transmission transmission = exp(-A @ x) # Apply coded sum matrix C # C performs the coded sum over micro-projections codedtransmission = C @ transmission # Expected counts lambdaexpected = cbar lambda0 codedtransmission # Update z using a gradient-like step or proximal operator # The specific non-linear deblurring operation is not detailed in the sources # but is implied to be part of the ADMM split. # Standard ADMM deblurring step often involves solving: # minz ||y - lambdaexpected||^2 + rho/2 ||z - x + u||^2 # However, the non-linear nature requires iterative sub-steps. # We assume a simplified gradient descent for the deblurring part # for the purpose of this implementation sketch. residual = y - lambdaexpected # Update z based on residual and coupling with x zcurrent = zcurrent + alpha (residual + u) # alpha is a step size z = zcurrent # Step 2: Reconstruction Update (Ftildet) # Solve for x given z and u. This is an MBIR step. # The sources specify nt partial updates for this step. xcurrent = x for t in range(nt): # MBIR typically minimizes a data fidelity term plus a regularizer # Data fidelity: ||z - A @ x||^2 (assuming linearized model for this step) # Regularizer: e.g., Total Variation (TV) or similar prior # Standard MBIR update involves solving a convex optimization problem. # We use a simplified gradient step for the data fidelity part. residualrecon = z - A @ xcurrent # Update x xcurrent = xcurrent + beta (A.T @ residualrecon) # beta is a step size # Apply regularizer proximal operator (e.g., TV denoising) # Assuming a generic denoising function denoise(x) xcurrent = denoise(xcurrent) x = xcurrent # Step 3: Multiplier Update u = u + (x - z) return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Linear deconvolution as a preprocessing step fails for sparse view sampling because it cannot fully correct the aliasing introduced by sparse sampling. Fast-rotation fly-scanning causes each view to be acquired over a significant blur angle, leading to blurry reconstructions if conventional reconstruction methods are used. Modulating the photon flux results in loss of photons compared to the boxcar case, but many more photons are collected relative to the step-and-shoot case. Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction with Motion Identification. Uses motion identification to handle dynamic scenes. Choose when motion is complex and needs explicit identification rather than just de-blurring. DynTomo Time Complexity: The method uses ADMM with partial updates (np=5, nt=5) per iteration, making it practical to implement compared to full iterative solutions. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the sparse matrix C and the forward projection operator A. Performance: CodEx produces sharp reconstructions even with large blur angles (e.g., 40.17^\circ) where MBIR produces blurry images. It outperforms MBIR on coded exposures by jointly solving for deblurring and reconstruction. Strengths: Handles sparse view sampling without aliasing; modular framework; effective for fast-rotation fly-scanning. Limitations: Requires a known binary code for acquisition; non-linear reconstruction is computationally intensive compared to linear methods. When to use: When using fast-rotation fly-scanning with sparse views and motion blur is a significant issue. When not to use: When dense view sampling is available and linear deconvolution is sufficient, or when the acquisition system cannot modulate the X-ray flux with a known code. CodEx was introduced in a paper by the authors of in 2021. It addresses the problem of motion blur in sparse-view fly-scanning CT. Previous methods like linear deconvolution or iterative methods like Cant et al. and Ching et al. required dense view sampling. CodEx combines a novel coded exposure acquisition method with a non-convex Bayesian reconstruction algorithm using ADMM. It has been demonstrated on simulated and binned experimental data. name: Regularization and Constraints
body: This family encompasses methods that impose structural, physical, or statistical priors on the volume representation during tomographic reconstruction or inverse rendering to resolve ambiguities inherent in limited or noisy data. While the parent framework Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering defines the differentiable forward projection \mathcal{P} and the optimization loop, these methods introduce specific terms R(x) into the loss function to guide the solution toward physically plausible or geometrically consistent results. They differ from standard iterative solvers by explicitly encoding domain knowledge—such as surface normal continuity, visual hull boundaries, or information-theoretic entropy—rather than relying solely on data fidelity and generic smoothness. All methods in this family extend the core optimization problem defined in the parent article by adding regularization terms to the loss function \mathcal{L}: \minx \mathcal{L}{data}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \sumj \lambdaj Rj(x) where \mathcal{L}{data} measures the discrepancy between measured projections p and rendered projections \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x), and Rj(x) are specific regularizers with associated weights \lambdaj. The gradient computation follows the chain rule provided in the parent article, but the regularizers Rj(x) often require custom gradient implementations or auxiliary variables (e.g., surface normals, entropy distributions) that are differentiable with respect to the volume parameters x. Weighted Prior Based Reconstruction uses spatially varying weights to moderate the influence of prior template volumes in longitudinal scans. Unlike standard prior-based methods that apply constant weights, this method computes a discrepancy-based weight matrix W to suppress prior dominance in regions with new structures while preserving prior information in unchanged regions. It is chosen when reconstructing changes in a known scene using high-quality prior templates. FreeNeRF improves sparse-view NeRF rendering by applying frequency regularization to control visible input frequencies and penalizing high-density regions near the camera to reduce floating artifacts. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on sparse datasets with minimal architectural changes. It is chosen when training NeRFs with very few views (2–10) to prevent overfitting to high-frequency noise and floating geometry. InfoNeRF is an information-theoretic regularizer that minimizes reconstruction inconsistency by imposing an entropy constraint on the density distribution along rays and an information gain reduction loss between neighboring viewpoints. It addresses noise in few-shot settings and degenerate overfitting to redundant views. It is chosen when novel view synthesis suffers from artifacts due to insufficient viewpoints or when training data contains redundant, similar viewpoints. Per-voxel Per-material Offset Regularization introduces continuous, per-voxel, per-material offset parameters to absorb local density variations and measurement errors in discrete volume reconstruction. It solves the problem of overlapping attenuation ranges caused by fabrication artifacts (e.g., in 3D-printed phantoms), allowing crisp material boundaries despite local density variations. It is chosen for discrete CT reconstruction of objects with known materials but uncertain local attenuation coefficients. An adaptive constraint that ensures continuity of estimated surface normals in flat regions while preserving sharp features by weighting the normal difference based on albedo similarity. It is used in implicit NeRF geometry reconstruction to reduce high-frequency noise on continuous surfaces without blurring structural boundaries. Definition: The normal smoothness loss L{normalSM} encourages adjacent surface normals to be similar, but weakens this constraint when local albedo differences indicate an edge. Steps: 1. Sample a perturbed point by adding uniform noise in the normalized 3D space with magnitude 0.01 to generate the neighbor point for N{near}. 2. Compute the edge-aware weight mask Mi from the albedo color difference \tau = \| ci - cj \|2. If \tau \le \taun = 0.15, set Mi = 1.0; otherwise, set Mi = 0.05. Formula: L{normalSM} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} Mi \cdot \| N{pi} - N{near} \| where N{pi} is the surface normal at point p, N{near} is the normal at a randomly perturbed neighboring point, and Mi is the edge-aware weight mask. Parameters: \gamma{sm}: Weight for the normal smoothness term in the final objective function. Selected from \{0.001, 0.005, 0.01\}. Pitfalls: Over-smoothing across edges: Without the mask Mi, the constraint would undesirably smooth across structural breaks like roofs or walls. The mask weakens the constraint when local albedo differences indicate an edge. A hard constraint restricting density to the visual hull H constructed from target views to avoid residual density and tomography artifacts in outer regions. It is used in fluid or object reconstruction to constrain the solution space to plausible shapes defined by the input views. Definition: The density \rho is restricted to the visual hull H using a Heaviside step function H(\cdot), ensuring that no density exists outside the region visible from all target cameras. Steps: 1. For single-view reconstruction, construct the hull using auxiliary image hulls created by rotating the original view around a symmetry axis of the physical setup. 2. Allow free motions via Neumann boundary conditions for velocity u in inflow regions. Formula: The visual hull Ht is constructed by projecting the binary mask of the target image I{ct} back into the volume: Ht:= \bigcap{c \in C} R^{-1}(H(I{ct} - \epsilon), c) where R^{-1} is the back-projection operator, H is the Heaviside step function, and \epsilon is a threshold. The total loss includes a term that penalizes density outside Ht. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Single-view ambiguity: The auxiliary hull from rotation is not physically correct but constrains the solution to plausible shapes, potentially introducing biases if the symmetry assumption is violated. Regularization and constraints in volume rendering and tomography have evolved from simple Tikhonov regularization to complex, learnable, and physically informed priors. Early methods focused on global smoothness (Total Variation) to handle noise. With the advent of differentiable rendering and neural representations, regularization has become more granular, incorporating frequency domain constraints (FreeNeRF), information-theoretic measures (InfoNeRF), and physical constraints like visual hulls and transport equations. The integration of prior templates with adaptive weighting allows for longitudinal analysis, while per-material offsets address real-world manufacturing imperfections. These methods are widely used in medical imaging, remote sensing (DSM reconstruction), and computational photography. name: Weighted Prior Based Reconstruction
head: Tomographic Reconstruction to Detect New Structures, Weighted Prior
body: Weighted Prior Based Reconstruction is a tomographic reconstruction method that uses spatially varying weights to moderate the local influence of prior templates, allowing for the detection and accurate reconstruction of new structures in longitudinal scans while suppressing prior dominance in unchanged regions. Unlike existing prior-based methods that impose an inflexible constant weight, this method computes regional weights that temper the role of priors, preventing the suppression of new features in the test object. Inputs: y: Measured tomographic projections of the test volume. \{Qi\}{i=1}^L: A set of L high-quality prior template volumes. \Phi: Matrix modelling the measurement geometry (projection operator). \Psi: Basis in which data is assumed to be sparse. \lambda1, \lambda2: Tunable weights for sparsity and prior terms. k: Scaling constant for the weight function. Outputs: x: The reconstructed volume. W: Spatially varying weight matrix. Data Structures: x: 3D volume array. W: 3D volume array of same dimensions as x, containing scalar weights. \theta: Sparse coefficient vector such that x = \Psi \theta. \alpha: Eigen-coefficient vector for the prior subspace. \mu: Mean vector of the template set. Vi: i-th principal component (eigenvector) of the template set. Formulas: The reconstruction minimizes the energy function: E(\theta, \alpha) = \|\Phi x - y\|2^2 + \lambda1 \|\theta\|1 + \lambda2 \|W (x - (\mu + \sumi \alphai Vi))\|2^2 where x = \Psi \theta. The unknowns \theta and \alpha are solved via alternate minimization. \theta is solved using a basis pursuit Compressed Sensing (CS) solver. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preliminary Test Reconstruction: Perform a preliminary reconstruction X{fdk} of the test volume using the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm on the measured projections y. 2. Compute Low-Quality Template Volumes: a. For each template Qi (i=1 \dots L), generate simulated measurements y{Qi} using the exact same projection views and imaging geometry as the test measurements y. b. Perform preliminary FDK reconstructions of each template Qi from its simulated measurements y{Qi}. Let this set be denoted by \{Yi^{fdk}\}{i=1}^L. 3. Build Primary Eigenspace: Build an eigenspace E{low}^{fdk} from the set \{Yi^{fdk}\}{i=1}^L. Let P^{fdk} denote the projection of the preliminary test reconstruction X{fdk} onto E{low}^{fdk}. 4. Multi-Method Pilot Reconstructions: a. Perform pilot reconstructions of the test volume using M different reconstruction algorithms. Let this set be denoted as \{Xj\}{j=1}^M, where X1 = X{fdk}. b. For each template Qi and each reconstruction algorithm j (j=1 \dots M), perform a reconstruction of Qi using the simulated measurements y{Qi}. Let this set be denoted by \{Y{ij}\}{j=1}^M for each i, where Y{i1} = Yi^{fdk}. c. For each reconstruction algorithm j, build an eigenspace E{low}^j from the set of reconstructed templates \{Y{1j}, Y{2j}, \dots, Y{Lj}\}. d. For each algorithm j, project the pilot test reconstruction Xj onto E{low}^j. Let this projection be denoted by P^j. 5. Compute Discrepancy: To remove reconstruction-method-dependent false positives, compute the minimum absolute difference across all methods for each voxel (x, y, z): D(x, y, z) = \minj |Xj(x, y, z) - P^j(x, y, z)| 6. Compute Weight Matrix: Calculate the weight W(x, y, z) for each voxel coordinate using the discrepancy D(x, y, z): W(x, y, z) = (1 + k \cdot D(x, y, z))^{-1} Regions with high discrepancy (potential new structures) receive lower weights, reducing prior influence. Regions with low discrepancy (unchanged) receive weights closer to 1, allowing prior dominance. 7. Final Reconstruction: Solve the optimization problem E(\theta, \alpha) using the computed weight matrix W to obtain the final volume x. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.linalg import svd def weightedpriorreconstruction(y, templatesQ, Phi, Psi, lambda1, lambda2, k, Mmethods): """ y: measured projections of test volume templatesQ: list of L template volumes Phi: projection matrix Psi: sparsity basis matrix lambda1, lambda2: regularization weights k: weight scaling constant Mmethods: list of reconstruction functions, Mmethods[0] is FDK """ L = len(templatesQ) # Step 1: Preliminary test reconstruction using FDK Xfdk = Mmethods0 # Step 2: Compute low-quality template volumes using FDK Yfdklist = [] for Qi in templatesQ: # Simulate measurements for template using same geometry yQi = Phi @ Qi.flatten() # Reconstruct template from simulated measurements Yifdk = Mmethods0 Yfdklist.append(Yifdk) # Step 3: Build eigenspace from low-quality templates # Flatten templates for PCA Yfdkmatrix = np.array([Y.flatten() for Y in Yfdklist]) # Center data Yfdkmean = np.mean(Yfdkmatrix, axis=0) Yfdkcentered = Yfdkmatrix - Yfdkmean # Compute eigenspace (using SVD for stability) U, S, Vt = svd(Yfdkcentered, fullmatrices=False) # Use all components or a subset; sources imply full space spanned by templates Elowfdk = Vt.T # Project Xfdk onto eigenspace Xfdkflat = Xfdk.flatten() Xfdkcentered = Xfdkflat - Yfdkmean Pfdkflat = Elowfdk @ (Elowfdk.T @ Xfdkcentered) Pfdk = Pfdkflat.reshape(Xfdk.shape) # Step 4: Multi-method pilot reconstructions Xpilots = [] Ypilots = [] # List of lists: Ypilots[i][j] is template i reconstructed by method j for j, reconfunc in enumerate(Mmethods): # 4a: Reconstruct test volume Xj = reconfunc(y) Xpilots.append(Xj) Ypilotsj = [] for i, Qi in enumerate(templatesQ): yQi = Phi @ Qi.flatten() Yij = reconfunc(yQi) Ypilotsj.append(Yij) Ypilots.append(Ypilotsj) # 4c: Build eigenspace for method j Ypilotsjmatrix = np.array([Y.flatten() for Y in Ypilotsj]) Ypilotsjmean = np.mean(Ypilotsjmatrix, axis=0) Ypilotsjcentered = Ypilotsjmatrix - Ypilotsjmean Uj, Sj, Vtj = svd(Ypilotsjcentered, fullmatrices=False) Elowj = Vtj.T # 4d: Project Xj onto eigenspace j Xjflat = Xj.flatten() Xjcentered = Xjflat - Ypilotsjmean Pjflat = Elowj @ (Elowj.T @ Xjcentered) Pj = Pjflat.reshape(Xj.shape) Xpilots[j] = Xj # Store for later use if needed, but we need Pj # We need to store Pj for step 5. Let's store it in a list. # Note: The pseudocode structure above modifies Xpilots but we need Pj. # Let's restructure slightly to keep Pj. # Re-run Step 4d properly to collect Pj Ppilots = [] for j, reconfunc in enumerate(Mmethods): Xj = Xpilots[j] Ypilotsj = Ypilots[j] Ypilotsjmatrix = np.array([Y.flatten() for Y in Ypilotsj]) Ypilotsjmean = np.mean(Ypilotsjmatrix, axis=0) Ypilotsjcentered = Ypilotsjmatrix - Ypilotsjmean Uj, Sj, Vtj = svd(Ypilotsjcentered, fullmatrices=False) Elowj = Vtj.T Xjflat = Xj.flatten() Xjcentered = Xjflat - Ypilotsjmean Pjflat = Elowj @ (Elowj.T @ Xjcentered) Pj = Pjflat.reshape(Xj.shape) Ppilots.append(Pj) # Step 5: Compute discrepancy # Initialize discrepancy volume with infinity discrepancy = np.full(Xfdk.shape, np.inf) for j in range(len(Mmethods)): Xj = Xpilots[j] Pj = Ppilots[j] diff = np.abs(Xj - Pj) discrepancy = np.minimum(discrepancy, diff) # Step 6: Compute weight matrix W = 1.0 / (1.0 + k discrepancy) # Step 7: Final Reconstruction # Solve E(theta, alpha) = ||Phi Psi theta - y||^2 + lambda1 ||theta||1 + lambda2 ||W (Psi theta - (mu + sum alphai Vi))||^2 # This requires an optimization solver. The source states theta is solved using basis pursuit CS solver # and alpha is solved via alternate minimization. # Implementation of the specific solver is not detailed in the source beyond "basis pursuit CS solver". # We assume a function solveoptimization exists that handles this specific energy function. # Compute mu and Vi from original high-quality templates Q Qmatrix = np.array([Q.flatten() for Q in templatesQ]) muflat = np.mean(Qmatrix, axis=0) Qcentered = Qmatrix - muflat Uq, Sq, Vtq = svd(Qcentered, fullmatrices=False) # Vi are the columns of Uq (or rows of Vtq transposed) # The source uses Vi as principal components. # Let's assume Vi corresponds to the eigenvectors of the template covariance. # Placeholder for the actual optimization step as the specific CS solver implementation details are not provided # in the source text beyond the name. xfinal = solveweightedprioroptimization(y, Phi, Psi, W, muflat, Vtq.T, lambda1, lambda2) return xfinal, W def solveweightedprioroptimization(y, Phi, Psi, W, mu, Vcomponents, lambda1, lambda2): """ Placeholder for the alternate minimization solver. The source specifies: 1. theta is solved using basis pursuit CS solver. 2. alpha is solved (implied least squares or similar given the quadratic term). 3. Alternate minimization. """ # This part is not fully specified in the source. # We return a dummy value to satisfy the "no placeholders" rule for the method's core definition. # However, the source does not give the algorithm for the solver, only that it uses "basis pursuit CS solver". # We must indicate this is not given. raise NotImplementedError("The specific algorithm for solving the alternate minimization problem is not given in the sources.") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alignment: If alignment is not present between scans, all template volumes must be pre-aligned before computing the eigenspace, and the test volume must be registered to the templates after its preliminary pilot reconstruction. False Positives: The use of multiple reconstruction methods and taking the minimum difference helps remove reconstruction-method-dependent false positives. Complexity: The method requires multiple preliminary reconstructions (FDK and M other methods) for both the test volume and L templates. This increases computational cost compared to single-pass reconstruction. Performance: Validated on synthetic and real volume data, specifically biological specimens in longitudinal studies (Potato dataset with 5% projection views, Okra dataset with 10% projection views). Strengths: Significantly improves overall quality of reconstructed data while minimizing the impact of priors on regions containing new information. Limitations: Requires a set of high-quality prior templates. Performance depends on the accuracy of the preliminary reconstructions and the choice of M methods. Origin: The method was introduced in "Learning from past scans: Tomographic reconstruction to detect new structures". History: Prior-based methods using eigenspaces were shown to better accommodate variation in the match of a test volume to a set of templates. However, global priors impose inflexible constant weights, leading to suppression of new features in longitudinal studies. This method addresses that limitation by computing regional weights. Usage: Longitudinal studies where the same object is scanned multiple times to monitor for small changes over time.
