name: Node-Local Support Guard
head: Guard, Parallel Support Guard, node-local guard
body: The Node-Local Support Guard is a defense mechanism for distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderers that clamps stored 3D Gaussian parameters into precomputed per-field coordinate boxes to prevent catastrophic corruption from single-bit upsets (SBUs). It ensures that no primitive's projected scale exceeds the largest trained scale, making frame-covering corruption impossible. Unlike error-correcting codes (ECC) which operate on memory words, the guard operates on the semantic range of parameters, catching errors that survive or bypass ECC, including those introduced after correction in registers or caches. The method consists of a one-time precomputation phase after training and a per-frame parallel clamping phase applied independently on each node before rendering. Inputs: \theta: The set of stored 3D Gaussian parameters for N primitives. Each primitive i has parameters \thetai organized into fields f and components c. Sp: The subset of primitives assigned to node p. M: The scrub interval (number of frames between guard re-applications). Outputs: Clamped parameters \theta' ready for rendering. A clamp count Cp for health monitoring. Support Box (Bf): For each field f, a pair of bounds (\ell{f,c}, h{f,c}) for each component c. \ell{f,c} = \mini \theta{i,f,c} h{f,c} = \maxi \theta{i,f,c} These bounds are computed once over all N primitives after training. Clamp Counter: A local integer clamp{sp} initialized to 0 for each node p per frame. \lambda: The bit flip rate per stored bit per frame. b: The total number of stored bits, scaling with the number of primitives N (b = \Theta(N)). M: The scrub interval. Derived from Corollary 2, the maximum interval to keep the expected dose below the catastrophic threshold \tau is M \le \Theta(N \alpha^{-1} \tau / \lambda). Selective Clamp Variant: Clamps only the scale and opacity fields. Cost: 1× memory, <0.1 ms/frame. 1. Precompute Support Box (One-time, post-training): For each field f and component c, compute the minimum and maximum values across all N primitives: \ell{f,c} \leftarrow \mini \theta{i,f,c} h{f,c} \leftarrow \maxi \theta{i,f,c} 2. Per-Frame Guard Application (Node p): For each frame, on node p holding primitive subset Sp: a. Initialize local clamp counter: clamp{sp} \leftarrow 0. b. Iterate over each primitive i \in Sp in parallel. c. For each field f and component c: i. Check if the value is out of bounds or non-finite: If \theta{i,f,c} \notin [\ell{f,c}, h{f,c}] or \theta{i,f,c} is non-finite: Clamp the value: \theta{i,f,c} \leftarrow \text{clamp}(\theta{i,f,c}, \ell{f,c}, h{f,c}). Increment counter: clamp{sp} \leftarrow clamp{sp} + 1. d. Render the subset Sp to the node's tile. e. Composite tiles across nodes. f. Check if the total clamp count across all nodes exceeds a health threshold. If so, raise a host parity/scrub alert to signal silent-data-corruption rather than masking the degrading device. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputesupportbox(theta, fields, components): bounds = {} for f in fields: for c in components: values = [theta[i][f][c] for i in range(len(theta))] bounds[(f, c)] = (min(values), max(values)) return bounds def nodelocalsupportguard(thetap, bounds, fields, components, healththreshold): clampcount = 0 for i in range(len(thetap)): for f in fields: for c in components: val = thetap[i][f][c] minval, maxval = bounds[(f, c)] # Check for out-of-bounds or non-finite values if not (minval <= val <= maxval) or not math.isfinite(val): # Clamp to the trained support box thetap[i][f][c] = max(minval, min(maxval, val)) clampcount += 1 # Render the subset to the node's tile and composite tiles across nodes # tile = renderprimitives(thetap) # compositetiles(tile) # Health check: surface errors rather than silently masking them # if clampcount > healththreshold: # raisealert("Silent Data Corruption Detected") return thetap, clampcount Residual Error: The guard does not bound the worst-case in-support residual error, only out-of-range flips. The residual error is bounded by the in-box spread and is measured to be perceptually negligible. Aggressive Optimization: If optimization grows very large primitives, the support box widens, admitting a larger guarded footprint and weakening primitive-locality assumptions. Inert Components: The guard skips inert higher-order spherical-harmonic coefficients, touching only a quarter of the parameter memory (14 of 59 components per primitive). A mitigation technique that clamps only the scale and opacity fields to prevent catastrophic upsets, relying on the fact that these fields carry almost all catastrophic mass. It is cheaper than the full support guard, with a cost of 1× memory and <0.1 ms/frame. Time Complexity: Per node, O(N/P) per frame, where N is total primitives and P is number of nodes. Steady-State Overhead: O(N/(P M)), amortized over the scrub interval M. Performance: On a system with 66 million primitives, the guard cost is 9.66 ms per frame (18.3% of render time), sustaining 5 megapixels per second and an effective parameter-read bandwidth of 763 GB/s. Memory Overhead: 1× memory (stores the bounds, which is negligible compared to primitive data). Strengths: Eliminates catastrophic failure mode (frame-covering corruption) requiring only one flip; no cross-node traffic or synchronization points; complementary to ECC. Limitations: Does not correct in-box errors; effectiveness depends on the tightness of the trained support box. When to Use: In distributed 3DGS rendering environments susceptible to single-bit upsets (e.g., high-altitude or space applications) where ECC is insufficient or too costly. The Node-Local Support Guard was introduced in the context of analyzing single-event upsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It addresses the finding that while most single-bit upsets in 3DGS are localized, a few critical bits can cause frame-covering corruption. The method was developed to provide a low-overhead, semantic-range defense that complements hardware ECC. name: Volumetric displays and holography
body: This family covers hardware systems and computational methods that render volumetric data directly into physical space, creating images visible from multiple viewpoints without headgear. It differs from standard rasterization by projecting light into a physical medium or light field rather than onto a 2D sensor. It is distinct from Voxel engines and games which simulate volume appearance on 2D displays, and from Scientific and medical visualization which typically uses 2D slice views or volume rendering on monitors. Renders volumetric images with arbitrary per-voxel colors by temporally synchronizing spatial voxel generation with a Liquid Crystal (LC) color filter. It solves multicolor volumetric display by mapping 3D voxel data to control signals for a galvanometer scanner, varifocal lens, and LC filter. Unlike monochromatic scanning methods, it explicitly calculates optimal scanning routes for color layers to minimize mechanical travel time while ensuring color fidelity through temporal multiplexing. It is chosen when full-color volumetric displays with precise spatial control are required. Physically separates the volume where voxels are generated (drawing space) from the observation volume (viewing space) using an optical re-projection system. This allows the drawing space to be filled with materials like xenon gas that lower the energy threshold for voxel generation and provide broadband emission, without creating a physical barrier. It enables the insertion of color filters in the re-projection path. It is chosen when the display medium requires specific environmental conditions (like gas discharge) incompatible with direct user viewing. Renders palm-sized 3D contents in real space by splitting a femtosecond laser into two paths: one using an LC-SLM for holographic voxel generation, and the other using a 3D laser scanner. It solves the limitation of single-path systems by cooperatively combining holographic multiplexing with galvanometric scanning to achieve higher voxel density and larger volumes. It is chosen for high-resolution, real-time volumetric displays in free space. Generates multi-view stereoscopic images of volumetric medical datasets for display on a multi-view lenticular screen, using the GPU for both rendering and compositing. It is chosen when hardware-accelerated, glasses-free stereoscopic visualization of medical volumes is required. Creates luminous image points in free space using a trapped particle illuminated by RGB lasers, forming images via persistence of vision. It solves the 'clipping' limitation of holographic displays by keeping image points physically separate from the scattering surface, allowing unconstrained viewing angles. It is chosen for free-space displays requiring large viewing geometries. Maps 3D voxel data to a physical 3D light field by computing the interference pattern (hologram) required to reconstruct the volume. It differs from sibling methods by using optical superposition (diffraction) rather than temporal persistence or scanning beams. It is chosen when wave optics modeling is needed to resolve viewing space vs. drawing space conflicts through phase modulation. Uses quantum dots (QDs) embedded in a polymer substrate to eliminate occlusion from electrical wiring. External light excites the QDs to emit light spontaneously, forming visible voxels without internal power connections. It is chosen for displays requiring high transparency and absence of internal wiring occlusion. Realizes a solid-state volumetric display by using the chromatic dispersion of a diffractive lens to image planar patterns from a projector. Each image plane's position is defined by a distinct wavelength from a narrowband polychromatic source. It is chosen for solid-state displays without moving parts in the viewing volume. Not given in the sources. Displays layered volumetric images by projecting optical patterns onto a rotating object composed of fan-shaped disks, using external high-speed cameras for tracking and a high-speed projector for rendering. It is chosen for interactive displays where users can freely move and rotate the physical object. Not given in the sources. A display system that eliminates the need for mental reconstruction by displaying the entire stack of tomographic images as a 3D image using a vibrating mirror with variable focal length optics. The speaker is made to vibrate at 30 Hz, and tomographic images are displayed one at a time on the CRT in synchrony with the mirror's motion. Due to the variable focal length, timing sequence, and retinal integration, the stack of 2D images appears as a virtual 3D image in the mirror. The mirror consists of an aluminized membrane stretched over a loud-speaker coupled to a CRT. A volumetric display using a drone equipped with 8 one-dimensional LEDs. The voxel generation capability is limited to the surface of a sphere, but the display space itself can move. A method using bubbles excited by lasers in liquid as voxels. By increasing liquid viscosity, slow-floating bubbles are generated and arranged to stack 2D cross-sections, realizing volumetric image display. This system has a very long voxel residence time, requiring time for image refresh, but can express complex shapes. A volumetric display that extends the Pepper's Ghost optical illusion to multiple stacked translucent planes, cumulatively giving volume to an initially two-dimensional projection. A plane of translucent material is placed at a certain angle on a light source so that it reflects towards the user the projection of an image superimposed on the perceived reality. This is repeated for multiple planes to create volume. It differs from persistence-of-vision displays that use moving parts or levitated particles by using static stacked planes. It is implemented as a layer-based painting tool, retro-gaming platform, text overlaying media player for subtitles, browser-based 3D scene renderer, and volumetric data visualizer. Layer thickness is evaluated alongside light reflection and transmission properties to optimize image quality, though the exact value is not specified. Holographic display methods for volume data have evolved to support cinematic volume rendering on light field displays. Modern implementations integrate visualization toolkits like VTK to generate quilt images and movies for holographic screens, enabling photo-realistic rendering of volumetric data such as CT scans for medical computing. Early volumetric display concepts included varifocal mirror systems for stereotactic neurosurgery planning, which used vibrating mirrors to stack tomographic images into a virtual 3D image. Free-space volumetric displays have also been explored using drones, trapped particles, and laser-excited bubbles to create images without physical screens. Additionally, static stacked-plane systems like SliceView extend traditional optical illusions for direct manipulation of 3D content. name: Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM)
head: Rotating Mirror Volumetric Display, Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (vdrm) optical simulation & encoding, vdrm optical simulation & encoding
body: VRDM is a volumetric display method that projects 3D voxel data onto a rotating mirror using surrounding LED screens, mapping 3D coordinates to 2D screen pixels via analytical mirror reflection matrices. It differs from standard ray marching by avoiding per-pixel ray tracing loops, instead computing direct projections for each rotation angle to drive the LED arrays synchronously. Inputs: 3D voxel grid (implicit or explicit), rotation angle \theta, mirror offset d, screen geometry parameters. Outputs: Frame buffer for surrounding LED screens, structured as AngleImage. Data Structures: AngleImage: Contiguous memory block of 772 bytes. Bytes 0-3: u32 angle value. Bytes 4-771: 192 rows of RGBH arrays. Each row is 4 bytes: R (u8), G (u8), B (u8), H (u8 representing depth/address). ScreenLinePixels: Array of WPIXELS Option<PixelColor> (u32 RGBA). ScreenLineAddr: Struct containing screenidx (usize) and addr (u32) for depth sorting. Parameters (Default Values): WPIXELS: 64 (screen width resolution). HPIXELS: 40 (screen height resolution). MIRROROFFSET: 1.0 per notes, but source code uses \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414. SCREENOFFSET: 0.25 per notes, but source code uses 0.05. SCREENXOFFSET: -0.75. SCREENZOFFSET: -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET. SCREENYOFFSET: -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET. NUMSCREENS: 3. TOTALANGLES: WPIXELS 8 = 512 angles. Steps: 1. Generate Pyramid Surface (Reference Geometry): For each pixel (x, y) in a W\PIXELS \times W\PIXELS grid: Compute r = W\PIXELS / 2. Compute h = |x - r| + |y - r|. If h \ge H\PIXELS, skip. Compute z = H\PIXELS - 1 - h. Assign color based on quadrant relative to center (r, r): x \ge r, y \ge r \to gray; x < r, y \ge r \to red; x < r, y < r \to green; x \ge r, y < r \to magenta. This creates a half-pyramid reference surface. 2. Mirror Transformation: To map a 3D point (x, y, z) to the mirror plane: Apply a 2D rotation matrix to (x, y) coordinates based on the current rotation angle \theta. Apply a fixed 45-degree rotation matrix to (y, z) coordinates to align the point with the mirror plane's normal. Apply the mirror reflection matrix M in homogeneous coordinates: M = \begin{bmatrix} \sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta & -2\sin\theta\cos\theta & 0 \\ -2\sin\theta\cos\theta & \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta & 0 \\ 2d\cos\theta & 2d\sin\theta & 1 \end{bmatrix} where \theta is the mirror angle in radians and d is MIRROROFFSET. Note: The source code implements mirrormat4 with specific sign conventions for sin/cos derived from column-major layout. 3. Encode Pixels per Angle: For each angle \thetak in the angle map (from codec.encode()): Initialize pixels array of size IMGHEIGHT (192) with None. For each voxel/point in the 3D volume: Transform the 3D point to 2D screen coordinates (u, v) using the mirror matrix and screen projection logic. Determine the target screen index and pixel address. If the pixel address is already occupied, keep the pixel with the smaller addr (closest depth). Store [r, g, b, p.addr as u8] in the pixels array. Z-depth Zeroing Pitfall: If the alpha channel of a pixel is zero (rgba & 0xFFFFFF00 == 0), force the computed z-depth (or H value) to 0 to prevent rendering artifacts from transparent voxels. 4. Output Assembly: Pack the pixels array into the AngleImage structure: [angle(4), R(1), G(1), B(1), H(1),...] repeated 192 times. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math WPIXELS = 64 HPIXELS = 40 IMGHEIGHT = 192 MIRROROFFSET = math.sqrt(2) # Source code uses sqrt(2); notes state 1.0 SCREENOFFSET = 0.05 # Source code uses 0.05; notes state 0.25 SCREENZOFFSET = -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET SCREENYOFFSET = -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET NUMSCREENS = 3 TOTALANGLES = WPIXELS 8 def generatepyramidsurface(): """Generates reference pyramid surface for encoding.""" surface = [] r = WPIXELS / 2 for x in range(WPIXELS): for y in range(WPIXELS): h = abs(x - r) + abs(y - r) if h >= HPIXELS: continue z = HPIXELS - 1 - h # Quadrant color assignment relative to center (r, r) if x >= r and y >= r: color = (128, 128, 128) # Gray elif x < r and y >= r: color = (255, 0, 0) # Red elif x < r and y < r: color = (0, 255, 0) # Green else: color = (255, 0, 255) # Magenta surface.append((x, y, z, color)) return surface def rotate2d(x, y, theta): """Applies 2D rotation matrix to (x, y).""" cost = math.cos(theta) sint = math.sin(theta) return x cost - y sint, x sint + y cost def rotateyz45(y, z): """Applies fixed 45-degree rotation matrix to (y, z).""" invsqrt2 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(2) return y invsqrt2 - z invsqrt2, y invsqrt2 + z invsqrt2 def applymirrormatrix(x, y, z, theta, d): """Applies the 3x3 mirror reflection matrix in homogeneous coordinates.""" sint = math.sin(theta) cost = math.cos(theta) sin2 = sint sint cos2 = cost cost sincos = sint cost # M [x, y, z]^T xnew = (sin2 - cos2) x - 2 sincos y ynew = -2 sincos x + (cos2 - sin2) y znew = 2 d cost x + 2 d sint y + z return xnew, ynew, znew def maptoscreencoords(x, y, z): """Maps transformed coordinates to screen pixel indices (u, v). Exact scaling/offsets use the source's caclviewpoint logic.""" # Linear scaling placeholder for demonstration; replace with exact screen geometry math scalex = WPIXELS / 2.0 scaley = IMGHEIGHT / 2.0 u = int((x + 1.0) scalex) v = int((y + 1.0) scaley) return u, v def encodeframe(voxels, theta): """Encodes a single frame for a given angle.""" # Initialize 192 rows, each row is a list of 64 pixels (None or (R,G,B,H)) pixels = [[None] WPIXELS for in range(IMGHEIGHT)] for voxel in voxels: x, y, z, rgba = voxel # 1. Mirror Transformation xrot, yrot = rotate2d(x, y, theta) yrot, zrot = rotateyz45(yrot, z) xproj, yproj, zproj = applymirrormatrix(xrot, yrot, zrot, theta, MIRROROFFSET) # 2. Project to screen grid u, v = maptoscreencoords(xproj, yproj, zproj) # Bounds check if not (0 <= u < WPIXELS and 0 <= v < IMGHEIGHT): continue # Extract RGBA components r = rgba & 0xFF g = (rgba >> 8) & 0xFF b = (rgba >> 16) & 0xFF a = (rgba >> 24) & 0xFF # 3. Z-depth Zeroing Pitfall if (rgba & 0xFFFFFF00) == 0: depthaddr = 0 else: depthaddr = int(abs(zproj) 100) & 0xFF # Scaled depth address as u8 # 4. Depth Sorting if pixels[v][u] is not None: existingaddr = pixels[v][u][3] if depthaddr < existingaddr: pixels[v][u] = (r, g, b, depthaddr) else: pixels[v][u] = (r, g, b, depthaddr) return pixels def assembleangleimage(angleval, pixels): """Assembles the 772-byte AngleImage structure.""" buffer = bytearray(772) # Pack angle (4 bytes) buffer[0:4] = angleval.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') # Pack 192 rows of RGBH offset = 4 for row in pixels: for pixel in row: if pixel is None: buffer[offset:offset+4] = bytes([0, 0, 0, 0]) else: r, g, b, h = pixel buffer[offset:offset+4] = bytes([r, g, b, h]) offset += 4 return buffer Defines mechanical geometry and dynamic balancing for a rotating double-helix reflector. Distinguished by its double-helix topology minimizing drag/vibration, enabling "walk-around" viewing. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot A), where N is the number of voxels and A is the number of angles (TOTALANGLES). Each voxel is projected to each angle frame. Memory Complexity: O(A \cdot H \cdot W) for the frame buffer storage, where H=192, W=64. Each frame is 772 bytes. Performance: The method avoids per-pixel ray tracing, using analytical matrices for direct projection, which is faster than iterative ray marching. Strengths: Real-time capable for low-resolution volumes; simple optical setup (one mirror, 3 screens). Limitations: Resolution limited by screen pixel count and mirror rotation speed; requires precise synchronization; artifacts from transparent voxels if Z-depth zeroing is not applied. VRDM was developed as an early-stage volumetric display concept using two spinning mirrors, later evolved to version 2.0 with one mirror and three surrounding LED screens. The simulation and encoding pipeline was implemented by hikaricai. hikaricai/vdrm, https://github.com/hikaricai/vdrm, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Helical Display Surface Geometry & Balancing
head: Double-Helix Reflector, Second-Generation Helix
body: This method defines the mechanical geometry and dynamic balancing strategy for a rotating double-helix reflector used in laser-based volumetric displays. It solves the problem of maintaining structural integrity and optical stability at high rotational speeds by utilizing axisymmetric contours to balance centrifugal forces and continuous curvature to maximize bending stiffness. It builds on Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM) and is distinguished from standard cylindrical or planar rotating mirrors by its specific double-helix topology, which minimizes aerodynamic drag and vibration while enabling "walk-around" viewing of the projected 3D volume. The method constructs a rotating optical surface from discrete segments, ensuring dynamic equilibrium through geometric symmetry and precise mass distribution. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Target imaging volume dimensions, rotational speed, material properties (polystyrene plastic), and structural constraints (shaft diameter, bearing type). Outputs: A fabricated double-helix reflector assembly with specific segment geometry, surface finish, and balancing weights, enclosed in a rotating housing. Data Structures and Layout The helix is constructed as a vertically stacked assembly of identical segments. Segment Geometry: Height: 1 inch. Thickness: Uniform 2 mm. Shape: Double-helix contour with continuous curvature. Center Feature: A 1/2-inch diameter concentric cylinder housing a center pin. Assembly: Total Segments: 18. Total Height: 18 inches. Bonding: Segments are vertically stacked and bonded together. Surface Finish: Upper Surface: Opaque white finish to enhance reflectivity and light diffusion. Rotor Assembly: Helix + Pin Weight: 5 pounds. Total Rotor Assembly Weight: 125 pounds. Housing: Transparent cylindrical housing rotating with the helix. Shaft: 2-inch steel shaft. Numbered Steps 1. Design Contour: Define a double-helix contour with a 36-inch diameter and 18-inch height. Ensure the contour is axisymmetric to sustain equilibrium of centrifugally-induced forces. 2. Fabricate Segments: Injection-mold 18 segments from polystyrene plastic. Each segment must have a uniform thickness of 2 mm and a height of 1 inch. 3. Integrate Center Pin: Incorporate a 1/2-inch diameter concentric cylinder into the segments to house a center pin. This pin aligns the plastic segments during assembly and centers the helix in its housing. 4. Assemble Helix: Vertically stack and bond the 18 segments. The resulting helix weighs 5 pounds. 5. Apply Surface Finish: Treat the upper surface of the helix with an opaque white finish to enhance reflectivity and light diffusion. 6. Enclose in Housing: Place the helix inside a transparent cylindrical housing that rotates with it. The housing supports the helix around its entire perimeter and shelters it from nonrotating objects. The housing is mounted on a circular turntable at the top of a 2-inch steel shaft. 7. Balance Assembly: Dynamically balance the total rotor assembly (125 pounds) to assure smooth performance. The assembly is designed for a first-critical natural frequency (f) greater than 33 Hz. 8. Mount Drive System: Attach a shaft-mounted drive pulley and encode disk to complete the rotor assembly. Support the rotor shaft with a pair of self-aligning cartridge bearings. Formulas and Parameters Operating Speed: 600 rpm. Natural Frequency Constraint: f > 33 \text{ Hz}. Addressable Volume: 10" \times 10" \times 15" (constrained by scanner optics and helix occlusions). Total Imaging Volume Potential: 10 cubic feet (36" diameter, 18" high). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Centrifugal Forces: Unbalanced centrifugal forces cause vibration. Solved by the axisymmetry of the double-helix contour. Structural Stiffness: Low bending stiffness leads to deformation. Solved by the continuous curvature of the helix. Aerodynamic Drag: Drag loads can destabilize rotation. Solved by enclosing the helix in a rotating transparent housing that entrains air, preventing drag load on the helix. Occlusion: The double-helix structure creates occlusions, reducing the usable volume. The addressable volume is limited to 10" \times 10" \times 15" despite a larger potential volume. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The system operates at 600 rpm with minimal noise and vibration. Scaling: The design displaces a potential cylindrical imaging volume of 10 cubic feet, but the addressable volume is constrained to 10" \times 10" \times 15" due to optical and geometric limitations. Strengths: Inherently free of low-frequency vibration due to unique shape and light weight; minimizes weight and aerodynamic drag; maximizes structural stiffness. Limitations: Addressable volume is reduced by helix occlusions; requires complex dynamic balancing of a 125-pound assembly. When to use: When a true 3D volumetric display with walk-around viewing is required, and mechanical stability at high speeds is critical. When not to use: When the full potential volume (10 cubic feet) is required without occlusion constraints, or when lower rotational speeds are acceptable for simpler geometries. The method originated from the NRaD team's development of second-generation 3-D technology, documented in a 1992 report with continuing development. It was designed to improve upon earlier volumetric display systems by addressing vibration and aerodynamic drag issues inherent in rotating mirror systems. The system uses ceiling-mounted mirrors to fold laser signals into a vertical attitude, allowing for "walk-around" viewing. name: Laser-based 3-D Volumetric Display (Rotating Helix with AO Scanner)
head: AO-Scanned Helix Display, Rotating Helix Volumetric Display, Helical Volumetric Display, Helix-based 3-D Volumetric Display, Double Helix Laser Display, Laser-based rotating double helix volumetric display, 3-D Volumetric Display (Helix-based Laser Projection), Rotating Helical Volumetric Display, Volumetric Display using Helical Surface, Helix-based 3-D Display, Helical Display System
body: A hardware-based volumetric display technique that projects 3-D image points (voxels) onto the surface of a rapidly rotating helical structure using computer-directed laser beams, creating a true 3-D image space visible to multiple viewers without eyewear. It solves the problem of displaying true 3-D data with physiological depth cues (accommodation, convergence, motion parallax) by forming physical light points in mid-air, unlike 2-D displays that rely on psychological cues. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Phase-Controlled Laser Pointing for Swept Displays by its use of random-access AO scanning for voxel placement rather than phase-synchronized continuous lines, and from Spot Size Reduction Methods by its reliance on the helical geometry and AO deflection rather than purely geometric optics for spot definition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3-D Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) for each desired voxel, a synchronization pulse from a sensor on the helix hub, and control signals for laser intensity. Output: A volumetric image composed of discrete voxels visible in real space, formed by laser light scattering from the rotating helix surface. Data Structures: Frame Buffer: Stores voxel coordinates. In second-generation systems, the z-axis is mapped from the spatial domain to a temporal domain (height maps to memory location). Control Memory: Capacity of 65,000 voxels per color in second-generation implementations. Addressability is 4096 \times 4096 per display volume. Scanner State: Tracks the current RF frequency sweep for X and Y deflectors to determine beam angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Translation: Translate raw (x, y, z) coordinates into the computer memory such that the z-axis (height) is mapped to a temporal domain corresponding to the helix's rotational phase. 2. Synchronization: Wait for a synchronization pulse from a sensor on the helix hub indicating a known rotational angle (e.g., top dead center). 3. Surface Position Calculation: Calculate the position of the rotating helix surface at the exact moment the point needs to be displayed based on the rotational speed and the target (x, y) coordinates. The vertical voxel position z is determined by the intersection of the beam and the helix surface, defined by the rotation angle \theta: z = f(x, y, \theta). 4. Beam Steering: Send (x, y) coordinate pairs to the Acousto-Optic (AO) scanner in sequence to address the correct radial position. The AO scanner uses two deflectors for independent X and Y deflection. 5. Intensity Modulation: Modulate the laser intensity to illuminate only specific voxels, leaving dark areas unaddressed. 6. Projection: The laser beam illuminates the corresponding discrete points on the rotating helix surface. Light scatters from the surface, making voxels appear to emanate from specific points in real space. 7. Refresh: Repeat at the refresh rate (typically 20 Hz) to maintain persistence of vision. Formulas: Voxel Rate: The maximum rate at which voxels can be addressed is limited by the access time of the AO deflector. \text{Voxel Rate} = \frac{1}{\text{Access Time}} For an access time of 10 \, \mu\text{sec}, the max voxel rate is 100,000 voxels/sec. Usable Voxels per Frame: \text{Usable Voxels per Frame} = \frac{\text{Voxel Rate}}{\text{Refresh Rate}} - \text{Dwell Time Voxels} For 100,000 voxels/sec and 20 Hz refresh, the theoretical max is 5,000 voxels. Half-Angle Scan Range: The deflection angle of an AO deflector. \theta{AO} = \frac{\lambda \Delta f}{vs} Where \lambda is optical wavelength, \Delta f is RF frequency sweep, and vs is acoustic velocity. Beam Divergence Constant: \theta = \frac{\lambda}{d} Where \theta is initial beam divergence angle and d is laser beam waist diameter. Vertical Velocity of Helix Surface: vz = \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{dz}{d\theta} \frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{h}{2\pi} \cdot 2\pi f = h f Where h is helix height and f is rotation rate. Parameters: Helix Dimensions: Laboratory model: 36-inch diameter, 18-inch height, 36-inch pitch, 2 mm blade thickness. Transportable/Commercial: 12-inch diameter, 8-inch height. Rotation Speed: 600 RPM for double-helix (2 blades) to achieve 20 Hz refresh (f = \text{Refresh Rate} / \text{Blades} = 20/2 = 10 rev/sec = 600 RPM). Single-spiral commercial variant: 1200 RPM. Refresh Rate: 20 Hz. Access Time: 10 \, \mu\text{sec} for single-channel; 5 \, \mu\text{sec} for four-channel systems (achieved by reducing beam diameter from 6 mm to 3 mm). Deflector Sweep Range: 75 to 125 MHz (\Delta f = 50 MHz). Acoustic Velocity (vs): 0.65 mm/ms. Input Beam Diameter: 1.6 mm at the scanner input. Voxel Size: 1.5 mm (24-inch system); 0.7 mm (compact 12-inch system). Brightness: 256 levels per color. Laser Sources: Green: 2x 250 mW diode-pumped doubled Nd:YAG (532 nm). Red: 8x 30 mW single-mode red diode lasers (633 nm) or HeNe (633 nm). Laser Safety: <15 mW average per image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time def waitseconds(t): time.sleep(t) def setaodeflectory(anglerad): # Convert angle to RF frequency; exact synthesis algorithm not given in sources pass def setaodeflectorx(anglerad): # Convert angle to RF frequency; exact synthesis algorithm not given in sources pass def setlaserintensity(level): # Set AO modulator intensity via RF drive pass def pulselaser(): # Trigger laser pulse synchronized with deflection pass def rendervolumetricdisplay(framebuffer, helixparams, scannerparams): PI = 3.141592653589793 hmm = helixparams['helixheightin'] 25.4 rpm = helixparams['rotationspeedrpm'] frps = rpm / 60.0 refreshrate = helixparams['refreshrate'] accesstimes = scannerparams['accesstimeus'] / 1e6 maxvoxelrate = 1.0 / accesstimes theoreticalmaxvoxels = maxvoxelrate / refreshrate waitseconds(0.1) # Wait for sync pulse from hub sensor for voxel in framebuffer: x, y, z, intensity = voxel thetarad = (2 PI z) / hmm omega = 2 PI frps timedelays = thetarad / omega waitseconds(timedelays) lambdam = scannerparams['wavelengthnm'] / 1e9 deltafhz = scannerparams['deflectorsweeprangeMHz'] 1e6 vsms = scannerparams['acousticvelocitymmms'] totaldeflectionrad = (2 lambdam deltafhz) / vsms anglexrad = x (totaldeflectionrad / 2) angleyrad = y (totaldeflectionrad / 2) setaodeflectory(angleyrad) setaodeflectorx(anglexrad) setlaserintensity(intensity) pulselaser() waitseconds(accesstimes) An interaction method that resolves the ambiguity of laser pointers projecting continuous lines by synchronizing pulse frequency with sweep frequency and adjusting phase offset via joystick for precise z-coordinate control. Choose when manual selection ray positioning is required. Optical and mechanical strategies to reduce laser spot diameter and addressable area, addressing excessive voxel size. Choose when higher spatial resolution is needed than the base AO scanner provides. Time Complexity: The voxel rate is limited by the AO access time. Single-channel systems achieve ~100,000 voxels/sec. Four-channel systems achieve ~200,000 voxels/sec per channel, totaling up to 1.6 million voxels/sec for the first commercial model or 3.2 million voxels/sec for the transportable dual-volume system. Memory Complexity: Frame buffer size is limited by control card memory, such as 65,000 voxels per color in second-generation systems. Measured Performance: The laboratory model (36-inch) produces 120,000 voxels per frame (RGB) at 2.4 million voxels/sec. The transportable model (12-inch) produces 160,000 total voxels per frame at 1.6 million voxels/sec. The measured spot size is ~4 ± 0.5 mm at the helix for the 36-inch system, and 0.7 mm for the 12-inch system. Scaling: Voxel count scales with the number of parallel AO scanner channels. Beam diameter reduction from 6 mm to 3 mm halves access time, doubling voxel throughput per channel. Strengths: The system provides true physiological depth cues (accommodation, convergence, motion parallax) for group viewing without eyewear. It is highly compatible with the human visual system compared to stereoscopic or holographic displays. Limitations: Reflective helix blades can block image portions, creating occlusion zones; this is mitigated by using a translucent helix and bottom projection. The center shaft creates a dead zone where voxels cannot be placed. Steep helical slope near the central axis causes spot elongation; primary image creation is restricted to regions midway between the center and the rim. The addressable volume is constrained by scanner optics and occlusions (e.g., 10" x 10" x 15" in second-generation systems). Early systems used ion lasers requiring water cooling, though solid-state lasers reduce power consumption by ~1000x. When to Use: Applications requiring true 3D visualization for multiple viewers, such as air traffic control, submarine navigation, battle management, and medical imaging. When Not to Use: Applications requiring extremely high spatial resolution (sub-millimeter) without hardware modification, or where the central dead zone is critical. The concept was invented by Professor Rüdiger Hartwig at the University of Stuttgart in the early 1980s. Feasibility was demonstrated by Dr. R. D. Williams and team at Texas Instruments in late 1989. R&D began at SSC San Diego (SPAWAR Systems Center, San Diego) in early 1990. First-generation prototypes were built by NCCOSC RDT&E Division in the early 1990s. Second-generation development objectives were established in mid-1992, with a report published in April 1995. The technology was commercialized via a 1995 CRADA with NEOS Technologies, Inc. and RGB Technology, Inc. for military and government use. It was deployed on the USS Stennis for the Joint Warrior Interoperability Demonstration (JWID 97) and installed in the SPAWAR Command Center of the Future. name: Phase-Controlled Laser Pointing for Swept Displays
head: Joystick-controlled depth pointing, Phase-controlled laser pointing
body: Phase-controlled laser pointing is an interaction method for swept volumetric displays that resolves the ambiguity of laser pointers projecting continuous lines across the volume. By synchronizing the laser pulse frequency with the display's sweep frequency and adjusting the phase offset via an analog joystick, the user can position a discrete laser dot at a specific height (z-coordinate) on the helical display surface. This method serves as an alternative to distance-controlled depth pointing, offering precise manual control over the selection ray's position rather than relying on physical proximity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Analog joystick position (phase control), display sweep frequency (typically 30 Hz). Output: A laser dot appearing at a specific vertical position on the rotating helical surface. Data Structures and Hardware Layout: The implementation relies on a specific hardware configuration: Microcontroller: Arduino Nano running Timer 1 at 16 MHz resolution. Power: 9V rechargeable battery. Laser: 1 mW red laser diode. Driver: 2N2222 transistor used to switch the laser diode. Interface: Analog joystick for phase adjustment. Parameters: Default Frequency: 30 Hz. Clock Resolution: 16 MHz (Timer 1 on Arduino Nano). Drift Rate: 5 mm per minute on a Voxon VX1 display under default conditions. Steps: 1. Synchronization Verification: The user observes the laser dot; if the dot is static and does not drift, the pointer is synchronized with the display's oscillation. 2. Frequency Configuration: The laser is configured to pulse at the same frequency as the display's oscillation. This frequency is typically set to 30 Hz but can be adjusted once per display by pressing a button to enter adjust mode and using the analog stick. 3. Phase Adjustment: The user moves the analog joystick to change the phase of the laser pulse relative to the display's sweep cycle. This phase shift determines the vertical position (height) of the laser dot on the helical surface. 4. Complex Patterns (Optional): More complex timing patterns, such as a dashed line with a dot at the pointing position, can be generated by modifying the pulse train logic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time DISPLAYFREQHZ = 30 CYCLEPERIODS = 1.0 / DISPLAYFREQHZ TIMERCLOCKHZ = 16000000 ADCRESOLUTION = 1024 def initializetimer1forfrequency(freqhz): # Configures Timer 1 on the microcontroller to generate interrupts at freqhz. # On an Arduino Nano (16 MHz), this involves setting a prescaler and an output compare register (OCR1A) # to match the desired period. The sources do not specify the exact register values. pass def initializelaserdriver(): # Configures the 2N2222 transistor GPIO pin as an output to switch the 1 mW laser diode. pass def initializejoystickadc(): # Configures the analog joystick GPIO pin as an input for the microcontroller's ADC. pass def readanalogjoystick(): # Returns an integer from 0 to ADCRESOLUTION-1 representing the joystick's current position. return 512 # Standard ADC read operation def waituntiltimerreaches(phaseoffsets): # Blocks execution until the microcontroller's internal timer reaches the specified phase offset. # This aligns the laser pulse with the display's sweep cycle. time.sleep(phaseoffsets) def turnonlaser(): # Sets the laser driver GPIO pin high, activating the 1 mW laser diode. pass def turnofflaser(): # Sets the laser driver GPIO pin low, deactivating the laser diode. pass def mainloop(): initializetimer1forfrequency(DISPLAYFREQHZ) initializelaserdriver() initializejoystickadc() while True: joystickval = readanalogjoystick() phaseoffsets = (joystickval / ADCRESOLUTION) CYCLEPERIODS waituntiltimerreaches(phaseoffsets) turnonlaser() turnofflaser() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frequency Drift: If the microcontroller clock is not perfectly stable, frequency drift occurs, causing the laser dot to drift vertically. The specified hardware (Arduino Nano at 16 MHz) exhibits a drift rate of 5 mm per minute on a Voxon VX1 display. Calibration: Frequency adjustment is required only once per display, not per session. Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing is an interaction method where the depth of the laser dot is determined by the physical distance between the pointer device and the display surface, creating a "lock ray" illusion. It uses an ultrasonic range sensor (HC-SR04) to measure distance and triggers the laser accordingly. It is chosen when a natural "point-and-shoot" interaction is preferred over manual phase adjustment, though it may interfere with other ultrasonic devices. See Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing. A hardware interaction technique that automatically projects a laser onto the first visible surface in the line of sight by combining a light detector, laser, and dichroic optics. It routes incoming light through an aperture and lens to a detector, amplifies the signal via an op-amp, and triggers the laser when light is detected. An analog joystick controls the time offset (to project above/below the surface) and sensor sensitivity. It fails on sparse volumetric graphics or surfaces composed of multiple small slices and requires manual light level adaptation per application. A deployment strategy allowing simultaneous use of multiple independent laser pointers on a single swept volumetric display without display-side communication. It enables single-user two-handed gestures (e.g., pinching for rotation) and multi-user role swapping. It supports lasers of different colors. However, multiple devices using ultrasonic distance measurement will interfere with each other. The method provides real-time interaction where latency is dominated by the display's sweep frequency (30 Hz) and the microcontroller's timer resolution. Memory complexity is minimal, requiring only timer registers and ADC readings. The default 30 Hz configuration results in a vertical drift of 5 mm per minute on a Voxon VX1 display. Strengths include precise manual control over the z-coordinate, simple hardware implementation, and compatibility with existing displays without modification. Limitations include the need for manual synchronization verification, susceptibility to clock drift, and per-display frequency adjustment requirements. It should be used when precise, manual control of the selection point's height is required or when the user prefers a joystick interface over distance-based interaction. It should not be used when automatic surface detection is preferred or when multiple users require independent distance-based tracking without interference. This method was introduced in the paper "PointerVol: A Laser Pointer for Swept Volumetric Displays" presented at UIST ’24 (October 13–16, 2024, Pittsburgh, PA, USA). It addresses the problem of depth ambiguity in swept volumetric displays where a standard laser pointer creates a visible line across the volume. The method is inspired by the "depth ray" and "lock ray" techniques used in other volumetric display systems. name: Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing
head: Ultrasonic distance-based pointing
body: Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing is an interaction method for swept volumetric displays where the depth of a laser dot along the intersection line is determined by the physical distance between the pointer device and the display surface. This creates the illusion that the dot appears at a fixed distance from the pointer, effectively implementing a "lock ray" technique where the marker's position is controlled by inputs from the pointer device rather than a phase offset. It provides an alternative to Phase-Controlled Laser Pointing for Swept Displays, which adjusts depth via phase offset controlled by an analog joystick. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Physical distance from the pointer to the display center, measured via an ultrasonic sensor. Output: Timing signal to trigger the laser diode at the correct phase of the display's sweep cycle to render the dot at the calculated depth. Data Structures: Sensor Configuration: Sensor Model: HC-SR04 ultrasonic range sensor. Sampling Rate: 150 samples per second at 1 meter distance. Default Field of View Angle: 15 degrees. Modified Field of View Angle: 25 degrees (achieved by increasing pulse voltage V{pp} from 5V to 30V). Microcontroller State: Reference Distance: A stored value representing the distance from the center of the display to the pointer at the moment of reset. Current Distance: The latest corrected reading from the sensor. Predicted Difuser Position: A calculated value based on the sinusoidal oscillation model of the display's difuser. Numbered Steps: 1. Measure Raw Distance: The ultrasonic sensor emits a sound pulse and measures the time of flight (t{tof}) for the echo to return. 2. Correct for Time of Flight: The raw distance reading is corrected to account for the time of flight of sound to ensure accuracy. 3. Reset Reference (Optional): If the user presses the reset button, the current corrected distance is saved as the new reference distance from the center of the display to the pointer. 4. Predict Difuser Position: The system predicts the position of the display's difuser assuming a sinusoidal oscillation. 5. Trigger Laser: The laser diode is triggered at the calculated phase to render the dot at the depth corresponding to the pointer's distance. Formulas: Distance Correction: The sources state that distances are corrected according to the time of flight of sound, but do not provide the specific mathematical formula for this correction. Difuser Position Prediction: The position is predicted assuming a sinusoidal oscillation of the difuser. The specific equation for this sinusoidal model is not provided in the sources. Parameters: Laser: 1 mW red laser diode. Driver: 2N2222 transistor. Microcontroller: Arduino Nano. Power: 9V rechargeable battery. Display Frequency: 30 Hz (default). Laser Pulse Voltage (V{pp}): 30 V (modified) or 5 V (default). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sensor Exposure: The difuser must be directly exposed to the ultrasonic sensor. A protective dome cannot be used because ultrasound requires direct exposure to propagate effectively. LIDAR Rejection: LIDAR sensors were explored but rejected due to low sampling rates (below 30 samples per second) and unreliability caused by the translucency of the difuser. Drift: With a default frequency of 30 Hz and an Arduino Nano (Timer 1 at 16 MHz resolution), the laser drifts only 5 mm per minute in a Voxon VX1 display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time SPEEDOFSOUND = 343.0 # m/s DISPLAYFREQHZ = 30.0 # Hz SAMPLERATEHZ = 150.0 # Hz referencedistancem = 0.0 currentdistancem = 0.0 def getcurrenttime(): """Returns current system time in seconds.""" return time.time() def buttonpressed(): """Checks if the reset button on the pointer device is pressed.""" # Hardware-specific GPIO check return False def measurerawdistance(): """Emits ultrasonic pulse and measures time of flight in seconds.""" # HC-SR04 trigger/echo interface return 0.0 def correctdistance(rawtimes): """Corrects raw time of flight to distance.""" # Formula not provided in sources return (rawtimes SPEEDOFSOUND) / 2.0 def predictdifuserposition(times): """Predicts difuser position assuming sinusoidal oscillation.""" # Specific equation not provided in sources return 0.0 def resetreference(): """Sets the current corrected distance as the reference distance from the center of the display to the pointer.""" global referencedistancem referencedistancem = currentdistancem def triggerlaser(): """Calculates laser trigger timing based on current distance and difuser position prediction.""" global currentdistancem # 1. Measure and correct distance rawtime = measurerawdistance() currentdistancem = correctdistance(rawtime) # 2. Predict difuser position difuserpos = predictdifuserposition(getcurrenttime()) # 3. Calculate phase offset based on distance # The depth is determined by the distance between pointer and display # Specific mapping from distance to phase is not provided # 4. Trigger laser # Laser switches on at configured frequency matching display oscillation # Hardware-specific trigger implementation required # Source does not specify the exact trigger mechanism def mainloop(): while True: if buttonpressed(): resetreference() triggerlaser() time.sleep(1.0 / SAMPLERATEHZ) Accuracy: The method provides a fixed-distance illusion relative to the pointer. Drift is minimal (5 mm per minute) when using a 30 Hz display and an Arduino Nano. Limitations: The method requires direct line-of-sight between the sensor and the difuser, preventing the use of protective domes. It is sensitive to the translucency of the difuser, which caused unreliability with LIDAR alternatives. Hardware Constraints: Relies on the HC-SR04 sensor, which has a maximum angle of 15 degrees (modifiable to 25 degrees with higher voltage). This method was introduced in the paper "PointerVol: A Laser Pointer for Swept Volumetric Displays" by Fernández et al., presented at UIST 2024. It is part of the development of laser-based 3-D volumetric displays using rotating helix geometry and AO scanners. The technique is equivalent to the "lock ray" technique previously shown to yield good results for volumetric displays. name: Spot Size Reduction Methods
head: Addressable Area Reduction
body: This method defines four optical and mechanical strategies to reduce the laser spot diameter and the corresponding addressable area on a rotating helical volumetric display. The original system produced a 4 mm spot diameter, which these methods aim to reduce to approximately 1.7–2.0 mm. Input: The existing scanner-helix optical train, characterized by a throw distance, output lens focal lengths, and scanner resolution (256 × 256 deflectors). Output: A reduced spot diameter (target ~1.7–1.8 mm) and a remapped addressable area (e.g., 13 × 13 or 24 × 24) within the 4095 × 4095 digital address space. The hardware state is defined by the following parameters: throwdistance: Distance from scanner to helix surface (mm). lensfocallength: Focal length of projection/output lenses (mm). scannerresolution: Number of addressable points per axis (integer). beamsize: Diameter of the laser beam within the deflectors (mm). spotdiameter: Resulting spot size at the helix surface (mm). addressablearea: The physical or logical grid size occupied by the beam (e.g., 13 × 13). The implementation involves selecting one of four mutually exclusive or combinable hardware modifications. 1. Method 1: Reduce Throw Distance Reduce the physical distance from the scanner to the helix by approximately half. Target throw distance: 1700 mm. Result: Spot diameter of 1.7 mm; addressable area reduces to 13+ × 13+. 2. Method 2: Insert Projection Lens Insert a single projection lens in front of the scanner. Select lens focal length from {500, 1000, 1500} mm. Result: Best spot size is 1.8 mm. Requires an 8-inch lens. Introduces optical aberrations. 3. Method 3: Change Output Lenses Modify the output optics to decrease angular magnification. Replace the last output lens with a focal length of approximately 110 mm (original was 60 mm). Remap voxel images to fill the 4095 × 4095 address space. Result: Spot size of 1.7 mm. 4. Method 4: Increase Scanner Resolution Increase the beam size in the deflectors to 6.4 mm. Increase scanner resolution from 256 × 256 to 512 × 512. Result: Spot size of 1.8 mm at 24 × 24 area. Sub-millimeter spots possible if optimized to 13 × 13 area. Penalty: Total voxel count reduces from 40,000 to 20,000. No explicit mathematical formulas are provided in the sources. Throw Distance: ~1700 mm. Projection Lens Focal Lengths: 500, 1000, or 1500 mm. Output Lens Focal Length: 60 mm (original) replaced by ~110 mm. Deflector Beam Size: 6.4 mm. Aberrations: Method 2 introduces optical aberrations that are difficult to remove. Voxel Count Reduction: Method 4 halves the total number of voxels (40,000 to 20,000), reducing image density. Misalignment: Slight misalignment of scanner optics (e.g., shifting the 80 mm collimating lens by ±1 mm) has negligible effect on spot size if the output lens is adjusted to achieve the minimum spot size. Lens Size: Method 2 requires an 8-inch lens, which is physically large. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatespotreductionmethods(): """ Evaluates four methods for reducing spot size on a helical volumetric display. Returns the recommended method based on source evaluation. """ results = [] # Method 1: Reduce throw distance method1 = { "name": "Reduce Throw Distance", "throwdistancemm": 1700, "spotdiametermm": 1.7, "addressablearea": "13+ x 13+", "pros": ["Direct", "Good spot size"], "cons": [] } results.append(method1) # Method 2: Insert projection lens method2 = { "name": "Insert Projection Lens", "lensfocallengthsmm": [500, 1000, 1500], "spotdiametermm": 1.8, "lenssizeinches": 8, "pros": [], "cons": ["Aberrations", "Large lens required", "Worse spot size than Method 1"] } results.append(method2) # Method 3: Change output lenses method3 = { "name": "Change Output Lenses", "oldoutputlensmm": 60, "newoutputlensmm": 110, "spotdiametermm": 1.7, "addressspace": "4095 x 4095", "pros": ["Cost-effective", "Straightforward", "Good spot size"], "cons": [] } results.append(method3) # Method 4: Increase scanner resolution method4 = { "name": "Increase Scanner Resolution", "oldresolution": "256 x 256", "newresolution": "512 x 512", "beamsizemm": 6.4, "spotdiametermm": 1.8, "addressablearea": "24 x 24", "totalvoxelsold": 40000, "totalvoxelsnew": 20000, "pros": ["Higher resolution"], "cons": ["Halved voxel count", "Larger area"] } results.append(method4) # Selection logic based on source evaluation # Method 3 is selected as most cost-effective and straightforward # Method 2 rejected due to aberrations and lens size # Method 4 penalized by halved voxel count recommendedmethod = method3 return recommendedmethod Adjusting lens positions to compensate for misalignment without degrading spot size. Using Gaussian beam traces for additional optical analysis. Performance: Method 3 achieves a 1.7 mm spot size, comparable to Method 1, but is preferred for its cost-effectiveness and simplicity. Trade-offs: Method 1 requires physical modification of the throw distance. Method 2 introduces aberrations and requires large optics. Method 4 reduces the total voxel count by 50%. Robustness: The system is tolerant to slight misalignments (±1 mm shift in collimating lens) if the output lens is re-focused. This method was developed for the Improved Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System. It addresses limitations in the initial design where the spot size was too large (4 mm) and the addressable area was insufficiently utilized. The goal was to reduce the spot size to approximately 2 mm or less while maintaining a high voxel count. DTIC ADA358303: Improved Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System. name: Varifocal Mirror Display
head: Sher's method, Variable Focal Length Mirror, Variable Focal Length Mirror Display, Variable-mirror-based 3D display, Varifocal Mirror, Varifocal Mirror 3D Display, Vibrating Mirror Display
body: The Varifocal Mirror Display is a volumetric display system that generates a true 3D image in space by reflecting a sequence of 2D images from a vibrating circular mirror with variable focal length. It solves the problem of mental reconstruction required by stacked 2D displays by using retinal integration to fuse rapidly changing images into a continuous volume. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Rotational Swept-Screen Projection by using a deformable mirror driven by audio signals rather than a mechanically rotating physical screen, and from Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering by using temporal multiplexing of static frames rather than continuous beam scanning. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of 2D tomographic images (frames) corresponding to depth slices, synchronized with the mirror's vibration phase. Output: A virtual 3D image floating in space in front of the viewer, viewable by multiple observers within a limited solid angle. Data Structures Refresher Buffer: A memory structure storing the display list of 3D points. Each point is defined by its (x, y) screen coordinates and its desired depth z. The scheduling of points in this buffer determines their apparent depth. Frame Sequence: A list of 2D images, one for each depth slice, displayed in synchrony with the mirror's motion. System Layout The hardware consists of a high-speed point-plotting CRT (or monitor) pointed at a flexible circular mirror. The mirror is an aluminized membrane stretched over the cone of a loudspeaker (woofer). The woofer is driven by an audio signal to vibrate the mirror. Parameters Drive Frequency: 30 Hz audio signal. Frame Rate: 30 frames per second (synchronized with the 30 Hz drive). Display Volume: Maximum 25 \times 25 \times 25 cm. Resolution: 128x128 points per frame. Position Accuracy: Points must be displayed within 0.1 inches of their desired position to appear correct. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize System: Attach the flexible circular mirror to the front of the woofer. Connect the monitor to the woofer's audio input or a synchronized controller. 2. Drive Mirror: Apply a 30 Hz sinusoidal audio signal to the woofer. This causes the mirror to vibrate, continuously changing its curvature and thus its focal length. 3. Synchronize Display: Display the tomographic images from the refresher buffer onto the CRT one at a time. The timing of each frame must be synchronized with the phase of the mirror's vibration. 4. Map Depth to Timing: Schedule each 3D point in the display list such that it is displayed when the mirror's focal length corresponds to the point's desired depth z. The position of the mirror (curvature) determines the apparent depth of the reflected point. 5. Reflect and Fuse: The viewer observes the reflection of the CRT screen on the vibrating mirror. Due to the variable focal length, different points appear at different physical locations in space. The human eye fuses the rapidly changing 2D images (30 fps) into a single 3D image via retinal integration. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. DRIVEFREQUENCYHZ = 30 FRAMERATE = 30 MAXVOLUMECM = 25 RESOLUTION = 128 POSITIONTOLERANCEINCHES = 0.1 class Point3D: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x # Screen coordinate self.y = y # Screen coordinate self.z = z # Desired depth in volume def varifocalmirrordisplay(points3d, monitor, mirrordriver): """ Renders a 3D point cloud using a varifocal mirror display. Args: points3d: List of Point3D objects. monitor: Object with method displayframe(frameindex, imagedata). mirrordriver: Object with method setaudiosignal(phase, amplitude). """ # 1. Initialize the mirror driver with a 30 Hz signal # The mirror vibrates continuously, changing focal length mirrordriver.startvibration(frequency=DRIVEFREQUENCYHZ) # 2. Prepare the display list # Sort points by depth if necessary, or schedule based on phase # The key is that the timing of the frame determines the apparent depth displaylist = points3d # 3. Render Loop while True: # Get current phase of the mirror vibration (0 to 2pi) # This phase corresponds to the current focal length currentphase = mirrordriver.getcurrentphase() # Map phase to depth slice index # Assuming one full vibration cycle corresponds to the full depth range # or a specific subset of the cycle is used for the volume depthsliceindex = mapphasetoslice(currentphase, totalslices=FRAMERATE) # 4. Select and Display Frame # Retrieve the 2D image for the current depth slice # This image contains all points scheduled for this specific depth currentframe = generateframeforslice(displaylist, depthsliceindex) # Display the frame on the CRT # The CRT must have fast phosphor decay to prevent smear monitor.displayframe(depthsliceindex, currentframe) # 5. Wait for next frame # Synchronize with the 30 Hz drive waitfornextframe(FRAMERATE) def mapphasetophase(phase, totalslices): """ Maps the continuous phase of the mirror vibration to a discrete frame index. In a real implementation, this mapping depends on the specific mechanical response of the mirror and the synchronization logic. """ # Normalize phase to 0-1 normalizedphase = phase % (2 3.14159) / (2 3.14159) # Map to frame index return int(normalizedphase totalslices) def generateframeforslice(points, sliceindex): """ Generates a 2D image for a specific depth slice. """ frame = createblankimage(RESOLUTION, RESOLUTION) for point in points: # Check if point belongs to this slice # In a real system, this is determined by the scheduling/timing if ispointinslice(point, sliceindex): # Plot point on the CRT # Position accuracy must be within 0.1 inches plotpoint(frame, point.x, point.y) return frame def ispointinslice(point, sliceindex): """ Determines if a 3D point should be displayed in the current frame. This is based on the scheduling of the point in the refresher buffer relative to the mirror's phase. """ # Placeholder for the specific scheduling logic # The point is displayed when the mirror's focal length matches its depth z return False # Implementation detail depends on synchronization hardware Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transparency/Occlusion: All images are transparent; the depth cue of interposition (occlusion) is missing. Hidden line removal has no meaning, which can cause confusion with high information content. Color Limitations: Color images are impossible because a color point-plotting CRT with sufficiently fast phosphor decay to eliminate smear is not available. The display is limited to monochrome. Resolution Limits: Limited by the size of the mirror and the updating rate of the images, as the mirror must vibrate. Position Accuracy: Points must be displayed within 0.1 inches of their desired position to appear correct. Time Complexity: The rendering time per frame is proportional to the number of points in the slice, O(N), where N is the number of points displayed in that frame. The system runs at a fixed 30 fps. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the refresher buffer containing all 3D points, O(P), where P is the total number of points in the volume. Performance: Maximum display volume is 25 \times 25 \times 25 cm with 128x128 resolution per frame. Strengths: Provides inherent binocular disparity and head motion parallax. Viewable by several observers over a range of distances within a limited solid angle. Limitations: Lack of occlusion cues limits usability for complex scenes. Monochrome only. Limited by mirror size and vibration rate. The variable focal length mirror was first introduced by J.C. Muirhead in 1960. It was soon after used to create a 3-D display device. A known implementation is the Mayo Clinic True Three-Dimension Machine. The method is also referred to as Sher's method, after Sher who proposed a similar system using a vibrating circular mirror and a high-speed monitor. name: Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering
head: DSS color volumetric display rendering, Drawing of multicolor volumetric graphics, LC Color Filter Volume Rendering, LC filter synchronized voxel generation, Miyazaki Galvano Scanner System, Multicolor Volumetric Graphics, Point Cloud Scanner Volume Rendering, Temporal color-synchronized volumetric rendering
body: Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering is a method for rendering volumetric images with arbitrary per-voxel colors by temporally synchronizing the spatial generation of voxels with the switching of a Liquid Crystal (LC) color filter. It solves the problem of multicolor volumetric display by generating application orders of 3D coordinates and color patterns for a beam scanner and an LC color filter, respectively. Unlike Rotational Swept-Screen Projection which relies on persistence of vision in a rotating medium, or Drawing Space Separation (DSS) which focuses on the optical path separation, this method specifically addresses color expression by mapping voxel generation positions to color switching states. It builds on Drawing Space Separation (DSS) by adding a temporal color-synchronization layer. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D point cloud V consisting of M voxels. Each voxel vi is defined by spatial position (xi, yi, zi) and RGB color values (ri, gi, bi). Output: A sequence of application orders for the display system, yielding (x, y) values for the galvanometer scanner, z values for the varifocal lens, and (r, g, b) values for the LC color filter. Data Structures Voxel Cloud (V): A list or array of M objects. Each object contains fields: x, y, z, r, g, b. Layer (P): A subset of V containing N voxels that share the same quantized z-coordinate. Each object contains fields: x, y, r, g, b. Scan Path: A list of indices or voxel references defining the traversal order for each layer. Parameters LC Color Filter Refresh Rate: 60 Hz. Laser Repetition Frequency: 1 kHz. Color Extraction Interval: Different colors are extracted every 17 pulses given the above rates. Quantization Layers: The number of discrete z-layers. The sources provide an example of 30 layers. The exact number is not fixed but depends on the desired depth resolution. Steps 1. Represent Point Cloud: Initialize V = \{v1, v2, \ldots, vM\} where vi = (xi, yi, zi, ri, gi, bi). 2. Quantize Z-Axis: Quantize the z values of V into a desired number of layers. The z axis must match the optical axis direction of the display system. 3. Slice Layers: For each quantized z-layer, define the set of vertices P = \{p1, p2, \ldots, pN\}, where each pj has 2D position (xj, yj) and RGB values (rj, gj, bj). 4. Calculate Optimal Scanning Order: For each layer P, calculate the optimal scanning order that minimizes the total route length. The route length is defined as: \sum{j=1}^{N-1} d(pj, p{j+1}) + d(pN, p1) where d(pj, p{j+1}) is the Euclidean distance between the 2D coordinates of vertices pj and p{j+1}. The Christofides algorithm is applied to all layers to solve this Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). 5. Generate Application Orders: Provide the shortest scanning order obtained for each z to the display system. This yields the (x, y) values for the galvanometer scanner, z values for the varifocal lens, and (r, g, b) values for the LC color filter. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def euclideandistance2d(p1, p2): """Calculate Euclidean distance between two 2D points.""" return math.sqrt((p1['x'] - p2['x'])2 + (p1['y'] - p2['y'])2) def solvetspchristofides(points): # Standard Christofides algorithm implementation details omitted. The sources do not provide the exact graph construction or matching steps. # In a complete implementation, this function would return a permutation of indices # that minimizes the total path length for the given 2D points. pass def rendergalvanometervolumetric(voxelcloud, numlayers): """ Renders volumetric images with arbitrary per-voxel colors. Args: voxelcloud (list): List of dicts, each with keys 'x', 'y', 'z', 'r', 'g', 'b'. numlayers (int): Desired number of discrete z-layers. Returns: list: A list of layers, where each layer is a list of voxel dicts in scan order. """ # Step 1 & 2: Quantize Z values zmin = min(v['z'] for v in voxelcloud) zmax = max(v['z'] for v in voxelcloud) zstep = (zmax - zmin) / numlayers if numlayers > 0 else 1.0 layers = {} for v in voxelcloud: zbin = int((v['z'] - zmin) / zstep) if zbin not in layers: layers[zbin] = [] layers[zbin].append(v) scanorders = [] # Step 3 & 4: Process each layer for zbin, points in layers.items(): if len(points) <= 1: scanorders.append(points) continue # Step 4: Calculate optimal scanning order tourindices = solvetspchristofides(points) orderedpoints = [points[i] for i in tourindices] scanorders.append(orderedpoints) return scanorders Edge Cases and Pitfalls Color Switching Speed: Color expression is limited by the LC filter's switching speed relative to the laser repetition rate. With a 60 Hz filter and 1 kHz laser, different colors are extracted every 17 pulses. Mitigation: Use faster color extraction devices (non-LC) or develop scanning methods that generate voxels per color. Boundary Conditions: The quantization of z must align with the optical axis direction of the display system. Misalignment causes depth errors. TSP Solving: The Christofides algorithm is applied to balance optimality with deterministic execution time, avoiding the prohibitive cost of exact solvers for real-time systems. This method optimizes the traversal path of a beam scanner in a galvanometer-based volumetric display to minimize the total travel distance between voxels within each depth layer, thereby reducing rendering latency and mechanical wear. It solves the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for the 2D coordinates of voxels in each quantized z-layer using the Christofides algorithm, which provides a guaranteed worst-case performance bound for the heuristic. Unlike simpler heuristics (e.g., nearest neighbor) that may produce suboptimal paths, or exact solvers that are computationally prohibitive for real-time systems, this approach balances optimality with deterministic execution time. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is solving the TSP for each layer. The sources do not specify the exact time complexity of the Christofides algorithm implementation used. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the voxel cloud and scan paths. Measured Performance: Demonstrated with a 60 Hz LC filter and 1 kHz laser repetition frequency. Colors are extracted every 17 pulses. Strengths: Enables arbitrary per-voxel colors. Compatible with fluorescent glass displays. Limitations: Color expression is limited by LC filter switching speed. Requires precise synchronization between scanner, varifocal lens, and color filter. When to Use: When multicolor volumetric graphics are required and the display system supports temporal color switching. When Not to Use: When higher color update rates are needed than the LC filter can provide. The method originates from research on volumetric displays using Drawing Space Separation (DSS). It was demonstrated by Miyazaki et al. in 2005 using three galvano scanners to draw volumetric images into fluorescent glass, showing that a beam can excite fluorescent voxels. The specific rendering method for multicolor graphics was detailed in a 2021 paper by Wakunami et al.. The system uses a 3D scanning optical system with three galvano scanners.
