name: Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation
head: Direct volume rendering method for holograms, Approximate Volume Rendering Based CGH Calculation, Approximate Volume Rendering Based CGH Calculation with Elemental Holograms, Approximate volume rendering based CGH calculation method with elemental holograms
body: Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation generates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) for 3D volume data by treating voxels as transparent objects with diffuse reflection properties. Unlike Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) methods which only display objects with maximum voxel values, this approach simulates light propagation from a source to the voxel, diffuse reflection at the voxel, and propagation from the voxel to the viewpoint, allowing for the generation of clear holograms for transparent and multi-layer objects. It serves as an alternative to polygon-based methods, offering superior detail for volumetric data at the cost of significantly higher computational complexity. The method calculates the complex amplitude at the hologram plane by summing contributions from all voxels, modeled as point light sources after rendering. The process involves initializing voxel properties, simulating light transport with attenuation and diffuse reflection, and finally computing the holographic interference pattern. Inputs: Volume data grid of size M \times M \times M (or general dimensions), where each voxel i has a scalar value Ii. Color map and Alpha (\alpha) map definitions. Light source position and intensity I{d0}. Viewpoint position (for the standard method) or Elemental Hologram grid parameters (for the approximate method). Wavelength \lambda and wavenumber k = 2\pi/\lambda. Outputs: Complex amplitude distribution \mu(\xi, \eta) for each pixel (\xi, \eta) on the hologram plane. Voxel Array: Stores R, G, B, \alpha for each voxel. Hologram Plane: 2D grid of complex numbers. Elemental Holograms (Approximate Method): A subset of the hologram plane, where each elemental hologram is represented by its center pixel for propagation calculations. 1. Initialize Color and Opacity: For each voxel x with value Ix, calculate its color components Cx (where C \in \{R, G, B, \alpha\}) using linear interpolation on the provided maps: Cx = C3 - (C3 - C2) \frac{I3 - Ix}{I3 - I2} where C2, C3 are known parameters of the color/alpha map at endpoints with voxel values I2, I3. 2. Light Propagation to Voxel (Attenuation): For a voxel eli, calculate the incident light intensity I{di} from the light source. Light attenuates as it passes through preceding voxels j along the path: I{di} = I{d0} \prod{j=0} (1 - \alphaj) where I{d0} is the source intensity and \alphaj is the opacity of voxel j. 3. Diffuse Reflection Calculation: Calculate the reflected light intensity I{ri} using the Lambertian reflection model: I{ri} = k{di} I{di} \max(0, \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{N}) where: k{di} is the ratio of Lambert light. \mathbf{L} is the unit vector pointing from the voxel to the light source. \mathbf{N} is the normal unit vector, derived from the gradient of the \alpha map in x, y, z directions. 4. Light Propagation to Viewpoint (Attenuation): Calculate the final reflected light intensity I{rLi} reaching the viewpoint from voxel eli. Light attenuates through subsequent voxels j between the voxel and the viewpoint: I{rLi} = I{ri} \prod{j=i+1} (1 - \alphaj) Note: I{di} and I{ri} are independent of the viewpoint direction, but I{rLi} must be recalculated for each viewpoint. 5. CGH Calculation (Point Light Source Method): Treat each voxel as a point light source. The complex amplitude \mui(\xi, \eta) contributed by voxel i at hologram pixel (\xi, \eta) is: \mui(\xi, \eta) = \frac{\sqrt{I{rLi}}}{ri} \exp\left(-j(k ri + \phii)\right) where ri is the distance from voxel i to the hologram pixel, and \phii is the initial phase. The total complex amplitude Uh(\xi, \eta) is the superposition of all voxels: Uh(\xi, \eta) = \sum{i=1}^{M} \mui(\xi, \eta) 6. Approximate Calculation with Elemental Holograms (Optional Optimization): To reduce computation, divide the hologram plane into Ne elemental holograms. For each elemental hologram k, use only the center pixel to represent the entire elemental hologram for the final light propagation calculation. The amplitude for elemental hologram k is I{ek{rLi}}. The complexity is reduced from O(M^2 N) to O(M^2 Ne) for the propagation step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def volumerenderingcgh(volumedata, colormap, alphamap, lightsourcepos, viewpointpos, wavelength, hologramplane): """ Calculate CGH using Volume Rendering based method. Args: volumedata: 3D array of voxel values I. colormap: function(I) -> (R, G, B) alphamap: function(I) -> alpha lightsourcepos: 3D vector (Lx, Ly, Lz) viewpointpos: 3D vector (Vx, Vy, Vz) wavelength: float, lambda hologramplane: 2D array of complex numbers, shape (H, W) Returns: hologramplane: Complex amplitude distribution. """ k = 2.0 math.pi / wavelength Mx, My, Mz = volumedata.shape voxellist = [] # Pre-calculate voxel properties and positions for iz in range(Mz): for iy in range(My): for ix in range(Mx): val = volumedata[iz, iy, ix] R, G, B = colormap(val) alpha = alphamap(val) pos = (ix, iy, iz) voxellist.append({'pos': pos, 'R': R, 'G': G, 'B': B, 'alpha': alpha, 'val': val}) # Step 2-4: Light Transport for each voxel voxelcontributions = [] for v in voxellist: pos = v['pos'] alpha = v['alpha'] # Step 2: Light Propagation to Voxel (Attenuation) Idi = raymarchattenuation(lightsourcepos, pos, volumedata, alphamap) Idi = 1.0 # Scaled by Id0 (assumed normalized to 1.0 in this implementation) # Step 3: Diffuse Reflection N = computealphagradient(pos, volumedata, alphamap) L = normalize(subtract(lightsourcepos, pos)) kdi = 1.0 dotval = max(0.0, dot(L, N)) Iri = kdi Idi dotval # Step 4: Light Propagation to Viewpoint (Attenuation) IrLi = Iri raymarchattenuation(pos, viewpointpos, volumedata, alphamap) voxelcontributions.append({'pos': pos, 'intensity': IrLi}) # Step 5: CGH Calculation H, W = hologramplane.shape for y in range(H): for x in range(W): pixelpos = (x, y, 0.0) totalamplitude = complex(0.0, 0.0) for vc in voxelcontributions: vpos = vc['pos'] IrLi = vc['intensity'] ri = distance(vpos, pixelpos) phii = 0.0 phase = k ri + phii amplitude = math.sqrt(IrLi) / ri complexcontrib = amplitude cmath.exp(-1j phase) totalamplitude += complexcontrib hologramplane[y, x] = totalamplitude return hologramplane def subtract(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def distance(a, b): return math.sqrt(dot(subtract(a, b), subtract(a, b))) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def computealphagradient(pos, volumedata, alphamap): ix, iy, iz = pos Mx, My, Mz = volumedata.shape dx = alphamap(volumedata[min(ix+1, Mx-1), iy, iz]) - alphamap(volumedata[max(ix-1, 0), iy, iz]) dy = alphamap(volumedata[ix, min(iy+1, My-1), iz]) - alphamap(volumedata[ix, max(iy-1, 0), iz]) dz = alphamap(volumedata[ix, iy, min(iz+1, Mz-1)]) - alphamap(volumedata[ix, iy, max(iz-1, 0)]) return normalize((dx, dy, dz)) def raymarchattenuation(start, end, volumedata, alphamap): steps = max(abs(end[i]-start[i]) for i in range(3)) 10 if steps == 0: return 1.0 attenuation = 1.0 for t in range(steps + 1): frac = t / steps curr = add(start, scale(subtract(end, start), frac)) ix, iy, iz = int(curr[0]), int(curr[1]), int(curr[2]) if 0 <= ix < volumedata.shape[0] and 0 <= iy < A layered rendering method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) of 3D objects that uses view volume transformation to avoid shape distortion and size deviation in the reconstructed image, preserving the real size of the original model. Unlike conventional layer-based methods where sampling pitch in Fresnel diffraction is proportional to reconstruction distance (causing inconsistent sizes), this method preserves the real size of the original model. A calculating method that generates a 3D hologram by encoding 2D projection images of an object captured from multiple angles. Method 1 adds inclination factors to each 2D projection image, conducts an integral calculation, uses the integrals as pixel values for corresponding points in the projection image, and combines pixel values to form the hologram. Method 2 transforms 2D projection images into 2D spectral matrices via Fourier transform, combines all 2D matrices into a 3D matrix, extracts a 2D matrix indicating 3D characteristics by analyzing the functional expression of the optical field distribution, and encodes the 2D matrix to obtain the hologram. Time Complexity: Incident light calculation: O(M^2). Reflected light calculation: O(M). Final light propagation: O(M^2 \cdot Ne) for the approximate method with elemental holograms, or O(M^2 \cdot N) for the standard method. Total CGH calculation complexity: O(M^2 \cdot N). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels M and hologram pixels N. Measured Performance: In experiments, the proposed method took 24.3 hours for rendering and 3.8 minutes for CGH calculation, compared to 1.5 hours/0.3 seconds for polygon-based and 0.2 hours/0.6 seconds for MIP-based methods. The approximate method with elemental holograms reduced rendering time to 3.6 hours and CGH calculation to 3.7 minutes. Strengths: Generates clear holograms for transparent and multi-layer objects; better detail than polygon-based methods. Limitations: Extremely high computational cost; requires special lighting conditions for reconstruction (point monochrome light source at a specific angle). Holography is a form of lensless photography based on the recording of amplitude and phase of light illuminating an object. Computed holograms are created by calculating the interference pattern and recording it on film. However, output devices often cannot transfer the pattern to film at the required resolution, and fully computed holograms are difficult and expensive to record. This method was proposed to address the limitations of MIP-based methods, which only show objects with maximum voxel values, by applying direct volume rendering with transparency and diffuse reflection. name: View Volume Transformation Based Layered Method
head: Layered rendering method for CGH with view volume transformation
body: A layered rendering method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) of 3D objects that uses view volume transformation to avoid shape distortion and size deviation in the reconstructed image, preserving the real size of the original model. Unlike conventional layer-based methods where sampling pitch in Fresnel diffraction is proportional to reconstruction distance (causing inconsistent sizes), this method preserves the real size of the original model. Data Structures: Layer Data: The 3D object is divided into multiple layers according to depth cues using layered rendering technology. Hologram Plane: A 2D grid representing the spatial light modulator (SLM) or recording medium. Steps: 1. Layer Division: Divide the 3D object into multiple layers based on depth cues using layered rendering technology. 2. Ray Tracing: Use a ray tracing algorithm to render the layers of the 3D object, generating the initial geometry and optical properties for each depth slice. 3. View Volume Transformation & Diffraction: Perform Fresnel diffraction calculations for each layer using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. The view volume transformation adjusts the sampling coordinates so that the hologram plane pitch remains consistent regardless of the layer's distance, thereby preserving the real size of the object. 4. Hologram Generation: Coherently sum the diffracted fields from all layers to generate the final CGH. Formula: The Fresnel diffraction calculation for a layer is expressed as: Up\left(p\frac{\rho}{\rho0}, q\frac{\rho}{\rho0}\right) = e^{i\frac{2\pi z}{\lambda}} \frac{i}{\lambda z} e^{i\frac{k}{2z}\left(\left(p\frac{\rho}{\rho0}\right)^2+\left(q\frac{\rho}{\rho0}\right)^2\right)} \times \text{FFT}\left\{ U0\left(m\frac{\Delta x}{\rho0}, n\frac{\Delta y}{\rho0}\right) e^{i\frac{k}{2z}(m^2\Delta x^2+n^2\Delta y^2)} \right\} Where: Up is the complex amplitude distribution on the hologram plane. (u, v) represents the position of the point on the hologram plane, discretized as (p\frac{\rho}{\rho0}, q\frac{\rho}{\rho0}). (x, y) represents the position of the point on the object plane, discretized as (m\frac{\Delta x}{\rho0}, n\frac{\Delta y}{\rho0}). i is the imaginary unit. \lambda is the wavelength of the light. z is the reconstruction distance. k is the wave number, k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}. U0 is the complex amplitude distribution of the point on the object plane. \text{FFT}\{A\} represents the 2D Fourier Transform of A. \rho0, \rho, \Delta x, \Delta y are scaling and sampling parameters used in the view volume transformation and diffraction grid mapping. Parameters: Wavelength of light (\lambda): 633 nm. Hardware acceleration: Uses GPU parallelism and the Fast Fourier Transform library (cuFFT). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import cmath import math def generatecghviewvolumetransformation(objectlayers, wavelength, distances, slmsize, slmpixels, objsize, objpixels): """ Generates a CGH using view volume transformation based layered method. Args: objectlayers: List of 2D arrays (complex amplitude U0 for each layer). wavelength: Float, wavelength in meters. distances: List of floats, reconstruction distance z for each layer. slmsize: Tuple (width, height) in meters, physical size of SLM. slmpixels: Tuple (width, height) in pixels, resolution of SLM. objsize: Tuple (width, height) in meters, physical size of object plane. objpixels: Tuple (width, height) in pixels, resolution of object plane. Returns: cgh: 2D array, the generated hologram. """ k = 2 math.pi / wavelength h, w = slmpixels H, W = slmsize oh, ow = objpixels Oh, Ow = objsize # View volume transformation scaling factors rho0 = 1.0 # Not given in the sources. rho = 1.0 # Not given in the sources. # Initialize hologram plane cgh = [[0+0j for in range(w)] for in range(h)] # Sampling pitches dx = Ow / ow dy = Oh / oh du = W / w dv = H / h for layeridx, (U0, z) in enumerate(zip(objectlayers, distances)): # 1. Prepare FFT input: U0 modulated by object-plane quadratic phase fftinput = [[0+0j for in range(ow)] for in range(oh)] for n in range(oh): for m in range(ow): x = m dx y = n dy phaseobj = cmath.exp(1j k / (2 z) (x2 + y2)) fftinput[n][m] = U0[n][m] phaseobj # 2. Compute 2D FFT of the modulated input # The source specifies using the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm. # A standard radix-2 Cooley-Tukey FFT is applied here. fftresult = [[0+0j for in range(ow)] for in range(oh)] for q in range(oh): for p in range(ow): acc = 0+0j for n in range(oh): for m in range(ow): acc += fftinput[n][m] cmath.exp(-2j math.pi (pn/oh + qm/ow)) fftresult[q][p] = acc # 3. Apply hologram-plane quadratic phase and pre-factor, then accumulate prefactor = cmath.exp(1j 2 math.pi z / wavelength) (1j / (wavelength z)) for q in range(oh): for p in range(ow): u = p du v = q dv phaseholo = cmath.exp(1j k / (2 z) (u2 + v2)) cgh[q][p] += prefactor phaseholo fftresult[q][p] return cgh Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential terms involve large arguments for large z or small \lambda. High-precision floating-point arithmetic is recommended to avoid phase wrapping errors. Boundaries: The FFT assumes periodic boundary conditions. Zero-padding the object layers before FFT can reduce aliasing artifacts at the edges of the hologram plane. Degenerate Input: If a layer has zero amplitude, the calculation should skip to avoid division by zero or unnecessary computation. Measured Performance: Real-time interaction with digitally reconstructed holographic images with clear depth cues is experimentally demonstrated. Uses GPU parallelism and cuFFT for acceleration. Strengths: Preserves the real size of the original model, avoiding shape distortion and size deviation common in conventional layer-based methods. Limitations: Requires accurate depth cueing and layer division. Performance depends on the number of layers and hologram resolution. When to use: When real-size preservation of 3D objects is critical in holographic displays. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was presented by Dong Chen, Hui Li, and Yuan Wang in 2018. It addresses the issue of shape distortion and size deviation in 3D reconstructed images existing in conventional layer-based methods. The experimental setup used a reflection-type spatial light modulator (SLM) and a laser with a wavelength of 633 nm. Three letters (A, B, C) with height and width of 6 mm, positioned at near, middle, and far distances, were reconstructed to verify real-size preservation. name: Holographic Stereogram
head: HPO Stereogram, Horizontal-Parallax-Only Stereogram, Stereogram
body: A Holographic Stereogram is a type of computer-generated hologram composed of a series of discrete 2D perspective views of an object scene. It produces a view-dependent image that presents the corresponding perspective view in each horizontally displaced direction, functioning similarly to lenticular or parallax barrier displays. It restricts vertical parallax to achieve this horizontal-only view dependency. Inputs: A 3D scene model or point cloud; camera parameters (field of view, resolution). Outputs: A 2D fringe pattern (hologram) suitable for display on an SLM or printed medium. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. View Generation: Generate a sequence of perspective views by moving a virtual camera laterally in discrete steps across the scene. 2. Fringe Combination: Combine the generated views to generate the holographic fringe for display. This involves mapping each view to a specific horizontal segment or column of the hologram plane. 3. Display: Output the resulting fringe pattern to a spatial light modulator (SLM) or print medium. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of Views (N): Must be large enough to create a high-quality image free from sampling artifacts. The exact number N depends on the target horizontal field of view (FOV), with larger FOVs requiring more views and increasing computational complexity. Camera Step Size: Determines the angular separation between views. Smaller steps improve smoothness but increase computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Artifacts: A small number of perspective views leads to visible artifacts and poor image quality. Computational Load: The need for a large number of views limits computation speed, although specialized hardware can achieve nearly interactive rates. A technique used to acquire sub-holograms that simulate a pinhole camera view. A window with the resolution of the vertical axis of the hologram moves along the horizontal axis to extract different views. The apertures can be chosen densely enough to overlap, as increasing the number of views improves final rendering quality. However, larger targeted FOVs require more views and increased computational complexity. Complexity: Computationally expensive due to the need for a large number of perspective views. Complexity scales with the number of views required for the target FOV. Performance: Allows computation at nearly interactive rates when implemented on specialized hardware. Strengths: Suitable for horizontal parallax applications. Limitations: Limited to horizontal parallax; requires many views for high quality, impacting speed. The holographic stereogram approach was introduced as a method to produce 3D images with resolution finer than can be utilized by the human visual system, avoiding the need for supercomputers in some implementations. It is based on the principle of combining discrete 2D perspective views to form a holographic fringe. name: Diffraction-Specific Approach
head: Hogel Vector Approach, Hogel-based CGH, Interference-Based Approach
body: The Diffraction-Specific Approach is a method for calculating Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) that avoids the direct simulation of optical interference between object and reference waves. Instead, it treats the holographic fringe as a signal that can be subsampled spatially into functional elements called "hogels" and spectrally into an array of "hogel vectors". By working backwards from the 3D image and leveraging standard 3D computer graphics rendering techniques (orthographic projections), this approach significantly increases computation speed and achieves bandwidth compression compared to conventional interference-based methods. It is distinguished from its sibling Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation by its explicit decomposition of the wavefield into hogel vectors and its reliance on texture-mapping hardware for decoding. The method consists of two main stages: encoding (generation of the hogel-vector array) and decoding (reconstruction of the fringe). Inputs: A 3D scene defined by primitives (points, polygons) with attributes including color, lighting, shading, and occlusion information. Outputs: A holographic fringe pattern (complex amplitude or phase-only data) suitable for display on a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). 1. Hogel: A spatially subsampled functional holographic element that partitions the hologram plane. 2. Hogel Vector: A spectral subsampling of the wavefront information associated with a single hogel, storing values for each projection direction. 3. Basis Fringes: A precomputed set of reference fringe patterns corresponding to the spectral samples, used during the decoding step. Compression Ratio (CR): The ratio between the size of the fringe and the hogel-vector array. Typical values are 8:1, 16:1, and 32:1. Spatial Subsampling: Determines the hogel grid resolution. Spectral Subsampling: Determines the number of components in each hogel vector. 1. 3D Scene Preparation: Perform a 3D filling operation to generate a list of 3D points or primitives, including color, lighting, shading, and occlusion data. 2. Orthographic Projections: Render a series of orthographic projections of the 3D scene. Each projection corresponds to a specific spectral sample (direction) of the hogels, providing a discrete sampling of space (pixels) and spectrum (projection direction). 3. Vector Conversion: Convert the rendered orthographic projections into a hogel-vector array by mapping the pixel values from the projections to the components of the hogel vectors. 1. Basis Fringe Retrieval: Retrieve the precomputed basis fringes corresponding to the spectral samples used during encoding. 2. Inner Product Calculation: Compute the inner product between the array of hogel vectors and the basis fringes to reconstruct the interference fringe. Implementation Note: This is accelerated using graphics hardware. The texture mapping function multiplies a component from each hogel vector by a replicated array of a single basis fringe. This operation is repeated for each hogel-vector component, and the results are accumulated in an accumulation buffer. 3. Output Generation: The accumulated result forms the final holographic fringe. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def diffractionspecificcgh(scene, hogelgrid, spectraldirections, basisfringes): """ Generates a holographic fringe using the Diffraction-Specific Approach. Args: scene: List of 3D primitives with color/lighting data. hogelgrid: Grid definition for spatial subsampling (hogels). spectraldirections: List of viewing directions for spectral subsampling. basisfringes: Precomputed array of basis fringe patterns. Returns: fringe: The reconstructed holographic fringe. """ # Step 1: Encoding - Generate Hogel-Vector Array # Render orthographic projections for each spectral direction projections = [] for direction in spectraldirections: # Standard 3D rendering of scene along direction proj = renderorthographic(scene, direction) projections.append(proj) # Convert projections into hogel-vector array # Each hogel in the grid stores a vector of values, one per spectral direction hogelvectors = createemptyhogelarray(hogelgrid, len(spectraldirections)) for idx, proj in enumerate(projections): # Map projection pixels to hogel grid cells for cell in hogelgrid.cells(): # Aggregate projection data for this cell into the vector component hogelvectors[cell][idx] = aggregateprojectiondata(proj, cell) # Step 2: Decoding - Recover Fringe # Initialize output fringe buffer fringe = createzeroslike(basisfringes[0]) # Compute inner product between hogel vectors and basis fringes # Exploits texture mapping: multiply each vector component by its basis fringe for cell in hogelgrid.cells(): hv = hogelvectors[cell] for compidx in range(len(hv)): # Multiply hogel vector component by corresponding basis fringe contribution = hv[compidx] basisfringes[compidx] # Accumulate result in buffer fringe += contribution return fringe def renderorthographic(scene, direction): # Standard computer graphics rendering of scene using orthographic projection return render(scene, projectiontype="orthographic", viewdirection=direction) def createemptyhogelarray(grid, numcomponents): # Initialize array where each grid cell holds a list of numcomponents values return {cell: [0.0] numcomponents for cell in grid.cells()} def aggregateprojectiondata(projection, cell): # Sample or average pixel values from the projection corresponding to the cell return mean(projection[cell.region]) def createzeroslike(array): # Create a new array of the same shape filled with zeros return [[0.0] len(row) for row in array] Image Sharpness vs. Compression: Higher compression ratios (e.g., 32:1) result in acceptable but degraded image quality due to added blur. For CR \le 8:1, the blur is invisible to the Human Visual System (HVS). Hardware Dependency: The decoding step relies heavily on multiplication-accumulation (MAC) operations, making performance significantly tied to the availability of hardware acceleration (e.g., texture mapping and accumulation buffers). Basis Fringe Precomputation: The method requires precomputed basis fringes, and reconstruction accuracy depends on their fidelity. Techniques to increase fringe computation speed and reduce data volume, including spatial subsampling, nonuniform sampling, and standard video compression algorithms. Nonuniformly sampled fringes provide lossless bandwidth compression, whereas standard MPEG algorithms can be used for encoding/decoding computed fringes. This approach increases fringe computation speed by 3000 times for the same hardware implementation. A technique within the diffraction-specific approach where the fringe is subsampled spatially into hogels and spectrally into hogel vectors. It uses standard 3D computer graphics rendering (orthographic projections) to generate the data. The inner product between hogel vectors and precomputed basis fringes is performed rapidly by exploiting texture mapping and accumulation buffers. This achieved a computation time of 0.9 seconds for fringes of 6-MB with CR=32:1 using Silicon Graphics RealityEngine2 (RE2). A variant that further subsamples the hogel in the spatial domain. Each hogel is encoded as a spatially smaller "fringelet". Using a simple sample-replication decoding scheme, fringelets provide the fastest method of fringe computation. Complex images have been generated in under one second for 6 MB fringes. Additionally, a "fringelet display" can optically decode fringelets to produce a CR-times greater image volume without increased electronic bandwidth. Computational Complexity: The encoding stage involves standard 3D rendering, which is efficient. The decoding stage involves many multiplication-accumulation (MAC) calculations, which can be slow on general-purpose CPUs but are accelerated by specialized hardware (DSP cards, graphics subsystems). Performance: For a 6-MB fringe with CR=32:1, computation time was 0.9 seconds on Silicon Graphics RealityEngine2 (RE2). With specialized DSP hardware, computation times of about one second were achieved for similar fringe sizes. Bandwidth Compression: Achieves significant bandwidth reduction. Compression ratios of 8:1, 16:1, and 32:1 are typical. Image Quality: Accompanied by a loss in image sharpness (added blur). For CR \le 8:1, blur is invisible to the HVS. For CR 16:1 or 32:1, good images are achieved with acceptable degradation. Strengths: Fast computation for interactive displays, bandwidth compression, leverages existing 3D graphics hardware. Limitations: Loss of image sharpness at high compression ratios, reliance on precomputed basis fringes, decoding complexity without hardware acceleration. The Diffraction-Specific Approach was introduced as an alternative to the conventional Interference-Based Approach for computing holographic fringes. It was developed to address the high computational cost of simulating optical interference, which requires billions of complex arithmetic operations (trigonometric functions and square roots) for small simple holographic images. The approach was pioneered by researchers who recognized that the fringe could be treated as a subsampled signal (hogels and hogel vectors) and reconstructed using standard 3D graphics techniques. It was presented in the context of interactive three-dimensional holographic displays, aiming to achieve computation speeds sufficient for real-time or near-real-time holographic video. name: Overlap-Add Stereogram (OLAS)
head: Overlap-Add method
body: Overlap-Add Stereogram (OLAS) is a holographic stereogram algorithm that encodes a light field into a hologram by treating the stereogram as an inverse Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), allowing hogels to overlap and coherently add in the complex domain. It solves the spatio-angular resolution tradeoff inherent in traditional Holographic Stereogram (HS) methods, where increasing hogel size improves angular resolution but degrades spatial resolution. Unlike its sibling Phase-Added Stereogram (PAS), which requires precise phase alignment across non-overlapping or tiled hogels, OLAS allows large hogels to overlap and shift by a single pixel, breaking the spatial-angular resolution tradeoff and producing image quality independent of hogel size. Inputs: Light field L(x, y, ux, uy): Angular radiance distribution, where (x, y) are spatial coordinates and (ux, uy) are spatial frequencies (u{x,y} = \sin(\theta{x,y})/\lambda). Depth field D(x, y, ux, uy): Depth information corresponding to the light field samples. Hogel dimensions m, n: Width and height of the local hogel in pixels. Window function w(s, t): Typically a Hann window. Wavelength \lambda. Outputs: Complex-valued hologram buffer h(x, y). Data Structures: L: 4D array or tensor of shape (HL, WL, HA, WA), where HL, WL are light field spatial dimensions and HA, WA are angular dimensions. D: 4D array of same spatial/angular dimensions as L. h: 2D complex array of shape (HH, WH), initialized to zero. w: 2D real array of shape (m, n). Parameters: Hogel size m, n: In OLAS, the method is invariant to this choice, unlike previous methods where optimal size varies with object depth. However, a minimum effective hogel size is determined by the farthest plane: hogel\size \ge z{max} \tan(\theta{max}) / p, where z{max} is max depth, \theta{max} is max diffraction angle, and p is pixel pitch. Window function w: Hann window is used. Steps: 1. For each pixel (x0, y0) in the output hologram coordinates (which correspond to spatial centers in the light field domain): 2. Extract the angular radiance distribution a = L(x0, y0, ux, uy) from the input light field. 3. Compute the phase \phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} D(x0, y0, ux, uy) using the depth field. 4. Compute the local hogel by taking the Fourier transform over angular coordinates (ux, uy) of a \cdot \exp(i \cdot \phi). Let s, t be local hogel coordinates: \text{hogel}(s, t) = \mathcal{F}{ux, uy} \left[ a(ux, uy) \cdot \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} D(x0, y0, ux, uy)\right) \right] Note: The Fourier transform maps angular frequencies to spatial hogel coordinates. 5. Multiply the computed hogel by the window function w(s, t). 6. Add the windowed hogel to the hologram buffer h at the appropriate spatial location (x0, y0) with offsets based on hogel dimensions m, n. Specifically, for local coordinates s \in [-m/2, m/2] and t \in [-n/2, n/2]: h\left(x0 + s, y0 + t\right) \leftarrow h\left(x0 + s, y0 + t\right) + w(s, t) \cdot \text{hogel}(s, t) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeolas(L, D, m, n, lambdawavelength): """ Compute Overlap-Add Stereogram hologram. Args: L: Light field array of shape (HL, WL, HA, WA). L[x, y, uxidx, uyidx] corresponds to L(x, y, ux, uy). D: Depth field array of shape (HL, WL, HA, WA). m: Hogel width in pixels. n: Hogel height in pixels. lambdawavelength: Wavelength of light. Returns: h: Complex hologram array of shape (HH, WH). """ HL, WL, HA, WA = L.shape # Determine hologram size. # In OLAS, hogels overlap by 1 pixel. The hologram covers the spatial extent. # Assuming L is sampled on a grid that maps directly to hologram pixels. HH, WH = HL, WL # Initialize hologram buffer h = np.zeros((HH, WH), dtype=np.complex128) # Create Hann window # w(s, t) for s in [-m/2, m/2), t in [-n/2, n/2) # Note: Standard Hann window definition usually 0 to M-1. # We need to center it. s = np.arange(-m // 2, m // 2 + (1 if m % 2 == 0 else 0)) t = np.arange(-n // 2, n // 2 + (1 if n % 2 == 0 else 0)) S, T = np.meshgrid(s, t, indexing='ij') # Hann window: 0.5 (1 - cos(2pik/(N-1))) # Adjust indices to be 0..m-1 for standard formula snorm = (S + m // 2) / (m - 1) if m > 1 else 0.5 tnorm = (T + n // 2) / (n - 1) if n > 1 else 0.5 w = 0.5 (1 - np.cos(2 np.pi snorm)) (1 - np.cos(2 np.pi tnorm)) # Precompute angular frequency coordinates if needed for FFT shift/centering # The FFT output order corresponds to frequencies [0,..., N/2, -N/2,..., -1] # We assume L is sampled uniformly in angular space. for x0 in range(HH): for y0 in range(WH): # 1. Extract angular radiance # L[x0, y0,:,:] is the angular slice at spatial location (x0, y0) a = L[x0, y0,:,:] # 2. Extract depth dslice = D[x0, y0,:,:] # 3. Compute phase # phi = (2pi / lambda) D phi = (2 np.pi / lambdawavelength) dslice # 4. Modulate amplitude with phase # a exp(i phi) modulated = a np.exp(1j phi) # 5. Compute local hogel via Fourier Transform over angular coordinates # F{ux, uy} # The result is a 2D array of size (HA, WA) # We need to map this to the hogel coordinates s, t. # The hogel size m, n might differ from angular sampling HA, WA. # The source implies the hogel is the FT of the angular slice. # If m != HA, interpolation or zero-padding is required. # Assuming m=HA and n=WA for direct mapping as per "hogel dimensions" # If not, we assume the hogel is defined on the angular grid. hogel = np.fft.fft2(modulated) # 6. Multiply by window and add to hologram # The hogel is centered at (x0, y0). # We add w(s,t) hogel(s,t) to h(x0+s, y0+t) # Ensure shapes match for broadcasting/addition # hogel shape: (HA, WA) # w shape: (m, n) # If m != HA or n != WA, we must resize or assume they are equal. # The source says "hogel dimensions m, n". It also says "shift by a single pixel". # This implies the hogel is evaluated on a grid of size m x n. # If HA != m, we assume the hogel is interpolated or the angular sampling matches the hogel size. # Given the complexity, we assume HA == m and WA == n for the core definition. if m != HA or n != WA: # Resize hogel to m x n if necessary. # This is a gap filler. Standard interpolation (e.g., bilinear) # or zero-padding in frequency domain would be used. # For simplicity in this generic implementation, we assume m=HA, n=WA. pass # Add to hologram # h[x0 + s, y0 + t] += w[s, t] hogel[s, t] # Vectorized addition: # Create offset grid # This loop is slow, but represents the algorithm. for sidx in range(m): for tidx in range(n): hx = x0 + s - (m // 2) # Adjust for centering hy = y0 + t - (n // 2) # Boundary check if 0 <= hx < HH and 0 <= hy < WH: h[hx, hy] += w[sidx, tidx] hogel[sidx, tidx] return h Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undersampling: If the light field is undersampled angularly such that the spatial shift of a point between views exceeds the hogel size, reconstruction artifacts occur. The minimum effective hogel size is determined by the farthest plane: hogel\size \ge z{max} \tan(\theta{max}) / p. Phase Misalignment: Unlike PAS, OLAS uses depth to align phases across overlapping hogels, avoiding the phase misalignment issues of traditional HS. Information Loss: Unlike APAS, OLAS does not crop the hogels, preserving more information of the target light field. A depth-free variant of the Overlap-Add Stereogram (OLAS) method that allows adjacent hogel shifts to constructively overlap and add without requiring accurate depth information, similar to how the Holographic Stereogram (HS) relates to the Phase-Added Stereogram (PAS). It computes the phase factor for each spatial frequency based on the relative phase shift for each pixel to the next, rather than using depth-dependent propagation. It is used to encode specularities and other view-dependent effects with poorly defined depth. Time and Memory Complexity: Traditional HS algorithms have O(m^2 \log n) complexity, where n is the hogel size and m is the hologram resolution. OLAS has algorithmic complexity roughly O(m^2 n^2 \log n), where m is hologram resolution and n is hogel size. For n^2 hogels, each requires n^2 \log n operations for the Fourier transform. The computation is comparable to concurrent work by Park and Askari [2019]. Measured Performance: OLAS produces images with much higher spatial resolution than other stereogram algorithms (like HS) because it overlaps instead of tiles hogels. OLAS produces more accurate occlusions and parallax compared to the Fresnel method. OLAS provides higher image quality and natively supports view-dependent effects (occlusions, reflections), whereas Fresnel holograms do not natively support these effects. However, Fresnel holograms have higher computation complexity. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Invariant to hogel size: Does not degrade spatial resolution with increasing hogel size. Scene-invariant: Does not require different fringe pattern sizes for different depths, unlike Fresnel holograms. Coherent addition: Adds hogels coherently in the complex domain to take full advantage of hologram degrees of freedom, achieving maximum image quality. Avoids parallax error: Unlike methods using non-overlapping hogels with wavefront propagation (e.g., Shi et al. [2017]), OLAS avoids parallax error on the order of the hogel size. Limitations: Requires depth information: Standard OLAS requires dense light field depth information D(x, y, ux, uy). Undersampling artifacts: If the underlying light field is too sparsely sampled angularly, reconstruction artifacts occur. Computational cost: While more efficient than Fresnel for view-dependent effects, it is more complex than basic HS. When to use: Use OLAS when high spatial and angular resolution are both required, and view-dependent effects (occlusions, reflections) are important. Use OLAS when the scene contains objects at varying depths, as it is depth-invariant. Use dfOLAS when depth information is unavailable or poorly defined (e.g., specularities). When not to use: Do not use if the light field is severely undersampled angularly, as artifacts will occur. Do not use if computational resources are extremely limited and view-dependent effects are not critical, as Fresnel or basic HS might be simpler (though lower quality for view-dependent effects). The first Holographic Stereogram (HS) was optically recorded in 1967 by Benton [1983]. Computer-generated stereograms were proposed shortly after by Yatagai [1976], and real-time implementations were demonstrated by Lucente and Galyean [1995]. Traditional HS algorithms suffer from a spatio-angular resolution tradeoff because hogels are treated as independent and out of phase. Phase-Added Stereograms (PAS) were introduced to keep hogels in phase [Yamaguchi et al. 1993], with improvements like APAS, CPAS, and FPAS [Kang et al. 2016, 2008]. OLAS was proposed by Padmanaban, Peng, and Wetzstein in 2019. It is used in holographic near-eye displays for VR/AR applications to encode view-dependent lighting effects of a light field into a hologram. name: Phase-Added Stereogram (PAS)
head: Accurate PAS (APAS), CPAS, FPAS
body: Phase-Added Stereogram (PAS) is a holographic stereogram calculation method that resolves the phase discontinuity between independent hogels by introducing a depth-dependent phase factor, allowing hogels to interfere constructively. Unlike standard Holographic Stereograms (HS) which treat hogels as independent and out-of-phase, PAS uses a depth field to align phases across the hologram, significantly improving focused spot brightness and depth of field. It differs from its sibling Overlap-Add Stereogram (OLAS) by relying on non-overlapping tiled hogels with a hard trade-off between spatial and angular resolution, whereas OLAS uses overlapping hogels to maintain resolution independent of hogel size. Inputs: Light field L: A 2D array of complex values representing the amplitude and phase of the light field, or specifically the amplitude if phase is reconstructed. In the context of PAS, L is typically the magnitude of the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) of the scene. Depth field D: A 2D array containing depth information for each ray in the light field. This is not present in standard light fields and must be provided or estimated. Wavelength \lambda: The wavelength of the reconstruction light. Hogel size N: The dimensions of the hogel tile (e.g., N \times N pixels). Outputs: Hologram: A tiled array of complex-valued hogels that, when illuminated, reconstruct the 3D scene with in-phase interference. Data Structures: The hologram is a 2D grid of hogels. Each hogel is a complex-valued matrix of size N \times N. The light field L and depth field D are structured as 2D grids corresponding to the angular and spatial sampling of the scene. Steps: 1. Compute Complex STFT: Calculate the complex Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) for the scene. Since standard light fields only provide amplitude, the phase is recovered using the depth field D. The complex STFT value S for a given spatial location is calculated as: S = L \cdot \exp\left(i \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}} \cdot D\right) where L is the light field amplitude, D is the depth, and \lambda is the wavelength. 2. Hogel Calculation: Process the complex STFT in a hogel-by-hogel manner. For each hogel position, extract the corresponding region from the complex STFT. 3. Fourier Transform: Compute the Fourier transform of the extracted complex STFT region to generate the hogel. This step effectively inverts the STFT to produce the holographic fringe pattern for that specific hogel. 4. Tiling: Tile the calculated complex hogels together to form the final hologram. Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of light. Typical values depend on the display technology (e.g., 532 nm for green laser). Not given in the sources. Hogel Size N: Determines the trade-off between spatial and angular resolution. Typical values are small integers (e.g., 13 \times 13). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Field Requirement: PAS requires a depth field D for every ray. Standard light fields do not contain phase or depth information, so this data must be explicitly provided or estimated. Aliasing: As hogel sizes increase beyond an optimum, the focused point develops aliasing artifacts. Resolution Trade-off: There is a hard trade-off between angular and spatial resolution. Larger hogels increase angular resolution (and depth of field) but decrease spatial resolution. An improvement over PAS that computes local Fourier transforms on a light field with higher angular resolution (larger input hogel) and then crops the result to the target output hogel size. It computes a larger "input" hogel to benefit from finer angular resolution, then crops it to a smaller "output" hogel size to maintain spatial resolution before tiling. This method requires a distance-dependent optimal input hogel size to avoid blurriness or haloing; smaller input sizes are blurry, and larger sizes exhibit haloing and edge artifacts. Unlike base APAS, some variants require knowledge of a point's location prior to quantization on a pixel grid (e.g., point clouds), though base APAS relies exclusively on light field and depth information. In contrast to OLAS, APAS performance degrades if the input hogel size is not optimally chosen for the distance, whereas OLAS is invariant to hogel size. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithmic complexity is roughly O(m^2 n^2 \log n), similar to other Fourier-based holographic methods. Memory usage is proportional to the size of the hologram and the intermediate complex STFT calculations. Measured Performance: PAS allows individual hogels to interfere constructively, resulting in a significantly brighter focused spot compared to HS. PAS provides improved focusing capabilities and depth of field compared to HS, which suffers from poor focusing due to out-of-phase hogels. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improves hologram quality over standard HS by aligning phases; allows for brighter reconstructions. Limitations: Requires a depth field; imposes a hard trade-off between spatial and angular resolution; larger hogels cause aliasing artifacts; APAS variants lose information during cropping. When to Use: Use PAS when phase alignment is critical for reconstruction quality and a depth field is available. Avoid PAS when hogel size flexibility is required without resolution trade-offs, in which case OLAS is preferred. Phase-Added Stereograms were introduced by Yamaguchi et al. in 1993 to address the phase discontinuity issue in Holographic Stereograms (HS). The method was developed to improve the quality of holographic displays by ensuring that hogels interfere constructively. Subsequent improvements, such as Accurate PAS (APAS) by Kang et al. in 2008, and other variants like Compensated PAS (CPAS) and Fast PAS (FPAS), have been proposed to further enhance wavefront approximation or computational complexity. PAS is primarily used in the context of Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) for volumetric displays and holography. name: Computational Phase Modulation (CGH Generation)
head: Fresnel Holography, Fresnel holograms, Lens Phase Function Method, ORA method, Optimization with Random Phase Algorithm, Point-based wavefront propagation
body:
Computational Phase Modulation generates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) by calculating the complex wavefield contributions of scene elements to a hologram plane, typically displayed on a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). It solves the problem of reconstructing 3D light fields from digital scene data by explicitly modeling the diffraction of light from source elements to the modulator plane. It is distinguished from Point-Cloud Based CGH Calculation by its specific reliance on the "lens phase function" abstraction for sub-holograms and the "point-wise integration" summation model, and from Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm by its direct point-to-plane propagation model rather than layer-by-layer accumulation. Inputs: Scene definition: A set of M object points \vec{o}j = (xj, yj, zj) with desired intensities aj. Hologram plane parameters: Resolution (W, H), pixel pitch p, wavelength \lambda. SLM constraints: Maximum supported spatial frequency, which determines the maximum radius of a sub-hologram. Outputs: A complex-valued hologram pattern H(\vec{p}) or phase-only pattern \phih(x,y) ready for SLM display. Data Structures: Hologram Plane: A 2D grid of complex values H(x,y) or phase values \phih(x,y), size W 	imes H. Sub-hologram Map: A mapping from hologram pixel coordinates \vec{p} to the set of object points 	ext{sp}(\vec{p}) whose sub-holograms cover \vec{p}. Method: The method computes the hologram by summing the contributions of all object points. Each object point j contributes a "lens phase function" fj(\vec{p}) to every hologram pixel \vec{p} that falls within its designated sub-hologram region. 1. Initialize the hologram plane H(\vec{p}) = 0 for all \vec{p}. 2. For each object point j in the scene: a. Determine Sub-hologram Region: Calculate the bounding box on the hologram plane that contains the spatial frequencies supported by the SLM for the distance zj and wavelength \lambda. b. For each pixel \vec{p} in the region: i. Calculate the distance r{j,\vec{p}} = \|\vec{p} - \vec{o}j\|. ii. Calculate the lens phase function contribution: fj(\vec{p}) = \exp\left(i \left(\phi{0,j} +  rac{2\pi}{\lambda} r{j,\vec{p}}ight)ight) where \phi{0,j} is an initial phase offset (typically 0). iii. Add the weighted contribution to the hologram plane: H(\vec{p}) \leftarrow H(\vec{p}) + aj fj(\vec{p}) 3. Post-processing (Optional): If the SLM is phase-only, convert the complex H(\vec{p}) to a phase-only pattern \phih(x,y) using an approximation method. Note: The source describes an iterative optimization (ORA) to refine phase \phih for uniform intensity spot arrays, which is a specific variant of this post-processing step. Formulas: Lens Phase Function: fo(\vec{p}) = e^{i(\phio +  rac{2\pi}{\lambda} \|\vec{p}-\vec{o}\|)} where \vec{o} is the object point, \vec{p} is the hologram pixel, \lambda is wavelength, and \phio is phase offset. Hologram Summation: H(\vec{p}) = \sum{j \in 	ext{sp}(\vec{p})} aj fj(\vec{p}) where 	ext{sp}(\vec{p}) is the set of object points whose sub-holograms include \vec{p}, and aj is the intensity weight. Reconstruction (Verification): Ur(
ux, 
uy) = \iint Uh(x, y) e^{-i 2\pi (x
ux + y
uy)} dx dy where Uh is the hologram pattern and Ur is the reconstructed complex amplitude. Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of reconstruction light. aj: Desired intensity of object point j. \phio: Phase offset, typically 0. Sub-hologram size: Determined by SLM spatial frequency limits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sub-hologram Overlap: Sub-holograms for different object points may overlap on the hologram plane. Spatial Frequency Limits: If a sub-hologram is too large, the phase gradient exceeds the SLM's Nyquist limit. Phase-Only Modulation: Most SLMs can only modulate phase or amplitude, not both simultaneously, requiring direct or iterative approximation methods for complex-valued fields. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecghphasemodulation(objectpoints, hologramwidth, hologramheight, pixelpitch, wavelength): """ Computes the complex hologram H(p) using the lens phase function method. Args: objectpoints: List of tuples (x, y, z, intensity) for each point in the scene. hologramwidth: Width of the hologram plane in pixels. hologramheight: Height of the hologram plane in pixels. pixelpitch: Physical size of one pixel (e.g., in meters). wavelength: Wavelength of the reconstruction laser (e.g., in meters). Returns: H: 2D numpy array of complex values representing the hologram plane. """ import numpy as np # Initialize hologram plane with zeros H = np.zeros((hologramheight, hologramwidth), dtype=np.complex128) # Create coordinate grids for the hologram plane xcoords = np.arange(hologramwidth) pixelpitch - (hologramwidth pixelpitch) / 2 ycoords = np.arange(hologramheight) pixelpitch - (hologramheight pixelpitch) / 2 X, Y = np.meshgrid(xcoords, ycoords) k = 2 np.pi / wavelength for point in objectpoints: ox, oy, oz, intensity = point # Calculate distance from object point to each hologram pixel dx = X - ox dy = Y - oy dz = -oz R = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Calculate lens phase function # fo(p) = exp(i (phi0 + k R)) # phi0 is set to 0 as per source phase = k R fo = np.exp(1j phase) # Add weighted contribution to hologram H += intensity fo return H def applyphaseonlyconstraint(H): """ Converts complex hologram to phase-only using Amplitude Discard method. """ phase = np.angle(H) return np.exp(1j phase) Uses phase-only CGHs on an LCOS-SLM to split a laser beam into multiple focal spots simultaneously, increasing voxel generation density for volumetric displays. It differs from single-point rendering by enabling parallel voxel generation, though it requires optimization of scanning trajectories and hardware constraints. Methods for encoding complex-valued object waves into phase-only holograms for LCSLMs without iterative optimization. Includes Amplitude Discard (simplest), Double Phase (encodes amplitude and phase into two adjacent values), and Binary Phase (quantizes to two levels). Trades image quality and energy efficiency for computational simplicity. Mitigates depth replicas in simultaneous color holography by exploiting the wavelength-dependent phase response of LCoS SLMs. Uses SLMs with phase ranges > 2\pi to break wavelength-depth ambiguity, differing from Computational Phase Modulation by addressing multi-wavelength crosstalk via physical device dispersion rather than algorithmic approximation. A model for the phase delay \phi\lambda imparted by an LCoS SLM, accounting for wavelength dispersion. The phase delay is \phi\lambda =  rac{2\pi d}{\lambda} n(s, \lambda), where d is the LC layer thickness, n(s, \lambda) is the refractive index controlled by digital input s and dependent on \lambda. Quantization errors increase with larger phase ranges, requiring at least 6 bits of granularity per 2\pi range to maintain PSNR/SSIM. Complexity: The naive point-wise integration scales with O(M \cdot N), where M is the number of object points and N is the number of hologram pixels. This is extremely expensive for high-resolution holograms and large scenes. Memory: Requires storing the complex hologram plane H(\vec{p}), size W 	imes H complex values. Strengths: Physically accurate modeling of diffraction from point sources; supports arbitrary 3D point distributions. Limitations: Computationally intensive for large scenes; sub-hologram overlap is handled by complex summation; phase-only SLMs require approximation methods since they cannot modulate amplitude and phase simultaneously. When to use: When high-fidelity point-source reconstruction is required and computational resources allow for direct summation. When not to use: For real-time applications with very large scenes or high-resolution SLMs without acceleration techniques (e.g., GPU parallelization, FFT-based approximations). Originating from the principles of Fresnel holography, this method was formalized in the context of holographic near-eye displays and volumetric graphics. The "lens phase function" and "point-wise integration" terminology was popularized by Maimone et al. for holographic projectors. The ORA (Optimization with Random Phase Algorithm) variant was developed by Hayasaki et al. for femtosecond laser processing and volumetric graphics. The extended phase range approach was introduced to address color crosstalk in simultaneous color holography. name: CGH-based parallel focal point generation
head: CGH-Based Multi-Voxel Generation, Computer Generated Hologram parallel voxel generation, Computer Generated Holography multi-point rendering
body: This method uses phase-only Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) displayed on a Liquid Crystal on Silicon Spatial Light Modulator (LCOS-SLM) to split a single laser beam into multiple focal spots simultaneously. It solves the bottleneck of low voxel generation density in holographic volumetric displays by increasing the number of voxels generated per frame. Unlike single-point rendering, it allows for parallel voxel generation, though it introduces trade-offs in scanning trajectory optimization and hardware constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target voxel distribution (number of focal points P), laser parameters (repetition frequency, pulse energy), LCOS-SLM specifications (maximum spatial frequency, grayscale range). Output: A phase-only CGH pattern displayed on the SLM, resulting in P simultaneous focal points in the drawing space. Data Structures: CGH Pattern: A 2D array of phase values. Layout: Grayscale values 0 to 255 (8-bit). Mapping: Grayscale value g \in [0, 255] maps linearly to phase modulation \phi \in [0, 2\pi]. Spatial Frequency Constraint: The encoded focal points must be arranged within a spatial frequency range up to 1/8 of the LCOS-SLM's maximum spatial frequency. Algorithm Steps: 1. CGH Generation: Generate a phase-only hologram to create P focal points. Use the Gerchberg–Saxton method with 50 Fourier iterative calculations to optimize the phase distribution. Ensure the spatial frequency of the generated pattern does not exceed 1/8 of the SLM's maximum spatial frequency. 2. SLM Display: Load the calculated CGH onto the LCOS-SLM. The SLM modulates the phase of the incident laser beam according to the grayscale values. 3. Optical Focusing: Pass the modulated beam through a lens (focal length f{lens}) and a varifocal lens. The lens focuses the light into separated focal points in the drawing space at an effective infinite distance. 4. Scanning: Apply the scanning trajectory to the beam. Note: If using a trajectory optimized for single-point rendering, blur may occur when rendering multiple spatially separated focal points. Optimizing the scanning trajectory for multi-point rendering is required to resolve this. Formulas: The estimated number of voxels generated per frame N is calculated as: N = \frac{P \cdot n}{fr} Where: P: Number of focal points (voxels) generated in parallel per pulse. n: Number of voxels generated in 1 second, dependent on the laser repetition frequency. fr: Refresh rate of the display system. Parameters (Typical Values from Sources): Lens Focal Length (f{lens}): 200 mm. Threshold Energy (E{th}): 0.004 mJ. Duty Cycle / Distribution Factor (D): 50%. Estimated Parallel Voxels (P): 708 (theoretical estimate based on D=50\% and E{th}). Actual Achieved Parallel Voxels (P): 4 (due to hardware constraints). Refresh Rate (fr): 20 Hz. Estimated Voxels per Frame (N): 35,400. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecghforparallelfocalpoints(targetpoints, slmwidth, slmheight, maxspatialfreq): """ Generates a phase-only CGH to create multiple focal points using Gerchberg-Saxton. targetpoints: list of (x, y) coordinates for desired focal spots. """ # Initialize phase array with uniform phase phase = [[0.0 for in range(slmwidth)] for in range(slmheight)] # Construct target intensity mask constrained by spatial frequency limit targetintensity = [[0.0 for in range(slmwidth)] for in range(slmheight)] for (x, y) in targetpoints: if abs(x) <= maxspatialfreq / 8 and abs(y) <= maxspatialfreq / 8: targetintensity[y][x] = 1.0 # Gerchberg-Saxton Iteration (50 steps) for iteration in range(50): # Forward 2D Fourier Transform to focal plane field = fft2(exp(1j phase)) # Apply amplitude constraint in focal plane amplitude = abs(field) phasefocal = angle(field) newamplitude = [sqrt(row) for row in targetintensity] # Reconstruct field in focal plane fieldfocal = [[newamplitude[i][j] exp(1j phasefocal[i][j]) for j in range(slmwidth)] for i in range(slmheight)] # Inverse 2D Fourier Transform back to SLM plane fieldslm = ifft2(fieldfocal) # Apply amplitude constraint in SLM plane (constant amplitude) phase = [[angle(fieldslm[i][j]) for j in range(slmwidth)] for i in range(slmheight)] # Map phase to 8-bit grayscale cghgrayscale = [[int(round(phase[i][j] / (2 3.14159) 255)) % 256 for j in range(slmwidth)] for i in range(slmheight)] return cghgrayscale def calculatevoxelsperframe(parallelpoints, voxelspersecond, refreshrate): """ Calculates N = P n / fr exactly as defined in the source. """ return (parallelpoints voxelspersecond) / refreshrate Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blur: Using a scanning trajectory optimized for single-point rendering causes increased blur when rendering multiple spatially separated focal points. The trajectory must be optimized for multi-point rendering. Hardware Damage: Actual parallelized voxels achieved (P=4) were significantly less than estimated (P=708) because irradiated pulse energy was reduced to prevent damage to the varifocal lens. Solution for Damage: Use a varifocal lens with higher light resistance or combine with dynamic optimization for CGH diffraction efficiency to improve P. Time Complexity: CGH generation requires 50 Fourier iterative calculations (Gerchberg–Saxton), which is computationally intensive but done offline or per-frame depending on system capability. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the CGH pattern (2D array of 8-bit values). Performance: Estimated: 35,400 voxels per frame at 20 Hz refresh rate with estimated P=708. Actual (Experimental): 4 parallel focal points achieved due to energy constraints. Strengths: Increases voxel generation density per frame; enables simultaneous multi-voxel rendering. Limitations: Requires careful scanning trajectory optimization to avoid blur; limited by varifocal lens damage thresholds; actual parallel count may be much lower than theoretical estimates. When to Use: When high voxel density is required and hardware can support the necessary pulse energy and lens resistance. When Not to Use: When single-point precision is critical and multi-point blur cannot be tolerated without trajectory optimization. This method was developed for holographic laser-excited volumetric display systems. It builds on Computational Phase Modulation (CGH Generation) [7284-computational-phase-modulation-cgh-generation.md]. The technique was demonstrated in experimental systems using femtosecond lasers and LCOS-SLMs to generate volumetric graphics in gas-filled cells. The CGH is optimized using 50 Fourier iterative calculations based on the Gerchberg–Saxton method. name: Phase-Only Hologram Approximations
head: Amplitude Discard Method, Binary Phase Method, DPE, Direct Amplitude Encoding, Double Phase Encoding, Double Phase Method, Double-phase holograms
body: Phase-only hologram approximations are methods for generating holograms compatible with Liquid Crystal Spatial Light Modulators (LCSLMs) that can only modulate the phase of light, not its amplitude. They solve the problem of encoding a complex-valued object wave O(x,y;c) into a phase-only hologram H without using computationally expensive iterative optimization. The Amplitude Discard Method is the simplest approach, retaining only the phase of the object wave, while the Double Phase Method explicitly encodes both amplitude and phase into two adjacent phase values. The Binary Phase Method quantizes the phase to two levels. These methods trade off image quality and energy efficiency for computational simplicity and real-time capability. Input: Complex-valued object wave O(x, y; c), where x, y are spatial coordinates and c is the color channel index. Output: Phase-only hologram H(x, y), representing the phase values to be displayed on the SLM. Object Wave: A 2D array of complex numbers, one per pixel per color channel. Hologram: A 2D array of phase values. For Amplitude Discard and Binary Phase: One phase value per pixel, quantized to L or 2 levels respectively. For Double Phase: Two phase values per logical pixel, typically arranged in a checkerboard pattern or sub-hologram block. This method discards the amplitude of the object wave and quantizes the phase. H(x, y; c) = Q \left( \frac{L}{2\pi} \arg \{ O(x, y; c) \} \right) \arg \{ O \}: The phase angle of the complex object wave. L: Number of discrete quantization levels (typically L=256). Q: A uniform mid-rise quantizer mapping the scaled phase to integer levels. Parameters: L=256. Characteristics: Does not produce unwanted diffraction order artifacts, so no spatial filter is required in the optical system. This method discards the amplitude and quantizes the phase to two levels. Formula: The phase is quantized to two discrete SLM levels. Parameters: 2 quantization levels. Characteristics: Requires temporal averaging and a single-sideband filter. This method encodes the complex value O into the sum of two complex numbers with constant amplitude and variable phase. O(x, y; c) = 0.5 e^{j \theta1(x, y; c)} + 0.5 e^{j \theta2(x, y; c)} \theta1, \theta2: The two phase values to be encoded. Derivation: Let O = a e^{j p}, where a = |O| is the amplitude and p = \arg \{ O \} is the phase. The two phase values are calculated as: Pa(r) = p - \arccos(a) Pb(r) = p + \arccos(a) where a \in [0, 1]. Parameters: Quantization levels L=256. Characteristics: Requires spatial filtering by a pupil aperture to remove unwanted diffraction orders. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def amplitudediscardhologram(objectwave, L=256): """ Generates a phase-only hologram using the Amplitude Discard Method. Args: objectwave: 2D numpy array of complex numbers representing O(x,y;c). L: Number of quantization levels (default 256). Returns: hologram: 2D numpy array of phase values in [0, 2pi). """ # Extract phase angle from complex object wave phase = np.angle(objectwave) # Scale phase to [-L/2, L/2) and quantize using uniform mid-rise quantizer Q scaledphase = (L / (2 np.pi)) phase quantized = np.round(scaledphase) # Map back to phase range [0, 2pi) hologram = (quantized / L) 2 np.pi hologram = hologram % (2 np.pi) return hologram def binaryphasehologram(objectwave, numlevels=2): """ Generates a phase-only hologram using the Binary Phase Method. Args: objectwave: 2D numpy array of complex numbers. numlevels: Number of phase levels (default 2). Returns: hologram: 2D numpy array of phase values. """ phase = np.angle(objectwave) # Shift phase to [0, 2pi] phaseshifted = phase % (2 np.pi) # Scale to [0, numlevels), quantize, and map back to phase range scaled = (numlevels / (2 np.pi)) phaseshifted quantized = np.round(scaled) % numlevels hologram = (quantized / numlevels) 2 np.pi return hologram def doublephasehologram(objectwave, L=256): """ Generates a double phase hologram using Direct Amplitude Encoding. Args: objectwave: 2D numpy array of complex numbers. L: Number of quantization levels (default 256). Returns: holograma: 2D numpy array of phase values Pa. hologramb: 2D numpy array of phase values Pb. """ # Extract amplitude and phase amplitude = np.abs(objectwave) phase = np.angle(objectwave) # Clamp amplitude to [0, 1] to satisfy arccos domain requirement amplitude = np.clip(amplitude, 0.0, 1.0) # Calculate Pa and Pb per S2 derivation acosa = np.arccos(amplitude) Pa = phase - acosa Pb = phase + acosa # Quantize to L levels and map back to phase range Pascaled = (L / (2 np.pi)) Pa Pbscaled = (L / (2 np.pi)) Pb Paquant = np.round(Pascaled) % L Pbquant = np.round(Pbscaled) % L holograma = (Paquant / L) 2 np.pi hologramb = (Pbquant / L) 2 np.pi return holograma, hologramb Amplitude > 1: The Double Phase Method requires |O| \le 1 for \arccos(|O|) to be real. Resolution Loss: The Double Phase Method requires two phase values for each complex value, leading to a corresponding loss in resolution. Ringing Artifacts: The Double Phase Method may produce subtle ringing artifacts. Simple Text Only: The Amplitude Discard Method may produce acceptable results only for simple text and symbology consisting of thin lines, as phase encodes high frequencies like object edges; it is not a practical general solution. Phase Wrapping: Real-world SLMs may have imperfections in phase wrapping from 2\pi back to 0. One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR) is a technique for generating phase-only holograms by replacing iterative phase optimization with random phase assignment, relying on temporal averaging to recover the target image intensity. It differs from standard amplitude discard methods by explicitly managing the resulting high-frequency noise through the rapid playback of multiple randomized sub-frames, rather than attempting to minimize noise within a single static hologram. Amplitude Discard: O(N) time and memory, where N is the number of pixels. Binary Phase: O(N) time and memory. Double Phase: O(N) time and memory. Iterative Methods: Not considered in these approximations due to high computational burden. PSNR (dB): Binary Phase: 25.2 dB. Double Phase: 27.6 dB, 30.57 dB (red), 30.05 dB (green), 27.26 dB (blue) in simulation. Amplitude Discard: 27.7 dB. Amplitude Holograms (for comparison): 40.2 dB at \Delta=0.5. SSIM: Binary Phase: 0.30. Double Phase: 0.40. Amplitude Discard: 0.62. Amplitude Holograms (for comparison): 0.97 at \Delta=0.5. Energy Efficiency: Amplitude Discard: 100%. Binary Phase: 50%. Double Phase: 21.6%. Amplitude Holograms: 1.4% at \Delta=0.5. Amplitude Discard: Strengths: Highest energy efficiency (100%), no spatial filter needed, simple computation. Limitations: Lower SSIM than binary phase, not practical for general images due to high-frequency noise. Binary Phase: Strengths: Superior SSIM compared to other phase methods due to temporal averaging reducing speckle noise. Limitations: Lower PSNR, requires temporal averaging and single-sideband filter, significant per-pixel error. Double Phase: Strengths: Higher contrast and less high-frequency noise than iterative methods, smooth phase profile. Limitations: Lowest energy efficiency (21.6%), requires spatial filtering, resolution loss, ringing artifacts. Use Amplitude Discard for simple text or symbology, or when maximum energy efficiency (100%) is required and no spatial filter is available. Use Binary Phase when structural preservation (SSIM) is more important than PSNR and temporal averaging is feasible. Use Double Phase when high contrast and smooth phase are required, and spatial filtering is available. The Amplitude Discard Method is described as the most trivial way of computing a phase-only hologram. The Double Phase Method was described by Hsueh and Sawchuk in 1978. These methods are used in holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality, where real-time embedded rendering is required. name: One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR)
head: Temporal averaging
body: One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR), also known as temporal averaging, generates phase-only holograms by playing back multiple sub-frames with randomized object phases to approximate a target complex wavefield. Unlike iterative methods that optimize phase to match a target amplitude, OSPR discards amplitude entirely and relies on the temporal averaging of uncorrelated pseudo-random noise patterns to reveal the target image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target complex object wavefield O(x,y) = A(x,y)e^{i\phio(x,y)}, where A is amplitude and \phio is phase. Output: A sequence of binary or multi-level phase-only hologram sub-frames Hk(x,y) displayed in rapid succession. Data Structures: Each hologram sub-frame is a 2D grid of phase values, typically quantized to binary levels (0, \pi) or a small discrete set, suitable for high-speed binary SLMs. Steps: 1. Randomize Object Phase: Instead of optimizing the object phase \phio to match the target amplitude, assign \phio(x,y) random values uniformly distributed over [0, 2\pi) for each sub-frame generation. 2. Generate Hologram Sub-frames: Compute the hologram Hk using the randomized phase \phio^{(k)}. The required amplitude on the hologram plane becomes a pseudo-random uniform noise pattern because the object phase is random. 3. Discard Amplitude: On playback, the amplitude information is discarded, leaving only the phase component of Hk to be displayed by the SLM. 4. Temporal Playback: Display the sequence of hologram sub-frames H1, H2, \dots, HN in random succession on a high-speed display. 5. Noise Averaging: The human eye or a low-pass optical system averages the intensity of these rapidly changing sub-frames. Since the noise patterns are uncorrelated across sub-frames, they average out, revealing the target image. Parameters: Number of sub-frames N: Several sub-frames must be calculated for each image frame. Display Switching Speed: Must be high enough to meet bandwidth requirements and prevent flicker. Pitfalls: Low contrast of noisy hologram sub-frames cannot be recovered by temporal averaging. Requires high bandwidth and switching speed from the display (SLM). Iteratively optimized holograms tend to include undesirable high frequency noise or speckle, which OSPR aims to mitigate through averaging. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generateosprsubframes(targetamplitude, targetphase, numsubframes): """Generates phase-only hologram sub-frames using OSPR.""" rows = len(targetamplitude) cols = len(targetamplitude[0]) subframes = [] for in range(numsubframes): # Step 1: Randomize object phase uniformly over [0, 2pi) randomphase = [[random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) for in range(cols)] for in range(rows)] # Step 2: Generate hologram sub-frame using randomized phase # The source indicates the hologram is computed from the randomized phase, # making the required amplitude a pseudo-random uniform noise pattern. # The exact hologram computation formula is not given in the sources. hologramphase = [[random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) for in range(cols)] for in range(rows)] # Step 3: Discard amplitude; output is phase-only subframes.append(hologramphase) return subframes def displayosprsequence(subframes, refreshratehz): """Plays back sub-frames in random succession on a high-speed SLM.""" frameduration = 1.0 / refreshratehz for frame in subframes: # Step 4: Display holograms in random succession # Step 5: Human eye or low-pass optical system averages intensity # Hardware-specific display call is omitted as it is implementation-specific pass This method models and mitigates phase noise inherent to liquid crystal amplitude-only Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) by analyzing the coupling between amplitude modulation and unwanted phase modulation. It establishes a mathematical framework using Jacobi-Anger expansions to separate signal terms from noise terms in the Fourier domain, allowing for the design of grating frequencies that prevent noise overlap with the reconstructed signal. It sets it apart from sibling methods by providing a rigorous analytical derivation of noise spectra based on the specific physical properties of the liquid crystal, rather than relying solely on empirical averaging or iterative phase retrieval. Time Complexity: Requires calculating multiple hologram sub-frames for each image frame, increasing computational load compared to single-frame methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The primary downside is that the low contrast of the noisy hologram sub-frames cannot be recovered by temporal averaging. Hardware Requirements: Requires high bandwidth and switching speed from the display (SLM). Binary phase holograms may be produced for playback on a high-speed binary SLM to facilitate these requirements. Strengths: Mitigates undesirable high-frequency noise or speckle associated with iteratively optimized holograms. Limitations: Cannot recover low contrast from noisy sub-frames; requires multiple sub-frames per image frame; dependent on high-speed display hardware. One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR), also known as temporal averaging, was introduced by Cable et al. in 2004. It is used in holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality to generate phase-only holograms that approximate complex wavefields by averaging out noise over time.
