name: Phase Noise Handling in Amplitude-Only SLMs
head: Phase Noise Mitigation in Amplitude-Only SLMs
body: This method models and mitigates phase noise inherent to liquid crystal amplitude-only Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) by analyzing the coupling between amplitude modulation and unwanted phase modulation. It establishes a mathematical framework using Jacobi-Anger expansions to separate signal terms from noise terms in the Fourier domain, allowing for the design of grating frequencies that prevent noise overlap with the reconstructed signal. It sets it apart from sibling methods by providing a rigorous analytical derivation of noise spectra based on the specific physical properties of the liquid crystal, rather than relying solely on empirical averaging or iterative phase retrieval. Inputs and Outputs Input: The amplitude modulation function f(x) applied to the SLM pixels. Output: A derived expression for the wave field at the SLM plane identifying signal and noise components, and a constraint on the grating phase frequency to avoid aliasing. Data Structures Amplitude Function: Represented as a Fourier series f(x) = \sumk Fk \cos(kx + \phik), where Fk are amplitude coefficients and \phik are phase coefficients for spatial frequency k. Phase Noise Model: Unwanted phase modulation is modeled as a second-order polynomial of the amplitude: \exp(i p1 f(x) + i p2 f(x)^2), where p1 and p2 are coefficients characterizing the liquid crystal's phase-amplitude coupling. Steps 1. Model the Wave Field: Define the complex wave field U(x) at the SLM plane as the product of the amplitude modulation and the unwanted phase modulation: U(x) = f(x) e^{i p1 f(x) + i p2 f(x)^2} 2. Expand Phase Terms: Apply the Jacobi-Anger expansion, e^{iz \cos \theta} = \sum{n=-\infty}^{\infty} i^n Jn(z) e^{in\theta}, to the exponential terms, where Jn(z) is the n-th Bessel function of the first kind. (Note: The source text contains an OCR typo in the summation limits; the standard identity is used here.) 3. Substitute Fourier Series: Substitute the Fourier series expansion of f(x) into the phase terms. 4. Derive Expanded Expression: The full expanded wave field is given by: U(x) = f(x) \prodk \sumn i^n Jn(p1 Fk) e^{in(kx + \phik)} \prod{k,l} \sumn i^n Jn\left(\frac{p2 Fk Fl}{2}\right) e^{in((k+l)x + \phik + \phil)} \prod{k,l} \sumn i^n Jn\left(\frac{p2 Fk Fl}{2}\right) e^{in((k-l)x + \phik - \phil)} 5. Approximate for Small Parameters: In typical experimental conditions, p1, p2, Fk < 1 and |n| \ll 1. Under these conditions, higher-order Bessel functions Jn(z) for |n| \gg 1 are negligible. The expression approximates to: U(x) \approx f(x) \prodk J0(p1 Fk) \prod{k,l} J0\left(\frac{p2 Fk Fl}{2}\right) \left[ \summ J1(p1 Fm) e^{i(mx + \phim)} + \sum{m,n} 2i J1\left(\frac{p2 Fm Fn}{2}\right) e^{i((m+n)x + \phim + \phin)} + O(p1 Fk^2) + O(p2 Fk^2) \right] Note: The source's Eq. (6) contains typographical errors in Bessel indices and Fourier coefficients; the corrected structure above preserves the derivation's intent for implementation. 6. Identify Noise Terms: Analyze the frequency components of the expanded expression. The signal term is typically the first-order diffraction e^{ik{prism}x}. Noise terms arise from higher-order interactions, such as e^{ik{pitch}x - 2ik{prism}x}, where k{pitch} is the wavenumber of the SLM pixel pitch and k{prism} is the grating frequency. 7. Set Grating Frequency Constraint: To ensure noise terms do not overlap with the signal term in the Fourier domain, set the grating phase frequency k{prism} to one-quarter or less of the spatial frequency of the pixel pitch k{pitch}: k{prism} \le \frac{1}{4} k{pitch} Parameters p1, p2: Phase noise coefficients. Values are typically < 1 in experimental setups. Fk: Fourier coefficients of the amplitude pattern. Values are typically < 1. Grating Frequency: Must be \le 1/4 of the pixel pitch spatial frequency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noise Overlap: If the grating phase frequency is set to one-third of the spatial frequency of the pixel pitch, the signal term e^{ik{prism}x} overlaps with the noise term e^{ik{pitch}x - 2ik{prism}x}, making the noise unfilterable. High-Order Terms: If p1 Fk or p2 Fk Fl are not small, the approximation in Step 5 fails, and higher-order Bessel terms must be retained, increasing computational complexity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.special import jv def calculatewavefieldspectrum(fouriercoeffs, p1, p2, kmax): """ Calculate spectral components of the wave field at an amplitude-only SLM with phase noise, using the Jacobi-Anger expansion. Parameters: fouriercoeffs: dict mapping spatial frequency k to (amplitude Fk, phase phik) p1: Phase noise linear coefficient p2: Phase noise quadratic coefficient kmax: Maximum spatial frequency to consider for truncation Returns: spectrum: dict mapping spatial frequency k to complex amplitude """ spectrum = {} ks = [k for k in fouriercoeffs.keys() if abs(k) <= kmax] # Global scaling factor from zero-order Bessel terms in the approximation # U0 = prodk J0(p1 Fk) prod{k,l} J0(p2 Fk Fl / 2) # This factor scales all spectral components uniformly. for k in ks: Fk, phik = fouriercoeffs[k] # Linear phase noise term (n=1 dominant) if abs(p1 Fk) < 1.0: coeff = jv(1, p1 Fk) freq = k phase = phik spectrum[freq] = spectrum.get(freq, 0) + coeff np.exp(1j phase) # Quadratic phase noise terms (n=1 dominant) for l in ks: Fl, phil = fouriercoeffs[l] arg = p2 Fk Fl / 2 if abs(arg) < 1.0: coeff = jv(1, arg) # (k+l) term freqsum = k + l phasesum = phik + phil spectrum[freqsum] = spectrum.get(freqsum, 0) + 2j coeff np.exp(1j phasesum) # (k-l) term freqdiff = k - l phasediff = phik - phil spectrum[freqdiff] = spectrum.get(freqdiff, 0) + 2j coeff np.exp(1j phasediff) return spectrum def checkgratingconstraint(kprism, kpitch): """ Verify grating frequency avoids noise overlap. """ return kprism <= 0.25 kpitch A method to obtain amplitude in a phase-only device by playing back several holograms with randomized object phases in random succession, allowing noise to average out. It sets itself apart by relying on temporal averaging rather than analytical spectral separation. Choose it when hardware supports rapid sequential hologram display and phase noise is stochastic rather than deterministic. Link A broader approach that uses the physical properties of the SLM and optical system to engineer the diffraction pattern, often incorporating phase noise models. It sets itself apart by treating the SLM's physical response as part of the optical transfer function rather than a defect to be filtered. Choose it when designing custom holographic displays with specific SLM hardware constraints. Link Time Complexity: The analytical derivation is O(1). The numerical evaluation of the spectrum depends on the number of Fourier components N. The pseudocode is O(N^2) due to the double loop over k and l. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the Fourier coefficients and the resulting spectrum. Measured Performance: In experiments using an IRIS-U62 LCoS SLM (3840 × 2160 resolution, 3.6 μm pixel pitch, binned 2×2 to 7.2 μm effective pitch), the method successfully mitigated phase noise by setting the grating frequency to \le 1/4 of the pixel pitch spatial frequency. The distance between minimum and maximum depths was set to 2 mm, with dispersion diameters of 25 (red), 20 (green), and 18 pixels (blue) under 2 mm light propagation. Strengths: Provides a rigorous physical model for phase noise; allows for precise design of grating frequencies to avoid aliasing; analytical solution avoids iterative computation. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that p1, p2, Fk < 1; higher-order terms may become significant for large amplitude modulations or strong phase coupling; requires accurate characterization of p1 and p2 for the specific SLM. When to Use: When using amplitude-only SLMs for holography and phase noise is a significant artifact; when analytical design of the grating frequency is preferred over empirical tuning. When Not to Use: When the SLM has negligible phase noise; when the amplitude modulation is large enough to violate the small argument approximation for Bessel functions. This method originates from research into diffraction-engineered holography, specifically addressing the limitations of amplitude-only SLMs in volumetric displays and holographic computer-generated holography. The work was published in Nature Communications in 2022 by researchers investigating the depth representation limit of holographic displays. Diffraction-engineered holography: Beyond the depth representation limit of holographic displays, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33728-5, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Extended Phase Range SLM Modulation
head: Depth Replica Removal via Extended Phase Range, Extended Phase Range, Extended Phase Range SLM for Depth Replica Reduction, Replica reduction, Wavelength-Dependent Phase SLM
body: Extended Phase Range SLM Modulation is a technique used in simultaneous color holography to mitigate depth replicas (ghost images) by exploiting the wavelength-dependent phase response of Liquid Crystal Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs). Unlike standard 0-2\pi SLMs which produce perfect intensity copies of the target image at specific replica planes, this method uses SLMs with extended phase ranges (greater than 2\pi) that vary significantly across RGB wavelengths to break the wavelength-depth ambiguity. This approach sets it apart from Computational Phase Modulation (CGH Generation) by specifically addressing the multi-wavelength crosstalk inherent in single-SLM color holography, and differs from Phase-Only Hologram Approximations by relying on physical device dispersion rather than algorithmic approximation to suppress artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target RGB image data; SLM physical parameters including LC layer thickness d, minimum refractive index n{min}, and wavelength-dependent maximum refractive index n{max}(\lambda). Output: Phase-only hologram pattern \phi(x,y) optimized for the specific SLM's wavelength-dependent phase response. Data Structures: SLM Model: A mapping function R(\lambda) returning the maximum phase shift \phi{max}(\lambda) for a given wavelength \lambda. Fields: wavelength (float, nm), phaserange (float, multiples of \pi). Typical values for Holoeye Pluto-2.1-Vis-016: Red (\lambda \approx 630 nm): 2.4\pi Green (\lambda \approx 532 nm): 5.9\pi Blue (\lambda \approx 450 nm): 7.4\pi Method Steps: 1. Characterize SLM Dispersion: Determine the phase response \phi\lambda for each primary color channel. The phase shift introduced by the LC layer is defined as: \phi\lambda = \frac{2\pi d \Delta n(\lambda)}{\lambda} where d is the LC layer thickness and \Delta n(\lambda) = n(\lambda) - n{min} is the change in refractive index relative to the minimum state. Note that n depends on \lambda due to material dispersion. 2. Analyze Wavelength Dependence: Calculate the derivative of phase with respect to wavelength to quantify replica suppression potential: \frac{d\phi}{d\lambda} A larger magnitude of this derivative indicates stronger wavelength dependence, which diminishes the coherence of replica planes across different colors. This derivative increases with larger \Delta n = n{max} - n{min} and higher dispersion -dn/d\lambda. 3. Generate Hologram: Compute the phase pattern \phi(x,y) using a standard CGH algorithm but constrain the phase values to the specific extended range [0, \phi{max}(\lambda)] for each channel during the optimization step. Unlike standard methods that wrap phase to 2\pi, this method allows the phase to exceed 2\pi according to the device's physical limits. 4. Quantization: Map the continuous phase values to the SLM's bit depth. Simulation indicates that PSNR and SSIM remain almost constant for 6 bits and above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeextendedphasehologram(targetrgb, slmthickness, nmin, nmaxlambda, wavelengths, bitdepth, maxiterations): # Initialize phase pattern with random values in [0, 2pi) phasepattern = [[random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Precompute maximum phase shift for each wavelength based on SLM physics maxphases = [] for lam in wavelengths: nmax = nmaxlambda[lam] deltan = nmax - nmin maxphases.append((2 math.pi slmthickness deltan) / lam) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Standard iterative Fourier transform algorithm (e.g., Gerchberg-Saxton) for c, lam in enumerate(wavelengths): # Apply wavelength-dependent phase scaling # Physical phase shift = phasepattern (maxphases[c] / (2 pi)) scaledphase = [[phasepattern[r][col] (maxphases[c] / (2 math.pi)) for col in range(width)] for r in range(height)] # [Comment] Propagate scaledphase to sensor plane using Fresnel diffraction integral # Replace amplitude with target amplitude sqrt(targetrgb[:,:, c]) # Backward propagate to SLM plane # Update phasepattern using angle of backward propagated field pass # Quantize phase to SLM bit depth levels = 2bitdepth - 1 quantizedphase = [[round(phase / (2 math.pi) levels) / levels (2 math.pi) for phase in row] for row in phasepattern] phasepattern = quantizedphase return phasepattern Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard SLM Behavior: If the SLM has a uniform 0-2\pi range across all colors, perfect copies (replicas) appear at specific depth planes, degrading image quality. Quantization Errors: As the phase range increases, the limited bit depth of the SLM becomes more noticeable, potentially increasing quantization noise. Dispersion Control: The user has minimal control over the absolute wavelength \lambda or the material dispersion -dn/d\lambda; these are fixed by the hardware. Generates multiple focal points simultaneously. It does not explicitly address wavelength-dependent replica reduction but may benefit from extended phase range to reduce crosstalk between focal planes. Choose this method when simultaneous multi-plane focusing is required rather than full-field holographic reconstruction. Link Uses algorithms to approximate complex fields with phase-only masks. Extended phase range is a hardware-specific modulation technique that can be combined with these approximations to improve quality. Choose this method when complex amplitude modulation is required but only phase-only SLMs are available. Link Time Complexity: Determined by the underlying CGH generation algorithm (e.g., Gerchberg-Saxton iterations). The extended phase range adds negligible computational overhead, primarily affecting the phase wrapping/constraint step. Memory Complexity: Standard for CGH generation. Measured Performance: Simulation using Holoeye Pluto-2.1-Vis-016 (Red: 2.4\pi, Green: 5.9\pi, Blue: 7.4\pi) showed substantial reduction in depth replicas compared to a uniform 2\pi SLM. This improves target plane hologram quality and creates defocused content at other depths, reducing high-frequency out-of-focus light at the sensor plane. Strengths: Effectively breaks wavelength-depth ambiguity; reduces ghost images in simultaneous color holography; improves accommodation cues. Limitations: Requires specific SLM hardware with high dispersion and extended phase range; quantization errors increase with phase range if bit depth is insufficient (though stable above 6 bits). When to use: Simultaneous color holography on single SLMs where depth replicas are a significant artifact. When not to use: Monochromatic holography (where wavelength dependence is irrelevant) or when using SLMs with uniform 0-2\pi response. The technique was proposed to address the limitation of placing content arbitrarily in 3D volume and the issue of in-focus images appearing at out-of-focus depths, which hinders accommodation. It builds on the understanding that standard 0-2\pi SLMs produce perfect copies at replica planes. The method leverages the physical properties of Liquid Crystal materials, specifically the refractive index difference \Delta n and dispersion -dn/d\lambda, to create wavelength-dependent phase shifts. The specific implementation details and simulation results were published by Kim et al. in 2023. name: Inverse Design Algorithm for Voxel-based CGVHs
head: Iterative Propagation Algorithm (IPA) for mode conversion
body: The Inverse Design Algorithm for Voxel-based Computer-Generated Volume Holograms (CGVHs) is a method for designing holographic structures that convert N mutually incoherent transverse input modes \{un\} into N target modes \{vn\} with a one-to-one mapping. It optimizes the refractive index distribution within a 3D volume to achieve specific mode conversion efficiencies. Unlike direct forward calculation methods, this algorithm uses an iterative approach to select voxel distributions that maximize the overlap between propagated fields and target modes. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a split-step Fourier Beam Propagation Method (BPM) and a local multi-objective criterion to select from a discrete set of pre-defined transverse voxel profiles. Inputs: N: Number of input/target mode pairs. \{un\}{n=1}^N: Input mode field distributions defined at plane z{in} = z1. \{vn\}{n=1}^N: Target mode field distributions defined at plane z{out} = z{K+1}. \lambdan: Wavelength associated with mode pair n. nn: Bulk refractive index of the sample at wavelength \lambdan. D: Number of available transverse voxel distributions \{\Delta RId\}{d=0}^D. \Delta RI0 is the null modification. I, J, K: Grid dimensions of the sample volume. Dx, Dy, Dz: Spatial extensions of sub-volumes v{ijk}. dx, dy, dz: Simulation spatial resolutions. Outputs: Selected voxel distribution index d^{ijk} for each sub-volume v{ijk} (1 \le i \le I, 1 \le j \le J, 1 \le k \le K). The sample volume is virtually split into sub-volumes v{ijk} acting as placeholders for elementary voxel distributions. Grid: 3D array of indices (i, j, k). Sub-volume v{ijk}: Defined by spatial extent Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Voxel Distributions: A discrete set of D+1 transverse refractive index change profiles \Delta RId(x,y). These are relative to the bulk index nn. Field Storage: Complex 2D arrays storing transverse field distributions u{ijk}^n and v{ijk}^n at each plane zk. Elementary Length: Dz = 10 \mu m (typical). Simulation Resolution: dx = dy = 0.25 \mu m, dz = 0.5 \mu m (typical). Coordinate System: Rectangular (O, x, y, z), with z as the propagation direction. Phase multiplication model: Crossing a layer of thickness dz through a homogeneous medium nn, followed by a local phase \phi{ijk}, is modeled as: \phi{ijk}(\lambdan) = \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi}{\lambdan} \Delta RI{ijk}^d(\lambdan) dz\right), \quad 0 \le d \le D. Maximization criterion: The squared l2 distance minimization O{min} = \min \sum{n=1}^N \|un - vn\|2^2 is transformed into a maximization problem for lossless designs (where \|un\|^2 and \|vn\|^2 are conserved): O{max} = \max{\Delta RI{ijk}^d} \sum{n=1}^N \int{z{out}} \Re(vn^ un). Local selection criterion: The optimal distribution for sub-volume v{ijk} maximizes: O{ijk}^{max} = \maxd \sum{n=1}^N \int{z{k+1}} \Re\left((v{ijk+1}^n)^ u{ijk+1}^n(d)\right) where u{ijk+1}^n(d) is the input mode propagated from zk to z{k+1} through \Delta RI{ijk}^d. 1. Initialization: Set all sub-volumes v{ijk} to the null distribution \Delta RI0. 2. Forward Propagation: Propagate input modes \{un\} from z1 to z{K+1} using split-step Fourier BPM with resolutions dx, dy, dz. Cross sub-volumes v{ijk} layer by layer for k from 1 to K. During propagation, save the transverse distributions \{un\} before crossing each v{ijk}, noting them \{u{ijk}^n\} for reference. Note \{zk\} as the common transverse planes where distributions are saved. 3. Convergence Check: Compute the final overlap criterion O{max} to monitor convergence. If satisfactory or stagnant, exit and consider the current selection optimal. 4. Backward Propagation and Voxel Selection: Iteratively backpropagate target modes \{vn\} from z{out}=z{K+1} to z{in}=z1. For a given k, select the distribution d that maximizes the local multi-objective criterion O{ijk}^{max}. To find d, try all distributions \{\Delta RI{ijk}^d\} for each sub-volume v{ijk} (k fixed). After selecting \{\Delta RI{ijk}^d\} for a given k, backpropagate target modes \{v{ijk+1}^n\} to plane zk, and repeat iteratively until k=1. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def splitstepbpm(fieldin, dz, nbulk, wavelength): """Standard split-step Fourier BPM propagation through homogeneous medium.""" k0 = 2 np.pi / wavelength # Propagation phase in frequency domain kx = np.fft.fftfreq(fieldin.shape[1], d=0.25e-6) 2 np.pi ky = np.fft.fftfreq(fieldin.shape[0], d=0.25e-6) 2 np.pi KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky) kz = np.sqrt((nbulk k0)2 - KX2 - KY2) phase = np.exp(1j kz dz) fieldfft = np.fft.fft2(fieldin) fieldfft = phase return np.fft.ifft2(fieldfft) def backpropagatelayer(fieldin, dz, deltari, wavelength, nb): """Reverse phase multiplication and reverse homogeneous propagation.""" phase = np.exp(-1j 2 np.pi / wavelength deltari dz) fieldprop = fieldin phase return splitstepbpm(fieldprop, -dz, nb, wavelength) def inversedesignCGVH(N, modesu, modesv, wavelengths, nbulk, voxeldistributions, I, J, K, Dz, dx, dy, dz): """ Inverse design algorithm for voxel-based CGVHs. """ H, W = modesu[0].shape selectedvoxels = np.zeros((I, J, K), dtype=int) # ufields[k][n] stores field at plane zk for mode n ufields = [np.zeros((I, J, N, H, W), dtype=complex) for in range(K + 1)] # vfields[k][n] stores field at plane zk for mode n vfields = [np.zeros((I, J, N, H, W), dtype=complex) for in range(K + 1)] prevoverlap = 0.0 maxiterations = 100 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Step 1: Forward Propagation for n in range(N): ufields[0][:,:, n,:,:] = modesu[n] for k in range(K): for i in range(I): for j in range(J): d = selectedvoxels[i, j, k] deltari = voxeldistributions[d] for n in range(N): # Propagate from zk to z{k+1} ufields[k+1][i, j, n,:,:] = splitstepbpm( ufields[k][i, j, n,:,:], dz, nbulk, wavelengths[n]) # Local phase multiplication phase = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi / wavelengths[n] deltari dz) ufields[k+1][i, j, n,:,:] = phase # Step 2: Convergence Check totaloverlap = 0.0 for n in range(N): overlap = np.sum(np.conj(modesv[n]) ufields[K][:,:, n,:,:]) totaloverlap += np.real(overlap) if iteration > 0 and abs(totaloverlap - prevoverlap) < 1e-6: break prevoverlap = totaloverlap # Step 3: Backward Propagation and Voxel Selection for n in range(N): vfields[K][:,:, n,:,:] = modesv[n] for k in range(K - 1, -1, -1): for i in range(I): for j in range(J): bestd = 0 bestcriterion = -np.inf uin = ufields[k][i, j,:,:,:] vtarget = vfields[k+1][i, j,:,:,:] for d in range(len(voxeldistributions)): deltari = voxeldistributions[d] localcriterion = 0.0 for n in range(N): unext = splitstepbpm(uin[n,:,:], dz, nbulk, wavelengths[n]) phase = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi / wavelengths[n] deltari dz) unext = phase overlap = np.real(np.sum(np.conj(vtarget[n,:,:]) unext)) localcriterion += overlap if localcriterion > bestcriterion: bestcriterion = localcriterion bestd = d selectedvoxels[i, j, k] = bestd deltaribest = voxeldistributions[bestd] for n in range(N): vfields[k][i, j, n,:,:] = backpropagatelayer( vtarget[n,:,:], dz, deltaribest, wavelengths[n], nbulk) return selectedvoxels Precision: The simulation resolution dx, dy, dz must be much smaller than the feature size to ensure numerical accuracy. Typical values are dx=dy=0.25 \mu m and dz=0.5 \mu m. Wavelength Dependence: The voxel distributions \Delta RId may be wavelength-dependent, requiring the algorithm to use the correct \Delta RId(\lambdan) for each mode n. Convergence Monitoring: The algorithm monitors stagnation of the overlap metric to determine termination. Complexity: Each iteration involves K forward propagation steps and K backward propagation steps. In each step, for each sub-volume, all D voxel distributions are tested. The complexity per iteration is O(K \cdot I \cdot J \cdot D \cdot N \cdot \text{BPM\cost}). Memory: Requires storing fields at all K+1 planes for all N modes, plus the voxel distributions. Memory complexity is O(K \cdot I \cdot J \cdot N \cdot H \cdot W). Strengths: Allows for the design of complex 3D structures for multi-mode conversion using a discrete set of transverse voxel profiles. Limitations: The solution depends on the initial guess (all null) and the set of available voxel distributions. The maximization criterion is derived specifically for lossless designs where \|un\|^2 and \|vn\|^2 are conserved. The algorithm was proposed in the context of designing computer-generated volume holograms (CGVHs) in glass for mode conversion. It is based on the Iterative Propagation Algorithm (IPA) [50], which maximizes the overlap integral between propagated fields and target fields. name: Multiple Wavefront Recording Planes (WRP) with Horizontal Parallax Only (HPO)
head: Fast CGH method for point clouds, HPO WRP method
body: This method generates computer-generated holograms (CGH) for point clouds by distributing the calculation across multiple parallel wavefront recording planes (WRPs) to handle occlusion and reduce computational load, specifically adapted for Horizontal Parallax Only (HPO) displays. It differs from full-parallax WRP methods by computing point contributions to 1D hololines rather than the full 2D plane, and from naive point-source summation by using pre-computed look-up tables (LUTs) and band-limited angular spectrum propagation to manage the high spatial bandwidth product (SBP) required for wide viewing angles. Inputs: Point cloud data: Set of M points, each with 3D coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and RGB color values. Display parameters: Pixel pitch px, py, resolution Nx, Ny, wavelength \lambda, and number of WRPs. Hologram geometry: HPO configuration where diffraction is computed only along horizontal lines (hololines). Outputs: Complex-valued hologram data for the HPO display. Data Structures: Point Cloud: Array of structures containing position (x, y, z) and color (R, G, B). Look-Up Table (LUT): Pre-computed complex propagation kernels for a specific distance z. The LUT stores the complex amplitude H(u, v; z) in the frequency domain, modified by a random phase mask for diffuse reflection modeling. Wavefront Recording Planes (WRPs): A set of parallel planes positioned between the object (point cloud) and the hologram plane. Each WRP holds a complex field representing the wavefront at that depth. Hololines: 1D arrays representing the hologram data for a single vertical row of the display. Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of reconstruction light (e.g., 640 nm). px, py: Horizontal and vertical pixel pitches (e.g., 0.55 µm, 23.4 µm). Nx, Ny: Resolution of the hologram plane (e.g., 32,768 × 768). z{min}: Minimum object-to-hologram distance to satisfy Shannon criterion, calculated as z{min} = \frac{N p^2}{\lambda}. \theta: Maximum diffraction angle, determined by \sin \theta = \frac{\lambda}{2p}. Steps: 1. Point Volume Attribution: Assign a Gaussian distribution profile to each point in the point cloud to model a continuous volume rather than a singular point. This generates smoother, continuous surface reconstructions. The amplitude Ai of point i at a distance r from its center is modeled as: Ai(r) = A{0,i} \exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where \sigma controls the spread [G: \sigma is typically chosen based on the desired surface smoothness and pixel pitch; not explicitly defined in sources, but implied by "Gaussian distribution profile"]. 2. LUT Generation (Source Plane to First WRP): Pre-compute the propagation kernel from the point source plane to the first WRP distance z{LUT}. Calculate the angular spectrum transfer function H(u, v; z{LUT}) using the Band-Limited Angular Spectrum Method (BL-ASM). Apply a random phase mask to the LUT content to account for diffuse reflections, scattering light over a wide angular range. Store the complex kernel H{LUT}(u, v) in the LUT. 3. Inter-WRP Propagation: Propagate the wavefield from one WRP to the next parallel WRP using BL-ASM. For each WRP pair separated by distance \Delta z, compute the transfer function H(u, v; \Delta z). Apply BL-ASM constraints: double the calculation window area in the source plane by padding with zeros, perform FFT, multiply by the transfer function, and IFFT, then crop the output to the original window size to avoid edge errors from circular convolution. 4. HPO Hololine Computation: Adapt the standard WRP method for HPO by computing contributions only to 1D hololines. For each point i, determine its contribution to the hololines on the hologram plane. Instead of propagating to the full 2D hologram plane, propagate the wavefield from the last WRP to the hologram plane along the horizontal direction only. Use inverted Gaussian filters during propagation to model occlusions, locally blocking light from points behind others. 5. Superposition: Sum the complex contributions from all points i onto the respective hololines of the hologram plane [G: Standard superposition principle for CGH]. 6. Color Channel Handling: For colour holograms, compute the hologram for a single reference wavelength (e.g., red, 640 nm) but assign RGB intensity values to the points. The final hologram consists of three channels computed with the same wavelength but different intensities per point to maintain colour information and wide viewing angle. 7. Quantization (Optional): If using a phase-only SLM, quantize the complex field Uh(x, y) to phase values 0 to 2\pi [G: Standard phase-only encoding techniques such as detour phase or error diffusion may be applied, but specific algorithm details are not provided in the source]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computetransferfunction(distance, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx): """Compute the band-limited angular spectrum transfer function H(u,v;z).""" u = np.fft.fftfreq(Nx, d=px) v = np.fft.fftfreq(Ny, d=px) U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v) # w calculation: w = (lambda^-2 - u^2 - v^2)^0.5 wsq = (1.0 / wavelength2) - U2 - V2 w = np.zeroslike(wsq) w[wsq >= 0] = np.sqrt(wsq[wsq >= 0]) H = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi w distance) # Band-limiting: H'(u,v;z) = H(u,v;z) rect(u/2ulimit) rect(v/2vlimit) ulimit = 1.0 / (2 px) vlimit = 1.0 / (2 px) rectu = np.abs(U) <= ulimit rectv = np.abs(V) <= vlimit H = H rectu rectv return H def propagateblasm2d(field, transferfunc, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx): """Band-Limited Angular Spectrum propagation with zero-padding and cropping.""" # Double the calculation window area by padding with zeros Nypad, Nxpad = 2 Ny, 2 Nx fieldpadded = np.zeros((Nypad, Nxpad), dtype=complex) fieldpadded[:Ny,:Nx] = field # Resize transfer function to match padded grid spacing upad = np.fft.fftfreq(Nxpad, d=px / 2) vpad = np.fft.fftfreq(Nypad, d=px / 2) Upad, Vpad = np.meshgrid(upad, vpad) wsqpad = (1.0 / wavelength2) - Upad2 - Vpad2 wpad = np.zeroslike(wsqpad) wpad[wsqpad >= 0] = np.sqrt(wsqpad[wsqpad >= 0]) Hpad = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi wpad transferfunc.shape[0] / Ny) # Scale distance proportionally ulimit = 1.0 / (2 (px / 2)) vlimit = 1.0 / (2 (px / 2)) Hpad = Hpad (np.abs(Upad) <= ulimit) (np.abs(Vpad) <= vlimit) # FFT, multiply, IFFT F = np.fft.fft2(fieldpadded) G = F Hpad fieldoutpadded = np.fft.ifft2(G) # Crop to original window size return fieldoutpadded[:Ny,:Nx] def propagateblasm1d(fieldrow, distance, wavelength, px, Nx): """1D BL-ASM propagation for HPO hololines.""" u = np.fft.fftfreq(Nx, d=px) U = u.reshape(1, -1) wsq = (1.0 / wavelength2) - U2 w = np.zeroslike(wsq) w[wsq >= 0] = np.sqrt(wsq[wsq >= 0]) H = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi w distance) # Band-limiting ulimit = 1.0 / (2 px) H = H (np.abs(U) <= ulimit) F = np.fft.fft(fieldrow) G = F H return np.fft.ifft(G) def applyinvertedgaussianocclusion(field, centerx, centery, sigma): """Locally block light using an inverted Gaussian filter to model occlusions.""" Ny, Nx = field.shape y, x = np.mgrid[0:Ny, 0:Nx] distsq = (x - centerx)2 + (y - centery)2 occlusion = 1.0 - np.exp(-distsq / (2 sigma2)) return field occlusion def generatehpowrpcgh(points, displayparams, wrpdistances, lutdistance): """ Generate HPO CGH using Multiple WRP method. Args: points: List of dicts with keys 'x', 'y', 'z', 'r', 'g', 'b'. displayparams: Dict with 'lambda', 'px', 'py', 'Nx', 'Ny'. wrpdistances: List of z-distances for each WRP plane. lutdistance: Distance for LUT generation. Returns: hologram: 2D array (Ny, Nx) of complex values. """ wavelength = displayparams['lambda'] px = displayparams['px'] Nx = displayparams['Nx'] Ny = displayparams['Ny'] # Initialize hologram plane hologram = np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=complex) # Step 1 & 2: LUT Generation lut = computetransferfunction(lutdistance, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) randomphase = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi np.random.rand(Ny, Nx)) lut = randomphase # Initialize WRPs wrpfields = [np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=complex) for in range(len(wrpdistances))] # Step 1: Project points to first WRP for point in points: dz = wrpdistances[0] - point['z'] if dz <= 0: continue # Map point to grid indices ix = int(point['x'] / px) iy = int(point['y'] / px) sigma = px # [G: Typical spread relative to pixel pitch] # Create sparse source field with Gaussian attribution sourcefield = np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=complex) y, x = np.mgrid[0:Ny, 0:Nx] distsq = (x - ix)2 + (y - iy)2 amp = point['r'] np.exp(-distsq px2 / (2 sigma2)) sourcefield = amp # Propagate to first WRP using LUT (BL-ASM) wrpfields[0] += propagateblasm2d(sourcefield, lut, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) # Step 3: Inter-WRP Propagation for i in range(len(wrpdistances) - 1): dz = wrpdistances[i+1] - wrpdistances[i] h = computetransferfunction(dz, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) wrpfields[i+1] = propagateblasm2d(wrpfields[i], h, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) # Step 4: HPO Hololine Computation & Step 5: Superposition dzfinal = displayparams['zhologram'] - wrpdistances[-1] for y in range(Ny): fieldrow = wrpfields[-1][y,:] # 1D BL-ASM propagation to hologram plane hologramrow = propagateblasm1d(fieldrow, dzfinal, wavelength, px, Nx) # Apply inverted Gaussian occlusion filter if needed # [G: Occlusion centers would be derived from point cloud depth ordering] hologramrow = applyinvertedgaussianocclusion(hologramrow, Nx//2, 0, px) hologram[y,:] += hologramrow return hologram POS-WRP is a rendering pipeline that encodes mesh-based 3D scenes into complex-valued wave fields with fine-grained textures, photo-realistic shadings, and perspective depth cues. It solves the problem of maintaining continuous depth cues and realistic illumination when projecting from perspective scene space to the orthogonal space of a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Unlike standard wave propagation which assumes paraxial orthogonal propagation, POS-WRP explicitly transforms mesh coordinates and textures to correct for projection discrepancies, delivering high-fidelity data with reduced speckle artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the point cloud, K WRP fields, and the LUT. Each WRP field is O(N) complex numbers. The LUT is O(N). Total memory is O(K \cdot N + N). For high-resolution holograms (e.g., 32,768 × 768), this can be significant. Measured Performance: Demonstrated on a Holografika HoloVizio 722RC light field display with 32,768 × 768 pixel resolution, 0.55 µm horizontal pitch, and 640 nm wavelength. The method supports a viewing angle of 70°. Strengths: Handles occlusion naturally through the WRP structure and inverted Gaussian filters. High-quality reconstructions with smooth surfaces due to Gaussian volume attribution. Wide field of view achieved through diffuse reflection modeling (random phase LUTs). Efficient for HPO by reducing 2D propagation to 1D hololines. Limitations: HPO results in constrained viewing zones and astigmatic output due to diminished vertical resolution. Small pixel pitch leads to strong light field diffusion beyond computation window borders, requiring BL-ASM and zero-padding, which increases computational overhead. Aperiodic functions cause edge errors in FFT, mitigated by BL-ASM but not eliminated. Limited to point clouds; mesh-based scenes require different handling (see POS-WRP). When to Use: Use for point cloud data on HPO displays requiring wide viewing angles and high resolution. When Not to Use: Avoid for full-parallax holography, mesh-based scenes with complex textures (use POS-WRP), or when computational resources are too limited for BL-ASM overhead. The Multiple WRP method was originally proposed for fast computation of holograms supporting full parallax. It was adapted for HPO displays to leverage the specific constraints of light field displays, such as the Holografika HoloVizio 722RC. The method builds on the Angular Spectrum method for wave propagation and incorporates Band-Limited Angular Spectrum (BL-ASM) to handle the high spatial bandwidth product of modern holographic displays. name: Phase-Only Wave Field Reconstruction/Propagation (POS-WRP)
head: POS-WRP, Perspective-to-Orthogonal Smooth Wave field Rendering Pipeline (POS-WRP)
body: POS-WRP is a rendering pipeline that encodes mesh-based 3D scenes into complex-valued wave fields with fine-grained textures, photo-realistic shadings, and perspective depth cues. It solves the problem of maintaining continuous depth cues and realistic illumination when projecting from perspective scene space to the orthogonal space of a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Unlike standard wave propagation which assumes paraxial orthogonal propagation, POS-WRP explicitly transforms mesh coordinates and textures to correct for projection discrepancies, delivering high-fidelity data with reduced speckle artifacts. Inputs: 3D scene data: Mesh geometry (vertices, faces) and lighting data captured through a perspective camera. Pre-defined output texture dimensions. Outputs: Complex-valued wave field representation of the scene at the hologram plane. Specifically, the amplitude is derived from baked textures, and the phase is processed for SLM compatibility. Data Structures: Mesh: Standard polygonal mesh representation. Texture: Output texture storing physical illumination values (amplitude). Wave Field: Complex-valued array U(x,y) representing the field at the SLM plane. Parameters: Processing time for POS-WRP component: 24.96 seconds per hologram. Spatial sampling rate: Assumed sufficient such that visual loss from ignoring diffraction at occlusion edges is negligible. Steps: 1. Input Acquisition: Load the 3D scene comprising meshes and lighting data from a perspective camera view. 2. Texture Baking (Amplitude Generation): Employ a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) pipeline to bake rendering outcomes onto a pre-defined output texture. The texture stores physical illumination, which serves as the amplitude A(x,y) of the wave field across mesh facets. Occlusion Handling: During baking, obstructed portions of a facet are rendered black (zero amplitude). This adheres to geometric optics principles. Diffraction at occlusion edges is not explicitly accounted for, relying on facet size and sampling rate to render visual loss negligible. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform mesh coordinates and textures from perspective scene space to orthogonal SLM space to maintain consistency with the orthogonal projection required for wave field propagation from the SLM. 4. Tilted Plane Propagation & Phase Smoothing: Process the transformed meshes and textures through tilted plane propagation. Incorporate an additional phase smoothing step to generate a relatively smooth target phase. This mitigates artifacts caused by SLM crosstalk. 5. Wave Field Propagation: Use spectral resampling and the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) to propagate each tilted facet of the mesh scene to the hologram plane. This creates the final complex-valued wave field representation of the entire scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def poswrppipeline(meshvertices, meshfaces, lightingdata, cameraintrinsics, textureresolution): """ Implements the Phase-Only Wave Field Reconstruction/Propagation (POS-WRP) pipeline. Args: meshvertices: List of 3D vertex coordinates. meshfaces: List of face indices referencing vertices. lightingdata: Light sources and environment map. cameraintrinsics: Perspective camera parameters (focal length, principal point). textureresolution: (width, height) of the output texture. Returns: complexwavefield: Complex-valued array representing the wave field at the hologram plane. """ # Step 1: Input 3D scene comprises meshes and lighting data captured through a perspective camera. # (Data is already in input variables) # Step 2: Texture Baking # Employ physically based rendering (PBR) pipelines to bake rendering outcomes onto a pre-defined output texture. # The texture contains physical illumination serving as the amplitude across mesh facets. amplitudetexture = bakepbrtexture(meshvertices, meshfaces, lightingdata, cameraintrinsics, textureresolution) # Occlusion handling is naturally integrated during baking. # Obstructed portions are rendered black (zero amplitude). # Note: Diffraction at occlusion edges is not explicitly accounted for. # Step 3: Coordinate Transformation # Transform mesh coordinates and textures from perspective scene space to orthogonal SLM space. # This ensures consistency with the orthogonal projection during wave field propagation. transformedvertices = perspectivetoorthogonaltransform(meshvertices, cameraintrinsics) transformedtexture = resampletexturetoorthogonal(amplitudetexture, cameraintrinsics, textureresolution) # Step 4: Tilted Plane Propagation and Phase Smoothing # Process transformed meshes and textures through tilted plane propagation. # Incorporate phase smoothing to mitigate SLM crosstalk artifacts. # This step generates a relatively smooth target phase. phasemap = computephasefromtiltedfacets(transformedvertices, transformedtexture) smoothedphase = applyphasesmoothing(phasemap) # Step 5: Wave Field Propagation using ASM # Use spectral resampling and Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) to propagate each tilted facet # to the hologram plane. complexwavefield = propagatewithasmspectralresampling(transformedvertices, transformedtexture, smoothedphase) return complexwavefield def bakepbrtexture(vertices, faces, lights, camera, resolution): """ Simulates PBR baking. Returns a 1D array of amplitude values. Obstructed areas are 0.0. """ # Standard rasterization and shading calculation. # For each pixel in the output texture: # 1. Ray trace from camera through pixel into scene. # 2. If intersection with mesh: # a. Calculate shading using PBR model (lights, material). # b. Store result as amplitude. # 3. Else (occluded or no intersection): # a. Store 0.0 (black). amplitude = [0.0] (resolution[0] resolution[1]) for y in range(resolution[1]): for x in range(resolution[0]): intersection = traceray(camera, x, y, vertices, faces) if intersection: amplitude[y resolution[0] + x] = computepbrshading(intersection, lights) else: amplitude[y resolution[0] + x] = 0.0 return amplitude def traceray(camera, x, y, vertices, faces): # Standard ray generation and triangle intersection logic return None def computepbrshading(intersection, lights): # Standard physically based rendering shading calculation return 1.0 def perspectivetoorthogonaltransform(vertices, camera): """ Transforms mesh vertices from perspective projection to orthogonal space compatible with SLM. """ # Apply inverse perspective projection and re-project to orthogonal coordinates. # The exact mathematical transformation depends on the specific camera-to-SLM mapping. # The source states this is done to maintain consistency with orthogonal propagation. transformed = [] for v in vertices: tx = (v.x - camera.cx) / camera.fx ty = (v.y - camera.cy) / camera.fy transformed.append((tx, ty, v.z)) return transformed def resampletexturetoorthogonal(texture, camera, resolution): """ Interpolates texture coordinates to match orthogonal projection grid. """ # Map orthogonal pixel coordinates back to perspective texture coordinates and sample. newtexture = [0.0] (resolution[0] resolution[1]) for y in range(resolution[1]): for x in range(resolution[0]): newtexture[y resolution[0] + x] = texture[y resolution[0] + x] return newtexture def computephasefromtiltedfacets(vertices, texture): """ Computes phase delay based on facet tilt and propagation distance. """ # The source mentions processing through tilted plane propagation but does not detail the phase extraction formula. # Typically, phase is computed as \phi = k \cdot z \cdot \cos(\theta) where \theta is the facet tilt angle. phase = [0.0] len(texture) for i in range(len(texture)): phase[i] = math.atan2(0, 1) # Placeholder for actual phase calculation from geometry return phase def applyphasesmoothing(phasemap): """ Applies phase smoothing to mitigate SLM crosstalk. """ # The source mentions an "additional phase smoothing step" but does not provide the algorithm. # This would typically involve low-pass filtering the phase map or optimizing phase continuity. smoothed = [0.0] len(phasemap) for i in range(len(phasemap)): smoothed[i] = phasemap[i] # Placeholder for actual smoothing kernel return smoothed def propagatewithasmspectralresampling(vertices, texture, phase): """ Propagates the wave field from the mesh plane to the hologram plane using ASM with spectral resampling. """ # Initialize complex field U = amplitude exp(i phase) field = [] for i in range(len(texture)): field.append(complex(texture[i] math.cos(phase[i]), texture[i] math.sin(phase[i]))) # FFT to frequency domain freqfield = fft2d(field) # Spectral resampling: interpolate frequency grid to match target propagation scale resampledfreq = spectralresample(freqfield, targetscale=1.0) # Angular Spectrum Method transfer function H(fx, fy) = exp(i kz z) # kz = sqrt(k^2 - (2pifx)^2 - (2pify)^2) k = 2 math.pi / 532e-9 # Wavelength 532nm example z = 0.1 # Propagation distance 10cm example H = [] for fy in range(freqfield.shape[1]): for fx in range(freqfield.shape[0]): kx = 2 math.pi fx / freqfield.shape[0] ky = 2 math.pi fy / freqfield.shape[1] kz = math.sqrt(max(k2 - kx2 - ky2, 0)) H.append(complex(math.cos(kz z), math.sin(kz z))) # Multiply and IFFT back to spatial domain propagatedfreq = [a b for a, b in zip(resampledfreq, H)] propagatedfield = ifft2d(propagatedfreq) return propagatedfield def fft2d(data): # Standard 2D discrete Fourier transform implementation return data def ifft2d(data): # Standard 2D inverse discrete Fourier transform implementation return data def spectralresample(data, targetscale): # Interpolate frequency domain data to adjust sampling rate for ASM return data Time Complexity: The POS-WRP component takes 24.96 seconds per hologram. The total time for generating one phase-only hologram (including the subsequent PAGD optimization) is 54.96 seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Delivers high-fidelity wave field data with continuous depth cues. Reduces speckle artifacts. Maintains perspective depth cues and realistic shadings which are typically lost in orthogonal propagation. Computationally efficient occlusion handling by using geometric optics (PBR) rather than wave-based masking. Limitations: Does not explicitly account for diffraction at occlusion edges, assuming visual loss is negligible due to sampling rate. Real-time hologram generation remains a goal for future exploration; current performance is not real-time. When to use: When high-fidelity, photo-realistic holographic reconstruction from mesh data is required, and continuous depth cues are critical. When not to use: When real-time performance is strictly required, or when diffraction effects at occlusion edges are visually significant for the specific resolution and scene scale. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Mesh-represented and learning-empowered hologram synthesis for full 3D holographic displays". Context: It is part of a framework that also includes the Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD) algorithm for encoding the complex wave field into phase-only holograms. Development: The method addresses challenges in end-to-end holographic display frameworks where tightly coupled approaches may lack robustness. It aims to bridge the disparity in wavefront propagation between simulation and physical display systems. name: Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm
head: Layer-Based Hologram Calculation, Layer-based CGH Calculation
body: The Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm calculates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGHs) by slicing a 3D scene into discrete parallel depth layers and numerically propagating their wavefields to the hologram plane. It distinguishes itself from point-cloud or volume-rendering methods by leveraging 2D Fourier transforms to efficiently compute the superposition of these layers, enabling real-time binocular color holography. Unlike continuous depth methods, it introduces visible separation artifacts at layer boundaries when applied to scenes with continuous depth ranges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D model represented as an 8-bit Computer Generated Depth Map (CGDM), where depth values range from 0 to 255. The model is sliced into L=256 parallel layers. Output: A complex amplitude distribution E{com}(x,y) on the holographic plane, which is subsequently quantized to a phase-only distribution Ep(x,y) for display on a phase-only Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Data Structures: Layer Amplitude Map Ul(x,y): A 2D array representing the amplitude of the l-th depth layer. Random Phase Map r(x,y): A 2D array of random phase values superposed on each layer to simulate the diffusive effect of the object surface. Layer Distance zl: The scalar distance between the l-th layer and the holographic plane. Parameters: L = 256: Number of layers, derived from the 8-bit CGDM. \lambda: Wavelength of the reconstruction light. u, v: Spatial frequencies defined as u = \frac{\cos \alpha}{\lambda} and v = \frac{\cos \beta}{\lambda}, where \alpha and \beta are the angles between the incident wave and the x- and y-directions, respectively. FT: Fourier Transform operator. FT^{-1}: Inverse Fourier Transform operator. Algorithm Steps: 1. Slicing: Divide the 3D model into 256 parallel layers based on the 8-bit CGDM. 2. Phase Superposition: For each layer l, superpose a random phase r(x,y) onto the layer's amplitude Ul(x,y) to simulate surface diffusion. 3. Propagation Calculation: Compute the complex amplitude distribution E{com}(x,y) on the holographic plane by summing the contributions of all layers. The contribution of each layer is calculated by transforming the modulated layer amplitude to the frequency domain, applying a phase shift term representing propagation, and transforming back: E{com}(x,y) = \sum{l=0}^{255} FT^{-1} \left\{ FT \left\{ Ul(x,y) \exp[i r(x,y)] \right\} \exp \left[ i \frac{2\pi}{zl} \left( 1 - \lambda u - \frac{\lambda v}{\lambda} \right) \right] \right\} 4. Phase Extraction: Extract the phase-only distribution Ep(x,y) = \arg(E{com}(x,y)) from the complex amplitude for use with a phase-only SLM. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath import random def layerbasedhologram(layers, zl, lambdawavelength, alpha, beta): """ Calculate hologram using layer-based algorithm. Args: layers: List of 2D arrays Ul(x,y) for l in 0..255. zl: List of distances zl for each layer. lambdawavelength: Scalar wavelength lambda. alpha: Angle between incident wave and x-direction. beta: Angle between incident wave and y-direction. Returns: Ep: Phase-only hologram distribution. """ L = 256 u = math.cos(alpha) / lambdawavelength v = math.cos(beta) / lambdawavelength # Initialize complex amplitude sum with zeros height = len(layers[0]) width = len(layers[0][0]) Ecom = [[0.0 + 0.0j] width for in range(height)] for l in range(L): Ul = layers[l] z = zl[l] # Generate random phase map r(x,y) in [0, 2pi) for this layer r = [[random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Modulate amplitude with random phase modulated = [[Ul[i][j] cmath.exp(1j r[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] # Forward 2D Fourier Transform (standard operation) freq = fft2(modulated) # Propagation phase shift # Source formula: exp[i (2pi/zl) (1 - lambdau - lambdav/lambda)] # Note: lambdav/lambda simplifies to v. phaseshift = cmath.exp(1j (2 math.pi / z) (1 - lambdawavelength u - v)) # Apply phase shift propagated = [[freq[i][j] phaseshift for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] # Inverse 2D Fourier Transform (standard operation) propagatedspace = ifft2(propagated) # Sum contributions for i in range(height): for j in range(width): Ecom[i][j] += propagatedspace[i][j] # Extract phase-only distribution Ep = [[cmath.phase(Ecom[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] return Ep def fft2(M): """Standard 2D discrete Fourier transform.""" # Represents standard FFT algorithm pass def ifft2(M): """Standard 2D inverse discrete Fourier transform.""" # Represents standard IFFT algorithm pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuous Depth Artifacts: When applied to VR scenes with continuous depth ranges, the discrete layering creates visible separation artifacts at layer boundaries. This makes the method suitable for AR content with isolated 3D models but not ideal for continuous VR scenes. Optical Misalignment: Experimental prototypes may suffer from reduced imaging quality due to optical component misalignment, geometric aberrations, and chromatic aberrations. Computes left and right holograms by propagating light waves from compensated depth layers to the hologram plane using 2D IFFTs. Distinguished by its specific reliance on 2D IFFTs for high-resolution binocular color holography on hardware accelerators. Performance: Capable of computing binocular color holograms at over 35 frames per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin embedded platform for a resolution of 2048 \times 1024. Strengths: Enables real-time, standalone holographic near-eye displays with full-color reconstruction and accurate focus cues. Reduces speckle noise when combined with SLED illumination. Limitations: Not suitable for scenes with continuous depth extents due to layer boundary artifacts. Limited field-of-view remains a challenge for holographic near-eye displays. Imaging quality may be lower than consumer stereoscopic displays due to optical imperfections. The method is described as a real-time hologram calculation technique for binocular color holograms. It employs an 8-bit CGDM to slice 3D models into 256 parallel layers. The approach is utilized in holographic near-eye displays and 3D display systems using depth maps generated by 2D-to-3D rendering. name: Layer-based diffraction
head: FFT-based holographic computation, Layer-based CGH Calculation, Layer-based hologram generation, Layer-based holographic rendering method, Layer-based method
body: Layer-based diffraction computes left and right holograms by numerically propagating light waves from compensated depth layers towards the hologram plane and summing them. It generates high-quality holographic patterns for a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) from RGB-D 3D scene data by computing optical field distributions on the eye lens plane using 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transforms (IFFTs). It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific reliance on 2D IFFTs for both the optical field distribution and hologram pattern computations, enabling high-resolution binocular color holography on hardware accelerators. Inputs and Outputs Input: RGB-D 3D image data representing the 3D image projected onto the viewer's retina plane. The data format consists of Red, Green, Blue, and Depth channels. Output: A single combined hologram pattern for the SLM, derived from simultaneously processed left and right eye images. Data Structures Complex Numbers: Stored in memory using exactly 32 bits. Number Representation: Fixed-point number representation is used for all data processing and IFFT multiplications. Hologram Levels: The amplitude-only hologram is quantized onto L=256 discrete levels. Steps 1. Receive Input: Obtain the RGB-D 3D image data from rendering software or a 3D camera. 2. Compute Optical Field: Compute the optical field distribution on the eye lens plane from the retina plane image. 3. Compute Hologram Patterns: Compute the holographic patterns to be applied to the SLM from the eye lens plane distributions. 4. Execute 2D IFFTs: Perform 2D IFFT computations for the field distribution and pattern computations. The 2D IFFTs are computed using the row-column method, where 1-D IFFTs are performed on rows and then columns. 5. Process Binocular Images: Process right and left eye images simultaneously. 6. Combine: Combine the two eye images into a single hologram. 7. Quantize: Obtain the amplitude-only hologram H by shifting, scaling, and quantizing the real part of the complex-valued object wave O onto L=256 discrete levels. Formulas The complex-valued object wave O(x, y; c) is the sum of propagated waves from Nz compensated depth layers: O(x, y; c) = \sum{i=0}^{Nz-1} P{\hat{z}i} \{ Ui \} (x, y; c) where c is the color channel. The propagation of a layer Ui from depth \hat{z}i is given by the Fourier transform: P{\hat{z}i} \{ Ui \} = \frac{\exp(j \lambdac \hat{z}i)}{j \lambdac \hat{z}i} \mathcal{F} \left\{ Ui(\xi, \eta; c) \exp\left( \frac{j \pi (\xi^2 + \eta^2)}{\lambdac \hat{z}i} \right) \exp\left( -\frac{j \pi (x^2 + y^2)}{\lambdac \hat{z}i} \right) \right\} where: \lambdac is the wavelength of color channel c. \mathcal{F} is the forward Fourier transform. \hat{z}i is the intermediate compensated layer depth. Ui(\xi, \eta; c) is the field at the layer. The final amplitude-only hologram H is: H(x, y; c) = Q(\Re \{ O(x, y; c) \}, L, \Delta) where \Re \{ O \} is the real part of the object wave, L=256 is the number of discrete levels, and Q represents the quantization operation. Parameters Output Resolution: 3840 × 2160 pixels. Refresh Rate: 30 frames per second (fps). Quantization Levels: L = 256. Pitfalls Hardware Complexity: FFT-based layer methods are traditionally unsuitable for CGH hardware accelerators because large-scale FFT processors are difficult to build. This implementation overcomes that using a highly parallel architecture and hardware-reducing techniques. Precision: Fixed-point arithmetic is used to minimize bit depth, requiring careful management of precision to avoid artifacts in the IFFT multiplications. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def layerbaseddiffraction(rgbddata, retinaplaneimage, eyelensparams, slmparams): """ Computes hologram from RGB-D data using layer-based diffraction. """ # Step 1: Receive Input (RGB-D format) # Step 2 & 3: Compute optical field on eye lens plane and SLM patterns # Step 5: Process right and left eyes simultaneously rightfield = computeeyelensfield(retinaplaneimage, eyelensparams, eye='right') rightpattern = computeslmpattern(rightfield, slmparams) leftfield = computeeyelensfield(retinaplaneimage, eyelensparams, eye='left') leftpattern = computeslmpattern(leftfield, slmparams) # Step 6: Combine into single hologram combinedhologram = combineholograms(rightpattern, leftpattern) # Step 7: Quantize to L=256 levels finalhologram = quantizehologram(combinedhologram, levels=256) return finalhologram def computeeyelensfield(retinaimage, params, eye): # Initialize complex field sum fieldsum = 0.0 + 0.0j Nz = params.numlayers for i in range(Nz): # Extract layer data Ui(xi, eta) for depth zhati Ui = getlayerdata(retinaimage, params.zhat[i]) # Propagate layer using diffraction formula propagated = propagatelayer(Ui, params.lambdac, params.zhat[i]) fieldsum += propagated return fieldsum def propagatelayer(Ui, lambdac, zhati): # Pre-computation phase factor phasefactor = math.exp(1j lambdac zhati) / (1j lambdac zhati) # Apply quadratic phase modulation to source coordinates (xi, eta) # The evidence formula includes a term with (x^2+y^2) inside the transform argument modulated = Ui math.exp(1j math.pi (Ui.coordsx2 + Ui.coordsy2) / (lambdac zhati)) modulated = math.exp(-1j math.pi (Ui.coordsx2 + Ui.coordsy2) / (lambdac zhati)) # Execute 2D IFFT/FFT as per row-column method fftresult = forwardfouriertransform(modulated) return phasefactor fftresult def forwardfouriertransform(data): # Standard 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (row-column method) rowtransformed = [fft1d(row) for row in data] coltransformed = [fft1d(col) for col in zip(rowtransformed)] return coltransformed def fft1d(signal): N = len(signal) result = [0.0 + 0.0j] N for k in range(N): for n in range(N): result[k] += signal[n] math.exp(-2j math.pi k n / N) return result def getlayerdata(retinaimage, depth): # Extract pixels matching the compensated layer depth zhati return retinaimage.filterbydepth(depth) def computeslmpattern(lensfield, slmparams): # FSU performs filtering, scaling, and pixel encoding # Pixel encoding converts complex number to integer using fixed-point representation encoded = pixelencodefixedpoint(lensfield) return encoded def pixelencodefixedpoint(complexval): # Fixed-point representation uses 32 bits for complex numbers # Convert real and imaginary parts to fixed-point integers realfixed = int(complexval.real (215)) & 0xFFFF imagfixed = int(complexval.imag (215)) & 0xFFFF return (realfixed << 16) | imagfixed def combineholograms(rightpattern, leftpattern): # Combine right and left eye images into a single hologram return rightpattern + leftpattern def quantizehologram(hologram, levels=256): # Shift, scale, and quantize the real part of O onto L discrete levels realpart = [[row.real for row in col] for col in hologram] minval = min(min(row) for row in realpart) maxval = max(max(row) for row in realpart) scale = (levels - 1) / (maxval - minval) if maxval != minval else 1.0 quantized = [[int((val - minval) scale) for val in row] for row in realpart] return quantized CGH algorithms that process the light field using Fresnel or other wavefront propagation methods. Unlike holographic stereograms, these can be applied globally or within hogels. Requires different propagation kernels for different depths, resulting in a different calculation per pixel, which may make parallelization more difficult. True depth-varying Fresnel method takes roughly O(m^4) operations. A single-plane approximation takes only O(m^2 \log m) operations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Complex numbers are stored using exactly 32 bits. Fixed-point representation is used to minimize bit depth. Measured Performance: A single-chip FPGA implementation generates binocular holographic colour images with 3840 × 2160 pixels at 30 fps. Scenes with 8 million voxels are rendered at 30 fps. Scaling: The method is implemented on a single-chip FPGA, suggesting scalability through parallel architecture. Strengths: Generates high-quality holograms for real scenes. Enables real-time embedded rendering. Limitations: Historically, FFT-based layer methods were considered unsuitable for CGH hardware accelerators due to the difficulty of building large-scale FFT processors. When to use: When high-quality binocular color holography is required for real scenes, and hardware acceleration via FPGA is available. When not: When computational resources are limited to CPUs without specialized FFT hardware, as large-scale FFT processors are difficult to build. Origin: The method is used in holographic near-eye displays and slim-panel holographic video displays. History: Layer-based methods using FFTs were traditionally considered unsuitable for CGH hardware accelerators because FFT processors were difficult to build in large scale. Recent implementations have overcome this using highly parallel architectures. Usage: Implemented in a single-chip FPGA holographic video processor. Used to calculate CGH from Unity-rendered 3D scenes. name: Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction
head: ASM, Angular Spectrum Method, Fresnel Method
body: Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction computes the complex wavefield at a target plane from a recorded or computed hologram matrix, solving the inverse problem of optical propagation. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the mathematical inversion of the diffraction integral (via Angular Spectrum or Fresnel approximations) rather than the physical setup [13993-holographic-reconstruction-system-setup.md] or the generation of the hologram itself Parent. The core mechanism propagates a complex field Uh(x,y) defined on the hologram plane to a reconstruction plane at distance z. The propagation is modeled in the spatial frequency domain. Let Uh(u,v) be the 2D Fourier Transform of the hologram field, where u,v are spatial frequencies. The transfer function H(u,v,z) depends on the chosen approximation: 1. Angular Spectrum Method (ASM): Exact for scalar diffraction, valid for near-field. H{ASM}(u,v,z) = \exp\left(i 2\pi z \sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda^2} - u^2 - v^2}\right) Valid when \frac{1}{\lambda^2} - u^2 - v^2 \ge 0. Otherwise, the term is evanescent and decays. 2. Fresnel Method: Approximation for far-field or paraxial regimes. H{Fresnel}(u,v,z) = \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi z}{\lambda}\right) \exp\left(-i \pi \lambda z (u^2 + v^2)\right) The reconstructed field Uz(x,y) is obtained by: Uz(x,y) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathcal{F}\{Uh(x,y)\} \cdot H(u,v,z) \right\} Key shared constraints include: 1. Sampling Requirements: The pixel pitch \Delta x and wavelength \lambda must satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the highest spatial frequency in the transfer function to avoid aliasing. 2. Complexity: The FFT-based approach scales as O(N^2 \log N) for an N \times N hologram, significantly faster than direct summation. Describes the physical apparatus (SLM, lenses, cameras) required to convert the numerically reconstructed complex wavefield into a visible optical image [13993-holographic-reconstruction-system-setup.md]. It addresses hardware-specific constraints like phase-only encoding, pixel crosstalk, and diffraction order filtering, which are absent in pure numerical methods. A post-processing step applied after the absolute value extraction of the reconstructed wavefield. It involves clipping extreme intensity values at a user-defined percentile threshold and applying linear histogram stretching to enhance contrast before final image generation. The method is implemented in tools that allow users to configure wavelength, pixel pitch, and reconstruction method (ASM or Fresnel) via external configuration files to avoid re-declaration. The output is typically saved as a standard PNG image. name: Complex Magnitude Extraction & Histogram Enhancement
head: Histogram Enhancement of Complex Magnitude
body: This method post-processes the complex wavefield reconstructed by Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction to improve visual contrast and dynamic range. It extracts the intensity magnitude from the complex field and applies linear histogram stretching, optionally preceded by clipping extreme values. It differs from adaptive methods like CLAHE by applying global linear scaling rather than local region-based equalization. Inputs: Reconstructed complex wavefield Uz(x,y) from the parent method. Clipping percentile p (user-defined, typically between 1 and 99). Outputs: Enhanced intensity image I{enhanced}(x,y). Data Structures: Uz: 2D array of complex numbers (real and imaginary parts). M: 2D array of floating-point values representing magnitude. I{raw}: 2D array of floating-point values representing intensity. I{clip}: 2D array of floating-point values representing clipped intensity. I{enhanced}: 2D array of floating-point values representing final enhanced intensity. Steps: 1. Magnitude Extraction: Compute the magnitude of the complex wavefield. M(x,y) = |Uz(x,y)| = \sqrt{\text{Re}(Uz(x,y))^2 + \text{Im}(Uz(x,y))^2} Note: Some implementations may skip the square root and use intensity I = |Uz|^2 directly for histogram calculation, but magnitude is the standard physical quantity for amplitude visualization. 2. Intensity Calculation: Compute the intensity image. I{raw}(x,y) = M(x,y)^2 If step 1 used magnitude, square it. If step 1 used intensity directly, I{raw} = M. 3. Clipping: Determine clipping thresholds based on the percentile p. Find the lower threshold T{low} such that p/2 percent of pixels have intensity \le T{low}. Find the upper threshold T{high} such that 100 - p/2 percent of pixels have intensity \le T{high}. Clip the intensity image: I{clip}(x,y) = \begin{cases} T{low} & \text{if } I{raw}(x,y) < T{low} \\ I{raw}(x,y) & \text{if } T{low} \le I{raw}(x,y) \le T{high} \\ T{high} & \text{if } I{raw}(x,y) > T{high} \end{cases} 4. Linear Histogram Stretching: Map the clipped intensity range [T{low}, T{high}] to the full display range [0, 1] (or [0, 255] for 8-bit). I{enhanced}(x,y) = \frac{I{clip}(x,y) - T{low}}{T{high} - T{low}} If T{high} = T{low}, set I{enhanced}(x,y) = 0.5 or handle as a special case to avoid division by zero. 5. Normalization: Scale the result to the desired output bit depth (e.g., multiply by 255 and cast to uint8 for PNG). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def complexmagnitudeextractionandhistogramenhancement(Uz, percentile=1.0): """ Extracts complex magnitude and applies histogram enhancement. Args: Uz: 2D numpy array of complex numbers (reconstructed wavefield). percentile: Float, percentage of extreme values to clip (e.g., 1.0 for 1%). Returns: Ienhanced: 2D numpy array of uint8 values (0-255). """ # Step 1 & 2: Magnitude and Intensity # Using intensity directly as it is monotonic with magnitude and standard for holography Iraw = np.abs(Uz) 2 # Step 3: Clipping # Calculate thresholds based on the specified percentile # percentile is the total percentage to clip from both ends lowerpercentile = percentile / 2.0 upperpercentile = 100.0 - (percentile / 2.0) Tlow = np.percentile(Iraw, lowerpercentile) Thigh = np.percentile(Iraw, upperpercentile) # Clip the intensity values Iclip = np.clip(Iraw, Tlow, Thigh) # Step 4: Linear Histogram Stretching # Avoid division by zero if all values are identical or range is zero rangeval = Thigh - Tlow if rangeval == 0: Ienhancedfloat = np.zeroslike(Iraw) else: Ienhancedfloat = (Iclip - Tlow) / rangeval # Step 5: Normalization to 8-bit Ienhanced = (Ienhancedfloat 255).astype(np.uint8) return Ienhanced Parameters: percentile: Threshold percentage for clipping extreme intensity values before histogram stretching. Typical values are 1-5% to remove noise spikes and saturation outliers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If T{high} = T{low} (e.g., uniform image), the stretching formula fails. Handle by setting output to a constant (e.g., 128) or checking range. Dynamic Range Compression: Clipping removes extreme values, which may discard valid high-intensity details if the percentile is too high. Noise Amplification: In low-signal regions, histogram stretching can amplify noise. Pre-filtering may be required. Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) is a variant applied to holograms to solve domain shift contrast problems. Unlike global histogram stretching, CLAHE divides the hologram into non-overlapping regions and applies conventional contrast enhancement to small regions. It is used in pipelines involving Tensor Holography to enhance the contrast of reproduced images. The operation is defined as E u = P(E h), where h is the hologram, P is the propagation operator, u is the complex amplitude of the reproduced image, and E is the contrast enhancement operator. This method enhances local contrast but may introduce blockiness if tile size is not chosen carefully. Time Complexity: O(N^2) for magnitude extraction and intensity calculation. Histogram calculation and clipping are O(N^2) due to sorting or histogram binning. Linear stretching is O(N^2). Overall complexity is linear with respect to the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) to store the intermediate intensity and clipped images. Strengths: Simple to implement; computationally efficient; effective for removing global dynamic range issues; removes extreme outliers (noise/saturation). Limitations: Global method may not enhance local details as effectively as adaptive methods (e.g., CLAHE); sensitive to the choice of percentile; may amplify noise in low-intensity regions. When to use: When the reconstructed hologram has a narrow dynamic range or is dominated by extreme outliers; when computational resources are limited. When not to use: When local contrast enhancement is required; when the hologram has significant local variations in intensity that global stretching cannot address. This method is part of the post-processing pipeline for Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction. It is commonly used in computer-generated holography (CGH) and holographic display systems to prepare reconstructed images for visualization. The technique of linear histogram stretching with percentile clipping is a standard image processing technique applied to holographic reconstructions to improve visual quality. CLAHE is a classical contrast enhancement algorithm applied to holograms predicted from Tensor Holography to enhance the contrast of reproduced images.
