name: Holographic Reconstruction System Setup
head: Experimental setup for holographic reconstruction, Optical setup for holographic reconstruction, Phase-Only Holographic Display
body: This article describes the physical optical apparatus required to reconstruct a complex wavefield computed numerically (see Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction) into a visible image. It converts digital hologram matrices into optical fields using spatial light modulators (SLMs), handling phase-only or amplitude-only modulation constraints, and filtering diffraction artifacts. It differs from pure numerical reconstruction by introducing physical components (lasers, lenses, SLMs, cameras) and their empirical calibration. The system converts a digital hologram into a physical wavefront using coherent illumination, spatial light modulation, and optical filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Digital hologram matrix (complex or real-valued), system parameters (wavelength, pixel pitch, distance). Output: Reconstructed wavefront captured by a camera or viewed by an eye. Data Structures: Hologram Matrix: 2D array of complex numbers Uh(x,y) or real-valued intensity/phase maps. SLM Pixel Map: 2D array of values mapped to SLM physical pixels. Steps: 1. Illumination Preparation: Filter the illumination laser beam by a pinhole and collimate it by a lens. To remove speckles caused by laser coherence, rotate a holographic diffuser at the focused spot of the laser beams. 2. Hologram Encoding (if Phase-Only SLM): If the SLM is phase-only but the hologram is complex-valued, use the Burch encoding method to project the complex wave field onto real values. For off-axis holograms, set the grating period to 0.25 of its maximum period to avoid unwanted noise. 3. SLM Modulation: Upload the encoded hologram to the SLM. If using an LCoS SLM with small pixel pitch, put the same pixel value in 2x2 nearest pixels to minimize pixel crosstalk. Calibrate the amplitude by measuring output values for each input pixel value, as modulated intensity nonlinearly depends on assigned pixel values. 4. Optical Propagation and Filtering: Illuminate the SLM with the collimated laser beam. Form the Fourier plane using a first lens group. Block zeroth order and higher order diffractions using an adjustable 2D slit. 5. Reconstruction and Capture: The reconstructed wavefront modulated by the CGH on the SLM is captured by a digital camera. The camera is placed at shooting distances of 155, 160, 165, and 170 mm. Alternatively, view directly with the human eye or a near-eye display system. Parameters: Wavelength (\lambda): Must match the recording or intended reconstruction wavelength. Common values: 638, 515, and 460 nm sequentially illuminated on the LCoS. Single wavelength example: 532 nm. Pixel Pitch (\Delta x): Determines spatial frequency sampling. Example: 3.6 \mum for IRIS-U62 LCoS, effectively 7.2 \mum when upsampled. Example: 3.74 \mum. Reconstruction Distance (z): Axial distance from SLM to camera/eye. Examples: 155, 160, 165, 170 mm. Minimum required: > 1.7 mm to avoid excessive defocus blur from pixel pitch diffraction. Grating Period: For off-axis holograms, set to 0.25 of maximum period. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pixel Crosstalk: Small pixel pitch on LCoS SLMs causes crosstalk. Mitigation: upsample by 2x2. Diffraction Orders: Zeroth and higher orders create noise. Mitigation: use a 2D slit at the Fourier plane. Speckle: Caused by laser coherence. Mitigation: rotate holographic diffuser. Defocus Blur: Pixel pitch diffraction causes blur. At 2 mm propagation, dispersion diameters are 25 pixels (red), 20 (green), 18 (blue). If max defocus blur diameter is 15 pixels, propagation must be > 1.7 mm. Nonlinear Response: SLM intensity response is nonlinear. Calibration is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configureholographicsetup(wavelength, slmpitch, slmresolution, reconstructiondistance): """ Configures physical parameters and procedural steps for holographic reconstruction setup. """ # 1. Illumination Preparation # Filter illumination laser beam by a pinhole and collimate it by a lens illumination = { "pinholefilter": True, "collimatinglens": True, "specklereduction": "rotateholographicdiffuseratfocusedspot" # } # 2. Hologram Encoding (if Phase-Only SLM) # Use Burch encoding to project complex wave field onto real values # For off-axis holograms, set grating period to 0.25 of maximum period encoding = { "method": "burchencoding", "gratingperiodratio": 0.25, "hologramtype": "off-axis" } # 3. SLM Modulation # Put same pixel value in 2x2 nearest pixels to minimize crosstalk # Calibrate amplitude: measure output intensity for each input pixel value slmconfig = { "upsamplefactor": 2, "amplitudecalibration": "measureoutputforeachinputpixel" } # 4. Optical Propagation and Filtering # Form Fourier plane using first lens group # Block zeroth order and higher order diffractions using adjustable 2D slit filtering = { "fourierplanelens": True, "slitfilter": "adjustable2dslit" } # 5. Capture Setup # Capture reconstructed wavefront with digital camera at shooting distance capture = { "cameratype": "digitalcamera", "shootingdistances": [155, 160, 165, 170] # mm } return { "illumination": illumination, "encoding": encoding, "slm": slmconfig, "filtering": filtering, "capture": capture } A user-driven calibration method for correcting optical aberrations in holographic near-eye displays by empirically determining coefficients of the holographic object point representation. It differs from automated alignment methods by relying on direct human visual feedback to optimize mathematical parameters rather than computer vision. Choose it when the display system has unknown or complex aggregate optical errors that cannot be modeled explicitly. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In one experiment, shooting distances of 155, 160, 165, and 170 mm were used to achieve 3D effects. Scaling: Propagation distance must be adjusted to avoid defocus blur from pixel pitch diffraction. Minimum distance > 1.7 mm for a 2 mm depth range. Strengths: Allows physical reconstruction of complex wavefields; calibration can correct for system-specific aberrations. Limitations: Requires precise optical alignment; sensitive to laser coherence (speckle); nonlinear SLM response requires calibration; diffraction orders must be filtered. When to Use: When physical holographic reconstruction is needed for volumetric displays or near-eye displays. When Not to Use: When purely numerical simulation is sufficient. Holographic reconstruction systems have been developed for various applications, including 2D-to-3D rendering and near-eye displays for VR/AR. Early systems used phase-only SLMs with Gaea-2 systems. More recent developments include diffraction-engineered holography using LCoS SLMs to overcome depth representation limits. Calibration techniques using user feedback have been proposed for correcting aberrations in holographic near-eye displays. name: Calibration via Coefficient Adjustment
head: Aberration Calibration
body: Calibration via Coefficient Adjustment is a user-in-the-loop method for correcting optical aberrations in holographic near-eye displays by empirically determining the coefficients of the holographic object point representation. It solves the problem of unknown or complex aggregate optical errors in the display and eye system without requiring explicit knowledge of the optical surfaces. It differs from automated alignment methods, such as Parallax-barrier and Lenticular Display Calibration, which use computer vision and homography to map physical components, by relying on direct human visual feedback to optimize mathematical parameters [S1, 19679-parallax-barrier-and-lenticular-display-calibration.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A holographic display system capable of rendering a single object point; a user. Output: A set of optimal coefficients a{jo} for the holographic representation function. Data Structures: The holographic representation of a single object point oi is defined by the function fz(\rho, \theta){oi}. This function is parameterized by a set of coefficients a{jo}. The specific internal layout of these coefficients is not detailed, but they correspond to orthogonal geometric operations such as scale, squash, and rotate. Steps: 1. Select Object Point: Choose a specific object point oi to calibrate. 2. Render Test Pattern: The display presents the single object point oi to the user, represented in the hologram as fz(\rho, \theta){oi}. 3. User Adjustment: The user adjusts the coefficients a{jo} of fz(\rho, \theta){oi}. 4. Feedback Loop: The user observes the resulting spot and adjusts coefficients until the most tightly focused spot is seen. 5. Repeat: Repeat steps 1-4 for additional object points oi across the display volume. 6. Interpolation: For true 3D holograms, perform calibration for a small number of focal positions (e.g., four) and interpolate the coefficients over the complete focal range. Interpolate coefficients for remaining spatial points, as aberrations vary smoothly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calibratecoefficients(display, userfeedback): """ Calibrate holographic coefficients via user feedback. Args: display: Object representing the holographic display hardware. userfeedback: Function that returns a quality metric or allows user input to adjust coefficients. Returns: dict: A mapping of (objectpointid, focalposition) to coefficient vectors ajo. """ # Define sparse set of object points to measure # For highly aberrated systems, ~15 points are sufficient # For low aberration, 1 point at center is sufficient measuredpoints = getsparseobjectpoints(display) # Define focal positions for 3D interpolation focalpositions = [z1, z2, z3, z4] calibrationdata = {} for oi in measuredpoints: for z in focalpositions: # Render single object point oi at focal position z # Representation: fz(rho, theta)oi # Initialize coefficients ajo currentcoefficients = initializecoefficients() # User adjusts coefficients until tightest focus is seen # This is an interactive loop, not automated optimization currentcoefficients = userfeedback.adjustuntilfocused( display, oi, z, currentcoefficients) calibrationdata[(oi, z)] = currentcoefficients # Interpolate coefficients for all other points and focal positions # Aberrations are assumed to be smoothly varying fullcoefficientmap = interpolatecoefficients(calibrationdata) return fullcoefficientmap Parameters: Number of measured points (highly aberrated): 15. Number of measured points (low aberration): 1 (center of display). Number of focal positions: 4 (example). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: It is impractical to measure fz(\rho, \theta){oi} for all object points because there are expected to be millions. The method relies on the assumption that aberrations are smoothly varying. A procedure to automatically calibrate the position of a parallax-barrier with respect to the underlying rear-projection image using a digital camera and homography. It differs from manual alignment by using a computer-guided laser-cut barrier and automated image processing to map projector sub-pixels to specific viewing angles. Time Complexity: The calibration process is interactive and user-dependent. The calculation of the hologram for a single point is fast, but the user adjustment loop dominates the time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing coefficients for a sparse set of points and focal positions, then interpolating. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Does not require knowledge of the specific optics of the display or eye; measures the aggregate effect of all components. The coefficients are applicable for any image content. Limitations: Requires user interaction; impractical for all millions of object points. Relies on smooth variation of aberrations for interpolation accuracy. When to use: When optical aberrations are significant and unknown, or when explicit optical modeling is intractable. This method is described in the context of Holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. It addresses the complexity of the Fresnel holographic model and the need for high-speed calculation while maintaining visual quality through aberration correction. Holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality, https://doi.org/10.1145/3072959.3073624, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Parallax-barrier and Lenticular Display Calibration
head: Automatic calibration of parallax-barrier
body: A procedure to automatically calibrate the position of a parallax-barrier with respect to the underlying rear-projection image using a digital camera and homography. It differs from manual alignment by using a computer-guided laser-cut barrier and automated image processing to map projector sub-pixels to specific viewing angles. Inputs: A rear-projection screen with a parallax-barrier mounted ~10 mm in front. A high-resolution digital camera (3K × 2K) positioned ~3 meters from the screen, facing the center. Multiple projectors covering the screen area. The physical barrier has slits 1 pixel wide, spaced 16 pixels apart, supporting 16 views. Outputs: A 3 × 3 homography matrix for each projector mapping display coordinates to camera pixels. A view assignment for every sub-pixel in each projector's image space. Data Structures: Homography matrix H: 3 × 3 matrix representing the projective transformation between the projector plane and the camera image plane. Slit line equation: ax + by + c = 0, derived via linear regression. View map: A 2D array matching the projector resolution, where each element stores an integer view index (0–15). Steps: 1. Homography Computation: Display checkerboard images on each projector. Capture corresponding images with the camera. Fit horizontal and vertical lines to the observed checkerboard patterns. Compute the intersection of each horizontal line with each vertical line analytically to obtain 48 coordinates of checkerboard corners in the camera image. Compute the 3 × 3 homography matrix H that maps points on the display to camera pixels using these corner correspondences. 2. Slit Detection in Camera Space: Project a white image on each projector to create a continuous bright surface. Capture a single image with the camera. Apply a Laplacian edge detector to the captured image. Threshold the result to isolate pixels belonging to the slits (high intensity areas). Perform a flood-fill operation to group pixels corresponding to each slit. Use linear regression on the pixels of each slit group to compute an analytical line equation for the slit. 3. Mapping to Projector Space: Transform the slit lines from camera space to the image space of each projector using the computed homographies H. The resulting slit lines in the projector images are roughly 16 pixels apart. 4. Interpolation and View Assignment: Interpolate the line equations for neighboring original slit lines to obtain slit lines for the remaining 15 views. Rasterize all lines for all 16 views. Entirely fill the projector image space so that each sub-pixel has a view assignment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calibrateparallaxbarrier(projectors, camera, barrierslitcount=16): """ Calibrate parallax barrier position relative to projectors. """ homographies = {} # Step 1: Compute Homographies for projector in projectors: # Display checkerboard on projector projector.displaycheckerboard() # Capture image cameraimage = camera.capture() # Detect lines horizontallines = fitlines(cameraimage, orientation='horizontal') verticallines = fitlines(cameraimage, orientation='vertical') # Compute corners corners = [] for hline in horizontallines: for vline in verticallines: corner = intersect(hline, vline) corners.append(corner) # Compute homography H mapping display points to camera pixels # Note: Display points are known from checkerboard pattern definition displaypoints = getcheckerboardpatternpoints() H = computehomography(displaypoints, corners) homographies[projector.id] = H # Step 2: Detect Slits in Camera Space # Project white image for projector in projectors: projector.displaywhite() # Capture single image whiteimage = camera.capture() # Edge detection and thresholding edges = laplacianedgedetector(whiteimage) thresholded = threshold(edges, value=0) # Threshold to isolate slits # Flood fill to group slit pixels slitgroups = floodfill(thresholded) # Linear regression for slit lines slitlinescamera = [] for group in slitgroups: line = linearregression(group) # Returns ax + by + c = 0 slitlinescamera.append(line) # Step 3: Transform Slits to Projector Space slitlinesprojector = {} for projid, H in homographies.items(): # Inverse homography to map from camera to projector Hinv = inverse(H) linesproj = [] for linecam in slitlinescamera: # Transform line equation from camera space to projector space lineproj = transformline(linecam, Hinv) linesproj.append(lineproj) slitlinesprojector[projid] = linesproj # Step 4: Interpolation and Rasterization viewmaps = {} for projid, linesproj in slitlinesprojector.items(): # Interpolate lines for all 16 views # Assuming linesproj contains the primary visible slits alllines = interpolatelines(linesproj, count=barrierslitcount) # Rasterize and assign views width, height = projector.resolution viewmap = emptyarray(width, height, dtype=int) for viewidx, line in enumerate(alllines): # Rasterize line and fill regions between lines with viewidx # This step assigns each sub-pixel a view assignviewtopixels(viewmap, line, viewidx, alllines) viewmaps[projid] = viewmap return homographies, viewmaps Parameters: Camera resolution: 3K × 2K. Camera distance: ~3 meters. Barrier slit width: 1 pixel. Barrier slit spacing: 16 pixels. Number of views: 16. Edge Cases: If the camera resolution is insufficient to detect slits, the Laplacian edge detection may fail. Degenerate checkerboard patterns (e.g., collinear points) will fail homography computation. Time Complexity: Dominated by line fitting and homography computation per projector. Linear in the number of pixels for edge detection and flood fill. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the camera and projector resolution for storing images and view maps. Strengths: Automated, high precision due to high-resolution camera and analytical line fitting. Limitations: Requires precise camera placement and high-resolution imaging. Originated in the context of distributed rendering for multiview parallax displays. The method uses a computer-guided laser to cut the parallax-barrier slits into a sheet of black Mylar polyester film, which is glued to a sheet of glass mounted ~10 mm in front of the rear-projection screen. Distributed rendering for multiview parallax displays, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.650171, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Polygon-based CGH generation
head: Polygon Plane Method
body: The Polygon-based CGH generation method synthesizes computer-generated holograms by decomposing a 3D scene into a set of 2D polygonal surfaces, treating each surface as a continuous light-emitting element rather than a collection of discrete points. It solves the computational bottleneck of point-cloud synthesis by reducing the number of scene elements required to approximate a geometry, thereby lowering the complexity of the wavefield superposition. Unlike point-cloud methods that sum contributions from thousands of individual emitters, this method integrates the wavefront contribution over the area of each polygon. It is distinguished from volume rendering approaches by its explicit geometric representation of surfaces and from layer-based methods by its handling of arbitrarily oriented planes rather than strictly horizontal slices. The method relies on plane-wave spectrum theory and spherical-wave diffraction theory to propagate the wavefield from the object plane to the hologram plane. The core challenge is that standard propagation algorithms assume the source plane is parallel to the hologram plane; therefore, the algorithm must transform arbitrarily oriented polygon planes into a local coordinate system aligned with the propagation direction. Inputs: A 3D scene defined by a mesh of N polygons. Each polygon is defined by its vertices in global coordinates (x, y, z). Wavelength of reconstruction light \lambda. Propagation distance d from the object plane to the hologram plane. Hologram plane dimensions and pixel pitch. Outputs: Complex amplitude distribution H(x, y) on the hologram plane. 1. Polygon Vertex List: A list of N polygons. Each polygon i contains a list of vertices V{i,j} = (x{i,j}, y{i,j}, z{i,j}). 2. Transformation Matrix T: A 3 \times 3 matrix used to map global coordinates to local coordinates for each polygon. T = \begin{bmatrix} a1 & a2 & a3 \\ a4 & a5 & a6 \\ a7 & a8 & a9 \end{bmatrix} The inverse transformation is given by k = T^{-1} \hat{k}, where k is the wave vector in global coordinates and \hat{k} is in local coordinates. 1. Scene Decomposition: Divide the 3D object into micro-polygon planes. Each plane is generally not parallel to the hologram plane. 2. Coordinate Transformation Setup: For each polygon, determine the transformation matrix T that aligns the polygon's normal with the propagation direction (z-axis). 3. Local Spectrum Calculation: Calculate the local spectrum of the polygon in its local coordinate system (\hat{u}, \hat{v}). The complex amplitude in the local domain is denoted as \hat{e}[\hat{u}(u,v), \hat{v}(u,v)]. 4. Jacobian Computation: Compute the Jacobian determinant J(u, v) to account for the coordinate transformation between global spatial frequencies (u, v) and local spatial frequencies (\hat{u}, \hat{v}). J(u, v) = \frac{\partial \hat{u}}{\partial u} \frac{\partial \hat{v}}{\partial v} - \frac{\partial \hat{u}}{\partial v} \frac{\partial \hat{v}}{\partial u} Using the matrix elements ai, this expands to: J(u, v) = (a2 a6 - a3 a5) \frac{\partial w}{\partial u} + (a3 a4 - a1 a6) \frac{\partial w}{\partial v} + (a1 a5 - a2 a4) where w represents the coordinate transformation function. 5. Wavefield Propagation Integration: Integrate the contribution of the polygon to the hologram plane using the plane-wave spectrum propagation formula: H(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{e}[\hat{u}(u,v), \hat{v}(u,v)] \exp \left[ i 2\pi ( \hat{u}(u,v) x + \hat{v}(u,v) y) \right] J(u,v) \exp \left[ i k d \sqrt{1 - \lambda^2 u^2 - \lambda^2 v^2} \right] du dv Where: k = 2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber. d is the propagation distance. \lambda is the wavelength. u, v are spatial frequencies in the global system. 6. Superposition: Sum the contributions Hi(x, y) from all N polygons to obtain the total hologram: H{total}(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Hi(x, y) 7. Quantization: Quantize the complex amplitude to phase values 0 to 2\pi if using a phase-only SLM. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polygonbasedcgh(scenepolygons, wavelength, propagationdistance, hologramresolution): """ Generates a CGH using the Polygon Plane Method. Args: scenepolygons: List of polygons. Each polygon is a list of vertices [(x1, y1, z1), (x2, y2, z2),...]. wavelength: Float, wavelength of light lambda. propagationdistance: Float, distance d from object to hologram. hologramresolution: Tuple (H, W), height and width of hologram in pixels. Returns: hologram: 2D array of complex amplitudes. """ k = 2 pi / wavelength hologram = zeros((H, W), dtype=complex) # Precompute hologram coordinates xcoords, ycoords = meshgrid(range(W), range(H)) for polygon in scenepolygons: # Step 1: Determine transformation matrix T for this polygon # T aligns the polygon normal with the z-axis. # Note: The exact construction of T depends on the polygon's orientation. # For a general polygon, T is derived from the normal vector n = (nx, ny, nz). # A common approach is to rotate n to (0, 0, 1). T = computetransformationmatrix(polygon) # Step 2: Define local spectrum function ehat(uhat, vhat) # This represents the complex amplitude distribution on the polygon surface. # For a uniform emitter, this is constant over the polygon area. # The limits of integration are determined by the polygon's projection # in the frequency domain. # Step 3: Numerical Integration # The integral is over spatial frequencies u, v. # We discretize the integration domain. # Define integration bounds for u, v based on polygon size and distance # Approximation: The spatial frequency support is limited by the polygon's # extent. Let Umax and Vmax be the max spatial frequencies. urange = linspace(-Umax, Umax, numintegrationsteps) vrange = linspace(-Vmax, Vmax, numintegrationsteps) polygoncontribution = zeros((H, W), dtype=complex) for u in urange: for v in vrange: # Calculate local frequencies uhat, vhat from global u, v # using the inverse transformation or geometric projection uhat, vhat = transformfrequencies(u, v, T) # Evaluate local spectrum # ehat is non-zero only if (uhat, vhat) corresponds to a point # within the polygon's spatial extent. if iswithinpolygonbounds(uhat, vhat, polygon): ehatval = getlocalspectrumvalue(uhat, vhat, polygon) # Calculate Jacobian J(u, v) # J depends on the derivatives of the coordinate transformation. # Using the formula provided in sources: # J = (a2a6 - a3a5)dw/du + (a3a4 - a1a6)dw/dv + (a1a5 - a2a4) # dw/du and dw/dv are partial derivatives of the transformation. Jval = computejacobian(u, v, T) # Propagation phase term # sqrt(1 - lambda^2 u^2 - lambda^2 v^2) # This term represents the z-component of the wave vector. # Guard against complex results if u,v are too large (evanescent waves) arg = 1 - wavelength2 (u2 + v2) if arg < 0: continue # Evanescent wave, decays rapidly propagationphase = exp(1j k propagationdistance sqrt(arg)) # Spatial phase term: exp(i 2pi (uhat x + vhat y)) # Note: The source formula uses uhat x + vhat y. # x, y are hologram coordinates. spatialphase = exp(1j 2 pi (uhat xcoords + vhat ycoords)) # Accumulate contribution integrand = ehatval spatialphase Jval propagationphase polygoncontribution += integrand du dv # du, dv are step sizes # Add to total hologram hologram += polygoncontribution return hologram def computetransformationmatrix(polygon): """ Computes the 3x3 transformation matrix T that rotates the polygon's normal vector to align with the z-axis (0,0,1). """ # Calculate normal vector n from polygon vertices v1 = polygon[1] - polygon[0] v2 = polygon[2] - polygon[0] n = cross(v1, v2) n = normalize(n) # Construct rotation matrix to align n with z-axis # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation requires # specific rotation axis and angle calculation. # T = [[a1, a2, a3], [a4, a5, a6], [a7, a8, a9]] # The elements a1..a9 are derived from the rotation matrix R such that R n = (0,0,1). # For the purpose of the algorithm, T is the rotation matrix. return constructrotationmatrixtoz(n) def computejacobian(u, v, T): """ Computes the Jacobian determinant J(u,v) for the coordinate transformation. """ # Extract elements from T a1, a2, a3 = T[0] a4, a5, a6 = T[1] a7, a8, a9 = T[2] # Calculate partial derivatives dw/du and dw/dv # These depend on the specific mapping between global and local coordinates. # In the context of plane-wave spectrum, this relates to the projection of the # polygon onto the frequency plane. # Assuming a linear transformation for small angles or specific approximations: dwdu =... # Placeholder for specific derivative calculation based on T dwdv =... # Placeholder for specific derivative calculation based on T J = (a2 a6 - a3 a5) dwdu + (a3 a4 - a1 a6) dwdv + (a1 a5 - a2 a4) return J Wavelength (\lambda): Typically 532 nm (green) or 633 nm (red) for visible holography. Propagation Distance (d): Depends on the scene depth and hologram setup. In the cited experiments, distances were sufficient to resolve the 3D cubic modules. Polygon Count: Varies by scene complexity. The method is efficient when the polygon count is significantly lower than the point cloud count. 1. Discrete Fourier Transformation Error: The use of discrete integration (DFT) introduces deviation errors in the calculated hologram. 2. Discrete Data Error: Discretization of the polygon surface and frequency domain causes calculation inaccuracies. 3. High Complexity Scenes: If the scene has a very high number of polygons, the computational cost increases significantly. Advanced acceleration techniques (e.g., LUTs) are required. 4. Hidden-Surface Removal: Determining which polygons are visible from the hologram plane can be computationally intensive, especially for complex scenes. 5. Evanescent Waves: The term \sqrt{1 - \lambda^2 u^2 - \lambda^2 v^2} becomes imaginary if spatial frequencies u, v exceed 1/\lambda. These evanescent waves decay exponentially and can be ignored for far-field holograms. Time Complexity: The complexity is proportional to N \times P \times I, where N is the number of polygons, P is the number of hologram pixels, and I is the number of integration steps in the frequency domain. This is generally faster than point-cloud synthesis (M \times P) where M (points) > N (polygons). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the complex amplitude for each polygon's contribution during integration. Memory usage scales with the number of polygons and hologram resolution. Measured Performance: In the cited study, a 3D cubic module took approximately 91-93 ms to calculate, while a triangle module took 53.8 ms. The total time for one plane in a more complex setup was around 15.8 ms, with the majority of time spent on 3D scene generation and light wave propagation. Strengths: Lower computational cost than point-cloud methods for simple geometries. Accurate representation of continuous surfaces. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-complexity scenes with many polygons. Hidden-surface removal is difficult and costly. Discretization errors affect accuracy. When to Use: Suitable for scenes with well-defined, smooth surfaces and moderate complexity. Not ideal for highly detailed, noisy, or point-heavy data without simplification. The Polygon Plane Method was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D real-time computer-generated holograms. It is based on plane-wave spectrum theory and spherical-wave diffraction theory. The method addresses the limitations of point-cloud synthesis by leveraging the geometric continuity of polygonal surfaces. It is part of the broader family of geometric-based CGH calculation methods, alongside ray-based and layer-based approaches. name: Point-Cloud Based CGH Calculation
head: Point Source Method, Point-Cloud Approach, Point-based CGH, Point-cloud based hologram calculation
body: Point-Cloud Based CGH Calculation generates computer-generated holograms by discretizing a 3D scene into a finite set of points, treating each as a coherent point light source, and summing their propagated wavefields on the hologram plane. It is distinguished from Polygon-based CGH generation and Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm by avoiding large-scale FFT circuits and complex mesh processing, making it highly suitable for hardware implementation. While computationally simpler than polygon-based or layer-based approaches, it suffers from high computational cost for large scenes and produces artifacts such as vivid boundaries and weak defocus blur compared to modern alternatives. Inputs: A set of N object points Pi = (xi, yi, zi) representing the 3D scene. Hologram plane dimensions W \times H (pixels). Wavelength \lambda of the reconstruction light. Distance z from the object plane to the hologram plane, or individual depths zi for each point. Outputs: A complex amplitude distribution Uh(x,y) on the hologram plane, which is subsequently encoded into a phase-only or amplitude-only hologram pattern. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of tuples containing coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and optional amplitude Ai and initial phase \phi{0,i} for each point i \in [1, N]. Hologram Buffer: A 2D complex array initialized to zero to accumulate contributions. Mathematical Model: The complex amplitude contribution of a single point source i at hologram pixel (x,y) is calculated using the spherical wave propagation formula or the Fresnel approximation. The distance ri from point i to pixel (x,y) is: ri = \sqrt{(x-xi)^2 + (y-yi)^2 + zi^2}. The phase is \phii(x,y) = k ri + \phi{0,i}, where k = 2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber. The total hologram is the superposition: Uh(x,y) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ai \exp\left(i \phii(x,y)\right). Steps: 1. Discretization: Represent the 3D object as a finite set of object points. 2. Propagation: For each point Pi, calculate its complex amplitude distribution on the hologram plane using the spherical wave formula or Fresnel approximation. 3. Superposition: Sum the complex amplitudes of all N points to obtain the total wave surface distribution Uh(x,y). 4. Occlusion Handling (Optional): Ignore backside wavefront contributions when backside and frontside wavefronts overlap. 5. Encoding: Encode Uh(x,y) into a format suitable for the Spatial Light Modulator (SLM), such as phase-only encoding or amplitude modulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatepointcloudcgh(points, width, height, wavelength): """ Calculate CGH using direct point-wise integration. Args: points: List of tuples (x, y, z, amplitude, phase) for N points. width: Width of hologram in pixels. height: Height of hologram in pixels. wavelength: Wavelength of light in meters. Returns: hologram: 2D list of complex numbers of size (height, width). """ k = 2.0 math.pi / wavelength hologram = [[0.0 + 0.0j for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ampsum = 0.0 + 0.0j for px, py, pz, amp, phi0 in points: dx = x - px dy = y - py dz = pz r = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) phase = k r + phi0 ampsum += amp complex(math.cos(phase), math.sin(phase)) hologram[y][x] = ampsum return hologram Parameters: Wavelength (\lambda): Typically 400-700 nm for visible light. Sub-hologram size: In optimized implementations using Look-Up Tables (LUTs) or Wavefront Recording Planes (WRP), the hologram is divided into sub-holograms. The runtime scales quadratically with the sub-hologram size. Point Density: The number of points N directly impacts complexity; 2 million points is a common benchmark for performance measurement. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Naive summation does not account for occlusion, leading to "see-through" artifacts; explicit occlusion handling increases computational cost. Depth Errors: Incorrect depth values in captured depth maps cause interference-induced black lines at object boundaries. Vivid Boundaries: Abrupt phase variations at interfaces of objects at different depths cause constructive/destructive interference, creating sharp boundaries instead of natural defocus blur. Hole Distortion: Holes in objects are distorted by depth differences between the object and background. Defocus Blur: Coherent propagation forms Fresnel diffraction patterns rather than natural defocus blur, distorting depth perception. Pre-calculates point contributions for specific depths and reuses them to reduce computation time, though it increases memory usage. Interposes an intermediate plane between the point cloud and hologram plane to reduce propagation distance and complexity. Approximates point-wise integration as a convolution with a spatially invariant kernel when the lens phase is fixed, reducing runtime from seconds to milliseconds but sacrificing spatial variance accuracy. A hardware-accelerated method for generating computer-generated holograms from point-cloud data using a dedicated FPGA pipeline. It solves the computational bottleneck by employing a normalized Fresnel approximation that enables integer arithmetic and incremental phase calculation, thereby eliminating the need for memory-intensive look-up tables for trigonometric operations. Unlike the layer method, which relies on FFTs and is unsuitable for hardware implementation, HORN-8 is optimized for localized models and achieves high parallelization through a memoryless pipeline architecture. Time Complexity: The naive point-wise integration method scales as O(N{obj} N{hol}). Runtime scales quadratically with the sub-hologram size. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the hologram buffer. LUT methods require O(D \cdot W{sub} \cdot H{sub}) memory for pre-calculated tables, where D is the number of depth levels. Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA GTX 980 Ti, NVIDIA V100. Runtime: 1 to tens of seconds for 2 million points on GTX 980 Ti, depending on sub-hologram size. Convolution methods can achieve milliseconds. Image Quality (nCGH): 512x512 dataset PSNR 22.5 dB, SSIM 0.756; FHD dataset PSNR 27.1 dB, SSIM 0.889. Strengths: Relatively simple calculations. Can handle real scenes acquired as point clouds. No need for complex polygon mesh processing. Suitable for hardware implementation. Limitations: High computational cost for large scenes. Weak defocus blur and vivid boundaries distort depth perception. Sensitive to depth map errors. Slower than convolution-based methods. When to Use: Small to medium-sized scenes where simplicity is prioritized. Localized models where hardware acceleration is preferred. Synthetic scenes with known point coordinates. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring high resolution and large point counts. Scenes requiring accurate depth cues and natural defocus blur. Applications with noisy or incomplete depth data. The point-cloud approach, also known as the object point scattering method, is a conventional CGH generation technique. In 2002, T. Shimobab et al. employed this method to construct a 3D diagram using a reflective LCD panel and LED reference light source. It is based on the superposition of spherical waves from point sources. It has been widely studied as a baseline for comparison with layer-based, polygon-based, and diffraction-engineered holography. Despite its simplicity, its computational inefficiency and optical artifacts have led to faster and higher-quality alternatives. name: HORN-8 Point-Cloud Hologram Generation
head: HORN-8 algorithm, HORN-8 pipeline
body: HORN-8 is a hardware-accelerated method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) from point-cloud data using a dedicated FPGA pipeline. It solves the computational bottleneck of point-cloud CGH by employing a normalized Fresnel approximation that enables integer arithmetic and incremental phase calculation, thereby eliminating the need for memory-intensive look-up tables for trigonometric operations. Unlike the layer method, which relies on FFTs and is unsuitable for hardware implementation, HORN-8 is optimized for localized models and achieves high parallelization through a memoryless pipeline architecture. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N{obj} object points, where each point j has a depth Zj. The hologram plane has dimensions N{hol} pixels. The system supports a maximum of 65,536 object points per calculation block. Output: A hologram intensity map I(X\alpha, Y\alpha) for all pixels \alpha on the acquisition plane. Data Structures The system is implemented on an FPGA with a specific pipeline structure: FPGA Board: Contains 7 parallel pipelines. Pipeline: Consists of 1 Basic Processing Unit (BPU) and 639 Additional Processing Units (APU). Total Cores: Each board has 640 \times 7 = 4,480 parallel calculation circuits (cores). Memory: The design is memoryless for the calculation pipeline itself, using Block RAM only for input/output data buffering. Formulas The core calculation uses the normalized Fresnel approximation. The intensity I(X\alpha, Y\alpha) at pixel (X\alpha, Y\alpha) is the sum of contributions from all object points: I ( X\alpha, Y\alpha) = \sum{j=1}^{N{obj}} \cos \left[ 2\pi \left( \frac{p}{2\lambda Zj} (X\alpha^2 + Y\alpha^2) \right) \right] = \sum{j=1}^{N{obj}} \cos (2\pi \theta{\alpha j}) Where: p is the hologram pixel pitch. \lambda is the wavelength of the reference light. Zj is the depth of object point j. X\alpha, Y\alpha are the pixel coordinates normalized by the pixel pitch p (i.e., integer indices). Aj (intensity of point j) is set to 1 and excluded from the equation. \theta{\alpha j} is the normalized phase term for point j at pixel \alpha: \theta{\alpha j} = \frac{p}{2\lambda Zj} (X\alpha^2 + Y\alpha^2). Parameters Operating Frequency (f): 0.25 GHz. Parallel Circuits (C): 4,480 per board. Max Points per Block: 65,536 (2^{16}). Algorithm Steps The calculation proceeds pixel by pixel across the hologram plane. For each pixel, the contributions of all active object points are summed. 1. Initialization (BPU): For the first pixel (X1, Y1), the Basic Processing Unit (BPU) calculates the initial phase \theta{1j} and the corresponding cosine value for each object point j. 2. Increment Calculation: Compute the phase difference increment \Deltaj = \frac{p}{2\lambda Zj} for each object point j. 3. Phase Update (APU): For subsequent pixels, the Additional Processing Units (APU) update the phase incrementally. The difference \Gamma = 2\Deltaj X\alpha between adjacent pixels is summed to create the next phase value. 4. Cosine Approximation: Calculate the cosine of the updated phase using a novel approximate algorithm implemented with two adder-subtractor gates. This avoids memory look-up tables, allowing the pipeline to be memoryless. 5. Summation: Sum the cosine contributions from all object points to determine the hologram pixel intensity. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-5 for all pixels in the hologram plane. 7. Block Processing: When a larger number of object points needs to be addressed, the object is divided into blocks for calculation. Pseudocode The following pseudocode represents the logic of a single pipeline core (BPU or APU) processing one object point's contribution to the hologram plane. Note that in the actual hardware, these operations are parallelized across 4,480 cores per board. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def horn8pipeline(objectpoints, hologramwidth, hologramheight, p, wavelength): """ Simulates the HORN-8 pipeline logic for a single object point contribution. In hardware, this is parallelized across many cores. """ hologram = [[0.0] hologramheight for in range(hologramwidth)] for x in range(hologramwidth): for y in range(hologramheight): intensity = 0.0 for pt in objectpoints: z = pt['z'] if z == 0: continue # Avoid division by zero delta = p / (2 wavelength z) if x == 0 and y == 0: # BPU: initial phase for first pixel phase = delta (x2 + y2) else: # APU: incremental phase update # Hardware sums Gamma = 2 delta Xalpha for X direction phase += 2 delta x # Hardware cosine approximation using two adder-subtractor gates cosval = math.cos(2 math.pi phase) intensity += cosval hologram[x][y] = intensity return hologram def theoreticaltime(Nobj, Nhol, f, C): """ Calculates the theoretical time for HORN-8 generation. """ return (Nobj Nhol) / (f C) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Memory Bottleneck: Previous systems used look-up tables for cosine operations, which consumed significant Block RAM (up to 94% usage) and limited parallelism. HORN-8 avoids this by using an approximate algorithm with adder-subtractors, keeping slice usage at 98% and Block RAM at 94% but freeing up memory for I/O. Object Size Limit: The maximum number of object points per calculation block is 65,536. When a larger number of object points needs to be addressed, the object is divided into blocks for calculation. Precision: The use of integer arithmetic and approximate cosine algorithms may introduce quantization errors, but the design prioritizes speed and hardware efficiency. Time and Memory Complexity Time Complexity: The theoretical calculation time for one board is T{horn} = \frac{N{obj} \times N{hol}}{f \times C}. Memory Complexity: The pipeline is memoryless for calculation, using Block RAM only for input/output data buffering. Measured Performance Single Board: Generating a 1,920x1,080 hologram (2 million pixels) from 10,000 points took 0.019 seconds (155 fps). This is 160x faster than a CPU (Core i7-6700K, 2.951 seconds) and 6x faster than a GPU (GTX TITAN X, 0.106 seconds). Cluster Performance: An 8-board cluster generated a 100-million-pixel hologram from 10,000 points in 100 ms (10 fps). Large-Scale Generation: Generating a 100-million-pixel hologram from 10-million points took 125 seconds on an 8-board cluster, with the object divided into 160 blocks of ~65,000 points each. Scaling Performance scales linearly with the number of parallel circuits (cores) and boards. The system is designed to output hologram data in parallel with calculation, concealing transfer time T{out}. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: High speed, suitable for hardware implementation, memoryless pipeline, effective for localized models (simulations, medical data). Limitations: Requires division of large objects into blocks, approximate cosine algorithm may have precision trade-offs, not suitable for complete spaces (real scenes) which are better handled by the layer method. HORN-8 was developed as a next-generation holographic imaging system to demonstrate real-time generation of large-scale holograms. It builds on the point-cloud based CGH calculation method, which is effective for localized models and suitable for hardware implementation due to its independence from FFTs. The system was designed to overcome the memory and speed limitations of previous HORN computers by implementing a memoryless pipeline with a novel cosine approximation algorithm. name: True 3D Hologram Calculation
head: Fresnel holography with phase correction
body: True 3D Hologram Calculation generates a hologram where scene elements are positioned at their actual 3D coordinates, providing accurate depth cues and parallax. It differs from planar hologram methods by explicitly correcting the object phase to maintain consistency across the hologram plane, preventing the noise and artifacts that arise when using a constant object phase for objects at varying depths. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A point cloud of object points \mathbf{o} derived from color and depth buffers, with occluded points culled from the viewer's eye position. The wavelength \lambda of the reconstruction light. The position of the hologram plane. Outputs: A phase-only or complex amplitude hologram pattern ready for upload to a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of 3D coordinates \mathbf{o} = (xo, yo, zo) and associated color/intensity values. Hologram Plane: A 2D grid of pixels (x, y) at a specific depth zh. Method Steps: 1. Point Cloud Generation: Form a point cloud from the viewer's eye position using standard rendering pipeline color and depth buffers, culling occluded points to ensure only visible surfaces contribute to the hologram. 2. Phase Correction Calculation: For each object point \mathbf{o}, calculate the corrected object phase \phio to ensure consistency across the sub-hologram associated with that point, mitigating the wide variation in phase that occurs with true 3D depth. 3. Hologram Synthesis: Calculate the total complex amplitude at each hologram pixel by summing the contributions of all object points, using the corrected phase \phio and the actual 3D position of each point in the wave propagation model. Formulas: The corrected object phase \phio is calculated as: \phio = -\frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left( |\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{r}| - |\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{o}| \right) Where: \lambda is the wavelength of the reconstruction light. k is the wavenumber (2\pi/\lambda). \mathbf{o} is the 3D position of the object point. \mathbf{p}c^o is the center point of the sub-hologram corresponding to object point \mathbf{o}. \mathbf{r} is a reference point (often on the optical axis) used to define the phase reference distance. Note: The source text contains OCR artifacts (kpc®o − l®k), which are corrected here to standard Euclidean distance notation to resolve symbol ambiguity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def calculatetrue3dhologram(pointcloud, wavelength, hologrampixels, subhologramcenters, referencepoint): """ Calculate a true 3D hologram with phase correction. Args: pointcloud: List of objects with attributes.pos (3D tuple) and.intensity (float). wavelength: Float, lambda of reconstruction light. hologrampixels: List of 3D pixel coordinates (x, y, zh). subhologramcenters: Dict mapping object index to 3D center point pc^o. referencepoint: 3D tuple for the reference position r. Returns: hologram: List of complex amplitudes corresponding to hologrampixels. """ k = 2.0 math.pi / wavelength hologram = [0.0 + 0.0j] len(hologrampixels) for idx, obj in enumerate(pointcloud): pco = subhologramcenters[idx] # Euclidean distance from sub-hologram center to object point distobj = math.sqrt(sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(pco, obj.pos))) # Euclidean distance from sub-hologram center to reference point distref = math.sqrt(sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(pco, referencepoint))) # Corrected object phase phio = -(2.0 math.pi / wavelength) (distref - distobj) for pxidx, px in enumerate(hologrampixels): # Distance from object point to hologram pixel dist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(px, obj.pos))) # Propagation phase phiprop = k dist # Total phase at pixel totalphase = phio + phiprop # Amplitude from point cloud data Ao = obj.intensity # Add contribution to hologram hologram[pxidx] += Ao cmath.exp(1j totalphase) return hologram Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Constant Phase Error: Using a constant object phase \phio for true 3D holograms results in widely varying object phase at the hologram plane, producing poor quality results with high noise. Intra-pupil Effects: The method assumes view-dependent effects are handled by head-tracked rendering and does not account for intra-pupil view-dependent effects, such as differences in occlusion or specular highlights between the left and right edges of the eye pupil. Holographic Defocus Blur Matching calculates the maximum propagation distance \Delta z and the diameter of the blur circle of a human eye CoC{eye} in display pixels. It ensures that the holographic defocus blur matches the optical defocus blur of the human eye. It sets itself apart by linking SLM and lens array optical constraints to the physiological limits of the human pupil, allowing for the determination of rendering camera aperture sizes that produce perceptually correct depth cues. This method achieves full 3D vectorial holography by decomposing a target 3D optical field into an array of quasi-non-diffracting beams, each with independently programmable axial intensity and polarization profiles. Unlike conventional holographic approaches using spatial light modulators (SLMs) or digital micromirror devices (DMDs), which are often restricted to 2D vectorial holography or lack depth control, this method coordinates the modulation of amplitude, depth, and polarization across an entire volume using longitudinally engineered beam arrays. Aberration-space holography is a method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) that simultaneously corrects spatially varying (anisoplanatic) aberrations across an entire Nyquist-limited volume or field of view. Unlike isoplanatic correction, which optimizes phase for a single local patch and fails outside it, this technique combines individual propagation kernels—each tailored to negate local aberration at a specific target point—into a single spatial light modulator (SLM) hologram. This enables diffraction-limited control of multiple optical beams in parallel across 2D fields and 3D volumes, overcoming the anisoplanatic limit that restricts parallel steering to small regions. A processing method that captures 2D elemental images via a micro lens array, calculates holograms using a corrected Iterative Fourier Transform Algorithm (IFTA), uploads them to an SLM, and reconstructs a 3D image using output-side micro lens array imaging. Implemented by Choi et al. (2005) to construct a full-parallax wide-viewing-angle 3D holographic display system. Steps: 1. Capture 2D elemental images of a 3D object using a CCD and input micro lens array. 2. Calculate the hologram of the elemental images using a corrected IFTA. 3. Upload the calculated hologram to an SLM. 4. Reconstruct the 3D image using image formation from the output micro lens array. This geometry separates the desired reconstruction from unwanted terms (twin images) by shifting them into different diffraction orders, enabling clean three-dimensional holograms. The reference beam meets the object beam at an angle. Developed by Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks after the availability of coherent laser sources. Complexity: The calculation scales with the number of object points and hologram pixels. For true 3D, every point contributes to every pixel, leading to O(N \cdot M) complexity where N is points and M is hologram pixels. Performance: Achieving good results with phase-only modulation is difficult without phase correction. The phase correction method allows for high-quality holograms with widely varying depth, but requires careful computation of the reference distances. Strengths: Provides accurate 3D depth cues and parallax. Corrects for phase inconsistencies inherent in naive true 3D Fresnel holography. Limitations: Computationally expensive. Does not account for intra-pupil view-dependent effects. The method is described in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. It addresses the challenge of generating high-quality true 3D holograms using phase-only modulation, where naive approaches fail due to phase variation across the hologram plane. The phase correction formula was introduced to improve consistency on the hologram plane. name: Holographic Defocus Blur Matching
head: Blur Circle Diameter Calculation, CoC Eye Matching, Determining the diameter of the blur circle
body: Holographic Defocus Blur Matching is a method for calculating the maximum propagation distance of a hologram (\Delta z) and the diameter of the blur circle of a human eye (CoC{eye}) in display pixels, ensuring that the holographic defocus blur matches the optical defocus blur of the human eye. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly linking the physical constraints of the spatial light modulator (SLM) and lens array optics to the physiological limits of the human pupil, allowing for the determination of rendering camera aperture sizes that produce perceptually correct depth cues. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Pixel pitch of the SLM (\Delta x), display resolution (res), system field of view (FoV), virtual image distance of the floating object (d), and human pupil diameter (A). Outputs: Maximum hologram propagation distance (\Delta z) and the eye's blur circle diameter in pixels (CoC{eye}). Data Structures No complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar geometric and optical parameters. Steps and Formulas 1. Calculate Maximum Propagation Distance (\Delta z): The maximum distance the hologram can propagate while still reconstructing a virtual image from distance d to infinity is determined by approximating the lens array as a thin lens. The formula is: \Delta z \approx \frac{1}{\Delta x^2 res^2} \frac{d}{4 \tan^2(FoV/2)} Where: \Delta x: Pixel pitch of the SLM. res: Resolution of the display. FoV: Field of view of the system. d: Virtual image distance of the floating object synthesized by the hologram. The virtual image distance of the display is assumed to be infinity. 2. Calculate Eye Blur Circle Diameter (CoC{eye}): Calculate the diameter of the blur circle of a human eye when focused at infinity, while the holographic object is at distance d, expressed in units of display pixels: CoC{eye} = \frac{A \cdot res}{2d \cdot \tan(FoV/2)} Where: A: Pupil diameter. 3. Determine Rendering Aperture: Set the aperture size of the rendering camera to satisfy the calculated CoC{eye} diameter to ensure the rendered images match the human eye's defocus blur. Parameters and Typical Values Pupil Diameter (A): Set to 1.5 mm. This value is chosen to avoid image degradation originating from a partially blocked wave field, as the pupil diameter is larger than 1.5 mm in the majority of cases. Typical Scenario: For a 55° FoV, 4K resolution, \Delta x = 7.2 \, \mu\text{m}, and d = 0.35 \, \text{m}: \Delta z = 2 \, \text{mm}. CoC{eye} = 15 \, \text{pixels}. Pitfalls and Edge Cases FoV Dependency: Achieving a blur circle equivalent to that of a human eye is only possible under a small FoV (~10°). Propagation Distance Trade-off: Increasing the propagation distance to enlarge the defocus blur diameter causes the virtual image distance (d) to come closer, which also increases CoC{eye}. Consequently, an increase in the diameter of the defocus blur under a fixed propagation distance is required to attain a human eye-equivalent defocus blur with a holographic display. Wave Field Blocking: If the wave field of the hologram is partially blocked by the iris, image quality degrades due to noise from the blocked wave field. Complexity: The method involves constant-time arithmetic operations and trigonometric functions. Strengths: Provides a direct mapping between hardware parameters (SLM, lens array) and perceptual parameters (pupil size, defocus), enabling physically accurate depth cue synthesis in volumetric displays. Limitations: The method's ability to match human eye defocus is constrained by the system's Field of View; it is difficult to match under small FoV conditions when adjusting propagation distance. Use Cases: Holographic optical tweezers, one-step volumetric printings, and volumetric displays requiring accurate depth perception. The method originates from research into diffraction-engineered holography, specifically addressing the depth representation limits of holographic displays. It was developed to support time applications such as holographic optical tweezers, one-step volumetric printings, and volumetric displays by ensuring that the synthesized holographic defocus matches the optical defocus of the human eye. The work was published in Nature Communications in 2022. name: Longitudinally Engineered Metasurface for 3D Vectorial Holography
head: 3D vectorial holography, longitudinally tunable beam arrays
body: This method achieves full 3D vectorial holography by decomposing a target 3D optical field into an array of quasi-non-diffracting beams, each with independently programmable axial intensity and polarization profiles. Unlike conventional holographic approaches using spatial light modulators (SLMs) or digital micromirror devices (DMDs), which are often restricted to 2D vectorial holography or lack depth control, this method coordinates the modulation of amplitude, depth, and polarization across an entire volume using longitudinally engineered beam arrays. Inputs and Outputs Input: Target 3D vectorial optical field defined by axial intensity profile F{p;q}(z) and polarization state for each beam (p,q) in the array; axial extent Z0; number of Bessel components N; free-space wavevector k0; lateral beam positions \rho{p;q}. Output: Metasurface unitary Jones matrix profile \tilde{U}{meta}(\rho, \phi), implemented via nanopillar geometry (dimensions Dx, Dy) and orientation \theta(\rho, \phi). Data Structures Beam Array: A 2D grid of beams indexed by (p,q). Longitudinal Response Function: For each beam (p,q), a complex-valued function \tilde{F}{p;q}(z) defined over z \in [0, Z0]. Bessel Coefficients: Complex coefficients A{Lp;q;m} and A{Rp;q;m} for m \in [-N, N]. Metasurface Pixel: Defined by local orientation \theta(\rho, \phi) and transmission parameters tx, ty, \phix, \phiy. Method Steps 1. Define Longitudinal Response Function: For each beam (p,q), define the longitudinal response function \tilde{F}{p;q}(z) as the product of a scalar axial intensity profile F{p;q}(z) and a Jones vectorial function describing the polarization state: \tilde{F}{p;q}(z) = F{p;q}(z) [a{Lp;q}(z)|L\rangle + a{Rp;q}(z)|R\rangle] where |L\rangle and |R\rangle are unit vectors for left- and right-circular polarization (LCP/RCP), and a{Lp;q}(z), a{Rp;q}(z) are z-dependent complex weighting coefficients satisfying the normalization condition |a{Lp;q}(z)|^2 + |a{Rp;q}(z)|^2 = 1. 2. Decompose into Spin-Dependent Channels: Decompose \tilde{F}{p;q}(z) into two spin-dependent complex value functions corresponding to the LCP and RCP channels: F{L}^{p;q}(z) = F{p;q}(z)a{Lp;q}(z) F{R}^{p;q}(z) = F{p;q}(z)a{Rp;q}(z) 3. Compute Bessel Coefficients via Fourier-like Synthesis: Calculate the complex weighting coefficients for the m-th Bessel beam component in the LCP or RCP channels by projecting the spin-dependent functions onto exponential basis functions: A{Lp;q;m} = \frac{1}{Z0} \int0^{Z0} F{L}^{p;q}(z) e^{-i \frac{2\pi}{Z0} m z} dz A{Rp;q;m} = \frac{1}{Z0} \int0^{Z0} F{R}^{p;q}(z) e^{-i \frac{2\pi}{Z0} m z} dz where Z0 is the axial extent, and the discrete spacing is \Delta kz = 2\pi/Z0. 4. Construct 3D Vectorial Light Field: The complete generated 3D vectorial light field \tilde{E}(\rho, z) is the coherent summation of all spin-dependent Bessel functions across the full beam array: \tilde{E}(\rho, z) = \sump \sumq \sum{m=-N}^{N} \left[ A{Lp;q;m} |L\rangle + A{Rp;q;m} |R\rangle \right] J0(k{\rho}^{m} |\rho - \rho{p;q}|) e^{i kz^m z} where J0 is the zeroth-order Bessel function of the first kind, \rho{p;q} is the lateral displacement, and the transverse and longitudinal wavevectors k{\rho}^m and kz^m satisfy the dispersion relation (k{\rho}^m)^2 + (kz^m)^2 = (k0)^2. 5. Determine Metasurface Jones Matrix: Substitute z=0 into the field expression to obtain the initial complex field distributions at the metasurface plane for both orthogonal polarization components. From these, determine the unitary Jones matrix profile \tilde{U}{meta}(\rho, \phi) required to realize the target longitudinal response function: \tilde{U}{meta}(\rho, \phi) = R(-\theta(\rho, \phi)) \begin{bmatrix} tx e^{i\phix(\rho,\phi)} & 0 \\ 0 & ty e^{i\phiy(\rho,\phi)} \end{bmatrix} R(\theta(\rho, \phi)) where R(\theta) is the rotation matrix for local nanopillar orientation \theta(\rho, \phi), and tx, ty, \phix, \phiy define the amplitude and phase transmission coefficients for linear polarization along x and y directions. 6. Implement via Dual-Matrix Holography: Tailor the geometry (Dx, Dy) and in-plane orientation \theta of each rectangular-shaped nanopillar to implement the designed matrix profile \tilde{U}{meta}(\rho, \phi) using a dual-matrix holography technique, enabling subwavelength control over both phase and polarization at each metasurface pixel. Parameters Z0: Axial extent of the modulated beam array. Determines the discrete spacing of Bessel components \Delta kz = 2\pi/Z0. N: Half the number of Bessel beam components in the superposition. Total components = 2N + 1. k0: Free-space wavevector. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Normalization: The weighting coefficients a{Lp;q}(z) and a{Rp;q}(z) must satisfy |a{Lp;q}(z)|^2 + |a{Rp;q}(z)|^2 = 1 to ensure physical realizability. Orthogonality: The discrete spacing \Delta kz = 2\pi/Z0 ensures mutual orthogonality of the Bessel basis components over the defined axial range Z0. Dispersion Relation: The wavevectors k{\rho}^m and kz^m must satisfy (k{\rho}^m)^2 + (kz^m)^2 = (k0)^2. Not given in the sources. This method was introduced by Le Tan, Pengcheng Huo, Peicheng Lin, et al. in the paper "Longitudinally engineered metasurfaces for 3D vectorial holography" published in Light: Science & Applications in 2026. It addresses the limitations of conventional holographic approaches (SLMs, DMDs) and previous metasurface holograms restricted to 2D vectorial holography by achieving full 3D vectorial holography.
