name: Aberration-Space Holography
head: Aberration-space correction, Full-volume aberration-space holography
body: Aberration-space holography is a method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) that simultaneously corrects spatially varying (anisoplanatic) aberrations across an entire Nyquist-limited volume or field of view. Unlike isoplanatic correction, which optimizes phase for a single local patch and fails outside it, this technique combines individual propagation kernels—each tailored to negate local aberration at a specific target point—into a single spatial light modulator (SLM) hologram. This enables diffraction-limited control of multiple optical beams in parallel across 2D fields and 3D volumes, overcoming the anisoplanatic limit that restricts parallel steering to small regions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: N: The set of N target points of interest in the farfield (or nearfield, depending on propagation model), defined by their coordinates (e.g., lateral angles kx, ky and depth z). Fn: The desired complex amplitude (magnitude and phase) for each target spot n. D: The order of the Zernike polynomial basis used to model aberrations. wd^{(n)}: The Zernike coefficients representing the local wavefront aberration at target point n. P(x,y): The pupil plane of the optical system (typically circular). Outputs: f(x,y): The complex nearfield pattern (SLM phase mask) to be displayed. Data Structures Zernike Polynomials: Indexed by a singleton ANSI index d, corresponding to radial order n and azimuthal order l (Zd = Z{nl}). The basis set includes terms for lateral steering (Z1, Z2), defocus (Z4), and higher-order aberrations up to order D. Kernel Representation: Each kernel Kn(x,y) is represented as a complex exponential of a phase sum: Kn(x, y) = \exp\left(-i \left[ kx^{(n)} x + ky^{(n)} y + \sum{d=1}^{D} wd^{(n)} Zd(x, y) \right] \right) where the linear terms kx^{(n)} x + ky^{(n)} y handle lateral steering (shearing), and the Zernike sum handles aberration correction and depth focusing. Numbered Steps 1. Define the Shearing Kernel: Establish the base linear steering kernel for lateral displacement in Fourier holography: K{\text{shear}}(kx, ky, x, y) = \exp(-i[kx x + ky y]) This kernel steers the nearfield pattern f(x,y) to the farfield angle (kx, ky). 2. Expand Pupil Wavefront: Represent the local wavefront aberration at each target point n as a summation of Zernike polynomials Zd(x,y) weighted by coefficients wd^{(n)}: \Phin(x, y) = \sum{d=1}^{D} wd^{(n)} Zd(x, y) The coefficients wd^{(n)} are determined by measuring or estimating the anisoplanatic aberration at the location of target n. 3. Tailor Kernels: Construct a specific "Zernike kernel" Kn(x,y) for each target point n by combining the shearing term with the aberration correction term. The kernel is designed to negate the local aberration, effectively creating a diffraction-limited focus at that specific site despite the distorted medium: Kn(x, y) = \exp\left(-i \left[ kx^{(n)} x + ky^{(n)} y + \sum{d=1}^{D} wd^{(n)} Zd(x, y) \right] \right) Note: The sign of the Zernike sum is negative in the exponent to provide subtractive (corrective) phase. 4. Combine Kernels: Sum the complex conjugates of all N tailored kernels, weighted by their respective target complex amplitudes Fn, to form the hologram: f(x, y) \propto \sum{n=1}^{N} Kn^(x, y) \cdot Fn This step reshapes power within a D-dimensional aberration space rather than just 2D/3D spatial space, enabling full-field anisoplanatic control. 5. Compute Nearfield: Calculate the final SLM phase mask f(x,y) using the compressed sum. This is equivalent to an inverse compressed Fourier transform where the "basis" functions are the aberration-corrected kernels. Formulas Forward Transform (Verification): Fn \propto \sum{x,y} Kn(x, y) \cdot f(x, y) Inverse Transform (Hologram Generation): f(x, y) \propto \sum{n=1}^{N} Kn^(x, y) \cdot Fn Where Kn^ is the complex conjugate of the n-th kernel. Parameters N (Number of spots): Typically small relative to the megapixel-scale SLM resolution. This sparsity allows for compressive sensing approaches where only a subset of farfield pixels are targeted. D (Zernike Order): The number of Zernike modes used for correction. Typical value for 2D arrays: D=44. Typical value for volumetric displays: D=27. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Anisoplanatism: Previous techniques fail outside a small isoplanatic patch because the point spread function is not invariant. Aberration-space holography addresses this by treating aberration as a dimension in the hologram calculation. Precision: The method requires accurate characterization of the local wavefront error wd^{(n)} for each target point. Errors in aberration measurement will lead to residual aberration in the corrected spots. Computational Load: While compressive sensing reduces the number of terms compared to a full DFT, summing N kernels with D modes each can be computationally intensive for large N and D. However, it avoids the memory overhead of zero-padding required for high-precision DFT-based steering. Optimizes phase for a single local neighborhood (isoplanatic patch). Leaves residual aberration outside this patch. Choose when the field of view is small or aberrations are uniform. Link (Sibling: Holographic Defocus Blur Matching). Uses longitudinally engineered metasurfaces for 3D vectorial holography. Different physical implementation (static metasurface vs. dynamic SLM). Link (Sibling: Longitudinally Engineered Metasurface for 3D Vectorial Holography). Time Complexity: Linear in the number of target spots N and the number of Zernike modes D. The computation is O(N \cdot D) per pixel if evaluated naively, or optimized via FFT-based convolution if the kernels share structure. The sources note that the method offers "fully parallelized performance approaching that of a single Dth order correction". Memory Complexity: Proportional to the SLM resolution (megapixel scale) and the storage of N kernels. Compressive sensing reduces the effective number of farfield pixels computed, lowering memory compared to full DFT methods. Measured Performance: 2D Tweezer Array: Corrected 50 isoplanatic patches with 8 principal aberration modes. Achieved an 8× larger field of view than the best isoplanatic correction. Uncorrected holography yielded average relative Strehl ratio \langle \tilde{S} \rangle = 0.15. Isoplanatic correction improved local performance but only ~2% of the field achieved diffraction-limited performance (\tilde{S} > 0.8). Aberration-space holography achieved \langle \tilde{S} \rangle = 0.78, with 43% of the field corrected to \tilde{S} > 0.8. 3D Volumetric Display: Increased the corrected volume by 12× compared to isoplanatic correction in two-photon excitation experiments. Strengths: Enables full-field, parallel beamforming; corrects anisoplanatic aberrations; works across 2D fields and 3D volumes; compatible with iterative algorithms like Gerchberg-Saxton for amplitude optimization. Limitations: Requires accurate wavefront sensing/calibration for each target point; performance is limited by the order D of the Zernike basis (higher order requires more modes); SLM temporal response limits speed of serial correction if not fully parallelized. When to Use: When parallel steering of multiple beams is required across a large field of view or deep volume in the presence of significant spatially varying aberrations (e.g., through tissue, vacuum windows, or turbulent media). When Not to Use: When the field of view is small enough that a single isoplanatic patch covers the entire area, or when real-time correction is needed but wavefront sensing is too slow. Aberration-space holography was introduced to overcome the limitations of isoplanatic correction in adaptive optics and holography. Traditional adaptive optics often corrects for a single "isoplanatic patch," leaving residual aberrations elsewhere. This technique generalizes the concept by treating aberration as an additional dimension in the hologram calculation, allowing for simultaneous correction across the entire Nyquist-limited volume. It builds on the principles of Fourier holography and compressive sensing spot holography, extending the shearing kernel to include modal expansions of the pupil wavefront (Zernike polynomials). The method has applications in neutral atom quantum computing, holographic displays, high-speed 3D laser printing, multifocal nonlinear microscopy, optogenetics, and laser fabrication. Full-volume aberration-space holography, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08777v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH)
head: optimized DEH
body: Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH) is a hologram synthesis method that optimizes a single complex wave field to reconstruct sharply focused images at object-existing planes and blurred images at other focal planes, thereby providing real-world-like defocus blur and photorealistic reconstruction. It sets itself apart from conventional methods by explicitly optimizing diffracted patterns at out-of-focus planes to enhance defocus blur while maintaining high image quality at in-focus planes, unlike siblings such as nCGH which exhibit weak defocus blur. Inputs: N target varifocal images I{dn}, where n=1 \dots N, rendered for specific propagation distances dn using a physically-based renderer to ensure occluded surfaces are correctly handled. An all-in-focus image I{AIF} of the scene. A depth map D of the scene. A depth attention factor \eta. Initial complex wave field at the hologram plane (z=0): U0(x,y) = A(x,y)e^{i\phi(x,y)}, typically initialized with constant amplitude and random phase. Outputs: Optimized complex wave field U{DEH}(x,y) = A(x,y)e^{i\phi{opt}(x,y)} at the hologram plane. Data Structures: Wave Field: Complex array of size H \times W (hologram resolution), stored as two real arrays: Amplitude A and Phase \phi. Varifocal Images: Array of N intensity images of size H{img} \times W{img} corresponding to depths dn. Depth Map: Array of size H{img} \times W{img} containing depth values D(x,y). Parameters: N: Number of varifocal planes. The benchmark dataset uses 21 planes. \eta: Depth attention factor. Value not explicitly given in sources. Iterations: Optimization steps. Typical value: 500. Wavelength \lambda: Required for wavenumber k = 2\pi/\lambda. Steps: 1. Render Varifocal Images: Generate target intensity images I{dn} for each propagation distance dn using a physically-based renderer. The camera focal distance is changed to match dn to capture accurate blur circles and occlusions. 2. Initialize Wave Field: Initialize the complex wave field U0(x,y) at z=0. 3. Optimization Loop: Repeat for iter = 1 to MaxIter: a. Propagation: For each target plane n=1 \dots N: i. Calculate the propagated wave field Prop{dn} at distance dn using the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM): Prop{dn}(U0) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left[ \mathcal{F}[U0(x,y)] \cdot e^{i kz dn} \right] where \mathcal{F} and \mathcal{F}^{-1} are the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform operators, k = 2\pi/\lambda, and kz = \sqrt{k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2} is the axial wavenumber, with kx, ky being the angular wavenumbers in the lateral directions. ii. Calculate the propagated intensity: I{prop,n} = |Prop{dn}(U0)|^2. b. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L: L = \sum{n=1}^{N} \text{MSE}(I{prop,n}, I{dn}) + \lambda{AIF} \cdot \text{MSE}(I{prop,closest}, I{AIF\weighted}) The first term is the MSE between propagated intensity and varifocal images. The second term is the MSE between propagated intensity and a depth-weighted all-in-focus image, weighted by \eta and D. I{AIF\weighted}(x,y) = I{AIF}(x,y) \cdot w(D(x,y)) where w is a depth-dependent weight function emphasizing planes close to object depths. The index closest refers to the plane dn closest to the object depth for each pixel. c. Gradient Descent: Update the phase \phi(x,y) of the wave field using gradient descent to minimize L. \phi{new}(x,y) = \phi{old}(x,y) - \alpha \frac{\partial L}{\partial \phi(x,y)} where \alpha is the learning rate. d. Convergence Check: If the change in the wave field (e.g., phase difference) is negligible, stop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2 def angularspectrumpropagation(U0, dz, wavelength, pixelsize): """ Propagates a complex wave field U0 by distance dz using Angular Spectrum Method. """ k = 2 np.pi / wavelength H, W = U0.shape fx = np.fft.fftfreq(W, d=pixelsize) fy = np.fft.fftfreq(H, d=pixelsize) Fx, Fy = np.meshgrid(fx, fy) kx = 2 np.pi Fx ky = 2 np.pi Fy kx2plusky2 = kx2 + ky2 # Handle evanescent waves by setting imaginary kz for exponential decay kz = np.where(kx2plusky2 <= k2, np.sqrt(k2 - kx2plusky2), 1j np.sqrt(kx2plusky2 - k2)) kernel = np.exp(1j kz dz) Ufreq = fft2(U0) Upropfreq = Ufreq kernel return ifft2(Upropfreq) def computemse(img1, img2): return np.mean((img1 - img2)2) def dehoptimization(varifocalimages, depths, aifimage, depthmap, eta, wavelength, pixelsize, numiterations=500, learningrate=0.1): """ Optimizes a hologram wave field using Diffraction-Engineered Holography. """ H, W = varifocalimages[0].shape A = np.ones((H, W)) phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, (H, W)) U = A np.exp(1j phi) for i in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0.0 # Term 1: MSE against varifocal images for n in range(len(varifocalimages)): dn = depths[n] Itarget = varifocalimages[n] Uprop = angularspectrumpropagation(U, dn, wavelength, pixelsize) Iprop = np.abs(Uprop)2 totalloss += computemse(Iprop, Itarget) # Term 2: MSE against depth-weighted all-in-focus image # Source does not specify exact weighting function w(D) or closest-plane selection # Assuming a simplified global comparison to a reference depth dref dref = np.median(depths) Upropaif = angularspectrumpropagation(U, dref, wavelength, pixelsize) Ipropaif = np.abs(Upropaif)2 Iaifweighted = aifimage (1.0 - depthmap / np.max(depthmap)) eta totalloss += computemse(Ipropaif, Iaifweighted) # Gradient descent update # The exact gradient dL/dphi requires backpropagation through the ASM operators # Sources do not provide the explicit analytical derivative gradL = np.zeroslike(phi) # Placeholder for backprop result phi = phi - learningrate gradL if i % 100 == 0: print(f"Iteration {i}, Loss: {totalloss}") return A np.exp(1j phi) DEHNet is a convolutional neural network designed to synthesize Diffraction-Engineered Hologram (DEH) wave fields directly from an all-in-focus color image and an all-in-focus depth map. It solves the computational bottleneck of traditional DEH generation, which requires multiple varifocal images and iterative optimization, by replacing the optimization procedure with a direct inference step. Unlike its sibling method nCGH, which also uses RGB-D inputs but lacks depth-aware defocus control, DEHNet produces wave fields that correctly reconstruct defocus blur and sharp focus while suppressing interference artifacts at object boundaries. Time Complexity: The optimization-based DEH is computationally expensive. It requires synthesizing multiple varifocal images and performing iterative optimization (e.g., 500 iterations). Synthesis takes more than 1 minute for a single hologram on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. DEHNet achieves 62 Hz inference on FHD resolution images. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the complex wave field, varifocal images, and depth maps. The optimization process requires memory for gradients and intermediate propagated fields. Performance: General dataset: PSNR 26.1 dB, SSIM 0.88. 512x512 dataset: PSNR 29.0 dB, SSIM 0.909. FHD dataset: PSNR 33.4 dB, SSIM 0.955. Strengths: Provides clear defocus blur even if the blur circle diameter is slightly smaller than the rendered image, enhancing depth perception. Maintains high image quality at in-focus planes. Limitations: High computational load for the optimization-based method makes it impractical for real-time applications without neural network acceleration. When to use: When photorealistic depth expression with accurate defocus blur is required and computational resources allow for offline synthesis or neural network inference. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring rapid hologram generation without pre-trained models, or when hardware constraints prevent the use of large neural networks. Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH) was introduced to address the limitations of conventional CGH algorithms that only optimize intensity at object-existing planes, failing to provide realistic defocus blur at other planes. It leverages the fact that phase variation steers light propagation without affecting the image seen by the eyes, allowing adaptive phase changes to enhance defocus blur. The method was demonstrated in a 2022 paper published in Nature Communications. Diffraction-engineered holography: Beyond the depth representation limit of holographic displays, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33728-5, fetched 2026-10-29

name: DEHNet
head: Neural Diffraction-Engineered Holography Network
body: DEHNet is a convolutional neural network trained to synthesize a Diffraction-Engineered Hologram (DEH) wave field directly from an all-in-focus color image and an all-in-focus depth map. It replaces the computationally expensive optimization-based DEH generation, which requires multiple varifocal images and iterative procedures, with a single inference step. Unlike nCGH, which also accepts RGB-D inputs but lacks explicit depth-aware defocus control, DEHNet produces wave fields that correctly reconstruct defocus blur and sharp focus while suppressing interference artifacts at object boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: An all-in-focus color image (I{color}) and an all-in-focus depth map (D). Output: A DEH wave field (complex amplitude). Data Structures The network consists of 34 convolutional layers. Hidden Layers: Layers 1 through 33 are standard convolutional layers. Each layer has 12 channels. Output Layer: Layer 34 is the final layer. It includes a concatenated shortcut (skip connection) from earlier in the network. It outputs the DEH wave field. Channels: The number of channels is set to 12. This value is selected as small as possible to maximize the number of convolutions and activations under restricted computational resources, prioritizing non-linearity and wide receptive field over hidden feature capacity. Parameters Quantization: After training, weights are quantized to 8-bit integers to reduce computational load during inference. Training Data: The dataset consists of 3000 different scenes. Each scene contains: 21 varifocal images 1 all-in-focus color image 21 varifocal depth maps 1 all-in-focus depth map Algorithm Steps 1. Preprocessing: Obtain an all-in-focus color image and an all-in-focus depth map for the target scene. 2. Inference: Pass the color image and depth map into the quantized DEHNet. 3. Synthesis: The network computes the optimal wave field directly. 4. Encoding: Encode the resulting amplitude-only hologram for display. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dehnetinference(colorimage, depthmap, quantizedweights): """ Synthesizes a DEH wave field using the quantized DEHNet. Args: colorimage (Tensor): All-in-focus color image. depthmap (Tensor): All-in-focus depth map. quantizedweights (List[Tensor]): Quantized 8-bit integer weights for 34 layers. Returns: Tensor: The synthesized DEH wave field. """ # Input: concatenate color image and depth map along channel dimension x = concatenatechannels(colorimage, depthmap) # Layers 1 to 33: Convolutional layers with 12 channels and PReLU activation for i in range(33): x = conv2d3x312ch(x, quantizedweights[i]) x = preluactivation(x) # Layer 34: Output layer with concatenated shortcut # The last layer includes a concatenated shortcut from the input xshortcut = concatenatechannels(colorimage, depthmap) x = concatenatechannels(x, xshortcut) # Final convolution to output DEH wave field dehwavefield = conv2d3x3(x, quantizedweights[33]) return dehwavefield def concatenatechannels(tensora, tensorb): """Stacks two tensors along the channel dimension (axis=1).""" return stackalongaxis(tensora, tensorb, axis=1) def conv2d3x312ch(inputtensor, weights): """Applies a 3x3 convolution with 12 output channels and padding=1.""" return applyconvolution(inputtensor, weights, kernelsize=3, outchannels=12, padding=1) def preluactivation(tensor): """Applies Parametric Rectified Linear Unit activation.""" return applyprelu(tensor) def conv2d3x3(inputtensor, weights): """Applies a 3x3 convolution with output channels matching the wave field.""" return applyconvolution(inputtensor, weights, kernelsize=3, padding=1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Map Errors: Real-world captured depth maps often contain incorrect values or depth holes. These errors induce severe noise and distort objects in the reconstructed hologram. Unlike nCGH, which produces interference-induced black lines at the boundaries of noisy depth, DEHNet suppresses this noise at boundaries. Occlusion: The method must handle occluded surfaces correctly to provide appropriate blur and sharp focus. Time and Memory Complexity Inference Time: DEHNet (quantized, qNET) achieves a frame rate of 62 Hz. Total Frame Rate: Including the encoding of amplitude-only holograms (0.89 ms), the total frame rate is 57 Hz. Comparison to Optimization: DEHNet is 8600 times faster than the optimization-based DEH method (OPT), which requires more than 1 minute per hologram. Comparison to nCGH: DEHNet is 70 times faster than nCGH. Measured Performance 512x512 Dataset: DEHNet (qNET): PSNR 28.5 dB, SSIM 0.894. nCGH: PSNR 22.5 dB, SSIM 0.756. DEHNet provides a 6.5 dB enhancement in PSNR and 0.15 enhancement in SSIM compared to nCGH. FHD Dataset: DEHNet (qNET): PSNR 32.7 dB, SSIM 0.939. nCGH: PSNR 27.1 dB, SSIM 0.889. DEHNet provides a 6.3 dB enhancement in PSNR and 0.07 enhancement in SSIM compared to nCGH. Comparison to OPT: DEHNet (qNET) has a PSNR of 28.5 dB, compared to OPT's 29.0 dB, representing a loss of only ~0.5 dB. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Real-time performance (62 Hz); superior image quality compared to nCGH; robustness to noisy depth maps from real-world sensors; correct depth perception and defocus blur. Limitations: Requires training data (3000 scenes); performance depends on the quality of the input depth map, though it is more robust than nCGH. DEHNet was introduced to address the impracticality of optimization-based DEH generation for real-time applications, which requires numerous varifocal images and extensive computation. It builds on the Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH) method, which synthesizes optimal wave fields for clear defocus blur and correct depth perception. The method was developed by the authors of the source paper, published in Nature Communications in 2022. Diffraction-engineered holography: Beyond the depth representation limit of holographic displays, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33728-5, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Holographic 3D display system based on SLM
head: Holographic 3D display system based on liquid crystal spatial light modulator or digital micromirror device, LC/DMD Holographic Display, SLM-based Holographic Display
body: This method uses a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) and a reference light source to physically reconstruct a computer-generated hologram. It converts calculated holographic data into a visible 3D optical field by modulating incident light via electro-optic effects (LC) or mechanical reflection (DMD). It differs from pure calculation methods by focusing on the physical reconstruction pipeline using readily available components like reflective LCDs and LEDs. Inputs: 1. Hologram Data: A 2D pattern generated by a CGH algorithm (e.g., object point scattering method). 2. Light Source: An LED or laser. 3. Modulator: A reflective LCD panel or DMD. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D diagram of the object. Data Structures: Hologram Plane: A 2D array of pixels corresponding to the active area of the SLM. Modulator State: For reflective LCDs, the data is uploaded as an image intensity or phase pattern. For DMDs, the data is uploaded as a binary bitmap controlling mirror states to switch light on/off. Steps: 1. Hologram Generation: The system computer generates a 3D diagram of the target object, typically using the object point scattering method. 2. Data Upload: The calculated hologram data is uploaded to the reflective LCD panel acting as the light modulator. 3. Illumination: An LED is used as the reference light source to illuminate the SLM. 4. Reconstruction: The modulated light diffracts, reconstructing the 3D diagram of the object in space. Pitfalls: Computational Load: The object point scattering method involves calculating the interference of every object point with every hologram pixel, resulting in high calculation amounts that hinder high-resolution reconstruction. Coherence Length: The use of LEDs as reference sources introduces a shorter coherence length compared to lasers, which degrades reconstruction quality. A variant that replaces standard SLM pixelation with a pseudorandom mask of pinholes to overcome narrow diffraction angle limits. A technique that reconstructs only the wavefront at eye positions to reduce processing load, using a subhologram approach where each 3D scene point is represented by a 30×30 pixel array. The 3D scene is located between the Fourier plane and the SLM or behind the SLM, providing Viewing Windows (VWs) for observers in the Fourier plane. It differs from prior art which reconstructs the scene around the Fourier plane and provides viewing regions behind it. A moderate pixel pitch of 50 μm can generate a VW with 20 mm size at a 2 m distance, making large-size holographic displays feasible with existing technology. Complexity: The calculation complexity is dominated by the object point scattering method, scaling poorly with resolution and object point count, making high-resolution reconstruction difficult. Hardware Constraints: LC-SLMs rely on the electro-optic effect to modulate incident light. DMDs consist of millions of micro-mirrors where the reflection direction is controlled through a voltage signal to complete the on/off state of light. Image Quality: Reconstruction quality is significantly affected by the coherence length of the light source. View Window Scaling: Using moderate pixel sizes (e.g., 50 μm) instead of typical ~1 μm pitches allows generating viewing windows of practical sizes (e.g., 20 mm at 2 m distance) without requiring nanoscale manufacturing. The specific system configuration was employed by T. Shimobaba et al. from Japan in 2002. It represents an early practical implementation of computer-generated holography using readily available components (LCDs and LEDs) rather than specialized laser interferometry setups. The method is cited in the context of advances in digital holography and 3D display technologies. Principle and Outlook of Holography, https://doi.org/10.2991/icmmita-16.2016.54, fetched 2026-10-26 Three-dimensional display technologies, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4269274, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Non-periodic Photon Sieve Holographic Display
head: Deterministic pseudorandom mask holography, Photon sieve display
body: The Non-periodic Photon Sieve Holographic Display is a flat-panel wavefront modulation technique that combines a transmissive liquid crystal display (LCD) with a deterministically generated pseudorandom mask of pinholes to generate large dynamic holographic images with a wide viewing angle. It solves the fundamental limitation of standard Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs), which are restricted to narrow diffraction angles and small space-bandwidth products due to pixel pitch constraints. By diffracting light at wide angles through the pinholes, the method expands the optical mode space significantly, enabling large-area projection and multi-color holography without the bulky complexity of SLM multiplexing or time-consuming calibration processes. Inputs: Collimated laser beams at specific wavelengths (Red: 639 nm, Green: 532 nm, Blue: 473 nm). Target 3D scene defined by desired focal positions (xf, yf, zf). LCD panel parameters: Resolution W \times H (e.g., 1024 \times 768), pixel pitch p. Photon sieve parameters: Pinhole size d, pinhole positions \mathbf{r}k, and LCD pixel positions \mathbf{p}k. Outputs: Phase modulation pattern displayed on the LCD panel. Reconstructed 3D holographic image in the volume between the observer and the screen. 1. LCD Panel: A 2D array of pixels with resolution W \times H. Each pixel k has a center position \mathbf{p}k = (xk, yk) in the x-y plane. 2. Photon Sieve Mask: A binary transmission mask defined by a set of pinholes. Layout: One-to-one correspondence with LCD pixels. There is exactly one pinhole per LCD pixel. Pinhole Position: The lateral displacement of the k-th pinhole from the center of the k-th LCD pixel follows a continuous uniform distribution. Pinhole Size: Diameter d (e.g., 2.2 μm). Orientation: Pseudo-randomly oriented to suppress spatial aliasing. 3. Optical Path Data: For each pinhole k and target focus j, the optical path length L{k,j} from the pinhole position to the focal point. 1. System Setup: Place the non-periodic photon sieve close to the transmissive LCD panel to maintain a small form factor. Illuminate the LCD panel with collimated laser beams. 2. Pattern Generation (for each target focus j): Calculate the required phase shift for each LCD pixel k to direct light from the pinhole k to the target focal position \mathbf{f}j = (xj, yj, zj). The phase value \phik is determined by the optical path length from the pinhole to the focus: \phik = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} L{k,j} where \lambda is the wavelength of the light. The optical path length L{k,j} is the Euclidean distance between the pinhole position and the focal point. 3. LCD Modulation: Convert the calculated phase values \phik into bias values suitable for the LCD panel. Display the bias values on the LCD panel. The LCD acts as a wavefront modulator; its non-ideal amplitude/phase response is scrambled by the photon sieve's randomness, allowing efficient modulation upon precise calibration. 4. Diffraction: Light passes through the LCD and the photon sieve pinholes. The pinholes act as a spectrally uncorrelated optical transformation, diffracting light at wide angles. 5. Projection: Project the holographic images onto a large volume. The images are formed in the space between the observer's eyes and the scattering surface (photon sieve) because the light is emitted from the screen. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computephasepattern(lcdwidth, lcdheight, pinholepositions, targetfocus, wavelength): """ Computes the phase pattern for a single focus and wavelength. Args: lcdwidth (int): Number of pixels in x-direction. lcdheight (int): Number of pixels in y-direction. pinholepositions (list of tuples): List of (x, y) coordinates for each pinhole. Length must equal lcdwidth lcdheight. Positions are pseudo-randomly displaced from pixel centers. targetfocus (tuple): (x, y, z) coordinates of the desired focal point. wavelength (float): Wavelength of the illumination laser in meters. Returns: list of lists: 2D array of phase values (radians) wrapped to [0, 2pi). """ numpixels = lcdwidth lcdheight # Initialize 2D array for LCD panel phasepattern = [[0.0] lcdwidth for in range(lcdheight)] fx, fy, fz = targetfocus for idx in range(numpixels): px, py = pinholepositions[idx] # Calculate optical path length from pinhole to focus dx = fx - px dy = fy - py dz = fz opticalpathlength = math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Calculate phase shift required phaseshift = (2 math.pi opticalpathlength) / wavelength # Map linear index to 2D coordinates and store wrapped phase row = idx // lcdwidth col = idx % lcdwidth phasepattern[row][col] = phaseshift % (2 math.pi) return phasepattern def displayandproject(phasepattern, lcdpanel, photonsieve, laser): """ Displays the pattern and projects the hologram. """ # Illuminate LCD with laser lcdpanel.illuminate(laser) # Display phase pattern on LCD lcdpanel.display(phasepattern) # Light passes through LCD and Photon Sieve # The sieve diffracts light at wide angles lightfield = photonsieve.transmit(lcdpanel.getoutput()) # Optical projection geometry is determined by the physical setup; # light propagates from the sieve to the volume between screen and observer. Pinhole Size (d): 2.2 μm (standard demonstration); variable sizes tested include 2 μm, 3 μm, and 5 μm. LCD Resolution: XGA (1024 \times 768 pixels), providing \sim 10^6 controlled optical modes. Wavelengths: Red (\lambda = 639 nm), Green (\lambda = 532 nm), Blue (\lambda = 473 nm). Numerical Aperture (NA): 0.75 (used in measurement system). Low Light Efficiency: The active area of the LCD pixel is confined by the pinhole size, resulting in low transmittance (e.g., 0.16% for 2.2 μm pinholes). Viewing Angle Reduction with Distance: When the distance between the screen and focus increases beyond a certain distance (Z{1,2}), the effective viewing angle decreases inversely proportional to the distance due to the limited supported spatial frequency range. Contrast Degradation with Multiple Foci: When a large number of optical modes are addressed simultaneously, the signal level decreases proportionally to the number of optical modes while background noise remains constant. Spatial Aliasing: If pinholes are periodically aligned, reconstructed holograms carry optical information only within the Nyquist frequency defined by pixel pitches, causing unwanted multiple cloned images. This is avoided by using pseudo-randomly oriented pinholes. Background Noise: Pseudo-random pinhole orientation suppresses image duplication but introduces background noise. Time Complexity: The calculation of the optimal pattern requires O(\sim 10^6) computations, equal to the number of LCD pixels, rather than O(>10^9) for the large optical mode space. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Viewing Angle: Approximately 30^\circ achieved with a single flat-panel wavefront modulator. Contrast Factor: Approximately 2.0 \times 10^5 achieved using all pixels in XGA resolution. Transmittance: 0.16% measured for a photon sieve with 2.2 μm sized pinholes. Enhancement: The product of screen size and diffraction angle was enhanced by a factor of \sim 1200 compared to using only a wavefront modulator with XGA resolution. Scaling: Larger pinhole sizes or a larger number of pinholes per LCD pixel increase transmittance but compromise viewing angles. The calculation burden increases linearly with the number of pinholes, requiring O(\sim 10^6) computations equal to the LCD pixel count, rather than O(>10^9) for the full optical mode space. A demonstration with 7.8 million pinholes successfully generated a holographic tetrahedron with 60 foci. Strengths: Wide viewing angle, large screen size, multi-color projection, small form factor, no time-consuming calibration. Limitations: Low light efficiency, contrast degradation with many foci, viewing angle reduction at large distances, background noise. When to Use: When a wide viewing angle and large holographic image area are required from a compact, flat-panel device without complex SLM multiplexing. When Not to Use: When high light efficiency is critical, or when complex holographic images requiring many simultaneous foci are needed without sacrificing contrast. Origin: Published in Nature Communications, 2019, Volume 10, Article 1304. History: The method addresses the limitations of standard SLMs, which have limited diffraction angles (\theta = 2\sin^{-1}(\lambda/2p)) and small space-bandwidth products. Unlike wavefront shaping through disordered systems, which requires time-consuming calibration, this method uses a deterministically generated pseudorandom mask. It overcomes the challenges of transmissive SLMs (narrow pixel pitch difficulties due to embedded electrodes) by using an off-the-shelf LCD combined with a photon sieve. name: Simultaneous Color Holography via End-to-End Optimization
head: Depth Division Holography, Depth division, Differentiable Hologram Optimization, Gradient Descent Hologram Synthesis, Optimization-based Simultaneous Color Hologram Generation, Simultaneous RGB Holography, Single SLM Pattern RGB Holography
body: This method generates a full RGB hologram using a single Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) pattern illuminated simultaneously by red, green, and blue light sources, eliminating the need for field sequential color or multiple SLMs. It sets itself apart from Depth Division Multiplexing by directly optimizing the output hologram end-to-end rather than assigning colors to different depths, and from Bit Division Multiplexing by using a flexible framework with a perceptual loss function for direct optimization rather than a two-step lookup table process. The method formulates hologram generation as an end-to-end differentiable optimization problem. It maps target RGB intensities to SLM voltage values by minimizing a perceptual loss function through gradient descent. Inputs and Outputs Input: Target RGB intensity image \hat{I}; SLM physical parameters (wavelengths \lambdar, \lambdag, \lambdab; phase range; learning rate; iteration count). Output: Optimized 8-bit digital SLM pattern s. Data Structures SLM Pattern s: 2D array of 8-bit integers controlling the SLM phase delay. Complex Wavefield g\lambda: 2D array of complex numbers representing the electric field at the SLM plane for each wavelength. Reconstructed Intensity I{z,\lambda}: 2D array of real numbers representing the intensity at the target plane z for each wavelength. Steps 1. Initialization: Choose a target depth d{target} and initialize the SLM pattern s and optimization parameters (learning rate, number of iterations). 2. SLM Modeling: For each wavelength \lambda \in \{r, g, b\}, compute the wavelength-dependent phase delay \phi\lambda(s) using the SLM model, which maps voltage values to a complex field via a learned cross-talk kernel and a linear lookup table. 3. Field Generation: Compute the electric field leaving the SLM for each wavelength: g\lambda = e^{i\phi\lambda(s)}. 4. Propagation: Propagate the electric field g\lambda to the target plane z using the propagation function f{prop} to obtain the reconstructed intensity: I{z,\lambda} = f{prop}(g\lambda, z, \lambda). The propagation model separates the zeroth and first diffraction orders and combines them through a U-Net architecture. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss by comparing the reconstructed intensities I{z,\lambda} with the target intensities \hat{I}{z,\lambda} using a pixel-wise perceptual loss function that weights luminance and chrominance based on human visual acuity: L = \sum{\lambda \in \{r,g,b\}} \mathcal{L}{perceptual}(\hat{I}{z,\lambda}, I{z,\lambda}). 6. Gradient Update: Calculate gradients of the loss with respect to the SLM pattern s using automatic differentiation and update s via gradient descent: s \leftarrow s - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial s}. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–6 until convergence or the maximum number of iterations is reached. Parameters SLM Phase Range: The method leverages the extended phase range of Liquid Crystal on Silicon (LCoS) SLMs, up to 10\pi, to create diversity in phase triplets for RGB. Perceptual Loss Weights: Scalars weighting luminance and chrominance channels based on human visual acuity. Learning Rate (\eta): Step size for gradient descent. Optimization Iterations: Number of optimization steps. Pitfalls Depth Replicas: Simultaneous color holography suffers from "depth replicas" artifacts due to the ambiguity between color and propagation distance. This is mitigated by using the extended phase range of the SLM. Wavelength Dependence: The SLM response varies with wavelength, requiring accurate modeling in the SLM model step. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizeslm(targetrgb, wavelengths, numiterations, learningrate): # Initialize SLM pattern s as a 2D array of 8-bit values s = randomuint8array(targetrgb.shape[:2]) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Step 2 & 3: SLM Model and Field Generation per wavelength fieldsslm = {} for lam in wavelengths: phase = slmphasemodel(s, lam) fieldsslm[lam] = complexexp(1j phase) # Step 4: Propagation to target plane z intensities = {} for lam in wavelengths: fieldsensor = propagationmodel(fieldsslm[lam], lam) intensities[lam] = abs(fieldsensor) 2 # Step 5: Perceptual Loss calculation loss = 0.0 for idx, lam in enumerate(wavelengths): loss += perceptualloss(intensities[lam], targetrgb[:,:,idx]) # Step 6: Gradient Update gradients = gradient(loss, s) s = s - learningrate gradients return s def slmphasemodel(s, lam): # Maps 8-bit digital SLM pattern to wavelength-dependent phase delay # using a learned cross-talk kernel and a linear lookup table phase = applycrosstalkkernel(s, lam) return phase + linearlookuptable(lam)[s] def propagationmodel(fieldslm, lam): # Propagates electric field to sensor plane using modified ASM model # that separates zeroth and first diffraction orders and combines them via U-Net orders = separatediffractionorders(fieldslm) return combinediffractionorders(orders) def perceptualloss(recon, target): # Computes pixel-wise loss weighting luminance and chrominance based on human visual acuity return meansquarederror(recon, target) def gradient(loss, variable): # Standard automatic differentiation backpropagation return computebackwardpass(loss, variable) Generates holograms for a full-color image across multiple depth planes using a single SLM pattern. It extends the base method by optimizing for a stack of target intensities at different depths instead of a single plane. Determines the optimal phase modulation range for each color channel to overcome depth-wavelength ambiguity in the propagation kernel. It sets itself apart by focusing on the magnitude of phase excursion per channel rather than the loss function or focal stack geometry. Addresses the overdetermined nature of single-SLM RGB holography by transforming the error metric into opponent color space and applying low-pass filters that mimic the human visual system's contrast sensitivity. It sets itself apart from standard RGB loss by shifting optimization error into imperceptible regions of the color space. Time Complexity: The optimization process is iterative and computationally expensive, scaling with the number of optimization iterations and the complexity of the U-Net propagation model. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SLM voltage matrix, complex wavefields at each step, and gradients for backpropagation. Strengths: Eliminates the need for field sequential color or multiple SLMs; allows for extended phase range utilization; improves color fidelity via perceptual loss. Limitations: Computationally intensive optimization; sensitive to accurate SLM and propagation models; potential for depth replica artifacts if phase range is not sufficiently extended. When to use: When a single SLM pattern is required for simultaneous RGB illumination, and computational resources for optimization are available. This method was introduced by researchers at Reality Labs Research, Meta, USA. It addresses the limitations of traditional color holography methods such as field sequential color, depth division multiplexing, and bit division multiplexing. The work builds on prior research in differentiable holography and perceptual loss functions for image optimization. It was validated experimentally on 2D and 3D content using a custom camera-calibrated model. name: Simultaneous Color Focal Stack Optimization
head: Learned Wave Propagation SLM Optimization, Multi-plane Focal Stack Optimization
body: Simultaneous Color Focal Stack Optimization is a method for generating computer-generated holograms that reconstruct a full-color image across multiple depth planes using a single spatial light modulator pattern illuminated simultaneously by red, green, and blue light sources. It extends Simultaneous Color Holography via End-to-End Optimization by jointly optimizing the SLM pattern for a stack of target intensities at different depths rather than a single plane. Unlike single-plane optimization, it iteratively propagates the optical field through a learned wave propagation model for each depth plane to compute gradients and update the pattern. Inputs: Learned wave propagation model Holo(\cdot) for the unfiltered holography system. Initial SLM pattern P{SLM}. Target intensity images I{target}[d] for each depth plane d in the focal stack. Outputs: Optimized SLM pattern P{SLM}. Captured simultaneous color focal stack FocalStack. Data Structures: P{SLM}: The phase or complex pattern on the SLM. I{target}[d]: A 2D array representing the desired intensity at depth d. FocalStack: A list of captured images, one for each depth plane. Algorithm: 1. Load the learned wave propagation model. 2. Initialize P{SLM} and define I{target} for each depth plane in the focal stack. 3. Iterate while P{SLM} has not converged. 4. For each depth plane d in the focal stack hologram: a. Clear previous gradients with respect to P{SLM}. b. Generate the field from the current P{SLM} and propagate it to depth plane d using the learned model: Field{out} = Holo(P{SLM}, \text{depth}=d) c. Compute loss using a custom perceptual loss function: Loss = LossFunc(Field{out}, I{target}[d]) d. Backpropagate the gradient of Loss with respect to P{SLM}. e. Update P{SLM} using the calculated gradients. 5. After convergence, capture the simultaneous color focal stack by moving the camera to each plane and capturing the image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SimultaneousColorFocalStackOptimization(learnedmodel, initialpslm, targetintensities): """ Optimizes an SLM pattern for a multi-plane focal stack using a learned wave propagation model. Args: learnedmodel: A callable Holo(PSLM, depth) that propagates the field to a specific depth. initialpslm: The initial SLM pattern (tensor/array). targetintensities: A list or dictionary of target intensity images Itarget[d] for each depth plane d. Returns: optimizedpslm: The optimized SLM pattern. focalstack: A list of captured images for each depth plane. """ pslm = initialpslm focalstack = [] # 1. Optimization Loop while not checkconvergence(pslm): for d in targetintensities: # 2. Clear gradients cleargradients(pslm) # 3. Forward propagation fieldout = learnedmodel(pslm, depth=d) # 4. Compute loss loss = perceptualloss(fieldout, targetintensities[d]) # 5. Backpropagation loss.backward() # 6. Update SLM pattern updateparameters(pslm) # 7. Capture (Experimental Step) for d in targetintensities: movecameratodepth(d) hologram = captureimage() focalstack.append(hologram) return pslm, focalstack def cleargradients(tensor): """Resets the gradient accumulator for the tensor.""" tensor.grad = None def perceptualloss(fieldout, target): """Custom perceptual loss function as referenced in the method.""" return sum((abs(fieldout) - target) 2) / len(fieldout) def updateparameters(tensor, learningrate=0.01): """Updates tensor values using gradient descent.""" tensor -= learningrate tensor.grad def checkconvergence(tensor): """Checks if optimization has converged. Logic not specified in sources.""" return False def movecameratodepth(depth): """Hardware operation to position camera at the specified depth plane.""" pass def captureimage(): """Hardware operation to capture image from the camera sensor.""" return None Parameters: Convergence Criteria: Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Failure: If the optimization fails to converge, or if the product of initial source power and weighting function exceeds 100% (during Source Power Optimization), the exposure time should be increased and the source power optimization restarted. Bit Depth Quantization: A significant drop-off in PSNR and SSIM occurs between 5 and 6 bits. An effective bit depth of at least 6 bits is required for adequate image quality. This method generates phase-only computer-generated holograms for multi-plane 3D targets by mapping spatial intensity distributions to depth-dependent reconstructions using a trainable Fourier transform layer. It explicitly addresses axial crosstalk by combining a physics-informed training strategy with a specialized network architecture that expands the receptive field. Unlike traditional iterative optimization methods, it achieves significant speedups while maintaining structural fidelity in sparse 3D volumes. An active camera-in-the-loop iterative process to optimize the power of each color channel of the SLED source for color fidelity. It is chosen when precise color balance is required and the source power cannot be perfectly calibrated beforehand. It sets the source power to an arbitrary value less than 100% across all three color channels. A baseline reference image is captured, debayered, and mapped to SLM space. Three learnable weighting parameters (one per color channel) are initialized to unity and applied to the captured reference image as a proxy for source power. The process iteratively captures an image, debayers it, maps it to SLM space, calculates loss against the target, and backpropagates through the weighting parameters' computational graph. The initial source power is updated by multiplying it by the updated weighting parameters, and the loop restarts with a new image capture. It repeats until the color weighting parameters converge, typically taking between 15 and 30 iterations. If convergence fails or the product of initial source power and weighting function exceeds 100%, the exposure time is increased and the optimization restarted. An analysis defining the effective bit depth as the number of bits contained in a 2\pi interval of the extended phase range. It determines the minimum quantization level required for adequate image quality. It simulates holograms by optimizing with gradient descent and then quantizing to the target bit depth. A significant drop-off in PSNR and SSIM is observed between 5 and 6 bits. The minimum effective bit depth required is 6 bits. For a 6-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 31.00 and SSIM is 0.856; for an 8-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 34.98 and SSIM is 0.943. No image quality improvement is achieved for simultaneous color holograms once each color channel has a bit depth of at least 6 bits across a 2\pi phase range. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: For a 6-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 31.00 and SSIM is 0.856. For an 8-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 34.98 and SSIM is 0.943. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for the creation of volumetric color displays using a single SLM and simultaneous RGB illumination. Uses a learned wave propagation model for the unfiltered holography system. Limitations: Requires a learned wave propagation model that must be trained for the specific unfiltered holography system. Requires experimental capture for validation, which involves moving the camera. Sensitive to source power calibration, requiring active optimization. When to use: When creating volumetric color holograms with a single SLM and simultaneous RGB illumination is desired, and a learned propagation model is available. When not to use: When high bit-depth SLMs are not available, as a minimum effective bit depth of 6 bits is required. The method was introduced by Markley et al. in "Simultaneous Color Computer Generated Holography". It addresses the challenges of near-eye holographic displays and volumetric imaging by enabling simultaneous color reconstruction across multiple depth planes. The approach relies on a learned wave propagation model for the unfiltered holography system, which accounts for system-specific aberrations and filtering effects. The research highlights the importance of source power optimization and SLM bit depth analysis for achieving high-fidelity color holograms. name: Physics-Informed Deep Learning Framework for Multi-Plane CGH
head: Multi-Plane Neural CGH with Physics-Informed Self-Supervision, Neural Multi-Plane CGH, Physics-Informed Neural Holography
body: This method generates phase-only computer-generated holograms (CGH) for multi-plane 3D targets by mapping spatial intensity distributions to depth-dependent reconstructions using a trainable Fourier transform layer. It explicitly addresses axial crosstalk (unwanted intensity diffraction from adjacent planes) by combining a physics-informed training strategy with a specialized network architecture that expands the receptive field. Unlike traditional iterative optimization methods, it achieves significant speedups while maintaining structural fidelity in sparse 3D volumes. Input: A discretized 3D target volume I{tar} with dimensions m \times m \times p, where m is the lateral resolution (matching the SLM pixel grid) and p is the number of axial depth planes. The input is a binary or sparse intensity stack representing the desired focal spots at each depth Zk. Output: A phase-only hologram \phi{SLM}(x, y) defined on the SLM plane, where x, y are lateral coordinates. The network processes the input as a tensor of shape (p, m, m) or (m, m, p) depending on channel ordering, but logically represents p channels of m \times m intensity values. The internal feature maps utilize space-to-depth (interleave) operations to reshape spatial regions into channel groups, effectively increasing the channel dimension while reducing spatial resolution to expand the receptive field. The model is a U-Net-style encoder-decoder architecture: 1. Encoder: Consists of six convolutional blocks. Instead of standard max-pooling, it uses space-to-depth (interleave) operations to preserve high-frequency fringe details and expand the receptive field for global diffraction modeling. 2. Bottleneck: A central structure that reduces feature map channels to enhance computational efficiency. 3. Decoder: Uses two up-sampling stages and depth-to-space (deinterleave) operations to restore spatial resolution. 4. Output Layer: Produces the complex optical field at the focal plane Z=0, denoted as U(X, Y; 0). The framework integrates a differentiable physics model within the training loop to constrain solutions to wave optics. 1. SLM Field: The complex field immediately after the SLM is defined as: U{SLM}(x, y) = \exp[i \phi{SLM}(x, y)] where the input beam has unit amplitude. 2. Propagation: The field at image space depth Z is calculated. In the far-field regime (valid when Z \ge f, where f is the focal length of the focusing lens), the field is expressed using the 2D Fourier transform \mathcal{F}: U(X, Y; Z) = A0 \times \mathcal{F}\{U{SLM}\} where the amplitude factor is: A0 = \frac{\exp(ikZ)\exp\left(\frac{ik(X^2+Y^2)}{2Z}\right)}{i\lambda Z} Here, k = 2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber and \lambda is the wavelength. 3. Intensity: The reconstructed intensity at each depth plane is: I(X, Y; Z) = |U(X, Y; Z)|^2. The training involves a two-phase strategy to balance initialization and physical consistency: 1. Phase 1 (Supervised): Reference holograms are computed using an angular spectrum-based CGH algorithm for the target volumes. These serve as supervisory targets for the network output during initial epochs. 2. Phase 2 (Self-Supervised): The reference targets are gradually phased out. The loss is evaluated directly on the reconstructed intensity volumes I{recon} generated by the physics model. The primary loss is the cosine similarity loss, which is scale-invariant and emphasizes structural similarity over absolute intensity: L = 1 - \frac{\langle I{tar}, I{recon} \rangle}{|I{tar}| |I{recon}|} where \langle \cdot \rangle is the inner product and |\cdot| is the modulus, computed across all pixels and all p depth planes. Regularization: A regularization term is applied to the reconstructed background lying outside a narrow mask defined around the target points to suppress background noise. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SpaceToDepth(nn.Module): """Reshuffles local spatial regions into separate channel groups.""" def init(self, blocksize=2): super().init() self.blocksize = blocksize def forward(self, x): b, c, h, w = x.size() bs = self.blocksize x = x.view(b, c, h // bs, bs, w // bs, bs) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 5, 2, 4).contiguous() x = x.view(b, c bs bs, h // bs, w // bs) return x class DepthToSpace(nn.Module): """Inverse of SpaceToDepth.""" def init(self, blocksize=2): super().init() self.blocksize = blocksize def forward(self, x): b, c, h, w = x.size() bs = self.blocksize cin = c // (bs bs) x = x.view(b, cin, bs, bs, h, w) x = x.permute(0, 1, 4, 2, 5, 3).contiguous() x = x.view(b, cin, h bs, w bs) return x class PhysicsInformedMultiPlaneCGH(nn.Module): def init(self, m, p, kernelsize=3): super().init() self.m = m self.p = p self.enc1 = nn.Conv2d(p, 64, kernelsize, padding=1) self.sto1 = SpaceToDepth() self.enc2 = nn.Conv2d(64 4, 128, kernelsize, padding=1) self.bottleneck = nn.Conv2d(128 4, 256, kernelsize, padding=1) self.d2 = nn.Conv2d(256, 128, kernelsize, padding=1) self.dto2 = DepthToSpace() self.d1 = nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernelsize, padding=1) self.dto1 = DepthToSpace() self.outconv = nn.Conv2d(64, 2, kernelsize, padding=1) self.initweights() def initweights(self): for m in self.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d): nn.init.kaimingnormal(m.weight, mode='fanout', nonlinearity='relu') def forward(self, targetvolume): x = self.enc1(targetvolume) x = F.relu(x) x = self.sto1(x) x = self.enc2(x) x = F.relu(x) x = self.bottleneck(x) x = F.relu(x) x = self.d2(x) x = F.relu(x) x = self.dto2(x) x = self.d1(x) x = F.relu(x) x = self.dto1(x) complexfieldz0 = self.outconv(x) return complexfieldz0 def computelossandtrain(network, targetvolume, optimizer, device, epoch, totalepochs): optimizer.zerograd() complexfieldz0 = network(targetvolume) ureal = complexfieldz0[:, 0,:,:] uimag = complexfieldz0[:, 1,:,:] uz0 = torch.complex(ureal, uimag) uslm = torch.fft.ifft2(uz0) numplanes = targetvolume.size(1) axialinterval = 0.01 # 10mm in meters zcoords = torch.tensor([i axialinterval for i in range(numplanes)], device=device) lam = 532e-9 k = 2 torch.pi / lam y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(targetvolume.size(2), device=device), torch.arange(targetvolume.size(3), device=device), indexing='ij') reconstructedintensities = [] for z in zcoords: A0 = torch.exp(1j k z) torch.exp(1j k (x2 + y2) / (2 z)) / (1j lam z) Uslmfft = torch.fft.fft2(uslm) Uz = A0 Uslmfft Iz = torch.abs(Uz)2 reconstructedintensities.append(Iz) Irecon = torch.stack(reconstructedintensities, dim=1) Itarflat = targetvolume.view(targetvolume.size(0), -1) Ireconflat = Irecon.view(Irecon.size(0), -1) dotproduct = torch.sum(Itarflat Ireconflat, dim=1) normtar = torch.norm(Itarflat, dim=1) normrecon = torch.norm(Ireconflat, dim=1) cosinesim = dotproduct / (normtar normrecon + 1e-8) loss = 1 - cosinesim.mean() # Regularization for background outside narrow mask around target points # Implementation depends on specific target geometry and mask definition. loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Weight Initialization: He initialization. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 8. Training Duration: 200 epochs. Dataset: 20,000 synthetically generated sparse 3D point cloud volumes distributed across five depth planes. Hardware/Implementation: PyTorch version 2.8.0. Sparse vs. Dense: The framework is optimized for sparse 3D structures (point clouds). Reconstruction of dense, continuous grayscale images may fail to preserve surface continuity and texture. Noise Sensitivity: The cosine similarity loss is scale-invariant and does not explicitly model noise. Performance may degrade in the presence of speckle or optical imperfections unless domain randomization with simulated speckle is incorporated. Far-Field Assumption: The Fourier transform layer relies on the far-field approximation (Z \ge f). If target planes are too close to the lens (near-field), the physics model becomes inaccurate. Time: The method is significantly faster than iterative optimization. For a five-plane hologram, the proposed method takes 0.13s compared to 1.38s for Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) and 14.40s for Iterative-SGD. Memory: The U-Net architecture with bottleneck reduces feature map channels, enhancing computational efficiency. Specific VRAM usage is not given. Hardware: Phase-only SLM (1920x1080 pixels, 8µm pixel size) at \lambda=532nm, NA=0.1, 10mm axial interval. Metrics (5-plane holograms): Proposed Method: PSNR 30.35 dB, SSIM 0.59, Time 0.13s. Gerchberg-Saxton (50 iters): PSNR 33.57 dB, SSIM 0.85, Time 1.38s. Iterative-SGD: PSNR 27.47 dB, SSIM 0.13, Time 14.40s. Crosstalk: Simulated and experimental results show bright, well-localized focal spots with minimal inter-plane leakage (axial crosstalk). Strengths: Orders-of-magnitude acceleration in computation compared to iterative methods; effective suppression of axial crosstalk for sparse targets; end-to-end differentiable physics integration. Limitations: Not suitable for dense, continuous grayscale images without loss function adaptation; sensitive to noise without explicit noise modeling in training. The method was published in Photonics 2026, 13, 252 (Received 24 January 2026, Published 4 March 2026). It builds upon the field of neural CGH, which leverages deep learning for high-speed hologram generation. It specifically addresses the limitations of traditional algorithms like Gerchberg-Saxton and iterative optimization, which suffer from high computational cost and axial crosstalk in multi-plane displays. The framework enables volumetric and near-eye displays, as well as holographic optical tweezer technologies. It is particularly suited for applications requiring discrete focal points, such as structured light projection or optical trapping. name: Phase Range Optimization for Simultaneous Color
head: Differentiated Phase Range RGB Holography, RGB Phase Range Optimization, SLM Phase Range Optimization
body: This method determines the optimal phase modulation range for each color channel (Red, Green, Blue) in a simultaneous color holography system to overcome the depth-wavelength ambiguity inherent in the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) kernel. It ensures that the holographic patterns for each wavelength are sufficiently distinct to reconstruct unique color channels, while minimizing the phase range to preserve effective bit depth and refresh rate. It builds on Simultaneous Color Holography via End-to-End Optimization by explicitly optimizing the phase excursion magnitude per channel. Inputs: Target RGB image I{\text{target}}, wavelengths \lambdaR, \lambdaG, \lambdaB, propagation distance z, SLM pixel pitch p, SLM resolution N \times N. Outputs: Optimal phase ranges \PhiR, \PhiG, \PhiB and the optimized SLM phase pattern \Phi{\text{SLM}}. Parameters: \PhiR fixed at 2\pi. \PhiB searched in [2\pi, 8\pi]. \PhiG = (\PhiR + \PhiB)/2. Loss function is the L2 norm between target and simulated hologram. Algorithm: 1. Initialize \PhiR = 2\pi and \PhiB = 2\pi. 2. Compute \PhiG = (\PhiR + \PhiB) / 2. 3. For the current phase ranges, optimize the SLM pattern \Phi{\text{SLM}} using gradient descent with a naive ASM forward model. 4. Compute the L2 norm loss L = \| I{\text{target}} - I{\text{sim}} \|2^2 between the target image and the ASM-simulated hologram. 5. If L falls below an empirical quality threshold, record the current \PhiB and terminate the search. 6. Increment \PhiB by a step (e.g., 0.1\pi) and repeat steps 2–5 until \PhiB reaches 8\pi. 7. Select the smallest \PhiB that met the quality threshold. For unnatural images (highly unique color channels), a minimum \PhiB of 5\pi is sufficient. For natural images (similar color channels), a phase difference of 4\pi (i.e., \PhiB = 6\pi) is adequate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def angularspectrumpropagation(field, wavelength, distance, pitch): """Standard ASM propagation using FFT.""" N = field.shape[0] fx = np.fft.fftfreq(N, pitch) fy = np.fft.fftfreq(N, pitch) fx, fy = np.meshgrid(fx, fy) H = np.exp(1j 2 math.pi distance np.sqrt((1/wavelength)2 - fx2 - fy2)) H[fx2 + fy2 > (1/wavelength)2] = 0 return np.abs(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(field) H))2 def optimizephaserange(targetimage, wavelengths, distance, pitch, resolution, imagetype="natural"): """ Determines optimal phase ranges for R, G, B channels via experimental search. """ phiR = 2 math.pi phiBmin = 2 math.pi phiBmax = 8 math.pi step = 0.1 math.pi # Empirical L2 loss thresholds for acceptable quality threshold = 0.05 if imagetype == "natural" else 0.05 bestphib = phiBmax bestslmpattern = None phiB = phiBmin while phiB <= phiBmax: phiG = (phiR + phiB) / 2 # Inner optimization: Gradient descent to minimize L2 loss slmphase = np.zeros((resolution, resolution)) learningrate = 0.01 epochs = 1000 # Standard iteration count for convergence for in range(epochs): # Phase modulation constrained to each channel's range phaseR = np.clip(slmphase, 0, phiR) phaseG = np.clip(slmphase, 0, phiG) phaseB = np.clip(slmphase, 0, phiB) # Simulate ASM reconstruction for each channel UR = angularspectrumpropagation(np.exp(1j phaseR), wavelengths[0], distance, pitch) UG = angularspectrumpropagation(np.exp(1j phaseG), wavelengths[1], distance, pitch) UB = angularspectrumpropagation(np.exp(1j phaseB), wavelengths[2], distance, pitch) # Incoherent intensity sum for color holography Isim = UR + UG + UB # L2 norm loss loss = np.sum((targetimage - Isim)2) # The sources do not specify the exact gradient formula; standard backpropagation applies. # grad =... # slmphase -= learningrate grad # Evaluate quality if loss < threshold: bestphib = phiB bestslmpattern = slmphase break phiB += step phiGfinal = (phiR + bestphib) / 2 return phiR, phiGfinal, bestphib, bestslmpattern Time Complexity: The method requires iterative gradient descent for each candidate phase range, making it computationally intensive but necessary to resolve the depth-wavelength ambiguity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Larger phase ranges degrade image quality by reducing effective bit depth and tend to have slower refresh rates on physical SLMs. Strengths: Overcomes depth-wavelength ambiguity; provides a systematic way to select SLMs or configure phase ranges for simultaneous color. Limitations: Requires empirical tuning or simulation to determine the "minimal" range; unnatural images require significantly larger phase ranges (5\pi) than natural images (4\pi difference). When to use: When using an SLM with extended phase range capability for simultaneous RGB holography, or when selecting an SLM for such a system. This method originates from research into Simultaneous Color Computer Generated Holography (CGH). It addresses the specific challenge that the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) kernel introduces depth-wavelength ambiguity, meaning different wavelengths can produce similar diffraction patterns for different depths. By ensuring the phase ranges are sufficiently different, unique holograms are produced for each color channel. The experimental procedure was detailed in studies involving Holoeye Pluto SLMs (Red: 2.4\pi, Green: 5.9\pi, Blue: 7.4\pi) and standard simulated SLMs (Red: 2\pi, Green: 2.7\pi, Blue: 3.4\pi), comparing performance against depth division and bit division methods. name: Perceptual Loss Function for Color Holography
head: Filtered RGB Loss, Opponent Color Space Loss, Perceptual Loss Function
body: This method addresses the overdetermined nature of generating full-color holograms with a single Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) illuminated by simultaneous red, green, and blue light sources, where the output contains three times the degrees of freedom of the SLM pattern. It reduces color deviations and desaturation by transforming the error metric into opponent color space and applying low-pass filters that mimic the human visual system's (HVS) contrast sensitivity, thereby de-prioritizing high-frequency chrominance errors. Unlike standard RGB loss, which treats all color channels equally, this approach shifts optimization error into imperceptible regions of the color space, resulting in visually less noisy holograms with superior color fidelity. Inputs and Outputs Input: Target RGB image I{\lambdar}, I{\lambdag}, I{\lambdab} at wavelengths \lambdar, \lambdag, \lambdab; initial SLM pattern s. Output: Optimized SLM phase pattern s that minimizes the perceptual loss. Data Structures Target Image: 2D array of shape (H, W, 3) containing normalized intensity values for Red, Green, and Blue channels. Opponent Channels: 2D arrays of shape (H, W) for Luminance (O1), Red-Green Chrominance (O2), and Blue-Yellow Chrominance (O3). Filters: 2D frequency-domain masks k1, k2, k3 representing low-pass filters in the Fourier domain. Parameters Luminance Filter Width (\gamma1): 0.75 (75% of Fourier space width). Chrominance Filter Width (\gamma2, \gamma3): 0.45 (45% of Fourier space width). System Constants: SLM pixel pitch p (e.g., 8 µm) and eyepiece focal length f (e.g., 36.6 mm). Numbered Steps 1. Forward Propagation: Compute the simulated hologram intensity I from the current SLM pattern s using a differentiable physical model (e.g., Fresnel propagation) for each wavelength \lambdar, \lambdag, \lambdab. 2. Color Space Transformation: Convert the RGB intensities of both the target image \hat{I} and the simulated hologram I into opponent color space channels O1, O2, O3 using the linear transformation defined below. 3. Filter Generation: Construct low-pass filters k1, k2, k3 in the Fourier domain. The filter width is defined as a fraction \gamma of the total Fourier space width. For a system with p=8 \mu m and f=36.6 mm, the cutoff frequencies are 30 cycles/deg for luminance and 18 cycles/deg for chrominance. 4. Frequency Domain Filtering: Apply the filters ki to the opponent channels of both the target and the simulation via 2D convolution (or multiplication in the Fourier domain). 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the pixel-wise loss (e.g., Mean Squared Error) between the filtered target channels and the filtered simulated channels for all three opponent components. 6. Optimization: Update the SLM pattern s using gradient descent to minimize the total loss. Formulas The opponent color channels are computed as: O1 = 0.299 \cdot I{\lambdar} + 0.587 \cdot I{\lambdag} + 0.114 \cdot I{\lambdab} O2 = I{\lambdar} - I{\lambdag} O3 = I{\lambdab} - I{\lambdar} - I{\lambdag} where O1 is luminance, O2 is red-green chrominance, and O3 is blue-yellow chrominance. The total loss function is: \arg\mins \sum{i=1}^3 L(\hat{O}i ki, Oi ki) where denotes 2D convolution, \hat{O}i and Oi are the i-th opponent channels of the target and simulated hologram respectively, and L is a pixel-wise loss function (typically MSE). The spatial frequency cutoff in cycles per degree is calculated as: \text{cutoff} = \frac{f}{\pi} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{2p} \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} where f is the focal length, p is the pixel pitch, and \gamma is the filter width fraction. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def opponentcolortransform(rgbimage): """ Converts RGB image to opponent color space (Luminance, Red-Green, Blue-Yellow). Args: rgbimage: np.array of shape (H, W, 3) with values in [0, 1]. Returns: opponentchannels: np.array of shape (H, W, 3) for O1, O2, O3. """ r = rgbimage[:,:, 0] g = rgbimage[:,:, 1] b = rgbimage[:,:, 2] # Luminance o1 = 0.299 r + 0.587 g + 0.114 b # Red-Green Chrominance o2 = r - g # Blue-Yellow Chrominance o3 = b - r - g return np.stack([o1, o2, o3], axis=-1) def createfourierlowpassfilter(shape, cutofffraction): """ Creates a 2D low-pass filter mask in the Fourier domain. Args: shape: Tuple (H, W) for the spatial domain size. cutofffraction: Float, fraction of the Fourier space width to keep (e.g., 0.75). Returns: filtermask: np.array of shape (H, W) with values 0 or 1. """ h, w = shape # Create coordinate grids centered at (0,0) in frequency space y, x = np.ogrid[:h,:w] y = y - h // 2 x = x - w // 2 # Calculate distance from center in normalized frequency units maxradius = min(h, w) / 2.0 radius = cutofffraction maxradius distance = np.sqrt(x2 + y2) # Create mask: 1 inside radius, 0 outside filtermask = (distance <= radius).astype(np.float32) return filtermask def applyfourierfilter(image, filtermask): """ Applies a frequency-domain filter to an image via FFT. Args: image: np.array of shape (H, W). filtermask: np.array of shape (H, W). Returns: filteredimage: np.array of shape (H, W). """ # FFT, shift to center, apply mask, shift back, IFFT fftimg = np.fft.fft2(image) fftshifted = np.fft.fftshift(fftimg) fftfiltered = fftshifted filtermask fftunshifted = np.fft.ifftshift(fftfiltered) filteredimg = np.fft.ifft2(fftunshifted).real return filteredimg def perceptuallossstep(targetrgb, simulatedrgb, cutofflum, cutoffchrom): """ Computes the perceptual loss between target and simulated holograms. Args: targetrgb: np.array (H, W, 3) target image. simulatedrgb: np.array (H, W, 3) simulated hologram output. cutofflum: Float, cutoff fraction for luminance (0.75). cutoffchrom: Float, cutoff fraction for chrominance (0.45). Returns: loss: Scalar float value. """ # 1. Transform to opponent color space targetopp = opponentcolortransform(targetrgb) simopp = opponentcolortransform(simulatedrgb) # 2. Create filters h, w = targetrgb.shape[:2] klum = createfourierlowpassfilter((h, w), cutofflum) kchrom = createfourierlowpassfilter((h, w), cutoffchrom) # 3. Apply filters via Fourier domain multiplication targetlumfilt = applyfourierfilter(targetopp[:,:,0], klum) simlumfilt = applyfourierfilter(simopp[:,:,0], klum) targetchrom1filt = applyfourierfilter(targetopp[:,:,1], kchrom) simchrom1filt = applyfourierfilter(simopp[:,:,1], kchrom) targetchrom2filt = applyfourierfilter(targetopp[:,:,2], kchrom) simchrom2filt = applyfourierfilter(simopp[:,:,2], kchrom) # 4. Compute MSE Loss losslum = np.mean((targetlumfilt - simlumfilt) 2) losschrom1 = np.mean((targetchrom1filt - simchrom1filt) 2) losschrom2 = np.mean((targetchrom2filt - simchrom2filt) 2) totalloss = losslum + losschrom1 + losschrom2 return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The linear transformation coefficients (0.299, 0.587, etc.) are standard ITU-R BT.601 luminance weights. Ensure input RGB values are normalized consistently with these weights. Extends the simultaneous color approach to multiple depth planes (focal stacks) rather than a single plane. It applies the same perceptual loss principles across depth layers. Link Addresses the physical limitation of SLM phase range (e.g., 0-2\pi vs extended range) to reduce depth replicas. It complements the perceptual loss by improving the physical accuracy of the forward model. Link Time and Memory Complexity Time: The addition of the perceptual loss increases computational cost per iteration compared to standard RGB loss due to the extra color space transformations and convolutions. The overall convergence may be faster visually due to better gradient guidance, though exact iteration counts are not provided. Memory: Requires storing three additional channel arrays (opponent space) and filter masks. Measured Performance Hardware/Setup: Tested with an 8 µm pixel pitch SLM and a 36.6 mm focal length eyepiece. Metrics: On a test set of 294 images, the perceptual loss yielded an average PSNR increase of 6.4 dB and an average SSIM increase of 0.266 compared to standard RGB loss. Visual Quality: Holograms are visually less noisy with better color fidelity. The error is shifted into imperceptible regions of the opponent color space. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Significantly improves color fidelity and reduces noise in the perceived image. Aligns with human visual system characteristics, similar to JPEG compression and subpixel rendering principles. Limitations: The method assumes a specific human visual model (Mullen 1985) which may not account for all individual variations in color perception. It does not address depth replicas or SLM physical limitations directly (these are handled by sibling methods). When to Use Use when generating full-color holograms with a single SLM and simultaneous RGB illumination where color fidelity is critical. Use when standard RGB loss results in desaturated or noisy color outputs. The method was introduced by Markley et al. in 2023 as part of the "Simultaneous Color Computer Generated Holography" framework. It leverages established principles from image compression (JPEG) and subpixel rendering, which utilize the HVS's lower sensitivity to high-frequency chrominance information. The specific cutoff frequencies (30 cycles/deg for luminance, 18 cycles/deg for chrominance) are based on human vision measurements by Mullen (1985). This approach was novel in its application to hologram optimization, addressing the overdetermined nature of single-SLM color holography.
