name: SHG-based Volumetric Display
head: Frequency upconversion volumetric display, Glass-Ceramic (GC) Volumetric Display, SHG Volumetric Display, Volumetric Display via Frequency Upconversion, Volumetric display via frequency upconversion (SHG) with laser scanning
body: A volumetric display technique that generates 3D images by rapidly scanning the focal point of a near-infrared laser inside a transparent composite material containing dispersed nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals. The NLO crystals generate visible light via Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG), creating localized, isotropic emission spots (voxels) without ghost images. Unlike its parent method, which relies on two-step fluorescence from rare-earth ions, this method uses the instantaneous nonlinear optical response of SHG to achieve ultrafast emission and full-color purity. Inputs and Outputs Input: A femtosecond (fs) laser source emitting at a fundamental wavelength \lambda{fund}; a transparent glass-ceramic (GC) composite containing dispersed NLO crystals; a scanning system (galvanometer mirrors and focusing lens). Output: A 3D volumetric image composed of visible light voxels emitted from the focal volume within the material. Data Structures The display medium is a Glass-Ceramic (GC) composite. Matrix: Glass (e.g., Ba2TiSi2O8 or BTS glass). Inclusions: NLO crystals (e.g., BTS crystals). Crystal Geometry: Spherulitic aggregates with radius R typically 50–300 nm. Volume Fraction: \varphi typically 0.01 to 0.2. Optical Properties: Refractive index of glass ng and crystal nc are closely matched to minimize scattering (e.g., ng=1.77, nc=1.76 at 632.8 nm). Numbered Steps 1. Laser Selection: Select a fundamental laser wavelength \lambda{fund} such that its second harmonic \lambda{fund}/2 corresponds to the desired visible color. Common mappings: 800 nm \rightarrow 400 nm (purple) 900 nm \rightarrow 450 nm (blue) 1080 nm \rightarrow 540 nm (green) 1230 nm \rightarrow 615 nm (red). 2. Beam Steering (XY): Direct the fundamental laser beam using two galvanometer mirrors to illuminate a specific 2D point (x, y) on the display volume. 3. Depth Positioning (Z): Specify the depth position z of the voxels by changing the distance between the GC sample and the galvanometer mirrors (or by moving the focus along the optical axis). 4. Emission Generation: Focus the laser into the GC material. At the focal point, the high intensity I0 induces Second-Harmonic Generation in the randomly oriented NLO crystals, emitting visible light at \lambda{fund}/2. 5. Scanning: Rapidly scan the focal point through the volume to construct moving 3D objects. The scanning frequency must be over 30 Hz to ensure image fusion. Formulas Scattering Turbidity: The light attenuation due to scattering in the GC material is estimated by: \sigma = \frac{14}{15\pi} \varphi(1 - \varphi) k^8 R^7 \left( \frac{\Delta n}{n} \right)^2 where \varphi is the volume fraction of the crystalline phase, R is the crystal radius, n is the refractive index of the crystal, \Delta n is the refractive index difference between the glassy and crystal phases, and k=2\pi/\lambda (\lambda is the wavelength of light). Voxel Dimension: The resolution is determined by the focal spot size, expressed as: d = \frac{4\lambda f}{\pi D} where \lambda is the wavelength, f is the focal length of the lens, and D is the diameter of the fundamental beam. Total SHG Intensity: The total intensity generated by dispersed crystals is: I{2,\text{tot}} = A f T2 T1^2 I0^2 L where A is a constant determined by crystal size and optical constants, f is the volume fraction of the crystalline phase, T1 and T2 are the fundamental beam and SHG signal transmissions, I0 is the fundamental beam intensity, and L is the sample thickness. Parameters Laser Source: Femtosecond laser. Example: 800 nm, 1 kHz repetition rate. Pumping Power (I0): Typical value 100 mW for a 1 mm^3 voxel. Crystal Size: ~100–300 nm. This size is smaller than the coherent length of BTS crystal (~10 \mum), preventing exact phase-matching for all particles and ensuring isotropic emission. Volume Fraction (f): 0.05 to 0.2 for solid displays, 0.01 for liquid colloidal displays. Sample Thickness (L): 0.02 m to 1 m depending on display type. Minimal Emission Energy: Calculated minimal energy to observe green light (540 nm) in a dimly lit room (assuming 1 \muW per 1 mm^3 spot): Solid-1 (0.02 m^3): 8 mW Solid-2 (0.1 m^3): 103 mW Liquid (1 m^3): 106 mW. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shgvolumetricdisplay(): # Configuration lambdafund = 1080e-9 # 1080 nm for green lambdavis = lambdafund / 2 # 540 nm flens = 0.1 # 10 cm focal length Dbeam = 0.01 # 1 cm beam diameter Lsample = 0.02 # 2 cm thickness phi = 0.05 # Volume fraction Rcrystal = 50e-9 # 50 nm radius ncrystal = 1.76 deltan = 0.01 # Index mismatch nglass = 1.77 # Calculate Voxel Size k = 2 pi / lambdafund voxelsize = (4 lambdafund flens) / (pi Dbeam) # Calculate Scattering Turbidity sigma = (14 / (15 pi)) phi (1 - phi) (k8) (Rcrystal7) ((deltan / ncrystal)2) # Calculate Required Power for Visibility # Assuming target intensity Itarget = 1 uW / mm^3 # Efficiency eta = 0.003% at 100 mW # I2tot = A phi T2 T1^2 I0^2 L # Simplified: Power scales with L^3 for full volume, L^2 for surface requiredpowermW = calculateminimalenergy(Lsample, phi, Rcrystal) # Scanning Loop for x, y, z in scanpath(volumedimensions): # Set Galvanometer Mirrors for XY setgalvanometer(x, y) # Set Z-position by moving sample or focus setzposition(z) # Emit Laser Pulse emitlaser(lambdafund, power=requiredpowermW) # Wait for refresh rate (>30 Hz) waitforrefresh() def calculateminimalenergy(L, phi, R): # Returns minimal emission energy in mW based on Table 1 data # For L=0.02, phi=0.05, R=20nm -> 8 mW # For L=0.1, phi=0.2, R=50nm -> 103 mW # For L=1.0, phi=0.01, R=50nm -> 106 mW # Interpolation or lookup table required based on specific parameters # Not given in the sources for arbitrary L. return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ghost Images: Avoided by using SHG (response time ~100 fs) instead of Rare-Earth ions (lifetime \mus to ms). Image Drift: Slight image drift occurs due to frequency upconversion along the light path before and after the focus. Mitigation: Use an optical lens with a large size and short focal length to create a large divergence angle. Mitigation: Use a laser system with smaller peak power to eliminate self-focusing and filamentation. Scattering Loss: High transparency is maintained if crystal size and volume fraction are controlled. For BTS GC with 5% crystalline phase and 50 nm crystals, scattering loss is <1% for a 10-mm-thick plate. Even with 200 nm crystals and 20% volume fraction, attenuation is <30%. Anisotropy: Single crystals are unsuitable because SHG emission is strongly anisotropic, causing image distortion. Dispersed randomly oriented NLO crystals ensure isotropic emission. Time Complexity: The emission is instantaneous (~100 fs response time). The frame rate is limited by the scanning hardware (galvanometer mirrors), typically requiring >30 Hz for image fusion. Memory Complexity: Not applicable (physical display). Scaling: Full-volume display requires laser power scaling with L^3, making large sizes unrealistic. Surface-only display scales with L^2, dramatically reducing required power. Strengths: Full-color capability with high color purity (near-monochromatic emissions); unlimited viewing angles (isotropic emission); no ghost images; viewable without glasses. Limitations: High laser power requirements for large volumes; image drift due to nonlinear effects along the beam path; limited by scanner hardware speed. When to use: Proof-of-concept 3D displays, head-up displays (2D transparent displays), applications requiring wide viewing angles and no glasses. Origin: Developed by researchers publishing in Advanced Materials (2017). History: The method utilizes Ba2TiSi2O8 (BTS) glass-ceramics, which offer high second-order optical nonlinearity and small index mismatch between glass and crystal phases. Usage: Demonstrated as a proof-of-concept for volumetric 3D displays viewable from any angle, and potential for 2D transparent displays. A volumetric full-color display realized by frequency upconversion of a transparent composite incorporating dispersed nonlinear optical crystals, https://doi.org/10.1038/am.2017.89, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Optical Addressing of Photochromic Mixtures
head: Colour-selective PM colouration, Geometrical optical intersection, Optical Addressing of Multi-Colour Photochromic Material Mixture, Optical Addressing of Photochromic Materials, Position- and colour-selective colouration, Position-selective PM colouration, Two-channel optical addressing
body: This method realizes a dynamic, full-colour volumetric display by exploiting the dual-light response of photochromic molecules (PMs) within a solid mixture. It solves the problem of 3D spatial addressing and colour selection in a single homogeneous medium by using the geometric intersection of two control light channels: ultraviolet (UV) light for colouration and visible (Vis) light for decolouration. Unlike sibling methods that rely on layered plates or complex 3D nanomaterial alignment, this approach uniformly mixes PM types, allowing high-density voxel arrangements determined by the molecular scale (~1 nm) and simple orthogonal optical geometry. Inputs: 1. PM Volume: A transparent solid block containing a mixture of photochromic molecules (diarylethenes) dissolved in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymer matrix. 2. UV Light Source: Monochromatic light at 302 nm for inducing colouration (open-ring to closed-ring transition). 3. Vis Light Source: Spatially modulated visible light (projector or SLM) for inducing decolouration (closed-ring to open-ring transition) and selecting colour via spectrum management. 4. Control Signals: Synchronization signals for two Spatial Light Modulators (SLM1 for UV, SLM2 for Vis). Outputs: A 3D image rendered within the volume, where voxels are coloured based on the local balance of UV and Vis irradiation. PM Volume Construction: Material: Diarylethene PMs dissolved in toluene, mixed with PDMS polymer. Dimensions: Approximately 1 \text{ cm} \times 1 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm} for single-colour demonstrations, or 1 \text{ cm} \times 1 \text{ cm} \times 2 \text{ cm} for multi-colour demonstrations. Preparation: Single-colour concentration: 2 mg PM per 1 mL toluene. Multi-colour concentration: 1 mg yellow PM and 1 mg blue PM per 2 mL toluene. Mixing ratio: 4.4 mL polymer to 2 mL PM solution. Solidification: Heated at 100 °C for approximately 3 hours. Optical Properties: The PM is transparent (open-ring) initially. UV irradiation turns it coloured (closed-ring). Vis irradiation returns it to transparent. Different PM types absorb different Vis wavelengths for decolouration. System Architecture: SLM1: Controls UV irradiation pattern for depth selection. SLM2: Controls Vis irradiation pattern for 2D spatial addressing and colour selection. Geometry: UV and Vis sources are arranged to irradiate the PM volume from different angles, typically orthogonal. 1. Initialization: Prepare the PM volume as described above. 2. Alignment: Ensure UV and Vis sources are aligned orthogonally to the volume. 3. Synchronization Setup: Configure SLM1 (UV) and SLM2 (Vis) to operate synchronously. Define the arrival time T and duration \Delta T for both channels. Strict synchronization is required to prevent unintended coloration. 4. Depth Scanning Loop: For each depth layer z from 1 to N (where N is the depth resolution): a. UV Modulation: SLM1 projects a pattern that irradiates only the target depth layer z with UV light. b. Vis Modulation: Simultaneously, SLM2 projects a 2D pattern corresponding to the desired image for layer z. The spectrum of this Vis light determines the colour of the voxels in this layer. c. Irradiation: Maintain irradiation for a duration \Delta t. d. Repeat: Increment z and repeat steps 4a–4c until all layers are scanned. Timing Constraints: Let T{UV} and T{Vis} be the arrival times of UV and Vis light, and \Delta T{UV} and \Delta T{Vis} be their durations. If T{UV} < T{Vis}, unintended coloration occurs during the interval [T{UV}, T{Vis}]. If T{UV} = T{Vis} and \Delta T{UV} > \Delta T{Vis}, unintended coloration occurs during [T{Vis} + \Delta T{Vis}, T{UV} + \Delta T{UV}]. Requirement: T{UV} \ge T{Vis} and \Delta T{UV} \le \Delta T{Vis} (or strict equality with precise hardware sync) to avoid artifacts. Performance Metrics: Total Scan Time: T{scan} = N \Delta t. Max Rendering Time per Layer: To suppress flicker at a frame rate of F{frame} \ge 60 \text{ Hz}, the time to render one layer must satisfy: \Delta t \le \frac{1}{F{frame} \cdot N} For F{frame} = 60 \text{ Hz}, \Delta t \le \frac{1}{60 N} seconds. Typical Parameters: UV Wavelength: 302 nm. UV Intensity: 0.84 mW/cm². Vis Intensity: 15.04 mW/cm². PM Purity: >99% HPLC purity. Projector Specs (Example): 500 ANSI Lumens, 1280 × 800 resolution, 30,000:1 contrast. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time def opticaladdressingpmdisplay(Ndepth, framerate, uvintensity, visintensity, layerdata): """ Implements the optical addressing scan for a photochromic mixture volumetric display. layerdata: list of tuples (uvmask, vispattern, visspectrum) for each depth layer. """ maxdt = 1.0 / (framerate Ndepth) TUV = 0.0 TVis = 0.0 DeltaTUV = 0.0 DeltaTVis = 0.0 for z in range(1, Ndepth + 1): uvmask, vispattern, visspectrum = layerdata[z - 1] # Configure SLM1 to irradiate only depth z with UV light # Configure SLM2 to project vispattern with visspectrum simultaneously # Hardware triggers ensure TUV == TVis and DeltaTUV == DeltaTVis # Apply light with specified intensities print(f"Applying UV ({uvintensity} mW/cm^2) and Vis ({visintensity} mW/cm^2) at depth {z}") # Duration must not exceed maxdt to maintain frame rate Deltat = min(maxdt, 0.001) time.sleep(Deltat) print(f"Stopped light at depth {z}") # Guard: verify timing constraints to prevent unintended coloration if TUV < TVis or (TUV == TVis and DeltaTUV > DeltaTVis): print("Warning: Timing mismatch detected. Unintended coloration risk.") 1. Timing Mismatch: If UV light arrives before Vis light (T{UV} < T{Vis}) or if UV duration exceeds Vis duration (\Delta T{UV} > \Delta T{Vis}), unintended coloration occurs in the overlap region. Strict hardware synchronization is mandatory. 2. Boundary Blurring: Boundaries between coloured and decoloured areas are blurred due to the spread of Vis light, causing extra decolouration at edges. This blurring is on a scale much larger than the wavelength of light. 3. Colour Artifacts at Boundaries: In multi-PM mixtures, if Vis light spreads, it may decolour one PM type more easily than another (e.g., yellow PM decolours more easily than blue PM), causing the boundary to appear blue instead of the intended colour. 4. Solution for Blurring: Use a highly directional light source, such as a laser-based projector, to minimize light spread. 5. Minimum Voxel Size: Theoretically limited by the size of a molecule (~1 nm), but practically limited by the diffraction limit of light and the resolution of the SLMs/projectors. Time Complexity: The total scan time is N \Delta t, where N is the depth resolution and \Delta t is the rendering time per layer. To achieve a flicker-free frame rate of 60 Hz, \Delta t \le 1/(60 N). Memory Complexity: Not applicable in the traditional sense, as the "memory" is the physical PM volume. The data structure for the 3D image is stored in the host system. Resolution: Depth (Z): Dominated by the resolution of SLM1 (UV) and the optical focusing/scanning mechanism. Lateral (X, Y): Dominated by the resolution of SLM2 (Vis) and the diffraction limit of light. Theoretical Limit: ~1 nm (molecular size). Strengths: Simple hardware structure (uniform mixture, no 3D alignment of voxels). High-density voxel arrangement possible. Full-colour capability via spectrum management. Dynamic rewriting capability. Limitations: Blurring at boundaries due to light spread. Frame rate limited by SLM speed, not molecular response time (picoseconds). Requires precise synchronization of UV and Vis sources. When to Use: Suitable for applications requiring dynamic, full-colour volumetric displays with simple hardware, such as information display and human-computer interaction. When Not to Use: When high-resolution boundaries are critical without post-processing or specialized optics, or when extremely high frame rates are required beyond SLM capabilities. Origin: Proposed and experimentally demonstrated by Hirayama R. et al. in 2016. Development: The method builds on the properties of P-type photochromic materials (diarylethenes), which are thermally irreversible and exhibit colour states dependent on both UV and Vis irradiation. Previous T-type PM displays required layered plates and suffered from voxel overlap restrictions. This P-type mixture approach allows uniform mixing, enabling simpler hardware and higher density. Usage: Fields of information display and human–computer interaction. name: Laser-Induced Plasma and Bubble Volumetric Displays
head: Laser-induced plasma display, Laser plasma displays, Laser-induced bubble display, Laser-Induced Plasma Volumetric Displays
body: Laser-induced plasma and bubble volumetric displays generate visible voxels in free space or within a liquid medium by focusing high-energy laser pulses to trigger nonlinear optical effects, such as air ionization or cavitation. Unlike swept-volume or light-field displays, these systems create self-emitting point sources at specific (x, y, z) coordinates without requiring a physical screen or moving macroscopic parts inside the image volume. They are distinguished from sibling methods like inkjet printing or quantum-dot displays by their ability to render in open air (plasma) or transparent fluids (bubbles) using laser energy rather than physical deposition or fluorescence from pre-doped solids. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: High-power pulsed laser source (femtosecond or nanosecond IR), 3D positioning system (galvanometer mirrors, linear motors, varifocal lenses), and optionally a spatial light modulator (SLM) for holographic generation. Outputs: Visible light emission (plasma glow) or refractive index changes (microbubbles) at targeted 3D coordinates. Data Structures: The system does not use a traditional voxel grid stored in memory. Instead, it uses a stream of target coordinates (x, y, z) and pulse timing parameters. Target List: A sequence of 3D coordinates \{Pi\} where Pi = (xi, yi, zi). Pulse Parameters: For each target, a pulse energy E and duration \tau are defined. Numbered Steps: 1. Beam Steering: The laser beam is directed through a galvanometer mirror system to control the x and y positions of the focal point. 2. Axial Focusing: A varifocal lens or linear motor adjusts the z position of the focal plane. 3. Excitation: A high-intensity laser pulse is emitted. When the intensity exceeds the threshold of the medium (air or liquid), nonlinear absorption occurs. For Plasma: The electric field of the laser ionizes the air molecules at the focal point, creating a micro-plasma that emits broadband visible light. For Bubbles: In a high-viscosity liquid, the laser induces optical breakdown, creating a cavitation bubble that scatters or emits light when illuminated. 4. Scanning: The system moves to the next coordinate in the target list. The persistence of the plasma glow or bubble formation allows the eye to perceive a continuous image. 5. Holographic Alternative (Optional): Instead of direct scanning, a computer-generated hologram (CGH) is calculated on an SLM to shape the wavefront, focusing multiple beams simultaneously to create voxel arrays. Formulas: Plasma Threshold: Plasma generation occurs when the peak intensity I exceeds the ionization threshold I{th} of the medium: I = \frac{2P}{\pi w0^2} > I{th} Where P is the peak pulse power and w0 is the beam waist radius at the focus. Voxel Generation Rate: The frame rate is limited by the pulse repetition rate. For early systems, this was approximately 100 pulses per second. Parameters: Laser Type: Femtosecond or nanosecond infrared lasers. Voxel Size (Plasma): Determined by the diffraction limit of the focusing optics and the ionization threshold. Voxel Size (Bubble): In high-viscosity liquids, microbubbles can be controlled in size and intensity via holographic laser drawing. Resolution: Limited by the scanning speed and the minimum spot size. Early plasma displays achieved roughly a cubic meter volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def laserplasmadisplay(targetpoints, laser, scanner, lens): """ Renders a 3D image using laser-induced plasma voxels. Args: targetpoints: List of (x, y, z) coordinates for voxels. laser: Object with method emitpulse(energy, duration). scanner: Object with method setxy(x, y). lens: Object with method setz(z). """ for point in targetpoints: x, y, z = point # 1. Position the focal point in 3D space scanner.setxy(x, y) lens.setz(z) # 2. Emit a high-power pulse to induce plasma # The pulse must exceed the ionization threshold of air laser.emitpulse(energy=HIGHENERGY, duration=FEMTOSECOND) # 3. Wait for plasma decay or persistence if required # Note: Plasma glow is transient; persistence relies on eye integration # or high repetition rates. waitfordecay() def laserbubbledisplay(targetpoints, liquidmedium, laser, scanner, lens): """ Renders a 3D image using laser-induced microbubbles in a high-viscosity liquid. Args: targetpoints: List of (x, y, z) coordinates. liquidmedium: The high-viscosity fluid containing the bubbles. laser: Femtosecond laser source. scanner: Galvanometer mirror system. lens: Varifocal lens. """ for point in targetpoints: x, y, z = point # 1. Position the focal point within the liquid scanner.setxy(x, y) lens.setz(z) # 2. Emit pulse to create cavitation bubble # The bubble acts as a voxel, scattering or emitting light laser.emitpulse(energy=CAVITATIONTHRESHOLD, duration=FEMTOSECOND) # 3. Control bubble geometry/intensity if using holographic method # This step is specific to advanced implementations using SLMs # applyholographicwavefront(laser, point) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aberration: High-speed changes in varifocal lenses can introduce optical aberrations, degrading voxel quality. Aperture Limits: The aperture of the objective lens limits the maximum working space and the angular range of the galvanometer mirror. Acoustic Noise: Plasma voxels produce an audible "popping" sound due to rapid air expansion. Eye Safety: The high energy density required for plasma generation near the focal point raises significant eye-safety concerns. A subclass of laser-induced displays that renders voxels in open air without any containing medium, resembling science-fiction holograms. It uses self-illuminating sources like plasma or photophoretic traps to levitate and illuminate particles. Unlike bubble displays, it operates in air, but suffers from monochrome output, audible noise, and strict scanning speed limits that constrain refresh rates. Commercial examples include Burton Inc.'s Aerial Burton (2011). Time Complexity: Frame rate is linearly dependent on the number of voxels and the pulse repetition rate. With ~100 pulses/second in early systems, complex scenes require multiplexing or parallel beam generation. Memory Complexity: Low; only the target coordinate list needs to be stored. No volumetric texture maps are required. Performance: Early 2006 techniques achieved ~100 pulses/second within a cubic meter volume. Modern femtosecond systems offer higher precision but remain limited by scanning mechanics. Strengths: True 3D voxels in free space; no glasses required; works with transparent media (air/liquid). Limitations: Monochrome (unless up-conversion crystals are used); audible noise; eye safety risks; limited color capability without complex multiplexing; occlusion is additive (back voxels bleed through front ones). When to Use: When true free-space volumetric presence is required and safety/acoustic constraints are manageable. When Not to Use: For high-color fidelity, silent operation, or dense opaque surfaces. The technique originated from the observation that strongly focused laser beams induce air plasma emission only near the focal point. Kimura et al. first demonstrated 2D images in air using galvanometric scanning mirrors, later extending this to 3D. Ochiai et al. proposed using femtosecond lasers with spatial light modulation for holographic rendering. The field expanded to include laser-induced bubbles in high-viscosity liquids (Kumagai et al.) and up-conversion crystals (Zhu et al., Mun et al.) to address color and resolution limitations. Commercial efforts like Burton Inc.'s Aerial Burton (2011) and research from Brigham Young University's Optical Trap Display have further explored free-space point-light displays. What is A Volumetric Display?, https://www.mobilepixels.us/pages/what-is-a-volumetric-display?srsltid=AYCX9vK8xrsJpADuue0kuBQrGLoGaAlKbDhSUiAQBf97hCstLFLUkQ-f, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volumetric 3D Display: Features and Classification, https://www.coppjournal.org/journal/view.html?uid=1568, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Three-dimensional display technologies, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4269274, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Rotational Swept-Screen Projection
body: Rotational swept-screen projection is a class of volumetric display systems that generates a continuous 3D image by projecting 2D image patterns onto a screen undergoing rotational motion. It solves the problem of creating a stationary, viewable 3D volume without requiring the light source itself to scan the entire volume mechanically, instead relying on the temporal integration of the human eye as the screen sweeps through space. It differs from translational swept-screen methods by utilizing rotational kinematics to define the volume, and from static multi-layer displays by physically moving the projection surface. The core mechanism involves a screen (reflective, transmissive, or emissive) rotating around a central axis. A projection system (LED array, laser, or projector) updates the image on the screen synchronously with the rotation angle. 1. Coordinate Mapping: The 3D world coordinates of a voxel are mapped to 2D screen coordinates and a specific frame index corresponding to the rotation angle. 2. Temporal Integration: The screen speed and frame rate are chosen such that the persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. 3. Synchronization: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. Misalignment between screen position and projected frame index results in Z-depth distortion [8515-multi-planar-volumetric-3d-display.md]. VRDM projects 3D voxel data onto a rotating mirror using surrounding LED screens, mapping 3D coordinates to 2D screen pixels via analytical mirror reflection matrices. It differs from standard ray marching by avoiding per-pixel ray tracing loops, instead computing direct projections for each rotation angle to drive the LED arrays synchronously. Choose this method when a reflective, pyramid-shaped volume is desired with high geometric precision. This system renders volumetric images by rotating a 2D LED panel array around a central axis and synchronously updating the panel content to match the rotation angle. It differs from laser-based swept-screen systems by generating voxels directly on an emissive surface without requiring external synchronization with electron beams or lasers. Choose this method for direct emissive volumetric rendering with high frame counts per rotation. This method projects a sequence of 2D image patterns onto a screen moving along the Z-axis to form a stack of spatial image planes, creating a true 3D image viewable without glasses. Unlike conventional 2D screens that rely on psychological depth cues, this method places voxels at their physical spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally to provide both physiological and psychological depth cues. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like the Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM) by utilizing linear or reciprocating screen motion rather than rotational sweep. Choose this method for planar volumetric displays requiring precise Z-depth layering. A volumetric display system that generates voxels by irradiating a fluorescent screen coated on a rotating plane with an electron beam. This is an early implementation of the rotational swept-screen principle, predating laser and LED variants. A cylindrical 3D display using a parallax barrier with multiple slits and a 1D LED array rotating along the slits. It utilizes the scanning of light rays when slit and LED positions change to reproduce multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. A 360-degree display using a moving projection surface (vertically oscillating diffuser) synchronized with a projection system. It relies on retinal persistence to create a full volumetric object. The system oscillates a diffuser vertically at high frequency, synchronizes the projection system with the diffuser's motion, and the viewer perceives the image as a full object due to retinal persistence. The high frequency precludes the diffuser from being seen, leading to general transparency. Occlusion from different parts of the image is not possible because the image is diffused in a large field of view, limiting the display to 'ghosted content' rather than true volumetric occlusion. The concept of rotational volumetric displays dates back to the 1950s and 1960s. In 1958, Withey proposed a system using a translating fluorescent screen inside a vacuum container. In the 1960s, Hartwig proposed laser irradiation of rotating screens, followed by a helical screen structure. In 1994, Blundell et al. proposed a system based on generating an image drawing space, and the "Cathode ray sphere" was proposed, using a 15 Hz rotating fluorescent plane. The 2000s saw a shift towards LED and laser excitation, with Hisatake proposing the rotation of lanthanide-mixed polymer sheets excited by a 410 nm laser. In 2004, Perlin et al. demonstrated volumetric imaging by irradiating dust in the air with lasers. In 2010, the Seelinder system was proposed, using a cylindrical parallax barrier with a rotating 1D LED array. Recent developments include holographic diffuser combinations that form multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. ボリュメトリックディスプレイ, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jvrsj/29/3/2927/pdf/-char/ja, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Multi-user volumetric 360° display based on retro-reflective transparent surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1364/oe.409181, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Holographic Defuser Light Field Display
head: Jones et al. holographic rotating diffuser, Jones light-field display, Rotating Screen Light Field Display, Rotating Screen Light Field Display with a High-Speed Projector, USC: Rotating Screen Light Field Display
body: A volumetric display system that generates a 360° horizontal light field by projecting images onto a rotating holographic diffuser screen. Unlike standard rotational swept-screen displays that diffuse light broadly, this method uses a diffuser with specific angular characteristics to reflect light within a narrow cone (1.25°), creating distinct viewpoints for multiple users simultaneously. It solves the limitation of occlusion in traditional ghosted volumetric displays, though it remains constrained to content without complex occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of N=288 pre-rendered 2D images; projector frame rate and screen rotation speed. Output: A 360° horizontal light field with 288 distinct viewpoints. Data Structures: Image Buffer: A sequence of N=288 images. Each image corresponds to a specific angular sector of the 360° field of view. Screen Geometry: A cylindrical or planar surface coated with a holographic diffuser material. Diffuser Property: A reflection profile limited to a range of \theta{max} = 1.25^\circ. Steps: 1. Synchronization Setup: Synchronize the projector's frame update with the angular position of the rotating screen. 2. Image Selection: For each projector frame k, select the image Ik corresponding to the current viewing angle \phik determined by the screen's rotation angle. 3. Projection: Project image Ik onto the screen surface. 4. Diffusion: The holographic diffuser reflects the projected light only within the narrow angular range of \pm 0.625^\circ (centered on the specular reflection direction). 5. Viewpoint Generation: As the screen rotates, the narrow reflection cone sweeps across the audience, delivering the correct perspective image to each viewer's position. 6. Temporal Integration: The screen speed and frame rate are chosen such that persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. Formulas: Viewpoint Count: N = 288. Angular Resolution: The angular width of each viewpoint is determined by the diffuser's reflection range, \Delta \theta = 1.25^\circ. Mapping: The image index k is mapped to the rotation angle \alpha such that k = \lfloor \frac{\alpha}{360^\circ} \times 288 \rfloor \pmod{288}. Parameters: Number of Images: 288. Horizontal Field of View: 360°. Reflection Angle Range: 1.25°. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: The system cannot render occlusion between objects in the scene because the light is diffused into a wide horizontal field of view for all viewers simultaneously. It is limited to "ghosted content" where objects do not block each other from different viewpoints. Viewer Position: Users must be at a specific height and distance from the device to receive the correct viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderholographicdisplay(images, rotationangledegrees): """ Selects and projects the correct image based on screen rotation. Args: images: List of 288 pre-rendered 2D images. rotationangledegrees: Current angle of the screen (0-360). Returns: The image to project. """ # Map rotation angle to image index normalizedangle = rotationangledegrees % 360.0 index = int((normalizedangle / 360.0) 288) % 288 return images[index] def checkdiffuserconstraint(viewerangledegrees, screennormalangledegrees): """ Checks if a viewer is within the narrow reflection cone. Args: viewerangledegrees: Angle of the viewer relative to the screen center. screennormalangledegrees: Angle of the screen's surface normal. Returns: True if viewer is in the 1.25 degree reflection cone. """ anglediff = abs(viewerangledegrees - screennormalangledegrees) # The reflection range is 1.25 degrees total, so the viewer must be within 0.625 degrees of the specular direction return anglediff <= 0.625 Uses a physical mirror to sweep a light source. Sets it apart by offering true occlusion. Choose for line-based volumetric rendering. Link Uses an array of LEDs on a rotating ring. Sets it apart by simpler hardware without light-field perspective correction. Choose for low-cost rotational displays. Link Projects onto a generic rotating screen. Sets it apart by lacking angular selectivity, resulting in ghosting for multiple viewers. Choose for single-viewer swept displays. Link Uses discrete planes. Sets it apart by lacking continuous 3D depth. Choose for planar volumetric scenes. Link Oscillates rather than rotates. Sets it apart by limited field of view. Choose for constrained rotational ranges. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Generates 288 images on a 360° horizontal field of view. The reflection angle is limited to 1.25°. Strengths: Allows multi-user sharing of the visual experience at a given height and distance. Provides a true 360° light field with distinct viewpoints. Limitations: Cannot render occlusion between objects, limiting content to "ghosted" scenes. Relies on rotating parts and scanning mechanisms, imposing physical limitations on display volume and forcing trade-offs between image quality and system complexity. When to use: For multi-user 360° displays where occlusion is not critical. When not to use: For scenes requiring complex depth interactions or occlusion. The system was proposed by Jones et al. to allow multi-user sharing of the visual experience at a given height and distance from the device. It addresses the limitation of traditional rotational swept-screen displays where broad diffusion prevents distinct viewpoints for multiple users. The concept builds on earlier work by Joens et al. in 2007, who combined a rotating holographic defuser with a high-speed projector to form multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. name: Cathode Ray Volumetric Display
head: Blundell implementation, Cathode Ray Sphere, Hirsch 1958 design, ITT Labs 1960 system, Ketchpel concept, Rotating Screen 3D Display with CRT
body: The Cathode Ray Volumetric Display (CRVD), also known as the Cathode Ray Sphere (CRS), is a volumetric 3D display that generates voxels by irradiating a fluorescent screen coated on a rotating plane with an electron beam. It addresses the problem of creating a true 3D volume of light without requiring the viewer to wear special glasses, by using temporal integration of discrete 2D slices projected onto a rapidly rotating surface. It differs from sibling swept-screen systems (e.g., Rotating Rigid Screen with Projector) by using direct electron beam excitation of phosphor rather than optical projection of light, allowing for high-intensity, high-contrast voxels in a vacuum environment. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (or point cloud) defining the desired image; rotation speed \omega of the screen; electron beam deflection coordinates (x, y); beam intensity I. Output: A visible 3D volume of light emitted from the rotating phosphor screen. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array V[x, y, z] where x, y are screen coordinates and z is the radial distance from the rotation axis. Not given in the sources. Beam Control Signal: A time-varying signal mapping rotation angle \theta(t) to beam deflection (x(t), y(t)) and intensity I(t). Numbered Steps: 1. Screen Rotation: A flat, phosphor-coated screen rotates around a central axis at a constant angular velocity \omega. The screen is enclosed in a vacuum chamber. 2. Beam Deflection: An electron gun generates a beam that is deflected by magnetic or electrostatic fields to strike a specific point (x, y) on the rotating screen. 3. Synchronization: The beam deflection and intensity are synchronized with the screen's angular position \theta(t) = \omega t. The beam must hit the target (x, y) at the precise moment the screen rotates into the correct radial position z corresponding to the desired voxel depth. 4. Voxel Generation: The electron beam excites the phosphor coating, causing it to emit light at the struck location, creating a single voxel. 5. Temporal Integration: As the screen rotates, the beam addresses multiple 2D slices at different radial distances. The persistence of vision blends these discrete slices into a continuous 3D volume. Formulas: Angular Position: \theta(t) = \omega t Radial Mapping: The radial distance r of a voxel from the center is fixed by the physical placement of the screen or the beam focus. For a flat screen rotating around its center, the radial distance r corresponds to the distance from the axis. The z-coordinate in the world frame is mapped to r on the screen. Not given in the sources. Beam Timing: The beam must be deflected to (x, y) when the screen angle \theta places the physical point (x, y) at the desired radial depth. Not given in the sources. Parameters: Rotation Speed: The screen rotates at high speed. Blundell's implementation used 15 Hz. Phosphor Decay Rate: Must be short enough to prevent blurring between slices but long enough to maintain brightness. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Phosphor Decay vs. Rotation Speed: Image quality is affected by the interaction between the phosphor decay rate and the speed of rotation. If decay is too slow, adjacent slices blur; if too fast, brightness is insufficient. Vacuum Integrity: The system requires a vacuum to allow electron beam travel. Clarity of the glass enclosure affects viewability. Screen Translucency: The view depends on the translucency of the rotating screen. If too opaque, internal voxels are obscured; if too transparent, contrast is lost. Dead Zones: Electron beams cannot be emitted in all directions simultaneously; blind spots may exist depending on the number of electron guns. Multiple guns can mitigate this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crvdrender(voxelgrid, rotationspeedhz, phosphordecaytimems): """ Generates the control signals for the electron beam to render a 3D volume. Args: voxelgrid: 3D array [x, y, z] representing the desired image. x, y are screen coordinates. z is radial distance from axis. rotationspeedhz: Rotation speed in Hz. phosphordecaytimems: Phosphor persistence in milliseconds. """ omega = 2 math.pi rotationspeedhz # Angular velocity in rad/s # Determine the time for one full rotation T = 1.0 / rotationspeedhz # Initialize beam control signals beamdeflectionx = [] beamdeflectiony = [] beamintensity = [] # Time resolution for simulation/control dt = 0.0001 # 100 microseconds t = 0 while t < T: # Current angular position theta = omega t # Map angular position to screen coordinates # For a flat screen rotating around its center, the physical point # at angle theta corresponds to a specific radial distance r. # However, the beam must hit a specific (x, y) on the screen. # The synchronization requires that when the screen point (x, y) # is at the correct radial depth, the beam is active. # Simplified model: The beam scans the screen surface. # The 'z' depth is determined by the radial distance of the hit point. # For a flat disk, all points are at the same radial distance from the center? # No, the screen is a plane. The rotation axis is perpendicular to the plane? # Or parallel? The sources say "flat rotating screen" and "vertical rotating screen". # If vertical, the axis is horizontal. The screen rotates like a wheel. # The radial distance r from the axis varies with the position on the screen. # Let's assume the screen is a disk rotating around its center axis. # The electron beam hits a point (x, y) on the disk. # The radial distance r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). # The voxel grid's z-coordinate maps to r. # To render a voxel at (xv, yv, zv): # The beam must hit (xv, yv) when the screen is at the correct angle? # No, the screen is rotating. The physical point (xv, yv) on the screen # moves in a circle. The radial distance r is constant for a given (xv, yv). # So, zv must equal r = sqrt(xv^2 + yv^2). # This implies that for a flat disk rotating around its center, # the z-depth is determined by the radial distance from the center. # This is a limitation: you cannot have two voxels at the same (x, y) but different z. # Unless the screen is not a flat disk but a curved surface or the axis is different. # The sources mention "flat rotating screen". # If the screen is flat and rotates around an axis perpendicular to it (like a record), # then all points are at the same distance from the axis? No, r varies. # But the z-axis of the volume is usually the axis of rotation. # So, a point (x, y) on the screen corresponds to a specific r. # The beam hits (x, y). The light is emitted. # The viewer sees the light from all angles as the screen rotates. # The depth z is perceived as the radial distance r. # Therefore, the voxel grid must be mapped such that z = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). # This is a significant constraint. # Let's assume the beam can be deflected to any (x, y) on the screen. # The intensity is set based on the voxel value at (x, y, z=sqrt(x^2+y^2)). xscreen = xv yscreen = yv r = math.sqrt(xscreen2 + yscreen2) zvoxel = r # Check if there is a voxel at this (x, y, z) if voxelgrid.hasvoxel(xscreen, yscreen, zvoxel): intensity = voxelgrid.getintensity(xscreen, yscreen, zvoxel) else: intensity = 0 beamdeflectionx.append(xscreen) beamdeflectiony.append(yscreen) beamintensity.append(intensity) t += dt return beamdeflectionx, beamdeflectiony, beamintensity The specific implementation by Ketchpel and Blundell using a spherical or cylindrical phosphor screen? The sources say "flat rotating screen" for Hirsch/ITT and "phosphor-coated target screen" for CRS. The term "Sphere" might be metaphorical or refer to the volume. The sources do not clarify if the screen is spherical or flat for CRS. It is linked to the same family. The original proposal using a relay mirror/prism system. The first reported implementation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and rotation speed. The beam must be updated at a high frequency to match the rotation. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid size. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Blundell's system operated at 15 Hz. Scaling: Limited by the size of the vacuum chamber and the precision of the electron beam deflection. Not given in the sources. Strengths: High brightness and contrast due to direct phosphor excitation; true volumetric display without glasses. Limitations: Requires vacuum; complex synchronization; limited depth resolution due to radial mapping constraint; phosphor decay issues; safety hazards from high voltage and X-rays. When to use: For high-end visualization where true 3D light is required and cost/complexity is not a barrier. When not: For consumer applications due to complexity and safety. The concept was proposed by Hirsch in 1958. It was reported by Aviation Week as developed by ITT Labs in 1960. The Cathode Ray Sphere (CRS) concept was originally developed by Ketchpel in the 1960s and later implemented by Blundell. Blundell et al. provided a comprehensive classification of volumetric display systems in 2000, including this method. name: Seelinder
head: Cylindrical 3D display with parallax barrier, Cylindrical Parallax Barrier Display, Rotating LED array volumetric display with parallax barrier
body: Seelinder is a 360° autostereoscopic volumetric display that generates a horizontal parallax barrier (HPO) viewing area using a rotating cylindrical parallax barrier and a 1D LED array. It solves the physical limitation of mounting a full 360° array of LED sources by rotating a single linear array synchronously with a slotted cylindrical barrier. Unlike static parallax barrier displays, Seelinder creates multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees by scanning light rays as the slit and LED positions change relative to each other. It builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection by using the barrier itself as the spatial multiplexing element rather than a continuous emissive screen. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of 2D view images corresponding to different horizontal viewing angles; rotation speed \omega; barrier geometry parameters. Output: A 3D volumetric image visible from any position surrounding the device (outward viewing) or inside it (inward viewing). Data Structures: The hardware consists of two primary rotating components: 1. Cylindrical Parallax Barrier: A cylinder with vertical slits. Barrier Interval (B): The center-to-center distance between adjacent slits. Aperture Width (A): The width of the open slit. Height (H): Vertical extent of the barrier. 2. LED Array: A 1D linear array of LEDs. LED Width (W{LED}): Physical width of each LED emitter. Position: Located at a fixed radial distance D from the cylinder axis, inside the barrier (for outward viewing) or outside (for inward viewing). Numbered Steps: 1. Synchronization Setup: The LED array and the cylindrical parallax barrier rotate together at a constant angular velocity \omega. In the standard "outward viewing" configuration, the barrier is outer and LEDs are inner. In the "inward viewing" variant, the viewer is inside the cylinder, barriers are inner, LEDs are outer, and both rotate together. 2. Viewpoint Mapping: The 360° horizontal field of view is divided into N discrete viewing zones (views). For a prototype, N > 70. Each zone corresponds to a specific angular interval \Delta \theta < 1^\circ. 3. Image Generation: For each rotation angle \theta(t), the system determines which LED in the 1D array is aligned with which slit in the barrier. The LED array displays the 2D image slice corresponding to the viewer's current angular position relative to the barrier slits. 4. Light Ray Scanning: As the assembly rotates, the relative motion between the slits and the LEDs scans light rays across the horizontal plane. This scanning reproduces multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. 5. Temporal Integration: The persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D slices projected through the moving slits into a continuous 3D volume. The refresh rate must be sufficient to maintain image stability. Formulas: Angular Parallax Interval: \Delta \theta = \frac{360^\circ}{N}, where N is the number of views. Pixel Viewing Angle: The source specifies a pixel viewing angle of 60^\circ divided into over 70 views. This implies the optical design ensures each LED pixel contributes to a specific angular sector. Synchronization Condition: The frame update rate f{frame} and rotation speed \omega must satisfy the condition that the image content updates in phase with the barrier slits passing the LEDs. If the barrier has M slits, the system may update frames or sub-images as slits align with LEDs. Parameters (Prototype Values): Diameter: 200 mm. Height: 256 mm. Resolution: 1254 circumferential pixels, 256 vertical pixels. Refresh Rate: 30 Hz. Views: Over 70 views. Key Design Parameters: Barrier interval (B), aperture width (A), LED width (W{LED}), and distance between LEDs and barriers (D). Pitfalls: Misalignment: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. Misalignment results in Z-depth distortion. Physical Limits: The number of LEDs is physically limited by the 1D array size; rotation is required to cover 360°. Viewing Zone Accuracy: Each viewing location (zone) must receive the appropriate view corresponding to the viewer's location. Incorrect mapping causes crosstalk or incorrect depth perception. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. name: Dynamic Projection Mapping for Rotating Volumetric Display
head: External Tracking of Rotating Objects, Handheld Volumetric Display Using Dynamic Projection Mapping
body: This method renders layered volumetric images by projecting optical patterns onto the surface of a manually rotated object composed of fan-shaped disks, using external high-speed cameras for tracking and a high-speed projector for rendering. It enables users to freely move and rotate the physical display while maintaining a stable perceived image, distinguishing itself from spiral swept-volume approaches by providing discrete physical depth planes, albeit with lower depth resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Target images for each layer (Ti), projector calibration matrix (P), real-time pose data of the rotating object (position, orientation, rotation angle \alpha). Outputs: Projected image frames on the rotating fan blades. Data Structures: Rotating Object: A stack of l disks. Each disk has n=3 fan-shaped blades. Blade radius: 50 mm. Blade thickness: 3 mm. Interval between adjacent disks: 10 mm. Angular offset between disks: 360^\circ / (3 \times l). Tracking Markers: Three retroreflective markers attached to the frontmost disk: 1. One at the geometric center. 2. Two along the bisector of the central angle of two blades, at distances 47 mm (outer) and 23.5 mm (inner) from the center. Numbered Steps: 1. Tracking: Use external high-speed cameras (e.g., OptiTrack PrimeX 13W1) to detect the marker positions. Calculate the object's model matrix M and the rotation angle \alpha [°] around the axis of rotation using the tracking API (e.g., OptiTrack Motive). 2. Layer Rotation: For each layer i (where i=1 is the frontmost layer) in an assembly with l layers, rotate the target image Ti by an angular offset of \frac{360(i-1)}{3 \times l} [°] relative to the frontmost layer. 3. Rotation Compensation: Counteract the physical rotation of the object by rotating the resulting image by -\alpha [°] so that the perceived orientation remains constant. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Calculate the homogeneous coordinates pp on the projector's frame for a point pr on the rotating object using the projector matrix P and the inverse model matrix M^{-1}: pp = P M^{-1} pr 5. Projection Delay Compensation: Measure the average projection delay da [ms] (typically ~12.5 ms). Calculate the predicted projection deviation \Delta ap [°] based on the current rotational speed s [RPM]: \Delta ap = \frac{360 \times da}{s \times 60000} Apply this angular offset to the projected pattern to align the image with the physical blade position at the time of light emission. 6. Rendering: Render the transformed and compensated image onto the projector frame and project it onto the rotating blades. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(targetimages, projectormatrix, modelmatrix, rotationangle, rotationalspeed, avgdelayms): """ Renders the projection frame for a rotating volumetric display. Args: targetimages: List of images for each layer, indexed 0 to l-1. projectormatrix: 4x4 calibration matrix P. modelmatrix: 4x4 object model matrix M. rotationangle: Current rotation angle alpha in degrees. rotationalspeed: Rotational speed s in RPM. avgdelayms: Average measured projection delay da in ms. Returns: projectedframe: The image to be sent to the projector. """ numlayers = len(targetimages) numblades = 3 projectedframe = None for i in range(numlayers): Ti = targetimages[i] layerindex1 = i + 1 layeroffsetdeg = (360 (layerindex1 - 1)) / (numblades numlayers) # Standard image rotation by layeroffsetdeg Tirotated = applyrotation(Ti, layeroffsetdeg) # Counteract physical rotation by -alpha Ticompensated = applyrotation(Tirotated, -rotationangle) # Predict projection deviation from average delay deltaapdeg = (360 avgdelayms) / (rotationalspeed 60000) # Apply delay compensation Tifinal = applyrotation(Ticompensated, deltaapdeg) # Standard compositing of layer images onto the projection buffer if projectedframe is None: projectedframe = Tifinal else: projectedframe = compositeimages(projectedframe, Tifinal) return projectedframe Parameters: Number of blades per disk: 3. Blade radius: 50 mm. Blade thickness: 3 mm. Interval between adjacent disks: 10 mm. Marker distance from center (outer): 47 mm. Marker distance from center (inner): 23.5 mm. Average projection delay: 12.5 ms (SD 1.30 ms) at 600–1200 RPM. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deceleration: Because the rotor is manually driven, contact with external objects causes rapid deceleration and stopping, requiring robust tracking updates. Precision: The system achieves a mean apparent projection delay of 0.147 ms (SD 1.02 ms) after compensation, compared to 12.5 ms before. Failure to compensate for delay results in visible misalignment. Depth Resolution: The discrete physical planes result in lower depth resolution compared to continuous swept-volume methods. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Dependent on camera frame rate, tracking API latency, and projector refresh rate. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Measured Performance: Average projection delay of 12.5 ms (SD 1.30 ms) was measured at rotational speeds between 600 and 1200 RPM. After compensation, the mean apparent projection delay was 0.147 ms (SD 1.02 ms, n=31). Hardware: Implemented with three high-speed cameras (PrimeX 13W1), Intel Core i7-13700KF CPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX3080 GPU, and a high-speed projector (DynaFlash2). Strengths: Allows users to freely move and rotate the object; no embedded rotation mechanism or light-emitting elements in the object. Limitations: Lower depth resolution compared to spiral swept-volume approaches. Manual rotation requires user supervision and can stop abruptly. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Mobile Volu-Me: Handheld Volumetric Display Using Dynamic Projection Mapping onto Rotating Fans". History: It builds on dynamic projection mapping technology, applying it to a handheld, manually rotated fan structure to enable portable volumetric displays. Usage: Used in prototypes with 3D-printed PLA fan assemblies (3-layer and 5-layer configurations) for user studies on perceived quality and depth representation. Uses mirrors to sweep a light sheet, offering continuous depth but requiring complex scanning mechanics. Separates the drawing space from the viewing space, allowing interaction without occlusion. Uses holography for high-resolution volumetric displays. Uses lenticular lenses to direct views to different angles. Traps particles in air using light to create the volume. Calculates holograms for volumetric display. Uses quantum dots for emission. Uses chromatic dispersion to create depth. Uses materials that emit light in 3D. Sweeps a screen continuously, offering continuous depth but potentially lower resolution per plane. name: Oscillating Diffuser Volumetric Display
head: Voxon volumetric display, moving projection surface display, oscillating diffuser display
body: An oscillating diffuser volumetric display is a 360-degree volumetric display that uses a vertically oscillating diffuser screen synchronized with a projection system to create a full volumetric object via retinal persistence. It is distinguished from rotational swept-screen systems by its linear vertical motion rather than rotation, and from holographic defuser displays by its reliance on simple diffusive scattering rather than light-field generation for occlusion. While it allows for multi-user viewing from various angles, it is limited to "ghosted content" because the large field of view prevents true occlusion between different parts of the image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D virtual scene or animation; a synchronization signal from the diffuser actuator or projector. Output: A projected 2D image stream on the oscillating diffuser, perceived by the viewer as a 3D volume. Data Structures: Frame Buffer: A standard 24-bit RGB image. In specific implementations (e.g., FlexiVol), multiple binary slices are packed into this single frame. Synchronization Signal: A periodic signal (e.g., sine wave) driving the actuator, sampled to determine phase. Steps: 1. Oscillation: A diffuser screen is driven to oscillate vertically at a high frequency. The frequency is chosen such that the human eye cannot perceive the motion of the screen itself, resulting in the screen appearing generally transparent. 2. Synchronization: The projection system updates its image synchronously with the diffuser's position. Synchronization can be achieved by: Using the actuator signal to trigger the renderer: The renderer samples the actuation signal phase before each frame, extrapolates the diffuser position for the upcoming slices, renders the content, and sends it. Using the projector as the master clock: The actuator is driven at the same frequency as the projector frame rate, requiring drift correction. 3. Projection: The projector displays 2D slices onto the moving diffuser. As the diffuser moves, the persistence of vision blends these discrete slices into a continuous 3D volume. 4. Perception: The viewer perceives a floating 3D object. Because the diffuser scatters light in a large field of view, multiple viewers can see the image from different angles. Parameters: Oscillation Frequency: High enough to prevent flicker and screen visibility. Not given in the sources. Frame Rate: Must match the oscillation frequency or be an integer multiple. Pitfalls: Occlusion: True volumetric occlusion is not possible because the image is diffused over a large field of view. The display is limited to "ghosted content" where objects do not block each other. Synchronization Drift: If the actuator and projector are not perfectly phase-locked, drift occurs, causing Z-depth distortion or blurring. A rendering method for a swept volumetric display using an elastic diffuser. It differs from standard implementations by packing multiple binary slices into a single color frame to increase data throughput or simplify transmission. Definition: A virtual scene is sliced along planes, and these slices are projected at high speed onto the oscillating diffuser. Steps: 1. Slice the virtual scene along planes. 2. Combine several slices into a single color image. 3. Send the combined color image to the projector via HDMI or Display Port. 4. Project the slices at high speed onto the oscillating diffuser. Parameters: Number of slices packed per frame: 24. Color depth per slice: Binary (1-bit per channel implied by 24 slices packed into 24-bit RGB). Layout: A regular 24-bit RGB image where 24 binary slices are packed. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of slices rendered per frame. Synchronization overhead depends on the sampling rate of the actuator signal. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only requires storing the current frame buffer and scene data. Performance: Efficient for displaying animated objects or figures. The high oscillating frequency precludes the diffuser from being seen, leading to general transparency. Strengths: 360-degree viewing; multi-user capability; simple optical setup compared to holographic methods. Limitations: No true occlusion between objects; limited to "ghosted content". When to use: When multi-user 360-degree visibility is required and true occlusion is not critical. When not to use: When true volumetric occlusion is required. The concept was developed to allow efficient 360-degree display of volumetric objects, particularly for animated figures, enabling group viewing. The commercial product Voxon is a notable example of this technology. Research by Jones et al. proposed using a holographic rotating diffuser to address the occlusion limitation, generating 288 images on a 360° horizontal field of view. More recent research has explored elastic diffusers (e.g., elastane, latex, silicone) to improve mechanical and optical properties. name: Radial Multiview Three-Dimensional Display
head: Perspecta display, Theta Parallax Only (TPO) display, circular display
body: The Radial Multiview Three-Dimensional Display creates opaque 3D imagery by projecting a sequence of 2D views onto a rotating optical diffuser screen, rather than volumetric slices. Unlike prior art omnidirectional volumetric displays that produce transparent imagery due to superimposition, this method uses an exit pupil with a limited horizontal viewing angle to render opaque features within specific viewing zones. It builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection by defining the content as angular views rather than spatial slices. Inputs: A 3D scene dataset rendered as a sequence of 2D images corresponding to distinct angular sectors (viewing zones) around the scene. Outputs: A perceived 3D volume with opaque features visible from specific horizontal angles. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a sequence of N 2D images. In the standard implementation, N=198, corresponding to 1-degree increments over 360 degrees. Each image has a resolution of 768 \times 768 pixels. Hardware Layout: 1. A stationary Digital Micromirror Device (DMD) projector (8). 2. A rotating assembly ("cake pan" 5) containing: Relay mirrors (6, 7). An isotropic diffuser screen (4). Optionally, a Fresnel lens (2). 3. A clear protective dome (22). Steps: 1. Scene Rendering: Generate a sequence of 2D images by rendering the 3D scene from an inward-facing camera or algorithm located on a circular track around the scene. Each image corresponds to a specific viewing zone. 2. Projection: The stationary DMD projector illuminates the relay mirrors. 3. Rotation: The cake pan rotates the relay mirrors, diffuser, and Fresnel lens together at a speed of 600–1000 rpm. 4. Sweeping: The relay mirrors direct the projected 2D images onto the rotating diffuser screen. As the screen rotates, the images sweep through space. 5. Temporal Integration: The human eye's persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D views into a unified 3D scene. 6. Viewing: The user perceives opaque 3D imagery within the exit pupil's limited horizontal viewing angle. Pitfalls: Transparency vs. Opacity: Prior art displays with omnidirectional diffusers cannot render opaque features because light from a voxel enters the eye from multiple angles simultaneously. This method avoids this by restricting the horizontal viewing angle. Synchronization: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. Misalignment results in Z-depth distortion [8515-multi-planar-volumetric-3d-display.md]. Rotation Speed: 600–1000 rpm. Resolution: 198 radially disposed views, with 768x768 pixels per view. Parallax: Full parallax is generated, but opacity is restricted to specific viewing zones defined by the exit pupil. Strengths: Creates high-resolution, opaque 3D imagery with full parallax, overcoming the transparency limitation of omnidirectional diffusers. Limitations: Requires precise synchronization between the stationary projector and the rotating screen [8515-multi-planar-volumetric-3d-display.md]. The Perspecta display is described in US Pat. No. 6,554,430. The present application (US 7,277,226 B2) claims priority to US provisional application 60/537,116, filed Jan. 16, 2004. It was developed by Actuality Systems, Inc.. name: Viewpoint-surrounding Hemisphere System
head: Holographic tabletop system, Tabletop display using space-division, Time-division tabletop display
body: The Viewpoint-surrounding Hemisphere System is a tabletop volumetric display method where viewpoints are created above a view volume in which virtual objects are formed. It is based on multi-view technology composed of multiple projection optics and can be implemented using space-division or time-division techniques. It differs from its siblings by specifically targeting the tabletop form factor with a hemispherical or conical screen geometry that directs light upward to intersect above the table surface, enabling 360-degree viewing without crosstalk. The method generates a 3D view volume above a tabletop by projecting elemental images onto a rotating or static screen geometry. There are four primary implementation variants described in the literature: Space-Division (fVisiOn), Time-Division (Takaki and Uchida), Time-Division (Kim et al.), and Holographic (Lim et al.). Inputs: 3D scene data or elemental image arrays; rotation speed (for time-division); projector parameters. Outputs: A 3D volumetric image visible from 360 degrees above the tabletop. The source does not specify a universal data structure. Implementation depends on the variant: Space-Division: An array of elemental images, one for each projector. Time-Division: A sequence of elemental images synchronized with rotation. Holographic: Holographic data (phase/amplitude) for the SLM. 1. Screen Setup: Position an anisotropic diffusing screen in the shape of a cone directly beneath the tabletop. 2. Projector Placement: Arrange N projectors evenly spaced along the circumference beneath the screen. The source specifies N=288 with a spacing interval of 1.25^\circ. 3. Projection: Project 2D elemental images onto the conic screen from each projector. 4. Optical Convergence: The conical screen provides a wide diffusing angle vertically and a narrow horizontal diffusing angle (approximately 0.4^\circ) to enable 360-degree viewpoints without crosstalk. 5. View Volume Formation: The optical axes of each projector intersect above the tabletop, forming a view volume observable from 360 degrees. 1. Setup: Position a high-speed projector along the table’s central axis. 2. Optics: Use a rotating decentered Fresnel lens. 3. Light Redirection: The decentered lens redirects light from each elemental image off-axis to converge at a point on the circumference above the tabletop. 4. Synchronization: The decentered lens rotates around the central axis. The high-speed projector synchronizes with the rotation. 5. Viewpoint Generation: This synchronization generates 800 viewpoints. 1. Setup: Use an inclined and off-axis anisotropic diffusing screen. 2. Projection: Project elemental images onto the rotating screen in the normal direction using folded high-speed projector optics. 3. Overlap: Lights emanating from each elemental image on the screen overlap each other above the tabletop. 4. View Volume: The overlap creates a view volume in the region above the table. 1. SLM: Use a high-speed spatial light modulator (SLM) to reconstruct holographic images. 2. Scanning: Employ rotation scanning optics and parabolic mirrors to create a 360-degree perspective. 3. Focusing: Use aspheric lenses or freeform mirror-based reflective optics to focus light waves. 4. Effect: This provides natural 3D images with accommodation effects at each viewpoint. Space-Division: Number of projectors: 288. Spacing interval: 1.25^\circ. Horizontal diffusing angle: \approx 0.4^\circ. Time-Division (Takaki/Uchida): Number of viewpoints: 800. Space-Division: Requires numerous projection optics, leading to alignment challenges. Time-Division: Suffers from mechanical vibrations, lack of optical brightness, and flickering problems. Space-Division: High hardware complexity (288 projectors in the cited example). Alignment is difficult. No flickering or mechanical vibration issues. Time-Division: Lower hardware count (single projector in cited examples). Issues include mechanical vibration, reduced brightness, and flickering. Holographic: Offers accommodation effects. Complexity lies in high-speed SLM and scanning optics. The system is described in the context of tabletop volumetric displays suitable for applications where viewpoints are created above the view volume. Representative systems include "fVisiOn" by Yoshida et al., time-division displays by Takaki and Uchida and Kim et al., and holographic systems by Lim et al. and Heo et al..
