name: Elastic Diffuser Swept Volumetric Display
head: Elastic Strip Diffuser Array, FlexiVol, FlexiVol Swept Volumetric Display with Elastic Diffuser
body: The Elastic Diffuser Swept Volumetric Display (FlexiVol) is a reach-through volumetric display that replaces the rigid optical diffuser of a planar swept-screen system with an array of elastic strips. This modification allows users to physically insert their hands into the display volume to interact with true-3D content without distorting the entire display or risking injury. It sets itself apart from rigid swept displays by enabling direct haptic interaction and from membrane-based displays by isolating deformation to individual strips, thereby preventing global volume distortion and excessive resistive forces. The system builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection but replaces the rigid screen with a deformable elastic strip array and integrates a hand-tracking pipeline for interaction. Inputs: User hand position (from cameras), virtual scene geometry, actuation signal phase. Outputs: Projected light pattern on the diffuser, rendered 3D hand model within the volume. 1. Diffuser Strip Array Geometry: Array of parallel strips. Strip Dimensions: Width w = 20 mm, Length L = 200 mm. Material: Elastic bands (selected for best compromise of mechanical, optical, and oscillatory properties among tested materials: projection screens, elastane, latex, silicone). Mounting: Cured or attached to a rigid acrylic sheet with a spacer defining the rest thickness. Elasticity: Maximum elongation \Delta L{max} = 50 mm (from rest length 185 mm to 235 mm). This limit approximates finger push depth on a 190 \times 190 \times 80 mm volume and prevents irreversible plastic deformation. 2. Hand Tracking Coordinates Source: Two webcams capturing the interaction space. Processing: Video streams processed via MediaPipe for keypoint detection. Transformation: 2D image coordinates triangulated and transformed into the volumetric display's 3D coordinate system. Transmission: Coordinates sent via UDP to the display rendering software. 3. Projected Image Buffer Format: 24-bit RGB image. Content Packing: Multiple temporal slices are combined into a single spatial frame. Example: 24 slices with binary color encoding are packed into one 24-bit RGB frame. Interface: HDMI or Display Port. 1. Fabric Preparation: Laser-cut elastic materials into 200 \times 20 mm strips along the elastic dimension. For curable materials (e.g., silicone), cure sheets of 0.8 mm thickness on an acrylic base with a spacer. 2. Hand Tracking & Triangulation: Capture video from two webcams. Process streams using MediaPipe to extract hand keypoints. Triangulate 3D hand position from the two camera views. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the triangulated hand coordinates from the camera frame to the volumetric display's world coordinate system. 4. Synchronization Sampling: Sample the actuation signal phase (e.g., from a 15 Hz sinusoidal driver) at the start of each projector frame to extrapolate the diffuser's instantaneous position. 5. Slice Rendering: Render the virtual scene slices corresponding to the diffuser's current position. If using binary color projection, reduce color information to binary patterns to multiply effective frame rate. 6. Image Packing: Pack the rendered slices into a single 24-bit RGB image. For example, pack 24 binary slices into the R, G, and B channels. 7. Projection: Send the packed image to the high-frame-rate projector (e.g., Voxon VX1). 8. Hand Visualization: Render the user's hand as a 3D object within the volume, spatially aligned with the virtual content using the transformed coordinates. 9. Interaction Processing: Navigation: Detect alternate swiping gestures on oscillating bands. If 4 index/middle finger switches are detected, move the camera/environment based on hand orientation. Wrap environment at limits for infinite exploration. Touch/Selection: Detect contact between hand and virtual objects. Trigger events (e.g., bells ringing, balloons popping). Rotation: Detect grasp (thumb + index/middle). Rotate object based on hand orientation change. Deformation: Detect push on deformable objects. Apply deformation up to a threshold, then split object (e.g., mushrooms popping). Avoidance/Capture: For dynamic objects (e.g., fish), calculate distance to hand. Move object away faster as distance decreases. If touched and hand stops, trigger interaction animation. Projector Frame Rate Requirement The required projector operating frequency f{proj} is determined by the number of slices N{slices} and the sweep frame rate f{sweep}: f{proj} = N{slices} \times f{sweep} Example: 100 slices at 30 Hz sweep requires 3000 Hz projector operation. Effective Frame Rate with Binary Color When using binary pattern multiplication, the effective frame rate f{eff} is: f{eff} = f{proj} \times N{bitplanes} Example: Voxon VX1 at 120 Hz with 24-bit color projects binary patterns at 2880 Hz (implying N{bitplanes} logic or specific time-multiplexing scheme described in source). Note: The source states "projects binary patterns at 2880 Hz" for a 120 Hz base with 24-bit color, which implies a specific multiplexing factor or that the 2880 Hz is the result of the binary projection strategy on the hardware limit. The source explicitly says: "For example, the Voxon VX1 projects 192 slices at 15 Hz (2880 Hz)... When operating at 120 Hz with 24-bit color depth, it projects binary patterns at 2880 Hz". This suggests the hardware limit or the binary projection constraint caps the effective slice rate. Strip Deformation Approximation The deformation of a single strip can be approximated by a sinusoid or parabola, unlike 2D membrane deformation which is complex and global. Strip Width: 20 mm. Chosen to match finger width. Smaller strips cause optical discontinuities; larger strips behave like membranes. Rest Length: 185 mm. Max Elongation: 50 mm (Total length 235 mm). Display Volume: 190 \times 190 \times 80 mm. Projector: Voxon VX1 (DLP). Actuation Signal: 15 Hz sinusoidal. Projector VSync: 120 Hz. Slices: 192 slices at 15 Hz sweep (2880 Hz effective). Resolution: 980x720 px (at 15 Hz) or 1280x800 px (at 120 Hz binary). Optical Discontinuities: Using strips narrower than 20 mm creates visible gaps or artifacts between strips. Plastic Deformation: Exceeding the 50 mm elongation limit causes irreversible damage to the elastic material. Synchronization Drift: Even with matched frequencies, drift occurs. The rendering system must sample the actuation signal phase every frame to extrapolate position. Force Feedback: Membranes exert high anisotropic forces on fingers; strips mitigate this but still require careful material selection to avoid discomfort. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mainloop(): # Initialization diffuser = ElasticStripArray(width=20.0, length=200.0, maxelongation=50.0) projector = DLPProjector(model="VoxonVX1", resolution=(1280, 800)) handtracker = MediaPipeHandTracker(cameracount=2) scene = VirtualScene() # Synchronization setup actuationsignal = getactuationsignal() # 15 Hz sinusoid vsyncfreq = 120.0 # Hz while True: # 1. Hand Tracking handkeypoints = handtracker.getkeypoints() if handkeypoints is not None: # Triangulate and transform to display coordinates handpos3d = triangulateandtransform(handkeypoints) else: handpos3d = None # 2. Synchronization # Sample actuation signal phase to determine diffuser position phase = actuationsignal.getphase() diffuserposition = extrapolatediffuserposition(phase) # 3. Interaction Logic interactionevents = [] if handpos3d is not None: # Navigation: Alternate swiping detection if detectalternateswipe(handkeypoints): navdelta = calculateorientationchange(handkeypoints) scene.navigate(navdelta) # Touch/Selection for obj in scene.objects: if istouching(handpos3d, obj): triggerevent(obj, "touch") # Rotation if isgrasping(handkeypoints): rotationdelta = calculategrasprotation(handkeypoints) scene.rotateactiveobject(rotationdelta) # Deformation for obj in scene.deformableobjects: if ispushing(handpos3d, obj): deformation = applypush(handpos3d, obj) if deformation > threshold: obj.split() # Dynamic Object Interaction (Fish) for fish in scene.fish: dist = distance(handpos3d, fish.pos) if dist < avoidanceradius: fish.avoid(handpos3d, dist) elif istouching(handpos3d, fish) and handisstill(handkeypoints): fish.interact() # 4. Rendering # Render slices based on diffuser position slices = scene.renderslices(diffuserposition) # Pack slices into binary color image # Example: 24 slices packed into 24-bit RGB packedimage = packslicesintorgb(slices, numslices=24) # 5. Projection projector.display(packedimage) # 6. Hand Visualization if handpos3d is not None: renderhandmodel(handpos3d) Uses holographic principles for light field generation, differing from the swept-scan mechanical approach. Link Uses electron beams on phosphor screens, lacking the direct reach-through interaction of elastic diffusers. Link A specific type of volumetric display, distinct in its optical path and interaction model. Link Focuses on projection mapping techniques for rotating screens, potentially using rigid screens. Link Uses oscillation instead of rotation, but may use rigid diffusers. Link Uses multiple views rather than temporal slicing on a single screen. Link Uses a hemisphere screen, differing in form factor and interaction space. Link The base parent method, using a non-deformable screen. Link Time Complexity: Rendering is linear with the number of slices N{slices}. Hand tracking is constant time per frame but requires significant CPU/GPU for MediaPipe processing. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of slices and image resolution. Performance: The Voxon VX1 projector can handle up to 2880 Hz effective frame rate with binary color projection. Strengths: Enables direct reach-through interaction; isolates deformation to local areas; avoids global volume distortion; safe for users. Limitations: Optical discontinuities between strips; limited deformation range (50 mm); requires precise synchronization; complex interaction logic for dynamic objects. When to Use: Applications requiring direct physical interaction with 3D content, such as education, training, or playful exploration. When Not to Use: Applications requiring high optical uniformity without strip artifacts, or where large-scale deformation of the display volume is needed. The Elastic Diffuser Swept Volumetric Display, known as FlexiVol, was introduced to address the lack of direct interaction in traditional swept volumetric displays, which use rigid diffusers. The concept was developed by researchers presenting at CHI EA '26 in Barcelona, Spain. The work builds on previous swept volumetric display technologies, replacing the rigid screen with an array of elastic strips to enable "come-and-interact" scenarios. The design choice of strips over membranes was driven by the need to prevent global volume distortion and excessive resistive forces on the user's fingers. name: Rotating Rigid Screen with Projector
head: Rotational Swept-Screen Projection with Projector
body: This method renders volumetric images by rotating a rigid reflective or transmissive screen around a central axis while a projector synchronously updates the 2D image content to match the rotation angle. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like the Holographic Defuser Light Field Display and Cathode Ray Volumetric Display by using a continuous rotational sweep rather than linear reciprocating motion or electron beam deflection, allowing for higher frame rates and larger display scales. The core mechanism involves a screen (reflective, transmissive, or emissive) rotating around a central axis. A projection system (LED array, laser, or projector) updates the image on the screen synchronously with the rotation angle. 1. Coordinate Mapping: The 3D world coordinates of a voxel are mapped to 2D screen coordinates and a specific frame index corresponding to the rotation angle. 2. Temporal Integration: The screen speed and frame rate are chosen such that the persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. 3. Synchronization: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. Misalignment between screen position and projected frame index results in Z-depth distortion [8515-multi-planar-volumetric-3d-display.md]. A 2D full-color LED array rotational display renders volumetric images by rotating a 2D LED panel array around a central axis and synchronously updating the panel content to match the rotation angle. It differs from laser-based swept-screen systems by generating voxels directly on an emissive surface without requiring external synchronization with electron beams or lasers. See 2D Full-Color LED Array Rotational Display. A multi-planar volumetric 3D display projects a sequence of 2D image patterns onto a screen moving along the Z-axis to form a stack of spatial image planes, creating a true 3D image viewable without glasses. Unlike conventional 2D screens that rely on psychological depth cues, this method places voxels at their physical spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally to provide both physiological and psychological depth cues. Builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM), 2D Full-Color LED Array Rotational Display, and Oscillating Swept Volume Display by utilizing linear or reciprocating screen motion rather than rotational sweep. See Multi-planar volumetric 3D display. Definition: A larger volumetric display variant using a rotating screen resembling a drill bit with ramps and drop-offs, and projectors positioned above, allowing for higher frame rates and larger projections. Steps: 1. Use a helical slicing algorithm instead of a linear slicing algorithm to process the 3D form. 2. Align three projectors (red, green, blue) into the same space. 3. Perform keystone calibration to align the projectors. Pitfalls: 1. A dead spot appears in the middle of the image where the surface is not moving fast enough to maintain the illusion, appearing as a vortex-like hole. 2. Keystone calibration complexity can result in pink fringing around icons. Comparison: The rotating display delivers higher frame rates compared to the reciprocating display, but is harder to scale up due to the difficulty of moving the glass fast enough for a solid illusion in larger sizes. Originating from work by Voxon Photonics and the Silverton team, this approach was developed to address the scaling limitations of reciprocating "glass shaker" volumetric displays. The rotating design allows for larger physical dimensions and higher frame rates, though it introduces complexities in multi-projector alignment and helical slicing. Voxon hologram volumetric display (2019), https://newatlas.com/vr/voxon-photonics-3d-hologram-volumetric-displays/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 2D Full-Color LED Array Rotational Display
head: LED Array Volumetric Display, Multivox Volumetric Display System, Rotational Volumetric Display
body: A 2D full-color LED array rotational display renders volumetric images by rotating a 2D LED panel array around a central axis and synchronously updating the panel content to match the rotation angle. It differs from laser-based swept-screen systems by generating voxels directly on an emissive surface without requiring external synchronization with electron beams or lasers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel buffer (volume data) and a target rotation speed. Output: A 3D volumetric image perceived by the human eye via persistence of vision. Data Structures: Voxel Buffer: A 3D array stored in shared memory, written by a client process and read by a driver process. LED Panel State: The current 2D image frame to be displayed on the HUB75 panels. Parameters: Images per rotation: 512 frames per full revolution. Rotation Speed: Several hundred RPM. Panel Type: HUB75 LED panels. Steps: 1. Initialization: Configure the GPIO memory-mapped access base address (BCMBASE) for the specific hardware (e.g., Raspberry Pi 4). Define GPIO mappings and panel layout in the driver configuration file. 2. Synchronization Setup: Establish a sync signal using a single GPIO pin connected to a photodiode or similar sensor. The signal is high for 180° of rotation and low for the other 180°. 3. Frame Calculation: For each rotation, calculate the 512 required 2D slices. Extract the 2D cross-section of the voxel buffer corresponding to the current rotation angle. 4. Buffer Update: Write the calculated 2D frame data into the shared memory voxel buffer. 5. Scanout: The driver reads the voxel buffer and drives the HUB75 LED panels in sync with the rotation angle detected by the sync signal. 6. Persistence: The rapid rotation and frame updates blend the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. BCMBASE = None # Base address for memory-mapped GPIO access FRAMESPERROTATION = 512 # SYNCPIN = None # GPIO pin for photodiode sync def initgpio(): # Memory-map GPIO access using BCMBASE # Configure SYNCPIN as input pass def readsync(): # Read digital state of SYNCPIN # Returns True for high (180°), False for low (180°) return True # def extractslice(buffer, k): # Compute angle theta = (k / FRAMESPERROTATION) 2 pi # Extract 2D cross-section of buffer at theta # Return 2D pixel array for HUB75 panels return [] def drivepanels(image): # Write image data to HUB75 panels # Supports ABCDE addressing or ABC shift register addressing pass def main(): initgpio() k = 0 while True: # Driver scans voxel buffer in sync with rotation slicedata = extractslice(voxelbuffer, k) drivepanels(slicedata) k = (k + 1) % FRAMESPERROTATION # Timing is managed by hardware sync signal and rotation speed Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Compatibility: The GPIO memory-mapped access assumes a Raspberry Pi 4. Using different Pi models requires changing BCMBASE and is untested. Synchronization: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. The photodiode sync signal must be correctly wired to distinguish the 180° high and low phases. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of voxels and frames per rotation. Memory complexity is proportional to the voxel buffer size. Performance: Requires high-speed GPIO updates and precise timing. The system runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 embedded in the spinning hardware. Strengths: Self-contained system; no external synchronization devices needed; full-color output. Limitations: Limited to the resolution of the LED panels; rotation speed limits the maximum volume size and frame rate; hardware-specific GPIO code. The concept of using rotating 2D full-color LED arrays for volumetric display was proposed by Xie et al. in 2009. This method was later categorized as a "free-space" volumetric display by Sumalley et al. in 2018. A hardware implementation uses two HUB75 LED panels controlled by a Raspberry Pi 4. name: Spinning Volumetric Display Control Pipeline
head: LED Volumetric Display Serial Protocol, Volumetric Pattern Encoding
body: This pipeline converts text-based volumetric patterns into polar coordinates, packs them into a serial data stream, and transmits them to an Arduino to drive a spinning 3D LED volumetric display. It bridges the gap between abstract 3D shape definitions and the hardware-specific timing requirements of a rotating rigid screen with a 2D full-color LED array [7246-2d-full-color-led-array-rotational-display]. Unlike real-time ray-casting or ray-marching methods, this is a pre-computed, static-pattern encoding scheme optimized for low-bandwidth serial transmission to embedded controllers. Inputs: 1. Configuration File: Text file containing volslices, vollayers, volradius, displaywipe, serialport, and baudrate. 2. Pattern File: Text file defining the 3D shape. Supports three modes: TOPDOWN: Cartesian grid iteration. FRONTBACK: Cartesian grid iteration with line-break markers. OUTSIDEIN: Direct polar coordinate iteration. Active voxels are marked with '0'. In FRONTBACK mode, 'E' marks a line break. Outputs: A raw binary serial stream sent to the Arduino via the specified serial port. Configuration Globals: volslices: int. Number of angular divisions. vollayers: int. Number of vertical layers. volradius: int. Maximum radial extent (excluding center). displaywipe: uint8t. Initial wipe command. serialport: char[32]. Port identifier (e.g., "/dev/ttyUSB0"). baudrate: int. Communication speed. Coordinate Objects: CartPnt: Stores height (int), x (int), y (int). PolPnt: Stores height (int), slice (int), radius (int), deg (int). Serial Data Buffer: serialData: 2D array of uint16t with dimensions [360][vollayers]. Indexed as serialData[slice][height]. Each uint16t acts as a bitmask representing active LEDs at a specific slice and height. 1. Parse Configuration: Read config.txt to initialize global variables volslices, vollayers, volradius, displaywipe, serialport, and baudrate. 2. Parse Pattern File: Read the mode string (TOPDOWN, FRONTBACK, or OUTSIDEIN). TOPDOWN/FRONTBACK: Iterate grid coordinates. For FRONTBACK, handle 'E' markers. Read character markers; if '0' and within volradius, create a CartPnt. OUTSIDEIN: Iterate radius, height, and slice indices directly. If marker is '0', create a PolPnt directly. Convert all CartPnt objects to PolPnt objects using the coordinate transformation formulas. 3. Pack Serial Data: Initialize serialData array to zero. For each PolPnt in the pattern: Calculate the radius bitmask: data = 2^(volradius - (radius - 1)). Update the buffer: serialData[polPnt.slice][polPnt.height] |= data. 4. Transmit Data: Open serial port with 8N1 settings, raw mode, no flow control. Send displaywipe (1 byte). Iterate through serialData by slice index i and layer index j. For each serialData[i][j] that is non-zero: Send 2 bytes of data (little-endian uint16t). Send 1 byte of slice index i. Send 1 byte of layer index j. Pause for 1 second every 20 bytes transmitted to prevent buffer overflow or timing issues. Close serial port. Cartesian to Polar Slice: \text{slice} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{atan2}(y, x) \times 180}{\pi} \right\rfloor \times \frac{\text{vol\slices}}{360.0} If \text{slice} < 0, then \text{slice} = \text{slice} + \text{vol\slices}. Cartesian to Polar Radius: \text{radius} = \text{round}\left(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right) Radius Bitmask Encoding: \text{data} = 2^{(\text{vol\radius} - (\text{radius} - 1))} This encodes the radius as a single bit within the 16-bit word. The bit position corresponds to the radial distance from the center. volslices: Number of angular divisions. Determines angular resolution. vollayers: Number of vertical layers. Determines vertical resolution. volradius: Maximum radial extent. Defines the size of the display volume. baudrate: Supported values: 4800, 9600, 14400, 19200, 28800, 38400, 57600, 115200. displaywipe: A single byte command sent at the start to clear the display. Radius Overflow: The radius encoding uses pow(2,...) cast to int. If radius exceeds volradius or is 0, the exponent becomes negative or large, potentially causing overflow or incorrect bitmasks. The code assumes radius is in [1, volradius]. Serial Framing: The transmission uses raw binary writes without framing or checksums. The Arduino expects exact byte sequences: 2 bytes data, 1 byte slice, 1 byte layer per active voxel. Precision: The slice calculation uses floating-point arithmetic for atan2 and division. Integer truncation occurs after multiplication by volslices/360.0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import struct import time import serial volslices = 360 vollayers = 10 volradius = 5 displaywipe = 0x00 serialport = "/dev/ttyUSB0" baudrate = 115200 def parseconfig(configpath): # Read config.txt and set global variables # Implementation details omitted for brevity pass def cartesiantopolar(x, y, height, volslices, volradius): sliceidx = int(math.floor((math.atan2(y, x) 180 / math.pi) (volslices / 360.0))) if sliceidx < 0: sliceidx += volslices radius = int(round(math.sqrt(x2 + y2))) return height, sliceidx, radius def packserialdata(patternpoints, volslices, vollayers, volradius): # Initialize 2D array [360][vollayers] with 0 serialdata = [[0 for in range(vollayers)] for in range(360)] for height, sliceidx, radius in patternpoints: # Clamp radius to valid range [1, volradius] if radius < 1: radius = 1 if radius > volradius: continue # Encode radius into bitmask # data = 2^(volradius - (radius - 1)) exponent = volradius - (radius - 1) data = 1 << exponent # Merge into buffer using bitwise OR serialdata[sliceidx][height] |= data return serialdata def transmitserialdata(serialdata, serialport, baudrate, displaywipe): ser = serial.Serial(serialport, baudrate, bytesize=serial.EIGHTBITS, parity=serial.PARITYNONE, stopbits=serial.STOPBITSONE, timeout=1) # Send display wipe ser.write(bytes([displaywipe])) bytecount = 0 for sliceidx in range(360): for layeridx in range(vollayers): dataval = serialdata[sliceidx][layeridx] if dataval != 0: # Send 2 bytes data (little-endian) ser.write(struct.pack('<H', dataval)) # Send 1 byte slice index ser.write(bytes([sliceidx])) # Send 1 byte layer index ser.write(bytes([layeridx])) bytecount += 4 # Pause every 20 bytes if bytecount % 20 == 0: time.sleep(1) ser.close() def main(): parseconfig("config.txt") # Example pattern points (height, slice, radius) # In reality, these are parsed from a text file patternpoints = [ (0, 0, 1), (1, 10, 2), (2, 20, 3) ] serialdata = packserialdata(patternpoints, volslices, vollayers, volradius) transmitserialdata(serialdata, serialport, baudrate, displaywipe) if name == "main": main() Time Complexity: Parsing is O(N) where N is the number of active voxels. Packing is O(N). Transmission is O(N) but dominated by I/O latency and the 1-second pause every 20 bytes. Memory Complexity: O(\text{vol\slices} \times \text{vol\layers}) for the serialData buffer. For typical values (360 slices, 10 layers), this is 7200 uint16t entries, which is negligible. Performance: The bottleneck is the serial transmission speed and the explicit pauses. At 115200 baud, transmitting 4 bytes takes ~0.35 ms. However, the 1-second pause every 20 bytes (80 bytes of data) dominates the runtime. Strengths: Simple implementation, low hardware requirements (Arduino + shift registers), deterministic output. Limitations: Static patterns only (no dynamic animation without re-transmission), low bandwidth due to serial protocol, no error checking, fixed resolution based on configuration. When to use: For simple, static 3D LED displays where cost and simplicity are prioritized over dynamic content or high resolution. When not to use: For real-time interactive applications, high-resolution displays, or scenes requiring frequent updates. This method originates from an open-source project by YangR13, which provides code for a spinning 3D volumetric display running off an Arduino. The project includes a computer-end interpreter (interpreter.cpp) that converts 3D shapes from text files into byte strings, and an Arduino-end sketch (voldisplay.ino) that reads these values and drives the LEDs via daisy-chained shift registers. The serial communication library (arduino-serial-lib) is based on work by Tod E. Kurt (2006-2013). The method is designed for educational and hobbyist purposes, demonstrating the principles of volumetric display control with minimal hardware. YangR13/voldisplay, https://github.com/YangR13/voldisplay, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-planar volumetric 3D display
head: Moving screen volumetric display, Swept-screen volumetric display, Temporal integration volumetric display
body: A multi-planar volumetric 3D display projects a sequence of 2D image patterns onto a screen moving along the Z-axis to form a stack of spatial image planes, creating a true 3D image viewable without glasses. Unlike conventional 2D screens that rely on psychological depth cues, this method places voxels at their physical spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally to provide both physiological and psychological depth cues. Builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM), 2D Full-Color LED Array Rotational Display, and Oscillating Swept Volume Display by utilizing linear or reciprocating screen motion rather than rotational sweep. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume defined by N 2D image frames (slices) corresponding to specific Z-depths, and a screen sweep frequency f{sweep}. Output: A continuous 3D volumetric image perceived by the human eye. Data Structures: Image Sequence: A list of N 2D frames \{I0, I1,..., I{N-1}\}, where each frame Ik corresponds to the image pattern projected when the screen is at position zk. Screen State: Defined by position z(t) and velocity v(t) along the Z-axis. Steps: 1. Initialize Sweep: The screen begins moving along the Z-axis in a back-and-forth motion at a frequency f{sweep} > 24 Hz. 2. Synchronize Projection: A high-speed 2D image projector updates its output synchronously with the screen's position. 3. Project Frames: During one complete sweep cycle (period T = 1/f{sweep}), the projector displays N distinct 2D image frames. 4. Intercept and Stack: The moving screen intercepts the projected light at different Z-positions. Each frame Ik is projected when the screen is at the corresponding depth zk, forming a stack of spatial image planes. 5. Temporal Integration: Due to persistence of vision and the high sweep frequency, the discrete 2D slices blend into a continuous 3D volume in the viewer's perception. Formulas: Sweep Frequency: f{sweep} > 24 Hz. Frame Rate: The projector must display N frames within T = 1/f{sweep}, requiring a frame rate R{proj} = N \cdot f{sweep}. Z-Position Mapping: For a sweep range [Z{min}, Z{max}], the position zk for frame k (k \in [0, N-1]) is mapped linearly or according to the screen's kinematic profile. Parameters: f{sweep}: Screen sweep frequency. Must be > 24 Hz to avoid flicker and ensure proper temporal integration. N: Number of 2D image frames projected per sweep cycle. Projector Type: High-speed 2D image projector (e.g., DLP) is preferred for high frame rates and quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flicker: If f{sweep} \le 24 Hz, the display may flicker, breaking the 3D illusion. Motion Blur: Excessive screen velocity relative to projector exposure time can cause blurring of the slices. A signal modulation technique that projects variable 1D patterns along the viewing line through the display volume by timing laser pulses. It provides depth context without the occlusion of full 3D shapes, serving as the 3D analog to the 0D dot used on 2D screens. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The system relies on high-speed DLP projection engines to achieve the necessary frame rates. Strengths: Displays voxels physically at their spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally, providing true physiological depth cues. Limitations: Requires precise synchronization between screen motion and projection. Limited by the mechanical speed of the screen and the frame rate of the projector. When to use: When true 3D spatial representation with physiological depth cues is required, and glasses-free viewing is necessary. When not to use: When high resolution is required without mechanical complexity, or when the scene requires static 3D display without motion. The multi-planar volumetric 3D display technique was developed to address the limitations of conventional 2D screens, which lack physical depth cues. It utilizes high-speed DLP projection engines to facilitate the rapid projection of 2D image patterns onto a moving screen. The method was highlighted in research focusing on the design of volumetric 3D displays based on high-speed DLP projection engines. A volumetric 3D display based on a DLP projection engine, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.displa.2012.11.001, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Line Patterns and 2D/3D Projection
head: Line Pattern Volumetric Display, Temporal Laser Line Projection
body: A signal modulation technique that projects variable 1D patterns along the viewing line through the display volume by timing laser pulses. It provides depth context without the occlusion of full 3D shapes, serving as the 3D analog to the 0D dot used on 2D screens. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Time-varying control signals (e.g., from a joystick or distance sensor) and the display's oscillation frequency. Output: A modulated laser beam forming 1D patterns (points, lines, dashed segments) within the volumetric display space. Data Structures: Control Signal: A time-indexed sequence of duty cycle or pulse-width values. Oscillation State: The current phase of the display screen's rotation/oscillation. Steps: 1. Synchronization: Align the laser control signal with the display's oscillation frequency. The phase of the signal relative to the oscillation determines the depth (Z-axis) where the pattern appears. 2. Pattern Generation: Modulate the laser's pulse width or duty cycle over time to create specific 1D shapes. Single Point: A short pulse duration. Continuous Line: A sustained pulse duration covering the desired length. Dashed Line/Segments: Alternating on/off states within the pulse window. 3. Depth Control: Adjust the phase offset of the control signal to move the pattern along the Z-axis. 4. Animation: Play temporal animations (e.g., moving segments) to encode direction or speed along the line. Formulas: Drift Error: The positional drift of the laser dot is a function of the frequency mismatch between the laser controller and the display. In a Voxon VX1 display with an Arduino Nano (16 MHz Timer 1), a default 30 Hz oscillation results in a drift of only 5 mm per minute. Parameters: Oscillation Frequency: Typically 30 Hz. Controller Resolution: 16 MHz timer resolution (e.g., Arduino Nano). Interaction Distance: 30 cm to 2 meters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatelasersignal(oscillationphase, patterntype, length, dashratio): """ Generates the duty cycle for the laser diode based on the current oscillation phase and desired pattern. Args: oscillationphase: Float [0, 1], representing the current position of the screen in its oscillation cycle. patterntype: String {'point', 'line', 'dashed'} length: Float [0, 1], relative length of the line segment. dashratio: Float [0, 1], ratio of 'on' time to total period for dashed lines. Returns: Float: Duty cycle (0.0 to 1.0) for the current sample. """ # Determine the 'on' window for the pattern relative to the phase # The phase maps to the Z-depth. The pattern extends along the line # passing through the volume at that depth. if patterntype == 'point': # Short pulse centered at the target phase pulsewidth = 0.05 # Arbitrary small width for a point center = oscillationphase if abs(oscillationphase - center) < pulsewidth / 2: return 1.0 else: return 0.0 elif patterntype == 'line': # Continuous line of specified length # The line extends along the viewing line through the volume. # In practice, this is a sustained pulse while the screen passes # through the relevant Z-range. return 1.0 # Simplified: Laser is on for the duration of the line's Z-span elif patterntype == 'dashed': # Dashed line with a dot at the pointing position # Modulate duty cycle to create dashes cycle = (oscillationphase 10) % 1.0 # Create repeating cycle if cycle < dashratio: return 1.0 else: return 0.0 return 0.0 def synchronizelaser(displayfreq, controllerfreq): """ Adjusts the controller to minimize drift. """ # Frequency needs to be adjusted only once per display # Default 30 Hz oscillation with 16 MHz timer resolution # yields 5mm/min drift # Not given in the sources: synchronization algorithm details pass Edge Cases: Hand Jittering: Hand jitter is less noticeable at distances of 30 cm to 2 meters. Arm Fatigue: A disadvantage inherited from traditional laser pointers. A visual pattern modification where the laser output is pulsed to create a dashed line with a solid dot at the pointing position, rather than a continuous line or single point. The laser is pulsed at the display's oscillation frequency, but the duty cycle or timing is modulated to produce the dashed appearance, with the solid dot appearing at the specific phase/height selected by the user. This pattern was employed in depth user studies. Strengths: Provides depth context without occlusion; allows for natural interaction (e.g., pinching, rotation) using wearable devices. Limitations: Hand jitter and arm fatigue are disadvantages. Higher-dimensional pointers (spheres, cubes) are considered beyond the scope of current laser pointer implementations. Performance: Drift is minimal (5 mm/min) with standard hardware (Arduino Nano, 30 Hz display). Originated with the PointerVol device, a laser pointer designed for swept volumetric displays. The concept draws an analogy between 2D screens (using 0D dots) and 3D volumes (using 1D line patterns). Future research directions include higher-dimensional pointers (spheres, cubes, arrows) and independent control of multiple pointers for complex 3D rotations. PointerVol: A Laser Pointer for Swept Volumetric Displays, https://doi.org/10.1145/3654777.3676432, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Oscillating Swept Volume Display
head: Oscivox, Undulating Volumetric Display
body: The Oscillating Swept Volume Display is a swept volume display that replaces linear or continuous rotation with an undulating (back-and-forth) motion to reduce mechanical jerk at the sweep endpoints. It builds on Multi-planar volumetric 3D display by projecting 2D image patterns onto a moving screen to form a stack of spatial images along the Z-axis, but uses sinusoidal oscillation instead of linear translation or continuous rotation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel buffer and a hardware synchronization signal (SPINSYNC) from the motion controller. Output: Pixel data sent to an LED matrix or projector, synchronized to the instantaneous angle of the oscillating screen. Data Structures: The voxel buffer is a 3D array of pixelt (8-bit RGB332) with dimensions X=64, Y=64, Z=32. Memory Layout: Row-major. VOXELXSTRIDE = 1 VOXELZSTRIDE = 64 VOXELYSTRIDE = 2048 Index formula: VOXELINDEX(x, y, z) = x + y 2048 + z 64. Total Voxels: 262,144. Double Buffer: The shared memory buffer is sized at 2 262,144 sizeof(pixelt) to allow frame swapping without tearing. Parameters: Pixel Format: RGB332 (8-bit). Red: 3 bits (mask 0xE0), Green: 3 bits (mask 0x1C), Blue: 2 bits (mask 0x03). Conversion macros: R332(p) = (((p) >> 5) & 7) 36 G332(p) = (((p) >> 2) & 7) 36 B332(p) = ((p) & 3) 85. Fixed-Point Precision: REVOLUTIONPRECISION = 20 (bits for frequency/period scaling). ANGLEPRECISION = 10 (bits for angle index). SINCOSPRECISION = 12 (bits for sine/cosine table values). Sine/Cosine Table: 1024 entries (1 << 10). Values are fixed-point integers scaled by 2^{12}. GPIO Mapping (Raspberry Pi BCM2711): RGB Data: Pins 12, 9, 6, 5, 8, 7, 21, 13, 20, 26, 19, 16. Row Select (A-E): Pins 4, 15, 18, 17, 14. Control: RGBBLANK=11, RGBCLOCK=0, RGBSTROBE=3, SPINSYNC=1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Sine/Cosine Table: Iterate i from 0 to 1023. Compute angle a = i \cdot \frac{2\pi}{1023}. Store round(cos(a) 4096) in sincosfixed[i][0] and round(sin(a) 4096) in sincosfixed[i][1]. 2. Initialize Span Offsets (Partial): Compute pitch ef / 64. Set vx = -ef/2, vy = de + \sqrt{bd^2 - ac^2}, vsh = 1/(pitch \cdot 0.8), vsv = 1/(pitch \cdot 0.8). Loop i from 0 to 1023: \theta = i \cdot \frac{2\pi}{1023}. Compute bx = \cos(\theta) \cdot ab - ac. Compute by = \sin(\theta) \cdot ab. Compute ddy = \sqrt{bd^2 - bx^2}. 3. Angle Tracking Loop (Real-time): Read the hardware timer (currenttick) and the sync pin state. On a rising edge of the sync pin: Measure the period: T = \text{current\tick} - \text{sync\prev\tick}. Clamp period: T = \max(2^{10}, T) to prevent division by zero or overflow. Compute revolution frequency: f = \frac{2^{20}}{T}. Update current angle: \theta = (\text{current\tick} - \text{sync\prev\tick}) \cdot f. 4. Projection: Map the current 3D voxel coordinates to 2D screen coordinates based on the instantaneous angle \theta derived from the oscillating motion. Project the corresponding slice onto the LED matrix. Synchronize the image update with the screen's position to ensure temporal integration blends the slices into a continuous volume. Pitfalls: Revolution period measurement can be zero or extremely small on startup or noise, causing division by zero or frequency overflow. Handled by clamping revolutionperiod = max(1<<10, revolutionperiod). File loading loop uses do-while(frames > 1) but frames is calculated as filesize / volumesize. If frames is 0 or 1, the loop still runs once. The rtot accumulator wraps at volumesize but the loop condition doesn't check rtot against volumesize for termination, relying on frames. syncprevtick # Clamp period to minimum 1<<10 to prevent division by zero if period < (1 << 10): period = 1 << 10 frequency = (1 << REVOLUTIONPRECISION) // period syncprevtick = tickcurr return syncprevtick, synclevel, period, frequency return syncprevtick, synclevel, revolutionperiod, (1 << REVOLUTIONPRECISION) // revolutionperiod def mainloop(): sincos = initsincostable() vx, vy, vsh, vsv, offsets = initspanoffsets(100, 50, 80, 10, 60) syncprevtick = 0 synclevel = 1 revolutionperiod = 1 << 26 revolutionfrequency = (1 << REVOLUTIONPRECISION) // revolutionperiod while True: tickcurr = gettimerus() # Simulate timeruS syncprevtick, synclevel, revolutionperiod, revolutionfrequency = angletrackingloop( tickcurr, syncprevtick, synclevel, revolutionperiod) # Compute current angle index for table lookup deltaticks = tickcurr - syncprevtick currentangleindex = (deltaticks revolutionfrequency) >> ANGLEPRECISION currentangleindex %= TABLESIZE # Projection mapping logic not fully detailed in the source; implement angle-to-screen coordinate transformation here. # Use sincos[currentangleindex] and offsets to map 3D voxel coordinates to 2D LED matrix positions. pass A volumetric display that creates 3D images by projecting horizontal layer slices onto a single piece of rear-projection glass moving back and forth in the air, synchronized with a high-speed projector. It breaks a 3D form into horizontal layer slices, moves the glass back and forth at 15 cycles per second using harmonic resonance springs, and tracks the glass location to synchronize with a 4,000 frames per second projector so each slice is projected at exactly the right height. The slices are stacked and re-stacked rapidly so the eye cannot track the motion, creating a floating object illusion. The image is redrawn on both the up and down swing of the glass to achieve a 30 frames per second hologram video refresh rate. Parameters include a glass movement frequency of 15 cycles per second, a projector frame rate of 4,000 frames per second, a video refresh rate of 30 frames per second, and a display volume of 18x18x8 cm (approx. 7x7x3 inches). Pitfalls include projector beam divergence, multiple color projections, and synchronization issues requiring advanced programming and processing. It is used in the Voxon VX1 table, sold for US10,000. Mechanical: Reduces jerk at endpoints compared to linear reciprocation or constant-velocity rotation with hard stops, potentially allowing for higher acceleration or longer mechanical life. Performance: Implemented on a Raspberry Pi 4 driving a 64x64 LED matrix. The driver exposes a memory-mapped voxel buffer compatible with the Multivox ecosystem. Limitations: The source notes the project was a test object and "didn't take it beyond this test object," implying limited performance data or optimization for large volumes. Precision: Fixed-point arithmetic is used for angle and frequency calculations to avoid floating-point overhead on the embedded controller. The Oscillating Swept Volume Display, also known as Oscivox, was developed by AncientJames as an experimental swept volume display. It was designed to explore the benefits of linear volume displays while mitigating the mechanical jerk associated with reversing direction in linear or rotational sweeps by using an undulating motion profile. The implementation is part of the Multivox ecosystem, providing a driver for Raspberry Pi-based volumetric displays. name: Moving Slit Display
head: Holotron
body: The Moving Slit Display is a volumetric 3D display technique that projects 2D image patterns onto a moving screen to form a stack of spatial images along the Z-axis, creating a true 3D image in space viewable without glasses. It is distinguished from its siblings by using a physical slit aperture that moves laterally in front of a high-speed display (typically a CRT) to multiplex multiple views into a sequence of partial images, rather than using static lenses or oscillating screens. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N distinct 2D views of a 3D scene. Output: A continuous volumetric image perceived by the viewer. Data Structures: The display system consists of a high-speed display device (historically a Cathode Ray Tube, CRT) and a mechanical slit aperture. Display Buffer: A frame buffer capable of high refresh rates. The buffer layout for a single frame consists of N columns of image data, where each column corresponds to one of the N views. Slit Aperture: A physical mask with a narrow vertical slit. The slit width determines the angular resolution and brightness trade-off. Steps: 1. View Multiplexing: For each frame, arrange the N views side-by-side in the display buffer. Specifically, the i-th column of the i-th view is placed adjacent to the others. This forms a "partial image" composed of N columns. 2. Beam Restriction: The horizontal deflection of the electron beam (in a CRT implementation) is restricted to the momentary position of the partial-image area. This ensures that only the relevant columns are illuminated at any given instant. 3. Slit Movement: The slit aperture moves laterally across the face of the display. The speed of the slit must be synchronized with the frame rate of the display. 4. Sequential Projection: As the slit moves, it exposes different parts of the display to the viewer. During a single pass of the slit, the display sequentially shows the set of N views as a sequence of partial images, each composed of N columns. 5. Persistence Integration: The phosphor persistence of the display (or the integration time of the human eye) blends these sequential partial images into a continuous volumetric image. Parameters: Number of Views (N): The number of distinct perspectives multiplexed. Higher N increases angular resolution but reduces brightness per view. Slit Width: Smaller apertures achieve denser distribution of virtual image sources but greatly reduce the brightness of each view. CRT Requirements: The sampling frequency and phosphor persistence must be sufficiently high to support the rapid sequential display of columns. If standard CRTs are insufficient, a multiple electron gun CRT in conjunction with a multiple moving-slit panel has been proposed to reduce these requirements. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def movingslitdisplay(nviews, slitspeed, displayrefreshrate): """ Simulates the control logic for a Moving Slit Display. Args: nviews (int): Number of views to multiplex. slitspeed (float): Speed of the slit movement (pixels per second). displayrefreshrate (float): Refresh rate of the display (Hz). """ # Calculate the number of columns per view # Assuming a square display for simplicity, width W, height H # Each view occupies W/nviews columns # Initialize display buffer # Buffer size: H x W displaybuffer = createbuffer(height=H, width=W) # Generate N views views = generatenviews(nviews) # Synchronize slit movement with display refresh # The slit moves continuously, but the display updates discretely while True: # Get current slit position slitx = getslitposition(time) # Determine which columns are currently behind the slit # The slit has a finite width, but for ideal multiplexing, # we assume it reveals one column set at a time or a small window # Update display buffer with multiplexed views # Place column i of view i at position (i colwidth,:) for i in range(nviews): colstart = i (W // nviews) colend = colstart + (W // nviews) displaybuffer[:, colstart:colend] = views[i][:, 0] # Render the display buffer render(displaybuffer) # Wait for next refresh waitforrefresh(displayrefreshrate) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Brightness vs. Resolution: Selecting a small aperture to achieve dense distribution of virtual image sources greatly reduces the brightness of each view. CRT Limitations: Standard CRTs may not have sufficient sampling frequency or phosphor persistence. This necessitates specialized hardware like multiple electron gun CRTs. Synchronization: Precise synchronization between the slit movement and the display refresh is critical to avoid image tearing or misalignment. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: The time complexity is dominated by the display refresh rate and the mechanical speed of the slit. The system must update the display buffer at a high frequency to match the slit movement. Memory Complexity: The memory requirement is proportional to the number of views N and the resolution of each view. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scaling to higher resolutions requires higher display refresh rates and faster slit movement mechanisms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a true volumetric image without the need for glasses. Can achieve a wide field of view. Limitations: Brightness is significantly reduced due to the slit aperture. Requires high-speed displays and precise mechanical synchronization. When to Use: Use when a glasses-free volumetric display is required and high brightness is not the primary concern. When Not to Use: Do not use when high brightness or low power consumption is critical. The Moving Slit Display, also known as the Holotron, was proposed by St. John. It is a variant of the multi-planar volumetric 3D display technique. The concept was developed to address the limitations of static parallax barriers and lenticular lenses by introducing motion to the aperture, allowing for a more flexible and potentially higher-quality volumetric image. name: Rotating Volumetric Display
head: Helical Screen Volumometric Sweep, Helical slicing display
body: A Rotating Volumetric Display renders 3D images by sweeping a helical screen surface through space while projecting synchronized 2D slices, creating a continuous volumetric illusion via temporal integration. It differs from linear reciprocating displays by using rotational motion to achieve higher frame rates, though it introduces a central "dead spot" where surface velocity is insufficient for the persistence of vision. It builds on Rotating Rigid Screen with Projector by replacing the flat or curved rigid screen with a helical geometry and employing a helical slicing algorithm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel model or volume dataset. Output: A continuous 3D volumetric image visible to the observer. Hardware Inputs: Angular position from a rotary encoder; control signals to a DC motor. Data Structures: Helical Screen Geometry: Defined by radius R and height H per revolution. The screen consists of N blades (typically N=3). Projection Buffer: A 2D image buffer corresponding to the projector's resolution. For binary-frame-warping systems, this may be a preloaded binary image containing geometric markers (e.g., three bright circles). Transformation Parameters: Affine or homography matrices mapping 3D world coordinates to 2D screen coordinates based on the current rotation angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Helical Slicing: Instead of linear slicing, compute the intersection of the 3D volume with the helical surface at the current rotation angle \theta. This determines which voxel data maps to which pixel on the screen. 2. Coordinate Mapping: Map the 3D world coordinates of the voxel to 2D screen coordinates (u, v) and a specific frame index corresponding to the rotation angle \theta. 3. Image Generation: Generate the 2D projection image for the current slice. Standard Projector: Render the slice directly to the projector buffer. Binary-Frame-Warping: Update the preloaded binary image using an affine transformation derived from the coordinate transformation parameters. 4. Keystone Calibration: Align multiple projectors (e.g., Red, Green, Blue) into the same physical space to ensure color registration. 5. Synchronization: Drive the DC motor using PID control based on feedback from the rotary encoder to maintain precise angular velocity. 6. Temporal Integration: The screen rotates at speed \omega such that the persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. The sweep frequency f{sweep} is the product of the blade count N and the rotation frequency f{rot}: f{sweep} = N \times f{rot} 7. Observer Interaction: The image is viewed via reflection from a half-mirror or directly, depending on the configuration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrotatingvolumetricdisplay(volumedata, helixparams, motorstate): """ Renders a frame for a rotating helical volumetric display. Args: volumedata: 3D array of voxel intensities. helixparams: Object containing radius R, height H, blade count N. motorstate: Object containing current angle theta, angular velocity omega. Returns: projectedimage: 2D array representing the projector input. """ # 1. Determine current slice geometry based on rotation angle # The helical surface is defined by z = (H / 2pi) theta + k (H/N) for blade k # Map 3D voxel coordinates to the helical surface at current theta slicegeometry = computehelicalintersection(volumedata, helixparams, motorstate.theta) # 2. Generate 2D projection for this slice # For standard projectors, render directly. # For binary-frame-warping, compute affine transform parameters. if usebinarywarping: # Preloaded binary image contains markers (e.g., 3 circles) # Update markers using affine transformation based on coordinate mapping affineparams = computeaffinetransform(slicegeometry, helixparams) projectedimage = applyaffinetobinaryimage(preloadedbinaryimage, affineparams) else: # Standard rendering: map voxels to screen pixels projectedimage = renderslicetoprojector(slicegeometry, helixparams) # 3. Apply keystone correction if using multiple projectors # This step is hardware/calibration dependent and often results in fringing projectedimage = applykeystonecorrection(projectedimage) return projectedimage def controlmotor(targetspeed, encoderfeedback): """ PID control loop for the DC motor. """ error = targetspeed - encoderfeedback.angularvelocity integral += error derivative = error - lasterror output = Kp error + Ki integral + Kd derivative lasterror = error setmotorvoltage(output) Parameters: Helical Screen Blade Count (N): 3. Rotation Speed (f{rot}): 5 rps (revolutions per second). Sweep Frequency (f{sweep}): 15 Hz. Helix Radius (R): 120 mm. Helix Height (H): 160 mm. Motor: Maxon A-MAX32 DC motor. Encoder: Autonics E40S-6-3600-3-N-24 rotary encoder. Control Method: PID control. Projector Types: ViaLUX V-7001 or binary-frame-warping projector (2469 Hz max update). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dead Spot: A vortex-like hole appears in the center of the image where the surface velocity is too low to maintain the persistence of vision illusion. Content must be created with this central void in mind. Keystone Fringing: Complex keystone calibration for multi-projector alignment can result in color fringing (e.g., pink fringing around icons). Precision: Misalignment between screen position and projected frame index results in Z-depth distortion [8515-multi-planar-volumetric-3d-display.md]. Uses preloaded binary images and affine transformations for high-speed updates (up to 2469 Hz) with reduced latency, sacrificing arbitrary image projection capability. Projects arbitrary images but at lower frame rates (e.g., ViaLUX V-7001), offering more flexibility in content but potentially higher latency. Time Complexity: Dependent on the complexity of the helical slicing algorithm and the affine transformation calculations. Binary-frame-warping reduces computational load by only sending affine parameters. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D volume data and the preloaded binary image (if using binary-warping). Measured Performance: Achieves a sweep frequency of 15 Hz with a 5 rps rotation speed and 3 blades. Binary-frame-warping projector supports up to 2469 Hz updates. Scaling: Rotating displays deliver higher frame rates than reciprocating displays but are harder to scale up due to the mechanical difficulty of moving large glass screens at sufficient speeds for a solid illusion. Strengths: Higher frame rates compared to reciprocating systems; compelling volumetric illusion; unedited physical hardware (no CGI/compositing required). Limitations: Central dead spot; complex keystone calibration; mechanical complexity and scaling limits. The Rotating Volumetric Display was developed by Voxon Photonics as an alternative to their linear "glass shaker" technology, aiming to overcome scaling limitations of reciprocating motion. The concept involves a screen resembling a drill bit with ramps and drop-offs, allowing projectors to be positioned above the display. A specific implementation using a helical screen with PID-controlled DC motor and rotary encoder was detailed in a 2024 ACM paper, demonstrating low-latency performance using binary-frame-warping techniques. name: Holographic Display System
head: HoloDis system, Holographic rendering system, IMEC HoloDis, IMEC Holographic Display, Scalable holographic display
body: A scalable hardware and software system for multi-user interactive computer graphics that uses an array of micro-displays and a holographic screen to emit light beams of different color and intensity in controlled directions, composing a continuous 3D view. It differs from pure computational CGH methods by relying on a specific optical geometry where a holographic screen performs the final wavefront transformation, enabling horizontal-only parallax without the massive computational load of full volumetric wavefront synthesis. Inputs: Graphics commands (OpenGL-compatible). DVI streams driving the micro-displays. Outputs: A 3D light field with horizontal parallax only. Data Structures: Micro-display Array: A specially arranged array of projectors. Each projector generates an array of pixels with controlled intensity and color. Holographic Screen: A passive optical element that transforms incident light beams into an asymmetrical pyramidal form. Steps: 1. Graphics Rendering: An OpenGL-compliant library on a client PC redefines OpenGL behavior to multicast graphics commands to server PCs. 2. Command Re-interpretation: Server PCs re-interpret commands for holographic rendering, generating DVI streams. 3. Projection: Projectors generate an array of pixels at controlled intensity and color onto the holographic screen. 4. Beam Generation: Each point of the holographic screen transmits different colored light beams into different directions in front of the screen. 5. Optical Transformation: The holographic screen transforms the incident light beams into an asymmetrical pyramidal form, creating horizontal-only parallax. Parameters: Field of View (FOV): 50 degrees. Angular Resolution: 0.8 degrees horizontal. Vertical Diffusion: 60 degrees. Horizontal Diffusion: 0.8 degrees. Prototype Resolution: 7.4M pixels. Refresh Rate: 10-15 Hz. Drive Interface: Three DVI streams. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertical Parallax: Not implemented in the prototype because it would require an order of magnitude increase in data size, rendering times, and system complexity for little gain in visual performance in standard settings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesystem(): """ Initialize the client-server architecture and OpenGL hooks. """ clientpc = ClientPC() serverpcs = [ServerPC() for in range(3)] # Driven by 3 DVI streams clientpc.hookopengl() # Redefines OpenGL behavior to multicast commands def renderframe(sceneobjects): """ Render a single frame of the holographic display. """ # 1. Multicast graphics commands to servers commands = clientpc.reinterpretopenglcommands(sceneobjects) # 2. Servers process commands and generate DVI streams dvistreams = [] for server in serverpcs: stream = server.processcommands(commands) dvistreams.append(stream) # 3. Projectors generate pixels on the holographic screen # The screen is an array of pixels with controlled intensity and color holographicscreen = HolographicScreen() for i, stream in enumerate(dvistreams): holographicscreen.project(stream) # 4. Holographic screen transforms beams # Each point on the screen emits light beams of different color/intensity # into different directions, creating horizontal-only parallax # The distribution is an asymmetrical pyramid: # Vertical size = vertical FOV (60 degrees) # Horizontal size = neighboring emitting directions (0.8 degrees resolution) lightfield = holographicscreen.transformbeams() return lightfield def main(): initializesystem() while True: scene = getnextscene() renderframe(scene) # Refresh rate is 10-15 Hz waitforrefresh() A nanoscale SiGe-MEMS chip with over 1 billion micro-diffractive nanodevices (DNDs) acting as visible-light-diffracting elements. It uses a pixel pitch of 500 nm to achieve a viewing angle of approximately 38° (19° off axis) with 635 nm illumination. The ultimate system targets a 60° diffraction angle and HD quality. The prototype described in the main text, using an array of micro-displays and a holographic screen for horizontal-only parallax. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in terms of algorithmic complexity, but rendering is driven by DVI streams at 10-15 Hz for 7.4M pixels. Memory/Complexity: Adding vertical parallax would increase data size, rendering times, and system complexity by an order of magnitude. Performance: Prototype achieved 7.4M pixels at 10-15 Hz refresh rate. Strengths: Scalable design for multi-user interactive graphics; controlled emission of light beams; horizontal-only parallax sufficient for standard settings. Limitations: No vertical parallax in the prototype; limited viewing angle (50° FOV, 0.8° angular resolution) compared to ultimate goals (60° diffraction angle). The system was presented by Balogh et al. in 2005. It targets multi-user interactive computer graphics applications. The feasibility was evaluated with a working hardware and software prototype. IMEC also developed a related nanoscale MEMS-based holographic display (HoloDis). A Scalable Hardware and Software System for the Holographic Display of Interactive Graphics Applications, https://doi.org/10.2312/egs.20051036, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Three-dimensional display technologies, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4269274, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Optical Projection and Reflection
body: Optical Projection and Reflection techniques generate volumetric or pseudo-volumetric images by reflecting light from a 2D display source onto semi-reflective surfaces, creating the illusion of floating 3D objects in free space. This family solves the problem of presenting 3D content with natural occlusion cues without requiring physical particles or scanning beams in the viewing volume. It differs from scanning methods (like Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering) by using static optical elements to create persistent images, and from holographic methods (like Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation) by relying on geometric reflection rather than wavefront interference. The core mechanism involves a display source emitting light that strikes a translucent or semi-reflective surface. The surface reflects a portion of the light toward the viewer while transmitting the remainder. By stacking multiple such surfaces or using specific geometries, distinct image slices are superimposed to create depth. Key Mathematical Principles: 1. Contrast and Occlusion: The perception of a floating volume relies on high contrast between the projected image and the real background. If I{img} is the intensity of the projected image and I{bg} is the intensity of the real background, the contrast C at the boundary is defined as: C = \frac{I{img} - I{bg}}{I{img} + I{bg}} High contrast (bright image, dark background) is essential for the "floating" effect. 2. Perspective Projection: To simulate virtual images located behind the physical drawing volume, the display content must be projected based on the viewer's position. For an observer at point E = (x0, y0, z0) and an image point X = (x, y, z), the perspective projection onto a plane P (perpendicular to the line EO, where O is the origin) is governed by the matrix S: S = \begin{bmatrix} -r^2 & r^2 x0 & 0 & 0 \\ -r x0 z0 & -r y0 z0 & r \rho^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & r \rho \\ -\rho x0 & -\rho y0 & -\rho z0 & r \rho \end{bmatrix} where: r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2 + z0^2}} \rho = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2}} 3. Rendering Steps: The system prepares image slices, applies perspective projection based on viewer position, emits light from the display source, and handles reflection/transmission at each layer to superimpose the final volume. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendersliceview(viewerpos, layers, displayparams): """ Render the SliceView volumetric display. Args: viewerpos: Tuple (x0, y0, z0) representing viewer position E. layers: List of dicts, each containing: 'image': 2D numpy array of the layer's content. 'z': Depth of the layer. 'R': Reflection coefficient. 'T': Transmission coefficient. displayparams: Dict containing optical parameters. Returns: None (displays images to respective layers) """ x0, y0, z0 = viewerpos # Calculate projection matrix components r = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02 + z02) rho = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02) # Construct projection matrix S S = [ [-r2, r2 x0, 0, 0], [-r x0 z0, -r y0 z0, r rho2, 0], [0, 0, 0, r rho], [-rho x0, -rho y0, -rho z0, r rho] ] for layer in layers: image = layer['image'] z = layer['z'] R = layer['R'] T = layer['T'] # Apply perspective projection to the image based on viewer position. # Sources do not specify the image warping algorithm; typically involves inverse mapping using the projection matrix. projectedimage = image # Display the projected image on the layer's display source. # Sources do not specify hardware emission control; typically involves driving the display panel with the projected image buffer. pass SliceView is a volumetric display system that extends the Pepper's Ghost optical illusion to multiple stacked translucent planes, cumulatively giving volume to an initially two-dimensional projection. It solves the problem of presenting 3D content in physical space without moving parts by superimposing distinct image slices at different depths, allowing the viewer to perceive a floating volume that occludes the real background. Unlike stereoscopic displays, it avoids vergence accommodation conflict (VAC) between the virtual object and the real background, and differs from persistence-of-vision displays by using static stacked planes rather than oscillating surfaces or levitated particles. Choose this method when natural occlusion and depth cues are required without mechanical scanning. Mechanically driven mirrors are beam deflectors used in volumetric displays to steer light beams toward specific points in a drawing volume. They solve the problem of directing light from a source to arbitrary (x, y, z) coordinates within a 3D space by physically rotating mirrors. They are distinguished from electro-optic deflectors by being essentially lossless but suffering from slower response times. Choose this method when high optical efficiency is prioritized over high-speed beam steering. This method provides a lensless magnification technique for holographic displays by using a diverging point light source to perform coarse beam steering, allowing a hologram to steer light at a finer angle to focus into an image. It solves the problem of achieving wide fields of view (60–100°) without the bulky refractive lenses required by conventional magnification. Unlike SliceView which relies on physical layer stacking, this method uses optical diffraction and divergence to create depth and magnification simultaneously. Choose this method when a wide field of view and lensless design are required. A technique to simulate virtual images (located behind the physical drawing volume) in freespace volumetric displays by projecting content onto a background image plane that moves and rotates to match the viewer's position, creating motion parallax cues consistent with a distant object. Definition: Simulates virtual images in freespace displays using time-varying perspective projection. Steps: 1. Define observer position E = (x0, y0, z0). 2. Define 3D image point X = (x, y, z). 3. Define background image plane P, typically perpendicular to line EO where O is origin. 4. Calculate intersection of line EX with plane P to determine pixel coordinate. Link: No separate article. A simple 360° display based on a conical semi-reflective surface that reflects an anamorphic image into a real undistorted aerial image. It has no moving parts. Definition: 360° display using conical semi-reflective surface. Steps: 1. Display an anamorphic image. 2. Reflect it off a 360° symmetrical conical semi-reflective surface. 3. Surface creates a real undistorted aerial image. 4. As viewer turns device, image changes to offer 360° interactive view. Pitfalls: Constrained to a limited number of viewers because only one point of view is displayed at a time. Link: No separate article. An analog electro-optic deflector using a series arrangement of electro-optic prisms. A light beam is deflected by varying the refractive index of each prism by applying an electric field to its top and bottom electroded faces. Pitfalls: The prism type suffers from high load capacitance, which limits random access times and increases complexity. Numbers: Better than 300-spot resolution has been demonstrated in the prism type of electro-optic deflector. Comparison: Unlike digital electro-optic deflectors which offer discrete beam positioning, this configuration yields an output continuously controllable in position. Link: No separate article. Optical projection and reflection techniques have roots in classical theatrical illusions, specifically Pepper's Ghost, which uses a large sheet of glass to reflect a hidden stage area into the main stage. SliceView was developed as an extension of Pepper's Ghost to multiple planes to create volumetric depth cues. Perspective Projection Backdrop was introduced in 2021 to simulate virtual images in optical trap displays (OTDs) by employing time-varying perspective projection. Pepper's Cone was proposed as a low-cost, efficient 360° display solution using conical surfaces. Mechanically driven mirrors were documented in early volumetric display studies (1970s) as a method for beam deflection, noting trade-offs between speed, hysteresis, and damping. These methods are used in research prototypes for volumetric displays, holography, and augmented reality interfaces where natural occlusion and parallax are desired without the complexity of scanning beams or particle traps.
