name: SliceView
head: Pepper's Ghost volumetric extension, Pepper's ghost display, Pepper's ghost effect, holographic display
body: SliceView is a volumetric display system that extends the Pepper's Ghost optical illusion to multiple stacked translucent planes, cumulatively giving volume to an initially two-dimensional projection. It solves the problem of presenting 3D content in physical space without moving parts by superimposing distinct image slices at different depths, allowing the viewer to perceive a floating volume that occludes the real background. Unlike stereoscopic displays, it avoids vergence accommodation conflict (VAC) between the virtual object and the real background, and differs from persistence-of-vision displays by using static stacked planes rather than oscillating surfaces or levitated particles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D image slices corresponding to different depth layers; viewer position E = (x0, y0, z0) for perspective correction; physical parameters of the display stack (layer thicknesses ti, reflection coefficients Ri, transmission coefficients Ti). Output: A perceived 3D volumetric image floating in space, superimposed on the real background. Data Structures: The system relies on a physical stack of N translucent planes. Each plane i (where i = 1 \dots N) is defined by: Position zi along the optical axis. Thickness ti. Optical properties: Reflection coefficient Ri and Transmission coefficient Ti. Content: A 2D image buffer Ii(x, y) with a black background. Numbered Steps: 1. Layer Preparation: For each layer i, generate or retrieve the 2D image Ii representing the cross-section of the 3D object at depth zi. The image must be surrounded by a black background to ensure high contrast. 2. Perspective Projection: Adjust the content of each layer Ii based on the viewer's position E to simulate a virtual image located at depth zi. The projection is governed by the matrix S: S = \begin{bmatrix} -r^2 & r^2 x0 & 0 & 0 \\ -r x0 z0 & -r y0 z0 & r \rho^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & r \rho \\ -\rho x0 & -\rho y0 & -\rho z0 & r \rho \end{bmatrix} where: r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2 + z0^2}} \rho = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2}} 3. Display Emission: Emit light from the display source (e.g., LCD/OLED panel or projector) for each layer i. 4. Reflection and Transmission: The semi-reflective surface reflects a portion of the light (Ri) towards the viewer and transmits the remainder (Ti) to the next layer or background. The viewer sees the virtual image appearing to float in space. 5. Superposition: The viewer perceives the superimposed images from all layers i=1 \dots N. The high contrast between the projected image intensity I{img} and the real background intensity I{bg} creates the perception of volume. The contrast C at the boundary is defined as: C = \frac{I{img} - I{bg}}{I{img} + I{bg}} Parameters: Layer Thickness (ti): Evaluated alongside light reflection and transmission properties to optimize image quality. Exact optimization formulas are not specified in the sources. Reflection/Transmission Coefficients (Ri, Ti): Critical for balancing brightness and depth perception. Ri + Ti \leq 1 (accounting for absorption). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vergence Accommodation Conflict (VAC): While stereoscopic displays suffer from VAC due to the gap between accommodation on a 2D display and 3D vergence sensation, SliceView avoids this because the virtual object and real background are at different optical distances, and the image is a reflection, not a focused 2D plane in the same way. Contrast Loss: If the background is not sufficiently dark, the contrast C decreases, reducing the "floating" effect and volume perception. Layer Alignment: Misalignment of the physical planes or the projected images can cause ghosting or misregistration of the volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendersliceview(viewerpos, layers, displayparams): """ Render the SliceView volumetric display. Args: viewerpos: Tuple (x0, y0, z0) representing viewer position E. layers: List of dicts, each containing: 'image': 2D numpy array of the layer's content. 'z': Depth of the layer. 'R': Reflection coefficient. 'T': Transmission coefficient. displayparams: Dict containing optical parameters. Returns: None (displays images to respective layers) """ x0, y0, z0 = viewerpos # Calculate projection matrix components r = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02 + z02) rho = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02) # Construct projection matrix S S = [ [-r2, r2 x0, 0, 0], [-r x0 z0, -r y0 z0, r rho2, 0], [0, 0, 0, r rho], [-rho x0, -rho y0, -rho z0, r rho] ] for layer in layers: image = layer['image'] z = layer['z'] R = layer['R'] T = layer['T'] # Apply perspective projection to the image # Sources do not specify the image warping algorithm; typically involves inverse mapping using the projection matrix. projectedimage = image # Display the projected image on the layer's display source # The semi-reflective surface will reflect R portion to viewer # and transmit T portion to subsequent layers/background # Sources do not specify hardware emission control; typically involves driving the display panel with the projected image buffer. pass A 360° volumetric display based on a transparent projection surface made of sparse cube corner distribution. It derives from the Pepper's Ghost configuration but uses a transparent retro-reflective surface to project a real image, avoiding the need for a display panel above the device. The surface reflects the image towards the viewer while remaining transparent. The image seen through the semi-reflective surface (or directly if configured as aerial) seems to float if surrounded by a black background. Occlusion between the bright image and the real background creates volume perception. Compared to classical Pepper's Ghost design, this solution avoids the presence of a display panel above the device and presents a brighter image. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids vergence accommodation conflict (VAC) between the virtual object and the real background; simple and cheap compared to complex solutions; provides a 360° view in the transparent retro-reflective variant; no moving parts in the projected volume. Limitations: Relies on high contrast between projected image and real background; layer thickness and optical properties require careful optimization; limited to static volumes or temporally varying multi-view perception. When to use: When a simple, low-cost volumetric display is needed for public demonstrations, retro-gaming, or data visualization. When not to use: When precise stereoscopic depth cues are required, or when the environment has high ambient light that reduces contrast. The Pepper's Ghost effect creates a virtual image from a display by reflection on a semi-reflective surface. SliceView specifically applies this to multiple stacked translucent planes to create a volumetric display. The transparent retro-reflective surface variant was developed in a laboratory and presented to the public during a symposium, aiming to provide a 360° volumetric display without the need for a display panel above the device. SliceView has been implemented as a layer-based painting tool, retro-gaming platform, text overlaying media player for subtitles, browser-based 3D scene renderer, and volumetric data visualizer. name: Mechanically Driven Mirrors
head: Galvanometer driven, Piezoelectrically driven
body: Mechanically driven mirrors are beam deflectors used in volumetric displays and holography to steer light beams. They are essentially lossless but suffer from slow response times compared to electro-optic alternatives. They differ from SliceView by using dynamic reflection rather than static semi-reflective layers, and from Holographic Magnification via Diverging Light by using physical inertia rather than liquid crystal phase arrays for beam steering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Commanded deflection angle \theta. Output: Reflected light beam at angle 2\theta (assuming normal incidence). Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Receive a command for a target deflection angle. 2. Actuate the mirror mechanism (galvanometer or piezoelectric) to rotate the mirror surface. 3. Reflect the incident light beam off the mirror surface. 4. Stabilize the mirror to the target angle before emitting the next spot or frame. Formulas: Natural frequency fn determines the time response in random access operation. Maximum spot capability N{max} for a refresh rate R{refresh} is derived from the natural frequency: N{max} \approx \frac{fn}{R{refresh}} Parameters: Piezoelectric units: Lowest natural frequency: \approx 12 \text{ KHz}. Maximum spot capability at 30 \text{ Hz} refresh: 400 spots. Galvanometer units: Lowest natural frequency: \approx 3 \text{ KHz}. Maximum spot capability at 30 \text{ Hz} refresh: 100 spots. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Hysteresis (Galvanometer): Galvanometer drives are susceptible to hysteresis effects as large as 4\%. To overcome this, the system must always approach a newly commanded deflection angle from the same direction. This requirement nearly doubles the random access time. Hysteresis (Piezoelectric): Piezoelectric drives circumvent hysteresis by using active position sensing. Underdamped Oscillation: High-response mechanical mirror drives often operate in a highly underdamped manner, producing slowly decaying oscillations about the mean orientation. This enlarges the apparent spot size, decreases boundary definition, and causes misregistration. Additional damping is required to prevent viewing degradation, which further decreases drive response. Pointing Accuracy: Pointing accuracies of 0.1 spot diameter are generally sufficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import time class MechanicallyDrivenMirror: def init(self, drivetype, naturalfrequencyhz): """ Initialize a mechanically driven mirror. Args: drivetype: 'galvanometer' or 'piezoelectric'. naturalfrequencyhz: The lowest natural frequency of the unit. """ self.drivetype = drivetype self.naturalfrequencyhz = naturalfrequencyhz self.currentangle = 0.0 self.lastdirection = None def settargetangle(self, targetangle): """ Command the mirror to a new deflection angle. Args: targetangle: The desired deflection angle in degrees. """ if self.drivetype == 'galvanometer': # Galvanometer hysteresis mitigation: # Always approach from the same direction to avoid 4% hysteresis error if self.lastdirection is not None: if (targetangle > self.currentangle) != (self.lastdirection > 0): # Direction change detected; full traversal required pass self.lastdirection = 1 if targetangle > self.currentangle else -1 # Actuate mirror hardware # Hardware-specific voltage/current control not given in sources self.actuate(targetangle) # Wait for settling based on natural frequency and damping settlingtime = self.calculatesettlingtime(targetangle) time.sleep(settlingtime) self.currentangle = targetangle def actuate(self, angle): """ Physically move the mirror to the target angle. Hardware actuation details not given in sources """ pass def calculatesettlingtime(self, angle): """ Estimate time required for the mirror to settle within 0.1 spot diameter accuracy. Damping characteristics not given in sources """ return 1.0 / self.naturalfrequencyhz def reflectbeam(self, incidentdirection): """ Reflect an incident beam off the current mirror orientation. Args: incidentdirection: List/tuple of 3 floats representing incident light direction. Returns: Reflected beam vector as list of 3 floats. """ # Mirror normal rotates with angle (assuming rotation around Y-axis) rad = math.radians(self.currentangle) normal = [math.sin(rad), 0.0, math.cos(rad)] # Vector reflection: R = I - 2(I·N)N dot = sum(i n for i, n in zip(incidentdirection, normal)) reflected = [i - 2 dot n for i, n in zip(incidentdirection, normal)] return reflected A liquid crystal-based transmission phase array that optically tilts coherent backlight beams to expand the holographic viewing angle. It differs from mechanical mirrors by using electro-optic phase shifts rather than physical inertia. Maximum steering angle is \sim 15^\circ with an angular resolution of 0.02^\circ at a wavelength of 520 \text{ nm}. A key pitfall is that the maximum steering angle decreases as the light source area increases due to etendue constraints. Time Complexity: Response time is limited by the mechanical natural frequency. Galvanometer units (\approx 3 \text{ KHz}) are slower than piezoelectric units (\approx 12 \text{ KHz}). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: At a 30 \text{ Hz} refresh rate, piezoelectric units support a maximum of 400 spots, while galvanometer units support 100 spots. Scaling: Scaling is limited by the trade-off between damping and response time; additional damping reduces oscillations but decreases drive response. Strengths: Essentially lossless efficiency. Limitations: Slow response time compared to electro-optic deflectors; susceptibility to hysteresis (galvanometer); underdamped oscillations causing misregistration. When to use: When high optical efficiency is required and the application can tolerate slower frame rates or spot counts. When not to use: When high-speed random access or high spot counts are required without the overhead of hysteresis compensation. Mechanically driven mirrors are among the simplest beam deflectors available for volumetric displays. They were studied in the context of 3D volumetric display systems in the 1970s. The technology distinguishes between galvanometer-driven and piezoelectric-driven units based on their actuation mechanisms and natural frequencies. name: Holographic Magnification via Diverging Light
head: Diverging Light Holographic Magnification
body: This method provides a lensless magnification technique for holographic displays by using a diverging point light source to perform coarse beam steering, allowing a hologram to steer light at a finer angle to focus into an image. It solves the problem of achieving wide fields of view (60–100°) without the bulky refractive lenses required by conventional magnification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) displaying a hologram pattern; a diverging point light source positioned at \vec{l}e; wavelength \lambda. Output: A magnified virtual image with an expanded field of view and a reduced exit pupil. Data Structures: SLM Pattern: A 2D array of phase values. The sub-hologram size corresponds to the effective exit pupil size. Light Source: Defined by position \vec{l}e relative to the SLM. Core Principles: The hologram acts as a series of superimposed diffraction gratings. The light deflection angle is determined by the grating equation: d(\sin\thetai + \sin\thetam) = \lambda where d is the grating pitch, \thetai is the light incidence angle, \thetam is the diffraction angle, and \lambda is the wavelength. The lens phase function for a sub-hologram is updated to handle diverging light. The phase \phi at position \vec{p} on the SLM, relative to the eye position \vec{o} and light source \vec{l}e, is calculated as: \phi(\vec{p}) = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left( |\vec{p} - \vec{l}e| + |\vec{p} - \vec{o}| \right) This phase function accounts for the path length difference from the diverging source to the SLM pixel and from the pixel to the observer's eye. Parameters: SLM Pixel Pitch: Typically 8 µm. Minimum Grating Pitch (d): 16 µm (derived from Nyquist sampling theorem on 8 µm pixels). Wavelength (\lambda): 532 nm (green light). Maximum Diffraction Angle (\thetam): \pm 1.9^\circ for normally incident light with d=16\mu m and \lambda=532nm. Field of View: 60–100° or more, limited only by the divergence of the point light source. Steps: 1. Define Geometry: Position the diverging point light source at \vec{l}e and the observer's eye at \vec{o} relative to the SLM. 2. Calculate Phase: For each pixel \vec{p} in the sub-hologram, calculate the phase \phi(\vec{p}) based on the path lengths from the light source to the pixel and from the pixel to the eye. 3. Compute Hologram: Generate the hologram pattern using the calculated phase values. 4. Display: Render the hologram on the SLM. 5. Illumination: Illuminate the SLM with the diverging light from \vec{l}e. 6. Diffraction & Steering: The hologram diffracts the light. The beam divergence performs coarse beam steering while the hologram steers light at a finer angle to focus the light into an image. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exit Pupil Reduction: As the projector is magnified with diverging light, the field of view increases, but the effective size of the exit pupil decreases. Sub-hologram Size: The sub-hologram size used in computation must match the size of the reduced exit pupil. Attempting to increase the sub-hologram size would require diffraction angles and spatial frequencies higher than the SLM can reproduce. Etendue: Unlike conventional displays, the etendue of a holographic projector is linked to the device resolution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Supports wide fields of view (60–100°). Strengths: Lensless magnification; avoids bulky refractive lenses; enables wide fields of view with smaller optics. Limitations: The exit pupil size decreases as magnification increases; etendue is limited by SLM resolution. When to use: When wide fields of view are required in VR/AR near-eye displays without bulky optics. This technique was developed to address the need for wide fields of view in VR and AR displays without the bulk of conventional refractive lenses. It builds on the principle that holographic displays can be magnified lenslessly using a diverging point light source, as cited from Makowski et al. [2012] and Qu et al. [2015] in. The method was detailed in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. Holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality, https://doi.org/10.1145/3072959.3073624, fetched 2026-10-30

name: 3D Light PAD
head: volumetric three-dimensional digital light photoactivatable dye display
body: 3D Light PAD is a chemically enabled volumetric 3D display that uses photoactivatable molecules and digital light processing (DLP) to generate structured light in three dimensions by simultaneously activating and exciting fluorophores in a spatial pattern defined by DLP. It differs from photoactivated localization microscopy, which sequentially activates subsets of fluorophores, by generating a viewable volumetric image through simultaneous activation and excitation. Unlike beam-addressable systems using upconversion or plasma which require expensive high-energy beams, 3D Light PAD uses DLP projectors and photoactivatable dyes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D image definition (spatial pattern), two light sources (ultraviolet for photoactivation, visible for excitation/emission), and a chemical medium consisting of photoactivatable dye dispersed in a low-scattering solvent with a base additive. Output: A 3D volumetric image composed of fluorescent voxels at the intersection of the structured light beams. Data Structures and Chemical Composition: The medium is a solution containing: 1. Photoactivatable Dye: N-phenyl spirolactam rhodamine B. 2. Solvent: Low-scattering solvent, specifically dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) in the reported implementation. 3. Base Additive: Triethylamine, used to increase reversibility and speed up thermal fading. Concentrations tested were 1 p.p.m. (7.2 mM), 5 p.p.m. (36 mM), and 15 p.p.m. (108 mM). Operating Principle: The dye exists in a non-fluorescent 'off' state (spirolactam form) and a fluorescent 'on' state (merocyanine form). Photoactivation: Ultraviolet light opens the spirolactam ring, converting the dye to the fluorescent 'on' state. Excitation/Emission: Visible light excites the 'on' state dye, causing it to emit fluorescence. Voxel Generation: A 3D voxel is generated at the intersection of the UV and visible light beams. Thermal Fading: The 'on' state is thermally reversible. The dye spontaneously returns to the 'off' state, allowing the voxel to fade and enabling dynamic updates. The base (triethylamine) accelerates this thermal fading. Parameters: Photoactivation Wavelength: Ultraviolet light. Specific wavelengths used in experiments include 254 nm, 315 nm, and 385 nm. Excitation Wavelength: Visible light. Specific wavelengths used include 532 nm and 556 nm. Emission Wavelength: 586 nm. Minimum Voxel Size: 0.68 \text{ mm}^3. Resolution: 200 mm (stated as such in the source, likely a typo for 200 µm or similar, but reported as 200 mm). Kinetics: The thermal fading (off-rate, k{obs}) follows single-exponential decay. The rate depends on the concentration of triethylamine: 1 p.p.m. triethylamine: k{obs} = 0.048 \text{ s}^{-1}. 5 p.p.m. triethylamine: k{obs} = 0.20 \text{ s}^{-1}. 15 p.p.m. triethylamine: k{obs} = 0.50 \text{ s}^{-1} [G: The increase in rate was observed to be linear with base concentration]. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Slow Fading/Irreversibility: Prolonged UV illumination or the use of certain solvents (e.g., chloroform CHCl3, deuterated chloroform CDCl3) can lead to slow thermal fading kinetics or irreversible coloration/fluorescence. Solvent Choice: Chlorinated solvents like chloroform (CHCl3) or deuterated chloroform (CDCl3) cause irreversible coloration and fluorescence under prolonged UV illumination, so dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) was used in the reported implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uvprojectoron(pattern): """Projects the UV pattern to photoactivate dye at intersection points.""" pass def uvprojectoroff(): """Stops UV projection.""" pass def visprojectoron(pattern): """Projects the visible pattern to excite activated dye.""" pass def visprojectoroff(): """Stops visible projection.""" pass def waitms(durationms): """Pauses execution for the specified duration.""" import time time.sleep(durationms / 1000.0) def initializedisplay(): # Define chemical medium parameters dyeconcentration = 5.0 # mM, as used in experiments solvent = "dichloromethane" base = "triethylamine" baseppm = 5.0 # Example concentration basemolarity = 36.0 # mM corresponding to 5 p.p.m. # Define optical parameters uvwavelength = 385 # nm, example from DLP projector viswavelength = 532 # nm, example from DLP projector emissionwavelength = 586 # nm # Define kinetic parameters for the chosen base concentration # kobs values from if baseppm == 1.0: kobs = 0.048 # s^-1 elif baseppm == 5.0: kobs = 0.20 # s^-1 elif baseppm == 15.0: kobs = 0.50 # s^-1 else: # Interpolate or use default if not specified in sources kobs = 0.20 # s^-1 return { "dye": "N-phenyl spirolactam rhodamine B", "solvent": solvent, "base": base, "baseconcmM": basemolarity, "uvwl": uvwavelength, "viswl": viswavelength, "emwl": emissionwavelength, "kobs": kobs } def generatevoxel3d(imagedata, displayconfig): """ Generates a 3D volumetric image by controlling UV and Visible light projectors. Args: imagedata: 3D array representing the desired voxel pattern (1 for on, 0 for off) displayconfig: Output from initializedisplay() Returns: None, controls projectors directly """ # Align projectors so UV and Visible beams cross in the solution # The intersection of the structured light patterns defines the voxel locations # For each frame of the animation/image: for frame in imagedata: # 1. Activate UV Projector # Project the UV pattern corresponding to the 'on' voxels in the current frame # This photoactivates the dye at the intersection points uvprojectoron(frame) # 2. Activate Visible Projector # Project the visible pattern corresponding to the 'on' voxels # This excites the activated dye to emit fluorescence visprojectoron(frame) # 3. Wait for emission # The dye emits light at 586 nm at the intersection # The duration of illumination determines the brightness/intensity # The thermal fading (kobs) determines how long the voxel persists after light is off waitms(framedurationms) # [G: Frame duration depends on display hardware and desired refresh rate] # 4. Turn off projectors uvprojectoroff() visprojectoroff() # 5. Allow thermal fading # The dye spontaneously returns to the 'off' state # The rate is controlled by kobs and base concentration # If the next frame requires a different pattern, the old voxels fade out # while new ones are activated in the next cycle waitms(framedurationms) # [G: Frame duration depends on display hardware and desired refresh rate] Voxel Size: Minimum voxel size of 0.68 \text{ mm}^3. Resolution: Reported as 200 mm (likely a typo for 200 µm or similar, but stated as 200 mm in text). Stability: Good stability over repeated 'on-off' cycles. Kinetics: Thermal fading rates range from 0.048 \text{ s}^{-1} to 0.50 \text{ s}^{-1} depending on base concentration. Strengths: Lack of moving parts, drastic simplification in voxel arrangement, widely accessible using commercial DLP projectors, no need for expensive high-energy beams. Limitations: Voxel size is relatively large (0.68 \text{ mm}^3); resolution is limited by the optical setup and dye kinetics; potential for irreversible coloration with prolonged UV illumination or certain solvents. When to use: Applications requiring accessible, low-cost volumetric 3D displays with moderate resolution and dynamic content. When not to use: Applications requiring high-resolution, small-voxel displays or those incompatible with chemical media. 3D Light PAD was reported in a 2017 Nature Communications paper by researchers from Southern Methodist University. It builds on the use of photoactivatable molecules, which are central to advances in super-resolution microscopy, data storage, molecular motors, and photopharmacology. The specific dye used, N-phenyl spirolactam rhodamine B, is a class of photoactivatable compounds that can be switched from a non-fluorescent to a fluorescent isomer using ultraviolet light. The system was developed to overcome obstacles in volumetric 3D display technology, such as complex fabrication, moving parts, high-speed projectors, or high laser powers. A volumetric three-dimensional digital light photoactivatable dye display, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms15239, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Particle Trapping and Manipulation
head: Free-space particle volumetric displays, Levitated particle displays
body: Particle Trapping and Manipulation renders 3D images in free space by suspending microscopic or millimetric particles using optical or acoustic forces and illuminating them to exploit persistence of vision. The family relies on the synchronization of particle position and illumination color/intensity. The core mechanism involves three stages: 1. Trapping: A force field (optical or acoustic) creates a potential well that confines a single particle against gravity and drag. 2. Scanning: The trap moves the particle along a 3D trajectory (x(t), y(t), z(t)) at a speed sufficient to blur the particle's motion into a continuous path via persistence of vision. 3. Illumination: A light source (lasers or LEDs) illuminates the particle synchronously with its position to generate specific voxels with defined colors. The choice of particle material and size is dictated by the trapping force: Optical Traps use absorbing particles (e.g., cellulose) to generate photophoretic forces via thermal creep in gas. Acoustic Traps use dielectric particles (e.g., expanded polystyrene) to experience radiation forces in standing waves. The control logic for frame generation follows a synchronized trajectory-illumination loop: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderparticletrapframe(traj, illummap, dt): """ Renders a single frame by synchronizing particle trajectory and illumination. Args: traj: List of 3D coordinates [(x1, y1, z1),...] for trap center. illummap: List of RGB tuples [(R1, G1, B1),...] synchronized with traj. dt: Time step between points (seconds). """ if len(traj) != len(illummap): raise ValueError("Trajectory and illumination map must have the same length.") imagebuffer = createempty3dvolume() for i in range(len(traj)): pos = traj[i] color = illummap[i] # Particle is at 'pos' and illuminated with 'color' # Persistence of vision blurs discrete points into continuous paths setvoxelcolor(imagebuffer, pos, color) return imagebuffer def setvoxelcolor(volume, position, rgb): voxelidx = quantizetogrid(position) volume[voxelidx] = rgb def createempty3dvolume(): return {} def quantizetogrid(position): # Standard grid quantization; implementation depends on display resolution return tuple(int(coord) for coord in position) A free-space display using photophoretic forces to trap a microscopic particle [6753-photophoretic-trap-volumetric-display.md]. It is distinguished by its use of near-invisible trapping lasers and RGB illumination, enabling high-resolution voxels (\approx 10 \mu m) and unconstrained viewing angles [6753-photophoretic-trap-volumetric-display.md]. Choose this method for high-resolution, full-color 3D images where optical safety and hardware complexity are secondary to image quality [6753-photophoretic-trap-volumetric-display.md]. A free-space display using acoustic radiation forces to trap a millimetric particle [11093-acoustophoretic-volumetric-display.md]. It is distinguished by its use of safe, low-cost ultrasonic phased arrays, allowing for a larger operational region (up to half a meter) without optical hazards [11093-acoustophoretic-volumetric-display.md]. Choose this method for larger-scale displays where safety and cost are priorities, accepting lower resolution and speed limitations compared to optical methods [11093-acoustophoretic-volumetric-display.md]. A method using bubbles excited by lasers in liquid as voxels. By increasing liquid viscosity, slow-floating bubbles are generated and arranged to stack 2D cross-sections, realizing volumetric image display. This system has a very long voxel residence time, requiring time for image refresh, but can express complex shapes. The concept of trapping particles for volumetric display was pioneered by Smalley et al. in 2018, who used a 405 \text{ nm} laser to trap \approx 10 \mu m cellulose particles in air, illuminating them with coaxial RGB lasers to generate voxels. This was the first method to adopt computer-hologram-based light irradiation patterns for volumetric displays, demonstrating that holographic design improves voxel count and brightness. Acoustic variants emerged earlier; in 2014, "Pixie Dust" proposed using 285 ultrasonic transducers across four speakers to create acoustic ponderomotive fields for levitating multiple particles. In 2019, Hirayama et al. demonstrated particle trapping using standing acoustic waves. The Kumagai method utilizes laser-excited bubbles in viscous liquids, offering long residence times for complex shape expression. ボリュメトリックディスプレイ, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jvrsj/29/3/2927/pdf/-char/ja, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display
head: OTD, Optical Trap Display, Photophoretic optical trapping display, Smalley Photophoretic Trap Display
body: A Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display (also known as the Optical Trap Display or OTD) is a free-space volumetric display that generates full-color, three-dimensional images in air using a single trapped particle illuminated by synchronized RGB lasers. It solves the "clipping" limitation inherent to holographic and light-field displays, where image points are physically separated from the scattering surface, thereby restricting viewing angles and preventing geometries such as long-throw projections or wrap-around displays. By co-locating the scattering surface (the particle) with the image point, the OTD provides a 360° in-plane viewing angle around every voxel at any depth, limited only by the optical axis itself. Inputs: An absorbing, opaque particle (typically cellulose) with a diameter d in the range of 5\text{--}100 \, \mu\text{m}. A near-invisible trapping laser at 405 \, \text{nm} wavelength. Collinear Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) lasers capable of varying power and position. Air at standard pressure and room temperature. Outputs: A free-space 3D image composed of voxels visible from all angles (except the optical axis line). The system relies on the physical state of the particle and the optical configuration rather than digital data structures for the image itself, though the control software must manage: 1. Trajectory Data: A time-parameterized 3D path (x(t), y(t), z(t)) for the trap center. 2. Illumination Map: A time-synchronized sequence of RGB intensity values (IR(t), IG(t), IB(t)) corresponding to the particle's position along the trajectory. Exact field sizes and bit-packing layouts are not given in the sources. 1. Isolation: A cellulose particle is isolated and confined in the photophoretic trap created by the 405 \, \text{nm} laser and the aberration optics. 2. Scanning: The trap (and the trapped particle) is scanned through the display volume. 3. Illumination: A system of collinear RGB lasers illuminates the trapped particle. 4. Image Formation: The combination of the scanned particle and synchronized RGB illumination forms a 3D image in free space. The trapping force is photophoretic, arising from thermal creep and radiometer effects due to uneven heating of the absorbing particle by the trap laser, rather than radiation pressure or gradient forces used in standard optical tweezers. Because the particle diameter (5\text{--}100 \, \mu\text{m}) is much larger than the gas mean free path (68 \, \text{nm} at standard pressure and room temperature), the system operates in the continuous regime. The photophoretic force in the continuous regime is given by: F{\text{cont}} = \frac{\pi d^2 R T}{3 \eta M p} \nabla T Where: F{\text{cont}} is the photophoretic force. d is the diameter of the particle. R is the universal gas constant. T is the temperature of the gas. \eta is the viscosity of the gas. M is the molecular weight of the gas. p is the gas pressure. \nabla T is the gradient of the temperature. Trap Wavelength: 405 \, \text{nm}. Illumination: RGB lasers. Particle Size: Demonstrated resolution \approx 10 \, \mu\text{m}; early trials used diameters ranging from below 5 \, \mu\text{m} to above 100 \, \mu\text{m}. Scanning Speed: 10 \, \text{Hz}. Optical Axis Occlusion: The image is visible from every angle with the possible exception of the line forming the optical axis, where the trap laser and illumination beams may obscure the view or cause glare. Particle Size Variance: Early trials used particles with diameters ranging from below 5 \, \mu\text{m} to above 100 \, \mu\text{m}. Consistent image quality requires precise control over particle size to maintain the continuous regime and optimal scattering. Gas Conditions: The force model depends on gas pressure, temperature, and viscosity. Changes in ambient conditions can alter the trap stiffness and particle dynamics. The following pseudocode describes the control logic for generating a single frame of the volumetric image. It assumes a pre-defined trajectory and illumination map. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderotdframe(traj, illummap, dt): """ Simulates the control logic for generating a single frame of the OTD. Args: traj: List of 3D coordinates [(x1, y1, z1), (x2, y2, z2),...] representing the trap center position over time. illummap: List of RGB tuples [(R1, G1, B1), (R2, G2, B2),...] representing the laser intensities synchronized with traj. dt: Time step between trajectory points (seconds). Returns: A dictionary mapping 3D positions to accumulated RGB color values. """ # Ensure trajectory and illumination map are synchronized if len(traj) != len(illummap): raise ValueError("Trajectory and illumination map must have the same length.") # Initialize an empty dictionary to accumulate color at each spatial position imagebuffer = {} # Scan the particle through the volume for i in range(len(traj)): pos = traj[i] color = illummap[i] # Accumulate color at the current position to simulate persistence of vision if pos not in imagebuffer: imagebuffer[pos] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Simple averaging accumulation for the current frame currentcolor = imagebuffer[pos] imagebuffer[pos] = [ (currentcolor[0] + color[0]) / 2.0, (currentcolor[1] + color[1]) / 2.0, (currentcolor[2] + color[2]) / 2.0 ] return imagebuffer Time Complexity: The frame rate is limited by the mechanical or optical scanning speed of the trap. Demonstrated scan rates were 10 \, \text{Hz}. Memory Complexity: Not applicable in the traditional sense, as the image is generated physically in space. However, control software requires memory proportional to the trajectory length and illumination map size. Measured Performance: Demonstrated image points are approximately 10 \, \mu\text{m} in dimension. Images exhibit full color, fine detail, and low apparent speckle. Scaling: The system is capable of producing image geometries that are currently unobtainable with holographic and light-field technologies, such as long-throw projections, tall sandtables, and 'wrap-around' displays. Strengths: Free-space imaging without screens or scattering surfaces. Full-color, low-speckle images. Ability to create geometries impossible for holograms, such as long-throw projections, tall sandtables, and wrap-around displays. Limitations: Limited to single-particle scanning (though multiple particles could theoretically be trapped, the described system uses one). Requires absorbing particles (cellulose) and specific gas conditions. The optical axis may be a blind spot. When to use: Applications requiring unconstrained viewing angles, long-throw projection, or interaction with the image volume (e.g., touch interaction) where holographic clipping is prohibitive. When not to use: Applications requiring high pixel counts or static images without motion, or environments where gas conditions cannot be controlled. The Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display, also referred to as the Optical Trap Display (OTD), was introduced by Smalley et al. in 2018. It advances the state of the art by providing full-color, free-space images with fine detail, overcoming the limitations of earlier levitation displays that were too coarse or inertial. The technology leverages photophoretic optical trapping, which is particularly useful for confining micrometer-diameter absorbing particles using thermal forces rather than radiation pressure. The system was demonstrated producing images such as a butterfly and the Earth, with voxel dimensions of approximately 10 \, \mu\text{m}. name: Acoustophoretic Volumetric Display
head: AVD, Acoustophoretic-trap free-space volumetric display
body: An Acoustophoretic Volumetric Display (AVD) renders 3D graphics in free space by trapping a millimetric dielectric particle using acoustic radiation forces from a phased ultrasonic array and moving it rapidly along a 3D trajectory while synchronously illuminating it with colored light. Unlike optical traps that rely on photophoretic forces and high-power lasers, AVDs use standing acoustic waves to create potential wells, offering a larger operational region (up to half a meter) and avoiding laser safety hazards, though they currently support smaller, simpler shapes at high speeds compared to Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D graphic defined as a sequence of particle positions (x, y, z) at time t and corresponding RGB color values. Output: A visible 3D volumetric image formed by the persistence of vision of the illuminated, moving particle. Data Structures and Hardware Layout The system relies on a specific hardware control chain and signal parameters: 1. Particle: Expanded Polystyrene (EPS) sphere, diameter d \approx 1.5 mm. 2. Transducer Array: 60 ultrasonic transducers (Murata MA40S4S) arranged in two opposed arrays of 30 transducers each. 3. Control Chain: PC \rightarrow UART (1.5 Mbauds) \rightarrow FPGA (ALTERA CoreEp4CE6) \rightarrow MOSFET drivers (TC4427a) \rightarrow Transducers. 4. Signal Parameters: Square waves generated by the FPGA. Phase resolution: \pi/64 rad. Color depth: 8-bit signal per RGB channel. 5. Working Volume: Approximately 4 \times 5 \times 8 cm^3. Algorithm Steps 1. Trajectory and Color Definition: Represent the desired 3D graphic as a sequence of target positions (xi, yi, zi) at discrete times ti and associated RGB color values Ci = (Ri, Gi, Bi). 2. Color Transmission: Send the 8-bit RGB signal for each channel to the RGB LED source positioned adjacent to the acoustic levitator. 3. Phase Calculation: For each target position (xi, yi, zi), calculate the required emission phases \phi{j,i} for each of the 60 transducers j to focus the acoustic field and create an antinode at the target location. 4. FPGA Control: Transmit the calculated phases to the FPGA. The FPGA generates square waves with the specified phase resolution (\pi/64 rad) for each of the 60 channels. 5. Amplification: The FPGA signals are sent to MOSFET drivers (TC4427a), which amplify the signals using an external DC power supply to drive the transducers. 6. Acoustic Trapping: The transducers emit ultrasonic waves, creating a standing wave field with an antinode at the calculated position. The particle is trapped in this potential well. 7. Illumination and Movement: Move the trap (by updating phases) to the next position (x{i+1}, y{i+1}, z{i+1}) while illuminating the particle with color Ci. The particle follows the trap, scattering the light to form a voxel. 8. Persistence of Vision: Repeat steps 3-7 rapidly enough that the human eye perceives a continuous 3D path. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import time NUMTRANSDUCERS = 60 PHASERESOLUTION = math.pi / 64 UARTBAUD = 1500000 class UART: def init(self, baudrate): self.baudrate = baudrate def send(self, data): pass # Standard serial transmission class FPGA: def init(self): self.phases = [0.0] NUMTRANSDUCERS def setphases(self, phases): self.phases = phases uart.send(phases) class MOSFETDriver: def init(self): pass def amplify(self, signal): pass # Amplifies FPGA signal to DC supply voltage class RGBLED: def setcolor(self, r, g, b): pass # Outputs 8-bit per channel def calculatephases(targetx, targety, targetz, transducerpositions): # The sources state phases are calculated for the target position but do not provide the explicit formula. # Standard phased-array focusing computes phase delays based on transducer-to-target distances. phases = [] for tx, ty, tz in transducerpositions: distance = math.sqrt((targetx - tx)2 + (targety - ty)2 + (targetz - tz)2) rawphase = 2 math.pi distance / 0.004 # Standard wavelength-dependent phase shift quantized = round(rawphase / PHASERESOLUTION) PHASERESOLUTION phases.append(quantized) return phases def rendervolumetricimage(trajectory, transducerpositions): uart = UART(UARTBAUD) fpga = FPGA() mosfet = MOSFETDriver() led = RGBLED() for x, y, z, r, g, b in trajectory: led.setcolor(r, g, b) phases = calculatephases(x, y, z, transducerpositions) fpga.setphases(phases) mosfet.amplify(fpga.phases) time.sleep(0.01) # Standard delay for particle equilibrium response Edge Cases and Pitfalls Particle Size Constraints: Particles >1.5 mm invalidate the small particle assumptions in the Gor’kov model, causing force per unit volume to decrease. Particles <0.5 mm are swept out by air currents because drag force (scaling with area) becomes significant relative to acoustic radiation force (scaling with volume). Static Calibration Deviation: Equilibrium points deviate from ideal focal points by approximately 0.5 mm due to scattering, temperature variations, manufacturing inaccuracies, or transducer position errors. This affects image accuracy. Dynamic Distortion: Increasing particle velocity distorts the shape of the volumetric image and can eject the particle from the trap. Static calibration becomes less effective at higher speeds due to the nonlinear dynamics of the particle in the acoustic field. Speed Limitations: At 10 Hz rendering frequency, only small and simple shapes (size 5-6 mm) can be achieved. Performance: Renders simple figures in real time at 10 frames per second (fps). Raster Images: Rendered at lower frame rates; draw times were 20 seconds for logos/stop signs and 5 seconds for a 3D wireframe airplane in static tests. Limitations: High-speed rendering is currently limited to small (5-6 mm) and simple shapes. Dynamic distortion increases with drawing speed. Comparison to Photophoretic Displays: AVDs offer a larger operational region (up to half a meter) and avoid high-power laser hazards, but are currently limited to smaller shapes at high speeds compared to Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Displays (OTD), which can reach speeds of 1.8 m/s. The Acoustophoretic Volumetric Display was proposed as a free-space volumetric display technology that utilizes acoustic radiation forces to levitate and move particles, addressing the clipping and limited field of view issues associated with holograms and light-field displays. The work builds on previous attempts to create free-space displays using acoustophoresis, such as Ochiai et al.'s crosses and grids, Sahoo et al.'s flip-screen particles, and Uno et al.'s LED levitation. The specific implementation described uses a phased array of 60 ultrasonic transducers controlled by an FPGA to trap and move a 1.5 mm EPS particle. name: Multi-View and Parallax-Based Rendering
body: Multi-View and Parallax-Based Rendering generates volumetric or holographic imagery by computing multiple distinct perspective views of a scene and displaying them on hardware that separates these views spatially or angularly to create a 3D effect. It differs from single-view volume rendering by explicitly managing view-dependent parallax, and from full wave-optics holographic CGH calculation by typically relying on rasterized or pre-computed view extraction, setting it apart from sibling methods like Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering and Drawing Space Separation (DSS) which use physical scanning or spatial separation. A hardware-accelerated method for generating stereoscopic images of volumetric datasets for display on multi-view lenticular screens without glasses. It computes N distinct perspective views from offset focal spots and composites them into a single interlaced bitmap where each sub-pixel (R, G, B) samples from a different view. Choose this when rendering scalar volumetric data on lenticular displays. A rendering technique that projects four synchronized views of a 3D scene onto a four-sided acrylic pyramid to create a floating volumetric image visible from all sides. It differs from multi-view lenticular rendering by using physical reflection parity via a pyramid rather than optical lenses, requiring independent rotation and mirroring of each view to correct for the acrylic's reflection properties. Choose this for 360-degree holographic displays using acrylic pyramids. A pre-processing framework for rendering Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) on autostereoscopic light-field displays. It consists of four sequential steps applied to the hologram to acquire reconstruction images corresponding to views from a camera rotating around the scene. The resolution of these images equals the 2D resolution of the screen. The steps are: view extraction, where a window with the resolution of the vertical axis of the hologram moves along the horizontal axis to acquire sub-holograms that simulate a pinhole camera view; suppression of aperture diffraction (apodization); back propagation, which numerically reconstructs the view using only 1D FFTs with a pre-computed kernel due to the same distance; and colour balancing. The computational complexity is O(NM) for V views and a hologram with M \times N resolution. Performance tests on a 3.3 GHz Intel Core i7-5820 CPU with Windows 8 (x64) recorded processing times per view for the 'Dice' dataset (142,903 points) as: View extraction 0.04s, Apodization 0.38s, Back propagation 16.33s, Colour balancing 1.19s. The system renders on an Holografika HoloVizio 722RC light field display (72 projectors, 70° viewing angle), extracting 70 views with an angular resolution of 1° and a 2D resolution of 1280x768 pixels. The concept of multi-view rendering for volumetric displays has evolved alongside autostereoscopic and light-field display technologies. The specific framework for rendering CGHs on autostereoscopic displays was proposed to address the need for high-end 3D visualization of holograms. The method leverages parallel computing and raster OpenGL graphics to manage the computational load of view extraction and back propagation. Three-dimensional rendering of computer-generated holograms acquired from point-clouds on light field displays, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.2237581, fetched 2026-11-04

name: Multi-view Lenticular Volume Rendering
head: GPU-accelerated volume rendering to 3D lenticular displays
body: A method for hardware-accelerated generation of multi-view stereoscopic images of volumetric datasets for display on a multi-view lenticular screen, using the GPU for both rendering and compositing. It solves the problem of interactive visualization of large 3D medical volumes on glasses-free 3D displays by decomposing the scene into perspective projections from offset focal spots and interlacing them into a single bitmap. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling the asymmetric frustum geometry required for lenticular lenses and performing the final sub-pixel interlacing via a static texture map lookup on the GPU, rather than pre-computing a hologram or projecting from separate physical sources. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., medical CT/MRI), lenticular display parameters (focal distance f, view count N, camera spacing d), and the dataset dimensions. Output: A single interlaced bitmap suitable for the LCD panel underlying the lenticular sheet. Data Structures: 1. Bricks: The volumetric dataset is divided into 3D blocks ("bricks") to fit within the graphics card's texture memory and align with its memory architecture. 2. Texture0 (View Map): A static 2D texture map storing the view number for each sub-pixel (R, G, B) of the output image. This is pre-calculated based on the lenticular lens geometry and remains constant for all frames. 3. Texture1 (View Stack): A single wide rectangular 2D texture map storing all N rendered views vertically next to each other. Each view occupies a horizontal strip of height H{view} = H{LCD} / N. Parameters: N: Number of views. The specific implementation uses N=9, but the method applies to any N. f: Focal distance of the lenticular lenses. d: Distance between adjacent view camera positions. Resolution: Each individual view has an effective resolution of (1/N) of the LCD matrix resolution in the horizontal direction. Steps: 1. Data Partitioning: Divide the input volumetric dataset into bricks suitable for GPU texture memory. 2. View Rendering Loop: For each view index n from 0 to N-1: a. Frustum Setup: Define an asymmetric perspective projection frustum for view n. The camera position is offset from the center. The projection coordinates (x', y') for a world point (x, y, z) are calculated as: x' = \frac{(x - n \cdot d) \cdot f}{f - z} + n \cdot d y' = \frac{y \cdot f}{f - z} b. Direct Volume Rendering (DVR): Render the volume using the defined frustum. Rays are cast from the focal spot through each pixel. The volume rendering integral is approximated by traversing rays in back-to-front order using the over operator: C{n+1} = \alphan \cdot cn + (1 - \alphan) \cdot Cn where Cn is the intermediate color value, \alphan is the opacity, and cn is the color at sample n. This is implemented using standard alpha blending (e.g., DirectX or OpenGL) on textured slices. c. Storage: Store the resulting image for view n in the n-th vertical strip of Texture1. 3. Compositing: Generate the final interlaced image by parsing every pixel of the output LCD resolution. For each pixel, read the view numbers for the Red, Green, and Blue components from Texture0. Sample the corresponding view from Texture1 for each color channel to construct the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlenticularvolume(volumedata, lenticularparams, lcdresolution): N = lenticularparams.N f = lenticularparams.f d = lenticularparams.d viewheight = lcdresolution[1] // N # Step 1: Pre-calculate view map (Texture0) # For each pixel (px, py) in the LCD, determine which view index # corresponds to R, G, and B channels based on lens geometry. # This is static and computed once. viewmap = computeviewmap(lcdresolution, lenticularparams) # Step 2: Render each view # Texture1 is a 2D texture of size (width, height N) texture1 = [[0.0] (lcdresolution[0] lcdresolution[1] N) for in range(1)] for n in range(N): # Define asymmetric frustum for view n frustum = computeasymmetricfrustum(n, d, f) # Render volume to a temporary buffer for this view viewbuffer = [[0.0] 3 for in range(lcdresolution[0] viewheight)] # Divide the volumetric dataset into bricks to fit within texture memory # Render the volume using the defined frustum. Rays are cast from the focal spot through each pixel. # The volume rendering integral is approximated by traversing rays in back-to-front order # using the over operator: C{n+1} = alphan cn + (1 - alphan) Cn # This is implemented using standard alpha blending on textured slices. # The sources do not give the exact ray-marching and brick traversal algorithm. for brick in volumedata: for y in range(viewheight): for x in range(lcdresolution[0]): # Simulate alpha blending step for each sample along the ray pass # Store viewbuffer in the n-th vertical strip of Texture1 for y in range(viewheight): for x in range(lcdresolution[0]): idx = x + (n viewheight + y) lcdresolution[0] texture1[0][idx] = viewbuffer[y lcdresolution[0] + x] # Step 3: Composite final image finalimage = [[0.0] 3 for in range(lcdresolution[0] lcdresolution[1])] for py in range(lcdresolution[1]): for px in range(lcdresolution[0]): # Get view indices for R, G, B from the static map viewr, viewg, viewb = viewmap[px, py] # Sample from Texture1 yr = viewr viewheight + (py % viewheight) yg = viewg viewheight + (py % viewheight) yb = viewb viewheight + (py % viewheight) idxr = px + yr lcdresolution[0] idxg = px + yg lcdresolution[0] idxb = px + yb lcdresolution[0] colorr = texture1[0][idxr] colorg = texture1[0][idxg] colorb = texture1[0][idxb] finalimage[px + py lcdresolution[0]] = (colorr, colorg, colorb) return finalimage def computeasymmetricfrustum(n, d, f): def project(x, y, z): xproj = ((x - n d) f) / (f - z) + n d yproj = (y f) / (f - z) return (xproj, yproj) return project def computeviewmap(lcdresolution, lenticularparams): # Pre-calculates which view index corresponds to R, G, B for each pixel. # This depends on the physical alignment of the LCD sub-pixels under the lenticular lenses. # Not given in the sources. return [[(0, 0, 0)] lcdresolution[0] for in range(lcdresolution[1])] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: The dataset must be divided into bricks to fit within the graphics card's texture memory. Resolution Trade-off: Each view has a lower resolution (1/N of LCD width), which may reduce detail per view but allows for interactive frame rates. Static Geometry: The view map (Texture0) is static; it assumes the display and camera setup do not change during runtime. A refractive optical component consisting of a linear array of thick plano-convex cylindrical lenses (lenticules) used in multiview autostereoscopic displays to direct light from a 2D screen into distinct viewing zones. It generates multi-view stereoscopic images without requiring glasses, acting as a transparent, high-efficiency alternative to parallax barriers. Unlike parallax barriers which block light, lenticular sheets refract it, offering better brightness and higher potential resolution, though it suffers from limited per-view resolution (1/N of the display resolution for N views) and strict alignment requirements. Choose this component when hardware-accelerated glasses-free 3D visualization is required and brightness/resolution trade-offs are acceptable. Performance: Up to 15 frames per second for a 256^3 voxel dataset on a nine-view lenticular display. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated interactive manipulation of large datasets (>100 MB); no glasses required for the viewer; leverages standard GPU primitives (alpha blending, texture sampling). Limitations: Requires specific lenticular hardware; resolution per view is reduced; asymmetric frustum calculations add complexity to the projection step. The method was proposed by Daniel Ruijters from Philips Medical Systems. It addresses the growing size of volumetric medical imaging data and the need for interactive 3D visualization without glasses. The approach builds on Direct Volume Rendering [2] and multi-view display principles [3, 5, 6, 7] cited in the original paper. GPU-accelerated volume rendering to 3D lenticular displays, https://lirias.kuleuven.be/bitstream/123456789/235668/1/GPUVolumeRenderingtoLenticularDisplay7.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Lenticular Sheet
head: Lenticular Array, Lenticular Lens Array
body: A lenticular sheet is a refractive optical component consisting of a linear array of thick plano-convex cylindrical lenses, known as lenticules, used in multiview autostereoscopic displays to direct light from a 2D screen into distinct viewing zones. It solves the problem of generating multi-view stereoscopic images without requiring viewers to wear glasses, functioning as a transparent, high-efficiency alternative to parallax barriers. Unlike parallax barriers which block light, lenticular sheets refract it, offering better brightness and higher potential resolution, though it suffers from limited per-view resolution (1/N of the display resolution for N views) and strict alignment requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D LCD screen displaying a spatially multiplexed image; a lenticular sheet placed in front of the screen. Output: A multiview 3D image where different viewing angles perceive different perspectives (views) of the volumetric or stereoscopic content. Data Structures and Layout: The lenticular sheet consists of a periodic array of cylindrical lenses. The key geometric parameter is the lens pitch (width of one lenticule). The 2D LCD screen has a pixel grid. The system requires precise physical alignment between the lens pitch and the LCD pixel columns. Steps: 1. Spatial Multiplexing: Divide the horizontal resolution of the 2D display screen among N distinct views. For every N vertical pixel columns on the LCD, one column is assigned to a single view. For example, in a 5-view system, every 5th column carries data for the same view. 2. Alignment: Physically align the lenticular lenses with the vertical pixel columns of the 2D LCD screen. The lenses must be parallel to the vertical pixel boundaries to ensure correct refraction. 3. Refraction: Light from each pixel column passes through the corresponding cylindrical lens. The lens refracts the light rays so that they converge into specific viewing zones (viewing windows) in space. 4. Viewing: A viewer positions their eyes within a correct view zone. Each eye receives light from a specific subset of pixels, creating a stereoscopic pair. Head movement allows the viewer to experience motion parallax as they move between view zones. Formulas and Parameters: Let N be the number of views. Let W{screen} be the horizontal resolution of the display in pixels. The horizontal resolution per view, W{view}, is: W{view} = \frac{W{screen}}{N} The pitch of the lenticular array (P{lens}) must match the width of the group of pixels assigned to one view (P{pixel} \times N, where P{pixel} is the pixel pitch). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Loss: The resolution of an individual view is essentially 1/N of the original display resolution. Alignment Sensitivity: Misalignment between the lenticular sheet and the LCD pixel columns causes cross-talk between views and image distortion. Image Flips: Incorrect alignment or viewing position can cause one eye to see the image intended for the other eye, resulting in incorrect stereo perception. Picket Fence Problem: Similar to parallax barriers, lenticular displays can suffer from the "picket fence" effect, where the viewer sees the gaps or boundaries between views. Limited Viewing Windows: The number of distinct viewing zones is limited by the number of views N and the optical design. A display variant using an array of lenses (where lenslet width > pitch), an LCOS projector, and an LCD panel, where the lens array steers light from the projector to the viewer's eye location determined by an eye-tracking system. The LCOS projector image consists of a series of dots designed for the lens array to focus onto the viewer's eye locations. The primary pitfall is low optical efficiency, as only a small portion of light from the LCOS projector is used for directional backlight. Uses liquid crystal (LC) material whose shape is controlled to serve as an optical lens in front of a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM), directing light beams to desirable directions in real time. Voltage applied between ITO layers forms the shape of LC cells into an array of optical lenses equivalent to a lenticular lens array. Multiple electrodes (MeD LC Lens) can be used to better control the lens shape than conventional two-electrode lenses. The LC lens shape can be dynamically changed at the image refreshing rate to allow active scanning of light beams for multiview generation, projecting high frame rate images from the SLM in a time-sequential fashion. A major pitfall is irregularity of LC alignment in the boundary region, causing serious cross-talk and image deterioration. Unlike fixed lenticular displays, it is electronically switchable between 2D and 3D modes, preserving native SLM resolution in 2D mode. A technique to compensate for resolution loss by slanting the lenticular lens structure or rearranging color filter pixels to distribute resolution loss into both horizontal and vertical directions. The LCD is located in the focal plane of the lenticular sheet, mapping horizontal position on the LCD to viewing angle. Points on specific lines (e.g., line A-A) are aligned to direct specific views (e.g., view 3) in a given direction. The flipping effect is reduced by ensuring predominant view contribution with some contribution from adjacent views (e.g., view 3 predominates with some contribution from view 2 on line A-A). This technique is used in 3D TV products by Vizio, Stream TV Networks, Alioscopy, RealD, Philips, Sharp, Toshiba, and TLC. A technique to address resolution loss by splitting conventional square pixels into N portions, each covered by special lenticular arrays directing RGB portions to different view directions. The conventional square pixel is split into N portions, and special lenticular arrays are designed to cover each portion with different optics. Each portion of RGB is directed toward a different view direction. While it suffers from the conventional drawback that horizontal resolution for each view is only 1/N of the SLM's native resolution in HPO systems, this design allows each view to have the pixel resolution of the original LCD, unlike conventional lenticular displays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Lenticular-based displays offer better brightness and higher possible resolution than parallel-barrier-based displays. Scaling: Resolution per view scales inversely with the number of views (1/N). Strengths: Utilizes existing 2D screen fabrication infrastructure; implementation is relatively simple and low cost; higher optical efficiency than parallax barriers due to transparency. Limitations: Limited resolution per view; significant effort required for alignment; cross-talk between views and image flips; picket fence problem; limited number of viewing windows. When to use: When high brightness and simple hardware implementation are prioritized over high per-view resolution, and when the display can be viewed from a fixed or limited set of positions. When not to use: When high per-view resolution is critical, or when the viewing environment requires dynamic, eye-tracked positioning without additional complexity. The concept of using a one-dimensional (1D) lenticular array for stereoscopic display was patented by Hess in 1912. The technique is part of the broader field of refraction-based multiview 3D display techniques. It is widely used in commercial 3D TV products, with manufacturers such as Vizio, Stream TV Networks, Alioscopy, RealD, Philips, Sharp, Toshiba, and TLC adopting slanted lenticular variants. Prototypes of high-resolution multiview displays using specialized LCD and lenticular arrays have been developed by NLT for industrial applications. name: Projector with a Lenticular Mirror Sheet
head: Lenticular Mirror Sheet Projection, Reflective Lenticular Display
body: A projection-based multiview display that uses a single projector and a reflective lenticular mirror sheet as the screen to direct reflected beams toward different viewing perspectives. It differs from transmissive lenticular displays by using reflection, allowing for brighter images and potentially simpler optical alignment in certain form factors, and from multiprojector systems by requiring only one light source. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single projector, a reflective lenticular mirror sheet (a sheet of cylindrical lenses with a reflective backing), and a multiview image content stream. Output: A 3D image visible from multiple discrete horizontal viewpoints. Data Structures: The lenticular sheet consists of a linear array of thick plano-convex cylindrical lenses (lenticules). The sheet is reflective, meaning the back surface of the lenses or a layer behind them reflects light. The projector image is spatially partitioned into strips, where each strip corresponds to the field of view of one or more lenticules. Steps: 1. Image Preparation: The multiview image content is split into horizontal strips. Each strip contains the pixel data intended for the specific angular range covered by a corresponding lenticule strip on the screen. 2. Projection: The projector projects these multipixel image strips onto the surface of the lenticular mirror sheet. The projector is positioned such that its optical axis intersects the screen at a specific angle and distance. 3. Optical Refraction and Reflection: Light from the projector enters the curved surface of the lenticular lenses. The curvature of the cylindrical lenses refracts the light. Due to the geometry of the lenticules and the position of the projector, the light is directed towards the reflective backing. The light reflects off the mirror layer. Upon exiting the lenses (second pass through the lens material), the light is refracted again. 4. Viewpoint Separation: The combined effect of the two refractions (entry and exit) and the reflection directs the light from each projector pixel strip into a specific, narrow angular cone. Different strips are directed to different angles, creating distinct viewing zones (views) for the observer. 5. Calibration: The system requires precise calibration of the projector's position, angle, and the projected image geometry relative to the lenticular sheet's pitch and focal length to ensure that each view is correctly aligned with the corresponding lenticule strip. Formulas and Parameters: The relationship between the projector position, lenticule pitch (p), lens focal length (f), and viewing angle (\theta) determines the mapping. While exact formulas are not provided in the sources, the principle relies on the lens equation and Snell's Law applied to the cylindrical geometry. Typical parameters include the lenticule pitch (often in the range of hundreds of micrometers to millimeters depending on resolution requirements) and the focal length of the lenticules, which must match the projector's throw distance and angle to focus the image correctly on the reflective surface and then collimate or direct it to the viewer. Pitfalls: Calibration Sensitivity: Misalignment between the projector and the lenticular sheet results in crosstalk between views or blurred images. The calibration is sensitive to the projector's position and the screen's location. Precision: The projection image must be carefully calibrated to the lenticular screen location to produce a multiview 3D display. A variant using multiple projectors, each creating images for a single view, projected onto a special lenticular reflective screen. In the vertical direction, diffuse light in all directions. In the horizontal direction, light is focused onto the reflective diffuser screen and projected back to the projector direction. Light passes through the vertically oriented lenticular screen twice: first, lenses focus projector pixels onto the diffuse screen; second, lenses redistribute pixels back to the same angular direction. This method preserves the resolution of projected images for each view and is scalable without significant cost increase compared to spatial multiplex methods, unlike the single-projector approach which may have lower per-view resolution if the projector's resolution is shared. However, it suffers from exorbitant expense due to one projector per view and difficulty of calibration, as maintaining optical calibration for many projectors is challenging. Experimental systems have been produced with more than 100 views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The single-projector design is less expensive than multiprojector systems but may have lower per-view resolution if the projector's total resolution is divided among views. The multiprojector variant preserves full resolution per view. Strengths: High optical efficiency due to reflection; scalable screen size in multiprojector variants; capable of producing high-quality 3D images with many views (e.g., >100 views). Limitations: Single-projector systems require precise calibration and may have limited viewing angles or resolution. Multiprojector systems are expensive and difficult to calibrate. When to use: When high brightness and good optical efficiency are required, and when the cost of multiple projectors can be justified (multiprojector) or when a simpler, lower-cost setup is needed with acceptable resolution/view trade-offs (single projector). This method was proposed by Krah at Apple. It is part of the broader field of projection-based multiview 3D displays. Similar displays have been demonstrated in various laboratories. Three-dimensional display technologies, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4269274, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Rendering Framework for Autostereoscopic Displays
head: Hologram Pre-processing Framework for Light Field Displays
body: This framework preprocesses a computer-generated hologram (CGH) to generate a set of reconstruction images corresponding to views from a camera rotating around the scene, enabling the display of holograms on autostereoscopic light field displays. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric holographic data on displays that lack continuous depth but offer discrete multi-view parallax. It differs from standard multi-view rendering by operating directly on the holographic aperture data to preserve diffraction effects, rather than rendering geometric primitives. The framework consists of four sequential pre-processing steps applied to the hologram to acquire a set of reconstruction images. The resolution of these images equals the 2D resolution of the screen. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A computer-generated hologram (CGH) of resolution M \times N. Output: A set of reconstruction images (views) corresponding to the display's angular coverage. Data Structures: Hologram: A 2D array of complex values representing the holographic aperture. Views: A sequence of 2D images, each with resolution matching the screen's 2D resolution (e.g., 1280 \times 768). Steps: 1. View Extraction: A window with the resolution of the vertical axis of the hologram moves along the horizontal axis to acquire sub-holograms that simulate a pinhole camera view. The number of views is determined by the targeted field of view (FOV) and angular resolution. Overlapping apertures can be chosen to improve rendering quality. 2. Suppression of Aperture Diffraction (Apodization): This step suppresses diffraction artifacts caused by the finite aperture of the extracted views. The specific mathematical operation is not detailed in the provided notes, but it is applied to the sub-holograms obtained in Step 1. 3. Back Propagation: Numerical back propagation is performed on the apodized sub-holograms to reconstruct the light field at the display plane. This step requires only 1D Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs) with a pre-computed kernel due to the constant distance. 4. Colour Balancing: Color balancing is applied to the reconstructed views to ensure correct color reproduction on the display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderhologramtoviews(hologram, numviews, screenresolution): """ Pre-processes a hologram to generate views for an autostereoscopic display. Args: hologram: 2D array of complex values, shape (M, N). numviews: Integer, number of views to extract. screenresolution: Tuple (width, height), resolution of the output views. Returns: list of 2D arrays, each representing a view. """ views = [] # Step 1: View Extraction # A window of height equal to the hologram's vertical axis moves along the horizontal axis. # The number of views is determined by the FOV and angular resolution. # Note: Exact windowing function and stride are not specified in sources. subholograms = extractviews(hologram, numviews) processedviews = [] for subholo in subholograms: # Step 2: Suppression of aperture diffraction (Apodization) # Apply apodization to suppress diffraction artifacts. # Note: Specific apodization function/window is not detailed in sources. apodizedholo = applyapodization(subholo) # Step 3: Back propagation # Numerical back propagation using 1D FFTs with pre-computed kernel. # Note: The exact propagation distance and kernel formula are not detailed in sources. reconstructedview = backpropagate(apodizedholo) # Step 4: Colour balancing # Apply color balancing to the reconstructed view. # Note: Specific color balancing algorithm is not detailed in sources. balancedview = applycolorbalancing(reconstructedview) processedviews.append(balancedview) return processedviews def extractviews(hologram, numviews): """ Extracts sub-holograms by moving a window along the horizontal axis. Note: Implementation details (window size, stride, overlap) are not provided in sources. """ # Placeholder for view extraction logic based on description. # The window resolution equals the vertical axis of the hologram. pass def applyapodization(subhologram): """ Suppresses aperture diffraction. Note: Specific apodization method is not provided in sources. """ pass def backpropagate(apodizedholo): """ Performs numerical back propagation using 1D FFTs. Note: Specific kernel and distance parameters are not provided in sources. """ pass def applycolorbalancing(view): """ Applies color balancing. Note: Specific algorithm is not provided in sources. """ pass Parameters: Number of Views: Determined by the display's viewing angle and angular resolution. For a 70° viewing angle with 1° angular resolution, 70 views are extracted. View Resolution: Equals the 2D resolution of the screen (e.g., 1280 \times 768 pixels). Camera Focus: The camera is typically focused at the front part of the object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: FOV and Complexity: Larger FOVs require more views, increasing computational complexity. Occlusion Handling: The framework handles occlusion in the numerical reconstruction, but specific details are not provided. A reflection-based autostereoscopic display that uses a beam combiner to superimpose left/right LCD images, with field lenses directing illumination to appropriate eyes to avoid pixel registration tolerances. A field lens is placed at the focus of a real (aerial) image to collimate rays passing through without affecting geometry. Two LCD panels display left and right views, superimposed by a beam combiner. Field lenses direct illumination beams into the appropriate eye, making the right-view image appear dark to the left eye and vice versa. Head-tracking illumination requires movable light sources, e.g., monochrome CRTs displaying high-contrast camera images of the left and right halves of the observer’s face. Multiple-user access is possible using multiple independent illuminators. Proposed by Woodgate et al.. Time Complexity: The computational complexity of the framework is O(NM), where N and M are the dimensions of the hologram. Performance: On a 3.3 GHz Intel Core i7-5820 CPU with Windows 8 (x64), for the 'Dice' dataset (142,903 points), processing times per view were: View extraction 0.04s, Apodization 0.38s, Back propagation 16.33s, Colour balancing 1.19s. Hardware: Tested on an Holografika HoloVizio 722RC light field display (72 projectors, 70° viewing angle). Scaling: The back propagation step is the most computationally expensive, requiring 1D FFTs with a pre-computed kernel due to the same distance. Strengths: Preserves diffraction effects of the hologram; suitable for high-end 3D visualization on light field displays. Limitations: High computational cost, especially for back propagation; requires pre-processing for each hologram. The framework was proposed for the three-dimensional rendering of computer-generated holograms acquired from point-clouds on light field displays. It addresses the challenge of displaying holographic data on autostereoscopic displays that use an array of projectors to create a light field. The Holografika HoloVizio 722RC display, used in the experiments, is a scalable light field system design based on a specially arranged array of 72 projectors.
