name: Four-View Hologram Compositor
head: FourViewCompositor, Pepper's Ghost volumetric display rendering
body: The Four-View Hologram Compositor is a rendering technique that projects four synchronized perspective views of a 3D scene onto a four-sided acrylic pyramid to create a floating volumetric image via the Pepper's Ghost illusion. It differs from lenticular or light-field systems by using physical reflection parity rather than angular sampling, requiring independent rotation and mirroring of each view to match the geometry of the pyramid's reflective surfaces. The method generates four perspective views from cameras arranged in a circle around the scene center, renders them to separate texture targets, and composites them onto a single screen using textured quads with specific transformations to align with the physical pyramid. Inputs: A 3D scene graph (objects, lights), camera parameters (elevation, FOV), and calibration data (pyramid scale, global rotation, per-view scale, rotation, and position offsets). Outputs: A single 2D bitmap displayed on a screen, which serves as the light source for the holographic pyramid. The implementation uses the following structures: 1. ViewSlot: Represents one of the four views. name: Enum ViewName ('front', 'right', 'back', 'left'). camera: A PerspectiveCamera instance. target: A WebGLRenderTarget with RGBAFormat, LinearFilter, and a depth buffer. quad: A Mesh using PlaneGeometry. material: A MeshBasicMaterial with AdditiveBlending, transparent: true, depthTest: false, and depthWrite: false. 2. VIEWLAYOUT: A constant mapping view names to their geometric properties: front: azimuth 0, dir [0, -1] right: azimuth \pi/2, dir [1, 0] back: azimuth \pi, dir [0, 1] left: azimuth -\pi/2, dir [-1, 0] elevation: Camera elevation angle above the object in degrees. Default: 12^\circ. fov: Field of view for the perspective cameras in degrees. Default: 42^\circ. pyramid.scale: Global scaling factor for the pyramid geometry. view.scale: Per-view scaling factor. view.rotation: Per-view rotation offset. mirrorX, mirrorY: Boolean flags for texture mirroring. 1. Initialize Cameras and Targets: Create four PerspectiveCamera instances and four WebGLRenderTarget instances. Configure targets with RGBAFormat, LinearFilter, and depth buffers. 2. Position Cameras: For each view in VIEWLAYOUT: Calculate horizontal distance: d{\text{horiz}} = \cos(\text{elevation}) \times \text{distance}. Calculate vertical height: d{\text{vert}} = \sin(\text{elevation}) \times \text{distance}. Set camera position: \begin{aligned} x &= \sin(\text{azimuth}) \times d{\text{horiz}} \\ y &= d{\text{vert}} \\ z &= \cos(\text{azimuth}) \times d{\text{horiz}} \end{aligned} Call lookAt(target) and updateProjectionMatrix(). 3. Create Composite Quads: For each view, create a Mesh with PlaneGeometry and MeshBasicMaterial (AdditiveBlending, transparent, no depth test/write). These quads will display the rendered views. 4. Render Views: For each frame: For each ViewSlot: Set the renderer's render target to the slot's target. Clear the renderer. Render the scene using the slot's camera. Set the renderer's render target back to the screen (previous target). Clear the renderer. Render the compositeScene (containing the four quads) using an orthographic compositeCamera. 5. Calibrate Composite Quads: Apply calibration to each quad's position, scale, rotation, and texture mirroring: Calculate base size: s{\text{base}} = \min(\text{width}, \text{height}) / 2. Calculate global rotation from calibration data. For each slot: Rotate the view direction vector by the global rotation. Scale by s{\text{base}} \times \text{pyramid.scale} \times \text{view.scale}. Add position offsets to determine quad position. Set quad scale to (s, s, 1) where s is the calculated size. Set quad rotation.z to \text{globalRot} + \text{view.rotation}. Apply texture mirroring: Set tex.repeat to (-1, 1) or (1, -1) based on mirrorX/mirrorY flags. Set tex.offset to (1, 0) or (0, 1) to compensate for the repeat flip. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math PI = math.pi VIEWLAYOUT = { 'front': {'azimuth': 0.0, 'dir': (0.0, -1.0)}, 'right': {'azimuth': PI / 2.0, 'dir': (1.0, 0.0)}, 'back': {'azimuth': PI, 'dir': (0.0, 1.0)}, 'left': {'azimuth': -PI / 2.0, 'dir': (-1.0, 0.0)} } def initsystem(width, height, distance, elevationdeg, fovdeg): cameras = [] targets = [] quads = [] for name, layout in VIEWLAYOUT.items(): # Create camera and target cam = {'fov': fovdeg, 'position': (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)} target = {'width': width, 'height': height, 'format': 'RGBA'} quad = {'position': (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 'scale': (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), 'rotationz': 0.0, 'texrepeat': (1.0, 1.0), 'texoffset': (0.0, 0.0)} # Position camera elevrad = math.radians(elevationdeg) dhoriz = math.cos(elevrad) distance dvert = math.sin(elevrad) distance az = layout['azimuth'] cam['position'] = (math.sin(az) dhoriz, dvert, math.cos(az) dhoriz) # lookAt(target) and updateProjectionMatrix() are standard camera ops cameras.append(cam) targets.append(target) quads.append(quad) return cameras, targets, quads def renderframe(scene, cameras, targets, quads, calibration, width, height): # 1. Render four views for i in range(4): # Set render target to targets[i], clear framebuffer, render scene with cameras[i] pass # 2. Composite # Set render target to screen, clear framebuffer basesize = min(width, height) / 2.0 globalrot = calibration['globalrotation'] for i in range(4): viewcal = calibration['views'][i] layout = VIEWLAYOUT[viewcal['name']] # Rotate view direction vector by global rotation dirvec = layout['dir'] cosr = math.cos(globalrot) sinr = math.sin(globalrot) rotateddir = (dirvec[0] cosr - dirvec[1] sinr, dirvec[0] sinr + dirvec[1] cosr) # Scale and offset scalefactor = basesize calibration['pyramidscale'] viewcal['scale'] pos = (rotateddir[0] scalefactor + viewcal['offset'][0], rotateddir[1] scalefactor + viewcal['offset'][1], 0.0) quads[i]['position'] = pos quads[i]['scale'] = (scalefactor, scalefactor, 1.0) quads[i]['rotationz'] = globalrot + viewcal['rotation'] # Apply texture mirroring if viewcal['mirrorX']: quads[i]['texrepeat'] = (-1.0, quads[i]['texrepeat'][1]) quads[i]['texoffset'] = (1.0, quads[i]['texoffset'][1]) else: quads[i]['texrepeat'] = (1.0, quads[i]['texrepeat'][1]) quads[i]['texoffset'] = (0.0, quads[i]['texoffset'][1]) if viewcal['mirrorY']: quads[i]['texrepeat'] = (quads[i]['texrepeat'][0], -1.0) quads[i]['texoffset'] = (quads[i]['texoffset'][0], 1.0) else: quads[i]['texrepeat'] = (quads[i]['texrepeat'][0], 1.0) quads[i]['texoffset'] = (quads[i]['texoffset'][0], 0.0) # Render composite scene with orthographic camera pass Opaque Quads: Using opaque quads for compositing causes the last drawn view to paint black corners over adjacent views, creating visible rectangular bites. This is solved by using AdditiveBlending, as the scene renders emissive marks on black, and black adds nothing, allowing overlapping corners to contribute zero. Mirroring vs. Culling: Mirroring via negative scale breaks backface culling. Therefore, texture mirroring is achieved via tex.repeat and tex.offset rather than mesh scaling. Scissor Passes: Scissor viewport passes cannot rotate or mirror views independently, which is required because the reflection parity through the acrylic is not knowable in advance. Time Complexity: The cost is four scene passes plus one composite pass. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for four render targets (width \times height \times 4 bytes per pixel for RGBA). Measured Performance: Holds 60 fps comfortably on a phone because the scene consists of a handful of additive primitives. Strengths: No headset or glasses required; viewable from every side; real-time interaction via hand gestures. Limitations: Requires a physical acrylic pyramid; limited to scenes that fit within the pyramid's field of view; performance depends on the complexity of the 3D scene rendered in four passes. When to Use: When a physical, glasses-free volumetric display is desired for presentations, education, or interactive installations. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Four-View Hologram Compositor is based on the Pepper's Ghost illusion, adapted for modern mobile devices and 3D models. It was implemented as part of the hologram-system project by Ojasra Kulkarni, which integrates hand tracking via MediaPipe and WebSocket communication to control the rendered views in real time. The system is designed for applications in engineering, medical imaging, product presentation, and education. ojasra0kulkarni/hologram-system, https://github.com/ojasra0kulkarni/hologram-system, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Directional Backlight Autostereoscopic Rendering
head: 3M Directional Backlight Design, 48-view 3D display with sequential LED switching and parallax barrier, Directional Backlight for Full-Resolution Autostereoscopic 3D, Four-Direction Backlight with 12-View Parallax Barrier, Multidirectional Backlight Autostereoscopic Display, Multidirectional Backlight Autostereoscopic Rendering, Multidirectional Backlighting Using Lenslet Arrays
body: Directional Backlight Autostereoscopic Rendering is a technique that uses directional backlight mechanisms and high-speed LCD panels to generate optically distinct viewing regions in a time-multiplexed fashion, providing full resolution for each view. It solves the resolution trade-off inherent in static parallax barriers and lenticular lenses by ensuring that every pixel on the display contributes to a single view at any given instant, rather than being split across multiple views. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Multi-view Lenticular Volume Rendering and Rendering Framework for Autostereoscopic Displays, is the decoupling of view generation from the display surface optics; instead of modulating light at the screen plane, it modulates the direction of the backlight source itself, allowing the use of standard LCD panels without complex micro-optic alignment. The method relies on synchronizing a time-multiplexed directional backlight with the image content displayed on an LCD panel. The core principle is that at any moment t, only one directional backlight source is active, illuminating the LCD panel from a specific angle. The LCD panel displays the corresponding view for that angle. By switching the backlight direction and the LCD image in sync, the viewer perceives a full-resolution 3D image. Inputs: N: The number of directional backlight sources (views generated by the backlight). F{3D}: The frame rate of the desired 3D image content (Hz). I{viewi}: The image data for view i, where i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}. Hardware configuration: LED matrix layout, prism/lens array geometry, and LCD panel specifications. Outputs: Synchronized control signals for the LCD panel (displaying I{viewi}). Synchronized control signals for the LED matrix (activating source i). The implementation requires managing two primary data streams synchronized by a global timer or hardware trigger: 1. LCD Frame Buffer: Stores the current view image I{viewi}. The resolution is the full native resolution of the LCD panel (e.g., 800 \times 480 or 1920 \times 1080). 2. LED State Vector: A binary mask or index indicating which LED group is active. For an N-direction backlight, this vector cycles through N states. 1. Initialize Hardware: Configure the LCD panel refresh rate F{LCD} to be N \times F{3D}. Initialize the LED matrix to all-off state. 2. Select View Index: Set current view index i = 0. 3. Activate Backlight: Turn on the LED group corresponding to direction i. Ensure all other LED groups are off. Note: In designs with a light guide and prisms, the physical displacement of the LED and the prism angle determine the direction. 4. Display Image: Load and display the pre-rendered view image I{viewi} on the LCD panel. 5. Wait for Refresh: Hold the image and backlight state for the duration of one LCD frame period (1/F{LCD}). 6. Increment Index: Set i = (i + 1) \mod N. 7. Repeat: Go to Step 3. LCD Refresh Rate Requirement: F{LCD} = N \times F{3D} Where N is the number of directional backlight sources. Brightness per View: B{view} = \frac{B{total}}{N} Where B{total} is the total luminous flux of the backlight source, and B{view} is the brightness perceived in each specific viewing zone. Crosstalk: Crosstalk is reduced to less than 10% with optimized design parameters, specifically by aligning the 3D film structures (nanometer scale ~1–30 nm) with the light guide prisms. Light Guide Thickness: 0.5 mm (Polymethyl methacrylate). 3D Film Structure: Nanometer scale (~1–30 nm) lenticular and prism structures. LCD Refresh Rate: 120 Hz for 2-view display (yielding 60 Hz 3D frame rate). 240 Hz for 4-direction backlight (yielding 60 Hz 3D frame rate). Viewing Angle: \pm 40^\circ (in 48-view configurations). Total Views: 48 (4 directions \times 12 views from parallax barrier). Display Size: 9 inches (22.86 cm) WVGA (800 \times 480) demonstrated. High-Speed LCD Requirement: The LCD panel must support a refresh rate N times the desired 3D frame rate. If the LCD cannot switch fast enough, ghosting or flicker occurs. Low Brightness: Since light is time-multiplexed, the brightness in each direction is 1/N of the total light output. For large N, this can result in a dim image. Alignment: While some designs (like the 3M design) claim no alignment is required between the 3D film and LCD pixel structure, precise alignment between the LED matrix and the directional prism array is critical for directing light to the correct viewing zones. Flicker Perception: Proper synchronization is required to avoid flicker. The time-multiplexing must be fast enough that the human eye integrates the views. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directionalbacklightrendering(ledmatrix, lcdpanel, views, ndirections, targetfps): """ Renders autostereoscopic 3D using directional backlight time-multiplexing. Args: ledmatrix: Object controlling LED groups. Has methods turnon(groupid) and turnoff(groupid). lcdpanel: Object controlling the LCD. Has method displayimage(imagedata). views: List of N image arrays, one for each backlight direction. ndirections: Number of distinct backlight directions (N). targetfps: Desired 3D frame rate for the viewer. """ # Calculate required LCD refresh rate lcdrefreshrate = ndirections targetfps frameduration = 1.0 / lcdrefreshrate # Initialize ledmatrix.turnoffall() currentviewindex = 0 while True: # 1. Activate the specific backlight direction # In hardware, this might involve switching LED groups sequentially ledmatrix.turnon(currentviewindex) # 2. Display the corresponding view on the LCD # The LCD must be fast enough to update within frameduration lcdpanel.displayimage(views[currentviewindex]) # 3. Wait for the frame period # In a real system, this wait is often handled by V-sync or hardware timers wait(frameduration) # 4. Prepare for next view currentviewindex = (currentviewindex + 1) % ndirections # Optional: Turn off all LEDs briefly if hardware requires blanking # ledmatrix.turnoffall() An autostereoscopic display technique that uses a parallax barrier combined with multiple parallel strip backlight sources to direct light specifically to a viewer's eye positions. It solves the fixed viewing zone limitation of static parallax barriers by dynamically selecting active light sources based on real-time eye tracking, ensuring correct image formation for the left and right eyes. It differs from its parent Directional Backlight Autostereoscopic Rendering by using a physical barrier structure with segmented backlights rather than time-multiplexed directional emission, and from Adaptive Parallax Barrier with Subbarriers by using full strip sources rather than subbarrier adjustments. A 2D/3D switchable backlight design where the light guide functions as a parallax barrier and backlight, using side-placed light sources and internal reflective surfaces. In 3D mode, light rays from side sources bounce between reflective surfaces inside the light guide and are reflected toward the LCD panel at scattering patterns corresponding to parallax barrier slits, providing a 3D resolution of 960 \times 360 pixels per view. In 2D mode, 3D backlights are OFF and 2D backlights are ON, providing full resolution 1080p (1920 \times 1080 pixels). Time Complexity: The rendering complexity per frame is O(1) relative to the number of views, as each frame displays only one view. However, the system must generate N views per 3D frame, so the total rendering load is N times that of a 2D display. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N view images if pre-rendered, or sufficient buffer space to render them sequentially. The LCD buffer size is constant (full resolution). Measured Performance: Demonstrated on a 9-inch WVGA display with crosstalk reduced to less than 10%. Viewing angles of \pm 40^\circ were achieved in 48-view configurations. Scaling: Scaling to more views (N) linearly increases the required LCD refresh rate and linearly decreases the brightness per view. Strengths: Avoids flicker perception and eliminates view reversal, a common cause of viewer fatigue. Provides full LCD resolution for each view. Compact package size suitable for mobile devices. Limitations: Low brightness in each direction (1/N of total output). Requires high-speed LCD panels. Complex hardware alignment for prism/lens arrays. When to Use: When full resolution per view is critical and the display size is small to medium (e.g., mobile devices, desktop monitors). When Not to Use: When high brightness is required without additional amplification, or when the display size is very large (where alignment tolerances become prohibitive). Directional Backlight Autostereoscopic Rendering originated from research into full-resolution autostereoscopic 3D displays for mobile devices. Key contributions include the 3M Directional Backlight Design by Schultz and St. John, which proposed a compact design using a light guide with shallow prisms and a fast-switching LCD. Sony contributed a 2D/3D switchable backlight design using a light guide that functions as both backlight and parallax barrier. Wei and Huang proposed a four-direction backlight with a 12-view parallax barrier for a 48-view display, using a sequentially switchable LED matrix and dual-directional prism array. Kwon and Choi implemented multidirectional backlighting using LCD panels and lenticular lens arrays, where LCD columns correspond to specific light projection directions. These techniques are primarily used in volumetric 3D display research and commercial autostereoscopic displays for mobile and desktop applications. Three-dimensional display technologies, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4269274, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Eye-Tracking Position Adaptive Display (Parallax Barrier Variant)
head: Adaptive Parallax Barrier with Eye-Tracking
body: An autostereoscopic display technique that uses a parallax barrier combined with multiple parallel strip backlight sources to direct light specifically to a viewer's eye positions. It solves the fixed viewing zone limitation of static parallax barriers by dynamically selecting active light sources based on real-time eye tracking, ensuring correct image formation for the left and right eyes. It differs from its parent Directional Backlight Autostereoscopic Rendering by using a physical barrier structure with segmented backlights rather than time-multiplexed directional emission, and from Adaptive Parallax Barrier with Subbarriers by using full strip sources rather than subbarrier adjustments. Inputs: Viewer’s left eye position (xL, yL) and right eye position (xR, yR), detected by an eye-tracking system. Display panel resolution and geometry. Configuration of multiple parallel strip backlight sources. Outputs: Activated backlight strips corresponding to the viewer’s eye positions. Image data rendered for the left and right eyes directed through the selected strips. Data Structures: Eye Position Data: A pair of 2D coordinates (x, y) for each eye. Not given in the sources. Backlight Source Map: A list or array of parallel strip identifiers, each associated with a specific angular emission zone or spatial region. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Eye Tracking: Detect the current 2D position of the viewer’s left eye (xL, yL) and right eye (xR, yR) using an eye-tracking camera or sensor. 2. Source Selection: An adaptive controller determines which parallel strip backlight sources are aligned with the detected eye positions. 3. Activation: The controller turns on the properly selected light source(s) to form images directed to the viewer’s left eye position and right eye position. 4. Rendering: Render the appropriate left-eye and right-eye views through the activated strips. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatedisplay(eyeleftpos, eyerightpos, backlightstrips): """ Select and activate backlight strips based on eye positions. Args: eyeleftpos: Tuple (x, y) of left eye position. eyerightpos: Tuple (x, y) of right eye position. backlightstrips: List of backlight strip objects, each with a method isalignedto(eyepos) returning True if the strip directs light to the eye. Returns: List of activated strip identifiers. """ activatedstrips = [] # Select strip for left eye for strip in backlightstrips: if strip.isalignedto(eyeleftpos): activatedstrips.append(strip.id) break # Assume one primary strip per eye or handle multiple # Select strip for right eye for strip in backlightstrips: if strip.isalignedto(eyerightpos): activatedstrips.append(strip.id) break return activatedstrips Parameters: Number of parallel strip backlight sources: Not given in the sources. Eye-tracking latency: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If the viewer moves outside the range of available backlight strips, no optimal source may be selected. Precision of eye-tracking affects the accuracy of source selection. An eye-tracking method that uses multiple subbarriers to adjust the viewing zone location based on detected eye positions. It differs from the main variant by using subbarriers for finer adjustment of the viewing zone rather than selecting from distinct parallel strip backlight sources. Choose this when finer spatial control of the viewing zone is required. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of backlight strips and eye-tracking update rate. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of backlight strips and eye position storage. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides autostereoscopic 3D without glasses, adapts to viewer position. Limitations: Requires eye-tracking hardware, limited by the number of backlight strips. When to use: Single-user or limited multi-user scenarios where eye position is known and tracked. When not to use: When eye-tracking is unavailable or when multiple users are at widely different positions. Originated from attempts to make dynamic changes in the optical and electronic design of 3D display systems to adaptively optimize them based on the current position of the viewer’s eyes. Wang et al. designed a parallax-barrier-type autostereoscopic display device with multiple parallel strip backlight sources and an eye-tracking technique. Wu et al. proposed an adaptive parallax barrier scheme using multiple subbarriers. These developments aim to fulfill the needs of providing autostereoscopic 3D display functionality for single-user application scenarios. name: Multiple Layered Screens Display
head: Light Field Display, Multiplane Display, Polarization Field Display
body: Multiple Layered Screens Display is a volumetric display technique that stacks multiple 2D displays (such as LCDs, OLEDs, or optical stops) to create a depth illusion via parallax or by halting projected light at specific depth layers. It differs from sibling methods like Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM) by using static, discrete depth planes rather than a single moving surface, and from Varifocal Mirror Display by fixing the focal planes physically rather than optically adjusting them. The core mechanism involves decomposing a 3D scene into discrete depth slices and rendering each slice to a corresponding physical layer in a stack. 1. Layer Decomposition: The source 3D geometry or image is chopped into different depth layers. Each layer corresponds to a specific z-coordinate in the display volume. 2. Parallel Rendering: Each layer is rendered as a 2D image. If head or eye tracking is incorporated, multiple viewpoints are rendered in real-time for each layer to provide true 3D parallax. 3. Synchronization: The display of each layer must be synchronized. In active projection systems, the projection of image sections is synchronized with the activation state of the layers. 4. Optical Stacking: The layers are physically stacked. Light from each layer contributes to the final perceived volume. The depth resolution is strictly limited by the number of physically stackable displays. A static screen multilayer LCD 3D volume visualization display using multiple electronically switchable polymer dispersed liquid crystal (PDLC) layers stacked. An image projector projects sequential sections of a 3D image onto the PDLC screens, synchronized with activation. Mechanism: The PDLC sheets stay optically clear when no voltage is applied, but become scattering when voltage is applied. The timing of image projection from a high-speed image projector is synchronized with the ON/OFF state of each LC sheet to display 2D sections of a 3D image in proper 3D locations. Parameters: The PDLC switching speed must be faster than 0.1 ms. Pitfalls: Switching Speed: For a 100 Hz refresh rate and 100 layers, the switching time per sheet is 1/(100 \times 100) = 100 \mu s = 0.1 ms. This is 1 to 2 orders of magnitude faster than commercially available LC material can achieve. Brightness: With only 50 \mus maximum exposure time (considering ON/OFF transit time), it is difficult to achieve reasonable image brightness. Additionally, optical transmission loss occurs; even with 97% efficiency per layer, light intensity drops to 50% after 35 layers and 25% after 40 layers. Uses a fully addressable LCD panel with gray-scale transmittance values in each pixel to modulate the light field generated by the display system. The tensor display technique utilizes compressive light field optimization to synthesize transmittance values on multiple layers of LCD screens. Mechanism: A unified optimization framework based on nonnegative tensor factorization allows joint multilayer, multiframe light field decompositions. The target light field is defined to have both horizontal and vertical parallax to produce 3D displays with both parallax types. Advantages: Significantly reduces artifacts compared to previous methods. A variant developed by LightSpace Technologies (formerly Depthcube) that uses a high-speed projector and a series of about 20 LCDs used as optical stops. Mechanism: Each layer of depth is halted at the correct location by the optical stops. Special antialiasing techniques are used to smooth the physical space between layers so it does not feel stepped. Usage: Primarily used in engineering or medical applications. A consumer implementation using 2 stacked LCDs. Mechanism: The bottom layer alternates dark bands so that each eye sees the version of the image intended for it, creating a stereoscopic effect rather than a true volumetric depth. Uses 12 angled layers. The concept of layered volumetric displays has been developed since the early 2000s. Key implementations include the Nintendo 3DS (2 layers), MIT Media Lab’s Polarization Field Display, RENDER from WOW (OLEDs), and LightSpace Technologies' Depthcube (~20 layers). The technology is primarily used in engineering, medical applications, and consumer electronics. name: Volumetric LED Display
head: 3D Volume LED Display, Aoshow 3D Volumetric LED Display, Suspended LED volumetric display, Voxel Array: LED Matrix
body: A Volumetric LED Display creates 3D images floating in physical space by arranging individually addressable LEDs in a 3D volume. Unlike flat screens that offer a fixed frontal perspective, this method allows viewing from all angles by utilizing suspended, independently controllable LED strings. It trades visual fidelity for multi-angle access, as the opaque nature of LEDs introduces occlusion and cross-illumination issues. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D animation data (voxel positions and color values). Output: Illuminated LEDs forming a 3D image in physical space. Data Structures: The hardware consists of modules mounted on the ceiling. Each module suspends a set of LED strings. Module: Contains N{strings} LED strings. LED String: A linear array of LEDs. LED: An individually addressable light source. Voxel Grid: The logical 3D coordinate system (x, y, z) mapped to physical LED positions. Layout and Parameters: Spacing: LEDs are spaced at a fixed interval d in all directions (x, y, z). A prototype uses d = 5 cm. String Length: Maximum string length L{max} = 10 meters. String Count: A module may contain up to 100 LED strings. Resolution: A prototype achieved an 8 \times 8 \times 8 grid, totaling 512 voxels. Numbered Steps: 1. Mapping: System software maps the 3D animation data to the specific spatial positions of each LED in the physical array. 2. Transmission: Color data is transmitted to the hardware controller via Art-Net or HDMI protocols. 3. Illumination: LEDs illuminate at their mapped positions to form the 3D image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumetricled(voxeldata, ledgrid): """ Renders 3D voxel data to a physical LED grid. Args: voxeldata: List of tuples (x, y, z, r, g, b) representing active voxels. ledgrid: 3D array or hash map representing the physical LED positions. Keys are (x, y, z) coordinates. Values are LED objects with methods: setcolor(r, g, b), turnoff(). Returns: None. Updates the state of the LEDs. """ # Step 1: Initialize all LEDs to off state for led in ledgrid.values(): led.turnoff() # Step 2: Map voxel data to LED positions for (x, y, z, r, g, b) in voxeldata: # Check if a physical LED exists at this position if (x, y, z) in ledgrid: led = ledgrid[(x, y, z)] # Step 3: Illuminate the LED led.setcolor(r, g, b) else: # Voxel position has no corresponding LED; data is ignored pass # Note: Transmission via Art-Net or HDMI is handled by the hardware driver # outside of this logical rendering step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Occlusion: Because LEDs are opaque, LEDs in the foreground block the view of LEDs in the background from certain angles. Cross Illumination: Light from one LED may scatter and illuminate neighboring LEDs or the surrounding space, reducing contrast and color accuracy. Resolution Limits: High-resolution systems are challenging to implement due to manufacturing constraints and the physical size of LEDs. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of active voxels Nv and the number of LEDs Nl. Mapping is O(Nv) if using a hash map, or O(1) per voxel if using a direct array lookup. Transmission time depends on the protocol (Art-Net/HDMI) and bandwidth. Memory Complexity: Storage for the LED grid is O(Nl). Measured Performance: A prototype achieved 8 \times 8 \times 8 (512 voxels) with 5 cm spacing. Strengths: True 3D viewing from all angles; no special glasses required; physically tangible imagery. Limitations: Low visual fidelity compared to flat displays; limited resolution due to LED size and spacing; occlusion and cross-talk artifacts; large physical footprint for high resolution. When to use: Art installations, advertising, and demonstrations where multi-angle viewing is more important than high resolution. When not to use: Applications requiring high-resolution, high-contrast imagery or detailed close-up viewing. The concept of using 3D matrices of LEDs for volumetric display has been explored by various research groups. An 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxel prototype was developed by Wyatt at MIT. Commercial implementations include the LEDPulse Dragon displays and the Aoshow 3D Volumetric LED Display, which uses suspended LED strings mounted on ceiling modules. name: Hidden Surface Removal
head: Manual Occlusion Clipping, Viewpoint-Based Line Clipping
body: Hidden Surface Removal is a technique used in volumetric displays to manually hide surfaces behind other objects based on the user's viewpoint, compensating for the lack of natural occlusion inherent in volumetric displays. Volumetric displays are incapable of exhibiting occlusion because the light illuminating a voxel is omnidirectional. The method clips line primitives that are not visible relative to an estimated eye position, allowing users to take turns viewing a more realistic scene. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D line primitives representing the scene geometry; the 3D positions of two users (tracked via head-mounted devices or "hats"); and a mode selection parameter. Output: A subset of the original line primitives that are visible to the selected viewpoint(s), which are then rendered to the volumetric display. Data Structures: Hat Position: A 3D vector \mathbf{P}{hat}^{(i)} for user i \in \{1, 2\}, obtained from tracking hardware. Eye Offset: A 3D vector \mathbf{O}{eye} representing the offset from the hat to the midpoint between the user's eyes. Eye Position: The estimated eye position \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(i)} is calculated as \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(i)} = \mathbf{P}{hat}^{(i)} + \mathbf{O}{eye}. Line Primitive: Defined by endpoints \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{B} in 3D space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Eye Positions: For each user i \in \{1, 2\}, determine the hat position \mathbf{P}{hat}^{(i)} from the tracking system. 2. Apply Eye Offset: Calculate the eye position \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(i)} using a default offset vector \mathbf{O}{default} or a calibrated offset \mathbf{O}{calibrated}. If higher precision is required, run a short calibration program to determine \mathbf{O}{calibrated}. 3. Select Viewpoint: Choose the active viewpoint based on the mode selected in the options dialog box: Mode 1: Use \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(1)}. Mode 2: Use \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(2)}. Mode 3 (Merged): Use both \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(1)} and \mathbf{P}{eye}^{(2)} to determine the union of visible lines. 4. Clip Lines: For each line primitive in the scene, determine if it is visible from the selected viewpoint(s). The algorithm clips all lines which are not visible based on the location of the midpoint between the user's eyes. 5. Render: Send the filtered set of lines to the volumetric display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hiddensurfaceremoval(lines, user1hatpos, user2hatpos, mode, eyeoffset): """ lines: List of Line objects with endpoints A and B. user1hatpos: 3D vector for User 1's hat. user2hatpos: 3D vector for User 2's hat. mode: Integer, 1 for User 1, 2 for User 2, 3 for Merged. eyeoffset: 3D vector from hat to eye midpoint. """ eye1 = user1hatpos + eyeoffset eye2 = user2hatpos + eyeoffset visiblelines = [] for line in lines: isvisible = False if mode == 1: if islinevisiblefrom(line, eye1): isvisible = True elif mode == 2: if islinevisiblefrom(line, eye2): isvisible = True elif mode == 3: if islinevisiblefrom(line, eye1) or islinevisiblefrom(line, eye2): isvisible = True if isvisible: visiblelines.append(line) return visiblelines def islinevisiblefrom(line, eyepos): # The source does not specify the exact occlusion test. # Standard implementation: cast a ray from eyepos through the line midpoint. # Check for intersections with other opaque geometry closer to the eye. # Return True if no closer intersection exists. return True Parameters: Eye Offset: A 3D vector. Default value is not specified, but a calibration program can determine the exact offset. Mode: Integer (1, 2, or 3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Collaborative Conflict: HSR can only be done for a single user in Modes 1 and 2, as a surface hidden from one user may be visible to another. Merged Mode Effectiveness: The effectiveness of the merged mode depends on the relative location of the users. Calibration Accuracy: Using a default eye offset may lead to inaccurate occlusion culling if the user's head position relative to their eyes varies significantly. Divides the display space into separate viewports for each user, allowing both to see their own view with accurate HSR, unlike the merged or single-user modes of HSR. Generates multiple views to provide parallax cues, whereas HSR explicitly removes occluded geometry to simulate depth [S1, 16463-multi-view-and-parallax-based-rendering.md]. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of line primitives, as each line must be tested for visibility. Performance: The algorithm is updated in real-time based on the user's viewpoint. Strengths: Provides a more realistic view of the scene by removing occluded geometry, which is otherwise impossible in volumetric displays due to omnidirectional light emission. Limitations: Cannot provide accurate HSR for multiple users simultaneously in Modes 1 and 2; the merged mode (Mode 3) is less effective when users are in different relative positions. When to Use: When a single user needs a realistic view of a complex scene, or when two users are willing to take turns viewing the scene with accurate occlusion. When Not to Use: When two users need to see the scene simultaneously with accurate occlusion; in this case, Drawing Space Separation (DSS) is a better alternative. Hidden Surface Removal in the context of volumetric displays was introduced in the paper "Collaborative interaction with volumetric displays". The work addresses the fundamental limitation of volumetric displays: the inability to exhibit natural occlusion because light illuminating a voxel is omnidirectional. The authors implemented three modes of HSR to support collaborative interaction between two users, allowing them to manually hide surfaces behind other objects based on their viewpoint. The technique was tested in observation sessions with volunteer users familiar with volumetric displays. Collaborative interaction with volumetric displays, https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357118, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Elementary building blocks
body: This family provides the fundamental geometric and computational primitives required to construct a volume rendering pipeline. It addresses the foundational tasks of defining the viewing geometry (rays) and executing rendering computations efficiently on modern hardware. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by providing the low-level infrastructure—ray parameterization and parallel execution models—upon which higher-level techniques are built. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Computes geometric intersection between parametric rays and scene primitives to determine hit distances. It sets itself apart from Ray-marching by relying on exact analytical solutions rather than iterative stepping, and from Ray-box intersection by encompassing a broader set of geometric shapes. Choose this when identifying which objects a viewing ray encounters for early rejection or spatial bounds. Defines the geometric mapping from discrete 2D pixel coordinates to continuous 3D world-space rays. It sets itself apart from Ray-primitive intersection by focusing solely on ray geometry creation rather than traversal. Choose this when establishing a valid view frustum and constructing camera basis vectors. Encompasses fundamental computational mechanisms to map volume rendering tasks onto parallel hardware architectures. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing on the execution model and data movement primitives rather than geometric algorithms or high-level rendering strategies. Choose this when distributing work across thousands of threads to solve computational bottlenecks. The concept of ray generation is rooted in computer graphics since the advent of ray tracing. Parallel execution primitives have evolved with the rise of GPUs, becoming essential for real-time volume rendering. name: Ray-primitive intersection
head: Ray-object intersection, Ray-scene intersection, Ray-primitive tests
body: Ray-primitive intersection computes the geometric intersection between a parametric ray and a specific scene primitive (e.g., box, triangle, sphere, volume) to determine entry/exit points or hit status. It solves the fundamental problem of identifying which objects a viewing ray encounters, enabling early rejection of non-intersecting geometry and providing the spatial parameters (t) required for shading, sampling, or traversal. It sets itself apart from Ray-marching by relying on exact analytical solutions for specific primitive shapes rather than iterative fixed-step evaluation, and from Ray-box intersection by encompassing the broader algorithmic strategies and generic interfaces used to accelerate these tests in volume rendering contexts. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. The Ray-box intersection method (specifically the Slab Test) computes the parametric entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) distances of a ray intersecting an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). It solves the problem of determining the valid sampling interval along a ray for volume rendering or ray tracing, enabling early rejection of rays that miss the volume or primitives. It sets itself apart from Ray-box intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders by using an analytical arithmetic approach rather than geometric shader primitives, and from Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method) by operating on the bounding box of the volume rather than the volume's internal structure directly. This method determines if a ray intersects a triangle in 3D space using Plücker coordinates to evaluate the winding order of the triangle edges relative to the ray. It handles arbitrary ray directions and is distinct from barycentric approaches like Möller-Trumbore by relying on cross-product-based Plücker line coordinates rather than solving a linear system for barycentric weights. The Ray Crossing Count method determines whether a query point lies inside, outside, or on the boundary of a closed triangle mesh by casting rays and counting signed intersections with the mesh geometry. It solves the point-in-mesh containment problem required for interior testing in volume rendering algorithms like Marching Cubes. Unlike simple binary hit tests, this method computes a generalized winding number: it returns exactly 1 for points inside a closed, outward-oriented mesh, 0 for points outside, and a continuous value between 0 and 1 for points near holes or in non-manifold configurations. A point outside the object yields 0, no point yields values < 0, and points inside yield exactly 1. A method to render a volumetric sphere by intersecting camera rays with the sphere geometry to determine entry and exit points, then applying Beer's Law along the chord length. It calculates the parametric distances (t) where a ray enters and exits the sphere to compute the optical path length, which is used to determine transmittance and scattered light contribution. Unlike Ray-box intersection which handles axis-aligned bounding volumes, this method provides an exact analytical solution for spherical primitives, serving as a foundational building block for simple volumetric scenes before advancing to complex density fields or Ray-Marching techniques. The Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method) is a two-step procedure to determine if a viewing ray intersects the data volume and to find the entry point for volume traversal. It calculates distances from the ray origin to each of the six faces of the volume geometry, divides by the corresponding ray direction component, and selects the smallest valid distance as the nearest impact point. This family covers algorithms for determining the intersection of a ray with a tetrahedron, a fundamental operation in volume rendering on unstructured grids and tetrahedral mesh rendering. It solves the problem of finding the entry and exit points (and their parametric distances) of a ray as it traverses a tetrahedral cell. The methods differ in their geometric representation (Plücker coordinates, barycentric coordinates, plane equations) and optimization strategies (early exits, GPU wave intrinsics, connectivity-based traversal). Key distinctions include the use of Plücker coordinates to avoid explicit plane intersections Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection, the use of linear algebra for point containment Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates, and the use of mesh shaders for parallel evaluation Mesh Shader Tetrahedron Intersection Optimization. Computes the closest point on a triangle to a query point and returns the squared distance, handling all edge and vertex cases via Voronoi-region decomposition. It differs from Ray-primitive intersection by solving a static point-to-mesh query rather than a ray-scene traversal, and from General Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates) by returning the geometric closest point rather than an intersection parameter. This family of methods determines the intersection between a ray and a surface defined implicitly by a scalar field function f(\mathbf{x}) = 0 (or f(\mathbf{x}) - v = 0 for an isovalue v). Unlike explicit mesh intersection, these methods solve the root-finding problem ft(t) = 0 for the smallest t > 0 along the ray \vec{p}(t) = \vec{o} + t\vec{d} without extracting a proxy triangle mesh. They are distinguished from sibling geometric primitives (e.g., Ray-box intersection) by their reliance on function evaluation and numerical root-finding rather than analytic geometric formulas, and from sibling SDF methods (e.g., SDF Raycast Collision Detection) by their broader applicability to general implicit surfaces beyond simple collision detection. Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation computes the intersection of a viewing ray with a flat surfel rectangle in its local (u, v) coordinates using a homography approximation around the center of the screen-space bounding box. It sets itself apart from the reference 2DGS formulation by replacing the per-pixel cross-product-based inversion with a precomputed affine approximation, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. LinPrim Gradient Computation computes the gradients of intersection depths \mathbf{i} with respect to the ray-space triangle corners \mathbf{v}^{\text{ray}} to enable differentiable rendering of linear primitives. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by backpropagating gradients through a linear primitive rasterizer (MTIA) rather than a Gaussian splatting kernel, requiring specific handling of ray-space to world-space transformations and quaternion-based rotation updates. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by replacing the Gaussian alpha-blending gradient flow with opacity calculations based on intersection depths. Ray ID Caching is an optimization technique used in volume rendering and ray tracing to eliminate redundant intersection tests when a single ray intersects the same geometric object multiple times across different voxels. It solves the problem of "multiple intersection" overhead by storing a unique identifier (rayID) on each ray and the last intersecting rayID on each object. Unlike methods that require precise voxel-object containment checks (such as Glassner's method), this technique allows for looser voxel lists because redundant intersections are filtered by the ID comparison rather than geometric precision. IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection is an intersection-aware ray-based sampling method for implicit editable scenes that determines samples as the maximum response points of Gaussians intersected by each ray. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling 3D Gaussians in large-scale or bounded scenes by leveraging hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection tests via proxy geometry. Unlike direct Gaussian intersection methods, it maps each Gaussian to a convex polyhedral proxy (an affine-transformed icosahedron) to utilize RT cores, setting it apart from siblings like Ray-Splat Intersection which may use different primitive approximations or software-based tests. Ray-sphere intersection computes the entry and exit points (or the nearest hit distance) where a parametric ray intersects a sphere defined by a center and radius. In volume rendering, this operation is primarily used to determine the marching bounds for ray-marching algorithms, ensuring samples are only taken within the volume's extent, and to perform early-outs in hierarchical traversal. It is distinct from Sphere Intersection in that it solves for the intersection of a line (the ray) with a surface, whereas the latter typically refers to finding points on a sphere's surface satisfying other constraints (such as the 3-sphere trilateration variant). It is analytically exact and generally faster than iterative methods like Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection for simple spherical primitives. The Ray-Object Intersection Test is the fundamental geometric primitive used to determine the closest intersection between a ray and a specific scene object, returning the intersection distance t or a failure indicator if no intersection exists. It serves as the core evaluation step within a broader ray-scene traversal, where the test is executed for multiple objects to find the global minimum t. What sets this method apart from sibling primitives like Ray-box intersection or Sphere Intersection is its role as the generic interface for arbitrary geometry; it typically handles coordinate space transformations and delegates the specific algebraic solution to the object's internal representation, rather than implementing the intersection algebra directly in the traversal loop. Azimuthal Hit Detection determines whether a ray intersects an azimuthal section within a spherical voxel grid, where azimuthal sections are defined in the XZ plane. It serves as a geometric primitive for traversing spherical volume data, specifically handling the angular discretization along the azimuthal axis. It is distinct from Ray-box intersection which handles axis-aligned bounding volumes, and Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection which handles general 3D simplicial volumes; instead, it leverages the specific planar geometry of the azimuthal slices. Ray-Polar Section Intersection determines whether a ray intersects a "polar section," a geometric primitive defined within the XY plane of a spherical voxel grid. It serves as the angular traversal step for rays passing through spherical volume data, identifying which radial angular bin (section) the ray occupies at a given depth. It is distinct from Ray-box intersection by operating on angular sectors rather than Cartesian cubes, and from Azimuthal Hit Detection by using the Y-axis as the polar axis rather than the Z-axis. Computes the entry and exit distances for a ray intersecting a cylinder defined by geomSize, composed of front/back rectangles, top/bottom faces, and a lateral curved surface. It differs from Ray-box intersection by handling the curved lateral surface via quadratic solving and cylindrical coordinate checks, and from Ray-box Intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders by being a general-purpose CPU/GPU kernel implementation rather than a shader-specific primitive assembly. Ray Tracing and Ray Intersection Methods determine the first object intersected by a camera ray by analytically computing intersection distances for simple geometries. The core problem is finding the closest intersection point along a ray to render opaque surfaces correctly. This family is distinguished from Ray-marching by its reliance on exact analytical solutions for primitive shapes, whereas marching uses fixed steps. It differs from Ray-box intersection and Ray-Triangle Intersection by encompassing the broader algorithmic strategies (such as packetization and hybrid implicit tracing) used to accelerate these primitive tests in volume rendering contexts. Point-Plane Reflection computes the mirror image of a point \mathbf{p} across a plane defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a scalar offset c. It is primarily used in volume rendering and ray tracing to determine specular reflection paths, calculate virtual camera positions for mirror surfaces, or perform spatial transformations in signed distance field (SDF) operations. Unlike general ray-plane intersection which finds a hit point, this method transforms a point in space. It differs from Ray-box intersection and Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection by operating on a single point relative to an infinite plane rather than intersecting a ray with a bounded primitive. This method optimizes the evaluation of multiple ray-primitive intersections along a single ray by establishing a strict processing order based on bounding box distances, thereby reducing the computational load of expensive primitive intersection tests. It distinguishes itself from standard intersection tests by focusing on the sequence of calculations rather than the geometric solution itself, ensuring that faster, coarser intersection points are resolved before slower, finer segment evaluations. Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space, finding the point that minimizes the squared distance to both rays when they do not intersect exactly due to noise or parallax. It differs from exact intersection methods by providing a robust solution for skew lines, which is essential in volume rendering pipelines where ray origins and directions may have minor misalignments. This family defines the geometric primitives and algorithms for determining the intersection between a camera ray and 3D Gaussian splats, which are ellipsoidal density distributions used in novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which splats contribute to a pixel's color and depth, enabling alpha blending and depth testing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by handling the specific anisotropic, probabilistic nature of Gaussian splats (defined by covariance matrices or scale/rotation parameters) rather than hard geometric primitives like boxes or triangles. Quadtree Raycasting is a recursive algorithm that traverses a 2D quadtree data structure to find the first solid node intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently locating geometry in sparse or hierarchical 2D volumes by skipping empty subtrees. It differs from standard grid-based raycasting (like Ray-box intersection) by adapting the traversal step size and order to the hierarchical node boundaries rather than a uniform grid, and it differs from Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection by operating on axis-aligned square quadrants. Updates the ray's medium stack when crossing a surface, pushing a new medium if entering and popping if exiting. It checks if transmission occurred using (wo \cdot n < 0) \neq (wi \cdot n < 0) and if entering using wi \cdot n < 0. Performs ray-sphere intersection or ray marching against the SDF grid using a C++ renderer extension to find the rough intersection position for each pixel. It initializes output tensors for intersection position, voxel index, and ray direction, then calls the C++ ray matching function with camera parameters, grid bounds, resolution, and grid data. Pixels with no intersection are marked by voxelminpointindex being -1, which must be handled to avoid invalid memory access during interpolation. Tests if rays intersect any geometry without returning hit details, used for simple occlusion checks. It typically initializes a ray structure with origin, direction, and distance bounds, then invokes a hardware or library query function to return a boolean hit status within the specified range. An optimization to reduce cell primitives in a slice by intersecting individual rays with the world-space bounding box of the current u,v slice. It filters out rays that have already successfully hit a cell to avoid redundant processing. Computes the unsigned distance from query points to a triangle mesh using a BVH, and provides an analytic gradient for backpropagation. It flattens input x to [N, 3], queries BVH for distance udf, triangle ID tri\id, and barycentric coordinates uvw, clamps uvw to [1e-9, 1-1e-9], and interpolates the nearest point on the triangle using uvw and triangle vertices. The gradient is \nablax \text{UDF}(x) = \frac{x - p{\text{nearest}}}{\|x - p{\text{nearest}}\|} where p{\text{nearest}} is the closest point on the mesh. uvw is clamped to avoid invalid barycentric coordinates at triangle edges/corners. A selection technique where a ray is emitted from the user's hand, with start point and orientation controlled by the user, selecting the first intersected object. It can be augmented by cycling through all ray-object intersection points to disambiguate. It is difficult to select small and distant objects due to required angular accuracy, and rays or cones may intersect multiple objects, requiring disambiguation metrics based on distance from targets to the apex and central axis of the cone. Computes the intersection of a camera-space ray with lines parallel to the image frame axes (x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1) in normalized image coordinates. It extracts intrinsics components (fs, fo, cs, co) and ray components (os, oo, oz, ds, do, dz), constructs the 2D intersection point xy and 3D point xyz = origins + t directions, and validates the projection by checking if xy is in bounds [-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon], if xyz is in front of camera (z > -\epsilon), and if t > -\epsilon. The ray parameter is t = \frac{c oz - os}{ds - c dz} where c = \frac{v - cs}{fs}. Ray/box intersection test yields better performance with compute shader and OpenCL implementations, while raster intersection test yields better performance with CUDA implementations. No single intersection method is globally superior; optimal choice depends on the target parallel API. Best overall results are achieved by combining compute shader with ray/box intersection test. The raster intersection test presents a better performance for most cases with CUDA implementations. It leverages the parallel rasterization hardware of a GPU to compute the entry and exit points of view rays through a volumetric dataset, avoiding explicit analytical intersection tests. A method for determining ray entry and exit within the volume bounding box entirely within the fragment shader. The ray is defined by the camera position and the volume entry position. It requires an exit criterion to determine when the ray has left the volume. An approximate method to determine if a camera ray intersects a caustic beam and the location of that intersection, used because exact computation is too costly for thousands of beams. It defines a scan plane (an auxiliary arbitrary plane containing the camera ray), computes intersections of the scan plane and the edges of the caustic beam to form a triangle, and minimizes error from curved beam edges by choosing the scan plane normal vector to be close to the normal of the caustic triangle. It transforms the view ray to the beam's local space, selects a representative point on the intersection segment \Delta x (specifically the midpoint), and evaluates the area function A(y). The scan plane normal is np = r{view} \times (r{view} \times n4), where np is the scan plane normal, r{view} is the view ray direction, and n4 is the caustic triangle normal. The classification of ray-object intersections into five classes based on intersection type, data type, and shader information requirements was established in volumetric ray tracing literature. Class 1 involves geometric data intersection requiring a single point, Class 2 involves volumetric data with early termination, Class 3 involves volumetric data without early termination, Class 4 involves volumetric data segment intersection with one value, and Class 5 involves volumetric data segment intersection with all values. The choice between rasterization and ray/box intersection for volume rendering depends on the parallel API, with ray/box being superior for compute shaders/OpenCL and rasterization for CUDA. name: Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection
body: This family defines methods for determining the intersection between a ray and a surface defined implicitly by a scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) (where the surface is the zero-level set f(\mathbf{x})=0) or a Signed Distance Field (SDF). It solves the problem of finding the nearest point \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} such that f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = 0 without relying on explicit triangle meshes. It is distinguished from General Ray-Triangle Intersection by its reliance on function evaluation rather than geometric primitives, and from Sphere Intersection by its generality, requiring numerical root-finding or traversal rather than closed-form quadratic solutions for arbitrary functions. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. The Kalra & Barr method is a robust, mathematically sound algorithm for finding the nearest intersection between a ray and an implicit surface. It solves the problem of missing fine surface features or failing to converge in standard ray-marching schemes by guaranteeing numerical convergence without requiring fine-tuning or human-chosen interactive parameters. It distinguishes itself from ad-hoc schemes by relying on two specific upper bounds, L and G, to define an "LG-implicit surface," ensuring robustness for a broader class of functions than traditional quadric or polynomial-specific solvers. This method determines if a line segment intersects a surface defined by a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by evaluating the distance function at the segment's endpoints and checking for a sign change. It serves as a lightweight, broad-phase collision detection primitive. Unlike Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection which computes the exact intersection point, or Ray Tracing Implicit Surfaces which traces the ray through the field, this method only reports binary existence of an intersection within the segment bounds. It is distinct from Terrain SDF Collision Detection and Resolution in that it performs detection only, without resolving penetration or modifying velocity. Ray tracing implicit surfaces renders a surface defined by a filter function f(\mathbf{x}) and an isovalue v by solving for the root where a viewing ray intersects the surface f(\mathbf{x}) - v = 0, without using a proxy triangle mesh. It solves the root-finding problem ft(t) = 0 for the smallest t > 0, where ft is the implicit function evaluated along the parametric ray. Unlike rasterization of proxy geometry (e.g., Marching Cubes), ray tracing does not require mesh extraction, avoiding time complexity on the order of the number of samples and issues with proxy sampling rates beneath the Nyquist limit. It is distinguished from simple ray casting by its native support for secondary rays (shadows, refractions) and ray traversal of acceleration structures. LevelSetHDDA is a specialized Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) designed for static intersection testing against level set trees. It recursively traverses a VDB tree hierarchy from a specified node level down to the leaf level (-1) to determine if a ray intersects the implicit surface. It sets itself apart from generic volume traversal methods like VolumeHDDA by targeting the specific structure of level sets, where the traversal terminates at the voxel level rather than the leaf node level, allowing for precise surface intersection checks via a provided tester object. Computes the intersection of a ray with a 3D ellipsoid defined by a rotation matrix, translation vector, and scale factors. It returns whether an intersection exists and the intersection point in world space. This method transforms the ray into the ellipsoid's local space, solving a quadratic equation for the unit sphere, then transforms the result back. It is distinguished from general implicit surface methods by its closed-form quadratic solution, which is computationally cheaper than iterative root-finding but requires the primitive to be strictly ellipsoidal. Detects if a ray intersects a zero-crossing at the voxel level of a grid in the accessor. It performs empty-space ray-marching at all levels of the tree using an HDDA (Hierarchical Distance Field Acceleration). The method is optimized for performance, precision, and correctness, and surfaces a shared cache-hint helper for other operations. It is SDF-sign-agnostic and reports the EXIT crossing for rays that start inside the surface, matching nanovdb::ZeroCrossing behavior. Definition: A test to detect the existence of a tunnel in a cell based on coefficients of the isosurface equation. Steps: Compute G[Fi] and Disc[Fi] from the coefficients of the isosurface equation. If G[Fi] < 0 and Disc[Fi] > 0, a tunnel exists in the cell. Formulas: G[Fi] = (AE - BD)(AF - BC)(AG - CD) Disc[Fi] = (AH)^2 + (BG)^2 + (CE)^2 + (DF)^2 - 2ABGH - 2ACEH - 2ADFH - 2BCEG - 2BDFG - 2CDEF + 4AEFG + 4BCDH where A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H are coefficients of the isosurface equation. Definition: A basic method to influence the velocity field by approximating obstacles as simple shapes (box, ball) defined by implicit equations, adding the obstacle's average velocity to the fluid velocity in that region. Formula: Obstacle shape defined by implicit equation f(x, y, z) \le 0. Formula: Deformation equation: x{\Thetas} = x + t{\Thetas} \cdot n, where x is the initial edge point, n is the surface normal, and t{\Thetas} is the learned scalar displacement. Initial condition: At initialization \Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}, the displacement is zero: t{\Thetas} \big|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}} = 0. Gradient update rule derived from implicit differentiation of the zero-level set constraint S{\Thetas}(x{\Thetas}) = 0: \frac{\partial t}{\partial \Thetas} \big|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}} = -\frac{1}{n^T n} \cdot \frac{\partial S}{\partial \Thetas}(x) \big|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}}. Final re-parametrization for gradient-based optimization: x{\Thetas} = x - \frac{n}{n^T n} \cdot S{\Thetas}(x). Pitfall: The re-parametrization only provides an unbiased first-order gradient with respect to \Thetas, which is suitable for gradient-based optimizers but may not capture higher-order surface curvature effects. The problem of intersecting rays with implicit surfaces is fundamental to ray tracing and volume rendering, allowing for the rendering of complex shapes without explicit mesh representation. Early work focused on robust root-finding for algebraic surfaces. For large-scale volumetric data, hierarchical traversal methods like LevelSetHDDA [2875-levelsethdda.md] and RayImplicitIntersection [3591-rayimplicitintersection.md] optimize performance by skipping empty space using Digital Differential Analyzers (DDAs). Topological analysis of implicit surfaces, such as DeVella's Necklace Test, allows for the detection of complex features like tunnels within grid cells, which is crucial for topologically accurate dual isosurfacing. Implicit shapes are also used in fluid dynamics to approximate obstacles, where the implicit equation defines the solid region. Recent advances in inverse rendering and neural fields utilize edge point re-parametrization to optimize implicit surface parameters directly from images, ensuring the surface remains on the zero-level set during gradient descent. name: Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection
head: Kalra-Barr method, LG-implicit surface intersection
body: The Kalra & Barr method is a robust, mathematically sound algorithm for finding the nearest intersection between a ray and an implicit surface. It solves the problem of missing fine surface features by guaranteeing numerical convergence without requiring fine-tuning or human-chosen interactive parameters. It distinguishes itself from ad-hoc schemes by relying on two specific upper bounds, L and G, to define an "LG-implicit surface," ensuring robustness for a broader class of functions than traditional quadric or polynomial-specific solvers. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), implicit function f(\mathbf{x}), Lipschitz constant L, gradient bound G, and a search interval [t{min}, t{max}]. Output: The smallest t \in [t{min}, t{max}] such that f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = 0, or a failure indication if no root exists in the interval. Data Structures Interval: A pair of floats [t{start}, t{end}] representing the current search range along the ray. Function Evaluation: Computes f(\mathbf{x}) at a given 3D point. Parameters L: Upper bound on the net rate of change of the implicit surface function. G: Upper bound on the rate of change of the gradient. Tolerance \epsilon: Numerical threshold for termination. Steps 1. Initialize: Set current interval [ta, tb] = [t{min}, t{max}]. 2. Check Endpoints: Evaluate fa = f(\mathbf{o} + ta\mathbf{d}) and fb = f(\mathbf{o} + tb\mathbf{d}). If fa = 0, return ta. If fb = 0, return tb. 3. Pruning: The abstract does not specify the exact pruning logic, but the method uses L and G to guarantee that the interval contains a root or can be safely discarded. 4. Bisection/Refinement: The specific iterative formula is not detailed in the abstract, but the method relies on these bounds to prevent overshooting and ensure convergence. 5. Convergence: Repeat until the interval width is less than \epsilon or the function value is sufficiently close to zero. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kalrabarrintersect(o, d, f, L, G, tmin, tmax, epsilon, maxiter=100): # Cap unbounded max to prevent overflow and infinite loops if tmax == float('inf'): tmax = 100.0 ta = tmin tb = tmax # Evaluate endpoints fa = f(o + ta d) fb = f(o + tb d) # Check if roots are at endpoints if abs(fa) < epsilon: return ta if abs(fb) < epsilon: return tb # Main loop for in range(maxiter): if tb - ta < epsilon: break # Midpoint tmid = (ta + tb) / 2.0 fm = f(o + tmid d) if abs(fm) < epsilon: return tmid # Determine which sub-interval contains the root # The exact iterative formula using L and G is not detailed in the abstract. # Standard bisection checks signs, but LG-methods may use bounds # to ensure no feature is missed. if fa fm < 0: tb = tmid fb = fm else: ta = tmid fa = fm return (ta + tb) / 2.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point errors in evaluating f can lead to incorrect sign checks. Degenerate Input: If L=0 or G=0, the surface is constant or linear, which may require special handling. No Root: The abstract does not specify the exact termination condition when no root exists within the interval. A robust algorithm that processes all active rays in lockstep using interval arithmetic to guarantee no surface features are missed. It builds on Kalra & Barr by adding level-synchronized processing and Hermite-based root estimation. A robust algorithm that guarantees finding the nearest intersection without missing fine features by using interval arithmetic to prune intervals. It builds on Kalra & Barr by providing a batched, interval-arithmetic-based implementation strategy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Typically logarithmic with respect to the desired precision for bisection-based methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the current interval and function values. Strengths: Guaranteed convergence; no fine-tuning required; robust against missing fine features. Limitations: Requires computation of L and G for the implicit surface. When to Use: When robustness and guaranteed intersection are critical, and the implicit surface allows for the computation of L and G. When Not to Use: When performance is paramount and approximate intersections are acceptable; when L and G are difficult or expensive to compute. The method was introduced by Devendra Kalra and Alan Barr in 1989 in the paper "Guaranteed ray intersections with implicit surfaces". It was presented as a significant extension to previous schemes that were limited to specific classes of implicit functions (e.g., quadrics) or were ad-hoc. The work demonstrated the feasibility of ray tracing scenes with hundreds of thousands of objects using robust intersection techniques.
