name: Level-synchronized bisection ray casting
head: Batch bisection, Iso-surface bisection, Ray Subdivision and Interval Processing
body: Level-synchronized bisection ray casting is a robust algorithm for rendering the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} by processing all active rays in lockstep using interval arithmetic to guarantee no surface features are missed. It solves the problem of missing fine surface details or grazing intersections inherent in standard discrete ray marching by bounding the function value over continuous segments and iteratively bisecting intervals until convergence. It builds on Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection and differs from Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion by its specific implementation of level-synchronized processing and Hermite-based root estimation. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^R, directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^R (normalized). Scene bounds [\mathbf{b}{min}, \mathbf{b}{max}] \subset \mathbb{R}^3. Implicit function f(\mathbf{p}) and an InclusionFunction object providing bounds over 3D axis-aligned boxes. Parameters: maxdepth (integer, default 40), threshold (float, default 10^{-5}). Outputs: TraceResult dataclass containing: hit: boolean array (R,), true if surface found. t: float64 array (R,), distance to hit. position: float64 array (R, 3), world position of hit. normal: float64 array (R, 3), surface normal at hit. depthcount: int array (R,), number of bisection steps. tlo, thi: float64 arrays (R,), final interval bounds. Data Structures: rayidx: Array of active ray indices. ivtlo, ivthi: Arrays of interval endpoints for active rays. hitmask: Boolean mask identifying rays intersecting the scene AABB. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize resulthit to False, resultt to inf, resulttlo to inf, resultthi to inf, resultdepth to 0. Compute ray-AABB intersection for all rays. Identify active rays where intersection exists and t{max} > t{min}. Set rayidx to indices of active rays. Set ivtlo to t{min} and ivthi to t{max} for active rays. 2. Ray Subdivision (Pre-processing): Subdivide the ray parameter space [t{min}, t{max}] into intervals. Subdivide further when switching between areas overlapped by primitive supports and areas not overlapped by any primitive support to avoid processing empty areas. For each resulting interval [t{begin}, t{end}], proceed to interval processing. 3. Level-Synchronized Bisection Loop: Iterate depth from 0 to maxdepth. If len(rayidx) == 0, break. Convert to 3D Boxes: For each active ray i, compute 3D axis-aligned boxes corresponding to the current interval [iv\t\lo[i], iv\t\hi[i]]: \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{o}i + iv\t\lo[i] \cdot \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{p}1 = \mathbf{o}i + iv\t\hi[i] \cdot \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{lo}{3d} = \min(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) \mathbf{hi}{3d} = \max(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) Inclusion Test: Evaluate inclusion bounds using inclusionfn.evaluate(lo3d, hi3d) to get [f{lo}, f{hi}]. Filter Active Rays: Determine if zero level set is present: \text{has\zero}[i] = (f{lo}[i] \le 0.0) \land (f{hi}[i] \ge 0.0) Update rayidx, ivtlo, ivthi to keep only rays where haszero is true. If len(rayidx) == 0, break. 4. Interval Processing (Per Active Ray): For each active ray interval [t{begin}, t{end}] with Hermite data \mathbf{h}b at t{begin} and \mathbf{h}e at t{end}: Initialize n \leftarrow 0, saved \leftarrow None. While n < 32: n \leftarrow n + 1. Estimate root t{root} \leftarrow \text{Oracle}(t{begin}, t{end}, i) using quadratic interpolation of Hermite data. If t{root} = \infty and saved is None, return false, \infty (no hit in this interval). If t{root} < \infty: Evaluate Hermite data at root: \mathbf{h}r \leftarrow \text{HermiteData}(t{root}). If |\mathbf{h}r.\text{val}| < \varepsilon, return true, t{root} (hit found). Determine primitive sign change: b{prim} \leftarrow (\mathbf{h}r.\text{prim} > 0) \land (\mathbf{h}b.\text{prim} < 0). If saved is None and \mathbf{h}r.\text{val} \ge 0 and \mathbf{h}e.\text{val} < 0 and b{prim}, store potential backtrack: saved \leftarrow [(t{root}, \mathbf{h}r), (t{end}, \mathbf{h}e)]. Update interval: If \mathbf{h}r.\text{val} < 0 or b{prim}, set t{end}, \mathbf{h}e \leftarrow t{root}, \mathbf{h}r; else set t{begin}, \mathbf{h}b \leftarrow t{root}, \mathbf{h}r. Else if saved is not None: Restore interval: (t{begin}, \mathbf{h}b), (t{end}, \mathbf{h}e) \leftarrow \text{saved}, saved \leftarrow None. If loop completes without hit, return false, \infty. 5. Result Update: For each valid hit with distance t{valid}: If t{valid} < \text{result\t}[\text{ray\idx}[i]]: \text{result\hit}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow \text{True} \text{result\t}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{valid} \text{result\t\lo}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{lo} \text{result\t\hi}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{hi} This ensures front-to-back rendering by keeping only the closest hit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class TraceResult: hit: np.ndarray t: np.ndarray position: np.ndarray normal: np.ndarray depthcount: np.ndarray tlo: np.ndarray thi: np.ndarray def levelsynchronizedbisectioncast(origins, directions, boundsmin, boundsmax, inclusionfn, maxdepth=40, threshold=1e-5): R = origins.shape[0] # Initialize results resulthit = np.zeros(R, dtype=bool) resultt = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resulttlo = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resultthi = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resultdepth = np.zeros(R, dtype=np.int32) # Ray-AABB intersection safedirs = np.where(directions == 0, 1.0, directions) tminvals = (boundsmin - origins) / safedirs tmaxvals = (boundsmax - origins) / safedirs # Fix: use np.max/min over axis=1 to get scalar tmin/tmax per ray tminarr = np.max(tminvals, axis=1) tmaxarr = np.min(tmaxvals, axis=1) hitmask = (tminarr < tmaxarr) & (tmaxarr > 0) rayidx = np.where(hitmask)[0] ivtlo = tminarr[rayidx] ivthi = tmaxarr[rayidx] # Pre-subdivision handled by scene structure; initial AABB bounds serve as starting intervals. for depth in range(maxdepth): if len(rayidx) == 0: break # Convert intervals to 3D boxes p0 = origins[rayidx] + ivtlo[:, np.newaxis] directions[rayidx] p1 = origins[rayidx] + ivthi[:, np.newaxis] directions[rayidx] lo3d = np.minimum(p0, p1) hi3d = np.maximum(p0, p1) # Evaluate inclusion bounds flo, fhi = inclusionfn.evaluate(lo3d, hi3d) # Filter active rays: haszero if flo <= 0 <= fhi haszero = (flo <= 0.0) & (fhi >= 0.0) rayidx = rayidx[haszero] ivtlo = ivtlo[haszero] ivthi = ivthi[haszero] if len(rayidx) == 0: break validhits = [] validrayindices = [] validtlo = [] validthi = [] for i in range(len(rayidx)): tbegin = ivtlo[i] tend = ivthi[i] # Standard evaluation returning function value and derivative for Hermite interpolation hb = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(origins[rayidx[i]] + tbegin directions[rayidx[i]]) he = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(origins[rayidx[i]] + tend directions[rayidx[i]]) saved = None hitfound = False hitt = np.inf for n in range(32): troot = oraclehermiteinterpolation(tbegin, tend, hb, he) if troot == np.inf: if saved is None: break else: (tbegin, hb), (tend, he) = saved saved = None continue proot = origins[rayidx[i]] + troot directions[rayidx[i]] hr = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(proot) if abs(hr.val) < threshold: hitfound = True hitt = troot break bprim = (hr.prim > 0) and (hb.prim < 0) if saved is None and hr.val >= 0 and he.val < 0 and bprim: saved = [(troot, hr), (tend, he)] if hr.val < 0 or bprim: tend = troot he = hr else: tbegin = troot hb = hr if hitfound: validhits.append(hitt) validrayindices.append(rayidx[i]) validtlo.append(tbegin) validthi.append(tend) if validhits: validhits = np.array(validhits) validrayindices = np.array(validrayindices) validtlo = np.array(validtlo) validthi = np.array(validthi) mask = validhits < resultt[validrayindices] resulthit[validrayindices[mask]] = True resultt[validrayindices[mask]] = validhits[mask] resulttlo[validrayindices[mask]] = validtlo[mask] resultthi[validrayindices[mask]] = validthi[mask] resultdepth[validrayindices[mask]] = depth + 1 positions = np.zeros((R, 3)) normals = np.zeros((R, 3)) hitindices = np.where(resulthit)[0] if len(hitindices) > 0: positions[hitindices] = origins[hitindices] + resultt[hitindices][:, np.newaxis] directions[hitindices] normals[hitindices] = inclusionfn.getnormals(positions[hitindices]) return TraceResult( hit=resulthit, t=resultt, position=positions, normal=normals, depthcount=resultdepth, tlo=resulttlo, thi=resultthi) def oraclehermiteinterpolation(tbegin, tend, hb, he): dt = tend - tbegin if dt == 0: return np.inf c = hb.val b = hb.prim dt a = 2 (he.val - hb.val) - (hb.prim + he.prim) dt if abs(a) < 1e-12: if abs(b) < 1e-12: return np.inf t = -c / b else: discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return np.inf sqrtdisc = np.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) if 0 <= t1 <= 1: t = t1 elif 0 <= t2 <= 1: t = t2 else: return np.inf return tbegin + t dt Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum number of bisection iterations allowed per ray. name: Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion
head: Level-Synchronized Interval Bisection
body: Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion is a robust ray casting algorithm that renders the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} using level-synchronized interval bisection. It guarantees no surface features are missed by using an inclusion function to bound f over axis-aligned boxes and pruning intervals that cannot contain a zero crossing. Inputs: origins (array of \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3), directions (array of \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, normalized), tmin and tmax (scalar bounds for the ray segment), hitmask (boolean array indicating active rays), inclusion (GradientInclusion instance), fnp (implicit function evaluator), maxdepth (integer, maximum bisection depth), threshold (float, bisection convergence threshold), lipschitz (float or 'auto', Lipschitz constant for the inclusion function), newtoniter (integer, optional Newton refinement steps), batchsize (integer, number of rays to process per batch; None processes all at once). Outputs: Final hit positions \mathbf{x} and depths t for all rays. Data Structures: Interval [f-, f+] representing the guaranteed range of f; ray state arrays tstart and tend tracking the current search interval for each ray. Parameters: maxdepth (maximum bisection depth), threshold (bisection convergence threshold), lipschitz (if 'auto', estimated by sampling gradient norms over the bounding box via torch.autograd), batchsize (number of rays to process per batch; None processes all at once). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize inclusion with f{np} and L. For each active ray, set [t{start}, t{end}] = [t{min}, t{max}]. 2. Level-Synchronized Bisection Loop: For step from 1 to maxdepth: Compute midpoint t{mid} = (t{start} + t{end}) / 2. Evaluate inclusion function: [f{min}, f{max}] = \text{inclusion.evaluate}(t{start}, t{end}). Pruning: If 0 \notin [f{min}, f{max}], deactivate the ray. Convergence: If |t{end} - t{start}| < \text{threshold}, deactivate the ray. Refinement: Evaluate f(t{start}) and f(t{mid}). If signs differ, set t{end} = t{mid}; otherwise set t{start} = t{mid}. 3. Newton Refinement: For converged rays, perform newtoniter steps: t{new} = t{old} - f(\mathbf{x}) / (\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{d}). 4. Output: Return final \mathbf{x} and t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def bisectiontracewithgradientinclusion(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, lipschitz, newtoniter, batchsize): # Initialize inclusion function as specified inclusion = GradientInclusion(fnp, lipschitz=lipschitz) return tracerays(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter, batchsize) def tracerays(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter, batchsize): tstart = np.fulllike(origins[..., 0], tmin) tend = np.fulllike(origins[..., 0], tmax) activeindices = np.where(hitmask)[0] if batchsize is not None: for bstart in range(0, len(activeindices), batchsize): bend = min(bstart + batchsize, len(activeindices)) processbatch(activeindices[bstart:bend], origins, directions, tstart, tend, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter) else: processbatch(activeindices, origins, directions, tstart, tend, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter) return tstart, origins + tstart[..., None] directions def processbatch(indices, origins, directions, tstart, tend, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, maxdepth, threshold, newtoniter): for step in range(maxdepth): activeinbatch = hitmask[indices] if not np.any(activeinbatch): break tmid = 0.5 (tstart[indices] + tend[indices]) fmin, fmax = inclusion.evaluate(tstart[indices], tend[indices]) # Pruning: intervals that cannot contain zero are deactivated nozero = (fmin > 0) | (fmax < 0) hitmask[indices[nozero]] = False activeinbatch = hitmask[indices] if not np.any(activeinbatch): break # Convergence check converged = (tend[indices] - tstart[indices]) < threshold hitmask[indices[converged]] = False remaining = activeinbatch & ~converged if np.any(remaining): remidx = indices[remaining] tmidrem = tmid[remaining] ptsmid = origins[remidx] + tmidrem[..., None] directions[remidx] fmid = fnp(ptsmid) ptsstart = origins[remidx] + tstart[remidx][..., None] directions[remidx] fstart = fnp(ptsstart) signchange = fstart fmid < 0 tend[remidx[signchange]] = tmidrem[signchange] tstart[remidx[~signchange]] = tmidrem[~signchange] # Newton refinement for converged rays convergedglobal = hitmask[indices] if np.any(convergedglobal): cidx = indices[convergedglobal] pts = origins[cidx] + tstart[cidx][..., None] directions[cidx] for in range(newtoniter): fval = fnp(pts) grad = computegradient(fnp, pts) dot = np.sum(grad directions[cidx][..., None], axis=-1) tstart[cidx] -= fval / dot pts = origins[cidx] + tstart[cidx][..., None] directions[cidx] def computegradient(fnp, points): # Standard gradient computation via automatic differentiation points = points.detach().requiresgrad(True) out = fnp(points) grad = torch.autograd.grad(out.sum(), points, creategraph=True)[0] return grad.detach().numpy() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Constant: If L is underestimated, the inclusion bounds are not guaranteed, risking missed surfaces. Degenerate Intervals: The threshold check prevents division by zero during Newton refinement. Multiple Crossings: The method finds the first zero crossing within the active interval. Provides the bounding functions used by this method. Choose GradientInclusion for a balance of tightness and generality, or AffineInclusion for symbolic functions requiring tighter bounds. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of rays and D is maxdepth. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing ray states. Performance: Robust against aliasing and missed surfaces, but slower than simple bisection due to inclusion overhead. Strengths: Guaranteed no-miss property; handles complex implicit functions well. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to interval arithmetic; requires Lipschitz constant estimation. The method is implemented in the iso-surface-rendering library by narnia-ai-mason. It builds on level-synchronized bisection ray casting, enhancing it with gradient-based inclusion strategies for improved accuracy and efficiency. name: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies
head: InclusionFunction strategies
body: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies compute conservative bounds on a scalar field function f over a spatial region, enabling the parent Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion to safely skip ray segments that cannot contain a zero-level set. They are distinguished by their trade-off between generality and bound tightness: black-box strategies work with any function but yield loose bounds, analytic strategies require symbolic formulas to produce tighter bounds, and gradient-based strategies use local derivatives for a middle ground. All strategies evaluate a scalar field f: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R} over a candidate step or bounding box to compute an inclusion bound [f-, f+] that guarantees f(\mathbf{x}) \in [f-, f+] for all \mathbf{x} in the domain. The renderer uses this bound to determine if the zero-level set intersects the region; if the interval does not contain zero, the region is pruned. The strategies are categorized by their required input information: black-box methods require only point evaluations and a Lipschitz constant, gradient-based methods require \nabla f, and analytic methods require the symbolic expression of f. What it is: A black-box baseline that estimates a global Lipschitz constant \lambda by sampling gradient norms over a bounding box, then uses \lambda to construct linear inclusion bounds. What sets it apart: It requires no symbolic access to f, making it the only viable option when only point evaluations are available. It yields the loosest bounds because it relies on a global maximum gradient rather than local information. When to choose: Use for black-box functions (e.g., neural networks or procedural shaders) where gradients or symbolic formulas are inaccessible. Link: SamplingInclusion What it is: The default strategy that computes tighter bounds by using the local gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) at the current ray position to approximate the function's rate of change. What sets it apart: It requires gradient access but no symbolic formula, providing tighter bounds than SamplingInclusion by adapting to local variation, while remaining less tight than analytic methods. When to choose: Use when f is differentiable and gradients are available via automatic differentiation or analytical derivatives, but symbolic propagation is not feasible. Link: GradientInclusion What it is: An analytic strategy that applies Natural Interval Arithmetic (NIA) directly to the symbolic formula of f, replacing real numbers with intervals and standard operations with their interval counterparts. What sets it apart: It provides tighter bounds than SamplingInclusion and GradientInclusion when the analytic formula is known, but suffers from the interval dependency problem where repeated variables are treated as independent. When to choose: Use when the symbolic formula of f is available and simple, and tighter bounds than gradient-based methods are needed without the overhead of Affine Arithmetic. Link: NaturalIntervalInclusion What it is: An analytic strategy that uses Affine Arithmetic (AA) on the symbolic formula of f, decomposing value intervals into affine combinations of independent unit interval symbols to track uncertainty sources. What sets it apart: It provides the tightest bounds among the four strategies by mitigating the dependency problem of NIA, significantly reducing bisection steps, at the cost of higher computational overhead. When to choose: Use when the symbolic formula of f is available, tightest possible bounds are required for performance, and the computational cost of AA is acceptable. Link: AffineInclusion A method that simplifies SDF expressions in specific regions by coupling pruning and rendering, using interval arithmetic to evaluate nodes in a construction tree. It relies on well-defined interval arithmetic queries for each node in the construction tree to determine pruning eligibility. It differs from Lipschitz pruning by using explicit interval arithmetic queries per node rather than treating primitives as black boxes with 1-Lipschitz bounds. The isoray library introduced four specific inclusion strategies for Python-based robust iso-surface rendering, emphasizing black-box compatibility while offering analytic optimizations for tighter bounds. Parallel Tape Reduction extends interval arithmetic to hierarchical SDF simplification, enabling real-time rendering of complex scenes with thousands of nodes by coupling pruning and rendering. Estimates the global Lipschitz constant \lambda for an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^d ightarrow \mathbb{R} by sampling gradient norms over a bounding box. This constant is required by the interval inclusion function to prune intervals that do not contain the zero-level set. It distinguishes itself from black-box sampling methods by utilizing gradient information to derive a tighter bound than point-evaluation differences alone. Inputs: Implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^d ightarrow \mathbb{R} and its gradient 
abla f. A bounding box \mathcal{B} defining the domain of interest. A parameter lipschitz: either a pre-computed float value or the string "auto". If lipschitz is a float, return it immediately. 2. If lipschitz is "auto", estimate \lambda by sampling the gradient magnitude \|
abla f(\mathbf{x})\| at multiple points \mathbf{x} within the bounding box \mathcal{B}. 3. The estimated constant is the maximum observed gradient norm: \lambda = \max{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{B}} \|

name: Local Lipschitz Bound Computation for Hierarchical Implicit Models
head: Hierarchical Lipschitz Bound Computation, Tree-based Lipschitz Bound
body:
This method computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for a segment \mathbf{e} within a hierarchical construction tree of implicit primitives and operators. It solves the problem of determining safe stepping distances in enhanced sphere tracing (Segment Tracing) by providing a tight bound on the gradient magnitude, which allows for larger, safe steps along the ray compared to conservative global bounds. It is distinguished from its parent Lipschitz Constant Estimation by operating on the specific geometric structure of the implicit model (the construction tree) rather than sampling the bounding box, and from its children by handling general hierarchical operators (Boolean, blending, affine, deformation) rather than specific primitive types. Inputs: A hierarchical construction tree where leaves are compactly supported skeletal primitives and nodes are operators (Boolean, blending, affine, deformation). A ray segment \mathbf{e} defined by parameter interval [t, t+\epsilon], with center c and radius r = \|\mathbf{e}\|/2. The ray direction unit vector \mathbf{u}. Outputs: The local Lipschitz bound \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for the segment \mathbf{e}. Data Structures: Hierarchical Construction Tree: A tree structure where leaves are compactly supported skeletal primitives and internal nodes store operator types and pointers to child nodes. Method: The computation traverses the tree recursively. For a node, the bound is computed based on the operator type. If the primitive or deformation is complex, coarser bounds may be used. 1. Base Case (Leaf Primitive): Compute \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for the skeletal primitive using the product of two terms: \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \|g' \circ d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e})\| \|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\| where: g is the falloff filter function. d is the Euclidean distance to the skeleton. \delta(\mathbf{e}) represents the ray parameterization over the segment. \mathbf{u} is the ray direction unit vector. Falloff Bound (\|g' \circ d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e})\|): Compute the interval image of the distance d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}). Approximate the distance interval using the 1-Lipschitz property of distance functions: d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \subset [d(c) - r, d(c) + r] where c is the segment center and r = \|\mathbf{e}\|/2. Bound g' using Interval Analysis on this distance interval. Gradient Bound (\|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\|): General Case: Use the bound 1, since \|
abla d\| = 1 for Euclidean distance to a skeleton (1-Lipschitz) and \|\mathbf{u}\|=1: \|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\| \leq 1 Tighter Bound (Points, Spheres, Line Segments): Compute the closed-form image of 
abla d \circ \delta \cdot \mathbf{u} over the segment \mathbf{e}. For a point primitive with center c, 
abla d(p) = (p-c)/\|p-c\|. The image is the interval [|
abla d \circ \delta(t) \cdot \mathbf{u}|, |
abla d \circ \delta(t+\epsilon) \cdot \mathbf{u}|]. 2. Coarser Bounds (Complex Primitives/Deformations): If exact computation is difficult, use global bounds for the supporting ray \Delta or bounding sphere S \supset \mathbf{e}: \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(\Delta) \quad 	ext{and} \quad \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(S) where \lambda(\Delta) and \lambda(S) are the Lipschitz bounds of f over the entire ray and sphere respectively. 3. Internal Nodes (Operators): Compute bounds for children and combine based on operator type: Blending (Additive): f = fA + fB \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = \lambdaA(\mathbf{e}) + \lambdaB(\mathbf{e}) Boolean Union/Intersection (Max/Min): fU = \max(fA, fB), fI = \min(fA, fB) \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = \max(\lambdaA(\mathbf{e}), \lambdaB(\mathbf{e})) Pasko Union: fU = fA + fB + \sqrt{fA^2 + fB^2} \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = 2(\lambdaA(\mathbf{e}) + \lambdaB(\mathbf{e})) 4. Affine Transformations: Let fD = fN \circ a, where a is the affine transformation. Transform segment \mathbf{e} to \mathbf{e}' = a^{-1}(\mathbf{e}). For translation/rotation (1-Lipschitz): \lambdaD(\mathbf{e}) = \lambdaN(\mathbf{e}') For scaling by factor \alpha: \lambdaD(\mathbf{e}) =  rac{1}{\alpha} \lambdaN(\mathbf{e}') 5. Deformations: Let fW = fN \circ \omega^{-1}, where \omega is the warping function. The gradient is 
abla fW = 
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}, where \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse warping function. Bound the Lipschitz constant by bounding the gradient norm and Jacobian norm: \|
abla fW\| \leq \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}\| \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\| Compute two local bounds for the transformed segment \mathbf{e}' = \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{e}): 1. Bound of the norm of the gradient \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{e}')\|. 2. Bound of the norm of the Jacobian \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}(\mathbf{e}')\|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelipschitzbound(node, segmente, raydirectionu): """ Computes the local Lipschitz bound lambda(e) for a segment e in a hierarchical tree. """ if node.isleaf(): return computeprimitivelipschitz(node.primitive, segmente, raydirectionu) operatortype = node.operatortype lambdaleft = computelipschitzbound(node.leftchild, segmente, raydirectionu) lambdaright = computelipschitzbound(node.rightchild, segmente, raydirectionu) if operatortype == "BLEND": return lambdaleft + lambdaright elif operatortype in ["BOOLEANUNION", "BOOLEANINTERSECTION"]: return max(lambdaleft, lambdaright) elif operatortype == "PASKOUNION": return 2 (lambdaleft + lambdaright) elif operatortype == "AFFINE": segmenteprime = node.affinetransform.inversetransform(segmente) childbound = computelipschitzbound(node.child, segmenteprime, raydirectionu) alpha = node.affinetransform.getscalingfactor() return childbound / alpha elif operatortype == "DEFORMATION": segmenteprime = node.warpingfunction.inversetransform(segmente) lambdagrad = computelipschitzbound(node.child, segmenteprime, raydirectionu) # Sources do not specify the exact Jacobian norm computation for arbitrary warping functions. lambdajacobian = computejacobiannormbound(node.warpingfunction, segmenteprime) return lambdagrad lambdajacobian else: # Fallback to coarser bounds if operator type is not explicitly handled # Sources do not specify the exact fallback mechanism. return 1.0 def computeprimitivelipschitz(primitive, segmente, raydirectionu): """ Computes the Lipschitz bound for a leaf skeletal primitive. lambda(e) <= ||g' o d o delta(e)|| ||grad(d) o delta(e). u|| """ # 1. Falloff Bound: ||g' o d o delta(e)|| dcenter = primitive.distance(segmente.center) r = segmente.radius distanceintervalmin = dcenter - r distanceintervalmax = dcenter + r # Standard interval arithmetic evaluation of the falloff derivative g' over the interval falloffbound = max(abs(primitive.gprime(distanceintervalmin)), abs(primitive.gprime(distanceintervalmax))) # 2. Gradient Bound: ||grad(d) o delta(e). u|| if primitive.type == "POINT": pstart = segmente.startpoint pend = segmente.endpoint graddotustart = abs(dot(primitive.gradient(pstart), raydirectionu)) graddotuend = abs(dot(primitive.gradient(pend), raydirectionu)) gradientbound = max(graddotustart, graddotuend) else: gradientbound = 1.0 return falloffbound gradientbound def computejacobiannormbound(warpingfunction, segmente): # Sources do not specify the exact Jacobian norm computation for arbitrary warping functions. return 1.0 Parameters: Typical falloff functions: Wyvill's C^1 sextic, Wyvill's C^2 sextic, C^1 quartic. Scaling factor \alpha for affine transformations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Primitives/Deformations: Exact computation of \lambda(\mathbf{e}) may be very complex. Use coarser bounds \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(\Delta) and \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(S) to ensure correctness and efficiency. Distance Interval Approximation: The approximation d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \subset [d(c) - r, d(c) + r] relies on the 1-Lipschitz property of distance. This is valid but may be loose for complex skeletons. Gradient Bound Tightness: The general bound of 1 for \|
abla d \circ \delta \cdot \mathbf{u}\| is not accurate. name: Lipschitz Bound Computation for Skeletal Primitives
head: Falloff Filter Function Lipschitz Bound Computation
body: This method computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda for skeletal primitives by evaluating the maximum absolute value of the derivative of the falloff filter function g(x) over a specific interval [a, b]. It solves the problem of determining safe stepping distances in enhanced sphere tracing by providing a tight bound on the gradient magnitude, which allows for larger, safe steps along the ray compared to conservative global bounds. It is distinguished from generic interval arithmetic strategies by relying on closed-form analytical solutions for specific standard falloff functions, avoiding numerical approximation errors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The falloff filter function g(x), the interval [a, b] representing the normalized distance range along the ray segment. Output: The Lipschitz bound \lambda, defined as \max{x \in [a,b]} |g'(x)|. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on pre-computed analytical roots and derivative formulas for specific primitive types. Steps: 1. Identify the falloff function type (Wyvill, Quadric, or Blobs). 2. Compute the root x^0 of the second-order derivative g''(x) = 0 within the unit interval [0, 1]. 3. Determine the bound \lambda based on the position of x^0 relative to the input interval [a, b]: If a \geq 1, then \lambda = 0. If x^0 \in [a, b], then \lambda = |g'(x^0)|. Otherwise, \lambda = \max(|g'(a)|, |g'(b)|). Formulas: For all functions, g(x) is defined for x < 1 and 0 otherwise. The derivatives are evaluated as follows: Wyvill Function: g(x) = (1 - x^2)^3 g'(x) = -6x(1-x^2)^2 g''(x) = -6(1-x^2)(1-5x^2) Root: x^0 = 1/\sqrt{5}. Bound: \lambda0 = 96\sqrt{5}/125 \leq 1.72. Quadric Function: g(x) = (1 - x^2)^2 g'(x) = -4x(1-x^2) g''(x) = -4(1-3x^2) Root: x^0 = 1/\sqrt{3}. Bound: \lambda0 = 8\sqrt{3}/9 \leq 1.54. Blobs Function: g(x) = -\frac{4}{9}x^6 + \frac{17}{9}x^4 - \frac{22}{9}x^2 + 1 g'(x) = -\frac{4}{9}x(x^2 - 1)(6x^2 - 11) g''(x) = -\frac{4}{9}(30x^4 - 51x^2 + 11) Root: x^0 = \frac{51 - \sqrt{1281}}{2\sqrt{15}}. Bound: \lambda0 = (17\sqrt{1281} + 453)\sqrt{\frac{17}{2278125} - \frac{\sqrt{1281}}{6834375}} \leq 1.59. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelipschitzboundwyvill(a, b): if a >= 1: return 0.0 xstar = 1.0 / math.sqrt(5.0) lambdastar = 96.0 math.sqrt(5.0) / 125.0 if a <= xstar <= b: return lambdastar else: def gprime(x): return abs(-6.0 x (1.0 - xx)2) return max(gprime(a), gprime(b)) def computelipschitzboundquadric(a, b): if a >= 1: return 0.0 xstar = 1.0 / math.sqrt(3.0) lambdastar = 8.0 math.sqrt(3.0) / 9.0 if a <= xstar <= b: return lambdastar else: def gprime(x): return abs(-4.0 x (1.0 - xx)) return max(gprime(a), gprime(b)) def computelipschitzboundblobs(a, b): if a >= 1: return 0.0 sqrt1281 = math.sqrt(1281.0) sqrt15 = math.sqrt(15.0) xstar = (51.0 - sqrt1281) / (2.0 sqrt15) term1 = 17.0 sqrt1281 + 453.0 term2 = 17.0 / 2278125.0 - sqrt1281 / 6834375.0 lambdastar = term1 math.sqrt(term2) if a <= xstar <= b: return lambdastar else: def gprime(x): return abs((-4.0/9.0) x (xx - 1.0) (6.0xx - 11.0)) return max(gprime(a), gprime(b)) Parameters: None. The method is deterministic based on the function type. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a \geq 1, the bound is exactly 0, as the falloff function is 0 and its derivative is 0 outside the unit interval. Floating-point precision in evaluating g'(x) near boundaries should be handled carefully, though the analytical forms are stable. The root x^0 must be checked against the interval [a, b] correctly; if the interval does not contain the peak of the derivative, the maximum occurs at one of the endpoints. Computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for a segment e within a hierarchical construction tree. This method provides the component-wise bound for skeletal primitives used within that larger hierarchical context. It is chosen when skeletal primitives are combined with other implicit operators in a construction tree, as it supplies the tight per-primitive gradient bounds required for the parent's hierarchical aggregation. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the constants for the specific function type. Strengths: Provides tight, accurate bounds that enable larger stepping distances in sphere tracing, reducing the number of field function queries. It avoids the overhead of numerical root-finding or interval arithmetic propagation for these specific primitives. Limitations: Only applicable to skeletal primitives with the specific falloff functions defined (Wyvill, Quadric, Blobs). Not applicable to arbitrary implicit functions. When to use: When using enhanced sphere tracing with skeletal primitives and needing to optimize ray marching steps. When not to use: For non-skeletal primitives or when the falloff function does not match the predefined analytical forms. The method originates from the analysis of falloff filter functions used in soft object rendering. The Wyvill function was introduced by Wyvill in 1986. The Quadric function is a standard C^1 variant. The Blobs function, described in [WMW86], modifies the quadric to satisfy specific boundary conditions. The specific Lipschitz bound computation for these functions was detailed in the context of segment tracing using local Lipschitz bounds. name: Forward Linear Inclusion Function
head: Linear Bounding Function, Linear Inclusion Function
body: The Forward Linear Inclusion Function is a method for computing valid, linear bounds on a scalar field function f(t) along a ray, used to determine safe step sizes in sphere tracing. It solves the problem of finding the maximum distance to the next surface intersection by constructing a bounding cone that is guaranteed to contain the true function values. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying solely on the function value and a global Lipschitz constant, offering black-box compatibility at the cost of potentially looser bounds compared to gradient-based or higher-order methods [S1, 1410-interval-arithmetic-inclusion-strategies.md]. Inputs and outputs: Input: The scalar field function f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} evaluated at the current ray position t0, denoted f(t0); the global Lipschitz constant \lambda for the field; the current ray parameter t0. Output: A step size \Delta t representing the maximum safe distance to the next zero-crossing, and the inclusion bounds [f-(t), f+(t)] for t > t0. Data structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values. Numbered steps: 1. Evaluate the scalar field at the current ray position t0 to obtain f(t0). 2. Define the forward linear inclusion function f for t > t0 as a pair of linear bounding lines starting at (t0, f(t0)). 3. The lower bound f-(t) and upper bound f+(t) are defined as: f-(t) = f(t0) - \lambda(t - t0) f+(t) = f(t0) + \lambda(t - t0) where \lambda is the Lipschitz constant such that |f(t) - f(t0)| \leq \lambda |t - t0| for all t. 4. To find the step size, solve for the intersection of the bounding lines with the zero threshold (v=0). Since the function value f(t0) indicates the distance to the surface in normalized space, the step size is determined by the intersection of the bound with zero. 5. The step size \Delta t is calculated as: \Delta t = \frac{|f(t0)|}{\lambda} The sign of f(t0) determines the direction of the surface relative to the ray, but the step size is always positive. Formulas: Inclusion bounds: f = f(t0) \pm \lambda(t - t0). Step size: \Delta t = f(t0) / \lambda (assuming f(t0) > 0 for exterior points). Parameters: \lambda: The Lipschitz constant of the scalar field. This must be known or estimated beforehand. Typical values depend on the specific noise function or implicit surface being rendered. Edge cases and pitfalls: If f(t0) = 0, the step size is 0, indicating the ray is exactly on the surface. If \lambda = 0, the function is constant, and no intersection can be found unless f(t0) = 0. The bound is only valid if \lambda is a true global Lipschitz constant for the field. Underestimating \lambda leads to invalid bounds and missed intersections. The linear bound may be loose for functions with high curvature, leading to smaller step sizes than necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardlinearinclusionstep(f, t0, lambdaval): """ Calculate the step size for sphere tracing using the Forward Linear Inclusion Function. Args: f (callable): The scalar field function f(t). t0 (float): The current ray parameter. lambdaval (float): The global Lipschitz constant of the field. Returns: float: The step size to advance the ray. """ # Evaluate the function at the current position ft0 = f(t0) # Handle the case where we are exactly on the surface if abs(ft0) < 1e-6: return 0.0 # Calculate step size using the linear inclusion bound intersection with zero # The bound is f(t0) +/- lambda (t - t0). # Intersection with 0: 0 = f(t0) + lambda (t - t0) => t - t0 = -f(t0)/lambda # We take the absolute value for the step size step = abs(ft0) / lambdaval return step The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function is a method for computing tighter, valid bounds on a scalar field function f(t) along a ray, used to determine safe step sizes in sphere tracing. Time complexity: O(1) per step, as it requires only one function evaluation and basic arithmetic. Memory complexity: O(1), requiring no additional storage beyond the current state. Measured performance: Performance depends heavily on the tightness of \lambda. A loose \lambda results in smaller step sizes and more evaluations, reducing performance. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of steps required to reach the surface. Strengths: Simple to implement, requires no gradient information, works with black-box functions. Limitations: Can produce loose bounds for functions with high curvature, leading to inefficient step sizes compared to quadratic or gradient-based methods. When to use: When gradient information is unavailable or too expensive to compute, and the Lipschitz constant is known. When not to use: When high performance is critical and the function has significant curvature, making linear bounds too loose. The Forward Linear Inclusion Function is based on the principles of interval arithmetic and Lipschitz continuity applied to ray tracing. It formalizes the step size calculation in sphere tracing by finding intersections of bounding functions with the threshold. The method is described in the context of fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise. Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70072, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function
head: Hybrid quadratic-linear bound, Improved Quad. Bounds, Improved Quadratic Taylor
body: The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function is a method for computing tighter, valid bounds on a scalar field function f(t) along a ray, used to determine safe step sizes in sphere tracing. It solves the problem where standard quadratic bounds violate the first-order Lipschitz constraint, causing the bound to grow too fast and result in smaller, inefficient step sizes than linear bounds. It sets itself apart by enforcing both first-order (\lambda) and second-order (\gamma) Lipschitz constraints simultaneously, switching to a linear bound when the quadratic derivative exceeds the first-order limit. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current ray parameter t0, function value f(t0), first derivative f'(t0), first-order Lipschitz constant \lambda, second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma. Output: Inclusion function f{\pm}(t) providing lower (f-) and upper (f+) bounds for t > t0. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic operations. Formulas: The improved inclusion function f{\pm}(t) is defined piecewise using a quadratic component q{\pm}(t) and a switch point t{\pm}: q{\pm}(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) \cdot \left( f'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2}\gamma(t - t0) \right) t{\pm} = t0 + \frac{\pm\lambda - f'(t0)}{\pm\gamma} The final bound is: f{\pm}(t) = \begin{cases} q{\pm}(t) & \forall t \in [t0, t{\pm}] \\ q{\pm}(t{\pm}) \pm \lambda \cdot (t - t{\pm}) & \forall t > t{\pm} \end{cases} Parameters: \lambda: First-order Lipschitz constant. \gamma: Second-order Lipschitz constant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvedquadraticinclusion(t0, ft0, fprimet0, lambdaval, gammaval): """ Computes the improved quadratic inclusion bounds for t > t0. Args: t0: Current ray parameter. ft0: Function value at t0. fprimet0: First derivative at t0. lambdaval: First-order Lipschitz constant. gammaval: Second-order Lipschitz constant. Returns: A function that takes t and returns (lowerbound, upperbound). """ # Calculate switch points for upper and lower bounds # tplus = t0 + (lambda - fprime) / gamma # tminus = t0 + (-lambda - fprime) / (-gamma) = t0 + (lambda + fprime) / gamma tplus = t0 + (lambdaval - fprimet0) / gammaval tminus = t0 + (lambdaval + fprimet0) / gammaval def bound(t): if t <= t0: return ft0, ft0 # Calculate quadratic components # qplus(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) (f'(t0) + 0.5 gamma (t - t0)) # qminus(t) = f(t0) + (t - t0) (f'(t0) - 0.5 gamma (t - t0)) dt = t - t0 qplus = ft0 + dt (fprimet0 + 0.5 gammaval dt) qminus = ft0 + dt (fprimet0 - 0.5 gammaval dt) # Determine if we are past the switch point for upper bound if t > tplus: # Switch to linear bound # fplus(t) = qplus(tplus) + lambda (t - tplus) dtswitch = tplus - t0 qplusatswitch = ft0 + dtswitch (fprimet0 + 0.5 gammaval dtswitch) upper = qplusatswitch + lambdaval (t - tplus) else: upper = qplus # Determine if we are past the switch point for lower bound if t > tminus: # Switch to linear bound # fminus(t) = qminus(tminus) - lambda (t - tminus) dtswitch = tminus - t0 qminusatswitch = ft0 + dtswitch (fprimet0 - 0.5 gammaval dtswitch) lower = qminusatswitch - lambdaval (t - tminus) else: lower = qminus return lower, upper return bound Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard quadratic bounds that do not enforce the first-order Lipschitz constraint, potentially leading to loose bounds. Use when \gamma is small and \lambda is not a limiting factor. Time and Memory Complexity: The computational cost is the same as regular quadratic inclusion functions. Measured Performance: On the Sponge scene with all enhancements (SS, ES+1): Both Regular Quad and Improved Quad achieve 70.0 avg steps, 651.1 avg octaves, and 16.3 ms time, providing a \times 4.0 speedup vs Linear. On Sponge (far) scene with all enhancements (SS, ES+1): Regular Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.8 ms time. Improved Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.7 ms time. Both provide a \times 1.7 speedup vs Linear. Without enhancements, improved quadratic bounds allow \times 1.2 and \times 1.1 reduction in steps compared to naive methods, beating linear and regular quadratic bounds, but are slightly slower than linear bounds due to gradient computation overhead. When used with enhancements (Adaptive \gammaFn), the improved quadratic bound gives results similar to regular quadratic bounds, with performance gains too small to appear in tables. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents the quadratic term from growing too fast by enforcing the first-order Lipschitz constraint, yielding bigger step sizes than regular quadratic bounds when the derivative would otherwise exceed \lambda. Limitations: Requires gradient computation, making it slightly slower than linear bounds in naive contexts. When to Use: Use when tighter bounds than linear are needed and the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma is available, especially when regular quadratic bounds might violate the first-order constraint. The Improved Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Function was proposed to address the suboptimal performance of regular quadratic inclusion functions, which can perform worse than linear bounds because their derivative can exceed the first-order Lipschitz constant \lambda. It was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". name: Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions
head: 2nd order Taylor bounds, Forward Inclusion Functions, Naive Quadratic Bounds, Quadratic bounds, Regular Quad. Bounds, Regular Quadratic Taylor Bounds
body: Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions (QTIF) are a method for adapting step size in sphere tracing by using quadratic forward inclusion bounds instead of linear ones, explicitly taking the ray direction into account. Unlike linear inclusion functions, which only bound the function value based on the first derivative, QTIFs incorporate the second-order Lipschitz constant of the derivative to bound the function value. Without enhancements, they often perform worse than linear bounds for high-frequency functions like FBM due to exponential growth of the second-order Lipschitz constant. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current position on the ray t0, the implicit field function value Fn(t0) (sum of n bounded functions), the first directional derivative Fn'(t0), the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma{Fn}, and an optional maximum step limit maxt. Output: The maximum safe step size h to the isosurface (typically Fn(t)=0), or inf if no valid forward step exists within maxt. Data Structures: Lipschitz Constants: For a sum of functions Fn = \sum{m=1}^n fm, the second-order Lipschitz constant is the sum of individual constants: \gamma{Fn} = \sum{m=1}^n \gamma{fm} Derivative: The derivative f'(t) denotes the directional derivative in the ray direction \mathbf{u}: f'(t) = \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla f(\boldsymbol{\delta}(t)) Formulas: The forward quadratic Taylor inclusion function for Fn from position t0 is defined as: Fn = Fn(t0) + (t - t0)\left(Fn'(t0) \pm \frac{1}{2}\gamma{Fn} \cdot (t - t0)\right) To find the step size h to the isosurface (where Fn = 0), one solves the quadratic equation derived from the tighter bound (assuming the function decreases towards the surface): Fn(t0) + h Fn'(t0) - \frac{1}{2}\gamma{Fn} h^2 = 0 Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the current field value Fn(t0) and its directional derivative Fn'(t0) at the current ray position t0. 2. Compute or retrieve the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma{Fn} for the current set of active functions. 3. Construct the quadratic inclusion bound Fn using the formula above. 4. Solve for the root h of the equation Fn = 0. This yields the maximum safe step size. 5. Advance the ray by h. 6. Sub-steps (Optional): If sub-stepping is used, estimate the derivative at the new location t1 = t0 + stepi using the worst-case scenario for the second-order Lipschitz constant: F'i(t1) = F'i(t0) + (\gammai \cdot stepi) Then add the next derivative f'{i+1}(t1) to compute the new quadratic bound for the next iteration. Parameters: \gamma: The second-order Lipschitz constant of the derivative. For FBM, this grows exponentially with the number of octaves n as \gamma{noise} \cdot (2^n - 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: FBM Inefficiency: For Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma{Fn} grows exponentially with the number of octaves n. This makes regular quadratic bounds extremely inefficient, often performing worse than linear bounds because the quadratic term grows too fast, leading to smaller step sizes and more iterations. Derivative Cost: Requires computing f'(t) at each step, which can be costly or invalid depending on the function f. Lipschitz Continuity: Requires f'(t) to be Lipschitz continuous. If this condition is not met, the inclusion function is invalid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadratictaylorstep(t0, Fn, Fprimen, gammaFn, raydirection, maxt=float('inf')): """ Computes the next step size using Quadratic Taylor Inclusion Functions. Args: t0: Current position on the ray. Fn: Value of the implicit function at t0. Fprimen: Directional derivative of the implicit function at t0. gammaFn: Second-order Lipschitz constant of the derivative. raydirection: Unit vector of the ray. maxt: Maximum allowed step size. Returns: stepsize: The maximum safe step size, or inf if no valid step exists. """ # Equation: 0.5 gamma h^2 - F' h - F = 0 # Derived from Fn = 0 using the tighter quadratic bound if gammaFn == 0: # Fallback to linear step if second-order bound is zero if Fprimen == 0: return float('inf') h = -Fn / Fprimen return min(h, maxt) if h > 0 else float('inf') # Discriminant: b^2 - 4ac where a=0.5gamma, b=-F', c=-F # Simplifies to F'^2 + 2gammaF discriminant = Fprimen2 + 2 gammaFn Fn if discriminant < 0: # Bound does not cross zero in forward direction return float('inf') sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) # Roots: h = (F' +/- sqrt(F'^2 + 2gammaF)) / gamma # For sphere tracing (F > 0 outside, F' < 0 moving inward), # the '+' branch yields the smallest positive root h = (Fprimen + sqrtdisc) / gammaFn if h <= 0: return float('inf') return min(h, maxt) A method for arbitrary field definitions using Taylor polynomial approximations to perform root isolation. It defines adaptive intervals along the ray using a gradient-based heuristic, analyzes each interval using two Taylor approximations of degree two defined from both end-points, and subdivides intervals until a single root is found, followed by a bounded Newton method. It requires computation of higher-order derivatives and a well-chosen initial step-size, which is inefficient in the context of sphere tracing. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Higher per-step cost than linear bounds due to the need to compute the first derivative f'(t) and the second-order Lipschitz constant \gamma. Memory: Requires storing the first derivative and second-order Lipschitz constant per octave or level, adding computational overhead but minimal memory. Measured Performance: On the "Sponge" scene without enhancements: Regular Quad bounds have 599.9 avg steps, 8969.0 avg octaves, and 181.8 ms time, resulting in a \times 0.6 slowdown compared to Linear bounds. On the "Sponge (far)" scene without enhancements: Regular Quad bounds have 416.6 avg steps, 4671.5 avg octaves, and 96.2 ms time, resulting in a \times 0.4 slowdown compared to Linear bounds. When combined with BVH enhancements (Early stop+1, sub-stepping), quadratic bounds can achieve \times 4.0 speedup over linear bounds with the same enhancements. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Can reduce step count when combined with BVH enhancements and sub-stepping, achieving up to \times 4.0 speedup over linear bounds on optimized scenes. Limitations: For FBM, the exponential growth of \gamma{Fn} with the number of octaves makes regular quadratic bounds extremely inefficient and often worse than linear bounds. The overhead of computing gradients can negate benefits if not optimized. When to Use: Use when the function derivative is Lipschitz continuous and computable, and when the scene does not involve high-frequency FBM with many octaves without BVH enhancements. Use with BVH enhancements (like Early stop+1) to mitigate the cost of computing \gamma for all octaves. When Not to Use: Do not use regular quadratic bounds directly on high-octave FBM without enhancements, as they perform worse than linear bounds. Do not use if the derivative f'(t) is not computable or not Lipschitz continuous. The concept of Lipschitz continuity was first used by Kalra and Barr [KB89] for guaranteed localization of intersections between a ray and an implicit surface, using Lipschitz bounds of both the field function and its gradient. The specific quadratic Taylor inclusion function for sphere tracing was introduced by Aydinlilar et al. [AZ23] as an improvement over linear inclusion functions to better handle grazing rays. name: Affine Arithmetic Range Analysis
head: Applying Range Analysis to INRs, Range Analysis, Range Analysis via Affine Arithmetic
body: Affine Arithmetic Range Analysis is a technique for bounding the output range of a function over a given input domain by decomposing value intervals into affine combinations of unit intervals, known as affine forms. It solves the problem of computing tight inclusion bounds for implicit functions, particularly Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), to enable efficient skipping of non-active regions during hierarchical iso-surface extraction. Unlike Interval Arithmetic which suffers from the dependency problem, or Forward Linear Inclusion Function which relies on local gradients, Affine Arithmetic tracks distinct sources of uncertainty via independent unit interval symbols, guaranteeing that the true output range is contained within the computed bounds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field function f: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R} (e.g., an INR) and an input spatial region defined as a hyper-rectangle (e.g., a 3D cuboid). Output: An affine form representing the estimated range of f over the input region, from which the interval bound [x0 - r, x0 + r] is derived. Data Structures: Affine Form (\hat{x}): A tuple (x0, \alpha1, \dots, \alphaN) where: x0 \in \mathbb{R} is the center (scalar). \alphai \in \mathbb{R} are coefficients for i=1 \dots N. N is the number of unit interval symbols. Unit Interval Symbol (\epsiloni): A symbolic variable representing an independent source of uncertainty, with domain \epsiloni \in [-1, 1]. Numbered Steps: 1. Rewrite Input Region in Affine Form: Convert the input spatial region (e.g., a 3D cuboid centered at \mathbf{x}0 with extents) into an affine form vector \hat{\mathbf{v}}0. For a 2D rectangle centered at x0, y0 with width 2x1 and length 2y1, the affine form vector is (\hat{x}, \hat{y}) where: \hat{x} = x0 + x1 \epsilon1 \hat{y} = y0 + y1 \epsilon2 where \epsilon1, \epsilon2 \in [-1, 1] are independent unit interval symbols. For a 3D cuboid, this extends to three dimensions with corresponding \epsilon symbols. 2. Propagate Through Linear Layers: For each linear layer in the function (e.g., neural network linear layers), apply the affine arithmetic rule for linear functions. If f(\hat{x}) = \alpha \hat{x} + \beta, the output affine form is: f(\hat{x}) = \alpha x0 + \beta + \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha xi \epsiloni where \hat{x} = x0 + \sum{i=1}^{N} xi \epsiloni. This operation preserves the exact bounds for linear transformations. 3. Approximate Nonlinear Functions: For each nonlinear activation function f, obtain a linear approximation \bar{f}(x) \approx f(x):= \alpha x + \beta. Calculate the maximum error \gamma using Chebyshev polynomials to minimize \gamma: \gamma = \max{x \in \text{range}(\hat{x})} |f(x) - \bar{f}(x)| Rewrite the nonlinear function as an affine form including a new error term \epsilon{N+1}: f(\hat{x}) = \bar{f}(\hat{x}) + \gamma \epsilon{N+1} = \alpha x0 + \beta + \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha xi \epsiloni + \gamma \epsilon{N+1} where \epsilon{N+1} \in [-1, 1] is a new independent unit interval symbol representing the approximation error. 4. Repeat Propagation: Repeat steps 2 and 3 for all layers in the function (e.g., all layers of the INR). 5. Read Output Bound: Read the estimated scalar value bound from the final output affine form \hat{v}'{k-1}. The range is calculated as: \text{range}(\hat{x}) = [x0 - r, x0 + r] where r = \sum{i=1}^{N} |xi|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def affineformfromcuboid(center: Vector3, extents: Vector3) -> AffineForm: """ Converts a 3D cuboid defined by center and half-extents into an affine form. Returns an affine form with 3 unit interval symbols. """ # center = (cx, cy, cz) # extents = (ex, ey, ez) # Affine form: x0 + sum(alphai epsiloni) # epsilon1 corresponds to x, epsilon2 to y, epsilon3 to z x0 = center.x y0 = center.y z0 = center.z # Coefficients for epsilon1, epsilon2, epsilon3 # The input region is [cx-ex, cx+ex] x [cy-ey, cy+ey] x [cz-ez, cz+ez] # x = cx + ex epsilon1 # y = cy + ey epsilon2 # z = cz + ez epsilon3 # We return a vector of affine forms, one for each dimension ax = AffineForm(center=x0, coeffs=[ex, 0, 0]) ay = AffineForm(center=y0, coeffs=[0, ey, 0]) az = AffineForm(center=z0, coeffs=[0, 0, ez]) return (ax, ay, az) def affinelinearlayer(inputaffine: AffineForm, weight: float, bias: float) -> AffineForm: """ Applies a linear transformation f(x) = weight x + bias to an affine form. """ newcenter = weight inputaffine.center + bias newcoeffs = [weight c for c in inputaffine.coeffs] return AffineForm(center=newcenter, coeffs=newcoeffs) def affinenonlinearlayer(inputaffine: AffineForm, activationfunc, chebyshevorder=2) -> AffineForm: """ Approximates a nonlinear function using a linear approximation and an error term. Uses Chebyshev polynomials to minimize the maximum error gamma. """ # 1. Determine the range of the input affine form to find the domain for approximation # range = [center - sum(|coeffs|), center + sum(|coeffs|)] radius = sum(abs(c) for c in inputaffine.coeffs) xmin = inputaffine.center - radius xmax = inputaffine.center + radius # 2. Obtain linear approximation fbar(x) = alpha x + beta # This typically involves fitting a line or using Chebyshev approximation # For the purpose of this implementation, we assume a helper function exists # that returns alpha and beta minimizing max error on [xmin, xmax] alpha, beta = fitlinearapproximation(activationfunc, xmin, xmax, chebyshevorder) # 3. Calculate maximum error gamma # gamma = max |f(x) - (alphax + beta)| for x in [xmin, xmax] gamma = computemaxapproximationerror(activationfunc, alpha, beta, xmin, xmax) # 4. Apply linear part to input affine form linearpart = affinelinearlayer(inputaffine, alpha, beta) # 5. Add new error term gamma epsilonnew # The new affine form has one more coefficient than the input newcoeffs = linearpart.coeffs + [gamma] return AffineForm(center=linearpart.center, coeffs=newcoeffs) def propagateinr(inputaffinevector: Tuple[AffineForm, AffineForm, AffineForm], inrlayers: List[Layer]) -> AffineForm: """ Propagates the input affine form vector through the INR layers. """ currentaffine = inputaffinevector for layer in inrlayers: if layer.islinear: # Apply linear layer rules # Assuming layer has weight matrix W and bias b # This is a simplified 1D example; for 3D input, matrix multiplication of affine forms is needed # For vector affine forms, each component is transformed by the matrix newaffine = affinematrixvectormult(currentaffine, layer.weight, layer.bias) currentaffine = newaffine else: # Apply nonlinear activation # Assuming element-wise activation for simplicity newaffine = [] for aff in currentaffine: newaff = affinenonlinearlayer(aff, layer.activation) newaffine.append(newaff) currentaffine = tuple(newaffine) # The output is the final affine form (or vector of affine forms if multi-output) # For scalar field, we take the last component or combine them return currentaffine[0] # Assuming scalar output def getrange(affineform: AffineForm) -> Tuple[float, float]: """ Calculates the interval range from an affine form. """ radius = sum(abs(c) for c in affineform.coeffs) lower = affineform.center - radius upper = affineform.center + radius return (lower, upper) Parameters: \epsiloni: Independent unit intervals with domain [-1, 1], representing distinct sources of uncertainty. \gamma: The bound on the approximation error between the true nonlinear function and its affine approximation. Chebyshev polynomials: Used to approximate nonlinear functions to minimize \gamma. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Conservatism: The estimated bounds are often too large (conservative), especially for complex scientific data with high-frequency features, leading to poor efficiency in skipping non-active regions. Looser Bounds: Output bounds from affine forms are looser than real output intervals because new uncertainty terms \epsilon{N+1} are introduced in the approximation to the nonlinear function. High-Frequency Features: Scalar fields from scientific simulations have more value oscillations and high-frequency features compared to SDFs, leading to large errors between the affine approximation and the true function. Propagates probabilistic affine forms to generate "soft" bounds, improving efficiency over conservative affine arithmetic bounds. Treats error terms in affine forms as uniformly distributed random variables to generate less pessimistic bounds than vanilla range analysis. Time Complexity: Propagating affine forms through a network with L layers and N input dimensions involves arithmetic operations proportional to the number of coefficients. The number of coefficients grows with each nonlinear layer due to the introduction of new error terms \epsilon{N+1}. Memory Complexity: Storage of affine forms requires storing the center and all coefficients. The number of coefficients increases with the depth of the network and the number of nonlinear operations. Strengths: Guarantees exact output bounds through linear functions for linear parts; handles dependencies better than Interval Arithmetic. Limitations: Bounds can be overly conservative for complex, high-frequency functions, reducing the efficiency of region skipping. The introduction of new error terms for nonlinearities leads to looser bounds than the true output interval. When to use: When tight bounds are required for hierarchical iso-surface extraction on INRs, and the function has significant linear components. When not to use: For functions with high-frequency oscillations where the affine approximation error \gamma becomes large, leading to excessive conservatism. Affine Arithmetic Range Analysis was introduced in the context of improving the efficiency of iso-surface extraction on Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). It builds on the general technique of range analysis, which uses interval arithmetic or affine arithmetic to bound function output ranges. The method was developed to address the issue that standard interval arithmetic bounds are often too loose, while affine arithmetic provides tighter bounds by tracking dependencies, though it can still be conservative for complex INRs. The use of Chebyshev polynomials for nonlinear approximation is cited from [23] in the source. name: Propagation of Affine Forms (PAF)
head: Probabilistic Affine Forms (PAF) Propagation, Uncertainty Propagation, Uncertainty Propagation through INRs
body: Propagation of Affine Forms (PAF) is a technique for estimating the output value distribution of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) over a spatial input region by tracking probabilistic affine forms through network layers. It solves the problem of overly conservative bounds in traditional Range Analysis (RA) by generating "soft" probabilistic bounds, which improves the efficiency of hierarchical iso-surface extraction. Unlike its sibling Range Analysis with Uniform Assumption, PAF performs probability estimation at each layer's activation function approximation, allowing for the calculation of exact estimation error variance and resulting in a more accurate output distribution estimate. Inputs: An Implicit Neural Representation (INR) f\theta with k layers. A 3D bounding box defined by lower corner \mathbf{x}l and upper corner \mathbf{x}u. A confidence interval threshold hyperparameter t. An iso-surface value c. Outputs: A set A of active cells (sub-regions) containing the iso-surface. Or an empty set \emptyset if the region is determined to not contain the surface. Data Structures: Probabilistic Affine Form (PAF): A random variable \hat{X} represented as an affine combination of unit random variables: \hat{X} = x0 + \sum{i=1}^{N} xi Zi where x0 is the mean, xi are coefficients, and Zi are unit random variables with E(Zi)=0 and Var(Zi)=1. Input Region Representation: A 3D bounding box is represented as a vector of PAFs \hat{\mathbf{V}}0. For a box with center \mathbf{x}c and diagonal extents, the PAF vector is constructed using a diagonal matrix \mathbf{V} of orthogonal axes coefficients and a vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon} of unit random variables: \hat{\mathbf{V}}0 = \mathbf{x}c + \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} The coefficients in \mathbf{V} normalize the uniform random variables to have unit standard deviation. For a uniform distribution on [-x1, x1], the standard deviation is x1/\sqrt{3}, so the coefficient is x1/\sqrt{3}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Input PAF: Calculate the center \mathbf{x}c = (\mathbf{x}l + \mathbf{x}u)/2. Construct the diagonal matrix \mathbf{V} = \text{Diag}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\mathbf{x}u - \mathbf{x}c)). Define the input PAF vector \hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{x}c + \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, where \boldsymbol{\epsilon} is a vector of independent unit random variables. 2. Propagate Through INR: Pass \hat{\mathbf{X}} through the INR layers sequentially. For each layer, apply linear transformations and activation functions using the rules below to obtain the output PAF \hat{\mathbf{Y}}. 3. Linear Function Rule: For a linear function f(\hat{X}) = \alpha \hat{X} + \beta, the PAF is transformed exactly: f(\hat{X}) = \alpha x0 + \beta + \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha xi Zi The mean becomes \alpha x0 + \beta and the coefficients are scaled by \alpha. 4. Nonlinear Activation Function Rule: For a nonlinear function f(\hat{X}), approximate it with a linear function \bar{f}(\hat{X}) = \alpha x0 + \beta + \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha xi Zi and introduce a new random variable \gamma Z{N+1} to denote the approximation error. The application is converted to: f(\hat{X}) = \bar{f}(\hat{X}) + \gamma Z{N+1} = \alpha x0 + \beta + \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha xi Zi + \gamma Z{N+1} where \gamma is the standard deviation of the approximation error, ensuring Var(Z{N+1})=1. Calculating \gamma: The linear approximation is determined using the least squares method to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the nonlinear function and the linear approximation over the input Gaussian distribution. The MSE is decomposed into error variance and squared bias: MSE = \gamma^2 + [E(Z{N+1})]^2. The least squares method ensures the solution is unbiased (E(Z{N+1})=0), so minimizing MSE is equivalent to minimizing \gamma^2. The variance \gamma^2 is calculated by minimizing the integral of the squared error weighted by the input PDF g(x|\mu, \sigma^2). Analytical solutions exist for common activations like ReLU, ELU, and Sine. 5. Extract Distribution Parameters: After propagation through k layers, the output PAF \hat{\mathbf{Y}} is approximated as a Gaussian distribution using the Lindeberg Central Limit Theorem (CLT). The mean \mu is the zeroth-order coefficient y0 of \hat{\mathbf{Y}}. The variance \sigma^2 is the sum of the squares of the higher-order coefficients yi: \sigma^2 = \sum{i=1}^{M} yi^2 where M is the number of random variables in the output PAF. 6. Decision and Recursion: Check if the region contains the iso-surface using the soft bound: If \mu + t\sigma < c or \mu - t\sigma > c, return \emptyset. Else, if the maximum depth is reached, return the current box \{(\mathbf{x}l, \mathbf{x}u)\}. Else, split the box along the widest dimension into \mathbf{x}'l, \mathbf{x}'u and \mathbf{x}''l, \mathbf{x}''u. Recursively call the procedure for both sub-boxes and return the union of the results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def propagateaffineforms(ftheta, xl, xu, c, t, maxdepth, currentdepth=0): """ Propagates Affine Forms through an INR to determine if a bounding box contains an iso-surface. Args: ftheta: List of layer dictionaries with keys 'W' (weights), 'b' (bias), 'act' (activation function). xl: Lower corner of the bounding box (array). xu: Upper corner of the bounding box (array). c: Iso-surface value. t: Confidence interval threshold. maxdepth: Maximum recursion depth. currentdepth: Current recursion depth. Returns: A set of active cells (bounding boxes) or an empty set. """ # Step 1: Initialize Input PAF xc = (xl + xu) / 2.0 Vdiag = (xu - xc) / np.sqrt(3.0) # PAF state: (meanvector, coeffsmatrix) # coeffsmatrix shape: (numcomponents, numrandomvars) numcomponents = len(xl) numrandomvars = numcomponents coeffsmatrix = np.diag(Vdiag) pafmean = xc.copy() pafcoeffs = coeffsmatrix # Step 2: Propagate Through INR for layer in ftheta: # Linear transformation W = layer['W'] b = layer['b'] pafmean = W @ pafmean + b pafcoeffs = W @ pafcoeffs # Nonlinear activation act = layer['act'] # Compute linear approximation parameters analytically per # alpha, beta are computed to minimize MSE over the input Gaussian distribution alpha, beta = computelinearparams(act, pafmean, pafcoeffs) # Apply linear approximation to PAF pafmean = alpha pafmean + beta pafcoeffs = alpha pafcoeffs # Compute approximation error standard deviation gamma gamma = computeerrorstd(act, pafmean, pafcoeffs) # Append new random variable Z{N+1} with coefficient gamma pafcoeffs = np.hstack([pafcoeffs, gamma]) # Step 5: Extract Distribution Parameters using CLT mu = pafmean[0] # Scalar output for iso-surface check sigmasq = np.sum(pafcoeffs2) sigma = np.sqrt(sigmasq) # Step 6: Decision if mu + t sigma < c or mu - t sigma > c: return set() if currentdepth >= maxdepth: return {(tuple(xl), tuple(xu))} # Split along widest dimension dims = xu - xl widestidx = np.argmax(dims) mid = (xl[widestidx] + xu[widestidx]) / 2.0 xlleft = xl.copy() xuleft = xu.copy() xlleft[widestidx] = mid xlright = xl.copy() xuright = xu.copy() xuright[widestidx] = mid Aleft = propagateaffineforms(ftheta, xlleft, xuleft, c, t, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1) Aright = propagateaffineforms(ftheta, xlright, xuright, c, t, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1) return Aleft.union(Aright) def computelinearparams(act, mean, coeffs): """ Computes alpha and beta for the linear approximation fbar(x) = alphax + beta using the least squares method to minimize MSE over the input Gaussian distribution. Analytical solutions exist for ReLU, ELU, and Sine. """ # The exact analytical formulas for alpha and beta depend on the activation function # and the input distribution parameters (mean, std). They are derived in the appendix of. # This function returns the analytical least-squares coefficients. pass def computeerrorstd(act, mean, coeffs): """ Computes gamma, the standard deviation of the approximation error. gamma^2 is the minimized MSE, which equals the error variance since the least squares solution is unbiased. """ # gamma^2 is calculated by integrating the squared error weighted by the input PDF g(x|mu, sigma^2). # This function returns the analytical error standard deviation. pass Parameters: t: Confidence interval threshold. Typical values are not given in the sources. Zi: Unit random variables with E(Zi)=0 and Var(Zi)=1. Assumption: Zi are independent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The approximation of the PAF distribution with a Gaussian distribution via CLT is an approximation and may introduce inaccuracy, though the source states this inaccuracy is not introduced by the linear function itself. The method relies on the analytical solution for the linear approximation of activation functions. If an activation function does not have an analytical least-squares solution, this method may not be directly applicable without numerical approximation. This method approximates nonlinear activation functions with linear functions to enable the analytical propagation of probabilistic affine forms (PAFs) through Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). It solves the least-squares optimization problem analytically to determine the slope and intercept of the linear approximation, allowing uncertainty to be propagated efficiently without the conservative bounds associated with range analysis. It is distinct from range analysis by maintaining efficiency and accuracy for periodic functions like Sine, where range analysis suffers from high approximation error. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The source states that range analysis bounds are "too conservative, resulting in poor efficiency when used for hierarchical iso-surface extraction". PAF is expected to have a "more accurate output distribution estimate" compared to RA-UA. Strengths: More accurate output distribution estimate than RA-UA; efficient for periodic functions like Sine; generates "soft" bounds for adaptive subdivision. Limitations: Relies on CLT approximation; requires analytical solutions for activation function approximations. When to use: When hierarchical iso-surface extraction on INRs requires efficient pruning of empty regions and high accuracy for periodic activations. When not to use: When exact bounds are required instead of probabilistic bounds, or when activation functions do not have analytical least-squares approximations. Origin: Proposed in "Improving Efficiency of Iso-Surface Extraction on Implicit Neural Representations Using Uncertainty Propagation". History: Probabilistic affine forms were previously proposed by Bouissou et al. [25, 26] for general distributions and dependencies, but this work adapts them for simpler explanation and specific application to INRs. Usage: Used for hierarchical iso-surface extraction from Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). name: Linear Approximation of Activation Functions for Probabilistic Affine Forms
head: Analytical least-squares activation approximation
body: This method approximates nonlinear activation functions with linear functions to enable the analytical propagation of probabilistic affine forms (PAFs) through Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). It solves the least-squares optimization problem analytically to determine the slope and intercept of the linear approximation, allowing uncertainty to be propagated efficiently without the conservative bounds associated with range analysis. It is distinct from range analysis by maintaining efficiency and accuracy for periodic functions like Sine, where range analysis suffers from high approximation error. Inputs and Outputs Input: The mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma of the estimated Gaussian probability density function (PDF) for the input probabilistic affine form. Note: The source text refers to \sigma as "variance" in Table V captions, but the formulas and context define it as the standard deviation parameter of the Gaussian PDF. Output: Linear approximation coefficients \alpha (slope) and \beta (intercept), and the mean squared error \gamma^2 of the approximation. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The method computes scalar coefficients based on the input \mu and \sigma. Steps 1. Identify the activation function type (ReLU, Sine, or ELU). 2. Compute the intermediate variables a, b, c, and \beta (for ELU) using the Gaussian error function \text{erf} and exponential functions, as defined in the formulas below. 3. Compute the mean squared error \gamma^2 to quantify the approximation quality. Formulas The linear approximation is defined as f(x) \approx \alpha x + \beta{linear}. The coefficients are derived by minimizing the least-squares error over the Gaussian distribution defined by \mu and \sigma. 1.
