name: Edge Point Re-parametrization
head: Implicit Surface Deformation via Re-parametrization, Learned Surface Displacement
body:
Edge Point Re-parametrization provides an explicit, closed-form re-parametrization of the surface point x for implicit surfaces, enabling gradients to flow through surface geometry during inverse rendering optimization. It solves the problem that the root of S(x)=0 is not directly differentiable in standard automatic differentiation frameworks when x is the output of a solver. Inputs and Outputs Input: An initial edge point x, the SDF function S{\Thetas} parameterized by \Thetas, and the surface normal n = 
abla S{\Thetas}(x). Output: A re-parametrized surface point x{\Thetas} that lies on the zero-level set of S{\Thetas} and is differentiable with respect to \Thetas. Data Structures x: 3D vector (x, y, z). n: 3D vector (nx, ny, nz), used in the dot product n^T n. S{\Thetas}(x): Scalar SDF value. \Thetas: Parameters of the implicit surface representation (e.g., MLP weights). Steps 1. Define Deformation Direction: The surface point moves along the surface normal n from the initial point x. The deformed point is defined as x{\Thetas} = x + t{\Thetas} \cdot n, where t{\Thetas} is a scalar displacement. 2. Initial Condition: At initialization \Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}, the displacement is zero, ensuring x{\Thetas} = x. 3. Zero-Level Set Constraint: The deformed point must satisfy S{\Thetas}(x{\Thetas}) = 0. 4. Implicit Differentiation: Differentiating the constraint with respect to \Thetas yields  rac{\partial S}{\partial \Thetas}(x{\Thetas}) + \left(  rac{\partial S}{\partial x{\Thetas}} ight)^T  rac{\partial x{\Thetas}}{\partial \Thetas} = 0. 5. Evaluate at Initialization: At \Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}, the gradient of the displacement is  rac{\partial t}{\partial \Thetas}  ig|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}} = - rac{1}{n^T n} \cdot  rac{\partial S}{\partial \Thetas}(x)  ig|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}}. 6. First-Order Approximation: The scalar displacement is approximated as t{\Thetas} \approx - rac{1}{n^T n} \cdot S{\Thetas}(x). 7. Final Re-parametrization: Substituting t{\Thetas} back yields x{\Thetas} = x -  rac{n}{n^T n} \cdot S{\Thetas}(x). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def edgepointreparametrization(x, Sval, n): """ Computes the re-parametrized surface point xtheta. Args: x: Initial 3D point (tensor). Sval: SDF value at x, Stheta(x) (scalar tensor). n: Surface normal vector (3D vector tensor). Returns: xtheta: Re-parametrized point on the zero-level set. """ ndotn = n[0]n[0] + n[1]n[1] + n[2]n[2] if ndotn < 1e-8: return x t = -Sval / ndotn xtheta = x + t n return xtheta Parameters x: Initial intersection estimate. S{\Thetas}(x): SDF value. n: Normal vector 
abla S{\Thetas}(x). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Normals: If n is zero, n^T n is zero, leading to division by zero. A guard is required. First-Order Approximation: The method provides an unbiased first-order gradient with respect to \Thetas, suitable for gradient-based optimizers, but may not capture higher-order surface curvature effects. Initialization: The method assumes the initial point x is close enough to the surface such that the first-order approximation is valid. Reparameterizes the surface intersection equation to make the surface point differentiable with respect to the SDF MLP parameters. It is chosen when differentiable rendering of complex materials and geometry is required simultaneously. Differentiable Surface Point Reparameterization Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per ray, assuming S{\Thetas}(x) and 
abla S{\Thetas}(x) are computed in O(1). Memory: O(1) additional memory per ray. Measured Performance Not given in the sources. Scaling Scales linearly with the number of rays. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Enables gradient-based optimization of implicit surfaces in inverse rendering. Limitations: First-order approximation may be inaccurate for large displacements or highly curved surfaces. When to Use Use when optimizing neural implicit surfaces (SDFs) for inverse rendering tasks where geometry needs to be updated via gradient descent. When Not to Use Do not use for static rendering where geometry is fixed. Do not use if high-order curvature accuracy is critical and the first-order approximation is insufficient. Originated in the context of inverse rendering and neural implicit surface optimization. The method was introduced in the IRON paper (2022) to enable differentiable ray-surface intersection for optimizing Neural SDFs and materials from photometric images. IRON: Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Neural SDFs and Materials from Photometric Images, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00548, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Differentiable Surface Point Reparameterization
head: Differentiable surface point, Reparameterized surface intersection
body:
This method reparameterizes the surface intersection equation to ensure the computed surface point is differentiable with respect to the parameters of the implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) MLP. It solves the problem of non-differentiable surface locations in inverse rendering and optimization, where standard root-finding or ray-marching yields points that do not propagate gradients back to the network weights. It differs from standard ray-marching by explicitly correcting the intersection point using the surface normal, and from discontinuity handling methods by focusing on the smooth zero-set case. Inputs: x: The 3D point on the ray (typically the last sample before or at the estimated intersection). \Thetag: The parameters of the SDF MLP. S{\Thetag}(x): The SDF value at x. Outputs: x{\Thetag}: The reparameterized surface point, differentiable w.r.t. \Thetag. Data Structures: No persistent data structures. The method is a point-wise operation. Steps: 1. Compute the surface normal n at point x by evaluating the gradient of the SDF: n = 
abla S{\Thetag}(x) 2. Compute the reparameterized surface point x{\Thetag} using the following equation: x{\Thetag} = x -  rac{S{\Thetag}(x)}{\|n\|^2} n Note: The source presents the formula as x -  rac{S{\Thetag}(x)}{n} n where n is the normal vector. In vector calculus, division by a vector is undefined. The standard Newton-Raphson step for finding the root of f(t)=0 along the normal direction is x{new} = x -  rac{f(x)}{
abla f(x) \cdot \hat{n}} \hat{n}. If n is the unit normal, \|n\|=1. If n is the raw gradient, the denominator is the squared norm. The source notation n in the denominator likely implies the dot product or normalization. Given n = 
abla S, the standard differentiable correction is x -  rac{S(x)}{\|
abla S(x)\|^2} 
abla S(x). We implement the standard differentiable form. 3. Return x{\Thetag}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterizesurfacepoint(x, sdfmlpparams): """ Computes the differentiable surface point from a ray sample x. Args: x: torch.Tensor, shape (3,), the 3D point on the ray. sdfmlpparams: The parameters of the SDF MLP. Returns: torch.Tensor, shape (3,), the reparameterized surface point. """ # 1. Evaluate SDF value and gradient # Sval is a scalar Sval, gradS = sdfmlpparams(x, computegradient=True) # 2. Compute the squared norm of the gradient # Using a small epsilon for numerical stability if needed, though not specified in source gradnormsq = torch.dot(gradS, gradS) # 3. Apply the reparameterization formula # xnew = x - (Sval / ||gradS||^2) gradS # This corresponds to one step of Newton's method towards the zero set # along the gradient direction. correction = (Sval / gradnormsq) gradS xnew = x - correction return xnew Parameters: None explicitly defined. The method relies on the SDF MLP parameters \Thetag. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If 
abla S{\Thetag}(x) \approx 0, the denominator becomes zero, causing numerical instability. This occurs at critical points of the SDF (minima, maxima, saddles) which are not on the surface. A guard should check for \|n\|^2 < \epsilon and fall back to x or handle the error. Non-unit Normal: The formula assumes the correction is along the gradient. If the gradient is not normalized, the step size is scaled by the gradient magnitude. The formula in is ambiguous regarding normalization. The implementation above uses the squared norm to ensure correct scaling for non-unit gradients. A method to differentiate discontinuities caused by object silhouettes or interior edges in implicitly defined geometry, extending the implicit function theorem from points on the zero set to discontinuities. It is chosen when the geometry involves non-smooth features like silhouettes or interior edges where standard differentiability fails. Unlike the smooth reparameterization, this method does not explicitly compute the discontinuity location xd in the forward pass; instead, the compiler expands a ray marching loop to approach the zero set, and in the backward pass, it samples the discontinuity by evaluating Boolean conditions and applies the implicit function theorem based on whether the ray intersects locally C^1 smooth geometry or not. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming the SDF evaluation and gradient computation are O(1) (dependent on MLP depth). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Enables end-to-end differentiable optimization of SDF parameters in inverse rendering tasks. Limitations: Only applicable to smooth surfaces (zero set of SDF). Does not handle discontinuities without the extension described in Subtopics. Sensitive to gradient magnitude near critical points. The method originates from work on Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues, specifically in the context of optimizing SDF-based representations for material decoupling and surface reconstruction. It builds on previous works [76, 85] cited in for differentiable surface point computation. The extension to discontinuities via the Implicit Function Theorem is motivated by [Yariv et al. 2020] and [Li et al. 2020], and extends results from [Gargallo et al. 2007] which were limited to C^1 continuous geometry. PIR: Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00055, fetched 2026-10-26 A δ, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530125, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Logit-based Root Finding (L-Tracing)
head: L-Tracing, Root Finding Surface Points, secant method for implicit surfaces
body:
L-Tracing is a root-finding method for determining the intersection distance d of a ray with an implicit surface defined by a neural network outputting logits. It solves the problem of locating the zero-crossing of a signed distance-like function in a differentiable rendering pipeline by combining a coarse grid search with a secant method refinement. It is distinguished from standard Signed Distance Function (SDF) intersection methods by its specific handling of neural network logits, where the convention is positive outside the surface and negative inside, and by its use of a cost-matrix-based sign-change detection to efficiently identify the first entry point along the ray. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: rayso: Tensor of ray origins, shape [B, Nrays, 3] or [Nrays, 3]. raysd: Tensor of ray directions, shape [B, Nrays, 3] or [Nrays, 3]. near: Scalar or tensor specifying the near plane distance. far: Scalar or tensor specifying the far plane distance. surfacequeryfn: A callable neural network that takes 3D points and returns logits. logittau: Scalar bias subtracted from network output to center logits. Nsteps: Integer, number of coarse samples along the ray (default 256). Nsecantsteps: Integer, number of secant iterations (passed to refinement). fillinf: Boolean, how to handle rays with no intersection. Outputs: ptpred: Tensor of 3D intersection points, shape [B, Nrays, 3]. dpred: Tensor of intersection distances, shape [B, Nrays]. Data Structures t: Linear space tensor of shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps, 1] with values in [0, 1]. dproposal: Tensor of proposed distances, shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps, 1]. pproposal: Tensor of query points, shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps, 3]. val: Tensor of logits, shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps]. sign: Sign matrix, shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps]. costmatrix: Matrix for finding the first sign change, shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps]. Parameters Nsteps: Default 256. Controls coarse grid resolution. logittau: Bias term. Not given in the sources. Nsecantsteps: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Batching: If batched is False, unsqueeze rayso and raysd at dimension 0 to ensure shape [1, Nrays, 3]. 2. Tensor Conversion: Convert scalar near and far to tensors matching the shape of rayso if they are not already tensors. 3. Coarse Sampling Grid: Create t as a linear space from 0.0 to 1.0 with Nsteps elements. Reshape t to [B, Nrays, Nsteps, 1]. 4. Propose Distances: Compute proposal distances: d{proposal} = near 	imes (1 - t) + far 	imes t Compute query points: p{proposal} = rayso + d{proposal} 	imes raysd 5. Network Query: Query the surface network at p{proposal} to get logits val{raw}. Center the values: val = surface\query n(p{proposal}) - logit	au Shape of val is [B, Nrays, Nsteps]. 6. Initial Occupancy Check: Check if the first sample point (index 0) is inside the surface. The convention is positive outside, negative inside. If val[..., 0] > 0, the first point is outside (not occupied). Let mask{0
ot\occupied} be the boolean mask where val[..., 0] > 0. 7. Sign Change Detection: Construct a sign matrix for adjacent pairs. For i < N{steps}-1: sign[i] = 	ext{sign}(val[i] 	imes val[i+1]) For the last element, set sign[N{steps}-1] = 1. Create a cost matrix by multiplying the sign matrix by descending indices [N{steps}, N{steps}-1, \dots, 1]. Find the minimum cost and its index for each ray. A negative minimum cost indicates a sign change occurred. 8. Masking Valid Rays: Identify rays with at least one sign change: mask{sign\change} = (values < 0). Verify the sign change is from positive (outside) to negative (inside). Check if the value at the identified index is positive: mask{pos	o
eg} = val[..., indices] > 0. Combine masks: mask = mask{sign\change} 	ext{ AND } mask{pos	o
eg} 	ext{ AND } mask{0
ot\occupied}. 9. Secant Method Refinement: Extract bounds for masked rays: d{high}, f{high}: Distance and value at the index where sign change was detected. d{low}, f{low}: Distance and value at the next index (clamped to N{steps}-1). Run the secant method using f{low}, f{high}, d{low}, d{high}, ray origins/directions, and the network function to find refined depth d{pred} for masked rays. 10. Compute Points: For masked rays: pt{pred} = rayso + d{pred} 	imes raysd. For unmasked rays: Initialize pt{pred} to ones (placeholder). 11. Handle No Intersection: If fillinf is false, set depth to far. If fillinf is true, set depth to np.inf. If the first point was occupied (mask{0
ot\occupied} == 0), set depth to 0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def ltracing(rayso, raysd, near, far, surfacequeryfn, logittau, Nsteps=256, Nsecantsteps=10, fillinf=False, batched=False): """ L-Tracing: Logit-based Root Finding for implicit surfaces. Args: rayso: Ray origins [B, Nrays, 3] or [Nrays, 3] raysd: Ray directions [B, Nrays, 3] or [Nrays, 3] near: Near plane distance (scalar or tensor) far: Far plane distance (scalar or tensor) surfacequeryfn: Neural network returning logits for 3D points logittau: Bias to subtract from logits Nsteps: Number of coarse samples Nsecantsteps: Number of secant iterations fillinf: If True, set no-intersection depth to inf, else far batched: If False, assume single batch dimension Returns: ptpred: Intersection points [B, Nrays, 3] dpred: Intersection distances [B, Nrays] """ # 1. Batching if not batched: rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(0) raysd = raysd.unsqueeze(0) B, Nrays, = rayso.shape # 2. Tensor Conversion if not isinstance(near, torch.Tensor): near = torch.full((B, Nrays), near, device=rayso.device) if not isinstance(far, torch.Tensor): far = torch.full((B, Nrays), far, device=rayso.device) # 3. Coarse Sampling Grid t = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, Nsteps, device=rayso.device).view(1, 1, Nsteps, 1) t = t.expand(B, Nrays, Nsteps, 1) # 4. Propose Distances dproposal = near (1 - t) + far t dproposal = dproposal.squeeze(-1) # Shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps] # Expand rays for broadcasting raysoexp = rayso.unsqueeze(2).expand(B, Nrays, Nsteps, 3) raysdexp = raysd.unsqueeze(2).expand(B, Nrays, Nsteps, 3) pproposal = raysoexp + dproposal.unsqueeze(-1) raysdexp # 5. Network Query # surfacequeryfn should handle batched points valraw = surfacequeryfn(pproposal) # Shape [B, Nrays, Nsteps] val = valraw - logittau # 6. Initial Occupancy Check # Positive outside, negative inside. First point outside means val > 0 mask0notoccupied = val[:,:, 0] > 0 # 7. Sign Change Detection # Sign of product of adjacent values signmatrix = torch.sign(val[:,:,:-1] val[:,:, 1:]) # Last element sign is 1 lastsign = torch.ones(B, Nrays, 1, device=rayso.device) signmatrix = torch.cat([signmatrix, lastsign], dim=-1) # Cost matrix: weight by descending index to find first sign change indices = torch.arange(Nsteps, 0, -1, device=rayso.device).view(1, 1, Nsteps) costmatrix = signmatrix indices # Find min cost and index mincost, indices = torch.min(costmatrix, dim=-1) # 8. Masking Valid Rays masksignchange = mincost < 0 # Check if value at index is positive (outside) -> entering surface # Gather values at detected indices # indices shape [B, Nrays], need to gather from val [B, Nrays, Nsteps] valatindex = torch.gather(val, 2, indices.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) maskpostoneg = valatindex > 0 mask = masksignchange & maskpostoneg & mask0notoccupied # 9. Secant Method Refinement dpred = torch.full((B, Nrays), float('inf'), device=rayso.device) if mask.any(): # Extract bounds # dhigh, fhigh at index dhigh = torch.gather(dproposal, 2, indices.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) fhigh = valatindex # dlow, flow at next index (clamped) nextindices = torch.clamp(indices + 1, max=Nsteps - 1) dlow = torch.gather(dproposal, 2, nextindices.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) flow = torch.gather(val, 2, nextindices.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # Run secant method for masked rays # This is a placeholder for the actual secant iteration loop # which would iterate Nsecantsteps times updating d based on flow, fhigh dpred[mask] = runsecantmethod( dlow[mask], flow[mask], dhigh[mask], fhigh[mask], rayso[mask], raysd[mask], surfacequeryfn, Nsecantsteps) # 10. Compute Points ptpred = torch.ones(B, Nrays, 3, device=rayso.device) if mask.any(): ptpred[mask] = rayso[mask] + dpred[mask].unsqueeze(-1) raysd[mask] # 11. Handle No Intersection if not fillinf: dpred[~mask] = far[~mask] else: dpred[~mask] = float('inf') # If first point was occupied, depth is 0 dpred[~mask0notoccupied] = 0 return ptpred, dpred def runsecantmethod(dlow, flow, dhigh, fhigh, rayso, raysd, surfacequeryfn, Nsecantsteps): """ Placeholder for secant method refinement. Iteratively refines the root between dlow and dhigh. """ dcurr = dlow.clone() fcurr = flow.clone() dprev = dhigh.clone() fprev = fhigh.clone() for in range(Nsecantsteps): # Secant step # dnext = dcurr - fcurr (dprev - dcurr) / (fprev - fcurr) # Guard against division by zero denom = fprev - fcurr denom = torch.where(denom == 0, torch.oneslike(denom) 1e-8, denom) dnext = dcurr - fcurr (dprev - dcurr) / denom # Query surface at new point pnext = rayso + dnext.unsqueeze(-1) raysd fnext = surfacequeryfn(pnext) - logittau # logittau must be accessible or passed # Update bounds # If fnext has same sign as fcurr, replace curr with next # Otherwise replace prev with next # Standard secant method updates both points dprev = dcurr.clone() fprev = fcurr.clone() dcurr = dnext.clone() fcurr = fnext.clone() return dcurr Subtopics Secant Method Refinement: A root-finding algorithm that approximates the root by drawing a secant line between two points. It converges faster than bisection but requires derivative-like information (slope) from two previous points. Choose when the function is smooth and differentiable. Coarse Grid Search: A uniform sampling of the ray interval to detect sign changes. It is robust but computationally expensive if N{steps} is large. Choose when the surface topology is complex or unknown. Time Complexity: O(B \cdot N{rays} \cdot N{steps}) for the coarse sampling and network query. The secant refinement is O(B \cdot N{rays} \cdot N{secant\steps}), which is typically negligible compared to the network query. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot N{rays} \cdot N{steps}) to store the coarse samples and logits. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and coarse steps. The neural network query is the bottleneck. Strengths: Handles implicit surfaces defined by neural networks efficiently. The cost-matrix approach allows vectorized sign-change detection. Limitations: Relies on the coarse grid to find the initial bracket. If the surface is very thin or the grid is too sparse, sign changes may be missed. Assumes the ray starts outside the surface. When to use: When rendering neural implicit surfaces where the output is logits rather than signed distances, and the surface is expected to be entered from outside. When not to use: When the ray origin is inside the surface, or when the surface is extremely thin relative to the coarse step size. L-Tracing was introduced in the context of neural implicit surface rendering, specifically for methods that use neural networks to represent surfaces via logits. The method is part of the L-Tracing framework, which aims to efficiently trace rays through these implicit representations. The approach leverages the properties of neural network outputs (logits) and uses a combination of coarse sampling and secant refinement to locate intersections. ziyc/L-Tracing, https://github.com/ziyc/L-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Density Cloud Intersection
head: Density Cloud, Density Cloud Intersection, Metaball / Density Cloud Intersection, Metaball Intersection
body: Ray-Density Cloud Intersection computes the intersection of a ray with a complex implicit surface defined by the fused intensity distribution of multiple atomic centers, typically modeled as Gaussian bumps. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric structures like electron clouds or metaballs where the surface is defined by a threshold of the summed density field. Unlike sibling methods that may perform culling during the rendering loop, this method incorporates culling into the enumeration phase to minimize overhead for large atom counts. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, a set of N atoms where each atom i has a center position \mathbf{c}i and a density profile function, and a threshold value \tau defining the surface. Output: Intersection distance t along the ray, or null if no intersection exists. Data Structures Atom: A structure containing the 3D position \mathbf{c}i and parameters for the density function (e.g., width/sigma for Gaussian). Sphere of Influence: For each atom, a bounding sphere is precomputed based on the allowable error threshold. This sphere encloses the region where the atom's density influence is above the threshold. Formulas The intensity distribution of each atom i is defined as a Gaussian bump: Di(\mathbf{p}) = Ai e^{-\frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}i\|^2}{2\sigmai^2}} where \mathbf{p} is a point in space, Ai is the amplitude, and \sigmai controls the spread. The total intensity at point \mathbf{p} is the summation over all atoms: D(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Di(\mathbf{p}) The surface is defined by the isosurface D(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. Parameters Allowable error threshold: A user-defined value that determines the sphere of influence for culling atoms. An atom is considered "close" if its density influence is above this threshold. Steps 1. Preprocessing (Enumeration Phase): For each atom, compute its sphere of influence based on the allowable error threshold. Enumerate voxels or spatial regions and associate them with atoms whose spheres of influence contain them. This allows culling of irrelevant atoms during ray intersection. 2. Ray Intersection Calculation: Since the equation D(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = \tau cannot be solved algebraically due to the summation of Gaussian functions, numerical methods are required. Use Regula Falsi and Newton iteration to find the root t. During the evaluation of D(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}), only include atoms whose spheres of influence contain the current point \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. This culling is performed during enumeration, not in the inner rendering loop. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raydensitycloudintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, atoms, threshold, tolerance=1e-6, maxiter=50): """ Computes the intersection of a ray with a density cloud surface. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray (normalized). atoms: List of Atom objects, each with position 'center' and 'sigma'. threshold: Float, the density threshold defining the surface. tolerance: Float, convergence tolerance for numerical solver. maxiter: Int, maximum iterations for Newton's method. Returns: Float: Intersection distance t, or None if no intersection. """ # Precompute spheres of influence for culling # An atom is included if its density at the point is above a cutoff. # The sphere of influence radius Ri is derived from the condition Di(p) >= cutoff. # For Gaussian: Ai exp(-Ri^2 / (2sigmai^2)) = cutoff # Ri = sigmai sqrt(-2 ln(cutoff / Ai)) # Note: The specific cutoff value is the "allowable error threshold". # For implementation, we assume a global cutoff or per-atom threshold is provided. # Here we assume a simple distance check against a precomputed radius for efficiency. def getinfluencingatoms(point): """Return atoms whose sphere of influence contains the point.""" influencing = [] for atom in atoms: # Check if point is within the sphere of influence # This check relies on precomputed radii based on the allowable error threshold if distancesq(point, atom.center) <= atom.influenceradiussq: influencing.append(atom) return influencing def totaldensity(point, influencingatoms): """Calculate total density at point using only influencing atoms.""" density = 0.0 for atom in influencingatoms: distsq = distancesq(point, atom.center) # Gaussian bump formula density += atom.amplitude exp(-distsq / (2 atom.sigma2)) return density def densityderivative(point, influencingatoms): """Calculate derivative of density along ray direction.""" # d/dt D(o + td) = grad(D). d # grad(Di) = Di (-2(p - ci) / (2sigma^2)) = -Di (p - ci) / sigma^2 deriv = 0.0 for atom in influencingatoms: diff = point - atom.center distsq = dot(diff, diff) dval = atom.amplitude exp(-distsq / (2 atom.sigma2)) # Gradient contribution gradcontrib = -dval diff / (atom.sigma2) deriv += dot(gradcontrib, raydirection) return deriv # Initial guess and bounds for Regula Falsi / Newton # We need to find t such that density(o + td) - threshold = 0 # Simple initial search to bracket the root or find a starting point # This part is not explicitly detailed in sources, so we use a standard approach tmin = 0.0 tmax = 1000.0 # Arbitrary large value, should be scene-dependent # Check if ray starts inside or outside startatoms = getinfluencingatoms(rayorigin) startdensity = totaldensity(rayorigin, startatoms) if abs(startdensity - threshold) < tolerance: return 0.0 # Find a bracketing interval [ta, tb] ta = 0.0 tb = 1.0 densitya = startdensity densityb = totaldensity(rayorigin + tb raydirection, getinfluencingatoms(rayorigin + tb raydirection)) # Expand interval if no sign change found while (densitya - threshold) (densityb - threshold) > 0 and tb < 10000.0: ta = tb densitya = densityb tb = 2 densityb = totaldensity(rayorigin + tb raydirection, getinfluencingatoms(rayorigin + tb raydirection)) if (densitya - threshold) (densityb - threshold) > 0: return None # No intersection found in range # Newton-Raphson iteration with Regula Falsi fallback or hybrid # Sources specify Regula Falsi and Newton iteration currentt = tb for i in range(maxiter): currentpoint = rayorigin + currentt raydirection influencing = getinfluencingatoms(currentpoint) fval = totaldensity(currentpoint, influencing) - threshold fderiv = densityderivative(currentpoint, influencing) if abs(fval) < tolerance: return currentt if abs(fderiv) < 1e-10: # Fallback to Regula Falsi if derivative is near zero # Regula Falsi: tnew = tb - f(tb) (ta - tb) / (f(tb) - f(ta)) # We need to track f(ta) and f(tb) pass # Newton step nextt = currentt - fval / fderiv # Clamp to interval to ensure convergence if nextt < ta or nextt > tb: nextt = (ta + tb) / 2.0 # Bisection step as safe fallback # Update interval nextpoint = rayorigin + nextt raydirection nextdensity = totaldensity(nextpoint, getinfluencingatoms(nextpoint)) if (nextdensity - threshold) (densitya - threshold) < 0: tb = nextt densityb = nextdensity else: ta = nextt densitya = nextdensity currentt = nextt return currentt if abs(totaldensity(rayorigin + currentt raydirection, getinfluencingatoms(rayorigin + currentt raydirection)) - threshold) < tolerance else None def distancesq(p1, p2): return (p1.x - p2.x)2 + (p1.y - p2.y)2 + (p1.z - p2.z)2 def dot(v1, v2): return v1.x v2.x + v1.y v2.y + v1.z v2.z def exp(x): import math return math.exp(x) Subtopics Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection: Uses marching cubes for isosurface extraction rather than ray intersection. Choose when rasterization is preferred over ray tracing. SDF Raycast Collision Detection: Uses Signed Distance Functions for collision detection. Choose when exact distance to surface is needed for physics, not just visual intersection. Ray Tracing Implicit Surfaces: General category for ray-implicit intersection. This method is a specific instance for density clouds. LevelSetHDDA: Uses Hierarchical Depth-First Approach for level sets. Choose for hierarchical data structures. Ray-Ellipsoid Intersection: Analytical intersection for ellipsoids. Choose for simple primitive shapes. RayImplicitIntersection: General implicit surface intersection. This method is a specific implementation for density clouds. Edge Point Re-parametrization: Technique for refining intersection points. Use as a post-processing step for accuracy. Logit-based Root Finding (L-Tracing): Alternative root-finding method. Choose for better stability in certain density profiles. Time Complexity: The intersection calculation is expensive because it requires numerical iteration (Regula Falsi and Newton) for each ray. The cost depends on the number of influencing atoms at each iteration step. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of atom positions and precomputed spheres of influence. Measured Performance: For a model with 64 atoms, culling time is less than 30% of total rendering time. For a model with 7,011 atoms (Brain density cloud), rendering took 45 minutes on a VAX 11/785, with 8 seconds of preprocessing. Enumeration time for the 7,011 atom model was less than 10 seconds, a negligible fraction of the total rendering time. Strengths: Culling is performed during the enumeration phase, which is more efficient than Blinn's scheme that performs culling in the inner rendering loop. This makes it scalable to larger atom counts. Limitations: Numerical solution is required, which is slower than algebraic solutions. The Gaussian function spreads to infinity, requiring careful culling. When to use: When rendering metaballs or density clouds where visual fidelity of fused surfaces is required. When not to use: When performance is critical and the number of atoms is very large, or when an algebraic solution is possible (e.g., using polynomial functions like biquadratic). The metaball or density cloud primitive was first introduced by Nishimura in the Links ray-tracing system. It was later independently introduced by Blinn in English-language literature. The method was implemented in the ART (Accelerated Ray-Tracing) system, where it was used to render complex structures like the "Brain" density cloud based on a DNA model. name: LinPrim Gradient Computation
head: Backpropagation through ray space intersection, Gradient propagation for LinPrim
body: LinPrim Gradient Computation computes the gradients of intersection depths \mathbf{i} with respect to the ray-space triangle corners \mathbf{v}^{\text{ray}} to enable differentiable rendering of linear primitives. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimization by backpropagating gradients through a linear primitive rasterizer (MTIA) rather than a Gaussian splatting kernel, requiring specific handling of ray-space to world-space transformations and rotation parameter updates. It builds on Ray-primitive intersection to compute the necessary gradients for intersection depths. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}, \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}}, \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}}: The three corners of the triangle in ray space, each a 3D vector (x, y, z). \mathbf{r}: The pixel ray coordinates in ray space, a 2D vector (rx, ry). d: The determinant of the triangle projection in ray space. u, v: The barycentric coordinates of the intersection point relative to the triangle corners. \mathbf{i}1, \mathbf{i}2: The near and far intersection depths of the ray with the primitive. \alpha: The opacity parameter of the primitive. \sigma(\cdot): The sigmoid function. \frac{\partial L}{\partial o}: The incoming gradient of the loss with respect to the final opacity o. Outputs: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}}: The gradient of the loss with respect to each ray-space corner \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}} for k \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Data Structures The method operates on standard 3D vectors and scalars. The barycentric coordinates u and v are scalars. The determinant d is a scalar. The ray coordinates \mathbf{r} are 2D vectors. The corners \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}} are 3D vectors. Bit packing details are Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Compute Opacity Gradient: Calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to the intersection depths \mathbf{i}1 and \mathbf{i}2 using the opacity formula: o(\mathbf{i}1, \mathbf{i}2) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\alpha) \cdot (\mathbf{i}2 - \mathbf{i}1)). Let \frac{\partial L}{\partial o} be the incoming gradient. The gradient with respect to the depth difference \Delta \mathbf{i} = \mathbf{i}2 - \mathbf{i}1 is: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \Delta \mathbf{i}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial o} \cdot \sigma(\alpha) \cdot \exp(-\sigma(\alpha) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{i}). Distribute this gradient to \mathbf{i}1 and \mathbf{i}2: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{i}1} = -\frac{\partial L}{\partial \Delta \mathbf{i}}, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{i}2} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \Delta \mathbf{i}}. 2. Compute Barycentric Coordinate Derivatives: Calculate the derivatives of the barycentric coordinates u and v with respect to the ray-space corners. Barycentric coordinates are invariant to depth, so they have only two non-zero components (x and y). For corner \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}: \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}} = \frac{1}{d} \left( \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{r}y \\ \mathbf{r}x - \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}} \end{pmatrix} - u \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}} \\ \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}} \end{pmatrix} \right) \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}} = \frac{1}{d} \left( \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{r}y - \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}} \\ \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{r}x \end{pmatrix} - v \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}} \\ \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}} - \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}} \end{pmatrix} \right). The derivatives for \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}} and \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}} are analogous, derived by symmetry or by applying the same formula with indices permuted. 3. Compute Intersection Depth Gradients w.r.t. Corners: Calculate the gradient of the intersection depth \mathbf{i} with respect to each ray-space corner \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}. The gradient \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}} is a 3D vector. For corner \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}: \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0^{\text{ray}}} = \begin{pmatrix} -\left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,x}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ - \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{0,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ 1 - u - v \end{pmatrix}. For corner \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}}: \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}1^{\text{ray}}} = \begin{pmatrix} -\left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ - \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{1,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ u \end{pmatrix} Note: The source text contains typos in indices for \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 (e.g., \partial u / \partial \mathbf{v}{1,x} appearing twice, vy used instead of v). The source formula for \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 is incomplete in the source text, showing only two rows. Implementers must infer the third component. Based on the linear combination \mathbf{p} = (1-u-v)\mathbf{v}0 + u\mathbf{v}1 + v\mathbf{v}2 and \mathbf{i} being the z-coordinate of \mathbf{p} in ray space, the z-component for \mathbf{v}1 is u and for \mathbf{v}2 is v. The x and y components follow the symmetric pattern of \mathbf{v}0 with permuted indices. For corner \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}}: \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}2^{\text{ray}}} = \begin{pmatrix} -\left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,x}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ - \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{v}{0,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{1,z}^{\text{ray}} + \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{v}{2,y}^{\text{ray}}} \cdot \mathbf{v}{2,z}^{\text{ray}} \\ v \end{pmatrix} Note: The source uses vy in partial derivatives, likely a typo for v. The third component is v based on symmetry with \mathbf{v}0. 4. Aggregate Gradients: Multiply the gradient of the loss with respect to the intersection depth \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{i}} by the gradient of the intersection depth with respect to the corner \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}} to get the gradient of the loss with respect to the corner: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{i}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{i}}{\partial \mathbf{v}k^{\text{ray}}}. This is a scalar-vector multiplication since \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{i}} is a scalar. 5. Transform Gradients to World Space: Gradient flow towards the ray space center follows the same process as to that of the corners. Undoing ray space and view-space transformations is straightforward as they are matrix multiplications. Transform the gradients from ray space to view space, and then from view space to world space using the inverse of the transformation matrices used in the forward pass. 6. Propagate to Primitive Parameters: Once the gradients have been mapped back into world space, propagate each corner's gradient into the primitive's distance and rotation parameters. Parameters Color learning rate: 2.5 \times 10^{-3}. SH Coefficients learning rate: 1.25 \times 10^{-4}. Opacity learning rate: 2.5 \times 10^{-2}. Rotation learning rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Distance learning rate: 2.6 \times 10^{-4}, scaled by the maximum distance between a known camera pose and the mean camera pose to ensure consistent behavior in scale-ambiguous settings. 2D filter kernel size: 0.1. For octahedra, the ray space vector is moved by half that amount (0.05), as the adjustment is mirrored on both sides. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Octahedron Negation: For octahedra, vertices are in positive or negative directions from the center. The gradient onto the actual ray space feature can be negated. This negation is omitted in the provided formulas for readability but must be applied in implementation. Density Normalization: Do not propagate gradients through the density normalization factor. Source Typos: The source text contains typos in indices for \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 (e.g., \partial u / \partial \mathbf{v}{1,x} appearing twice, vy used instead of v). Implementers should derive analogous formulas for \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 based on symmetry or correct the typos. Missing Z-Components: The source formula for \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 is incomplete, showing only two rows. Implementers must infer the third component based on symmetry with \mathbf{v}0. Assuming \mathbf{i} is the z-coordinate of the intersection point in ray space, the third component for \mathbf{v}1 is u and for \mathbf{v}2 is v. LinPrim Optimization is the training procedure for Linear Primitives, using differentiable rendering to adjust primitive attributes (center, covariance, opacity, color) by backpropagating gradients from a composite L1 and SSIM loss through the entire rendering pipeline. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly handling the backpropagation through the Linear Primitive Intersection Algorithm (MTIA) and preprocessing steps, including specific handling for ray-space to world-space transformation and adaptive learning rates based on scene scale. Choose it when training linear primitives for differentiable volumetric rendering. Time and Memory Complexity The method involves computing barycentric coordinates and their derivatives, which are constant time operations per triangle. The transformation to world space is also constant time. The overall complexity is linear with respect to the number of primitives. Measured Performance On ScanNet++ scene 39f36da05b (rendered on an RTX 3090), the average rendering time with the ray space approximation is 15.87ms, with rasterization taking 14.60ms. Removing the ray space approximation increases the rendering time to 29.15ms, with rasterization increasing to 28.34ms. This increase comes solely from the rasterization step. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of primitives. The ray space approximation significantly improves performance by reducing rasterization time. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Enables differentiable rendering of linear primitives. The ray space approximation provides a significant speedup. Limitations: The method is sensitive to initialization. Removing the ray space approximation increases rendering time significantly. The method struggles with certain classes like Storage Cabinet and Computer Tower compared to 3DGS. When to Use Use this method when differentiable rendering of linear primitives is required and performance is a concern, allowing the use of the ray space approximation. When Not to Use Do not use if high accuracy on complex geometry is required and performance constraints are loose, as removing the ray space approximation improves quality but at a high computational cost. LinPrim Gradient Computation is part of the LinPrim method for differentiable volumetric rendering, which uses linear primitives (triangles) instead of Gaussians. The method was introduced in the paper "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering". The gradient computation is designed to work with the MTIA rasterizer. The method is evaluated on ScanNet++ and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets. LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16312, fetched 2026-10-26

name: LinPrim Optimization
head: X-Gaussian Optimization, X-Gaussian Training
body: LinPrim Optimization is the training procedure for Linear Primitives, using differentiable rendering to adjust primitive attributes (center, covariance, opacity, color) by backpropagating gradients from a composite L1 and SSIM loss through the entire rendering pipeline. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly handling the backpropagation through the Linear Primitive Intersection Algorithm (MTIA) and preprocessing steps, including specific handling for ray-space to world-space transformation and adaptive learning rates based on scene scale. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of Np linear primitives, each defined by attributes \boldsymbol{\mu}i (center), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i (covariance), \alphai (opacity), and \mathbf{f}i (color/features). Ground-truth images from known views. Outputs: Optimized primitive attributes \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, \alphai, \mathbf{f}i. Data Structures: Primitive Attributes: Each primitive i stores: \boldsymbol{\mu}i: 3D position vector. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: 3 \times 3 covariance matrix (or equivalent parameterization). \alphai: Scalar opacity. \mathbf{f}i: Color/feature vector. Ray Space Geometry: Primitives are transformed into ray space for intersection computation, where the position of corners depends on the ray space center and offsets to it. Numbered Steps: 1. Forward Rendering: Render the scene using the current primitive attributes. Compute the intersection depths \mathbf{i} using the Linear Primitive Intersection Algorithm (MTIA). 2. Loss Computation: Calculate the training objective \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of L1 loss \mathcal{L}1 and SSIM loss \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} between the rendered image and the ground-truth image: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \gamma)\mathcal{L}1 + \gamma\mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} where \gamma is a hyperparameter balancing the two loss terms. 3. Rasterization Backpropagation: Backpropagate through the alpha blending process to obtain gradients with respect to each primitive's alpha \alphai and color \mathbf{f}i. The gradient of alpha \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alphai} indicates whether the primitive should be more or less transparent, implying whether the intersections should move closer together or farther apart along the pixel's ray. Propagate gradients through the MTIA to obtain gradients with respect to the intersection depths \mathbf{i}. Aggregate gradients over the triangle corners and both intersections to propagate gradients from alpha to the geometric features (primitive center and vertices). The intersection depth is influenced by the position of each corner of the triangle. 4. Preprocessing Backpropagation: The gradients obtained in Step 3 are in ray space. Reverse the projection and view transformations to yield world space gradients. Compute final center gradients by combining the propagated ray space center gradients with the impact of the position on the ray space approximation and view-dependent color. Split the gradient flow with respect to the corners when undoing the rotation, propagating gradients onto quaternion and distance features respectively. 5. Learning Rate Adjustment: Approximate the scene size using the maximum distance between two training cameras. Adjust the learning rates for position and distance features accordingly to handle scene scale ambiguity. 6. Parameter Update: Optimize the attributes using the ADAM optimizer. Adjust the number of primitives Np using adaptive control (e.g., cloning/splitting based on gradient magnitude or opacity, as adapted from 3DGS). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linprimoptimization(primitives, groundtruthimages, cameras, gamma, numepochs, lrposbase, lrdistbase): # Approximate scene size for learning rate adjustment scenesize = max(camera.position.norm() for camera in cameras) lrpos = lrposbase scenesize lrdist = lrdistbase scenesize # Initialize optimizer state for ADAM optimizerstate = {p: {'m': 0.0, 'v': 0.0} for p in primitives} for epoch in range(numepochs): totalloss = 0.0 for image, camera in zip(groundtruthimages, cameras): # 1. Forward Rendering: Transform primitives to ray space, compute intersections via MTIA, rasterize rayspaceprims = [transformtorayspace(p, camera) for p in primitives] renderedimage = rasterizelinprims(rayspaceprims, camera) # 2. Loss Computation l1loss = sum((renderedimage - image).abs()) / renderedimage.numel() ssimloss = computessimwindow(renderedimage, image) loss = (1 - gamma) l1loss + gamma ssimloss # 3. Rasterization Backpropagation # Backprop through blending to get dalpha and dcolor dalpha, dcolor = backpropblending(loss, renderedimage) # Alpha gradient indicates transparency change, implying intersection depth adjustments dintersection = backpropmtia(dalpha, rayspaceprims) # Aggregate over corners and intersections to get geometric gradients in ray space dgeometricray = aggregategeometricgradients(dintersection, rayspaceprims) # 4. Preprocessing Backpropagation # Reverse projection and view transformations to yield world space gradients dgeometricworld = backproppreprocessing(dgeometricray, camera) # Combine ray space center gradients with position impact on approximation and color dmuworld = combinecentergradients(dgeometricworld, primitives, camera) # Split gradient flow w.r.t corners when undoing rotation onto quaternion and distance dquat, ddist = splitcornergradients(dgeometricworld, primitives) # 5. Update Gradients primitives.mu.grad = dmuworld primitives.quat.grad = dquat primitives.dist.grad = ddist primitives.alpha.grad = dalpha primitives.f.grad = dcolor totalloss += loss.item() # 6. Parameter Update updateadamstep(primitives, optimizerstate, lrpos, lrdist) # Adaptive control for population Np primitives.adaptivecontrol() return primitives Parameters: \gamma: Hyperparameter balancing L1 and SSIM loss. Typical value not given in sources. Learning rates: Adjusted based on scene size (max distance between training cameras). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene Scale Ambiguity: The method explicitly addresses scale ambiguity by adjusting learning rates based on the maximum distance between training cameras. Ray Space vs. World Space: Gradients must be correctly transformed from ray space (where intersection occurs) to world space (where primitives are stored). Rotation Handling: Gradient flow splits when undoing rotation onto quaternion and distance features, requiring careful implementation of the inverse rotation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method mentions "cheaper training costs and faster inference speed" compared to RGB rasterization in 3DGS due to avoiding complex view direction computations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable rendering allows end-to-end optimization. Explicit handling of ray-space to world-space gradients and scene scale adaptation. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of the backpropagation through the MTIA and preprocessing steps. When to use: When optimizing linear primitives for differentiable volumetric rendering, particularly in X-ray or similar modalities where view direction computations can be simplified. Origin: LinPrim Optimization is part of the LinPrim method, introduced in "LinPrim: Linear Primitives for Differentiable Volumetric Rendering". It builds on the differentiable rendering framework of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). History: The method adapts the population control and optimization strategies from 3DGS to linear primitives. Usage: Used for differentiable volumetric rendering, with specific application in X-ray novel view synthesis (Radiative Gaussian Splatting). name: Ray ID Caching
head: RayID Culling, RayID Technique for Avoiding Multiple Intersections
body: Ray ID Caching is an optimization technique used in volume rendering and ray tracing to eliminate redundant intersection tests when a single ray intersects the same geometric object multiple times across different voxels. It solves the multiple intersection overhead by storing a unique identifier (rayID) on each ray and the last intersecting rayID on each object. Unlike methods that require precise voxel-object containment checks (such as Glassner's method), this technique allows for looser voxel lists because redundant intersections are filtered by the ID comparison rather than geometric precision. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of rays, each with a unique rayID; a set of objects, each with a stored objectrayID; and a voxel traversal structure providing candidate objects for each ray. Output: A reduced set of actual intersection tests performed, skipping those where the object has already been tested by the current ray. Data Structures 1. Ray Structure: rayID: An integer variable holding a unique value for that specific ray. 2. Object Structure: objectrayID: An integer variable storing the rayID of the ray that most recently performed an intersection test with this object. Initialization: objectrayID is initialized to 0. No valid ray is ever allowed to have a rayID of 0. Algorithm Steps 1. For each ray r with rayID R, iterate through the list of candidate objects o provided by the voxel traversal. 2. Let O be the objectrayID stored in object o. 3. Compare R and O: If R == O: The object o has already been intersected (or tested) by ray r. Skip the intersection test for o. If R \neq O: Perform the geometric intersection test between ray r and object o. 4. After the comparison and potential test, update the object's stored ID: Set o.\text{object\rayID} = R. 5. If the intersection test succeeds, process the hit according to the rendering pipeline. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyrayidcaching(ray, candidateobjects): """ ray: object with attribute rayID (int) candidateobjects: list of objects, each with attribute objectrayID (int) Returns: list of objects that actually required an intersection test. """ currentrayid = ray.rayID testedobjects = [] for obj in candidateobjects: # Step 1: Compare rayID with object's stored rayID if obj.objectrayID == currentrayid: # Object already tested by this ray; skip intersection test continue # Step 2: Perform intersection test # The source implies the test is performed if IDs don't match. intersectionhit = intersectrayobject(ray, obj) # Step 3: Update object's stored rayID # This marks the object as "tested" by the current ray. # This prevents redundant tests in the same traversal pass. obj.objectrayID = currentrayid # Step 4: Process hit if successful if intersectionhit: testedobjects.append(obj) return testedobjects def intersectrayobject(ray, obj): """ Standard geometric intersection routine. Returns True if ray intersects obj, False otherwise. """ # Implementation varies by primitive type (triangle, sphere, etc.) return False Parameters rayID: Unique integer identifier for each ray. objectrayID: Integer identifier for the last ray that tested the object. Initial objectrayID: 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Initialization: objectrayID must be reset to 0 (or a value distinct from any valid rayID) between frame renders or traversal passes to ensure correctness. Precision: The method relies on integer comparison, avoiding floating-point precision issues associated with geometric containment checks. Memory: Requires storing an additional integer per object. Time Complexity: Adds one integer comparison per potential intersection. This is negligible compared to the cost of a full geometric intersection test, which is typically several orders of magnitude more expensive. Memory Complexity: Adds one integer field per object. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of objects that must be intersected, especially as grid subdivision increases and objects span more voxels. In test scenes with up to 3540 objects, the number of actual intersections remained small. Strengths: Allows for looser voxel lists (faster voxelization/traversal setup) because redundant intersections are filtered by ID rather than requiring tight voxel-object containment. The technique was described in the context of "Fast Voxel Traversal for Ray Tracing". It addresses the "multiple intersection problem" where a ray intersects the same object multiple times as it traverses different voxels. The paper contrasts this with Glassner's method, which required computing the exact voxels an object occupies—a non-trivial task for complicated objects. The implementation was tested on a Sun 3/75 running Unix, with scenes rendered at 512x512 resolution. Future research directions mentioned include reducing reliance on floating-point calculations and adapting the algorithm to other space partitioning structures. name: Ray Occlusion Test
head: hitSomething, hitSomething8, rtcOccluded1, rtcOccluded8
body: The Ray Occlusion Test determines whether a ray intersects any geometry within a specified distance range, returning only a binary result rather than detailed intersection data. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, minimum distance t{near}, maximum distance t{far} (typically infinity), and an acceleration structure context. Output: Boolean indicating if any geometry was intersected within [t{near}, t{far}]. Data Structures The method uses a ray structure (e.g., RTCRay or RTCRay8) containing: origin: 3D vector (x, y, z) direction: 3D vector (x, y, z), typically normalized. tnear: float, minimum intersection distance. tfar: float, maximum intersection distance. hit: boolean or flag indicating intersection status. Steps 1. Initialize the ray structure with origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Set t{near} to the specified minimum distance. 3. Set t{far} to the maximum valid distance (typically infinity). 4. Initialize the acceleration structure context if not already done. 5. Invoke the occlusion query function (rtcOccluded1 for single rays or rtcOccluded8 for batched rays). 6. Return true if an intersection occurred within the range, false otherwise. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayocclusiontest(origin, direction, mindist, maxdist, context): # Initialize ray structure ray = {'origin': origin, 'direction': direction, 'tnear': mindist, 'tfar': maxdist, 'hit': False} # Initialize context if not already done if context is None: context = {} # # Invoke occlusion query function (e.g., rtcOccluded1 or rtcOccluded8) # This queries the acceleration structure for any intersection # Implementation depends on the specific ray tracing kernel # Standard library call to update ray state ray['hit'] = queryaccelerationstructure(ray, context) # Return result based on intersection status return ray['tfar'] < 0.0 Parameters mindist: Minimum ray distance for intersection. Edge Cases If t{near} > t{far}, the test should return false immediately. Degenerate rays (zero-length direction) should be handled or rejected. An optimized variant using pre-generated sampling masks to efficiently update occlusion values along a ray direction, designed to accelerate local density averages in 3D volumes. name: Ray-cast Occlusion with Sampling Masks
head: Slab-based Occlusion Accumulation, VolumeManager::calcOcclusion, VolumeManager::initSlice, calcOcclusion, initSlice
body: Ray-cast Occlusion with Sampling Masks is an optimized method for calculating volume occlusion values by using pre-generated sampling masks to efficiently update occlusion values along a ray direction, rather than re-sampling the entire sphere for each voxel. It builds on Ray Occlusion Test by providing the actual occlusion intensity values required for ray casting, specifically designed to accelerate the computation of local density averages in 3D volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume data structure (mvolume), a sampling radius (rad or radius), pre-computed sampling masks (idxadd and idxremove), and a direction vector (dir) with step increment (stepInc). Output: An occlusion value for each voxel, stored in mocclusion. Data Structures: mvolume: The 3D volume grid, accessed via getVoxel(mvolume, pos). idxadd and idxremove: osg::Vec3Array objects containing offset vectors for voxels entering and leaving the sampling sphere as the ray progresses. occprev: An array storing the occlusion value for the previous slice along the primary accumulation axis (e.g., y-slice or x-slice). addprev, subtprev: Accumulators for the net voxel intensity entering and leaving the sampling window along the secondary axes. msphereSamples: The count of voxels actually inside the sampling sphere. Formulas: Total voxels in cubic bounding box: w = (2 \cdot rad + 1)^3. Net difference in intensity: diff = \frac{add - rem}{m\sphereSamples}. The source specifies dividing by w in intermediate slab-based updates, but the final formula section specifies dividing by m\sphereSamples (the actual voxel count inside the sphere). Parameters: rad: The radius of the spherical sampling kernel, determining the window size for occlusion calculation. radius: The radius of the sampling sphere. dir: The direction vector of the ray along which occlusion is accumulated. stepInc: The starting coordinate offset for the ray. Steps: The method typically involves initialization and incremental updates using masks. The implementation iterates through volume dimensions z from 0 to mvolume->r(), x from 0 to mvolume->s(), and y from 0 to mvolume->t(). 1. Initialization: Initialize occprev[y] to store occlusion for the previous y-slice. Initialize addprev and subtprev to 0. For the base case (x=0, y=0), compute the full occlusion for the first voxel by summing all voxels in the sphere centered at pos. Store this in occprev[0] and set mocclusion for that voxel. This step also sets msphereSamples. 2. First Column Update (x=0, y>0): Calculate the difference between voxels entering the sphere at the top (y+rad) and leaving at the bottom (y-rad) along the y-axis. Sum these into temporary accumulators add and subt. Compute diff = \frac{add - subt}{w}. Update occlusion: occ = diff + occprev[y-1]. Store result in occprev[y] and set mocclusion voxel. 3. First Row Reset (y=0, x>0): Reset addprev and subtprev to 0. Calculate the difference between voxels entering at the right (x+rad) and leaving at the left (x-rad) along the x-axis for the current z-slice. This prepares the accumulators for the main loop. 4. Main Loop Update (x>0, y>0): Update addprev by adding voxels entering at x+rad and subtracting voxels leaving at x-rad for each z in [-rad, rad]. Update subtprev similarly. This effectively slides the sampling window along the x-axis. Compute final occlusion for current voxel: diff = \frac{addprev - subtprev}{w}. occ = occprev[y] + diff. Set mocclusion voxel and update occprev[y] for the next y iteration. 5. Alternative Mask-Based Update: For each voxel at pos (iterating y from 0 to t(), x from 0 to s()): Base case (x=0): Compute initial occlusion using getOcclusion(pos, radius). Set mocclusion and store in occold. Update case (x>0): Define prev position as (x-1, y, stepInc). Initialize add=0, rem=0. Subtract old voxels: Iterate through remmask (equivalent to idxremove). For each offset, calculate tmp = prev + offset. Add getVoxel(mvolume, tmp) to rem. Add new voxels: Iterate through addmask (equivalent to idxadd). For each offset, calculate tmp = pos + offset. Add getVoxel(mvolume, tmp) to add. Compute diff = \frac{add - rem}{m\sphereSamples}. Update occlusion based on previous value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeocclusionmasks(volume, radius, idxadd, idxremove, stepinc): occprev = [0.0] volume.t() addprev = 0.0 subtprev = 0.0 mspheresamples = 0 occold = 0.0 for z in range(volume.r()): for x in range(volume.s()): for y in range(volume.t()): pos = (x, y, z) # Base case: first voxel if x == 0 and y == 0: occold = getocclusion(pos, radius, volume) occprev[0] = occold volume.setocclusion(pos, occold) continue # Alternative mask-based update (simplified view from source) if x == 0: occold = getocclusion(pos, radius, volume) volume.setocclusion(pos, occold) continue # Update case (x > 0) prevpos = (x - 1, y, stepinc) addval = 0.0 remval = 0.0 # Subtract old voxels for offset in idxremove: tmp = (prevpos[0] + offset.x, prevpos[1] + offset.y, prevpos[2] + offset.z) remval += volume.getvoxel(tmp) # Add new voxels for offset in idxadd: tmp = (pos[0] + offset.x, pos[1] + offset.y, pos[2] + offset.z) addval += volume.getvoxel(tmp) # Compute difference and update occlusion diff = (addval - remval) / mspheresamples occ = occold + diff volume.setocclusion(pos, occ) occold = occ Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Specific if/else branches are required for x=0 and y=0 to handle the initialization of the sliding window accumulators correctly, preventing out-of-bounds access or incorrect accumulation logic. Normalization: msphereSamples is set by getOcclusion and represents the number of voxels in the sampling sphere, used as the divisor for the difference calculation. A method to calculate occlusion values for a volume, serving as the base case for the incremental mask-based method. It computes the average intensity of all voxels within a sphere of radius rad centered at pos. Definition: Computes res by iterating through a cube bounding the sphere (x, y, z from -rad to rad), incrementing msphereSamples for each valid voxel inside the sphere, and summing their values. Returns res / msphereSamples. Parameters: radius (sphere radius), dir (direction vector for sampling in calcOcclusion), stepInc (step increment, default 1). Usage: Implemented in VolumeManager.cpp, used by the VolumeManager singleton to provide occlusion data for the ray casting renderer and to initialize values for the faster mask-based method. Not given in the sources. The method originates from the volume-occlusion-editor project by MPanknin. It is designed to support ray casting renderers by providing efficient local density estimates. name: Point-Plane Reflection
head: Reflect Point Across Plane, Space Reflection
body: Point-Plane Reflection computes the mirror image of a point \mathbf{p} across a plane defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a scalar offset c. It serves as a fundamental geometric primitive for ray-primitive intersection, specifically for determining specular reflection directions or mirroring geometry in volumetric and differentiable rendering contexts. It is distinct from Mirror, which applies this reflection operation to entire volumetric datasets for symmetry filling, whereas Point-Plane Reflection operates on individual geometric entities. Inputs and Outputs Input: Point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, plane normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3, plane offset c \in \mathbb{R}. Output: Modified point \mathbf{p}' (the reflected point) and a signed distance indicator s = \text{sign}(t). Data Structures \mathbf{p}: 3-component floating-point vector. \mathbf{n}: 3-component floating-point vector. c: Single floating-point scalar. t: Single floating-point scalar representing the signed distance. Steps 1. Compute the signed distance t from the point to the plane using the dot product and offset: t = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + c 2. Check if the point lies on the negative side of the plane relative to the normal. If t < 0: Reflect the point across the plane by subtracting twice the signed distance along the normal: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} - 2t\mathbf{n} 3. Return the sign of t: s = \text{sign}(t) where \text{sign}(t) is -1 if t < 0, 0 if t = 0, and 1 if t > 0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointplanereflection(p, n, c): # Step 1: Compute signed distance t t = p[0]n[0] + p[1]n[1] + p[2]n[2] + c # Step 2: Reflect if t < 0 if t < 0: p[0] = p[0] - 2.0 t n[0] p[1] = p[1] - 2.0 t n[1] p[2] = p[2] - 2.0 t n[2] # Step 3: Return sign of t signt = -1 if t < 0 else (1 if t > 0 else 0) return p, signt Parameters Normalization of \mathbf{n}: The formula assumes \mathbf{n} is a unit vector. If \mathbf{n} is not normalized, the offset c and the distance t are scaled by \|\mathbf{n}\|, and the reflection vector 2t\mathbf{n} becomes geometrically incorrect unless \mathbf{n} is normalized first. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-normalized Normal: If \mathbf{n} is not normalized, the reflection is geometrically incorrect. Precision: For points very close to the plane (t \approx 0), floating-point errors may cause oscillation if this operation is repeated iteratively. Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{n} is the zero vector, the plane is undefined. The Mirror method is a volumetric filling tool that copies content from a source region to a target region across a user-defined reflection plane. It is designed to exploit symmetry in structures, such as the human body or head, by allowing users to interactively define a plane that divides the volume into two parts. Unlike the parent Point-Plane Reflection which reflects a single point, Mirror operates on volumetric data, copying material values from one side of the plane to the other. The Image Method for Specular Reflection is a geometric technique to determine the specular hit point and path length by mirroring the receiver (or source) across the reflecting surface, converting the broken path into a straight line. It provides a deterministic, closed-form solution for the hit point and angles without iterative optimization, unlike angle search methods. Formula The path length \ell(h) is given by: \ell(h) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + (2h - yS - yR)^2} where h is the wall height, yS and yR are source and receiver y-coordinates, and \Delta x is the horizontal distance. The hit point xB is: xB = xS + \frac{(h - yS)(xR - xS)}{2h - yS - yR} The reflection angle \thetai = \thetar is: \thetai = \thetar = \arctan\left[ \frac{|xR - xS|}{|2h - yS - yR|} \right] Pitfall The derivative \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial h} = \frac{2(2h - yS - yR)}{\ell(h)} applies only to a nonzero-length path while the same valid reflection branch is retained. If the path topology changes (e.g., hit point moves off the surface), the derivative is invalid. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per point reflection. The operation involves a dot product, a few multiplications, and a conditional update. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space. Measured Performance Not given in the sources. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of points to be reflected. It is highly suitable for parallel execution on GPUs, as each point reflection is independent. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Exact, closed-form solution; computationally inexpensive; easy to implement. Limitations: Only applicable to planar surfaces; requires normalized normal vector; does not handle curved or complex geometries directly. When to Use Use when reflecting points across flat planes, such as in specular reflection calculations, symmetry operations, or simple geometric transformations. When Not to Use Do not use for curved surfaces, non-planar boundaries, or when the normal vector is not available or not normalized. The Point-Plane Reflection method is a standard geometric transformation used in computer graphics, particularly in ray tracing and volume rendering for specular reflections and symmetry operations. It is derived from basic linear algebra and vector geometry. The Image Method variant is used in differentiable ray tracing to compute specular paths deterministically. tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differentiable ray tracing — from paths to gradients | Bai Liping, https://bailiping.com/differentiable-ray-tracing/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Image Method for Specular Reflection
head: Image Method (IM), Method of Images, Unfolded reflection
body: The Image Method (IM) is a geometric technique that determines the specular hit point and path length on a planar surface by mirroring the receiver (or source) across the reflecting plane, thereby converting the broken emitter–surface–receiver path into a straight line. Unlike angle search methods, IM provides a deterministic, closed-form solution for the hit point and angles without iterative optimization. It is limited to specular reflections on planar surfaces, whereas methods like Fermat-Path-Tracing (FPT) and Min-Path-Tracing (MPT) can simulate arbitrary numbers of diffractions or reflections. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Source position S = (xS, yS). Receiver position R = (xR, yR). Reflecting plane defined by height h (for a horizontal plane at y=h). In the general case, the plane is defined by a normal vector and offset, but the primary formula provided assumes a horizontal wall. Horizontal distance \Delta x = |xR - xS|. Outputs: Hit point xB on the surface. Path length \ell(h). Incident/Reflected angle \thetai = \thetar. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar coordinates and basic geometric primitives. Steps 1. Mirror the Receiver: Reflect the receiver position R across the plane to obtain the image point R'. For a horizontal plane at height h, the vertical coordinate of the image is y{R'} = 2h - yR. The horizontal coordinate remains x{R'} = xR. 2. Construct Straight Line: Form a straight line segment from the source S to the image R'. 3. Calculate Path Length: The path length \ell(h) is the Euclidean distance between S and R': \ell(h) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + (2h - yS - yR)^2} where \Delta x = |xR - xS|. 4. Determine Hit Point: The specular hit point xB is the intersection of the line segment S \to R' with the plane y=h: xB = xS + \frac{(h - yS)(xR - xS)}{2h - yS - yR}. 5. Calculate Angles: The incident and reflected angles are equal and determined by the geometry: \thetai = \thetar = \arctan\left( \frac{|xR - xS|}{|2h - yS - yR|} \right). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imagemethodspecularreflection(xs, ys, xr, yr, h): """ Calculate specular reflection hit point and path length using the Image Method. Args: xs, ys: Source coordinates. xr, yr: Receiver coordinates. h: Height of the horizontal reflecting plane. Returns: xb: Hit point x-coordinate on the plane. pathlength: Total path length S -> Surface -> R. angle: Incident/reflected angle in radians. """ # Horizontal distance deltax = abs(xr - xs) # Vertical term in the unfolded path # This represents the vertical distance between source and mirrored receiver verticaldiff = 2 h - ys - yr # Path length: Euclidean distance from S to R' (mirrored R) pathlength = (deltax2 + verticaldiff2)0.5 # Hit point x-coordinate # Intersection of line S->R' with y=h # Avoid division by zero if source and receiver are at same vertical level relative to plane center if verticaldiff == 0: # Degenerate case: source and receiver are symmetric with respect to the plane height # The hit point is the midpoint horizontally xb = (xs + xr) / 2.0 else: xb = xs + ((h - ys) (xr - xs)) / verticaldiff # Angle of incidence/reflection # atan2 handles the quadrant correctly, but here we use absolute values for magnitude # The angle is with respect to the normal (vertical) or surface? # The formula uses atan(|dx|/|dy|), which is the angle with the normal if dy is vertical. # Standard definition: angle with normal. angle = abs(atan2(deltax, abs(verticaldiff))) return xb, pathlength, angle Parameters and Typical Values h: Plane height. Must be such that the hit point lies on the physical surface if the surface is bounded. \Delta x: Horizontal separation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Derivative Validity: The derivative \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial h} = \frac{2(2h - yS - yR)}{\ell(h)} applies only to a nonzero-length path while the same valid reflection branch is retained. If the path topology changes (e.g., the hit point moves off the surface), the derivative is invalid. Degenerate Input: If 2h - yS - yR = 0, the denominator in the hit point calculation becomes zero. This corresponds to the source and receiver being symmetric with respect to the plane's height, resulting in a horizontal path segment parallel to the plane's normal projection? No, it means the source and mirrored receiver have the same y-coordinate, so the line connecting them is horizontal. If the plane is horizontal, they never intersect unless they are on the plane. In this case, the hit point is the midpoint. Time Complexity: O(1), as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables. Strengths: Deterministic, closed-form solution; no iterative optimization required; differentiable with respect to geometric parameters. Limitations: Limited to specular reflections on planar surfaces. Cannot handle multiple reflections or diffractions directly. When to Use: When simulating single specular reflections on flat surfaces where performance and differentiability are critical. When Not to Use: For complex scenes with multiple reflections, diffractions, or non-planar surfaces. The Image Method is a classical technique in electromagnetics and optics for solving boundary value problems. In the context of differentiable ray tracing, it has been adapted to provide analytical gradients for path lengths and hit points, facilitating optimization of geometry and material parameters in radio network simulations. It is implemented in frameworks like Sionna RT for differentiable ray tracing.
