name: Mirror
head: Mirror Tool, Mirroring tool
body: The Mirror method is a volumetric filling tool that copies content from a source region to a target region across a user-defined reflection plane. It is designed to exploit symmetry in structures, such as the human body or head, by allowing users to interactively define a plane that divides the volume into two parts. Unlike the parent Point-Plane Reflection which reflects a single point, Mirror operates on volumetric data, copying material values from one side of the plane to the other. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a user-defined reflection plane (position and orientation), and a mirroring direction. Output: A modified volume where the target region contains copied material from the source region. Data Structures: The implementation uses a texture-based system. The volume data is stored in VolumeTex (3D texture). A SculptMap (3D texture) acts as a mask representing visibility and inserted material, using the alpha channel (Col.a) for visibility and the blue channel (Col.b) for inserted material. A PolygonCoord (2D texture) provides texture coordinates for sampling the volume data. Steps: 1. The user interactively selects the position and orientation of the reflection plane. 2. The direction of mirroring, represented by an arrow on the plane, defines the target area for copying. The opposite direction defines the source region. 3. For each voxel V in the selected part of the volume, calculate the coordinates of its reflected voxel V'. Let P be the orthogonal projection of V onto the reflection plane. Let d be the distance between voxel V and its orthogonal projection P. The mirrored voxel V' is located at an absolute distance |d| from P, in the same direction as the vector \vec{v}(V-p). 4. Access the voxel at V' in the source region. 5. If visible material exists at V', copy its content to V. Formula: Let d be the distance between voxel V and its orthogonal projection P on the reflection plane. The mirrored voxel V' is located at absolute distance |d| from P, in the same direction as the vector \vec{v}(V-p). Pseudocode: The source provides a fragment shader implementation (FSMirror) applied to proxy geometry fragments, noting it considers a plane moving along the X axis. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def FSMirror(v2fTexCoord, P, SculptMap, PolygonCoord, VolumeTex): # Map fragment to volume coordinates via 2D texture sampling texCoord = PolygonCoord.sample(v2fTexCoord) # Get current volume voxel value via 3D texture sampling volumevoxel = VolumeTex.sample(texCoord.xyz) # Get current mask state (visibility in alpha, insertion in blue) Col = SculptMap.sample(texCoord.xyz) # Calculate 3D Euclidean distance from the plane point P to the current voxel # P.a is used as a divisor for normalization or scaling D = ((P.x - texCoord.x)2 + (P.y - texCoord.y)2 + (P.z - texCoord.z)2)0.5 / P.a # Check if the voxel is within the influence of the mirror tool if D < Col.a: # Do not overwrite existing material if it is not background # Col.a == 0.0 implies no visibility/mask active # volumevoxel.r == 0.0 implies background/no material if volumevoxel.r == 0.0 or Col.a == 0.0: # Mark this voxel as having inserted material (using blue channel) Col.b = 1.0 return Col Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overwriting: The tool does not overwrite existing material. It checks the current value of voxels; they are filled only if they have background values (e.g., volumevoxel.r == 0.0). Visibility: The tool relies on a visibility mask (Col.a) to determine which voxels are affected. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exploits symmetry in structures like the human body, reducing manual effort for symmetric modeling. Integrated into a texture-based volume rendering system, allowing users to manipulate only a 3D mask before concluding the sculpting process. Limitations: Limited to structures with symmetry. Does not overwrite existing material, which may require pre-cleaning of the target region. When to Use: Use when working with symmetric anatomical structures (e.g., human head) and when the target region is empty or contains background values. The Mirror tool was developed as part of a volume sculpting system based on geometric tools, specifically integrated with 3D Clipper and Digger tools. It was designed to provide direct insertion of material in voxels by exploiting the existing symmetry of many structures of the human body. The implementation uses specific shaders (FSMirror) applied to fragments of proxy geometry within a texture-based volume rendering pipeline. The tool was assessed in a practical application reported in Section 7 of the source paper. Volume sculpting based on geometric tools, https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03194498, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ray Cursor
head: Ray Cursor Selection, laser gun selection
body: Ray Cursor is a 3D selection technique where a virtual ray is emitted from a user-controlled source (typically the hand or finger) to identify and select objects in a scene. It solves the problem of selecting specific models in volumetric or immersive 3D environments where traditional 2D input devices are insufficient. Unlike Ray Occlusion Test, which defines the ray by the vector between the eye and hand, Ray Cursor allows the user to independently control the ray's origin and orientation, offering greater flexibility but requiring higher angular accuracy. Inputs and Outputs Input: User hand position \mathbf{p}{hand} and orientation (defining direction \mathbf{d}); scene geometry (list of objects). Output: Selected object identifier; visual feedback (highlighting). Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{p}{hand} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}. Intersection List: A list of intersection points \{ \mathbf{i}1, \mathbf{i}2, \dots, \mathbf{i}n \} sorted by distance from \mathbf{o}. Steps 1. Emit Ray: The system generates a ray starting at the user's hand position \mathbf{p}{hand} with direction \mathbf{d} determined by hand orientation. 2. Intersect: Perform ray-object intersection tests against all scene objects. 3. Sort: Sort intersection points by distance from the ray origin \mathbf{o}. 4. Highlight: Highlight the closest intersected object (first in the sorted list) by changing its color (e.g., to yellow). 5. Cycle (Optional): If multiple objects are intersected, allow the user to cycle through them by moving the hand forward (selecting further objects) or backward (selecting closer objects). 6. Select: Upon a trigger gesture, select the currently highlighted object (turning it blue). Formulas Ray Equation: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where t \ge 0. Distance Metric for Cone Disambiguation (Spotlight Selection): If using a cone instead of a ray, select the object based on the distance from the target to the apex and central axis of the cone. Parameters Ray Color: Yellow for highlighting, Blue for selected. Cone Apex: Located at the user's hand. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Angular Accuracy: Selecting small and distant objects is difficult due to the required precision in hand orientation. Multiple Intersections: A ray may intersect multiple objects. The system must disambiguate which object to select. Occlusion: If the user cannot see the hand or ray clearly, selection may fail. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycursorselect(handposition, handorientation, sceneobjects): # Define ray origin and direction rayorigin = handposition raydirection = normalize(handorientation) # Find all intersections intersections = [] for obj in sceneobjects: hitpoint, hitdistance = intersectrayobject(rayorigin, raydirection, obj) if hitpoint is not None: intersections.append((hitdistance, obj, hitpoint)) # Sort by distance intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) if not intersections: return None # Highlight the closest object closestdistance, closestobj, closestpoint = intersections[0] highlightobject(closestobj, color="yellow") # If cycling is enabled, allow user to select further objects # This is handled by user input loop, not shown here return closestobj Uses a cone instead of a ray to accommodate angular error. Selects the object closest to the cone's central axis and apex. Choose when high angular precision is difficult. Defines the ray by the vector between the eye and hand. Choose when the user wants to select objects behind their hand. Time Complexity: O(N) for intersection tests against N objects, plus O(M \log M) for sorting M intersections. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store intersection points. Strengths: Intuitive for 3D environments; allows selection of near and distant objects. Limitations: High angular accuracy required for small/distant objects; multiple intersections require disambiguation. When to Use: Immersive 3D environments with volumetric displays or VR. When Not to Use: 2D interfaces; scenes with high object density where disambiguation is complex. Ray Cursor selection was implemented by Liang and Green in 1994 as "laser gun" selection for immersive 3D environments. It was designed to allow users to select both near and distant objects by emitting a ray from the user's hand. The technique was later explored in volumetric displays, where it was found to be more effective than other techniques for static selection tasks. Hinckley suggested augmenting the technique with cycling through intersection points. name: Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection
body: This family defines the geometric intersection between a camera ray and 3D Gaussian splats, which are ellipsoidal primitives used in novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of accurately determining which splats contribute to a pixel and at what depth, enabling alpha blending and depth-based operations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by handling the specific quadratic nature of Gaussian density fields, supporting both exact ellipsoid intersection and numerical stabilization for degenerate cases, unlike Sphere Intersection which assumes constant radius or Ray-Triangle Intersection which handles planar surfaces. The shared principles are inherited from Ray-primitive intersection. Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation computes the precise intersection point of a viewing ray with a flat surfel rectangle in the surfel's local (u, v) coordinates. It solves the problem of determining where a pixel's ray hits the surfel plane to evaluate the 2D Gaussian opacity, avoiding the per-pixel cross products and divisions required by the original 2DGS formulation. It sets itself apart from Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection by using a homography approximation around the screen-space bounding box center to replace the exact ray-plane intersection with a rational function, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. SPaGS is a real-time rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that supports arbitrary spherical camera models, specifically equirectangular panoramas, by replacing the standard local affine approximation with a numerically stable ray-splat intersection approach. It solves the problem of rendering artifacts and numerical instability inherent in standard 3DGS when applied to wide-field-of-view or distorted panoramic views, where first-order affine projections fail to accurately represent the Gaussian distribution. Unlike ODGS, which uses suboptimal tangent plane approximations, or 3DGUT, which relies on the Unscented Transform, SPaGS achieves higher quality and speed by representing each viewing ray as the intersection of two perpendicular planes in camera space, thereby avoiding matrix inversion of the covariance. Ray-Splat Intersection determines which 3D Gaussian splats in a scene are intersected by a camera ray, returning the closest hit for depth testing, picking, or alpha blending. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by supporting both approximate spherical intersection (for performance) and true ellipsoid intersection (for geometric accuracy) within a hierarchical Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) structure. Unlike Splat Raycasting Dispatch, which focuses on the parallel dispatch mechanism, this method defines the geometric traversal and intersection logic itself. Splat Raycasting Dispatch manages the buffer preparation and dispatch call for ray-splat intersection tests, returning hit distances and splat indices. It operates on pre-transformed, packed buffer structures optimized for batched processing, distinguishing it from Ray-Splat Intersection, and targets standard Euclidean camera models rather than spherical panoramas like Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS). This method computes the intersection depths between camera rays and quadric splats, providing a numerically stable solution when the quadratic coefficient is near zero. It differs from standard quadratic solvers by detecting degenerate cases where the quadric surface is nearly flat or the ray is nearly perpendicular to the principal axes, switching to a linear approximation to prevent floating-point overflow. It builds on Ray-Splat/gaussian Intersection by handling the specific numerical instability inherent in second-order primitives. Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS) is a surface reconstruction method that replaces static Gaussian primitives with deformable quadric surfaces (specifically paraboloids) to capture intricate geometry. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which uses Euclidean distance for density modeling, QGS employs geodesic distance-based density distributions to maintain spatial coherence during deformation. It sets itself apart from its siblings by generalizing 3D Gaussian primitives to higher-order surfaces, allowing adaptive curvature modeling while retaining the efficiency of ray-splat intersection. The Ray-Point Distance Test is a fragment shader technique that tests whether a viewing ray passes within a specified radius of up to 10 pre-selected 3D points, outputting a binary highlight color to indicate selection proximity. It differs from general ray-primitive intersection methods by operating on a discrete, small constant number of points rather than continuous geometric primitives, and by explicitly using the ray segment endpoints to compute perpendicular distance. Intersect the RBFs of the density representation with slices of thickness \Delta x that are perpendicular to the view direction. Render the slices from far to near using alpha blending with GLONE and GLSRCALPHA. Render the bounding quad of all intersections with the RBFs in each slice. For each pixel, retrieve D(x) and Lx from 3D textures. Set the RGB channels of the output to D(x)Lx. Set the alpha channel to the differential transmittance of the slice, computed as \exp(-\frac{\tau}{t} D(x) \Delta x). A technique to discard Gaussians that do not directly intersect with the ray, based on the intersection points identified during depth reinitialization. Identify \mathcal{I}{max}, the collection of all indexes i{max}(x) for all pixels x. Retain only Gaussians whose index i is in \mathcal{I}{max}. \mathcal{G}^{int} = \{\mathcal{G}i | i \in \mathcal{I}{max} \wedge i \in [1, N]\}, where \mathcal{G}^{int} is the set of intersected Gaussians and \mathcal{I}{max} is the collection of all indexes i{max}(x) in the rendered indexes. The concept of ray-splat intersection evolved from the need to render 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) efficiently in real-time. Standard 3DGS uses a rasterization-based approach that approximates the projection of Gaussians onto the image plane. For wide-field-of-view cameras or spherical panoramas, this first-order affine approximation introduces significant artifacts, leading to Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS) which uses exact ray-splat intersection with perpendicular planes to avoid covariance matrix inversion. Concurrently, Ray-Splat Intersection introduced BVH-based traversal for more complex scenes, supporting both spherical approximations and true ellipsoid intersections. Numerical stability issues in quadratic solvers for quadric splats led to Ray-splat Intersection with Numerical Stabilization, which switches to linear approximations when the quadratic coefficient is negligible. Quadratic Gaussian Splatting further generalized this by using paraboloids and geodesic distances for surface reconstruction. Additionally, Intersection Preserving discards Gaussians that do not directly intersect with the ray based on depth reinitialization, while Ray Marching with RBF Intersection intersects RBFs with slices perpendicular to the view direction for volume rendering. name: Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation
head: 2DGS Ray-Surfel Intersection, Homography-based Ray-Surfel Intersection, Screen-space Homography Surfel Intersection
body: Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation computes the precise intersection point of a viewing ray with a flat surfel rectangle in the surfel's local (u, v) coordinates. It solves the problem of determining where a pixel's ray hits the surfel plane to evaluate the 2D Gaussian opacity, avoiding the per-pixel cross products and divisions required by the original 2DGS formulation. It sets itself apart from Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection by using a homography approximation around the screen-space bounding box center to replace the exact ray-plane intersection with a rational function, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Surfel-to-world homogeneous transformation matrix H \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times4}. World-to-screen homogeneous transformation matrix W \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times4}. Pixel coordinates (xp, yp) in screen space. Surfel center (u0, v0) in local coordinates. Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J} of the homography approximation. Offset vector \Delta from the bounding box center to the pixel. Ray direction vector d (used in the denominator term). Base opacity oi. Outputs: Local intersection coordinates (uj, vj). Per-pixel opacity \alphai. Data Structures Matrices: H and W are 4\times4 homogeneous transformation matrices. H maps local surfel coordinates (u, v, 1, 1)^\top to world space. W maps world space to screen space. Vectors: \mathbf{h}x, \mathbf{h}y, \mathbf{h}u, \mathbf{h}v are 4D homogeneous plane vectors. \mathbf{J} is a 2\times2 Jacobian matrix. \Delta is a 2D offset vector. Steps 1. Define Screen-Space Planes: Construct two plane vectors representing the pixel boundaries in screen space: \mathbf{h}x = (-1, 0, 0, xp)^\top \mathbf{h}y = (0, -1, 0, yp)^\top 2. Transform to Surfel-Local Frame: Transform these planes into the surfel's local coordinate system using the combined transformation WH. Note that the transformation is applied via the transpose of the inverse (or adjoint) of the matrix product, effectively transforming planes: \mathbf{h}u = (WH)^\top \mathbf{h}x \mathbf{h}v = (WH)^\top \mathbf{h}y 3. Compute Intersection Coordinates: Solve the 2\times2 linear system derived from the intersection of the ray with the surfel plane defined by \mathbf{h}u and \mathbf{h}v. Let hu^i and hv^i denote the i-th component of vectors \mathbf{h}u and \mathbf{h}v respectively (1-indexed): uj = \frac{hu^2 hv^4 - hu^4 hv^2}{hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1} vj = \frac{hu^4 hv^1 - hu^1 hv^4}{hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1} Alternative Approximation (Homography): For hardware rasterization or performance optimization, the intersection can be approximated using a homography expansion around the center of the screen-space bounding box (u0, v0): u = u0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)u}{1 + d^\top\Delta} v = v0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)v}{1 + d^\top\Delta} Here, \Delta is the offset from the bounding box center, \mathbf{J} is the precomputed Jacobian, and d is the ray direction. This avoids per-pixel cross products and divisions. 4. Evaluate Opacity: Compute the per-pixel opacity using the 2D Gaussian falloff in the local frame: \alphai = oi \exp\left(-\frac{uj^2 + vj^2}{2}\right) Parameters Gaussian Variance: The exponent uses a variance of 1 (implicit in the formula -(u^2+v^2)/2). Base Opacity oi: A scalar parameter per surfel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: In the exact formulation, the denominator hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1 represents the determinant of the system. If this is zero, the ray is parallel to the surfel plane or the planes are degenerate. Precision: The homography approximation is valid near the center of the bounding box. Far from the center, the rational function may deviate from the exact intersection. Hardware Rasterization: When using the homography approximation with hardware rasterization, the comparison with 2DGS was timed only on the CUDA renderer because the hardware rasterizer does not have a native ray-surfel variant. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exactraysurfelintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, H, W, xp, yp, oi): """ Computes exact ray-surfel intersection using plane transformation. Args: rayorigin: (3,) list, ray origin. raydirection: (3,) list, normalized ray direction. H: (4, 4) list of lists, surfel-to-world homogeneous matrix. W: (4, 4) list of lists, world-to-screen homogeneous matrix. xp: float, pixel x coordinate. yp: float, pixel y coordinate. oi: float, base opacity. Returns: alpha: float, per-pixel opacity. """ # Step 1: Define screen-space planes hx = [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, xp] hy = [0.0, -1.0, 0.0, yp] # Step 2: Transform to surfel-local frame # Note: (WH)^T transforms planes from screen to local WH = [[sum(W[i][k] H[k][j] for k in range(4)) for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)] WHT = [[WH[j][i] for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)] def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] hu = matvecmul(WHT, hx) hv = matvecmul(WHT, hy) # Step 3: Solve 2x2 system for uj, vj # Denominator: hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1 (1-indexed) # In 0-indexed Python: hu[0] hv[1] - hu[1] hv[0] denom = hu[0] hv[1] - hu[1] hv[0] if abs(denom) < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: ray parallel to surfel or invalid geometry return 0.0 # Formula indices 1,2,4 -> Python indices 0,1,3 uj = (hu[1] hv[3] - hu[3] hv[1]) / denom vj = (hu[3] hv[0] - hu[0] hv[3]) / denom # Step 4: Evaluate opacity import math alpha = oi math.exp(-(uj2 + vj2) / 2.0) return alpha def homographyraysurfelintersection(u0, v0, J, delta, d, oi): """ Computes approximate ray-surfel intersection using homography. Args: u0: float, center u coordinate of bounding box. v0: float, center v coordinate of bounding box. J: (2, 2) list of lists, Jacobian matrix. delta: (2,) list, offset from center. d: (3,) list, ray direction (used in denominator term). oi: float, base opacity. Returns: alpha: float, per-pixel opacity. """ import math # Compute denominator term: 1 + d^T delta # delta is 2D, d is 3D. We pad delta with 0 for the dot product. delta3d = delta + [0.0] dotproduct = sum(d[i] delta3d[i] for i in range(3)) denomterm = 1.0 + dotproduct if abs(denomterm) < 1e-9: return 0.0 # Compute J delta Jdelta = [sum(J[i][j] delta[j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)] u = u0 + Jdelta[0] / denomterm v = v0 + Jdelta[1] / denomterm alpha = oi math.exp(-(u2 + v2) / 2.0) return alpha A rasterization technique for planar surfels that computes screen-space texture coordinates (u, v) using an algebraically exact rational function of pixel position, avoiding per-pixel cross products and vector constructions. It sets itself apart from the reference 2DGS formulation by replacing the per-pixel cross-product-based inversion with a precomputed affine approximation, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. It is chosen for fragment-bound scenes where the saving per fragment yields significant performance gains (+47% on stump and flowers scenes) compared to scenes bound by sorting and binning (+20% on train scene). The hardware rasterizer has no ray–surfel variant, so performance comparisons were made on the CUDA renderer. Time Complexity: The exact method involves matrix-vector multiplications and a 2\times2 solve, which is constant time O(1) per pixel per surfel. The homography approximation reduces this to a few multiplications and additions, also O(1) but with a smaller constant factor. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 4\times4 matrices H and W per surfel or globally, and per-pixel temporary vectors. Memory usage is low and constant per surfel. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, the hardware rasterizer implementation achieved 2698, 3016, and 4413 FPS respectively, which is 1.8× faster than the CUDA software rasterizer implementation. The method remains 1.1–1.5× faster than Speedy-Splat at lower LPIPS on matched hardware rasterizers. Strengths: Avoids expensive per-pixel cross products and divisions of the original 2DGS method. Compatible with hardware rasterization for significant speedups. Limitations: The homography approximation is local to the bounding box center; accuracy may degrade far from the center. The exact method still requires more computation than simple splatting if not optimized. When to Use: Use when high-quality surfel rendering is required and performance is critical, especially on hardware rasterizers. Use the exact method when precision is paramount and the homography approximation is insufficient. The method originates from 2DGS (2D Gaussian Splatting), which introduced the surfel parameterization and ray-plane intersection for evaluating Gaussian opacity. Fourier Splatting inherits this ray-surfel intersection method but replaces the fixed Gaussian falloff with Fourier encoded boundaries. The homography-based approximation was introduced in "Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting" to enable hardware rasterization of surfels by leveraging perspective-correct texturing principles. name: Closed-form perspective-correct surfel rasterization
head: homography-based surfel projection, rational interpolation for surfels
body: A rasterization technique for planar surfels that computes screen-space texture coordinates (u, v) using an algebraically exact rational function of pixel position, avoiding per-pixel cross products and vector constructions. It sets itself apart from the reference 2DGS formulation by replacing the per-pixel cross-product-based inversion with a precomputed affine approximation, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A surfel defined in camera space, the current camera projection matrix, and the screen-space bounding box of the surfel. Output: For each pixel (x, y) within the bounding box, the interpolated texture coordinates (u, v) and a validity flag. Data Structures: The method precomputes eight coefficients per surfel per frame. These are stored in a structure with the following layout: u0, v0: float16 (FP16). The intersection coordinates at the center of the screen-space bounding box. Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv: float16 (FP16). Elements of the Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J}, representing the rate of change of u and v per pixel offset. opacity, shape: float16 (FP16). Surfels' opacity and shape parameters (contextual, not part of the coordinate formula but stored alongside). dx, dy: float32 (FP32). Components of the perspective denominator gradient vector \mathbf{d}. Stored in FP32 because they span several orders of magnitude; errors here scale across the entire surfel. Numbered Steps: 1. Determine the screen-space bounding box of the surfel. 2. Compute the center of this bounding box, (xc, yc). 3. Evaluate the surfel intersection at the center to obtain (u0, v0). 4. Compute the Jacobian \mathbf{J} and the denominator gradient \mathbf{d} at the center. 5. Store the eight coefficients: (u0, v0), \mathbf{J}, and \mathbf{d}. 6. For each pixel (x, y) in the bounding box, calculate the pixel offset from the center: \Delta = (x - xc, y - yc). 7. Compute the perspective denominator: denom = 1 + \mathbf{d}^{\top}\Delta. 8. Edge Case/Pitfall: If denom \le 0, the plane is parallel to or behind the camera for this pixel. Skip the fragment. 9. Compute the numerator corrections: numu = (\mathbf{J}\Delta)u and numv = (\mathbf{J}\Delta)v. 10. Evaluate the final coordinates: u = u0 + \frac{numu}{denom} and v = v0 + \frac{numv}{denom}. Formula: The core interpolation formula is: u = u0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)u}{1 + \mathbf{d}^{\top}\Delta}, \quad v = v0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)v}{1 + \mathbf{d}^{\top}\Delta} Where: \Delta is the pixel offset from the bounding box center. (u0, v0) is the intersection at the center. \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian (rate of change per pixel). \mathbf{d} is the gradient of the perspective denominator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def precomputesurfelcoefficients(Tu, Tv, Tw, xc, yc): # p = Tu x Tv - y(Tu x Tw) - x(Tw x Tv) # px = -(Tw x Tv) = Tv x Tw # py = -(Tu x Tw) = Tw x Tu p0 = cross(Tu, Tv) px = cross(Tv, Tw) py = cross(Tw, Tu) # Evaluate vector p at center pc = [p0[i] + xc px[i] + yc py[i] for i in range(3)] pcz = pc[2] # u0, v0 u0 = pc[0] / pcz v0 = pc[1] / pcz # Jacobian J and gradient d Juu = px[0] / pcz Juv = py[0] / pcz Jvu = px[1] / pcz Jvv = py[1] / pcz dx = px[2] / pcz dy = py[2] / pcz return u0, v0, Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv, dx, dy def rasterizesurfelpixel(u0, v0, Juu, Juv, Jvu, Jvv, dx, dy, deltax, deltay): denom = 1.0 + (dx deltax + dy deltay) if denom <= 0.0: return None, None, False numu = Juu deltax + Juv deltay numv = Jvu deltax + Jvv deltay u = u0 + numu / denom v = v0 + numv / denom return u, v, True Parameters: Precision Split: (u0, v0), \mathbf{J}, opacity, and shape are stored as FP16. The denominator gradient \mathbf{d} is stored as FP32. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Denominator \le 0: Pixels with a non-positive denominator look at the plane from behind the camera and must be skipped. Floating-Point Reassociation: Near the alpha cutoff, floating-point reassociation can flip whether a fragment is drawn, causing non-byte-identical renders between the closed-form and reference methods (59–66 dB PSNR difference), though visual quality remains high. Precision Sensitivity: Errors in \mathbf{d} scale across the whole surfel, necessitating FP32 storage. Time Complexity: Per pixel, the method requires about 10 fused multiply-adds and one division, compared to roughly 15 fused multiply-adds and two divisions in the reference method. Memory Complexity: The precomputation stores 8 coefficients per surfel. The staging changes no arithmetic, only the shared-memory layout. Measured Performance: 32% higher mean frame rate than 2DGS on tested scenes. Quality: The renders match the 2DGS formulation to within 0.03 dB PSNR and 0.0002 LPIPS on 13 scenes. Strengths: No per-pixel cross product, making it computationally cheaper and numerically safer than packing plane rows at reduced precision (which costs 0.05–0.7 dB due to error amplification). Limitations: Not byte-identical to the reference method due to floating-point differences near alpha cutoffs. This method is described in "Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting". It builds on the homography projection properties of planar surfels, exploiting the fact that (u, v) is a ratio of two linear functions of the pixel position, similar to perspective-correct texturing in rasterizers. Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.13808, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS)
head: Fast and Accurate 3D Gaussian Splatting for Spherical Panoramas, HTGS extended to spherical camera model, SPaGS (Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting), SPaGS Ray-Plane Intersection, omnidirectional Ray-Splat Intersection
body: SPaGS is a real-time rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that supports arbitrary spherical camera models, specifically equirectangular panoramas, by replacing the standard local affine approximation with a numerically stable ray-splat intersection approach. It solves the problem of rendering artifacts and numerical instability inherent in standard 3DGS when applied to wide-field-of-view or distorted panoramic views, where first-order affine projections fail to accurately represent the Gaussian distribution. Unlike ODGS, which uses suboptimal tangent plane approximations, or 3DGUT, which relies on the Unscented Transform, SPaGS achieves higher quality and speed by representing each viewing ray as the intersection of two perpendicular planes in camera space, thereby avoiding matrix inversion of the covariance. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene represented by a set of 3D Gaussian splats; an equirectangular image of width W and height H; a background color \mathbf{c}{background}. Output: A rendered equirectangular image with per-pixel color \mathbf{C}. Data Structures Each 3D Gaussian splat i is defined by the following fields: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position (center) of the Gaussian. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation represented as a quaternion. s{u,i}, s{v,i}, s{w,i} \in \mathbb{R}: Scale factors along the local axes. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity (scalar). \mathbf{c}i: View-dependent color, represented by Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients of degree 3. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix, derived from \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{q}i, s{u,i}, s{v,i}, s{w,i}. Transformation Matrices M \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}: World-to-camera transformation matrix. T \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}: Local-to-world transformation matrix for a splat, defined by its scaling, rotation, and position parameters. T^{-1}: Inverse of the local-to-world matrix, used to transform camera-space vectors into the splat's local coordinate system. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Direction Computation: For each pixel (x, y) in the equirectangular image (0 \le x < W, 0 \le y < H), compute the ray direction \mathbf{d} in camera space. The direction is derived from the pixel coordinates assuming the image plane is a unit sphere mapped to equirectangular coordinates: \begin{aligned} \theta &= \frac{2\pi x}{W} \\ \phi &= \frac{\pi y}{H} \\ dx &= \cos(\theta) \cos(\phi) \\ dy &= \sin(\phi) \\ dz &= \sin(\theta) \cos(\phi) \end{aligned} The source defines spherical coordinates \theta, \phi from a camera vector \mathbf{c} as \theta = \text{atan2}(cz, cx) and \phi = \text{asin}(cy / \|\mathbf{c}\|). The direction \mathbf{d} corresponds to the vector from the camera origin through the pixel. 2. Plane Normal Calculation: Compute the normals \mathbf{n}x and \mathbf{n}y of two perpendicular planes \pix and \piy that contain the ray direction \mathbf{d} and the camera origin. These planes are computed directly in camera space using the image dimensions W and H. The source cites Eqs. (6)-(10) for this calculation. Since the planes contain the camera origin (0,0,0)^\top, they are represented in homogeneous coordinates as \pi{x/y} = (\mathbf{n}{x/y}, 0)^\top. 3. Plane Transformation: Transform the planes \pix and \piy from camera space into the local coordinate system of each 3D Gaussian splat i. This is achieved by applying the inverse transformation T^{-1} (which incorporates M) to the plane representations. Let the transformed planes in local space be \pi'{x,i} and \pi'{y,i}. 4. Ray-Splat Intersection: Perform the intersection test in the splat's local coordinate system. The ray is represented by the intersection of the two transformed planes \pi'{x,i} and \pi'{y,i}. This approach avoids the explicit inversion of the covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, ensuring numerical stability even for degenerate Gaussians. Compute the squared Mahalanobis distance \rhoi(\mathbf{x})^2 at the intersection point \mathbf{x}. 5. Alpha Evaluation: Calculate the alpha value \alphai for the splat at the intersection point using the Gaussian's opacity oi and the computed distance \rhoi(\mathbf{x})^2: \alphai = oi \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} \rhoi(\mathbf{x})^2\right) (Note: The exact form of Eq. (3) is referenced but not fully expanded in the snippet, but this is the standard Gaussian alpha evaluation consistent with the context). 6. Hybrid Transparency Blending: Core: Sort the contributing splats by depth. Apply standard \alpha-blending to the first K splats (the "core"). Tail: Combine the remaining splats (the "tail") without sorting. Compute the combined tail color \mathbf{c}{tail} and remaining opacity T{tail}. Final Color: Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{C}: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{c}{tail} + (1 - T{tail}) \mathbf{c}{background} Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return [v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l] def rendersphericalpanorama(splats, W, H, K, cbackground): """ Renders an equirectangular panorama using SPaGS. Args: splats: List of Gaussian splats, each with attributes: mu (3,), q (4,), scale (3,), opacity (float), shcoeffs (degree 3), Tinv (4x4 matrix as list of lists) W: Image width H: Image height K: Number of splats in the core blend cbackground: Background color vector [r, g, b] Returns: Image buffer of shape (H, W, 3) """ image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Step 1: Compute ray direction in camera space theta = 2.0 math.pi x / W phi = math.pi y / H d = [math.cos(theta) math.cos(phi), math.sin(phi), math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi)] # Step 2: Compute plane normals nx, ny in camera space up = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] if abs(d[1]) > 0.9: up = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] nx = normalize(cross(d, up)) ny = normalize(cross(d, nx)) # Bounding box culling not detailed in the sources candidates = [s for s in splats if True] contributions = [] for s in candidates: # Step 3: Transform planes to splat local space Rinv = [row[:3] for row in s.Tinv] nprimex = [dot(Rinv[0], nx), dot(Rinv[1], nx), dot(Rinv[2], nx)] nprimey = [dot(Rinv[0], ny), dot(Rinv[1], ny), dot(Rinv[2], ny)] # Ray in local space: origin olocal = Tinv[:3, 3], direction dlocal = Rinv @ d olocal = [s.Tinv[0][3], s.Tinv[1][3], s.Tinv[2][3]] dlocal = [dot(Rinv[0], d[0]), dot(Rinv[1], d[1]), dot(Rinv[2], d[2])] dlocal = normalize(dlocal) # Step 4 & 5: Intersection in local space & Alpha Evaluation # Compute alpha at the point on the ray closest to the Gaussian center diff = [s.mu[0] - olocal[0], s.mu[1] - olocal[1], s.mu[2] - olocal[2]] proj = dot(diff, dlocal) closest = [olocal[0] + proj dlocal[0], olocal[1] + proj dlocal[1], olocal[2] + proj dlocal[2]] vec = [s.mu[0] - closest[0], s.mu[1] - closest[1], s.mu[2] - closest[2]] rhosq = (vec[0]s.scale[0])2 + (vec[1]s.scale[1])2 + (vec[2]s.scale[2])2 alpha = s.opacity math.exp(-0.5 rhosq) if alpha > 0.0: # SH evaluation not detailed in the sources color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] depth = dot(dlocal, s.mu) contributions.append((alpha, color, depth)) # Step 6: Hybrid Blending contributions.sort(key=lambda k: k[2]) # Core blending corecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] corealpha = 0.0 for i in range(min(K, len(contributions))): a, c, = contributions[i] corecolor = [corecolor[j](1-a) + c[j]a for j in range(3)] corealpha += a (1 - corealpha) # Tail blending (unsorted accumulation as per source) tailcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tailalpha = 0.0 for i in range(K, len(contributions)): a, c, = contributions[i] tailcolor = [tailcolor[j](1-a) + c[j]a for j in range(3)] tailalpha += a (1 - tailalpha) # Final color: C = ctail + (1 - Ttail) cbackground finalcolor = [tailcolor[j] + (1 - tailalpha) cbackground[j] for j in range(3)] finalcolor = [finalcolor[j](1-corealpha) + corecolor[j]corealpha for j in range(3)] image[y][x] = finalcolor return image Parameters K: The number of depth-sorted splats included in the 'core' part of hybrid transparency blending. The remaining splats form the 'tail'. Degree of Spherical Harmonics: Set to 3 for view-dependent color representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Gaussians: Standard covariance-based rasterization can become numerically unstable for degenerate Gaussians (e.g., very thin or flat). Wide-Field-of-View Artifacts: Standard 3DGS uses a first-order affine approximation for projection, leading to residual errors and noticeable rendering artifacts in wide-FoV views. Spherical Distortion: The equirectangular projection causes non-linear distortion. A two-stage method to calculate an axis-aligned screen-space bounding box for 3D Gaussians in spherical panoramas, addressing deformation caused by omnidirectional pixel distribution and non-linear spherical projection. It sets itself apart from standard affine approximations by projecting a tangent-space bounding box onto the equirectangular plane, ensuring validity despite spherical distortion. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS, storing position, rotation, scale, opacity, and SH coefficients. Measured Performance: SPaGS achieves sharper reconstructions on large-scale scenes (e.g., Zip-NeRF) compared to other real-time methods. Strengths: Numerical stability for degenerate Gaussians; accurate rendering for wide-FoV and distorted panoramic inputs; real-time performance. Limitations: More complex than standard 3DGS due to the ray-splat intersection and plane transformations. When to use: Real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas, specifically equirectangular images, supporting distorted panoramic inputs. When not to use: Standard perspective cameras without distortion, where standard 3DGS is sufficient and faster. SPaGS was introduced by Huang et al. (2024) and Bai et al. (2024) in the context of error analysis and optimal projection strategies for 3DGS. It extends the approach of Hahlbohm et al. [HFW25] to spherical camera models. The method addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS, which only supports undistorted perspective camera models, by providing a numerically stable ray-splat intersection approach. It is used for real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas. SPaGS: Fast and Accurate 3D Gaussian Splatting for Spherical Panoramas, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70171, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Tangent Plane-Based Bounding Box Calculation
head: SPaGS Bounding Box, Two-Stage Bounding Box
body: A two-stage method to calculate an axis-aligned screen-space bounding box for 3D Gaussians in spherical panoramas, addressing deformation caused by omnidirectional pixel distribution and non-linear spherical projection. It sets itself apart from standard affine rasterization by projecting a tangent-space bounding box onto the equirectangular plane, ensuring validity despite spherical distortion. It builds on Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS). Inputs: 3D Gaussian splat parameters (mean \mathbf{m} in camera space); spherical camera projection parameters (equirectangular image dimensions W \times H). Outputs: Axis-aligned 2D bounding box (p{x,\min}, p{y,\min}, p{x,\max}, p{y,\max}) on the equirectangular image plane. Data Structures: Tangent Space Basis: Three normalized vectors \hat{\mathbf{t}} (tangent), \hat{\mathbf{b}} (bitangent), \hat{\mathbf{n}} (normal) representing the local x, y, z axes of the tangent space. Tangent Space Bounding Box: Four floats (t{x,\min}, t{x,\max}, t{y,\min}, t{y,\max}) defining the rectangle in the tangent plane z=1. Camera Space Coordinates: Derived from tangent coordinates using transformation matrix. Steps: 1. Define Tangent Space: For each splat, compute the normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} from the covariance matrix. Determine the reference vector \mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} to avoid singularity at poles: if the mean \mathbf{m} lies on the vector of the two poles, use \mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} = (1, 0, 0)^T, otherwise use \mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} = (0, 0, 1)^T. Compute \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{r}{\text{ref}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}}) and \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \hat{\mathbf{t}}. The origin of the tangent space is the camera space origin. The tangent plane is defined as z=1. 2. Transform to Tangent Space: Construct the transformation matrix M from camera space to tangent space: M = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{t}}^T \\ \hat{\mathbf{b}}^T \\ \hat{\mathbf{n}}^T \end{bmatrix} Transform the splat into tangent space. 3. Calculate Tangent Space Bounding Box: Compute the 2D axis-aligned bounding box (t{x,\min}, t{x,\max}, t{y,\min}, t{y,\max}) on the tangent plane using the standard HTGS approach [HFW25] on the transformed splat parameters. Let the box be represented by points t = (tx, ty, 1) where tx \in [t{x,\min}, t{x,\max}] and ty \in [t{y,\min}, t{y,\max}]. 4. Project to Camera Space: Inverse the tangent space transformation to get camera space coordinates (cx, cy, cz) for any point on the tangent plane: \begin{bmatrix} cx \\ cy \\ cz \end{bmatrix} = M^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} tx \\ ty \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Specifically, \mathbf{c} = tx \hat{\mathbf{t}} + ty \hat{\mathbf{b}} + 1 \hat{\mathbf{n}}, where \mathbf{c} = (cx, cy, cz)^T is the point in camera space corresponding to (tx, ty) on the tangent plane z=1. 5. Project to Equirectangular Plane (Stage 2): Calculate the minimum and maximum py (latitude) and px (longitude) on the equirectangular plane. Latitude (py): Using the monotonically increasing property of \arcsin, calculate p{y,\min} and p{y,\max} by evaluating the four corners of the tangent bounding box: py = \arcsin\left(\frac{cy}{\sqrt{cx^2 + cy^2 + cz^2}}\right) p{y,\min} = \min{(tx, ty) \in \text{corners}} \arcsin\left(\frac{cy(tx, ty)}{\|\mathbf{c}(tx, ty)\|}\right) p{y,\max} = \max{(tx, ty) \in \text{corners}} \arcsin\left(\frac{cy(tx, ty)}{\|\mathbf{c}(tx, ty)\|}\right) Longitude (px): To overcome the singularity and discontinuity of \text{atan2}, calculate the maximized differential angle \Delta \phi instead of directly computing longitude. The final p{x,\min} and p{x,\max} are derived from the center longitude \phic and \Delta \phi: p{x,\min} = \phic - \Delta \phi, \quad p{x,\max} = \phic + \Delta \phi 6. Handle Pole Coverage: If the projected bounding box covers the north or south pole (determined by checking if the latitude range includes \pm \pi/2), calculate p{y,\min} and p{y,\max} similarly for the projection center on the respective sphere. Set p{x,\min} = -\pi and p{x,\max} = \pi (full image width) since the pole is fully covered. If the projection center lies exactly on a pole, use the same method with simplified expressions. 7. Load Balancing: Apply a load balancing scheme similar to Radl et al. [RSP24] to address the impact of occasional large bounding boxes on Gaussian/tile instance creation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def tangentplaneboundingbox(splatmean, splatcov, imagewidth, imageheight): # Step 1: Define Tangent Space # Compute normal from covariance (principal component) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(splatcov) nhat = eigenvectors[:, np.argmin(eigenvalues)] nhat = nhat / np.linalg.norm(nhat) # Reference vector to avoid singularity refvec = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) if abs(np.dot(splatmean, refvec)) > 1 - 1e-6: refvec = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) that = np.cross(refvec, nhat) that = that / np.linalg.norm(that) bhat = np.cross(nhat, that) # Step 2: Transform to Tangent Space M = np.array([that, bhat, nhat]) covt = M @ splatcov @ M.T # Step 3: Calculate Tangent Space Bounding Box # Standard 2D Gaussian bounding box calculation (e.g., 3-sigma) txmin, txmax = -3.0 math.sqrt(covt[0, 0]), 3.0 math.sqrt(covt[0, 0]) tymin, tymax = -3.0 math.sqrt(covt[1, 1]), 3.0 math.sqrt(covt[1, 1]) # Step 4 & 5: Project to Equirectangular Plane cornerst = [ (txmin, tymin), (txmin, tymax), (txmax, tymin), (txmax, tymax) ] cornersc = [] for tx, ty in cornerst: c = tx that + ty bhat + 1.0 nhat cornersc.append(c) # Calculate pymin, pymax pyvalues = [] for c in cornersc: normc = np.linalg.norm(c) if normc == 0: continue py = math.asin(c[1] / normc) pyvalues.append(py) pymin = min(pyvalues) pymax = max(pyvalues) # Calculate pxmin, pxmax using differential angle meanc = np.mean(cornersc, axis=0) normmean = np.linalg.norm(meanc) if normmean == 0: phic = 0.0 else: phic = math.atan2(meanc[0], meanc[2]) # Compute max differential angle from corners pxvalues = [] for c in cornersc: normc = np.linalg.norm(c) if normc == 0: continue px = math.atan2(c[0], c[2]) pxvalues.append(px) # Handle wrap-around for px pxvalues.sort() maxgap = 0 for i in range(len(pxvalues) - 1): gap = pxvalues[i+1] - pxvalues[i] if gap > maxgap: maxgap = gap if maxgap > math.pi: pxmin = -math.pi pxmax = math.pi else: pxmin = pxvalues[0] pxmax = pxvalues[-1] # Step 6: Handle Pole Coverage if pymax > math.pi/2 - 1e-6 or pymin < -math.pi/2 + 1e-6: pxmin = -math.pi pxmax = math.pi return (pxmin, pymin, pxmax, pymax) Computes a tight 2D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS) primitives by approximating the primitive's boundary with tangent planes, avoiding the loose approximation of projecting 3D bounding box vertices. It addresses the inefficiency caused by QGS concave cases and the lack of an elementary inverse for the geodesic distance function, which makes analytical determination of the rendered portion difficult. It builds on Tangent Plane-Based Bounding Box Calculation. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat, as it involves a fixed number of matrix operations and trigonometric functions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per splat, storing only the bounding box coordinates. Strengths: Handles spherical projection distortion accurately; numerically stable at poles; avoids loose approximations of 3D bounding box projections. Limitations: Requires careful handling of pole singularities; load balancing is necessary due to occasional large bounding boxes. When to use: Real-time rendering of 3D Gaussians on spherical panoramas (e.g., VR, 360° video) where standard affine rasterization fails due to non-linear projection. Originated in the SPaGS paper to enable real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian splats on spherical panoramas. It addresses the limitations of standard 3DGS rasterization, which assumes a local affine approximation, by introducing a numerically stable ray-splat intersection approach suitable for arbitrary spherical camera models. SPaGS: Fast and Accurate 3D Gaussian Splatting for Spherical Panoramas, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70171, fetched 2026-11-01 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Tight Bounding Box Calculation for Quadric Gaussians
head: QGS Bounding Box, Quadric Gaussian Bounding Box
body: This method computes a tight 2D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS) primitives by approximating the primitive's boundary with tangent planes, avoiding the loose approximation of projecting 3D bounding box vertices. It addresses the inefficiency caused by QGS concave cases and the lack of an elementary inverse for the geodesic distance function, which makes analytical determination of the rendered portion difficult. It builds on Tangent Plane-Based Bounding Box Calculation. Inputs: Quadratic coefficient a of the geodesic function. Variance \sigma0(\theta) of the Gaussian distribution along the major axis (\theta=0) and minor axis (\theta=\pi/2). Outputs: 2D AABB dimensions defined by x1 and x2 (half-widths/heights in the tangent plane projection). Data Structures: No complex data structures required; calculation is analytical/algebraic. Steps: 1. Approximate Geodesic Function: Scale the geodesic function l(a, \rho) to a quadratic polynomial approximation \hat{l}(a, \rho): \hat{l}(a, \rho) = \frac{4|a|\rho^2 + 6\rho}{7} where \rho is the horizontal distance from the primitive's vertex. 2. Solve for Horizontal Distance (\rho): For a given direction \theta0 with variance \sigma0(\theta0), solve \hat{l}(a, \rho) - \sigma0 = 0 for \rho. The quadratic formula yields two roots: \rho{0,1} = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{36 + 112|a|\sigma0}}{8|a|} Since the function passes through the origin, take the positive root to represent the horizontal distance. 3. Compute Major and Minor Axis Distances: Calculate \rho1 for the major axis (\theta = 0) and \rho2 for the minor axis (\theta = \pi/2) using the variance \sigma0(0) and \sigma0(\pi/2) respectively. 4. Define Quadric Points: Obtain four points on the quadric surface in the local coordinate system: (\pm\rho1, 0, \rho1^2) and (0, \pm\rho2, \rho2^2). 5. Compute Tangent Plane Intersections: Compute the intersection of the tangent planes at these four points with the plane z=0 to determine the bounding box extents x1 and x2. Let s1 and s2 be the slopes of the tangent planes at the points corresponding to \rho1 and \rho2 respectively. The intersections are calculated as: x1 = \pm \frac{\rho1 s1 - \rho1^2}{s1}, \quad x2 = \pm \frac{\rho2 s2 - \rho2^2}{s2} The resulting 3D shape is a truncated pyramid with top dimensions \rho1 \times \rho2, bottom dimensions x1 \times x2, and height determined by the z-coordinate of the tangent plane intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeqgsboundingbox(a, sigmamajor, sigmaminor): """ Computes the tight bounding box extents x1 and x2 for a Quadratic Gaussian. Args: a (float): Quadratic coefficient of the geodesic function. sigmamajor (float): Variance along the major axis (theta=0). sigmaminor (float): Variance along the minor axis (theta=pi/2). Returns: tuple: (x1, x2) representing the half-width and half-height of the AABB. """ absa = abs(a) # Step 1 & 2: Solve for rho using the positive root of the quadratic approximation # rho = (-6 + sqrt(36 + 112 |a| sigma)) / (8 |a|) # Calculate rho1 for major axis discriminant1 = 36 + 112 absa sigmamajor rho1 = (-6 + math.sqrt(discriminant1)) / (8 absa) # Calculate rho2 for minor axis discriminant2 = 36 + 112 absa sigmaminor rho2 = (-6 + math.sqrt(discriminant2)) / (8 absa) # Step 4 & 5: Compute tangent plane intersections # The source defines x1 and x2 using slopes s1 and s2. # For the quadric points (±ρ1, 0, ρ1^2) and (0, ±ρ2, ρ2^2), the surface is z = ρ^2. # The slope of the tangent plane in the radial direction is s = dz/dρ = 2ρ. s1 = 2 rho1 s2 = 2 rho2 # Avoid division by zero if slope is zero if abs(s1) < 1e-9: x1 = rho1 else: x1 = (rho1 s1 - rho12) / s1 if abs(s2) < 1e-9: x2 = rho2 else: x2 = (rho2 s2 - rho22) / s2 return abs(x1), abs(x2) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: QGS includes concave cases, which complicates the analytical determination of the rendered portion during preprocessing. The geodesic function lacks an elementary inverse, requiring numerical or approximate solutions for the equipotential \rho(\theta0) = \{l^{-1}(l0): l0 = \sigma(\theta0)\}. Even with an analytical solution, equipotential lines in non-Euclidean space may not fully enclose the primitive, requiring extra boundary calculations. Precision issues may arise if a is very small, leading to division by near-zero values in the root calculation or slope determination. Time Complexity: The calculation involves basic arithmetic operations and square roots, making it O(1) per primitive. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, QGS with this tight bounding box (QGS w/ TB) achieved 14.15 FPS compared to 7.92 FPS for standard QGS, with reduced storage (641MB vs 688MB). On the TNT dataset, it achieved 25.36 FPS vs 13.27 FPS. Strengths: Significantly tighter bounding box than projecting 3D vertices, leading to higher rendering FPS and lower storage overhead. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the quadratic approximation of the geodesic function. Origin: Introduced in "Quadratic Gaussian Splatting: High Quality Surface Reconstruction with Second-Order Geometric Primitives" (ICCV 2025). Development: Developed to address the limitations of 2DGS/3DGS where Gaussian primitives are convex, making bounding box computation straightforward. QGS introduces concave cases and non-Euclidean geodesic distances, necessitating a more sophisticated bounding box calculation. Usage: Used in high-quality surface reconstruction with second-order geometric primitives. name: Ray-Splat Intersection
head: IntersectionTester, Raycaster Splat Intersection, Raycaster.castRayAtSplatTreeNode, Raycaster.intersectSplatMesh, Raycasting via BVH, Splat Picking
body: Ray-Splat Intersection determines which 3D Gaussian splats in a scene are intersected by a camera ray, returning the closest hit for depth testing, picking, or alpha blending. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by supporting both approximate spherical intersection (for performance) and true ellipsoid intersection (for geometric accuracy) within a hierarchical Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) structure. Unlike Splat Raycasting Dispatch, which focuses on the parallel dispatch mechanism, this method defines the geometric traversal and intersection logic itself. Inputs: Camera parameters: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), projection type (Perspective/Orthographic), and screen coordinates (x, y) for ray generation. Scene data: A collection of splats, each defined by center \mathbf{c}, scale vector \mathbf{s} = (sx, sy, sz), rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, and opacity \alpha (stored in color channel w). BVH: A Bounding Volume Hierarchy constructed from axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) of the splats. Flags: raycastAgainstTrueSplatEllipsoid (boolean), splatRenderMode (TwoD or ThreeD), and scaleEpsilon. Outputs: A sorted list of hit records, each containing the splat index, intersection distance t, hit point \mathbf{p}, and normal \mathbf{n} (if required). Splat Data: center: vec3 (world space position). scale: vec3 (local scale factors). rotation: quat (local orientation). color: vec4 (RGB + opacity \alpha in w). BVH Node: boundingBox: AABB (min/max extents in local subtree space). indexes: uint32[] (list of splat indices contained in this leaf or subtree). subTrees: Node[] (children, if internal node). Hit Record: splatIndex: uint32. distance: float (from ray origin to hit point). hitPoint: vec3 (world space). normal: vec3 (world space, optional). scaleEpsilon: 0.0000001. Threshold for ignoring degenerate splats. maxDistance: 100.0. Maximum ray length for approximate sampling in. resolution: 1.0. Step size for sampling in. raycastAgainstTrueSplatEllipsoid: true for accurate ellipsoid intersection, false for spherical approximation. 1. Ray Generation: Perspective Camera: 1. Compute Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): \text{ndc}x = \frac{x}{\text{width}} \cdot 2.0 - 1.0 \text{ndc}y = \left( \frac{\text{height} - y}{\text{height}} \right) \cdot 2.0 - 1.0 2. Set ray origin \mathbf{o} to the camera world position. 3. Unproject NDC coordinates to world space to get a point \mathbf{p}{\text{ndc}}. 4. Set ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{\text{ndc}} - \mathbf{o}). Orthographic Camera: 1. Unproject NDC coordinates with z derived from camera near/far planes using z = \frac{\text{near} + \text{far}}{\text{near} - \text{far}}. 2. Set ray origin \mathbf{o} to the unprojected point. 3. Set ray direction \mathbf{d} to the camera's forward vector (0,0,-1) transformed by the camera's world rotation matrix. 2. BVH Construction (if not pre-built): 1. Iterate over all splat offsets. 2. Extract each splat's bounds into a boxes array. 3. Compute a global bounding box. 4. Construct a BVH from the boxes array. 3. Traversal: 1. For each root node of the splat tree (or subtree): 1. Compute fromLocal (world matrix \times scene transform if dynamic) and toLocal (inverse of fromLocal). 2. Transform ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} to local space. 3. Call castRayAtSplatTreeNode with local ray, tree, subtree root node, and output hits array. 4. Node Intersection (castRayAtSplatTreeNode): 1. Check if ray intersects node bounding box: if (!ray.intersectBox(node.boundingBox)) return;. 2. If leaf node: 1. Iterate over node.data.indexes. 2. For each splat global index, get scene index and check if scene is visible. If not visible, continue. 3. Retrieve splat color, center, scale, and rotation. 4. Degeneracy Check: If any scale component is \le \text{scaleEpsilon}, or if ThreeD mode and sz \le \text{scaleEpsilon}, skip splat. 5. Intersection Test: Approximate Sphere (if raycastAgainstTrueSplatEllipsoid is false): 1. Compute radius: r = \frac{sx + sy}{2}. 2. If ThreeD mode: r = \frac{sx + sy + sz}{3}. 3. Check intersection with sphere at \mathbf{c} with radius r. True Ellipsoid (if raycastAgainstTrueSplatEllipsoid is true): 1. Construct a scale matrix from the splat's scale vector. 2. Construct a rotation matrix from the splat's quaternion. 3. Calculate a uniform scale factor from the splat's opacity: k = \log{10}(\alpha) \cdot 2.0. 4. Construct a uniform scale matrix and combine it with rotation and scale matrices to form the transformation from sphere space to world space: M{\text{world}} = U \cdot R \cdot S. 5. Compute the inverse transformation matrix to map from world space to sphere space: M{\text{sphere}} = M{\text{world}}^{-1}. 6. Transform the ray origin to sphere space: \mathbf{o}{\text{sphere}} = M{\text{sphere}} \cdot (\mathbf{o}{\text{local}} - \mathbf{c}). 7. Transform the ray direction to sphere space: \mathbf{d}{\text{sphere}} = \text{normalize}(M{\text{sphere}} \cdot (\mathbf{o}{\text{local}} + \mathbf{d}{\text{local}} - \mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{o}{\text{sphere}}). 8. Perform a ray-sphere intersection test in sphere space with radius 1.0. 9. If it intersects, transform the hit point back to world space using the forward matrix and splat center, then record the hit. 3. If internal node: 1. Recursively call castRayAtSplatTreeNode for each child. 5. Post-Processing: 1. Transform hit origins and normals back to world space using fromLocal. 2. Compute distance as length of vector from ray origin to hit origin. 3. Sort all hits by distance ascending. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raysplatintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, splattree, camera, usetrueellipsoid=True, scaleepsilon=1e-7, rendermode="TwoD"): """ Intersects a ray against a splat mesh using a BVH. Returns a list of hits sorted by distance. """ hits = [] # 1. Ray Generation (Simplified for Perspective) # In practice, this depends on camera model. # Assuming rayorigin and raydirection are already provided in world space. # 2. Traverse Tree for subtree in splattree.subtrees: # Compute local transforms worldmatrix = subtree.worldmatrix if subtree.dynamicmode: worldmatrix = worldmatrix @ subtree.scenetransform tolocal = inverse(worldmatrix) fromlocal = worldmatrix # Transform ray to local space olocal = transformpoint(tolocal, rayorigin) dlocal = normalize(transformvector(tolocal, raydirection)) localray = Ray(olocal, dlocal) # Recursively cast castrayatnode(localray, subtree.rootnode, fromlocal, hits, scaleepsilon, rendermode, usetrueellipsoid) # 3. Sort Hits hits.sort(key=lambda h: h.distance) return hits def castrayatnode(ray, node, fromlocal, hits, scaleepsilon, rendermode, usetrueellipsoid): """ Recursive BVH traversal. """ # Check bounding box intersection if not rayintersectsbox(ray.origin, ray.direction, node.boundingbox): return if node.isleaf: for splatindex in node.indexes: splat = getsplatdata(splatindex) # Degeneracy check if any(s <= scaleepsilon for s in splat.scale): continue if rendermode == "ThreeD" and splat.scale.z <= scaleepsilon: continue hit = None if not usetrueellipsoid: # Approximate Sphere radius = (splat.scale.x + splat.scale.y) / 2.0 if rendermode == "ThreeD": radius = (splat.scale.x + splat.scale.y + splat.scale.z) / 3.0 hit = raysphereintersection(ray, splat.center, radius) else: # True Ellipsoid # Compute opacity-based uniform scale opacity = splat.color.w uniformscalefactor = log10(opacity) 2.0 # Construct matrices scalemat = diag(splat.scale.x, splat.scale.y, splat.scale.z) rotmat = quaterniontomatrix(splat.rotation) # Standard quaternion-to-rotation matrix conversion uniformmat = diag(uniformscalefactor, uniformscalefactor, uniformscalefactor) # World to Sphere transformation # Mworld = U R S # Msphere = Mworld^-1 mworld = uniformmat @ rotmat @ scalemat msphere = inverse(mworld) # Transform ray to sphere space # osphere = Msphere (olocal - c) osphere = transformpoint(msphere, ray.origin - splat.center) # dsphere = normalize(Msphere (olocal + d - c) - osphere) dendlocal = ray.origin + ray.direction dendsphere = transformpoint(msphere, dendlocal - splat.center) dsphere = normalize(dendsphere - osphere) localraysphere = Ray(osphere, dsphere) hit = raysphereintersection(localraysphere, vec3(0,0,0), 1.0) if hit: # Transform hit point back to world space hitpointsphere = hit.point hitpointworld = transformpoint(mworld, hitpointsphere) + splat.center hit.distance = length(hitpointworld - ray.origin) hit.point = hitpointworld hit.normal = transformvector(fromlocal, hit.normal) if hit: hits.append(hit) else: # Internal node: recurse for child in node.children: castrayatnode(ray, child, fromlocal, hits, scaleepsilon, rendermode, usetrueellipsoid) def raysphereintersection(rayorigin, spherecenter, radius): """ Standard ray-sphere intersection. Returns hit record or None. """ oc = rayorigin - spherecenter a = dot(ray.direction, ray.direction) b = 2.0 dot(oc, ray.direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius radius discriminant = b b - 4.0 a c if discriminant < 0: return None sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t = t1 if t1 > 0 else t2 if t < 0: return None point = rayorigin + ray.direction t normal = normalize(point - spherecenter) return HitRecord(distance=t, point=point, normal=normal) class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction class HitRecord: def init(self, distance, point, normal): self.distance = distance self.point = point self.normal = normal def transformpoint(matrix, point): # Standard 4x4 matrix-vector multiplication for homogeneous coordinates w = matrix[3][0]point.x + matrix[3][1]point.y + matrix[3][2]point.z + matrix[3][3] return vec3( (matrix[0][0]point.x + matrix[0][1]point.y + matrix[0][2]point.z + matrix[0][3]) / w, (matrix[1][0]point.x + matrix[1][1]point.y + matrix[1][2]point.z + matrix[1][3]) / w, (matrix[2][0]point.x + matrix[2][1]point.y + matrix[2][2]point.z + matrix[2][3]) / w) def transformvector(matrix, vector): # Standard 4x4 matrix-vector multiplication for direction (w=0) return vec3( matrix[0][0]vector.x + matrix[0][1]vector.y + matrix[0][2]vector.z, matrix[1][0]vector.x + matrix[1][1]vector.y + matrix[1][2]vector.z, matrix[2][0]vector.x + matrix[2][1]vector.y + matrix[2][2]vector.z) def rayintersectsbox(origin, direction, box): # Standard AABB-ray intersection test # Returns True if ray intersects the axis-aligned bounding box pass def diag(x, y, z): return [[x, 0, 0, 0], [0, y, 0, 0], [0, 0, z, 0], [0, 0, 0, 1]] def log10(x): import math return math.log10(x) def length(v): return (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2)0.5 def normalize(v): l = length(v) if l == 0: return vec3(0,0,0) return vec3(v.x/l, v.y/l, v.z/l) def dot(v1, v2): return v1.xv2.x + v1.yv2.y + v1.zv2.z class vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def sub(self, other): return vec3(self.x-other.x, self.y-other.y, self.z-other.z) def add(self, other): return vec3(self.x+other.x, self.y+other.y, self.z+other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return vec3(self.xscalar, self.yscalar, self.zscalar) Degenerate Splats: Splats with scale components \le \text{scaleEpsilon} (10^{-7}) are skipped to prevent division by zero or invalid geometry during matrix inversion. Null Data: If renderData or camera is null, the intersection test returns null and logs an error. BVH Failure: If BVH construction fails (bvh === null), the test returns null and logs an error. Vertex Count Changes: If the number of vertices changes between calls, a warning is logged, but execution continues. Precision: Using log10 for opacity scaling assumes opacity is in (0, 1]. Opacity of 0 results in -\infty, which should be handled or clamped. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports both approximate and exact intersection; efficient culling via BVH; handles dynamic scenes via local space transformation. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Ray-Splat Intersection is a core component of real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers, particularly those implemented in JavaScript/WebGL for browser-based viewing. It was developed to enable efficient picking and depth testing in large-scale Gaussian splat scenes. The method leverages BVH structures to accelerate ray-primitive intersection, a technique common in ray tracing but adapted here for the specific geometry of 3D Gaussians. mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) huggingface/gsplat.js, https://github.com/huggingface/gsplat.js, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splat Raycasting Dispatch
body: Splat Raycasting Dispatch manages the buffer preparation and dispatch call for ray-splat intersection tests, returning hit distances and splat indices. It operates on pre-transformed, packed buffer structures optimized for batched processing, distinguishing it from Ray-Splat Intersection, and targets standard Euclidean camera models rather than spherical panoramas like Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS). Inputs: splats: A flat array of u32 values representing splat data, size at least 4 count. splats2: A secondary buffer of u32 values, size 4 count. originx, originy, originz: Ray origin coordinates as f32. dirx, diry, dirz: Ray direction vector components as f32. minopacity: Minimum opacity threshold as f32. near: Near plane distance as f32. far: Far plane distance as f32. tables: Precomputed lookup tables of type RaycastTables. Outputs: distances: A Vec<f32> of size RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT containing intersection distances. indices: A Vec<u32> of capacity RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT containing original splat indices for hits. The implementation uses a fixed-capacity buffer structure to manage memory. RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT: usize constant set to 65536, defining the maximum number of splats per dispatch batch. RaycastBuffers: Contains splats (Vec<u32>, size RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT 4), splats2 (Vec<u32>, size RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT 4), distances (Vec<f32>, size RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT), indices (Vec<u32>, capacity RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT), and tables (RaycastTables). 1. Clear the distances and indices buffers. 2. Extract subbuffers splats[0..(4 count)] and splats2[0..(4 count)]. 3. Validate that count as usize does not exceed RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT; throw an error if it does. 4. Call raycastsplatellipsoids(subbuffer, subbuffer2, distances, indices, [originx, originy, originz], [dirx, diry, dirz], minopacity, tables, near, far). 5. Return distances as a Float32Array view. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatraycastingdispatch(splats, splats2, count, origin, direction, minopacity, near, far, tables): RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT = 65536 if count > RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT: raise ValueError(f"Count {count} exceeds buffer capacity {RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT}") distances = [float('inf')] RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT indices = [0] RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT subbuffersplats = splats[0: 4 count] subbuffersplats2 = splats2[0: 4 count] raycastsplatellipsoids( subbuffersplats, subbuffersplats2, distances, indices, origin[0], origin[1], origin[2], direction[0], direction[1], direction[2], minopacity, tables, near, far) return distances Buffer Overflow: count as usize must not exceed RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT (65536); exceeding this limit throws an error. Opacity Threshold: minopacity must be strictly less than 1.0. Precision: Not given in the sources. This variant describes the higher-level integration of the dispatch kernel within a JavaScript/WASM environment. Process: 1. Transform ray origin and direction from world to mesh space using the inverse of matrixWorld, storing results in raycastOrigin and raycastDirection. 2. Iterate over splat ranges via splats.forEachRaycastRange; for each range, copy splat records into buffers using splats.copySplatRecords, mapping original indices to raycastVisibleIndices, and flush to WASM when buffer capacity is reached. 3. On flush, call raycastsplatbuffers with raycastOrigin, raycastDirection, minRaycastOpacity, near, far, and count, then retrieve distances and hitIndices from WASM. 4. For each hit, compute the world point via ray.at(distance) and store the distance, point, object, and original splat index in intersects. Data Structures: raycastVisibleIndices is a Uint32Array mapping buffer slot indices to original splat indices, sized to buffer.length / 4, and is reallocated if capacity changes. Parameters: minRaycastOpacity is the threshold for raycast inclusion, defaulting to 0.1, and must be strictly less than 1.0. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is optimized for batched processing on WASM, leveraging SIMD instructions via RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+simd128,+bulk-memory". Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Fixed buffer size limits the maximum batch size to RAYCASTBUFFERCOUNT. Splat Raycasting Dispatch is part of the Gaussian-Splat-Lite project, which builds 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations for WebAssembly. It builds on the geometric principles of ray-splat intersection defined in the parent article Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection.
