name: Volume Bounds Computation
head: computeVolumeBounds
body: Volume Bounds Computation computes an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) that encloses a set of 3D points, with optional padding in world units on all sides. It serves as the foundational step for initializing voxel grids and spatial samplers by defining the spatial extent of the scene. Unlike Bounding Cube Creation, which forces a cubic aspect ratio, or Character Bounding Box Initialization, which targets specific skeletal hierarchies, this method produces a rectangular prism tailored to the input point distribution, with configurable padding in world units on all sides. Inputs: points: An array of 3D points, where each point is a tuple or vector [x, y, z]. padding: A scalar value representing the padding to add to all sides of the bounding box in world units. If not specified, defaults to 0.0. Outputs: VolumeBounds: An object containing: min: [number, number, number] — The minimum coordinates of the AABB. max: [number, number, number] — The maximum coordinates of the AABB. size: [number, number, number] — The dimensions of the AABB (max - min). center: [number, number, number] — The geometric center of the AABB. Data Structures: The VolumeBounds object is a flat structure with four fields, each being a 3-element array of floating-point numbers. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize min to [Infinity, Infinity, Infinity] and max to [-Infinity, -Infinity, -Infinity]. 2. Iterate through each point p in points: a. Update min.x = min(min.x, p.x), min.y = min(min.y, p.y), min.z = min(min.z, p.z). b. Update max.x = max(max.x, p.x), max.y = max(max.y, p.y), max.z = max(max.z, p.z). 3. Apply padding: a. min.x -= padding, min.y -= padding, min.z -= padding. b. max.x += padding, max.y += padding, max.z += padding. 4. Compute size: a. size.x = max.x - min.x. b. size.y = max.y - min.y. c. size.z = max.z - min.z. 5. Compute center: a. center.x = (min.x + max.x) / 2. b. center.y = (min.y + max.y) / 2. c. center.z = (min.z + max.z) / 2. 6. Return VolumeBounds object with min, max, size, and center. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumebounds(points: list[tuple[float, float, float]], padding: float = 0.0) -> dict: # Initialize min and max with extreme values minval = [float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')] maxval = [float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')] # Iterate over all input points to find min and max coordinates for p in points: if p[0] < minval[0]: minval[0] = p[0] if p[1] < minval[1]: minval[1] = p[1] if p[2] < minval[2]: minval[2] = p[2] if p[0] > maxval[0]: maxval[0] = p[0] if p[1] > maxval[1]: maxval[1] = p[1] if p[2] > maxval[2]: maxval[2] = p[2] # Apply configurable padding in world units to all sides minval[0] -= padding minval[1] -= padding minval[2] -= padding maxval[0] += padding maxval[1] += padding maxval[2] += padding # Compute size and center size = [ maxval[0] - minval[0], maxval[1] - minval[1], maxval[2] - minval[2] ] center = [ (minval[0] + maxval[0]) / 2.0, (minval[1] + maxval[1]) / 2.0, (minval[2] + maxval[2]) / 2.0 ] return { "min": minval, "max": maxval, "size": size, "center": center } Parameters: padding: Configurable padding in world units. Typical value: 0.0 for tight bounds, >0.0 for safety margins. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Input: If points is empty, min remains [inf, inf, inf] and max remains [-inf, -inf, -inf]. The caller must check for this case before using the result. Precision: Using float('inf') ensures correct initialization regardless of the scale of the input data, avoiding underflow/overflow issues with arbitrary initial values. Degenerate Input: If all points are identical, size will be [0, 0, 0]. Padding ensures the box has non-zero volume if padding > 0. Silhouette-based Bounding Box Initialization computes an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) that tightly encloses the visible geometry of a scene by projecting ground truth silhouettes from training cameras onto the scene space. It serves as a robust initialization step for volume rendering, particularly when the scene is dense or when precise spatial bounds are required before adaptive learning or sparse voxel grid construction begins. Unlike simple extent-based methods, it accounts for camera visibility and occlusion, ensuring the bounding volume only encompasses regions actually observed by the training set. Silhouette-Based Bounding Box Estimation computes a 3D volume that strictly encloses a target object by intersecting the back-projected foreground regions from multiple binary segmentation masks. It differs from Octree-based Bounding Volume Computation by relying solely on 2D image masks rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning, and from Silhouette-based Bounding Box Initialization by explicitly constructing the full volumetric hull rather than just an initial box. Octree-based Bounding Volume Computation computes a convex bounding volume for a signed distance field (SDF) by adaptively decomposing space into an octree and extracting the convex hull from cubes that straddle the surface. It serves as an alternative to Sphere Carving, trading higher SDF evaluation costs for potentially faster convergence on shapes with significant anisotropy in the field values. Unlike Sphere Carving, which provides strict bounding guarantees, this approach does not guarantee that the resulting volume encloses the entire surface. Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) Computation computes an oriented bounding box (OBB) that tightly encloses a set of 3D points or sub-boxes by fitting an ellipsoid via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the covariance matrix of the vertices. Unlike its sibling Volume Bounds Computation, which produces axis-aligned boxes, this method determines optimal orientation and extent, providing tighter bounds for rotated instances. It is primarily used in 3D cuboid detection for instance segmentation and conservative culling in SDF-based rendering. Selective Bounding Volume (SBV) is a 3D extension of the 2D bounding box method used to identify and extract a Volume of Interest (VOI) from a 3D medical image by ignoring blank slices and confining coordinates to active portions. It sets itself apart from shape-adaptive methods by refusing to discard any active portions in any slices, thereby preserving clinically significant background details that other methods might remove. Robust Bounding Box Computation is a method to compute a bounding box for a 3DGS scene by clipping outliers using percentiles, preventing distant 'floater' splats from dominating the AABB. It differs from the standard method by ignoring extreme values in the coordinate distribution. Definition: Computes a bounding box by sorting splat centers and selecting coordinates at percentile boundaries. Steps: 1. Collect all X, Y, and Z coordinates of the splat centers into separate arrays. 2. Sort each coordinate array in ascending order. 3. Calculate the lower index as floor(p (N - 1)) and the upper index as ceil((1 - p) (N - 1)), where N is the number of splats and p is bboxPercentile. 4. Construct the bounding box using the coordinates at the lower and upper indices for each axis. Parameters: bboxPercentile: The fraction of splats to clip from each end of the distribution per axis. Typical value: 0.02 (clip outer 2%). Complexity: O(N log N) due to sorting, where N is the number of splats. Time Complexity: O(N) for the standard AABB computation, where N is the number of input points. O(N log N) for the Robust Bounding Box Computation due to sorting. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the input points and coordinate arrays for the robust method. The standard method uses O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple, fast, and predictable performance for static datasets. The robust variant effectively handles outliers common in neural rendering scenes (e.g., 3DGS floaters). Limitations: The standard AABB may be too loose if the scene has significant anisotropy or outliers. Silhouette-based methods require accurate camera poses and masks. OBB computation is more expensive and complex. When to use: Use standard AABB for general point clouds and mesh bounds. Use robust bounding box for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes with potential outliers. Use silhouette-based when no 3D geometry is available. Use OBB when tight fitting for oriented instances is required. Volume Bounds Computation is a fundamental technique in computer graphics for defining the spatial extent of a scene or object. It is widely used in volume rendering to initialize voxel grids, splat carvers, and raymarchers. The method is often a precursor to more complex bounding volume hierarchies or spatial partitioning structures. In the context of neural rendering and 3D Gaussian Splatting, robust variants have been developed to handle the specific challenges of outlier splats. Silhouette-based methods are common in NeRF-like pipelines where explicit geometry is not available. feat: 3D IDW interpolation volume and voxel visualisation, https://github.com/darkmine-oss/baselode/pull/50, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Silhouette-based Bounding Box Initialization
body: Silhouette-based Bounding Box Initialization computes an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) that encloses a scene by projecting ground truth silhouettes from training cameras. It sets itself apart from extent-based or octree methods by using silhouette union to define spatial bounds before adaptive learning or sparse voxel grid construction begins. Inputs: traincameras (camera poses and intrinsics), groundTruth (silhouette masks), scene (target scene object), datasetSize (number of views), silhouetteRadius (expansion radius), issparse (boolean flag for scene sparsity), skipIndex and skips (view indices to exclude), configs->silhouetteInitial (enable flag). Outputs: scene.bboxdepthmax/min, scene.bboxheightmax/min, scene.bboxwidthmax/min (AABB limits), scene.adaptiveLRDevice (learning rate parameters). Camera: Contains projection matrix cameraKernel[9], translation translateMat[3], and image dimensions targetImageSize[2]. Scene: Contains bounding box limits (bboxdepthmax/min, bboxheightmax/min, bboxwidthmax/min) and device memory for learning rates (adaptiveLRDevice). 1. Check configs->silhouetteInitial. If false, create tempScene, initialize it, compute bbox, copy limits to scene, and free tempScene. 2. If true and issparse is false, call bboxsilhouette directly on scene with issparse=false. 3. If true and issparse is true, create tempScene, initialize it with parameters sceneWidth, sceneHeight, sceneDepth, true, true, 0.1, -10., 0.5, 1., call bboxsilhouette on tempScene with issparse=true, copy bbox limits and adaptiveLRDevice to scene, and free tempScene. 4. The bboxsilhouette step projects silhouettes, expands by silhouetteRadius, and computes the union to update the scene's bounding box fields. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Scene: def init(self): self.bboxdepthmax = self.bboxdepthmin = 0.0 self.bboxheightmax = self.bboxheightmin = 0.0 self.bboxwidthmax = self.bboxwidthmin = 0.0 self.adaptivelrdevice = [] self.width = self.height = self.depth = 0.0 def initself(self, w, h, d, f1, f2, p1, p2, p3, p4): self.width, self.height, self.depth = w, h, d # Internal flags and parameters initialized as per source def freeself(self): del self.adaptivelrdevice def computebboxfromsilhouettes(cameras, groundtruth, targetscene, datasetsize, radius, issparse, skipidx, skips): # Projects silhouettes, expands by radius, computes union, updates targetscene bbox fields pass def copybboxes(src, dst): dst.bboxdepthmax, dst.bboxdepthmin = src.bboxdepthmax, src.bboxdepthmin dst.bboxheightmax, dst.bboxheightmin = src.bboxheightmax, src.bboxheightmin dst.bboxwidthmax, dst.bboxwidthmin = src.bboxwidthmax, src.bboxwidthmin def silhouettebasedbboxinit(traincameras, groundtruth, scene, datasetsize, silhouetteradius, issparse, skipindex, skips, configs): if not configs.silhouetteinitial: tempscene = Scene() tempscene.initself(scene.width, scene.height, scene.depth, True, True, 0.1, -10.0, 0.5, 1.0) computebboxfromsilhouettes(traincameras, groundtruth, tempscene, datasetsize, silhouetteradius, True, skipindex, skips) copybboxes(tempscene, scene) tempscene.freeself() elif not issparse: computebboxfromsilhouettes(traincameras, groundtruth, scene, datasetsize, silhouetteradius, False, skipindex, skips) else: tempscene = Scene() tempscene.initself(scene.width, scene.height, scene.depth, True, True, 0.1, -10.0, 0.5, 1.0) computebboxfromsilhouettes(traincameras, groundtruth, tempscene, datasetsize, silhouetteradius, True, skipindex, skips) copybboxes(tempscene, scene) scene.adaptivelrdevice = tempscene.adaptivelrdevice.copy() # standard device memory copy tempscene.freeself() silhouetteRadius: Expansion radius for silhouette projections. skipIndex: Single view index to exclude. skips: List of view indices to exclude. configs->silhouetteInitial: Boolean flag enabling the method. Sparse scenes require a temporary scene with specific padding parameters (0.1, -10., 0.5, 1.0) to compute bounds correctly. Large-scale scenes may exceed GPU memory limits during simultaneous processing, necessitating sub-scene decomposition. A spatial decomposition methodology that assigns cameras to sub-scenes to facilitate precise resource allocation and spatial indexing for large-scale scene reconstruction. It computes the initial bounding box for a sub-scene as the union of the individual camera projection bounding boxes associated with that sub-scene, then refines the region by computing the minimum bounding rectangle that encompasses the entire scene range observed by all cameras in the sub-scene. This resulting rectangle is used as the scene bounding box for the sub-scene. It uses Instant-NGP as the baseline model for training sub-scene models, chosen for its speed to meet near-real-time requirements for large-scale reconstruction. Default parameters include MaxNum (maximum cameras per sub-scene) of 113 to prevent GPU memory overflow on 24GB GPUs, TopNum (initial maximum cameras per cluster) of 90, and Training iterations of 5 \times 10^3. The method handles sparse and dense representations differently by routing sparse scenes through a temporary scene structure with explicit padding parameters. Sub-scene decomposition limits peak memory usage by restricting the number of cameras processed simultaneously (e.g., MaxNum=113). The sub-scene variant uses Instant-NGP as a baseline to meet near-real-time reconstruction requirements. The method was employed in Clear-plenoxels for initializing bounding boxes and adaptive learning rates using silhouette information. The sub-scene decomposition variant was introduced in BirdNeRF for fast neural reconstruction of large-scale scenes from aerial imagery, addressing GPU memory constraints and enabling near-real-time reconstruction. nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) BirdNeRF: fast neural reconstruction of large-scale scenes from aerial imagery., https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-21206-z, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Silhouette-Based Bounding Box Estimation
head: Visual Hull, shape-from-silhouette
body: Silhouette-Based Bounding Box Estimation computes a 3D volume that strictly encloses a target object by intersecting the back-projected foreground regions from multiple binary segmentation masks. It differs from Octree-based Bounding Volume Computation by relying solely on 2D image masks rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning. Inputs: traincameras: Array of camera poses (extrinsics) and intrinsics for N training views. masks: Array of binary foreground-background segmentation masks, one per view. silhouetteRadius: Scalar expansion radius for the final bounds. skipIndex/skips: Optional indices and strides for subsampling views. Outputs: scene.bboxdepthmin/max, scene.bboxwidthmin/max, scene.bboxheightmin/max: The final axis-aligned bounding box coordinates. Data Structures: Mask: Binary array of size H \times W, where 1 indicates foreground and 0 indicates background. Camera Pose: 4 \times 4 matrix containing rotation and translation; S2 uses camera-to-world or world-to-camera conventions. Voxel Grid: Optional intermediate representation; S1 uses a 400 \times 400 \times 400 voxel grid to store the hull. Steps: 1. Initialize Bounds: Set global minimums (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) to +\infty and maximums (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) to -\infty. 2. Iterate Views: Loop through each training view, applying skipIndex/skips if provided. 3. Extract Mask: Retrieve the binary mask Mi for view i. Masks are derived from alpha channels if available, or via background separation (e.g., OpenCV for white backgrounds) or segmentation models. 4. Backproject Silhouette: For each pixel (u, v) in Mi where Mi[u, v] == 1, construct the ray r originating from the camera center Ci and passing through the pixel using camera intrinsics. The ray represents a cone of possible object locations. 5. Accumulate Volume: Backproject mask pixels into 3D space and accumulate 3D points or mark voxels along the rays. S1 implements this by casting rays into a coarse voxel grid and marking intersected voxels as occupied. 6. Compute Min/Max: Determine the bounding box enclosing all accumulated 3D points or occupied voxels along the X, Y, and Z axes. 7. Expand Bounds: Apply silhouetteRadius to the computed bounds to account for discretization and ensure the object is fully contained. 8. Store: Write the final bounds to scene.bboxdepthmin/max, scene.bboxwidthmin/max, scene.bboxheightmin/max. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesilhouettebbox(traincameras, masks, silhouetteradius, maxdepth=10.0, skipindex=None): """ Computes a bounding box enclosing the visual hull of an object. Args: traincameras: List of dicts with 'intrinsics' (3x3), 'extrinsics' (4x4 W2C). masks: List of 2D binary arrays (H, W). silhouetteradius: Float expansion factor. maxdepth: Float, maximum ray length for point accumulation. skipindex: Optional list of view indices. Returns: dict: {'bboxmin': [x, y, z], 'bboxmax': [x, y, z]} """ globalmin = [float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')] globalmax = [float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')] indices = skipindex if skipindex is not None else range(len(traincameras)) for i in indices: cam = traincameras[i] mask = masks[i] K = cam['intrinsics'] R = [row[:3] for row in cam['extrinsics']] t = [cam['extrinsics'][j][3] for j in range(3)] # Camera center in world space: Cw = -R^T t Cw = [-sum(R[j][k] t[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] invK = invert3x3(K) foregroundpixels = [(u, v) for v in range(len(mask)) for u in range(len(mask[0])) if mask[v][u] > 0] for u, v in foregroundpixels: # Ray direction in camera space: dcam = invK [u, v, 1] dcam = [ invK[0][0]u + invK[0][1]v + invK[0][2], invK[1][0]u + invK[1][1]v + invK[1][2], invK[2][0]u + invK[2][1]v + invK[2][2] ] # Transform direction to world space: dw = R^T dcam dw = [ R[0][0]dcam[0] + R[1][0]dcam[1] + R[2][0]dcam[2], R[0][1]dcam[0] + R[1][1]dcam[1] + R[2][1]dcam[2], R[0][2]dcam[0] + R[1][2]dcam[1] + R[2][2]dcam[2] ] # Normalize direction norm = (dw[0]2 + dw[1]2 + dw[2]2)0.5 dw = [d / norm for d in dw] # Accumulate points along the ray up to maxdepth for depth in range(1, int(maxdepth) + 1): point = [Cw[j] + depth dw[j] for j in range(3)] for j in range(3): if point[j] < globalmin[j]: globalmin[j] = point[j] if point[j] > globalmax[j]: globalmax[j] = point[j] globalmin = [m - silhouetteradius for m in globalmin] globalmax = [m + silhouetteradius for m in globalmax] return {'bboxmin': globalmin, 'bboxmax': globalmax} def invert3x3(M): invdet = 1.0 / (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) return [ [(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])invdet], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])invdet], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])invdet] ] Parameters: silhouetteRadius: Expansion radius to ensure the object is fully contained. Typical value: Not given in the sources. skipIndex: Indices of views to skip for subsampling. voxelResolution: S1 uses 400 \times 400 \times 400. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convex Shapes: The visual hull cannot restore dented parts (undercuts) of non-convex shapes, but it never overcuts and contains 100% of the object. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of views and P is the number of foreground pixels or voxels processed. S1 notes it can fit 100 images in about 10 seconds using JAX. Memory Complexity: O(V) for voxel-based implementation, where V is the number of voxels (e.g., 400^3). Performance: Provides a 2-8x speedup in NeRF training by eliminating unnecessary network evaluations outside the hull. Strengths: Fast, simple, guarantees the object is fully contained (100% recall). Limitations: Cannot represent concavities; requires accurate segmentation masks. Origin: Visual Hull is a classic 3D reconstruction technique based on shape-from-silhouette. History: It predates NeRF and has been applied in many classic 3D reconstruction contexts. Usage: Recently revisited in VaxNeRF to accelerate NeRF training by providing a coarse in-out field separation. name: Octree-based Bounding Volume Computation
head: Convex Hull from Straddling Cubes, Octree-based Bounding Volume
body: This method computes a convex bounding volume for a signed distance field (SDF) by adaptively decomposing space into an octree and extracting the convex hull from cubes that straddle the surface. It serves as an alternative to Sphere Carving, typically requiring significantly more SDF evaluations to obtain a good convex hull, but potentially converging faster for shapes with significant anisotropy in f values. Unlike Sphere Carving, this approach does not provide bounding guarantees that the resulting volume encloses the entire surface. Inputs: A signed distance function f(\mathbf{x}). An initial large cube C{\text{root}} enclosing the region of interest. Outputs: A convex hull H approximating the surface boundary. Data Structures: Octree Node: Represents a cube in 3D space. center: 3D vector \mathbf{c}, the geometric center of the cube. diagonal: scalar d, the length of the cube's space diagonal. children: list of 8 child nodes or None if leaf. vertices: list of 8 corner points of the cube. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the root node with the initial large cube C{\text{root}}. 2. Recursive Subdivision: For each node, evaluate f(\mathbf{c}) at the cube center. If f(\mathbf{c}) \ge d, the cube does not straddle the surface; stop subdivision for this branch. If f(\mathbf{c}) < d, the cube may straddle the surface; subdivide it into 8 equal child cubes and process each recursively. 3. Straddling Detection: Identify straddling cubes as the octree leaves reached during traversal where f(\mathbf{c}) < d. 4. Convex Hull Construction: Collect the eight vertices of all detected straddling cubes. Compute the convex hull H of this point set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeoctreeboundingvolume(f, initialcube): """ Computes a convex bounding volume for an SDF f using an octree. Args: f: Signed distance function. initialcube: A cube object with attributes 'center' (vec3), 'diagonal' (float), 'sidelength' (float), and 'vertices' (list of 8 vec3). Returns: H: Convex hull of the straddling cubes' vertices. """ straddlingvertices = [] def recurse(cube): fval = f(cube.center) # If f(c) >= diagonal, the cube does not straddle the surface. if fval >= cube.diagonal: return # Sources do not specify a termination condition other than f(c) >= d. # In practice, a minimum cube size or max depth is required. if cube.sidelength < 1e-6: straddlingvertices.extend(cube.vertices) return # Subdivide into 8 children for child in cube.subdivide(): recurse(child) recurse(initialcube) # Sources do not specify the convex hull algorithm. H = convexhull(straddlingvertices) return H Parameters: Initial cube size: Not given in the sources. Max depth / Min cube size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coplanar Points: The final point set may contain numerous coplanar points, especially for flat surface parts, slowing convex hull computation as all points may contribute to the convex envelope. No Bounding Guarantees: The octree approach does not provide any bounding guarantees that the resulting volume encloses the entire surface. Infinite Recursion: If the SDF value at the center remains less than the diagonal indefinitely (e.g., exactly on the surface where f(\mathbf{c})=0), the recursion may not terminate without a minimum cube size or maximum depth. Time Complexity: Requires significantly more SDF evaluations than Sphere Carving to accurately obtain a good convex hull. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: For shapes with significant anisotropy in f values, the method may converge faster. For very conservative functions, the computational advantage of Sphere Carving may be offset by the cost of intersecting many spheres. Strengths: May converge faster for shapes with significant anisotropy in f values. Limitations: Does not provide bounding guarantees; requires more SDF evaluations; coplanar points can slow convex hull computation. When to use: When the shape has significant anisotropy in the SDF values and bounding guarantees are not critical. When not to use: When strict bounding guarantees are required or when the SDF is very conservative and Sphere Carving is more efficient. Origin: The method is described as an alternative strategy for computing convex bounding volumes for implicit surfaces defined by SDFs. History: The octree decomposition variant is attributed to Hart [Hart 1996]. Usage: Used in volume rendering and implicit surface processing as an alternative to Sphere Carving. name: Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) Computation
head: 3D Cuboid Detection, PCA-based Bounding Box, SdfBoundingBox::merge
body: Computes an oriented bounding box (OBB) that encloses a set of 3D points or sub-boxes by fitting an ellipsoid via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the covariance matrix of the vertices. Unlike its sibling Volume Bounds Computation, which produces axis-aligned boxes, this method determines optimal orientation and extent. It is primarily used in 3D cuboid detection for instance segmentation and for merging sub-boxes in signed distance field trees. Inputs: 1. A set of 3D points assigned to an instance (for PCA-based detection). 2. A list of subboxes, where each sub-box provides a transformation matrix and 8 local vertices (for SDF-based merge). Outputs: 1. An OBB defined by a center, orientation (rotation basis), and scale (extent). 2. For SDF implementation: newbboxmat (transformation matrix), fullinverse, and transinverse. Data Structures: vertmat: A matrix of shape (V \times 4) where V is the total number of vertices (e.g., subboxes.len() 8), stored in homogeneous coordinates. covarmat: A 3 \times 3 covariance matrix derived from the spatial coordinates of the centered vertices. eigenbasis: A 4 \times 4 matrix representing the rotation/translation basis in homogeneous coordinates. Steps: 1. Handle Empty Input: If subboxes is empty, return a zero bounding box. 2. Construct Vertex Matrix: Extract the 8 vertices of each subbox and transform them by subbox.matrix to populate vertmat. If using raw points directly, pad them to 4D with w=1. 3. Compute Mean: Calculate the mean of all vertices: \text{vert\mean} = \text{column\mean}(\text{vert\mat}). 4. Center Vertices: Subtract \text{vert\mean} from each column in vertmat: \text{vert\mat}{\text{centered}} = \text{vert\mat} - \text{vert\mean}. 5. Compute Covariance Matrix: Compute the covariance using the centered spatial coordinates: \text{covar\mat} = \frac{1}{V-1} \text{vert\mat}{\text{centered}}[:,:3]^T \text{vert\mat}{\text{centered}}[:,:3]. Only the top-left 3 \times 3 block is used for PCA orientation. 6. Principal Component Analysis (PCA): Compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \text{covar\mat}. Construct eigenbasis from the top 3 eigenvectors as the rotation basis. Force the 4th row and 4th column of eigenbasis to [0, 0, 0, 1] to ensure valid homogeneous coordinates: \text{eigen\basis}[3,:] = [0, 0, 0, 1] and \text{eigen\basis}[:, 3] = [0, 0, 0, 1]^T. 7. Project Vertices: Project the centered vertices onto the eigenbasis: \text{vert\proj\mat} = \text{eigen\basis} \times \text{vert\mat}{\text{centered}}^T. This aligns the data with the principal axes. 8. Calculate Extents: Find the minimum and maximum coordinates of the projected vertices along each axis: \text{box\min} = \min(\text{vert\proj\mat}[:3,:]), \text{box\max} = \max(\text{vert\proj\mat}[:3,:]). 9. Calculate Centroid and Scale: Calculate centroid in the local projected space: \text{centroid} = (\text{box\max} + \text{box\min}) / 2.0. Calculate scale: \text{scale} = \text{box\max} - \text{centroid}. Calculate reciprocal scale: \text{scale\recip} = 1.0 / \text{scale}. 10. Construct Bounding Box Matrix: Combine translation, rotation, and scaling: \text{new\bbox\mat} = T(\text{vert\mean}) \times \text{eigen\basis} \times S(\text{scale}) \times T(\text{centroid}). Where T is translation and S is non-uniform scaling. 11. Compute Inverses: Compute fullinverse as the inverse of newbboxmat. Compute transinverse as the inverse of the translation-rotation part: \text{trans\inverse} = (T(\text{vert\mean}) \times \text{eigen\basis})^{-1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class SdfBoundingBox: def init(self, newbboxmat, fullinverse, transinverse, centroid, scale): self.newbboxmat = newbboxmat self.fullinverse = fullinverse self.transinverse = transinverse self.centroid = centroid self.scale = scale @staticmethod def zero(): return SdfBoundingBox(np.eye(4), np.eye(4), np.eye(4), np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3)) def computeobb(subboxes): """ Compute OBB from a list of subboxes. Each subbox has a 'matrix' (4x4) and 8 vertices in local space. """ if not subboxes: return SdfBoundingBox.zero() # Step 2: Construct vertex matrix vertices = [] for subbox in subboxes: for localv in subbox.localvertices: worldv = subbox.matrix @ localv vertices.append(worldv) vertmat = np.array(vertices) # Shape: (N, 4) numvertices = vertmat.shape[0] # Step 3: Compute mean vertmean = np.mean(vertmat, axis=0) # Step 4: Center vertices vertmatcentered = vertmat - vertmean # Step 5: Compute covariance matrix (3x3) xyzcentered = vertmatcentered[:,:3] covarmat = (xyzcentered.T @ xyzcentered) / (numvertices - 1) # Step 6: PCA eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covarmat) idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] # Construct eigenbasis (4x4) eigenbasis = np.eye(4) eigenbasis[:3,:3] = eigenvectors.T # Force 4th row and column to identity basis eigenbasis[3,:] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] eigenbasis[:, 3] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Step 7: Project vertices vertprojmat = eigenbasis @ vertmatcentered.T # Shape: (4, N) # Extract xyz projections xyzproj = vertprojmat[:3,:] # Step 8: Calculate extents boxmin = np.min(xyzproj, axis=1) boxmax = np.max(xyzproj, axis=1) # Step 9: Calculate centroid and scale centroid = (boxmax + boxmin) / 2.0 scale = boxmax - centroid scalerecip = 1.0 / scale # Step 10: Construct new bounding box matrix T1 = np.eye(4) T1[:3, 3] = vertmean[:3] S = np.eye(4) S[0, 0] = scale[0] S[1, 1] = scale[1] S[2, 2] = scale[2] T2 = np.eye(4) T2[:3, 3] = centroid newbboxmat = T1 @ eigenbasis @ S @ T2 # Step 11: Compute inverses fullinverse = np.linalg.inv(newbboxmat) transpart = T1 @ eigenbasis transinverse = np.linalg.inv(transpart) return SdfBoundingBox(newbboxmat, fullinverse, transinverse, centroid, scale) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Input: Handled by returning a zero bounding box. Degenerate Covariance: If all points are collinear or coplanar, the covariance matrix will be singular, causing PCA to fail or produce arbitrary orientations. Precision: Homogeneous coordinate forcing and matrix inversion can accumulate floating-point errors; use double precision for construction if high accuracy is required. Scale Reciprocal: The source computes scalerecip but does not apply it in the matrix construction; it is retained for potential downstream normalization or inverse transformations. Originated in 3D computer vision for instance segmentation and cuboid detection. The SUDS paper (2023) applies PCA to the convex hull of points belonging to each instance to derive oriented bounding boxes. The SDF implementation adapts this for merging sub-boxes in a signed distance field tree. name: Selective Bounding Volume (SBV)
body: Selective Bounding Volume (SBV) is a 3D extension of the 2D bounding box method used to identify and extract a Volume of Interest (VOI) from a 3D medical image by ignoring blank slices and confining coordinates to active portions. It sets itself apart from shape-adaptive methods by refusing to discard any active portions in any slices, thereby preserving clinically significant background details that other methods might remove. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D medical image X with dimensions [x, y, z] (width, height, depth). Output: An extracted sub-volume VOI containing only the active region. Data Structures: tempcoordinates: An array of 4 integers [x1, x2, x3, x4] initialized to zero. These store the bounding box coordinates (min\row, min\col, max\row, max\col) for each non-blank slice. RowMin, ColumnMin, RowMax, ColumnMax: Integer variables storing the global minimum and maximum coordinates across all active slices. z1, z2: Integer indices marking the first and last non-zero slices. Steps: 1. Get Dimensions: Determine the size of the input image X as [x, y, z]. 2. Initialize: Declare RowMin, ColumnMin, RowMax, ColumnMax as integers. Initialize tempcoordinates [x1, x2, x3, x4] to [0, 0, 0, 0]. 3. Identify Active Z-Range: Iterate through all z-slices to search for zero-intensity (blank) slices. Identify z1 as the index of the first non-zero slice and z2 as the index of the last non-zero slice. Blank slices at the foremost and end of the volume are ignored to prevent them from affecting the bounding volume calculation. 4. Compute Slice Bounding Boxes: For each slice z from z1 to z2: Apply 2D bounding box operations on the slice to find its local active region. Update tempcoordinates with the local bounding box coordinates [x1, x2, x3, x4] for that slice. 5. Compute Global Bounds: Determine the global bounding box by taking the minimum and maximum of the accumulated coordinates: RowMin = \min(x1), ColumnMin = \min(x2), RowMax = \max(x3), ColumnMax = \max(x4), where the min/max functions operate over all slices from z1 to z2. 6. Extract VOI: Iterate through the volume using the global bounds: For k from z1 to z2, for i from RowMin to RowMax, for j from ColumnMin to ColumnMax, assign VOI \leftarrow X(i, j, k). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectiveboundingvolume(X): # X is a 3D array of shape (depth, height, width) # Step 1: Get dimensions zdim, ydim, xdim = len(X), len(X[0]), len(X[0][0]) # Step 2: Initialize # tempcoordinates stores [minrow, mincol, maxrow, maxcol] for each active slice tempcoordinates = [] z1 = None z2 = None # Step 3: Identify active Z-range for k in range(zdim): if not isblankslice(X[k]): if z1 is None: z1 = k z2 = k if z1 is None: return None # Step 4: Compute slice bounding boxes for k in range(z1, z2 + 1): box = compute2dboundingbox(X[k]) tempcoordinates.append(box) # Step 5: Compute global bounds # x1=minrow, x2=mincol, x3=maxrow, x4=maxcol allx1 = [b[0] for b in tempcoordinates] allx2 = [b[1] for b in tempcoordinates] allx3 = [b[2] for b in tempcoordinates] allx4 = [b[3] for b in tempcoordinates] RowMin = min(allx1) ColumnMin = min(allx2) RowMax = max(allx3) ColumnMax = max(allx4) # Step 6: Extract VOI outz = z2 - z1 + 1 outy = RowMax - RowMin + 1 outx = ColumnMax - ColumnMin + 1 VOI = [[[0 for in range(outx)] for in range(outy)] for in range(outz)] for k in range(z1, z2 + 1): for i in range(RowMin, RowMax + 1): for j in range(ColumnMin, ColumnMax + 1): VOI[k - z1][i - RowMin][j - ColumnMin] = X[k][i][j] return VOI def isblankslice(slice2d): return all(val == 0 for row in slice2d for val in row) def compute2dboundingbox(slice2d): rows, cols = [], [] for r, row in enumerate(slice2d): for c, val in enumerate(row): if val != 0: rows.append(r) cols.append(c) if not rows: return [0, 0, 0, 0] return [min(rows), min(cols), max(rows), max(cols)] Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blank Slices: The method explicitly ignores blank slices (null image slices) at the foremost and end of the volume. If the entire volume is blank, the algorithm should handle the case where z1 is never set. Active Portions: Unlike shape-adaptive methods, SBV does not discard any active portions in any slices. This preserves clinically significant background details but may result in a larger bounding volume if the object is sparse within the active slices. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Preserves all active portions in any slices, including clinically significant background details, which shape-adaptive methods might discard. It is an automated morphological operation-based object detection technique. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Use when extracting a VOI from 3D medical images where preserving all active background details is critical, and blank slices exist at the boundaries of the volume. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The Selective Bounding Volume (SBV) method was proposed in the paper "On a hybrid lossless compression technique for three‐dimensional medical images". History and Development: The method is described as a 3D extension of the Bounding Box method. It was developed to overcome issues with existing techniques that discarded non-object details. Where it is Used: 3D medical imaging, specifically for object detection and as a preprocessing step for lossless compression. On a hybrid lossless compression technique for three‐dimensional medical images, https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.12960, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Bounding Box and Camera Center Calculation
head: AABB and Camera Setup, CenteredView Calculation, Scene Center and Radius Calculation
body: This method computes the geometric center and bounding radius of a voxel grid or mesh to position cameras and define clipping planes for volume rendering. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly deriving camera parameters (such as position and field of view) from the scene's spatial extent, whereas siblings like Bounding Cube Creation or Volume Bounds Computation focus solely on spatial bounds without camera integration. It builds on Mesh Bounding Box Calculation by using the computed AABB to derive a centered view configuration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid or set of vertices with known minimum and maximum bounds (bounds\min, bounds\max). Output: A camera center position (C) and, optionally, a bounding radius (R) and transform matrix. Data Structures: CenteredView: A structure containing a transformation matrix (transform) and a camera center vector (cameracenter). VoxelGrid: A data structure containing boundsmin and boundsmax vectors. Steps: 1. Retrieve the minimum and maximum bounds of the scene. If starting from vertices, iterate through all vertices to find the minimum and maximum coordinates for each axis (x, y, z). 2. Calculate the center coordinates (Cx, Cy, Cz) as the average of the minimum and maximum bounds for each axis. 3. Calculate the edge lengths (dx, dy, dz) as the differences between maximum and minimum bounds. 4. Compute the bounding radius (R) as half the Euclidean diagonal of the bounding box. 5. Determine the camera center position. Two common approaches exist: Approach A (Radius-based): Use the center calculated in Step 2. The radius is used for clipping plane calculations. Approach B (FOV-based): For orthographic or perspective cameras with a specific field of view (e.g., 45 degrees), calculate the camera Z position (Cz) relative to the maximum Z bound (Z{max}) and the maximum X or Y edge length (E{max}). Formulas: Center: Cx = \frac{bounds\min.x + bounds\max.x}{2.0} Cy = \frac{bounds\min.y + bounds\max.y}{2.0} Cz = \frac{bounds\min.z + bounds\max.z}{2.0} Radius: R = \frac{\sqrt{(bounds\max.x - bounds\min.x)^2 + (bounds\max.y - bounds\min.y)^2 + (bounds\max.z - bounds\min.z)^2}}{2.0} Camera Z (FOV-based): Cz = Z{max} + \frac{E{max}}{\tan(\frac{FOV}{2})} Where E{max} = \max(bounds\max.x - bounds\min.x, bounds\max.y - bounds\min.y) and FOV = 45^\circ. Parameters: Field of View (FOV): Typically 45^\circ for the FOV-based approach. Grid: The voxel data structure containing bounds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Bounds: If the scene has zero volume (all vertices at the same point), the radius is zero, and division by zero may occur in FOV calculations if not guarded. Precision: Use floating-point arithmetic for center and radius calculations to avoid integer truncation errors. Coordinate Systems: Ensure consistency between the bounding box coordinate system and the camera coordinate system. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateboundingboxandcameracenter(verticesorbounds): """ Calculate the center, radius, and camera center for a voxel grid or mesh. Args: verticesorbounds: Either a list of vertices (x, y, z) or a structure with boundsmin and boundsmax. name: Host-side Bounding Box Computation
head: ComputeBoundHost, UnionBoundHost
body: Computes the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for each triangle in a mesh on the CPU host, producing separate arrays for minimum and maximum coordinates. It serves as a prerequisite step for GPU-based voxelization by providing the spatial extent of each primitive before ray-primitive intersection or volume rasterization. It differs from Mesh Bounding Box Calculation, which computes a single global AABB for the entire mesh, by maintaining per-triangle bounds. Inputs: vertices: Pointer to an array of float values representing vertex positions. The layout is contiguous triples (x, y, z), indexed by triangle indices. triangles: Pointer to an array of int indices. Each triangle consists of 3 indices into the vertices array. N: The number of triangles in the mesh. ncores: The number of CPU threads to use for parallel execution. Outputs: bbox0: Output array of float of size at least 3 \times N. Stores the minimum coordinates (minx, miny, minz) for each triangle. bbox1: Output array of float of size at least 3 \times N. Stores the maximum coordinates (maxx, maxy, maxz) for each triangle. Data Structure Layout: The output arrays use a Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout optimized for component-wise access. For triangle index i (0 \le i < N): bbox0[i] stores \minx bbox0[i + N] stores \miny bbox0[i + 2N] stores \minz bbox1[i] stores \maxx bbox1[i + N] stores \maxy bbox1[i + 2N] stores \maxz. Algorithm Steps: 1. Dispatch: Check if ncores > 1. If true, call ComputeBoundParallel with begin=0 and end=N. If false, call ComputeBoundSerial with begin=0 and end=N. 2. Serial Execution (ComputeBoundSerial): Iterate triidx from begin to end. Initialize bbox0 and bbox1 entries for triidx to extreme values: For c \in \{0, 1, 2\}: c\idx = tri\idx + c \times N bbox0[c\idx] = \text{FLT\MAX} bbox1[c\idx] = -\text{FLT\MAX}. For each vertex component c \in \{0, 1, 2\} of the triangle: Retrieve vertex index: idx = triangles[tri\idx + c \times N]. Retrieve vertex pointer: ptr = &vertices[3 \times idx]. val = ptr[c] c\idx = tri\idx + c \times N Update bounds: If val < bbox0[c\idx], set bbox0[c\idx] = val. If val > bbox1[c\idx], set bbox1[c\idx] = val. 3. Parallel Execution (ComputeBoundParallel): Calculate threadsize = N / nthreads (default n\threads = 4). Create nthreads - 1 threads, each processing a chunk of threadsize triangles starting from begin. The last thread processes the remaining triangles from begin + (nthreads - 1) \times threadsize to end. Each thread executes the logic of ComputeBoundSerial for its assigned range. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading def computeboundhost(vertices, triangles, N, ncores=1): # Initialize output arrays of size 3N bbox0 = [float('inf')] (3 N) bbox1 = [float('-inf')] (3 N) if ncores > 1: computeboundparallel(vertices, triangles, N, bbox0, bbox1, ncores) else: computeboundserial(vertices, triangles, N, 0, N, bbox0, bbox1) return bbox0, bbox1 def computeboundserial(vertices, triangles, N, begin, end, bbox0, bbox1): for triidx in range(begin, end): # Initialize bounds for this triangle for c in range(3): cidx = triidx + c N bbox0[cidx] = float('inf') bbox1[cidx] = float('-inf') # Process 3 vertices of the triangle for c in range(3): # Retrieve vertex index and pointer per evidence vertidx = triangles[triidx + c N] basevertidx = vertidx 3 # Update bounds for component c val = vertices[basevertidx + c] cidx = triidx + c N if val < bbox0[cidx]: bbox0[cidx] = val if val > bbox1[cidx]: bbox1[cidx] = val def computeboundparallel(vertices, triangles, N, bbox0, bbox1, ncores): nthreads = ncores threadsize = N // nthreads threads = [] # Create nthreads - 1 threads for t in range(nthreads - 1): startidx = t threadsize endidx = (t + 1) threadsize thread = threading.Thread( target=computeboundserial, args=(vertices, triangles, N, startidx, endidx, bbox0, bbox1)) threads.append(thread) thread.start() # Last thread processes the remainder laststart = (nthreads - 1) threadsize lastend = N thread = threading.Thread( target=computeboundserial, args=(vertices, triangles, N, laststart, lastend, bbox0, bbox1)) threads.append(thread) thread.start() for thread in threads: thread.join() Parameters: vertices: Array of floats. Layout is contiguous triples (x,y,z) per vertex. triangles: Array of integers. Indices into vertices. N: Integer, number of triangles. ncores: Integer, number of CPU threads. Default 4 in source implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If N < 1, UnionBoundHost returns immediately without processing, avoiding division by zero or invalid memory access in subsequent logic if called directly, though ComputeBoundHost does not explicitly check N < 1 before calling parallel/serial versions. ComputeBoundSerial loops triidx from begin to end, so if begin >= end, it does nothing, which safely handles the last thread in parallel execution when N is not evenly divisible by ncores. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of triangles. Each triangle is processed exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output arrays bbox0 and bbox1. Performance: Parallel execution scales with ncores. The source implementation uses a simple chunking strategy. No specific hardware benchmarks are provided in the sources. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and easy to parallelize. Provides per-triangle bounds necessary for efficient voxelization culling. Limitations: Does not compute a global mesh bound. Requires host-side memory allocation for output arrays. This method is part of the host-side preprocessing pipeline for GPU-based voxelization, specifically from the hpsoar/voxelizer project. It prepares the geometric data for the voxelizekernel which runs on the GPU device. The method is distinct from global bounding box computation, focusing on per-primitive bounds to enable efficient spatial partitioning during rasterization. hpsoar/voxelizer, https://github.com/hpsoar/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 2D Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) Intersection
head: Rect, Rect Intersection, Rectangle Overlap Test
body: This method determines whether two 2D axis-aligned rectangles overlap in space. It solves the problem of spatial culling and collision detection in 2D graphics by checking for separation along the X and Y axes. It is distinguished from its parent Ray-box intersection by operating on two static bounding volumes rather than a ray and a volume, and from Two-stage Accurate Intersection Test (TAIT) by using a simple overlap test rather than a two-stage approximation for projected Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two rectangles, R1 and R2, each defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. Output: A boolean value true if the rectangles overlap (including edge/touching cases), false otherwise. Data Structures: The rectangles are represented using integer coordinates. The layout is a struct containing two 2D integer vectors: min: A Vec2i representing the lower-left corner (min.x, min.y). max: A Vec2i representing the upper-right corner (max.x, max.y). Formulas: The width and height of a rectangle are inclusive: width = max.x - min.x + 1 height = max.y - min.y + 1 Algorithm: The intersection test checks for overlap along both axes independently. Two rectangles do not intersect if one is completely to the left, right, above, or below the other. The intersection is true if none of these separation conditions are met. Separation conditions: 1. R1 is to the left of R2: R1.max.x < R2.min.x 2. R1 is to the right of R2: R1.min.x > R2.max.x 3. R1 is below R2: R1.max.y < R2.min.y 4. R1 is above R2: R1.min.y > R2.max.y Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersects(r1, r2): """ Check if two 2D AABBs overlap. r1, r2: Objects with attributes min (Vec2i) and max (Vec2i). Returns: True if overlapping, False otherwise. """ return not (r1.max.x < r2.min.x or r1.max.y < r2.min.y or r1.min.x > r2.max.x or r1.min.y > r2.max.y) Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Touching Edges: If rectangles share an edge or corner (e.g., R1.max.x == R2.min.x), the test returns true (overlap) because the condition R1.max.x < R2.min.x is false. This is consistent with inclusive bounds. Degenerate Rectangles: If min == max (a point), the logic still holds. A point overlaps a rectangle if it lies within or on the boundary of the rectangle. Computes the distance along a ray direction from a given point to the nearest intersection with an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). It returns -1 if the starting point is inside the box or if the ray points away from the box. TAIT is a two-stage culling method used in 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization to accurately determine overlaps between projected Gaussians and rasterization tiles, reducing false positives from the standard Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) test which overestimates coverage. It builds on 2D Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) Intersection by introducing a tighter bounding box approximation in Stage 1 and a geometric line-distance check in Stage 2, balancing accuracy and computational cost. Determines whether two axis-aligned bounding boxes overlap in 3D space by checking independent overlap along the X, Y, and Z axes. Check overlap along X: min.x \le other.max.x \land max.x \ge other.min.x. Check overlap along Y: min.y \le other.max.y \land max.y \ge other.min.y. Check overlap along Z: min.z \le other.max.z \land max.z \ge other.min.z. Return true only if all three axes overlap. Formula: min.x \le other.max.x \land max.x \ge other.min.x \land min.y \le other.max.y \land max.y \ge other.min.y \land min.z \le other.max.z \land max.z \ge other.min.z. Time Complexity: O(1). The test involves a fixed number of comparisons (4 comparisons). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is allocated. Strengths: Extremely fast, branch-predictable, and simple to implement. Limitations: Only works for axis-aligned rectangles. Rotated rectangles require different methods (e.g., SAT with rotated axes). When to use: 2D collision detection, spatial partitioning culling, UI hit testing. When not to use: Rotated objects, non-axis-aligned volumes. The method is a fundamental primitive in computational geometry and computer graphics. name: AABB Ray Distance
head: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Intersection Distance
body: Computes the distance along a ray direction from a given point to the nearest intersection with an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). It returns -1 if the starting point is inside the box or if the ray points away from the box. Inputs: point: The starting position of the ray (3D vector). direction: The ray direction vector (3D vector). boundingboxmin: Minimum coordinates of the AABB (3D vector). boundingboxmax: Maximum coordinates of the AABB (3D vector). Outputs: dist: The distance to the nearest intersection. Returns -1 if no valid intersection exists (point inside or ray misses). Data Structures: Vectors are treated as 3-element arrays or tuples (x, y, z). Coordinates are in world space. Steps: 1. Normalize the ray direction vector \vec{d} to unit length. Let \vec{d} = (dx, dy, dz). 2. Initialize dist to -1. 3. Iterate over each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. Let v be the coordinate of point on axis i. b. Let d be the component of direction on axis i. c. Let mini and maxi be the minimum and maximum extents of the AABB on axis i. d. If dist is -1: If v < mini and d > 0: Set dist = (mini - v) / d. If v > maxi and d < 0: Set dist = (maxi - v) / d. e. Else (dist is not -1): If v < mini and d > 0: Set dist = \max(\text{dist}, (mini - v) / d). If v > maxi and d < 0: Set dist = \max(\text{dist}, (maxi - v) / d). 4. Return dist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbraydistance(point, direction, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax): # 1. Normalize direction length = sqrt(direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2) if length == 0: return -1 dx = direction[0] / length dy = direction[1] / length dz = direction[2] / length dist = -1 # Process X axis v = point[0] d = dx if dist == -1: if v < boundingboxmin[0] and d > 0: dist = (boundingboxmin[0] - v) / d if v > boundingboxmax[0] and d < 0: dist = (boundingboxmax[0] - v) / d else: if v < boundingboxmin[0] and d > 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmin[0] - v) / d) if v > boundingboxmax[0] and d < 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmax[0] - v) / d) # Process Y axis v = point[1] d = dy if dist == -1: if v < boundingboxmin[1] and d > 0: dist = (boundingboxmin[1] - v) / d if v > boundingboxmax[1] and d < 0: dist = (boundingboxmax[1] - v) / d else: if v < boundingboxmin[1] and d > 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmin[1] - v) / d) if v > boundingboxmax[1] and d < 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmax[1] - v) / d) # Process Z axis v = point[2] d = dz if dist == -1: if v < boundingboxmin[2] and d > 0: dist = (boundingboxmin[2] - v) / d if v > boundingboxmax[2] and d < 0: dist = (boundingboxmax[2] - v) / d else: if v < boundingboxmin[2] and d > 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmin[2] - v) / d) if v > boundingboxmax[2] and d < 0: dist = max(dist, (boundingboxmax[2] - v) / d) return dist Parameters: boundingboxmin/maxx/y/z: World coordinates defining the AABB extents. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm uses max (or fmaxf) to keep the largest positive distance when multiple axes yield intersections, effectively finding the entry point into the box. It returns -1 if the starting point is inside the box or if the ray points away from the box. Precision issues may arise if the ray direction is very close to zero on an axis; normalization handles this, but division by near-zero direction components should be guarded against in robust implementations. name: Analytical AABB Fog Feathering via Case Classification
head: Analytical AABB Fog Feathering, Case-Based Fog Integration
body: This method computes the optical density (fog amount) for a ray intersecting an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) with edge feathering, where fog density increases linearly from zero at the boundary to a constant value in the interior. It solves the problem of analytically integrating this variable density profile by classifying the ray's geometric relationship to the box into specific cases (miss, parallel pass, corner entry, etc.) and summing their contributions. It differs from standard ray-box intersection by returning a scalar fog value rather than just hit distances, and from ray marching by attempting to provide a closed-form solution, though it is noted to be complex due to numerous corner cases. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). AABB defined by min corner B{min} and max corner B{max}. Feather parameter f: the distance from the AABB boundary into the volume over which fog density ramps from 0 to 1. Outputs: Fog amount (optical density) F. Data Structures: The AABB is treated as a 3D box. The ray is parameterized as R(t) = O + tD. Steps: 1. Compute Ray-Box Intersection: Calculate the intersection of the ray with the AABB. This involves finding the entry and exit distances t{entry} and t{exit}. If the ray misses the box, compute the closest distance d{miss} from the ray to the box and the parameter t{closest} where this minimum occurs. 2. Classify Case: Use the intersection results (t{entry}, t{exit}) or the miss parameters (d{miss}, t{closest}) to determine which geometric case applies. The source identifies the following primary cases: Miss: Ray does not intersect the box. Parallel Pass: Ray runs parallel to the constant fog region, passing only through the non-constant (feathered) region. Corner Intersection: Ray passes through the non-constant density region at a corner of the bounding region. Partial Entry: Fragment is partially inside the non-constant fog. Full Entry: Ray goes completely from zero to constant fog density. Start Inside: Ray starts inside the non-constant region. 3. Compute Fog Contribution: Calculate the fog value F based on the classified case. The total fog is the sum of contributions from the relevant geometric segments. Formulas: The fog density \rho(t) is assumed to increase linearly from 0 to \rho{max} over the feather distance f. The optical density is the integral of \rho(t) along the ray path. Case: Full Entry (Zero to Constant): If the view ray goes completely from zero density to constant density, the integrated fog value is directly related to the constant fog value by a factor of 1/2. F = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \text{ConstantFogValue} This holds because the area under the linear ramp is half the area of the corresponding rectangle. The angle of incidence does not change this ratio, as the rate of change remains constant relative to the path length. Case: Partial Entry: If a fragment is partially inside the non-constant fog, the value is related by a ratio of the distance between the pixel and the edge of the constant region. For example, if the pixel is halfway through the non-constant fog, the value is 1/2 of 1/2, or 1/4 of the full constant fog value. F = \text{Ratio} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \text{ConstantFogValue} Where \text{Ratio} is the fraction of the feather distance traversed. Case: Parallel Pass (Camera Outside): If the camera is outside the fog and the view vector is parallel to the constant fog region, passing only through the non-constant fog, the non-constant fog is essentially constant but at a lowered density. This lowered density is related to the ratio of the distance from the constant density fog. The region has a changing section that increases until the lowered density, then remains constant until it saturates or exits through another changing region. Case: Corner Intersection (Zero Density Region): If the view ray passes through the non-constant density region at a corner of the bounding region and the fragment is in a zero density region, the fog calculation equals the constant density region value. The constant density is related to the distance of the constant bounding region from the view ray (line-to-box distance). It equals the constant calculation because it passes through an increasing section and a decreasing section of equal size. Thus, it is 2 \times 1/2 of the constant value, effectively equaling the constant value. Case: Miss: For misses, the method returns the distance of the ray from the box and a time T along the ray where the ray is closest to the box or intersects it. The fog value is derived from these parameters, likely involving the distance d{miss} relative to the feather distance f. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns fogamount. """ # 1. Assuming linear ramp logic similar to partial entry fogamount = ratio 0.5 # Placeholder for exact miss formula else: fogamount = 0.0 return fogamount # Hit case # Determine entry and exit points tentry = max(tmin, 0.0) texit = tmax # Calculate path length inside the box pathlength = texit - tentry # Classify case based on geometry relative to feather distance # Case: Full Entry (entire path is within feather zone or constant zone) # If the ray enters and exits within the feathered region or fully in constant # The source distinguishes "completely from zero to constant" # Check if ray stays entirely within the feathered boundary # This requires checking if the entry and exit points are within 'feather' distance of the surface # Simplified classification logic based on source description: # Case: Partial Entry (ray enters feather zone but doesn't reach constant, or exits before) # Or ray is partially inside non-constant fog # Ratio of distance between pixel and edge of constant region # Case: Parallel Pass # Ray parallel to constant fog, passing only through non-constant # Lowered density related to distance from constant density fog # Equals constant calculation distfromconstant = computelinetoboxdistance(rayorigin, raydir, aabbmin, aabbmax) # Related to distance of constant bounding region from view ray fogamount = computeconstantfogvalue(distfromconstant, feather) else: # General case: Full or Partial Entry # Calculate length of path in feathered region vs constant region lengthinfeather = computelengthinfeatherzone(rayorigin, raydir, aabbmin, aabbmax, feather) lengthinconstant = pathlength - lengthinfeather # Full entry contribution: 1/2 of constant value for the feather part # Partial entry: ratio based fogamount = (lengthinfeather 0.5) + (lengthinconstant 1.0) return fogamount def rayboxintersect(origin, dir, minb, maxb): # Standard implementation tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if dir[i] == 0: if origin[i] < minb[i] or origin[i] > maxb[i]: return None, None, False else: t1 = (minb[i] - origin[i]) / dir[i] t2 = (maxb[i] - origin[i]) / dir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None, False return tmin, tmax, True def raytoaabbdistance(origin, dir, minb, maxb): # Check if ray is parallel to the constant fog region # Constant fog region is the inner box shrunk by feather pass def iscornerintersection(origin, dir, minb, maxb, feather): # Check if ray passes through non-constant region at a corner pass def computelengthinfeatherzone(origin, dir, minb, maxb, feather): # Compute length of ray segment within the feathered boundary pass def computeconstantfogvalue(distfromconstant, feather): # Relate distance to constant fog value pass Parameters: feather: Represents how far the feathering should be applied inside the volume. Typical values depend on the scene scale, but must be positive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method involves numerous corner cases (parallel passes, corner intersections, starting inside, etc.), making it complex and error-prone. Precision issues may arise when the ray is nearly parallel to the box faces or when the feather distance is very small relative to the box size. The source notes that due to the high number of corner cases, switching to a ray-marched implementation is recommended as a more attractive solution. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables for intermediate calculations. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Does not scale with resolution or sample count, as it is a single evaluation per ray. Strengths: Provides an exact analytical solution without sampling noise. Limitations: Extremely complex to implement correctly due to the many corner cases. The source explicitly states that a ray-marched implementation is often more attractive. When to use: When a noise-free, analytical fog solution is required and the implementation complexity can be managed. When not to use: When performance is critical and the overhead of case classification is prohibitive, or when the volume shape is complex and ray marching is already in use. name: Optimized Ray-Box Distance for Parallel Projections
head: Distance Computation for Entry and Exit Points, Parallel Projection Ray-Box Distance
body: This method optimizes the calculation of the Euclidean distance between ray entry and exit points within an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for parallel projection volume rendering. It avoids the computationally expensive square root operation inherent in the standard distance formula by exploiting the geometric constraints of parallel rays and octree structures. It differs from general ray-box intersection methods by precomputing direction cosines and using case-specific arithmetic shortcuts based on the octree level. Inputs: Ray direction vector \vec{r} = (rx, ry, rz). Bounding box defined by minimum corner min = (minx, miny, minz) and maximum corner max = (maxx, maxy, maxz). Entry point a = (ax, ay, az) and exit point b = (bx, by, bz) on the box surface. Octree level i of the node (where i=0 is the root). d0: Intersection length of the ray with the entire dataset's bounding box (precomputed). Outputs: Distance d along the ray from a to b. Data Structures: Direction cosines: \cos \alpha, \cos \beta, \cos \gamma. These are derived from the normalized ray direction. Coordinates of entry a and exit b. Steps: 1. Compute Direction Cosines: Calculate the magnitude of the ray direction: |\vec{r}| = \sqrt{rx^2 + ry^2 + rz^2}. Compute cosines: \cos \alpha = \frac{rx}{|\vec{r}|}, \quad \cos \beta = \frac{ry}{|\vec{r}|}, \quad \cos \gamma = \frac{rz}{|\vec{r}|} Ensure |\vec{r}| is not zero to avoid division by zero. 2. Detect Intersection Case: Determine if the ray passes through opposite faces or adjacent faces sharing an edge. Case 1 (Opposite Faces): The entry point a has at least two coordinates equal to the corresponding coordinates of the box's minimum corner (min), AND the exit point b has at least two coordinates equal to the corresponding coordinates of the box's maximum corner (max). Case 2 (Adjacent Faces): The ray intersects two faces sharing a common edge. This is the default if Case 1 is false. 3. Calculate Distance: If Case 1: Use the octree level formula: d = \frac{d0}{i + 1} This relies on the property that intersection length is inversely proportional to the node level in a uniform octree. If Case 2: Determine which axis the shared edge is parallel to. The shared edge is parallel to the axis where the coordinate difference between a and b is zero (or negligible due to precision). If the edge is parallel to the X-axis (i.e., ay = by and az = bz): d = (bx - ax) \cos \alpha If the edge is parallel to the Y-axis (i.e., ax = bx and az = bz): d = (by - ay) \cos \beta If the edge is parallel to the Z-axis (i.e., ax = bx and ay = by): d = (bz - az) \cos \gamma Note: The source formulas (10-12) use the coordinate difference multiplied by the cosine of the angle with the respective axis. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedrayboxdistance(a, b, mincorner, maxcorner, i, d0, raydir): """ a: tuple (ax, ay, az) entry point b: tuple (bx, by, bz) exit point mincorner: tuple (minx, miny, minz) maxcorner: tuple (maxx, maxy, maxz) i: int, octree level d0: float, root box intersection length raydir: tuple (rx, ry, rz) """ # Step 1: Compute direction cosines mag = (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return 0.0 # Guard against zero-length ray cosalpha = raydir[0] / mag cosbeta = raydir[1] / mag cosgamma = raydir[2] / mag # Step 2: Detect Case 1 (Opposite Faces) # Check if a matches mincorner in at least 2 dimensions amatchmin = sum(1 for k in range(3) if abs(a[k] - mincorner[k]) < 1e-9) # Check if b matches maxcorner in at least 2 dimensions bmatchmax = sum(1 for k in range(3) if abs(b[k] - maxcorner[k]) < 1e-9) if amatchmin >= 2 and bmatchmax >= 2: # Case 1: Opposite faces return d0 / (i + 1) else: # Case 2: Adjacent faces sharing an edge # Determine which axis the edge is parallel to # The edge is parallel to the axis where the coordinate does not change # i.e., a[k] == b[k] # Check X-axis parallel (edge along X, so Y and Z are constant) if abs(a[1] - b[1]) < 1e-9 and abs(a[2] - b[2]) < 1e-9: return (b[0] - a[0]) cosalpha # Check Y-axis parallel (edge along Y, so X and Z are constant) elif abs(a[0] - b[0]) < 1e-9 and abs(a[2] - b[2]) < 1e-9: return (b[1] - a[1]) cosbeta # Check Z-axis parallel (edge along Z, so X and Y are constant) elif abs(a[0] - b[0]) < 1e-9 and abs(a[1] - b[1]) < 1e-9: return (b[2] - a[2]) cosgamma else: # Fallback or error: Should not happen for valid box intersections # Compute standard Euclidean distance as fallback return ((b[0]-a[0])2 + (b[1]-a[1])2 + (b[2]-a[2])2)0.5 Parameters: d0: Precomputed intersection length with the root bounding box. i: Octree level index, starting at 0 for the root. \cos \alpha, \cos \beta, \cos \gamma: Direction cosines of the parallel ray. Edge Cases: Zero Ray Length: If the ray direction is zero, the distance is undefined. A guard is required. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for coordinate equality (e.g., ay = by) should use a small epsilon tolerance to handle numerical inaccuracies. Degenerate Boxes: If the box has zero volume, the distance is zero. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray-box intersection. It replaces a square root and three subtractions/squarings with simple arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional storage for direction cosines. Strengths: Significantly faster than the standard Euclidean distance formula, which is critical for interactive rendering of large volume datasets. Limitations: Only applicable to parallel projections. Not valid for perspective projections where rays diverge. Requires precomputation of d0 and direction cosines. When to Use: Interactive volume rendering using parallel projection and octree-based spatial subdivision. When Not to Use: Perspective projection, non-octree structures, or when high precision is required for non-axis-aligned cases not covered by the two defined cases. This method was introduced in the context of an octree-based multiresolution approach for interactive rendering of very large volume data sets. It addresses the computational bottleneck of calculating ray-box intersection lengths during traversal of the octree structure. The approach leverages the uniformity of parallel rays and the hierarchical nature of the octree to simplify distance calculations. name: Two-stage Accurate Intersection Test (TAIT)
head: Coarse-to-fine intersection test
body: TAIT is a two-stage culling method used in 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization to accurately determine overlaps between projected Gaussians and rasterization tiles, reducing false positives from the standard Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) test which overestimates coverage. It builds on 2D Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) Intersection by introducing a tighter bounding box approximation in Stage 1 and a geometric line-distance check in Stage 2, balancing accuracy and computational cost. Inputs: Projected Gaussian center (cx, cy). Original opacity oi. Eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 of the 2D projection covariance matrix, with \lambda1 > \lambda2. Diagonal components \Sigma'X, \Sigma'Y of the projection covariance matrix in the x and y directions. Tile geometry (center coordinates, width, height). Outputs: Boolean flag indicating if the Gaussian intersects the tile. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values derived from the Gaussian's projection and tile geometry. Parameters: Opacity threshold \tau = 1/255. Tile circumcircle radius r. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Coarse Bounding Box Calculation Model the opacity falloff of the Gaussian as a function of distance d from its projected center: \alphai = oi e^{-d^2 / 2\lambda} Calculate the effective semi-major axis R{major} and semi-minor axis R{minor} lengths, defined as the distances at which opacity decays to \tau: R{major} = \sqrt{2 \lambda1 \ln(oi / \tau)} R{minor} = \sqrt{2 \lambda2 \ln(oi / \tau)} Calculate the width W and height H of the tight bounding box for the ellipse using R{major} and the covariance components: W = 2 R{major} \sqrt{\Sigma'X / \lambda1} H = 2 R{major} \sqrt{\Sigma'Y / \lambda2} Perform a standard AABB test using the bounding box defined by W and H centered at (cx, cy). If the tile does not intersect this box, discard the pair. 2. Stage 2: Fine Geometric Culling For tiles passing Stage 1, perform a finer check to eliminate false positives caused by the mismatch between the elliptical Gaussian shape and the rectangular bounding box. Define l as the vector connecting the center of the tile to the center of the ellipse. Define \theta as the angle between l and the semi-minor axis of the ellipse. Define r as the circumcircle radius of the tile. Classify the tile as non-intersecting if: |l| \cos \theta + r > R{minor} If the condition is not met, the Gaussian intersects the tile. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def taitintersection(cx, cy, oi, lambda1, lambda2, sigmax, sigmay, tx, ty, tw, th): """ Two-stage Accurate Intersection Test. cx, cy: float, Gaussian center oi: float, original opacity lambda1, lambda2: float, eigenvalues (lambda1 > lambda2) sigmax, sigmay: float, diagonal covariance components tx, ty: float, tile center tw, th: float, tile width and height (full extents) Returns: True if intersecting, False otherwise. """ tau = 1.0 / 255.0 # Stage 1: Effective axes and tight bounding box rmajor = math.sqrt(2 lambda1 math.log(oi / tau)) rminor = math.sqrt(2 lambda2 math.log(oi / tau)) w = 2 rmajor math.sqrt(sigmax / lambda1) h = 2 rmajor math.sqrt(sigmay / lambda2) # AABB check against tight bounding box if cx + w / 2 < tx - tw / 2 or cx - w / 2 > tx + tw / 2: return False if cy + h / 2 < ty - th / 2 or cy - h / 2 > ty + th / 2: return False # Stage 2: Fine geometric culling # Vector from tile center to Gaussian center dx = cx - tx dy = cy - ty ldist = math.sqrt(dx dx + dy dy) # Compute unit vector of semi-minor axis # For 2x2 symmetric covariance C = [[cxx, cxy], [cxy, cyy]], # eigenvector for lambda2 is [lambda2 - cyy, cxy]. # Assuming axis-aligned covariance (cxy = 0) based on provided inputs. if lambda2 > sigmay: ux, uy = 1.0, 0.0 else: ux, uy = 0.0, 1.0 # cos(theta) between center vector and minor axis if ldist == 0: costheta = 1.0 else: costheta = (dx ux + dy uy) / ldist # Tile circumcircle radius r = 0.5 math.sqrt(tw tw + th th) # Non-intersection condition if ldist abs(costheta) + r > rminor: return False return True A variant that retains substantially fewer Gaussian-tile pairs than GSCore’s OOBB bounding box and introduces negligible redundancy compared to FlashGS while significantly reducing computational cost. It uses the same Stage 1 bounding box calculation but defines Stage 2 culling using the line l connecting the tile center to the ellipse center projected onto the short axis, classifying non-intersection if |l| \cos \theta + r > R{minor}. Time Complexity: Minimal computational cost per test, involving square roots, logarithms, and a single distance comparison. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per test. Performance: Achieves optimal speedup across various scenes by reducing false positives compared to standard AABB and GSCore’s OOBB, while avoiding the high cost of complex geometric operations used in FlashGS. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of Gaussian-tile pairs processed in later stages, mitigating kernel idle caused by load imbalance. Limitations: Requires calculation of eigenvalues and covariance components, adding overhead compared to simple AABB. TAIT was proposed to address the inefficiencies of standard AABB tests in 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, which overestimate coverage and cause excessive tile assignments. It was introduced in the paper "No Redundancy, No Stall: Lightweight Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-time Rendering".
