name: AABB Representation (Min/Max)
head: AABB Data Structure, Axis-Aligned Bounding Box data structure, Min/Max corners, Slab representation
body: The Min/Max AABB representation defines an axis-aligned bounding box by explicitly storing the minimum and maximum coordinate values along each of the three spatial axes. It treats the box as the intersection of three orthogonal "slabs" (infinite regions bounded by parallel planes). This representation is preferred over point-plus-dimensions (centroid + size) because merging two boxes is a trivial component-wise min/max operation, whereas the latter requires extra arithmetic. Data Structures: The representation occupies 6 floating-point values. Two common layouts are cited: 1. Array-based (Slab) Layout: Three arrays of two floats each. xminmax[2]: xmin at index 0, xmax at index 1. yminmax[2]: ymin at index 0, ymax at index 1. zminmax[2]: zmin at index 0, zmax at index 1. Total size: 6 floats. 2. Vector-based Layout: Two 3D vectors. lb (lower bound): (xmin, ymin, zmin). ub (upper bound): (xmax, ymax, zmax). Total size: 6 floats. Constructors: Common initialization methods include default initialization, construction from coordinates (lbx, lby, lbz, ubx, uby, ubz), construction from Eigen vectors, construction from a sphere (pos, radius), construction from a triangle (v1, v2, v3), and merging two AABBs. Merging Logic: To compute the bounding box enclosing two AABBs (b0 and b1), the new bounds are calculated component-wise: \begin{aligned} x{min} &= \min(b0.x{min}, b1.x{min}) \\ x{max} &= \max(b0.x{max}, b1.x{max}) \\ y{min} &= \min(b0.y{min}, b1.y{min}) \\ y{max} &= \max(b0.y{max}, b1.y{max}) \\ z{min} &= \min(b0.z{min}, b1.z{min}) \\ z{max} &= \max(b0.z{max}, b1.z{max}) \end{aligned} This is significantly simpler than the point-plus-dimensions representation, which requires recalculating the centroid and dimensions from the combined extents. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class AABB: def init(self, lb=None, ub=None): # Default constructor initializes to empty/infinite bounds or requires explicit assignment. if lb is None or ub is None: self.lb = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.ub = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: self.lb = list(lb) self.ub = list(ub) @classmethod def fromcoords(cls, lbx, lby, lbz, ubx, uby, ubz): return cls(lb=[lbx, lby, lbz], ub=[ubx, uby, ubz]) @classmethod def fromsphere(cls, center, radius): # Sphere bounding box: min = center - radius, max = center + radius return cls( lb=[center[0] - radius, center[1] - radius, center[2] - radius], ub=[center[0] + radius, center[1] + radius, center[2] + radius]) @classmethod def fromtriangle(cls, v1, v2, v3): # Triangle bounding box: component-wise min/max across vertices xvals = [v1[0], v2[0], v3[0]] yvals = [v1[1], v2[1], v3[1]] zvals = [v1[2], v2[2], v3[2]] return cls( lb=[min(xvals), min(yvals), min(zvals)], ub=[max(xvals), max(yvals), max(zvals)]) @classmethod def merge(cls, a, b): # Computes the bounding box enclosing both AABB 'a' and 'b' lb = [ min(a.lb[0], b.lb[0]), min(a.lb[1], b.lb[1]), min(a.lb[2], b.lb[2]) ] ub = [ max(a.ub[0], b.ub[0]), max(a.ub[1], b.ub[1]), max(a.ub[2], b.ub[2]) ] return cls(lb=lb, ub=ub) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Boxes: If min > max for any axis, the box is invalid. Merging logic must handle empty or invalid boxes explicitly to prevent propagation of invalid bounds. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for containment or intersection should account for epsilon errors if exact boundaries are critical. Axis Alignment: The representation assumes the box is axis-aligned. If the box is rotated, this representation is invalid; an OBB (Oriented Bounding Box) representation is required instead. Memory: Fixed size of 6 floats (24 bytes on standard 32-bit float systems). Time Complexity: Merging two AABBs is O(1). Strengths: Trivial to merge, simple to implement, and directly compatible with slab-based ray-box intersection algorithms. Limitations: Does not support rotation. For rotated objects, the AABB must be recomputed or an OBB used. The Min/Max representation is a standard data structure in computer graphics, particularly in ray tracing and spatial acceleration structures. It is explicitly used in Peter Shirley's raytracing series. It serves as the foundational primitive for the Ray-box intersection method, where the box is treated as the intersection of three slabs. name: Ray-AABB Intersection (Slab/Min-Max)
head: BuildChunkSegments, Min-Max Method, Multi-Chunk Ray-Box Intersection and Segment Building, Ray-Box Intersection for Volume Traversal, Slab Method, Slab Method for Ray-AABB Intersection, Slab Test, Slab/Min-Max
body: The Slab/Min-Max method computes the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of a ray with an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) by evaluating the ray against the box's six defining planes (slabs). It solves the problem of efficiently culling rays that miss a volume primitive or defining the valid traversal range for ray marching. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz). Ray direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). AABB defined by minimum corner \mathbf{b}{min} = (b{min,x}, b{min,y}, b{min,z}) and maximum corner \mathbf{b}{max} = (b{max,x}, b{max,y}, b{max,z}). Outputs: Boolean hit status. Intersection interval [t{near}, t{far}]. Intersection point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t{near}\mathbf{d}. Data Structures: Vectors are 3-component floating-point arrays. The AABB is stored as two 3D points representing the min and max corners. Steps: 1. Compute Inverse Direction: Calculate \mathbf{d}{inv} = 1.0 / \mathbf{d}. Handle zero direction components by checking against a tolerance \epsilon and using a large constant or skipping the axis constraint. 2. Compute Slab Intersections: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}, calculate the parameter t where the ray intersects the min and max planes: t{min,i} = (b{min,i} - oi) \cdot d{inv,i} t{max,i} = (b{max,i} - oi) \cdot d{inv,i} 3. Determine Local Interval: For each axis, the ray is inside the slab between the smaller and larger of the two computed t values: t{1,i} = \min(t{min,i}, t{max,i}) t{2,i} = \max(t{min,i}, t{max,i}) 4. Compute Global Interval: The ray is inside the box only when it is inside all slabs simultaneously. The entry distance t{near} is the maximum of the local entry distances, and the exit distance t{far} is the minimum of the local exit distances: t{near} = \max(t{1,x}, t{1,y}, t{1,z}) t{far} = \min(t{2,x}, t{2,y}, t{2,z}) 5. Check Intersection: An intersection exists if the interval is valid and in front of the ray origin: t{near} \le t{far} \quad \text{and} \quad t{near} \ge 0 6. Calculate Intersection Point: If an intersection exists, the entry point is: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t{near} \mathbf{d} Parameters: voxelsize: The size of the voxels (AABBs) if the box is derived from a voxel grid. epsilon: Floating-point tolerance used for approximate equality checks and boundary margin validation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Component: If di = 0, division produces infinity or NaN. If the ray origin is outside the slab (oi < b{min,i} or oi > b{max,i}), the ray misses. If the origin is inside, the ray is parallel to the slab and effectively ignores the constraint. NaN Propagation: NaNs from zero-direction divisions can propagate through min/max operations, causing false negatives. Branchless variants use sign masks to select bounds and suppress NaN propagation. Grazing Rays: Rays parallel to a face or lying exactly on a boundary may miss due to precision issues. Watertight fixes treat BVH boxes as closed sets to guarantee consistent intersection decisions for axis-parallel rays on face planes. Hollow Objects: When ray marching inside hollow objects, the gradient at the start of the ray may be zero if the ray starts "inside the material" because gradient calculation uses data before the ray start. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayaabbslabintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax, epsilon=1e-10): """ Computes the intersection of a ray with an AABB using the slab method. Args: rayorigin: tuple (ox, oy, oz) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) boxmin: tuple (bminx, bminy, bminz) boxmax: tuple (bmaxx, bmaxy, bmaxz) epsilon: tolerance for zero direction check Returns: tuple (hit: bool, tnear: float, tfar: float, point: tuple or None) """ ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydirection bminx, bminy, bminz = boxmin bmaxx, bmaxy, bmaxz = boxmax # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero # Sources use infinity or a large constant (BigNumber) for near-zero directions invdx = 1.0 / dx if abs(dx) > epsilon else float('inf') invdy = 1.0 / dy if abs(dy) > epsilon else float('inf') invdz = 1.0 / dz if abs(dz) > epsilon else float('inf') # Compute t values for min and max planes along each axis tminx = (bminx - ox) invdx tmaxx = (bmaxx - ox) invdx tminy = (bminy - oy) invdy tmaxy = (bmaxy - oy) invdy tminz = (bminz - oz) invdz tmaxz = (bmaxz - oz) invdz # Determine local min and max intervals for each axis t1x = min(tminx, tmaxx) t2x = max(tminx, tmaxx) t1y = min(tminy, tmaxy) t2y = max(tminy, tmaxy) t1z = min(tminz, tmaxz) t2z = max(tminz, tmaxz) # Compute global near and far intersection distances tnear = max(t1x, t1y, t1z) tfar = min(t2x, t2y, t2z) # Check for valid intersection if tnear <= tfar and tnear >= 0: hit = True px = ox + tnear dx py = oy + tnear dy pz = oz + tnear dz point = (px, py, pz) else: hit = False tnear = float('inf') tfar = float('-inf') point = None return hit, tnear, tfar, point This method computes the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of camera rays with a scene bounding box (AABB), clamps these intervals to near/far clipping planes, and generates a set of query points along each ray for volume rendering. It solves the problem of determining valid spatial extents for ray marching and preparing structured sample coordinates (including ray IDs and step indices) for downstream neural radiance field evaluation. It differs from its sibling Ray-Cube Intersection by supporting arbitrary axis-aligned bounding boxes rather than just cubes, and from Branchless Ray/AABB Intersection with NaN Handling by explicitly handling the generation of sample points and metadata (ray/step IDs) rather than just returning boolean intersection results. This method computes the intersection of a ray with an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a branchless algorithm that correctly handles IEEE 754 floating-point edge cases, specifically NaNs generated when a ray direction component is zero. It builds on Ray-AABB Intersection (Slab/Min-Max) by replacing conditional checks for zero direction with precomputed inverse directions and nested min/max operations that suppress NaN propagation. Unlike the standard branchless slab method, this variant guarantees robustness for degenerate cases where the ray origin lies exactly on a box boundary or the ray is parallel to an axis, preventing false positives caused by NaN propagation. The Ray-OBB Intersection Test determines if a ray intersects an Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) and computes the distance to the nearest intersection point. It extends the slab method by projecting the ray onto the OBB's local axes to compute intersection intervals (slabs) along each axis. Unlike Ray-box intersection which assumes axis alignment, this method handles arbitrary orientations by testing intersection with pairs of parallel planes perpendicular to the OBB's local axes. AABB Intersection via Face Traversal is a method to determine the entry (front) and exit (back) points of a ray intersecting an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) by explicitly testing the ray against each of the six faces of the box. Unlike the standard slab method which computes intersection intervals along axes, this approach decomposes the AABB into six planar faces and performs individual ray-face intersection tests. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit geometric decomposition into faces and triangles, making it computationally more expensive than the slab method. Determines if a line segment defined by endpoints a and b intersects an axis-aligned box defined by lower corner lo and upper corner hi, considering a spherical radius r around the segment. It sets itself apart from standard ray-box intersection by treating the segment as a capsule (cylinder with hemispherical caps) rather than an infinitely thin line, allowing for collision detection with thickness. This method fixes a robustness bug in shared slab tests where a ray with a zero direction component lying exactly in the plane of a box face misses the box on one side. It ensures that grazing rays, such as orthographic camera rays landing exactly on a bound, correctly intersect triangles whose edges they touch, by treating BVH boxes as closed sets. Unlike standard slab tests which may compute an empty slab for t > 0 due to zero-inversion artifacts, this fix guarantees consistent intersection decisions for axis-parallel rays on face planes. This family implements the standard algorithm for determining the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] between a ray and an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) by computing intersections with the box's six defining planes (slabs). It solves the fundamental problem of efficiently culling rays that miss a volume primitive or determining the precise entry and exit distances for ray marching. It is distinguished from Ray-Cube Intersection by returning scalar t-intervals rather than 3D coordinates and face indices, and from AABB Intersection via Face Traversal by computing the full interval upfront rather than stepping through voxels. A bounding box is used to determine ray entry and exit from the volumetric dataset, accelerating calculation by skipping rays that miss the volume and enabling 'cutting' the volume to look inside. When looking inside a hollow object (like the Stanford Bunny), the gradient at the start of the ray may be 0 if the ray starts 'inside the material' because gradient calculation uses data before the ray start. A bounding volume defined as the intersection of slabs, where slabs are formed by the intersection of two half-spaces extending in opposite directions. Utilizing slabs significantly speeds up the evaluation of the signed distance function he by dividing the number of scalar products by two. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Ray-Bounding Box Intersection and Sampling Preparation
head: Ray Sampling with AABB Clipping and Cyclic Wrapping, Ray-Bounding Box Intersection and Sampling
body: This method computes the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of camera rays with a scene bounding box (AABB), clamps these intervals to near/far clipping planes, and generates a set of query points along each ray for volume rendering. It solves the problem of determining valid spatial extents for ray marching and preparing structured sample coordinates (including ray IDs and step indices) for downstream neural radiance field evaluation. It differs from its sibling Ray-Cube Intersection by supporting arbitrary axis-aligned bounding boxes rather than just cubes, and from Branchless Ray/AABB Intersection with NaN Handling by explicitly handling the generation of sample points and metadata (ray/step IDs) rather than just returning boolean intersection results. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (N, 3), float32. raysd: Ray directions, shape (N, 3), float32. xyzmin: Bounding box minimum corner, shape (3), float32. xyzmax: Bounding box maximum corner, shape (3), float32. near: Near clipping plane distance, float32 scalar. far: Far clipping plane distance, float32 scalar. stepsize: Number of voxels per sample step, float32 scalar. voxelsize: Physical size of a single voxel, float32 scalar. Outputs: rayspts: Sampled query points, shape (total\len, 3), float32. maskoutbbox: Boolean mask for points outside the bounding box, shape (total\len). rayid: Ray index for each point, shape (total\len), int32. stepid: Step index within each ray, shape (total\len), int32. Nsteps: Number of samples per ray, shape (N), int32. tmin: Clamped entry distance per ray, shape (N), float32. tmax: Clamped exit distance per ray, shape (N), float32. Data Structures: Tensors are typically contiguous in memory. rayso and raysd are reshaped to (-1, 3) if necessary. rayid is constructed via cumulative sum of a marker array to assign ray indices to the flattened point list. Parameters: stepsize: Number of voxels per sample step. near: Near clipping plane distance. far: Far clipping plane distance. Typically set to 10^9 to prevent rays from stopping early when hitting the scene bounding box. voxelsize: Physical size of a single voxel. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Ensure rayso and raysd are contiguous and reshaped to (-1, 3). Replace any zero components in raysd with 10^{-6} to prevent division by zero during intersection calculation. Let the modified direction be vec. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute intermediate rates for each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}: axi = \frac{xyz{max}[i] - rayso[i]}{vec[i]} bxi = \frac{xyz{min}[i] - rayso[i]}{vec[i]} Compute unclamped t{min} and t{max} for each ray: t{min}^{raw} = \max(\min(ax0, bx0), \min(ax1, bx1), \min(ax2, bx2)) t{max}^{raw} = \min(\max(ax0, bx0), \max(ax1, bx1), \max(ax2, bx2)) Clamp to near/far planes: t{min} = \max(\min(t{min}^{raw}, far), near) t{max} = \max(\min(t{max}^{raw}, far), near) 3. Sample Count Calculation: Compute step distance: stepdist = stepsize \times voxel\size. Compute ray direction norm: r{norm} = \sqrt{raysd[0]^2 + raysd[1]^2 + raysd[2]^2}. Calculate number of samples per ray: n{samples} = \max\left(\left\lceil \frac{(t{max} - t{min}) \times r{norm}}{stepdist} \right\rceil, 1\right) Store n{samples} as N{steps}. 4. Point Generation: Compute total number of points: total\len = \sum N{steps}. Compute ray start position: rays{start} = rayso + raysd \times t{min}. Compute normalized direction: rays{dir} = raysd / r{norm}. Generate base step distances: distk = stepdist \times k for k = 0, \dots, n{samples}-1. Compute query points: p = rays{start} + rays{dir} \times distk 5. Masking and Metadata: Compute maskoutbbox: True if any coordinate of p is outside [xyz{min}, xyz{max}]. Construct rayid: Initialize array of zeros length total\len. Set rayid[Nstepscumsum[i-1]] = 1 for i > 0. Perform cumulative sum. Construct stepid: For index idx, let rid = rayid[idx]. Then step\id[idx] = idx - (N{steps\cumsum}[rid-1] \text{ if } rid \neq 0 \text{ else } 0). Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs if a ray direction component is exactly zero; clamping to 10^{-6} prevents this. Points may fall outside the bounding box due to discretization or floating-point inaccuracies; they must be explicitly masked out using maskoutbbox. Rays with t{min} \ge t{max} after clamping yield zero or negative sample counts; the \max(\dots, 1) ensures at least one sample per ray to simplify downstream indexing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def raybboxintersectionandsampling( rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax, near, far, stepsize, voxelsize): # Convert inputs to tensors if necessary rayso = torch.astensor(rayso, dtype=torch.float32) raysd = torch.astensor(raysd, dtype=torch.float32) xyzmin = torch.astensor(xyzmin, dtype=torch.float32) xyzmax = torch.astensor(xyzmax, dtype=torch.float32) N = rayso.shape[0] rayso = rayso.contiguous().reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.contiguous().reshape(-1, 3) # Replace zero direction components with 1e-6 to avoid division by zero vec = torch.where(raysd == 0, torch.fulllike(raysd, 1e-6), raysd) # Compute intersection rates ax = (xyzmax.unsqueeze(0) - rayso) / vec.unsqueeze(0) bx = (xyzmin.unsqueeze(0) - rayso) / vec.unsqueeze(0) # Standard slab method for tmin and tmax tminraw = torch.max(torch.min(ax, bx), dim=1).values tmaxraw = torch.min(torch.max(ax, bx), dim=1).values # Clamp to near/far planes tmin = torch.clamp(tminraw, min=near, max=far) tmax = torch.clamp(tmaxraw, min=near, max=far) # Compute ray direction norm and step distance rnorm = torch.norm(raysd, dim=1, keepdim=True) stepdist = stepsize voxelsize # Calculate number of samples per ray, ensuring at least 1 nsamplesfloat = (tmax - tmin) rnorm / stepdist Nsteps = torch.clamp(torch.ceil(nsamplesfloat).long(), min=1) totallen = int(Nsteps.sum().item()) if totallen == 0: return { 'rayspts': torch.empty(0, 3), 'maskoutbbox': torch.empty(0, dtype=torch.bool), 'rayid': torch.empty(0, dtype=torch.long), 'stepid': torch.empty(0, dtype=torch.long), 'Nsteps': Nsteps, 'tmin': tmin, 'tmax': tmax } # Compute ray start position and normalized direction raysstart = rayso + raysd tmin.unsqueeze(1) raysdir = raysd / rnorm # Generate step indices and distances maxsteps = int(Nsteps.max().item()) steps = torch.arange(maxsteps, device=rayso.device) validmask = steps.unsqueeze(0) < Nsteps.unsqueeze(1) dists = steps.float() stepdist # Compute query points raysstartexp = raysstart.unsqueeze(1) raysdirexp = raysdir.unsqueeze(1) distsexp = dists.unsqueeze(2) raysptsunmasked = raysstartexp + raysdirexp distsexp rayspts = raysptsunmasked[validmask] # Compute maskoutbbox maskx = (rayspts[:, 0] < xyzmin[0]) | (rayspts[:, 0] > xyzmax[0]) masky = (rayspts[:, 1] < xyzmin[1]) | (rayspts[:, 1] > xyzmax[1]) maskz = (rayspts[:, 2] < xyzmin[2]) | (rayspts[:, 2] > xyzmax[2]) maskoutbbox = maskx | masky | maskz # Construct rayid Nstepscumsum = torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.long, device=Nsteps.device), Nsteps.cumsum(0)[:-1]]) rayid = torch.zeros(totallen, dtype=torch.long, device=Nsteps.device) rayid[Nstepscumsum[1:]] = 1 rayid = rayid.cumsum(0) # Construct stepid stepid = torch.arange(totallen, dtype=torch.long, device=Nsteps.device) offsets = Nstepscumsum[rayid] stepid = stepid - offsets return { 'rayspts': rayspts, 'maskoutbbox': maskoutbbox, 'rayid': rayid, 'stepid': stepid, 'Nsteps': Nsteps, 'tmin': tmin, 'tmax': tmax } Computes the bounding box in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space from a set of rays by calculating the minimum and maximum of ray origins and endpoints, then stacking them. This is used when rendering in NDC space to define the volume extent for sampling. Performance: Efficiently implemented in CUDA for batched processing, often splitting rays into batches (e.g., 10,000) to manage memory. Strengths: Handles arbitrary bounding boxes and provides structured metadata (ray/step IDs) for efficient downstream processing. Limitations: Requires careful handling of zero-direction components to avoid division by zero. The fixed step size may lead to over-sampling in sparse regions or under-sampling in dense regions if not combined with importance sampling. When to use: When rendering neural radiance fields with a defined bounding box. This method is commonly used in neural radiance field (NeRF) implementations, particularly those dealing with unbounded scenes or specific bounding box constraints. It builds on the standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection [Parent] and extends it to prepare samples for volume rendering. sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, https://github.com/sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, https://github.com/sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, https://github.com/Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) https://github.com/ZhenyangLiu/Collaborative-Neural-Radiance-Fields-for-Novel-View-Synthesis, https://github.com/ZhenyangLiu/Collaborative-Neural-Radiance-Fields-for-Novel-View-Synthesis, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

body: Ray Point Sampling generates query points along camera rays for volume rendering by distributing samples within a defined spatial region, typically the scene's bounding box. It solves the problem of discretizing continuous ray paths into discrete evaluation locations for neural radiance fields or voxel grids. Unlike Background Point Sampling which targets infinite space outside the scene, or Uncertainty-guided Point Sampling which targets high-error regions, this method provides a baseline uniform or importance-weighted distribution within the foreground volume. It builds on Ray-Bounding Box Intersection and Sampling Preparation which computes the intersection bounds and step distances. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, contiguous. raysd: Ray directions, contiguous. xyzmin: Bounding box minimum, shape (3). xyzmax: Bounding box maximum, shape (3). near: Near clipping distance, scalar. far: Far clipping distance, scalar. Set to 10^9. stepsize: Base step size, scalar. voxelsize: Voxel grid resolution size, scalar. isunbounded: Boolean flag indicating if the scene is unbounded (e.g., DTU dataset). Outputs: raypts: Sample points, shape (N{total}, 3). rayid: Ray indices for each point, shape (N{total}). stepid: Step indices for each point, shape (N{total}). Data Structures: Points are stored in a flat array raypts with fields x, y, z (float32). rayid and stepid are integer arrays mapping each point to its source ray and sequential step index. Parameters: stepdist = stepsize voxelsize. Uniform samples per ray: 64. Importance samples per ray: 32. Unbounded extra samples: 32. Maximum batch size: 512 \times 64 \times 32 points. Steps: 1. Ensure rayso and raysd are contiguous in memory. 2. Calculate the effective step distance: stepdist = stepsize \times voxel\size 3. Sample points along rays using a kernel that distributes points at intervals of stepdist from near to far, returning raypts, maskoutbbox, rayid, stepid, Nsteps, tmin, and tmax. 4. Filter points inside the bounding box: mask\inbbox = \neg mask\outbbox 5. Apply maskinbbox to raypts, rayid, and stepid to discard out-of-bounds points. 6. Return the filtered raypts, rayid, and stepid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raypointsampling(rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax, near, far, stepsize, voxelsize, isunbounded): # Ensure contiguous memory layout rayso = [list(o) for o in rayso] raysd = [list(d) for d in raysd] # Calculate effective step distance stepdist = stepsize voxelsize # Sample points along rays at stepdist intervals from near to far # (Standard uniform ray sampling logic replaces the CUDA kernel call) raypts, rayid, stepid = [], [], [] for i, (o, d) in enumerate(zip(rayso, raysd)): t = near step = 0 while t <= far: pt = [o[j] + t d[j] for j in range(3)] raypts.append(pt) rayid.append(i) stepid.append(step) t += stepdist step += 1 # Filter points inside bounding box maskoutbbox = [any(pt[j] < xyzmin[j] or pt[j] > xyzmax[j] for j in range(3)) for pt in raypts] maskinbbox = [not m for m in maskoutbbox] # Apply mask raypts = [pt for pt, m in zip(raypts, maskinbbox) if m] rayid = [rid for rid, m in zip(rayid, maskinbbox) if m] stepid = [sid for sid, m in zip(stepid, maskinbbox) if m] return raypts, rayid, stepid Edge Cases: If the scene is unbounded (e.g., DTU), 32 additional points are sampled in contracted space. Filters out rays that do not intersect known free space. Adjusts near- and far-bounds (t{near}, t{far}) to the endpoints of the ray-box intersection. Does not adjust t{near} if the ray origin x0 is already inside the BBox. Retrieves samples lying on an edge defined by two vertices by filtering samples based on their distance from the ray origin. Calculates distances from vertices v1, v2 to ray origin. Iterates through samples, adding those where dist(v1, R.origin) \le dist(s.position, R.origin) \le dist(v2, R.origin). Generates uniformly distributed random points within a specified 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defined by minimum and maximum bounds. It solves the problem of initializing ray origins or query points for volume rendering and neural field training by ensuring spatial coverage without bias. Unlike Background Point Sampling which targets empty space, or Uncertainty-guided Point Sampling which targets high-error regions, this method provides a baseline uniform distribution. Background Point Sampling generates sample points along rays for background regions, defined as the space outside the scene's bounding box. It employs a specific non-uniform sampling distribution controlled by a bgpreserve parameter to balance between uniform angular sampling and uniform radial sampling. This method is distinct from sibling methods like Random Point Sampling in Bounds, which typically samples uniformly within a defined volume, by specifically targeting the infinite or large-distance background region with a distribution that adapts based on the ray's geometry relative to the bounding box. Uncertainty-guided point sampling selects 2D coordinates within bounding boxes by prioritizing regions of high prediction uncertainty. It oversamples points randomly, selects a fraction via an uncertainty function, and fills the remainder with random points. Maximum batch size is 512 \times 64 \times 32 points. Strengths: Simple, uniform coverage of the foreground volume. Limitations: May waste samples in empty space if not combined with free-space skipping. body: Generates uniformly distributed random points within a specified 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defined by minimum and maximum bounds. It solves the problem of initializing ray origins or query points for volume rendering and neural field training by ensuring spatial coverage without bias. Unlike Background Point Sampling which targets empty space, or Uncertainty-guided Point Sampling which targets high-error regions, this method provides a baseline uniform distribution. Inputs: numpoints: Integer, the number of random points to generate. bounds: A tuple or list containing two arrays/tensors: minbounds (shape [3] or [batch, 3]) and maxbounds (shape [3] or [batch, 3]). device: The computational device (e.g., 'cpu', 'cuda'). Data Structures: minbounds: torch.Tensor, stores the minimum coordinates of the bounding box. maxbounds: torch.Tensor, stores the maximum coordinates of the bounding box. numberofsamples: int, stores the count of points to generate. Steps: 1. Initialization: Store numpoints in numberofsamples. Convert minbounds and maxbounds to tensors on the specified device. If the inputs are not batched, add a batch dimension (unsqueeze) to ensure consistent tensor shapes for vectorized operations. 2. Uniform Generation: Generate numpoints random points in the unit cube [0, 1]^3 by sampling three independent uniform random values for each point. u \sim \mathcal{U}([0, 1])^3 3. Scaling and Shifting: Transform the unit cube samples to the target bounding box. Let w = \text{max\bounds} - \text{min\bounds} be the width vector. The final point p is calculated as: p = u \cdot w + \text{min\bounds} This linear mapping preserves uniformity. Alternative Voxel-Centric Formulation: Some implementations define the bounds relative to a voxel center c and size vector s. In this case, random values r are sampled from \mathcal{U}(-1, 1)^3, scaled by s, and added to c: p = c + r \cdot s where c is the voxel center, s is the voxel size vector, and r \sim \mathcal{U}(-1, 1)^3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def samplerandompointsinbounds(numpoints, minbounds, maxbounds, device='cpu'): """ Generates uniformly distributed random points within a 3D bounding box. Args: numpoints (int): Number of points to generate. minbounds (tensor-like): Minimum bounds of the box, shape (3,) or (batch, 3). maxbounds (tensor-like): Maximum bounds of the box, shape (3,) or (batch, 3). device (str): Target device for tensors. Returns: torch.Tensor: Sampled points of shape (numpoints, 3). """ # Convert inputs to tensors and ensure they are on the correct device minb = torch.astensor(minbounds, device=device).float() maxb = torch.astensor(maxbounds, device=device).float() # Add batch dimension if not present to handle vectorized operations uniformly if minb.dim() == 1: minb = minb.unsqueeze(0) maxb = maxb.unsqueeze(0) # Generate uniform random numbers in 0, 1) # Shape: (numpoints, 3) u = torch.rand((numpoints, 3), device=device) # Calculate box dimensions width = maxb - minb # Scale and shift to the bounding box p = u width + minb return p Parameters: numpoints: Typical values range from thousands to millions depending on training batch sizes. bounds: Defined by the scene or voxel grid geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Cubic Voxels: If the sampling domain is conceptualized as a voxel, scaling a uniform distribution over (-1,1)^3 correctly covers the volume, but the density per unit world-space volume remains uniform. However, if spherical sampling is expected within a non-cubic voxel, this method produces non-uniform density relative to the sphere. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for large bounding boxes may introduce precision errors in the least significant bits of the coordinates. Empty Bounds: If minbounds equals maxbounds, the width is zero, resulting in all points collapsing to the single boundary point. A set of specialized sampling strategies for generating position-direction (p, v) tuples for [Directed Distance Fields (DDFs) within a bounding box B. Uniform (U): Samples p \sim \mathcal{U}[B] and v \sim \mathcal{U}[S^2]. At-surface (A): Samples a surface point q0 \sim \mathcal{U}[S] (areaweighted) and direction v0 \sim \mathcal{U}[S^2]. Samples p on the line segment between q0 and its intersection with B along v0. Sets v = -v0. Bounding (B): Samples p \sim \mathcal{U}[\partial B] (boundary) and v \sim \mathcal{U}[S^2], restricted to point into the interior of B. Surface (S): Samples p \sim \mathcal{U}[S] and v \sim \mathcal{U}[S^2]. Tangent (T): Same as A-type, but enforces v0 to lie in the tangent plane T{q0}(S). Offset (O): Takes a T-type (p, v) and updates p \leftarrow p + \varsigmaO \epsilonO n0, where n0 is the normal at q0, \epsilonO = 0.05, and \varsigmaO \sim \mathcal{U}[\{-1, 1\}]. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of points, as it involves generating 3N random numbers and performing 3N multiplications and additions. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the resulting points. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to vectorized tensor operations (torch.rand, broadcasting). Strengths: Simple to implement; guarantees uniform spatial coverage; no bias towards any region of the box. Limitations: Does not account for scene geometry or uncertainty; may waste samples in empty space compared to Background Point Sampling. When to use: Initial training phases, baseline comparisons, or when uniform spatial coverage is required regardless of content. When not to use: When focusing on surface details or high-uncertainty regions. Uniform sampling within bounding volumes is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics. It is used in neural field training for initializing ray origins and query data. The specific implementation details using PyTorch tensors are documented in repositories for Neural Surfaces and VF-NeRF. name: Background Point Sampling
body: Background Point Sampling generates sample points along rays for background regions, defined as the space outside the scene's bounding box. It employs a specific non-uniform sampling distribution controlled by a bgpreserve parameter to balance between uniform angular sampling and uniform radial sampling. This method is distinct from sibling methods like Random Point Sampling in Bounds, which typically samples uniformly within a defined volume, by specifically targeting the infinite or large-distance background region with a distribution that adapts based on the ray's geometry relative to the bounding box. Inputs: rayso: Origin coordinates for all rays, shape (Nrays, 3). raysd: Direction vectors for all rays, shape (Nrays, 3). tmax: Array of maximum t-values (intersection distances) for each ray, shape (Nrays,). Nsamples: Integer, number of background samples to generate per ray. bgpreserve: Float parameter controlling the sampling distribution blend, typically in [0, 1]. Outputs: bgpts: Sample point coordinates in the original world space, shape (Nrays Nsamples, 3). bgt: Sample distances from the ray origin, shape (Nrays Nsamples,). Data Structures: The implementation flattens the ray-sample grid into a 1D array for efficient GPU processing. The index idx maps to a specific ray and sample step: iray = idx // Nsamples istep = idx % Nsamples Steps: 1. For each sample index idx from 0 to N{rays} \times N{samples} - 1: 2. Calculate the ray index iray and step index istep as defined above. 3. Retrieve the maximum t-value for the current ray: t{inner} = t{max}[i{ray}]. 4. Calculate the original outer t-coordinate: t{outer}^{orig} = t{inner} - 1.0 + \frac{1.0}{1.0 - \frac{i{step}}{N{samples}}} 5. Calculate the original 3D point coordinates in world space using the ray origin and direction scaled by t{outer}^{orig}: \mathbf{p}{orig} = \mathbf{o}{ray} + \mathbf{d}{ray} \times t{outer}^{orig} where \mathbf{o}{ray} = \text{rays\o}[i{ray}] and \mathbf{d}{ray} = \text{rays\d}[i{ray}]. Let components be x, y, z. 6. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the origin: t{outer} = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} 7. Calculate the maximum absolute coordinate component: m = \max(|x|, |y|, |z|) 8. Calculate the radius factor: R{outer} = \frac{t{outer}}{m} 9. Calculate the scaling factor o2ip using bgpreserve: o2ip = \left(\frac{R{outer}^2}{t{outer}^2}\right) (1 - \text{bg\preserve}) + \left(\frac{R{outer}}{t{outer}}\right) \text{bg\preserve} 10. Scale the original point coordinates to get the final background point: \mathbf{p}{final} = \mathbf{p}{orig} \times o2ip 11. Store \mathbf{p}{final} and t{outer} for the current idx. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backgroundpointsampling(rayso, raysd, tmax, Nsamples, bgpreserve): Nrays = len(rayso) totalsamples = Nrays Nsamples bgpts = [None] totalsamples bgt = [0.0] totalsamples for idx in range(totalsamples): iray = idx // Nsamples istep = idx % Nsamples tinner = tmax[iray] touterorig = tinner - 1.0 + 1.0 / (1.0 - istep / Nsamples) rayo = rayso[iray] rayd = raysd[iray] orirayptsx = rayo[0] + rayd[0] touterorig orirayptsy = rayo[1] + rayd[1] touterorig orirayptsz = rayo[2] + rayd[2] touterorig touter = (orirayptsx2 + orirayptsy2 + orirayptsz2)0.5 orirayptsm = max(abs(orirayptsx), abs(orirayptsy), abs(orirayptsz)) if orirayptsm == 0.0: Router = 0.0 else: Router = touter / orirayptsm if touter == 0.0: o2ip = 0.0 else: o2ip = (Router2 / touter2) (1.0 - bgpreserve) + (Router / touter) bgpreserve finalx = orirayptsx o2ip finaly = orirayptsy o2ip finalz = orirayptsz o2ip bgpts[idx] = (finalx, finaly, finalz) bgt[idx] = touter return bgpts, bgt Parameters: bgpreserve: Float, typically between 0 and 1. Controls the blend between sampling distributions. Nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If orirayptsm is 0 (point at origin), Router is undefined. A guard returning 0.0 is required. Denominator Zero: In the calculation of touterorig, if istep == Nsamples, the denominator 1.0 - (istep / Nsamples) becomes zero. Since istep ranges from 0 to N{samples}-1, this case is avoided. If Nsamples is 0, the loop does not execute. Precision: Floating point precision issues may arise when touter is very large or very small. The scaling factor o2ip can become unstable if touter is close to zero. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \times N{samples}). Each sample requires a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \times N{samples}) to store the output points and distances. Strengths: Provides a structured way to sample the background, which is crucial for NeRF-based methods that need to account for background color and depth. The bgpreserve parameter allows tuning the sampling density. Limitations: The non-uniform distribution may require more samples to achieve the same variance reduction as uniform sampling in certain scenarios. Computationally more expensive than simple uniform sampling due to the per-sample geometric calculations. When to Use: When rendering scenes with significant background content that needs to be modeled explicitly. When Not to Use: If the background is simple (e.g., constant color) and does not require detailed sampling. If computational resources are extremely limited and a simpler background approximation suffices. Background Point Sampling is used in volume rendering to handle the background region by generating samples outside the bounding box of the scene. It originates from the DirectVoxGO implementation. sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, https://github.com/sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Uncertainty-guided Point Sampling
head: Uncertainty-guided point sampling with oversampling, importance sampling with oversampling, uncertain point sampling
body: Uncertainty-guided point sampling selects 2D coordinates within bounding boxes by prioritizing regions of high prediction uncertainty. It oversamples points randomly, selects a fraction via an uncertainty function, and fills the remainder with random points. Inputs: coarselogits: A tensor of shape (numboxes, C, Hcoarse, Wcoarse) containing coarse network predictions. numpoints: The desired number of final samples per box. oversampleratio: An integer \ge 1 determining the initial oversampling factor. importancesampleratio: A float in [0, 1] determining the fraction of final points selected via uncertainty. uncertaintyfunc: A function mapping logits to scalar uncertainty values. Outputs: pointcoords: A tensor of shape (numboxes, numpoints, 2) containing the selected 2D coordinates. Data Structures: pointcoords: Stores the final selected coordinates. pointlogits: Intermediate tensor storing logits at sampled locations. pointuncertainties: Tensor storing uncertainty scores. Steps: 1. Validate parameters: Assert oversampleratio >= 1 and 0 <= importancesampleratio <= 1. 2. Compute numboxes as the first dimension of coarselogits. 3. Compute the number of initial random samples: numsampled = int(numpoints oversampleratio). 4. Generate numsampled random 2D coordinates for each box: pointcoords = torch.rand(numboxes, numsampled, 2, device=coarselogits.device). 5. Sample the coarse logits at these random coordinates using bilinear interpolation with aligncorners=False. 6. Compute uncertainty for each sampled point: pointuncertainties = uncertaintyfunc(pointlogits). 7. Calculate the number of points to select based on uncertainty and the remainder for random sampling: numuncertainpoints = int(importancesampleratio numpoints) and numrandompoints = numpoints - numuncertainpoints. 8. Select the top-k points with the highest uncertainty for each box: idx = torch.topk(pointuncertainties[:, 0,:], k=numuncertainpoints, dim=1)[1]. 9. Flatten the indices to a global index space by adding a box offset: shift = numsampled torch.arange(numboxes, dtype=torch.long, device=coarselogits.device). 10. Apply the offset: idx += shift[:, None]. 11. Gather the corresponding coordinates from the initial random set: pointcoords = pointcoords.view(-1, 2)[idx.view(-1),:].view(numboxes, numuncertainpoints, 2). 12. If numrandompoints > 0, generate additional random coordinates of shape (numboxes, numrandompoints, 2) and concatenate them to the uncertain coordinates. 13. Return the combined pointcoords. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def uncertaintyguidedpointsampling(coarselogits, numpoints, oversampleratio, importancesampleratio, uncertaintyfunc): # 1. Validate parameters assert oversampleratio >= 1 assert 0 <= importancesampleratio <= 1 numboxes = coarselogits.shape[0] numsampled = int(numpoints oversampleratio) # 2. Generate initial random coordinates in [0, 1] pointcoords = torch.rand(numboxes, numsampled, 2, device=coarselogits.device) # 3. Sample logits at these coordinates # Standard bilinear interpolation: normalize to [-1, 1], apply gridsample, return (numboxes, numsampled, C) coordsnorm = 2.0 pointcoords - 1.0 gridcoords = coordsnorm.permute(0, 2, 1).unsqueeze(2) pointlogits = F.gridsample(coarselogits, gridcoords, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False, paddingmode='zeros') pointlogits = pointlogits.squeeze(-1).transpose(1, 2) # 4. Compute uncertainties pointuncertainties = uncertaintyfunc(pointlogits) # 5. Determine counts numuncertainpoints = int(importancesampleratio numpoints) numrandompoints = numpoints - numuncertainpoints # 6. Select top-k uncertain points # Assumes pointuncertainties has shape (numboxes, 1, numsampled) or (numboxes, C, numsampled) idx = torch.topk(pointuncertainties[:, 0,:], k=numuncertainpoints, dim=1)[1] # 7. Flatten indices with box offset shift = numsampled torch.arange(numboxes, dtype=torch.long, device=coarselogits.device) idx += shift[:, None] # 8. Gather coordinates pointcoords = pointcoords.view(-1, 2)[idx.view(-1),:].view(numboxes, numuncertainpoints, 2) # 9. Add random points if needed if numrandompoints > 0: randomcoords = torch.rand(numboxes, numrandompoints, 2, device=coarselogits.device) pointcoords = torch.cat([pointcoords, randomcoords], dim=1) return pointcoords Parameters: oversampleratio: Integer factor to increase initial random samples before filtering. Must be \ge 1. importancesampleratio: Float fraction of final points selected via uncertainty. Range: [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pre-computation Error: Calculating uncertainty on coarse predictions before sampling yields incorrect values. If uncertaintyfunc(logits) = -|logits|, a point sampled between logits -1 and 1 might have 0 logits, resulting in 0 uncertainty. Pre-computing coarse uncertainties would assign -1 to that point, biasing the selection. Uncertainty must be computed on the logits sampled at the specific random coordinates. Generates uniformly distributed points within specified bounds. Use when no prior knowledge of uncertainty is available or for baseline comparison. Link Samples points in regions predicted to be empty/background. Use when the goal is to accelerate rendering by skipping empty space. Link Not given in the sources. Uncertainty-guided point sampling was introduced in the pixel-nerf repository for pixel-wise neural rendering. It leverages the principle that regions with high prediction variance contain more information that needs to be resolved. sxyu/pixel-nerf, https://github.com/sxyu/pixel-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Clipping Distance Computation via Volume Corners
head: IJK to RAS Corner Projection, Volume Bounding Box Clipping
body: Computes the near and far clipping distances for ray marching by projecting the eight corners of the volume bounding box onto the camera view direction, then taking the minimum and maximum of these projected distances. This method ensures that all sample points generated along a ray fall within the volume's spatial extent, preventing out-of-bounds memory access and unnecessary computation outside the volume. Inputs: Camera matrix M{cam} (4x4). Volume bounding box dimensions in IJK space: I, J, K (number of voxels along each axis). IJK-to-RAS transformation matrix M{ijk2ras} (4x4). Margin parameter \delta (default 30.0 mm). Outputs: Near clipping distance d{near}. Far clipping distance d{far}. Data Structures: Camera matrix M{cam}: 4x4 matrix. If the norm of the translation column (last column, first 3 rows) is less than 1.0, it is treated as a world-to-camera matrix and inverted to obtain the camera-to-world matrix M{world}; otherwise, it is used directly. Volume corners in IJK space: 8 points (i, j, k) where i \in \{0, I-1\}, j \in \{0, J-1\}, k \in \{0, K-1\}. Volume corners in RAS space: 8 points \mathbf{p}{ras}^{(n)} for n=0..7. Steps: 1. Extract Camera Pose: Determine the camera position \mathbf{c} and view direction \mathbf{v} from M{cam}. If \|M{cam}[0:3, 3]\| < 1.0, invert M{cam} to get M{world}. Extract \mathbf{c} and \mathbf{v} from M{world} and normalize \mathbf{v}. 2. Generate IJK Corners: Create the 8 corners of the volume bounding box in IJK space using indices 0 and I-1, 0 and J-1, and 0 and K-1. 3. Transform to RAS Space: For each corner \mathbf{p}{ijk} = (i, j, k, 1)^T, compute \mathbf{p}{ras} = M{ijk2ras} \cdot \mathbf{p}{ijk} and take the first three components to get the 3D position in RAS space. 4. Project Corners: For each RAS corner \mathbf{p}{ras}^{(n)}, compute the vector \mathbf{d}^{(n)} = \mathbf{p}{ras}^{(n)} - \mathbf{c} and project this vector onto the normalized view direction \mathbf{v} to get the scalar distance t^{(n)} = \mathbf{d}^{(n)} \cdot \mathbf{v}. 5. Compute Clipping Distances: Set t{min} = \minn(t^{(n)}) and t{max} = \maxn(t^{(n)}). Set d{near} = t{min} - \delta and d{far} = t{max} + \delta. Clamp d{near} to a minimum of 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeclippingdistances(cameramatrix, ijk2ras, volumedims, margin=30.0): """ Compute near and far clipping distances for volume ray marching. Expects cameramatrix and ijk2ras as list of lists (4x4). volumedims is a tuple (I, J, K). """ I, J, K = volumedims # Step 1: Extract Camera Pose # Get translation column (last column, first 3 rows) translation = [cameramatrix[0][3], cameramatrix[1][3], cameramatrix[2][3]] translationnorm = math.sqrt(sum(t t for t in translation)) # Invert if world-to-camera (norm < 1.0), else use directly. # The source uses a boolean mask and torch.where to avoid branching. if translationnorm < 1.0: cameramatrixworld = invert4x4(cameramatrix) else: cameramatrixworld = cameramatrix # Extract camera position campos = [cameramatrixworld[0][3], cameramatrixworld[1][3], cameramatrixworld[2][3]] # Extract view direction (standard convention uses negative Z-axis of the world matrix) viewdir = [-cameramatrixworld[0][2], -cameramatrixworld[1][2], -cameramatrixworld[2][2]] vnorm = math.sqrt(sum(v v for v in viewdir)) viewdir = [v / vnorm for v in viewdir] # Step 2: Generate IJK Corners cornersijk = [] for i in [0, I - 1]: for j in [0, J - 1]: for k in [0, K - 1]: cornersijk.append([float(i), float(j), float(k)]) # Step 3: Transform to RAS Space cornersras = [] for p in cornersijk: x, y, z = p # Homogeneous multiplication: pras = M [x, y, z, 1]^T wx = ijk2ras[0][0] x + ijk2ras[0][1] y + ijk2ras[0][2] z + ijk2ras[0][3] wy = ijk2ras[1][0] x + ijk2ras[1][1] y + ijk2ras[1][2] z + ijk2ras[1][3] wz = ijk2ras[2][0] x + ijk2ras[2][1] y + ijk2ras[2][2] z + ijk2ras[2][3] cornersras.append([wx, wy, wz]) # Step 4: Project Corners distances = [] for p in cornersras: dx = p[0] - campos[0] dy = p[1] - campos[1] dz = p[2] - campos[2] t = dx viewdir[0] + dy viewdir[1] + dz viewdir[2] distances.append(t) # Step 5: Compute Clipping Distances tmin = min(distances) tmax = max(distances) dnear = tmin - margin dfar = tmax + margin dnear = max(dnear, 0.1) return dnear, dfar def invert4x4(m): """Standard 4x4 matrix inverse implementation.""" # Cofactor expansion for 4x4 matrix inverse def minor(mat, r, c): return [[mat[i][j] for j in range(4) if j != c] for i in range(4) if i != r] cofactors = [[0]4 for in range(4)] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): cofactors[i][j] = ((-1)(i+j)) det3x3(minor(m, i, j)) # Transpose cofactors to get adjugate, then divide by determinant det = sum(m[0][j] cofactors[0][j] for j in range(4)) invdet = 1.0 / det return [[cofactors[j][i] invdet for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)] def det3x3(m): return (m[0][0] (m[1][1]m[2][2] - m[1][2]m[2][1]) - m[0][1] (m[1][0]m[2][2] - m[1][2]m[2][0]) + m[0][2] (m[1][0]m[2][1] - m[1][1]m[2][0])) Parameters: margin: Safety margin added to near/far distances in mm. Default value is 30.0. Positive values expand the clipping range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The clamping of d{near} to 0.1 prevents zero or negative distances, which could cause division by zero or sampling errors. The method assumes a standard camera convention where the view direction aligns with the negative Z-axis of the world matrix; deviations require adjusting the view direction extraction. A vertex shader implementation that projects the world-space axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of a fire volume to enable fragment shader ray marching. It transforms volume-space corners (unit cube [0,1]^3) to world space using a volumetoworld matrix, then to clip space using view and projection matrices. It outputs the world position of the corners for use in the fragment shader. This variant uses GPU-based rendering pipelines with push constants and shaders. Time Complexity: O(1) with respect to volume resolution, as it processes a fixed 8 corners. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only 8 corners and a few scalar values. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays if applied per-ray, but since the volume bounds are global, it can be computed once per volume and reused for all rays. Strengths: Simple, robust, and efficient. Ensures all samples are within the volume bounds. Limitations: Assumes the volume is axis-aligned in IJK space and convex. Does not account for internal structures or non-convex shapes. When to use: When a quick and reliable method to determine ray clipping bounds is needed for volume rendering. When not to use: For non-convex volumes or when more precise ray-box intersection is required. This method is used in differentiable volume raycasting for digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs). The approach is based on projecting the volume bounding box corners onto the camera view direction to determine the integration range for ray marching. pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, https://github.com/migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: CUDA Extension Interface for Ray Sampling and Rendering
body: This module provides a PyTorch C++ extension containing CUDA kernels for ray sampling, alpha calculation, and weight accumulation in volume rendering. It exposes low-level tensor operations for batched ray processing, enabling efficient GPU execution of point sampling, masking, and differentiable alpha blending. The interface consists of multiple CUDA kernels exposed via pybind11. Each kernel accepts PyTorch tensors as inputs and returns PyTorch tensors or vectors of tensors as outputs. All tensors are assumed to be on the same CUDA device. The data structures are implicit in the tensor shapes defined by the kernel signatures. Rays: Defined by origin rayso (shape [Nrays, 3]) and direction raysd (shape [Nrays, 3]). Bounding Box: Defined by xyzmin and xyzmax (shape [3]). Mask Cache: A 3D tensor world (shape [D, H, W]) representing a binary occupancy grid. Density/Alpha: 1D tensors of shape [Nsamples] or [Nrays Nsamples]. The extension provides the following CUDA kernels: Computes the entry (tmin) and exit (tmax) distances of each ray with the axis-aligned bounding box defined by xyzmin and xyzmax. Inputs: rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax (tensors), near, far (floats). Outputs: tmin, tmax (tensors). Logic: For each ray, the standard slab method computes intersections with the six planes of the bounding box. The minimum of the maximum entry distances and the maximum of the minimum exit distances yields tmin and tmax. Results are clamped to [near, far]. Determines the number of sample points required for each ray based on a fixed step distance. Inputs: raysd, tmin, tmax (tensors), stepdist (float). Outputs: nsamples (tensor). Logic: Computes the ray segment length Li = t{max, i} - t{min, i} and sets n\samples[i] = \lceil Li / stepdist \rceil. Prepares the starting point and direction for sampling. Inputs: rayso, raysd, tmin (tensors). Outputs: startpoints, dirs (tensors). Logic: Computes start\points[i] = rays\o[i] + t{min, i} \cdot rays\d[i] and copies rays\d[i] to dirs[i]. Generates the 3D coordinates of sample points along each ray. Inputs: rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax (tensors), near, far, stepdist (floats). Outputs: pts, tvals, validmask (tensors). Logic: Computes sample positions t{val, i, k} = t{min, i} + (k + 0.5) \cdot stepdist and converts them to world coordinates pts[i, k] = rays\o[i] + t{val, i, k} \cdot rays\d[i]. Samples points in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). Inputs: rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax (tensors), Nsamples (int). Outputs: pts, tvals (tensors). Logic: Distributes N\samples points uniformly along the ray segment within the bounding box. Samples points in the background region to handle occlusion and background color estimation. Inputs: rayso, raysd, tmax (tensors), bgpreserve (float), Nsamples (int). Outputs: bgpts (tensor). Logic: Extends sampling beyond t{max} using a spacing strategy controlled by bgpreserve. Checks if sample points fall within known free space to skip rendering. Inputs: world (3D tensor), xyz (2D tensor, last dim 3), xyz2ijkscale, xyz2ijkshift (tensors). Outputs: mask (tensor). Logic: Converts world coordinates to grid indices via ijk = (xyz \cdot xyz2ijk\scale) + xyz2ijk\shift, clamps to grid bounds, and performs trilinear interpolation or nearest-neighbor lookup on world. Converts raw density values to alpha (opacity) values. Inputs: density (1D tensor), shift (float), interval (float). Outputs: alpha, expdensity (tensors). Logic: Computes \sigma' = \max(density + shift, 0), then \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma' \cdot interval) and stores \exp(-\sigma' \cdot interval) in expdensity. Same as raw2alpha but supports per-sample intervals. Inputs: density (1D tensor), shift (float), interval (tensor). Outputs: alpha, expdensity (tensors). Logic: Applies the same formula element-wise using the per-sample interval tensor. Computes the contribution weight of each sample point in the volume rendering integral. Inputs: alpha, rayid (1D tensors), nrays (int). Outputs: weight, T, alphainvlast (tensors). Logic: Computes transmittance T[i, k] = \prod{j=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha[i, j]) and weight W[i, k] = T[i, k] \cdot \alpha[i, k] for each ray. raw2alphabackward: Computes gradients of density given gradients of alpha and expdensity. raw2alphanonunibackward: Same as above but with per-sample interval. alpha2weightbackward: Computes gradients of alpha given gradients of weight by propagating gradients backward through the transmittance product. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def alpha2weightforward(alpha: torch.Tensor, rayid: torch.Tensor, nrays: int): """ alpha: [Nrays Nsamples] rayid: [Nrays Nsamples] nrays: int """ Ntotal = alpha.size(0) Nsamples = Ntotal // nrays T = torch.zeros(Ntotal, device=alpha.device) weight = torch.zeros(Ntotal, device=alpha.device) alphainvlast = torch.zeros(nrays, device=alpha.device) # Initialize transmittance for the start of each ray for r in range(nrays): T[r Nsamples] = 1.0 # Compute transmittance and weights sequentially per ray for r in range(nrays): start = r Nsamples for k in range(1, Nsamples): T[start + k] = T[start + k - 1] (1.0 - alpha[start + k - 1]) for k in range(Nsamples): weight[start + k] = T[start + k] alpha[start + k] alphainvlast[r] = T[start + Nsamples - 1] (1.0 - alpha[start + Nsamples - 1]) return weight, T, alphainvlast Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) for sampling and accumulation. The parallel prefix sum in alpha2weight is O(\log N{samples}) per ray on GPU. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) for storing points, transmittance, and weights. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU execution via CUDA kernels, avoiding CPU-GPU data transfer overhead. Performance scales with the number of rays and samples, limited by memory bandwidth for large volumes. Strengths: Efficient batched processing, differentiable, supports non-uniform sampling. Limitations: Requires careful handling of padding for rays with different sample counts. This interface is part of the UnboundedNeRFPytorch implementation, an unofficial PyTorch port of NeRF-related methods for unbounded scenes. It extends standard NeRF rendering pipelines by providing specialized kernels for ray-box intersection and sampling, which are crucial for handling large, unbounded volumes efficiently. The code is based on the renderutils.cpp module from the original NeRF implementations, adapted for PyTorch's autograd system. sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, https://github.com/sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Branchless Ray/AABB Intersection with NaN Handling
head: Branchless Ray-AABB Intersection, Fast Branchless Ray/Bounding Box Intersection Part 2, NaN-safe Ray-AABB Intersection, Ray-AABB Intersection (Branchless), checkHit
body: This method computes the intersection of a ray with an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a branchless algorithm that correctly handles IEEE 754 floating-point edge cases, specifically NaNs generated when a ray direction component is zero. It builds on Ray-AABB Intersection (Slab/Min-Max) by replacing conditional checks for zero direction with precomputed inverse directions and nested min/max operations that suppress NaN propagation. Unlike the standard branchless slab method, this variant guarantees robustness for degenerate cases where the ray origin lies exactly on a box boundary or the ray is parallel to an axis, preventing false positives caused by NaN propagation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz), ray direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz), AABB bounds \mathbf{min} = (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}), \mathbf{max} = (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Output: Boolean indicating intersection, and optionally entry time t{min}, exit time t{max}, and side vectors \mathbf{sideMin}, \mathbf{sideMax}. Data Structures: Ray: Struct containing origin (float3) and dir (float3). AABB: Struct containing min (float3) and max (float3). Precomputation: Compute the inverse direction components \text{dir\inv}i = 1.0 / di. If di = 0, IEEE 754 specifies \text{dir\inv}i = \pm \infty. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize t{min} and t{max} using the first dimension (i=0) without bounds checking: t1 = (x{min} - ox) \cdot \text{dir\inv}x t2 = (x{max} - ox) \cdot \text{dir\inv}x t{min} = \min(t1, t2) t{max} = \max(t1, t2) 2. Loop over dimensions i \in \{1, 2\} (y and z axes): a. Compute slab intersections for the current axis: t1 = (\text{min}i - oi) \cdot \text{dir\inv}i t2 = (\text{max}i - oi) \cdot \text{dir\inv}i b. Update t{min} to suppress NaNs from the current slab: t{min} = \max(t{min}, \min(\min(t1, t2), t{max})) This uses the property that \min(\text{NaN}, t{max}) returns t{max} if t{max} is not NaN, effectively ignoring the NaN slab contribution. c. Update t{max} to suppress NaNs from the current slab: t{max} = \min(t{max}, \max(\max(t1, t2), t{min})) This uses the property that \max(\text{NaN}, t{min}) returns t{min} if t{min} is not NaN, effectively ignoring the NaN slab contribution. 3. Return true if t{max} > \max(t{min}, 0.0), otherwise return false. This checks for a valid intersection interval that starts after or at the ray origin. Using \ge instead of > is required for degenerate boxes with zero thickness or to handle floating-point precision issues where t{max} == t{min} at edges/corners. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayaabbintersectbranchlessnansafe(origin, dir, minbound, maxbound): # Precompute inverse direction components (IEEE 754 handles 1.0/0.0 as ±inf) dirinv = [1.0 / d for d in dir] # Dimension 0 (X) t1 = (minbound[0] - origin[0]) dirinv[0] t2 = (maxbound[0] - origin[0]) dirinv[0] tmin = math.fmin(t1, t2) tmax = math.fmax(t1, t2) # Dimensions 1 (Y) and 2 (Z) for i in range(1, 3): t1 = (minbound[i] - origin[i]) dirinv[i] t2 = (maxbound[i] - origin[i]) dirinv[i] # NaN suppression logic using math.fmin/fmax to match SSE minps/maxps behavior # If t1 or t2 is NaN, math.fmin(t1, t2) returns the non-NaN operand tmin = math.fmax(tmin, math.fmin(math.fmin(t1, t2), tmax)) tmax = math.fmin(tmax, math.fmax(math.fmax(t1, t2), tmin)) # Check intersection interval return tmax > math.fmax(tmin, 0.0) Side Vector Calculation (Optional): To determine which faces are intersected, the algorithm can be extended as shown in. This requires the AABB to be defined by center and minSize/maxSize or derived from min/max. 1. Compute isPositive vector: \text{isPositive}i = 1.0 if \text{dir\inv}i > 0, else 0.0. 2. Compute isNegative vector: \text{isNegative}i = 1.0 - \text{isPositive}i. 3. Compute leftSide and rightSide vectors: \text{leftSide}i = \text{center}i + \text{isPositive}i \cdot \text{minSize}i + \text{isNegative}i \cdot \text{maxSize}i \text{rightSide}i = \text{center}i + \text{isPositive}i \cdot \text{maxSize}i + \text{isNegative}i \cdot \text{minSize}i (Note: minSize and maxSize refer to the distance from center to min/max bounds, effectively half-extents if centered, or adjusted based on the specific AABB representation.) 4. Compute time vectors: \text{leftSideTimesOneOverDir}i = (\text{leftSide}i - oi) \cdot \text{dir\inv}i \text{rightSideTimesOneOverDir}i = (\text{rightSide}i - oi) \cdot \text{dir\inv}i 5. Compute t{min} and t{max} from these vectors: t{min} = \max(\text{leftSideTimesOneOverDir}x, \max(\text{leftSideTimesOneOverDir}y, \text{leftSideTimesOneOverDir}z)) t{max} = \min(\text{rightSideTimesOneOverDir}x, \min(\text{rightSideTimesOneOverDir}y, \text{rightSideTimesOneOverDir}z)) 6. Compute side vectors: \text{directionSign}i = \text{sign}(\text{dir\inv}i) \text{sideMin}i = (\text{leftSideTimesOneOverDir}i == t{min}) \cdot \text{directionSign}i \text{sideMax}i = (\text{rightSideTimesOneOverDir}i == t{max}) \cdot \text{directionSign}i The side vectors are signed to correctly identify entry/exit faces relative to the viewer, compensating for floating-point precision errors. Parameters: No tunable parameters. Relies on IEEE 754 standard behavior for min/max with NaNs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction: If di = 0, \text{dir\inv}i = \pm \infty. If the ray origin is inside the box along that axis, t1 and t2 become \pm \infty. The NaN suppression logic handles this by ignoring the NaN/Inf results from that slab. Ray on Boundary: If the ray origin lies exactly on a box face, t1 or t2 may be NaN (0 \infty). The nested min/max suppresses these NaNs. Degenerate Boxes: For boxes with zero thickness (e.g., planes), use \ge in the final return condition to avoid false negatives due to precision. Precision Errors: Floating-point inaccuracies may cause t{max} == t{min} at edges/corners. Using \ge helps mitigate this. Time Complexity: O(1) with a fixed number of operations (unrolled loop for 3 dimensions). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar registers. Performance: On GCC 4.9.2 at -O3, the NaN-safe implementation handles just over 93 million rays per second, taking around 30 clock cycles per ray without vectorization. Scaling: Performance is independent of scene complexity as it operates on a single AABB. Strengths: Branchless execution improves pipeline efficiency on modern CPUs/GPUs. Robust handling of NaNs prevents visual artifacts in practice if the ray/object intersection functions are implemented correctly. Limitations: Approximately 30% slower than the fastest version that ignores NaN consistency, and 15% slower than the version without explicit NaN handling, due to extra min/max operations and handling of floating-point special cases (infinities, NaNs). When to use: When robustness is critical, especially in BVH traversal where degenerate rays or boxes might occur. When visual artifacts from NaN propagation are unacceptable. When not to use: In performance-critical paths where the risk of degenerate cases is negligible and the 15-30% overhead is prohibitive, and the application can tolerate potential false positives in rare degenerate cases. The branchless approach originated with Brian Smits (1998) and was implemented by Amy Williams et al. (2005). The specific NaN handling workaround using nested min/max was applied by Thierry Berger-Perrin. The method is used in ray tracing for efficient ray-primitive intersection tests.
