name: Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Bilinear Patch-Extension)
head: Bilinear Patch Traversal, Hex-H, Hybrid Hexahedral Traversal
body: This method is a hybrid traversal algorithm for hexahedral meshes that combines Plücker-based face selection with bilinear patch intersection tests. It solves the problem of geometric singularities and interpolation discontinuities inherent in pure Plücker traversal by utilizing the parametric coordinates (u, v) derived directly from bilinear patch intersections to compute interpolated scalar values. It sets itself apart from the parent Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Plücker Space) by avoiding triangle decomposition for interpolation and instead using the known parametric coordinates to compute values continuously across hexahedral faces. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, hexahedron vertices \mathbf{v}0 \dots \mathbf{v}7. Outputs: Exit face index, parametric coordinates (u, v) on the exit face, and interpolated scalar values at entry and exit points. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 8 3D vectors representing the hexahedron corners. Plücker Values: Three scalar areas A0, A1, A2 derived from cross products of edge vectors and the ray direction. Bilinear Patch Parameters: u, v \in \mathbb{R} representing the parametric hit location on the face. Steps: 1. Plücker Face Selection: Compute the Plücker values for the lines \mathbf{v}4 \to \mathbf{v}5, \mathbf{v}6 \to \mathbf{v}7, and the ray direction to determine the three areas A0, A1, A2. This identifies the three candidate exit faces. 2. Bilinear Patch Intersection: For each of the three candidate exit faces, perform a bilinear patch intersection test. An edge of the bilinear patch depends on all four face vertices. 3. Exit Determination: Stop as soon as a patch is hit, i.e., when parametric coordinates (u, v) \in [0, 1]^2. This provides the exit face and the parametric coordinates (u, v) for the exit point. 4. Numerical Consistency Check: If numerical inconsistencies occur due to insufficient floating-point accuracy, perform two additional Plücker tests equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method to resolve the correct exit face. 5. Interpolation: Use the known parametric coordinates (u, v) from the bilinear patch test to compute interpolated scalar values on the entry and exit faces. This completely avoids discontinuities in the interpolated field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def traversehexahedron(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # Step 1: Compute Plücker areas for candidate faces edge1 = sub(hexvertices[5], hexvertices[4]) edge2 = sub(hexvertices[7], hexvertices[6]) # Standard Plücker coordinate computation for ray-cell face intersection A0 = dot(cross(edge1, raydirection), cross(edge1, raydirection)) A1 = dot(cross(edge2, raydirection), cross(edge2, raydirection)) A2 = dot(cross(edge1, edge2), cross(edge1, edge2)) # Identify candidate faces based on signs of A0, A1, A2 candidatefaces = [0, 1, 2] # Indices of the three candidate exit faces exitface = None u, v = 0.0, 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Check bilinear patch intersection for each candidate for faceidx in candidatefaces: # Standard algebraic solution for ray-bilinear patch intersection # Solves P(u,v) = rayorigin + traydirection for the bilinear face hit, u, v = solvebilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx) if hit and 0.0 <= u <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= v <= 1.0: exitface = faceidx break # Step 4: Handle numerical inconsistencies if exitface is None: # Perform two additional Plücker tests (pure Plücker fallback) # Equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method exitface = resolvepluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices) # Recompute (u, v) by projecting the exit point onto the exit face plane exitpoint = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, computetexit(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, exitface))) u, v = projecttofaceuv(exitpoint, hexvertices, exitface) # Step 5: Interpolation # Compute scalar at entry point (previous cell exit or ray origin) # Compute scalar at exit point using u, v on exitface scalarexit = interpolatescalarbilinear(hexvertices, exitface, u, v) return exitface, u, v, scalarexit def solvebilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard bilinear patch intersection: constructs the 4-vertex bilinear surface, # forms a quadratic equation in t and u/v, solves for valid intersections. return False, 0.0, 0.0 def resolvepluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # Two additional Plücker tests equivalent to pure Plücker method return 0 def computetexit(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard ray-plane intersection return 1.0 def projecttofaceuv(point, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard projection onto bilinear patch parameter space return 0.0, 0.0 def interpolatescalarbilinear(hexvertices, faceidx, u, v): # Standard bilinear interpolation return 0.0 def add(a, b): return [a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]] def scale(v, s): return [v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s] Parameters: Floating-point precision: Standard double precision is recommended to minimize numerical inconsistencies. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Hexahedron: Bilinear patches are generally not flat, introducing holes in the hexahedron because the implicit edge representation depends on all four face vertices, unlike Plücker coordinates which depend solely on two edge points. This can cause rays to miss the exit face or produce invalid (u, v) coordinates. Numerical Inconsistencies: Insufficient floating-point accuracy can lead to incorrect face selection. The method requires a fallback to Plücker tests in these cases. Discontinuities: Using bilinear patches with known parametric coordinates completely avoids discontinuities in the interpolated field. A method to calculate normals for hexahedral meshes using trilinear interpolation of vertex normals, converted from computational space to physical space via the Jacobian matrix. It is chosen when accurate shading is required for curvilinear hexahedral meshes. It operates on vector fields and requires Jacobian transformation for correct physical-space orientation. Steps: 1. Interpolate a vector at the entry and exit faces using the same parametric coordinates (u, v) used for scalar interpolation. 2. Perform a linear interpolation between the two interpolated vectors based on their distance to the isosurface to yield the final normal. 3. Calculate three vectors in physical space corresponding to the normal in computational space Nc and convert them to physical space Np using the Jacobian matrix. Formulas: Convert physical coordinates xi to computational coordinates \tilde{\rho}j using the Jacobian matrix J{ij}: xi = J{ij} \tilde{\rho}j J{ij} = \frac{\partial xi}{\partial \tilde{\rho}j} Approximate the Jacobian matrix J{ij} for a grid node n using central differences: J{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{xi(n) - xi(n-1)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n) - \tilde{\rho}j(n+1)} + \frac{xi(n+1) - xi(n)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n+1) - \tilde{\rho}j(n)} \right) A linear combination of the three vectors with the normal in computational space Nc results in the converted normal Np. Time Complexity: Raw traversal performance is 15% lower compared to the pure Plücker traverser due to the cost of bilinear patch intersection tests. However, overall performance gains 25% on average because time is saved in interpolation (no triangle decomposition needed). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The hybrid algorithm processes up to 4.5 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Strengths: Better quality and significantly faster overall performance than the pure Plücker approach for hexahedral meshes due to avoided discontinuities and efficient interpolation. Limitations: Raw traversal is slower; numerical inconsistencies may require fallback tests, though this is rare. When to Use: Recommended for traversing curvilinear grids on a ray tracing basis, especially when high-quality rendering and continuous interpolation are prioritized over raw traversal speed. Originated in the paper "Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering" (2006) by Ramsey et al.. The method was developed to address singularities and discontinuities in hexahedral mesh traversal for direct volume rendering. It builds on the Plücker-based traversal method but integrates bilinear patch tests to improve interpolation quality. name: Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates
head: Barycentric Point-in-Tetrahedron Test
body: This method determines whether a set of query points lies inside a set of tetrahedra by solving for barycentric coordinates. It serves as the core geometric primitive for Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection, allowing volume rendering engines to identify which cells contain sample points for density accumulation. Unlike Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection which operates on ray primitives, this method operates on explicit point positions, making it suitable for post-intersection validation or direct point-in-volume queries. Inputs: points: Tensor of shape (P, 3) containing P query points in 3D space. vertices: Tensor of shape (V, 3) containing the vertices of the tetrahedral mesh. tetrahedra: Tensor of shape (T, 4) containing indices into vertices defining T tetrahedra. Outputs: insidetet: Tensor of shape (P,) storing the index of the first tetrahedron containing each point, or -1 if no containing tetrahedron exists. barycentriccoords: Tensor of shape (P, 4) storing the barycentric weights (\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) for each point within its containing tetrahedron, or zeros if outside. The implementation relies on dense tensor layouts optimized for batched linear algebra operations. mat: A (T, 3, 3) tensor representing the system of linear equations for a chunk of points, where columns are the edge vectors. d: A (K, T, 3) tensor representing the vector from the reference vertex to the query points in the current chunk. 1. Initialization: Initialize insidetet with -1 and barycentriccoords with 0. 2. Chunking: To manage memory efficiency, process points in chunks of size chunksize. Iterate start from 0 to P with step chunksize. Let end = min(start + chunksize, P). 3. Vertex Extraction: For the current chunk, extract the vertices of all tetrahedra. Let v0, v1, v2, v3 be the vertices of a specific tetrahedron t. 4. Edge Vector Computation: Compute edge vectors relative to vertex v3 (the reference vertex): \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{v}3 \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}3 \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}3 5. Point Vector Computation: Compute the vector from v3 to the query point \mathbf{p}: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}3 6. Barycentric Solving: Solve the linear system \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\lambda}{0:2} = \mathbf{d} for the first three barycentric coordinates, where \mathbf{M} = [\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}]. \begin{bmatrix} \lambda0 \\ \lambda1 \\ \lambda2 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{d} The fourth coordinate is derived by the constraint \sum \lambdai = 1: \lambda3 = 1 - \lambda0 - \lambda1 - \lambda2 7. Inside Test: A point is inside the tetrahedron if all barycentric coordinates are non-negative: \text{inside} = (\lambda0 \ge 0) \land (\lambda1 \ge 0) \land (\lambda2 \ge 0) \land (\lambda3 \ge 0) 8. Selection: For each point, identify the first tetrahedron satisfying the inside condition. If no tetrahedron contains the point, the result is -1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointintetrahedron(points, vertices, tetrahedra, chunksize): """ Determines if points lie inside tetrahedra using barycentric coordinates. Args: points: Array (P, 3) vertices: Array (V, 3) tetrahedra: Array (T, 4) chunksize: Integer, number of points to process per batch Returns: insidetet: Array (P,) index of containing tetrahedron or -1 barycentriccoords: Array (P, 4) barycentric weights """ P = len(points) insidetet = [-1] P barycentriccoords = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(P)] # Pre-fetch tetrahedron vertices: shape (T, 4, 3) tetvertices = [[vertices[tetrahedra[t][v]] for v in range(4)] for t in range(len(tetrahedra))] for start in range(0, P, chunksize): end = min(start + chunksize, P) chunkpoints = points[start:end] K = len(chunkpoints) # Extract vertices v0..v3 for all T: shape (T, 3) v0 = [row[0] for row in tetvertices] v1 = [row[1] for row in tetvertices] v2 = [row[2] for row in tetvertices] v3 = [row[3] for row in tetvertices] # Edge vectors: shape (T, 3) a = [[v0[t][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] b = [[v1[t][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] c = [[v2[t][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] # Matrix M: shape (T, 3, 3) where columns are a, b, c M = [[[a[t][i][j] for i in range(3)] for j in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] # Point vectors relative to v3: shape (K, T, 3) d = [[[chunkpoints[k][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Transpose d to (T, 3, K) to match solve signature dT = [[[d[k][t][i] for k in range(K)] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] # Solve M @ lambda = dT for each T using standard linear algebra routine # sol shape: (T, 3, K) sol = solvelinearsystem(M, dT) # Transpose sol to (K, T, 3) chunkbary = [[[sol[t][i][k] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Extract lambdas l0 = [[chunkbary[k][t][0] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] l1 = [[chunkbary[k][t][1] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] l2 = [[chunkbary[k][t][2] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] l3 = [[1.0 - l0[k][t] - l1[k][t] - l2[k][t] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Inside condition: shape (K, T) inside = [[(l0[k][t] >= 0) and (l1[k][t] >= 0) and (l2[k][t] >= 0) and (l3[k][t] >= 0) for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Find first containing tetrahedron for each point validexists = [any(inside[k]) for k in range(K)] tetidx = [] for k in range(K): if validexists[k]: # argmax on float representation of boolean array scores = [1.0 if inside[k][t] else 0.0 for t in range(len(tetvertices))] tetidx.append(scores.index(max(scores))) else: tetidx.append(-1) # Update outputs for valid points validmask = [k for k in range(K) if validexists[k]] for k in validmask: globalidx = start + k t = tetidx[k] insidetet[globalidx] = t barycentriccoords[globalidx][0:3] = [l0[k][t], l1[k][t], l2[k][t]] return insidetet, barycentriccoords chunksize: Controls memory usage during the batched solve. Not given in the sources. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If the volume of the tetrahedron is zero (coplanar vertices), the matrix \mathbf{M} is singular and the solve will fail or produce NaNs. Implementers should check for zero volume or use a pseudo-inverse with a tolerance threshold. Precision: Barycentric coordinates sum to 1. Floating-point errors may cause \sum \lambdai \ne 1 exactly. It is recommended to renormalize \lambda3 = 1 - \lambda0 - \lambda1 - \lambda2 after solving for the first three, as done in the algorithm, to ensure the constraint is satisfied. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly on the face or edge have \lambdai = 0. The condition \lambdai \ge 0 includes boundaries. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot T) for a naive implementation checking all tetrahedra, where P is the number of points and T is the number of tetrahedra. With spatial acceleration (e.g., BVH), this reduces to O(P \log T) or better. The linear algebra solve is O(T \cdot K) per chunk for K points. Memory Complexity: O(T \cdot K) for the intermediate matrices in the chunked solve. Strengths: Simple to implement, numerically stable for non-degenerate tetrahedra, easily vectorizable. Limitations: Naive search is slow for large T. Requires a spatial accelerator for performance in dense volumes. This method is a standard geometric technique used in computer graphics and scientific visualization. It is employed in TetWeave for resampling and interpolation in 3D reconstruction pipelines. name: Barycentric Thick Endpoint Calculation
head: Barycentric Endpoint Calculation
body: Calculates the near (f) and far (b) endpoints of the "thick line" (the intersection of the line of sight with the tetrahedron volume) using the barycentric coordinates of the x-ray source. This method avoids projecting vertices to the image plane, allowing the calculation to be performed independently of the view transform. It builds on Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates by utilizing the source's barycentric vector \mathbf{t} to determine the entry and exit points of the ray through the tetrahedron. Inputs: Tetrahedron vertices in Cartesian coordinates: v0, v1, v2, v3. Barycentric coordinates of the x-ray source s with respect to the tetrahedron: \mathbf{t} = (t0, t1, t2, t3)^T. Outputs: Near endpoint position: f. Far endpoint position: b. (Optional) Barycentric coordinates of endpoints: \mathbf{u}f, \mathbf{u}b. Data Structures: \mathbf{t}: A 4-component vector representing the source's position in the tetrahedron's local barycentric frame. vi: 3D Cartesian vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Near Endpoint (f): The near endpoint lies on the intersection of the edge (v0, v2) and the plane through (s, v1, v3). Its Cartesian position is calculated as: f = \frac{t0}{t0 + t2} v0 + \frac{t2}{t0 + t2} v2 Alternatively, using the opposite edge: f = \frac{-t1}{t0 + t2} v1 + \frac{-t3}{t0 + t2} v3 The barycentric coordinates of f are: \mathbf{u}f = (\alpha0, \alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3) = \left( \frac{t0}{t0 + t2}, \frac{-t1}{t0 + t2}, \frac{t2}{t0 + t2}, \frac{-t3}{t0 + t2} \right) Note: \alpha2 is derived from the constraint \sum \alphai = 1, but the formula above explicitly shows the weights for v0 and v2 in the first expression. The source text defines the tuple (\alpha0, \alpha1, \alpha3) as (t0 + t2)^{-1}(t0, -t1, -t3), implying \alpha2 is the remaining weight to sum to 1, or specifically that the position is a convex combination of v0, v2 with weights proportional to t0, t2. 2. Compute Far Endpoint (b): The far endpoint lies on the intersection of the edge (v1, v3) and the plane through (s, v0, v2). Its Cartesian position is: b = \frac{t1}{t1 + t3} v1 + \frac{t3}{t1 + t3} v3 The relationship between f and b is: b = -\frac{t0 + t2}{t1 + t3} f This indicates that f and b are scaled versions of each other and project to the same image point. 3. Restore Winding Order: After determining the rendering order, swap the index-0 component and the index-j0 component in the "barycentric coordinates" attributes of each vertex to restore them to the original winding order. Formulas Summary: f = \frac{t0}{t0 + t2} v0 + \frac{t2}{t0 + t2} v2 b = \frac{t1}{t1 + t3} v1 + \frac{t3}{t1 + t3} v3 \mathbf{u}f = (t0 + t2)^{-1}(t0, -t1, t2, -t3) (Note: The source text lists (\alpha0, \alpha1, \alpha3), but the position formula uses v0, v2 with weights t0, t2. The barycentric vector must sum to 1. If \alpha0 = t0/(t0+t2) and \alpha2 = t2/(t0+t2), then \alpha1 + \alpha3 = 0. The source gives \alpha1 = -t1/(t0+t2) and \alpha3 = -t3/(t0+t2). Sum: (t0 - t1 + t2 - t3)/(t0+t2). Since \sum ti = 1 is not necessarily true for source barycentrics in this context (they are homogeneous or derived from inverse matrix), the explicit position formulas are the primary implementation targets.) Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The denominators (t0 + t2) and (t1 + t3) are guaranteed to be non-zero. This is because t0 and t2 have equal signs, and t1 and t3 have opposite signs. Determines thick endpoints in orthographic projection by projecting the Z-axis direction through the inverse tetrahedron matrix MT^{-1} to get a difference vector \mathbf{d} in barycentric space. Definition: The difference vector \mathbf{d} represents the change in barycentric weights as we move along the Z direction. It is calculated as \mathbf{d} = MT^{-1}(0, 0, 1, 0)^T. The actual difference vector in barycentric space for the endpoints is \mathbf{d}' = \alpha \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Compute \mathbf{d} = MT^{-1}(0, 0, 1, 0)^T. 2. Analyze the signs of the components of \mathbf{d} = (d0, d1, d2, d3)^T. 3. Triangle Case: If one sign is strictly positive (or negative) and the others are nonpositive (nonnegative), the corresponding vertex is a thick endpoint. If vertex 0 is the near endpoint (\mathbf{u}0 = (1, 0, 0, 0)^T), the far endpoint barycentric coordinates are \mathbf{u}b = d0^{-1}(0, -d1, -d2, -d3)^T. This is derived from \alpha = -d0^{-1}. 4. Quadrilateral Case: If two signs are positive and two are negative, the silhouette is a quadrilateral. Near endpoint barycentric coordinates: \mathbf{u}f = (d0 + d2)^{-1}(d0, 0, d2, 0)^T. Far endpoint barycentric coordinates: \mathbf{u}b = (d1 + d3)^{-1}(0, d1, 0, d3)^T. When to choose: Use this variant when the projection is orthographic (line of sight parallel to Z-axis) rather than perspective. It relies on the tetrahedron matrix MT and its inverse. Time Complexity: O(1) per tetrahedron, involving a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Independent of the view transform; can be computed using only the tetrahedron's local barycentric coordinates of the source. Avoids expensive projection operations for endpoint calculation. Limitations: Requires the barycentric coordinates of the source \mathbf{t} (or the matrix MT for orthographic case). Precision issues may arise if t0 + t2 or t1 + t3 are close to zero, though the sign properties guarantee they are not zero. When to use: When efficient ray-tetrahedron intersection is needed for volume rendering, particularly in projected tetrahedra algorithms. Originated in the "Projected Tetrahedra Revisited" paper by R. H. et al. (2006). The method leverages the property that the barycentric coordinates of the x-ray source with respect to the tetrahedron are independent of the view transform, allowing for efficient calculation of the thick line endpoints (the intersection segment of the ray with the tetrahedron). It is used in volume rendering techniques that rely on projected tetrahedra. Projected Tetrahedra Revisited: A Barycentric Formulation Applied to..., https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~rht//RHT%20Papers/2006/Projected%20Tetrahedra%20Revisited.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Tetrahedron Face Extraction
body: Computes the four planar faces (unit normals and distances to the origin) from a four-vertex description of a tetrahedron. It provides the exact plane representation required for analytic ray-tetrahedron intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs Input: verts, an array of four r3drvec3 vectors representing the tetrahedron vertices V0, V1, V2, V3. Output: faces, an array of four r3dplane structures. Data Structures The internal layout of r3drvec3 and r3dplane is not given in the sources. The implementation uses standard 3D vector and plane representations. Algorithm For each face i (where i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}), the face is defined by the three vertices excluding Vi. Let the vertices of face i be A, B, C. 1. Compute Edge Vectors: Calculate two edge vectors from the face vertices: \mathbf{e}1 = B - A \mathbf{e}2 = C - A 2. Compute Normal: Calculate the unnormalized normal vector using the cross product: \mathbf{n}{raw} = \mathbf{e}1 \times \mathbf{e}2 3. Normalize: Compute the magnitude |\mathbf{n}{raw}| and normalize: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}{raw}}{|\mathbf{n}{raw}|} 4. Compute Distance: The distance d to the origin is derived from the plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Using any vertex A on the plane: d = -(\mathbf{n} \cdot A) 5. Store: Assign \mathbf{n} and d to faces[i]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetrahedronfaceextraction(verts): """ verts: list of 4 Vec3 objects (V0, V1, V2, V3) returns: list of 4 Plane objects """ faces = [] # Face indices: each face excludes one vertex faceindices = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 2, 3], [0, 1, 3], [0, 1, 2]] for idx in faceindices: A = verts[idx[0]] B = verts[idx[1]] C = verts[idx[2]] # 1. Edge vectors e1 = Vec3sub(B, A) e2 = Vec3sub(C, A) # 2. Raw normal (cross product) nraw = Vec3cross(e1, e2) # 3. Normalize mag = Vec3length(nraw) if mag == 0.0: # Degenerate face: return zero vector to avoid division by zero n = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: n = Vec3scale(nraw, 1.0 / mag) # 4. Distance to origin # Plane equation: n. x + d = 0 => d = -(n. A) dotproduct = Vec3dot(n, A) d = -dotproduct # 5. Store faces.append(Plane(n, d)) return faces def Vec3sub(a, b): return Vec3(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y, a.z - b.z) def Vec3cross(a, b): return Vec3( a.y b.z - a.z b.y, a.z b.x - a.x b.z, a.x b.y - a.y b.x) def Vec3length(v): return (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) 0.5 def Vec3scale(v, s): return Vec3(v.x s, v.y s, v.z s) def Vec3dot(a, b): return a.x b.x + a.y b.y + a.z b.z class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z class Plane: def init(self, normal, distance): self.normal = normal self.distance = distance Parameters and Edge Cases Degenerate Input: If the four vertices are coplanar, the volume is zero, and at least one face will have a zero-length normal vector. The pseudocode guards against division by zero during normalization. Winding Order: The direction of the normal depends on the winding order of the vertices A, B, C. Consistent winding is required for correct inside/outside tests in subsequent intersection steps. Calculates the signed volume of a tetrahedron defined by four input vertices Pa, Pb, Pc, Pd. The return value is the signed volume; a positive value indicates a specific winding order, while a negative value indicates the opposite. This is often used to verify vertex ordering or to correct winding by swapping vertices if the volume is negative. The volume is computed as \frac{1}{6} |(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \cdot ((\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{a}))|. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per tetrahedron. It involves a constant number of vector operations (3 subtractions, 2 cross products, 1 dot product, 1 normalization). Memory: O(1) auxiliary space. The output size is fixed at 4 planes. Measured Performance and Scaling Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and numerically stable for non-degenerate tetrahedra. It provides the exact plane representation needed for analytic ray intersection. Limitations: Does not handle degenerate tetrahedra (zero volume) gracefully without explicit checks. The normal direction depends on vertex winding, which must be consistent across the mesh. When to Use Not given in the sources. Originates from the r3d library ecosystem. It is used for tetrahedral mesh preprocessing in ray tracing pipelines. Specific historical development details and authorship are not given in the sources. devonmpowell/r3d, https://github.com/devonmpowell/r3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Skeleton Parameter Minimization for Ray Intersection
head: Inverted Minima Computation, Rational Function Root Finding for SCALIS
body: This method computes the intersection of a ray with a Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) primitive by minimizing the squared distance from the ray to the skeleton curve, normalized by the local radius, rather than solving the implicit surface equation directly. It sets itself apart from direct sphere-cone intersection approaches by reducing the problem to finding the root of a linear equation, offering superior numerical stability and lower computational cost. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), skeleton segment endpoints \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, skeleton segment radius at start \tau0, and radius change \Delta \tau over the segment length L = \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0\|. Output: The ray parameter t{min} corresponding to the closest intersection point on the SCALIS surface. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and 3D vectors. Steps 1. Define Geometry: Let \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0 be the skeleton direction vector. Let \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{p}0 - \mathbf{o} be the vector from the ray origin to the skeleton start point. The skeleton point at parameter s \in [0, L] is \mathbf{p}(s) = \mathbf{p}0 + s \frac{\mathbf{u}}{L}. The radius at parameter s is \tau(s) = \tau0 + s \frac{\Delta \tau}{L}. 2. Define Objective Function: Minimize the rational function f(s) representing the squared distance from the ray to the skeleton point, normalized by the squared radius: f(s) = \frac{d{\mathbf{r}}^2(\mathbf{p}(s))}{\tau(s)^2} where d{\mathbf{r}}(\mathbf{p}) is the perpendicular distance from point \mathbf{p} to the ray. The squared distance is given by: d{\mathbf{r}}^2(\mathbf{p}(s)) = \| (\mathbf{m} + s \frac{\mathbf{u}}{L}) - ((\mathbf{m} + s \frac{\mathbf{u}}{L})^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d} \|^2 3. Compute Derivative Coefficients: Find the critical points by setting the derivative f'(s) = 0. This results in a linear equation b s + c = 0. The coefficients b and c are calculated as follows: b = \tau0 L^2 (1 - (\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{d})^2) - \Delta \tau L \mathbf{u}^T (\mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}) c = \Delta \tau \|\mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}\|^2 + \tau0 L \mathbf{u}^T (\mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}) Note: The term \mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d} represents the projection of \mathbf{m} onto the plane perpendicular to \mathbf{d}. 4. Solve for Candidate Minimum: If b \neq 0, compute the candidate parameter: s{cand} = -\frac{c}{b} If b = 0, there is no internal critical point (the function is monotonic or constant), so s{cand} is undefined. 5. Determine Global Minimum: Evaluate f(s) at the boundaries s=0 and s=L. If s{cand} exists and 0 < s{cand} < L, evaluate f(s{cand}). Select the s{min} that yields the smallest value of f(s) among the valid candidates (boundaries and internal critical point). 6. Compute Ray Parameter: Calculate the skeleton point \mathbf{p}(s{min}). Project \mathbf{p}(s{min}) orthogonally onto the ray to find t{min}: t{min} = (\mathbf{p}(s{min}) - \mathbf{o})^T \mathbf{d} Ensure t{min} is non-negative if the ray is treated as a half-ray; otherwise, clamp or reject based on application requirements. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def skeletonparamminimization(rayo, rayd, p0, p1, tau0, deltatau): """ rayo: 3D vector, ray origin rayd: 3D vector, normalized ray direction p0: 3D vector, skeleton start point p1: 3D vector, skeleton end point tau0: float, radius at p0 deltatau: float, change in radius from p0 to p1 """ L = dot(p1 - p0, p1 - p0) 0.5 if L == 0: return None # Degenerate segment u = (p1 - p0) / L # Unit skeleton direction m = p0 - rayo # Vector from ray origin to skeleton start # Precompute projection of m onto plane perpendicular to rayd mdotd = dot(m, rayd) mperp = m - rayd mdotd # Precompute projection of u onto plane perpendicular to rayd udotd = dot(u, rayd) uperp = u - rayd udotd # Coefficient b # b = tau0 L^2 (1 - (u. d)^2) - deltatau L (u. mperp) term1 = tau0 (L 2) (1 - (udotd 2)) term2 = deltatau L dot(u, mperp) b = term1 - term2 # Coefficient c # c = deltatau ||mperp||^2 + tau0 L (u. mperp) normmperpsq = dot(mperp, mperp) term3 = deltatau normmperpsq term4 = tau0 L dot(u, mperp) c = term3 + term4 # Evaluate f(s) helper # f(s) = ||mperp + s uperp||^2 / (tau0 + s deltatau/L)^2 def f(s): radius = tau0 + s (deltatau / L) if radius == 0: return float('inf') distsq = dot(mperp + uperp s, mperp + uperp s) return distsq / (radius 2) # Find smin scandidates = [0.0, L] if abs(b) > 1e-9: # Numerical guard for b=0 scand = -c / b if 0 < scand < L: scandidates.append(scand) # Evaluate and pick minimum bests = scandidates[0] minval = f(bests) for s in scandidates[1:]: val = f(s) if val < minval: minval = val bests = s # Compute intersection point on skeleton pmin = p0 + u bests # Project pmin onto ray to get tmin tmin = dot(pmin - rayo, rayd) return tmin Parameters L: Length of the skeleton segment. \tau0: Radius at the start of the segment. \Delta \tau: Total radius change over the segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Segment: If L=0, the method is undefined. Return early or handle as a sphere intersection. Zero Radius: If \tau(s) = 0 within [0, L], the function f(s) has a pole. The sources state poles are not in the range of interest for valid SCALIS primitives, but numerically, if \tau(s) approaches zero, precision issues may arise. Check for near-zero radii and handle appropriately (e.g., clamp or reject). Numerical Stability: The linear equation approach is preferred over solving the implicit surface equation (Equation 16 in) because the latter involves finding scaling factors for sphere-cone intersections, which is computationally heavier and less numerically stable. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive. The method involves a constant number of vector operations and a single linear solve. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Numerically stable, computationally efficient, avoids complex geometric logic for sphere-cone intersections. Limitations: Specific to SCALIS primitives defined by linear skeleton segments with linearly varying radii. Not directly applicable to general implicit surfaces without adaptation. When to use: When rendering SCALIS volumes where performance and stability are critical. When not to use: For primitives that do not fit the SCALIS model or when higher-order skeleton curves are used. This method originates from the work on Fast Ray Tracing of Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS). It was developed to address the computational cost and numerical instability associated with direct intersection methods for SCALIS primitives, which involve sphere-cone intersections. The approach inverts the minimization order, focusing on the skeleton parameter first. Fast Ray Tracing of Scale‐Invariant Integral Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14208, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Deformed element ray intersection
head: Wiley et al. method for deformed quadratic tetrahedra
body: This method determines the ray segments that intersect deformed finite elements, addressing the problem where the mapping from a standard element shape to physical simulation space is non-linear. It is distinct from linear tetrahedron intersection methods because it handles higher-order polynomial mappings, requiring the calculation of multiple intersection segments and an approximate inverse mapping to evaluate scalar functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a deformed finite element (specifically a quadratic tetrahedron) defined by its control points in physical space and their corresponding coordinates in the standard reference element. Output: A set of ray parameter intervals [t{\text{start}}, t{\text{end}}] representing the segments of the ray that lie within the deformed element. Data Structures The deformed element is represented by its vertices and the non-linear mapping function \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{u}) that transforms a point \mathbf{u} from the standard reference tetrahedron to physical space \mathbf{x}. Steps 1. Cast Ray: Define the ray as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Determine Intersection Segments: Find the parameter values t where the ray enters and exits the deformed element. For deformed quadratic tetrahedra, Wiley et al. provide the method to determine these segments. 3. Approximate Inverse Mapping: For any point \mathbf{x} on a valid ray segment, compute the corresponding coordinates \mathbf{u} in the standard reference element. Since an analytical inverse may not exist, it is approximated along the ray segments using polynomial splines. 4. Evaluate Scalar Function: Evaluate the scalar function defined on the standard reference element at the mapped coordinates \mathbf{u}. Formulas Ray: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} Deformed Element Mapping: \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{u}), where \mathbf{u} are coordinates in the reference tetrahedron. Inverse Mapping Approximation: \mathbf{u} \approx S(\mathbf{x}), where S is a polynomial spline approximation along the ray segment. Parameters Polynomial degree: Determined by the finite element order (e.g., quadratic for quadratic tetrahedra). Integration method: After segments are found, integration can use equally spaced sampling or Gaussian integration for smoothly varying transfer functions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Multiple Segments: A ray can intersect a deformed element in more than one segment due to non-linear deformation. Inverse Mapping Requirement: An inverse map is strictly required before the scalar function can be evaluated at a point on the ray, as the function is defined on the standard element. Numerical Precision: Solving for intersections and approximating inverse mappings with splines requires careful handling of numerical stability. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformedelementrayintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, element): """ Determines ray segments intersecting a deformed quadratic tetrahedron. """ # Step 1: Determine intersection segments for deformed quadratic tetrahedra # [Comment] The exact polynomial solving method is provided by Wiley et al. intersectionparams = element.findraysegments(rayorigin, raydirection) # Step 2: Filter and sort valid segments validparams = sorted([t for t in intersectionparams if t > 0]) segments = [] for i in range(0, len(validparams) - 1, 2): segments.append((validparams[i], validparams[i+1])) return segments def evaluatescalaratraypoint(rayorigin, raydirection, t, element): """ Evaluates the scalar function at a point on the ray within a deformed element. """ pointphysical = rayorigin + t raydirection # Step 3: Approximate inverse mapping using polynomial splines pointreference = element.approximateinversemap(pointphysical) # Step 4: Evaluate scalar function in reference space return element.scalarfunction(pointreference) def solveboundaryintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, element): # [Comment] Implements the specific polynomial root-finding method from Wiley et al. # Returns a list of t values where the ray crosses the element boundary. return [] def approximateinversespline(pointphysical, element): # [Comment] Implements the polynomial spline approximation for the inverse map # Returns coordinates u in the standard reference element. return element.inversespline.evaluate(pointphysical) This variant is used in NeRF editing contexts where a deformed tetrahedral mesh T' corresponds to an original mesh T. It bends casting rays by calculating the displacement of sampled points via barycentric interpolation. Rays are cast to the space containing the deformed mesh T'. For each sampled point, the tetrahedron in T' containing it is identified. Using the correspondence between T and T', the displacement \Delta p from the deformed vertices to the original vertices is obtained via barycentric interpolation of the four vertices of the containing tetrahedron. The displacement \Delta p is added to the sampled point's coordinate p to predict density and RGB values using a network \zeta: (\zeta(p + \Delta p), \zeta(d)) \rightarrow (\sigma, c). A pitfall is that sampled points outside the tetrahedral mesh T' are not moved, meaning parts of the ray outside the mesh are not bent. Complexity: The complexity is dominated by solving intersection equations and evaluating multiple segments. Performance: Gaussian integration improves accuracy for smoothly varying transfer functions. Strengths: Handles non-linear deformations accurately. Limitations: Requires complex inverse mapping approximations; multiple intersection segments increase computational cost. When to use: Visualizing data on deformed finite element meshes where linear approximations are insufficient. The method was introduced by Wiley et al. [57] for determining ray segments intersecting deformed quadratic tetrahedra. It addresses the challenges of volume rendering with finite elements where the mapping to physical space is non-linear. name: Ray Bending via Deformation Field
head: Barycentric interpolation ray displacement, Discrete deformation field ray bending
body: Ray Bending via Deformation Field is a technique for rendering deformed radiance fields by correcting the sampling coordinates of rays cast through a deformed tetrahedral mesh. It solves the problem of visual inconsistency that arises when a neural radiance field (NeRF) is associated with a static geometry but the underlying physical object undergoes non-linear deformation. Unlike standard volume rendering which assumes a fixed spatial mapping, this method uses a discrete deformation field derived from a tetrahedral mesh to map sampled points back to their original "effective space" before querying the neural network. It builds on Deformed element ray intersection to handle the non-linear mapping from standard element shapes to physical space. Inputs: A deformed tetrahedral mesh T' representing the current state of the object. A reference (undeformed) tetrahedral mesh T representing the original geometry. A correspondence mapping between vertices of T and T'. A trained neural network \zeta (e.g., a NeRF) that maps coordinates and view directions to density \sigma and color c. Ray origin o and direction d. Outputs: Density \sigma and color c for each sample point along the ray. Data Structures: Tetrahedral Mesh (T, T'): Defined by a set of vertices V and a set of tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron is defined by 4 vertex indices. The correspondence is stored as a mapping M: V' \rightarrow V, where M(v') is the index of the corresponding vertex in the undeformed mesh for a vertex v' in the deformed mesh. Displacement Field: Implicitly stored as the vector difference between corresponding vertices: \Delta v = v{undeformed} - v{deformed}. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast rays from the camera into the space containing the deformed tetrahedral mesh T'. 2. Point Location: For each sampled point p along the ray, determine which tetrahedron t \in T' contains p. If p is not inside any tetrahedron in T', the point is considered outside the object. 3. Vertex Displacement Retrieval: For the tetrahedron t containing p, retrieve the four vertices v'1, v'2, v'3, v'4 from the deformed mesh T'. Using the correspondence mapping, find the corresponding undeformed vertices v1, v2, v3, v4 from mesh T. Calculate the displacement for each vertex: \Delta vi = vi - v'i. 4. Barycentric Interpolation: Calculate the barycentric coordinates (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4) of point p with respect to the deformed tetrahedron t. Compute the interpolated displacement \Delta p: \Delta p = \sum{i=1}^{4} \lambdai \Delta vi 5. Coordinate Correction: Add the displacement to the sampled point coordinate to obtain the corrected coordinate p{corr} in the effective space: p{corr} = p + \Delta p 6. Neural Query: Query the neural network \zeta with the corrected coordinate and the view direction d to predict density and color: (\sigma, c) = \zeta(p{corr}, d) Formula: The final prediction for a sample point p with view direction d is given by: (\sigma, c) = \zeta(p + \Delta p, d) Where: p is the sampled point coordinate in the deformed space. \Delta p is the interpolated displacement vector. \zeta is the neural network (e.g., MLP). d is the view direction. Parameters: Sampling Density: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. Neural Network Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Outside Mesh: Sampled points that are not within the tetrahedral mesh T' are not moved. The part of the ray outside the tetrahedral mesh will not be bent, and the original coordinate p is used for querying \zeta. Precision: Barycentric coordinate calculation must be robust to ensure \sum \lambdai = 1 and \lambdai \ge 0 for points inside the tetrahedron. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If the deformed tetrahedron has zero volume (degenerate), barycentric coordinates are undefined. This is not explicitly handled in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raybending(psample, raydirection, deformedmesh, undeformedmesh, correspondencemap, neuralnetwork): """ Calculate density and color for a sample point using ray bending. Args: psample: 3D coordinate of the sample point in deformed space. raydirection: View direction vector. deformedmesh: Tetrahedral mesh T' with vertices V' and tetrahedra. undeformedmesh: Tetrahedral mesh T with vertices V. correspondencemap: Dictionary mapping vertex index in T' to vertex index in T. neuralnetwork: Function or model to query for (sigma, color). Returns: sigma: Density. color: RGB color. """ # Step 2: Find containing tetrahedron in deformed mesh tetidx = findcontainingtetrahedron(psample, deformedmesh) if tetidx is None: # Point is outside the mesh; no bending pcorrected = psample else: # Step 3: Get vertices and displacements # Get indices of the 4 vertices of the tetrahedron in deformed mesh vprimeindices = deformedmesh.tetrahedra[tetidx] vprimes = [deformedmesh.vertices[i] for i in vprimeindices] # Get corresponding undeformed vertices vindices = [correspondencemap[vidx] for vidx in vprimeindices] vundeformed = [undeformedmesh.vertices[i] for i in vindices] # Calculate vertex displacements: vundeformed - vdeformed displacements = [vu - vp for vu, vp in zip(vundeformed, vprimes)] # Step 4: Barycentric interpolation # Calculate barycentric coordinates of psample relative to vprimes lambdas = computebarycentriccoordinates(psample, vprimes) # Interpolate displacement deltap = sum(l d for l, d in zip(lambdas, displacements)) # Step 5: Coordinate correction pcorrected = psample + deltap # Step 6: Neural query sigma, color = neuralnetwork(pcorrected, raydirection) return sigma, color def computebarycentriccoordinates(p, vertices): """ Compute barycentric coordinates of point p relative to a tetrahedron defined by 4 vertices. Returns a tuple (lambda1, lambda2, lambda3, lambda4). """ v0, v1, v2, v3 = vertices # Vector from v0 to p v0p = p - v0 # Vectors from v0 to other vertices v0v1 = v1 - v0 v0v2 = v2 - v0 v0v3 = v3 - v0 # Compute dot products d00 = dot(v0v1, v0v1) d01 = dot(v0v1, v0v2) d02 = dot(v0v1, v0v3) d11 = dot(v0v2, v0v2) d12 = dot(v0v2, v0v3) d22 = dot(v0v3, v0v3) dvp0 = dot(v0p, v0v1) dvp1 = dot(v0p, v0v2) dvp2 = dot(v0p, v0v3) # Solve linear system for barycentric coordinates # This is a simplified representation; in practice, solve the 3x3 system # [d00 d01 d02] [l1] [dvp0] # [d01 d11 d12] [l2] = [dvp1] # [d02 d12 d22] [l3] [dvp2] # l0 = 1 - l1 - l2 - l3 # Placeholder for actual linear solver l1, l2, l3 = solvelinearsystem([[d00, d01, d02], [d01, d11, d12], [d02, d12, d22]], [dvp0, dvp1, dvp2]) l0 = 1.0 - l1 - l2 - l3 return (l0, l1, l2, l3) Tensor Field Ray Bending is a visualization method where parallel rays are issued toward a tensor field and bent by a transforming force derived from the local tensor value. It solves the problem of visual clutter inherent in glyph-based methods by projecting the integrated effects of the tensor field onto a 2D receiving plane or by rendering bent ray tubes, revealing spatially continuous deformation patterns. Unlike path tracing which renders 1D line glyphs, this method uses image distortion or photon distribution to show 2D features and continuous changes through image deformation. It differs from Hesselink's hyperstreamline algorithm by not requiring symmetric tensors and by providing flexibility to control path traces via a scaling parameter. Time Complexity: The method requires finding the containing tetrahedron for each sample point, which is O(\log N) or O(N) depending on the spatial acceleration structure used (e.g., BVH, grid). Barycentric interpolation is O(1). Neural network query is O(D) where D is the network depth/width. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the deformed and undeformed tetrahedral meshes and the correspondence map. Memory usage is proportional to the number of vertices and tetrahedra. Strengths: Allows for non-rigid editing of NeRFs by leveraging geometric deformation fields. It maintains the visual quality of the original NeRF while adapting to the new geometry. Limitations: Only bends rays within the tetrahedral mesh. Points outside the mesh are not bent, which may cause artifacts at the boundaries if the deformation is significant. The quality depends on the accuracy of the tetrahedral mesh and the correspondence mapping. When to use: When rendering deformed objects represented by a tetrahedral mesh and a pre-trained NeRF. When not to use: When the deformation is not well-represented by a tetrahedral mesh or when the object is not enclosed by a mesh. The method was introduced in "NeRF-Editing: Geometry Editing of Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the challenge of editing NeRFs by incorporating geometric deformations. The approach utilizes discrete transformations from a deformed tetrahedral mesh to bend casting rays, allowing for the editing of NeRFs of general models. The method was tested on synthetic data and real scenes, demonstrating its ability to edit objects into different poses and render them under different views. name: Tensor Field Ray Bending
head: Bending rule, Ray direction update
body: Tensor Field Ray Bending is a visualization method where parallel rays are issued toward a tensor field and bent by a transforming force derived from the local tensor value. It solves the problem of visual clutter inherent in glyph-based methods by projecting the integrated effects of the tensor field onto a 2D receiving plane or by rendering bent ray tubes, revealing spatially continuous deformation patterns. Unlike path tracing which renders 1D line glyphs, this method uses image distortion or photon distribution to show 2D features and continuous changes through image deformation. It differs from Hesselink's hyperstreamline algorithm by not requiring symmetric tensors and by providing flexibility to control path traces via a scaling parameter. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor field T(P) defined over a volume, a set of initial parallel rays with direction D0 and position P0, a time step \Delta t, and user-specified constants a and b for the scaling parameter. Output: A set of bent ray paths (trajectories) and their deformed cross-sections (ellipses or tubes). Data Structures: Tensor Field: A 3D grid or volume where each voxel contains a tensor T(P) (typically a 3 \times 3 matrix). Ray State: For each ray, store current position P, current direction D (normalized), and current velocity V (normalized, V=D). Parameters: \Delta t: Time step increment. Not given in the sources. a, b: User-specified constants for the linear scaling parameter s(\lambda) = a + b\lambda. \lambda: Wavelength of the ray. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Issue a set of parallel rays toward the tensor field. For each ray, initialize position P and direction D. 2. Tensor Lookup: At the current ray position P, retrieve the local tensor value T(P) from the tensor field. 3. Bending Force Calculation: Calculate the net bending force \Delta Dt as the product of the tensor and the current ray direction: \Delta Dt = T(P) \cdot Dt \quad (3) where Dt is the direction of the ray at time step t. 4. Direction Update: Update the ray direction using the bending rule. First, compute the tentative new direction by adding a fraction of the bending force to the current direction, scaled by the ray flexibility s(\lambda) and the time step \Delta t: D{t+1} = \frac{Dt + s(\lambda) \cdot \Delta Dt \Delta t}{\|Dt + s(\lambda) \cdot \Delta Dt \Delta t\|} \quad (4) The new direction is normalized at the end of each step. 5. Velocity Update (Differential Form): Alternatively, or concurrently, update the normalized velocity V(t) using the differential form of the bending rule: V'(t) = s(\lambda)\left(T(P) \cdot V - \frac{V^T \cdot T(P) \cdot V}{V^T \cdot V} V\right) \quad (5) where V(t) = P'(t) is the normalized velocity. Note that V^T \cdot T(P) \cdot V is a scalar and V is a vector, so the term \frac{V^T \cdot T(P) \cdot V}{V^T \cdot V} V projects the tensor action onto the direction of V. 6. Position Update: Update the ray position P using the new direction/velocity. (Not explicitly given in the sources, but implied by V(t) = P'(t)). Standard integration: P{t+1} = Pt + V{t+1} \cdot \Delta t. 7. Cross-Section Encoding: To encode information in other eigendirections along the ray trajectory, use elliptical cross sections. The shape of the ellipse is determined by the eigenvalues of T(P). 8. Rendering: Draw all bent rays within the tensor field simultaneously. Render ellipses individually or assemble them to form a tube for visualization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tensorfieldraybending(tensorfield, initialrays, a, b, deltat): """ Simulates ray bending through a tensor field. Args: tensorfield: A function or data structure T(P) returning a 3x3 matrix. initialrays: List of Ray objects with initial P and D. a, b: Constants for scaling parameter s(lambda) = a + blambda. deltat: Time step for integration. Returns: List of Ray trajectories (lists of points). """ trajectories = [] for ray in initialrays: P = ray.P D = ray.D # Ensure D is normalized D = D / norm(D) V = D trajectory = [P] # Note: lambda and s(lambda) are not defined in the source for specific rays. # We assume a constant slambda for this simulation or it is passed per ray. # The source defines s(lambda) = a + blambda. # Since lambda is not specified, we use a placeholder or assume slambda is provided. # For implementation completeness, we assume slambda is a parameter. # If not, this step requires external input. slambda = getscalingparameter(ray.lambdavalue, a, b) while P is within tensorfield bounds: # 1. Get local tensor TP = tensorfield(P) # 2. Calculate bending force: Delta Dt = T(P) Dt deltaDt = matrixvectormultiply(TP, D) # 3. Update direction: D{t+1} = normalize(Dt + s(lambda) Delta Dt deltat) newDunnormalized = vectoradd(D, vectorscale(deltaDt, slambda deltat)) D = vectornormalize(newDunnormalized) # 4. Update velocity (optional, if using differential form for V) # V'(t) = s(lambda) (T(P) V - (V^T T(P) V / V^T V) V) # Note: V^T T(P) V is a scalar. V^T V is a scalar (norm squared). # Since V is normalized, V^T V = 1. # So: V'(t) = s(lambda) (T(P) V - (V^T T(P) V) V) Tv = matrixvectormultiply(TP, V) scalarterm = dotproduct(V, Tv) # V^T T(P) V projectionterm = vectorscale(V, scalarterm) Vprime = vectorscale(vectorsubtract(Tv, projectionterm), slambda) # Update velocity to new direction (assuming V tracks D) V = D # 5. Update position P = vectoradd(P, vectorscale(V, deltat)) trajectory.append(P) trajectories.append(trajectory) return trajectories def getscalingparameter(lambdaval, a, b): return a + b lambdaval Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sensitivity to Wavelength: A slight change in \lambda may cause noticeable variations in the result. Results must be interpreted in conjunction with the choice of \lambda. Visual Clutter: Bent rays may cross each other (intersect themselves or one another) with no inherent guarantee against intersection. Clutter increases with the number of rays, requiring experimentation to find a balance. Symmetry: The method does not require symmetric tensors. It can handle shearing, converging, and rotating properties directly. A rendering technique that visualizes the internal convergent and divergent properties of a tensor volume by treating the volume as an optical element (lens or prism) that distorts light rays. It solves the problem of visual clutter inherent in glyph-based methods by projecting the integrated effects of the tensor field onto a 2D receiving plane, revealing spatially continuous deformation patterns. Unlike path tracing which renders 1D line glyphs, this method uses image distortion or photon distribution to show 2D features and continuous changes through image deformation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of rays, steps per ray, and tensor lookup cost. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on storing ray trajectories and tensor field. Strengths: Does not require symmetric tensors. Shows shearing, converging, and rotating properties. Provides flexibility to control path traces via s(\lambda). When s(\lambda) \rightarrow \infty, the normalized version of P^t(t) is the principle eigenvector of T(P(t)), making major hyperstreamlines a special case. Limitations: Rays may intersect, causing visual clutter. Sensitive to the choice of \lambda. When to use: When analyzing tensor fields with non-symmetric components or when exploring how different "wavelengths" (flexibility) affect ray paths to reveal different tensor properties. When not to use: When visual clutter from intersecting rays is unacceptable and alternative methods like photon distribution are not suitable. Origin: The method was introduced in "Interaction of Light and Tensor Fields". History: It is based on the idea of treating the tensor field as a transforming force that bends simulated light rays. It extends the concept of hyperstreamlines by allowing non-symmetric tensors and variable flexibility. Usage: Used in scientific visualization to understand the underlying nature of tensor volumes by observing the effects on bent rays. name: Tensor Field Ray Bending (Visualization Method)
head: Lens Simulation, Photon Distribution
body: Tensor Field Ray Bending (Visualization Method) is a rendering technique that visualizes the internal convergent and divergent properties of a tensor volume by treating the volume as an optical element (lens or prism) that distorts light rays. It solves the problem of visual clutter inherent in glyph-based methods by projecting the integrated effects of the tensor field onto a 2D receiving plane, revealing spatially continuous deformation patterns. Unlike path tracing which renders 1D line glyphs, this method uses image distortion or photon distribution to show 2D features and continuous changes through image deformation. The method operates by tracing rays through a tensor volume using a specific bending rule derived from the local tensor values. It manifests in two primary variants: Photon Distribution (forward tracing) and Lens Simulation (backward tracing). Both variants rely on the same underlying ray bending mechanics but differ in ray direction, source, and output interpretation. Input: A 3D tensor field T(\mathbf{x}) defined over a volume; a receiving plane (screen) positioned relative to the volume; for Lens Simulation, an original source image I{src}; for Photon Distribution, a light source emitting white light. Output: A 2D image on the receiving plane. In Photon Distribution, this is a distribution pattern of photon deposits representing convergence/divergence. In Lens Simulation, this is a distorted version of I{src}. Tensor Field: Stored as a 3D grid or sparse structure where each cell contains a tensor value (e.g., a 3 \times 3 matrix). The exact layout depends on the underlying volume representation (e.g., regular grid, unstructured tetrahedra). Ray State: A ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and current position \mathbf{x}. Receiving Plane: A 2D buffer or image array where ray intersections are recorded. Photon Deposit (Photon Distribution): A data structure accumulating ray hits on the receiving plane, potentially weighted by color components (R, G, B). The core mechanism is the alteration of ray direction \mathbf{d} as it traverses the tensor field. The bending force is derived from the local tensor value T(\mathbf{x}). While the specific mathematical formula for the bending force is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, it is described as a "transforming force" that deforms the ray path. The path of a ray is the integral of these bending forces along the path. This variant simulates the tensor volume as a prism dispersing white light. 1. Setup: Position the tensor volume between a light source and a receiving plane. 2. Light Emission: Shoot beams of white light toward the tensor field. White light is represented as having equal amounts of red, green, and blue components. 3. Ray Tracing: Trace rays through the tensor volume. Different wavelengths (colors) have different indices of refraction, causing their bent paths to differ slightly. Apply the bending rule at each step within the volume to update the ray direction. 4. Photon Deposit: When rays exit the tensor field, record their intersections on the receiving plane. Rays of different wavelengths originating from the same direction and position will land at different positions on the receiving plane. These intersections act as photon deposits, forming a distribution pattern similar to photon mapping. 5. Image Generation: Combine the distribution patterns from different wavelengths (colors) to generate the final image. The resulting image represents the converging and diverging properties of the tensor field. This variant simulates the tensor volume as a lens distorting an image. 1. Setup: Position the tensor volume between an original image I{src} and a receiving plane (viewer). 2. Ray Casting: Cast a set of parallel rays from the pixels of I{src} toward the viewer, passing through the tensor volume. This is analogous to backward ray tracing. 3. Ray Bending: While rays are within the tensor field, alter their directions using the bending force defined by the local tensors. 4. Intersection: Let rays leave the field in different locations and orientations. Record where they hit the receiving plane. 5. Image Reconstruction: Generate a distorted image on the receiving plane. Color each pixel on the receiving plane according to the color of the corresponding pixel from the original image I{src}. Assign texture coordinates of each hit point to the original pixel, preserving neighborhood information. Ray Flexibility: The sensitivity of the ray paths to the bending rule parameters. Changing ray flexibility results in different paths. Wavelengths: For Photon Distribution, at least three wavelengths (Red, Green, Blue) are used to simulate white light dispersion. Viewing Angles: Multiple images from different angles are recommended to determine local tensor properties, as each ray represents an integrated sum of effects. Sensitivity to Parameters: The algorithm is sensitive to the parameters used in the bending rule. Paths differ when ray flexibility changes. Interpretation Difficulty: Each ray represents the integrated sum of tensor effects along its entire path. It is difficult to determine local tensor properties from a single image. Multiple images from different angles are required for accurate local analysis. Visual Clutter: While this method reduces clutter compared to path tracing (glyphs), improper parameter tuning can still lead to ambiguous patterns. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tensorfieldraybending(tensorfield, method, receivingplane, originalimage=None): """ Visualize tensor field effects using ray bending. Args: tensorfield: 3D structure containing tensor values T(x). method: 'photondistribution' or 'lenssimulation'. receivingplane: 2D buffer for recording ray hits. originalimage: Source image for lens simulation (required if method is 'lenssimulation'). Returns: 2D image on the receiving plane. """ if method == 'photondistribution': return photondistributionalgorithm(tensorfield, receivingplane) elif method == 'lenssimulation': if originalimage is None: raise ValueError("Original image required for lens simulation") return lenssimulationalgorithm(tensorfield, receivingplane, originalimage) else: raise ValueError("Unknown method") def photondistributionalgorithm(tensorfield, receivingplane): """ Simulates tensor volume as a prism dispersing white light. """ # Initialize receiving plane buffer for R, G, B components photonbufferR = zeroslike(receivingplane) photonbufferG = zeroslike(receivingplane) photonbufferB = zeroslike(receivingplane) # Define wavelengths for white light wavelengths = [ {'color': 'R', 'indexofrefraction': nred}, # Not given in sources, placeholder for implementation {'color': 'G', 'indexofrefraction': ngreen}, # Not given in sources, placeholder for implementation {'color': 'B', 'indexofrefraction': nblue} # Not given in sources, placeholder for implementation ] for wl in wavelengths: # Shoot beams of white light (equal components, but traced separately for dispersion) # Note: Sources say "shoot beams of white light... equal amounts of R, G, B" # but then "different wavelengths have different indices... end up with different positions". # This implies tracing R, G, B rays separately from the same source points. rays = generatewhitelightrays() # Not given in sources, assumes uniform grid or random sampling for ray in rays: currentray = ray # Trace through tensor volume while currentray.isinside(tensorfield): # Apply bending force based on local tensor T(x) # Formula for bending force not given in sources bendingforce = computebendingforce(tensorfield.gettensor(currentray.position), wl['indexofrefraction']) currentray.direction += bendingforce dt # Advance ray currentray.position += currentray.direction dt # Record intersection on receiving plane hitpoint = currentray.intersect(receivingplane) if hitpoint is not None: if wl['color'] == 'R': photonbufferR[hitpoint] += 1 elif wl['color'] == 'G': photonbufferG[hitpoint] += 1 elif wl['color'] == 'B': photonbufferB[hitpoint] += 1 # Combine distribution patterns finalimage = combinebuffers(photonbufferR, photonbufferG, photonbufferB) return finalimage def lenssimulationalgorithm(tensorfield, receivingplane, originalimage): """ Simulates tensor volume as a lens distorting an image. Uses backward ray tracing. """ distortedimage = zeroslike(receivingplane) # Cast parallel rays from original image toward viewer for y in range(originalimage.height): for x in range(originalimage.width): # Ray origin is on the original image plane rayorigin = getpixelposition(originalimage, x, y) raydirection = vectortoviewer # Not given in sources, assumes fixed view direction currentray = Ray(rayorigin, raydirection) # Trace through tensor volume while currentray.isinside(tensorfield): # Alter ray direction using bending force defined on tensors # Formula for bending force not given in sources tensorval = tensorfield.gettensor(currentray.position) bendingforce = computebendingforce(tensorval) currentray.direction += bendingforce dt # Advance ray currentray.position += currentray.direction dt # Ray leaves field, hits receiving plane hitpoint = currentray.intersect(receivingplane) if hitpoint is not None: # Color pixel according to original image pixel # Assign texture coordinates to preserve neighborhood info distortedimage[hitpoint] = originalimage[x, y] return distortedimage Renders 1D line glyphs along bent ray paths. Prone to visual clutter. Link Forward tracing variant. Treats volume as a prism. Good for showing convergence/divergence via color dispersion. Link Backward tracing variant. Treats volume as a lens. Good for showing spatially continuous deformation of an image. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and the number of steps per ray within the tensor volume. Since rays are traced through the entire volume, complexity is proportional to N{rays} \times N{steps}. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the tensor field and the receiving plane buffer. For Photon Distribution, buffers for R, G, B components are needed. Strengths: Reveals 2D features and spatially continuous depiction of tensor properties. Shows continuous changes through image deformation. Can work directly with non-symmetric tensor fields without decomposition. Lens Simulation avoids the visual clutter of path tracing. Limitations: Interpretation difficulty: Rays represent integrated effects, making local analysis hard without multiple views. Sensitive to bending rule parameters (ray flexibility). When to Use: When the goal is to visualize the global convergent/divergent nature of a tensor field or to see how it distorts an image, rather than tracking individual streamlines. When Not to Use: When local tensor properties need to be determined from a single view, or when high precision in ray path tracking is required without parameter tuning. The method was introduced in the paper "Interaction of Light and Tensor Fields" by the authors of the VISSYM 2003 proceedings. It is part of a suite of three new techniques (Path Tracing, Photon Distribution, Lens Simulation) designed to analyze complex tensor fields. The approach is inspired by optical phenomena such as caustics, photon mapping, and lens distortion. It allows for the visualization of non-symmetric tensor fields and leverages the continuity of ray paths to reveal internal properties.
