name: Mesh Shader Tetrahedron Intersection Optimization
head: Accelerated intersections using wave intrinsics within a mesh shader, Optimized Cyrus-Beck for tetrahedra
body: This method optimizes the ray-tetrahedron intersection test by leveraging mesh shader wave intrinsics to share geometric data among the four vertices of a single tetrahedron. It reduces redundant memory loads by a factor of four and lowers the computational cost of the intersection routine to approximately 12 floating-point operations (FLOPs). Unlike naive implementations that load tetrahedron data independently for each vertex, this approach precomputes plane parameters in the mesh shader and computes final distances in the fragment shader, building on the standard Cyrus-Beck algorithm. The method splits the intersection calculation between a mesh shader (for precomputation) and a fragment shader (for final distance calculation). It assumes a tetrahedron is defined by four vertices and four outward-facing triangular faces. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, passed as uniform or per-ray data. Vertex positions of the tetrahedron, accessible via wave intrinsics. tetVertexId: An identifier for the current vertex within the tetrahedron (0–3). Outputs: planeN: A vector of four numerators for the plane equations, one per face. planeD: A vector of four denominators for the plane equations, one per face. Static Lookup Table (kTetTriangles) A constant array of 4 uint4 vectors defining the vertex indices for the 4 faces of a tetrahedron. The indices are ordered to ensure outward-facing normals. \text{kTetTriangles} = \begin{bmatrix} 0, 2, 1, 3 \\ 1, 2, 3, 0 \\ 0, 3, 2, 1 \\ 3, 0, 1, 2 \end{bmatrix} Each row i corresponds to the face opposite vertex i. The three indices define the triangle vertices. 1. Face Index Retrieval: For the current vertex tetVertexId, retrieve the face index tri from kTetTriangles[tetVertexId]. 2. Normal Computation: Compute the outward-facing normal \mathbf{n} for the triangle defined by tri. The vertices of the triangle are accessed using wave intrinsics to read the positions of the other lanes in the wave group. \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[2]} - \mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[0]}) \times (\mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[1]} - \mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[0]}) Where \mathbf{v}{\text{idx}} is the position of the vertex with index idx, retrieved via WaveReadLaneAt. 3. Plane Numerator: Compute the numerator for the plane equation. Let \mathbf{v}0 be the position of the first vertex of the triangle (tri[0]). \text{num} = \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{o}) Broadcast this scalar num to all lanes in the wave group to populate the planeN vector. 4. Plane Denominator: Compute the denominator for each lane. The normal \mathbf{n} is broadcasted to the specific lane. \text{planeD}{\text{lane}} = \mathbf{n}{\text{lane}} \cdot \mathbf{d} 5. Normalization: In the fragment shader, normalize the denominator by the length of the ray direction \mathbf{d}. \text{planeD}' = \frac{\text{planeD}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} 6. Intersection Parameters: Compute the intersection parameter t for each plane. ti = \frac{\text{planeN}i}{\text{planeD}'i} 7. Entry and Exit Distances: t{\text{enter}} = \max \{ ti \mid \text{planeD}'i > 0 \}. If no such i exists, t{\text{enter}} = -\infty. t{\text{exit}} = \min \{ ti \mid \text{planeD}'i < 0 \}. If no such i exists, t{\text{exit}} = +\infty. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshshaderintersect(rayorigin, raydir, tetvertexid, vertexpositions): # Static lookup table for outward-facing faces kTetTriangles = [ (0, 2, 1, 3), (1, 2, 3, 0), (0, 3, 2, 1), (3, 0, 1, 2) ] # Base lane index for this tetrahedron baselane = (wavegetlaneindex() // 4) 4 # Helper to read vertex position from another lane def getvertex(idx): return wavereadlaneat(vertexpositions, baselane + idx) # Get face indices for the current vertex tri = kTetTriangles[tetvertexid] # Compute outward facing normal n v0 = getvertex(tri[0]) v1 = getvertex(tri[1]) v2 = getvertex(tri[2]) edge1 = v2 - v0 edge2 = v1 - v0 n = cross(edge1, edge2) # Compute numerator num = dot(n, v0 - rayorigin) num = dot(n, v0 - rayorigin) # Each lane constructs a vector of 4 numerators by reading num from all 4 lanes planeN = [wavereadlaneat(num, baselane + i) for i in range(4)] # Each lane constructs a vector of 4 denominators by reading n from all 4 lanes and dotting with raydir planeD = [dot(wavereadlaneat(n, baselane + i), raydir) for i in range(4)] return planeN, planeD def fragmentshaderintersect(planeN, planeD, raydir): # Normalize denominator by ray direction length dlen = length(raydir) planeDnorm = [d / dlen for d in planeD] # Compute t for each plane allt = [n / d for n, d in zip(planeN, planeDnorm)] # Compute tenter: max t where planeD > 0 tenter = float('-inf') for i in range(4): if planeDnorm[i] > 0.0: if allt[i] > tenter: tenter = allt[i] # Compute texit: min t where planeD < 0 texit = float('inf') for i in range(4): if planeDnorm[i] < 0.0: if allt[i] < texit: texit = allt[i] return tenter, texit kTetTriangles: Static constant array. Values are fixed as shown in the Data Structures section. Redundant Loads: The naive version loads tetrahedron information for each of the 4 vertices separately, leading to redundant memory loads. This method avoids this by sharing information between vertices in the mesh shader. Wave Size: The method assumes a wave size of at least 4 to accommodate the 4 vertices of a tetrahedron. Parallel Gather Semantics: The pseudocode uses list comprehensions for clarity, but in hardware these operations execute in parallel across the wave lanes to gather num and n values. Time Complexity: The optimized implementation reduces the runtime cost to only 12 FLOPs for the intersection calculation. Memory Access: Reduces memory loads by a factor of four compared to the naive version by leveraging wave intrinsics to share data among vertices. Strengths: Significant reduction in computational cost and memory bandwidth usage for tetrahedral mesh rendering. Limitations: Requires hardware support for mesh shaders and wave intrinsics. The method is specific to tetrahedral primitives. This method addresses the inefficiency of naive ray-tetrahedron intersection tests in volumetric rendering by exploiting the parallel execution model of mesh shaders. It is a specialized application of the Cyrus-Beck algorithm. Radiance Meshes for Volumetric Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04076v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Raytracing Cell-Organized Irregular Volumes
head: Cell-based volume raytracing, Raytracing irregular volume data
body: This method renders volumetric data defined by unstructured or irregular cell grids (such as tetrahedra or hexahedra) by traversing the cell structure along a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently visiting cells intersected by a ray in non-uniform geometries where regular grid acceleration structures are not applicable. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly handling the topological connectivity of irregular cells and managing concave dataset boundaries, which can cause rays to exit and re-enter the volume multiple times. The method traverses a cell-organized irregular volume by stepping from cell to cell along a ray. It relies on the geometric intersection of the ray with the faces of the cells to determine entry and exit points. Input: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{d} and direction \mathbf{c}; irregular volume dataset composed of cells (e.g., tetrahedra, hexahedra) with associated vertex positions and face connectivity; scalar or vector field values at vertices. Output: Integrated optical properties (color, opacity) along the ray path within the volume. Cell: Contains a list of vertices and a list of faces. Face: Defined by three vertices for tetrahedra or four for hexahedra; for tetrahedra, a face is a triangle. The face stores the precomputed cross product of its edge vectors to accelerate intersection tests. Exposed Faces: The set of faces on the boundary of the dataset that are not shared with another cell. These define the entry and exit points for the ray when it leaves the volume. 1. Initial Intersection: Intersect the ray against all exposed faces of the dataset to find the first entry point. 2. Cell Traversal: Identify the cell adjacent to the current face. Intersect the ray with all faces of the current cell to find the exit face. Use the barycentric coordinate test to verify if the intersection point lies within the triangular face. If the intersection point is inside the face, the ray passes through to the adjacent cell. If the face is not shared by another cell, the ray has exited the dataset. 3. Re-entry Handling: If the ray exits the dataset, intersect the ray against all remaining exposed faces to find a new entry point. This is necessary because irregular volumes can be concave, allowing the ray to intersect the surface in multiple locations. 4. Integration: For each cell traversed, integrate the volume properties along the segment inside the cell. 5. Termination: Stop when the ray has exited the dataset and no further re-entries are found, or when the ray direction parameter exceeds a maximum distance. Plane Intersection: The intersection parameter t for a ray defined by point \mathbf{d} (origin) and vector \mathbf{c} (direction) with a plane defined by points \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} (where \mathbf{c} is also used as a point on the plane in the source notation) is given by: t = \frac{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac}) \cdot \mathbf{a} - (\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac}) \cdot \mathbf{d}}{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac}) \cdot \mathbf{c}} where \mathbf{Ab} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{Ac} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}. The cross product \mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac} is the plane normal and can be precomputed and stored with the face. Barycentric Coordinate Test: To verify if an intersection point lies inside a triangular face defined by \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} and ray direction \mathbf{e}, calculate: u = \frac{(\mathbf{Ac} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{d} - (\mathbf{Ac} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{a}}{(\mathbf{Ac} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{b}} v = \frac{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{d} - (\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{a}}{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{c}} where \mathbf{d} denotes the intersection point in this context. If u > 0, v > 0, and u + v < 1, the point is inside the face. Tessellation: For hexahedral cells, if symmetric tessellation is not possible, add a new vertex at the center of each face and subdivide into twenty-four tetrahedra. Concave Volumes: Rays may exit and re-enter the dataset. After exiting, re-intersect with all exposed faces to find new entry points. Degenerate Tetrahedra (Coincident Vertices): Two zero-area triangles and two non-degenerate triangles. Ignore zero-area triangles. If the ray enters through a non-degenerate face, it exits through the other. The distance difference dt=0, so no integration is required. Degenerate Tetrahedra (Planar): All face intersection distances are the same. Determine which two triangular faces the ray passes through the interior of (entry and exit). dt=0, so no integration is required. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytraceirregularvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volume): # Constants INF = float('inf') EPS = 1e-9 # Precomputed adjacency map: face -> cell celladjacency = {face: cell for cell in volume.cells for face in cell.faces} # 1. Initial Intersection: Find first entry point among exposed faces mint = INF entryface = None for face in volume.exposedfaces: t = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > EPS and t < mint: mint = t entryface = face if entryface is None: return None # Ray does not hit volume currentt = mint currentface = entryface accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 while True: # 2. Identify current cell adjacent to the entry face cell = celladjacency[currentface] # 3. Find exit face among cell faces exitface = None exitt = INF for face in cell.faces: if face is currentface: continue t = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > currentt + EPS: intersectionpoint = rayorigin + t raydirection if ispointintriangle(intersectionpoint, face.vertices, raydirection): if t < exitt: exitt = t exitface = face # 4. Handle exit from volume if exitface is None: # Ray exited the dataset; re-intersect with all exposed faces reentryt = INF reentryface = None for face in volume.exposedfaces: t = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > currentt + EPS and t < reentryt: reentryt = t reentryface = face if reentryface is not None: currentt = reentryt currentface = reentryface continue else: break # No further intersections # 5. Integrate through the cell dt = exitt - currentt if dt > EPS: # Integration method depends on the specific volume data representation color, opacity = integratecellproperties(cell, rayorigin, raydirection, currentt, exitt) # Standard alpha compositing accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + color (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) # 6. Move to next cell currentt = exitt currentface = exitface return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face): # Source formula: t = ((Ab x Ac). a - (Ab x Ac). d) / ((Ab x Ac). c) # Note: Source uses d for ray origin and c for ray direction (and plane point) a, b, c = face.vertices Ab = b - a Ac = c - a N = cross(Ab, Ac) # Denominator uses raydirection (source calls it c) denom = dot(N, raydirection) if abs(denom) < EPS: return INF # Numerator: N. a - N. rayorigin num = dot(N, a) - dot(N, rayorigin) return num / denom def ispointintriangle(point, vertices, raydirection): a, b, c = vertices Ab = b - a Ac = c - a e = raydirection d = point # Intersection point term1 = cross(Ac, e) unum = dot(term1, d) - dot(term1, a) uden = dot(term1, b) term2 = cross(Ab, e) vnum = dot(term2, d) - dot(term2, a) vden = dot(term2, c) if abs(uden) < EPS or abs(vden) < EPS: return False u = unum / uden v = vnum / vden return u > 0 and v > 0 and (u + v) < 1 def integratecellproperties(cell, rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend): # Integration logic depends on the specific scalar/vector field representation return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 Time Complexity: Depends on the number of cells intersected by the ray. In the worst case, this is proportional to the number of cells in the volume. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of cells and faces in the volume. Strengths: Handles irregular and unstructured grids efficiently. Can handle concave volumes correctly by re-entering the dataset. Limitations: Requires explicit connectivity information. Degenerate cells must be handled explicitly. Performance may degrade for highly complex or concave geometries due to multiple re-entries. This method was introduced in the paper "Raytracing irregular volume data". It addresses the need for rendering techniques that can handle non-uniform volumetric data, such as those arising from finite element analysis or geological modeling, where regular grid structures are not suitable. Raytracing irregular volume data, https://doi.org/10.1145/99307.99316, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Point Calculus Faceted Solid Raycasting
head: Faceted Solid Intersection in Point Calculus, Point Calculus Ray Marching, Ray-Solid Intersection via Point Calculus Edge Cases, Tetrahedron/Prism Raycasting via Point Calculus, Visualization of Geometric Models of Faceted Solids in Point Calculus
body: A GPU-accelerated raycasting method for visualizing faceted solids (e.g., tetrahedrons, prisms) defined as a three-parameter set of points in 3D space using point calculus. It determines ray-solid intersections by solving systems of equations via the Newton method, specifically by fixing edge parameters of the solid's parametric equation to 0 or 1. Unlike standard analytic distance functions or triangle rasterization, this approach aims for a complete absence of visual artifacts on faceted solids by treating the solid as a continuous parametric volume. It is distinct from Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection by using iterative numerical solving of parametric systems rather than algebraic line-plane intersections, and from Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates by computing entry/exit intervals directly through parametric edge constraints rather than discrete containment tests. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Solid definition: Four vertices of a 3D simplex A, B, C, D (coordinates \mathbf{x}A, \dots, \mathbf{x}D) and parametric functions p(u,v,w), q(u,v,w), r(u,v,w), s(u,v,w) such that p+q+r+s=1. For faceted solids like tetrahedrons, these are linear: M = Auv\bar{w} + B\bar{v}\bar{w} + C\bar{u}\bar{v}\bar{w} + Dw where \bar{u}=1-u, etc.. Camera parameters: Eye position P, target T, and screen pixel coordinates (px, py) normalized to [0,1]. Constants: Maximum tracing distance d{max}=100, numerical step \Delta=10^{-3}, max Newton iterations N{max}=100. Outputs: Color of the pixel, determined by whether the ray segment PQ lies inside the solid and Lambertian shading. Data Structures Simplex Vertices: Array of 4 vectors \{A, B, C, D\}, each 3 floats. Ray Segment: Two vectors P (origin) and Q (end). Newton State: Vector \sigma = \{x, y, z\} representing the current approximation of the unknown parameters (u, v, w, t) mapped to 3 variables. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Generation: Compute the ray direction basis vectors \vec{k}, \vec{i}, \vec{j} from the camera position P and target T: \vec{k} = \frac{T - P}{|T - P|} \vec{i} = \frac{\{0,1,0\} \times \vec{k}}{|\{0,1,0\} \times \vec{k}|} \vec{j} = \vec{i} \times \vec{k} Calculate the ray endpoint Q using pixel coordinates px, py and max distance d{max}: Q = P + \frac{\vec{i} \cdot px + \vec{j} \cdot py + \vec{k}}{|\vec{i} \cdot px + \vec{j} \cdot py + \vec{k}|} d{max} 2. Barycentric Coordinate Calculation (Tetrahedron Specific): For a tetrahedron defined by simplex ABCD, calculate the barycentric coordinates for points P and Q. First, compute the volume of the simplex V{ABCD} using the determinant: V{ABCD} = \det \begin{pmatrix} xA - xD & yA - yD & zA - zD \\ xB - xD & yB - yD & zB - zD \\ xC - xD & yC - yD & zC - zD \end{pmatrix} Compute volumes for sub-tetrahedra (e.g., V{PBCD}) similarly by replacing the first vertex with P or Q. The barycentric coordinates for P are: pP = \frac{V{PBCD}}{V{ABCD}}, \quad qP = \frac{V{APCD}}{V{ABCD}}, \quad rP = \frac{V{ABPD}}{V{ABCD}}, \quad sP = 1 - pP - qP - rP Repeat for Q to get pQ, qQ, rQ, sQ. Note: The factor 1/6 in volume calculation is omitted as it cancels out in the ratio. 3. Intersection Interval Determination (Tetrahedron Specific): Determine the parameter \lambda along the segment PQ where the ray intersects the faces. The intersection point S on face BCD (where p=0) is found at: \lambda = \frac{pP}{pP - pQ} The point S is: S = P \frac{pQ}{pQ - pP} + Q \frac{pP}{pP - pQ} Similarly, calculate \lambda for other faces. The ray segment lies inside the tetrahedron if \lambda falls within the interval defined by the entry and exit faces: \lambda \in \left[ \frac{rP}{rP - rQ}; \frac{pP}{pP - pQ} \right] If \lambda is outside this interval, the ray does not intersect the solid volume. 4. General Faceted Solid Intersection (Newton Method): For general faceted solids defined by M = A p + B q + C r + D s, equate the ray equation to the solid equation: P\bar{t} + Qt = A p(u,v,w) + B q(u,v,w) + C r(u,v,w) + D s(u,v,w) This yields a system of 3 scalar equations (x, y, z) with 4 unknowns (u, v, w, t). To solve, fix one parameter to an edge value (0 or 1) for each of the 6 systems corresponding to the solid's shells: 1. u=0, x=v, y=w, z=t 2. u=1, x=v, y=w, z=t 3. v=0, x=u, y=w, z=t 4. v=1, x=u, y=w, z=t 5. w=0, x=u, y=v, z=t 6. w=1, x=u, y=v, z=t For each system, solve for the remaining 3 unknowns using Newton's method: \sigma^{(i)} = \sigma^{(i-1)} - J(\sigma^{(i-1)})^{-1} F(\sigma^{(i-1)}) where \sigma = \{x, y, z\} maps to the specific unknowns for that system, and t is always mapped to z. Jacobian Calculation: Compute the Jacobian matrix J numerically using central differences with step \Delta = 10^{-3}: \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(\sigma) = \frac{F(\{x + \Delta, y, z\}) - F(\{x - \Delta, y, z\})}{2\Delta} The full Jacobian is: J(\sigma) = \begin{pmatrix} \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(\sigma) \right)x & \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}(\sigma) \right)x & \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}(\sigma) \right)x \\ \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(\sigma) \right)y & \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}(\sigma) \right)y & \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}(\sigma) \right)y \\ \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(\sigma) \right)z & \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}(\sigma) \right)z & \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}(\sigma) \right)z \end{pmatrix} Initialization and Degeneracy Handling: Initialize \sigma^{(0)} = \{0, 0, 0\}. Check if J(\sigma^{(0)}) is degenerate. If so, substitute the identity matrix for J to correct the first approximation. Stopping Conditions: 1. Accuracy: \sqrt{(x^{(i)} - x^{(i-1)})^2 + (y^{(i)} - y^{(i-1)})^2 + (z^{(i)} - z^{(i-1)})^2} < \Delta. 2. Max Iterations: i > 100. 5. Solution Validation: For each of the 6 systems, check if the resulting parameters (u, v, w, t) are all within the range [0, 1]. Discard solutions outside this range. If two valid solutions exist with t \in [0, 1], the ray passes through the solid. The segment between the corresponding t values is inside. If one valid solution exists, the ray touches the solid. If no valid solutions exist, there is no intersection. 6. Shading: Calculate the normal vector \vec{n} for Lambertian shading using the gradient of the distance function \delta (distance to the solid on segment PQ) via finite differences: \vec{d} = \{\delta(P + \vec{i} \cdot \Delta, Q) - \delta(P, Q), \delta(P + \vec{j} \cdot \Delta, Q) - \delta(P, Q), \delta(P + \vec{k} \cdot \Delta, Q) - \delta(P, Q)\} \vec{n} = \frac{\vec{d}}{|\vec{d}|} Apply lighting model using \vec{n} and light direction. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointcalculusfacetedsolidraycasting(A, B, C, D, pfunc, qfunc, rfunc, sfunc, Peye, Ttarget, px, py, dmax=100.0, delta=1e-3, maxiter=100): # 1. Ray Generation k = normalize(Ttarget - Peye) i = normalize(cross(vec3(0, 1, 0), k)) j = cross(i, k) raydir = normalize(i px + j py + k) Qend = Peye + raydir dmax # 2. Tetrahedron Specific Check (if solid is tetrahedron) # Calculate volumes VABCD = det(vec3(A.x-D.x, A.y-D.y, A.z-D.z), vec3(B.x-D.x, B.y-D.y, B.z-D.z), vec3(C.x-D.x, C.y-D.y, C.z-D.z)) # Helper to get barycentric coords def getbarycentric(Ppoint, Apt, Bpt, Cpt, Dpt, VABCD): VPBCD = det(vec3(Ppoint.x-Dpt.x, Ppoint.y-Dpt.y, Ppoint.z-Dpt.z), vec3(Bpt.x-Dpt.x, Bpt.y-Dpt.y, Bpt.z-Dpt.z), vec3(Cpt.x-Dpt.x, Cpt.y-Dpt.y, Cpt.z-Dpt.z)) VAPCD = det(vec3(Apt.x-Ppoint.x, Apt.y-Ppoint.y, Apt.z-Ppoint.z), vec3(Cpt.x-Dpt.x, Cpt.y-Dpt.y, Cpt.z-Dpt.z), vec3(Bpt.x-Dpt.x, Bpt.y-Dpt.y, Bpt.z-Dpt.z)) # Note: order matters for sign VABPD = det(vec3(Apt.x-Dpt.x, Apt.y-Dpt.y, Apt.z-Dpt.z), vec3(Bpt.x-Ppoint.x, Bpt.y-Ppoint.y, Bpt.z-Ppoint.z), vec3(Cpt.x-Dpt.x, Cpt.y-Dpt.y, Cpt.z-Dpt.z)) p = VPBCD / VABCD q = VAPCD / VABCD r = VABPD / VABCD s = 1.0 - p - q - r return p, q, r, s pP, qP, rP, sP = getbarycentric(Peye, A, B, C, D, VABCD) pQ, qQ, rQ, sQ = getbarycentric(Qend, A, B, C, D, VABCD) # Check intersection interval for tetrahedron # Interval [rP/(rP - rQ), pP/(pP - pQ)] # Note: This assumes specific face ordering. General case uses Newton below. # For general implementation, proceed to Newton method for robustness across solids. # 3. General Faceted Solid Intersection via Newton Method validintersections = [] # Define the 6 systems systems = [ {'fixed': ('u', 0), 'vars': ('v', 'w', 't')}, {'fixed': ('u', 1), 'vars': ('v', 'w', 't')}, {'fixed': ('v', 0), 'vars': ('u', 'w', 't')}, {'fixed': ('v', 1), 'vars': ('u', 'w', 't')}, {'fixed': ('w', 0), 'vars': ('u', 'v', 't')}, {'fixed': ('w', 1), 'vars': ('u', 'v', 't')} ] for sys in systems: fixedparam, fixedval = sys['fixed'] xvar, yvar, zvar = sys['vars'] # Initial guess sigma = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(maxiter): # Map sigma to u, v, w, t u, v, w, t = mapsigmatoparams(sigma, fixedparam, fixedval, xvar, yvar, zvar) # Evaluate F(sigma) = Ray(u,v,w,t) - Solid(u,v,w,t) # Ray point: P + t(Q-P) raypoint = Peye + t (Qend - Peye) # Solid point pval = pfunc(u, v, w) qval = qfunc(u, v, w) rval = rfunc(u, v, w) sval = sfunc(u, v, w) solidpoint = A pval + B qval + C rval + D sval Fval = raypoint - solidpoint # Check convergence if length(Fval) < delta: # Simplified convergence check based on residual # Check if parameters are in [0,1] if 0 <= u <= 1 and 0 <= v <= 1 and 0 <= w <= 1 and 0 <= t <= 1: validintersections.append(t) break # Compute Jacobian numerically J = computejacobiannumerical(sigma, fixedparam, fixedval, xvar, yvar, zvar, pfunc, qfunc, rfunc, sfunc, A, B, C, D, Peye, Qend, delta) # Check for degeneracy if isdegenerate(J): J = identitymatrix() # Newton step deltasigma = solvelinearsystem(J, Fval) sigma = sigma - deltasigma else: # Max iterations reached, no solution for this system pass # 4. Determine if inside # If two valid t values exist, the segment between them is inside if len(validintersections) >= 2: tmin = min(validintersections) tmax = max(validintersections) # Calculate normal at intersection point for shading #... (calculate normal using distance function gradient) return colorwithshading(tmin) else: return backgroundcolor def mapsigmatoparams(sigma, fixedparam, fixedval, xvar, yvar, zvar): u, v, w, t = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 if fixedparam == 'u': u = fixedval elif fixedparam == 'v': v = fixedval elif fixedparam == 'w': w = fixedval if xvar == 'u': u = sigma.x elif xvar == 'v': v = sigma.x elif xvar == 'w': w = sigma.x elif xvar == 't': t = sigma.x if yvar == 'u': u = sigma.y elif yvar == 'v': v = sigma.y elif yvar == 'w': w = sigma.y elif yvar == 't': t = sigma.y if zvar == 'u': u = sigma.z elif zvar == 'v': v = sigma.z elif zvar == 'w': w = sigma.z elif zvar == 't': t = sigma.z return u, v, w, t def computejacobiannumerical(sigma, fixedparam, fixedval, xvar, yvar, zvar, pfunc, qfunc, rfunc, sfunc, A, B, C, D, Peye, Qend, delta): # Helper to get F value for a given sigma def getF(s): u, v, w, t = mapsigmatoparams(s, fixedparam, fixedval, xvar, yvar, zvar) raypoint = Peye + t (Qend - Peye) pval = pfunc(u, v, w) qval = qfunc(u, v, w) rval = rfunc(u, v, w) sval = sfunc(u, v, w) solidpoint = A pval + B qval + C rval + D sval return raypoint - solidpoint J = mat3(0.0) # Column 1: dF/dx splus = sigma splus.x += delta sminus = sigma sminus.x -= delta J[0][0] = (getF(splus).x - getF(sminus).x) / (2 delta) J[1][0] = (getF(splus).y - getF(sminus).y) / (2 delta) J[2][0] = (getF(splus).z - getF(sminus).z) / (2 delta) # Column 2: dF/dy splus = sigma splus.y += delta sminus = sigma sminus.y -= delta J[0][1] = (getF(splus).x - getF(sminus).x) / (2 delta) J[1][1] = (getF(splus).y - getF(sminus).y) / (2 delta) J[2][1] = (getF(splus).z - getF(sminus).z) / (2 delta) # Column 3: dF/dz splus = sigma splus.z += delta sminus = sigma sminus.z -= delta J[0][2] = (getF(splus).x - getF(sminus).x) / (2 delta) J[1][2] = (getF(splus).y - getF(sminus).y) / (2 delta) J[2][2] = (getF(splus).z - getF(sminus).z) / (2 delta) return J def isdegenerate(J): # Check determinant or condition number det = J[0][0] (J[1][1]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][1]) - \ J[0][1] (J[1][0]J[2][2] - J[1][2]J[2][0]) + \ J[0][2] (J[1][0]J[2][1] - J[1][1]J[2][0]) return abs(det) < 1e-10 Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, but with a high constant factor due to solving 6 systems of equations, each requiring multiple Newton iterations (average 7-10 steps). Each iteration involves evaluating the parametric functions and computing a 3x3 Jacobian via finite differences (6 function evaluations per Jacobian). Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread. Only vertex coordinates and a few temporary vectors are stored. Measured Performance: ~60 frames per second on general-purpose monitors using GPU acceleration (ShaderToy/GLSL). Strengths: High image fidelity with complete absence of visual artifacts on faceted solids. Handles complex parametric definitions of solids. Limitations: Produces artifacts for curvilinear solids because Newton's method lacks sufficient accuracy for numerical solutions of non-linear systems in those cases. Degenerate Jacobians at the first iteration can cause loss of solution if not handled. Some edge case systems may have no solution or solutions outside [0,1]. When to use: Rendering faceted solids (tetrahedrons, prisms) where artifact-free visualization is critical and the solid can be defined in point calculus. When not to use: Rendering curvilinear solids or when high performance is required for complex scenes with many solids, due to the iterative nature and lack of convergence guarantees for non-faceted shapes. The method was introduced in the paper "Visualization of Geometric Models of Faceted Solids in Point Calculus" by Konopatskiy, Ryabinin, and Bezdytniy. It builds on the concept of defining geometric solids as a three-parameter set of points in 3D space, originally formulated in earlier works [1, 2, 3] cited in. The approach uses point calculus mathematical apparatus to solve the intersection problem analytically/numerically, leveraging modern GPU hardware acceleration via ray marching. It was implemented in GLSL and demonstrated on ShaderToy. The method is part of the broader effort to integrate scientific visualization systems like SciVi. name: Barycentric Tetrahedral Isosurface Ray Intersection
head: Unstructured mesh ray intersection
body: This method intersects a ray with an isosurface implicitly defined within a tetrahedral cell of an unstructured mesh using barycentric interpolation. It solves for the intersection parameter t by reducing the density constraint to a linear equation, distinguishing it from methods that may require quadratic solutions or explicit surface reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{a}, ray direction \vec{b} (assumed normalized), tetrahedron vertices \mathbf{p}i = (xi, yi, zi) for i=0..3, vertex densities \rhoi, and isovalue \rho{\text{iso}}. Output: Intersection parameter t, intersection point \mathbf{p}(t), and normal vector \vec{\mathbf{N}}. If no valid intersection exists, the method returns failure. Data Structures The tetrahedron is defined by four vertices. Each vertex \mathbf{p}i has associated scalar density \rhoi. Precomputed plane equations fi(\mathbf{p}) are required for efficient barycentric coordinate calculation. Plane Equation Definition For each face i opposite vertex \mathbf{p}i, define a plane equation fi(\mathbf{p}) such that fi(\mathbf{p}i) = 1 and fi(\mathbf{p}j) = 0 for j \neq i. The equation takes the form: fi(\mathbf{p}) = \vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}i) where \vec{\mathbf{n}}i is the normal vector and \mathbf{q}i is a point on the plane. The barycentric coordinate \alphai for any point \mathbf{p} is simply fi(\mathbf{p}). Steps 1. Precompute Plane Parameters: For each vertex i, determine \vec{\mathbf{n}}i and \mathbf{q}i such that fi(\mathbf{p}) = \vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}i) satisfies the barycentric conditions. Note that \vec{\mathbf{n}}i is constant for the tetrahedron. 2. Formulate Linear Equation: Substitute the ray equation \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\vec{b} into the density interpolation formula: \rho(t) = \sum{i=0}^3 fi(\mathbf{a} + t\vec{b})\rhoi = \rho{\text{iso}} Since fi(\mathbf{a} + t\vec{b}) = \vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot (\mathbf{a} + t\vec{b} - \mathbf{q}i) = \vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{q}i) + t (\vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot \vec{b}), the equation becomes linear in t: t \left( \sum{i=0}^3 \rhoi (\vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot \vec{b}) \right) + \sum{i=0}^3 \rhoi (\vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{q}i)) = \rho{\text{iso}} Let A = \sum{i=0}^3 \rhoi (\vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot \vec{b}) and B = \sum{i=0}^3 \rhoi (\vec{\mathbf{n}}i \cdot (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{q}i)) - \rho{\text{iso}}. The equation is A t + B = 0. 3. Solve for t: If |A| < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small epsilon, e.g., 10^{-30} for stability with large coefficients), the ray is parallel to the isosurface gradient or the solution is degenerate. Handle as no intersection or special case. Otherwise, t = -B / A. 4. Validate Intersection: Calculate the intersection point \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\vec{b}. Compute barycentric coordinates \alphai = fi(\mathbf{p}(t)) for all i=0..3. If \alphai > 0 for all i, the intersection is inside the tetrahedron and is accepted. Otherwise, reject. 5. Compute Normal: If accepted, compute the normal vector \vec{\mathbf{N}} as: \vec{\mathbf{N}} = \sum{i=0}^3 \rhoi \vec{\mathbf{n}}i This normal is constant within the tetrahedron for linear barycentric interpolation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def barycentrictetraisosurfaceintersect(rayorigin, raydir, tetravertices, vertexdensities, rhoiso): # Precomputed plane normals and points for the tetrahedron # n[i] is the normal vector for face i # q[i] is a point on face i # These must be precomputed such that fi(p) = dot(n[i], p - q[i]) # and fi(pj) = 1 if i==j else 0 A = 0.0 B = 0.0 for i in range(4): # Calculate dot products ndotb = dot(tetraplanenormals[i], raydir) ndotaminusq = dot(tetraplanenormals[i], rayorigin - tetraplanepoints[i]) A += vertexdensities[i] ndotb B += vertexdensities[i] ndotaminusq B -= rhoiso # Check for degenerate case where A is near zero if abs(A) < 1e-30: return None # No unique solution or parallel t = -B / A # Calculate intersection point p = rayorigin + t raydir # Check if point is inside tetrahedron using barycentric coordinates for i in range(4): alphai = dot(tetraplanenormals[i], p - tetraplanepoints[i]) if alphai <= 0: return None # Outside tetrahedron # Compute normal normal = vec3(0, 0, 0) for i in range(4): normal += vertexdensities[i] tetraplanenormals[i] return { 't': t, 'point': p, 'normal': normalize(normal) } Parameters \epsilon: Epsilon for stability check. Source suggests 10^{-30} for maximum stability with large coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate A: If A \approx 0, the ray direction is orthogonal to the effective gradient of the density field within the cell, or the density variation is negligible. The source code modifies special cases for linear or quadratic solutions, assuming A is nonzero in the standard derivation. Precision: Use high-precision arithmetic for plane equation evaluations if coefficients are large to avoid numerical instability. Uses convex hulls to accelerate ray traversal, differing in its use of explicit polygonal approximations rather than implicit barycentric interpolation. Uses Plücker coordinates for intersection tests, offering a different algebraic approach to ray-tetrahedron intersection. Provides the fundamental geometric test used in step 4 of this method. Details the geometry of tetrahedron faces, relevant for precomputing plane equations. Optimizes ray intersection by reducing the search space, a complementary optimization technique. Handles non-linear or deformed elements, whereas this method assumes linear barycentric interpolation. Focuses on GPU-specific optimizations for this type of intersection. Discusses acceleration structures for unstructured meshes, which this method operates on. An alternative approach to raycasting on unstructured grids using point calculus. Time Complexity: O(1) per tetrahedron, involving a constant number of dot products and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per tetrahedron, assuming plane parameters are precomputed and stored with the mesh. Strengths: Simple linear solution; robust with proper epsilon handling; naturally provides normals. Limitations: Assumes linear density variation within the tetrahedron; requires precomputed plane equations; sensitive to numerical precision if coefficients are large. When to Use: Ideal for unstructured tetrahedral meshes with linearly interpolated scalar fields where isosurface extraction is required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for higher-order interpolation schemes without modification; less efficient than hierarchical acceleration structures for large volumes. This method is based on the work of Schwarze, as cited in the source. The approach was implemented with modifications for stability, specifically handling cases where the linear coefficient A might be zero and using a very small epsilon (10^{-30}) for numerical stability. It is part of the broader field of interactive ray tracing for volume visualization on unstructured meshes. name: Ray-Object Intersection Test
head: Child Ray Intersection with Transformation, Ray Intersection Update, Ray-Object Intersection, raytrace
body: The Ray-Object Intersection Test determines if and where a ray intersects a specific scene object, returning the closest valid intersection distance or a failure indicator. It serves as the core decision unit in ray tracing and volume rendering pipelines, filtering out non-intersections and self-intersections via epsilon thresholds to ensure robustness. Unlike sibling primitives that solve for specific analytic shapes (e.g., Sphere Intersection), this test is a generic interface that may involve coordinate space transformations to handle arbitrary object orientations and positions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and an object (geometry definition, optional transformation matrix \mathbf{M}). Output: Distance t to the closest intersection point, hit status, object index, and surface normal. Data Structures The ray state is maintained in a structure containing: origin: Vector3D (x, y, z) direction: Vector3D (x, y, z), typically normalized. normal: Vector3D, the surface normal at the hit point. t: Float, the current closest hit distance. hit: Boolean, indicating if a valid hit has been recorded. Steps 1. Transformation (Optional): If the object has a transformation matrix \mathbf{M}, transform the ray into the object's local coordinate space. New origin: \mathbf{o}' = \mathbf{M} \cdot [\mathbf{o}, 1]^T New direction: \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{M} \cdot [\mathbf{d}, 0]^T 2. Intersection Solve: Solve the system of equations representing the ray and the object's surface geometry to find potential intersection parameters t{obj}. 3. Filtering: Check if the computed t{obj} is valid: t{obj} > \epsilon (where \epsilon is 1.0 \times 10^{-5} or 0.001) to prevent self-intersection or near-origin artifacts. t{obj} < t{current} (if tracking the closest hit among multiple objects). 4. Update: If valid, update the ray's hit state: Set hit = true. Set t = t{obj}. Store the object index. Transform the normal back to world space using the matrix transpose: \mathbf{n}{world} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{M}^\top \cdot [\mathbf{n}{local}, 1]^T). 5. Return: Return the boolean hit status and the distance t. Formulas Ray Equation: \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}^+. Unit Sphere Surface: \{(x, y, z) \mid x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\}. Optimization Criterion: Find object o that minimizes t such that t = \text{intersection test}(\mathbf{r}, o) and t > 0. Parameters \epsilon (SMALLESTDIST): Minimum distance threshold to accept a hit. Typical values are 1.0 \times 10^{-5} or 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Self-Intersection: Intersections very close to the ray origin or previous hit point (t \le \epsilon) must be discarded to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Rays: If \mathbf{d} is not normalized, t does not represent Euclidean distance. Transformation Precision: Normal transformation uses the matrix transpose, not the inverse-transpose, to map local normals to world space per the provided implementation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayobjectintersection(ray, objects, epsilon=1e-5): """ Finds the closest intersection between a ray and a list of objects. """ closestt = float('inf') hitindex = -1 for index, obj in enumerate(objects): # 1. Transform ray to object's local space if matrix M exists if hasattr(obj, 'transform'): M = obj.transform localo = M.transformpoint(ray.origin) locald = M.transformvector(ray.direction) else: localo = ray.origin locald = ray.direction # 2. Solve system of equations between the ray and the object geometry # Returns distance tobj or None if no intersection tobj = solveintersection(localo, locald, obj.geometry) # 3. Filter: must be in front of ray origin and closer than current best if tobj is not None and tobj > epsilon and tobj < closestt: closestt = tobj hitindex = index # 4. Update ray state if a valid hit was found if hitindex != -1: ray.t = closestt ray.hit = True ray.objindex = hitindex # Transform normal back to world space using matrix transpose if hasattr(objects[hitindex], 'transform'): M = objects[hitindex].transform localn = computenormal(objects[hitindex].geometry, closestt) worldn = M.transpose().transformvector(localn) ray.normal = normalize(worldn) else: localn = computenormal(objects[hitindex].geometry, closestt) ray.normal = normalize(localn) return ray.hit, ray.t def solveintersection(o, d, geometry): # Solves the parametric ray equation p(t) = o + td against the object's implicit/surface equation. # The sources do not give the specific solver implementation for arbitrary geometry. return None def computenormal(geometry, t): # Computes the surface normal at the intersection point. # The sources do not give the specific normal computation implementation. return Vector3(0, 0, 1) A recursive ray traversal algorithm for a binary bounding box tree (BBNode) that determines the closest surface intersection by testing the node's bounding box, then recursing into left and right children, and finally comparing hit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the nearest primitive in a hierarchical scene structure by pruning branches whose bounding volumes do not intersect the ray. Unlike Ray-Object Intersection Test which tests a single object, this method navigates a tree structure to find the global minimum intersection distance among all contained primitives. Time Complexity: O(1) per object for analytic primitives (spheres, planes, triangles). O(N) for a naive test against N objects. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per test. Strengths: Core decision unit for ray tracing and volume rendering; handles coordinate transformations; robust with epsilon filtering. Limitations: Linear scan does not scale to large scenes. When to use: For small scenes, debugging, or as the leaf node test in acceleration structures. When not to use: For large-scale rendering without acceleration; for complex CSG operations without decomposition. The concept originates from early ray tracing algorithms, where the intersection of a ray with primitive shapes (spheres, planes) was solved analytically. The term "raytrace" in this context refers to the iterative process of casting rays and updating intersection states. The use of epsilon thresholds to prevent self-intersection is a standard practice in computer graphics to handle floating-point precision errors. name: Bounding Box Node Intersection
head: BBNode::intersect
body: Bounding Box Node Intersection is a recursive ray traversal algorithm for a binary bounding box tree that determines the closest surface intersection by testing the node's bounding box, then recursing into left and right children, and finally comparing hit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the nearest primitive in a hierarchical scene structure by pruning branches whose bounding volumes do not intersect the ray. Unlike Ray-Object Intersection Test which tests a single object, this method navigates a tree structure to find the global minimum intersection distance among all contained primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray R (origin O, direction D), a reference to the current BBNode, and a mutable best-hit tracker best initialized to (\infty, \text{None}). Output: Updates best with the closest intersection distance t and corresponding primitive, or leaves it unchanged if no intersection is found within the subtree. Data Structures: The BBNode (or BVH node) structure contains the following fields: min / low: A 3D vector representing the minimum corner of the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). max / high: A 3D vector representing the maximum corner of the AABB. left / childl: A reference to the left child node. right / childr: A reference to the right child node. nprims: A 16-bit unsigned integer storing the number of primitives in a leaf node. data: An array of primitives (e.g., triangles) stored in a leaf node. getType() / type tag: Indicates if the node is an Interior (internal) or Leaf type. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bounding Box Test: Test if the ray intersects the current node's AABB defined by min and max. If the ray does not intersect the AABB, return immediately without updating best. 2. Node Type Check: Determine if the current node is an Interior or a Leaf. 3. Interior Recursion: If the node is Interior, recursively call the intersection function on the left child, then on the right child. 4. Leaf Primitive Test: If the node is Leaf, iterate over each primitive t in data. Test if the ray intersects t and if the intersection distance is less than best[0]. If both conditions hold, update best to (\text{distmin}(R, t), t). 5. Precision Handling: When comparing hit distances, add a small epsilon constant \epsilon = 0.001f to the left hit distance before comparison to mitigate floating-point precision errors. Formulas: Slab intersection for axis i: t1 = (mini - Oi) / Di, t2 = (maxi - Oi) / Di. Intersection interval: t{min} = \maxi(\min(t{1,i}, t{2,i})), t{max} = \mini(\max(t{1,i}, t{2,i})). Ray intersects AABB if t{min} \le t{max} and t{min} \ge 0. Distance comparison with epsilon: t{hit} + \epsilon < best[0]. Parameters: \epsilon: Floating-point precision guard for hit distance comparison, typically 0.001f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-Point Precision: Direct comparison of hit distances can lead to incorrect pruning due to precision errors. The algorithm explicitly adds \epsilon = 0.001f to the left hit distance before comparison to mitigate this. Grazing Rays / Parallel Slabs: When a ray direction component is zero, the ray is parallel to the slab faces. The intersection test must verify the ray origin lies within the slab bounds along that axis; otherwise, it returns no intersection. Empty Children / Leaf Nodes: The algorithm checks the node type and primitive count before recursion or iteration, handling leaf nodes or incomplete trees gracefully. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bbnodeintersect(ray, node, best): # 1. Bounding Box Test (slab intersection) tmin, tmax = rayaabbintersect(ray, node.min, node.max) if tmin is None: return # 2. Node Type Check if node.isinterior(): # 3. Interior Recursion bbnodeintersect(ray, node.left, best) bbnodeintersect(ray, node.right, best) else: # 4. Leaf Primitive Test for prim in node.data: thit = raytriangleintersect(ray, prim) # 5. Precision Handling: add epsilon to left hit distance before comparison if thit is not None and (thit + 0.001) < best[0]: best[0] = thit best[1] = prim def rayaabbintersect(ray, minv, maxv): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if ray.d[i] == 0.0: if ray.o[i] < minv[i] or ray.o[i] > maxv[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (minv[i] - ray.o[i]) / ray.d[i] t2 = (maxv[i] - ray.o[i]) / ray.d[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def raytriangleintersect(ray, tri): # Standard Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection v1, v2, v3 = tri.p0, tri.p1, tri.p2 e1 = (v1[0]-v2[0], v1[1]-v2[1], v1[2]-v2[2]) e2 = (v1[0]-v3[0], v1[1]-v3[1], v1[2]-v3[2]) h = (ray.d[1]e2[2]-ray.d[2]e2[1], ray.d[2]e2[0]-ray.d[0]e2[2], ray.d[0]e2[1]-ray.d[1]e2[0]) a = e1[0]h[0] + e1[1]h[1] + e1[2]h[2] if -0.00001 < a < 0.00001: return None f = 1.0 / a s = (ray.o[0]-v1[0], ray.o[1]-v1[1], ray.o[2]-v1[2]) u = f (s[0]h[0] + s[1]h[1] + s[2]h[2]) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return None q = (s[0]e1[2]-s[2]e1[1], s[2]e1[0]-s[0]e1[2], s[0]e1[1]-s[1]e1[0]) v = f (ray.d[0]q[0] + ray.d[1]q[1] + ray.d[2]q[2]) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return None t = f (e1[0]q[0] + e1[1]q[1] + e1[2]q[2]) if t > 0.00001: return t return None Generalizes this node intersection test to arbitrary bounding volumes and hierarchical traversal, adapting to spatial distribution rather than uniform grids. It is chosen when scene geometry is highly non-uniform or when dynamic updates require frequent tree rebuilds, trading off traversal simplicity for better spatial coherence. Time Complexity: O(\log N) on average for balanced trees, where N is the number of primitives, but degrades to O(N) in worst-case scenarios (e.g., highly unbalanced trees or rays intersecting many nodes). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the tree structure and bounding boxes. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of primitive intersection tests compared to brute-force linear search by pruning non-intersecting branches. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the quality of the bounding volume hierarchy construction and the spatial distribution of primitives. When to use: Ideal for scenes with many static primitives where acceleration structures can be precomputed, or when ray traversal overhead must be minimized. The method originates from standard ray tracing acceleration techniques and is formally specified in logical BVH specifications. Early implementations detailed recursive traversal logic for binary bounding box trees with explicit epsilon handling for precision. It builds on the concept of Ray-Object Intersection Test by applying it recursively within a tree hierarchy. cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15028, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV)
head: Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVH)
body: Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) is an acceleration structure for ray-primitive intersection that organizes scene primitives into a tree of nested bounding volumes to reduce the number of expensive primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of linear search complexity in brute-force ray tracing by allowing rays to quickly discard large portions of the scene that do not intersect the current bounding volume. Unlike regular 3D grids which partition space uniformly, HBV adapts its structure to the spatial distribution of primitives, typically storing primitives only at leaf nodes and partitioning the primitive set at internal nodes. Inputs: A set of primitives P (e.g., triangles, spheres); a ray r = (o, d) where o is the origin and d is the direction. Outputs: A list of intersection hits, sorted by distance from o. Data Structures: The HBV is a tree where each node N contains: 1. Bounding Volume (BV): A geometric enclosure B that contains all primitives in the subtree rooted at N. Common types include Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB), Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBB), or spheres. 2. Primitives: A list of primitives PN associated with the node. In standard implementations, internal nodes do not store primitives; primitives are stored only at leaf nodes. 3. Children: Pointers to child nodes (for binary trees) or an array of children (for higher arity). Parameters: BV Type: The shape of the bounding volume (e.g., AABB, Sphere, OBB). Arity: The number of children per internal node. Stopping Criterion: The maximum number of primitives allowed in a leaf node (e.g., default <4 primitives). Partitioning Criterion: The heuristic used to split primitives during construction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construction (Preprocessing): If a model hierarchy exists, derive the tree from it. Otherwise, use automatic clustering. A standard top-down approach computes a tight bounding box around all primitives, splits along the centroid of the longest axis, and recurses until the stopping criterion is met. Other methods include bottom-up clustering or iterative insertion. 2. Traversal (Intersection Test): The traversal determines which primitives intersect the ray r. The standard recursive depth-first approach is defined as follows: python def intersect(node, ray, hits): if rayintersectsbv(node.bound, ray): if node.isleaf: intersectprimitives(node.prims, ray, hits) else: for child in node.children: intersect(child, ray, hits) def rayintersectsbv(bv, ray): # Standard slab method for AABB intersection # Returns True if ray intersects bv for t >= 0 # Handles di = 0 by checking ray origin against bounds tmin = max((bv.min[i] - ray.o[i]) / ray.d[i] if ray.d[i] != 0 else (0.0 if ray.o[i] < bv.min[i] else float('inf')) for i in range(3)) tmax = min((bv.max[i] - ray.o[i]) / ray.d[i] if ray.d[i] != 0 else (0.0 if ray.o[i] > bv.max[i] else float('inf')) for i in range(3)) return tmin <= tmax and tmax >= 0 def intersectprimitives(prims, ray, hits): for prim in prims: t = rayprimitiveintersection(ray, prim) if t is not None and t >= 0: hits.append((t, prim)) hits.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) Priority Queue Traversal (Optimization): Pure depth-first search (DFS) order depends only on tree topology, not spatial layout. To improve efficiency, a priority queue (heap) can be used to visit nodes in order of their distance to the ray origin. 1. Initialize a min-heap with the root node. 2. While the heap is not empty: a. Extract the node N with the smallest distance t{BV} from the ray origin to its BV intersection. b. If t{BV} is greater than the distance t{hit} of the closest primitive intersection found so far, discard N and its subtree (pruning). c. Otherwise, if N is a leaf, test its primitives and update t{hit} if a closer intersection is found. d. If N is internal, calculate the intersection distance for each child, and insert valid children into the heap. e. A complete ordering among all BVs is not required; only the ability to extract the minimum element is needed, which a heap provides in O(\log n) time per operation. Formulas: Ray-BV Intersection: For an AABB defined by [minx, maxx] \times [miny, maxy] \times [minz, maxz], the ray o + t \cdot d intersects if: t{min} = \max \left( \frac{minx - ox}{dx}, \frac{miny - oy}{dy}, \frac{minz - oz}{dz} \right) t{max} = \min \left( \frac{maxx - ox}{dx}, \frac{maxy - oy}{dy}, \frac{maxz - oz}{dz} \right) Intersection exists if t{min} \le t{max} and t{max} \ge 0. Heap Complexity: Insertion and extraction of the minimal element cost O(\log n). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: False Positives: A "false positive" occurs when the BV is hit but the object inside is not. This requires further testing of the primitives within the node. Ordering Ambiguity: The closest ray-BV intersection and the closest ray-primitive intersection can happen in different BVs. The priority queue must handle this correctly by not assuming that the closest BV contains the closest primitive. Precision: Numerical stability in ray-BV intersection tests can affect pruning efficiency. This method accelerates the computation of physically-based indirect illumination for Gaussian splatting representations by treating Gaussians as ellipsoidal surfels and organizing them into a BVH. It solves the problem of unnatural indirect lighting in unconstrained spherical harmonic (SH) methods by enforcing physical constraints via ray tracing. Unlike standard Gaussian splatting which uses screen-space rasterization, this approach explicitly traces rays through the 3D Gaussian field to calculate visibility and accumulated radiance, enabling true inverse rendering and relighting. This method constructs a BVH using a recursive top-down approach that optimizes a cost function based on surface area and object count, rather than seeking the mathematically optimal partition which is computationally infeasible. It distinguishes itself from iterative bottom-up methods by generally yielding better BVH quality, and from exact optimal partitioning by using a heuristic plane-sweep strategy to find a near-optimal split. It builds on Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV). Median Cut BVH Construction is a top-down heuristic method for building a BVH by recursively partitioning a set of primitives based on their spatial centroids. It solves the problem of organizing geometry for efficient ray-primitive intersection by creating a balanced binary tree. It is distinguished from Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep) by its simplicity and deterministic partitioning via sorting, rather than optimizing surface area or using plane-sweep algorithms. It builds on Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV). The choice of bounding volume affects the trade-off between construction time, traversal speed, and tightness of fit. Common types include AABBs, Spheres, OBBs, and convex hulls. A traversal algorithm that uses a priority queue (heap) to visit BV nodes in order of their distance to the ray origin, improving upon pure depth-first search. It calculates the distance between the ray origin and the intersection point of the ray with the currently visited BV. If this distance is greater than the distance to an already found intersection with an object, the BV and its subtree are ignored. Otherwise, it recurses into the children. All remaining BVs are sorted by their distance to the ray origin in a heap, and the closest BV is always selected as the next candidate. The pitfall is that the closest ray-BV intersection and the closest ray-primitive intersection can happen in different BVs, so a complete ordering among BVs is not needed, only the ability to extract the closest one. Time Complexity: Construction: Depends on the heuristic. Traversal: Worst-case O(n) if the tree is unbalanced or the ray passes through all nodes. Average case is significantly better, often O(\log n) for well-balanced trees. Priority queue traversal adds O(\log n) overhead per node visit, where n is the number of elements in the heap. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of nodes and primitives. Measured Performance: For a scene with 66,430 spheres, brute-force rendering took 24,891.0 seconds, while a Goldsmith/Salmon BVH took 7.4 seconds on an Athlon XP 1900+. This demonstrates a significant speedup for large scenes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Adapts to scene density; reduces intersection tests significantly for sparse scenes; flexible BV types. Limitations: False positives still require primitive tests. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Bounding Volume Hierarchy was introduced as an acceleration data structure for ray tracing to save costs by precomputations on the scene and filtering of rays during run-time. The concept of using bounding volumes to filter rays dates back to early ray tracing research. The specific term "Bounding Volume Hierarchy" and its application to hierarchical scene graphs became prominent in the 1980s and 1990s. Rubin and Whitted pioneered hierarchical bounding volume structures in 1980. Goldsmith and Salmon (1987) proposed an iterative insertion method for BVHs. The structure is widely used in modern ray tracers and global illumination engines. name: BVH for Gaussian Surfels
head: BVH over ellipses representing Gaussians, Gaussian Surfels BVH, Indirect illumination via BVH ray tracing, Physically-based Illumination with Raytracing
body: This method accelerates physically-based indirect illumination computation for Gaussian splatting representations by treating Gaussians as ellipsoidal surfels organized in a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It replaces unnatural indirect lighting from unconstrained spherical harmonic methods with physically constrained ray tracing through the learned radiance field. Unlike screen-space rasterization, it explicitly traces rays to compute visibility and accumulated radiance for inverse rendering and relighting. Inputs: A set of N Gaussians, each defined by center \mathbf{x}, covariance matrix (defining ellipse shape/orientation), color c, and transparency \alpha. Visibility threshold \epsilon = 0.8. Sampling count K for directions. View direction \omegao and environment map for direct illumination. Outputs: Outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) per Gaussian vertex. Data Structures: BVH: A hierarchical tree where each node contains an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing its children, and leaf nodes store the Gaussian surfels. Exact layout and bit-packing details are Not given in the sources. Gaussian Representation: Each Gaussian is treated as an ellipse for intersection purposes. The axis lengths of these ellipses are scaled by a factor of three to ensure robust intersection testing. Steps: 1. BVH Construction: Construct a BVH over the set of Gaussians. Represent each Gaussian as an ellipse and scale its axis lengths by a factor of three before insertion. 2. Hemisphere Definition: For each Gaussian vertex \mathbf{x} with geometry normal \mathbf{n}, define the upper hemisphere \Omega relative to \mathbf{n}. 3. Direction Sampling: Uniformly sample K directions \{\omega{ik}\}{k=1}^K within \Omega. 4. Ray Emission: For each sampled direction \omega{ik}, emit a ray R(t) = \mathbf{x} + t\omega{ik} starting from the Gaussian center \mathbf{x}. 5. BVH Query: Query the BVH to find intersecting Gaussians along the ray. 6. Accumulation: Accumulate transmittance T and indirect radiance Li^{ind} as the ray traverses the scene. 7. Visibility: Compute visibility V(\mathbf{x}, \omegai): V(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } T \le \epsilon \\ 1 & \text{if } T > \epsilon \end{cases} where \epsilon = 0.8. 8. Indirect Radiance: Compute indirect incoming radiance Li^{ind}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) by summing contributions of intersected Gaussians: Li^{ind}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = \sum{l=0}^{n} cl \alphal Tl where cl is color, \alphal is transparency, and Tl is transmittance up to Gaussian l. 9. Total Incoming Radiance: Compute Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = Li^{dir}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai)V(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) + Li^{ind}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai), where Li^{dir} is direct illumination from the environment map. 10. Outgoing Radiance: Compute Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) using the rendering equation: Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) = \int{\Omega} f(\mathbf{x}, a, r, \omegai, \omegao) Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}) d\omegai where f is the Disney Principled BRDF, a is albedo, r is roughness, and \omegao is the view direction. This integral is approximated by the sum over the K sampled directions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def samplehemisphere(normal, k): """Uniformly sample k directions on the upper hemisphere defined by normal.""" directions = [] # Construct orthonormal basis from normal v = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) if abs(normal[2]) < 0.9 else np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) u = np.cross(normal, v) u /= np.linalg.norm(u) v = np.cross(normal, u) v /= np.linalg.norm(v) for in range(k): phi = 2.0 math.pi np.random.uniform(0, 1) costheta = np.random.uniform(0, 1) sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) localdir = np.array([sintheta math.cos(phi), sintheta math.sin(phi), costheta]) directions.append(u localdir[0] + v localdir[1] + normal localdir[2]) return directions def rayellipseintersection(rayo, rayd, ellipse): """Analytic intersection of ray with ellipse. Returns t or None.""" c = ellipse.center S = ellipse.shapematrix A = np.dot(rayd, np.dot(S, rayd)) B = 2.0 np.dot(rayd, np.dot(S, rayo - c)) C = np.dot(rayo - c, np.dot(S, rayo - c)) - 1.0 disc = BB - 4AC if disc < 0: return None sqrtd = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-B - sqrtd) / (2A) t2 = (-B + sqrtd) / (2A) t = t1 if t1 > 0 else (t2 if t2 > 0 else None) return t def traceray(rayo, rayd, bvh, epsilon): """Trace ray through BVH, return visibility V and indirect radiance Lind.""" hits = bvh.query(rayo, rayd) hits.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) transmittance = 1.0 Lind = 0.0 for g, t in hits: Lind += g.color g.alpha transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - g.alpha) if transmittance < 1e-6: break V = 0.0 if transmittance <= epsilon else 1.0 return V, Lind def computeglobalillumination(gaussians, bvh, K, epsilon, omegao, envmap): """Compute outgoing radiance for all Gaussians.""" results = [] for g in gaussians: center = g.center normal = g.normal directions = samplehemisphere(normal, K) Losum = 0.0 for omegai in directions: V, Lind = traceray(center, omegai, bvh, epsilon) Ldir = envmap.sample(omegai) Li = Ldir V + Lind # Disney Principled BRDF evaluation f = 1.0 dot = max(0.0, np.dot(omegai, normal)) Losum += f Li dot Lo = Losum / K results.append(Lo) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The visibility threshold \epsilon = 0.8 is a fixed heuristic. Axis scaling by a factor of three is required for robust intersection testing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables physically-based indirect illumination and relighting, which is not possible with standard SH-based Gaussian splatting. The BVH acceleration makes ray tracing through the Gaussian field feasible. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to ray tracing and sampling. The visibility threshold \epsilon=0.8 is a heuristic. When to use: When physically-based inverse rendering and relighting are required for Gaussian splatting scenes. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "SVG-IR: Spatially-Varying Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering". It addresses the limitation of previous unconstrained SH-based methods which produce unnatural indirect lighting. By introducing physically-based illumination via ray tracing through a learned radiance field represented by Gaussians, it enforces physical constraints. The BVH over ellipses is used to accelerate ray tracing. SVG-IR: Spatially-Varying Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01505, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep)
head: Heuristic Aufbau einer BVH, Top-down BVH construction
body: This method constructs a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) using a recursive top-down approach that optimizes a cost function based on surface area and object count, rather than seeking the mathematically optimal partition which is computationally infeasible. It distinguishes itself from iterative bottom-up methods by generally yielding better BVH quality, and from exact optimal partitioning by using a heuristic plane-sweep strategy to find a near-optimal split. It builds on Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) by computing the bounding volume for a given set of objects before partitioning. Inputs: A set of n geometric primitives (e.g., triangles) B. Outputs: A root node of a BVH tree representing the bounding volume of B. Data Structures: Primitive Representation: Each primitive is represented by its centroid (center point) ci. Bounding Volume (BV): An axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing a set of primitives. For a single primitive bj, the elementary BV is the bounding box of that primitive. For a set, it is the union of its children's BVs. Cost Function: A scalar value estimating the rendering cost (e.g., ray intersection probability). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Parent BV: Compute the bounding volume B for the current set of objects. 2. Base Case / Leaf Check: If the set contains a single primitive, create a leaf node containing that primitive and return. 3. Select Split Axis: Determine the axis (x, y, or z) with the greatest extent (largest dimension) of the current bounding volume B. 4. Sort Primitives: Sort the primitives in the current set based on the centroid coordinates along the selected axis. Let the sorted list be p1, p2, \dots, pn. 5. Plane-Sweep for Optimal Split: Initialize the left set bounding box BL to the elementary BV of p1. Iterate through split index j from 1 to n-1: Update BL to include pj. Compute the bounding box of the right set BR (primitives p{j+1} \dots pn). Calculate the cost for the split at j: Cost(j) = \frac{\text{Area}(BL)}{\text{Area}(B)} \cdot j + \frac{\text{Area}(BR)}{\text{Area}(B)} \cdot (n-j) where \text{Area}(\cdot) is the surface area of the bounding box, and j and n-j are the number of objects in the left and right child sets, respectively. Track the minimum cost and the corresponding split index k. Note: The formula implies a cost model where the probability of a ray hitting a child is proportional to its surface area relative to the parent, and the cost of traversing that child is proportional to the number of primitives it contains. If multiple splits yield identical minimum costs, apply an alternative heuristic such as the number of triangles in the subtree to break the tie. 6. Partition: Split the primitives into two subsets B1 = \{p1, \dots, pk\} and B2 = \{p{k+1}, \dots, pn\} based on the optimal split index k. 7. Recursive Construction: Recursively construct the BVH for each of the resulting subsets. 8. Non-Binary Fallback (Heuristic Check): If the resulting children nodes result in prohibitively high costs (e.g., the area increase is approximately 90% of the parent's area), attach the primitives directly as children of the current node instead of creating binary children. This allows the BVH to be non-binary. 9. Return Node: Create a node with the bounding volume B and children. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class AABB: def init(self, minpt, maxpt): self.min = minpt self.max = maxpt class Node: def init(self, bv, children): self.bv = bv self.children = children def surfacearea(aabb): dx = aabb.max[0] - aabb.min[0] dy = aabb.max[1] - aabb.min[1] dz = aabb.max[2] - aabb.min[2] return 2.0 (dx dy + dy dz + dz dx) def union(aabb1, aabb2): return AABB( (min(aabb1.min[0], aabb2.min[0]), min(aabb1.min[1], aabb2.min[1]), min(aabb1.min[2], aabb2.min[2])), (max(aabb1.max[0], aabb2.max[0]), max(aabb1.max[1], aabb2.max[1]), max(aabb1.max[2], aabb2.max[2]))) def computebv(primitives): if not primitives: return AABB((0,0,0), (0,0,0)) minpt = (min(p.centroid[0] for p in primitives), min(p.centroid[1] for p in primitives), min(p.centroid[2] for p in primitives)) maxpt = (max(p.centroid[0] for p in primitives), max(p.centroid[1] for p in primitives), max(p.centroid[2] for p in primitives)) return AABB(minpt, maxpt) def buildbvhtopdown(primitives): if not primitives: return None parentbv = computebv(primitives) if len(primitives) == 1: return Node(parentbv, primitives) extent = (parentbv.max[0] - parentbv.min[0], parentbv.max[1] - parentbv.min[1], parentbv.max[2] - parentbv.min[2]) axis = extent.index(max(extent)) sortedprimitives = sorted(primitives, key=lambda p: p.centroid[axis]) n = len(sortedprimitives) # Precompute right BVs for O(1) access during sweep rightbvs = [None] (n + 1) rightbvs[n] = AABB((float('inf'),)3, (float('-inf'),)3) for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): rightbvs[i] = union(rightbvs[i+1], computebv([sortedprimitives[i]])) leftbv = computebv([sortedprimitives[0]]) rightbv = rightbvs[1] mincost = float('inf') bestk = -1 parentarea = surfacearea(parentbv) for j in range(1, n): cost = (surfacearea(leftbv) / parentarea) j + (surfacearea(rightbv) / parentarea) (n - j) if cost < mincost: mincost = cost bestk = j if j < n - 1: leftbv = union(leftbv, computebv([sortedprimitives[j]])) rightbv = rightbvs[j+1] # Fallback: attach directly if area increase is ~90% of parent area if (surfacearea(leftbv) + surfacearea(rightbv)) > 0.9 parentarea: return Node(parentbv, sortedprimitives) leftprimitives = sortedprimitives[:bestk] rightprimitives = sortedprimitives[bestk:] leftchild = buildbvhtopdown(leftprimitives) rightchild = buildbvhtopdown(rightprimitives) return Node(parentbv, [leftchild, rightchild]) Time Complexity: O(n \log^2 n), derived from the recurrence T(n) = T(\alpha n) + T((1-\alpha)n) + O(n \log n). The O(n \log n) term comes from sorting the primitives at each node. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Top-down methods generally yield better BVHs than iterative methods. Strengths: Heuristic approach is computationally feasible compared to exact optimal partitioning. Limitations: The mathematically optimal partition is not practical, so this method is a heuristic approximation. When to use: When a good quality BVH is needed and O(n \log^2 n) is acceptable. When not to use: When exact optimal partitioning is required (infeasible) or when O(n \log n) is strictly required (consider SAH or other methods). This method is described in the context of "Advanced Computer Graphics" lectures by G. Zachmann. It is based on the work of Salmon and Goldsmith, as referenced in the source. The source also references a comparison of data structures by Havran. name: Median Cut BVH Construction
head: Median Cut BVH, Median Split BVH Construction
body: Median Cut BVH Construction is a top-down heuristic method for building a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) by recursively partitioning a set of primitives based on their spatial centroids. It solves the problem of organizing geometry for efficient ray-primitive intersection by creating a balanced binary tree. It is distinguished from Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep) by its simplicity and deterministic partitioning via sorting, rather than optimizing surface area or using plane-sweep algorithms. It builds on Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV). Inputs: A list of N primitives, each with an associated bounding volume (BV) and a centroid position. Outputs: A BVH tree structure where leaf nodes contain a subset of primitives and internal nodes contain bounding volumes enclosing their children. Data Structures: Primitive: Contains a bounding box (min, max) and a centroid (center point). BBox: Contains min and max vectors. LeafNode: Contains a bounding box and a list of primitives. InternalNode: Contains a bounding box, a left child, and a right child. Steps: 1. Construct BV: Create a bounding volume enclosing all objects in the current set. 2. Select Axis: Choose an axis (x, y, or z) for partitioning. Variant A: Cyclically choose a different axis on each level. Variant B: Choose the axis with the longest extent. 3. Sort: Sort all objects according to their center along the selected axis. 4. Partition: Partition the scene along the median on the selected axis; assign half of the objects to the left and right subtrees. 5. Recurse: Repeat steps 1-4 recursively. 6. Terminate: Stop recursion when a node contains less than n objects. Formulas: Centroid: C = \frac{B{\min} + B{\max}}{2}. Median split index: m = \lfloor N/2 \rfloor. Left subset: primitives [0, m-1]. Right subset: primitives [m, N-1]. Parameters: n: Leaf node size threshold. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Input: If all primitives have identical centroids, sorting order is arbitrary. Precision: Sorting stability may affect tree balance if centroids are identical. Use a stable sort or secondary key (e.g., primitive ID) to ensure deterministic behavior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeunionbbox(bboxes): mincoord = min(b.min for b in bboxes) maxcoord = max(b.max for b in bboxes) return BBox(mincoord, maxcoord) class BBox: def init(self, min, max): self.min = min self.max = max class LeafNode: def init(self, primitives): self.bbox = computeunionbbox([p.bbox for p in primitives]) self.primitives = primitives class InternalNode: def init(self, bbox, left, right): self.bbox = bbox self.left = left self.right = right def mediancutbvh(primitives, depth=0, leafthreshold=2): if len(primitives) <= leafthreshold: return LeafNode(primitives) currentbbox = computeunionbbox([p.bbox for p in primitives]) # Variant A: Cyclically choose axis axis = depth % 3 # Variant B: Choose axis with longest extent # extents = currentbbox.max - currentbbox.min # axis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: extents[i]) sortedprimitives = sorted(primitives, key=lambda p: p.centroid[axis]) mid = len(sortedprimitives) // 2 leftprimitives = sortedprimitives[:mid] rightprimitives = sortedprimitives[mid:] leftchild = mediancutbvh(leftprimitives, depth + 1, leafthreshold) rightchild = mediancutbvh(rightprimitives, depth + 1, leafthreshold) internalbbox = computeunionbbox([leftchild.bbox, rightchild.bbox]) return InternalNode(internalbbox, leftchild, rightchild) This variant handles raw triangle soup input (vertex and index arrays) before applying the median cut recursion. It involves an initial preprocessing step to convert raw indices into a primitive array with explicit vertex references and type tags. The steps are: calculate trinum = idxnum / 3; create a primitive array prim of size trinum; loop i from 0 to trinum-1 and j from 0 to 2; set prim[i].v[j] = v[idx[3i+j]]; set prim[i].type = primitive::TRI; create an intersector from prim and trinum; delete prim. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per level due to sorting, leading to O(N \log^2 N) total construction time for a balanced tree. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the tree nodes and primitive lists. Performance: Fast to implement and predictably balanced. However, it does not optimize for ray traversal efficiency (e.g., SAH), so the resulting BVH may have more overlap and lower traversal performance compared to Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep). Strengths: Simplicity, deterministic output, good balance. Limitations: Suboptimal tree quality for ray tracing; sensitive to centroid distribution. When to use: When construction speed is critical and traversal performance is secondary, or for debugging/prototyping. When not to use: For high-performance ray tracing where BVH quality directly impacts frame rate. Originated as a simple heuristic for top-down BVH construction in computer graphics. It is described in lecture materials for Advanced Computer Graphics by G. Zachmann. It is a variant of the general Median Cut algorithm applied to spatial partitioning.
