name: Volume BVH
head: Volume Bounding Volume Hierarchy, Scene-level Volume BVH
body: Volume BVH is a hierarchical acceleration structure for volume rendering that handles multiple objects, instances, and transformations by using bounding boxes to quickly identify which volume instances overlap a given ray segment. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which potentially transformed or instanced volume sources contribute to a specific ray, serving as a coarse-level filter before detailed voxel traversal. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the scene-level management of multiple distinct volume objects and instances, rather than optimizing the construction of a single object's hierarchy or handling specific primitive types like Gaussian surfels. The family relies on a tree of axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) where each node contains a bounding volume enclosing its children. The traversal mechanism follows these steps: first, construct a BVH using the bounding boxes of each object to find instances overlapping a ray segment from point A to B. Second, gather the list of overlapping objects into an array in the kernel before volume shading begins. Third, optionally refine the BVH by replacing full object bounding boxes with inner or leaf node bounding boxes to reduce false positives. Fourth, optionally extend traversal down to the voxel level using an algorithm like HDDA. Key shared properties include storing AABBs in nodes, robustly detecting overlap for rotated, scaled, or instanced objects, and operating orthogonally to internal voxel traversal. Optimizes BVH construction and traversal specifically for Gaussian surfel primitives, differing from the general object-instance focus of the main Volume BVH. Provides a specific algorithm for building the BVH tree using plane-sweep heuristics, which can be applied to Volume BVH construction but is not unique to it. The concept was proposed for Blender's Cycles renderer to optimize volume stepping and replace or augment the current shadevolume kernel logic. It addresses the limitation of existing tree structures like OpenVDB or NanoVDB, which store volumes hierarchically but lack scene-level instance overlap detection for transformed or instanced objects. #92570 - Cycles: volume sampling improvements - blender - Blender Projects, https://projects.blender.org/blender/blender/issues/92570, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Bit-stealing for Strand-Based Geometry
head: Mixed Bounding Volume Strategy, Woop et al. mixed BVH
body: Bit-stealing for strand-based geometry is a heterogeneous Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) representation designed for hair and fur, which combines Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) near the root for fast traversal with Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) at deeper levels for tighter volume fits. It distinguishes itself from standard BVHs by using bit-field exploitation to encode node type, primitive counts, and offsets within a single 64-bit index, while leveraging a merged-parent quantization frame for OBB children to reduce memory footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Bezier segments representing hair/fur strands. Output: A BVH tree stored in a compact, bit-packed layout using indirect addressing. Data Structures: The BVH is defined by the type BVHm, which supports three node variants: AABBNode, OBBNode, and Leaf. 1. Index Layout (I): A 64-bit unsigned integer (u64) serves as the node identifier. The bits are partitioned as follows: Bits 0–1: Node type discriminator. Bits 1–4: Primitive count (nprims) for Leaf nodes; unused for interior nodes. Bits 5–63: Offset. For Leaf nodes, this is the primitive offset into the primitive buffer. For interior nodes, this is the offset into the respective interior node buffer (AABBs or OBBs). 2. Node Variants: AABBNode: Stores uncompressed 32-bit floating-point bounds (low: f32x3x4, high: f32x3x4) and four child pointers (C: u64x4). OBBNode: Stores a merged-parent bounding volume (mlo: f32x3, mex: f32x3), per-child quantized offsets (qlo: u8x3x4, qhi: u8x3x4), a shared quantized orientation matrix (qo: i8x4x3), and four child pointers (C: u64x4). Leaf: Stores a primitive count (nprims: u4) and an array of BezierSegment data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construct Tree: Build a BVH where the top levels use AABBs and deeper levels transition to OBBs. 2. Encode Index: For each node, compute the 64-bit index I by setting bits 0–1 to the node type code, bits 1–4 to the primitive count (if leaf), and bits 5–63 to the memory offset. 3. Store Interior Nodes: If AABBNode, store low, high, and C in the AABB indirect group. If OBBNode, store mlo, mex, qlo, qhi, qo, and C in the OBB indirect group. 4. Store Primitives: Store BezierSegment data in the primitive buffer, indexed by the leaf offset. 5. Traverse: Decode I to determine node type and offset. If Leaf, access primitives using the offset. If AABBNode, access bounds and children from the AABB buffer. If OBBNode, access merged bounds and quantized data from the OBB buffer. Dequantize child bounds using mlo, mex, qlo, qhi, and qo to perform intersection tests. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodeindex(I: int) -> dict: return {'type': I & 0x3, 'nprims': (I >> 1) & 0xF, 'offset': I >> 5} def traverse(nodeindex: int, rayorigin: tuple, raydirection: tuple, primbuf: list, aabbbuf: list, obbbuf: list) -> bool: info = decodeindex(nodeindex) if info['type'] == 2: # LEAFTYPE primitives = primbuf[info['offset']:info['offset'] + info['nprims']] for prim in primitives: # Standard ray-Bezier intersection test pass return False elif info['type'] == 0: # AABBTYPE aabbdata = aabbbuf[info['offset']] # Standard ray-AABB slab test for i in range(3): if rayorigin[i] < aabbdata.low[i] or rayorigin[i] > aabbdata.high[i]: return False for childidx in aabbdata.C: if traverse(childidx, rayorigin, raydirection, primbuf, aabbbuf, obbbuf): return True return False elif info['type'] == 1: # OBBTYPE obbdata = obbbuf[info['offset']] # Dequantize child bounds using merged parent frame # Note: Exact dequantization formulas are not provided in sources for i in range(4): childlow = dequantize(obbdata.mlo, obbdata.mex, obbdata.qlo[i], obbdata.qo) childhigh = dequantize(obbdata.mlo, obbdata.mex, obbdata.qhi[i], obbdata.qo) # Standard ray-OBB intersection test pass return False return False def dequantize(mlo, mex, q, qo): # Standard dequantization logic return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Parameters and Edge Cases: Quantization: OBB bounds are quantized to 8-bit integers (u8) relative to a merged parent frame. Orientation: The orientation matrix qo is quantized to 8-bit signed integers (i8) and shared among all four children of an OBB node. Pitfall: The specific dequantization functions for OBB bounds and orientation are not defined in the source specification. Implementers must derive these from Woop et al. [105, Sec 3.5]. Memory: Reduces memory footprint by using quantized 8-bit offsets and shared orientation matrices for OBBs, compared to storing full 32-bit floats for every child bound. Performance: AABBs at the root provide fast, simple traversal, while OBBs at deeper levels offer tighter bounds for complex strand geometry, improving culling efficiency. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Compact representation for high-primitive-count hair/fur; flexible layout decoupling. Limitations: Requires complex dequantization logic for OBBs; bit-stealing requires careful index management. The method is based on the mixed bounding volume strategy from Woop et al. [105], which addresses the challenges of ray tracing hair and fur, such as high primitive counts and poor spatial coherence. It is implemented in the Scion language to demonstrate decoupling data layouts from BVH structures. name: BVH with 8-bit Quantized Bounds and Indirect Interior Storage
head: bvh8-q8-ci, bvh8i, qbvh8i
body: This method defines an 8-ary Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) layout optimized for memory efficiency and traversal speed by storing interior node bounds in a separate indirect array and quantizing child bounding boxes to 8-bit integers. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth consumption and cache pressure during ray traversal by reducing the footprint of interior nodes and leveraging SIMD-friendly integer arithmetic for intersection tests. It differs from its sibling BVH for Gaussian Surfels by targeting triangle primitives with a specific 8-ary topology, and from Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep) by defining the storage layout and quantization scheme rather than the construction heuristic. It extends Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) by introducing indirect interior storage and 8-bit quantization. Inputs: A set of geometric primitives (specifically triangles) and a target BVH topology (8-ary). Outputs: A serialized BVH structure containing a primitive array and an indirect interior array, along with a root index. The layout is defined by two main groups: Interiors and the main indexed group. 1. Global Header: primitivecount: u32 primitives: Array of Triangle of size primitivecount interiorcount: u32 2. Indirect Interior Group (Interiors): Size: interiorcount Fields per node: mlo: f32x3 (Merged Low bounds of children) mex: f32x3 (Merged Extent of children, mhi - mlo) childbounds: qbox3x8 (Quantized bounds for 8 children) children: u32x8 (Pointers/indices to children) Derived fields (for traversal logic): lo = \text{dequantize\bounds\lo}(mlo, mex, child\bounds) hi = \text{dequantize\bounds\hi}(mlo, mex, child\bounds) 3. Main Indexed Group (indexed by I): Default root index I is 1. The index I is a 32-bit integer split as follows: Bit 0: Tag bit. 1 indicates an Interior node; 0 indicates a Leaf node. Bits 1-31: Payload. If Tag is 1 (Interior): Bits 2-31 store the index into the Interiors array. If Tag is 0 (Leaf): Bits 7-31 store the primitive offset O. Bits 2-6 store nprims - 1. 4. Quantized Box (qbox3): Represents a 3D bounding box quantized to 8 bits per axis. Fields: lo: u8x3, hi: u8x3. Values are clamped to [0, 255]. 5. Quantized Box Array (qbox3x8): Array of 8 qbox3 structures, one for each child of an interior node. 1. Quantization of Child Bounds For each interior node with 8 children, the bounds are quantized relative to the merged bounds of all children. Merged Bounds: mlo = \mini(lowi) mhi = \maxi(highi) mex = mhi - mlo Where i \in [0, 7] indexes the children. Reciprocal: rcp = \frac{255.0}{mex} Quantization Function: For each child i and axis d \in \{x, y, z\}: q{lo}^{(i,d)} = \text{tfloor}((lowi^{(d)} - mlo^{(d)}) \times rcp^{(d)}) q{hi}^{(i,d)} = \text{tceil}((highi^{(d)} - mlo^{(d)}) \times rcp^{(d)}) Where \text{tfloor}(v) and \text{tceil}(v) clamp the result to [0, 255]. Dequantization (for intersection tests): lo^{(i,d)} = mlo^{(d)} + (q{lo}^{(i,d)} \times rcp^{(d)}) \times mex^{(d)} hi^{(i,d)} = mlo^{(d)} + (q{hi}^{(i,d)} \times rcp^{(d)}) \times mex^{(d)} The formula in the notes is \text{lo} = \text{mlo} + (\text{bound.lo} \times \text{rcp}) \times \text{mex}. This implies the stored bound.lo is the integer index, and it is scaled back to float space. 2. Index Packing Interior Node Index: I = (\text{interior\array\index} \ll 2) \mid 1 Leaf Node Index: I = (\text{primitive\offset} \ll 7) \mid ((\text{nprims} - 1) \ll 2) \mid 0 3. Build Procedure The build process constructs the tree bottom-up or via a specified topology, generating the packed indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tfloor(v): """Floor and clamp to [0, 255]""" return max(0, min(int(math.floor(v)), 255)) def tceil(v): """Ceil and clamp to [0, 255]""" return max(0, min(int(math.ceil(v)), 255)) def computemergedlow(lows): """Compute element-wise minimum across 8 children's low bounds.""" mlo = list(lows[0]) for i in range(1, 8): for d in range(3): if lows[i][d] < mlo[d]: mlo[d] = lows[i][d] return mlo def computemergedextent(lows, highs): """Compute max(high) - min(low) across 8 children.""" mlo = computemergedlow(lows) mhi = list(highs[0]) for i in range(1, 8): for d in range(3): if highs[i][d] > mhi[d]: mhi[d] = highs[i][d] return [mhi[d] - mlo[d] for d in range(3)] def quantizebounds(lows, highs): """Quantize 8 children's bounds to 8-bit integers.""" mlo = computemergedlow(lows) mex = computemergedextent(lows, highs) rcp = [255.0 / mex[d] for d in range(3)] childbounds = [] for i in range(8): qlo = [tfloor((lows[i][d] - mlo[d]) rcp[d]) for d in range(3)] qhi = [tceil((highs[i][d] - mlo[d]) rcp[d]) for d in range(3)] childbounds.append({'lo': qlo, 'hi': qhi}) return childbounds def buildinteriornode(childrenindices, lows, highs, interiorsarray): """ Build an interior node. Returns the packed index for this node. """ mlo = computemergedlow(lows) mex = computemergedextent(lows, highs) childbounds = quantizebounds(lows, highs) interiorindex = len(interiorsarray) interiorsarray.append({ 'mlo': mlo, 'mex': mex, 'childbounds': childbounds, 'children': childrenindices }) return (interiorindex << 2) | 1 def buildleafnode(primitives, nprims, primitivearray): """ Build a leaf node. Returns the packed index for this node. """ offset = len(primitivearray) for i in range(nprims): primitivearray.append(primitives[i]) return (offset << 7) | ((nprims - 1) << 2) | 0 4. Intersection Method For the quantized layout, the Möller-Trumbore algorithm is used for ray-triangle intersection. The dequantized bounds are used for the BVH traversal step (AABB intersection), and the quantized bounds may be used for early rejection or SIMD optimization if the hardware supports integer AABB tests. Zero Extent: If mex is zero (degenerate bounding box), division by zero occurs in rcp. The implementation must handle this, likely by treating the extent as a small epsilon or skipping quantization. Quantization Error: Quantization to 8 bits introduces error. The dequantized bounds are an approximation. This may lead to false negatives in intersection tests if the approximation is too coarse, though the source notes that Möller-Trumbore is used for the final primitive test, mitigating this risk for correctness. Index Overflow: The leaf index packs nprims - 1 into 5 bits (bits 2-6), limiting nprims to 32 primitives per leaf. The interior index is stored in 30 bits (bits 2-31), allowing for 2^{30} interior nodes. Memory Footprint: Significantly reduced compared to unquantized layouts (e.g., bvh8i) because child bounds are stored as 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats, and interior nodes are stored in a separate compact array. The source notes that qbvh8i uses less memory than bvh8i. Traversal Speed: The use of 8-bit quantization and integer arithmetic can improve SIMD performance. The source notes that qbvh8i has lower latency per ray than bvh8i in some configurations. Construction Time: The build procedure involves additional floating-point operations for quantization and dequantization setup. The source notes that fully replicating Embree's construction strategy is impractical, implying construction is complex. Scalability: The 8-ary tree structure reduces tree height, potentially improving cache locality. The indirect interior storage allows for better memory layout optimization. Limitations: Limited to 32 primitives per leaf. Quantization error may affect precision, though the final primitive test is accurate. This layout is part of Intel Embree's 8-ary BVH layouts, specifically qbvh8i for quantized representations. It represents over a decade of production engineering effort by domain experts. It is used in production rendering systems for its balance of memory efficiency and traversal speed. The source "Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies" compares this layout with other BVH implementations. Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15028, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Ray Tracing and Ray Intersection Methods
head: Ray Intersection Methods
body: Ray tracing is a surface rendering technique that determines the first object intersected by a camera ray by analytically computing intersection distances for explicit geometry. It solves the problem of finding the exact point where a ray meets a surface in a single evaluation, providing mathematically correct intersections limited only by floating-point precision. Unlike Ray Tracing which advances a ray in repeated steps to approximate intersections, ray tracing solves specific mathematical equations (e.g., quadratics for spheres, barycentric tests for triangles) to find the hit point directly. It differs from simple Ray Casting by explicitly supporting recursive light paths for reflections, refractions, and shadows, generating more realistic images at higher computational cost. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \hat{\mathbf{d}}; a scene representation consisting of explicit geometry (e.g., triangle meshes) and an acceleration structure (e.g., BVH). Output: The smallest positive distance t along the ray to the first intersected primitive, and the intersection point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\hat{\mathbf{d}}. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \hat{\mathbf{d}}. Acceleration Structure: Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) or kd-tree. Nodes contain bounding boxes; leaf nodes contain lists of primitives (e.g., triangles). Primitive: For triangles, defined by vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Steps 1. Ray Definition: Define the parametric ray equation: \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\hat{\mathbf{d}} where t > 0 is the distance along the ray. 2. Acceleration Structure Traversal: Traverse the BVH to identify candidate primitives. If a ray misses a bounding box, skip all primitives inside it. 3. Primitive Intersection: For each candidate primitive, solve the intersection equation: Sphere: For a sphere at center \mathbf{c} with radius r, solve \|\mathbf{o} + t\hat{\mathbf{d}} - \mathbf{c}\|^2 = r^2 for the smallest positive root. Triangle: Test the ray against the plane containing the triangle, then use barycentric coordinates to determine if the intersection point lies inside the triangle edges. 4. Closest Hit Selection: Select the primitive with the smallest positive t. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, scene): """ Trace a ray against a scene to find the closest intersection. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, normalized direction of the ray. scene: Object containing acceleration structure and primitives. Returns: thit: Distance to closest intersection, or infinity if no hit. hitpoint: 3D vector, intersection point. hitprimitive: Identifier of the hit primitive. """ thit = float('inf') hitpoint = None hitprimitive = None # Step 1: Traverse acceleration structure to find candidate primitives # Standard BVH traversal: recursively test ray against bounding boxes, # collecting primitives from intersected leaf nodes. candidates = [] # Implementation depends on BVH/kd-tree layout # Step 2: Test each candidate primitive for primitive in candidates: # Step 3: Solve intersection equation for primitive type # Sphere: solve ||o + td - c||^2 = r^2 for smallest positive t # Triangle: test ray against plane, then check barycentric coordinates t = solveprimitiveintersection(primitive, rayorigin, raydirection) # Step 4: Update closest hit if this intersection is closer if 0 < t < thit: thit = t hitpoint = rayorigin + t raydirection hitprimitive = primitive return thit, hitpoint, hitprimitive Parameters Acceleration Structure: BVHs or kd-trees are required for large scenes to avoid testing every triangle. Epsilon: Small values to handle precision issues (e.g., 10^{-5} for intersection, 10^{-3} for ray marching step size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Complex Geometry: Fails when object geometry is too complex for analytical intersection solutions. Procedural Geometry: Awkward to handle; requires tessellation into triangles (losing precision) or custom intersection shaders. Deformation: Moving or twisting geometry requires updating the mesh and rebuilding the acceleration structure, which is expensive. Memory: Detailed triangle meshes and acceleration structures can consume gigabytes of memory. Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction approximates the position of an isosurface between two sample points by iteratively halving the interval based on scalar field values. It locates the zero-crossing of a scalar field along a ray using a fixed number of iterative bisection steps to refine the hit position. It sets itself apart from Trilinear Isosurface Intersection by avoiding analytical cubic polynomial solving in favor of iterative subdivision, and is chosen when exact algebraic solutions are unstable or unavailable. Trilinear Isosurface Intersection computes the intersection point between a ray and an isosurface defined by a threshold value within a single hexahedral voxel of a scalar grid. It solves the problem of finding the precise surface location by formulating the intersection as a cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, which is then solved analytically or via robust numerical methods. It sets itself apart from Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction by providing closed-form or direct numerical solutions rather than iterative bisection, and is chosen when high precision within structured grids is required. Neubauer Iso-surface Ray Casting is a visibility testing method used to determine which parts of extracted line loops or sparse surface features are occluded by the isosurface, avoiding the computational cost of extracting and rendering the entire isosurface mesh. It sets itself apart from siblings like Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction and Trilinear Isosurface Intersection by focusing on binary occlusion checks for specific vertices rather than precise surface point extraction, and differs from Ray Tracing by using a coarse macro-cell traversal structure optimized for sparse feature visibility. The Hybrid Packetization Strategy is a ray-triangle intersection method designed to improve SIMD utilization on GPUs when standard packetization is inefficient due to sparse acceleration structures with high primitive density per leaf. It solves the problem of lost coherence in warp-level computations by dynamically switching between standard warp-level intersection and parallel processing of individual rays based on workload. It sets itself apart from standard packetization by distributing the work of a single ray across multiple threads when the number of intersection candidates is high, thereby maintaining throughput even when rays traverse cells with varying densities. Classic ray tracing (Whitted-style) is a rendering model that captures shadows, specular reflection, refraction, and diffuse surface shading by placing an image plane in the scene and sending rays through each pixel. It entails ray casting with the additional tracing of secondary rays for shadows and refractions. It sets itself apart from basic intersection methods by explicitly managing recursive light paths and secondary ray generation, and is chosen when physically accurate global illumination effects are required. This method casts a primary ray against a fixed set of spheres to find the closest intersection and computes unshadowed diffuse lighting from multiple point lights. It omits recursive shadow rays and reflections, distinguishing it from full ray tracing implementations. It sets itself apart by restricting the scene to explicit spheres and direct illumination only, and is chosen for lightweight, deterministic lighting in constrained environments. Screen-Space Ray Tracing with Depth Buffer (SSRT) is a technique to trace rays in screen space against a depth buffer to find surface intersections, supporting up to four depth layers per pixel. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-surface intersections for effects like reflections, refractions, and ambient occlusion without traversing complex scene graphs or voxel structures. What sets it apart from Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction and Trilinear Isosurface Intersection is that it operates directly on the rendered depth buffer rather than a volumetric or implicit representation, allowing it to capture any geometry already present in the frame buffer. Unlike Ray Tracing which traverses acceleration structures, SSRT traverses the 2D screen grid, making it highly parallelizable on GPUs but limited to visible surfaces. Parabolic Ray Tracing is a method for computing light ray trajectories in media with spatially varying Refractive Index Fields (RIF) by approximating the RIF such that ray paths are second-order polynomials within tetrahedral cells. It solves the problem of exact intersection computation with cell boundaries, which is difficult when ray trajectories involve transcendental functions, by reducing the intersection problem to solving quadratic equations. It differs from linear ray tracing methods by accounting for continuous curvature within cells, and from general non-linear solvers by providing closed-form analytical solutions for the trajectory. The Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) is a cost model used to determine the optimal partitioning of primitives in Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) construction, both for top-down recursive splitting and iterative insertion. It minimizes the estimated ray tracing cost by leveraging the probability that a ray intersects a bounding volume, which is proportional to its surface area. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction or Trilinear Isosurface Intersection by operating on the acceleration structure's topology rather than the geometric intersection logic itself, providing a general framework for spatial partitioning efficiency. Packet Ray List Merging is an optimization where lists of adjacent pixels (typically 2x2 groups) are combined into a single list. This exploits spatial coherence where adjacent pixels share common visible blocks, reducing the number of lists generated and processed. In Phase I, the BONO tree is traversed, and lists are created for each packet of rays instead of individual pixels. If a group of pixels overlaps with the projection of the current node, the group's list is processed. The upper bound k on the list size for grouped pixels is increased compared to single pixels; best performance is achieved when k is around 20 for packets, compared to 12 for single pixels. The Geometry Integrator is a direct illumination integrator for scene geometry that uses a hardcoded two-sided diffuse BSDF with red reflectance [0.8, 0.2, 0.2]. It performs ray intersection against the scene (itx: SurfaceInteraction3f = scene.rayintersect(ray)), adjusts the normal direction to point against the ray direction (itx.n = dr.select(dr.dot(itx.n, ray.d) < 0, itx.n, -itx.n)), loads the BSDF, checks visibility using a shadow ray intersected against the scene (itxshadow: mi.SurfaceInteraction3f = scene.rayintersect(rayL)), and accumulates direct illumination if both primary and secondary rays are valid (L += dr.select(validray, Li, black)). Measured Performance: Modern GPUs accelerate ray-triangle intersection with dedicated hardware (RT cores), making real-time ray tracing feasible for games and interactive applications. Strengths: Exact intersections; no stepping artifacts; hardware acceleration; mesh compatibility. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than ray casting and ray marching; procedural geometry is awkward; deformation is expensive; high memory usage for large scenes. When to Use: When exact intersections are required, and the scene consists of explicit geometry (e.g., triangle meshes). When Not to Use: When the scene is defined by procedural functions or SDFs, or when performance is critical and approximate intersections are acceptable. Ray tracing originated as a surface rendering technique to determine the first object intersected by a camera ray. It was developed as a more sophisticated algorithm than ray casting, involving diffraction and reflection to generate more realistic images. The method computes rays not only from the camera to the object, but also from the object to the light source to check for lighting, and implements reflection and diffraction. It is computationally more expensive than ray casting and ray marching. Modern implementations leverage acceleration structures like BVHs and kd-trees to handle large scenes efficiently. name: Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction
head: Bisection Isosurface Extraction, Isosurface Raycasting with Bisection, Isovalue Stepping, RayEvaluationSteppingIso
body: Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction approximates the position of an isosurface between two sample points by iteratively halving the interval based on scalar field values. It locates the zero-crossing of a scalar field along a ray using a fixed number of iterative bisection steps to refine the hit position. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: left (3D point where the scalar field value is less than or equal to the isovalue), right (3D point where the scalar field value is greater than the isovalue), texVol (volume texture object providing scalar field samples), iso (target isovalue, scalar or batched tensor). Output: surf (3D position of the isosurface intersection, calculated as the midpoint of the final interval). Data Structures: vec3: A 3-component vector type representing 3D coordinates. float: Scalar floating-point type for volume values. cudaTextureObjectt: Handle for accessing the volume texture on the GPU. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the recursion depth limit recdepth to 5. 2. Loop iter from 0 to recdepth - 1: a. Compute the midpoint: mid = \frac{right + left}{2.0}. b. Sample the volume scalar value at the midpoint: curIso = texture(texVol, mid).x. c. If curIso \le iso, set left = mid. d. Else, set right = mid. 3. Set the output surface point: surf = \frac{right + left}{2.0}. Formulas: Midpoint calculation: mid = \frac{left + right}{2}. Bisection condition: if f(mid) \le iso, the interval becomes [mid, right]; otherwise it becomes [left, mid]. Final position: surf = \frac{left + right}{2}. Parameters: recdepth: Fixed number of bisection iterations. Default value is 5. binarySearchSteps: Number of binary search steps to refine hit position. Range 0–20. Default 0. isocontourRange: Range of values [-v, +v] for surface feature mapping. Range 0.01–500.0. Default 5.0. selectedSurfaceFeature: Enum for shading features (OFF, FIRSTPRINCIPALCURVATURE, SECONDPRINCIPALCURVATURE, MEANCURVATURE, GAUSSIANCURVATURE). Default OFF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: With recdepth=5, the interval is reduced by a factor of 2^5 = 32. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes left and right correctly bracket the isovalue. Adaptive Sampling: The method can apply adaptive sampling to handle small features or silhouette regions where standard sampling fails. Performance: Refining already detected intersections has virtually no impact on performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binarysearchisosurfaceextraction(left, right, texvol, iso, recdepth=5): """ Approximates the position of an isosurface between two sample points by iteratively halving the interval based on scalar field values. Args: left (vec3): Start point where scalar <= iso. right (vec3): End point where scalar > iso. texvol (TextureObject): Volume texture for sampling. iso (float): Target isovalue. recdepth (int): Number of bisection iterations. Default 5. Returns: vec3: The estimated surface intersection point. """ # texture(tex, coord) samples volume scalar field at coord for in range(recdepth): # Compute midpoint mid = (right + left) / 2.0 # Sample scalar value at midpoint curiso = texture(texvol, mid).x # Bisection step if curiso <= iso: left = mid else: right = mid # Return final midpoint surf = (right + left) / 2.0 return surf This method locates isosurface intersections as a function of the scalar field values at the segment endpoints along a ray to eliminate coverage gaps that cause aliasing artifacts. It builds on Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction by using endpoint values to determine surface presence without intermediate sampling checks. Isocontour Shading with Curvature is a shading method for isosurfaces that uses surface features including first curvature (k1), second curvature (k2), mean curvature ((k1+k2)/2), Gaussian curvature (k1 \cdot k2), or a curvature texture. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Surface Location via Segment Endpoint Values and Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces by explicitly incorporating curvature data and multi-level isocontour highlighting into the shading kernel. The method builds on Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction to refine surface positions before applying the curvature-aware shading pass. Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces adapts the Fast Shaded Isosurfaces method for PC hardware using multi-stage rasterization and 2D textures to efficiently render shaded isosurfaces. It replaces iterative ray-marching with a two-pass register combiner pipeline that interpolates voxel gradients and computes dot-product lighting, extracting a specific isosurface boundary instead of integrating opacity. IsoSurface Ray Marching is a ray casting technique that renders an isosurface by sampling a 3D volume scalar field and detecting zero crossings relative to a threshold value. It avoids explicit polygon extraction by refining intersection positions via bisection and shading with Phong lighting. Unlike its sibling Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction, which approximates position by iteratively halving an interval, this method integrates the marching process directly into the ray traversal loop with a fixed step size, refining only upon crossing detection. A ray function that computes whether a given isovalue \sigma exists along the ray. Produces the same result as marching cubes but with higher accuracy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: At sampling distance 1.0, performance is 24 fps; at sampling distance 5.0, performance is 66 fps. Strengths: Virtually no impact on performance for refinement; improves accuracy for small features and silhouette regions. Limitations: Fixed number of steps does not adapt to feature size; requires initial bracketing of the isosurface. When to Use: When high accuracy is needed for already detected intersections. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction is a technique used in GPU-based volume raycasting to refine isosurface intersections. It was discussed in the context of advanced illumination techniques for volume rendering. The method optionally supports coloring the surface based on curvature features via a selected surface feature parameter. It provides a higher accuracy alternative to marching cubes for ray-casted isosurfaces. name: Surface Location via Segment Endpoint Values
head: Endpoint-based surface location, Segment endpoint surface intersection
body: This method locates isosurface intersections as a function of the scalar field values at the segment endpoints along a ray to eliminate coverage gaps that cause aliasing artifacts. It builds on Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction by using endpoint values to determine surface presence without intermediate sampling checks. Inputs: Ray segment defined by two endpoints P0 and P1. Scalar field values at endpoints: v0 = f(P0) and v1 = f(P1). Isosurface value v{iso}. Outputs: Boolean flag indicating if an isosurface intersection exists within the segment. Data Structures: Two scalar values v0, v1 representing the field at the ray segment endpoints. Steps: 1. Evaluate the scalar field f at the ray segment endpoints P0 and P1 to obtain v0 and v1. 2. Check if the isosurface value v{iso} lies between v0 and v1. 3. If an intersection is detected, the segment is passed to the binary search routine for precise location. Formulas: Intersection condition: (v0 - v{iso}) \cdot (v1 - v{iso}) \le 0, where v0 and v1 are the scalar field values at the segment endpoints, and v{iso} is the target isosurface value. Parameters: v{iso}: The target isosurface value. Typical values depend on the data domain (e.g., 0.5 for normalized density). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: If the sampling step size is too large, the field values v0 and v1 may both be on the same side of v{iso} even if the surface passes through the segment, leading to missed intersections (coverage gaps). Precision: Floating-point precision errors near the threshold v{iso} may cause incorrect sign checks. Guard clauses or epsilon comparisons may be required. A technique to allow smaller particle radii by inserting separating entry and exit points only when contiguous empty voxels span a world-space distance greater than a threshold g. It optimizes splatting by marking only voxels that overlap the surface of each particle sphere instead of all voxels inside the particle spheres. To avoid repetitive distance computations, it computes a lower bound of the number of voxels corresponding to g for each part of a voxel column in a boundary region. Actual world-space distance between two successive set voxels is computed only if this lower bound is exceeded. Cells with partially filled neighbors are not skipped to avoid cutting off detailed boundary surfaces formed by overlapping particles. Parameter: g: Threshold distance in world space for detecting contiguous empty voxels that require separating surfaces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates aliasing artifacts caused by coverage gaps between sampling points. Limitations: Highly dependent on sampling density; if the segment is too long, the method fails to detect intersections. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of volumetric rendering techniques for displaying three-dimensional aerodynamic flow field data. The original strategy of sampling at even steps along each ray produced pronounced aliasing artifacts due to gaps in coverage between sampling points. Locating surfaces as a function of segment endpoint values was proposed to eliminate this problem. The number of voxels in the data volume affects the degree of spatial aliasing, with higher voxel counts exhibiting fewer artifacts. DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Memory-Efficient On-The-Fly Voxelization of Particle Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/pgv.20151150, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Isocontour Shading with Curvature
head: RayEvaluationSteppingIso
body: Isocontour Shading with Curvature is a shading method for isosurfaces that uses surface features including first curvature (k1), second curvature (k2), mean curvature ((k1+k2)/2), Gaussian curvature (k1 \cdot k2), or a curvature texture. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Surface Location via Segment Endpoint Values and Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces by explicitly incorporating curvature data and multi-level isocontour highlighting into the shading kernel. The method builds on Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction to refine surface positions before applying the curvature-aware shading pass. Inputs: 1. rayDirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3). 2. normals: Tensor of shape (N, 3). 3. curvature: Optional tensor of shape (N, 2). 4. isovalue: Scalar threshold for extraction, default 0.5. 5. binarySearchSteps: Number of binary search steps, default 0. 6. numIsocontours: Number of isocontours to highlight, default 5. 7. isocontourRange: Range for isocontour highlighting, default 5. Outputs: 1. colors: Tensor of shape (N, 4). 1. Isocontour Texture (isocontourTextureObject): Layout: CUDA array isocontourTextureArray. Channel Descriptor: (32, 32, 32, 32, cudaChannelFormatKindFloat). Size: ISOCONTOURTEXTURERESOLUTION. Addressing: Clamp. Filtering: Linear. Coordinates: Normalized. 2. Curvature Texture (curvatureTextureObject): Layout: CUDA array curvatureTextureArray. Channel Descriptor: (8, 8, 8, 8, cudaChannelFormatKindUnsigned). Size: textureWidth \times textureHeight. Source: Loaded from shaders/curvature-texture.png (RGBA 8-bit). Addressing: Clamp. Filtering: Linear. Read Mode: Normalized float. ISOWIDTH: Constant value 20. COLORNEGATIVE: Magenta. COLORZERO: White. COLORPOSITIVE: Green. COLORISOZERO: Dark blue. COLORISOOTHER: Black. KERNELDOUBLEPRECISION: Integer flag (1 for double, 0 for single). RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGSURFACEFEATURE: Integer enum indicating the selected surface feature. The shading kernel RayEvaluationIsoShadingCurvature executes the following logic for each ray: 1. Generate Isocontour Texture Coordinate & Base Color: For each index i in [0, \text{ISOCONTOUR\TEXTURE\RESOLUTION}), convert to v1 in [-1, +1] via v1 = \frac{2i}{\text{ISOCONTOUR\TEXTURE\RESOLUTION} - 1} - 1. Compute base color: if v1 < 0, \text{lerp}(\text{COLOR\NEGATIVE}, \text{COLOR\ZERO}, v1 + 1); else \text{lerp}(\text{COLOR\ZERO}, \text{COLOR\POSITIVE}, v1). 2. Apply Isocontour Highlighting: If \text{numIsocontours\} > 0, compute v2 = v1 \cdot \text{numIsocontours\}, \text{closestIsovalue} = \text{round}(v2), \text{distanceToIso} = |v2 - \text{closestIsovalue}|, \text{isoBlend} = \max(0.0, 1.0 - \text{ISO\WIDTH} \cdot \text{distanceToIso}) where \text{ISO\WIDTH} = 20. Blend with isocolor: if \text{closestIsovalue} == 0, \text{isocolor} = \text{COLOR\ISO\ZERO}; else \text{isocolor} = \text{COLOR\ISO\OTHER}. Final \text{rgb} = \text{lerp}(\text{rgb}, \text{isocolor}, \text{isoBlend}). 3. Shading Kernel Launch: Kernel name is RayEvaluationIsoShadingCurvature. Inputs are rayDirections (N, 3), normals (N, 3), and optionally curvature (N, 2). Output is colors (N, 4). Defines passed: KERNELDOUBLEPRECISION (1 if double, 0 otherwise), RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGSURFACEFEATURE (int of selected feature). 4. Kernel Arguments: virtualsize (N, 1, 1), accNormals, accCurvature (or empty if not provided), accRayDirections, accColors, isocontourRange, and texture object (curvatureTextureObject if CURVATURETEXTURE feature selected, else isocontourTextureObject). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayevaluationisoshadingcurvature( v1values, # Array of N normalized scalar values in [-1, 1] raydirections, # Array of N vectors (N, 3) normals, # Array of N vectors (N, 3) curvature, # Array of N vectors (N, 2) or None numisocontours, # int, default 5 isocontourtexture, # Texture object for isocontour curvaturetexture, # Texture object for curvature (optional) surfacefeature # int, 0 for OFF, 1 for CURVATURETEXTURE, 2 for MEAN, 3 for GAUSSIAN): N = len(v1values) colors = [] ISOWIDTH = 20.0 COLORNEGATIVE = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Magenta COLORZERO = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # White COLORPOSITIVE = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Green COLORISOZERO = [0.0, 0.0, 0.5] # Dark blue COLORISOOTHER = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Black requirescurvature = surfacefeature != 0 if requirescurvature and curvature is None: raise RuntimeError("A surface feature requiring curvature is needed, but no curvature tensor is passed") for i in range(N): v1 = v1values[i] # 1. Base color from isocontour mapping if v1 < 0: basecolor = lerp(COLORNEGATIVE, COLORZERO, v1 + 1.0) else: basecolor = lerp(COLORZERO, COLORPOSITIVE, v1) # 2. Isocontour highlighting finalcolor = basecolor if numisocontours > 0: v2 = v1 numisocontours closestiso = round(v2) disttoiso = abs(v2 - closestiso) isoblend = max(0.0, 1.0 - ISOWIDTH disttoiso) if closestiso == 0: isocolor = COLORISOZERO else: isocolor = COLORISOOTHER finalcolor = lerp(basecolor, isocolor, isoblend) # 3. Curvature modulation if requirescurvature: if surfacefeature == 1: # CURVATURETEXTURE curval = curvaturetexture.sample(v1, v1) else: k1, k2 = curvature[i] if surfacefeature == 2: # FEATUREMEAN curval = (k1 + k2) / 2.0 elif surfacefeature == 3: # FEATUREGAUSSIAN curval = k1 k2 else: curval = 1.0 finalcolor = [c curval for c in finalcolor] colors.append(finalcolor + [1.0]) # RGBA return colors def lerp(a, b, t): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) return [a[j] + t (b[j] - a[j]) for j in range(len(a))] Missing Curvature: If selectedSurfaceFeature is not OFF and no curvature tensor is provided, the method throws a runtime error: "A surface feature requiring curvature is needed, but no curvature tensor is passed". Batched Isovalues: If isovalue is a tensor (batched), getBatches returns the size of the first dimension of the tensor; otherwise, it returns an empty optional. Precision: The method supports double precision via the KERNELDOUBLEPRECISION flag. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is part of the fV-SRN (Feature Volume - Scene Reconstruction Networks) project, an unofficial implementation by shamanDevel. It is designed to work with Scene Reconstruction Networks (SRNs) that use tensor cores for volume interpolation. The shading method is implemented in CUDA and integrated into the rendererrayevaluationsteppingiso.cuh module. shamanDevel/fV-SRN, https://github.com/shamanDevel/fV-SRN, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces
head: Fast Shaded Isosurfaces adaptation
body: Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces adapts the Fast Shaded Isosurfaces method for PC hardware using multi-stage rasterization and 2D textures to efficiently render shaded isosurfaces. It replaces iterative ray-marching with a two-pass register combiner pipeline that interpolates voxel gradients and computes dot-product lighting, extracting a specific isosurface boundary instead of integrating opacity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset represented as a sequence of 2D slices containing scalar values and pre-computed voxel gradients. Output: A shaded 2D image of the isosurface projected onto the screen. Data Structures: The volume is decomposed into 2D textures. Texture 0: Stores the voxel gradients in its RGB components. Texture 1: Stores the scalar intensity values in its Alpha component. Constant Color Registers: Store the light direction vector in register 2, the diffuse light color, and the ambient light color. Numbered Steps: 1. Gradient and Intensity Encoding: Compute the voxel gradient for each voxel and write it to the RGB components of a 2D texture representing the volume. Code the scalar intensity into the Alpha component of the texture. 2. First Pass: Interpolation (General Combiner 0): Apply the first general combiner stage to interpolate intermediate slices. Map the RGB output of Texture 0 (gradient \tilde{n}) to variable A. The combiner interpolates the gradient vector across the screen space based on the fragment's position relative to the slice boundaries. The result is the interpolated normal \tilde{n}{interp}. 3. Second Pass: Lighting Calculation (General Combiner 1): Enable the second general combiner to compute the dot product A \bullet B. Map the RGB output of Combiner 0 (the interpolated normal \tilde{n}{interp}) to variable A. Map Constant Color Register 2 (the light vector \tilde{l}) to variable B. The operation computes the dot product D = \tilde{n}{interp} \cdot \tilde{l} in the RGB portion. The Alpha component is not modified by Combiner 1 and remains the interpolated intensity. 4. Final Compositing: Combine the diffuse lighting term with ambient lighting. The final combiner calculates the output color using the dot product and the constant color registers for diffuse and ambient light. Formulas: \tilde{n}: voxel gradient vector. \tilde{l}: light direction vector. I: scalar intensity value. \alpha: interpolation factor between slice i and slice i+1. D: dot product \tilde{n}{interp} \cdot \tilde{l}. C{diffuse}, C{ambient}: RGB light color vectors. C{final}: output pixel color. Parameters and Typical Values: Light Vector \tilde{l}: Direction depends on camera or scene setup. Light Colors: C{diffuse} and C{ambient} are RGB vectors. Signed Fixed-Point: The hardware supports signed fixed-point values for combiner inputs, allowing direct storage of negative gradient components without scaling and biasing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single Light Source: The method is restricted to a single light source due to the fixed-function dot product calculation in the combiner pipeline. Monochrome Display: The algorithm is restricted to monochrome display only. Gradient Accuracy: The quality of the shading depends on the accuracy of the pre-computed voxel gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendershadedisosurface(slices, lightvector, diffusecolor, ambientcolor, alpha): """ Simulates the multi-stage register combiner pipeline for shaded isosurfaces. slices: list of 2D arrays, each (H, W, 4). RGB=gradient, Alpha=intensity. lightvector: (3,) array. Mapped to constant color register 2. diffusecolor, ambientcolor: (3,) arrays. alpha: float, interpolation factor between slice i and i+1. """ finalimage = None for i in range(len(slices) - 1): scurr = slices[i] snext = slices[i + 1] # Combiner 0: Interpolate intermediate slices # Input A: RGB from Texture 0 (gradient n) ncurr = scurr[:,:,:3] nnext = snext[:,:,:3] ninterp = (1.0 - alpha) ncurr + alpha nnext # Alpha output: interpolated intensity icurr = scurr[:,:, 3] inext = snext[:,:, 3] iinterp = (1.0 - alpha) icurr + alpha inext # Combiner 1: Compute dot product A. B # Input A: ninterp, Input B: lightvector (const color register 2) # RGB portion calculates dot product, Alpha portion is unused/unchanged D = ninterp[:,:, 0] lightvector[0] + ninterp[:,:, 1] lightvector[1] + ninterp[:,:, 2] lightvector[2] # Final Combiner: Cfinal = D Cdiffuse + Cambient finalrgb = D[:,:, None] diffusecolor + ambientcolor finalimage = finalrgb return finalimage Extracts flat-shaded isosurfaces by adapting the K-Buffer rasterization technique to replace 3D pre-integrated volume tables with a 2D lookup table for boolean detection between front and back scalar values. It is chosen when simple, fast hardware boolean extraction is preferred over continuous gradient-based shading. See K-Buffer Isosurface Extraction. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the screen space projection. Performance: Enables interactive frame rates for shaded isosurfaces on standard PC hardware. Strengths: Efficient use of fixed-function GPU hardware; avoids software ray-marching. Limitations: Restricted to single light sources; limited to monochrome display; requires pre-computation of gradients. The method is an adaptation of the "Fast Shaded Isosurfaces" algorithm, designed to leverage the capabilities of standard PC graphics hardware (specifically OpenGL register combiners) for volume visualization. It was developed to provide efficient rendering of shaded isosurfaces at interactive frame rates. Interactive Volume Rendering on Standard PC Graphics Hardware, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/VolVisforPCHardware.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: K-Buffer Isosurface Extraction
body: K-Buffer Isosurface Extraction is a framework for extracting flat-shaded isosurfaces from volumetric data by adapting the K-Buffer rasterization technique. It replaces the 3D pre-integrated volume integral table used in standard volume rendering with a 2D lookup table. This method distinguishes itself from its parent, Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces, by explicitly utilizing a 2D texture-based lookup table for boolean isosurface detection between front and back scalar values, enabling a simple and fast extraction process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset, a contour value c, and a K-Buffer containing depth-sorted fragments. Output: A flat-shaded isosurface mesh. Data Structures: 1. K-Buffer: Stores depth-sorted fragments. Each entry k contains the fragment's scalar value and the x and y components of its normal vector. The z component of the normal is not stored but computed later. 2. Isosurface Lookup Table (LUT): A 2D texture stored on the GPU. It is indexed by the front scalar value v^1 and the back scalar value v^2. It stores a boolean result (1 or 0) indicating whether the isosurface passes between the two scalar values. The LUT is regenerated whenever the contour value c changes. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Normals): Compute the gradient of the volume for each vertex v in the mesh to enable direct lighting. Extract the x and y components of the normal vector and store them in the K-Buffer entries corresponding to the fragments. 2. LUT Generation: Regenerate the 2D lookup table whenever the contour value c changes. 3. Rasterization: Rasterize the volume data into the K-Buffer, sorting fragments by depth. 4. Fragment Processing: For every rasterized fragment, determine v^1 and v^2 from the K-Buffer. Test if an isosurface passes between the fragments using the lookup table with inputs (v^1, v^2). 5. Normal Completion: Compute the z component of the normal vector based on the stored x and y components. Formulas: Boolean Test: The lookup table returns 1 if v^1 \leq c \leq v^2 or v^1 \geq c \geq v^2, and 0 otherwise. Here, v^1 is the front scalar value and v^2 is the back scalar value. Normal Z-Component: The specific formula for computing the z component from the x and y components is not provided in the sources. Parameters: c: The contour value used for the boolean test in the lookup table. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Contour Change: The lookup table must be regenerated every time the contour value c changes to maintain correctness. Normal Precision: The z component of the normal is derived rather than stored, but the exact derivation formula is not given. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: The algorithm is described as a simple, fast, and extensible approach to volume rendering. It provides a simple way to compute a flat shaded isosurface. When to use it and when not: Suitable when a simple, fast isosurface extraction is required and direct lighting via precomputed gradients is desired. Origin: The method is described in the context of the K-Buffer and its applications to volume rendering. History and development: The approach builds on the general idea of using a 2D lookup table for isosurface extraction instead of the 3D pre-integrated volume integral table. It references prior work [59] for the lookup table implementation. Where it is used: Volume rendering and isosurface extraction on GPU hardware. THE K-BUFFER AND ITS APPLICATIONS TO VOLUME RENDERING, https://ctsilva.github.io/thesis/steve-callahan-ms-thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: IsoSurface Ray Marching
head: Pseudo Iso Surface, Pseudo IsoSurface Rendering using Ray Casting, Shader Type 3: Iso Surface with RAY CASTING Method
body: IsoSurface Ray Marching is a ray casting technique that renders an isosurface by sampling a 3D volume scalar field and comparing values against a threshold. It avoids explicit polygon extraction by detecting zero crossings during ray traversal, refining hit positions via bisection, and shading with Phong lighting. Unlike Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction, which approximates position by iteratively halving an interval, this method integrates the marching process directly into the ray traversal loop with a fixed step size, refining only upon crossing detection. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume texture (uVolume3DSampler), camera position (ucameraPosition), step size (ustepSize), isovalue threshold (uisoValue), and vertex attributes providing 3D texture coordinates (oTexCoords). Output: A fragment color (FragColor) representing the shaded isosurface. Data Structures Volume Texture: 3D texture object bound to unit 0, sampled using sampler3D. Uniforms: uMVPMatrix: Model-View-Projection matrix. uVolume3DSampler: Sampler for the 3D volume. ucameraPosition: Camera position in world space. ustepSize: Step vector for ray advancement, typically (1.0f/XDIM, 1.0f/YDIM, 1.0f/ZDIM). uisoValue: Integer threshold, normalized in the shader by dividing by 255.0. Constants: MAXSAMPLES: 300. DELTA: 0.01 (used for gradient calculation). Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Compile and link vertex and fragment shaders from.glsl files. Bind attribute aPosition. Retrieve uniform locations for uMVPMatrix, uVolume3DSampler, ucameraPosition, and ustepSize. 2. Rendering Setup: Enable blending. Set the shader program. Pass the Model-View-Projection matrix, camera position, step size, and isovalue. Bind the 3D volume texture to unit 0. Draw a unit cube using 36 unsigned short indices. 3. Ray Initialization: Initialize ray origin dataPosition from interpolated 3D texture coordinates oTexCoords. 4. Ray Direction: Calculate geometryDirection by subtracting 0.5 from oTexCoords, subtracting ucameraPosition, and normalizing the result. 5. Step Vector: Calculate directionStep by multiplying geometryDirection with ustepSize. 6. Ray Marching Loop: Loop i from 0 to MAXSAMPLES (300): a. Advance dataPosition by directionStep. b. Boundary Check: If dot(sign(dataPosition - texMin), sign(texMax - dataPosition)) < 3.0, break the loop. This condition triggers if any component of dataPosition falls outside the [0, 1] bounds. c. Sampling: Sample the volume at current dataPosition (fSample) and next position dataPosition + directionStep (fSample2). d. Zero Crossing Detection: If (fSample - isoValue) < 0 AND (fSample2 - isoValue) >= 0.0, refine the intersection. e. Refinement: Call Bisection(xN, xF, isoValue) where xN is dataPosition and xF is dataPosition + directionStep. The bisection loop runs 4 times, halving the interval [left, right] based on the sample value relative to iso. f. Normal Calculation: Calculate normal N at the refined position tc using GetGradient(tc). GetGradient uses central finite difference with DELTA and normalizes the result. g. Shading: Compute final color using PhongLighting(L, N, V, 250, vec3(0.5)) and assign to FragColor. Break the loop. Formulas Gradient Approximation: N = \text{normalize}\left(\frac{S{-} - S{+}}{2.0}\right) Where S{-} and S{+} are samples at uvw - \Delta and uvw + \Delta along each axis. Phong Lighting: C = (\max(L \cdot N, 0) \cdot C{diffuse} + \max(0.00001, (\frac{L+V}{|L+V|} \cdot N))^p) \cdot 1.0 Where L is light direction, N is normal, V is view direction, p is shininess (250), and C{diffuse} is diffuse color (vec3(0.5)). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(aPosition, uMVPMatrix): glPosition = uMVPMatrix vec4(aPosition, 1.0) oTexCoords = aPosition # Unit cube vertices map directly to [0,1] texture coordinates def fragmentshader(oTexCoords, uVolume3DSampler, ucameraPosition, ustepSize, uisoValue, ulightDirection, uviewDirection): iso = uisoValue / 255.0 # Normalize integer isoValue MAXSAMPLES = 300 DELTA = 0.01 texMin = vec3(0.0) texMax = vec3(1.0) # Ray Initialization dataPosition = oTexCoords geometryDirection = normalize(oTexCoords - 0.5 - ucameraPosition) directionStep = geometryDirection ustepSize for i in range(MAXSAMPLES): # Advance dataPosition += directionStep # Boundary Check if dot(sign(dataPosition - texMin), sign(texMax - dataPosition)) < 3.0: break # Sampling fSample = samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, dataPosition) fSample2 = samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, dataPosition + directionStep) # Zero Crossing Detection if (fSample - iso) < 0 and (fSample2 - iso) >= 0.0: # Refine Intersection tc = bisection(dataPosition, dataPosition + directionStep, iso, uVolume3DSampler) # Calculate Normal N = getgradient(tc, DELTA, uVolume3DSampler) # Shading L = ulightDirection V = uviewDirection diffuse = max(dot(L, N), 0.0) vec3(0.5) halfvec = normalize(L + V) specular = pow(max(dot(halfvec, N), 0.00001), 250.0) FragColor = vec4((diffuse + specular) 1.0, 1.0) return FragColor # If no intersection found, return background or black FragColor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return FragColor def bisection(xN, xF, iso, uVolume3DSampler): left = xN right = xF for in range(4): mid = (left + right) / 2.0 sample = samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, mid) if sample < iso: left = mid else: right = mid return (left + right) / 2.0 def getgradient(tc, DELTA, uVolume3DSampler): # Central finite difference grad = vec3(0.0) grad.x = samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, tc + vec3(DELTA, 0.0, 0.0)) - samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, tc - vec3(DELTA, 0.0, 0.0)) grad.y = samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, tc + vec3(0.0, DELTA, 0.0)) - samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, tc - vec3(0.0, DELTA, 0.0)) grad.z = samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, tc + vec3(0.0, 0.0, DELTA)) - samplevolume(uVolume3DSampler, tc - vec3(0.0, 0.0, DELTA)) return normalize(grad / 2.0) def samplevolume(sampler, pos): # Standard 3D texture sampling returning a scalar value return texture(sampler, pos).r Parameters uisoValue: Uniform integer representing the isovalue threshold. Normalized in shader by dividing by 255.0. MAXSAMPLES: Constant integer defining the maximum number of ray march steps per ray. Value: 300. DELTA: Constant float defining the step size for gradient calculation using finite differences. Value: 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Check: The boundary check uses dot(sign(dataPosition - texMin), sign(texMax - dataPosition)) < 3.0. If any component is out of bounds [0,1], the sign product becomes negative or zero, reducing the dot product below 3, triggering termination. Note that sign(0) evaluates to 0, which can cause premature termination if the ray exactly hits a volume boundary. Precision: The bisection is limited to 4 iterations, which may not provide high precision for all cases. Lighting: The source does not specify how light direction L and view direction V are computed in the shader, which is a gap for implementation. They are passed as uniforms in the pseudocode. Step Size: A fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed surfaces if the step size is too large relative to volume features. Subtopics Surface Location via Segment Endpoint Values: Determines surface location based on values at segment endpoints. Choose when endpoint values are sufficient for accurate surface approximation. Link Isocontour Shading with Curvature: Enhances shading by incorporating curvature information. Choose when surface detail and curvature-based shading are required. Link Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces: Uses multiple rasterization passes for shading. Choose when complex shading effects are needed and performance allows for multiple passes. Link Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays (pixels). Each ray marches up to MAXSAMPLES (300) steps, with bisection adding a constant overhead (4 iterations) upon crossing detection. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the 3D volume texture storage. The shader uses minimal additional memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution (number of rays) and volume size (texture memory). The fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed surfaces if the step size is too large relative to volume features. Strengths: Simple implementation, no explicit mesh generation, real-time capable with fixed step size. Limitations: Fixed step size can lead to inaccuracies or missed surfaces; boundary check logic is specific to the [0,1] texture coordinate space; lighting calculation details are missing. When to use: Real-time visualization of isosurfaces where explicit mesh generation is undesirable or too costly. When not to use: When high precision is required, or when the volume has features smaller than the step size. Origin: The method is described in the "Volumetric Render Engine" GitHub repository by mikejernil. History and Development: The code is part of a larger volumetric rendering application that includes multiple rendering modes (slicing, raycasting, colormap classification, marching tetrahedra). Usage: Used in the "Volumetric Render Engine" for rendering isosurfaces from 3D volume data. name: Bisection Isosurface Extraction
head: BEM Isosurface Computation Implementation, Isovalue Stepping, RayEvaluationSteppingIso
body: Bisection Isosurface Extraction is a meshfree method for locating isosurfaces within scalar fields by performing a line search using the bisection algorithm. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by decoupling the field evaluation from the meshing process, using an octree to identify relevant regions and applying bisection only along specific search lines to find intersection points, thereby significantly reducing computational costs compared to volume-meshed approaches. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar field function (e.g., electric potential) computable at arbitrary points; an octree structure defining the spatial domain (inner and outer octrees); a target isovalue. Output: A set of points on the isosurface, which are subsequently meshed into triangular elements. Data Structures Octree: A hierarchical structure dividing space into cubes. The implementation uses an inner octree and an outer octree. The outer octree adds one additional layer of cubes to the inner octree to account for field values outside the bounding box of the object. Relevant Cubes: A subset of octree cubes selected for detailed computation. In the reference implementation, 28 cubes from the inner octree and 16 from the outer octree were selected, representing 1.3% of the total cubes. Search Line: A line segment along which the bisection is performed to find the isovalue. Parameters Convergence Error: The bisection stops when the interval width or function value difference is below a threshold. The source notes an average of 20 iterations are needed to find the point with a defined isovalue and relatively small error. Solver Settings (for field computation): GMRES with Jacobi preconditioner, convergence error < 10^{-6}, achieved in 56 iteration steps. Matrix Compression: Fast Multipole Method (FMM) with L = 12. Steps 1. Construct Octree: Build an inner octree and an outer octree (with one additional layer) covering the domain. 2. Determine Data Range: Calculate the range of the scalar field for each cube in the octree. 3. Select Relevant Cubes: Identify cubes where the isovalue lies within the data range. Select these cubes for detailed computation. 4. Define Search Lines: Define search lines within or crossing the relevant cubes. 5. Bisection Line Search: For each search line, apply the bisection method to find the point where the scalar field equals the target isovalue. Let f(x) be the scalar field value at point x. Let v{target} be the target isovalue. Initialize interval [a, b] on the line such that f(a) - v{target} and f(b) - v{target} have opposite signs. Iterate: 1. c = (a + b) / 2 2. If |f(c) - v{target}| < \epsilon or |b - a| < \delta, stop. 3. If (f(a) - v{target}) \cdot (f(c) - v{target}) < 0, set b = c. 4. Else, set a = c. The source notes an average of 20 iterations are required. 6. Collect Points: Gather the intersection points found via bisection. 7. Meshing: Merge the isosurface segments into a common element container. Renumber element nodes. 8. Output: Transfer the element set to visualization software. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bisectionisosurfaceextraction(fieldfunction, targetisovalue, octree, searchlines): """ Extracts isosurface points using bisection along search lines. Args: fieldfunction: Callable that returns scalar value at (x, y, z). targetisovalue: The scalar value defining the isosurface. octree: Octree structure with inner and outer layers. searchlines: List of line segments (start, end) for bisection. Returns: List of 3D points on the isosurface. """ isosurfacepoints = [] # Step 1-3: Select relevant cubes based on octree data range # Note: In the source, this selection is done by determining data range per cube # and selecting 28 inner + 16 outer cubes. relevantcubes = selectrelevantcubes(octree, targetisovalue) # Step 4-5: Perform bisection on search lines for line in searchlines: startpoint = line.start endpoint = line.end # Evaluate endpoints valstart = fieldfunction(startpoint) valend = fieldfunction(endpoint) # Check if isovalue exists in this interval if (valstart - targetisovalue) (valend - targetisovalue) > 0: continue # Bisection loop a = startpoint b = endpoint vala = valstart valb = valend # Average 20 iterations as per source for in range(20): c = (a + b) / 2.0 valc = fieldfunction(c) if abs(valc - targetisovalue) < 1e-6: # Convergence threshold isosurfacepoints.append(c) break if (vala - targetisovalue) (valc - targetisovalue) < 0: b = c valb = valc else: a = c vala = valc # Step 6-8: Meshing and output # Merge segments, renumber nodes, and return points return isosurfacepoints def selectrelevantcubes(octree, targetisovalue): """ Selects cubes where the scalar field range includes the target isovalue. """ relevant = [] for cube in octree.allcubes: minval, maxval = cube.datarange if minval <= targetisovalue <= maxval: relevant.append(cube) return relevant Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Conditions: The outer octree layer is necessary to capture field values outside the bounding box, preventing errors in isosurface location near boundaries. Precision: The method relies on the accuracy of the scalar field function. In the source, the field was computed using a BEM solver with GMRES convergence error < 10^{-6}. Refinement: Without refinement, the octree structure may be visible in the isosurface, leading to non-smooth results. Determines surface position based on scalar values at segment endpoints without iterative bisection. Choose when computational resources are extremely limited and lower precision is acceptable. Surface Location via Segment Endpoint Values Focuses on shading techniques for isosurfaces, potentially using curvature information. Choose when visual quality and shading accuracy are prioritized over extraction speed. Isocontour Shading with Curvature Uses rasterization techniques for isosurface rendering. Choose when GPU acceleration is available and rasterization pipelines are preferred over ray-based methods. Multi-Stage Rasterization for Shaded Isosurfaces Advances along rays to find isosurface intersections. Choose when a simpler, step-based approach is sufficient and bisection overhead is undesirable. IsoSurface Ray Marching Time Complexity: The method reduces computational costs by performing detailed computations in only 1.3% of the cubes. In the reference example, 29,984 potential computations were required for a coarse isosurface, taking ~10 minutes on a single core. Memory Complexity: Uses an octree structure. The inner octree had 3,209 cubes and the outer had 65 cubes. Performance: The source reports 29,984 computations for a coarse isosurface (168 nodes, 80 elements) taking ~10 minutes on a single core Intel Xeon CPU E3-1275v5. Strengths: Significant reduction in computational costs and storage requirements compared to volume-meshed post-processing. High flexibility due to meshfree nature. Limitations: Performance optimization was omitted in the source implementation, focusing on accuracy and resource testing. Coarse isosurfaces may lack smoothness without refinement. When to Use: When high-quality, meshfree isosurfaces are needed and computational resources allow for iterative field evaluations. Particularly suitable for post-processing of BEM results. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the overhead of field evaluation and bisection is prohibitive. The method was presented by A. Buchau et al. in 2017 as an innovative approach for meshfree computation of isosurfaces. It combines octree-based isovalue search methods, FMM accelerated BEMs, and advancing front meshing algorithms. The implementation was done in C# using the.NET library for an in-house post-processing BEM software. A meshfree isosurface computation method for boundary element methods, https://doi.org/10.2495/cmem-v5-n5-647-658, fetched 2026-10-26
