name: Trilinear Isosurface Intersection
head: Analytical cubic solution, Isosurface Intersection via Cubic Polynomial
body:
Trilinear Isosurface Intersection computes the intersection point between a ray and an isosurface defined by a threshold value within a single hexahedral voxel of a scalar grid. It solves the problem of finding the precise surface location by formulating the intersection as a cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, which is then solved analytically or via robust numerical methods. This method builds on Ray Tracing and Ray Intersection Methods by providing the specific algebraic mechanism for hexahedral cells. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D}. Voxel corner scalar values v{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Isovalue I (threshold). Outputs: Intersection distance t (if an intersection exists within the voxel bounds). Intersection point \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D}. Data Structures: The method operates on the eight scalar values associated with the voxel corners. No additional geometric data structures (like normals or Hermite data) are required for the intersection calculation itself. Steps: 1. Culling: Compute the minimum (v{min}) and maximum (v{max}) of the eight corner values v{ijk}. If I < v{min} or I > v{max}, the isosurface does not intersect the voxel (or the ray does not hit it within this cell's scalar range). Terminate. 2. Formulate Trilinear Equation: Define the trilinear interpolant f(u, v, w) over the parametric domain (u, v, w) \in [0, 1]^3. The value at any point is: f(u, v, w) = \sum{i=0}^1 \sum{j=0}^1 \sum{k=0}^1 (1 - Ui)(1 - Vj)(1 - Wk) v{ijk} where U0 = 1-u, U1 = u, V0 = 1-v, V1 = v, W0 = 1-w, W1 = w. The isosurface is defined by f(u, v, w) = I. 3. Substitute Ray Parametrization: For a general ray passing through the voxel, map the ray \mathbf{R}(t) = \mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D} into the voxel's local coordinate system. Let the voxel span from \mathbf{C}{min} to \mathbf{C}{max}. The parametric coordinates (u(t), v(t), w(t)) are linear functions of t: u(t) =  rac{Ox + t Dx - C{min,x}}{C{max,x} - C{min,x}}, \quad v(t) =  rac{Oy + t Dy - C{min,y}}{C{max,y} - C{min,y}}, \quad w(t) =  rac{Oz + t Dz - C{min,z}}{C{max,z} - C{min,z}} Substituting these linear expressions into the trilinear equation f(u(t), v(t), w(t)) - I = 0 yields a cubic polynomial in t: G3 t^3 + G2 t^2 + G1 t + G0 = 0 The coefficients G0, G1, G2, G3 are derived from the corner values v{ijk} and the ray direction components scaled by the voxel dimensions. 4. Solve Cubic Polynomial: Solve for real roots t of the cubic equation. If G3 
eq 0, use Cardano's method or a robust numerical solver (e.g., Newton-Raphson) to find roots. If G3 = 0, it reduces to a quadratic equation G2 t^2 + G1 t + G0 = 0. Solve using the quadratic formula. Discriminant Analysis (for Cardano's method): Compute the discriminant D3 to determine the nature of the roots: \delta^2 =  rac{G2^2 - 3G3G1}{9G3^2} xN = - rac{G2}{3G3} yN = G3 xN^3 + G2 xN^2 + G1 xN + G0 D3 = yN^2 - 4 G3^2 \delta^3 If D3 > 0: One real root, two complex conjugate roots. If D3 = 0: If yN = 0: Three equal real roots. If yN 
eq 0: One distinct real root and two equal real roots. If D3 < 0: Three distinct real roots. For the quadratic case (G3=0, G2 
eq 0), compute D2 = G1^2 - 4G2G0. If D2 < 0, no real roots. 5. Select Valid Root: Filter roots t such that t > 0 (assuming forward ray) and the intersection point lies within the voxel bounds. Select the smallest positive t as the first intersection. 6. Compute Intersection Point: Evaluate \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{O} + t\mathbf{D}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cbrt(x): """Compute the real cube root of x.""" return math.copysign(abs(x)(1.0/3.0), x) def trilinearisosurfaceintersection(O, D, voxelmin, voxelmax, cornervalues, isovalue): """ O: Ray origin (vec3) D: Ray direction (vec3) voxelmin: Voxel minimum corner (vec3) voxelmax: Voxel maximum corner (vec3) cornervalues: Array of 8 floats [v000, v001, v010, v011, v100, v101, v110, v111] isovalue: Threshold scalar Returns: t (float) if intersection found, else None """ # 1. Culling vmin = min(cornervalues) vmax = max(cornervalues) if isovalue < vmin or isovalue > vmax: return None # 2. Compute voxel dimensions and ray parametric derivatives dx = voxelmax.x - voxelmin.x dy = voxelmax.y - voxelmin.y dz = voxelmax.z - voxelmin.z # u(t) = u0 + tdu, v(t) = v0 + tdv, w(t) = w0 + tdw u0 = (O.x - voxelmin.x) / dx du = D.x / dx v0 = (O.y - voxelmin.y) / dy dv = D.y / dy w0 = (O.z - voxelmin.z) / dz dw = D.z / dz # 3. Compute trilinear coefficients c0..c7 # f(u,v,w) = c0 + c1u + c2v + c3w + c4uv + c5uw + c6vw + c7uvw c0 = cornervalues[0] c1 = cornervalues[4] - cornervalues[0] c2 = cornervalues[2] - cornervalues[0] c3 = cornervalues[1] - cornervalues[0] c4 = cornervalues[0] - cornervalues[4] - cornervalues[2] + cornervalues[6] c5 = cornervalues[0] - cornervalues[4] - cornervalues[1] + cornervalues[5] c6 = cornervalues[0] - cornervalues[2] - cornervalues[1] + cornervalues[3] c7 = cornervalues[0] - cornervalues[4] - cornervalues[2] - cornervalues[1] + cornervalues[6] + cornervalues[5] + cornervalues[3] - cornervalues[7] # 4. Compute cubic coefficients G3, G2, G1, G0 for f(u(t),v(t),w(t)) - isovalue = 0 G3 = c7 du dv dw G2 = (c4 du dv) + (c5 du dw) + (c6 dv dw) + \ c7 (du dv w0 + du dw v0 + dv dw u0) G1 = (c1 du) + (c2 dv) + (c3 dw) + \ (c4 (u0 dv + v0 du)) + \ (c5 (u0 dw + w0 du)) + \ (c6 (v0 dw + w0 dv)) + \ c7 (u0 v0 dw + u0 w0 dv + v0 w0 du) G0 = c0 + (c1 u0) + (c2 v0) + (c3 w0) + \ (c4 u0 v0) + (c5 u0 w0) + (c6 v0 w0) + \ (c7 u0 v0 w0) - isovalue # 5. Solve Cubic roots = [] EPS = 1e-9 if abs(G3) < EPS: # Quadratic or lower if abs(G2) < EPS: # Linear G1t + G0 = 0 if abs(G1) > EPS: roots.append(-G0 / G1) else: # Quadratic G2t^2 + G1t + G0 = 0 D2 = G1G1 - 4G2G0 if D2 >= 0: sqrtD2 = math.sqrt(D2) roots.append((-G1 + sqrtD2) / (2G2)) roots.append((-G1 - sqrtD2) / (2G2)) else: # Cubic G3t^3 + G2t^2 + G1t + G0 = 0 # Normalize to t^3 + at^2 + bt + c = 0 a = G2 / G3 b = G1 / G3 c = G0 / G3 # Cardano's method p = b - (a a) / 3.0 q = (2 a a a) / 27.0 - (a b) / 3.0 + c delta = (qq)/4.0 + (ppp)/27.0 if delta > EPS: # One real root sqrtdelta = math.sqrt(delta) u = cbrt(-q/2.0 + sqrtdelta) v = cbrt(-q/2.0 - sqrtdelta) t = u + v - a/3.0 roots.append(t) elif delta > -EPS: # Multiple roots (delta approx 0) if abs(q) < EPS: t = -a/3.0 roots.append(t) # Triple root else: u = cbrt(-q/2.0) t1 = 2u - a/3.0 t2 = -u - a/3.0 roots.append(t1) roots.append(t2) else: # 3 distinct real roots (delta < 0) # Use trigonometric solution r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27.0) costheta = -q / (2r) # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) theta = math.acos(costheta) m = 2 cbrt(r) t1 = m math.cos(theta/3.0) - a/3.0 t2 = m math.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3.0) - a/3.0 t3 = m math.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3.0) - a/3.0 roots.append(t1) roots.append(t2) roots.append(t3) # 6. Filter and return smallest positive t validroots = [t for t in roots if t > 1e-6] if not validroots: return None return min(validroots) Parameters: epsilon: Intersection threshold. A rule of thumb is 1% of the smallest voxel size to accurately encompass the surface area. iso: Isosurface threshold value, defaults to 0.0f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Cubic: If G3 \approx 0, the equation is quadratic. If G2 \approx 0 as well, it is linear. Robust implementations must check for these conditions to avoid division by zero. Precision: Single-precision arithmetic may yield numerical instability in root finding. The Neubauer iterative method is noted to yield single-precision, numerically stable results compared to some analytical solvers. Ambiguous Faces: In topological analysis (e.g., for dual contouring or polygonization), faces with four same-sign ended diagonals and four (+/-) edges are ambiguous. The sign is determined by the asymptotic decider. Analytic Voxel Intersection is a method for computing the intersection between a ray and the isosurface defined by the zero level set of a signed distance function (SDF) within a single voxel of an SDF grid. It solves the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation of the corner signed distances to find the exact intersection distance t. Unlike sphere tracing, which requires iterative stepping that slows down near the surface, this method provides a direct solution, avoiding iterative step reduction and offering superior performance for silhouette and secondary rays. Monotone Path Construction is an algorithm used to determine the start (low) and end (high) vertices of a monotone path passing through a specific sample point within a trilinear cell. It solves the problem of identifying the relevant arcs in a contour tree by mapping a continuous sample position to discrete mesh vertices, enabling the traversal of the contour tree's branch decomposition. It differs from analytic methods by relying on a deterministic, axis-parallel greedy descent/ascent strategy rather than solving polynomial roots for the exact intersection. A normalization technique for cubes with no body saddles, mapping the theoretical saddle point m into the block via linear scaling and analyzing gradients to constrain topology. Compute theoretical midpoint m = (-c/a - d/a, -b/a). If m is outside the block, apply linear transformations to scale the block so m is inside. Assume m is in block and T{mmm} = 0. Gradients along midpoint lines are constant: ax/a, ay/a, az/a. Assume all positive (apply axis reflection if negative). Let function values at positive ends be \alpha,  eta, \gamma > 0. A rendering technique that uses fast trilinear interpolation for ray intersection search but uses the gradient from tricubic interpolation for normal calculation to avoid visual discontinuities at node boundaries. Perform ray intersection search using the trilinear interpolant, which is faster to compute than tricubic. Store tricubic coefficients only at nodes containing the isosurface. Calculate surface normals using the gradient of the tricubic interpolant instead of the trilinear gradient to ensure smoothness. Trilinear interpolation guarantees shape continuity but not gradient continuity, causing visual discontinuities (grid patterns) at node boundaries if used for normals. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel intersection, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations to compute coefficients and solve a cubic equation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per intersection. Performance: Iterative methods like Neubauer's root finder are slightly faster than analytical solvers and yield single-precision, numerically stable results. GPU implementations can optimize coefficient extraction by fetching as few as 4 data samples per voxel. Strengths: Computes intersection points directly from the cubic polynomial; avoids iterative step reduction near surfaces; suitable for secondary rays where precision is critical. Limitations: Cubic solver complexity; potential numerical instability in single precision if not handled carefully; only applicable to hexahedral/trilinear grids. When to use: When exact surface location is required, or when performance of iterative marching is insufficient. When not to use: For non-hexahedral grids, or when approximate intersection is sufficient and simpler linear traversal is preferred. Trilinear Isosurface Intersection originates from the need to accurately render isosurfaces in volume data using ray tracing techniques. It leverages the fact that trilinear interpolation within a voxel results in a cubic polynomial along any ray passing through it. Early implementations used analytical cubic solvers (Schwarze's cubic solver), while later optimizations explored iterative root finders (Neubauer) for stability and speed. The method is also used in dual isosurfacing to compute interior points without requiring Hermite data, contrasting with dual contouring which does require it. name: Analytic Voxel Intersection
head: Cubic Voxel Intersection, SDF Grid Ray Tracing
body: Analytic Voxel Intersection is a method for computing the intersection between a ray and the isosurface defined by the zero level set of a signed distance function (SDF) within a single voxel of an SDF grid. It solves the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation of the corner signed distances to find the exact intersection distance t. Unlike sphere tracing, which requires iterative stepping that slows down near the surface, this method provides a direct solution, avoiding iterative step reduction and offering superior performance for silhouette and secondary rays. The method computes the intersection by solving the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation of the corner signed distances. Inputs: Ray origin o = (ox, oy, oz) and direction d = (dx, dy, dz) in world space. Voxel bounds in world space to compute entry and exit points. Signed distances at the eight corners of the voxel: s{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}, where s{000} is the corner at (0,0,0) in canonical space. Outputs: Intersection distance t \in [0, t{far}], where t{far} is the distance to the voxel exit. If no intersection exists, the method returns no hit. Data Structures: The voxel is treated as a unit cube in canonical space [0, 1]^3. Constants ki (i=0..7) and intermediate variables mj (j=0..5) are computed once per voxel/ray pair. Cubic coefficients ci (i=0..3). Step 1: Ray-Voxel Box Intersection Compute the intersection of the ray with the voxel bounding box to determine the entry point and t{far}. 1. If the ray origin is inside the box, set the new origin o{new} = o. 2. Otherwise, compute the entry point o{new} on the box surface. 3. Compute t{far} as the distance from o{new} to the exit point on the box surface. 4. Transform o{new} and d into the canonical voxel space [0, 1]^3. Note that d remains unchanged if the voxel is axis-aligned and unit-sized, but o must be shifted to the local corner. Let the transformed origin be o and direction be d for subsequent steps. Step 2: Compute Polynomial Constants Calculate the constants ki from the corner signed distances s{ijk}: \begin{aligned} k0 &= s{000} \\ k1 &= s{100} - s{000} \\ k2 &= s{010} - s{000} \\ k3 &= s{110} - s{010} - k1 \\ a &= s{101} - s{001} \\ k4 &= k0 - s{001} \\ k5 &= k1 - a \\ k6 &= k2 - (s{011} - s{001}) \\ k7 &= k3 - (s{111} - s{011} - a) \end{aligned} Calculate the intermediate variables mj using the transformed ray origin o and direction d: \begin{aligned} m0 &= ox oy \\ m1 &= dx dy \\ m2 &= ox dy + oy dx \\ m3 &= k5 oz - k1 \\ m4 &= k6 oz - k2 \\ m5 &= k7 oz - k3 \end{aligned} Step 3: Compute Cubic Coefficients Compute the coefficients ci of the cubic equation c3 t^3 + c2 t^2 + c1 t + c0 = 0: \begin{aligned} c0 &= (k4 oz - k0) + ox m3 + oy m4 + m0 m5 \\ c1 &= dx m3 + dy m4 + m2 m5 + dz (k4 + k5 ox + k6 oy + k7 m0) \\ c2 &= m1 m5 + dz (k5 dx + k6 dy + k7 m2) \\ c3 &= k7 m1 dz \end{aligned} This computation requires 37 operations (counting FMA as one). Step 4: Solve for Intersection Solve the cubic equation for the smallest real root t such that t \in [0, t{far}]. Two primary approaches are described: Approach A: Analytic Solver Use an analytic cubic root solver (e.g., Vieta's approach) to find all real roots and select the smallest valid t. This is the fastest voxel intersection method. Approach B: Numerical (Marmitt et al. + Newton-Raphson) 1. Differentiate the cubic: g'(t) = 3c3 t^2 + 2c2 t + c1 = 0. 2. Solve the quadratic g'(t)=0 to find critical points. 3. Split the interval [0, t{far}] into subintervals based on these critical points. 4. Process subintervals from t=0 to t{far}. For each subinterval [t{start}, t{end}], check if g(t{start})g(t{end}) \le 0. 5. If a sign change is detected, a root exists in the interval. 6. Refine the root using Newton-Raphson iteration: Initialize t using linear interpolation: t = \frac{g(t{end})t{start} - g(t{start})t{end}}{g(t{end}) - g(t{start})}. Iterate: \begin{aligned} t{prev} &= t \\ t &= t - \frac{g(t)}{g'(t)} \end{aligned} Stop when |t - t{prev}| < \epsilon or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-point imprecision: Rays may "sneak" between neighboring voxel surfaces, causing visible cracks. Mitigation: Add a test: if the ray origin is on a voxel face and f(ox, oy, oz) < 0, return an immediate hit to make the surface solid. Derivative Magnitude: In Newton-Raphson, if the starting point is on the cubic curve and the derivative magnitude is small, convergence may be slow or unstable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def analyticvoxelintersection(o, d, scorners, voxelmin, voxelmax): # 1. Ray-box intersection (standard slab method) tnear, tfar = rayboxintersect(o, d, voxelmin, voxelmax) if tnear > tfar or tfar < 0: return None if tnear == 0: olocal = o - voxelmin dlocal = d (voxelmax - voxelmin) else: olocal = o + d tnear - voxelmin dlocal = d (voxelmax - voxelmin) tfar = tfar - tnear # 2. Compute k constants k0 = scorners[0,0,0] k1 = scorners[1,0,0] - k0 k2 = scorners[0,1,0] - k0 k3 = scorners[1,1,0] - scorners[0,1,0] - k1 a = scorners[1,0,1] - scorners[0,0,1] k4 = k0 - scorners[0,0,1] k5 = k1 - a k6 = k2 - (scorners[0,1,1] - scorners[0,0,1]) k7 = k3 - (scorners[1,1,1] - scorners[0,1,1] - a) # 3. Compute m variables m0 = olocal.x olocal.y m1 = dlocal.x dlocal.y m2 = olocal.x dlocal.y + olocal.y dlocal.x m3 = k5 olocal.z - k1 m4 = k6 olocal.z - k2 m5 = k7 olocal.z - k3 # 4. Compute cubic coefficients c0 = (k4 olocal.z - k0) + olocal.x m3 + olocal.y m4 + m0 m5 c1 = dlocal.x m3 + dlocal.y m4 + m2 m5 + dlocal.z (k4 + k5 olocal.x + k6 olocal.y + k7 m0) c2 = m1 m5 + dlocal.z (k5 dlocal.x + k6 dlocal.y + k7 m2) c3 = k7 m1 dlocal.z # 5. Solve cubic for smallest real root in [0, tfar] # Analytic cubic root solver (e.g., Vieta's approach) roots = solvecubicanalytic(c3, c2, c1, c0) validroots = [t for t in roots if 0 <= t <= tfar] if not validroots: return None thit = min(validroots) # 6. Edge case: floating-point cracks mitigation if thit == 0 and f(olocal.x, olocal.y, olocal.z) < 0: return 0.0 return thit Time Complexity: The coefficient computation is constant time, O(1), with 37 operations. Solving the cubic is also O(1). The analytic solver is generally faster than the numerical Newton-Raphson approach, which depends on convergence speed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for constants and coefficients. Performance: The analytic test (A) is the fastest voxel intersection method. In benchmarks, it outperforms sphere tracing and numerical methods, especially near silhouettes and for secondary rays. Strengths: Direct solution avoids iterative step reduction; high performance; continuous normals can be computed via the gradient of the trilinear function. Limitations: Requires solving a cubic equation; floating-point errors can cause cracks without additional tests; complex to implement compared to simple sphere tracing. When to use: When performance is critical, especially for SDF grids where rays frequently intersect surfaces at grazing angles or for path tracing secondary rays. When not to use: For simple scenes where sphere tracing is sufficient and implementation complexity is a concern; if hardware acceleration for ray-box intersection is not available and traversal overhead dominates. The method was presented in "Ray tracing of signed distance function grids". It builds on the work of Parker et al. [1998], who derived the third-order polynomial for trilinear interpolation of SDFs but used a brute-force method requiring ~161 operations. The authors of optimized the coefficient computation to 37 operations and provided a remedy for discontinuous normals between voxels, which Parker et al. did not address. The method is used in real-time rendering and path tracing of SDF grids to improve performance over sphere tracing. name: Monotone Path Construction in Trilinear Cells
head: Axis-Parallel Monotone Path
body: Monotone Path Construction is an algorithm to find the start (low) and end (high) vertices of a monotone path passing through a sample point inside a trilinear cell. It solves the problem of mapping a continuous sample position to discrete mesh vertices to identify the corresponding arc in a contour tree subgraph. It differs from analytic voxel intersection methods by using a deterministic, axis-parallel greedy descent and ascent strategy rather than solving polynomial roots for exact intersections. Inputs: t: The trilinear interpolant function defined on the domain [0, 1]^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}. p: The sample position vector (x, y, z) inside the trilinear cell, where p \in [0, 1]^3. Outputs: p{lo}: The position of the mesh vertex representing the lower endpoint of the monotone path. p{hi}: The position of the mesh vertex representing the higher endpoint of the monotone path. Helper Functions: \text{roundDown}(\text{axis}, p): Returns a new position vector identical to p, except the component corresponding to \text{axis} is replaced with 0. \text{roundUp}(\text{axis}, p): Returns a new position vector identical to p, except the component corresponding to \text{axis} is replaced with 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize along X-axis: Set p{lo} = \text{roundDown}(x, p) and p{hi} = \text{roundUp}(x, p). If t(p{lo}) > t(p{hi}), swap p{lo} and p{hi} to ensure p{lo} is the lower-value endpoint. 2. Complete descending path to mesh vertex along Y-axis (for p{lo}): Set \text{temp} = \text{roundUp}(y, p{lo}) and p{lo} = \text{roundDown}(y, p{lo}). If t(p{lo}) > t(\text{temp}), swap p{lo} and \text{temp}. 3. Complete descending path to mesh vertex along Z-axis (for p{lo}): Set \text{temp} = \text{roundUp}(z, p{lo}) and p{lo} = \text{roundDown}(z, p{lo}). If t(p{lo}) > t(\text{temp}), swap p{lo} and \text{temp}. 4. Complete ascending path to mesh vertex along Y-axis (for p{hi}): Set \text{temp} = \text{roundUp}(y, p{hi}) and p{hi} = \text{roundDown}(y, p{hi}). If t(p{hi}) < t(\text{temp}), swap p{hi} and \text{temp}. 5. Complete ascending path to mesh vertex along Z-axis (for p{hi}): Set \text{temp} = \text{roundUp}(z, p{hi}) and p{hi} = \text{roundDown}(z, p{hi}). If t(p{hi}) < t(\text{temp}), swap p{hi} and \text{temp}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rounddown(axis, p): """Returns p with the component corresponding to axis set to 0.""" if axis == 'x': return (0, p[1], p[2]) elif axis == 'y': return (p[0], 0, p[2]) elif axis == 'z': return (p[0], p[1], 0) def roundup(axis, p): """Returns p with the component corresponding to axis set to 1.""" if axis == 'x': return (1, p[1], p[2]) elif axis == 'y': return (p[0], 1, p[2]) elif axis == 'z': return (p[0], p[1], 1) def monotonepathconstruction(t, p): """ t: function mapping (x,y,z) to scalar value p: tuple (x, y, z) in [0,1]^3 Returns: (plo, phi) """ # Step 1: Initialize along X plo = rounddown('x', p) phi = roundup('x', p) if t(plo) > t(phi): plo, phi = phi, plo # Step 2: Descending path for plo along Y temp = roundup('y', plo) plo = rounddown('y', plo) if t(plo) > t(temp): plo, temp = temp, plo # Step 3: Descending path for plo along Z temp = roundup('z', plo) plo = rounddown('z', plo) if t(plo) > t(temp): plo, temp = temp, plo # Step 4: Ascending path for phi along Y temp = roundup('y', phi) phi = rounddown('y', phi) if t(phi) < t(temp): phi, temp = temp, phi # Step 5: Ascending path for phi along Z temp = roundup('z', phi) phi = rounddown('z', phi) if t(phi) < t(temp): phi, temp = temp, phi return plo, phi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Values: If t(p{lo}) == t(p{hi}) or intermediate comparisons result in equality, the swap condition evaluates to false and the current vertex is retained. Boundary Conditions: The roundDown and roundUp functions explicitly map to 0 or 1, ensuring the output vertices are always mesh vertices (corners of the cell). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Deterministic execution with a fixed sequence of conditional swaps. Limitations: It constructs an approximate monotone path to vertices rather than finding the exact isosurface intersection. The method was introduced to find the arc in the contour tree corresponding to the region containing the sample point. Once the high and low vertices are determined, the algorithm looks up the corresponding arcs and walks from the high arc towards the low arc in the branch decomposition (a rooted tree) to find the path between branches. name: Face Saddle Detection
head: Bilinear face saddle criterion, Saddle Point Detection on Shared Face, Trilinear Face Saddle Detection
body: Face Saddle Detection determines whether a critical point located on the shared face between two adjacent trilinear cells is a true saddle point of the piecewise trilinear interpolant or merely a regular point. While a point on a shared face is always a saddle of the 2D bilinear interpolant defined on that face, it is only a saddle of the full 3D trilinear field if the connectivity of the isosurface regions matches across the boundary. This method distinguishes true 3D saddles from false positives arising from the planar constraint of the face, ensuring correct topological classification during isosurface extraction. Inputs: Function values at the 8 vertices of two adjacent cells sharing a face. The coordinates of the critical point p on the shared face. Outputs: Boolean: True if p is a saddle point of the trilinear interpolant; False otherwise. Data Structures: The method requires the function values at the vertices of the two cells. Let the shared face be perpendicular to the x-axis. The vertices are labeled as follows: Shared Face Vertices: A, B, C, D. These are the four vertices of the face common to both cells. Adjacent Cell 1 Vertices: A1, B1, C1, D1. These are the vertices of the first cell connected to A, B, C, D respectively, extending in the positive x direction. Adjacent Cell 2 Vertices: A{-1}, B{-1}, C{-1}, D{-1}. These are the vertices of the second cell connected to A, B, C, D respectively, extending in the negative x direction. Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Verify Bilinear Saddle: Check if p is a saddle point of the bilinear interpolant defined on the shared face. If p is not a saddle of the face's bilinear interpolant, it is a regular point of the trilinear interpolant. 2. Rotate Cell Notation: Rotate the labeling of the vertices on the shared face such that vertices A and C have function values larger than the saddle value f(p), and vertices B and D have function values smaller than f(p). This ensures that A+C - B - D > 0. 3. Compute Connectivity Derivatives: Calculate the derivative of the connectivity term Ax Cx - Bx Dx with respect to x at x=0 for both adjacent cells. This derivative determines the sign of the connectivity for small x > 0 (for Cell 1) and small x < 0 (for Cell 2). For Cell 1 (positive x direction), compute S1: S1 = C(A1 - A) + A(C1 - C) - D(B1 - B) - B(D1 - D) For Cell 2 (negative x direction), compute S2: S2 = C(A{-1} - A) + A(C{-1} - C) - D(B{-1} - B) - B(D{-1} - D) Note: The expression Ax Cx - Bx Dx determines connectivity. If positive, negative values are connected; if negative, positive values are connected. The derivative at x=0 provides the sign of this term for infinitesimal x. 4. Check Sign Consistency: Compare the signs of S1 and S2. If \text{sign}(S1) == \text{sign}(S2), then p is a saddle point of the trilinear interpolant. If \text{sign}(S1) \neq \text{sign}(S2), then p is a regular point of the trilinear interpolant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isfacesaddle(A, B, C, D, A1, B1, C1, D1, Aminus1, Bminus1, Cminus1, Dminus1): """ Determines if a point p on the shared face between two cells is a saddle point. Parameters: A, B, C, D: Function values at the shared face vertices. Must be rotated such that A and C > saddlevalue and B, D < saddlevalue. A1, B1, C1, D1: Function values at the vertices of the adjacent cell in the +x direction. Aminus1, Bminus1, Cminus1, Dminus1: Function values at the vertices of the adjacent cell in the -x direction. Returns: True if p is a trilinear saddle, False otherwise. """ # Step 1: Check if p is a bilinear saddle on the face. # This check is assumed to be performed by the caller or a preceding step. # If not a bilinear saddle, return False. if not isbilinearsaddleonface(A, B, C, D): return False # Step 2: Compute S1 for the cell in the +x direction # Formula: C(A1 - A) + A(C1 - C) - D(B1 - B) - B(D1 - D) S1 = C (A1 - A) + A (C1 - C) - D (B1 - B) - B (D1 - D) # Step 3: Compute S2 for the cell in the -x direction # Formula: C(A-1 - A) + A(C-1 - C) - D(B-1 - B) - B(D-1 - D) S2 = C (Aminus1 - A) + A (Cminus1 - C) - D (Bminus1 - B) - B (Dminus1 - D) # Step 4: Check sign consistency # If S1 and S2 have the same sign, it is a saddle. # Note: If S1 or S2 is 0, it implies bilinear variation in the cube, which is considered # not possible if there are different values along edges. # We use strict sign comparison. signS1 = 1 if S1 > 0 else (-1 if S1 < 0 else 0) signS2 = 1 if S2 > 0 else (-1 if S2 < 0 else 0) if signS1 == 0 or signS2 == 0: # This case implies bilinear variation in the cube. # According to, this is not possible if there are different values along edges. # If it occurs, it is treated as a degenerate case. # Based on the logic that 0 implies no connectivity change direction, # it does not satisfy the "same sign" condition for a saddle in the strict sense # of connecting regions in both cubes consistently with non-zero derivatives. # However, the lemma states "have the same sign". 0 is not a sign in the context # of connecting positive/negative regions in the proof. # We return False as it fails the strict sign match required for the saddle classification # in the presence of non-zero derivatives. return False return signS1 == signS2 def isbilinearsaddleonface(A, B, C, D): """ Checks if the point p (implicitly defined by the saddle value) is a saddle of the bilinear interpolant on the face. For a bilinear patch with corners A, B, C, D (ordered around the face), a saddle exists if (A - B)(C - D) < 0 and (A - D)(C - B) < 0. This assumes A and C are opposite, B and D are opposite. """ # Assuming A, B, C, D are ordered such that A-C and B-D are diagonals # The condition for a saddle in a bilinear patch is that the product of # differences along diagonals is negative. return (A - C) (B - D) < 0 Parameters: A, C: Function values on the shared face vertices that are larger than the saddle value. B, D: Function values on the shared face vertices that are smaller than the saddle value. A1, C1, B1, D1: Function values of the vertices in the first adjacent cell. A{-1}, C{-1}, B{-1}, D{-1}: Function values of the vertices in the second adjacent cell. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Derivative: If the calculated derivative value (S1 or S2) is 0, it implies bilinear variation in the cube. The source states this is considered not possible if there are different values along edges. In implementation, this should be treated as a degenerate case, likely returning False or handling via higher-order checks, as the sign is undefined. Sign Ambiguity: The criterion relies on the strict sign of the derivatives. If the signs differ, the connectivity of positive/negative regions does not match across the face, meaning the point is not a critical point of the piecewise trilinear interpolant. Computes the exact intersection of a ray with the isosurface inside a single voxel using the roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation. It does not explicitly classify critical points but finds the intersection distance. Analytic Voxel Intersection Constructs a monotone path through the cell to guide the ray marching or intersection search, ensuring convergence to the correct root. It handles the topology but does not explicitly detect face saddles. Monotone Path Construction in Trilinear Cells Time Complexity: O(1) per face saddle check. It involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, multiplications, additions). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional data structures are required beyond the vertex values. Strengths: Provides an exact topological classification of critical points on cell boundaries, which is crucial for correct isosurface extraction and topology preservation. It avoids the need for numerical refinement at these specific points. Limitations: Requires access to the function values of both adjacent cells and their neighbors. It is only applicable to points lying exactly on the shared faces of the grid. When to use: Use when extracting isosurfaces from trilinearly interpolated scalar fields and topological correctness is required, particularly when critical points may lie on cell boundaries. The method originates from the analysis of critical points in piecewise trilinear interpolation. It is formally stated as Lemma 4 in the work by. The lemma builds on the idea that a face saddle is a saddle of the trilinear interpolant if and only if the connectivity of the isosurface regions (positive and negative) is consistent across the shared face. This consistency is determined by the sign of the derivative of the connectivity term Ax Cx - Bx Dx with respect to the axis perpendicular to the face. The work references Nielson and Hamann [20] for the connectivity criterion and Chernyaev [4] for the idea of using the derivative to determine connectivity direction. Exploring Scalar Fields Using Critical Isovalues, https://escholarship.org/content/qt8h5134ht/qt8h5134ht.pdf?t=ptt27g, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Neubauer Iso-surface Ray Casting
head: Kd-Jump, Neubauer method, Ray Casting Visibility Test, Ray tracing for occlusion
body: Neubauer Iso-surface Ray Casting is a visibility testing method used to determine which parts of extracted line loops or sparse surface features are occluded by the isosurface, avoiding the computational cost of extracting and rendering the entire isosurface mesh. It sets itself apart from siblings like Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction and Trilinear Isosurface Intersection by focusing on binary occlusion checks for specific vertices rather than precise surface point extraction, and differs from Ray Tracing by using a coarse macro-cell traversal structure optimized for sparse feature visibility. Inputs: A scalar volume dataset. A set of vertices representing features (e.g., line loop vertices) to be tested for visibility. Camera position. Macro-cell size parameter m. Outputs: A boolean mask indicating which vertices are occluded by the isosurface. Data Structures: 1. Macro-Cell Grid: The volume is subdivided into a 3D grid of macro-cells, each of size m \times m \times m voxels. 2. Min/Max Octree: Built from the macro-cells. Each leaf node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values found within its corresponding macro-cell. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: 1. Subdivide the complete data set into macro-cells of size m^3. 2. Build a min/max octree from these macro-cells. 3. Set the macro-cell size parameter m, typically between 4 and 10. 2. Visibility Test for Each Vertex: For each vertex in the rendered feature set: 1. Define a ray originating at the vertex and directed towards the camera position. 2. Apply a depth offset heuristic to the ray origin to prevent immediate self-intersection detection. 3. Traverse the min/max octree using the ray: at each traversal step, check the stored min/max values to determine if boundary-cells belong to the next sub-tree. 4. At a leaf node, project/rasterize the boundaries of the macro-cell onto the image plane to yield a hexagonal footprint. 5. As the ray passes through each cell, determine whether it intersects the isosurface by examining the intersection of the ray with the face by which it leaves the cell. 6. At that intersection, use linear interpolation from the four corners to determine the function value and check if it has changed sign (indicating the ray passed from outside to inside the isosurface). 7. If the sign has changed, mark the originating vertex as occluded. Parameters: m: Macro-cell size dimension. Typical values are between 4 and 10. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: Tracing a ray from a vertex on the surface directly to the camera may immediately detect the surface itself as an occluder. This is mitigated by using a "depth offset" heuristic, moving the ray origin slightly away from the vertex. Precision: Linear interpolation at the cell boundary assumes the scalar field is well-behaved within the macro-cell. This method computes the ray-isosurface intersection for metaballs by representing the scalar density field along a ray as a polynomial in Bézier form and applying Bézier clipping to find the root. It builds on Neubauer Iso-surface Ray Casting. A distributed implementation of the Neubauer method optimized for large datasets using a cluster of render nodes. It sets itself apart by scaling performance linearly with the number of nodes, addressing the scalability limitations of the single-node Neubauer approach. It is chosen when rendering very large datasets (e.g., 428 MB Visible Female) where single-node performance is insufficient. Performance is almost five times slower than Wald's approach for the Visible Female dataset on a single PC, but scales effectively on clusters. Time Complexity: Asymptotically O(n^2) for a volume of size n^3. The number of vertices rendered is O(n), and the number of cells touched by an average ray is also O(n). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the min/max octree, which consumes much less additional memory for acceleration structures compared to alternatives like kd-trees. Measured Performance: Single PIV 1.9 GHz, 512x512 resolution: Average frame rate of 0.8 fps. Visible Female dataset (428 MB): 1 fps with 1 render node, up to 22 fps with 32 nodes. Compared to Wald's approach (~8.1 fps on single PC), Neubauer is ~5x slower on the Visible Female dataset on a single machine. Strengths: Avoids the cost of full isosurface extraction; suitable for sparse features; low memory overhead for acceleration structures. Limitations: Does not scale well for real-time rendering of large datasets on single nodes; asymptotically expensive compared to z-buffer approaches for dense features; precision limited by macro-cell size and linear interpolation. When to use: When only sparse features (lines, loops) need visibility testing and full mesh extraction is too costly. When not to use: When real-time performance on large, dense volumes is required on a single CPU; when precise surface point extraction is needed rather than binary occlusion. The method was introduced by Neubauer et al. in 2002. It was developed as a solution for rendering line drawings from volume data, specifically to determine occlusion for extracted loops without generating the full isosurface mesh. It has been used as a baseline for comparison in single-kernel rendering pipelines, such as in the Kd-Jump implementation. name: Interactive Large Iso-Surface Ray Tracing
head: Brute-force ray tracing for isosurfaces, DeMarle approach, Direct ray-isosurface intersection, Interactive Ray Tracing for Isosurface Rendering, Out-of-core iso-surface ray tracing
body: This method renders isosurfaces from large rectilinear scalar fields by tracing rays through the volume and performing analytic intersections, thereby avoiding the explicit generation of polygonal surface meshes (such as Marching Cubes). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Neubauer Iso-surface Ray Casting by computing the exact intersection point analytically within each voxel rather than extracting line segments and testing for occlusion, and from Bézier Clipping for Metaball Ray Casting by targeting rectilinear grid data rather than implicit metaball fields. Inputs: A rectilinear scalar field \rho with even grid point spacing, an isovalue \rho{\text{iso}}, and a set of camera rays defined by origin \vec{a} and direction \vec{b}. Outputs: The color of the first isosurface intersection for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Volume Data: Rectilinear array of scalar values. 2. Bricks: The volume is partitioned into 3D tiles ("bricks") to improve cache locality. Brick dimensions are independent of the hierarchy cell sizes. Neither the number of atomic voxels nor the number of bricks needs to be a power of two. 3. Spatial Hierarchy: A tri-level hierarchy is used to accelerate traversal of empty cells. Level 0: Top-level cell covering the entire volume. Level 1 & 2: Intermediate macrocells. Level 3: Data cells (voxels). Each macrocell stores the minimum and maximum data values of its children. The storage overhead is negligible (< 0.5% of data size). 4. Work Queue: A queue of screen-space tiles for dynamic load balancing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Split the screen into tiles of 32 pixels width by 4 pixels height. Add all tiles to a work queue. 2. Tile Processing: For each tile assigned to a processor: a. For each pixel in the tile, construct the ray \vec{r}(t) = \vec{a} + t\vec{b}. b. Traversal: Use the Amanatides and Woo incremental method to traverse the ray through the volume cells. i. At each step, check the current macrocell's min/max values. ii. If \rho{\text{iso}} \notin [\min, \max], skip the macrocell and advance to the next cell in the traversal order. iii. If \rho{\text{iso}} \in [\min, \max], descend into the hierarchy or proceed to the specific voxel cell. c. Intersection: When a voxel containing the isosurface is encountered, solve for the intersection parameter t. The density \rho is approximated using trilinear interpolation between the 8 grid points of the voxel. This results in a cubic polynomial in t: \rho(xa + txb, ya + tyb, za + tzb) - \rho{\text{iso}} = 0 Solve this cubic polynomial in closed form to find roots t. d. Root Selection: i. Discard roots that are not contained within the current cell's parameter range. ii. If multiple valid roots exist, select the smallest t (closest to the eye). iii. If no valid roots exist, the ray misses the isosurface in this cell; continue traversal. e. Shading: Compute the color at the intersection point using the selected t. This may involve normal estimation via the gradient of the trilinear interpolation. 3. Load Balancing: Processors pull tiles from the queue. Initially, large chunks are assigned to reduce contention. As the frame completes, smaller chunks are assigned to balance the load. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tilecoords, volume, hierarchy, isovalue, camera): """ Renders a single tile of the image. tilecoords: (xstart, ystart, width, height) volume: 3D array of scalar values hierarchy: 3-level tree storing min/max per node isovalue: float camera: object with getray(x, y) method """ imagebuffer = emptyarray(width, height) for y in range(ystart, ystart + height): for x in range(xstart, xstart + width): ray = camera.getray(x, y) intersectiont = None # Phase 1 & 2: Traverse and Intersect currentcell = hierarchy.root tcurrent = ray.origin while currentcell is not None: # Check if isovalue is within the bounds of the current macrocell if not (hierarchy.getmin(currentcell) <= isovalue <= hierarchy.getmax(currentcell)): # Skip this macrocell, advance ray to next cell boundary tcurrent = ray.advancetonextcellboundary(tcurrent, currentcell) currentcell = hierarchy.getnextcell(currentcell, tcurrent) continue # If we are at the leaf level (data cells), perform analytic intersection if currentcell.isleaf(): # Get the 8 corner values of the voxel voxelvalues = volume.getvoxelvalues(currentcell) # Solve cubic polynomial for trilinear interpolation intersection # Equation: rho(ray(t)) - isovalue = 0 roots = solvecubictrilinearintersection(ray, voxelvalues, isovalue) # Filter roots: must be within the cell's t-range validroots = [t for t in roots if ray.isincell(t, currentcell)] if validroots: # Select closest intersection intersectiont = min(validroots) break # Advance to next cell in hierarchy or volume tcurrent = ray.advancetonextcellboundary(tcurrent, currentcell) currentcell = hierarchy.getnextcell(currentcell, tcurrent) # Phase 3: Shade if intersectiont is not None: point = ray.origin + intersectiont ray.direction color = shade(point, ray, volume, hierarchy) imagebuffer[y - ystart][x - xstart] = color else: imagebuffer[y - ystart][x - xstart] = backgroundcolor return imagebuffer def solvecubictrilinearintersection(ray, voxelvalues, isovalue): """ Solves for t in rho(x(t), y(t), z(t)) = isovalue using trilinear interpolation. Returns list of real roots. """ # Define trilinear interpolation coefficients based on ray direction and voxel corners # rho(t) = c0 + c1t + c2t^2 + c3t^3 # The coefficients c0..c3 are derived from the 8 voxel values and ray direction components # This is a standard expansion of trilinear interpolation along a line coeffs = computetrilinearcoeffs(ray, voxelvalues) # Solve cubic equation c3t^3 + c2t^2 + c1t + (c0 - isovalue) = 0 roots = solvecubicequation(coeffs[3], coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] - isovalue) return roots Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Solving the cubic polynomial requires careful handling of numerical precision to avoid missing intersections or finding false ones near cell boundaries. Multiple Roots: A ray may intersect the same isosurface multiple times within a single voxel (e.g., a thin structure passing through). The algorithm must select the smallest t. Worst Case Complexity: If the isosurface is highly complex and fills the volume, the hierarchy provides little benefit, and complexity approaches O(n). Time Complexity: Average complexity with a three-level hierarchy is O(\sqrt[3]{n}), where n is the number of voxels. Worst case is O(n). Memory Complexity: The hierarchy overhead is negligible (< 0.5% of data size). Performance: On an SGI Reality Monster (64 CPUs), the Visible Woman dataset (910 MB, 1734 slices, 512x512, 16-bit) achieves 7-15 FPS for skin isosurface (\rho=600.5) and 6-15 FPS for bone isosurface (\rho=1224.5). Time Distribution: For skin, traversal takes 55%, intersection 22%, shading 23%. For bone, traversal takes 66%, intersection 21%, shading 13%. Scalability: On 128 processors, efficiency is 91% for View 1 and 80% for View 2. Efficiency drops for >64 processors due to load imbalance and synchronization overhead. Strengths: Simplicity, scalability on distributed/shared-memory multiprocessors, no need for explicit mesh generation, correct front-to-back compositing order for transparency. Limitations: High intrinsic computational cost compared to optimized ray-tracing methods (e.g., Wald's approach is ~5x faster on similar datasets). Performance is sensitive to load imbalance in complex views. The method was introduced by DeMarle et al. in "Interactive Ray Tracing for Isosurface Rendering". It was designed to render the Visible Woman dataset (CT data from the National Library of Medicine Visible Human Project) interactively on high-end systems. The approach leverages the scalability of brute-force ray tracing when combined with optimizations like bricking and spatial hierarchies. name: Bézier Clipping for Metaball Ray Casting
head: Nishita et al. method, Ray-isosurface test using Bézier form
body: This method computes the ray-isosurface intersection for metaballs by representing the scalar density field along a viewing ray as a polynomial in Bézier form and applying Bézier clipping to find the root. It builds on Neubauer Iso-surface Ray Casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A viewing ray defined by origin and direction; a set of N metaballs (spheres) with centers (xi, yi, zi) and effective radii Ri in the viewing coordinate system; a target isosurface value \tau; and a parameter interval s \in [0, 1] representing the ray segment. Output: The intersection point(s) on the isosurface, or null if no intersection exists in the interval. Data Structures: Bézier Coefficients: For each metaball i, a set of coefficients \{dm^i\} representing the density function fi(s) of degree M. Combined Density: The sum of individual metaball densities, also represented in Bézier form. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection Test: For each metaball i, determine if the ray intersects the sphere. Calculate the determinant Di of the quadratic equation for the ray-sphere intersection. If no intersection, skip the metaball. Define the parameter ai as: ai = \frac{Di}{Ri} where Ri is the effective radius of metaball i. 2. Compute Bézier Coefficients for Single Metaball: Calculate the coefficients \{dm^i\} for the density function fi(s) of degree M based on the polynomial degree used for the metaball definition. For Quartic Polynomial (Degree 4): d0^i = d1^i = d3^i = d4^i = 0 d2^i = \frac{8}{3} ai^2 For Degree-Six Polynomial (Degree 6): d0^i = d1^i = d5^i = d6^i = 0 d2^i = d4^i = \frac{16}{27} ai^2 d3^i = \frac{8(8ai + 5)ai^2}{45} 3. Clipping for Combined Density: For N metaballs intersecting the ray in the given interval, compute the coefficients of the total density function. The total density is the sum of individual densities. To maintain the Bézier form and enable clipping, apply de Casteljau's algorithm to clip the Bézier curve defined by \{dm^i\} for each metaball to the current interval, then sum the resulting control points. Let the combined Bézier coefficients be \{Dm\}. 4. Ray-Isosurface Test: Substitute the combined density function in Bézier form into the ray-isosurface test equation to obtain the equation for the ray-isosurface test at that interval. This yields a polynomial equation in Bézier form representing the distance from the isosurface. 5. Bézier Clipping: Apply Bézier clipping to the resulting polynomial to isolate roots within s \in [0, 1]. This involves iteratively clipping the domain based on the convex hull property of the Bézier curve until the root is found or the interval is discarded. Bounding Rectangle Calculation (Culling): To efficiently cull metaballs that do not intersect the screen, calculate the bounding rectangle of the sphere's projection on the screen. Let (xi, yi, zi) be the center of sphere i in the viewing coordinate system, Ri its radius, and z{\text{screen}} the distance from the viewpoint to the screen. The x and y coordinates of the bounding rectangle are: x = \frac{z{\text{screen}}(xi zi \pm Ri \sqrt{xi^2 + zi^2 - Ri^2})}{zi^2 - Ri^2} y = \frac{z{\text{screen}}(yi zi \pm Ri \sqrt{yi^2 + zi^2 - Ri^2})}{zi^2 - Ri^2} Render squares covering this region using point sprites for visualization or culling purposes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def bezierclippingmetaballraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, metaballs, isosurfacethreshold, zscreen): """ rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) metaballs: list of dicts with 'center' (cx, cy, cz) and 'radius' R isosurfacethreshold: float zscreen: float """ # 1. Culling and Setup candidates = [] for ball in metaballs: cx, cy, cz = ball['center'] R = ball['radius'] denomx = cz cz - R R if abs(denomx) < 1e-9: continue radtermx = R math.sqrt(cx cx + cz cz - R R) xmin = (zscreen (cx cz - radtermx)) / denomx xmax = (zscreen (cx cz + radtermx)) / denomx denomy = cz cz - R R if abs(denomy) < 1e-9: continue radtermy = R math.sqrt(cy cy + cz cz - R R) ymin = (zscreen (cy cz - radtermy)) / denomy ymax = (zscreen (cy cz + radtermy)) / denomy candidates.append(ball) # 2. Ray-Sphere Intersection and Coefficient Calculation combinedbeziercoeffs = [0.0] 7 # Max degree 6 + 1 for ball in candidates: cx, cy, cz = ball['center'] R = ball['radius'] Lx = rayorigin[0] - cx Ly = rayorigin[1] - cy Lz = rayorigin[2] - cz a = 1.0 b = 2.0 (raydirection[0] Lx + raydirection[1] Ly + raydirection[2] Lz) c = Lx Lx + Ly Ly + Lz Lz - R R discriminant = b b - 4 a c if discriminant < 0: continue Di = discriminant ai = Di / R d = [0.0] 7 d[2] = (16.0 / 27.0) (ai 2) d[3] = (8.0 (8.0 ai + 5.0) (ai 2)) / 45.0 d[4] = (16.0 / 27.0) (ai 2) for m in range(7): combinedbeziercoeffs[m] += d[m] # 3. Ray-Isosurface Test: F(s) - tau = 0 # In Bézier form, subtracting a constant tau from the curve means # subtracting tau from all control points. for m in range(7): combinedbeziercoeffs[m] -= isosurfacethreshold # 4. Bézier Clipping (Standard implementation) def bezierclip(coeffs, u, v): # Iteratively clip the interval [u, v] based on convex hull bounds while v - u > 1e-6: mincp = min(coeffs) maxcp = max(coeffs) if maxcp < 0 or mincp > 0: return None # No root in interval # Find clipping parameter t where hull crosses 0 tleft = 0.0 tright = 1.0 for i in range(len(coeffs) - 1): if coeffs[i] <= 0 <= coeffs[i+1]: t = coeffs[i] / (coeffs[i] - coeffs[i+1]) tleft = max(tleft, t) elif coeffs[i+1] <= 0 <= coeffs[i]: t = coeffs[i] / (coeffs[i] - coeffs[i+1]) tright = min(tright, t) if tleft >= tright: return None u = u + tleft (v - u) v = u + tright (v - u) return u roots = bezierclip(combinedbeziercoeffs, 0.0, 1.0) if roots is None: return None return rayorigin[0] + roots raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + roots raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + roots raydirection[2] Time Complexity: Depends on the degree of the polynomial and the number of clipping iterations. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of metaballs N for storing coefficients. Strengths: Robust against multiple intersections; no derivative calculation required; handles high-degree density functions naturally. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the Bézier clipping implementation; potential numerical instability if coefficients are large or small. When to use: When rendering large numbers of metaballs with high-quality isosurfaces and robust intersection testing is required. Originating from Nishita et al. [NN94], this method was adapted for GPU-based fast ray casting for metaballs. It leverages the properties of Bézier curves to perform robust root finding for the implicit surface defined by the metaball density field. name: Hybrid Packetization Strategy
head: Hybrid Intersector, Hybrid Packetization, Hybrid Packetization for Triangle Intersection, Hybrid Ray-Triangle Intersection
body: The Hybrid Packetization Strategy is a ray-triangle intersection method designed to improve SIMD utilization on GPUs when standard packetization is inefficient due to sparse acceleration structures with high primitive density per leaf. It solves the problem of lost coherence in warp-level computations by dynamically switching between standard warp-level intersection and parallel processing of individual rays based on workload. It sets itself apart from standard packetization by distributing the work of a single ray across multiple threads when the number of intersection candidates is high, thereby maintaining throughput even when rays traverse cells with varying densities. The method operates within a GPU warp (SIMD unit of 32 threads) during the ray-triangle intersection stage of ray traversal. It adapts its execution path based on the number of intersection candidates (workload) for the rays in the warp. Inputs: A warp of 32 rays, each with a current traversal state and a list of intersection candidates (primitive indices) for the current cell. Outputs: The closest intersection distance for each ray, stored in thread-local memory. Shared Memory Buffer: Stores entries for rays with high workload. Each entry contains: rayindex: The index of the ray within the warp (0–31). firstcandidateindex: The index of the first primitive in the ray's candidate list. Note: The indices of the remaining primitives are consecutive, so only the first needs to be stored. Shared Memory Arrays: Used for reduction of intersection distances. High Workload Threshold: 16 intersection candidates. Standard Intersection Fallback Threshold: 20 active rays with high workload. Parallelization Granularity: Pairs of rays (2 rays per thread pair). 1. Check Uniformity: Determine if all 32 rays in the warp have intersection candidates. If yes, proceed with standard ray-triangle intersection. If no, proceed to step 2. 2. Check High Workload Count: Count the number of rays with at least 16 intersection candidates (high workload). 3. Fallback Decision: If the count is greater than 20, proceed with the standard intersection routine. This maps better to Fermi GPUs because they support more Boolean operations at the warp level in hardware. If the count is 20 or fewer, proceed to step 4. 4. Buffer High Workload Rays: For each ray with high workload (≥16 candidates), use an atomic increment on a shared counter to get a unique position in the shared memory buffer. Store the rayindex and firstcandidateindex in the buffer at that position. 5. Process Buffered Rays: Iterate through the entries in the shared memory buffer, taking two entries at a time. For each pair of rays, perform 32 intersection tests in parallel. 6. Reduce Results: Combine results by performing a reduction on the arrays containing intersection distances, which are shared between threads. 7. Store Results: The thread responsible for tracing each ray records the closest intersection (if any) in thread-local memory. 8. Process Remaining Rays: When all rays with high workload have been processed, perform the remaining intersection tests one by one for all rays as usual. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridpacketizationintersect(warprays): # warprays: list of 32 Ray objects # Each Ray has.candidates (list of int) and.closestdist (float, init to inf) # Step 1: Check if all rays have intersection candidates allhavecandidates = all(len(r.candidates) > 0 for r in warprays) if allhavecandidates: # Standard warp-level ray-triangle intersection return warprays # Step 2: Count rays with high workload (>= 16 candidates) highworkloadthreshold = 16 fallbackthreshold = 20 highworkloadrays = [(i, r) for i, r in enumerate(warprays) if len(r.candidates) >= highworkloadthreshold] numhigh = len(highworkloadrays) # Step 3: Fallback if too many high-workload rays if numhigh > fallbackthreshold: # Standard intersection routine (optimized for Fermi Boolean ops) return warprays # Step 4: Buffer high workload rays # Atomic increment on a shared counter to get unique position buffer = [] for idx, ray in highworkloadrays: pos = len(buffer) # Simulates atomic increment on shared counter buffer.append((idx, ray.candidates[0])) # Step 5: Process buffered rays in pairs for i in range(0, len(buffer), 2): if i + 1 < len(buffer): idx1, = buffer[i] idx2, = buffer[i + 1] ray1 = warprays[idx1] ray2 = warprays[idx2] # Perform 32 intersection tests for a pair of rays in parallel shareddists = [float('inf')] 32 allcands = ray1.candidates + ray2.candidates numcands = len(allcands) for t in range(32): for k in range(t, numcands, 32): primidx = allcands[k] # Standard ray-triangle intersection test pass # Step 6: Reduce results on shared distance arrays mindist = min(shareddists) # Step 7: Record closest intersection in thread local memory warprays[idx1].closestdist = mindist warprays[idx2].closestdist = mindist else: # Odd ray in buffer, process alone idx, = buffer[i] ray = warprays[idx] mindist = float('inf') for primidx in ray.candidates: # Standard ray-triangle intersection test pass warprays[idx].closestdist = mindist # Step 8: Process remaining low-workload rays one by one for idx, ray in enumerate(warprays): if len(ray.candidates) < highworkloadthreshold: mindist = float('inf') for primidx in ray.candidates: # Standard ray-triangle intersection test pass warprays[idx].closestdist = mindist return warprays Coherence Loss: SIMD efficiency is tied to ray coherence. It is lost as soon as some rays traverse a full cell while others pass through an empty one. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The method assumes a warp size of 32 threads. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of intersection candidates and the number of high-workload rays. Memory Complexity: Uses shared memory for the buffer and reduction arrays. The buffer holds at most 20 entries; if more than 20 high-workload rays exist, the algorithm falls back to the standard routine instead of using the buffer. Measured Performance: Tested on NVIDIA GeForce GTX 285, GTX 280, and GTX 470. Performance scales with the number of primitive references, which is scene-dependent. Strengths: Improves SIMD utilization for sparse grids with many primitives per leaf. Limitations: Requires benchmarking to determine the optimal fallback threshold (20). The actual SIMD width of 32 was considered too big for processing more than 2 rays at a time due to overhead. When to Use: When standard packetization is inefficient due to sparse acceleration structures with high primitive density per leaf. When Not to Use: When the number of high-workload rays exceeds 20, or when rays are highly coherent. The Hybrid Packetization Strategy was introduced in the paper "Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing on GPUs" by J. Kalojanov, M. Billeter, and P. Slusallek. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of standard packetization in the context of two-level grids, which are sparse and contain many primitives per leaf. The method was tested on NVIDIA GPUs, specifically Fermi architecture (GTX 285, GTX 470) and earlier (GTX 280). name: Ray Tracing
head: Classic ray tracing, Whitted-style Ray Tracing
body: Classic ray tracing (Whitted-style) is a rendering model that captures shadows, specular reflection, refraction, and diffuse surface shading by placing an image plane in the scene and sending rays through each pixel. It entails ray casting with the additional tracing of secondary rays for shadows and refractions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene description containing geometric primitives, material properties, light sources, and a camera model defining an image plane. Output: A 2D image where each pixel value represents the accumulated lighting information gathered by rays intersecting objects. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by an origin point \mathbf{o} and a direction vector \mathbf{d}. Intersection Record: Contains the hit point \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, material properties, and distance t from origin. Scene: Contains objects, lights, and a method to find the closest intersection along a ray. Algorithm Steps: The rendering process traces rays recursively. For each pixel, a primary ray is generated. The function TraceRay(ray, depth) proceeds as follows: 1. Intersection Test: Find the closest intersection between ray and any object in the scene. If no intersection occurs, return the background color. 2. Diffuse Shading: Calculate the diffuse component of the surface color based on the material's diffuse reflectivity and illumination from visible light sources. 3. Shadow Testing: For each light source, cast a shadow ray from the intersection point \mathbf{p} toward the light source. If this ray intersects any object before reaching the light, the point is blocked; otherwise, it is illuminated. 4. Reflection: If the material has non-zero reflectivity, spawn a reflection ray. The direction \mathbf{r} is calculated using the surface normal \mathbf{n} and incident direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} Recursively call TraceRay(r, depth + 1). 5. Refraction: If the material has non-zero refractivity, spawn a refraction ray. The direction \mathbf{t} is calculated using Snell's Law, accounting for the indices of refraction of the current medium and the material. Recursively call TraceRay(t, depth + 1). 6. Accumulation: Combine the diffuse, reflected, and refracted contributions according to the material's shading model to produce the final color for the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction class HitRecord: def init(self, point, normal, material, distance): self.point = point self.normal = normal self.material = material self.distance = distance EPSILON = 1e-4 BACKGROUNDCOLOR = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) return tuple(x / length for x in v) def reflect(direction, normal): return tuple(d - 2 dot(direction, normal) n for d, n in zip(direction, normal)) def refract(direction, normal, etaratio): costhetai = -dot(normalize(direction), normalize(normal)) sinthetaisq = 1.0 - costhetai 2 if etaratio 2 sinthetaisq > 1.0: return None costhetat = math.sqrt(1.0 - etaratio 2 sinthetaisq) return tuple(etaratio d + (etaratio costhetai - costhetat) n for d, n in zip(direction, normal)) def traceray(ray, scene, maxdepth): if maxdepth <= 0: return BACKGROUNDCOLOR hit = scene.intersect(ray) if hit is None: return BACKGROUNDCOLOR color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for light in scene.lights: lightdir = normalize(tuple(l - p for l, p in zip(light.position, hit.point))) shadowray = Ray(origin=tuple(h + EPSILON n for h, n in zip(hit.point, hit.normal)), direction=lightdir) shadowhit = scene.intersect(shadowray) lightdist = dot(lightdir, tuple(l - p for l, p in zip(light.position, hit.point))) if shadowhit is None or shadowhit.distance > lightdist: diffuse = hit.material.diffuse max(0.0, dot(hit.normal, lightdir)) color = tuple(c + d l for c, d, l in zip(color, diffuse, light.intensity)) if hit.material.reflectivity > 0: reflectdir = reflect(ray.direction, hit.normal) reflectray = Ray(origin=tuple(h + EPSILON n for h, n in zip(hit.point, hit.normal)), direction=reflectdir) reflcolor = traceray(reflectray, scene, maxdepth - 1) color = tuple(c + r m for c, r, m in zip(color, reflcolor, hit.material.reflectivity)) if hit.material.refractivity > 0: eta = hit.material.ior refractdir = refract(ray.direction, hit.normal, eta) if refractdir is not None: refractray = Ray(origin=tuple(h - EPSILON n for h, n in zip(hit.point, hit.normal)), direction=refractdir) refractcolor = traceray(refractray, scene, maxdepth - 1) color = tuple(c + r m for c, r, m in zip(color, refractcolor, hit.material.refractivity)) return color Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum recursion depth for secondary rays. Typical values are Not given in the sources. epsilon: Small offset value added to intersection points to prevent self-intersection artifacts when spawning secondary rays. Typical values are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Total Internal Reflection: When the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle during refraction, no refracted ray exists; only reflection occurs. Infinite Recursion: Caused by perfect mirrors or transparent objects in a closed loop. Mitigated by maxdepth and energy attenuation per bounce. Precision Errors: Floating-point inaccuracies can cause rays to miss intersections or intersect the same surface they originated from. Offset vectors (epsilon) are required. Not given in the sources. Origin: First proposed by Whitted. History: Extends Appel's earlier ray casting work by introducing secondary rays for shadows and refractions. Usage: Not given in the sources. name: Multi-Sphere Ray Tracing with Diffuse Lighting
head: Primary Ray Tracing Loop, sphIntrAll
body: This method casts a primary ray against a fixed set of spheres to find the closest intersection and computes unshadowed diffuse lighting from multiple point lights. It omits recursive shadow rays and reflections, distinguishing it from full ray tracing implementations. Inputs: Ray origin org, ray direction dir, array of spheres S with count sphCnt, array of lights L with count lightCnt. Outputs: Final color color (vec4). Data Structures: struct intr: bool is (hit status), float t (distance to hit), vec3 N (surface normal at hit). struct material: vec3 kd (diffuse color coefficient), float l (unused). struct light: vec3 p (position), float intensiv (intensity). struct sph: float r (radius), vec3 c (center), material m (material). Steps: 1. Initialize closest hit mint with is=false, t=1000, N=vec3(0). 2. Loop over all spheres i from 0 to sphCnt-1. 3. Compute intersection of ray (org, dir) with sphere S[i] using sphInt. 4. If intersect.is is true and intersect.t < mint.t, update mint = intersect, store material mm = S[i].m, and set color = vec4(mm.kd, 1). 5. If mint.is is true, initialize difInt = 0. 6. Loop over all lights i from 0 to lightCnt-1. 7. Compute hit point P = org + dir mint.t. 8. Compute light direction ld = normalize(L[i].p - P). (The original source code incorrectly normalizes P instead of the direction vector; this step corrects that to match the formula and standard practice). 9. Accumulate diffuse contribution: difInt += L[i].intensiv max(0., dot(ld, mint.N)). 10. Set final color: color = vec4(mm.kd difInt, 1). 11. Return color. Formula: The final color C is calculated as: C = \mathbf{k}d \sum{j=1}^{L} Ij \max(0, \mathbf{d}j \cdot \mathbf{N}) Where \mathbf{k}d is the diffuse color coefficient, L is the number of lights, Ij is the intensity of light j, \mathbf{d}j is the normalized direction from the hit point to light j, and \mathbf{N} is the surface normal at the hit point. Parameters: sphCnt: Number of spheres. Typical value: 3. lightCnt: Number of lights processed. Typical value: 1 (array contains 2). mint.t: Initial maximum ray distance. Typical value: 1000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multispherediffuse(org, dir, S, sphCnt, L, lightCnt): mintis = False mintt = 1000.0 mintN = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) mmkd = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(sphCnt): intersect = sphInt(S[i], org, dir) if intersect[0] and intersect[1] < mintt: mintis = True mintt = intersect[1] mintN = intersect[2] mmkd = S[i].m.kd if mintis: difInt = 0.0 hitpoint = (org[0] + dir[0] mintt, org[1] + dir[1] mintt, org[2] + dir[2] mintt) for j in range(lightCnt): ld = normalize((L[j].p[0] - hitpoint[0], L[j].p[1] - hitpoint[1], L[j].p[2] - hitpoint[2])) difInt += L[j].intensiv max(0.0, dot(ld, mintN)) color = (mmkd[0] difInt, mmkd[1] difInt, mmkd[2] difInt, 1.0) else: color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return color def sphInt(sph, org, dir): oc = (org[0] - sph.c[0], org[1] - sph.c[1], org[2] - sph.c[2]) a = dot(dir, dir) b = 2.0 dot(oc, dir) c = dot(oc, oc) - sph.r sph.r disc = b b - 4 a c if disc < 0: return (False, 1000.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) sqrtdisc = sqrt(max(0.0, disc)) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t = t1 if t1 > 0.0 else t2 if t < 0.0: return (False, 1000.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) hitpt = (org[0] + dir[0] t, org[1] + dir[1] t, org[2] + dir[2] t) N = normalize((hitpt[0] - sph.c[0], hitpt[1] - sph.c[1], hitpt[2] - sph.c[2])) return (True, t, N) def normalize(v): l = sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def sqrt(x): return x0.5 Edge Cases: No Hit: If no sphere is intersected, the method returns a default color (implementation dependent, often black or background). Precision: Using a large initial mint.t (1000) may cause precision issues if the scene is scaled differently. Light Direction: The light direction is computed from the hit point to the light position, not from the light to the hit point, to ensure correct dot product sign for diffuse shading. The core primitive test. See Ray Tracing and Ray Intersection Methods. The shading model used. See Ray Tracing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, no recursion, suitable for static scenes with few primitives. Limitations: No shadows, reflections, or refractions. When to Use: Educational purposes, simple demos, or scenes with very few objects and lights. When Not to Use: Complex scenes, real-time rendering, or when accurate lighting (shadows, reflections) is required. This method is a basic ray tracing technique often used in introductory computer graphics courses and simple renderers. It demonstrates the fundamental concepts of ray-primitive intersection and diffuse shading without the complexity of recursive ray tracing. trimesh33/sdf, https://github.com/trimesh33/sdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
