name: Screen-Space Ray Tracing with Depth Buffer
head: SSRT, Single depth-buffer tracing
body: Screen-Space Ray Tracing with Depth Buffer (SSRT) traces rays in screen space against a depth buffer to find surface intersections, supporting up to four depth layers per pixel. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-surface intersections for effects like reflections, refractions, and ambient occlusion without traversing complex scene graphs or voxel structures. What sets it apart from Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction and Trilinear Isosurface Intersection is that it operates directly on the rendered depth buffer rather than a volumetric or implicit representation, allowing it to capture any geometry already present in the frame buffer. Unlike Ray Tracing which traverses acceleration structures, SSRT traverses the 2D screen grid, making it highly parallelizable on GPUs but limited to visible surfaces. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: csOrig: Camera-space ray origin (vec3). csDir: Camera-space ray direction (vec3). proj: Matrix projecting from camera-space position to pixel screen position (mat4x4). nearPlaneZ: Explicit negative near plane Z value (float). csZBuffer: The depth buffer (sampler2D). csZBufferSize: Dimensions of the depth buffer (vec2). csZBufferIsHyperbolic: Boolean flag indicating if the depth buffer uses hyperbolic encoding (bool). zThickness: Camera-space Z thickness ascribed to each point in the depth buffer (float). maxDistance: Maximum trace distance in camera-space (float). maxSteps: Maximum number of steps to trace (float/int). stride: Step size multiplier in screen space (float). jitter: Random value in [0,1] used to conceal banding (float). clipInfo: Information used for reconstructing camera-space Z from hyperbolic depth values (vec3). Outputs: hitPixel: Screen-space coordinates of the hit (out point2). hitLayer: Index of the hit layer in the depth buffer (out int). csHitPoint: Camera-space hit point (out point3). Return value: Boolean indicating if the hit pixel is within buffer bounds. Data Structures The method tracks up to four depth-buffer layers in sceneZMax at each pixel. If csZBufferIsHyperbolic is true, the buffer contains hyperbolically encoded depth values; otherwise, it is assumed to contain precomputed negative camera-space Z values for performance. Algorithm Steps 1. Clip to Near Plane: Calculate the ray length within the valid range. If the ray endpoint exceeds the near plane, clip it. \text{rayLength} = \begin{cases} \frac{\text{nearPlaneZ} - \text{csOrig}.z}{\text{csDir}.z} & \text{if } (\text{csOrig}.z + \text{csDir}.z \times \text{maxDistance}) > \text{nearPlaneZ} \\ \text{maxDistance} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute the clipped endpoint: \text{csEndPoint} = \text{csOrig} + \text{csDir} \times \text{rayLength}. 2. Project to Screen Space: Convert endpoints to homogeneous coordinates and then to screen space. H0 = \text{proj} \times \text{vec4}(\text{csOrig}, 1.0), \quad H1 = \text{proj} \times \text{vec4}(\text{csEndPoint}, 1.0) k0 = \frac{1.0}{H0.w}, \quad k1 = \frac{1.0}{H1.w} P0 = H0.xy \times k0, \quad P1 = H1.xy \times k1 Q0 = \text{csOrig} \times k0, \quad Q1 = \text{csEndPoint} \times k1 Here, P represents screen-space coordinates and Q represents camera-space coordinates scaled by 1/w. 3. Handle Single-Pixel Lines: Ensure the ray has a non-zero delta to avoid division by zero. P1 += \text{vec2}((\text{distanceSquared}(P0, P1) < 0.0001) ? 0.01: 0.0). 4. Determine Traversal Direction and Derivatives: Compute delta: \Delta = P1 - P0. If |\Delta.x| < |\Delta.y|, permute coordinates (swap x/y for P0, P1, \Delta) and set permute = true. Compute step direction and inverse delta x: \text{stepDir} = \text{sign}(\Delta.x), \quad \text{invdx} = \frac{\text{stepDir}}{\Delta.x} Compute derivatives per unit step in the dominant axis: dP = \text{vec2}(\text{stepDir}, \Delta.y \times \text{invdx}) \times \text{stride} dQ = (Q1 - Q0) \times \text{invdx} \times \text{stride} dk = (k1 - k0) \times \text{invdx} \times \text{stride}. 5. Apply Jitter: Bump the starting position to conceal banding artifacts caused by stride > 1. P0 += dP \times \text{jitter}, \quad Q0 += dQ \times \text{jitter}, \quad k0 += dk \times \text{jitter}. 6. Initialize Loop Variables: \text{prevZMaxEstimate} = \text{csOrig}.z Q = Q0, \quad k = k0, \quad \text{stepCount} = 0.0 \text{end} = P1.x \times \text{stepDir}. 7. Loop Over Pixels: Iterate while the ray is within bounds and steps remain. Condition: (P.x \times \text{stepDir}) \le \text{end} \land \text{stepCount} < \text{maxSteps} Update: P += dP, \quad Q.z += dQ.z, \quad k += dk, \quad \text{stepCount} += 1.0. 8. Inside Loop - Compute Ray Z Bounds: Compute ray Z bounds for the current step. The ray covers the interval [\text{rayZMin}, \text{rayZMax}]. \text{rayZMin} = \text{prevZMaxEstimate} \text{rayZMax} = \frac{dQ.z \times 0.5 + Q.z}{dk \times 0.5 + k} \text{prevZMaxEstimate} = \text{rayZMax} If \text{rayZMin} > \text{rayZMax}, swap them. 9. Inside Loop - Fetch Depth & Check Intersection: Determine hit pixel coordinates: \text{hitPixel} = \text{permute} ? P.yx: P. Fetch depth values: \text{sceneZMax} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{csZBuffer}, \text{int2}(\text{hitPixel}), 0). If csZBufferIsHyperbolic is true, reconstruct camera-space Z for each layer: \text{sceneZMax}[L] = \text{reconstructCSZ}(\text{sceneZMax}[L], \text{clipInfo}) \quad \text{for } L \in [0, 3]. Compute scene Z bounds: \text{sceneZMin} = \text{sceneZMax} - \text{zThickness}. Check for overlap with any layer L: If (\text{rayZMax} \ge \text{sceneZMin}[L] \land \text{rayZMin} \le \text{sceneZMax}[L]) \lor (\text{sceneZMax}[L] == 0), then a hit is found. Set hitLayer = L and break out of both loops. 10. Post-Loop - Compute Hit Point: Advance Q.xy based on steps taken: Q.xy += dQ.xy \times \text{stepCount} Compute final hit point: \text{hitPoint} = Q \times \frac{1.0}{k}. 11. Return Result: Check if hitPixel is within buffer bounds: \text{return all}(\text{lessThanEqual}(|\text{hitPixel} - (\text{csZBufferSize} \times 0.5)|, \text{csZBufferSize} \times 0.5)). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec2: def init(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y def add(self, o): return Vec2(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y) def sub(self, o): return Vec2(self.x - o.x, self.y - o.y) def mul(self, s): return Vec2(self.x s, self.y s) def truediv(self, s): return Vec2(self.x / s, self.y / s) def abs(self): return Vec2(abs(self.x), abs(self.y)) @property def yx(self): return Vec2(self.y, self.x) @property def xy(self): return Vec2(self.x, self.y) class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vec3(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y, self.z + o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x - o.x, self.y - o.y, self.z - o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def truediv(self, s): return Vec3(self.x / s, self.y / s, self.z / s) @property def xy(self): return Vec2(self.x, self.y) @xy.setter def xy(self, v): self.x, self.y = v.x, v.y class Vec4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def add(self, o): return Vec4(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y, self.z + o.z, self.w + o.w) def sub(self, o): return Vec4(self.x - o.x, self.y - o.y, self.z - o.z, self.w - o.w) def mul(self, s): return Vec4(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s, self.w s) def tracescreenspaceray(csOrig, csDir, proj, csZBuffer, csZBufferSize, zThickness, csZBufferIsHyperbolic, clipInfo, nearPlaneZ, stride, jitter, maxSteps, maxDistance): def distancesquared(a, b): return (a.x - b.x)2 + (a.y - b.y)2 def int2(v): return (int(v.x), int(v.y)) def swap(a, b): return b, a def texelfetch(tex, coord, level): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for texture fetch def reconstructcsz(depth, clipInfo): # Formula for reconstructing camera-space Z from hyperbolic depth not provided in sources return depth # 1. Clip to near plane if (csOrig.z + csDir.z maxDistance) > nearPlaneZ: rayLength = (nearPlaneZ - csOrig.z) / csDir.z else: rayLength = maxDistance csEndPoint = csOrig + csDir rayLength # 2. Project to screen space H0 = proj Vec4(csOrig.x, csOrig.y, csOrig.z, 1.0) H1 = proj Vec4(csEndPoint.x, csEndPoint.y, csEndPoint.z, 1.0) k0 = 1.0 / H0.w k1 = 1.0 / H1.w Q0 = Vec3(csOrig.x k0, csOrig.y k0, csOrig.z k0) Q1 = Vec3(csEndPoint.x k1, csEndPoint.y k1, csEndPoint.z k1) P0 = Vec2(H0.x k0, H0.y k0) P1 = Vec2(H1.x k1, H1.y k1) # 3. Handle single-pixel lines if distancesquared(P0, P1) < 0.0001: P1 = P1 + Vec2(0.01) delta = P1 - P0 permute = False if abs(delta.x) < abs(delta.y): permute = True delta = delta.yx P0 = P0.yx P1 = P1.yx stepDir = 1.0 if delta.x > 0 else (-1.0 if delta.x < 0 else 0.0) invdx = stepDir / delta.x dP = Vec2(stepDir, delta.y invdx) stride dQ = (Q1 - Q0) invdx stride dk = (k1 - k0) invdx stride # 4. Apply jitter P0 = P0 + dP jitter Q0 = Q0 + dQ jitter k0 = k0 + dk jitter # 5. Initialize loop variables prevZMaxEstimate = csOrig.z Q = Q0 k = k0 stepCount = 0.0 end = P1.x stepDir hitPixel = Vec2(-1, -1) hitLayer = -1 csHitPoint = Vec3(0, 0, 0) # 6. Loop over pixels P = P0 while (P.x stepDir) <= end and stepCount < maxSteps: # Compute ray Z bounds rayZMin = prevZMaxEstimate rayZMax = (dQ.z 0.5 + Q.z) / (dk 0.5 + k) prevZMaxEstimate = rayZMax if rayZMin > rayZMax: rayZMin, rayZMax = swap(rayZMin, rayZMax) # Determine hit pixel hitPixel = P.yx if permute else P # Fetch depth buffer sceneZMax = texelfetch(csZBuffer, int2(hitPixel), 0) if csZBufferIsHyperbolic: for layer in range(4): sceneZMax[layer] = reconstructcsz(sceneZMax[layer], clipInfo) # Check intersection sceneZMin = [sceneZMax[i] - zThickness for i in range(4)] hitfound = False for L in range(4): if (rayZMax >= sceneZMin[L] and rayZMin <= sceneZMax[L]) or (sceneZMax[L] == 0): hitLayer = L hitfound = True break if hitfound: break # Update loop variables P = P + dP Q.z = Q.z + dQ.z k = k + dk stepCount = stepCount + 1.0 # 7. Post-Loop - Compute Hit Point Q.xy = Q.xy + dQ.xy stepCount csHitPoint = Vec3(Q.x (1.0 / k), Q.y (1.0 / k), Q.z (1.0 / k)) # 8. Return Result boundscheck = all(abs(hitPixel.x - (csZBufferSize.x 0.5)) <= (csZBufferSize.x 0.5)) and all(abs(hitPixel.y - (csZBufferSize.y 0.5)) <= (csZBufferSize.y 0.5)) return boundscheck, hitPixel, hitLayer, csHitPoint Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: Avoided because the ray is clipped to the near plane (no w=0 singularity) and delta.x is guaranteed non-zero for single-pixel lines. Coordinate System: The method assumes pixel (0,0) is the upper-left corner. To switch to lower-left, modify the final hit point by hitPoint.y = csZBufferSize.y - hitPoint.y. Performance: Converting hyperbolic depth values per iteration is expensive. It is preferred to use a floating-point buffer of precomputed negative camera-space values. Miss Handling: Rays that miss the depth buffer (travel farther than maxDistance or towards the camera) require a fallback strategy, such as sparse voxels or environment cube maps. Time and Memory Complexity The time complexity is linear with respect to the number of iterations before a hit is encountered or the maxDistance is reached. The method tracks up to four depth-buffer layers in sceneZMax at each pixel. Measured Performance At 1920x1080 resolution, casting a diagonal ray for 25 iterations per pixel costs 1.2 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce Titan and 6.4 ms on a MacBook NVIDIA GeForce 650M. Ambient occlusion and radiosity examples, which cast 25 rays per pixel, spend about 30 ms on ray casts, making them not viable for real-time pipelines with other tasks. Scaling Performance scales linearly with resolution and the number of rays per pixel. Using stride > 1 reduces the number of samples, improving performance at the cost of quality. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Efficient for single-ray-per-pixel effects like reflections and refractions. Captures any geometry present in the depth buffer without additional scene traversal. Limitations: Limited to visible surfaces. High ray counts (e.g., for global illumination) are too slow for real-time. Stride > 1 introduces banding artifacts. When to Use Use for reflection and refraction (one ray cast per pixel) where real-time performance is critical. Not recommended for ambient occlusion or radiosity if other graphics tasks are present. Origin The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient GPU screen-space ray tracing". It is a feature of the G3D Innovation Engine. History and Development The technique has been used in commercial games such as Killzone: Shadow Fall for reflections and volumetrics. It was presented at SIGGRAPH Advances in Real-Time Rendering in Games course. Usage It is used for reflection and refraction (one ray cast per pixel) and ambient occlusion/radiosity (25 rays per pixel). Efficient GPU screen-space ray tracing, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Parabolic Ray Tracing in Heterogeneous Media
head: Non-linear ray tracing, Piecewise polynomial ray tracing
body: Parabolic Ray Tracing computes light ray trajectories in media with spatially varying Refractive Index Fields (RIF) by modeling the squared RIF as a linear function within tetrahedral cells, yielding second-order polynomial ray paths. It solves the problem of exact intersection computation with cell boundaries, which is otherwise difficult when trajectories involve transcendental functions, by reducing boundary crossings to solving quadratic equations. It differs from linear ray tracing by accounting for continuous curvature within cells, and from general non-linear solvers by providing closed-form analytical solutions for the trajectory. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh defining the spatial domain. A Refractive Index Field (RIF) \eta(\mathbf{x}) defined per cell. A ray origin \mathbf{x}0 and initial direction \mathbf{p}0 satisfying the Eikonal equation. Outputs: The trajectory of the ray as it traverses the medium. Intersection points with cell boundaries. Data Structures: Cell Coefficients: For each tetrahedral cell, the squared RIF is defined as a linear function: \eta^2(\mathbf{x}) = A0 + A1 \mathbf{x}x + A2 \mathbf{x}y + A3 \mathbf{x}z = A0 + \boldsymbol{\gamma} \cdot \mathbf{x} where \boldsymbol{\gamma} = [A1, A2, A3]^T is the constant gradient of the squared RIF, and A0 is a scalar offset. Ray State: Position \mathbf{x}(\tau) and direction \mathbf{p}(\tau) at parameter \tau. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ray State: Set initial position \mathbf{x}0 and initial direction \mathbf{p}0. Ensure \|\mathbf{p}0\| = \eta(\mathbf{x}0) to satisfy the Eikonal equation. 2. Determine Current Cell: Identify the tetrahedral cell containing the current ray position \mathbf{x}(\tau). 3. Compute Cell Coefficients: Retrieve \boldsymbol{\gamma} and A0 for the current cell based on the RIF definition. 4. Compute Ray Trajectory within Cell: The ray trajectory \mathbf{x}(\tau) and direction \mathbf{p}(\tau) are second-order polynomials in the parameter \tau: \mathbf{x}(\tau) = \frac{1}{4}\boldsymbol{\gamma} \tau^2 + \mathbf{p}0\tau + \mathbf{x}0 \mathbf{p}(\tau) = \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\gamma} \tau + \mathbf{p}0 where \tau is a parameter related to arc length s by ds = \eta d\tau. 5. Intersect with Cell Boundary: Intersect the polynomial ray subsection with a cell boundary by solving a quadratic equation exactly. Let the cell boundary be defined by a plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Substitute \mathbf{x}(\tau) into the plane equation: \mathbf{n} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{4}\boldsymbol{\gamma} \tau^2 + \mathbf{p}0\tau + \mathbf{x}0 \right) + d = 0 Rearrange into standard quadratic form a\tau^2 + b\tau + c = 0: a = \frac{1}{4} (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}) b = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}0 c = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}0 + d Solve for \tau using the quadratic formula. Select the smallest positive \tau that corresponds to the exit point from the current cell. 6. Update Ray State: Update position: \mathbf{x}{new} = \mathbf{x}(\tau{exit}). Update direction: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p}(\tau{exit}). Reset \tau to 0 for the next cell, adjusting \mathbf{x}0 and \mathbf{p}0 accordingly. 7. Traverse to Next Cell: Move to the adjacent tetrahedral cell sharing the exit face and repeat steps 2-6 until the ray exits the medium or reaches a termination condition. 8. Intersect Scene Geometry (SDF): For intersecting the panel's signed distance field (SDF), step naively along the computed parabolic ray trajectory, similar to regular sphere tracing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def norm(a): return math.sqrt(dot(a, a)) def solvequadratic(a, b, c): """Solve ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Returns smallest positive root or None.""" if abs(a) < 1e-12: if abs(b) < 1e-12: return None root = -c / b return root if root > 0 else None discriminant = b b - 4 a c if discriminant < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) root1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) root2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) roots = [r for r in [root1, root2] if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else None def pointintetrahedron(v0, v1, v2, v3, p): """Check if point p is inside tetrahedron defined by 4 vertices using barycentric coordinates.""" v0v1 = [v1[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0v2 = [v2[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0v3 = [v3[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0p = [p[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)] d00 = dot(v0v1, v0v1) d01 = dot(v0v1, v0v2) d02 = dot(v0v1, v0v3) d11 = dot(v0v2, v0v2) d12 = dot(v0v2, v0v3) d22 = dot(v0v3, v0v3) d30 = dot(v0p, v0v1) d31 = dot(v0p, v0v2) d32 = dot(v0p, v0v3) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 if abs(denom) < 1e-12: return False b0 = (d11 d22 - d12 d12) d30 + (d02 d12 - d01 d22) d31 + (d01 d12 - d02 d11) d32 b1 = (d00 d22 - d02 d02) d31 + (d12 d02 - d00 d22) d30 + (d00 d12 - d01 d02) d32 b2 = (d00 d11 - d01 d01) d32 + (d01 d02 - d00 d11) d31 + (d11 d02 - d01 d12) d30 b3 = 1.0 - (b0 + b1 + b2) / denom return b0 >= 0 and b1 >= 0 and b2 >= 0 and b3 >= 0 def getadjacenttetrahedron(tetmesh, currenttetidx, exitfaceidx): """Return index of tetrahedron sharing exitfaceidx with currenttetidx.""" # Assumes tetmesh stores adjacency or face-to-tet mapping. # Standard mesh traversal: look up neighbor via face index. return tetmesh[currenttetidx].adjacent[exitfaceidx] def parabolicraytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, tetmesh, riffunction): """ Trace a ray through a tetrahedral mesh with a piecewise linear squared RIF. Args: rayorigin: Initial position x0. raydirection: Initial direction p0. tetmesh: List of tetrahedra, each with vertices, faces, and adjacency list. riffunction: Function returning (gamma, A0) for a given position. Returns: List of intersection points. """ x = list(rayorigin) p = list(raydirection) intersections = [] # Ensure initial direction satisfies Eikonal equation gammainit, A0init = riffunction(x) etainit = math.sqrt(A0init + dot(gammainit, x)) pnorm = norm(p) p = [val (etainit / pnorm) for val in p] # Find initial tetrahedron currenttetidx = None for i, tet in enumerate(tetmesh): if pointintetrahedron(tet.vertices, x): currenttetidx = i break while currenttetidx is not None: currenttet = tetmesh[currenttetidx] gamma, A0 = riffunction(x) # Find exit point from current tetrahedron mintau = float('inf') exitfaceidx = None for faceidx, face in enumerate(currenttet.faces): n = face.normal d = -dot(n, face.vertices[0]) # Coefficients for quadratic equation a = 0.25 dot(n, gamma) b = dot(n, p) c = dot(n, x) + d tau = solvequadratic(a, b, c) if tau is not None and tau < mintau: mintau = tau exitfaceidx = faceidx if mintau == float('inf'): break # Compute exit position and direction exitx = [0.25 gamma[i] (mintau 2) + p[i] mintau + x[i] for i in range(3)] exitp = [0.5 gamma[i] mintau + p[i] for i in range(3)] intersections.append(exitx) # Update state for next cell (reset tau to 0 implicitly by using new x, p) x = exitx p = exitp # Find next tetrahedron currenttetidx = getadjacenttetrahedron(tetmesh, currenttetidx, exitfaceidx) return intersections Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Eikonal Equation: The initial direction must satisfy \|\mathbf{p}0\| = \eta(\mathbf{x}0) to ensure physical correctness. SDF Intersection: Stepping naively along the parabolic trajectory for SDF intersection requires careful step sizing to avoid missing geometry, similar to standard sphere tracing. Degenerate Cells: If a tetrahedron is degenerate (zero volume), the barycentric test fails and the ray may escape the mesh; mesh quality checks are required. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of cells traversed, with constant time per cell for intersection computation (solving a quadratic equation). Memory Complexity: Linear in the size of the tetrahedral mesh and RIF data. Strengths: Exact intersection computation with cell boundaries; analytical solutions for ray trajectories within cells. Limitations: Limited to media where the squared RIF can be approximated as a linear function within tetrahedral cells; may require fine mesh resolution for accurate RIF representation. When to Use: When accurate ray tracing in heterogeneous media with smooth refractive index variations is required, and the medium can be discretized into tetrahedral cells with linear squared RIF profiles. When Not to Use: When the RIF varies rapidly or non-linearly within cells, or when the medium is not naturally represented as a tetrahedral mesh. Parabolic Ray Tracing was introduced in the context of seismic wave propagation, where Virieux and Farra demonstrated that a well-chosen expression for the slowness profile within tetrahedral cells yields simple second-order polynomial solutions for ray trajectories. This approach was later adapted for computer graphics to model light propagation in heterogeneous media, such as old glass, by assembling multiple tetrahedral cells and tracing piecewise polynomial rays. It generalizes the concept of ray differentials used in computer graphics for building two-point tracing methods. Parabolic Sphere Tracing of Signed Distance Fields for Old Glass Modelling and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3613853, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Surface Area Heuristic (SAH)
head: Crofton’s Theorem based cost model, Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) / Crofton’s Theorem
body: The Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) is a cost model used to determine the optimal partitioning of primitives in Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) construction, both for top-down recursive splitting and iterative insertion. It minimizes the estimated ray tracing cost by leveraging the probability that a ray intersects a bounding volume, which is proportional to its surface area. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of primitives P enclosed in a parent Bounding Volume B. Output: A partition of P into subsets B1 and B2 (and potentially more) that minimizes the SAH cost function, or the decision to attach a primitive directly to the current node in iterative insertion. Data Structures: Bounding Volume (BV): Typically an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). The layout includes minimum and maximum coordinates defining the volume. The surface area is calculated from these extents. Primitive Set: A list of primitives associated with each node. Core Formula: The cost C(B) of a node containing a set of polygons B is estimated by the weighted sum of the surface areas of its children multiplied by the number of primitives they contain: C(B) = \min{B \subseteq P(B)} \left[ Area(B1) \cdot N(B1) + Area(B2) \cdot N(B2) \right] Where: B is the set of polygons in the parent BV. B1 and B2 are the subsets of primitives assigned to the left and right children, respectively. Area(Bi) is the surface area of the bounding volume enclosing subset Bi. N(Bi) is the number of primitives in subset Bi. Theoretical Basis: The heuristic relies on Crofton’s Theorem, which states that for a convex body, the total number of rays hitting an object is proportional to its surface area. Consequently, the probability of a ray hitting an object completely inside a cell is proportional to the object's surface area relative to the cell's properties. The cost model assumes that the traversal cost is proportional to the surface area of the bounding volumes tested. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bounding Volume Calculation: Calculate the bounding volume for the given set of objects. 2. Partitioning (Top-Down): Partition the set of objects into two (or more) subsets. Calculate the bounding volumes for each subset. Compute the cost C(B) for the partition using the formula above. Seek the optimal split that minimizes this cost. Exhaustively searching all possible partitions is not practical. Heuristic approaches represent objects by their centroids, determine the axis of largest extent, sort points along this axis, and use a plane-sweep to find the minimum cost split. 3. Recursive Construction: Recursively construct BVHs for each subset. 4. Iterative Insertion (Goldsmith/Salmon): For each new object, propagate it into the subtree that causes the smallest cost increase for ray tracing. Tie-Breaking: If both subtrees cause equal costs (e.g., 0), use a secondary heuristic, such as the number of triangles in the subtree. Non-Binary Fallback: If all subtrees cause too high costs (e.g., area increase reaches 90% of the parent's area), attach the object as a direct child of the current node, allowing for non-binary BVHs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Node: def init(self, primitives=None, bv=None): self.primitives = primitives if primitives is not None else [] self.bv = bv self.children = [] def computeboundingvolume(primitives): if not primitives: return {'min': (0, 0, 0), 'max': (0, 0, 0)} minx, miny, minz = float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf') maxx, maxy, maxz = float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf') for p in primitives: minx = min(minx, p.min[0]); miny = min(miny, p.min[1]); minz = min(minz, p.min[2]) maxx = max(maxx, p.max[0]); maxy = max(maxy, p.max[1]); maxz = max(maxz, p.max[2]) return {'min': (minx, miny, minz), 'max': (maxx, maxy, maxz)} def surfacearea(bv): d = (bv['max'][0] - oldcost if costincrease < minincrease: minincrease = costincrease bestchild = child parentarea = surfacearea(node.bv) newbvarea = surfacearea(computeboundingvolume(bestchild.primitives + [primitive])) if newbvarea > 0.9 parentarea: node.children.append(Node([primitive])) return insertiterative(bestchild, primitive) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exhaustive Search: Finding the true global minimum split is computationally expensive and not practical. Heuristics like plane-sweep on sorted centroids are necessary. Non-Binary Trees: The heuristic allows for non-binary BVHs if the cost of splitting is too high (e.g., >90% area increase). Tie-Breaking: Equal costs require a secondary heuristic, such as primitive count. A cost model for ray intersection with a subset of the scene enclosed in a Bounding Volume (BV), used to evaluate the trade-off between BV simplicity and compactness. The total cost T is defined as T = n \cdot B + m \cdot I, where n is the number of rays tested against the BV, B is the cost for one ray-BV intersection test, m is the number of rays that actually intersect the BV, and I is the cost for testing the objects in the BV. The goal is to minimize T. Simple BVs (e.g., sphere or box) have small intersection costs B but usually result in a large number of ray hits m, while compact BVs (e.g., exact convex hull) have small m but high intersection costs B. Time Complexity: The cost calculation for a single split is O(N) where N is the number of primitives. Finding the optimal split via plane-sweep is O(N \log N) due to sorting. Memory Complexity: Depends on the BVH structure; typically O(N) for N primitives. Strengths: Provides a robust, geometry-independent metric for balancing the BVH tree, leading to efficient ray traversal. Limitations: The heuristic assumes uniform ray distribution and may not be optimal for all scene types or ray distributions. Exhaustive optimization is impractical. When to use: Standard choice for BVH construction in ray tracers. When not to use: When scene-specific heuristics are known to be more accurate, or when build time is extremely constrained and simpler splits are acceptable. The Surface Area Heuristic is based on Crofton’s Theorem, which relates the number of rays hitting an object to its surface area. It was popularized in the context of BVH construction by Goldsmith and Salmon for iterative insertion and is widely used in top-down construction methods. It addresses the problem of efficiently organizing primitives for ray tracing by minimizing the expected number of intersection tests. name: Ray-Primitive and Segment Intersection
head: Intersection Ordering Optimization, Ray-Primitive and Segment Intersection Ordering
body: This method optimizes the evaluation of volumetric ray primitives by determining the correct processing order of intersection points and segments along a ray. It also provides the geometric primitives for intersecting rays with line segments. It solves the problem of redundant or incorrect shading calculations when multiple objects or data structures intersect a single ray. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sphere Intersection and Ray-Triangle Intersection by focusing on the ordering and culling of intersection results rather than the analytic solution of a single primitive, and from Voxel selection via pick ray intersection by handling general bounding box hierarchies rather than specific voxel grid traversal. The method consists of two distinct components: an optimization strategy for ordering intersection evaluations based on bounding boxes, and the geometric algorithm for intersecting a ray with a line segment. Inputs: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz) and direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). List of objects, each with an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). For segment intersection: Segment endpoints \mathbf{A} = (ax, ay) and \mathbf{B} = (bx, by). Outputs: Sorted list of intersection points and segments to be processed by the shader. For segment intersection: Intersection parameter t, segment parameter s, and validity flag. 1. Intersection Point List (P): Contains objects classified as Class 1 (surface intersections). Each entry stores the object ID and the distance to the entry point of its bounding box. 2. Intersection Segment List (S): Contains objects classified as Class 2 or 3 (volumetric/average/max-value projections). Each entry stores the object ID and the distance to the exit point of its bounding box. 3. Bounding Box: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. Used to compute entry and exit distances for the ray. 1. Bounding Box Intersection: For each object, compute the entry and exit points of the ray with its bounding box. Determine if the ray intersects the box. 2. Classification: Class 1: Surface intersection objects. Distance metric is the entry point of the bounding box. Class 2: Average-value projection objects. Distance metric is the exit point of the bounding box. Class 3: Max-value projection objects. Distance metric is the exit point of the bounding box. 3. Sorting: Sort the lists P and S by distance. P is sorted by entry distance. S is sorted by exit distance. The sources imply a unified processing order where Class 1 points are processed before Class 2/3 segments that might contain them, or segments that are occluded by closer Class 1 points. 4. Initialize Tracker: Set D{min} = \infty. This variable tracks the closest intersection point found so far. 5. Process Intersection Points (Class 1): Iterate through the sorted list P. For each point, if its distance is less than D{min}, update D{min} to this distance. This establishes the closest surface intersection Pt. 6. Process Intersection Segments (Class 2/3): Iterate through the sorted list S. Use D{min} to cull or terminate calculations: If a Class 1 intersection occurs within a Class 4 segment, compute the average value only for the sub-segment outside the Class 1 intersection, not the entire segment. If a Class 1 intersection occurs after a Class 2 or 3 intersection start, perform the Class 1 calculation first. This reduces the segment length for the Class 2/3 calculation or allows early termination of Class 3. Class 3 Early Termination: For max-value projection, if the maximum value encountered along the ray up to point Pt is vt, the Class 3 calculation can terminate as soon as a value v2 is encountered such that v2 > vt. This requires the Class 1 calculation to be performed first to establish Pt. 1. Compute Segment Vector: \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A} = (sx, sy). 2. Compute Denominator: denom = dx sy - dy sx. 3. Check Parallelism: If |denom| < \epsilon, the ray and segment are parallel. Return invalid/null. 4. Compute Parameters: t = \frac{(ax - ox) sy - (ay - oy) sx}{denom} s = \frac{(ax - ox) dy - (ay - oy) dx}{denom} 5. Validate: The intersection is valid if t \ge 0 (ray direction) AND 0 \le s \le 1 (segment bounds). 6. Compute Intersection Point: \mathbf{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. Ray-Segment Intersection Parameters: sx = bx - ax sy = by - ay denom = dx sy - dy sx t = \frac{(ax - ox) sy - (ay - oy) sx}{denom} s = \frac{(ax - ox) dy - (ay - oy) dx}{denom} valid = (t \ge 0) \land (0 \le s \le 1) hitx = ox + dx t hity = oy + dy t Ray-AABB Intersection Distances: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: t{1,i} = \frac{bbox{min,i} - oi}{di} t{2,i} = \frac{bbox{max,i} - oi}{di} t{enter,i} = \min(t{1,i}, t{2,i}) t{exit,i} = \max(t{1,i}, t{2,i}) t{min} = \maxi(t{enter,i}) t{max} = \mini(t{exit,i}) Intersection exists if t{min} \le t{max} and t{max} \ge 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raysegmentintersect2d(ox, oy, dx, dy, ax, ay, bx, by): """ Computes intersection between ray (O, D) and segment (A, B) in 2D. Returns dict with t, s, x, y, valid or None if parallel. """ sx = bx - ax sy = by - ay denom = dx sy - dy sx # Check for parallelism if math.isclose(denom, 0.0, abstol=1e-9): return None t = ((ax - ox) sy - (ay - oy) sx) / denom s = ((ax - ox) dy - (ay - oy) dx) / denom valid = (t >= 0) and (s >= 0) and (s <= 1) hitx = ox + dx t hity = oy + dy t return { "t": t, "s": s, "x": hitx, "y": hity, "valid": valid } def computerayaabbintersection(origin, direction, bbox): """ Computes tmin and tmax for ray-AABB intersection. bbox: {'min': (x,y,z), 'max': (x,y,z)} Returns (tmin, tmax) or None if no intersection. """ tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bbox['min'][i] or origin[i] > bbox['max'][i]: return None # No intersection else: t1 = (bbox['min'][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bbox['max'][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None # Ray behind box or invalid interval return (tmin, tmax) def processintersectionordering(rayorigin, raydir, objects): """ Optimizes processing order of intersection points and segments. objects: list of dicts with 'bbox' (min, max), 'class' (1, 2, 3), 'id'. Returns sorted lists of points and segments to process. """ points = [] # Class 1 segments = [] # Class 2, 3 for obj in objects: # Compute ray-AABB intersection result = computerayaabbintersection(rayorigin, raydir, obj['bbox']) if result is None: continue tmin, tmax = result if obj['class'] == 1: # Class 1: Surface. Distance is entry point. points.append({ 'id': obj['id'], 'distance': tmin, 'tmin': tmin, 'tmax': tmax }) else: # Class 2/3: Volumetric. Distance is exit point. segments.append({ 'id': obj['id'], 'class': obj['class'], 'distance': tmax, 'tmin': tmin, 'tmax': tmax }) # Sort points by entry distance points.sort(key=lambda p: p['distance']) # Sort segments by exit distance segments.sort(key=lambda s: s['distance']) # Process Points to find closest intersection dmin = float('inf') closestpoint = None for p in points: if p['distance'] < dmin: dmin = p['distance'] closestpoint = p # Process Segments with culling processedsegments = [] for seg in segments: # Check if segment is completely behind the closest point if seg['tmax'] < dmin: continue # Cull # Check if segment contains the closest point if seg['tmin'] <= dmin <= seg['tmax']: # The closest point is inside this segment. # If Class 1, it overrides the segment value at that point. # For Class 2 (Average), compute average for sub-segments outside the point. # For Class 3 (Max), check early termination logic. # Note: Exact sub-segment calculation depends on specific shader requirements processedsegments.append({ 'id': seg['id'], 'type': 'partial', 'tstart': seg['tmin'], 'tend': dmin, 'tstart2': dmin, 'tend2': seg['tmax'] }) else: # Segment is entirely before or after the closest point processedsegments.append({ 'id': seg['id'], 'type': 'full', 'tmin': seg['tmin'], 'tmax': seg['tmax'] }) return points, processedsegments Inside Ray: If a ray starts inside a solid, it must report the exit point to prevent holes or inside-out meshes from passing as outside intersections. Class 1 vs Class 2/3: Class 1 calculations are generally faster and should be performed first to reduce segment lengths or enable early termination for Class 3. Linear Edge Intersection determines the precise position where an isosurface intersects a grid edge by linearly interpolating between the scalar field values at the two vertices defining that edge. It solves the problem of locating surface geometry within a discrete voxel grid, serving as the fundamental geometric primitive for contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes and ray-marching isosurface extraction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by assuming a strictly linear variation of the scalar field along the edge, providing an exact algebraic solution for the intersection point under that assumption, whereas Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement uses numerical approximation and Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction uses gradient data for higher-order accuracy. This method extracts spatial information from a simulation by mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D voxel indices, serving as a direct manipulation interface for tasks such as segmentation seed selection. It computes the corresponding seed voxel from user clicks and drags on the image plane. Computes the intersection between a 2D ray (origin O, direction D) and a line segment (endpoints A, B), returning the intersection point and validity parameters t and s. It is distinguished from Linear Edge Intersection by its explicit handling of the ray's forward direction constraint and the segment's bounded domain via Cramer's rule, rather than solving for infinite lines. Boundary Segment Validity Conditions define the geometric and topological constraints required for a line segment connecting two points on a polygonal mesh to be classified as a valid spatial boundary segment. These conditions ensure that the segment represents a true visibility boundary rather than a segment penetrating the geometry. This method is distinct from sibling methods like Linear Edge Intersection and Voxel selection via pick ray intersection by explicitly validating the segment against mesh normals and intersection geometry to prevent penetration artifacts. Ordering Optimization: Sorting the intersection lists takes O(N \log N) where N is the number of objects intersected by the ray. The processing step is O(N). Ray-Segment Intersection: O(1) per segment. Specific performance metrics are not given in the sources. However, the method is designed to reduce total computation by avoiding unnecessary segment evaluations. The method scales with the number of objects intersected by the ray. Efficient bounding box hierarchies (BVH) are implied to reduce the number of bounding box tests. Strengths: Reduces redundant shading calculations; enables early termination for max-value projections; handles complex ordering of surface and volumetric intersections. Limitations: Requires classification of objects into classes; relies on accurate bounding box intersection; does not solve the analytic intersection itself but orders the results. Use when rendering scenes with multiple overlapping volumetric objects or mixed surface/volume data where shading costs are high and early termination is possible. Use when ray-segment intersection is required for 2D grid traversal or wall detection. Use when only a single primitive intersection is needed (use sibling methods). The intersection ordering optimization was introduced by Sobierajski et al. in "Volumetric Ray Tracing". The ray-segment intersection formula is a standard 2D geometric primitive often implemented in raycasting tutorials. The ray query interface for general shapes was developed as part of the EBGeometry project. The method evolved from the need to optimize volumetric ray tracing, where shading calculations are expensive. By ordering intersections and culling segments, significant performance gains are achieved. The ray-segment intersection is a foundational component in 2D raycasting engines. The EBGeometry project extended ray queries to support various shape types with device-callable interfaces. Volumetric ray tracers. 2D raycasting engines and maze renderers. General-purpose geometry libraries supporting ray queries on meshes and distance fields. name: Linear Edge Intersection
head: Edge Intersection for Isosurface Extraction, Linear Edge Interpolation, Marching Cububes Edge Crossing
body: Linear Edge Intersection determines the precise position where an isosurface intersects a grid edge by linearly interpolating between the scalar field values at the two vertices defining that edge. It solves the problem of locating surface geometry within a discrete voxel grid, serving as the fundamental geometric primitive for contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes and ray-marching isosurface extraction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by assuming a strictly linear variation of the scalar field along the edge, providing an exact algebraic solution for the intersection point under that assumption, whereas Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement uses numerical approximation and Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction uses gradient data for higher-order accuracy. Inputs: Two edge endpoints: \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 (3D coordinates). Scalar field values at endpoints: v1 = f(\mathbf{p}1) and v2 = f(\mathbf{p}2). Target isovalue (threshold): iso (or k, T, Y). Outputs: Intersection point \mathbf{p} on the edge segment [\mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2]. Data Structures: Points are represented as 3D vectors (x, y, z). Scalar values are floating-point numbers. Steps: 1. Identify Intersection: Check if the edge crosses the isosurface. This occurs if (v1 - iso) and (v2 - iso) have opposite signs. If both values are on the same side of the isovalue, there is no intersection on this edge segment. 2. Handle Degeneracy: If the scalar values are nearly identical (|v1 - v2| < \epsilon), the denominator in the interpolation formula approaches zero. In this case, return \mathbf{p}1 to avoid division by zero. Typical \epsilon values are 10^{-7} or 10^{-5}. 3. Calculate Interpolation Factor: Compute the normalized distance t (or \mu, \alpha, k) from \mathbf{p}1 to the intersection point: t = \frac{iso - v1}{v2 - v1} Alternatively, using signed distances d1 = v1 - iso and d2 = v2 - iso (where d1 and d2 have opposite signs): \mathbf{p} = \frac{d1 \mathbf{p}2 - d2 \mathbf{p}1}{d1 - d2} This signed-distance form is numerically more stable when vertices are near the plane. 4. Compute Position: Calculate the intersection point using vector interpolation: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}1 + t (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}1) Or in component form: \mathbf{p} = (1 - t) \mathbf{p}1 + t \mathbf{p}2 5. Clamping (Optional but Recommended): To handle floating-point inaccuracies where t might slightly exceed [0, 1], clamp t to [0, 1] before computing \mathbf{p}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearedgeintersection(p1, p2, v1, v2, iso, epsilon=1e-7): """ Calculates the intersection point of an isosurface with an edge. Args: p1: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the first endpoint. p2: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the second endpoint. v1: Scalar value at p1. v2: Scalar value at p2. iso: Target isovalue. epsilon: Threshold for degenerate case detection. Returns: 3D vector representing the intersection point. """ # Check for degenerate case where endpoints have same scalar value if abs(v2 - v1) < epsilon: return p1 # Calculate interpolation factor t t = (iso - v1) / (v2 - v1) # Clamp t to [0, 1] to handle floating point errors t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Compute intersection point: p = p1 + t (p2 - p1) px = p1[0] + t (p2[0] - p1[0]) py = p1[1] + t (p2[1] - p1[1]) pz = p1[2] + t (p2[2] - p1[2]) return (px, py, pz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If v1 = v2, the denominator is zero. This must be guarded against. Numerical Stability: When vertices are very close to the isosurface, standard interpolation can suffer from cancellation errors. Using signed distances (d0, d1) as in improves stability. Multiple Roots: Linear interpolation assumes a single root per edge. If the scalar field has multiple roots within the voxel (e.g., a thin structure passing through), linear interpolation will fail to detect all intersections. Vertex Ordering: In some implementations (e.g.,), consistent ordering of P1 and P2 (e.g., by coordinate value) is required to ensure correct triangle generation and normal orientation. Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is a post-detection technique used to accurately locate the intersection point of a viewing ray with an isosurface within a volume dataset. It solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in coarse adaptive sampling or sphere tracing by iteratively narrowing the interval known to contain the root. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on repeated linear interpolation (bisection) to refine the position, offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Linear Intersection Approximation (also known as Midpoint Intersection) estimates the intersection point of an isosurface with a grid edge by calculating the geometric midpoint of the edge, rather than performing linear interpolation based on scalar values. It differs from its parent, Linear Edge Intersection, by ignoring endpoint scalar values entirely, and from its sibling, Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement, by using a single fixed geometric step instead of recursive refinement. This method computes the precise intersection point on a triangle edge where a scalar field equals a threshold, using linear interpolation between two grid vertices. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement by avoiding iterative convergence, instead applying a deterministic "snap" heuristic to vertices near the threshold to stabilize the interpolation result. It serves as the geometric foundation for Triangle Point Sampling, which requires robust point generation to ensure uniform spatial distribution. Inverse Linear Interpolation calculates the non-integer position x corresponding to a specific scalar value v between two known values v1 and v2 at positions x1 and x2. It solves the inverse interpolation problem for isosurface extraction by determining the exact location along a grid line segment where an interpolated scalar field takes on a specific isosurface value Tm. Unlike forward linear interpolation which estimates a value at a known position, this method inverts the relationship to find the exact position for a known value, which is necessary for precise isosurface mesh generation. It builds on Linear Edge Intersection by providing the specific arithmetic to resolve the intersection point analytically. Hermite interpolation for isosurface extraction determines the precise position of an isovertex along a zero-crossing edge by utilizing both scalar field values and gradient information (Hermite data) at the edge endpoints. Unlike Linear Edge Intersection, which assumes linear variation and produces artifacts on non-linear implicit functions, this method fits higher-order polynomials to the local field behavior, significantly improving surface accuracy. It is primarily used in contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes where gradient data is available or can be approximated. This method estimates the positional error introduced by linear interpolation when determining the intersection of a scalar field with an isovalue on a grid edge. It leverages Taylor series expansion to bound the difference between the true root and the linear approximation without solving a linear system. It distinguishes itself from Linear Edge Intersection by providing a quantitative error metric rather than just the position, and from Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement by offering an analytical estimate rather than a numerical refinement. Approximates the zero-crossing position along an edge by sampling discrete points and selecting the one with minimum absolute density. It initializes a minimum value and iterates through a fixed number of steps (e.g., 8) along the edge, updating the best position if a lower absolute density is found. Clips wall edges to a screen or player boundary (e.g., y < 1) using linear interpolation to find the intersection point. If an endpoint is behind the boundary, it calculates the interpolation factor t and updates the coordinates to lie exactly on the boundary plane. An interpolation method between linear interpolation and midpoint selection used to calculate the intersection point of an edge and an iso-surface. It normalizes the interpolation ratio k based on thresholds m and n: if |k| < m, |k| is set to q; if |k| > n, |k| is set to p; otherwise, |k| is set to 0.5. This reduces artifacts in specific topological configurations. A method to find the point where the SDF assumes the isovalue c=0 along an edge exhibiting a material change, reduced to finding a value t \in [0,1]. It applies binary search with a limit of 8 iterations and a sub-interval size threshold of 10^{-6}. Handles cases where the surface intersects a grid edge more than once. It identifies a point where the gradient is perpendicular to the edge and deforms the surface to ensure only single edge intersections remain, using linear interpolation in the direction of the gradient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Linear interpolation is fast and simple, offering advantages in terms of speed and mathematical model simplicity. However, it is significantly more costly than the midpoint algorithm because it requires computing scalar values at ray entry and exit points. Accuracy: Provides an exact solution under the assumption of linear field variation. Accuracy degrades if the scalar field is highly non-linear within the voxel. Strengths: Simplicity, speed, and numerical stability when implemented with signed distances. Limitations: Cannot resolve multiple roots within a single edge or voxel. May produce artifacts if the underlying field is not smooth or linear. When to Use: When performance is critical and the scalar field is relatively smooth or linear within voxels. When Not to Use: When high geometric accuracy is required for highly non-linear fields, or when multiple intersections per voxel are expected. Not given in the sources. body: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is a post-detection technique used to accurately locate the intersection point of a viewing ray with an isosurface within a volume dataset. It solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in coarse adaptive sampling or sphere tracing by iteratively narrowing the interval known to contain the root. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on repeated linear interpolation (bisection) to refine the position, offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}] (or [x{near}, x{far}]) where a sign change in the scalar field value has been detected, the scalar field values at the interval endpoints d{prev} and d{curr} (or f{near}, f{far}), and the target isovalue \rho. Outputs: The refined intersection parameter t{hit} (or position \mathbf{x}{hit}). Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and 3D coordinates. No complex data structures are required beyond the ray parameters and the scalar field texture/volume access function. Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the search interval. Let L (or x{near}) be the point outside the isovalue (where f(L) < \rho) and R (or x{far}) be the point inside or at the isovalue (where f(R) \ge \rho). In adaptive sampling contexts, these correspond to t{prev} and t{curr} respectively. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat for a fixed number of iterations N (typically 4 to 10): a. Linear Interpolation: Compute the new candidate point \mathbf{x}{new} (or parameter M) using linear interpolation between the current bounds. The position is calculated as: \mathbf{x}{new} = (\mathbf{x}{far} - \mathbf{x}{near}) \frac{\rho - f{near}}{f{far} - f{near}} + \mathbf{x}{near} Alternatively, in parameter space t: t{new} = t{near} + (t{far} - t{near}) \frac{\rho - f{near}}{f{far} - f{near}} b. Sampling: Evaluate the scalar field value f{new} at \mathbf{x}{new} (or dM at t{new}). c. Interval Update: Compare f{new} with \rho: If f{new} < \rho (the new point is outside the isovalue), update the lower bound: set x{near} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{near} = f{new}. If f{new} \ge \rho (the new point is inside or at the isovalue), update the upper bound: set x{far} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{far} = f{new}. Note: Some implementations use strict inequality for the upper bound update (dM > 0) and lower bound update (dM < 0) assuming centered zero-level sets. While the method is named "bisection", it primarily uses linear interpolation, though some variants use strict midpoint bisection (M = (L+R)/2). 3. Termination: After N iterations, the refined intersection position is \mathbf{x}{new} (or t{new}). If N=0, return the midpoint of the final interval (t{min} + t{max}) / 2. 4. Shading: The refined point is shaded using the appropriate lighting model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplescalarfield(pos): """Standard volume lookup. Returns scalar value at pos.""" return volumelookup(pos) def intersectdomainbox(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax): """Standard ray-AABB intersection. Returns (tmin, tmax).""" tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) < 1e-9: if origin[i] < domainmin[i] or origin[i] > domainmax[i]: return (float('inf'), -float('inf')) else: t1 = (domainmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (domainmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def refineisohitbisection(origin, direction, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, isovalue, numiterations=5): """ Refines the intersection of a ray with an isosurface using bisection. """ tnear = tprev tfar = tcurr fnear = dprev ffar = dcurr # Guard: ensure valid interval for bisection if fnear >= isovalue or ffar < isovalue: return (tnear + tfar) / 2.0 for in range(numiterations): denom = ffar - fnear if abs(denom) < 1e-9: tnew = (tnear + tfar) / 2.0 else: tnew = tnear + (tfar - tnear) (isovalue - fnear) / denom posnew = origin + tnew direction fnew = samplescalarfield(posnew) # Update bounds based on S4 if fnew < isovalue: tnear = tnew fnear = fnew else: tfar = tnew ffar = fnew return tnew def raymarchwithrefinement(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax, isovalue, stepsize, numrefineiters=5): """ Adaptive ray marching with iterative bisection refinement. """ tmin, tmax = intersectdomainbox(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax) if tmax <= tmin: return None tprev = tmin dprev = samplescalarfield(origin + tprev direction) tcurr = tprev + stepsize while tcurr <= tmax: dcurr = samplescalarfield(origin + tcurr direction) # Check for sign change (outside to inside) if (dprev < isovalue) and (dcurr >= isovalue): thit = refineisohitbisection( origin, direction, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, isovalue, numrefineiters) phit = origin + thit direction # Shading is application-specific; return hit point for shading pipeline return phit tprev = tcurr dprev = dcurr tcurr += stepsize return None Parameters: numiterations (or uRefinementIterations): The number of bisection steps. Typical values range from 4 to 10, with 5 being common. More iterations improve accuracy at the cost of additional scalar field evaluations. isovalue (\rho): The scalar threshold defining the surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{far} \approx f{near}, the linear interpolation formula divides by zero. The pseudocode handles this by falling back to the midpoint. Sign Change Assumption: The method assumes a single root within the interval. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in f{new} comparisons can cause infinite loops if not bounded by iteration count. Using a fixed iteration count avoids this. Neubauer's algorithm is a method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the problem of locating the precise root of the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by using repeated linear interpolation to refine the intersection position within the ray segment containing the root. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or root isolation techniques (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d along a ray where a signed distance function (SDF) or occupancy logit crosses a specific threshold. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement by using linear interpolation between two bracketing points to estimate the next probe point, rather than simply halving the interval. The Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm that determines the exact intersection point of a ray with an implicit surface within a segment known to contain an intersection. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines. The method systematically halves the search interval at each step until the midpoint evaluates to zero. Hitpoint Refinement is an iterative technique to achieve higher quality in detecting surface intersections without reducing rendering speed. It allows for coarser initial sampling steps to increase rendering speed, refining the detected intersection point through a specific heuristic procedure. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a "half-step back, then check direction" adjustment rather than standard bisection or secant methods, enabling significant speedups when paired with large initial sampling distances. Windowed Bisection for Isosurface Refinement refines the isosurface position along a ray using 4 iterations of bisection with windowing, ensuring correctness across brick boundaries by using sampleWithIndirection. It initializes lo = tLow and hi = tHigh, then loops 4 times to calculate the midpoint mid = (lo + hi) 0.5, position pos = rayOrigin + rayDir mid, and voxel coordinates voxel = normalizedToVoxel(pos,...). It samples density, normalizes it to [0,1] using uniforms.floatMin and uniforms.floatMax, then applies windowing: density = applyWindow(normalizedDensity, windowCenter, windowWidth);. It updates bounds: if density >= isoValue, set hi = mid; else lo = mid, and returns (lo + hi) 0.5. Time Complexity: O(N) scalar field evaluations per intersection, where N is the number of refinement iterations. This is significantly cheaper than solving cubic polynomials for exact trilinear intersection but more expensive than a single-step detection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Measured Performance: A fixed number of 4 iterations is empirically sufficient for high-quality positions in many datasets. Increasing iterations improves accuracy at the cost of additional evaluations. Strengths: Provides a more accurate hit position than a single-step midpoint detection. Empirically, a fixed number of iterations yields high-quality positions. Limitations: Potential artifacts in complex topologies if the initial step size is too large. When to Use: When adaptive sampling is used and high precision is needed without the cost of analytic inversion. When Not to Use: When the scalar field is extremely noisy or discontinuous, or when exact geometric precision is required for subsequent physics simulations. The method originates from real-time volume graphics research, specifically in the context of isosurface rendering. It is commonly used in GPU-based volume raycasting pipelines where adaptive sampling is employed to balance performance and quality. shalu-007-git/isosurface-ray-casting, https://github.com/shalu-007-git/isosurface-ray-casting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Ray-Casting and Advanced Shading of Discrete Isosurfaces, https://cgl.ethz.ch/people/archive/siggc/publications/eg05.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Adding Refined Isosurface Rendering and Shadow Mapping to vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper, https://insight-journal.org/pdfs/880.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Show HN: Kiln – WebGPU-native out-of-core volume rendering for multi-GB datasets, https://github.com/MPanknin/kiln-render, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neubauer's Ray-Voxel Intersection Algorithm
head: Neubauer, Neubauer's Approximative Intersection, Neubauer's Method, Repeated Linear Interpolation
body: Neubauer's algorithm is a fast, approximate method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the root-finding problem for the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by repeatedly applying linear interpolation to narrow down the segment containing the root. It is distinguished from sibling methods by relying solely on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or derivative-based root isolation (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), trading mathematical exactness for computational speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray R(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, the interval [t{in}, t{out}] where the ray overlaps the voxel, scalar field values \rho{ijk} at the eight voxel vertices, the iso-value \rho{iso}, and the iteration count N (typically 2–3). Output: The hit distance t{hit} along the ray, or a "NO HIT" status if no intersection is found within the voxel. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on scalar variables for the interval bounds t0, t1, the interpolated density values \rho0, \rho1, and the candidate parameter t. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the search interval boundaries and evaluate densities at the endpoints: t0:= t{in}, \quad t1:= t{out} \rho0:= \rho(R(t0)), \quad \rho1:= \rho(R(t1)) where \rho(R(t)) is computed via trilinear interpolation of the voxel's vertex data. 2. Initial Sign Check: If \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho1 - \rho{iso}), return NO HIT. This indicates the iso-surface does not cross the ray segment within the voxel, or crosses an even number of times, which the method cannot detect. 3. Iterative Refinement (Repeated Linear Interpolation): For i = 1 to N: a. Compute the candidate intersection parameter using linear interpolation: t:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} b. Evaluate the density at the candidate point: \rho{new}:= \rho(R(t)). c. Determine which sub-segment contains the root by comparing signs: If \text{sign}(\rho{new} - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}), the root lies in [t, t1]; update t0:= t, \rho0:= \rho{new}. Else, the root lies in [t0, t]; update t1:= t, \rho1:= \rho{new}. 4. Final Result: After N iterations, compute the final hit distance: t{hit}:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} Return t{hit}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NeubauerRayVoxelIntersection(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelbounds, voxeldata, rhoiso, N=3): """ rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) voxelbounds: tuple (x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1) voxeldata: list/tuple of 8 floats representing density at voxel corners rhoiso: float, the iso-surface value N: int, number of interpolation iterations """ # 1. Calculate ray-voxel overlap interval [tin, tout] using slab method x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1 = voxelbounds tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): p = rayorigin[axis] d = raydirection[axis] b0 = [x0, y0, z0][axis] b1 = [x1, y1, z1][axis] if abs(d) < 1e-12: if p < b0 or p > b1: return None else: t1 = (b0 - p) / d t2 = (b1 - p) / d if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None tin, tout = tmin, tmax # Helper to evaluate trilinear interpolation def evaluatedensity(t): px = rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0] py = rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1] pz = rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2] u = (px - x0) / (x1 - x0) v = (py - y0) / (y1 - y0) w = (pz - z0) / (z1 - z0) u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, w)) d000 = voxeldata[0]; d100 = voxeldata[1] d010 = voxeldata[2]; d110 = voxeldata[3] d001 = voxeldata[4]; d101 = voxeldata[5] d011 = voxeldata[6]; d111 = voxeldata[7] d00 = d000 (1 - u) + d100 u d10 = d010 (1 - u) + d110 u d01 = d001 (1 - u) + d101 u d11 = d011 (1 - u) + d111 u d0 = d00 (1 - v) + d10 v d1 = d01 (1 - v) + d11 v return d0 (1 - w) + d1 w # 2. Initialize interval t0 = tin t1 = tout rho0 = evaluatedensity(t0) rho1 = evaluatedensity(t1) # 3. Initial sign check def sign(val): if val > 0: return 1 elif val < 0: return -1 else: return 0 if sign(rho0 - rhoiso) == sign(rho1 - rhoiso): return None # 4. Iterative refinement for i in range(N): t = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) rhonew = evaluatedensity(t) if sign(rhonew - rhoiso) == sign(rho0 - rhoiso): t0 = t rho0 = rhonew else: t1 = t rho1 = rhonew # 5. Final result thit = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) return thit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: The algorithm assumes a single root within the segment defined by differing signs. It can falsely return the last intersection point if three intersections are contained within a voxel but two of them are within the first ray segment. Complex Topologies: In cases where the function has two roots, the entry and exit densities may be on the same side of \rho{iso}, causing the initial sign check to return NO HIT incorrectly. SIMD Compatibility: The control flow involves conditional updates to t0, t1, \rho0, \rho1 based on sign comparisons. This inconsistent decision-making on which segment to handle makes the base algorithm less suitable for SIMD than methods with uniform control flow, although it remains functional and faster than exact solvers in parallel contexts. Approximation Errors: As an iterative approximation, it linearly approximates the trilinear function, making it error-prone and prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations. Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial resulting from substituting the ray equation into the trilinear interpolation function to find the precise root. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Neubauer's algorithm by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions (Cardano's formula) rather than iterative refinement or isolation techniques, offering mathematical exactness at the cost of significant computational expense and numerical instability. Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm for iso-surfaces that combines the speed of Neubauer's method with the correctness guarantees of Schwarze's method. It solves the problem of finding the first intersection of a ray with a cubic polynomial within a voxel by first isolating the root interval using the polynomial's extrema, then refining the location via iterative root finding. Unlike Neubauer's method, which can fail or return incorrect intersections when multiple roots exist in a segment, this method guarantees that the final interval contains exactly one root, ensuring the first valid intersection is found. Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection computes the point where a ray intersects an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation within a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. Unlike analytical cubic solvers (e.g., Schwarze’s method), this approach is slightly faster and yields single-precision, numerically stable results. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of iterations N (typically 2–3). Each iteration requires one trilinear interpolation evaluation. Trilinear interpolation is O(1) with a constant number of arithmetic operations. Thus, the time complexity per ray-voxel intersection is O(N), which is effectively constant. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar variables. Measured Performance: On a 1.8GHz AMD Opteron CPU, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-voxel intersections per second in synthetic setups (Table 1). In SIMD mode on synthetic setups, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-cell intersections per second (Table 2). On real-world datasets (Bonsai, Aneurism, Engine), Neubauer achieves approximately 2.93–2.94 million intersections per second (Table 3). In SIMD mode on real-world datasets, Neubauer achieves 6.94–7.65 million intersections per second, a speedup of factor 2.3–2.6 over sequential code (Table 4). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Computationally very cheap and faster than the accurate but slow Schwarze algorithm. Better suited for SIMD implementation than Schwarze due to simpler control flow. Integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system. Limitations: Prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations. Can fail to locate valid intersections in cases with multiple roots or specific topological configurations. Less numerically stable than isolation-based methods. When to Use: Use when computational speed is prioritized over exactness and the voxel data topology is relatively simple. The method is well-suited for scenarios where an approximate intersection is acceptable and exact solvers are too slow. When Not to Use: Avoid when high accuracy is required or when the iso-surface may contain multiple intersections within a single voxel, as the method is error-prone and may miss valid intersections. Neubauer's algorithm was proposed by Neubauer et al. in 2002. It was analyzed and compared with other ray-voxel intersection techniques (including Schwarze's method and linear interpolation) in the context of iso-surface volume rendering by Wald et al. in 2004. The method is integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system for iso-surface volume rendering, where it serves as a fast, approximate intersection primitive.
