name: Iterative Bisection for Zero-Crossing
head: Bisection Zero-Crossing, Zero Crossing Approximation
body: This method finds the precise location along a grid edge where a Signed Distance Function (SDF) crosses a specific isovalue (typically c=0), indicating a material boundary between solid and air. It solves the root-finding problem f(t) = 0 for t \in [0,1], where t is the relative position along the edge. It is distinguished from Linear Edge Intersection by using iterative numerical approximation rather than analytic linear interpolation, allowing it to handle non-linear SDF variations at the cost of higher computational overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two grid vertices V1, V2 with known world positions and SDF values d1, d2. The edge is valid only if one vertex is solid (d \le c) and the other is air (d > c), indicating a material change. Output: A scalar t \in [0,1] representing the relative intersection point. Data Structures: No complex structures are required. The algorithm operates on scalar values and simple interval bounds. Parameters: Maximum iterations: N{max} = 8. Sub-interval size threshold: \epsilon{size} = 10^{-6}. Density value bias: \epsilon{val} = 10^{-2}. Steps: 1. Initialize the search interval [t{min}, t{max}] = [0, 1]. 2. Loop for i from 1 to N{max}: a. Calculate midpoint: t{mid} = (t{min} + t{max}) / 2. b. Sample the SDF at the corresponding world position to get d{mid}. c. Check for termination conditions: i. If |d{mid}| \le \epsilon{val}, return t{mid}. ii. If (t{max} - t{min}) \le \epsilon{size}, return t{mid}. d. Determine the new sub-interval: i. If d{mid} and d1 have opposite signs (or d{mid} \le c vs d1 > c logic depending on sign convention), set t{max} = t{mid}. ii. Else, set t{min} = t{mid}. 3. If the loop completes without early termination, return the last calculated t{mid}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativebisectionzerocrossing(v1pos, v2pos, v1sdf, v2sdf, isovalue=0.0): # Check for material change # Solid: sdf <= isovalue, Air: sdf > isovalue isv1solid = v1sdf <= isovalue isv2solid = v2sdf <= isovalue if isv1solid == isv2solid: return None # No zero crossing on this edge tmin = 0.0 tmax = 1.0 tmid = 0.5 # Safeguards maxiter = 8 sizethresh = 1e-6 valthresh = 1e-2 for in range(maxiter): # Calculate midpoint position # Linear interpolation of position is standard for sampling location midpos = v1pos + tmid (v2pos - v1pos) # Sample SDF at midpoint midsdf = samplesdf(midpos) # Check value threshold if abs(midsdf - isovalue) <= valthresh: return tmid # Check interval size threshold if (tmax - tmin) <= sizethresh: return tmid # Determine which half contains the root # If midsdf is on the same side as v1sdf relative to isovalue, # the root is in the right half [tmid, tmax] # Otherwise, it is in the left half [tmin, tmid] # Logic: if (midsdf - isovalue) and (v1sdf - isovalue) have same sign middiff = midsdf - isovalue v1diff = v1sdf - isovalue if (middiff > 0 and v1diff > 0) or (middiff < 0 and v1diff < 0): tmin = tmid else: tmax = tmid tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2 # Return last calculated midpoint if limit breached return tmid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Crossings: The method assumes only one material change per edge. If the grid resolution is insufficient to capture smaller details, multiple zero-crossings on a single edge will be lost, and only the first or dominant one is found. Precision: Rounding errors in floating-point arithmetic may prevent the function from ever reaching exactly zero, necessitating the bias threshold. A variant used in ray-marching contexts (e.g., dipole sum reconstruction) rather than grid-edge extraction. It identifies the first zero-crossing along a camera ray by placing 1024 dense samples between near and far limits. If found, it refines the region with 24 sparse samples before the crossing, 48 dense samples around the crossing, and 8 sparse samples after. If no crossing is found, it places 80 uniform samples. This approach optimizes sample density around the surface for inverse rendering efficiency. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of iterations (constant 8 in this implementation). Each step requires one SDF evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1). Performance: The method converges slowly compared to Newton-Raphson but is robust and guaranteed to converge for continuous functions. The limit of 8 steps provides a good trade-off between accuracy and performance for terrain rendering. Strengths: Robustness; handles non-linear SDFs better than linear interpolation; simple to implement. Limitations: Slower convergence; requires SDF sampling (which may be expensive if the SDF is not analytic); loses sub-grid detail if resolution is low. When to use: When the SDF is not analytically differentiable or when robustness against non-linearities is prioritized over speed. When not to use: When high-frequency details are expected but grid resolution is low, as multiple crossings will be missed. The method originates from volumetric terrain rendering techniques using WebGL, where efficient isosurface extraction from SDF grids was required. It relies on the bisection method (binary search), described in literature as one of the most effective methods for finding real zeros of continuous functions ]. The specific safeguards (8 iterations, 10^{-6} size threshold, 10^{-2} value bias) were introduced to handle the limitations of computer number representation and to ensure early termination in real-time rendering contexts. name: Vertex Handling for Grid Vertices
head: F >= 0 Handling, Strictly Positive Field at Vertices
body: Vertex Handling for Grid Vertices resolves topological ambiguities in isosurface extraction when the scalar field value at a grid vertex equals the threshold exactly. It sets the convention that the field is considered strictly positive when F \ge 0, ensuring consistent connectivity for the marching cubes/tetrahedra algorithm. This method is distinct from refinement techniques like Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement or approximation methods like Linear Intersection Approximation because it relies on a deterministic sign convention rather than geometric correction or iterative solving. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar field values F(v) at grid vertices v. Output: A consistent boolean classification of vertices as "inside" (F < 0) or "outside" (F \ge 0). Data Structures: No additional data structures are required. The method modifies the interpretation of existing scalar values. Steps: 1. For every vertex v in the grid, evaluate the scalar field value F(v). 2. Compare F(v) against the isosurface threshold T (typically 0 for signed distance fields or zero-crossings). 3. Apply the strict inequality rule: If F(v) < T, classify vertex as inside. If P(v) \ge T, classify vertex as outside. 4. Use these classifications to determine edge crossings via Linear Edge Intersection. Formulas: \text{Class}(v) = \begin{cases} \text{Inside} & \text{if } F(v) < T \\ \text{Outside} & \text{if } F(v) \ge T \end{cases} Parameters: Threshold T: Typically 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If F(v) = T, the standard floating-point comparison might be unstable. The strict F \ge 0 rule provides a deterministic tie-breaker, preventing ambiguous cases where a vertex could be counted as both inside and outside depending on rounding errors. Precision: This method assumes that the scalar field is well-defined at vertices. It does not handle cases where the surface passes through an edge multiple times (which requires gradient analysis as noted in). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifyvertex(fieldvalue, threshold): """ Classifies a vertex based on the strict positive field convention. Args: fieldvalue (float): The scalar value F(v) at the vertex. threshold (float): The isosurface threshold T. Returns: bool: True if the vertex is considered 'Outside' (F >= T), False if 'Inside' (F < T). """ # Strictly positive field handling: F >= 0 is treated as positive/outside return fieldvalue >= threshold A vertex ordering regimen to ensure consistent planar coefficients and signed area cross products for shared facets, mitigating numeric inaccuracies in nearly parallel ray/cell intersections. Within a cell, vertices of adjacent facets are numbered in opposite directions (CW or CCW) to attain consistent vector directions. Adjacent facets sharing a 'corner' leg also order vertices in opposite directions. Adjacent cells are classified as 'even' and 'odd' in all three logical mesh dimensions (checkerboard pattern). The vertex order direction for facets of an odd cell is set opposite to that of even cells. These directed line segments generate planar coefficients and signed area cross products for the ray-through-facet test. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per vertex. Memory: O(1) additional memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with the number of vertices. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Deterministic; eliminates topological ambiguities at vertices; simple to implement. Limitations: Does not resolve cases where the surface intersects an edge multiple times (requires gradient analysis); relies on the assumption that the field is well-behaved at vertices. When to use it: Use when extracting isosurfaces from grid-based scalar fields where vertex values may exactly match the threshold. When not: Do not use if the surface intersects edges multiple times within a single cell, as this requires more complex handling. Origin: Isotopic approximation of implicit curves and surfaces (2004) and Ray tracing through a hexahedral mesh in HADES (2004). The method is used in isosurface extraction algorithms (e.g., Marching Cubes) to handle the case where the surface passes through grid vertices. Isotopic approximation of implicit curves and surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1145/1057432.1057465, fetched 2026-10-29 Ray tracing through a hexahedral mesh in HADES, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1413331/?q=segment tracing, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Linear Interpolation
head: Inverse Linear Interpolation for Isosurface Location, Inverse interpolation problem, Isosurface location calculation, Linear Interpolation Position
body:
Inverse Linear Interpolation calculates the non-integer position x corresponding to a specific scalar value v between two known values v1 and v2 at positions x1 and x2. It solves the inverse interpolation problem for isosurface extraction by determining the exact location along a grid line segment where an interpolated scalar field takes on a specific isosurface value Tm. Unlike forward linear interpolation which estimates a value at a known position, this method inverts the relationship to find the exact position for a known value, which is necessary for precise isosurface mesh generation. It builds on Linear Edge Intersection by providing the specific arithmetic to resolve the intersection point analytically. Inputs: x1, x2: The coordinates of the two endpoints of the grid line segment. T1, T2: The scalar data values at x1 and x2 respectively. Tm: The target isosurface level value. Outputs: xm: The interpolated coordinate along the segment where the scalar value equals Tm. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method operates on scalar values and coordinates. If implemented within a grid context, x1 and x2 are often derived from grid indices i, j, k and cell dimensions. Steps: 1. Validate Monotonicity: Check if Tm lies between T1 and T2. 2. Check for Degeneracy: Check if T1 = T2. 3. Compute Interpolation Parameter \alpha: Calculate the normalized distance parameter \alpha using the formula: \alpha =  rac{Tm - T1}{T2 - T1} This parameter represents the fractional distance from x1 to x2. 4. Compute Intersection Position xm: Calculate the final position using the weighted average of the endpoints: xm = (1 - \alpha)x1 + \alpha x2 Alternatively, this can be computed directly as: xm = x1 + (x2 - x1) 	imes  rac{Tm - T1}{T2 - T1} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverselinearinterpolation(x1: float, x2: float, t1: float, t2: float, tm: float) -> float: """ Calculates the position xm along the segment [x1, x2] where the scalar value equals tm. Args: x1: Start coordinate of the segment. x2: End coordinate of the segment. t1: Scalar value at x1. t2: Scalar value at x2. tm: Target isosurface value. Returns: The coordinate xm where the interpolated value is tm. Raises: ValueError: If t1 equals t2 (division by zero). """ # Sources do not specify boundary checks; standard practice validates T1 <= Tm <= T2 and T1 != T2 if t1 == t2: raise ValueError("Division by zero: t1 equals t2. No unique intersection point.") alpha = (tm - t1) / (t2 - t1) return x1 + (x2 - x1) alpha Sensitivity and Error Analysis: The position xm is sensitive to uncertainties \Delta T1 and \Delta T2 in the data values. The error \Delta xm is given by: \Delta xm =  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T1} \Delta T1 +  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T2} \Delta T2 The partial derivatives are:  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T1} =  rac{Tm - T2}{(T2 - T1)^2}(x2 - x1)  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T2} =  rac{T1 - Tm}{(T2 - T1)^2}(x2 - x1) The relative error can be expressed as:  rac{\Delta xm}{x2 - x1} = -\left(1 - \alphaight) rac{\Delta T1}{T2 - T1} + \alpha  rac{\Delta T2}{T2 - T1} The error bound is: |\Delta xm| \le |x2 - x1|  rac{\max(|\Delta T1|, |\Delta T2|)}{|T2 - T1|} Uncertainty in isosurface location is proportional to the magnitude of data uncertainty and inversely proportional to the data variation |T2 - T1|. A variant that uses Newton-Raphson iteration to refine the intersection point by projecting a sample point onto the isosurface using the gradient. It calculates a displacement parameter t =  rac{fI - f(x0)}{
abla f(x0) \cdot 
abla f(x0)} and updates the point p'\lambda = x0 + t 
abla f(x0). It applies a displacement criterion \Delta d (based on cell dimensions) to discard points projected too far, avoiding convergence to distant roots near local extrema. Time Complexity: O(1). The method involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtraction, division, multiplication, addition). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the input variables. Strengths: Exact analytical solution for linear interpolation. Extremely fast computation, suitable for real-time rendering or large-scale mesh generation. Assumes linear variation between grid points. Limitations: Accuracy degrades if the scalar field varies non-linearly within the cell. Numerical instability or division by zero when T1 = T2 (zero gradient). Sensitivity to data noise increases as |T2 - T1| approaches zero. When to use: Standard isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) where linear interpolation is the standard assumption. Real-time volume rendering requiring precise ray-primitive intersection. When not to use: When high-order continuity or non-linear field behavior is critical and higher-order interpolation (e.g., Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction) is available Siblings: [Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction]. When the gradient is known to be zero or near-zero, requiring fallback logic. Inverse Linear Interpolation is a fundamental technique in scientific visualization and computer graphics, particularly in isosurface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes. The method is formally described in the verification guide for Smokeview (Version 6), a tool for visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation data, where it is referred to as the "inverse interpolation problem". The sensitivity analysis provided in highlights the importance of understanding error propagation in isosurface location due to data uncertainty. A basic implementation appears in open-source volume rendering code. joshcodd/volume-rendering, https://github.com/joshcodd/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume III: Verification Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-3, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Iso-splatting: a point-based alternative to isosurface visualization, https://doi.org/10.1109/pccga.2003.1238274, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction
head: Hermite contouring, Hermite interpolation
body:
Hermite interpolation for isosurface extraction determines the precise position of an isovertex along a zero-crossing edge by utilizing both scalar field values and gradient information (Hermite data) at the edge endpoints. Unlike Linear Edge Intersection, which assumes linear variation and produces artifacts on non-linear implicit functions, this method fits higher-order polynomials to the local field behavior, significantly improving surface accuracy. It is primarily used in contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes where gradient data is available or can be approximated. Inputs: Edge endpoints \mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1 \in \mathbb{R}^3, scalar field values v0 = F(\mathbf{x}0) and v1 = F(\mathbf{x}1), gradient vectors 
abla F0 = 
abla F(\mathbf{x}0) and 
abla F1 = 
abla F(\mathbf{x}1), and target isovalue T (typically 0). Outputs: Isovertex position \mathbf{x}{iso} along the edge such that F(\mathbf{x}{iso}) \approx T. Not given in the sources. 1. Normalize the Edge Interval: Map the physical edge segment [\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1] to the parametric interval [0, 1] by defining e = \mathbf{x}1 - \mathbf{x}0 and L = \|e\|. 2. Compute Directional Derivatives: Calculate the derivative of the scalar field along the edge direction at each endpoint as f'0 =  rac{
abla F0 \cdot e}{\|e\|^2} and f'1 =  rac{
abla F1 \cdot e}{\|e\|^2}. If the edge is axis-aligned, f' is simply the corresponding component of 
abla F. 3. Scale Derivatives for Unit Interval: Scale the directional derivatives by the edge length to obtain derivatives for the normalized interval: d0 = f'0 \cdot L and d1 = f'1 \cdot L. 4. Adjust Values for Target Isovalue: Shift the function values to target the zero-crossing: v0 \leftarrow v0 - T and v1 \leftarrow v1 - T. 5. Select Interpolation Order and Solve: Choose between Cubic or Quadratic Hermite interpolation based on the implicit function's nature. Cubic Hermite Interpolation: Fit p(t) = a0 + a1 t + a2 t^2 + a3 t^3 satisfying p(0)=v0, p'(0)=d0, p(1)=v1, p'(1)=d1. The coefficients are uniquely determined as a0 = v0, a1 = d0, a2 = 3v1 - 3v0 - 2d0 - d1, and a3 = 2v0 - 2v1 + d0 + d1. Quadratic Hermite Interpolation: Use when the implicit function is known to be quadratic (e.g., PSR with B-splines). Fit p(t) = a0 + a1 t + a2 t^2 by interpolating values exactly (a0 = v0, a0 + a1 + a2 = v1) and fitting derivatives in a least-squares sense. The coefficients are a1 =  rac{d0 - d1}{2} + v1 - v0 and a2 =  rac{d1 - d0}{2}. 6. Compute Isovertex Position: Solve p(t) = 0 for t \in [0, 1] and compute \mathbf{x}{iso} = \mathbf{x}0 + t \cdot e. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cbrt(x): if x >= 0: return x (1/3) else: return -((-x) (1/3)) def hermiteisovertex(x0, x1, v0, v1, grad0, grad1, T=0.0): """ Calculate isovertex position using Hermite interpolation. Args: x0, x1: Endpoints of the edge (vectors). v0, v1: Scalar field values at endpoints. grad0, grad1: Gradient vectors at endpoints. T: Target isovalue. Returns: xiso: Position of the isovertex. """ # 1. Edge vector and length e = [x1[i] - x0[i] for i in range(3)] Lsq = dot(e, e) # Handle degenerate edge if Lsq < 1e-12: return x0 L = math.sqrt(Lsq) # 2. Directional derivatives (projected onto edge direction) # f' = (grad. e) / ||e||^2 df0 = dot(grad0, e) / Lsq df1 = dot(grad1, e) / Lsq # 3. Scale derivatives for unit interval [0, 1] # d = df L d0 = df0 L d1 = df1 L # 4. Adjust values for target isovalue v0adj = v0 - T v1adj = v1 - T # 5. Solve for t # Using Cubic Hermite as the general robust method a0 = v0adj a1 = d0 a2 = 3 v1adj - 3 v0adj - 2 d0 - d1 a3 = 2 v0adj - 2 v1adj + d0 + d1 # Solve cubic a3t^3 + a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 t = solvecubicrootinrange(a3, a2, a1, a0, 0.0, 1.0) if t is None: # Fallback to linear if cubic fails to find root in range # Linear interpolation: t = -v0 / (v1 - v0) denom = v1adj - v0adj if abs(denom) < 1e-12: return x0 t = -v0adj / denom t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # 6. Compute position xiso = [x0[i] + t e[i] for i in range(3)] return xiso def solvecubicrootinrange(a3, a2, a1, a0, low, high): """ Finds a real root of a3t^3 + a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 within [low, high]. Returns the root or None if no root exists in range. """ # Normalize if a3 is 0 (quadratic) if abs(a3) < 1e-12: if abs(a2) < 1e-12: # Linear: a1t + a0 = 0 if abs(a1) > 1e-12: t = -a0 / a1 if low <= t <= high: return t return None else: # Quadratic: a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 disc = a1a1 - 4a2a0 if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-a1 + sqrtdisc) / (2 a2) t2 = (-a1 - sqrtdisc) / (2 a2) if low <= t1 <= high: return t1 if low <= t2 <= high: return t2 return None # Cubic case # Convert to depressed cubic u^3 + pu + q = 0 # t = u - a2/(3a3) p = (3a3a1 - a2a2) / (3a3a3) q = (2a2a2a2 - 9a3a2a1 + 27a3a3a0) / (27a3a3a3) # Discriminant delta = (qq/4 + ppp/27) if delta > 0: # One real root sqrtdelta = math.sqrt(delta) u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrtdelta) + cbrt(-q/2 - sqrtdelta) t = u - a2 / (3 a3) if low <= t <= high: return t elif delta == 0: # Multiple roots if p == 0 and q == 0: t = -a2 / (3 a3) # Triple root if low <= t <= high: return t else: u = cbrt(-q/2) t1 = 2u - a2/(3a3) t2 = -u - a2/(3a3) if low <= t1 <= high: return t1 if low <= t2 <= high: return t2 else: # Three real roots (casus irreducibilis) r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27) theta = math.acos(-q / (2 r)) m = 2 math.cbrt(r) t1 = m math.cos(theta/3) - a2/(3a3) t2 = m math.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - a2/(3a3) t3 = m math.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - a2/(3a3) candidates = [t1, t2, t3] for t in candidates: if low <= t <= high: return t return None Target Isovalue (T): Typically 0. Interpolation Order: Cubic is the default for general implicit functions; Quadratic is used for known quadratic fields (e.g., B-splines). Degenerate Edges: If \|\mathbf{x}0 - \mathbf{x}1\| \approx 0, the derivative calculation involves division by zero. Multiple Roots: A cubic polynomial can have up to three real roots. To uniquely define the position of an isovertex, we observe that there must be an odd number of roots along a zero-crossing edge. Least-Squares Pitfall: Do not use the standard least-squares solution for all four constraints (values and derivatives) in the quadratic case, because it does not guarantee that the polynomial p(t) has a root along the edge even if F(t) does. The value-interpolating, derivative-least-squares approach is preferred. Gradient Availability: Hermite data (gradients) may not be available in all datasets; the approach remains effective even when gradients are approximated using finite differences. Cubic Hermite Interpolation fits a cubic polynomial to the four Hermite constraints (two values, two derivatives). It is the general-purpose method for non-linear implicit functions, offering higher accuracy than linear interpolation by reducing artifacts. It requires solving a cubic equation, which may yield up to three roots, necessitating a strategy to select the correct isovertex. Choose this when the implicit function is not known to be quadratic and high accuracy is required. See Cubic Hermite Interpolation. This variant fits a quadratic polynomial that interpolates the endpoint values exactly and fits the endpoint derivatives in a least-squares sense. It is specifically designed for implicit functions known to be quadratic, such as those represented by linear combinations of second-order B-splines (e.g., PSR). It is computationally cheaper than cubic interpolation (solving a quadratic vs. cubic equation) and avoids the multiple-root ambiguity of cubics. Choose this when the underlying field is known to be quadratic. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge. Cubic interpolation involves solving a cubic equation (constant number of operations). Quadratic interpolation involves solving a quadratic equation (constant number of operations). Memory Complexity: O(1) per edge. No additional storage is required beyond the input values and gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of edges in the mesh. Strengths: Significantly reduces reconstruction artifacts compared to linear interpolation for non-linear implicit functions. Provides mathematically precise isovertex positions given gradient data. Limitations: Requires gradient data (Hermite data), which may need to be computed via finite differences if not available, adding overhead and potential noise. Cubic interpolation can have multiple roots, requiring careful selection logic. When to Use: When high-quality isosurfaces are required for non-linear implicit functions and gradient information is available or can be efficiently approximated. When Not to Use: When gradient data is unavailable and finite difference approximation is too expensive or noisy, or when the implicit function is strictly linear (linear interpolation is sufficient and faster). Hermite interpolation for isosurface extraction was proposed to address the inaccuracies of linear interpolation in contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes when applied to non-linear implicit functions. The method utilizes the gradient of the implicit function to generate more accurate isosurfaces by means of higher-order interpolation techniques. The approach was demonstrated to provide clear quality improvements, even when Hermite data is not directly available and gradients are approximated using finite differences. Accurate Isosurface Interpolation with Hermite Data, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7335492/, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Cubic Hermite Interpolation
head: Third Order Polynomial, Cubic polynomial interpolation
body: Cubic Hermite Interpolation is a method for determining precise isovertex positions along zero-crossing edges in contouring algorithms by fitting a cubic polynomial to both function values and gradients (Hermite data) at the edge endpoints. It improves upon linear interpolation by reducing artifacts caused by the non-linear nature of implicit functions, offering higher accuracy at the cost of solving for polynomial coefficients and finding cubic roots. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar field values v0 = f(x0) and v1 = f(x1) at edge endpoints x0 and x1; two derivative estimates d0 = f'(x0) and d1 = f'(x1); and the target isovalue k. Outputs: The position x^ along the edge where the interpolated function equals k. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and a single cubic polynomial defined by four coefficients. Steps: 1. Compute Coefficients: Determine the coefficients a0, a1, a2, a3 of the cubic polynomial p(x) = a0 + a1 x + a2 x^2 + a3 x^3 such that it satisfies the Hermite constraints: \begin{aligned} p(x0) &= v0 \\ p(x1) &= v1 \\ p'(x0) &= d0 \\ p'(x1) &= d1 \end{aligned} The closed-form solution for these coefficients is: \begin{aligned} a0 &= v0 \\ a1 &= d0 \\ a2 &= 3v1 - 3v0 - 2d0 - d1 \\ a3 &= 2v0 - 2v1 + d0 + d1 \end{aligned} These formulas assume the edge is parameterized such that x0=0 and x1=1. 2. Solve for Roots: Find all real roots of the equation p(x) = k, which is equivalent to finding roots of q(x) = a0 + a1 x + a2 x^2 + a3 x^3 - k = 0. 3. Select Isovertex: If multiple real roots exist within the edge interval, select the "middle" root to uniquely define the isovertex position. This choice is based on the observation that a zero-crossing edge must contain an odd number of roots, and the middle root best represents the primary crossing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cubichermiteinterpolation(v0, v1, d0, d1, k): """ Computes the isovertex position along an edge [0, 1] using cubic Hermite interpolation. Args: v0: Function value at x=0 v1: Function value at x=1 d0: Derivative estimate at x=0 d1: Derivative estimate at x=1 k: Target isovalue Returns: xstar: The position of the isovertex along the edge [0, 1] """ # Step 1: Compute cubic coefficients # p(x) = a0 + a1x + a2x^2 + a3x^3 a0 = v0 a1 = d0 a2 = 3 v1 - 3 v0 - 2 d0 - d1 a3 = 2 v0 - 2 v1 + d0 + d1 # Adjust for isovalue k: solve a0 + a1x + a2x^2 + a3x^3 = k # Equivalent to: a3x^3 + a2x^2 + a1x + (a0 - k) = 0 c3 = a3 c2 = a2 c1 = a1 c0 = a0 - k # Step 2: Find real roots of the cubic equation roots = solvecubicreal(c0, c1, c2, c3) # Step 3: Filter roots within the edge interval [0, 1] validroots = [r for r in roots if 0.0 <= r <= 1.0] if not validroots: # Fallback: If no roots found, return midpoint or handle error # This can happen if the cubic approximation fails to capture the crossing return 0.5 if len(validroots) == 1: return validroots[0] # Select the middle root if multiple roots exist validroots.sort() return validroots[len(validroots) // 2] def solvecubicreal(c0, c1, c2, c3): """ Solves c3x^3 + c2x^2 + c1x + c0 = 0 for real roots. Uses Cardano's method with robust sign handling for cube roots. """ if c3 == 0: if c2 == 0: if c1 == 0: return [] return [-c0 / c1] disc = c12 - 4 c2 c0 if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) return [(-c1 - sqrtdisc) / (2 c2), (-c1 + sqrtdisc) / (2 c2)] a = c2 / c3 b = c1 / c3 c = c0 / c3 p = b - a2 / 3 q = 2 a3 / 27 - a b / 3 + c disc = q2 / 4 + p3 / 27 roots = [] if disc > 0: # One real root uval = -q / 2 + math.sqrt(disc) vval = -q / 2 - math.sqrt(disc) u = math.copysign(abs(uval)(1/3), uval) v = math.copysign(abs(vval)(1/3), vval) roots.append(u + v - a / 3) elif disc == 0: # Multiple real roots if q == 0: roots.append(-a / 3) else: uval = -q / 2 u = math.copysign(abs(uval)(1/3), uval) roots.append(2 u - a / 3) roots.append(-u - a / 3) else: # Three distinct real roots r = math.sqrt(-p3 / 27) theta = math.acos(-q / (2 r)) m = 2 r(1/3) roots.append(m math.cos(theta / 3) - a / 3) roots.append(m math.cos((theta + 2 math.pi) / 3) - a / 3) roots.append(m math.cos((theta + 4 math.pi) / 3) - a / 3) return roots Parameters: Derivative Estimation: Derivatives f'(x0) and f'(x1) are often not directly available and must be approximated using finite difference methods. The quality of these estimates significantly impacts accuracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Roots: A cubic polynomial can have up to three real roots. The location and count of these roots may be sensitive to small perturbations in function coefficients. Root Selection: If multiple roots exist, the "middle" root is selected to ensure a unique isovertex position. Missing Roots: If the cubic polynomial p(x) does not have a root along the edge despite f(x) having a zero-crossing, the interpolation fails to capture the crossing. This can occur if the derivative estimates are poor or the function is highly non-linear. Kochanek-Bartels spline interpolation is an interpolation method used to generate smooth tour paths through a series of keyframes in Smokeview. Each interval is uniquely specified using a function value and a derivative at both endpoints, requiring four data values. Derivatives at endpoints are computed in terms of three parameters: bias, continuity, and tension. Each parameter ranges from -1 to 1 with a default value of 0, though bias and continuity are set to zero internally by Smokeview. A tension value of 1 results in a linear spline, removing smoothness. Unlike standard cubic splines, Kochanek-Bartels allows local control via bias, continuity, and tension parameters to adjust path smoothness or create abrupt changes. Solving the 4x4 system is constant time O(1) per edge due to the closed-form solution. Finding cubic roots is also O(1) but involves more arithmetic operations than linear interpolation. Memory complexity is O(1) additional memory per edge. The method provides higher accuracy than linear interpolation, especially for non-linear implicit functions. It is sensitive to derivative estimation errors. It may fail to find a root if the cubic approximation is poor. It should be used when high accuracy is required and derivative information (or good estimates) is available. Cubic Hermite Interpolation was proposed as a higher-order interpolation method to improve the accuracy of level crossing detection in isosurface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes. It builds on the concept of Hermite interpolation, which uses both function values and derivatives to construct a polynomial. The specific closed-form coefficients for the edge case are detailed in, while the broader context of high-order interpolation methods is discussed in. name: Edge-Crossing Error Approximation
head: Linear interpolation error estimation, Taylor series error approximation
body: This method estimates the positional error introduced by linear interpolation when determining the intersection of a scalar field with an isovalue on a grid edge. It leverages Taylor series expansion to bound the difference between the true root and the linear approximation without solving a linear system. Inputs: Scalar field values at grid vertices xi, x{i+1}, the isovalue k, and the linear crossing position \bar{x}^ computed via Linear Edge Intersection. Outputs: The estimated edge-crossing error e (or bound eb). Data Structures: The method requires the first-order divided differences U[i, i+1] and second-order divided differences U[i-1, i+1] and U[i, i+2]. U[i] = f(xi) U[i, i+1] = \frac{U[i+1] - U[i]}{x{i+1} - xi} U[i-1, i+1] = \frac{U[i, i+1] - U[i-1, i]}{x{i+1} - x{i-1}} U[i, i+2] = \frac{U[i+1, i+2] - U[i, i+1]}{x{i+2} - xi} Steps: 1. Compute the divided differences U[i, i+1], U[i-1, i+1], and U[i, i+2] using the scalar values at vertices x{i-1}, xi, x{i+1}, x{i+2}. 2. Calculate the maximum second-order divided difference magnitude: M = \max(|U[i-1, i+1]|, |U[i, i+2]|). 3. Compute the tighter vertex approximation error estimate e using the linear crossing position \bar{x}^: e = \frac{M}{U[i, i+1]} (\bar{x}^ - xi)(\bar{x}^ - x{i+1}) 4. (Optional) Compute the standard bound approximation eb for a conservative upper bound: eb = \frac{M}{U[i, i+1]} (xi - x{i+1})^2 Formulas: The theoretical error bound is derived from the Taylor series remainder: |x^ - \bar{x}^| \le \frac{\max{\xi \in [xi, x{i+1}]} |f''(\xi)|}{2 U[i, i+1]} (x^ - xi)(x^ - x{i+1}) where x^ is the true root and \xi is an unknown point in the interval. Since f''(\xi) and x^ are unknown, they are approximated as described in Steps 2-3. Parameters: Grid spacing: Implicit in xi coordinates. Typical performance: Error computation takes <1ms for the Tangle dataset, compared to seconds for isosurface comparison methods. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If U[i, i+1] \approx 0, the denominator becomes small, leading to large error estimates or numerical instability. This occurs when the scalar values at the edge endpoints are equal. Overestimation: The standard bound eb tends to significantly overestimate the error compared to the measured error. The vertex approximation e is much tighter. Hidden Features: Linear interpolation may miss isosurface patches (hidden features) entirely. This method estimates error on existing crossings but does not detect missing features; see Hidden Features Detection and Reconstruction for that capability. This variant detects and reconstructs isosurface patches (hidden features) not captured by standard linear interpolation by analyzing slopes on cell edges. Definition: Identifies cells where linear interpolation fails to capture topology changes due to opposite slopes surrounding a feature. Detection Condition: A hidden feature is detected in a cell if for any of its edges, two of the three slopes (divided differences) of neighboring edges have opposite signs. In 1D, this is indicated by U[i-1, i+1] \cdot U[i+1, i+2] < 0. Reconstruction: The detected cell is subdivided into smaller subcells using tri-cubic Lagrange polynomial interpolation. Linear interpolation for refinement does not recover these features. The Marching Cubes (or Squares) algorithm is then applied to each subcell. Pitfalls: Cell refinements lead to cracks in the reconstructed isosurface where refined cells meet unrefined neighbors. Crack-free techniques from adaptive mesh refinement are required to resolve these mismatches. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and divided difference calculations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per edge, requiring storage of local scalar values and divided differences. Performance: The approximated error computation is computationally efficient, taking less than 1ms for the Tangle example, whereas measuring error via isosurface comparison takes a few seconds. Strengths: Provides quick insight into isosurface quality without additional sampling or solving linear systems. The vertex approximation e is significantly closer to the measured error than the standard bound eb. Limitations: It only estimates error for existing crossings; it does not detect missing features (hidden features) on its own. The standard bound eb is a loose overestimate. The method originates from the analysis of interpolation errors in volume rendering and isosurface extraction. It builds on the observation that Taylor series expansion can estimate local function error. Previous work by Moller et al. used Taylor series for smooth filters and error estimation in volume data approximation. This specific application to edge-crossing error in Marching Cubes algorithms was proposed to visualize isosurface discrepancies and guide decisions on using higher-order interpolation or higher-resolution data. Estimation and Visualization of Isosurface Uncertainty from Linear and High-Order Interpolation Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00043v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Voxel selection via pick ray intersection
head: Basic picker, Pick ray intersection for voxel selection, Voxel Picking with Bresenham's Algorithm, Voxel Selecting
body: This method extracts spatial information from a simulation by mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D voxel indices, serving as a direct manipulation interface for tasks such as segmentation seed selection. It computes the corresponding seed voxel from user clicks and drags on the image plane. Inputs: Screen coordinates (x{screen}, y{screen}) from mouse clicks or drags. Orthographic camera projection parameters. Volume bounding box (rectangular solid). Outputs: 3D voxel index (i, j, k). Data Structures: Pick Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Volume Bounding Box: Axis-aligned box defining the volume extents. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Construct the pick ray from screen coordinates. For orthographic projection, map (x{screen}, y{screen}) to world space coordinates on the camera's near plane to determine ray origin \mathbf{o}. The ray direction \mathbf{d} is constant and aligned with the view direction. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Perform intersection tests similar to ray tracing to find the closest point of intersection between the pick ray and the volume's rectangular solid. 3. Voxel Selection: If an intersection exists, determine the voxel index (i, j, k) at the intersection point. This can be implemented using a modified Bresenham's Algorithm to traverse the voxel grid, or via direct coordinate conversion from the intersection point. 4. Return Index: Output the integer voxel coordinates (i, j, k). Formulas: Not given in the sources. Standard ray-box intersection and coordinate conversion are used. Parameters: Projection Type: Orthographic only. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Projection: The described implementation does not support perspective projections; it is limited to orthographic views. Out-of-Bounds: If the screen coordinate does not intersect the volume bounding box, no voxel is selected. Precision: Integer voxel indices must be clamped to valid grid ranges [0, Nx-1], [0, Ny-1], [0, Nz-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def selectvoxel(screenx, screeny, camera, volumebounds, voxelsize): # Step 1: Generate pick ray (Orthographic only) # Map screen coordinates to world space on near plane aspect = camera.viewportwidth / camera.viewportheight nx = (2.0 screenx / camera.viewportwidth) - 1.0 ny = (2.0 screeny / camera.viewportheight) - 1.0 viewwidth = camera.orthowidth viewheight = viewwidth / aspect rayorigin = camera.position + \ (nx viewwidth 0.5) camera.right + \ (ny viewheight 0.5) camera.up raydirection = -camera.forward # Orthographic ray direction is constant # Step 2: Ray-Box Intersection (Standard slab method) tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if abs(raydirection[axis]) < 1e-8: if rayorigin[axis] < volumebounds.min[axis] or rayorigin[axis] > volumebounds.max[axis]: return None else: invd = 1.0 / raydirection[axis] t1 = (volumebounds.min[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) invd t2 = (volumebounds.max[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) invd tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None if tmax < 0: return None # Use closest intersection point t = tmin if tmin > 0 else 0.0 intersectionpoint = rayorigin + t raydirection # Step 3: Convert intersection point to voxel index voxelx = math.floor((intersectionpoint.x - volumebounds.min.x) / voxelsize.x) voxely = math.floor((intersectionpoint.y - volumebounds.min.y) / voxelsize.y) voxelz = math.floor((intersectionpoint.z - volumebounds.min.z) / voxelsize.z) # Clamp to valid range voxelx = max(0, min(voxelx, volumebounds.resolution.x - 1)) voxely = max(0, min(voxely, volumebounds.resolution.y - 1)) voxelz = max(0, min(voxelz, volumebounds.resolution.z - 1)) return (voxelx, voxely, voxelz) Uses a pre-computed index texture for direct lookup from screen to voxel, avoiding runtime ray casting. Choose when performance is critical and memory allows for the index map. A CPU-side controller for voxel painting and erasing that uses DDA raycasting to determine brush position and normal on the voxel grid. Choose when dynamic editing of voxel data is required. Determines the 3D location within a simulation volume where a user intends to inject smoke or voxels based on 2D mouse input. Choose when the geometric intersection point is more important than the specific voxel index. Determines voxel coordinates intersected by a pick ray by transforming the intersection point into local space and identifying the hit face based on axis fractional offsets. Choose when working with voxelized meshes rather than regular grids. Time Complexity: O(1) for ray-box intersection and coordinate conversion. Bresenham's traversal is O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed, but typically only the entry voxel is needed for seed selection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Quick and reliable for orthographic views. Strengths: Intuitive user interface for segmentation; simple implementation for orthographic projections. Limitations: Does not support perspective projections. Accuracy depends on voxel grid alignment. The method originated in the context of volume visualization and segmentation applications, specifically the SIV system. It was also independently implemented in homebrew voxel engines for real-time simulation interaction. The technique leverages the regular structure of voxel grids to simplify ray-primitive intersection, often employing Bresenham's algorithm for grid traversal. It is used in medical imaging and scientific visualization for seed point selection during isosurface segmentation. name: Reverse Index Map for Voxel Location
head: P->V Mapping
body: The Reverse Index Map (P->V) is a technique used to determine the 3D voxel location in volume coordinates from a 2D fragment location in the framebuffer and a current slice z-offset. It serves as the inverse of the forward mapping used during texture sampling, enabling direct manipulation and segmentation by linking screen pixels to volumetric data. Inputs: 1. Fragment location in the framebuffer (x{fb}, y{fb}). 2. Current slice z-offset (z{slice}). Outputs: 1. Voxel location in volume coordinates (V = (xv, yv, zv)). Data Structures: Reverse Index Texture: A 2D texture mapping packed coordinates (P) to volume coordinates (V). The texture stores the 3D voxel coordinates corresponding to each 2D screen position. The layout typically stores xv, yv, zv as components (e.g., RGBA or RGB with one component unused or packed) in the texture units. Steps: 1. Retrieve the fragment's 2D coordinates (x{fb}, y{fb}) from the framebuffer. 2. Combine these coordinates with the current slice z-offset to form the packed coordinate P. In the context of slice-based rendering, P typically represents the 2D screen position (x{fb}, y{fb}) which indexes into the Reverse Index Texture. 3. Sample the Reverse Index Texture at P to retrieve the volume coordinates V. V = \text{TextureLookup}(\text{ReverseIndexTexture}, P) 4. Use V as the seed voxel for subsequent ray integration or segmentation operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxellocation(fragmentx, fragmenty, slicezoffset, reverseindextexture): """ Determines the 3D voxel location from 2D framebuffer coordinates. Args: fragmentx (int): X coordinate in the framebuffer. fragmenty (int): Y coordinate in the framebuffer. slicezoffset (float): The current z-offset for the slice being rendered. reverseindextexture (Texture): A 2D texture mapping 2D screen coords to 3D volume coords. Returns: tuple: (xv, yv, zv) volume coordinates. """ # Packed coordinates P are derived from the fragment location. # In slice-based rendering, P typically corresponds to (fragmentx, fragmenty). p = (fragmentx, fragmenty) # Sample the reverse index texture to get volume coordinates V. # The texture stores (xv, yv, zv) for each 2D position. v = reverseindextexture[p] # v is expected to be a vector (xv, yv, zv). return v Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the voxel location depends on the resolution of the Reverse Index Texture. Boundaries: Fragments outside the volume bounds will return invalid or undefined coordinates. Slice Offset: The slice z-offset must be consistent with the data used to generate the Reverse Index Texture. A technique used during ray integration to map volume coordinates to packed texture coordinates via a forward mapping index texture (V \to P). It is the inverse of the Reverse Index Map. While the Reverse Index Map is used for interaction (screen to volume), the Forward Index Map is used for sampling (volume to texture). The layout is a texture mapping volume coordinates (V) to packed texture coordinates (P). A method to map 2D mouse clicks on a Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) image to 3D voxel coordinates by maintaining a depth buffer of the current projection. Unlike the Reverse Index Map which uses a pre-computed texture, this method maintains a 2D buffer Z(i, j) = (x, y, z) that records the voxel position for each projected MIP value or surface color. When a user selects a point [i, j] in the MIP, the appropriate voxel address (x, y, z) is looked up from the buffer. This is used to redefine slice positions in orthogonal viewers or provide initial points for analysis. To prevent depth ambiguity (where the projected value comes from brighter values in front of or behind the vessel of interest), a limited MIP is used where only voxels between two planes z{min} and z{max} parallel to the view plane are projected. The depth range (z{max} - z{min}) should be reduced to about the size of the voxel dimensionality (e.g., 1mm) to generate oblique slices. The technique is part of an approach to interleaving rendering and interaction, where the rendering is updated incrementally to allow user interaction. The Reverse Index Map was introduced in the context of Local Ambient Occlusion in Direct Volume Rendering by Hernell et al.. It was developed to support interactive rendering by allowing rapid determination of voxel locations from fragment positions. The technique is part of a broader approach to interleaving rendering and interaction, where the rendering is updated incrementally to allow user interaction. The Forward Index Map is used in conjunction with the Reverse Index Map to handle texture indirection during ray integration. The MIP Depth Buffer Lookup method was developed in the context of the Angiotool for interactive visualization of MRI vector and tensor fields. name: BrushController
head: BrushController::DDAVoxelRaycast, BrushController::UpdateFromMouse
body: A CPU-side controller for voxel painting and erasing that uses Digital Differential Analysis (DDA) raycasting to determine brush position and normal on the voxel grid, with a fallback to ray-AABB intersection if voxel data is unavailable. It solves the problem of translating 2D user input into precise 3D spatial edits within a discrete volumetric representation. Unlike static voxelization, it supports dynamic editing where the system computes the adjacent empty voxel position for addition or the current voxel position for removal based on the raycast hit normal. It differs from Volume Painting for Selection by directly modifying the underlying voxel data structure rather than generating a selection mask for later processing. Inputs: Camera state: cameraPos (vec3), cameraForward (vec3), cameraRight (vec3), cameraUp (vec3). Viewport parameters: fov (field of view in radians), aspectRatio (width/height). Input state: mouseNDC (vec2, range [-1, 1]), leftButtonDown (bool), rightButtonDown (bool), scrollDelta (float). Voxel grid data: voxelGridData (pointer/struct), voxelGridSize (vec3, uint32t), gridMin (vec3), gridMax (vec3). Constants: maxDist (1024.0f), maxSteps (512), epsilon (1e-6f). Outputs: mbrushPosition (vec3): World-space center of the brush. misPainting (bool): True if left mouse button is down. misErasing (bool): True if right mouse button is down. mradius (float): Brush radius. mmaterial (uint32t): Material ID to paint (0 for erase/air). Data Structures: The BrushConstants struct is used to pass state to shaders or internal logic. Its layout is: positionX: float positionY: float positionZ: float radius: float material: uint32t mode: uint32t shape: uint32t strength: float gridSizeX: uint32t gridSizeY: uint32t gridSizeZ: uint32t seed: uint32t. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Brush State: Set default values: mbrushPosition = (64.0f, 64.0f, 64.0f), mmaterial = 3 (Stone), mradius = 5.0f, mmode = Paint, mshape = Sphere. 2. Update Input State: Set misPainting = leftButtonDown and misErasing = rightButtonDown. 3. Adjust Radius: If scrollDelta != 0.0f, update radius: mradius = mradius + scrollDelta. 4. Calculate Ray Direction: Compute the ray direction in world space from Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): \text{tanHalfFov} = \tan(\text{fov} \times 0.5f) \text{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\text{cameraForward} + \text{cameraRight} \times \text{mouseNDC}.x \times \text{tanHalfFov} \times \text{aspectRatio} + \text{cameraUp} \times \text{mouseNDC}.y \times \text{tanHalfFov}). 5. Raycast and Determine Target Voxel: Check if voxelGridData is not null and voxelGridSize > 0. Case A: Voxel Data Available (DDA Raycast). Perform a DDA voxel traversal from cameraPos along rayDir. Calculate inverse ray direction components. If abs(rayDir.x) < epsilon, use 1e6f instead of 1/rayDir.x to prevent division by zero. Initialize sideDist (distance to next grid boundary) and deltaDist (distance to cross one voxel) based on ray direction and voxel size. Iterate up to maxSteps: 1. Add a small epsilon (1e-4f) to startPos before flooring to voxelPos to handle precision issues at grid boundaries. 2. Query voxel material at voxelPos. 3. If material is non-zero (hit): Set hitVoxel = voxelPos. Determine hitNormal based on the face crossed (e.g., if crossing X face, normal is (-step.x, 0, 0)). Break loop. 4. Advance ray to next voxel: Compare sideDist components to find the smallest distance. Add deltaDist of the smallest component to sideDist. Increment voxelPos in the corresponding axis by step (1 or -1). Update hitNormal for the new face. 5. If dist > maxDist, break loop. Determine targetVoxel: If erasing (misErasing): targetVoxel = hitVoxel. If painting (misPainting): targetVoxel = hitVoxel + hitNormal. Case B: Voxel Data Unavailable (Fallback). Perform Ray-Box Intersection with the grid bounds. If hit: Set t = max(tMin, 0.0f) + 10.0f. Calculate hitPos = cameraPos + rayDir t. Clamp hitPos to grid bounds. Set targetVoxel = hitPos. 6. Set Brush Position: Set mbrushPosition = targetVoxel + (0.5f, 0.5f, 0.5f). Clamp mbrushPosition to [mgridMin + 0.5f, mgridMax - 0.5f]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. startpos.x) invray.x, (voxelpos.y + (1.0 if raydir.y > 0 else 0.0) - startpos.y) invray.y, (voxelpos.z + (1.0 if raydir.z > 0 else 0.0) - startpos.z) invray.z) deltadist = abs(invray) step = vec3( 1.0 if raydir.x > 0 else -1.0, 1.0 if raydir.y > 0 else -1.0, 1.0 if raydir.z > 0 else -1.0) hitvoxel = vec3(0) hitnormal = vec3(0) hit = False dist = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): voxel = getvoxelat(voxelpos, voxelgriddata, voxelgridsize) materialval = getmaterialfromvoxel(voxel) if materialval != 0: hitvoxel = voxelpos hit = True break if sidedist.x < sidedist.y: if sidedist.x < sidedist.z: sidedist.x += deltadist.x voxelpos.x += step.x hitnormal = vec3(-step.x, 0, 0) dist += deltadist.x else: sidedist.z += deltadist.z voxelpos.z += step.z hitnormal = vec3(0, 0, -step.z) dist += deltadist.z else: if sidedist.y < sidedist.z: sidedist.y += deltadist.y voxelpos.y += step.y hitnormal = vec3(0, -step.y, 0) dist += deltadist.y else: sidedist.z += deltadist.z voxelpos.z += step.z hitnormal = vec3(0, 0, -step.z) dist += deltadist.z if dist > maxdist: break if hit: if iserasing: targetvoxel = hitvoxel else: targetvoxel = hitvoxel + hitnormal else: tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(camerapos, raydir, gridmin, gridmax) if tmin is not None: t = max(tmin, 0.0) + 10.0 hitpos = camerapos + raydir t hitpos = clamp(hitpos, gridmin, gridmax) targetvoxel = hitpos brushpos = targetvoxel + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) brushpos = clamp(brushpos, gridmin + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), gridmax - body: This method enables real-time modification of a voxel grid by casting rays from screen-space mouse coordinates into the 3D world to determine interaction points. It solves the problem of translating 2D user input into precise 3D spatial edits (addition or removal of voxels) within a discrete volumetric representation. Inputs: rayOrigin: World-space origin of the pick ray, derived from camera position and screen coordinates. rayDirection: Direction vector of the pick ray. brushsize: Radius of the spherical brush mask in voxel units. brushvoxel: The voxel type/color to place; 0 indicates break/destroy mode. add: Boolean flag; true for adding voxels, false for removing them. Outputs: Modified voxel grid state (voxels added or removed). Updated hover state for visual feedback. Data Structures: Chunk: A block of voxels. Contains locX, locY, locZ (chunk coordinates) and CHUNKSIZE (dimension). Voxel Data: Accessed via a 3D array within a chunk: voxelData[x][y][z]. Hit Info: hitPosition (world coordinates of intersection), hitNormal (surface normal at intersection). Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Compute rayOrigin and rayDirection from the current mouse position and camera projection/view matrices. 2. Raycasting for Hit: Cast the ray into the voxel world to find the first solid voxel or surface. If add is true, the raycast seeks an empty space adjacent to a solid voxel. If add is false, the raycast seeks an existing solid voxel to remove. The raycast returns hitPosition and hitNormal. 3. Hit Adjustment: If add is true, offset hitPosition by the hitNormal to ensure the new voxel is placed outside the existing geometry (e.g., hitPosition += hitNormal 0.01f). 4. Brush Application: Apply a spherical brush mask centered at hitPosition with radius brushsize. Iterate over voxels within the bounding box of the sphere. For each voxel, check if it lies within the sphere distance from hitPosition. If brushvoxel is non-zero, set the voxel to brushvoxel. If brushvoxel is zero, destroy the voxel. 5. State Update: Refresh the hover state to reflect the modification. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelgridedit(rayorigin, raydirection, add, brushsize, brushvoxel, voxelgrid, chunks): """ Edit voxel grid using raycasting and spherical brush. Args: rayorigin: vec3, world space origin of the ray raydirection: vec3, direction of the ray add: bool, True to add voxels, False to remove brushsize: float, radius of the brush in voxel units brushvoxel: int, voxel type to place (0 for break) voxelgrid: 3D array of voxel states chunks: list of chunk objects with locX, locY, locZ, CHUNKSIZE """ hitposition, hitnormal = raycastvoxelgrid(rayorigin, raydirection, add, voxelgrid, chunks) if hitposition is None: return if add: hitposition = hitposition + hitnormal 0.01 minx = int(hitposition.x - brushsize) maxx = int(hitposition.x + brushsize) miny = int(hitposition.y - brushsize) maxy = int(hitposition.y + brushsize) minz = int(hitposition.z - brushsize) maxz = int(hitposition.z + brushsize) for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): distsq = (x - hitposition.x)2 + (y - hitposition.y)2 + (z - hitposition.z)2 if distsq <= brushsize2: if brushvoxel != 0: voxelgrid[x][y][z] = brushvoxel else: voxelgrid[x][y][z] = 0 updatehoveredvoxel(rayorigin, raydirection) def raycastvoxelgrid(rayorigin, raydirection, add, voxelgrid, chunks): """ March ray to find hit position and normal. Uses fixed-step advancement to avoid division by zero on axis-aligned rays. """ lastpos = None for in range(100): rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection 0.2 chunk = chunks[int(rayorigin.x / 16)][int(rayorigin.y / 16)][int(rayorigin.z / 16)] localpos = vec3( rayorigin.x - chunk.locX chunk.CHUNKSIZE, rayorigin.y - chunk.locY chunk.CHUNKSIZE, rayorigin.z - chunk.locZ chunk.CHUNKSIZE) if localpos == lastpos: continue lastpos = localpos if -1 < localpos.x < chunk.CHUNKSIZE and \ -1 < localpos.y < chunk.CHUNKSIZE and \ -1 < localpos.z < chunk.CHUNKSIZE: voxel = voxelgrid[localpos.x][localpos.y][localpos.z] if voxel and not add: return localpos, vec3(0, 1, 0) if not voxel and add: return localpos, vec3(0, 1, 0) return None, None def updatehoveredvoxel(origin, direction): """Refreshes hover state after modification.""" pass Parameters: brushsize: Radius of the brush. brushvoxel: Voxel type to place; 0 for break. add: Boolean flag equivalent to BuildOrBreak. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point inaccuracies in raycasting may cause missed voxels or incorrect normals. Using a small offset (0.01f) when adding helps avoid placing voxels inside existing geometry. Boundaries: Ensure voxel coordinates are within valid chunk bounds before access. Degenerate Input: If the ray does not hit any voxel, the edit operation should be skipped. Modifies voxel density values in a local radius around a raycast hit point and triggers chunk regeneration. Unlike static voxelization, this approach supports real-time editing where the user selects a target face on an existing voxel, and the system computes the adjacent empty voxel position for addition or the current voxel position for removal. Performance: Real-time editing is feasible with efficient raycasting and spatial partitioning (e.g., chunks, octrees). Strengths: Intuitive user interaction and real-time feedback. Limitations: Performance may degrade with very large brush sizes or complex scenes without spatial acceleration structures. name: Raycast-based Voxel Editing
head: Chunk Noise Modification, Marching Cubes Voxel Sculpting
body: This method modifies voxel density values in a local radius around a raycast hit point and triggers chunk regeneration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera screen coordinates (mouse position), current voxel chunk grid state, edit parameters (radius, edit value). Output: Modified voxel density values in affected chunks, regenerated mesh geometry for those chunks. Data Structures: Chunk Grid: A 3D array of ChunkMatrix objects indexed by global chunk coordinates. Hit Point: A Vector3 position in world space where the ray intersects a mesh. Chunk Indices: A 3-tuple (cx, cy, cz) identifying the chunk containing the hit point, computed via GetCurrentChunkFromPos. Local Voxel Indices: A 3-tuple (vx, vy, vz) identifying the specific voxel within the chunk, computed via GetCurrentCubeInChunkFromPos. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast a ray from the camera through the mouse screen position with a maximum distance of 20 units. 2. Hit Validation: Check if the ray hits a transform tagged "Mesh". 3. Position Conversion: Extract the world-space hit point and compute the global chunk indices using GetCurrentChunkFromPos(hitPos). 4. Local Index Calculation: Compute the local voxel indices within the identified chunk using GetCurrentCubeInChunkFromPos(hitPos). 5. Direction Determination: Determine the edit direction: dir = 1 for left mouse button (add), dir = -1 for right mouse button (subtract). 6. Voxel Modification: Call SetNoiseValues on the hit chunk, passing the local voxel indices, dir editValue, and radius to modify noise in the affected area. 7. Mesh Regeneration: Call UpdateSurroundingChunks with the hit chunk's global indices to regenerate affected meshes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def handlevoxeledit(screenpos, camera, chunks, editvalue, radius, mousebutton, chunksize, voxelsize): # Step 1: Cast ray rayorigin, raydirection = computecameraray(screenpos, camera) maxdistance = 20.0 # Standard ray-mesh intersection; returns hit dict or None hit = castraytomesh(rayorigin, raydirection, maxdistance) # Step 2: Hit validation if hit is None or hit.get("tag") != "Mesh": return hitpos = hit["point"] # Step 3: Position to chunk indices cx = int(hitpos[0] // chunksize) cy = int(hitpos[1] // chunksize) cz = int(hitpos[2] // chunksize) # Step 4: Position to local voxel indices vx = int(((hitpos[0] - cx chunksize) / voxelsize) % chunksize) vy = int(((hitpos[1] - cy chunksize) / voxelsize) % chunksize) vz = int(((hitpos[2] - cz chunksize) / voxelsize) % chunksize) # Step 5: Direction dir = 1 if mousebutton == "left" else -1 # Step 6: Modify voxels hitchunk = chunks[cx, cy, cz] setnoisevalues(hitchunk, vx, vy, vz, dir editvalue, radius, voxelsize) # Step 7: Regenerate meshes updatesurroundingchunks(chunks, cx, cy, cz) def computecameraray(screenpos, camera): ndcx = (2.0 screenpos[0] / camera.width) - 1.0 ndcy = (2.0 screenpos[1] / camera.height) - 1.0 raydir = [ndcx camera.aspect, ndcy, -1.0] raydir = normalize(raydir) return camera.position, raydir def setnoisevalues(chunk, centervx, centervy, centervz, value, radius, voxelsize): halfr = int(radius / voxelsize) for dx in range(-halfr, halfr + 1): for dy in range(-halfr, halfr + 1): for dz in range(-halfr, halfr + 1): x, y, z = centervx + dx, centervy + dy, centervz + dz if not (0 <= x < chunk.width and 0 <= y < chunk.height and 0 <= z < chunk.depth): continue distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq <= (radius / voxelsize) 2: chunk.noisematrix[x, y, z] += value def updatesurroundingchunks(chunks, cx, cy, cz): for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): nx, ny, nz = cx + dx, cy + dy, cz + dz if 0 <= nx < len(chunks) and 0 <= ny < len(chunks[0]) and 0 <= nz < len(chunks[0][0]): # Standard mesh regeneration from noise matrix regeneratemesh(chunks[nx, ny, nz]) Parameters: Max Ray Distance: 20 units. Edit Value: Not given in the sources. Typical values depend on density scale. Radius: Not given in the sources. Typical values are 1-5 voxels. Chunk Size & Voxel Size: Not given in the sources. Values depend on the underlying grid layout. Edge Cases: Ray Miss: If the ray does not hit a "Mesh" tagged object, the function returns immediately without modifying data. Chunk Boundaries: GetCurrentCubeInChunkFromPos must correctly handle voxels on chunk boundaries using modulo arithmetic. Precision: Floating-point precision in hit.point and subsequent index calculations can lead to jitter if not handled carefully. Rounding or epsilon checks may be needed. Time Complexity: Raycasting is O(1) per interaction. Voxel modification is O(r^3) where r is the brush radius. Mesh regeneration is O(v) where v is the number of voxels in the affected chunk and its immediate neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for the edit operation, assuming in-place modification of the chunk's noise matrix. Strengths: Interactive, immediate feedback. Simple to implement. Limitations: Limited to local edits. Performance may degrade if many chunks are regenerated simultaneously. When to Use: Interactive voxel sculpting tools. When Not to Use: Large-scale, non-interactive terrain generation. This method is described in an unofficial voxel sculpting implementation that modifies noise density values based on raycast hits and regenerates chunks. name: Voxel Grid Editing (Add/Remove)
head: Interactive voxel manipulation, Raycast-based Voxel Interaction, Screen-to-Voxel Mapping, Voxel Click Handling, Voxel Interaction and Grid Snapping
body: This method enables dynamic modification of a voxel grid by adding or removing individual voxels at specific positions determined by raycasting from screen-space mouse input. It solves the problem of translating 2D user interaction into 3D volumetric changes, allowing for real-time sculpting or construction in voxel-based environments. Unlike static voxelization tools, this approach focuses on interactive feedback loops where mesh regeneration or spatial index updates occur immediately after a click. It differs from Raycast-based Voxel Editing by emphasizing the specific logic of grid snapping and face-normal determination for single-voxel operations rather than bulk brush strokes. Inputs: Screen-space mouse coordinates (pixel position). Camera projection matrix and view direction. Current voxel grid data structure (Octree or Voxel Array). Material/type identifier for new voxels. Outputs: Modified voxel grid (added/removed voxel). Updated visual representation (regenerated mesh or updated node visibility). The implementation uses specific structures to track interaction state and grid topology. 1. Hover Info / Hit State (C++/General) Stores the result of the raycast before modification. hasHit (bool): True if the ray intersected a valid voxel face. node (Pointer/Reference): Reference to the octree node or voxel object hit. position (vec3): The 3D world coordinate of the intersection point. normal (vec3): The surface normal of the hit face, indicating the direction of the click relative to the voxel. depth (int): The octree depth of the hit node. Default Constructor: hasHit = false, node = nullptr, depth = 0. 2. Player Interaction Component State (Unity/C#) Holds persistent state for the interaction system. tree (Octree): The underlying spatial data structure. targetVoxelCursor (GameObject): Visual indicator for the selected voxel. normalCursor (GameObject): Visual indicator for the face normal. hitMask (LayerMask): Physics layer mask to restrict raycasting to voxel objects. blockBreak (ParticleSystem): Visual effect for removal. hitVoxelPosition (Vector3): The grid position of the voxel currently under the cursor. neighborVoxelPosition (Vector3): The grid position of the adjacent voxel in the direction of the normal. 1. Ray Generation: Convert the screen-space mouse position (u, v) into a 3D ray originating from the camera. This is typically done using the camera's ScreenPointToRay function, which computes the ray origin and direction based on the viewport and projection matrix. Input: Mouse pixel coordinates (u, v). Output: Ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera position and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. 2. Physics Raycast: Cast the generated ray into the scene against the voxel geometry. Perform a raycast with a maximum distance of 3.0 units in Unity examples. Filter results using a layer mask to ignore non-voxel objects. If no hit occurs, terminate the operation. If a hit occurs, retrieve the hit point \mathbf{p}{hit} and the face normal \mathbf{n} from the collision data. 3. Grid Snapping (Hit Voxel Determination): Determine the integer grid coordinates of the voxel that was physically hit. The hit point \mathbf{p}{hit} is in world space. Snap to the grid center of the hit voxel using the centered convention. Formula: \mathbf{v}{hit} = \lfloor \mathbf{p}{hit} - \mathbf{n} \times 0.5 \rfloor + 0.5 Where \lfloor \cdot \rfloor is the component-wise floor function. 4. Target Voxel Calculation (Neighbor Determination): Determine the position of the voxel to be added or removed based on the face normal. The normal \mathbf{n} points out of the hit voxel face. The adjacent voxel position \mathbf{v}{adj} is calculated by adding the normal vector to the hit voxel's position. Formula: \mathbf{v}{adj} = \mathbf{v}{hit} + \mathbf{n}. This \mathbf{v}{adj} represents the empty space adjacent to the hit face, which is the target for addition, or the hit voxel itself for removal, depending on the mode. 5. Operation Execution: Perform the add or remove action based on user input (e.g., Left Click vs. Right Click, or Mode flags). Removal Mode: Target: The hit voxel \mathbf{v}{hit}. Action: Remove the voxel from the octree/grid at \mathbf{v}{hit}. Trigger: tree.RemoveVoxel(vhit). Addition Mode: Target: The adjacent voxel \mathbf{v}{adj}. Action: Insert a new voxel into the octree/grid at \mathbf{v}{adj} with the current material/type. Trigger: tree.InsertVoxel(vadj, material). Note on Inverted Worlds: Some implementations swap the target logic if the world coordinate system is inverted, calling Click(neighbor, hit, 0, 1) for removal and Click(hit, neighbor, 1, 0) for addition. 6. Feedback and Regeneration: Update visual cursors to reflect the new hit state. Play particle effects (e.g., block break) if a voxel was removed. Trigger mesh regeneration or spatial index update. In mesh-based renderers: Call the mesh builder function to reconstruct the geometry from the modified grid. In octree-based renderers: Call CubicQuery or similar neighbor update functions to ensure connectivity and visibility are correct. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def handlevoxeledit(mousepos, camera, voxeltree, editmode, button): """ Handles voxel addition or removal based on mouse click. Args: mousepos: (x, y) screen coordinates. camera: Camera object with screenpointtoray method. voxeltree: Octree or VoxelGrid instance. editmode: Boolean, True for Edit/Add-Remove mode, False for Navigation. button: Integer, 0 for left click, 2 for right click. Returns: None """ if not editmode: return # Step 1: Ray Generation rayorigin, raydirection = camera.screenpointtoray(mousepos) # Step 2: Physics Raycast hit = traceray(rayorigin, raydirection, maxdistance=3.0, layermask=VOXELLAYER) if hit is None: return hitpoint = hit.point hitnormal = hit.normal # Step 3: Grid Snapping # Determine the voxel that was physically hit using centered convention snappedpoint = hitpoint - (hitnormal 0.5) hitvoxelcoords = floorvector(snappedpoint) + 0.5 # Step 4: Target Voxel Calculation # The adjacent voxel is in the direction of the normal targetvoxelcoords = hitvoxelcoords + hitnormal # Step 5: Operation Execution if button == 0: # Remove the hit voxel voxeltree.removevoxel(hitvoxelcoords) playparticleeffect(hitvoxelcoords, type="BREAK") elif button == 2: # Add voxel to the adjacent position voxeltree.insertvoxel(targetvoxelcoords, currentmaterial) playparticleeffect(targetvoxelcoords, type="PLACE") # Step 6: Feedback and Regeneration updatecursors(hitvoxelcoords, targetvoxelcoords) voxeltree.rebuildmeshorupdateneighbors() def floorvector(v): """Component-wise floor function for vector.""" return (int(v[0]), int(v[1]), int(v[2])) def traceray(origin, direction, maxdistance, layermask): """Simulates a physics raycast returning a hit dict or None.""" # Standard raycast implementation stub pass def updatecursors(hitpos, neighborpos): """Updates visual cursor positions.""" pass def playparticleeffect(pos, type): """Plays a particle system at the given position.""" pass VOXELLAYER = 1 currentmaterial = "default" Ray Distance: The maximum distance for the raycast is set to 3.0 units in Unity implementations. Grid Alignment: The offset of 0.5 in the snapping formula assumes voxel centers are at integer + 0.5 coordinates. Precision: Floating-point errors in raycast hit points can cause jitter when snapping. Degenerate Input: If the ray hits an edge or vertex shared by multiple voxels, the normal may be ambiguous. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Real-time interaction is feasible if mesh regeneration is optimized. Full mesh rebuilds on every click can cause frame drops in large scenes. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Single-voxel granularity can be slow for large-scale edits. This method originated from the need for interactive voxel editors in game development and 3D modeling tools. Early implementations in Unity-based voxel games (e.g., VoxelCaverns) popularized the "screen-to-raycast-to-grid" pattern for player interaction. It is widely used in voxel-based sandbox games (e.g., Minecraft clones), 3D model voxelization tools, and procedural generation editors. The technique bridges the gap between 2D screen input and 3D volumetric data, enabling real-time sculpting and construction.
