name: 3D Ring Visibility & Occlusion Test
head: ring depth test, ring raster validation
body: The 3D Ring Visibility & Occlusion Test is a screen-space rasterization technique that projects 3D ring boundary segments to screen space, computes depth via inverse-linear interpolation, and validates visibility against a voxel depth buffer. It differs from sibling methods like Change of Integration Variable for Boundary Segments by operating in screen space using rasterization primitives rather than analytical integration in world space. Inputs: Ring center \mathbf{c}, eye position \mathbf{e}, radius r, near plane distance n, focal length f, screen width w, screen height h, camera basis vectors \mathbf{right}, \mathbf{up}, \mathbf{forward}, and a voxel depth buffer. Outputs: Updated voxel masks (support, visible, definite, possible, edge, contact). Data Structures: The ring is discretized into 3 orientations (indices 0..2) and 32 sub-segments per orientation (indices 0..31). Each sub-segment connects two consecutive angular positions. Steps: 1. Iterate ring index k \in \{0, 1, 2\} and segment index i \in \{0, \dots, 31\}. 2. Compute angle \theta = i \times 0.1963495408. 3. Compute displacement vectors \mathbf{\delta}1 and \mathbf{\delta}2 for angles \theta and \theta + 0.1963495408 using the ring-specific layout: (c, s, 0), (c, 0, s), or (0, c, s) where c = r \cos(\theta), s = r \sin(\theta). 4. Compute world direction vectors \mathbf{d}1 = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{\delta}1 - \mathbf{e} and \mathbf{d}2 = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{\delta}2 - \mathbf{e}. 5. Project to camera space: \mathbf{a} = [\mathbf{d}1 \cdot \mathbf{right}, \mathbf{d}1 \cdot \mathbf{up}, \mathbf{d}1 \cdot \mathbf{forward}] and \mathbf{b} = [\mathbf{d}2 \cdot \mathbf{right}, \mathbf{d}2 \cdot \mathbf{up}, \mathbf{d}2 \cdot \mathbf{forward}]. 6. If \max(az, bz) < n, skip the segment. 7. If \min(az, bz) < n, clip the segment to the near plane by interpolating the cut point. 8. Project endpoints to screen coordinates: px = \frac{w}{2} + f \frac{ax}{az}, py = \frac{h}{2} - f \frac{ay}{az} (and similarly for q from \mathbf{b}). 9. Compute bounding box [x{\min}, x{\max}] \times [y{\min}, y{\max}] covering the segment. 10. For each pixel (xx, yy) in the bounding box: Compute screen-space delta \Delta = (qx - px, qy - py) and squared length L^2 = \Deltax^2 + \Deltay^2. If L^2 < 10^{-6}, skip the pixel. Compute projection parameter t = \text{clip}\left( \frac{(xx + 0.5 - px)\Deltax + (yy + 0.5 - py)\Deltay}{L^2}, 0, 1 \right). Compute 2D distance from pixel center to the segment. If distance \le 0.75, mark as stroke. 11. Compute depth z at parameter t using inverse-linear interpolation: z = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{az} + t \left(\frac{1}{bz} - \frac{1}{az}\right)}. 12. Compute normalized depth: \text{depth} = 1 - \frac{n}{\max(n, z - 0.0001)}. 13. Update voxel masks based on stroke status and computed depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ringvisibilitytest(center, eye, radius, near, focal, width, height, right, up, forward): anglestep = 0.1963495408 epsilon = 0.0001 for ringidx in range(3): for segidx in range(32): angle = segidx anglestep c1 = radius math.cos(angle) s1 = radius math.sin(angle) c2 = radius math.cos(angle + anglestep) s2 = radius math.sin(angle + anglestep) if ringidx == 0: delta1 = (c1, s1, 0) delta2 = (c2, s2, 0) elif ringidx == 1: delta1 = (c1, 0, s1) delta2 = (c2, 0, s2) else: delta1 = (0, c1, s1) delta2 = (0, c2, s2) d1 = (center[0] + delta1[0] - eye[0], center[1] + delta1[1] - eye[1], center[2] + delta1[2] - eye[2]) d2 = (center[0] + delta2[0] - eye[0], center[1] + delta2[1] - eye[1], center[2] + delta2[2] - eye[2]) a = (d1[0]right[0] + d1[1]right[1] + d1[2]right[2], d1[0]up[0] + d1[1]up[1] + d1[2]up[2], d1[0]forward[0] + d1[1]forward[1] + d1[2]forward[2]) b = (d2[0]right[0] + d2[1]right[1] + d2[2]right[2], d2[0]up[0] + d2[1]up[1] + d2[2]up[2], d2[0]forward[0] + d2[1]forward[1] + d2[2]forward[2]) if max(a[2], b[2]) < near: continue if min(a[2], b[2]) < near: tclip = (near - a[2]) / (b[2] - a[2]) a = (a[0] + tclip (b[0] - a[0]), a[1] + tclip (b[1] - a[1]), near) px = width / 2.0 + focal a[0] / a[2] py = height / 2.0 - focal a[1] / a[2] qx = width / 2.0 + focal b[0] / b[2] qy = height / 2.0 - focal b[1] / b[2] xmin, xmax = int(math.floor(min(px, qx))), int(math.ceil(max(px, qx))) ymin, ymax = int(math.floor(min(py, qy))), int(math.ceil(max(py, qy))) dx = qx - px dy = qy - py squared = dx dx + dy dy if squared < 1e-6: continue for xx in range(xmin, xmax + 1): for yy in range(ymin, ymax + 1): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, ((xx + 0.5 - px) dx + (yy + 0.5 - py) dy) / squared)) projx = px + t dx projy = py + t dy dist = math.sqrt((xx + 0.5 - projx)2 + (yy + 0.5 - projy)2) if dist <= 0.75: z = 1.0 / (1.0 / a[2] + t (1.0 / b[2] - 1.0 / a[2])) depth = 1.0 - near / max(near, z - epsilon) # Update masks (support, visible, definite, possible, edge, contact) based on depth and stroke status Pitfalls: Degenerate segments (squared length < 10^{-6}) are skipped. Near clipping is handled by checking min/max z against the near plane and interpolating the cut point. Division by zero in depth calculation is avoided by \max(\text{near}, \dots). Not given in the sources. The method originates from the bend-voxel rendering pipeline. aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: 4D Convex Polytope Line Segment Culling
head: 4D Line Clipping, 4D Line Culling, 4D Wireframe Occlusion Culling, Block4d Algorithm, Hyperplane Clipping for 4D
body: This algorithm culls wireframe line segments in 4D space that are occluded by the faces of a convex 4D polytope when the camera is located outside the polytope. It solves the occlusion detection problem in non-rasterized 4D rendering where a depth buffer is unavailable by constructing an occlusion cone from the polytope's front-facing hyperplanes to determine which parts of a line segment remain visible. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling 4D geometric topology (identifying turning edges and conical occlusion regions) rather than relying on coordinate-aligned simplifications or integration variable changes. Inputs: A 4D line segment defined by endpoints A and B, parameterized by t \in [0, 1]. A convex 4D polytope defined by its (n-1)-dimensional faces (hyperplanes) and their outward-pointing normals. Camera position C. Outputs: A list of valid sub-segments representing the visible portions of the input segment. Data Structures: Hyperplane Array P: An array of hyperplanes forming the occlusion cone. Each hyperplane p is defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n}p and a scalar dp such that a point \mathbf{x} is inside (unoccluded side) if \mathbf{n}p \cdot \mathbf{x} + dp \ge 0. Occluded Interval [a, b]: A pair of floats representing the parameter range [a, b] \subseteq [0, 1] that is currently known to be occluded. The visible regions are the complementary intervals [0, a] and [b, 1]. Steps: 1. Identify Front-Facing Faces: For each (n-1)-dimensional face of the 4D convex polytope, determine if it is front-facing relative to the camera using its normal vector. 2. Construct Occlusion Cone: Identify "turning edges" (n-2 dimensional edges, i.e., 2D faces in 4D) where a front-facing face meets a back-facing face. These edges define the boundary of the occlusion region. Collect all hyperplanes corresponding to front-facing faces into the array P. 3. Initialize Occluded Interval: Set a = 0 and b = 1. This represents that the entire segment is initially considered occluded. 4. Iterate Hyperplanes: Loop through each hyperplane p in array P. Calculate the signed distance of endpoints A and B from hyperplane p: valA = \mathbf{n}p \cdot A + dp and valB = \mathbf{n}p \cdot B + dp. Case 1: Both endpoints outside. If both A and B are on the outside (occluded) side (valA < 0 and valB < 0), the entire segment is occluded by this hyperplane. Terminate the algorithm immediately. Case 2: A outside, B inside. If A is outside (valA < 0) and B is inside (valB \ge 0), calculate the intersection parameter t{int} = \frac{-valA}{valB - valA}. If t{int} > a, update a = t{int} to shrink the occluded region from the left. Case 3: B outside, A inside. If B is outside (valB < 0) and A is inside (valA \ge 0), calculate t{int} = \frac{-valA}{valB - valA}. If t{int} < b, update b = t{int} to shrink the occluded region from the right. Case 4: Both inside. If both A and B are inside (valA \ge 0 and valB \ge 0), no occlusion information is gained from this hyperplane. Continue to the next hyperplane. 5. Handle Multiple Objects: If the scene contains multiple polytopes, apply this culling iteratively on the remaining segments. If the final result satisfies 0 < a < b < 1, the segment is split into two parts: [0, a] and [b, 1]. These two resulting segments are treated as separate segments for subsequent culling against other cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cullsegment4doutside(A, B, hyperplanesP, epsilon=1e-6): """ Culls a 4D line segment against a convex polytope when the camera is outside. Args: A: 4D vector, start point (t=0) B: 4D vector, end point (t=1) hyperplanesP: List of tuples (normal: 4D vector, dist: float) Normals point OUTWARD. Inside is dot(n, x) + d >= 0. epsilon: Small value to inset faces and prevent floating-point errors Returns: List of tuples (tstart, tend) representing visible sub-segments. """ # Initialize occluded interval [a, b] to [0, 1] (fully occluded) a = 0.0 b = 1.0 for (normal, dist) in hyperplanesP: # Calculate signed distances valA = dot(normal, A) + dist valB = dot(normal, B) + dist # Apply epsilon inset to handle floating-point precision isAinside = valA >= -epsilon isBinside = valB >= -epsilon if not isAinside and not isBinside: # Case 1: Both endpoints outside -> Entire segment occluded return [] if isAinside and isBinside: # Case 4: Both endpoints inside -> No change to occluded interval continue if not isAinside and isBinside: # Case 2: A outside, B inside denom = valB - valA if abs(denom) < 1e-9: continue # Degenerate case tint = -valA / denom if tint > a: a = tint if isAinside and not isBinside: # Case 3: B outside, A inside denom = valB - valA if abs(denom) < 1e-9: continue tint = -valA / denom if tint < b: b = tint # After processing all hyperplanes, return visible sub-segments if a < b: return [(0.0, a), (b, 1.0)] else: return [] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera Inside: If the camera is inside the polytope, the occlusion logic reverses. The region outside the hyperplanes is occluded, and the algorithm must be adjusted to initialize [a, b] = [0, 1] as fully safe and shrink it. See 4D Convex Polytope Line Segment Culling (Camera Inside). Floating-Point Errors: Floating-point errors may cause edges to be incorrectly culled. To prevent this, shrink the faces of the polytope inward by a small epsilon value before calculating occlusion. Endpoints on Hyperplane: If both endpoints of the line segment lie exactly on a hyperplane, no valid information is gained. The algorithm does nothing for this case and continues to the next hyperplane. Multiple Objects: The algorithm must be applied iteratively. A segment may be split into two parts ([0, a] and [b, 1]) if 0 < a < b < 1. These parts are then processed against subsequent polytopes. A variant of the culling algorithm used when the camera is inside the polytope. In this case, the hyperplane array P is empty for the outside logic, and the culling logic is inverted. The clipped regions become the outside (occluded) regions, and the middle region becomes the safe (unoccluded) area. The safe interval [a, b] is initialized to [0, 1] (fully unoccluded) and is compressed from both ends as hyperplanes are processed. The structure is: Left Endpoint A(0) -- Occluded -- a -- Safe -- b -- Occluded -- Right Endpoint B(1). For each hyperplane, if both endpoints are outside, the line is occluded. If one is inside and one outside, the intersection x is calculated, and a or b is updated to shrink the safe interval based on which side is being occluded. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of front-facing hyperplanes in the occlusion cone. For each segment, it iterates through the array P. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of hyperplanes in the occlusion cone. Performance: The complex culling logic for wireframe rendering is easy to implement on the CPU but difficult to port to the GPU. No parallelized algorithm has been found for this specific logic. Strengths: Provides exact analytic occlusion culling for 4D wireframes without a depth buffer. Limitations: Difficult to parallelize on GPU. Limited optimizations can be made using hierarchical data structures like bounding boxes. Arbitrary 2D face culling (in 3D projections) is complex, though coordinate-aligned hypercubes simplify it. When to use: When rendering 4D wireframes in a non-rasterized environment where depth buffering is not available or feasible. When not to use: When high-performance GPU parallelization is required, or when the scene consists of arbitrary 2D faces in 3D (which is described as complex). The algorithm originates from the implementation 'dearsip' in the context of 4D computer graphics, specifically for rendering 4D polytopes (like hypercubes). The implementation achieved 3D cell-to-2D face occlusion culling, which was possible because the scene mostly consisted of hypercubes aligned with coordinate axes, making 2D face culling easier. Arbitrary 2D face culling is described as complex. The method was developed to solve the problem of occlusion in 4D wireframe rendering where traditional rasterization techniques (like depth buffers) are not applicable. 四维计算机图形学：渲染篇, https://wxyhly.github.io/archives/cg4d/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Plane/Rectangle Intersection
body: This family computes the intersection of a ray with planar primitives, ranging from infinite planes to bounded rectangles and squares. It solves the problem of determining entry and exit points for volume rendering traversal or hit testing for surface rendering. It is distinguished from curved primitives (like Sphere Intersection) by relying on linear algebra and plane equations rather than quadratic surface definitions, and from general mesh intersection by operating on simple, analytically defined patches. See Ray-Primitive Intersection (Analytic/Geometric). Computes entry and exit distances for spherical volumes using a closed-form quadratic solution. It is chosen when bounding spherical primitives or sampling within spherical volumes, avoiding the barycentric checks of triangles or iterative root-finding of implicit surfaces. Computes entry and exit distances for cylinders by decomposing them into planar faces and a curved lateral surface solved via quadratic equations. It is chosen for cylindrical primitives where bounding box approximations are insufficient. Computes intersection distance and point for unbounded planes, rejecting if parallel or outside segment bounds. It is chosen for ground planes, sky domes, or clipping planes kept separate from scene BVHs. Determines hits on finite, axis-aligned rectangular patches by solving a fixed-axis plane equation and checking two free coordinates against bounds. It is chosen for fast, branch-minimized hit testing on planar surfaces aligned with coordinate axes. Computes the volume of the irregular polyhedron formed by a plane intersecting a cube, constructing an ordered list of face vertices for volume calculation. It is chosen in computational astrophysics for determining partial cell ionization or burning front coverage. Ray-squared plane intersection test that computes intersection with a square primitive defined by corner, v1, v2, and normal. Compute intersection point: p = ray.o + ray.d tHit. Check if point is inside square: planarhitptvector = p - corner, alpha = dot(w, cross(planarhitptvector, v2)), beta = dot(w, cross(v1, planarhitptvector)), where w = cross(v1, v2) / dot(cross(v1, v2), cross(v1, v2)). Return false if !(alpha > 0.0 && alpha < 1.0) || !(beta > 0.0 && beta < 1.0). The analytical intersection of rays with planes is a foundational technique in computer graphics, dating back to the early days of ray tracing. The infinite plane test is derived directly from the plane equation \mathbf{N} \cdot (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{P}0) = 0. Bounded variants, such as axis-aligned rectangles and squares, add spatial constraints to this basic test. ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, https://github.com/ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Sphere Intersection
head: Analytical ray-sphere intersection, Ball Ray Intersection, Quadratic Ray-Sphere Intersection, Ray-Ball Intersection, Sphere Ray Intersection, Sphere-Ray Intersection Check, SphereCollider.forward, Spherical Volume Intersection
body: Ray-sphere intersection computes the entry and exit distances (t) where a ray intersects a sphere, defining the valid sampling interval for volume rendering within that spherical volume. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the geometric bounds of a spherical primitive to limit raymarching steps. Unlike Ray-Plane/Rectangle Intersection, which handles flat boundaries, this method solves a quadratic equation to account for the sphere's curvature. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (vec3), ray direction \mathbf{d} (vec3, typically normalized but not required), sphere center \mathbf{c} (vec3), sphere radius r (float). Optional: transformation matrices to convert world-space ray to local space. Outputs: Boolean hit status, intersection distances t{near} and t{far} (floats), and optionally the hit point and surface normal. Data Structures: Sphere: Defined by center \mathbf{c} and radius r. In some implementations, the sphere is defined by quaternion coefficients \alphaw, \betaw, \gammaw for use in kernel space or Möbius transformations. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Transform to Local Space (Optional): If the sphere is defined in a local coordinate system (e.g., via a transformation matrix), transform the ray origin and direction into that space. Let the transformed ray be \mathbf{r}o, \mathbf{r}d. If the sphere is centered at the origin, \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}. Otherwise, compute the vector from the ray origin to the sphere center: \mathbf{oc} = \mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}. 2. Compute Quadratic Coefficients: Substitute the ray equation \mathbf{q}(t) = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d}t into the sphere equation |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}|^2 = r^2. This yields the quadratic equation At^2 + Bt + C = 0. The coefficients are: \begin{aligned} A &= \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d} \\ B &= 2 (\mathbf{oc} \cdot \mathbf{d}) \\ C &= (\mathbf{oc} \cdot \mathbf{oc}) - r^2 \end{aligned} Note: Some implementations use a half-coefficient form to avoid the factor of 2 in B, defining b = \mathbf{oc} \cdot \mathbf{d} and solving At^2 + 2bt + C = 0. 3. Compute Discriminant: Calculate the discriminant \Delta: \Delta = B^2 - 4AC Alternatively, using the half-coefficient form: \Delta = 4(b^2 - AC). If \Delta < 0, the ray does not intersect the sphere (miss). 4. Solve for t: If \Delta \ge 0, compute the roots: t{1,2} = \frac{-B \pm \sqrt{\Delta}}{2A} Using the half-coefficient form: t{1,2} = -b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - AC}. Ensure t1 \le t2 by swapping if necessary. 5. Filter Roots: If both t1 and t2 are negative, the sphere is behind the ray origin (miss). If t1 < 0 and t2 \ge 0, the ray origin is inside the sphere. The entry distance is clamped to 0 and the exit distance is t2. If t1 \ge 0, both intersections are in front of the ray. The entry distance is t1 and the exit distance is t2. Clamp distances to the ray segment bounds [t{min}, t{max}] if applicable. 6. Compute Hit Point and Normal (Optional): Hit point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t. Surface normal: \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}). Note: Some implementations compute the normal as \text{normalize}(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}) depending on the desired orientation (inward vs outward). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raysphereintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecenter, sphereradius): """ Computes the intersection of a ray with a sphere. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydirection: vec3, direction of the ray (does not need to be normalized). spherecenter: vec3, center of the sphere. sphereradius: float, radius of the sphere. Returns: tuple: (hit: bool, tnear: float, tfar: float, hitpoint: vec3, normal: vec3) hitpoint and normal are None if no hit. """ # Vector from ray origin to sphere center oc = rayorigin - spherecenter # Quadratic coefficients a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) c = dot(oc, oc) - sphereradius sphereradius # Discriminant discriminant = b b - 4.0 a c if discriminant < 0: return (False, 0.0, 0.0, None, None) sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) # Calculate the two t values t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) # Ensure t1 is the smaller value if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 # Determine the valid intersection interval # If both t are negative, the sphere is behind the ray if t1 < 0 and t2 < 0: return (False, 0.0, 0.0, None, None) # If t1 is negative, the ray origin is inside the sphere if t1 < 0: tnear = 0.0 tfar = t2 else: tnear = t1 tfar = t2 # Compute hit point and normal at tnear hitpoint = rayorigin + raydirection tnear normal = normalize(hitpoint - spherecenter) return (True, tnear, tfar, hitpoint, normal) Parameters: radius: Float, default 1.0. nearplane: Float, default 0.0, used to clamp the minimum near distance to avoid self-intersection or z-fighting. softintersection: Boolean, default False. If True, the distance between near and far is always 2 \times radius. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Origin Inside Sphere: If the ray origin is inside the sphere, t1 will be negative. The entry distance should be clamped to 0.0 or handled specifically for volume rendering to allow sampling from the inside. Tangent Ray: If \Delta = 0, the ray is tangent to the sphere. t1 = t2. This is a valid hit but may cause numerical instability if not handled. Numerical Precision: Negative discriminants due to floating-point errors for tangent rays should be clamped to 0.0. Uninitialized Variables: In some implementations, the normal calculation references an uninitialized t variable, leading to garbage values. Self-Intersection: A threshold (e.g., 0.0001) is often used to prevent self-intersection artifacts. The 3-Sphere Intersection method computes the geometric intersection points of the surfaces of three spheres, generating new sample points on the boundary of a carved volume. It solves the system of equations defined by the sphere boundaries to find positions that lie on all three surfaces simultaneously. Unlike Ray-Sphere Intersection, which finds where a ray enters or exits a single sphere, this method determines the specific vertices formed by the mutual overlap of three distinct spheres, a process essential for advancing the surface boundary in sphere carving algorithms. This method performs a ray-splat intersection test by approximating the true Gaussian splat ellipsoid with a sphere. It solves the problem of efficiently determining visibility for splat-based rendering without the computational cost of exact ellipsoid-ray intersection. It is distinguished from its parent Ray-Sphere Intersection by its specific application to Gaussian splatting parameters, and from its sibling Fast Sphere Rendering via Ray-Sphere Test by its integration into the broader splat rendering pipeline context where it serves as a fallback or optimization when true ellipsoid testing is disabled. Spherical Medium Density Integration computes the optical depth along a ray segment passing through a sphere where density decreases quadratically from the center to the edge. It solves the problem of analytically integrating a spatially varying density function within a spherical volume, avoiding numerical sampling. It differs from its parent Ray-Sphere Intersection by providing the accumulated density value rather than just geometric hit points, and from siblings like Ray-Splat Intersection by using an exact quadratic falloff rather than a Gaussian or constant approximation. The Pulsar Forward Pass is a GPU-accelerated ray-sphere intersection and rendering method designed for differentiable sphere-based neural rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which spheres contribute to each pixel and computing their color contributions while simultaneously preparing data for a backward pass. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing a shared memory buffer for sphere draw information and using a fixed-size priority queue to track the closest five spheres per pixel, enabling a highly optimized backward pass that avoids redundant intersection searches. Inverse Transforming Spheres computes the coefficients (\alpha', \beta', \gamma') of a sphere in kernel space given the coefficients (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) of that sphere in world space after a quaternionic Möbius transformation. This allows a ray tracer to test if a world-space sphere intersects a kernel distance function by transforming the sphere into kernel space and performing a standard ray-sphere intersection. It differs from forward transformation by solving for the pre-image coefficients directly via algebraic expansion of the quaternionic Möbius map, avoiding iterative root-finding. Time Complexity: O(1) per sphere. The method involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (dot products, square root, division). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Only a few scalar variables are needed to store the coefficients and roots. Measured Performance: The analytical solution is significantly faster than discrete raymarching approaches, which require multiple iterations and distance queries. For example, in sparse voxel representations, ray-sphere intersection is used to quickly determine entry and exit depths for points treated as spheres. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of spheres if tested against a list, but each individual test is constant time. GPU implementations can batch these tests for many rays and spheres simultaneously. Strengths: Exact solution, no iteration required, robust for most cases, efficient for bounding volume hierarchies (BVH) or scene bounding spheres. Limitations: Does not handle non-spherical primitives. Numerical instability can occur for rays tangent to the sphere or rays originating very close to the surface. When to Use: When the scene contains spherical primitives or when a spherical bounding volume is used to cull rays. When Not to Use: When higher precision is required for non-spherical shapes, or when the sphere is part of a complex mesh that requires triangle intersection. The analytical ray-sphere intersection is a fundamental technique in computer graphics, originating from the need to efficiently test for collisions between rays and simple geometric primitives. It is widely used in ray tracing, volume rendering, and collision detection. The method is based on solving the quadratic equation derived from the intersection of a line (ray) and a sphere. ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, https://github.com/ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) hexhowells/GoTracer, https://github.com/hexhowells/GoTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Kernel-Reflection Sequences, https://doi.org/10.2312/stag.20161364, fetched 2026-10-26 autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) HectorArellanoDev/WebGPUVoxelConeTracing, https://github.com/HectorArellanoDev/WebGPUVoxelConeTracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, https://github.com/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) trimesh33/sdf, https://github.com/trimesh33/sdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, https://github.com/ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volumetric Rendering - Alan Zucconi, https://www.alanzucconi.com/2016/07/01/volumetric-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: 3-Sphere Intersection (Trilateration)
head: Sphere Trilateration, Trilateration
body: The 3-Sphere Intersection method computes the geometric intersection points of the surfaces of three spheres, generating new sample points on the boundary of a carved volume. It solves the system of equations defined by the sphere boundaries to find positions that lie on all three surfaces simultaneously. Unlike Ray-Sphere Intersection, which finds where a ray enters or exits a single sphere, this method determines the specific vertices formed by the mutual overlap of three distinct spheres, a process essential for advancing the surface boundary in sphere carving algorithms. Inputs: Three spheres S0, S1, S2, defined by their centers \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2 and radii r0, r1, r2. Outputs: A set of intersection points \mathbf{p}. The solution formula yields two points symmetric with respect to the plane defined by the centers, or none if the spheres do not intersect at a common point. Steps: 1. Define Local Frame: Construct an orthonormal basis (\mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z) aligned with the plane passing through the centers \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2. Compute \mathbf{e}z = \frac{(\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \times (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0)}{\|(\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0) \times (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0)\|} and \mathbf{e}x = \frac{\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0}{\|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0\|}. The source text explicitly defines \mathbf{e}y = \mathbf{e}x \times \mathbf{e}x, which evaluates to a zero vector due to a typographical error. Implementation should use the standard right-handed completion \mathbf{e}y = \mathbf{e}z \times \mathbf{e}x. 2. Compute Local Coordinates of Centers: Calculate the scalar projections of the center vectors into the local frame: a = \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0\| b = (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0) \cdot \mathbf{e}x c = (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0) \cdot \mathbf{e}y 3. Solve for Local Coordinates (x, y, z): The system of equations in the local frame is x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r0^2, (x - a)^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r1^2, and (x - b)^2 + (y - c)^2 + z^2 = r2^2. Solving the system yields: x = \frac{r0^2 - r1^2 + a^2}{2a} y = \frac{r1^2 - r2^2 - (x - a)^2 + (x - b)^2 + c^2}{2c} z = \sqrt{r0^2 - x^2 - y^2} The source specifies that computing z is valid only if the term under the radical is positive, indicating that a common intersection exists. If the term is negative, the spheres do not share a common intersection point. Implementation should guard against division by zero when c \approx 0. 4. Transform Back to Original Frame: Map the local coordinates back to world space using the constructed basis: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}0 + x \cdot \mathbf{e}x + y \cdot \mathbf{e}y \pm z \cdot \mathbf{e}z Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple def cross(v1: List[float], v2: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [ v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0] ] def dot(v1: List[float], v2: List[float]) -> float: return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def sub(v1: List[float], v2: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [v1[0]-v2[0], v1[1]-v2[1], v1[2]-v2[2]] def add(v1: List[float], v2: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [v1[0]+v2[0], v1[1]+v2[1], v1[2]+v2[2]] def scale(v: List[float], s: float) -> List[float]: return [v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s] def norm(v: List[float]) -> float: return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def normalize(v: List[float]) -> List[float]: n = norm(v) if n == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return scale(v, 1.0/n) def spheretrilateration(p0: List[float], r0: float, p1: List[float], r1: float, p2: List[float], r2: float) -> List[List[float]]: """ Computes the intersection points of three spheres. Returns a list of intersection points (0, 1, or 2 points). """ # Step 1: Define Local Frame v1 = sub(p1, p0) v2 = sub(p2, p0) crossprod = cross(v1, v2) normcross = norm(crossprod) if normcross < 1e-9: return [] # Degenerate: centers are collinear ez = normalize(crossprod) normv1 = norm(v1) if normv1 < 1e-9: return [] # Degenerate: p0 and p1 are identical ex = normalize(v1) ey = cross(ez, ex) # Corrected from source typo (ex x ex) # Step 2: Compute Local Coordinates a = normv1 b = dot(v2, ex) c = dot(v2, ey) # Step 3: Solve for x, y, z x = (r02 - r12 + a2) / (2 a) if abs(c) < 1e-9: return [] # Degenerate: p2 lies on the local x-axis y = (r12 - r22 - (x - a)2 + (x - b)2 + c2) / (2 c) rad = r02 - x2 - y2 if rad < 0: return [] # No common intersection z = math.sqrt(rad) # Step 4: Transform back to original frame termxy = add(scale(ex, x), scale(ey, y)) pplus = add(p0, add(termxy, scale(ez, z))) pminus = add(p0, add(termxy, scale(ez, -z))) return [pplus, pminus] Parameters: a = \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0\| b = (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0) \cdot \mathbf{e}x c = (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}0) \cdot \mathbf{e}y Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Collinear or Identical Centers: If the centers are collinear or identical, the basis vectors become undefined or zero, requiring early termination. Degenerate Local Y: If c \approx 0, the denominator in the y calculation becomes zero, requiring a guard. No Intersection: If r0^2 - x^2 - y^2 < 0, the spheres do not share a common intersection point. What it is: Approximates a primitive using a sphere for intersection testing. Difference: Uses a single sphere for ray intersection, whereas 3-Sphere Intersection finds the vertex of three spheres. When to choose: When performance is critical and approximate bounds are sufficient. Link: Ray-Splat Intersection (Sphere Approximation) What it is: Integrates density along a ray through a spherical medium. Difference: Focuses on volume integration (transmittance/absorption) rather than geometric surface intersection. When to choose: For rendering participating media within spherical volumes. Link: Spherical Medium Density Integration What it is: A rendering pass that intersects spheres and draws them. Difference: Uses sphere intersection for rasterization/visibility, not for computing boundary points via trilateration. When to choose: For forward rendering of point-based or sphere-based primitives. Link: Pulsar Forward Pass (Sphere Intersection and Draw) What it is: Applies inverse transformations to spheres. Difference: Deals with coordinate space transformation of the primitive itself, not the intersection of multiple primitives. When to choose: When spheres are defined in a local space and need to be tested in world or view space. Link: Inverse Transforming Spheres Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides exact geometric intersection points, ensuring convergence in sphere carving algorithms by placing new spheres on the boundary. Limitations: Requires the term under the radical to be non-negative for a valid intersection. When to use: When generating new sample points on the boundary of a carved volume defined by a set of spheres. When not: When spheres do not intersect at a common point. The method originates from the Sphere Carving algorithm, introduced by Cédric Zanni in 2024. It is used to compute the set of points Pk on the surface of the carved volume Vk by finding the intersections of three spheres from the current set Sk. This technique ensures that new spheres placed at these intersections will create new intersections in the next step, facilitating the convergence of the carving process towards the target shape. The specific trilateration formulas are detailed in Appendix A.2 of the source paper. name: Ray-Splat Intersection (Sphere Approximation)
head: Approximate Sphere Splat Intersection, Splat Sphere Hit Test
body: This method approximates a Gaussian splat's true ellipsoid with a sphere to perform a faster ray-splat intersection test. It serves as a performance optimization when exact ellipsoid intersection is disabled, trading geometric fidelity for speed. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Splat center \mathbf{c} (world space). Splat scale components \mathbf{s} = (sx, sy, sz). Rendering mode flag indicating 2D or 3D splatting. Boolean flag raycastAgainstTrueSplatEllipsoid. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If intersected: hit distance t, hit position \mathbf{p}, and splat global index. Data Structures: Splat attributes are typically stored in a flat array or buffer. The relevant fields are center (vec3) and scale (vec3). Steps: 1. Check Mode: If raycastAgainstTrueSplatEllipsoid is true, this method is not used; the exact ellipsoid intersection method is invoked instead. 2. Calculate Approximate Radius: Compute the radius r of the approximating sphere based on the splat's scale components and the current rendering mode: For 2D mode: r = \frac{sx + sy}{2} For 3D mode (SplatRenderMode.ThreeD): r = \frac{sx + sy + sz}{3} 3. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Perform a standard ray-sphere intersection test using the calculated radius r and the splat center \mathbf{c}. Let \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}. Calculate t{ca} = \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{d}. Calculate d^2 = \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{L} - t{ca}^2. If d^2 > r^2, there is no intersection. Otherwise, calculate t{hc} = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}. The hit distance is t = t{ca} - t{hc} (for the front face). If t < 0, the sphere is behind the ray origin. 4. Record Hit: If an intersection is found, record the hit point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and the splat's global index. Pitfalls: This method is less accurate than the true ellipsoid intersection because it ignores the anisotropy of the Gaussian splat. It should only be used when performance is prioritized over geometric fidelity or when the splats are roughly isotropic. Precision issues may arise if the scale components vary significantly, leading to large discrepancies between the approximated sphere and the actual splat extent. Floating-point errors in d^2 may cause false misses if not clamped to zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raysplatintersectionsphereapprox(rayorigin, raydir, splatcenter, splatscale, is3dmode, splatindex): """ Performs ray-splat intersection using sphere approximation. Args: rayorigin: tuple(float, float, float), ray origin raydir: tuple(float, float, float), normalized ray direction splatcenter: tuple(float, float, float), world space center of the splat splatscale: tuple(float, float, float), scale components (sx, sy, sz) is3dmode: bool, True for 3D splatting, False for 2D splatindex: int, global index of the splat in the buffer Returns: tuple: (hit: bool, t: float, hitpoint: tuple or None, index: int) """ # Step 1: Calculate approximate radius sx, sy, sz = splatscale if is3dmode: radius = (sx + sy + sz) / 3.0 else: radius = (sx + sy) / 2.0 # Step 2: Ray-sphere intersection Lx, Ly, Lz = splatcenter[0] - rayorigin[0], splatcenter[1] - rayorigin[1], splatcenter[2] - rayorigin[2] Dx, Dy, Dz = raydir[0], raydir[1], raydir[2] tca = Lx Dx + Ly Dy + Lz Dz dsq = (Lx Lx + Ly Ly + Lz Lz) - tca tca # Guard against precision errors causing negative values under sqrt if dsq < 0.0: dsq = 0.0 # Check if ray misses the sphere if dsq > radius radius: return (False, float('inf'), None, splatindex) # Calculate hit distance thc = (radius radius - dsq) 0.5 t = tca - thc # Check if hit is behind the ray origin if t < 0.0: return (False, float('inf'), None, splatindex) # Calculate hit point hitpoint = (rayorigin[0] + Dx t, rayorigin[1] + Dy t, rayorigin[2] + Dz t) # Splat index is provided by the caller's iteration loop return (True, t, hitpoint, splatindex) A method to render spheres using only their radii and centers, avoiding polygon tessellation. It distinguishes itself from direct tessellation approaches by evaluating proxy-based ray casting techniques and adaptive vertex distribution methods. Choose it when rendering a rectangular region tightly fitting the perspective-projected sphere on screen. Time Complexity: O(1) per splat. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Significantly faster than exact ellipsoid intersection because it avoids solving a quadratic equation derived from the inverse covariance matrix. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally cheap, suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs where instruction count matters. Limitations: Geometrically inaccurate for highly anisotropic splats. May cause visual artifacts such as incorrect occlusion or missing splats that are actually visible but outside the approximated sphere. When to use: When rendering large numbers of splats and performance is critical, or when splats are expected to be roughly spherical. When not to use: When high geometric fidelity is required, or when splats are highly elongated. This method is used in the context of Gaussian Splatting rendering, specifically in implementations like GaussianSplats3D. It serves as a simplified alternative to the more accurate but computationally expensive ellipsoid-ray intersection. The approach leverages the fact that for many practical purposes, a sphere can provide a reasonable approximation of a splat's extent, especially when the splat's scale components are similar. mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fast Sphere Rendering via Ray-Sphere Test
head: Projected sphere rendering
body: A method to render spheres using only their radii and centers, avoiding polygon tessellation. It renders a rectangular region tightly fitting the perspective-projected sphere on the screen and performs a ray-sphere intersection test in the fragment shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sphere center \mathbf{c}, sphere radius r, viewing ray origin \mathbf{o}, viewing ray direction \mathbf{d}, and the previous intersection parameter t{\text{prev}} from the depth peeling pass. Output: Fragment color or depth; the fragment is discarded if no valid intersection exists. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. In the vertex shader, specify the rectangular region that tightly fits the perspective-projected sphere on the screen. 2. For each fragment in this region, perform an intersection test for the viewing ray and the sphere in the fragment shader. 3. Discard the fragment if there is no intersection. 4. Render only the front or back face of the sphere, whichever is farther away from the previous intersection point, as depth peeling does not require both. Formulas: Ray-sphere intersection: Given ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and sphere center \mathbf{c} with radius r, solve for t in |\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}|^2 = r^2. Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayspheretest(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecenter, sphereradius, prevt): oc = rayorigin - spherecenter a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) c = dot(oc, oc) - sphereradius sphereradius discriminant = b b - 4 a c if discriminant < 0: return None # Discard fragment sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) # Select the face farther from the previous intersection point candidates = [] if t1 > prevt: candidates.append(t1) if t2 > prevt: candidates.append(t2) if not candidates: return None # Discard fragment return max(candidates) This family characterizes scalability and performance for drawing spherical glyphs in 3D space using proxy geometry for pixel-perfect ray casting. It distinguishes itself from direct tessellation approaches by evaluating various proxy-based ray casting techniques and adaptive vertex distribution methods. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: The method avoids polygon tessellation, which reduces overhead for large numbers of spheres. However, rendering effective spheres multiple times during depth peeling can become computationally expensive for a large number of metaballs. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method originates from GPU-based Fast Ray Casting for a Large Number of Metaballs. History and development: It is part of a broader GPU-based ray casting approach for metaballs, specifically optimizing depth peeling and isosurface tests. Where it is used: It is used for rendering metaballs and spherical glyphs in 3D space. name: Sphere Ray Casting Benchmark Methods
head: Spherical glyph ray casting
body: This benchmark family evaluates scalability and rendering performance for drawing spherical glyphs in 3D space using proxy geometry for pixel-perfect ray casting. It distinguishes itself from direct tessellation approaches by comparing various proxy-based ray casting techniques (instanced triangles, instanced quads, geometry-shader-generated polygons) alongside adaptive vertex distribution methods. All methods in this family approximate spherical particles with simple proxy geometry and perform a ray-sphere intersection test to determine pixel coverage. The family focuses on efficient rendering of large particle counts, such as those in molecular dynamics simulations, while maintaining pixel-perfect accuracy. Key shared characteristics: Proxy Geometry: Spheres are rendered as simple geometric primitives that serve as a basis for subsequent ray casting. Adaptive Detail: Adaptive techniques compute the number of vertices created for each particle based on the distance to the camera. Platform Constraints: Performance measurements must account for hardware limitations, as tessellation shaders could not be made to run on the UWP on the Xbox, restricting tessellation-based measurements to desktop machines. Computes the number of vertices for each particle based on camera distance. The hemisphere variant distributes vertices on the hemisphere facing the camera, whereas the sphere variant distributes them over the whole surface. Choose when dynamic level-of-detail is required for spherical particles. Uses instanced triangle geometry as the proxy for ray casting. Choose for minimal vertex overhead when ray casting on simple proxies. Uses instanced quad geometry as the proxy for ray casting. Choose when quad proxies offer better coverage or performance characteristics than triangles. Uses geometry shaders to generate quads or polygons on the fly for ray casting. Choose when dynamic proxy generation is preferred over pre-baked instanced buffers. Creates spherical geometry on the fly using tessellation shaders. Note: This method was only measured on desktop machines due to UWP Xbox limitations. Choose when actual spherical geometry is preferred over flat proxies, provided the target platform supports tessellation shaders. The benchmark family was introduced to characterize scalability for spherical glyph rendering across varying input parameters and computing resources. The methods build on earlier work by Gumhold (2003) regarding pixel-perfect sphere ray casting using proxy geometry. The benchmarks were tested using real-world molecular dynamics data sets (a time step from the formation of a liquid layer and a time step from a laser ablation simulation) and uniformly distributed random particles positioned in a 10^3 unit domain. A significant constraint noted during development was the inability to run tessellation shaders on the UWP platform for Xbox, which limited the scope of tessellation-based measurements to desktop environments. name: Spherical Medium Density Integration
head: Quadratic Spherical Density, Spherical Density Integration
body: Spherical Medium Density Integration computes the optical depth along a ray segment passing through a sphere where density decreases quadratically from the center to the edge. It solves the problem of analytically integrating a spatially varying density function within a spherical volume, avoiding numerical sampling. It differs from its parent Ray-Sphere Intersection by providing the accumulated density value rather than just geometric hit points, and from siblings like Ray-Splat Intersection by using an exact quadratic falloff rather than a Gaussian or constant approximation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction \boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized), ray maximum distance D > 0, sphere center \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3, sphere radius R > 0, density factor \varrho' \ge 0. Outputs: Integrated density (optical depth) P(\mathbf{x}{2D}). Data Structures: No complex structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic and vector dot products. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Parameters: Calculate B = \langle \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o} \rangle and C = \|\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}\|^2 - R^2. Calculate discriminant \Delta = B^2 - C. If \Delta < 0, the ray does not intersect the sphere; return P = 0. Calculate bounds t1 = \max(0, -B - \sqrt{\Delta}) and t2 = \min(D, -B + \sqrt{\Delta}). If t1 \ge t2, the ray misses the sphere or is tangent; return P = 0. 2. Integrate Density: The density function is \varrho(\mathbf{x}') = \varrho' \cdot (1 - \|\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{o}\|^2/R^2) if \|\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{o}\| \leq R, else 0. The integrated density is P(\mathbf{x}{2D}) = -\varrho' \cdot R^{-2} \cdot \left( \frac{t2^3 - t1^3}{3} + B(t2^2 - t1^2) + C(t2 - t1) \right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalmediumdensityintegration(c, omega, D, o, R, rhoprime): # Vector subtraction: c - o diff = [c[i] - o[i] for i in range(3)] # B = <omega, c - o> B = omega[0]diff[0] + omega[1]diff[1] + omega[2]diff[2] # C = ||c - o||^2 - R^2 C = diff[0]2 + diff[1]2 + diff[2]2 - R2 # Discriminant delta = B2 - C # No intersection if delta < 0: return 0.0 sqrtdelta = delta0.5 # Intersection bounds t1 = max(0.0, -B - sqrtdelta) t2 = min(D, -B + sqrtdelta) # No valid segment inside sphere if t1 >= t2: return 0.0 # Integrate density term1 = (t23 - t13) / 3.0 term2 = B (t22 - t12) term3 = C (t2 - t1) P = -rhoprime (1.0 / (R2)) (term1 + term2 + term3) return P Parameters: R: Radius of the sphere. Must be > 0. \mathbf{o}: Center of the sphere. \varrho': Density factor. Must be \ge 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Clamp \Delta to 0 if slightly negative (e.g., < -10^{-9}) to avoid domain errors in square root. Boundary: The formula assumes the ray segment is clipped to [0, D]; if the sphere is entirely behind the camera (t2 < 0), t1 = \max(0, \dots) handles it correctly. Sign Consistency: B must be defined as \langle \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o} \rangle consistently in both intersection and integration steps. A variant where the density function is \rho(x) = \frac{1 - r^2}{|x|^2} if 1 - r^2 > 0, else 0, where r = |x| is the distance from the center. This creates a sphere with soft edges where density tapers at the edges. The color is constant white \mathbf{c}(x) = (1, 1, 1). Time Complexity: O(1); the method involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (dot products, square root, polynomial evaluation). Memory Complexity: O(1); no additional memory is allocated. Performance: Significantly faster than numerical integration (e.g., quadrature) or ray marching, as it provides an exact analytical solution. Strengths: Exact result; no aliasing artifacts from sampling; efficient for real-time rendering. Limitations: Only applicable to spherical volumes with quadratic density falloff; cannot handle complex shapes or non-quadratic density functions. When to use: When rendering participating media confined to spherical volumes with smooth, quadratic density gradients. When not to use: For non-spherical volumes, or when the density function does not match the quadratic model. The method derives from the analytical integration of participating media for spherical volumes with quadratic density falloff, originally derived by Quílez [2015]. It appears in Tomás Ize's thesis "Real-Time Light Transport in Analytically Integrable Participating Media" (2015). The "Soft White Sphere" variant appears in production volume rendering contexts, such as Clemson University's production volume rendering reports. name: Pulsar Forward Pass (Sphere Intersection and Draw)
body: The Pulsar Forward Pass is a GPU-accelerated ray-sphere intersection and rendering method designed for differentiable sphere-based neural rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which spheres contribute to each pixel and computing their color contributions while simultaneously preparing data for a backward pass. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing a shared memory buffer for sphere draw information and using a fixed-size priority queue to track the closest five spheres per pixel, enabling a highly optimized backward pass that avoids redundant intersection searches. Inputs: A list of N spheres, each defined by center \mathbf{c}i, radius ri, and color/opacity parameters. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction vectors for each pixel). Rendering resolution (width W, height H). Early termination threshold n (default 1%). Outputs: Rendered image (color and optionally depth/normal). Gradients for sphere parameters and camera parameters (if backward pass is enabled). 1. Sphere List: Array of sphere parameters. 2. Block-wide Shared Memory Buffer: Stores sphere draw information with intersections. Size is a multiple of the block size to always accommodate all sphere hits. 3. Backward Pass Buffer: Per-pixel storage containing the normalization factor, and the intersection depths and IDs of the closest 5 spheres. 4. Priority Queue: Per-pixel, fixed-size (5 elements) optimized priority queue tracking the IDs and intersection depths of the closest spheres for the backward pass. 5. Gradient Buffers: Sphere-specific gradients buffer and camera gradient buffer per sphere. Block Size: 16 \times 16 = 256 threads (8 warps per block). Early Termination Threshold (n): Default 1%. Max Tracked Spheres: 5 (fixed at compile time). Camera Gradient Normalization Constant: 1 \times 10^{-3}. 1. Sorting and Bounding: Sort spheres to find an arbitrary number of closest spheres to the camera. Manual sorting is used instead of OPTIX to avoid the runtime hit and because OPTIX does not provide access to the acceleration structure. During sorting, find the enclosing rectangle for all visible spheres and use this information for tighter bounds of the region to draw. 2. Block-wise Intersection Search: Launch GPU blocks of 16 \times 16 threads. Implement intersection search through coalesced loading of the intersection information structures and testing of the limits of the current pixel block. Write access to the shared memory buffer needs to be properly synchronized. If the buffer becomes too full or the spheres are exhausted, Step 3 execution is invoked to clear it. 3. Draw Operation (Step 2): Each pixel thread works autonomously. The draw operation is executed for each pixel separately and for each sphere draw information that has been loaded into the shared memory buffer. Because every pixel is processed by its own thread, write conflicts for the channel information are avoided and each pixel thread can work through the list of loaded draw information at full speed. Track intersection depths for each sphere using a small optimized priority queue to track the IDs and intersection depths of the closest five spheres for the backward pass. Update the denominator of the rendering equation to continuously track the minimum required depth that a sphere must have for an n percent contribution to the color channels. Each pixel thread can vote whether it is 'done' with processing spheres and future spheres would have not enough impact; if all pixels in a block vote 'done', execution is terminated. The vote is implemented through a thread-warp-block stage-wise reduction operation. If a backward pass is intended, write information from the forward pass into a buffer. 4. Backward Pass (Optional): Parallelize the backward pass over the pixels. Each thread only processes the spheres that have been detected at the pixel position, but requires synchronization for gradient accumulation for each sphere. Reserve memory to store all sphere specific gradients. Accumulate sphere gradients through synchronized access from each pixel thread. Allocate a buffer for the camera gradient information per sphere. Accumulate camera gradients sphere-wise and run a device-wide reduction as a post-processing step, because synchronizing the accumulation of camera gradients causes too much memory pressure. Normalize sphere gradients by averaging over the number of pixels from which they are computed. Normalize camera gradients by taking the area that each sphere covers in the image as a normalization factor, together with a constant 1 \times 10^{-3}. Gradient computation for each gradient is only performed if the gradients are required by the PyTorch autodiff framework. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math BLOCKSIZE = 256 # 16x16 threads, 8 warps per block MAXTRACKEDSPHERES = 5 # Fixed at compile time EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD = 0.01 # Default 1% CAMERAGRADNORMCONSTANT = 1e-3 # class Sphere: def init(self, center, radius, color, opacity, sphereid): self.center = center self.radius = radius self.color = color self.opacity = opacity self.sphereid = sphereid def raysphereintersect(origin, direction, sphere): # Standard ray-sphere intersection oc = [origin[i] - sphere.center[i] for i in range(3)] a = sum(dd for d in direction) b = sum(oc[i]direction[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i]oc[i] for i in range(3)) - sphere.radius2 disc = bb - ac if disc < 0: return None t = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / a if t < 0: return None hitpoint = [origin[i] + tdirection[i] for i in range(3)] normal = [(hitpoint[i] - sphere.center[i])/sphere.radius for i in range(3)] return t, hitpoint, normal def sphereintersectsblock(sphere, bx, by, bw, bh): # Axis-aligned bounding box test against block bounds return (sphere.center[0] - sphere.radius <= bx + bw and sphere.center[0] + sphere.radius >= bx and sphere.center[1] - sphere.radius <= by + bh and sphere.center[1] + sphere.radius >= by) def pulsarforwardpass(spheres, cameraorigin, cameradirections, W, H): # Step 1: Sorting and Bounding sortedspheres = sorted(enumerate(spheres), key=lambda x: math.dist(cameraorigin, x[1].center)) # Compute enclosing rectangle for visible spheres # (Sources do not specify exact bounding box algorithm) # Initialize buffers image = [[0.0]3 for in range(H)] backwardbuffers = [[None]W for in range(H)] spheregradients = [0.0]len(spheres) cameragradients = [0.0]len(spheres) # Step 2 & 3: Block-wise Intersection and Draw for by in range(0, H, 16): for bx in range(0, W, 16): sharedbuffer = [] # Coalesced loading and intersection search for idx, sphere in sortedspheres: if sphereintersectsblock(sphere, bx, by, 16, 16): sharedbuffer.append((idx, sphere)) # Draw Operation: each pixel thread works autonomously for y in range(by, min(by + 16, H)): for x in range(bx, min(bx + 16, W)): raydir = cameradirections[y][x] pq = [] # Priority queue for closest 5 spheres denom = 1.0 # Denominator of rendering equation done = False for idx, sphere in sharedbuffer: if done: break hit = raysphereintersect(cameraorigin, raydir, sphere) if hit: depth, point, normal = hit # Priority Queue Update pq.append((depth, idx)) pq.sort(key=lambda p: p[0]) if len(pq) > MAXTRACKEDSPHERES: pq.pop() # Update rendering equation denominator denom += sphere.opacity # Compute color contribution image[y][x] = [image[y][x][i] + sphere.color[i]sphere.opacity for i in range(3)] # Early termination check if depth > denom EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD: done = True # Backward Pass Buffer Write backwardbuffers[y][x] = { 'normfactor': denom, 'depths': [d for d, in pq], 'ids': [i for, i in pq] } # Early termination vote via thread-warp-block reduction # If all pixels in block vote done, terminate block loop # (Sources do not specify exact reduction implementation) # Step 4: Backward Pass (Optional) # Gradient computation only if required by autodiff framework # Parallelize over pixels for y in range(H): for x in range(W): state = backwardbuffers[y][x] if state is None: continue for d, sid in state['depths']: # Sphere gradient accumulation via synchronized access # (Sources do not specify exact atomic/sync mechanism) pass # Camera gradient accumulation sphere-wise pass # Normalize sphere gradients by averaging over pixel count # Normalize camera gradients by area CAMERAGRADNORMCONSTANT return image, spheregradients, cameragradients Buffer Overflow: The shared memory buffer must be synchronized and cleared if it becomes full or spheres are exhausted. Memory Pressure: Synchronizing camera gradient accumulation per pixel causes too much memory pressure; use sphere-wise accumulation and device-wide reduction. Precision: Use double precision for intersection calculations if necessary to avoid artifacts, though not explicitly stated, standard practice in ray tracing. Degenerate Input: Empty sphere list or zero-radius spheres should be handled gracefully. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Camera gradient accumulation reduction takes 0.6 ms for 1,000,000 spheres. Scaling: Scales favorably with future GPU generations due to block size optimization. Scales well with image resolution and the number of spheres. Strengths: Fast execution, robust to large spheres, efficient backward pass by avoiding redundant intersection searches. Limitations: Requires manual sorting because OPTIX does not provide access to the acceleration structure. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Pulsar Forward Pass was introduced in the paper "Pulsar: Efficient Sphere-based Neural Rendering". It was developed to address the limitations of existing methods like OPTIX, which do not provide access to the acceleration structure for manual sorting and arbitrary closest sphere queries. The method was designed to be efficient and differentiable, enabling optimization of sphere parameters and camera parameters using gradient descent. It has been used in neural rendering applications where sphere-based representations are advantageous. name: Inverse Transforming Spheres
head: Inverse Möbius Transformation of Spheres, Inverse Quaternion Möbius Transform for Spheres
body: Inverse Transforming Spheres computes the coefficients (\alpha', \beta', \gamma') of a sphere in kernel space given the coefficients (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) of that sphere in world space after a quaternionic Möbius transformation. This allows a ray tracer to test if a world-space sphere intersects a kernel distance function by transforming the sphere into kernel space and performing a standard ray-sphere intersection. It differs from forward transformation by solving for the pre-image coefficients directly via algebraic expansion of the quaternionic Möbius map, avoiding iterative root-finding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sphere coefficients in world space \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \beta \in \mathbb{H}0 (pure quaternion), \gamma \in \mathbb{R}, and Möbius transformation matrix coefficients a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{H}. Outputs: Sphere coefficients in kernel space \alpha' \in \mathbb{R}, \beta' \in \mathbb{H}0, \gamma' \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: Quaternions are represented as 4-component tuples (w, x, y, z). \mathbb{H}0 denotes pure quaternions where the scalar part w is zero. \bar{q} denotes the quaternion conjugate (w, -x, -y, -z). q\bar{q} denotes the squared norm w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2. \text{Re}(q) denotes the scalar part w. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute conjugates \bar{a}, \bar{b}, \bar{c}, \bar{d}, \bar{\beta}. 2. Compute scalar products a\bar{a}, c\bar{c}, b\bar{b}, and d\bar{d}. 3. Compute quaternion products \bar{c}\beta a, \bar{b}a, \bar{d}\beta a, \bar{b}\bar{\beta}c, \bar{d}\bar{c}, and \bar{d}\beta b. 4. Extract real parts of \bar{c}\beta a and \bar{d}\beta b. 5. Assemble \alpha', \beta', and \gamma' using the linear combinations of the computed terms. Formulas: The implicit equation of a sphere or plane in quaternion space is: \alpha(q\bar{q}) + \beta q + \bar{q}\bar{\beta} + \gamma = 0 where q \in \mathbb{H}. For a sphere of radius \rho centered at \kappa, the coefficients are \alpha = 1, \beta = \kappa, and \gamma = |\kappa|^2 - \rho^2. The Möbius transformation is defined as \mathcal{L}(q) = (aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1}. Substituting \mathcal{L}(q) into the sphere equation and clearing denominators by multiplying by (cq+d) from the left and (cq+d) from the right yields the original sphere coefficients: \alpha' = \alpha a \bar{a} + 2 \text{Re}(\bar{c} \beta a) + \gamma \bar{c} c \beta' = \alpha \bar{b} a + \bar{d} \beta a + \bar{b} \bar{\beta} c + \gamma \bar{d} \bar{c} \gamma' = \alpha b \bar{b} + 2 \text{Re}(\bar{d} \beta b) + \gamma d \bar{d}. Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical precision: Quaternion multiplication involves multiple floating-point operations, and accumulated error may affect the accuracy of the intersection test in kernel space. Pure quaternion constraint: \beta and \beta' must be pure quaternions (scalar part 0). Numerical errors might introduce a small scalar component in \beta', which should be zeroed out. Boundaries and degenerate input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inversetransformsphere(alpha, beta, gamma, a, b, c, d): """ Computes the coefficients (alphaprime, betaprime, gammaprime) of the original sphere in kernel space, given world-space coefficients and Möbius matrix elements a, b, c, d. Inputs: alpha, gamma: float (real numbers) beta: tuple (w, x, y, z) representing a pure quaternion (w=0) a, b, c, d: tuple (w, x, y, z) representing quaternions Outputs: alphaprime: float betaprime: tuple (w, x, y, z) representing a pure quaternion gammaprime: float """ # Helper: Quaternion conjugate def conj(q): return (q[0], -q[1], -q[2], -q[3]) # Helper: Quaternion multiplication def qmul(q1, q2): w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1 w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2 return ( w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2) # Helper: Real part of quaternion def re(q): return q[0] # Helper: Scalar multiplication of quaternion def smul(s, q): return (s q[0], s q[1], s q[2], s q[3]) # Helper: Add two quaternions def qadd(q1, q2): return (q1[0]+q2[0], q1[1]+q2[1], q1[2]+q2[2], q1[3]+q2[3]) # Conjugates abar = conj(a) bbar = conj(b) cbar = conj(c) dbar = conj(d) betabar = conj(beta) # Calculate alpha' # alpha' = alpha a abar + 2 Re(cbar beta a) + gamma cbar c scalaraa = qmul(a, abar)[0] term2alphaq = qmul(cbar, qmul(beta, a)) scalarcc = qmul(cbar, c)[0] alphaprime = alpha scalaraa + 2 re(term2alphaq) + gamma scalarcc # Calculate beta' # beta' = alpha bbar a + dbar beta a + bbar betabar c + gamma dbar cbar term1beta = smul(alpha, qmul(bbar, a)) term2beta = qmul(dbar, qmul(beta, a)) term3beta = qmul(bbar, qmul(betabar, c)) term4beta = smul(gamma, qmul(dbar, cbar)) betaprime = qadd(qadd(qadd(term1beta, term2beta), term3beta), term4beta) # Calculate gamma' # gamma' = alpha b bbar + 2 Re(dbar beta b) + gamma d dbar scalarbb = qmul(b, bbar)[0] term2gammaq = qmul(dbar, qmul(beta, b)) scalardd = qmul(d, dbar)[0] gammaprime = alpha scalarbb + 2 re(term2gammaq) + gamma scalardd return alphaprime, betaprime, gammaprime Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per sphere, involving a fixed number of quaternion multiplications and additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Exact algebraic solution; no iterative approximation; enables efficient culling of spheres against kernel distance functions. Limitations: Requires the Möbius transformation to be invertible; only applicable to spheres/planes; quaternion arithmetic is more expensive than standard 3D vector math. When to use: When rendering Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) or other conformally transformed implicit surfaces where spheres need to be tested against the kernel. When not to use: For non-spherical primitives or when the transformation is not a Möbius transformation. The method originates from the work on Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS). It was introduced to allow efficient ray tracing of complex natural scenes by conformally distorting expansion levels. The technique leverages the properties of quaternionic Möbius transformations to map spheres in world space to spheres (or planes) in kernel space, enabling the use of standard ray-sphere intersection algorithms. name: Ray-Cylinder Intersection
body: Computes the entry and exit distances for a ray intersecting a finite cylinder aligned along the Y-axis, defined by radius, top Y, and bottom Y. It decomposes the cylinder into front/back rectangles, top/bottom faces, and a lateral curved surface to test intersections. Unlike Ray-Sphere Intersection which relies on a single quadratic solution, this method requires intersection tests against multiple geometric primitives. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (not necessarily normalized), cylinder geometry size geomSize (a vector where geomSize.x is the radius, geomSize.y is the height along the Y-axis, and geomSize.z is the depth/width along the Z-axis). Outputs: Entry distance inAbs, exit distance outAbs. Returns true if an intersection exists, false otherwise. Data Structures geomSize: float3 containing (r, h, w). rayOrig: float3 ray origin. rayVect: float3 ray direction. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize inAbsVal = 0, outAbsVal = 0, inAbsFound = false, outAbsFound = false. 2. Intersect Front Rectangle: Define points P0 = (0, 0, 0), P1 = (geomSize.x, 0, 0), P2 = (0, geomSize.z, 0). Compute normal \mathbf{n} = (P1 - P0) \times (P2 - P0). Compute dot product d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. If d \neq 0, compute s = \mathbf{n} \cdot (P0 - \mathbf{o}) / d. Compute intersection point P = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}. Check bounds P.x \ge 0, P.x \le geomSize.x, P.y \ge 0, P.y \le geomSize.z. If d > 0, update outAbsVal with s (maximize); if d < 0, update inAbsVal with s (minimize). 3. Intersect Back Rectangle: Define points P0 = (lastPoint.x, 0, lastPoint.z), P1 = (0, 0, 0), P2 = (0, geomSize.z, 0), where lastPoint is derived from cylToCart(geomSize). Compute normal \mathbf{n}, dot d, and s. Check bounds using projected coordinate x = \mathbf{P} \cdot (P0 - P1) / \|P0 - P1\|. Check bounds x \ge 0, x \le geomSize.x, P.y \ge 0, P.y \le geomSize.z. Update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d. 4. Intersect Top Face: Define point P0 = (0, geomSize.z, 0) and normal \mathbf{n} = (0, 1, 0). Compute s. Convert intersection point to cylindrical coordinates P = \text{cartToCyl}(\mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}). Check if P.x \le geomSize.x and P.y \le geomSize.y. Update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d. 5. Intersect Bottom Face: Define point P0 = (0, 0, 0) and normal \mathbf{n} = (0, -1, 0). Compute s. Convert to cylindrical coordinates. Check bounds. Update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d. 6. Intersect Lateral Face: Solve quadratic equation for cylinder radius geomSize.x. Compute a = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}, b = 2 \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}, c = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} - (\text{geomSize.x})^2, where \mathbf{u} = (\mathbf{d}.x, \mathbf{d}.z) and \mathbf{v} = (\mathbf{o}.x, \mathbf{o}.z). If discriminant \Delta \ge 0, compute roots s0, s1. Convert points to cylindrical P{\text{Cyl}}. Check if P{\text{Cyl}}.y \le \text{geomSize.y} and P{\text{Cyl}}.z \ge 0 and P{\text{Cyl}}.z \le \text{geomSize.z}. Update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on dot product d[i]. 7. Handle Degenerate Cases: If only entry found, set outAbsVal = inAbsVal + 2 geomSize.x / \| \mathbf{d} \|. If only exit found, set inAbsVal = outAbsVal - 2 geomSize.x / \| \mathbf{d} \|. 8. Return: true if outAbsVal >= inAbsVal and both outAbsFound and inAbsFound are true. Formulas Quadratic coefficients for the lateral face: a = dx^2 + dz^2, b = 2(dx ox + dz oz), c = ox^2 + oz^2 - r^2. Discriminant \Delta = b^2 - 4ac. Parameters geomType: Character indicating geometry type; if geomType == 'c', use this method. Pitfalls If y < bottom or y > top, the intersection is outside the finite cylinder bounds; return -1.0. Precision issues may occur near boundaries; degenerate cases where only entry or exit is found require fallback calculations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayintersectcylinder(rayorig, raydir, geomsize): """ rayorig: tuple (x, y, z) raydir: tuple (x, y, z) geomsize: tuple (radius, height, width) Returns: (inabs, outabs, hit) """ import math R = geomsize[0] H = geomsize[1] W = geomsize[2] inabsval = 0.0 outabsval = 0.0 inabsfound = False outabsfound = False def carttocyl(p): r = (p[0]2 + p[2]2)0.5 theta = math.atan2(p[2], p[0]) y = p[1] return (r, theta, y) # 1. Front Rectangle P0 = (0, 0, 0) P1 = (R, 0, 0) P2 = (0, W, 0) n = (P1[1]P2[2] - P1[2]P2[1], P1[2]P2[0] - P1[0]P2[2], P1[0]P2[1] - P1[1]P2[0]) d = n[0]raydir[0] + n[1]raydir[1] + n[2]raydir[2] if d != 0: s = (n[0](P0[0]-rayorig[0]) + n[1](P0[1]-rayorig[1]) + n[2](P0[2]-rayorig[2])) / d P = (rayorig[0] + sraydir[0], rayorig[1] + sraydir[1], rayorig[2] + sraydir[2]) if P[0] >= 0 and P[0] <= R and P[1] >= 0 and P[1] <= W: if d > 0: outabsval = max(outabsval, s) if outabsfound else s outabsfound = True else: inabsval = min(inabsval, s) if inabsfound else s inabsfound = True # 2. Back Rectangle lastpoint = (R, H, W) # Derived from cylToCart(geomSize) P0 = (lastpoint[0], 0, lastpoint[2]) P1 = (0, 0, 0) P2 = (0, W, 0) n = (P1[1]P2[2] - P1[2]P2[1], P1[2]P2[0] - P1[0]P2[2], P1[0]P2[1] - P1[1]P2[0]) d = n[0]raydir[0] + n[1]raydir[1] + n[2]raydir[2] if d != 0: s = (n[0](P0[0]-rayorig[0]) + n[1](P0[1]-rayorig[1]) + n[2](P0[2]-rayorig[2])) / d P = (rayorig[0] + sraydir[0], rayorig[1] + sraydir[1], rayorig[2] + sraydir[2]) vec = (P0[0]-P1[0], P0[1]-P1[1], P0[2]-P1[2]) lenvec = (vec[0]2 + vec[1]2 + vec[2]2)0.5 if lenvec > 0: xproj = (P[0]vec[0] + P[1]vec[1] + P[2]vec[2]) / lenvec if xproj >= 0 and xproj <= R and P[1] >= 0 and P[1] <= W: if d > 0: outabsval = max(outabsval, s) if outabsfound else s outabsfound = True else: inabsval = min(inabsval, s) if inabsfound else s inabsfound = True # 3. Top Face P0 = (0, H, 0) n = (0, 1, 0) d = n[0]raydir[0] + n[1]raydir[1] + n[2]raydir[2] if d != 0: s = (n[0](P0[0]-rayorig[0]) + n[1](P0[1]-rayorig[1]) + n[2](P0[2]-rayorig[2])) / d P = (rayorig[0] + sraydir[0], rayorig[1] + sraydir[1], rayorig[2] + sraydir[2]) cylp = carttocyl(P) if cylp[0] <= R and cylp[2] >= 0 and cylp[2] <= H: if d > 0: outabsval = max(outabsval, s) if outabsfound else s outabsfound = True else: inabsval = min(inabsval, s) if inabsfound else s inabsfound = True # 4. Bottom Face P0 = (0, 0, 0) n = (0, -1, 0) d = n[0]raydir[0] + n[1]raydir[1] + n[2]raydir[2] if d != 0: s = (n[0](P0[0]-rayorig[0]) + n[1](P0[1]-rayorig[1]) + n[2](P0[2]-rayorig[2])) / d P = (rayorig[0] + sraydir[0], rayorig[1] + sraydir[1], rayorig[2] + sraydir[2]) cylp = carttocyl(P) if cylp[0] <= R and cylp[2] >= 0 and cylp[2] <= H: if d > 0: outabsval = max(outabsval, s) if outabsfound else s outabsfound = True else: inabsval = min(inabsval, s) if inabsfound else s inabsfound = True # 5. Lateral Face u = (raydir[0], raydir[2]) v = (rayorig[0], rayorig[2]) a = u[0]2 + u[1]2 b = 2 (u[0]v[0] + u[1]v[1]) c = v[0]2 + v[1]2 - (R R) delta = bb - 4ac if delta >= 0: sqrtdelta = delta0.5 s0 = (-b - sqrtdelta) / (2 a) s1 = (-b + sqrtdelta) / (2 a) for s in [s0, s1]: P = (rayorig[0] + sraydir[0], rayorig[1] + sraydir[1], rayorig[2] + sraydir[2]) cylp = carttocyl(P) if cylp[0] <= R and cylp[2] >= 0 and cylp[2] <= H: normal = (P[0] / R, 0, P[2] / R) dotnd = normal[0]raydir[0] + normal[1]raydir[1] + normal[2]raydir[2] if dotnd > 0: outabsval = max(outabsval, s) if outabsfound else s outabsfound = True else: inabsval = min(inabsval, s) if inabsfound else s inabsfound = True # 6. Degenerate Cases if inabsfound and not outabsfound: outabsval = inabsval + 2 R / (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 if outabsfound and not inabsfound: inabsval = outabsval - 2 R / (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 hit = outabsval >= inabsval and outabsfound and inabsfound return inabsval, outabsval, hit Determines the query cylinder's radius rc for particle querying in discrete media. The parameter k in the radius formula determines the percentage of the pixel's footprint at the nearest boundary of the medium. Typical value range for k is [0.5, 1]. Setting k too large produces undesirable aliasing and overly blurred volumetric glints, although overall brightness remains similar. Setting k too small misses many particles during querying, leading to inefficiency, especially in very sparse media (e.g., N{tot} = 10^4). Time Complexity: Constant time per ray, as it performs a fixed number of intersection tests against planar and quadratic surfaces. Memory Complexity: Constant, requiring only a few scalar variables for state. Strengths: Accurate intersection for cylindrical primitives; handles degenerate cases where only entry or exit is found. Limitations: More complex than sphere intersection due to multiple face tests; requires careful handling of coordinate transformations. When to use: When rendering scenes with cylindrical primitives or when using query cylinders for sparse particle systems. The method is derived from CUDA-based volume rendering implementations. It is used in the context of rendering discrete participating media using geometrical optics approximation, where query cylinders are used to efficiently sample particles.
