name: Infinite Plane Ray Intersection
head: Analytical ray-plane intersection, Infinite Ground Plane, InfinitePlan::rayIntersect, InfinitePlan::rayIntersectP, Matrix-Based Plane Intersection, Ray-Plane Intersection, planeIntr
body: Computes the intersection of a ray with an infinite plane defined by a point and a normal, returning the intersection distance and point, or rejecting if the ray is parallel or outside the valid segment bounds. It is commonly used for ground planes kept separate from the scene's BVH. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, plane point \mathbf{P}, plane normal \mathbf{N}, minimum distance t{min}, maximum distance t{max}. Output: Boolean success flag, intersection distance t, intersection point \mathbf{p}, and plane normal \mathbf{N}. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The plane is defined by point \mathbf{P} and normal \mathbf{N}. The ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps 1. Compute the denominator D = \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 2. Check for parallelism: If |D| < \epsilon, the ray is parallel to the plane. Return failure. 3. Compute the intersection distance t: t = \frac{\mathbf{N} \cdot (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{o})}{\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{d}} 4. Check bounds: If t < t{min} or t > t{max}, the intersection is outside the valid ray segment. Return failure. 5. Compute the intersection point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} 6. Return success with t, \mathbf{p}, and \mathbf{N}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def intersectinfiniteplane(rayo, rayd, planep, planen, tmin, tmax, epsilon=1e-6): denominator = dot(planen, rayd) if abs(denominator) < epsilon: return False, 0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = dot((planep[0]-rayo[0], planep[1]-rayo[1], planep[2]-rayo[2]), planen) / denominator if t < tmin or t > tmax: return False, 0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) p = (rayo[0] + trayd[0], rayo[1] + trayd[1], rayo[2] + trayd[2]) return True, t, p Parameters epsilon: Threshold for parallel ray/plane test. Value not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Parallel Rays: If the ray direction is perpendicular to the plane normal, the denominator is zero, causing division by zero. This must be checked to avoid invalid results. Intersects a ray with a finite plane segment. It is distinct from the infinite plane method by requiring additional bounds tests to ensure the intersection point lies within the segment. Choose it when the plane has finite extent. See Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test. A specific application of the infinite plane intersection used as a scene base. It is distinct by being kept separate from the scene's BVH for performance. Choose it for ground planes in path tracers. See Infinite Ground Plane. Time complexity: O(1) constant time, requiring only a few dot products and a division. Memory complexity: O(1) constant space, requiring no additional data structures. Measured performance with hardware, resolution, and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extremely fast and simple to implement. Limitations: Only works for infinite planes. When to use: Ideal for ground planes or sky domes in path tracers. When not to use: When the plane has finite bounds or when the scene contains many planes that can be efficiently accelerated with a BVH. The analytical ray-plane intersection is a fundamental technique in computer graphics. It is widely used in path tracers and real-time renderers for its simplicity and speed. The infinite ground plane pattern is commonly used in offline renderers, where it is kept separate from the BVH for efficiency. name: Ray-Square Intersection
head: Quad Plane Intersection, Square Ray Intersection, Square::rayIntersect, castRayAgainstQuads
body: Ray-square intersection computes whether a ray intersects a finite square primitive (quad) defined by a corner point and two edge vectors, or by a transformation matrix and a canonical unit square. It solves the problem of determining precise hit locations on planar square surfaces, which is essential for rendering flat geometry, light sources, and texture planes in volume rendering and path tracing. It differs from Ray-Plane/Rectangle Intersection by enforcing strict square boundary checks (equal edge lengths, orthogonal or specific basis constraints) and often optimizing for batched or canonical representations. Inputs: 1. Ray: Origin \mathbf{o}, Direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). 2. Square Definition: One of the following: Explicit Basis: Corner \mathbf{c}, Edge Vectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, and Normal \mathbf{n}. Transform Matrix: World-to-local transformation matrix \mathbf{M}{world \to local} and a canonical square in local space spanning [-0.5, 0.5] \times [-0.5, 0.5] at z=0. 3. (Optional) Batch: Array of transformation matrices for multiple squares. Outputs: Boolean hit: True if intersection occurs within the square bounds. Float t: Distance along the ray to the intersection point. Vector2 uv: Local coordinates on the square (typically [0,1] or [-0.5, 0.5]). Vector3 point: World-space intersection point. Ray: Struct with origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). Square (Explicit): Struct with corner (vec3), v1 (vec3), v2 (vec3), normal (vec3). Square (Transform): Struct with worldToLocal (mat4x4). Batch: Array of worldToLocal matrices. This method computes the intersection with the infinite plane defined by the square, then checks if the point lies within the square boundaries using barycentric-like coordinates. 1. Compute Plane Normal: \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}1 \times \mathbf{v}2 If \|\mathbf{w}\| \approx 0, the square is degenerate; return no hit. \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|} 2. Ray-Plane Intersection: Compute the denominator: denom = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} If |denom| < \epsilon (ray parallel to plane), return no hit. Compute distance t: t = \frac{\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o})}{denom} If t < \epsilon (intersection behind ray origin), return no hit. 3. Intersection Point: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} 4. Boundary Check: Compute vector from corner to point: \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} Compute coordinates \alpha, \beta using the cross-product method described in: \alpha = \frac{\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{p}{local} \times \mathbf{v}2)}{\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{w}} \beta = \frac{\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{v}1 \times \mathbf{p}{local})}{\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{w}} The point is inside the square if: 0 < \alpha < 1 \quad \text{and} \quad 0 < \beta < 1 (Note: Strict inequality excludes edges; use \le if edges are included. uses strict inequalities). 5. UV Coordinates: u = \alpha, \quad v = \beta This method transforms the ray into the local space of the square, where the square is a unit square centered at the origin in the xy-plane (z=0), spanning [-0.5, 0.5]. This is efficient for batched rendering. 1. Transform Ray: Transform ray origin and direction to local space using \mathbf{M}{world \to local}: \mathbf{o}{local} = \mathbf{M}{world \to local} \cdot [\mathbf{o}, 1]^T \mathbf{d}{local} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{M}{world \to local} \cdot [\mathbf{d}, 0]^T) Note: The w component of the origin becomes the local z coordinate. The direction is transformed as a vector (ignoring translation) and normalized. 2. Ray-Plane Intersection (Local): The plane is at z=0. t = \frac{-\mathbf{o}{local}.z}{\mathbf{d}{local}.z} Check validity: \mathbf{d}{local}.z > \epsilon (ray points towards positive z, assuming square faces +z? Or check against specific orientation). checks localStart.z < 0 and localDirec.z > 0, implying the ray starts behind the plane (z<0) and moves towards it (z>0). t > \epsilon (intersection in front of ray). 3. Hit Position: \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{o}{local} + t \mathbf{d}{local} 4. Boundary Check: Check if \mathbf{p}{local}.x and \mathbf{p}{local}.y are within [-0.5, 0.5]: -0.5 \le \mathbf{p}{local}.x \le 0.5 \quad \text{and} \quad -0.5 \le \mathbf{p}{local}.y \le 0.5 5. UV Coordinates: u = \mathbf{p}{local}.x + 0.5 v = \mathbf{p}{local}.y + 0.5 (Mapping [-0.5, 0.5] to [0, 1]). 6. Back-Transform (Optional): If world-space point is needed: \mathbf{p}{world} = \mathbf{M}{local \to world} \cdot [\mathbf{p}{local}.x, \mathbf{p}{local}.y, 0, 1]^T Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raysquareintersectexplicit(rayo, rayd, corner, v1, v2): """ Intersect ray with square defined by corner, v1, v2. Returns (hit, t, u, v, point) """ # 1. Compute normal w = cross(v1, v2) wdotw = dot(w, w) if wdotw < 1e-9: return False, 0, 0, 0, None # Degenerate square n = w / sqrt(wdotw) # 2. Ray-plane intersection denom = dot(n, rayd) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return False, 0, 0, 0, None # Parallel t = dot(n, corner - rayo) / denom if t < 1e-9: return False, 0, 0, 0, None # Behind ray # 3. Intersection point p = rayo + t rayd # 4. Boundary check plocal = p - corner alpha = dot(w, cross(plocal, v2)) / wdotw beta = dot(w, cross(v1, plocal)) / wdotw # Check bounds (strictly inside as per) if alpha > 0.0 and alpha < 1.0 and beta > 0.0 and beta < 1.0: return True, t, alpha, beta, p else: return False, 0, 0, 0, None def raysquareintersecttransform(rayo, rayd, worldtolocal): """ Intersect ray with canonical square in local space [-0.5, 0.5]x[-0.5, 0.5] at z=0. Uses transform matrix. Returns (hit, t, u, v, point) """ # 1. Transform ray to local space # Transform origin (w=1) olocalx = dot(worldtolocal[0], vec4(rayo, 1.0)) olocaly = dot(worldtolocal[1], vec4(rayo, 1.0)) olocalz = dot(worldtolocal[2], vec4(rayo, 1.0)) olocal = vec3(olocalx, olocaly, olocalz) # Transform direction (w=0) dlocalx = dot(worldtolocal[0], vec4(rayd, 0.0)) dlocaly = dot(worldtolocal[1], vec4(rayd, 0.0)) dlocalz = dot(worldtolocal[2], vec4(rayd, 0.0)) dlocal = normalize(vec3(dlocalx, dlocaly, dlocalz)) # 2. Ray-plane intersection at z=0 # Check if ray points towards plane (z>0) and starts behind (z<0) if dlocal.z <= 1e-9 or olocal.z >= -1e-9: return False, 0, 0, 0, None t = -olocal.z / dlocal.z if t < 1e-9: return False, 0, 0, 0, None # 3. Hit position in local space plocalx = olocal.x + t dlocal.x plocaly = olocal.y + t dlocal.y # plocalz is 0 # 4. Boundary check if -0.5 <= plocalx <= 0.5 and -0.5 <= plocaly <= 0.5: u = plocalx + 0.5 v = plocaly + 0.5 # Transform point back to world space if needed # pworld = localtoworld vec4(plocal, 0, 1) return True, t, u, v, None # Return local point or transform back else: return False, 0, 0, 0, None \epsilon: Epsilon for floating-point comparisons. Typical value: 10^{-9} to 10^{-7}. leastT: In batched scenarios, the minimum t found so far. Initialized to infinity or a large value (e.g., 1000). 1. Degenerate Squares: If \mathbf{v}1 and \mathbf{v}2 are parallel or zero, the normal is undefined. Check \|\mathbf{v}1 \times \mathbf{v}2\| < \epsilon. 2. Parallel Ray: If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} \approx 0, the ray is parallel to the plane. No intersection. 3. Back-face Culling: The sign of \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} determines if the ray hits the front or back face. Depending on the application, back faces may be ignored. assumes a specific orientation (z>0 direction). 4. Precision: When checking boundaries, use a small epsilon to avoid missing hits due to floating-point errors at the edges. 5. Transform Normalization: When transforming the ray direction, it must be normalized after transformation because the transformation matrix may include non-uniform scaling. Time Complexity: O(1) per square. For N squares, O(N) if tested individually. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Analytic solution is exact and fast. Transform-based method allows efficient batching and GPU-friendly code. Explicit method handles arbitrary oriented squares without matrix inversion. Limitations: Only works for planar squares. Transform method requires pre-computed world-to-local matrices. Precision issues near edges or parallel rays. When to Use: Rendering flat geometry, light sources, or skyboxes composed of quads. When high performance is required for large numbers of small planar primitives. When Not to Use: For curved surfaces (use sphere, cylinder, etc.). For non-planar or deformed quads (use triangle decomposition or higher-order primitives). Ray-square intersection is a fundamental primitive test in computer graphics, particularly in ray tracing and path tracing. It is often implemented as part of a broader ray-primitive intersection module. The explicit basis method is derived from standard computational geometry techniques for point-in-convex-polygon tests. The transform-based method is common in modern rendering engines and GPU shaders, where objects are often defined in local space and transformed to world space. name: Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test
head: Plane-Rectangle Intersection, XYRect/XZRect/YZRect Hit
body: The Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test determines whether a ray intersects a finite rectangle lying on an axis-aligned plane. It solves the problem of bounding infinite plane intersections to a specific 2D extent, which is essential for modeling flat surfaces in ray tracing. It differs from Infinite Plane Ray Intersection by adding boundary checks for the rectangle's edges, and from Plane-Cube Intersection by handling a single planar face rather than a volumetric solid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, a minimum distance t{min}, a maximum distance t{max}, and a rectangle object. Output: A boolean indicating hit status, and a HitRecord structure populated with intersection distance t, point \mathbf{p}, normal \mathbf{n}, and material. Data Structures: Rectangles are defined by structs containing bounds on two axes, a constant coordinate on the third axis, and a material. XYRect: Fields X0, X1 (x-bounds), Y0, Y1 (y-bounds), K (z-coordinate), Mat (material). XZRect: Fields X0, X1 (x-bounds), Z0, Z1 (z-bounds), K (y-coordinate), Mat (material). YZRect: Fields Y0, Y1 (y-bounds), Z0, Z1 (z-bounds), K (x-coordinate), Mat (material). Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Parameter (t): Solve the plane equation for the fixed axis. For an XYRect (normal along Z), the plane equation is z = K. Substituting the ray equation z(t) = oz + t \cdot dz, we get: t = \frac{K - oz}{dz} For XZRect (normal along Y): t = \frac{K - oy}{dy}. For YZRect (normal along X): t = \frac{K - ox}{dx}. 2. Check Depth Bounds: If t < t{min} or t > t{max}, the intersection is outside the valid ray segment. Return false. 3. Compute Transverse Coordinates: Calculate the coordinates on the plane's axes at parameter t. For XYRect: x = ox + t \cdot dx y = oy + t \cdot dy (Analogous formulas apply for other orientations). 4. Check Boundary Bounds: Verify if the transverse coordinates lie within the rectangle's extents using direct comparisons. For XYRect: x < X0 \text{ or } x > X1 \text{ or } y < Y0 \text{ or } y > Y1 If any coordinate is out of bounds, return false. 5. Populate HitRecord: Set t{rec} = t, set \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}, determine the outward normal (e.g., \mathbf{n}{out} = (0, 0, 1) for XYRect), orient the normal against the ray direction using a standard face-normal routine, and assign the material from the rectangle object. Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the ray direction component along the fixed axis is zero (e.g., dz = 0 for XYRect), division by zero occurs. The result is NaN or Inf, which typically fails the t{min}/t{max} bounds check, but explicit guards are omitted in the source implementation. Coordinate Ordering: Bounds X0, X1 are not guaranteed to be sorted (X0 < X1). The implementation relies on direct < and > comparisons rather than min/max functions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vector(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin, self.direction = origin, direction def at(self, t): return self.origin + self.direction t class HitRecord: def init(self): self.t, self.p, self.normal, self.frontface, self.mat = 0.0, None, None, False, None def setfacenormal(self, ray, outwardnormal): self.frontface = ray.direction.dot(outwardnormal) < 0 self.normal = -outwardnormal if self.frontface else outwardnormal def hitxyrect(rect, ray, tmin, tmax): denom = ray.direction.z t = (rect.K - ray.origin.z) / denom if t < tmin or t > tmax: return False x = ray.origin.x + t ray.direction.x y = ray.origin.y + t ray.direction.y if x < rect.X0 or x > rect.X1 or y < rect.Y0 or y > rect.Y1: return False rec = HitRecord() rec.t = t rec.p = ray.at(t) outwardnormal = Vector(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) rec.setfacenormal(ray, outwardnormal) rec.mat = rect.Mat return True Intersects a ray with an axis-aligned plane defined by an anchor point, extent, and direction index d. It returns the intersection distance t and barycentric-like coordinates u, v. The method uses a direction index to permute coordinate axes, aligning the plane normal with a single axis to simplify the intersection calculation. It sets itself apart by generalizing to any axis-aligned plane rather than a bounded rectangle, and is chosen when only the plane intersection is needed without 2D extent checks. An algorithm to determine if a rectangular tile needs rendering by checking if a projected Gaussian ellipse intersects with it, used to reduce false positives compared to bounding box checks. It improves upon the Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test by performing exact geometric intersection tests rather than conservative bounding volume checks, thereby reducing overdraw in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It sets itself apart by handling elliptical projections instead of flat rectangles, and is chosen when rendering 3D Gaussian splats. Time Complexity: O(1). The method involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required beyond the input ray and rectangle definitions. Strengths: Extremely fast and numerically stable for axis-aligned primitives. Ideal for bounding boxes and planar surfaces in scene graphs. Limitations: Only applicable to axis-aligned rectangles. Requires separate implementations for different orientations (XY, XZ, YZ) or a generalized permutation approach. When to use: When rendering flat, axis-aligned surfaces or as part of bounding volume hierarchies (BVH) leaf nodes. When not to use: For rotated rectangles or non-planar shapes. The method is a standard component in educational ray tracers and simple rendering engines. It is derived from the analytic intersection of a ray with a plane, constrained by rectangular bounds. The implementation follows a struct-based design with method receivers, typical of Go-based educational ray tracer repositories. hexhowells/GoTracer, https://github.com/hexhowells/GoTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Axis-Aligned Plane Intersection
body: Intersects a ray with an axis-aligned plane defined by an anchor point, extent, and direction index d. It returns the intersection distance t and barycentric-like coordinates u, v. The method uses a direction index to permute coordinate axes, aligning the plane normal with a single axis to simplify the intersection calculation. Inputs: ray: Ray defined by origin O and direction D (3D vectors). anchor: Corner of the plane/rectangle (3D vector). extent: Size of the plane/rectangle along its local axes (3D vector). d: Integer direction index (0–5) mapping to specific axis permutations. frame: Context object providing eyenear (near clip distance w and origin xyz). Outputs: t: Intersection distance along the ray. u, v: Local coordinates on the plane, normalized to [0, 1]. Boolean success flag. Data Structures: Vectors are 3D floats. d is an integer index mapping to specific axis permutations. Steps: 1. Axis Permutation: Select eye, origin, and ray components based on d to align the plane normal with the X-axis of the permuted space. If d < 2: Use axes (x, y, z). If 2 <= d < 4: Use axes (y, x, z). If d >= 4: Use axes (z, x, y). Specifically: eye = appearanceaxes(frame.eyenear.xyz, d), origin = appearanceaxes(anchor, d), delta = appearanceaxes(ray, d). 2. Plane Constant: Compute the plane offset along the normal. plane = origin.x + (1.0 \text{ if } (d \& 1) \text{ else } 0.0) 3. Distance Numerator: distance = plane - eye.x 4. Parallel Check: If delta.x is zero, the ray is parallel to the plane. 5. Intersection Distance: t = \frac{distance}{delta.x} 6. Local Coordinates Numerator: Compute unnormalized local coordinates using the Y and Z components of the permuted space. uNumerator = eye.y + t \cdot delta.y - origin.y vNumerator = eye.z + t \cdot delta.z - origin.z 7. Normalization: u = \frac{uNumerator}{extent.x} v = \frac{vNumerator}{extent.y} (Note: extent.x and extent.y refer to the U and V dimensions in the permuted coordinate space.) 8. Validity Checks: If t is NaN or Inf, or if t < frame.eyenear.w (near clip), return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def axisalignedplaneintersection(rayorigin, raydir, anchor, extent, d, eyenearw): import math # Permutation mapping based on d if d < 2: perm = (0, 1, 2) elif d < 4: perm = (1, 0, 2) else: perm = (2, 0, 1) # Extract components in permuted order eyex = rayorigin[perm[0]] eyey = rayorigin[perm[1]] eyez = rayorigin[perm[2]] deltax = raydir[perm[0]] deltay = raydir[perm[1]] deltaz = raydir[perm[2]] originx = anchor[perm[0]] originy = anchor[perm[1]] originz = anchor[perm[2]] # Permute extent to match the coordinate space extx = extent[perm[0]] exty = extent[perm[1]] # Plane constant plane = originx + (1.0 if (d & 1) else 0.0) distance = plane - eyex # Parallel check if deltax == 0.0: return False, None, None t = distance / deltax # Validity checks if math.isnan(t) or math.isinf(t) or t < eyenearw: return False, None, None # Local coordinates uNumerator = eyey + t deltay - originy vNumerator = eyez + t deltaz - originz # Normalize u = uNumerator / extx v = vNumerator / exty return True, t, u, v Determines the 3D integer voxel cell coordinate and the 3D intersection point given the ray intersection with an axis-aligned plane. It builds on axisalignedplaneintersection. 1. Call axisalignedplaneintersection to get t, u, v. If it fails, return false. 2. Compute local coordinates in world units: localU = u extent.x, localV = v extent.y. 3. Compute cell offset: offset = clamp(floor(vec2(localU, localV)), vec2(0.0), extent - 1.0). 4. Initialize cell with anchor: cell = uvec3(anchor). 5. Add offset to cell based on direction d: if d < 2, add to cell.y and cell.z; if 2 <= d < 4, add to cell.x and cell.z; if d >= 4, add to cell.x and cell.y. 6. Compute 3D point: point = frame.eyenear.xyz + ray t. Time Complexity: O(1). Fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No dynamic allocation. Strengths: Extremely fast; avoids branching on face normal by using a direction index; handles all 6 faces of an AABB uniformly. Limitations: Only works for axis-aligned planes; requires pre-computed direction index d; precision issues may occur if t is very large or deltax is very small. When to use: Ray casting against voxel grids, AABBs, or any set of axis-aligned planes where the face index is known or easily derived. Originated in the bend-voxel project. The method leverages axis-aligned properties to simplify intersection tests, a common optimization in volume rendering and voxel-based rendering. aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Precise Rectangle-Ellipse Intersection Test
head: Precise Rectangle-Ellipse Intersection, Algebraic Simplification for Intersection
body: An algorithm to determine if a rectangular tile needs rendering by checking if a projected Gaussian ellipse intersects with it, used to reduce false positives compared to bounding box checks. It improves upon the Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test by performing exact geometric intersection tests rather than conservative bounding volume checks, thereby reducing overdraw in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Inputs: A rectangle R defined by its four edges (segments). An ellipse E defined by its center and conic coefficients (implicitly via the quadratic form derived from the Gaussian projection). Outputs: Boolean: true if the rectangle and ellipse intersect (or the rectangle center is inside the ellipse), false otherwise. Data Structures: Rectangle edges are treated as line segments [ai, bi] on lines containing the rectangle boundaries. Ellipse intersection with a line is determined by solving a quadratic equation AX^2 + BX + C = 0, where A, B, C are coefficients derived from the ellipse equation and the line equation. Steps: 1. Center Check: Check if the center point of the rectangle lies inside the ellipse. If true, return true. 2. Edge Iteration: For each edge of the rectangle: a. Define the line containing the segment. b. Determine if the line intersects the ellipse. This involves solving the quadratic equation formed by substituting the line equation into the ellipse equation. c. If the line intersects the ellipse, calculate the intersection points (roots of the quadratic). d. Check if any intersection points lie on the rectangle edge segment [ai, bi]. e. If an intersection is found on the segment, return true. 3. Result: If no intersection is found after checking all edges, return false. Algebraic Simplification for Intersection: To avoid high-cost operations (division and square roots) when checking if a tile edge intersects an ellipse, the root check is transformed into algebraic inequalities. Formulas: Quadratic Equation: AX^2 + BX + C = 0. Discriminant: DELTA = B^2 - 4AC. Assume A > 0. Define expressions: e1 = 2Aai + B e2 = 2Abi + B The condition for the line segment [ai, bi] to intersect the ellipse roots \frac{-B \pm \sqrt{DELTA}}{2A} is: ai \leq \frac{-B + \sqrt{DELTA}}{2A} \quad \& \quad bi \geq \frac{-B - \sqrt{DELTA}}{2A} Optimized check avoiding sqrt/div: (e1 \leq 0 \parallel e1^2 \leq DELTA) \quad \& \quad (e2 \geq 0 \parallel e2^2 \leq DELTA) Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Plane-Cube Intersection
head: Plane-Cube Intersection Volume, Volume from a plane slicing a cube
body: This method computes the volume of the irregular polygon formed by the intersection of a plane and a cube. It is designed for scenarios where a planar boundary slices through a volumetric cell, such as determining the fraction of a cell that is partially ionized or covered by a burning front in computational astrophysics. It differs from standard ray-cube intersection by outputting the resulting volume rather than just intersection points, and extends the approach of Salama & Kolb (2005) by explicitly constructing an ordered list of face vertices to facilitate this volume calculation. Inputs: A unit cube defined by 8 vertices \mathbf{V}1 through \mathbf{V}8, enumerated and ordered as specified by the source. A plane parameterized by spherical angles \theta and \phi and the normal ray length dl. Outputs: The volume of the intersection polygon. The set of intersection points on the cube edges. Data Structures: Vertices \mathbf{V}i: 3D Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). Edges E{i \rightarrow j}: Defined by pairs of vertex indices (i, j). Intersection points: 3D coordinates derived from the edge intersection logic. Steps: 1. Define the Plane Normal: Compute the Cartesian coordinates of the normal ray \mathbf{n} using spherical angles \theta and \phi and length dl: \mathbf{n} = [dl \cos(\theta), \ dl \sin(\theta)\sin(\phi), \ dl \cos(\phi) ] Derive the unit normal vector \mathbf{\hat{n}} = \mathbf{n} / \|\mathbf{n}\|. 2. Define the Plane Equation: The plane equation is given by: dl = \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot \mathbf{x} where \mathbf{x} represents the Cartesian coordinates of any point lying on the plane. 3. Iterate Over Cube Edges: For each edge E{i \rightarrow j} connecting vertex \mathbf{V}i to \mathbf{V}j: a. Define the edge line parametrically: E{i \rightarrow j} = \mathbf{V}i + \lambda (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i) b. Calculate the intersection parameter \lambda: \lambda = \frac{ dl - \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot \mathbf{V}i }{\mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i) } c. Check validity: An intersection exists on the segment if and only if 0 \le \lambda \le 1. d. If valid, compute the intersection point \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{V}i + \lambda (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i). 4. Construct the Polygon: Collect all valid intersection points. The resulting shape is an inscribed irregular polygon with 3 to 6 vertices. 5. Compute Volume: Construct an ordered list of the face vertices of the resulting polygon. Use this ordered list to compute the volume of the irregular polygon. The specific algorithm for ordering vertices and calculating the volume from the list is not detailed in the source. Parameters: \theta: Spherical angle, 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi. \phi: Spherical angle, 0 \le \phi \le \pi. dl: Length of the normal ray (distance from origin). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Intersections: If \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i) = 0, the edge is parallel to the plane. Numerically, a guard is required to avoid division by zero. Vertex Ordering: The volume calculation depends on an "ordered list of face vertices". Incorrect ordering will yield incorrect volumes or self-intersecting meshes. The source implies a specific enumeration of the cube vertices \mathbf{V}1 to \mathbf{V}8 is required, but does not provide the coordinate mapping. Polygon Complexity: The number of vertices of the intersecting polygon can vary between 3 and 6, showing "wild patterns" as \theta and \phi change, even if the volume changes smoothly. Computes intersection points between a plane and the 12 edges of a unit cube. Iterates over the 12 edges and computes the parameter t using the plane equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0. If 0 < t < 2, the intersection point is computed and added to the result. The parameter is calculated as t = -\frac{A x0 + B y0 + C z0 + D}{A (x1 - x0) + B (y1 - y0) + C (z1 - z0)}. A known pitfall is that the condition t>0 \ \&\& \ t<2 allows intersections slightly outside the unit cube since the edge length is 2 in this parameterization. The method operates in constant time O(1) and constant space O(1) relative to scene size, as it processes a single cube with a fixed number of edges. It provides an exact analytical volume for planar cuts through cubic cells, which is useful for adaptive mesh refinement or astrophysical simulations involving partial cell coverage. It requires careful handling of vertex ordering for volume integration. The complexity of the intersection polygon topology (3 to 6 vertices) may require case-specific logic for robust mesh generation. Use this method when a planar boundary intersects a cubic volume element and the exact volume of the intersection is required. Do not use it for non-planar cuts or non-cubic primitives. The method was introduced by F.X. Timmes in the context of computational astrophysics, specifically for calculating the fraction of a cell that may be partially ionized or covered by a burning front. It extends the ideas presented by Salama & Kolb in 2005. name: Ray-Triangle Intersection
body: Computes the intersection of a ray with a single triangle in 3D space, determining if the ray hits the triangle's interior and returning the intersection distance. Unlike Sphere Intersection which uses algebraic distance checks, or Ray-Plane/Rectangle Intersection which handles infinite or axis-aligned bounds, this method explicitly tests against a finite, arbitrary triangular surface using barycentric coordinate validation. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (typically normalized), triangle vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection; if true, the distance t along the ray to the intersection point. Data Structures Vertices are stored as 3D vectors (\mathbb{R}^3). Ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters weighttolerance: A small value (e.g., 10^{-4}) used to relax the barycentric coordinate check, allowing rays to pass slightly outside the triangle edges to prevent gaps between adjacent triangles. smallt: A minimum distance threshold to avoid self-intersection or self-shadowing bugs. Steps 1. Compute Triangle Normal: Calculate the normal vector \mathbf{n} of the triangle plane. \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}0)) 2. Ray-Plane Intersection: Calculate the numerator and denominator for the intersection distance t. \text{numerator} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{o}) \text{denominator} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{d}) 3. Parallel Check: If denominator is zero, the ray is parallel to the triangle plane. 4. Distance Check: Compute t = \text{numerator} / \text{denominator}. If t < \text{small\t}, the intersection is too close (behind the ray origin or self-intersecting). 5. Intersection Point: Compute the intersection point \mathbf{p}. \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d} 6. Barycentric Coordinates: Compute the barycentric coordinates (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) of \mathbf{p} relative to the triangle. \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0 \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}0 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}0 \text{dot00} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}1) \text{dot01} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2) \text{dot02} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{v}) \text{dot11} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}2, \mathbf{e}2) \text{dot12} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}2, \mathbf{v}) \text{invDenom} = 1 / (\text{dot00} \cdot \text{dot11} - \text{dot01} \cdot \text{dot01}) \alpha = (\text{dot11} \cdot \text{dot02} - \text{dot01} \cdot \text{dot12}) \cdot \text{invDenom} \beta = (\text{dot00} \cdot \text{dot12} - \text{dot01} \cdot \text{dot02}) \cdot \text{invDenom} \gamma = 1 - \alpha - \beta 7. Inside Check: Check if the barycentric coordinates are within the valid range, relaxed by weighttolerance. \text{if } \alpha \ge -\text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \beta \ge -\text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \gamma \ge -\text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \alpha \le 1 + \text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \beta \le 1 + \text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \gamma \le 1 + \text{weight\tolerance} Return true. Otherwise, return false. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytriangleintersect(o, d, v0, v1, v2, smallt=0.0, weighttolerance=1e-4): # Step 1: Compute triangle normal e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 n = normalize(cross(e1, e2)) # Step 2: Ray-plane intersection parameters numerator = dot(n, v0 - o) denominator = dot(n, d) # Step 3: Parallel check if denominator == 0: return False, 0.0 # Step 4: Distance check t = numerator / denominator if t < smallt: return False, 0.0 # Step 5: Intersection point p = o + t d # Step 6: Barycentric coordinates v = p - v0 dot00 = dot(e1, e1) dot01 = dot(e1, e2) dot02 = dot(e1, v) dot11 = dot(e2, e2) dot12 = dot(e2, v) invDenom = 1.0 / (dot00 dot11 - dot01 dot01) alpha = (dot11 dot02 - dot01 dot12) invDenom beta = (dot00 dot12 - dot01 dot02) invDenom gamma = 1.0 - alpha - beta # Step 7: Inside check with tolerance if (alpha >= -weighttolerance and beta >= -weighttolerance and gamma >= -weighttolerance and alpha <= 1.0 + weighttolerance and beta <= 1.0 + weighttolerance and gamma <= 1.0 + weighttolerance): return True, t else: return False, 0.0 This method determines if a ray intersects a triangle in 3D space using Plücker coordinates to handle arbitrary ray directions. It solves the ray-primitive intersection problem by combining a front-face culling test based on the ray-triangle normal dot product with a winding-order consistency check derived from edge Plücker coordinates. Computes the closest point on a triangle to a query point and the squared distance between them. It solves the problem of finding the minimum Euclidean distance from a 3D point to a triangular surface patch, which is a fundamental primitive for signed distance field (SDF) generation, collision detection, and mesh sampling. It sets itself apart from Ray-Triangle Intersection by solving a minimization problem over the triangle's interior and boundary rather than finding a scalar parameter t along a ray. The Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test determines whether two triangles in 3D space intersect (share any common points) using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). It solves the problem of detecting collisions between triangular primitives, which is a fundamental building block for mesh intersection, voxelization, and constructive solid geometry. Unlike Ray-Triangle Intersection, which tests a ray against a single triangle, this method tests two arbitrary triangles against each other without a predefined viewing direction. This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid by dispatching a compute shader where each thread corresponds to a voxel cell. It determines voxel solidity by testing each cell against every mesh triangle using a Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) broad-phase test followed by a Möller-Trumbore ray-triangle intersection. It differs from hierarchical voxelization by using a brute-force per-voxel, per-triangle approach, making it simple to implement but computationally expensive for high-resolution grids or complex meshes. A faster method to find intersections by projecting 3D vertices to 2D based on a swizzle mode and checking 2D point-in-triangle containment. For each face, the 3D vertices are swizzled according to the template mode, and a 2D point-in-triangle test is called to check if the point is inside the triangle, returning the distance d if true. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The number of operations is constant, involving a few vector cross products, dot products, and divisions. Performance scales linearly with the number of triangles tested. On GPUs, parallel execution across threads allows testing many triangles simultaneously. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for most standard ray tracing scenarios, handles arbitrary triangle orientations. Limitations: Sensitive to numerical precision near triangle edges, which is mitigated by weighttolerance. Not suitable for hierarchical acceleration structures without additional bounding volume checks. When to Use: When testing a ray against a single triangle or a small set of triangles. When Not to Use: When testing against large meshes; use acceleration structures like BVH or KD-trees instead. The method is a fundamental building block in ray tracing and volume rendering, enabling the intersection of rays with triangular mesh geometry. name: General Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates)
head: Triangle Ray Intersection, rayIntersectsTriangle
body: This method determines if a ray intersects a triangle in 3D space using Plücker coordinates to handle arbitrary ray directions. It solves the ray-primitive intersection problem by combining a front-face culling test based on the ray-triangle normal dot product with a winding-order consistency check derived from edge Plücker coordinates. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, triangle vertices \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. Data Structures: vec3f: 3D vector type with components x, y, z. float: 32-bit floating point number. Steps: 1. Normal Calculation: Compute the triangle normal \mathbf{n}. 2. Front-Face Culling: Calculate the dot product between the normal and the ray direction: \cos ND = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} If \cos ND == 0, return false. This ignores the case where the ray lies in the triangle's plane. 3. Intersection Parameter: If the intersection distance t is required, calculate it: t = \frac{-\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{a})}{\cos ND}. 4. Coordinate Translation: Translate the triangle vertices to the ray origin space: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{o} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{o} \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}. 5. Plücker Coordinate Calculation: Compute the Plücker coordinates for the three edges of the triangle relative to the ray direction. The Plücker coordinate function is defined as: \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{a}0, \mathbf{a}1, \mathbf{b}0, \mathbf{b}1) = \mathbf{a}1 \cdot (\mathbf{b}1 \times \mathbf{b}0) + \mathbf{b}1 \cdot (\mathbf{a}1 \times \mathbf{a}0). Apply this to the edges: sx = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) sy = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) sz = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}). 6. Winding Order Check: Determine intersection based on the signs of sx, sy, sz. If \min(sx, sy, sz) \ge 0 or \max(sx, sy, sz) \le 0, return true (intersection). Otherwise, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytriangleintersectionplucker(rayorigin, raydir, tria, trib, tric): # 1. Calculate normal edge1 = trib - tria edge2 = tric - tria normal = cross(edge1, edge2) # 2. Front-face culling cosnd = dot(normal, raydir) if cosnd == 0.0: return False # 3. Calculate t t = -dot(rayorigin - tria, normal) / cosnd # 4. Translate vertices to ray origin space a = tria - rayorigin b = trib - rayorigin c = tric - rayorigin # 5. Compute Plücker coordinates def pluecker(a0, a1, b0, b1): return dot(a1 - a0, cross(b1, b0)) + dot(b1 - b0, cross(a1, a0)) sx = pluecker(vec3f(0.0), raydir, a, b) sy = pluecker(vec3f(0.0), raydir, b, c) sz = pluecker(vec3f(0.0), raydir, c, a) # 6. Check winding order if min(sx, sy, sz) >= 0.0 or max(sx, sy, sz) <= 0.0: return True else: return False Parameters: cosnd threshold: Strictly 0.0 check. Edge Cases: Ray in Plane: If \cos ND == 0, the method returns false, ignoring the possibility of the ray lying in the triangle's plane. Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle area is zero, the normal is zero, leading to division by zero or undefined behavior. Precision: Floating point precision issues may arise near the edges of the triangle. An algorithm to determine if a ray intersects a triangle, optimized for axis-aligned rays using Plücker coordinates to simplify cross products. The Möller-Trumbore algorithm computes the intersection of a ray with a triangle by solving for the parametric distance t and barycentric coordinates (u, v) directly, avoiding the explicit calculation of the triangle's plane equation. It sets itself apart from general analytic methods by using Cramer's rule to derive these parameters in a single step, which minimizes storage requirements and computational overhead. Unlike the Plücker method, which relies on Plücker coordinates to handle arbitrary ray directions with a different algebraic structure, Möller-Trumbore operates directly in Cartesian space using cross and dot products. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The method is efficient for general rays. Strengths: Handles arbitrary ray directions. Limitations: Does not handle rays lying in the triangle's plane. When to use: When intersecting general rays against triangles and only the boolean intersection result is needed. The method is described in the context of general ray-triangle intersection using Plücker coordinates. Plücker coordinates are a representation of lines in projective geometry, often used in computer graphics for efficient line-line and line-plane intersection tests. name: Axis-Aligned Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates)
head: rayIntersectsTriangle (AxisAlignedRay)
body: An algorithm to determine if a ray intersects a triangle, optimized for axis-aligned rays using Plücker coordinates to simplify cross products. Inputs: org: Ray origin (float3). dir: Ray direction (float3), constrained to be axis-aligned. a, b, c: Triangle vertices (float3). n: Triangle normal (float3). Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. Data Structures: Standard 3D vectors and scalars. Steps: 1. Calculate the dot product of the triangle normal and ray direction: \text{cosND} = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{dir}. 2. Calculate the intersection distance t along the ray: t = -\mathbf{n} \cdot (\text{org} - \mathbf{a}) / \text{cosND}. 3. Transform the triangle vertices into the coordinate space centered at the ray origin: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a} - \text{org}, \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} - \text{org}, \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} - \text{org}. 4. Compute Plücker coordinates for the three triangle edges relative to the ray direction using the helper function \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{a}0, \mathbf{a}1, \mathbf{b}0, \mathbf{b}1) = (\mathbf{a}1 - \mathbf{a}0) \cdot (\mathbf{b}1 \times \mathbf{b}0) + (\mathbf{b}1 - \mathbf{b}0) \cdot (\mathbf{a}1 \times \mathbf{a}0). The calls are \text{sx} = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{dir}, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}), \text{sy} = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{dir}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}), and \text{sz} = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{dir}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}). 5. Determine if the ray is inside the triangle by checking if all Plücker coordinates have the same sign: if \min(\text{sx}, \text{sy}, \text{sz}) \ge 0 or \max(\text{sx}, \text{sy}, \text{sz}) \le 0, return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(u, v): return u[0]v[0] + u[1]v[1] + u[2]v[2] def cross(u, v): return (u[1]v[2] - u[2]v[1], u[2]v[0] - u[0]v[2], u[0]v[1] - u[1]v[0]) def pluecker(a0, a1, b0, b1): return dot((a1[0]-a0[0], a1[1]-a0[1], a1[2]-a0[2]), cross(b1, b0)) + \ dot((b1[0]-b0[0], b1[1]-b0[1], b1[2]-b0[2]), cross(a1, a0)) def axisalignedraytriangleintersection(org, dir, a, b, c, n): cosND = dot(n, dir) t = -dot(n, (org[0]-a[0], org[1]-a[1], org[2]-a[2])) / cosND a = (a[0]-org[0], a[1]-org[1], a[2]-org[2]) b = (b[0]-org[0], b[1]-org[1], b[2]-org[2]) c = (c[0]-org[0], c[1]-org[1], c[2]-org[2]) sx = pluecker((0, 0, 0), dir, a, b) sy = pluecker((0, 0, 0), dir, b, c) sz = pluecker((0, 0, 0), dir, c, a) if min(sx, sy, sz) >= 0.0 or max(sx, sy, sz) <= 0.0: return True return False Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the ray is perfectly parallel to the triangle plane (\text{cosND} == 0), the function returns false, ignoring the edge case where the ray might lie in the same 2D plane. name: Möller-Trumbore Ray-Triangle Intersection
head: Möller-Trumbore, MT Algorithm, MT intersection, Ray-Triangle Intersection (Möller-Trumbore), Triangle-Ray Intersection (Möller-Trumbore), Moeller-Trumbore Ray-Triangle Intersection (Embree)
body: The Möller-Trumbore algorithm computes the intersection of a ray with a triangle by solving for the parametric distance t and barycentric coordinates (u, v) directly, avoiding the explicit calculation of the triangle's plane equation. It translates the ray origin and changes the vector basis to yield a vector (t, u, v)^T, minimizing storage requirements and computational overhead. It operates directly in Cartesian space using cross and dot products. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} (3D vector) Ray direction \mathbf{D} (3D vector) Triangle vertices \mathbf{V}1, \mathbf{V}2, \mathbf{V}3 (3D vectors) Epsilon threshold \epsilon for numerical stability (typically 10^{-6} to 10^{-7}) Outputs: Intersection distance t (scalar) Barycentric coordinates u, v (scalars) Boolean success flag or None/false if no intersection Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{pvec}, \mathbf{qvec} are 3D floating-point vectors Scalars det, inv\det, u, v, t are floating-point numbers Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors of the triangle: \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{V}2 - \mathbf{V}1 \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{V}3 - \mathbf{V}1 2. Compute the vector from \mathbf{V}1 to the ray origin: \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{O} - \mathbf{V}1 3. Compute the cross product of the ray direction and the second edge: \mathbf{pvec} = \mathbf{D} \times \mathbf{e}2 4. Compute the determinant of the system: det = \mathbf{e}1 \cdot \mathbf{pvec} 5. Check for parallelism: If |det| < \epsilon, the ray is parallel to the triangle plane (or lies in it). Return no intersection. Compute the inverse determinant: inv\det = 1.0 / det 6. Compute the first barycentric coordinate u: u = (\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{pvec}) \times inv\det If u < 0.0 or u > 1.0, the intersection point lies outside the triangle edge. Return no intersection. 7. Compute the cross product of \mathbf{T} and the first edge: \mathbf{qvec} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{e}1 8. Compute the second barycentric coordinate v: v = (\mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{qvec}) \times inv\det If v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0, the intersection point lies outside the triangle. Return no intersection. 9. Compute the intersection distance t: t = (\mathbf{e}2 \cdot \mathbf{qvec}) \times inv\det If t < \epsilon (or t \le 0), the intersection is behind the ray origin or at the origin. Return no intersection. 10. Return success with t, u, v. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mullertrumbore(rayorigin, raydirection, v1, v2, v3, epsilon=1e-7): # Step 1: Edge vectors e1 = v2 - v1 e2 = v3 - v1 # Step 2: Vector from V1 to ray origin tvec = rayorigin - v1 # Step 3: Cross product of ray direction and second edge pvec = cross(raydirection, e2) # Step 4: Determinant det = dot(e1, pvec) # Step 5: Check for parallelism if abs(det) < epsilon: return None invdet = 1.0 / det # Step 6: Compute u u = dot(tvec, pvec) invdet if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return None # Step 7: Cross product of tvec and first edge qvec = cross(tvec, e1) # Step 8: Compute v v = dot(raydirection, qvec) invdet if v < 0.0 or (u + v) > 1.0: return None # Step 9: Compute t t = dot(e2, qvec) invdet if t < epsilon: return None return {'t': t, 'u': u, 'v': v} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If the determinant is near zero, division by zero occurs. The check |det| < \epsilon prevents this. Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle vertices are collinear, the area is zero, and the determinant may be zero or near-zero. Back-Facing Triangles: The algorithm returns intersections for both front and back faces. Numerical Precision: Using a small epsilon is critical for robustness, especially when rays align with mesh vertices or edges. Eliminates vertical slice artifacts in mesh voxelization by introducing a small, direction-aware offset to ray origins before performing ray-triangle intersection tests. It specifically addresses numerical instability in the Möller-Trumbore algorithm when rays align exactly with mesh vertices or edges, a common issue in meshes with regular grid topology such as terrain height maps. Unlike alternative approaches that bypass ray-tracing entirely (e.g., using Signed Distance Fields), this technique preserves the geometric fidelity of the original mesh while ensuring robust intersection detection. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: It is considered one of the fastest ray-triangle intersection routines for triangles without precomputed plane equations. Optimized variants exist that delay division or handle sign checks differently, but the core logic remains the same. Strengths: Minimal storage, no need to compute plane equations, robust handling of barycentric coordinates directly. Limitations: Does not inherently handle back-face culling (requires caller intervention). The algorithm was introduced by Tomas Möller and Ben Trumbore in 1997 in the paper "Fast, Minimum Storage Ray/Triangle Intersection". It is widely used in volume rendering for mesh voxelization and ray-triangle intersection tests. idealab-isu/GPView, https://github.com/idealab-isu/GPView, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, https://github.com/bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Mesh Voxelization - GitHub, https://github.com/davidstutz/mesh-voxelization, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) lijiemark/floating-islands-generator, https://github.com/lijiemark/floating-islands-generator, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, https://github.com/matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) yeataro/TD-Raymarching-System, https://github.com/yeataro/TD-Raymarching-System, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, https://github.com/ojaisnielsen/dtu-2010-cuda-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) abhishektrip/SliceBasedVolumeRendering, https://github.com/abhishektrip/SliceBasedVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, https://github.com/migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) (PDF) Axis‐Normalized Ray‐Box Intersection - ResearchGate, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/390921688Axis-NormalizedRay-BoxIntersection, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Ray Origin Jitter for Mesh Voxelization
head: Jittered Ray Origins, STL Voxelization Artifacts Fix
body: This method eliminates vertical slice artifacts in mesh voxelization by adding a small offset to ray origins before performing ray-triangle intersection tests Möller-Trumbore Ray-Triangle Intersection. It specifically addresses numerical instability in the Möller-Trumbore algorithm when rays align exactly with mesh vertices or edges, which is common in meshes with regular grid topology such as terrain height maps. An alternative approach to avoid this coplanarity issue is to use Signed Distance Field (SDF) files, which bypass ray-tracing entirely. Inputs and Outputs Input: Voxel grid position (xyz), an initial offset vector (offset), and the ray direction axis (direction). Output: A jittered ray origin vector (rorigin) for the subsequent Möller-Trumbore intersection test. Data Structures xyz: Three-dimensional coordinates of the voxel position. offset: Vector displacement from the voxel center to the ray start point. direction: Integer axis index (0, 1, or 2 for X, Y, Z respectively) indicating the primary ray direction. Steps 1. Calculate the base ray origin by adding the voxel position and the predefined offset: r{\text{origin}} = \text{position}(xyz) + \text{offset} 2. Define the jitter magnitude constant as 0.001 times the voxel size. 3. Add jitter to the components of r{\text{origin}} that are perpendicular to the ray direction. The jitter is applied to component N only if the ray direction is not aligned with axis N (\text{direction} \neq N). Parameters jitter: The magnitude of the offset added to ray origins. The standard value is 0.001 \times \text{voxel\size}, representing 0.1\% of the voxel size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Regular Grid Topology: The primary failure case occurs with meshes generated from height maps or regular grids (e.g., hill.stl with 421 Y-aligned planes) where vertices lie on exact coordinates. Without jitter, rays often start exactly on vertex planes, leading to undefined intersection results or missed voxels. Precision: The 0.1\% offset is empirically shown to be imperceptible in the final simulation while effectively solving the coplanarity issue. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jitterrayorigin(positionxyz, offset, direction, voxelsize): # positionxyz and offset are 3D vectors rorigin = positionxyz + offset jitter = 0.001 voxelsize if direction != 0: rorigin.x += jitter if direction != 1: rorigin.y += jitter if direction != 2: rorigin.z += jitter return rorigin Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively eliminates vertical slice artifacts in voxelized terrain and regular meshes. Simple to integrate into existing ray-triangle intersection kernels. Limitations: Only addresses coplanarity issues related to ray origins. Requires knowledge of the ray direction and voxel size. When to use: Use this method when voxelizing STL meshes (especially terrain/heightmap data) using ray-triangle intersection and observing vertical gaps or missing voxels. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique was proposed in a GitHub pull request to the FluidX3D project, a lattice Boltzmann CFD software, to fix vertical slice artifacts in STL mesh voxelization. The issue was identified when voxelizing terrain meshes with regular grid structures, where the Möller-Trumbore algorithm failed due to rays aligning exactly with mesh vertices. The solution, introduced by user meet-brad-ch in December 2025, adds a small jitter to ray origins perpendicular to the ray direction. It was tested on a hill.stl terrain mesh with 421 Y-aligned planes, showing a transition from visible artifacts to clean voxelization. Fix vertical slice artifacts in mesh voxelization, https://github.com/ProjectPhysX/FluidX3D/pull/323, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Point-Triangle Distance
head: Closest Point on Triangle, Point to Triangle Distance, closestPointOnTriangleToPoint, pointToTriangleDistSqr
body: Computes the closest point on a triangle to a query point and returns the squared distance, utilizing barycentric coordinates and Voronoi-region decomposition to handle edge and vertex cases. The source implementation provides two distinct functions: one returning the closest point and barycentric coordinates, and another returning the squared distance. It differs from Ray-Triangle Intersection by solving a proximity minimization problem rather than a ray-primitive intersection, and from Unsigned Triangle Distance by explicitly returning the barycentric coordinates of the closest point alongside the distance. Inputs: Triangle vertices v0, v1, v2 (3D vectors). Query point p (3D vector). Outputs: Closest point on the triangle surface. Barycentric coordinates t0, t1 such that closest = v0 + t0(v1 - v0) + t1(v2 - v0). Squared distance from p to the closest point. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector type supporting arithmetic operations and dot product. Scalar floating-point type for parameters t0, t1. Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors: edge0 = v1 - v0 edge1 = v2 - v0 2. Compute vector from triangle vertex to query point: w = v0 - p 3. Compute dot products: a = edge0 \cdot edge0 b = edge0 \cdot edge1 c = edge1 \cdot edge1 d = edge0 \cdot w e = edge1 \cdot w 4. Compute determinant and parameters: det = a \cdot c - b \cdot b s = b \cdot e - c \cdot d t = b \cdot d - a \cdot e 5. Determine region based on s + t relative to det: Case A: s + t < det (Closest point is inside the triangle or on an edge/vertex) If s < 0 and t < 0: If d < 0: s = \text{clamp}(-d / a, 0, 1) t = 0 Else: s = 0 t = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) If s < 0 and t \ge 0: s = \text{clamp}(-d / a, 0, 1) t = 0 If s \ge 0 and t < 0: s = 0 t = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) Case B: s + t \ge det (Closest point is outside the triangle's edge opposite vertex 0) If s < 0: Let tmp0 = b + d Let tmp1 = c + e If tmp1 > tmp0: s = \text{clamp}((tmp1 - tmp0) / (a - 2b + c), 0, 1) t = 1 - s Else: s = 0 t = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) If s \ge 0 and t < 0: If a + d > b + e: s = \text{clamp}((c + e - b - d) / (a - 2b + c), 0, 1) t = 1 - s Else: s = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) t = 0 6. Compute closest point: closest = v0 + s \cdot edge0 + t \cdot edge1 7. Return squared distance: dist^2 = \|closest - p\|^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(u, v): return u.x v.x + u.y v.y + u.z v.z def clamp(x, minval, maxval): if x < minval: return minval if x > maxval: return maxval return x def closestpointontriangle(v0, v1, v2, p): edge0 = v1 - v0 edge1 = v2 - v0 w = v0 - p a = dot(edge0, edge0) b = dot(edge0, edge1) c = dot(edge1, edge1) d = dot(edge0, w) e = dot(edge1, w) det = a c - b b s = b e - c d t = b d - a e if s + t < det: if s < 0 and t < 0: if d < 0: s = clamp(-d / a, 0.0, 1.0) t = 0.0 else: s = 0.0 t = clamp(-e / c, 0.0, 1.0) elif s < 0: s = clamp(-d / a, 0.0, 1.0) t = 0.0 elif t < 0: s = 0.0 t = clamp(-e / c, 0.0, 1.0) else: if s < 0: tmp0 = b + d tmp1 = c + e if tmp1 > tmp0: denom = a - 2 b + c s = clamp((tmp1 - tmp0) / denom, 0.0, 1.0) t = 1.0 - s else: s = 0.0 t = clamp(-e / c, 0.0, 1.0) elif t < 0: if a + d > b + e: denom = a - 2 b + c s = clamp((c + e - b - d) / denom, 0.0, 1.0) t = 1.0 - s else: s = clamp(-e / c, 0.0, 1.0) t = 0.0 closest = v0 + s edge0 + t edge1 distsq = dot(closest - p, closest - p) return closest, distsq, s, t Parameters: Vec3T: Any vector type supporting arithmetic and dot product. v0, v1, v2: Triangle vertices. p: Query point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate triangles (zero area, collinear or coincident vertices) are handled implicitly: the face-interior test naturally fails and the code falls through to the nearest edge or vertex result. Computes the unsigned distance from a query point to a triangle defined by three vertices a, b, c. It checks if the point projects inside the triangle to decide between computing the minimum edge distance or the plane distance. Mesh SDF Sampling constructs a callable signed distance field (SDF) sampler function from a THREE.BufferGeometry instance and a world transform matrix. It solves the problem of evaluating the shortest signed distance from arbitrary world-space coordinates to a triangle mesh surface, where negative values indicate interior points and positive values indicate exterior points. It differs from raw mesh intersection tests by providing continuous distance gradients essential for smooth shading and anti-aliasing. This method voxelizes watertight triangular meshes into Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or occupancy grids by computing distances from voxel reference points to mesh faces or by testing for geometric intersection between triangles and voxel boxes. It distinguishes itself from pure SDF-based occupancy derivation by using explicit triangle-box intersection tests to guarantee that any voxel intersecting the mesh surface is marked as occupied, avoiding voxels that might be missed by SDF-only approaches. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance for SDF computation. Computes the barycentric coordinates of a 3D point relative to a triangle defined by three vertices. It solves the problem of expressing a point's position within a triangle's local coordinate system, which is a prerequisite for Point-Triangle Distance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the geometric projection and area-based calculation rather than distance minimization or mesh sampling. The Triangle Coverage Test verifies whether a triangle T is completely contained within the union of three spheres centered at its vertices, with radii determined by a scalar field function f evaluated at those vertices. It solves the problem of ensuring that a discrete sampling of an implicit volume is dense enough to guarantee no gaps exist between the approximating spheres, which is critical for sphere carving algorithms. Unlike general ray-triangle intersection which determines visibility, this test determines topological completeness of the volume approximation. It is distinct from Point-Triangle Distance by focusing on set containment rather than proximity, and from Barycentric Coordinate Calculation by using barycentric logic only implicitly to define the triangle domain. Zero Set Initialization of Meshes is a method for initializing the signed distance field (SDF) of a triangular mesh by identifying samples that lie on or near the mesh surface (the "zero set") and assigning them initial signs. It solves the problem of establishing an accurate initial distance field from a polygonal mesh without relying on global topological information. It differs from its sibling Unsigned Triangle Distance by computing signed distances and from Mesh SDF Sampling by focusing specifically on the initialization phase for distance transforms rather than general sampling. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance to determine geometric proximity. Computes the unsigned distance from a point to a quadrilateral defined by four vertices a, b, c, d. It checks if the point is inside the projected quad to decide between edge distance and plane distance. If the point is inside the quad (sum of signs < 3), return the minimum squared distance to the four edges. Otherwise, return the squared distance to the plane containing the quad. Edge distance uses projection: \text{proj}{ba}(pa) = ba \cdot \text{clamp}(\frac{ba \cdot pa}{\|ba\|^2}, 0, 1). Parameters: a, b, c, d: vec3, the four vertices of the quadrilateral in order. Identifies the nearest triangle to a burr head from a triangle cache. Determines the plane on which this nearest triangle lies and calculates the distance (d) from the burr center to that plane. If d > burr radius (r), no collision has occurred. If d \le r, collision is recorded and two values are computed: force vector is set to the nearest triangle's normal, and link distance is calculated as burr radius minus burr centre's distance from the plane. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance and hardware scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. Originating from Ericson's "Real-Time Collision Detection" (Sec. 5.1.5), the method uses Voronoi-region decomposition to efficiently find the closest point on a triangle. It is used in collision detection and signed distance field computations. name: Unsigned Triangle Distance
head: Unsigned Triangle, udTriangle
body: Computes the unsigned distance from a query point to a triangle defined by three vertices a, b, c. It checks if the point projects inside the triangle to decide between computing the minimum edge distance or the plane distance. Inputs: p: Query point (vec3). a, b, c: Triangle vertices (vec3). Outputs: d: Unsigned distance (float). Data Structures: Intermediate vectors ba, pa, cb, pb, ac, pc, nor (all vec3). Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors and point-to-vertex vectors: ba = b - a, \quad pa = p - a cb = c - b, \quad pb = p - b ac = a - c, \quad pc = p - c. 2. Compute the triangle normal: nor = ba \times ac. 3. Determine if the point projects inside the triangle by summing the signs of the cross products of each edge with the normal against the corresponding point vector: inside = (\text{sign}(\text{dot}(\text{cross}(ba, nor), pa)) + \text{sign}(\text{dot}(\text{cross}(cb, nor), pb)) + \text{sign}(\text{dot}(\text{cross}(ac, nor), pc))) < 2.0. 4. If inside, compute the minimum squared distance to the three edges. For each edge (e.g., ba), project pa onto ba clamped to [0, 1]: proj = ba \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{ba \cdot pa}{\|ba\|^2}, 0.0, 1.0\right) dist^2 = \|proj - pa\|^2. 5. If not inside, compute the squared distance to the plane containing the triangle: dist^2 = \frac{(nor \cdot pa)^2}{\|nor\|^2}. 6. Return \sqrt{dist^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def cross(v1, v2): return (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def sign(x): return 1 if x > 0 else (-1 if x < 0 else 0) def dot2(v): return dot(v, v) def udTriangle(p, a, b, c): ba = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]) pa = (p[0]-a[0], p[1]-a[1], p[2]-a[2]) cb = (c[0]-b[0], c[1]-b[1], c[2]-b[2]) pb = (p[0]-b[0], p[1]-b[1], p[2]-b[2]) ac = (a[0]-c[0], a[1]-c[1], a[2]-c[2]) pc = (p[0]-c[0], p[1]-c[1], p[2]-c[2]) nor = cross(ba, ac) s1 = sign(dot(cross(ba, nor), pa)) s2 = sign(dot(cross(cb, nor), pb)) s3 = sign(dot(cross(ac, nor), pc)) inside = (s1 + s2 + s3) < 2.0 if inside: projba = (ba[0]clamp(dot(ba, pa)/dot2(ba), 0.0, 1.0), ba[1]clamp(dot(ba, pa)/dot2(ba), 0.0, 1.0), ba[2]clamp(dot(ba, pa)/dot2(ba), 0.0, 1.0)) distba = dot2((projba[0]-pa[0], projba[1]-pa[1], projba[2]-pa[2])) projcb = (cb[0]clamp(dot(cb, pb)/dot2(cb), 0.0, 1.0), cb[1]clamp(dot(cb, pb)/dot2(cb), 0.0, 1.0), cb[2]clamp(dot(cb, pb)/dot2(cb), 0.0, 1.0)) distcb = dot2((projcb[0]-pb[0], projcb[1]-pb[1], projcb[2]-pb[2])) projac = (ac[0]clamp(dot(ac, pc)/dot2(ac), 0.0, 1.0), ac[1]clamp(dot(ac, pc)/dot2(ac), 0.0, 1.0), ac[2]clamp(dot(ac, pc)/dot2(ac), 0.0, 1.0)) distac = dot2((projac[0]-pc[0], projac[1]-pc[1], projac[2]-pc[2])) return math.sqrt(min(distba, min(distcb, distac))) else: return math.sqrt(dot(nor, pa)dot(nor, pa) / dot2(nor)) Parameters: a, b, c: vec3. Vertices of the triangle. Order does not affect unsigned distance magnitude, but affects normal direction (used only for the inside check logic which is robust to winding). Edge Cases: Degenerate Triangle: If a, b, c are collinear, nor is zero. The plane distance formula divides by \|nor\|^2, causing division by zero. A guard should check dot2(nor) < epsilon and fallback to point-to-segment distance on the longest edge. Point on Plane: If the point lies on the plane but outside the triangle, the plane distance formula yields 0 because nor \cdot pa = 0. This correctly represents the distance to the infinite plane, though the point is outside the triangle boundary. Precision: Clamping prevents extrapolation errors on edges. Computes the center and radius of the unique circle passing through three non-collinear vertices a, b, c of a triangle. This method is primarily used in volume rendering to define the bounding sphere (splat) for triangle-based leaf nodes, as described in Unsigned Triangle Distance. It is distinguished by its formulation using vector cross products and coordinate differences, which minimizes numerical error for vertices far from the origin, and by a specific fallback strategy for obtuse triangles. Time Complexity: O(1). Fixed number of vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No dynamic allocation. Strengths: Robust handling of edge/vertex proximity without explicit case branching for barycentric coordinates. Fast execution suitable for ray marching. Limitations: Does not provide signed distance (orientation). Degenerate triangles cause division by zero. When to use: When only magnitude of distance is needed, e.g., for blending or collision response. When not to use: When surface normal orientation is required (use Signed Triangle Distance). Originated in the GLSL SDF primitives library by Marklundin. It is a standard primitive in ray marching and distance field rendering. marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Circum-Center Calculation
head: Circum-center, Circumcircle Center
body: Computes the circum-center and circum-radius of a triangle defined by three vertices a, b, c. It is used to derive bounding spheres for triangle-based leaf nodes in volume rendering. Inputs: Three vertices a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Absolute circum-center C and circum-radius R. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors relative to a: ab = b - a, ac = c - a. 2. Compute A(b, c) = ab \times ac. Evaluate the denominator 2|A(b, c)|^2. If near zero, the vertices are co-linear (degenerate). 3. For non-degenerate triangles, determine if the triangle is obtuse. If obtuse, approximate the circum-center as the midpoint of the longest edge and the circum-radius as half the length of that edge. 4. For non-obtuse triangles, compute the relative circum-center m{tri} using the analytic formula. 5. Compute the absolute center C = a + m{tri} and the radius R = |m{tri}|. Formula: Let A(u, v) = (u - a) \times (v - a). The relative circum-center m{tri} is: m{tri} = \frac{|c - a|^2 A(b, c) \times (b - a) + |b - a|^2 (c - a) \times A(b, c)}{2 |A(b, c)|^2} Where: | \cdot | denotes the Euclidean norm. \times denotes the cross product. The denominator is 2 |A(b, c)|^2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degeneracy: The denominator vanishes when vertices are co-linear. Numerical Stability: The formula uses differences of coordinates rather than absolute values, which reduces relative error since vertices are typically closer to each other than to the origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Tuple, List def crossproduct(u: List[float], v: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [ u[1]v[2] - u[2]v[1], u[2]v[0] - u[0]v[2], u[0]v[1] - u[1]v[0] ] def dotproduct(u: List[float], v: List[float]) -> float: return u[0]v[0] + u[1]v[1] + u[2]v[2] def vectorsub(u: List[float], v: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [u[0]-v[0], u[1]-v[1], u[2]-v[2]] def vectornormsq(u: List[float]) -> float: return dotproduct(u, u) def trianglecircumcenter(a: List[float], b: List[float], c: List[float]) -> Tuple[List[float], float]: ab = vectorsub(b, a) ac = vectorsub(c, a) Abc = crossproduct(ab, ac) denomsq = 2.0 vectornormsq(Abc) # Fallback for degenerate (co-linear) vertices if denomsq < 1e-12: lenab = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ab)) lenac = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ac)) lenbc = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(vectorsub(c, b))) maxlen = max(lenab, lenac, lenbc) if maxlen == lenab: return [(a[0]+b[0])/2, (a[1]+b[1])/2, (a[2]+b[2])/2], lenab / 2.0 elif maxlen == lenac: return [(a[0]+c[0])/2, (a[1]+c[1])/2, (a[2]+c[2])/2], lenac / 2.0 else: return [(b[0]+c[0])/2, (b[1]+c[1])/2, (b[2]+c[2])/2], lenbc / 2.0 # Check for obtuse triangle ba = vectorsub(a, b) bc = vectorsub(c, b) ca = vectorsub(a, c) cb = vectorsub(b, c) dota = dotproduct(ab, ac) dotb = dotproduct(ba, bc) dotc = dotproduct(ca, cb) if dota < 0 or dotb < 0 or dotc < 0: lenab = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ab)) lenac = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ac)) lenbc = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(bc)) maxlen = max(lenab, lenac, lenbc) if maxlen == lenab: return [(a[0]+b[0])/2, (a[1]+b[1])/2, (a[2]+b[2])/2], lenab / 2.0 elif maxlen == lenac: return [(a[0]+c[0])/2, (a[1]+c[1])/2, (a[2]+c[2])/2], lenac / 2.0 else: return [(b[0]+c[0])/2, (b[1]+c[1])/2, (b[2]+c[2])/2], lenbc / 2.0 term1vec = crossproduct(Abc, ab) term2vec = crossproduct(ac, Abc) term1 = vectornormsq(ac) term1vec term2 = vectornormsq(ab) term2vec numerator = [term1[0] + term2[0], term1[1] + term2[1], term1[2] + term2[2]] mtri = [numerator[0] / denomsq, numerator[1] / denomsq, numerator[2] / denomsq] center = [a[0] + mtri[0], a[1] + mtri[1], a[2] + mtri[2]] radius = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(mtri)) return center, radius Computes the center and radius of the sphere passing through four vertices a, b, c, d. It is chosen when tetrahedral primitives are used instead of triangles. The relative circum-center m{tet} is: m{tet} = \frac{|d - a|^2 A(b, c) + |c - a|^2 A(d, b) + |b - a|^2 A(c, d)}{2 \det\begin{pmatrix} [b-a]x & [b-a]y & [b-a]z \\ [c-a]x & [c-a]y & [c-a]z \\ [d-a]x & [d-a]y & [d-a]z \end{pmatrix}} Where A(u, v) = (u - a) \times (v - a) and [u]k is the k-th component. The absolute center is a + m{tet} and radius is |m{tet}|. Using differences of coordinates rather than absolute values reduces relative error, as vertices are usually nearer to each other than to the origin. The formula becomes unstable if the denominator vanishes, which occurs when the tetrahedron is nearly degenerate (flat or needle-shaped). Constant-time evaluation per primitive. Numerically stable for non-degenerate triangles when using coordinate differences. Unstable for degenerate inputs. Not given in the sources for measured performance or scaling behavior. Originated in the TetSplat paper by Museth and Lombeyda (2004) for real-time rendering and volume clipping of large meshes. The method is adapted from reference [19] in the original paper. It is used to derive leaf nodes for hierarchical volume representations from triangle meshes.
