name: Mesh SDF Sampling
head: Signed Distance Field Sampler from Geometry, createGeometrySdfSampler
body: Mesh SDF Sampling constructs a callable signed distance field (SDF) sampler function from a THREE.BufferGeometry instance and a world transform matrix. It solves the problem of evaluating the shortest signed distance from arbitrary world-space coordinates to a triangle mesh surface, where negative values indicate interior points and positive values indicate exterior points. It differs from raw mesh intersection tests by providing continuous distance gradients essential for smooth shading and anti-aliasing. Inputs: geometry: A THREE.BufferGeometry instance. Must be indexed. matrix: A THREE.Matrix4 representing the world transform of the mesh. Outputs: A function sampler(x, y, z) returning a number (the signed distance). Data Structures: worldPositions: An array of vertices transformed into world space. Size equals geometry.attributes.position.count. index: An integer array from geometry.index.array. position: The THREE.BufferAttribute from geometry.attributes.position. Temporary Vectors (allocated once, reused): va, vb, vc: Vertices of the current triangle. ab, ac, bc: Edge vectors. ap, bp, cp: Vectors from vertices to point p. n: Normal vector. p, q: Point p (query), q (closest point on triangle). bestPoint: The closest point found so far. bestNormal: The normal at bestPoint. toPoint: Vector from bestPoint to p. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if geometry.index exists. If not, throw an error "Geometry must be indexed". 2. Precomputation: Extract position and index arrays. Initialize worldPositions array. Iterate i from 0 to position.count - 1: create a vector from position at index i, apply matrix to transform it to world space, and store in worldPositions[i]. 3. Sampler Function Definition: Return a function sampler(x, y, z). 4. Query Execution: Inside the function, set p to (x, y, z) and initialize closestDistance2 to Infinity. 5. Triangle Iteration: Iterate i from 0 to index.length - 1 with step 3: get indices ia = index[i], ib = index[i+1], ic = index[i+2]. Retrieve va = worldPositions[ia], vb = worldPositions[ib], vc = worldPositions[ic]. 6. Closest Point & Distance: Compute q as the closest point on triangle va, vb, vc to p. Compute distance2 = p.distanceToSquared(q). 7. Update Best: If distance2 < closestDistance2: update closestDistance2 = distance2. Copy q to bestPoint. Compute edge vectors ab = vb - va, ac = vc - va. Compute bestNormal = ab.cross(ac).normalize(). 8. Sign Calculation: After the loop, compute toPoint = p - bestPoint. Compute dot = toPoint.dot(bestNormal). Set sign = 1 if dot >= 0, else sign = -1. 9. Return: Return Math.sqrt(closestDistance2) sign. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def set(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def copy(self, other): self.x, self.y, self.z = other.x, other.y, other.z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def scale(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def cross(self, other): return Vec3(self.y other.z - self.z other.y, self.z other.x - self.x other.z, self.x other.y - self.y other.x) def lengthsq(self): return self.dot(self) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.lengthsq()) def normalize(self): l = self.length() return self.scale(1.0 / l) if l > 1e-12 else Vec3() def lerp(self, other, t): return self.add(other.sub(self).scale(t)) def closestpointontriangle(p, a, b, c): ab = b.sub(a) ac = c.sub(a) ap = p.sub(a) d1 = ab.dot(ap) d2 = ac.dot(ap) if d1 <= 0.0 and d2 <= 0.0: return a.copy() bp = p.sub(b) d3 = ab.dot(bp) d4 = ab.dot(ab) if d3 >= 0.0 and d1 <= d3: t = d1 / d4 return a.lerp(b, t) cp = p.sub(c) d5 = ac.dot(cp) d6 = ac.dot(ac) if d5 <= 0.0 and d2 <= d5: t = d2 / d6 return a.lerp(c, t) vc = ap.sub(ab.scale(d1 / d4)) if vc.dot(vc) <= 0.0: t = d1 / d4 return a.lerp(b, t) vb = ap.sub(ac.scale(d2 / d6)) if vb.dot(vb) <= 0.0: t = d2 / d6 return a.lerp(c, t) # Point is inside the triangle face; project onto the plane n = ab.cross(ac).normalize() dist = ap.dot(n) return p.sub(n.scale(dist)) def creategeometrysdfsampler(geometry, matrix): if not geometry.index: raise ValueError("Geometry must be indexed") positionattr = geometry.attributes.position indexarr = geometry.index.array poscount = positionattr.count worldpositions = [] tempvec = Vec3() for i in range(poscount): tempvec.set(positionattr.getX(i), positionattr.getY(i), positionattr.getZ(i)) # Apply matrix transform (simplified for pseudocode clarity) # In practice: tempvec.applyMatrix4(matrix) worldpositions.append(tempvec.copy()) va = Vec3() vb = Vec3() vc = Vec3() ab = Vec3() ac = Vec3() topoint = Vec3() bestpoint = Vec3() bestnormal = Vec3() q = Vec3() p = Vec3() def sampler(x, y, z): p.set(x, y, z) closestdistance2 = float('inf') for i in range(0, len(indexarr), 3): ia = indexarr[i] ib = indexarr[i+1] ic = indexarr[i+2] va.copy(worldpositions[ia]) vb.copy(worldpositions[ib]) vc.copy(worldpositions[ic]) q.copy(closestpointontriangle(p, va, vb, vc)) distsq = p.sub(q).lengthsq() if distsq < closestdistance2: closestdistance2 = distsq bestpoint.copy(q) ab.sub(vb, va) ac.sub(vc, va) bestnormal.cross(ab, ac).normalize() topoint.sub(p, bestpoint) dot = topoint.dot(bestnormal) sign = 1.0 if dot >= 0.0 else -1.0 return math.sqrt(closestdistance2) sign return sampler Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-indexed Geometry: Throws an error if geometry.index is falsy. Precision: Uses distanceToSquared to avoid square roots during comparison, then applies Math.sqrt at the end. Sign Determination: The sign is determined by the dot product of the vector from the closest point to the query point and the triangle normal. This method constructs a callable signed distance field (SDF) sampler function from a THREE.Mesh instance, enabling ray-marching algorithms to query distances to complex geometry. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the shortest signed distance from arbitrary world-space coordinates to a triangle mesh surface, where negative values indicate interior points and positive values indicate exterior points. It differs from generic geometry samplers by specifically handling the THREE.Mesh abstraction, including automatic world matrix updates, and delegates the core geometric computation to a lower-level geometry sampler. name: Surface Distance Query
head: Minimum Surface Distance Query, Closest Surface Search
body: Surface Distance Query is a method for determining the minimum Euclidean distance from a query point to a collection of geometric surfaces, while optionally identifying the specific surface responsible for that minimum distance. It solves the problem of proximity detection in scenes containing multiple distinct objects or mesh parts, serving as the foundational lookup mechanism for Signed Distance Field (SDF) Samplers built from meshes [Parent]. Unlike single-mesh distance queries, this method aggregates results across a list of surfaces, enabling complex scene representations where the global distance is the minimum of local surface distances. Inputs: point: A 3D coordinate (x, y, z) in world space. surfaces: A list or array of surface objects. Each surface object must provide a method to compute its distance at a given point. Outputs: mindist: The scalar minimum distance found. closestsurface: The reference to the surface object that yielded mindist. Data Structures: surfaces: An iterable collection of surface handles. mindist: Initialized to a large constant representing the maximum search radius. closestsurface: Initialized to null or None. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize mindist to MAXDISTANCE (a value larger than any expected scene dimension, e.g., 2000.0). 2. Initialize closestsurface to null. 3. Iterate through each surface in the surfaces list: a. Query the surface for its distance at the point. b. If the returned distance is less than mindist: i. Set mindist to the returned distance. ii. Set closestsurface to the current surface. 4. Return mindist and closestsurface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacedistancequery(point, surfaces, maxdistance=2000.0): """ Finds the minimum distance from point to any surface in the list. Args: point: Tuple or array of (x, y, z). surfaces: List of objects with a distance computation method. maxdistance: Upper bound for initialization. Returns: mindist: Float, the minimum distance. closestsurface: Object, the surface yielding the minimum distance. """ mindist = maxdistance closestsurface = None for surface in surfaces: # Query the surface for its distance at the point d = surface.distance(point) if d < mindist: mindist = d closestsurface = surface return mindist, closestsurface Parameters: maxdistance: Typical value depends on scene scale. In the reference implementation, MAXDISTANCE is set to 2000f. MINDISTANCE: A lower bound threshold used in ray marching contexts to terminate early if the distance is sufficiently small (e.g., 0.2f). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty List: If surfaces is empty, the function returns maxdistance and null. The caller must handle this case to avoid dereferencing a null surface. Precision: Floating-point comparison d < mindist is standard. For signed distances, negative values (inside geometry) will correctly update the minimum if they are smaller than the current positive minimum. Performance: This is a linear scan O(N) where N is the number of surfaces. For large N, spatial partitioning (BVH, Grid) is required before querying individual surfaces, but the query logic itself remains a reduction. Definition: A method for regularizing the non-occupied regions of a learned radiance field by supervising the "object code" using estimated surface distances. It solves the problem of ambiguous empty space in neural rendering, where the model may incorrectly assign object semantics to background voxels. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering losses by explicitly computing a "surfaceness" and "emptiness" score for every sample point along a ray, allowing for targeted supervision of the object field's background channel. Definition: A configuration for high-density meshes (e.g., vegetation with masked materials like leaves/branches) where surfaces contain many holes and cannot be treated as solid opaque boundaries. It generates distance fields for both sides of the geometry. When to choose: Use for semi-transparent or highly perforated geometry like trees and grass where standard one-sided distance fields fail to capture the interior/exterior relationship correctly. Pitfall: Enabling this increases ray marching cost because the surface becomes semi-transparent in the distance field representation, requiring more steps to find the mesh intersection compared to opaque surfaces. Definition: A technique that renders a surface colored by the geodesic (mesh-path) distance from a query point, computed via Dijkstra's algorithm on the surface mesh. Steps: Find the closest mesh vertex to the query point using a spatial locator. Run Dijkstra's algorithm on the surface mesh from the closest vertex to a dummy end vertex (0) to compute cumulative edge weights. Extract cumulative weights as a numpy array and replace uncomputed/infinite distances with -1.0. Normalize distances based on climmax (default 'ptile95'): supports 'max', 'mean', 'median', 'ptileN' (percentile), or a float; divide by climmax, scale to 0-255, clip, and mark negatives as -1. Construct a 257-entry LUT: index 0 is white with specified alpha; indices 1-256 map to the colormap. Create a polydata mapper, set input, override scalar range to (-1.0, maxdatarange), and bind the LUT. Parameters: climmax: Normalization target, default 'ptile95'. Layout: vtk.vtkLookupTable: 257 entries. Pitfall: Unreachable mesh regions or uncomputed Dijkstra weights exceed VTKDOUBLEMAX/10.0 and must be explicitly replaced with -1.0 to avoid rendering artifacts. Definition: The closest point query (CPQ) finds the nearest surface point to a given query position. Steps: Tree construction uses top-down recursive partitioning with binned surface area heuristic (SAH) splits: primitives are distributed into spatial buckets along each axis, and sweep operations compute partition costs to select optimal splits. Distance-based node sorting is implemented, which visits children in an order determined by proximity to the query point. Queries are issued as 100,000 randomly sampled queries within each scene’s bounding volume, executed single-threaded. Parameters: Query count: 100,000 randomly sampled queries per scene. Pitfall: Scion checks for SENTINEL nodes because some layouts may have invalid children, whereas FCPW assumes sentinels do not exist and elides this check, causing a performance difference. Numbers: On ARM, Scion is 4% slower than FCPW (geomean). On x86, Scion is 5% faster than FCPW (geomean). Worst case performance is 0.89x on the white-oak scene. Definition: A metric that computes the displacements between each point in a compared point cloud and the nearest facet of a reference mesh. It provides signed distances if mesh normals are considered. Steps: For each point in the compared point cloud, search for the nearest triangle in the reference mesh. Calculate the nearest Euclidean distance between the point and the triangle facet. Optionally assign a sign to the distance based on the triangle normal. Parameters: Reference mesh: A high-accuracy ground truth mesh (e.g., from Structured Light Imaging) used as the baseline for distance calculations. Time Complexity: O(N) per query, where N is the number of surfaces in the list. Each surface distance calculation is O(1) for analytic primitives or O(M) for mesh queries depending on the surface implementation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the list of surface references. No additional temporary memory is required beyond scalar variables. Strengths: Simple to implement and agnostic to the underlying surface representation as long as a distance method exists. Limitations: Linear scan does not scale to scenes with thousands of surfaces without spatial acceleration structures. Does not handle self-occlusion or visibility; it returns the geometric minimum, not the visible minimum. When to use: Small to medium-sized scenes, or as a backend for SDF samplers where the number of constituent meshes is manageable [Parent, S1]. When not to use: Large-scale open worlds with millions of objects; use spatial hashing or BVH-based distance queries instead. The method originates from basic ray-marching shader implementations where multiple surface types are queried per pixel to determine the closest hit. It is a core component of the "Signed Distance Field Sampler from Mesh" pipeline, allowing a single sampler function to abstract over a THREE.Mesh instance composed of multiple geometries [Parent]. The specific implementation details (MAXDISTANCE=2000f, MINDISTANCE=0.2f) come from a Java-based ray marching engine. The variant "Geodesic Distance Rendering" utilizes VTK's Dijkstra implementation for path-based distance visualization. conradplake/ray-marching-shader, https://github.com/conradplake/ray-marching-shader, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 虚幻引擎网格体距离场, https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/mesh-distance-fields-in-unreal-engine?lang=zh-CN, fetched 2026-10-30 Volume Renderer with VTK - yuta-hi, https://github.com/yuta-hi/volume-renderer, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15028, fetched 2026-10-29 GEOMETRIC ACCURACY ANALYSIS BETWEEN NEURAL RADIANCE FIELDS (NERFS) AND TERRESTRIAL LASER SCANNING (TLS), https://doi.org/10.5194/isprs-archives-xlviii-1-w3-2023-153-2023, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Empty Space Supervision
body: 3D Empty Space Supervision is a method for regularizing the non-occupied regions of a learned radiance field by supervising the "object code" using estimated surface distances. It solves the problem of ambiguous empty space in neural rendering, where the model may incorrectly assign object semantics to background voxels. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering losses by explicitly computing a "surfaceness" and "emptiness" score for every sample point along a ray, allowing for targeted supervision of the object field's background channel. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K 3D sample points \{pk\}{k=1}^K along a query ray; the learned density \sigmak and distance intervals \deltak for each sample; the camera-to-sample distance dk; the hyperparameter \Delta d; the object code vector ok \in \mathbb{R}^{H+1} for each sample point. Outputs: The 3D empty space loss \ell{3d\empty} and the 3D object field loss \ell{3d\obj}, which are combined with 2D losses to optimize the object field MLP. Data Structures: Object Code (ok): A one-hot vector of dimension H+1. The first H dimensions represent specific object classes, and the (H+1)-th dimension represents the "empty" or "background" class. Sample Point Data: For each k \in \{1, \dots, K\}: dk: Distance from camera center to sample point k. \sigmak: Learned density at sample point k. \deltak: Distance between sample point k and k+1 (or to the ray end). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Compute Transmittance and Alpha: For each sample point k, compute the transmittance Tk and alpha \alphak using the explicit volume rendering equations: Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{i=1}^{k-1} \sigmai \deltai\right) \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak) Note: T1 = 1. 2. Estimate Surface Distance (d): Calculate the approximate distance from the camera center to the surface hit point along the ray: d = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak \deltak 3. Compute Surfaceness Score (sk): For each sample point k, compute the surfaceness score, which measures how close the sample is to the estimated surface distance d: sk = \exp\left(-(dk - d)^2\right) 4. Compute Emptiness Score (ek): For each sample point k, compute the emptiness score. This score is high for points in front of the surface (empty space) and zero for points behind the surface: ek = (1 - sk) \cdot \mathbbm{1}(d - \Delta d - dk > 0) Where \mathbbm{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function: 1 if the condition is true, 0 otherwise. \Delta d is a hyperparameter compensating for distance estimation inaccuracy. 5. Compute 3D Empty Loss (\ell{3d\empty}): Supervise the last dimension of the object code (o^{H+1}k), which corresponds to the empty class: \ell{3d\empty} = -\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \Big ( ek \log(o^{H+1}k) + sk \log(1 - o^{H+1}k) \Big) Note: The term sk \log(1 - o^{H+1}k) encourages the empty class probability to be low at the surface. 6. Compute 3D Object Field Loss (\ell{3d\obj}): Push the first H dimensions of the object code (o^hk for h=1 \dots H) to zero in empty space: \ell{3d\obj} = - \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \Big ( ek \sum{h=1}^H \log(1 - o^hk) \Big) 7. Total Loss: The total object field loss is the sum of the 2D object loss (\ell{2d\obj}), the 3D empty loss, and the 3D object field loss: \ell = \ell{2d\obj} + \ell{3d\empty} + \ell{3d\obj} Parameters: \Delta d: Hyperparameter to compensate for inaccuracy in the estimated surface distance d. Typical value: 0.05 meters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compute3demptysupervision(dk, sigma, delta, objectcode, deltad=0.05): """ Computes 3D empty space supervision losses for a single ray. Args: dk: List of floats, distance from camera to each sample point. sigma: List of floats, learned density at each sample point. delta: List of floats, distance between consecutive sample points. objectcode: List of lists, object code for each sample point. Last dimension (H+1) is the empty/background class. deltad: Float, hyperparameter for distance inaccuracy compensation. Returns: loss3dempty: Float, emptiness supervision loss. loss3dobj: Float, object field suppression loss in empty space. """ K = len(sigma) H = len(objectcode[0]) - 1 eps = 1e-7 # Step 1: Compute Transmittance Tk # Tk = exp(-sum{i=1}^{k-1} sigmai deltai) T = [1.0] K currentsum = 0.0 for k in range(1, K): currentsum += sigma[k-1] delta[k-1] T[k] = math.exp(-currentsum) # Step 2: Compute Alpha alphak alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[k] delta[k]) for k in range(K)] # Step 3: Estimate Surface Distance d # d = sum{k=1}^K Tk alphak deltak d = sum(T[k] alpha[k] delta[k] for k in range(K)) # Step 4: Compute Surfaceness Score sk s = [math.exp(-(dk[k] - d)2) for k in range(K)] # Step 5: Compute Emptiness Score ek e = [(1.0 - s[k]) (1.0 if (d - deltad - dk[k] > 0) else 0.0) for k in range(K)] # Step 6: Compute Losses # Extract object code dimensions oempty = [objectcode[k][H] for k in range(K)] oobjects = [[objectcode[k][h] for h in range(H)] for k in range(K)] # l3dempty = -1/K sum( ek log(ok^{H+1}) + sk log(1 - ok^{H+1})) loss3dempty = 0.0 for k in range(K): loss3dempty += e[k] math.log(oempty[k] + eps) + s[k] math.log(1.0 - oempty[k] + eps) loss3dempty = -loss3dempty / K # l3dobj = -1/K sum( ek sum{h=1}^H log(1 - ok^h)) loss3dobj = 0.0 for k in range(K): sumh = sum(math.log(1.0 - oobjects[k][h] + eps) for h in range(H)) loss3dobj += e[k] sumh loss3dobj = -loss3dobj / K return loss3dempty, loss3dobj Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The indicator function \mathbbm{1}(d - \Delta d - dk > 0) creates a hard boundary. The hyperparameter \Delta d compensates for distance estimation inaccuracy. Degenerate Input: If \sigmak = 0 for all k, then Tk=1, \alphak=0, d=0. Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes K samples are sufficient to capture the surface. If the surface is between samples, d is an approximation. A supervision signal using HD map ground height fields to guide density field reconstruction, partitioning ray termination into uncertain, ground, and certain regions to avoid applying supervision where map data is unreliable. It differs from 3D Empty Space Supervision by using external map data (height fields) rather than estimated surface distances from the radiance field itself. It is chosen when high-definition maps are available for driving scenes. The method partitions the ray termination distribution into: 1) Uncertain region (obstacles not in map), 2) Ground region (surface within error tolerance \epsilon \approx 30cm), 3) Certain region (beneath ground). It generates a dense triangle mesh Mc from the ground height map M using Delaunay triangulation and renders it to get pseudo ground truth depth D{pgt}. The loss is: L{gd} = \mathbb{E}{r \in Ii} \left[ \int{D{pgt} - \epsilon}^{D{pgt} + \epsilon} h(t) \frac{(t - D{pgt})^2}{2\epsilon^2} \exp\left(-\frac{(t - D{pgt})^2}{2\epsilon^2}\right) dt + \int{D{pgt} + \epsilon}^{\infty} h(t)^2 dt \right] where h(t) is the ray termination distribution, and \epsilon is the uncertainty parameter (typical average error ~30cm). It also improves smoothness by sampling 2x2 patches for depth gradient computation. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples K per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storing K samples of density, distance, and object codes. Strengths: Explicitly handles empty space, preventing the model from assigning object semantics to background. Complements 2D supervision by providing 3D geometric constraints. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the estimated surface distance d. If the density field is poor, d is inaccurate, leading to incorrect emptiness scores. When to use: When learning object fields in scenes with significant empty space and 2D object masks are available. When not to use: When no object field representation is used, or when high-quality 3D ground truth geometry is available (in which case direct geometric losses might be preferred). 3D Empty Space Supervision was introduced in DM-NeRF (Deep Model-based Neural Radiance Fields) by Liu et al., published at ICLR 2023. The method addresses the limitation of standard NeRF which only optimizes for photometric consistency, often resulting in ambiguous geometry in empty regions. By introducing an object field and supervising it with 3D emptiness scores derived from estimated surface distances, DM-NeRF enables 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images. DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07227v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros55552.2023.10341681, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Triangle-Box Intersection Voxelization
head: Mesh Voxelization via SDF and Occupancy, Triangle-Point Distance Voxelization, Watertight Mesh Voxelization
body: This method voxelizes watertight triangular meshes into Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or occupancy grids by computing distances from voxel reference points to mesh faces or by testing for geometric intersection between triangles and voxel boxes. It distinguishes itself from pure SDF-based occupancy derivation by using explicit triangle-box intersection tests to guarantee that any voxel intersecting the mesh surface is marked as occupied, avoiding voxels that might be missed by SDF-only approaches. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance for SDF computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight triangular mesh in OFF format (or a directory of such files). Output: An HDF5 tensor of shape N \times C \times H \times W \times D (or C \times H \times W \times D for a single file), where N is the number of input meshes, C=2 is the number of channels, H is height (y-axis), W is width (x-axis), and D is depth (z-axis). Optional Output: If the --color flag is set, an additional [int]color.h5 file stores original face colors, indexed by face IDs stored in the occupancy grid. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array indexed by (h, w, d) corresponding to spatial coordinates. Mesh Representation: A list of triangles, each defined by 3 vertices (x, y, z). HDF5 Tensor: Dimensions [N, C, H, W, D]. C=2 holds SDF sign/distance or occupancy/color data. Values are signed distances in SDF mode, or 0/face IDs in occupancy mode. Formulas: Voxel size: \Delta x = \frac{1}{W}, \Delta y = \frac{1}{H}, \Delta z = \frac{1}{D}. Voxel bounds for index (h, w, d): x \in [w\Delta x, (w+1)\Delta x], y \in [h\Delta y, (h+1)\Delta y], z \in [d\Delta z, (d+1)\Delta z]. Voxel center: cx = (w+0.5)\Delta x, cy = (h+0.5)\Delta y, cz = (d+0.5)\Delta z. SDF sign: d{signed} = -d{min} if point is interior, d{signed} = d{min} if exterior. Parameters: --mode: 'occ' (default) or 'sdf'. --height, --width, --depth: Resolution H, W, D. Default 32 \times 32 \times 32. --center: Boolean. If set, use voxel centers for SDF computation; otherwise, use voxel corners (default). --color: Boolean. If set, store face IDs in occupancy grid and save colors to a separate file. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing and Scaling: Load the input mesh. Normalize the mesh to [-0.5, 0.5]^3. Scale and translate the mesh to fit the volume bounds [0, H] \times [0, W] \times [0, D]. The coordinate system assumes x= right, y= up, z= forward. The output volume maps H \to y, W \to x, D \to z. 2. Voxelization Loop: Iterate over each voxel (h, w, d) in the grid. Determine the reference point P: if --center is false, P is the voxel corner (e.g., top-left-front); if true, P is the voxel center. If --mode is 'sdf': Compute the distance from P to the nearest triangle face using the triangle-point distance algorithm. Determine the sign: negative if P is inside the mesh, positive if outside. Store the signed distance in the output tensor. If --mode is 'occ': Perform a triangle-box intersection test between the voxel box (defined by center and half-size) and all mesh triangles. If any intersection is detected, mark the voxel as occupied. If --color is set, store the ID of the intersecting face instead of a simple binary 1. 3. Output Generation: Save the resulting tensor to an HDF5 file. If --color is set, save the face colors to [int]color.h5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizemesh(meshtriangles, height, width, depth, mode='occ', usecenter=False, color=False): # Initialize output tensor: N=1, C=2, H, W, D outputtensor = [[[[[0.0 for in range(depth)] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for in range(2)] for in range(1)] colordata = {} dx, dy, dz = 1.0 / width, 1.0 / height, 1.0 / depth for h in range(height): for w in range(width): for d in range(depth): # Voxel bounds in world space [0, H]x[0, W]x[0, D] # y maps to h, x maps to w, z maps to d miny, maxy = h dy, (h + 1) dy minx, maxx = w dx, (w + 1) dx minz, maxz = d dz, (d + 1) dz centery = (miny + maxy) / 2.0 centerx = (minx + maxx) / 2.0 centerz = (minz + maxz) / 2.0 halfy, halfx, halfz = dy / 2.0, dx / 2.0, dz / 2.0 if usecenter: refpoint = (centerx, centery, centerz) voxelcenter = (centerx, centery, centerz) voxelhalf = (halfx, halfy, halfz) else: refpoint = (minx, miny, minz) voxelcenter = (centerx, centery, centerz) voxelhalf = (halfx, halfy, halfz) if mode == 'sdf': mindist = float('inf') for tri in meshtriangles: dist = pointtriangledistance(refpoint, tri) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist # Determine sign: inside if ray from refpoint intersects odd number of triangles isinside = raycastintersection(refpoint, meshtriangles) signeddist = -mindist if isinside else mindist outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = signeddist elif mode == 'occ': isoccupied = False intersectingfaceid = -1 for triidx, tri in enumerate(meshtriangles): if triboxoverlap(voxelcenter, voxelhalf, tri): isoccupied = True if color: intersectingfaceid = triidx break if isoccupied: if color: outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = intersectingfaceid if intersectingfaceid not in colordata: colordata[intersectingfaceid] = getfacecolor(triidx) else: outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = 1.0 else: outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = 0.0 return outputtensor, colordata def pointtriangledistance(p, tri): # Standard point-triangle distance using barycentric coordinates v0, v1, v2 = tri edge1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) edge2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) diff = (p[0]-v0[0], p[1]-v0[1], p[2]-v0[2]) a = edge1[0]2 + edge1[1]2 + edge1[2]2 b = edge1[0]edge2[0] + edge1[1]edge2[1] + edge1[2]edge2[2] c = edge2[0]2 + edge2[1]2 + edge2[2]2 d = edge1[0]diff[0] + edge1[1]diff[1] + edge1[2]diff[2] e = edge2[0]diff[0] + edge2[1]diff[1] + edge2[2]diff[2] D = ac - bb s = (be - cd) / D t = (ae - bd) / D if s + t <= 1: if s < 0: s = 0 if t < 0: t = 0 if s + t > 1: if d < 0: s = 0 elif e < 0: t = 0 else: num = b - d den = a - 2b + c if num/den >= 0: s = num/den else: s = 0 t = 1 - s q = (diff[0] - sedge1[0] - tedge2[0])2 + (diff[1] - sedge1[1] - tedge2[1])2 + (diff[2] - sedge1[2] - tedge2[2])2 return math.sqrt(q) if s < 0: s = 0 if t < 0: t = 0 if s + t > 1: if d < 0: s = 0 elif e < 0: t = 0 else: num = b - d den = a - 2b + c if num/den >= 0: s = num/den else: s = 0 t = 1 - s q = (diff[0] - sedge1[0] - tedge2[0])2 + (diff[1] - sedge1[1] - tedge2[1])2 + (diff[2] - sedge1[2] - tedge2[2])2 return math.sqrt(q) def triboxoverlap(center, halfsize, tri): # Axis-aligned bounding box overlap test v0, v1, v2 = tri mintri = (min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) maxtri = (max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) minbox = (center[0]-halfsize[0], center[1]-halfsize[1], center[2]-halfsize[2]) maxbox = (center[0]+halfsize[0], center[1]+halfsize[1], center[2]+halfsize[2]) if mintri[0] > maxbox[0] or maxtri[0] < minbox[0]: return False if mintri[1] > maxbox[1] or maxtri[1] < minbox[1]: return False if mintri[2] > maxbox[2] or maxtri[2] < minbox[2]: return False return True def raycastintersection(point, triangles): # Standard ray casting: cast ray along +x, count intersections count = 0 for tri in triangles: # Check intersection of ray (point, (1,0,0)) with tri # Simplified: returns True if odd intersections pass # Standard algorithm return count % 2 == 1 def getfacecolor(faceidx): # Returns color for face index return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight Meshes: The method assumes watertight meshes. Non-watertight meshes may produce incorrect SDFs (no negative values) or occupancy. Simplification using a semi-convex hull algorithm is suggested but is crude. Coordinate System Mismatch: The input OFF files assume x= right, y= up, z= forward. The output volume maps height (y) to the first dimension, width (x) to the second, and depth (z) to the third. SDF Reference Point: The choice between voxel corner and center affects the marching cubes implementation used for conversion. Standard marching cubes (e.g., PyMCubes) expect corner-based SDFs. Samples SDF values from a mesh. Chosen when continuous distance fields are needed for smooth interpolation or gradient-based optimization, rather than discrete voxel occupancy. Computes the distance to the nearest triangle without sign. Chosen when interior/exterior distinction is not required, or for collision detection where only proximity matters. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot T), where V is the number of voxels (H \times W \times D) and T is the number of triangles. Naive implementation checks all triangles for all voxels. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W \times D) for the output grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Resolution defaults to 32^3. Higher resolutions (e.g., 64^3) improve reconstruction quality. Strengths: Guarantees watertight occupancy via explicit intersection tests. Supports color preservation. Simple to implement using existing geometric primitives. Limitations: Requires watertight input. Naive implementation is slow for high-resolution grids or complex meshes. Coordinate system swaps can cause confusion. When to use: When a discrete, watertight representation of a mesh is needed for 3D shape completion or volumetric processing, especially when SDF-based occupancy is insufficient due to leakage. When not to use: For non-watertight meshes without preprocessing. When continuous SDF gradients are needed for optimization. When performance is critical and the mesh is highly complex. The method was introduced by David Stutz and Andreas Geiger in 2018 at CVPR for the paper "Learning 3D Shape Completion from Laser Scan Data with Weak Supervision". It builds on prior work from 2017 on shape completion from bounding boxes. The implementation is a parallel C++ tool that uses external libraries for triangle-point distance (christopherbatty/SDFGen) and triangle-box intersection (Tomas Akenine-Möller). name: Barycentric Coordinate Calculation
head: Barycentric Coordinates, Point-in-Triangle Barycentric Coordinates
body: Computes the barycentric coordinates of a 3D point relative to a triangle defined by three vertices. It solves the problem of expressing a point's position within a triangle's local coordinate system, which is a prerequisite for Point-Triangle Distance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the geometric projection and area-based calculation rather than distance minimization or mesh sampling. Inputs: A 3D point P, and three triangle vertices p1, p2, p3. Outputs: A 3D vector (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) representing the barycentric coordinates. Data Structures: Vector3: A 3-component floating-point vector. norm, pointProj: 3D vectors. a1, a2, a3: Scalar floats representing sub-triangle areas. Steps: 1. Compute the triangle normal: \text{norm} = \text{Cross}(p2 - p1, p3 - p1). 2. Project the point P onto the triangle's plane to handle points not exactly on the plane: \text{pointProj} = P - \frac{\text{Dot}(P - p1, \text{norm})}{\|\text{norm}\|^2} \text{norm}. If \|\text{norm}\|^2 is zero, the triangle is degenerate and the method fails. 3. Calculate the area of the sub-triangle opposite p1 (formed by \text{pointProj}, p2, p3): a1 = \text{Area}(\text{pointProj}, p2, p3). 4. Calculate the area of the sub-triangle opposite p2 (formed by p1, \text{pointProj}, p3): a2 = \text{Area}(p1, \text{pointProj}, p3). 5. Calculate the area of the sub-triangle opposite p3 (formed by p1, p2, \text{pointProj}): a3 = \text{Area}(p1, p2, \text{pointProj}). 6. Return the normalized barycentric coordinates: (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) = \frac{(a1, a2, a3)}{a1 + a2 + a3}. Formula: The area of a triangle with vertices A, B, C is calculated as: \text{Area} = \frac{\|\text{Cross}(B - A, C - A)\|}{2}. Pitfalls: If the point is not on the triangle's plane, it is projected onto the plane before area calculation. If the triangle is degenerate (area zero), division by zero occurs in the final normalization step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def cross(v1, v2): return (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) def calculatetrianglearea(p1, p2, p3): """Returns the area of the triangle defined by p1, p2, p3.""" v1 = (p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1], p2[2]-p1[2]) v2 = (p3[0]-p1[0], p3[1]-p1[1], p3[2]-p1[2]) c = cross(v1, v2) return math.sqrt(dot(c, c)) / 2.0 def tobarycentriccoordinates(point, p1, p2, p3): """ Computes barycentric coordinates of point relative to triangle p1, p2, p3. Returns (lambda1, lambda2, lambda3). """ # 1. Compute triangle normal v1 = (p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1], p2[2]-p1[2]) v2 = (p3[0]-p1[0], p3[1]-p1[1], p3[2]-p1[2]) norm = cross(v1, v2) # 2. Project point onto triangle's plane dotval = dot((point[0]-p1[0], point[1]-p1[1], point[2]-p1[2]), norm) normsq = dot(norm, norm) if normsq == 0: raise ValueError("Degenerate triangle: zero area.") pointproj = (point[0] - (dotval / normsq) norm[0], point[1] - (dotval / normsq) norm[1], point[2] - (dotval / normsq) norm[2]) # 3. Calculate areas of sub-triangles a1 = calculatetrianglearea(pointproj, p2, p3) a2 = calculatetrianglearea(p1, pointproj, p3) a3 = calculatetrianglearea(p1, p2, pointproj) # 4. Normalize totalarea = a1 + a2 + a3 if totalarea == 0: raise ValueError("Total sub-triangle area is zero.") return (a1 / totalarea, a2 / totalarea, a3 / totalarea) A method to calculate rasterization derivatives using barycentric coordinates to overcome occlusion discontinuity by treating shapes as locally planar. It calculates barycentric coordinates of each triangle with respect to each pixel, introducing negative values for the barycentric coordinates of pixels lying outside the triangle border. This approximation allows shapes to be treated as locally planar to approximate occlusion boundaries. However, this approximation poses problems when optimizing for translation or occlusion. Time complexity: O(1) per point-triangle pair. Memory complexity: O(1). Strengths: Simple geometric interpretation; handles off-plane points via projection. Limitations: Fails on degenerate triangles; projection step adds computational cost compared to planar-only methods. Origin: Standard computational geometry technique. History: Used in graphics for interpolation, texture mapping, and point-in-triangle tests. Usage: Found in Point-Triangle Distance and differentiable rendering pipelines. xandergos/unity-sparse-voxel-octrees, https://github.com/xandergos/unity-sparse-voxel-octrees, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differentiable Rendering: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2006.12057, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Coverage Test
body: The Triangle Coverage Test verifies whether a triangle T is completely covered by three spheres centered at its vertices, with radii determined by a scalar field function f evaluated at those vertices. It solves the problem of ensuring that a discrete sampling of an implicit volume is dense enough to guarantee no gaps exist between the approximating spheres, which is critical for sphere carving algorithms. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Triangle T defined by three vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a scalar field function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Output: Boolean True if the triangle is completely covered by the spheres; False otherwise. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 3 vectors \mathbf{v}i. Radii: Array of 3 floats ri = f(\mathbf{v}i). Circles: Implicitly defined by center \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{v}i and radius ri in the plane of T. Numbered Steps: 1. Evaluate radii ri = f(\mathbf{v}i) for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. 2. Check disjointness: If any pair of circles is disjoint, the test fails and returns False. 3. Check intersection points: For each pair of circles, compute their intersection points. If any intersection point lies inside T and outside the third circle, the test fails and returns False. 4. Return True if neither disjointness nor uncovered intersection points are found. Formulas: Sphere coverage condition: \forall \mathbf{p} \in T, \exists i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}i\| < f(\mathbf{v}i), where \mathbf{p} is any point on the triangle, \mathbf{v}i are the vertices, and f(\mathbf{v}i) are the sphere radii. Disjointness condition: \|\mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{v}j\| > ri + rj. Parameters: The test relies on the property that the initial volume sampling is dense enough to create sphere intersections. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate triangles (collinear vertices) have zero area and require explicit handling. Floating-point precision errors in intersection calculations may cause false negatives; epsilon thresholds should be used for comparisons. The test specifically checks for intersection points of two circles that lie inside the triangle but outside the third circle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trianglecoveragetest(v0, v1, v2, f): # Step 1: Evaluate radii r = [f(v0), f(v1), f(v2)] verts = [v0, v1, v2] # Helper: Euclidean distance def dist(a, b): return math.sqrt(sum((a[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(3))) # Step 2: Check disjointness for i in range(3): for j in range(i + 1, 3): if dist(verts[i], verts[j]) > r[i] + r[j]: return False # Compute triangle normal for 3D circle intersection v01 = [verts[1][k] - verts[0][k] for k in range(3)] v02 = [verts[2][k] - verts[0][k] for k in range(3)] normal = [ v01[1]v02[2] - v01[2]v02[1], v01[2]v02[0] - v01[0]v02[2], v01[0]v02[1] - v01[1]v02[0] ] nlen = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in normal)) if nlen < 1e-9: return True # Degenerate triangle, assume covered normal = [x / nlen for x in normal] # Helper: Point-in-triangle using barycentric coordinates def pointintriangle(p): v0v1 = [verts[1][k] - verts[0][k] for k in range(3)] v0v2 = [verts[2][k] - verts[0][k] for k in range(3)] v0p = [p[k] - verts[0][k] for k in range(3)] d00 = sum(v0v1[k]v0v1[k] for k in range(3)) d01 = sum(v0v1[k]v0v2[k] for k in range(3)) d11 = sum(v0v2[k]v0v2[k] for k in range(3)) d20 = sum(v0p[k]v0v1[k] for k in range(3)) d21 = sum(v0p[k]v0v2[k] for k in range(3)) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return False v = (d11 d20 - d01 d21) / denom w = (d00 d21 - d01 d20) / denom u = 1.0 - v - w return u >= 0 and v >= 0 and w >= 0 # Helper: Circle-circle intersection in 3D def circleintersection(p1, r1, p2, r2, n): d = dist(p1, p2) if d > r1 + r2 or d < abs(r1 - r2): return [] if d == 0: return [] a = (r12 - r22 + d2) / (2 d) hsq = r12 - a2 if hsq < 0: return [] h = math.sqrt(hsq) p2vec = [p2[k] - p1[k] for k in range(3)] pbase = [p1[k] + a p2vec[k] / d for k in range(3)] u = [p2vec[k] / d for k in range(3)] v = [n[1]u[2] - n[2]u[1], n[2]u[0] - n[0]u[2], n[0]u[1] - n[1]u[0]] vlen = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) if vlen < 1e-9: return [] v = [x / vlen for x in v] return [[pbase[k] + h v[k] for k in range(3)], [pbase[k] - h v[k] for k in range(3)]] # Step 3: Check intersection points for i in range(3): for j in range(i + 1, 3): k = 3 - i - j pts = circleintersection(verts[i], r[i], verts[j], r[j], normal) for p in pts: if pointintriangle(p): if dist(p, verts[k]) > r[k]: return False return True Computes the distance from a point to a triangle without sign. Use when you need metric distance rather than coverage. Samples SDF values on a mesh. Use when generating the input f for the coverage test. Voxelizes a triangle. Use when rasterizing rather than checking sphere coverage. Computes barycentric coordinates. Use as a helper for point-in-triangle tests within the coverage test. Initializes SDF zero sets. Use when setting up the initial volume for sphere carving. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently verifies volume completeness without dense sampling. Limitations: Relies on dense initial sampling; fails if spheres are too small or sparse. When to use: Sphere carving algorithms, implicit volume reconstruction. When not to use: When spheres are not dense enough or when exact SDF values are not available. The Triangle Coverage Test was introduced by Cédric Zanni in 2024 as part of the Sphere Carving algorithm for bounding volumes of signed distance fields. It addresses the need to ensure that the discrete sampling of an implicit volume is dense enough to create sphere intersections, preventing gaps in the reconstructed volume. The method is based on the observation that a triangle is not covered if either one circle is disjoint from the others or an intersection point of two circles lies inside the triangle but outside the third. name: Zero Set Initialization of Meshes
body: Zero Set Initialization of Meshes initializes the closest points for triangle meshes by operating on individual triangles without using edge or vertex adjacency information. It establishes an initial signed distance field from a polygonal mesh by identifying samples near the surface and assigning them signs. It differs from Unsigned Triangle Distance by computing signed distances and from Mesh SDF Sampling by focusing on the initialization phase for distance transforms. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance to determine geometric proximity. Inputs: A triangular mesh (list of triangles), a 3D grid of samples, and cell-width (the distance between adjacent samples in x, y, and z directions). Outputs: A queue of zero set samples, each with an associated sign, a duplication flag, and a distance value. Data Structures: Sample: Represents a grid point. Fields: position (3D vector), distance (scalar, initialized to infinity), sign (scalar, +1 or -1), queued (boolean, default false), ambiguous (boolean, default false). Triangle: Defined by three vertices v0, v1, v2 and normal n. Steps: 1. Bounding Box Adjustment: For every triangle T in the mesh: Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of T: (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) to (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Expand the box by cell-width: x'{min} = x{min} - \text{cell-width}, \quad x'{max} = x{max} + \text{cell-width} (Similarly for y and z). 2. Sample Evaluation: For each sample s within the adjusted bounding box: Compute the closest point cp(s) on triangle T to s. Determine the type of closest point: face, edge, or vertex. Calculate the distance \delta = \|s - cp(s)\|. If \delta \le \sqrt{3} \cdot \text{cell-width} and \delta < s.distance: Place s on the zero set queue. Set s.queued = \text{true} to prohibit duplication. Update s.distance = \delta. Compute s.sign based on the closest point type (see Sign Computation below). If the closest point is a vertex and signs are ambiguous, set s.ambiguous = \text{true} and s.sign = 0. Sign Computation: The sign determines whether the sample is inside or outside the mesh. Face Case: If cp(s) lies on the face of T, the sign is determined by the dot product of the triangle normal n' and the vector v = s - cp(s): \text{sign} = \text{sign}(n' \cdot v) where \text{sign}(x) is +1 if x \ge 0 and -1 if x < 0. Edge Case: If cp(s) lies on an edge shared by two triangles T1 and T2, compute dot products d1 = n1 \cdot v and d2 = n2 \cdot v. The sign is taken from the triangle with the larger absolute dot product: \text{sign} = \text{sign}(di) \quad \text{where } |di| = \max(|d1|, |d2|). Vertex Case: If cp(s) coincides with a vertex shared by multiple triangles, compute dot products for all adjacent triangles. If the dot products have mixed signs (some positive, some negative), the sample is marked as ambiguous. No sign is propagated initially (s.sign = 0). Post-Processing for Ambiguity: After the initial pass and any subsequent distance transform steps, ambiguous samples are revisited. The signs of the 26-neighbors of the ambiguous sample are examined. The sign of the majority of the neighbors is assigned to the ambiguous sample. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def zerosetinitialization(mesh, grid, cellwidth): def closestpointontriangle(tri, p): # Barycentric projection to find closest point on triangle v0, v1, v2 = tri.vertices e1, e2 = v1 - v0, v2 - v0 d1, d2 = (p - v0) @ e1, (p - v0) @ e2 a, b, c = e1 @ e1, e1 @ e2, e2 @ e2 det = a c - b b s = (c d1 - b d2) / max(det, 1e-12) t = (a d2 - b d1) / max(det, 1e-12) if s + t <= 1: if s >= 0 and t >= 0: return v0 + s e1 + t e2, 'face' elif s < 0: return v0 + max(0, min(1, t)) e2, 'edge' elif t < 0: return v0 + max(0, min(1, s)) e1, 'edge' # Fallback to edges/vertices if projection outside return v0, 'vertex' # Simplified for self-containment; for tri in mesh: bboxmin, bboxmax = tri.boundingbox() expandedmin = bboxmin - cellwidth expandedmax = bboxmax + cellwidth for s in grid.samplesinbox(expandedmin, expandedmax): if s.queued: continue cp, cptype = closestpointontriangle(tri, s.position) delta = math.dist(cp, s.position) if delta <= math.sqrt(3) cellwidth and delta < s.distance: s.queued = True s.distance = delta v = s.position - cp if cptype == 'face': s.sign = 1 if tri.normal @ v >= 0 else -1 elif cptype == 'edge': # Source specifies computing dot products for adjacent triangles sharing the edge # Adjacency lookup omitted per source constraint; d1 = tri.normal @ v s.sign = 1 if d1 >= 0 else -1 elif cptype == 'vertex': # Source specifies checking adjacent triangles for mixed signs # Adjacency lookup omitted per source constraint; d = tri.normal @ v if d >= 0: s.sign = 1 else: s.sign = -1 # Ambiguity resolution deferred to post-processing A naive baseline method that builds correspondence between an extracted triangular mesh and continuous volume space by finding the closest point on the mesh surface for each sampled point and using its displacement directly as the sampled point's displacement. Unlike Zero Set Initialization, it does not explicitly manage a queue or sign propagation for distance transforms, serving as a simpler geometric proxy. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of triangles and M is the number of samples within the expanded bounding boxes of all triangles. In practice, spatial indexing (e.g., voxelization) is often used to limit M. Memory Complexity: O(G), where G is the number of grid samples, to store distance, sign, and queue flags. Strengths: Efficiently identifies the zero set without requiring complex topological data structures or adjacency information for the entire mesh. It is robust for local curvature regions. Limitations: Vertex ambiguity requires post-processing. The \sqrt{3} \cdot \text{cell-width} threshold is heuristic; tighter bounds may miss samples, while looser bounds increase computational cost. It does not guarantee a globally consistent sign field without the neighbor-heuristic resolution. When to use: When initializing SDFs for distance transforms on triangle meshes where topological information is unavailable or expensive to compute. When not to use: When high precision is required without post-processing ambiguity resolution, or when the mesh has complex non-manifold geometry where vertex ambiguity is frequent. The method originates from research on distance field generation for triangle meshes. It is designed to operate on individual triangles without using edge or vertex adjacency information, making it suitable for compressed or simplified mesh representations. The technique is noted as being very similar to the method proposed by Huang et al.. It is primarily used in computer graphics for generating signed distance fields from polygonal meshes for rendering and simulation. name: Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test
head: SAT Triangle Intersection, Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) for triangles, testIntersection
body: The Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test determines whether two triangles in 3D space intersect using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). It solves the problem of detecting collisions between triangular primitives by projecting them onto potential separating axes and checking for interval overlap. Unlike Ray-Triangle Intersection, which tests a ray against a single triangle, this method tests two arbitrary triangles against each other without a predefined viewing direction. It is distinct from General Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates) in that it relies on interval projection rather than line-plane duality, and from Point-Triangle Distance as it returns a boolean intersection status rather than a distance metric. Input: Two triangles, T1 and T2. Output: A boolean value: true (or 1) if the triangles intersect, false (or 0) if they do not. Each triangle is defined by three vertices in 3D space, stored in a vt[3][3] array where each row is a 3D float vector. Vertices are indexed 0, 1, 2. The test projects both triangles onto a set of potential separating axes. If the projections (intervals) on any axis are disjoint, the triangles do not intersect. If all tested axes show overlap, the triangles intersect. 1. Compute Edge Vectors: For each triangle Ti (i \in \{1, 2\}), compute the three edge vectors: e{i,0} = Ti.vt[1] - Ti.vt[0], e{i,1} = Ti.vt[2] - Ti.vt[1], e{i,2} = Ti.vt[0] - Ti.vt[2]. 2. Compute Face Normals: Compute the unnormalized face normals: n1 = e{1,0} \times e{1,1} and n2 = e{2,0} \times e{2,1}. 3. Check for Co-planarity: Compute n = n1 \times n2. If n is the zero vector, the triangles are co-planar. Co-planar Case: Check if the triangles lie in the same plane by comparing n1 \cdot T1.vt[0] and n1 \cdot T2.vt[0]. If n1 \cdot T1.vt[0] \neq n1 \cdot T2.vt[0], the planes are distinct and the triangles do not intersect; return false. If they are in the same plane, test separation along the 6 edge normals: n1 \times e{1,i} and n2 \times e{2,i} for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. If any axis separates the triangles, return false; otherwise return true. Non-Co-planar Case: Test separation along the face normals n1 and n2. If either separates them, return false. Test separation along the 9 cross products of every edge of T1 with every edge of T2: axis{i,j} = e{1,i} \times e{2,j} for i,j \in \{0, 1, 2\}. If any separates them, return false. If no axis separates the triangles, return true. 4. Projection and Separation Check: For each candidate axis A, project both triangles to min/max intervals: min1 = A \cdot T1.vt[0], max1 = min1; loop k \in \{1, 2\}: temp = A \cdot T1.vt[k]; update min1 = \min(min1, temp), max1 = \max(max1, temp); repeat for T2. If any axis shows disjoint intervals (min1 \ge max2 or min2 \ge max1), return false; else return true. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triangletriangleintersect(t1, t2, epsilon=1e-5): # 1. Compute edge vectors e1 = [t1.vt[1] - t1.vt[0], t1.vt[2] - t1.vt[1], t1.vt[0] - t1.vt[2]] e2 = [t2.vt[1] - t2.vt[0], t2.vt[2] - t2.vt[1], t2.vt[0] - t2.vt[2]] # 2. Compute face normals n1 = cross(e1[0], e1[1]) n2 = cross(e2[0], e2[1]) # 3. Check co-planarity n = cross(n1, n2) if iszerovector(n, epsilon): # Co-planar case if dot(n1, t1.vt[0]) != dot(n1, t2.vt[0]): return False axes = [] for i in range(3): axes.append(cross(n1, e1[i])) axes.append(cross(n2, e2[i])) for axis in axes: if testseparation(axis, t1, t2, epsilon): return False return True else: # Non-co-planar case if testseparation(n1, t1, t2, epsilon): return False if testseparation(n2, t1, t2, epsilon): return False for i in range(3): for j in range(3): axis = cross(e1[i], e2[j]) if testseparation(axis, t1, t2, epsilon): return False return True def testseparation(axis, t1, t2, epsilon): min1 = dot(axis, t1.vt[0]) max1 = min1 for k in range(1, 3): proj = dot(axis, t1.vt[k]) if proj < min1: min1 = proj if proj > max1: max1 = proj min2 = dot(axis, t2.vt[0]) max2 = min2 for k in range(1, 3): proj = dot(axis, t2.vt[k]) if proj < min2: min2 = proj if proj > max2: max2 = proj if min1 > max2 + epsilon or min2 > max1 + epsilon: return True return False def iszerovector(v, epsilon): return abs(v.x) < epsilon and abs(v.y) < epsilon and abs(v.z) < epsilon Note: dot and cross are standard vector operations. Epsilon: A small floating-point tolerance (e.g., 0.00001f) used to handle numerical instability in separation checks and zero-vector detection. Co-planar Triangles: Handling co-planar triangles correctly is critical. Some implementations use a hack where co-planar triangles are explicitly regarded as not intersecting to avoid degenerate cases. The full SAT test requires testing the 6 edge normals in the co-planar case. Numerical Precision: Floating-point errors can cause false negatives or positives. Using an epsilon in the separation check (min1 > max2 + \epsilon) helps mitigate this. Degenerate Triangles: If a triangle has zero area (collinear vertices), its normal is zero. The algorithm assumes non-degenerate triangles; degenerate inputs may require pre-validation. An early-out optimization where the axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) of the two triangles are tested for intersection. If the AABBs do not intersect, the triangles do not intersect. This is an O(1) check that can save the more expensive SAT test. An extension of the intersection test that computes the area of intersection between two triangles, useful for rendering and physics. Time Complexity: O(1) per pair of triangles. The algorithm tests at most 11 axes (2 face normals + 9 edge-edge cross products) for non-co-planar triangles, and up to 6 axes for co-planar triangles. Memory Complexity: O(1). Only a few temporary vectors and scalars are required. Measured Performance: The SAT method is generally fast and robust for single pair tests. Strengths: No division by zero issues; handles all relative orientations; robust with epsilon tuning. Limitations: Does not provide the intersection curve or area; co-planar cases require special handling; less efficient than bounding volume hierarchies for large scenes. When to Use: When testing a small number of triangle pairs, or as a leaf-node test in a spatial partitioning structure. When Not to Use: For large-scale scene intersection, use a BVH or grid-based approach. For ray-triangle intersection, use Ray-Triangle Intersection. The Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test using SAT is a standard technique in computational geometry and computer graphics. It is implemented in various open-source dual contouring and mesh processing libraries, including work by Tao Ju. The method relies on the Separating Axis Theorem, which states that two convex objects are disjoint if and only if there exists a plane (axis) onto which their projections do not overlap. For triangles, the potential separating axes are the face normals and the cross products of their edges. aewallin/dualcontouring, https://github.com/aewallin/dualcontouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jbayardo/tao-ju-dual-contouring, https://github.com/jbayardo/tao-ju-dual-contouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Mesh Voxelization via SAT Ray Casting
head: Ray-Triangle Intersection for Voxelization, UnityGPUMeshVoxelizer, VoxelizeMesh
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid by dispatching a compute shader where each thread corresponds to a voxel cell. It determines voxel solidity by testing each cell against every mesh triangle using a Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) broad-phase test followed by a Möller-Trumbore ray-triangle intersection. It differs from hierarchical voxelization by using a brute-force per-voxel, per-triangle approach, making it simple to implement but computationally expensive for high-resolution grids or complex meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions and triangle indices. Input: Voxel grid dimensions (W, H, D) and cell size (s). Input: World-space bounds of the voxelization volume. Output: A structured buffer of voxels, each containing a position and a boolean isSolid flag. Data Structures: The implementation uses the following structures in HLSL/C#: 1. Voxel: hlsl struct Voxel { Vector3 position; // World-space center of the voxel float isSolid; // 1.0 if solid, 0.0 otherwise }; Stored in a RWStructuredBuffer<Voxel>. 2. Triangle: hlsl struct Triangle { float3 a, b, c; // Vertices in world space }; Triangles are not stored as a single struct buffer but are fetched from vertex and index buffers. 3. Mesh Buffers: MeshVertices: StructuredBuffer<float3>, size Nv (number of vertices). MeshTriangleIndices: StructuredBuffer<int>, size Nt \times 3 (number of triangles \times 3). 4. Grid Parameters: GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth: Integers defining the voxel count per axis. CellHalfSize: Float, half the side length of a voxel (default 0.05f). BoundsMin: Float3, minimum corner of the voxel grid in world space. WorldToLocalMatrix: Matrix, transforms world coordinates to local mesh coordinates. TriangleCount: Integer, total number of triangles. Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Calculate grid dimensions from the mesh collider bounds and CellHalfSize. W = \lceil \frac{\text{bounds.extents.x}}{\text{CellHalfSize} \times 2} \rceil H = \lceil \frac{\text{bounds.extents.y}}{\text{CellHalfSize} \times 2} \rceil D = \lceil \frac{\text{bounds.extents.z}}{\text{CellHalfSize} \times 2} \rceil Allocate voxelsBuffer of size W \times H \times D. 2. Buffer Upload: Upload mesh vertices to MeshVertices and indices to MeshTriangleIndices. 3. Compute Dispatch: Dispatch the VoxelizeMesh kernel with thread groups: \text{Groups}x = \lceil \frac{W}{\text{GroupSize}} \rceil, \quad \text{Groups}y = \lceil \frac{H}{\text{GroupSize}} \rceil, \quad \text{Groups}z = \lceil \frac{D}{\text{GroupSize}} \rceil. 4. Voxelization Kernel (VoxelizeMesh): For each thread with global ID (id.x, id.y, id.z): a. Bounds Check: If id.x \ge W or id.y \ge H or id.z \ge D, return. b. Compute Cell Center: \text{cellSize} = \text{CellHalfSize} \times 2.0 \text{centerPos} = (id.x \times \text{cellSize} + \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{BoundsMin}.x, \dots) (Repeat for y and z components). c. Initialize Solidity: Set isSolid = 0. d. Triangle Iteration: Iterate through all triangles i from 0 to TriangleCount - 1. i. Fetch vertices A, B, C from MeshVertices using indices from MeshTriangleIndices. ii. SAT Broad-Phase: Test if the voxel AABB (centered at centerPos, extents CellHalfSize) intersects the triangle's AABB. iii. Ray-Triangle Intersection: If SAT passes, cast a ray from centerPos towards the triangle centroid (or use the Möller-Trumbore algorithm directly if the SAT is considered part of the intersection logic). If a hit is found, set isSolid = 1 and break. e. Write Output: Write the voxel to voxelsBuffer[id.z W H + id.y W + id.x]. 5. Fill Volume (Optional): Dispatch a subsequent kernel to propagate solidity to neighboring empty voxels if a "filled" volume is required rather than a surface shell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EPSILON = 0.0000001 def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, tria, trib, tric): ab = (trib[0]-tria[0], trib[1]-tria[1], trib[2]-tria[2]) ac = (tric[0]-tria[0], tric[1]-tria[1], tric[2]-tria[2]) h = cross(raydirection, ac) a = dot(ab, h) if a > -EPSILON and a < EPSILON: return False f = 1.0 / a s = (rayorigin[0]-tria[0], rayorigin[1]-tria[1], rayorigin[2]-tria[2]) u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return False q = cross(s, ab) v = f dot(raydirection, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return False t = f dot(ac, q) if t <= EPSILON: return False return True def sattest(voxelcenter, voxelextents, tria, trib, tric): axes = [ (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1), cross((trib[0]-tria[0], trib[1]-tria[1], trib[2]-tria[2]), (tric[0]-tria[0], tric[1]-tria[1], tric[2]-tria[2])) ] for axis in axes: p0 = dot(tria, axis) p1 = dot(trib, axis) p2 = dot(tric, axis) maxP = max(p0, max(p1, p2)) minP = min(p0, min(p1, p2)) r = voxelextents[0]abs(axis[0]) + voxelextents[1]abs(axis[1]) + voxelextents[2]abs(axis[2]) if max(-maxP, minP) > r: return False return True def voxelizemeshkernel(idx, idy, idz, gridw, gridh, gridd, cellhalfsize, boundsmin, meshvertices, meshindices, trianglecount, voxelsbuffer): if idx >= gridw or idy >= gridh or idz >= gridd: return cellsize = cellhalfsize 2.0 centerpos = ( idx cellsize + cellhalfsize + boundsmin[0], idy cellsize + cellhalfsize + boundsmin[1], idz cellsize + cellhalfsize + boundsmin[2]) issolid = 0.0 voxelextents = (cellhalfsize, cellhalfsize, cellhalfsize) for i in range(trianglecount): idx0 = meshindices[i 3] idx1 = meshindices[i 3 + 1] idx2 = meshindices[i 3 + 2] tria = meshvertices[idx0] trib = meshvertices[idx1] tric = meshvertices[idx2] if not sattest(centerpos, voxelextents, tria, trib, tric): continue centroid = ((tria[0]+trib[0]+tric[0])/3.0, (tria[1]+trib[1]+tric[1])/3.0, (tria[2]+trib[2]+tric[2])/3.0) direction = centroid lensq = direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2 if lensq > 0.0: lensqinv = 1.0 / (lensq 0.5) direction = (direction[0]lensqinv, direction[1]lensqinv, direction[2]lensqinv) else: direction = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) if raytriangleintersect(centerpos, direction, tria, trib, tric): issolid = 1.0 break voxelsbuffer[idz gridw gridh + idy gridw + idx] = (centerpos, issolid) Parameters: CellHalfSize: Default 0.05f. Determines voxel resolution. GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth: Derived from mesh bounds and CellHalfSize. BoundsMin: World-space minimum corner of the voxelization volume. WorldToLocalMatrix: Used if mesh vertices are in local space and need transformation to world space for intersection tests. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Parallel to Triangle: If the ray direction is parallel to the triangle plane, the denominator a in Möller-Trumbore becomes zero. Handled by checking if (a > -epsilon && a < epsilon) return false;. Barycentric Coordinates: If u or v are outside [0, 1] or u+v > 1, the ray misses the triangle. Handled by explicit bounds checks. Back-facing/Degenerate Hits: Hits with t \le \epsilon are rejected to avoid self-intersection or degenerate cases. Handled by return t > epsilon;. Time Complexity: O(V \times T), where V is the total number of voxels (W \times H \times D) and T is the number of triangles. Each voxel thread iterates over all triangles. Memory Complexity: O(V + V{mesh} + T{mesh}), where V is the voxel buffer size, V{mesh} is the vertex buffer size, and T{mesh} is the index buffer size. Performance: Performance degrades linearly with grid resolution and triangle count. Suitable for real-time visualization of moderate-resolution grids on modern GPUs. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structures required, fully parallelizable. Limitations: No spatial acceleration, leading to poor performance on dense meshes or high-resolution grids. This method is implemented in the Unity engine using ComputeShaders and Graphics.DrawProceduralIndirect / Graphics.DrawMeshInstancedIndirect for visualization. It is part of the "UnityGPUMeshVoxelizer" project series. bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, https://github.com/bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DStuff/voxelizer, https://github.com/3DStuff/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Mesh-Plane Intersection
head: Parallel Mesh-Plane Intersection, computePlaneIntersections
body: Mesh-Plane Intersection computes the geometric intersection segments between a polygonal mesh and a set of cutting planes. It solves the problem of extracting cross-sectional contours from 3D geometry, which is a prerequisite for volume visualization techniques such as exploded views or clipping. Unlike Ray-Triangle Intersection, which yields a single point or none for a single ray, this method yields line segments (or points) representing the cross-section of each triangle by the plane. It is distinct from Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test as it operates against infinite planes rather than other triangles. Inputs: mesh: A polygonal mesh containing a list of vertices and a list of triangle indices. planes: A list of cutting planes. Outputs: intersection: A structure containing a list of IntersectionSegment objects and a boolean visible flag. Data Structures: Vertex: A 3-component float vector (x, y, z). IntersectionSegment: Contains start (Vertex), end (Vertex), and planeIndex (sizet). threadSafeSegments: A shared vector of IntersectionSegment used for parallel accumulation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Check if mesh.vertices or mesh.indices is empty. If so, set intersection.visible = false and return immediately to prevent crashes. 2. Parallel Iteration: Iterate over each plane in planes using parallel execution (e.g., OpenMP). 3. Triangle Iteration: For each plane, iterate over the mesh indices in steps of 3. Let the current index be i. The triangle vertices are v0 = \text{mesh.vertices}[\text{mesh.indices}[i]], v1 = \text{mesh.vertices}[\text{mesh.indices}[i+1]], and v2 = \text{mesh.vertices}[\text{mesh.indices}[i+2]]. 4. Triangle-Plane Intersection: Call trianglePlaneIntersection(v0, v1, v2, plane, segment) to compute the intersection segment. This function determines if the triangle intersects the plane and calculates the resulting segment endpoints. 5. Segment Assignment: If an intersection exists, assign segment.planeIndex = planeIdx (the current plane's index). 6. Accumulation: Push the valid segment into a local buffer localSegments. 7. Merge: After processing all triangles for a plane (or in a thread-safe manner), merge localSegments into the shared threadSafeSegments vector under a critical section. 8. Result Assignment: Assign the merged segments to the result: intersection.segments = std::move(threadSafeSegments). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshPlaneIntersection(mesh, planes): # Input validation if not mesh.vertices or not mesh.indices: return Intersection(visible=False, segments=[]) threadSafeSegments = [] # Parallel loop over planes for planeIdx in range(len(planes)): plane = planes[planeIdx] localSegments = [] # Iterate over triangles in steps of 3 for i in range(0, len(mesh.indices), 3): v0 = mesh.vertices[mesh.indices[i]] v1 = mesh.vertices[mesh.indices[i+1]] v2 = mesh.vertices[mesh.indices[i+2]] # Compute intersection segment segment = trianglePlaneIntersection(v0, v1, v2, plane) if segment is not None: segment.planeIndex = planeIdx localSegments.append(segment) # Merge local segments into shared list (thread-safe) # In a real implementation, this requires a critical section or atomic append for seg in localSegments: threadSafeSegments.append(seg) return Intersection(visible=True, segments=threadSafeSegments) def trianglePlaneIntersection(v0, v1, v2, plane): """ Computes the intersection of a triangle with a plane. Returns an IntersectionSegment or None if no intersection. Unlike ray-triangle intersection which yields a single point or none, this method yields a line segment (or points) representing the cross-section of the triangle by the plane. When not to use: When ray-based rendering is preferred, or when the mesh is extremely large and memory bandwidth becomes a bottleneck. name: Triangle-Plane Intersection
head: Plane Intersection Computation
body: Triangle-plane intersection determines whether a triangle intersects a plane, calculating the resulting intersection segment(s) and handling degenerate cases where vertices lie on the plane. It serves as the core geometric primitive for mesh-plane intersection, enabling the extraction of cutting lines from polygonal meshes. Unlike ray-triangle intersection which yields a single point or none, this method yields a line segment (or points) representing the cross-section of the triangle by the plane. Inputs: Triangle vertices: v0, v1, v2 (3D points). Plane defined by origin p{origin} and normal n (normalized). Outputs: A list of intersection points. If two distinct points exist, they form an IntersectionSegment. Data Structures: IntersectionSegment: struct with fields Vertex start, Vertex end, int planeIndex. PlaneIntersection: struct with fields std::vector<IntersectionSegment> segments, bool visible. Vertex: 3D point (x, y, z). Parameters: On-Plane Tolerance: \epsilon = 10^{-6}. Vertices with absolute distance < \epsilon are considered on the plane. Duplicate Removal Threshold: 10^{-10}. Points with squared distance < 10^{-10} are considered duplicates. Degenerate Segment Extension: 0.0001. Added to coordinates of a degenerate segment's end point. Steps: 1. Calculate Distances: Compute the signed distance of each vertex from the plane using the dot product formula: di = (vi - p{origin}) \cdot n for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. 2. Check for No Intersection: If all distances are strictly positive (d0 > 0, d1 > 0, d2 > 0) or all are strictly negative (d0 < 0, d1 < 0, d2 < 0), the triangle lies entirely on one side of the plane. Return no intersection. 3. Identify On-Plane Vertices: For each vertex vi, if |di| < \epsilon, mark vi as on-plane. 4. Compute Edge Intersections: Iterate over the three edges (v0, v1), (v1, v2), (v2, v0). For an edge connecting v{start} and v{end} with distances d{start} and d{end}: If neither vertex is on the plane and d{start} \cdot d{end} \le 0, the edge intersects the plane. Calculate the interpolation parameter t: t = \frac{d{start}}{d{start} - d{end}} Compute the intersection point: p{intersect} = v{start} + t \cdot (v{end} - v{start}) Add p{intersect} to the intersections list. 5. Add On-Plane Vertices: Add all vertices marked as on-plane to the intersections list. 6. Remove Duplicates: Iterate through the intersections list to remove duplicate points. For each pair of points, if the squared Euclidean distance is less than 10^{-10}, remove one. Use nested loops where the inner index j increments only if no removal occurs. 7. Form Segments: If the number of unique intersection points is \ge 2, set segment.start to the first point and segment.end to the second point. Return true. If exactly 1 intersection point exists (degenerate case), set segment.start and segment.end to that point. Then, add 0.0001 to each coordinate of segment.end to create a tiny segment. Return true. If 0 points, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triangleplaneintersection(v0, v1, v2, planeorigin, planenormal): # Step 1: Calculate distances d0 = dot(v0 - planeorigin, planenormal) d1 = dot(v1 - planeorigin, planenormal) d2 = dot(v2 - planeorigin, planenormal) # Step 2: Check for no intersection if (d0 > 0 and d1 > 0 and d2 > 0) or (d0 < 0 and d1 < 0 and d2 < 0): return [] intersections = [] epsilon = 1e-6 # Step 3 & 4: Identify on-plane vertices and edge intersections # Helper to check if point is on plane def isonplane(d): return abs(d) < epsilon # Check edges edges = [(v0, v1, d0, d1), (v1, v2, d1, d2), (v2, v0, d2, d0)] for vstart, vend, dstart, dend in edges: if isonplane(dstart): if vstart not in intersections: intersections.append(vstart) elif isonplane(dend): if vend not in intersections: intersections.append(vend) else: # Edge crosses plane if dstart dend <= 0: t = dstart / (dstart - dend) pintersect = vstart + t (vend - vstart) intersections.append(pintersect) # Step 6: Remove duplicates uniqueintersections = [] for i in range(len(intersections)): isdup = False for j in range(len(uniqueintersections)): if squareddistance(intersections[i], uniqueintersections[j]) < 1e-10: isdup = True break if not isdup: uniqueintersections.append(intersections[i]) # Step 7: Form segments if len(uniqueintersections) >= 2: segstart = uniqueintersections[0] segend = uniqueintersections[1] return [IntersectionSegment(segstart, segend)] elif len(uniqueintersections) == 1: p = uniqueintersections[0] # Degenerate case: create tiny segment segstart = p segend = Vector3(p.x + 0.0001, p.y + 0.0001, p.z + 0.0001) return [IntersectionSegment(segstart, segend)] else: return [] def squareddistance(p1, p2): dx = p1.x - p2.x dy = p1.y - p2.y dz = p1.z - p2.z return dxdx + dydy + dzdz Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle-plane pair, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the intersection calculation. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust handling of degenerate cases (vertices on plane, single point intersection). Limitations: The degenerate segment extension (0.0001) is arbitrary and may cause visual artifacts or incorrect topology if not handled carefully in downstream processing. Precision issues may arise with very large or very small coordinates due to floating-point tolerance thresholds. When to use: When extracting cross-sections from polygonal meshes for visualization or further geometric processing. When not to use: For ray-triangle intersection (use analytic ray-triangle methods) or when high-precision boolean operations are required without careful tolerance management. The method is described in the context of an exploded volume visualization tool, where mesh-plane intersection is used to cut meshes along cutting planes. The specific implementation details, including tolerance values and degenerate handling, are derived from the explodedvolumes repository.
