name: Coordinate System and Parametric Intersection
body: Coordinate System and Parametric Intersection provides geometric primitives for determining ray intersections within structured voxel grids and for computing approximate intersections with complex volumetric structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection by its specific handling of spherical grid topology and from Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation by its reliance on angular decomposition and scan-plane approximations. Determines whether a ray intersects an azimuthal section within a spherical voxel grid. An azimuthal section is defined as a surface segment living in the XZ plane, bounded by radial and polar extents. This method serves as the core primitive intersection test for the azimuthal dimension, complementing radial and polar hit detection. It is distinguished from Ray-Polar Section Intersection by operating on the XZ plane geometry rather than the XY plane, and from Ray-Ray Intersection by specifically handling the curved, sector-based boundaries of spherical coordinates rather than straight line segments. Choose it when traversing spherical voxel grids requiring azimuthal boundary checks. See Azimuthal Hit Detection. Determines whether a ray intersects a polar section, which is a volumetric primitive defined within the XY plane of a spherical voxel grid. It serves as the specific implementation for polar coordinates within the broader Ray-Primitive Intersection framework. It distinguishes itself from Azimuthal Hit Detection by operating on the Y-axis plane rather than the Z-axis, and from Ray-Ray Intersection by handling planar sector boundaries rather than linear line segments. Choose it when traversing spherical voxel grids requiring polar boundary checks. See Ray-Polar Section Intersection. Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. Used when rays do not intersect exactly due to noise or parallax, finding the point that minimizes the squared distance to both rays. It differs from exact intersection methods by providing a robust estimate for skew lines, which is essential in volumetric reconstruction where ray origins and directions are derived from noisy camera poses. Choose it when resolving non-intersecting lines in 3D space. See Ray-Ray Intersection. An approximate method to determine if a camera ray intersects a caustic beam and the location of that intersection, used because exact computation is too costly for thousands of beams. Definition: An approximate method to determine if a camera ray intersects a caustic beam and the location of that intersection, used because exact computation is too costly for thousands of beams. Steps: 1. Define a scan plane, which is an auxiliary arbitrary plane containing the camera ray. 2. Compute the intersections of the scan plane and the edges of the caustic beam to form a triangle. 3. Minimize error from curved beam edges by choosing the scan plane normal vector to be close to the normal of the caustic triangle. 4. Transform the view ray to the beam's local space. 5. Select a representative point on the intersection segment \Delta x (specifically the midpoint) and evaluate the area function A(y). 6. Compute the fraction of light scattered towards the viewer based on the cross-section area (determining radiance scaling) and scattering in the participating medium. Formula: The scan plane normal \mathbf{n}p is computed as \mathbf{n}p = \mathbf{r}{view} \times (\mathbf{r}{view} \times \mathbf{n}4), where \mathbf{r}{view} is the view ray direction and \mathbf{n}4 is the caustic triangle normal. Choose it when rendering real-time volume caustics where exact ray-bilinear patch intersection is too expensive. The spherical coordinate intersection methods are part of the infrastructure for spherical voxel grid traversal, often used in global illumination and caustic rendering where spherical symmetry or specific grid structures are advantageous. The Ray-Ray intersection method is a standard technique in computer graphics for finding the closest approach between skew lines, frequently used in ray tracing acceleration structures and multi-view geometry. The Scan Plane Beam Intersection method originates from real-time volume caustics rendering, where exact ray-bilinear patch intersection is too expensive for the large number of caustic beams present in typical scenes. name: Azimuthal Hit Detection
head: azimuthalHit
body: Azimuthal Hit Detection determines whether an azimuthal hit occurs for a given ray. An azimuthal hit is an intersection between the ray and an azimuthal section, where azimuthal sections live in the XZ plane. This method projects the 3D ray and voxel boundaries onto the XZ plane to perform 2D intersection tests, serving as one of the two angular components required to traverse a spherical volume. It differs from Ray-Polar Section Intersection by operating on the XZ plane rather than the XY plane, and from Ray-Ray Intersection by handling curved grid boundaries via planar projection. Inputs: grid: The spherical voxel grid object containing bounds, center, and angular resolution. ray: The ray being tested, containing origin, direction, and segment endpoints. currentazimuthalvoxel: The integer index of the current azimuthal voxel being traversed. collineartimes: Output container for collinear intersection times. t: Output parameter for the intersection distance. maxt: Maximum valid intersection distance. raysegment: Ray segment object with.P1() (start point) and.vector() (direction vector) methods. Outputs: Boolean indicating if an azimuthal hit occurred. Updated t and collineartimes if a hit is found. Data Structures: BoundVec3: A 3D vector structure where the Y-component is explicitly set to 0.0 for azimuthal calculations. grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(v): Returns a BoundVec3 representing the boundary vector for voxel v. grid.pMaxAzimuthal(v): Returns a structure with fields P1 and P2 representing the azimuthal bounds for voxel v. Steps: 1. Calculate pone: BoundVec3 with x = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P1, y = 0.0, z = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P2. 2. Calculate ptwo: BoundVec3 with x = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P1, y = 0.0, z = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P2. 3. Set umin pointer to &grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel). 4. Set umax pointer to &grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1). 5. Calculate wmin = pone - raysegment.P1(). 6. Calculate wmax = ptwo - raysegment.P1(). 7. Calculate perpuvmin = umin->x() raysegment.vector().z() - umin->z() raysegment.vector().x(). 8. Calculate perpuvmax = umax->x() raysegment.vector().z() - umax->z() raysegment.vector().x(). 9. Calculate perpuwmin = umin->x() wmin.z() - umin->z() wmin.x(). 10. Calculate perpuwmax = umax->x() wmax.z() - umax->z() wmax.x(). 11. Calculate perpvwmin = raysegment.vector().x() wmin.z() - raysegment.vector().z() wmin.x(). 12. Calculate perpvwmax = raysegment.vector().x() wmax.z() - raysegment.vector().z() wmax.x(). 13. Return angularHit(grid, ray, perpuvmin, perpuvmax, perpuwmin, perpuwmax, perpvwmin, perpvwmax, raysegment, collineartimes, t, maxt, ray.direction().z(), grid.sphereCenter().z(), grid.pMaxAzimuthal(), currentazimuthalvoxel). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class RaySegment: def init(self, start, direction): self.start = start self.dir = direction def P1(self): return self.start def vector(self): return self.dir def azimuthalHit(grid, ray, currentazimuthalvoxel, collineartimes, t, maxt, raysegment): # 1. Define boundary points in XZ plane (y=0) pone = Vec3(grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P1, 0.0, grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P2) ptwo = Vec3(grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P1, 0.0, grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P2) # 2. Get boundary vectors umin = grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel) umax = grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1) # 3. Displacement vectors from ray start raystart = raysegment.P1() rayvec = raysegment.vector() wmin = Vec3(pone.x - raystart.x, 0.0, pone.z - raystart.z) wmax = Vec3(ptwo.x - raystart.x, 0.0, ptwo.z - raystart.z) # 4. 2D Cross Products in XZ plane perpuvmin = umin.x rayvec.z - umin.z rayvec.x perpuvmax = umax.x rayvec.z - umax.z rayvec.x perpuwmin = umin.x wmin.z - umin.z wmin.x perpuwmax = umax.x wmax.z - umax.z wmax.x perpvwmin = rayvec.x wmin.z - rayvec.z wmin.x perpvwmax = rayvec.x wmax.z - rayvec.z wmax.x # 5. Call generalized angular hit handler # The sources do not provide the implementation of angularHit; it handles the actual intersection logic using the computed perpendicular components. # return angularHit(grid, ray, perpuvmin, perpuvmax, perpuwmin, perpuwmax, perpvwmin, perpvwmax, raysegment, collineartimes, t, maxt, ray.direction().z(), grid.sphereCenter().z(), grid.pMaxAzimuthal(), currentazimuthalvoxel) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Collinearity: If the ray is parallel to the azimuthal boundary, the cross products will be zero, and the angular hit handler updates collineartimes accordingly. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for equality should use a tolerance epsilon if exact equality is not guaranteed by the grid construction. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes currentazimuthalvoxel + 1 is a valid index; bounds checking mechanism is not given in the sources. Computes intersections in the XY plane for polar angles, setting it apart by operating on the XY plane rather than XZ. Choose when traversing the polar dimension of a spherical grid. Ray-Polar Section Intersection Handles intersections between two rays, setting it apart by not dealing with grid boundaries. Choose when determining ray-ray crossings. Ray-Ray Intersection Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently reduces 3D spherical intersection to 2D planar geometry and integrates with the generalized angular traversal framework. Limitations: Requires accurate pre-computation of azimuthal bounds. When to use: During spherical voxel grid traversal when crossing azimuthal boundaries. When not to use: When traversing radial or polar boundaries, or when the grid is not spherical. The method is part of the Spherical Volume Rendering (SVR) algorithm, implemented in the svr-algorithm repository. It follows the mathematical principles of decomposing spherical intersections into planar components for efficient traversal. spherical-volume-rendering/svr-algorithm, https://github.com/spherical-volume-rendering/svr-algorithm, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Polar Section Intersection
head: Polar Hit Detection, polarHit
body: Determines whether a ray intersects a polar section of a spherical voxel grid, where polar sections are defined within the XY plane. It differs from Azimuthal Hit Detection by operating on the polar coordinate boundaries (Y-axis projection) rather than azimuthal ones (Z-axis projection), and from Ray-Ray Intersection by utilizing precomputed grid boundary vectors rather than solving for arbitrary line-line crossings. Inputs: A ray segment (defined by origin P1 and direction vector \vec{v}), the current polar voxel index i, the spherical voxel grid data (including pMaxPolar boundary definitions and centerToPolarBound mappings), and traversal parameters (t, max\t, collinear times). Outputs: Boolean or status indicating a polar hit, with updated intersection parameters. Data Structures: BoundVec3: A 3D vector structure where the Z component is explicitly set to 0.0 for polar calculations. LineSegment: Defined by points P1 and P2. raysegment: Contains P1 (origin) and \vec{v} (direction vector). Steps: 1. Retrieve Boundary Points: Let P{1, i} be grid.pMaxPolar(i).P1 and P{2, i} be grid.pMaxPolar(i).P2. Let P{1, i+1} be grid.pMaxPolar(i+1).P1 and P{2, i+1} be grid.pMaxPolar(i+1).P2. Construct 2D vectors in the XY plane (Z=0): \vec{p}{one} = (P{1, i}, P{2, i}, 0.0) \vec{p}{two} = (P{1, i+1}, P{2, i+1}, 0.0) 2. Retrieve Center-to-Bound Vectors: Let \vec{u}{min} be the vector pointed to by grid.centerToPolarBound(i). Let \vec{u}{max} be the vector pointed to by grid.centerToPolarBound(i+1). 3. Calculate Displacement Vectors: Let \vec{w}{min} = \vec{p}{one} - ray\segment.P1. Let \vec{w}{max} = \vec{p}{two} - ray\segment.P1. 4. Calculate Perpendicular Components (2D Cross Products): These values represent the signed area of parallelograms formed by the vectors in the XY plane. perp\uv\min = u{min}.x \cdot v.y - u{min}.y \cdot v.x perp\uv\max = u{max}.x \cdot v.y - u{max}.y \cdot v.x perp\uw\min = u{min}.x \cdot w{min}.y - u{min}.y \cdot w{min}.x perp\uw\max = u{max}.x \cdot w{max}.y - u{max}.y \cdot w{max}.x perp\vw\min = v.x \cdot w{min}.y - v.y \cdot w{min}.x perp\vw\max = v.x \cdot w{max}.y - v.y \cdot w{max}.x 5. Invoke Generalized Angular Hit Logic: Pass the calculated perpendicular components to angularHit along with grid context, ray data, and traversal state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Construct pone and ptwo vectors (Z=0) pone = BoundVec3(x=p1curr, y=p2curr, z=0.0) ptwo = BoundVec3(x=p1next, y=p2next, z=0.0) # 3. Calculate w vectors wmin = pone - raysegment.P1() wmax = ptwo - raysegment.P1() # 5. name: Ray-Ray Intersection
head: Least-squares ray intersection, Ray vs. Ray Intersection
body: Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. It is used when rays do not intersect exactly (e.g., due to noise or parallax), finding the point that minimizes the squared distance to both rays. It sets itself apart from standard ray-casting which assumes exact intersection by minimizing the squared distance to both rays, making it robust to noise or parallax errors. Inputs: origins: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) containing the origins of the two rays. directions: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) containing the direction vectors of the two rays. eps: Float threshold for detecting parallel rays (default 1e-5). infval: Float value returned for parallel ray intersections (default 1e10). Outputs: result: Tensor of shape (shape, 3) containing the least-squares intersection points; parallel ray pairs are assigned infval. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on batched tensors where shape represents the batch dimensions (e.g., number of ray pairs). Intermediate tensor n has shape (2, shape, 3, 3) representing the matrix n{r,b,i,j}. Intermediate tensor lhs has shape (shape, 3, 3). Intermediate tensor rhs has shape (shape, 3). Steps: 1. Broadcast origins and directions to a common shape. 2. Stack origins and directions into tensors of shape (2, shape, 3). 3. Detect parallel rays by computing the dot product of the direction vectors for each ray pair; a pair is considered parallel if the dot product exceeds 1 - \text{eps}. 4. Filter out parallel rays from the origins and directions tensors. 5. Compute the outer product matrix n{r,b,i,j} = d{r,b,i} d{r,b,j} - \delta{i,j} for each ray, where d is the direction vector and \delta is the Kronecker delta (identity matrix). 6. Compute the left-hand side L{b,i,j} = \sum{r=0}^{1} n{r,b,i,j} by summing n over the ray dimension. 7. Compute the right-hand side R{b,i} = \sum{r=0}^{1} \sum{j=0}^{2} n{r,b,i,j} o{r,b,j} by multiplying n with the origins o and summing over the ray and inner indices. 8. Solve the linear system L p = R for p using least squares. 9. Initialize the output tensor with infval. 10. Assign the computed solution p to the non-parallel indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def intersectrays(origins, directions, eps=1e-5, infval=1e10): """ Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. Args: origins: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) directions: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) eps: Threshold for parallel ray detection infval: Value for parallel ray results Returns: result: Tensor of shape (shape, 3) """ origins = torch.astensor(origins, dtype=torch.float32) directions = torch.astensor(directions, dtype=torch.float32) shape = origins.shape[1:-1] # Step 3: Detect parallel rays dotproduct = torch.sum(directions[0] directions[1], dim=-1) parallel = dotproduct > (1.0 - eps) # Step 4: Filter parallel rays nonparallelmask = ~parallel if not torch.any(nonparallelmask): return torch.full((shape, 3), infval, dtype=origins.dtype, device=origins.device) # Flatten batch dimensions for indexing (not in sources) originsflat = origins.reshape(2, -1, 3) directionsflat = directions.reshape(2, -1, 3) parallelflat = parallel.reshape(-1) nonparallelflat = ~parallelflat originsfiltered = originsflat[:, nonparallelflat,:] directionsfiltered = directionsflat[:, nonparallelflat,:] # Step 5: Compute n n = torch.einsum("r b i, r b j -> r b i j", directionsfiltered, directionsfiltered) eye3 = torch.eye(3, dtype=n.dtype, device=n.device) n = n - eye3.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # Step 6: Compute LHS lhs = torch.sum(n, dim=0) # Step 7: Compute RHS rhstemp = torch.einsum("r b i j, r b j -> r b i", n, originsfiltered) rhs = torch.sum(rhstemp, dim=0) # Step 8: Solve linear system solution = torch.linalg.lstsq(lhs, rhs).solution # Step 9 & 10: Initialize and assign results result = torch.full((shape, 3), infval, dtype=origins.dtype, device=origins.device) resultflat = result.reshape(-1, 3) resultflat[nonparallelflat,:] = solution result = resultflat.reshape(shape, 3) return result Parameters: eps: Float, default 1e-5. Threshold for detecting parallel rays based on dot product proximity to 1. infval: Float, default 1e10. Value returned for parallel ray intersections. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If rays are parallel, the dot product threshold detects them and the algorithm returns infval. Degenerate Input: If origins or directions contain NaN or Inf, standard floating-point propagation rules apply. It extends Ray-Ray Intersection by batching the computation over multiple pixel locations and handling the transformation from camera to world space. It is distinct from standard ray-casting which assumes exact intersection; this method minimizes the squared distance to both rays, making it robust to noise or parallax errors. A filter to eliminate inaccurate correspondences by computing the minimal distance between two rays; true correspondences should converge at a single point (distance ~ 0). It discards paired rays where d{ray} > \tau{ray}. The distance d{ray} is computed as \|o1 - o2 + m d1 - n d2\|2, where o1, o2 are origins, d1, d2 are directions, and m, n are distances from origins to the closest points on the respective rays. The values m and n are solved from the system: \begin{cases} m(d1 \cdot d2) - n(d1 \cdot d2) = d1 \cdot o2 - d1 \cdot o1 \\ m(d1 \cdot d2) - n(d2 \cdot d2) = d2 \cdot o2 - d2 \cdot o1 \end{cases} The solution is: m = \frac{be + cf - cg - bd}{ab - c^2}, \quad n = \frac{ce + af - cd - ag}{ab - c^2} where a = d1 \cdot d1, b = d2 \cdot d2, c = d1 \cdot d2, d = d1 \cdot o1, e = d1 \cdot o2, f = d2 \cdot o1, g = d2 \cdot o2. name: Ray Casting and Intersection
head: Least-squares ray intersection, Ray intersection via least squares
body: Computes 3D ray origins and directions from 2D pixel coordinates and camera parameters, and finds the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. It extends Ray-Ray Intersection by batching the computation over multiple pixel locations and handling the transformation from camera to world space. It minimizes the squared distance to both rays, making it robust to calibration errors or parallax when rays do not intersect exactly. Inputs: intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrices K (typically 3 \times 3). extrinsics: Camera extrinsic matrices T (typically 4 \times 4), containing rotation R and translation t. pixelcoords: 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) for the rays to be cast. eps: Epsilon for detecting parallel rays (default 10^{-5}). infval: Value used to represent infinity for parallel ray intersections (default 10^{10}). Outputs: intersectionpoints: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) of the least-squares intersection points for each ray pair. Data Structures: Ray directions are stored as unit vectors in world space. Ray origins are stored as 3D points (camera centers). Matrices N are 3 \times 3 matrices derived from ray directions. Steps: 1. Unproject to Camera Space: Convert 2D pixel coordinates to homogeneous coordinates \mathbf{p}{cam} = [u, v, 1]^T. Multiply by the inverse intrinsic matrix K^{-1} to get unprojected direction vectors in camera space, then normalize by the z-component to obtain unit vectors. 2. Transform to World Space: Transform the ray directions from camera space to world space using the rotation component R of the extrinsic matrix. 3. Compute Ray Origins: Set ray origins to the camera center (translation part of extrinsics), tiled to match the ray direction shape. 4. Detect Parallel Rays: Check if the dot product of the two ray directions is greater than 1 - \text{eps}. 5. Construct Matrices: For each ray i with direction \mathbf{u}i, compute Ni = \mathbf{u}i \mathbf{u}i^T - I, where I is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. 6. Compute LHS: Sum N over the ray dimension to form the left-hand side of the least-squares equation: A = \sumi Ni. 7. Compute RHS: Multiply N with origins and sum over the ray dimension to form the right-hand side: \mathbf{b} = \sumi Ni \mathbf{o}i. 8. Filter Parallel Rays: Remove parallel rays from the batch before solving the linear system. 9. Solve: Solve for the intersection point \mathbf{p} using least squares: \mathbf{p} = \text{argmin}{\mathbf{x}} \| A \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \|^2. 10. Handle Parallel Rays: Set the result for parallel rays to infval to indicate no valid intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def raycastingandintersection( intrinsics1: torch.Tensor, extrinsics1: torch.Tensor, intrinsics2: torch.Tensor, extrinsics2: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords1: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords2: torch.Tensor, eps: float = 1e-5, infval: float = 1e10) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the least-squares intersection of two rays cast from pixel coordinates. Args: intrinsics1: (B, 3, 3) Camera intrinsic matrices for ray set 1. extrinsics1: (B, 4, 4) Camera extrinsic matrices for ray set 1. intrinsics2: (B, 3, 3) Camera intrinsic matrices for ray set 2. extrinsics2: (B, 4, 4) Camera extrinsic matrices for ray set 2. pixelcoords1: (B, 2) Pixel coordinates for ray set 1. pixelcoords2: (B, 2) Pixel coordinates for ray set 2. eps: Epsilon for parallel ray detection. infval: Value for parallel ray results. Returns: intersectionpoints: (B, 3) 3D intersection points. """ # Step 1: Unproject to camera space ones1 = torch.oneslike(pixelcoords1[...,:1]) pcam1 = torch.cat([pixelcoords1, ones1], dim=-1) dcam1 = torch.bmm(intrinsics1.inverse(), pcam1.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) dcam1 = dcam1 / dcam1[..., 2:3] ones2 = torch.oneslike(pixelcoords2[...,:1]) pcam2 = torch.cat([pixelcoords2, ones2], dim=-1) dcam2 = torch.bmm(intrinsics2.inverse(), pcam2.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) dcam2 = dcam2 / dcam2[..., 2:3] # Step 2: Transform to world space R1 = extrinsics1[:,:3,:3] dworld1 = torch.bmm(R1, dcam1.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) u1 = dworld1 / dworld1.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) R2 = extrinsics2[:,:3,:3] dworld2 = torch.bmm(R2, dcam2.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) u2 = dworld2 / dworld2.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Step 3: Compute origins origins1 = extrinsics1[:,:3, 3] origins2 = extrinsics2[:,:3, 3] # Step 4: Detect parallel rays dotproducts = torch.sum(u1 u2, dim=-1) isparallel = dotproducts > (1.0 - eps) # Step 5: Construct matrices Ni = ui ui^T - I u1ext = u1.unsqueeze(-1) u1T = u1.unsqueeze(-2) N1 = torch.bmm(u1ext, u1T) - torch.eye(3, device=u1.device).unsqueeze(0) u2ext = u2.unsqueeze(-1) u2T = u2.unsqueeze(-2) N2 = torch.bmm(u2ext, u2T) - torch.eye(3, device=u2.device).unsqueeze(0) # Step 6 & 7: Compute LHS and RHS A = N1 + N2 b = torch.bmm(N1, origins1.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) + torch.bmm(N2, origins2.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # Step 8 & 9: Solve least squares for non-parallel rays result = torch.full((A.shape[0], 3), infval, device=A.device) mask = ~isparallel if mask.any(): Anp = A[mask] bnp = b[mask] sol = torch.linalg.lstsq(Anp, bnp).solution result[mask] = sol return result Not given in the sources. name: Window Refraction (Slab Geometry)
head: Slab Refraction, Parallel-Sided Window Refraction
body: This method models the propagation of light rays through a parallel-sided glass slab (such as a window), calculating refraction at the first interface, linear propagation through the medium, and refraction at the second interface. It distinguishes itself from simple transmission or single-surface refraction by explicitly handling the displacement and angular change caused by traversing a finite thickness of material with a different refractive index. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Incident rays defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized); slab geometry defined by two parallel planes (left and right interfaces); refractive indices n{ext} (external) and n{glass} (internal). Outputs: Refracted rays with updated origins (exit points), updated directions, and transmission coefficients. Data Structures Rays are represented as tensors containing: origins: (N, 3) tensor of 3D coordinates. directions: (N, 3) tensor of normalized direction vectors. luminosities: (N,) tensor of intensity values. meta: Additional metadata (e.g., wavelength, ID). Parameters n{ext}: Refractive index of the external medium. n{glass}: Refractive index of the slab material. \mu = n{glass} / n{ext}: Relative refractive index ratio. Steps 1. Interface Intersection: Calculate the intersection parameter t for the ray with both the left and right interfaces of the slab. Let t{left} and t{right} be these values. 2. Entry Point Selection: Determine the entry point t{entry} as the minimum of t{left} and t{right}, excluding invalid intersections (e.g., rays originating inside or behind the slab). If an intersection is invalid, set t to NaN. 3. Masking: Create a boolean mask validmask identifying rays that successfully intersect the first interface (t{entry} is not NaN). 4. Internal Ray Construction: For valid rays, compute the entry point \mathbf{p}{entry} = \mathbf{o} + t{entry} \mathbf{d} and the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the entry interface. 5. First Refraction: Compute the refracted direction \mathbf{d}{glass} inside the slab using Snell's Law: c = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} \text{tmp} = 1 - \mu^2 (1 - c^2) \mathbf{d}{glass} = \sqrt{\text{tmp}} \mathbf{n} + \mu (\mathbf{d} - c \mathbf{n}) Note: If \text{tmp} < 0, total internal reflection occurs, and the ray is considered lost or reflected (not refracted through the slab). 6. Exit Intersection: Calculate the intersection parameter t{exit} for the internal ray (origin \mathbf{p}{entry}, direction \mathbf{d}{glass}) with the second interface. 7. Validity Check: Update the mask. If t{exit} is NaN (ray misses the second interface or total internal reflection occurred), the ray is discarded from the refracted output. 8. Exit Point and Second Refraction: For rays passing the validity check: Compute exit point: \mathbf{p}{exit} = \mathbf{p}{entry} + t{exit} \mathbf{d}{glass}. Compute exit normal \mathbf{n}{exit} (parallel to \mathbf{n} but pointing outward). Compute final refracted direction \mathbf{d}{out} using Snell's Law with ratio 1/\mu. 9. Transmission Coefficient: Calculate the transmission coefficient T using the Fresnel equations based on the incident angle at the first interface: T = \text{fresnel\transmission}(\arccos(c), n{ext}, n{glass}) 10. Output Assembly: Return new rays with: Origin: \mathbf{p}{exit} Direction: \mathbf{d}{out} Luminosity: L{out} = L{in} \times T Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def windowrefractionslab( origins: torch.Tensor, # (N, 3) directions: torch.Tensor, # (N, 3), normalized luminosities: torch.Tensor, # (N,) next: float, nglass: float, getrayintersectionleftinterface, # Function returning t for left plane getrayintersectionrightinterface, # Function returning t for right plane getraysinsidewindow # Function returning (rayinglass, normal)): """ Models refraction through a parallel-sided slab. """ # 1. Calculate intersection times with left and right interfaces tleft = getrayintersectionleftinterface(origins, directions) tright = getrayintersectionrightinterface(origins, directions) # 2. Select minimum t; set inf/invalid to NaN # Assuming getrayintersection returns NaN for no intersection tentry = torch.where(tright < tleft, tright, tleft) # 3. Filter rays that intersect the first interface mask = ~torch.isnan(tentry) if not mask.any(): return origins, directions, luminosities, mask # No valid rays # 4. Compute rays inside the window # This helper typically computes entry point and normal # Returns: (originsinside, directionsinside, normals) originsinside, directionsinside, normals = getraysinsidewindow( origins[mask], directions[mask], tentry[mask]) # 5. Calculate intersection with second interface # gettmin finds the smallest positive t for the second plane texit = gettmin(originsinside, directionsinside) # 6. Update mask for rays that hit the second interface validexit = ~torch.isnan(texit) finalmask = mask & validexit # 7. Compute refracted properties for valid rays # Extract valid data vorigins = origins[finalmask] vdirs = directions[finalmask] vlum = luminosities[finalmask] vnormals = normals[validexit] # Corresponding normals for valid exit rays # Relative refractive index mu = nglass / next # Snell's Law components # c = n. d (dot product of normal and incident direction) c = torch.sum(vnormals vdirs, dim=1) # tmp = 1 - mu^2 (1 - c^2) tmp = 1.0 - (mu 2) (1.0 - (c 2)) # Handle total internal reflection (tmp < 0) # In this specific slab implementation, if tmp < 0, the ray doesn't refract # We assume getraysinsidewindow or texit logic already handles # rays that don't propagate, but we safeguard here. validrefraction = tmp >= 0 finalmask = finalmask & validrefraction # Refracted direction inside glass # dglass = sqrt(tmp) n + mu (d - c n) dglass = torch.sqrt(tmp.unsqueeze(1)) vnormals + mu (vdirs - c.unsqueeze(1) vnormals) # Exit point calculation # texit is already computed for the internal ray # pexit = pentry + texit dglass # Note: originsinside are the entry points pexit = originsinside[validrefraction] + texit[validrefraction].unsqueeze(1) dglass[validrefraction] # Second refraction (Glass to External) # Normal at exit is same as entry normal but pointing outward? # For parallel slab, normal vector direction relative to ray matters. # Assuming normals passed are consistent with entry. # For exit, we refract from nglass to next. Ratio is 1/mu. muexit = 1.0 / mu # Dot product with exit normal (assuming normal points out of glass) # If normals are stored as entry normals, we might need to flip them for exit calculation # depending on convention. Assuming getraysinsidewindow provides normals # oriented for the internal propagation context or we handle sign. # Standard Snell's law vector form for exit: # cexit = nexit. dglass # If nexit is parallel to nentry, and dglass is entering the second surface: cexit = torch.sum(vnormals[validrefraction] dglass[validrefraction], dim=1) tmpexit = 1.0 - (muexit 2) (1.0 - (cexit 2)) validexitrefraction = tmpexit >= 0 finalmask = finalmask & validexitrefraction dout = torch.sqrt(tmpexit.unsqueeze(1)) vnormals[validrefraction] + muexit (dglass[validrefraction] - cexit.unsqueeze(1) vnormals[validrefraction]) # Transmission coefficient # Incident angle thetai = acos(c) thetai = torch.acos(torch.clamp(c[validrefraction], -1.0, 1.0)) transcoeff = fresnelcoeff(thetai, nglass, next) # Update luminosities newluminosities = vlum[validrefraction] transcoeff # Return new Rays neworigins = pexit[validrefraction] newdirections = dout[validrefraction] return neworigins, newdirections, newluminosities, finalmask def fresnelcoeff(thetai, n1, n2): """ Simplified transmission coefficient calculation. Uses Fresnel equations for unpolarized light. """ # Snell's law: n1 sin(thetai) = n2 sin(thetat) sinthetat = (n1 / n2) torch.sin(thetai) costhetat = torch.sqrt(1.0 - sinthetat 2) # Fresnel transmission for unpolarized light # T = 0.5 (Ts + Tp) # Ts = 1 - ((n1 cos(thetai) - n2 cos(thetat)) / (n1 cos(thetai) + n2 cos(thetat)))^2 # Tp = 1 - ((n1 cos(thetat) - n2 cos(thetai)) / (n1 cos(thetat) + n2 cos(thetai)))^2 costhetai = torch.cos(thetai) nums = n1 costhetai - n2 costhetat dens = n1 costhetai + n2 costhetat Ts = 1.0 - (nums / dens) 2 nump = n1 costhetat - n2 costhetai denp = n1 costhetat + n2 costhetai Tp = 1.0 - (nump / denp) 2 return 0.5 (Ts + Tp) Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. The cost is dominated by a constant number of vector operations and trigonometric functions per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store ray attributes and intermediate tensors. Strengths: Physically accurate for parallel-sided transparent objects; handles batched ray processing efficiently on GPUs. Limitations: Assumes ideal parallel planes; does not account for dispersion (wavelength-dependent refraction) unless extended; total internal reflection results in ray loss unless handled by a reflection model. When to use: Simulating windows, glass panes, or planar optical elements in ray tracing. When not to use: Curved glass surfaces (use Sphere Intersection or general mesh intersection) or when dispersion is critical. This method is implemented in the gradoptics library, part of the MAGIS (Matter-gravity Interferometer with Atomic Sensing) project infrastructure, used for simulating optical systems in precision measurement experiments. It provides a specialized primitive for ray-tracing through planar dielectric interfaces. magis-slac/gradoptics, https://github.com/magis-slac/gradoptics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Topological/Inside Tests
body: Topological/Inside Tests evaluate the topological relationship between a query point and a boundary to determine if the point lies inside or outside a volume or mesh. They serve as a preprocessing step for sculpting applications and boolean operations. Unlike Ray-primitive intersection, which computes geometric hit points, these tests return a boolean state or winding number for a static point. See Ray-primitive intersection. Determines if a point is inside a closed triangle mesh by counting ray-surface intersections. It solves the topological "inside/outside" ambiguity that plagues simpler depth-based tests. Unlike Region Nesting Merge, which relies on hierarchical containment logic, this method uses a direct parity or signed accumulation of ray-triangle hits. Choose this for general point-in-mesh queries on closed meshes. A post-processing step that removes nested inner regions from a sorted list of ray samples. It solves the problem of redundant geometry resulting from boolean unions or subtractions where one volume is entirely contained within another. It differs from Ray Crossing Count (Winding Number) by using a simple nesting depth counter based on normal direction rather than a cumulative winding number, making it suitable for specific sculpting and boolean contexts where only the outermost boundary of nested structures is required. Choose this when processing pre-computed ray samples for sculpting or boolean operations. A procedure that checks if a vertex is inside or outside the volume by finding the closest sample along the ray and checking its normal direction. Step 1. Calculate the signed distance between the vertex v and the ray origin. 2. Find the sample s in R.list where the distance from s.position to R.origin is less than or equal to the vertex distance and is the maximum such distance. 3. If the dot product of s.normal and R.direction is less than 0, return False (outside). Code Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def IsInside(Ray R, Vertex v): dist = Dist(v, R.origin) # signed dist. between 2 points s = None maxdist = -float('inf') for sample in R.list: d = Dist(sample.position, R.origin) if d <= dist and d > maxdist: maxdist = d s = sample if s is None: return False if Dot(s.normal, R.direction) < 0: return False else: return True A method to detect if a triangle is inverted (facing the inside of the object) by checking the dot product of the triangle normal and the field function gradients at its vertices. Formula n \cdot F'(a) > 0 \text{ AND } n \cdot F'(b) > 0 \text{ AND } n \cdot F'(c) > 0. Pitfalls Discrete integration can let points cross an edge and create a fold. Edge collapsing may invert a neighboring triangle. Surface projection constraints may invert triangles when projecting points to the surface. Edge subdivision inherently inserts new inverted elements when subdividing an edge belonging to an inverted triangle. User interaction or surface animation may modify particle positions too fast for the mechanical system to follow them. The methods discussed in provide better visual quality for sculpting applications by reducing distance error compared to other algorithms. Cubical marching squares and associated data structures are utilized to improve visual quality and distance error in these applications. The methods allow for efficient visual quality improvements in sculpting by providing robust inside/outside tests for vertices and samples. name: Ray Crossing Count (Winding Number)
head: Crossing Count Ray Query, Even-Odd Rule for Classification, Ray-Triangle Crossing Count, Winding Number Classification, Winding Number Rule for Classification, winding number via crossing count
body: The Ray Crossing Count method determines whether a 3D point lies inside or outside a closed triangle mesh by casting a ray and counting surface intersections. It solves the topological "inside/outside" ambiguity that plagues simpler depth-based tests, which can fail when a ray intersects the same triangle multiple times or hits edges/vertices, causing sign-flipping artifacts. Builds on Topological/Inside Tests. Unlike the Region Nesting Merge sibling, which relies on hierarchical containment logic, this method uses a direct parity or signed accumulation of ray-triangle hits. Input: A query point P = (Px, Py, Pz) and a triangle mesh \mathcal{M} consisting of N triangles. Each triangle Ti is defined by vertices \mathbf{v}{i,0}, \mathbf{v}{i,1}, \mathbf{v}{i,2} and an outward-facing normal \mathbf{n}i. Output: A boolean indicating if P is inside the mesh, or an integer/float winding number. 1. Triangle List: An array of N triangles, where each triangle stores vertex positions and precomputed normals. 2. Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH): A tree structure where each node stores an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) enclosing its child triangles, and leaves contain indices to the triangle list. 3. 2D Grid (Optional Optimization): For axis-aligned ray casting, a 2D grid of size W \times H stores lists of triangles intersecting each grid cell, along with their intersection z-values. 1. Initialize crossingCount = 0 and totalCount = 0. 2. Cast a ray from P along direction \mathbf{d}. 3. Traverse the BVH to find every triangle whose bounding box intersects the given ray. 4. For each candidate triangle, compute the ray-triangle intersection. 5. If the intersection occurs at a positive distance t > 0, increment totalCount. 6. Update crossingCount by adding +1 if \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0, otherwise adding -1. 7. Classify the point: if using parity, odd totalCount means inside and even means outside. If using signed winding, outside yields 0 and inside yields +1 for a closed outward-oriented mesh. 8. For degenerate cases, cast rays in six directions (±x, ±y, ±z) and take a majority vote of the inside/outside results. 9. For open meshes or triangle soups, the signed crossing count provides a generalized value between 0 and 1. Signed Winding Update: \text{crossingCount} \leftarrow \text{crossingCount} + \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Parity Classification: \text{Inside} \iff \text{totalCount} \bmod 2 = 1. Signed Classification: \text{Inside} \iff \text{crossingCount} = 1 (closed outward mesh). Generalized Winding: \text{Value} \in [0, 1] for meshes with holes or soups. Ray Direction: Typically aligned with a principal axis (e.g., +z) for the 2D grid optimization, or arbitrary directions for robustness. Intersection Algorithm: Müller-Trombose intersection algorithm. Grid Resolution: Example given is 128 \times 128 for the 2D projection optimization. Edge/Vertex Hits: Rays hitting triangle edges or vertices may double-count triangles, making the theoretical crossing count unreliable for single rays. Closed Mesh Requirement: The parity method is only meaningful for closed meshes. Numerical Precision: Floating-point errors near the surface can cause inconsistent results; a small epsilon guard is required for intersection checks. Performance Scaling: Brute-force checking all triangles is O(N). The 2D grid optimization reduces the query search space from checking 128^3 points to 128^2 points by pre-calculating intersections. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, v0, v1, v2): edge1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) edge2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) normal = cross(edge1, edge2) denom = dot(normal, direction) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: return None t = dot(normal, (v0[0]-origin[0], v0[1]-origin[1], v0[2]-origin[2])) / denom if t <= 0: return None hit = (origin[0]+direction[0]t, origin[1]+direction[1]t, origin[2]+direction[2]t) v0v1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) v0v2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) v0p = (hit[0]-v0[0], hit[1]-v0[1], hit[2]-v0[2]) d00 = dot(v0v1, v0v1) d01 = dot(v0v1, v0v2) d02 = dot(v0v1, v0p) d11 = dot(v0v2, v0v2) d12 = dot(v0v2, v0p) invDenom = 1.0 / (d00 d11 - d01 d01) u = (d11 d02 - d01 d12) invDenom v = (d00 d12 - d01 d02) invDenom if u >= 0.0 and v >= 0.0 and (u + v) <= 1.0: return (t, hit) return None def traversebvhcandidates(bvh, origin, direction): # Standard BVH traversal: check AABB intersection, recurse to children, collect leaf triangle indices # Returns list of triangle indices whose bounding boxes intersect the ray. return [] # Placeholder for BVH traversal implementation def raycrossingcount(querypoint, triangles, bvh, usesigned=True): rayorigin = querypoint raydirection = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) crossingcount = 0 totalcount = 0 candidateindices = traversebvhcandidates(bvh, rayorigin, raydirection) for idx in candidateindices: tri = triangles[idx] hit = raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2) if hit is not None: totalcount += 1 if usesigned: dotproduct = dot(tri.normal, raydirection) crossingcount += 1 if dotproduct > 0.0 else -1 else: crossingcount += 1 if usesigned: return crossingcount else: return (crossingcount % 2) == 1 Time Complexity: O(N) for brute-force ray-triangle intersection. Traversing a BVH prunes non-intersecting triangles. The 2D grid optimization reduces the query search space from 128^3 points to 128^2 points. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing triangles. O(H \cdot W) for the 2D grid optimization. Measured Performance: The overhead of the raycast step is small when performed simultaneously with Signed Distance Field (SDF) calculation. Strengths: Robust against sign-flipping artifacts caused by depth-based tests. Provides generalized winding numbers for non-closed meshes. Limitations: Sensitive to degenerate ray hits (edges/vertices) without mitigation. Requires closed meshes for simple parity interpretation. When to Use: When topological correctness is critical, especially in Marching Cubes implementations where incorrect inside/outside tests cause artifacts. When dealing with meshes that may have holes or non-manifold geometry, the signed winding number is preferred. The Ray Crossing Count method is a fundamental technique in computational geometry for point-in-polyhedron tests. It is widely used in volume rendering, particularly in Marching Cubes implementations, to correctly determine the interior of a mesh. The specific implementation using signed crossing counts to fix artifacts in Marching Cubes 33 was detailed by Vega et al. in "A Fast and Memory-Saving Marching Cubes 33 Implementation with the Correct Interior Test" (JCGT 2019). The 2D grid optimization approach is discussed in community forums as a way to reduce computational complexity for voxel-based rendering. name: Region Nesting Merge
head: MergeRegion
body: Region Nesting Merge is a post-processing step for topological ray operations that removes nested inner regions from a sorted list of ray samples. It solves the problem of redundant or invalid geometry resulting from boolean unions or subtractions, where one volumetric region is contained entirely within another. It differs from Ray Crossing Count by relying on the orientation of surface normals relative to the ray direction to determine nesting depth, rather than counting geometric intersections. It is a core component of Ray Union and Ray Subtraction. Inputs and Outputs The input is a ray R containing a list of samples R.list sorted by position along the ray. Each sample s contains a position and a normal vector s.normal. The ray contains a direction vector R.direction. The output updates R.list to contain only the samples defining the outermost boundaries of the volumetric regions, effectively removing any samples that define regions strictly inside other regions. Data Structures The ray structure holds a direction vector and a list of samples. Each sample structure holds a position and a normal vector. A temporary list T is allocated to accumulate the surviving samples. Algorithm The procedure iterates through the sorted samples while maintaining a nesting level counter. The logic treats a sample with a normal pointing against the ray direction as an entry into a volume, and a normal pointing with the ray direction as an exit. 1. Initialize a nesting level counter level = 0. 2. Initialize an empty output list T. 3. For each sample s in the sorted input list R.list: a. Calculate the dot product D = \mathbf{n}s \cdot \mathbf{d}R. b. If D < 0 (normal opposes ray direction, entering a region): decrement level by 1. If level == 0, add s to T. c. Else (D \ge 0, normal aligns with ray direction, leaving a region): if level == 0, add s to T. Increment level by 1. 4. Replace R.list with T. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def MergeRegion(R): level = 0 T = [] for s in R.list: dotproduct = dot(s.normal, R.direction) if dotproduct < 0: level = level - 1 if level == 0: T.append(s) else: if level == 0: T.append(s) level = level + 1 R.list = T Parameters R.direction is the direction vector of the ray. s.normal is the normal vector of the sample. The normals must be consistent with the topological definition of the volume, typically outward-facing for standard union logic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls The input list R.list must be strictly sorted by position along the ray, otherwise the nesting logic fails. The algorithm relies on the convention that normals pointing against the ray direction denote entry, which must be maintained across all samples. In Ray Subtraction, the normals of the subtracted volume are inverted before merging to satisfy this convention for the subtraction logic. If the list is empty, the output is empty. If the nesting level does not return to 0 at the end of the list, the input data is topologically inconsistent (e.g., an unpaired entry or exit). Ray subtraction is a boolean operation that removes material from a target ray (Ray A) using a source ray (Ray B). The time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of samples in R.list, as the algorithm performs a single pass through the list. The memory complexity is O(N) in the worst case, as a new list T is created. The method is simple, efficient, and robust for boolean operations on ray-based volumetric representations. It assumes a specific normal orientation convention and requires pre-sorted input. It does not handle complex self-intersections or non-manifold geometry that violates the entry/exit pairing assumption. Region Nesting Merge was introduced in the context of detail sculpting using cubical marching squares. It serves as the core mechanism for resolving topological conflicts in ray-based boolean operations. The method is part of a family of topological inside tests that use normal orientation to determine volumetric inclusion. name: Ray Subtraction
head: RaySubstraction
body: Ray subtraction is a boolean operation that removes material from a target ray (Ray A) using a source ray (Ray B). It solves the problem of sculpting or editing volumetric data by allowing users to delete specific regions, such as removing a sphere from a cube. It differs from Ray Union by inverting the normals of the source samples before merging, which causes the MergeRegion procedure to treat the source region as an "inside" void rather than an added volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray A (target), Ray B (source). Output: Ray A modified in place to represent the material of A minus B. Data Structures: Ray.list: A list of samples. Each sample s contains a position (implied by sorting) and a normal vector. Ray.direction: The viewing direction vector. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through every sample s in Ray B.list. 2. Negate the normal of sample s: s.normal \leftarrow -s.normal. 3. Append the modified sample s to Ray A.list. 4. Sort Ray A.list by depth (typically z-value or distance along the ray). 5. Call MergeRegion on Ray A to remove inner regions based on the inverted normals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RaySubstraction(A, B): for s in B.list: s.normal = -s.normal A.list.append(s) A.list.sort(key=lambda s: dot(s.position, A.direction)) MergeRegion(A) def MergeRegion(R): level = 0 T = [] for s in R.list: if dot(s.normal, R.direction) < 0: level -= 1 if level == 0: T.append(s) else: if level == 0: T.append(s) level += 1 R.list = T Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision errors in sorting or dot products may lead to incorrect nesting levels if samples are coplanar or nearly parallel to the ray. A procedure for handling occlusion when removing an object part that is in front of another one. Instead of simple boolean subtraction, it zeros out the first mode of density along the ray. The first mode of density is defined as starting at the first point with non-zero density up to the first subsequent point with zero density. This procedure is effective but can be slow and may leave artifacts of incomplete removal. A technique to remove occluding structures by skipping ray integration steps that intersect with a specified geometric shape (e.g., sphere, cone, cylinder). It uses an Init shader to compute start and stopping coordinates of the carving shape. If the ray intersects the shape, the integration start position (currentDistance) is adjusted to the intersection point. Parameters: interactionPoint1: A user-defined 3D coordinate used to determine the center of the carving shape (e.g., sphere). currentDistance: A built-in variable specifying the next integration position along the ray. sphereRadius: The radius of the carving sphere. Pseudocode (Volume Carving Init Shader): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. centerDir = interactionPoint1 - rayStart centerProjDist = dot(centerDir, rayDir) centerProj = rayStart + rayDir centerProjDist distCenterProjCenter = length(centerProj - interactionPoint1) if distCenterProjCenter < sphereRadius: dcpc2 = distCenterProjCenter distCenterProjCenter sr2 = sphereRadius sphereRadius intersectDistance = centerProjDist + sqrt(sr2 - dcpc2) if intersectDistance > 0.0: currentDistance = intersectDistance Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step, O(N \log N) where N is the total number of samples in both rays, plus the linear scan of MergeRegion, O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the merged list. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages existing union and merge logic. Limitations: The basic boolean subtraction does not handle occlusion well (e.g., removing a front object while keeping a back object) without additional density zeroing techniques. The volume carving variant can be slow and may leave artifacts. When to use: When performing boolean sculpting on ray lists where topological correctness is required. When not to use: When occlusion handling is critical and performance is constrained, or when the geometry is complex enough that simple ray list manipulation fails to capture the visual intent. The method originates from work on detail sculpting using cubical marching squares. It was introduced as Algorithm 3 in the paper "Detail sculpting using cubical marching squares". The technique is similar to Ray Union but relies on normal inversion to achieve subtraction semantics. Variants like Volume Carving were later explored in the context of interactive GPU volume rendering shaders using frameworks like PRISM, and occlusion-aware removal was discussed in the context of editing Conditional Radiance Fields. name: Ray-Mesh Intersection Sampling with Priority Material Assignment
head: Mesh-Based Material Assignment, Priority Rule Assignment
body: This method determines the material composition at each sample point along a view ray by intersecting the ray with a set of organ meshes, decomposing the ray into segments, and assigning materials based on a strict priority hierarchy to resolve overlaps. It differs from voxel-level segmentation approaches by ensuring smooth boundaries between organs, thereby avoiding the "staircase" artifacts common in grid-based segmentation. Inputs: A grid-based MRI scalar volumetric dataset. A set of triangle meshes representing internal organs and the external skin. The specific dataset described consists of: 1 skin mesh. 23 bone meshes. 17 muscle meshes. 10 tendon meshes. 6 ligament capsule meshes. Outputs: For each ray, a sequence of samples with assigned materials, colors (C), and opacities (\alpha) ready for compositing. Data Structures: Meshes: Triangle meshes for each organ type. No specific bit-packing or layout is given beyond the count of meshes per organ type. Ray Segments: A list of intervals [t{start}, t{end}] along the ray parameter t, defined by consecutive intersection points. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} into the volume. 2. Intersection Computation: Compute all intersection points between the ray and every mesh in the set (skin, bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments). 3. Sorting: Sort the intersection points by their distance from the camera (increasing t). 4. Segmentation: Decompose the ray into segments between consecutive sorted intersection points. The first intersection defines the start of sampling, and the last intersection defines the end. This ignores empty space outside the hand, accelerating rendering and ignoring MRI noise. 5. Material Assignment: For each segment, determine which meshes contain the segment's interior. Apply the priority rule to assign a single material to the entire segment. The priority hierarchy is: \text{bone} > \text{tendon} > \text{muscle} > \text{ligament} > \text{fat} "Fat" is defined as locations inside the skin mesh but not inside any other organ mesh (bone, tendon, muscle, or ligament). 6. Sampling: Evaluate MRI values at discrete sample positions along the ray. MRI values are obtained by trilinear interpolation from the discrete grid points. 7. Jittering: Apply stochastic jittering to sample positions to avoid "wood-grain artifacts" caused by equidistant sampling discretization. 8. Opacity Correction: If stochastic jittering changes the effective sample spacing from \Delta x0 (equidistant) to \Delta x, correct the opacity \alpha of the sampled points. If \alpha{equidistant} is the opacity under equidistant sampling, the corrected opacity is: \alpha{corrected} = \alpha{equidistant} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta x0}. 9. Transfer Function Application: Apply the transfer function corresponding to the assigned material to the MRI value to obtain color C and opacity \alpha. 10. Compositing: Composite the resulting colors and opacities using back-to-front order along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, meshes, volumegrid, transferfunctions): # Step 1 & 2: Compute intersections intersections = [] for mesh in meshes: # Compute intersection of ray with mesh triangles # Returns list of t values where ray intersects mesh tvals = intersectraymesh(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh) for t in tvals: intersections.append(t) # Step 3: Sort intersections intersections.sort() if not intersections: return None # No intersection with hand # Step 4: Define sampling range tstart = intersections[0] tend = intersections[-1] # Step 5: Decompose into segments and assign materials # Note: In practice, one might sample continuously, but the method # assigns material per segment defined by intersections. # For implementation, we iterate through segments. segments = [] for i in range(len(intersections) - 1): tsegstart = intersections[i] tsegend = intersections[i+1] # Pick a representative point in the segment to determine containment tmid = (tsegstart + tsegend) / 2.0 point = rayorigin + raydirection tmid # Determine which meshes contain this point # This requires a point-in-mesh test for each mesh containingmeshes = [] for mesh in meshes: if ispointinsidemesh(point, mesh): containingmeshes.append(mesh) # Apply Priority Rule material = assignprioritymaterial(containingmeshes) segments.append({ 'tstart': tsegstart, 'tend': tsegend, 'material': material }) # Step 6, 7, 8, 9: Sample and composite # Approximate volume integral using discrete samples # Back-to-front compositing color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alphaaccumulated = 0.0 # Iterate segments from back to front (decreasing t) for segment in reversed(segments): ts = segment['tstart'] te = segment['tend'] material = segment['material'] # Determine number of samples for this segment # Or use a fixed step size deltax # Let's assume a fixed step size for simplicity, adjusted by jitter numsamples = int((te - ts) / stepsize) + 1 for k in range(numsamples): # Stochastic jittering jitter = random.uniform(0, stepsize) tsample = ts + k stepsize + jitter # Ensure within segment bounds if tsample > te: continue # Sample position pos = rayorigin + raydirection tsample # Trilinear interpolation from volume grid mrivalue = trilinearinterpolate(volumegrid, pos) # Get transfer function for material tf = transferfunctions[material] # Apply transfer function Craw, alpharaw = tf(mrivalue) # Opacity correction for jittering # Assuming stepsize corresponds to deltax0 # If jitter changes effective spacing, correct alpha # The source formula: alphacorrected = alphaequidistant (dx / dx0) # Here, if we treat the sample as representing a volume element # proportional to the step size, and jitter affects the effective # coverage, we apply the correction. # Note: The exact application of this formula in discrete sampling # requires careful handling of the "equidistant" baseline. # We assume alpharaw is computed for equidistant spacing. alphacorrected = alpharaw (stepsize / stepsize) # Simplified if stepsize is constant # Back-to-front compositing # Cout = Cin + Csample alphasample (1 - alphaaccumulated) # alphaout = alphaaccumulated + alphasample (1 - alphaaccumulated) weight = alphacorrected (1.0 - alphaaccumulated) color = color + Craw weight alphaaccumulated = alphaaccumulated + alphacorrected (1.0 - alphaaccumulated) if alphaaccumulated >= 1.0: break return color def assignprioritymaterial(containingmeshes): # Priority: bone > tendon > muscle > ligament > fat # Check for highest priority mesh present if any(mesh.type == 'bone' for mesh in containingmeshes): return 'bone' if any(mesh.type == 'tendon' for mesh in containingmeshes): return 'tendon' if any(mesh.type == 'muscle' for mesh in containingmeshes): return 'muscle' if any(mesh.type == 'ligament' for mesh in containingmeshes): return 'ligament' # Fat is inside skin but not other organs # If we are here, we are inside skin (checked by caller or implicit) # and not in bone, tendon, muscle, ligament return 'fat' def ispointinsidemesh(point, mesh): # Standard ray casting or winding number algorithm for point-in-mesh # Returns True if point is inside the mesh volume pass def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): # Trilinear interpolation of scalar value at point in grid pass Parameters: Step Size: Not explicitly given, but determines sample density. Priority Hierarchy: bone > tendon > muscle > ligament > fat. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mesh Overlaps: Segmentation errors cause mesh overlaps (e.g., organs inside skin, ligaments intersecting phalanges). The priority rule resolves this ambiguity. Wood-Grain Artifacts: Equidistant sampling leads to artifacts. Stochastic jittering is required. Opacity Correction: When using jittering, opacity must be corrected to maintain energy conservation/accuracy. Time Complexity: Dominated by ray-mesh intersection tests. With N meshes and T triangles per mesh, intersection is O(N \cdot T) per ray. Sorting intersections is O(K \log K) where K is the number of intersections. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the volume grid and mesh data structures. Strengths: Avoids "staircase" artifacts common in voxel-level segmentation by ensuring smooth boundaries between organs. Improves image quality by ignoring MRI noise outside the hand. Limitations: Requires pre-computed, accurate mesh segmentation. Computationally expensive due to numerous ray-mesh intersections. When to use: When high-quality visualization of complex, overlapping anatomical structures is required, and mesh data is available. When not to use: When mesh data is not available, or real-time performance is critical and mesh intersection costs are prohibitive. This method was described in the context of volume rendering human hand anatomy from MRI data. It was proposed to improve upon voxel-level segmentation techniques by using mesh-based material assignment. The approach was applied to a dataset consisting of 1 skin, 23 bones, 17 muscles, 10 tendons, and 6 ligament capsules. name: Ray generation and camera models
body: Ray generation and camera models define the geometric mapping from discrete 2D pixel coordinates to continuous 3D world-space rays, serving as the foundational input for volume rendering, ray marching, and ray tracing pipelines. This family solves the problem of establishing a valid view frustum by constructing camera basis vectors and projecting pixel locations onto a virtual image plane. It differs from sibling methods like Ray-primitive intersection by focusing solely on the creation of the ray geometry rather than its traversal, and from Parallel and GPU primitives by defining the logical data flow rather than the hardware execution model. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Sky Gradient generates a background color for rays that miss the primary volume or reach infinite distance by interpolating between a horizon color and a zenith color based on the ray's vertical direction component. It is a lightweight, non-geometry effect often implemented as a handful of sine waves or simple color blending in a sky shader. The Arcball Camera is an interactive camera control technique that maps 2D screen coordinates to a 3D virtual sphere to compute rotation quaternions for smooth orbiting around a center point. It decouples 2D input from 3D orientation, allowing intuitive rotation without gimbal lock. It differs from First-Person Camera Control by orbiting a fixed center rather than moving the eye position directly. Uniform Sphere Sampling generates a random direction vector uniformly distributed over the surface of a unit sphere. It solves the problem of creating isotropic ray directions for global illumination, sky sampling, or volume scattering where no preferred direction exists. It sets itself apart from Random Hemisphere Sampling by covering the full 4\pi steradians rather than restricting samples to a half-sphere, and from Rejection Sampling for Uniform Sphere Sampling by using a direct transformation method that avoids discarding samples. First-Person Camera Control manages camera position, orientation (yaw and pitch), and projection parameters, translating discrete user input (mouse movement, keyboard presses) into continuous 3D transformations. It packs these state variables into a GPU-friendly structure to minimize bandwidth overhead during rendering passes. The Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector is a CT geometry type that allows the user to define the 3D location and orientation of every individual source-detector pair, overriding standard geometric assumptions. It supports flexible specification including arbitrary 3D detector shifts and non-equispaced projection angles, covering planar or curved detectors (axial) and arbitrary source/detector placement (flexible). It differs from fixed-camera models by explicitly defining every source-detector pair, supporting complex trajectories and parameterized detector surfaces while maintaining exact cell-constant integration. The Camera Class Structure defines the geometric state and rendering parameters required to generate rays for volume rendering. It serves as the primary interface between the application's scene graph and the ray generation kernel, encapsulating position, orientation, field of view, and clipping boundaries. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific sampling strategies or traversal setups, this structure provides the foundational data layout necessary to compute ray origins and directions for any camera model. Ray Angle Computation calculates the geometric angular relationship between a query ray and reference rays intersecting the same 3D point. It is primarily used in multi-view stereo and NeRF-based methods to generate features that encode viewing geometry. Unlike methods that rely solely on coordinate transformations, this approach explicitly computes the dot product and difference vectors between ray directions to capture angular similarity. The Sky Radiance Model generates background illumination for ray-traced scenes by sampling a precomputed equirectangular sky texture and adding a direct sun disk contribution based on ray direction relative to the sun direction. It solves the problem of providing sky lighting without performing real-time atmospheric integration per ray. It differs from the Sky Gradient by using a high-resolution precomputed texture for complex atmospheric effects rather than a simple analytic gradient, and from the Uniform Sphere Sampling by including directional sun intensity and atmospheric attenuation. This method initializes the compute shader pipeline for volumetric ray marching, specifically handling camera ray reconstruction and dispatch parameters for a voxel-based smoke renderer. It differs from general ray generation by explicitly detailing the reconstruction of world-space rays from screen coordinates via inverse projection matrices and the two-stage marching logic (empty-space skipping vs. density accumulation). It serves as the computational core that bridges the camera model and the voxel data structures. The Grid Ray Sampler generates camera rays by mapping pixel coordinates from an image grid to 3D space, producing either a uniform set of rays covering the entire resolution or a random subset of rays for sparse sampling. It differs from its siblings by providing the foundational geometric mapping from 2D pixel indices to 3D ray origins and directions, whereas methods like Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera focus on specific camera models or environmental lighting, and Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling builds upon this uniform base by re-weighting samples based on opacity. Fisheye Distortion Correction eliminates the visual bowing of flat surfaces in ray-cast scenes caused by using raw Euclidean ray lengths for perspective projection. It replaces the naive distance with the perpendicular distance to the projection plane, ensuring that a flat wall renders as a straight line across the entire field of view. Unlike Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera which define viewing geometry, this method specifically corrects the depth value used for screen-space projection in planar scenes. Ray casting is the fundamental image synthesis technique that generates primary rays through image pixels to determine visible geometry and accumulate light contributions, serving as the base layer for more complex ray tracing algorithms. It is distinguished from full ray tracing by its exclusive use of primary (viewing) rays, omitting secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions. This family defines the geometric mapping from discrete pixel coordinates to continuous 3D rays, establishing the camera's extrinsic parameters and projection model. It solves the problem of generating valid ray origins and directions for volume rendering by constructing an orthonormal basis from eye/target/up vectors and applying the appropriate projection, differing from sibling methods by focusing on fundamental algebraic construction rather than traversal optimizations or control interfaces. This family implements optical effects that deviate from the ideal pinhole camera model, primarily depth of field (blur based on focal distance) and geometric lens distortions. It sets itself apart from sibling ray generation methods by introducing a finite aperture for ray origins, requiring sampling over a 2D area rather than a single point, and by modifying ray directions to simulate optical phenomena like magnification or shift. Camera Trajectory and Path Generation defines the sequence of camera poses (positions and orientations) used to sample rays for volume rendering or novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of determining where to place virtual cameras to capture a scene from desired viewpoints, ranging from static orbits to complex helical fly-throughs. It differs from Ray generation and camera models by focusing on the temporal/spatial sequence of poses rather than the instantaneous ray construction, and from Novel View Synthesis Rendering by excluding the actual rendering and encoding steps, providing only the geometric path. Camera Ray Generation computes the 3D origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for primary rays corresponding to each pixel (or sample) in an image, mapping 2D raster coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. It differs from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection (converging rays) and from Pinhole Camera Ray Generation by explicitly constructing and utilizing camera parameters (intrinsic/extrinsic or basis vectors) rather than assuming a canonical pinhole model. It serves as the foundational step for Ray Casting and Ray Marching. Definition: Minimizes aliasing caused by ray divergence by adjusting the distance between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane, reducing the angle between neighboring rays. Steps: Increase the distance between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane. As distance increases, the angle of divergence between rays decreases. As distance approaches infinity, ray divergence approaches zero. Steps: Initialize bounds with scene.sceneBounds. Iterate over scene.splatSets, merging each set's bounds into bounds using MergeBounds. If bounds is invalid, return default view with center {0, 0, 2.5} and radius 1.0. Otherwise, return view with center = ComputeAabbCenter(bounds) and radius = max(ComputeAabbRadius(bounds), 0.5f). Call EstimateSceneView(scene) to get view. Calculate aspect = width / height. Calculate distance = max(view.radius 2.5f, 1.5f). Set eye = {view.center.x, view.center.y, view.center.z - distance}. Set input.view = LookAt(eye, view.center, {0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f}). Set input.proj = Perspective(1.0f, aspect, 0.01f, max(100.0f, distance + view.radius 4.0f)). Set input.cameraPosition = eye. Set input.viewportWidth = width, input.viewportHeight = height. Set input.nearPlane = 0.01f. Set input.farPlane = max(100.0f, distance + view.radius 4.0f). Set input.frameIndex = frameIndex. Set input.settings.antialiasing = true, input.settings.fastCulling = true. The pinhole camera model, which simulates depth by positioning the eye behind the image plane at a distance f (focal length), is the standard geometric foundation for ray generation in computer graphics. Early implementations in ray marching focused on simple perspective projection to create depth illusions, moving beyond orthographic parallel casting. The field has expanded to include arbitrary source-detector geometries for medical imaging (CT).
