name: Sky Gradient
head: Aurora Rendering, Aurora curtains, Horizon-Zenith Gradient, Neon Sky, Sky gradient texture, Synthwave Sky Gradient, getSky
body: Sky Gradient generates a background color for rays that do not intersect the primary volume, interpolating between a horizon color and a zenith color based on the ray's vertical direction component. It differs from SkyboxRendering by lacking time-dependent sun/moon arcs or procedural starfields in its core definition. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray direction vector \mathbf{d} (typically normalized). Input: Horizon color \mathbf{C}{horizon} (RGB). Input: Zenith color \mathbf{C}{zenith} (RGB). Input: Optional transition parameters (bounds, power, glow intensity). Output: Background color \mathbf{C}{sky} (RGB). Data Structures No persistent data structures are required. The method is a pure function of the ray direction and uniform color parameters. Steps 1. Normalize Direction: Ensure the ray direction \mathbf{d} is normalized. If the input is a point \mathbf{p} relative to the camera, compute \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Compute Vertical Component: Extract the vertical component y = \mathbf{d}y (the y-component of the normalized direction vector). 3. Compute Interpolation Factor: Calculate a factor t that maps the vertical range to [0, 1]. Two common variations exist: Linear Mapping: t = 0.5 \times (y + 1.0). This maps y=-1 (nadir) to t=0 and y=1 (zenith) to t=1. Smoothstep Mapping: t = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.7, y). This creates a smooth transition starting at y=0 and completing at y=0.7. Clamped Linear: h = \text{clamp}(0.5 \times y + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Apply Power (Optional): Some implementations apply a power function to the factor to adjust the gradient curve. For example, use h^{0.55} instead of h. 5. Interpolate Colors: Compute the base sky color using linear interpolation (mix): \mathbf{C}{base} = (1 - t) \mathbf{C}{horizon} + t \mathbf{C}{zenith} Or using the power-adjusted factor h: \mathbf{C}{base} = (1 - h^p) \mathbf{C}{horizon} + h^p \mathbf{C}{zenith} where p is the mix power (e.g., 0.55). 6. Add Ground Glow (Optional): Enhance the horizon with a glow effect. Compute the glow intensity based on the distance from the horizon: \mathbf{C}{glow} = \mathbf{C}{horizon} \times I \times (1.0 - |y|)^g where I is intensity (e.g., 0.4) and g is the glow power (e.g., 6.0). 7. Combine: Add the glow to the base color: \mathbf{C}{sky} = \mathbf{C}{base} + \mathbf{C}{glow}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def mix(a, b, t): return (a[0](1.0-t) + b[0]t, a[1](1.0-t) + b[1]t, a[2](1.0-t) + b[2]t) def clamp(x, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, x)) def skygradient(direction, horizon, zenith, usesmoothstep=False, smoothstepmax=0.7, mixpower=1.0, glowintensity=0.0, glowpower=6.0): d = normalize(direction) y = d[1] if usesmoothstep: t = smoothstep(0.0, smoothstepmax, y) else: t = 0.5 (y + 1.0) t = clamp(t, 0.0, 1.0) tpow = t mixpower basecolor = mix(horizon, zenith, tpow) if glowintensity > 0.0: glowfactor = (1.0 - abs(y)) glowpower glowcolor = (horizon[0]glowintensityglowfactor, horizon[1]glowintensityglowfactor, horizon[2]glowintensityglowfactor) basecolor = (basecolor[0]+glowcolor[0], basecolor[1]+glowcolor[1], basecolor[2]+glowcolor[2]) return basecolor Parameters Horizon Color: RGB vector. Example: (0.80, 0.90, 1.0), (0.55, 0.06, 0.32), (255, 100, 80). Zenith Color: RGB vector. Example: (0.35, 0.60, 0.95), (0.02, 0.01, 0.05), (10, 20, 60). Smoothstep Bounds: Transition range for d.y. Example: (0.0, 0.7). Mix Power: Exponent for interpolation factor. Example: 0.55. Default: 1.0. Glow Intensity: Multiplier for ground glow. Example: 0.4. Default: 0.0. Glow Power: Exponent for glow falloff. Example: 6.0. Default: 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-normalized Input: If the direction vector is not normalized, the y-component will not accurately represent the vertical angle, leading to incorrect gradient placement. Always normalize. Precision: When y is close to 0 or 1, floating-point precision errors might cause slight color shifts. Clamping t to [0, 1] mitigates this. Degenerate Input: If horizon and zenith colors are identical, the result is constant regardless of direction. Generates a dynamic sky color with time-dependent sun/moon arcs, day/night palettes, and a hashed starfield. Choose when you need a realistic day/night cycle or starfield. Uses a learnable/procedural 3D grid sampled on spherical shells with volumetric attenuation. Choose when you need density-based background sampling or volumetric fog effects in the background. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray. The computation involves a few arithmetic operations and trigonometric functions (if normalization is required). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the input parameters. Performance: Extremely fast. Suitable for real-time rendering on any hardware. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, easy to tune visually. Limitations: Lacks physical accuracy (no scattering, no sun position), no temporal variation (static unless manually animated), no starfields or complex atmospheric effects. When to Use: Simple backgrounds, stylized rendering, performance-critical applications, or as a base for more complex sky models. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy is required, when dynamic sun/moon positions are needed, or when volumetric background effects are desired. Variations include "Aurora Rendering" which adds sine-wave based aurora effects, and implementations featuring ground glow and specific color palettes. name: SkyboxRendering
head: NoisyStarField, Procedural sky, SampleStars, Sky Gradient with Day/Night Cycle, Sky Shader, Skybox, Skybox Rendering with Day/Night Cycle, StableStarField
body: SkyboxRendering generates a dynamic sky color for a ray or fragment based on the viewing direction, simulating a day/night cycle with sun position, atmospheric blending, and a procedural starfield. It differs from the parent Sky Gradient by introducing time-dependent sun/moon arcs, distinct day/night color palettes blended via light direction, and a hashed starfield component. Inputs: raydir: Normalized ray direction in world space (\mathbf{r}). sundir: Normalized direction to the sun (\mathbf{s}). time: Current simulation time (for star twinkle). Outputs: skycolor: Final RGB color of the sky. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: SunSize: Exponent for sun disk falloff. Default: 10.0. StarThreshold: Hash threshold for star presence. Default: 0.99514. StarGridScale: Scaling factor for star coordinate mapping. Default: 4096.0. Day/Night Colors: Pre-defined RGB vectors for zenith and horizon for both cycles. Blend Bounds: Smoothstep boundaries for vertical blending. Default: -0.5 to 1.5. Steps: 1. Calculate Day/Night Blend Factor: Determine the intensity of daylight based on the sun's vertical position or dot product with the world up vector (\mathbf{y} = (0,1,0)): Using sun direction Y component: \text{mixFactor} = 1.0 - (1.0 - \mathbf{s}y)^4 Or using light dot normalization: \text{lightDot} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y}) \text{lightDotNormalized} = \frac{\text{lightDot} + 1.0}{2.0} \text{cycleBlendValue} = 1.0 - \text{lightDotNormalized} 2. Compute Day Sky Gradient: Interpolate between day bottom and top colors based on ray vertical component \mathbf{r}y: \text{day} = \text{mix}(\text{DayBottomColor}, \text{DayTopColor}, \text{smoothstep}(D{start}, D{end}, \mathbf{r}y + 0.5)) Where D{start} = -0.5, D{end} = 1.5. 3. Compute Night Sky Gradient: Interpolate between night bottom and top colors: \text{night} = \text{mix}(\text{NightBottomColor}, \text{NightTopColor}, \text{smoothstep}(N{start}, N{end}, \mathbf{r}y + 0.5)) Where N{start} = -0.5, N{end} = 1.5. 4. Compute Sun Contribution: Calculate the dot product between the ray and sun direction: \text{sundot} = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{s}), 0.0, 1.0) \text{sun} = \text{SunColor} \times \text{pow}(\text{sundot}, \text{SunSize}) \text{SunColor} may vary based on time of day (e.g., mix between down/up sun colors). 5. Blend Day and Night: Combine the day and night gradients using the cycle blend value: \text{cycleColor} = \text{mix}(\text{day}, \text{night}, \text{cycleBlendValue}) 6. Add Sun to Cycle Color: Blend the sun contribution into the cycle color: \text{cycleColor} = \text{mix}(\text{cycleColor} + \text{sun}, \text{sun}, \text{clamp}(\text{pow}(\text{sundot}, \text{SunSize}), 0, 1)) 7. Generate Starfield: Coordinate Mapping: Convert ray direction to 2D UV for hashing: u = \text{fract}\left(0.5 + \frac{\text{atan2}(\mathbf{r}z, \mathbf{r}x)}{2\pi}\right) v = (\mathbf{r}y \times 0.5) + 0.5 \text{sample\pos} = (u \times 4096.0, v \times 4096.0) Stable Sampling: Use bilinear interpolation of a noisy hash field to prevent star flickering. 1. Calculate integer base coordinates: \text{base} = \text{floor}(\text{sample\pos}). 2. Calculate fractional parts: \text{fract\x} = \text{fract}(\text{sample\pos}x), \text{fract\y} = \text{fract}(\text{sample\pos}y). 3. Sample NoisyStarField at four corners: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) relative to base. 4. Bilinearly interpolate the results using \text{fract\x} and \text{fract\y}. NoisyStarField Logic: 1. Hash the integer position to get a value h \in 0, 1). 2. If h \ge \text{threshold} (0.99514), return \text{pow}\left(\frac{h - \text{threshold}}{1.0 - \text{threshold}}, 6.0\right), else return 0.0. Fade Stars: Apply horizon fade and night fade: \text{horizonFade} = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.2, \mathbf{r}y) \text{nightFade} = \text{smoothstep}(1.0, 0.0, \text{mixFactor}) \text{starValue} = \text{StableStarField}(\text{sample\pos}) \times \text{horizonFade} \times \text{nightFade} 8. Final [Color Composition: Mix ground and sky colors if ground is visible (ray \mathbf{r}y is low): \text{groundColor} = \text{mix}(\text{NIGHT\GROUND\COLOR}, \text{DAY\GROUND\COLOR}, \text{mixFactor}) \text{skyColor} = \text{mix}(\text{NIGHT\SKY\COLOR}, \text{DAY\SKY\COLOR}, \text{mixFactor}) \text{baseColor} = \text{mix}(\text{groundColor}, \text{skyColor}, \mathbf{r}y) \text{finalColor} = \text{baseColor} + \text{starValue} 9. Post-Processing (Optional): Apply contrast and saturation adjustments: \text{contrast} = \text{rgb} \times \text{rgb} \times (3.0 - 2.0 \times \text{rgb}) \text{saturation} = \text{rgb} \times (1.0 + \text{sat}) - \text{sat} \times \text{dot}(\text{rgb}, (0.33, 0.33, 0.33)) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def fract(x): return x - math.floor(x) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def clamp(x, mn, mx): return max(mn, min(mx, x)) def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def vec2(x, y): return (x, y) def Hash2D(pos): # Standard hash implementation p = vec2(dot(pos, vec2(127.1, 311.7)), dot(pos, vec2(269.5, 183.3))) return fract(math.sin(p[0]) 43758.5453123) def NoisyStarField(pos, threshold): val = Hash2D(pos) if val >= threshold: return pow((val - threshold) / (1.0 - threshold), 6.0) return 0.0 def StableStarField(samplepos, threshold): basex = math.floor(samplepos[0]) basey = math.floor(samplepos[1]) fx = fract(samplepos[0]) fy = fract(samplepos[1]) h00 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex, basey), threshold) h10 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex + 1, basey), threshold) h01 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex, basey + 1), threshold) h11 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex + 1, basey + 1), threshold) return mix(mix(h00, h10, fx), mix(h01, h11, fx), fy) def SkyboxRendering(raydir, sundir, time): # 1. Day/Night Blend Factor mixfactor = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - sundir[1], 4.0) lightdot = dot(sundir, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) lightdotnormalized = (lightdot + 1.0) / 2.0 cycleblendvalue = 1.0 - lightdotnormalized # 2. Day Sky Gradient daybottom = vec3(205.0, 200.0, 252.0) / 255.0 1.3 daytop = vec3(85.0, 105.0, 170.0) / 255.0 day = mix(daybottom, daytop, smoothstep(-0.5, 1.5, raydir[1] + 0.5)) # 3. Night Sky Gradient nightbottom = vec3(205.0, 220.0, 255.0) / 255.0 0.5 nighttop = vec3(0.0, 10.0, 51.0) / 255.0 0.7 night = mix(nightbottom, nighttop, smoothstep(-0.5, 1.5, raydir[1] + 0.5)) # 4. Sun Contribution sundot = clamp(dot(raydir, sundir), 0.0, 1.0) suncolordown = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) 0.7 suncolorup = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) 0.8 suncolor = mix(suncolordown, suncolorup, 1.0 - smoothstep(1.0, 0.5, lightdotnormalized)) sunsize = 10.0 sun = suncolor pow(sundot, sunsize) # 5. Blend Day and Night cyclecolor = mix(day, night, cycleblendvalue) # 6. Add Sun cyclecolor = mix(cyclecolor + sun, sun, clamp(pow(sundot, sunsize), 0.0, 1.0)) # 7. Starfield u = fract(0.5 + math.atan2(raydir[2], raydir[0]) / (2.0 3.14159265)) v = (raydir[1] 0.5) + 0.5 samplepos = vec2(u 4096.0, v 4096.0) threshold = 0.99514 starval = StableStarField(samplepos, threshold) # Fade Stars horizonfade = smoothstep(0.0, 0.2, raydir[1]) nightfade = smoothstep(1.0, 0.0, mixfactor) starval = horizonfade nightfade # 8. Final Color nightground = vec3(0.1, 0.1, 0.2) dayground = vec3(0.5, 0.4, 0.3) groundcolor = mix(nightground, dayground, mixfactor) skycolor = mix(nightground, dayground, mixfactor) basecolor = mix(groundcolor, skycolor, raydir[1]) finalcolor = basecolor + starval return finalcolor A procedural star field generated by hashing sky directions into cells, with a sparse probability of holding a star, jittered position within the cell, and twinkle animation. It differs from the StableStarField by using a single hash lookup per cell rather than bilinear interpolation, resulting in sharper but potentially flickering stars if not animated. Choose this when visual sharpness is prioritized over temporal stability, or when twinkle effects are desired. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: No texture memory usage, fully procedural, supports dynamic day/night cycles. Limitations: Not given in the sources. SkyboxRendering is a common technique in real-time graphics, particularly in voxel engines and raymarched scenes, to provide a dynamic background without loading large skybox textures. The specific implementation details provided here are derived from various open-source voxel raymarching projects and voxel engines. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) SamCZ/RayTracer, https://github.com/SamCZ/RayTracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, https://github.com/DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, https://github.com/PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hashed Star Field
head: Procedural Stars
body: A procedural star field generated by hashing sky directions into cells, with a sparse probability of holding a star, jittered position within the cell, and twinkle animation. It provides a deterministic, low-memory background for raymarched scenes without requiring external texture assets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray direction rd (normalized), time uniform uTime (seconds). Output: Star brightness vec3 (typically white or tinted). Data Structures: No persistent data structures. The method is stateless and computes star presence/position on-the-fly using integer hashing. Steps: 1. Horizon Culling: If the ray's vertical component rd.y is less than 0.04, return black (no stars below the horizon). 2. Projection: Calculate a 2D screen-space-like coordinate sp from the ray direction to map the sphere to a plane for hashing: sp = \left( \frac{rd.xz}{rd.y + 0.35} \right) \times 42.0 Here, rd.xz is the vector (rd.x, rd.z). 3. Cell Identification: Determine the integer grid cell containing the ray: cell = \lfloor sp \rfloor 4. Hashing: Hash the cell coordinates to produce a unique integer hs. The specific hash function is not detailed in the source, but it must be deterministic and produce a high-entropy integer. 5. Star Presence Check: Extract the first byte of the hash, hByte(hs, 0). If this value (normalized to 0.0–1.0 range, i.e., hByte(hs, 0) / 255.0) is greater than or equal to 0.985, return black. This results in approximately 1.5% of cells containing a star. 6. Star Position: Calculate the jittered position of the star within the cell using subsequent bytes of the hash: starPos = \left( \frac{hByte(hs, 8)}{255.0}, \frac{hByte(hs, 16)}{255.0} \right) This maps the star to a point in the unit square [0, 1] within the cell. 7. Distance Calculation: Calculate the distance from the ray's projected position to the star's jittered position. Use fract(sp) to get the fractional part of the projected coordinate within the cell. Apply smoothstep to create a soft falloff: dot = \text{smoothstep}(0.14, 0.0, \| \text{fract}(sp) - starPos \|) This creates a star with a radius of approximately 0.14 units in the projected space. 8. Twinkle: Calculate a time-varying brightness factor using the hash to ensure each star twinkles independently: twinkle = 0.7 + 0.3 \times \sin(uTime \times 2.0 + (hs \ \& \ 63)) The bitwise AND with 63 extracts the lower 6 bits of the hash, providing a unique phase offset. 9. Final Compositing: Combine the distance falloff, twinkle, and a horizon fade-out: \text{result} = vec3(dot) \times twinkle \times 0.7 \times \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.25, rd.y) The final brightness is scaled by 0.7 and fades out smoothly as rd.y approaches 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hashedstarfield(rd: vec3, uTime: float) -> vec3: # 1. Horizon culling if rd.y < 0.04: return vec3(0.0) # 2. Projection sp = vec2(rd.x, rd.z) / (rd.y + 0.35) 42.0 # 3. Cell identification cell = floor(sp) # 4. Hashing # Note: The specific hash function is not defined in the source. # A common choice for integer hashing is a multiplicative hash or # a bit-mixing function. We assume a deterministic hash function # that takes a vec2 and returns an integer. hs = hashinteger(cell) # 5. Star presence check # hByte(hs, 0) extracts the most significant byte or a specific byte. # Assuming standard byte extraction where value is 0-255. # The source uses hByte(hs, 0) >= 0.985, implying normalization. byte0 = (hs >> 24) & 0xFF # Example extraction, adjust based on actual hash implementation if byte0 / 255.0 >= 0.985: return vec3(0.0) # 6. Star position byte8 = (hs >> 16) & 0xFF byte16 = (hs >> 8) & 0xFF starPos = vec2(byte8 / 255.0, byte16 / 255.0) # 7. Distance calculation fracsp = fract(sp) dist = length(fracsp - starPos) dot = smoothstep(0.14, 0.0, dist) # 8. Twinkle # hs & 63 extracts lower 6 bits phase = hs & 63 twinkle = 0.7 + 0.3 sin(uTime 2.0 + float(phase)) # 9. Final compositing horizonfade = smoothstep(0.0, 0.25, rd.y) return vec3(dot) twinkle 0.7 horizonfade def hashinteger(v: vec2) -> int: # Simple integer hash for demonstration p = vec2(239.0, 113.0) h = int(dot(v, p)) h = (h ^ (h >> 16)) 0x85ebca6b h = (h ^ (h >> 13)) 0xc2b2ae35 h = h ^ (h >> 16) return h Parameters: Star Density: ~1.5% of cells hold a star (threshold 0.985 on normalized byte). Star Size: Soft radius of 0.14 in projected space. Twinkle Frequency: uTime 2.0. Horizon Cutoff: rd.y < 0.04. Horizon Fade: smoothstep(0.0, 0.25, rd.y). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The hash function must be deterministic and consistent across platforms. Standard integer hashing may vary; use a fixed, portable hash implementation. Boundaries: The projection formula rd.xz / (rd.y + 0.35) avoids division by zero since rd.y is clamped or checked. The constant 0.35 prevents singularity at the zenith. Degenerate Input: Rays with rd.y <= 0 are handled by the horizon culling step. An additive high-frequency point layer for stars, supporting procedural hash-fields or catalog buffers, with a non-destructive transform stack and an aggregate-to-ambient lighting operator. It rasterizes as sharp points for appearance but integrates to smooth ambient for lighting, demonstrating the 'same data, two operators' principle. Definition: Supports two source types: procedural hash-field (default, cheap, no assets) or a catalog buffer containing {dir(RA/Dec), magnitude, B–V color, parallax, proper-motion}. Steps: 1. Source Generation: Use a procedural hash-field or catalog buffer. 2. Transform Stack: Apply an ordered set of nodes over (dir, mag, color) in a compute pre-pass on the immutable source buffer. Nodes include: Rotate, Precess, SwirlWarp(noise), Lens(center, strength), MagnitudeCurve (= limiting-magnitude / light-pollution), ColorLUT, Cull(class/distance), ProperMotionScrub(t). 3. Optional 3D Reprojection: Support observer relocation using parallax-to-distance conversion. 4. Aggregate-to-Ambient: Reduce the point layer to feed the diffuse channel of the lighting system (Seam B). 5. Masked Distortion: Support regional distortion by reusing importance-painting. Parameters: Noise: Use deterministic seeded noise only. Comparison: The star buffer rasterizes as sharp points for appearance but integrates to smooth ambient for lighting, demonstrating the 'same data, two operators' principle. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and a hash lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1), no persistent data structures are required for the basic procedural version. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time raymarching. The source is part of a sphere-traced raymarcher, implying it is executed per pixel per ray. Strengths: Deterministic, low memory footprint, no external assets required, supports twinkle animation. Limitations: Limited to a simple point distribution; cannot represent complex star catalogs or realistic spectral variations without the extended transform stack variant. When to Use: When a simple, procedural, animated starfield is needed for a raymarched scene without the overhead of texture lookups or large data structures. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity astronomical accuracy, catalog-based stars, or complex lighting integration is required. The method originates from the "neon-raymarcher" project by PIGJET, which implements a procedural synthwave neon city using sphere-tracing. It is used as a background element in this raymarched scene. The extended variant with transform stacks is part of a broader Spherical-Gaussian sky and authorable environment lighting system. name: Background Rendering
body:
Background Rendering renders the environment behind a volume by sampling a 3D grid representing the background field along concentric spheres. It handles infinite distance or skybox-like backgrounds by mapping spherical coordinates to a 2D equirectangular texture. Unlike standard equirectangular sampling which may alias distant features, this method uses a structured traversal of background layers to mitigate aliasing. It serves as the final compositing stage, accumulating color from background layers and adding a constant ambient term based on remaining transmission. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin ray.origin, ray direction ray.dir, background grid resolution grid.backgroundreso, number of background layers grid.backgroundnlayers, background data grid grid.backgrounddata (density and color), log-transmittance logtransmit from the volume pass, optimization options opt (including stepsize, stopthresh, backgroundbrightness), and ray world step size ray.worldstep. Outputs: Background color out (RGB) and updated log-transmittance. Data Structures: grid.backgrounddata: A 3D grid of size backgroundreso x backgroundreso x backgroundnlayers. Each voxel stores 4 channels: 3 for color (RGB) and 1 for density (\sigma). ray.l: Integer lattice indices for trilinear interpolation. ray.pos: Fractional offsets for trilinear interpolation. layers} / 	ext{opt.step\size} floor + 2. C0: Spherical Harmonic DC factor, typically  rac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}. Steps: 1. name: Background Rendering Kernel (Forward)
body: A CUDA kernel that renders the background color for rays that have transmitted through the volume. It composites the background environment onto the accumulated volume color for rays that have not been fully occluded. Inputs and Outputs: grid: Background environment data structure. rayspec: Ray origins and directions. options: Rendering configuration parameters. logtransmit: Per-ray logarithmic transmission values. output: Buffer for the resulting background color. Data Structures: logtransmit: Array of floats, indexed by rayid. Stores the natural logarithm of the accumulated transmission along the ray through the volume. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray Specification: Extract ray origins and directions from the input buffers for the current thread's rayid. 2. Find Background Bounds: Call rayfindboundsbg to determine the intersection interval of the ray with the background environment bounds. 3. Check Occlusion: If logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0, the ray is considered highly occluded and the thread returns early, skipping background rendering. 4. Render Background Forward: Call renderbackgroundforward with the grid, rayspec, options, logtransmit, and output buffers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. body: This method renders the background environment for rays that have transmitted through the volume by sampling a layered spherical map. It differs from standard equirectangular sampling by using concentric spheres to distribute samples, which helps mitigate aliasing and provides a structured traversal of the background layers. It serves as the final compositing stage in the background rendering kernel, accumulating color from the background layers and adding a constant ambient term based on remaining transmission. Inputs: ray.origin: 3D vector, ray origin. ray.dir: 3D vector, ray direction. grid.backgroundlinks: Array of integers defining the connectivity or structure of the background data layers. grid.backgrounddata: Array of floats containing the background density (\sigma) and color values. grid.backgroundreso: Integer, resolution of the background spherical map (W \times H). grid.backgroundnlayers: Integer, number of layers in the background representation. opt.stepsize: Float, control parameter for step count calculation. opt.stopthresh: Float, termination threshold for transmission. opt.backgroundbrightness: Float, constant color added at the end. Outputs: outv[3]: Accumulated background color (RGB). logtransmit: Logarithmic transmission factor updated during the loop. out[3]: Final output color updated after the loop. The background data is stored in a 3D lattice structure implied by grid.backgrounddata. The interpolation function trilerpbgone assumes a layout where the first two dimensions correspond to the equirectangular map (W \times H) and the third dimension corresponds to the layers (N{layers}). Calculate nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2. Initialize outv[3] = {0, 0, 0}. Initialize logtransmit = 0.0. Initialize invrlast = 1.0 / innerradius. 2. Calculate position ray.pos = ray.origin + t ray.dir. Calculate invrmid = 1.0 / length(ray.pos). Normalize position: ray.pos = invrmid. Convert to equirectangular coordinates: unitvec2equirect(ray.pos, grid.backgroundreso, ray.pos). Calculate layer index ray.pos[2] = clamp((1.0 - invrmid) grid.backgroundnlayers - 0.5, 0.0, grid.backgroundnlayers - 1). Convert to integer lattice ray.l[j] = floor(ray.pos[j]) for j \in \{0, 1, 2\}. name: Skybox Rendering with Procedural Shading
head: Procedural Sky, Shader-based Sky
body: A procedural sky rendered on a back-face culled sphere using a custom shader material, combining horizon/zenith gradients, ground reflection, tiling noise clouds, and a sun disk with glow. It differs from kernel-based forward rendering by computing the background color per-fragment via analytical functions and noise sampling rather than precomputing or accumulating contributions in a separate pass. Inputs and outputs: Input: Camera view direction vector \mathbf{dir} (normalized). Input: Sun direction vector \mathbf{sunDir} (normalized). Input: Cloud texture (2D noise map). Input: Color constants for horizon, zenith, ground, and sun. Output: Final background color \mathbf{col}. Data structures: Sphere geometry: Radius R = 440 units, resolution 32 \times 16 segments, render order -1000 (renders behind everything), depth write disabled, fog disabled, frustum culling disabled. Parameters: Horizon blend exponent: 0.55. Ground blend threshold: 0.25 (smoothstep range start). Cloud UV scale: 0.22. Cloud UV offset: (0.31, 0.17). Cloud noise threshold: 0.5 to 0.78. Cloud vertical fade: 0.02 to 0.22. Cloud opacity multiplier: 0.85. Cloud color mix threshold: 0.55 to 0.9. Sun glow exponents: 12 (weight 0.25), 220 (weight 0.6). Sun disk smoothstep: 0.99935 to 0.9997. Sun disk intensity multiplier: 18. Cloud masking factor for sun: 0.8. Steps: 1. Calculate normalized camera direction \mathbf{dir}. 2. Compute vertical component y = \mathbf{dir}.y. 3. Determine sun direction \mathbf{sunDir}. 4. Calculate horizon blend factor up = \max(y, 0). 5. Mix horizon and zenith colors: \mathbf{col} = \text{mix}(\text{color}(\text{HORIZON}), \text{color}(\text{ZENITH}), \text{pow}(up, 0.55)). 6. Blend with ground color based on negative y: \mathbf{col} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{col}, \text{color}(\text{GROUND}), \text{smoothstep}(0, 0.25, -y)). 7. Generate cloud layer by projecting direction onto a high plane. Calculate UVs: \mathbf{cuv} = (\mathbf{dir}.xz / (y + 0.12)) \times 0.22 + (0.31, 0.17). 8. Sample tiling noise texture n = \text{texture}(\text{cloudTexture}, \mathbf{cuv}).r. 9. Compute cloud opacity: \mathbf{cloud} = \text{smoothstep}(0.5, 0.78, n) \times \text{smoothstep}(0.02, 0.22, y) \times 0.85. 10. Compute cloud color based on noise: \mathbf{cloudCol} = \text{mix}((0.82, 0.86, 0.93), (1.15, 1.15, 1.15), \text{smoothstep}(0.55, 0.9, n)). 11. Blend cloud into sky: \mathbf{col} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{col}, \mathbf{cloudCol}, \mathbf{cloud}). 12. Render sun disk and glow. Calculate dot product s = \max(\mathbf{dir} \cdot \mathbf{sunDir}, 0). 13. Compute glow using power functions: \mathbf{glow} = \text{pow}(s, 12) \times 0.25 + \text{pow}(s, 220) \times 0.6. 14. Compute disk using smoothstep threshold: \mathbf{disk} = \text{smoothstep}(0.99935, 0.9997, s) \times (1 - \mathbf{cloud} \times 0.8) \times 18. 15. Add sun color to sky: \mathbf{col} = \mathbf{col} + \text{color}(\text{SUN\COLOR}) \times (\mathbf{glow} + \mathbf{disk}). Pitfalls: Sun disk must be masked by clouds to avoid rendering through them. Implemented by multiplying disk intensity by 1 - \mathbf{cloud} \times 0.8. Precision issues may arise near the horizon due to the y+0.12 term in cloud UV calculation; ensure y does not cause division by zero or extreme UV stretching. The sphere must be rendered with depth write disabled and behind all other geometry (render order -1000) to avoid z-fighting with foreground objects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderskybox(dirx, diry, dirz, sunDirx, sunDiry, sunDirz, cloudsamplefn): # Constants from HORIZON = (0.5, 0.7, 0.9) ZENITH = (0.1, 0.3, 0.6) GROUND = (0.4, 0.3, 0.2) SUNCOLOR = (1.0, 0.9, 0.7) def mix(a, b, t): return tuple(ai + (bi - ai) t for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def smoothstep(e0, e1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - e0) / (e1 - e0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] y = diry up = max(y, 0.0) col = mix(HORIZON, ZENITH, up 0.55) col = mix(col, GROUND, smoothstep(0.0, 0.25, -y)) uvx = dirx / (y + 0.12) 0.22 + 0.31 uvy = dirz / (y + 0.12) 0.22 + 0.17 n = cloudsamplefn(uvx, uvy) cloud = smoothstep(0.5, 0.78, n) smoothstep(0.02, 0.22, y) 0.85 cloudcol = mix((0.82, 0.86, 0.93), (1.15, 1.15, 1.15), smoothstep(0.55, 0.9, n)) col = mix(col, cloudcol, cloud) sunDir = (sunDirx, sunDiry, sunDirz) s = max(dot((dirx, diry, dirz), sunDir), 0.0) glow = (s 12) 0.25 + (s 220) 0.6 disk = smoothstep(0.99935, 0.9997, s) (1.0 - cloud 0.8) 18.0 col = tuple(ci + SUNCOLOR[i] (glow + disk) for i, ci in enumerate(col)) return col Procedural background with sky gradient, sun glow, volumetric light shafts, and vignette. name: Background Color Resolution
body: Background Color Resolution determines the final background color for rays that do not intersect any foreground geometry or volumetric scene elements. It serves as the fallback color in the compositing equation, ensuring that empty space is rendered with a consistent appearance. It differs from Background Rendering by focusing specifically on the scalar or tensor resolution of the background value itself, rather than the procedural generation of sky gradients or sun glow, and from Background Rendering Kernel (Forward) by handling the logical selection and expansion of the background color tensor before it is composited. Inputs: backgroundcolor: The desired background color. Can be a string key, a tensor, or a special flag. shape: The target output shape (e.g., [batchsize, numrays, 3]). device: The target device (e.g., CPU or GPU). BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE: An optional global override value. Outputs: bgcolor: A tensor of shape shape with 3 channels (RGB), dtype float32. Data Structures: colors.COLORSDICT: A dictionary mapping string keys to RGB color values. Steps: 1. Validation: Assert that backgroundcolor is not the special string 'lastsample' or 'random'. Assert that the last dimension of the backgroundcolor tensor (if it is a tensor) is 3, representing RGB channels. 2. Override Check: If BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE is not None, set backgroundcolor to this override value and skip further processing. 3. String Resolution: If backgroundcolor is a string, check if it exists in colors.COLORSDICT. If it does, replace backgroundcolor with the corresponding RGB value from the dictionary. 4. Expansion and Placement: Expand the backgroundcolor tensor to match the target shape using broadcasting or replication. Move the resulting tensor to the specified device. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resolvebackgroundcolor(backgroundcolor, shape, device, BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE=None): # Step 1: Validation if isinstance(backgroundcolor, str): if backgroundcolor in ['lastsample', 'random']: raise ValueError("backgroundcolor cannot be 'lastsample' or 'random'") # Step 2: Override Check if BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE is not None: bgcolor = BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE else: bgcolor = backgroundcolor # Step 3: String Resolution if isinstance(bgcolor, str): if bgcolor in colors.COLORSDICT: bgcolor = colors.COLORSDICT[bgcolor] else: # Handle unknown string keys if necessary, or raise error raise KeyError(f"Unknown background color key: {bgcolor}") # Step 4: Tensor Handling and Expansion if not isinstance(bgcolor, torch.Tensor): bgcolor = torch.tensor(bgcolor, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) # Assert last dimension is 3 if bgcolor.shape[-1] != 3: raise ValueError("Background color must have 3 channels (RGB)") # Expand to target shape # Note: Broadcasting rules apply. If bgcolor is (3,), it broadcasts to (..., 3) # If bgcolor is (1, 3), it broadcasts to (..., 3) # We assume bgcolor is already on the correct device or move it bgcolor = bgcolor.to(device) # Expand dimensions to match shape # If shape is [B, R, 3] and bgcolor is [3], we need to expand to [B, R, 3] # torch.fulllike or expanddims can be used. # A robust way: create a tensor of the target shape and fill it. # However, if bgcolor is a constant tensor, we can use broadcasting. # Let's assume we want to replicate the color across all rays. # If bgcolor is a single color vector (3,), we expand it to the target shape if bgcolor.ndim == 1: # Expand from (3,) to (..., 3) # We need to prepend dimensions to match shape[:-1] newshape = list(shape[:-1]) + [3] bgcolor = bgcolor.view(1, 1, 3) # Start with minimal broadcastable shape bgcolor = bgcolor.expand(newshape) else: # If it's already a tensor with shape compatible for broadcasting bgcolor = bgcolor.expand(shape) return bgcolor Parameters: BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE: If provided, this value takes precedence over any other setting. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Flags: Passing 'lastsample' or 'random' as a string will raise an assertion error. Dimension Mismatch: If the input tensor does not have 3 channels in the last dimension, an assertion error is raised. Unknown Keys: If a string key is not found in colors.COLORSDICT, behavior is not explicitly defined in the notes, but typically raises a KeyError. Uses a constant, hardcoded background color for all rays. In NeRF implementations, a white background is commonly used to match ShapeNet renderings, while a black background is used for the DTU setup. This method is chosen when the scene requires a uniform backdrop to isolate geometry or match specific dataset conventions. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) for string lookup and override checks; O(N) for tensor expansion where N is the number of rays, due to broadcasting/replication. Memory: O(N) to store the expanded background color tensor. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays due to tensor expansion. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and fast for constant colors. Limitations: Cannot handle dynamic or procedural backgrounds without additional logic. When to Use: Use when a uniform background is sufficient. Use when integrating with datasets that require specific background colors (e.g., ShapeNet, DTU). When Not to Use: Do not use when procedural sky gradients, sun glow, or volumetric light shafts are required; use Background Rendering instead. This method is part of the nerfstudio project, specifically within the camera transformation and rendering helper code. It is used in NeRF implementations to handle background colors for datasets like ShapeNet and DTU. The approach of using fixed background colors (white for ShapeNet, black for DTU) was established in early NeRF literature to match training data conventions. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) pixelNeRF: Neural Radiance Fields from One or Few Images, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00455, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF Background Rendering
head: Background Rendering with Occupancy Grid and Density Function
body: This method renders the background behind the primary scene geometry using a separate occupancy grid and density function, distinct from the foreground scene representation. It addresses the limitation of constant background colors by allowing the background to be modeled as a distinct volumetric entity, while still supporting a fallback constant color for rays that do not intersect the background geometry. It builds on Background Color Resolution by providing a learned volumetric background component. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins (t{origins}), ray directions (t{dirs}), ray indices (ray\indices), and the primary scene's bounding box intersection distance (t{max}). Outputs: A dictionary containing comprgb (composite RGB), opacity, depth, raysvalid, numsamples. In training mode, it also returns weights, points, intervals, and rayindices. Data Structures: geometrybg: A neural network or implicit function that takes 3D positions and returns density (\sigma) and features (f). texturebg: A neural network that takes features (f) and ray directions (t{dirs}) to return RGB color. occupancygridbg: A sparse grid used for efficient ray marching culling. backgroundcolor: A constant 3D vector used as the fallback background color. Parameters: nearplanebg: The minimum distance for background ray marching, used when rays do not intersect the scene bounding box. farplanebg: The maximum distance for background ray marching. renderstepsizebg: The step size for background ray marching, controlling sampling granularity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define Density Query Function: Create a function sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) that: Extracts ray origins and directions using rayindices. Computes midpoints: positions = t{origins} + t{dirs} \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2}. Returns density from self.geometrybg(positions). 2. Determine Ray Bounds: For each ray, determine the near plane for background sampling: If the ray intersects the scene AABB (t{max} > 10^9), set the near plane to t{max}. Otherwise, set the near plane to self.nearplanebg. 3. Ray Marching: Perform ray marching using raymarching with: sigmafn nearplane (computed in Step 2) farplane=self.farplanebg renderstepsize=self.renderstepsizebg Optional occupancy grid self.occupancygridbg. This returns t{starts}, t{ends}, and ray\indices for the sampled intervals. 4. Compute Sample Positions: Calculate sample midpoints and 3D positions: midpoints = \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} positions = t{origins} + t{dirs} \times midpoints 5. Query Geometry and Texture: Query background geometry for density and features: density, feature = self.geometrybg(positions) Compute RGB from features and ray directions: rgb = self.texturebg(feature, t{dirs}) 6. Compute Rendering Weights: Calculate weights from density using renderweightfromdensity: weights = render\weight\from\density(t{starts}, t{ends}, density[..., None], ray\indices=ray\indices, n\rays=n\rays) 7. Accumulate Along Rays: Accumulate opacity, depth, and RGB along rays using accumulatealongrays with the computed weights to get initial comprgb, opacity, and depth. 8. Blend with Constant Background: Add the constant background color to the accumulated RGB for rays with zero opacity: comp\rgb = comp\rgb + self.background\color \times (1.0 - opacity) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbackground(torigins, tdirs, rayindices, tmax, nrays): # Step 1: Define density query function def sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices): # Extract ray origins and directions using rayindices origins = torigins[rayindices] dirs = tdirs[rayindices] # Compute midpoints midpoints = (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 positions = origins + dirs midpoints # Return density from background geometry density, = self.geometrybg(positions) return density # Step 2: Determine Ray Bounds # If ray intersects scene AABB (tmax > 1e9), use tmax; else use nearplanebg nearplanes = torch.where(tmax > 1e9, tmax, torch.fulllike(tmax, self.nearplanebg)) # Step 3: Ray Marching # Perform ray marching with sigmafn, nearplanes, farplanebg, renderstepsizebg, occupancygridbg tstarts, tends, rayindices = raymarching( sigmafn=sigmafn, nearplane=nearplanes, farplane=self.farplanebg, renderstepsize=self.renderstepsizebg, occupancygrid=self.occupancygridbg, rayindices=rayindices) # Step 4: Compute Sample Positions midpoints = (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 origins = torigins[rayindices] dirs = tdirs[rayindices] positions = origins + dirs midpoints # Step 5: Query Geometry and Texture density, feature = self.geometrybg(positions) rgb = self.texturebg(feature, dirs) # Step 6: Compute Rendering Weights # density[..., None] adds a dimension for broadcasting weights = renderweightfromdensity( tstarts, tends, density[..., None], rayindices=rayindices, nrays=nrays) # Step 7: Accumulate Along Rays comprgb, opacity, depth = accumulatealongrays( weights, rgb, tstarts, tends, rayindices, nrays) # Step 8: Blend with Constant Background # Add constant background color for rays with zero opacity comprgb = comprgb + self.backgroundcolor (1.0 - opacity) return { 'comprgb': comprgb, 'opacity': opacity, 'depth': depth, 'raysvalid': torch.ones(nrays, dtype=torch.bool), # Assuming all rays valid if not specified 'numsamples': tstarts.shape[0] // nrays # Approximation if not explicitly returned } A NeRF variant that combines primary scene rendering with a separate learned background rendering pass, blending the results based on the primary scene's opacity. It addresses the limitation of constant background colors by allowing the background to be modeled as a distinct volumetric entity, while still supporting a fallback constant color for rays that do not intersect the background geometry. Time and Memory Complexity: The complexity depends on the number of samples per ray, which is determined by renderstepsizebg and the distance between nearplanebg and farplanebg. The occupancy grid occupancygridbg accelerates ray marching by skipping empty space, reducing the number of density queries. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows for a learned, potentially complex background rather than a flat color, improving realism for scenes with detailed backgrounds. The occupancy grid provides efficiency gains. Limitations: Requires additional memory for the background geometry and texture networks. If the background is truly distant and uniform, a constant color may be more efficient and sufficient. When to Use: Use when the background contains significant detail that cannot be captured by a constant color, and when the computational budget allows for an additional volumetric rendering pass. This method is part of the GSDF (Gaussian Splatting with Density Fields) framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting by incorporating density fields for background rendering. It was introduced in the city-super/GSDF repository. GSDF, https://github.com/city-super/GSDF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeRF with Learned Background
head: Learned Background NeRF
body: A NeRF variant that combines primary scene rendering with a separate learned background rendering pass, blending the results based on the primary scene's opacity. It addresses the limitation of constant background colors by allowing the background to be modeled as a distinct volumetric entity, while still supporting a fallback constant color for rays that do not intersect the background geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins and directions (rays), primary scene model parameters, background model parameters (if separate), and a boolean flag learnedbackground. Outputs: A dictionary comprgb containing the final composited RGB color, opacity (accumulated alpha), and sample counts. Data Structures: out: Dictionary from primary scene forward pass containing comprgb, opacity, numsamples, raysvalid. outbg: Dictionary from background forward pass containing comprgb, opacity, numsamples. self.backgroundcolor: A constant RGB vector used as a fallback. Steps: 1. Primary Rendering: Execute the primary scene forward pass (e.g., forward) to obtain out. This yields the primary color out['comprgb'] and primary opacity out['opacity']. 2. Background Selection: Check the configuration flag self.config.learnedbackground. If true: Execute the background forward pass self.forwardbg(rays) to obtain outbg. If false: Construct a dummy outbg where comprgb is set to self.backgroundcolor, and opacity and numsamples are zero. 3. Compositing: Combine the primary and background results. The final comprgb is calculated as: \text{comp\rgb} = \text{out}['\text{comp\rgb}'] + \text{out\bg}['\text{comp\rgb}'] \times (1.0 - \text{out}['\text{opacity}]) This assumes the background is rendered behind the primary scene, with the background contribution weighted by the transparency of the primary scene. 4. Aggregation: Sum or combine numsamples and raysvalid from both out and outbg to reflect the total computational cost and valid ray count. Parameters: self.backgroundcolor: A constant color vector. Used when learnedbackground is false or for rays that fail to intersect the background geometry. Pitfalls: If learnedbackground is enabled but the background model is not properly trained, artifacts may appear in the background region. The blending formula assumes the primary scene's opacity correctly represents the transmittance of the foreground. If the primary scene's opacity is inaccurate, the background bleed will be incorrect. A supervision strategy for textureless sky and background rays using semantic masks and a free-space penalty loss to prevent spherical shell reconstructions. It uses an L1 loss for rendered color (L{COLOR}) and an eikonal term for SDF regularization (L{REG}). A free-space penalty loss (L{MASK}) is applied with a small weight to remove sky while keeping foreground structures intact, as semantic masks for the background are imperfect and may contain foreground structures. Directly using a background NeRF for foreground-background separation on textureless sky (which lacks motion parallax) leads to reconstructions contained in spherical shells. Time and Memory Complexity: Adds the computational cost of a second volume rendering pass (or a constant color lookup if disabled) to the primary scene rendering. Memory usage increases if a separate background model (e.g., MLP or grid) is stored. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the complexity of the background model. If a constant color is used, scaling is negligible. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows for realistic, non-uniform backgrounds that can be learned from data. Limitations: Requires additional training data or supervision for the background. If not learned, it falls back to a constant color. When to use it and when not: Use when the background is complex, textured, or varies across views. Do not use when the background is uniform or when computational resources are extremely limited, as a constant color fallback is available. Originated as a variant in NeRF-based reconstruction pipelines to handle backgrounds that are not part of the primary scene geometry. It builds on NeRF Background Rendering by allowing the background to be learned rather than just using a separate occupancy grid with a constant color. city-super/GSDF, https://github.com/city-super/GSDF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Neural 3D Reconstruction in the Wild, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528233.3530718, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Environment Rendering Setup
head: Daytime Lighting System, Sky and Fog Configuration
body: Configures the global lighting, atmospheric fog, and shadow parameters for a bright, saturated daytime look, typically targeting mobile-specific quality adjustments. It sets up the sky dome, directional sun, hemisphere light, and fog density, distinct from sibling methods like SkyboxRendering which use pre-rendered cubemaps, or Background Rendering which handles static backdrops without volumetric interaction. Inputs: Scene object, camera object, platform type (mobile/desktop), and optional anisotropy parameters for fog. Outputs: Configured scene with sky dome, lights, fog, and shadow settings. Data Structures: Color: 24-bit integer (0xRRGGBB) or RGB tuple. Vector3: Normalized direction vector (x, y, z). ShadowCamera: Defines frustum bounds [-H, H] for left/right/top/bottom, near plane n=1, far plane f=260. Fog: Linear or exponential height fog with near distance d{near} and far distance d{far}. Parameters: Zenith Color: 0x2a78e0. Horizon Color: 0xb6daf5. Ground Color: 0xb9cfdc. Sun Color: 0xfff2dc. Sun Direction: (0.36, 0.7, 0.6) normalized. Hemisphere Sky Color: 0xcfe4ff. Hemisphere Ground Color: 0x8d7a5c. Hemisphere Intensity: 1.35. Sun Intensity: 3.2. Shadow Map Size: 2048 \times 2048 (mobile), 4096 \times 4096 (desktop). Shadow Camera Half-Size H: 32 (mobile), 48 (desktop). Shadow Bias: -0.0004. Shadow Normal Bias: 0.04. Shadow Radius (Softness): 2. Tone Mapping: ACES Filmic. Exposure: 1.1. Pixel Ratio Cap: 1.25 (mobile), 1.5 (desktop). Steps: 1. Background: Set the scene background color to the Horizon Color (0xb6daf5). 2. Fog: Configure scene fog using the Horizon Color. Set near distance d{near} = 70 and far distance d{far} = 330. 3. Hemisphere Light: Create a hemisphere light with sky color 0xcfe4ff, ground color 0x8d7a5c, and intensity 1.35. Add to scene. 4. Sun Light: a. Create a directional light with color 0xfff2dc and intensity 3.2. b. Enable shadows. c. Set shadow map size based on platform: 2048^2 for mobile, 4096^2 for desktop. d. Configure shadow camera frustum: bounds [-H, H] for left/right/top/bottom, near 1, far 260, where H is 32 (mobile) or 48 (desktop). e. Set shadow bias parameters: bias -0.0004, normal bias 0.04, radius 2. f. Add sun light and its target to the scene. 5. Sky Dome: Create the sky dome using the sky() method (which interpolates between Zenith and Horizon colors based on ray vertical component, building on Sky Gradient). Add to scene. 6. Post-Processing: Apply ACES Filmic tone mapping with exposure 1.1. 7. Pixel Ratio: Cap pixel ratio to 1.25 (mobile) or 1.5 (desktop). Pitfalls: Shadow Camera Snapping: The shadow camera position must be snapped to whole shadow texels to prevent shadow edges from "crawling" or jittering as the camera moves. This is achieved by aligning the camera bounds to the shadow map grid. A configuration for controlling global fog density and color via Anisotropy and Radial blend parameters in the Environment Editor. It distinguishes between atmospheric fog (isotropic, low anisotropy) and sun radial scattering (anisotropic, high anisotropy). The Radial blend factor (range 0–1) blends these components: 0.0 shows atmosphere only, 1.0 shows radial only. Anisotropy controls the directionality of light scattering. Performance: Mobile targets 2048^2 shadow maps and lower pixel ratios (1.25) for real-time performance on constrained hardware. Desktop targets 4096^2 maps and higher ratios (1.5) for quality. Memory: Shadow map memory scales with resolution (2048^2 vs 4096^2). Strengths: Provides a consistent, bright daytime look with integrated volumetric fog and shadowing. Limitations: Specific to mobile/desktop presets; not a general-purpose lighting solver. Originated in the Voxel Wars project, an unofficial voxel-based game engine, providing a standardized daytime lighting setup. The volumetric fog aspects are documented in CRYENGINE 5 documentation, linking the setup to analytical and ray-marched volumetric fog techniques. sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, https://github.com/sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) CRYENGINE | Documentation - Volumetric Fog, https://www.cryengine.com/docs/static/engines/cryengine-5/categories/23756816/pages/26215326, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Viewing Plane Distance Adjustment
head: Divergence minimization, Ray Divergence Reduction via Viewing Plane Distance
body: Viewing Plane Distance Adjustment minimizes aliasing artifacts caused by ray divergence in volume rendering by increasing the distance between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane. By reducing the angle between neighboring rays, it ensures adjacent pixels sample adjacent regions of the data volume. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera eye position \mathbf{o}, viewing plane distance d, and pixel grid dimensions. Output: Adjusted viewing plane distance d{adj} and updated ray directions. Data Structures Standard camera parameters (eye position, viewing plane distance, pixel grid dimensions). Steps 1. Calculate Ray Divergence: Determine the angular separation between rays passing through adjacent pixels using standard geometric projection. 2. Adjust Distance: Increase the distance d between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane. 3. Convergence Check: As d increases, the angle of divergence between rays decreases. Continue increasing d until the divergence angle is sufficiently small to prevent sampling gaps. 4. Ray Generation: Generate rays using the adjusted distance. Formulas For small angles, the divergence angle \alpha between neighboring rays is approximated by \alpha \approx \text{pixel\pitch} / d. Parameters Typical Distance: In the source example, a 512 \times 512 pixel image plane was set at a distance of 5000 units from the viewer's eye. Resulting Divergence: With the above configuration, the maximum divergence between neighboring rays was 0.011^\circ. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point precision may limit the maximum usable distance. Degenerate Input: If the viewing plane distance is zero or negative, ray generation is undefined. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import Tuple import math class Ray: def init(self, origin: Tuple[float, float, float], direction: Tuple[float, float, float]): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def adjustviewingplanedistance(pixelpitch: float, targetdivergenceanglerad: float) -> float: # Step 1-3: Increase distance until divergence angle is sufficiently small if targetdivergenceanglerad <= 0: raise ValueError("Target divergence angle must be positive.") # Standard geometric approximation: distance ≈ pixelpitch / divergenceangle return pixelpitch / targetdivergenceanglerad def generateray(eyepos: Tuple[float, float, float], pixelpos3d: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Ray: # Step 4: Generate rays using the adjusted distance dx = pixelpos3d[0] - eyepos[0] dy = pixelpos3d[1] - eyepos[1] dz = pixelpos3d[2] - eyepos[2] length = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if length == 0: raise ValueError("Eye position and pixel position cannot be identical.") return Ray(eyepos, (dx/length, dy/length, dz/length)) A flat field lens exploiting spatial anisotropy to gather diffracted light and reduce the minimum viewing distance required for pixel overlap in holographic displays. It uses a Geometric Phase Lens (GPL) with 98% diffraction efficiency across the visible spectrum. The minimum viewing distance is calculated as D = 0.5 \times L / \tan(\theta/2), where L is the horizontal display length and \theta is the viewing angle. For a 10-inch display (L \approx 22 cm) and \theta = 0.25^\circ, the distance is reduced from ~25 m to ~1 m (25× reduction) using a 1 m focal length GPL. Time Complexity: O(1) for distance adjustment calculation. Ray generation remains O(N) for N pixels. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for distance parameter. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Described in a DTIC report on volumetric rendering techniques for aerodynamic flow field data, it addresses the problem of rays diverging and failing to sample adjacent pixels. The technique is applied in the context of subvolume isolation via cutting plane methods. DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Slim-panel holographic video display, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19298-4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Camera Class Structure
head: Camera Layout, Camera Struct, Camera fields layout
body: The Camera Class Structure defines the geometric state and rendering parameters required to generate rays for volume rendering. It serves as the primary interface between the application's scene graph and the ray generation kernel, encapsulating position, orientation, field of view, and clipping boundaries. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific sampling strategies or traversal setups, this structure provides the foundational data layout necessary to compute ray origins and directions for any camera model. The structure aggregates scalar and vector fields to define the camera's pose and frustum. Implementations vary in their internal representation of orientation (e.g., quaternion vs. basis vectors) and auxiliary data (e.g., view matrices, lighting directions). Two distinct layouts are observed in source implementations. Layout A (Quaternion-based) Defined in, this layout uses a #[repr(C, align(16))] struct with the following fields: 1. position: Vec3<f32> (12 bytes). The camera eye position. 2. fov: f32 (4 bytes). Field of view angle. 3. orientation: Quat<f32> (16 bytes). Rotation quaternion. 4. clipnear: f32 (4 bytes). Near clipping plane distance. 5. clipfar: f32 (4 bytes). Far clipping plane distance. Total size: 40 bytes. Layout B (Basis/Matrix-based) Defined in, this layout includes additional auxiliary fields: 1. forward: vec3. Forward vector. 2. up: vec3. Up vector. 3. position: vec3. Camera position. 4. zoom: vec3. Zoom parameters. 5. view: mat4. View transformation matrix. 6. lightDir: vec3. Direction to the primary light source. 7. volumeCentre: vec3. Center of the volume being rendered. 8. volumeScale: vec3. Scale of the volume. The camera is initialized with its core geometric parameters. For Layout A, the constructor is: Camera::new(fov, position, orientation, clipnear, clipfar). The camera structure feeds into the Ray Origin and Direction Setup method. The position field directly sets the ray origin \mathbf{o}. The orientation (or basis vectors) and fov are used to compute the ray direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel. The clipnear and clipfar values define the integration interval [t{\min}, t{\max}] for ray marching. Alignment: In Layout A, the struct is explicitly aligned to 16 bytes to ensure efficient GPU memory access. Redundancy: Layout B stores both explicit vectors (forward, up) and a full matrix (view), requiring careful synchronization during updates. Volume Context: Layout B includes volume-specific data (volumeCentre, volumeScale), coupling the camera to the scene geometry. Memory: Layout A is compact (40 bytes), suitable for uniform buffers. Layout B is larger due to the inclusion of matrices and auxiliary vectors. Performance: Smaller structs reduce bandwidth when updating camera state per frame. Flexibility: Layout A is more generic. Layout B is tailored for specific volume rendering pipelines where volume bounds are tightly coupled with camera setup. The camera structure is a fundamental component in graphics programming, evolving from simple pinhole models to complex state containers. The specific layouts cited here are from modern GPU-based ray marching implementations. unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) fraserlove/ossium, https://github.com/fraserlove/ossium, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Camera Augmentation
head: Intrinsic/Extrinsic perturbation, Perspective Augmentation
body: Camera augmentation perturbs camera parameters during training to improve robustness against small image misalignments and promote diversity in generated views. It deviates from the fixed camera assumptions of EG3D by introducing stochastic variations in intrinsic and extrinsic properties. While EG3D assumes a fixed camera radius of 2.7, focal length of 18.83, zero roll, and a central principal point, this method samples these values from specific distributions. Inputs: Base camera parameters (focal length f, radius r, principal point (cx, cy), roll angle \theta{\text{roll}}), dataset type (FFHQ or AFHQ), current training epoch e, and maximum schedule epoch E{\text{max}} (typically 100). Outputs: Perturbed camera parameters used for ray generation. Data Structures: The method modifies the following scalar parameters: f: Focal length (float). r: Camera radius (float). cx, cy: Principal point coordinates (float). \theta{\text{roll}}: Camera roll angle in degrees (float). \theta{\text{persp}}: Perspective augmentation angle in degrees (float). Steps: 1. Determine Augmentation Schedule (Perspective Augmentation): Calculate the current maximum angle range based on the training epoch. The range expands linearly from [0^\circ, 0^\circ] to [-15^\circ, 15^\circ] over 100 epochs. \theta{\max}(e) = 15^\circ \times \min\left(1, \frac{e}{E{\text{max}}}\right) Randomly and independently sample an angle \theta{\text{persp}} from the current range [-\theta{\max}, \theta{\max}]. This angle is applied as a perspective distortion along the height axis. The corresponding rotation matrix Rz is defined as: Rz = \begin{pmatrix} \cos \thetaz & -\sin \thetaz & 0 \\ \sin \thetaz & \cos \thetaz & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where \thetaz denotes the sampled perspective angle. Direct optimization of Euler angles is avoided in SinGRAF due to discontinuities at \theta=0; instead, cosine and sine values are carried for rotation parameterization. 2. Sample Intrinsic and Extrinsic Perturbations: For each training step, sample the following parameters from normal distributions. The parameters depend on the dataset. For FFHQ: Focal length f \sim \mathcal{N}(18.83, 1.0^2). Camera radius r \sim \mathcal{N}(2.7, 0.1^2). Principal point cx, cy \sim \mathcal{N}(256, 14^2). Camera roll \theta{\text{roll}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0^\circ, 2^\circ). For AFHQ: Focal length f \sim \mathcal{N}(18.83, 1.5^2). Camera radius r \sim \mathcal{N}(2.7, 0.1^2). Principal point cx, cy \sim \mathcal{N}(256, 25^2). Camera roll \theta{\text{roll}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0^\circ, 6^\circ). 3. Apply Perturbations: Combine the sampled parameters to form the augmented camera matrix. Apply the perspective distortion along the height axis using the sampled angle. The final camera pose and intrinsics are then used for ray generation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def samplecameraaugmentation(datasettype: str, epoch: int, maxepochs: int = 100) -> dict: """ Samples augmented camera parameters based on dataset and training progress. Args: datasettype: 'FFHQ' or 'AFHQ' epoch: Current training epoch maxepochs: Total epochs for linear schedule (default 100) Returns: dict with keys: 'focallength', 'radius', 'principalpointx', 'principalpointy', 'roll', 'perspectiveangle' """ basefocal = 18.83 baseradius = 2.7 baseprincipal = 256.0 if datasettype == 'FFHQ': stdfocal = 1.0 stdradius = 0.1 stdprincipal = 14.0 stdroll = 2.0 elif datasettype == 'AFHQ': stdfocal = 1.5 stdradius = 0.1 stdprincipal = 25.0 stdroll = 6.0 else: raise ValueError("Unknown dataset type") focallength = random.gauss(basefocal, stdfocal) radius = random.gauss(baseradius, stdradius) principalpointx = random.gauss(baseprincipal, stdprincipal) principalpointy = random.gauss(baseprincipal, stdprincipal) roll = random.gauss(0.0, stdroll) currentmaxangle = 15.0 min(1.0, epoch / maxepochs) perspectiveangle = random.uniform(-currentmaxangle, currentmaxangle) return { 'focallength': focallength, 'radius': radius, 'principalpointx': principalpointx, 'principalpointy': principalpointy, 'roll': roll, 'perspectiveangle': perspectiveangle } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The linear schedule for perspective augmentation assumes a fixed maxepochs of 100. If training exceeds this, the angle remains capped at 15^\circ. Principal point sampling is centered at 256. Direct optimization of Euler angles is avoided in SinGRAF due to discontinuities at \theta=0. A training technique that perturbs camera poses during the generation of 3D-aware models to address the lack of capability to model precise 3D structures from different vertical angles. It sets itself apart from standard fixed-camera training by explicitly oversampling vertical perspectives, ensuring better coverage of varied vertical perspectives than the base dataset distribution. Choose it when vertical angle coverage is critical for the target dataset. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves robustness to misalignment and increases view diversity without requiring additional data. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Use when training 3D-aware generative models on single images where ground-truth multi-view data is unavailable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Camera augmentation was introduced to address the limitations of fixed camera models in generative radiance fields, specifically EG3D. It was adopted in Real-Time Radiance Fields for Single-Image Portrait View Synthesis to handle real image misalignments. SinGRAF also employs a similar perspective augmentation technique to promote diversity in 3D generative radiance fields. The technique is particularly relevant for single-image view synthesis where ground-truth multi-view data is unavailable. name: Pose Augmentation for FFHQ
head: Pose Distribution Augmentation
body: A training technique that perturbs camera poses during the generation of 3D-aware models to address the lack of capability to model precise 3D structures from different vertical angles. It sets itself apart from standard fixed-camera training by explicitly oversampling vertical perspectives, ensuring better coverage of varied vertical perspectives than the base dataset distribution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The standard FFHQ dataset pose statistics (standard deviations for yaw and pitch). Output: A modified training loop where camera poses are sampled from an augmented distribution with probability 0.5. Data Structures: Pose parameters: Yaw (\thetay) and Pitch (\thetap). Distribution parameters: \sigma{yaw} and \sigma{pitch}, derived from the FFHQ dataset statistics. Steps: 1. During training, for each batch or sample, generate a random probability p \in [0, 1]. 2. If p < 0.5, sample the pose from the augmented distribution defined below. Otherwise, use the original dataset pose distribution. 3. Sample the yaw angle \thetay from a Normal distribution: \thetay \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma{yaw}) 4. Sample the pitch angle \thetap from a Uniform distribution: \thetap \sim \mathcal{U}(-3\sigma{pitch}, 3\sigma{pitch}) 5. Construct the camera pose using the sampled \thetay and \thetap. Parameters: Probability of augmentation: 0.5. Yaw distribution: Normal \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma{yaw}). Pitch distribution: Uniform \mathcal{U}(-3\sigma{pitch}, 3\sigma{pitch}). Typical range for multi-view synthesis evaluation: Yaw in [-0.4, 0.4] radians and Pitch in [-0.4, 0.1] radians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sampleaugmentedpose(sigmayaw, sigmapitch): """ Samples a pose from the augmented distribution. Args: sigmayaw (float): Standard deviation of yaw from FFHQ dataset. sigmapitch (float): Standard deviation of pitch from FFHQ dataset. Returns: tuple: (yaw, pitch) sampled from the augmented distribution. """ # Sample yaw from Normal distribution N(0, sigmayaw) yaw = np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=sigmayaw) # Sample pitch from Uniform distribution U(-3sigmapitch, 3sigmapitch) lowerbound = -3.0 sigmapitch upperbound = 3.0 sigmapitch pitch = np.random.uniform(low=lowerbound, high=upperbound) return yaw, pitch def gettrainingpose(sigmayaw, sigmapitch): """ Determines the pose for a training step based on augmentation probability. Args: sigmayaw (float): Standard deviation of yaw from FFHQ dataset. sigmapitch (float): Standard deviation of pitch from FFHQ dataset. Returns: tuple: (yaw, pitch) for the current training step. """ # Probability of augmentation is 0.5 if np.random.random() < 0.5: return sampleaugmentedpose(sigmayaw, sigmapitch) else: # Return original dataset pose distribution # Note: The specific implementation of the original distribution is not given in the sources. # This is a placeholder for the standard FFHQ pose sampling logic. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The sources do not specify how the original dataset pose distribution is sampled when augmentation is not applied. The uniform distribution for pitch extends to \pm 3\sigma{pitch}, which may exceed typical natural head rotation ranges if \sigma{pitch} is large, potentially leading to unrealistic poses if not clamped. A modification of Adaptive Discriminator Augmentation (ADA) where both the input image and the camera pose are augmented with the same geometric transformation (scale, translation, rotation), and the discriminator is conditioned on the augmented pose. It is chosen to prevent artifacts caused by 2D-only augmentation in 3D-aware models. Standard ADA is not 3D-aware because augmentations are only carried out in image space while the discriminator is conditioned on the original camera pose, leading to artifacts such as objects appearing concave. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method ensures better coverage of images with varied vertical perspectives. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Addresses the lack of capability to model precise 3D structures from different vertical angles. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When training on the FFHQ dataset to improve 3D consistency in vertical perspectives. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in GSGAN (Gaussian Splatting GAN) for the FFHQ dataset. The authors observed that training on FFHQ lacked the capability to accurately model precise structures of 3D scenes, particularly for structures viewed from different vertical angles. The method was introduced as a training trick to address this specific limitation.
