name: Ray Angle Computation
head: Angular Difference Computation, Ray-to-Ray Angle Calculation
body: Ray Angle Computation determines the geometric relationship between a query ray and reference rays by calculating the angular difference between their directions at a shared 3D point. It solves the problem of encoding multi-view consistency by quantifying directional changes between a target camera and training cameras for a specific spatial location. Unlike sibling methods that generate features via coordinate transformation or uniform sampling, this method explicitly computes the dot product and difference vector between normalized ray directions to capture angular similarity. Inputs: xyz: A tensor of shape (N, 3) representing N 3D points. trainposes: A tensor of shape (M, 4, 4) representing 4 \times 4 transformation matrices for M training cameras. querypose: A tensor of shape (1, 4, 4) representing the 4 \times 4 transformation matrix for the query camera. Outputs: raydiffdot: A tensor of shape (N, M) containing the dot product between the query and training ray directions. raydiffnorm: A tensor of shape (N, M) containing the Euclidean norm of the difference vector between the directions. Data Structures: Points are stored as floating-point vectors (x, y, z). Poses are stored as 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrices. The camera origin is extracted from the fourth column at indices [:,:3, 3]. Steps: 1. Extract Camera Centers: Extract origins from pose matrices: C{\text{train}} = \text{train\poses}[:,:3, 3] and C{\text{query}} = \text{query\pose}[:,:3, 3]. 2. Compute Direction Vectors: Calculate vectors from camera centers to points: \mathbf{v}{\text{query}} = C{\text{query}} - \mathbf{xyz} and \mathbf{v}{\text{train}} = C{\text{train}} - \mathbf{xyz}. These vectors point from the point to the camera, which preserves angular relationships for subsequent calculations. 3. Normalize Directions: Normalize vectors to unit length: \mathbf{d}{\text{query}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{query}} / (\|\mathbf{v}{\text{query}}\| + \epsilon) and \mathbf{d}{\text{train}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{train}} / (\|\mathbf{v}{\text{train}}\| + \epsilon). 4. Compute Difference Vector: Calculate the element-wise difference: \mathbf{d}{\text{diff}} = \mathbf{d}{\text{query}} - \mathbf{d}{\text{train}}. 5. Compute Metrics: Calculate the Euclidean norm \text{ray\diff\norm} = \|\mathbf{d}{\text{diff}}\| and the dot product \text{ray\diff\dot} = \sum (\mathbf{d}{\text{query}} \cdot \mathbf{d}{\text{train}}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computerayangles(xyz, trainposes, querypose, epsilon=1e-6): # 1. Extract camera origins traincenters = trainposes[:,:3, 3] # (M, 3) querycenter = querypose[:,:3, 3] # (1, 3) # 2. Compute vectors from camera center to point vecquery = querycenter - xyz # (N, 3) vectrain = traincenters - xyz # (N, M, 3) via broadcasting # 3. Normalize directions normquery = torch.norm(vecquery, dim=1, keepdim=True) # (N, 1) normtrain = torch.norm(vectrain, dim=2, keepdim=True) # (N, M, 1) dquery = vecquery / (normquery + epsilon) # (N, 3) dtrain = vectrain / (normtrain + epsilon) # (N, M, 3) # 4. Compute difference vector dqueryexpanded = dquery.unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 3) ddiff = dqueryexpanded - dtrain # (N, M, 3) # 5. Compute metrics raydiffnorm = torch.norm(ddiff, dim=2) # (N, M) raydiffdot = torch.sum(dqueryexpanded dtrain, dim=2) # (N, M) return raydiffdot, raydiffnorm Parameters: epsilon: 10^{-6}, added to prevent division by zero during normalization. Edge Cases: Zero Vector: If a point coincides with a camera center, the vector norm is zero; the \epsilon term prevents NaN values. Degenerate Input: If xyz or poses are not aligned in the same coordinate system, the computed angles will be meaningless. Creates explicit feature vectors from angular differences for multi-view stereo. It builds on this method by converting the computed dot products and norms into feature embeddings. Choose this when you need to inject viewing geometry into a neural network for novel view synthesis. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. The operations are vectorizable and parallelizable on GPUs. Sensitivity to pose and coordinate precision is inherent to the calculation. Occlusion and visibility are not accounted for. The origin, specific project name, and development history are not given in the sources. The method is used in neural rendering pipelines to encode geometric relationships between rays and cameras. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Angle Feature Generation
body: Angle Feature Generation creates features based on the angular relationship between rays and camera positions for multi-view stereo rendering. It builds on Ray Angle Computation by converting angular differences into explicit feature vectors that encode viewing geometry. Unlike Direction Feature Generation, which relies on coordinate transformation, this method explicitly computes the dot product between ray directions to capture angular similarity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Reference ray direction, ray directions from source/training cameras, and camera positions for direction computation. Output: A feature vector containing the computed angle features (dot products). Data Structures: Feature vector: A 1D array or tensor where each element corresponds to a computed angular metric for a specific source view. Ray directions: 3D unit vectors representing the direction of the ray. Steps: 1. Compute Directions: Determine the direction vectors from the camera centers to the ray points. For a ray originating at camera center \mathbf{C} and passing through point \mathbf{P}, the direction is \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{C}}{\|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{C}\|}. 2. Compute Dot Products: Calculate the dot product between the reference ray direction \mathbf{d}{\text{ref}} and each source ray direction \mathbf{d}{\text{src}}. The angle feature f is given by: f = \mathbf{d}{\text{ref}} \cdot \mathbf{d}{\text{src}} This value represents the cosine of the angle between the two rays. 3. Aggregate Features: Collect these dot products for all source views to form the final angle feature vector. Parameters: Number of source views: Determines the length of the output feature vector. Normalization: Directions are normalized to unit length before dot product computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-length rays: If the point coincides with a camera center, the direction is undefined; guard against division by zero. Precision: Dot products are sensitive to floating-point precision; ensure directions are normalized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def genanglefeature(refcampos, srccampos, point): """ Compute angle features based on dot products between ray directions. Args: refcampos: (3,) tensor, reference camera position in world space srccampos: (N, 3) tensor, source camera positions in world space point: (3,) tensor, 3D point in world space Returns: features: (N,) tensor, angle features (dot products) """ # Step 1: Compute reference ray direction refdir = point - refcampos refdir = refdir / (torch.norm(refdir) + 1e-8) features = [] for i in range(len(srccampos)): # Step 1: Compute source ray direction srcdir = point - srccampos[i] srcdir = srcdir / (torch.norm(srcdir) + 1e-8) # Step 2: Compute dot product dotproduct = torch.dot(refdir, srcdir) features.append(dotproduct) return torch.stack(features) Generates features based on the direction of rays in the reference camera coordinate system. It sets itself apart by transforming ray directions using the world-to-camera rotation matrix rather than computing dot products between multiple rays. Choose this method when explicit angular similarity metrics are less important than absolute directional encoding in the reference frame. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Not given in the sources. Memory: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of multi-view stereo rendering. It is used to enhance geometric understanding in neural rendering by providing explicit angular features. Xharlie/pointnerf, https://github.com/Xharlie/pointnerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Confidence Modeling
head: Ray-confidence modeling with target degree-of-freedom regularization

Ray-confidence modeling estimates the reliability of volumetric primitives based on ray coverage to adaptively control their shape and regularization strength. It solves the problem of over-smoothing or artifacts in sparse-view reconstruction by assigning higher confidence (and thus sharper, Gaussian-like shapes) to well-observed regions and lower confidence (heavier tails) to occluded or sparsely sampled areas. It differs from sibling methods like Angle Feature Generation by directly influencing the primitive's statistical distribution parameters rather than just providing angular features for downstream networks. A sensor model that incorporates angular uncertainty, improving reconstruction of thin objects and surfaces compared to a model that disregards it. On the Newer College dataset, it significantly improves the ability to reconstruct surfaces and thin objects at higher resolutions. Compared to 'ours (rays)' (which disregards angular uncertainty), 'ours (beams)' produces larger maps (30-70% increase) and higher runtime (50% increase) but offers better quality for thin objects and surfaces, especially in noisy real-world data. A sensor model that disregards angular uncertainty. On the Panoptic Flat dataset (no noise), there is no difference in performance between 'ours (rays)' and 'ours (beams)'. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but the uncertainty-aware model ('ours (beams)') has a 50% increase in runtime compared to the uncertainty-agnostic model ('ours (rays)'). Memory Complexity: The uncertainty-aware model produces larger maps by 30-70% depending on resolution. Performance: On the Newer College dataset, the uncertainty-aware model performs on par with TSDF-based methods (voxblox) in surface reconstruction and superior in thin object reconstruction. On the Panoptic Flat dataset (no noise), performance is identical to the uncertainty-agnostic model. Strengths: Better reconstruction of thin objects and surfaces in noisy data; good general performance in memory and runtime with potential for multi-threading improvements. Limitations: Higher memory and runtime costs for the uncertainty-aware variant; performance gain is negligible in noise-free scenarios. The ray-confidence modeling method is part of the TR-GS framework, which uses Student’s t primitives for volumetric representation. The framework was introduced in "TR-GS: High-Fidelity Sparse-View CT Volumetric Rendering via t-Distribution Gaussian Splatting and Ray-Confidence Modeling". The uncertainty-aware sensor model ('ours (beams)') is described in "Efficient volumetric mapping of multi-scale environments using wavelet-based compression". name: Uncertainty-aware sensor model (beams)
head: Continuous occupancy measurement model, continuous sensor model, ours (beams)
body: The uncertainty-aware sensor model (beams) is a volumetric measurement integration method that models sensor observations as soft beams with angular and range uncertainty, rather than infinitely thin rays. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts and poor reconstruction of thin structures (e.g., branches, cables) that arise when ray density is low relative to voxel resolution or when discrete/TSDF models are used. It is distinguished from its sibling Uncertainty-aware sensor model (rays) by explicitly incorporating angular uncertainty, which improves surface and thin-object fidelity at the cost of increased memory and runtime. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical map representation (specifically using Haar wavelets for compression and multi-resolution access). Sensor measurements consisting of range values and associated angular uncertainties derived from sensor calibration and pose estimation. Output: Updated volumetric map with continuous occupancy values, reflecting sub-voxel accuracy and reduced entropy in free space. Data Structures: The method relies on a Haar wavelet-based representation of the volume. This structure allows for efficient coarse-to-fine integration and compression. The specific bit-packing or field layout of the wavelet coefficients is not detailed in the sources, but the structure supports hierarchical access to skip unnecessary work during updates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Beam Definition: For each sensor measurement, define a "soft beam" volume instead of a line. The beam's geometry is determined by the sensor's range measurement and its angular uncertainty cone. 2. Uncertainty Incorporation: Map the angular uncertainty (from calibration/pose) and range uncertainty into the beam's cross-sectional width or probability distribution along the ray path. 3. Hierarchical Integration: Perform a specialized measurement integration algorithm that exploits the hierarchical nature of the map. Start at the coarsest resolution level. Determine if the beam intersects the current voxel or region. If the region is fully free or fully occupied at the current resolution, apply the update and skip children. If the region is partially occupied or the beam passes through, recurse to finer levels. This guarantees identical results to a naive integrator applying updates at the highest resolution throughout the field of view, but with significant speedup. 4. Occupancy Update: Update the wavelet coefficients (or underlying voxel values) based on the continuous occupancy model, accounting for the probability of occupancy within the soft beam volume. Formulas and Parameters: The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the continuous occupancy measurement model or the beam geometry. They reference inspiration from work [16] (not provided in the source list) for the continuous model. Angular Uncertainty: Derived from sensor calibration and pose estimation. Range Uncertainty: Incorporated into the model. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Ray Density: The model specifically addresses aliasing artifacts that occur in regions where ray density is low compared to voxel resolution. Thin Objects: Discrete models fail here; this model succeeds by allowing sub-voxel accuracy. High Entropy: Traditional thin-ray models create high-entropy free space regions that are hard to compress; this model mitigates that. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integratemeasurement(map, measurement): """ Integrates a single sensor measurement into the wavelet-based map. measurement: object containing range, angularuncertainty, and pose info. map: Hierarchical Haar wavelet map structure. """ # Define the soft beam geometry based on measurement uncertainty # Note: Exact geometric formulation of the "soft beam" is not provided in sources beam = createsoftbeam(measurement.range, measurement.angularuncertainty) # Start hierarchical integration from the root (coarsest level) integraterecursive(map.root, beam) def integraterecursive(voxel, beam): """ Recursively updates the map, skipping fully determined regions. """ # Check if the beam intersects this voxel's spatial extent if not intersects(voxel.bounds, beam): return # If the voxel is at the finest resolution, apply the continuous occupancy update if voxel.isleaf(): # Update occupancy based on the beam's probability distribution # Note: Specific update rule for continuous occupancy is not detailed in sources voxel.updateoccupancy(beam) return # If the voxel is fully free or fully occupied at this resolution, # we can potentially skip or apply a coarse update. # The sources state the algorithm guarantees identical results to naive integration # while skipping unnecessary work. # Recurse to children for child in voxel.children: integraterecursive(child, beam) Memory: Produces larger maps than the ray-based variant, with an increase of 30% to 70% depending on resolution. This is due to the need to update more voxels and store more fine details/partial occupancy values. Runtime: Approximately 50% increase in runtime compared to the ray-based variant. The hierarchical integration algorithm speeds up the process, but the uncertainty-aware model is inherently more costly. Quality: Significantly improves the reconstruction of surfaces and thin objects (branches, cables, fences) compared to discrete occupancy, TSDFs, and the ray-based uncertainty model. Performs on par with TSDF-based methods (like Voxblox) for general surface reconstruction but superior for thin structures. Compression: The wavelet representation enables good compression, mitigating some of the memory overhead. Scalability: The wall time could be reduced significantly using multi-threading, as voxel updates are independent. The method is described in the context of efficient volumetric mapping of multi-scale environments using wavelet-based compression. It was developed to address limitations in existing multi-resolution mapping frameworks, such as Octomap (discrete, poor thin object reconstruction) and Voxblox (TSDF-based, struggles with thin objects). The continuous occupancy measurement model is inspired by prior work [16] (not in source list). The method was evaluated on the Newer College dataset (Cloister sequence) using FastLIO2 for odometry and point cloud generation. name: Sky Radiance Model
head: atmospheric scattering
body: The Sky Radiance Model provides background illumination by sampling a precomputed sky view texture and adding a discrete sun disk contribution based on the ray direction relative to the sun direction. It solves the problem of generating sky lighting without performing expensive real-time atmospheric scattering integrals, relying instead on a baked lookup texture. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), sun direction \mathbf{s} (normalized), sun color \mathbf{C}{sun}, sky view texture \mathcal{T}{sky}, solar angular radius. Output: Radiance \mathbf{L}{sky} (RGB vector). Data Structures Sky View Texture (\mathcal{T}{sky}): A 2D texture of size W \times H (default 400 \times 400) storing RGB radiance values. Sun Direction (\mathbf{s}): A normalized 3D vector representing the sun's position. Sun Color (\mathbf{C}{sun}): A 4D vector float4(100.f, 100.f, 100.f, 0.f) where the RGB components define intensity and the W component is zero. Parameters VXSKYLUTWIDTH: 400. VXSKYLUTHEIGHT: 400. VXSKYSOLARRADIUSRAD: Angular radius of the sun disk in radians. VXSKYPLANETRADIUS: 6371e3f. VXSKYPLANETCENTER: float3(0.f, -VXSKYPLANETRADIUS, 0.f). VXSKYHEIGHT: 100e3f. VXSKYRAYLEIGHHEIGHT: VXSKYHEIGHT 0.08f. VXSKYMIEHEIGHT: VXSKYHEIGHT 0.012f. VXSKYRAYLEIGHS: float3(5.802e-6f, 13.558e-6f, 33.100e-6f). VXSKYMIES: float3(3.996e-6f, 3.996e-6f, 3.996e-6f). VXSKYMIEA: float3(4.40e-6f, 4.40e-6f, 4.40e-6f). VXSKYOZONEA: float3(0.650e-6f, 1.881e-6f, 0.085e-6f). Steps 1. Convert ray direction \mathbf{d} to 2D UV coordinates (u, v) using a helper function skyviewraydirtouv. 2. Sample the sky view texture at (u, v) using a linear sampler at mip level 0 to obtain base radiance \mathbf{L}{base}: \mathbf{L}{base} = \mathcal{T}{sky}.SampleLevel(\mathbf{d}{uv}, 0.0).rgb 3. Compute the cosine of the solar radius: \cos \theta{max} = \cos(\text{VX\SKY\SOLAR\RADIUS\RAD}) 4. Check sun disk intersection: if \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{s} \ge \cos \theta{max}, add the sun contribution to the radiance: \mathbf{L}{sky} = \mathbf{L}{base} + \frac{\mathbf{C}{sun}.rgb}{\sqrt{1.0 - \cos \theta{max}}} Otherwise, \mathbf{L}{sky} = \mathbf{L}{base}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeskyradiance(raydir: tuple, sundir: tuple, suncolor: tuple, solarradiusrad: float) -> tuple: # Standard equirectangular projection for skyviewraydirtouv u = 0.5 + math.atan2(raydir[2], raydir[0]) / (2.0 math.pi) v = 0.5 - math.asin(raydir[1]) / math.pi # A step the sources do not give is a comment saying so. # Texture sample: radiance = skyviewtex.SampleLevel(skyviewsampler, (u, v), 0.0).rgb baseradiance = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) costhetamax = math.cos(solarradiusrad) dotproduct = raydir[0]sundir[0] + raydir[1]sundir[1] + raydir[2]sundir[2] if dotproduct >= costhetamax: invsqrt = 1.0 / math.sqrt(1.0 - costhetamax) suncontribution = (suncolor[0] invsqrt, suncolor[1] invsqrt, suncolor[2] invsqrt) finalradiance = (baseradiance[0] + suncontribution[0], baseradiance[1] + suncontribution[1], baseradiance[2] + suncontribution[2]) else: finalradiance = baseradiance return finalradiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls UV Mapping: The function skyviewraydirtouv is not defined in the sources. Implementers must ensure the UV mapping matches the coordinate system used to generate the sky view texture. Division by Zero: If VXSKYSOLARRADIUSRAD is zero, the term \sqrt{1.0 - \cos \theta{max}} approaches zero, potentially causing division by zero or numerical instability. The sources do not specify a guard for this case. An Earth-like atmosphere model that bakes single-scattered sunlight (Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering) into an equirectangular map sampled by environmentlight, with sun irradiance attenuated by air along its direction. It differs from the base Sky Radiance Model by explicitly modeling spectral attenuation and scattering physics rather than relying solely on a precomputed view texture and simple sun disk addition. A constant environment lighting term baked into a uniform sky parameter. It is chosen for simplicity and performance when directional sky variation is not needed, serving as a fallback or base ambient term. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, dominated by texture sampling and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the sky view texture, where W=400 and H=400 by default. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory footprint, provides directional sky lighting. Limitations: Relies on a precomputed texture, limiting dynamic sky changes without regeneration. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The model appears in a pull request for a PBR renderer aiming for a MagicaVoxel look, where it is combined with a uniform sky and an infinite ground plane. The renderer adds the sun radiance to the escaped radiance from the sky model. It is part of the VXRay renderer ecosystem. name: Sky Atmosphere
head: Rayleigh + Mie + ozone, physically based sky
body: An Earth-like atmosphere model that bakes single-scattered sunlight (Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering) into an equirectangular map sampled by environmentlight, with sun irradiance attenuated by air along its direction. It differs from its parent Sky Radiance Model by explicitly modeling the spectral attenuation and scattering physics of an Earth-like atmosphere rather than relying solely on a precomputed view texture and simple sun disk addition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sun direction vector, atmospheric parameters (Rayleigh, Mie, ozone coefficients), and the geometry of the atmosphere (implied Earth-like spherical shell). Output: An equirectangular environment map containing the baked sky radiance. Data Structures: Equirectangular Map: A 2D texture mapping longitude to the x-axis and latitude to the y-axis, requiring one byte per cell. Atmospheric Parameters: Coefficients for Rayleigh scattering, Mie scattering, and ozone absorption. Steps: 1. Calculate Single-Scattered Sunlight: Compute the contributions from Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering for sunlight interacting with an Earth-like atmosphere. 2. Bake Contributions: Store these computed radiance values into an equirectangular map. 3. Sample Map: Use an environmentlight sampler to retrieve sky radiance based on the ray direction. 4. Attenuate Sun Irradiance: Modulate the sun's direct irradiance by the air along its direction to redden low suns. Formulas and Parameters: The sources describe the baking process conceptually but do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the scattering coefficients or atmospheric integration. The attenuation of the sun's irradiance is described qualitatively as being "attenuated by the air along its direction". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Sun Angles: The method specifically handles the reddening effect of low suns by attenuating irradiance based on the air path. Precision: No specific precision requirements are given for the baking process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def bakeskyatmosphere(sundirection, atmosphereparams): """ Bakes single-scattered sunlight into an equirectangular map. Args: sundirection: tuple(float, float, float), direction of the sun. atmosphereparams: dict containing Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone coefficients. Returns: list[list[list[float]]]: Equirectangular map of sky radiance (height x width x 3). """ width = 2048 height = 1024 skymap = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Convert pixel coordinates to spherical coordinates longitude = (x / width) 2.0 math.pi latitude = (y / height) math.pi - math.pi / 2.0 # Convert to Cartesian direction vector dirvec = ( math.cos(latitude) math.cos(longitude), math.sin(latitude), math.cos(latitude) math.sin(longitude)) # Calculate single-scattered sunlight contributions radiance = calculatesinglescattering(dirvec, sundirection, atmosphereparams) # Store in the equirectangular map skymap[y][x] = radiance return skymap def sampleskyatmosphere(raydirection, skymap, sundirection, atmosphereparams): """ Samples the baked sky atmosphere for a given ray direction. Args: raydirection: tuple(float, float, float), direction of the ray. skymap: list[list[list[float]]], the baked equirectangular map. sundirection: tuple(float, float, float), direction of the sun. atmosphereparams: dict containing atmospheric coefficients. Returns: list[float]: The sky radiance for the given direction. """ # Convert ray direction to equirectangular coordinates longitude = math.atan2(raydirection[2], raydirection[0]) latitude = math.asin(raydirection[1]) # Map to texture coordinates x = int(((longitude + math.pi) / (2.0 math.pi)) len(skymap[0])) y = int(((latitude + math.pi / 2.0) / math.pi) len(skymap)) # Clamp coordinates to valid range x = max(0, min(x, len(skymap[0]) - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, len(skymap) - 1)) # Sample the baked sky radiance skyradiance = skymap[y][x] # Attenuate sun irradiance by air along its direction sunattenuation = calculatesunattenuation(sundirection, atmosphereparams) # Combine sky radiance and attenuated sun contribution finalradiance = [ skyradiance[i] + sunattenuation[i] for i in range(3) ] return finalradiance def calculatesinglescattering(dirvec, sundirection, params): """Standard single-scattering approximation for Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone.""" costheta = dirvec[0]sundirection[0] + dirvec[1]sundirection[1] + dirvec[2]sundirection[2] rayleighphase = 3.0 / (16.0 math.pi) (1.0 + costheta2) mieg = params.get('mieg', 0.8) miephase = 3.0 / (8.0 math.pi) ((1.0 + costheta2) / (1.0 + mieg2 - 2.0 mieg costheta)) ozonefactor = params.get('ozonefactor', 0.5) return [ rayleighphase params.get('rayleigh', 0.0025) ozonefactor, miephase params.get('mie', 0.0010) ozonefactor, rayleighphase params.get('rayleigh', 0.0025) ozonefactor ] def calculatesunattenuation(sundirection, params): """Calculates the attenuation of the sun's irradiance due to atmospheric scattering.""" pathlength = 1.0 / max(math.sin(sundirection[1]), 0.01) attenuation = math.exp(-pathlength params.get('totalextinction', 0.003)) return [ attenuation 1.0, attenuation 0.8, attenuation 0.6 ] A general illumination model for atmospheric effects (blue skies, sunsets, rainbows, shafts of light) based on the A-cube, modeling the atmosphere by particles of different sizes and using volume sampling techniques. The A-cube or atmospheric cube limits the modeling space to a finite volume. The atmospheric model handles absorption, scattering (Rayleigh and Mie) and geometric optics (refractive dispersion) but operating in the RGB colour model. Density and phase functions of the scattering particles inside the cube can vary from point to point. For complex atmospheric descriptions, the A-cube can be subdivided into a number of voxels to store pre-computed data. Time Complexity: The baking step is performed offline, and the sampling step is O(1) per ray if the map is precomputed. Memory Complexity: Depends on the resolution of the equirectangular map, with the sources specifying one byte per cell. Strengths: Physically based representation of Earth-like sky colors and sun attenuation. Limitations: Limited to single scattering and Earth-like atmospheres. When to use: When a physically based, Earth-like sky is required with minimal runtime cost. When not to use: When complex atmospheric effects like rainbows or non-Earth-like atmospheres are needed. The method is associated with the implementation of MagicaVoxel, specifically in the context of adding a physically based sky with Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering. The A-cube model was introduced by Inakage as a general illumination model for atmospheric effects. name: Compute Shader Ray Marching Setup
head: Ray Marching Setup
body: This method establishes the computational pipeline for rendering volumetric smoke by launching a compute shader that marches rays through a voxel grid, accumulating density which is then composited over a camera feed. It differs from standard ray generation by explicitly handling the resolution scaling (downsampling) and the two-stage marching logic (empty-space skipping vs. density accumulation) within the setup phase, deferring the actual ray direction calculation to the generation kernel. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Screen resolution (Screen.width, Screen.height), camera transform (cam.transform.position), inverse projection matrix (invProjectionMatrix), camera-to-world matrix (CamToWorldMatrix), maximum ray length (RayMaxLength, default 50.0), density smoothing factor (smoothing), density multiplier (densityMUlt), and a pre-generated Worley noise texture. Outputs: A RenderTexture (smokeTexture) with format ARGB64, linear color space, and random write access, containing the accumulated smoke density. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Stored in a ComputeBuffer. 3D coordinates (x, y, z) are flattened to linear indices using index = z \cdot (X \cdot Y) + y \cdot X + x, where X, Y are grid dimensions. Out-of-bounds access returns -1. Noise Texture: A RWTexture2D storing Worley noise values, sampled per pixel. Result Texture: RWTexture2D<float4> ResultTexture with ARGB64 format. Steps: 1. Calculate Render Resolution: Compute the target width and height for the compute shader dispatch by dividing the screen dimensions by 8 and rounding up: width = \lceil \frac{Screen.width}{8} \rceil, \quad height = \lceil \frac{Screen.height}{8} \rceil 2. Initialize Output Texture: Create a RenderTexture with the calculated dimensions, format ARGB64, and linear color space. 3. Configure Shader Matrices: Pass CamToWorldMatrix and invProjectionMatrix to the compute shader. 4. Set Camera Position: Pass the camera's world-space position (camPosWS) to the shader. 5. Dispatch Compute Shader: Launch the ray marching kernel with thread groups sized according to the calculated resolution: dispatch(kernelIndex, \frac{width}{8}, \frac{height}{8}, 1) Pseudocode (Setup Phase): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. width = ceil(Screen.width / 8) height = ceil(Screen.height / 8) smokeTexture = RenderTexture(width, height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.ARGB64, RenderTextureReadWrite.Linear) shader.SetMatrix("CamToWorldMatrix", cam.transform.worldToLocalMatrix.inverse) shader.SetMatrix("invProjectionMatrix", camera.projectionMatrix.inverse) shader.SetVector("CamPosWS", cam.transform.position) shader.SetFloat("RayMaxLength", 50.0) shader.SetFloat("smoothing", smoothingfactor) shader.SetFloat("densityMUlt", densitymultiplier) shader.Dispatch(0, width // 8, height // 8, 1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sampling Bug: The reference implementation samples the noise texture using screen-space UV coordinates (uv) rather than world-space positions. This causes the noise pattern to remain fixed to the screen rather than the volume, creating a "swimming" artifact as the camera moves. The correct approach is to sample noise using the 3D world position of the ray sample point. Volume Bounds: The accumulation loop (Stage Two) runs for a fixed number of steps (e.g., 40) regardless of whether the ray has exited the voxel grid, potentially causing smoke to bleed outside the intended volume bounds. Color Reassignment: In the debug visualization fragment shader, the color variable col is reassigned every iteration, which is inefficient and incorrect for accumulation logic. Generates initial camera rays per pixel using a pinhole model, converting thread indices to UV coordinates and applying focal length and rotation transformations. Handles the sampling of the voxel grid during the march, including empty-space skipping logic. Time Complexity: The setup phase is O(1) relative to resolution, but the dispatch scales with \frac{W \cdot H}{64} thread groups. The marching cost depends on the density of the volume; empty-space skipping reduces cost for rays outside the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the voxel grid (ComputeBuffer), the noise texture (RWTexture2D), and the output render texture (ARGB64, 32 bits per pixel). Strengths: Efficiently handles large volumes by skipping empty space; uses procedural noise to avoid texture memory overhead for the density field. Limitations: The reference implementation has a significant bug where noise is sampled in screen space, breaking spatial coherence; fixed-step accumulation ignores volume boundaries. When to use: Suitable for real-time volumetric effects where performance is critical and the volume is sparse or well-contained. When not to use: Not suitable for high-fidelity volumetrics requiring accurate 3D noise sampling or precise boundary adherence without modification. This method is derived from a GitHub repository by Schokolasbotter, which demonstrates a real-time volumetric smoke raymarching implementation in Unity using compute shaders. It combines voxelization, procedural Worley noise generation, and a two-stage ray marcher to achieve real-time performance. name: Compute Shader Ray Generation
head: Basic GPU Ray Generation via Compute Shader, CUDA Ray Generation, Kamera-Strahl-Erzeugung im Compute-Shader, Ray Generation Program
body: This method generates initial camera rays for a frame by launching a compute shader with one thread per pixel. It converts thread indices into normalized UV coordinates and computes ray directions using a pinhole camera model defined by a focal length. It differs from standard perspective projection implementations by explicitly detailing the normalization to [-1, 1] and the specific focal length derivation from the field of view, while deferring camera orientation (rotation) to subsequent transformation steps. Inputs and Outputs: Window width W and height H (integers). Field of view angle \alpha (radians). Camera orientation angles \phi (rotation around x-axis) and \theta (rotation around y-axis). Outputs: Ray origin \vec{o} (world space, camera position) and ray direction \vec{rd} (world space, normalized). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required for ray generation itself. The compute shader state relies on the hardware-provided DispatchThreadID (global thread ID) and GroupThreadID/GroupID for coordinate mapping. Numbered Steps: 1. Determine the pixel coordinates (x, y) from the thread ID within the block and the block ID within the grid. 2. Scale the integer pixel coordinates to the range [0, 1] by dividing by window dimensions. 3. Center the coordinates so the screen center is (0,0), mapping the top-left pixel to [-1, 1] and the bottom-right to [1, -1]. 4. Calculate the focal length f from the field of view \alpha. 5. Compute the initial unoriented ray direction \vec{rd}^0 in a local coordinate system where the camera looks along the positive Z-axis. 6. Set the ray origin. In the local coordinate system, it is \vec{o}{origin} = [0, 0, -f]^T. In world space, it corresponds to the camera position \vec{ro}. 7. Transform \vec{rd}^0 and \vec{o}{origin} into world space using rotation matrices defined by camera angles \phi and \theta. Formulas: Pixel scaling: \vec{v}{scaledPixelCoord} = (x/W, y/H). UV centering: \vec{uv} = \vec{v}{scaledPixelCoord} \cdot 2 - \vec{1}, where u = \vec{uv}x and v = \vec{uv}y. Focal length: f = 1 / \tan(\alpha / 2). Local direction: \vec{rd}^0 = [u, v, f]^T / \sqrt{u^2 + v^2 + f^2}. Source describes an equivalent vector subtraction method where the origin is \vec{o}{origin} = [0, 0, -f]^T and the direction is \vec{p}{direction} = [u, v, 0]^T - [0, 0, -f]^T = [u, v, f]^T, which yields the same direction vector before normalization. World orientation: \vec{rd} = Ry(\theta) \cdot Rx(\phi) \cdot \vec{rd}^0 and \vec{o} = Ry(\theta) \cdot Rx(\phi) \cdot \vec{o}{origin}. Rotation matrices: Ry(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} and Rx(\phi) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\phi & -\sin\phi \\ 0 & \sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{bmatrix}. Parameters: Thread block size: 8 \times 8 threads (64 threads per group). Focal length f: Derived from \alpha. Near plane width v{nearPlaneWidth}: Set to 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If W or H is zero, normalization fails. Ensure W, H > 0. Precision: Using integer arithmetic for thread ID calculation is safe. Floating point precision for u, v depends on the window size. For very large resolutions, u^2 + v^2 + f^2 may suffer from precision loss if f is very small or very large. Boundary Pixels: The mapping ensures all pixels from (0,0) to (W-1, H-1) are covered. The window is divided into 8 \times 8 squares, and the dispatch arguments are the number of squares in the X and Y directions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateray(groupidx, groupidy, groupthreadidx, groupthreadidy, W, H, alpha, phi, theta): # 1. Determine pixel coordinates x = groupidx 8 + groupthreadidx y = groupidy 8 + groupthreadidy # 2. Normalize to [0, 1] uscaled = x / W vscaled = y / H # 3. Center to [-1, 1] u = uscaled 2.0 - 1.0 v = vscaled 2.0 - 1.0 # 4. Calculate focal length f = 1.0 / math.tan(alpha / 2.0) # 5. Calculate local direction vector [u, v, f] and normalize rdlocalx = u rdlocaly = v rdlocalz = f rdlocallen = math.sqrt(rdlocalx2 + rdlocaly2 + rdlocalz2) rdlocalx /= rdlocallen rdlocaly /= rdlocallen rdlocalz /= rdlocallen # 6. Set local origin originlocalx = 0.0 originlocaly = 0.0 originlocalz = -f # 7. Apply rotation matrices for camera orientation costheta = math.cos(theta) sintheta = math.sin(theta) cosphi = math.cos(phi) sinphi = math.sin(phi) # Apply Rx(phi) rdxtemp = rdlocalx rdytemp = rdlocaly cosphi - rdlocalz sinphi rdztemp = rdlocaly sinphi + rdlocalz cosphi originxtemp = originlocalx originytemp = originlocaly cosphi - originlocalz sinphi originztemp = originlocaly sinphi + originlocalz cosphi # Apply Ry(theta) rdworldx = rdxtemp costheta + rdztemp sintheta rdworldy = rdytemp rdworldz = -rdxtemp sintheta + rdztemp costheta originworldx = originxtemp costheta + originztemp sintheta originworldy = originytemp originworldz = -originxtemp sintheta + originztemp costheta return (originworldx, originworldy, originworldz), (rdworldx, rdworldy, rdworldz) Generates view rays for each framebuffer pixel by bilinearly interpolating four pre-computed world-space corner rays of the camera's view frustum, then traces them through a 3D voxel or Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) texture to produce a color image. It differs from standard perspective projection by avoiding per-pixel matrix-vector multiplication for ray direction generation, instead relying on spatial interpolation of boundary vectors. Choose this method when minimizing arithmetic intensity per pixel is critical and the camera is static or moves slowly. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel. The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (normalization, trigonometry, normalization). Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread. No additional memory is allocated for ray generation. Performance: Highly parallelizable. The 8 \times 8 thread block size aligns with typical GPU warp/wavefront sizes (32 or 64 threads), ensuring efficient SIMD execution. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and low overhead. Suitable for real-time applications where ray generation is a small fraction of the total rendering cost. Limitations: Assumes a pinhole camera model. Does not account for lens effects (bokeh, distortion) without extension. Requires explicit rotation handling for non-axis-aligned cameras. This method originates from implementations of GPU-based raycasting and raymarching, specifically those utilizing compute shaders for general-purpose rendering tasks. It is detailed in works on CUDA-based distance field raymarching and voxel raycasting implementations. The approach of mapping thread IDs to pixel coordinates and generating rays via a pinhole model is a standard technique in GPU ray tracing pipelines. name: Compute Shader Voxel Raycasting with Corner Ray Interpolation
head: Corner Ray Interpolation Raycasting
body: This method generates view rays for each framebuffer pixel by bilinearly interpolating four pre-computed world-space corner rays of the camera's view frustum, then traces them through a 3D voxel or Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) texture to produce a color image. It differs from standard perspective projection by avoiding per-pixel matrix-vector multiplication for ray direction generation, instead relying on spatial interpolation of boundary vectors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Integer pixel coordinates px (from glGlobalInvocationID.xy), camera eye position eye, four world-space corner direction vectors (ray00, ray01, ray10, ray11) defining the frustum corners, framebuffer dimensions size, and a 3D voxel texture containing the scene data. Outputs: An RGB color with alpha 1.0 stored in the framebuffer image at px. Data Structures: Voxel Texture: A 3D OpenGL texture (GLTEXTURE3D) storing the SVO or volume data, uploaded via SVO.uploadTexture(textureSize, svo.getTextureData()). Framebuffer: An OpenGL image (framebufferImage) bound at a specific binding point for write access via imageStore. Uniforms: textureSize is a vec3 uniform set to (texSize, 1.0/texSize, 1.0/(2.0texSize)), providing the texture resolution and its reciprocals for coordinate normalization. invNumberOfIndGrids is a float uniform set to 2.0 / texSize, used to scale indirection grid lookups. Algorithm Steps: 1. Boundary Check: Determine the framebuffer size using the built-in imageSize function. If the current global invocation ID px exceeds size in any dimension, terminate the shader execution to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. 2. Normalize Pixel Coordinate: Calculate the normalized pixel coordinate p in the interval (0, 1) by adding 0.5 to the integer pixel index px, casting to vec2, and dividing by the framebuffer size: p = \frac{\text{vec2}(px) + \text{vec2}(0.5)}{\text{vec2}(size)} 3. Interpolate Ray Direction: Compute the world-space ray direction dir by bilinearly interpolating the four corner rays using p.x and p.y: \text{dir} = \text{mix}(\text{mix}(\text{ray00}, \text{ray01}, p.y), \text{mix}(\text{ray10}, \text{ray11}, p.y), p.x) Here, ray00, ray01, ray10, and ray11 represent the world-space direction vectors from the eye to the four corners of the view frustum. 4. Normalize Direction: Normalize the interpolated dir vector to ensure it is a unit vector. This is critical because the bilinearly interpolated direction is not guaranteed to be of unit length, and normalization ensures consistent step sizes or intersection calculations during tracing. 5. Trace Ray: Trace the ray starting at the eye position along the normalized dir through the voxel texture. The traversal samples the 3D texture and accumulates color until an opaque voxel is found or the maximum depth is reached. 6. Store Result: Store the resulting RGB color with an alpha of 1.0 into the framebuffer image at the current pixel index px. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): px = glGlobalInvocationID.xy size = framebufferimage.shape # if px[0] >= size[0] or px[1] >= size[1]: return # p = (np.array(px, dtype=float) + 0.5) / size # dir = mix(mix(ray00, ray01, p[1]), mix(ray10, ray11, p[1]), p[0]) # dir = normalize(dir) # color = trace(eye, dir) # # The internal ray traversal and texture sampling logic is not given in the sources. framebufferimage[px[0], px[1]] = np.array([color[0], color[1], color[2], 1.0]) # Note: mix, normalize, and vector arithmetic are standard math/vector operations. glGlobalInvocationID.xy provides the pixel coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Unit Direction: The interpolated dir vector is not guaranteed to be unit length. Failing to normalize it before tracing can lead to incorrect step sizes in the ray marching algorithm or inaccurate intersection calculations. Out-of-Bounds Execution: Compute shaders often require work group sizes that are powers of two. If the framebuffer dimensions are not powers of two, extra work items may be launched. A boundary check against imageSize is required to prevent writing to unallocated memory. Not given in the sources. It represents a practical approach to integrating ray generation with sparse voxel octree traversal in a compute shader environment. name: Cubemap Ray Marching (Combined)
body: Cubemap Ray Marching (Combined) is a compute shader dispatch setup method for rendering volumetric effects across a cube map environment. It configures the required shader resources and dispatches the CSRAYMARCH kernel to process multiple cube map faces in parallel. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-object constant buffer, per-frame constant buffer, sample resolution constant buffer (CBSAMPLERES), grid dimensions (mgridSize), cube map LOD (mcubeMapLOD), cube face count (mcubeFaceCount), color shader resource view (SRV), optional spherical harmonic coefficient SRV (mcoeffSH), and optional cube face culling constant buffer view (CBV) controlled by CPUCUBEFACECULL. Outputs: Unordered Access View (UAV) for the cube map at the specified LOD. Data Structures: mgridSize: 3D vector containing the simulation grid dimensions. mcubeMapLOD: Integer specifying the mip level for the cube map. mcubeFaceCount: Integer specifying the number of cube map faces to process. CBSAMPLERES: Constant buffer holding sample resolution parameters. Steps: 1. Set the compute shader to CSRAYMARCH. 2. Bind the UAV for the cube map at LOD mcubeMapLOD. 3. Bind CBVs for per-object, per-frame, and sample resolution (CBSAMPLERES). 4. Conditionally bind a CBV for cube face culling or a list if the CPUCUBEFACECULL macro is set to 1 or 2. 5. Bind the SRV for colors at descriptor index 0. 6. If mcoeffSH is present, bind the SRV for spherical harmonic coefficients at descriptor index 1. 7. Bind a LINEARCLAMP sampler. 8. Calculate the compute shader dispatch group counts by shifting mgridSize.x and mgridSize.y right by mcubeMapLOD, then dividing by 8 for the x and y group counts, while the z group count equals mcubeFaceCount. 9. Dispatch the compute shader with the calculated group counts. Formulas: x{\text{groups}} = \lfloor (m\gridSize.x \gg m\cubeMapLOD) / 8 \rfloor y{\text{groups}} = \lfloor (m\gridSize.y \gg m\cubeMapLOD) / 8 \rfloor z{\text{groups}} = m\cubeFaceCount Where \gg denotes a bitwise right shift. Parameters: mgridSize.x, mgridSize.y: Grid dimensions. mcubeMapLOD: Cube map LOD level. mcubeFaceCount: Number of cube faces. CPUCUBEFACECULL: Macro controlling face culling behavior (1 or 2). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If mcoeffSH is not present, the SRV for spherical harmonic coefficients is skipped. The face culling CBV is only bound when CPUCUBEFACECULL equals 1 or 2. Division by 8 assumes a thread group width of 8; if the hardware group size differs, the divisor must match the actual thread group dimensions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupcubemapraymarching(mgridSize, mcubeMapLOD, mcubeFaceCount, CPUCUBEFACECULL, mcoeffSHpresent): # 1. Set compute shader to CSRAYMARCH activeshader = "CSRAYMARCH" # 2. Bind UAV for cube map at specific LOD uavstate = {"resource": "cubemap", "lod": mcubeMapLOD} # 3. Bind CBVs for per-object, per-frame, and sample resolution cbvstate = [ {"type": "perobject"}, {"type": "perframe"}, {"type": "sampleresolution", "name": "CBSAMPLERES"} ] # 4. Conditionally bind CBV for cube face culling if CPUCUBEFACECULL in (1, 2): cbvstate.append({"type": "cubefaceculling"}) # 5. Bind SRV for colors at index 0 srvstate = [{"index": 0, "type": "colors"}] # 6. Bind SRV for spherical harmonic coefficients at index 1 if present if mcoeffSHpresent: srvstate.append({"index": 1, "type": "shcoefficients"}) # 7. Bind LINEARCLAMP sampler samplerstate = {"filter": "LINEARCLAMP"} # 8. Calculate dispatch group counts xraw = mgridSize.x >> mcubeMapLOD yraw = mgridSize.y >> mcubeMapLOD xgroups = xraw // 8 ygroups = yraw // 8 zgroups = mcubeFaceCount # 9. Dispatch compute shader dispatchgroups = (xgroups, ygroups, zgroups) A method to cast volumetric shadows in all directions from a single light source by using a CubeCamera to capture depth from six directions, overcoming the limitation of a single directional light camera. Unlike the single-direction light camera approach which requires the light camera to point at the viewer to maximize shadow map coverage, the cube camera captures shadows in all directions but is considered a 'hack' with lower quality than other examples. Not given in the sources. This method is part of the FluidX12 sample, which demonstrates real-time fluid simulation and rendering using DirectX 12. name: Cube Camera Volumetric Shadows
body: A method to cast volumetric shadows in all directions from a single light source by using a CubeCamera to capture depth from six directions, overcoming the limitation of a single directional light camera. Unlike the single-direction light camera approach which requires the light camera to point at the viewer to maximize shadow map coverage, the cube camera captures shadows in all directions but is considered a 'hack' with lower quality than other examples. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry, light position, light far plane distance (shadowFar), cube render target dimensions (SHADOWMAPSIZE). Output: A cube texture containing normalized depth values in the red channel, used by the volumetric lighting effect's fragment shader. Data Structures: 1. Cube Render Target: Stores the depth data as a floating-point RGBA texture. Format: RGBA Type: 32-bit float Mipmaps: Disabled Filtering: Linear Depth Buffer: Enabled 2. Cube Camera: Captures the scene from six orthogonal directions. Near plane: CUBECAMERANEAR Far plane: CUBECAMERAFAR Target: The cube render target 3. Shadow Material: A custom shader material used to render depth. Vertex Shader: Outputs vWorldPosition (world space position of the vertex) Fragment Shader: Computes normalized distance to the light Uniforms: lightPosition (vec3), shadowFar (float) Steps: 1. Create a cube render target with the specified size, RGBA format, float type, no mipmaps, linear filtering, and depth buffer enabled. 2. Initialize a cube camera with near and far clipping planes, targeting the created cube render target. 3. Create a custom shadow material that calculates the linear distance from the vertex's world position to the light position. 4. Normalize the distance to the range [0, 1] by dividing by the shadow far plane and clamping the result. 5. Output the normalized distance to the red channel of the fragment color, leaving other channels zero. 6. Replace all scene object materials with the shadow material before rendering the cube camera snapshot. 7. Render the scene using the cube camera to capture the depth texture. 8. Restore the original scene materials after capturing the depth texture. 9. Pass the resulting cube shadow map to the volumetric lighting effect's fragment shader to calculate shadows in all directions. Formulas: The normalized distance d{\text{norm}} for a fragment at world position \mathbf{p} relative to light position \mathbf{l} and far plane F is: d{\text{norm}} = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{l}\|}{F}, 0.0, 1.0 \right) In the provided implementation, the light position is assumed to be the origin or handled such that length(vWorldPosition) represents the distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. shadowcuberendertarget = allocatecubetexture( size=SHADOWMAPSIZE, format=RGBAFLOAT32, generatemipmaps=False, minfilter=LINEAR, magfilter=LINEAR, depthbuffer=True) shadowcubecamera = createcubecamera( near=CUBECAMERANEAR, far=CUBECAMERAFAR, target=shadowcuberendertarget) shadowmaterial = createshadermaterial( vertexshader=""" varying vec3 vWorldPosition; void main() { vec4 worldPosition = modelMatrix vec4(position, 1.0); vWorldPosition = worldPosition.xyz; glPosition = projectionMatrix viewMatrix worldPosition; } """, fragmentshader=""" uniform vec3 lightPosition; uniform float shadowFar; varying vec3 vWorldPosition; void main() { float distance = length(vWorldPosition - lightPosition); float normalizedDistance = clamp(distance / shadowFar, 0.0, 1.0); glFragColor = vec4(normalizedDistance, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); } """, side=DUALSIDED, uniforms={ "lightPosition": lightpositionvector, "shadowFar": CUBECAMERAFAR }) originalmaterials = [] for object in scene.objects: originalmaterials.append(object.material) object.material = shadowmaterial for faceindex in range(6): shadowcubecamera.setactiveface(faceindex) renderer.render(scene, shadowcubecamera) for i, object in enumerate(scene.objects): object.material = originalmaterials[i] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Native Cube Depth Texture: Three.js does not provide a native CubeDepthTexture, requiring a custom depth extraction method using a color buffer. Flickering Artifacts: Shadow beams may flicker due to shadow map resolution. This is a side-effect of the resolution and tends to happen in scenes with a large number of objects occluding the light, even with simple geometries. Increasing the resolution stabilizes the effect. Performance: Scaling to multiple light sources requires extra code for each new source (new light camera, new shadow FBO, passing textures/matrices, calculating shadows/scattering/accumulation). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scaling to multiple light sources is described as requiring extra code for each new source of light, including a new light camera, new shadow FBO, passing textures and matrices, and calculating shadows, light scattering, and accumulation. Strengths: Captures shadows in all directions from a single light source without needing to orient the light camera towards the viewer. Limitations: Considered a 'hack' with lower quality than other examples. Prone to flickering artifacts at lower resolutions. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in a blog post by Maxime Heckel. History: It is part of an exploration of volumetric lighting techniques, specifically addressing the limitation of single-direction light cameras. Usage: Used in real-time volumetric lighting with post-processing and raymarching, particularly in WebGL/Three.js environments. On Shaping Light: Real-Time Volumetric Lighting with Post-Processing..., https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/shaping-light-volumetric-lighting-with-post-processing-and-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Smoke Raymarching with Voxel Grid and FBM Noise
head: Raymarcher smoke rendering, VoxelShader compute shader
body: A GPU-based volumetric rendering technique that renders smoke clouds using a voxel grid density field combined with procedural Fractional Brownian Motion (FBM) noise, performing raymarching with Henyey-Greenstein scattering and Beer-Lambert absorption. It differs from pure procedural noise renderers by using a voxel grid for base density and from pure voxel renderers by adding high-frequency FBM detail, combined via a sphere Signed Distance Function (SDF) falloff. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, camera-to-world matrix, inverse projection matrix, scene depth texture (DepthTex), voxel grid structured buffer, smoke sphere parameters (origin, max radius, normalized time), and rendering settings (steps, multipliers, colors). Outputs: RWTexture2DArray<float4> SmokesArrayResult (accumulated color) and RWTexture2DArray<float> SmokeDepthResult (distance traveled), indexed by SmokeArrayIndex. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: StructuredBuffer<float> voxelGrid. Flattened 3D array. Access function: hlsl uint flatten(int3 pos) { return pos.x + pos.y VoxelResolution.x + pos.z VoxelResolution.x VoxelResolution.y; } Voxel Resolution: int3 VoxelResolution defining grid dimensions. Bounds: float3 boundsMin, float3 boundsMax defining the AABB of the voxel grid in world space. Parameters: marchSteps: Number of raymarching steps per ray. lightmarchSteps: Number of steps for the light march. stepSize: Step size for the main raymarch loop. lightStepSize: Step size for the light march loop. densityMultiplier: Multiplier for sampled density. inScatterMultiplier: Controls in-scattering contribution in Beer's law. outScatterMultiplier: Controls out-scattering contribution in Beer's law. forwardScatter (g{fwd}): Asymmetry parameter for forward scattering. backwardScatter (g{bwd}): Asymmetry parameter for backward scattering. scatterMultiplier: Multiplier for the scattering term. brightness: Base brightness multiplier. transmitThreshold: Minimum transmittance value for clamping. scale: Frequency multiplier for FBM noise. noiseAmplitude: Amplitude multiplier for FBM noise. densityOffset: Threshold subtracted from FBM noise. cloudSpeed: Vector3 for animating smoke position. normalizedTime: Used to calculate expanding radius. maxRadius: Maximum radius of the smoke sphere. SmokeOrigin: Center point of the smoke sphere in world space. MAXDISTANCE: 200.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CSMain(id: int3): # id.xy is pixel coordinate, id.z is array slice index uv = id.xy / BufferSize # Calculate Ray rayorigin = CameraWorldPos raydirection = inverseprojectionmatrix float4(uv 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) raydirection = mul(CameraToWorld, raydirection) raydirection = normalize(raydirection) viewlength = length(raydirection) # Or derived from projection # Scene Depth scenedepthlinear = lineareyedepth(sampletexture(DepthTex, uv)) scenedepth = scenedepthlinear viewlength # Initialize Raymarch raydist = 0.0 transmit = 1.0 I = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Advance to voxel box or scene depth samplepos = rayorigin while raydist < MAXDISTANCE and raydist < scenedepth: # Check if inside voxel box bounds if isinsidebounds(samplepos): break samplepos += raydirection 0.4 raydist += 0.4 if raydist >= scenedepth: # Ray did not intersect voxel box within scene depth writecolor(SmokesArrayResult, id, float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) writedepth(SmokeDepthResult, id, raydist) return # Calculate Scattering Term lightdir = normalize(WorldSpaceLightDir) scatter = calculatescatter(raydirection, lightdir) # Raymarch Loop for i in range(marchSteps): raydist += stepSize samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection raydist if raydist >= scenedepth: break # Calculate Density density = densityatposition(samplepos) densityMultiplier # Accumulate Illumination lightdensity = lightmarch(samplepos) I += density transmit lightdensity scatter # Update Transmission # Note: inScatterMultiplier modifies the optical depth calculation opticaldepth = density (1.0 - inScatterMultiplier) transmit = exp(-opticaldepth) # Final Color color = I LightColor0.rgb scatterColor alpha = 1.0 - transmit writecolor(SmokesArrayResult, id, float4(color brightness, alpha)) writedepth(SmokeDepthResult, id, raydist) def densityatposition(pos: float3) -> float: # Calculate Sphere SDF Falloff disttocenter = length(pos - SmokeOrigin) radius = normalizedTime maxRadius sdf = disttocenter - radius # Voxel Density voxelpos = worldtovoxel(pos) if not isinsidevoxelbounds(voxelpos): return 0.0 # Trilinear Interpolation (Custom Implementation from Source) vi = floor(voxelpos) vf = frac(voxelpos) # Source uses a custom weight calculation: weight = 1 - min(abs(seedPos - (vi + i)), VoxelResolution) # This appears to be a specific implementation detail or potential bug in the source, # but is implemented as follows for fidelity: weights = calculatecustomtrilinearweights(voxelpos, vi, vf, VoxelResolution) v = trilinearsample(voxelGrid, voxelpos, weights) # FBM Noise noisepos = pos + cloudSpeed Time.x fbmval = fbm(noisepos scale) # Combine # D = saturate(v) (1 - saturate(SDF(dist, radius))) # Note: The source formula D = saturate(v) (1 - saturate(SDF(dist, radius))) # implies the voxel density is modulated by the sphere falloff. # However, the FBM is added/subtracted? The source says "combined via a sphere SDF falloff". # The specific combination of Voxel and FBM is not explicitly defined as a sum/diff in the formula list, # but densityAtPosition usually returns the final density. # Assuming the FBM is applied to the voxel density or added to it before falloff. # Given "D = saturate(v) (1 - saturate(SDF...))", v likely includes FBM. # Re-reading source: "Calculate sample density... using densityAtPosition". # And "FBM Noise: Sum of weighted noise octaves". # And "Density at position: D = saturate(v) (1 - saturate(SDF...))". # It is implied that v is the base density (voxel + noise). basedensity = v + noiseAmplitude max(0.0, fbmval - densityOffset) falloff = 1.0 - saturate(sdf) return saturate(basedensity) falloff def lightmarch(pos: float3) -> float: density = 0.0 lightpos = pos for i in range(lightmarchSteps): lightpos += normalize(WorldSpaceLightDir) lightStepSize d = densityatposition(lightpos) lightStepSize densityMultiplier density += max(0.0, d) opticaldepth = density (1.0 - outScatterMultiplier) transmit = exp(-opticaldepth) # Clamp low transmittance return lerp(transmit, 1.0, transmitThreshold) def calculatescatter(raydir: float3, lightdir: float3) -> float: costheta = dot(raydir, lightdir) hfwd = heneygreenstein(forwardScatter, costheta) hbwd = heneygreenstein(-backwardScatter, costheta) return (hfwd + hbwd) / 2.0 def heneygreenstein(g: float, costheta: float) -> float: gsq = g g num = 1.0 - gsq den = 1.0 + gsq - 2.0 g costheta return num / (4.0 3.14159265 pow(den, 1.5)) def fbm(p: float3) -> float: # Sum of weighted noise octaves n1 = noise(p) n2 = noise(p 3.02) n3 = noise(p 3.03) n4 = noise(p 3.01) n5 = noise(p 3.02) n6 = noise(p 3.03) return 0.5 n1 + 0.25 n2 + 0.125 n3 + 0.0625 n4 + 0.03125 n5 + 0.015625 n6 def calculatecustomtrilinearweights(seedpos: float3, vi: int3, vf: float3, res: int3) -> float4: # Source: weight = 1 - min(abs(seedPos - (vi + i)), VoxelResolution) # This is non-standard. Standard trilinear uses vf. # Implementing exactly as source describes for fidelity. # Assuming 'i' iterates over 8 corners? Or is this a simplified 1D weight? # The source snippet is ambiguous on the exact loop for weights. # However, standard trilinear is: w000 = (1-vf.x)(1-vf.y)(1-vf.z) w100 = vf.x(1-vf.y)(1-vf.z) w010 = (1-vf.x)vf.y(1-vf.z) w110 = vf.xvf.y(1-vf.z) w001 = (1-vf.x)(1-vf.y)vf.z w101 = vf.x(1-vf.y)vf.z w011 = (1-vf.x)vf.yvf.z w111 = vf.xvf.yvf.z return float4(w000, w100, w010, w110) # Placeholder for 8 weights, source implementation unclear # Standard trilinear interpolation is used here as the source's "custom" description # is syntactically incomplete for 3D weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene Depth Occlusion: If the raymarch distance exceeds the scene depth (distanceTraveled >= sceneDepth), the ray must be terminated and black returned to prevent rendering smoke behind opaque geometry. Voxel Bounds: Voxel access must be bounded by boundsMin and boundsMax. If the sample position is outside these bounds, return 0 density. Trilinear Interpolation: The source mentions a custom weight calculation weight = 1 - min(abs(seedPos - (vi + i)), VoxelResolution) which may be incorrect for standard trilinear interpolation. Implementers should verify this against the actual shader code or use standard trilinear interpolation if the custom method produces artifacts. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot M \cdot L), where P is the number of pixels, M is marchSteps, and L is lightmarchSteps. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the voxel grid, where V is the total number of voxels. Output textures require O(P) memory. Performance: Dispatches compute shader with thread groups of 8 \times 8 \times 1. Number of groups is \lceil \text{width} / 8 \rceil \times \lceil \text{height} / 8 \rceil \times 1. Strengths: Combines the structural control of voxel grids with the high-frequency detail of procedural noise. Efficiently handles dynamic smoke via FBM animation. Limitations: Dependent on voxel grid resolution for base density. Performance scales linearly with march steps and light march steps. Custom trilinear interpolation may introduce artifacts. This method is derived from an unofficial GitHub repository "Voltonik/VolumetricSmoke". It is used in real-time graphics applications, specifically within Unity compute shader pipelines, to render dynamic volumetric smoke effects such as smoke grenades. name: Fisheye Distortion Correction
head: fisheye fix, perpendicular distance correction
body: Fisheye Distortion Correction eliminates the visual bowing of flat surfaces in ray-cast scenes caused by using raw Euclidean ray lengths for perspective projection. It replaces the naive distance with the perpendicular distance to the projection plane, ensuring that a flat wall renders as a straight line across the entire field of view. Inputs and Outputs Input: Field of view angle (\text{fov}), distance to the target plane along the center axis (D0), and the ray's angle from the center axis (\delta). Output: Corrected perpendicular distance (D{\perp}) and screen-space projection parameters. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values per ray or per pixel column. Steps 1. Calculate Naive Distance: Compute the raw Euclidean length of the ray to the plane. For a ray fired at angle \delta from the center, the naive distance is: \text{naive}(\delta) = \frac{D0}{\cos(\delta)} This value increases as \delta moves away from 0, causing the "fisheye" bow. 2. Apply Correction: Multiply the naive distance by \cos(\delta) to project it onto the forward axis: \text{corrected}(\delta) = \text{naive}(\delta) \cdot \cos(\delta) = D0 This yields the constant perpendicular distance D0 for all angles, flattening the surface. 3. Compute Projection Plane Distance: Determine the distance from the camera to the virtual projection plane (\text{projPlaneDist}) based on screen width (\text{screenW}) and field of view: \text{projPlaneDist} = \frac{\text{screenW} / 2}{\tan(\text{fov} / 2)} 4. Calculate Screen Height: Use the corrected distance to determine the vertical size of objects on screen: \text{lineHeight} = \frac{\text{wallHeight} \cdot \text{projPlaneDist}}{\text{distance}} Where \text{distance} is the corrected perpendicular distance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def correctfisheyedistance(D0, delta): """ Corrects the Euclidean ray distance to the perpendicular distance. Args: D0 (float): Distance to the wall along the center axis. delta (float): Angle of the ray from the center axis in radians. Returns: float: The corrected perpendicular distance (always D0). """ cosdelta = math.cos(delta) if abs(cosdelta) < 1e-9: return float('inf') naivedist = D0 / cosdelta correcteddist = naivedist cosdelta return correcteddist def calculatescreenheight(wallheight, screenwidth, fovdeg, correcteddistance): """ Calculates the height of a wall segment on the screen. Args: wallheight (float): Real-world height of the wall. screenwidth (float): Width of the screen in pixels or units. fovdeg (float): Field of view in degrees. correcteddistance (float): The perpendicular distance to the wall. Returns: float: The height of the wall in screen units. """ fovrad = math.radians(fovdeg) projplanedist = (screenwidth / 2.0) / math.tan(fovrad / 2.0) if correcteddistance == 0: return float('inf') lineheight = (wallheight projplanedist) / correcteddistance return lineheight Parameters D0: Distance to the wall. Typical values depend on scene scale. \text{fov}: Field of view. Not given in the sources. \text{screenW}: Screen width. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If \delta = \pm \pi/2, \cos(\delta) = 0. The naive distance becomes infinite. In practice, FOV is limited to < 180^\circ, so \delta stays within (-\pi/2, \pi/2). Precision: For very large D0 or very small \delta, floating-point precision may cause minor artifacts, but the multiplication by \cos(\delta) generally stabilizes the result to D0. Non-Planar Surfaces: This correction assumes a flat wall perpendicular to the view axis. Calculates the vertical pixel height of a wall segment on the screen based on the wall's real-world height, the projection plane distance, and the corrected perpendicular distance. It is chosen when rendering 2D sprites or textured planes in a 3D ray-cast environment. Formula: \text{lineHeight} = (\text{wallHeight} \cdot \text{projPlaneDist}) / \text{distance}. A lens model where the distance from a pixel P to the center is proportional to the viewing angle \alpha, supporting up to 360-degree views with less distortion than hemispherical fisheye. It requires a special transform from pixel coordinates to 3D polar coordinates to calculate ray direction. Implementation typically uses four GPU fragment passes: RayDirection, RayTfrontback, RayCasting, and Rendering. Real-time algorithms used to counteract optical distortions caused by projection geometry, specifically keystoning and the rotation of the SLM image in the plane of the projection screen. The system projects the SLM image at a 45º angle onto the rotating screen, requiring proprietary optics to ensure good focus across the screen. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray/pixel for the correction calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Negligible computational overhead compared to ray casting itself. The primary cost is the trigonometric functions (\cos, \tan), which are fast on modern GPUs. Strengths: Eliminates geometric distortion of flat surfaces; simple to implement; works with any ray casting engine. Limitations: Only corrects for planar surfaces perpendicular to the view axis. Does not handle general 3D scene distortion (e.g., curved walls, spherical objects) without additional per-surface corrections. When to use: Essential for ray-casted 2D/3D hybrids (like classic FPS engines) or any scene where flat walls must appear straight. When not to use: Not needed for perspective-corrected rasterization pipelines that handle depth automatically, or for non-planar fisheye effects where distortion is desired. The fisheye effect in ray casting was identified as a geometric artifact where naive Euclidean distances cause flat walls to appear bowed. The correction method, multiplying by \cos(\delta), is a standard technique in ray casting tutorials and implementations to maintain visual fidelity for planar geometry.
