name: Wall Height Projection
head: 1D Texture Mapping, Vertical Strip Rendering, screen height calculation
body: Wall Height Projection calculates the vertical pixel extent of a wall segment on the screen based on the wall's real-world height, the projection plane distance, and the corrected perpendicular distance to the wall. It renders the scene as vertical strips per pixel column, drawing the wall strip and filling the remaining screen space with ceiling and floor colors. This method solves the problem of rendering flat walls with correct perspective scaling after fisheye distortion has been corrected, ensuring that the wall appears straight and properly sized relative to the viewer's position. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: wallHeight: The real-world height of the wall segment (e.g., 5 units). distance: The corrected perpendicular distance from the camera to the wall. screenHeight: The total height of the screen in pixels. screenW: The screen width in pixels (set to 320 in the reference implementation). fov: The field of view angle in radians. Outputs: For each column i, the vertical screen coordinates for the wall, floor, and ceiling strips. Data Structures Not given in the sources. The method operates on scalar values per column. Steps 1. Calculate Projection Plane Distance: Compute the distance from the camera to the projection plane using the screen width and field of view. \text{projPlaneDist} = \frac{\text{screenW} / 2}{\tan(\text{fov} / 2)} 2. Calculate Screen-Space Wall Height: Compute the height of the wall in pixels using the real-world wall height, the projection plane distance, and the corrected perpendicular distance. \text{lineHeight} = \frac{\text{wallHeight} \cdot \text{projPlaneDist}}{\text{distance}} Source uses a simplified hardcoded variant wallHeight = ((1 5) / distance) 177, where 5 is the wall height and 177 is a screen scaling factor. 3. Draw Vertical Strips: For each column i from 0 to screenW - 1: Wall: Draw a 1-pixel wide strip centered vertically. y{\text{start}} = \frac{\text{screenHeight}}{2} - \frac{\text{lineHeight}}{2} y{\text{end}} = \frac{\text{screenHeight}}{2} + \frac{\text{lineHeight}}{2} Draw from ystart to yend. Floor: Draw a 1-pixel wide strip below the wall. y{\text{start}} = \frac{\text{screenHeight}}{2} + \frac{\text{lineHeight}}{2} y{\text{end}} = \text{screenHeight} Draw from ystart to yend. Ceiling: Draw a 1-pixel wide strip above the wall. y{\text{start}} = 0 y{\text{end}} = \frac{\text{screenHeight}}{2} - \frac{\text{lineHeight}}{2} Draw from ystart to yend. 4. Shading: Apply shading based on wall orientation. Vertical hits (side=0 or 1) use a darker color than horizontal hits to simulate lighting. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def wallheightprojection(screenw, screenh, fov, wallheightreal, correcteddistance, sidehit): # Step 1: Calculate projection plane distance projplanedist = (screenw / 2) / math.tan(fov / 2) # Step 2: Calculate screen-space wall height lineheight = (wallheightreal projplanedist) / correcteddistance # Step 3: Draw vertical strips centery = screenh / 2 halfwall = lineheight / 2 walltop = centery - halfwall wallbottom = centery + halfwall floortop = wallbottom floorbottom = screenh ceilingtop = 0 ceilingbottom = walltop # Determine wall color based on orientation if sidehit == 0 or sidehit == 1: wallcolor = 'darkcolor' else: wallcolor = 'basecolor' # Initialize screen buffer screen = [[None] screenh for in range(screenw)] for i in range(screenw): # Draw wall strip for y in range(int(walltop), int(wallbottom)): screen[i][y] = wallcolor # Draw floor strip for y in range(int(floortop), int(floorbottom)): screen[i][y] = 'floorcolor' # Draw ceiling strip for y in range(int(ceilingtop), int(ceilingbottom)): screen[i][y] = 'ceilingcolor' Parameters projPlaneDist: The distance from the camera to the projection plane. wallHeight: Real-world height of the wall. distance: Corrected perpendicular distance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Ensure distance is not zero to avoid division by zero. Boundaries: Ensure lineheight does not exceed screenheight. Shading: Correctly identifying wall orientation (vertical vs. horizontal hits) is necessary for proper shading. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the screen width, as each column is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(1) per column, as only scalar values are needed. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally efficient, corrects fisheye distortion for flat walls. Limitations: Only suitable for flat walls, requires pre-computed corrected distances. When to Use: When rendering flat walls with correct perspective after fisheye correction. When Not to Use: For non-flat surfaces or complex 3D scenes without additional processing. Wall Height Projection is a technique used in raycasting engines to render flat walls with correct perspective scaling. It is often used in conjunction with fisheye distortion correction to ensure that walls appear straight and properly sized. The method is derived from the principles of perspective projection and is commonly used in early 3D games and educational raycasting demos. mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, https://github.com/mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Raycasting Prototype with DDA - GitHub, https://github.com/GPMLAD/raycasting, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation
body: This family defines the geometric mapping between world coordinates, camera-local coordinates, and normalized device coordinates (NDC) to enable accurate ray generation for volume rendering. It solves the problem of establishing a consistent coordinate frame for rays, ensuring that ray origins and directions are correctly oriented relative to the scene and the image plane. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera is its focus on the fundamental linear algebra and coordinate system conversions required before any specific sampling strategy (e.g., depth, disparity, or angular) can be applied. It provides the mathematical foundation for Camera Ray Generation. The core mechanism of this family is the application of affine transformations to map points and vectors between different reference frames. All methods in this family rely on the definition of a camera pose, typically represented by a 4 \times 4 matrix or a set of basis vectors (eye, center, up). 1. Coordinate Frames: World Space: The global coordinate system in which the scene geometry is defined. Camera (View) Space: A local coordinate system attached to the camera, typically with the origin at the eye position, the Z-axis aligned with the viewing direction (often -Z or +Z), and the X/Y axes aligned with the image plane. Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): A canonical cube, typically [-1, 1]^3, used to standardize ray directions and origins for uniform sampling, particularly in forward-facing scenes. 2. Transformation Matrices: World-to-View (M{w2v}): Transforms world coordinates to camera space. It is constructed from the camera's basis vectors and position. Camera-to-World (M{c2w}): The inverse of the world-to-view matrix. It transforms camera-space rays (origins and directions) into world space for intersection tests with scene geometry. Projection/NDC Mapping: Transforms camera-space coordinates into NDC space, often involving perspective division or disparity-based reparameterization. 3. Ray Representation: Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. When transforming rays, origins are treated as points (using homogeneous coordinate w=1), while directions are treated as vectors (using w=0) to ensure translation does not affect direction. 4. Basis Construction: The camera basis vectors (Right/Up/Forward) are derived from the eye position, target point, and an up vector using cross products to ensure orthogonality. Maps camera-space rays into a normalized device coordinate (NDC) cube [-1, 1]^3 to enable uniform sampling in disparity (inverse depth) for forward-facing scenes with unbounded depth. Unlike standard ray generation which samples metric depth linearly, this method shifts ray origins to the near plane and projects them such that linear sampling in the transformed NDC parameter t' corresponds to linear sampling in disparity from the near plane to infinity. This allows rendering scenes extending to infinity within a fixed bounding volume, a requirement for real-world forward-facing captures like those in the LLFF dataset. Builds on the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model from Ray generation and camera models. Builds a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix that maps coordinates from world space to camera (view) space, or conversely transforms rays from view space to world space, given an eye position, a target center, and an up vector. It solves the problem of defining a canonical camera coordinate frame for ray generation and volume rendering. Unlike other pose methods, this constructs the basis from scratch using look-at parameters rather than applying a pre-defined rigid transform. The Point to Camera Transformation converts 3D points from world coordinates into the camera's local coordinate system. It establishes the relative position of scene geometry with respect to the viewer, serving as a foundational step for ray generation and visibility checks. Unlike NDC Ray Transformation, which maps pixels to rays, or View Matrix Construction, which builds the full affine transform matrix, this method explicitly computes the rotated and translated position of individual points to facilitate downstream operations like depth sampling or projection. A flexible CT forward/backward projection model that allows the user to define the 3D location and orientation of every individual source-detector pair, overriding standard geometric assumptions. It supports planar or curved detectors and arbitrary source/detector placement, enabling complex trajectories and non-equispaced projection angles. Unlike standard Radon models which assume parallel rays, this geometry handles point-source cone-beam and fan-beam configurations where projection lines are non-parallel. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation by mapping world-space voxel intersections to arbitrary detector coordinates. Models complex, multi-piece glass objects by mapping UV coordinates from a mesh face to a specific 3D section of a source panel. Unlike standard texture mapping, it maps the full physical properties of the source panel—including geometric displacement, bubble distribution, and varying index of refraction—onto a 3D facet using a rigid affine transformation. It solves the problem of intersecting rays with composite glass objects where each facet corresponds to a distinct region of a physical glass panel, allowing for accurate caustic estimation and transmission lighting in a unified local space. It differs from NDC Ray Transformation by operating on local facet frames rather than global camera coordinates. Definition: A coordinate transformation that maps 3D points to (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) where \alpha specifies the epipolar slice, \beta is the angle of the view ray relative to the light direction, and \gamma is the distance from the light ray through the eye point. This allows view rays and light rays to be indexed independently along orthogonal axes. Step: To handle the epipole singularity, render results within a small ring (about two degrees) around the epipole using a standard ray marcher, and apply the epipolar algorithm only to the remainder of the image. Pitfall: At the epipole (where view rays and light rays are parallel), the rectification mapping is singular and the derivative ds/d\gamma goes to infinity. This causes large values that disrupt the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Complexity: Rectification of the camera depth map and unrectification take O(sr) time, and rectification of the shadow map takes O(sd) time, where s is the number of slices, r is the average number of camera rays per slice, and d is the number of light rays. Definition: Transforms Gaussian parameters predicted in camera space into world space for rendering, using a 4 \times 4 camera-to-world extrinsics matrix \mathbf{T} containing rotation \mathbf{R} and translation \mathbf{t}. Formula: The world-space mean is transformed as \mu{\text{world}} = \mathbf{T}\mu{\text{cam}}, applying the full 4 \times 4 transformation matrix. The world-space covariance is transformed as \Sigma{\text{world}} = \mathbf{R}\Sigma{\text{cam}}\mathbf{R}^T, using only the 3 \times 3 rotation component \mathbf{R}. The world-space opacity is unchanged: \alpha{\text{world}} = \alpha{\text{cam}}. The world-space scale is transformed as \mathbf{s}{\text{world}} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{s}{\text{cam}}, where \mathbf{D} is a block-diagonal matrix of Wigner D matrices that rotates spherical harmonics coefficients. Parameter: The library e3nn is used to compute the Wigner D matrices (\mathbf{D}) and to recompile the original 3D Gaussian splatting code base to follow e3nn's conventions. Definition: A strategy to rotate visible camera view directions so they look at the center of a sub-region S, and align their distances to the center of S with a specific radius r, to ensure points inside S can be warped to meaningful coordinates. Parameter: r: The aligned distance to the region center, empirically set as the mean distance to the region center among the 1/4 nearest visible cameras. Pitfall: Visible cameras are not suitable for direct perspective warping because some do not fully cover the region or look at it obliquely, leading to meaningless warp coordinates. Definition: Converts a stack of viewpoint cameras (with projection matrices and world view transforms) into Open3D PinholeCameraParameters objects. Step: For each viewpoint, construct an NDC-to-pixel transformation matrix ndc2pix of shape (3,4): [[W/2, 0, 0, (W-1)/2], [0, H/2, 0, (H-1)/2], [0, 0, 0, 1]]. Compute the intrinsic matrix by multiplying the projection matrix by ndc2pix and transposing the result, then taking the top-left 3 \times 3: intrins = (viewpointcam.projectionmatrix @ ndc2pix)[:3,:3].T. Extract intrinsic parameters: cx = intrins[0,2], cy = intrins[1,2], fx = intrins[0,0], fy = intrins[1,1]. Create an Open3D PinholeCameraIntrinsic object with width, height, and the extracted fx, fy, cx, cy. Compute the extrinsic matrix as the transpose of the world view transform: extrinsic = np.asarray((viewpointcam.worldviewtransform.T).cpu().numpy()). Create an Open3D PinholeCameraParameters object, set its intrinsic and extrinsic attributes, and append to the trajectory list. Definition: Rendering performed only for parallel projections, assuming all casted rays have the same direction. Pitfall: Perspective projection ray casting is not supported. It would require modification of the system and additional memory requirements to store different ray parameters for each pixel. The concept of the view matrix and coordinate transformation originates from classical computer graphics and photogrammetry. The specific application of NDC transformations for disparity sampling in forward-facing scenes was introduced to handle unbounded depth ranges. The transformation of Gaussian parameters for 3D Gaussian Splatting, as detailed in PixelSplat, extends these linear algebra concepts to handle the covariance and spherical harmonics of Gaussian primitives. Camera rectification strategies for multi-view stereo and NeRF training, as seen in F2-NeRF, further refine these transformations to optimize sampling efficiency in specific sub-regions. The hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm utilizes coordinate rectification to index view and light rays independently. Open3D compatibility tools provide standardized conversion routines for camera parameters. name: NDC Ray Transformation
head: NDC Ray Conversion, NDC Ray Conversion for Forward-Facing Scenes, NDC Rays, Non-Deterministic Coordinates (NDC) Ray Transformation, Non-Dominated Coordinates (NDC) Ray Transformation, Normalized Device Coordinates Ray Transform, Unbounded Scene Ray Transformation
body: The NDC Ray Transformation maps camera-space rays into a canonical bounding cube [-1, 1]^3 to enable uniform sampling in disparity (inverse depth) for forward-facing, unbounded scenes. Unlike standard ray generation which assumes bounded metric depth, this method shifts ray origins to the near plane and projects them such that linear sampling in the transformed space corresponds to linear sampling in disparity from the near plane to infinity. It is primarily used for real-world captures (e.g., LLFF) where the scene extends to infinity, whereas standard ray generation is reserved for synthetic bounded scenes (e.g., Blender). Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 in camera space. Camera intrinsics: focal length f{cam}, image width W, image height H. Near plane distance n (scalar). Far plane distance f (scalar, typically \infty for forward-facing scenes). Outputs: Transformed ray origins \mathbf{o}' \in \mathbb{R}^3 and directions \mathbf{d}' \in \mathbb{R}^3 in NDC space. Data Structures: Rays are stored as tensors of shape (N, 3) for origins and directions, where N is the number of rays. Steps: 1. Shift Origin to Near Plane: Calculate the parameter tn to move the ray origin \mathbf{o} to the intersection with the near plane z = -n. tn = -\frac{n + oz}{dz} Update the origin: \mathbf{o}{shifted} = \mathbf{o} + tn \mathbf{d} Note: This step ensures that t'=0 in NDC space corresponds to the near plane in world space, allowing linear sampling of t' \in [0, 1] to cover disparity from n to \infty. 2. Compute Projection Constants: Define the scaling factors based on the pinhole camera model. ax = -\frac{f{cam}}{W/2} ay = -\frac{f{cam}}{H/2} For unbounded scenes (far plane f \to \infty), the Z-constants simplify to: az = 1 bz = 2n If a finite far plane f is required, use the standard perspective projection constants: az = \frac{f+n}{f-n} bz = \frac{2fn}{f-n} 3. Project Origin to NDC: Compute the NDC origin \mathbf{o}' using the shifted origin \mathbf{o}{shifted} (denoted as \mathbf{o} in the final formulas below for brevity, assuming the shift has occurred). o'x = ax \frac{ox}{oz} o'y = ay \frac{oy}{oz} o'z = az + \frac{bz}{oz} Substituting the simplified constants for unbounded scenes: o'x = -\frac{f{cam}}{W/2} \frac{ox}{oz} o'y = -\frac{f{cam}}{H/2} \frac{oy}{oz} o'z = 1 + \frac{2n}{oz} 4. Project Direction to NDC: Compute the NDC direction \mathbf{d}'. d'x = ax \left( \frac{dx}{dz} - \frac{ox}{oz} \right) d'y = ay \left( \frac{dy}{dz} - \frac{oy}{oz} \right) d'z = -\frac{bz}{oz} Substituting the simplified constants for unbounded scenes: d'x = -\frac{f{cam}}{W/2} \left( \frac{dx}{dz} - \frac{ox}{oz} \right) d'y = -\frac{f{cam}}{H/2} \left( \frac{dy}{dz} - \frac{oy}{oz} \right) d'z = -\frac{2n}{oz} 5. Reparameterization Mapping: The parameter t' in NDC space is related to the original parameter t by: t' = \frac{t dz}{oz + t dz} This maps t=0 to t'=0 and t \to \infty to t'=1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def ndcrays(o, d, focal, W, H, near, far=None): """ Transforms camera-space rays to NDC space. Args: o: Tensor of shape (..., 3), ray origins in camera space. d: Tensor of shape (..., 3), ray directions in camera space. focal: Scalar, focal length. W: Scalar, image width in pixels. H: Scalar, image height in pixels. near: Scalar, near plane distance. far: Scalar, far plane distance. If None, assumes infinity. Returns: ondc: Tensor of shape (..., 3), NDC origins. dndc: Tensor of shape (..., 3), NDC directions. """ # 1. Shift origin to near plane # tn = -(near + oz) / dz # oshifted = o + tn d # Note: We perform the shift before projection. # The formulas in S1 assume o is already at the near plane intersection. # Calculate tn tn = -(near + o[..., 2]) / d[..., 2] # Expand tn for broadcasting tn = tn.unsqueeze(-1) # Shift origin oshifted = o + tn d # 2. Compute constants # ax, ay ax = -focal / (W / 2.0) ay = -focal / (H / 2.0) # az, bz if far is None: az = 1.0 bz = 2.0 near else: az = (far + near) / (far - near) bz = (2.0 far near) / (far - near) # 3. Project Origin # o'x = ax (ox / oz) # o'y = ay (oy / oz) # o'z = az + bz / oz oxoz = oshifted[..., 0] / oshifted[..., 2] oyoz = oshifted[..., 1] / oshifted[..., 2] ondcx = ax oxoz ondcy = ay oyoz ondcz = az + bz / oshifted[..., 2] ondc = torch.stack([ondcx, ondcy, ondcz], dim=-1) # 4. Project Direction # d'x = ax (dx/dz - ox/oz) # d'y = ay (dy/dz - oy/oz) # d'z = -bz / oz dxdz = d[..., 0] / d[..., 2] dydz = d[..., 1] / d[..., 2] dndcx = ax (dxdz - oxoz) dndcy = ay (dydz - oyoz) dndcz = -bz / oshifted[..., 2] dndc = torch.stack([dndcx, dndcy, dndcz], dim=-1) return ondc, dndc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If dz = 0, the ray is parallel to the near plane and cannot be shifted to it. In practice, rays are generated from pixel centers, so dz is rarely exactly zero, but numerical stability should be considered. Unbounded Scenes: NDC is only suitable for unbounded scenes. Coordinate System: The derivation assumes the camera looks in the -Z direction. General NDC Ray Conversion maps camera-space rays into a normalized device coordinate (NDC) space to fix the near and far clipping planes at constant values, removing the need for scene-dependent depth bounds in non-spherical datasets. Unlike Blender-specific NDC conventions that assume fixed intrinsics and sign conventions, this method handles arbitrary camera parameters by explicitly shifting ray origins to the near plane and projecting them based on focal length and image dimensions. It is primarily used for forward-facing scenes where depth ranges are large, enabling uniform sampling in NDC space to correspond to inverse depth (disparity) sampling in the original world space. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. The transformation involves basic arithmetic operations per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the transformed rays. Strengths: Allows rendering of unbounded scenes within a fixed bounding volume [-1, 1]^3. Enables uniform sampling in disparity, which is crucial for forward-facing real-world captures where depth varies significantly. Limitations: Not suitable for bounded scenes or scenes with significant depth variation that is not forward-facing. Requires accurate near plane estimation. When to Use: Forward-facing real-world scenes (e.g., LLFF dataset) where the background extends to infinity. When Not to Use: Synthetic bounded scenes (e.g., Blender datasets) where standard ray generation is sufficient. The NDC Ray Transformation was introduced in the NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020) to handle real-world forward-facing captures where the scene extends to infinity. It adapts the normalized device coordinates used in triangle rasterization pipelines to neural radiance fields, mapping the perspective rays to parallel rays in the transformed volume and using disparity instead of metric depth. This allows the neural network to learn a bounded representation for unbounded scenes. head: General NDC, NDC Ray Conversion, NDC Rays, NDC projection, Normalized Device Coordinate rays
body:
General NDC Ray Conversion transforms camera-space rays into Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space, mapping the viewing frustum to a canonical cube (typically [-1, 1]^3). This technique fixes the near and far clipping planes to constant values (e.g., 0 and 1 or -1 and 1), removing the need for scene-dependent depth bounds and enabling uniform sampling strategies for forward-facing scenes. It differs from Pinhole Camera Projection by producing a full ray for traversal rather than a single point, and from Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates by specifically handling the normalization of depth bounds rather than just generating world-space rays. The resulting directionsndc are not unit length, and the projection of the original ray does not equal the NDC ray (projection(origins + t directions) 
eq originsndc + t directionsndc). Inputs: rayso: Ray origins in camera space, shape (batchsize, 3) or (H, W, 3). raysd: Ray directions in camera space, shape (batchsize, 3) or (H, W, 3). focal: Focal length of the pinhole camera (float). W: Image width in pixels (int). H: Image height in pixels (int). near: Near plane distance along the negative z-axis (float). Default is 1.0. Outputs: raysondc: Transformed origins in NDC space, shape (batchsize, 3) or (H, W, 3). raysdndc: Transformed directions in NDC space, shape (batchsize, 3) or (H, W, 3). Data Structures: The inputs and outputs are dense floating-point arrays. The z-component of the origin in NDC space maps the near plane to a constant value (typically 1 or 0 depending on convention) and infinity to another constant (typically 3 or 1). Steps: 1. Shift Origins to Near Plane: Calculate the shift factor t to move the ray origin to the near plane (z = -near in standard camera coordinates). t = - rac{near + rays\o[..., 2]}{rays\d[..., 2]} Update origins: rays\o = rays\o + t[..., 	ext{None}] \cdot rays\d Some implementations use t =  rac{near - rays\o[..., 2]}{rays\d[..., 2]} due to different sign conventions (e.g., Blender vs. OpenGL). 2. Project Origins to NDC: Compute the NDC coordinates for the shifted origins. The x and y components are scaled by the focal length and image dimensions. The z component maps the depth to the NDC range. o0 = - rac{1}{W / (2 \cdot focal)} \cdot  rac{rays\o[..., 0]}{rays\o[..., 2]} o1 = - rac{1}{H / (2 \cdot focal)} \cdot  rac{rays\o[..., 1]}{rays\o[..., 2]} o2 = 1 + 2 \cdot  rac{near}{rays\o[..., 2]} At the near plane (rays\o[..., 2] = -near), o2 = -1. As rays\o[..., 2] 	o -\infty, o2 	o 1, mapping the depth range to [-1, 1]. 3. Project Directions to NDC: Compute the NDC direction components, which accounts for the perspective division difference between the origin and the point at infinity. d0 = - rac{1}{W / (2 \cdot focal)} \cdot \left(  rac{rays\d[..., 0]}{rays\d[..., 2]} -  rac{rays\o[..., 0]}{rays\o[..., 2]} ight) d1 = - rac{1}{H / (2 \cdot focal)} \cdot \left(  rac{rays\d[..., 1]}{rays\d[..., 2]} -  rac{rays\o[..., 1]}{rays\o[..., 2]} ight) d2 = -2 \cdot  rac{near}{rays\o[..., 2]} The direction z-component d2 ensures that the ray in NDC space points towards the correct depth range. At the near plane, d2 = 2. As z 	o -\infty, d2 	o 0. 4. Stack Results: Concatenate the components to form the final NDC rays. rays\o
dc = [o0, o1, o2] rays\d
dc = [d0, d1, d2] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def converttondc(rayso, raysd, focal, W, H, near=1.0): """ Convert camera-space rays to NDC space. Args: rayso: (..., 3) ray origins in camera space. raysd: (..., 3) ray directions in camera space. focal: float, focal length. W: int, image width. H: int, image height. near: float, near plane distance. Returns: raysondc: (..., 3) NDC origins. raysdndc: (..., 3) NDC directions. """ # Step 1: Shift origins to the near plane # t = -(near + raysoz) / raysdz t = -(near + rayso[..., 2:3]) / raysd[..., 2:3] raysoshifted = rayso + t raysd # Step 2: Project origins to NDC # o0 = -1 / (W / (2focal)) (ox / oz) # o1 = -1 / (H / (2focal)) (oy / oz) # o2 = 1 + 2 near / oz invhw = np.array([W / (2.0 focal), H / (2.0 focal)]) o0 = -1.0 / invhw[0] (raysoshifted[..., 0:1] / raysoshifted[..., 2:3]) o1 = -1.0 / invhw[1] (raysoshifted[..., 1:2] / raysoshifted[..., 2:3]) o2 = 1.0 + 2.0 near / raysoshifted[..., 2:3] raysondc = np.concatenate([o0, o1, o2], axis=-1) # Step 3: Project directions to NDC # d0 = -1 / (W / (2focal)) (dx/dz - ox/oz) # d1 = -1 / (H / (2focal)) (dy/dz - oy/oz) # d2 = -2 near / oz oxoz = raysoshifted[..., 0:1] / raysoshifted[..., 2:3] oyoz = raysoshifted[..., 1:2] / raysoshifted[..., 2:3] dxdz = raysd[..., 0:1] / raysd[..., 2:3] dydz = raysd[..., 1:2] / raysd[..., 2:3] d0 = -1.0 / invhw[0] (dxdz - oxoz) d1 = -1.0 / invhw[1] (dydz - oyoz) d2 = -2.0 near / raysoshifted[..., 2:3] raysdndc = np.concatenate([d0, d1, d2], axis=-1) return raysondc, raysdndc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Z: If raysd[..., 2] is zero, the shift factor t becomes infinite. This occurs for rays parallel to the near plane. In practice, this should be handled by clamping or checking for zero denominators. Sign Conventions: Different libraries (e.g., Blender vs. OpenGL) use different camera coordinate systems. Blender uses a right-handed system where the camera looks down +z, while OpenGL uses a left-handed system where the camera looks down -z. The formula for t and the signs in the projection must be adjusted accordingly. Spherical Poses: NDC assumes a forward-facing scene. For spherical or omnidirectional scenes, NDC can clip geometry or distort depth significantly. A sphericposes flag is often used to bypass NDC conversion and use scene bounds instead. Generates world-space rays from pixel indices. It typically precedes NDC conversion if the scene requires NDC sampling. Projects pixels to camera-space rays. This is the immediate predecessor to NDC conversion. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. The operations are element-wise arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the transformed rays. Performance: The transformation is computationally inexpensive compared to ray marching or volume rendering. It is typically performed once per ray batch. Strengths: Simplifies sampling strategies by fixing the depth range to [0, 1] or [-1, 1]. Enables uniform sampling in NDC space to correspond to inverse depth sampling in world space, which is beneficial for forward-facing scenes with large depth variations. Limitations: Not suitable for non-forward-facing or spherical scenes, as it distorts depth and can clip geometry. Requires accurate focal length and image dimensions. When to Use: Forward-facing scenes (e.g., LLFF dataset) where depth range is large and uniform sampling is desired. When Not to Use: Spherical scenes, scenes with significant camera rotation around the object, or when exact world-space depth is required for other processing steps. General NDC Ray Conversion was introduced in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) to handle forward-facing scenes efficiently. The technique maps the perspective frustum to a canonical cube, allowing for simpler and more robust sampling strategies. name: Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates
head: Beaming Rays, Camera Raycasting, Pixel to Ray Unprojection, Ray Direction Calculation, Ray Generation from Camera/NDC, Ray Generation from Pixels, Ray Generation from Screen Coordinates
body: Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates converts 2D screen pixel coordinates into 3D world-space ray origins and directions, serving as the foundational step for raymarching and volume rendering. It solves the problem of "lifting" 2D image data into 3D space by establishing the geometric relationship between the camera sensor and the world. Unlike Pinhole Camera Projection (Pixel to Camera), which focuses on the algebraic backprojection to camera space, this method explicitly constructs world-space rays, often leveraging the inverse Projection-View matrix or explicit NDC-to-world transformations. It builds on General NDC Ray Conversion by handling the final mapping from pixel indices to the specific camera model's world coordinates. Inputs: Pixel coordinates (u, v) or a grid of pixel indices. Image resolution (W, H). Camera parameters: Intrinsic matrix K (or focal length f, principal point cx, cy), Extrinsics (Rotation R, Translation T), and Projection matrix P (or View-Projection matrix VP). Field of View (FOV) and aspect ratio, if using explicit geometric construction. Outputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (typically the camera center). Ray directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized vectors pointing from origin through the pixel). Data Structures: RayBundle: A structure containing tensors for origins and directions. rayso: Shape (N, 3), where N = W \times H (or batch size \times N). raysd: Shape (N, 3), normalized direction vectors. samplepoints: Shape (N, K, 3), initialized to zeros for marching steps. Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Grid: Create a grid of pixel coordinates (u, v) for all pixels in the image. u \in [0, W-1], v \in [0, H-1]. Note: Coordinate systems vary. Metal uses top-left (0,0), while some implementations assume center (0,0). 2. Convert to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): Map pixel coordinates to NDC space [-1, 1]. Formula: x{ndc} = \frac{2 u}{W} - 1 y{ndc} = \frac{2 v}{H} - 1 For a point on the near plane at Z=1 (in camera/NDC space), the 3D NDC point is \mathbf{p}{ndc} = [x{ndc}, y{ndc}, 1.0]^T. Alternative (Explicit FOV): If not using matrix inversion, calculate centered UVs: xy = [u - W/2.0, v - H/2.0] z = \frac{H}{2 \tan(\text{FOV}{vertical} / 2)} \mathbf{d}{cam} = \text{normalize}([xyx, xyy, -z]). 3. Unproject to World Space: Method A: Inverse Projection-View Matrix: Form homogeneous NDC point: \mathbf{p}{ndc}^{hom} = [x{ndc}, y{ndc}, 1.0, 1.0]^T. Compute inverse matrix M^{-1} = (VP)^{-1}. Transform: \mathbf{p}{world}^{hom} = M^{-1} \mathbf{p}{ndc}^{hom}. Perform perspective division: \mathbf{p}{world} = \mathbf{p}{world}^{hom} / w, where w is the fourth component of \mathbf{p}{world}^{hom}. This yields a point on the image plane in world space. Method B: Camera Unproject API: Use a library function (e.g., camera.unprojectpoints) that takes NDC points and returns world coordinates, handling the matrix inversion internally. 4. Determine Ray Origin: The ray origin is the camera center in world space. \mathbf{o} = \text{camera.getcameracenter()}. If using extrinsics R, T, the camera center is -\mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{T}. 5. Compute Ray Direction: Calculate the vector from the origin to the unprojected world point on the image plane. \mathbf{d}{raw} = \mathbf{p}{world} - \mathbf{o}. Normalize the direction: \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{d}{raw}\|}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def generateraysfrompixels(imagesize, camera): """ Generates ray origins and directions for all pixels in an image. Args: imagesize: Tuple (W, H) camera: Camera object with methods getcameracenter() and unprojectpoints() Returns: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3) raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3) """ W, H = imagesize N = W H # Step 1: Generate pixel coordinates # Create meshgrid of pixel indices # Note: meshgrid(y, x) creates grids where first dim is y (rows) and second is x (cols) yindices, xindices = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') # Flatten to list of (x, y) pairs # Shape: (N, 2) pixelcoords = torch.stack([xindices.flatten(), yindices.flatten()], dim=-1).float() # Step 2: Convert to NDC # Map [0, W-1] -> [-1, 1] ndcx = (2.0 pixelcoords[:, 0]) / W - 1.0 ndcy = (2.0 pixelcoords[:, 1]) / H - 1.0 # Construct NDC points on the near plane (Z=1 in camera/NDC space) # Shape: (N, 3) ndcpoints = torch.stack([ndcx, ndcy, torch.oneslike(ndcx)], dim=-1) # Step 3: Unproject to World Space # Append homogeneous coordinate 1.0 ndcpointshom = torch.cat([ndcpoints, torch.oneslike(ndcpoints[...,:1])], dim=-1) # Shape: (N, 4) # Use camera's unproject method. # Assumes camera handles the inverse VP matrix multiplication and perspective division. # fromndc=True indicates input is in NDC space [-1, 1] worldpoints = camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpointshom, fromndc=True) # Shape: (N, 3) # Step 4: Get Ray Origin # Get camera center in world space camcenter = camera.getcameracenter() # Shape: (3,) # Expand to match number of rays rayso = camcenter.expand(N, -1) # Shape: (N, 3) # Step 5: Compute Ray Direction # Vector from origin to world point on image plane raysd = worldpoints - rayso # Shape: (N, 3) # Normalize directions raysd = F.normalize(raysd, dim=-1) # Shape: (N, 3) return rayso, raysd Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Origin: Metal/OpenGL uses top-left (0,0) for pixels, while some mathematical derivations assume center (0,0). Implementations must adjust fragCoord by subtracting size / 2.0 if using the explicit FOV method. Homogeneous Dimension: When appending the homogeneous coordinate, ensure the shape matches the expected input of the unprojection function. Some APIs expect (N, 4), others handle (N, 3) NDC internally. Device Agnosticism: Hardcoding.cuda() breaks execution on CPU or other devices. Use camera.device. Aspect Ratio: If the explicit FOV method is used, the vertical FOV must be combined with the aspect ratio (implicitly via W/H in the xy calculation) to prevent distortion. Converts 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) and depth z into 3D homogeneous coordinates in the camera frame using the intrinsic matrix. It implements the backprojection operator \pi^{-1}, mapping a pixel p and depth z to a 3D point xc via z K^{-1} \bar{p}. It is the inverse of the forward camera projection operator \pi(xc) \approx K xc, building on Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates and distinct from NDC-to-World Ray Generation. NDC-to-World Ray Generation computes the world-space origin of a ray for a given Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) pixel, assuming a pinhole camera model where the camera is at the origin in view space, facing the positive Z axis, with a near plane at Z=1. It differs from sibling methods like Pinhole Camera Projection (Pixel to Camera) by explicitly constructing the ray origin in world space based on the field of view and aspect ratio, rather than just transforming pixel coordinates to camera space. A common pitfall in implementation is incorrectly offsetting the ray origin by screen-space coordinates, which causes field-of-view distortion and curvature artifacts. Transforms a camera from normalized device coordinates (NDC) space to screen pixel coordinates for rasterization. It calculates screen focal length as f{screen} = f \cdot \min(W, H) / 2.0 and sets the principal point to (W/2, H/2). This is the inverse operation of the projection step in ray generation, used for rendering rather than raycasting. Time Complexity: O(N), where N = W \times H. The operations (grid generation, matrix multiplication, normalization) are vectorizable and parallelizable across pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store origins and directions. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to tensor operations. The bottleneck is typically the matrix inversion if done per-frame (though VP is usually constant per camera pose) or the unprojection API call overhead. Strengths: Generalizable to any camera model supported by the unprojection API; handles arbitrary extrinsics and intrinsics. Limitations: Requires accurate camera calibration. If the inverse matrix is singular (e.g., camera at infinity), it fails. Ray generation from pixel coordinates is a fundamental technique in computer graphics. It is used in volume rendering, neural radiance fields (NeRF), and 3D Gaussian Splatting. The specific implementation using NDC and inverse Projection-View matrices is standard in modern graphics APIs (OpenGL, Vulkan, Metal) and deep learning frameworks (PyTorch3D, DiffRast). name: Pinhole Camera Projection (Pixel to Camera)
head: Pixel to Camera, Inverse Projection, Inverse Camera Projection for 3D Positioning, Camera Ray Lifting
body: This method converts 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) and a depth value z into 3D homogeneous coordinates in the camera coordinate frame using the camera intrinsic matrix. It implements the backprojection operator \pi^{-1}, mapping a pixel p and depth z to a 3D point xc via z K^{-1} \bar{p}. It is the inverse of the forward camera projection operator \pi(xc) \approx K xc, building on Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates and distinct from NDC-to-World Ray Generation. Inputs: intrinsics: A 3 \times 3 matrix K containing focal lengths, principal point offsets, and optionally a skew coefficient. pixelcoords: 2D coordinates (u, v) or (x, y) representing pixel locations. depth: Depth value z (distance from the camera center along the optical axis). Outputs: cameracoords: An array of shape (..., 4) containing homogeneous 3D coordinates [Xc, Yc, Zc, 1]^T in the camera frame. Data Structures: The intrinsic matrix K is typically stored as: K = \begin{bmatrix} fx & s & cx \\ 0 & fy & cy \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where fx, fy are focal lengths in pixels, (cx, cy) is the principal point, and s is the skew coefficient. Steps: 1. Extract intrinsic parameters from the matrix K: fx = K[0, 0] fy = K[1, 1] cx = K[0, 2] cy = K[1, 2] s = K[0, 1] (skew). 2. Compute the unnormalized camera space coordinates X{lift} and Y{lift} using the backprojection formula: X{lift} = \frac{u - cx + \frac{cy \cdot s}{fy} - \frac{s \cdot v}{fy}}{fx} \cdot z Y{lift} = \frac{v - cy}{fy} \cdot z Some implementations assume zero skew (s=0), simplifying X{lift} to (u - cx) z / fx. 3. Set Z{lift} = z. 4. Construct the homogeneous coordinate vector by stacking [X{lift}, Y{lift}, Z{lift}, 1] along the last dimension. 5. (Optional) Generate a validity mask where depth z > 0 to filter out invalid points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pixeltocamera(intrinsics, u, v, z): """ Lifts pixel coordinates and depth to camera space homogeneous coordinates. Args: intrinsics: Array of shape (..., 3, 3) containing the camera intrinsic matrix K. u: Array of shape (...,) containing x-pixel coordinates. v: Array of shape (...,) containing y-pixel coordinates. z: Array of shape (...,) containing depth values. Returns: Array of shape (..., 4) containing homogeneous camera coordinates [X, Y, Z, 1]. """ # Extract intrinsics fx = intrinsics[..., 0, 0] fy = intrinsics[..., 1, 1] cx = intrinsics[..., 0, 2] cy = intrinsics[..., 1, 2] skew = intrinsics[..., 0, 1] # Compute X coordinate in camera space xlift = ((u - cx + cy skew / fy - skew v / fy) / fx) z # Compute Y coordinate in camera space ylift = ((v - cy) / fy) z # Z is simply the depth zlift = z # Stack into homogeneous coordinates [x, y, z, 1] ones = [1.0] len(z) if hasattr(z, 'len') else [1.0] cameracoords = list(zip(xlift, ylift, zlift, ones)) return cameracoords Parameters: intrinsics: 3 \times 3 matrix. Typical values depend on resolution and lens, e.g., fx \approx 500-1000 for standard lenses. depth: Positive float. Must be >0 for valid backprojection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Depth: Division by zero or invalid geometry if z=0. A validity mask (z>0) should be applied. Skew: If the source assumes zero skew but the matrix contains non-zero skew, the X{lift} calculation will be incorrect if the skew term is omitted. Pixel Centering: The formula assumes pixel coordinates refer to the top-left corner or center depending on convention. The "Continuous-to-Discrete" variant explicitly assumes pixel centers are at integer + 0.5. If using integer pixel indices directly, ensure consistency with the intrinsic definition. Coordinate System: The output is in the camera frame. To get world coordinates, it must be multiplied by the extrinsic matrix [R|t]. A method to convert continuous image coordinates (\mu'x, \mu'y) to discrete pixel coordinates (pi, pj). It assumes the pixel center is at the center of a unit area box, leading to the relation pi + 0.5 = fx \cdot tx / tz + cx and pj + 0.5 = fy \cdot ty / tz + cy. This is the forward projection step often used to map 3D points to 2D pixels, whereas the main method performs the inverse. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels/points, as it involves only element-wise arithmetic operations. Strengths: Simple, differentiable, and efficient. It directly maps depth maps to 3D points without iterative solvers. Limitations: Requires accurate depth and intrinsics. Errors in intrinsics (especially principal point or focal length) propagate linearly to 3D errors. Does not handle occlusions or missing depth values inherently (requires masking). When to use: When generating rays for volume rendering from a known depth map and camera pose. The projection operator \pi(xc) \approx K xc and its inverse \pi^{-1}(p, z) = z K^{-1} \bar{p} are standard formulations in camera geometry. The method is used in NeRF-based approaches and Gaussian Splatting pipelines to initialize 3D points from 2D observations. Implementations may simplify the backprojection by assuming zero skew for modern sensors. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Renderable Neural Radiance Map for Visual Navigation, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00878, fetched 2026-10-26 SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00408, fetched 2026-10-26 NVlabs/InstantSplat, https://github.com/NVlabs/InstantSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2409.06765, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: NDC-to-World Ray Generation
head: Camera Raycasting, View Space Ray Origin
body: NDC-to-World Ray Generation computes the world-space position of a ray origin for a given Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) pixel, assuming a pinhole camera model where the camera is at the origin in view space, facing the positive Z axis, with a near plane at Z=1. It builds on Ray Generation from Pixel Coordinates by explicitly constructing the ray origin in world space based on the near-plane geometry defined by the field of view and aspect ratio, rather than just transforming pixel coordinates to camera space. It differs from the sibling method Pinhole Camera Projection (Pixel to Camera) by outputting the world-space origin directly instead of returning camera-space coordinates. A common implementation pitfall is incorrectly offsetting the ray origin by screen-space coordinates, which causes field-of-view distortion and curvature artifacts. Inputs: ndcx, ndcy: Normalized Device Coordinates of the pixel in the range [0, 1]. halffovradx: Horizontal half-field of view in radians. aspect: Screen aspect ratio (width divided by height). camerapos: World-space position of the camera. cameraforward, cameraup, cameraright: Camera orientation basis vectors. Outputs: worldpos: The world-space origin of the ray. Data Structures: Vector3d: A 3D vector structure with fields x, y, z. Steps: 1. Initialize camera basis vectors in view space: forward = (0, 0, 1), up = (0, 1, 0), and right = cross(up, forward). 2. Rotate the camera basis vectors around a specified axis (x, y, or z) by a given angle in degrees, updating each vector independently. 3. Calculate the near-plane dimensions using the horizontal half-field of view and aspect ratio. 4. Calculate the view-space position by offsetting the forward vector along the right and up axes based on the NDC coordinates. 5. Transform the view-space position to world space by adding the camera position. Formulas: near\plane\width = 2.0 \cdot \tan(\text{half\fov\rad\x}). near\plane\height = \frac{near\plane\width}{\text{aspect}}. \text{view\pos} = \text{forward} + \text{right} \cdot (\text{ndc\x} - 0.5) \cdot near\plane\width + \text{up} \cdot (\text{ndc\y} - 0.5) \cdot near\plane\height. \text{world\pos} = \text{view\pos} + \text{camera\pos}. Parameters: halffovradx: Horizontal half-field of view in radians, derived from degrees via (\text{deg} \cdot \pi) / 180.0. aspect: Screen aspect ratio used to scale the near-plane height. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The formula assumes NDC coordinates are in the range [0, 1]. Adding screen-space coordinates (e.g., vec3(x, y, 0)) to the ray origin while also adding the direction vector results in an incorrect effective field of view that varies with pixel position, leading to distortion and curvature artifacts, especially when the camera is close to objects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ndctoworldray(ndcx, ndcy, halffovradx, aspect, camerapos, cameraforward, cameraup, cameraright): """Computes the world-space ray origin for a given NDC pixel.""" nearplanewidth = 2.0 math.tan(halffovradx) nearplaneheight = nearplanewidth / aspect viewpos = cameraforward + cameraright (ndcx - 0.5) nearplanewidth + cameraup (ndcy - 0.5) nearplaneheight worldpos = viewpos + camerapos return worldpos A correction for raymarching where the ray origin is incorrectly initialized with screen-space pixel coordinates, causing field-of-view distortion and curvature artifacts when the camera is close to objects. The correct method initializes the ray origin raypos to the camera position campos only, without adding screen-space coordinates. Specifically, one should not add the screen-space vector vec3(x, y, 0) to the ray origin before adding the ray direction r. Adding vec3(x, y, 0) to the ray origin while also adding the direction vector r (which already contains screen-space information) results in an incorrect effective field of view that varies with pixel position, leading to distortion. Standard raymarching leaves the ray origin at the camera position (or world origin relative to camera) and varies only the direction based on fragment coordinates, whereas the flawed approach adds pixel offsets to the origin. Not given in the sources. The method is derived from the implementation of a terminal-based signed distance field renderer. The specific pitfall of adding screen-space coordinates to the ray origin was identified in a discussion on avoiding curvature artifacts in raytracers. The source provides the core formula for calculating the ray origin based on NDC coordinates, field of view, and aspect ratio. The source highlights the common mistake of offsetting the ray origin, which leads to distortion. name: View Matrix Construction
head: Camera View Matrix Computation, Look-at view matrix construction, LookAt Matrix, LookAt Matrix Construction, viewmatrix
body: View Matrix Construction computes a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix that maps coordinates or rays between world space and camera (view) space, given an eye position, a target point, and an up vector. It solves the problem of defining a camera's orientation and position in 3D space to enable ray generation for volume rendering. It differs from NDC Ray Transformation by establishing the initial world-to-view or view-to-world basis rather than mapping to normalized device coordinates, and from Camera Pose Transformation by deriving the basis vectors from geometric primitives (eye, target, up) rather than applying pre-computed rotation and translation operations to existing pose parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: eye: A 3D vector representing the camera position in world space. center (or target): A 3D vector representing the point the camera is looking at in world space. up: A 3D vector representing the desired upward direction in world space, typically (0, 1, 0). Outputs: A 4 \times 4 matrix. The interpretation depends on the desired direction of transformation: Camera-to-World (C2W): Used to transform view-space rays (origins and directions) into world space for intersection tests. The basis vectors form the rotation part, and the eye position forms the translation part. World-to-View (W2V): Used to transform world coordinates into camera space. This is the inverse of the C2W matrix. Data Structures: Matrix Layout: The sources predominantly describe a 4 \times 4 matrix structure where the first three columns are the orthonormal basis vectors (Right, Up, Forward) and the fourth column contains the translation (eye position). Column 0: Right vector (\mathbf{s}). Column 1: Up vector (\mathbf{u}). Column 2: Forward vector (-\mathbf{f}). Column 3: Eye position (\mathbf{eye}). Row 3: (0, 0, 0, 1). Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate Forward Vector: Compute the direction from the eye to the center. Normalize this vector to obtain the forward axis \mathbf{f}. \mathbf{f} = \text{normalize}(\text{center} - \text{eye}) Note: Some conventions define the camera looking down the negative Z-axis in view space, so the world-space forward direction used in the basis might be -\mathbf{f}. 2. Calculate Right Vector: Compute the side vector \mathbf{s} by taking the cross product of the forward vector \mathbf{f} and the input up vector. Normalize the result. \mathbf{s} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{f}, \text{up})) This ensures the right vector is orthogonal to the viewing direction and the original up vector. 3. Calculate True Up Vector: Compute the corrected up vector \mathbf{u} by taking the cross product of the right vector \mathbf{s} and the forward vector \mathbf{f}. \mathbf{u} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{f}) This vector is guaranteed to be orthogonal to both \mathbf{s} and \mathbf{f}, forming an orthonormal basis. If the inputs are normalized and orthogonal, \mathbf{u} remains unit length. 4. Construct Matrix: Assemble the 4 \times 4 matrix. For a Camera-to-World matrix (transforming view-space to world-space): M{c2w} = \begin{bmatrix} sx & ux & -fx & 0 \\ sy & uy & -fy & 0 \\ sz & uz & -fz & 0 \\ \text{eye}x & \text{eye}y & \text{eye}z & 1 \end{bmatrix} (Assuming column-major storage where columns are \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{u}, -\mathbf{f}, \text{eye}). For a World-to-View matrix (transforming world-space to view-space): The rotation part is the transpose of the C2W rotation part (since it is orthonormal), and the translation part is -R^T \cdot \text{eye}. M{w2v} = \begin{bmatrix} sx & sy & sz & -\text{dot}(\mathbf{s}, \text{eye}) \\ ux & uy & uz & -\text{dot}(\mathbf{u}, \text{eye}) \\ -fx & -fy & -fz & \text{dot}(\mathbf{f}, \text{eye}) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} (Assuming row-major storage or explicit row definition). Formulas: Normalization: \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}. Cross Product: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}. Dot Product: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}. Parameters: eye: Camera position. Example: (0.0, 1000.0, -130.0) in RAS coordinates. center: Target point. Example: Volume center. up: Up vector. Example: (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) or (0.0, 1.0, 0.0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the eye and center are identical, the forward vector is zero, and normalization fails. A guard should check for this and return an identity matrix or raise an error. Parallel Up Vector: If the up vector is parallel (or anti-parallel) to the forward vector \mathbf{f}, the cross product for the right vector \mathbf{s} will be zero. This results in a singular matrix. A common fix is to use a default up vector (e.g., (0,1,0)) if the provided up vector is too close to parallel with \mathbf{f}. Axis Convention: The matrix assumes the camera looks down the negative Z-axis in view space when calculating ray marching directions. When transforming a direction vector from view space to world space, use w=0.0 to ensure translation does not affect the direction. Row vs Column Major: The mathematical definition of the basis vectors is consistent, but their placement in the matrix (rows vs columns) depends on the memory layout (row-major vs column-major) and the multiplication order (vector \times matrix vs matrix \times vector). Sources like explicitly define the matrix with basis vectors as rows in the code snippet, while describe them as columns. Implementers must align with their specific graphics API or math library conventions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructviewmatrix(eye, center, up, mode='c2w'): """ Constructs a 4x4 view matrix. Args: eye (tuple): Camera position (x, y, z). center (tuple): Target point (x, y, z). up (tuple): Up vector (x, y, z). mode (str): 'c2w' for Camera-to-World, 'w2v' for World-to-View. Returns: list: 4x4 matrix as a list of 4 lists (rows). """ # Step 1: Forward vector fx = center[0] - eye[0] fy = center[1] - eye[1] fz = center[2] - eye[2] # Normalize forward lengthf = (fx2 + fy2 + fz2)0.5 if lengthf == 0: raise ValueError("Eye and center are identical") fx = fx / lengthf fy = fy / lengthf fz = fz / lengthf # Step 2: Right vector (Side) # Cross product of f and up sx = fy up[2] - fz up[1] sy = fz up[0] - fx up[2] sz = fx up[1] - fy up[0] # Normalize side lengths = (sx2 + sy2 + sz2)0.5 if lengths == 0: raise ValueError("Up vector is parallel to forward vector") sx /= lengths sy /= lengths sz /= lengths # Step 3: True Up vector # Cross product of s and f ux = sy fz - sz fy uy = sz fx - sx fz uz = sx fy - sy fx # Step 4: Construct Matrix if mode == 'c2w': # Camera-to-World: Basis vectors are columns. # Col 0: Right (s), Col 1: Up (u), Col 2: -Forward (-f), Col 3: Eye # Row-major representation of this column-major matrix: # Row 0: s.x, u.x, -f.x, 0 # Row 1: s.y, u.y, -f.y, 0 # Row 2: s.z, u.z, -f.z, 0 # Row 3: eye.x, eye.y, eye.z, 1 return [ [sx, ux, -fx, 0.0], [sy, uy, -fy, 0.0], [sz, uz, -fz, 0.0], [eye[0], eye[1], eye[2], 1.0] ] elif mode == 'w2v': # World-to-View: Inverse of C2W. # Rotation part is transpose of C2W rotation. # Translation part is -R^T eye # Row 0: s.x, s.y, s.z, -dot(s, eye) # Row 1: u.x, u.y, u.z, -dot(u, eye) # Row 2: -f.x, -f.y, -f.z, dot(f, eye) # Row 3: 0, 0, 0, 1 dotseye = sx eye[0] + sy eye[1] + sz eye[2] dotueye = ux eye[0] + uy eye[1] + uz eye[2] dotfeye = fx eye[0] + fy eye[1] + fz eye[2] return [ [sx, sy, sz, -dotseye], [ux, uy, uz, -dotueye], [-fx, -fy, -fz, dotfeye], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] ] else: raise ValueError("Mode must be 'c2w' or 'w2v'") Average Pose Calculation computes a single representative camera pose from a set of input poses, providing a stable reference frame for subsequent volume rendering operations. It differs from Focus Point Calculation by averaging origins and directions rather than minimizing perpendicular distance to viewing rays, and from Bounding Sphere Estimation by yielding a transformation matrix rather than a scalar radius. It serves as the geometric anchor for View Matrix Construction when a global coordinate system is required. Camera Pose Transformation applies geometric operations—specifically translation and rotation—to camera-to-world (c2w) pose matrices or 3D points to align the virtual camera with a desired viewing configuration or to normalize a set of poses for volume rendering. It solves the problem of mapping coordinates between different reference frames (e.g., converting COLMAP's world-to-camera outputs to camera-to-world formats, or centering a scene at the origin) while preserving the rigid body structure of the camera. It differs from View Matrix Construction by focusing on the explicit manipulation of pose parameters (rotation angles, translation vectors) rather than constructing the final view matrix from basis vectors, and from Average Pose Calculation by operating on individual poses or specific transformations rather than computing statistical averages. Orbit Camera Basis Computation calculates an orthonormal camera basis (eye position, forward, right, and up vectors) for a camera that orbits around a fixed target center using spherical coordinates (yaw, pitch, and radius). It solves the problem of determining the viewing direction and position for interactive 3D navigation, ensuring the camera maintains a stable orientation relative to the world up vector while avoiding singularities. It differs from standard look-at methods by explicitly deriving the eye position from parametric spherical angles rather than accepting a pre-computed position, and from arcball controls by using direct angle-to-position mapping instead of quaternion rotations. This method defines a perspective projection where both the camera eye and the projection plane are displaced from the world origin, ensuring the Jacobian of the transformation is the identity at the center of the visibility bounding box (Vbb). It solves the problem of geometric distortion and floating-point precision loss in screen-z values that occurs when standard perspective projections (with the eye at the origin) are applied to scenes where the center of interest is far from the origin. Unlike standard parallel projections which preserve relative screen space, this method creates an illusion of depth by causing background objects to occupy less screen space than foreground objects of the same size. View Transformations define the sequence of affine and projective mappings that convert volume data from its native object coordinate system into the final image coordinate system. This method manages four distinct transformation matrices—modeling, viewing, projection, and viewport—to handle spatial positioning, camera orientation, and rasterization bounds. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit support for a multi-stage pipeline (Object \to World \to Eye \to Clip \to Image) and its integration with light direction vector transformation, ensuring shading calculations occur in the correct coordinate space. Copies the inverse view matrix (3 float4s, 12 floats) to device symbol for ray direction transformation. It copies 12 floats (3x4 matrix) to invViewMatrix symbol. Defines a fixed up vector t = {0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f} and camera position w = camPosition. It normalizes w, computes right vector u = normalize(cross(t, w)), and forward vector v = normalize(cross(w, u)). It builds a translation matrix matT with Change offsets, a rotation matrix temp from u, v, w columns, inverts temp to get rev, extracts axes X, Y, Z from rev, builds world-to-camera rotation w2cr and translation w2ct, combines to w2c = w2cr w2ct, transforms camera position adjustedvec = matT w2c camPosition, builds camera-to-world rotation c2wr and translation c2wt, combines to c2w = c2wr c2wt, and updates camPosition with c2w adjustedvec. name: Average Pose Calculation
head: Average Camera Pose, Average Pose, Average Pose Computation, mean pose via SVD
body: Average Pose Calculation computes a single representative camera pose from a set of input poses, providing a stable reference frame for subsequent volume rendering operations. It differs from Focus Point Calculation by averaging origins and directions rather than minimizing perpendicular distance to viewing rays, and from Bounding Sphere Estimation by yielding a transformation matrix rather than a scalar radius. It serves as the geometric anchor for View Matrix Construction when a global coordinate system is required. The method aggregates translation and rotation components from a collection of poses. Two distinct approaches exist in the literature: a vector-averaging approach and an SVD-based rotation averaging approach. Input: poses, a set of N camera poses. Format is either [N, 3, 4] (rotation 3\times3 + translation 3\times1) or [N, 4, 4] (homogeneous). Output: avgpose, a single 4\times4 transformation matrix representing the average pose. poses: Array of shape (N, 3, 4) or (N, 4, 4). Indices [:,:3, 3] denote the translation vectors (origins). Indices [:,:3, 2] denote the viewing direction vectors (z-axis). Indices [:,:3, 1] denote the up vectors (y-axis). Indices [:,:3,:3] denote the rotation matrices. This method averages the position, viewing direction, and up vector directly. 1. Extract Intrinsic Scaling (Optional): If required by the downstream pipeline, extract the focal length scaling factor hwf from the first pose's intrinsic parameters. 2. Compute Average Position: Calculate the centroid of the camera origins. \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{t}i where \mathbf{t}i is the translation vector of the i-th pose. 3. Compute Average Viewing Direction: Sum the z-axis vectors and normalize the result. \mathbf{z}{avg} = \text{normalize}\left( \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{z}i \right) where \mathbf{z}i is the third column of the rotation matrix of the i-th pose. 4. Compute Average Up Vector: Sum the up vectors and normalize the result. \mathbf{u}{avg} = \text{normalize}\left( \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{u}i \right) where \mathbf{u}i is the second column of the rotation matrix of the i-th pose. 5. Construct Pose: Call viewmatrix(zaxis, up, position) to build the camera-to-world matrix using the computed \mathbf{z}{avg}, \mathbf{u}{avg}, and \mathbf{c}. This method ensures the resulting rotation matrix is orthogonal by applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the mean rotation matrix. 1. Compute Average Translation: \mathbf{c} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{t}i 2. Compute Mean Rotation: \mathbf{R}{mean} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{R}i where \mathbf{R}i is the 3\times3 rotation submatrix of the i-th pose. 3. SVD Decomposition: Perform SVD on \mathbf{R}{mean}: \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{\Sigma}, \mathbf{V}^T = \text{svd}(\mathbf{R}{mean}) 4. Compute Orthogonal Rotation: \mathbf{R}{avg} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{V}^T This step projects the mean rotation onto the Special Orthogonal group SO(3). 5. Construct Pose: Concatenate \mathbf{R}{avg} and the reshaped translation vector \mathbf{c} to form the final 4\times4 matrix. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def viewmatrix(zaxis, up, position): """Constructs a 4x4 camera-to-world matrix from z-axis, up vector, and position.""" x = np.cross(zaxis, up) x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) y = np.cross(x, zaxis) rot = np.eye(4) rot[:3, 0] = x rot[:3, 1] = y rot[:3, 2] = zaxis trans = np.eye(4) trans[:3, 3] = position return trans @ rot def averageposesvd(poses): """ Computes average pose using SVD for rotation averaging. Args: poses: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3, 4) or (N, 4, 4) Returns: avgpose: np.ndarray of shape (4, 4) """ if poses.shape[1] == 4: poses = poses[:,:3,:] N = poses.shape[0] center = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 3], axis=0) meanrot = np.mean(poses[:,:3,:3], axis=0) U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(meanrot) avgrot = U @ Vt avgpose = np.hstack((avgrot, center.reshape(-1, 1))) avgpose = np.vstack((avgpose, np.array([[0, 0, 0, 1]]))) return avgpose def averageposevector(poses): """ Computes average pose using vector averaging. Args: poses: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3, 4) or (N, 4, 4) Returns: avgpose: np.ndarray of shape (4, 4) """ if poses.shape[1] == 4: poses = poses[:,:3,:] center = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 3], axis=0) zsum = np.sum(poses[:,:3, 2], axis=0) zaxis = zsum / np.linalg.norm(zsum) upsum = np.sum(poses[:,:3, 1], axis=0) up = upsum / np.linalg.norm(upsum) avgpose = viewmatrix(zaxis, up, center) return avgpose Input Format: The method accepts inputs of shape [N, 3, 4] or [N, 4, 4]. Degenerate Configurations: If all camera origins are identical, the average position is trivial. If all viewing directions are identical, the z-axis is well-defined. If the up vectors are collinear with the z-axis or sum to zero, normalization fails. A guard should check for zero-norm vectors before normalization. Estimates the center and radius of a bounding sphere for a scene based on a set of camera poses. It differs from Focus Point Calculation by explicitly deriving a scalar radius representing the scene's extent, which is critical for normalizing depth values and initializing volume rendering bounds. Focus Point Calculation finds the 3D point that minimizes the distance to all camera focal axes in a set of poses. It serves as a geometric center for a camera rig, often used to define the center of rotation or the origin for subsequent coordinate transformations. It differs from Average Pose Calculation by minimizing perpendicular distance to viewing rays rather than averaging origins and directions, and from Bounding Sphere Estimation by providing a single point rather than a volume. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) implementations, where an average pose is used to define the coordinate system for the scene. The SVD approach is a standard technique in computer vision for averaging rotation matrices, ensuring the result remains in SO(3).
