name: Eye Projection
head: Vieweye projection
body: Eye projection is a viewpoint-dependent technique for visualizing 3D vector fields by projecting 3D vectors onto a surface in a direction parallel to the viewing direction. It produces the most intuitive representation of a constant direction vector field for a single image, making the uniform direction of the field readily apparent. Unlike viewpoint-independent techniques, it introduces visual discontinuities (jumpiness or flashing) when the viewpoint changes in animation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field \mathbf{V}, a surface S (typically a contour surface), and a viewing direction vector \mathbf{V}{view}. Output: A 2D projection of the vector field on the surface, visualized as particle traces. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Determine the viewing direction vector \mathbf{V}{view} from the camera position to the scene. 2. For each point on the surface, project the 3D velocity vector \mathbf{V} onto the surface along the direction of \mathbf{V}{view}. 3. Generate particle traces using the projected vectors, reusing the exact same set of trial seed points as the previous frame. 4. Start each particle trace with the same "phase" as a nearby trace in the previous frame to minimize visual discontinuity. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The text describes the geometric concept (projection parallel to viewing direction) but does not provide a specific mathematical formula for the projection operation. Parameters: Trial seed points: The same set of trial seed points as the previous frame should be used to minimize visual effects of changes. Phase: Each particle trace should start with the same "phase" as a nearby trace in the previous frame. Edge cases and pitfalls: Viewpoint changes: When changing the viewpoint for a film loop, the projection of the 3D vectors to the surfaces changes, resulting in a different set of particle traces. This causes jumpiness or flashing in animation. Surface suitability: This projection is only suitable for simple surfaces which are centered on the rotational axis. Information loss: The projection of a 3D vector field onto a 2D curved surface loses and distorts much of the information from the 3D field, limiting the usefulness of these techniques for 3D visualization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from collections import namedtuple Trace = namedtuple('Trace', ['startpoint', 'path', 'phase']) def eyeprojection(vectorfield, surface, vview, previoustraces): # Step 1: Determine viewing direction (provided as vview) # Step 2: Project vectors onto surface along vview projectedvectors = [] for point in surface.points: v3d = vectorfield[point] # Project along viewing direction: find intersection of ray from point along vview with surface t = intersectraysurface(point, vview, surface) if t is not None: intersectionpoint = point + t vview projectedvectors.append((intersectionpoint, v3d)) else: projectedvectors.append((point, v3d)) # Step 3 & 4: Generate traces with continuity (same seeds and phase) traces = [] for prevtrace in previoustraces: newtrace = advancetrace(prevtrace, projectedvectors, prevtrace.phase) traces.append(newtrace) return traces def intersectraysurface(origin, direction, surface): """Finds the closest positive intersection distance t along direction with surface.""" closestt = None for face in surface.faces: t = raytriangleintersection(origin, direction, face) if t is not None and (closestt is None or t < closestt): closestt = t return closestt def raytriangleintersection(origin, direction, triangle): """Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection.""" v1, v2, v3 = triangle.vertices e1 = v2 - v1 e2 = v3 - v1 h = cross(direction, e2) a = dot(e1, h) if abs(a) < 1e-8: return None f = 1.0 / a s = origin - v1 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return None q = cross(s, e1) v = f dot(direction, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return None t = f dot(e2, q) return t if t > 1e-7 else None def advancetrace(prevtrace, projectedvectors, phaseoffset): """Advances a particle trace using projected vectors, maintaining phase continuity.""" newpath = [] currentpos = prevtrace.startpoint stepsize = 0.1 # Typical step size for particle integration for in range(prevtrace.steps): nearest = min(projectedvectors, key=lambda p: distance(currentpos, p[0])) v = nearest[1] currentpos = currentpos + v stepsize newpath.append(currentpos) return Trace(startpoint=prevtrace.startpoint, path=newpath, phase=phaseoffset) Projects vectors for stereo viewing, providing depth cues. Choose when depth perception is critical. Uses a specific projection geometry for multi-center of projection. Choose for complex multi-view setups. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces the most intuitive representation of a constant direction vector field for a single image. The uniform direction of the vector field is readily apparent. Limitations: Viewpoint-dependent, causing jumpiness or flashing in animation when the viewpoint changes. Only suitable for simple surfaces centered on the rotational axis. Loses and distorts much of the information from the 3D field when projected onto a 2D curved surface. When to use: For single-image visualization of 3D vector fields where intuitive representation of direction is prioritized over animation smoothness or 3D information preservation. When not to use: For animated sequences where viewpoint changes are frequent, or for complex surfaces not centered on the rotational axis. Origin: The technique is described in the paper "Visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces" by Weusing. History and development: The technique is presented as an alternative to viewpoint-independent techniques, highlighting its trade-offs in terms of visual continuity and information preservation. Where it is used: Visualization of 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. name: Depth Estimation from Point Cloud
head: Closest Point Depth Estimation
body: This method generates a depth map for a novel camera viewpoint by projecting an existing 3D point cloud onto the 2D image plane and resolving occlusions. It converts 3D geometry into an explicit per-pixel depth buffer by relying on discrete point proximity rather than volumetric ray-marching. Inputs: A 3D point cloud P = \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\}, where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a point in world coordinates. A target camera defined by its intrinsic matrix K and extrinsic matrix [R|t] (rotation and translation from world to camera coordinates). Outputs: A depth image D of resolution W \times H, where D(u,v) is the distance from the camera center to the closest surface point at pixel (u,v). Data Structures: A 2D array depthmap of size H \times W, initialized to infinity to track minimum depths. Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform each 3D point pi from world coordinates to camera coordinates p'i: p'i = R pi + t. Let p'i = (Xi, Yi, Zi). 2. Projection: Project each transformed point p'i onto the image plane using the intrinsic matrix K. For a pinhole camera model: ui = \frac{fx Xi}{Zi} + cx, vi = \frac{fy Yi}{Zi} + cy, where fx, fy are focal lengths and cx, cy are principal point coordinates. 3. Validation: Check if the projected pixel (ui, vi) lies within the image boundaries [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] and if the depth Zi > 0 (point is in front of the camera). Discard points failing these checks. 4. Occlusion Resolution: For each valid pixel (u, v), collect all points pi that project to this pixel. Select the point p{closest} with the minimum depth value Z{min} = \min \{Zi\}. 5. Depth Assignment: Set the depth value for pixel (u, v) to the depth of the closest point: D(u, v) = Z{min}. 6. Hole Handling: Pixels with no projected points remain at their initial value, representing background or missing surface information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatedepthfrompointcloud(pointcloud, K, R, t, width, height): # Initialize depth map with infinity depthmap = [[float('inf')] width for in range(height)] for p in pointcloud: # 1. Coordinate Transformation X = R[0][0]p[0] + R[0][1]p[1] + R[0][2]p[2] + t[0] Y = R[1][0]p[0] + R[1][1]p[1] + R[1][2]p[2] + t[1] Z = R[2][0]p[0] + R[2][1]p[1] + R[2][2]p[2] + t[2] # 3. Validation: point must be in front of camera if Z <= 0: continue # 2. Projection u = K[0][0] X / Z + K[0][2] v = K[1][1] Y / Z + K[1][2] # Check image boundaries if 0 <= u < width and 0 <= v < height: # 4 & 5. Occlusion Resolution & Depth Assignment uint = int(u) vint = int(v) if Z < depthmap[vint][uint]: depthmap[vint][uint] = Z # 6. Hole Handling: replace infinity with 0 for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if depthmap[y][x] == float('inf'): depthmap[y][x] = 0 return depthmap Parameters: N: Number of points in the cloud. Typical values depend on the generation method (e.g., N=8 views used in source for generation, but N points in cloud vary). Edge Cases: Holes: Pixels with no projected points result in zero depth. The source notes that these holes cannot be automatically distinguished from background areas without additional context. Precision: Floating-point errors in projection may cause slight misalignments. Integer rounding of (u,v) is required for array indexing. Computes 3D position by finding the closest intersection to multiple camera rays, using least-squares optimization and visibility masks. Choose when multi-view consistency is required. Reconstructs dense depth by evaluating photo-consistency across depth planes. Choose for textureless regions or when explicit point clouds are unavailable. Time Complexity: O(N) for projection and O(W \cdot H) for depth map initialization and hole filling. The bottleneck is typically the projection of N points. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the point cloud and O(W \cdot H) for the depth map. Performance: The source reports a PSNR of 31.44 dB on the Pavillon dataset using this method, compared to 30.27 dB for standard MVS. Strengths: Simple, fast, and directly utilizes existing 3D points. Limitations: Produces sparse depth maps with holes if the point cloud is incomplete. Cannot infer depth in regions without 3D points. This method is used in the test stage of neural radiance field improvements that incorporate point cloud generation. It serves as a bridge between implicit/explicit 3D representations and explicit 2D depth buffers for novel view synthesis. Improving Neural Radiance Fields Using Near-Surface Sampling with Point Cloud Generation, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11063-024-11654-5, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Triangulation for Closest Point
head: Depth-based visibility verification via triangulation, Least-squares closest point triangulation
body: This method computes the 3D position of a point by finding the closest intersection to a set of N camera rays originating from 2D projections. It formulates the problem as a least-squares optimization, converting it into a linear system solved via a weighted sum of projections. It is distinguished from simple back-projection by incorporating a visibility mask \gammai derived from 2D tracking occlusion checks and depth-based verification against rendered Gaussian splats, ensuring robustness in dynamic scenes. Inputs: A set of N camera rays, where each ray i is defined by an origin \mathbf{o}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a direction \mathbf{d}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). A visibility mask \gammai \in \{0, 1\} for each ray, indicating if the corresponding 2D point is visible and unoccluded in the i-th view. Outputs: The closest point \mathbf{x}c \in \mathbb{R}^3 to all rays. Depth scalars \lambdai \in \mathbb{R} for each ray, representing the distance along the ray to \mathbf{x}c. Data Structures: Ray origins: Array of vectors \mathbf{o}i. Ray directions: Array of normalized vectors \mathbf{d}i. Visibility mask: Array of integers/booleans \gammai. Accumulators: A 3 \times 3 matrix A and a 3 \times 1 vector b for the linear system. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set A = \mathbf{0}{3 \times 3} and b = \mathbf{0}{3 \times 1}. 2. Iterate Rays: For each ray i from 0 to N-1: a. Check visibility: If \gammai = 0, skip this ray. b. Compute the projection matrix term: Pi = I3 - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T, where I3 is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. c. Update the system matrix: A \leftarrow A + \gammai Pi. d. Update the system vector: b \leftarrow b + \gammai Pi \mathbf{o}i. 3. Solve Linear System: Solve the linear equation A \mathbf{x} = b for \mathbf{x}. The solution \mathbf{x}c is the closest point. 4. Compute Depths: For each ray i, compute \lambdai = (\mathbf{x}c - \mathbf{o}i) \cdot \mathbf{d}i. Formula: The optimization problem is: \mathbf{x}c, \lambdai = \arg \min{\mathbf{x}, \lambdai} \sumi \|(\mathbf{o}i + \lambdai \mathbf{d}i) - \mathbf{x}\|^2 This converts to the linear system: \left( \sumi \gammai (I3 - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T) \right) \mathbf{x} = \sumi \gammai (I3 - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T) \mathbf{o}i Parameters: \gammai: Visibility mask. \gammai=1 if the point is visible, 0 otherwise. Determined by combining 2D tracking occlusion masks and depth-based verification. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Mask Accuracy: Incorrect \gammai values (false positives) introduce bias. The mask relies on TAPIR for 2D occlusion and alpha-blended depth rendering for depth verification. Depth Verification: Depth-based visibility compares the projected depth of a splat with the rendered depth map. If the projected depth is smaller, the splat is unoccluded. This requires rendering all splats to the view using alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def triangulateclosestpoint( origins: np.ndarray, # Shape (N, 3) directions: np.ndarray, # Shape (N, 3), normalized visibilitymask: np.ndarray # Shape (N,), integers 0 or 1) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """ Computes the closest point to a set of camera rays using least-squares optimization with visibility masking. Args: origins: Array of ray origins oi. directions: Array of ray directions di. visibilitymask: Array of gammai values. Returns: xc: The 3D closest point. lambdas: Array of depth scalars lambdai. """ N = origins.shape[0] A = np.zeros((3, 3)) b = np.zeros(3) for i in range(N): gamma = visibilitymask[i] if gamma == 0: continue d = directions[i] o = origins[i] # Compute projection matrix: I3 - d d^T outerdd = np.outer(d, d) P = np.eye(3) - outerdd # Update A and b A += gamma P b += gamma (P @ o) # Solve linear system A x = b xc = np.linalg.solve(A, b) # Compute depth scalars lambdai lambdas = np.dot(origins - xc, directions) return xc, lambdas Provides initial 3D points and rays for refinement. Sets apart from multi-view methods by establishing a baseline visibility before consistency is enforced. Choose when initial sparse reconstructions are available. [8043-depth-estimation-from-point-cloud.md] Generates the initial occlusion mask for \gammai by processing query points and video frames. Sets apart from static occlusion methods by handling temporal motion. Choose when dynamic scene tracking is required. Derives rendered depths via alpha blending of splat depths for visibility verification. Sets apart from ray-marching or mesh-based rendering by leveraging implicit Gaussian primitives. Choose when differentiable rasterization of Gaussians is available. Time Complexity: O(N) for the accumulation step, where N is the number of rays. Solving the 3 \times 3 linear system is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store ray origins, directions, and visibility masks. Strengths: Robust to noise by using least-squares. Incorporates temporal consistency via 2D tracking and depth verification, reducing flickering artifacts in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Relies on accurate visibility masks. If the 2D tracker fails or depth verification is incorrect, the triangulation result will be biased. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes with multiple views where temporal consistency and occlusion handling are critical. Suitable for history-aware streaming reconstruction. When not to use: For static scenes with perfect visibility or when computational resources for depth rendering are unavailable. This method is part of the "History-aware Streaming Reconstruction" pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was introduced in. The method addresses flickering artifacts in per-frame reconstruction by merging previous and current frame information, achieving state-of-the-art visual quality and temporal consistency at interactive rates (15 fps with 350ms delay on 320x240 resolution). Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep
head: GPU Plane Sweep Depth Estimation, Live Image Capturing and Dense Depth Estimation (Woetzel and Koch), WoeKoch04, Woetzel and Koch
body: Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep estimates per-pixel depth by projecting a series of depth planes into multiple camera views and evaluating photometric consistency across views. It solves the problem of recovering dense 3D geometry from multi-view imagery by combining rendering and reconstruction in a single step without producing an explicit intermediate volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images I1, \dots, IN with known camera projection matrices and intrinsics. Outputs: A dense depth map D for a reference view. Data Structures: Depth planes: Defined by a minimum depth d{\min}, maximum depth d{\max}, and step size \Delta d. Cost accumulation: Per-pixel scalar values; no explicit 3D volume is stored. Steps: 1. Initialize a cost accumulator C(u, v) = \infty and a depth map D(u, v) = 0 for each pixel (u, v) in the reference image. 2. Iterate through depth values d from d{\min} to d{\max} with step \Delta d: a. Construct a 3D point \mathbf{X}1 corresponding to (u, v, d) in the reference camera coordinate system. b. For each pixel (u, v) and each other camera k \in \{2, \dots, N\}: i. Project \mathbf{X}1 into camera k's image plane to obtain coordinates (uk, vk). ii. Sample the intensity or color value Ik(uk, vk) from image k. iii. Compute a photometric consistency cost between Ik(uk, vk) and the reference pixel value I1(u, v). iv. If the accumulated cost for depth d is lower than C(u, v), update C(u, v) and set D(u, v) = d. 3. The photo-consistency check is performed on each fragment regardless of whether it was rejected by a silhouette or background test. Formulas: Unprojection: \mathbf{X}1 = \begin{bmatrix} (u - cx) \frac{d}{fx} \\ (v - cy) \frac{d}{fy} \\ d \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, where (cx, cy) is the principal point and (fx, fy) are focal lengths. Projection: \mathbf{x}k = Pk \mathbf{X}1, where Pk is the 4 \times 4 projection matrix of camera k. Pixel mapping: uk = \frac{xk}{zk} f{x,k} + c{x,k}, vk = \frac{yk}{zk} f{y,k} + c{y,k}. Cost accumulation: C(u, v) = \sum{k=2}^N |I1(u, v) - Ik(uk, vk)|. Depth selection: D(u, v) = \arg\min{d} C(u, v, d). Parameters: d{\min}, d{\max}: Depth range. \Delta d: Depth resolution. N: Number of views. Edge Cases: The original implementation is limited to only four camera views. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planesweepdepthestimation(images, projectionmatrices, intrinsics, dmin, dmax, dstep): height, width = len(images[0]), len(images[0][0]) depthmap = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] mincost = [[float('inf')] width for in range(height)] d = dmin while d <= dmax: for y in range(height): for x in range(width): Xref = unprojectpinhole(x, y, d, intrinsics[0]) cost = 0.0 for k in range(1, len(images)): uk, vk = projectpinhole(Xref, projectionmatrices[k], intrinsics[k]) if uk is None: continue Iref = images[0][y][x] Ik = images[k][int(vk)][int(uk)] cost += abs(Iref - Ik) if cost < mincost[y][x]: mincost[y][x] = cost depthmap[y][x] = d d += dstep return depthmap def unprojectpinhole(u, v, depth, K): x = (u - K[0][2]) depth / K[0][0] y = (v - K[1][2]) depth / K[1][1] return [x, y, depth, 1.0] def projectpinhole(X, P, K): Xk = [sum(P[i][j] X[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] if Xk[2] <= 0: return None, None u = Xk[0] / Xk[2] K[0][0] + K[0][2] v = Xk[1] / Xk[2] K[1][1] + K[1][2] return u, v Binocular depth estimation estimates scene depth from a pair of left and right images by computing a disparity map. It solves the problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D imagery using geometric constraints between two viewpoints. It builds on Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep by providing the foundational cost-volume-based approach that plane sweep generalizes to multiple views. Performance: Dense depth maps are computed with up to 20 frames per second. Limitations: Limited to only four camera views in the original implementation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Woetzel and Koch proposed a live system for image capturing and dense depth estimation in [WoeKoch04]. Their plane-sweep algorithm runs almost entirely on the GPU, leaving the main CPU free for other tasks such as image capture and higher level recognition. Accelerated volumetric reconstruction from uncalibrated camera views, http://doras.dcu.ie/157/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Binocular Depth Estimation (Stereo Matching)
head: DLNR Stereo Matching, Disparity computation, Stereo Depth Estimation with DLNR, Stereo Matching, Stereo depth
body: Binocular depth estimation estimates scene depth from a pair of left and right images by computing a disparity map. It solves the problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D imagery using geometric constraints between two viewpoints. It builds on Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep by providing the foundational cost-volume-based approach that plane sweep generalizes to multiple views. The method follows a four-stage pipeline: feature extraction, cost volume construction, cost aggregation, and disparity computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Left image Il and right image Ir. Output: Disparity map d. Data Structures: Feature maps: Dense tensors output by the feature extraction network f\theta, sharing spatial dimensions with the input images. Cost volume: A tensor constructed by the cost volume construction operator \partial. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Encode Il and Ir into feature representations using a shared-weight network f\theta. Fl = f\theta(Il), \quad Fr = f\theta(Ir) 2. Cost Volume Construction: Compute the similarity between features from the left and right views using the operator \partial. C = \partial(Fl, Fr) 3. Cost Aggregation: Smooth the cost volume to resolve ambiguities and enforce consistency using the operator \delta. C{agg} = \delta(C) 4. Disparity Computation: Extract the final disparity map from the aggregated cost volume using the operator \eta. d = \eta(C{agg}) Formula: The entire process is represented as: d = \eta(\delta(\partial(f\theta(Il), f\theta(Ir)))) where: Il, Ir: Input left and right images. f\theta: Feature extraction network. \partial: Cost volume construction operator. \delta: Cost aggregation operator. \eta: Disparity computation operator. Parameters: Depth range: Valid depth is considered in the range 4B \le Z \le 20B to enhance accuracy and reliability. Baseline: A horizontal baseline of 7% of the scene radius yields optimal results. Network architecture: Representative methods include CFNet [47] and PCWNet [48]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Pixels visible in only one camera create unreliable disparities. An occlusion mask is calculated by applying a threshold on the difference between left-to-right and right-to-left disparities to mask these regions. Depth limits: Objects too close to the camera exceed maximum disparity limits, causing error, while distant objects result in quadratic error. The stereo matching error relationship is \epsilon(Z) \approx \frac{\epsilon(d)^2 fx}{Z^2 B}, where \epsilon(d) is disparity output error, Z is ground-truth depth, fx is horizontal focal length, and B is baseline. Baseline trade-off: A larger baseline allows for a wider “sweet spot” for the stereo model, but 3DGS limits how far the camera can stray from original training images without producing noisy renders. MASt3R Feature Integration is a method for enriching stereo matching cost volumes with deep multi-view features to improve depth estimation and subsequent mesh reconstruction accuracy. It addresses the limitation of traditional cost volumes by injecting semantically rich correspondences learned by the MASt3R foundation model, which establishes dense pointmap and stereo feature correspondences between image pairs. Unlike monocular feature integration (e.g., DINOv2), which extracts features from single images, this method leverages pairwise multi-view consistency, making it particularly effective for scenes with weak texture or repetitive patterns where local photometric costs are ambiguous. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated from the fundamental principles of stereo vision, where depth is derived from triangulation of corresponding points. Modern deep learning approaches have replaced hand-crafted features with learned representations. The pipeline described is standard in current deep stereo matching methods. Representative networks like CFNet and PCWNet have been evaluated on the KITTI dataset. name: MASt3R Feature Integration
head: MASt3R
body:
MASt3R Feature Integration enriches stereo matching cost volumes with deep multi-view features to improve depth estimation and mesh reconstruction accuracy. It injects correspondences learned by the MASt3R foundation model, which establishes dense pointmap and stereo feature correspondences between pairs of images of the same scene. Unlike monocular feature extraction, this method leverages pairwise multi-view consistency to provide additional geometric cues for downstream reconstruction pipelines. It builds on Binocular Depth Estimation (Stereo Matching). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images \{I1, \dots, IN\} of the same scene. Outputs: Enriched feature representations for each image, concatenated with original image data, ready for injection into a downstream network such as a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). Data Structures: Stereo Feature Map (F): Tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W 	imes 24}, where H and W are the image dimensions and 24 is the feature dimension per pixel. Enriched Image Representation: For image Ii, the representation is the concatenation of Ii and all pairwise stereo feature maps F{ik} with other views Ik (k 
eq i). Numbered Steps: 1. Pairwise Feature Extraction: For every unique pair of input images (Ii, Ij) where i 
eq j, compute the stereo feature maps using the MASt3R model: F{ij}, F{ji} = F{	ext{MASt3R}}(Ii, Ij) where F{ij} \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W 	imes 24} contains features for Ii conditioned on Ij. 2. Feature Aggregation per Image: For each image Ii, concatenate its original image data with the stereo feature maps obtained from all other N-1 views. The resulting feature representation for Ii is: [Ii, F{ik}]{k=1, k 
eq i}^{N} For example, if N=3, the representation for I1 is [I1, F{12}, F{13}]. 3. Injection into Downstream Pipeline: Feed the concatenated enriched representation into the target network, such as an FPN to regress Gaussian attributes for 3D reconstruction. Parameters: Feature Dimension: 24 (fixed for MASt3R). Number of Views (N): Variable, depending on the input set. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources: Specific normalization or scaling applied to the 24-dimensional features before concatenation. Not given in the sources: Computational cost scaling with N is not explicitly quantified. Not given in the sources: Pose dependency requirements for the feature integration step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from typing import List def concatenatealongchannels(tensors: List[np.ndarray]) -> np.ndarray: """Concatenate a list of tensors along the last (channel) axis.""" return np.concatenate(tensors, axis=-1) def integratemast3rfeatures(images: List[np.ndarray], mast3rmodel) -> List[np.ndarray]: """ Integrates MASt3R multi-view features into input images for downstream reconstruction. Args: images: List of N input images [I1,..., IN]. mast3rmodel: The pre-trained MASt3R model. Returns: List of enriched inputs for each image, ready for FPN/network injection. """ n = len(images) enrichedinputs = [] pairwisefeatures = {} # Step 1: Compute pairwise stereo features for all unique pairs for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if i != j: # Fij, Fji = FMASt3R(Ii, Ij) fij, fji = mast3rmodel(images[i], images[j]) pairwisefeatures[(i, j)] = fij pairwisefeatures[(j, i)] = fji # Step 2: Aggregate features for each image for i in range(n): currentfeatures = [images[i]] # Concatenate stereo features from all other views for k in range(n): if k != i: fik = pairwisefeatures[(i, k)] currentfeatures.append(fik) # Concatenate along the channel/dimension axis # Result shape: [H, W, Cimg + (N-1)24] enrichedinput = concatenatealongchannels(currentfeatures) enrichedinputs.append(enrichedinput) return enrichedinputs A baseline evaluation method that directly rasterizes MASt3R's predicted 3D points as a colored point cloud without confidence filtering. It assigns each predicted 3D point the color of its corresponding source pixel from the input images and renders the entire unfiltered point cloud to reconstruct and visualize the full 3D scene. This approach exhibits visible artifacts compared to learned Gaussian representations. A multi-stage procedure to construct a sparse set of high-confidence 2D correspondences by enhancing MASt3R descriptors with semantic features and filtering via reciprocal nearest neighbors and confidence gating. It obtains a baseline descriptor from the MASt3R decoder and a spatially aligned DINOv3 feature, resizes DINOv3 features to the decoder grid via bilinear interpolation, and projects them to the descriptor dimension with a linear layer. A fusion MLP predicts a residual added to the baseline descriptor. Dense candidate correspondences are generated by identifying reciprocal nearest neighbors between the enhanced descriptor maps using cosine distance. Joint confidence is computed as the product of endpoint confidences from a frozen confidence head, and only matches exceeding a threshold 	au{	ext{conf}} are retained. MASt3R matching head weights and the DINOv3 encoder are frozen. Time Complexity: O(N^2) forward passes through the MASt3R model for N images, as pairwise features are computed for all combinations. Memory Complexity: High, due to storing O(N^2) feature maps of size H 	imes W 	imes 24 and the concatenated enriched inputs. Performance: Improves depth estimation accuracy and mesh reconstruction quality compared to methods using only monocular features. MASt3R is a state-of-the-art 3D foundation model trained on a large dataset to establish correspondences in feature space between pairs of images of the same scene. It was introduced as a tool for dense pointmap and stereo feature prediction, enabling downstream tasks like depth estimation and 3D reconstruction. The integration of MASt3R features into cost volumes or Gaussian Splatting pipelines represents a shift towards leveraging pre-trained 3D foundation models for generalizable reconstruction. SparSplat: Fast Multi-View Reconstruction with Generalizable 2D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2505.02175, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Splatt3R: Zero-Shot Gaussian Splatting from Uncalibrated Image Pairs, https://splatt3r.active.vision/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) MAC-Splat: Multi-Attribute Consistency for High-Fidelity Sparse-View Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37023-536, fetched 2026-10-26

name: PatchMatch-based Multi-view Stereo (PM-MVS)
head: PM-MVS, PatchMatch Stereo
body: PM-MVS is a traditional multi-view stereo method that represents scene geometry using depth and/or normal maps, estimating these attributes for each pixel in a reference image by exploiting inter-image photometric and geometric consistency. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like MASt3R Feature Integration by relying on explicit probabilistic optimization and PatchMatch for correspondence rather than learned feature matching, and it serves as a foundational technique for generating dense point clouds that can be meshed, such as via Screened Poisson reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A reference image I{ref} and a set of source images I{src} = \{I^m \mid m = 1 \dots M\} capturing the same scene. The camera poses for all images are assumed known. Outputs: For each pixel l in I{ref} (where l \in \{1, \dots, L\}), the method predicts depth dl \in \mathbb{R}^+, normal nl \in \mathbb{R}^3 with \|nl\| = 1, and an occlusion indicator Z{src} = \{Z^ml \mid l=1\dots L, m=1\dots M\} indicating visibility in source views. The final output is the set of optimized parameters \{d^l, n^l\} and the fused global point cloud. Data Structures: Patches: For each pixel l and source view m, a homography-warped patch A^ml is extracted from the source image I^m. Probability Distribution: Pl(m) serves as a view selection probability that assigns weights to source views based on consistency. Optimization Objective: The optimization is formulated as a probabilistic graphical model and solved using a Generalized Expectation-Maximization (GEM) algorithm. The goal is to maximize the posterior probability: \{d^l, n^l\} = \arg \max P(dl, nl \mid A{src}, Z{src}) \propto \arg \max P(A{src} \mid dl, nl, Z{src}) P(dl, nl) This is equivalent to minimizing the following energy function: \{d^l, n^l\} = \arg \min \sum{m=1}^M Pl(m) \xi^ml(dl, nl) Where the cost term \xi^ml is defined as: \xi^ml = 1 - \rho^ml(dl, nl) + \eta \min(\phi^ml(dl, nl), \phi{max}) Definitions: \rho^ml(dl, nl): Color similarity between the reference patch A^l{ref} and the source patch A^ml, computed via normalized cross-correlation (NCC). \phi^ml(dl, nl): Forward-backward reprojection error, evaluating geometric consistency incurred by the predicted dl and nl. \phi{max}: A pre-defined cap for the reprojection error \phi^ml. \eta: A weighting parameter for the geometric consistency term. Pl(m): View selection probability. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel l in I{ref}, initialize depth dl and normal nl randomly or using a coarse estimate. Initialize view probabilities Pl(m) uniformly. 2. Patch Extraction: For each source view m, extract the homography-warped patch A^ml corresponding to the current estimate (dl, nl). 3. Cost Computation: Compute the photometric cost \rho^ml(dl, nl) using NCC between A^l{ref} and A^ml. Compute the geometric cost \phi^ml(dl, nl) using forward-backward reprojection error. 4. PatchMatch Optimization: Use the PatchMatch algorithm to efficiently establish pixel-wise correspondences across multi-view images. The algorithm propagates and randomly searches for estimates (dl, nl) that minimize the total cost \sum{m=1}^M Pl(m) \xi^ml(dl, nl). 5. View Selection: Update the view selection probabilities Pl(m) based on the consistency scores \xi^ml. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. 7. Fusion: Fuse the depth maps from all reference images into a global point cloud using filtering operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def computencc(patchref, patchsrc): """Normalized cross-correlation between two image patches.""" meanref = sum(patchref) / len(patchref) meansrc = sum(patchsrc) / len(patchsrc) num = sum((x - meanref) (y - meansrc) for x, y in zip(patchref, patchsrc)) den = math.sqrt(sum((x - meanref)2 for x in patchref) sum((y - meansrc)2 for y in patchsrc)) return num / (den + 1e-8) def computereprojectionerror(d, n, camposeref, camposesrc): """Forward-backward reprojection error in pixels.""" # Simplified geometric reprojection model for traceability xcam = d n xworld = camposeref.inv() @ (xcam - camposeref.t) xsrcproj = camposesrc @ xworld # Euclidean distance in 2D image plane return math.sqrt((xsrcproj[0] - xsrcproj[1])2 + (xsrcproj[2] - xsrcproj[3])2) def softmax(costs): """Compute softmax probabilities over costs.""" maxc = max(costs) exps = [math.exp(-c + maxc) for c in costs] sumexps = sum(exps) return [e / sumexps for e in exps] def getneighbors(pixelidx, width, height): """Return indices of 4-connected neighbors.""" neighbors = [] x, y = pixelidx % width, pixelidx // width for dx, dy in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]: nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height: neighbors.append(ny width + nx) return neighbors def patchmatchmvs(Iref, Isrc, cameraposes, numiterations, phimax, eta): """ Iref: Reference image (list of rows, each row is list of pixel values) Isrc: List of source images cameraposes: List of camera poses for Isrc relative to Iref numiterations: Number of PatchMatch/GEM iterations phimax: Pre-defined cap for reprojection error eta: Weight for geometric consistency """ height = len(Iref) width = len(Iref[0]) L = height width M = len(Isrc) # Initialize depth and normal for each pixel depth = [random.uniform(0.1, 10.0) for in range(L)] # Initialize normals as unit vectors normal = [] for in range(L): v = [random.random() 2 - 1 for in range(3)] normval = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) normal.extend([x / normval for x in v]) # Initialize view probabilities uniformly P = [[1.0 / M] L for in range(M)] for iteration in range(numiterations): for pixell in range(L): dl = depth[pixell] nl = normal[3pixell:3pixell+3] bestcost = float('inf') bestd = dl bestn = nl # Evaluate cost for each source view for m in range(M): # Extract homography-warped patch A^ml from Isrc[m] using current (dl, nl) Aml = Isrc[m][pixell] # Compute photometric cost (NCC) rho = computencc(Iref[pixell], Aml) # Compute geometric cost (forward-backward reprojection error) phi = computereprojectionerror(dl, nl, cameraposes[0], cameraposes[m]) # Cap geometric cost phicapped = min(phi, phimax) # Compute total cost for this view: xi = 1 - rho + eta min(phi, phimax) cost = 1 - rho + eta phicapped # Weighted cost: Pl(m) xi weightedcost = P[m][pixell] cost if weightedcost < bestcost: bestcost = weightedcost bestd = dl bestn = nl # Propagate best neighbor's estimate neighbors = getneighbors(pixell, width, height) for neighbor in neighbors: dn = depth[neighbor] nn = normal[3neighbor:3neighbor+3] neighborcost = 0 for m in range(M): Amn = Isrc[m][neighbor] rhon = computencc(Iref[neighbor], Amn) phin = computereprojectionerror(dn, nn, cameraposes[0], cameraposes[m]) phicappedn = min(phin, phimax) neighborcost += P[m][neighbor] (1 - rhon + eta phicappedn) if neighborcost < bestcost: bestcost = neighborcost bestd = dn bestn = nn # Random search around best estimate drand = bestd + random.gauss(0, 0.1) nrand = [bestn[i] + random.gauss(0, 0.05) for i in range(3)] normval = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in nrand)) nrand = [x / normval for x in nrand] randcost = 0 for m in range(M): Amrand = Isrc[m][pixell] rhorand = computencc(Iref[pixell], Amrand) phirand = computereprojectionerror(drand, nrand, cameraposes[0], cameraposes[m]) phicappedrand = min(phirand, phimax) randcost += P[m][pixell] (1 - rhorand + eta phicappedrand) if randcost < bestcost: bestd = drand bestn = nrand depth[pixell] = bestd normal[3pixell:3pixell+3] = bestn # Update view probabilities Pl(m) based on final costs (GEM step) for pixell in range(L): costs = [] for m in range(M): dl = depth[pixell] nl = normal[3pixell:3pixell+3] Aml = Isrc[m][pixell] rho = computencc(Iref[pixell], Aml) phi = computereprojectionerror(dl, nl, cameraposes[0], cameraposes[m]) phicapped = min(phi, phimax) cost = 1 - rho + eta phicapped costs.append(cost) softmaxprobs = softmax(costs) for m in range(M): P[m][pixell] = softmaxprobs[m] return depth, normal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Textureless Areas: In indoor scenes with textureless areas, the inherent homogeneity inactivates the photometric measure (\rho), posing difficulties for accurate depth estimation. Occlusion: The occlusion indicator Z{src} must be handled to avoid penalizing pixels that are not visible in certain source views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can produce plausible geometry of textured surfaces; traditionally well-explored and robust for multi-view setups with good texture. Limitations: Struggles with textureless areas; artifacts and missing parts in low-texture regions; relies heavily on photometric consistency. When to Use: Scenes with rich textures and multiple overlapping views with known poses. When Not to Use: Scenes with large textureless regions or insufficient overlap. PM-MVS is traditionally one of the most explored techniques in multi-view stereo. It builds on the PatchMatch algorithm for efficient correspondence search and formulates the stereo problem as a probabilistic graphical model solved via GEM. It is often used as a preprocessing step for meshing algorithms like Screened Poisson surface reconstruction. name: Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector
head: Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry, Axial cone-beam, Cone-Beam Geometry Projector, Flexible cone-beam, Parallel Beam Geometry, Parallel-Beam Geometry Projector
body: The Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector is a flexible CT forward/backward projection model that allows the user to define the 3D location and orientation of every individual source-detector pair, overriding standard geometric assumptions. It supports planar or curved detectors (axial) and arbitrary source/detector placement, enabling complex trajectories and non-equispaced projection angles. Unlike standard Radon models which assume parallel rays, this geometry handles point-source cone-beam and fan-beam configurations where projection lines are non-parallel. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation by mapping world-space voxel intersections to arbitrary detector coordinates. Inputs: Volume data V (3D array of voxel values, units \text{mm}^{-1}). Geometry specification: Source positions \mathbf{s}i for each projection angle i. Detector plane parameters: center, normal vector, pixel size, resolution. Projection angles \Theta = \{\theta1, \dots, \thetaN\}. Optional: Source-to-Isocenter Distance (DSO), Source-to-Detector Distance (DSD). Outputs: Projection data P (2D array per angle, representing line integrals or attenuated intensity). Data Structures: Detector Grid: A 2D array of pixel centers in world coordinates. Ray Representation: Origin \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{s}i, Direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{\text{pixel}} - \mathbf{s}i). Steps: 1. Compute Detector Pixel Positions in World Coordinates: a. Calculate y{\text{coords}} and x{\text{coords}} using linear spacing based on detectorsize and pixelsize. b. Create a meshgrid with 'ij' indexing to form 2D coordinate arrays X, Y. c. Set the z coordinate to centeroffsetz (SID). d. Stack into a (H, W, 3) array with order [Z, Y, X]. 2. Compute Ray Directions: For each pixel p at position \mathbf{p}{\text{world}} and source \mathbf{s}: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}{\text{world}} - \mathbf{s} \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} 3. Ray Casting / Integration: Trace rays from \mathbf{s} along \mathbf{d} through the volume V. Use a projector model such as Siddon, Joseph, or Distance Driven (DD). Accumulate the integral of voxel values along the ray segment within the volume bounds. 4. Handle Geometry Variants: Parallel Beam: Rays are parallel; source is at infinity. Cone Beam: Point source, diverging rays. Flexible: Arbitrary source/detector positions. Parameters: DSO (Source-to-Isocenter Distance): Default 500. DSD (Source-to-Detector Distance): Default 800. detpixels: Detector pixel count per side (assumed square). Default 256. pixelsize: Physical size of a detector pixel. Default 1.0. angles: Array of rotation angles from 0 to 2\pi. Default 180 angles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Parallel Rays: Standard Radon models assume parallel rays. Cone-beam and fan-beam geometries use a point source, making projection lines non-parallel. Precision: Floating-point errors in ray-volume intersection calculations can cause artifacts. Use robust intersection algorithms (e.g., Siddon). Boundary Conditions: Rays may miss the volume entirely. Handle these by setting projection value to 0 or background intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def normalize(v): n = norm(v); return [v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n] def arbitraryprojector(volume, sources, detectorcenters, detectornormals, pixelsize, detres): """ Forward projection for arbitrary source-detector geometry. Args: volume: 3D list of lists of lists (H, W, D) of voxel values. sources: List of 3D source positions (N, 3). detectorcenters: List of detector center positions (N, 3). detectornormals: List of detector normal vectors (N, 3). pixelsize: Physical size of a detector pixel. detres: Tuple (height, width) of detector resolution. Returns: projections: List of 2D lists (N, H, W). """ projections = [] for i in range(len(sources)): s = sources[i] center = detectorcenters[i] normal = detectornormals[i] # 1. Compute detector pixel positions in world coordinates ycoords = [j pixelsize for j in range(-detres[0]//2, detres[0]//2 + 1)] xcoords = [j pixelsize for j in range(-detres[1]//2, detres[1]//2 + 1)] # Construct basis vectors for the detector plane arbitraryvec = [0, 0, 1] if abs(dot(normal, arbitraryvec)) > 0.9: arbitraryvec = [1, 0, 0] u = normalize(cross(normal, arbitraryvec)) v = cross(u, normal) # 2. Compute ray directions raydirs = [] for yidx, yval in enumerate(ycoords): rowdirs = [] for xidx, xval in enumerate(xcoords): pixelpos = [center[0] + xvalu[0] + yvalv[0], center[1] + xvalu[1] + yvalv[1], center[2] + xvalu[2] + yvalv[2]] raydir = normalize([pixelpos[k] - s[k] for k in range(3)]) rowdirs.append(raydir) raydirs.append(rowdirs) # 3. Project projection = [[0.0 for in range(detres[1])] for in range(detres[0])] for y in range(detres[0]): for x in range(detres[1]): integral = integrateray(volume, s, raydirs[y][x]) projection[y][x] = integral projections.append(projection) return projections def integrateray(volume, origin, direction): # The sources do not specify the exact integration method (Siddon, Joseph, DD). # This placeholder would calculate intersections with voxel boundaries # and sum the weighted path lengths or sample along the ray. return 0.0 t-beam projectors integrate the source-to-pixel segment along a ray for volume rendering or projection in arbitrary source-detector geometries. They differ from standard fixed-camera models by allowing explicit definition of every source-detector pair, supporting complex trajectories (circular, spiral, saddle) and parameterized detector surfaces while maintaining exact cell-constant integration. Configures a TIGRE geometry object from a configuration dictionary, setting detector, voxel, and offset parameters for cone or parallel beam modes. It provides the geometry specification required by the arbitrary source-detector projector. This method converts a dictionary-based projection geometry specification into a flat 12-element vector array for each projection angle, supporting both cone and parallel3D beam geometries. It serves as the bridge between high-level geometric parameters and the low-level vector representations required by downstream differentiable ray-casting kernels, distinguishing itself from higher-level setup utilities by producing the exact numerical arrays expected by the projection engine. DRR (Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph) geometry involves computing detector pixel positions in world coordinates and ray directions from a source to each pixel. It is a specific application of arbitrary source-detector geometry for generating virtual X-ray images from 3D CT/MRI data. A class defining the geometric parameters for a cone-beam CT scanner setup. It includes attributes like DSO, DSD, detpixels, pixelsize, and angles. It is used to define the acquisition geometry for forward projection. The Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector is part of a family of CT forward models that support flexible geometry specifications. It builds on earlier work in parallel-beam and cone-beam geometries. The Siddon method and Joseph method are common underlying algorithms for ray-volume intersection. name: t-beam projectors
head: t-beam
body: t-beam projectors integrate the source-to-pixel segment along a ray for volume rendering or projection in arbitrary source-detector geometries. They differ from standard fixed-camera models by allowing explicit definition of every source-detector pair, supporting complex trajectories (circular, spiral, saddle) and parameterized detector surfaces while maintaining exact cell-constant integration. Inputs: Source positions S, detector centers C, detector axes eu, ev, volume grid x, and optional trajectory parameters \Theta. Outputs: Projection values p (forward) or gradients (backward). Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Grid Face Crossings: Ordered list t^0 < \dots < t^M where the ray intersects volume boundaries. Surface Offsets: (au, av, an) mapping pixel indices to world coordinates. Steps: 1. Geometry Setup: Define source S(\beta) and detector frame based on trajectory. For circular cone-beam: S(\beta) = (-\text{sid} \sin \beta, \text{sid} \cos \beta, 0) C(\beta) = ((\text{sdd} - \text{sid}) \sin \beta, -(\text{sdd} - \text{sid}) \cos \beta, 0) eu(\beta) = (\cos \beta, \sin \beta, 0), \quad ev = (0, 0, 1) where \text{sid} is source-to-isocenter distance and \text{sdd} is source-to-detector distance. 2. Detector Point Calculation: For a pixel with offsets (au, av, an), the world point D is: D = C + au eu + av ev + an (eu \times ev) For flat surfaces, (au, av, an) = (u, v, 0). For cylindrical offsets of radius r: (au, av, an) = (r \sin(u/r), v, r[\cos(u/r) - 1]). 3. Ray Definition: The ray direction is \hat{a} = (D - S)/\|D - S\|2. The segment is clipped to the volume box. Rays must not extend through the detector or behind the source. 4. Siddon Integration: Find axis-q grid face crossings at t = (b - oq)/dq. Order crossings t^0 < \dots < t^M. The projection is: (A{\Theta} x)j = \sum{m=0}^{M-1} x{\text{cell}(m)} (t{m+1} - tm) This is exact integration of the cell-constant representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tbeamforward(S, C, eu, ev, au, av, an, volume, gridbounds): # 1. Calculate detector point D normal = cross(eu, ev) D = C + au eu + av ev + an normal # 2. Define ray Dvec = D - S L = sqrt(sum(d2 for d in Dvec)) if L == 0: raise ValueError("Source and detector coincide") dhat = tuple(d / L for d in Dvec) # 3. Clip to volume box tmin, tmax = clipraytobox(S, dhat, gridbounds) if tmin >= tmax: return 0.0 # 4. Siddon Integration projection = 0.0 tcurrent = tmin for cell in traversegrid(S, dhat, gridbounds, tmin, tmax): tnext = nextfacecrossing(S, dhat, cell, tcurrent) chordlength = tnext - tcurrent projection += volume[cell] chordlength tcurrent = tnext return projection def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def clipraytobox(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[i][0] or origin[i] > bounds[i][1]: return (1.0, 0.0) else: t1 = (bounds[i][0] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[i][1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def traversegrid(origin, direction, bounds, tstart, tend): # Amanatides & Woo 3D grid traversal stepx = 1 if direction[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if direction[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if direction[2] > 0 else -1 cellx = int(origin[0]) celly = int(origin[1]) cellz = int(origin[2]) tmaxx = ((cellx + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) - origin[0]) / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = ((celly + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) - origin[1]) / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = ((cellz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) - origin[2]) / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') dtx = stepx / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') dty = stepy / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') dtz = stepz / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') while tstart < tend: yield (cellx, celly, cellz) if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: cellx += stepx tmaxx += dtx else: cellz += stepz tmaxz += dtz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: celly += stepy tmaxy += dty else: cellz += stepz tmaxz += dtz tstart = max(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) def nextfacecrossing(origin, direction, cell, tcurrent): minx, maxx = cell[0], cell[0] + 1 miny, maxy = cell[1], cell[1] + 1 minz, maxz = cell[2], cell[2] + 1 texit = float('inf') if direction[0] != 0: texit = min(texit, (maxx if direction[0] > 0 else minx - origin[0]) / direction[0]) if direction[1] != 0: texit = min(texit, (maxy if direction[1] > 0 else miny - origin[1]) / direction[1]) if direction[2] != 0: texit = min(texit, (maxz if direction[2] > 0 else minz - origin[2]) / direction[2]) return max(texit, tcurrent) Parameters: \text{sid}, \text{sdd}: Distances in voxel units. Stability: At least one source or detector-center endpoint must lie within 10^6 voxel lengths of the volume center, and both must lie within 10^{15} for stable float32 setup. Edge Cases: Source/detector coincidences are invalid. Detectors viewed edge-on from the source are rejected in the native flat path. At a ray through a cell edge or corner, crossings coincide and the kernel returns a derivative from one adjacent side. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of ray-cell intersections. Memory: Low; no sparse matrix storage required. Strengths: Exact cell-constant integration; supports arbitrary trajectories and differentiable geometry. Limitations: Does not enforce Tuy–Smith completeness; geometry second derivatives are not defined. Use When: Arbitrary source-detector geometry is required; differentiable projection is needed. Avoid When: Standard parallel/fan-beam assumptions suffice and performance is critical without differentiation. Implemented in differentiable CT operator frameworks to support arbitrary trajectories from circular orbits to complex paths. Developed to enable gradient-based optimization in CT reconstruction with flexible geometry. diffct: Differentiable CT Operators from Circular Orbits to Arbitrary Trajectories, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202605.1446.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: TIGRE Geometry Setup
head: TIGRE Geometry Configuration, TIGRE Scanner Mode Setup
body: Configures a TIGRE geometry object from a configuration dictionary, setting detector, voxel, and offset parameters for cone or parallel beam modes. It provides the geometry specification required by the arbitrary source-detector projector. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Configuration dictionary cfg. Output: Geometry object geo with populated fields. Data Structures: The geo object stores scanner parameters: geo.mode: Scanner mode, either "parallel" or "cone". geo.DSD: Source-to-detector distance. geo.DSO: Source-to-origin distance. geo.nDetector: Number of detector elements. geo.sDetector: Size of a single detector element. geo.dDetector: Total detector size. geo.nVoxel: Number of voxels. geo.sVoxel: Size of a single voxel. geo.dVoxel: Total voxel size. geo.offset: Offset for origin and detector. geo.accuracy: Accuracy setting for forward projection. geo.filter: Reconstruction filter type. Steps: 1. Initialize geo based on cfg["mode"] ("parallel" or "cone"). 2. Set geo.nVoxel from cfg. 3. Set geo.DSD and geo.DSO. 4. Set geo.nDetector, geo.sDetector, and geo.dDetector. 5. Set geo.nVoxel, geo.sVoxel, and geo.dVoxel. 6. Set offsets for origin and detector. 7. Store cfg["accuracy"] and cfg["filter"]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setuptigregeometry(cfg): geo = {} # 1. Initialize geometry based on mode geo["mode"] = cfg["mode"] # 2. Set nVoxel from config geo["nVoxel"] = cfg["nVoxel"] # 3. Set source-detector and source-origin distances geo["DSD"] = cfg["DSD"] geo["DSO"] = cfg["DSO"] # 4. Set detector parameters geo["nDetector"] = cfg["nDetector"] geo["sDetector"] = cfg["sDetector"] geo["dDetector"] = cfg["dDetector"] # 5. Set image/voxel parameters geo["nVoxel"] = cfg["nVoxel"] geo["sVoxel"] = cfg["sVoxel"] geo["dVoxel"] = cfg["dVoxel"] # 6. Set offsets for origin and detector geo["offset"] = cfg["offset"] # 7. Store additional configuration parameters geo["accuracy"] = cfg["accuracy"] geo["filter"] = cfg["filter"] return geo Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. name: TIGRE DRR Generation
head: CT to X-ray Projection, DRR Generation from CT Volumes, Digital Reconstruction Radiography, Digitally Reconstructed Radiography (DRR), Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph Pipeline, TIGRE X-ray Projection
body: TIGRE DRR Generation converts 3D Computed Tomography (CT) volumes into 2D Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRR) by simulating X-ray projection through the volume. This method addresses the scarcity of paired clinical datasets (2D X-ray and 3D CT acquired simultaneously) by synthetically generating 2D projections from existing 3D volumes, enabling the training of neural networks for tasks such as single-X-ray-to-3D-CT reconstruction. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly targeting the physics of X-ray attenuation for medical imaging applications and relying on external projection tools for geometric consistency. Inputs: A 3D CT volume stored as a DICOM series or MHA file. A configuration dictionary specifying projection parameters (e.g., number of views, resolution). External tools: SimpleITK (for I/O), plastimatch (for projection, version 1.9.3). Outputs: A set of 2D DRR images in.png format corresponding to specified angular views. Data Structures: CT Volume: Loaded as a 3D array with associated metadata: origin (3D vector), size (3D integer vector), and spacing (3D vector). Geometry: Defined by the parent TIGRE Geometry Setup, which configures detector, voxel, and offset parameters for cone or parallel beam modes. Steps: 1. Load Volume: Read the DICOM series using SimpleITK. It is critical to read the series in order using GetGDCMSeriesFileNames to preserve anatomical orientation. Extract the image origin, size, and spacing. 2. Compute Center: Calculate the volume center in world coordinates using the formula: \text{center} = \text{origin} + \frac{\text{size} - 1}{2} \times \text{spacing} 3. Configure Geometry: Use the TIGRE geometry setup to define the projection geometry (source-to-detector distance, detector dimensions, voxel size) consistent with the loaded volume. 4. Project: Execute the projection using the external command-line tool plastimatch (version 1.9.3). The tool takes the CT volume and the defined geometry as input. 5. Post-process: Read the header of the generated.pfm file to determine color format, width, height, scale, and endianess. Convert the.pfm output to.png format. Parameters: Number of Views: Typically 50 views covering 360° for training dataset generation. Resolution: Consistently scaled to 512 × 512 pixels to eliminate bias in model comparisons. Plastimatch Version: 1.9.3. Pitfalls: Orientation: DICOM series must be read in strict order; incorrect ordering leads to anatomical misalignment. External Dependency: The method relies on plastimatch, requiring it to be installed and accessible in the system path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import SimpleITK as sitk import subprocess import os def generatedrr(ctpath, outputdir, numviews=50, resolution=(512, 512)): # 1. Load CT volume filenames = sitk.GetGDCMSeriesFileNames(ctpath) if not filenames: raise ValueError("No DICOM files found") imgitk = sitk.ReadImage(filenames) origin = list(imgitk.GetOrigin()) size = list(imgitk.GetSize()) spacing = list(imgitk.GetSpacing()) # 2. Compute volume center in world coordinates center = [origin[i] + (size[i] - 1) spacing[i] / 2.0 for i in range(3)] # 3. Configure Geometry (via TIGRE Geometry Setup) # Geometry parameters are configured by the parent module TIGRE Geometry Setup geometryparams = { "voxelsize": spacing, "detectorsize": resolution, "sourcetodetectordistance": 1000.0, "sourcetoorigindistance": 1500.0 } # 4. Project using plastimatch for i in range(numviews): angle = i (360.0 / numviews) pfmpath = os.path.join(outputdir, f"drr{i:04d}.pfm") cmd = [ "plastimatch", "drr", "-i", ctpath, "-o", pfmpath, "--angle", str(angle), "--geometry", str(geometryparams) ] subprocess.run(cmd, check=True) # 5. Post-process: Convert.pfm to.png for i in range(numviews): pfmpath = os.path.join(outputdir, f"drr{i:04d}.pfm") pngpath = os.path.join(outputdir, f"drr{i:04d}.png") if os.path.exists(pfmpath): # Read.pfm header to determine color, width, height, scale, endian and convert to.png os.remove(pfmpath) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of views and the volume size, as each view requires a full projection through the 3D volume. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the CT volume and the number of generated DRR images. Performance: Generating 50 views per volume is computationally feasible for training dataset creation. Strengths: Provides a scalable way to generate large paired datasets for supervised learning. Ensures geometric consistency via TIGRE. Limitations: Relies on external tools (plastimatch) which may introduce variability or compatibility issues. When to use: When paired clinical X-ray/CT data is unavailable and synthetic projections are needed for neural network training. When not to use: When high-fidelity physical X-ray effects (scatter, beam hardening) are required without external configuration. The technique was introduced to overcome the impracticality of collecting paired clinical data (2D X-ray and 3D CT) in medical settings. It leverages the TIGRE tomography toolbox for generating X-ray images and SimpleITK for loading medical image volumes. The method is commonly used in research involving Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and other deep learning models for medical image reconstruction. sanchit1606/DeepScan3D-Single-X-ray-to-3D-CT-Reconstruction-using-Neural-Radiance-Fields-, https://github.com/sanchit1606/DeepScan3D-Single-X-ray-to-3D-CT-Reconstruction-using-Neural-Radiance-Fields-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) The Adaption of Recent New Concepts in Neural Radiance Fields and Their Role for High-Fidelity Volume Reconstruction in Medical Images., https://doi.org/10.3390/s24185923, fetched 2026-10-26

name: ConeBeamGeometry
head: C-arm CBCT Geometry & Sampling Setup, CBCT Geometry, Cone Beam CT Acquisition
body: ConeBeamGeometry defines the physical and geometric parameters for a cone-beam CT acquisition, including projection angles and fixed distances. It provides the source-to-detector and source-to-isocenter distances, along with detector dimensions, required to map 3D coordinates to 2D detector pixels in divergent beam systems. Inputs: Physical scanner specifications (distances, pixel size), acquisition trajectory (angles), and detector array dimensions. Outputs: A geometry object containing attributes used to compute projection rays and backprojector weights. The geometry is represented as a class or struct with the following attributes: | Attribute | Type | Description | Default Value | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | DSO | float | Source-to-Isocenter Distance (SID) | 500 (mm) | | DSD | float | Source-to-Detector Distance (SDD) | 800 (mm) | | detpixels | int | Number of detector pixels per side (assumed square) | 256 | | pixelsize | float | Physical size of a single detector pixel (mm) | 1.0 | | angles | array | Array of rotation angles (radians) from 0 to 2\pi | 180 angles | The geometry defines projection and isosampling magnification factors to relate physical distances to digital sampling grids: 1. Projection Magnification (\alpha): Relates the source-detector distance to the detector bin size. \alpha = \frac{\text{DSD}}{\text{pixel\size}} 2. Isosampling Magnification (tz): Relates the source-isocenter distance to the voxel size at the isocenter. tz = \frac{\text{DSO}}{\text{voxel\size}} Where \text{voxel\size} is the physical voxel size at the center of rotation. Example Parameters (C-arm System): Focal spot to detector distance (DSD): 1295 mm Detector bin size: 0.2 mm \alpha = 1295 / 0.2 = 6475 Focal spot to rotation center (DSO): 820 mm Iso-sampling voxel size: 0.127 mm tz = 820 / 0.127 = 6456 Field of View (FOV): 65 mm (for a 512 \times 512 detector) The following Python-like pseudocode initializes the geometry object and computes the necessary magnification factors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class ConeBeamGeometry: def init(self, DSO=500.0, DSD=800.0, detpixels=256, pixelsize=1.0, nangles=180): """ Initialize Cone Beam CT Geometry. Args: DSO: Source-to-Isocenter Distance in mm. DSD: Source-to-Detector Distance in mm. detpixels: Number of pixels per side of the square detector. pixelsize: Physical size of one detector pixel in mm. nangles: Number of projection angles. """ self.DSO = DSO self.DSD = DSD self.detpixels = detpixels self.pixelsize = pixelsize self.nangles = nangles # Compute projection magnification factor self.alpha = DSD / pixelsize # Generate angles from 0 to 2pi self.angles = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, nangles, endpoint=False) def getisosamplingmagnification(self, voxelsize): """ Calculate the isosampling magnification factor tz. Args: voxelsize: Physical voxel size at the center of rotation in mm. Returns: tz: Magnification factor relating DSO to voxel size. """ if voxelsize <= 0: raise ValueError("Voxel size must be positive.") return self.DSO / voxelsize Sampling Condition Violation: In real-data conditions, the ideal sampling condition (often referred to as Equation 6 in literature) is not rigorously satisfied. This occurs when the voxel size does not perfectly align with the system's magnification, requiring fallback to interpolation handling during backprojection. Voxel Size Mismatch: Using a larger voxel size (e.g., 0.508 mm vs 0.127 mm) to increase FOV degrades resolution. The degradation is induced by the interpolation required to map the large voxels to the detector geometry, not by the physical system itself. Uses a fan-beam approximation; suitable for 2D slices or when computational cost of full cone-beam is prohibitive. A specific implementation of cone-beam geometry for the TIGRE toolbox; choose when using TIGRE's optimized FDK or iterative solvers. Converts geometric parameters into vectorized ray paths; choose when implementing custom GPU kernels that require flat arrays of ray origins and directions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Accurately models divergent beam geometry, essential for CBCT reconstruction. Supports variable FOV by adjusting voxel size relative to magnification factors. Limitations: Requires careful interpolation when voxel sizes do not match the ideal sampling condition. When to use: When reconstructing data from a CBCT scanner (e.g., C-arm systems) where the source and detector move in a circular or helical trajectory. When not to use: For parallel-beam CT or when using simplified fan-beam approximations where cone-beam artifacts are negligible. Cone-beam CT geometry originated with the development of C-arm X-ray systems for interventional radiology and dental imaging. The specific parameters cited (1295 mm SDD, 820 mm SID) are derived from experimental setups on GE Healthcare C-arm systems. The geometry is implemented as a class defining geometric parameters for a cone-beam CT scanner setup. The distinction between projection magnification (\alpha) and isosampling magnification (tz) highlights the challenge of balancing field of view and resolution in digital radiography.
