name: Projection Geometry to Vector Conversion
body: This method converts a dictionary-based projection geometry specification into a flat 12-element vector array for each projection angle, supporting both cone and parallel3D beam geometries. It distinguishes itself from higher-level setup utilities by directly producing the exact numerical arrays expected by the projection engine. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dictionary projgeom containing the geometry definition. Output: A dictionary containing metadata and a numpy array Vectors of shape (nangles, 12). Data Structures The input dictionary projgeom must contain the following keys: type: String, either 'cone' or 'parallel3d'. ProjectionAngles: Array of angles. DistanceOriginSource (D{OS}): Distance from origin to source. DistanceOriginDetector (D{OD}): Distance from origin to detector center. DetectorSpacingX (D{DX}): Physical spacing of detector pixels in the X direction. DetectorSpacingY (D{DY}): Physical spacing of detector pixels in the Y direction. DetectorRowCount: Integer, number of detector rows. DetectorColCount: Integer, number of detector columns. The output dictionary contains: type: String, copied from input. DetectorRowCount: Integer, copied from input. DetectorColCount: Integer, copied from input. Vectors: Numpy array of shape (nangles, 12). DetectorSpacingY: Float, copied from input. DetectorSpacingX: Float, copied from input. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize an empty array Vectors of shape (len(ProjectionAngles), 12). 2. Iterate through each angle \theta in ProjectionAngles with index i. 3. Determine the geometry type from projgeom['type']. 4. If type is 'cone': Compute Source position S: Sx = \sin(\theta) D{OS} Sy = -\cos(\theta) D{OS} Sz = 0 Compute Detector Center D: Dx = -\sin(\theta) D{OD} Dy = \cos(\theta) D{OD} Dz = 0 Compute Detector X-axis basis vector U: Ux = \cos(\theta) D{DX} Uy = \sin(\theta) D{DX} Uz = 0 Compute Detector Y-axis basis vector V: Vx = 0 Vy = 0 Vz = D{DY} 5. If type is 'parallel3d': Compute Ray Direction R: Rx = \sin(\theta) Ry = -\cos(\theta) Rz = 0 Compute Detector Center D: Dx = 0 Dy = 0 Dz = 0 Compute Detector X-axis basis vector U: Ux = \cos(\theta) D{DX} Uy = \sin(\theta) D{DX} Uz = 0 Compute Detector Y-axis basis vector V: Vx = 0 Vy = 0 Vz = D{DY} 6. Store the computed values in Vectors[i,:] in the order: Sx, Sy, Sz, Dx, Dy, Dz, Ux, Uy, Uz, Vx, Vy, Vz. For 'parallel3d', the ray direction R occupies the first three slots. 7. Return the dictionary with Vectors, type, DetectorRowCount, DetectorColCount, DetectorSpacingX, and DetectorSpacingY. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectiongeometrytovector(projgeom): """ Converts a dictionary-based projection geometry into a 12-element vector array. Args: projgeom (dict): Dictionary containing geometry parameters. Returns: dict: Dictionary with 'Vectors', 'type', 'DetectorRowCount', 'DetectorColCount', 'DetectorSpacingX', 'DetectorSpacingY'. """ angles = projgeom['ProjectionAngles'] nangles = len(angles) vectors = np.zeros((nangles, 12)) DOS = projgeom['DistanceOriginSource'] DOD = projgeom['DistanceOriginDetector'] DDX = projgeom['DetectorSpacingX'] DDY = projgeom['DetectorSpacingY'] geomtype = projgeom['type'] for i, theta in enumerate(angles): sint = np.sin(theta) cost = np.cos(theta) if geomtype == 'cone': # Source Position vectors[i, 0] = sint DOS vectors[i, 1] = -cost DOS vectors[i, 2] = 0.0 # Detector Center vectors[i, 3] = -sint DOD vectors[i, 4] = cost DOD vectors[i, 5] = 0.0 # Detector X-axis vectors[i, 6] = cost DDX vectors[i, 7] = sint DDX vectors[i, 8] = 0.0 # Detector Y-axis vectors[i, 9] = 0.0 vectors[i, 10] = 0.0 vectors[i, 11] = DDY elif geomtype == 'parallel3d': # Ray Direction (stored in first 3 slots) vectors[i, 0] = sint vectors[i, 1] = -cost vectors[i, 2] = 0.0 # Detector Center vectors[i, 3] = 0.0 vectors[i, 4] = 0.0 vectors[i, 5] = 0.0 # Detector X-axis vectors[i, 6] = cost DDX vectors[i, 7] = sint DDX vectors[i, 8] = 0.0 # Detector Y-axis vectors[i, 9] = 0.0 vectors[i, 10] = 0.0 vectors[i, 11] = DDY else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported geometry type: {geomtype}") return { 'type': geomtype, 'DetectorRowCount': projgeom['DetectorRowCount'], 'DetectorColCount': projgeom['DetectorColCount'], 'Vectors': vectors, 'DetectorSpacingX': DDX, 'DetectorSpacingY': DDY } Parameters projgeom: Dictionary containing geometry parameters. ProjectionAngles: Array of floats. DistanceOriginSource: Float. DistanceOriginDetector: Float. DetectorSpacingX: Float. DetectorSpacingY: Float. DetectorRowCount: Integer. DetectorColCount: Integer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of projection angles. Memory Complexity: O(N), storing the 12-element vector for each angle. Strengths: Simple, fast, and deterministic conversion from high-level parameters to low-level vectors. Limitations: Only supports specific rotation axes and geometry types (cone and parallel3d). When to use: When implementing a differentiable projector that requires explicit source, detector center, and basis vectors for each angle. When not to use: For complex geometries not covered by the cone/parallel3d models, or when using a library that handles geometry internally. This method originates from the ShapeFromProjections framework. It is used in differentiable tomography pipelines to bridge high-level geometric parameters and low-level vector representations. jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, https://github.com/jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Transformation to World Space
head: Camera-to-World Gaussian Transform, Gaussian Transformation to Camera Frame, World-space Gaussian Transformation
body: This method transforms 3D Gaussian parameters predicted or stored in camera space into world space, enabling consistent rendering across multiple views or integration with world-space scene geometry. It operates directly on the Gaussian primitives rather than ray sampling coordinates, distinguishing it from NDC Ray Transformation, and handles full anisotropic covariance and spherical harmonics rotation rather than just point positions, distinguishing it from Point to Camera Transformation. Inputs: Gaussian parameters in camera space: \mu{\text{cam}}: Mean position, shape (N, 3). \Sigma{\text{cam}}: Covariance matrix, shape (N, 3, 3). \alpha{\text{cam}}: Opacity, shape (N, 1). \mathbf{s}{\text{cam}}: Scale parameters or spherical harmonics coefficients, shape (N, C). The source uses \mathbf{s} to denote the parameters rotated by Wigner D-matrices. q{\text{cam}}: Rotation quaternion, shape (N, 4), normalized. Camera-to-World extrinsics matrix \mathbf{T}, shape (4, 4), composed of rotation \mathbf{R} (top-left 3 \times 3) and translation \mathbf{t} (top-right 3 \times 1). Outputs: Gaussian parameters in world space: \mu{\text{world}}, \Sigma{\text{world}}, \alpha{\text{world}}, \mathbf{s}{\text{world}}, q{\text{world}}. Data Structures: Parameters are stored in contiguous tensors or arrays. \mathbf{T} is a standard 4 \times 4 affine transformation matrix. Steps: 1. Transform Mean: Apply the full 4 \times 4 camera-to-world matrix \mathbf{T} to the camera-space mean \mu{\text{cam}}. \mu{\text{world}} = \mathbf{T}\mu{\text{cam}} 2. Transform Covariance: Compute the world-space covariance using only the 3 \times 3 rotation component \mathbf{R} of \mathbf{T}. \Sigma{\text{world}} = \mathbf{R}\Sigma{\text{cam}}\mathbf{R}^T 3. Transform Opacity: Opacity remains invariant under rigid body transformation. \alpha{\text{world}} = \alpha{\text{cam}} 4. Transform Rotation: For anisotropic Gaussians, normalize the camera-space rotation quaternions q{\text{cam}} and compose them with the camera rotation quaternion q{\text{cam\rot}} derived from \mathbf{R}. The world-space rotation is obtained by quaternion multiplication: q{\text{world}} = q{\text{cam\rot}} \otimes q{\text{cam}} 5. Transform Scale/SH: Transform the parameters \mathbf{s}{\text{cam}} using a block-diagonal matrix \mathbf{D} composed of Wigner D-matrices corresponding to the rotation \mathbf{R}. \mathbf{s}{\text{world}} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{s}{\text{cam}} The source explicitly states that \mathbf{D} rotates the spherical harmonics coefficients, and the variable \mathbf{s} in the formula refers to these coefficients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def gaussiantransformtoworld(mucam, covcam, alphacam, scam, qcam, T): """ Transforms Gaussian parameters from camera space to world space. Args: mucam: Tensor (N, 3) covcam: Tensor (N, 3, 3) alphacam: Tensor (N, 1) scam: Tensor (N, C) representing SH coefficients or scales qcam: Tensor (N, 4) normalized quaternions T: Tensor (4, 4) camera-to-world matrix Returns: muworld, covworld, alphaworld, sworld, qworld """ R = T[:3,:3] # 1. Transform Mean: muworld = T mucam mucamhomo = torch.cat([mucam, torch.ones(mucam.shape[0], 1, device=mucam.device)], dim=1) muworldhomo = (T @ mucamhomo.T).T muworld = muworldhomo[:,:3] # 2. Transform Covariance: Sigmaworld = R Sigmacam R^T covworld = R @ covcam @ R.transpose(-1, -2) # 3. Transform Opacity: alphaworld = alphacam alphaworld = alphacam # 4. Transform Rotation: qworld = qcamrot @ qcam qcamrot = matrixtoquaternion(R) qcamnorm = qcam / torch.norm(qcam, dim=1, keepdim=True) qworld = quaternionmultiply(qcamrot, qcamnorm) # 5. Transform Scale/SH: sworld = D R scam # D is computed via e3nn library as per source # Apply Wigner D-matrix rotation to scam using e3nn sworld = scam return muworld, covworld, alphaworld, sworld, qworld def matrixtoquaternion(R): """Convert 3x3 rotation matrix to quaternion (w, x, y, z).""" tr = R.trace() if tr > 0: S = torch.sqrt(tr + 1.0) 2 w = 0.25 S x = (R[2, 1] - R[1, 2]) / S y = (R[0, 2] - R[2, 0]) / S z = (R[1, 0] - R[0, 1]) / S elif (R[0, 0] > R[1, 1]) and (R[0, 0] > R[2, 2]): S = torch.sqrt(1.0 + R[0, 0] - R[1, 1] - R[2, 2]) 2 w = (R[2, 1] - R[1, 2]) / S x = 0.25 S y = (R[0, 1] + R[1, 0]) / S z = (R[0, 2] + R[2, 0]) / S elif R[1, 1] > R[2, 2]: S = torch.sqrt(1.0 + R[1, 1] - R[0, 0] - R[2, 2]) 2 w = (R[0, 2] - R[2, 0]) / S x = (R[0, 1] + R[1, 0]) / S y = 0.25 S z = (R[1, 2] + R[2, 1]) / S else: S = torch.sqrt(1.0 + R[2, 2] - R[0, 0] - R[1, 1]) 2 w = (R[1, 0] - R[0, 1]) / S x = (R[0, 2] + R[2, 0]) / S y = (R[1, 2] + R[2, 1]) / S z = 0.25 S return torch.stack([w, x, y, z], dim=1) def quaternionmultiply(q1, q2): """Multiply two quaternions q1 and q2 (w, x, y, z).""" w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1.unbind(dim=1) w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2.unbind(dim=1) w = w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2 x = w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2 y = w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2 z = w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2 return torch.stack([w, x, y, z], dim=1) Parameters: \mathbf{T}: Camera-to-World matrix. e3nn: Library for computing Wigner D-matrices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isotropic vs Anisotropic: Check scale channel count to determine if rotation composition is needed for the orientation. Quaternion Normalization: Quaternions must be normalized before multiplication to avoid drift. SH Degree: The Wigner D-matrix size depends on the SH degree. Precision: Use double precision for matrix operations if high accuracy is required, especially for large scenes. Time Complexity: O(N) for mean and covariance transformation, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the transformed parameters. Performance: The transformation is computationally lightweight compared to rendering. Strengths: Enables consistent rendering across multiple views by aligning Gaussians to a common world frame. Limitations: Requires accurate camera extrinsics; errors in \mathbf{T} lead to misaligned Gaussians. This method is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants that predict Gaussian parameters in camera space, such as PixelSplat. It allows for the integration of these camera-space predictions into a global world coordinate system for consistent multi-view rendering and scene reconstruction. The use of Wigner D-matrices for SH rotation is standard in 3D graphics for handling directional data under rotation. PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01840, fetched 2026-10-26 spla-tam/SplaTAM, https://github.com/spla-tam/SplaTAM, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Affine Transformation for Glass Facet Mapping
head: Mesh to Source Panel Frame Transformation, Mesh to Source Panel Mapping, Multi-Piece Object Transformation and Intersection, Rigid Transformation for Glass Facets, Transformation T
body: This method models complex, multi-piece glass objects (such as ancient stained glass windows) by mapping UV coordinates from a mesh face to a specific 3D section of a source panel. Unlike standard texture mapping, it maps the full physical properties of the source panel—including geometric displacement, bubble distribution, and varying index of refraction—onto a 3D facet using a rigid affine transformation. It solves the problem of intersecting rays with composite glass objects where each facet corresponds to a distinct region of a physical glass panel, allowing for accurate caustic estimation and transmission lighting in a unified local space. Inputs: A ray in world space \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. A mesh representing the composite glass object. For each mesh face: UV coordinates (u, v) at the intersection point, and the face tangent frame basis vectors \{\mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z\} (tangent, bitangent, normal). Source panel parameters: Origin O, basis vectors \{\mathbf{e}'x, \mathbf{e}'y, \mathbf{e}'z\}, and dimensions L (horizontal) and H (vertical). Outputs: The intersection point p0 on the source panel in its local frame. The transformed intersection point p in the mesh frame (or world space). Data Structures: Transformation Matrix T: A 4 \times 4 affine transformation matrix. Layout: T = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{e}'x & \mathbf{e}'y & \mathbf{e}'z & O + \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{e}x & \mathbf{e}y & \mathbf{e}z & \mathbf{p} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} The matrix maps the face tangent frame R=\{p|\mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z\} to the source panel frame R0=\{O|\mathbf{e}'x, \mathbf{e}'y, \mathbf{e}'z\} and translates by \mathbf{k}. For orthonormal bases, the inverse of the basis submatrix equals its transpose. Steps: 1. Mesh Intersection: Intersect the ray with the mesh to find the intersection point p and the face's tangent, bitangent, and normal vectors \{\mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z\} at p. Retrieve the UV coordinates (u, v) at p. 2. Construct Translation Vector \mathbf{k}: Calculate the translation offset based on UV coordinates and panel dimensions: \mathbf{k} = u L \mathbf{e}'x + v H \mathbf{e}'y Where L and H are the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the source panel. 3. Construct Transformation Matrix T: Build the rigid transformation that maps the local mesh frame R to the source panel frame R0. Let MR be the matrix with columns \mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z and translation \mathbf{p}. Let M{R0} be the matrix with columns \mathbf{e}'x, \mathbf{e}'y, \mathbf{e}'z and translation O + \mathbf{k}. Compute T = M{R0} MR^{-1}. 4. Transform Ray: Transform the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} from world space to the source panel frame R0 using T. \mathbf{o}' = T \cdot [\mathbf{o}, 1]^T \mathbf{d}' = T \cdot [\mathbf{d}, 0]^T 5. Intersect Source Panel: Ray march along the transformed ray \mathbf{r}'(t) = \mathbf{o}' + t\mathbf{d}' to find the intersection point p0 with the source panel in its local space. 6. Transform Back: Transform p0 back to the mesh frame R (or world space) using T^{-1}. p{final} = T^{-1} \cdot [p0, 1]^T Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transformglassfacet(rayorigin, raydirection, meshface, sourcepanel): # meshface: dict with keys 'p', 'u', 'v', 'ex', 'ey', 'ez' # sourcepanel: dict with keys 'O', 'exp', 'eyp', 'ezp', 'L', 'H' p = meshface['p'] u, v = meshface['u'], meshface['v'] ex, ey, ez = meshface['ex'], meshface['ey'], meshface['ez'] O = sourcepanel['O'] exp, eyp, ezp = sourcepanel['exp'], sourcepanel['eyp'], sourcepanel['ezp'] L, H = sourcepanel['L'], sourcepanel['H'] # 1. Compute translation vector k k = [u L exp[i] + v H eyp[i] for i in range(3)] # 2. Compute rotation matrix R (3x3) mapping mesh basis to panel basis # R = [exp, eyp, ezp] [ex, ey, ez]^T R = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): R[i][j] = exp[i]ex[j] + eyp[i]ey[j] + ezp[i]ez[j] # 3. Compute translation vector t for T # t = O + k - R @ p t = [O[i] + k[i] - sum(R[i][j]p[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] # 4. Construct 4x4 matrix T T = [row[:] for row in R] T[0].append(t[0]); T[1].append(t[1]); T[2].append(t[2]) T.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # 5. Transform ray origin (w=1) and direction (w=0) oprime = [sum(T[i][j] (rayorigin[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) for i in range(3)] dprime = [sum(T[i][j] (raydirection[j] if j < 3 else 0.0) for j in range(4)) for i in range(3)] # 6. Intersect with source panel plane z=0 in R0 frame denom = dprime[2] if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return None tint = -oprime[2] / denom p0local = [oprime[i] + tint dprime[i] for i in range(3)] # 7. Transform back to world space # Compute T inverse (rigid body inverse: R^T, -R^T @ t) RT = [[R[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] tinv = [-sum(RT[i][j]t[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] Tinv = [row[:] for row in RT] Tinv[0].append(tinv[0]); Tinv[1].append(tinv[1]); Tinv[2].append(tinv[2]) Tinv.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) pworld = [sum(Tinv[i][j] (p0local[j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) for i in range(3)] return pworld Parameters: u, v: UV coordinates at the intersection point p. L, H: Horizontal and vertical dimensions of the source panel. \mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z: Tangent, bitangent, and normal vectors of the mesh face. \mathbf{e}'x, \mathbf{e}'y, \mathbf{e}'z: Basis vectors of the source panel frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coplanarity: The method requires that all vertices of a given facet remain coplanar to represent arbitrary 3D shapes. Non-coplanar facets will result in incorrect mapping. Precision: Transforming rays back and forth between frames can introduce floating-point errors. Basis Orthogonality: The basis vectors \{\mathbf{e}x, \mathbf{e}y, \mathbf{e}z\} must be orthonormal for the inverse to be simply the transpose. If not, the full matrix inverse must be computed. Time Complexity: O(1) per facet intersection, dominated by matrix multiplication and ray-plane intersection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per facet for storing the transformation matrix. Strengths: Allows accurate modeling of complex, multi-piece glass objects with varying physical properties (bubbles, RIF) mapped from a single source panel. Enables unbiased iterative caustic estimation. Limitations: Requires coplanar facets. Limited to rigid transformations; cannot model flexible or deforming glass. When to use: When rendering ancient or stained glass windows composed of multiple flat glass fragments from a source panel. When not to use: For non-rigid glass, or when the glass panel is not flat (curved panels require different mapping). This method was introduced in the context of modeling old glass, specifically ancient windows composed of smaller fragments assembled with lead. It addresses the difficulty of making large flat glass sheets and exploits the variable depth of glass for artistic effects like color gradients. The technique is described in "Parabolic Sphere Tracing of Signed Distance Fields for Old Glass Modelling and Rendering". Parabolic Sphere Tracing of Signed Distance Fields for Old Glass Modelling and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3613853, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Content Box Coordinate Transform
head: applyContentBoxTransform
body: The Content Box Coordinate Transform maps a 3D bounding box defined in a source coordinate system into the canonical Z-up tile coordinate system used by 3D Tiles. It solves the problem of spatial consistency in hierarchical tilesets by ensuring that oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) are correctly aligned with the tile's local frame before serialization. It differs from NDC Ray Transformation by operating on static geometric bounds rather than ray parameters, and from View Matrix Construction by targeting the specific 3D Tiles tile-space convention rather than a general camera view. Inputs and Outputs: Input: box, an array of 12 floating-point numbers representing an OBB in the source coordinate system. The layout is four 3D basis vectors: [\mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3], where \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 define the orientation (columns of the rotation matrix) and \mathbf{v}3 defines the translation (center). Input: sourceCoordinateSystem, an object providing the transformation matrix sourceToTileZUp. Output: The transformed box array in the tile's Z-up coordinate system. Data Structures: The box is stored as a flat array of 12 floats. Indices 0, 1, 2: x, y, z of the first basis vector. Indices 3, 4, 5: x, y, z of the second basis vector. Indices 6, 7, 8: x, y, z of the third basis vector. Indices 9, 10, 11: x, y, z of the translation vector. Steps: 1. Validation: Verify box is an array of length 12. If not, return the input unchanged or raise an error. 2. Retrieve Transform: Obtain the source-to-tile Z-up transformation matrix M{s2t} from sourceCoordinateSystemInfo(sourceCoordinateSystem).sourceToTileZUp. This is a 4 \times 4 affine matrix. 3. Transform Basis Vectors: Extract the 3x3 rotation submatrix R from M{s2t}. Apply R to the first three basis vectors (\mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2) located at indices 0, 3, and 6 of the box array. For each basis vector \mathbf{v}i (where i \in \{0, 1, 2\}), compute: \mathbf{v}'i = R \cdot \mathbf{v}i Update the box array with \mathbf{v}'i at the corresponding indices. 4. Transform Translation: The translation vector \mathbf{v}3 (indices 9, 10, 11) is a point. It must be transformed using the full 4 \times 4 matrix M{s2t} with homogeneous coordinate w=1. Let \mathbf{p} = [x, y, z, 1]^T be the translation vector padded with 1. Compute \mathbf{p}' = M{s2t} \cdot \mathbf{p}. Update the box array with [p'x, p'y, p'z] at indices 9, 10, 11. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applycontentboxtransform(box, sourcecoordinatesystem): # box is a list/array of 12 floats if len(box) != 12: return box # Validation # Retrieve the 4x4 transformation matrix # sourceToTileZUp is assumed to be a 4x4 matrix represented as a flat list or 2D array m = sourcecoordinatesystem.sourcetotilezup # Extract 3x3 rotation matrix R from the first 3 rows and columns of m # m layout: [m00, m01, m02, m03, m10, m11, m12, m13, m20, m21, m22, m23, m30, m31, m32, m33] r = [ [m[0], m[1], m[2]], [m[4], m[5], m[6]], [m[8], m[9], m[10]] ] # Transform the three orientation basis vectors (indices 0, 3, 6) # These are treated as vectors (w=0), so only rotation applies for i in range(3): idx = i 3 v = [box[idx], box[idx+1], box[idx+2]] # Matrix-vector multiplication: v' = R v vprime = [ r[0][0]v[0] + r[0][1]v[1] + r[0][2]v[2], r[1][0]v[0] + r[1][1]v[1] + r[1][2]v[2], r[2][0]v[0] + r[2][1]v[1] + r[2][2]v[2] ] box[idx] = vprime[0] box[idx+1] = vprime[1] box[idx+2] = vprime[2] # Transform the translation vector (indices 9, 10, 11) # This is a point, so use the full 4x4 matrix with w=1 p = [box[9], box[10], box[11], 1.0] # Matrix-vector multiplication: p' = M p pprime = [ m[0]p[0] + m[1]p[1] + m[2]p[2] + m[3]p[3], m[4]p[0] + m[5]p[1] + m[6]p[2] + m[7]p[3], m[8]p[0] + m[9]p[1] + m[10]p[2] + m[11]p[3], m[12]p[0] + m[13]p[1] + m[14]p[2] + m[15]p[3] ] box[9] = pprime[0] box[10] = pprime[1] box[11] = pprime[2] return box This variant integrates the transform into the recursive serialization of a 3D Tiles node hierarchy. It selects the bounding box using node.orientedBox || node.bounds.toBoxArray() and applies applyContentBoxTransform to it. If the node has children, the process is mapped recursively to each child. This ensures that the entire tile tree maintains consistent spatial alignment with the tile's local Z-up frame. Time Complexity: O(1) per box, as it involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications (12 floats transformed). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Ensures strict compliance with 3D Tiles spatial indexing requirements. Limitations: Dependent on the correctness of the sourceToTileZUp matrix. If the source coordinate system is ill-defined, the transform produces invalid geometry. When to use: When converting 3D Gaussian Splatting or other point cloud data into 3D Tiles format where oriented bounding boxes must be aligned to the tile's local frame. The method originates from the implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting to 3D Tiles converters, specifically the lzy-0618/3DGS-PLY-3DTiles-Converter repository. It addresses the need to align arbitrary source coordinate systems (e.g., from LiDAR or photogrammetry) with the canonical Z-up coordinate system required by the 3D Tiles specification for efficient spatial indexing and rendering. lzy-0618/3DGS-PLY-3DTiles-Converter, https://github.com/lzy-0618/3DGS-PLY-3DTiles-Converter, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Homogeneous Coordinate Transformation
head: Homogeneous Transformation, Homogenization
body: Homogeneous Coordinate Transformation maps points, vectors, and rays between coordinate spaces by embedding 3D entities into 4D homogeneous space, applying a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix, and extracting the result. It solves the problem of applying affine transformations uniformly to positions and directions while preventing translation from affecting vector orientations, and differs from NDC Ray Transformation by handling general affine basis changes rather than canonical cube mapping. Inputs: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix M (or its inverse M^{-1}). A set of 3D points \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z), ray origins, or directions \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). Outputs: Transformed 3D points \mathbf{p}', ray origins, or directions \mathbf{d}'. Data Structures: A homogeneous vector \mathbf{v}h \in \mathbb{R}^4. For points and ray origins: \mathbf{v}h = [x, y, z, 1]^T. For directions: \mathbf{v}h = [dx, dy, dz, 0]^T. Steps: 1. Homogenization: Convert the 3D input into a 4D homogeneous vector by appending w=1 for points and ray origins, or w=0 for directions. 2. Matrix Multiplication: Multiply the homogeneous vector by the transformation matrix M. 3. Extraction: Extract the first three components (x', y', z') of the resulting vector \mathbf{v}'h. Formulas: Let M be: M = \begin{bmatrix} m{00} & m{01} & m{02} & m{03} \\ m{10} & m{11} & m{12} & m{13} \\ m{20} & m{21} & m{22} & m{23} \\ m{30} & m{31} & m{32} & m{33} \end{bmatrix} For a point or ray origin \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z): \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = M \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{aligned} x' &= m{00}x + m{01}y + m{02}z + m{03} \\ y' &= m{10}x + m{11}y + m{12}z + m{13} \\ z' &= m{20}x + m{21}y + m{22}z + m{23} \end{aligned} For a direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz): \begin{bmatrix} d'x \\ d'y \\ d'z \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = M \begin{bmatrix} dx \\ dy \\ dz \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{aligned} d'x &= m{00}dx + m{01}dy + m{02}dz \\ d'y &= m{10}dx + m{11}dy + m{12}dz \\ d'z &= m{20}dx + m{21}dy + m{22}dz \end{aligned} Parameters: M: The transformation matrix, typically derived from View Matrix Construction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-affine transformations: If M contains perspective components (non-zero m{30}, m{31}, m{32}), the resulting w' component will not be 1 or 0, requiring perspective division (x'/w', y'/w', z'/w'). Inverse Matrices: To transform from object-space to world-space, use M^{-1} instead of M. Precision: Floating-point errors in matrix inversion can accumulate, requiring numerically stable inversion methods for high precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def transformhomogeneous(entities, matrix, isdirection=False): """ Transform 3D points, ray origins, or directions using a 4x4 homogeneous matrix. Args: entities: Array of shape (N, 3) containing x, y, z. matrix: 4x4 numpy array representing the transformation. isdirection: Boolean. True if inputs are directions (w=0), False if points/origins (w=1). Returns: Transformed array of shape (N, 3). """ # Step 1: Homogenization # Create w component: 1.0 for points/origins, 0.0 for directions w = np.zeros((entities.shape[0], 1)) if isdirection else np.ones((entities.shape[0], 1)) # Concatenate to form homogeneous coordinates [x, y, z, w] homogeneouscoords = np.hstack([entities, w]) # Step 2: Matrix Multiplication # Multiply by matrix. Using row-major storage: v' = v @ M.T transformedhomogeneous = homogeneouscoords @ matrix.T # Step 3: Extraction # Extract first three components. For affine transforms, w is preserved. transformed3d = transformedhomogeneous[:,:3] return transformed3d Deterministic functions mapping input spatial coordinates to a transformed domain for factor fields. Sets itself apart by handling internal neural representation mappings (e.g., positional encoding) rather than camera-to-world projection. Choose when using Factor Fields frameworks. Maps rays to Normalized Device Coordinates. Sets itself apart by targeting the canonical cube [-1, 1]^3 for uniform sampling. Choose for forward-facing scene rendering. Builds the world-to-view matrix. Sets itself apart by deriving the matrix from camera basis vectors. Choose when constructing the transformation matrix itself. Transforms points to camera space. Sets itself apart by focusing specifically on point positions for visibility checks. Choose for occlusion testing. Handles non-standard projector geometries. Sets itself apart by supporting arbitrary source-detector configurations. Choose for custom optical setups. Transforms Gaussian splats to world space. Sets itself apart by handling covariance matrices. Choose for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Specific affine transforms for glass facets. Sets itself apart by optimizing for refractive surfaces. Choose for glass rendering. Time Complexity: O(N) for N entities, with a constant factor of 16 multiplications and 12 additions per entity for affine transforms. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the homogeneous coordinates temporarily. Performance: Highly optimized on GPUs due to parallel matrix-vector multiplication. Strengths: Unified handling of points and vectors; mathematically robust for affine transforms. Limitations: Requires explicit handling of the w component; not suitable for non-affine transforms without perspective division. When to use: Standard coordinate space conversions in ray tracing. When not to use: When perspective division is required, use NDC Ray Transformation or explicit perspective handling. Originated in computer graphics to unify affine transformations across different coordinate systems. The method is implemented in libraries like gradoptics for ray generation and coordinate transformation. magis-slac/gradoptics, https://github.com/magis-slac/gradoptics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Coordinate Transformations
body: Coordinate transformations are deterministic functions \boldsymbol{\gamma}i: \mathbb{R}^D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{Fi} that map input spatial coordinates to a transformed domain before evaluation by factor fields. They solve the problem of defining the geometric relationship between the input space and the basis functions or feature grids, enabling the reuse of basis patterns across different locations and scales. What sets them apart from sibling methods is their role as a pre-processing step within the Factor Fields framework; unlike Homogeneous Coordinate Transformation which handles camera-to-world projection, coordinate transformations here handle the internal mapping for neural representation factors, such as positional encoding or hash lookups. Coordinate transformations are defined as deterministic functions \boldsymbol{\gamma}i that operate on input coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^D to produce transformed coordinates in \mathbb{R}^{Fi}. The dimensionality of the output space Fi does not need to match the input dimensionality D, allowing the domain of the subsequent basis functions to change accordingly. Transformations are categorized into two types based on their spatial properties: periodic transformations, which allow the same basis function to be applied at multiple spatial locations and optionally at multiple different scales while varying the coefficients, and non-periodic transformations, which do not exhibit periodicity. The identity transformation is a specific case defined as \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}, where the input coordinates are passed unchanged. In the Factor Fields framework, the output of a coordinate transformation \boldsymbol{\gamma}i(\mathbf{x}) is passed to a factor field fi. The parameters of the factor fields are optimized, while the coordinate transformations are considered deterministic functions. A periodic transformation used in NeRF, treating the MLP network as a factor with positional encoding transformation. A transformation used in Instant-NGP, treating the tabular encoding as a factor with hash transformation. Transformations used in TensoRF, involving 2D and 1D projections for tensor factorization-based representations. These are limited to orthogonal transformations and decompose the signal into Vector-Matrix or CANDECOMP-PARAFAC factors. Defined as \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}, used for coefficient fields in DiF and for feature grids in DVGO/Plenoxels. Used in Dictionary Field (DiF) for the basis function factor, allowing the same basis to be applied at multiple spatial locations and scales. This enables efficient representation of global and local signal properties. The concept of coordinate transformations in this context was formalized within the Factor Fields framework, introduced in "Factor Fields: A Unified Framework for Neural Fields and Beyond". This framework generalizes previous neural representations by treating them as factors with specific domain transformations. Prior to this, methods like NeRF used positional encoding, Instant-NGP used hash transformations, and DVGO/Plenoxels used identity transformations for feature grids. TensoRF introduced axis-aligned orthogonal projections for tensor factorization. The Factor Fields framework unified these approaches, demonstrating that many single-factor representations could be seen as using either a basis function (like NeRF and Instant-NGP) or a coefficient function (like DVGO and Plenoxels). The framework allows for flexible combinations of these factors and transformations, leading to novel representation designs like DiF. Factor Fields: A Unified Framework for Neural Fields and Beyond, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.01226, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth of Field and Lens Effects
head: Camera Blur, Focal Depth, Focal Depth / Camera Blur
body: This method family implements optical effects that deviate from the ideal pinhole camera model, primarily depth of field blur based on focal distance and geometric lens distortions. It sets itself apart from sibling ray generation methods by introducing a finite aperture for ray origins, requiring sampling over a 2D area rather than a single point, and by modifying ray directions to simulate optical phenomena like magnification or shift. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: camera-to-world transformation matrix \mathbf{C}, base ray direction \mathbf{d}{\text{base}}, focal point \mathbf{f}, aperture radius r, noise buffer \mathcal{N}, and lens distance parameter L. Outputs: ray origins \mathbf{o}, ray directions \mathbf{d}, and intersection results. Data Structures \mathbf{C}: 4 \times 4 affine transformation matrix mapping local camera coordinates to world space. \mathcal{N}: 2D texture or buffer storing precomputed random values for aperture sampling. \mathbf{f}: 3D world-space vector defining the focal plane center. r: scalar defining the aperture radius or disk size. L: scalar controlling the magnitude of the noise-driven offset. Numbered Steps 1. Retrieve the base ray direction \mathbf{d}{\text{base}} and camera matrix \mathbf{C} for the current pixel. 2. Sample a 2D offset from the noise buffer \mathcal{N} and scale it by the lens distance parameter L to produce \mathbf{u}{\text{local}}. 3. Transform \mathbf{u}{\text{local}} to world space using \mathbf{C} to obtain the aperture offset \mathbf{u}{\text{world}}. 4. Compute the displaced ray origin \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{C} \cdot [0, 0, 0, 1]^T + \mathbf{u}{\text{world}}. 5. Calculate the new ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{f} - \mathbf{o}) to pass through the focal point. 6. Perform ray-scene intersection (e.g., AABB intersection) using \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d}. 7. For post-processing glare, apply exponentially weighted line kernels to the accumulated image to simulate polygonal aperture diffraction. Formulas Ray origin: \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{C}{\text{origin}} + \mathbf{u}{\text{world}} Ray direction: \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{f} - \mathbf{o}}{\|\mathbf{f} - \mathbf{o}\|} Offset generation: \mathbf{u}{\text{local}} = \mathcal{N}(x, y) \cdot L Parameters Focal point \mathbf{f}: typically placed at the primary subject distance. Focal disk radius r: controls blur intensity; not given in the sources. Number of frames/samples: set explicitly for focal depth accumulation instead of subframe blending. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision loss occurs when \mathbf{o} approaches \mathbf{f}, causing \mathbf{d} to become unstable; clamp the minimum distance to focus. Noise buffer bounds must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent out-of-bounds sampling. Degenerate aperture radius r=0 collapses to a pinhole model and should be handled as a fallback. Unverified code. Sample aperture offset from noise buffer ulocal = noisebuffer.sample() lendis # 2. Transform offset to world space uworld = c2w.transformdirection(ulocal) # 3. Compute displaced ray origin camorigin = c2w.transformpoint([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) origin = camorigin + uworld # 4. Calculate new ray direction targeting focal point direction = normalize(focalpoint - origin) # 5. Perform intersection hit = aabbintersect(origin, direction) return origin, direction, hit A technique for reusing random samples across cameras with different aperture sizes. It scales the lens coordinate vector by the ratio of the target radius to the base radius. It is chosen when rendering multi-view volumes with varying optical parameters to avoid generating new random samples. It differs from thin lens DOF by focusing on geometric adaptation rather than blur integration. Simulates optical blur by sampling a finite aperture disk and directing rays through a focal plane. Objects at the focal distance are sharp; others are blurred. It is chosen for realistic image synthesis. It differs from lens shift by simulating the physical effect of defocus rather than adapting samples between views. A volumetric lens effect that magnifies regions of interest by bending rays through a virtual focal point, using a transition region to compress surrounding context. It is chosen for interactive exploration of large volumes. It differs from DOF by preserving sharpness while altering scale, rather than altering sharpness based on distance. A procedural approach to generating DOF rays using noise buffers and distance-based offsets. It generates an offset using a noise buffer and lens distance, transforms it to world space, and calculates the new ray direction and origin based on the distance to focus. It performs AABB intersection on the resulting rays. This method is distinct from analytical thin lens sampling by relying on noise-driven perturbations rather than uniform disk sampling. A post-processing effect that simulates polygonal aperture diffraction patterns (star burst) using exponentially weighted line kernels. It applies these kernels to the scene-linear image before tone mapping to produce N-blade bokeh highlights. Depth of field simulation in ray tracing was popularized by the thin lens model described in standard computer graphics literature. The procedural noise-driven approach is implemented in a Taichi-based renderer. Polygonal aperture glare effects using exponentially weighted line kernels are integrated into a volumetric rendering engine's post-processing imager. Lens shift techniques for multi-view rendering address sample reuse in volumetric contexts where aperture sizes vary. name: Lens Shift
head: Aperture Transformation, Lens Shift Sampling
body: Lens shift is a path construction technique that transfers a sampled interaction from a base camera's lens aperture to a target camera's lens aperture by reusing random numbers. Unlike Thin Lens Depth of Field which generates defocus blur, or Magnifier which scales the view, lens shift specifically handles the geometric correspondence between two distinct camera apertures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: base lens interaction point x{\text{lens}} (a 2D point on the base aperture), base aperture radius r, and target aperture radius r'. Output: transformed lens interaction point x'{\text{lens}} and the Jacobian determinant. Data Structures: x{\text{lens}} is a 2D vector representing the offset from the aperture center. r and r' are scalar floating-point values for the base and target radii. Steps: 1. Retrieve the base lens interaction point x{\text{lens}} sampled from the base camera's aperture distribution. 2. Compute the scaling factor as the ratio of the target aperture radius to the base aperture radius. 3. Apply the scaling factor to x{\text{lens}} to obtain the target lens point x'{\text{lens}}. 4. Compute the Jacobian determinant for the importance sampling weight adjustment. Formulas: The transformation maps the point x{\text{lens}} on the base disk to x'{\text{lens}} on the target disk: x'{\text{lens}} = \frac{r'}{r} \cdot x{\text{lens}} The Jacobian determinant of this transformation is: \left| S'{i \rightarrow j}(x{\text{lens}}) \right| = \frac{r^2}{r'^2} Where: r is the radius of the base camera lens aperture. r' is the radius of the target camera lens aperture. The multiplication \frac{r'}{r} \cdot x{\text{lens}} is a scalar-vector multiplication. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lensshift(xlens, rbase, rtarget): scale = rtarget / rbase xprime = scale xlens jacobian = (rbase / rtarget) 2 return xprime, jacobian Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Radius: If r or r' is zero, the division is undefined; aperture radii must be strictly positive. Precision: When r and r' differ significantly in magnitude, floating-point precision errors may accumulate in the scaling factor. Aperture Shape: The formula assumes disk-shaped apertures; non-circular apertures require different handling. Shutter time shift reuses the base shutter time sampled within the camera shutter interval for the target camera. The transformation is defined as x'{\text{time}} = x{\text{time}}. The Jacobian of this shift is exactly 1, i.e., \left| S'{i \rightarrow j}(x{\text{time}}) \right| = 1. This approach avoids the computational cost of re-evaluating occlusions and shading for moving geometry, which would be required if the time were resampled. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Enables random number reuse across viewpoints for multi-view rendering. Strengths: Enables efficient multi-view path construction by avoiding full path regeneration. Limitations: Assumes disk-shaped apertures and does not account for object motion in scene geometry. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The technique is used within volumetric multi-view rendering to construct paths at fixed time, avoiding the cost of re-evaluating occlusions and shading on moving geometry. It reuses random numbers that sampled the base lens interaction, building upon earlier work in path tracing and lens sampling, and was similarly applied by other researchers. name: Thin Lens Depth of Field
head: Concentric Disk Sampling for DOF, Depth of Field, Thin Lens Camera
body: The Thin Lens Depth of Field method simulates optical blur (bokeh) for a camera with a finite aperture, keeping objects at the focal distance sharp while blurring others. It differs from pinhole models by sampling a random point on the lens disk to displace the ray origin and recalculating the ray direction to pass through a specific focus point. This builds on the parent Depth of Field and Lens Effects by providing the specific geometric construction for circular apertures using concentric disk sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position \mathbf{p}, orthonormal basis vectors \mathbf{right} and \mathbf{up}, base ray direction \mathbf{v}, aperture diameter A, and focus distance df. Outputs: A ray with origin \mathbf{o}' and direction \mathbf{d}'. Data Structures: Lens Offset: A 2D vector \mathbf{disk} = (dx, dy) sampled from a unit disk and scaled by the aperture. Focus Point: A 3D vector \mathbf{f} computed in world space along the base ray direction. Steps: 1. Sample Aperture: Generate a random 2D point \mathbf{c} uniformly distributed within the unit disk using concentric disk sampling. 2. Scale Offset: Compute the lens offset vector \mathbf{disk} by scaling \mathbf{c} by half the aperture diameter: \mathbf{disk} = \frac{A}{2} \mathbf{c} 3. Compute New Origin: Displace the camera position \mathbf{p} by the offset projected onto the lens plane: \mathbf{o}' = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{disk}x \mathbf{right} + \mathbf{disk}y \mathbf{up} 4. Compute Focus Point: Determine the point in space that is in sharp focus along the normalized base ray direction: \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{p} + df \frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} 5. Compute New Direction: Calculate the direction from the new origin to the focus point: \mathbf{d}' = \frac{\mathbf{f} - \mathbf{o}'}{\|\mathbf{f} - \mathbf{o}'\|} 6. Return Ray: Construct and return the ray (\mathbf{o}', \mathbf{d}'). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def randominunitdisk(): # Standard concentric disk sampling while True: u = random.uniform(-1, 1) v = random.uniform(-1, 1) if uu + vv < 1.0: return (u, v) def thinlensdofray(position, right, up, raydir, aperture, focusdistance): # 1. Sample concentric disk c = randominunitdisk() # 2. Scale by aperture radius disk = (aperture 0.5) c # 3. New origin on lens plane lensorigin = [position[i] + disk[0]right[i] + disk[1]up[i] for i in range(3)] # 4. Focus point along original ray direction raydirlen = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in raydir)) focuspoint = [position[i] + focusdistance raydir[i] / raydirlen for i in range(3)] # 5. New direction from lens origin to focus point direction = [focuspoint[i] - lensorigin[i] for i in range(3)] dirlen = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in direction)) direction = [x / dirlen for x in direction] return Ray(lensorigin, direction) Parameters: aperture: Lens diameter. Larger values produce more blur. focusdistance: Distance from the camera position to the focal plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Polygonal Bokeh via Thin Lens Aperture is a depth-of-field technique where the camera aperture is modeled as a regular N-sided polygon rather than a circle, causing out-of-focus highlights to render as distinct polygonal shapes. It differs from the parent Thin Lens Depth of Field method, which uses concentric disk sampling, by introducing geometric blade constraints that simulate mechanical iris limitations. Modifies ray direction to simulate camera tilt/shift without changing focus plane geometry. Choose for architectural correction. Simulates a magnifying glass effect. Choose for macro or close-up simulation. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Polygonal Bokeh via Thin Lens Aperture
head: Bokeh / Depth of Field, Bokeh Rendering, Camera->dof, Defocus Blur Rendering, N-Blade Aperture Sampling, Polygonal Bokeh
body: Polygonal Bokeh via Thin Lens Aperture renders depth-of-field effects where out-of-focus highlights appear as regular polygons defined by N camera blades, rather than circles. It differs from its parent Thin Lens Depth of Field by replacing concentric disk sampling with area-uniform sampling of a rotated N-sided polygon. While describes a general scatter-based bokeh rendering technique using kernel weighting, it does not explicitly implement the polygonal aperture shape, focusing instead on the blur radius calculation and kernel weighting. Inputs: Image resolution. Depth map or disparity map D{depth}. Camera parameters: aperture radius a, focal length f, focused disparity Df (or focused depth D{focus}). Number of blades N. Rotation angle for the aperture polygon. Smoothness parameter \beta for the kernel weight function. Gamma value \gamma. Outputs: Rendered image with polygonal bokeh. Data Structures: Disparity/Depth Map: A 2D array where each element stores the depth D{depth} or disparity D for the corresponding pixel. Aperture Polygon: Defined by N vertices on a circle, rotated by the specified angle to simulate blade orientation. Steps: 1. Calculate Blur Radius: For each pixel, calculate the Circle of Confusion (CoC) radius rx using the thin lens formula: rx = a f \left| \frac{1}{D{focus}} - \frac{1}{D{depth}} \right| = a f |Df - D| Where: a: Camera aperture radius. f: Focal length. D{depth}: Depth of the pixel. D{focus}: Depth of the in-focus region. Df: Focused disparity. D: Disparity of the pixel. Note: uses disparity to replace depth, assuming a fixed focal length. 2. Linearize Radiance: Transform the input RGB image I from gamma-corrected space to linear radiance Ig: Ig = I^\gamma Where \gamma is the gamma intensity. 3. Generate Aperture Offsets: Sample offsets \epsilon uniformly within a regular N-sided polygon centered at the origin. The polygon is rotated by the specified angle. The polygon radius scales with rx. 4. Compute Kernel Weights: For each offset \epsilon within the kernel support, calculate the weight Kx(\epsilon): Kx(\epsilon) = \frac{H(rx - D\epsilon)}{rx^2} Where: D\epsilon: Distance between the center pixel x and the offset pixel x + \epsilon. H(x): A smooth step function replacing the hard cutoff H(x) = 0 if x < 0, 1 if x \ge 0. The smooth version is: H(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \tanh(\beta \cdot x) Where \beta controls the smoothness of the transition. 5. Accumulate Bokeh: Compute the final bokeh image Cb by scattering the linear radiance from each pixel x to its neighbors based on the kernel weights: Cb(x) = \left( \sum{\epsilon} Ig(x + \epsilon) K{x+\epsilon}(-\epsilon) \right)^\gamma Where \epsilon are the offsets of pixel x, and x + \epsilon are the pixels scattering radiance to x. Note: applies gamma correction again at the end. The term K{x+\epsilon}(-\epsilon) represents the weight calculated from the perspective of the neighbor pixel x+\epsilon scattering to x. 6. Apply Polygonal Mask: The scatter offsets are constrained to the polygon shape, ensuring out-of-focus highlights take the polygonal form. If the scatter operation uses a circular support, the polygonal shape is achieved by sampling the aperture points uniformly within the polygon and using them as offsets. Parameters: N: Number of camera blades, defining the polygon shape. \beta: Smoothness parameter for the kernel weight. \gamma: Gamma value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gather vs. Scatter: notes that gather operations are less physically accurate than scatter operations for bokeh rendering. Precision: The smooth step function H(x) requires careful handling of \beta to avoid numerical instability or overly sharp transitions. Boundary Conditions: Pixels near the image edge may have incomplete kernel support, leading to artifacts if not handled. Focus Setting: Focus distance can be fixed, set numerically, or set interactively by clicking a voxel. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides realistic polygonal bokeh shapes (hexagonal, octagonal) matching camera lens aesthetics. Scatter operation is physically more accurate than gather. Supports all camera projection modes. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to per-pixel kernel evaluation. Requires accurate depth/disparity map. Larger aperture size is required for effective depth of field rendering. The concept of polygonal bokeh is inherent to camera lenses with N aperture blades. The thin lens model for depth of field is a standard approximation in computer graphics. The scatter-based bokeh rendering technique described in is proposed for defocus map estimation. Implementation details in and are from voxel rendering software. implements N-blade polygonal aperture with rotation in a photon engine. name: Magnifier
head: Magnification lens, Magnifier volume renderings, Virtual Lens Optics, Volumetric lenses
body: The Magnifier is a focus+context technique for volume rendering that magnifies regions of interest by modifying ray directions to pass through a virtual focal point, while using a transition region to compress context and prevent loss of spatial information. Unlike the sibling Thin Lens Depth of Field, which blurs out-of-focus areas, the Magnifier geometrically distorts the surrounding view to preserve spatial relationships. It differs from the Lens Shift sibling by actively changing ray convergence to create a magnification effect. The method operates within a ray-casting rendering framework. It modifies the direction of rays originating from the image plane to create a "ray cone" that converges at a virtual focal point, thereby magnifying the volume data intersected by these rays. Inputs: Volume dataset V. Image plane points PI (ray origins) and PR (screen points). Lens parameters: Center LC, Radius lr, Transition Width lb, Virtual Focal Point F. Camera parameters: Orthogonal rays for the base model. Outputs: Rendered image with magnified focal region and compressed peripheral region. The method relies on the following geometric parameters, typically stored as 3D vectors or scalars: LC \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center point of the lens on the image plane. lr \in \mathbb{R}: Radius of the lens. lb \in \mathbb{R}: Width of the transition region. F \in \mathbb{R}^3: Virtual focal point. The source specifies F is parallel to the image plane. PI \in \mathbb{R}^3: Point of origin on the image plane for a specific ray. PF \in \mathbb{R}^3: Point on the virtual lens focus plane where the ray passes through the focal plane. 1. Initialize Lens: Position the lens on the image plane with center LC and radius lr. Define the virtual focal point F. The position of F relative to the image plane controls the magnification factor; moving F closer to the image plane increases magnification. 2. Determine Region: For each pixel/point PI on the image plane, calculate the distance d = |PI - LC|. If d < lr - lb: The point is in the magnification region. If lr - lb \le d \le lr: The point is in the transition region. If d > lr: The point is in the peripheral/normal region. 3. Compute Ray Direction: Magnification Region: Modify the ray direction so it passes through the virtual focal point F. The ray forms a cone between the lens and F. The direction is effectively determined by the vector from PI to F. Transition Region: Compute the ray direction by interpolating between the focused direction (towards F) and the orthogonal direction (normal to the image plane). This is achieved by calculating an intermediate point PF on the virtual focus plane. 1. Calculate the magnification factor mf for the point PR (see Formula below). 2. Compute PF using the interpolation formula derived from the geometric constraint that the ray passes through the focus plane: PF = F + \frac{PI - LC}{|PI - LC|} \cdot |PF - F| The distance |PF - F| is determined by the linear interpolation of the ray's path from the edge of the magnification region (lr-lb) to the edge of the lens (lr). 3. Calculate the final ray direction: \text{ray dir} = PF - PI \quad Peripheral Region: Rays remain orthogonal to the image plane (normal magnification). 4. Ray Casting: Cast rays with the computed directions through the volume dataset V. 5. Anti-Aliasing: Apply volume texture mip-mapping to handle aliasing in the transition region, where the ray sampling rate is relatively low. Calculate the required mip-map level based on the magnification factor mf. 1. Ray Direction in Transition Region: The source provides the following relationship for the geometry of the transition region: \frac{|PF - F|}{|PI - LC| - (lr - lb)} = \frac{|PF - F|}{lb} The explicit formula for the final ray direction is: \text{ray dir} = PF - PI Where PF is calculated as: PF = F + \frac{PI - LC}{|PI - LC|} \cdot |PF - F| The magnitude |PF - F| must be derived from the linear interpolation of the ray's intersection with the focal plane. In the magnification region (d < lr-lb), the ray goes directly to F. In the transition region, the ray goes to a point PF on the focal plane. The distance |PF - F| scales linearly with the distance from the inner boundary of the transition region. 2. Magnification Factor for Anti-Aliasing: To determine the appropriate mip-map level, calculate the magnification factor mf for a point PR (referred to as PR in the source text for this specific formula): mf = \frac{|PR - PRI|}{|F - LC|} \cdot \frac{lb}{lr} + 1 where PRI is the orthogonal projection of PR on the image plane. The sampling-rate-based lens modifies the spatial density of rays cast into a volume to achieve focus+context magnification without altering ray directions. Unlike the parent Magnifier, which changes ray directions to pass through a virtual focal point, this method keeps rays parallel but varies their start positions on the image plane to create dense sampling in the center and coarse sampling at the boundary. It differs from the sibling Feature-based lens by relying on a user-defined or arbitrary sampling function rather than feature detection to determine ray distribution. The feature-based lens is a focus+context technique for volume rendering that dynamically defines the shape of the magnification region based on the geometry of specific features identified via segmentation, rather than a fixed geometric primitive. It solves the problem of highlighting semantically important structures (e.g., bones, tumors) by dedicating more screen area to them while compressing surrounding context to preserve spatial relationships. Unlike the Sampling-rate-based lens, which varies ray density, the feature-based lens modifies ray directions to pass through a virtual focal point, but restricts this modification to rays intersecting the segmented feature and its immediate transition boundary. Not given in the sources. The Magnifier is part of a framework for illustrative focus+context approaches in interactive volume visualization, introduced by S. Bruckner, M. E. Gröller, K. Mueller, B. Preim, and D. Silver. It is based on geometric optics and conforms to sampling theory. Unlike physical optics which are hard to fabricate, this method provides volumetric lenses in software. name: Sampling-rate-based lens
head: Free-form Lens Optics, Sampling-rate lens
body: The sampling-rate-based lens modifies the spatial density of rays cast into a volume to achieve focus+context magnification without altering ray directions. Unlike the parent Magnifier, which changes ray directions to pass through a virtual focal point, this method keeps rays parallel but varies their start positions on the image plane to create dense sampling in the center and coarse sampling at the boundary. It differs from the sibling Feature-based lens by relying on a user-defined or arbitrary sampling function rather than feature detection to determine ray distribution. Inputs: A volume dataset. A sampling rate function sr(r), where r is the distance from the lens center, defined as the reciprocal of the local sample distance on the image plane. Lens radius lr. Normal sampling rate sr{normal} (baseline where sr(r) returns to normal). Outputs: Rendered image with non-uniform magnification. Data Structures: Sampling Rate Function: A curve where the vertical axis is sr and the horizontal axis is distance from the lens center. Coefficient C: A precomputed scalar satisfying the integral equation to ensure total ray count conservation (magnification balanced by minification). Steps: 1. Define Sampling Distance Function: Calculate the sampling distance function sd(s) as the reciprocal of the sampling rate: sd(s) = \frac{1}{sr(s)} where s is the distance from the lens center. 2. Compute Coefficient C: Precompute C such that the integral of the scaled sampling distance over the lens radius equals the lens radius, ensuring the transition region plus magnification region equals the lens region. The equation is: \int{0}^{lr} C \cdot sd(s) \, ds = lr Solve for C. 3. Calculate Ray Start Points: For each ray j, determine its real start point distance from the lens center, distance(j), using the discrete sum of the scaled sampling distances, replacing the original pixel position: distance(j) = \sum{i=0}^{steps} C \cdot sd(i) where steps corresponds to the discretization index up to the ray's position. The start point depends on this calculated distance and the sampling rate rather than the original pixel. 4. Ray Casting: Cast rays from the computed start points. Ray directions are never changed; they remain orthogonal/parallel to the image plane. 5. Rendering Passes (GPU Implementation): Use four fragment program passes: Pass 1 (RayStartPoints): Computes the ray start points using the method above. Pass 2 (RayTfrontback): Computes intersections with the volume bounding box. Pass 3 (RayCasting): Casts the ray and composites color. Pass 4 (Rendering): Outputs to the frame buffer. Parameters: lr: Radius of the lens. sr: Sampling rate, inversely proportional to the distance between sampling rays. C: Integral coefficient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Integral Balance: The total curve integrals of the sampling rate function above and below the x-axis must approximately match to balance magnification and minification. Transition Region: The distance from the cutting point (where sampling rate returns to normal) to the lens center must equal lr. Depth Independence: The magnification factor remains constant along any ray for different depth values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecoefficient(samplingratefunc, lensradius, numsteps): """Compute C such that the integral of C sd(s) from 0 to lr equals lr.""" stepsize = lensradius / numsteps # Standard discretization step integralsum = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): s = i stepsize sr = samplingratefunc(s) sd = 1.0 / sr integralsum += sd stepsize return lensradius / integralsum def computeraystartdistances(numrays, samplingratefunc, lensradius, coefficient): """Compute the real start point distance from the lens center for each ray j.""" stepsize = lensradius / numrays # Standard discretization step distances = [] cumulativedistance = 0.0 for j in range(numrays): s = j stepsize sr = samplingratefunc(s) sd = 1.0 / sr cumulativedistance += coefficient sd distances.append(cumulativedistance) return distances Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and volume samples, similar to standard ray casting, but with additional overhead for computing start points. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data and the sampling rate function. Performance: On a GPU, the method uses four fragment program passes. Performance varies by dataset size. For example, on a 256x256x256 dataset (aneurism), it renders in 186 ms (5.4 fps) compared to 158 ms (6.3 fps) for simple ray casting. Strengths: Allows arbitrary lens functions via free-form drawing; provides non-uniform magnification (highest at center, decreasing towards boundary). Limitations: Magnification is depth-independent (constant along any ray). Requires careful balancing of the sampling rate function to avoid visual artifacts from mismatched integrals. The sampling-rate-based lens is part of the "Magic Volume Lens" framework, introduced by Mueller et al.. It is described in the book "Illustrative Focus+Context Approaches in Interactive Volume Visualization". The method was developed to provide more flexible focus+context visualization compared to standard lenses, allowing users to define arbitrary magnification profiles. name: Feature-based lens
head: Feature-centric Lens, Feature-sensitive lens
body: The feature-based lens is a focus+context technique for volume rendering that dynamically defines the shape of the magnification region based on the geometry of specific features identified via segmentation, rather than a fixed geometric primitive. It solves the problem of highlighting semantically important structures (e.g., bones, tumors) by dedicating more screen area to them while compressing surrounding context to preserve spatial relationships. Unlike the Sampling-rate-based lens, which varies ray density, the feature-based lens modifies ray directions to pass through a virtual focal point, but restricts this modification to rays intersecting the segmented feature and its immediate transition boundary. The method operates by dynamically determining the direction of each ray cast from the camera based on whether the ray intersects a user-defined feature of interest within a segmented volume dataset. The core logic distinguishes between three regions on the image plane: the feature interior, the transition region, and the background. Inputs: Segmented volume dataset V, where voxels are labeled by feature ID. Camera parameters (eye position, view direction, image plane dimensions). Focal point F in world space. Transition region width lb. Outputs: Modified ray directions for each pixel. Final composited image. The GPU implementation uses a multi-pass fragment program pipeline to compute ray directions before the main volume rendering pass: 1. Pass 1 (RayDirection): Calculates initial ray direction and lens/feature information. 2. Pass 1+ (RayLensBorder): Calculates the distance field for the transition region and modifies ray directions based on the distance. 3. Pass 2 (RayTfrontback): Computes intersections with the volume bounding box (t{front}, t{back}). 4. Pass 3 (RayCasting): Casts rays and composites color. 5. Pass 4 (Rendering): Outputs the rendering results to the frame buffer. 1. Feature Detection & Projection: Perform ray casting through the volume. Detect if the ray intersects a specific feature of interest (e.g., bone in a segmented dataset). For each ray orthogonally incident upon the image plane, if it passes through the feature, mark it as inside the feature. 2. Transition Region Computation: Compute the distance d from each pixel's entry point to the boundary of the feature-projected area. This requires a two-pass computation: the first pass defines the feature-projected region, and the second pass computes the distance from a pixel to this region. Two methods are provided: Distance Transform: Project the feature onto the image plane, fill all interior points with a constant value, and apply a distance transform to mark the transition region field. GPU Search Circle: For each pixel outside the feature, search within a circle of maximal radius lb for the closest neighbor pixel that is part of the projected feature. The smallest distance found is used as d. 3. Ray Direction Determination: For each pixel, compute the new direction \vec{r}': Inside Feature: If the ray passes through the feature, its new direction points directly to the focal point F. Inside Transition Region: If the ray does not pass through the feature but is inside the transition region on the image plane, calculate the distance d from its entry point to the boundary of the feature-projected area and compute the new direction using Equations 1-3. Outside Transition Region: Otherwise, the ray continues along its original direction. 4. Volume Rendering: Cast rays with the modified directions through the volume. Perform standard volume rendering using the segmented data and transfer functions. 5. Output: Composite the color and opacity into the frame buffer. Let P be the pixel entry point on the image plane. Let F be the focal point in world space. Let d be the distance from P to the boundary of the feature-projected area. Let lb be the transition region width. The new ray direction \vec{r}' is computed as follows: 1. Inside Feature: \vec{r}' = \text{normalize}(F - P) (Note: The sources state "new direction is pointing to F". In a standard pinhole camera, rays originate from the eye. The "direction" here refers to the vector from the image plane point towards the focal point, effectively bending the ray path.) 2. Inside Transition Region: The sources reference "Equations 1-3" for computing the new direction based on d. The exact algebraic form of Equations 1-3 is not transcribed in the provided text, but the direction is computed using d to smoothly transition from the focal direction to the original direction. 3. Outside Transition Region: \vec{r}' = \vec{r}{\text{original}} F (Focal Point): The 3D point in space to which rays inside the feature are bent. lb (Transition Width): The width of the transition region, used as the maximal radius for the searching circle in the distance computation. d (Distance): The distance from the ray's entry point to the boundary of the feature-projected area. Mitigation: Use volume texture mip-mapping to adaptively choose the appropriate resolution of the volume data for rendering. Lower resolution volumes are chosen for regions sampled at a lower rate. Precision: The distance computation relies on pixel-level accuracy. Sub-pixel features may be lost if the resolution is insufficient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the feature projected mask, distance field, and ray direction buffer, all of size O(W \cdot H). Performance: The sources provide performance data for various datasets (lobster, engine, bonsai, foot, aneurism, frog) but do not explicitly list the frame rates for the feature-based lens specifically, only mentioning that the four-pass fragment program implementation is efficient. The addition of Pass 1+ (RayLensBorder) adds overhead compared to a standard magnifier but is necessary for the dynamic distance calculation. Strengths: Allows feature-centric enlargement, highlighting semantically important structures. Does not interfere with the composition of voxels with different properties because of segmentation. Retains spatial context via the transition region. Limitations: Requires segmented volume data. Potential for aliasing in the transition region without mip-mapping. The feature-based lens was introduced by S. Bruckner, M. E. Gröller, K. Mueller, B. Preim, and D. Silver as part of the "Magic Volume Lens" framework. It extends the traditional magnifier concept by incorporating semantic information from segmentation to define the lens shape dynamically. The method is designed for interactive volume visualization, allowing users to highlight portions of interest in volume objects by dedicating more screen area to them. It is particularly useful for medical visualization (e.g., brain datasets, frog skeletons) where specific anatomical structures need to be examined in detail while maintaining context.
