name: Perfect Lens (Thin Lens Approximation)
body: The Perfect Lens method models a thin lens using the paraxial approximation to simulate depth of field effects in volume rendering. It maps incident rays from world space to a lens plane, intersects them with a defined plane of focus, and then refracts them through the optical center to a camera plane. This approach differs from sibling methods like Thin Lens Depth of Field by explicitly calculating the geometric intersection path through the lens center to determine the final ray direction, ensuring precise focus control based on magnification and numerical aperture. Inputs: origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray origins in world space. directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray directions in world space. f: Focal length (float). na: Numerical aperture (float), defined as the inverse of the f-number. m: Lens magnification (float). eps: Numerical stability parameter (float, default 10^{-15}). Outputs: neworigins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) representing the intersection points on the lens plane. newdirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3) representing the refracted ray directions. validmask: Boolean tensor of shape (N,) indicating which rays passed the aperture validation. Ray Tensor: A batched tensor where each row is a 3D vector (x, y, z). Lens Parameters: Stored as scalar floats. Plane of Focus (POF): A plane perpendicular to the optical axis (x-axis) at distance pof from the lens center. 1. Transform to Lens Space: Transform ray origins and directions from world space to lens space using the inverse camera transform. In this implementation, the lens is centered at the origin with the optical axis aligned to the x-axis. 2. Calculate Intersection with Lens Plane: Compute the intersection time t with the lens plane at x=0. t = \frac{-\text{origins}x}{\text{directions}x + \epsilon} Calculate the intersection coordinates (y, z) on the lens plane: y = \text{origins}y + t \cdot \text{directions}y z = \text{origins}z + t \cdot \text{directions}z 3. Validate Aperture: Check if the intersection point lies within the lens radius r{lens}. r{lens} = \frac{f \cdot na}{2} The ray is valid if: t > 0 \quad \text{AND} \quad y^2 + z^2 < r{lens}^2 If invalid, set t to NaN and mark the ray as invalid. 4. Calculate Plane of Focus (POF): Determine the distance of the plane of focus from the lens center. pof = \frac{f \cdot (m + 1)}{m} Adjust the sign of pof to place it on the same side as the object relative to the lens. If the object is at x{objects}, then: pof = pof \cdot \text{sign}(x{objects}) 5. Intersect with Plane of Focus: Calculate the intersection point x\star on the plane of focus. x0 = \text{origins} + t \cdot \text{directions} t{pof} = \frac{x{0,x} - pof}{\text{directions}x + \epsilon} t{pof} = -t{pof} x\star = x0 + t{pof} \cdot \text{directions} 6. Calculate Camera Position: Determine the camera position on the opposite side of the lens. \text{camera\pos} = -f \cdot (1 + m) \cdot \text{sign}(x{objects}) 7. Intersect with Camera Plane: Calculate the final intersection point xv on the camera plane passing through the optical center. d = -x\star t{cam} = \frac{\text{camera\pos} - x{\star,x}}{dx + \epsilon} xv = x\star + t{cam} \cdot d 8. Compute New Direction: The new direction is the vector from the lens intersection point x0 to the camera intersection point xv. \text{new\direction} = xv - x0 Normalize the new direction. 9. Set New Origin: The new origin is the intersection point on the lens plane x0. 10. Return Results: Return the new origins, new directions, and the validity mask. To sample points uniformly on the lens disk for Monte Carlo integration: 1. Generate r{squared} = \text{rand()} \cdot r{lens}^2. 2. Generate \theta = \text{rand()} \cdot 2\pi. 3. Convert to Cartesian coordinates: y = \sqrt{r{squared}} \cdot \cos(\theta) z = \sqrt{r{squared}} \cdot \sin(\theta) 4. The probability density is p(A) = \frac{1}{\pi r{lens}^2}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def perfectlensstep(origins, directions, f, na, m, eps=1e-15): """ Performs one step of the Perfect Lens approximation. Args: origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) f: Focal length (float) na: Numerical aperture (float) m: Magnification (float) eps: Numerical stability parameter (float) Returns: neworigins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) newdirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3) validmask: Tensor of shape (N,) """ # Step 1: Calculate intersection with lens plane at x=0 # t = (-origins[:, 0]) / (directions[:, 0] + eps) t = -origins[:, 0] / (directions[:, 0] + eps) # y = origins[:, 1] + t directions[:, 1] # z = origins[:, 2] + t directions[:, 2] y = origins[:, 1] + t directions[:, 1] z = origins[:, 2] + t directions[:, 2] # Step 2: Validate aperture # lensradius = f na / 2 lensradius = f na / 2.0 radiussq = y2 + z2 validt = (t > 0) & (radiussq < lensradius2) # Set t to NaN for invalid rays tvalid = torch.where(validt, t, torch.tensor(float('nan'), device=t.device)) # Step 3: Calculate intersection point on lens plane x0 # x0 = origins + t.unsqueeze(1) directions # Note: Use tvalid for calculation, but keep original origins for invalid rays if needed # However, for invalid rays, the direction is undefined, so we can set it to zero or keep original # Let's assume we only process valid rays for direction calculation, but return full batch x0 = origins + tvalid.unsqueeze(1) directions # Step 4: Calculate Plane of Focus (POF) # pof = f (m + 1) / m # We need the sign of the object position. Assuming xobjects is the x-coordinate of the object. # In this context, xobjects is typically the x-coordinate of the ray origin or a specified object plane. # Let's assume xobjects is the x-coordinate of the ray origin for simplicity, or passed as a parameter. # Based on the source, xobjects is calculated in intersect(). Let's assume it's the x-coordinate of the origin. xobjects = origins[:, 0] pof = f (m + 1) / m pof = pof torch.sign(xobjects) # Step 5: Intersect with Plane of Focus # tpof = (x0[:, 0] - pof) / (directions[:, 0] + eps) # tpof = -tpof # xstar = x0 + tpof.unsqueeze(1) directions tpof = (x0[:, 0] - pof) / (directions[:, 0] + eps) tpof = -tpof xstar = x0 + tpof.unsqueeze(1) directions # Step 6: Calculate Camera Position # camerapos = -f (1 + m) torch.sign(xobjects) camerapos = -f (1 + m) torch.sign(xobjects) # Step 7: Intersect with Camera Plane # d = -xstar # tcam = (camerapos - xstar[:, 0]) / (d[:, 0] + eps) # xv = xstar + tcam.unsqueeze(1) d d = -xstar tcam = (camerapos - xstar[:, 0]) / (d[:, 0] + eps) xv = xstar + tcam.unsqueeze(1) d # Step 8: Compute New Direction # newdirection = xv - x0 newdirection = xv - x0 # Normalize newdirection newdirection = newdirection / (torch.norm(newdirection, dim=1, keepdim=True) + eps) # Step 9: Set New Origin neworigins = x0 # Step 10: Handle Invalid Rays # For invalid rays, set newdirection to zero or original direction? # The source says "Return transformed rays with new directions and boolean mask of all True (valid rays)" # This implies we return the mask separately. # For invalid rays, the direction is not physically meaningful in this model. # We can set it to zero or keep the original. Let's set to zero for clarity. newdirection = torch.where(validt.unsqueeze(1), newdirection, torch.zeroslike(newdirection)) neworigins = torch.where(validt.unsqueeze(1), neworigins, origins) # Keep original origin for invalid rays? Or set to NaN? # The source says "set t to NaN" for invalid rays. # If t is NaN, x0 is NaN. # Let's use the tvalid to mask the results. # Re-calculate x0 with tvalid to ensure NaN for invalid rays x0invalid = origins + tvalid.unsqueeze(1) directions # If tvalid is False, tvalid is NaN, so x0invalid will be NaN # But torch.where with NaN might propagate NaN. # Let's just return the mask and the calculated values. return neworigins, newdirection, validt def samplelensdisk(lensradius, numsamples, device='cpu'): """ Samples points uniformly on the lens disk. Args: lensradius: Radius of the lens (float) numsamples: Number of samples (int) device: Device to create tensors on Returns: points: Tensor of shape (numsamples, 3) with y and z coordinates pdf: Probability density (float) """ # rsquared = rand() lensradius^2 rsquared = torch.rand(numsamples, device=device) lensradius2 # theta = rand() 2pi theta = torch.rand(numsamples, device=device) 2 math.pi # y = sqrt(rsquared) cos(theta) # z = sqrt(rsquared) sin(theta) y = torch.sqrt(rsquared) torch.cos(theta) z = torch.sqrt(rsquared) torch.sin(theta) # points[:, 0] = 0 (on the lens plane) # points[:, 1] = y # points[:, 2] = z points = torch.zeros((numsamples, 3), device=device) points[:, 1] = y points[:, 2] = z # pdf = 1 / (pi lensradius^2) pdf = 1.0 / (math.pi lensradius2) return points, pdf f: Focal length (float). na: Numerical aperture (float). m: Lens magnification (float). eps: Numerical stability parameter (float, default 10^{-15}). Division by Zero: The calculation of t involves division by the x-component of the direction. A small epsilon is added to prevent division by zero. Invalid Rays: Rays that do not intersect the lens plane within the aperture are marked as invalid. Their directions are set to zero or kept as original, depending on implementation. Sign of Object Position: The sign of the object position determines the side of the lens for the plane of focus and camera position. Incorrect sign handling can lead to incorrect focus. Numerical Stability: The use of epsilon is crucial for numerical stability, especially when dealing with rays parallel to the lens plane. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. Each ray is processed independently with a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the ray origins, directions, and intermediate calculations. Strengths: Provides precise control over depth of field through explicit geometric calculations. Efficient for batched ray processing. Limitations: Assumes paraxial approximation, which may not be accurate for wide-angle lenses or large apertures. Does not account for lens aberrations. When to Use: Suitable for volume rendering applications requiring depth of field effects with a thin lens model. When Not to Use: Not suitable for simulating complex lens effects such as aberrations, distortion, or non-paraxial behavior. The Perfect Lens method is based on the thin lens approximation, a common model in optics for simulating depth of field. It is implemented in the gradoptics library, which focuses on gradient-based optics simulations. The method is particularly useful in scientific visualization and volume rendering where precise control over focus is required. magis-slac/gradoptics, https://github.com/magis-slac/gradoptics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Depth of Field for Bitrate Control
head: Aperture-based bitrate control, Varying depth of field for graceful degradation
body: This method controls video bitrate in cloud rendering by dynamically adjusting the camera's aperture to vary the depth of field (DoF). A narrow depth of field blurs the background, reducing image detail and entropy, which lowers the encoded video bitrate and file size. It is distinct from standard optical DoF techniques because it treats aperture as a compression control knob rather than solely an artistic or optical parameter, leveraging the server-side 3D scene knowledge to simulate blur before streaming. Inputs: 3D scene geometry and camera parameters (position, orientation, focal length). Target or adjustable aperture value (f-number). Video encoding settings (codec, resolution). Outputs: Rendered video frames with variable depth of field blur. Corresponding video bitrate and file size. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard cloud rendering pipeline architecture: 1. Server Side: Unity game engine holds the 3D scene state and camera parameters. 2. Transmission: WebRTC framework handles real-time video stream transmission. 3. Client Side: Chrome web browser receives and displays the video stream. Steps: 1. Initialize Cloud Rendering System: Set up the Unity engine to render the 3D scene and configure WebRTC for video streaming to the client browser. 2. Expose Aperture Control: Implement a user interface control (e.g., a slider knob) in the Unity game controls that maps user input to the virtual camera's aperture setting. 3. Adjust Aperture: When the user adjusts the slider, update the virtual camera's f-number parameter. Lower f-numbers (e.g., 0.1) create a narrow depth of field; higher f-numbers (e.g., 10) create a larger depth of field. 4. Render with Depth of Field: Use a physics-based path tracing engine (such as Blender Cycles) to render the scene. The engine simulates the camera aperture, blurring out-of-focus regions (typically the background) based on the current f-number. 5. Stream Video: Transmit the rendered frames via WebRTC to the client browser. 6. Monitor Bitrate: Observe the video bitrate on the client side. As the aperture increases (depth of field narrows), the bitrate decreases due to reduced background detail. Parameters: F-stop (f-number): Controls the aperture size. Typical range: 0.1 to 10. Value 0.1: Narrow depth of field, high blur, low bitrate. Value 10: Large depth of field, low blur, high bitrate. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The relationship between f-number and bitrate is empirical, as demonstrated by the measured reductions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the rendering engine's ability to accurately simulate depth of field. Inaccurate simulation may not yield the expected bitrate reduction. Degenerate Input: If the scene has no depth variation (e.g., a flat plane), changing the aperture may not significantly affect the bitrate. Latency: Dynamic adjustment of DoF and subsequent encoding may introduce latency, though WebRTC is designed for real-time communication. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Rendering time may increase with narrower depth of field due to increased sampling requirements for blur, but this is not explicitly stated. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Image size at F10 is 65% bigger than at F0.1 (Blender Cycles, HDR environment map). Video size at F10 is 53% greater than at F0.1 (2-second videos, Blender). Video bitrate can reduce by four times when aperture sizes increase (simple game, input-controlled box moving through a forest). Strengths: Reduces video bitrate and file size. Improves quality of experience metrics such as video quality and delay. Leverages existing 3D scene information in cloud rendering. Limitations: Requires cloud rendering infrastructure with 3D scene knowledge. May not be suitable for all types of content (e.g., content where background detail is critical). When to use: Cloud rendering scenarios where bitrate reduction is prioritized and background detail can be sacrificed. When not to use: Local rendering without 3D scene access, or when high background detail is required. This technique was presented by Sarag Bharadwaj in an unofficial video presentation titled "Varying depth of field for graceful degradation and superior compression of...". The work explores the use of depth of field as a mechanism for bitrate control in cloud rendering, specifically using Unity and WebRTC. It builds on the premise that video frames with a narrow depth of field have fewer details in the background, leading to lower bitrates. name: Camera Trajectory and Path Generation
head: Camera Path Generation, Trajectory Sampling, Novel View Trajectory
body: This family defines methods for generating sequences of camera poses (position and orientation) for volume rendering, novel view synthesis, and 3D reconstruction. It solves the problem of determining valid viewing geometries when real-world capture data is unavailable, insufficient, or requires optimization for specific computational constraints. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera is the focus on generating temporal sequences or structured multi-view sets rather than interactive single-view controls or static background models. It differs from Camera Ray Generation by operating at the pose level (defining the camera's world transform) rather than the ray level (defining individual pixel rays), although it feeds directly into ray generation. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Generates multi-view camera poses for large-scale outdoor elongated structures (e.g., ancient city walls) from a 3D point cloud. It fits a principal axis via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the point cloud's XY coordinates, samples stations along this axis, and validates positions against a density grid to ensure coverage. It replaces indoor room-centric hardcoded poses with data-driven trajectories aligned to the structure's geometry. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by following a linear principal axis rather than a helical path, and from Orbit Camera Path Generation by maintaining a fixed distance from a linear centerline rather than orbiting a central point. Generates a continuous video of novel views by traversing a predefined camera trajectory (typically a spiral path) and rendering each frame using a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It differs from static novel view synthesis by outputting a temporal sequence (MP4) rather than a single image, and from diffusion-based methods like iNVS by relying on volumetric ray marching through a learned implicit representation rather than warping and inpainting. Reduces the computational load of trajectory-based rendering methods by selecting a subset of frames from a full trajectory based on a predefined mapping file. It serves as a preprocessing step for algorithms like 2D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for efficient training or rendering on hardware with limited memory or compute resources by skipping redundant or intermediate camera poses. Unlike continuous path generation methods such as Spiral Camera Path Generation or Orbit Camera Path Generation, this method operates on discrete, existing trajectory data, acting as a filter rather than a generator. Creates a sequence of camera poses for volume rendering or novel view synthesis when real-world capture data is unavailable or insufficient. It solves the problem of defining valid viewing geometries by sampling positions and orientations from a structured distribution, typically using low-discrepancy sequences like Sobol samplers to ensure uniform coverage of the scene volume. It differs from spiral or orbit generation by decoupling position and direction sampling to allow arbitrary spherical coverage, and from random pose selection by providing deterministic, space-filling trajectories rather than stochastic samples. Creates training data for volume rendering and 3D reconstruction models by simulating sensor observations in computer-generated environments. It solves the problem of lacking real-world labeled data by providing ground-truth geometry, semantic labels, and controlled noise characteristics. Unlike methods that generate camera trajectories for active planning or reconstruct scenes from sparse inputs, this method focuses on the pipeline of rendering, augmenting, and cleaning synthetic data to match the statistical properties of real sensors. It differs from Elongated Structure Camera Trajectory Generation by prioritizing data quality and label correctness over trajectory coverage, and from Novel View Synthesis Rendering by providing explicit geometric and semantic ground truth rather than just photometric consistency. Constructs camera trajectories by evaluating explicit mathematical functions of a scalar parameter (typically angle or time) to produce a sequence of camera poses. It solves the problem of generating smooth, continuous novel views from a sparse set of training images by defining the geometry of the path analytically rather than interpolating between discrete keyframes. It differs from Sparse Trajectory Generation by relying on closed-form equations for position and orientation, and from Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by deriving parameters directly from scene statistics (e.g., camera bounding boxes) rather than arbitrary artistic constraints. An initialization method for the transformation T \in SE(3) between Scene A and Scene B. It generates good camera viewpoints for Scene A using its Viewshed Field (VFA), transforms them by candidate T, and scores them based on their viewshed likelihood in Scene B (VFB). Generate a set of N good camera viewpoints CA for Scene A using VFA. For a candidate transformation T, transform each camera Ci in CA to get T(Ci). Calculate the viewshed score for all oriented points p originating from these transformed cameras in Scene B. Sample multiple random transformations T. Select the T with the highest Score{init} as the initialization. Calculate the initialization score for T as the median over all transformed cameras of the sum of viewshed values in Scene B: Score{init}(CA; T) = Median{CA}(\sum{p \in T(Ci)} VFB(p)). A method proposing multi-timestep sampling for multi-stage scene-level generation. Multi-timestep sampling is used for multi-stage scene-level generation. Surrounding environment, ground, and objects are synthesized. A method to generate two distinct camera paths for stereoscopic visualization by calculating a second eye position based on a separation angle and the primary view vector. Define the primary camera position c, look-at point l, and sky vector s. Calculate the viewing vector v = l - c. Calculate the right direction vector r using the cross product: r = S × v. Calculate the orthogonal component S of the sky vector s using: S = s - \cos(\alpha) v \frac{|s|}{|v|}, where \alpha is the angle between s and v. Calculate \cos(\alpha) using: \cos(\alpha) = \frac{v \cdot s}{|v| |s|}. Calculate the right eye position C using: C = c + \frac{r}{|r|} \frac{\beta 2\pi}{360} |v|, where \beta is the separation angle. The sky vector s does not need to be orthogonal to the view vector v for Splotch, but orthogonalization is performed for the stereo calculation. Creates a smooth spline path between input keyframe camera poses using multidimensional B-spline interpolation. Convert poses to (position, lookat, up) format using posestopoints(poses, dist=rotweight). Run multidimensional B-spline interpolation via scipy.interpolate.splprep on reshaped points with degree k and smoothness s. Evaluate spline at ninterp(points.shape[0]-1) points using splev. Reshape back to (n, 3, 3) format. Convert back to pose matrices using pointstoposes(newpoints). Parameters: ninterp (interpolation factor per segment), splinedegree (polynomial degree, default 5), smoothness (smoothing factor, default 0.03), rotweight (relative weighting of rotation/translation, default 0.1). Initialize camera selection scores: selected cameras get s=1.0, others get s=0.0. Apply temporal filtering to scores si^t to get weights wi^t using the exponential moving average formula with \lambda=0.05. Select the N views with the highest updated weights wi^t for rendering. Refine weights across all views using element-wise subtraction of the minimum weight, followed by normalization, to ensure zero weight for views entering/leaving the set and move C0 discontinuity to C1. Formula: wi^t = \lambda si^t + (1.0 - \lambda) wi^{t-1}. Formula: w^{CS} = \frac{w - \mini wi}{\sum (w - \mini wi)}. Parameters: \lambda (temporal filtering adaptation speed, typical 0.05), N (number of highest weighted views, typical 9). Pitfall: Temporal instability when cameras appear/disappear. Handled by smooth fading and weight refinement to ensure gradients of weights become discontinuous instead of actual values. Camera trajectory generation is fundamental to novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction, where the goal is to render views from angles not captured during data acquisition. Early methods relied on manual keyframe definition or simple geometric paths (spirals, orbits). With the advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting, the demand for high-quality, dense, and uniformly distributed camera poses increased to ensure robust training and rendering. For specific applications like stereoscopic visualization, specialized paths are required to maintain correct interocular geometry. In large-scale outdoor scenarios, data-driven approaches using PCA on point clouds have been developed to align trajectories with elongated structures. Furthermore, computational efficiency has led to sparse trajectory selection methods to reduce training time for large datasets. body: The Arcball Camera is a camera control technique that maps 2D screen coordinates to a 3D virtual sphere to compute rotation quaternions for smooth orbiting around a center point. It differs from First-Person Camera Control by decoupling rotation from the camera's local forward vector, instead rotating the view around a fixed center. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation to apply the resulting rotation to the view matrix. Inputs: Mouse position (x, y) in screen/pixel coordinates. Viewport dimensions: width W, height H. Previous mouse position (x{prev}, y{prev}) and previous arcball state (rotation quaternion q{old}). Camera configuration: eye position \mathbf{e}, center point \mathbf{c}, up vector \mathbf{u}, zoom speed k{zoom}, minimum/maximum camera distance d{min}, d{max}. Outputs: Updated camera view matrix M{cam}. Updated rotation quaternion q{new}. Updated translation vector for zoom/pan. ArcballState rotation: Quaternion q (w, x, y, z), normalized. translation: 4x4 matrix T or vector \mathbf{t}, representing zoom/pan offset. centerTranslation: 4x4 matrix Tc, representing the translation to the orbit center. invCamera: 4x4 matrix, inverse of the current camera matrix. invScreen: Array [1/W, 1/H] used to normalize pixel coordinates. lastPosition: 2D vector (x{prev}, y{prev}). isRotating: Boolean flag. CameraConfig eye: 3D vector \mathbf{e}. center: 3D vector \mathbf{c}. up: 3D vector \mathbf{u} (typically [0, 1, 0]). zoomSpeed: Scalar k{zoom} (e.g., 0.1). minDist: Float d{min} (e.g., 1.25). maxDist: Float d{max} (e.g., 8.0). 1. Initialize Camera Basis: Compute the camera's local coordinate system. \mathbf{z}{axis} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{e}) \mathbf{x}{axis} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{z}{axis}, \mathbf{u})) \mathbf{y}{axis} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{x}{axis}, \mathbf{z}{axis})) Construct the rotation matrix R from these axes and convert to initial quaternion q. Store translation \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{e} - \mathbf{c}. 2. Normalize Mouse Coordinates: Convert screen pixel coordinates to normalized device coordinates in the range [-1, 1]. u = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{2x}{W} - 1, -1, 1 \right) v = \text{clamp}\left( 1 - \frac{2y}{H}, -1, 1 \right) The y-axis inversion accounts for top-left origin screen coordinates. 3. Project to Arcball Surface (Screen-to-Arcball): Map the 2D point (u, v) to a 3D point \mathbf{p} on the virtual trackball. Calculate squared distance from center: d^2 = u^2 + v^2. If d^2 \le 1.0: The point is inside the unit circle. Project onto the upper hemisphere of the sphere: pz = \sqrt{1.0 - d^2} \mathbf{p} = (u, v, pz) If d^2 > 1.0: The point is outside the unit circle. Normalize the XY components and set z = 0. \mathbf{p}{xy} = \text{normalize}((u, v)) pz = 0 \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{xy} Some implementations use a spherical cap projection where z = \cos(\frac{\pi}{2} \min(d, 1)), or a hyperboloid fallback z = 1/\sqrt{u^2+v^2} for constant angular velocity. 4. Compute Rotation Delta: Let \mathbf{p}{prev} be the arcball point from the previous frame and \mathbf{p}{curr} be the current point. Compute the rotation axis \mathbf{a} and angle \theta between these two vectors. \mathbf{a} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{p}{prev}, \mathbf{p}{curr}) d = \text{dot}(\mathbf{p}{prev}, \mathbf{p}{curr}) Edge Case Handling: If d > 1 - \epsilon: Vectors are parallel. Return identity quaternion. If d < -1 + \epsilon: Vectors are anti-parallel. Find an orthogonal axis to \mathbf{p}{prev} by crossing with [1,0,0] or [0,1,0], normalize, and create a 180-degree quaternion. Else: Normalize \mathbf{a} and construct delta quaternion q{\Delta} = [1+d, \mathbf{a}], then normalize q{\Delta}. 5. Update Rotation Quaternion: q{new} = q{\Delta} \times q{old} Normalize q{new}. 6. Update Camera Matrix: Convert q{new} to rotation matrix R{quat}. The camera matrix M{cam} is constructed as: M{cam} = T{trans} \cdot R{quat} \cdot T{center}^{-1} Where T{center} translates the center \mathbf{c} to the origin, R{quat} applies the rotation, and T{trans} translates the eye back to its position relative to the center. 7. Handle Zoom and Pan: Zoom: Compute translation vector \mathbf{v}{zoom} = [0, 0, \text{amount} \cdot k{zoom}]. Update T{trans} and clamp the distance component to [d{min}, d{max}] to prevent passing through the center. Pan: Compute delta in screen space, transform to world space using M{cam}^{-1}, and update T{center} or the eye position relative to the center. Unverified code. A[i][k] B[k][j] return C class ArcballCamera: def init(self, eye, center, up, width, height): self.eye = eye self.center = center self.up = up self.width = width self.height = height zaxis = normalize([center[0]-eye[0], center[1]-eye[1], center[2]-eye[2]]) xaxis = normalize(cross(zaxis, up)) yaxis = normalize(cross(xaxis, zaxis)) self.rotation = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.translation = [eye[0]-center[0], eye[1]-center[1], eye[2]-center[2]] self.lastmouse = [0, 0] self.lastarcball = screentoarcball(0, 0, width, height) def updaterotation(self, x, y): currarcball = screentoarcball(x, y, self.width, self.height) deltaquat = rotationbetweenvectors(self.lastarcball, currarcball) self.rotation = quatmul(deltaquat, self.rotation) self.lastmouse = [x, y] self.lastarcball = currarcball def updatezoom(self, amount, zoomspeed, mindist, maxdist): zoomfactor = amount zoomspeed viewdir = normalize([self.center[0]-self.eye[0], self.center[1]-self.eye[1], self.center[2]-self.eye[2]]) neweye = [ self.eye[0] + viewdir[0] zoomfactor, self.eye[1] + viewdir[1] zoomfactor, self.eye[2] + viewdir[2] zoomfactor ] dist = math.sqrt((neweye[0]-self.center[0])2 + (neweye[1]-self.center[1])2 + (neweye[2]-self.center[2])scale] elif dist > maxdist: scale = maxdist / dist neweye = [self.center[0] + (neweye[0]-self.center[0])scale, self.center[1] + (neweye[1]-self.center[1])scale, self.center[2] + (neweye[2]-self.center[2])scale] self.eye = neweye self.translation = [neweye[0]-self.center[0], neweye[1]-self.center[1], neweye[2]-self.center[2]] def getcameramatrix(self): R = quattomat4(self.rotation) T = [ [1, 0, 0, self.translation[0]], [0, 1, 0, self.translation[1]], [0, 0, 1, self.translation[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1] ] Tcinv = [ [1, 0, 0, -self.center[0]], [0, 1, 0, -self.center[1]], [0, 0, 1, -self.center[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1] ] return mat4mul(T, mat4mul(R, Tcinv)) width, height: Viewport dimensions in pixels. zoomSpeed: Scalar multiplier for zoom magnitude (e.g., 0.1). minDist, maxDist: Minimum and maximum camera distance from center (e.g., 1.25, 8.0). eye, center, up: Initial camera position, target, and up vector. Gimbal Lock: Avoided by using quaternions instead of Euler angles. Parallel/Anti-parallel Vectors: When the mouse moves such that the arcball vectors are parallel or anti-parallel, the cross product is zero. Handle by checking the dot product against thresholds (1-\epsilon, -1+\epsilon) and using a fallback orthogonal axis for 180-degree rotations. Boundary Clamping: Mouse coordinates must be clamped to [-1, 1] before projection to prevent artifacts at screen edges. Zoom Clamping: The camera distance must be clamped to prevent the eye from passing through the center point. Projection Boundary: For points outside the unit circle, the provided sources normalize the XY components and set z=0 in their code. Alternative projections use a spherical cap z = \cos(\frac{\pi}{2} \min(d, 1)) or a hyperboloid z = 1/\sqrt{u^2+v^2}. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for rotation update. Memory Complexity: O(1) for state storage (quaternion, translation, matrices). Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time interaction. Strengths: Intuitive control, no gimbal lock, smooth rotation. Limitations: Can be disorienting if the center point is not visible or if the rotation axis is not aligned with user expectations. When to use: Interactive volume exploration and medical imaging viewers. When not to use: When precise, axis-aligned rotation is required, or when the camera needs to follow a specific path. name: First-Person Camera Control
head: Camera Control, Camera Controller, Camera State & GPU Data Packing, Input Handler, Mouse and Keyboard Input Controller
body: First-Person Camera Control manages the position, orientation (yaw/pitch), and projection parameters of a virtual camera, mapping user input (mouse/keyboard) to transformations for 3D rendering. It differs from spherical or arcball models by maintaining a fixed "up" vector and allowing free translation along the camera's local axes, which is essential for immersive exploration or precise volumetric inspection. It builds on Ray generation and camera models by providing the specific \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d} generation logic for a perspective view. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Mouse movement deltas (\Delta x, \Delta y), keyboard state (active keys), time delta (\Delta t), and initial camera state (position, yaw, pitch). Outputs: Updated camera position, orientation vectors (front, right, up), and a packed GPU buffer containing these parameters for ray generation shaders. Data Structures: The camera state is typically maintained in CPU memory for logic and packed into a GPU-friendly struct for rendering passes. CPU State (S3, unofficial): position: vec3 (x, y, z) front: vec3 (normalized direction vector) right: vec3 (normalized right vector) up: vec3 (normalized up vector) yaw: float (horizontal rotation, default \pi/2) pitch: float (vertical rotation, default 0.0) speed: float (movement speed) sensitivity: float (mouse sensitivity) zoom: float (field of view factor) aspectRatio: float nearPlane: float farPlane: float worldUp: vec3 (default (0, 1, 0)) GPU Struct (S1, unofficial): position: array<f32, 4> (xyz position, w unused or padding) rot: array<array<f32, 4>, 3> (3 rows of 4 floats, representing the rotation matrix columns or basis vectors) sinhalfvfov: f32 framecount: u32 width: f32 height: f32 prevposition: array<f32, 4> Parameters (Typical Values): Vertical Field of View (vfov): \pi/2 radians (90^\circ). Movement Speed: 1.0 units/sec. Mouse Sensitivity/Rotation Factor: 0.01 or 0.0025. Pan Factor: 1.0. Zoom Factor: 0.0025. Algorithm Steps: 1. Process Input: Read mouse deltas (\Delta x, \Delta y) and active keyboard keys. If mouse button is left and Control key is held, update lighting parameters (if applicable). If mouse button is left and Control is not held, update rotation: \Delta \text{yaw} = \Delta x \times \text{ROTATION\FACTOR} \Delta \text{pitch} = \Delta y \times \text{ROTATION\FACTOR} If mouse button is right, update pan (position offset): \Delta \text{pan}x = \Delta x \times \text{PAN\FACTOR} \Delta \text{pan}y = \Delta y \times \text{PAN\FACTOR} Store active keys on key-down; clear on key-up. 2. Update Orientation (Yaw/Pitch): Apply rotation deltas to yaw and pitch. Clamp pitch to [-\pi/2 + \epsilon, \pi/2 - \epsilon] to prevent gimbal lock or flipping. Recalculate basis vectors using the new angles: \text{front}x = \cos(\text{pitch}) \sin(\text{yaw}) \text{front}y = -\sin(\text{pitch}) \text{front}z = \cos(\text{pitch}) \cos(\text{yaw}) \text{front} = \text{normalize}(\text{front}) \text{right} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{front}, \text{worldUp})) \text{up} = \text{cross}(\text{right}, \text{front}) Note: Some implementations compute vecx and vecy from vecz (front) using cross products with a fixed up vector. 3. Update Position: Determine movement direction based on active keys (WASD/Arrows). Calculate displacement vector \mathbf{v}: \mathbf{v} = (\text{forward} \times \text{front} + \text{right} \times \text{right} + \text{up} \times \text{up}) \times \text{speed} \times \Delta t Update position: \text{position} = \text{position} + \mathbf{v} Note: If pan mode is active (right mouse), apply \Delta \text{pan} to position directly or relative to view plane. 4. Pack GPU Data: Compute sinhalfvfov = sin(0.5 vfov). Construct the rotation matrix rows/columns from front, right, up. Fill CameraGpuData struct with position, rot, sinhalfvfov, framecount, width, height, and prevposition. Upload to GPU buffer (e.g., Uniform Buffer Object or Storage Buffer). a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0] ] def processmouse(self, dx, dy): self.yaw += dx self.sensitivity self.pitch += dy self.sensitivity # Clamp pitch to avoid flipping if self.pitch > 89.0 math.pi / 180.0: self.pitch = 89.0 math.pi / 180.0 if self.pitch < -89.0 math.pi / 180.0: self.pitch = -89.0 math.pi / 180.0 self.updatevectors() def processkeyboard(self, direction, deltatime): velocity = self.speed deltatime if direction == 'FORWARD': self.position[0] += self.front[0] velocity self.position[1] += self.front[1] velocity self.position[2] += self.front[2] velocity elif direction == 'BACKWARD': self.position[0] -= self.front[0] velocity self.position[1] -= self.front[1] velocity self.position[2] -= self.front[2] velocity elif direction == 'RIGHT': self.position[0] += self.right[0] velocity self.position[1] += self.right[1] velocity self.position[2] += self.right[2] velocity elif direction == 'LEFT': self.position[0] -= self.right[0] velocity self.position[1] -= self.right[1] velocity self.position[2] -= self.right[2] velocity def getgpudata(self, width, height, framecount): sinhalfvfov = math.sin(self.vfov / 2.0) # Rotation matrix rows (or columns depending on shader expectation) # Here we pack basis vectors as rows for simplicity rot = [ self.front, # Row 0 self.right, # Row 1 self.up # Row 2 ] # Pad to 4 floats per row if required by struct rotpacked = [ self.front + [0.0], self.right + [0.0], self.up + [0.0] ] return { "position": self.position + [0.0], "rot": rotpacked, "sinhalfvfov": sinhalfvfov, "framecount": framecount, "width": float(width), "height": float(height), "prevposition": self.position + [0.0] # Update prev in actual loop } The Cinematic Camera Metaphor is a navigation technique for non-immersive 3D environments where user input manipulates the position and orientation of a virtual camera to control the viewpoint. It enables users to "tumble, track, and dolly" the view, allowing for precise framing of the scene. It is distinguished from direct manipulation metaphors (like Scene-in-Hand) by treating the camera as an independent entity controlled via standard input devices, often requiring modifier keys or specific gestures to invoke different camera motions. A programmatic interface for setting camera state, often used in scientific visualization toolkits (e.g., VTK.js). It handles synchronization between requested state and applied state, ensuring that changes are only applied if they differ from the last request. It supports setting position, focal point, view up, and zoom (parallel scale). A key pitfall is handling XR mode, where headset pose should override programmatic control, and ensuring that unchanged camera steps do not reset the view unexpectedly. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for input processing and matrix updates. Memory Complexity: O(1) for camera state storage. Performance: Highly efficient; the primary cost is the CPU-to-GPU upload of the camera uniform buffer, which can be batched or updated only when state changes. Strengths: Intuitive for exploration; supports free movement and rotation; standard in FPS games and medical imaging viewers. Limitations: Prone to gimbal lock if not implemented with quaternions or careful clamping (though yaw/pitch avoids singularity at poles, it restricts full spherical rotation). Not suitable for orbiting around a specific point without additional logic (pan/trackball hybrid). When to use: Immersive navigation, medical volume inspection, FPS-style viewers. When not to use: When a fixed orbit around a center point is required (use Arcball) or when spherical sampling is needed (use Uniform Sphere Sampling). body: The Cinematic Camera Metaphor is a navigation technique for non-immersive 3D environments where user input manipulates the position and orientation of a virtual camera to control the user's viewpoint. It enables users to tumble, track, and dolly the view for precise scene framing. It is distinguished from direct manipulation metaphors by treating the camera as an independent entity controlled via standard input devices, often requiring modifier keys or specific gestures to invoke different camera motions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Mouse movements with modifier keys, or 6DoF input device position/orientation. Output: Updated virtual camera position and orientation applied to the rendering pipeline. Data Structures: CameraState: Holds position (vec3), orientation (quat or euler angles), and projectionparams (fov, aspect ratio). InputEvent: Holds deltaposition (vec2/vec3), buttonstate (bool), modifierkeys (bitmask), and device pose data. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set CameraState to an initial view. 2. Read Input: Capture InputEvent from mouse or 6DoF device. 3. Map Input to Motion: If using mouse + keys: Map specific key combinations to tumble (rotation), track (pan), or dolly (zoom) operations. If using 6DoF device: Map device position directly to camera position for Eyeball-in-Hand, or map input to spatial/angular velocity for Flying Vehicle. 4. Update Camera: Apply the calculated transformation to CameraState. 5. Render: Use updated CameraState to generate the view matrix for ray generation. Parameters: Mapping Mode: Absolute or Relative. Relative mapping requires a button press to activate movement. Gestures: Specific mouse movements or button sequences can invoke predefined camera paths or positions (e.g., StyleCam). Pitfalls: Relative Mapping Confusion: Using relative mapping for eyeball-in-hand navigation can destroy the user's mental model of a fixed, invisible scene, leading to confusion. KEYTUMBLE = 0x01 KEYTRACK = 0x02 KEYDOLLY = 0x04 def updatecinematiccamera(camera: dict, inputevent: dict) -> dict: """ Updates the camera state based on input using the Cinematic Camera Metaphor. camera: dict with 'position' (list[float]), 'orientation' (list[float]), 'projectionparams' (dict) inputevent: dict with 'devicetype' (str), 'deltaposition' (list[float]), 'buttonpressed' (bool), 'modifierkeys' (int), 'deviceposition' (list[float]), 'deviceorientation' (list[float]) """ if inputevent["devicetype"] == "MOUSE": if inputevent["modifierkeys"] & KEYTUMBLE: camera["orientation"][0] += inputevent["deltaposition"][0] camera["orientation"][1] += inputevent["deltaposition"][1] elif inputevent["modifierkeys"] & KEYTRACK: camera["position"][0] += inputevent["deltaposition"][0] camera["position"][1] += inputevent["deltaposition"][1] elif inputevent["modifierkeys"] & KEYDOLLY: camera["position"][2] += inputevent["deltaposition"][1] elif inputevent["devicetype"] == "6DOF": if inputevent.get("relativemode", False): if inputevent["buttonpressed"]: camera["position"] = [camera["position"][i] + inputevent["deltaposition"][i] for i in range(3)] camera["orientation"] = [camera["orientation"][i] + inputevent.get("deltaorientation", [0,0,0])[i] for i in range(3)] else: camera["position"] = inputevent["deviceposition"] camera["orientation"] = inputevent["deviceorientation"] return camera A variant where the input device's position is directly mapped to the virtual camera's position. It supports absolute mapping (continuous control) or relative mapping (movement only when a button is depressed). Absolute mapping is preferred to maintain the user's mental model of a fixed scene; relative mapping can cause confusion. Example: Chameleon display device. The scene is perceived from the position and orientation of a virtual vehicle. The input device controls the spatial and angular velocity of this vehicle, allowing it to move through the scene. Commonly used in 3D games where the "player position" is the vehicle. Enhancements include rapid and controlled movement techniques. The 3D world moves in correspondence with the 6DoF input device. Rotating the device clockwise rotates the scene clockwise. Large movements can be achieved by ratcheting using a button as a clutch. Useful for hierarchical scenes. An extension, "World-in-Miniature," involves manipulating a hand-held miniature copy of the virtual environment. Strengths: Intuitive for users familiar with standard 2D mouse interactions; allows for precise control over framing and composition (tumble, track, dolly). Limitations: Can be less applicable for immersive 3D environments compared to other navigation tasks; relative mapping can break spatial awareness. Usage: Implemented in Unicam (mouse + single button + gestures) and StyleCam (tailored camera positions/paths). The Cinematic Camera Metaphor was introduced in the context of non-immersive 3D environments, such as 3D graphics and animation programs. It is based on the concept of tumbling, tracking, and dollying a viewpoint, as described by Burtnyk et al.. Variations using 6DoF input devices were explored by Ware and Osborne. Specific implementations include Unicam by Zeleznik and Forsberg and StyleCam by Burtnyk et al.. The Eyeball-in-Hand and Scene-in-Hand metaphors were also discussed by Ware and Osborne, with the Chameleon device by Fitzmaurice and World-in-Miniature by Stoakley et al. serving as examples. name: Scene-in-Hand Metaphor
head: World-in-Miniature, Eyeball-in-Hand
body: The Scene-in-Hand Metaphor is a navigation technique where the three-dimensional world moves in correspondence with a six degree-of-freedom (6DoF) input device. It sets itself apart from parent techniques like the Cinematic Camera Metaphor by treating the scene as a manipulable object rather than the camera as a free-moving entity, making it particularly useful for changing viewpoints in hierarchical scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 6DoF input device (e.g., a chameleon-style tracker) providing position and orientation data. Output: A transformation applied to the scene graph or camera matrix such that the scene rotates/transforms in the same direction as the device. Data Structures: Device State: A 6DoF pose vector P{dev} = [x, y, z, rx, ry, rz] representing the physical device's position and orientation relative to a base frame. Scene Transform: A 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix M{scene} applied to all scene objects. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set the initial scene transform M{scene} to the identity matrix I or the current view state. 2. Read Input: Acquire the current 6DoF pose P{dev} from the input device. 3. Compute Rotation: Extract the rotational component R{dev} from P{dev}. 4. Apply Rotation: Update the scene's orientation by multiplying the current scene matrix by the device's rotation: M{scene} \leftarrow M{scene} \times R{dev}. If the device is rotated clockwise, the scene rotates clockwise. 5. Handle Large Movements (Ratcheting): If a button on the device is pressed, it acts as a clutch, allowing the user to ratchet through large movements without continuous tracking drift. 6. Render: Render the scene using the updated M{scene}. Parameters: Clutch Button: A boolean flag on the input device. When true, rotation updates are accumulated or scaled differently to allow coarse navigation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Drift: Continuous integration of device rotation can lead to drift if the device's orientation sensor is noisy. Ratcheting mitigates this by allowing discrete updates. Hierarchy: The metaphor is specifically noted as useful for hierarchical scenes, implying that the transformation should respect the scene graph structure. A uniform scaling technique requiring both index fingers to be placed on and dragged along the display surface. Sliding fingers apart increases scale; sliding them together decreases it. Scaling stops when either finger is lifted. It is chosen when precise, uniform scaling of a volumetric model is required using direct touch interaction. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for pose reading and matrix multiplication. Memory Complexity: O(1) for storing the device pose and scene transform. Strengths: Intuitive mapping between device motion and scene motion; effective for hierarchical navigation. Limitations: Requires 6DoF hardware; potential for drift without ratcheting. When to use: When navigating complex, hierarchical 3D structures where direct manipulation of the scene is preferred over camera movement. When not to use: When only 2D input is available or when precise, isolated object manipulation is needed without moving the entire context. The technique was discussed in the context of volumetric display interaction, where traditional mouse-based navigation was found confusing. It builds on earlier work with the "chameleon" device, which provided "eyeball in hand" navigation. Stoakley et al. extended this concept with the "World-in-Miniature" metaphor, allowing users to manipulate a hand-held miniature copy of the virtual environment. name: Elongated Structure Camera Trajectory Generation
head: Elongated-structure trajectory generator, PCA-based Camera Path Generation, PCA-based multi-view trajectory generation, Principal Axis Camera Trajectory
body:
This method generates multi-view camera poses for large-scale outdoor elongated structures (e.g., ancient city walls) from a 3D point cloud by fitting a principal axis via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), sampling stations along it, and validating positions against a density grid. It replaces indoor room-centric hardcoded poses with data-driven trajectories aligned to the structure's geometry. Inputs: xyz: A tensor of shape [N, 3] containing 3D point cloud coordinates. config: A configuration object (see TrajectoryConfig below). Outputs: A list of CameraPose objects, each containing: extrinsics: A 4 	imes 4 world-to-camera matrix. intrinsics: A vector [fx, fy, cx, cy]. position: Camera center (x, y, z) in world space. target: Look-at target in world space. pitchdeg: The pitch angle used. Data Structures: TrajectoryConfig: numstations: int, default 10. Number of camera stations along the principal axis. distance: float, default 15.0. Primary distance from the wall surface in metres. fardistance: float, default 0.0. Optional farther distance for wide-coverage views. If set, generates an additional set of views. pitchanglesdeg: Tuple[float,...], default (-30.0, 0.0, 30.0). List of pitch angles in degrees (0 = horizontal, positive = camera looks downward). yawoffsetdeg: float, default 0.0. Additional yaw offset added to each station (0 = perpendicular to wall axis). fovydeg: float, default 60.0. Vertical field of view in degrees. imagewidth: int, default 640. Output image resolution in pixels. imageheight: int, default 480. Output image resolution in pixels. viewbothsides: bool, default True. Whether to place cameras on both sides of the wall. marginfactor: float, default 1.1. Extra margin beyond actual point cloud bounds (1.0 = exact bounds, 1.1 = 10% extra). Density Grid: A 2D tensor of shape [grid
x, grid
y] storing point counts per bin, populated by bucketizing point XY coordinates into bins defined by x ins and y ins, then accumulating ones via indexput. Steps: 1. Compute OBB and Bounds: Extract XY coordinates from xyz. Compute the covariance matrix of the XY points. Perform Eigenvalue Decomposition on the covariance matrix. Sort eigenvalues and eigenvectors in descending order. Let \mathbf{e}0 be the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue (principal axis). Let \mathbf{e}1 be the second. Project all XY points onto \mathbf{e}0 and \mathbf{e}1 to find projected min/max ranges. Compute the center of the point cloud in XY: \mathbf{c}{xy} = 	ext{mean}(xy). Compute global bounding box limits: x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}, z{min}, z{max}. Compute z{centre} = (z{min} + z{max}) / 2. Ensure consistent axis orientation: if \mathbf{e}1[0] < 0, negate both \mathbf{e}0 and \mathbf{e}1. Set \mathbf{main\axis} = \mathbf{e}0 and \mathbf{perp\axis} = \mathbf{e}1. 2. Compute Intrinsics: Convert fovydeg to radians: 	ext{fov}y = 	ext{fov\y\deg} 	imes \pi / 180. Compute focal length: f =  rac{	ext{height}}{2 	an(	ext{fov}y / 2)}. Set intrinsics vector: [f, f, 	ext{width}/2, 	ext{height}/2]. 3. Sample Stations: Calculate extent bounds along the principal axis: 	ext{extent}{min} = 	ext{proj}{min}[0] 	imes 	ext{margin actor}. 	ext{extent}{max} = 	ext{proj}{max}[0] 	imes 	ext{margin actor}. For i from 0 to numstations - 1: Compute parameter t = 	ext{extent}{min} + (	ext{extent}{max} - 	ext{extent}{min}) 	imes  rac{i}{\max(	ext{num\stations} - 1, 1)}. Compute point on axis: \mathbf{p}{axis} = \mathbf{c}{xy} + t 	imes \mathbf{main\axis}. Clamp p{axis}[0] to [x{min}, x{max}] and p{axis}[1] to [y{min}, y{max}]. Store (	ext{clamped}x, 	ext{clamped}y) as a station. 4. Build Density Grid: Determine maxdist = max(distance, fardistance if fardistance > 0 else 0). Set grid resolution gridres = 5.0 metres. Set padding gridpad = maxdist + 2 	imes gridres. Calculate grid dimensions: grid
x = \max(3, \lfloor (x{max} - x{min} + 2 	imes grid\pad) / grides floor). grid
y = \max(3, \lfloor (y{max} - y{min} + 2 	imes grid\pad) / grides floor). Define bin edges: x ins linearly spaced from x{min} - grid\pad to x{min} - grid\pad + grid
x 	imes grides. y ins linearly spaced from y{min} - grid\pad to y{min} - grid\pad + grid
y 	imes grides. Map points to grid indices using bucketization. Initialize density tensor of shape [grid
x, grid
y] to zeros. Accumulate counts: for each valid point index (xi, yi), increment density[xi, yi]. 5. Generate Camera Poses: Define distances list: [distance]. If fardistance > 0 and fardistance != distance, append fardistance. Define sides list: [1.0, -1.0] if viewbothsides is True, else [1.0]. For each dist in distances: For each sidesign in sides: For each station (sx, sy): Compute camera XY: cam\x = sx + \mathbf{perp\axis}[0] 	imes dist 	imes side\sign. cam\y = sy + \mathbf{perp\axis}[1] 	imes dist 	imes side\sign. Set cam\z = z{centre}. Compute radius for validation: r = \max(15.0, dist 	imes 0.5). Check if any points exist within radius r of (cam\x, cam\y) using the density grid. If not, skip this pose. For each pitchdeg in pitchanglesdeg: Convert pitchdeg to radians: 	ext{pitchad} = 	ext{pitch\deg} 	imes \pi / 180. Compute target Z: target\z = cam\z - 	an(	ext{pitchad}) 	imes dist. Compute target XY: The target lies along the camera's forward vector at distance dist. Since the camera is perpendicular to the wall axis (yaw offset 0), the target XY is the station XY (sx, sy). Construct camera-to-world rotation matrix \mathbf{R}{c2w} using lookatcv(campos, target): \mathbf{forward} = 	ext{target} - 	ext{campos}, normalized. Handle singularity: if |\mathbf{forward} \cdot \mathbf{up}| > 0.999 (where \mathbf{up}=[0,0,1]), set reference axis to \mathbf{x}=[1,0,0]. Else, use \mathbf{up}. \mathbf{right} = 	ext{reference} 	imes \mathbf{forward}, normalized. \mathbf{up}{corrected} = \mathbf{forward} 	imes \mathbf{right}, normalized. \mathbf{R}{c2w} = [\mathbf{right}, \mathbf{up}{corrected}, \mathbf{forward}]. Compute world-to-camera extrinsics \mathbf{E}: \mathbf{R}{w2c} = \mathbf{R}{c2w}^T. \mathbf{t} = -\mathbf{R}{w2c} 	imes 	ext{campos}. \mathbf{E} =  egin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}{w2c} & \mathbf{t} \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Create CameraPose with extrinsics=\mathbf{E}, intrinsics, position=(cam\x, cam\y, cam\z), target=(sx, sy, target\z), and pitchdeg. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch from typing import List, Tuple class CameraPose: extrinsics: torch.Tensor intrinsics: torch.Tensor position: Tuple[float, float, float] target: Tuple[float, float, float] pitchdeg: float class TrajectoryConfig: numstations: int = 10 distance: float = 15.0 fardistance: float = 0.0 pitchanglesdeg: Tuple[float,...] = (-30.0, 0.0, 30.0) yawoffsetdeg: float = 0.0 fovydeg: float = 60.0 imagewidth: int = 640 imageheight: int = 480 viewbothsides: bool = True marginfactor: float = 1.1 def generatetrajectory(xyz: torch.Tensor, config: TrajectoryConfig) -> List[CameraPose]: device = xyz.device # 1. Compute OBB and Bounds xy = xyz[:,:2] centrexy = xy.mean(dim=0) cov = torch.cov(xy) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = torch.linalg.eigh(cov) eigenvalues = eigenvalues.flip(0) eigenvectors = eigenvectors.flip(1) mainaxis = eigenvectors[:, 0] perpaxis = eigenvectors[:, 1] if perpaxis[0] < 0: perpaxis = -perpaxis mainaxis = -mainaxis xmin, xmax = float(xyz[:, 0].min()), float(xyz[:, 0].max()) ymin, ymax = float(xyz[:, 1].min()), float(xyz[:, 1].max()) zmin, zmax = float(xyz[:, 2].min()), float(xyz[:, 2].max()) zcentre = (zmin + zmax) / 2.0 proj = xy @ mainaxis projmin = float(proj.min()) projmax = float(proj.max()) # 2. Intrinsics fovy = math.radians(config.fovydeg) focal = config.imageheight / (2.0 math.tan(fovy / 2.0)) intrinsics = torch.tensor([focal, focal, config.imagewidth / 2.0, config.imageheight / 2.0], device=device) # 3. Stations margin = config.marginfactor extentmin = projmin margin extentmax = projmax margin stationsxy = [] denom = max(config.numstations - 1, 1) for i in range(config.numstations): t = extentmin + (extentmax - extentmin) i / denom onwall = centrexy + t mainaxis sx = float(torch.clamp(onwall[0], xmin, xmax)) sy = float(torch.clamp(onwall[1], ymin, ymax)) stationsxy.append((sx, sy)) # 4. Density Grid alldists = [config.distance] if config.fardistance > 0 and config.fardistance != config.distance: alldists.append(config.fardistance) maxdist = max(alldists) gridres = 5.0 gridpad = maxdist + 2.0 gridres gridnx = max(3, int((xmax - xmin + 2 gridpad) / gridres)) gridny = max(3, int((ymax - ymin + 2 gridpad) / gridres)) xbins = torch.linspace(xmin - gridpad, xmin - gridpad + gridnx gridres, gridnx + 1, device=device) ybins = torch.linspace(ymin - gridpad, ymin - gridpad + gridny gridres, gridny + 1, device=device) xidx = torch.bucketize(xyz[:, 0], xbins) - 1 yidx = torch.bucketize(xyz[:, 1], ybins) - 1 valid = (xidx >= 0) & (xidx < gridnx) & (yidx >= 0) & (yidx < gridny) xidx, yidx = xidx[valid], yidx[valid] density = torch.zeros(gridnx, gridny, device=device) density.indexput((xidx, yidx), torch.ones(xidx.shape[0], device=device), accumulate=True) def haspointsnear(cx: float, cy: float, radius: float) -> bool: # Grid window query approximation to check density within radius gx = int((cx - (xmin - gridpad)) / gridres) gy = int((cy - (ymin - gridpad)) / gridres) mingx = max(0, gx - int(radius / gridres) - 1) maxgx = min(gridnx - 1, gx + int(radius / gridres) + 1) mingy = max(0, gy - int(radius / gridres) - 1) maxgy = min(gridny - 1, gy + int(radius / gridres) + 1) return density[mingx:maxgx+1, mingy:maxgy+1].sum() > 0 poses = [] sides = [1.0, -1.0] if config.viewbothsides else [1.0] for dist in alldists: for sidesign in sides: for sx, sy in stationsxy: camx = sx + float(perpaxis[0]) dist sidesign camy = sy + float(perpaxis[1]) dist sidesign camz = zcentre radius = max(15.0, dist 0.5) if not haspointsnear(camx, camy, radius): continue for pitchdeg in config.pitchanglesdeg: pitchrad = math.radians(pitchdeg) targetz = camz - math.tan(pitchrad) dist targetx, targety = sx, sy campos = torch.tensor([camx, camy, camz], device=device) tgt = torch.tensor([targetx, targety, targetz], device=device) extrinsics = makeextrinsics(campos, tgt) poses.append(CameraPose( extrinsics=extrinsics, intrinsics=intrinsics, position=(camx, camy, camz), target=(targetx, targety, targetz), pitchdeg=pitchdeg)) return poses def makeextrinsics(campos: torch.Tensor, target: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: up = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], dtype=campos.dtype, device=campos.device) forward = target - campos forward = forward / (forward.norm() + 1e-12) cosangle = torch.abs(torch.dot(forward, up)) if cosangle > 0.999: refaxis = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0], dtype=campos.dtype, device=campos.device) else: refaxis = up right = torch.cross(refaxis, forward) right = right / (right.norm() + 1e-12) upcorrected = torch.cross(forward, right) upcorrected = upcorrected / (upcorrected.norm() + 1e-12) Rc2w = torch.stack([right, upcorrected, forward], dim=1) Rw2c = Rc2w.T extr = torch.eye(4, dtype=campos.dtype, device=campos.device) extr[:3,:3] = Rw2c extr[:3, 3] = -(Rw2c @ campos) return extr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: When the forward vector is nearly parallel to the world up vector (e.g., overhead cameras), the cross product for the right vector vanishes. This is handled by checking |\mathbf{forward} \cdot \mathbf{up}| > 0.999 and switching the reference axis to world X [1, 0, 0]. Division by Zero: If numstations is 1, the denominator in station interpolation becomes 0. This is handled by using \max(	ext{num\stations} - 1, 1). Boundary Clamping: Stations are clamped to the actual point cloud bounding box to ensure they remain within the data extent. Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the context of the Point-Splatting Multi-View 2D Rendering Pipeline for rendering large-scale outdoor point clouds, specifically ancient city walls. It replaces the hardcoded, room-centric camera poses used in earlier methods like Virtual-Multi-View-Fusion with a data-driven approach based on Principal Component Analysis. name: Sparse Trajectory Generation
head: Mapping-based Trajectory Selection
body: Sparse Trajectory Generation reduces a dense camera path to a subset of frames by filtering based on a predefined mapping file. It differs from Parametric Path Generation by relying on discrete frame indices rather than continuous mathematical functions. It differs from Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by acting as a post-processing filter rather than a generative model. Inputs and Outputs Input: ftrajectory, a list of camera frames; mapping, a list of entries where each entry contains a frame index. Output: sparsetraj, a list of camera frames corresponding to the selected indices. Data Structures ftrajectory: A sequence of frame objects. mapping: A sequence of entries. Each entry m is structured such that m[1] holds the 1-based frame index. sparsetraj: A dynamic list of frame objects. Steps 1. Initialize an empty list sparsetraj. 2. Iterate through each entry m in mapping. 3. Convert m[1] to an integer, then subtract 1 to adjust for 0-based indexing. 4. Append ftrajectory[index] to sparsetraj. 5. Return sparsetraj. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatesparsetrajectory(ftrajectory, mapping): sparsetraj = [] for m in mapping: frameindex1based = int(m[1]) index = frameindex1based - 1 sparsetraj.append(ftrajectory[index]) return sparsetraj Parameters and Edge Cases If mapping is empty, the result is an empty list. If index is out of bounds for ftrajectory, a robust implementation should check bounds before access. The 1600-frame threshold for optional sparsification applies only to the alignment variant, not the general generation method. Aligns a sparse camera trajectory to a ground truth trajectory using RANSAC-based point cloud registration. It differs from standard global alignment by handling sparse, potentially noisy inputs through iterative sampling, and optionally sparsifies the input trajectory if a mapping file is provided and the trajectory length exceeds 1600 frames. For the Waymo dataset, generates testing views by translating the camera by 2 to 3 meters or rotating it by 10 to 15 degrees horizontally. For LLFF and Mip-NeRF 360, partitions the full trajectory into training and testing sets to ensure ground truth images exist for extrapolated views. For scenes lacking obvious extrapolated trajectories, sparsifies the training views to create relative extrapolated trajectories. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the size of the mapping list, O(N), where N is the number of entries. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of selected frames, O(K), where K is the length of sparsetraj. Strengths: Simple to implement; computationally inexpensive; deterministic based on the mapping file. Limitations: Does not optimize for view coverage or redundancy; relies entirely on the quality of the provided mapping file. When to use: When a specific subset of frames is known a priori to be sufficient or required. name: Trajectory Alignment (RANSAC)
head: RANSAC Trajectory Alignment, Trajectory Alignment via RANSAC
body: Aligns a sparse camera trajectory to a ground truth trajectory using RANSAC-based point cloud registration. It differs from standard global alignment by handling sparse, potentially noisy inputs through iterative sampling, and optionally sparsifies the input trajectory if a mapping file is provided and the trajectory length exceeds 1600 frames. Inputs: gttrajcol: Ground truth trajectory (column-major format). mapfile: Optional mapping file containing nsampledframes, ntotalframes, and a mapping array where each row is [frameindex, totalframeindex]. gttrans: Optional transformation matrix to apply to the ground truth point cloud. randomvar: Noise magnitude multiplier. Default: 0.0. If < 1e-5, no noise is added. Outputs: Aligned trajectory poses. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A set of 3D points derived from trajectory camera positions. Correspondence Vector: A list of index pairs [i, i] indicating self-correspondence between the source and target point clouds. Steps: 1. Parse Mapping: If mapfile exists, parse nsampledframes, ntotalframes, and the mapping array. 2. Sparsify (Conditional): If mapfile is provided AND the trajectory length > 1600, use the mapping to select specific frames. If trajectory length <= 1600 or no mapfile is present, use the full trajectory. 3. Convert to Point Cloud: Convert the selected ground truth trajectory gttrajcol into a point cloud trajpcdcol. 4. Transform Ground Truth: If gttrans is provided, apply it to trajpcdcol. 5. Create Correspondences: Generate a correspondence vector corres where each point in the source trajectory corresponds to itself in the target trajectory: corres = [[0,0], [1,1],..., [N-1, N-1]]. 6. RANSAC Alignment: Perform RANSAC registration using trajpcdcol and the source trajectory point cloud with the following parameters: maxiteration: 100,000. maxvalidation: 100,000. Add noise to the source points scaled by randomvar if randomvar >= 1e-5. 7. Apply Transformation: Apply the best-fit transformation found by RANSAC to the source trajectory. Args: gttrajcol: Ground truth trajectory in column-major format. mapfile: Optional path to mapping file. gttrans: Optional transformation matrix for ground truth. randomvar: Noise magnitude multiplier. Returns: Aligned trajectory. """ # Step 1 & 2: Parse mapping and sparsify if necessary # Note: Implementation details for mapfile parsing depend on specific file format. # Assuming a helper function exists or the data is pre-loaded. # If mapfile is provided and len(gttrajcol) > 1600, select frames based on mapping. # Otherwise, use full trajectory. # Placeholder for actual file parsing logic not detailed in source. if mapfile is not None and len(gttrajcol) > 1600: # Parse mapfile to get indices # indices = parsemappingfile(mapfile) # selectedtraj = gttrajcol[indices] selectedtraj = gttrajcol # Placeholder else: selectedtraj = gttrajcol # Step 3: Convert to point cloud # Assuming converttrajectorytopointcloud extracts positions from trajectory. trajpcdcol = converttrajectorytopointcloud(selectedtraj) # Step 4: Transform ground truth if provided if gttrans is not None: trajpcdcol.transform(gttrans) # Step 5: Create correspondence vector # Correspondence is self-matching: point i in source matches point i in target npoints = len(selectedtraj) corresindices = np.array([[i, i] for i in range(npoints)]) corres = o3d.utility.Vector2iVector(corresindices) # Step 6: RANSAC Alignment # Assuming sourcetrajpcd is the trajectory to be aligned. # sourcetrajpcd = converttrajectorytopointcloud(sourcetrajectory) # Add noise if randomvar >= 1e-5 if randomvar >= 1e-5: # Add Gaussian noise scaled by randomvar to source points pass # Perform RANSAC registration # open3d.registrationransacbasedoncorrespondence is used here. # maxcorrespondencedistance and other criteria are not specified in sources. # Using default values or typical values for point cloud registration. # maxiteration=100000, maxvalidation=100000 are specified. # result = o3d.registration.registrationransacbasedoncorrespondence( # sourcetrajpcd, # trajpcdcol, # corres, # maxcorrespondencedistance=0.1, # Not given in sources. Typical value. # estimationmethod=o3d.pipelines.registration.TransformationEstimationPointToPoint(), # ransacn=3, # Not given. Typical for point-to-point. # checks=100000, # criteria=o3d.pipelines.registration.RANSACConvergenceCriteria(100000, 100000) #) # Apply result transformation to source trajectory # alignedtraj = applytransformation(sourcetrajectory, result.transformation) return selectedtraj # Placeholder return def converttrajectorytopointcloud(traj): """ Converts a trajectory to a point cloud. Implementation detail not provided in source. Assumes extraction of 3D positions. """ pcd = o3d.geometry.PointCloud() # Extract positions from traj # pcd.points = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(trajpositions) return pcd For fewer than 9 input views, performs alignment by sampling every possible pair of cameras in one set, computing the Sim(3) transformation relating it to the same camera pair in the other trajectory. The global Sim(3) transformation leading to the lowest average camera alignment error is kept. For 9 or more views, it uses the standard Umeyama algorithm. Time Complexity: High for the RANSAC variant due to 100,000 iterations and validation steps. The RANSAC-inspired variant for <9 views involves checking all camera pairs, which is O(N^2) for N views. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of trajectory points for point cloud storage. Strengths: Robust to noise and outliers in sparse trajectories. Handles very few views (<9) where standard algorithms fail. Limitations: Unstable for very few views if not using the RANSAC-inspired approach. Sparsification is only applied if trajectory length > 1600. When to use: When aligning sparse, noisy trajectories where standard global alignment (e.g., Umeyama) is unstable due to insufficient views. Originated in the context of 2D Gaussian Splatting and sparse pose alignment for NeRF reconstruction. The RANSAC-based approach was adopted to handle the instability of standard alignment methods (like Umeyama) when dealing with very few input views (<9).
