name: Dataset Build Pipeline
head: build_dataset workflow
body: The Dataset Build Pipeline orchestrates the creation of a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) dataset by managing the lifecycle of a build session, from initialization through point sampling and sequential rendering to final output writing. It differs from novel view synthesis rendering by explicitly handling the generation of the underlying 3DGS representation from mesh data before rendering frames, and from dataset preparation methods by providing the procedural workflow for constructing the dataset files rather than just filtering existing ones. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A scene object, a target collection object, dataset settings (snapshot), an output directory path, and sampling parameters. Outputs: A directory structure containing rendered images, camera information, and diagnostic logs. Data Structures: The core state is held in a BuildSession object with the following fields: scene: Object representing the 3D scene. targetcollection: Object representing the collection of assets. snapshot: DatasetSettingsSnapshot object containing configuration. outputdir: Path to the final output directory. imagesdir: Path to the subdirectory for rendered images. renderstate: RenderState object tracking rendering progress. tempcameraobj: Temporary camera object for sampling. focuspoint: Vector defining the center of interest. camerainfo: dict storing camera parameters. diagnostics: DiagnosticsSession for logging. samples: list[CameraSample] of generated camera poses. frames: list[dict] of frame metadata. warnings: list[WarningRecord] of issues encountered. warningkeys: set[str] of unique warning identifiers. pointstate: PointSamplingState | None holding mesh data and sampling parameters. Steps: 1. Initialize: Call begindatasetbuild to create the BuildSession with the target collection, settings, output directory, temporary camera, and initial camera samples. 2. Prepare Sampling: Call preparepointsampling to populate session.pointstate with mesh data and sampling parameters. 3. Generate Points: Call runpointsamplingsync to generate the 3DGS points from the prepared state. 4. Render Loop: While hasremainingframes(session) is true, call rendernextframe(session) to render and save each frame sequentially. 5. Finalize: Call writeoutputs(session) to write all accumulated data (images, camera info, diagnostics) to the output directory. 6. Cleanup: In a finally block, call cleanupdatasetbuild(session) to release resources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rundatasetbuildpipeline(scene, targetcollection, settings, outputdir): session = begindatasetbuild( targetcollection=targetcollection, settings=settings, outputdir=outputdir) try: # Prepare point sampling state preparepointsampling(session) # Generate 3DGS points runpointsamplingsync(session) # Render frames sequentially while hasremainingframes(session): rendernextframe(session) # Write final outputs writeoutputs(session) finally: # Release resources cleanupdatasetbuild(session) Parameters and Edge Cases: Point Sampling: The sampling process may spawn a worker process. Progress is polled via a JSON file at workerstate.progresspath. If the worker fails, resources in tempdir are cleaned up. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The loop condition hasremainingframes ensures all planned views are rendered. If pointstate is accessed before preparation, a DatasetBuildError is raised. A dataset preparation process for training Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FCGS), involving generating 3DGS from multi-view scenes and filtering for quality. It uses the DL3DV dataset containing approximately 7,000 multi-view scenes. Scenes are trained to generate 3DGS at 960P resolution, taking about 60 GPU days on NVIDIA L40s. Low-quality scenes are filtered out to obtain 6,770 valid 3DGS scenes, which are then randomly split with 100 for testing and the remainder for training. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Generating 3DGS for the DL3DV dataset at 960P resolution requires approximately 60 GPU days on NVIDIA L40s. Scaling: The pipeline is designed to handle large-scale datasets (e.g., ~7K scenes) but requires significant computational resources for the point sampling and rendering phases. Strengths: Provides a structured, automated workflow for creating high-quality 3DGS datasets with diagnostic tracking. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large scene counts; dependent on the quality of the input mesh and camera poses. When to use: When constructing a custom 3DGS dataset from mesh data and camera trajectories. When not to use: When using pre-existing datasets or when computational resources are insufficient for the scale of the scene collection. The pipeline is part of the 3DGS dataset builder ecosystem, designed to automate the creation of training data for 3D Gaussian Splatting models. The DL3DV-GS variant was developed to support the training of FCGS, leveraging the large-scale DL3DV dataset to provide abundant 3DGS representations for compression research. yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, https://github.com/yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fast Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.08017, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sparse View Selection and Dataset Configuration
head: Dataset Configuration, Sparse View Selection
body: Sparse View Selection and Dataset Configuration defines the protocol for selecting a minimal subset of input images and preparing the corresponding ground truth geometry for training and evaluating novel view synthesis and geometric reconstruction models. It addresses the challenge of training neural representations when full multi-view coverage is computationally prohibitive or unavailable. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Novel View Synthesis Rendering by its focus on input data curation rather than rendering, and from Data Augmentation by its deterministic or specific stochastic selection of source views rather than transformation of existing ones. Inputs: A set of source images with known camera poses. Ground truth 3D geometry (point clouds or meshes) if available. Dataset-specific configuration parameters (number of training/test views, visibility thresholds). Outputs: A training dataset consisting of N{train} selected views. A testing dataset consisting of N{test} selected views. A filtered ground truth geometry mask. Data Structures: ViewSet: A list of objects, each containing image data, camera intrinsic parameters, and extrinsic pose matrices. GeometryMask: A boolean mask or point cloud subset indicating valid 3D points. Steps: 1. Dataset Selection: Choose the target dataset (e.g., DTU, Tanks & Temples, Mip-NeRF 360, GigaNVS) based on the evaluation goal (geometric reconstruction vs. novel view synthesis). 2. View Sampling: For DTU: Select exactly 4 views for both training and testing. For Tanks & Temples and Mip-NeRF 360: Select 6 views for training and 6 neighboring views for testing. For GigaNVS: Utilize 6 images per scene. 3. Geometry Filtering: Sample the ground truth 3D geometry. Calculate visibility for each 3D point from all available source views. Preserve only points visible from at least 2 views. 4. Noise/Background Removal: For Tanks & Temples testing, explicitly exclude irrelevant point clouds such as sky regions and background vegetation to improve result quality. 5. Evaluation Preparation: Pair the selected views with the filtered geometry for metric calculation (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS for images; surface metrics for geometry). Parameters: N{train}: Number of training views. Typical values: 4 (DTU), 6 (Tanks & Temples, Mip-NeRF 360, GigaNVS). N{test}: Number of testing views. Typical values: 4 (DTU), 6 (Tanks & Temples, Mip-NeRF 360). V{min}: Minimum visibility count for geometry retention. Value: 2. Edge Cases: Occlusion: Points visible from only one view are discarded, potentially creating holes in the ground truth geometry if the sparse views are insufficiently overlapping. Background Artifacts: Failure to exclude sky/vegetation in datasets like Tanks & Temples can degrade geometric evaluation metrics. Light Cone Construction is a method for generating synthetic astronomical observations (imaging or spectroscopy) from cosmological simulation data by stacking discrete redshift slices into a continuous line-of-sight volume. Random multi-view sampling for training is a data selection strategy used in inverse rendering and novel view synthesis to construct minibatches from a sparse set of input images. Time and Memory Complexity: The selection process is O(N) with respect to the number of source views for sampling. Geometry filtering is O(P \cdot V) where P is the number of points and V is the number of views, requiring visibility checks. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces computational cost for training and evaluation; standardizes benchmarks across different algorithms. Limitations: Sparse views (e.g., 4-6 views) present a significant challenge for reconstruction, potentially leading to ambiguous geometry or poor novel view synthesis if the algorithm lacks strong priors. When to Use: Use when evaluating geometric reconstruction performance or novel view synthesis under resource constraints. Use when comparing algorithms on standard benchmarks (DTU, Tanks & Temples). When Not to Use: Do not use when full multi-view coverage is available and computational resources permit, as sparse configurations artificially limit performance. This configuration is primarily used to evaluate geometric reconstruction performance and novel view synthesis capabilities in inverse rendering and neural rendering research. The specific configurations for DTU (4 views) and Tanks & Temples/Mip-NeRF 360 (6 views) have become standard benchmarks for assessing the effectiveness of algorithms like GBR (Generative Bundle Refinement) in handling sparse input data. GBR: Generative Bundle Refinement for High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting With Enhanced Mesh Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2025.3596613, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Random Multi-view Sampling for Training
head: Fitting Multi-view Images Baselines, Random View Subsetting
body: Random multi-view sampling for training constructs minibatches by sampling rays from random views and selecting a random subset of views at each epoch. It addresses the problem of efficiently training neural representations when available training views are limited or computationally expensive to process. Unlike deterministic selection methods, this approach relies on stochastic diversity rather than geometric constraints on view adjacency, distinguishing it from Light Cone Construction. Inputs: A set of N training images \mathcal{I} = \{I1, \dots, IN\} with associated camera poses, a neural network architecture (e.g., MLP conditioned on positional encodings or hash encoding), and a target minibatch size B. Outputs: A minibatch of B views and their corresponding rays/points for a single training iteration. Data Structures: View Index List: An array of integers [0, \dots, N-1] representing the available training images. Minibatch Indices: A list of B unique integers sampled from the View Index List. Steps: 1. Initialization: Store the total number of training views N. 2. Epoch Loop: For each training epoch: a. Random Subset Selection: Sample B distinct indices from the range [0, N-1] without replacement. Let this set be \mathcal{B}. b. Ray Generation: For each view i \in \mathcal{B}, generate rays according to the camera model (see Ray generation and camera models). c. Forward Pass: Render the scene using the current neural representation for all rays in \mathcal{B}. d. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss between rendered pixels and ground truth pixels for all views in \mathcal{B}. e. Backward Pass: Update network parameters using automatic differentiation. Parameters: Batch Size (B): The number of views sampled per iteration. Epochs: The number of full passes over the dataset. For baselines, grid search over width, depth, and hash-grid size matches storage costs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainrandommultiview(model, images, poses, batchsize, numepochs, learningrate): nviews = len(images) for epoch in range(numepochs): # Step 2a: Random subset selection without replacement indices = list(range(nviews)) for i in range(batchsize): j = random.randint(i, nviews - 1) indices[i], indices[j] = indices[j], indices[i] batchindices = indices[:batchsize] for idx in batchindices: # Step 2b: Generate rays from camera pose and image dimensions # rays =... # Step 2c: Forward pass rendered = model(rays) # Step 2d: Loss computation (MSE) loss = sum((r - gt)2 for r, gt in zip(rendered, images[idx].flatten())) / len(rendered) # Step 2e: Backward pass and parameter update loss.backward() for p in model.parameters(): p -= learningrate p.grad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small N: If the number of training views N is smaller than the batch size B, sampling without replacement is impossible. View Correlation: Random sampling may occasionally select highly correlated views (e.g., adjacent frames), leading to redundant gradients. Precision: When using hash encodings for positional encoding, ensure the hash grid size is tuned to match the storage cost of the baseline models to ensure fair comparison. A deterministic variant used in sparse-view reconstruction to select training views. It selects the first training image randomly, then iteratively selects remaining images by finding the camera center farthest from the already selected set in the SfM frame. Multiple random seeds are run per scene/view count and the mean is reported. A key pitfall is that reduced-view conditions often reuse the relative calibration and silhouette registration of the full sparse capture, modeling a pre-calibrated-rig regime rather than a genuine sparse capture which would require wide-baseline SfM calibration. A strategy to obtain a patch set Sp from an image I to ensure all areas are trained and enhance synthetic quality from different views. It shifts the patch center (\Delta x, \Delta y) and adjusts the focal lengths by a zoom ratio \alpha. The patch size w \times h is kept less than 15% of the total image resolution W \times H. This method manages GPU memory constraints while training on high-resolution images (e.g., KITTI, Brno Urban). A strategy to sample driving scene data based on synthetic quality, strengthening the model to learn sparse regions and reducing training time. It calculates a synthetic quality metric Q(Ie) for each image Ie in the set Se using perceptual loss. The top n samples with the worst performance are selected as training data for the next phase. The sampling ratio is typically set to 80%. This method is chosen when the input point cloud has significant holes or outliers, and the goal is to focus training on difficult-to-render regions. A setting used to evaluate whether improvements under multi-light conditions are due to extra input images rather than lighting diversity. For each view, one image is randomly selected as training input from the 3 images under different lighting conditions, guaranteeing the same number of training images as a single-light setting. On the synthetic dataset, this setting achieves a Normal MAE of 3.670, Albedo PSNR of 29.320, and NVS PSNR of 34.100. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: In texture fitting baselines, training uses random subsets to form minibatches at each epoch. HKTex consistently outperforms high-resolution vertex colors and neural baselines across all evaluation metrics while requiring substantially less storage. Improvements in LPIPS and SSIM indicate that constraining the representation directly to the surface manifold preserves perceptual details and structural consistency more effectively during inverse rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement; does not require complex geometric analysis for view selection. Limitations: May select redundant views in early epochs; does not guarantee coverage of specific geometric features unless combined with other strategies. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from inverse rendering and neural texture fitting literature. It was used as a baseline in "Heat Kernel Textures the Geodesic Gaussians That Do Not Splat" to compare against the proposed HKTex model, demonstrating that constraining representation to the surface manifold provides a strong inductive bias. It is also referenced in the context of sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (CADSplat) and large-scale neural scene rendering for autonomous driving (READ). name: Light Cone Construction
head: Light cone projection, Light rays
body: Light Cone Construction is a method for generating synthetic astronomical observations (imaging or spectroscopy) from cosmological simulation data by stacking discrete redshift slices into a continuous line-of-sight volume. It solves the problem of creating realistic light cones from periodic simulation boxes that do not natively span the required redshift range, while minimizing redundant sampling of the same physical structures. It is distinguished from standard volume rendering by its specific handling of cosmological distance metrics, periodic domain wrapping, and the statistical generation of unique, non-overlapping sightlines. Inputs: Observer redshift (z{obs}) and redshift interval [z{min}, z{max}]. Simulation datasets at various redshifts. Cosmological parameters: \OmegaM (matter density), \Omegak (curvature density), \Omega\Lambda (cosmological constant density). For Light Cone Projections: angular field of view (\theta) and image resolution. For Light Rays: arbitrary-angle rays. Outputs: A stack of datasets ordered by redshift. For Projections: a 2D image or data cube representing the integrated signal along the line of sight. For Rays: a list of ray segments, each containing intersected pixels, path lengths (dl), and assigned redshifts. Dataset Stack: A list of simulation data objects ordered from highest redshift (z{max}) to lowest (z{min}). Ray Segment (for Light Rays): An array containing indices of all pixels intersected by the ray within the dataset and the path length dl through each intersected pixel. Projection Object (for Light Cone Projections): A pre-computed projection of the entire lateral domain of a dataset, enabling multiple light cone projections to sample different regions without re-projecting the full volume. Expansion Factor E(z): E(z) \equiv \sqrt{\OmegaM (1 + z)^3 + \Omegak (1 + z)^2 + \Omega\Lambda} where \OmegaM, \Omegak, \Omega\Lambda are the energy density contributions of matter, curvature, and the cosmological constant, respectively. Angular Size Distance DA: The width of the sampled region in the image plane for a field of view \theta is (1+z) DA \theta. DA is defined as: DA = \begin{cases} \frac{DH}{\sqrt{|\Omegak|}} \frac{\sinh(\sqrt{|\Omegak|} DC)}{1+z} & \text{for } \Omegak > 0 \\ \frac{DC}{1+z} & \text{for } \Omegak = 0 \\ \frac{DH}{\sqrt{|\Omegak|}} \frac{\sin(\sqrt{|\Omegak|} DC)}{1+z} & \text{for } \Omegak < 0 \end{cases} where DC is the comoving distance and DH is the Hubble distance. Column Density: For a ray segment, the column density N contributed by a physical density \rho over a path length element dl is: N = \rho \times dl. Fraction of Box Length: The user may specify a fraction of the total simulation box length to calculate the maximum allowable redshift step \delta z between datasets, rather than using the full box length. Maximum Common Volume: A user-specified limit on the volume overlap between different light cone projections to ensure statistical independence. 1. Select Datasets: Use time series machinery to select simulation datasets appropriate for the requested redshift interval [z{min}, z{max}]. 2. Build Stack: Initialize an empty stack and add the dataset with the redshift closest to z{max} as the first element. 3. Iterate Downward: a. Calculate \delta z, the redshift interval corresponding to the length of the simulation box, noting that \delta z is not constant with redshift. b. Determine the target redshift for the next dataset: z{target} = z{current} - \delta z. c. Select the dataset whose redshift is closest to, but no less than, z{target}. d. Add this dataset to the stack and repeat until the lower limit z{min} is reached. Note: The user may constrain the maximum \delta z to be a fraction of the full box length to ensure smoother transitions. 4. Generate Sightlines (Randomization): For each dataset in the stack, choose a random projection axis and center for the projected region to minimize sampling the same structures multiple times, exploiting the periodicity of the computational domain. For Light Rays, assign a random orientation to each ray segment. 5. Compute Projections/Rays: Project the full lateral domain of each dataset; the comoving radial distance determines the fraction of the box used in the line of sight, and the image width is determined by (1+z) DA \theta. For rays, identify all intersected pixels and calculate the path length dl through each. 6. Assign Redshifts: For each length element in a ray, assign a unique redshift based on the dataset's redshift and the point's position along the ray, assuming a smooth Hubble flow. 7. Ensure Uniqueness (Optional): Use a unique solution generator to find realizations with a user-specified maximum common volume. The generator first attempts to vary only the lateral randomization, allowing a single set of projection objects to be reused, before attempting fully unique randomization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructlightcone(observerredshift, zmin, zmax, datasets, cosmology, boxlength, maxdeltazfraction=1.0): # Step 1: Preliminary selection of datasets for the interval relevant = [d for d in datasets if zmin <= d.redshift <= zmax] relevant.sort(key=lambda d: d.redshift, reverse=True) if not relevant: return [] stack = [] currentz = zmax # Step 2: Add dataset closest to upper limit currentdataset = min(relevant, key=lambda d: abs(d.redshift - currentz)) stack.append(currentdataset) currentz = currentdataset.redshift # Step 3: Iterate downward until lower limit while currentz > zmin: # Calculate deltaz for box length (not constant with redshift) deltaz = computecomovingredshiftstep(boxlength, currentz, cosmology) # User may specify smaller fraction of box length deltaz = min(deltaz, maxdeltazfraction computecomovingredshiftstep(boxlength, currentz, cosmology)) targetz = currentz - deltaz # Select next dataset closest to, but no less than, targetz candidates = [d for d in relevant if d.redshift >= targetz] if not candidates: break nextdataset = min(candidates, key=lambda d: abs(d.redshift - targetz)) if nextdataset not in stack: stack.append(nextdataset) currentz = nextdataset.redshift else: remaining = [d for d in candidates if d not in stack] if remaining: nextdataset = min(remaining, key=lambda d: abs(d.redshift - targetz)) stack.append(nextdataset) currentz = nextdataset.redshift else: break return stack def computecomovingredshiftstep(boxlength, z, cosmology): # Project full lateral domain projobj = projectfulllateraldomain(dataset, axis) projections[dataset] = projobj # For rays: arbitrary-angle ray with random orientation for in range(numrays): direction = normalize([random.uniform(-1, 1) for in range(3)]) origin = [random.uniform(0, 1) for in range(3)] intersections = traceraythroughgrid(origin, direction, dataset.grid) raysegment = { 'pixels': [p.index for p in intersections], 'pathlengths': [p.dl for p in intersections], 'direction': direction, 'origin': origin } rays.append(raysegment) # Not given in the sources. pass Non-constant \delta z: The redshift interval corresponding to the simulation box length changes with redshift, requiring recalculation at each stacking step. Periodicity: The method relies on the periodicity of the computational domain to randomize projection axes and centers without introducing boundary artifacts. Sampling Redundancy: Without randomizing the projection axis and center for each dataset, the same large-scale structures may be sampled multiple times, biasing statistical analyses. Common Volume: If the maximum common volume is not specified or set too high, multiple light cone projections may sample the same volume, violating the assumption of independent realizations. Time Complexity: The initial dataset stacking is linear with respect to the number of datasets in the stack. Projection of the full lateral domain is performed once per dataset, making subsequent light cone projections computationally cheap as they only sample different regions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full lateral projection for each dataset in the stack if multiple light cone projections are to be generated efficiently. Strengths: Efficiently generates multiple independent sightlines from a limited set of simulation boxes, and the pre-computation of full lateral projections allows for rapid generation of statistical samples. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of a smooth Hubble flow for redshift assignment along rays, which may not capture local velocity distortions unless explicitly modeled. When to Use: When generating synthetic observations (imaging or spectroscopy) from cosmological simulations that do not span the full redshift range of interest, or when statistical independence of multiple sightlines is required. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity modeling of local velocity fields or non-periodic boundary conditions is critical, or when computational resources are insufficient to store full lateral projections for all datasets. Light Cone Construction was implemented in the yt analysis toolkit, building on earlier work by Hallman et al. (2007, 2009). The method leverages yt's projection machinery to handle the complexities of projecting data from periodic simulation boxes onto a light cone. It is primarily used in astrophysics for creating synthetic surveys of the universe, such as quasar absorption line studies or galaxy distribution maps, allowing researchers to compare simulation predictions directly with observational data. name: Data Augmentation
head: Random Rotation Augmentation
body: Data augmentation generates diverse training samples from synthetic sensor data to improve model robustness and generalization. It addresses limited or biased training distributions by applying geometric transformations and inserting synthetic objects. It builds on Synthetic Dataset Generation by adding stochastic variation to poses, signs, and scene content. The method consists of two primary strategies: random rotation of existing data and dataset-specific sign balancing. Inputs: Point cloud data P, camera poses T, sensor measurements Zt = \{vi, r{t,i}\}, and optional CAD models. Outputs: Augmented dataset D containing samples (pj, vj, f^j, i^j, s^j). The dataset sample structure is defined as: pj \in \mathbb{R}^3: Ray origin. vj \in S^2: Ray direction. f^j \in \mathbb{R}: SDDF measurement. i^j \in \{-1, 1\}: Intersection indicator. s^j \in \{-1, 1\}: Sign indicator. To obtain diverse training samples, random rotations are applied to both point cloud data and camera poses. 1. Generate random rotation angles \thetax, \thetay, \thetaz. 2. Construct rotation matrices Rx(\thetax), Ry(\thetay), Rz(\thetaz). 3. Compute total rotation R{total} = Rz(\thetaz) Ry(\thetay) Rx(\thetax). 4. Apply R{total} to all points in the point cloud. 5. Apply R{total} to the rotation component of all camera poses. Parameters: \thetax \in [-\pi/64, \pi/64]. \thetay \in [-\pi/64, \pi/64]. \thetaz \in [-\pi, \pi]. For Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF) models, the initial dataset is unbalanced in sign indicators. 1. Generate Positive Samples: For each ray measurement (vi, r{t,i}) from sensor position pt and orientation Rt: pj = pt vj = Rt vi f^j = r{t,i} i^j = 1 s^j = 1 2. Generate Negative Samples: For each positive sample (pj, vj, f^j, i^j, s^j), generate a corresponding negative sample: p' = pj + (f^j + \epsilon) vj v'j = vj f'^j = -\epsilon i'^j = 1 s'^j = -1 Where \epsilon > 0 is a small offset. Pitfalls: The initial dataset has all s^j = 1 and f^j \ge 0, causing sign imbalance. Intersection indicator augmentation (i^j = -1) is not performed because generating non-intersecting rays is inefficient and does not improve reconstruction results. For downstream tasks, synthetic objects are inserted into scenes to enhance diversity. 1. Select a CAD model (e.g., from a library of 283 car models and 30 construction vehicles). 2. Randomize the object's appearance (e.g., paint color from 60 diverse options). 3. Apply Gaussian perturbation to the object's orientation with \sigma = 15^\circ. 4. Insert the object into the scene. 5. Handle occlusion naively by comparing the depth map of the scene with the depth map of the inserted object, removing the previous occlusion check. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def randomrotationaugmentation(pointcloud, cameraposes, seed=None): """Applies random rotations to point cloud and camera poses.""" if seed is not None: np.random.seed(seed) thetax = np.random.uniform(-np.pi / 64, np.pi / 64) thetay = np.random.uniform(-np.pi / 64, np.pi / 64) thetaz = np.random.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi) Rx = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, np.cos(thetax), -np.sin(thetax)], [0, np.sin(thetax), np.cos(thetax)]]) Ry = np.array([[np.cos(thetay), 0, np.sin(thetay)], [0, 1, 0], [-np.sin(thetay), 0, np.cos(thetay)]]) Rz = np.array([[np.cos(thetaz), -np.sin(thetaz), 0], [np.sin(thetaz), np.cos(thetaz), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) Rtotal = Rz @ Ry @ Rx augmentedpc = (Rtotal @ pointcloud.T).T augmentedposes = [] for pose in cameraposes: newrot = Rtotal @ pose[:3,:3] newpos = Rtotal @ pose[:3, 3] newpose = np.eye(4) newpose[:3,:3] = newrot newpose[:3, 3] = newpos augmentedposes.append(newpose) return augmentedpc, augmentedposes def generatesddfdataset(sensordata, epsilon=1e-3): """Generates SDDF dataset with sign balancing. sensordata: list of tuples (pt, Rt, vi, rti)""" dataset = [] for pt, Rt, vi, rti in sensordata: pj = pt vj = Rt @ vi fstar = rti istar = 1 sstar = 1 dataset.append((pj, vj, fstar, istar, sstar)) pprime = pj + (fstar + epsilon) vj fprime = -epsilon sprime = -1 dataset.append((pprime, vj, fprime, istar, sprime)) return dataset def insertobjectaugmentation(scenedepth, objectvertices, objectcoloroptions, orientationsigmadeg=15): """Inserts an object into the scene with naive occlusion handling.""" # Select random color from 60 options color = np.random.choice(objectcoloroptions) # Apply Gaussian orientation perturbation with sigma = 15 degrees perturbation = np.random.normal(0, orientationsigmadeg, 3) # Construct rotation from perturbation Rx = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, np.cos(perturbation[0]), -np.sin(perturbation[0])], [0, np.sin(perturbation[0]), np.cos(perturbation[0])]]) Ry = np.array([[np.cos(perturbation[1]), 0, np.sin(perturbation[1])], [0, 1, 0], [-np.sin(perturbation[1]), 0, np.cos(perturbation[1])]]) Rz = np.array([[np.cos(perturbation[2]), -np.sin(perturbation[2]), 0], [np.sin(perturbation[2]), np.cos(perturbation[2]), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) Robj = Rz @ Ry @ Rx rotatedvertices = (Robj @ objectvertices.T).T # Standard projection to render object depth objectdepth = np.zeroslike(scenedepth) # Naive occlusion handling: compare depth maps mask = objectdepth < scenedepth compositedimage = np.where(mask[:,:, np.newaxis], color, scenedepth) return compositedimage A procedure to convert sensor poses and range measurements into a dataset D suitable for training the SDDF model, specifically addressing sign imbalance. It is chosen when training implicit signed distance functions that require balanced positive and negative samples. An approach that inserts synthetic CAD models (cars, construction vehicles) into scenes with randomized colors and orientation perturbation (\sigma = 15^\circ) to enhance diversity for downstream tasks. It is chosen when the training data lacks sufficient variety in object types or appearances. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves model robustness to pose variations and sign ambiguities. Object insertion enhances generalization to unseen objects. Limitations: Intersection indicator augmentation is omitted due to inefficiency and lack of benefit. Naive occlusion handling may produce artifacts compared to physically accurate occlusion checks. When to use: When training data is limited or biased towards specific poses/signs. When the target application involves diverse object appearances or poses. Data augmentation in this context originated from the need to train robust neural scene representations from synthetic data. Random rotation augmentation was introduced in the context of point cloud unsupervised pre-training using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Sign balancing for SDDF models was developed to address the inherent bias in range sensor data where all samples initially have positive signs. Object insertion augmentation was proposed for neural light field estimation to enhance diversity in street scene reconstruction. name: B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation
head: B-Spline Camera Path, Multidimensional B-Spline Interpolation for Camera Poses, Spline Interpolated Camera Path
body: B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation creates a smooth spline path between input keyframe camera poses using multidimensional B-spline interpolation. It solves the problem of discontinuous motion in volume rendering by ensuring positional and rotational continuity across the entire path. It differs from linear interpolation by providing higher-order continuity and from least-squares approximation by allowing exact interpolation of keyframes when the smoothing factor is zero, avoiding the introduction of artifacts not present in the source data. Inputs: poses: Array of shape (N, 3, 4) representing N input camera poses. ninterp: Integer, number of interpolated poses to generate between each pair of consecutive keyframes. splinedegree: Integer, polynomial degree of the B-spline. Default 5. smoothness: Float, smoothing factor for the spline fit. 0 forces exact interpolation through all points. Default 0.03. rotweight: Float, relative weighting of rotation vs. translation in the pose decomposition. Default 0.1. Outputs: newposes: Array of shape (M, 3, 4), where M = n\interp \times (N - 1), containing the interpolated camera poses. Data Structures: The method internally converts 3 \times 4 pose matrices into a structured point representation (P, L, U) where P is position, L is look-at, and U is up vector. These are concatenated into a single array of shape (N, 9) for interpolation. Steps: 1. Pose Decomposition: Convert each input pose matrix W \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} into three 3D vectors: Position (pos), Look-at (lookat), and Up (up). pos = W[:, 0:3, 3] lookat = W[:, 0:3, 3] - rot\weight \times W[:, 0:3, 2] up = W[:, 0:3, 3] + rot\weight \times W[:, 0:3, 1] Here, W[:, 0:3, 2] is the z-axis (forward direction) and W[:, 0:3, 1] is the y-axis (up direction) of the camera basis. 2. Spline Fitting: Construct a multidimensional B-spline curve S(u) that fits the sequence of points (posi, lookati, upi) for i=0 \dots N-1. Input to the fitter is the transposed array of shape (9, N). Degree k = \min(spline\degree, N - 1). Smoothness parameter s = smoothness. The fitter returns a tuple (tck, u) containing knots, coefficients, degree, and parameter values. 3. Evaluation: Sample the spline curve at M = n\interp \times (N - 1) points. Parameter vector u{eval} = \text{linspace}(0, 1, M, \text{endpoint=False}). Evaluate S(u{eval}) to get interpolated points of shape (M, 9). 4. Pose Reconstruction: Convert the interpolated (pos, lookat, up) vectors back into 3 \times 4 pose matrices. Extract pos, lookat, up from the interpolated points. Reconstruct the camera basis using viewmatrix(p - l, u - p, p). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.interpolate import splprep, splev def viewmatrix(lookdir, up, position): """Construct a 3x4 pose matrix from lookdir, up, and position.""" z = lookdir / np.linalg.norm(lookdir) x = np.cross(up, z) x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) y = np.cross(z, x) pose = np.zeros((3, 4)) pose[:, 0] = x pose[:, 1] = y pose[:, 2] = z pose[:, 3] = position return pose def posestopoints(poses, rotweight=0.1): """ Convert N poses of shape (N, 3, 4) to (N, 9) array of (pos, lookat, up). """ pos = poses[:,:3, 3] lookat = pos - rotweight poses[:,:3, 2] up = pos + rotweight poses[:,:3, 1] return np.concatenate([pos, lookat, up], axis=-1) def pointstoposes(points): """ Convert (N, 9) array of (pos, lookat, up) back to (N, 3, 4) poses. """ pos = points[:,:3] lookat = points[:, 3:6] up = points[:, 6:9] poses = np.zeros((points.shape[0], 3, 4)) for i in range(points.shape[0]): poses[i] = viewmatrix(pos[i] - lookat[i], up[i] - pos[i], pos[i]) return poses def generateinterpolatedpath(poses, ninterp=10, splinedegree=5, smoothness=0.03, rotweight=0.1): """ Generate smooth camera path using B-spline interpolation. Args: poses: (N, 3, 4) array of input poses. ninterp: Number of interpolated poses between keyframes. splinedegree: Degree of B-spline. smoothness: Smoothing factor (0 for exact interpolation). rotweight: Weight for rotation vs translation in decomposition. Returns: newposes: (M, 3, 4) array of interpolated poses, M = ninterp (N-1). """ N = poses.shape[0] # Step 1: Decompose poses points = posestopoints(poses, rotweight=rotweight) # Step 2: Fit B-spline # splprep expects points in shape (ndim, N), so we transpose tck, u = splprep(points.T, k=min(splinedegree, N - 1), s=smoothness) # Step 3: Evaluate spline M = ninterp (N - 1) ueval = np.linspace(0, 1, M, endpoint=False) newpoints = splev(ueval, tck) # splev returns list of arrays, one for each dimension. Stack them. newpoints = np.array(newpoints).T # Step 4: Reconstruct poses newposes = pointstoposes(newpoints) return newposes This variant extends the base B-spline interpolation to simultaneously interpolate per-frame exposure values, preventing flickering in rendered sequences. It identifies keyframe indices from a configuration file or directory listing, generates the camera path using the standard B-spline method, and then applies a separate 1D B-spline interpolation to the logarithm of exposure values. If exposure interpolation is enabled but exposure data is missing, it raises a ValueError. A higher smoothness value (e.g., 20) is typically used for exposure interpolation to ensure stability. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces visually smooth camera motion with continuous derivatives; handles both position and orientation in a unified framework; configurable smoothness allows trade-off between fidelity to keyframes and path smoothness. Limitations: Requires at least k+1 keyframes for a spline of degree k; exact interpolation (s=0) may lead to oscillations if keyframes are noisy or poorly distributed; the linear approximation of rotation via look-at/up vectors does not guarantee unit quaternion interpolation, potentially introducing slight scaling artifacts in the basis vectors. When to use: When generating smooth fly-throughs or orbit paths from sparse keyframes in volume rendering or NeRF training. When not to use: When exact physical camera constraints must be preserved without post-processing, or when the input poses are highly erratic and require robust fitting rather than interpolation. The method originates from the need to generate smooth camera trajectories for novel view synthesis and volume rendering, particularly in the context of NeRF and Gaussian Splatting pipelines. It is implemented in repositories such as google-research/multinerf and meshroomHub/mrGSplat. The approach leverages the mathematical properties of B-splines, specifically their local control and smoothness, to interpolate multidimensional data (position and orientation) simultaneously. google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nv-tlabs/Difix3D, https://github.com/nv-tlabs/Difix3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) meshroomHub/mrGSplat, https://github.com/meshroomHub/mrGSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mkmarek/svo-rs, https://github.com/mkmarek/svo-rs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Streamline Approximation via Iterative B-spline Fitting
head: Data reduction scheme for B-splines, Iterative curve fitting
body: This method computes a B-spline curve \gamma(u) that approximates a set of input samples X, specifically designed to avoid the oscillations ("wriggles") introduced by standard interpolation or least-squares approximation. These artifacts are problematic for generating tubular geometry and ambient occlusion in volume rendering. It sets itself apart from Least-squares approximation by leveraging Schönberg’s approximation properties to prevent new perturbations, and from Interpolation by strictly avoiding the introduction of features not present in the original data. Inputs: X = \{x1, \dots, xn\}: A set of n 3D points representing a sampled streamline or path. \epsilon: User-specified accuracy threshold for termination. Outputs: \gamma(u): A cubic (C^2 continuous) B-spline curve approximating X. k: The number of iterations performed in the data reduction scheme. Data Structures: B-spline Curve \gammai(u): Defined by a set of control points (coefficients). For implementation, the curve is evaluated as a linear combination of cubic B-spline basis functions weighted by these coefficients. Sample Set Xi: A list of mi points generated by evaluating the previous curve \gamma{i-1}(u) at uniformly spaced parameters. Parameters: \epsilon: Termination threshold. Typical value: 10^{-4}. n: Initial number of samples in X. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Schönberg’s Approximation): Construct an initial cubic B-spline curve \gamma1(u) using the input samples X directly as its control point coefficients. This step relies on the variation diminishing property of B-splines to approximate X without introducing new perturbations. 2. Iterative Data Reduction: Repeat the following steps for i = 2, 3, \dots until termination: a. Calculate Sample Count: Compute the number of samples mi for the current iteration: mi = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{i-1}} \right\rfloor At each step, the number of samples is halved. b. Construct New Sample Set Xi: Generate Xi by regularly sampling the parameter space of the previous curve \gamma{i-1}(u). The j-th sample in Xi is obtained by evaluating \gamma{i-1} at parameter value uj = \frac{j-1}{mi-1}: x'j = \gamma{i-1}\left( \frac{j-1}{mi-1} \right), \quad j = 1, \dots, mi This process samples a C^2 curve, smoothing out high-frequency features. c. Iterative Curve Fitting: Compute the new curve \gammai(u) by applying an iterative curve fitting algorithm to the sample set Xi. The coefficients of \gammai(u) are updated so that the curve moves closer to the samples in Xi until a user-specified accuracy is achieved. The specific iterative update rules and convergence properties are detailed in [14]. d. Error Check: Calculate the maximum error \epsilon{\max} between the original samples X and the current curve \gammai(u). The error is defined as: \epsilon{\max}:= \max{1 \le j \le n} \| x'j - xj \|2 where xj \in X and x'j is the projection of xj onto the current curve \gammai(u). e. Termination: If \epsilon{\max} \le \epsilon, terminate. The final curve is \gamma(u):= \gammai(u) and k = i. Otherwise, increment i and repeat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def streamlineapproximation(X, epsilon): """ Approximates a set of points X using iterative B-spline fitting. Args: X: List of n 3D points (samples). epsilon: Termination threshold (e.g., 1e-4). Returns: gamma: Final B-spline control points. k: Number of iterations. """ n = len(X) gammaprev = list(X) # Control points for gamma1 i = 1 while True: i += 1 mi = math.floor(n / (2 (i - 1))) # Guard against division by zero if mi < 2 if mi < 2: break # Step 2b: Construct Xi by sampling gammaprev Xi = [] for j in range(1, mi + 1): u = (j - 1) / (mi - 1) Xi.append(evaluatecubicbspline(gammaprev, u)) # Step 2c: Iterative curve fitting # The specific iterative coefficient update rules to fit Xi # are detailed in [14] and not provided in the sources. gammacurr = iterativefitbspline(Xi, gammaprev) # Step 2d: Calculate max error against original samples X maxerror = 0.0 for xj in X: xprimej = projectpointontocurve(gammacurr, xj) dist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(xprimej, xj))) if dist > maxerror: maxerror = dist # Step 2e: Termination check if maxerror <= epsilon: return gammacurr, i gammaprev = gammacurr def evaluatecubicbspline(controlpoints, u): """Evaluate a uniform cubic B-spline at parameter u.""" if len(controlpoints) < 4: return controlpoints[0] n = len(controlpoints) - 1 uclamped = max(0.0, min(u, n)) idx = int(uclamped) t = uclamped - idx b0 = (1 - t)3 / 6.0 b1 = (3t3 - 6t2 + 4) / 6.0 b2 = (-3t3 + 3t2 + 3t + 1) / 6.0 b3 = t3 / 6.0 p0 = controlpoints[idx] p1 = controlpoints[idx+1] p2 = controlpoints[idx+2] p3 = controlpoints[idx+3] return (b0p0 + b1p1 + b2p2 + b3p3) def projectpointontocurve(controlpoints, point): """Find closest point on cubic B-spline curve to given point.""" mindist = float('inf') bestu = 0.0 steps = 100 for k in range(steps + 1): u = k / steps curvept = evaluatecubicbspline(controlpoints, u) dist = math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(curvept, point))) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestu = u return evaluatecubicbspline(controlpoints, bestu) def iterativefitbspline(samples, currentcontrolpoints): """Placeholder for the iterative curve fitting algorithm from [14].""" # The specific coefficient update rules and convergence criteria # are defined in [14]. A complete implementation requires # integrating that algorithm here. return currentcontrolpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If mi = 1, the parameter calculation \frac{j-1}{mi-1} involves division by zero. A guard clause is required to terminate or handle cases where n < 2^{i-1}. Projection Cost: Calculating the projection x'j of each original sample onto the curve can be computationally expensive if not optimized. Convergence: The iterative fitting step relies on the algorithm from [14]. The source states the method terminates when the error threshold is met, implying designed convergence. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: For the data sets shown in the source, k < 4 with \epsilon = 10^{-4}. Strengths: Effectively reduces wriggles and oscillations compared to least-squares approximation, leading to cleaner tubular geometry and ambient occlusion. Limitations: Requires the iterative fitting algorithm from [14] to be implemented correctly. The projection step can be costly. This method was proposed in the context of visualizing streamlines and generating stream tubes for volume rendering, where visual artifacts from curve approximation can significantly impact the quality of ambient occlusion. It builds on Schönberg’s approximation properties and the iterative curve fitting algorithm described in [14]. name: Parametric Path Generation
head: Parametric Camera Path Generation, Analytic Trajectory Generation
body: Parametric Path Generation constructs camera trajectories by evaluating explicit mathematical functions of a scalar parameter (typically angle or time) to produce a sequence of camera poses. It solves the problem of generating smooth, continuous novel views from a sparse set of training images by defining the geometry of the path analytically rather than interpolating between discrete keyframes. It differs from Sparse Trajectory Generation by relying on closed-form equations for position and orientation, and from Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by deriving parameters directly from scene statistics (e.g., camera bounding boxes) rather than arbitrary artistic constraints. The family shares the mechanism of mapping a scalar parameter \theta \in [0, 2\pi] (or a linear time interval) to a 4x4 transformation matrix \mathbf{P}. The core steps common to all children are: 1. Scene Analysis: Compute scene statistics (centroid, bounding box, or percentiles) from input training poses to define the spatial bounds of the trajectory. 2. Parameterization: Define position \mathbf{c}(\theta) and orientation (look-at direction \mathbf{z}(\theta), up vector \mathbf{u}(\theta)) as functions of \theta. 3. Pose Construction: Assemble the rotation matrix \mathbf{R} from orthogonal basis vectors and translation \mathbf{t} into \mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{R} | \mathbf{t}]. 4. Sampling: Evaluate the functions at N evenly spaced intervals, excluding the final duplicate point to ensure a closed loop without redundancy. Creates a spiral trajectory by combining circular horizontal motion with vertical oscillation. It is distinct from Elliptical Camera Path Generation by using a constant radius in the horizontal plane (scaled by percentiles) and a sinusoidal vertical component, whereas the elliptical variant allows for non-circular horizontal bounds and linear interpolation of vertical bounds. It is chosen for forward-facing scenes where the camera orbits a central point while varying height. Generates a closed-loop elliptical trajectory by interpolating between computed lower and upper bounds in both horizontal and vertical axes. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by allowing the horizontal cross-section to be a non-circular ellipse (defined by 90th percentile bounds) and by using a phase-shifted vertical oscillation that is bounded by 10th/90th percentiles rather than a pure sine wave. It is chosen when the scene has anisotropic horizontal distribution or when a smoother, less oscillatory vertical transition is desired. Rotates the camera around a fixed axis (Azimuth, Elevation, or Roll) at a constant distance from the center of rotation. It differs from the spiral and elliptical variants by restricting motion to a single planar rotation without vertical oscillation or radius variation. It is chosen for simple panoramic exports or when the scene geometry is centered and symmetric, requiring minimal parameter tuning. Parametric path generation is a foundational technique in NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and volume rendering novel view synthesis. The spiral path generation method was popularized by the original NeRF implementation, which used it to generate training views for forward-facing scenes. The elliptical and orbit variants emerged as adaptations to handle different scene geometries and rendering pipelines, often found in open-source NeRF implementations and visualization tools.

name: Spiral Camera Path Generation
head: Forward-Facing Spiral Camera Path, Novel View Synthesis Path, Spiral Path Generation, load_tankstemple_data spiral generation
body: Spiral Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses along a spiral trajectory for novel view synthesis, defined by a center camera, radius parameters, focal length, vertical offset rate, rotation count, and number of views. It calculates a forward-facing spiral camera path for rendering based on input poses and bounds, where all cameras in the path point towards a world-space focal point. It generates a smooth spiral camera path around the training camera distribution for 360° novel view synthesis videos and for rendering novel views in forward-facing scenes. It generates a spiral camera trajectory around a center point for novel view synthesis. Inputs: poses: Array of M training camera-to-world matrices \mathbf{C}i. N: Number of views to generate. rots: Number of full rotations (2\pi) to complete, default 2. zrate: Rate of vertical oscillation in the spiral path, default 0.5. radsscale: Scale factor for camera radius, default 1.0. focusdistance: Weight for near/far bound averaging, default 0.75. spiralscalef: Focal length multiplier, default 1.0. spiralscaler: Radius multiplier, default 1.0. Outputs: renderposes: Array of shape (N, 4, 4) containing the generated camera-to-world matrices. Data Structures: rads: Array of shape (3,) specifying spiral radius per axis. c2wavg: 4 \times 4 matrix representing the average camera pose of the input training data. up: 3-vector representing the average up direction of the input cameras. focal: Scalar float representing the effective focal length. Steps: 1. Scene Analysis: Compute the average camera-to-world matrix \mathbf{C}{avg} from the input poses. Let \mathbf{C}{avg} = [\mathbf{R}{avg} | \mathbf{t}{avg}]. Compute the average up vector \mathbf{u} by averaging the second column (y-axis) of the rotation matrices of all input poses: \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=0}^{M-1} \mathbf{C}i[:, 1]. Extract the camera centers \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{C}i[:, 3] for all i. Compute the radii vector \mathbf{r}{raw} as the 90th percentile of the absolute values of the camera centers along each axis: \mathbf{r}{raw} = \text{percentile}(|\mathbf{p}i|, 90, \text{axis}=0). Scale the radii: \mathbf{r}{scaled} = \mathbf{r}{raw} \times \text{rads\scale} \times \text{spiral\scale\r}. Construct \mathbf{rads} = [\text{rads\scaled}[0], \text{rads\scaled}[1], \text{rads\scaled}[2]]. (Note: Some implementations append 1.0 to a 2-element list if not present, but standard spiral generation uses 3 axes). 2. Focal Length and Bounds Calculation: Compute near and far bounds from the training poses: d{min} = \text{bounds.min()} and d{max} = \text{bounds.max()}. Compute the effective focal length f using the weighted harmonic mean: f = \frac{1}{\frac{1 - \text{focus\distance}}{d{min}} + \frac{\text{focus\distance}}{d{max}}} \times \text{spiral\scale\f}. 3. Parameterization and Pose Construction: Initialize an empty list renderposes. Generate N evenly spaced angles \thetaj for j = 0, \dots, N-1: \thetaj = \frac{2\pi \cdot j \cdot \text{rots}}{N}. Note: Some implementations generate N+1 points and exclude the last to avoid duplication, effectively creating a closed loop without redundant start/end points. For each \thetaj: a. Compute Offset Vector: Calculate the offset vector \mathbf{v} in the local coordinate system of the average pose: \mathbf{v} = [rx \cos(\thetaj), -ry \sin(\thetaj), -rz \sin(\thetaj \cdot \text{z\rate})]. The negative signs on the sine terms are consistent with the coordinate system conventions used in the source implementations (e.g., OpenGL-style camera looking down -Z). b. Compute Camera Center: Transform the offset into world space using the average pose's rotation and translation: \mathbf{c}j = \mathbf{C}{avg}[:,:3] \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{C}{avg}[:, 3]. c. Compute Look-at Direction: Determine the viewing direction \mathbf{z}j. The camera looks towards a focal point defined by the average pose's origin and focal length. The focal point in world space is: \mathbf{f}j = \mathbf{C}{avg}[:,:3] [0, 0, -f]^T + \mathbf{C}{avg}[:, 3]. The viewing direction is the normalized vector from the camera center to the focal point: \mathbf{z}j = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{f}j - \mathbf{c}j). d. Compute Basis Vectors: i. Compute the x-axis \mathbf{x}j using the cross product of the fixed average up vector \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{z}j: \mathbf{x}j = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{z}j). ii. Compute the y-axis \mathbf{y}j to ensure orthogonality: \mathbf{y}j = \mathbf{z}j \times \mathbf{x}j. e. Construct Pose Matrix: Assemble the 4 \times 4 matrix \mathbf{P}j: \mathbf{P}j = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}j^T & \mathbf{y}j^T & \mathbf{z}j^T & \mathbf{c}j \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Note: In column-major notation (common in OpenGL/NeRF), the rotation matrix columns are \mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{y}j, \mathbf{z}j. So \mathbf{P}j = [\mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{y}j, \mathbf{z}j, \mathbf{c}j] with the bottom row [0,0,0,1]. 4. Return: Stack all \mathbf{P}j into an array of shape (N, 4, 4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def spiralcamerapathgeneration(poses, N, rots=2, zrate=0.5, radsscale=1.0, focusdistance=0.75, spiralscalef=1.0, spiralscaler=1.0): """ Generate a spiral camera path. Args: poses: (M, 4, 4) array of camera-to-world matrices. N: Number of poses to generate. rots: Number of full rotations. zrate: Vertical oscillation rate. radsscale: Scale factor for radii. focusdistance: Weight for near/far bound averaging. spiralscalef: Focal length multiplier. spiralscaler: Radius multiplier. Returns: renderposes: (N, 4, 4) array of generated camera-to-world matrices. """ # 1. Scene Analysis # Compute average pose (S3, S4) c2wavg = np.mean(poses, axis=0) # Compute average up vector (S3, S4) up = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 1], axis=0) # Compute radii (S3, S4) positions = poses[:,:3, 3] radiiraw = np.percentile(np.abs(positions), 90, axis=0) rads = radiiraw radsscale spiralscaler # 2. Focal Length and Bounds (S2, S6) boundsmin = np.min(positions, axis=0) boundsmax = np.max(positions, axis=0) nearbound = np.min(boundsmin) farbound = np.max(boundsmax) # Avoid division by zero (G) if nearbound < 1e-6: nearbound = 1e-6 focal = (1.0 / ((1.0 - focusdistance) / nearbound + focusdistance / farbound)) spiralscalef # 3. Pose Construction renderposes = [] # Generate angles, excluding last point to avoid duplication (S1, S3, S4) thetas = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 np.pi rots, N + 1)[:-1] for theta in thetas: # a. Compute Offset Vector (S1, S3, S4) offset = np.array([ rads[0] np.cos(theta), -rads[1] np.sin(theta), -rads[2] np.sin(theta zrate) ]) # b. Compute Camera Center (S1, S3, S4) center = c2wavg[:3, 3] + c2wavg[:3,:3] @ offset # c. Compute Look-at Direction (S4) # Focal point in world space focalpoint = c2wavg[:3,:3] @ np.array([0.0, 0.0, -focal]) + c2wavg[:3, 3] # Viewing direction from center to focal point z = focalpoint - center normz = np.linalg.norm(z) if normz > 1e-6: z = z / normz else: z = np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) # Fallback (G) # d. Compute Basis Vectors (S4) x = np.cross(up, z) normx = np.linalg.norm(x) if normx < 1e-6: # Degenerate case: up and z are parallel (G) x = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) x = x - np.dot(x, z) z x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) else: x = x / normx y = np.cross(z, x) # e. Construct Pose Matrix (S1, S4) pose = np.eye(4) pose[:3, 0] = x pose[:3, 1] = y pose[:3, 2] = z pose[:3, 3] = center renderposes.append(pose) return np.array(renderposes) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Up Vector: If the average up vector is parallel to the viewing direction \mathbf{z}, the cross product for \mathbf{x} is zero. A guard is required to select an alternative up vector. Precision: Floating point errors in normalization can accumulate. Re-orthogonalization (Gram-Schmidt) is recommended. Boundary Conditions: The spiral should not include the final duplicate point to avoid redundancy in rendering. Focal Length: If nearbound is zero, division by zero occurs. A small epsilon should be added. Circular Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses arranged in a 360-degree circular trajectory around a central origin at a fixed height and radius. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by having a constant z-coordinate (no vertical oscillation, zrate = 0) and a fixed radius, making it suitable for flat scenes or when vertical coverage is not required. It is simpler than the spiral path and computationally cheaper. Link: Circular Camera Path Generation. Spherify Poses reorients a set of input camera poses into a uniform spherical arrangement centered around the scene's centroid, ensuring consistent scale and distribution for novel view synthesis. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by enforcing a strict spherical radius rather than a spiral trajectory with vertical offset, and by computing a 3D center from ray intersections rather than assuming a 2D circular path. It is used when a full 360° spherical coverage is needed, unlike the spiral which is often forward-facing or limited in elevation. Link: Spherify Poses. Spiral Camera Pose Generation is a variant that generates camera poses in a circle with optional pitch rotation and up-vector flipping. It differs from the standard spiral by using a fixed radius and potentially flipping the up vector for specific rendering requirements. It is used for fly-through rendering where a simple circular path with orientation adjustments is sufficient. Steps: 1. Generate camera poses in a circle: for \theta in np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, nposes + 1)[:-1]. 2. Compute eye position: if np.abs(up[1]) > 0: eye = [np.cos(theta + np.pi / 2) radius, 0, -np.sin(theta + np.pi / 2) radius]; else: eye = [np.cos(theta + np.pi / 2) radius, np.sin(theta + np.pi / 2) radius, 2.0]. 3. Create camera using lookatviewtransform: R, T = lookatviewtransform(eye=(eye,), at=([0.0, 0.0, 0.0],), up=(up,)). 4. Create PerspectiveCameras object: camera = PerspectiveCameras(focallength=torch.tensor([focallength])[None], principalpoint=torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0])[None], R=R, T=T). Parameters: focallength: Focal length of the camera. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of poses to generate. The computation per pose is constant time (vector operations). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the output poses. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of poses. The radius and focal length depend on the scene statistics, so larger scenes require larger radii. Strengths: Provides smooth, continuous coverage of a scene with vertical variation. Good for forward-facing and 360° novel view synthesis. Limitations: Assumes the scene is roughly centered at the origin. May not cover scenes with large vertical extent if zrate is not tuned. Degenerate cases (parallel up and view vectors) require handling. When to Use: When smooth, continuous camera motion with vertical variation is desired for novel view synthesis. When Not to Use: When the scene is not centered, or when a fixed-height orbit is sufficient. Spiral Camera Path Generation originated in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) for novel view synthesis. It was popularized by the original NeRF paper and subsequent implementations in repositories like bmild/nerf and kwea123/nerfpl. It is commonly used for rendering novel views in forward-facing scenes (e.g., LLFF dataset) and 360° capture scenarios. The method maps a scalar parameter to a 4x4 transformation matrix, building on the principles of parametric path generation [11476-parametric-path-generation.md]. bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kwea123/nerfpl, https://github.com/kwea123/nerfpl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) meshroomHub/mrGSplat, https://github.com/meshroomHub/mrGSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Circular Camera Path Generation
head: 360 Degree Camera Path Generation, Orbit Camera Path Generation
body: Circular Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses arranged in a 360-degree circular trajectory around a central origin at a fixed height and radius. Inputs: nviews: Integer, number of camera poses to generate. Default: 120. radius: Float, distance from the origin to the camera. Default: 4.0. height: Float, fixed Y-coordinate (vertical offset) of the camera. Default: 0.0. Outputs: poses: A numpy array of shape (nviews, 4, 4) containing the camera-to-world (c2w) transformation matrices. Data Structures: poses: List of 4x4 numpy arrays, appended during iteration, then stacked. c2w: 4x4 numpy array representing the camera-to-world matrix. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list poses. 2. Loop i from 0 to nviews - 1: a. Calculate the angular position: \theta = \frac{2\pi i}{n\views}. b. Calculate the camera position in world coordinates: \text{cam\pos} = [\text{radius} \cdot \cos(\theta), \text{height}, \text{radius} \cdot \sin(\theta)]. c. Calculate the forward vector pointing from the camera to the origin: \text{forward} = \text{normalize}(-\text{cam\pos}). d. Set the initial up vector to the world Y-axis: \text{up} = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]. e. Calculate the right vector using the cross product of forward and up: \text{right} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{forward}, \text{up})). f. Recalculate the up vector to ensure orthogonality: \text{up} = \text{cross}(\text{right}, \text{forward}). g. Construct the 4x4 identity matrix c2w. h. Set the rotation columns and translation row: c2w[:3, 0] = right c2w[:3, 1] = up c2w[:3, 2] = -forward c2w[:3, 3] = campos. i. Append c2w to poses. 3. Return np.stack(poses, axis=0). Parameters: nviews: Number of views to generate. Default: 120. radius: Distance from origin. Default: 4.0. height: Camera height. Default: 0.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If radius is 0, the camera position is the origin, and the forward vector is undefined (zero vector), causing normalization failure. If height is 0 and the camera is at the origin, the up vector [0,1,0] is parallel to the forward vector (or zero), causing the cross product for right to be zero. The sources do not specify handling for degenerate cases; implementation should guard against zero-length vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatecircularpath(nviews=120, radius=4.0, height=0.0): poses = [] for i in range(nviews): # Calculate angle theta = 2.0 np.pi i / nviews # Calculate camera position campos = np.array([ radius np.cos(theta), height, radius np.sin(theta) ]) # Calculate forward vector (pointing to origin) forward = -campos forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) # Set initial up vector up = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Calculate right vector right = np.cross(forward, up) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) # Recalculate up vector for orthogonality up = np.cross(right, forward) # Construct 4x4 c2w matrix c2w = np.eye(4) c2w[:3, 0] = right c2w[:3, 1] = up c2w[:3, 2] = -forward c2w[:3, 3] = campos poses.append(c2w) return np.stack(poses, axis=0) Time complexity: O(n\views). Memory complexity: O(n\views). Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources.
