name: Spherify Poses
head: Pose Spherification, Spherical Path Centering, Spherical Pose Reorganization
body: Spherify Poses reorients a set of input camera poses into a uniform spherical arrangement centered around the scene's centroid, ensuring consistent scale and distribution for novel view synthesis. It differs from Circular Camera Path Generation by computing a 3D center from ray intersections rather than assuming a 2D circular path, and from Spiral Camera Path Generation by enforcing a strict spherical radius rather than a spiral trajectory with vertical offset. Inputs: poses: Array of shape [N{\text{orig}}, 4, 4] representing input camera poses in world coordinates, where poses[:,:3,2:3] stores ray directions and poses[:,:3,3] stores camera positions. bds: Bounding box data (optional, used for scaling reference). N: Integer, the number of new poses to generate. Outputs: posesspherical: Array of shape [N, 4, 4] containing the new camera poses arranged on a sphere. Data Structures: raysd: Array of shape [N{\text{orig}}, 3, 1] containing unit ray directions extracted from poses. rayso: Array of shape [N{\text{orig}}, 3, 1] containing ray origins (camera positions) extracted from poses. Ai: Matrix of shape [3, 3] for each ray i, defined as I - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T. bi: Vector of shape [3, 1] for each ray i, defined as -Ai \mathbf{o}i. Steps: 1. Extract Rays: Extract ray directions \mathbf{d}i and origins \mathbf{o}i from the input poses matrix. \mathbf{d}i = \text{poses}[i,:3, 2:3] \mathbf{o}i = \text{poses}[i,:3, 3:4] 2. Compute Sphere Center: Calculate the point \mathbf{p}{\text{mindist}} that minimizes the distance to all camera rays by solving a least-squares problem. Ai = I - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T bi = -Ai \mathbf{o}i \mathbf{p}{\text{mindist}} = -\left( \frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} Ai^T Ai \right)^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} bi \right) Set \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{p}{\text{mindist}}. 3. Compute Up Vector: Calculate the mean vector from the center to the camera positions to define the initial "up" direction. \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} (\text{poses}[i,:3, 3] - \mathbf{c}) 4. Construct Local Coordinate System: Normalize \mathbf{u} to get \mathbf{vec}0. Compute \mathbf{vec}1 by crossing \mathbf{vec}0 with a fixed arbitrary vector \mathbf{v}{\text{fix}} = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]^T to avoid degeneracy if \mathbf{u} is parallel to the world up. Compute \mathbf{vec}2 by crossing \mathbf{vec}0 and \mathbf{vec}1. \mathbf{vec}0 = \frac{\mathbf{u}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|} \mathbf{vec}1 = \frac{\mathbf{v}{\text{fix}} \times \mathbf{vec}0}{\|\mathbf{v}{\text{fix}} \times \mathbf{vec}0\|} \mathbf{vec}2 = \frac{\mathbf{vec}0 \times \mathbf{vec}1}{\|\mathbf{vec}0 \times \mathbf{vec}1\|} 5. Reset Poses: Construct a transformation matrix T using the basis vectors and the center. T = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{vec}1 & \mathbf{vec}2 & \mathbf{vec}0 & \mathbf{c} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Apply this transformation to all input poses to get posesreset. 6. Compute Radius and Scale: Calculate the radius r of the centered poses. r = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} \|\text{poses\reset}[i,:3, 3]\|^2} Compute scale factor s = 1/r. Apply this scale to posesreset and bds. 7. Compute Spherical Parameters: Calculate the centroid of the scaled poses. Extract the z-coordinate of the centroid, zh. zh = \text{centroid}[2] Compute the radius of the circle in the xy-plane, r{\text{circle}}. r{\text{circle}} = \sqrt{r^2 - zh^2} 8. Generate New Poses: Iterate \theta from 0 to 2\pi with N steps. For each \theta: \mathbf{camorigin} = [r{\text{circle}} \cos(\theta), r{\text{circle}} \sin(\theta), zh] Construct a new local basis for the camera orientation: \mathbf{vec}2' = \frac{\mathbf{camorigin}}{\|\mathbf{camorigin}\|} \mathbf{vec}0' = \frac{\mathbf{vec}2' \times [0, 0, -1]^T}{\|\mathbf{vec}2' \times [0, 0, -1]^T\|} \mathbf{vec}1' = \frac{\mathbf{vec}2' \times \mathbf{vec}0'}{\|\mathbf{vec}2' \times \mathbf{vec}0'\|} Set the pose matrix P with columns \mathbf{vec}0', \mathbf{vec}1', \mathbf{vec}2' and translation \mathbf{camorigin}. P = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{vec}0' & \mathbf{vec}1' & \mathbf{vec}2' & \mathbf{camorigin} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} 9. Append Homogeneous Row: Append the original pose's w-row (typically poses[0,:3,-1:]) to the new poses to maintain homogeneous coordinate structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def spherifyposes(poses, N): """ Reorients camera poses to a spherical arrangement. Args: poses: np.array of shape (Norig, 4, 4) N: int, number of new poses to generate Returns: posesspherical: np.array of shape (N, 4, 4) """ # 1. Extract rays raysd = poses[:,:3, 2:3] # Shape (Norig, 3, 1) rayso = poses[:,:3, 3:4] # Shape (Norig, 3, 1) # 2. Compute sphere center I = np.eye(3) # Ai = I - di di^T Ai = I - (raysd @ raysd.transpose(0, 2, 1)) # bi = -Ai oi bi = -Ai @ rayso # ptmindist = -inv(mean(Ai^T @ Ai)) @ mean(bi) meanA = np.mean(Ai.transpose(0, 2, 1) @ Ai, axis=0) meanb = np.mean(bi, axis=0) ptmindist = -np.linalg.inv(meanA) @ meanb.flatten() center = ptmindist # 3. Compute up vector campositions = poses[:,:3, 3] up = np.mean(campositions - center, axis=0) # 4. Construct local coordinate system vec0 = up / np.linalg.norm(up) vfix = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]) vec1 = np.cross(vfix, vec0) vec1 = vec1 / np.linalg.norm(vec1) vec2 = np.cross(vec0, vec1) vec2 = vec2 / np.linalg.norm(vec2) # 5. Reset poses # c2w = [vec1, vec2, vec0, pos=center] R = np.columnstack((vec1, vec2, vec0)) T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = R T[:3, 3] = center # Apply transformation to all input poses posesreset = np.zeroslike(poses) for i in range(poses.shape[0]): posesreset[i] = T @ poses[i] # 6. Compute radius and scale positions = posesreset[:,:3, 3] rad = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum(positions2, axis=-1))) sc = 1.0 / rad posesreset[:,:3, 3] = sc # Apply scale to posesreset # 7. Compute spherical parameters centroid = np.mean(posesreset[:,:3, 3], axis=0) zh = centroid[2] radcircle = np.sqrt(rad2 - zh2) # 8. Generate new poses thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, N, endpoint=False) posesspherical = np.zeros((N, 4, 4)) for i, th in enumerate(thetas): camorigin = np.array([radcircle np.cos(th), radcircle np.sin(th), zh]) vec2prime = camorigin / np.linalg.norm(camorigin) vec0prime = np.cross(vec2prime, np.array([0, 0, -1])) vec0prime = vec0prime / np.linalg.norm(vec0prime) vec1prime = np.cross(vec2prime, vec0prime) vec1prime = vec1prime / np.linalg.norm(vec1prime) posesspherical[i,:3, 0] = vec0prime posesspherical[i,:3, 1] = vec1prime posesspherical[i,:3, 2] = vec2prime posesspherical[i,:3, 3] = camorigin posesspherical[i, 3,:] = poses[0, 3,:] # Append original w-row return posesspherical Parameters: N: Number of poses to generate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Up Vector: If the mean up vector is zero (cameras are symmetric around the center), normalization fails. Guard against this by checking np.linalg.norm(up) < epsilon. Parallel Ray Directions: If all rays are parallel, Ai becomes singular, and the least-squares solution for the center is unstable. Check for collinearity of ray directions. Complexity of Cross Product: If \mathbf{vec}0 is parallel to \mathbf{v}{\text{fix}}, the cross product for \mathbf{vec}1 is zero. The fixed vector [0.1, 0.2, 0.3] is chosen to be unlikely to be parallel to typical scene up vectors, but a fallback is recommended. Radius Calculation: The formula for r{\text{circle}} assumes r \ge |zh|. If the scene is not roughly spherical or the centering is poor, this may result in a NaN. Check for r^2 < zh^2. Generates poses on a 2D circle. Choose when the scene is planar or when a simple orbit is sufficient. Spherify is chosen for 3D volumetric scenes requiring full spherical coverage. Time Complexity: O(N) for extracting rays and computing the center. O(N) for generating new poses. Overall linear in the number of input poses and output poses. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store rays, intermediate matrices, and output poses. Strengths: Provides a robust, data-driven center for spherical sampling, which is crucial for NeRF training on unstructured data. Ensures uniform distribution of views. Limitations: Assumes the scene is roughly spherical. If the scene is elongated or has a specific orientation, the spherical path may not cover all parts of the scene uniformly. The fixed vector for cross product is arbitrary. When to Use: When preparing unstructured image collections for NeRF training where a spherical camera path is desired. When Not to Use: When the scene is known to be planar or when a specific trajectory (e.g., spiral, linear) is required for artistic or physical reasons. The method originates from the NerfingMVS project. It is used in the context of novel view synthesis, specifically for reorganizing camera poses from arbitrary viewpoints into a structured spherical path to facilitate training and rendering. weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Elliptical Camera Path Generation
head: Elliptical Camera Path with Y Variation, Elliptical Path Generation, Elliptical Render Path (Y Variation), Elliptical Render Path Generation, elliptical camera trajectory
body: Generates a closed-loop elliptical camera trajectory centered on a focal point derived from input training poses, with optional asymmetric height variation along the vertical axis. It differs from Orbit Camera Path Generation by allowing independent scaling of the ellipse axes and non-circular vertical oscillation, and from Spiral Camera Path Generation by maintaining a constant radius (or bounded height range) rather than a continuously expanding or contracting radius. Inputs: poses: Array of shape (N, 4, 4) containing N input camera poses. nframes: Integer, number of output frames. Default 120. zvariation: Float, amplitude of height variation. Default 0. zphase: Float, phase shift for height variation. Default 0. constspeed: Boolean, whether to resample for constant velocity. Default True. Outputs: path: Array of shape (n\frames, 4, 4) containing the generated camera poses. Data Structures: center: Vector of shape (3,) representing the focal point. offset: Vector of shape (3,) defining the center of the ellipse bounds. sc: Vector of shape (3,) representing the semi-axis lengths (scaling factors). low, high: Vectors of shape (3,) defining the bounding box of the ellipse. zlow, zhigh: Scalars defining the vertical bounds. up: Vector of shape (3,) defining the camera up direction. positions: Array of shape (n\frames, 3) for intermediate position calculation. Steps: 1. Scene Analysis: Compute the focal point center using a function focuspointfn(poses). 2. Offset and Scaling: Determine the offset vector. For the primary X-Y plane variant, offset = [center[0], center[1], 0]. Compute scaling factors sc using the 90th percentile of the absolute distances of camera positions from offset: \text{sc} = \text{percentile}(|\text{poses}[:,:3, 3] - \text{offset}|, 90, \text{axis}=0). Define ellipse bounds: \text{low} = -\text{sc} + \text{offset} \text{high} = \text{sc} + \text{offset}. 3. Vertical Bounds: Compute zlow and zhigh using the 10th and 90th percentiles of the z-coordinates of the camera positions: \text{z\low} = \text{percentile}(\text{poses}[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 10, \text{axis}=0) \text{z\high} = \text{percentile}(\text{poses}[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 90, \text{axis}=0). 4. Position Parameterization: Define a function getpositions(theta) that returns the 3D position for a given angle \theta \in [0, 2\pi]: x(\theta) = \text{low}[0] + (\text{high}[0] - \text{low}[0]) \cdot (\cos(\theta) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) y(\theta) = \text{low}[1] + (\text{high}[1] - \text{low}[1]) \cdot (\sin(\theta) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) z(\theta) = \text{z\variation} \cdot (\text{z\low}[2] + (\text{z\high}[2] - \text{z\low}[2]) \cdot (\cos(\theta + 2\pi \cdot \text{z\phase}) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5)). 5. Sampling: Generate \theta values: \theta = \text{linspace}(0, 2\pi, n\frames + 1, \text{endpoint}=\text{True}). Evaluate getpositions(theta) for all \theta to get positions of shape (n\frames + 1, 3). Remove the last duplicate point (where \theta = 2\pi) to close the loop without redundancy: \text{positions} = \text{positions}[0:n\frames]. 6. Constant Speed Resampling (Optional): If constspeed is true, calculate the arc lengths between consecutive positions and resample \theta to ensure uniform spacing. Calculate lengths: \text{lengths}i = \| \text{positions}{i+1} - \text{positions}i \|2. Resample \theta using cumulative arc length interpolation to maintain constant velocity. 7. Up Vector Determination: Compute the average up vector from input poses: \text{avg\up} = \text{mean}(\text{poses}[:,:3, 1], \text{axis}=0). Normalize avgup. Find the index indup of the maximum absolute component of avgup. Set the up vector: \text{up} = \mathbf{e}{\text{ind\up}} \cdot \text{sign}(\text{avg\up}[\text{ind\up}]) where \mathbf{e}{\text{ind\up}} is the basis vector with 1 at indup and 0 elsewhere. 8. Pose Construction: For each position p in positions, construct a view matrix using viewmatrix(p - center, up, p). Stack all poses into the output path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def focuspointfn(poses): """Calculate the focal point (center) of the camera poses. Typically the mean of the camera positions.""" return np.mean(poses[:,:3, 3], axis=0) def viewmatrix(lookat, up, position): """Construct a view matrix from look-at direction, up vector, and position. lookat: direction the camera looks towards (from position). up: up vector. position: camera position. Returns a 4x4 matrix.""" z = lookat / np.linalg.norm(lookat) x = np.cross(up, z) # Guard against parallel up and lookat if np.linalg.norm(x) < 1e-6: x = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) y = np.cross(z, x) R = np.columnstack((x, y, z)) t = -R.T @ position P = np.eye(4) P[:3,:3] = R P[:3, 3] = t return P def generateellipsepath(poses, nframes, zvariation=0.0, zphase=0.0, constspeed=True): """Generate an elliptical camera path.""" # 1. Scene Analysis center = focuspointfn(poses) # 2. Offset and Scaling offset = np.array([center[0], center[1], 0.0]) sc = np.percentile(np.abs(poses[:,:3, 3] - offset), 90, axis=0) low = -sc + offset high = sc + offset # 3. Vertical Bounds zlow = np.percentile(poses[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 10, axis=0) zhigh = np.percentile(poses[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 90, axis=0) # 4. Position Parameterization def getpositions(theta): x = low[0] + (high[0] - low[0]) (np.cos(theta) 0.5 + 0.5) y = low[1] + (high[1] - low[1]) (np.sin(theta) 0.5 + 0.5) z = zvariation (zlow[2] + (zhigh[2] - zlow[2]) (np.cos(theta + 2 np.pi zphase) 0.5 + 0.5)) return np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) # 5. Sampling theta = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, nframes + 1, endpoint=True) positions = getpositions(theta) positions = positions[:-1] # 6. Constant Speed Resampling (Optional) if constspeed: lengths = np.linalg.norm(positions[1:] - positions[:-1], axis=-1) cumlengths = np.insert(np.cumsum(lengths), 0, 0.0) uniformt = np.linspace(0, cumlengths[-1], nframes) theta = np.interp(uniformt, cumlengths, theta) positions = getpositions(theta) # 7. Up Vector Determination avgup = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 1], axis=0) norm = np.linalg.norm(avgup) # Guard against zero-length average up vector if norm > 1e-6: avgup = avgup / norm indup = np.argmax(np.abs(avgup)) up = np.eye(3)[indup] np.sign(avgup[indup]) # 8. Pose Construction path = np.stack([viewmatrix(p - center, up, p) for p in positions]) return path Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If all input poses are collinear or identical, sc may be zero or avgup may be undefined. Guard against division by zero in normalization. Boundary Conditions: The mapping from \theta to position uses a shifted cosine/sine, ensuring the path starts and ends at the same point without discontinuity. Axis Variation: The coordinate axes can be swapped (e.g., X-Z plane with Y variation) depending on the specific variant implementation. Generates a path with a continuously changing radius, suitable for capturing scenes with depth variation. Choose when the scene has significant depth and a circular orbit is insufficient. Generates a circular path around a center point. Choose when the scene is roughly spherical and a constant radius is appropriate. Strengths: Simple to implement, provides smooth and symmetric paths, allows for controlled height variation. Limitations: Assumes the scene is roughly centered and bounded by the input poses. When to Use: When a smooth, closed-loop camera path is needed for novel view synthesis or visualization, and the scene is well-contained within the input poses. When Not to Use: When the scene is very large or unbounded, or when the camera needs to follow a specific non-elliptical trajectory. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the NeRF and multi-NeRF literature, specifically implemented in the multinerf repository by Google Research. It has been adopted and adapted in various other neural rendering frameworks such as mrGSplat, VolSplat, and VoLoDSplat for generating training or evaluation camera paths. google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) meshroomHub/mrGSplat, https://github.com/meshroomHub/mrGSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ziplab/VolSplat, https://github.com/ziplab/VolSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, https://github.com/pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Orbit Camera Path Generation
head: Camera Orbit Animation, Camera Orbit Generation, Circular Camera Path, Orbit Camera Trajectory Generation, Rotating Mesh Video Rendering, Rotation animation camera setup, Turntable Mode
body: Orbit Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of rendered frames by incrementally rotating the camera around a fixed focal point, producing a smooth circular visualization effect. It differs from its siblings, Spiral and Elliptical path generation, by constraining the camera trajectory to a single plane perpendicular to the rotation axis at a constant radius, ensuring uniform angular velocity and no change in elevation or distance. Inputs: activecamera: The camera object or state to be transformed. framecount: Total number of frames to generate (default 36). azimuthincrement: Degrees to rotate the camera around the view-up axis per frame (default 10). rotateaxis: Integer specifying the rotation axis: 0 for Elevation, 1 for Roll, 2 for Azimuth. rotateangles: Optional list of float angles in degrees to rotate the camera at each step. resolution: Output image dimensions (default [1000, 800]). outputdir: Directory path for saving rendered frames (default outputs/preview). Outputs: A sequence of rendered frames saved as a PNG image sequence or a 4D NumPy array. Data Structures: renderedimage: A 4D NumPy array of shape (framecount, height, width, 3) with dtype uint8, initialized to zeros. imagefilter: A VTK vtkWindowToImageFilter instance used to convert the render window to an image buffer. Steps: 1. Initialize: Obtain the active camera object and configure the rendering window with the specified resolution. 2. Loop: Iterate i from 0 to framecount - 1. 3. Compute Angle: If rotateangles is provided, set angle = rotateangles[i]. Otherwise, set angle = azimuthincrement. 4. Apply Rotation: Rotate the camera using the rotateaxis specification. For azimuth rotation (axis 2), call camera.Azimuth(angle). 5. Render: Trigger the rendering pipeline. If using VTK, call imagefilter.Modified() and imagefilter.Update(), then window.Render(). 6. Capture: Extract the rendered image data. In VTK, convert imagefilter.GetOutput() to a NumPy array. 7. Store: Assign the captured image to renderedimage[i,:,:,:]. 8. Reset (Optional): Apply the inverse rotation camera.Azimuth(-angle) after capture to prevent cumulative drift. 9. Save: Write the frame to outputdir with a sequential filename (e.g., frame%03d.png). Formulas: For a circular orbit in the XY plane around a center \mathbf{c} = (cx, cy, cz) at radius r: \thetai = \frac{2\pi \cdot i}{\text{num\frames}} xi = cx + r \cdot \cos(\thetai) yi = cy + r \cdot \sin(\thetai) zi = cz + \text{elevation} The look-at direction is \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}i, where \mathbf{p}i = (xi, yi, zi). Camera orientation angles are computed as \text{rot}z = \arctan2(dy, dx) - \frac{\pi}{2} and \text{rot}x = -\arctan2(dz, \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}). The optimal focal length is f = \max(f{\text{base}}, r \cdot 0.5). Parameters: azimuthincrement: Typical value 10 degrees. framecount: Typical value 36. resolution: Typical value [1000, 800]. rotateaxis: 0 (Elevation), 1 (Roll), 2 (Azimuth). Edge Cases: Cumulative Error: Repeated floating-point rotations can accumulate orientation drift. Using rotateangles with explicit values or resetting the camera orientation periodically mitigates this. Axis Ambiguity: The rotateaxis parameter must be consistently interpreted by the camera API. VTK uses 0, 1, 2 for Elevation, Roll, Azimuth respectively. Empty Grid: If the input grid is empty, the function returns early to prevent invalid camera setup or division by zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import os def generateorbitframes(activecamera, framecount, azimuthincrement, rotateaxis, resolution, outputdir, rotateangles=None): """Generates orbit camera frames.""" os.makedirs(outputdir, existok=True) height, width = resolution renderedimage = np.zeros((framecount, height, width, 3), dtype=np.uint8) for i in range(framecount): if rotateangles is not None: angle = rotateangles[i] else: angle = azimuthincrement if rotateaxis == 2: activecamera.Azimuth(angle) elif rotateaxis == 0: activecamera.Elevation(angle) elif rotateaxis == 1: activecamera.Roll(angle) # Trigger renderer and extract pixel buffer to NumPy array frame = np.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=np.uint8) renderedimage[i] = frame # Write frame to disk using standard image library filename = os.path.join(outputdir, f"frame{i:03d}.png") # Reset rotation to prevent cumulative drift if rotateaxis == 2: activecamera.Azimuth(-angle) elif rotateaxis == 0: activecamera.Elevation(-angle) elif rotateaxis == 1: activecamera.Roll(-angle) return renderedimage A method for 3D reconstruction that uses a fine-tuned image-to-video model to generate turn-table style video sequences (orbit paths) from a single image, which are then used for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It differs by generating the path content via a video model rather than geometric camera transforms. Time Complexity: O(F), where F is the number of frames, as each frame requires one rotation and one render operation. Memory Complexity: O(F \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C) when pre-allocating the frame buffer. Performance: Rendering time depends on the scene complexity and resolution. Typical resolution [1000, 800] with 36 frames is feasible for real-time preview but may require batch processing for high-res volume rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement; produces smooth, continuous rotation ideal for visualizing symmetric or centrally focused data. Limitations: Does not provide elevation changes (unlike Spiral) or aspect variation (unlike Elliptical), potentially hiding features located above or below the equatorial plane. The method is commonly implemented in scientific visualization pipelines using VTK and ParaView. It is utilized for exporting animation sequences (e.g., PNG frames) that can be stitched into videos using tools like ffmpeg. The approach is foundational in volume rendering workflows for creating turn-table style visualizations. ashawkey/stable-dreamfusion, https://github.com/ashawkey/stable-dreamfusion, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) cjcamp16/sciviz-paraview, https://github.com/cjcamp16/sciviz-paraview, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MagicaVoxel.vox, https://ephtracy.github.io/, fetched 2026-10-26 Laityperfect7/GaussianScan-Recon, https://github.com/Laityperfect7/GaussianScan-Recon, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) nath54/NaxelEditor, https://github.com/nath54/NaxelEditor, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Renderer with VTK - yuta-hi, https://github.com/yuta-hi/volume-renderer, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: IM-3D
body: IM-3D is a 3D reconstruction method that fine-tunes an image-to-video model based on Emu to generate a turn-table style video rotating around an object, which is subsequently used as input for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction. It builds on Orbit Camera Path Generation by generating the orbiting frames via a learned video model rather than explicit camera trajectory sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single source image of the target object. Output: A 3D Gaussian Splatting representation of the object. Data Structures: Fine-tuned Image-to-Video Model: An Emu-based architecture adapted for turn-table video generation. Generated Video: A sequence of frames simulating a camera orbiting the object. 3DGS Representation: The final output structure containing Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, color, opacity) derived from the video frames. Steps: 1. Fine-tuning: The Emu-based image-to-video model is fine-tuned. 2. Video Generation: The fine-tuned model takes the single input image and generates a video sequence where the camera rotates around the object. 3. 3DGS Reconstruction: The generated video frames are extracted and fed into a 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction pipeline to recover the 3D scene. Parameters: Rotation Angle: Not given in the sources. Video Length: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. IM-3D was introduced in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds upon the Emu image-to-video model and applies it to the task of single-image 3D reconstruction via intermediate video generation. name: Camera Motion Trajectory Approximation
head: Lie Algebra SE(3) Interpolation, SE(3) Camera Trajectory Approximation
body: This method approximates the continuous camera trajectory during a finite shutter exposure time by interpolating between known discrete poses within the Lie algebra of the special Euclidean group SE(3). It solves the problem of modeling motion blur in differentiable rendering by providing a smooth, differentiable parameterization of camera motion that respects the non-commutative nature of 3D rigid body transformations. It distinguishes itself from Euclidean linear interpolation by preserving the SE(3) manifold structure, and supports higher-order differentiable optimization via Bézier curves. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Start pose T0 \in SE(3), end pose T1 \in SE(3), shutter duration \tau, and current time t \in [0, \tau]. For higher-order methods, additional control points Tj and interpolation order K are required. Outputs: Interpolated camera pose Tt \in SE(3) at time t. Data Structures Pose (T): A 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix representing rotation and translation in SE(3). Lie Algebra Element (\xi): A 6-dimensional vector representing the logarithm of a rotation matrix, packed as [\omegax, \omegay, \omegaz, vx, vy, vz]^T. Mathematical Primitives Logarithm (\log): Maps T \in SE(3) to its Lie algebra element \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3). Exponential (\exp): Maps \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3) back to T \in SE(3). Matrix Multiplication (\cdot): Standard 4 \times 4 matrix multiplication. Interpolation Methods 1. Linear Interpolation Suitable for short shutter times and small motion amplitudes. Given start T0 and end T1: Tt = T0 \cdot \exp\left( \log(T0^{-1} \cdot T1) \frac{t}{\tau} \right) where t \in [0, \tau] and \tau is the shutter time. 2. Cubic Spline Interpolation Requires four control points T0, T1, T2, T3. Let u = t/\tau \in [0, 1]. The basis function matrix \tilde{B}(u) is: \tilde{B}(u) = C \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ u \\ u^2 \\ u^3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} The interpolated pose is computed as: T(u) = T0 \cdot \prod{j=0}^{2} \exp\left( \tilde{B}{j+1}(u) \cdot \Omegaj \right) where \Omegaj are the Lie algebra elements corresponding to the control points Tj. The notation \tilde{B}{j+1} refers to the (j+1)-th entry of the basis vector result. 3. Bézier Curve Interpolation Uses K+1 control points T0, \dots, TK and order K. The source implementation uses K=7. Let u = t/\tau \in [0, 1]. The interpolated pose is: Tt = \prod{j=0}^{K} \exp\left( \binom{K}{j} (1-u)^{K-j} u^j \log(Tj) \right) This formulation applies De Casteljau’s algorithm in the Lie algebra representation, ensuring differentiability with respect to control points Tj. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def se3log(T): """Computes the 6-vector Lie algebra element from a 4x4 SE(3) matrix.""" R = T[:3,:3] tvec = T[:3, 3] theta = np.arccos(np.clip((np.trace(R) - 1) / 2, -1.0, 1.0)) if theta < 1e-6: omega = np.zeros(3) Vinv = np.eye(3) else: k = np.array([R[2,1]-R[1,2], R[0,2]-R[2,0], R[1,0]-R[0,1]]) / (2 np.sin(theta)) omega = theta k Kskew = np.array([[0, -k[2], k[1]], [k[2], 0, -k[0]], [-k[1], k[0], 0]]) V = np.eye(3) + ((1 - np.cos(theta)) / (theta2)) Kskew + ((theta - np.sin(theta)) / (theta3)) (Kskew @ Kskew) Vinv = np.linalg.inv(V) v = Vinv @ tvec return np.concatenate([omega, v]) def se3exp(xi): """Computes the 4x4 SE(3) matrix from a 6-vector Lie algebra element.""" omega = xi[:3] v = xi[3:] theta = np.linalg.norm(omega) if theta < 1e-6: R = np.eye(3) V = np.eye(3) else: k = omega / theta Kskew = np.array([[0, -k[2], k[1]], [k[2], 0, -k[0]], [-k[1], k[0], 0]]) R = np.eye(3) + np.sin(theta) Kskew + (1 - np.cos(theta)) (Kskew @ Kskew) V = np.eye(3) + ((1 - np.cos(theta)) / (theta2)) Kskew + ((theta - np.sin(theta)) / (theta3)) (Kskew @ Kskew) tvec = V @ v T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = R T[:3, 3] = tvec return T def linearse3interpolation(T0, T1, t, tau): """Linear interpolation in SE(3) Lie algebra.""" deltaT = np.linalg.inv(T0) @ T1 xi = se3log(deltaT) xiscaled = xi (t / tau) expdelta = se3exp(xiscaled) return T0 @ expdelta def bezierse3interpolation(controlpoints, K, t, tau): """Bézier interpolation in SE(3) Lie algebra.""" u = t / tau result = np.eye(4) for j in range(K + 1): binom = math.comb(K, j) weight = binom ((1 - u)(K - j)) (uj) xij = se3log(controlpoints[j]) xiscaled = xij weight expterm = se3exp(xiscaled) result = result @ expterm return result Parameters Order K: The degree of the Bézier curve. The source uses K=7. Shutter Time \tau: The duration of the exposure. Time t: The current timestamp within the exposure, t \in [0, \tau]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Identity Rotation: When \theta \approx 0, the logarithm and exponential functions must handle the singularity gracefully to avoid division by zero. Degenerate Input: If control points are identical, the trajectory remains static. The source notes that control points overlap during initialization before optimization. Precision: The composition of many exponentials in high-order Bézier curves can accumulate numerical error. Guard clauses for small angles are required. Defines the mathematical parameterization of camera motion trajectories. Linear interpolation is sufficient for synthetic scenes with short time intervals, while cubic B-splines are required for real captured scenes with longer exposure times and complex motions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard evaluation is O(1) for linear and O(K) for Bézier. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard storage is O(1) for linear and O(K) for Bézier control points. Performance: The method is differentiable, allowing joint optimization of scene and camera parameters using gradient descent (e.g., Adam optimizer). Strengths: Ensures valid SE(3) poses; differentiable; handles arbitrary smooth motion. Limitations: Requires initialization of control points (e.g., via COLMAP); higher-order curves increase computational cost. When to use: When motion blur needs to be modeled in differentiable rendering pipelines, particularly for deblurring or novel view synthesis from blurred images. The method originates from "Deblur-GS: 3D Gaussian Splatting from Camera Motion Blurred Images". It builds on the principle that camera motion during shutter time can be parameterized in SE(3) and approximated using interpolation in its Lie algebra. The approach allows for the optimization of motion blurring by optimizing the control points of the trajectory. name: Camera Trajectory Representations
head: Camera trajectory interpolation, SE(3) trajectory parameterization, Trajectory Representations for Camera Motion
body: This family defines the mathematical parameterization of camera motion trajectories used to approximate camera movement during shutter exposure time for motion blur synthesis. It solves the problem of how to interpolate between known camera poses to generate intermediate virtual views. The choice of representation is primarily driven by the complexity of the motion and the duration of the exposure: linear interpolation is sufficient for synthetic scenes with short time intervals, while cubic B-splines are required for real captured scenes with longer exposure times and complex motions. Builds on Camera Motion Trajectory Approximation. All representations in this family operate within the Lie group SE(3) to ensure valid rigid body transformations. The core mechanism involves optimizing a set of parameters to define the path between camera poses. The trajectory is typically discretized into n intermediate virtual images to balance rendering performance and training efficiency, with n=10 being a common empirical choice. The optimization targets the camera poses themselves, rather than just the trajectory shape, allowing the model to adapt to the specific blur characteristics of the input data. Linear interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by optimizing only the start pose \mathbf{T}{start} and the end pose \mathbf{T}{end}. The intermediate poses are generated by linearly interpolating between these two endpoints. This method is computationally efficient and sufficient for synthetic datasets where camera motions are simpler and exposure times are effectively shorter. It is employed for synthetic datasets such as those from Deblur-NeRF-S and MBA-VO. Cubic B-spline interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by jointly optimizing four control knots: \mathbf{T}1, \mathbf{T}2, \mathbf{T}3, and \mathbf{T}4. This higher-order spline allows for the modeling of more complex camera motions and nuances over longer time intervals. It outperforms linear interpolation in real captured scenes, particularly due to the longer exposure times inherent in real-world image capture. It is employed for real datasets, such as the 10 real captured scenes from Deblur-NeRF. This variant uses a differentially flat dynamical model of a quadrotor for camera trajectory generation. The flat outputs consist of 3D Euclidean position and yaw, with pitch treated as an additional independent state, resulting in 5-dimensional waypoints. Between successive waypoints \mathbf{x}t \to \mathbf{x}{t+\Delta t}, trajectories are calculated using Dijkstra's algorithm combined with rotorpy to solve a quadratic optimization problem. The flat outputs are parameterized using a 7th-order polynomial to minimize the integral of the squared snap. Camera pitch is linearly interpolated along the trajectory since it is independent of the quadrotor dynamics. An additional 2\pi yaw rotation with pitch modulation is performed at the end of the trajectory to provide extra information for NeRF training and target spotting. The distinction between linear and higher-order spline representations for camera trajectories in the context of neural rendering and deblurring was formalized in the BAD-Gaussians paper. The authors conducted experiments on both synthetic datasets (Deblur-NeRF-S, MBA-VO) and real datasets (Deblur-NeRF) to assess the impact of trajectory representations. They found that while linear interpolation performed comparably to cubic B-splines on synthetic data, the latter was necessary for real data to handle complex motions and longer exposure times effectively. The specific mathematical details of the cubic B-spline implementation are referenced from external literature. BAD-Gaussians: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72698-914, fetched 2026-10-26 Active Scout: Multi-Target Tracking Using Neural Radiance Fields in Dense Urban Environments, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros58592.2024.10802565, fetched 2026-10-26

name: User Viewport Predictor
head: Viewport trajectory prediction
body: The User Viewport Predictor estimates future camera poses (6DoF) from recent interaction history to enable proactive resource allocation in volume rendering and 3D scene delivery. It differs from synthetic or spline-based trajectory generators by relying on empirical user data rather than predefined geometric paths. It serves as a lightweight, short-term forecasting module that can be replaced by more complex models like deep learning predictors. The method uses linear regression to predict the next N frames based on a sliding window of recent observations. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of 6DoF viewport poses \mathbf{P}t = [xt, yt, zt, \alphat, \betat, \gammat] for t in the history window hw. Output: Predicted 6DoF poses for the prediction window pw. Data Structures History Window (hw): A buffer storing recent viewport samples. Prediction Window (pw): The temporal range into the future to predict. Linear Model: For each of the 6 degrees of freedom, a separate linear regression model y = mx + c is maintained. Parameters hw = 0.5 seconds. pw = 1 second. Steps 1. Re-center Angular Data: Before fitting, handle the cyclical nature of rotation angles (\alpha, \beta, \gamma). Set the angle of the first point in hw as 0. Calculate subsequent angles relative to this reference, increasing clockwise and decreasing counter-clockwise, resulting in a range of [-180, 180]. 2. Fit Linear Model: For each of the 6 features independently, treat the feature value as the dependent variable yi and its relative order in the sequence compared to the first point in hw as the independent variable xi. Compute the linear regression coefficients (slope m and intercept c) for the set \{(xi, yi)\}. 3. Forecast: For each future time step k in pw, calculate the relative time index x{pred} from the start of hw and predict the feature value y{pred} = m \cdot x{pred} + c. 4. Update: Continuously slide the hw window forward as new viewport data arrives and re-fit the models. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class UserViewportPredictor: def init(self, historywindowsec=0.5, predwindowsec=1.0, fps=36): self.historywindowsec = historywindowsec self.predwindowsec = predwindowsec self.fps = fps self.historylen = int(historywindowsec fps) self.predlen = int(predwindowsec fps) # Buffer for 6DoF: [x, y, z, alpha, beta, gamma] self.historybuffer = [None] self.historylen self.modelparams = [[0.0, 0.0] for in range(6)] # [slope, intercept] per DOF self.filledcount = 0 def recenterangles(self, angles): """Re-center angular data relative to the first point in the window.""" if not angles or len(angles) == 0: return angles first = angles[0] # Relative angles, range [-180, 180] implied by source return [math.degrees(math.atan2(math.sin(math.radians(a - first)), math.cos(math.radians(a - first)))) for a in angles] def linearregression(self, xvals, yvals): """Compute slope (m) and intercept (c) for y = mx + c.""" n = len(xvals) if n < 2: return 0.0, 0.0 sumx = sum(xvals) sumy = sum(yvals) sumxy = sum(x y for x, y in zip(xvals, yvals)) sumx2 = sum(x x for x in xvals) denom = n sumx2 - sumx sumx if denom == 0: return 0.0, sumy / n m = (n sumxy - sumx sumy) / denom c = (sumy - m sumx) / n return m, c def update(self, newpose): """Add a new viewport pose and re-fit models.""" # Shift buffer and append new pose self.historybuffer.pop(0) self.historybuffer.append(newpose) self.filledcount = min(self.filledcount + 1, self.historylen) # Fit models for each DOF for dof in range(6): # Extract valid samples samples = [self.historybuffer[i][dof] for i in range(self.filledcount)] xvals = list(range(self.filledcount)) # Handle angles (dofs 3, 4, 5) if dof >= 3: samples = self.recenterangles(samples) m, c = self.linearregression(xvals, samples) self.modelparams[dof] = [m, c] def predict(self): """Predict future viewports for the prediction window.""" if self.filledcount < 2: return None # Relative time indices for prediction continue from history startx = self.filledcount xpred = list(range(startx, startx + self.predlen)) predictions = [] for k in range(self.predlen): row = [] for dof in range(6): m, c = self.modelparams[dof] ypred = m xpred[k] + c row.append(ypred) predictions.append(row) return predictions Edge Cases and Pitfalls Angular Discontinuity: The cyclical nature of angles (0^\circ \equiv 360^\circ) can cause large errors in linear regression if not handled. The method requires re-centering relative to the first point in the history window. Non-Linear Motion: Linear regression assumes constant velocity/rotation. Sudden user movements may lead to prediction errors. A module that processes user interaction data to evaluate the type, parameters, speed, and duration of engagement, potentially predicting consecutive viewpoints or regions of interest. It serves as a bridge between raw input events and the visualization system's response, specifically feeding into the User Viewport Predictor to inform future camera trajectory decisions. It is distinguished from the predictor itself by its role in quantifying the quality and intent of the current interaction (e.g., zooming vs. panning) rather than just fitting a linear regression to historical pose data. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for fitting, as the number of features (6) and history window size (fixed at 0.5 s) are constant. Memory Complexity: O(hw \cdot 6), where hw is the history window size in samples. Performance: Simple and fast, suitable for real-time systems. Accuracy: Reasonable accuracy for short-term forecasting. Limitations: Assumes linear motion; may fail during rapid or non-linear user interactions. The method was introduced in the context of L3GS (Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery). It was chosen for its simplicity, speed, and reasonable accuracy in short-term forecasting, similar to its use in other viewport-adaptive systems. The modular design allows for future replacement with more sophisticated models like deep learning predictors. name: Engagement Estimation
head: Engagement Estimation Timer, Viewport Predictor with Engagement Statistics
body: Engagement Estimation is a module that processes user interaction data to evaluate the type, parameters, speed, and duration of engagement, potentially predicting consecutive viewpoints or regions of interest. It serves as a bridge between raw input events and the visualization system's response, specifically feeding into the User Viewport Predictor [15801-user-viewport-predictor.md] to inform future camera trajectory decisions. It is distinguished from the predictor itself by its role in quantifying the quality and intent of the current interaction (e.g., zooming vs. panning) rather than just fitting a linear regression to historical pose data. The module calculates engagement metrics for three primary interaction types: rotation, panning, and zooming. It utilizes a timer to measure the duration of these interactions and outputs specific parameters relevant to the interaction type. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Raw interaction events (rotation, panning, zooming), current time, previous interaction state. Outputs: Engagement duration (scalar). Interaction speed (scalar). Interaction type (enum/flag). For zooming: Coordinates of the user-interaction point (the position of initial interaction on the object). For rotation/panning: No additional semantic-dependent navigation coordinates are output by default, though this may be added. Data Structures: Timer: A scalar value tracking the elapsed time of the current interaction. LastInteractionDuration: A scalar storing the duration of the most recently completed interaction. InteractionPoint: A 3D vector storing the initial interaction coordinates for zooming events. Steps: 1. Initialize Timer: When an interaction event (rotation, panning, or zooming) begins, initialize the Timer to zero. 2. Update Timer: During the interaction, increment the Timer based on the elapsed time since the start of the interaction. 3. Evaluate Speed: Calculate the speed of interaction based on the change in camera parameters (e.g., rotation angle, pan distance, zoom factor) divided by the Timer duration. 4. Capture Zoom Point: If the interaction type is zooming, record the 3D coordinates of the object point corresponding to the initial interaction event as the InteractionPoint. 5. Finalize Interaction: When the user finishes the interaction (event ends): Store the current Timer value into LastInteractionDuration. Zero the Timer for the next interaction. 6. Incorporate Statistics: Use the LastInteractionDuration, interaction speed, and type to evaluate engagement. For zooming, this includes the duration of interaction with a particular region of an object from the viewpoint. 7. Predict Viewpoints: Use the evaluated engagement parameters to make predictions about consecutive viewpoints or regions of interest. Formulas: Engagement Duration: D = t{end} - t{start}. Interaction Speed: V = \frac{\Delta P}{D}, where \Delta P is the magnitude of the change in interaction parameters (e.g., rotation angle, pan distance). Engagement Score (for Animation): An exponential function is used to estimate user interaction, where S(t{current}) is the score at current time t. The exact formula for S(t) is not provided in the sources, but it maps duration to an interval [0, 1], where 0 indicates no interaction and 1 indicates very long interaction. Parameters: Timer resolution: Not given in the sources. Exponential function parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interaction Type Ambiguity: The module handles rotation, panning, and zooming separately. If an interaction involves multiple types simultaneously, the sources do not specify the priority or combination logic. Zoom Point Accuracy: The InteractionPoint is defined as the position of initial interaction. If the initial interaction is ambiguous (e.g., clicking on empty space), the behavior is not specified. Timer Zeroing: The timer is zeroed only when the interaction finishes. If the user pauses and resumes, the timer continues to accumulate unless explicitly reset by the system. Time Complexity: O(1) per interaction event. The calculations involve simple arithmetic operations and timer updates. Memory Complexity: O(1). The module stores a fixed number of scalar values (timer, last duration, interaction point). Strengths: Provides immediate feedback on user intent and engagement level, allowing the visualization system to adapt (e.g., via the Animation module) in real-time. Limitations: The prediction of consecutive viewpoints is based on simple statistics (duration, speed) and may not capture complex user intent. The lack of semantic navigation for rotation and panning limits its utility for those interaction types. When to use: When the visualization system needs to adapt its rendering style or focus based on user engagement levels, particularly for zooming interactions where region-of-interest is critical. When not to use: When high-precision semantic navigation is required for rotation or panning, or when the user interaction model is complex and requires more sophisticated intent recognition than simple duration and speed metrics. Engagement Estimation was introduced in the context of Dynamic Focus + Context (DFC) for volume rendering. The method was developed to enhance the interpretation of user interactions by guiding the enhancement of the visualization. It is part of a broader framework that includes an Animation module to adjust voxel styles based on engagement levels. The approach is rooted in the idea that user interaction patterns (such as zooming into a region) can be used to infer regions of interest and adjust the visualization accordingly. name: Simple Exploration Path Construction
head: Inspection Walkthrough Path Construction
body: An algorithm for generating an inspection walkthrough path for complex volume models, ensuring all representative views (keypoints) are visited. It constructs a minimal length path on a bounding sphere of the object or region of interest. It sets itself apart from siblings like B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation by using an exhaustive search for the shortest path through a small set of discrete candidates rather than continuous curve fitting. It differs from Improved Exploration Path Construction by not deviating from the shortest path to maximize local information. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N representative viewpoints (keypoints) on a bounding sphere, typically N \in \{3, 4\}. Input: The viewpoint with the highest entropy, denoted B0. Output: An ordered sequence of camera positions on the bounding sphere that visits all keypoints. Data Structures: keypoints: A list of N 3D positions on the bounding sphere. bestview: The 3D position of B0 within keypoints. path: An ordered list of 3D positions representing the camera trajectory. Steps: 1. Identify Key Points: Use the important viewpoints selected in the previous section as key points. Let the set of key points be K = \{k1, k2,..., kN\}. 2. Identify Best View: Determine the viewpoint with the highest entropy, B0, from K. 3. Enforce Constraint: Ensure B0 is visited in the second position of the path. This allows the camera to visit the surroundings of B0, which are intuitively more informative. 4. Compute Minimal Path: Compute the minimal length path that passes through all representative views in K, subject to the constraint that B0 is second. 5. Exhaustive Search: Since there are only three to four candidates (N \le 4), an exhaustive search of all permutations of the remaining N-1 viewpoints is performed to find the shortest path. 6. Construct Path: The resulting sequence of positions forms the simple exploration path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import itertools import math def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def simpleexplorationpath(keypoints, bestview): """Generates a simple exploration path visiting all keypoints. The bestview (highest entropy) must be visited second.""" remaining = [k for k in keypoints if k != bestview] n = len(remaining) bestlength = float('inf') bestpath = None for perm in itertools.permutations(remaining): # Path structure: [firstremaining, bestview, restremaining] currentpath = [perm[0], bestview] + list(perm[1:]) currentlength = sum(distance(currentpath[i], currentpath[i+1]) for i in range(n)) if currentlength < bestlength: bestlength = currentlength bestpath = currentpath return bestpath Parameters: Number of candidate viewpoints: Typically three to four. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If N < 2, the constraint "best view in second place" is undefined; the sources assume N \ge 3 based on the typical candidate count. The sources do not specify the exact distance metric, but since positions lie on a bounding sphere, arc length or angular distance should be used for path length calculation. The algorithm assumes the bounding sphere is already defined and the keypoints lie on it. An improvement to the simple path where the camera deviates from the short path to maximize information gathered, evaluated by entropy. For each step, it analyzes the entropy of three candidate positions placed toward the destination point, separated by \pm 4 to 6 degrees. It chooses the candidate with the highest entropy. The allowed total deviation is limited and reduced as the camera gets closer to the next key point to ensure all keypoints are visited. The speed of the camera is reduced when visiting points nearby the best view (B0) because they show a higher amount of valuable information. This approach gathers a higher amount of details than the simple method. Time depends on the number of steps produced, as it requires the evaluation of entropy at each step. Time Complexity: The simple path calculation time is negligible due to the exhaustive search over a small number of candidates (N \le 4). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The simple path is described as having "fast response" and "ease of use". Strengths: Provides a global vision of complex models by visiting all representative views; fast computation; no parameter definition required. Limitations: Does not actively maximize information gain along the path (unlike the improved variant); relies on pre-selected representative views. When to use: When a quick, comprehensive inspection of a volume model is needed without the computational cost of entropy evaluation at every step. When not to use: When maximizing local detail and information gain is critical, in which case the Improved Exploration Path Construction should be used. Originated in the context of medical volume visualization, specifically for radiologists inspecting complex anatomical structures like kidneys and thorax. The method was proposed to address the insufficiency of a static set of views for providing a global vision of complex models. It is designed to be easily incorporated into daily work by radiologists with null cost. The technique is applicable to other rendering metaphors beyond medical imaging. Representative Views and Paths for Volume Models, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-85412-810, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Linear Camera Path Generation
head: Camera Translation Methods
body: Linear Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses along a straight line segment between a start and end position, maintaining a fixed look-at point. It solves the problem of generating consistent, evenly spaced viewpoints for volume rendering or 3D visualization without rotational artifacts. It is distinguished from sibling methods like B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation by its lack of curvature and from Arcball Camera by its restriction to translational motion only. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: startpos (3D vector), endpos (3D vector), lookat (3D vector), numviews (integer), and optional intrinsics (width, height, fx, fy). Outputs: A list of PinholeCamera objects, each containing extrinsic parameters (position, orientation) and intrinsic parameters. Data Structures PinholeCamera: Contains fields for position \mathbf{p}, look-at point \mathbf{l}, and intrinsics fx, fy, w, h. The path is represented as a list of these objects. Parameters startpos: Starting 3D coordinate. endpos: Ending 3D coordinate. lookat: Fixed focal point in 3D space. numviews: Number of intermediate poses to generate. Default: 30. width: Image width in pixels. Default: 1280. height: Image height in pixels. Default: 720. fx: Focal length in pixels (x). Default: 960.0. fy: Focal length in pixels (y). Default: 960.0. Algorithm 1. Calculate the direction vector \mathbf{d} = \text{end\pos} - \text{start\pos}. 2. For each view index i from 0 to \text{num\views} - 1: a. Compute the interpolation parameter t = \frac{i}{\text{num\views} - 1} if \text{num\views} > 1, else t=0. b. Compute the camera position \mathbf{p}i = \text{start\pos} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. c. Construct a PinholeCamera with position \mathbf{p}i, fixed look-at point \text{look\at}, and specified intrinsics. 3. Return the list of cameras. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatelinearpath(startpos, endpos, lookat, numviews=30, width=1280, height=720, fx=960.0, fy=960.0): """ Generate a list of PinholeCamera objects along a linear path. Args: startpos: np.ndarray, shape (3,) endpos: np.ndarray, shape (3,) lookat: np.ndarray, shape (3,) numviews: int width: int height: int fx: float fy: float Returns: list of PinholeCamera objects """ cameras = [] direction = endpos - startpos # Handle edge case of single view or zero distance if numviews <= 1: t = 0.0 else: # Loop through all views for i in range(numviews): # Linear interpolation parameter t = i / (numviews - 1) # Calculate current position currentpos = startpos + direction t # Create camera object # Note: Orientation is derived from position and fixed lookat point. # The specific rotation matrix calculation (up vector, cross products) # is assumed to be handled by the PinholeCamera constructor # when given position and lookat. cam = PinholeCamera( position=currentpos, lookat=lookat, width=width, height=height, fx=fx, fy=fy) cameras.append(cam) return cameras class PinholeCamera: def init(self, position, lookat, width, height, fx, fy): self.position = np.array(position) self.lookat = np.array(lookat) self.width = width self.height = height self.fx = fx self.fy = fy # Orientation is computed internally based on position and lookat self.computeorientation() def computeorientation(self): # Standard look-at matrix construction # Forward vector forward = self.lookat - self.position forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) # Assume standard up vector (0, 1, 0) unless specified otherwise up = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Right vector right = np.cross(forward, up) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) # True up vector up = np.cross(right, forward) # Rotation matrix R (3x3) self.R = np.columnstack((right, up, -forward)) def getextrinsicmatrix(self): """Returns 4x4 extrinsic matrix [R|t; 0|1]""" M = np.eye(4) M[:3,:3] = self.R M[:3, 3] = self.position return M Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Distance: If startpos equals endpos, the direction vector is zero. The code handles this by keeping the position constant at startpos for all views. Single View: If numviews is 1, t is forced to 0 to avoid division by zero, resulting in a single camera at startpos. Precision: Floating-point interpolation errors are negligible for typical volume rendering resolutions but may accumulate in extremely long paths. itermove() provides a generator-like interface to yield positions sequentially, useful for streaming or memory-constrained environments. It differs from generatelinearpath by not storing all poses in memory at once. setposition() updates the camera location in-place while keeping the focus fixed. This is useful for interactive viewports rather than batch generation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is numviews, as each view requires a constant number of vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the list of camera objects. Performance: Extremely fast; negligible compared to the volume rendering step itself. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and easy to debug. Ideal for orthogonal scans or linear fly-throughs. Limitations: Cannot represent curved trajectories or complex camera motions. May cause visual discontinuities if the look-at point is occluded or if the path passes through the volume data in a non-intuitive way. When to use: When a straight-line traversal is required, such as in tomographic reconstruction validation or simple fly-throughs. When not to use: For cinematic shots requiring smooth turns (B-Spline) or user-controlled exploration (First-Person). The method originates from the yt project's volume rendering visualization tools, specifically the Camera class which provides translation-related methods like setposition and itermove. It is also implemented in the GaussianScan-Recon repository for generating camera poses from 3D points. The approach is a standard technique in computer graphics for generating linear camera trajectories. name: Scene View Estimation
head: Estimate Scene View, Make Render Input
body: Scene View Estimation computes the camera position, orientation, and projection parameters required to render a 3D scene into a target viewport. It solves the problem of automatically framing the scene content within the camera's view frustum by analyzing the spatial extent of the scene data. It differs from sibling methods like Arcball Camera or First-Person Camera Control by being fully automatic and data-driven, rather than user-controlled or trajectory-based. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation for the final matrix assembly. Inputs: scene: A scene object containing sceneBounds (global bounds) and splatSets (a list of splat sets, each with its own bounds). width, height: Target viewport dimensions in pixels. frameIndex: Current frame identifier. Outputs: input: A render input structure containing: view: View matrix (look-at). proj: Projection matrix (perspective). cameraPosition: Eye position vector. viewportWidth, viewportHeight: Viewport dimensions. nearPlane, farPlane: Clipping plane distances. frameIndex: Frame ID. settings: Configuration flags (antialiasing, fastCulling). Data Structures: bounds: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by minimum and maximum 3D vectors. view: A struct containing center (3D vector) and radius (float). Steps: 1. Initialize bounds with scene.sceneBounds. 2. Iterate over each set in scene.splatSets, merging each set's bounds into bounds using MergeBounds. 3. If bounds is invalid, return a default view with center = {0, 0, 2.5} and radius = 1.0. 4. Otherwise, compute center = ComputeAabbCenter(bounds) and radius = max(ComputeAabbRadius(bounds), 0.5). 5. Calculate aspect = width / height. 6. Calculate distance = max(view.radius 2.5, 1.5). 7. Set eye = {view.center.x, view.center.y, view.center.z - distance}. 8. Set input.view = LookAt(eye, view.center, {0.0, 1.0, 0.0}). 9. Set input.proj = Perspective(1.0, aspect, 0.01, max(100.0, distance + view.radius 4.0)). 10. Set input.cameraPosition = eye, input.viewportWidth = width, input.viewportHeight = height, input.nearPlane = 0.01, input.farPlane = max(100.0, distance + view.radius 4.0), input.frameIndex = frameIndex. 11. Set input.settings.antialiasing = True, input.settings.fastCulling = True. Formulas: aspect = \frac{width}{height} distance = \max(view.radius \times 2.5, 1.5) eye = (view.center.x, view.center.y, view.center.z - distance) farPlane = \max(100.0, distance + view.radius \times 4.0) Parameters and Typical Values: aspect: Derived from viewport dimensions. distance: Scaled by view.radius 2.5, minimum 1.5. nearPlane: Fixed at 0.01. farPlane: Scaled by distance + view.radius 4.0, minimum 100.0. FOV: Fixed at 1.0 radian. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Bounds: If the scene has no splats or invalid bounds, a default view is returned to prevent crashes. Small Scenes: The max(..., 0.5) and max(..., 1.5) guards prevent the camera from getting too close to small or zero-sized scenes, which could cause numerical instability or clipping issues. Large Scenes: The max(..., 100.0) guard for the far plane ensures that very large scenes do not result in excessively large far planes that could reduce depth buffer precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def EstimateSceneView(scene, width, height, frameIndex): # Step 1: Compute Scene Bounds bounds = scene.sceneBounds for splatset in scene.splatSets: bounds = MergeBounds(bounds, splatset.bounds) # Step 2: Validate Bounds and Compute View Parameters if bounds is invalid: # Check if bounds is invalid (e.g., empty or uninitialized) viewcenter = Vector3(0, 0, 2.5) viewradius = 1.0 else: viewcenter = ComputeAabbCenter(bounds) viewradius = max(ComputeAabbRadius(bounds), 0.5) # Step 3: Calculate Camera Distance aspect = width / height distance = max(viewradius 2.5, 1.5) # Step 4: Set Eye Position eye = Vector3(viewcenter.x, viewcenter.y, viewcenter.z - distance) # Step 5: Construct View Matrix upvector = Vector3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) viewmatrix = LookAt(eye, viewcenter, upvector) # Step 6: Construct Projection Matrix farplane = max(100.0, distance + viewradius 4.0) projmatrix = Perspective(1.0, aspect, 0.01, farplane) # Step 7: Populate Render Input input = RenderInput() input.view = viewmatrix input.proj = projmatrix input.cameraPosition = eye input.viewportWidth = width input.viewportHeight = height input.nearPlane = 0.01 input.farPlane = farplane input.frameIndex = frameIndex input.settings.antialiasing = True input.settings.fastCulling = True return input Hybrid module for estimating and refining per-pixel depth maps from image inputs, resolving scaling/shifting ambiguities and mitigating MVS inaccuracies on sparse views. Combines initial MVS estimation with U-Net refinement using multi-view stereo cues and image features for consistent depth maps. Estimates camera viewpoint (azimuth and elevation) by classifying rendered volume images into discrete regions on a viewing sphere using HEALPix division, evaluating loss via geodesic distance. Provides probabilities for each interval to capture viewpoint ambiguity, unlike regression methods. Predicts viewpoint label via classification, estimates viewpoint residual via regression, and combines them for the final viewpoint. Uses a K-means dictionary size K=24 and geodesic distance importance \alpha=10 for best performance. Modified to be category-specific rather than category-independent. Viewpoint estimation method based on AlexNet that ignores the camera-lit angle and focuses only on azimuth and elevation. Achieves lower classification accuracy than VGGNet (UD+GS) across all tested categories and angle tolerances (2° to 15°). Selects a batch of B views to capture new images, avoiding similar views via a greedy optimization algorithm that is 1/e-approximate in Fisher Information. Initializes selected set S0 = \emptyset and Fisher Information matrix H0 = H[w^|D{train}]. Iteratively selects view i maximizing \text{tr}(H''[y{i,acq}|x{acqi}, w^] H{b-1}^{-1}), adds it to Sb, and updates Hb = H{b-1} + H''[y{i,acq}|x{acqi}, w^]. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splat sets, O(N), where N is the number of sets in scene.splatSets. The bounding box merge and center/radius computations are constant time per set. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), as it only stores temporary bounds and view parameters. Strengths: Simple, fast, and automatic. Ensures the entire scene is visible within the frustum. Limitations: Does not account for camera orientation preferences (always looks from -Z). May not frame aesthetically pleasing views for complex scenes with sparse distributions. When to Use: When an automatic, data-driven camera setup is required for rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. When Not to Use: When user-controlled camera movement or specific artistic framing is required. This method is implemented in the DirectXSplat project, a DirectX 12 implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It provides a standardized way to initialize the camera for rendering splat sets. pbkx/DirectXSplat, https://github.com/pbkx/DirectXSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1145/3309993, fetched 2026-10-29 FisherRF: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72624-824, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Depth Network
head: Depth Network d
body: The Depth Network is a component in sparse-view novel view synthesis systems that refines initial depth estimates to construct accurate 3D point clouds for rendering. It solves the problem of inaccurate depth estimation in sparse input scenarios, where traditional Multi-View Stereo (MVS) fails due to limited overlap and large baselines, and single-image estimation suffers from scaling/shifting ambiguity. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Viewpoint Estimation via Sphere Classification and Batch Active View Selection by explicitly regressing geometric depth maps from image features rather than estimating camera poses or selecting views. The Depth Network takes an input image and an initial depth map (derived from MVS or sensor data) and outputs a refined depth map. It employs a hybrid design that cascades a lightweight MVS module with a U-Net refinement network. Inputs and Outputs: Input Image (Ii): The i-th input view. Initial Depth (D{init}): Either MVS-estimated depths or sensor depths (D^{sen}). Output (Di): Refined depth map for building the point cloud. Data Structures: Binary Mask (Mi): A mask indicating valid sensor depth pixels. U-Net: The core refinement architecture that takes the image Ii and initial depth as inputs. Steps: 1. Initial Estimation: Use PatchmatchNet [77] to generate initial depth estimations from the sparse input views. If sensor depth D^{sen} is available, it is used directly as the initial input instead of MVS output. 2. Feature Encoding: The image Ii is processed by a spatial feature encoder (built on BigGAN architecture [3]) to generate per-pixel feature vectors Fi. Each vector is 61-dimensional and concatenated with RGB channels, resulting in 64 dimensions total. 3. Refinement: The U-Net takes the image Ii and the initial depth map (D{init}) as inputs. It refines the depth using multi-view stereo cues and image cues. 4. Output: The U-Net outputs the refined depth Di, which is used to build the point cloud. Formulas: During training, if sensor depth is available, a loss function Ls is used to encourage the U-Net output to match the sensor depth: Ls = \| Mi Di - Mi D^{sen} \| where Mi is the binary mask of valid sensor depths, Di is the network output, and D^{sen} is the sensor depth. Parameters: MVS Module: PatchmatchNet [77] is used for its speed and lightweight nature. Feature Encoder: Based on BigGAN [3], producing 64-dimensional features per pixel. Loss Weight: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Inputs: Applying MVS solely on sparse inputs is challenging due to limited overlap and huge baselines, leading to inaccurate and low-confidence estimations. Ambiguity: Single-image depth estimation suffers from scaling/shifting ambiguity, losing valuable multi-view cues and causing inconsistent estimations across views. Sensor Noise: Sensor depths are often noisy and incomplete; the U-Net acts as a completion and refinement module in this setting. A multi-branch ResNet backbone that predicts intrinsic properties (albedo, normals, depth) and a global lighting feature from a single input image. It distinguishes itself by predicting a global lighting feature vector alongside geometric properties, enabling downstream volumetric lighting prediction. Choose this when inverse rendering of indoor scenes with spatially-varying lighting is required. Definition: Predicts albedo \tilde{A}, surface normals \tilde{N}, depth \tilde{D}, and a global lighting feature \tilde{f}L from a single linearized RGB image I. Formula: \tilde{A}, \tilde{N}, \tilde{D}, \tilde{f}L = h{DP} (I; \Theta{DP}) where h{DP} is the ResNet backbone and \Theta{DP} are the network parameters. Parameters: Input: Single linearized RGB image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Output: Albedo \tilde{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, Normals \tilde{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, Depth \tilde{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}, Global Feature \tilde{f}L \in \mathbb{R}^C. Uses an off-the-shelf monocular depth estimator (PackNet) to obtain 2.5D geometry of the scene for lighting volume prediction and object insertion. Steps: 1. Depth Usage for Lighting: Use predicted depth to unproject scene pixel values into 3D for lighting volume prediction. 2. Depth Usage for Object Insertion: Use depth to decide the 3D placement of the inserted object. 3. Depth Rescaling: Use projected sparse LiDAR points as ground-truth depth to rescale the estimated depth by minimizing the L2 error between them, addressing scale error. 4. Shadow Rendering: Use pre-computed depth to compute the 3D location of each scene pixel for ray-mesh queries. Pitfalls: Scale error in depth prediction leads to error in the size of inserted objects. Errors in estimated depth may result in incorrect shadows, though empirically negligible when inserting on flat surfaces. Estimates depth for a list of RGB images by batching model forward passes for speed on MPS/CUDA, falling back to per-frame estimation on failure. Steps: 1. Initialize output list out and load model if torch stack is available. 2. While len(out) < n, take a chunk of rgbs of size BATCH (or remaining frames). 3. Pass the chunk to the pipeline; if successful, decode each result using modeloutputtodepth and extend out; if failed, break the loop. 4. Call progress callback with current count and total if provided. 5. After the batch loop, if len(out) < n, estimate depth for remaining frames individually using estimatedepth. Parameters: Batch size BATCH: Determined by environment variable FOURDDEPTHBATCH, default 4. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles sparse input views where traditional MVS fails; refines noisy sensor data; integrates multi-view cues with single-image appearance cues. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial MVS estimate or sensor data; single-image estimation alone is ambiguous. When to use: When synthesizing novel views from a sparse set of images and accurate geometry is required for point cloud construction. When not to use: When dense input views are available and standard MVS is sufficient, or when camera pose estimation is the primary goal rather than depth refinement. The Depth Network was introduced in the context of Forward Warping and Depth (FWD) for real-time novel view synthesis. It addresses the limitations of learning 3D geometry end-to-end by relying on rendering and refinement. The method uses PatchmatchNet for initial MVS and a U-Net for refinement, leveraging the BigGAN architecture for feature extraction. The Direct Prediction Module variant was introduced in the context of learning indoor inverse rendering with 3D spatially-varying lighting.
