name: GPS-Gaussian Network Architecture
head: GPS-Gaussian, Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: The GPS-Gaussian Network Architecture is a regression method that predicts pixel-wise 3D Gaussian parameter maps (position, rotation, scaling, opacity, and color) to enable real-time novel view synthesis. While primarily described as a single-image approach, the implementation actually selects two adjacent source views for binocular depth estimation based on view vector similarity. It distinguishes itself from classic binocular stereo methods by making the image encoder independent from the depth estimator and re-indexing the correlation volume for both lookup procedures, achieving a compact parallelized implementation with over 30% efficiency gain. Inputs and Outputs Input: A source image I of resolution 1024 \times 1024. Output: Five pixel-wise maps: Position map Mp, Rotation map Mr, Scaling map Ms, Opacity map M\alpha, and Color map Mc. Data Structures Correlation Volume C: A 3D tensor used for depth estimation, re-indexed to support both reference and target view lookups in a single parallelized pass. Feature Maps: Intermediate representations fS (source image features) and depth features. Gaussian Feature \Gamma: The decoded pixel-wise feature vector before final parameter prediction. Algorithm Steps 1. Image Encoding: The input image I is processed by an image encoder to produce image features fS. This encoder is designed to be independent from the depth estimator. 2. Depth Estimation: The features are processed by a depth estimator that re-indexes the correlation volume C to allow efficient lookup for both reference and target view operations. A refinement module iteratively refines the depth map for T = 3 iterations, chosen as a trade-off between performance and computational cost. The output is a predicted depth map D. Depth prediction operates on a lower resolution and is upsampled to the full image resolution (1024 \times 1024). 3. Depth Encoding: The predicted depth map D is passed through a depth encoder E{depth}, which has an identical architecture to the image encoder. 4. Feature Aggregation: Image features and depth features are aggregated into a U-Net-like Gaussian parameter decoder D{parm} via skip connections. 5. Parameter Prediction: The decoder outputs a pixel-wise Gaussian feature \Gamma. Three specific prediction heads process \Gamma to produce the rotation map Mr, scaling map Ms, and opacity map M\alpha. The position map Mp is computed directly from the predicted depth map D. The color map Mc is directly borrowed from the RGB values of the input image I. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageencoder(I): # Trained CNN encoder producing features fS return I def depthestimator(F, C, T): # Depth estimator with re-indexed correlation volume C and T refinement iterations return F def depthencoder(D): # Trained depth encoder Edepth with identical architecture to imageencoder return D def gaussianparameterdecoder(Fimg, Fdepth): # U-Net-like decoder Dparm with skip connections return Fimg def rotationhead(G): # Prediction head for rotation map Mr return G def scalinghead(G): # Prediction head for scaling map Ms return G def opacityhead(G): # Prediction head for opacity map Malpha return G def depthtoposition(D): # Computes position map Mp directly from depth map D return D def gpsgaussiannetwork(sourceimage: list) -> dict: """ Predicts 3D Gaussian parameters from source images. Args: sourceimage: RGB image tensor of shape (3, 1024, 1024). Returns: Dictionary containing maps Mp, Mr, Ms, Malpha, Mc. """ # 1. Image Encoding imagefeatures = imageencoder(sourceimage) # 2. Depth Estimation # Re-index correlation volume C for parallelized lookup # Refinement runs for T=3 iterations depthmap = depthestimator(imagefeatures, C=[], T=3) # 3. Depth Encoding # Edepth has identical architecture to imageencoder depthfeatures = depthencoder(depthmap) # 4. Feature Aggregation # Concatenate image and depth features, pass through U-Net decoder gaussianfeature = gaussianparameterdecoder(imagefeatures, depthfeatures) # 5. Parameter Prediction # Predict rotation, scaling, and opacity from Gaussian feature rotationmap = rotationhead(gaussianfeature) scalingmap = scalinghead(gaussianfeature) opacitymap = opacityhead(gaussianfeature) # Position is derived directly from depth positionmap = depthtoposition(depthmap) # Color is borrowed directly from input colormap = sourceimage return { "Mp": positionmap, "Mr": rotationmap, "Ms": scalingmap, "Malpha": opacitymap, "Mc": colormap } Parameters T = 3: Number of refinement iterations in the depth estimator. Input Resolution: 1024 \times 1024 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Upsampling Artifacts: Depth prediction operates on low resolution and is upsampled to full resolution, causing drastically changed depth in margin areas (e.g., crossed limbs, legs), leading to ambiguous predictions and rendering noise. Ambiguous Depth Handling: The network handles ambiguous depth predictions at margins by jointly regressing extremely low opacity values for outlier Gaussian points, making them invisible in novel view rendering. Generalization: The model is trained on uniformly placed 8-camera setups but generalizes to random camera setups with pitch in [-20^\circ, +20^\circ] and yaw in [-25^\circ, +25^\circ]. Performance may degrade outside these ranges, requiring re-training with synthetic data covering those setups. Time Complexity: The method is designed for real-time performance. On an RTX 3090 GPU, source view processing takes 14 ms, each novel view takes 5 ms, and the total is 27 ms. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The re-indexing of the correlation volume and independent encoder design provide an efficiency increase exceeding 30% compared to classic binocular stereo methods that do not share these optimizations. Strengths: Real-time novel view synthesis from a single image; robust handling of ambiguous depth via learned opacity; efficient parallelized implementation. Limitations: Depth upsampling artifacts in complex geometries (margins); generalization limited to specific camera angle ranges unless re-trained; relies on accurate single-image depth estimation. When to use: Real-time novel view synthesis from a single source image. When not to use: When high-precision geometry is required in complex margin areas without opacity masking; when camera poses are outside the trained distribution [-20^\circ, +20^\circ] pitch and [-25^\circ, +25^\circ] yaw without re-training. The GPS-Gaussian architecture was introduced in the paper "GPS-Gaussian: Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Human Novel View Synthesis". It builds upon the Depth Network module, which estimates depth from a single image using a hybrid design to resolve scaling/shifting ambiguity and inconsistent estimations across views [Parent]. The method was tested with randomly placed camera setups to demonstrate generalization capabilities. name: Viewpoint Estimation via Sphere Classification
head: Geodesic loss viewpoint estimation, HEALPix-based viewpoint classification
body: This method estimates the camera viewpoint (azimuth and elevation) of a rendered volume image by classifying the image into discrete regions on a viewing sphere, rather than regressing continuous angles. It differs from previous classification methods that divide azimuth and elevation domains independently by dividing the sphere uniformly using HEALPix, allowing loss evaluation via geodesic distance. It differs from regression methods, which fail to capture viewpoint ambiguity (e.g., similar rendered images for nearby viewpoints), by providing probabilities for each interval. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A rendered volume image. Output: A predicted viewpoint label corresponding to one of N discrete regions on the viewing sphere, or a probability distribution over these regions. Data Structures: Viewpoint Label: The viewing sphere is discretized into N uniform regions using HEALPix, which serve as viewpoint labels. Viewpoint Parameterization: A viewpoint is parameterized as a tuple (\theta, \phi), where \theta is the azimuth (longitude) angle and \phi is the elevation (latitude) angle. The viewing sphere is centered at the volume center. Algorithm Steps: 1. Dataset Generation (Training Phase): Select a category of volumes (e.g., head, engine). For each volume in the category, generate a large number of rendered images with viewpoint annotations. Viewpoint Sampling: Sample viewpoints uniformly on the viewing sphere using HEALPix. These sampled viewpoints serve as the ground-truth labels for the generated images. Rendering Parameter Variation: For each viewpoint label, render images with varying parameters to ensure robustness: Camera-Tilt: Randomly rotate the camera-tilt angle for each image to handle CNN's lack of rotation invariance. Projection Type: Randomly select between parallel and perspective projection for each image. Background Color: Randomly choose black or white for each image to account for alpha blending effects. Scale: Uniformly sample scale from 1 to 1.8 for rendering volumes to reduce scale influence. Lighting Mode: Mode 1: Environment light only. Mode 2: Environment light + one headlight at camera position; headlight intensity sampled uniformly from 0.7 to 1. Mode 3: Environment light + headlight + scene light; scene light position sampled on a sphere with radius 3-5x the viewing sphere radius; headlight and scene light intensities sampled uniformly from 0.35 to 0.5. Transfer Functions: Opacity: Manually designed to highlight specific features (e.g., skin, skull, tooth) rather than randomly generated, to avoid missing important features. Add a small random disturbance: for each feature, move the keypoint of the 1D transfer function left or right by distance d \sim N(0, 1). Color: Randomly sample color for each feature for each image, biased towards high contrast with the background. Train a category-specific CNN on this dataset. 2. Inference (Testing Phase): Input a new rendered volume image into the trained CNN. The CNN outputs a classification result, identifying the HEALPix region (viewpoint label) most likely to have generated the image. The predicted viewpoint is the center (or representative point) of the predicted HEALPix region. Formulas: The loss is computed using the geodesic distance between the predicted viewpoint label and the ground-truth viewpoint label. Let y be the ground-truth label and \hat{y} be the predicted label (or probability distribution). The loss L is based on the geodesic distance dG(y, \hat{y}) on the sphere. Parameters: Camera-Tilt Angle: Randomly rotated for each rendered image during training. Projection Type: Randomly selected between parallel and perspective projection for each rendered image. Background Color: Randomly chosen as black or white for each rendered image. Scale: Uniformly sampled from 1 to 1.8 for rendering volumes. Lighting Mode 1: Environment light only. Lighting Mode 2: Environment light + one headlight at camera position; headlight intensity sampled uniformly from 0.7 to 1. Lighting Mode 3: Environment light + headlight + scene light; scene light position sampled on sphere with radius 3-5x viewing sphere radius; intensities sampled from 0.35 to 0.5. Phong Coefficients: Ambient=1 (fixed); Diffuse sampled from 0.25 to 0.75; Specular sampled from 0.5 to 1; Shininess sampled from 20 to 100. Opacity Disturbance: For each feature, the keypoint of the 1D transfer function is moved left or right by distance d \sim N(0, 1). Color Transfer Function: Color of each feature randomly sampled for each image, biased towards high contrast with background. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Keypoint-based methods are unsuitable: They require known camera intrinsic parameters to solve perspective-n-point, whereas this method estimates viewpoints with unknown/different intrinsic parameters (parallel vs perspective). Random Opacity Transfer Functions: Randomly generated opacity functions may miss important features completely, reducing performance. Azimuth/Elevation Non-Uniformity: Previous methods dividing azimuth and elevation independently fail because these are not uniform units of measure and cannot directly evaluate distance. A loss function for viewpoint estimation that modifies the Softmax loss by incorporating geometric constraints between neighbor viewpoints to exploit continuity on the viewing sphere. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments show that classification performance is better than regression performance for viewpoint estimation. Strengths: Captures viewpoint ambiguity by providing probabilities for each interval, unlike regression which returns only predicted parameters. Handles different intrinsic parameters (parallel vs perspective projection). Uses geodesic distance for loss, which correctly evaluates distance on the sphere, unlike independent azimuth/elevation classification. Limitations: Requires a large number of viewpoint-annotated images to avoid overfitting deep CNNs. Requires generating a training dataset via "Render for CNN" approach since no public training dataset exists for this specific problem. Performance may depend on the specific category of volumes (e.g., head vs engine). When to use: When estimating viewpoint for volume visualization where camera intrinsics are unknown or variable, and when capturing viewpoint ambiguity is important. When not to use: When keypoints are available and camera intrinsics are known (keypoint-based methods may be more suitable). Origin: The method was introduced in "CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization". History: It uses HEALPix [7] for sphere pixelization and references the 'Render for CNN' [35] approach for dataset generation. It addresses limitations of previous classification methods that divided azimuth and elevation independently and regression methods that failed to capture ambiguity. Usage: Used for viewpoint estimation of rendered volume images in volume visualization contexts. name: Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function
head: GS Loss
body: The Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function (GS Loss) is a classification loss for viewpoint estimation that modifies the standard Softmax loss by incorporating geometric constraints between neighboring viewpoints on the viewing sphere. Unlike standard Softmax, which treats all incorrect classes as equally wrong, GS Loss assigns non-zero weights to neighbor viewpoints based on their geodesic distance from the ground truth, explicitly exploiting the continuity and correlation inherent in spherical camera parameterizations. Inputs and Outputs Input: A rendered volume image s and its ground-truth viewpoint label vs from a discrete set of viewpoints V. Output: A scalar loss value L{vp}(s) used to update the neural network weights. Data Structures Viewpoint Set (V): A discrete set of viewpoints covering the viewing sphere, where neighbor relationships are defined by the chosen sphere discretization (e.g., HEALPix). Neighbor Viewpoint Set (V(vs, n)): A subset of V containing viewpoints within a relative distance bandwidth n of the ground-truth viewpoint vs. Ground-Truth Distribution (q): A vector of weights over the viewpoint set V, where q(v) is the target probability weight for viewpoint v. Parameters Bandwidth Parameter (n): Determines the size of the neighbor set V(vs, n). Typical Value: n=1. Effect: Includes the ground-truth viewpoint and its first-order neighbors; n=0 includes only the ground truth. Geodesic Distance (d): The distance metric between two viewpoints on the sphere, d: V \times V \to \mathbb{R}. Algorithm The loss is computed in three steps: 1. Determine Neighbor Set: Identify the set of viewpoints V(vs, n) surrounding the ground-truth viewpoint vs based on the bandwidth parameter n. 2. Compute Ground-Truth Distribution Weights: Calculate the weight q(v) for each viewpoint v \in V(vs, n) using the exponential decay of the geodesic distance: q(v) = e^{-d(v, vs)} For viewpoints outside the neighbor set, q(v) = 0. 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the weighted cross-entropy loss using the predicted probabilities Pv(s) and the weights q(v): L{vp}(s) = - \sum{v \in V(vs, n)} q(v) \log Pv(s) Where Pv(s) is the probability that image s is classified as viewpoint v. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def geometricstructureawareloss(predictedprobs, groundtruthlabel, neighborlabels): """ Computes the Geometric Structure-Aware Loss. Args: predictedprobs: dict mapping viewpoint labels to probabilities Pv(s). groundtruthlabel: The label of the ground-truth viewpoint vs. neighborlabels: List of viewpoint labels in V(vs, n). Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ loss = 0.0 # Step 1 & 2: Iterate over the neighbor set and compute weights for v in neighborlabels: # Compute geodesic distance d(v, vs) # Assumes viewpoints are represented as unit vectors or coordinates # where a standard geodesic distance function is available. dist = geodesicdistance(v, groundtruthlabel) # Calculate weight q(v) = exp(-d) weight = math.exp(-dist) # Get predicted probability Pv(s) prob = predictedprobs[v] # Guard against log(0) if prob <= 0: prob = 1e-9 # Add to loss: -q(v) log(Pv(s)) loss -= weight math.log(prob) return loss def geodesicdistance(viewpointa, viewpointb): """Computes geodesic distance between two viewpoints.""" # Standard implementation for unit vectors on a sphere dot = sum(a b for a, b in zip(viewpointa, viewpointb)) dot = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot)) # Clamp for numerical stability return math.acos(dot) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Probability: If Pv(s) = 0 for any v with q(v) > 0, the log term becomes undefined. Standard practice is to clamp probabilities or add a small epsilon before taking the logarithm. Neighbor Definition: The definition of "neighbor" is strictly tied to the sphere discretization (e.g., HEALPix). Bandwidth Selection: The choice of n determines how many neighbors contribute to the loss; n=1 is used in experiments to include the ground truth and its first-order neighbors. Complexity: The complexity is proportional to the size of the neighbor set |V(vs, n)|, which remains constant relative to the total number of viewpoints |V| for a fixed bandwidth n. Performance: In experiments on volume visualization datasets (engine, fish, head, tooth, tree, vessel), GS Loss with n=1 improved prediction accuracy compared to standard Softmax loss. Strengths: Explicitly models the continuity of the viewing sphere, preventing the model from treating distant viewpoints as equally "wrong" as immediate neighbors. Limitations: Requires a discretization scheme that provides neighbor relationships and is not directly applicable to continuous regression without discretization. The Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function was introduced in the context of CNN-based viewpoint estimation for volume visualization. It addresses the limitation of standard classification losses that ignore the geometric structure of the viewing sphere. The method leverages the fact that neighboring viewpoints share significant geometric information, which is particularly important for viewpoint estimation. The approach was evaluated on six volume categories extracted from public databases (VolVis, The Volume Library). name: Batch Active View Selection
head: Greedy Batch Selection
body: Batch Active View Selection selects a batch of B camera views to capture new images for volume reconstruction, avoiding the selection of highly similar views by using a greedy optimization algorithm based on Fisher Information. It differs from single-view selection methods by planning a trajectory for an agent to acquire multiple training views simultaneously, addressing the combinatorial explosion of directly maximizing expected information gain across a batch. The method uses a greedy approximation to maximize the trace of the product of the new view's Hessian and the inverse of the accumulated Fisher Information matrix, providing a 1/e-approximation of the optimal solution. Inputs: D{pool}: The pool of candidate acquisition views. H''[w^ | D{train}]: The Fisher Information matrix (Hessian) computed from the initial training dataset D{train} at the current optimal weights w^. B: The number of views to select in the batch. Outputs: SB: The set of B selected views. Data Structures: Sb: A set containing the indices of views selected in steps 0 to b. Hb: The accumulated Fisher Information matrix after step b. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the selected set S0 to the empty set \emptyset. 2. Initialize the accumulated Fisher Information matrix H0 to the Hessian of the training data: H0 \leftarrow H''[w^ | D{train}]. 3. For each batch step b from 1 to B: a. Identify the candidate view i from the remaining pool D{pool} \setminus S{b-1} that maximizes the trace of the product of its Hessian and the inverse of the current accumulated matrix: i \leftarrow \arg \max{x{acq} \in D{pool} \setminus S{b-1}} \text{tr} \left( H''[y{i{acq}} | x{acqi}, w^] H{b-1}^{-1} \right) where H''[y{i{acq}} | x{acqi}, w^] is the Hessian (Fisher Information contribution) of the candidate view i. b. Add the selected view i to the set: Sb \leftarrow S{b-1} \cup \{i\}. c. Update the accumulated Fisher Information matrix by adding the selected view's Hessian: Hb \leftarrow H{b-1} + H''[y{i{acq}} | x{acqi}, w^]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def batchactiveviewselection(candidatepool, Htrain, B): """ Selects B views from candidatepool using greedy Fisher Information maximization. Args: candidatepool: List of view indices. Htrain: Initial Fisher Information matrix (2D list) from training data. B: Number of views to select. Returns: selected: List of selected view indices. """ selected = [] Hacc = [row[:] for row in Htrain] # Deep copy of Htrain Hinv = inversematrix(Hacc) for b in range(1, B + 1): bestview = None maxtrace = -float('inf') for viewidx in candidatepool: if viewidx in selected: continue # Standard operation to compute or retrieve H''[yiacq | xacqi, w] Hview = computehessian(viewidx) product = matmul(Hview, Hinv) currenttrace = trace(product) if currenttrace > maxtrace: maxtrace = currenttrace bestview = viewidx selected.append(bestview) Hviewbest = computehessian(bestview) Hacc = matadd(Hacc, Hviewbest) Hinv = inversematrix(Hacc) return selected def trace(M): return sum(M[i][i] for i in range(len(M))) def matmul(A, B): n, m, p = len(A), len(B[0]), len(B) return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(p)) for j in range(m)] for i in range(n)] def matadd(A, B): return [[A[i][j] + B[i][j] for j in range(len(A[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def inversematrix(M): # Standard matrix inversion; in practice, Cholesky or LU decomposition is used for stability. pass # Implementation omitted; use standard linear algebra routine. def computehessian(viewidx): # Standard operation to compute the Hessian of the candidate view at current weights w. pass # Implementation omitted; depends on scene representation and loss function. Parameters: B: Batch size. When B=1, the algorithm is equivalent to single-view active selection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pool Exhaustion: If the candidate pool D{pool} becomes empty before B views are selected, the loop terminates early. Numerical Stability: The trace operation sums eigenvalues; numerical instability may occur if H{b-1} is ill-conditioned. In practice, maintaining the inverse explicitly or using Cholesky decomposition updates is recommended for stability and speed. Greedy Representative View Selection is a method for selecting a small, diverse subset of camera views to represent a 3D scene, ensuring that selected views capture information not present in previously chosen ones. It solves the problem of redundant view selection by maximizing geometric diversity among a candidate set. It differs from global maximization approaches by offering a linear-time approximation that yields similar results with significantly lower computational cost. Greedy Representative View Selection Approximation Guarantee: The greedy selection provides a 1/e-approximation of the optimal Fisher Information objective. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids the combinatorial explosion of directly maximizing expected information gain between training and acquisition samples. It is designed for real-world scenarios where an agent plans a trajectory to acquire multiple training views simultaneously. Limitations: Greedy optimization may yield suboptimal global solutions compared to exhaustive search, though the approximation bound mitigates this. When to use: When batch acquisition is required and computational cost of global optimization is prohibitive. The method was introduced in the context of active mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting and Radiance Fields, specifically in the paper "FisherRF: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information". It addresses the problem of selecting informative views for reconstruction by leveraging Fisher Information to quantify the information gain of potential new views. The approach is designed to avoid the combinatorial explosion of directly maximizing expected information gain between training and acquisition samples. name: Greedy Representative View Selection
body: Greedy Representative View Selection is a greedy scheme to select a set of views that show information not captured in the best view, avoiding similar information under different directions. It differs from global maximization approaches by yielding similar results with linear cost instead of quadratic cost in the number of views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of candidate views, a distance metric d(X, Y) between two views, and the desired number of representative views M. Output: A subset of M representative views. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Similarity Metric: The distance d(X, Y) between two views is computed using the Normalized Compression Distance (NCD). NCD is chosen because simple image metrics like Mean Squared Error are sensitive to transformations such as rotation or translation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Select the best view B0 with an adaptive algorithm. 2. Measure the distances from B0 to the remaining views. 3. Select the next representer view B1 as the one at the highest distance from B0. 4. For subsequent views, compute distances from remaining views against all previously selected views and choose the view X that maximizes the geometric average of the distances to the selected views. Parameters: M: Number of representative views. Usually three or four are enough for most models. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedyrepresentativeviews(candidates, distfunc, m): """ Select m representative views from candidates using greedy geometric average distance. Args: candidates: List of view identifiers. distfunc: Function d(X, Y) returning distance between two views. m: Number of representative views to select. Returns: List of selected view identifiers. """ if not candidates: return [] # Step 1: Select B0 using an adaptive algorithm. # Source does not specify the adaptive algorithm for B0 selection. b0 = candidates[0] selected = [b0] remaining = [v for v in candidates if v != b0] if m == 1: return selected # Step 2: Measure distances from B0 to remaining views. # Step 3: Select B1 as the view furthest from B0. maxdist = -1.0 b1 = None for v in remaining: d = distfunc(b0, v) if d > maxdist: maxdist = d b1 = v selected.append(b1) remaining = [v for v in remaining if v != b1] if m == 2: return selected # Step 4: Iteratively select remaining views by maximizing geometric average distance to selected views. for k in range(2, m): bestview = None maxgeoavg = -1.0 for v in remaining: product = 1.0 for b in selected: product = distfunc(v, b) geoavg = product (1.0 / len(selected)) if geoavg > maxgeoavg: maxgeoavg = geoavg bestview = v selected.append(bestview) remaining = [v for v in remaining if v != bestview] return selected Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A supervision strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that favors target cameras with optical axes significantly different from input cameras to constrain Gaussian scales and orientations. It prunes Gaussians with opacity below \tau\alpha from the voxel-based scene G{vox} to yield G^0 = \{(\mu^0m, \xi^0m)\}{m=1}^M. Candidate target views v are scored by their angular separation from the nearest input direction i \in C: a(v, C) = \min{i \in C} \arccos(fv^\top fi), where fv = Rv^\star (0, 0, 1)^\top is the unit optical axis in the common reference frame. The target set T is sampled with a bias toward larger scores a(v, C). Supervision is applied to renderings of G^0 from both input views and T, using GT-depth warp masks to restrict loss to valid regions with depth-consistent support. Opacity pruning threshold \tau\alpha values tested include 0.01, 0.02, and 0.05. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of views, as the comparison process is the most costly part, but each step only compares remaining views against the fixed set of selected views. Global maximization has a quadratic cost in the number of views. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids redundant information capture; computationally efficient compared to global optimization; robust to image transformations via NCD. Limitations: Greedy approach may not find the globally optimal set of views; relies on the quality of the similarity metric. When to use: When a small, diverse set of views is needed for volume model representation or initialization, and computational resources are limited. When not to use: When the globally optimal view set is required and computational cost is not a constraint. The method was proposed in the context of generating representative views and paths for volume models, aiming to avoid preprocessing steps like segmentation. It was developed to address the limitations of simple image metrics (like MSE) which are sensitive to rotations and translations, and to improve upon methods like those by Bordoloi and Shen which use Jensen-Shannon divergence but do not exploit dataset symmetry. Representative Views and Paths for Volume Models, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-85412-810, fetched 2026-10-26 InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20341, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Stereo Rendering
head: Anaglyph Stereo, Red-Blue (Anaglyph) Stereo, Red-cyan stereo, Red-green stereo
body: Stereo rendering generates a pair of images to simulate binocular parallax, where each eye sees a slightly different picture to determine depth. It differs from standard rendering by requiring two distinct camera viewpoints separated by an inter-ocular distance. Unlike Depth of Field and Lens Effects which simulates focus, stereo rendering simulates disparity. The presentation method determines how these images are combined and viewed. Inputs: Scene geometry, camera parameters (position, orientation, frustum), eye separation distance, and display type (single vs. dual). Outputs: A stereo image pair (either separate buffers, a combined anaglyph, or interlaced frames). The implementation relies on standard camera frustum data structures extended with stereo parameters. Camera Frustum: Defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and projection matrix. For single-display systems, the frustum must be sheared to account for the non-perpendicular view plane relative to the combined image. Image Buffers: Standard RGB uses 24 bits per pixel (8 bits per channel). Stereo double buffering requires quad buffering (Left Front, Left Back, Right Front, Right Back). Memory for a 1Kx1K display with 24-bit RGB, 24-bit back buffer color, and 24-bit z-buffer per view is 144 bits per pixel or 18 MB total. 1. Calculate Eye Positions: Determine left and right eye origins based on the center eye position and eye separation distance. 2. Set Camera Configuration: For two-display systems, perform camera azimuths to reach the left and right eye positions. For single-display systems, translate and shear the camera's viewing frustum to handle the non-perpendicular view plane. 3. Generate Images: Render the scene from both eye positions to generate the left and right eye images. 4. Convert to Intensity: Convert the RGB values of both views into grayscale intensities. 5. Combine Channels (Anaglyph): Create the resulting image where red values are taken from left eye image intensities and blue values (mixture of blue and green) are taken from right eye image intensities. 6. Display: Invoke stereo rendering mode on the render window. The anaglyph channel mapping converts intensities IL (left) and IR (right) into output channels: R{out} = IL B{out} = IR G{out} = IR \quad \text{(Red-green variant utilizes eye sensitivity to green)} This discards original hue and saturation. Eye Separation Distance: The distance between the left and right eye positions. Controlling this amount directly controls the generated parallax. Typical values approximate human inter-ocular distance (~6.5 cm) but are often adjusted for virtual scale. Precision: High bits-per-pixel requirements for double-buffered stereo can exhaust video memory (e.g., 144 bits/pixel for 1Kx1K). Screen Coverage: Time-multiplexed techniques require the application to take up the entire screen while rendering. Color Loss: Anaglyph methods discard original hue and saturation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupstereorendering(renderwindow, stereotype="RedBlue"): renderwindow.StereoRenderOn() if stereotype == "RedBlue": renderwindow.SetStereoTypeToRedBlue() # Further rendering will be done in stereo Generates a stereo pair from a pre-existing 2D image stack to simulate binocular parallax and volumetric depth perception using standard web technologies. It is distinguished from full ray-casting volume rendering by relying on image overlay and CSS positioning rather than per-pixel shading, and from single-slice viewers by allowing simultaneous visibility of multiple depth layers. Choose when visualizing scientific volumetric data in a browser without specialized hardware. Stereo Pseudo 3D Rendering via Image Stacks Each eye is updated at the original refresh rate (e.g., 60Hz) with full horizontal resolution but half vertical resolution. Renders the left eye image to the top half of the screen and the right eye image to the bottom half, then enters a special stereo mode on the graphics card to double the monitor's refresh rate (e.g., from 60Hz to 120Hz). Choose when full horizontal resolution is prioritized over vertical resolution and screen takeover is acceptable. Uses TV standards (NTSC/PAL) interlacing, rendering left eye to even lines and right eye to odd lines. Viewed with liquid crystal shutter glasses synchronized to the interlacing rate. Choose for television display compatibility, though it suffers from low resolution and flicker because each eye is updated at half the refresh rate. Displays both left and right images simultaneously on two separate screens (one per eye). Requires two graphics cards or one card with two outputs. Choose when simultaneous full-resolution views are required and hardware cost is not a constraint. Preserves all color information by separating views using polarized light: one eye's image projected through a vertical filter, the other through a horizontal filter. User wears glasses with a vertical filter over one eye and a horizontal filter over the other. Choose when color fidelity is critical and polarized projection hardware is available. Uses separate left and right image buffers, allowing stereo rendering without taking over the entire screen. Requires more memory or lower resolution (e.g., 144 bits per pixel for 1Kx1K with quad buffering). Choose for high-quality interactive applications on supported hardware without full-screen takeover. Displays both views in a single image using repeating dot patterns, where depth is incorporated by changing the interval between patterns. Viewed by focusing in front of or behind the image until two triangular cutouts in the top appear as one. Choose for static, depth-only images requiring no special hardware. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to pixels and scene complexity, multiplied by the number of eyes (typically 2). Memory Complexity: Increases significantly for double-buffered stereo; quad buffering can require up to 144 bits per pixel. Performance: Time multiplexed methods halve vertical resolution per eye. Interlaced methods halve vertical resolution and suffer from flicker. Anaglyph methods have minimal performance overhead but poor color fidelity. Scaling: Resolution scales with display hardware; interlaced and split-screen methods halve vertical resolution per eye, while dual buffer maintains full resolution at the cost of memory. Strengths: Anaglyph is low-cost and works on any display (monitor, paper, or film) with inexpensive glasses. Dual buffer preserves full resolution and color but requires hardware support. Limitations: Anaglyph loses color. Interlaced has low resolution and flicker. Time parallel requires expensive hardware. SIRDS requires user effort to focus and loses texture/color. When to use: Use Anaglyph for low-cost distribution. Use Dual Buffer for high-quality interactive applications with supported hardware. Use SIRDS for static depth-only images. Stereo rendering originated from the need to simulate binocular vision in computer graphics. Foundational concepts of camera azimuths for two-display systems and frustum shearing for single-display systems were detailed in early computer graphics literature, specifically in the context of the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) and general advanced computer graphics textbooks. The term encompasses various methods including anaglyph, interlaced, and polarized techniques, adapted from television and display technologies. Chapter 7 - Advanced Computer Graphics - VTK, https://examples.vtk.org/site/VTKBook/07Chapter7/, fetched 2026-10-29 (book)

name: Stereo Pseudo 3D Rendering via Image Stacks
head: Pseudo Stereo Pair Generation, Stereo Pseudo 3D, Web-based Stereo Pseudo 3D
body:
This method generates a stereo pair of images from a pre-existing 2D image stack to simulate binocular parallax and volumetric depth perception using standard web technologies. It solves the problem of visualizing scientific volumetric data in a browser without specialized hardware or client-side rendering engines. It is distinguished from full ray-casting volume rendering by relying on image overlay and CSS positioning rather than per-pixel shading, and from single-slice viewers like BrainMaps.org by allowing simultaneous visibility of multiple depth layers. Inputs and Outputs Input: A stack of N 2D images (e.g., PNG slices) representing cross-sections of a volume. Output: Two HTML DOM trees (stacks) containing positioned elements that produce a 3D effect when viewed with stereo merging. Data Structures The implementation relies on the HTML Document Object Model (DOM). Containers: Two
elements with position: absolute CSS styling. One serves as the base stack (imgstacks), the other as the offset stack (imgoffsets). Image Elements: nodes created dynamically. Each has position: absolute, and explicit top, left, width, and height style properties. Preprocessing: Input images must have alpha channels added, with background pixels set to transparent to allow proper overlay blending. Numbered Steps 1. Preprocess Images: Convert input slices to PNG format with transparent backgrounds. Generate a single semi-opaque white image (e.g., 180x180 pixels, 10% opacity) to be reused for distance attenuation. 2. Initialize DOM: Create two absolute-positioned
containers in the HTML structure: one for the base stack and one for the offset stack. 3. Generate Base Stack: Iterate through the image stack from i = 0 to N-1. For each data slice i: create an element, set src to the data slice, set position to absolute, and set top and left to the base coordinates (e.g., 0,0 relative to container). Append to the base stack container. Insert the semi-opaque white image between every pair of data slices to simulate distance attenuation (aerial perspective). 4. Generate Offset Stack: Iterate through the image stack from i = 0 to N-1. For each data slice i: create an element, set src to the data slice, set position to absolute, calculate horizontal position: xi = x{i-1} + \Delta x, where for the first slice x0 is the base left position, set left to xi, keep top identical to the base stack, and append to the offset stack container. Insert the semi-opaque white image between every pair of data slices in the offset stack as well. 5. Display: Load both stacks into the browser. The combined result is viewed with stereo merging to perceive the 3D effect. Formulas Horizontal offset accumulation: xi = x{i-1} + \Delta x for i > 0, with x0 = x{\text{base}}. Distance attenuation: achieved by interleaving a semi-opaque layer with opacity \alpha between data slices. Parameters Opacity of interleaving layer (\alpha): Typically 10% (0.1) for the semi-opaque white image. Horizontal offset per slice (\Delta x): Typically 1 pixel relative to the previous slice's position. Eye separation: Approximately 6 cm, used to calculate horizontal disparities for stereoscopic depth perception. Image Resolution: Example usage subsampled to 180x180 pixels from 512x512 source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Pseudo-Accuracy: Fixed linear offsetting produces "pseudo" accurate stereo pairs, not fully accurate geometric projections. Nonlinear offsetting based on a depth function can improve accuracy but is not implemented in the basic method. Viewpoint Rigidity: The viewpoint is predetermined by the image stack organization. Interactive viewpoint changes (rotation, zoom) are not supported on the fly. Viewer Strain: Stereo merging requires the user to perform cross-viewing or parallel viewing, which can cause eye strain. Optical aids (mirrors/prisms) may be required. Performance Scaling: Memory and load time scale linearly with the number of images. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class DOMElement: def init(self, tag, attrs=None): self.tag = tag self.attrs = attrs or {} self.children = [] def append(self, child): self.children.append(child) def generatestereopseudo3d(imagestack, numslices, offsetperslice=1, opacity=0.1): """ Generates DOM structures for stereo pseudo 3D rendering. imagestack: List of image data/paths. numslices: Number of data slices N. offsetperslice: Horizontal pixel shift per slice depth. opacity: Opacity of the interleaving attenuation layer. """ # 1. Preprocessing assumed done: images are transparent PNGs. # Generate a single semi-opaque white image for attenuation. attenuationimage = {"src": "attenuation10pct.png", "opacity": opacity} # 2. Initialize DOM containers basecontainer = DOMElement("div", {"id": "imgstacks", "position": "absolute"}) offsetcontainer = DOMElement("div", {"id": "imgoffsets", "position": "absolute"}) contentcontainer = DOMElement("div", {"id": "imgcontent", "position": "absolute"}) contentcontainer.append(basecontainer) contentcontainer.append(offsetcontainer) # 3. Build Base Stack currenttop = 0 currentleft = 0 for i in range(numslices): # Add data slice imgelem = DOMElement("img", {"src": imagestack[i], "position": "absolute", "top": str(currenttop) + "px", "left": str(currentleft) + "px"}) basecontainer.append(imgelem) # Add attenuation layer between slices (except after the last one) if i < numslices - 1: attimg = DOMElement("img", {"src": attenuationimage["src"], "position": "absolute", "top": str(currenttop) + "px", "left": str(currentleft) + "px"}) basecontainer.append(attimg) # 4. Build Offset Stack offsettop = 0 offsetleft = 0 for i in range(numslices): # Add data slice with cumulative horizontal offset currentoffsetx = offsetleft + i offsetperslice imgelem = DOMElement("img", {"src": imagestack[i], "position": "absolute", "top": str(offsettop) + "px", "left": str(currentoffsetx) + "px"}) offsetcontainer.append(imgelem) # Add attenuation layer if i < numslices - 1: attimg = DOMElement("img", {"src": attenuationimage["src"], "position": "absolute", "top": str(offsettop) + "px", "left": str(currentoffsetx) + "px"}) offsetcontainer.append(attimg) return contentcontainer Time Complexity: Linear O(N) with respect to the number of images N for loading and DOM construction. Memory Complexity: Linear O(N), as each image is stored in the browser cache and DOM. Measured Performance: On a 1.7 GHz PC with 1GB RAM, displaying 50 overlayed images took approximately 3 seconds after download. Load time and memory usage scaled linearly for 15, 30, and 50 images (95kB–126kB each) on Firefox 2.0 and IE 7.0. Strengths: Requires no specialized software, hardware, or client-side computation; works in standard web browsers with CSS/JS support. Allows viewing multiple stacked images simultaneously to perceive volumetric structures. Limitations: No interactive viewpoint changes; stereo accuracy is approximate; requires user ability to merge stereo images; potential eye strain. When to Use: Web-based display of static scientific volumetric data where interactive 3D rendering is not feasible or necessary. When Not to Use: When interactive viewpoint changes or high-precision geometric stereo are required. The method was developed by D. C.-Y. Eng and Y. Choe and presented at the Pacific Graphics 2008 conference. It was applied to visualize 50 slices of mouse spinal cord scans from the KESM dataset, where blood vessels were stained with India ink. The approach contrasts with BrainMaps.org, which displays one slide at a time, and other web-based 3D approaches that require specialized software or hardware. Stereo Pseudo 3D Rendering for Web-based Display of Scientific Volumetric Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg-pbg08/073-080, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Camera Model with Radial/Tangential Distortion
head: nerfies Camera
body: This camera model defines the geometric relationship between 2D pixel coordinates and 3D world rays, incorporating standard pinhole camera intrinsics (focal length, principal point, skew, aspect ratio) and lens distortion (radial and tangential). It is used to convert between pixel coordinates and 3D world rays or points. It distinguishes itself from simple pinhole models by including an iterative undistortion step to recover ideal normalized coordinates from distorted pixel measurements. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Pixel coordinates with shape [..., 2] and camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: Normalized ray directions in world coordinates with shape [..., 3]. Data Structures: The Camera object stores the following fields: orientation: 3 \times 3 matrix (world-to-camera rotation). position: 3-vector (camera center in world coordinates). focallength: float. principalpoint: 2-vector [u0, v0]. skew: float. pixelaspectratio: float. radialdistortion: 3-vector [k1, k2, k3]. tangentialdistortion: 2-vector [p1, p2]. imagesize: 2-vector [width, height] (uint32). dtype: data type (e.g., float32). Formulas: 1. Pixel to Local Undistorted Coordinates: The mapping from ideal normalized coordinates (x, y) to distorted pixel coordinates (u, v) is: u = f \cdot x + s \cdot y + u0 v = f \cdot \text{aspect} \cdot y + v0 Where f is focal length, s is skew, and \text{aspect} is pixel aspect ratio. 2. Radial Distortion Factor: r^2 = x^2 + y^2 d(r) = 1 + r^2 (k1 + r^2 (k2 + k3 r^2)) 3. Tangential and Radial Distortion Application: The distorted coordinates (xd, yd) are related to ideal coordinates (x, y) by: xd = x \cdot d(r) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2) yd = y \cdot d(r) + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r^2 + 2 y^2) 4. World Ray Direction: \mathbf{d}{\text{world}} = \text{Orientation}^\top \mathbf{d}{\text{local}} Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Ensure pixel coordinates have a last dimension of 2 and match the camera's dtype. 2. Reshape: Flatten pixel coordinates to (-1, 2) for batch processing. 3. Normalize to Principal Point: Calculate intermediate y and x values: y = \frac{v - v0}{f \cdot \text{aspect}} x = \frac{u - u0 - s \cdot y}{f} 4. Undistortion: If radial or tangential distortion parameters are non-zero, apply radialandtangentialundistort to (x, y) using Newton's method to solve for ideal (x, y) given distorted (xd, yd). 5. Local Ray Direction: Stack [x, y, 1] and normalize by L2 norm. 6. World Transformation: Multiply local directions by the transpose of the orientation matrix. 7. Final Normalization: Normalize the resulting world directions by L2 norm. 8. Reshape: Restore the original batch shape plus (3,). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeresidualandjacobian(x, y, xd, yd, k1, k2, k3, p1, p2): """Computes residuals and Jacobian for undistortion.""" r = x x + y y d = 1.0 + r (k1 + r (k2 + k3 r)) # Distorted projection equations fx = d x + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r + 2 x x) - xd fy = d y + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r + 2 y y) - yd # Derivatives of d dr = k1 + r (2.0 k2 + 3.0 k3 r) dx = 2.0 x dr dy = 2.0 y dr # Jacobian entries fxx = d + dx x + 2 p1 y + 6 p2 x fxy = dx y + 2 p1 x + 2 p2 y fyx = dx y + 2 p2 y + 2 p1 x fyy = d + dy y + 2 p2 x + 6 p1 y return fx, fy, fxx, fxy, fyx, fyy def radialandtangentialundistort(xd, yd, k1=0.0, k2=0.0, k3=0.0, p1=0.0, p2=0.0, eps=1e-9, maxiterations=10): """Undistorts pixel coordinates using Newton's method.""" x = xd.copy() y = yd.copy() for in range(maxiterations): fx, fy, fxx, fxy, fyx, fyy = computeresidualandjacobian( x, y, xd, yd, k1, k2, k3, p1, p2) denominator = fyx fxy - fxx fyy xnumerator = fx fyy - fy fxy ynumerator = fy fxx - fx fyx # Avoid division by zero stepx = np.where(np.abs(denominator) > eps, xnumerator / denominator, 0.0) stepy = np.where(np.abs(denominator) > eps, ynumerator / denominator, 0.0) x = x + stepx y = y + stepy return x, y def pixelstorays(pixels, camera): """ Convert pixel coordinates to world-space ray directions. Args: pixels: np.ndarray of shape (..., 2) camera: Camera object with attributes orientation, position, focallength, principalpoint, skew, pixelaspectratio, radialdistortion, tangentialdistortion. Returns: np.ndarray of shape (..., 3) containing normalized ray directions. """ # 1. Validation if pixels.shape[-1] != 2: raise ValueError("Pixels must have shape (..., 2)") pixels = pixels.astype(camera.dtype) # 2. Reshape originalshape = pixels.shape pixelsflat = pixels.reshape(-1, 2) # 3. Normalize to principal point u = pixelsflat[:, 0] v = pixelsflat[:, 1] scalefactorx = camera.focallength scalefactory = camera.focallength camera.pixelaspectratio u0, v0 = camera.principalpoint s = camera.skew y = (v - v0) / scalefactory x = (u - u0 - s y) / scalefactorx # 4. Undistortion if np.any(camera.radialdistortion) or np.any(camera.tangentialdistortion): k1, k2, k3 = camera.radialdistortion p1, p2 = camera.tangentialdistortion x, y = radialandtangentialundistort(x, y, k1, k2, k3, p1, p2) # 5. Local Ray Direction dirs = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1) dirs = dirs / np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # 6. World Transformation raysdir = np.matmul(camera.orientation.T, dirs[..., np.newaxis]).squeeze(-1) # 7. Final Normalization raysdir = raysdir / np.linalg.norm(raysdir, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # 8. Reshape return raysdir.reshape(originalshape[:-1] + (3,)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Denominator: In undistortion, if the Jacobian determinant is near zero, the step is clamped to zero to prevent NaNs. Degenerate Look-At: If the look-at vector and up vector are parallel, the right vector calculation fails (norm < eps). Cropping: If cropping the camera domain results in non-positive resolution, an error is raised. A parameterization variant where pixel-valued parameters (focal length, principal point) are scaled by the initial camera focal length f. This encodes camera residual parameters as world coordinates, making additive biases invariant to the absolute scale of the scene. For example, a residual \Delta u0 is applied as u0' = u0 + f \Delta u0. Not given in the sources. The camera model is implemented in the Nerfies library by Google. It is based on standard computer vision camera models with radial and tangential distortion. The Pixel Scale variant is described in the CamP paper for camera preconditioning in neural radiance fields. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CamP: Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3618321, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Camera Ray Projection
head: Camera Ray Generation with Distortion Models, Inverse Projection with Distortion, Pixel to Ray Conversion with Distortion
body: Camera Ray Projection converts 2D pixel coordinates into 3D world-space rays by applying inverse intrinsic mapping, radial/tangential distortion correction, and extrinsic transformation. It solves the inverse camera distortion equations to map distorted normalized coordinates to undistorted ones using Newton-Raphson iteration, then constructs normalized ray directions. It differs from its sibling Camera Model with Radial/Tangential Distortion by explicitly handling the iterative inversion of the distortion model and providing the final world-space ray geometry (origins, directions, and optional radii) required for volume rendering sampling. Inputs: Pixel coordinates: P = (u, v), shape (H, W) or batched. Intrinsics: Focal length fx, fy, principal point (cx, cy), skew s, pixel aspect ratio r. Distortion parameters: Radial k1, k2, k3 (and optionally k4), Tangential p1, p2. Extrinsics: Camera orientation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and position T \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or camera-to-world matrix C2W). Optional: Camera type (Perspective/Fisheye), NDC inverse intrinsic matrix. Outputs: Rays dataclass containing: origins: Camera positions in world space, shape (..., 3). directions: Unnormalized ray directions in world space, shape (..., 3). viewdirs: Normalized ray directions, shape (..., 3). radii: Optional cone radii for mip-NeRF, shape (..., 1). imageplane: Original pixel coordinates, shape (..., 2). Data Structures: Distortion coefficients are stored as floats. Default values are 0.0 for all ki, pi. Camera orientation is a 3 \times 3 orthonormal matrix. Pixel coordinates are typically integer indices; half-pixel offset is applied to target pixel centers. Steps: 1. Pixel to Normalized Coordinates: Compute pixel centers by adding 0.5 to integer indices. Convert to normalized image plane coordinates (x{raw}, y{raw}) using intrinsics: y{raw} = \frac{v - cy}{fy \cdot r} x{raw} = \frac{u - cx - s \cdot y{raw}}{fx} 2. Inverse Distortion (Undistortion): Solve for undistorted normalized coordinates (x, y) from distorted (xd, yd) = (x{raw}, y{raw}) using Newton-Raphson. Distortion Model: The forward distortion maps undistorted (x, y) to distorted (xd, yd): r^2 = x^2 + y^2 d(x, y) = 1 + k1 r^2 + k2 r^4 + k3 r^6 \quad (\text{or } 1 + k4 r^8 \text{ if } k4 \text{ is present}) xd = x \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2) yd = y \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r^2 + 2 y^2) Newton-Raphson Iteration: Initialize x = xd, y = yd. Iterate up to maxiterations (default 10 or 100): a. Compute residuals fx, fy: fx = x \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2) - xd fy = y \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r^2 + 2 y^2) - yd b. Compute Jacobian elements J{xx}, J{xy}, J{yx}, J{yy}: Let d' = \frac{d(d)}{d(r^2)} = k1 + 2 k2 r^2 + 3 k3 r^4. J{xx} = d + 2 x^2 d' + 2 p1 y + 6 p2 x J{xy} = 2 x y d' + 2 p1 x + 2 p2 y J{yx} = J{xy} J{yy} = d + 2 y^2 d' + 6 p1 y + 2 p2 x c. Compute Newton step using Cramer's rule: \text{det} = J{xx} J{yy} - J{xy} J{yx} \Delta x = \frac{fx J{yy} - fy J{xy}}{\text{det}} \Delta y = \frac{fy J{xx} - fx J{yx}}{\text{det}} d. Handle singular Jacobian: If |\text{det}| < \epsilon (default 10^{-9} or 10^{-12}), set \Delta x = 0, \Delta y = 0. e. Trust Region: Compute step norm squared S = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2. If S > \max(r^2 \cdot k{RelStepRadius}^2, k{StepRadius}^2) (defaults 0.1), scale step: \text{scale} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{radiusSqr}}{S}} \Delta x \leftarrow \Delta x \cdot \text{scale}, \quad \Delta y \leftarrow \Delta y \cdot \text{scale} f. Update: x \leftarrow x + \Delta x y \leftarrow y + \Delta y g. Convergence: If step norm squared < 10^{-10} or max iterations reached, break. 3. Local Ray Direction Construction: Stack undistorted coordinates with z=1: \mathbf{v}{local} = [x, y, 1]^T Normalize: \mathbf{v}{local} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{v}{local}}{\|\mathbf{v}{local}\|} 4. Fisheye Correction (Optional): If camera type is FISHEYE: \theta = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} Clamp \theta to \pi. \text{scale} = \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\theta} x \leftarrow x \cdot \text{scale}, \quad y \leftarrow y \cdot \text{scale} z = \cos(\theta) Reconstruct and normalize \mathbf{v}{local} = [x, y, z]^T. 5. Coordinate System Flip: Flip from OpenCV to OpenGL convention if necessary: \mathbf{v}{local} \leftarrow \text{diag}(1, -1, -1) \cdot \mathbf{v}{local} 6. World Space Transformation: Apply camera rotation R (orientation matrix): \mathbf{v}{world} = R \cdot \mathbf{v}{local} Normalize: \mathbf{v}{world} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{v}{world}}{\|\mathbf{v}{world}\|} 7. Ray Origins: Set origins to camera position T (from extrinsics). 8. Ray Radii (Optional): For mip-NeRF, compute radii using neighbor rays. Compute directions for right neighbor (u+1, v) and bottom neighbor (u, v+1). dx{norm} = \|\mathbf{v}{right} - \mathbf{v}{current}\| dy{norm} = \|\mathbf{v}{bottom} - \mathbf{v}{current}\| \text{radii} = 0.5 \cdot (dx{norm} + dy{norm}) \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{12}} If NDC space is used, compute radii from NDC origin differences. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def camerarayprojection( pixels: np.ndarray, # Shape (H, W, 2) or (N, 2), integer pixel coords fx: float, # Focal length x fy: float, # Focal length y cx: float, # Principal point x cy: float, # Principal point y skew: float = 0.0, # Skew aspectratio: float = 1.0,# Pixel aspect ratio k1: float = 0.0, # Radial distortion k1 k2: float = 0.0, # Radial distortion k2 k3: float = 0.0, # Radial distortion k3 p1: float = 0.0, # Tangential distortion p1 p2: float = 0.0, # Tangential distortion p2 R: np.ndarray = None, # 3x3 Rotation matrix (world from camera) T: np.ndarray = None, # 3x1 Translation vector (camera position in world) maxiterations: int = 10, # Max Newton iterations eps: float = 1e-9 # Epsilon for Jacobian check): """ Projects pixel coordinates to world-space rays with distortion correction. Returns origins, directions, viewdirs. """ # 1. Pixel to Normalized Coordinates u = pixels[..., 0] + 0.5 v = pixels[..., 1] + 0.5 yraw = (v - cy) / (fy aspectratio) xraw = (u - cx - skew yraw) / fx # 2. Inverse Distortion x = xraw.copy() y = yraw.copy() for in range(maxiterations): r2 = xx + yy # Distortion factor d d = 1.0 + r2 (k1 + r2 (k2 + r2 k3)) # Residuals resx = x d + 2.0 p1 x y + p2 (r2 + 2.0 xx) - xraw resy = y d + 2.0 p2 x y + p1 (r2 + 2.0 yy) - yraw # Jacobian derivative of d w.r.t r2 dddr2 = k1 + r2 (2.0 k2 + 3.0 r2 k3) # Jacobian elements jxx = d + 2.0 xx dddr2 + 2.0 p1 y + 6.0 p2 x jxy = 2.0 x y dddr2 + 2.0 p1 x + 2.0 p2 y jyx = jxy jyy = d + 2.0 yy dddr2 + 6.0 p1 y + 2.0 p2 x # Determinant det = jxx jyy - jxy jyx # Newton Step if np.abs(det) > eps: dx = (resx jyy - resy jxy) / det dy = (resy jxx - resx jyx) / det else: dx = 0.0 dy = 0.0 # Trust Region stepsqr = dxdx + dydy radiussqr = max(r2 0.01, 0.01) # kRelStepRadius=0.1, kStepRadius=0.1 per if stepsqr > radiussqr: scale = np.sqrt(radiussqr / stepsqr) dx = scale dy = scale x = x + dx y = y + dy # Convergence check if dxdx + dydy < 1e-10: break # 3. Local Ray Direction dirslocal = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1) norms = np.linalg.norm(dirslocal, axis=-1, keepdims=True) dirslocal = dirslocal / norms # 4. World Space Transformation if R is not None: dirsworld = np.matmul(dirslocal, R.T) else: dirsworld = dirslocal normsworld = np.linalg.norm(dirsworld, axis=-1, keepdims=True) viewdirs = dirsworld / normsworld # 5. Origins if T is not None: origins = np.broadcastto(T, (dirsworld.shape[:-1], 3)) else: origins = np.zeroslike(dirsworld) return origins, dirsworld, viewdirs Time Complexity: O(N \cdot I) where N is number of pixels and I is number of Newton iterations (typically 10-100). The Jacobian computation is constant time per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing ray origins, directions, and residuals. Performance: Newton-Raphson converges quadratically near the solution. For small distortions, 5-10 iterations are sufficient. For large distortions (e.g., wide-angle lenses), up to 100 iterations may be needed. Strengths: Handles arbitrary radial/tangential distortion models. Provides accurate ray directions for volume rendering. Limitations: Iterative solver can be slow on CPU. Singular Jacobians (rare, near optical center with high distortion) require fallback. When to use: When camera calibration includes non-zero distortion coefficients. When not to use: For pinhole cameras with negligible distortion, skip undistortion for performance. The inverse distortion method originates from computer vision camera calibration models and is widely used in photogrammetry and SLAM. In volume rendering, it is used by frameworks like NeRF and its variants to handle real-world camera distortions. The Newton-Raphson approach is standard for inverting the polynomial distortion model. name: Multicam Ray Generation
head: Ray Generation (Multicam)
body: Multicam Ray Generation constructs ray origins and directions for a multi-camera dataset by applying per-image metadata (intrinsic and extrinsic matrices) stored in a JSON file. It differs from single-camera models by iterating over a collection of distinct camera poses, allowing the synthesis of views from multiple physical or virtual sensors. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A list of camera metadata dictionaries (loaded from metadata.json), each containing pix2cam (3x3 intrinsic matrix), cam2world (4x4 extrinsic matrix), width, height, lossmult, near, and far. Outputs: Two tensors of shape (H, W, 3) for origins and viewdirs, and scalar attributes broadcasted to (H, W) for lossmult, near, and far. Data Structures pix2cam: 3x3 matrix mapping pixel coordinates to camera frame directions. cam2world: 4x4 matrix mapping camera frame to world frame. res2grid(w, h): Generates a meshgrid of pixel centers. Using indexing='xy', it returns coordinates (x+0.5, y+0.5) for x \in [0, W-1] and y \in [0, H-1]. Steps 1. Load Metadata: Parse metadata.json to extract pix2cam, cam2world, width, height, lossmult, near, and far for the current image. 2. Create Pixel Grid: Generate pixel coordinates using res2grid(width, height). 3. Compute Camera Directions: Construct pixel direction vectors: \mathbf{p} = [x, y, 1]. Transform to camera frame: \mathbf{d}{cam} = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{K}^T, where \mathbf{K} = \text{pix2cam}[:3,:3]. 4. Transform to World Space: Rotate directions: \mathbf{d}{world} = \mathbf{d}{cam} \cdot \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{R} = \text{cam2world}[:3,:3]. Set origins: \mathbf{o} = \text{broadcast}(\text{cam2world}[:3, -1]) to match the shape of \mathbf{d}{world}. 5. Normalize Directions: Compute \mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{world}}{\|\mathbf{d}{world}\|} to obtain viewdirs. 6. Calculate Radii: Compute \Delta x, the distance between adjacent direction vectors, for each image. Pad the last element of \Delta x to match the spatial dimensions. Calculate radii: r = \frac{\Delta x \cdot 2}{\sqrt{12}}. 7. Broadcast Attributes: Expand lossmult, near, and far from scalars to tensors of shape (H, W). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def res2grid(w, h): """Returns meshgrid of (x+0.5, y+0.5) with indexing='xy'.""" x = torch.arange(w, dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5 y = torch.arange(h, dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5 return torch.meshgrid(x, y, indexing='xy') def generaterays(metadata): """ Generate rays for a single camera from metadata. metadata: dict with keys 'pix2cam', 'cam2world', 'width', 'height', 'lossmult', 'near', 'far'. """ # 1. Load metadata K = metadata['pix2cam'][:3,:3] # 3x3 R = metadata['cam2world'][:3,:3] # 3x3 T = metadata['cam2world'][:3, 3] # 3x1 H, W = metadata['height'], metadata['width'] # 2. Create pixel grid x, y = res2grid(W, H) # Shape (H, W) # 3. Compute camera directions # pixeldirs shape: (H, W, 3) -> [x, y, 1] pixeldirs = torch.stack([x, y, torch.oneslike(x)], dim=-1) # cameradirs = pixeldirs @ K.T cameradirs = torch.matmul(pixeldirs, K.T) # 4. Transform to world space # directions = cameradirs @ R.T directions = torch.matmul(cameradirs, R.T) # origins = broadcast(T) origins = torch.broadcastto(T, directions.shape) # 5. Normalize directions viewdirs = directions / torch.norm(directions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # 6. Calculate radii # dx: distance between adjacent direction vectors # Approximation: compute norm of difference between adjacent viewdirs # Note: The source mentions calculating dx for each image and padding. # A robust implementation computes the angular separation. # For simplicity, assuming dx is derived from the grid spacing in direction space. # The source formula: radii = dx 2 / sqrt(12) # Compute dx as the norm of the difference between adjacent normalized directions # along the x-axis (or average of x and y) # This step requires careful handling of boundaries. # Source says: "Calculate dx... and pad the last element" # Example implementation for dx (x-direction): dxx = torch.norm(viewdirs[:, 1:,:] - viewdirs[:,:-1,:], dim=-1) dxx = torch.cat([dxx, dxx[:, -1:]], dim=1) # Pad last element # Example implementation for dx (y-direction): dxy = torch.norm(viewdirs[1:,:,:] - viewdirs[:-1,:,:], dim=-1) dxy = torch.cat([dxy, dxy[-1:,:]], dim=0) # Pad last element # Average dx dx = (dxx + dxy) / 2.0 radii = dx 2.0 / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(12.0)) # 7. Broadcast attributes lossmult = torch.full((H, W), metadata['lossmult']) near = torch.full((H, W), metadata['near']) far = torch.full((H, W), metadata['far']) return origins, viewdirs, radii, lossmult, near, far Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Normalization of directions must be performed after rotation to ensure unit length. Boundaries: Padding is required for dx calculation to maintain spatial dimensions. Degenerate Input: If pix2cam or cam2world are singular, ray generation will fail. A variant where the image width must be exactly twice the height (W = 2H) to support correct equirectangular projection. This constraint ensures proper mapping of spherical coordinates to the 2D image plane. Time Complexity: O(N) where N = H \times W, as each pixel is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store origins, directions, and attributes. Strengths: Efficiently handles multiple cameras by reusing the same ray generation logic with different metadata. Limitations: Requires pre-computed metadata for each camera. When to Use: Multi-view reconstruction, NeRF training with multiple cameras. When Not to Use: Single-camera scenarios where simpler ray generation suffices. Originating from the CaSE-NeRF project, this method adapts standard NeRF ray generation for multi-camera datasets. It relies on JSON-stored metadata for flexibility across different camera setups. name: Parallel Projection Ray Casting
head: Volume Rendering with Parallel Projection, Orthographic Ray Casting
body: Parallel projection ray casting is a volume rendering technique where all cast rays are parallel to each other and aligned with a single viewing direction. It is preferred for scientific visualization because it preserves accurate sizes and relative positions of structures without perspective distortion. Unlike perspective projection, which requires storing different ray parameters for each pixel, parallel projection assumes a uniform ray direction, simplifying the geometric setup. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset (voxels), image resolution (W, H), and viewing angles (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) representing rotations around the Z, Y, and X axes respectively. Output: A 2D image where each pixel (i, j) corresponds to a ray traversing the volume. Data Structures Rotation Matrices: Three 3 \times 3 matrices are used to define the viewing direction: Mx(\gamma) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos \gamma & -\sin \gamma \\ 0 & \sin \gamma & \cos \gamma \end{pmatrix} My(\beta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos \beta & 0 & \sin \beta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin \beta & 0 & \cos \beta \end{pmatrix} Mz(\alpha) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos \alpha & -\sin \alpha & 0 \\ \sin \alpha & \cos \alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where \alpha, \beta, \gamma are the rotation angles. Base Plane: A rectangular plane initially aligned with one of the coordinate planes (XOY, YOZ, or XOZ) passing through the origin. Points are placed on this plane corresponding to image pixels, scaled by a coefficient determining the distance between rays. Steps 1. Initialize Base Plane: Select a coordinate plane (e.g., XOY) and place sample points on it corresponding to the image resolution (W, H), centered at the origin. 2. Compute Viewing Direction: Apply rotation matrices to the normal vector of the base plane to achieve the desired viewing angle. The combined rotation matrix M is typically M = Mz(\alpha) My(\beta) Mx(\gamma) (order may vary based on convention, but sources specify these three matrices define the orientation). 3. Generate Rays: For each pixel (i, j), define a ray origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} on the rotated base plane and a direction \mathbf{d} equal to the rotated normal vector of the base plane. All rays share the same direction \mathbf{d}. 4. Ray Marching: For each ray, iterate through the volume. Sample voxel values along the ray path. 5. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using a compositing function (e.g., front-to-back or back-to-front) until the ray exits the volume or opacity reaches 1.0. 6. Render: Draw the final accumulated color to the pixel (i, j). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Mx(gamma): return [[1, 0, 0], [0, cos(gamma), -sin(gamma)], [0, sin(gamma), cos(gamma)]] def My(beta): return [[cos(beta), 0, sin(beta)], [0, 1, 0], [-sin(beta), 0, cos(beta)]] def Mz(alpha): return [[cos(alpha), -sin(alpha), 0], [sin(alpha), cos(alpha), 0], [0, 0, 1]] def parallelprojectionraycast(volume, width, height, alpha, beta, gamma): # 1. Compute combined rotation matrix for viewing direction # Note: Source lists matrices but does not explicitly specify multiplication order. # Standard convention is often applied, but exact order is "Not given in the sources." M = multiplymatrices(Mz(alpha), My(beta), Mx(gamma)) # 2. Determine viewing direction vector (normal of the rotated base plane) # Assuming initial base plane is XOY, normal is (0,0,1) initialnormal = [0, 0, 1] viewdirection = matrixvectormultiply(M, initialnormal) viewdirection = normalize(viewdirection) # 3. Initialize output image image = zeros((height, width, 3)) # 4. Iterate over pixels for j in range(height): for i in range(width): # Define ray origin on the base plane # Source mentions placing points on the plane aligned with coordinate axes # and scaling by a coefficient. Exact mapping from pixel (i,j) to 3D point # depends on the specific base plane selection and scaling factor. # Assuming a standard orthographic projection setup where the base plane # is the image plane itself in world coordinates, or mapped via the inverse rotation. # For simplicity, we assume the ray origin is computed based on the camera setup. rayorigin = computerayorigin(i, j, width, height, M) # Initialize compositing state color = [0, 0, 0] opacity = 0.0 # Ray marching t = 0.0 stepsize = getstepsize() # Depends on volume resolution and scale while t < volumeextent: currentpos = rayorigin + t viewdirection if not insidevolume(currentpos): break # Sample volume voxelvalue = samplevolume(volume, currentpos) voxelcolor, voxelopacity = transferfunction(voxelvalue) # Compositing (Front-to-Back) # Source mentions "Compositing(cur-prop, vox-prop, Normal)" # Standard front-to-back alpha blending: alphaterm = voxelopacity exp(-opacity) color += voxelcolor alphaterm opacity += alphaterm if opacity >= 1.0: break t += stepsize image[j, i] = color return image Parameters Rotation Angles: \alpha (Z-axis), \beta (Y-axis), \gamma (X-axis). Typical values depend on the desired view. Step Size: Determines the distance between samples along the ray. Scaling is achieved by changing this step size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Perspective Projection: This method does not support perspective projection. Implementing it would require modifying the system to store different ray parameters for each pixel, increasing memory requirements. Rounding Errors: In integer-based ray casting, rounding errors can cause adjacent rays to have different forms despite having the same slope. A variant that uses integer-based rays and templates to exploit coherence among parallel rays, speeding up rendering of binary voxel models for interactive decision making. Definition: Uses discrete line algorithms to generate integer rays. The form of the rays is calculated once and stored in a template to avoid re-performing the line algorithm for each pixel due to rounding errors. Base Plane Selection: Rays are cast from a base plane, which is one of the six volume faces with the largest projection area on the screen and closer to the viewer. Ray Type: Integer-based rays are used because the volume is binary, voxel values are constant/uniform, and speed is crucial. Interpolation does not improve quality for such volumes, and integer rays are faster than floating-point rays. Template Choice: A 26-ray template is chosen over a 6-ray template because it contains fewer voxels and samples the voxel space uniformly, ensuring adjacent voxels are joined by a vertex rather than just a face. Comparison: Integer rays use discrete line algorithms and sample nearest voxels. Floating point rays use continuous generation and higher-order interpolation. Integer rays are chosen for speed and sufficient quality in binary/uniform contexts. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of samples per ray. Template-based variants reduce overhead by caching ray paths. Memory Complexity: Lower than perspective ray casting because a single direction vector is shared among all rays, rather than storing unique origins and directions for each pixel. However, template-based methods require additional memory to store ray templates. Strengths: Preserves accurate sizes and relative positions of structures; no perspective distortion; efficient for scientific visualization where metric accuracy is required. Limitations: Cannot represent perspective effects; requires re-traversal of the dataset if the view changes significantly in some implementations (e.g., combined slices). When to Use: Scientific visualization, medical imaging (CT/MRI) where measurements are critical, and interactive design evaluation of binary models. When Not to Use: Artistic visualization requiring realistic depth cues or perspective distortion. Parallel projection has been a standard technique in volume rendering for scientific visualization since the early days of the field. It is widely supported in visualization toolkits such as ParaView, where it can be enabled via a "Camera Parallel Projection" checkbox. The technique is particularly prevalent in X-ray computed tomography (CT) visualization, where accurate representation of internal structures is paramount. Variations like template-based ray casting were developed in the 1990s to address performance issues in interactive design environments, specifically for die casting part evaluation.
