name: Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) for Volumetric Subsurface Scattering
head: Latent Variable Model for Sphere-Tracing
body: This method uses a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to statistically model and sample the complex scattering behavior of light within a translucent volume during sphere-tracing. It solves the problem of efficiently computing in-scattered direct illumination by bypassing the explicit simulation of every internal scattering event. Instead of tracing a ray through the medium point-by-point, the method infers the number of scattering events, the exit position and direction, and a representative internal scattering event in a single pass. It is distinguished from standard path tracing by its use of learned probabilistic models to approximate the distribution of scattering paths, and from sibling methods like Learning Multiple-Scattering Solutions for Sphere-Tracing by its specific decomposition into three distinct CVAE modules (LENGTHGEN, PATHGEN, EVENTGEN) optimized for GPU shader execution. The method operates on a sphere of radius r{sphere} centered at the ray origin. The inputs are the medium's extinction coefficient \sigmat, the Henyey-Greenstein anisotropy factor g, and the albedo \varphi. The outputs are sampled parameters defining the bypassed path section: the number of scattering events N, the exit position x and direction \omega, and a representative internal scattering event (X, W) for next-event estimation. The method consists of three separate CVAE models: LENGTHGEN, PATHGEN, and EVENTGEN. Each model is a neural network defined by: P{in}: Number of input parameters. P{out}: Number of output parameters (dimension of predicted variables). L: Latent space dimension. D: Depth (number of hidden layers). W: Nodes per layer. Architecture Constraints: Hidden layers use the Softplus activation function: \text{Softplus}(x) = \log(1 + \exp(x)). Final layers output mean \mu and log-covariance \log(\Sigma) without non-linear activation. To optimize GPU matrix multiplication (which operates on 4 \times 4 blocks), W is chosen as a multiple of four. L is chosen such that the decoder input size P{in} + L is a multiple of four. D is kept small to minimize sequential computation penalties. Hyperparameter Settings (from): | Model | P{in} | P{out} | D | W | L | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | LENGTHGEN | 2 | 3 | 7 | 1 | 3 | | PATHGEN | 6 | 3 | 1 | 8 | 5 | | EVENTGEN | 1 | 3 | 1 | 12 | 5 | Note: The source notes that for PATHGEN and EVENTGEN, D, W, L were examined from sets \{1,2,3\}, \{4,8,12,16\}, \{2,6\}, \{5,9\} respectively, but the values above are the empirically selected final settings. The encoder Enc(x, c) and decoder Dec(z, c) are trained jointly to maximize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): L = -KL(q{Enc}(z | x, c) || \mathcal{N}(0, I)) + \langle \log p{Dec}(x | z, c) \rangle{q{Enc}} Encoder: Outputs mean \mu{Enc} and diagonal covariance \Sigma{Enc} for the latent distribution q{Enc}(z | x, c). Decoder: Outputs mean \mu{Dec} and diagonal covariance \Sigma{Dec} for the data distribution p{Dec}(x | z, c). Reparameterization: During training, latent samples are drawn via the reparameterization trick to ensure gradient flow. At render time, the encoder is discarded. The process is sequential: 1. Preprocessing: Rescale the extinction coefficient to account for sphere radius: \sigmat' = \sigmat r{sphere}. This is justified by the homogeneity of the medium. 2. LENGTHGEN (Number of Events): Inputs: \sigmat', g, latent sample z^{(LL)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I{LL}), noise \epsilon^{(1)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I1). Output: N, the number of scattering events. Implementation: LENGTHGEN(σt', g, z^(LL), ε^(1)) → N. 3. Absorption Check: Sample absorption variable A from a Bernoulli distribution conditioned on N and albedo \varphi: pA(A | N, \varphi) = q(N, \varphi)^A (1 - q(N, \varphi))^{1-A} where q(N, \varphi) = 1 - \varphi^N. If A=1, the path is absorbed. The path is rejected immediately, and no further models are evaluated. 4. PATHGEN (Exit Position and Direction): Inputs: \sigmat', g, N, latent sample z^{(LP)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I{LP}), noise \epsilon^{(3)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I3). Output: (\theta, \beta, \alpha). Implementation: PATHGEN(σt', g, N, z^(LP), ε^(3)) → (θ, β, α). Parameterization: The exit position x on the sphere surface is defined by spherical coordinates (r{sphere}, \theta, \psi). \theta is the angle between the incoming direction \omega{in} and the exit position. Due to the rotation invariance of the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, the distribution p{x,\omega} is invariant to rotations around \omega{in}. Therefore, \psi is sampled uniformly from [0, 2\pi] and is not predicted by the CVAE. The CVAE predicts \theta. The direction \omega is derived from \theta and the uniform \psi. Construction of x: 1. Define a local reference frame where \omega{in} maps to (0,0,1). 2. Sample \tilde{x} = (\sin(\theta), 0, \cos(\theta)). 3. Apply a rotation R\psi around the z-axis by angle \psi. 4. Transform back to real space using rotation matrix R{CVAE}: x = r{sphere} R{CVAE} R\psi \tilde{x} 5. The outgoing direction \omega is normalized x relative to the center, or derived from the scattering geometry. The source notes \omega is parameterized as (\theta, \alpha, \beta) in the shader signature, but the text describes \theta and \psi for position. The direction \omega is typically the normalized vector from the sphere center to x for exit, or determined by the scattering event. The source states PATHGEN outputs (\theta, \beta, \alpha). We assume \theta is the polar angle, and \alpha, \beta define the azimuthal orientation or local frame rotation, but given the invariance argument, \psi is uniform. The specific mapping of \alpha, \beta to the final direction vector \omega requires constructing the local basis. A standard approach is: \omega is the direction of x from the center. The angles \alpha, \beta might refer to the local coordinate system for the next step or are redundant if \psi handles rotation. However, the shader signature explicitly lists them. We implement the output as the tuple (\theta, \beta, \alpha) and use \psi \sim U[0, 2\pi] for the final rotation if needed, or interpret \alpha, \beta as the azimuthal components if the invariance is handled differently. Correction based on text: The text says "restrict the CVAE learning space to only the \theta coordinate, while \psi is sampled uniformly". It then says PATHGEN outputs (\theta, \beta, \alpha). This implies \beta, \alpha might be unused or define the local frame for W. Given the invariance, \psi is the key rotational degree of freedom. We will assume the CVAE outputs \theta and potentially parameters for the local frame, but the primary geometric variable is \theta. For implementation, we treat the output as (\theta, \beta, \alpha) and use \psi for the final rotation of the position vector. 5. EVENTGEN (Representative Scattering Event): Used for next-event estimation of in-scattered direct illumination. Inputs: \sigmat', g, \varphi, \theta, \alpha, \beta, N, latent sample z^{(LE)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I{LE}), noise \epsilon^{(6)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I6). Output: (X, W), the position and direction of a representative internal scattering event. Implementation: EVENTGEN(σt', g, φ, θ, α, β, N, z^(LE), ε^(6)) → (X, W). X is the position inside the sphere, W is the direction of the ray arriving at X. These are transformed to real-space coordinates using the appropriate rotation matrix and scaling. Unverified code. name: Spherical Coordinate Test Data Generation
body: A coordinate transformation method to generate concentric spherical test data for validating the sampling process in volume rendering pipelines. It serves as a visual validation tool to ensure that the structure of input data grids is retained during the sampling process, allowing multiple spheres to be viewed simultaneously by assigning different data values to each shell. It differs from sibling methods like Random Hemisphere Sampling by providing deterministic, structured geometric primitives rather than stochastic samples, and from Rejection Sampling for Uniform Sphere Sampling by focusing on data grid integrity verification rather than probability distribution correctness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of discrete radius values r, and angular ranges for \theta and \phi. Output: A 3D Cartesian grid (x, y, z) representing concentric spherical shells. Data Structures: A 3D array or grid where each cell corresponds to a Cartesian coordinate. The value stored at each grid point is arbitrary for validation purposes, but distinct values are assigned to different radii to distinguish shells. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty 3D grid. 2. For each integer radius r starting from 1: a. Iterate through discrete angular samples for \theta in (0, 2\pi). b. Iterate through discrete angular samples for \phi in (0, \pi). c. Compute x, y, z using the formulas below. d. Map (x, y, z) to the nearest grid index. e. Assign a unique data value to this shell to allow visual distinction from other spheres. 3. Render or process the resulting grid to verify that the spherical structure is maintained during sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatesphericaltestdata(gridshape, maxradius, numtheta, numphi): grid = np.zeros(gridshape) for r in range(1, maxradius + 1): shellvalue = r for theta in np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numtheta, endpoint=False): for phi in np.linspace(0, np.pi, numphi, endpoint=False): x = r np.cos(theta) np.sin(phi) y = r np.sin(theta) np.sin(phi) z = r np.cos(phi) ix, iy, iz = int(round(x)), int(round(y)), int(round(z)) if 0 <= ix < gridshape[0] and 0 <= iy < gridshape[1] and 0 <= iz < gridshape[2]: grid[ix, iy, iz] = shellvalue return grid Formulas: The transformation from spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi) to Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) is defined as: x = r \cos(\theta) \sin(\phi) y = r \sin(\theta) \sin(\phi) z = r \cos(\phi) Parameters: r: Starts at 1 and increases by units of 1 (e.g., r = 1, 2, 3, \dots) to obtain a series of concentric spheres. \theta: Azimuthal angle, range (0, 2\pi). \phi: Polar angle, range (0, \pi). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision errors in trigonometric functions may cause gaps or overlaps in the shells if the angular resolution is too low. The boundary conditions \theta = 0, 2\pi and \phi = 0, \pi must be handled to avoid duplicate points at the poles or prime meridian. The value of the data items is not important for the structural validation, but distinct values are required for visual differentiation. A coordinate transformation method to generate cylindrical and truncated conic shell test data for validating the sampling process. It uses the same validation purpose as the spherical variant but employs cylindrical coordinates. The transformation is defined as: x = r \cos(\theta) y = r \sin(\theta) z = z Where 0 < \theta < 2\pi and r increases by units of 1 starting at 1 to obtain cylindrical shells. For truncated cones, r varies linearly as a function of z. This allows validation of internal and external structure visibility in cylindrical geometries, similar to the spherical case. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of grid points generated. The generation is deterministic and fast, suitable for pre-computation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the volume of the bounding box of the largest sphere or cylinder. Strengths: Provides clear visual confirmation that the sampling process preserves geometric structure. Allows simultaneous viewing of internal and external structures. Limitations: Only validates structural integrity, not statistical distribution or density accuracy. When to use: During the initial development and testing of volume rendering pipelines to ensure data grid retention during sampling. When not to use: For performance benchmarking or validation of statistical sampling properties. Originated in the context of volume visualization validation, specifically in the work by Dr. Phil Webster at the Wright Research and Development Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. The method was part of a broader visual validation process that included fabricated data sets (spheres, cylinders, truncated cones) and actual simulation data from finite-element analysis. The goal was to ensure that the structure of the input data grid was retained during the sampling process onto rectangular grids. name: Grid Ray Sampler
head: Primary Ray Sampling with Reparameterization, Reparameterized Primary Ray Sampling
body: The Grid Ray Sampler generates a set of 3D camera rays by mapping pixel coordinates from an image grid to world space using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. It solves the problem of sampling primary rays for a sensor, optionally applying a reparameterization function to the image-space positions to enable differentiable rendering with respect to camera or scene parameters. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the geometric transformation from 2D pixel indices to 3D ray vectors, whereas methods like Near-Far Linear Ray Generation focus on depth discretization along those rays, and Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling focuses on adaptive depth sampling based on prior weights. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: intrinsic (camera intrinsic matrix), pose (world-to-object or camera-to-world transformation matrix), resolution (image dimensions H \times W), numrays (target ray count), fullgrid (boolean flag for uniform vs random sampling), framerate.count() (accumulated sample count per pixel for coherence handling). Outputs: rayso (ray origins tensor), raysd (ray directions tensor). Data Structures Ray Buffer: A contiguous memory block storing origins and directions. Pixel Coordinates: Integer tensors i, j representing row and column indices, generated via meshgrid. Steps 1. Determine Ray Count: N = \text{num\rays} if fullgrid is false, otherwise N = H \times W. 2. Generate Pixel Indices: Create 2D grids of pixel coordinates i \in [0, H-1] and j \in [0, W-1] using torch.meshgrid with indexing="ij". 3. Select Indices: If fullgrid is false, generate random indices selectinds of size N from the range [0, H \times W - 1]. Gather the corresponding i and j values using selectinds. Reshape and expand i and j to match batch dimensions. 4. Lift to Camera Space: Convert 2D pixel coordinates to 3D points in the camera coordinate system using a lift function with intrinsics: pixelpointscam = lift(i, j, torch.oneslike(i), intrinsics=intrinsic). 5. Transform to World Space: Apply the pose transformation to get world coordinates: worldcoords = torch.bmm(pose, pixelpointscam).transpose(-1, -2)[...,:3]. 6. Compute Ray Origins: Extract ray origins from the pose matrix: rayso = pose[...,:3, 3]. 7. Compute Ray Directions: Calculate raw directions by subtracting origins from world coordinates: raysd = worldcoords - rayso[..., None,:]. 8. Normalize Directions: Normalize the direction vectors: raysd = F.normalize(raysd, dim=-1). 9. Expand Origins: Expand ray origins to match ray directions shape: rayso = rayso[..., None,:].expandas(raysd). Formulas Ray origin: \mathbf{o} = \text{pose}[:,:,:3, 3]. Ray direction: \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{p}{\text{world}} - \mathbf{o}}{\|\mathbf{p}{\text{world}} - \mathbf{o}\|2}. Parameters resolution: Integer defining image dimensions. Typical value: 512. framerate.count(): uint32t representing accumulated samples per pixel, passed to ray generator for coherence handling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Reparameterization requires the film to sample borders and the filter to not be a box filter. Precision handling for matrix operations and coordinate transformations is required to avoid artifacts. Boundary conditions for pixel coordinates must be handled to prevent out-of-bounds access. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def gridraysampler(intrinsic, pose, resolution, numrays, fullgrid=False, batchsize=1): """ Generate camera rays from pixel grid. Args: intrinsic: (3, 3) Camera intrinsic matrix K. pose: (4, 4) Camera-to-world transformation matrix. resolution: (H, W) Image dimensions. numrays: int Number of rays if fullgrid is False. fullgrid: bool If True, generate HW rays. batchsize: int Number of camera views. Returns: rayso: (batchsize, N, 3) Ray origins. raysd: (batchsize, N, 3) Ray directions. """ H, W = resolution N = H W if fullgrid else numrays # 1. Generate pixel coordinates i, j = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') # 2. Reshape and expand to match batch dimensions i = i.reshape(-1).unsqueeze(0).expand(batchsize, -1) j = j.reshape(-1).unsqueeze(0).expand(batchsize, -1) # 3. Select indices if not full grid if not fullgrid: selectinds = torch.randint(0, H W, size=(N,), device=i.device) i = i[:, selectinds] j = j[:, selectinds] # 4. Lift to camera space ones = torch.oneslike(i) pixelpointscam = torch.stack([j.float(), i.float(), ones], dim=-1) # Apply inverse intrinsic to lift to camera space Kinv = torch.inverse(intrinsic) pixelpointscam = torch.bmm(pixelpointscam, Kinv.T) # 5. Transform to world coordinates pixelpointscamhom = torch.cat([pixelpointscam, torch.ones(batchsize, N, 1, device=i.device)], dim=-1) worldcoordshom = torch.bmm(pose, pixelpointscamhom.transpose(-1, -2)) worldcoords = worldcoordshom[...,:3,:].transpose(-1, -2) # 6. Compute ray origins rayso = pose[...,:3, 3] rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(1).expandas(worldcoords) # 7. Compute ray directions raysd = worldcoords - rayso # 8. Normalize directions raysd = F.normalize(raysd, dim=-1) return rayso, raysd This method generates camera rays from pixel coordinates, passes them through an implicit neural renderer, and extracts rendered features (such as color or geometry) into image tensors. It differs from the parent Grid Ray Sampler by handling the complete inference pipeline—transforming pixel grids into ray bundles, executing the neural network forward pass, and reshaping the output—rather than just sampling ray origins and directions. Choose it when building a full differentiable neural rendering pipeline rather than a standalone ray generator. Near-Middle-Far Ray Generation divides a camera ray into two distinct segments: a linear interpolation from the near plane to a middle point, and a disparity (inverse-linear) interpolation from the middle point to the far plane. It allocates a configurable fraction of samples to the near-middle segment and the remainder to the middle-far segment. Choose it when depth resolution needs to be non-uniformly distributed across the viewing frustum. Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling generates refined ray samples for volume rendering by sampling new depth positions based on previous iteration's weights, then computing segment lengths and midpoints for rendering. It builds on the coarse sampling provided by the Grid Ray Sampler by adaptively drawing new samples from the distribution defined by prior weights. Choose it when variance reduction is needed by concentrating samples on high-contribution regions. Near-Far Linear Ray Generation generates a list of 3D sampling points along a camera ray segment defined by near (t{min}) and far (t{max}) distances for a specified number of samples. It solves the problem of discretizing the continuous ray domain into a finite set of query points for volume rendering or neural radiance field evaluation. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing the foundational uniform or disparity-based spacing logic upon which stratified, probabilistic, or depth-guided variants build. Unlike Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which adapts density to learned probabilities, or Depth-Guided Supersampling which uses external depth priors, this method relies on fixed geometric intervals. Choose it for standard uniform discretization along a ray segment. Batch Stratified Pixel Sampling is a ray generation method used in neural reconstruction pipelines to select a subset of pixels for optimization at each training iteration. It solves the problem of efficiently computing gradients by avoiding the memory overhead of processing the entire image grid while ensuring uniform coverage through stratification. It differs from its sibling Grid-based Stratified Camera Sampling by focusing on batched pixel selection for ground-truth retrieval via bilinear interpolation, rather than generating continuous camera rays for volumetric traversal. Choose it when training memory is constrained and pixel-level gradient updates are required. Grid-based Stratified Camera Sampling generates camera rays by uniformly covering the scene volume using a 3D stratified grid for camera positions, combined with random selection of training view orientations. It differs from the parent Grid Ray Sampler by explicitly stratifying the camera position space across the scene bounds rather than just the pixel grid, and from siblings like Near-Middle-Far Ray Generation by decoupling position stratification from view orientation selection. Choose it when novel view synthesis requires diverse camera poses rather than fixed viewpoints. This method generates stratified cosine-weighted diffuse rays for bounded one-bounce voxel global illumination, sampling from primary hit positions. It differs from its siblings by specifically targeting the second bounce (GI) in a voxel-based pipeline, using stratified sampling to reduce variance compared to pure random generation, while restricting rays to a fixed maximum distance for performance. Choose it for efficient first-bounce global illumination in voxel-based rendering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Grid Ray Sampler is a fundamental component in computer graphics and neural rendering pipelines for generating camera rays from pixel coordinates. It is widely used in NeRF-based methods and differentiable rendering frameworks. The method relies on standard pinhole camera models and homogeneous coordinate transformations. body: This method generates camera rays from pixel coordinates, passes them through an implicit neural renderer, and extracts rendered features (such as color or geometry) into image tensors. It differs from the parent Grid Ray Sampler by handling the complete inference pipeline—transforming pixel grids into ray bundles, executing the neural network forward pass, and reshaping the output—rather than just sampling ray origins and directions. Inputs: Camera parameters (intrinsic/extrinsic matrices, image size). Light location (optional, for lighting calculations). Neural model instance (implicit renderer). Feature key (feat): specifies the output channel to render, typically 'color' or 'geometry'. Outputs: Rendered image tensor of shape [height, width, 3] containing RGB values or geometry data. Data Structures: RayBundle: Contains origins (shape [numrays, 3]) and directions (shape [numrays, 3]). out: Dictionary-like output from the model, where out['color'] or out['geometry'] has shape [batchsize, numrays, 3]. Steps: 1. Initialize Model: Set the neural model to evaluation mode and move to the target device (e.g., GPU). \text{model} \leftarrow \text{Model}(\text{cfg}) \text{model} \leftarrow \text{model.to}(\text{device}) \text{model}.\text{eval}() 2. Compute Light Direction (Optional): If lighting is required, compute the direction from the light source to the scene origin. This assumes the object is centered at the origin. \mathbf{d}{\text{light}} = \mathbf{l}{\text{loc}} - \mathbf{o}{\text{origin}} \mathbf{d}{\text{light}} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{\text{light}}}{\|\mathbf{d}{\text{light}}\|} Note: The source code flags a potential issue if the object is not at the origin. 3. Reshape Output: Extract the specified feature tensor and reshape it from [batchsize, numrays, 3] to [height, width, 3]. \mathbf{I} = \mathbf{O}[\text{feat}].\text{view}(\text{height}, \text{width}, 3) 7. body: A procedure to render RGB, Depth, and Accumulation maps for a set of latent codes and camera poses using a pre-trained NeRF generator. It handles batching and post-processing of outputs, reshaping them into image tensors. It differs from standard ray marching by operating on a batch of latent vectors and camera poses simultaneously, optimizing throughput for inference. Inputs: Latent codes z: Tensor of shape (N, Dz), where N is the number of samples and Dz is the latent dimension. Camera poses: Optional tensor or list of camera extrinsics. If not provided, rays are set to None. Generator: A pre-trained neural network capable of querying color and density given a latent code and ray. batchsize: Integer controlling the chunking of latent codes and rays. imgsize: Spatial dimensions (H, W) of the output image. Outputs: RGB: Tensor of shape (N, 3, H, W). Depth: Tensor of shape (N, 1, H, W). Accumulation: Tensor of shape (N, 1, H, W). Data Structures: Rays: Input rays are structured as (B, 2, H \times W, C) where B is the batch size, 2 represents the ray origin and direction, H \times W is the number of pixels, and C=3 is the dimensionality of origin/direction vectors. Intermediate Query Output: The generator returns tensors of shape (N \times H \times W, C{out}) where C{out} includes RGB, Disparity, Accumulation, and other outputs. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the generator to evaluation mode to disable training-specific updates. Determine the computation device. 2. Batch Splitting: Split the latent codes z into batches of size batchsize. 3. Ray Generation: If camera poses are provided, generate rays for each pose using a ray sampler (e.g., valraysampler), stack them, and split into batches matching the latent code batches. If no poses are provided, the rays list is None. 4. Iteration: Iterate through each batch of latent codes zi and rays raysi. 5. Gradient Disabling: Disable gradient computation for the forward pass. 6. Ray Preprocessing: Permute and flatten the rays tensor from shape (B, 2, H, W, C) to (2, B \times H \times W, 3). This flattens the spatial dimensions to query the network pixel-by-pixel within the batch. 7. Network Query: Pass the latent code zi and preprocessed rays raysi to the generator. Retrieve RGB, Disparity, Accumulation, and other outputs. 8. Reshaping: Reshape the outputs from (N \times H \times W, C) to (N, C, H, W). 9. Collection: Append the reshaped tensors to lists for RGB, Disparity, and Accumulation. 10. Concatenation: Concatenate all batch results along the first dimension to form the final tensors. 11. Depth Conversion: Convert disparity maps to depth maps. 12. Return: Return the final RGB, Depth, and Accumulation tensors. Formulas: Disparity to Depth Conversion: depth = \frac{1}{\max(10^{-10}, disparity)} Undefined values (where disparity equals 10^{10}) are set to the far plane value. Depth Normalization (for visualization): depth{norm} = \frac{depth - near}{far - near} Where near and far are the near and far plane distances retrieved from generator.renderkwargstest. Parameters: near: Near plane distance, retrieved from generator.renderkwargstest['near']. far: Far plane distance, retrieved from generator.renderkwargstest['far']. batchsize: Controls chunking. imgsize: Spatial dimensions, e.g., 64. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def batchedraysamplingandneuralrendering(generator, latentcodes, poses, batchsize, imgsize, near, far): """ Renders RGB, Depth, and Accumulation for a batch of latent codes and poses. Args: generator: Pre-trained NeRF generator model. latentcodes: List of latent vectors of shape (N, Dz). poses: List of camera pose matrices or None. batchsize: Integer for batching. imgsize: Integer, spatial dimension (H=W). near: Near plane distance. far: Far plane distance. Returns: rgb: Array (N, 3, H, W) depth: Array (N, 1, H, W) acc: Array (N, 1, H, W) """ generator.eval() N = len(latentcodes) # Split latent codes into batches zbatches = [latentcodes[i:i+batchsize] for i in range(0, N, batchsize)] # Generate rays if poses are provided raysbatches = None if poses is not None: allrays = [] for pose in poses: # valraysampler returns rays for a single pose rays = generator.valraysampler(imgsize, imgsize, generator.focal, pose)[0] allrays.append(rays) allrays = stack(allrays, axis=0) # Shape: (N, 2, H, W, C) raysbatches = [allrays[i:i+batchsize] for i in range(0, N, batchsize)] rgblist = [] displist = [] acclist = [] for i, zi in enumerate(zbatches): raysi = raysbatches[i] if raysbatches is not None else None bs = len(zi) # Disable gradients with nograd(): # Preprocess rays: Bx2x(HxW)xC -> 2x(BxHxW)x3 if raysi is not None: # Permute to (B, H, W, 2, C) then flatten spatial and view dims raysi = permute(raysi, axes=(0, 2, 3, 1, 4)) raysi = reshape(raysi, (bs imgsize imgsize, 2, 3)) raysi = permute(raysi, axes=(1, 0, 2)) # Query generator rgbi, dispi, acci, = generator(zi, rays=raysi) # Reshape outputs from (NHW, C) to (N, C, H, W) reshapefn = lambda x: permute(reshape(x, (bs, imgsize, imgsize, x.shape[1])), axes=(0, 3, 1, 2)) rgblist.append(reshapefn(rgbi)) displist.append(reshapefn(dispi)) acclist.append(reshapefn(acci)) # Concatenate results rgb = concatenate(rgblist, axis=0) disp = concatenate(displist, axis=0) acc = concatenate(acclist, axis=0) # Handle undefined disparity values (10^10) disp = where(disp == 1e10, far, disp) # Depth = 1 / max(1e-10, disp) depth = 1.0 / clamp(disp, min=1e-10) return rgb, depth, acc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undefined Disparity: Disparity values equal to 10^{10} indicate undefined depth (e.g., background) and must be explicitly handled by setting them to the far plane value before the inverse operation. Precision: Use \max(10^{-10}, disparity) to avoid division by zero or numerical instability with very small disparity values. Missing Poses: If poses are not provided, rays must be handled correctly as None to avoid errors in the generator query. Performance: Measured performance depends on the generator's complexity and hardware. For example, on a GPU with \le10GB memory, an image size of 64x64 is recommended. Strengths: Efficient for generating multiple views or latent samples and handles batching automatically. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained generator. When to Use: When rendering multiple images from a NeRF model, especially for evaluation metrics like FID/KID or video generation. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method is part of the evaluation and inference pipeline for these models. name: Near-Middle-Far Ray Generation
body: Near-Middle-Far Ray Generation divides a camera ray into two distinct segments: a linear interpolation from the near plane to a middle point, and a disparity (inverse-linear) interpolation from the middle point to the far plane. It allocates a configurable fraction of samples to the near-middle segment and the remainder to the middle-far segment. Inputs: near: float or tensor, the distance to the near clipping plane. far: float or tensor, the distance to the far clipping plane. middle: float or tensor, the distance to the middle point where the sampling strategy switches. pointcount: int, the total number of sample points to generate along the ray. middlesplit: float, the fraction of pointcount allocated to the near-middle segment (default 0.6). jitter: float in [0, 1), a fraction of the step length used to perturb sample positions. campos: tensor, the camera position. raydir: tensor, the ray direction. Outputs: raypos: tensor of sample positions along the ray. valid: tensor of ones indicating all samples are valid. Data Structures: t0, t1: tensors of linearly spaced values in [0, 1] with sizes N0 and N1. d0, d1: tensors of computed distances for the near-middle and middle-far segments. tvals: concatenated distance tensor of shape (batch, height, width, N0 + N1). segmentlength: tensor of truncated, jittered segment lengths of shape (batch, height, width, pointcount). endpointts: tensor of cumulative end-point distances of shape (batch, height, width, pointcount + 1). middlepointts: tensor of midpoint distances of shape (batch, height, width, pointcount). Steps: 1. Calculate point counts: N0 = \lfloor \text{point\count} \times \text{middle\split} \rfloor + 1 and N1 = \lfloor \text{point\count} \times (1 - \text{middle\split}) \rfloor + 2. 2. Generate linear parameter values: t0 = linspace(0, 1, N0) and t1 = linspace(0, 1, N1). 3. Compute near-middle distances: d0 = near (1 - t0) + middle t0. 4. Compute middle-far distances: d1 = 1.0 / (1.0/middle (1 - t1) + 1.0/far t1). 5. Concatenate distances along the sample dimension: tvals = cat([d0, d1], dim=2). 6. Compute raw segment lengths: diffs = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1]. 7. Apply jitter: jittered = diffs (1.0 + jitter (randlike(diffs) - 0.5)). 8. Truncate to pointcount samples: segmentlength = jittered[...,:pointcount]. 9. Compute cumulative distances, prepend zeros, and add near offset: endpointts = near + cat([zeroslike(segmentlength[...,:1]), cumsum(segmentlength)], dim=2). 10. Compute middle-point distances: middlepointts = (endpointts[...,:-1] + endpointts[..., 1:]) / 2.0. 11. Compute ray positions: raypos = campos + raydir middlepointts. 12. Set validity mask: valid = oneslike(middlepointts). Formulas: Linear interpolation: d0 = \text{near} \times (1 - t) + \text{middle} \times t. Disparity interpolation: d1 = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\text{middle}} \times (1 - t) + \frac{1}{\text{far}} \times t}. Jittered segment length: \Delta = \Delta{\text{raw}} \times (1 + \text{jitter} \times (u - 0.5)), where u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1). Midpoint distance: t{\text{mid}} = \frac{t{\text{end}, i} + t{\text{end}, i+1}}{2}. Parameters: middlesplit: float, default 0.6. jitter: float in [0, 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If middle is not strictly between near and far, the disparity formula may yield invalid or inverted distances. If pointcount exceeds N0 + N1 - 1, the truncation step discards samples; the source assumes N0 + N1 - 1 \ge \text{point\count}. Division by zero occurs if middle or far is zero in the disparity formula. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def nearmiddlefarraygeneration(near, far, middle, pointcount, middlesplit=0.6, jitter=0.0, campos=None, raydir=None): # 1. Calculate point counts N0 = int(pointcount middlesplit) + 1 N1 = int(pointcount (1 - middlesplit)) + 2 # 2. Generate linear parameter values [0, 1] t0 = torch.linspace(0, 1, N0) t1 = torch.linspace(0, 1, N1) # 3. Compute near-middle distances (linear) d0 = near (1.0 - t0) + middle t0 # 4. Compute middle-far distances (disparity) invmiddle = 1.0 / middle invfar = 1.0 / far d1 = 1.0 / (invmiddle (1.0 - t1) + invfar t1) # 5. Concatenate distances along the sample dimension tvals = torch.cat([d0, d1], dim=2) # 6. Compute raw segment lengths diffs = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] # 7. Apply jitter randomvals = torch.randlike(diffs) jittered = diffs (1.0 + jitter (randomvals - 0.5)) # 8. Truncate to pointcount samples segmentlength = jittered[...,:pointcount] # 9. Compute cumulative distances, prepend zeros, add near offset cumsumlengths = torch.cumsum(segmentlength, dim=2) zeros = torch.zeroslike(segmentlength[...,:1]) endpointts = near + torch.cat([zeros, cumsumlengths], dim=2) # 10. Compute middle-point distances middlepointts = (endpointts[...,:-1] + endpointts[..., 1:]) / 2.0 # 11. Compute ray positions if campos is not None and raydir is not None: raypos = campos + raydir middlepointts else: raypos = middlepointts # 12. Set validity mask valid = torch.oneslike(middlepointts) return raypos, valid Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling
head: NeRF Ray Refinement Sampling, Refine Ray Generation, Refined Ray Generation
body: Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling generates refined ray samples for volume rendering by sampling new depth positions based on previous iteration's weights, then computing segment lengths and midpoints for rendering. It builds on the coarse sampling provided by the Grid Ray Sampler by adaptively drawing new samples from the distribution defined by prior weights. The method takes previous depth samples and their associated weights, samples new depth positions using a probability density function routine, and computes the geometric properties required for volume rendering. Inputs: prevts: Tensor of shape (N, Rays, PrevSamples) containing the previous sample distances. prevweights: Tensor of shape (N, Rays, PrevSamples) containing the previous sample weights. pointcount: Integer specifying the number of new samples to generate per ray. campos: Camera position vector. raydir: Ray direction vector. jitter: Boolean flag indicating whether to add uniform noise to samples. Outputs: raypos: Tensor of shape (N, Rays, pointcount) containing the 3D world positions of the new sample points. segmentlength: Tensor of shape (N, Rays, pointcount) containing the length of each segment along the ray. validitymask: Boolean tensor indicating valid samples. prevts: Float tensor storing depth values t. prevweights: Float tensor storing weights w. endpointts: Float tensor storing the new depth samples. middlepointts: Float tensor storing the midpoints of the segments defined by endpointts. segmentlength: Float tensor storing the distance between consecutive endpoints. 1. Sample New Depths: Draw pointcount + 1 new depth values from the distribution defined by prevts and prevweights using a PDF sampling routine (samplepdf) with a jitter condition. 2. Reshape: Reshape endpointts to remove the last dimension added by samplepdf, resulting in shape (N, Rays, pointcount + 1). 3. Compute Segment Lengths: Calculate the difference between consecutive depth values: \text{segment\length}i = \text{end\point\ts}i - \text{end\point\ts}{i-1} for i = 1 \dots \text{point\count}. 4. Scale Segment Lengths: Multiply the depth differences by the norm of the ray direction vector \|\mathbf{d}\| to convert depth distance to Euclidean distance: \text{segment\length}i^{\text{euclidean}} = \text{segment\length}i \times \|\mathbf{d}\|. 5. Compute Midpoints: Calculate the midpoint depth for each segment: \text{middle\point\ts}i = \frac{\text{end\point\ts}i + \text{end\point\ts}{i-1}}{2}. 6. Compute Ray Positions: Calculate the 3D world position for each midpoint: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{c} + \text{middle\point\ts}i \times \mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{c} is campos and \mathbf{d} is raydir. 7. Initialize Validity Mask: Create a boolean mask of ones with the same dtype and device as middlepointts. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def samplepdf(bins, weights, nsamples, jitter=True): """ PDF sampling from bins and weights. bins: (..., N) depth values weights: (..., N) importance weights nsamples: int, number of samples to draw jitter: bool, add uniform noise Returns: (..., nsamples) sampled depths """ # Pad weights with zeros at start and end to define full range weights = F.pad(weights, (1, 0), 'constant', 0.0) # Compute CDF cdf = torch.cumsum(weights, dim=-1) cdf = cdf[...,:-1] cdf = cdf / cdf[..., -1:] # Sample uniform random numbers u = torch.rand(list(weights.shape[:-1]) + [nsamples], device=weights.device) if jitter: u = u (1.0 / nsamples) + torch.randlike(u) / nsamples # Invert CDF indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='left') binsg = bins.gather(-1, indices) binsl = bins.gather(-1, indices - 1) cdfg = cdf.gather(-1, indices) cdfl = cdf.gather(-1, indices - 1) # Interpolate t = (u - cdfl) / (cdfg - cdfl + 1e-5) samples = binsl + t (binsg - binsl) return samples def refinedraygeneration(prevts, prevweights, pointcount, campos, raydir, jitter=True): """ prevts: (N, Rays, PrevSamples) prevweights: (N, Rays, PrevSamples) """ # Step 1: Sample new end-point ts endpointts = samplepdf(prevts, prevweights, pointcount + 1, jitter) # Step 2: Reshape endpointts to remove the last dimension added by samplepdf if endpointts.dim() > 3: endpointts = endpointts.squeeze(-1) # Step 3: Compute segment lengths segmentlength = endpointts[:,:, 1:] - endpointts[:,:,:-1] # Step 4: Compute middle-point ts middlepointts = (endpointts[:,:,:-1] + endpointts[:,:, 1:]) / 2.0 # Step 5: Compute ray positions raypos = campos.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) + raydir.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) middlepointts.unsqueeze(-1) # Step 6: Multiply segmentlength by ray direction norm raydirnorm = torch.norm(raydir, dim=-1, keepdim=True) segmentlength = segmentlength raydirnorm # Step 7: Initialize validity mask validitymask = torch.oneslike(middlepointts, dtype=torch.bool) return raypos, segmentlength, validitymask pointcount: The number of refined samples per ray. jitter: Boolean flag indicating whether to add uniform noise to samples. Reshape Requirement: The samplepdf routine may return an extra trailing dimension that must be explicitly removed before computing differences. Direction Norm Scaling: Segment lengths computed from depth differences must be scaled by the ray direction norm to yield correct Euclidean distances. Mask Initialization: The validity mask must be initialized to ones with the exact same dtype and device as middlepointts to ensure correct broadcasting and device placement. Extends NeRF ray refinement by restricting samples to a cube domain defined by domainsize, marking points outside as invalid. It calls the base refineraygeneration to obtain initial raypos, segmentlength, and middlepointts, then computes a validity mask by checking if all coordinates of raypos fall within (-\text{domain\size}, \text{domain\size}). Combines pixel-guided and depth-guided sampling distributions using a weight parameter \beta that increments from 0 to 0.5 across training iterations. The final sampling probability is computed as P{samp}(u, v) = \beta P'c(u, v) + (1 - \beta)P'd(u, v), where P'c is the normalized pixel-guided probability and P'd is the normalized depth-guided probability. Rays are sampled based on this fused distribution during training. Not given in the sources. This method is used in PointNeRF. It was introduced to improve the efficiency of volume rendering by adaptively sampling along rays based on previous iteration weights. name: CDF-based Ray Resampling
head: CDF Resampling Kernel, CDF Resampling for Ray Points, midpoint resampling
body:
CDF-based Ray Resampling redistributes a set of input ray samples into a new, fixed-number set of samples by sampling from the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of the volumetric rendering weights. It differs from standard implementations by sampling the midpoints of the resampled intervals rather than the start or end points, and by explicitly adding a background interval to the CDF to allow samples to be assigned to the background when foreground density is low. This method builds on Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling by providing a deterministic, weight-aware resampling strategy that preserves the total energy of the ray while adapting sample density to the signal. The method takes a set of rays with varying numbers of input samples and resamples each ray to a target number of output samples (steps). It operates on a per-ray basis using a CUDA kernel, but the logical steps are defined below. Inputs: packedinfo: Tensor of shape [nrays, 2]. Column 0 is the base index in the flat arrays for each ray. Column 1 is the number of input samples (numsteps) for each ray. tstarts: Tensor of shape [nsamplesin, 1]. The start positions (t{start}) of the input frustum-shaped samples along each ray. tends: Tensor of shape [nsamplesin, 1]. The end positions (t{end}) of the input frustum-shaped samples along each ray. weights: Tensor of shape [nsamplesin]. The volumetric rendering weights (wi) for each input sample. steps: Integer. The target number of resampled points per ray. Outputs: resamplets: Tensor of shape [totalresampledsamples, 1]. The t-coordinates (midpoints) of the resampled samples. resampleoffsets: Tensor of shape [totalresampledsamples, 1]. The offset of each resampled midpoint relative to the start of its assigned input interval. resampleindices: Tensor of shape [totalresampledsamples] (int64). The index of the input interval (from weights) that each resampled sample falls into. resamplefgcounts: Tensor of shape [nsamplesin] (int32). The number of resampled samples assigned to each input foreground interval. resamplebgcounts: Tensor of shape [nrays] (int32). The number of resampled samples assigned to the background for each ray. resamplepackedinfo: Tensor of shape [nrays, 2]. Column 0 is the start index in the output arrays. Column 1 is the end index (exclusive) in the output arrays. The algorithm uses flat tensors for efficiency. The packedinfo structure allows random access to ray segments without iterating through a jagged array. The output arrays are pre-allocated based on the total number of resampled steps to avoid dynamic resizing. 1. Validation: Assert that nsamples (the number of input samples per ray, assumed uniform or handled via packedinfo) is greater than 1. If nsamples == 1, the method is undefined. 2. Pre-computation: Calculate totalsamples: Sum of numsteps for all rays (from packedinfo). Calculate resamplenumsteps: For each ray, the number of steps to resample. In the reference implementation, this is often uniform (steps), but the logic supports variable counts. Let N{out} be the target steps per ray. Calculate resamplecumsteps: Cumulative sum of resamplenumsteps across rays. This defines the boundaries in the output tensors. Allocate output tensors: totalsteps = Sum of resamplenumsteps. resamplets, resampleoffsets of size totalsteps. resampleindices of size totalsteps. resamplefgcounts of size totalsamples. resamplebgcounts of size nrays. 3. Per-Ray Processing (Kernel): For each ray i: Locate Segment: Get base index Bi = 	ext{packed\info}[i, 0] and step count Si = 	ext{packed\info}[i, 1]. Compute Total Weight: Sum foreground weights: W{fg} = \sum{j=0}^{Si-1} w{Bi+j}. Compute background weight: W{bg} = \max(1.0 - W{fg}, 0.0). Total weight: W{total} = W{fg} + W{bg}. Calculate CDF Step Size: Let N{out} be the number of resampled steps for this ray. cdf\step\size =  rac{1.0 -  rac{1.0}{N{out}}}{N{out} - 1}. This formula ensures that the sampling points are uniformly distributed in CDF space, excluding the very end of the CDF to handle the background interval correctly. Initialize Pointers: cdf\prev = 0.0. cdf
ext =  rac{w{Bi}}{W{total}}. cdf\u =  rac{1.0}{2 \cdot N{out}}. This is the first sampling position in CDF space (midpoint of the first bin). Resample Loop: For k = 0 to N{out} - 1: Find Interval: While cdf\u > cdf
ext and cdf
ext < 1.0: cdf\prev = cdf
ext. If cdf\prev + cdf\step\size < 1.0: cdf
ext = cdf\prev + cdf\step\size. Else: cdf
ext = 1.0. Note: The reference implementation uses a specific logic where cdfnext is updated based on the weight sum. A more robust interpretation based on the notes: Iterate through input weights wj (where j is the index in the ray's segment). Accumulate weight sum. If cdf\u falls within the cumulative weight range of an input interval, assign the sample to that interval. Assign Sample: If cdf\u corresponds to the background interval (i.e., it exceeds the sum of all foreground weights): Assign to background. t{mid} = t{end, last} + 10000.0 (fixed offset for background, as per). Increment resamplebgcounts[i]. Set resampleindices to a special value or handle separately. Else: Identify the input interval m such that CDF(m-1) \le cdf\u \le CDF(m). Calculate the local position within the interval: local\u =  rac{cdf\u - CDF(m-1)}{wm}. Calculate midpoint: t{mid} =  rac{t{start, m} + t{end, m}}{2}. (Note: The notes specify sampling midpoints. If the CDF sampling lands in an interval, the output t is the midpoint of that input interval, or potentially interpolated. The notes say "sample midpoints instead of start/end points", implying the output t is the midpoint of the resampled interval? No, it says "sample midpoints... of the resampled frustum-shape samples". Given the input is frustum-shaped, the output is likely the midpoint of the input interval that the CDF sample falls into, or a linear interpolation. The notes explicitly state: "Calculate the number of steps per ray... Compute cumulative sum... Construct resamplepackedinfo... Allocate output tensors... Launch kernel". The kernel calculates resamplets. The pitfall is nsamples > 1. The key distinction is "sampling midpoints". This usually means if a sample falls in interval [ti, t{i+1}], its t value is (ti + t{i+1})/2. Calculate offset: offset = t{mid} - t{start, m}. Increment resamplefgcounts[m]. Store t{mid} in resamplets, offset in resampleoffsets, and m in resampleindices. Advance CDF: cdf\u += cdf\step\size. 4. Finalize: Fill remaining points in the last interval (background) if the loop ends with j < num ins (this part of the note is slightly ambiguous, but implies handling the tail of the CDF). Return the populated tensors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def cdfresamplingkernel(packedinfo, tstarts, tends, weights, steps): """ Simulates the CDF-based Ray Resampling kernel logic. Note: This is a Python simulation for clarity. The actual implementation is in CUDA. """ nrays = packedinfo.shape[0] resamplets = [] resampleoffsets = [] resampleindices = [] resamplefgcounts = torch.zeros(weights.shape[0], dtype=torch.int32) resamplebgcounts = torch.zeros(nrays, dtype=torch.int32) resamplepackedinfo = [] currentoutidx = 0 for i in range(nrays): baseidx = packedinfo[i, 0].item() numsteps = packedinfo[i, 1].item() # Extract ray-specific data rayweights = weights[baseidx: baseidx + numsteps] raytstarts = tstarts[baseidx: baseidx + numsteps] raytends = tends[baseidx: baseidx + numsteps] # Compute total weight including background wfgsum = rayweights.sum().item() wbg = max(1.0 - wfgsum, 0.0) wtotal = wfgsum + wbg if wtotal == 0: # Degenerate case: no density. Assign all to background? # Or uniform? The notes imply background handling when foreground is low. # If wtotal is 0, CDF is undefined. Assume uniform or skip. # For robustness, let's assume uniform distribution over background. pass # CDF Step Size # cdfstepsize = (1.0 - 1.0 / numbins) / (numbins - 1) # Here numbins = steps if steps <= 1: raise ValueError("steps must be > 1") cdfstepsize = (1.0 - 1.0 / steps) / (steps - 1) # Initialize CDF pointers cdfprev = 0.0 # cdfnext is the cumulative weight up to the current interval # We iterate through intervals cdfu = 1.0 / (2 steps) # First sample midpoint in CDF space rayresampledts = [] rayresampledoffsets = [] rayresampledindices = [] # Build CDF of foreground weights cdffg = torch.cumsum(rayweights, dim=0) for k in range(steps): # Determine which interval cdfu falls into # Normalize cdfu to [0, wtotal] # Actually, cdfu is in [0, 1] relative to wtotal? # The notes say: cdfnext = weights[0] / weightssum. # So cdfu is in [0, 1]. # Find index m such that cdffg[m-1]/wtotal < cdfu <= cdffg[m]/wtotal # Handle background if cdfu > (wfgsum / wtotal) if wtotal > 0 else 0: # Background sample # Fixed offset 10000.f added to ends[steps-1] lasttend = raytends[-1].item() tmid = lasttend + 10000.0 offset = 10000.0 # Offset from last end? Or relative to start? # Notes say "offsets of the resampled midpoints with respect to the starts of the sampled intervals" # If it's background, there is no "interval" in the foreground sense. # Let's assume offset is 0 or handled separately. # The notes say "fill remaining points in the last interval (background) with fixed offset 10000.f added to ends[steps-1]" # This implies the t value is ends[-1] + 10000. # Offset might be 10000. rayresampledts.append(tmid) rayresampledoffsets.append(10000.0) rayresampledindices.append(-1) # Special index for background resamplebgcounts[i] += 1 else: # Foreground sample # Find interval # cdfu wtotal targetweight = cdfu wtotal # Find first index where cdffg >= targetweight # Use searchsorted m = torch.searchsorted(cdffg, targetweight, side='right').item() # Clamp m m = min(m, numsteps - 1) # Get interval bounds tstart = raytstarts[m].item() tend = raytends[m].item() # Sample midpoint tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 # Offset from start offset = tmid - tstart rayresampledts.append(tmid) rayresampledoffsets.append(offset) rayresampledindices.append(baseidx + m) resamplefgcounts[baseidx + m] += 1 # Advance CDF cdfu += cdfstepsize # Store results resamplets.extend(rayresampledts) resampleoffsets.extend(rayresampledoffsets) resampleindices.extend(rayresampledindices) # Packed info for output resamplepackedinfo.append([currentoutidx, currentoutidx + steps]) currentoutidx += steps return ( torch.tensor(resamplets, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1), torch.tensor(resampleoffsets, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1), torch.tensor(resampleindices, dtype=torch.int64), resamplefgcounts, resamplebgcounts, torch.tensor(resamplepackedinfo, dtype=torch.int64)) steps: Target number of resampled points per ray. Must be greater than 1. packedinfo: Tensor of shape [nrays, 2]. weights: Tensor of shape [nsamplesin]. tstarts, tends: Tensors of shape [nsamplesin, 1]. nsamples == 1: The CUDA kernel does not handle rays with only 1 input sample. The Python wrapper asserts nsamples > 1. Zero Weight: If all weights are zero, W{total} = 0. The CDF is undefined. The implementation should handle this by assigning all samples to the background or distributing them uniformly. The notes mention max(1.0 - weightssum, 0.0), which handles the case where foreground weight is low but not zero. If foreground is exactly zero, background is 1.0. Background Interval: The background interval is handled by adding a fixed offset of 10000.0 to the last end position. This is a heuristic to push background samples far away from the foreground. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{out}) for the resampling step, where N{out} is the number of resampled steps per ray. The CDF construction is O(N{in}) per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N{in} + N{out}) for storing input and output tensors. Strengths: Deterministic resampling based on weight distribution. Handles background explicitly. Efficient CUDA implementation. Limitations: Requires nsamples > 1. The fixed background offset is a heuristic. When to use: When you need to adapt the number of samples per ray based on the signal density, while maintaining a fixed output size for downstream processing. This method is implemented in the RISE-SDF repository. It is a specialized ray resampling technique for volume rendering, specifically designed to work with frustum-shaped samples and to handle background contributions explicitly. dehezhang2/RISE-SDF, https://github.com/dehezhang2/RISE-SDF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Stochastic Filtering Using Opacity
head: Importance Sampling Filtering
body: Stochastic Filtering Using Opacity is a ray sampling refinement technique used in Explicit Radiance Field (ERF) reconstruction to reduce computational cost during optimization. It filters a pre-sampled set of ray points by querying the Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) for opacity estimates, then applies importance sampling to retain only the samples most likely to be near true scene surfaces. It differs from CDF-based Ray Resampling by using a simple additive weight model (c + o) rather than cumulative distribution functions, and from its parent Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling by operating on a fixed budget of previously stratified samples rather than generating new samples from a PDF. Inputs: A set of limited ray sampling points s'{r,i} for ray r, resulting from a previous stratified sampling step. The current SVO geometry estimate. A user-defined constant c. Outputs: A further reduced set of ray sampling points s''{r,i} with count N{max,r} < N{max}. Data Structures: SVO Opacity Query: The SVO stores opacity values. Access requires 4D interpolation (spatial x,y,z and temporal t) as defined in Eq. 5 of the source. The exact interpolation kernel is not detailed in the provided notes, but standard trilinear or higher-order interpolation over the voxel grid is implied by "4D interpolation scheme". Sampling Weights: A scalar weight w{s,r}(t{i,k}) is computed for each sample point at depth t{i,k}. Steps: 1. Opacity Query: For each sample point t{i,k} in the limited set s'{r,i}, query the SVO to obtain the opacity sample o(t{i,k}) using 4D interpolation. 2. Weight Calculation: Compute the sampling weight for each point using the formula: w{s,r}(t{i,k}) = c + o(t{i,k}) where c is a constant and o(t{i,k}) is the queried opacity. 3. Importance Sampling: Use the weights w{s,r}(t{i,k}) to perform importance sampling. Select a subset of points s''{r,i} \subset s'{r,i} such that the final count N{max,r} does not exceed the secondary budget limit. Points with higher opacity (closer to surfaces) are preferentially retained. 4. Radiance Retrieval: Use the final reduced set s''{r,i} to retrieve outgoing SLF radiance samples from the SVO. Parameters: Constant c: Set to 0.05. This ensures that the entire ray is sampled at least infrequently, handling intermediate false free space regions where opacity is low but gradients are still needed. Sample Budgets: N{max}: Maximum samples per ray after initial stratified sampling. Typical value: 256. N{max,r}: Maximum samples per ray after stochastic filtering. Typical value: 32. Samples per node edge length \alpha: Set to 8. Pitfalls: Gradient Noise: Randomly skipping sampling points induces noise on loss gradients. However, the optimizer (Adam/SGD) is robust to this noise. False Occluders: This method helps avoid false occluders consistently blocking true surface points, which would otherwise result in missing gradients for correct reconstruction. Optimization Only: This stochastic limiting is primarily required to limit gradient computation costs during optimization. It is optional for final rendering once the SVO is built, as no loss gradients are computed and SVO nodes tightly bound observed surfaces. This variant refers to the initial random subsampling step that occurs before opacity filtering. It randomly selects a subset of stratified samples to fit within a budget N{max}. It exploits the fact that Adam tracks gradient histories, allowing dense ray sampling to be deferred over multiple iterations. Skipping points randomly induces gradient noise, but SGD is robust against it. Crucially, it prevents false occluders from consistently occluding true surface points, which would cause missing gradients. This step precedes the opacity-based filtering described in the main method. Time Complexity: Dominated by SVO opacity queries (4D interpolation) and the sorting/selection step for importance sampling. The reduction from N{max} to N{max,r} significantly reduces subsequent radiance retrieval costs. Memory Complexity: Requires storing weights for all intermediate samples before selection. The use of a capped budget N{max} prevents unbounded memory growth on GPU. Performance: Reduces the number of samples used for gradient computation from 256 to 32 per ray in typical configurations, lowering optimization cost. Strengths: Efficiently focuses computational resources on surface-proximate regions. Handles false free space via the constant c. Limitations: Introduces gradient noise. Not suitable for final rendering where full sampling may be preferred for quality, though the source notes it is optional in that phase. The method originates from the Explicit Radiance Field (ERF) reconstruction framework. It was introduced to manage the high computational cost of gradient-based optimization in neural radiance fields by using explicit voxel structures (SVO) and stochastic sampling strategies. The approach leverages the properties of the Adam optimizer to tolerate noisy gradients from subsampled rays. ERF: Explicit Radiance Field Reconstruction From Scratch, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00051v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Near-Far Linear Ray Generation
head: NeRF Near-Far Linear Ray Generation, Near-Far Disparity Linear Ray Generation
body: Near-Far Linear Ray Generation generates a list of 3D sampling points along a camera ray segment defined by near (t{min}) and far (t{max}) distances for a specified number of samples. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing the foundational uniform or disparity-based spacing logic upon which stratified, probabilistic, or depth-guided variants build. Unlike Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which adapts density to learned probabilities, or Depth-Guided Supersampling which uses external depth priors, this method relies on fixed geometric intervals. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (N{rays}, 3). raysd: Ray directions, shape (N{rays}, 3). near: Near plane distances, shape (N{rays}, 1). far: Far plane distances, shape (N{rays}, 1). Nsamples: Integer, number of depth samples per ray. lindisp: Boolean. If True, samples in disparity space (1/z); if False, samples in linear depth space. perturb: Float. Amount of random jitter to add to samples (0.0 for no jitter). bbox3D: Optional 3D Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) for clipping. Outputs: xyzcoarsesampled: 3D coordinates of sampled points, shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 3). Data Structures: Tensors for ray parameters and sampled depths are used, typically standard floating-point formats. Steps: 1. Decompose Ray Parameters: Extract origins, directions, near, and far values from the input tensor. \text{rays}o, \text{rays}d = \text{rays}[:, 0:3], \text{rays}[:, 3:6] \text{near}, \text{far} = \text{rays}[:, 6:7], \text{rays}[:, 7:8] 2. Generate Normalized Depth Steps: Create a linearly spaced vector from 0 to 1 with N{samples} steps. z{steps} = \text{linspace}(0, 1, N{samples}) 3. Compute Depth Values (z{vals}): If lindisp is False (linear depth): z{vals} = \text{near} \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + \text{far} \cdot z{steps} If lindisp is True (linear disparity): z{vals} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\text{near}} \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + \frac{1}{\text{far}} \cdot z{steps}} 4. Expand Dimensions: Expand z{vals} to match the batch dimension of rays. z{vals} = \text{expand}(z{vals}, (N{rays}, N{samples})) 5. Apply Bounding Box Clipping (Optional): If bbox3D is provided, compute intersection intervals using the slab method (DDA) and clamp z{vals} to valid ranges. Compute inverse direction: \text{inv\rays\d} = 1.0 / (\text{rays}d + \epsilon). Calculate t{min}, t{max} for the AABB and clamp to [\text{near}, \text{far}]. Note: If clipping alters the valid range, z{vals} must be re-sampled or interpolated within the new bounds. The sources describe clipping as a constraint step but do not provide the explicit re-sampling formula for clipped rays in the main linear generation block. 6. Perturb Samples (Optional): If perturb > 0, add uniform random noise to break sampling symmetry. Compute interval midpoints: z{vals\mid} = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:,:-1] + z{vals}[:, 1:]) Define interval bounds: \text{upper} = \text{concat}([z{vals\mid}, z{vals}[:, -1:]], \text{dim}=-1) \text{lower} = \text{concat}([z{vals}[:,:1], z{vals\mid}], \text{dim}=-1) Generate random noise: \text{perturb\rand} = \text{perturb} \cdot \text{rand}(z{vals}.shape) Apply jitter: z{vals} = \text{lower} + (\text{upper} - \text{lower}) \cdot \text{perturb\rand} 7. Compute 3D Coordinates: Combine ray origin, direction, and sampled depths. \text{xyz\coarse\sampled} = \text{rays}o.\text{unsqueeze}(1) + \text{rays}d.\text{unsqueeze}(1) \cdot z{vals}.\text{unsqueeze}(2) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def nearfarlinearraygeneration(rays, Nsamples, lindisp=False, perturb=1.0, bbox3d=None): """ Generate 3D sampling points along camera rays. Args: rays: Tensor of shape (Nrays, 8). Columns 0-2: origin (x,y,z), Columns 3-5: direction (x,y,z), Column 6: near distance, Column 7: far distance. Nsamples: int, number of samples per ray. lindisp: bool, if True sample in disparity space. perturb: float, amount of jitter (0.0 to disable). bbox3d: tuple (minxyz, maxxyz) or None. Returns: xyzcoarsesampled: Tensor of shape (Nrays, Nsamples, 3). """ # 1. Decompose ray parameters rayso = rays[:, 0:3] # (Nrays, 3) raysd = rays[:, 3:6] # (Nrays, 3) near = rays[:, 6:7] # (Nrays, 1) far = rays[:, 7:8] # (Nrays, 1) # 2. Generate normalized depth steps zsteps = torch.linspace(0, 1, Nsamples, device=rays.device) # (Nsamples,) # 3. Compute depth values if not lindisp: # Linear depth zvals = near (1 - zsteps) + far zsteps else: # Linear disparity zvals = 1.0 / (1.0 / near (1 - zsteps) + 1.0 / far zsteps) # 4. Apply Bounding Box Clipping (Optional) # The sources describe AABB clipping via DDA but do not provide the full re-sampling logic for clipped rays in this specific function. if bbox3d is not None: invraysd = 1.0 / (raysd + 1e-6) # Standard slab method to compute tmin/tmax for AABB intersection would go here # zvals would then be clamped to the valid range [tmin, tmax] # 5. Perturb samples if perturb > 0: # Compute midpoints zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[:,:-1] + zvals[:, 1:]) # (Nrays, Nsamples - 1) # Compute upper and lower bounds upper = torch.cat([zvalsmid, zvals[:, -1:]], dim=-1) # (Nrays, Nsamples) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], zvalsmid], dim=-1) # (Nrays, Nsamples) # Generate random noise perturbrand = perturb torch.rand(zvals.shape, device=rays.device) # Apply jitter zvals = lower + (upper - lower) perturbrand # 6. Compute 3D coordinates xyzcoarsesampled = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) return xyzcoarsesampled Parameters: Nsamples: Default 64. lindisp: Default False (linear depth). perturb: Default 1.0 (full jitter). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: When computing disparity (1/z), if near is 0, division by zero occurs. Add a small epsilon (\epsilon) to denominators. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when near and far differ significantly in magnitude, especially in disparity space. Boundary Conditions: If bbox3D is used, rays that do not intersect the box must be handled (e.g., by discarding or clamping to the box boundaries). Constrains ray sampling intervals to a specified viewing volume defined by fixed global near and far distances. Ensures samples are only generated within valid bounds, preventing rays from sampling empty space beyond the far plane or artifacts near the camera origin. Applies rigid, uniform bounds to all rays. Choose when rigid viewing volume constraints are required. Samples points along rays using inverse CDF sampling based on probability distributions associated with depth intervals. Maps uniform random noise to depth intervals using the cumulative distribution function derived from per-hit probabilities. Replaces uniform spacing with probability-weighted stratification. Choose when adaptive density based on learned scene probabilities is needed. Generates sample points along camera rays by sampling z-values (depths) either linearly or in disparity space, with optional stratification to reduce variance. Extends the base method by supporting disparity-based spacing and depth-guided supersampling. Choose when variance reduction via stratification is desired. Generates sample positions along a ray by perturbing a depth estimate with Gaussian noise, encouraging the renderer to sample around the estimated surface location. Relies on an external depth prior rather than a learned density distribution. Choose when external depth priors are available. Computes the near and far clipping planes for ray sampling based on the dataset type and Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) configuration. Ensures that the ray sampler operates within a geometrically valid range appropriate for the scene's scale and projection model. Choose when dataset-specific parameterization is required. Samples a fixed number of points along each ray globally, then filters out samples that fall outside of occupied Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) cells. Prioritizes a uniform global sampling density, using the SPC structure solely as a validity mask. Choose when uniform global density is prioritized over cell-specific sampling. Generates ray samples along a near-far segment by dividing the depth range into equal intervals and drawing one uniform random sample from each interval, ensuring low-discrepancy coverage. Guarantees that every sub-interval contributes exactly one sample, reducing variance. Choose when low-discrepancy coverage is required. Generates ray samples using disparity spacing with random jitter within segments, similar to NeRF's sampling but with explicit segment length calculation. It creates linear t{vals} from 0 to 1 with pointcount steps, converts them to disparity space using t{vals} = 1. / (1. / \text{near} \cdot (1 - t{vals}) + 1. / \text{far} \cdot t{vals}), and applies jitter if jitter > 0 by computing midpoints, upper/lower bounds, and random t{rand} to jitter t{vals}. Segment lengths are computed by differencing t{vals}, appending a large value (1e10), and multiplying by ray direction norm. Ray positions are computed directly from t{vals} or middle-point ts as \text{raypos} = \text{campos} + \text{raydir} \cdot t{vals}. A method to generate seed points along a line segment between mstartPt and mendPt. It calculates delta as (\text{m\endPt} - \text{m\startPt}) / \text{count} and loops i from 0 to count - 1, setting \text{m\h\seeds}[i] = \text{m\startPt} + i \cdot \text{delta}. The parameter count specifies the number of seed points to generate. Generates samples in NDC space by initializing sample count N{samples}, retrieving near/far clipping planes, and generating linearly spaced depth values interpx between near and far. If training, uniform random noise is added to interpx scaled by step size (\text{far}-\text{near})/N{samples}. Linear depth is converted to NDC depth using \text{ndc\depth} = 2 \cdot \text{ndc\near\plane} / (1 - \text{ndc\near\plane} - \text{interpx}). The depth is then rescaled to simulated Euclidean depth using util.gradrescale(interpx, ndcdepth). Ray points are computed using either simulated or linear depth, and a mask is generated to check if points are outside the AABB defined by self.aabb[0] and self.aabb[1]. The parameter ndcnearplane is typically 1.0. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) for generating depth values and 3D coordinates. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) to store the sampled points. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides uniform coverage of the ray segment; disparity sampling is beneficial for scenes with large depth variations. Limitations: Uniform sampling may waste samples in empty space; disparity sampling can introduce precision issues near the camera. When to use: When a simple, uniform sampling strategy is sufficient. When not to use: When the scene has complex geometry requiring adaptive sampling; when computational resources are limited and stratified or importance sampling is preferred. Near-Far Linear Ray Generation is a fundamental technique in volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRF) for discretizing camera rays into sample points. It was popularized by the NeRF paper and is widely used in various implementations such as TensoRF and PointNeRF. The method allows for efficient evaluation of neural networks along rays to render images or extract 3D structures.
