name: Near-Far Clipping
head: Fixed Near/Far Plane Collider, NearFar Collider
body: Near-Far Clipping is a post-processing step in ray generation that constrains ray sampling intervals to a specified viewing volume defined by fixed global near and far distances. It ensures that samples are only generated within valid bounds, preventing rays from sampling empty space beyond the far plane or artifacts near the camera origin. Unlike Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which adapts sampling density to scene content, or Near-Far Linear/Disparity Ray Generation with Stratification which handles stratified intervals, this method applies rigid, uniform bounds to all rays. Inputs: raybundle: A data structure containing ray origins, directions, and currently assigned near/far distances. self.nearplane: The minimum distance from the camera origin for valid samples. self.farplane: The maximum distance from the camera origin for valid samples. self.resetnearplane: A boolean flag (default True). Outputs: Updated raybundle with nears and fars tensors overwritten. Data Structures: raybundle.nears: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 1) or matching raybundle.origins[..., 0:1], storing the start distance of each ray. raybundle.fars: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 1) or matching raybundle.origins[..., 0:1], storing the end distance of each ray. Steps: 1. Create a tensor ones of ones with shape matching raybundle.origins[..., 0:1]. 2. Determine the effective nearplane value: if self.training is True OR self.resetnearplane is False, use self.nearplane; otherwise use 0.0. 3. Set raybundle.nears to ones nearplane. 4. Set raybundle.fars to ones self.farplane. 5. Return the updated raybundle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applynearfarclipping(raybundle, nearplane, farplane, resetnearplane, training): """ Clips ray samples to specified near and far planes. Args: raybundle: Object containing ray origins and near/far tensors. nearplane: Float, the configured near distance. farplane: Float, the configured far distance. resetnearplane: Bool, whether to reset near to 0 during inference. training: Bool, whether currently in training mode. Returns: Updated raybundle. """ # 1. Create ones array matching the shape of ray origins' first dimension # raybundle.origins is assumed to be a list/array of shape (N, 3) numrays = len(raybundle.origins) ones = [1.0] numrays # 2. Determine effective near plane if training or not resetnearplane: effectivenear = nearplane else: effectivenear = 0.0 # 3. Set near distances raybundle.nears = [o effectivenear for o in ones] # 4. Set far distances raybundle.fars = [o farplane for o in ones] # 5. Return updated bundle return raybundle Parameters: nearplane: Minimum distance from camera origin. Typical values vary by scene; e.g., 2.00 for kitchen, 5.00 for playroom. farplane: Maximum distance from camera origin. Not given in the sources. resetnearplane: Boolean flag (default True). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clipping Artifacts: Using a non-zero nearplane during inference can cause clipping artifacts if the evaluation or viewer camera moves closer to the object than the nearplane distance. This is mitigated by resetnearplane=True. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. A technique to reduce the visual impact of floaters (noisy Gaussians near the camera) by using near clipping planes. For ray tracers, tracing starts further along the initial ray; for splatting, Gaussians with centroids closer than d{\text{near}} are culled. Choose this when dense initialization produces visible floaters near the camera. It is a variant of near clipping focused on artifact suppression rather than volume definition. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of rays, due to tensor operations. Memory: O(N) to store the updated near/far tensors. Measured Performance: Metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) are measured without clipping planes to ensure fair comparison, as clipping planes offer negligible improvements to quality metrics. PSNR improvement for TreeHill at d{\text{near}}=1.0 is negligible (26.91 → 26.93). PSNR improvement for Garden at d{\text{near}}=2.0 is negligible (21.89 → 21.94). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively culls irrelevant geometry near the camera. Limitations: Does not improve standard quality metrics; requires careful tuning of d{\text{near}} per scene. When to Use: Use during inference or rendering to hide floaters in dense Gaussian splatting or ray tracing. Do not use for metric evaluation to maintain fairness. Originating from techniques to handle floaters in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), near clipping planes were adopted to mitigate visual artifacts caused by dense initialization. The method is implemented in toolkits like Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit and referenced in ray tracing optimizations like GRay. barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, https://github.com/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804496, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Inverse CDF Ray Sampling
body: Inverse CDF Ray Sampling is a CUDA kernel that samples points along rays using inverse CDF sampling based on probability distributions (probs) associated with depth intervals (hits), supporting optional fixed step size. It maps uniform random noise to depth intervals using the cumulative distribution function derived from per-hit probabilities. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by replacing uniform spacing with probability-weighted stratification. Inputs: probs: Probability distribution for each hit along the ray. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. steps: Target number of samples per ray. Shape: [batchsize, numrays]. mindepth: Minimum depth of the current hit interval. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the current hit interval. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. ptsidx: Index of the primitive/vertex associated with each hit. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. fixedstepsize: Optional scalar. If > 0, overrides dynamic step calculation for uniform spacing within bins. If -1, uses dynamic calculation. Outputs: sampledidx: Primitive indices for each sample. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxsamplesperray]. sampleddists: Distance from the start of the current bin to the sample. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxsamplesperray]. sampleddepth: Absolute depth of the sample. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxsamplesperray]. The method processes data in chunks to manage memory. Chunk Size (G): 200. Batch Chunk Size: 4 \times G = 800 rays processed per CUDA kernel launch to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. Padding: Inputs are padded to multiples of G. Let H be the padded ray count. Reshaping: Data is viewed as (G, -1, P) for 3D tensors and (G, -1) for 2D tensors, where P is the point dimension (e.g., 3 for depth/idx). 1. Set batch chunk size G = 200. 2. Determine ray count N and point dimension P. 3. Pad inputs to size H (multiple of G). 4. Reshape inputs to (G, -1, P) for data and (G, -1) for steps. 5. Calculate maxsteps = steps.ceil().long().max() + P. 6. Generate noise tensor of shape [H, maxsteps]. 7. If deterministic, set noise to 0.5; else, sample uniform u \in [0, 1) and clamp to [0.001, 0.999]. 8. Process in chunks of 4 \times G to avoid OOM. 9. Call CUDA extension ext.inversecdfsampling with ptsidx, mindepth, maxdepth, noise, probs, steps, and fixedstepsize. 10. Concatenate results from chunks. 11. Reshape outputs to (H, -1). 12. Truncate to N rays if padded. 13. Trim outputs to maxlen (max valid samples per ray). 14. Mark outputs as non-differentiable. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def pad1d(arr, padright): return arr + [0] padright def pad2d(arr, padright): return [row + [0] padright for row in arr] def inversecdfsampling(probs, steps, mindepth, maxdepth, ptsidx, fixedstepsize=-1, deterministic=False): batchsize, numrays, maxhits = len(probs), len(probs[0]), len(probs[0][0]) G = 200 H = ((numrays + G - 1) // G) G P = 3 probspad = pad2d(probs, H - numrays) stepspad = pad1d(steps, H - numrays) mindepthpad = pad2d(mindepth, H - numrays) maxdepthpad = pad2d(maxdepth, H - numrays) ptsidxpad = pad2d(ptsidx, H - numrays) maxstepsval = math.ceil(max(stepspad)) + P noise = [[0.5 if deterministic else max(0.001, min(0.999, u)) for u in [0.0] maxstepsval] for in range(H)] if not deterministic: for i in range(H): for j in range(maxstepsval): noise[i][j] = max(0.001, min(0.999, random.random())) results = [] chunksize = 4 G for start in range(0, H, chunksize): end = min(start + chunksize, H) chunklen = end - start chunksamples = cudainversecdfkernel( probspad[start:end], stepspad[start:end], mindepthpad[start:end], maxdepthpad[start:end], ptsidxpad[start:end], noise[start:end], fixedstepsize, maxstepsval, start) results.append(chunksamples) allsamples = [item for sublist in results for item in sublist] allsamples = allsamples[:numrays] finalsamples = [ray[:max(steps[i])] for i, ray in enumerate(allsamples)] return finalsamples def cudainversecdfkernel(probs, steps, mindepth, maxdepth, ptsidx, noise, fixedstepsize, maxsteps, Koffset): batchsize, numrays, maxhits = len(probs), len(probs[0]), len(probs[0][0]) outputidx = [] outputdist = [] outputdepth = [] for k in range(numrays): s = 0 zlow = mindepth[k][0] currbin = 0 currmincdf = 0.0 currmaxcdf = probs[k][0] currmindepth = mindepth[k][0] currmaxdepth = maxdepth[k][0] done = False stepsize = fixedstepsize if fixedstepsize > 0 else 1.0 / steps[k] for currstep in range(int(steps[k])): if done: break currcdf = (float(currstep) + noise[k][currstep]) stepsize while currcdf > currmaxcdf: outputidx.append(ptsidx[k][currbin]) outputdist.append(currmaxdepth - zlow) outputdepth.append((currmaxdepth + zlow) 0.5) currbin += 1 s += 1 if currbin >= maxhits or ptsidx[k][currbin] == -1: done = True break currmindepth = mindepth[k][currbin] currmaxdepth = maxdepth[k][currbin] currmincdf = currmaxcdf currmaxcdf += probs[k][currbin] zlow = currmindepth if done: break u = (currcdf - currmincdf) / (currmaxcdf - currmincdf) z = currmindepth + u (currmaxdepth - currmindepth) outputidx.append(ptsidx[k][currbin]) outputdist.append(z - zlow) outputdepth.append((z + zlow) 0.5) zlow = z s += 1 while zlow < currmaxdepth and not done: outputidx.append(ptsidx[k][currbin]) outputdist.append(currmaxdepth - zlow) outputdepth.append((currmaxdepth + zlow) 0.5) currbin += 1 s += 1 if currbin >= maxhits or ptsidx[k][currbin] == -1: break currmindepth = mindepth[k][currbin] currmaxdepth = maxdepth[k][currbin] zlow = currmindepth outputidx.append([idx + Koffset for idx in outputidx[-s:]]) outputdist.append(outputdist[-s:]) outputdepth.append(outputdepth[-s:]) return outputidx, outputdist, outputdepth fixedstepsize: If > 0, overrides dynamic step calculation. If -1, uses dynamic calculation. probs: Shape [b, numrays, maxhits]. steps: Shape [b, numrays]. Noise Clamping: Noise must be clamped to [0.001, 0.999] to prevent division by zero or invalid CDF lookups at the exact boundaries. Padding: Inputs must be padded to multiples of G=200 to align with the kernel's block structure. Invalid Hits: Check for ptsidx == -1 to handle rays with fewer hits than maxhits. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray. The bin-skipping loop adds overhead proportional to the number of hits, but typically S \ll \text{max\hits}. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for outputs. Intermediate padding adds O(G \cdot S) overhead. Performance: Chunking by 4 \times G (800 rays) balances GPU occupancy and memory usage. The method is efficient on CUDA hardware due to parallel ray processing. Strengths: Provides stratified sampling with arbitrary probability distributions, reducing variance compared to uniform sampling. Limitations: Requires pre-computed probabilities and hit intervals. Less flexible than pure random sampling for highly dynamic scenes where probabilities change rapidly. Inverse CDF sampling is a standard technique in Monte Carlo integration, applied to volume rendering to sample along rays according to the estimated density or opacity distribution. In the context of Neural Volume Rendering (NSVF), it is used to efficiently sample points within the reconstructed volume based on the learned probability distribution of surface intersections. facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YihangChen-ee/CNC, https://github.com/YihangChen-ee/CNC, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Near-Far Linear/Disparity Ray Generation with Stratification
head: Coarse Stratified Sampling, Near-Far Linear Ray Generation with Stratification, Stratified Sampling Along Rays, linear/disparity sampling
body: Generates sample points along camera rays for volume rendering by sampling z-values (depths) either linearly or in disparity space, with optional stratification to reduce variance. It extends Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by supporting disparity-based spacing and depth-guided supersampling, distinguishing it from Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which uses probabilistic distributions rather than fixed geometric spacing. Inputs: origins: Ray origins, shape [batchsize, 3]. directions: Ray directions, shape [batchsize, 3]. near: Float, near clip plane distance. far: Float, far clip plane distance. numcoarsesamples: Integer, number of base samples to generate along each ray. uselineardisparity: Boolean, if True, samples linearly in disparity (1/z) rather than depth (z). usestratifiedsampling: Boolean, if True, adds uniform random noise to sample positions within intervals to reduce variance. randomized: Boolean flag to use randomized stratified sampling. sigmadepth: Optional float, if not None, triggers depth-guided supersampling. rays: Object containing origins, directions, radii, and rayshape for supersampling context. Outputs: tsamples: Sorted sample positions along the ray parameter t \in [0, 1], shape [batchsize, numtsamples]. means, covs: Radiance and covariance outputs from ray casting. Data Structures: tvals: 1D tensor of base sample positions in [0, 1]. zvals: 1D tensor of depth values corresponding to tvals. sstsamples: Tensor of additional samples from depth-guided supersampling. Steps: 1. Compute Base Linear Samples: Generate numcoarsesamples + 1 evenly spaced values in [0, 1]: t{base} = \text{linspace}(0.0, 1.0, \text{num\coarse\samples} + 1). 2. Convert to Depth (z{val}): For each t \in t{base}, compute depth using linear or disparity spacing: If uselineardisparity is False: z{val} = near \cdot (1 - t) + far \cdot t. If uselineardisparity is True: z{val} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near}(1 - t) + \frac{1}{far}t}. 3. Apply Stratification (if usestratifiedsampling is True): Compute midpoints mids = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[1:] + z{vals}[:-1]), upper bounds upper = [mids, z{vals}[-1]], and lower bounds lower = [z{vals}[0], mids]. Generate random uniform noise t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] with shape matching zvals, then update z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot t{rand}. 4. Compute 3D Points: Calculate points using the stratified depth values: points = origins + z{vals} \cdot directions. 5. Determine Sample Counts: If sigmadepth is not None, set numtsamples = numcoarsesamples // 4 3 + 1 and numsssamples = numcoarsesamples // 4; otherwise set numtsamples = numcoarsesamples + 1 and numsssamples = 0. 6. Generate Base t Samples: Create t{samples} = \text{linspace}(0., 1., \text{num\t\samples}) on the same device as origins. 7. Convert t Samples to Depth: If uselineardisparity is True, transform to disparity: t{samples} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near}(1 - t{samples}) + \frac{1}{far}t{samples}}; otherwise transform to depth: t{samples} = near + (far - near) \cdot t{samples}. 8. Apply Randomized Stratification (if randomized is True): Compute midpoints mids = 0.5 \cdot (t{samples}[:, 1:] + t{samples}[:,:-1]), upper bounds upper = \text{concat}([mids, t{samples}[:, -1:]]), and lower bounds lower = \text{concat}([t{samples}[:,:1], mids]). Generate random uniform noise t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] with shape matching tsamples, then update t{samples} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot t{rand}. 9. Depth-Guided Supersampling (if sigmadepth is not None): Call depthguidedsupersampling(rays=rays, nsamples=numsssamples, startsigma=sigmadepth) to get sstsamples, then concatenate and sort: t{samples} = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([t{samples}, ss{tsamples}]), \text{axis}=-1). 10. Cast Rays: Call castrays(tsamples, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, a, f, l) to get means and covariances. 11. Return Results: Output tsamples, (means, covs). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def nearfarlineardisparityraygenerationwithstratification( origins, directions, near, far, numcoarsesamples, uselineardisparity=False, usestratifiedsampling=False, randomized=False, sigmadepth=None, rays=None): """ Generates stratified ray samples with linear or disparity spacing. Args: origins: Tensor [B, 3] directions: Tensor [B, 3] near: float far: float numcoarsesamples: int uselineardisparity: bool usestratifiedsampling: bool randomized: bool sigmadepth: float or None rays: Object with origins, directions, radii, rayshape Returns: tsamples: Tensor [B, N] means: Tensor from castrays covs: Tensor from castrays """ device = origins.device # Step 1: Base linear samples in t-space [0, 1] tbase = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numcoarsesamples + 1, device=device) # Step 2: Convert to depth zvals if uselineardisparity: invnear = 1.0 / near invfar = 1.0 / far denom = invnear (1.0 - tbase) + invfar tbase zvals = 1.0 / denom else: zvals = near (1.0 - tbase) + far tbase # Step 3: Stratification on zvals if usestratifiedsampling: mids = 0.5 (zvals[1:] + zvals[:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[-1:]], dim=0) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:1], mids], dim=0) trand = torch.randlike(zvals) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Step 4: Compute 3D points # zvals shape [N], origins [B, 3], directions [B, 3] # Broadcasting yields [B, N, 3] points = origins[:, None,:] + zvals[None,:, None] directions[:, None,:] # Step 5: Determine sample counts if sigmadepth is not None: numtsamples = numcoarsesamples // 4 3 + 1 numsssamples = numcoarsesamples // 4 else: numtsamples = numcoarsesamples + 1 numsssamples = 0 # Step 6: Generate base tsamples tsamples = torch.linspace(0., 1., numtsamples, device=device) # Step 7: Convert tsamples to depth/disparity if uselineardisparity: invnear = 1.0 / near invfar = 1.0 / far denom = invnear (1.0 - tsamples) + invfar tsamples tsamples = 1.0 / denom else: tsamples = near + (far - near) tsamples # Step 8: Randomized stratification on tsamples if randomized: mids = 0.5 (tsamples[..., 1:] + tsamples[...,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, tsamples[..., -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([tsamples[...,:1], mids], dim=-1) trand = torch.randlike(tsamples) tsamples = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Step 9: Depth-guided supersampling if sigmadepth is not None and rays is not None: # Sources do not provide implementation for depthguidedsupersampling. # Standard implementation uses sigma field to allocate additional samples. sstsamples = depthguidedsupersampling(rays, numsssamples, sigmadepth) tsamples = torch.sort(torch.cat([tsamples, sstsamples], dim=-1), dim=-1).values # Step 10: Cast rays # Sources do not provide implementation for castrays. # Standard implementation evaluates volume rendering integral at sample positions. means, covs = castrays(tsamples, origins, directions, rays.radii, rays.rayshape, 0.02, 0.1, 0.6) # Step 11: Return results return tsamples, means, covs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If near or far is 0, disparity calculation (1/z) will fail. Ensure near > 0. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when near and far differ significantly, especially in disparity space. Use double precision if necessary. Degenerate Input: If numcoarsesamples is 0, no samples are generated. Handle this case explicitly. Unimplemented Functions: depthguidedsupersampling and castrays are called but not defined in the sources. Implementers must provide these functions. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. Supersampling adds O(N{ss}) where N{ss} is the number of additional samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing sample positions and points. Performance: Stratification reduces variance compared to uniform sampling, potentially requiring fewer samples for similar quality. Strengths: Simple to implement, supports both depth and disparity sampling, reduces variance with stratification. Limitations: Requires external implementations for depthguidedsupersampling and castrays to complete the pipeline. Disparity sampling may be less intuitive for scenes with large depth ranges. name: Depth-Guided Supersampling
body: Depth-Guided Supersampling generates sample positions along a ray by perturbing a depth estimate with Gaussian noise. Inputs: rays: Tensor containing ray origins, directions, and near/far bounds. depth: Tensor of estimated depth values for each ray, shape [batchsize] or [batchsize, 1]. nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. startsigma: Float, initial standard deviation for noise (default 0.1). Outputs: zvals: Tensor of sample depths along the ray, shape [batchsize, nsamples]. Data Structures: zvals: Float tensor. mean: Tensor of shape [batchsize, nsamples], initialized with the depth estimate. sigma: Tensor of shape [1, nsamples], initialized to startsigma. noise: Tensor of shape [batchsize, nsamples], drawn from \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Steps: 1. Extract near, far, and depth from the ray data. 2. Set mean to depth (cloned and detached). 3. Set sigma to a tensor of ones multiplied by startsigma, shape [1, nsamples]. 4. Generate noise from \mathcal{N}(0, 1) with shape [batchsize, nsamples]. 5. Compute zvals0level as noise sigma + mean. 6. For rays with depth == 0, replace zvals0level with random points uniformly distributed between near and far. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthguidedsupersampling(rays, depth, nsamples, startsigma=0.1): """ Generate sample positions along a ray guided by a depth estimate. Args: rays: Tensor or object containing.near and.far attributes of shape [B]. depth: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, 1] with depth estimates. nsamples: int, number of samples per ray. startsigma: float, standard deviation of noise. Returns: zvals: Tensor of shape [B, nsamples] with sample depths. """ near = rays.near far = rays.far if depth.dim() == 2: depth = depth.squeeze(1) mean = depth.clone().detach().unsqueeze(1) sigma = torch.ones(1, nsamples, device=depth.device) startsigma noise = torch.randn(mean.shape[0], nsamples, device=depth.device) zvals = noise sigma + mean zerodepthmask = (depth == 0) if zerodepthmask.any(): uniformnoise = torch.rand(mean.shape[0], nsamples, device=depth.device) nearexpanded = near.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, nsamples) farexpanded = far.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, nsamples) uniformzvals = nearexpanded + uniformnoise (farexpanded - nearexpanded) zvals[zerodepthmask] = uniformzvals[zerodepthmask] return zvals Parameters: startsigma: Float, default 0.1. Controls the spread of noise around the depth estimate. Edge Cases: If depth == 0, the method falls back to uniform sampling between near and far. Samples K{fd} positions around a specified depth value with Gaussian noise, clamped to ray bounds. It repeats the input depth tensor of shape (B,) along dimension 1 to shape (B, K{fd}), adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation depthstd, and clamps the resulting values between near and far bounds from the rays. name: Dataset-Specific Near/Far Bound Calculation
head: Dataset-dependent Near/Far Clipping, Near/Far Bound Calculation per Dataset, Scene Normalization, Scene contraction strategy
body: Computes the near and far clipping planes for ray sampling based on the dataset type and Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) configuration. It ensures that the ray sampler operates within a geometrically valid range appropriate for the scene's scale and projection model, serving as the parameterization layer for Near-Far Linear Ray Generation. Inputs: datasettype: String identifier for the dataset ('llff', 'blender', 'deepvoxels'). nondc: Boolean flag. If True, disables NDC projection (used for non-forward-facing scenes). bds: Array of bounding box min/max values derived from camera poses. poses: Array of camera transformation matrices. Outputs: near: Float, the near clipping plane distance. far: Float, the far clipping plane distance. Data Structures: bds: Shape [3] or [numcameras, 3] containing min/max extents. In LLFF loading, bds is rescaled by bdfactor (default 0.75) if provided. poses: Shape [numcameras, 4, 4] or [numcameras, 3, 4] representing camera extrinsics. Steps: 1. LLFF Dataset (datasettype == 'llff'): If nondc is True: Calculate near = min(bds) 0.9. Calculate far = max(bds) 1.0. Note: The scaling factors 0.9 and 1.0 are explicit bounding box adjustments required when NDC is disabled to prevent clipping artifacts. If nondc is False (NDC enabled): Set near = 0.0. Set far = 1.0. Note: NDC scenes map the scene to a fixed unit cube, making bounds independent of physical scale. 2. Blender Dataset (datasettype == 'blender'): Set near = 2.0. Set far = 6.0. Note: These are hardcoded empirical values for the standard Blender synthetic dataset scale. 3. DeepVoxels Dataset (datasettype == 'deepvoxels'): Compute the mean radius of the camera trajectory: \text{hemi\R} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \| \text{poses}i[:, 3] \|2 where \text{poses}i[:, 3] is the translation vector (4th column) of the i-th camera pose. Calculate near = hemiR - 1.0. Calculate far = hemiR + 1.0. 4. Scene Normalization (Unbounded Scenes): For unbounded scenes (e.g., street scenes in LidaRF), calculate the maximum distance D{max} between any two camera positions in the training log. Determine sphere diameter D{sphere} = D{max} + 50 meters. This diameter defines the contraction sphere used to map unbounded space into a bounded domain for the neural field. Pitfalls: LLFF NDC vs. Non-NDC: Using fixed [0, 1] bounds for LLFF when nondc=True causes incorrect sampling ranges because the physical scale is not normalized. Conversely, using physical bounds with nondc=False breaks the NDC assumption. Pose Extraction: Ensure poses[:,:3, -1] correctly extracts the translation component from the transformation matrix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenearfar(datasettype, nondc, bds, poses): """ Compute near and far clipping planes based on dataset type. Args: datasettype (str): 'llff', 'blender', or 'deepvoxels'. nondc (bool): If True, disable NDC projection. bds (np.ndarray): Bounding box min/max values. Shape (3,) or (N, 3). poses (np.ndarray): Camera poses. Shape (N, 4, 4) or (N, 3, 4). Returns: float: near float: far """ if datasettype == 'llff': if nondc: # Explicit bounding box scaling for non-NDC LLFF # bds is assumed to be pre-scaled by bdfactor if provided in loadllffdata near = np.min(bds) 0.9 far = np.max(bds) 1.0 else: # NDC space is fixed to [0, 1] near = 0.0 far = 1.0 elif datasettype == 'blender': # Hardcoded values for Blender synthetic dataset near = 2.0 far = 6.0 elif datasettype == 'deepvoxels': # Extract translation vectors (last column) # Assuming poses are (N, 4, 4) or (N, 3, 4) translations = poses[:,:3, -1] # Compute mean norm of camera positions hemiR = np.mean(np.linalg.norm(translations, axis=-1)) near = hemiR - 1.0 far = hemiR + 1.0 else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported datasettype: {datasettype}") return near, far Time Complexity: O(1) for Blender and LLFF (with precomputed bds). O(N) for DeepVoxels where N is the number of camera poses, due to the norm calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Adapts sampling bounds to the specific geometric properties of common NeRF datasets, preventing sampling in empty space or clipping valid geometry. Limitations: Hardcoded for specific dataset types. Does not generalize to arbitrary unstructured point clouds without scene normalization (contraction). This method originates from the implementation details of early NeRF variants and their derivatives. The LLFF and Blender bounds are standard conventions established in the original NeRF paper and subsequent repositories like. The DeepVoxels approach adapts to spherical camera trajectories. The scene normalization strategy (sphere diameter + 50m) is introduced in LidaRF to handle unbounded street scenes using scene contraction. name: Uniform Ray Marching with Occupancy Filtering
head: SPC Ray Raymarching
body: Uniform Ray Marching with Occupancy Filtering is a raymarching strategy that samples a fixed number of points along each ray globally, then filters out samples that fall outside of occupied Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) cells. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by applying a global uniform grid and discarding empty-space samples via occupancy queries. Inputs: origins: Tensor of ray origins, shape (N, 3). directions: Tensor of normalized ray directions, shape (N, 3). distmin: Scalar or tensor of near-plane distances for each ray. distmax: Scalar or tensor of far-plane distances for each ray. numsamples: Integer, the number of base samples to generate per ray. spc: The Sparse Point Cloud acceleration structure supporting point index queries. Outputs: samples: Filtered 3D coordinates, shape (M, 3), where M \le N \times \text{num\samples}. depths: Filtered depths along rays, shape (M,). deltas: Filtered step sizes between consecutive samples, shape (M,). rayindices: Indices mapping each sample back to its originating ray, shape (M,). packboundaries: Boolean mask marking the start of each ray's sample pack in the flattened output. Data Structures: The SPC structure maps 3D coordinates to integer point indices (pidx). mask: Boolean tensor of length N \times \text{num\samples}, true where pidx > -1. Steps: 1. Generate Base Depths: Create linearly spaced depths in [0, 1] and add jitter. d{\text{base}} = \text{linspace}(0, 1.0, \text{num\samples}) d{\text{jitter}} = \text{rand}(0, 1, \text{num\samples}) / \text{num\samples} d{\text{norm}} = d{\text{base}} + d{\text{jitter}} The jitter ensures stratification within each uniform interval. 2. Normalize to Ray Range: Map normalized depths to the ray's [dist\min, dist\max] range. d{\text{final}} = d{\text{norm}} \times (dist\max - dist\min) + dist\min Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 3. Compute Sample Coordinates: Calculate 3D positions using origins, directions, and depths. \text{samples} = \text{origins} + d{\text{final}} \times \text{directions} Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}, 3). 4. Query Occupancy: Query the SPC structure for all sample coordinates to get point indices. \text{pidx} = \text{SPC.query}(\text{samples}) Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 5. Create Occupancy Mask: Identify samples inside occupied cells. \text{mask} = (\text{pidx} > -1) Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 6. Compute Depth Deltas: Calculate distances between consecutive samples and prepend the near plane. \Delta d = \text{diff}(d{\text{final}}, \text{axis}=1) \Delta d{\text{full}} = [dist\min, \Delta d{0}, \Delta d{1}, \dots] Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 7. Filter Samples: Flatten tensors and filter using the mask. \text{flat\samples} = \text{flatten}(\text{samples}) \text{flat\depths} = \text{flatten}(d{\text{final}}) \text{flat\deltas} = \text{flatten}(\Delta d{\text{full}}) \text{flat\ray\idx} = \text{repeat}(0..N-1, \text{num\samples}) \text{flat\mask} = \text{flatten}(\text{mask}) Apply fastfiltermethod to keep only elements where flatmask is true. \text{out\samples} = \text{flat\samples}[\text{flat\mask}] \text{out\depths} = \text{flat\depths}[\text{flat\mask}] \text{out\deltas} = \text{flat\deltas}[\text{flat\mask}] \text{out\ray\idx} = \text{flat\ray\idx}[\text{flat\mask}] 8. Mark Pack Boundaries: Identify the start of each ray's samples in the filtered output. Boundaries are marked where the ray index changes or at the first element. Parameters: numsamples: Number of samples generated per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Occupancy: If NUMHITSAMPLES (the count of true values in mask) is 0, the output tensors will be empty. Precision: Jitter addition must be performed carefully to avoid precision loss when distmax - distmin is very large or very small. Boundary Conditions: The first delta is explicitly set to distmin. Ensure distmin is correctly passed for rays that may have varying near planes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformraymarchingwithoccupancyfilter( origins: torch.Tensor, directions: torch.Tensor, distmin: torch.Tensor, distmax: torch.Tensor, numsamples: int, spcqueryfunc) -> dict: """ Performs uniform ray marching with occupancy filtering. Args: origins: (N, 3) Ray origins. directions: (N, 3) Normalized ray directions. distmin: (N,) or scalar Near plane distance. distmax: (N,) or scalar Far plane distance. numsamples: int Number of samples per ray. spcqueryfunc: Callable that takes (N numsamples, 3) coordinates and returns (N numsamples,) pidx. Returns: Dictionary containing filtered samples, depths, deltas, rayindices, and packboundaries. """ N = origins.shape[0] # 1. Generate base depths with jitter basedepths = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples, device=origins.device) jitter = torch.rand(numsamples, device=origins.device) / numsamples normdepths = basedepths + jitter # (numsamples,) # 2. Normalize to ray range normdepths = normdepths.unsqueeze(0) # (1, numsamples) distminexp = distmin.unsqueeze(1) if distmin.dim() == 1 else distmin distmaxexp = distmax.unsqueeze(1) if distmax.dim() == 1 else distmax depths = normdepths (distmaxexp - distminexp) + distminexp # (N, numsamples) # 3. Compute sample coordinates depths3d = depths.unsqueeze(2) # (N, numsamples, 1) samples = origins.unsqueeze(1) + depths3d directions.unsqueeze(1) # (N, numsamples, 3) # 4. Query SPC flatsamples = samples.reshape(-1, 3) # (N numsamples, 3) pidx = spcqueryfunc(flatsamples) # (N numsamples,) # 5. Create mask mask = pidx > -1 # (N numsamples,) # 6. Compute deltas deltasdiff = torch.diff(depths, dim=1) # (N, numsamples - 1) deltas = torch.cat([distminexp, deltasdiff], dim=1) # (N, numsamples) # 7. Filter flatdepths = depths.reshape(-1) flatdeltas = deltas.reshape(-1) flatrayindices = torch.arange(N, device=origins.device).repeatinterleave(numsamples) validsamples = flatsamples[mask] validdepths = flatdepths[mask] validdeltas = flatdeltas[mask] validrayindices = flatrayindices[mask] # 8. Mark pack boundaries shiftedrayindices = torch.roll(validrayindices, 1) shiftedrayindices[0] = -1 packboundaries = validrayindices != shiftedrayindices return { "samples": validsamples, "depths": validdepths, "deltas": validdeltas, "rayindices": validrayindices, "packboundaries": packboundaries } A raymarching strategy that intersects rays with SPC cells and samples points at uniform distances determined by the cell geometry. It calls raytrace(rays, level, withexit=True) to get intersection depths. It calculates stepsize as 2\sqrt{3} / \text{num\samples}, scales it to an integer scale, and normalizes stepsize to 1.0/\text{scale}. It calculates interval counts for each intersection by scaling depth intervals and taking the ceiling difference. It filters out intersections with zero interval counts. It computes an inclusive sum of interval counts for indexing. It calls uniformsamplecuda kernel with scale, filtered indices, depths, and inclusive sum. It computes deltas as constant stepsize for all samples. It computes sample coordinates using ray origins, directions, and depth samples. Parameter: numsamples determines the uniform step distance, calculated as 2\sqrt{3}/\text{num\samples} initially. Pitfall: NUMINTERSECTIONS can be 0. A raymarching strategy that first intersects rays with Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) cells, then samples a fixed number of points within each intersected cell. It calls raytrace(rays, level, withexit=True) to get ray indices (ridx), point indices (pidx), and depth intervals (depth) for each intersection. It generates depth samples within each interval by calling samplefromdepthintervals(depth, numsamples) and appending a dimension. It computes depth deltas by taking the difference of depthsamples along the last dimension, prepending the start depth of the interval. It computes sample coordinates by adding the product of ray origins/directions and depth samples using torch.addcmul. It creates a boundary mask marking the start of each sample pack by expanding the first-hit mask of each intersection. It flattens ridx, samples, and depthsamples to a single list of size numintersections numsamples. Parameter: numsamples is the number of samples generated per voxel intersection. Pitfall: NUMINTERSECTIONS can be 0, meaning no cells were hit by any ray. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for generating samples and querying the SPC, where N is the number of rays and S is numsamples. Filtering is O(N \cdot S). The SPC query cost depends on the structure. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for storing intermediate tensors before filtering. The output size is variable but bounded by N \cdot S. Performance: Efficient for scenes with high occupancy where most samples are valid. In sparse scenes, the filtering step discards many samples, but the initial generation cost remains. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides uniform sampling density in space; jitter reduces banding. Limitations: Wastes computation on empty space if the scene is sparse; numsamples must be chosen to balance coverage and performance; potential for NUMHITSAMPLES = 0 in empty scenes. When to use: When a uniform sampling distribution is desired and the scene has significant occupied volume. When not to use: In very sparse scenes where most rays hit empty space, as the filtering overhead may not justify the uniform sampling benefit; consider SPC Voxel Raymarching instead. This method is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp framework, specifically within the wisp.tracers module, designed for efficient neural radiance field rendering. It builds on the concept of uniform ray sampling but integrates occupancy filtering via Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) structures to optimize computation in sparse environments. name: Near-Far Linear Ray Generation with Stratified Sampling
body: This method generates ray samples along a near-far segment by dividing the depth range into intervals and drawing one uniform random sample from each interval. It differs from uniform jittered sampling by guaranteeing that every sub-interval contributes exactly one sample. Inputs: tmin: Near plane distance (scalar or tensor). tmax: Far plane distance (scalar or tensor). numsamples: Integer count of samples per ray (e.g., 384). depthmode: String specifying interpolation space: 'linear', 'geometric', or 'harmonic'. epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero or log(0) in non-linear modes. Default: 10^{-3}. rayorigin: 3D camera origin position. raydirection: Normalized ray direction vector. Outputs: samples: Tensor of shape [..., numsamples, 3] containing the final 3D positions along the ray. Data Structures: ts: Intermediate tensor of shape [..., numsamples] storing interpolated depth values. trand: Tensor of shape [..., numsamples] storing uniform random noise in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Base Timestamps: Generate base timestamps using linear spacing from 0 to 1, reshaped to broadcast with batch dimensions: ts = linspace(0, 1, numsamples) reshaped to [..., numsamples]. 2. Interpolation: Compute interpolated timestamps ts based on depthmode: Linear: ts = tmin (1.0 - ts) + tmax ts. Geometric: Interpolate in log-space: ts = (clamp(tmin, epsilon).log() (1.0 - ts) + clamp(tmax, epsilon).log() ts).exp(). This samples closer points more densely. Harmonic: Interpolate in inverse-space: ts = 1.0 / (1.0 / clamp(tmin, epsilon) (1.0 - ts) + 1.0 / clamp(tmax, epsilon) ts). Recommended for spherical scenes. 3. Midpoints: Compute interval midpoints: mids = 0.5 (ts[..., 1:] + ts[...,:-1]). 4. Interval Bounds: Define the boundaries of each stratified interval: Lower bounds: lower = cat([tmin, mids], dim=-1). Upper bounds: upper = cat([mids, tmax], dim=-1). 5. Stratified Sampling: Draw uniform random noise trand in [0, 1] with the same shape as ts. Compute final depth values: ts = lower + (upper - lower) trand. 6. Position Calculation: Compute sample position: position = rayorigin + raydirection ts[..., None]. (Note: describes an alternative loop-based approach where t = tmin + dt (i + random()) and position = rayorigin + raydirection t, but the vectorized formulation above is standard for batched execution). 7. Output: Return positions unsqueezed at the last dimension: samples = ts.unsqueeze(-1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def stratifiedsampleray(tmin, tmax, numsamples, depthmode='linear', epsilon=1e-3, rayorigin=None, raydirection=None): # 1. Base timestamps ts = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples, device=tmin.device) # Reshape to broadcast: [..., numsamples] ts = ts.view([1] tmin.dim() + [numsamples]) # 2. Interpolate based on depthmode if depthmode == 'linear': ts = tmin (1.0 - ts) + tmax ts elif depthmode == 'geometric': tminc = torch.clamp(tmin, min=epsilon) tmaxc = torch.clamp(tmax, min=epsilon) ts = torch.exp(torch.log(tminc) (1.0 - ts) + torch.log(tmaxc) ts) elif depthmode == 'harmonic': tminc = torch.clamp(tmin, min=epsilon) tmaxc = torch.clamp(tmax, min=epsilon) invtmin = 1.0 / tminc invtmax = 1.0 / tmaxc ts = 1.0 / (invtmin (1.0 - ts) + invtmax ts) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown depthmode: {depthmode}") # 3. Midpoints mids = 0.5 (ts[..., 1:] + ts[...,:-1]) # 4. Interval bounds lower = torch.cat([tmin.unsqueeze(-1), mids], dim=-1) upper = torch.cat([mids, tmax.unsqueeze(-1)], dim=-1) # 5. Stratified sampling trand = torch.randlike(ts) ts = lower + (upper - lower) trand # 6. Position calculation if rayorigin is not None and raydirection is not None: samples = rayorigin + raydirection ts.unsqueeze(-1) else: samples = ts.unsqueeze(-1) return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Harmonic Interpolation: Edge cases occur when the observer crosses from the inner to outer volume, potentially causing discontinuities. Zero Distance: If t{min} = 0, geometric and harmonic modes require clamping to \epsilon to avoid \log(0) or 1/0. Ordering: The method assumes t{min} < t{max}. If not, results are undefined. Filters samples outside the viewing frustum. Use when rays must be discarded before marching. Samples based on a learned or analytical distribution. Use when importance sampling is required. Extends stratification to disparity space. Use for stereo or multi-view consistency. Adaptive sampling based on depth variance. Use for high-detail regions. Computes t{min}, t{max} from scene data. Use when bounds are not known a priori. Skips empty space. Use with stratified sampling to improve efficiency in sparse volumes. Samples rays with specific spacing constraints. Use when regular grid alignment is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Typical numsamples is 384. Strengths: Simple to implement; supports multiple interpolation modes. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene content; harmonic mode can be unstable near zero. When to Use: General-purpose volume rendering where uniform coverage is desired; spherical scenes (use harmonic mode). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is implemented in modern neural rendering frameworks. (gsgen3d/gsgen) uses it for 3D generation, supporting linear, geometric, and harmonic modes. (OctaNeRF) uses a loop-based variant for distillation. gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mdmubarak/OctaNeRF, https://github.com/mdmubarak/OctaNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SpacedSampler
body: The SpacedSampler samples points along a ray according to a user-defined spacing function and its inverse. It generalizes linear and disparity sampling by performing uniform stratified sampling in a transformed spacing space and mapping the results back to Euclidean space. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by allowing arbitrary non-linear spacing functions rather than restricting interpolation to linear distance. Inputs: near: Tensor of shape (numrays,) containing near-plane distances. far: Tensor of shape (numrays,) containing far-plane distances. numsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. spacingfn: Callable mapping Euclidean distance to spacing coordinate. spacingfninv: Callable mapping spacing coordinate back to Euclidean distance. trainstratified: Boolean, default True. singlejitter: Boolean, default False. Outputs: RaySamples object containing: starts: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with Euclidean start positions. ends: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with Euclidean end positions. spacingstarts: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with spacing-space start positions. spacingends: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with spacing-space end positions. spacingtoeuclideanfn: Helper function for interpolation. Data Structures: bins: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples + 1) in spacing space. bincenters: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) in spacing space. binlower, binupper: Tensors of shape (numrays, numsamples) in spacing space. trand: Random jitter tensor. Steps: 1. Compute uniform bins in spacing space: bins = linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples + 1). 2. Generate stratified jitter if training and stratified sampling is enabled: trand is drawn from a uniform distribution U(0, 1). If singlejitter is True, trand has shape (numrays, 1); otherwise trand has shape (numrays, numsamples + 1). 3. Calculate bin centers in spacing space: bincenters = (bins[..., 1:] + bins[...,:-1]) / 2.0. 4. Construct bin lower and upper bounds in spacing space: binlower = cat([bins[...,:1], bincenters], -1) and binupper = cat([bincenters, bins[..., -1:]], -1). 5. Apply stratified jitter to bins: bins = binlower + (binupper - binlower) trand. 6. Transform ray near and far distances into spacing space: snear = spacingfn(near) and sfar = spacingfn(far). 7. Define helper function spacingtoeuclideanfn(x) = spacingfninv(x sfar + (1 - x) snear) to interpolate in spacing space and map back to Euclidean. 8. Map the spacing-space bins to Euclidean space: euclideanbins = spacingtoeuclideanfn(bins). 9. Create RaySamples using the Euclidean bin starts and ends, and the spacing bin starts and ends, along with the helper function. Formulas: Uniform bins: \text{bins} = \text{linspace}(0.0, 1.0, \text{num\samples} + 1). Bin centers: \text{bin\centers} = \frac{\text{bins}[:, 1:] + \text{bins}[:,:-1]}{2.0}. Bin bounds: \text{bin\lower} = \text{cat}([\text{bins}[:,:1], \text{bin\centers}], \text{axis}=-1), \text{bin\upper} = \text{cat}([\text{bin\centers}, \text{bins}[:, -1:]], \text{axis}=-1). Stratified jitter: \text{bins} = \text{bin\lower} + (\text{bin\upper} - \text{bin\lower}) \times \text{t\rand}. Spacing transformation: s{\text{near}} = \text{spacing\fn}(\text{near}), s{\text{far}} = \text{spacing\fn}(\text{far}). Spacing-to-Euclidean mapping: \text{spacing\to\euclidean\fn}(x) = \text{spacing\fn\inv}(x \cdot s{\text{far}} + (1 - x) \cdot s{\text{near}}). Parameters: spacingfn: A callable that maps Euclidean distance to spacing coordinate. spacingfninv: A callable that maps spacing coordinate back to Euclidean distance. trainstratified: Boolean flag, default True, to use stratified sampling during training. singlejitter: Boolean flag, default False, to use a single random jitter value for all samples along a ray instead of one per sample. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When spacingfn or spacingfninv involve logarithms or square roots, ensure inputs are positive to avoid NaNs or complex numbers. Boundaries: Ensure near and far are positive and near < far. Degenerate Input: If numsamples is 0, the method should return empty tensors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def spacedsampler(near, far, numsamples, spacingfn, spacingfninv, trainstratified=True, singlejitter=False): """ Samples points along a ray using a user-defined spacing function. Args: near: Tensor of shape (numrays,) with near-plane distances. far: Tensor of shape (numrays,) with far-plane distances. numsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. spacingfn: Callable mapping Euclidean distance to spacing coordinate. spacingfninv: Callable mapping spacing coordinate to Euclidean distance. trainstratified: Boolean, default True. singlejitter: Boolean, default False. Returns: Dictionary with starts, ends, spacingstarts, spacingends, and spacingtoeuclideanfn. """ numrays = near.shape[0] # Step 1: Compute uniform bins in spacing space bins = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples + 1, device=near.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(numrays, -1) # Step 2: Generate stratified jitter if trainstratified: if singlejitter: trand = torch.rand(numrays, 1, device=near.device) else: trand = torch.rand(numrays, numsamples + 1, device=near.device) else: trand = torch.zeroslike(bins) # Step 3: Calculate bin centers bincenters = (bins[..., 1:] + bins[...,:-1]) / 2.0 # Step 4: Construct bin lower and upper bounds binlower = torch.cat([bins[...,:1], bincenters], dim=-1) binupper = torch.cat([bincenters, bins[..., -1:]], dim=-1) # Step 5: Apply stratified jitter to bins bins = binlower + (binupper - binlower) trand # Step 6: Transform ray near and far distances into spacing space snear = spacingfn(near) sfar = spacingfn(far) # Step 7: Define helper function def spacingtoeuclideanfn(x): snearexpanded = snear.unsqueeze(-1) sfarexpanded = sfar.unsqueeze(-1) sinterp = x sfarexpanded + (1 - x) snearexpanded return spacingfninv(sinterp) # Step 8: Map the spacing-space bins to Euclidean space euclideanbins = spacingtoeuclideanfn(bins) # Step 9: Create RaySamples euclideanstarts = spacingtoeuclideanfn(binlower) euclideanends = spacingtoeuclideanfn(binupper) spacingstarts = binlower spacingends = binupper return { 'starts': euclideanstarts, 'ends': euclideanends, 'spacingstarts': spacingstarts, 'spacingends': spacingends, 'spacingtoeuclideanfn': spacingtoeuclideanfn } A piecewise sampler that allocates the first half of samples uniformly and the second half using linearly in disparity spacing. It uses the spacing function s(x) = x/2 if x < 1 else 1 - 1/(2x) and its inverse s^{-1}(s) = 2s if s < 0.5 else 1/(2 - 2s). Parameters: numsamples, trainstratified (default True), singlejitter (default False). Samples points uniformly along a ray in Euclidean space. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = lambda x: x and spacingfninv = lambda x: x. Samples points linearly in disparity (inverse depth) along a ray. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = lambda x: 1/x and spacingfninv = lambda x: 1/x. Samples points using a square root spacing function along a ray. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = torch.sqrt and spacingfninv = lambda x: x2. Samples points using a logarithmic spacing function along a ray. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = torch.log and spacingfninv = torch.exp. Not given in the sources. The SpacedSampler is implemented in the nerfstudio project, a collaboration-friendly studio for NeRFs. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Batch Stratified Pixel Sampling
head: Pixel Sampling and Ground Truth Retrieval
body: Batch Stratified Pixel Sampling is a method used in neural reconstruction pipelines to select a subset of pixels for optimization at each training iteration. Inputs: Target image (texture) containing ground-truth color values. Batch size Nb. Image dimensions W \times H. Outputs: A set of Nb pixel coordinates (u, v) and their corresponding ground-truth color values. Data Structures: Pixel coordinates: Floating-point pairs (u, v) representing sub-pixel locations. Ground-truth values: Floating-point vectors (e.g., RGB) retrieved via interpolation. Steps: 1. Stratified Sampling: Divide the image grid into a grid of strata and sample pixel coordinates within each stratum. 2. Ground-Truth Retrieval: Obtain ground-truth values at the sampled coordinates via bilinear interpolation on the target image. 3. Efficient Lookup: Implement the bilinear interpolation as a CUDA texture lookup for hardware-accelerated efficiency. Parameters: Batch size Nb: Number of pixels to sample. Strata count: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases: Boundary conditions and precision behavior: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def batchstratifiedpixelsampling(targetimage, batchsize, width, height): """ Samples a batch of pixels using stratified sampling and retrieves ground truth. Args: targetimage: 2D array of pixel values. batchsize: Number of pixels to sample. width: Image width in pixels. height: Image height in pixels. Returns: pixels: List of (u, v) coordinates. gtvalues: List of interpolated color values. """ pixels = [] gtvalues = [] # Standard stratified sampling: divide image into strata grid strataside = int(round(batchsize 0.5)) if strataside strataside < batchsize: strataside += 1 strataw = width / strataside stratah = height / strataside for i in range(strataside): for j in range(strataside): if len(pixels) >= batchsize: break # Sample uniform sub-pixel coordinate within stratum u = (i + random.uniform(0, 1)) strataw v = (j + random.uniform(0, 1)) stratah # Clip to image bounds u = max(0.0, min(u, float(width - 1))) v = max(0.0, min(v, float(height - 1))) pixels.append((u, v)) # Bilinear interpolation via CUDA texture lookup gtvalues.append(bilinearinterpolate(targetimage, u, v, width, height)) if len(pixels) >= batchsize: break return pixels, gtvalues def bilinearinterpolate(image, x, y, width, height): x0, y0 = int(x), int(y) x1, y1 = min(x0 + 1, width - 1), min(y0 + 1, height - 1) dx, dy = x - x0, y - y0 c00 = image[y0][x0] c01 = image[y0][x1] c10 = image[y1][x0] c11 = image[y1][x1] return (1 - dx) (1 - dy) c00 + dx (1 - dy) c01 + (1 - dx) dy c10 + dx dy c11 A variant used in interaction-aware pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It selects view-pixel pairs by sampling around projected Gaussian centers and their neighbors to evaluate opacity responses, rather than using uniform stratified sampling. Definition: Selects a set of view-pixel pairs Pb for a block Cb by sampling around projected Gaussian centers and their neighbors. Steps: 1. Initialize Pb \leftarrow \emptyset and D \leftarrow \{(0, 0), (\pm0.5, 0), (0, \pm0.5), (\pm0.35, \pm0.35)\}. 2. For each selected view v: a. Obtain projected centers u{vi} and screen radii h{vi} for i \in Cb. b. Generate pixel locations p = \text{round}(u{vi} + \max(h{vi}, 1)\delta) for h{vi} > 0 and \delta \in D. c. Remove duplicate pixels and discard those outside the image boundaries. d. Add remaining view-pixel pairs (v, p) to Pb. 3. Return Pb. Formula: Candidate locations: u{vi} + \max(h{vi}, 1)\delta, where \delta \in D = \{(0, 0), (\pm0.5, 0), (0, \pm0.5), (\pm0.35, \pm0.35)\}. Parameters: D: Set of 9 offset vectors (center + 8 neighbors) used for pixel sampling. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Grid-based Stratified Camera Sampling
head: Grid-based Stratified Sampler, Stratified Scene Sampling
body: Grid-based Stratified Camera Sampling generates camera rays by uniformly covering the scene volume using a 3D stratified grid for camera positions, combined with random selection of training view orientations. It differs from the parent Grid Ray Sampler by explicitly stratifying the camera position space across the scene bounds rather than just the pixel grid, and from siblings like Near-Middle-Far Ray Generation by decoupling position stratification from view orientation selection. Inputs: colmapdata: A pickled dictionary loaded via joblib.load containing camera parameters indexed by view keys. datasettrain: A collection of training views used to sample camera orientations. bins: List of integers defining grid resolution, default [16, 16, 16]. minpoint, maxpoint: 3D vectors defining the bounding box of the scene volume. znear, zfar: Clipping plane distances, default 0.01 and 100.0. Outputs: samplestate: Object containing pos (camera position), quat (camera orientation quaternion), and center (used to compute gaze direction). sampleparams: Object containing lod (Level of Detail parameter). Data Structures: samplestate: pos: 3D vector (float). quat: 4D vector (float), normalized quaternion. center: List or array of points, accessed as center[0].x and center[0].y. sampleparams: lod: Float in range [0.0, 1.0]. Steps: 1. Define the stratified grid resolution bins (default [16, 16, 16]). 2. Generate stratified random positions within the scene bounds defined by minpoint and maxpoint using stratifiedrandom(np.stack((minpoint, maxpoint), axis=1), bins). 3. Iterate over all bin combinations using itertools.product(range(bins[0]), range(bins[1]), range(bins[2])). 4. For each bin, assign the sampled position to samplestate.pos. 5. Randomly select a camera index from datasettrain to determine orientation: cameraindex = np.random.randint(len(datasettrain)). 6. Convert COLMAP camera data to world coordinates using convertcolmapcamera. 7. Compute the gaze direction using the camera matrix and principal point: \text{gaze\dir} = \text{get\gaze\dir\global}(\text{cam\mat}, \text{proj\mat}, \text{np.array}([\text{center}[0].x, \text{center}[0].y])). 8. Set samplestate.quat and gazedir from the selected camera data. 9. Generate a random LOD value: \text{random\lod} = \text{uniform}(0.0, 1.0) and assign it to sampleparams.lod. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import itertools import numpy as np import random def gridbasedstratifiedcamerasampling( colmapdata, datasettrain, bins=[16, 16, 16], minpoint=np.array([-1.0, -1.0, -1.0]), maxpoint=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), znear=0.01, zfar=100.0): """ Generates camera samples using grid-based stratified sampling for positions and random training view selection for orientations. """ def stratifiedrandom(bounds, bins): """Generates stratified random points within the given bounds.""" samples = [] minpt, maxpt = bounds[0], bounds[1] for i in range(bins[0]): for j in range(bins[1]): for k in range(bins[2]): x = minpt[0] + (maxpt[0] - minpt[0]) (i + random.random()) / bins[0] y = minpt[1] + (maxpt[1] - minpt[1]) (j + random.random()) / bins[1] z = minpt[2] + (maxpt[2] - minpt[2]) (k + random.random()) / bins[2] samples.append(np.array([x, y, z])) return samples positions = stratifiedrandom(np.stack((minpoint, maxpoint), axis=1), bins) for i, j, k in itertools.product(range(bins[0]), range(bins[1]), range(bins[2])): samplestate = type('SampleState', (), {})() sampleparams = type('SampleParams', (), {})() idx = i bins[1] bins[2] + j bins[2] + k samplestate.pos = positions[idx] cameraindex = np.random.randint(len(datasettrain)) keys = list(colmapdata.keys()) cameradata = colmapdata[keys[cameraindex % len(keys)]] # Standard center point for gaze computation samplestate.center = [type('Point', (), {'x': 0.5, 'y': 0.5})()] # Standard gaze direction computation def getgazedirglobal(cammat, projmat, center): return np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) gazedir = getgazedirglobal( cameradata["cammat"], cameradata["projmat"], np.array([samplestate.center[0].x, samplestate.center[0].y])) samplestate.quat = cameradata.get("quat", np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0])) samplestate.gazedir = gazedir randomlod = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) sampleparams.lod = randomlod yield samplestate, sampleparams Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in coordinate transformations may affect ray accuracy. Boundaries: Ensure minpoint and maxpoint correctly enclose the scene volume to avoid sampling outside the region of interest. Degenerate Input: If datasettrain is empty, camera orientation selection will fail. Camera Data Structure: The structure of colmapdata and datasettrain must be consistent with the assumptions in the pseudocode. A broader pipeline context. Uses fixed depth planes for ray generation. Uses probability density functions for importance sampling. Linearly interpolates between near and far planes. Time Complexity: O(B0 \cdot B1 \cdot B2) where Bi are the bin dimensions, due to iterating over all bin combinations. Memory Complexity: O(B0 \cdot B1 \cdot B2) to store the stratified positions. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Uniform coverage of the scene volume for camera positions. Limitations: May not adapt to scene complexity or importance. When to use: When uniform coverage of camera positions is desired. When not to use: When importance sampling based on scene content is needed. This method is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting training to generate diverse camera views for rendering. facebookresearch/CLOD-3DGS, https://github.com/facebookresearch/CLOD-3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Stratified Cosine-Weighted Diffuse Ray Generation
head: Stratified Cosine-Weighted Diffuse Ray Generation for One-Bounce Voxel GI, bounded one-bounce voxel GI ray gen
body: This method generates stratified cosine-weighted diffuse rays for bounded one-bounce voxel global illumination, sampling from primary hit positions. It builds on Grid Ray Sampler and differs from its siblings by specifically targeting the second bounce in a voxel-based pipeline and restricting rays to a fixed maximum distance. Inputs: globalIndex: The unique compute dispatch thread ID. primarybuffer: An array of primary hit results indexed by pixel. activeSamples: The number of active samples per pixel for the current frame. kMaximumGiSamples: The maximum number of GI samples per pixel. gGiFrameSeed: The seed for the PCG random number generator. gGlobalIlluminationMaxDistanceMeters: The maximum ray distance in meters. gShadowBiasMeters: The shadow bias in meters. voxelscale: The conversion factor from meters to voxel units. totalCapacity: The total number of threads dispatched. Outputs: outputbuffer: An array of TraceRay structures containing the generated GI rays. Data Structures: TraceRay: Contains fields hit (uint, 0 if miss, non-zero if hit), origin (float3), direction (float3), maxDistance (float), and id (uint). randomPair: A pair of floats (u, v) representing the stratified sample coordinates. Numbered Steps & Formulas: 1. Map the dispatch thread ID to pixel and sample indices: pixelIndex = globalIndex // kMaximumGiSamples and sampleIndex = globalIndex % kMaximumGiSamples. If globalIndex >= totalCapacity, return an empty TraceRay. 2. Fetch the primary trace result for pixelIndex. If primary.hit == 0 or sampleIndex >= activeSamples, return an empty TraceRay. 3. Compute the stratified sample coordinates: hashVal = PcgHash(pixelIndex ^ gGiFrameSeed) and randomPair = RotatedHammersley2D(sampleIndex, activeSamples, hashVal). 4. Set the ray direction using cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling relative to the surface normal at the primary hit point: ray.direction = CosineWeightedHemisphereSample(primary.normal, randomPair). 5. Set ray.maxDistance to gGlobalIlluminationMaxDistanceMeters converted to voxel units, assign ray.id = globalIndex, and write the result to outputbuffer. Parameters: kMaximumGiSamples: Fixed at 16. gGiPrimaryRayCount: Number of primary rays processed in the previous pass. gGiFrameSeed: Seed for the PCG random number generator. gGlobalIlluminationMode: Controls GI activation; GI is active when equal to kGlobalIlluminationVoxelOneBounce. gGlobalIlluminationSamples: User-requested number of GI samples per pixel. gShadowBiasMeters: Shadow bias in meters, converted to voxel units for ray origin offset. gGlobalIlluminationMaxDistanceMeters: Maximum distance for GI rays in meters, converted to voxel units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If activeSamples is less than sampleIndex, the ray is discarded. Precision issues may arise if gShadowBiasMeters is too small relative to voxelscale, causing self-intersection. Non-unit cell sizes require explicit voxelscale multiplication for distance and bias values. Degenerate surface normals (zero length) must be normalized before hemisphere sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class TraceRay: def init(self, hit, origin, direction, maxDistance, id): self.hit = hit self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.maxDistance = maxDistance self.id = id def generategiray(globalindex, primarybuffer, activesamples, kmaximumgisamples, ggiframeseed, gshadowbiasmeters, gglobalilluminationmaxdistancemeters, voxelscale, totalcapacity): # Step 1: Map thread ID pixelindex = globalindex // kmaximumgisamples sampleindex = globalindex % kmaximumgisamples if globalindex >= totalcapacity: return TraceRay(hit=0, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), maxDistance=0.0, id=0) # Step 2: Fetch primary result primary = primarybuffer[pixelindex] if primary.hit == 0 or sampleindex >= activesamples: return TraceRay(hit=0, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), maxDistance=0.0, id=0) # Step 3: Compute stratified sample hashval = pcghash(pixelindex ^ ggiframeseed) randompair = rotatedhammersley2d(sampleindex, activesamples, hashval) # Step 4: Sample direction raydirection = cosineweightedhemispheresample(primary.normal, randompair) # Step 5: Set ray properties maxdistancevoxel = gglobalilluminationmaxdistancemeters voxelscale originoffset = primary.normal gshadowbiasmeters voxelscale rayorigin = (primary.origin[0] + originoffset[0], primary.origin[1] + originoffset[1], primary.origin[2] + originoffset[2]) return TraceRay(hit=1, origin=rayorigin, direction=raydirection, maxDistance=maxdistancevoxel, id=globalindex) def pcghash(x): # Standard PCG32 state transformation x = ((x >> 16) ^ x) 0x45d9f3b x = ((x >> 16) ^ x) 0x45d9f3b x = (x >> 16) ^ x return x def rotatedhammersley2d(sampleidx, activesamples, seed): # Standard Hammersley sequence with simple hash rotation u = (sampleidx + 0.5) / activesamples v = (seed + sampleidx 2654435761) & 0xFFFFFFFF v = ((v >> 1) ^ (-(v & 1))) & 0xFFFFFFFF v = (v 0x21f0aaad) & 0xFFFFFFFF v = (v 0xd35a2d97) & 0xFFFFFFFF return (u, v / 4294967296.0) def cosineweightedhemispheresample(normal, randompair): # Cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling u1, u2 = randompair x = math.sqrt(1.0 - u1) math.cos(2.0 math.pi u2) y = math.sqrt(1.0 - u1) math.sin(2.0 math.pi u2) z = math.sqrt(u1) # Construct orthonormal basis from normal if abs(normal[2]) < 0.9999: up = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: up = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) tangent = mathnormalize(mathcross(up, normal)) bitangent = mathcross(normal, tangent) return (tangent[0]x + bitangent[0]y + normal[0]z, tangent[1]x + bitangent[1]y + normal[1]z, tangent[2]x + bitangent[2]y + normal[2]z) def mathnormalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def mathcross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) Time complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Ray Casting
head: Primary Ray Tracing, Ray casting and compositing
body: Ray casting is the fundamental image synthesis technique that determines the color of each pixel by casting primary rays from a camera through the image plane into the scene and computing the first intersection with visible geometry. It differs from full ray tracing by excluding secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions, serving as the base visibility computation upon which advanced effects are built. In volume rendering, it specifically refers to ray casting and compositing of even-spaced samples along primary viewing rays. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A camera model defining the origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel; a scene representation containing geometric primitives or a volumetric grid. Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel (u, v) contains the color computed at the closest intersection point or the accumulated opacity along the corresponding ray. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Primitive/Volume: Stores geometric parameters (e.g., sphere center \mathbf{c} and radius r) or scalar/color grid data, and provides intersection or sampling functions. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the image, generate a primary ray R(t) using the camera model. 2. Intersection Testing: For each primitive in the scene, calculate the intersection parameter t between the ray and the primitive. 3. Closest Hit Selection: Identify the primitive with the smallest positive t (closest to the camera origin). 4. Color Computation: Compute the color at the intersection point \mathbf{p} = R(t{min}) based on the primitive's material properties or distance from the camera. Formulas The ray equation is defined as: R(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin, \mathbf{d} is the direction vector, and t is the parameter along the ray. For a sphere with center \mathbf{c} and radius r, the intersection is found by solving for t in: |\mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}|^2 = r^2 Expanding this yields a quadratic equation: t^2 (\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}) + 2t (\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c})) + (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) - r^2 = 0 Let A = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}, B = 2 \mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}), and C = (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) - r^2. The solutions are: t = \frac{-B \pm \sqrt{B^2 - 4AC}}{2A} If the discriminant B^2 - 4AC < 0, there is no intersection. The algorithm picks the closest intersection point to determine pixel color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycast(scene, camera, width, height): image = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin = camera.getorigin(x, y) raydirection = camera.getdirection(x, y) raydirection = normalize(raydirection) closestt = float('inf') hitprimitive = None for primitive in scene.primitives: t = primitive.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if t > 0 and t < closestt: closestt = t hitprimitive = primitive if hitprimitive is not None: hitpoint = rayorigin + closestt raydirection image[y][x] = hitprimitive.computecolor(hitpoint) else: image[y][x] = backgroundcolor return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lens Distortion: Calibration models with polynomials up to degree five are not trivially invertible, which complicates ray generation. Sampling Interval: For volume rendering, samples should be spaced at equal distances \Delta s, where \Delta s = 1 (one voxel length) if frequency content is unknown, following the Nyquist theorem. Early Termination: Rays can be terminated when accumulated opacity reaches a value close to unity to accelerate volume rendering. Precision: Floating-point errors in the discriminant calculation can cause false negatives for grazing intersections. Scaling: The method scales with the number of pixels and the number of primitives to intersect with. Strengths: Simple implementation; produces correct visibility for opaque objects; serves as the foundation for more complex rendering techniques. Limitations: Does not handle transparency, shadows, or reflections inherently; performance degrades linearly with scene complexity without acceleration structures. When to Use: Basic visibility checks; educational purposes; as a base for ray marching in volume rendering where analytical intersections are not feasible. Ray casting was introduced as the basic form of ray tracing, considering only primary rays without secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions. It is a physically-based image synthesis technique that generates primary rays through pixels to determine visible objects and accumulates contributions along the ray to compute light distribution. The method is widely used in computer graphics for its simplicity and correctness in determining visibility. In volume visualization, it has been extensively applied to volumetric datasets arising in biomedical imaging and scientific visualization applications.
