name: Camera Ray Generation
head: unproject, Ray Unprojection
body: Camera Ray Generation computes the 3D world-space origin and direction vectors for viewing rays corresponding to each pixel in a raster image, given explicit camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. It solves the problem of mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. Unlike Pinhole Camera Ray Generation, which often derives rays directly from geometric primitives such as field of view (FOV) and camera basis vectors, this method relies on explicit intrinsic (K) and extrinsic (c2w) matrices to define the projection geometry. It builds on Ray Sampling and Generation by providing the specific geometric unprojection logic required to initialize the parallel execution model. Inputs: Image dimensions: width W, height H. Pixel coordinates: integer grid (i, j) where 0 \le i < W and 0 \le j < H. Camera Intrinsics: 3 \times 3 matrix K containing focal lengths (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). Camera Extrinsic: 4 \times 4 matrix c2w (camera-to-world) containing rotation R and translation T. Optional: Sub-pixel offsets (sx, sy) for anti-aliasing. Optional: Depth values z if unprojecting specific 3D points rather than directions. Outputs: Ray Origins: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3) representing world-space positions. Ray Directions: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3) representing normalized world-space vectors. Data Structures: RayBundle or Rays namedtuple/struct containing fields: origins (float32), directions (float32), viewdirs (float32). In some implementations, a Ray struct contains origin and direction (normalized). Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create a meshgrid of pixel indices i (width) and j (height). i \in [0, W-1], j \in [0, H-1]. Apply flips if specified (e.g., flipx, flipy) to match coordinate system conventions. Adjust coordinates based on mode: 'center' adds 0.5 to pixel centers, 'random' adds uniform noise. 2. Compute Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) or Camera Space Coordinates: Method A (Matrix-based): Homogenize 2D coordinates by appending a 1.0 component to form vectors \mathbf{p}{2d} = [i, j, 1]^T. Method B (Geometric): Compute aspect-corrected UV coordinates in [-1, 1] with y-up: \text{uv}x = \frac{i + sx + 0.5}{W} \cdot 2 - 1 \text{uv}y = \frac{j + sy + 0.5}{H} \cdot 2 - 1 \text{uv}x \leftarrow \text{uv}x \cdot \frac{W}{H}. Note: Vulkan's flipped Y-axis in clip space may require negating Y during reconstruction. 3. Unproject to Camera Space: Using Intrinsics K: Multiply by the inverse intrinsic matrix to get ray directions in camera space \mathbf{d}{cam}. \mathbf{d}{cam} = K^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} i - cx \\ j - cy \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. Alternatively, using FOV and Basis Vectors: \mathbf{d}{cam} = \text{normalize}(\text{uv}x \cdot \mathbf{u}{right} + \text{uv}y \cdot \mathbf{u}{up} - \mathbf{u}{forward}). Here \mathbf{u}{right}, \mathbf{u}{up}, \mathbf{u}{forward} are the camera basis vectors. 4. Normalize Directions: Normalize the camera-space direction vectors to unit length: \mathbf{d}{cam} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{d}{cam}}{\|\mathbf{d}{cam}\|}. 5. Transform to World Space: Rotate the camera-space directions using the rotation part of the extrinsic matrix R (top-left 3 \times 3 of c2w). \mathbf{d}{world} = R \cdot \mathbf{d}{cam}. Extract the ray origin from the translation part of the extrinsic matrix T (last column of c2w). \mathbf{o}{world} = T. Broadcast \mathbf{o}{world} to match the shape of \mathbf{d}{world}. 6. Optional: Depth Unprojection: If 3D points are required instead of directions, scale the unprojected camera-space directions by the depth z: \mathbf{p}{cam} = \mathbf{d}{cam} \cdot z. Transform \mathbf{p}{cam} to world space using c2w. 7. Front-of-Camera Check: Verify that points in camera space have z > -\epsilon (where \epsilon = 10^{-6}) to ensure they are in front of the camera. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatecamerarays(W, H, K, c2w, subpixeloffsets=None, mode='center'): """ Generate camera rays for volume rendering. Args: W: Image width. H: Image height. K: 3x3 intrinsic matrix [[fx, 0, cx], [0, fy, cy], [0, 0, 1]]. c2w: 4x4 camera-to-world transformation matrix. subpixeloffsets: Optional tuple (sx, sy) for anti-aliasing. mode: 'center' (pixel centers), 'lefttop' (corners), 'random' (jitter). Returns: origins: (H, W, 3) array of world-space ray origins. directions: (H, W, 3) array of normalized world-space ray directions. """ # 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H), indexing='ij') # 2. Adjust for mode and subpixel offsets if mode == 'center': i = i.astype(np.float32) + 0.5 j = j.astype(np.float32) + 0.5 elif mode == 'random': i = i.astype(np.float32) + np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=(H, W)) j = j.astype(np.float32) + np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=(H, W)) if subpixeloffsets is not None: sx, sy = subpixeloffsets i += sx j += sy # 3. Unproject to Camera Space using Intrinsics # Extract intrinsic parameters fx = K[0, 0] fy = K[1, 1] cx = K[0, 2] cy = K[1, 2] # Compute normalized coordinates relative to principal point # Note: Coordinate system conventions vary. This assumes standard pinhole model. # If inversey is true, j is flipped. u = (i - cx) / fx v = (j - cy) / fy # Construct direction vectors in camera space (z=1 plane) # Shape: (H, W, 3) directionscam = np.stack([u, v, np.oneslike(u)], axis=-1) # 4. Normalize Directions norms = np.linalg.norm(directionscam, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Avoid division by zero norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-6) directionscam = directionscam / norms # 5. Transform to World Space # Extract rotation and translation from c2w R = c2w[:3,:3] T = c2w[:3, 3] # Rotate directions: (H, W, 3) @ (3, 3) -> (H, W, 3) # Using einsum or matmul directionsworld = np.einsum('ijk,kl->ijl', directionscam, R) # 6. Set Origins # Broadcast translation T to (H, W, 3) originsworld = np.broadcastto(T, (H, W, 3)) return originsworld, directionsworld Parameters with Typical Values: K: Depends on camera calibration. Typical fx, fy \approx 500-1000 pixels for standard lenses. c2w: Identity for world-aligned cameras; varies for tracked cameras. \epsilon: 10^{-6} for front-of-camera check. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Mismatch: The 3D texture/model may be centered at different coordinates than the camera's reference frame, requiring remapping of camera movements into voxel coordinates. Vulkan Y-Axis: Vulkan's flipped Y-axis in clip space requires negating Y during view-space reconstruction. Degenerate Matrices: Check for zero viewport height or singular intrinsic matrices to avoid NaNs. Aspect Ratio: Handle varying aspect ratios and viewport sizes correctly. Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation constructs initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. This method differs from perspective ray generation by maintaining parallel rays, eliminating vanishing points and depth-dependent field-of-view scaling. Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation regenerates ray geometry (origin and direction) from stored pixel indices and camera parameters, enabling sample streaming and resumption in volume rendering pipelines. It maps pixel coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) and unprojects them to world space to compute unit-length direction vectors. Unlike static ray generation, this method is designed for payloads that persist across frames or batches, allowing rays to be reconstructed on-demand from minimal state. This method implements the ray generation and initial traversal setup for volume rendering within the NVIDIA OptiX 7 API. It computes pixel rays, initializes the random number generator (RNG) for anti-aliasing, and dispatches volume tracing via optixTrace. It differs from generic ray generation methods by integrating specific OptiX 7 launch parameters, SBT indexing, and visibility masks to restrict traversal to volume geometry. Object Space Ray Setup constructs ray origins and directions within the local coordinate system of a mesh, ensuring that the raytraced volume moves, scales, and rotates rigidly with the object's transform. Unlike world-space ray generation, which treats the volume as a static window into the world, this method embeds the object's transformation directly into the ray parameters, allowing the raytraced geometry to behave like a physical part of the mesh. It serves as the foundational step for Camera Ray Generation when the rendering target is a specific object rather than the entire scene. This method generates per-pixel ray directions for volume rendering by encoding the index of pre-computed frustum corner vectors into the Z-coordinate of a full-screen quad's vertices, allowing the vertex shader to look up the correct ray direction from a uniform array. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding per-fragment matrix multiplications for direction calculation, instead using a discrete lookup based on vertex attributes. It differs from Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader by performing the direction selection in the vertex shader rather than the fragment shader, reducing redundant calculations for adjacent pixels sharing the same vertex. Ray Origin Offset Noise is a technique that perturbs the starting position of a ray march to avoid banding artifacts. It differs from its sibling Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by adding stochastic variation to the ray origin rather than strictly adhering to pixel centers, and from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by focusing on initialization jitter rather than payload management during traversal. Camera Matrix Ray Generation computes the 3D world-space origin and direction vectors for viewing rays corresponding to each pixel in a raster image, given explicit camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. It solves the problem of mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. Unlike Pinhole Camera Ray Generation, which often derives rays directly from geometric primitives such as field of view (FOV) and camera basis vectors, this method relies on explicit intrinsic (K) and extrinsic (c2w) matrices to define the projection geometry. This method generates camera rays for ray tracing by rendering a single quad to the screen, allowing the fragment shader to compute the ray origin and direction for each pixel using interpolated vertex coordinates. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding explicit matrix multiplications in favor of geometric basis vectors derived from camera parameters, and from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection through a viewing plane distance. Ray Position Calculation computes the 3D spatial coordinates of sample points (query points) along a bundle of rays defined by their origins and directions, constrained within a specific depth range. It solves the problem of mapping 1D depth samples to 3D Euclidean space for volume rendering or neural rendering pipelines. It differs from Camera Ray Generation by assuming the ray origins and directions are already computed; it focuses solely on the linear interpolation along the ray vector to determine sample locations. Epipolar Ray Intersection lifts 2D image points to 3D space by intersecting rays constructed from those points with a set of input world-space rays. It solves the problem of finding the precise 3D positions and depths corresponding to specified 2D coordinates on epipolar lines defined by camera origins and directions. It differs from sibling methods like Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by explicitly handling the intersection of two distinct ray sets (image-space and world-space) rather than generating rays from a single camera model, and from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by focusing on geometric reprojection via epipolar constraints rather than payload streaming. Flattened Ray Generation for Training is a data preparation method that converts a batch of training images into a single, flat tensor of rays and corresponding pixel colors, optimized for stochastic gradient descent in neural volume rendering. Unlike Camera Ray Generation, which generates rays on-the-fly per batch or view, this method pre-aggregates rays from all training poses into a unified structure, enabling efficient random sampling of individual rays across the entire dataset during training. It differs from Precomputed Ray Buffering by typically handling the flattening and indexing logic within the training loop or a dedicated sampler rather than storing the entire dataset in CPU RAM, though both aim to decouple ray generation from the forward pass. A camera that glides forward along a procedural road centerline, yawing to follow bends and banking gently, producing an orthonormal ray basis for the shader. Steps: Update position z += \text{speed} \cdot dt; Compute eye position [roadX(z), \text{height}, z]; Compute target [roadX(z + \text{lookAhead}), \text{lookHeight}, z + \text{lookAhead}]; Compute forward \text{normalize}(\text{target} - \text{position}); Compute right \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{forward}, \text{WORLD\UP})); Compute up \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{right}, \text{forward})). Parameters: Eye height: 3.5 world units; Look-ahead distance: 15 world units; Look height: 1.5 world units; World up vector: [0, 1, 0]. Camera orientation convention: Z-axis along optical axis (orthogonal to image plane), X-axis pointing towards bottom/ground, Y-axis according to right-hand rule. Parameters: RES: 0.02f; RANGEMAX: 100000.0f; HFOV: M\PI \cdot 160.0f / 180.0f; VFOV: M\PI \cdot 160.0f / 180.0f; HSIZE: 6; VSIZE: 4. Spherical Ray Casting generates camera rays by mapping a 2D grid of pixel coordinates to spherical angles (\theta, \phi), creating a cylindrical-spherical projection suitable for 360-degree video and dome-based presentations. Differs from standard pinhole models by using angular spacing rather than linear perspective projection, and from orthographic models by maintaining a central viewpoint with varying ray density. A 2D sculpting tool that removes voxels inside a selection volume defined by perspective projection from the user's point of view through a circular cursor on the view plane. Steps: Set cursor as a circle aligned with the view plane; set virtual pointer origin to user's point of view; set direction vector (line of sight) from point of view to cursor center; set cursor radius r and 2D position P via user selection of a screen pixel. For each voxel, project its center onto the view plane using perspective projection; calculate 2D Euclidean distance d from projected voxel center V to cursor center P; if d < r, remove the voxel. Formula: Selection condition: d < r, where d is the 2D Euclidean distance on the view plane between the projected voxel center and cursor center P, and r is the cursor radius. Pitfall: Perspective projection causes the selection volume to be a cone with apex at the point of view, making the tool dependent on viewing parameters. Orthographic projection yields a cylinder, which is preferred for 3D tools to detach from the point of view. Selects a point on a plane surface of the volume cube aligned with two of the three primary axes (e.g., Y and Z) and casts a ray down to the third axis (e.g., X-axis) to determine the ray path. Steps: Derive four ray representations: 1) An image pair co-planar to the ray in the other two axes (e.g., X-Z and X-Y planes). 2) An intensity profile along the ray. 3) The corresponding SOI label profile. 4) Location coordinates of entry and exit points. Parameters: Number of rays: 64 rays per axis, 192 total per volume. Checks if 3D points in camera space are in front of the camera (Z > -\epsilon). Steps: Check if the Z coordinate (last element) is > -\epsilon: return \text{xyz}[..., -1] > -\epsilon. Parameters: \epsilon: float = 10^{-6} (tolerance for front-of-camera check). Voxel Picking is a volume rendering interaction technique that selects a specific position along a camera ray based on the sample that contributes most significantly to the final pixel color. Unlike methods that select the maximum data value or opacity threshold, this approach targets the sample with the highest accumulated contribution to the rendered image. It is distinct from Camera Ray Generation by adding a selection criterion to the generated ray, and differs from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by focusing on contribution-based selection rather than geometric projection alone. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for generating rays for all pixels, where W and H are image dimensions. Each ray computation is O(1) involving matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot 3) to store origins and directions. Strengths: Flexible camera models via explicit matrices; supports arbitrary camera movements and poses. Limitations: Requires accurate camera calibration (intrinsics/extrinsics); sensitive to coordinate system mismatches. When to Use: When camera parameters are known from calibration or tracking (e.g., NeRF, SLAM outputs). When Not to Use: When simple geometric primitives (e.g., fixed FOV) are sufficient and matrix overhead is undesirable. Camera Ray Generation is a fundamental technique in computer graphics, originating from the need to map rasterized screen coordinates to 3D space for ray tracing and volume rendering. It is widely used in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and other view synthesis methods where camera poses are estimated from images. The method relies on the pinhole camera model and its matrix representation, which has been standard since the early days of computer vision and graphics. name: Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation
head: Orthographic ray casting, Parallel Ray Casting, Parallel Ray Generation, PlaneParallelLens
body: Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation constructs initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. This method models a camera at infinity where all rays are parallel to one viewing vector, commonly used in applications like biomedicine that do not benefit from perspective distortion. Inputs: eye: Camera position reference in world space (3D vector). target: Look-at target point in world space (3D vector). up: World up vector (3D vector, typically (0,1,0)). width, height: Image resolution in pixels. extent: Half-size of the viewing region in world units along both right and up axes (scalar, default 1.0). Outputs: origins: Array of ray origins distributed on a grid perpendicular to the viewing direction. directions: Array of identical normalized directions for the orthographic camera. Data Structures: origins and directions: Dense arrays matching the pixel grid dimensions, populated via broadcasting. Steps: 1. Compute Camera Basis: Calculate the forward, right, and camera-up vectors using a standard look-at routine camerabasis(eye, target, up). forward = normalize(target - eye). right = normalize(cross(forward, up)). camup = cross(right, forward). 2. Compute Image Plane Dimensions: Determine the half-width and half-height of the viewing region in world units. aspect = width / height. halfw = extent aspect. halfh = extent. 3. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create a meshgrid of pixel indices i (row, 0 \dots height-1) and j (column, 0 \dots width-1). Map these to normalized coordinates u and v on the image plane: u = \left( \frac{2.0 \cdot (j + 0.5)}{width} - 1.0 \right) \cdot half\w. v = \left( 1.0 - \frac{2.0 \cdot (i + 0.5)}{height} \right) \cdot half\h. Note: The v formula uses (1.0 - \dots) to align the image plane's vertical axis with the camera's up vector, assuming standard screen coordinates where i=0 is the top. 4. Compute Origins: Calculate the world-space origin for each ray by offsetting the eye position by the scaled basis vectors: origin{i,j} = eye + u{i,j} \cdot right + v{i,j} \cdot cam\up. 5. Set Directions: Broadcast the normalized forward vector to match the shape of origins. All rays share this identical direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def orthographicraygeneration(eye, target, up, width, height, extent=1.0): """ Generates orthographic camera rays. Args: eye: (3,) array-like, camera position reference. target: (3,) array-like, look-at target. up: (3,) array-like, world up vector. width: int, image width. height: int, image height. extent: float, half-size of viewing region in world units. Returns: origins: (height, width, 3) array of ray origins. directions: (height, width, 3) array of ray directions. """ eye = np.asarray(eye, dtype=np.float32) target = np.asarray(target, dtype=np.float32) up = np.asarray(up, dtype=np.float32) # 1. Compute Camera Basis forward = target - eye forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) right = np.cross(forward, up) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) camup = np.cross(right, forward) # 2. Compute Image Plane Dimensions aspect = width / height halfw = extent aspect halfh = extent # 3. Generate Pixel Coordinates # Create meshgrid of indices j, i = np.meshgrid(np.arange(width), np.arange(height)) # Map to world coordinates on the image plane u = (2.0 (j + 0.5) / width - 1.0) halfw v = (1.0 - 2.0 (i + 0.5) / height) halfh # 4. Compute Origins # Expand dimensions for broadcasting: eye (3,), right (3,), camup (3,) # u (H, W), v (H, W) origins = (eye[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] + u[:,:, np.newaxis] right[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] + v[:,:, np.newaxis] camup[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:]) # 5. Set Directions # Broadcast forward vector to (H, W, 3) directions = np.broadcastto(forward[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:], (height, width, 3)) return origins, directions Parameters: extent: Half-size of the viewing region in world units along both right and up axes. Default value is 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Basis: If eye equals target, the forward vector is zero, causing normalization failure. A guard should check for this distance. Up Vector Alignment: If up is parallel to forward, the right vector becomes zero. The camerabasis helper must handle this by rotating the up vector or using a default right vector. Precision: Using float32 for large extent values may cause precision loss in origin calculation. Use float64 for large scenes or high-precision requirements. Viewing Plane Ray Generation constructs the initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. It generates parallel rays, contrasting with perspective ray generation which supports non-parallel viewing. Choose it when metric-preserving, distortion-free projection is required. Orthographic Projection is a size-preserving projection where objects in the foreground take up the same amount of screen space as objects in the background, and parallel lines in the 3D scene remain parallel when drawn on the screen. Choose it for technical drawings, CAD, and scientific visualizations where accurate spatial relationships are critical. Orthographic Camera Handling for Point Clouds alternates the camera type from Orthographic to PerspectiveCamera with a similar viewing scope to enable rendering. It is used when differentiable rendering of point clouds requires perspective effects or specific focal length adjustments for zooming. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate all ray origins and directions, where W and H are image width and height. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the origin and direction arrays. Performance: Very fast ray generation as it involves simple vector additions and broadcasts, with no division by depth required. Strengths: No perspective distortion; uniform sampling density across the image plane; suitable for scientific visualization where metric accuracy is required. Limitations: Does not simulate depth perception via foreshortening; field of view is fixed by extent and aspect ratio, not by a focal length. When to use: Scientific visualization, CAD, architectural rendering, or any scenario requiring metric-preserving projections. When not to use: When realistic human-like vision or depth cues from perspective are required. Orthographic projection is a fundamental concept in computer graphics, historically used in technical drawing and CAD. In the context of volume rendering, it provides a consistent sampling grid. The method generates parallel rays for applications like biomedicine where perspective distortion is undesirable. The PlaneParallelLens is the standard lens type for this projection. In differentiable rendering pipelines, it may be alternated with perspective cameras for specific point cloud tasks. name: Viewing Plane Ray Generation
head: Projection Plane Raycasting
body: Viewing Plane Ray Generation constructs the initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. This method generates parallel rays, contrasting with perspective ray generation which supports non-parallel viewing. Inputs: Image resolution: W \times H (width, height). Viewing direction vector: \mathbf{d}{view} (normalized). Transformation matrix: \mathbf{M} (combined translation, rotation, and scaling). Camera scale factor: S{cam} (typically 0.25). Sample period: P{sample} (typically 2.0). Outputs: A set of rays, each defined by an origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} and direction \mathbf{d}{ray}. Data Structures: ViewingPlane: A 2D grid of size W \times H. mdata: A std::vector<vec3> of size W \times H. Each element at index k = i + j \cdot W stores a 2D screen coordinate normalized to [-1, 1] for x and y, with z=0. mmat: The combined transformation matrix \mathbf{M}. Steps: 1. Initialize Normalized Grid Points: For each pixel (i, j) where 0 \le i < W and 0 \le j < H: x{norm} = \frac{2(i + 0.5)}{W} - 1 y{norm} = \frac{2(j + 0.5)}{H} - 1 Store \mathbf{p}{norm} = [x{norm}, y{norm}, 0]^T in mdata at index k. 2. Compute Ray Direction: Define three reference points in local space: Origin \mathbf{a} = [0, 0, 0]^T Rightmost \mathbf{b} = [1, 0, 0]^T Upmost \mathbf{c} = [0, 1, 0]^T Transform these points using \mathbf{M}: \mathbf{a}' = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}' = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}' = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{c} Compute the ray direction as the normalized cross product of the transformed right and up vectors: \mathbf{d}{ray} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{b}' - \mathbf{a}', \mathbf{c}' - \mathbf{a}')) 3. Compute Ray Origins: For each pixel (i, j) with normalized coordinate \mathbf{p}{norm} = [x{norm}, y{norm}, 0]^T: Scale the coordinate by S{cam}: \mathbf{p}{scaled} = [x{norm} \cdot S{cam}, y{norm} \cdot S{cam}, 0]^T Transform \mathbf{p}{scaled} by \mathbf{M} to get the world-space origin: \mathbf{o}{i,j} = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{p}{scaled} 4. Cast Rays: For each pixel (i, j), cast a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o}{i,j} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}{ray} into the volume data. Resample volume data planes in top-to-bottom order and cast rays in the viewing direction inside the projection planes to produce the image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateviewingplanerays(W, H, M, Scam=0.25, Psample=2.0): """ Generate rays for an orthographic viewing plane. Args: W: Image width H: Image height M: 4x4 transformation matrix (translation rotation scaling) Scam: Camera scale factor Psample: Sample period (used in ray marching, not generation) Returns: origins: List of vec3, size WH directions: List of vec3, size WH (all identical) """ def cross(u, v): return (u[1]v[2] - u[2]v[1], u[2]v[0] - u[0]v[2], u[0]v[1] - u[1]v[0]) def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def matvecmul(M, v): return ( M[0][0]v[0] + M[0][1]v[1] + M[0][2]v[2] + M[0][3], M[1][0]v[0] + M[1][1]v[1] + M[1][2]v[2] + M[1][3], M[2][0]v[0] + M[2][1]v[1] + M[2][2]v[2] + M[2][3]) origins = [] directions = [] # Step 2: Compute ray direction from transformation matrix a = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) b = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) c = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) aprime = matvecmul(M, a) bprime = matvecmul(M, b) cprime = matvecmul(M, c) rightvec = (bprime[0]-aprime[0], bprime[1]-aprime[1], bprime[2]-aprime[2]) upvec = (cprime[0]-aprime[0], cprime[1]-aprime[1], cprime[2]-aprime[2]) raydir = normalize(rightvec) # Step 1 & 3: Generate origins for each pixel for j in range(H): for i in range(W): xnorm = 2.0 (i + 0.5) / W - 1.0 ynorm = 2.0 (j + 0.5) / H - 1.0 xscaled = xnorm Scam yscaled = ynorm Scam pscaled = (xscaled, yscaled, 0.0) origin = matvecmul(M, pscaled) origins.append(origin) directions.append(raydir) # Ray marching and volume accumulation are not specified in the sources. return origins, directions Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \mathbf{M} is singular or degenerate, the cross product may yield a zero vector. Guard against this by checking the magnitude of the cross product before normalization. The normalization to [-1, 1] assumes a centered projection plane. Off-center cameras require an offset in the transformation matrix. Precision issues may arise if S{cam} is very small or very large, affecting the spatial distribution of origins. A specific instance of viewing plane ray generation for isometric views, defined by a height parameter. It generates parallel rays where the viewing direction is determined by the height setting, typically used for voxel-based rendering. Choose this when an isometric perspective is required without perspective distortion. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate all ray origins and directions. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the origins and directions. Performance: Linear scaling with image resolution. The direction computation is constant time per ray (all rays share the same direction in orthographic mode). Strengths: Simple, deterministic, no perspective distortion, efficient for parallel processing. Limitations: No depth cueing from perspective, limited to orthographic views. When to use: Isometric views, technical visualizations, voxel rendering where perspective is not desired. When not to use: Perspective views, scenes requiring depth-based field of view. The concept of projection plane raycasting originates from early volume rendering architectures, such as the VIRIM system, which used hardware-accelerated resampling and ray casting. The method was formalized in architectures for real-time volume rendering, emphasizing the separation of geometry resampling and ray casting. The specific implementation details, including the transformation matrix approach and normalization, are derived from modern implementations in procedural noise and voxel rendering libraries. name: Orthographic Projection
head: Parallel Projection, Size-Preserving Projection
body: Orthographic projection is a size-preserving mapping that flattens a 3D scene onto a 2D plane such that objects in the foreground occupy the same screen space as identical objects in the background, and parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the projection. It differs from perspective projection, which creates depth by scaling objects smaller with distance. It is a sibling to Viewing Plane Ray Generation and builds on Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Six clipping plane coordinates defining the view volume: fleft, fright (left/right), fdown, fup (bottom/top), fnear, ffar (near/far). Outputs: A projection matrix or transformed coordinates that map 3D world coordinates to the 2D viewport, discarding geometry outside the defined box. Data Structures: The view volume is defined as a box bounded by the six clipping planes. Steps: 1. Define the six clipping parameters: fleft, fright, fdown, fup, fnear, ffar. 2. Construct the orthographic projection matrix. 3. Apply the matrix to vertex coordinates, converting to homogeneous space if necessary. 4. Points outside the box defined by the clipping planes are clipped and not drawn. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orthographicprojectionmatrix(fleft, fright, fdown, fup, fnear, ffar): dx = fright - fleft dy = fup - fdown dz = ffar - fnear return [ [2.0 / dx, 0.0, 0.0, -(fright + fleft) / dx], [0.0, 2.0 / dy, 0.0, -(fup + fdown) / dy], [0.0, 0.0, -2.0 / dz, -(ffar + fnear) / dz], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] ] def applyprojection(matrix, point): x, y, z, w = point[0], point[1], point[2], point[3] newx = matrix[0][0] x + matrix[0][3] w newy = matrix[1][1] y + matrix[1][3] w newz = matrix[2][2] z + matrix[2][3] w neww = matrix[3][3] w return [newx / neww, newy / neww, newz / neww, neww] Parameters: fleft, fright: Left and right clipping plane x-coordinates. fdown, fup: Bottom and top clipping plane y-coordinates. fnear, ffar: Near and far clipping plane z-coordinates. Edge Cases: Clipping: Drawing does not occur outside the 3D region defined by the six clipping planes. Additional clipping: Up to six additional clipping planes parallel to the x, y, and z axes may be activated to hide geometry. A projection method that creates an illusion of depth by causing objects in the background to take up less screen space than the same sized object drawn in the foreground. It is selected via the View section of the Motion/View dialog box in Smokeview. It uses glFrustum with the same six clipping plane parameters (fleft, fright, fdown, fup, fnear, ffar) to define a truncated pyramid view frustum. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Size-preserving; objects maintain consistent screen space regardless of depth, making it suitable for technical visualization where scale accuracy is critical. Limitations: Objects are drawn at the same size regardless of distance, which differs from perspective projection that shortens objects at a distance. When to use: When visualizing data where relative sizes at different depths must remain accurate (e.g., fire dynamics simulation data). When not to use: When a realistic illusion of depth is required. Orthographic projection is a standard technique in computer graphics, implemented in OpenGL via glOrtho. It is used in Smokeview, a tool for visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation (FDS) data, to allow users to toggle between perspective and size-preserving views via the Motion/View dialog box. The implementation relies on the six clipping plane parameters to define the view volume. name: Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation
head: Ray Direction Computation, SampleStreamingPayload, Ray Generation from Pixels
body: Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation regenerates ray geometry (origin and direction) from stored pixel indices and camera parameters, enabling sample streaming and resumption in volume rendering pipelines. It maps pixel coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) and unprojects them to world space to compute unit-length direction vectors. Unlike static ray generation, this method is designed for payloads that persist across frames or batches, allowing rays to be reconstructed on-demand from minimal state. Inputs: pixelindex: Integer identifier for the pixel (often derived from framebuffer index). framesize: Tuple (W, H) representing image width and height. camera: Object or structure containing camera parameters, including: position: Camera origin in world space. direction, horizontal, vertical: Basis vectors defining the view frustum. c2w: Camera-to-world transformation matrix (4x4). focallength: Focal length parameter. unprojectpoints: Function/method to map NDC points to world space. getcameracenter: Function/method to retrieve camera origin. params: Configuration object containing light direction for shadow rays. Outputs: RayBundle or Ray structure containing: origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (numcameras, N, 3). directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (numcameras, N, 3) with unit length. samplepoints, samplelengths: Zero-initialized tensors for volume integration. Data Structures: RayBundle: A container holding origins, directions, and sample metadata. In PyTorch implementations, these are typically torch.Tensor objects. Ray (C++ style): Struct with fields org (vec3f), dir (vec3f), alpha (float), color (vec3f). Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create 2D grids of column (i) and row (j) indices. For streaming/pixel index approach: Compute ix and iy from pixelindex: ix = \text{pixel\index} \pmod W iy = \lfloor \text{pixel\index} / W \rfloor For full image generation: Create arrays x and y using np.linspace(0, W, endpoint=False) and np.linspace(0, H, endpoint=False). 2. Normalize to NDC Space: Map pixel coordinates to NDC space [-1, 1]. Using pixel indices: \text{screen}x = \frac{ix + 0.5}{W} \text{screen}y = \frac{iy + 0.5}{H} \text{ndc}x = 2 \cdot \text{screen}x - 1 \text{ndc}y = 2 \cdot \text{screen}y - 1 Using meshgrid: Stack y and x grids, reverse dimensions to shape (WH, 2), negate, and append 1 for homogeneous coordinates. 3. Unproject to World Space: Method A (Using Unproject Function): Concatenate 1 to NDC points to form homogeneous coordinates. Call camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpoints, fromndc=True) to get world space points worldpts. Get camera center rayso via camera.getcameracenter(). Repeat rayso for all pixels. Method B (Using Camera Basis): Compute raw directions in camera space: x = \frac{i - W/2}{f} y = -\frac{j - H/2}{f} z = -1 Combine with camera basis vectors u (x-axis), v (y-axis), w (z-axis): \text{raw\dir} = x \cdot u + y \cdot v + w 4. Compute Ray Origins: Method A: rayso is the camera center, broadcasted to match the number of rays. Method B: rayso is the translation part of the c2w matrix (last column). 5. Compute Ray Directions: Method A: \text{raw\dir} = \text{world\pts} - \text{rays\o} Method B: Rotate rawdir to world space using the upper-left 3x3 rotation submatrix of c2w: \text{rays\d} = \text{raw\dir} \cdot \text{c2w}{3\times3} 6. Normalize Directions: Compute L2 norm and divide: \text{norm} = \sqrt{\sum{k=1}^3 \text{rays\d}k^2} \text{rays\d} = \frac{\text{rays\d}}{\text{norm}} 7. Initialize Payload (Optional for Streaming): Set ray.alpha = alpha (passed parameter), ray.color = 0.f (shadow) or color (main), and initialize sample points/lengths to zero. Pseudocode (PyTorch-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computeraysfrompixels(pixelindices, imagesize, camera): """ Compute ray origins and directions from pixel indices. Args: pixelindices: Tensor of shape (N,) containing pixel indices. imagesize: Tuple (W, H). camera: Object with attributes: c2w: Tensor (4, 4) camera-to-world matrix. focallength: Float. getcameracenter(): Returns Tensor (3,) camera position. unprojectpoints(ndcpoints, fromndc=True): Returns Tensor (N, 3) world points. Returns: origins: Tensor (N, 3) directions: Tensor (N, 3) """ W, H = imagesize # Step 1: Compute screen coordinates from pixel index ix = pixelindices % W iy = pixelindices // W # Step 2: Normalize to NDC [-1, 1] # Add 0.5 for pixel center, then scale to [0, 1], then to [-1, 1] ndcx = 2.0 ((ix.float() + 0.5) / W) - 1.0 ndcy = 2.0 ((iy.float() + 0.5) / H) - 1.0 # Stack to (N, 2) ndcpoints2d = torch.stack([ndcx, ndcy], dim=-1) # Step 3: Unproject to world space # Append 1 for homogeneous coordinates ndcpointshomogeneous = torch.cat([ndcpoints2d, torch.oneslike(ndcpoints2d[..., -1:])], dim=-1) # Use camera's unproject function worldpts = camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpointshomogeneous, fromndc=True) # Step 4: Get camera origin rayso = camera.getcameracenter() # Broadcast origin to match number of rays rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(0).expand(worldpts.shape[0], -1) # Step 5: Compute directions raysd = worldpts - rayso # Step 6: Normalize directions norms = torch.linalg.norm(raysd, dim=1, keepdim=True) raysd = raysd / norms return rayso, raysd def computeraysfromgrid(imagesize, camera): """ Compute rays for all pixels in an image using grid generation. """ W, H = imagesize # Step 1: Create pixel grids x = torch.linspace(0, W, W, endpoint=False) y = torch.linspace(0, H, H, endpoint=False) # Step 2: Meshgrid and reshape # torch.meshgrid returns (H, W) grids. Stack and reshape to (WH, 2) ygrid, xgrid = torch.meshgrid(y, x, indexing='xy') xygrid = torch.stack([xgrid, ygrid], dim=-1).view(-1, 2) # Step 3: Normalize to NDC ndcx = 2.0 (xygrid[:, 0] / W) - 1.0 ndcy = 2.0 (xygrid[:, 1] / H) - 1.0 ndcpoints2d = torch.stack([ndcx, ndcy], dim=-1) # Step 4: Unproject ndcpointshomogeneous = torch.cat([ndcpoints2d, torch.oneslike(ndcpoints2d[..., -1:])], dim=-1) worldpts = camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpointshomogeneous, fromndc=True) # Step 5: Origins rayso = camera.getcameracenter() rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(0).expand(worldpts.shape[0], -1) # Step 6: Directions raysd = worldpts - rayso norms = torch.linalg.norm(raysd, dim=1, keepdim=True) raysd = raysd / norms return rayso, raysd Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in normalization can cause directions to deviate slightly from unit length. Re-normalization is recommended. Coordinate System: Ensure NDC space matches the camera's expected input (e.g., y-axis direction). Some implementations negate the NDC y-coordinate. The method originates from implementations in neural volume rendering and NeRF pipelines, where efficient ray generation is critical for training and rendering. The SampleStreamingPayload concept is used in instantVNR for resuming volume rendering tasks. The pixel-to-ray mapping via NDC unprojection is a standard technique in computer graphics, adapted here for deep learning-based volume rendering. name: OptiX Ray Generation & Traversal Setup
head: OptiX 7 Ray Generation, OptiX Ray Generation, Ray Generation Program
body: This method implements the ray generation and initial traversal setup for volume rendering within the NVIDIA OptiX 7 API. It computes pixel rays, initializes the random number generator (RNG) for anti-aliasing, and dispatches volume tracing via optixTrace. It differs from generic ray generation methods by integrating specific OptiX 7 launch parameters, SBT indexing, and visibility masks to restrict traversal to volume geometry. Inputs: Frame buffer dimensions: width w, height h. Camera parameters: position \mathbf{e}, direction vector, horizontal basis \mathbf{r}, vertical basis \mathbf{u}, focal length f, rotation angles \phi (phi) and \theta (theta). Launch parameters: frameindex, frame.size, camera struct. OptiX constants: VISIBILITYMASKVOLUME, MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE, MethodOptiX::RAYTYPECOUNT. Outputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel. Payload for optixTrace. Data Structures: RandomTEA: RNG state initialized with frameindex and fbIndex. vec2f/vec3f: 2D and 3D floating-point vectors for screen coordinates and ray data. uint32t payload: Packed pointer data for ray payload. Steps: 1. Thread Launch: Launch a CUDA kernel with w \times h threads. Threads are grouped into 8 \times 8 tiled blocks, consisting of two 32-thread wraps computed as SIMD vectors. 2. Pixel Indexing: Compute the framebuffer index: fbIndex = ix + iy frame.size.x. 3. RNG Initialization: Initialize the RNG state: rngstate = RandomTEA(frameindex, fbIndex). 4. Screen Coordinates: Determine 2D screen space coordinates. Compute normalized screen position: screen = vec2f((float)ix + 0.5, (float)iy + 0.5) / vec2f(frame.size). Convert to UV coordinates where top-left is [-1, 1] and bottom-right is [1, -1]. 5. name: Object Space Ray Setup
head: Camera Space Transformation for Ray Origin, Local Space Ray Setup, Object Space Ray Casting, Ray Origin Calculation for Near Plane Quad, Ray Casting Vertex Shader, RayCasterShaderCodeTester::NearPlaneVertexShader
body: Object Space Ray Setup constructs ray origins and directions within the local coordinate system of a mesh, ensuring that the raytraced volume moves, scales, and rotates rigidly with the object's transform. Unlike world-space ray generation, which treats the volume as a static window into the world, this method embeds the object's transformation directly into the ray parameters, allowing the raytraced geometry to behave like a physical part of the mesh. Inputs: v.vertex: The vertex position in local/object space. WorldSpaceCameraPos or ucamera: The camera position in world space. unityWorldToObject or inverse(modelMatrix): The matrix transforming world coordinates to object space. Outputs: rayOrigin: The starting point of the ray in object space. rayDirection: The direction of the ray in object space. Data Structures: The vertex shader output struct (v2f) contains: position (SVPOSITION): Clip-space position for rasterization. localPosition (TEXCOORD0, float4): The vertex position in local space, used as the ray origin. viewDirection (TEXCOORD1, float4): The unnormalized view vector in local space. Steps: 1. Transform the world-space camera position to object space by multiplying it with the world-to-object matrix. The w-component of the camera position vector must be 1.0 to include translation. 2. Set the ray origin to the vertex's local position. 3. Compute the unnormalized view direction by subtracting the object-space camera position from the local vertex position. 4. Pass localPosition and viewDirection to the fragment shader for interpolation. 5. In the fragment shader, normalize the view direction. Normalization must occur here, not in the vertex shader, because linear interpolation of vectors distorts their length, particularly on low-poly meshes or at close camera distances. Formulas: \mathbf{c}{obj} = \mathbf{M}{world \to obj} \times \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}{world} \\ 1.0 \end{bmatrix} Where \mathbf{c}{obj} is the camera position in object space, \mathbf{M}{world \to obj} is the inverse model matrix, and \mathbf{c}{world} is the camera position in world space. \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{v}{local} Where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin and \mathbf{v}{local} is the vertex position in local space. \mathbf{d}{raw} = \mathbf{v}{local} - \mathbf{c}{obj} Where \mathbf{d}{raw} is the raw unnormalized view direction vector. \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{d}{raw}\|} Where \mathbf{d} is the normalized ray direction. Parameters: Typical values for ray marching step count and step size are not specified by this setup method; they depend on the downstream marching algorithm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: W-Component Error: If the camera position is transformed with a w-component of 0, the translation component of the inverse matrix is ignored, resulting in incorrect ray origins that only account for rotation and scale. Interpolation Distortion: Normalizing the view direction in the vertex shader leads to incorrect angles in the fragment shader due to perspective-correct interpolation artifacts, especially visible on low-poly objects or close camera distances. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vertexsetup(vertexlocal, cameraworld, worldtoobjectmatrix): # Compute clip-space position for rasterization # clipposition =... # Store local position as ray origin localposition = vertexlocal # Transform camera world position to object space # w-component must be 1.0 to include translation # cameraobj = worldtoobjectmatrix vec4(cameraworld, 1.0) cameraobj = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Matrix-vector multiplication # Compute unnormalized view direction in local space viewdirection = vertexlocal - cameraobj return { 'clipposition': None, 'localposition': localposition, 'viewdirection': viewdirection } def fragmentsetup(vertexoutput): # Normalize direction in fragment shader to avoid interpolation distortion rawdir = vertexoutput['viewdirection'] length = math.sqrt(sum(c c for c in rawdir)) dir = [c / length for c in rawdir] # Use local position as ray origin rayorigin = vertexoutput['localposition'] return rayorigin, dir This variant explicitly details the construction of the ray origin in volume texture space by transforming a vertex from the near plane quad through inverse view and model transformations, followed by scaling and translation to align with the volume grid. It differs from camera-space ray setup by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Strengths: Ensures the raytraced volume is rigidly attached to the mesh, simplifying animation and transformation logic. Intuitive for single-object rendering. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method originates from basic sphere tracing and ray marching tutorials, where object-space rendering is preferred for its simplicity and intuitive handling of object transformations. head: Ray Origin Calculation for Near Plane Quad, RayCasterShaderCodeTester::NearPlaneVertexShader
body: This method calculates the ray origin in volume texture space for a given vertex on the near plane quad, used for testing ray casting shaders. It transforms a vertex from view space to world space using the inverse model-view matrix, then translates and scales it into the local volume coordinate system. It differs from camera-space ray setup [4179-object-space-ray-setup-camera-space-transformation-for-ray-o.md] by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Inputs: glvertex: Vertex position in view space (4D vector). inversemodelviewmatrix: 4×4 matrix transforming view space to world space. voltranslation: 3D translation vector of the volume in world space. volscale: Scalar scale factor of the volume in world space. projectionmatrix: 4×4 projection matrix for clipping. Outputs: glposition: Clip-space position for rasterization. rayposition: Ray origin in volume texture space (normalized 0–1 range, 4D vector). Data Structures: Vectors and matrices are standard 3D/4D floating-point arrays. Matrix multiplication uses standard linear algebra conventions. Steps: 1. Compute the clip-space position: glposition = projectionmatrix @ glvertex. 2. Transform the vertex from view space to world space: worldpos = inversemodelviewmatrix @ glvertex. 3. Extract the 3D position: rayposition = worldpos[:3]. 4. Translate the position to volume-local space: rayposition = rayposition - voltranslation. 5. Scale the position to volume-local space: rayposition = rayposition / volscale. 6. Offset the position to center it in texture coordinates: rayposition = rayposition + 0.5. 7. Pack the result into a 4D vector: rayposition = [rayposition[0], rayposition[1], rayposition[2], 1.0]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NearPlaneVertexShader(glvertex, inversemodelviewmatrix, voltranslation, volscale, projectionmatrix): # Step 1: Compute clip-space position glposition = projectionmatrix @ glvertex # Step 2: Transform vertex from view space to world space worldpos = inversemodelviewmatrix @ glvertex # Step 3: Extract 3D position rayposition = worldpos[:3] # Step 4: Translate to volume-local space rayposition = rayposition - voltranslation # Step 5: Scale to volume-local space rayposition = rayposition / volscale # Step 6: Offset to center in texture coordinates rayposition = rayposition + 0.5 # Step 7: Pack result rayposition = [rayposition[0], rayposition[1], rayposition[2], 1.0] return glposition, rayposition Parameters: VolTranslation: 3D translation vector of the volume in world space. VolScale: Scalar scale factor of the volume in world space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise if the volume is very large or very small. Boundaries: The method assumes the volume is a unit cube centered at the origin in texture space. If the volume is not a unit cube, the offset and scale may need adjustment. Degenerate Input: If VolScale is zero, division by zero will occur. This method establishes the geometric foundation for GPU-based volume raycasting by mapping a 3D bounding box (typically a unit cube) to screen space while simultaneously computing normalized 3D texture coordinates for each fragment. It solves the problem of translating object-space vertex positions into both clip-space positions for rasterization and valid texture lookup coordinates for the fragment shader. It differs from camera-space ray setup [4179-object-space-ray-setup-camera-space-transformation-for-ray-o.md] by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the VoxVizThesis repository. It is used in the context of volume rendering, specifically for testing ray casting shaders. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Object Space Ray Setup via Vertex Shader UV Computation
head: GPU Raycasting (Vertex Shader UV Computation), Raycasting Bounding Box & Sample Position Setup, Vertex Shader UV Computation
body: This method establishes the geometric foundation for GPU-based volume raycasting by mapping a 3D bounding box to screen space while simultaneously computing normalized 3D texture coordinates for each fragment. It solves the problem of translating object-space vertex positions into both clip-space positions for rasterization and valid texture lookup coordinates for the fragment shader. It differs from camera-space ray setup [4179-object-space-ray-setup-camera-space-transformation-for-ray-o.md] by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Object-space vertex positions (vVertex), Model-View-Projection matrix (MVP). Output: Clip-space position (glPosition), 3D texture coordinates (vUV). Data Structures: Vertex Buffer Object (VBO): Stores vertex positions with layout totalVertices sizeof(glm::vec3). Index Buffer Object (IBO): Stores triangle indices with layout totalIndices sizeof(GLuint). Vertex Array Object (VAO): Binds the VBO and IBO, enabling the vertex attribute array for vVertex at location 0 with 3 components, GLFLOAT, normalized false, stride 0, offset 0. Steps: 1. Buffer Initialization: Generate and bind a VAO. Allocate memory for vertices and indices. Fill the vertex buffer with the bounding box geometry (e.g., a cube centered at the origin with bounds [-0.5, 0.5]). Fill the index buffer with triangle indices. Enable the vertex attribute array for vVertex and bind the index buffer. 2. Vertex Shader Execution: For each vertex, compute the clip-space position by multiplying the MVP matrix with the homogeneous vertex position: \text{gl\Position} = \text{MVP} \times \begin{bmatrix} \text{vVertex}.xyz \\ 1.0 \end{bmatrix}. Compute the 3D texture coordinates by adding 0.5 to each component of the object-space vertex position, shifting the range from [-0.5, 0.5] to [0.0, 1.0] for normalized texture lookups: \text{vUV} = \text{vVertex}.xyz + 0.5. Declare vUV as smooth out vec3 to enable hardware interpolation across the primitive. 3. Fragment Shader Input: The fragment shader receives the interpolated vUV values, which represent the position within the volume texture space for direct sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevertexsetup(vVertex: tuple[float, float, float], MVP: list[list[float]]) -> tuple[tuple[float, float, float, float], tuple[float, float, float]]: """ Computes clip-space position and 3D texture coordinates for a single vertex. Args: vVertex: Object-space vertex position (x, y, z). MVP: Combined Model-View-Projection matrix (4x4 list of lists). Returns: glPosition: Clip-space position (x, y, z, w). vUV: 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w). """ # Homogeneous vertex position vertexh = (vVertex[0], vVertex[1], vVertex[2], 1.0) # Matrix-vector multiplication for clip space glPosition = tuple( sum(MVP[row][col] vertexh[col] for col in range(4)) for row in range(4)) # Shift unit cube coordinates from [-0.5, 0.5] to [0, 1] vUV = (vVertex[0] + 0.5, vVertex[1] + 0.5, vVertex[2] + 0.5) return glPosition, vUV Parameters: MVP: Combined Model-View-Projection matrix, passed as a uniform mat4. vVertex: Object-space vertex position, declared as layout(location = 0) in vec3. vUV: 3D texture coordinates, declared as smooth out vec3 in the vertex shader and smooth in vec3 in the fragment shader. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Range: The unit cube is typically centered at the origin with bounds [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5] to [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]. Failing to add 0.5 to the vertex coordinates will result in texture coordinates outside the [0, 1] range, causing incorrect sampling or clamping artifacts. Not given in the sources. This method is used in GPU-based volume raycasting implementations, particularly in educational and open-source projects. It relies on standard OpenGL features such as vertex shaders, fragment shaders, and texture sampling. The approach of using a unit cube and shifting coordinates is a common technique in computer graphics for simplifying texture coordinate generation. mversiotech/volume-rendering-demo, https://github.com/mversiotech/volume-rendering-demo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) aashish24/vtkvolume, https://github.com/aashish24/vtkvolume, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Custom Frustum Ray Generation via Vertex Z-Index
head: CustomGraphicsBlit, Frustum Corner Indexing, Ray Direction Assignment via Frustum Corners
body: This method generates per-pixel ray directions for volume rendering by encoding the index of pre-computed frustum corner vectors into the Z-coordinate of a full-screen quad's vertices, allowing the vertex shader to look up the correct ray direction from a uniform array. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding per-fragment matrix multiplications for direction calculation, instead using a discrete lookup based on vertex attributes. It differs from Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader by performing the direction selection in the vertex shader rather than the fragment shader, reducing redundant calculations for adjacent pixels sharing the same vertex. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A full-screen quad (typically two triangles or one quad) with UV coordinates (u,v) \in [0,1]^2. The quad vertices carry a custom Z-coordinate representing an index. Uniforms: FrustumCornersES: A float4x4 (or array of float3) containing the eye-space coordinates of the four frustum corners. CameraInvViewMatrix: A float4x4 inverse view matrix to transform eye-space rays to world-space. MainTexTexelSize: A float4 containing texture dimensions, used to detect UV orientation. Output: A fragment shader input ray (world-space direction vector) and standard position/UV attributes. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer: Contains 4 vertices. Each vertex has: position: float3 (or float4). X and Y are screen-space UVs (0 or 1). Z is the corner index (0-3). uv: float2 (0 or 1). Uniform Array FrustumCornersES: Index 0: Top-Left (TL) corner direction in eye-space. Index 1: Top-Right (TR) corner direction in eye-space. Index 2: Bottom-Right (BR) corner direction in eye-space. Index 3: Bottom-Left (BL) corner direction in eye-space. Note: The mapping of indices to corners depends on the specific blit implementation. The source uses indices 3, 2, 1, 0 for vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1) respectively, mapping to BL, BR, TR, TL. Numbered Steps: 1. Prepare Frustum Corners (CPU Side): Calculate the four frustum corner directions in camera space for the current camera using Camera.CalculateFrustumCorners with a full-screen rect (0,0,1,1). These vectors are passed to the shader as FrustumCornersES. 2. Issue Full-Screen Quad with Custom Z-Indices (CPU/GPU API Side): Draw a full-screen quad. For each of the four vertices, set the Z-coordinate of the vertex position to the index of the corresponding frustum corner. Vertex 1: UV (0,0), Z = 3 (BL) Vertex 2: UV (1,0), Z = 2 (BR) Vertex 3: UV (1,1), Z = 1 (TR) Vertex 4: UV (0,1), Z = 0 (TL) Note: An orthographic projection matrix is used to ensure these Z-values are passed through unchanged to the vertex shader. 3. Vertex Shader Processing: For each vertex: a. Extract the index from the vertex Z-coordinate: index = v.vertex.z. b. Reset the vertex Z-coordinate to a standard depth value (e.g., 0.1) to ensure correct projection and depth buffering: v.vertex.z = 0.1. c. Transform the vertex position using the model-view-projection matrix: o.pos = mul(UNITYMATRIXMVP, v.vertex). d. Pass the UV coordinates to the fragment shader. If the texture starts at the top (detected by MainTexTexelSize.y < 0), flip the Y-coordinate: o.uv.y = 1 - o.uv.y. e. Look up the eye-space ray direction using the extracted index: o.rayes = FrustumCornersES[(int)index].xyz. The retrieved eye-space ray is normalized. f. Transform the eye-space ray direction to world-space: o.rayws = mul(CameraInvViewMatrix, float4(o.rayes, 0)). Since it is a direction, the translation component of the inverse view matrix is zeroed out by the homogeneous coordinate. 4. Fragment Shader: Interpolate the ray vector across the screen. Use this world-space direction for raymarching. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def customgraphicsblit(source, destination, material, passidx): RenderTexture.active = destination material.SetPass(passidx) material.SetMatrix("FrustumCornersES", getfrustumcornerseyespace()) material.SetMatrix("CameraInvViewMatrix", camera.inverseviewmatrix) beginquads() setuv(0.0, 0.0); setvertex(0.0, 0.0, 3.0) setuv(1.0, 0.0); setvertex(1.0, 0.0, 2.0) setuv(1.0, 1.0); setvertex(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) setuv(0.0, 1.0); setvertex(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) endquads() RenderTexture.active = None def vertexshader(vertex, uv, frustumcornerses, camerainvviewmatrix, texelsize): index = int(vertex.z) vertex.z = 0.1 pos = matmul(UNITYMATRIXMVP, vertex) outuv = uv.xy if texelsize.y < 0: outuv.y = 1.0 - outuv.y rayes = frustumcornerses[index][:3] rayws = matmul(camerainvviewmatrix, (rayes[0], rayes[1], rayes[2], 0.0))[:3] return pos, outuv, rayws Parameters: FrustumCornersES: float4x4 uniform. Contains 4 vectors representing the eye-space directions to the four corners of the frustum. CameraInvViewMatrix: float4x4 uniform. The inverse of the camera's view matrix. MainTexTexelSize: float4 uniform. Used to detect UV orientation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: UV Orientation: On some platforms, textures may start at the top-left, requiring Y-flipping of UVs. This is handled by checking MainTexTexelSize.y < 0. Index Mapping: The mapping between vertex Z-index and frustum corner must be consistent between the CPU-side quad generation and the shader's lookup table. Precision: Using Z-coordinate for index storage relies on the vertex shader receiving the exact integer value. Floating-point precision issues are unlikely for small integers (0-3) in standard vertex formats. Degenerate Input: If the camera has no frustum (e.g., invalid projection), the corner vectors may be undefined. A method to compute the four frustum corner directions in camera space using Camera.CalculateFrustumCorners with a full-screen rect (0,0,1,1), far clip plane, and mono eye. The corners are then transformed from camera space to world space using only rotation (via TransformDirection), as rays are directions, not points. The resulting four world-space direction vectors (FrustumCornerTR, FrustumCornerBR, FrustumCornerTL, FrustumCornerBL) are passed to the shader as uniform vectors. This variant pre-computes world-space directions directly, potentially simplifying the vertex shader by removing the need for CameraInvViewMatrix multiplication. A geometry shader-based approach that generates a full-screen quad representing the projection plane of the sensor (e.g., Kinect) in world space. The quad is generated by creating 4 vertices with normalized device coordinates (e.g., -1.0, 1.0, 0.01, 1.0) and calculating the world space position by multiplying half-window size coordinates with the inverse view matrix: Pos = mul(float4(-cb\f2HalfWinSize.x, cb\f2HalfWinSize.y, 1, 1), cb\mInvView). Texture coordinates are set to map screen space (0,0) to (WinReso.x, WinReso.y). Parameters include cbf2HalfWinSize (half resolution) and cbmInvView (inverse view matrix). This method is more explicit about world-space positioning but requires a geometry shader stage. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for ray direction calculation, as it is a simple array lookup and matrix multiplication in the vertex shader, interpolated to fragments. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the 4 frustum corner vectors and the inverse view matrix. Strengths: Simple implementation, minimal GPU overhead, works well with standard image effect pipelines. Limitations: Only supports 4 discrete ray directions (corners), which may cause visible artifacts if the frustum is highly distorted or if high precision is required across the screen. When to use: When rendering volume data with a perspective camera and performance is critical, and the 4-corner approximation is sufficient for the visual quality required. This technique was popularized in the context of Unity game engine image effects and raymarching shaders. It is described in Adrian Bolboaca's blog post "Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation". The method leverages the flexibility of custom blit functions in Unity to pass additional data (the corner index) via the vertex Z-coordinate, which is otherwise unused in a standard orthographic blit. It is a common pattern in real-time raymarching for volumetric effects and distance field rendering. name: Ray Origin Offset Noise
head: Noise Generation for Ray Offset, Ray Offset Noise
body: Ray Origin Offset Noise is a technique that perturbs the starting position of a ray march to avoid banding artifacts. It differs from its sibling Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by adding stochastic variation to the ray origin rather than strictly adhering to pixel centers, and from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by focusing on initialization jitter rather than payload management during traversal. Inputs: uv: A 2D vector representing the normalized screen or grid coordinates of the current sample. unitVector: A constant 2D vector used to break spatial correlation. Outputs: r: A pseudo-random floating-point value in the range [0, 1). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required; the function is stateless and computes the random value on demand based on input coordinates. Steps: 1. Scale unitVector by the constant 79.30408. 2. Compute the dot product of uv and the scaled vector. 3. Apply the sine function to the dot product result. 4. Multiply the sine output by 43758.5453. 5. Extract the fractional part of the product to yield r. Formula: r = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(uv, \text{unitVector} \times 79.30408)) \times 43758.5453) Where: \text{dot}(a, b) is the dot product of vectors a and b. \text{fract}(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor. \text{unitVector} is a constant 2D vector; its specific components are not detailed in the source. Parameters: unitVector: A constant 2D vector. 79.30408: A constant scaling factor applied to unitVector. 43758.5453: A constant multiplier. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of sine and large constants can lead to precision issues on some hardware; intermediate calculations should maintain sufficient precision to avoid pattern repetition. Correlation: The choice of unitVector and the scaling factor is critical to minimize spatial correlation between adjacent samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayoriginoffsetnoise(uv: tuple, unitvector: tuple) -> float: """Generates a pseudo-random value to offset the ray origin.""" scale = 79.30408 dotproduct = uv[0] (unitvector[0] scale) + uv[1] (unitvector[1] scale) sinval = math.sin(dotproduct) multiplied = sinval 43758.5453 fractionalpart = multiplied - math.floor(multiplied) return fractionalpart A hash-based pseudo-random number generator maps integer or floating-point coordinates to a deterministic pseudo-random value in the range [0, 1) or [-1, 1] using transcendental functions (typically sine) or multiplicative mixing. It generates independent values based on spatial coordinates, ensuring that the same coordinate always yields the same random value across different frames and devices. body: Deterministic LCG Noise Generation is a pseudo-random number generator that produces normalized floating-point values in the range [-1, 1] using linear congruential recurrence and bit-shifting normalization. It is used in volume rendering to provide deterministic noise for ray origin offsetting, thereby avoiding banding artifacts during ray marching [Parent]. It differs from hash-based pseudo-random number generators by relying on sequential state updates rather than spatial hashing, and from incremental random number generation methods by its fixed modular arithmetic structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A seed value representing the initial state. Output: A normalized float v in the range [-1, 1) or [-1, 1] depending on the variant. Data Structures: The generator maintains a single state variable. Two variants are documented: 1. 32-bit variant: A single 32-bit unsigned integer (u32) state field. 2. 64-bit variant: A single 64-bit unsigned integer (u64) state field. Parameters: 32-bit constants: Multiplier a = 1664525, Increment c = 1013904223. 64-bit constants: Multiplier a = 6364136223846793005, Increment c = 1442695040888963407. These are the Numerical Recipes constants. Modulus: Implicitly 2^{32} for the 32-bit variant and 2^{64} for the 64-bit variant, implemented via wrapping arithmetic. Steps: 1. Update State: Compute the next state using the linear congruential formula: x{n+1} = (xn \cdot a + c) \pmod M where M = 2^{32} or 2^{64}, and arithmetic is performed with wrapping (modulo 2^k). 2. Extract Bits: For the 32-bit variant: Shift the state right by 8 bits (state >> 8) to extract the top 24 bits. For the 64-bit variant: Shift the state right by 40 bits (state >> 40) to extract the top 24 bits. 3. Normalize: Convert the extracted integer bits to a float in [-1, 1). For the 32-bit variant: Scale the 24-bit integer to [0, 1) and then to [-1, 1] via v = (\text{bits} / 2^{24}) \cdot 2.0 - 1.0. For the 64-bit variant: Cast the shifted value to f32 and divide by 8388608.0 (2^{23}), then subtract 1.0: v = (\text{bits} / 8388608.0) - 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Produces values in [-1, 1]. Produces values in [-1, 1). Uses Numerical Recipes constants. """ state = seed & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF # Step 1: Update state with wrapping arithmetic state = (state 6364136223846793005 + 1442695040888963407) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF # Step 2: Extract top 24 bits bits = state >> 40 # Step 3: Normalize to [-1, 1) val = (bits / 8388608.0) - 1.0 return val Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The 64-bit variant casts to f32 after shifting, which preserves the top 24 bits but discards lower precision. body: A hash-based pseudo-random number generator maps integer or floating-point coordinates to a deterministic pseudo-random value in the range [0, 1) or [-1, 1] using arithmetic operations. It solves the problem of generating unique, seemingly random offsets for ray origins or lattice indices without storing large lookup tables. It is distinguished from Incremental Random Number Generation by its coordinate-based determinism rather than state-based iteration, and from Deterministic Integer Hashing by its reliance on floating-point sine functions rather than bitwise integer operations. Inputs: A coordinate vector p (typically vec2 or vec3). Outputs: A single floating-point value r \in 0, 1). Data Structures: None. Pure arithmetic functions. Parameters: Constants for the sine-based hash: C1 = 127.1, C2 = 311.7 (for 2D); C3 = 74.7 (for 3D); Multiplier M = 43758.5453123. Constants for the sin-free hash: K = 0.1031, B = 33.33. Steps (Sin-based variant): 1. Compute the dot product of the input coordinate p and a constant vector c: h = p \cdot c. 2. Apply the sine function: s = \sin(h). 3. Scale by the multiplier: v = s \times M. 4. Extract the fractional part: r = v - \lfloor v \rfloor. Steps (Sin-free variant): 1. Scale the input p by K: p' = p \times K. 2. Compute a dot product of p' with itself plus a bias: d = p' \cdot (p' + B). 3. Combine components and extract the fractional part. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Constants from.""" h = px 127.1 + py 311.7 s = math.sin(h) v = s 43758.5453123 return v - math.floor(v) def hashsin3d(px: float, py: float, pz: float) -> float: """Sin-based hash for 3D coordinates. Constants from.""" h = px 127.1 + py 311.7 + pz 74.7 s = math.sin(h) v = s 43758.5453123 return v - math.floor(v) def hashsinfree2d(px: float, py: float) -> float: """Sin-free hash for 2D coordinates. Constants from.""" # vec3 p3 = fract(vec3(p.xyx).1031) p3x = px 0.1031 - math.floor(px 0.1031) p3y = py 0.1031 - math.floor(py 0.1031) p3z = px 0.1031 - math.floor(px 0.1031) # p.xyx -> x, y, x # p3 += dot(p3, p3.yzx + 33.33) # p3.yzx maps to (p3y, p3z, p3x) dotval = p3x (p3y + 33.33) + p3y (p3z + 33.33) + p3z (p3x + 33.33) p3x += dotval p3y += dotval p3z += dotval # return fract((p3.x + p3.y) p3.z) return (p3x + p3y) p3z - math.floor((p3x + p3y) p3z) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Sensitivity: The sin-based hash relies on the precision of the sine function and floating-point multiplication. When not to use: High-quality Monte Carlo integration, cryptographic applications, or when bit-exact reproducibility across different hardware architectures is required. body: Deterministic integer hashing provides a platform-independent method for generating pseudo-random integers from integer coordinates, ensuring identical bit-exact results between CPU (TypeScript) and GPU (GLSL) environments. It solves the reproducibility problem in procedural content generation where floating-point sine-based hashing drifts due to library implementation differences. Unlike floating-point sine hashing, this method uses only 32-bit bitwise operations and multiplication, guaranteeing consistent wrapping behavior for negative coordinates. Inputs and Outputs: uhash takes a 32-bit unsigned integer x and returns a 32-bit unsigned integer h. hashCell takes three 32-bit signed integers cx, cy, cz and returns a 32-bit unsigned integer h. hashToFloat takes a 32-bit unsigned integer h and returns a 32-bit float f in 0, 1). Data Structures: All intermediate values are 32-bit unsigned integers (uint32). Multiplication uses 32-bit wrapping semantics (modulo 2^{32}). Parameters: uhash multipliers are M{u1} = \text{0x7feb352d} and M{u2} = \text{0x846ca68b}. hashCell multipliers are M{cx} = \text{0x9e3779b9}, M{cy} = \text{0x85ebca6b}, and M{cz} = \text{0xc2b2ae35}. computehash constants are M0 = 2860486313\text{U} and M1 = 3267000013\text{U}. Steps: 1. Base Mixer (uhash): Mix the input integer x using a sequence of XOR shifts and multiplications: \begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow x \oplus (x \gg 16) \\ x &\leftarrow x \times M{u1} \\ x &\leftarrow x \oplus (x \gg 15) \\ x &\leftarrow x \times M{u2} \\ x &\leftarrow x \oplus (x \gg 16) \\ \text{return } x \gg 0 \end{aligned} The final >>> 0 or x >> 0 ensures the result is treated as an unsigned 32-bit integer, masking out any sign extension if the language treats shifts differently on signed types. 2. 3D [Coordinate Hashing (hashCell): Combine three integer coordinates into a single hash: \begin{aligned} h &\leftarrow \text{uhash}(cx \times M{cx}) \\ h &\leftarrow \text{uhash}(h \oplus (cy \times M{cy})) \\ h &\leftarrow \text{uhash}(h \oplus (cz \times M{cz})) \\ \text{return } h \gg 0 \end{aligned} Negative coordinates are handled naturally because the multiplication and XOR operations on 32-bit integers wrap identically to GLSL's uint(int) cast. 3. Float Conversion (hashToFloat): Map the integer hash to a float in 0, 1): f = \frac{h \gg 8}{16777216.0} Shifting right by 8 bits discards the lower 8 bits, leaving the top 24 bits. This ensures the value fits within the 24-bit mantissa of a 32-bit IEEE 754 float without precision loss during conversion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uhash(x: int) -> int: x = x & 0xFFFFFFFF x ^= (x >> 16) x = (x 0x7feb352d) & 0xFFFFFFFF x ^= (x >> 15) x = (x 0x846ca68b) & 0xFFFFFFFF x ^= (x >> 16) return x & 0xFFFFFFFF def hashCell(cx: int, cy: int, cz: int) -> int: MCX = 0x9e3779b9 MCY = 0x85ebca6b MCZ = 0xc2b2ae35 h = uhash(cx MCX) h = uhash(h ^ (cy MCY)) h = uhash(h ^ (cz MCZ)) return h def hashToFloat(h: int) -> float: return (h >> 8) / 16777216.0 def computehashbyteslice(data: list) -> int: M0 = 2860486313 M1 = 3267000013 h = M0 for b in data: h = ((h ^ b) M1) & 0xFFFFFFFF return h Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Integer hashing handles negative inputs correctly because 32-bit two's complement arithmetic wraps consistently across platforms. Precision Loss: Using the full 32-bit integer directly in a float conversion would lose precision because the mantissa only holds 24 bits. The >> 8 shift is critical. Platform Drift: Avoid sin() or cos() for hashing if CPU and GPU code share the same hash function, as math library implementations may differ slightly.
