name: Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader
head: Fragment shader ray tracing, Fragment Shader Ray Generation, Ray Tracing Fragment Shader
body: This method generates camera rays for ray tracing by rendering a single quad to the screen, allowing the fragment shader to compute the ray origin and direction for each pixel using interpolated vertex coordinates. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding explicit matrix multiplications in favor of geometric basis vectors derived from camera parameters, and from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection through a viewing plane distance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Window resolution (iResolution), camera position (iRayOrigin), camera facing direction (iRayDir), camera up direction (iRayUp), distance to viewing plane (iPlaneDist), and interpolated texture coordinates (texCoord) ranging from (0,0) to (1,1) across the quad. Outputs: A ray (origin and direction) for each pixel, which is then used for intersection testing and shading. Data Structures: Uniforms: iResolution (vec2), iRayOrigin (vec3), iRayDir (vec3), iRayUp (vec3), iPlaneDist (float). Varying/Input: texCoord (vec2) interpolated from vertex attributes (0,0) to (1,1). Steps: 1. Setup Geometry: Render a single quad (two triangles covering the screen) using a minimal vertex shader that performs no transformations. 2. Compute Normalized Coordinates: In the fragment shader, convert the interpolated texCoord (range [0,1]) to a normalized device coordinate p (range [-1,1]): p = 2.0 \cdot \text{texCoord} - 1.0 3. Apply Aspect Ratio: Scale the x-component of p by the aspect ratio to prevent distortion: p.x = p.x \cdot \frac{\text{iResolution}.x}{\text{iResolution}.y} 4. Compute Camera Basis Vectors: Calculate the camera's right vector (camSide) using the cross product of the forward (iRayDir) and up (iRayUp) vectors: \text{camSide} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{iRayDir}, \text{iRayUp})) 5. Calculate Ray Direction: Compute the ray direction by combining the basis vectors scaled by p and the viewing plane distance: \text{raydir} = \text{normalize}(p.x \cdot \text{camSide} + p.y \cdot \text{iRayUp} + \text{iPlaneDist} \cdot \text{iRayDir}) 6. Set Ray Origin: The ray origin is the camera position: \text{rayorig} = \text{iRayOrigin} 7. Trace and Shade: Use the generated ray to perform intersection tests (e.g., sphere tracing) and compute the final color. Apply Lambertian shading with albedo 0.8, light intensity 8.0, light direction vec3(-0.2, 1.0, -0.3), and shadow bias 0.0001. Formulas: Normalized coordinates: p = 2.0 \cdot \text{texCoord} - 1.0. Aspect-scaled coordinates: p.x = p.x \cdot \frac{\text{iResolution}.x}{\text{iResolution}.y}. Ray direction: \text{raydir} = \text{normalize}(p.x \cdot \text{camSide} + p.y \cdot \text{iRayUp} + \text{iPlaneDist} \cdot \text{iRayDir}). Sphere intersection parameter: t = \begin{cases} t1 & \text{if } t1 < t2 \land t1 \ge 0 \\ t2 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, where t1 = -OdotD + \sqrt{\text{base}}, t2 = -OdotD - \sqrt{\text{base}}, \text{base} = OdotD^2 - OdotO + \text{radius}^2, OdotD = \text{dot}(\text{rayorig} - \text{pos}, \text{raydir}), and OdotO = \text{dot}(\text{rayorig} - \text{pos}, \text{rayorig} - \text{pos}). Lambertian diffuse shading: L = \frac{\text{albedo}}{\pi} \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot -\mathbf{l}) I{\text{light}}. Parameters: iPlaneDist: Controls the field of view. A smaller value results in a wider FOV. iResolution: Window dimensions in pixels. albedo: 0.8. lightintensity: 8.0. lightdirection: vec3(-0.2, 1.0, -0.3). shadowbias: 0.0001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aspect Ratio Distortion: Failing to scale the x-coordinate by the aspect ratio (width/height) will distort the field of view, making circles appear as ellipses. Camera Basis Orthogonality: The camSide vector is computed via cross(iRayDir, iRayUp). If iRayUp is not orthogonal to iRayDir, the resulting basis is not orthonormal, leading to skewed rays. Winding Order: The quad's vertex winding order determines the interpolation direction of texCoord. Ensure the quad covers the screen correctly (e.g., vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1)) and that the interpolation maps to screen space correctly (bottom-left to top-right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeraydirection(texcoord, resolution, raydir, rayup, planedist): p = [2.0 texcoord[0] - 1.0, 2.0 texcoord[1] - 1.0] p[0] = resolution[0] / resolution[1] camside = normalize(cross(raydir, rayup)) raydir = normalize([p[0] camside[0] + p[1] rayup[0] + planedist raydir[0], p[0] camside[1] + p[1] rayup[1] + planedist raydir[1], p[0] camside[2] + p[1] rayup[2] + planedist raydir[2]]) return raydir def tracesphere(rayorig, raydir, pos, radius): OdotD = dot(rayorig, raydir) - dot(pos, raydir) OdotO = dot(rayorig, rayorig) - 2.0 dot(rayorig, pos) + dot(pos, pos) base = OdotD OdotD - OdotO + radius radius if base >= 0: root = math.sqrt(base) t1 = -OdotD + root t2 = -OdotD - root if t1 >= 0 or t2 >= 0: t = t1 if (t1 < t2 and t1 >= 0) else t2 pt = [rayorig[i] + raydir[i] t for i in range(3)] normal = normalize([pt[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)]) return {"point": pt, "normal": normal, "t": t, "hit": True} return {"point": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "normal": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "t": -1.0, "hit": False} def shadelambertian(hitpoint, normal, lightdir, albedo, lightintensity, shadowbias): lightdirnorm = normalize(lightdir) diff = max(0.0, dot(normal, [-lightdirnorm[i] for i in range(3)])) return (albedo / math.pi) diff lightintensity def main(): rayorig = iRayOrigin raydir = computeraydirection(texCoord, iResolution, iRayDir, iRayUp, iPlaneDist) hit = tracesphere(rayorig, raydir, spherepos, sphereradius) if hit["hit"]: lightdir = [-0.2, 1.0, -0.3] color = shadelambertian(hit["point"], hit["normal"], lightdir, 0.8, 8.0, 0.0001) else: color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] fragColor = [color[0], color[1], color[2], 1.0] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, leverages GPU interpolation, minimal geometry overhead. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This technique is a fundamental approach to GPU ray tracing, popularized by educational resources and demos. It allows developers to implement ray tracing in the fragment shader without complex vertex transformations, making it accessible for learning and simple applications. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) mxbrt/svo, https://github.com/mxbrt/svo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Further Graphics - University of Cambridge, https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1819/FGraphics/1.%20Ray%20Marching%20and%20Signed%20Distance%20Fields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Position Calculation
head: Depth to 3D Points Conversion (Ray-based), Query Point Sampling, Ray-based Point Reconstruction, Rendered Point Cloud Reconstruction
body: Ray Position Calculation computes the 3D spatial coordinates of sampling points (query points) along camera rays within specified near and far depth bounds. It solves the problem of discretizing a continuous ray into a finite set of 3D locations for volume rendering or neural radiance field evaluation. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by taking generated rays and sampling specific positions along them rather than producing the ray vectors themselves. It differs from World Space Position Reconstruction by generating positions along a parametric ray direction rather than reconstructing a single point from depth buffers. Inputs: rayorigins: torch.Tensor of shape (W, H, 3), containing the 3D origin for each pixel's ray. raydirections: torch.Tensor of shape (W, H, 3), containing the normalized direction vector for each pixel's ray. nearthresh: float, the nearest depth coordinate of interest. farthresh: float, the farthest depth coordinate of interest. numsamples: int, the number of samples drawn along each ray. randomize: bool, default True. If True, adds random noise to depth values. Outputs: querypoints: torch.Tensor of shape (W, H, num\samples, 3), containing the 3D coordinates of the sampling points. Data Structures: depthvalues: 1D tensor of shape (num\samples) containing the sampled distances along the ray. Steps: 1. Generate a linearly spaced array of distances between nearthresh and farthresh with numsamples elements, denoted as d. 2. If randomize is True, add uniform noise to each di to jitter the samples. The noise is typically sampled from U(0, \frac{far\thresh - near\thresh}{num\samples}). 3. Compute the query points using the ray equation: Q{w,h,s} = O{w,h} + ds \cdot D{w,h} Where: Q{w,h,s} is the query point at pixel (w,h) and sample index s. O{w,h} is the ray origin at pixel (w,h). D{w,h} is the ray direction at pixel (w,h). ds is the distance value for sample s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def raypositioncalculation(rayorigins: torch.Tensor, raydirections: torch.Tensor, nearthresh: float, farthresh: float, numsamples: int, randomize: bool = True) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes 3D query points along rays within near and far bounds. """ # Step 1: Create linearly spaced depth values depthvalues = torch.linspace(nearthresh, farthresh, numsamples, device=rayorigins.device) # Step 2: Optional jittering if randomize: # Add uniform noise to depth values stepsize = (farthresh - nearthresh) / numsamples noise = torch.randlike(depthvalues) stepsize depthvalues = depthvalues + noise # Step 3: Expand dimensions for broadcasting # rayorigins: (W, H, 1, 3) # raydirections: (W, H, 1, 3) # depthvalues: (1, 1, numsamples, 1) rayoriginsexp = rayorigins.unsqueeze(2) raydirectionsexp = raydirections.unsqueeze(2) depthvaluesexp = depthvalues.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(3) # Step 4: Compute query points: Q = O + d D querypoints = rayoriginsexp + raydirectionsexp depthvaluesexp return querypoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When numsamples is very large, depthvalues may suffer from floating-point precision issues if nearthresh and farthresh are large. Ensure nearthresh and farthresh are consistent with the coordinate system scale. Zero Direction: If raydirections contains zero vectors, the result will be invalid. Ray directions should be normalized before this step. Near/Far Order: If nearthresh > farthresh, torch.linspace will produce decreasing values, which is mathematically valid but semantically incorrect for ray marching. Validate nearthresh < farthresh. Reconstructs 3D world-space positions from 2D screen-space UV coordinates and depth values. It differs from direct ray generation by first establishing the precise 3D location of the current fragment in the world, which serves as the origin for subsequent raymarching steps. Choose this when working with post-processing raymarching or deferred rendering pipelines where depth buffers are available, rather than parametric camera rays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The operation scales linearly with W \cdot H \cdot N. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The output tensor requires O(W \cdot H \cdot N \cdot 3) memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple, differentiable, and easily vectorized. Supports jittering for anti-aliasing. Limitations: Does not handle ray-object intersections or adaptive sampling. It assumes a uniform or linear spacing along the ray unless modified. When to use: Standard volume rendering and NeRF training requiring fixed-step ray marching. When not to use: When adaptive sampling based on scene complexity is required, or when ray-object intersection is needed before sampling. body: World Space Position Reconstruction is a method to reconstruct 3D world-space positions from 2D screen-space UV coordinates and depth values, enabling raymarching in post-processing by converting screen space to world space. It differs from direct ray generation by first establishing the precise 3D location of the current fragment in the world, which serves as the origin for subsequent raymarching steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: uv: UV coordinate of the current fragment in the post-processing pass. depth: Depth value of the underlying scene sampled at uv. projectionMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera projection matrix. viewMatrixInverse: Inverse of the view matrix (equivalent to camera.matrixWorld). CameraPosition: The 3D position of the camera. ViewDir: The view direction vector for the current pixel. Outputs: worldSpace: The reconstructed 3D position in world coordinates. Data Structures: Clip Space Vector: A 4D vector {xNDC, yNDC, zNDC, 1.0}. View Space Vector: A 4D vector resulting from matrix multiplication. World Space Vector: A 4D vector resulting from matrix multiplication, requiring perspective division. Depth Texture Index: An integer 3-vector (int3) constructed from the pixel's screen-space x and y coordinates and a z of 0, used for direct texture loading. Steps: 1. Convert UV to NDC: Calculate Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) for x and y. 2. Convert Depth to NDC Z: Transform the linear or depth-buffer value to NDC Z. 3. Construct Clip Space Vector: Assemble the 4D clip-space vector. 4. Transform to View Space: Multiply the clip-space vector by the inverse projection matrix. 5. Transform to World Space: Multiply the view-space vector by the inverse view matrix. 6. Perspective Divide: Divide the x, y, and z components by the w component to obtain the final world position. Formulas: Matrix-based reconstruction pipeline: x{NDC} = uv.x \times 2.0 - 1.0 y{NDC} = uv.y \times 2.0 - 1.0 z{NDC} = depth \times 2.0 - 1.0 clipSpace = \{x{NDC}, y{NDC}, z{NDC}, 1.0\} view = projectionMatrixInverse \times clipSpace world = viewMatrixInverse \times view worldSpace = \frac{world.xyz}{world.w} Linear depth reconstruction alternative: Position{WS} = Depth{linear} \times ViewDir + CameraPosition Parameters: uv: UV coordinate of the current fragment in the post-processing pass. depth: Depth texture of the underlying scene sampled at the same UV. projectionMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera projection matrix, used to convert clip-space to view-space. viewMatrixInverse: Inverse of the view matrix (camera.matrixWorld), transforms view space to world space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Filtering: Hardware texture filtering must not be used for depth sampling in this context because it interpolates across edges of different blocks, leading to incorrect depth values. Point filtering (e.g., Texture.Load) must be used instead. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed for matrix operations. Degenerate inputs (e.g., world.w being zero) should be handled, though not explicitly detailed in sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. body: Epipolar Ray Intersection lifts 2D image points to 3D space by intersecting rays constructed from those points with a set of input world-space rays. It solves the problem of finding the precise 3D positions and depths corresponding to specified 2D coordinates on epipolar lines defined by camera origins and directions. Inputs and Outputs: origins: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3) representing ray origins in world space. directions: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3) representing ray directions in world space. xy: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 2) representing 2D image coordinates. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 4, 4) representing camera extrinsic matrices. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3, 3) representing camera intrinsic matrices. Output xyz: Float tensor representing the lifted 3D points. Output depth: Float tensor representing the distance from the camera origin to the 3D point. Data Structures: The method uses standard 3D vector and matrix operations. The getworldrays helper constructs ray origins and directions from 2D points using camera parameters. The intersectrays helper computes the intersection between two rays. Steps: 1. Construct World Rays from 2D Points: Convert the 2D image coordinates xy and camera parameters (extrinsics, intrinsics) into world-space ray origins (xyorigins) and directions (xydirections) using the getworldrays function. 2. Intersect Rays: Intersect the input world-space rays (origins, directions) with the newly constructed world rays (xyorigins, xydirections) using the intersectrays function to find the 3D point xyz. 3. Compute Depth: Calculate the depth as the L2 norm (Euclidean distance) between the lifted 3D point xyz and the input ray origins. Formulas: The depth is computed as: \text{depth} = \| \text{xyz} - \text{origins} \| where \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from typing import Tuple def getworldrays( xy: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, intrinsics: torch.Tensor) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Converts 2D image coordinates to world-space ray origins and directions. Args: xy: Float tensor of shape (batch, 2), 2D image coordinates. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 4, 4), camera extrinsics. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3, 3), camera intrinsics. Returns: xyorigins: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray origins in world space. xydirections: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray directions in world space. """ # Homogeneous coordinates for xy (add 1s) xyhom = torch.cat([xy, torch.oneslike(xy[...,:1])], dim=-1) # (batch, 3) # Invert intrinsics to go from pixel to camera coordinates Kinv = torch.inverse(intrinsics) # (batch, 3, 3) # Camera space directions (assuming origin at camera center) directionscam = torch.bmm(Kinv, xyhom.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # (batch, 3) # Normalize directions directionscam = directionscam / torch.norm(directionscam, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Transform directions to world space using rotation part of extrinsics R = extrinsics[...,:3,:3] # (batch, 3, 3) t = extrinsics[...,:3, 3] # (batch, 3) directionsworld = torch.bmm(R, directionscam.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # (batch, 3) # Origins are the camera centers in world space originsworld = t # (batch, 3) return originsworld, directionsworld def intersectrays( origins1: torch.Tensor, directions1: torch.Tensor, origins2: torch.Tensor, directions2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the intersection point of two rays in 3D space. Finds the point that minimizes the distance between the two rays. Args: origins1: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), first ray origins. directions1: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), first ray directions. origins2: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), second ray origins. directions2: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), second ray directions. Returns: intersection: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), the 3D intersection point. """ # Normalize directions d1 = directions1 / torch.norm(directions1, dim=-1, keepdim=True) d2 = directions2 / torch.norm(directions2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Cross product of directions n = torch.cross(d1, d2, dim=-1) # (batch, 3) nnormsq = torch.sum(n n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # (batch, 1) # Avoid division by zero for parallel rays nnormsq = torch.clamp(nnormsq, min=1e-8) # Vector between origins v = origins2 - origins1 # (batch, 3) # Project v onto the normal vector n c1 = torch.sum(v n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) / nnormsq # (batch, 1) # Intersection point on ray 1 intersection = origins1 + d1 c1 # (batch, 3) return intersection def liftto3d( origins: torch.Tensor, directions: torch.Tensor, xy: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, intrinsics: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Lifts 2D points to 3D space via epipolar ray intersection. Args: origins: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), input ray origins. directions: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), input ray directions. xy: Float tensor of shape (batch, 2), 2D image coordinates. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 4, 4), camera extrinsics. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3, 3), camera intrinsics. Returns: xyz: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), lifted 3D points. """ # Step 1: Get world rays from 2D points xyorigins, xydirections = getworldrays(xy, extrinsics, intrinsics) # Step 2: Intersect input rays with world rays xyz = intersectrays(origins, directions, xyorigins, xydirections) return xyz def getdepth( xyz: torch.Tensor, origins: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes depth as the L2 norm of the difference between the 3D point and the ray origin. Args: xyz: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), 3D points. origins: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray origins. Returns: depth: Float tensor of shape (batch), depth values. """ diff = xyz - origins depth = torch.norm(diff, dim=-1) return depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If the input ray and the constructed world ray are parallel, the cross product in intersectrays will be zero, leading to division by zero. The pseudocode handles this by clamping the denominator to a small epsilon. Out-of-Bounds Coordinates: The 2D coordinates xy should be within the valid image bounds. Implementations verify xy >= -epsilon and xy <= 1 + epsilon for normalized coordinates. Points Behind Camera: The Z coordinate of the lifted point in the camera frame should be positive (in front of the camera). Checks like Z > -epsilon can be used to validate this. Negative Ray Parameter: The intersection parameter t should be positive, indicating the intersection is in the direction of the ray. Verification uses t > -epsilon. The depth is computed as the Euclidean distance from the camera center to the 3D point: depth = (xyz - extrinsics[0,:3, 3]).norm(dim=-1). Finally, it renders depth labels along the epipolar line with white backer rectangles and rotated text. This variant focuses on validating the projection of points onto epipolar lines. It checks if XY coordinates are in bounds (normalized 0 to 1) by verifying xy >= -epsilon and xy <= 1 + epsilon for all dimensions. It also checks if points are in front of the camera by verifying the Z coordinate is greater than -epsilon. Additionally, it verifies if the ray parameter t is positive by checking t > -epsilon. When Not to Use: Avoid if camera parameters are inaccurate or if the rays are likely to be parallel. body: This method converts a 2D depth map and associated pseudo-focal lengths into a 3D point cloud in absolute coordinates. It solves the problem of mapping per-pixel depth values from a 2D image plane into 3D space. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth values into 3D space. It builds on Epipolar Ray Intersection. Inputs: depth: Depth map of shape (B, H, W) or (B, H, W, n). pseudofocal: Pseudo focal lengths of shape [B, H, W], [B, 2, H, W], or [B, 1, H, W]. pp (optional): Principal point coordinates. If None, defaults are used. Outputs: A 3D point cloud represented as coordinates (x, y, z) for each pixel in the depth map. Data Structures: Grid coordinates gridx, gridy: 2D arrays of shape (H, W) representing pixel indices. pseudofocalx, pseudofocaly: Extracted focal length components from pseudofocal. Steps: 1. Generate grid coordinates gridx and gridy using an xygrid function, which creates coordinate matrices for the image dimensions H \times W. 2. Adjust grid coordinates by subtracting the principal point. If pp is provided, subtract pp; otherwise, subtract (W-1)/2 for x and (H-1)/2 for y. 3. Extract pseudofocalx and pseudofocaly from pseudofocal based on its shape. 4. Compute the x coordinate: x = \text{depth} \times \text{grid\x} / \text{pseudo\focalx}. 5. Compute the y coordinate: y = \text{depth} \times \text{grid\y} / \text{pseudo\focaly}. 6. Compute the z coordinate: z = \text{depth}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def depthto3dpoints(depth, pseudofocal, pp=None): """ Converts a depth map and pseudo-focal lengths to a 3D point cloud. Args: depth: np.ndarray of shape (B, H, W) or (B, H, W, n) pseudofocal: np.ndarray of shape [B, H, W], [B, 2, H, W], or [B, 1, H, W] pp: tuple (px, py) for principal point. If None, uses image center. Returns: points: np.ndarray of shape (B, H, W, 3) containing x, y, z coordinates """ # Get dimensions B, H, W = depth.shape[:3] # 1. Generate grid coordinates yindices, xindices = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') # 2. Adjust grid coordinates by subtracting principal point if pp is None: px = (W - 1) / 2.0 py = (H - 1) / 2.0 else: px, py = pp gridx = xindices.astype(np.float32) - px gridy = yindices.astype(np.float32) - py # 3. Extract pseudo focal lengths if pseudofocal.ndim == 4: if pseudofocal.shape[1] == 2: pseudofocalx = pseudofocal[:, 0,:,:] pseudofocaly = pseudofocal[:, 1,:,:] else: pseudofocalx = pseudofocal[:, 0,:,:] pseudofocaly = pseudofocal[:, 0,:,:] else: pseudofocalx = pseudofocal pseudofocaly = pseudofocal # 4-6. Compute coordinates x = depth gridx / pseudofocalx y = depth gridy / pseudofocaly z = depth # Stack into (B, H, W, 3) points = np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) return points Parameters: depth: Depth map of shape (B, H, W) or (B, H, W, n). pseudofocal: Pseudo focal lengths of shape [B, H, W], [B, 2, H, W], or [B, 1, H, W]. pp: Principal point. If None, defaults to image center (W-1)/2, (H-1)/2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero if pseudofocalx or pseudofocaly is zero. Guard against zero focal lengths. Shape mismatches between depth and pseudofocal. Ensure broadcasting compatibility. Principal point offset if not centered. Use provided pp or default to center. body: This method converts 2D depth maps into 3D point clouds in absolute coordinates using camera intrinsics and poses. It solves the problem of mapping per-pixel depth values from a 2D image plane into 3D world coordinates. It builds on Depth to 3D Points Conversion by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. Inputs: depth: A tensor of shape (H, W) or (B, H, W) containing depth values z (distance from camera center). intrinsics: A 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix K. K{0,0} = fx (focal length in x) K{1,1} = fy (focal length in y) K{0,2} = cx (principal point x) K{1,2} = cy (principal point y) K{2,2} = 1 extrinsic (optional): A 4x4 world-to-camera transformation matrix W2C. If omitted, points remain in camera space. Outputs: points: A tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (B, H \times W, 3) containing 3D coordinates in world space. Data Structures: Pixel grid indices xx, yy: 1D tensors of shape (H \times W) representing column and row indices. Homogeneous coordinate vector pixones: 1D tensor of shape (H \times W, 1) filled with ones. Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Grid: For a depth map of size H \times W, generate coordinates u \in [0, W-1] and v \in [0, H-1]. Flatten these into 1D arrays xx and yy of length H \times W. 2. Compute Camera Space Coordinates: For each pixel (u, v) with depth z, compute xc = (u - cx) \frac{z}{fx}, yc = (v - cy) \frac{z}{fy}, and zc = z. Stack these into a tensor ptscam of shape (H \times W, 3). 3. Transform to World Space (Optional): If extrinsic is provided, construct homogeneous coordinates pts4 by appending a column of ones to ptscam. Compute the camera-to-world matrix C2W = (W2C)^{-1}. Transform points: P{world} = C2W \times pts4^T. Extract the first three rows to get Cartesian world coordinates. 4. Depth Scaling Variant: Some pipelines normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] and apply depth scaling s{d{i,j}} = \frac{f1 d{i,j} + f2}{d{i,j}} using elements f1, f2 from the projection matrix. The adjusted coordinates are transformed via the inverse projection matrix T to world space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthmaptoabsolutecameracoordinates(depth, intrinsics, extrinsic=None): """ Converts a depth map to 3D world coordinates. Args: depth: Tensor of shape (B, H, W) or (H, W). Depth values in meters. intrinsics: Tensor of shape (B, 3, 3) or (3, 3). Camera intrinsic matrix K. extrinsic: Tensor of shape (B, 4, 4) or (4, 4). World-to-Camera matrix W2C. Optional. Returns: points: Tensor of shape (B, HW, 3). 3D points in world space. """ # Handle batch dimension if depth.dim() == 2: depth = depth.unsqueeze(0) intrinsics = intrinsics.unsqueeze(0) if extrinsic is not None: extrinsic = extrinsic.unsqueeze(0) B, H, W = depth.shape # 1. Generate pixel grid indices u = torch.arange(0, W, device=depth.device).float() v = torch.arange(0, H, device=depth.device).float() uu, vv = torch.meshgrid(u, v, indexing='xy') # Flatten to 1D xx = uu.reshape(-1) # Column indices (u) yy = vv.reshape(-1) # Row indices (v) # Repeat for batch dimension if needed, or broadcast xx = xx.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) yy = yy.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) zdepth = depth.reshape(B, -1) # 2. Extract intrinsics fx = intrinsics[:, 0, 0] fy = intrinsics[:, 1, 1] cx = intrinsics[:, 0, 2] cy = intrinsics[:, 1, 2] # 3. Compute camera space coordinates xcam = (xx - cx.unsqueeze(1)) zdepth / fx.unsqueeze(1) ycam = (yy - cy.unsqueeze(1)) zdepth / fy.unsqueeze(1) zcam = zdepth # Stack into (B, HW, 3) ptscam = torch.stack([xcam, ycam, zcam], dim=-1) # 4. Transform to world space if extrinsic is provided if extrinsic is not None: # Compute C2W = inv(W2C) c2w = torch.inverse(extrinsic) # Append homogeneous coordinate 1 ones = torch.ones(B, ptscam.shape[1], 1, device=ptscam.device) pts4 = torch.cat([ptscam, ones], dim=-1) # (B, HW, 4) # Transform: Pworld = C2W @ Pcamhom ptsworldhom = torch.bmm(c2w, pts4.transpose(1, 2)) # (B, 4, HW) ptsworldhom = ptsworldhom.transpose(1, 2) # (B, HW, 4) # Discard homogeneous coordinate pts = ptsworldhom[:,:,:3] else: pts = ptscam return pts Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Depth: Pixels with z=0 result in division by zero; clamp or mask invalid depths. Invalid Intrinsics: Ensure fx, fy > 0. Coordinate System: Verify if the depth map represents distance along the optical axis or Euclidean distance from the camera center. name: Point Cloud Construction
head: Depth and Feature Unprojection, Multi-view Point Cloud Generation
body: Point Cloud Construction converts 2D input views into 3D point clouds containing geometric positions and view-dependent semantic features. It solves the problem of representing complex scenes in a memory-efficient and scalable format, serving as the foundational representation for subsequent differentiable rendering and multi-view fusion. Unlike sibling methods that rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth and learned feature vectors into 3D space, preserving high-dimensional semantic information alongside geometry [S1, 16278-virtual-laser-scan-for-point-cloud-generation.md]. Inputs: Input view Ii. Camera intrinsics matrix K. Estimated depth map Di. Raw spatial feature vectors Fi^0. Outputs: Point cloud Pi, a set of points where each point contains 3D coordinates and a 64-dimensional feature vector. Data Structures: Point Cloud Pi: An array of points. Each point stores 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) derived from depth and intrinsics, and a feature vector F \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. Feature Vector Layout: Dimensions 0-60 (61 dims) store semantic features from the spatial encoder, and dimensions 61-63 (3 dims) store RGB color channels from Ii. Steps: 1. Depth and Feature Estimation: For each input view Ii, estimate the per-pixel depth map Di and raw feature vectors Fi^0. 2. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate each 61-dimensional feature vector Fi^0 with the 3 RGB channels of Ii to form the final 64-dimensional feature vector Fi. 3. 3D Unprojection: For each pixel (u, v) with depth d{uv} and feature F{uv}, convert pixel coordinates to normalized camera coordinates using K^{-1}, then scale by depth to obtain camera-space coordinates. 4. World Transformation: Transform camera-space coordinates to world coordinates using the parent method [7984-depth-map-to-absolute-camera-coordinates.md]. 5. Assembly: Create a point p = (X, Y, Z, F{uv}) and append it to Pi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructpointcloud(Ii, K, Di, Firaw): """ Constructs a 3D point cloud from a single view. Args: Ii: Input image (H, W, 3) with RGB values. K: Camera intrinsic matrix (3, 3). Di: Estimated depth map (H, W). Firaw: Spatial feature vectors (H, W, 61). Returns: Pi: List of points, each being a tuple (X, Y, Z, F64). """ H, W = len(Di), len(Di[0]) Pi = [] Kinv = inverse3x3(K) # Standard linear algebra operation for y in range(H): for x in range(W): depth = Di[y][x] if depth is None or depth <= 0: continue featraw = Firaw[y][x] rgb = Ii[y][x] featfull = featraw + rgb # Concatenate 61-dim and 3-dim pixelhom = [x, y, 1.0] camcoordshom = matvecmul(Kinv, pixelhom) camcoords = [c depth for c in camcoordshom[:3]] worldcoords = transformtoworld(camcoords) # Parent method [7984-depth-map-to-absolute-camera-coordinates.md] Pi.append((worldcoords[0], worldcoords[1], worldcoords[2], featfull)) return Pi Parameters: Feature vector base dimension: 61. Total feature dimension per point: 64 (61 + 3 RGB). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Single-image depth estimation suffers from scaling/shifting ambiguity, which can lead to inconsistent 3D points across views. The method relies on the depth network d to mitigate this, often using multi-view stereo cues. Missing Depth: Pixels with invalid or missing depth values must be excluded from the point cloud to prevent geometric artifacts. Coordinate System Consistency: Depth values and intrinsics must align with the camera coordinate system defined by K and the parent transformation [S1, 7984-depth-map-to-absolute-camera-coordinates.md]. Projects 2D features from a source view to a target view using estimated depth and camera poses. It differs from standard geometric warping by explicitly handling depth uncertainty through a depth volume, allowing feature aggregation across multiple depth hypotheses rather than a single plane. Choose this variant when multi-view consistency checks or feature aggregation for depth estimation are required. Finds valid observations \{f(\omegam|p)\} for each surface point p from captured multi-view images. It projects p to the 2D camera plane as p0 = K [R|t] p to verify field of view. It resolves occlusions by projecting all points to the image plane and keeping only the nearest point at each image position. It defines a valid observation cone around the surface normal n with angle \delta to filter back-facing and extreme-angle views. For valid cameras, it extracts pixel values via linear interpolation. Generates synthetic 2D views from a 3D point cloud using virtual cameras and Hidden Point Removal (HPR) to ensure geometric alignment and physical realism. It places uniformly distributed virtual camera poses on a bounding sphere centered at the point cloud’s centroid, oriented toward the object. It projects the point cloud onto the virtual image plane using a pinhole model, inheriting RGB attributes directly. It applies HPR to compute a hemispherical depth map and dynamically cull background points occluded by the foreground, resolving penetration artifacts from naive projection. Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of pixels, O(H \times W) per view, as each pixel is processed independently during unprojection. Memory complexity is proportional to the pixel count times the feature dimension, O(H \times W \times 64) for the point cloud data. Strengths include efficiency, compact memory usage, and scalability to complex scenes compared to dense voxel grids. Limitations include reliance on depth estimation accuracy, where scaling/shifting ambiguity or sparse inputs with large baselines can cause geometric errors. It is used when a compact, semantically rich 3D representation is needed for differentiable rendering or novel view synthesis. When high-precision geometric reconstruction without semantic features is required, or when depth estimation is unreliable, alternative methods should be used. The method originates from the FWD (Forward Warping and Depth) model for real-time novel view synthesis. It was introduced to leverage the efficiency and scalability of point clouds for representing scenes with complex geometry and view-dependent appearance. The approach integrates a differentiable neural point cloud renderer, enabling end-to-end training with photometric and perceptual losses. name: Depth-aware Feature Warping
body: Depth-aware Feature Warping projects 2D features from a source view to a target view using estimated depth and camera poses, enabling multi-view consistency checks or feature aggregation for depth estimation. Inputs: Source feature map Fs \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times H \times W}. Source camera intrinsics K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times 3}. Relative pose from source to target view P \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 4 \times 4}, composed of rotation R \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times 3} and translation t \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times 1}. Depth volume D \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times D \times H \times W}, where D is the number of depth candidates. Outputs: Warped feature map Fw \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times D \times H \times W}. Data Structures: Homogeneous pixel coordinate grid: Shape [B, 3, H, W]. 3D points in camera space: Shape [B, 3, H \times W]. Transformed 3D points: Shape [B, 3, D, H \times W]. Sampling grid: Shape [B, D, H \times W, 2]. Parameters: clampmindepth: Minimum depth value for clamping z during reprojection to prevent division by zero. Default is 10^{-3}. Steps: 1. Generate a homogeneous pixel coordinate grid of shape [B, 3, H, W] by appending a ones channel to pixel coordinates. 2. Back-project pixels to 3D camera space by multiplying the inverse intrinsics with the flattened grid, resulting in shape [B, 3, H \times W]. 3. Transform 3D points to the target view's coordinate system using the rotation component of the pose matrix, repeat across depth channels, and scale by depth values, resulting in shape [B, 3, D, H \times W]. 4. Translate the points by the translation component of the pose, maintaining shape [B, 3, D, H \times W]. 5. Reproject the 3D points to the target 2D image plane by multiplying with intrinsics and reshaping, resulting in shape [B, 3, D, H \times W]. 6. Compute normalized pixel coordinates by dividing x and y by z (depth), clamping z to clampmindepth to avoid division by zero, resulting in shape [B, 2, D, H \times W]. 7. Normalize pixel coordinates to the range [-1, 1] required by gridsample, resulting in shape [B, D, H \times W] for each coordinate. 8. Stack x and y grids into a sampling grid of shape [B, D, H \times W, 2]. 9. Sample features from the source feature map using bilinear interpolation and zero padding on out-of-bounds pixels, resulting in shape [B, C, D, H, W]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def warpwithposedepthcandidates(feature1, intrinsics, pose, depth, clampmindepth=1e-3): B, C, H, W = feature1.shape D = depth.shape[1] # 1. Generate homogeneous pixel coordinate grid [B, 3, H, W] u = torch.arange(W, device=feature1.device).float().view(1, 1, 1, W) v = torch.arange(H, device=feature1.device).float().view(1, 1, H, 1) ones = torch.oneslike(u) grid = torch.cat([u, v, ones], dim=1).expand(B, -1, -1, -1) # 2. Back-project to 3D camera space [B, 3, HW] points = torch.inverse(intrinsics).bmm(grid.view(B, 3, -1)) # 3. Transform to target coordinate system [B, 3, D, HW] R = pose[:,:3,:3] points = torch.bmm(R, points).unsqueeze(2).repeat(1, 1, D, 1) depth.view(B, 1, D, H W) # 4. Translate by pose translation [B, 3, D, HW] t = pose[:,:3, -1:].unsqueeze(-1) points = points + t # 5. Reproject to target image plane [B, 3, D, HW] points = torch.bmm(intrinsics, points.view(B, 3, -1)).view(B, 3, D, H W) # 6. Compute normalized pixel coordinates [B, 2, D, HW] pixelcoords = points[:,:2] / points[:, -1:].clamp(min=clampmindepth) # 7. Normalize to [-1, 1] range [B, D, HW] xgrid = 2 pixelcoords[:, 0] / (W - 1) - 1 ygrid = 2 pixelcoords[:, 1] / (H - 1) - 1 # 8. Stack into sampling grid [B, D, HW, 2] gridsample = torch.stack([xgrid, ygrid], dim=-1) # 9. Sample features [B, C, D, H, W] warpedfeature = F.gridsample( feature1, gridsample.view(B, D H, W, 2), mode="bilinear", paddingmode="zeros", aligncorners=True) return warpedfeature Pitfalls: Large feature maps (>1,000,000 elements) cause CUDNN errors in gridsample; the code disables CUDNN for gridsample in this case. Division by zero must be handled via clamping z to clampmindepth. Coordinate system conventions (e.g., origin at center vs. corner, axis directions) must be consistent between back-projection and reprojection. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables multi-view consistency checks and feature aggregation across multiple depth hypotheses rather than a single depth plane. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution images and large depth volumes; sensitive to errors in depth estimation and camera pose accuracy. When to use: Multi-view stereo depth estimation and feature alignment tasks requiring cross-view aggregation. When not to use: Real-time applications with strict latency constraints and limited depth uncertainty. Depth-aware Feature Warping is a technique in deep learning-based multi-view stereo (MVS) and novel view synthesis that aligns features from multiple viewpoints into a common coordinate system. It is implemented in frameworks such as DepthSplat for efficient depth estimation and feature aggregation. cvg/depthsplat, https://github.com/cvg/depthsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Virtual Laser Scan for Point Cloud Generation
head: Scan class, get_surface_point_cloud via scan
body: A method to generate a point cloud with normals from a mesh by rendering normal and depth buffers from a specific camera viewpoint and reprojecting the buffer data into world space. It differs from direct mesh sampling by relying on rasterization to handle visibility and occlusion, effectively acting as a "virtual laser scan" from a single viewpoint. It builds on Depth Map to Absolute Camera Coordinates by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. Inputs: mesh: The input 3D mesh object. cameratransform: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix representing the camera's pose in world space. resolution: Integer, width and height of the rendered buffers (default 400). calculatenormals: Boolean, whether to compute and store normals (default True). fov: Field of view in radians (default 1). znear: Near plane distance (default 0.1). zfar: Far plane distance (default 10). Outputs: self.points: Array of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates in world space. self.normals: Array of shape (N, 3) containing unit normals in world space (if calculatenormals is True). Data Structures: depthbuffer: Rendered depth values from the graphics API. colorbuffer: Rendered normal buffer (RGB8 format) if calculatenormals is True. projectionmatrix: 4 \times 4 matrix derived from camera intrinsics. cameraposition: 3 \times 1 vector derived from cameratransform. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera: Compute cameraposition from cameratransform: \text{camera\position} = (\text{camera\transform} \times [0, 0, 0, 1]^T)[:3] Create a perspective camera with yfov=fov, aspectRatio=1.0, znear=znear, zfar=zfar. Extract the projectionmatrix. 2. Render Buffers: Render the mesh using the camera. Obtain depthbuffer and colorbuffer (if calculatenormals is True) at the specified resolution. 3. Filter Valid Pixels: Find indices where depth is non-zero: \text{indices} = \text{argwhere}(\text{depth\buffer} \neq 0) Set depth values equal to 0 to infinity to exclude them from further processing: \text{depth\buffer}[\text{depth\buffer} == 0] = \infty 4. Revert Depth Processing: Revert to linear clip-space depth z{clip} using: z{clip} = \frac{z{far} + z{near} - \frac{2 z{near} z{far}}{depth{buffer}}}{z{far} - z{near}} Store this as self.depth. 5. Map to Clip Space: Create a points array of shape (N, 4) initialized with ones in the w-component. Map pixel indices to normalized device coordinates (NDC) clip space: \text{points}[:, [1, 0]] = \frac{\text{indices}}{\text{resolution} - 1} \times 2 - 1 Negate the y-component to account for coordinate system differences (e.g., screen vs. clip space): \text{points}[:, 1] = -1 Set the z-component to the calculated clip-space depth: \text{points}[:, 2] = \text{self.depth}[\text{indices}[:, 0], \text{indices}[:, 1]] 6. Transform to World Space: Compute the clipping-to-world matrix: \text{clipping\to\world} = \text{camera\transform} \times \text{inv}(\text{projection\matrix}) Transform points: \text{points} = \text{points} \times \text{clipping\to\world}^T Perform perspective divide: \text{points} = \text{points} / \text{points}[:, 3][:, \text{newaxis}] Store the final 3D points: \text{self.points} = \text{points}[:,:3] 7. Compute Normals (Optional): If calculatenormals is True: Decode normals from the color buffer (assuming RGB8 encoding where [0, 255] maps to [-1, 1]): \text{normals} = \frac{\text{color\buffer}[\text{indices}[:, 0], \text{indices}[:, 1]]}{255} \times 2 - 1 Compute vector from camera to points: \text{camera\to\points} = \text{camera\position} - \text{self.points} Determine orientation via dot product: \text{normal\orientation} = \text{einsum}('ij,ij->i', \text{camera\to\points}, \text{normals}) Flip normals pointing away from the camera: \text{normals}[\text{normal\orientation} < 0] = -1 Store normals: \text{self.normals} = \text{normals} Pitfalls: If the camera is inside the model, the visibility check in isvisible must account for depth comparison against the stored depth buffer to determine if a point is occluded. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class Scan: def init(self, mesh, cameratransform, resolution=400, calculatenormals=True, fov=1.0, znear=0.1, zfar=10.0): self.mesh = mesh self.cameratransform = cameratransform self.resolution = resolution self.calculatenormals = calculatenormals self.znear = znear self.zfar = zfar # Compute camera position self.cameraposition = np.matmul(self.cameratransform, np.array([0, 0, 0, 1]))[:3] # Sources do not provide the graphics API implementation for camera creation and rendering. self.projectionmatrix = np.eye(4) depthbuffer, colorbuffer = self.renderbuffers() # Filter valid pixels indices = np.argwhere(depthbuffer != 0) depthbuffer[depthbuffer == 0] = float('inf') if indices.size == 0: self.points = np.empty((0, 3)) self.normals = None return # Revert depth processing to get clip-space depth self.depth = (zfar + znear - (2.0 znear zfar) / depthbuffer) / (zfar - znear) # Map pixel indices to clip space coordinates points = np.ones((indices.shape[0], 4)) points[:, [1, 0]] = indices.astype(float) / (resolution - 1) 2 - 1 points[:, 1] = -1 # Negate y points[:, 2] = self.depth[indices[:, 0], indices[:, 1]] # Transform to world space clippingtoworld = np.matmul(self.cameratransform, np.linalg.inv(self.projectionmatrix)) points = np.matmul(points, clippingtoworld.transpose()) # Perspective divide points /= points[:, 3][:, np.newaxis] self.points = points[:,:3] if calculatenormals: # Decode normals from color buffer normals = colorbuffer[indices[:, 0], indices[:, 1]] / 255.0 2.0 - 1.0 # Compute vector from camera to points cameratopoints = self.cameraposition - self.points # Determine normal orientation normalorientation = np.einsum('ij,ij->i', cameratopoints, normals) # Flip normals pointing away from camera normals[normalorientation < 0] = -1 self.normals = normals else: self.normals = None def renderbuffers(self): # Sources do not give the rendering implementation; typically handled by a graphics API. return np.zeros((self.resolution, self.resolution)), np.zeros((self.resolution, self.resolution, 3)) def isvisible(self, points): # Sources do not give the full implementation of isvisible. # If the camera is inside the model, the visibility check must account for depth comparison # against the stored depth buffer to determine if a point is occluded. return np.ones(points.shape[0], dtype=bool) A variant that generates a complete surface point cloud by aggregating scans from multiple viewpoints. It uses a Fibonacci sphere distribution to generate camera angles, ensuring uniform coverage. For each angle, a Scan object is created with specific parameters: fov=1.0472, znear=boundingradius, zfar=3boundingradius, and resolution=400. The points and normals from all scans are concatenated to form the final SurfacePointCloud. Not given in the sources. Originated in the meshtosdf library by marian42, which uses virtual laser scans to generate point clouds for Signed Distance Field (SDF) reconstruction. meshtosdf, https://github.com/marian42/meshtosdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Lidar Depth Generation
body: Lidar Depth Generation converts accumulated 3D LiDAR points into pixel-aligned depth maps for synchronized RGB images. It projects LiDAR points from multiple time steps onto the 2D image plane, selecting the nearest point per pixel to handle sparsity. Inputs: Target image frame timestamp. Camera intrinsics K (3×3 matrix). Camera-to-world pose T{cam}^{world} (4×4 matrix). Set of LiDAR frames, each containing a timestamp, 3D points in sensor coordinates, and LiDAR-to-world pose T{lidar}^{world} (4×4 matrix). Image dimensions H \times W. Outputs: Depth map D of size H \times W, where D{u,v} is the depth value for pixel (u, v). Data Structures: Depth map: 2D array initialized to infinity to indicate no depth. Steps: 1. Select the 10 closest LiDAR frames to the target image frame. 2. Transform the selected LiDAR points into world coordinates. 3. Project the world-coordinate LiDAR points onto the image coordinates. 4. Compute the depth value as the distance along the ray from the camera center to each LiDAR point. 5. When multiple LiDAR points project to the same pixel, derive the depth value from the nearest LiDAR point. Formulas: Camera-relative point: p{cam} = T{cam}^{world^{-1}} p{world}. Pixel coordinates: u = \frac{K{00} p{cam,x} + K{02}}{p{cam,z}}, v = \frac{K{11} p{cam,y} + K{12}}{p{cam,z}}. Depth: d = \|p{cam}\|2 = \sqrt{p{cam,x}^2 + p{cam,y}^2 + p{cam,z}^2}. Aggregation: D{u,v} = \min(D{u,v}, d). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatelidardepth(imagetimestamp, K, campose, lidarframes, imageheight, imagewidth, numframes=10): # 1. Select closest frames timediffs = [(abs(frame[0] - imagetimestamp), i) for i, frame in enumerate(lidarframes)] timediffs.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) selectedframes = [lidarframes[idx] for, idx in timediffs[:numframes]] # Initialize depth map with infinity depthmap = [[float('inf')] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] # Inverse camera pose caminv = invert4x4(campose) # Standard linear algebra for frame in selectedframes:, points, lidarpose = frame for p in points: # 2. Transform to world coordinates phomo = [p[0], p[1], p[2], 1.0] wp = [sum(lidarpose[i][j] phomo[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] pworld = wp[:3] # 3. Project to image coordinates wphomo = [pworld[0], pworld[1], pworld[2], 1.0] cphomo = [sum(caminv[i][j] wphomo[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] pcam = cphomo[:3] if pcam[2] <= 0: continue u = (K[0][0] pcam[0] + K[0][2]) / pcam[2] v = (K[1][1] pcam[1] + K[1][2]) / pcam[2] if 0 <= u < imagewidth and 0 <= v < imageheight: # 4. Compute depth d = (pcam[0]2 + pcam[1]2 + pcam[2]2)0.5 # 5. Update depth map with minimum depth ui, vi = int(u), int(v) if d < depthmap[vi][ui]: depthmap[vi][ui] = d return depthmap def invert4x4(M): # Standard 4x4 matrix inversion via Gaussian elimination or adjugate method # Not given in the sources. pass Parameters: numframes: 10. Edge Cases: No LiDAR points: If no points project to a pixel, the depth remains infinity. Multiple points: The nearest point (smallest depth) is chosen, handling occlusions. Precision: Floating-point precision in depth calculation should be sufficient to distinguish close points. Simulates real LiDAR sensor rays by defining ray origin and direction based on sensor parameters and ego-vehicle motion to generate 3D points. It differs from standard ray casting by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of the sensor origin due to vehicle velocity and incorporating a learned "raydrop" probability to mimic real-world signal loss, rather than assuming perfect reflection. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot W), where N is the number of LiDAR points in the selected frames and W is the number of frames. Projection and aggregation are linear in the number of points. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the depth map, plus storage for the selected LiDAR points. Strengths: Provides accurate depth supervision by leveraging LiDAR's direct range measurement. Handles sparse LiDAR data by accumulating points over time. Limitations: Requires synchronized LiDAR and camera data. Performance depends on the density of LiDAR points and the number of frames used. Occlusions may still result in missing depth if the nearest point is not captured. When to use: When generating depth maps for neural rendering or vision tasks where LiDAR data is available but sparse. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and LiDAR data is not available or too sparse. Lidar Depth Generation is a technique used in datasets like PandaSet to provide depth supervision for neural radiance fields and vision tasks. It addresses unbounded scenes by normalizing the scene based on the camera trajectory radius. name: LiDAR Ray Simulation
head: NeRF-LiDAR Ray Simulation
body: Simulates real LiDAR sensor rays by defining ray origin and direction based on sensor parameters and ego-vehicle motion to generate 3D points. It differs from standard ray casting by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of the sensor origin due to vehicle velocity and incorporating a learned "raydrop" probability to mimic real-world signal loss, rather than assuming perfect reflection. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Implicit NeRF representation (for distance \hat{D}), LiDAR sensor parameters (channels, field of view, spin rate), ego-vehicle velocity v, and time interval \Delta t. Outputs: A set of 3D points p and their associated semantic/depth labels, forming a simulated LiDAR frame \hat{P}. Data Structures Ray Parameters: Defined by azimuth \theta and vertical angle \phi. Equirectangular Grid: A 2D image grid of resolution H \times W used for point-wise alignment. For a 32-channel LiDAR (e.g., nuScenes), this is 32 \times 1024. Numbered Steps 1. Determine Ray Direction: For each laser channel, calculate the azimuth \theta and vertical angle \phi based on the LiDAR's mechanical settings and the time interval \Delta t within the scan cycle. Compute the direction vector d using: d = (\cos \theta \cos \phi, \sin \theta \sin \phi, \cos \phi)^T 2. Update Ray Origin: Calculate the current sensor origin o by updating the previous origin o0 with the ego-vehicle's velocity v over the time interval \Delta t: o = o0 + \Delta t \cdot v 3. Query NeRF for Distance: Cast the ray defined by o and d into the NeRF to render the distance \hat{D} from the sensor to the nearest surface. 4. Compute 3D Point: Calculate the simulated point p in 3D space: p = o + \hat{D}d 5. Apply Raydrop (Optional/Learned): To match real-world sensor behavior where points are dropped due to low reflectance or incidence angle, apply a learned probability mask. This is achieved by projecting both the real point cloud P and simulated point cloud \hat{P} into 2D equirectangular grids to establish point-wise correspondence P \simeq \hat{P}. Parameters LiDAR spinning speed: 20 Hz (e.g., Velodyne HDL32E in nuScenes). Field of view: -30.67° to 10.67° across 32 channels. Time interval \Delta t: Determined by the LiDAR frame rate (e.g., 20 Hz for nuScenes). Points per frame: 20,000 to 40,000 for a standard 32-channel LiDAR. Pseudocode Unverified code. name: Distance-from-Center (DFC) Map Generation
head: DFC maps
body: Distance-from-Center (DFC) map generation converts per-view depth maps into a global radial distance representation relative to a scene center. It solves the problem of separating foreground and background elements in outdoor scenes by providing a unified metric that is invariant to camera position. Unlike sibling methods that operate in local camera coordinates or raw point clouds, DFC maps express depth in a common global reference frame, enabling a single distance threshold to segment foreground and background regions across all views. Inputs: Camera poses (extrinsics) for N views. Depth maps Dv for each view v. Camera intrinsics (standard pinhole model). Outputs: A set of DFC maps, one per view, where each pixel stores the Euclidean distance from the unprojected 3D point to O. Data Structures: Scene Center O: A 3D vector (Ox, Oy, Oz). DFC Map Mv: A 2D array of floats, same dimensions as Dv. Mv(u, v) stores the distance. Steps: 1. For each view v and each pixel (u, v) in Dv: Retrieve depth d = Dv(u, v). If d \le 0 or invalid, mark Mv(u, v) as invalid and continue. Unproject (u, v) and d using intrinsics and the camera pose to obtain the 3D point P in world coordinates. 2. Compute the Euclidean distance from P to O: \text{dist} = \| P - O \|2 = \sqrt{(Px - Ox)^2 + (Py - Oy)^2 + (Pz - Oz)^2}. 3. Store \text{dist} in Mv(u, v). Parameters: Scene Center O: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Depth: Pixels with missing or non-positive depth must be excluded to prevent invalid distances. Coordinate System Alignment: Camera poses and depth maps must share the same world coordinate frame for O to be valid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatedfcmaps(depthmaps, poses, intrinsics, scenecenter): """ depthmaps: list of 2D arrays, shape (H, W), depth in meters. poses: list of 4x4 arrays, camera-to-world transformation matrices. intrinsics: 3x3 array, camera intrinsic matrix K. scenecenter: 1D array, shape (3,), coordinates of O. Returns: list of 2D arrays, DFC maps. """ dfcmaps = [] for depthmap, Tcam2world in zip(depthmaps, poses): H, W = depthmap.shape dfcmap = np.full((H, W), np.nan) u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H)) # Unproject to camera space rays xcam = (u - intrinsics[0, 2]) / intrinsics[0, 0] ycam = (v - intrinsics[1, 2]) / intrinsics[1, 1] rayscam = np.stack([xcam, ycam, np.oneslike(u)], axis=-1) # Transform to world space R = Tcam2world[:3,:3] raysworld = np.einsum('ijk,ljk->ijl', rayscam, R) Cworld = Tcam2world[:3, 3] # Filter valid depth valid = (depthmap > 0) Pworld = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) Pworld[valid] = Cworld + depthmap[valid,:, np.newaxis] raysworld[valid] # Compute distance to scene center diff = Pworld - scenecenter[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] dists = np.sqrt(np.sum(diff2, axis=-1)) dfcmap[valid] = dists[valid] dfcmaps.append(dfcmap) return dfcmaps This variant uses the DFC maps to automatically determine a threshold for separating foreground and background. It estimates the histogram of DFC values from the original point cloud with a binning interval of 10 meters. The threshold Ri is set at the first bin interval where the point count is less than 2.5% of the total reconstructed points. This threshold is then used to generate masked background images (removing foreground pixels) and filtered foreground points (keeping points within distance Ri from the center). The parameter Ri is scene-dependent but the heuristic is robust; manual override is possible. Changing Ri within reasonable ranges has minimal impact on novel view synthesis metrics but may affect reconstruction detail in moved regions. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W), where N is the number of views, and H, W are image dimensions. Each pixel is processed once for unprojection and distance calculation. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) to store the DFC maps. Strengths: Provides a global, view-invariant metric for depth, simplifying foreground/background segmentation in outdoor scenes. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth maps and camera poses. The heuristic for Ri may fail in scenes with unusual depth distributions. When to use: Outdoor scene reconstruction where background separation is critical, such as in Gaussian Splatting with environment map baking. When not to use: Indoor scenes with complex lighting or where global center is ambiguous. The DFC map generation method was introduced in the context of EnvMap-GS, a two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction method that bakes background into an environment map. It was proposed by D. Pintani et al. to address the challenge of separating foreground and background in outdoor scenes for 3D Gaussian Splatting. name: Gaussian Seeding
head: Gaussian Seeding and Sampling, New Gaussian Seeding
body: Gaussian Seeding initializes the 3D Gaussian primitives for a SLAM or reconstruction system by sampling points from a ground truth depth map and camera pose. It solves the problem of establishing an initial point cloud representation that balances uniform spatial coverage with high-frequency detail preservation. It differs from simple uniform sampling by incorporating gradient-based pixel selection and handles submap initialization logic to manage memory constraints during incremental mapping. Inputs: gtcolor: Ground truth color image. gtdepth: Ground truth depth map. intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix. c2w: Estimated camera-to-world transformation matrix. seedingmask: Boolean mask indicating valid pixels for seeding. isnewsubmap: Boolean flag indicating if a new submap is being initialized. newsubmappointsnum: Target number of points for a new submap. newsubmapgradientpointsnum: Number of gradient-based points for a new submap. newframesamplesize: Target number of points for a new frame (if not new submap). Outputs: points: A tensor of 3D coordinates in world space, cast to float32. Data Structures: pts: 3D point cloud tensor of shape (H \times W, 3), where N is the number of valid pixels. validids: 1D tensor of flat indices corresponding to pixels where seedingmask is true and depth is valid. sampleids: 1D tensor of selected indices to generate the final Gaussian set. Steps: 1. Point Cloud Creation: Convert the ground truth depth map to 3D points in world coordinates using camera intrinsics and the estimated camera-to-world matrix. The depth is scaled by a factor of 1.005 to account for sensor bias or offset. Let pts be the resulting tensor of shape (H \times W, 3). 2. Masking: Flatten the ground truth depth and create a boolean mask nonzerodepthmask where depth > 0. This filters out invalid depth values (e.g., infinity or zero). 3. Valid ID Identification: Identify validids as the flat indices of non-zero elements in seedingmask. These are the candidate pixels for seeding. 4. Sampling Strategy Selection: Case A: New Submap (isnewsubmap is True): If newsubmappointsnum < 0, select all indices from pts.shape[0]. Otherwise, sample newsubmappointsnum unique indices from the total pixel count without replacement. Let this set be uniformids. Sample newsubmapgradientpointsnum pixel indices based on the image gradient magnitude of gtcolor. Let this set be gradientids. Concatenate uniformids and gradientids. Combine with validids and take the unique values to form the final sampleids. Case B: New Frame / Existing Submap (isnewsubmap is False): If newframesamplesize < 0 or the number of validids is less than newframesamplesize, use all validids. Otherwise, randomly sample newframesamplesize unique indices from validids without replacement. Set sampleids to these selected indices. 5. Filtering: Filter sampleids to ensure they correspond only to pixels where nonzerodepthmask is true. This ensures no NaN or invalid coordinates are included. 6. Output: Return the 3D points pts[sample\ids], cast to float32. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianseeding(gtcolor, gtdepth, intrinsics, c2w, seedingmask, isnewsubmap, newsubmappointsnum, newsubmapgradientpointsnum, newframesamplesize): # Step 1: Create point cloud from ground truth # Depth is scaled by 1.005 pts = createpointcloud(gtcolor, 1.005 gtdepth, intrinsics, c2w) # Step 2: Flatten depth and create mask for valid depths flatgtdepth = gtdepth.flatten() nonzerodepthmask = flatgtdepth > 0 # Step 3: Get valid IDs from seeding mask validids = flatnonzero(seedingmask.flatten()) sampleids = None if isnewsubmap: # Step 4A: New Submap Logic # Uniform sampling if newsubmappointsnum < 0: uniformids = arange(pts.shape[0]) else: uniformids = randomsamplewithoutreplacement(pts.shape[0], newsubmappointsnum) # Gradient sampling gradientids = samplepixelsbasedongradient(gtcolor, newsubmapgradientpointsnum) # Combine and unique combinedids = concatenate([uniformids, gradientids, validids]) sampleids = unique(combinedids) else: # Step 4B: New Frame / Existing Submap Logic numvalid = len(validids) if newframesamplesize < 0 or numvalid < newframesamplesize: sampleids = validids else: # Sample from validids without replacement perm = randomsamplewithoutreplacement(numvalid, newframesamplesize) sampleids = validids[perm] # Step 5: Filter by non-zero depth mask validdepthmask = nonzerodepthmask[sampleids] finalids = sampleids[validdepthmask] # Step 6: Return points return pts[finalids].astype('float32') def createpointcloud(color, depth, intrinsics, c2w): # Standard back-projection: pixel coords -> camera frame -> world frame h, w = depth.shape u, v = meshgrid(arange(w), arange(h)) fx, fy = intrinsics[0, 0], intrinsics[1, 1] cx, cy = intrinsics[0, 2], intrinsics[1, 2] xcam = (u - cx) depth / fx ycam = (v - cy) depth / fy zcam = depth ptscam = stack([xcam, ycam, zcam], axis=-1) # Apply camera-to-world transform (assuming 4x4 matrix) ptsworld = (c2w[:3,:3] @ ptscam.reshape(-1, 3).T).T + c2w[:3, 3] return ptsworld.reshape(h, w, 3) def samplepixelsbasedongradient(color, numpoints): # Compute gradient magnitude (Sobel or simple difference) gradx = abs(color[:, 1:] - color[:,:-1]) grady = abs(color[1:,:] - color[:-1,:]) gradmag = mean(gradx, axis=-1) + mean(grady, axis=-1) # Pad to match original size gradmag = pad(gradmag, ((0, 1), (0, 1)), mode='edge') # Normalize to probabilities prob = gradmag / (sum(gradmag) + 1e-8) # Sample indices indices = randomchoice(prob.flatten(), size=numpoints, replace=False) return indices Parameters: 1.005: Depth scaling factor. newsubmappointsnum: Controls uniform sampling density for new submaps. Negative values imply "all points". newsubmapgradientpointsnum: Number of high-detail points sampled via gradient. newframesamplesize: Controls sampling density for incremental frames. Edge Cases: If validids is empty, the output is an empty tensor. If sampleids contains indices where depth is zero or invalid, they are removed in Step 5. Precision: Output is explicitly cast to float32. Time Complexity: Dominated by the point cloud creation (O(H \times W)) and sorting/unique operations on indices (O(N \log N) where N is the number of selected pixels). Gradient sampling adds overhead proportional to image size. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) for storing the full point cloud before sampling. Strengths: Combines global coverage (uniform) with local detail (gradient), ensuring robust initialization for SLAM systems. Limitations: Relies on accurate ground truth depth and camera pose. If c2w is poor, the seeded Gaussians will be misaligned. Gaussian Seeding is a method used in Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems, specifically referenced in the context of the Gaussian-SLAM project. It serves as the initialization step for creating the 3D Gaussian representation from monocular or stereo depth inputs. name: Point Cloud Generation and Refinement
head: Depth-guided Point Cloud Refinement
body: An offline process that generates and refines a 3D point cloud from a subset of training images to improve depth estimation accuracy for novel views in neural rendering. It differs from standard Multi-View Stereo (MVS) by iteratively validating points against ground-truth depth from adjacent views, allowing it to generate a denser, more accurate point cloud for similar computational time, which leads to higher rendering quality (PSNR). Inputs: A subset of training images with known camera poses and ground-truth depth maps. A threshold parameter \tau controlling the tolerance for depth consistency. Outputs: A refined 3D point cloud. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of 3D points P = \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\} in absolute coordinates. Depth Map: A 2D array of ground-truth depth values d{GT} for each pixel in the training views. Steps: 1. Initialization: Select a subset of training views with sufficient and uniform distance between adjacent viewpoints to ensure efficiency. 2. Iterative Generation: For each viewpoint Vi in the subset, sequentially follow the trajectory: a. Generate: Create an initial point cloud using the depth image from viewpoint Vi. b. Project: Project the 3D points of the generated point cloud onto the image plane of the next viewpoint V{i+1}. c. Calculate Distance: For each projected point, calculate the distance \tilde{d} between the 3D point and the camera location of V{i+1} using multiple view geometry. d. Validate: Compare \tilde{d} with the ground-truth depth value d{GT} of the corresponding pixel in V{i+1}'s depth map. Check if the condition is satisfied: |\tilde{d} - d{GT}| \le \tau where \tilde{d} is the calculated distance, d{GT} is the ground-truth depth, and \tau is the specified threshold. e. Refine: If the condition is not satisfied, discard the current point and generate a new 3D point by back-projecting the pixel with value d{GT} from V{i+1}. 3. Finalization: Repeat the iteration for all viewpoints in the subset to produce the final refined point cloud. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateandrefinepointcloud(trainingviews, tau): """ Generate and refine a 3D point cloud from a subset of training views. Args: trainingviews: List of view objects containing camera intrinsics (K), inverse intrinsics (Kinv), rotation (R), translation (t), position, width, height, and depthmap. tau: Threshold for depth consistency check. Returns: pointcloud: List of 3D points. """ pointcloud = [] # Iterate through the subset of training views sequentially for i in range(len(trainingviews) - 1): currentview = trainingviews[i] nextview = trainingviews[i + 1] # Step 1: Generate initial point cloud from current view's depth currentpoints = [] for y in range(currentview.height): for x in range(currentview.width): d = currentview.depthmap[y][x] if d > 0: p = backprojectpixel(x, y, d, currentview) currentpoints.append(p) # Step 2 & 3: Project to next view, calculate distance, validate for p in currentpoints: u, v = projecttopixel(p, nextview) # Check bounds if 0 <= u < nextview.width and 0 <= v < nextview.height: dgt = nextview.depthmap[int(v)][int(u)] # Calculate Euclidean distance to next camera center dtilde = distancetocamera(p, nextview.position) # Step 4: Validate against threshold if abs(dtilde - dgt) <= tau: pointcloud.append(p) else: # Generate new point from ground truth depth newp = backprojectpixel(int(u), int(v), dgt, nextview) pointcloud.append(newp) return pointcloud def backprojectpixel(u, v, depth, camera): # Standard pinhole back-projection: P = Kinv [u, v, 1] depth ray = [u, v, 1.0] localp = multiplymatrixvector(camera.Kinv, ray) localp = [x depth for x in localp] # Apply extrinsics (R, t) camp = multiplymatrixvector(camera.R, localp) return [camp[i] + camera.t[i] for i in range(3)] def projecttopixel(point, camera): # Transform to camera space: Pcam = R^T (P - t) camp = [point[i] - camera.t[i] for i in range(3)] camp = multiplymatrixvector(camera.R.T, camp) # Project: [u, v, w] = K Pcam proj = multiplymatrixvector(camera.K, camp) return proj[0] / proj[2], proj[1] / proj[2] def distancetocamera(point, camerapos): return ((point[0]-camerapos[0])2 + (point[1]-camerapos[1])2 + (point[2]-camerapos[2])2)0.5 def multiplymatrixvector(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] Parameters: \tau: Threshold for comparing calculated distance and ground-truth depth. Controls point cloud density and hole filling. Too large: fewer points, faster rendering, more holes. Too small: overlapping points, slower rendering, fewer holes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Selection: An inappropriate \tau leads to either excessive holes (if too large) or overlapping points causing slow rendering (if too small). Background Filling: If the hole-filling kernel size \kappa (used in subsequent refinement) is too small, holes in background areas may be filled, blurring the depth image. Subset Selection: Using the entire training view set is less efficient; a subset with uniform spacing is recommended. A strategy that uses sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and dense PatchMatch Stereo point clouds to guide depth prediction in few-shot novel view synthesis, preventing overfitting to training views. It differs from standard depth-supervised methods by computing adaptive weights based on multiview color consistency to mitigate inaccuracies in estimated 3D points, and by restricting its application to early training stages. A post-processing technique that enhances the geometric fidelity of depth maps projected from a 3D point cloud, addressing the loss of fine details and scale ambiguity inherent in initial projections. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Depth-Guided Optimization by explicitly integrating high-resolution RGB priors via diffusion models to recover high-frequency geometric details, rather than relying solely on geometric consistency or optimization constraints. It obtains accurate depth images for novel views by refining a rough depth image projected from a 3D point cloud, specifically by removing unnecessary points and filling holes. Generates 3D point locations and confidence using multi-view stereo, then optimizes features and geometry for radiance field training. It generates 3D point locations and confidence using deep MVS methods with deep 3D CNNs, uses a 2D CNN to extract feature maps from images, aligns them with the generated points, and describes per-point features, then performs point growing and pruning procedures to eliminate outliers and holes, ensuring rendering quality. Time Complexity: Similar to standard MVS. On a GPU with 20 views, processing time is approximately 87.12 s, compared to 86.78 s for standard MVS. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Generates more points than standard MVS for similar computational time, leading to higher PSNR (31.44 dB vs 30.27 dB on the Pavillon dataset). Strengths: Improves rendering quality by providing a denser, more accurate point cloud. Limitations: Requires ground-truth depth maps for training views; performance is sensitive to the threshold \tau. When to use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is required and ground-truth depth data is available for training views. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and slight quality degradation is acceptable, or when ground-truth depth is unavailable. Originated in the work by H. B. Yoo et al., titled "Improving Neural Radiance Fields Using Near-Surface Sampling with Point Cloud Generation". The method was developed to improve depth estimation accuracy for novel views by iteratively correcting point positions based on depth consistency across training views. It leverages multiple view geometry to iteratively correct point positions based on depth consistency across training views.
