name: RaySamples
head: ColorSamples, ColorSamplesVec, DepthSamples, DepthSamplesVec, Pixel Rendering, Ray/Depth/Color Sample Data Structures, RaySamples Data Structure, RaySamplesVec
body: RaySamples is a data structure used in volume rendering and neural rendering pipelines to store geometric and radiometric attributes for a batch of ray samples. It serves as the primary container for intermediate results during ray marching, holding origins, directions, and predicted scene properties such as signed distance fields, density, or color for each sample point along the ray. Unlike sibling methods that focus on generation or specific sampling patterns, RaySamples focuses on the storage and manipulation of these samples, enabling efficient batched operations for integration and gradient computation. The RaySamples structure aggregates tensors representing the state of rays sampled through a scene. It is typically populated by a ray sampler and consumed by an integrator. Input: A set of rays defined by origins and directions, often generated from camera parameters and lens models. Output: A structured batch of samples containing geometric positions, surface normals, and predicted neural network outputs such as SDF, density, and color. The core implementation is a C++ struct wrapping seven PyTorch tensors. All fields are torch::Tensor objects, and operations include a numel() > 0 guard to prevent processing empty tensors. RaySamples Layout: origin: [N, 3] — World-space origin of each ray sample. direction: [N, 3] — Normalized direction vector of each ray sample. zdirnorm: [N, 1] — Cosine of the angle between the ray direction and a reference normal, used for importance sampling or shading. predxyz: [N, 3] — Predicted 3D coordinates from a neural network prior or refinement. predsdf: [N, 1] — Predicted Signed Distance Field value. predisigma: [N, 1] — Predicted inverse density or opacity parameter. ridx: [N] — Ray indices mapping each sample back to its originating pixel or ray. Variants: DepthSamples: Extends RaySamples with xyz [N, 3], depth [N, 1], and raysdf [N, 1]. ColorSamples: Extends RaySamples with rgb [N, 3]. Vec Variants: RaySamplesVec, DepthSamplesVec, and ColorSamplesVec store the same fields as vectors of tensors, supporting variable-length batches or specific memory layouts. The following steps describe the generation of rays and computation of intensities as detailed in. This process involves sensor sampling, lens modeling, and optical corrections. 1. Sample Ray Origins on Sensor: Generate origins on the sensor plane for each pixel (pxi, pxj) and sample count. python rayorigins, pa1 = sensor.sampleonpixels(samplesperpixel, pxi, pxj, device=device) rayorigins = rayorigins.reshape(-1, 3) rayorigins = rayorigins.unsqueeze(0).expand([directionspersample] + list(rayorigins.shape)).transpose(0, 1).reshape(-1, 3) 2. Sample Points on Lens: Generate points on the lens aperture to simulate depth of field or aperture effects. python pprime, pa2 = lens.samplepointsonlens(rayorigins.shape[0], device=device) 3. Compute Ray Directions: Calculate the direction from the sensor origin to the lens point. python raydirections = optics.batchvector( pprime[:, 0] - rayorigins[:, 0], pprime[:, 1] - rayorigins[:, 1], pprime[:, 2] - rayorigins[:, 2]) 4. Compute Cosine Theta: Calculate the cosine of the angle between the sensor normal and the ray direction for vignetting/falloff correction. python sensornormal = (lens.transform.transform[:-1, -1] - torch.tensor(sensor.position)).to(device) sensornormal = 1. / torch.norm(sensornormal) costheta = optics.optics.vector.costheta(sensornormal[None,...], raydirections) 5. Create Rays Object: Assemble the rays with metadata. python rays = Rays(origin=rayorigins, direction=raydirections, meta={'costheta': costheta}) 6. Backward Ray Tracing: Trace rays through the scene using an integrator. python intensities, variances = backwardraytracing(rays, scene, lightsource, integrator, maxiterations=maxiterations) if not integrator.withvar: intensities = backwardraytracing(rays, scene, lightsource, integrator, maxiterations=maxiterations) 7. Compute Final Intensities and Variances: Apply optical corrections and average over samples. Let z be the distance from the lens center to the sensor center: z = \sqrt{\sum((lens.transform.transform[:3, -1] - sensor.c2w.transform[:3, -1])^2)} The final intensity for each pixel is: I = \frac{\text{mean}{samples}(\text{mean}{dirs}(\cos\theta^4 \cdot I{raw}))}{z^2 \cdot p{a1} \cdot p{a2}} The final variance is: V = \frac{\text{mean}{samples}(\text{mean}{dirs}(\cos\theta^8 \cdot V{raw}))}{z^4 \cdot p{a1}^2 \cdot p{a2}^2} If the integrator does not compute variance, return only intensities. samplesperpixel: Number of samples per pixel. directionspersample: Number of directions sampled per pixel location for lens effects. maxiterations: Maximum number of bounces or ray marching steps (default: 3). Empty Tensors: The numel() > 0 guard is critical to avoid runtime errors in PyTorch/C++ when a pixel or batch dimension is empty. Precision: Optical calculations involving z^2 and z^4 in denominators can lead to numerical instability if z is very small, requiring consistent coordinate systems for sensor.position and lens.transform. What it is: A variant of RaySamples that includes an rgb tensor [N, 3] representing the color contribution of each sample. What sets it apart: It adds radiometric data to the geometric base without altering the underlying tensor manipulation methods. When to choose it: Use it when the rendering pipeline outputs color directly per sample, such as in path tracing or neural radiance field rendering, and needs to accumulate color. Link: Inherits all methods from RaySamples, including index, slice, and cat, with safety checks applied to the rgb field. What it is: A utility for extracting pixel values from an input image corresponding to sampled rays. What sets it apart: It focuses on image-space retrieval rather than world-space ray storage. When to choose it: Use it in supervised training where rendered rays need to be compared against ground-truth image patches. Link: Uses a ray sampler to get indices or coordinates, applying direct indexing or bilinear grid sampling to extract RGB values. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples N for storage and basic operations such as indexing and slicing. The ray tracing step depends on the scene complexity and integrator. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of samples, requiring 7 \times N \times \text{dtype\size} bytes for the base structure plus variants. Performance: Efficient on GPU due to the PyTorch tensor backend, allowing high throughput through batched operations. Strengths: Provides a unified data structure for geometric and neural predictions. Limitations: Memory overhead for storing all intermediate predictions for every sample. When to use: Neural rendering pipelines that require joint optimization of geometry and appearance. The RaySamples structure enables the integration of LiDAR data with visual rendering by providing a common data format for ray-sample interactions. The specific implementation with predxyz, predsdf, and predisigma fields is characteristic of systems like GS-SDF, which unify Gaussian Splatting and SDF-based reconstruction. The optical sampling model originates from computational photography and gradient optics, applying physical lens models to neural rendering. name: Abstract Light Source Interface
head: Base Light Source
body: The Abstract Light Source Interface defines the contract for light source objects in volume rendering pipelines, specifically enabling backward ray tracing by providing a geometric bounding shape and methods for ray sampling. It distinguishes itself from sibling samplers like Camera Ray Generation by focusing on emission geometry rather than camera projection, requiring implementations to define how rays originate from a light volume. The interface mandates that all concrete light source implementations must provide a bounding shape for intersection tests and implement specific methods for generating and visualizing rays. Bounding Shape A bounding shape is required if the light source is used with backward ray tracing. This shape defines the spatial extent from which rays are emitted. If not provided, the default is None. Ray Sampling Implementations must provide a method to sample rays from the light source. This method takes the number of rays to generate and the target device as arguments and returns a collection of Rays objects. Visualization Implementations must provide a method to plot the light source position on a given matplotlib axis. Samples rays uniformly from a spherical light source. Choose when the light source is isotropic and spherical. Samples rays from a grid-based light distribution. Choose when the light source has a structured, grid-aligned geometry. General ray casting from a light source. Choose for basic forward rendering scenarios. Generates rays from the camera eye. Not a light source, but a sibling in ray generation. General ray sample generation utilities. Choose for low-level sample manipulation. Data structure for ray samples. Choose when handling the output of sampling operations. The interface originates from the gradoptics library by SLAC. It was designed to support backward ray tracing in optical simulations, where light sources must be defined by their bounding geometry to facilitate intersection calculations with incident rays. magis-slac/gradoptics, https://github.com/magis-slac/gradoptics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Raw Camera Measurement Model
head: RawNeRF Camera Model, Sensor Noise Model
body: The Raw Camera Measurement Model describes the physical process by which a camera sensor converts incoming photon flux into a high-bit-depth digital signal, serving as the input domain for methods like RawNeRF. It distinguishes itself from standard rendering pipelines by explicitly modeling the noise characteristics (shot and read noise) and the linear, high-dynamic-range nature of raw sensor data, rather than assuming a tone-mapped or gamma-corrected output. Inputs and Outputs Input: The expected number of photons arriving at a pixel during the shutter open time, denoted as xi (proportional to irradiance). Output: A noisy digital measurement yi, typically stored as a 10- to 14-bit integer. Data Structures The raw image is represented as a 2D array of unsigned integers. The bit depth is typically 10, 12, or 14 bits. The values are offset by a "black level" to accommodate negative noise components. Steps 1. Photon Capture: Photons hit the sensor pixels and are converted into an electrical charge proportional to the incident light intensity. 2. Digitization: The analog electrical charge is recorded as a high bit-depth digital signal. 3. Black Level Offset: The raw values are offset by a fixed "black level" value. This offset ensures that the digital representation can handle negative deviations caused by noise without clipping to zero immediately. 4. Noise Addition: Noise is added to the signal. The combined effect of photon arrival statistics (shot noise) and readout circuitry noise (read noise) is modeled. 5. Measurement: The final value yi is obtained. To recover the underlying signal, the black level is subtracted from yi. Formulas The relationship between the noisy measurement yi and the expected photon count xi is defined by the noise distribution. The error yi - xi is zero-mean. The noise distribution is modeled as Gaussian, where the variance \sigma^2 is an affine function of the mean xi: yi \sim \mathcal{N}(xi, \sigma^2(xi)) Where the variance is given by: \sigma^2(xi) = \alpha xi + \beta \alpha: Represents the gain related to shot noise (Poisson process variance). \beta: Represents the variance of the read noise. Parameters Bit Depth: Typical raw sensor data uses 10 to 14 bits. Black Level: A constant offset value specific to the sensor, required to allow for negative measurements due to noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Raw data preserves dynamic range, but the noise variance increases with signal intensity (affine variance). Negative Values: Because of the black level offset, raw values can be small positive integers that correspond to negative physical quantities after subtraction. Non-Linearity: While raw data is linear with respect to photon count, subsequent pipeline stages (white balance, tone mapping) are non-linear and corrupt the noise distribution. A model demonstrating that pixel brightness is directly related to specific intensity inside a camera, assuming a properly focused imaging system. It establishes the geometric link between scene radiance and the sensor signal. Complexity: The measurement model itself is O(1) per pixel for noise simulation, involving simple arithmetic operations. Memory: Requires storage for high-bit-depth images (10-14 bits per channel). Strengths: Preserves maximum dynamic range and allows for flexible post-processing (exposure, white balance). Accurately models the statistical properties of real-world sensor data. Limitations: Requires access to raw sensor data, which is not always available. The noise model parameters (\alpha, \beta) must be calibrated for the specific sensor. The model originates from the work on "NeRF in the Dark," which introduced the use of noisy raw images for high dynamic range view synthesis. It builds upon the understanding that raw camera measurements are a noisy, linear representation of photon flux, distinct from processed images. The connection between specific intensity and pixel brightness is rooted in classical imaging theory, such as that described by Horn and Sjoberg. name: Cylindrical Slit-Scan Rendering
head: Cylindrical Panorama Rendering, Slit-Scan Rendering
body: Cylindrical Slit-Scan Rendering generates a cylindrical environment map by performing a series of narrow vertical rendering passes, each capturing a single column of the final panorama. This method eliminates horizontal perspective distortion by ensuring the camera's optical axis remains perpendicular to the projection plane for every column. It is distinct from standard panoramic cameras or single-pass equirectangular projections by decoupling the horizontal view angle from the vertical field of view, allowing for precise control over the vertical frustum while maintaining a consistent horizon. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scene (e.g., Gaussian Splatting or mesh-based scene), vertical field of view (FoVY), target width w, and target height h. Output: A cylindrical perspective map of dimensions w \times h. Data Structures Cylindrical Map: A 2D image buffer of size w \times h. Rendering Strip: A temporary buffer of size 16 \times h (or similar narrow width) used for intermediate rasterization. Parameters Vertical Field of View (FoVY): Fixed at 120^\circ. Strip Width: 16 pixels. Up Vector: [0, 1, 0]. Steps 1. Scene Alignment: Align the scene's vertical axis to the up-vector [0, 1, 0]. 2. Camera Positioning: Position a virtual camera at the center of the scene (origin \mathbf{o} = [0, 0, 0]). 3. Iterative Rendering: For each column index i from 0 to w-1: a. Calculate the horizontal angle \thetai: \thetai = \frac{2\pi \cdot i}{w} + \pi b. Set the camera view direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{d} = [\sin(\thetai), 0, \cos(\thetai)] c. Set the camera up vector to [0, 1, 0] to maintain a consistent horizontal horizon. d. Render a narrow vertical strip of width 16 pixels centered on the column corresponding to i, using the fixed FoVY of 120^\circ. e. Extract the central column of pixels from the rendered strip. 4. Assembly: Concatenate the extracted columns in order of i to form the final w \times h Cylindrical Perspective Map. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cylindricalslitscanrender(scene, w, h, fovydegrees=120): """ Generates a cylindrical panorama using slit-scan rendering. Args: scene: The 3D scene data structure. w: Width of the output cylindrical map. h: Height of the output cylindrical map. fovydegrees: Vertical field of view in degrees (default 120). Returns: cylindricalmap: A 2D array of shape (w, h) containing the rendered pixels. """ # Initialize output buffer cylindricalmap = empty2darray(w, h) # Camera setup cameraorigin = [0, 0, 0] upvector = [0, 1, 0] fovyrad = radians(fovydegrees) # Render each column for i in range(w): # Calculate horizontal angle thetai = (2 PI i / w) + PI # Calculate view direction viewdirection = [sin(thetai), 0, cos(thetai)] # Configure camera for this pass # Note: The specific rasterizer API is abstracted here. # The camera is positioned at origin, looking at viewdirection, # with upvector [0,1,0] and vertical FOV fovyrad. camera = Camera( origin=cameraorigin, direction=viewdirection, up=upvector, fovy=fovyrad, aspectratio=1.0 # Assumed for narrow strip processing) # Render a narrow strip (e.g., 16 pixels wide) # The strip is centered around the column i stripwidth = 16 stripxstart = i - stripwidth // 2 stripxend = i + stripwidth // 2 # Render the strip to a temporary buffer # The rasterizer handles the projection and shading stripbuffer = renderscene(scene, camera, xrange=[stripxstart, stripxend], yrange=[0, h]) # Extract the central column from the strip # Assuming stripbuffer has width 'stripwidth' centercolindex = stripwidth // 2 centralcolumn = stripbuffer[:, centercolindex] # Place the column in the final map cylindricalmap[i,:] = centralcolumn return cylindricalmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls Horizontal Boundaries: The method naturally handles the wrap-around from i=w-1 to i=0 due to the periodic nature of the sine/cosine functions, but care must be taken if the scene is not centered or if the camera origin is not truly central. Vertical FoV Limitation: The fixed 120^\circ vertical field of view means that polar regions (zenith and nadir) are not covered by the cylindrical map, resulting in empty areas. This variant extends the cylindrical map to a full spherical equirectangular projection. It involves mapping cylindrical coordinates to equirectangular coordinates and filling the empty polar regions using generative inpainting. For each pixel (x', y') in the target equirectangular image, the source vertical coordinate v{source} in the cylindrical map is calculated as v{source} = \tan(\phi) / \tan(FoVY / 2), where \phi is the vertical angle corresponding to y' and FoVY is 120^\circ. The polar regions, which are empty due to the limited vertical FoV, are filled using generative inpainting (e.g., Stable Diffusion via Krita Generative AI plugin) with prompts such as "realistic sky". To avoid seams at horizontal boundaries, an offset is applied and a second inpainting pass is performed. Additionally, regions containing extra elongated Gaussians in the foreground (which may cover the bottom part of the map) are painted black to be filled by the inpainting process. Time Complexity: O(w \cdot h \cdot r), where r is the cost of rendering a single narrow strip. Since w passes are performed, the total time is proportional to the width of the panorama. Memory Complexity: O(w \cdot h) for the final map, plus O(16 \cdot h) for the temporary strip buffer. Strengths: Eliminates horizontal perspective distortion, which is critical for accurate environment mapping in certain applications. Simple to implement using standard rasterizers. Limitations: Does not cover the full sphere (polar regions are missing). Requires multiple rendering passes, which can be slower than a single-pass method for very wide panoramas. When to Use: When horizontal perspective accuracy is paramount and the scene is centered. Suitable for generating environment maps for Gaussian Splatting or other novel view synthesis techniques. When Not to Use: When full spherical coverage is required without post-processing, or when computational efficiency is critical and horizontal distortion is acceptable. The method was introduced by D. Pintani et al. in the paper "EnvMap-GS: two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction with background-to-environment map baking". It was developed to facilitate the integration of cylindrical environment maps into existing renderers, particularly for outdoor Gaussian reconstruction tasks where background elements like sky and distant buildings need to be accurately represented. The approach leverages the fact that cylindrical projections eliminate horizontal perspective distortion, making them suitable for certain visualization and reconstruction pipelines. name: Parallel and GPU primitives
head: GPU acceleration primitives, parallel rendering primitives
body: This family encompasses the low-level algorithms and hardware mechanisms used to execute volume rendering computations on parallel architectures, primarily GPUs and multi-core CPUs. It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential ray casting and compositing by distributing work across thousands of threads. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Ray-primitive intersection and Ray generation and camera models is its focus on the execution model, memory synchronization, and data parallelism infrastructure rather than the geometric or optical mathematics of the ray itself. The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores). Common principles include: 1. Thread Mapping: Assigning one or more threads to process specific data elements (e.g., one thread per pixel or one thread per voxel sample). 2. Memory Hierarchy Utilization: Leveraging global memory for large datasets, shared/local memory for intermediate results (reductions), and registers for per-thread state. 3. Synchronization: Managing concurrency conflicts using atomic operations, barriers, or spatial partitioning (tiles) to ensure data consistency without excessive serialization. 4. Data Parallelism: Performing identical operations on different data elements simultaneously, often requiring coalesced memory access patterns to maximize bandwidth. A rendering strategy that divides the framebuffer into disjoint spatial tiles to enable lock-free, zero-synchronization parallel processing of semi-transparent primitives. It solves the concurrency conflict inherent in alpha compositing by ensuring that each tile is written to by only one thread, eliminating the need for atomics or locks. This approach is distinct from Parallel Direct Compositing which may use global atomic counters, and from Y-Bucket Parallelization which groups pixels by depth rather than spatial locality. A GPU compute shader kernel is a program executed on the GPU that processes data in parallel using thread IDs to map work items to data elements. It serves as a fundamental primitive for general-purpose GPU (GPGPU) computing, such as generating gradient textures or performing initial volume data preprocessing. It differs from higher-level volume rendering techniques by operating at the raw hardware execution level, requiring manual management of thread indexing and memory access patterns. CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability is a mechanism that allows CUDA kernels to read from and write to OpenGL resources (textures, buffers) directly in GPU memory, eliminating the need for CPU-mediated data transfers. It solves the bottleneck of copying rendered volume data or simulation results from CUDA device memory back to system memory for display. It sets itself apart from standard interop methods by supporting both read-only access (via mapped arrays/texture objects) and write access (via surface objects or direct buffer pointers), enabling zero-copy rendering pipelines. Y-Bucket Parallelization is a two-pass parallel algorithm for direct volume rendering that processes polygonal representations of isosurfaces or volume slices by grouping them into scanline-based "y-buckets". It solves the problem of efficiently rendering irregular and multiple grids in software by maximizing spatial coherence and avoiding the computational difficulties associated with ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. Atomic Fragment List Insertion is a GPU-side algorithm for building a per-pixel linked list of fragments using atomic operations to handle concurrent writes from multiple fragments without locks. It solves the problem of accumulating geometry fragments into a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) for subsequent compositing or ray processing. It differs from brute-force ray marching by avoiding empty space evaluation and from Tiled Parallel Compositing by using a global atomic counter for list construction rather than tiled accumulation buffers. Hardware and Platform Specific methods execute volume rendering algorithms directly on the GPU using shader languages (GLSL/HLSL) or compute models (CUDA/OpenCL), bypassing the CPU for the heavy lifting of ray marching and compositing. This approach solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based ray casting by leveraging massive parallelism. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Tiled Parallel Compositing and Compute Shader Kernel by its specific reliance on the graphics pipeline's fragment/vertex shaders or specific vendor APIs (CUDA) rather than generic compute abstractions or tile-based memory optimizations. Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) Orchestration is a GPU-based method for computing prefix sums (scans) of an input array using a multi-timestep iterative reduction strategy with ping-pong buffers. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating data across parallel threads without race conditions, serving as a foundational primitive for operations like voxel compaction and vertex indexing in volume rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Tiled Parallel Compositing by focusing on the low-level data movement and synchronization required for global aggregation, rather than high-level compositing logic. A multi-core parallel rendering method that divides screen space into contiguous regions for Phase I (BONO tree traversal to build block lists) and partitions ray casting tasks into Z-ordered tiles grouped by weight for Phase II (dynamic load-balanced ray casting). It sets itself apart from static tile allocation methods by using dynamic, weight-based grouping of Z-ordered tiles to achieve better load balancing and cache performance while minimizing synchronization overhead. Parallel Vector Multiplication is a fundamental GPU primitive where each thread independently multiplies corresponding elements from two input arrays to produce an output array. It solves the problem of element-wise vector scaling or Hadamard product computation at massive scale by mapping one thread per data element. It is distinct from sibling primitives like Parallel Prefix Sum (which requires inter-thread dependency) or Atomic Fragment List Insertion (which requires synchronization), as it involves no communication between threads. A parallel volume rendering technique where image compositing is performed directly across processors in a distributed memory environment, specifically analyzed for block data subdivision on a bidirectional torus topology. A lifecycle management technique for Buffer Objects (BOs) shared between OpenGL and CUDA. After allocation in OpenGL, the buffer is registered with CUDA. It alternates accessibility for integration (CUDA) or rendering (OpenGL). Operations performed across a subgroup (NVIDIA warp, AMD wave), which are hardware-synchronized groups of threads. Unlike atomics, they do not involve global memory synchronization and are faster. A technique to safely write to global memory from multiple GPU threads simultaneously by avoiding race conditions (collisions) using atomic operations. A warp-level reduction technique using warp shuffling operations (Kepler+) to communicate register values, allocating a single float4 buffer from the register space of each thread. step: Bind renderPipeline with descriptor set indices {0, currentImageIndex}. Push width and height as uint32t[2] constants. Transition swapchain image layout from eUndefined to eGeneral. Dispatch compute shader: (width + 15) / 16 by (height + 15) / 16 workgroups. Transition image layout to eColorAttachmentOptimal if GUI is enabled, else ePresentSrcKHR. If GUI enabled, draw ImGui, then transition from eColorAttachmentOptimal back to ePresentSrcKHR. code: Render pass dispatch and layout transitions. definition: Calculation of vector dot products using NVIDIA's CUDA CUBLAS library. A method to calculate vector dot products using point-wise multiplication followed by a parallel reduction operation within each thread block. step: Create a dot product handler. Calculate the dot product of arbitrary sized vectors using the cublasSDot function with necessary parameters. Write the result into device memory. Point-wise multiplication is performed in the kernel, storing results in shared memory sized to the number of threads in the block. Parallel reduction is performed using a tree-based approach within each thread block to sum the multiplied values. layout: Shared memory is used to store intermediate results for each variable, with each block maintaining its own copy. complexity: Complexity of parallel reduction is O(log n), compared to O(n) for traditional summation. definition: A parallel scheme exploiting parallelism in object space by dividing the volume into p subvolumes assigned to processors. step: Divide the volume into p subvolumes. Assign tasks associated with each subvolume to processors. Parallel render each subvolume to generate p distributed subimages. Merge subimages into the final image via image compositing. Parallel and GPU primitives have evolved alongside the development of General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPGPU). Early volume rendering relied on CPU-based ray casting, which was computationally prohibitive for high-resolution volumes. The introduction of programmable shaders (GLSL/HLSL) and compute APIs (CUDA, OpenCL) allowed for massive parallelization of the ray marching and compositing steps. Techniques like tiled compositing and atomic fragment lists emerged to solve specific concurrency issues in alpha blending and fragment accumulation. Object parallel rendering was developed to handle large-scale datasets by distributing volume data across processors, contrasting with screen-space parallelism. Modern implementations leverage hardware-specific features like warp shuffling and subgroup operations for efficient intra-thread-block communication. name: Tiled Parallel Compositing
body: Tiled parallel compositing partitions the output framebuffer into disjoint spatial tiles, enabling independent, parallel processing of each tile with zero synchronization, no atomics, and no locks. It solves concurrency conflicts in parallel volume rendering or splatting by ensuring each thread writes exclusively to its assigned pixel region. It sets itself apart from Atomic Fragment List Insertion by avoiding atomic contention, and from Parallel Direct Compositing by relying on spatial partitioning rather than data partitioning for parallelism. Inputs: wi, hi: Framebuffer width and height in pixels. TILEW, TILEH: Tile dimensions in pixels. bins.offsets: An array of size numtiles + 1 defining the start and end indices of splats assigned to each tile. projected: An array of projected splat data (position, covariance, color) indexed by splat ID. fb: A framebuffer buffer storing color and alpha values (e.g., Vec3 color and f32 alpha). Data Structures: ScratchBuffers: Reusable memory for intermediate calculations. sortaux: Vec<Projected>: Auxiliary storage for sorting or temporary projection data. tiles: TileBins: Structure containing the offsets array mapping tiles to splat ranges. FbPtr: A Send + Sync wrapper around mut (Vec3, f32) that enables safe concurrent mutable access to the framebuffer across threads, relying on the geometric guarantee that tile (tx, ty) only writes to pixels [tx \cdot TILE\W.. (tx+1) \cdot TILE\W, ty \cdot TILE\H.. (ty+1) \cdot TILE\H]. Parameters: TILEW, TILEH: Tile grid dimensions in pixels. AlphaThreshold: Minimum alpha value required to contribute to the framebuffer, used to skip transparent pixels during compositing. Steps: 1. Parallel Iteration: Iterate over all tile indices t in parallel using a thread pool or parallel iterator. 2. Tile Bounds Calculation: For each tile index t, determine grid coordinates (tx, ty) and pixel bounds: \begin{aligned} px0 &= tx \cdot TILE\W \\ py0 &= ty \cdot TILE\H \\ px1 &= \min(px0 + TILE\W - 1, wi - 1) \\ py1 &= \min(py0 + TILE\H - 1, hi - 1) \end{aligned}. 3. Validity Check: If px0 > px1 or py0 > py1, the tile is invalid or outside bounds; return immediately. 4. Splat Range Retrieval: Retrieve the splat index range for this tile: \begin{aligned} start &= bins.offsets[t] \\ end &= bins.offsets[t + 1] \end{aligned}. 5. Empty Check: If start == end, the tile has no splats; return immediately. 6. Splat Processing: For each splat ID sid in the range [start, end): a. Retrieve the projected splat p using projected.getunchecked(sid). b. Calculate the intersection of the splat's bounding box [bx0, by0, bx1, by1] with the tile's pixel bounds [px0, py0, px1, py1]: \begin{aligned} x0 &= \max(bx0, px0) \\ y0 &= \max(by0, py0) \\ x1 &= \min(bx1, px1) \\ y1 &= \min(by1, py1) \end{aligned}. c. If x0 > x1 or y0 > y1, the splat does not intersect the tile; continue to the next splat. d. Call compositesplatregion(p, fb, wi, x0, y0, x1, y1) to render the splat into the intersecting pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tiledparallelcompositing(wi, hi, TILEW, TILEH, bins, projected, fb): numtilesx = (wi + TILEW - 1) // TILEW numtilesy = (hi + TILEH - 1) // TILEH numtiles = numtilesx numtilesy # Parallel loop over tile indices for t in range(numtiles): # 1. Calculate tile coordinates and pixel bounds tx = t % numtilesx ty = t // numtilesx px0 = tx TILEW py0 = ty TILEH px1 = min(px0 + TILEW - 1, wi - 1) py1 = min(py0 + TILEH - 1, hi - 1) # 2. Check validity if px0 > px1 or py0 > py1: continue # 3. Get splat range start = bins.offsets[t] end = bins.offsets[t + 1] # 4. Check if empty if start == end: continue # 5. Process splats in this tile for sid in range(start, end): # Get projected splat data p = projected[sid] # Calculate intersection with tile bounds x0 = max(p.bx0, px0) y0 = max(p.by0, py0) x1 = min(p.bx1, px1) y1 = min(p.by1, py1) # Check intersection validity if x0 > x1 or y0 > y1: continue # Composite splat into framebuffer compositesplatregion(p, fb, wi, x0, y0, x1, y1) def compositesplatregion(p, fb, width, x0, y0, x1, y1): # Standard front-to-back alpha compositing for the intersecting region for y in range(y0, y1 + 1): for x in range(x0, x1 + 1): idx = y width + x # Blend splat color/alpha into framebuffer at (x, y) fb[idx].color = blend(fb[idx].color, p.color, p.alpha) fb[idx].alpha = blendalpha(fb[idx].alpha, p.alpha) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Borrow Checker/Concurrency: In languages like Rust, multiple threads cannot hold &mut references to the same buffer. This is handled by wrapping the raw framebuffer pointer in a Send + Sync newtype (FbPtr) and using unsafe blocks, relying on the disjoint tile geometry to guarantee no data races. Tile Bounds: Tiles at the image boundary must clamp pixel bounds to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Empty Tiles: Tiles with no overlapping geometry must be skipped early to avoid unnecessary overhead. Tile-Based Alpha Compositing blends multiple semi-transparent primitives into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest within disjoint tiles. It is distinguished from back-to-front compositing by its tile-based parallelization, which allows independent processing of each tile without synchronization. Choose this when rendering overlapping splats or Gaussians that require strict depth ordering per tile. Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue splits screen space into tiles and assigns them to processors via a shared queue to ensure high processor utilization over a wide range of views. It addresses the unpredictability of isosurface extraction complexity per pixel, which static partitioning cannot handle efficiently. It sets itself apart from static partitioning by dynamically adjusting task granularity to balance load and reduce contention. A strategy to select between two tile dimensions (16x16 and 16x32) based on the number of pixels to render to optimize performance. It sets itself apart from fixed-size tiling by adapting to resolution, reducing duplicated Gaussians at high resolutions while avoiding excessive sequential load per tile at low resolutions. Choose this when rendering at variable resolutions. This method initializes the data structures required for tiled parallel compositing by computing the spatial extent (boundaries) of each tile within the framebuffer. It solves the problem of determining which input primitives or data elements contribute to which output tiles, enabling subsequent parallel processing stages to operate on disjoint subsets of the image without synchronization. It differs from sibling methods like Coarse Raster by focusing on the setup of the boundary metadata itself rather than the rasterization of geometry, and from Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by being a static setup phase rather than a runtime scheduling mechanism. Parallel Image Assembly is the final step in spatial decomposition volume rendering where sub-images rendered by independent threads or processes are combined into a single final image. It solves the problem of merging disjoint spatial data portions into a coherent visual output by placing sub-images at their correct spatial coordinates and blending them along the z-axis using front-to-back alpha compositing. Unlike temporal sequencing, which has minimal overhead, spatial compositing incurs significant overhead due to the data collection and blending requirements. Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering is a parallelization strategy that divides the screen height into tiles and processes each tile in a separate thread to parallelize the rasterization workload. It differs from Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by focusing on the rasterization phase itself rather than just compositing pre-rasterized fragments, and from Screen Parallel Rendering by dividing the screen into tiles processed by threads on a single machine rather than subscreens distributed across multiple processors. Manages tile assignment and synchronization across worker threads using wave indices and tokens. It sets itself apart from lock-free tiling by providing explicit synchronization points for tasks requiring global consistency or progress tracking. Choose this when implementing a path tracer or ray caster that requires wave-based synchronization. Parallel Binary-Swap Compositing is a method for combining independently rendered image tiles from multiple processors in a massively parallel environment. It solves the synchronization and communication bottlenecks of naive parallel compositing by reducing the data volume at each step, ensuring all processors remain busy with useful work. Unlike approaches where communication dominates or processors idle, this method maintains full processor utilization by pairing processors in a binary-swap fashion. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of tiles and available threads, provided the workload is balanced. Strengths: Zero synchronization overhead, no atomics, no locks, effective on CPU. Simple to implement with standard parallel loops. Limitations: Load imbalance occurs if geometry clusters in specific tiles. When to use: When rendering large numbers of independent primitives (e.g., Gaussians, splats) with minimal inter-tile dependencies. When not to use: When global synchronization is required between tiles. Tiled parallel compositing is a standard spatial decomposition technique for parallel rendering. It leverages spatial decomposition to enable lock-free parallelism. The approach has been adapted for various hardware architectures, including CPU multi-threading (e.g., using rayon in Rust) and GPU compute shaders. name: Tile-Based Alpha Compositing
head: Tsplat compositing
body: Tile-Based Alpha Compositing is a rendering technique that blends multiple semi-transparent primitives (such as 2D Gaussians or splats) into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest within disjoint tiles. It is distinguished from back-to-front compositing by its tile-based parallelization, which allows independent processing of each tile without synchronization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of splats, each defined by a 2D center (sx, sy), an inverse 2D covariance matrix cov2d\inv, an opacity \alpha{splat}, and a color C{splat}. Output: A framebuffer containing accumulated color C{accum} and accumulated opacity \alpha{accum} for each pixel. Data Structures: Framebuffer: Parallel arrays or a 2D array of structs for C{accum} (RGB floats) and \alpha{accum} (float). Initialized to (0, 0, 0) and 0 respectively. Splat: Struct containing: sx, sy: Float center coordinates in pixel space. cov2d\inv: 2x2 inverse covariance matrix represented by elements a, b, d where cov2d\inv = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}. \alpha{splat}: Float opacity. C{splat}: RGB color vector. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the framebuffer's C{accum} to (0, 0, 0) and \alpha{accum} to 0 for all pixels. 2. Sorting: Sort all splats by depth (distance from camera) in descending order (front-to-back). 3. Tile Processing: Divide the image into disjoint tiles. For each tile: 4. Splat Rasterization: For each splat overlapping the tile: 5. Bounding Box: Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the splat's 2D Gaussian projection within the tile. 6. Pixel Loop: Iterate over each pixel (px, py) within the AABB: 7. Displacement: Calculate dx = px - sx and dy = py - sy. 8. Optimization: For a fixed row py, dy is constant. Precompute coefficients for the quadratic form in dx to optimize the inner loop. 9. Gaussian Evaluation: Compute the power term: power = -\frac{1}{2} (a \cdot dx^2 + 2b \cdot dx \cdot dy + d \cdot dy^2) where a = cov2d\inv.x\axis.x, b = cov2d\inv.x\axis.y, d = cov2d\inv.y\axis.y. 10. Alpha Calculation: Compute the splat's alpha at this pixel: \alpha = \alpha{splat} \cdot \exp(power). 11. Clamping: Clamp \alpha to [0, 1]. 12. Compositing: Update the framebuffer using front-to-back alpha blending: T = 1 - \alpha{accum} contrib = T \cdot \alpha C{accum} += contrib \cdot C{splat} \alpha{accum} += contrib. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tilebasedalphacompositing(splats, width, height, tilesize=16): # Initialize framebuffer accumcolor = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] accumalpha = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Sort splats front-to-back sortedsplats = sorted(splats, key=lambda s: s.depth, reverse=True) # Process tiles for ty in range(0, height, tilesize): for tx in range(0, width, tilesize): tileendy = min(ty + tilesize, height) tileendx = min(tx + tilesize, width) for splat in sortedsplats: # Compute bounding box from covariance # Approximate 3-sigma bounds from inverse covariance eigenvalues trace = splat.cov2dinv[0][0] + splat.cov2dinv[1][1] det = splat.cov2dinv[0][0] splat.cov2dinv[1][1] - splat.cov2dinv[0][1] 2 if det <= 0: continue sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(trace trace - 4 det) lambda1 = (trace + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - sqrtdisc) / 2 radius = 3.0 math.sqrt(1.0 / min(lambda1, lambda2)) xmin, xmax = int(splat.sx - radius), int(splat.sx + radius) ymin, ymax = int(splat.sy - radius), int(splat.sy + radius) # Clip to tile bounds clipxmin = max(tx, xmin) clipxmax = min(tileendx, xmax) clipymin = max(ty, ymin) clipymax = min(tileendy, ymax) if clipxmin >= clipxmax or clipymin >= clipymax: continue a = splat.cov2dinv[0][0] b = splat.cov2dinv[0][1] d = splat.cov2dinv[1][1] for py in range(clipymin, clipymax): dy = py - splat.sy term1 = d dy dy term2 = 2.0 b dy for px in range(clipxmin, clipxmax): # Skip if pixel is already fully opaque if accumalpha[py][px] >= 1.0: continue dx = px - splat.sx power = -0.5 (a dx dx + term2 dx + term1) alpha = splat.opacity math.exp(power) alpha = max(0.0, min(1.0, alpha)) if alpha < 1e-6: continue T = 1.0 - accumalpha[py][px] contrib = T alpha r, g, bval = accumcolor[py][px] cr, cg, cb = splat.color accumcolor[py][px] = (r + contrib cr, g + contrib cg, bval + contrib cb) accumalpha[py][px] += contrib Front-to-Back Alpha Compositing is a rendering technique that blends multiple semi-transparent primitives (such as 2D Gaussians or splats) into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest, ensuring correct occlusion where near primitives paint over far ones. It is distinguished from back-to-front compositing by its ability to use early termination: once the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold, the pixel is considered fully opaque and remaining splats are skipped, providing a significant computational speedup. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) where N is the number of splats and K is the average number of pixels per splat's bounding box. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the framebuffer, where W, H are image dimensions. Strengths: Parallelizable across tiles; no synchronization needed between tiles; effective on CPU architectures. Limitations: Requires sorting splats by depth; performance depends on splat density and overlap. When to use: Real-time rendering of large numbers of semi-transparent primitives, especially on CPU or GPU where tile-based parallelism is beneficial. When not to use: Scenes with very low opacity where early termination is ineffective; when strict back-to-front order is required for specific artistic effects. Tile-Based Alpha Compositing is implemented in the Tsplat renderer. The method leverages the spatial coherence of splats and the efficiency of tile-based processing to minimize overhead and maximize throughput. name: Front-to-Back Alpha Compositing
head: Alpha Compositing with Front-to-Back Blending, Front-to-Back Blending, Over Operator, Porter-Duff Over, Running Transmittance Compositing
body: Front-to-Back Alpha Compositing is a rendering technique that combines multiple semi-transparent primitives (such as 2D Gaussians or splats) into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest, ensuring correct occlusion where near primitives paint over far ones. Unlike back-to-front compositing, which requires processing all primitives to compute the final color, front-to-back compositing allows for early termination once the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold, providing a significant speedup for dense scenes. It builds on Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by defining the core blending logic applied within each tile. Inputs: A set of N splats (Gaussians), each defined by center position in screen space \mathbf{x}i = (ui, vi). Inverse 2D covariance matrix \Sigma'^{-1}i describing the ellipse shape and orientation. Intrinsic opacity scalar \alphai \in [0, 1]. Color vector \mathbf{c}i (typically RGB). Depth value Zc used for sorting. A pixel coordinate \mathbf{x} = (u, v). Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}. Remaining transmittance T indicating background visibility. Data Structures: Splat list sorted by depth Zc in ascending order (nearest first). Running transmittance scalar T, initialized to 1.0. Accumulated color vector \mathbf{C}, initialized to \mathbf{0}. Formulas: 1. Effective Per-Pixel Alpha: The influence of a splat at a specific pixel \mathbf{x} is determined by its 2D Gaussian falloff: \alphai(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \cdot \exp\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i)^\top \Sigma'^{-1}i (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i)\right) Here, \alphai(\mathbf{x}) is the effective alpha, \alphai is the intrinsic opacity, and the exponential term represents the Gaussian coverage Gi(\mathbf{x}). 2. Accumulated Transmittance: The fraction of light surviving all splats in front of splat i: Ti = \prod{j < i}(1 - \alphaj(\mathbf{x})) where T1 = 1. 3. Final Pixel Color: The sum of each splat's color weighted by its effective alpha and the transmittance reaching it: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i} \mathbf{c}i \alphai(\mathbf{x}) Ti Parameters: \epsilon (epsilon): Early termination threshold. Typical value: 10^{-4}. Steps: 1. Sort: Sort all splats affecting the pixel by their center depth Zc in ascending order (nearest to farthest). 2. Initialize: Set running transmittance T \leftarrow 1 and accumulated color \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{0}. 3. Iterate: For each splat i in sorted order: a. Calculate effective alpha \alphai(\mathbf{x}) using the Gaussian formula. b. If \alphai(\mathbf{x}) \approx 0, skip to next splat. c. Update accumulated color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + T \cdot \alphai(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i. d. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai(\mathbf{x})). e. Early Termination: If T < \epsilon, break the loop. 4. Result: Return \mathbf{C}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fronttobackcompositing(splatssorted, pixelx, epsilon=1e-4): """ Composites splats for a single pixel using front-to-back alpha blending. Args: splatssorted: List of splat objects sorted by depth (nearest first). Each splat has attributes: center (u, v), invcov (2x2 matrix), opacity (alpha), color (RGB vector). pixelx: Tuple (u, v) representing the pixel coordinate. epsilon: Threshold for early termination. Returns: C: Final accumulated color vector. """ T = 1.0 C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for splat in splatssorted: dx = pixelx[0] - splat.center[0] dy = pixelx[1] - splat.center[1] invcov = splat.invcov quadform = invcov[0][0] dx dx + (invcov[0][1] + invcov[1][0]) dx dy + invcov[1][1] dy dy alphaeff = splat.opacity math.exp(-0.5 quadform) if alphaeff <= 0.0: continue C[0] += T alphaeff splat.color[0] C[1] += T alphaeff splat.color[1] C[2] += T alphaeff splat.color[2] T = (1.0 - alphaeff) if T < epsilon: break return C Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sort-Order Flips: 3DGS sorts splats by center depth Zc. Since splats are 3D blobs with extent, overlapping splats can swap order as the camera moves, causing flickering ("popping artifacts"). This is a speed/quality trade-off. Incorrect Order: If splats are processed far-to-near without adjusting the compositing math, occlusion inverts, causing far splats to wrongly paint over near ones. Precision: The transmittance T decays exponentially. Using a threshold \epsilon prevents unnecessary computation for deeply occluded pixels. A Python/NumPy implementation of front-to-back alpha compositing that processes all pixels in an image simultaneously using vectorized operations, rather than per-pixel loops. Unlike GPU implementations that can perform per-pixel early termination, this NumPy version processes all splats for all pixels regardless of opacity, trading computational efficiency for code simplicity and gradient stability. A method that maps alpha-blending and sorting operations to a sequence of General Matrix Multiplications (GEMMs). The per-tile blending becomes a matrix multiplication C = AB where A contains the Gaussian attributes and B the pixel-wise accumulation weights. The process of rendering ordered grid patches using standard DVR algorithms and compositing them into a final image. Patches are rendered as RGB images with an alpha channel and composited using an 'over' operation, either in software or in hardware as an alpha-blending operation. In texture-mapping based hardware-assisted DVR algorithms, compositing is performed implicitly by rendering all grid patches into the same frame buffer. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) in the worst case, where N is the number of splats and P is the number of pixels. However, with early termination, the average case is significantly faster, often processing only 2–4 splats per pixel in dense scenes. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store splat attributes and sorted lists. Performance: The early termination optimization provides a significant speedup, especially for dense scenes where pixels become fully opaque quickly. Tiling further optimizes this by reducing the number of splats considered per pixel. Strengths: Correct occlusion handling, efficient early termination, simple algebraic formulation. Limitations: Sort-order flips can cause visual artifacts (popping). Requires sorting, which can be expensive if not optimized (e.g., via tiling or GPU primitives). When to Use: When correct occlusion is required and the scene has varying density, allowing early termination to save computation. When Not to Use: When sort-order artifacts are unacceptable and more complex depth handling is needed, or when hardware acceleration for sorting is unavailable. Front-to-back alpha compositing is a fundamental technique in computer graphics, originally derived from the Porter-Duff "over" operator used in image compositing. It is widely used in Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to render 2D Gaussian splats into a 2D image. The method is also analogous to ray marching in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and traditional volume rendering, where transmittance is accumulated along a ray. The compositing pipeline is designed to be differentiable, enabling backward passes for training splat parameters. 3DGS-101/textbook/05-alpha-compositing.md at main - GitHub, https://github.com/Chamud/3DGS-101/blob/main/textbook/05-alpha-compositing.md, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) 3D Gaussian Splatting 入门原创, https://blog.csdn.net/qq35831906/article/details/143322205, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Remote Interactive Direct Volume Rendering of AMR Data, https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/799586, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Vectorized Front-to-Back Compositing
head: NumPy Front-to-Back Compositing, Per-tile sorting, Tiled Rasterization, Vectorized Alpha Compositing
body: A Python/NumPy implementation of front-to-back alpha compositing that processes all pixels in an image simultaneously using vectorized operations, rather than per-pixel loops. Unlike GPU implementations that can perform per-pixel early termination, this NumPy version processes all splats for all pixels regardless of opacity, trading computational efficiency for code simplicity and gradient stability. Inputs: A list of splats, each defined by center (u, v) in pixel coordinates, a 2 \times 2 covariance matrix \Sigma' (or its inverse \Sigma'^{-1}), RGB color \mathbf{c}, stored opacity \alpha{\text{stored}}, and depth Zc. Image dimensions H \times W. Background color \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}}. Outputs: Final image \mathbf{C} of shape (H, W, 3). Data Structures: pix: Array of shape (H, W, 2) containing pixel coordinates (u, v). C: Accumulated color array of shape (H, W, 3), initialized to zeros. T: Transmittance array of shape (H, W), initialized to ones. Steps: 1. Sort Splats: Sort the list of splats by depth Zc in ascending order (near to far). 2. Initialize: Set \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{0} and T = \mathbf{1} for all pixels. 3. Iterate: For each splat i in sorted order: a. Compute pixel offsets: \mathbf{d} = \text{pix} - \text{center}i. b. Compute quadratic form: q = \mathbf{d}^T \Sigma'^{-1}i \mathbf{d}. c. Compute Gaussian falloff: G = \exp(-0.5 \cdot q). The normalization constant \frac{1}{2\pi|\Sigma'|} is omitted or absorbed. d. Compute effective alpha: \alphai = \alpha{\text{stored}, i} \cdot G. e. Clip alpha: \alphai = \min(\alphai, 0.999) to prevent \alpha=1.0. f. Compute weight: w = \alphai \cdot T. g. Update color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + w \cdot \mathbf{c}i. h. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai). 4. Background: Add background contribution: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + T \cdot \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}}. Formulas: Gaussian falloff: G = e^{-\frac{1}{2} d^T \Sigma'^{-1} d}. Effective alpha: \alphai(\mathbf{x}) = \alphai \cdot Gi(\mathbf{x}). Color accumulation: \mathbf{C} = \sumi \mathbf{c}i \alphai Ti, where Ti = \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj). Parameters: Alpha clipping upper bound: 0.999. Background color: [0.05, 0.05, 0.08] (dark navy). Low alpha threshold: \approx 0.004 (1/255). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vectorizedfronttobackcompositing(splats, H, W, backgroundcolor): """ splats: list of dicts with keys 'center' (2,), 'inv' (2x2), 'color' (3,), 'opacity' (float), 'depth' (float) H, W: int backgroundcolor: array (3,) """ # 1. Sort splats by depth (near first) splatssorted = sorted(splats, key=lambda g: g["depth"]) # 2. Initialize pixel grid and accumulators vv, uu = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W] pix = np.stack([uu, vv], axis=-1).astype(float) # (H, W, 2) C = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) # Accumulated color T = np.ones((H, W)) # Accumulated transmittance # 3. Iterate over splats for g in splatssorted: # a. Pixel offsets d = pix - g["center"] # (H, W, 2) # b. Quadratic form d^T Sigma'^-1 d q = np.einsum('...i,ij,...j->...', d, g["inv"], d) # c. Gaussian falloff G = np.exp(-0.5 q) # (H, W) # d. Effective alpha alpha = g["opacity"] G # e. Clip alpha to prevent gradient vanishing alpha = np.clip(alpha, 0.0, 0.999) # f. Weight w = alpha T # (H, W) # g. Update color C += w[:,:, None] g["color"] # Broadcasting color to (H, W, 3) # h. Update transmittance T = (1.0 - alpha) # Skip splats with very low alpha to save computation and gradient traffic if np.max(alpha) < 0.004: continue # 4. Add background C += T[:,:, None] backgroundcolor # Clip final image img = np.clip(C, 0, 1) return img Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha = 1.0: If \alpha reaches exactly 1.0, T becomes 0, stopping further contributions. This is acceptable for forward rendering but causes vanishing gradients during backpropagation. Clamping to 0.999 prevents this. Low Alpha: Effective alpha below 1/255 \approx 0.004 contributes nothing to 8-bit pixels. Evaluating these splats wastes computation and gradient traffic. Real implementations skip these. No Early Termination: Unlike GPU implementations, this vectorized approach cannot break the loop early when T < \epsilon for specific pixels. All pixels process all splats regardless of opacity. Time and memory complexity, measured performance, scaling, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are Not given in the sources. The method processes all splats for all pixels without per-pixel early termination, unlike GPU implementations. Described in an unofficial GitHub repository "3DGS-101" by Chamud. The underlying tiled sorting and compositing pipeline is implemented in the reference CUDA rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting and libraries like gsplat. 3DGS-101/textbook/05-alpha-compositing.md at main - GitHub, https://github.com/Chamud/3DGS-101/blob/main/textbook/05-alpha-compositing.md, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue
head: Parallel Volume Rendering (Screen Space Partitioning), Tile Queue Load Balancing
body: Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue is a parallel processing scheme that splits screen space into tiles and assigns them to processors via a shared queue to ensure high processor utilization over a wide range of views. It addresses the unpredictability of isosurface extraction complexity per pixel, which static partitioning cannot handle efficiently. It sets itself apart from static partitioning by dynamically adjusting task granularity to balance load and reduce contention. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset, a camera view, and a set of P processors. Output: A rendered image (framebuffer). Data Structures: Tile: A rectangular region of the image. In the reference implementation, tiles are 32 pixels wide by 4 pixels high. The width ensures tiles do not share a cache line with neighboring tiles. Queue: A shared data structure containing tile assignments. The queue supports atomic "pull" operations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Split the screen space into tiles in image space. At the beginning of a frame, each tile becomes an assignment in the shared queue. 2. Work Pulling: Each processor pulls a range of assignments from the queue. 3. Processing: The processor performs the assigned work (ray-tracing/isosurface extraction) for the tiles in the pulled range. 4. Iteration & Granularity Adjustment: After completing the work, the processor returns to the queue to pull more assignments. Assignments are initially doled out in large chunks, getting smaller as the frame nears completion to reduce contention early and balance load efficiently late. 5. Task Redistribution: If a node cannot finish its task before a time-out stamp, it takes the remnant, re-partitions it, and re-distributes it. Nodes may also steal smaller tasks from other nodes once they have completed their own tasks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time import threading tilequeue = [] queuelock = threading.Lock() TIMEOUT = 1.0 # seconds def initializeframe(tiles): # Order tasks in decreasing size for better load balancing tiles.sort(key=lambda t: t.complexity, reverse=True) tilequeue.extend(tiles) def pullwork(maxcount): with queuelock: chunk = tilequeue[:maxcount] del tilequeue[:maxcount] return chunk def rendertile(tile): # Perform ray-marching/compositing for the tile pass def processorloop(): while True: # Granularity: large chunks early, small chunks late chunksize = max(1, len(tilequeue) // 2) tiles = pullwork(chunksize) if not tiles: break start = time.time() for i, tile in enumerate(tiles): rendertile(tile) # Time-out: re-partition and redistribute remnant if time.time() - start > TIMEOUT: with queuelock: tilequeue.extend(tiles[i:]) break Parameters: Tile Dimensions: 32 pixels wide by 4 pixels high. Queue Ordering: Tasks ordered in decreasing size/complexity to achieve better load balancing. Granularity Strategy: Starts large, decreases as the frame completes. Exact formula for size reduction is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Contention: High contention for the queue can occur if chunk sizes are too small early in the frame. The large initial chunk size mitigates this. Load Imbalance: If the workload is extremely uneven, processors may finish early and idle. The decreasing chunk size helps balance this late in the frame. Synchronization Overhead: Synchronizing processors at the required frame rate can reduce efficiency, especially with large numbers of processors (> 64). Scanline Interleaving is an image-space partitioning strategy that distributes pixels across processors in a striped, round-robin pattern to balance the computational load of ray-merging operations. It addresses variations in depth complexity caused by local variations in cell sizes by dispersing ray-merging computations evenly across the screen. Load-Balanced Cell Assignment (PA) distributes the ray-segment merging workload in tiled parallel volume rendering by assigning coarse 2D mesh-cells to processors. It solves the problem of balancing computational load during the Local Pixel Merging (LPM) phase, where ray-segments generated by different processors for the same pixel must be combined into an atomic task per mesh-cell. Unlike Scanline Interleaving, which assumes neighbor mesh-cells have equal workload, PA explicitly models each mesh-cell's computational load based on its global ray-segment count to achieve a balanced distribution. Farm on Demand (FD) is a parallel isosurface extraction algorithm that achieves dynamic load balancing by subdividing a volumetric dataset into a large number of fine-grained tasks and distributing them to worker processes on demand. It builds on Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by applying the processor farm paradigm to volume data, where the master assigns small intervals of slices to workers as they become available, rather than using static partitioning. Unlike its sibling Load Balanced Cell Assignment (LBC), which uses static contiguous partitions, FD provides near-perfect computational load balancing for uneven isosurface distributions but probabilistically produces a significantly higher number of shared vertices due to non-contiguous task assignment. Hybrid Image Partitioning is a dynamic load balancing scheme for parallel volume rendering that combines static block assignment with dynamic tile grabbing to balance load distribution and minimize overlapping voxel accesses. It sets itself apart from static contiguous partitioning by avoiding poor load distribution caused by varying image complexity, and from static interleaved partitioning by minimizing excessive overlapping voxel accesses through spatial locality. It builds on Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by distributing the queue management across processors to avoid the bottleneck of a centralized point of control. Central Queue Load Balancing introduces a central queue of work where processors grab pending loads as soon as they become available. Processors use a shared queue containing a front-to-back sorted list of bricks, rendering corresponding bricks to a shared frame buffer. Race conditions are solved by having each processor render each brick to a private buffer, then moving to a complete work queue, blending from the private buffer onto the shared buffer only once all dependent bricks are in the completed work queue. However, choosing a central dispatching mechanism serializes the program, creating a single point of control that becomes a bottleneck as the number of processors increases. The Dynamic Mapping Problem is the problem of mapping image sources to display tiles through an ordered sequence of image compositing operations. It is formulated as embedding an interdependency graph (logical pipelines) into a fixed host graph (network topology) without exhausting bandwidth. The general problem is NP-complete, and solving it dynamically per frame requires assumptions allowing efficient polynomial time solution. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The algorithm is dynamic, so time complexity depends on the workload distribution and queue contention. Memory: Memory usage is proportional to the number of tiles in the queue and any private buffers used in variants. Measured Performance: Hardware: 128 CPUs. Scene: Bone isosurface in the Visible Human dataset. Resolution: 512x512 image. Results: View 1 (nearly 100% pixel coverage): 20.49 FPS, 91% efficiency. View 2 (approx 75% pixel coverage): 39.98 FPS, 80% efficiency. Scalability: Efficiency drops with larger numbers of processors (> 64) due to load imbalances and synchronization time. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High processor utilization over a wide range of views; adapts to unpredictable isosurface complexity; reduces contention with large initial chunks. Limitations: Synchronization overhead at high processor counts; requires a shared queue mechanism which can become a bottleneck if not distributed. Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue was introduced in the context of large-scale isosurface extraction methods for large image data sets. It was developed to address the challenges of real-time ray-tracing on large datasets, specifically the Visible Human dataset. The method was part of a broader effort to optimize parallel volume rendering on CPU clusters, leveraging cache locality through bricking and spatial hierarchies. name: Scanline Interleaving
body: Scanline Interleaving is an image-space partitioning strategy that distributes pixels across processors in a striped, round-robin pattern to balance the computational load of ray-merging operations. It addresses the problem of uneven depth complexity caused by local variations in cell sizes within unstructured meshes. It operates on the image plane rather than the volume data space, distinguishing it from Load-Balanced Cell Assignment, and uses static cyclic assignment rather than dynamic task queuing, distinguishing it from Farm on Demand (FD). The volumetric rendering integral for each sub-part is calculated independently on different processors, and the final image is reconstructed by placing these sub-images side-by-side according to their positions. Inputs: Image dimensions: width W, height H (number of scanlines). Number of processors: P. Outputs: Assignment of each pixel to a processor. Final merged pixel values (color and opacity). Data Structures: Per-pixel linked list of ray segments maintained at each pixel location, which are merged to form the final pixel value. Steps: 1. Partition the image space such that rows (scanlines) are distributed cyclically among processors. 2. Assign successive scanlines to processors in round-robin fashion using the formula \text{processor\id} = y \pmod P, where y is the scanline index (0 \le y < H) and P is the number of processors. 3. Each processor scan-converts its local cells to produce ray segments, which are routed to their final destinations in image space for merging. 4. At each pixel location, maintain a linked list of ray segments, which are merged to form the final pixel value. 5. Reconstruct the final image by placing the independently calculated sub-images side-by-side according to their positions. Parameters: P: Number of processors. H: Vertical resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance degrades if the vertical resolution is not several times larger than the number of processors. Suffers from load imbalance due to transparent pixels in the final image. A single data block may be accessed by multiple processors to calculate a single image, requiring data sharing between processors, which is exacerbated when the viewpoint changes. When using numerous processors, finer-grained pixel interleaving is required to more effectively distribute high-density regions over more processors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assignscanlines(width, height, numprocessors): """ Assigns each pixel in the image to a processor using scanline interleaving. Args: width (int): Number of columns (x-resolution). height (int): Number of rows (y-resolution). numprocessors (int): Total number of processors P. Returns: dict: A dictionary mapping (x, y) coordinates to processor IDs. """ assignment = {} for y in range(height): processorid = y % numprocessors for x in range(width): assignment[(x, y)] = processorid return assignment A finer-grained variant that assigns individual pixels or small blocks in round-robin order rather than entire scanlines. It sets itself apart by distributing high-density regions more effectively across many processors. Choose it when using numerous processors or when scanline granularity is insufficient. Combines multiple partitioning strategies to handle varying scene complexities. Choose it when a single static scheme fails to balance load across diverse views. Hybrid Image Partitioning Measured Performance: Pixel interleaving speeds up overall rendering by nearly 10 percent on large systems compared to coarser partitioning. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively disperses ray-merging operations when vertical resolution is high relative to processor count. Limitations: Performance degrades if vertical resolution is not several times larger than processor count. Suffers from load imbalance due to transparent pixels. Requires data sharing between processors. When to Use: When vertical resolution is several times larger than the number of processors and depth complexity is relatively uniform vertically. When Not to Use: When the number of processors is large relative to vertical resolution, or when depth complexity is highly localized. Use finer-grained pixel interleaving instead. Developed as part of a scalable parallel cell-projection volume rendering algorithm for three-dimensional unstructured data. It is used in conjunction with cell-projection rendering algorithms, where cells are scan-converted into ray segments and routed to image space for merging. The approach addresses local variations in cell sizes leading to variations in depth complexity in image space. name: Load-Balanced Cell Assignment
head: Pixel Assignment
body: Load-Balanced Cell Assignment (PA) distributes the ray-segment merging workload in tiled parallel volume rendering by assigning coarse 2D mesh-cells to processors. It solves the problem of balancing computational load during the Local Pixel Merging (LPM) phase, where ray-segments generated by different processors for the same pixel must be combined into an atomic task per mesh-cell. Unlike Scanline Interleaving, which assumes neighbor mesh-cells have equal workload, PA explicitly models each mesh-cell's computational load based on its global ray-segment count to achieve a balanced distribution. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of processors \{P1, \dots, Pr\}; a 2D coarse mesh imposed on the image screen; for each mesh-cell m, the subset of processors Pm \subseteq \{P1, \dots, Pr\} that generated ray-segments for pixels in m during the local rendering phase; the local ray-segment count r{km} for each processor Pk \in Pm; and the global ray-segment count Rm. Output: An assignment mapping each mesh-cell m to a single processor P{\text{assign}}(m). Data Structures Mesh: A 2D grid of cells covering the image screen. Cells should be close to square shapes to ensure scalability of the decomposition. Definitions Let Pm be the subset of processors that generated ray-segments for pixels in mesh-cell m. Let r{km} be the local ray-segment count of processor Pk for mesh-cell m. Let Rm be the global ray-segment count of mesh-cell m, defined as: Rm = \sum{Pk \in Pm} r{km} The computational load of m during the LPM step is assumed to be proportional to Rm. Algorithm Steps 1. Impose a 2D coarse mesh on the image screen, ensuring cells are close to square for scalability. 2. For each mesh-cell m, identify the subset of processors Pm that generated ray-segments for its pixels during the local rendering phase. 3. Compute the local ray-segment count r{km} for each processor Pk \in Pm and the global ray-segment count Rm = \sum{Pk \in Pm} r{km}. 4. Assign the atomic task of merging ray-segments for mesh-cell m to a single processor, using Rm as the computational load metric. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assigncells(meshcells, processors): """ Assigns mesh-cells to processors to balance load based on global ray-segment counts. meshcells: list of dicts with keys 'id', 'Rm' (global ray-segment count) processors: list of processor IDs """ # Initialize load tracker for each processor processorloads = {p: 0 for p in processors} assignment = {} # Assign each mesh-cell to the processor with the current minimum load # The source does not specify a sorting or scheduling heuristic for cell in meshcells: targetproc = min(processorloads, key=processorloads.get) assignment[cell['id']] = targetproc processorloads[targetproc] += cell['Rm'] return assignment Parameters and Edge Cases Mesh Shape: Mesh-cells should be close to square shapes for scalability. Granularity: The overhead of the assignment step must be kept minimal because of the fine granularity of the pixel merging operations. BLMCA is a load-balanced cell assignment method for tiled parallel volume rendering that simultaneously minimizes inter-processor communication volume and load imbalance. It improves upon pure Minimized-Communication Assignment (MCA) and pure Best-Fit Decreasing (BFD) load balancing by incorporating MCA’s greedy communication criterion into the BFD heuristic, prioritizing the assignment of heavily loaded mesh-cells to reduce communication overhead while maintaining balanced workloads. Choose BLMCA when both communication volume and load balance are critical, as it balances the trade-off that pure MCA or pure BFD neglect. Complexity: The source does not provide explicit time or memory complexity for the assignment algorithm itself, only noting that the overhead must be minimal. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scalability of the decomposition depends on mesh-cells being close to square shapes. Strengths: Explicitly minimizes load imbalance by using Rm as the load metric, avoiding the communication overhead issues of Scanline Interleaving (SCA) which lacks explicit communication minimization. Limitations: The source does not detail communication volume minimization for PA itself, only for MCA and BLMCA. PA is described as simple but distinct from SCA's assumption that neighbor cells have equal workload. When to use/not use: Use PA when computational load varies significantly across the image and must be explicitly balanced per mesh-cell; avoid it when neighbor cells can be assumed to have equal workload and zero-communication assignment is preferred. The method is proposed in research on parallel direct volume rendering of unstructured grids based on object-space decomposition. It addresses the Local Pixel Merging (LPM) phase where ray-segments generated by different processors must be merged, reducing the merging problem to an assignment problem on a 2D coarse mesh imposed on the image screen.
