name: Balanced-Load Minimized-Communication Assignment (BLMCA)
head: Minimized-Communication Assignment, Minimum-Communication Assignment (MCA)
body: BLMCA is a hybrid mesh-cell assignment heuristic for tiled parallel volume rendering that simultaneously minimizes communication volume during the Ray-Segment Migration (RSM) step and mitigates load imbalance during the Local Pixel Merging (LPM) step. It improves upon pure Minimum-Communication Assignment (MCA) by incorporating load-balancing constraints, and improves upon pure Best-Fit Decreasing (BFD) load balancing by prioritizing communication efficiency for heavily loaded cells. This scheme considers both the volume of communication in the RSM step and the load imbalance in the LPM step for minimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N mesh-cells \mathcal{M} = \{m1, \dots, mN\}, a set of P processors \mathcal{P} = \{P0, \dots, P{P-1}\}, and local workload data. Output: An assignment map A: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}, where A(m) is the processor assigned to mesh-cell m. Data Structures: 1. Local Workload Matrix (WL{local}): A matrix of size N \times P. Entry WL{local}[m, k] stores the number of ray-segments for mesh-cell m currently residing on processor Pk. 2. Global Workload Vector (WL{global}): A vector of size N. Entry WL{global}[m] stores the total number of ray-segments for mesh-cell m across all processors. 3. Processor Load Vector (Load): A vector of size P. Entry Load[k] stores the current cumulative load (sum of global ray-segment counts of assigned mesh-cells) of processor Pk. 4. Maximum Part Size (C{max}): The maximum allowable load capacity for any single processor, determined by a load balance criterion. Pre-computation (Parallel Phase): Before the assignment algorithm runs, each processor Pk must compute the necessary global statistics. This is done in parallel by all processors simultaneously: 1. Each processor Pk traverses its local RayBuffer to populate WL{local}[m, k] for all m \in \mathcal{M}. 2. A global-maximum operation is performed on WL{local} across all processors. This determines, for each mesh-cell m, the index k^ = \arg\maxk WL{local}[m, k] of the processor holding the most local ray-segments for m. 3. A global-sum operation is performed on WL{local} across all processors. This computes the total ray-segment count Rm for each mesh-cell m. 4. After these "fold and expand" communication steps, every processor holds the complete WL{global} vector and the index of the processor with the maximum local count for each mesh-cell. Assignment Algorithm (Sequential/Parallel Phase): Each processor runs the following logic to determine the final assignment A. The logic is identical on all processors, ensuring consistency. 1. Sort: Sort mesh-cells \mathcal{M} in decreasing order of their global ray-segment counts WL{global}[m]. 2. Initialize: Set Load[k] = 0 for all k \in \{0, \dots, P-1\}. 3. Iterate: For each mesh-cell m in the sorted order: a. Let k{max} be the index of the processor with the maximum local ray-segment count for m (obtained in the pre-computation phase). b. Check feasibility: If Load[k{max}] + Rm \le C{max}: i. Assign A(m) = k{max}. ii. Update load: Load[k{max}] \leftarrow Load[k{max}] + Rm. c. Else (if assigning to k{max} exceeds capacity): i. Find k{min}, the index of the minimally loaded processor: k{min} = \arg\mink Load[k]. ii. Assign A(m) = k{min}. iii. Update load: Load[k{min}] \leftarrow Load[k{min}] + Rm. Communication Volume Formula: The communication volume incurred by assigning mesh-cell m to processor Pi is given by: V(m, Pi) = Rm - r{km} Where: Rm is the global ray-segment count for mesh-cell m (WL{global}[m]). r{km} is the local ray-segment count of mesh-cell m on the processor Pk that currently holds the maximum local count for m (i.e., WL{local}[m, k{max}]). Note: If m is assigned to P{k{max}}, the communication volume is minimized to Rm - r{k{max}m}, which is the volume of segments that must be migrated from other processors to P{k{max}}. If m is assigned to a different processor Pj, the communication volume is higher, as segments from P{k{max}} must also be migrated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def BLMCA(meshcells, numprocessors, maxpartsize): """ meshcells: List of objects, each having: id: unique identifier localcounts: list of integers, localcounts[k] is ray-segment count on processor k numprocessors: int P maxpartsize: float Cmax Returns: assignment: dict mapping meshcell.id -> processorindex loads: list of floats, loads[k] is final load of processor k """ P = numprocessors # Pre-computation: Global Sum and Global Max # In a real parallel implementation, this uses MPIAllreduce or similar globalcounts = [] maxlocalindices = [] for m in meshcells: Rm = sum(m.localcounts) globalcounts.append(Rm) # Find processor with max local count kmax = 0 maxval = m.localcounts[0] for k in range(1, P): if m.localcounts[k] > maxval: maxval = m.localcounts[k] kmax = k maxlocalindices.append(kmax) # Create list of (globalcount, meshcell, kmax) celldata = [] for i, m in enumerate(meshcells): celldata.append({ 'id': m.id, 'globalcount': globalcounts[i], 'kmax': maxlocalindices[i] }) # Sort by global count descending celldata.sort(key=lambda x: x['globalcount'], reverse=True) # Initialize loads loads = [0.0] P assignment = {} for item in celldata: mid = item['id'] Rm = item['globalcount'] kmax = item['kmax'] # Check if assigning to kmax keeps load within capacity if loads[kmax] + Rm <= maxpartsize: assignment[mid] = kmax loads[kmax] += Rm else: # Find minimally loaded processor kmin = 0 minload = loads[0] for k in range(1, P): if loads[k] < minload: minload = loads[k] kmin = k assignment[mid] = kmin loads[kmin] += Rm return assignment, loads Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Load values are sums of integer ray-segment counts, so floating-point precision issues are minimal unless C{max} is derived from non-integer metrics. Tie Breaking: The \arg\min and \arg\max operations may have ties. The sources do not specify a tie-breaking rule. Implementers should choose a deterministic rule (e.g., lowest index) to ensure reproducibility. Degenerate Input: If a mesh-cell has zero ray-segments, it contributes zero load and zero communication. It can be assigned to any processor without affecting the objective functions significantly. Assigns each mesh-cell to the processor with the maximum local ray-segment count, minimizing communication volume but ignoring load balance. Used when communication is the primary bottleneck. Assigns mesh-cells in decreasing order of global load to the minimally loaded processor. Used as a heuristic for the n-way number-partitioning problem in load balancing. Time Complexity: The parallel pre-computation requires O(N \cdot P) work for local traversal and O(N \log P) or O(N) for global reduction depending on the communication topology. The sorting step is O(N \log N). The assignment loop is O(N \cdot P) if finding the min/max load naively, or O(N \log P) with a heap. Overall complexity is dominated by sorting and global reductions. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot P) for the local workload matrix if stored explicitly, though typically only the global counts and max indices are needed after reduction, reducing it to O(N + P). Measured Performance: The sources do not provide specific numerical performance benchmarks (e.g., speedup factors) for BLMCA compared to MCA or BFD alone. Strengths: Explicitly addresses both communication and load imbalance. The greedy strategy for heavily loaded cells ensures that the largest potential communication savings are captured first. Limitations: The load balancing component is a heuristic for an NP-hard problem (n-way number partitioning), so it does not guarantee optimal load balance. When to use: This scheme considers both the volume of communication in the RSM step and the load imbalance in the LPM step for minimization. When not to use: If communication is negligible compared to computation, pure BFD may be simpler. If load balance is perfect by construction, pure MCA is optimal for communication. BLMCA was proposed in the context of parallel direct volume rendering of unstructured grids based on object-space decomposition. It addresses the deficiencies of the Minimum-Communication Assignment (MCA) scheme, which ignores load balancing for the Local Pixel Merging (LPM) step. The method combines the greedy communication minimization of MCA with the Best-Fit Decreasing (BFD) heuristic from bin-packing theory to solve the n-way number-partitioning problem for load balancing. name: Farm on Demand (FD)
head: FD Algorithm, processor farm paradigm with on-demand distribution
body: Farm on Demand (FD) is a parallel isosurface extraction algorithm that achieves dynamic load balancing by subdividing a volumetric dataset into a large number of fine-grained tasks and distributing them to worker processes on demand. It builds on Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by applying the processor farm paradigm to volume data, where the master assigns small intervals of slices to workers as they become available, rather than using static partitioning. Unlike its sibling Load Balanced Cell Assignment (LBC), which uses static contiguous partitions, FD provides near-perfect computational load balancing for uneven isosurface distributions but probabilistically produces a significantly higher number of shared vertices due to non-contiguous task assignment. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset in the same format as the sequential algorithm. Output: An isosurface partitioned among parallel processes. Each process produces distinct Vertex, Triangle, and Index tables for each task interval it treats. Data Structures: Tasks: The dataset is subdivided into nT intervals of slices. Each task corresponds to a specific range of Z-slices. Shared State: A task pool managed by the master process, containing the list of available tasks. Worker State: Each worker maintains output tables (Vertex, Triangle, Index) for each task it processes. Parameters: nT: Total number of tasks (intervals of slices). nT > numW. numW: Number of worker processes. Task size: Normally Z{max} / nT slices, with the last task possibly containing a different amount. Steps: 1. Initialization: The master process shares a node with one worker process. The master subdivides the dataset into nT tasks. 2. Task Distribution: The master randomly assigns tasks to worker processes. This assignment is non-deterministic and non-contiguous. 3. On-Demand Request: Workers execute the isosurface extraction algorithm (identical to the one used in LBC) for their assigned tasks. Upon completing a task, a worker requests a new task from the master. 4. Data Acquisition: Workers acquire the data for their assigned tasks in multiple I/O chunks, rather than a single contiguous read. 5. Computation: Workers compute the isosurface for the assigned cells. The computation is balanced implicitly because workers with tasks containing fewer active cells finish faster and request new tasks sooner. 6. Output Generation: For each task, workers produce Vertex, Triangle, and Index tables. These are written to distinct files or buffers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class FarmOnDemand: def init(self, dataset, numworkers, numtasks): self.dataset = dataset self.numworkers = numworkers self.numtasks = numtasks self.tasks = self.subdividedataset(dataset, numtasks) self.taskpool = list(self.tasks) random.shuffle(self.taskpool) def subdividedataset(self, dataset, n): zmax = dataset.zdimension tasks = [] slicespertask = zmax / n for i in range(n): startslice = int(i slicespertask) endslice = int((i + 1) slicespertask) if i == n - 1: endslice = zmax tasks.append(Task(slicerange=(startslice, endslice))) return tasks def run(self): workers = [Worker(i, self.dataset) for i in range(self.numworkers)] for worker in workers: if self.taskpool: task = self.taskpool.pop(0) worker.assigntask(task) while any(not w.isidle() for w in workers): for worker in workers: if worker.isidle() and self.taskpool: task = self.taskpool.pop(0) worker.assigntask(task) allvertices, alltriangles, allindices = [], [], [] for worker in workers: allvertices.extend(worker.vertextables) alltriangles.extend(worker.triangletables) allindices.extend(worker.indextables) return Isosurface(vertices=allvertices, triangles=alltriangles, indices=allindices) class Worker: def init(self, id, dataset): self.id = id self.dataset = dataset self.currenttask = None self.vertextables = [] self.triangletables = [] self.indextables = [] self.busy = False def assigntask(self, task): self.currenttask = task self.busy = True self.executetask() def executetask(self): datachunks = self.dataset.readchunks(self.currenttask.slicerange) vertices, triangles, indices = marchingcubes(datachunks, threshold=0.5) self.vertextables.append(vertices) self.triangletables.append(triangles) self.indextables.append(indices) self.busy = False def isidle(self): return not For example, in the FC-1000 dataset, FD produced 1,007,205 shared vertices compared to 195,804 for LBC. Mesh Quality: The suitability of the isosurface partitioning is rarely completely satisfactory due to the high number of shared vertices, which may necessitate mesh redistribution. LBAC is a parallel isosurface extraction algorithm that partitions a 3D volume into contiguous regions along the Z-axis and dynamically balances the computational workload by equalizing the number of active cells (cells containing isosurface intersections) among worker processes. Unlike its sibling Load Balanced on Cells (LBC), which distributes the total number of cells evenly but suffers from unpredictable active cell distribution, LBAC ensures near-perfect load balancing for the triangulation phase by performing a preliminary analysis of active slice weights. It builds on Farm on Demand (FD) by using a static, contiguous Z-axis partitioning strategy rather than FD's random task assignment, which minimizes shared vertex overhead but requires a two-phase approach to achieve balance. Time Complexity: Theoretical load balancing is almost perfect and cheap, as balancing is obtained dynamically without explicit active cell counting. Speed up depends on the isosurface distribution; generally provides good performance if the grain size is suitable. Memory Complexity: Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Measured Performance: For small-medium isosurfaces, FD is often the best possibility, especially when considering I/O cost, due to the uneven distribution of isosurfaces and their small size. For large isosurfaces, LBAC provides better results. Strengths: Excellent computational load balancing for uneven isosurface distributions; good performance for small-medium isosurfaces. Limitations: Probabilistically produces many more shared vertices than LBC and LBAC; high I/O overhead due to multi-chunk data acquisition; mesh partitioning quality is often unsatisfactory. When to Use: Suitable when load-balanced computation is prioritized over mesh partitioning quality, particularly for small-medium isosurfaces with uneven distributions. When Not to Use: When mesh quality (low shared vertices) is critical, or for large isosurfaces where LBAC outperforms FD. Origin: The Farm on Demand (FD) algorithm was proposed by D. D'Agostino, A. Clematis, and V. Gianuzzi. History: It represents the fourth class of parallel isosurface extraction algorithms, based on the processor farm paradigm. It is similar to the algorithm proposed in [44] but differs in that the random task distribution among workers is made on demand, making the distribution nondeterministic. name: Load Balanced on Active Cells (LBAC)
head: LBAC Algorithm, LBC Algorithm, Load Balanced on Cells
body: LBAC is a parallel isosurface extraction algorithm that partitions a 3D volume into contiguous regions along the Z-axis and dynamically balances the computational workload by equalizing the number of active cells among worker processes. Unlike its sibling Load Balanced on Cells (LBC), which distributes the total number of cells evenly but suffers from unpredictable active cell distribution, LBAC ensures near-perfect load balancing for the triangulation phase by performing a preliminary analysis of active slice weights. It builds on Farm on Demand (FD) by using a static, contiguous Z-axis partitioning strategy rather than FD's random task assignment, which minimizes shared vertex overhead but requires a two-phase approach to achieve balance. Inputs: A 3D volumetric dataset, an isovalue, and the number of parallel processes numP. Outputs: A partitioned isosurface mesh consisting of a Vertex table, a Triangle table, and an Index table containing indices of shared vertices. Data Structures: weight[w]: An array of size numW (workers), storing the number of intersections (active cells) found in the slices assigned to worker w during the Analysis phase. start[w], stop[w]: Arrays of size numW, defining the Z-axis slice interval boundaries assigned to each worker for the Isoextraction phase. numW: The number of worker processes, calculated as numP - 1 (where one process acts as the coordinator). Algorithm Steps: The algorithm logically subdivides numP processes into one coordinator and numW workers. It executes three distinct phases: 1. Analysis Phase (Data Parallel): The volume is partitioned into numP intervals of approximately Zmax / numP slices, identical to the LBC partitioning strategy. Each worker independently processes its assigned interval. Workers perform a lightweight "Cell Classification" equivalent to identify active slices (slices containing at least one intersection). Each worker counts the number of intersections in its interval and sends this count as weight[w] to the coordinator. If the coordinator receives zero active slices from all workers, the algorithm terminates early, as no isosurface exists. 2. Balancing Phase (Coordinator): The coordinator receives the weight array from all workers. It performs ActiveSliceBalancing(weight, &start, &stop) to redistribute the slices. The goal is to assign contiguous slice intervals to each worker such that the sum of active cells in each worker's interval is approximately equal. The granularity of this balancing is the single slice, allowing for fine-grained load distribution. The coordinator communicates the new interval boundaries (start[w], stop[w]) to each worker. 3. Isoextraction Phase (Data Parallel): Each worker executes the standard isosurface extraction algorithm (based on WWMC, modified for shared vertices) on its newly assigned slice interval. Workers produce a Vertex table, a Triangle table, and an Index table containing indices of shared vertices on the boundaries of their intervals. Shared vertices are communicated to neighboring processes to ensure topological consistency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lbacalgorithm(volume, isovalue, numP): """ Simulates the LBAC parallel isosurface extraction algorithm. volume: 3D array of dimensions (X, Y, Z) isovalue: float threshold for extraction numP: number of parallel processes """ numW = numP - 1 coordinatorid = 0 zmax = volume.shape[2] # Phase 1: Analysis (Data Parallel) # Each worker processes its initial interval weights = [0] numW for w in range(numW): initialstart = w (zmax // numP) initialstop = (w + 1) (zmax // numP) activecount = 0 for z in range(initialstart, initialstop): # Lightweight classification: count intersections in slice z # Standard edge-vertex intersection check for marching cubes activecount += countintersectionsinslice(volume, z, isovalue) weights[w] = activecount # Coordinator checks for empty isosurface if sum(weights) == 0: return None # Early termination # Phase 2: Balancing (Coordinator) # Distribute slices to balance active cell counts starts = [0] numW stops = [0] numW activeslicebalancing(weights, starts, stops) # Phase 3: Isoextraction (Data Parallel) results = [None] numW for w in range(numW): newstart = starts[w] newstop = stops[w] vertextable = [] triangletable = [] indextable = [] for z in range(newstart, newstop): # Extract triangles for slice z using modified WWMC # Standard isosurface extraction step triangles = extractslicetriangles(volume, z, isovalue) triangletable.extend(triangles) # Generate index table for shared vertices at interval boundaries # Standard shared vertex handling step indextable = generatesharedvertexindices(vertextable, newstart, newstop) results[w] = { "vertices": vertextable, "triangles": triangletable, "indices": indextable } return results def activeslicebalancing(weights, starts, stops): """ Distributes slice intervals to balance active cell counts. Uses single-slice granularity. """ totalactive = sum(weights) if totalactive == 0: return targetload = totalactive / len(weights) currentload = 0 currentstart = 0 for w in range(len(weights)): # Accumulate slices until target load is reached while currentload < targetload and currentstart < len(weights): # Standard load balancing accumulation step currentload += weights[currentstart] currentstart += 1 starts[w] = currentstart stops[w] = currentstart # Placeholder for exact interval end logic based on evidence currentload = 0 Parameters: numP: Number of parallel processes. Determines the initial slice interval size. numW: Number of worker processes (numP - 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Execution Overhead: The Cell Classification operation (or its lightweight equivalent) is performed twice: once in the Analysis phase and again in the Isoextraction phase. Empty Isosurfaces: If the Analysis phase finds no active slices, the algorithm terminates early. I/O Contiguity: The algorithm assumes contiguous slice access. Shared Vertices: While LBAC balances triangles well, it produces more shared vertices than LBC because the rebalancing may split contiguous regions differently, though fewer than FD. Partitions volume by total cell count. Simpler but suffers from uneven active cell distribution. Choose when isosurfaces are homogeneous or when avoiding the Analysis phase overhead is critical. LBC Uses random task assignment for fine-grained balancing. Produces more shared vertices and higher I/O overhead for contiguous data. Choose when data is already partitioned into scattered blocks or when extreme heterogeneity requires dynamic task stealing. FD Time and Memory Complexity: The speedup depends heavily on the percentage of active cells. Achievable speedup depends on the incidence of the double execution of the input acquisition and the Cell Classification operations on the whole execution time, which is inversely related to the size of resulting isosurfaces. For small-to-medium isosurfaces, the overhead of the Analysis phase and the double execution of input acquisition/Cell Classification degrade performance, making LBAC less efficient than LBC. Measured Performance: On dataset 1NKW-3018 (large, homogeneous) with 16 processes: LBC spends 0.30s on I/O and 0.66s on CPU computation, outperforming LBAC due to lower I/O overhead from single contiguous acquisition. On dataset XT-25 (medium, large isosurface) with 16 processes: LBAC spends 10.2s on CPU and 9.1s on I/O. On dataset XT-180, LBAC spends 6.0s on CPU. On dataset FC-1000 (non-homogeneous): LBC was severely unbalanced (process 5 had 7x the load of others). LBAC achieved nearly perfect balance (5.5% to 6.4% load per worker) but produced 318,472 shared vertices (vs. 195,804 for LBC). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Achieves near-perfect load balancing of triangles and handles non-homogeneous isosurfaces effectively, while producing fewer shared vertices than FD. Limitations: Higher overhead for small/medium isosurfaces; sensitive to I/O patterns (requires contiguous slice storage); requires a coordinator process. When to use: Large datasets with large, non-homogeneous isosurfaces where perfect load balancing is required. When not to use: Small-to-medium isosurfaces (overhead dominates); datasets stored in scattered blocks (I/O penalty). LBAC was introduced by D. D’Agostino, A. Clematis, and V. Gianuzzi in their 2000 paper "Parallel Isosurface Extraction for 3D Data Analysis Workflows in Distributed Environments". It represents the third class of parallel algorithms in their classification, improving upon the LBC algorithm (first class) by adding a dynamic load balancing strategy based on active cell counts. It is distinct from the Farm on Demand (FD) algorithm (fourth class) by using a static, contiguous Z-axis partitioning rather than dynamic task distribution. name: Hybrid Image Partitioning
head: Task Queue Image Partitioning, distributed task queue
body: Hybrid Image Partitioning is a dynamic load balancing scheme for parallel volume rendering that combines static block assignment with dynamic tile grabbing to balance load distribution and minimize overlapping voxel accesses. It sets itself apart from static contiguous partitioning by avoiding poor load distribution caused by varying image complexity, and from static interleaved partitioning by minimizing excessive overlapping voxel accesses through spatial locality. It builds on Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by distributing the queue management across processors to avoid the bottleneck of a centralized point of control. Inputs: Image plane dimensions. Number of processors P. Volume dataset. Ray tracing parameters. Outputs: Rendered image. Data Structures: Image Plane: Divided into P contiguous rectangular blocks of comparable size. Image Tiles: Each block is divided into fixed-size square image tiles. Task Queues: One queue per processor, distributed across the system. Each queue contains the image tiles assigned to that processor. Steps: 1. Static Partitioning: Divide the image plane into P contiguous rectangular blocks of comparable size. 2. Tiling: Divide each image block into fixed-size square image tiles. 3. Assignment: Statically assign each image block to one processor. Each processor initializes its local task queue with the tiles in its assigned block. 4. Initial Processing: Each processor begins ray tracing the tiles in its assigned block in scan line order. 5. Dynamic Grabbing: When a processor finishes all tiles in its assigned block, it grabs an unprocessed image tile from the next processor in scan line order that has not yet finished its block. 6. Continuation: Processors continue to grab tiles from other processors' queues until all tiles are completed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridimagepartitioning(imagewidth, imageheight, volume, P, tilesize): # Step 1 & 2: Static Partitioning and Tiling blockwidth = imagewidth // P blocks = [] for i in range(P): left = i blockwidth right = (i + 1) blockwidth if i < P - 1 else imagewidth blocks.append((left, 0, right - left, imageheight)) # Divide each block into fixed-size square image tiles queues = [] initialtilecounts = [] for i in range(P): left, top, w, h = blocks[i] tiles = [] for y in range(top, top + h, tilesize): for x in range(left, left + w, tilesize): tiles.append((x, y, tilesize, tilesize)) queues.append(tiles) initialtilecounts.append(len(tiles)) # Step 3: Assignment blockdone = [False] P tilesprocessed = [0] P # Step 4 & 5: Initial Processing and Dynamic Grabbing def processorwork(i): while True: tile = None # Process own block first if queues[i]: tile = queues[i].pop(0) tilesprocessed[i] += 1 if tilesprocessed[i] == initialtilecounts[i]: blockdone[i] = True # When own block is done, grab from next processor else: nextproc = (i + 1) % P if not blockdone[nextproc] and queues[nextproc]: tile = queues[nextproc].pop(0) if tile is None: # Check termination: all queues empty and all blocks done if all(len(q) == 0 for q in queues) and all(blockdone): break continue # Yield/wait for work # Standard ray marching for the given tile region pass # Step 6: Continuation # Processors continue grabbing until all tiles completed # (Executed concurrently on P processors) for i in range(P): processorwork(i) Parameters: Tile Size: Fixed-size square tiles. The exact pixel dimensions are not given in the sources. w{max}: Size of adaptive image sampling regions in pixels. Rays are cast only from the four corner pixels of each region. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Centralized Bottleneck: Centralized dynamic partitioning becomes a bottleneck as processor count increases. This method avoids that by distributing queue management across processors (one queue per processor). Pixel Sharing in Adaptive Sampling: Adaptive image sampling creates dependencies between adjacent tiles because they share corner pixel values. If adjacent tiles are processed by different processors, synchronization or replicated computation is required. The hybrid scheme minimizes this by keeping spatially adjacent tiles with the same processor initially. Boundary Conditions: When a processor grabs from the next processor, it must ensure the next processor has not finished its block. If the next processor has finished, it may have already grabbed from the one after it. The source specifies grabbing from the "next processor in scan line order that has not yet finished its block". Ray Queue Scheduling is a dynamic load balancing method for distributed volume rendering that manages ray processing at the granularity of spatial cells (flex-blocks) rather than static image tiles or bricks. It solves the problem of uneven computational load in distributed ray tracing by maintaining a queue of pending rays for each cell and processing cells one at a time based on availability. It sets itself apart from static partitioning by dynamically assigning work to idle processors and from pure tile-based approaches by focusing on spatial coherence and cell-level traversal, building on Hybrid Image Partitioning. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Better scalability than centralized dynamic schemes because queue management is distributed (one queue per processor). Strengths: Good load distribution compared to static schemes; reduced overlapping voxel accesses compared to interleaved schemes; avoids centralized bottleneck. Limitations: Synchronization overhead for adaptive image sampling if adjacent tiles are processed by different processors (though minimized). When to use: When image complexity varies significantly across the image plane and viewing position, and when overlapping voxel accesses are a concern. When not: Not given in the sources. Originated in 1992 by researchers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, presented at the 1992 Workshop on Volume Visualization. The method was implemented on the DASH architecture. It addresses the limitations of static contiguous partitioning (poor load distribution) and static interleaved partitioning (excessive overlapping voxel accesses). name: Ray Queue Scheduling
head: Cell-Based Ray Queue, Dynamic Ray-Task Scheduling
body: Ray Queue Scheduling is a hybrid load-balancing scheme for distributed ray tracing that dynamically updates task assignments within the local partition of each render node. It addresses uneven computational loads by processing one cell at a time and routing rays to the queues of their next intersected cells. The method builds on Hybrid Image Partitioning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A distributed volumetric scene partitioned into flex-blocks (cells); a set of active rays; local memory of each render node. Output: Completed ray traces; updated ray queues reflecting the new positions of rays in the scene. Data Structures: Flex-blocks: The spatial subdivision units, each with defined data extents. Ray Queue: A data structure holding pending rays for each cell. Cell State: Indicates whether a cell is in main memory and ready for processing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Distribute the initial set of rays into the ray queues of the cells they initially intersect. 2. Cell Selection: Choose a cell to process using a greedy max-work approach. 3. Ray Traversal: If the selected cell is in main memory, trace all rays currently in its corresponding ray queue through the cell. Space skipping is automated using the data extents of the flex-block. 4. Ray Propagation: When a spawned ray exits the current cell, determine the next cell it intersects and place the ray on that cell's queue. 5. Queue Management: If the queue for the current cell is emptied, return to Step 2 to choose another cell. 6. Iteration: Repeat until all rays are completed or the rendering pass is finished. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Revisits: The same cell may be revisited by a ray and its descendants any number of times. Delayed Generation: Descendants may not be generated until the cell has been processed within another cell, complicating optimization. Scheduling Difficulty: Optimizing ray traversal is difficult due to the dynamic and non-deterministic nature of ray generation and cell revisits. A technique by Reinhard et al. that combines pyramid clipping with demand-driven scheduling of shadow ray tracing. Each processor handles both data parallel and shadow ray tasks, with data parallel tasks given higher priority. A pyramid is constructed around a bundle of rays and intersected with an octree subdivision of the volume to determine relevant cells. Clusters of rays are gathered to improve coherence. Dynamic Task Scheduling is a load-balancing method that dynamically schedules subvolumes or ray tasks within each render node. It addresses the NP-Complete problem of determining the optimum order in which cells are cached by adaptively assigning work using ray queues and neighbor communication. It is chosen for distributed ray tracing contexts and deferred workload mechanisms in game engines, and for GPU rendering of Kernel-Reflection Sequences where it breaks ray evaluation into variable-length tasks to handle differing convergence times. See Dynamic Task Scheduling. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Not given in the sources. Memory: Requires memory for ray queues per cell and the storage of flex-blocks in main memory when processed. Performance and Scaling: Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles uneven computational loads in distributed environments. Limitations: Optimization is difficult due to frequent cell revisits and delayed descendant generation. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originating from research on distributed volume visualization, the method addresses load balancing challenges in distributed ray tracing systems. It builds on the concept of flex-block partitioning and dynamic task scheduling to handle massive datasets like the Visible Korean data set. The approach is part of a broader framework for volumetric ray tracing that includes global illumination effects. Massive Data Management for Distributed Volume Visualization, http://hdl.handle.net/1951/47671, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic Task Scheduling
head: Deferred Work Scheduling, Dynamic Ray-Task Scheduling, Job Scheduling (Tick Events), Scheduler Tick Events
body: Dynamic Task Scheduling is a load-balancing method that dynamically schedules subvolumes (flex-bricks) or ray tasks within each render node. It addresses the NP-Complete problem of determining the optimum order in which cells are cached by adaptively assigning work using ray queues and neighbor communication. The method operates in distributed ray tracing contexts and as a deferred workload mechanism in game engines. For GPU rendering of Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS), it breaks ray evaluation into variable-length tasks to handle differing convergence times. Inputs: Massive volume dataset partitioned into render nodes; flex-block dependency graph; initial ray set. Outputs: Rendered image contributions from each node. Data Structures: Ray Queue: Holds pending rays for each cell. Flex-Block Dependency Graph: Determines the next neighbor to enter, selected by the direction of the ray segment. Task Buffer: Holds tasks for each component type in KRS models. Per-Component Free Distances: Array storing the remaining distance to travel for each ray component. Sorted Index: Small sorted index for faster minimum selection among components. Steps (Distributed Ray Tracing): 1. Each node calculates the ray contributions for the portion of data statically assigned to it. 2. Initialize a ray queue for each cell in the local partition to hold pending rays. 3. Process one cell at a time. When a cell is in main memory, trace all rays currently in its queue through the cell's data. 4. If a spawned ray exits the current cell, determine the next intersecting cell using the dependency graph and place the ray on that cell's queue. 5. Each node communicates ray information to neighboring nodes to update their respective queues. 6. Repeat until all rays have converged or exited the volume. Steps (GPU Scheduling for KRS): 1. Break ray evaluation into tasks, each evaluating a few sphere tracing iterations. 2. Maintain per-component free distances for every ray and a small sorted index for faster minimum selection. 3. Before every turn, for every ray, choose the component with the minimal free distance. 4. Insert a task into the respective buffer or store the intersection point if the ray has converged. 5. Process all task buffers sequentially. 6. When a task finishes, update the free distance and the index. 7. For primary rays, exploit coherence by performing the first few steps of sphere tracing at a lower resolution, advancing the current point only as far as the frustum of the low-res pixel is entirely covered by the unbounding sphere. 8. Repeat until all rays are converged, then perform shading for all intersection points in a deferred manner. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamictaskschedulingraytracing(localcells, dependencygraph, initialrays): rayqueues = {cell: [] for cell in localcells} for ray in initialrays: rayqueues[dependencygraph.getstartcell(ray)].append(ray) convergedpoints = [] while any(rayqueues.values()): nextcell = dependencygraph.selectnextcell(rayqueues) celldata = loadcelldata(nextcell) nextupdates = {} for ray in rayqueues[nextcell]: hit, exitpoint, remaining = traceray(ray, celldata) if hit: convergedpoints.append((ray.id, hit)) elif remaining is not None: nextcellid = dependencygraph.getnextcell(ray, exitpoint) if nextcellid not in localcells: sendraytoneighbor(nextcellid, remaining) else: nextupdates.setdefault(nextcellid, []).append(remaining) rayqueues[nextcell] = [] for cellid, rays in nextupdates.items(): rayqueues[cellid].extend(rays) return convergedpoints def gpukrsscheduling(rays, krsmodels): taskbuffers = {comp: [] for comp in krsmodels} freedistances = {ray.id: {comp: ray.length for comp in krsmodels} for ray in rays} sortedindex = [(ray.id, comp, freedistances[ray.id][comp]) for ray in rays for comp in krsmodels] sortedindex.sort(key=lambda x: x[2]) convergedpoints = {} for ray in rays: if ray.isprimary: lowresstep = performlowresspheretracing(ray) ray.currentpoint = lowresstep.point ray.remaininglength = lowresstep.remaininglength while any(taskbuffers.values()): for comp, buffer in taskbuffers.items(): newbuffer result.remaining sortedindex = [(r.id, c, freedistances[r.id][c]) for r in rays for c in krsmodels] sortedindex.sort(key=lambda x: x[2]) nextcomp = sortedindex[0][1] Strengths: Handles variable workloads effectively; reduces cache misses in distributed systems by following data locality; improves GPU utilization for complex models. Limitations: Adds implementation complexity; requires communication overhead in distributed settings; task management overhead on GPU. When to Use: When static load balancing is insufficient due to uneven data distribution or variable ray convergence times. When Not to Use: For simple, uniform volumes where static partitioning is sufficient and overhead is not justified. name: Dynamic Work Assignment
head: Dynamic scheduling
body: Dynamic work assignment is a parallel rendering technique that redistributes uneven computational tasks to improve resource utilization and overall performance compared to static assignment. It addresses idle resources caused by uneven tile lists, variable pixel traversal, or large block sizes that lead to poor load balancing in static methods. Instead of fixed mappings, it distributes work units dynamically, either based on current demand or historical rendering cost. Inputs: A set of work units (e.g., volume blocks or screen regions). A pool of available processing threads or nodes. (For cost-based variants) Historical rendering time for previous frames. Outputs: Completed rendered image or volume data. Updated cost metrics for subsequent frames (if applicable). Data Structures: Work Queue: A shared data structure containing unassigned work units. The specific layout is not detailed in the sources. Cost History: An array or map storing the rendering time of regions/blocks from the previous frame. Steps: 1. Initialization: Populate the work queue with all work units (volume blocks or screen regions). 2. Assignment: Threads or a master GPU dynamically assign work units from the queue. For cost-based variants, regions are distributed in order of descending cost, where cost is the time taken to render the region in the previous frame. 3. Processing: Each assigned unit is processed (e.g., ray casting, compositing, or Gaussian splatting). 4. Synchronization: Threads synchronize only upon completion of their assigned unit, avoiding the idle time associated with static "sync" variants that force synchronization at fixed block boundaries. 5. Cost Update (Optional): After a frame completes, record the time taken for each region/block to update the cost history for the next frame. Formulas: Cost Metric: Costi = Time{render, i}^{previous}, where Time{render, i} is the time taken to render region/block i in the previous frame. Performance Gain: Assignment based on descending cost provides approximately a 10-20% increase in frame rate under most conditions compared to other methods. Parameters: Region Size (for screen partitioning): 65x65 pixels. Replicated Edges: Two edges of replicated rays are included in each region to support adaptive sampling without seams. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Sync Failure: Static work assignment with forced synchronization ("sync" variant) performs poorly due to load imbalance and is abandoned in favor of dynamic assignment. Cache Coherence: Smaller block sizes in static assignment may lead to lower temporal cache coherence and higher L2 cache misses. Dynamic assignment mitigates this by allowing threads to process units that fit their cache state better, though Z-ordered memory layout is noted as beneficial for cache performance. Adaptive Sampling Incompatibility: Scanline-based assignment precludes adaptive sampling because screen areas, not lines, produce the greatest adaptive-sampling efficiency. Warp Divergence: Static mappings are prone to warp divergence due to footprint coverage and early termination, which dynamic scheduling mitigates by redistributing work through dynamic tile assignment. A parallel rendering load balancing technique where a master GPU dynamically assigns screen regions to ray casting nodes to adjust load balance. It offers two assignment methods: 1. Scanline Mode: The master assigns sequential scan lines to nodes on a first-come-first-serve (FCFS) basis. This provides good balance but precludes adaptive sampling. 2. Square Region Mode: The master distributes 65x65-pixel screen regions to nodes on an FCFS basis. Regions are distributed in order of descending cost, where cost is the time taken to render the region in the previous frame. This method provides approximately a 10-20% increase in frame rate under most conditions compared to other methods. The region size includes two edges of replicated rays to support adaptive sampling without seams. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but dynamic assignment reduces overall runtime by improving load balancing compared to static assignment. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Z-ordered memory layout is noted to result in consistently better performance due to better use of the memory hierarchy and lower L2 cache misses. Performance: Dynamic work assignment shows better overall performance than static work assignment. Static "sync" variant performed so poorly it was abandoned. Cost-based assignment provides a 10-20% frame rate increase. Balanced 3DGS redistributes work through dynamic tile assignment to improve SIMT utilization. Strengths: Better load balancing, especially when block sizes are large or scene coverage varies. Supports adaptive sampling when using square regions. Redistributes uneven tasks to address idle resources from variable pixel traversal. Limitations: Scanline assignment is incompatible with adaptive sampling. Static mappings are prone to warp divergence due to footprint coverage and early termination. When to use: When scene density varies significantly or when using large block sizes that cause load imbalance in static assignment. When uneven tile lists or variable pixel traversal cause SIMT idle resources. When not to use: When adaptive sampling is required and scanline assignment is used. Dynamic work assignment was developed as an optimization for parallel raycasting volume rendering. It was introduced to address the limitations of static work assignment, particularly the "sync" variant which forced synchronization at block levels and suffered from poor load balancing. The method is part of a broader effort to optimize multi-core and many-core shared-memory parallel raycasting. The screen region partitioning variant was implemented in the VISTAnet system for interactive multimodal volume visualization. In modern Gaussian splatting pipelines, dynamic scheduling redistributes uneven tasks to improve SIMT utilization and mitigate warp divergence. name: Load Balancing
body: Load balancing is a technique applied in both point assignment and image assignment to balance computational workload in parallel rendering systems. It serves as a core component of dynamic work assignment algorithms, improving overall performance over static assignment by adapting to varying primitive costs or image patch complexities. Load balancing dynamically assigns computational tasks to available processing units based on estimated task costs. Inputs: A set of computational tasks (e.g., 3D Gaussian primitives, image patches) with associated costs (e.g., projected ellipse size, resolution) and a set of processing resources (e.g., GPU threads, distributed nodes). Outputs: An assignment map linking each task to a specific resource. 1. Task Queue: Stores tasks with properties such as Gaussian parameters or bounding box dimensions. 2. Resource Pool: Tracks available processing units (threads or warps). 3. Cost Estimator: A function mapping task properties to an estimated computational cost, typically the number of tiles the projected ellipse intersects. 1. Partitioning (Offline): Divide the global dataset into initial chunks using a graph partitioning algorithm (e.g., METIS) to ensure spatial locality and reduce communication overhead. 2. Cost Estimation: For each task, estimate the computational cost based on the projected ellipse size or patch resolution. 3. Assignment (Online): Point Assignment: Use an online scheduling technique (e.g., Linear Sum Assignment) to assign points to machines or GPUs based on the partitioning and current load. Image Assignment: Split large images into smaller patches to allow flexible assignment to available resources. Adaptive Scheduling (GPU): If a Gaussian's projected ellipse is small and covers only one tile, assign the intersection task to the current thread. If the ellipse is large, remap the workload to a thread group (warp) to balance synchronization overhead. 4. Execution: Process tasks. Threads or warps pull tasks from the queue until completion. Cost Estimation (Gaussian): Ci = \text{number of tiles intersected by ellipse}i. Warp Size: 32 threads, chosen because the projected ellipse seldom covers more than 32 tiles. Partitioning Algorithm: METIS (bipartite graph partitioning). Communication Dominance: In distributed settings, communication time may dominate the overall runtime, making the performance gain from load balancing modest. Small Impact: Removing load balancing causes performance reductions ranging from 1% to 14%, indicating it is less critical than other optimizations like hierarchical assignment or patching. Large Ellipses: The adaptive warp-based scheduling assumes ellipses seldom cover more than 32 tiles; larger ellipses require different handling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assigntasks(tasks): """ Assigns tasks to processing units using adaptive scheduling. tasks: List of dicts with 'ellipsesize' (number of tiles). """ assignment = {} threadqueue = [f"thread{i}" for i in range(8)] warpqueue = [f"warp{i}" for i in range(4)] for task in tasks: cost = task['ellipsesize'] if cost == 1: # Small ellipse: assign to single thread if not threadqueue: threadqueue = [f"thread{i}" for i in range(8)] thread = threadqueue.pop(0) assignment[task] = {'type': 'singlethread', 'unit': thread} else: # Large ellipse: assign to warp # Assumes cost <= 32 tiles if not warpqueue: warpqueue = [f"warp{i}" for i in range(4)] warp = warpqueue.pop(0) assignment[task] = {'type': 'warp', 'unit': warp} return assignment An online scheduling technique paired with offline METIS partitioning to assign points or images, reducing communication overhead. It introduces no significant overhead, as indicated by end-to-end speedups across scenes. A strategy to balance workload by assigning single-tile intersection tasks to individual threads and multi-tile tasks to a warp, based on the size of the projected Gaussian ellipse. If the ellipse is small and covers only one tile, the current thread handles the precise intersection. If the ellipse is large, the workload is remapped to a thread group (warp) to balance synchronization overhead. The warp size is chosen because the size of the ellipse seldom covers more than 32 tiles. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance Impact: Removing load balancing causes performance reductions ranging from 1% to 14%. Hierarchical assignment and patching have larger impacts (16% to 35% and 10% to 52% respectively). Strengths: Reduces idle time in heterogeneous workloads; adapts to varying primitive sizes. Limitations: Modest effect in communication-bound distributed systems; assumes ellipses are small enough for warp-based scheduling. When to Use: When workload is uneven (e.g., varying Gaussian sizes, image resolutions) and communication overhead is manageable. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Load balancing in parallel rendering has evolved from static grid-based partitioning to dynamic, cost-aware assignment. Early methods used fixed grid partitions, which led to load imbalance when data density varied. Modern approaches, such as those in and, integrate graph partitioning (METIS) with online scheduling and adaptive GPU kernels to handle the irregularity of 3D Gaussian splatting and large-scale scenes. The technique is particularly relevant in distributed rendering systems where communication costs must be minimized alongside computational load. name: Adaptive Tile Sizing
head: Dynamic Tile Sizing
body: Adaptive Tile Sizing is a strategy for selecting tile dimensions in tiled parallel compositing based on the total number of pixels to render, aiming to optimize performance by balancing memory access patterns and computational load. It differs from sibling methods like Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by treating tile dimensions as tunable parameters subject to empirical thresholds rather than fixed constants, addressing the trade-off where larger tiles reduce duplicated primitive processing but increase sequential load per tile. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Total number of pixels to render (N{pix}). Input: Memory indexing scheme (column-major or row-major). Output: Selected tile dimensions (W \times H). Data Structures: Tile dimensions are represented as a pair of integers (W, H). The method evaluates two candidate configurations: Small tile: 16 \times 16 pixels. Large tile: 16 \times 32 pixels. Parameters: Threshold (T): 1,500,000 pixels. This value is determined experimentally. Steps: 1. Calculate the total number of pixels N{pix} to be rendered in the current frame or batch. 2. Compare N{pix} against the threshold T. 3. If N{pix} < T, select the 16 \times 32 tile configuration. 4. If N{pix} \ge T, select the 16 \times 16 tile configuration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selecttiledimensions(numpixels: int, indexing: str) -> tuple[int, int]: """ Selects tile dimensions based on pixel count and memory indexing. Args: numpixels: Total number of pixels to render. indexing: Memory indexing scheme, either 'column-major' or 'row-major'. Returns: A tuple (width, height) representing the selected tile dimensions. """ threshold = 1500000 # Base selection based on pixel count threshold if numpixels < threshold: width, height = 16, 32 else: width, height = 16, 16 # Adjust orientation based on memory indexing # Column-major: 16x32 is efficient (contiguous memory access along height) # Row-major: 32x16 is efficient (contiguous memory access along width) if indexing == 'row-major': # Swap dimensions to align the larger dimension with the row stride width, height = height, width return width, height Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Indexing Dependency: The performance advantage of 16 \times 32 over 32 \times 16 (or vice versa) is strictly dependent on memory indexing. In column-major indexing, 16 \times 32 outperforms 32 \times 16 because the larger dimension (32) aligns with the contiguous memory stride. In row-major indexing, this relationship is reversed. Implementers must swap dimensions if the rendering backend uses row-major storage. Resolution Sensitivity: The threshold of 1.5 million pixels is specific to the hardware and implementation context described in the source. Blindly using 16 \times 16 tiles for all resolutions can lead to suboptimal performance, as larger tiles are not always faster. Performance Degradation: Using larger tiles (e.g., 16 \times 32) on low-resolution scenes can increase render time. For example, on the Bicycle scene at low resolution, using 16 \times 32 tiles increased average render time to 9.77 ms, demonstrating that larger tiles are not universally superior. Image-Space Partitioning divides the output image into rectangular tiles to distribute ray-casting work among parallel threads, balancing the trade-off between mutex contention (small tiles) and load imbalance (large tiles). It differs from sibling methods by explicitly treating tile dimensions as tunable parameters subject to empirical sweep, rather than fixed constants, to identify performance "sweet spots" on specific hardware. An adaptive tiling method based on hybrid saliency detection that divides each Group of Frames (GoF) into fine-grained uniform tiles, extracts static and dynamic saliency metrics, fuses them into a distribution map, and clusters tiles to group salient regions into larger tiles for higher quality representation. It divides each GoF into fine-grained uniform tiles. It extracts static saliency consisting of: 1) Intra-tile dispersion (SI) capturing geometric features within tiles. 2) Inter-tile variability (SE) capturing geometric features between tiles. It extracts dynamic saliency (SD) by comparing matching tiles between the first and last frames to represent motion changes. It computes a weighted fusion of SI, SE, and SD to yield a comprehensive saliency distribution map for all tiles within a single GoF. It employs a clustering algorithm to group tiles with similar saliency values. Tiles with high saliency and proximal distances are prioritized and merged into larger tiles representing regions of greater user interest. Time Complexity: The selection logic is O(1), involving a single comparison and potential dimension swap. The impact on overall render time depends on the chosen tile size's efficiency in reducing duplicated Gaussian processing versus increasing sequential load per tile. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the selection logic. The tile size choice affects the granularity of shared memory usage and cache efficiency, but no additional data structures are required for the selection itself. Measured Performance: On the Bicycle scene, using 16 \times 32 tiles at low resolution resulted in an average render time of 9.77 ms, which was slower than the alternative, indicating that larger tiles are not always faster. The threshold of 1.5 million pixels was determined experimentally to optimize performance across varying resolutions. Strengths: Adapts to resolution changes without manual tuning; accounts for memory indexing architecture; reduces duplicated Gaussian processing at higher resolutions. Limitations: The threshold is hardware-specific and may not generalize across all architectures; requires knowledge of memory indexing scheme; may not account for scene complexity or content distribution. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) or similar tile-based compositing workloads where resolution varies significantly and memory access patterns are critical. Adaptive Tile Sizing was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering performance. The method addresses the inefficiency of fixed tile sizes by empirically determining a pixel-count threshold that balances the benefits of larger tiles (reduced duplicate processing) against their costs (increased sequential load). The specific threshold of 1.5 million pixels and the 16 \times 16 vs. 16 \times 32 configurations were derived from experiments on the Bicycle scene using a Julia-based implementation. The importance of memory indexing (column-major vs. row-major) was also highlighted as a critical factor in tile orientation performance. name: Image-Space Partitioning (Tile Size Optimization)
head: Image Tile Sizing and Work Assignment Strategy, Image Tile Tuning, Work Block Sizing
body: Image-Space Partitioning divides the output image into rectangular tiles to distribute ray-casting work among parallel threads, balancing the trade-off between mutex contention (small tiles) and load imbalance (large tiles). It differs from sibling methods by explicitly treating tile dimensions as tunable parameters subject to empirical sweep, rather than fixed constants, to identify performance "sweet spots" on specific hardware. The method builds on Adaptive Tile Sizing. Inputs: Image dimensions (W \times H). Hardware constraints (e.g., maximum threads per block and register memory limits). Memory layout (e.g., row-major ordering). Outputs: Optimal tile width (Tw) and height (Th). Work assignment strategy (static or dynamic). Data Structures: Work List: A queue of tiles to be processed, protected by a mutex for dynamic thread access. Tile Grid: The image decomposed into a grid of tiles, where boundary tiles are handled by clamping coordinates or processing partial tiles. Steps: 1. Define Search Space: Select ranges for tile width and height, typically using powers of two: \{1, 2, 4, \dots, 256, 512\}. 2. Filter Invalid Configurations: Exclude combinations that result in fewer than 2 total work blocks, as they prevent effective parallelization. 3. Benchmark: For each valid (Tw, Th) pair, render multiple views (e.g., 30 views) using the chosen work assignment strategy and measure the Frame Rendering Time (FRT). 4. Normalize Performance: Calculate normalized FRT for each configuration: \text{Normalized FRT} = \frac{\text{FRT}{config}}{\min(\text{FRT}{all})} Values range from 1.0 (optimal) to \infty. 5. Identify Sweet Spot: Select the configuration with the lowest normalized FRT. 6. Select Work Assignment: Use static assignment for the smallest block sizes, but prefer dynamic assignment for medium and large block sizes (e.g., 32 \times 32) due to better load balance. Parameters: Optimal Tile Size (CPU): 32 \times 32 pixels. Optimal Thread Block Size (GPU, FX5800): 4 \times 2 threads. GPU Constraints: Maximum 512 threads per block and 16KB register memory per block. Pitfalls: Small Tiles: Cause serialized access to the work list via mutex, degrading performance. Large Tiles: Result in insufficient tiles for good load balance. Cache Misses: Block widths of 1, 2, and 4 exhibit poor performance due to high L1, L2, and TLB cache miss rates caused by degraded spatial/temporal locality in row-major memory layouts. Invalid Decompositions: Configurations yielding 1 or 2 total blocks are invalid for parallelization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findoptimaltilesize(imagewidth, imageheight, maxthreadsperblock, registermemorylimit): """ Sweeps tile dimensions to find the configuration with the minimum normalized FRT. Returns (optimalw, optimalh, strategy). """ # Define search space: powers of two up to image dimensions widths = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512] heights = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512] # Filter dimensions to not exceed image size widths = [w for w in widths if w <= imagewidth] heights = [h for h in heights if h <= imageheight] minfrt = float('inf') bestconfig = None for w in widths: for h in heights: # Calculate total number of tiles using ceiling division numtilesw = (imagewidth + w - 1) // w numtilesh = (imageheight + h - 1) // h totaltiles = numtilesw numtilesh # Filter invalid configurations (< 2 blocks) if totaltiles < 2: continue # Filter GPU hardware constraints if w h > maxthreadsperblock: continue frts = [] for in range(30): # Sweep over 30 views # Initialize work list with tile coordinates worklist = [(x, y) for x in range(numtilesw) for y in range(numtilesh)] # Threads pop from worklist protected by a mutex for dynamic assignment rendertime = measureframerenderingtime(worklist) frts.append(rendertime) currentfrt = min(frts) # Minimum times represent optimal, contention-free conditions if currentfrt < minfrt: minfrt = currentfrt bestconfig = (w, h) # Determine work assignment strategy # Dynamic is preferred for medium/large tiles for better load balance strategy = "dynamic" if bestconfig[0] bestconfig[1] >= 3232 else "static" return bestconfig, strategy def measureframerenderingtime(worklist): # Executes the raycasting kernel over the provided tile grid return 0.0 Tests block sizes ranging from 4 to 128 threads per block. Best overall results are obtained by combining compute shaders with ray/box intersection tests. Squared block configurations yield superior results compared to rectangular blocks because they enable more coalesced accesses to the volume texture. A parallelization subdivision where different parts of the image are computed on different machines. Achieves good scalability with the size of the output image but does not allow processing larger data sets. Performance Variation: The worst-performing tile size can be up to 3.0 times slower than the best configuration, with a maximum normalized FRT of approximately 3.0. Complexity: The optimization phase requires O(N \cdot V \cdot T) operations, where N is the number of tile configurations, V is the number of views, and T is the render time per view. Strengths: Identifies hardware-specific optimal parameters and handles load imbalance effectively for medium and large tiles using dynamic assignment. Limitations: Requires empirical tuning, suffers from mutex overhead on small tiles, suffers from load imbalance on large tiles, and experiences high cache miss rates for specific tile shapes due to row-major memory layouts. When to Use: Deploy to specific hardware architectures where tile size significantly impacts cache behavior and synchronization overhead. The method originates from studies on hybrid parallelism for volume rendering on multi-core systems, specifically analyzing shared-memory raycasting on AMD Opteron CPUs and CUDA GPUs (FX5800). It addresses the need to balance parallel efficiency with memory access patterns in image-space partitioning. name: Tile Boundary Computation Setup
head: Tile Boundary Buffer Setup, Tile Boundary Generation
body: This method initializes the data structures required for tiled parallel compositing by computing the spatial extent (boundaries) of each tile within the framebuffer. It allocates and prepares a storage buffer for tile boundary indices, applies necessary GPU pipeline barriers, and dispatches a compute shader to populate the boundaries. Inputs: Swapchain extent (width W, height H) in pixels. numInstances representing the number of data elements or primitives to process. Outputs: tileBoundaryBuffer: A storage buffer containing boundary indices for each tile. Data Structures: tileBoundaryBuffer: A storage buffer sized T{tilesX} \times T{tilesY} \times 2 \times \text{sizeof(uint32t)}. Layout: For each tile (i, j), the buffer stores two uint32t values with a stride of 2 uint32s per tile. Total size: T{tilesX} \times T{tilesY} \times 8 bytes. The exact semantic meaning of the two values per tile is implied by the name "boundary" but not explicitly defined in the source beyond the storage size. Steps: 1. Calculate Tile Grid Dimensions: Compute the number of tiles in the X and Y directions using ceiling division: T{tilesX} = (W + 15) / 16 and T{tilesY} = (H + 15) / 16. 2. Allocate Buffer: Allocate tileBoundaryBuffer with size T{tilesX} \times T{tilesY} \times 2 \times \text{sizeof(uint32t)}. 3. Initialize Buffer: Zero out tileBoundaryBuffer using fillBuffer. 4. Synchronization: Apply a pipeline barrier transitioning tileBoundaryBuffer from eTransfer to eComputeShader access. 5. Bind Resources: Bind the sorted key buffer (sortKBufferEven) and tileBoundaryBuffer to the compute pipeline descriptor set. 6. Dispatch Compute Shader: Bind tileBoundaryPipeline and dispatch with numInstances as a push constant. 7. Dispatch Size: Calculate workgroup count as (numInstances + 255) / 256 workgroups. 8. Final Synchronization: Apply a compute write/read barrier on tileBoundaryBuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setuptileboundaries(swapchainwidth, swapchainheight, numinstances): # 1. Calculate tile grid dimensions tilex = (swapchainwidth + 15) // 16 tiley = (swapchainheight + 15) // 16 # 2. Allocate tile boundary storage buffer buffersize = tilex tiley 2 4 # 2 uint32t per tile tileboundarybuffer = [0] buffersize # 3. Initialize buffer using fillBuffer # (Buffer is already zero-initialized in Python list allocation) # 4. Apply pipeline barrier from eTransfer to eComputeShader for tileBoundaryBuffer # (Synchronization step: ensures transfer writes are visible to compute shaders) # 5. Bind sorted key buffer (sortKBufferEven) and tile boundary buffer to compute pipeline descriptor set # (Descriptor binding step: maps buffers to shader resource slots) # 6. Bind tileBoundaryPipeline and dispatch with numInstances as push constant # Workgroup size is 256 threads numworkgroups = (numinstances + 255) // 256 # dispatch(numworkgroups, 1, 1) # 7. Apply compute write/read barrier on tileBoundaryBuffer # (Synchronization step: ensures compute writes are visible to subsequent reads) return tileboundarybuffer, tilex, tiley, numworkgroups Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If swapchain dimensions are not multiples of 16, the last tiles in X and Y are partially filled, requiring the boundary computation to handle them correctly. Integer division for tile count calculation must use ceiling logic to cover partial tiles at the edges. The Coarse Rasterizer performs triangle setup and emits a conservative list of all triangles touching each tile in a tiled volume rendering pipeline. It differs from typical chunkers by avoiding per-tile queues and expensive tile coverage tests during the setup phase, instead relying on a global radix-sort to organize triangle-tile relationships. This approach minimizes inter-thread communication and leverages the high compute-to-bandwidth ratio of modern GPUs by recomputing setup data per tile rather than caching it. This method is a two-pass compute shader pipeline that classifies 8x4 pixel tiles based on the neural material (MLP) index used by their pixels, separating them into uniform tiles (single MLP) and mixed tiles (multiple MLPs), then sorts mixed tiles to ensure uniform MLP usage per tile for efficient hardware matrix multiplication. It solves the problem of thread divergence in cooperative vector matrix multiplication by ensuring all pixels in a same workgroup use the same base matrix. Unlike Coarse Raster, which focuses on early visibility culling, this method operates on the output of the Visibility pass to reorganize pixel data for the Lighting pass. Fix a tile t and define its pixel space rectangle \Omegat = x{\min}, x{\max}) \times [y{\min}, y{\max}). Index four slab pairs by i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} with normals ni = \epsilon{i,0}c0 + \epsilon{i,1}c1 + \epsilon{i,2}c2, where \epsilon{i,0}=+1 and \epsilon{i,1}, \epsilon{i,2} \in \{+1, -1\}. For each slab pair with n{i,z} \neq 0, solve |ni \cdot (\Delta x, \Delta y, \tau)| \le 1 for \tau to get bounds s{i,lo}(x,y) and s{i,hi}(x,y). Compute mi(x,y) and hi from these bounds. Memory Complexity: O(T{tilesX} \times T{tilesY}) for the tileBoundaryBuffer. Time Complexity: The setup phase is dominated by the compute shader dispatch, which scales proportionally to numInstances. name: Coarse Raster
head: Coarse Rasterizer
body: The Coarse Rasterizer performs triangle setup and emits a conservative list of all triangles touching each tile in a tiled volume rendering pipeline. It differs from typical chunkers by avoiding per-tile queues and expensive tile coverage tests during the setup phase, instead relying on a global radix-sort to organize triangle-tile relationships. This approach minimizes inter-thread communication and leverages the high compute-to-bandwidth ratio of modern GPUs by recomputing setup data per tile rather than caching it. The method consists of three main phases: Triangle Setup, Tile Sorting, and Tile Splitting. Input: A list of triangles defined in world or voxel space. Output: A set of virtual tiles, each containing a bounded number of triangles, ready for the Fine Raster stage. 1. Triangle Descriptor: A word-sized integer used for sorting. Bits [0:1]: Dominant axis of the triangle (2 bits). Bits [2:31]: Tile ID (remaining bits). 2. Unsorted List: An array of pairs (triangleindex, descriptor). 3. Per-Tile Ranges: After sorting, a compact list of (begin, end) indices into the sorted list for each physical tile. 4. Virtual Tile Arena: Memory allocated per virtual tile during the fine raster stage. M{tile}: The maximum number of triangles allowed in a virtual tile. 1. Triangle Setup and Emission For each triangle, a single CUDA thread processes the triangle. a. Compute the integer bounding box of the triangle. b. Determine the dominant axis of the triangle. c. Identify all physical tiles whose voxel grid intersects the triangle's integer bounding box. This is a conservative estimate; expensive precise coverage tests are skipped. d. For each touched tile, compute the 12 floats required for the cheapest 6-separating triangle-voxel coverage test. These floats are recomputed for each tile rather than computed once and reused, optimizing for GPU compute-to-bandwidth ratios. e. Construct the descriptor: combine the dominant axis (2 bits) and the tile ID. f. Emit a pair (triangleindex, descriptor) to a global unsorted list. 2. Tile Sorting a. Perform a global radix sort on the unsorted list of (triangleindex, descriptor) pairs based on the descriptor. b. The sorting groups triangles by tile ID, and within each tile, by dominant axis. This grouping increases SIMD efficiency in the subsequent fine raster stage. c. Generate a compact list of per-tile (begin, end) ranges that point to the start and end indices of each tile's triangles in the sorted array. 3. Tile Splitting a. Iterate through the physical tiles. b. If a physical tile contains more than M{tile} triangles, split it into multiple virtual tiles. c. Each virtual tile contains at most M{tile} triangles. d. Virtual tiles may overlap on the voxel grid. During the fine raster stage, a separate memory arena is created for each virtual tile. A final merging pass blends the results of all virtual tiles mapping to the same physical framebuffer entry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarseraster(triangles, Mtile): # Phase 1: Triangle Setup and Emission outputlist = [] for tri in triangles: # 1. Compute integer bounding box bboxmin = [int(tri.min[i]) for i in range(3)] bboxmax = [int(tri.max[i]) for i in range(3)] # 2. Determine dominant axis (0=x, 1=y, 2=z) extents = [bboxmax[i] - bboxmin[i] for i in range(3)] dominantaxis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: extents[i]) # 3. Find all tiles intersecting the bounding box touchedtiles = [] for x in range(bboxmin[0], bboxmax[0] + 1): for y in range(bboxmin[1], bboxmax[1] + 1): for z in range(bboxmin[2], bboxmax[2] + 1): touchedtiles.append((x, y, z)) # 4. Emit for each touched tile for tileid in touchedtiles: # Recompute 12 floats for this specific tile setupdata = computesetupfloats(tri, tileid) # Construct descriptor: 2 bits for axis, rest for tile ID descriptor = (tileid << 2) | dominantaxis outputlist.append((tri.id, descriptor)) # Phase 2: Tile Sorting # Represents the global radix sort counting and scattering phase sortedlist = sorted(outputlist, key=lambda x: x[1]) tileranges = {} currenttile = -1 startidx = 0 for i, (triidx, descriptor) in enumerate(sortedlist): tileid = descriptor >> 2 if tileid != currenttile: if currenttile != -1: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, i) currenttile = tileid startidx = i if currenttile != -1: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, len(sortedlist)) # Phase 3: Tile Splitting virtualtiles = [] for tileid, (start, end) in tileranges.items(): numtriangles = end - start if numtriangles <= Mtile: virtualtiles.append({ 'physicaltileid': tileid, 'triangles': sortedlist[start:end], 'isvirtual': False }) else: numsplits = (numtriangles + Mtile - 1) // Mtile for i in range(numsplits): chunkstart = start + i Mtile chunkend = min(start + (i + 1) Mtile, end) virtualtiles.append({ 'physicaltileid': tileid, 'triangles': sortedlist[chunkstart:chunkend], 'isvirtual': True, 'virtualindex': i }) return virtualtiles, tileranges def computesetupfloats(triangle, tileid): # Recompute the 12 floats required for the cheapest 6-separating triangle-voxel coverage test # for the specific tile. Implementation uses standard geometric calculations. return [0.0] 12 Low-resolution voxelizations: May have too few occupied tiles to fill the GPU machine, or skewed triangle distributions. Tile splitting addresses this by creating more virtual tiles to improve load balancing. Degenerate ranges: If a scanline range is degenerate, it does not intersect the triangle. The coarse rasterizer avoids this by using conservative bounding box tests, potentially emitting triangles to tiles they do not strictly intersect, which is handled by the fine rasterizer's precise tests. Time Complexity: Efficient due to low data amplification; triangles often touch one or a few tiles only. The sorting phase dominates complexity, typically O(N \log N) or O(N) with radix sort, where N is the number of triangle-tile pairs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the unsorted list, sorted list, and per-tile ranges. Virtual tile arenas are allocated during fine raster. Strengths: Avoids inter-thread communication primitives like per-tile queues by using global radix-sort counting and scattering. The recomputation of setup data exploits high compute-to-bandwidth ratios. Sorting by dominant axis improves SIMD efficiency in the fine raster stage. Limitations: Conservative bounding box tests may emit more triangles than necessary, increasing the workload for the fine rasterizer. The need for a global sort adds latency compared to queue-based approaches if the number of triangle-tile pairs is small. When to use: When running on GPUs with high compute-to-bandwidth ratios and when tile sizes are large enough that triangles touch few tiles. Especially useful for low-resolution voxelizations where load balancing is critical. The Coarse Rasterizer is part of the VoxelPipe pipeline. It was designed to address the inefficiencies of previous tiled volume rendering approaches that relied on per-tile queues and inter-thread communication. The method leverages the parallel sorting capabilities of GPUs to efficiently organize triangle data for subsequent rasterization stages.
