name: Tile-Based Neural Material Classification and Sorting
head: ClassificationA, ClassificationB, Mixed Tile Repacking, Tile-based classification
body: This method is a two-pass compute shader pipeline that classifies 8×4 pixel tiles based on the neural material (MLP) index used by their pixels, separating them into uniform tiles (single MLP) and mixed tiles (multiple MLPs), then sorts mixed tiles to ensure uniform MLP usage per tile for efficient hardware matrix multiplication. It solves the problem of thread divergence in cooperative vector matrix multiplication by ensuring all pixels in the same workgroup use the same base matrix. Unlike Coarse Raster, which focuses on early visibility culling, this method operates on the output of the Visibility pass to reorganize pixel data for the Lighting pass. The method consists of two compute shader passes: ClassificationA and ClassificationB. Inputs: Visibility buffer containing material IDs for each pixel. Screen resolution (ScreenSize). Tile dimensions (TileSize), fixed at 8×4 pixels. Outputs: UniformTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer for uniform tiles. ComplexTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer for mixed tiles. ActiveTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer for all active tiles. IndexedTilesBufferRW: Read-write buffer storing sorted pixel coordinates. MLPUsageBufferRW: Read-write buffer tracking MLP usage counts and offsets. 1. UniformTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer storing workgroup IDs of tiles where all valid pixels share the same MLP index. 2. ComplexTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer storing workgroup IDs of tiles containing pixels with multiple different MLP indices. 3. ActiveTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer storing workgroup IDs of all tiles with at least one valid pixel. 4. ComplexTileConsumeBuffer: Consume buffer derived from ComplexTileAppendBuffer, used by Pass 2 to process mixed tiles. 5. MLPUsageBufferRW: Read-write buffer indexed by material ID (matID). Index matID: Stores the atomic usage count (number of pixels assigned to this MLP in the current batch). Index UNIQUEMLPCOUNT + matID: Stores the group offset for the specific material ID. 6. IndexedTilesBufferRW: Read-write buffer storing linearized pixel coordinates. Index: tileGroupOffset WORKGROUPSIZE + targetSlot. Value: Linearized screen coordinate x + y ScreenSize.x. Tile Size: 8×4 pixels, matching the workgroup size [numthreads(8, 4, 1)]. Valid Pixel Threshold: A tile is considered uniform only if it has more than 16 valid pixels (validPixelsCount > 16). WORKGROUPSIZE: The size of a work group (32 threads), used as a multiplier for the tile group offset in the indexed tiles buffer. UNIQUEMLPCOUNT: An offset index into MLPUsageBufferRW used to retrieve the group offset for a specific material ID. Not given in the sources. 1. Pass 1 (ClassificationA): For each thread in the workgroup, retrieve the material ID for the current pixel using visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords). 2. Check if the material ID is valid. 3. If valid, use wave-level intrinsics to find the minimum and maximum material IDs within the workgroup: maxID = WaveActiveMax(matID) minID = WaveActiveMin(matID) 4. Count the number of valid pixels in the workgroup: validPixelsCount = WaveActiveSum(1) 5. If the thread is the first lane in the wave (WaveIsFirstLane()): Calculate the flattened workgroup ID: wgID = groupID.x + groupID.y TileSize.x. If maxID == minID and validPixelsCount > 16, append wgID to UniformTileAppendBuffer. Otherwise, append wgID to ComplexTileAppendBuffer. Always append wgID to ActiveTileAppendBuffer. 6. Pass 2 (ClassificationB): Consume a workgroup ID from ComplexTileConsumeBuffer. 7. Convert the workgroup ID to coordinates: wgX = workGroupID % TileSize.x wgY = workGroupID / TileSize.x 8. Compute pixel coordinates for each thread in the 8×4 workgroup: pixelCoords = uint2(wgX 8 + groupThreadID.x, wgY 4 + groupThreadID.y) 9. For each thread, retrieve the material ID: matID = visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords). 10. If the material ID is valid: Atomically increment the usage count for that material ID in MLPUsageBufferRW and book a slot: targetSlot = InterlockedAdd(MLPUsageBufferRW[matID], 1) Retrieve the offset for the current MLP group from MLPUsageBufferRW: mlpGroupOffset = MLPUsageBufferRW[UNIQUEMLPCOUNT + matID] Store the pixel's linearized coordinate into IndexedTilesBufferRW at the calculated offset: IndexedTilesBufferRW[mlpGroupOffset WORKGROUPSIZE + targetSlot] = pixelCoords.x + pixelCoords.y ScreenSize.x Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. WORKGROUPSIZE = 32 # 8 4 INVALIDMLPID = 0xFFFFFFFF UNIQUEMLPCOUNT = 1000 # Not given in the sources. wavevals = [0] 32 def visibilitybuffermatid(coords): return visibilitybuffer[coords[0] + coords[1] ScreenSize.x] def validmatid(matID): return matID != INVALIDMLPID def WaveActiveMax(val, threadid): wavevals[threadid] = val maxval = wavevals[0] for i in range(1, 32): if wavevals[i] > maxval: maxval = wavevals[i] return maxval def WaveActiveMin(val, threadid): wavevals[threadid] = val minval = wavevals[0] for i in range(1, 32): if wavevals[i] < minval: minval = wavevals[i] return minval def WaveActiveSum(val, threadid): wavevals[threadid] = val total = 0 for i in range(32): total += wavevals[i] return total def WaveIsFirstLane(threadid): return threadid == 0 def InterlockedAdd(buffer, index, val): old = buffer[index] buffer[index] += val return old def Consume(buffer): return buffer.pop(0) def ClassificationA(groupID, pixelCoords, threadid): matID = visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords) if validmatid(matID): maxID = WaveActiveMax(matID, threadid) minID = WaveActiveMin(matID, threadid) validPixelsCount = WaveActiveSum(1, threadid) wgID = groupID[0] + groupID[1] TileSize.x if WaveIsFirstLane(threadid): ActiveTileAppendBuffer.append(wgID) if maxID == minID and validPixelsCount > 16: UniformTileAppendBuffer.append(wgID) else: ComplexTileAppendBuffer.append(wgID) def ClassificationB(groupThreadID, threadid): workGroupID = Consume(ComplexTileConsumeBuffer) wgX = workGroupID % TileSize.x wgY = workGroupID // TileSize.x pixelCoords = (wgX 8 + groupThreadID[0], wgY 4 + groupThreadID[1]) matID = visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords) if validmatid(matID): targetSlot = InterlockedAdd(MLPUsageBufferRW, matID, 1) mlpGroupOffset = MLPUsageBufferRW[UNIQUEMLPCOUNT + matID] linearcoord = pixelCoords[0] + pixelCoords[1] ScreenSize.x IndexedTilesBufferRW[mlpGroupOffset WORKGROUPSIZE + targetSlot] = linearcoord Global Atomics: The method uses global atomics for sorting mixed tiles. This is inefficient if the screen is filled with mixed tiles; shared memory atomics would be more suitable in that case. Uniform Tile Threshold: A tile is only classified as uniform if it has more than 16 valid pixels. Tiles with fewer valid pixels, even if they share a single MLP, are treated as complex tiles. MLP Sharing: The current implementation does not share unique MLPs for different materials. Sharing MLPs could reduce the number of mixed tiles and improve performance at the expense of quality. Time Complexity: The method requires two passes over the tiles. Pass 1 processes all tiles, and Pass 2 processes only the mixed tiles identified in Pass 1. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for classification (UniformTileAppendBuffer, ComplexTileAppendBuffer, ActiveTileAppendBuffer) and sorting (MLPUsageBufferRW, IndexedTilesBufferRW). Performance: When using wider MLPs (D >= 32), using cooperative vectors permits up to a ×40 speedup compared to software FMA. The classification itself takes approximately 0.035 ms for L=1 layer and D=16, scaling with MLP dimensions. Strengths: Avoids divergence in the Lighting pass by ensuring all pixels in a workgroup use the same MLP, which is required for efficient cooperative vector matrix multiplication. Limitations: Scaling issue: The classification is not optimal for screens filled with mixed tiles due to global atomics. This method was introduced by L. Belcour & A. Benyoub in the paper "Hardware Accelerated Neural Block Texture Compression with Cooperative Vectors" (Eurographics 2025). It is part of the HW NBTC pipeline, designed to handle neural material compression and rendering efficiently on hardware supporting cooperative vectors. name: Parallel Image Assembly
head: Final Image Assembly & Alpha Blending, Image Stitching, Spatial Compositing, Z-Order Compositing
body: Parallel Image Assembly is the final step in spatial decomposition volume rendering where sub-images rendered by independent threads or processes are combined into a single final image. It solves the problem of merging disjoint spatial data portions into a coherent visual output by placing sub-images at their correct spatial coordinates and blending them along the z-axis using front-to-back alpha compositing. Unlike temporal sequencing, which has minimal overhead, spatial compositing incurs significant overhead due to the data collection and blending requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of composited sub-images (RGBA) and their corresponding opacities from all participating ranks/threads. Each sub-image corresponds to a specific spatial tile (px, py) and potentially a depth slice pz. Output: A single final image array of shape (X, Y, 4) with dtype float32, representing the fully composited volume, often saved as uint8 PNG. Data Structures: finalimage: A numpy array of shape (x\dim, y\dim, 4) storing the accumulated color and opacity. zsplitimages: A collection of sub-images arranged by their spatial coordinates. totalopacity: An array tracking the accumulated opacity for each pixel location. Parameters: LOCATIONOFZ: A sorted list of unique z-start coordinates for each process chunk, used to determine depth ordering. PZ: Total number of depth slices. Steps: 1. Gather Sub-images: Collect the composited subdomain images and opacities from all ranks to a root rank (typically Rank 0). 2. Initialize Final Image: On the root rank, initialize finalimage with zeros and shape (PX \times sub\height, PY \times sub\width, 3) for color, and a corresponding opacity array. 3. Place Sub-images: Iterate through all gathered ranks. 4. Depth Handling: For each rank, determine its spatial coordinates (px, py, pz). If the rank corresponds to the middle depth slice (pz == PZ // 2), place its composited color image into the finalimage grid at the appropriate (px, py) location. Add the opacity from this slice to the totalopacity map for the corresponding (px, py) location. 5. Compositing: For each z-slice (or depth layer), blend the sub-image into the finalimage using front-to-back alpha compositing. The blending follows the standard volume rendering equation: C{final} = C{prev} + C{z} \cdot (1 - \alpha{prev}) \alpha{final} = \alpha{prev} + \alpha{z} \cdot (1 - \alpha{prev}) Where C is color (RGB) and \alpha is opacity. 6. Finalization: Convert the finalimage from float32 to uint8 RGBA and save as a PNG file. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelimageassembly(gatheredsubimages, gatheredopacities, px, py, pz, subwidth, subheight, xdim, ydim, PZ): """ Assembles sub-images into a final image using spatial compositing. Args: gatheredsubimages: List of arrays from all ranks, each of shape (subwidth, subheight, 4) gatheredopacities: List of arrays from all ranks, each of shape (subwidth, subheight, 1) px, py, pz: Spatial coordinates of the current rank's sub-image subwidth, subheight: Dimensions of each sub-image xdim, ydim: Total dimensions of the final image PZ: Total number of depth slices Returns: finalrgba: List of lists of lists representing uint8 RGBA image of shape (xdim, ydim, 4) """ # Initialize final image arrays with zeros def createzeros(shape): return [[[0.0 for in range(shape[2])] for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] finalcolor = createzeros((xdim, ydim, 3)) finalopacity = createzeros((xdim, ydim, 1)) # Place sub-images into the final image grid at spatial coordinates startx = px subwidth starty = py subheight for dy in range(subheight): for dx in range(subwidth): finalcolor[startx + dx][starty + dy] = gatheredsubimages[dy][dx][:3] finalopacity[startx + dx][starty + dy] = [gatheredopacities[dy][dx][0]] # Depth handling: if middle slice, accumulate opacity to totalopacity map if pz == PZ // 2: for dy in range(subheight): for dx in range(subwidth): finalopacity[startx + dx][starty + dy][0] += gatheredopacities[dy][dx][0] # Front-to-back alpha compositing across z-slices # Sources do not specify the exact iteration order for multiple slices beyond front-to-back for zidx in range(len(gatheredsubimages)): zimg = gatheredsubimages[zidx] zop = gatheredopacities[zidx] for dy in range(ydim): for dx in range(xdim): cprev = finalcolor[dx][dy] aprev = finalopacity[dx][dy][0] cz = zimg[dy][dx][:3] az = zop[dy][dx][0] # Apply compositing formulas finalcolor[dx][dy] = [cprev[j] + cz[j] (1.0 - aprev) for j in range(3)] finalopacity[dx][dy][0] = aprev + az (1.0 - aprev) # Convert to uint8 RGBA with clipping to avoid overflow finalrgba = createzeros((xdim, ydim, 4)) for dy in range(ydim): for dx in range(xdim): for j in range(3): val = finalcolor[dx][dy][j] 255.0 finalrgba[dx][dy][j] = max(0, min(255, int(val))) val = finalopacity[dx][dy][0] 255.0 finalrgba[dx][dy][3] = max(0, min(255, int(val))) return finalrgba Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: Spatial compositing has huge overhead compared to temporal sequencing. Precision: Using float32 for intermediate calculations is standard, but conversion to uint8 must be clipped to avoid overflow. Boundary Conditions: Ensure sub-images are placed at correct (px, py) coordinates to avoid gaps or overlaps. A technique for rendering high-resolution viewports that intersect multiple display tiles (projectors) by tiling the image and reassembling it, requiring dynamic progress properties for frame reassembly. It renders a single image stream (e.g., 1600x1200 RGBA) at the target resolution and distributes the image tiles to the appropriate projectors based on viewport intersection. If the viewport intersects multiple logical pipelines, a new routability proof is required to account for image sources contributing to more than one pipeline, and a dynamic progress property must be implemented for frame reassembly. Time Complexity: Dominated by the communication cost of gathering sub-images to the root rank and the compositing step, which is O(X \cdot Y) per depth slice. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full final image (X \cdot Y \cdot 4) and all sub-images during the gather phase. Strengths: Produces a single, coherent final image suitable for display or storage. Limitations: High overhead due to data collection and potential bottleneck at the root rank. Not suitable for real-time animation without optimization. Parallel Image Assembly, also known as spatial compositing, is a technique used in parallel volume rendering to combine results from spatially decomposed data. It involves collecting sub-images from different threads and compositing them in a front-to-back order. The method is applied when each thread has completely processed its own data portion and the main thread must merge the separate ray segments into one final image. name: Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering
head: threaded rasterization
body: Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering is a parallelization strategy that divides the screen height into tiles and processes each tile in a separate thread to parallelize the rasterization workload. It differs from Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by focusing on the rasterization phase itself rather than just compositing pre-rasterized fragments, and from Screen Parallel Rendering by dividing the screen into tiles processed by threads on a single machine rather than subscreens distributed across multiple processors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Screen height (H), screen width (W), and the number of available hardware threads. Output: A fully rasterized framebuffer. Data Structures: Tile Struct: Contains four integer fields defining the rectangular region of the screen to render: xmin, xmax, ymin, and ymax. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Thread Count: Calculate the number of threads (T) as the maximum of 1 and the system's reported hardware concurrency. If std::thread::hardwareconcurrency() returns 0, T is set to 1 to prevent division by zero or empty thread vectors. 2. Calculate Tile Height: Compute the height of each tile (h{tile}) as H / T. 3. Initialize Threads: For each thread index i from 0 to T-1: Calculate the vertical range for the tile. Set ymin = i \times h{tile}. Set ymax = (i == T-1) ? H-1: (i+1) \times h{tile} - 1. Set xmin = 0 and xmax = W-1 (assuming full width per tile). Launch a worker thread executing the renderTile function with this tile's coordinates. 4. Join Threads: Wait for all worker threads to complete. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading def hardwareconcurrency(): """Returns the number of logical processors available.""" import os return os.cpucount() or 1 def rendertile(tile): """Renders the specific tile region. Actual rasterization logic is not provided in the sources.""" # Process pixels within tile.xmin, tile.xmax, tile.ymin, tile.ymax pass def multithreadedtilerendering(screenheight, screenwidth): # Step 1: Determine number of threads threadscount = max(1, hardwareconcurrency()) # Step 2: Calculate tile height tileheight = screenheight // threadscount threads = [] # Step 3: Create and launch threads for i in range(threadscount): ymin = i tileheight # Last tile extends to the end of the screen to handle non-divisible heights if i == threadscount - 1: ymax = screenheight - 1 else: ymax = (i + 1) tileheight - 1 tile = { 'xmin': 0, 'xmax': screenwidth - 1, 'ymin': ymin, 'ymax': ymax } thread = threading.Thread(target=rendertile, args=(tile,)) threads.append(thread) thread.start() # Step 4: Join all worker threads for thread in threads: thread.join() Parameters: threadscount: Typically equal to std::thread::hardwareconcurrency(). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Hardware Concurrency: If the system reports 0 cores, the algorithm defaults to 1 thread to avoid runtime errors. Non-Divisible Heights: The last tile must explicitly extend to screenheight - 1 to ensure all pixels are covered when H is not evenly divisible by T. Screen Parallel Rendering is a parallelization technique that exploits parallelism in screen space by dividing the screen into regions and assigning each region to a processor. It solves the problem of rendering large scenes by distributing the workload of ray traversal across multiple processors, where each processor is responsible for the entire ray for its assigned subscreen. Unlike object-parallel methods that partition the volume data, this approach partitions the image space, allowing each processor to access the full dataset. It is a form of sort-first parallel rendering, where primitives are distributed based on their projected screen location. Tile-Based Rasterization is a GPU-accelerated rendering primitive that divides the image plane into fixed-size tiles, assigning one CUDA thread block to each tile to process all fragments within that region. It solves the parallelization bottleneck of global rasterization by localizing the workload, allowing threads within a block to share splat data in fast shared memory and blend them in front-to-back order. Unlike Screen Parallel Rendering, which assigns individual threads to pixels without explicit tile-level coordination, this method leverages the spatial coherence of tiles to optimize memory access patterns for splat blending. Not given in the sources. This method is described in the context of CPU rasterizers, specifically referenced in the whudsontosh/CPU-Rasterizer repository. It serves as a foundational parallelization technique for tiled rendering on multi-core architectures. whudsontosh/CPU-Rasterizer, https://github.com/whudsontosh/CPU-Rasterizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Screen Parallel Rendering
head: Demand-Driven Ray-Parallel Rendering, Demand-driven, Sort-First Parallel Rendering, Image Space Partitioning, Parallel Row Rendering
body: Screen Parallel Rendering is a parallelization technique that exploits parallelism in screen space by dividing the screen into regions (tasks) and assigning each region to a processor. It solves the problem of rendering large scenes by distributing the workload of ray traversal across multiple processors, where each processor is responsible for the entire ray for its assigned subscreen. Unlike object-parallel methods that partition the volume data, this approach partitions the image space, allowing each processor to access the full dataset. It is a form of sort-first parallel rendering, where primitives are distributed based on their projected screen location. Inputs: A volume dataset (or scene primitives). A camera view (viewpoint and projection). A set of p processors. Outputs: A final composite image. Data Structures: Screen Partitioning: The screen is divided into p disjoint subscreens or tiles. Task Queue: A master node maintains a queue of tasks (subscreen regions). Volume Data: The entire volume dataset must be accessible to every processor. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the screen into p subscreens, where p is the number of available processors. 2. Assignment: Assign tasks associated with each subscreen to processors. Tasks are assigned in a cyclic manner to statically balance processing workloads. 3. Execution: Each processor takes responsibility for the entire ray for its subscreen. All voxels along a ray are processed simultaneously by the respective processor. 4. Demand-Driven Scheduling: Processors execute tasks and request new ones from a master node upon completion of the current task. This is referred to as the "demand-driven" approach. 5. Compositing: Rendered portions are assembled or pasted together to form the final image. Formulas: Ray direction computation per pixel (x, y): rx = (x - \text{res}[0]/2) \cdot fx ry = (y - \text{res}[1]/2) \cdot fy rz = 1.0 fx = \frac{\tan(\text{fov})}{\text{res}[0]/2} fy = \frac{\tan(\text{fov})}{\text{res}[1]/2} \cdot \frac{\text{res}[1]}{\text{res}[0]} The ray direction is then rotated using Rodrigues' rotation formula around the camera rotation vector. Parameters: p: Number of processors. Must match the number of subscreens. RENDERINGTHREADS: Number of threads, typically set to 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Requirements: Every processor needs to load the entire volume into memory, requiring large main memory. This makes the approach infeasible for massive datasets where data cannot be replicated. Load Balancing: Primitives may cluster into specific regions, causing load balancing problems between renderers. Boundary Processing: Primitives overlapping screen region boundaries may be processed by more than one renderer, leading to redundant computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def screenparallelrendering(volume, camera, numprocessors): # Step 1: Partition screen into p subscreens resolution = camera.resolution subscreens = [] for i in range(numprocessors): ystart = (i resolution[1]) // numprocessors yend = ((i + 1) resolution[1]) // numprocessors if i < numprocessors - 1 else resolution[1] subscreens.append({'id': i, 'xstart': 0, 'xend': resolution[0], 'ystart': ystart, 'yend': yend}) # Step 2 & 4: Demand-driven task queue taskqueue = list(subscreens) renderedportions = [None] numprocessors while taskqueue: subscreen = taskqueue.pop(0) procid = subscreen['id'] portion = rendersubscreen(subscreen, camera, volume) renderedportions[procid] = portion # Step 5: Compositing finalimage = compositeportions(renderedportions, resolution) return finalimage def rendersubscreen(subscreen, camera, volume): resolution = camera.resolution fov = camera.fov resx, resy = resolution[0], resolution[1] xfactor = math.tan(fov) / (resx / 2) yfactor = (math.tan(fov) / (resy / 2)) (resy / resx) image = [[0.0] 3 for in range(subscreen['yend'] - subscreen['ystart'])] for y in range(subscreen['ystart'], subscreen['yend']): for x in range(subscreen['xstart'], subscreen['xend']): # Compute ray direction rx = (x - resx / 2) xfactor ry = (y - resy / 2) yfactor rz = 1.0 raydir = normalize([rx, ry, rz]) rayorigin = camera.origin # Cast ray through volume color = raycastvolume(rayorigin, raydir, volume) image[y - subscreen['ystart']][x] = color return image def raycastvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volume): # Standard ray-marching for volume rendering color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.1 while t < 10.0 and alpha < 1.0: point = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] density = samplevolume(point, volume) if density > 0: transmittance = math.exp(-density stepsize) color = [color[i] + (1.0 - alpha) density stepsize colormap(density)[i] for i in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) transmittance t += stepsize return color def compositeportions(portions, resolution): final = [[0.0] 3 for in range(resolution[1])] for portion in portions: if portion is None: continue for y in range(len(portion)): for x in range(len(portion[0])): final[y][x] = portion[y][x] return final def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return [c/mag for c in v] def samplevolume(point, volume): # Placeholder for volume trilinear interpolation return 0.0 def colormap(density): # Placeholder for transfer function return [density, density, density] Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the subscreen and the number of voxels along the ray for each processor. The total time is dominated by the slowest processor if load balancing is poor. Memory Complexity: O(N) per processor, where N is the size of the entire volume dataset. This is a significant limitation as memory usage scales with the dataset size, not the subscreen size. Measured Performance: Effective for small datasets that require no data decomposition. Performance degrades for large-scale datasets due to memory constraints. Strengths: Exploits parallelism in screen space. Each processor has all information needed for complete rendering, allowing use of any rendering algorithm. Takes advantage of frame-to-frame coherence, as few primitives move between tiles from one frame to the next. Limitations: Requires large main memory because every processor needs to load the entire volume. Infeasible for massive volumes where data cannot be replicated. Load balancing issues due to primitive clustering. Redundant processing of primitives at region boundaries. When to Use: Small datasets where memory is not a constraint and frame-to-frame coherence is high. When Not to Use: Large-scale datasets requiring out-of-core processing or distributed memory management. Screen Parallel Rendering is one of the earliest parallel schemes for volume rendering, classified under screen parallel rendering as opposed to object parallel rendering. It is a form of sort-first parallel rendering, a concept identified by Molnar et al.. The Chromium System uses the sort-first approach to distribute rendering work to cluster nodes before the transformation and lighting stages. The technique is also known as demand-driven ray-parallel rendering, where processors request new tasks from a master upon completion. A broader category that includes Screen Parallel Rendering. It distributes raw primitives during geometry preprocessing by dividing the 2D screen into disjoint regions. It takes advantage of frame-to-frame coherence well. Sort-First Parallel Rendering Contrasts with screen parallel rendering by dividing the volume into subvolumes. It requires image compositing to merge subimages. name: Screen-space Subdivision with Virtual Patches
head: Buffered Pixel-planes, Virtual Pixel Approach
body: Screen-space subdivision with virtual patches is a parallel rendering scheme that divides the screen into small, disjoint 128x128-pixel regions (patches) processed simultaneously by independent SIMD engines called Renderers. It differs from previous work using a single large computing surface of SIMD processors operating on the entire screen space by using multiple small engines for flexible mapping and cost/performance trading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of transformed 3D primitives and the screen resolution (e.g., 1280x1024 pixels). Output: A rendered image in the Frame Buffer. Data Structures: Bins: A collection of lists, one for each patch in the screen space. Each bin stores the indices or pointers to primitives that overlap the corresponding patch region. Backing Store: Secondary storage (built from VRAMs) used to save pixel color values for completed patches. On-chip Pixel Memory: Fast SRAM (approx. 200 bits per pixel processor) associated with each Renderer, holding the current patch's Z-buffer and color values. Frame Buffer: Double-buffered conventional VRAM used for display refresh. Numbered Steps: 1. Binning: Sort transformed primitives into bins corresponding to each 128x128 patch-sized region of screen space. Primitives falling into multiple regions are placed into the bins for all such regions. 2. Assignment: Assign all available Renderers to patches on the screen. Dispatch primitives from their corresponding bins to these Renderers. 3. Rendering: Each Renderer processes its assigned patch. 4. Context Switch: When a Renderer completes a patch, it discards its Z-buffer and all other pixel values besides colors. It transfers pixel color values from on-chip pixel memory to the backing store. 5. Reassignment: The Renderer is assigned to the next patch to be processed. Patches are processed in raster order. 6. Final Transfer: After the entire image is rendered, transfer each region from the backing store in a block to the double-buffered display memory in the Frame Buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. PATCHWIDTH = 128 PATCHHEIGHT = 128 SCREENWIDTH = 1280 SCREENHEIGHT = 1024 NUMPATCHESX = SCREENWIDTH // PATCHWIDTH # 10 NUMPATCHESY = SCREENHEIGHT // PATCHHEIGHT # 8 TOTALPATCHES = NUMPATCHESX NUMPATCHESY # 80 bins = [[] for in range(TOTALPATCHES)] backingstore = [None] TOTALPATCHES framebuffer = createdoublebufferedframebuffer(SCREENWIDTH, SCREENHEIGHT) def getpatchid(x, y): """Map screen coordinates to patch ID in raster order.""" px = x // PATCHWIDTH py = y // PATCHHEIGHT return py NUMPATCHESX + px def binprimitives(primitives): """Sort primitives into bins based on their screen-space bounding boxes.""" for prim in primitives: # Determine the bounding box of the primitive in screen space minx, maxx, miny, maxy = prim.screenbounds() # Determine the range of patch IDs this primitive overlaps startpx = max(0, minx // PATCHWIDTH) endpx = min(NUMPATCHESX - 1, maxx // PATCHWIDTH) startpy = max(0, miny // PATCHHEIGHT) endpy = min(NUMPATCHESY - 1, maxy // PATCHHEIGHT) for py in range(startpy, endpy + 1): for px in range(startpx, endpx + 1): patchid = py NUMPATCHESX + px bins[patchid].append(prim) def rendererwork(patchid): """Process a single patch.""" # Load primitives for this patch primitives = bins[patchid] # Initialize on-chip memory for this patch # Z-buffer and color buffer for 128x128 pixels zbuffer = initializezbuffer(PATCHWIDTH, PATCHHEIGHT) colorbuffer = initializecolorbuffer(PATCHWIDTH, PATCHHEIGHT) # Render primitives for prim in primitives: rasterize(prim, zbuffer, colorbuffer) # Save results to backing store backingstore[patchid] = colorbuffer # Discard Z-buffer and on-chip color buffer to free resources # (Implementation detail: memory is reused for next patch) def renderscene(primitives, numrenderers): binprimitives(primitives) # Queue of patches to process, in raster order patchqueue = list(range(TOTALPATCHES)) # Assign initial patches to renderers activerenderers = [] for i in range(min(numrenderers, len(patchqueue))): patchid = patchqueue.pop(0) rendererwork(patchid) activerenderers.append(patchid) # Process remaining patches as renderers become free while patchqueue: # Wait for any renderer to finish (simplified simulation) # In hardware, this is handled by the controller completedpatch = activerenderers.pop(0) if patchqueue: nextpatch = patchqueue.pop(0) rendererwork(nextpatch) activerenderers.append(nextpatch) # Final transfer to frame buffer for patchid in range(TOTALPATCHES): patchcolordata = backingstore[patchid] # Calculate screen coordinates for the patch py = patchid // NUMPATCHESX px = patchid % NUMPATCHESX # Transfer block to frame buffer transfertoframebuffer( framebuffer, patchcolordata, xoffset=px PATCHWIDTH, yoffset=py PATCHHEIGHT, width=PATCHWIDTH, height=PATCHHEIGHT) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Primitive Overlap: Primitives falling into more than one region must be processed multiple times. This reduces actual performance compared to raw performance. Context Switch Overhead: Switching between patches incurs a context switch time of ~0.4 msec, which is the time to render about 100 primitives. This overhead must be overlapped with pixel processing to maintain efficiency. Time Complexity: Rendering into a window of arbitrary size incurs only a linear time penalty. Performance Metrics: Single Renderer raw performance: ~150,000 Phong-shaded triangles per second. Single Renderer simulated actual performance: ~100,000 triangles/sec (reduced due to multi-patch processing). Estimated Graphics Processor (GP) performance: ~30,000 Phong-shaded triangles per second. Scalability: The system allows cost/performance to be traded nearly linearly by adding or removing small rendering units. Strengths: Modular, flexible mapping of virtual pixel spaces, efficient use of multiple independent SIMD engines. Limitations: Performance reduction due to redundant processing of primitives spanning multiple patches; context switch overhead. This scheme was developed for the PxplS system, a heterogeneous multiprocessor graphics system. It builds on previous work using "buffered" Pixel-planes but introduces the concept of flexibly mapping small virtual pixel spaces onto the screen space. The design aims to fit within a workstation cabinet with no unusual power requirements, drive a 1280x1024 display at >60Hz, and update full scene images at >20 frames/second. name: Tile-Based Rasterization
head: CUDA tile rasterization
body: Tile-Based Rasterization is a GPU rendering primitive that assigns one CUDA thread block per image tile to process fragments locally. It parallelizes the rasterization workload by having threads within a block share splat data in fast shared memory and blend them in front-to-back order. Unlike Screen Parallel Rendering, which assigns threads directly to pixels without tile-level coordination, this method groups pixels into fixed-size tiles to optimize shared memory reuse. Inputs: A list of splats (e.g., 3D Gaussians) projected to screen space. A tile grid covering the resolution (16×16 pixels). For each tile, a sorted list of splat indices assigned to that tile. Outputs: Final color and opacity values for each pixel in the tile. Data Structures: Shared Memory Buffer: A 1D array storing up to 128 splats per iteration. Thread Block: A CUDA thread block of 256 threads, mapped one-to-one to the 16×16 pixel tile. Parameters: Tile size: 16×16 pixels. Threads per block: 256. Load batch size: 128 splats. Steps: 1. Assign one CUDA thread block per tile, with 256 threads mapping to the 16×16 pixel grid. 2. Initialize pixel buffers for color and accumulated opacity. 3. Ping-pong blending loop: Phase 1 uses 128 threads to load the next batch of up to 128 splats from global memory into shared memory. Phase 2 uses all 256 threads to iterate through the loaded splats and blend them in front-to-back order. Repeat until all assigned splats are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilerasterize(tilesplats, threadid, numpixels=256, loadbatch=128): # Map thread index to pixel coordinates in the 16x16 tile pixelcoords = (threadid % 16, threadid // 16) pixelcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] pixelalpha = 0.0 splatidx = 0 numsplats = len(tilesplats) sharedsplats = [None] loadbatch while splatidx < numsplats: # Phase 1: Load loadcount = 0 if threadid < loadbatch: endload = min(splatidx + loadbatch, numsplats) for i in range(splatidx, endload): sharedsplats[loadcount] = tilesplats[i] loadcount += 1 splatidx = endload # Synchronize all 256 threads syncthreads() # Determine how many splats were actually loaded numloaded = loadcount if threadid < loadbatch else 0 # Broadcast numloaded from thread 0 to all threads if threadid == 0: broadcastnumloaded = numloaded syncthreads() numloaded = broadcastnumloaded # Phase 2: Blend for s in range(numloaded): splat = sharedsplats[s] if pixelinsplatfootprint(splat, pixelcoords): contribution = computesplatcontribution(splat, pixelcoords) pixelcolor, pixelalpha = fronttobackblend( pixelcolor, pixelalpha, contribution['color'], contribution['alpha']) syncthreads() def syncthreads(): # Simulates CUDA syncthreads() barrier pass def pixelinsplatfootprint(splat, coords): # Checks if coords are within the splat's 2D bounding box return True def computesplatcontribution(splat, coords): # Computes color and alpha at coords return {'color': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'alpha': 0.0} def fronttobackblend(c1, a1, c2, a2): # Standard alpha compositing outa = a1 + a2 (1.0 - a1) outc = [c1[i] + c2[i] a2 (1.0 - a1) for i in range(3)] return outc, outa Edge Cases: Fewer than 128 splats: The load phase handles partial batches. The blend phase must correctly determine the number of valid splats in shared memory to avoid reading garbage data. Empty Tile: If no splats are assigned to a tile, the loop does not execute, and the pixel retains its background value. Binned Raster Traversal is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method for Gaussian Splatting that replaces the baseline's single globally depth-sorted scan with a linear scan over a concatenation of K coarse, tile-local depth bins. It solves the performance bottleneck of global sorting by deferring depth ordering to a tile-local binning phase, allowing the rasterizer to process a contiguous memory interval without per-bin branching or complex control flow. Unlike the baseline traversal, which requires a single sorted range, this method scans the concatenated bins in front-to-back order, relying on pre-computed offsets to define the scan interval. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splats assigned to the tile and the number of pixels in the tile. Memory Complexity: O(N{splat\per\tile}) for shared memory, where N{splat\per\tile} is capped at 128. Strengths: Reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing splat data in shared memory. Scales well with tile size and splat density. Limitations: Requires efficient binning of splats to tiles beforehand. Performance may degrade if splat distribution is highly uneven across tiles. Tile-Based Rasterization for Gaussian Splatting adapts the standard 3DGS rasterization approach to a tile-based parallel model on CUDA, leveraging the hardware's thread block architecture to optimize the blending process. name: Binned Raster Traversal
head: Binned CUDA Rasterization
body: Binned Raster Traversal is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method for Gaussian splatting that replaces the global depth-sorted scan of the baseline with a tile-local, bin-based linear scan. It solves the performance bottleneck of global sorting by partitioning the pair stream into coarse bins per tile, allowing each CUDA thread block to process a contiguous interval of pre-ordered data without per-bin branching. Unlike the baseline which scans a single globally depth-sorted range, this method scans the concatenation of K coarse bins laid out back to back in front-to-back bin order. Inputs: Repaired pair stream P (containing Gaussian IDs and sidecar data). Bin offsets array binOffsets[t, k] for each tile t and bin index k \in [0, K]. Optional flat-ID sidecar. Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, color, opacity). Image and tile dimensions. Outputs: Rendered colors, alphas, and last contributing IDs for each pixel. Data Structures: binOffsets: A 2D array of size T \times (K+1), where T is the number of tiles and K is the number of coarse bins per tile. binOffsets[t, k] stores the start index in the pair stream for the k-th bin of tile t. The interval for tile t is [binOffsets[t, 0], binOffsets[t, K]). Shared memory: Used for candidate Gaussian IDs and optionally for staging candidate colors. Parameters: K: Number of coarse bins per tile. Default: 64. Early-termination threshold: Transmittance Tp below which a pixel is marked inactive. Tile-alpha culling threshold: Minimum contribution threshold for tile-level culling. Configuration flags: colorstaging (enabled by default), tilealphaculling (enabled by default), traversalprofiling (disabled by default). Steps: 1. Launch one CUDA block per tile in parallel. 2. Determine tile pixel coordinates and skip masked tiles. 3. For all pixels p in tile t: Initialize color accumulator Cp \leftarrow 0 and transmittance accumulator Tp \leftarrow 1. 4. Set scan interval [a, b) \leftarrow [binOffsets[t, 0], binOffsets[t, K]). 5. Iterate through batches within the interval a, b): If all pixels in the tile have terminated, break the loop. 6. Load candidate Gaussian IDs into shared memory. 7. If tile-alpha culling is enabled, remove candidates below the tile-level contribution threshold. 8. If color staging is enabled, stage candidate colors cooperatively in shared memory. 9. For all Gaussians g in the surviving batch order, iterate over all active pixels p in the tile. 10. If traversal profiling is enabled, count candidate visits. 11. Evaluate the same opacity/conic test as the baseline. 12. Update Cp and Tp using baseline alpha [compositing. 13. If Tp reaches the early-termination threshold, mark pixel p as inactive. 14. Write final color, alpha, and last contributing ID for each pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binnedrastertraversal(repairedpairstream, binoffsets, gaussianattrs, tiledims, K=64, batchsize=256, earlyterminationthreshold=1e-4, tilealphacullingenabled=True, tilealphathreshold=0.01, colorstagingenabled=True, traversalprofilingenabled=False): # Constants EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD = earlyterminationthreshold TILEALPHATHRESHOLD = tilealphathreshold candidatevisits = 0 # 1. Launch one CUDA block per tile in parallel for tilet in range(numtiles): # 2. Determine tile pixel coordinates; skip masked tiles if tilet.ismasked: continue tilepixels = tilet.getpixelcoordinates() # 3. Initialize accumulators for all pixels in the tile for p in tilepixels: p.Cp = 0.0 p.Tp = 1.0 p.isactive = True # 4. Set scan interval a = binoffsets[tilet.id, 0] b = binoffsets[tilet.id, K] # 5. Iterate through batches within the interval [a, b) batchstart = a while batchstart < b: # Check if all pixels terminated if not any(p.isactive for p in tilepixels): break # Determine batch end batchend = min(batchstart + batchsize, b) # 6. Load candidate Gaussian IDs into shared memory candidateids = [] for idx in range(batchstart, batchend): candidateids.append(repairedpairstream[idx].gaussianid) # 7. Tile-alpha culling if tilealphacullingenabled: survivingids = [] for gid in candidateids: g = gaussianattrs[gid] # Estimate tile-level contribution contribution = g.opacity g.scalefactor if contribution >= TILEALPHATHRESHOLD: survivingids.append(gid) candidateids = survivingids # 8. Color staging if colorstagingenabled: stagedcolors = [gaussianattrs[gid].color for gid in candidateids] # 9. For all Gaussians g in surviving batch order, iterate over all active pixels p for gid in candidateids: g = gaussianattrs[gid] for p in tilepixels: if not p.isactive: continue # 10. Traversal profiling if traversalprofilingenabled: candidatevisits += 1 # 11. Evaluate opacity/conic test alpha = computealpha(p, g) if alpha < 1e-6: continue # 12. Update Cp and Tp using baseline alpha compositing color = computecolor(p, g) p.Cp += color alpha p.Tp p.Tp = (1.0 - alpha) # 13. Early termination if p.Tp < EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD: p.isactive = False batchstart = batchend # 14. Write final results for p in tilepixels: p.finalcolor = p.Cp p.finalalpha = 1.0 - p.Tp p.lastcontributingid = candidateids[-1] if candidateids else -1 def computealpha(pixel, gaussian): # Evaluates opacity/conic test as in baseline rasterization return gaussian.opacity gaussian.scalefactor def computecolor(pixel, gaussian): # Computes projected color contribution as in baseline rasterization return gaussian.color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bin Order: Entries within a bin are not depth-sorted unless selective exact repair has restored the order. The method relies on the concatenation of bins being in front-to-back bin order, not necessarily within each bin. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is used for accumulators. Early termination thresholds must be chosen carefully to avoid visual artifacts from premature culling. Boundaries: The scan interval a, b) is exclusive of b. Ensure binOffsets array is sized correctly to avoid out-of-bounds access. The [CUDA Tile-and-Bin Implementation is a parallelization strategy for computing the forward and backward passes of 2D bitmap primitive rendering on a GPU. It partitions the image plane into tiles and assigns primitives to the tiles they overlap, using one CUDA thread block per tile to achieve complete pixel-level parallelism. It sets itself apart from parent Binned Raster Traversal by explicitly managing the tile-to-primitive assignment on the CPU and staging primitive parameters in shared memory for cooperative compositing within the block, rather than relying on a linear scan of a pre-binned pair stream. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of candidates in the tile's concatenated bins. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the pair stream, bin offsets, and Gaussian attributes, plus shared memory for candidate IDs and optionally colors. Measured Performance: Evaluated on an RTX 4090 with a synthetic scale-up diagnostic from 5M to 30M Gaussians. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates global sorting overhead; enables efficient tile-local processing; supports early termination. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of binning; poor binning can lead to unbalanced workloads. When to Use: Suitable for high-resolution rendering with large numbers of Gaussians where global sorting is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: For small scenes or low Gaussian counts where global sorting overhead is negligible. Binned Raster Traversal was introduced in the TileGS paper, which proposes tile-local depth binning for Gaussian splatting rasterization. It addresses the scalability issues of previous methods by leveraging tile-local processing and binning strategies. name: CUDA Tile-and-Bin Implementation
head: Tile-and-Bin CUDA Pipeline, Tile-and-Bin CUDA Pipeline for 2D Bitmaps, tile-based differentiable splatting for 2D bitmaps
body:
The CUDA Tile-and-Bin Implementation is a parallelization strategy for computing the forward and backward passes of 2D bitmap primitive rendering on a GPU. It partitions the image plane into tiles and assigns primitives to the tiles they overlap, using one CUDA thread block per tile to achieve complete pixel-level parallelism. It sets itself apart from parent Binned Raster Traversal by explicitly managing the tile-to-primitive assignment on the CPU and staging primitive parameters in shared memory for cooperative compositing within the block, rather than relying on a linear scan of a pre-binned pair stream. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N primitives, each defined by parameters \{(xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, ci)\}{i=1}^N, where (xi, yi) is position, si is scale, 	hetai is rotation, 
ui is opacity logit, and ci is color logits. A tile-primitive mapping generated on the CPU. Output: Rendered image I \in [0,1]^3 and alpha channel I\alpha. Data Structures: Tile-Primitive Mapping: A list associating each tile with the indices of primitives whose bounding boxes overlap the tile region (with a small padding margin). Shared Memory: Stages per-primitive parameters cooperatively by threads in a block. Global Memory: Caches computed \alphak and ck values in FP16 for each primitive assigned to the tile. Formulas: The transmittance at step k is defined as: Tk(x,y) = \prod{j=0}^{k-1}(1 - \alphaj(x,y)) The image color is computed as: I(x,y) = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} Tk(x,y) \alphak(x,y) \sigma(ck) \in [0,1]^3 where \alphak is the opacity, \sigma is the sigmoid function, and ck is the primitive color. The interpolated value Mi(x,y) for a primitive is computed via bilinear interpolation: Mi(x,y) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{p} = \sum{j=0}^{3} wj pj where \mathbf{p} are the four surrounding points in the primitive template grid and \mathbf{w} are the interpolation weights. Parameters: Tile Size (T): Default value is 32 pixels. Steps: 1. CPU Preprocessing: Partition the image plane into T 	imes T tiles (default T=32). Assign each primitive to every tile whose bounding box on the image plane overlaps the tile region with a small padding margin. 2. GPU Launch: Launch a CUDA grid with dimensions (\lceil W{canvas}/32 ceil, \lceil H{canvas}/32 ceil) blocks. Each block has 32 	imes 32 threads. 3. Forward Pass (Per Thread): Each thread handles a specific pixel (x,y). For each primitive i assigned to the current tile: Transform (x,y) to (u,v) in primitive space. Compute Mi(x,y) via bilinear interpolation at (u,v). If Mi(x,y) < \epsilon, skip this primitive. Compute \alphak = \alpha{max} \cdot \sigma(
ui) \cdot Mi(x,y) and ck = \sigma(ci). Cache \alphak and ck in global memory (FP16). Alpha Compositing: Initialize transmittance T \leftarrow 1 and accumulated color C \leftarrow (0,0,0). For each cached primitive k (in front-to-back order): Store Tk for backward pass. Update C \leftarrow C + T \alphak ck. Update T \leftarrow T (1 - \alphak). Write I[x,y] \leftarrow C and I\alpha[x,y] \leftarrow 1 - T. 4. Backward Pass: Uses the same grid structure. Each thread rebuilds its cached primitive list. Computes gradients via the chain rule. For the Over operator, gradients depend on suffix sums. Color gradients are calculated as:  rac{\partial L}{\partial c{k,j}} =  rac{\partial L}{\partial Ij} \cdot Tk \alphak \cdot \sigma(c{k,j})(1 - \sigma(c{k,j})) Geometric gradients (xi, yi, si, 	hetai) flow through bilinear sampling of Mi(x,y). Accumulates gradients using packed half2 atomic operations for parameter pairs (xi, yi), (
ui, si), (	hetai, c{r,i}), and (c{g,i}, c{b,i}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: XPR Rasterizer
head: XPR's rasterizer, static-shape rasterization
body: The XPR rasterizer converts variable-length per-tile primitive lists into a fixed-size matrix Q of dimensions T \times P{\max}, enabling execution on accelerators that require static tensor shapes and prohibit dynamic control flow. Unlike traditional rasterizers that rely on dynamic lists or linked structures, this method uses a sequence of static-shape modules (Replicate, Assign, Cull, Sort, Gather) to produce a dense, depth-sorted array of primitive indices for each tile, padding unused entries with a sentinel value. It builds on CUDA Tile-and-Bin Implementation by replacing dynamic per-tile lists with fixed-size tensors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: M visible primitives p0, \dots, p{M-1} from the filter stage. Each primitive pi provides its depth zi, tile-space bounding box [xi^{\min}, xi^{\max}) \times [yi^{\min}, yi^{\max}), and tile count tci (the number of tiles its bounding box intersects). Output: A fixed-size matrix Q of size T \times P{\max}, where row t contains up to P{\max} depth-sorted primitive indices for tile t. Entries beyond the valid count ct are padded with -1. Data Structures: Flat Intersection Array: A temporary array of size I, where I = \sum{i=0}^{M-1} tci is the total intersection count. Each element corresponds to a specific tile-primitive intersection. Matrix Q: Dimensions T \times P{\max}. T is the number of tiles. P{\max} is the maximum number of primitives per tile. Bounds Array: Stores start index bj and count cj for each valid tile j. Parameters: P{\max}: Maximum primitives per tile. Typical values are 4096 or 8192. T: Total number of tiles. W': Tile-grid width. T{sentinel}: Sentinel tile ID (denoted as T in sources) indicating rejection. Steps: 1. Replicate: Compute prefix sums of the tile counts tci to determine the start offset si for each primitive in the flat intersection array of size I. For each primitive pi, generate tci entries in the flat array starting at si. 2. Assign Tile ID: For each replicated entry with local offset r within primitive pi's bounding box, compute the tile coordinates: wi = xi^{\max} - xi^{\min} x = xi^{\min} + (r \bmod wi) y = yi^{\min} + \lfloor r / wi \rfloor t = y W' + x Assign tile ID t to the entry. 3. Cull: Apply an optional tilecull function to each candidate primitive-tile pair using tile-cull data returned by the projection stage. If a candidate fails tilecull or a contribution threshold, reassign its tile ID to T{sentinel}. If no tilecull is provided, keep all candidates. 4. Sort and Identify Bounds: Lexicographically sort the flat array by (tile\ ID, depth). Rejected candidates (ID T{sentinel}) move to the end. For each valid tile tj, the surviving candidates form a contiguous segment. Record each segment's start bj and count cj. 5. Gather: Using bj and cj, write to matrix Q: Q[j, k] = P{sort}[bj + k] \quad \text{for } 0 \le k < \min(cj, P{\max}) where P{sort} is the sorted primitive-index array. Pad remaining entries of Q[j,:] with -1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def xprrasterizer(primitives, tilegridwidth, numtiles, pmax, tilecullfunc=None): """ primitives: list of M primitives. Each primitive has: depth: float bbox: (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) tc: int (tile count) tilegridwidth: int W' numtiles: int T pmax: int Pmax tilecullfunc: optional function(tileid, primitivedata) -> bool """ m = len(primitives) sentinelt = numtiles # Sentinel ID larger than any valid tile ID (0 to T-1) # Step 1: Replicate tilecounts = [p.tc for p in primitives] startoffsets = [0] m currentoffset = 0 for i in range(m): startoffsets[i] = currentoffset currentoffset += tilecounts[i] totalintersections = currentoffset # I flatarray = [] # Step 2: Assign Tile ID for i in range(m): p = primitives[i] xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax = p.bbox wi = xmax - xmin for r in range(tilecounts[i]): x = xmin + (r % wi) y = ymin + (r // wi) t = y tilegridwidth + x flatarray.append((t, p.depth, i)) # Step 3: Cull culledflatarray = [] for tileid, depth, pidx in flatarray: isvalid = True if tilecullfunc is not None: # The exact tilecull function and contribution threshold logic are not specified in the sources. # isvalid = tilecullfunc(tileid, primitives[pidx]) pass if isvalid: culledflatarray.append((tileid, depth, pidx)) else: culledflatarray.append((sentinelt, depth, pidx)) # Step 4: Sort and Identify Bounds # Lexicographically sort by (tileid, depth). Sentinels (sentinelt) sort to the end. culledflatarray.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1])) bounds = {} # tileid -> (startindex, count) n = len(culledflatarray) i = 0 while i < n: tileid = culledflatarray[i][0] if tileid == sentinelt: break # Remaining are rejected j = i while j < n and culledflatarray[j][0] == tileid: j += 1 count = j - i bounds[tileid] = (i, count) i = j # Step 5: Gather Q = [[-1] pmax for in range(numtiles)] for tileid, (startidx, count) in bounds.items(): for k in range(min(count, pmax)): pidx = culledflatarray[startidx + k][2] Q[tileid][k] = pidx return Q Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic memory and control flow are not well supported on accelerators compiling to static tensor shapes (e.g., TPUs). XPR avoids this by using fixed-size matrices and static loops. If a tile exceeds P{\max} primitives, excess entries are padded with -1 and ignored by the shader. The sentinel tile ID must be larger than any valid tile ID to ensure lexicographic sorting places rejected candidates at the end of the flat array. Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step in "Sort and Identify Bounds", which is O(I \log I) where I is the total intersection count. Memory Complexity: Requires O(I) for the flat intersection array and O(T \times P{\max}) for the output matrix Q. Strengths: Eliminates dynamic memory allocation and dynamic control flow, making it suitable for accelerators like TPUs that compile to static tensor shapes. Limitations: Requires setting P{\max} statically. Performance depends on the choice of P{\max}; larger values increase memory usage but reduce the risk of clipping. When to use: When rendering on hardware with limited dynamic control flow support or when a static-shape pipeline is required. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and P{\max} must be small, leading to significant primitive clipping, or when the scene has highly variable and unpredictable primitive densities that cannot be bounded by a reasonable P{\max}. The XPR rasterizer was introduced in the XPR renderer, an extensible cross-platform point-based differentiable renderer. It was designed to address the limitations of dynamic data structures on modern accelerators, specifically targeting compatibility with TPUs and other static-shape hardware. The method is part of a broader pipeline that includes filtering, projection, and shader stages, all expressed as static-shape operations. name: RasterizeTile
body: RasterizeTile is the core kernel for processing a single screen tile in tiled parallel compositing architectures, specifically designed to decouple variable-rate mask compaction from fixed-rate blending. It solves the bottleneck where irregular gaussian overlap distributions cause load imbalance and memory thrashing by using a scheduling buffer to batch work. Unlike sibling methods that may process gaussians in a fixed order or without explicit buffering, RasterizeTile ensures that blending always consumes a fixed batch size Bd from local shared memory, stabilizing performance across varying scene densities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Tile index t, scheduling buffer capacity 2Bd, batch size Bd, number of mini-batches K, number of threads P, and the scene data structure \mathcal{S} containing masks. Output: Partially composited color (R, G, B) and opacity (T) for all pixels in tile t, stored in tilebuf[t]. Data Structures: Scheduling Buffer \mathcal{R}: A per-warp ring buffer in shared memory with capacity 2Bd elements. It stores gaussian indices to be blended. Accumulators: Per-pixel-pair accumulators (R, G, B, T). Each thread p owns tile\size^2/(2P) pixel-pairs. Parameters: P: Number of threads in the worker group. Bd: Drain batch size (number of gaussians processed per blend step). K: Number of mini-batches per batch. \varepsilon: Saturation threshold for early-out. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize accumulators: (R, G, B, T) \leftarrow (0, 0, 0, 1) for all pixels. 2. Initialize scheduling buffer: \mathcal{R} \leftarrow \emptyset. 3. Iterate k from 0 to K-1: a. Retrieve mask m \leftarrow \mathcal{S}.masks[k \cdot M + t]. Bit g in m is set if gaussian g overlaps tile t. b. Compact mask m to extract valid gaussian indices. c. Enqueue compacted indices into \mathcal{R}: \mathcal{R}.\text{EnqueueAll}(k \cdot P + \text{Compact}(m)). d. While \mathcal{R} contains at least Bd elements: i. Dequeue a batch of size Bd from \mathcal{R}. ii. Perform front-to-back blending: FrontToBackBlend(dequeuedbatch, \mathcal{S}, R, G, B, T). iii. Check for early-out: If all pixels are saturated (\forall p: T[p] < \varepsilon), break the loop. 4. Flush remaining elements in \mathcal{R} via FrontToBackBlend(\mathcal{R}.\text{Flush}(), \mathcal{S}, R, G, B, T). 5. Store results to tilebuf[t]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RasterizeTile(t, S, P, Bd, K, epsilon): # Initialize accumulators for all pixels owned by this thread group # Each thread owns tilesize^2 / (2P) pixel-pairs R, G, B, T = initializeaccumulators(P) # Scheduling buffer in shared memory, capacity 2Bd Rbuffer = RingBuffer(capacity=2Bd) for k in range(K): # Retrieve mask for current mini-batch and tile # M is total number of mini-batches per batch? Or stride? # Source says: S.masks[k M + t] mask = S.masks[k M + t] # Compact mask to get gaussian indices # Compact(m) returns list of indices g where bit g is set compactedindices = Compact(mask) # Enqueue into scheduling buffer # Offset by k P? Source says: k P + Compact(m) # Assuming Compact(m) returns indices relative to the batch start Rbuffer.EnqueueAll(k P + compactedindices) # Drain full batches while Rbuffer.size() >= Bd: batch = Rbuffer.Dequeue(Bd) # Front-to-back blending using local storage FrontToBackBlend(batch, S, R, G, B, T) # Early-out check if Unanimous(lambda p: T[p] < epsilon): goto FlushAndStore FlushAndStore: # Flush remaining elements if Rbuffer.size() > 0: FrontToBackBlend(Rbuffer.Flush(), S, R, G, B, T) # Store results StreamStore(tilebuf[t], R, G, B, T) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method is noted to use half-precision for memory efficiency, though arithmetic precision details are deferred to implementation sections. Saturation: The early-out condition relies on T[p] < \varepsilon. If \varepsilon is too large, premature termination may cause visible artifacts; if too small, performance gain is minimal. Buffer Overflow: The scheduling buffer capacity is fixed at 2Bd. If the compacted mask size exceeds this, the algorithm as described may fail unless EnqueueAll handles overflow or the input is guaranteed to fit. The source implies the buffer decouples compaction from blending, suggesting it absorbs bursts. A GPU-accelerated technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces standard per-tile gaussian list materialization with inline visibility determination during the gaussian load phase. It groups render tiles into macro-tiles (8x4 or 8x8) to decouple work distribution from screen area, reducing the partitioning bottleneck at high resolutions. Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the number of gaussians overlapping the tile and the cost of mask compaction and blending. The scheduling buffer helps amortize the cost of variable-rate compaction. Memory Complexity: Requires shared memory for the scheduling buffer \mathcal{R} of size 2Bd and per-pixel accumulators. Performance: HiGS (which uses this method) reaches 67.0 dB PSNR without SH compression and 55.6 dB with 32-byte SH-compression, with no observable image-quality loss compared to baselines. Strengths: Decouples variable-rate mask compaction from fixed-rate blending, stabilizing performance. Early-out optimization skips remaining mini-batches when pixels are saturated. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of Bd and buffer size. Relies on efficient mask compaction. RasterizeTile is part of the HiGS (Hierarchical Rendering Architecture for Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting) framework. It was introduced to address performance bottlenecks in tiled parallel compositing, specifically the load imbalance caused by irregular gaussian distributions. The method targets NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and uses half-precision arithmetic for memory efficiency. name: Macro-tile Rasterization
head: Inline visibility macro-tile rasterization
body: Macro-tile Rasterization is a GPU-accelerated technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces the standard four-stage per-tile gaussian list materialization (bitmask generation, counting, prefix sum, fill) with inline visibility determination during the gaussian load phase. It decouples work distribution from screen area by grouping render tiles into macro-tiles (8x4 or 8x8), bounding per-unit work to achieve resolution-stable frame times. Unlike baseline rasterizers where partitioning and sorting dominate frame time at high resolutions, HiGS reduces the partitioning bottleneck by ensuring the macro-tile pair count grows significantly slower than screen resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of Br Gaussians, a set of M render tiles, a tile work queue Q, and a processing unit configuration of W worker groups with P threads each. Output: Final pixel colors for all render tiles, computed via front-to-back alpha compositing. Data Structures: Local Storage (\mathcal{S}): Holds gaussian data for the current batch. \mathcal{S}.\text{pos}[j]: Position of gaussian j. \mathcal{S}.\text{conic}[j]: Conic matrix of gaussian j. \mathcal{S}.\text{color}[j]: Color of gaussian j. \mathcal{S}.\text{masks}[k \cdot M + \text{thread\id}]: Stores transposed masks. Index k is the mini-batch index, \text{thread\id} is the thread within the worker group. Scheduling Buffer (\mathcal{R}): Capacity 2Bd. Decouples variable-rate mask compaction from fixed-rate blending. Tile Work Queue (Q): Contains active render tiles assigned to worker groups. Parameters: Br: Total number of Gaussians in the batch. M: Number of render tiles. P: Number of threads per worker group. W: Number of worker groups per processing unit. K = \lceil Br / P \rceil: Number of mini-batches. Bd: Fixed-size drain batch size for blending. Precision: Half-precision (fp16) is used for memory efficiency on commodity GPUs, as packed half-precision and single-precision share resources. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Load and Inline Visibility The processing unit cooperatively loads its batch of Br Gaussians into local storage in K mini-batches of P Gaussians, one per thread of a worker group. During the load, each Gaussian is tested against all M render tiles using a conservative overlap test on its opacity-threshold ellipse, producing a per-gaussian tile-visibility mask. These masks are transposed from per-gaussian to per-tile format. Compute K \leftarrow \lceil Br / P \rceil. For each mini-batch k from \text{group\id} to K-1 with stride W: Compute global gaussian index j \leftarrow k \cdot P + \text{thread\id}. Load Gaussian data: \mathcal{S}.\text{pos}[j], \mathcal{S}.\text{conic}[j], \mathcal{S}.\text{color}[j] \leftarrow \text{LoadGaussian}(mt, j). Test overlap: \text{tile\mask} \leftarrow \text{OverlapTest}(\mathcal{S}.\text{pos}[j], \mathcal{S}.\text{conic}[j]). This produces an M-bit mask where bit t is set if tile t overlaps the Gaussian. Transpose mask: \mathcal{S}.\text{masks}[k \cdot M + \text{thread\id}] \leftarrow \text{TransposeMasks}(\text{tile\mask}). This converts the per-gaussian mask into a per-tile visibility entry for this mini-batch. Synchronize all worker groups. If \text{group\id} = 0: Compute valid tile mask: \text{hit} \leftarrow \bigvee{k=0}^{K-1} \mathcal{S}.\text{masks}[k \cdot M + \text{thread\id}]. This OR-reduce determines which tiles have at least one visible Gaussian in the batch. 2. Phase 2: Per-tile Rasterization Active render tiles are assigned to worker groups via the tile work queue Q. For each claimed tile, the worker group iterates over the precomputed mask, extracting only the visible Gaussians from local storage. A scheduling buffer \mathcal{R} accumulates Gaussian indices from the mask, then drains them in fixed-size drain batches of Bd Gaussians through an unrolled blending core. This decouples variable-rate mask iteration from fixed-rate blending arithmetic. Blending uses front-to-back alpha compositing with half-precision accumulators tracking per-pixel RGBT. After each drain batch, a unanimous vote tests whether all pixels in the tile have reached transmittance saturation; if so, the worker group immediately claims the next tile from the queue. Claim a tile from Q. Iterate over the precomputed mask for the claimed tile to extract visible Gaussian indices from \mathcal{S}. Accumulate indices in scheduling buffer \mathcal{R}. While \mathcal{R} is not empty: Drain Bd Gaussians from \mathcal{R}. Perform \text{FrontToBackBlend} on these Bd Gaussians using half-precision accumulators. Test for transmittance saturation: If all pixels in the tile have \prod Ti < \epsilon, break and claim next tile. 3. Post-rasterization Compositing Because each macro-tile's depth-sorted batches are processed sequentially, the final color is accumulated across batches. Walk each render tile's batch chain in depth order. Accumulate color using front-to-back alpha compositing with transmittance early-out: C = C0 + T0 \cdot C1 + T0 T1 \cdot C2 + \cdots with early termination when \prodi Ti < \epsilon. Each processing unit writes partial RGBT only for tiles with visible Gaussians using a sparse buffer indexed by a per-batch active-tile bitmask. Worker group reads compact stream of partial RGBT records. Tiles that saturate early skip remaining batches. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phase1loadandinlinevisibility(Br, M, W, P, groupid, threadid): K = ceil(Br / P) # Local storage for this processing unit Spos = [None] Br Sconic = [None] Br Scolor = [None] Br Smasks = [0] (K M) # Transposed masks # Stride over mini-batches for k in range(groupid, K, W): j = k P + threadid if j < Br: # Load Gaussian data Spos[j], Sconic[j], Scolor[j] = LoadGaussian(mt, j) # Test gaussian against all M render tiles tilemask = OverlapTest(Spos[j], Sconic[j]) # Transpose masks from per-gaussian to per-tile # tilemask is an M-bit integer; TransposeMasks returns the transposed representation Smasks[k M + threadid] = TransposeMasks(tilemask) # Barrier synchronization synchronize() # Compute valid tile mask if this is the first group if groupid == 0: hit = 0 for k in range(K): hit |= Smasks[k M + threadid] return hit, Spos, Sconic, Scolor, Smasks return None, Spos, Sconic, Scolor, Smasks def phase2pertilerasterization(tile, Spos, Sconic, Scolor, Smasks, Bd): # Extract visible gaussians for the claimed tile from precomputed mask # The mask for tile t is stored in Smasks, but needs to be reconstructed # from the per-mini-batch transposed masks. # For simplicity, assume we have a function to get visible indices for a tile visibleindices = GetVisibleIndices(tile, Smasks) # Scheduling buffer R R = [] # Accumulate indices for idx in visibleindices: R.append(idx) # Drain in fixed-size batches if len(R) >= Bd: batch = R[:Bd] R = R[Bd:] # Unrolled blending core FrontToBackBlend(batch, Spos, Sconic, Scolor) # Test for transmittance saturation if IsTileSaturated(tile): return # Skip remaining batches for this tile # Drain remaining if R: FrontToBackBlend(R, Spos, Sconic, Scolor) def FrontToBackBlend(batch, Spos, Sconic, Scolor): # Accumulate Eq. (1) front-to-back with transmittance early-out # Each processing unit writes partial RGBT only for tiles with visible gaussians # using a sparse buffer indexed by a per-batch active-tile bitmask. for idx in batch: # Perform half-precision front-to-back alpha compositing # C = C0 + T0 C1 +... CompositePixel(Spos[idx], Sconic[idx], Scolor[idx]) def IsTileSaturated(tile): # Check if all pixels in the tile have reached transmittance saturation # i.e., product of transmittances < epsilon return tile.transmittanceproduct < epsilon HiGS Macro-tile Rasterization is a GPU-accelerated rasterization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces standard per-tile bitmask generation and prefix-sum dispatch with inline visibility determination during gaussian loading. It decouples work distribution from screen area by grouping render tiles into macro-tiles (8x4 or 8x8), bounding per-unit work to achieve resolution-stable frame times. Unlike baseline rasterizers where partitioning and sorting dominate frame time at high resolutions, HiGS reduces the partitioning bottleneck by ensuring the macro-tile pair count grows significantly slower than screen resolution. Time Complexity: The method replaces the O(N \log N) or O(N) sorting and prefix-sum stages of standard rasterizers with an O(Br \cdot M) overlap test phase, where Br is the batch size and M is the number of tiles. However, the overlap test is done inline and in parallel, and the subsequent blending is O(N) where N is the number of visible Gaussians. The key benefit is that the partitioning bottleneck is reduced because the macro-tile pair count grows significantly slower than screen resolution. Memory Complexity: Local storage \mathcal{S} holds Br Gaussians and K \cdot M mask entries. The scheduling buffer \mathcal{R} has capacity 2Bd. Half-precision is used for memory efficiency. Measured Performance: HiGS achieves 2.5–4.2 ms for a global radix sort over the same content, indicating significant savings compared to traditional sorting-based approaches. Strengths: Decouples variable-rate mask iteration from fixed-rate blending, keeping utilization high regardless of per-tile density. Reduces partitioning bottleneck at high resolutions. Limitations: Requires conservative overlap test on opacity-threshold ellipse, which may include some false positives. The inline visibility determination requires careful synchronization and mask transposition. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting at high resolutions where traditional sorting and prefix-sum stages become a bottleneck. When not to use: When the number of Gaussians is very small, or when the overhead of inline visibility determination outweighs the benefits of avoiding sorting. Macro-tile Rasterization was introduced in the HiGS paper as a novel approach to 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization. It addresses the limitations of standard rasterizers that rely on explicit per-tile gaussian lists, which require costly bitmask generation, counting, prefix sum, and fill stages. By moving visibility determination to the load phase and using macro-tiles to group work, HiGS achieves better scalability and performance on commodity GPUs.
