name: HiGS Macro-tile Rasterization
head: HiGS rasterizer, macro-tile rasterization, HiGS tile rasterization
body: HiGS Macro-tile Rasterization is a GPU-accelerated rasterization technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces standard per-tile bitmask generation and prefix-sum dispatch with inline visibility determination during gaussian loading. It decouples work distribution from screen area by grouping render tiles into macro-tiles (8x4 or 8x8), bounding per-unit work to achieve resolution-stable frame times. Unlike baseline rasterizers where partitioning and sorting dominate frame time at high resolutions, HiGS reduces the partitioning bottleneck by ensuring the macro-tile pair count grows significantly slower than screen resolution. Inputs: A batch of 3D Gaussians defined by position, covariance (Cholesky factor C), opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Camera projection parameters. Macro-tile layout configuration (8x4 or 8x8 render tiles per macro-tile). Global memory tile buffer (preallocated). Outputs: Partial RGBT (Red, Green, Blue, Transmittance) results stored in a global-memory sparse tile buffer. An active-tile bitmask indicating which render tiles within the macro-tile received gaussian contributions. 1. Global-Memory Tile Buffer: A preallocated dense array indexed by (macro-tile batch, render tile within macro-tile). Size: 16 KB per batch slot at default 8x8 render-tile size. Calculation: 32 tiles per macro-tile \times 64 pixels per tile \times 4 RGBT channels \times 2 bytes (half precision). Total Footprint: 16B KB for B macro-tile gaussian batches. 2. Active Mask: A per-batch 32-bit integer stored out-of-band. Flags which render tiles received gaussians. 3. Shared Memory Ring Buffer: A 2B-entry ring buffer storing gaussian indices, where B is the batch size. 4. Register Storage: 32x32 bit matrix for mask transpose (one word per warp lane). Gaussian attributes packed as half2 to halve shared memory occupancy and register pressure. Macro-tile Layout: 8x4 or 8x8 render tiles. For 8x4 layout, pixel coordinates (x, y) relative to the macro-tile center satisfy |x| \le 4 and |y| \le 2. Prescaling Factor: Cholesky factors are prescaled to absorb log2 base conversion and coordinate scaling: \tilde{C}'{ij} = C{ij} \times \frac{\text{tile\size}}{2} \times \frac{\text{tile\size}}{2} \times \text{tile\size} This allows the rasterizer to evaluate opacity using a single half-precision exp2 instruction without runtime base conversion. Batch Size (B): Number of gaussians in a macro-tile batch. 1. Mask Transpose: Each thread in a warp holds a 32x32 bit matrix in registers, where bit j indicates if gaussian j overlaps tile i. Perform a 5-stage warp-shuffle butterfly operation to transpose the matrix in registers. After transpose, lane i holds a word where bit j indicates gaussian j overlaps tile i. This avoids atomics and shared-memory bank conflicts. 2. Build Tile Work Queue: Warp 0 builds a work queue against a single shared-memory counter. Contention is kept warp-local. 3. Execute Blending Loop: Drain gaussian indices from the shared memory ring buffer in batches of B. Hoist position delta dx and base Cholesky term C{base\0} = C0 \cdot dx outside the pixel-pair loop. For each gaussian: Load 4 shared-memory values (using half2 packing). Execute inner loop (~11 half2 operations per pixel-pair). Evaluate opacity: \text{opacity} \times \text{exp2}(-\tilde{C}) where \tilde{C} is the prescaled Cholesky factor. Each gaussian requires exactly 4 shared-memory loads regardless of the number of pixel-pairs owned by the thread. 4. Check Saturation: After draining each batch, perform a warp-unanimous ballot vote to test if all pixel-pairs have saturated transmittance. If saturated, the warp immediately claims the next tile. 5. Write Partial Results: Write partial RGBT results to the global-memory tile buffer. Use cache-bypassing streaming stores to prevent evicting reused gaussian data from cache. 6. Post-Rasterization Compositing: A separate kernel assigns one warp per render tile. Walk parent macro-tile batches in depth order. Read partial RGBT from the sparse tile buffer only if the per-batch active-tile bitmask has the tile's bit set. Accumulate using front-to-back alpha blending with transmittance early-out. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def higsmacrotilerasterization(gaussians, camera, macrotileconfig): """ Main rasterization kernel for a single macro-tile batch. """ # 1. Mask Transpose # Each thread holds a 32x32 bit matrix in registers. # bitmatrix[i][j] = 1 if gaussian j overlaps tile i bitmatrix = computeoverlapmask(gaussians, camera, macrotileconfig) # Transpose 32x32 bit matrix using 5-stage warp-shuffle butterfly # After transpose: lane i holds word where bit j indicates gaussian j overlaps tile i transposedmatrix = warpshufflebutterfly(bitmatrix) # 2. Build Tile Work Queue # Warp 0 builds queue against shared-memory counter if threadid == 0: workqueue = buildworkqueue(transposedmatrix, sharedcounter) # 3. Execute Blending Loop # Shared memory ring buffer for gaussian indices ringbuffer = loadgaussianindicesfromglobaltoshared() while not ringbufferempty(): # Drain batch of B gaussians batch = ringbuffer.readbatch(B) for gaussian in batch: # Hoist invariant calculations dx = gaussian.position - macrotilecenter Cbase0 = gaussian.C[0] dx # Load gaussian attributes (half2 packed) # Requires 4 shared-memory loads per gaussian attrs = loadgaussianattributes(gaussian.id) # Inner blending loop (~11 half2 ops per pixel-pair) for pixelpair in activepixelpairs: # Evaluate opacity using prescaled Cholesky factor # opacity exp2(-Ctilde) Ctilde = computeprescaledchol(gaussian.C, dx, macrotileconfig) alpha = gaussian.opacity exp2(-Ctilde) # Accumulate RGBT accumulatepixel(pixelpair, alpha, gaussian.color, gaussian.sh) # 4. Check Saturation # Warp-unanimous ballot vote allsaturated = ballotall(saturatedtransmittance) if allsaturated: # Claim next tile immediately claimnexttile() break # 5. Write Partial Results # Use cache-bypassing streaming stores writepartialresultstoglobalbuffer(partialrgbt, cachebypass=True) # 6. Update Active Mask # Set bits for tiles that received gaussians activemask = computeactivemask(transposedmatrix) writeactivemask(activemask) def postrasterizationcompositing(activemasks, tilebuffer, macrotilebatches): """ Separate kernel for final compositing. """ # Assign one warp per render tile tileid = gettileid() # Walk batches in depth order for batch in macrotilebatches: # Check if this tile was active in this batch if activemasks[batch] & (1 << tileid): # Read partial RGBT from sparse tile buffer partialrgbt = readtilebuffer(batch, tileid) # Front-to-back alpha blending composite(partialrgbt) # Transmittance early-out if transmittancesaturated(): break Shared Memory Pressure: half2 packing halves shared memory occupancy for gaussian attributes and doubles the blending loop read rate, while also halving register pressure. Precision: The prescaling and tile-relative coordinates keep operands below the fp16 range limit, avoiding overflow during Mahalanobis evaluation. Cache Eviction: Writing partial results without cache-bypassing would evict reused gaussian data from cache, degrading performance. Time Complexity: The macro-tile pair count grows only 1.3–1.8x from 1080p to 4K, compared to 2.5–3.4x for render-tile schemes. Memory Complexity: The global-memory tile buffer footprint is 16B KB for B macro-tile gaussian batches. Performance: At 1080p 8x8 tiles, HiGS is 4.8x faster than gsplat (0.52 ms vs 2.49 ms mean). At 4K 8x8 tiles, HiGS is 8.4x faster (0.82 ms vs 6.92 ms mean). Sort stage accounts for 30–41% of intersection+sort time and under 0.08 ms even at 4K. Strengths: Resolution-stable frame times; reduced partitioning bottleneck; efficient use of fp16 and shared memory. Limitations: Requires preallocation of global-memory tile buffer; complex warp-shuffle implementation for mask transpose. When to Use: High-resolution rendering (4K+) where baseline rasterizers suffer from partitioning bottlenecks. When Not to Use: Low-resolution rendering where the overhead of macro-tile management may not be justified; scenes with extremely sparse gaussian distributions where tile saturation is rare. HiGS Macro-tile Rasterization was introduced in the HiGS paper (2026) as part of a hierarchical rendering architecture for real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitations of baseline rasterizers like gsplat, where partitioning and sorting dominate frame time at high resolutions. The method builds on the concept of macro-tiles to decouple work distribution from screen area, enabling resolution-stable performance. name: Tile-Based Wave Synchronization
head: Wavefront Rendering
body: Tile-Based Wave Synchronization manages tile assignment and synchronization across worker threads using wave indices and tokens. It serves as a synchronization primitive within tiled parallel compositing, ensuring that threads progress through discrete "waves" of work, allowing for coordinated state updates and potential cache coherency benefits. It differs from pure dynamic load balancing by enforcing synchronization barriers at wave boundaries, which can induce temporal cache coherency but risks load imbalance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A configuration specifying numwaves, numworkers, and tilesize. Output: Completed image tiles, with synchronization managed via internal provider state. Data Structures: Token: Holds a tileindex, waveindex, and jobid. Created by TileProvider::next(). Tile Wave Map (mtilewave): Maps tile indices to their current wave index. Configuration: Includes unsigned int numwaves, unsigned int numworkers, and imagesizet tilesize. Steps: 1. Token Acquisition: A worker thread calls TileProvider::next() to obtain a Token containing the assigned tile index and wave index. 2. Processing: The worker processes the assigned tile. 3. Wave Completion: Upon destruction of the Token, the provider updates the tile wave map: mtp.mtilewave[midx] = mwaveidx. 4. Notification: The provider notifies all waiting threads via mtp.mtilewave[midx].notifyall(). 5. Synchronization: Workers wait for the next wave index to be available before proceeding to new tiles. 6. Graceful Shutdown: Workers can call stopatnextwave() to finish their current wave before terminating. Formulas: ETA Calculation: Used for progress tracking: \text{avg\progress\rate} = \frac{\text{progress}}{\text{elapsed\time}} \text{eta} = \frac{1 - \text{progress}}{\text{avg\progress\rate}} Parameters: numwaves: Number of synchronization waves. numworkers: Number of worker threads. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Load Imbalance: If tiles have varying amounts of volume coverage, some threads may finish significantly earlier than others, causing idle time at synchronization barriers. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TileProvider: def init(self, numwaves, numworkers, tilecount): self.numwaves = numwaves self.numworkers = numworkers self.tilecount = tilecount self.tilewave = {} # Maps tileidx -> waveidx self.lock = Lock() self.condition = Condition(self.lock) self.currentwave = 0 self.finishedinwave = 0 def next(self): """Acquire a tile and wave index for a worker.""" with self.lock: # Simple round-robin or hash-based assignment could be used here # For wave sync, we assign tiles to waves tileidx = self.finishedinwave % self.tilecount waveidx = self.currentwave # Wait if this tile is not yet assigned to the current wave # In a real implementation, this would involve more complex state # to ensure all threads are in the same wave before proceeding while tileidx not in self.tilewave or self.tilewave[tileidx] != waveidx: self.condition.wait() return Token(tileidx, waveidx) def ontokendestroy(self, token): """Called when a worker finishes a tile.""" with self.lock: self.tilewave[token.tileidx] = token.waveidx self.finishedinwave += 1 # Notify waiting threads self.condition.notifyall() # Check if wave is complete if self.finishedinwave % self.numworkers == 0: self.currentwave += 1 class Token: def init(self, tileidx, waveidx): self.tileidx = tileidx self.waveidx = waveidx def del(self): # This is a simplification; in C++, destructors are explicit # In Python, we might use a context manager or explicit finish() pass class Worker: def init(self, provider): self.provider = provider self.stoprequested = False def run(self): while not self.stoprequested: token = self.provider.next() try: self.processtile(token.tileidx) finally: # Simulate token destruction triggering sync self.provider.ontokendestroy(token) def processtile(self, tileidx): # Ray casting logic pass def stopatnextwave(self): self.stoprequested = True A static work assignment algorithm that forces all threads to synchronize at the block level to induce temporal cache coherency by accessing nearby memory locations synchronously. This method performs poorly and was abandoned due to load imbalance, particularly when image tiles have less coverage of the 3D volume and calculate substantially fewer ray integration steps. Time Complexity: Synchronization overhead increases with the number of waves and the disparity in tile processing times. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the tile wave map and token state. Measured Performance: Static synchronization ("sync") performed poorly compared to dynamic assignment, with higher runtimes and L2 cache misses in some configurations. Z-ordered memory layout resulted in consistently better performance due to better use of the memory hierarchy. Strengths: Can induce temporal cache coherency. Limitations: Prone to load imbalance, especially with uneven volume coverage. When to use: When cache coherency is critical and tile workloads are uniform. When not to use: When tile workloads vary significantly (e.g., sparse volumes). The method is implemented in the Shibodd/volumepathtracer repository. The concept of static work assignment with synchronization was investigated in research on multi-core and many-core shared-memory parallel raycasting volume rendering optimization. name: Tile-Grouping Architecture
head: GS-TG
body: Tile-Grouping Architecture (GS-TG) is a GPU-optimized rasterization strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that merges adjacent tiles into larger work units to reduce redundant sorting overhead and improve data reuse within streaming multiprocessors. It distinguishes itself from standard tiled compositing by sharing the visibility sorting order across neighboring tiles while rasterizing each tile independently, thereby bypassing the need for per-tile CUDA radix sorts. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by center \mathbf{c}, covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, and color attributes; a camera projection matrix; and a framebuffer divided into a grid of tiles. Outputs: A rasterized image where each pixel contains the final blended color and depth. 1. Gaussian-Tile Association List: A list of tuples (g, t) where g is a Gaussian index and t is a tile index. This list is generated by intersecting Gaussian bounding spheres with tile bounding boxes. 2. Shared Sort Order: A single sorted list of Gaussians for a group of adjacent tiles, ordered by depth relative to the camera plane. This order is reused for all tiles within the group. 3. Tile State: Per-tile accumulators for color and depth, initialized to transparent/background values. 1. Tile Grouping: Divide the framebuffer into groups of adjacent tiles (e.g., 2 \times 2 or 4 \times 4 blocks). The group size is chosen to fit within the shared memory or cache hierarchy of a Streaming Multiprocessor (SM). 2. Association: For each Gaussian, determine which tiles it overlaps. Add entries to the Gaussian-Tile Association List. 3. Group Sorting: For each tile group, collect all Gaussians associated with any tile in the group. Sort these Gaussians by depth (front-to-back) once for the entire group. This replaces the per-tile sort. 4. Independent Rasterization: For each tile in the group: a. Initialize tile accumulators. b. Iterate through the shared sorted Gaussian list. c. For each Gaussian, check if it overlaps the current tile. d. If it overlaps, project the Gaussian to screen space and compute its contribution to the tile's pixels using alpha compositing. e. Skip Gaussians that are fully occluded or outside the tile bounds. 5. Assembly: Combine the results from all tiles to form the final image. Depth Sorting Key: For a Gaussian i, the depth key di is the distance from the camera center to the Gaussian center projected onto the view direction: di = \mathbf{v} \cdot (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{p}{cam}) where \mathbf{v} is the view direction, \mathbf{c}i is the Gaussian center, and \mathbf{p}{cam} is the camera position. Alpha Compositing: For a pixel p in tile t, the final color Ct is computed as: Ct = \sum{i \in \text{sorted}} \alphai \cdot ci \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity of Gaussian i at pixel p, and ci is its color. Group Size: Typically 2 \times 2 to 4 \times 4 tiles. Not given in the sources. Sort Algorithm: Hardware-accelerated depth test or radix sort for the group. Not given in the sources. Precision: Depth sorting precision may vary across tiles in a group if the depth range is large. Use high-precision depth values for sorting. Boundary Conditions: Gaussians on tile boundaries must be correctly assigned to avoid double-counting or gaps. The association step must handle boundary pixels consistently. Degenerate Input: If a tile group has no overlapping Gaussians, skip sorting and rasterization for that group. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilegroupingrasterize(gaussians, camera, tiles, groupsize): # Step 1: Group tiles tilegroups = createtilegroups(tiles, groupsize) # Step 2: Create Gaussian-Tile associations associations = [] for g in gaussians: for t in tiles: if intersects(g.boundingsphere, t.boundingbox): associations.append((g, t)) # Step 3 & 4: Process each group for group in tilegroups: # Collect Gaussians for this group groupgaussians = [g for g, t in associations if t in group] # Sort Gaussians by depth for the group sortedgaussians = sortbydepth(groupgaussians, camera) # Rasterize each tile independently using the shared order for tile in group: tilecolor = inittileaccumulator(tile) for g in sortedgaussians: if g.overlaps(tile): tilecolor = composite(tilecolor, g, camera) writetiletoframebuffer(tile, tilecolor) return framebuffer The parent method that divides the framebuffer into disjoint tiles for parallel processing. GS-TG builds on this by grouping tiles to share sorting work. A sibling method that performs alpha compositing per tile. GS-TG differs by sharing the sort order across multiple tiles. A sibling method that uses a queue to balance load. GS-TG uses static grouping, which may lead to load imbalance if tile complexity varies significantly. A sibling method that adjusts tile size based on scene complexity. GS-TG uses fixed-size groups, which may not adapt to varying Gaussian density. A sibling method that computes tile boundaries. GS-TG assumes pre-computed tile boundaries for grouping. A sibling method that assembles the final image from tiles. GS-TG includes this as the final step. A sibling method that uses multiple threads per tile. GS-TG uses multiple tiles per thread group. A sibling method that synchronizes waves of tiles. GS-TG avoids synchronization by sharing sort order. A sibling method that uses binary-swap for compositing. GS-TG uses standard alpha compositing with shared sorting. Time Complexity: Sorting is performed once per tile group instead of per tile, reducing sorting complexity from O(N \log N \cdot T) to O(N \log N \cdot \frac{T}{G}), where N is the number of Gaussians, T is the number of tiles, and G is the group size. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the shared sort order and tile accumulators. Memory usage is proportional to the number of Gaussians and tiles. Measured Performance: Achieves significant speedup by reducing redundant sorting work. Specific benchmarks are not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of tiles if the group size is optimized for the hardware cache hierarchy. Strengths: Reduces sorting overhead, improves data reuse, and leverages GPU hardware acceleration for depth testing. Limitations: May suffer from load imbalance if tile complexity varies. Fixed group size may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When sorting overhead is a bottleneck and tile complexity is relatively uniform. When not to use: When tile complexity varies significantly, leading to load imbalance. GS-TG was proposed in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization to address the high cost of per-tile sorting on GPUs. It is part of a broader trend of hardware-algorithm co-design for Gaussian rendering, alongside methods like GauRast, GSAcc, and GEMM-GS. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06157, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Parallel Binary-Swap Compositing
body: Parallel Binary-Swap Compositing is a method for combining independently rendered image tiles from multiple processors in a massively parallel environment. It solves the synchronization and communication bottlenecks of naive parallel compositing by reducing the data volume at each step, ensuring all processors remain busy with useful work. Unlike approaches where communication dominates or processors idle, this method maintains full processor utilization by pairing processors in a binary-swap fashion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N independent rendered image tiles, one per processor. Output: A single composite image. Data Structures: The method utilizes a k-D tree structure to manage the compositing tree and data distribution. Steps: 1. Initialization: Each processor holds its own independently rendered tile. 2. Pairing: Processors pair based on a binary-swap pattern. Processor i pairs with processor i \oplus 2^k, where k is the current step index starting from 0. 3. Compositing and Reduction: The receiver composites its current image with the image received from the sender. The image size for sending and compositing decreases at each step. The sender transmits its tile to the receiver. The sender becomes inactive for this step. 4. Iteration: The number of active processors is halved (N \leftarrow N/2). The step index increments. The process repeats until only one processor remains. 5. Termination: The single remaining processor holds the final composite image. Parameters: N: Number of processors. Initial tile dimensions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The sources do not specify handling for non-power-of-two processor counts or precision limits during accumulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. currentimage = localimage activecount = N step = 0 while activecount > 1: swapdist = 1 << step partner = procid ^ swapdist # Check if partner exists in the current active set. # activecount holds the number of active processors at the start of this step. if partner < activecount: if procid < partner: # Receiver: composite with partner's image partnerimage = receivedata(partner) currentimage = alphacomposite(currentimage, partnerimage) else: # Sender: transmit current image transmitdata(partner, currentimage) activecount >>= 1 step += 1 # The image size for sending and compositing decreases at each step finalimage = currentimage A parallel image compositing technique designed to combine independently rendered image tiles from multiple processors in a distributed-memory environment. It solves the limitation of standard Parallel Binary-Swap Compositing, which requires the number of processors N to be a power of two, by allowing any integer number of processors to participate. Unlike its parent method, it does not enforce a strict binary tree structure, instead grouping processors into pairs or triplets to facilitate data exchange. Choose this variant when N is not a power of two or when a distributed-memory architecture requires flexible grouping. Time Complexity: The method reduces active processors and image size at each step, completing in \log2 N iterations. Memory Complexity: Each processor stores its local image tile. Total memory scales with N and the initial tile size. Performance: Efficient because it decreases the image size for sending and compositing at each step, reducing communication overhead. It keeps all processors busy, avoiding idle time. Strengths: Simple implementation using a k-D tree structure. High efficiency in massively parallel environments. Limitations: The sources do not specify constraints on N or precision limits. The method was developed for parallel volume ray-tracing algorithms. It was implemented on the CM-5 and a network of scientific workstations. The tests used 32 high-performance workstations, including IBM RS/6000-550, HP9000/730, and Sun Sparc-10/30 machines. The algorithm divides both computation and memory load across all processors, allowing it to render data sets too large for a single uniprocessor. A data distributed, parallel algorithm for ray-traced volume..., https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/papers/PRS93.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: 2-3 Swap Compositing
head: 2-3 Swap, 2-3 Swap Image Compositing
body: 2-3 Swap Compositing is a parallel image compositing algorithm designed to combine independently rendered image tiles from multiple processors into a single final image, specifically addressing the limitation that the number of processors N must be a power of two in standard Binary Swap Compositing. It allows an arbitrary number of processors to be used while maintaining the O(N \log N) message complexity of binary swap, ensuring that all participating processors are fully utilized without idle stages. Unlike Direct Send, which suffers from network congestion and O(N^2) messages, 2-3 Swap limits communication to at most four neighbors per stage, making it suitable for massively parallel environments with thousands of processors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N processors, where N > 1 is an arbitrary integer. Each processor holds a partial image (tile) corresponding to a specific region of the final output image. The final image size is P pixels. Output: A single composited image constructed by tiling the partial images from all processors in scanline order. Data Structures: Compositing Tree: A recursive tree structure where each non-leaf node has either two or three children. The root represents the entire set of N processors. Leaf nodes represent individual processors. Processor List: A global ordered list of processor indices, initialized as [1, 2, \dots, N]. Image Partition: The final image is treated as a 1D pixel array in scanline order. At any stage, the image space is divided into contiguous partitions assigned to groups of processors. Algorithm Steps: 1. Tree Construction: Determine the number of stages S = \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor. Let K be such that 2^{K-1} \le N < 2^K. Construct the compositing tree recursively using ConstructCompositingTree(root, N, K-1). python class Node: def init(self): self.children = [] self.processors = [] def ConstructCompositingTree(node, n, d, proccounter): """ Recursively builds the compositing tree. node: The current tree node. n: The number of processors in this subtree. d: The depth remaining (distance to leaf). proccounter: Mutable list holding the global processor index counter. """ if d == 0: # Leaf node: assign the next available processor index node.processors = [proccounter[0]] proccounter[0] += 1 else: # Internal node: split n into 2 or 3 children l = n // 2 r = (n + 1) // 2 # ceil(n/2) if r < 2 d: # Split into 2 children node.children = [Node(), Node()] ConstructCompositingTree(node.children[0], l, d - 1, proccounter) ConstructCompositingTree(node.children[1], r, d - 1, proccounter) else: # Split into 3 children # The case (n mod 3) == 2 is mathematically impossible under the invariant 2^d <= n < 2^(d+1) l = n // 3 m = l r = n - 2 l node.children = [Node(), Node(), Node()] ConstructCompositingTree(node.children[0], l, d - 1, proccounter) ConstructCompositingTree(node.children[1], m, d - 1, proccounter) ConstructCompositingTree(node.children[2], r, d - 1, proccounter) 2. Order Assignment: Call OrderAssignment(root) to determine the processor order for image partitioning at each node. At leaf nodes, the order is the processor index. At internal nodes, the order is formed by interleaving the orders of the children. When merging groups (children) into a parent group: Rule 1: A group with a larger number of processors (smaller partitions) in the previous stage gets its order first. Rule 2: If group sizes are equal, the group with smaller processor indices gets its order first. python def OrderAssignment(node): if not node.children: return node.processors # Recursively get children orders childorders = [OrderAssignment(child) for child in node.children] # Sort children: larger processor count first, then smaller min index childorders.sort(key=lambda order: (-len(order), order[0])) # Concatenate in sorted order node.processors = [] for order in childorders: node.processors.extend(order) return node.processors 3. Compositing Stages: Execute S = \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor stages. In stage i (from 1 to S): Identify the groups of processors corresponding to the nodes at depth S - i + 1. Within each group, processors exchange pixel data. Partitioning: The image space is divided evenly among the M processors in the current group. Each processor is responsible for P/M pixels. Communication: Each processor sends its current partial image data to other processors in the same group and receives data from them. The number of neighbors is at most 4. Blending: After exchange, each processor blends the received pixels with its own local pixels using standard alpha compositing: C{out} = C{src} \alpha{src} + C{dst} (1 - \alpha{src}). 4. Gathering: After the final compositing stage, each processor holds a portion of the final composited image. Each processor sends its final partial image to a designated host processor, which tiles them to produce the final image. Formulas: Total Compositing Time: T{comp} = \sum{i=1}^{S} T{compi} where T{compi} = T{exchangei} + T{blendi}. Exchange Time per Stage (Full-Duplex): T{exchangei} = \max(L{sendi} + T{sendi}, L{recvi} + T{recvi}) where: L{sendi} = N{sendi} \times l{sendrecv} T{sendi} = \frac{P{sendi}}{B{sendi}} L{recvi} = N{recvi} \times l{sendrecv} T{recvi} = \frac{P{recvi}}{B{recvi}} l{sendrecv}: Latency per message. B{send/recv}: Network bandwidth. N{send/recv}: Number of send/receive operations. P{send/recv}: Size of pixel data sent/received. Blending Time: T{blendi} = \frac{P{blendi}}{B{blend}} where B{blend} is the blending bandwidth. Bounds for 2-3 Swap: Number of messages: N{sendrecv} \le 4 \times \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor. Pixel sending/receiving size: P{sendrecv} \le \frac{3}{4} \times P (theoretical bound; actual maximum \approx 1.23 P). Pixel blending size: P{blend} \le 2 \times P. Parameters: N: Number of processors. P: Size of the final image in pixels. S: Number of stages, \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Power-of-Two N: If N is not a power of two, the tree is complete but not full. This can cause workload imbalance. The worst-case timing is at most two times that of Binary Swap. Partition Alignment: Image partitions may not be perfectly aligned if processor counts are not evenly split (e.g., M vs M+1). However, analysis shows that cases where one partition overlaps three others are impossible, bounding communication to 4 neighbors. Idle Processors: Unlike Reduced Binary Swap, 2-3 Swap ensures no processors are idle at any stage. A generalization that divides communication into multiple rounds with variable group sizes ki, where \prod ki = N. It combines the flexibility of direct send with the performance of binary swap. Choose this when the network topology or communication patterns benefit from variable group sizes rather than the fixed 2-3 structure. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) messages exchanged. The number of stages is S = \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor. Memory Complexity: Each processor stores a fraction of the image. Total pixel data exchanged is bounded by 1.23 P for sending/receiving and 2.0 P for blending in the worst case. Performance: Scales well in massively parallel environments (thousands of processors). Outperforms Direct Send and Reduced Binary Swap in timing stability and efficiency. When N is a power of two, performance matches Binary Swap (the lower bound for 2-3 Swap). When N is not a power of two, timing is at most 2x that of Binary Swap. Average communication count is 1.98 \times \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor, significantly better than the worst-case bound of 4 \times \lfloor \log2 N \rfloor. Approximately 80% of communication cases involve 1 or 2 neighbors. Strengths: Supports arbitrary N. No idle processors. Low network congestion (max 4 neighbors). Suitable for simulation-time visualization. Limitations: Workload imbalance can occur for non-power-of-two N, leading to a difference ratio in total compositing time of up to 57% (observed at 1021 processors). Implementation complexity is higher than Direct Send due to tree construction and order assignment. 2-3 Swap Compositing was introduced by Yu et al. to overcome the limitation of Binary Swap Compositing, which requires the number of processors to be a power of two. The algorithm was designed for massively parallel volume rendering, specifically for simulation-time data visualization on supercomputers. It was tested on a supercomputer with up to 1024 processors and applied to a Richtmyer-Meshkov Instability (RMI) dataset of 2TB with 2048×2048×1920 spatial resolution, generating 4096² output images. The method is a generalization of binary swap, decomposing N into a summation of twos and threes to ensure full processor utilization. name: Radix-k Compositing
head: Radix-k
body: Radix-k Compositing is a distributed-memory compositing strategy that combines the flexibility of direct send with the performance of binary swap. It allows any number of processors N to participate in the compositing phase, solving the power-of-two restriction of binary-swap methods. It sets itself apart from its parent 2-3 Swap Compositing by generalizing the group size per round, whereas 2-3 swap is restricted to groups of two or three. It shows good scaling up to 16,000-way concurrency and is compatible with hybrid parallel systems. Inputs: N: Total number of processors involved in compositing. P: Set of processors, indexed 0 \dots N-1. Image data: Each processor holds a region of the current partial image to be composited. Outputs: A fully composited image distributed across the processors or gathered to a specific node, depending on the higher-level scheme. Data Structures: Standard image buffers partitioned among processors; each processor owns a specific region of the current image. No specific bit-packing is defined in the sources; standard image buffers are assumed. Steps: 1. Factorization: Determine a sequence of group sizes k1, k2, \dots, km such that: \prod{i=1}^{m} ki = N The factors ki are typically small integers (e.g., 2s and 3s). 2. Round Execution: For each round i from 1 to m: a. Divide the N processors into groups of size ki. b. Within each group, processors exchange their current image regions using a direct send method. c. Each processor composites the received data with its own local image data to update its region. 3. Completion: After m rounds, the compositing is complete. Parameters: ki: Group size for round i. The choice of factors affects the number of communication rounds (m) and the volume of data sent per round. N: Number of processors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If N is prime, the only valid factorization is k1 = N, resulting in a single round of all-to-all communication. The algorithm requires a valid factorization of N; if N is prime, the single-round all-to-all pattern may increase communication volume compared to multi-round strategies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositefronttoback(img1, img2): """Standard front-to-back volume compositing.""" return img1 (1.0 - img2.alpha) + img2 def radixkcompositing(N, myid, myimage, allimages): """ Perform Radix-k compositing. N: Total number of processors. myid: ID of this processor (0 to N-1). myimage: The partial image held by this processor. allimages: List of images held by all processors (simulated for algorithm clarity). """ # Step 1: Factorize N into group sizes ki # Note: The sources do not specify the exact factorization algorithm. factors = [] ntemp = N for k in [2, 3, 5, 7]: while ntemp % k == 0: factors.append(k) ntemp //= k if ntemp > 1: factors.append(ntemp) # Step 2: Execute rounds currentimages = list(allimages) currentimages[myid] = myimage for k in factors: # Determine group boundaries for this processor groupid = myid // k groupstart = groupid k groupend = groupstart + k # Collect images from all processors in this group # In a distributed system, this corresponds to the direct send exchange groupimages = [currentimages[p] for p in range(groupstart, groupend)] # Composite all images in the group combined = groupimages[0] for img in groupimages[1:]: combined = compositefronttoback(combined, img) # Update local image currentimages[myid] = combined return currentimages[myid] Binary All-to-All Communication is an optimized distributed communication algorithm used to maintain an up-to-date image of the entire cluster memory state on each rendering node, replacing pre-determined page positions. It sets itself apart from the classical logical ring approach by reducing the number of communication steps from P-1 to \log(P), thereby improving scalability and reducing sensitivity to communication latency. Binary-Tree Compositing is a compositing strategy for combining partial images from processing nodes, initially implemented as a simple binary-tree step. It sets itself apart from Radix-k by using a fixed hierarchical tree structure rather than configurable group sizes per round. It may be replaced later with more elaborate algorithms like binary-swap. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Scales to 16,000-way concurrency. Compatible with hybrid parallel systems, potentially leading to faster compositing times than MPI Alltoallv-based approaches. Strengths: Allows any number of processors. Combines direct send flexibility with binary swap performance. Limitations: Performance depends on the factorization of N. Not given in the sources. Radix-k Compositing was proposed by Peterka et al.. It was introduced in a paper demonstrating good scaling up to 16,000-way concurrency. The method is part of a hybrid distributed-memory parallel volume rendering scheme that combines object-order and image-order approaches to reduce load imbalance. name: Binary All-to-All Communication
head: Binary swap algorithm, Recursive doubling allgather
body: Binary All-to-All Communication is an optimized distributed communication algorithm used to maintain an up-to-date image of the entire cluster memory state (an array of keys) on each rendering node, replacing pre-determined page positions. It sets itself apart from the classical logical ring approach by reducing the number of communication steps from P-1 to \log(P), thereby improving scalability and reducing sensitivity to communication latency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of keys stored in the local buffer of each node. Output: An array containing all keys stored in the memory of the entire cluster, present on every node. Data Structures: Each node maintains a local buffer (array) of keys. The size of the buffer exchanged grows exponentially with each step. Parameters: P: Total number of nodes in the cluster. size: Size of the data chunk transferred per step. latency: Network latency per message. bandwidth: Network bandwidth. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Each node i starts with an array containing the keys stored in its local buffer. 2. Iterative Exchange: The algorithm proceeds in \log2(P) steps. In step k (where k ranges from 0 to \log2(P)-1): Each node i identifies its partner node j by XORing the node index with 2^k: j = i \oplus 2^k. Node i and Node j exchange their current accumulated buffers. Each node merges the received buffer with its own, effectively doubling the amount of unique data known to each node. 3. Completion: After \log2(P) steps, each node holds an array containing all keys stored in the memory of the cluster. Formulas: The execution time for the binary all-to-all communication is given by: T{binary} = \frac{(P - 1) \cdot size}{bandwidth} + \log(P) \cdot latency Where size is the total size of the data to be gathered, latency is the network latency, bandwidth is the network bandwidth, and \log is the logarithm to base 10 as specified in the source. For comparison, the logical ring approach has complexity O(P-1) and execution time: T{logical\ring} = \frac{(P - 1) \cdot size}{bandwidth} + (P - 1) \cdot latency Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binaryalltoall(localkeys, myid, numnodes): """ Performs binary all-to-all communication to gather all keys from all nodes. Args: localkeys: List of keys initially stored on this node. myid: Integer ID of this node (0 to numnodes - 1). numnodes: Total number of nodes (P). Returns: List of all keys from all nodes. """ buffer = list(localkeys) steps = numnodes.bitlength() - 1 for k in range(steps): partnerid = myid ^ (1 << k) # Synchronous point-to-point network exchange with partnerid receivedbuffer = networkexchange(buffer, partnerid) buffer = list(set(buffer + receivedbuffer)) return buffer def networkexchange(localbuf, partnerid): # Placeholder for actual network I/O (e.g., MPISendrecv); # returns the partner's current buffer state. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Latency Sensitivity: The algorithm is sensitive to communication latency, as more communication steps increase sensitivity. Boundary Conditions: The standard binary swap pairing assumes a power-of-two number of nodes; non-power-of-two clusters require dummy nodes or adjusted pairing logic. Precision: Not given in the sources. A scalable distributed protocol to detect when a frame is complete, avoiding the linear time and host coordination of straightforward approaches. Because each processor knows exactly how many ray segments it has sent to each of the other processors, a binary-swap summing process results in the total number of ray segments each processor should eventually receive. At the end of this globally synchronous process, each processor holds exactly the number of segments it needs. If this number equals the number of segments the processor has actually received, the processor can stop receiving. The algorithm runs in logarithmic time and does not involve the host, making it more efficient and scalable to a larger number of processors. Compared to a designated node coordinating termination by collecting local messages and broadcasting a global signal (which prolongs termination on large systems), this binary-swap approach is more scalable. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: O(\log(P)) communication steps, compared to O(P-1) for the logical ring. Memory Complexity: Each node must store the entire cluster's key array, so memory usage per node is O(P \cdot size). Measured Performance: The binary all-to-all communication reduces the latency term in the execution time from (P-1) \cdot latency to \log(P) \cdot latency. The main advantage is scalability thanks to the \log(P) complexity. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Better scalability than logical ring; fully overlapped with rendering in some implementations. Limitations: More sensitive to communication latency than methods with fewer steps; requires all nodes to participate synchronously in the exchange steps. When to Use: Use when maintaining an up-to-date image of the entire cluster memory state is required and scalability is a concern. Use when the number of nodes P is large, making the O(P-1) ring approach too slow due to latency. When Not to Use: Avoid when the cluster size is very small and latency is negligible compared to bandwidth. Avoid when a centralized host coordination is acceptable and simpler to implement. Binary All-to-All Communication is inspired by the binary swap algorithm. It is used in the context of distributed shared memory for roaming large volumes. The algorithm is used in parallel volume rendering systems to replace pre-determined page positions with a dynamic memory buffer. It is similar in spirit to the recursive doubling allgather operation used in many implementations. name: Compute Shader Kernel
head: CSMain
body: A Compute Shader Kernel is a GPU compute shader entry point that executes a user-defined function in parallel across a grid of threads. It serves as a basic example of GPU parallel execution by writing a gradient texture based on thread IDs. Inputs and Outputs: The kernel receives a dispatch grid defined by the host application. It writes results to a writable 2D texture. Data Structures: Output Buffer: RWTexture2D<float4> Result, a writable 2D texture of 4-component floats. Thread ID: The global thread index within the dispatch grid, accessed via hardware/runtime built-in variables. Parameters: Resolution: A float variable used to normalize thread IDs to the [0, 1] range. Thread Group Size: 8 \times 8 \times 1 threads per group. Steps: 1. Retrieve the global thread ID id. 2. Calculate normalized x coordinate: x = \frac{id.x}{\text{Resolution}}. 3. Calculate normalized y coordinate: y = \frac{id.y}{\text{Resolution}}. 4. Write the result to the texture at id.xy with RGB values (x, y, 0.0) and alpha 0.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computekernel(threadid, resolution, outputtexture): idx = threadid.x idy = threadid.y x = idx / resolution y = idy / resolution color = (x, y, 0.0, 0.0) outputtexture[idy, idx] = color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. name: Register-form kernels with staged shell data
head: Staged shell data optimization
body: This method optimizes GPU compute shader kernels for atomic orbital (AO) evaluations by staging shell metadata and coefficient data into groupshared memory, thereby eliminating dependent global memory loads during the inner loop evaluation. It builds on Compute Shader Kernel by restructuring data access patterns to improve occupancy and reduce latency for AO evaluations. Inputs: A list of Gaussian-type orbital (GTO) shells, each defined by centre, cutoff, angular momentum l, AO count, and primitive coefficients. A set of evaluation points (vertices or corners). Outputs: Evaluated function values and gradients at the points. Data Structures: Exact layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. Groupshared memory stores staged shell data (centre, cutoff, l, AO count, primitives) and rows of coefficient matrix C for the current chunk. Vertex values are kept in registers during computation. Steps: 1. Pack Chunks: Group shells into chunks containing at most 256 primitives. 2. Stage Data: Load shell metadata and rows of C into groupshared memory for the current chunk. 3. Filter Shells: For each evaluation point, skip shells that are out of reach in all three dimensions. 4. Evaluate: Execute the inner loop using the staged groupshared memory, avoiding dependent global loads per shell. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Maximum primitives per chunk: 256. Maximum primitives per shell: 64 (shells exceeding this are refused). Pitfalls: Shells with more than 64 primitives are refused by the set. Precision issues may arise if not handled; however, specific precision guards are not detailed in the sources. This variant optimizes the evaluation of Cartesian monomials by computing them at once per angular momentum l in mdgto's order, with AO normalization folded into the staged rows of C, which are read as float4. A single function accumulates the shell's polynomial and multiplies by the radial part once. The groupshared rows are sized per F (number of channels), ensuring that narrow kernels maintain high occupancy. Performance: Eliminates dependent global loads in the inner loop, improving throughput. Memory: Uses groupshared memory for staging, reducing global memory bandwidth pressure. Occupancy: Row sizing per F helps maintain occupancy for narrow kernels. Limitations: Shells with more than 64 primitives are unsupported. This optimization is part of the mdgtoisogpu implementation in mdlib, focusing on efficient GPU isosurface extraction. It addresses the bottleneck of loading shell data from global memory for every evaluation point. mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability
head: CUDA-GL Interop, CUDA-to-OpenGL PBO write, OpenGL-CUDA Interoperability via Pixel Buffer Object (PBO), PBO-based rendering
body: CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability is a method for sharing GPU memory between CUDA computational kernels and the OpenGL rendering pipeline without CPU-mediated data transfers. It solves the bottleneck where the CPU issues draw calls or copies data between host and device memory, which limits frame rates in real-time volume rendering. Unlike traditional raster engines that rely on draw calls and shader binding, this method allows CUDA kernels to write directly to OpenGL resources (such as Pixel Buffer Objects or 3D textures) or read from them via mapped CUDA arrays, enabling zero-copy data sharing between simulation and rendering. The method establishes a bridge between the CUDA and OpenGL contexts using the cudaGraphicsRegister API family. It supports two primary resource types: Pixel Buffer Objects (PBOs) for image output and OpenGL Textures (2D/3D) for data input or output via surface objects. Inputs: OpenGL resource IDs (texture IDs, buffer IDs), OpenGL context handle, CUDA device ID. Outputs: CUDA graphics resource handles (cudaGraphicsResourcet), CUDA array views (cudaArrayt), CUDA surface objects (cudaSurfaceObjectt), or device pointers (void). CUDA Graphics Resource Handle: An opaque handle returned by registration functions, used to map/unmap the resource. Type: cudaGraphicsResourcet. CUDA Array View: A linear memory structure representing the OpenGL texture data, accessible via texture/surface references. Type: cudaArrayt. CUDA Surface Object: A writable view of a CUDA array, allowing direct per-voxel/pixel writes from kernels. Type: cudaSurfaceObjectt. CudaGlTexture3D Class Layout (Example Implementation): mresource (cudaGraphicsResourcet), mwidth (int), mheight (int), mdepth (int). 1. Registration: Create the OpenGL resource (PBO, 3D/2D Texture, or VBO). Register it with CUDA using cudaGraphicsGLRegisterImage for textures or cudaGraphicsGLRegisterBuffer for buffers. Specify flags: cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsSurfaceLoadStore for writable textures, cudaGraphicsMapFlagsReadOnly for read-only textures, or cudaGraphicsMapFlagsNone for buffers. 2. Mapping: Call cudaGraphicsMapResources to gain CUDA access and synchronize contexts. For textures, call cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray to retrieve the cudaArrayt. Bind it to a CUDA texture object via cudaBindTextureToArray or to a surface object via cudaBindSurfaceToArray. For buffers, call cudaGraphicsResourceGetMappedPointer to retrieve the raw device pointer. 3. Computation: Launch the CUDA kernel to read from mapped textures or write to mapped arrays/pointers. Synchronize with cudaDeviceSynchronize() to ensure completion before OpenGL access. 4. Unmapping & Rendering: Call cudaGraphicsUnmapResources to release CUDA access. Display via PBO (bind to GLPIXELUNPACKBUFFER and draw a quad, or use an explicit FBO), or bind the texture and draw a quad. For VBOs, bind buffers and call glDrawArrays. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initcudaglinterop(pboid): # Register the OpenGL PBO with the CUDA runtime to enable zero-copy sharing cudaresource = registeropenglbufferwithcuda(pboid, flags=MAPFLAGSNONE) return cudaresource def renderframe(cudaresource, width, height, computekernel): # Gain CUDA access to the mapped OpenGL resource mapresources(1, cudaresource, stream=0) # Retrieve the device pointer to the PBO memory deviceptr, bytescount = getmappedpointer(cudaresource) # Launch the volume rendering kernel blockdim = (16, 16, 1) griddim = ((width + 15) // 16, (height + 15) // 16, 1) computekernel(griddim, blockdim, deviceptr, width, height) # Ensure kernel completion before OpenGL access synchronizedevice() # Release CUDA access to the resource unmapresources(1, cudaresource, stream=0) # Transfer PBO data to a display texture and render bindtextureunit(GLTEXTURE0) bindtexture(GLTEXTURE2D, displaytextureid) copypbototexture(GLTEXTURE2D, 0, 0, 0, width, height, GLRGBA, GLUNSIGNEDBYTE, deviceptr) drawscreenquad() swapframebuffers() Block Dimension: Typically dim3(16, 16, 1) for 2D image rendering. Grid Dimension: Calculated as (Width + blockdim.x) / blockdim.x for x, (Height + blockdim.y) / blockdim.y for y, and 1 for z. Interpolation Filter: Hamming windowed-sinc filter with width 5 is used to minimize artifacts in resampling operations. Zero-Padding: 100% zero-padding increases memory requirements by a factor of 8 but suppresses overlapping artifacts in Fourier-based methods. Context Switching: Direct access to CUDA address space memory from OpenGL is not possible; data must be transferred via shared buffers like PBOs. Switching between off-screen OpenGL contexts and CUDA contexts must be handled carefully to avoid resource conflicts. Premature Access: Accessing mapped VBO/PBO memory with OpenGL before unmapping causes program failure. Error Handling: If cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray fails, the surface object is not created, preventing kernel launch. Code must check cudaSuccess before creating surfaces. Performance: Reading device memory via global memory is less performant than via texture fetches due to texture cache optimization for 2D spatial locality. Typo Risk: Variable naming errors (e.g., cosntantNCP vs constantNCP) can lead to incorrect constant memory updates. Bindless Textures in CUDA is a method for managing and accessing texture data directly from CUDA kernels without the per-frame binding and mapping overhead of OpenGL-CUDA interoperability. It solves the performance bottlenecks and resource limits of traditional OpenGL-CUDA texture sharing, where textures must be bound, mapped to CUDA resources, and unmapped every frame. Unlike CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write, which focuses on surface buffers, this method addresses texture sampling by allowing a dynamic number of textures to be exposed simultaneously to the kernel at runtime. A technique to allow CUDA kernels to write directly to OpenGL 3D textures using CUDA surface objects. It writes directly to an OpenGL texture from a CUDA kernel using CUDA graphics interop, avoiding intermediate device buffers. This method is distinct from CUDA-OpenGL Interop Texture Copy which uses cudaMemcpy3D for bulk transfers rather than per-voxel kernel writes. A display routine that updates the view matrix, renders the volume, clears the screen, copies data from the CUDA PBO to an OpenGL texture, and draws a textured quad. It builds the inverse view matrix by extracting and transposing the model-view matrix components from OpenGL, binds the PBO pbo and copies its contents to the 2D texture tex using glTexSubImage2D with format GLRGBA and type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE, draws a textured quad covering the screen coordinates (0,0) to (1,1) using glBegin(GLQUADS), and swaps buffers. Time Complexity: The core interop operations (register, map, unmap) are constant time relative to data size but involve API overhead. The rendering loop performance is dominated by the CUDA kernel execution time. Memory Complexity: Zero-copy sharing eliminates four serial copies and four redundant texture objects compared to high-level libraries like SFML, reducing memory footprint. However, zero-padding in Fourier methods can increase VRAM usage by a factor of 8. Measured Performance: On a 512^3 dataset, the pure GPU implementation using CUDA-OpenGL interop outperformed the hybrid (CPU-GPU) one by a factor of 117x for the entire pipeline and 29x for the rendering loop. On NVIDIA GeForce GT 640, the entire pipeline took 693.365 ms; on NVIDIA QUADRO K5000, it took 164.4 ms. Scaling: The method scales with GPU compute power. Trilinear interpolation has almost the same performance as nearest-neighbour for slice sizes ≤ 512^2, but incurs higher performance cost for larger volumes. Strengths: Eliminates CPU bottlenecks from draw calls and API overhead. Eliminates four serial copies and four redundant texture objects compared to high-level libraries like SFML. Allows greater control over buffer bit depth. Limitations: Requires manual management of OpenGL and CUDA contexts. Context switching can be complex. Using SFML for display results in frame latencies >20 ms for 1080p textures, limiting framerate to under 60 fps, whereas PBO/FBO approach reduces this significantly. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where CPU overhead is a bottleneck, and direct GPU-side computation and display are required. When Not to Use: Simple applications where CPU-GPU transfer overhead is negligible, or when using higher-level frameworks that abstract away these details and performance is not critical. The method originated from the need to overcome CPU bottlenecks in traditional raster engines, where the host issues draw calls faster than the device can complete work. Early implementations used libraries like SFML, which introduced significant copy overhead. The shift to CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability allowed for direct GPU-side rendering pipelines, as demonstrated in frameworks like VRCUDA and Fourier Volume Rendering. name: Bindless Textures in CUDA
head: Bindless Textures, BindlessTexture objects
body: Bindless Textures in CUDA is a method for managing and accessing texture data directly from CUDA kernels without the per-frame binding and mapping overhead of OpenGL-CUDA interoperability. It solves the performance bottlenecks and resource limits of traditional OpenGL-CUDA texture sharing, where textures must be bound, mapped to CUDA resources, and unmapped every frame. Unlike CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write, which focuses on surface buffers, this method addresses texture sampling by allowing a dynamic number of textures to be exposed simultaneously to the kernel at runtime. Inputs: Raw texture data and format specifications (channel type, internal format). Outputs: BindlessTexture objects stored in device-accessible memory, enabling simultaneous texture exposure to the kernel. Data Structures: 1. BindlessTexture Object: A C++ templated class wrapping the CUDA texture object descriptor, supporting formats like unsigned char, unsigned short, and internal formats like float1, float4, uchar4. 2. Texture Registry: A linked list tracking all loaded BindlessTexture objects and their mipmap arrays for cleanup on program closure. Steps: 1. Create mipmapped texture objects in VRAM using the CUDA API. 2. Launch a simple CUDA kernel asynchronously to compute mipmaps for each texture during loading. 3. Wrap the created texture objects in BindlessTexture instances using C++ templates to match the data format. 4. Append each BindlessTexture to a linked list to track objects and mipmap arrays for later deallocation. 5. Sample textures in device code using only the tex variable descriptor associated with the BindlessTexture object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class BindlessTexture: """C++ templated wrapper for a CUDA texture object descriptor.""" def init(self, textureobject, formattype, internalformat): self.textureobject = textureobject self.formattype = formattype self.internalformat = internalformat self.mipmaps = [] def sample(self, coords, lod=0): """Sample texture at coords using the tex descriptor.""" # Standard CUDA texture sampling uses the bound texture object descriptor. return sampletexturedescriptor(self.textureobject, coords, lod) def free(self): """Free mipmap arrays and the texture object.""" for mipmap in self.mipmaps: freedevicememory(mipmap) destroytextureobject(self.textureobject) textureregistry = [] def loadbindlesstexture(rawdata, width, height, formattype, internalformat): """Load texture into VRAM and register it.""" # 1. Create mipmapped texture object textureobject = createtextureobject(rawdata, width, height, formattype, internalformat) # 2. Asynchronously compute mipmaps launchmipmapkernel(textureobject) synchronizestreams() # 3. Wrap and register bindlesstex = BindlessTexture(textureobject, formattype, internalformat) textureregistry.append(bindlesstex) return bindlesstex def cleanupbindlesstextures(): """Free all tracked textures.""" for tex in textureregistry: tex.free() textureregistry.clear() def createtextureobject(data, w, h, fmt, intfmt): """ Allocates VRAM and creates a CUDA texture object descriptor.""" return {"data": data, "width": w, "height": h, "format": fmt, "internal": intfmt} def launchmipmapkernel(texobj): """ Launches a CUDA kernel to generate mipmap levels asynchronously.""" pass def synchronizestreams(): """ Waits for asynchronous kernel completion.""" pass def sampletexturedescriptor(texobj, coords, lod): """ Performs bilinear/trilinear sampling on the texture object descriptor.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def freedevicememory(ptr): """ Frees device memory allocation.""" pass def destroytextureobject(texobj): """ Destroys the CUDA texture object descriptor.""" pass Parameters: tex: The variable name used to read a texture from device code; only this descriptor value needs to be known by the kernel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: Traditional OpenGL-CUDA mapping requires binding every frame, mapping to a CUDA resource prior to kernel launch, and unbinding/unmapping after, which adds significant overhead. Resource Limits: The traditional method limits the number of textures that can be simultaneously loaded. Hardcoding: The traditional method requires all CUDA resources to be declared in global scope, meaning the number of textures used must be hardcoded. Cleanup: Textures and their mipmap arrays must be explicitly freed on program closure or when no longer needed to prevent memory leaks. Time and Memory Complexity: Loading: Not given in the sources. Sampling: Not given in the sources. Memory: VRAM usage scales with the total size of loaded textures and their mipmap arrays. Measured Performance: Eliminates the per-frame binding and mapping overhead associated with OpenGL-CUDA interoperability. Allows a dynamic number of textures to be specified at runtime. Allows all textures to be exposed to the kernel simultaneously. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High performance due to elimination of binding overhead; flexibility in the number of textures; no need to hardcode texture counts in global scope. Limitations: Requires careful memory management via a linked list for cleanup; relies on the CUDA API for texture creation rather than OpenGL. When to Use: Use when rendering scenes with a dynamic or large number of textures that need to be accessed from CUDA kernels. Use when performance is critical and the overhead of OpenGL-CUDA binding is unacceptable. When Not to Use: Use CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write if the primary goal is to write surface buffers directly to OpenGL for immediate display without complex texture sampling. Use traditional OpenGL-CUDA interoperability if the number of textures is small, fixed, and known at compile time, and if the simplicity of OpenGL texture management is preferred over the performance gains. Bindless Textures in CUDA were introduced as a more performant design to replace the drawbacks of using OpenGL to manage textures for CUDA kernels. The traditional method, similar to typical raster-based renderers, was found unsuitable for advanced raymarching renderers due to binding overhead, limited simultaneous texture counts, and the need to hardcode texture numbers in global scope. The bindless approach utilizes an object-oriented design with C++ templating to support various formats and internal formats, enabling dynamic runtime specification and simultaneous exposure of all textures to the kernel. name: CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write
head: Direct GL Texture Write from CUDA, Surface Write via CUDA Interop
body: A technique to allow CUDA kernels to write directly to OpenGL 3D textures using CUDA surface objects. It writes directly to an OpenGL texture from a CUDA kernel using CUDA graphics interop, avoiding intermediate device buffers. This method is distinct from CUDA-OpenGL Interop Texture Copy, which uses cudaMemcpy3D for bulk transfers rather than per-voxel kernel writes. Inputs: OpenGL texture ID, CUDA module containing the surface reference, voxel coordinates, and color/value data. Outputs: Updated OpenGL 3D texture contents. Data Structures: Host-side: GLuint glTex: OpenGL texture object. CUgraphicsResource cudaTex: Registered CUDA graphics resource. CUarray cudaArray: Mapped CUDA array representing the texture memory. CUsurfref cudaSurfRef: Surface reference object linked to the array. Device-side: surface voxelGrid: A device-scope surface object bound to the mapped array. Steps: 1. Create OpenGL Texture: Generate a texture using glGenTextures and bind it as GLTEXTURE3D. Set minification and magnification filters to GLNEAREST. Allocate storage using glTexImage3D with internal format GLR8, format GLRED, and type GLFLOAT. Note: Source describes creating an RGBA8 texture instead. 2. Register with CUDA: Call cuGraphicsGLRegisterImage passing the OpenGL texture ID, target GLTEXTURE3D, and flags CUGRAPHICSREGISTERFLAGSSURFACELDST. Source uses cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsSurfaceLoadStore or cudaGraphicsRegisterFlagsWriteDiscard depending on usage. 3. Map Resource: Call cuGraphicsMapResources (or cudaGraphicsMapResources) with the registered resource. Retrieve the mapped CUDA array using cuGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray (or cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray). Unmap immediately if not needed by host code using cuGraphicsUnmapResources. 4. Bind Surface: Obtain the surface reference from the CUDA module using cuModuleGetSurfRef. Set the mapped array to this reference using cuSurfRefSetArray. 5. Launch Kernel: Launch a CUDA kernel where the device surface voxelGrid is active. The kernel writes data directly to the texture coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocategltexture(): """Allocates a new OpenGL texture object ID.""" return 1 def bindgltexture3d(texid): """Binds the texture object as a 3D texture target.""" pass def setglfilter(texid, target, filtermode): """Sets the minification/magnification filter for the texture.""" pass def allocategltexture3d(texid, internalformat, width, height, depth, format, datatype): """Allocates storage for a 3D texture with specified dimensions and formats.""" pass def registergltexturewithcuda(texid, target, flags): """Registers an OpenGL texture with the CUDA graphics interop layer.""" return 0 # cudaGraphicsResource handle def mapcudaresource(resource): """Maps the registered CUDA resource for device access.""" pass def getmappedcudaarray(resource, level, miplevel): """Retrieves the CUDA array object mapped to the resource.""" return 0 # cudaArray handle def unmapcudaresource(resource): """Unmaps the CUDA resource, releasing host access.""" pass def getsurfacereffrommodule(module, name): """Retrieves a surface reference object from a compiled CUDA module.""" return 0 # CUsurfref handle def setsurfacearray(surfref, array, level): """Binds a CUDA array to a surface reference.""" pass glTex = allocategltexture() bindgltexture3d(glTex) setglfilter(glTex, "GLTEXTUREMINFILTER", "GLNEAREST") setglfilter(glTex, "GLTEXTUREMAGFILTER", "GLNEAREST") allocategltexture3d(glTex, "GLR8", size, size, size, 0, "GLRED", "GLFLOAT") cudaTex = registergltexturewithcuda(glTex, "GLTEXTURE3D", "CUGRAPHICSREGISTERFLAGSSURFACELDST") mapcudaresource(cudaTex) cudaArray = getmappedcudaarray(cudaTex, 0, 0) unmapcudaresource(cudaTex) cudaSurfRef = getsurfacereffrommodule(module, "voxelGrid") setsurfacearray(cudaSurfRef, cudaArray, 0) Formulas: Surface Write Operation: C{x,y,z} = \text{surf3Dwrite}(color, \text{voxelGrid}, x, y, z). Parameters: Texture Format: GLR8 / GLRED / GLFLOAT. Flags: CUGRAPHICSREGISTERFLAGSSURFACELDST. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The source code example uses GLFLOAT type with GLR8 internal format, which is contradictory in standard OpenGL (R8 implies 8-bit integer). Implementers should verify driver behavior or use consistent formats like GLR32F for float data. Resource State: The resource must be unmapped before the OpenGL context uses the texture for rendering, and unmapped before CUDA writes if mapped by another context, though the example unmaps immediately after getting the array. Copies a 3D volume of float data from device memory into a registered OpenGL 3D texture via CUDA interop, mapping the resource, performing a 3D memory copy, and unmapping. Steps: 1. Map resource: cudaGraphicsMapResources(1, &mresource). 2. Get mapped array: cudaGraphicsSubResourceGetMappedArray(&array, mresource, 0, 0). 3. Configure copy: srcPtr from makecudaPitchedPtr(sourcePointer, widthsizeof(float), width, width, height), dstArray from mapped array, extent from makeextent(width, height, depth), kind = cudaMemcpyDeviceToDevice. 4. Execute: cudaMemcpy3D(&copy). 5. Unmap: cudaGraphicsUnmapResources(1, &mresource). Pitfalls: Source pointer must not be null and resource must be registered; throws std::logicerror if either condition fails. Strengths: Avoids copying the final image to a temporary device buffer and then to OpenGL, reducing latency and memory bandwidth usage for direct rendering. Limitations: Requires CUDA and OpenGL interop support. Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. Used in real-time volume rendering engines and scientific visualization tools where high-performance voxelization or ray casting is performed on the GPU and the result is displayed via OpenGL.
