name: PBO to Texture Copy for Display
head: OpenGL Display via PBO and Texture, OpenGL PBO Texture Upload & Display, PBO to Texture Copy, fullscreen quad render
body: This method transfers the final rendered image from a CUDA-registered Pixel Buffer Object (PBO) into an OpenGL texture and displays it on screen. It solves the problem of presenting GPU-computed volume data without incurring the latency of copying data back to the CPU system memory. It differs from Bindless Textures in CUDA by using explicit buffer-object synchronization rather than direct device pointers, and from CUDA-OpenGL Interop Surface Write by writing to a buffer object rather than a surface object, requiring an explicit texture upload step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A CUDA-registered PBO (mempboout or pbo) containing the rendered image data (typically GLRGBA or GLBGRA, GLUNSIGNEDBYTE). Input: OpenGL context with double buffering enabled. Output: The display window showing the volume rendering. Data Structures: texscreen: A 2D OpenGL texture object. pbo: A GLPIXELUNPACKBUFFER object. cinvViewMatrix: A constant buffer in CUDA containing the inverse view matrix, derived from the OpenGL model-view matrix. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the PBO with size width height 4 bytes (assuming 4-channel unsigned byte). Register the PBO with CUDA using cudaGraphicsGLRegisterBuffer. Create a 2D texture texscreen with nearest-neighbor filtering. 2. Per-Frame Rendering Loop: 1. Update View Matrix: Extract the model-view matrix from OpenGL, compute its inverse, and upload it to the CUDA constant buffer cinvViewMatrix. 2. Render Volume: Launch the CUDA volume rendering kernel. The kernel writes the final pixel colors directly into the registered PBO. 3. Synchronize: Ensure CUDA completion before accessing the PBO for display. 4. Copy to Texture: Bind the PBO as GLPIXELUNPACKBUFFER. Bind the texture texscreen. Call glTexSubImage2D with data pointer set to NULL (or 0). This tells OpenGL to read the texture data from the currently bound PBO. Parameters: width, height, format GLRGBA (or GLBGRA depending on kernel output), type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. 5. Display: Unbind the PBO and texture. Draw a fullscreen quad. The quad vertices are typically (-1,-1), (1,-1), (1,1), (-1,1). Texture coordinates map the image aspect ratio. If the image resolution is resx, resy and the texture is 2048x2048, the texture coordinates are (0,0), (resx/2048.0, 0), (resx/2048.0, resy/2048.0), (0, resy/2048.0). Alternatively, draw a quad from (0,0) to (1,1) in screen space if the texture covers the full viewport. 6. Swap Buffers: Call glutSwapBuffers() or equivalent to present the frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def displayframe(glcontext, cudastream, pbo, tex, width, height): # 1. Update inverse view matrix in CUDA constant memory # Extract model-view matrix from OpenGL, invert, transpose, upload to cinvViewMatrix invviewmatrix = getopenglinverseviewmatrix() setcudaconstant('cinvViewMatrix', invviewmatrix) # 2. Launch CUDA volume rendering kernel # Kernel writes to the registered PBO launchvolumerenderkernel(pbo, width, height, cudastream) # 3. Synchronize CUDA to ensure PBO is written # Standard CUDA synchronization cudastreamsynchronize(cudastream) # 4. Copy PBO data to OpenGL Texture # Bind PBO as unpack buffer glBindBuffer(GLPIXELUNPACKBUFFER, pbo) # Bind texture glBindTexture(GLTEXTURE2D, tex) # Upload data from PBO to texture # Format is GLRGBA or GLBGRA, type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE glTexSubImage2D( GLTEXTURE2D, 0, 0, 0, width, height, GLRGBA, GLUNSIGNEDBYTE, None # NULL pointer indicates data is in PBO) # Unbind PBO to avoid conflicts glBindBuffer(GLPIXELUNPACKBUFFER, 0) # 5. Render Fullscreen Quad # Set up projection and modelview for orthographic screen space glMatrixMode(GLPROJECTION) glLoadIdentity() glOrtho(0, width, 0, height, -1, 1) glMatrixMode(GLMODELVIEW) glLoadIdentity() # Calculate texture coordinates for aspect ratio correction tx = float(width) / 2048.0 ty = float(height) / 2048.0 # Draw quad with vertices and texture coordinates glBegin(GLQUADS) glTexCoord2f(0.0, 0.0); glVertex2f(-1.0, -1.0) glTexCoord2f(tx, 0.0); glVertex2f(1.0, -1.0) glTexCoord2f(tx, ty); glVertex2f(1.0, 1.0) glTexCoord2f(0.0, ty); glVertex2f(-1.0, 1.0) glEnd() # Swap buffers glutSwapBuffers() Parameters: width, height: Image resolution. 2048: Texture size used in for aspect ratio calculation. GLRGBA / GLBGRA: Color format. uses GLBGRA, uses GLRGBA. GLUNSIGNEDBYTE: Data type. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Format Mismatch: Ensure the format used in glTexSubImage2D matches the data layout written by the CUDA kernel. uses GLBGRA while uses GLRGBA. Mismatch causes color channel swapping or corruption. Aspect Ratio: If the texture is square (e.g., 2048x2048) but the image is not, texture coordinates must be scaled to prevent distortion. Synchronization: Failing to synchronize CUDA before accessing the PBO results in displaying stale or corrupted data. Time Complexity: O(1) for the copy and display steps relative to scene complexity, but O(WH) for the data transfer size. The dominant cost is the volume rendering kernel itself. Memory Complexity: O(WH) for the PBO and texture storage. Performance: Avoids CPU-GPU round-trip latency for the final image. The glTexSubImage2D with a PBO is efficient as it keeps data on the GPU. Strengths: Simple integration with existing OpenGL rendering pipelines; avoids CPU overhead. Limitations: Requires OpenGL 2.0+ and GLARBpixelbufferobject extension. Synchronization overhead between CUDA and OpenGL can limit frame rate if not managed carefully. This technique is part of the CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability suite, enabling GPU-accelerated volume rendering to be displayed in standard OpenGL windows. It was demonstrated in NVIDIA's CUDA SDK Volume Rendering sample and in open-source implementations like Sparse-Voxel-Octree-Raycasting. sp4cerat/Sparse-Voxel-Octree-Raycasting, https://github.com/sp4cerat/Sparse-Voxel-Octree-Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) RubbishKing0624/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/RubbishKing0624/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Atomic Fragment List Insertion
head: Atomic Counter Voxelization, Linked List Voxel Output, LinkedListGather, PPLL Gather, ST-7
body: Atomic Fragment List Insertion is a GPU-side algorithm for building a per-pixel linked list of fragments using atomic operations to handle concurrent writes from multiple fragments without locks. It solves the problem of dynamically collecting variable numbers of geometry or volume fragments into a single pixel's output buffer in a parallel environment. It differs from Tiled Parallel Compositing by avoiding tile-based sorting and compositing in favor of a global atomic counter and linked list structure, and from A-buffer linked-list creation and ray processing by relying on a global atomic counter for list construction rather than geometry shader-based quad generation and explicit ray-primitive intersection checks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Fragment color (vec4), fragment depth/distance (float), pixel coordinates (from glFragCoord). Output: Updated global atomic counter, updated per-pixel head pointers, updated fragment buffer. Data Structures: 1. uFragCounter: A single global atomic counter (uint) tracking the next available linear index in the fragment buffer. 2. uStartOffsetTex: A 2D texture storing the head pointer for each pixel. Layout: uvec4 where r holds the head index (uint), g, b, a are unused. Initialized to 0xFFFFFFFF (sentinel for empty list). 3. uFragmentBufferTex: A 2D texture acting as the fragment node storage. Width FRAGBUFFERW (typically 2048). Node Layout (uvec4): r: Packed color (rgba 10/10/10/10 bit format). g: Depth (float bits converted to uint). b: Next pointer (uint, index of next node in list). a: Unused (0). Parameters: FRAGBUFFERW: Width of the fragment buffer image in texels. Typical value: 2048. uLinkedListSize: Total capacity of the fragment buffer (derived from texture dimensions). Steps: 1. Early Exit: If fragment depth a < 1e-4 or color alpha color.a < 1e-4, return immediately. 2. Coordinate Extraction: Calculate pixel coordinates x = int(glFragCoord.x) and y = int(glFragCoord.y). 3. Atomic Index Allocation: Atomically increment uFragCounter to get a unique linear index: insertIndex = atomicCounterIncrement(uFragCounter). 4. Buffer Overflow Check: If insertIndex >= uLinkedListSize, silently drop the fragment (buffer full). 5. Head Pointer Swap: Atomically exchange the head pointer for pixel (x, y) in uStartOffsetTex with insertIndex. The return value oldHead is the previous head, which becomes the new node's next pointer: oldHead = imageAtomicExchange(uStartOffsetTex, ivec2(x, y), insertIndex). 6. Address Calculation: Calculate the 2D texture coordinates for the fragment node: fragAddr = ivec2(int(insertIndex) % FRAGBUFFERW, int(insertIndex) / FRAGBUFFERW). 7. Node Construction: Build the fragment node: frag.r = packColor(color) (packed rgba 10/10/10/10), frag.g = floatBitsToUint(depth), frag.b = oldHead, frag.a = 0. 8. Store Node: Write frag to uFragmentBufferTex at fragAddr. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def insertfragment(color: list, depth: float): # Early exit for transparent/near-zero depth fragments if color[3] < 1e-4 or depth < 1e-4: return # Get pixel coordinates x = int(glFragCoord.x) y = int(glFragCoord.y) # Allocate unique index insertindex = atomicCounterIncrement(uFragCounter) # Check buffer capacity if insertindex >= uLinkedListSize: return # Atomically swap head pointer; oldhead is the previous head oldhead = imageAtomicExchange(uStartOffsetTex, (x, y), insertindex) # Calculate buffer address fragx = insertindex % FRAGBUFFERW fragy = insertindex // FRAGBUFFERW fragaddr = (fragx, fragy) # Construct node # Pack color into 10/10/10/10 format (implementation dependent, assumed available) packedcolor = packrgba10101010(color) node = ( packedcolor, int(depth), # floatBitsToUint(depth) oldhead, 0) # Store node imageStore(uFragmentBufferTex, fragaddr, node) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Race Conditions: Using imageAtomicExchange ensures that two concurrent inserts do not read the same old head and overwrite each other, which would orphan the first fragment. Buffer Overflow: If the fragment buffer is full, fragments are silently dropped. Sentinel Value: The head pointer texture must be initialized to 0xFFFFFFFF (or -1u) to indicate an empty list. The PPLL Resolve Pass is a fragment shader pass that resolves a linked list of fragments per pixel into a final color by sorting and front-to-back blending. It takes the raw fragment data collected by the Atomic Fragment List Insertion method and produces the final image, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like A-buffer linked-list creation and ray processing by using per-pixel atomic exchange on a start offset texture for list construction rather than a global counter. This method constructs a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) on the GPU to efficiently identify which segment primitives overlap a given ray, avoiding the evaluation of empty space in expensive field computations. It differs from brute-force ray marching by using a geometry shader to generate quads covering primitive supports and a fragment shader to compute ray-support intersections, storing entry/exit points in a linked list. Unlike [Bru19], which requires explicit cutoff of primitive influences, this approach leverages compact support kernels (specifically clipped sphere-cones for Cauchy kernels) to naturally limit the interaction domain. A fullscreen quad render pass that initializes the per-pixel linked list start offset texture. It writes the sentinel value 0xFFFFFFFF (-1u) to indicate an empty list. For each pixel (x, y), if x < uViewportW and y < uViewportH, it writes uvec4(0xFFFFFFFF, 0, 0, 0) to uStartOffsetTex. A mechanism to manage a list of voxel fragments appended by thousands of concurrent threads, using an atomic counter to track the index of the next available entry and the count of fragments. The atomic counter is a 32-bit integer value stored in a buffer object. Atomic counters are preferred over generic atomicInc or atomicAdd because they are optimized for high performance when all threads operate on the same static memory region, whereas generic operations allow dynamic indexing. Atomic counters were introduced with OpenGL 4.2. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for insertion. The resolve pass complexity is Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(F) where F is the total number of fragments in the buffer. Requires storage for uStartOffsetTex (W x H) and uFragmentBufferTex (F nodes). Performance: Performance degrades if the buffer is frequently full, leading to dropped fragments. Atomic contention behavior is Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, no need for complex sorting hardware or shared memory management during insertion. Limitations: Buffer size must be pre-allocated and may be insufficient for complex scenes. Dropped fragments are lost. When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering where fragment counts are predictable and moderate. This method is part of the Parallel Per-Pixel Linked List (PPLL) family. It is used in the HexVolumeRenderer project for efficient fragment collection in volume rendering and ray casting contexts. name: PPLL Resolve Pass
head: Parallel Prefix List List Resolve
body: The PPLL Resolve Pass is a fragment shader pass that resolves a linked list of fragments per pixel into a final color by sorting and front-to-back blending. It takes the raw fragment data collected by the Atomic Fragment List Insertion method and produces the final image, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like A-buffer linked-list creation and ray processing by using per-pixel atomic exchange on a start offset texture for list construction rather than a global counter. Inputs: uStartOffsetTex: A texture storing the head pointer (fragment index) for each pixel, initialized to 0xFFFFFFFFu (end of list) by the Clear Pass. uFragmentBufferTex: A texture storing the fragment nodes, with RGBA32UI layout and dimensions FRAGBUFFERW × FRAGBUFFERH. uViewportW, uViewportH: Viewport dimensions. FRAGBUFFERW: Width of the fragment buffer texture (constant, typically 2048). MAXNUMFRAGS: Maximum number of fragments to process per pixel (constant, typically 32). Outputs: glFragColor: The final color for the current pixel. Per-pixel local storage: colorList[MAXNUMFRAGS]: Array of uint storing packed fragment colors. depthList[MAXNUMFRAGS]: Array of float storing fragment depths. Total size: 32 \times 12 bytes = 384 bytes. 1. Boundary Check: Get pixel coordinates x, y. If x >= uViewportW or y >= uViewportH, discard. 2. Load Head: Load the starting offset (head pointer) from uStartOffsetTex at (x, y) into fragOffset. 3. Initialize: Set numFrags = 0. 4. Traverse List: Loop i from 0 to MAXNUMFRAGS - 1: If fragOffset == 0xFFFFFFFFu, break (end of list). Calculate address ivec2(int(fragOffset) % FRAGBUFFERW, int(fragOffset) / FRAGBUFFERW). Load frag from uFragmentBufferTex at the calculated address. Update fragOffset = frag.b (the next pointer). Store frag.r in colorList[i]. Store uintBitsToFloat(frag.g) in depthList[i]. Increment numFrags. 5. Empty Check: If numFrags == 0, discard. 6. Sort: Insertion sort colorList and depthList by depthList ascending. Loop i from 1 to numFrags - 1. Store fragColor = colorList[i], fragDepth = depthList[i]. Loop j from i down to 1: If depthList[j-1] > fragDepth, shift colorList[j-1] to colorList[j] and depthList[j-1] to depthList[j]. Decrement j. Place fragColor and fragDepth at j. 7. Blend: Initialize outColor = vec4(0.0). Loop i from 0 to MAXNUMFRAGS - 1: If i >= numFrags, break. Unpack src = unpackColor(colorList[i]). Update outColor.rgb = outColor.rgb + (1.0 - outColor.a) src.a src.rgb. Update outColor.a = outColor.a + (1.0 - outColor.a) src.a. If outColor.a > 0.995, break (early-out optimization). 8. Convert: If outColor.a > 1e-4, divide outColor.rgb by outColor.a (premultiplied to straight alpha conversion). 9. Output: Output outColor to glFragColor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct def uintbitstofloat(val): return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', val & 0xFFFFFFFF))[0] def unpackcolor(packed): # Assumes 10:10:10:2 packing as per source comment r = ((packed >> 20) & 0x3FF) / 1023.0 g = ((packed >> 10) & 0x3FF) / 1023.0 b = (packed & 0x3FF) / 1023.0 a = ((packed >> 30) & 0x3) / 3.0 return [r, g, b, a] def resolvepass(x, y): if x >= uViewportW or y >= uViewportH: return None fragoffset = texelfetch(uStartOffsetTex, (x, y))[0] numfrags = 0 colorlist = [0] MAXNUMFRAGS depthlist = [0.0] MAXNUMFRAGS i = 0 while i < MAXNUMFRAGS and fragoffset != 0xFFFFFFFF: bufx = fragoffset % FRAGBUFFERW bufy = fragoffset // FRAGBUFFERW frag = texelfetch(uFragmentBufferTex, (bufx, bufy)) fragoffset = frag[1] colorlist[i] = frag[0] depthlist[i] = uintbitstofloat(frag[2]) i += 1 numfrags += 1 if numfrags == 0: return None for i in range(1, numfrags): fragcolor = colorlist[i] fragdepth = depthlist[i] j = i while j > 0 and depthlist[j-1] > fragdepth: colorlist[j] = colorlist[j-1] depthlist[j] = depthlist[j-1] j -= 1 colorlist[j] = fragcolor depthlist[j] = fragdepth outcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numfrags): src = unpackcolor(colorlist[i]) outcolor[0] += (1.0 - outcolor[3]) src[3] src[0] outcolor[1] += (1.0 - outcolor[3]) src[3] src[1] outcolor[2] += (1.0 - outcolor[3]) src[3] src[2] outcolor[3] += (1.0 - outcolor[3]) src[3] if outcolor[3] > 0.995: break if outcolor[3] > 1e-4: outcolor[0] /= outcolor[3] outcolor[1] /= outcolor[3] outcolor[2] /= outcolor[3] return outcolor MAXNUMFRAGS: Maximum number of fragments to process per pixel. Typical value: 32. FRAGBUFFERW: Width of the fragment buffer texture. Typical value: 2048. Early-out optimization: The blend loop breaks if outColor.a > 0.995 to save computation when the pixel is effectively opaque. Empty list handling: If no fragments are collected (numFrags == 0), the fragment is discarded. Buffer Full: If the fragment buffer is full, fragments are silently dropped during the gather phase, which may result in missing fragments in the resolve pass. Precision: Depth is stored as uintBitsToFloat(frag.g), implying a specific bit-packing scheme for depth in the fragment node. Time Complexity: O(N^2) per pixel due to insertion sort, where N = \text{MAX\NUM\FRAGS}. Traversal is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) per pixel for local storage, where N = \text{MAX\NUM\FRAGS}. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient for low fragment counts per pixel. Limitations: Insertion sort becomes inefficient for high fragment counts. Buffer overflow can occur if the gather phase exceeds capacity. When to use: Suitable for scenes with moderate fragment density per pixel. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes with very high fragment density per pixel where sorting overhead becomes significant. The PPLL Resolve Pass is part of the Parallel Prefix List List (PPLL) method for volume rendering. It was described in the context of a WebGL2-based volume renderer. The method relies on atomic operations for fragment list construction and a subsequent resolve pass for final color computation. name: A-buffer linked-list creation and ray processing
head: A-buffer linked-list creation, Ray processing with A-buffer linked-list
body: This method constructs a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) on the GPU to efficiently identify which segment primitives overlap a given ray, avoiding the evaluation of empty space in expensive field computations. It differs from brute-force ray marching by using a geometry shader to generate quads covering primitive supports and a fragment shader to compute ray-support intersections, storing entry/exit points in a linked list. Unlike [Bru19], which requires explicit cutoff of primitive influences, this approach leverages compact support kernels (specifically clipped sphere-cones for Cauchy kernels) to naturally limit the interaction domain. Inputs: Skeleton geometry defined as a set of segment primitives. Kernel parameters (e.g., scale \sigma, clipping radius). View ray (i, j) for each pixel. Optional occluding depth buffer for output sensitivity. Outputs: Isosurface intersection point or null if no intersection is found within bounds. Data Structures: 1. A-Buffer Linked List: Stores fragments per pixel. Each fragment contains: Entry depth (z{in}) along the ray. Exit depth (z{out}) along the ray. Primitive ID. The list is sorted by entry depth z{in}. 2. Processing Heaps (per ray): primitives: A min-heap (or sorted list) of active primitives, keyed by their exit depth (z{out}). Stores tuples (z{out}, \text{segId}). argmins: A min-heap storing the minimum field value (or derivative metric) contributed by each active primitive at the current ray position. Stores tuples (\text{argmin\val}, \text{segId}). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize primitives and argmins as empty heaps. Unlike [Bru19], which requires explicit cutoff of primitive influences, this approach leverages compact support kernels (specifically clipped sphere-cones for Cauchy kernels) to naturally limit the interaction domain. The A-Buffer Visibility Pass is a GPU fragment-stage algorithm that generates an approximate visibility function \tilde{v}(xe, x) for each view ray by storing depth and visibility control points in an A-Buffer. It solves the problem of efficiently representing volumetric occlusion along semi-transparent view rays to enable optimized illumination calculations, such as determining entry points for light rays or approximating multiple scattering. Unlike sibling methods that may focus on primitive intersection or general buffer construction, this method specifically targets the generation of a sparse, error-thresholded visibility function using a fixed maximum number of layers, similar in concept to deep shadow maps but applied to view-space volumetric visibility. Limitations: Numerical instability at field boundaries requires sphere tracing steps; blending artifacts may require under-relaxation; larger kernel footprints (e.g., Cauchy) increase computational time and A-buffer overflow risk. name: GPU A-Buffer Construction for Ray-Primitive Intersection
head: Dynamic Data Structure for Ray Processing, Dynamic Linked List for Primitive Supports, Sphere-Cone A-Buffer
body: This method constructs a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) on the GPU to efficiently identify which segment primitives overlap a given ray, avoiding the evaluation of empty space in expensive field computations. It differs from brute-force ray marching by using a geometry shader to generate quads covering primitive supports and a fragment shader to compute ray-support intersections, storing entry/exit points in a linked list. Unlike [Bru19], which requires explicit cutoff of primitive influences, this approach leverages compact support kernels (specifically clipped sphere-cones for Cauchy kernels) to naturally limit the interaction domain. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Skeleton segment primitives, each defined by a center line segment and a radius function (potentially varying). Kernel parameters: For Cauchy kernels, a clipping scaling factor \sigma{\text{clipping}} is computed to guarantee a maximal error \varepsilon{\text{clipping}}. Outputs: A linked list per ray containing sorted entry and exit points of the ray within each primitive's support, along with the associated primitive ID. Data Structures: A-Buffer Linked List: Stores tuples of (t{\text{entry}}, t{\text{exit}}, \text{primitive\id}) sorted by t{\text{entry}}. Quad: Generated per skeleton segment to cover the projected primitive support. The quad is segment-aligned. Steps: 1. Geometry Shader Execution: For each skeleton segment, generate a quad that covers the projected support of the primitive. The quad is computed using the method from [SWBG06], adapted for segment-aligned quads to minimize fragment generation, particularly for primitives with small radii relative to segment length. 2. Fragment Shader Execution: For each fragment generated by the quad, compute the intersection of the ray with the primitive's support (a sphere-cone). 3. Intersection Calculation: Determine the entry (t{\text{entry}}) and exit (t{\text{exit}}) points of the ray within the support. 4. Atomic Insertion: Insert the tuple (t{\text{entry}}, t{\text{exit}}, \text{primitive\id}) into the A-buffer linked list for the current ray using atomic operations. 5. Sorting: Sort the fragments in the linked list on the fly according to the depth of the entry point t{\text{entry}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildabuffer(rayorigin, raydirection, segments): # Initialize per-ray linked list for (tentry, texit, primitiveid) abuffer = [] for seg in segments: # 1. Geometry shader: generate segment-aligned quad covering projected support # Adapted from [SWBG06] to minimize fragment generation quad = projectsupporttoquad(seg.center, seg.radiusfunction) # 2. Fragment shader: compute ray-support intersection # Support is a sphere-cone; clipped by sigmaclipping for Cauchy kernels tentry, texit = solveraysphereconequadratic( rayorigin, raydirection, quad, seg.sigmaclipping) if tentry is not None: # 3. Insert entry/exit and primitive ID into A-buffer linked list # Hardware uses atomic operations for concurrent writes abuffer.append((tentry, texit, seg.id)) # 4. Sort on the fly by tentry depth # Final sort if hardware does not guarantee order abuffer.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return abuffer def projectsupporttoquad(center, radiusfunction): # Project the 3D segment support onto the 2D screen space return {"center": center, "radiusfunc": radiusfunction} def solveraysphereconequadratic(rayo, rayd, quad, sigmaclipping): # Solve quadratic equation for ray intersection with sphere-cone support # sigmaclipping scales the support to guarantee max error epsilonclipping # Returns (tentry, texit) or None return (0.0, 1.0) # Standard quadratic solution Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in intersection calculations may affect the accuracy of t{\text{entry}} and t{\text{exit}}, potentially leading to gaps or overlaps in the linked list. Boundary Conditions: Ensure that the quad generation covers the entire support, especially for primitives with varying radii. Degenerate Input: Handle cases where the ray is parallel to the segment or the support is degenerate (e.g., zero radius). Time Complexity: The construction time is correlated with the number of primitives influencing a given point along the ray. The use of a compact support kernel reduces the number of primitives to consider, improving performance. Memory Complexity: The A-buffer stores entry/exit points and primitive IDs for each ray. The memory usage depends on the number of overlapping primitives per ray. Strengths: Efficiently avoids processing empty areas and limits compulsory field evaluations. The use of compact support kernels simplifies the A-buffer construction by avoiding explicit cutoff of primitive influences. Limitations: The performance is highly correlated with the number of primitives influencing a given point. The method may require significant memory for rays with many overlapping primitives. When to Use: Suitable for large skeletons with compact kernels where field evaluations are expensive. The method extends the approach proposed by [Bru19], which relies on a dynamic data structure efficiently rebuilt at each frame using the GPU rendering pipeline. The original approach used a GPU-based quadric visualization algorithm [SWBG06] to compute a linked list of intersection points with supports of each primitive. This extension adapts the method for segment primitives with varying radius, specifically handling sphere-cone supports. The use of compact support kernels, such as the Cauchy kernel, allows for the clipping of primitive supports by a sphere-cone, ensuring a maximal error \varepsilon{\text{clipping}}. name: A-Buffer Visibility Pass
head: Approximate Visibility Function Generation, Approximate Visibility Pass, Deep Shadow Map Generation, GPU Visibility Pass, Visibility Pass (A-Buffer), Visibility Pass Implementation, Visibility buffer generation
body: The A-Buffer Visibility Pass is a GPU fragment-stage algorithm that generates an approximate visibility function \tilde{v}(xe, x) for each view ray by storing depth and visibility control points in an A-Buffer. It solves the problem of efficiently representing volumetric occlusion along semi-transparent view rays to enable optimized illumination calculations, such as determining entry points for light rays or approximating multiple scattering. Unlike sibling methods that focus on primitive intersection or general buffer construction, this method specifically targets the generation of a sparse, error-thresholded visibility function using a fixed maximum number of layers, similar in concept to deep shadow maps but applied to view-space volumetric visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data (voxels with color/opacity), camera ray definition (origin, direction, length), A-Buffer storage structure, error threshold for accumulated opacity difference, maximum layer count. Output: An A-Buffer containing control points (depth d, visibility v) for each pixel, and textures storing the first and last hit points of the volume traversal. Data Structures: A-Buffer: A 2D texture array. Each texture in the array corresponds to a specific layer index (up to a maximum of 32). Each texture has two channels: 1. Depth to camera (d) in volume space. 2. Visibility (v), defined as 1 - \text{accumulated opacity}. Hit Point Textures: Two separate textures storing the first and last hit points (coordinates) for each ray. Parameters: Maximum Layers: 32. Sampling Frequency: One sample per voxel during the unshaded raycasting pass. Storage Threshold: An error threshold for the difference in accumulated opacity; a new control point is added when this threshold is exceeded. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Define a ray from front to back (from the camera) for each pixel. 2. Ray Marching: Iterate through all samples s along the ray at a frequency of one sample per voxel. 3. Voxel Classification: Read and classify the voxel at sample s to obtain color and opacity c. 4. Compositing: If the opacity in c is greater than 0, perform front-to-back compositing along the ray into the accumulated result r. 5. Threshold Check: If the difference in accumulated opacity exceeds the a-buffer storage threshold: a. Calculate the distance to the camera d in volume space. b. Calculate the visibility v = 1 - r.a, where r.a is the accumulated opacity. c. Buffer Management: If the A-Buffer is full (reached maximum layers): i. Perform an iterative merging process to decimate existing control points. Remove the control point that introduces the smallest difference to make room for the new point. d. Store v and d as the next entry in the A-Buffer. e. Write the visibility value lv to the write cache. 6. Termination Check: Determine the next position. If the end of the ray is reached or the accumulated opacity is considered opaque, end the loop. 7. Hit Point Storage: After the loop, write the first and last hit points into two separate textures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def visibilitypass(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, raylength, threshold, maxlayers, width, height): # A-Buffer: 2D texture array [width, height, maxlayers] # Channel 0: depth d, Channel 1: visibility v abuffer = [[[[0.0, 0.0] for in range(maxlayers)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] firsthittexture = [[None for in range(height)] for in range(width)] lasthittexture = [[None for in range(height)] for in range(width)] writecache = [] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): currentlayer = 0 accopacity = 0.0 prevaccopacity = 0.0 firsthit = None lasthit = None numsamples = int(raylength / voxelsize) for i in range(numsamples): t = i voxelsize samplepos = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t) # Read/classify voxel at s to color/opacity c standard volume access copacity = 0.0 # Standard volume sampling would query the voxel grid here if copacity > 0.0: # Perform compositing front-to-back along ray into r accopacity = 1.0 - (1.0 - accopacity) (1.0 - copacity) # Check difference in accumulated opacity against threshold opacitydiff = accopacity - prevaccopacity if opacitydiff > threshold: # Calculate distance to camera d (volume space) d = t # Calculate visibility v = 1 - r.a v = 1.0 - accopacity # If a-buffer is full, merge smallest threshold distance if currentlayer < maxlayers: currentlayer += 1 # The first control point of the visibility function is not stored if currentlayer > 1: abuffer[x][y][currentlayer - 2][0] = d abuffer[x][y][currentlayer - 2][1] = v else: # Iterative merging: decimate existing control points by removing the one introducing the smallest difference to make room for the new point pass # Write lv to write cache writecache.append(v) # Track hit points if firsthit is None: firsthit = samplepos lasthit = samplepos prevaccopacity = accopacity # Termination check: end of ray or accumulated opacity considered opaque if accopacity >= 1.0: break firsthittexture[x][y] = firsthit lasthittexture[x][y] = lasthit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Buffer Fullness: If the visibility map is full when a new control point is needed, an iterative merging process is used. This increases computation time if peak finding is used for higher accuracy. First Control Point: The first control point of the visibility function is not stored because the first hit point results in the first visibility change. Precision: Using peak finding similar to [48] increases accuracy but also increases computation time. Time Complexity: The base pass is O(N) per ray where N is the number of voxels sampled (one sample per voxel). The merging process adds overhead when the buffer is full, potentially increasing complexity depending on the number of merges required. Peak finding can further increase computation time. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times L) where W, H are image dimensions and L is the maximum number of layers (32). Each layer stores 2 channels (depth, visibility). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows representation of transparency effects from high depth complexity with a low number of control points. Enables optimized entry points for light rays by projecting first/last hit points into light space. Limitations: Approximate nature may lose detail if the number of layers is too low or threshold is too high. Merging process can be computationally expensive. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The A-Buffer Visibility Pass is based on the work of Sundén et al. in "Multimodal Volume Illumination" (2015). It builds on the concept of approximate visibility functions using a low number of control points, as shown by Salvi et al. [39, cited in S1, unofficial]. The method is similar to deep shadow maps [52, cited in S1, unofficial] but applies the A-Buffer concept to view-space volumetric visibility rather than shadow occlusion. It is used in multimodal volume rendering to account for multiple scattering effects and to optimize illumination computations by providing entry points for light rays. name: Hardware and Platform Specific
head: GPU (GLSL/HLSL shader), GPU Shader Rendering
body: This family encompasses volume rendering techniques that offload the computational workload to parallel hardware accelerators, primarily GPUs, using shading languages (GLSL/HLSL) or compute APIs (CUDA/OpenCL). It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based volume rendering by leveraging massive parallelism to process pixels or voxels simultaneously. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Tiled Parallel Compositing by focusing on the low-level mapping of rendering tasks to hardware execution units (shaders, cores, or warps) rather than high-level algorithmic partitioning strategies, and differs from Multi-core BONO Tree Traversal and Ray Casting with Dynamic Tile Grouping by targeting GPU architectures rather than multi-core CPUs. The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores). Common principles include: 1. Thread Mapping: Assigning one or more threads to process specific data elements (e.g., one thread per pixel or one thread per voxel sample). 2. Memory Hierarchy Utilization: Leveraging global memory for large datasets, shared/local memory for intermediate results (reductions), and registers for per-thread state. 3. Synchronization: Managing concurrency conflicts using atomic operations, barriers, or spatial partitioning (tiles) to ensure data consistency without excessive serialization. 4. Data Parallelism: Performing identical operations on different data elements simultaneously, often requiring coalesced memory access patterns to maximize bandwidth. This method is a GPU-based ray-casting algorithm designed for the volume rendering of unstructured grid data, specifically guaranteeing accurate rendering results for non-convex meshes. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping irregular unstructured grid geometry to GPU hardware while maintaining topological accuracy, which is often lost in simpler projection methods. It sets itself apart from siblings like CUDA Volume Ray Casting by explicitly handling non-convexity through per-pixel intersection lists, and differs from VOGUE Architecture by relying on a ray-casting approach rather than a voxelization-based one. It builds on Hardware and Platform Specific principles by optimizing work distribution for modern GPU architectures. CUDA Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering method that parallelizes the ray casting algorithm on the NVIDIA GPU using the CUDA programming model, avoiding intermediate geometric entities to directly generate 2D images from 3D datasets. It assigns one thread per pixel to cast rays through a 3D volume texture, sampling scalar values, mapping them to color and opacity via a transfer function, and compositing the result using front-to-back alpha blending with early termination. It sets itself apart from standard OpenGL shader-based approaches by providing explicit control over memory hierarchy (textures, surfaces, and global memory) and kernel launch parameters, often yielding performance improvements over generic GPU-based implementations. VOGUE is a modular, add-on hardware accelerator designed for interactive volume ray-casting on single-user workstations. It solves the problem of limited memory bandwidth and rendering speed in high-resolution volume visualization by mapping an efficient image-order ray-casting algorithm directly onto a fully pipelined architecture. Unlike VIRIM, which replicates volume memory across parallel units, VOGUE partitions the dataset and distributes subvolumes among multiple interconnected units, offering a trade-off between machine size and performance. WebGL Volume Rendering performs direct volume rendering (DVR) using ray casting executed within the fragment shader of a WebGL context. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields in web browsers without requiring native plugins or server-side rendering. It is distinguished from CPU-based WebGL approaches by performing the heavy ray-casting computation on the GPU, and from desktop GPU methods (like CUDA) by its constraint to the WebGL API and browser security model. This article describes two distinct implementations sharing the name "Efficient Ray Casting Pipeline," which differ fundamentally in their rendering targets and hardware acceleration models. The first is a CPU-based 2D raycasting engine for pseudo-3D first-person views, optimized for minimal per-pixel arithmetic and direct framebuffer manipulation. The second is a multi-pass Direct3D 11 pipeline for 3D volume raycasting, utilizing geometry shaders for active brick detection and ray generation. Both methods prioritize predictable, low-latency operations over complex mathematical approximations to achieve real-time performance on their respective platforms. GPU Raycasting is a volume rendering technique that generates 2D images from 3D data fields by casting rays through the volume, where the calculation of resampling and image synthesis is processed by the GPU fragment shader for parallel calculation. It approximates the volume rendering integral by sampling at a finite number of positions along each ray. Unlike parent methods that may rely on complex hierarchical structures or visibility ordering, this approach maps the ray traversal directly to the GPU's parallel execution units, leveraging the graphics pipeline's texture sampling and blending capabilities. It differs from its sibling CUDA Volume Ray Casting by typically utilizing the fixed-function or programmable fragment shader pipeline of standard graphics APIs (like OpenGL) rather than general-purpose compute shaders, and from WebGL Volume Rendering by often assuming higher-end consumer or professional graphics hardware capabilities. GPU-Driven Architecture is a rendering paradigm where the residency octree and the mixed-resolution multi-volume renderer are fully implemented on the GPU, while the CPU handles only high-level orchestration. It solves the bottleneck of traditional raster engines where the host CPU controls data assembly via draw calls, eliminating data transfer and API call overhead between the host and device. It builds on Hardware and Platform Specific by fully implementing the residency octree and renderer on the GPU, while the CPU handles only high-level orchestration such as loading data and switching contexts. A ray-casting method that relies on auxiliary data structures and reads the volume from texture, which cannot benefit from VBOs and continuous streaming. While some descriptions claim it avoids sorting volume cells, HAVS is noted for performing accurate visibility sorting. Pinned Memory Data Transfer utilizes page-locked (pinned) host memory to enable direct, high-throughput Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfers between the CPU and GPU, bypassing the system's physical page table mechanisms. Unlike standard pageable host memory, which requires the GPU driver to stage data through a temporary pinned buffer, pinned memory allows the PCIe bus to access host memory addresses directly. This method is distinct from CUDA Unified Memory (introduced in CUDA 7.x), which uses a demand-paged, transparent memory management system, whereas pinned memory requires explicit allocation and management. OpenCL Staging Buffer Commit Flow manages data synchronization between CPU and GPU using a staging buffer in system RAM and parallel copy mechanisms. It addresses the bottleneck of CPU-GPU data transfer by hiding the copy time behind GPU compute work, requiring careful synchronization via two OpenCL command queues and events. Parameters include PCIe 3.0 bandwidth (~16 GB/s), internal GPU memory bandwidth (~320 GB/s), OpenCL 1.2 compatibility, and a maximum of 8192 bricks synchronized per frame. OpenCL Acceleration attempts to speed up parallel computations using OpenCL FFT and custom implementations on hardware like the Nvidia Quadro FX 1800. It is chosen when specific long parallel computations can balance the data-to-device transfer overhead, though speed increases are limited to cases where the graphics card is sufficiently utilized. The term "GPU (GLSL/HLSL shader)" refers to rendering implementations using these shading languages, supporting hardware from NVIDIA, AMD, and mobile processors, with shader support for OpenGL/ES 3.0+ and Shader Model 3. The approach has been tested on systems ranging from single-core CPUs to 32-core Opterons, with GPU versions enabling performance gains on desktop and mobile GPUs. name: GPU-based Ray-casting for Unstructured Grids
head: GPU Ray-Casting for Unstructured Grids, Ours, Per-pixel intersection list method
body: This method is a GPU-based ray-casting algorithm for volume rendering unstructured grid data that guarantees accurate results for non-convex meshes by employing per-pixel intersection lists. It solves the difficulty of mapping irregular unstructured grid data efficiently to GPU hardware by leveraging coherent sample placement and flat array storage, avoiding the cell-ordering bottlenecks of direct ray-casting. It sets itself apart from siblings like CUDA Volume Ray Casting by explicitly handling non-convexity through per-pixel intersection lists, and differs from VOGUE Architecture by relying on a ray-casting approach rather than a voxelization-based one. It builds on Hardware and Platform Specific principles by optimizing work distribution for modern GPU architectures. Inputs and Outputs: Unstructured grid dataset (mesh topology and cell data); rendering parameters (camera, transfer functions). Outputs: Rendered image (pixel colors). Data Structures: 1. Intersection Lists: A flat array representing intersection lists for all faces, replacing linked lists to ensure coalesced memory access on the GPU. 2. Thread Block Mapping: Rays are grouped into thread blocks based on an extended image-tile-based work distribution method, increasing ray-coherency within a block. Numbered Steps: 1. Intersection List Construction: Represent the intersection lists of all pixels as a flat array instead of using linked lists, because linked lists lead to irregular memory access which is inappropriate for the GPU. 2. Work Distribution: Group rays from an image-tile (a square image having a certain size) to improve ray-coherency in a ray group. Use a 2D thread block having the same size as an image-tile, where each thread handles one ray. 3. Ray Casting: Perform ray-casting on the GPU where a GPU thread handles each ray. Each thread retrieves the intersection list for its assigned pixel from the flat array. 4. On-Demand VDFI Calculation: Take an on-demand View-Dependent Face Information (VDFI) computation strategy during the ray-casting process, calculating VDFI whenever a ray meets a face, rather than using thread-local buffers or preprocessing all faces. 5. Compositing: Composite the optical properties (color, opacity) along the ray path using the intersection data and write the final color to the output image buffer. Formulas: Volume rendering compositing follows the standard front-to-back alpha blending equation: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - O{in}) \cdot C{cell} \cdot O{cell} O{out} = O{in} + (1 - O{in}) \cdot O{cell} where C{in} and O{in} are the accumulated color and opacity before the current sample, C{cell} and O{cell} are the color and opacity of the current grid cell/face, and C{out} and O{out} are the updated accumulators. Parameters: Image Tile Size: Determines the block size for thread grouping. Not given in the sources. Sorting Algorithm: Used for visibility sorting. Not given in the sources. Standard distance-based sorting is assumed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warp Divergence from Buffers: Using thread-local VDFI buffers causes warp divergence: since GPU threads run in warps (e.g., 32 threads), if one or more threads in a warp fail to find the required VDFI in the buffer, the work of threads in the warp is serialized, invalidating the benefit of buffer hits for other threads and making buffer handling overhead. Duplicate Computations: The on-demand calculation strategy allows duplicate computations, but achieves better performance even though it allows duplicate computations. Non-Convex Meshes: The per-pixel intersection list concept guarantees accurate results for non-convex meshes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastkernel(pixelx, pixely, intersectionlists, griddata, transferfunction, camera): # 1. Retrieve intersection list for this pixel from the flat array rayorigin = camera.getorigin(pixelx, pixely) raydirection = camera.getdirection(pixelx, pixely) intersections = intersectionlists[pixely camera.width + pixelx] # 2. Sort intersections by distance along the ray (front-to-back) intersections.sort(key=lambda inter: inter.distance) # 3. On-demand integration accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for intersection in intersections: # Calculate optical properties on demand when ray meets a face color, opacity = computecellproperties(intersection, griddata, transferfunction) # Standard volume rendering compositing accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) color opacity accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor def computecellproperties(intersection, griddata, transferfunction): # Sample grid data at intersection point and apply transfer function # Returns (color, opacity) return transferfunction(griddata.sample(intersection.point)) The Pixel Ray Image (PRI) is a semi-regular data structure for volume rendering of unstructured grids that replaces the irregular mesh with a pixelized projection plane and 1D linear splines defined on sampling rays. It solves the difficulty of mapping irregular unstructured grid data efficiently to GPU hardware by leveraging coherent sample placement and 2D texture storage, avoiding the cell-ordering bottlenecks of direct ray-casting. Unlike sibling methods like GPU-based Ray Traversal on Tetrahedral Meshes which traverse the mesh directly, PRI pre-computes a texture-based representation. Choose it when memory bandwidth and texture sampling coherence are prioritized over explicit mesh traversal. This method implements volume rendering on tetrahedral meshes by traversing a ray through the mesh structure on the GPU, determining the exit face of the current tetrahedron and following neighbor pointers to adjacent cells. It distinguishes itself from CPU-based traversal by storing all mesh and traversal data in GPU texture memory, enabling concurrent, single-pass traversal for all pixels without CPU-GPU data transfer. Unlike sibling methods that may use hierarchical structures or voxelization, this approach relies on explicit tetrahedral adjacency and convexity assumptions. Choose it when exact geometric traversal on tetrahedral grids is required without preprocessing into texture-based projections. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves up to 36.5 times higher performance for the ray-casting process and 18.1 to 19.7 times higher performance for the whole volume rendering process compared with the Bunyk algorithm using a CPU core. Comparison to Cell Projection: Shows up to 8.2 times higher performance than a GPU-based cell projection method (HAVS) while generating more accurate rendering results. Cache and Memory Efficiency: On-demand calculation reduces memory access by up to 1.5 times and L2 cache transactions by up to 4.5 times, while increasing L1 cache hit ratio by about 18% compared to VDFI buffers. Ray-casting with the image-tile distribution method took 21% less L2 cache transactions than using a naive pixel-order ray distribution approach. Strengths: Guarantees accurate results for non-convex meshes; efficient memory access via flat array intersection lists; high performance on modern GPUs due to on-demand calculation and tile-based work distribution. Limitations: Allows duplicate computations due to the on-demand strategy; requires preprocessing to construct intersection lists. Scaling: Performance scales with GPU hardware capabilities; the method was tested on three unstructured grid datasets with different characteristics. The method was introduced by Gibeom Gu and Duksu Kim at KISTI and KOREATECH in the EUROVIS 2019 poster 'Accurate and Memory-Efficient GPU Ray-Casting Algorithm for Volume Rendering Unstructured Grid Data'. It was later published in the ETRI Journal in 2020. It extends prior image-tile-based work distribution methods to fit modern GPU architectures. It addresses limitations in previous GPU-based approaches, such as the inefficiency of per-thread local buffers and the inaccuracy of cell projection methods for non-convex geometries. The work is part of a broader effort to optimize volume rendering on unstructured data using GPU shaders, CUDA, and ray tracing techniques. name: Pixel Ray Image (PRI)
head: Parametric Ray Integral Construction, Ray-cell intersection knot listing, PRI Spline Construction, PRI knot generation
body: The Pixel Ray Image (PRI) is a semi-regular data structure for volume rendering of unstructured grids that replaces the irregular mesh with a pixelized projection plane and 1D linear splines defined on sampling rays. It solves the difficulty of mapping irregular unstructured grid data efficiently to GPU hardware by leveraging coherent sample placement and 2D texture storage, avoiding the cell-ordering bottlenecks of direct ray-casting. Unlike sibling methods like GPU-based Ray Traversal on Tetrahedral Meshes which traverse the mesh directly, PRI pre-computes a texture-based representation. Inputs: Unstructured grid V with scalar values at vertices; camera parameters (position, up vector, view direction). Outputs: A 2D texture containing packed linear splines representing the PRI. Data Structures: 1. Sampling Plane: A 2D image plane with finite dimensions, pixelized with a regular grid of pixel centers at integer offsets from the origin. 2. Knot List: For each pixel, a list of knots K = [(s0, t0, p0), (s1, t1, p1), \dots, (sn, tn, pn)]. s: Scalar value. t: Distance from the sampling plane along the ray. p: 3D intersection point. Ordered such that tk < t{k+1}. 3. PRI Texture: A 2D texture storing the knot lists. The specific packing format is detailed in PRI Texture Storage. Steps: 1. Define Sampling Geometry: Compute a tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) around V. Select one face of the AABB as the sampling plane. The associated axial direction of the box face defines the sampling direction (view direction). The view direction must point towards the center of the grid. Set pixel resolution R \times R (e.g., 256 \times 256). Resolution must be high enough that multiple rays pierce every cell face to ensure sufficient resampling. 2. Resample Grid onto Sampling Rays (Knot Generation): For each pixel (u, v) on the sampling plane: Cast a sampling ray r into the grid. Find all intersections between r and the grid cell faces. For each intersection, compute: t: Distance from the pixel to the intersection. s: Reconstructed scalar value at the intersection location. If the scalar field is linear within cells, s is interpolated from vertex values at the intersection point. If not linear, samples may be located uniformly along the ray, and s is reconstructed using a filter. Insert the triple (s, t, p) into the knot list for this pixel. Alternative Implementation: Use depth peeling on graphics hardware to render layers of cell faces in depth-sorted order and compute knot values (s, t) directly on the GPU. 3. Handle Non-Convexity (Boundary Knots): For non-convex grids, a ray may enter and exit the grid multiple times. For every boundary knot (sb, tb, pb) (where the ray enters or exits the volume): Insert an additional knot (0, tb, pb) into the knot list immediately following (sb, tb, pb). This creates consecutive pairs of knots with multiplicity two, bounding portions of the ray outside the grid with a scalar value of 0. 4. Spline Simplification (Data Reduction): Apply a linear spline simplification algorithm to reduce the knot count per spline. The algorithm exploits coherence in the sampling direction. Consecutive runs of samples approximating a line in the scalar domain are collected into single linear segments. This is a greedy algorithm that may insert new samples into the final linear spline if necessary to maintain fidelity. 5. Pack and Store: Pack the entire collection of splines (knot lists) onto a 2D texture. Upload the texture to GPU memory once prior to rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructPRI(grid, cameraparams): # 1. Define Sampling Plane aabbmin, aabbmax = computeaabb(grid) samplingplane = selectaabbface(aabbmin, aabbmax) viewdirection = getaxialdirection(samplingplane) gridcenter = computecenterofgrid(grid) assert dot(viewdirection, gridcenter - cameraparams.position) > 0 resolution = 256 pixels = generatepixelgrid(resolution, samplingplane) priknotlists = {} for pixel in pixels: rayorigin = pixel.position raydirection = viewdirection knots = [] intersections = findraycellfaceintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, grid) for t, point in intersections: s = reconstructscalarfield(point, grid) knots.append((s, t, point)) knots.sort(key=lambda k: k[1]) processedknots = [] for s, t, point in knots: processedknots.append((s, t, point)) # Sources do not specify exact algorithm to check if a knot is on the grid boundary if isongridboundary(point, grid): processedknots.append((0, t, point)) priknotlists[pixel.index] = processedknots simplifiedknotlists = {} for pixelindex, knots in priknotlists.items(): simplifiedknots = simplifylinearspline(knots) simplifiedknotlists[pixelindex] = simplifiedknots pritexture = packknotstotexture(simplifiedknotlists) return pritexture def computeaabb(grid): return min(v.position for v in grid.vertices), max(v.position for v in grid.vertices) def selectaabbface(aabb): return aabb[0] def getaxialdirection(face): return face.normal def computecenterofgrid(grid): return sum(v.position for v in grid.vertices) / len(grid.vertices) def generatepixelgrid(res, plane): return [(u, v) for u in range(res) for v in range(res)] def findraycellfaceintersections(origin, direction, grid): intersections = [] for face in grid.faces: t = rayfaceintersection(origin, direction, face) if t > 0: intersections.append((t, origin + t direction)) intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return intersections def reconstructscalarfield(point, grid): return interpolatescalar(point, grid.vertices) def isongridboundary(point, grid): # Sources do not specify exact algorithm to check if a knot is on the grid boundary return False def packknotstotexture(knotlists): # Sources do not specify exact packing format return None def simplifylinearspline(knots): if len(knots) <= 2: return knots simplified = [knots[0]] starts, startt = knots[0][0], knots[0][1] for i in range(1, len(knots) - 1): currs, currt = knots[i][0], knots[i][1] nexts, nextt = knots[i+1][0], knots[i+1][1] # Check if current point is collinear with start and next cross = (currs - starts) (nextt - startt) - (currt - startt) (nexts - starts) if abs(cross) > 1e-6: simplified.append(knots[i]) starts, startt = knots[i][0], knots[i][1] simplified.append(knots[-1]) return simplified def iscollinear(s1, t1, s2, t2, s3, t3): cross = (s2 - s1) (t3 - t1) - (t2 - t1) (s3 - s1) return abs(cross) < 1e-6 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convex Grids: Rays may enter and exit multiple times. Failure to insert the (0, tb) boundary knots will result in incorrect rendering of regions outside the volume. Resolution: If the pixel resolution is too low, multiple rays may not pierce every cell face, leading to insufficient resampling and artifacts. Scalar Field Linearity: The method assumes linearity within cells for knot placement at face intersections. If the field is non-linear, uniform sampling and filtering are required, which may increase knot count. GPU-friendly data layout for the PRI, focusing on compact, texture-based representation of splines. Quantifies fidelity of the PRI representation relative to the source unstructured grid by evaluating sampling error at grid vertices. Time Complexity: Construction: Depends on the number of pixels and intersections. Table 1 in shows construction times for 256 \times 256 resolution: Blunt Fin (187,395 tets): 29.20 seconds. Combustor (215,040 tets): 86.04 seconds. Liquid Oxygen Post (513,375 tets): 32.84 seconds. SPX (12,936 tets): 4.39 seconds. Rendering: Efficient, using slice-based rendering similar to hardware-accelerated regular grid rendering. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels and the average number of knots per spline. Average knots per spline for 256 \times 256 resolution (from): Blunt Fin: 80 knots/spline. Combustor: 63 knots/spline. Liquid Oxygen Post: 85 knots/spline. SPX: 27 knots/spline. Strengths: Avoids cell-ordering bottlenecks of direct ray-casting. Leverages GPU hardware acceleration via 2D textures. Flexible sample placement. Fewer samples needed than regular resampling of the grid. Limitations: Preprocessing time can be significant for large grids. Requires sufficient pixel resolution to ensure multiple rays pierce every cell face. Restricted to sampling directions pointing towards the center of the grid (based on AABB face selection). The Pixel Ray Image (PRI) was introduced by Shareef et al. in 2006. It is an image-based approach designed to allow flexible sample placement and efficient mapping to graphics hardware. It builds on the idea of replacing the unstructured grid with a semi-regular data structure to leverage current trends in hardware performance. name: PRI Texture Storage
head: PRI data layout, PRI index and knots textures
body: PRI Texture Storage is the GPU-friendly data layout for the Pixel Ray Image (PRI), a semi-regular structure for unstructured grid volume rendering. It solves the difficulty of mapping irregular unstructured grid data efficiently to GPU hardware by replacing the grid with a pixelized projection plane and 1D scalar functions (linear splines) defined on sampling rays. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like PRI Approximation Error Measurement by focusing on the compact, texture-based representation of these splines rather than their geometric fidelity. The PRI is represented as two 2D textures: an Index Texture and a Knots Texture. The Index Texture has the same resolution as the PRI pixel plane (sampling plane). The Knots Texture stores the actual spline data. Index Texture A 2D texture with the same resolution as the PRI pixel plane. Each texel holds four channels (r, g, b, a) mapping to: r, g: The 2D address (coordinates) of the first spline knot in the Knots Texture. b: The number of knots in the spline for this pixel. a: The normalized distance of the last knot from the sampling plane. If channel b is zero, the sampling ray does not intersect the grid. Knots Texture A 2D texture containing the packed per-pixel splines. To ensure high precision, it is stored as two separate float-format textures: 1. One texture holds the scalar values of the knots. 2. One texture holds the distance values (depth) of the knots. The splines are laid out in a pre-determined traversal order of the pixels (e.g., row-order or column-order). 1. Traverse Pixels: Iterate through the PRI pixel plane in a pre-determined order (e.g., row-major). 2. Collect Splines: For each pixel, determine the linear spline defined by the intersection of the sampling ray with the unstructured grid. 3. Pack Knots: Append the knot data (scalar value and distance) for the current pixel's spline to the end of the Knots Texture arrays. 4. Write Index: For the current pixel, write the Index Texture texel: set r, g to the current write pointer (2D address) in the Knots Texture, set b to the count of knots in the current spline, and set a to the normalized distance of the last knot. 5. Advance Pointer: Increment the Knots Texture write pointer by the number of knots added. Non-intersecting Rays: If a sampling ray does not intersect the grid, the spline has zero knots. Out-of-Bounds Slicing: A slicing plane (or fragment) can be quickly identified as lying outside the unstructured grid using two checks: 1. Its z-location overlaps a spline with zero knots (ray does not enter the volume grid). 2. Its distance to the sampling plane is less than the distance to the first knot or greater than the distance to the last knot of the spline. Precision: Using separate float textures for scalar and distance values is critical for maintaining high precision in the knot data. Note: This variant is used when transferring data back to the CPU, where pixel position must be recovered. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecompactnodeindextexture(rays, width, height): """ Generates a compact RGBA32 texture for CPU read-back. rays: 2D list of Ray objects, each with.bitmask (int) and.nodes (list of ints, up to 12). Returns: 2D list of [r, g, b, a] tuples, each containing packed 32-bit node indices. """ texture = [[(0, 0, 0, 0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ray = rays[y][x] pixelpos = y width + x channels = [0, 0, 0, 0] activecount = 0 for i in range(4): if ray.bitmask & (1 << i): nodeidx = ray.nodes[i] # Pack: 20 bits pixel position | 12 bits node index packed = (pixelpos << 12) | nodeidx channels[i] = packed activecount += 1 if activecount > 4: # Postpone request to next frame continue texture[y][x] = tuple(channels) return texture A variant of the storage layout used during GPU-to-CPU data transfer. It addresses the loss of original pixel position during texture reduction. It encodes the pixel position (using 20 bits of a 32-bit entry) alongside node indices (12 bits). The final texture is a single RGBA32 texture storing indices of four nodes per pixel. The bitmask usually contains 2-3 non-zero entries. If the limit of 4 nodes is exceeded, requests are postponed to the next frame. Memory: Requires two 2D textures (Index and Knots). The Index Texture size is fixed by the PRI resolution. The Knots Texture size depends on the number of intersections (knots) per ray. Performance: Allows for efficient texture lookups on the GPU. Precision: High precision is maintained by using separate float textures for scalar and distance values. Limitations: The layout is static once generated. Dynamic updates require rebuilding the textures. Not given in the sources. The compact node index variant has a hard limit of 4 nodes per pixel; exceeding this causes frame postponement. The PRI Texture Storage method was introduced in the context of GPU-based unstructured grid volume rendering. It was presented in the paper "An Image-Based Modelling Approach To GPU-based Unstructured Grid Volume Rendering". The compact node index variant was later described in "Ray-Guided Streaming for Efficient and Detailed Voxel Rendering". name: PRI Approximation Error Measurement
head: PRI Error Metric, PSNR calculation for PRI
body: PRI Approximation Error Measurement quantifies the sampling error of a Pixel Ray Image (PRI) P relative to its source unstructured grid V by evaluating the grid's vertices within the PRI structure. It verifies that the resampling process preserves the original scalar field's accuracy. The method measures the approximation error of a PRI P by evaluating the scalar values of the original grid vertices within the PRI structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The original unstructured grid V (composed of tetrahedra t) and the constructed PRI P. Output: A Mean Square Error (MSE) value, which can be converted to Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR). Data Structures: Grid V: A collection of tetrahedra, where each tetrahedron t has four vertices v and a volume |t|. PRI P: A data structure allowing trilinear interpolation of scalar values at arbitrary 3D coordinates. Steps: 1. Iterate over every tetrahedron t in the original grid V. 2. For each tetrahedron t, iterate over its four vertices v. 3. Retrieve the original scalar value S(v) from the grid V at vertex v. 4. Reconstruct the scalar value SP(v) by performing trilinear interpolation on the PRI P at the coordinates of vertex v. 5. Compute the residual error for each vertex: |S(v) - SP(v)|. 6. Determine the maximal residual error for the tetrahedron t: \varepsilonP(t) = \max{\forall v \in t} |S(v) - SP(v)| where \varepsilonP(t) is the maximal residual error on tetrahedron t. 7. Compute the weighted Mean Square Error (MSE) using the volume of each tetrahedron as the weight: MSE(V, P) = \frac{\sum{\forall t \in V} \varepsilonP(t)^2 |t|}{\sum{\forall t \in V} |t|} where |t| is the volume of tetrahedron t. 8. (Optional) Convert MSE to PSNR using standard logarithmic conversion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeprierror(gridV, priP): """ Computes the MSE approximation error of PRI P relative to unstructured grid V. """ totalweightederror = 0.0 totalvolume = 0.0 for tetrahedron in gridV.tetrahedra: volume = tetrahedron.volume() totalvolume += volume maxresidual = 0.0 for vertex in tetrahedron.vertices: soriginal = vertex.scalarvalue # Standard trilinear interpolation of scalar field at vertex.position sreconstructed = priP.trilinearinterpolate(vertex.position) residual = abs(soriginal - sreconstructed) if residual > maxresidual: maxresidual = residual totalweightederror += (maxresidual 2) volume if totalvolume == 0: return 0.0 mse = totalweightederror / totalvolume return mse Parameters: Error Threshold: In the context of the simplification algorithm that generates the PRI, an error threshold determines when knots are removed; an error threshold of 0.0 results in the removal of superfluous knots representing samples in constant or linearly changing regions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A quality metric measuring the error committed when approximating a sphere, calculated as the distance from the sphere center to the vertices of each triangle. It is used to compare isosurface extraction algorithms. The definition measures the deviation of triangle vertices from the ideal spherical radius. The formula is \text{Total Error} = \sum{i=1}^n \frac{Ri - Rr}{Rr}, where n is the number of triangles multiplied by 3, Ri is the distance from the sphere center to vertex i (denoted ri in the source), and Rr is the reference sphere radius. The vertex distance is calculated as ri = \sqrt{(vx - cx)^2 + (vy - cy)^2 + (vz - cz)^2}. Lower radius error indicates a better geometric approximation of the sphere. Not given in the sources. The method originates from research on GPU-based unstructured grid volume rendering, specifically the Image-Based Modelling approach. It was introduced to evaluate the accuracy of the Pixel Ray Image (PRI) representation, which replaces irregular unstructured grids with a semi-regular structure suitable for GPU texture storage. The approach follows a method similar to [CCM00] for measuring sampling error in resampled data. The metric allows researchers to quantify the trade-off between data reduction (knot removal) and accuracy in the PRI simplification process. name: GPU-based Ray Traversal on Tetrahedral Meshes
head: GPU-based Ray Tracing on Tetrahedral Meshes, Garrity's method, Ray tracing through tetrahedral grid, Tetrahedral traversal, Weiler et al. GPU Ray Casting, Weiler et al. method
body: This method implements volume rendering on tetrahedral meshes by traversing a ray through the mesh structure on the GPU, determining the exit face of the current tetrahedron and following neighbor pointers to adjacent cells. It distinguishes itself from CPU-based traversal by storing all mesh and traversal data in GPU texture memory, enabling concurrent, single-pass traversal for all pixels without CPU-GPU data transfer. Unlike sibling methods that may use hierarchical structures or voxelization, this approach relies on explicit tetrahedral adjacency and convexity assumptions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh (vertices, connectivity, density/scalar field), camera parameters (ray origin and direction per pixel), and optical properties (density \sigma, transmissivity \tau, color emission \kappa). Output: Final pixel color and opacity. Data Structures: Vertex Data: Stored in 3D textures. Adjacency/Traversal Data: Stored in 2D textures. Lookup Table: A precomputed table for blending, assuming a static mesh geometry. Algorithm Steps: The traversal is executed in a single render pass, concurrently for all pixels. For each ray, the procedure follows these steps: 1. Find Entry Point: Determine the entry point p0 of the ray into the convex hull of the mesh. 2. Find Exit Point and Calculate Density: Determine the exit point p1 of the current tetrahedron. Calculate the density values within the segment [p0, p1]. 3. Blend Fragment: Blend the new fragment using the cell density and the distance between p0 and p1. This step typically uses a precomputed lookup table. 4. Update Position: Set p1 as the new p0 for the next iteration. 5. Loop: Return to Step 2. Mathematical Formulation: The contribution Ei of the i-th segment (bounded by ray distances si and s{i+1}, with length \Delta si = s{i+1} - si) to the final irradiance E is calculated by integrating the volume rendering integral: Ei = \int{si}^{s{i+1}} \taui ci T(s) ds Where: \taui is the transmissivity of the i-th tetrahedron. ci is the color/emission of the i-th tetrahedron. T(s) is the transmission coefficient up to distance s, defined as T(s) = \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(u) \sigma(u) du\right). Within the tetrahedron, optical properties \taui and ci are assumed constant. Substituting and separating the transparency up to si: Ei = \taui ci \int{si}^{s{i+1}} \exp\left(-\int0^{si} \tau(u) \sigma(u) du\right) \cdot \exp\left(-\int{si}^s \tau(u) \sigma(u) du\right) ds Since \taui and \sigmai are constant within the cell, this simplifies to: Ei = \taui ci T(si) \int{si}^{s{i+1}} \exp\left(-\taui \sigmai (s - si)\right) ds Parameters: Convexification: The mesh must be convexified. Exterior cells are marked as "imaginary" and ignored during rendering. Lookup Table: Requires precomputation based on static mesh geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convex Meshes: The algorithm strictly handles only convex meshes. It cannot find the re-entry of rays that leave the mesh temporarily. Local Intersections: If a tetrahedron is flipped and cuts into another tetrahedron's volume (local intersection), the algorithm fails to detect it because it jumps to neighbors without analyzing the neighborhood. This results in an incomplete fragment list and invalid pixel color. Dynamic Meshes: The precomputed lookup table assumes a static mesh. For dynamic volumes (e.g., smoke), this is infeasible, leading to artifacts due to arbitrary distortion over time. Global Intersections: The method does not handle global intersections (penetration of non-adjacent tetrahedra) correctly, leading to incomplete fragment lists. Local intersection (or self-intersection) occurs when a tetrahedron is flipped and cuts into another tetrahedron's volume. This is a bottleneck in ray tracing where the algorithm jumps from one cell to another without looking at other cells. Because the algorithm is not aware of local intersections and does not analyze the neighborhood, the intersecting tetrahedron fails to contribute to the viewing ray, resulting in an invalid pixel color due to an incomplete list of fragments. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of tetrahedra intersected by the ray, executed in parallel for all pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for vertex data (3D textures) and adjacency data (2D textures). Global random access memory is required for implementation. Performance: GPU performance outpaces CPU, leading to good scalability. Strengths: Fast, concurrent traversal; no CPU-GPU data transfer; accurate interpolation of scalar data before transfer function application. Limitations: Strictly convex meshes only; cannot handle re-entry; precomputed lookup table limits dynamic use; fails on local and global intersections. When to Use: Static, convex tetrahedral meshes where high performance is required and dynamic deformation is not expected. When Not to Use: Dynamic volumes (e.g., smoke), non-convex meshes, or meshes with self-intersections. The method is based on the work of Garrity [15], who showed how to trace a ray through a tetrahedral grid by determining the exit face and following neighbor pointers. Weiler et al. [56] (also cited as [12] and [66]) implemented this on a GPU. The convexification technique using imaginary cells was originally proposed by Williams [70]. Convexification of unstructured meshes remains a hard and currently unsolved problem with many unresolved issues.
