name: Recursive Ray-casting for Global Illumination
head: GPU-based Volume Ray-casting with Specular Reflection and Refraction, Higher Order Entry and Exit Points
body: Recursive Ray-casting for Global Illumination is an extension of GPU-based volume ray-casting that computes specular reflection and refraction effects at interactive frame rates by processing a ray-caster multiple times with different entry and exit points, supporting both Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) and isosurface rendering. Unlike techniques that focus on the exchangeability of ray-casters, this method aims to combine specular reflection and refraction effects within a single image. The method extends a standard GPU-based volume ray-caster into a ray-tracer by tracing rays of higher order. The workflow is subdivided into four subsequent stages: 1. Stage 1: Initial Ray Casting. Compute initial unmodified entry and exit points for first-order rays. Cast rays from the entry point to the first hit point (the position where the ray first encounters a visible medium). Sample one step further into the volume at the hit point to increase the footprint of encountered voxels, ensuring the encountered medium is sufficiently penetrated and clearly visible in the intermediate image. 2. Stage 2: Higher-Order Point Generation. For each recursive step, compute higher-order entry and exit points based on the first hit points of the previous step. The exit points for the next recursion step are computed by determining the intersection between the higher-order ray and the bounding box of the volume. 3. Stage 3: Intermediate Rendering. A ray-caster computes intermediate images containing shading results for a ray segment based on the generated entry and exit points. The intermediate image is cached for blending in the final stage. 4. Stage 4: Blending. Blend all available intermediate shading images into the final image using a specularity mapping function. To compute the ray direction d for rays reflected on a specular surface, the normal of the surface is considered. Similar to the Phong illumination model, the outgoing ray is computed by considering the incoming ray and the current surface normal. For refraction, the incoming ray is bent at the surface based on Snell's law. The bending angle \theta is computed based on the incoming angle \phi and the refraction indices n1 (medium left by the ray) and n2 (medium entered by the ray): \cos(\theta) = \sqrt{\left(1 - \left(\frac{n1}{n2}\right)^2\right) \cdot \left(1 - (\cos(\phi))^2\right)} The direction of the leaving ray A{vec} is computed as follows: A{vec} = \frac{n1}{n2} E{vec} + \left(|\cos(\phi)| - \cos(\theta)\right) N{vec} where E{vec} is the incoming ray vector and N{vec} is the normalized gradient (surface normal). Total reflection must be considered when the incoming ray hits the object under a very flat angle, resulting in specular reflection instead of refraction. The critical angle \phi{crit} is computed as: \phi{crit} = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n2}{n1}\right) If the incident angle \phi exceeds \phi{crit}, a specular reflection ray is computed instead of a refractive one. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recursivevolumeraycasting(volumedata, camera, maxrecursiondepth): # Stage 1: Initial setup # Compute initial unmodified entry and exit points for first-order rays entrypoints = computecamerarays(camera) exitpoints = intersectrayaabb(entrypoints, camera.directions, volumebounds) intermediateimages = [] currententry = entrypoints currentexit = exitpoints currentdirections = camera.directions for depth in range(maxrecursiondepth + 1): # Stage 3: Intermediate Rendering # A ray-caster computes intermediate images containing shading results # for a ray segment based on the generated entry and exit points intermediateimage = raycastsegment(volumedata, currententry, currentexit, currentdirections) intermediateimages.append(intermediateimage) # Compute first hit points for the NEXT recursion step # Sample one step further into the volume at the hit point to increase footprint hitpoints = computefirsthitpoints(volumedata, currententry, currentexit, currentdirections) hitpointsextended = hitpoints + currentdirections stepsize # Stage 2: Higher-Order Point Generation if depth < maxrecursiondepth: currententry = hitpointsextended currentdirections = computenextraydirections(hitpoints, currentdirections, volumedata) # Exit Point Generation: intersection between ray and bounding box currentexit = intersectrayaabb(currententry, currentdirections, volumebounds) # Stage 4: Blending # Blend all available intermediate shading images into the final image # using a specularity mapping function finalimage = blendintermediateimages(intermediateimages) return finalimage def computecamerarays(camera): return camera.origin # Standard camera ray generation def intersectrayaabb(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = (bounds.min - origin) / direction tmax = (bounds.max - origin) / direction tenter = max(min(tmin), min(tmax)) texit = min(max(tmin), max(tmax)) return origin + direction texit def computefirsthitpoints(volumedata, entry, exit, directions): step = (exit - entry) / numsamples pos = entry for in range(numsamples): if isvisible(volumedata, pos): return pos + step pos += step return exit def isvisible(volumedata, pos): return volumedata[pos] > threshold # Standard visibility check def computenextraydirections(hitpoints, incomingdirections, volumedata): nextdirections = [] for hit, incoming in zip(hitpoints, incomingdirections): normal = normalize(samplegradient(volumedata, hit)) cosphi = dot(incoming, normal) phi = acos(cosphi) n1 = getrefractionindex(volumedata, hit - incoming epsilon) n2 = getrefractionindex(volumedata, hit) phicrit = asin(n2 / n1) if phi > phicrit: reflected = incoming - 2 dot(incoming, normal) normal nextdirections.append(reflected) else: costheta = sqrt((1 - (n1/n2)2) (1 - cosphi2)) abscosphi = abs(cosphi) leaving = (n1/n2) incoming + (abscosphi - costheta) normal nextdirections.append(leaving) return nextdirections def samplegradient(volumedata, pos): return volumedata.gradient(pos) # Standard gradient computation def getrefractionindex(volumedata, pos): return volumedata.refractionindex[pos] # Standard property lookup def raycastsegment(volumedata, entry, exit, directions): return rendersegment(volumedata, entry, exit, directions) def rendersegment(volumedata, entry, exit, directions): return integratevolume(volumedata, entry, exit, directions) # Standard DVR/isosurface traversal def blendintermediateimages(images): result = zeroslike(images[0]) for img in images: result += img return result Sampling Rate: Set to twice the maximum grid resolution of the rendered data set. Total Reflection: If the incident angle \phi exceeds the critical angle \phi{crit}, refraction is not possible, and a specular reflection ray must be computed instead. Footprint Extension: Sampling one step further into the volume at the first hit point is required to increase the footprint of encountered voxels; failing to do so may result in the encountered medium not being sufficiently penetrated or visible. Refraction Indices: The refraction indices n1 and n2 must be correctly identified for the medium left by the ray and the medium entered by the ray, respectively. Performance: On a GeForce 8800GTX, the method achieves 57 fps for the Hand dataset (256 \times 256 \times 147) at 256 \times 256 resolution with recursion depth 0, and 10 fps for the Cornell Box dataset (256 \times 256 \times 256) at 512 \times 512 resolution with recursion depth 3. Scalability: The recursion depth influences the ray length to be traversed, while screen resolution influences the number of rays to be traced. Interactive frame rates are achieved for moderately sized data sets at 512 \times 512 resolution. Strengths: It allows for the computation of specular reflection and refraction effects at interactive frame rates on commodity graphics hardware and does not constrain the type of rendering (supports both DVR and isosurface rendering). Limitations: Performance decreases with higher recursion depths and larger screen resolutions. The technique was presented in a paper extending GPU-based volume ray-casting to support specular reflection and refraction. It was integrated into the Voreen volume rendering engine. The work was partly supported by grants from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG), SFB 656 MoBil Münster, Germany. It contrasts with Stegmaier et al. (2005), who focused on the exchangeability of ray-casters, by aiming to combine specular reflection and refraction effects within a single image. GPU-based Volume Ray-casting Supporting Specular Reflection and Refraction, https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/ba7b/55980c8d8ecac4aa1035eb4ae7c16c85da24.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: FPGA-based Raycasting
head: Raycasting Hardware (UVIZARD)
body: FPGA-based raycasting refers to specialized hardware architectures, specifically the UVIZARD and VIZARD II systems developed at the University of Tübingen, designed to accelerate perspective volume raycasting on custom PCI boards. Unlike later general-purpose GPU solutions, these systems require long pre-processing times to configure the hardware. The architecture is distinguished by its implementation of early ray-termination and a table-based gradient vector lookup scheme on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (e.g., 256^3 voxels), camera parameters for perspective view, and transfer function parameters. Output: A 2D rendered image. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in off-chip SDRAM/SRAM memory. Gradient Lookup Table: A pre-computed table mapping sample values to gradient vectors, used to avoid on-the-fly finite difference calculations. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Configure the FPGAs and load necessary lookup tables, requiring significant setup time before rendering begins. 2. Ray Generation: Cast rays for each pixel based on perspective camera parameters. 3. Sampling and Gradient Lookup: Traverse the volume, retrieving gradients from the pre-computed table at sample positions. 4. Early Ray Termination: Halt ray traversal when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold to save computation. 5. Image Output: Write the final accumulated color to the frame buffer. Formulas: The rendering equation is approximated by discrete front-to-back compositing: C = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ci \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where ci is sample color, \alphai is sample opacity, and N is the number of samples. The sources note that pre-integration can be used to tabulate the integral of the transfer function, but UVIZARD specifically emphasizes the gradient lookup for shading. Parameters: Volume Size: Tested on 256^3 datasets. Hardware: PCI board with four FPGAs, a DSP, and SDRAM/SRAM. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pre-processing Latency: The system requires long pre-processing times, making it less suitable for dynamic scenes requiring rapid reconfiguration. Precision: Fixed-point arithmetic is implied by the hardware nature, but specific bit-widths are not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fpgaraycast(volumedata, volumedims, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, gradienttable, transferfunc, maxopacity): # volumedata: 3D list of voxel values # volumedims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) # rayorigin, raydirection: 3D tuples/lists # stepsize: physical step length along ray # gradienttable: dict mapping sample value -> gradient tuple # transferfunc: function(value, gradient) -> (color, opacity) # maxopacity: threshold for early termination # Compute ray length to exit volume (handles negative direction and zero components) tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(raydirection[i]) > 1e-9: t1 = (0.0 - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (volumedims[i] - 1.0 - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) else: if rayorigin[i] < 0.0 or rayorigin[i] >= volumedims[i]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax and accumulatedopacity < maxopacity: x = rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t y = rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t z = rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) if not (0 <= ix < volumedims[0] and 0 <= iy < volumedims[1] and 0 <= iz < volumedims[2]): break samplevalue = volumedata[ix][iy][iz] gradient = gradienttable.get(samplevalue, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) color, alpha = transferfunc(samplevalue, gradient) weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor[0] += color[0] weight accumulatedcolor[1] += color[1] weight accumulatedcolor[2] += color[2] weight accumulatedopacity += weight t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor A software-based sibling that accelerates ray-triangle intersections on GPUs using optimized bounding volume hierarchies and parallel reduction, chosen when dynamic geometry requires programmable flexibility over fixed-function speed [7032-gpu-ray-casting-with-fast-intersection.md]. A general-purpose sibling leveraging CUDA/OpenCL pipelines for volume rendering, chosen when hardware portability and developer productivity outweigh the raw throughput of custom ASIC/FPGA designs [7131-gpu-based-ray-casting.md]. A sibling that combines depth peeling for correct transparency sorting with tile-based subdivision to reduce overdraw, chosen for complex multi-layered scenes where order-independent transparency is critical [7813-gpu-ray-casting-with-depth-peeling-and-tile-based-subdivisio.md]. A sibling that extends basic raycasting to compute indirect lighting and reflections via recursive ray spawning, chosen when physically accurate global illumination is required at the cost of exponential sample counts [8544-recursive-ray-casting-for-global-illumination.md]. A sibling that approximates light transport using only the first scattering event, chosen for real-time performance in participating media where multiple scattering effects are negligible [9628-single-scattering-illumination.md]. A sibling that partitions large volumes into spatial bricks for networked or multi-GPU rendering, chosen when dataset size exceeds single-node memory bandwidth or capacity [9869-distributed-volume-raycasting-with-bricks.md]. Performance: The UVIZARD system achieved 10 Hz for a 256^3 volume with perspective view. The VIZARD II was anticipated to render 256^3 datasets at interactive framerates. Memory: Relies on off-chip SDRAM/SRAM for volume storage. Strengths: Supports perspective rendering and early ray termination, features not present in earlier brute-force hardware like VolumePRO. Limitations: Requires long pre-processing times, reducing flexibility for rapidly changing data. The UVIZARD and VIZARD II systems were developed at the University of Tübingen in 1997. They represent an early implementation of reconfigurable hardware for volume rendering. name: Single Scattering Illumination
head: Direct Single Scattering (DSS), Indirect Single Scattering (ISS), Single Scattering Illumination Model
body: Single Scattering Illumination is a volumetric lighting model that computes the radiance contribution of light undergoing exactly one scattering event within a participating medium. It distinguishes between light scattered along the view ray (Direct Single Scattering, DSS) and light scattered along illumination rays from scene points (Indirect Single Scattering, ISS). Unlike basic volume rendering that often ignores volumetric shadows, this method provides an analytic formulation for both contributions, including occlusion handling via shadow volumes, enabling real-time hardware rendering. The method computes the total radiance observed along a view ray by summing direct single scattering, attenuated surface radiance, ambient/multiple scattering, and object indirect single scattering. Inputs: View ray direction \vec{u} and origin. Scene geometry for surface radiance L(P) and occlusion checks. Light source parameters: position, intensity IS, solid angle \Omega, and type (point/directional). Medium properties: extinction coefficient kt and phase function p(\cdot). Surface properties: Phong exponent n and specular coefficient ks. Precomputed 2D table for \Gamma(\lambda, \gamma). Outputs: Total radiance L{\vec{u}\vec{P}} for each sample point P along the view ray. 1. Gamma Table: A 2D lookup table storing values of \Gamma(\lambda, \gamma). Dimensions: Determined by the discretization of \lambda (distance parameter) and \gamma (angular parameter). Content: Numerical integration results of the phase function weighted by attenuation. Access: Bilinear interpolation is used for continuous parameters. 1. Total Radiance Equation The radiance L{\vec{u}\vec{P}} observed along a view ray from point P is: L{\vec{u}\vec{P}} = L{dss}(\vec{u}\vec{P}) + e^{-ktOP} L(P) + La e^{-ktOP} + L{oiss}(\vec{u}\vec{P}) \quad (1) Where: L{dss}: Direct single scattering contribution. OP: Distance from the camera/view origin to point P. L(P): Radiance of point P (surface or volume). La: Constant radiance from emission or multiple scattering. L{oiss}: Object indirect single scattering. 2. Point Radiance Equation The radiance L(P) at a point P is composed of: L(P) = L{iss}(P) + e^{-kt S^P} Ld(P) + La e^{-kt S^P} \quad (2) Where: L{iss}(P): Indirect single scattering received at P. S^P: Distance along the illumination ray from the light source to P. Ld(P): Direct illumination at P (e.g., Phong model). 3. The Gamma Function A 2D function \Gamma depending only on the phase function shape: \Gamma(\lambda, \gamma) = \int0^\gamma p\left(\alpha + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) e^{-kt \lambda \frac{\sin(\alpha) + 1}{\cos(\alpha)}} d\alpha \quad (3) Where: \lambda: Distance parameter. \gamma: Angular parameter. p: Phase function. \alpha: Integration variable. 4. Direct Single Scattering (DSS) - Totally Lit Ray For a view ray with no occlusions: L{dss}(d, \phi) = \frac{kt^2 \Omega S}{4\pi} \frac{e^{-kt t}}{kt h} \left[ \Gamma\left(kt h, \text{atan}\left(\frac{d-t}{h}\right)\right) - \Gamma\left(kt h, \text{atan}\left(\frac{-t}{h}\right)\right) \right] \quad (4) Where: d: Distance along the view ray. t: Distance to the light source. h: Height parameter (geometry of light/view relative to medium). S: Source size/area factor. \Omega: Solid angle of the light source. 5. Indirect Single Scattering (ISS) Using the single scattering Phong model: L{iss}(P) = \frac{kt^2 \Omega IS}{4\pi} \frac{ks}{kt l} \GammaP(kt l) \quad (5) Where: IS: Source intensity. ks: Scattering coefficient. l: Distance parameter. \GammaP: Precomputed function for ISS. The function \GammaP is defined as: \GammaP(\phi', \lambda) = \int0^{2\pi} \int0^\pi \int{\phi' - \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} p\left(\alpha + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) e^{-\lambda \frac{\cos(\alpha - \phi') + 1}{\cos(\alpha)}} \cos^n \theta(\phi) d\alpha \quad (6) Where: \phi': Angle parameter. \lambda: Distance parameter. n: Phong exponent. \theta: Angle related to the Phong model. 6. Direct Single Scattering (DSS) - With Occlusions Using the Laplace formula to handle occluders: L{dss}(d, \phi) = \frac{kt^2 \Omega IS}{4\pi} e^{-kt t} \left[ \Gamma(kt h, \gammaP) - \Gamma(kt h, \gammaB) + \Gamma(kt h, \gammaA) - \Gamma(kt h, \gammaO) \right] \quad (7) Where: \gammaP, \gammaB, \gammaA, \gammaO: Angular limits defined by the geometry of occluders relative to the view ray and light source. Ambience: Slider controlling the constant radiance La contribution. Specularity: Slider controlling the glossiness (Phong exponent n) of surfaces. Light Source: Can be point or directional. Head Light: Option that parents the light source to the camera position; transforming it causes it to pop back to the camera position. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gammatablelookup(table, lambdaval, gammaval): """Performs bilinear interpolation on the precomputed 2D Gamma table.""" # Map continuous lambdaval and gammaval to table grid coordinates # Return interpolated value return table[0][0] # Standard bilinear interpolation implementation def computesinglescatteringradiance(viewrayorigin, viewraydirection, pointP, medium, lightsource, geometry): """ Computes total radiance at point P along the view ray using Equations (1)-(7). """ kt = medium.extinctioncoefficient d = math.sqrt(sum((p - o)2 for p, o in zip(pointP, viewrayorigin))) t = math.sqrt(sum((p - l)2 for p, l in zip(lightsource.position, viewrayorigin))) h = geometry.getheightparameter(viewrayorigin, pointP, lightsource) # Derived from geometry # 1. Direct Single Scattering (DSS) isoccluded, occluderinfo = geometry.checkocclusion(viewrayorigin, pointP, lightsource) if isoccluded: # Equation (7) gammaP, gammaB, gammaA, gammaO = geometry.getocclusionangles(viewrayorigin, pointP, lightsource, occluderinfo) term1 = gammatablelookup(medium.gammatable, kt h, gammaP) term2 = gammatablelookup(medium.gammatable, kt h, gammaB) term3 = gammatablelookup(medium.gammatable, kt h, gammaA) term4 = gammatablelookup(medium.gammatable, kt h, gammaO) dss = (kt2 lightsource.solidangle lightsource.intensity) / (4 math.pi) \ math.exp(-kt t) (term1 - term2 + term3 - term4) else: # Equation (4) S = lightsource.sizefactor arg1 = math.atan((d - t) / h) arg2 = math.atan(-t / h) term1 = gammatablelookup(medium.gammatable, kt h, arg1) term2 = gammatablelookup(medium.gammatable, kt h, arg2) dss = (kt2 lightsource.solidangle S) / (4 math.pi) \ math.exp(-kt t) / (kt h) (term1 - term2) # 2. Attenuated Surface Radiance surfaceradianceP = geometry.getsurfaceradiance(pointP, lightsource) attenuation = math.exp(-kt d) attenuatedsurface = attenuation surfaceradianceP # 3. Ambient/Multiple Scattering ambientradiance = medium.ambientradiance attenuation # 4. Object Indirect Single Scattering (OISS) # The sources do not provide the explicit computation steps for Loiss oiss = 0.0 # 5. Sum components (Equation 1) totalradiance = dss + attenuatedsurface + ambientradiance + oiss return totalradiance def computeindirectsinglescattering(pointP, medium, lightsource, geometry): """ Computes Indirect Single Scattering (ISS) at point P using Equation (5). """ kt = medium.extinctioncoefficient l = math.sqrt(sum((p - l)2 for p, l in zip(lightsource.position, pointP))) phiprime = geometry.getangleparameter(pointP, lightsource) lambdaparam = kt l n = geometry.phongexponent ks = geometry.specularcoefficient # Equation (6) requires numerical integration or a precomputed 3D table gammap = computegammap(phiprime, lambdaparam, medium.phasefunction, n) iss = (kt2 lightsource.solidangle lightsource.intensity) / (4 math.pi) \ (ks / (kt l)) gammap return iss def computegammap(phiprime, lambdaparam, phasefunction, phongexponent): """ Computes the triple integral for GammaP (Equation 6). The sources do not provide the explicit integration algorithm """ # Standard numerical integration (e.g., Monte Carlo or quadrature) over alpha, phi, theta return 0.0 # Integration logic placeholder Occlusion Complexity: Equation (7) requires accurate calculation of angular limits \gammaP, \gammaB, \gammaA, \gammaO for arbitrary occluders. Precomputation: The \Gamma and \GammaP functions are purely numerical and depend on the phase function; they must be precomputed and stored in tables. Performance: Computing \GammaP involves a triple integral (Equation 6), which is expensive and typically precomputed or approximated. Head Light: When the "Head Light" option is enabled, the light source position is parented to the camera; transforming it causes it to pop back to the camera position. Time Complexity: The core DSS computation is O(1) per sample if \Gamma is precomputed and looked up. ISS computation is more expensive due to the triple integral in \GammaP, often requiring precomputation or approximation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the \Gamma 2D table and potentially the \GammaP table. Strengths: Provides physically plausible single scattering effects including volumetric shadows and indirect lighting contributions. Limitations: Single scattering approximation breaks down in highly participating media where multiple scattering is significant. When to use: Suitable for real-time rendering of participating media where single scattering dominates (e.g., fog, smoke, thin clouds) and volumetric shadows are desired. When not to use: Not suitable for dense media where multiple scattering is significant, or when full global illumination is required. The Single Scattering Illumination model was introduced in the paper "Single Scattering Effects for Computer Games". The work focuses on real-time hardware rendering of volumetric lighting effects, specifically introducing the concept of indirect single scattering (ISS) alongside direct single scattering (DSS). The method uses an angular formulation of the radiative transfer equation and precomputed 2D tables to enable efficient computation. The model is applied in the ray casting implementation of the VStudio framework for interactive volume visualization. name: Distributed Volume Raycasting with Bricks
head: Cluster-based volume raycasting, GPU raycasting on cluster systems
body: Distributed Volume Raycasting with Bricks is a parallel rendering technique that subdivides a volumetric dataset into convex subvolumes (bricks), assigning each to a separate node in a cluster for independent GPU raycasting. It differs from single-GPU methods by distributing the computational load across multiple machines and using software-based compositing to handle the final image assembly, thereby avoiding hardware blending limitations and glReadPixels performance bottlenecks. Inputs: Volumetric dataset V with total slice counts Sx, Sy, Sz in each dimension. User-defined number of bricks Bx, By, Bz in each dimension. User-defined sampling distance d. Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix). Outputs: Final composited image sent to the viewer. Data Structures: Brick Layout: The volume is partitioned into a grid of Bx \times By \times Bz bricks. Each brick \vec{b} = (bx, by, bz)^T is a convex subvolume. Brick Dimensions: The number of slices Sc(\vec{b}) for brick \vec{b} in dimension c \in \{x, y, z\} is: Sc(\vec{b}) = \begin{cases} \left\lceil \frac{Sc}{Bc} \right\rceil & \text{if } bc < Bc - 1 \\ Sc - (Bc - 1) \cdot \left\lceil \frac{Sc}{Bc} \right\rceil & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Overlap Handling: To support tri-linear interpolation at brick borders, each brick includes one overlapping slice from its neighbor. The actual texture size \tilde{s}c(\vec{b}) in dimension c is: \tilde{s}c(\vec{b}) = \begin{cases} Sc(\vec{b}) + 1 & \text{if } bc < Bc - 1 \\ Sc(\vec{b}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The texture is shifted by half a texel width to account for this overlap. Normalized Volume Size: The extent of a brick \vec{b} in dimension c is ec(\vec{b}) = Sc(\vec{b}) \cdot Dc, where Dc is the extent of a full-size brick. The normalized volume size is: Ec(\vec{b}) = \frac{ec(\vec{b})}{\max\{ex^b, ey^b, ez^b\}} Algorithm Steps: 1. Subdivision: Subdivide the volume dataset into bricks using a kd-tree to ensure convex partitions. 2. Assignment: Assign bricks to render nodes in the cluster. 3. Request: The viewer sends a render request containing necessary setup information to a designated master node. 4. Broadcast: The master node broadcasts the request to all render nodes via MPI. 5. Raycasting: Each render node raycasts its assigned bricks independently on its GPU. Vertex Shader: Computes ray direction vectors and passes them as additional texture coordinates to the fragment shader. This avoids recomputing directions in the fragment shader and ensures correct interpolation across brick boundaries. Fragment Shader: Performs raycasting within texture space [0,1] for each brick. Sampling Distance Adjustment: The user-defined sampling distance d must be scaled depending on the number of bricks to prevent an increase in the total number of sampling points, as raycasting happens in normalized texture space per brick. 6. Compositing: Nodes send their rendered images to a compositing node (or the viewer). Compositing is performed in software using the Direct-Send communication scheme. Empty-Space Skipping: An sl-sparse system based on the projection of bounding boxes is used to prevent blending empty pixels and mitigate glReadPixels performance issues. 7. Transfer: The final image is sent to the viewer. Compression: The image may be compressed using LZO real-time compression before transmission over the "last mile" (cluster to viewer). Computation time is extremely low, and compressed size is typically ~10% of the original. Transfer Methods: 1. Collect all images on one node and send one large package (uses fast interconnect, efficient for slow last-mile). 2. Send partial images directly from each node to the viewer (less idle time, but n smaller packages). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distributedvolumeraycasting(volumedata, cameraparams, Bx, By, Bz, d): # 1. Subdivision: Subdivide volume into bricks using a kd-tree for convex partitions # Source does not specify kd-tree implementation; standard spatial partitioning assumed. bricks = [(bx, by, bz) for bx in range(Bx) for by in range(By) for bz in range(Bz)] # 2. Assignment: Assign bricks to render nodes numnodes = len(bricks) rendernodes = [[] for in range(numnodes)] for i, brick in enumerate(bricks): rendernodes[i % numnodes].append(brick) # 3. Request & 4. Broadcast: Viewer sends request to master, master broadcasts via MPI masternode = rendernodes[0] request = {"camera": cameraparams, "bricks": bricks, "d": d} # MPI broadcast abstracted as per source description # 5. Parallel Raycasting: Each node raycasts assigned bricks independently noderesults = [] for nodeidx, nodebricks in enumerate(rendernodes): nodeimages = [] for brick in nodebricks: bx, by, bz = brick B = (Bx, By, Bz) S = (volumedata.Sx, volumedata.Sy, volumedata.Sz) # Compute brick slice counts def calcslices(c, bc, Bc, Sc): return math.ceil(Sc / Bc) if bc < Bc - 1 else Sc - (Bc - 1) math.ceil(Sc / Bc) Sb = tuple(calcslices(dim, bc, Bc, Sc) for dim, (bc, Bc, Sc) in enumerate(zip(brick, B, S))) # Overlap handling: replicate adjacent slice, shift texture by half texel tildes = tuple(s + 1 if b < B - 1 else s for s, b, B in zip(Sb, brick, B)) textureshift = 0.5 # half texel width # Sampling distance scaling: scale d by number of bricks to prevent increased sampling points totalbricks = Bx By Bz adjustedd = d / math.sqrt(totalbricks) # Standard scaling heuristic implied by source # Vertex shader computes ray direction, passes as texture coords # Source states vertex shader computes ray direction and passes it as texture coordinates. raydir = computeraydirection(cameraparams, brick) # Fragment shader raycasts in texture space [0,1] # Source states raycasting happens in texture space [0,1]. Standard raymarching loop. image = raycastbrick(volumedata, brick, Sb, tildes, textureshift, adjustedd, raydir) nodeimages.append(image) # 6. Compositing: Software compositing using Direct-Send # Empty-space skipping via sl-sparse bounding box projection composited = softwarecompositedirectsend(nodeimages) noderesults.append(composited) # 7. Transfer: Send final image to viewer # Method 1: Collect on one node, send large package finalimage = softwarecompositedirectsend(noderesults) # 8. Compression: LZO compression on "last mile" (cluster to viewer) # Computation time extremely low, size ~10% of original compressedimage = lzocompress(finalimage) return compressedimage def computeraydirection(cameraparams, brick): # Standard vertex shader operation: transforms view ray through camera matrix return (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) def raycastbrick(vol, brick, Sb, tildes, shift, d, raydir): # Standard fragment shader operation: marches ray in [0,1] texture space # Accumulates color/opacity using tri-linear interpolation with overlap shift return [0.0] 100 def softwarecompositedirectsend(images): # Standard software compositing: blends images using Direct-Send scheme return [0.0] 100 def lzocompress(data): # Standard LZO compression algorithm call return data Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and sampling points, distributed across N nodes. The sampling distance must be scaled with the number of bricks to keep the total sampling cost constant. Memory Complexity: Each node stores only its assigned bricks. Overlap slices increase local memory usage slightly. Performance: Compositing in software avoids the performance penalty of glReadPixels and hardware blending of empty pixels. LZO compression adds negligible computation time while reducing bandwidth usage by ~90%. Strengths: Scalability across cluster nodes; efficient use of fast interconnects for internal compositing; reduced bandwidth requirements for the final image transfer. Limitations: Requires MPI infrastructure and software compositing logic; communication overhead between nodes and viewer; potential load imbalance if bricks vary significantly in complexity (though convex partitioning helps). When to use: Large volume datasets that exceed single-GPU memory or compute capacity; environments with cluster infrastructure and MPI support. The method was introduced in the paper "Optimized volume raycasting for graphics-hardware-based cluster systems" (2006). It addresses the limitations of single-GPU raycasting by leveraging cluster computing. The approach builds on earlier CPU-based empty-space-skipping techniques [Lev90] but adapts them for GPU hardware and distributed software compositing. name: GPU-Driven Architecture
head: GPU-Driven Rendering
body: GPU-Driven Architecture is a rendering paradigm where the residency octree and the mixed-resolution multi-volume renderer are fully implemented on the GPU, while the CPU handles only high-level orchestration. It minimizes CPU-to-GPU data transfer bottlenecks by keeping buffer copies small and limiting cache misses per frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: High-level rendering commands from the CPU, brick data streamed from a server, and the current camera/view state. Output: The final rendered image frame. Data Structures: Residency Octree: Stored entirely in GPU memory. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Brick Cache: A GPU-side buffer holding active volume bricks. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. CPU Orchestration: The CPU initializes the rendering context and dispatches rendering and memory management commands to the GPU. 2. Ray-Guided Traversal: The GPU executes the renderer; during ray traversal through the residency octree, if a node is missing from the GPU cache, it generates a request for the missing data to be streamed in from the server. This makes the method ray-guided. 3. CPU Request Handling: The CPU receives brick requests generated by the GPU traversal and forwards them to the server. 4. Data Upload: The CPU uploads the bricks received from the server to the GPU. 5. Rendering: The GPU continues rendering using the newly uploaded bricks. Parameters: Global Cache Miss Limit: A global limit on the number of recorded cache misses per frame is specified to keep buffer copies from the GPU to the CPU small. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and boundary conditions are not detailed in the sources. Excessive cache misses can cause performance degradation due to increased CPU-GPU communication. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cpuorchestrate(): while renderingactive: # 1. CPU dispatches rendering and memory management commands to GPU gpu.executecommands() # 2. CPU forwards brick requests to server and uploads received bricks requests = gpu.collectbrickrequests() for req in requests: data = fetchfromserver(req) # Not detailed in sources gpu.upload(data) def gpurenderer(): for ray in rays: # 3. Ray-guided traversal through residency octree node = traverseoctree(ray) # Not detailed in sources if node is None: # 4. Missing node generates a request for missing data streamed from server gpu.submitbrickrequest(nodeid) # Not detailed in sources else: # 5. Continue rendering with newly uploaded bricks samplevolume(ray, node.brick) # Not detailed in sources The CUDA Raymarching Pipeline is a rendering architecture where the majority of processing, including computational kernels and rendering contexts, resides on the GPU device. This design eliminates data transfer and API call bottlenecks between the host CPU and the device GPU, which are common in traditional raster engines where the host controls data assembly via draw calls. It builds on GPU-Driven Architecture by fully implementing the residency octree and renderer on the GPU, while the CPU handles only high-level orchestration such as loading data and switching contexts. A GPU architecture designed for Sphere Tracing that uses independent cores rather than multi-ALU SIMD with lockstepping, handling threading natively via a storage manager. It differs from sibling architectures like the CUDA Raymarching Pipeline by replacing warp-based scheduling with a global double-ended queue managed by a storage manager, allowing arbitrary thread spawning and termination. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Minimizes CPU-to-GPU data transfer bottlenecks by limiting cache misses per frame. Strengths: Reduced CPU overhead and efficient handling of large datasets via ray-guided streaming. Limitations: Requires careful management of cache misses to avoid excessive CPU-GPU communication. When to use: Suitable for large-scale volume rendering where data cannot fit entirely in GPU memory and streaming is necessary. When not to use: Not suitable for small datasets where the overhead of orchestration outweighs the benefits. The GPU-Driven Architecture is part of a multi-channel page-table hierarchy system for volume rendering. It moves rendering logic entirely to the GPU to improve performance and scalability. name: CUDA Raymarching Pipeline
head: Full GPU-Based FVR Pipeline, GPU-based pre-processing (CUDA)
body: The CUDA Raymarching Pipeline is a rendering architecture where the majority of processing, including computational kernels and rendering contexts, resides on the GPU device. This design eliminates data transfer and API call bottlenecks between the host CPU and the device GPU, which are common in traditional raster engines where the host controls data assembly via draw calls. It builds on GPU-Driven Architecture by fully implementing the residency octree and renderer on the GPU, while the CPU handles only high-level orchestration such as loading data and switching contexts. It addresses the performance drop on discrete GPUs caused by CPU-to-GPU memory transfers and excessive draw calls by executing pre-processing tasks like partitioning and packing concurrently on the GPU. It differs from Custom GPU Architecture for Sphere Tracing by integrating Fourier-based volume rendering steps directly into the GPU pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset (loaded on CPU), light and object data (stored in vectors on host CPU). Output: Final reconstructed image displayed on screen. Data Structures: Host Memory: Vectors for light and object data; volume dataset before upload. Device Global Memory: Volume dataset, spectral volume (complex array), intermediate images. Device Texture Memory: 3D texture for spectral volume, 2D texture for projection-slice and final image. Pixel Buffer Object (PBO): Shared buffer between CUDA and OpenGL contexts to avoid CPU round-trips. Frame Buffer Object (FBO): Attached to a 2D texture for off-screen rendering. Numbered Steps: 1. Host Initialization: Store light and object data in vectors on the host CPU. Load the volume dataset on the CPU. 2. Data Upload: Copy light and object data from host memory to device memory once per frame. Copy the volume directly to GPU global memory using cudaMemcpy. Upload textures into VRAM. 3. Context Setup: Create and activate a CUDA context on the GPU. Expose uploaded textures using a texture object descriptor. 4. Spatial Centering: Execute the FFTSHIFT3DREAL kernel to center the 3D spatial volume. 5. 3D FFT: Invoke CUDAFFT3D to obtain the 3D frequency spectrum of the input spatial volume. 6. Spectral Centering: Invoke FFTSHIFT3DCOMPLEX to center the spectral volume at the origin of k-space. 7. Format Conversion: Convert the complex array to a format compatible with an OpenGL 3D texture (two components) using the REPACKARRAY kernel. 8. Interoperability Setup: Solve the interoperability issue between CUDA and OpenGL by using an OpenGL Pixel Buffer Object (PBO) registered in the CUDA memory space to share the spectral array. This avoids copying data back to the CPU and re-uploading, which is inefficient. 9. Projection-Slice Extraction: Map the shared spectral array to the OpenGL off-screen rendering context for projection-slice extraction. Extract the projection-slice via intersection with a proxy quadrant (same as hybrid method). 10. 2D Texture Packing: Pack the projection-slice into a 2D texture attached to an FBO. 11. CUDA Mapping: Map the 2D texture to a CUDA array for processing. 12. Resampling: Execute the RESAMPLESLICE kernel on the GPU to resample the slice. 13. Inverse 2D FFT: Execute the CUDAFFT2D kernel to perform the inverse 2D FFT. 14. Image Shifting: Execute the FFTSHIFT2DREAL kernel to shift the resulting image. 15. Final Display: Pack the final image into a 2D OpenGL texture and upload to GPU memory. Activate the on-screen rendering context and display the texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Data Upload # Copy light and object data to device memory (once per frame) dlightdata = allocatedevicememorylike(lightdata) copyhosttodevice(dlightdata, lightdata) dobjectdata = allocatedevicememorylike(objectdata) copyhosttodevice(dobjectdata, objectdata) # Copy volume to GPU global memory dvolume = allocatedevicememory(volumedata.shape) copyhosttodevice(dvolume, volumedata) # 3. Context Setup # Create and activate a CUDA context on the GPU cudacontext = createcudacontext() activatecudacontext(cudacontext) # 4. Spatial Centering # Execute the FFTSHIFT3DREAL kernel to center the 3D spatial volume dvolumecentered = allocatedevicememorylike(dvolume) executekernel(fftshift3dreal, dvolume, dvolumecentered) # 5. 3D FFT # Invoke CUDAFFT3D to obtain the 3D frequency spectrum dspectrum = executefft3d(dvolumecentered) # 6. Spectral Centering # Invoke FFTSHIFT3DCOMPLEX to center the spectral volume at the origin of k-space dspectrumcentered = allocatedevicememorylike(dspectrum) executekernel(fftshift3dcomplex, dspectrum, dspectrumcentered) # 7. Format Conversion # Convert the complex array to a format compatible with an OpenGL 3D texture (two components) using the REPACKARRAY kernel dspectrumrepacked = executekernel(repackarray, dspectrumcentered) # 8. Interoperability Setup # Solve the interoperability issue by using an OpenGL Pixel Buffer Object (PBO) registered in the CUDA memory space to share the spectral array pbo = createpboregisteredwithcuda() copydevicetodevice(pbo, dspectrumrepacked) # 9. Projection-Slice Extraction # Map the shared spectral array to the OpenGL off-screen rendering context for projection-slice extraction gloffscreencontext = createoffscreencontext() activateglcontext(gloffscreencontext) # Map PBO to OpenGL texture gltexture3d = create3dtexturefrompbo(pbo) # Extract the projection-slice via intersection with a proxy quadrant (same as hybrid method) bindfbo(fbo) bindtexture(gltexture3d) drawproxyquadrant() unbindfbo() # 10. 2D Texture Packing # Projection-slice is now in FBO's attached 2D texture d2dtextureref = gettexturereference(fbo) # 11. CUDA Mapping # Map the 2D texture to a CUDA array for processing cudaarray2d = mapgltexturetocudaarray(d2dtextureref) # 12. Resampling # Execute the RESAMPLESLICE kernel on the GPU to resample the slice dresampledslice = executekernel(resampleslice, cudaarray2d) # 13. Inverse 2D FFT # Execute the CUDAFFT2D kernel to perform the inverse 2D FFT dimagefreq = executefft2d(dresampledslice, inverse=True) # 14. Image Shifting # Execute the FFTSHIFT2DREAL kernel to shift the resulting image dimageshifted = allocatedevicememorylike(dimagefreq) executekernel(fftshift2dreal, dimagefreq, dimageshifted) # 15. Final Display # Pack the final image into a 2D OpenGL texture and upload to GPU memory gltexture2dfinal = create2dtexturefromcudaarray(dimageshifted) # Activate the on-screen rendering context and display the texture glonscreencontext = createonscreencontext() activateglcontext(glonscreencontext) displaytexture(gltexture2dfinal) def allocatedevicememorylike(data): return allocatedevicememory(data.shape) def allocatedevicememory(shape): # Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CUDA address space arrays cannot be accessed directly by OpenGL. Copying back to CPU and re-uploading is inefficient. This is solved by using an OpenGL PBO registered in the CUDA memory space. Performance drop on discrete GPUs caused by CPU-to-GPU memory transfers and excessive draw calls is addressed by keeping geometric data entirely resident in video memory. Strengths and Limitations: Eliminates data transfer and API call bottlenecks from host to device. The hybrid implementation lacked interactivity due to bottlenecks, which this full GPU-based pipeline aims to suppress. When to Use: When minimizing data transfer overhead is critical and the entire pipeline can be executed on the GPU. When Not to Use: When CPU-based control is required for complex scene management not easily offloaded to GPU. Origin: The pipeline was developed to address bottlenecks in raymarching engines, which were largely unexplored in terms of pipeline architecture compared to ray tracing and raster engines. It was presented in the context of High Performance GPU-Based Fourier Volume Rendering. History and Development: The approach reuses OpenGL rendering contexts from a previous hybrid implementation but reimplements the computational context in CUDA. It utilizes CUFFT library functions for FFT operations. Where it is Used: Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR). name: Custom GPU Architecture for Sphere Tracing
head: Thread Execution Model
body: A GPU architecture designed for Sphere Tracing that uses independent cores rather than multi-ALU SIMD with lockstepping, handling threading natively via a storage manager. It differs from sibling architectures like the CUDA Raymarching Pipeline by replacing warp-based scheduling with a global double-ended queue managed by a storage manager, allowing arbitrary thread spawning and termination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Immutable instruction memory (shared across all cores), immutable data memory (shared across all cores), and a global storage manager. Output: Frame buffer (via pushf instruction). Data Structures: 1. Storage Manager: Implemented as a double-ended queue (deque). It holds all non-running threads and supports coarse-grained execution priority control. 2. Core State: Each core maintains: Instruction Pointer (IP): Points to the current instruction in the immutable instruction memory. Mutable Registers: 16 registers per thread. DFU Stack: A stack for arithmetic operations within the Data Flow Unit (DFU). 3. Thread State: A thread consists of an instruction pointer and 16 mutable registers. Registers are loaded on start, saved on pause, and copied when spawning a child. Instruction Set: val: Assigns immediate values into the DFU (currently used for assigning distance function IDs). setval: Changes the value of a register. pack: Reads the value of a register. pushq: Spawns a new thread. Copies all 16 registers and pushes them onto the global queue (storage manager) for later execution by any core. drop: Terminates the current thread and discards all registers. pushf: Terminates the current thread and sends the pixel pointer (register r1) and color register (r2) to the frame buffer. next and accum: Accelerate finding the minimum distance for a set of distance functions using a built-in accumulator. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The storage manager is initialized as an empty double-ended queue. All cores are idle. 2. Dispatch: The storage manager selects a core that is ready to receive a thread. If multiple cores are ready, one is chosen arbitrarily. A thread is popped from the storage manager and sent to the core. 3. Execution: The core loads the thread's 16 registers and instruction pointer. The core executes instructions from the immutable instruction memory. Arithmetic operations use the DFU stack. Control flow is managed via pushq, drop, and pushf. 4. Thread Spawning (pushq): When pushq is executed, the core copies the current state (16 registers + IP) and pushes it to the storage manager. The current thread continues execution. 5. Thread Termination (drop): The thread is removed from the core, registers are discarded, and the core requests a new thread from the storage manager. 6. Frame Buffer Output (pushf): The thread is removed from the core. The values in r1 (pixel pointer) and r2 (color) are written to the frame buffer. The core requests a new thread. 7. Distance Function Acceleration: The next and accum instructions are used to find the minimum distance among a set of distance functions, reducing the size of individual distance function code. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import collections class StorageManager: def init(self): self.queue = collections.deque() def push(self, threaddata): self.queue.append(threaddata) def pop(self): return self.queue.popleft() if self.queue else None class Core: def init(self, storagemanager, instructionmemory, datamemory): self.storagemanager = storagemanager self.instructionmemory = instructionmemory self.datamemory = datamemory self.ip = 0 self.registers = [0] 16 self.dfustack = [] self.isbusy = False def execute(self): if not self.isbusy: thread = self.storagemanager.pop() if thread: self.ip, self.registers = thread self.isbusy = True self.runthread() def runthread(self): while self.isbusy: instr = self.instructionmemory[self.ip] self.ip += 1 op = instr['op'] if op == 'setval': self.registers[instr['r']] = instr['v'] elif op == 'pack': self.dfustack.append(self.registers[instr['r']]) elif op == 'val': self.dfustack.append(instr['v']) elif op == 'pushq': self.storagemanager.push((self.ip, self.registers.copy())) elif op == 'drop': self.isbusy = False self.registers = [0] 16 self.ip = 0 self.execute() elif op == 'pushf': framebuffer.write(self.registers[1], self.registers[2]) self.isbusy = False self.registers = [0] 16 self.ip = 0 self.execute() elif op == 'next': pass elif op == 'accum': pass else: # Arithmetic operations use the DFU stack. Specific instructions not given in the sources. pass class FrameBuffer: def write(self, pixelptr, color): pass storage = StorageManager() fb = FrameBuffer() cores = [Core(storage, instructionmem, datamem) for in range(N)] Parameters: Registers per thread: 16. Memory: Immutable instruction and data memory mirrored across all cores. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary Core Selection: If multiple cores are ready, one is chosen arbitrarily, which may affect performance predictability. Instruction Predictability: The instruction set is restrictive to make instruction memory accesses predictable. Square Root Precision: Calculating distances is integral to the algorithm, requiring a robust square root implementation for performance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Native threading support, coarse-grained priority control via deque, predictable instruction memory access, reduced code size for distance functions via next/accum. Limitations: Arbitrary core selection, potentially complex hardware implementation for storage manager and DFU. When to use: When implementing a custom GPU architecture specifically optimized for Sphere Tracing with native threading requirements. The architecture was described in a thesis evaluating the Sphere Tracing algorithm and a GPU designed to run it. It was written in CλaSH, a functional hardware description language based on Haskell. The design focuses on handling threading natively with light-weight threads, using a storage manager for scheduling. name: Pinned Memory Data Transfer
head: cudaMallocHost, Page-locked Host Memory Transfer, Pinned Memory Optimization
body: Pinned Memory Data Transfer uses page-locked host memory allocated via cudaMallocHost or cudaHostAlloc to enable direct DMA transfers between the CPU and GPU, improving host-to-device and device-to-host throughput. In legacy CUDA versions prior to 7.x, it served as the explicit mechanism for fast data movement before the introduction of CUDA-managed unified memory. Inputs: Host-side data buffer (e.g., mesh vertices); transfer size in bytes. Outputs: Device-side buffer populated with data; host-side pinned memory handle. Data Structures: 1. Host Pinned Buffer: Allocated via cudaHostAlloc or cudaMallocHost. Layout is contiguous in virtual memory. 2. Device Buffer: Allocated via cudaMalloc. Layout is contiguous in device global memory. 3. Transfer Descriptor: Not strictly required if using cudaMemcpyDefault, but logically represents the source pointer, destination pointer, and byte count. Steps: 1. Allocate Pinned Host Memory: Request page-locked memory from the CUDA runtime. This memory is not swappable by the OS. 2. Populate Host Data: Copy or generate the source data into the pinned host buffer. 3. Allocate Device Memory: Reserve space in GPU global memory. 4. Execute Transfer: Initiate the DMA transfer from the pinned host buffer to the device buffer using cudaMemcpyDefault. Formulas: Memory Constraint: Pinned memory consumes physical RAM that cannot be paged to disk. Parameters: cudaHostAllocDefault: Standard flag for pinned memory allocation. cudaMemcpyDefault: Transfer kind flag used to initiate the DMA operation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Exhaustion: Excessive use of pinned memory can starve the host OS of pageable memory, leading to system instability or thrashing. Alignment: Data should be aligned to cache line boundaries (typically 64 bytes) for optimal DMA performance. Legacy vs. Modern: In CUDA < 7.x, explicit pinned memory was the primary method for fast transfers. CUDA 7.x introduced unified memory as an alternative. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocatepinnedmemory(n): return [0] n # cudaHostAlloc def allocatedevicememory(n): return [0] n # cudaMalloc def freepinnedmemory(p): pass # cudaFreeHost def freedevicememory(p): pass # cudaFree def memcpy(dst, src, n): dst[:] = src[:] # cudaMemcpy hdata = allocatepinnedmemory(sizebytes) memcpy(hdata, sourcebuffer, sizebytes) ddata = allocatedevicememory(sizebytes) memcpy(ddata, hdata, sizebytes) # cudaMemcpyDefault freepinnedmemory(hdata) freedevicememory(ddata) Introduced in CUDA 7.x, it provides a transparent memory management system that automatically pages data between host and device. Allows the GPU to access host memory directly without copying. It is useful for small, irregular accesses but suffers from lower bandwidth than pinned memory transfers due to PCIe latency. Throughput: Improves host-to-device and device-to-host transfer rates compared to pageable memory. Latency: Setup latency is low, but the actual transfer is limited by PCIe bandwidth. Memory Cost: Consumes physical RAM that cannot be paged to disk. Use Case: Suitable for transferring structured data like triangle meshes to the GPU for processing. The technique was the primary method for explicit fast data movement in CUDA versions prior to 7.x, before the introduction of CUDA-managed unified memory. It remains relevant in legacy codebases and specific high-performance computing workflows where explicit control over host memory locking is required. wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, https://github.com/wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - Forceflow/cudavoxelizer: CUDA Voxelizer to convert polygon..., https://github.com/Forceflow/cudavoxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hardware Architectures Considerations
head: Hardware and Platform Specific Considerations
body: This article outlines the hardware constraints and architectural trends that dictate the efficiency of volume rendering and ray tracing implementations. It addresses the problem of mapping computational tasks to modern parallel hardware (CPUs and GPUs) by highlighting the trade-offs between compute intensity and memory latency. What sets this family apart is its focus on the physical limitations of execution units—such as restricted branching in GPU fragment programs and the unsuitability of complex traversal algorithms for GPUs—rather than just algorithmic complexity. The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores). Common principles include: 1. Thread Mapping: Assigning one or more threads to process specific data elements (e.g., one thread per pixel or one thread per voxel sample). 2. Memory Hierarchy Utilization: Leveraging global memory for large datasets, shared/local memory for intermediate results (reductions), and registers for per-thread state. 3. Synchronization: Managing concurrency conflicts using atomic operations, barriers, or spatial partitioning (tiles) to ensure data consistency without excessive serialization. 4. Data Parallelism: Performing identical operations on different data elements simultaneously, often requiring coalesced memory access patterns to maximize bandwidth. This family does not define specific algorithmic variants but rather establishes the hardware context for its children. Adapts ray casting for unstructured data on GPUs, requiring careful handling of the limited dependent texture fetch levels and branching restrictions. Leverages the streaming compute model and multi-core architecture of NVIDIA GPUs, emphasizing coalesced memory access and local memory maximization. A specific hardware-aware architecture that exploits the SIMD/MIMD settings mentioned in the background. Operates within the strict constraints of fragment programs, particularly the prohibition of data-dependent branching. Focuses on reducing memory accesses through compact data structures, a key requirement for the streaming compute model. Implements ray tracing on programmable graphics hardware, addressing the challenge that traversal algorithms are generally unsuited for GPU computation. Utilizes GPU compute capabilities, navigating the limitations of branching and memory access patterns inherent to GPU fragment programs. The current trend in CPU and GPU hardware design is towards three concepts: a streaming compute model, vector-like SIMD units, and multi-core architectures. These new architectures combine more and more parallel computations, where fast local computations are contrasted with slow memory access times. This hardware reality leads to favoring methods that reduce memory accesses (e.g., compact data structures, compression, multiresolution), maximize local memory accesses, and can be easily parallelized, especially in SIMD/MIMD settings. For example, memory layouts (i.e., bricking [PPL99]) should have big and bigger importance in order to improve performance, especially for the streaming compute model supported by nowadays hardware. Moreover, the current trend is to implement rendering methods on GPUs. However, GPUs present some limitations. For example, fragment programs are not allowed to perform data-dependent branching and have a more restricted memory access (i.e., the number of levels of dependent texture fetch is limited). Purcell et al. [PBMH02] showed that it is possible to do ray tracing with programmable graphics hardware. Further works have been made by using different data structures such as kd-tree or BVH. Results showed that ray tracing so far does not fully utilize GPU. The traversal algorithm is unsuited for GPU computation, and branching is unavoidable. Today, for ray tracing, CPUs seem to be more suitable than GPUs. name: Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) Orchestration
head: Blelloch Scan, Exclusive/Inclusive Scan via Ping-Pong, Parallel Prefix Sum, Prefix Sum (Scan), Up-Sweep Down-Sweep Scan, Work-Efficient GPU Scan
body: Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) Orchestration computes prefix sums of an input array on the GPU using a multi-timestep iterative reduction strategy with a ping-pong buffer swap. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating data (such as vertex counts or fragment indices) into a sequential format for subsequent parallel processing steps like stream compaction or indirect dispatch. Unlike naive iterative approaches that may require multiple kernel launches per level or fixed-size assumptions, this orchestration explicitly manages the up-sweep and down-sweep phases of a work-efficient tree-based scan across discrete timesteps, handling arbitrary input sizes via padding and ensuring memory consistency through strict barrier synchronization between ping-pong buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array I of N elements (typically integers or floats) representing values to be summed. Output: An array O of prefix sums. The method can produce either an exclusive scan (O[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} I[j] with O[0]=0) or an inclusive scan (O[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i} I[j]), depending on post-processing or specific kernel configuration. Data Structures: 1. Ping-Pong Buffers (prefixSumPingBuffer, prefixSumPongBuffer): Two storage buffers (e.g., std430 in Vulkan or cudaBuffer in CUDA) of size equal to the padded input length (next power of two). They hold intermediate results during the up-sweep and down-sweep phases and are swapped each iteration with explicit read/write barriers to prevent race conditions. 2. Push Constant (timestep): A 32-bit integer indicating the current iteration step of the scan algorithm, used to determine the stride and operation within the kernel. 3. Host Buffer (totalSumBufferHost): A host-accessible buffer used to retrieve the final total sum from the last element (N-1) of the active ping-pong buffer after computation completes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Padding: Pad the input array size N to the next power of two, N{p2}. 2. Initialization: Allocate prefixSumPingBuffer and prefixSumPongBuffer of size N{p2}. Copy input data to prefixSumPingBuffer and zero-initialize prefixSumPongBuffer. 3. Iteration Count: Calculate the number of timesteps required: T = \lceil \log2(N) \rceil. 4. Loop over Timesteps (t = 0 to T-1): a. Dispatch: Launch a compute shader/kernel with workgroup size 256 \times 1 \times 1 and grid size \lceil N{p2} / 256 \rceil. Pass timestep = t as a push constant. b. Kernel Execution: Each thread computes its global index idx = \text{gl\GlobalInvocationID.x}. Bounds Check: If idx \ge N{p2}, return immediately. Update Logic: If t is even: if idx < 2^t, dst[idx] = src[idx]; else dst[idx] = src[idx] + src[idx - 2^t]. If t is odd: if idx < 2^t, src[idx] = dst[idx]; else src[idx] = dst[idx] + dst[idx - 2^t]. c. Swap Buffers: Swap prefixSumPingBuffer and prefixSumPongBuffer. Apply synchronization barriers matching the timestep parity to prevent GPU read/write conflicts. 5. Finalization: Copy the final sum from the last element (N{p2}-1) of the active buffer to totalSumBufferHost using a buffer copy region. Convert to an exclusive scan if needed by shifting the inclusive result right by one position and setting O[0]=0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def scankernelstep(src, dst, timestep, np2): stride = 1 << timestep for idx in range(np2): if idx >= np2: continue if timestep % 2 == 0: if idx < stride: dst[idx] = src[idx] else: dst[idx] = src[idx] + src[idx - stride] else: if idx < stride: src[idx] = dst[idx] else: src[idx] = dst[idx] + dst[idx - stride] return src, dst def parallelprefixsumorchestration(inputarray, N): if N <= 0: return [], 0 # 1. Padding np2 = 1 while np2 < N: np2 = 2 # 2. Initialization src = list(inputarray) + [0] (np2 - N) dst = [0] np2 # 3. Iteration Count iters = math.ceil(math.log2(N)) # 4. Loop over Timesteps for t in range(iters): src, dst = scankernelstep(src, dst, t, np2) # Swap ping-pong buffers src, dst = dst, src # Apply synchronization barriers here in real implementation # 5. Finalization totalsum = src[np2 - 1] # Optional: Convert to exclusive scan # exclusivescan = [0] + src[:-1] return src, totalsum Parameters: timestep: Integer push constant, current iteration step t. numGroups: Number of compute shader workgroups, calculated as \lceil N{p2} / 256 \rceil. iters: Number of iterations, \lceil \log2(N) \rceil. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Power-of-Two Inputs: Must be padded to the next power of two. Elements beyond N should be initialized to 0 to avoid affecting the sum. Barrier Ordering: The ping-pong swap direction and barrier placement must strictly match the timestep parity to prevent GPU read/write conflicts. Power Calculation: Using a naive loop for 2^t is inefficient; bit shifting (1 << t) should be used. Bounds Checking: Threads with idx \ge N{p2} must return immediately to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Solves the duplicate vertex calculation problem in GPU-based parallel isosurface extraction by using an exclusive prefix sum to compute correct global vertex indices for vertices found by parallel threads. Unlike sibling methods that may only apply stream compaction to triangles, this approach applies scan-based indexing to both vertices and triangles, ensuring unique global indices without expensive post-processing merging. A parallel sorting algorithm designed for GPU execution that avoids inter-workgroup spin-waiting by using a hierarchical Blelloch scan to compute element positions, ensuring consistent behavior across heterogeneous GPU schedulers. It differs from naive parallel prefix sum approaches by explicitly decoupling the global position calculation from the scatter phase via a two-level hierarchical scan, allowing each level to be executed as an independent compute dispatch without cross-workgroup polling. A parallel shell list compaction method used in GPU-based isosurface extraction that replaces sequential processing by thread 0 with a parallel prefix sum approach. It coordinates with the octree to derive block offsets from the first active octree nodes (AOs) in each shell. Computes an output array O from an input array I such that each element O[i] is the sum of all input elements preceding index i (O[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} I[j]), with O[0]=0. In volume rendering, this primitive maps parallel voxel culling decisions to sequential indices in a compacted list, allowing culled voxels to be removed in parallel without data races. It differs from its siblings by serving as the fundamental indexing engine for stream compaction and hierarchical subdivision, whereas CUDA-based Exclusive Prefix Sum for Vertex Indexing targets specific vertex buffer layouts and Naive Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) lacks the work-efficient tree-based optimization. A GPU-based algorithm for computing the inclusive prefix sum of an array using global memory and multiple kernel invocations. It serves as a baseline implementation compatible with arbitrary input sizes, distinguishing itself from work-efficient variants by its iterative, level-by-level reduction approach which results in higher computational work (O(n \log n)) but simpler synchronization logic within each kernel launch. Unlike in-place tree-based methods, it avoids race conditions by double-buffering data between two device arrays across iterations. A two-pass GPU compute system that gathers visible splat counts per proxy and computes prefix sums to generate indirect dispatch and draw arguments for global Phase-3 rendering passes. It aggregates per-proxy visibility data into a global array and prepares execution parameters for subsequent geometry generation and indexing stages. Python-bound CUDA functions for chunked inclusive/exclusive prefix sums and products that support normalization and backward passes for gradients. Parameters include chunkstarts (start indices for each chunk), chunkcnts (counts of elements in each chunk), inputs (input tensor), normalize (flag to normalize the output), and backward (flag to compute backward pass/gradients). Time Complexity: O(\log N) parallel steps for the tree-based scan, with O(N) work per step distributed across threads. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input and output arrays, plus O(N) for the ping-pong buffers. Performance: Work-efficient variants (Blelloch) perform 2N additions for up-sweep and 2N for down-sweep, totaling 4N operations. Naive iterative approaches serve as a baseline with higher computational work (O(n \log n)) but simpler synchronization logic. Strengths: Handles arbitrary input sizes, work-efficient, suitable for GPU architectures with shared memory and barriers. Limitations: Requires padding to power of two, complex synchronization logic, potential for race conditions if barriers are mismanaged. When to Use: When stream compaction, indirect dispatch, or parallel aggregation is needed in volume rendering or isosurface extraction. When Not to Use: For small arrays where CPU sequential scan is faster, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained and O(N) extra storage is prohibitive. The parallel prefix sum is a fundamental primitive in parallel computing, with origins in the 1970s. The Blelloch scan algorithm, introduced by Guy E. Blelloch in 1990, is a work-efficient method using up-sweep and down-sweep phases. It has become a standard for GPU implementations due to its balance of work efficiency and memory access patterns. In volume rendering, it is used for tasks like fragment list compaction, vertex indexing, and indirect draw call generation.
