name: CUDA-based Exclusive Prefix Sum for Vertex Indexing
head: Exclusive scan vertex indexing, Scan-based vertex deduplication
body: This method solves the duplicate vertex calculation problem in GPU-based parallel isosurface extraction by using an exclusive prefix sum (scan) to compute correct global vertex indices for vertices found by parallel threads. Unlike sibling methods that may only apply stream compaction to triangles, this approach applies scan-based indexing to both vertices and triangles, ensuring that vertices identified by different threads are assigned unique, non-overlapping global indices without requiring expensive post-processing merging. Inputs: A pair of volume slices (lower and upper) of size W \times H (typically 512 \times 512 to 2048 \times 2048). A grid of threads, where each thread processes one cell in the slice pair. Outputs: Compacted arrays of unique vertex coordinates (resvert) and triangle counts (restrinumvect). Global vertex indices assigned to each detected vertex. The method requires five sets of matrices for vertex coordinates and labels, and corresponding scan output matrices, plus triangle storage structures. All matrices are of size W \times H, corresponding to the number of cells in the slice pair. 1. Vertex Coordinate Matrices: xvert, yvert: Store coordinates for edges along the X and Y axes of the lower slice. Xvert, Yvert: Store coordinates for edges along the X and Y axes of the upper slice. zvert: Store coordinates for edges along the Z axis (connecting lower and upper slices). 2. Label Matrices: xlabel, ylabel, Xlabel, Ylabel, zlabel: Corresponding label matrices for the coordinate matrices above. Initially, all labels are set to 1 to indicate vertex presence. 3. Scan Output Matrices: xscan, yscan, Xscan, Yscan, zscan: Output of the exclusive prefix sum operation on the label matrices. These serve as input for stream compaction and index calculation. 4. Triangle Storage: trinumvect: Stores the number of triangles created for each cell. restrinumvect: Compacted array storing the number of created triangles. Triangle array size is proportional to slice size, as at most 5 triangles are created per cell. 1. Initialization: For each cell in the slice pair, a dedicated thread executes the VerticesCalc kernel. The thread identifies vertices on the cell's edges and writes their coordinates to the respective xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, and zvert matrices. It also writes a label of 1 to the corresponding label matrix (xlabel, etc.) to mark the vertex's presence. 2. Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan): Perform an exclusive prefix sum operation on each of the five label matrices (xlabel through zlabel) using the CUDPP library. The output is stored in the corresponding scan matrices (xscan through zscan). The exclusive scan is defined as: V{out}[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} V{in}[j] Example: If xlabel contains \{5, 6, 2, 4, 0, 2, 0, 1\}, then xscan contains \{0, 5, 11, 13, 17, 17, 19, 19\}. 3. Index Assignment: The value in the scan matrix at a given cell's position indicates the number of vertices of that type found in all preceding cells. This value serves as the base global index for the vertices found in the current cell. If thread k finds N vertices, and the scan output for its cell is S, the global indices for these vertices are S, S+1, \dots, S+N-1. The total number of vertices is obtained by summing the last elements of the input label vector and the output scan vector (e.g., 1 + 19 = 20). 4. Stream Compaction (Vertices): Execute the VerticesCompact kernel to compact the vertex coordinate matrices into a single contiguous array resvert. The scan output matrices (xscan through zscan) are used to determine the write positions in resvert. Vertices are stored in a specific order: xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, zvert. The global index of a vertex in the final mesh is calculated by summing the counts of previous edge types. For example, if 100 vertices were found previously, and the current cell has 10 X-edges, 20 Y-edges, and 7 Z-edges, the first Z-vertex gets global index 100 + 10 + 20 = 130. However, its position in the compacted resvert vector is based on local offsets within the current cell's contribution, specifically position 30 (10+20) relative to the start of the current cell's block in the compacted array. 5. Stream Compaction (Triangles): Execute a second compaction kernel to process the trinumvect array into restrinumvect. This step also uses the scan operation to process result vectors and produce smaller vectors containing only the non-empty elements. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def VerticesCalc(celli, cellj, volumelower, volumeupper, xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, zvert, xlabel, ylabel, Xlabel, Ylabel, zlabel): # Determine vertex presence on each of the 12 edges of the cell # (Isosurface criteria not specified in sources) # Write coordinates and label 1 if vertex exists, else 0 if vertexexistsonlowerxedge: xvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) xlabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: xlabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonloweryedge: yvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) ylabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: ylabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonupperxedge: Xvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) Xlabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: Xlabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonupperyedge: Yvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) Ylabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: Ylabel[celli, cellj] = 0 if vertexexistsonzedge: zvert[celli, cellj] = computevertexcoord(...) zlabel[celli, cellj] = 1 else: zlabel[celli, cellj] = 0 def VerticesCompact(celli, cellj, xvert, yvert, Xvert, Yvert, zvert, xlabel, ylabel, Xlabel, Ylabel, zlabel, xscan, yscan, Xscan, Yscan, zscan, resvert): # Calculate base indices for this cell based on scan results basex = xscan[celli, cellj] basey = yscan[celli, cellj] baseX = Xscan[celli, cellj] baseY = Yscan[celli, cellj] basez = zscan[celli, cellj] # Determine how many vertices of each type were found in this cell countx = xlabel[celli, cellj] county = ylabel[celli, cellj] countX = Xlabel[celli, cellj] countY = Ylabel[celli, cellj] countz = zlabel[celli, cellj] # Calculate flat write position in resvert by summing all scan bases flatstart = basex + basey + baseX + baseY + basez offset = 0 # Write X vertices for k in range(countx): resvert[flatstart + offset] = xvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write Y vertices for k in range(county): resvert[flatstart + offset] = yvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write X (upper) vertices for k in range(countX): resvert[flatstart + offset] = Xvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write Y (upper) vertices for k in range(countY): resvert[flatstart + offset] = Yvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 # Write Z vertices for k in range(countz): resvert[flatstart + offset] = zvert[celli, cellj] offset += 1 def main(): # 1. Launch VerticesCalc kernel for all cells # Grid size: (W, H, 1) VerticesCalc<<<grid, block>>>(...) # 2. Perform Exclusive Prefix Sum on label matrices using CUDPP # CUDPPscan(xlabel, xlabel, WH, ADD) # CUDPPscan(ylabel, ylabel, WH, ADD) # CUDPPscan(Xlabel, Xlabel, WH, ADD) # CUDPPscan(Ylabel, Ylabel, WH, ADD) # CUDPPscan(zlabel, zlabel, WH, ADD) # 3. Launch VerticesCompact kernel VerticesCompact<<<grid, block>>>(...) # 4. Perform Stream Compaction for triangles (similar scan + compact steps) # (Implementation details for triangle compaction not specified in sources) Slice Size: Common dataset slice sizes are 512 \times 512 to 2048 \times 2048. Memory Occupancy: The auxiliary structures consume 78 to 1168 MB of GPU memory depending on slice size. Minimum GPU Memory: 512 MB is required to process 512 \times 512 slices. GPU Memory Limitation: The large size of auxiliary data structures for large slices (up to 1168 MB) necessitates processing one pair of slices at a time. Data Transfer Overhead: The effective number of vertices and triangles is much lower than the size of the data structures, leading to expensive data transfers. Stream compaction is critical to mitigate this. Search Structures: Search structures are disregarded because they also consume GPU memory, which is limited. Time Complexity: The method involves four kernels: two for vertex/triangle computation and two for stream compaction and scan operations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the slice size W \times H. For 512 \times 512 to 2048 \times 2048 slices, memory occupancy ranges from 78 to 1168 MB. Strengths: Solves the duplicate vertex calculation problem efficiently without post-processing merging. Reduces data transfer overhead via stream compaction. Compatible with standard CUDA devices with at least 512 MB of memory. Limitations: Memory-intensive, limiting the maximum slice size that can be processed at once. Data transfer between host and device remains a significant part of the execution time. When to Use: Suitable for GPU-based isosurface extraction where memory allows for processing slice pairs and high parallelism is desired. When Not to Use: Not suitable for volumes with very large slices that exceed available GPU memory, or when search structures are preferred despite memory costs. Origin: This method was introduced in the paper "A parallel isosurface extraction component for visualization pipelines executing on GPU clusters". Development: It extends previous work [25] which only used stream compaction for triangles, by applying it to both vertices and triangles to address duplicate vertex calculation. Usage: It is used in GPU-based visualization pipelines for isosurface extraction from volume data. name: Wait-Free Radix Sort
head: Hierarchical Blelloch Scan Sort
body: A parallel sorting algorithm designed for GPU execution that avoids inter-workgroup spin-waiting by using a hierarchical Blelloch scan to compute element positions, ensuring consistent behavior across heterogeneous GPU schedulers. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Global Accumulator + Compaction by eliminating cross-workgroup polling and busy-waits, which can degenerate into wasted cycles on devices without fixed scheduling guarantees. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes an array of N elements with 32-bit integer keys as input and produces the same elements sorted by key as output. It requires auxiliary storage buffers for tile sums and intermediate scan results, sized O(N/wg) where wg is the workgroup size. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains an indicator stream representing the presence of a specific digit value d for each element, a tile sums array of length N/wg storing the sum of counts for each workgroup tile, and prefix buffers storing the results of the upsweep and downsweep passes. Parameters: The radix size is fixed at 256 (8 bits per pass). A full 32-bit sort requires exactly 4 consecutive passes. The workgroup size wg is not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: The full 32-bit sort is performed by executing four consecutive passes of an 8-bit radix sort, starting from the least significant bits. In the k-th pass (k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}), the algorithm processes bits k \times 8 to (k + 1) \times 8 - 1 of the key. Each pass consists of three sequential steps: 1. Local Histogram: Each workgroup counts the frequencies of the current digit value d within its local elements. 2. Prefix Scan: A hierarchical Blelloch scan processes the histograms to compute the global base offset \text{base}d and the inter-workgroup prefix \text{prefix}{wg}. Forward Pass (Upsweep): Level l0 performs an exclusive scan inside each workgroup tile of size wg over the indicator stream for digit d, producing tile sums that form an array of length N/wg. Level l1 runs the same Blelloch scan on the tile sums array to obtain prefixes across tiles, and the process recurses until a single level remains. \text{base}d is read from the last level as the sum of counts of digits smaller than d. Backward Pass (Downsweep): The prefixes computed at level l1 are added back to their corresponding l0 tiles, and then to individual elements, yielding the inter-workgroup offset \text{prefix}{wg}. Each level is executed as an independent compute dispatch consuming the previous level's buffers, with only intra-workgroup barriers inside a tile. 3. Scatter: Each element is written to its new position \text{pos} in the sorted array. Formulas: The final position \text{pos} for an element originally at index i is calculated as: \text{pos} = \text{base}d + \text{rank}i where d is the specific digit value of the element, \text{base}d is the global offset equal to the total count of all elements with a digit value less than d, and \text{rank}i is the count of elements appearing before index i sharing the same digit value d. The rank \text{rank}i is decomposed into: \text{rank}i = \text{prefix}{wg} + \text{rank}{\text{local}i} where \text{prefix}{wg} is the inter-workgroup rank (total count of elements with digit d in all workgroups processed before the current one) and \text{rank}{\text{local}i} is the intra-workgroup rank (number of elements with digit d within the current workgroup before i). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def waitfreeradixsort(keys, values, N, wg): # 4 passes for 32-bit keys, processing LSB to MSB for k in range(4): # Extract 8-bit digit for each element digits = [(keys[i] >> (k 8)) & 0xFF for i in range(N)] # Step 1: Local Histogram # Each workgroup counts frequencies of digit d in its local elements localhistograms = [[0] 256 for in range(N // wg)] for i in range(N): localhistograms[i // wg][digits[i]] += 1 # Step 2: Prefix Scan (Hierarchical Blelloch) # Forward pass (upsweep) tilesums = [sum(hist) for hist in localhistograms] # Recursively scan tile sums until single level remains globalcounts = blellochupsweep(tilesums) # based is sum of counts of digits smaller than d baseoffsets = [sum(globalcounts[:d]) for d in range(256)] # Backward pass (downsweep) # Add prefixes from higher levels back to l0 tiles and elements interworkgroupprefixes = blellochdownsweep(localhistograms, globalcounts, N, wg) # Step 3: Scatter for i in range(N): d = digits[i] wgid = i // wg localidx = i % wg # ranklocali: count of digit d in current WG before index i ranklocali = sum(1 for j in range(localidx) if digits[j] == d) prefixwg = interworkgroupprefixes[wgid][d] ranki = prefixwg + ranklocali pos = baseoffsets[d] + ranki outputkeys[pos] = keys[i] outputvalues[pos] = values[i] # Swap buffers for next pass keys, values = outputkeys, outputvalues def blellochupsweep(arr): # Standard recursive Blelloch upsweep: pairwise reduction if len(arr) == 1: return arr tilesums = [] for i in range(0, len(arr), 2): tilesums.append(arr[i] + arr[i+1]) return blellochupsweep(tilesums) def blellochdownsweep(localhistograms, globalcounts, N, wg): # Standard Blelloch downsweep: propagate prefixes back to tiles and elements interworkgroupprefixes = [[0] 256 for in range(N // wg)] for wgid in range(N // wg): for d in range(256): # prefixwg is the cumulative sum of tile sums for workgroups before this one prefixwg = sum(sum(localhistograms[j][d]) for j in range(wgid)) interworkgroupprefixes[wgid][d] = prefixwg return interworkgroupprefixes Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The algorithm assumes N is divisible by wg or handles remainder workgroups appropriately. Degenerate Input: The algorithm handles any input distribution as it relies on histogram counts. This method performs a single pass of a radix sort on 64-bit keys by processing one 8-bit chunk per iteration, designed for GPU execution within a wait-free orchestration framework[3368-subgroup-based-radix-sort-partition.md][10404-radix-sort-gpu.md]. It is designed for WebGPU and Vulkan compute shaders, ensuring consistent behavior across heterogeneous GPU schedulers by avoiding race conditions inherent in atomic-based sorting. Unlike Subgroup-based Radix Sort Partition which minimizes atomic contention via subgroup ballots, or Radix Sort (GPU) which separates counting and scattering into distinct shader passes, this method integrates the scan and scatter within a ping-pong buffer architecture to handle arbitrary data types and key spaces[3368-subgroup-based-radix-sort-partition.md][10404-radix-sort-gpu.md]. This method modifies the shuffle steps of radix sorting to achieve coalesced memory access, addressing the performance penalty of random-like scattering patterns in global memory writes. It sets itself apart from standard element-wise mapping by performing local shuffling in shared memory to cluster same-radix elements, followed by a coalesced cluster-wise mapping to global memory, ensuring that the i-th thread outputs data to the i-th position in a 128-byte aligned region. Time Complexity: Linear work O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N/wg) auxiliary storage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids spin waiting across heterogeneous GPU schedulers; consistent behavior across devices; linear work complexity. Limitations: Requires multiple compute dispatches for each level of the scan; may have higher overhead for small N due to dispatch costs. When to use: When running on heterogeneous GPU hardware where scheduling order is not guaranteed, and avoiding busy-waits is critical. When not to use: When hardware-specific optimizations (like CUDA's warp-level primitives) are available and scheduling is deterministic. Introduced in the WebSplatter paper for depth sorting within a Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipeline. The method addresses the issue of inter-workgroup spin-waiting in prior parallel sorting approaches that assumed a fixed scheduling order and degenerated into busy-waits on devices without such guarantees. name: 8-bit Radix Sort
head: Bitwise radix sort
body: 8-bit Radix Sort is a parallel sorting algorithm that processes 64-bit sort keys by iterating through eight 8-bit chunks (digits), using a hierarchical Blelloch scan to compute element positions without inter-workgroup spin-waiting [Parent]. It is designed for Vulkan compute shaders, ensuring consistent behavior across heterogeneous GPU schedulers by avoiding race conditions inherent in atomic-based sorting [Parent]. Unlike Subgroup-based Radix Sort Partition which minimizes atomic contention via subgroup ballots, or Radix Sort (GPU) which separates counting and scattering into distinct shader passes, this method uses two separate compute pipelines per pass (histogram and scatter/scan) coordinated via ping-pong buffers to handle arbitrary data types and key spaces. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Array of 64-bit keys (sortKBuffer) and associated 32-bit values (sortVBuffer). Output: Sorted keys and values in the alternate ping-pong buffer. Parameters: numInstances (number of elements to sort), numRadixSortBlocksPerWorkgroup (number of sort blocks per compute workgroup, used to calculate invocation count). Data Structures: RadixSortPushConstants: A 16-byte structure containing four uint32t fields: gnumelements, gnumblocksperworkgroup, gshift, gnumworkgroups. Buffers: sortKBufferEven, sortKBufferOdd: Storage buffers for 64-bit keys, sized numInstances sizeof(uint64t). sortVBufferEven, sortVBufferOdd: Storage buffers for 32-bit values, sized numInstances sizeof(uint32t). sortHistBuffer: Histogram buffer for digit counting, sized numWorkgroups 256 sizeof(uint32t). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate globalInvocationSize as (numInstances + numRadixSortBlocksPerWorkgroup - 1) / numRadixSortBlocksPerWorkgroup, then align to 256 threads: (globalInvocationSize + 255) / 256. Calculate numWorkgroups based on the aligned invocation size. 2. Loop 8 times (once for each 8-bit chunk of the 64-bit key): a. Histogram Pass: Bind histogram pipeline sortHistPipeline and dispatch with ping-pong index i % 2 == 0 ? 0: 1. Dispatch histogram shader to count digit frequencies per workgroup. Barrier on sortHistBuffer to ensure histogram data is visible. b. Scan and Scatter Pass: Bind scatter/scan pipeline sortPipeline and dispatch with the same push constants and ping-pong index. This pass performs the parallel prefix sum (scan) on the histogram and scatters elements to their correct positions in the output buffer. c. Ping-Pong Barrier: If i % 2 == 0, barrier on sortKBufferOdd and sortVBufferOdd; else barrier on sortKBufferEven and sortVBufferEven. This ensures the next iteration reads from the buffer written in the current iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def radixsort8bit(numinstances, numradixsortblocksperworkgroup, sortbuffersizemultiplier, scenenumvertices): # Dynamic buffer resizing check if numinstances > scenenumvertices sortbuffersizemultiplier: while numinstances > scenenumvertices sortbuffersizemultiplier: sortbuffersizemultiplier += 1 # Reallocate buffers sortkbuffereven = allocatebuffer(scenenumvertices 8 sortbuffersizemultiplier) sortkbufferodd = allocatebuffer(scenenumvertices 8 sortbuffersizemultiplier) sortvbuffereven = allocatebuffer(scenenumvertices 4 sortbuffersizemultiplier) sortvbufferodd = allocatebuffer(scenenumvertices 4 sortbuffersizemultiplier) # Recalculate workgroups and histogram buffer size globalinvocationsize = (numinstances + numradixsortblocksperworkgroup - 1) // numradixsortblocksperworkgroup globalinvocationsize = (globalinvocationsize + 255) // 256 numworkgroups = (globalinvocationsize + 255) // 256 sorthistbuffer = allocatebuffer(numworkgroups 256 4) recordpreprocesscommandbuffer() return False # Skip current render pass # Main sort loop for i in range(8): shift = i 8 # Histogram Pass bindpipeline(sorthistpipeline) dispatchpushconstants( gnumelements=numinstances, gnumblocksperworkgroup=numradixsortblocksperworkgroup, gshift=shift, gnumworkgroups=numworkgroups, pingpongindex=i % 2) barrier(sorthistbuffer) # Scan and Scatter Pass bindpipeline(sortpipeline) dispatchpushconstants( gnumelements=numinstances, gnumblocksperworkgroup=numradixsortblocksperworkgroup, gshift=shift, gnumworkgroups=numworkgroups, pingpongindex=i % 2) # Ping-Pong Barrier if i % 2 == 0: barrier(sortkbufferodd) barrier(sortvbufferodd) else: barrier(sortkbuffereven) barrier(sortvbuffereven) def allocatebuffer(sizebytes): return [0] (sizebytes // 4) # Simulated storage buffer def calculatenumworkgroups(globalinvocationsize): return (globalinvocationsize + 255) // 256 def recordpreprocesscommandbuffer(): pass # Records command buffer state def bindpipeline(pipeline): pass # Sets active compute pipeline def dispatchpushconstants(gnumelements, gnumblocksperworkgroup, gshift, gnumworkgroups, pingpongindex): pass # Dispatches compute shader with push constants def barrier(buffer): pass # Synchronizes workgroups on buffer visibility Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Buffer Overflow: If numInstances exceeds the initial buffer capacity, dynamic resizing is required. Failure to resize leads to out-of-bounds writes. Precision: Uses uint64t for keys and uint32t for values. Boundary Conditions: The alignment to 256 threads ensures workgroup boundaries are respected, but numInstances may not be a multiple of the total thread count, requiring careful handling of out-of-bounds threads in shaders. Performs a single pass of radix sort for a partition (typically 4096 elements) using GPU subgroup ballot operations to compute local offsets, minimizing atomic contention on shared memory. It builds on 8-bit Radix Sort by replacing per-element atomic updates with subgroup-level exclusive scans, making it suitable for high-throughput sorting in compute shaders where subgroup size is known and fixed. A GPU-based integer sorting algorithm implemented via four compute shader passes: histogram counting, prefix sum, digit prefix sum, and scatter. It sorts keys by processing digits in a specific order, using parallel prefix sum (scan) as a subroutine to determine output positions. It is distinct from subgroup-based partitioning methods by explicitly separating the counting, offset calculation, and scattering phases into dedicated shader invocations. A hardware-optimized parallel implementation of the radix sort algorithm for GPUs that processes two bits per iteration (radix 4) to sort elements, lifting limitations on element count and precision compared to previous GPU sorters. It reduces the number of passes by half compared to binary-radix sort, eliminating restrictions on key space and supporting arbitrary data types. Unlike 8-bit Radix Sort which processes one bit at a time, this method clusters numbers with the same radix combination bits inside a block to enable coalesced memory writing, addressing the non-coalesced scattering bottleneck of element-wise mapping. A variant that dynamically scales the sort buffer capacity based on the scene size. It checks if numInstances > scene->getNumVertices() sortBufferSizeMultiplier. If true, it increments sortBufferSizeMultiplier in a while loop until the condition fails, then reallocates key buffers (sortKBufferEven/Odd) and value buffers (sortVBufferEven/Odd) to scene->getNumVertices() sizeof(uint64t) sortBufferSizeMultiplier. It recalculates globalInvocationSize and numWorkgroups for the histogram buffer and reallocates sortHistBuffer to numWorkgroups 256 sizeof(uint32t). Finally, it calls recordPreprocessCommandBuffer() and returns false to skip the current render pass. Time Complexity: O(8 \cdot N) where N is the number of elements, as it performs 8 passes (one per 8-bit digit) with linear work per pass. Memory Complexity: O(N) for key and value buffers, plus O(W \cdot 256) for the histogram buffer where W is the number of workgroups. Performance: Measured performance depends on GPU architecture and subgroup size. The ping-pong buffer approach avoids global memory contention for intermediate results but requires careful synchronization. Strengths: Works across heterogeneous GPU schedulers without spin-waiting; supports arbitrary 64-bit keys; dynamic buffer resizing handles varying scene sizes [Parent]. Limitations: Fixed 8-bit digit size may not be optimal for all data distributions; requires multiple buffer allocations for ping-pong. When to Use: Suitable for general-purpose sorting in Vulkan/WebGPU applications where key size is 64-bit and hardware atomic support is limited or inconsistent [Parent]. When Not to Use: For small datasets or when subgroup operations are heavily optimized and available, Subgroup-based Radix Sort Partition may offer better throughput. Originated in the context of performant, cross-platform Gaussian Splatting implementations using Vulkan. It was developed to address the challenges of sorting large numbers of Gaussian splats efficiently on GPUs with varying capabilities, particularly avoiding the pitfalls of inter-workgroup synchronization. The method leverages the Blelloch scan algorithm for position computation, a technique common in parallel prefix sum implementations, adapted for radix sorting [Parent]. name: Subgroup-based Radix Sort Partition
head: GLSL Subgroup Histogram Sort, Subgroup Radix Sort
body: This method performs a single pass of a radix sort for a partition of elements (typically 4096) using GPU subgroup ballot operations to compute local offsets, thereby minimizing atomic contention on shared memory. It builds on 8-bit Radix Sort by replacing per-element atomic updates with subgroup-level exclusive scans, making it suitable for high-throughput sorting in compute shaders where subgroup size is known and fixed. Inputs: keys: Array of 32-bit unsigned integers to sort. values: Array of 32-bit unsigned integers (or other data) to be permuted with keys. elementcount: Total number of valid elements in the partition. pass: Current radix pass index (0–3 for 32-bit keys). inoffset: Offset into the input arrays for the current workgroup. outoffset: Offset into the output arrays for the current workgroup. globalhistogram: Global memory array storing cumulative histogram sums across partitions. partitionhistogram: Global memory array storing histogram sums for the current partition. Outputs: keys: Sorted keys written to global memory. values: Corresponding values written to global memory. Data Structures: localhistogram: uint array of size SHMEMSIZE (4096). Layout: localhistogram[glNumSubgroups radix + subgroupindex]. Stores per-subgroup, per-radix bin counts. localhistogramsum: uint array of size RADIX (256). Stores the sum of bin counts across subgroups for a specific radix. localkeys: uint array of size PARTITIONSIZE (4096). localvalues: uint array of size PARTITIONSIZE (4096). localoffsets: uint array of size PARTITIONSIZE (4096). Stores local destination offsets for each element. subgrouphistogram: uint array of size glNumSubgroups. Stores per-subgroup histogram sums. Parameters: PARTITIONSIZE: 4096. RADIX: 256 (2^8). pass: 0, 1, 2, or 3. Steps: 1. Initialize Local Histograms: For each radix index i from 0 to RADIX-1, iterate over all subgroups and set localhistogram[glNumSubgroups i + subgroupindex] = 0. 2. Load Keys and Values: For each element i in the partition, calculate global index: globalindex = glGlobalInvocationID.x + inoffset. If globalindex < elementcount, load localkeys[i] = keys[keyindex + inoffset] and localvalues[i] = values[keyindex + inoffset]. Else, load 0xffffffff for keys and 0 for values. 3. Extract Radix Digit: For each element i, compute digit = bitfieldExtract(localkeys[i], pass 8, 8). 4. Compute Subgroup Ballot Masks: For each element i, initialize mask = subgroupBallot(true). For each bit j from 0 to 7, compute ballot = subgroupBallot(digit == (1 << j)) and update mask &= uvec4(digit - 1) ^ ballot. This creates a mask where bits are set if the corresponding radix digit matches the current element's digit. 5. Compute Subgroup Offset and Count: For each element i, compute subgroupoffset = subgroupBallotExclusiveBitCount(mask) and radixcount = subgroupBallotBitCount(mask). 6. Reduce Local Histogram Across Subgroups: For each index i in localhistogram with stride WORKGROUPSIZE, compute sum = subgroupAdd(v) and excl = subgroupExclusiveAdd(v). Store excl in localhistogram[i]. If threadindex == 0, store sum in localhistogramsum[i / glSubgroupSize]. 7. Reduce localhistogramsum Across Subgroups (128 elements): For each index i from 0 to intermediateoffset-1 (where intermediateoffset = RADIX glNumSubgroups / glSubgroupSize), compute sum and excl. Store excl in localhistogramsum[index]. If threadindex == 0, store sum in localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + index / glSubgroupSize]. 8. Reduce localhistogramsum Further (4 or 1 elements): For each index i from 0 to intermediatesize-1, compute excl = subgroupExclusiveAdd(v) and store in localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + index]. 9. Add Reduced Sums Back to localhistogramsum: For each index i from 0 to intermediateoffset-1, add localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + index / glSubgroupSize] to localhistogramsum[index]. 10. Add Reduced Sums to localhistogram: For each index i in localhistogram with stride WORKGROUPSIZE, add localhistogramsum[i / glSubgroupSize] to localhistogram[i]. 11. Post-Scan Stage: Update Local Offsets: For each element i, add localhistogram[glNumSubgroups radix + subgroupindex] to localoffsets[i]. Then, if subgrouphistogram[i] > 0, atomicAdd subgrouphistogram[i] to localhistogram[glNumSubgroups radix + subgroupindex]. 12. Compute Global Offsets: For each index i from 0 to RADIX-1, compute v = index == 0 ? 0: localhistogram[glNumSubgroups index - 1]. Set localhistogramsum[index] = globalhistogram[RADIX pass + index] + partitionhistogram[RADIX partitionindex + index] - v. 13. Rearrange Keys into localhistogram (Aliasing Memory): For each element i, set localhistogram[localoffsets[i]] = localkeys[i]. 14. Binning: Write Keys to Global Memory: For each element i, extract radix from localhistogram[i], compute dstoffset = localhistogramsum[radix] + i. If dstoffset < elementcount, write keys[dstoffset + outoffset] = key. Store dstoffset in localkeys[i / WORKGROUPSIZE]. 15. Rearrange Values into localhistogram: For each element i, set localhistogram[localoffsets[i]] = localvalues[i]. 16. Binning: Write Values to Global Memory: For each element i, get value from localhistogram[i], get dstoffset from localkeys[i / WORKGROUPSIZE]. If dstoffset < elementcount, write values[dstoffset + outoffset] = value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Initialize Local Histograms for radix in range(RADIX): for sg in range(glNumSubgroups): localhistogram[glNumSubgroups radix + sg] = 0 # 2. Load Keys and Values for i in range(PARTITIONSIZE): globalindex = glGlobalInvocationIDx + inoffset if globalindex < elementcount: localkeys[i] = keys[globalindex] localvalues[i] = values[globalindex] else: localkeys[i] = 0xFFFFFFFF localvalues[i] = 0 # 3. Extract Radix Digit digit = bitfieldextract(localkeys[i], passidx 8, 8) # 4. Compute Subgroup Ballot Masks mask = subgroupballot(True) for j in range(8): ballot = subgroupballot(digit == (1 << j)) mask &= (digit - 1) ^ ballot # 5. Compute Subgroup Offset and Count subgroupoffset = subgroupballotexclusivebitcount(mask) radixcount = subgroupballotbitcount(mask) # 6. Reduce Local Histogram Across Subgroups for i in range(0, PARTITIONSIZE, WORKGROUPSIZE): v = localhistogram[i] sumval = subgroupadd(v) excl = subgroupexclusiveadd(v) localhistogram[i] = excl if threadindex == 0: localhistogramsum[i // glSubgroupSize] = sumval # 7. Reduce localhistogramsum Across Subgroups intermediateoffset = RADIX glNumSubgroups // glSubgroupSize for i in range(intermediateoffset): v = localhistogramsum[i] sumval = subgroupadd(v) excl = subgroupexclusiveadd(v) localhistogramsum[i] = excl if threadindex == 0: localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + i // glSubgroupSize] = sumval # 8. Reduce localhistogramsum Further intermediatesize = intermediateoffset // glSubgroupSize for i in range(intermediatesize): v = localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + i] excl = subgroupexclusiveadd(v) localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + i] = excl # 9. Add Reduced Sums Back to localhistogramsum for i in range(intermediateoffset): localhistogramsum[i] += localhistogramsum[intermediateoffset + i // glSubgroupSize] # 10. Add Reduced Sums to localhistogram for i in range(0, PARTITIONSIZE, WORKGROUPSIZE): localhistogram[i] += localhistogramsum[i // glSubgroupSize] # 11. Post-Scan Stage: Update Local Offsets for i in range(PARTITIONSIZE): localoffsets[i] += localhistogram[glNumSubgroups passidx + subgroupindex] if subgrouphistogram[subgroupindex] > 0: atomicadd(localhistogram[glNumSubgroups passidx + subgroupindex], subgrouphistogram[subgroupindex]) # 12. Compute Global Offsets for i in range(RADIX): v = 0 if i == 0 else localhistogram[glNumSubgroups i - 1] localhistogramsum[i] = globalhistogram[RADIX passidx + i] + \ partitionhistogram[RADIX partitionindex + i] - v # 13. Rearrange Keys into localhistogram (Aliasing Memory) for i in range(PARTITIONSIZE): localhistogram[localoffsets[i]] = localkeys[i] barrier() # Ensure histogram data is consumed before overwriting # 14. Binning: Write Keys to Global Memory for i in range(PARTITIONSIZE): radix = bitfieldextract(localhistogram[i], passidx 8, 8) dstoffset = localhistogramsum[radix] + i if dstoffset < elementcount: keys[dstoffset + outoffset] = localhistogram[i] localkeys[i // WORKGROUPSIZE] = dstoffset # 15. Rearrange Values into localhistogram for i in range(PARTITIONSIZE): localhistogram[localoffsets[i]] = localvalues[i] # 16. Binning: Write Values to Global Memory for i in range(PARTITIONSIZE): value = localhistogram[i] dstoffset = localkeys[i // WORKGROUPSIZE] if dstoffset < elementcount: values[dstoffset + outoffset] = value Note: subgroupballot, subgroupadd, subgroupexclusiveadd, subgroupballotexclusivebitcount, subgroupballotbitcount, bitfieldextract, atomicadd, and barrier() are standard GLSL subgroup and memory operations. Pitfalls: Boundary Check: When loading keys/values, if keyindex >= elementcount, load 0xffffffff for keys and 0 for values to prevent out-of-bounds access and ensure invalid elements are sorted to the end. Memory Aliasing: localhistogram is reused for storing keys after the histogram reduction phase to save shared memory. This requires barriers to ensure all histogram data is consumed before overwriting. Time Complexity: O(N) per radix pass, where N is the partition size. The use of subgroup ballot operations reduces the constant factor compared to atomic-based approaches. Memory Complexity: O(PARTITIONSIZE) shared memory for keys, values, and histogram buffers. Strengths: Minimizes atomic contention by using subgroup-level exclusive scans. Efficient for small to medium partition sizes where subgroup operations are fast. Limitations: Requires fixed subgroup size. Performance may degrade if subgroup size is not a power of two or if the hardware does not support efficient ballot operations. When to Use: High-throughput sorting in compute shaders where subgroup size is known and fixed, and atomic contention is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When subgroup size is variable or unknown, or when sorting very large partitions where global memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck. This method is derived from the implementation in the Godot Gaussian Splatting project, which uses subgroup ballot operations to optimize radix sort partitions. It is an adaptation of parallel radix sort techniques to leverage GPU subgroup primitives for improved performance. name: Radix Sort (GPU)
head: RadixSortCountCS, RadixSortDigitPrefixSumCS, RadixSortPrefixSumCS, RadixSortScatterCS
body: A GPU-based integer sorting algorithm implemented via four compute shader passes: histogram counting, prefix sum, digit prefix sum, and scatter. It uses a parallel prefix sum (scan) implementation as a subroutine to compute output positions for each radix digit. The method operates on the following buffers and parameters, all defined in the source shader signatures: Input Keys: SrcKeys (SRV StructuredBuffer<uint>) Input Values: SrcVals (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>) Output Keys: DstKeys (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>) Output Values: DstVals (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>) Histogram: HistogramBuffer (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>) Digit Offsets: DigitOffsetBuffer (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>) Sort Parameters: SortParams (SRV StructuredBuffer<uint>) containing RadixShift, Count, NumTiles, UseIndirectSort. The parameters are passed via the SortParams structured buffer or directly as shader constants. The RadixShift parameter specifies the bit shift amount for the current radix digit being processed. Count specifies the total number of elements to sort. NumTiles specifies the number of tiles used for parallel histogramming. UseIndirectSort is a flag indicating whether indirect dispatch is used. 1. Histogram Counting (RadixSortCountCS) Input: SrcKeys, SortParams. Output: HistogramBuffer. Logic: Each thread block processes a tile of elements. For each element, extract the current 8-bit radix digit using (key >> RadixShift) & 0xFF. Increment the corresponding bin in the global histogram buffer using an atomic operation. Parameters: RadixShift, Count, NumTiles, UseIndirectSort. 2. Prefix Sum (RadixSortPrefixSumCS) Input: HistogramBuffer, DigitOffsetBuffer, SortParams, NumTiles, UseIndirectSort. Output: DigitOffsetBuffer. Logic: Perform a parallel prefix sum (scan) on the HistogramBuffer to compute the starting offsets for each digit bin. The result is stored in DigitOffsetBuffer. Parameters: NumTiles, UseIndirectSort. 3. Digit Prefix Sum (RadixSortDigitPrefixSumCS) Input: DigitOffsetBuffer. Output: DigitOffsetBuffer (updated). Logic: This pass refines or finalizes the offsets for the scatter phase. The exact transformation logic is not detailed in the sources. Parameters: None explicitly listed beyond the buffer itself. 4. Scatter (RadixSortScatterCS) Input: SrcKeys, SrcVals, DstKeys, DstVals, HistogramBuffer, DigitOffsetBuffer, SortParams, RadixShift, Count, NumTiles, UseIndirectSort. Output: DstKeys, DstVals. Logic: For each element, extract the current radix digit. Use the DigitOffsetBuffer to find the starting position for that digit. Scatter the key and value to the correct location in DstKeys and DstVals. Increment the offset for the next element with the same digit using an atomic add or pre-computed position. Parameters: RadixShift, Count, NumTiles, UseIndirectSort. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scan(arr): # Standard inclusive prefix sum result = [0] len(arr) result[0] = arr[0] for i in range(1, len(arr)): result[i] = result[i-1] + arr[i] return result def atomicadd(buffer, index, value): # Simulates GPU atomic add old = buffer[index] buffer[index] += value return old def RadixSortCountCS(SrcKeys, SortParams, HistogramBuffer): RadixShift = SortParams['RadixShift'] Count = SortParams['Count'] for i in range(256): HistogramBuffer[i] = 0 for idx in range(Count): key = SrcKeys[idx] digit = (key >> RadixShift) & 0xFF atomicadd(HistogramBuffer, digit, 1) def RadixSortPrefixSumCS(HistogramBuffer, DigitOffsetBuffer, SortParams): DigitOffsetBuffer[:] = scan(HistogramBuffer[:]) def RadixSortDigitPrefixSumCS(DigitOffsetBuffer): # Exact logic not detailed in sources pass def RadixSortScatterCS(SrcKeys, SrcVals, DstKeys, DstVals, HistogramBuffer, DigitOffsetBuffer, SortParams): RadixShift = SortParams['RadixShift'] Count = SortParams['Count'] for idx in range(Count): key = SrcKeys[idx] val = SrcVals[idx] digit = (key >> RadixShift) & 0xFF pos = atomicadd(DigitOffsetBuffer, digit, 1) DstKeys[pos] = key DstVals[pos] = val DX11 UAV Limit: DX11 has a strict limit on the number of simultaneous UAVs, which may prevent running the full pipeline if not optimized. Indirect Dispatch: The UseIndirectSort flag indicates that indirect dispatch may be required for certain configurations. Precision: Using uint32 for keys and values ensures no precision loss for standard integer types. Boundaries: The algorithm assumes Count is accurate and SrcKeys/SrcVals are valid. name: Binning State Allocation and Sorting
head: Radix Sort on Point List Keys
body: This method allocates and initializes the BinningState structure and performs a radix sort on point list keys. It serves as a specialized orchestration step within GPU-based volume rendering pipelines to reorder point cloud data. Inputs: P (number of points), binning (context holding BinningState fields). Outputs: Sorted binning.pointlistkeys and permuted binning.pointlist. Data Structures: The BinningState is a struct containing pointers to device memory. Its fields are allocated via obtain. The layout is: pointlist: uint32t, size P. pointlistunsorted: uint32t, size P. pointlistkeys: uint32t, size P. pointlistkeysunsorted: uint32t, size P. listsortingspace: char, dynamic size from sort. Steps: 1. Allocate the BinningState structure and its device memory buffers using obtain. 2. Initialize pointlistkeysunsorted and pointlistunsorted with raw point data. 3. Perform radix sort on pairs of keys and indices using cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs. 4. The sort reorders pointlistkeys in ascending order and permutes pointlist accordingly. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocatedevicememory(size, dtype): return [0] size def radixsortpairs32(keysin, keysout, valuesin, valuesout, numitems): # Standard 32-bit radix sort for pairs pairs = list(zip(keysin, valuesin)) for shift in range(0, 32, 8): buckets = [[] for in range(256)] for k, v in pairs: byteval = (k >> shift) & 0xFF buckets[byteval].append((k, v)) pairs = [item for bucket in buckets for item in bucket] for i in range(numitems): keysout[i] = pairs[i][0] valuesout[i] = pairs[i][1] def binningstateallocationandsorting(P, binning): # Step 1: Allocate BinningState fields via obtain binning.pointlist = allocatedevicememory(P, 'uint32t') binning.pointlistunsorted = allocatedevicememory(P, 'uint32t') binning.pointlistkeys = allocatedevicememory(P, 'uint32t') binning.pointlistkeysunsorted = allocatedevicememory(P, 'uint32t') # Temporary space size is dynamic; exact formula not given in sources sortingsize = P 4 binning.listsortingspace = allocatedevicememory(sortingsize, 'char') binning.sortingsize = sortingsize # Step 2: Initialize unsorted arrays with raw point data # binning.pointlistkeysunsorted[:] = rawkeys # binning.pointlistunsorted[:] = rawindices # Step 3: Perform radix sort on pairs of keys and indices # The sources provide a CUDA C++ API call: cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs(nullptr, binning.sortingsize, binning.pointlistkeysunsorted, binning.pointlistkeys, binning.pointlistunsorted, binning.pointlist, P) radixsortpairs32( keysin=binning.pointlistkeysunsorted, keysout=binning.pointlistkeys, valuesin=binning.pointlistunsorted, valuesout=binning.pointlist, numitems=P) Parameters: P: Number of points. name: 4-way Parallel Radix Sort
head: 2-bit-radix sort, 4-way parallel radix sorting, 4-way radix sort, Fast 4-way parallel radix sorting on GPUs, Four-way radix sorting
body: A hardware-optimized parallel implementation of the radix sort algorithm for GPUs that processes two bits per iteration (radix 4) to sort elements, lifting limitations on element count and precision compared to previous GPU sorters. It reduces the number of passes by half compared to binary-radix sort, eliminating restrictions on key space and supporting arbitrary data types. Unlike 8-bit Radix Sort which processes one bit at a time, this method clusters numbers with the same radix combination bits inside a block to enable coalesced memory writing, addressing the non-coalesced scattering bottleneck of element-wise mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of N keys (32-bit integers, floats, or mapped floats) and an optional array of values/indices to be permuted in parallel. Output: The keys and associated data sorted in ascending order. Data Structures: blockSize: Integer, typically 256 (128 threads \times 2 elements per thread). blockSumArray: Array of size \lceil N / blockSize \rceil \times 4. Stores the total count of elements for each of the 4 digits (0-3) per block. localPrefixSumArray: Array of size N. Stores the local prefix sum for the specific digit of each element, using a single array instead of four separate ones to reduce memory requirements. sharedMemory: Size sufficient for blockSize elements. Parameters: radixWidth: 2 bits. keyBits: 32 bits (loop runs for bits 0 to 30). blockSize: 256. threadsPerBlock: 128. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Floating Point): If keys are floating-point numbers, map them to integers using the method by Terdiman to preserve order for negative and positive numbers. 2. Initialization: Set blockSize = 256 and allocate and initialize blockSumArray on GPU memory to zero. 3. Main Loop: Iterate bit from 0 to 30 (inclusive), incrementing by 2. 1. Order Check: Perform a parallel reduction to check if the current input array is already sorted. If sorted, terminate the loop immediately. 2. Block Division: Divide the input data into equal blocks. 3. Parallel Block Processing (for all blocks in parallel): 1. Load Data: Load blockSize elements into shared memory (sdata). 2. Bit Extraction: Each thread extracts the 2-bit radix pair from its assigned elements at the current bit position. 3. Counting: Initialize four counting arrays cnt[0..3] in shared memory. For each element, set the corresponding counter bit to 1 if the extracted radix matches the digit index. 4. Local Prefix Sum: Perform a parallel optimized prefix sum (scan) on the four counting combinations simultaneously in shared memory. This computes the local frequency and position of each element within its block relative to its digit. 5. Shuffle: Reorder elements in shared memory so that elements with the same radix digit are clustered together in sorted order. This ensures that subsequent global writes are coalesced. 6. Store Local Prefix: Write the local prefix sum value for each element to localPrefixSumArray at the element's original global index. 7. Store Block Sum: Write the total count of elements for each of the 4 digits to the corresponding entry in blockSumArray for this block. 4. Global Prefix Sum: Perform a parallel prefix sum (scan) on the blockSumArray to compute global starting positions for each block and digit combination. 5. Mapping: For each element, calculate its final sorted position using the formula: \text{Sorted Position} = Pd[n] + m Where: d is the 2-bit radix digit of the element. n is the block index containing the element. Pd[n] is the global prefix block sum for digit d at block n (from the global scan of blockSumArray). m is the local prefix sum value for the element (from localPrefixSumArray). Permute the elements from the shared memory shuffle buffer to their calculated global positions in the output array. This mapping is cluster-wise, ensuring coalesced global memory writes. 6. Increment bit by 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fourwayradixsort(keys, values, n): blockSize = 256 threadsPerBlock = 128 numBlocks = (n + blockSize - 1) // blockSize blockSumArray = [0] (numBlocks 4) localPrefixSumArray = [0] n outputKeys = [0] n outputValues = [0] n currKeys = keys currValues = values nextKeys = outputKeys nextValues = outputValues for bit in range(0, 31, 2): # Order check (GPU uses optimized reduction) if issorted(currKeys, n): break for block in range(numBlocks): startIdx = block blockSize endIdx = min(startIdx + blockSize, n) localSize = endIdx - startIdx sdata = [0] blockSize cnt = [[0] threadsPerBlock for in range(4)] # Load data for i in range(localSize): tid = i % threadsPerBlock sdata[tid] = currKeys[startIdx + i] # Extract bits and count for tid in range(threadsPerBlock): if tid < localSize: val = sdata[tid] radix = (val >> bit) & 3 for b in range(4): cnt[b][tid] = 1 if b == radix else 0 # Local Prefix Sum (scan) on counters (GPU uses shared-memory scan) for b in range(4): scaninplace(cnt[b]) # Store local prefix sum for tid in range(threadsPerBlock): if tid < localSize: radix = (sdata[tid] >> bit) & 3 localPrefixSumArray[startIdx + tid] = cnt[radix][tid] # In-block shuffle: scatter elements to positions based on local rank shuffleddata = [0] localSize for tid in range(threadsPerBlock): if tid < localSize: radix = (sdata[tid] >> bit) & 3 pos = cnt[radix][tid] shuffleddata[pos] = sdata[tid] # Store block sums for b in range(4): blockSumArray[block 4 + b] = cnt[b][threadsPerBlock - 1] # Write shuffled data to temporary buffer for tid in range(localSize): nextKeys[startIdx + tid] = shuffleddata[tid] # Global Prefix Sum on blockSumArray scaninplace(blockSumArray) # Final Mapping for i in range(n): val = nextKeys[i] # Read from shuffled buffer radix = (val >> bit) & 3 block = i // blockSize m = localPrefixSumArray[i] base = blockSumArray[block 4 + radix] finalPos = base + m outputKeys[finalPos] = val outputValues[finalPos] = currValues[i] # Swap buffers currKeys, nextKeys = nextKeys, currKeys currValues, nextValues = nextValues, currValues def issorted(arr, n): return all(arr[i] <= arr[i+1] for i in range(n-1)) def scaninplace(arr): for i in range(1, len(arr)): arr[i] += arr[i-1] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-coalesced Scattering: Standard radix sort scatters elements to global memory based on individual indices, causing uncoalesced writes. This method uses in-block shuffling to cluster elements with the same radix, enabling coalesced global writes. Floating Point Mapping: Floating point numbers must be mapped to integers to preserve order. The Terdiman method is used. Block Size: The block size (256) is chosen to be a multiple of the warp size (32) to ensure coalesced memory access and to hide global memory latency while fitting in shared memory/cache. Order Checking: The order check is performed at the start of each pass. If the array is already sorted, the loop terminates early, saving passes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot \lceil 32/2 \rceil) = O(16N), where N is the number of elements. The algorithm processes 2 bits per pass, requiring 16 passes for 32-bit keys. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input/output arrays, plus O(N/R) for the block sum array and O(N) for the local prefix sum array. Performance: Outperforms all known GPU-based sorting systems by about a factor of two at the time of publication. It is almost twice as fast as the fastest known approaches (Sintorn/Assarsson, Sengupta, Le Grand). Strengths: Eliminates restrictions on key space and supports arbitrary data types (floats, negatives, pointers). Reduces the number of passes by half compared to binary-radix sort. Early termination if the array is already sorted. Coalesced global memory writes via in-block shuffling. Limitations: Requires shared memory for the in-block shuffle, limiting the maximum block size. The order check adds a small overhead (approx. 0.1% of sorting time) but is negligible. When to Use: Ideal for GPU-based sorting of large datasets where performance is critical, especially in physics simulations, collision detection, and scenes with thousands of objects or millions of particles. The algorithm was presented by Linh Ha, Jens Krüger, and Cláudio T. Silva from the University of Utah in a paper submitted to COMPUTER GRAPHICS Forum in February 2009. It addresses the challenge of efficient parallel sorting on GPUs, overcoming limitations of previous approaches like CUDPP (binary-radix sort) and Sintorn/Assarsson (atomic counting). The work was motivated by the need for fast sorting in physics-based simulations for computer games and virtual environments, such as collision detection for falling chairs, particle systems, and n-body galaxy problems. name: In-block shuffle and coalesced mapping
head: Coalesced Cluster-wise Mapping, In-block shuffle radix counting with coalesced cluster-wise mapping, Modified non-coalesced element-wise mapping
body: This method modifies the shuffle steps of radix sorting to achieve coalesced memory access, addressing the performance penalty of random-like scattering patterns in global memory writes. It sets itself apart from standard element-wise mapping by performing local shuffling in shared memory to cluster same-radix elements, followed by a coalesced cluster-wise mapping to global memory, ensuring that the i-th thread outputs data to the i-th position in a 128-byte aligned region. Inputs: An array of values (and optionally indices) residing in global memory, partitioned into blocks processed by a thread block. Outputs: The sorted array in global memory. Data Structures: Shared Memory Buffer: A temporary buffer sized to hold one block of data. Cluster Start Positions: An array storing the global memory offset of the first element for each unique radix combination (cluster) present in the block. The size of this array equals the number of unique radix combinations (e.g., 16 for 4-bit radix, 256 for 8-bit). Algorithm Steps: The procedure is executed per radix digit pass. Let N be the number of elements in the block, B be the block size (number of threads), and R be the radix size (number of possible digit values). 1. Read to Shared Memory: All threads in the block read their assigned elements from global memory into the shared memory buffer. 2. Compute Cluster Start Positions: Each thread determines the radix digit of its element. Using a parallel prefix sum (scan) or atomic operations within the block, compute the starting global memory offset for each radix cluster. Crucially, only the start position of the first element in each cluster is stored. The position of subsequent elements in the same cluster is defined implicitly based on the order of appearance in the input (due to the stability of LSD radix sort). 3. Determine Thread-to-Cluster Mapping: For each thread, identify which cluster its element belongs to. Determine the corresponding thread index that will handle the output for the specific position in the global memory output buffer. This step ensures that consecutive threads in the warp write to consecutive memory addresses. 4. Coalesced Cluster-wise Mapping: Each thread reads its element from the shared memory buffer. The thread calculates the final global memory destination address. This address is derived from the cluster start position (computed in Step 2) plus the implicit offset of the element within its cluster. The thread writes its element to the calculated global memory address. This step is performed in parallel by all threads, once for each radix combination, ensuring that the i-th thread outputs data to the i-th position in a 128-byte aligned region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inblockshufflecoalescedmapping(data, globalout, sharedmem, clusterstarts, RADIXSIZE, BLOCKSIZE): tid = threadIdx.x # Standard GPU thread identifier # Step 1: Read data in block to shared memory sharedmem[tid] = data[tid] syncthreads() # Standard thread block synchronization # Step 2: Compute the position of first elements in a cluster and corresponding thread r = extractradix(sharedmem[tid]) # Compute cluster start positions using a parallel prefix sum clusterstarts = prefixsum(r, RADIXSIZE) # Compute implicit offset within cluster by counting preceding elements with same radix offset = 0 for k in range(tid): if extractradix(sharedmem[k]) == r: offset += 1 destaddr = clusterstarts[r] + offset # Map to coalesced thread index: thread i writes to base + i targettid = destaddr % BLOCKSIZE # Reorder numbers in shared memory to align with target thread indices tempshared = [0] BLOCKSIZE tempshared[targettid] = sharedmem[tid] syncthreads() # Step 3: Each thread outputs corresponding data to global memory output # Each thread writes its element to the calculated global memory address # Since data was reordered, thread i now holds the element for globalout[base + i] globalout[clusterstarts[extractradix(tempshared[tid])] + computeoffset(tid, tempshared, extractradix(tempshared[tid]))] = tempshared[tid] syncthreads() Parameters: Alignment Requirement: Global memory output must be 128-byte aligned to satisfy the coalesced writing condition. Radix Size: Typically 4-bit (16 buckets) or 8-bit (256 buckets) depending on the hardware and data type. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Footprint: By storing only the first position of each cluster, the memory footprint for tracking positions is reduced compared to storing all mapping positions. Stability Assumption: The method relies on the stability of the LSD radix sort. If the sort is not stable, the implicit offset calculation will be incorrect. Shared Memory Contention: High contention on shared memory during the read and cluster start computation steps can reduce performance. Time Complexity: The method adds an O(N) shuffling step in shared memory but reduces the global memory write latency by ensuring coalesced accesses. Memory Complexity: Requires O(N) shared memory for the block data and O(R) shared memory for cluster start positions, where R is the radix size. Performance: Provides a 50% performance improvement on graphics cards supporting CUDA 1.0 and 1.1 (e.g., G80 and GeForce Quadro FX generation). On newer cards (e.g., GTX 280), it provides a 10% improvement. Strengths: Significantly reduces the penalty of non-coalesced writing, which can account for up to 36% of sorting time in standard implementations. Limitations: Requires additional logic to compute cluster start positions and implicit offsets. The benefit diminishes on newer hardware with better memory controllers. This technique was proposed to address the inefficiency of random-like scattering patterns in GPU radix sorting, which lead to non-coalesced writing. It is based on the observation that LSD radix sorting is stable, preserving the order of numbers with the same radix combination bits. The method is implemented as an implicit four-way radix counting with an additional in-block shuffle step. name: Group Prefix Sum for Shell Lists
body: Group Prefix Sum for Shell Lists is a parallel shell list compaction method used in GPU-based isosurface extraction. It replaces sequential processing by thread 0 with a parallel prefix sum approach. It coordinates with the octree to derive block offsets from the first active octree nodes (AOs) in each shell. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Shell lists for a block of 128 functions containing AO offsets and coefficient data. Output: Compacted shell lists with updated AO offsets. Auxiliary: Octree block offsets derived from the first AO in each shell. Data Structures: Shell list entries: Contain AO offsets and coefficient matrix rows (C). Groupshared memory: Stores chunks of at most 32 AOs, with coefficient rows staged for simultaneous thread access. Octree offsets: Derived from the first AO of each shell in a block. Steps: 1. Pack shell data into chunks of at most 32 AOs per block of 128 functions. 2. Stage rows of coefficient matrices (C) into groupshared memory for simultaneous reading by all threads. 3. Upload all 16 field records per thread. 4. Clamp loads from groupshared indices to handle inactive lanes (llvmpipe compatibility). 5. Compute the parallel prefix sum (isogroupprefix) across the shell list entries. 6. Extract AO offsets from the first AOs of each shell to determine octree block offsets. 7. Update shell list entries with compacted positions based on the prefix sum results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def groupprefixsumshelllists(shelldata, groupsize=128, chunksize=32): # 1. Pack shell data into chunks of at most 32 AOs per block of 128 functions chunks = [shelldata[i:i+chunksize] for i in range(0, len(shelldata), chunksize)] # 2. Stage rows of coefficient matrices (C) into groupshared memory # Not given in the sources. groupsharedC = [chunk[1] for chunk in chunks] # 3. Upload all 16 field records per thread # Not given in the sources. records = [row for chunk in groupsharedC for row in chunk[:16]] # 4. Clamp loads from groupshared indices to handle inactive lanes (llvmpipe) # Not given in the sources. clamped = [max(0, min(idx, len(groupsharedC)-1)) for idx in range(len(groupsharedC))] # 5. Compute parallel prefix sum (isogroupprefix) across shell list entries # Not given in the sources. aooffsets = [chunk[0] for chunk in chunks] flatoffsets = [ao for chunk in aooffsets for ao in chunk] prefixsums = [sum(flatoffsets[:i]) for i in range(len(flatoffsets))] # 6. Extract AO offsets from the first AOs of each shell for octree block offsets blockoffsets = [chunk[0][0] for chunk in chunks] # 7. Update shell list entries with compacted positions compacted = [] for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks): for j, ao in enumerate(chunk[0]): compacted.append((ao + prefixsums[i chunksize + j], chunk[1])) return compacted, blockoffsets Parameters: Group size: 128 functions per block. Chunk size: Maximum 32 AOs per chunk. Field records: 16 per thread. Edge Cases: Inactive lanes: Loads from groupshared memory must be clamped to prevent out-of-bounds access. llvmpipe compatibility: Special handling required for inactive lane loads. Orbital padding: Orbital sets no longer pad their functions to even indices. Empty shells: Not given in the sources. A compact data structure storing partial sums for O(\log n) point updates and prefix-sum queries. It differs from standard complete binary trees by storing only 1.5n elements instead of 2n, since prefix-sum queries from index 0 never require right children, halving memory and update costs. Choose it for dynamic environments requiring incremental light transport integration in volume rendering. Parallel processing replaces sequential thread-0 compaction, improving throughput. Groupshared memory staging reduces global memory bandwidth by allowing simultaneous thread access to coefficient matrix rows. Inactive lane clamping introduces minor overhead for llvmpipe compatibility. Not given in the sources: measured performance metrics, scaling behavior, or specific hardware benchmarks. Originates from the mdgtoisogpu optimization in the mdlib repository by Scanberg. It shifts shell list compaction from sequential thread-0 processing to a parallel prefix sum approach in GPU-based isosurface extraction. The implementation handles llvmpipe compatibility via index clamping and uses environment variables GTOISORELAXFIRST=0 and GTOISOCORNERSV2=0 to revert to legacy forms. mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
head: Fenwick tree variant, Half-tree, Hierarchical Integration (Partial Sum Tree), Partial Sum Tree
body: The Fenwick Tree (also known as the Half-tree or Partial Sum Tree) is a compact data structure that stores partial sums to enable O(\log n) point updates and prefix-sum queries. It solves the problem of efficiently maintaining cumulative sums in dynamic environments, such as the incremental integration of light transport in volume rendering. Unlike a standard complete binary tree which requires 2n nodes for n leaves, the Fenwick Tree variant exploits the fact that prefix-sum queries starting from index 0 never require the right child of any node, storing only 1.5n elements. This reduces memory usage and the number of nodes modified during updates by half compared to the full tree representation. It builds on Group Prefix Sum for Shell Lists. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of n values (e.g., light ray contributions b[\gamma]). Output: A compact tree structure supporting UPDATE(index, value) and QUERY(index) operations. Parameters: n is the number of data elements (light rays). Data Structures and Layout: The tree is stored as a contiguous array of size 1.5n. Lowest Level (Leaves): The complete lowest level of the tree is stored fully, containing n elements. This allows direct access to the next element for interpolation queries without a full tree traversal. Internal Levels: All higher levels store only half the nodes of a complete binary tree, totaling 0.5n elements. Total Size: 1.5n elements. Algorithms: 1. BUILD-TREE: Construct the tree from the input array. Start with the input array at the leaves. Recursively sum children to compute parent values up to the root. This can be done in linear time O(n). 2. UPDATE: Modify a leaf node and propagate changes to the root. Set the leaf node at the specified index to the new value (or zero). Recursively update each parent node up to the root by recomputing the sum of its children. Complexity: O(\log n). 3. QUERY: Compute the prefix sum \sum{k=0}^{q} b[k]. Check if the query index q is within the interval represented by the current node. If q is within the interval, the result is the value of the left child plus the recursive prefix sum of the right child. If q is outside the interval range, terminate recursion and return the value of the current node. Complexity: O(\log n). Formulas: Prefix Sum Query: Pq = \sum{k=0}^{q} b[k]. Interpolation for Floating-Point Depth: R[\beta] = Bi[\beta] \cdot \left( \text{QUERY}(\lfloor D[\beta] \rfloor) \cdot (1 - f) + \text{QUERY}(\lceil D[\beta] \rceil) \cdot f \right), where f = D[\beta] - \lfloor D[\beta] \rfloor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing Artifacts: Discretization can cause aliasing artifacts. To mitigate this, the depth D[\beta] is stored as a float. The algorithm queries the tree at \lfloor D[\beta] \rfloor and \lceil D[\beta] \rceil, then linearly interpolates the results. Interpolation Access: The query for \lceil D[\beta] \rceil accesses the next element in the complete lowest level of the tree. This requires storing the complete lowest level (unlike other levels which are halved) to allow direct lookup of the next element rather than performing a full tree query. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the usage of the Fenwick Tree in the context of incremental hierarchical integration for volume rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def INTEGRATESLICE(D, S, Bi, Gammai): # D contains lengths of view rays along gamma # S contains lengths of light rays along beta # Bi contains SVD factors for view rays # Gammai represents the set of light rays # Mark where light rays terminate terminationdepths = [[] for in range(len(S))] for gamma in range(len(S)): terminationdepths[S[gamma]].append(gamma) # Initialize the incremental counter, tree, and result tree = buildtree(Gammai) results = [0.0] len(D) # Walk over view rays for beta in range(len(D)): # Set the counter to zero for light rays that terminate at this beta for gamma in terminationdepths[beta]: updatetree(tree, gamma) # sets the gamma node to zero # Query two nearest results for interpolation flooridx = int(D[beta]) ceilidx = flooridx + 1 res1 = querytree(tree, flooridx) res2 = querytree(tree, ceilidx) # Lerp results and multiply by SVD factors Bi frac = D[beta] - flooridx results[beta] = Bi[beta] (res1 (1.0 - frac) + res2 frac) return results def buildtree(Gammai): # Not given in the sources. Standard construction: # Initialize array of size 1.5n, place Gammai at leaves, # recursively sum children to compute parents up to root. pass def updatetree(tree, index): # Not given in the sources. Standard implementation: # Set leaf at index to 0, then traverse up to root updating sums. pass def querytree(tree, q): # Not given in the sources. Standard implementation: # Check if q is in current node's interval. # If yes, return left child value + recursive query on right child. # If no, return node value. pass Time Complexity: Update and query operations each take O(\log n). The total integration time is O(s(r + d) \log d), where s is the number of slices, r is the number of view samples per slice, and d is the number of light rays. Memory Complexity: The structure requires 1.5n elements, where n is the number of data elements (light rays). Performance: The sr \log d term represents the number of queries, and sd \log d represents the number of updates. These terms dominate the O(s(r + d)) rectification cost. Comparison: Brute force ray marching requires O(srd) time. The Fenwick Tree approach is significantly faster when d is large, as \log d \ll d. Strengths: Reduced memory footprint (1.5n vs 2n) and reduced update cost (half the nodes modified on average) compared to a standard partial sum tree. Limitations: Requires careful handling of floating-point depths to avoid aliasing; relies on the assumption that prefix sums always start from index 0 (the eye). The Fenwick Tree, also known as the Half-tree, was introduced by Fenwick in 1994. The observation that an efficient data structure is possible with only half of the tree nodes stems from the fact that recursive prefix-sum queries starting from index 0 never use the right child of any node (leaf or internal). This structure is used in hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithms for single scattering to optimize the integration of light transport. name: Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan)
head: CPU Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan), Exclusive Sum, StreamCompaction::CPU::scan, exclusive scan
body: The Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan) computes an output array O from an input array I such that each element O[i] is the sum of all input elements preceding index i (O[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} I[j]), with O[0]=0. In volume rendering, this primitive maps parallel voxel culling decisions to sequential indices in a compacted list, allowing culled voxels to be removed in parallel without data races. It differs from its siblings by serving as the fundamental indexing engine for stream compaction and hierarchical subdivision, whereas CUDA-based Exclusive Prefix Sum for Vertex Indexing targets specific vertex buffer layouts and Naive Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) lacks the work-efficient tree-based optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Array I of n integers (typically 0/1 for culling flags or weights). Output: Array O of n integers representing the exclusive prefix sums. Data Structures: For CPU: Two contiguous integer arrays of size n. For GPU (Work-Efficient): Two ping-pong buffers (devdata1, devdata2) in global memory, sized to the next power of two greater than or equal to n. Algorithm (Work-Efficient GPU Implementation): This method uses a tree-based up-sweep (reduce) and down-sweep (scan) phase. 1. Padding: If n is not a power of two, compute n{p2} = 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil}. 2. Initialization: Copy I to the input buffer and zero-pad the buffer from index n to n{p2}-1. 3. Up-Sweep (Reduce): Perform a parallel reduction to compute inclusive sums in a tree structure. Loop d from 0 to \lceil \log2 n{p2} \rceil - 1: Calculate stride d1 = 2^d and d2 = 2^{d+1}. Launch kernel where threads at indices k \cdot d2 add the value at k \cdot d2 + d1 - 1 to k \cdot d2 + d2 - 1. 4. Root Reset: Set the root element (last element of the buffer, index n{p2}-1) to 0. 5. Down-Sweep (Scan): Perform the exclusive scan by propagating sums down the tree. Loop d from \lceil \log2 n{p2} \rceil - 1 down to 0: Calculate stride d1 = 2^d and d2 = 2^{d+1}. Launch kernel where threads at indices k \cdot d2 save the value at k \cdot d2 + d1 - 1, set that position to the value at k \cdot d2 + d2 - 1, and add the saved value to k \cdot d2 + d2 - 1. 6. Finalization: Copy the first n elements of the result buffer to the output array O. Algorithm (CPU Sequential Implementation): For verification or small n, a simple loop suffices: 1. Set O[0] = 0. 2. For i from 1 to n-1: O[i] = O[i-1] + I[i-1]. Formula: O[i] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = 0 \\ \sum{j=0}^{i-1} I[j] & \text{if } i > 0 \end{cases} Parameters: n: Number of elements. ThreadReduction: Compile-time flag (0 or 1). If 1, reduces thread count by a stride factor to avoid boundary checks; if 0, uses full grid with modulo checks. blockSize: CUDA block size (e.g., 256). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-power-of-two sizes: Must be zero-padded to the next power of two before processing. Only the first n results are valid; the rest are artifacts of padding. Empty Input: If n \le 0, return immediately. Precision: Linear sums may underflow for transmittance calculations; use logarithmic-space variants when opacity values are small. Pseudocode (GPU Work-Efficient, ThreadReduction == 0): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def exclusivescangpu(n, idata): if n <= 0: return [] # 1. Pad to next power of two np2 = 1 while np2 < n: np2 = 2 # 2. Initialize buffer with input and zero-padding devdata = [0] np2 for i in range(n): devdata[i] = idata[i] # 3. Up-Sweep (Reduce) numlevels = int(math.log2(np2)) for d in range(numlevels): stride = 1 << d d2 = 1 << (d + 1) for index in range(0, np2, d2): devdata[index + d2 - 1] += devdata[index + stride - 1] # 4. Reset Root devdata[np2 - 1] = 0 # 5. Down-Sweep (Scan) for d in range(numlevels - 1, -1, -1): stride = 1 << d d2 = 1 << (d + 1) for index in range(0, np2, d2): t = devdata[index + stride - 1] devdata[index + stride - 1] = devdata[index + d2 - 1] devdata[index + d2 - 1] += t # 6. Copy result odata = [0] n for i in range(n): odata[i] = devdata[i] return odata This method computes the exclusive cumulative sum of transmittance values in logarithmic space to avoid underflow and enable efficient scatter-add operations for alpha compositing weights. It differs from standard linear-space exclusive scans by operating on \log(1-\alpha), which preserves precision for small alpha values, and by explicitly handling ray-segment boundaries to reset cumulative state between independent rays. It builds on Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan). CPU Stream Compaction with Scan removes zero-valued elements from an integer array on the CPU by mapping input data to a binary mask, computing an exclusive prefix sum on that mask, and scattering the retained elements to their computed output indices. It sets itself apart from CPU Stream Compaction without Scan by using a scan operation to determine output indices rather than a simple sequential counter, making it suitable for scenarios where parallel reduction primitives are available or when preparing data structures for subsequent parallel processing. Thrust Scan is a GPU-accelerated implementation of the exclusive prefix sum (scan) operation that leverages the NVIDIA Thrust library to perform parallel reduction on device memory. It solves the problem of efficiently computing cumulative sums for large datasets on the GPU by abstracting the underlying kernel launch and memory management details. It is distinguished from custom CUDA implementations by its reliance on a highly optimized, library-based approach rather than hand-written kernels, and it is typically used as a component within larger stream compaction pipelines. A cumulative product function that computes the product of elements up to but not including the current element, used for calculating transmission (opacity accumulation) in DVR. It is implemented via cumprodexclusive utilities. Time Complexity: O(\log n) parallel steps for the tree-based GPU implementation, O(n) total work. The CPU naive implementation is O(n) sequential steps. Memory Complexity: O(n) device memory for the ping-pong buffers in the GPU work-efficient version. O(1) auxiliary space for the CPU version if reusing input/output arrays, or O(n) if allocating temporary buffers for compaction. Performance: On arrays of size 2^{27}, the work-efficient GPU scan takes ~26ms, outperforming the naive GPU scan (~35ms) and significantly beating CPU scan (~190ms). Thrust consistently outperforms custom naive and work-efficient implementations across block sizes. Strengths: Enables parallel stream compaction and hierarchical subdivision without atomic conflicts. Work-efficient versions minimize redundant memory accesses compared to naive approaches. Limitations: Requires power-of-two padding for standard tree algorithms, wasting memory for arbitrary sizes. Non-power-of-two inputs require careful boundary handling. The exclusive prefix sum is a fundamental parallel primitive introduced by Blelloch [1990]. It is widely used in volume rendering for sparse voxelization and stream compaction, as described in Harris et al. [2007]. The work-efficient GPU implementation using up-sweep and down-sweep phases is a standard technique for optimizing parallel reductions on GPUs.
