name: Log-space Exclusive Cumulative Sum for Transmittance
head: Log-space Exclusive Cumulative Sum, Log-space Exclusive Scan for Transmittance
body: This method computes the exclusive cumulative sum of transmittance values in logarithmic space to avoid underflow and enable efficient scatter-add operations for alpha compositing weights. It differs from standard linear-space exclusive scans by operating on \log(1-\alpha), which preserves precision for small alpha values, and by explicitly handling ray-segment boundaries to reset cumulative state between independent rays. It builds on Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan). Inputs: alphas: Array of alpha values for each intersection, shape [M]. rayindices: Array of ray IDs corresponding to each intersection, shape [M], integer type. Outputs: transmittances: Array of transmittance values Ti, shape [M]. weights: Array of compositing weights wi = Ti \cdot \alphai, shape [M]. Data Structures: logoma: Float array [M], storing \log(1-\alphai). logcumsum: Float array [M], storing inclusive cumulative sum of logoma. logexclusive: Float array [M], storing exclusive cumulative sum of logoma. isstart: Boolean array [M], marking the first intersection of each ray. segmentids: Integer array [M], identifying the segment (ray) index for each element. correctionscompact: Float array [K], where K is the number of segments, storing the exclusive cumulative sum value at the start of each segment. Steps: 1. Log-Transform: Compute the log of one-minus-alpha for each intersection to stabilize values near zero. \text{log\oma}i = \log(1 - \alphai) Pitfall: If \alphai = 1, \log(0) results in -\infty. Clamp \alphai to a maximum value slightly less than 1 (e.g., 1 - \epsilon) before logging. 2. Inclusive Scan: Compute the global inclusive cumulative sum of logoma. \text{log\cumsum}i = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{log\oma}j 3. Exclusive Shift: Convert the inclusive sum to an exclusive sum by shifting the array right and prepending zero. \text{log\exclusive}i = \begin{cases} 0 & i=0 \\ \text{log\cumsum}{i-1} & i>0 \end{cases} 4. Boundary Detection: Identify the start of each new ray by comparing the current ray index with the previous ray index. Create shiftedrays by concatenating a dummy value (rayindices[0] - 1) to the front of rayindices[:-1]. Compute isstart: \text{is\start}i = (\text{ray\indices}i \neq \text{shifted\rays}i) 5. Segment ID Assignment: Compute a unique ID for each ray segment using the cumulative sum of the start mask. \text{segment\ids}i = \left(\sum{j=0}^{i} \text{is\start}j\right) - 1 Note: This assumes isstart is cast to integer (0 or 1) before summation. 6. Correction Value Extraction: Extract the exclusive cumulative sum value at the start of each segment. These values represent the offset that must be subtracted to reset the cumulative sum to zero at each ray boundary. Let correctionscompact be the values of logexclusive at indices where isstart is true. Gather the correction for each element: \text{correction}i = \text{corrections\compact}{\text{segment\ids}i} 7. Boundary Reset: Subtract the correction from the exclusive cumulative sum to ensure transmittance starts at 1.0 (log 0) for each new ray. \text{log\transmittance}i = \text{log\exclusive}i - \text{correction}i 8. Exponentiation: Convert back to linear space. \text{transmittances}i = \exp(\text{log\transmittance}i) 9. Weight Calculation: Compute the final compositing weights. \text{weights}i = \text{transmittances}i \cdot \alphai Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def logspaceexclusivecumsum(alphas, rayindices): """ Compute transmittance and weights using log-space exclusive cumulative sum. Args: alphas: np.array of shape [M], float32, values in [0, 1). rayindices: np.array of shape [M], int32, ray IDs. Returns: transmittances: np.array of shape [M], float32. weights: np.array of shape [M], float32. """ # Step 1: Log-transform # Clamp alphas to avoid log(0) if necessary. logoma = np.log(1.0 - alphas) # Step 2: Inclusive cumulative sum logcumsum = np.cumsum(logoma) # Step 3: Convert to exclusive by shifting # Prepend 0.0, drop last element logexclusive = np.concatenate([np.zeros(1), logcumsum[:-1]]) # Step 4: Identify segment boundaries # Shift rayindices right by 1, filling first element with a value != rayindices[0] shiftedrays = np.concatenate([rayindices[:1] - 1, rayindices[:-1]]) isstart = rayindices != shiftedrays # Step 5: Compute per-segment correction IDs # Cast bool to int32 for cumsum segmentids = np.cumsum(isstart.astype(np.int32)) - 1 # Step 6: Gather correction values # correctionscompact contains logexclusive values at the start of each segment startmaskindices = np.where(isstart)[0] correctionscompact = logexclusive[startmaskindices] # Gather correction for each element corrections = correctionscompact[segmentids] # Step 7: Reset boundary values logtransmittance = logexclusive - corrections # Step 8: Exponentiate transmittances = np.exp(logtransmittance) # Step 9: Compute weights weights = transmittances alphas return transmittances, weights Parameters: No explicit tuning parameters. Precision depends on floating-point type (typically float32 or float64). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha = 1.0: \log(1-1) = -\infty. This breaks the cumulative sum. Clamp \alpha to 1-\epsilon. Not given in the sources. This method is used in differentiable Gaussian splatting rasterization, specifically in implementations like gsplat-mlx, to compute transmittance and weights for alpha compositing. It addresses the numerical instability of standard alpha compositing when dealing with many small alpha values, which can lead to underflow in linear space. By working in log space, the method ensures that transmittance values remain representable and accurate. name: CPU Stream Compaction with Scan
head: Prefix Sum based Compaction, StreamCompaction::CPU::compactWithScan
body: CPU Stream Compaction with Scan removes zero-valued elements from an integer array on the CPU by mapping input data to a binary mask, computing an exclusive prefix sum on that mask, and scattering the retained elements to their computed output indices. It sets itself apart from CPU Stream Compaction without Scan by using a scan operation to determine output indices rather than a simple sequential counter. This approach is suitable for scenarios where parallel reduction primitives are available or when preparing data structures for subsequent parallel processing. Inputs and Outputs: idata: Pointer to the constant input array of n integers. odata: Pointer to the output buffer for compacted elements. n: Number of elements in the input array. Return value: The count of non-zero elements (result count). Data Structures: 1. temp: An integer array of size n that stores the binary mask where temp[i] = 1 if idata[i] != 0, else 0. 2. scanArray: An integer array of size n that stores the exclusive prefix sum of temp. Steps: 1. Map: Convert the input integer array into a boolean array (stored as integers 0/1) where non-zero elements map to 1 and zero elements map to 0. Formula: M[i] = (I[i] == 0 ? 0: 1). 2. Scan: Compute the exclusive prefix sum of the boolean array M. Formula: S[0] = 0, S[i] = S[i-1] + M[i-1] for i > 0. This step relies on the parent method Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan). 3. Scatter: Iterate through the original input array and place each non-zero element into the output array at the index specified by the corresponding value in the scanned array. Output index for I[i] is S[i] if M[i]=1. 4. Result Count: Compute resultCount = scanArray[n-1] + temp[n-1]. 5. Cleanup: Free temp and scanArray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: GPU Stream Compaction with Scan
head: Map-Scan-Scatter, Stream Compaction via Scan, GPU Stream Compaction (Work-Efficient)
body: GPU Stream Compaction with Scan filters an input array of integers based on a boolean flag array, returning only elements where the flag is true into an output array while preserving their relative order. It efficiently compacts data by mapping input values to a binary mask, computing an exclusive prefix sum on the mask to generate output indices, and scattering the retained elements to those indices. It sets itself apart from CPU-based compaction by leveraging the GPU's parallel architecture and a work-efficient parallel scan algorithm, achieving performance improvements of over 4x for large arrays. Inputs and Outputs: idata: Pointer to the constant input array of integers (size n). odata: Pointer to the output buffer (size at least n). n: Number of elements in the input array. Output: The resulting compacted array of size M (where M \le N). Data Structures: The algorithm requires four device arrays, all allocated with size N = 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil} (the next power of two greater than or equal to n): 1. devidata: int array of size N. Stores the input data, zero-padded from index n to N-1. 2. devtemp: int array of size N. Stores the binary mask (1 for keep, 0 for discard). 3. devscanArr: int array of size N. Stores the exclusive prefix sum of the mask, representing output indices. 4. devodata: int array of size N. Stores the compacted output. Formal Specification: Given Input of integers and Flag of booleans of size N, the output Output of size M satisfies: \forall j. 0 \le j < M: \text{Output}[j] = t \Rightarrow \exists i. 0 \le i < N: \text{Input}[i] = t \land \text{Flag}[i] \forall i. 0 \le i < N: \text{Input}[i] = t \land \text{Flag}[i] \Rightarrow \exists j. 0 \le j < M: \text{Output}[j] = t \forall i, j. 0 \le i, j < N: (\text{Flag}[i] \land \text{Flag}[j] \land i < j \iff \exists k, l. 0 \le k, l < M: \text{Output}[k] = \text{Input}[i] \land \text{Output}[l] = \text{Input}[j] \land k < l). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Zero-Padding): Compute N = 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil}. Allocate devidata, devodata, devtemp, and devscanArr of size N. Copy idata to devidata for the first n elements. Zero-pad devidata from index n to N-1. 2. Map (Kernel kernMapToBoolean): For each thread i in [0, N): If devidata[i] != 0, set devtemp[i] = 1. Else, set devtemp[i] = 0. 3. Scan (Exclusive Prefix Sum): Perform a work-efficient parallel exclusive scan on devtemp to produce devscanArr. The work-efficient scan proceeds in three phases: an Up-Sweep pass to compute inclusive sums in a tree structure, a root reset setting the final element to 0, and a Down-Sweep pass to compute exclusive sums. The padded zeros do not affect the sum but ensure the tree structure remains complete. 4. Scatter (Kernel kernScatter): For each thread i in [0, N): If devtemp[i] == 1: Let idx = devscanArr[i]. Set devodata[idx] = devidata[i]. Else: Skip the thread; no write occurs. 5. Result Count: The number of remaining elements is derived from the scan result. The total count of kept elements equals the sum of the mask, which can be computed as devscanArr[N-1] + devtemp[N-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gpustreamcompactionwithscan(idata, n): if n == 0: return [], 0 # Step 1: Preprocessing N = 1 << (math.ceil(math.log2(n)) if n > 1 else 0) devidata = [0] N devodata = [0] N devtemp = [0] N devscanArr = [0] N for i in range(n): devidata[i] = idata[i] # Step 2: Map to Boolean for i in range(N): devtemp[i] = 1 if devidata[i] != 0 else 0 # Step 3: Exclusive Scan (Work-Efficient Simulation) # Up-Sweep (Inclusive) inclusive = [0] N inclusive[0] = devtemp[0] for i in range(1, N): inclusive[i] = inclusive[i-1] + devtemp[i] # Root Reset & Down-Sweep (Exclusive) devscanArr[0] = 0 for i in range(1, N): devscanArr[i] = inclusive[i-1] # Step 4: Scatter for i in range(N): if devtemp[i] == 1: idx = devscanArr[i] devodata[idx] = devidata[i] # Step 5: Count count = devscanArr[N-1] + devtemp[N-1] return devodata[:count], count Parameters: n: Number of elements in the input array. blockSize: Thread block size for CUDA kernels (e.g., 1024). gridSize: Calculated as (N + blockSize - 1) / blockSize. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-power-of-two sizes: Input arrays must be zero-padded to the next power of two to ensure the work-efficient scan tree is complete. Precision: Integer types are used for indices and counts, avoiding floating-point precision issues. Boundaries: The exclusive prefix sum values must be within the valid range of the Output array (0 to M-1) to be used safely as indices, which is guaranteed because for elements where Flag[i]=1, the exclusive prefix sum is strictly less than the total sum of flags (M). Time Complexity: O(N) work and O(\log N) depth for the scan, where N is the next power of two greater than or equal to n. Memory Complexity: O(N) additional memory for devtemp and devscanArr. Measured Performance: On an RTX 2060 Super, for an array size of 2^{27}, the work-efficient compact took 58.4025ms for power-of-two and 48.5331ms for non-power-of-two, over 4x faster than the CPU version (886.643ms). Strengths: High performance on GPU, handles arbitrary input sizes via padding, work-efficient scan minimizes redundant operations. Limitations: Requires additional memory for intermediate arrays, padding overhead for non-power-of-two sizes. When to use: When compacting large arrays on GPU and performance is critical. When not to use: For small arrays where CPU overhead is negligible, or when memory is constrained. body: CPU Stream Compaction without Scan removes zero-valued elements from an integer array on the CPU by iterating through the input and writing non-zero elements sequentially to an output buffer. It solves the problem of filtering data without the overhead of computing an exclusive prefix sum. Unlike its sibling CPU Stream Compaction with Scan, which requires a scan operation to determine output indices, this method maintains a simple counter, making it suitable for sequential CPU execution. Inputs and Outputs: idata: Pointer to the constant input array of integers. n: Number of elements in the input array. odata: Pointer to the output buffer for compacted elements. Data Structures: The method uses two contiguous memory blocks: the input array idata of size n and the output array odata of size at least n. No auxiliary data structures are required. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize a counter variable cnt to 0. This counter tracks the number of non-zero elements found and serves as the write index for odata. 2. Iterate through the input array idata with an index i from 0 to n-1. 3. For each element idata[i], check if it is non-zero. 4. If idata[i] is not equal to 0, write idata[i] to odata[cnt] and increment cnt by 1. 5. After the loop completes, cnt holds the total number of non-zero elements, which is the new size of the compacted array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the input array contains no non-zero elements, cnt remains 0, and odata is not written to. If all elements are non-zero, odata becomes a copy of idata. The output buffer odata must be allocated with a size of at least n to prevent buffer overflows, as the worst-case scenario requires full capacity. body: Thrust Scan is a GPU-accelerated exclusive prefix sum wrapper that delegates computation to the NVIDIA Thrust library. It solves the problem of efficiently computing cumulative sums for large datasets on the GPU by abstracting kernel launch and memory management details. It is distinguished from custom CUDA implementations by its reliance on a highly optimized, library-based approach rather than hand-written kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pointer to an array of n elements on the host (idata) and a pointer to an output array (odata) of size n. Output: The exclusive prefix sum of idata stored in odata. For an input array A, the output B satisfies B[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} A[j] for i > 0, and B[0] = 0. Data Structures: thrust::devicevector<T>: A container that manages memory on the GPU device. It is used to ensure that the data resides in device memory before the scan operation begins, thereby excluding memory transfer times from the performance measurement of the scan itself. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a thrust::devicevector<int> dvin initialized with the input range idata to idata + n, and a thrust::devicevector<int> dvout initialized with the output range odata to odata + n. Alternatively, construct dvin via a temporary thrust::hostvector cast to guarantee GPU allocation. 2. Execution: Call thrust::exclusivescan(dvin.begin(), dvin.end(), dvout.begin()) to perform the exclusive prefix sum on the device. 3. Result Retrieval: Copy the results from dvout back to the host output array odata using thrust::copy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def thrustscan(n, idata, odata): """ Performs exclusive prefix sum on idata using Thrust. idata: list or array of n integers (host) odata: list or array of n integers (host, for results) """ if n <= 0: return # Step 1: Initialize device vectors on GPU dvin = thrust.devicevector(n) for i in range(n): dvin[i] = idata[i] dvout = thrust.devicevector(n) # Step 2: Perform exclusive scan on device # thrust::exclusivescan(first, last, result) thrust.exclusivescan(dvin.begin(), dvin.end(), dvout.begin()) # Step 3: Copy results back to host for i in range(n): odata[i] = dvout[i] Parameters: n: The number of elements to scan. thrust::exclusivescan: The specific Thrust function used. It performs an exclusive scan by default. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Elements: If n \le 0, the function should return immediately without performing any operations. Timing: To accurately measure the performance of the scan algorithm itself, memory transfer operations (host-to-device and device-to-host) should be excluded from timing measurements. body: The Naive Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) is a GPU-based algorithm for computing the inclusive prefix sum of an array using global memory and multiple kernel invocations. It serves as a baseline implementation compatible with arbitrary input sizes, distinguishing itself from work-efficient variants by its iterative, level-by-level reduction approach which results in higher computational work (O(n \log n)) but simpler synchronization logic within each kernel launch. Unlike in-place tree-based methods, it avoids race conditions by double-buffering data between two device arrays across iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of n integers idata on the host. Output: An array of n integers odata on the host containing the exclusive prefix sum. Data Structures: Two device arrays, devdata1 and devdata2, of size n to double-buffer results and prevent race conditions, as threads are not guaranteed to run simultaneously. The algorithm processes the input in chunks fitting within a single thread block. If n exceeds the block size, the array is split into multiple blocks, and intermediate kernels propagate block sums to combine results. Parameters: blockSize: Number of threads per block. Typically 256 or 512. ilog2ceil(n): The ceiling of the base-2 logarithm of n, determining the number of kernel launches. Steps: 1. Allocation: Allocate two device arrays of size n. Copy idata to the first device array. 2. Iteration Loop: Calculate iterations L = \lceil \log2(\min(n, \text{blockSize})) \rceil. For each iteration d from 1 to L: Launch a kernel with blocksPerGrid = \lceil n / blockSize \rceil and blockSize threads. The kernel parameter offset is 2^{d-1}. Inside the kernel for each thread with global index id: Copy data[id] to a local buffer buffer[id]. Synchronize threads within the block. If threadIdx.x >= offset, update the value: buffer[id] = data[id - offset] + data[id]. Synchronize threads. Write buffer[id] back to data[id]. Synchronize threads. Swap devdata1 and devdata2 pointers after each kernel launch to double-buffer results. 3. Post-Processing (Exclusive Scan): The result in devdata1 is an inclusive scan. Convert to exclusive scan: Set odata[0] = 0. Copy devdata1[1...n-1] to odata[1...n-1]. If the input size n was larger than the block size, additional kernels (kernExtractLastElementPerBlock, kernAddOffsetPerBlock, kernShiftToExclusive) are used to combine block results and shift to exclusive. Pitfalls: The algorithm suffers from warp divergence and uncoalesced global memory accesses due to interleaved thread utilization patterns. Must be tested with non-power-of-two sized arrays to ensure correctness. The original pseudocode and CUDA code in GPU Gems 3 Chapter 39 contain known errors (superscripting, missing braces, bad indentation). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ilog2ceil(x): """Ceiling of base-2 logarithm.""" if x <= 1: return 0 lg = 0 while x > 1: x >>= 1 lg += 1 return lg def kernNaiveScan(data, buffer, n, blocksize): """Kernel logic for a single thread.""" id = blockIdx.x blocksize + threadIdx.x tx = threadIdx.x if id < n: log2n = ilog2ceil(min(n, blocksize)) for d in range(1, log2n + 1): offset = 1 << (d - 1) buffer[id] = data[id] # syncthreads() if tx >= offset: buffer[id] = data[id - offset] + data[id] # syncthreads() data[id] = buffer[id] # syncthreads() def naivescan(n, idata, blocksize): # 1. Allocation and Initialization devdata1 = list(idata) devdata2 = [0] n # 2. Iterative Kernel Launches (simulated) log2n = ilog2ceil(min(n, blocksize)) blockspergrid = (n + blocksize - 1) // blocksize for d in range(1, log2n + 1): offset = 1 << (d - 1) for b in range(blockspergrid): for t in range(blocksize): id = b blocksize + t if id < n: devdata2[id] = devdata1[id] # syncthreads() if t >= offset: devdata2[id] = devdata1[id - offset] + devdata1[id] # syncthreads() devdata1[id] = devdata2[id] # syncthreads() # Swap buffers for next iteration devdata1, devdata2 = devdata2, devdata1 # 3. Convert Inclusive to Exclusive odata = [0] n if n > 1: odata[1:] = devdata1[1:] return odata A parallel algorithm that computes the inclusive prefix sum of an array in O(n) total work and O(\log n) parallel depth, significantly improving upon the O(n \log n) work complexity of naive parallel scan. It achieves this efficiency by decomposing the computation into an upsweep (reduction) phase and a downsweep (scan) phase, operating on a binary tree structure. Unlike the Kogge-Stone algorithm, which is inherently inclusive and computes all prefix sums simultaneously via fixed-distance dependencies, the Work-Efficient Scan explicitly constructs exclusive intermediate values before converting them to inclusive results, making it suitable for operations where the current element must not influence its own prefix result during intermediate steps. A parallel prefix sum algorithm that concurrently generates binary masks for each radix combination, computes local prefix sums, merges results, and outputs total counts per block. It generates binary masks for each radix combination, computes the local prefix sum of the mask, merges the prefix sum results for all combinations, and sends the total number of each radix combination in each block to the output block sum array. Time Complexity: O(\log n) per block, but requires multiple kernel launches for arrays larger than block size, leading to higher overhead. When not to use: For large arrays where performance is critical, or when work efficiency is required. The Naive Parallel Prefix Sum algorithm is described in GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, Section 39.2.1. name: Work-Efficient Scan
head: Work-Efficient Parallel Scan, Work-Efficient Parallel Inclusive Scan, Work-Efficient Inclusive Scan
body: The Work-Efficient Scan is a parallel algorithm that computes the inclusive prefix sum of an array in O(n) total work and O(\log n) parallel depth, significantly improving upon the O(n \log n) work complexity of naive parallel scan. It achieves this efficiency by decomposing the computation into an upsweep (reduction) phase and a downsweep (scan) phase, operating on a binary tree structure. Unlike the Kogge-Stone algorithm, which is inherently inclusive and computes all prefix sums simultaneously via fixed-distance dependencies, the Work-Efficient Scan explicitly constructs exclusive intermediate values before converting them to inclusive results, making it suitable for operations where the current element must not influence its own prefix result during intermediate steps. For a single block, it operates in-place on a device array. For arrays larger than a single block, it uses multiple kernel launches across hierarchical levels. It requires the input size to be padded to the next power of two for internal tree operations, though the final output matches the original size. Input: Array idata of size n (arbitrary integer or floating-point type). Output: Array odata of size n containing the inclusive prefix sum. Auxiliary: For multi-block execution, arrays devidata, devbuffer, and devodata of size numscans are used to manage hierarchical reduction levels. For multi-block execution: devidata: Array of pointers to device memory, size numscans. devidata[i] holds the input for level i. devbuffer: Array of pointers to device memory, size numscans. devbuffer[i] holds intermediate results for level i. devodata: Array of pointers to device memory, size numscans. devodata[i] holds the final exclusive results for level i. arraysizes: Array of integers, size numscans. arraysizes[i] is the number of elements at level i. gridsizes: Array of integers, size numscans. gridsizes[i] is the number of blocks at level i. blocksize: CUDA block size. Profiling indicates optimal performance at 128 threads per block, though 512 is also cited as optimal in other contexts. Values like 1024 are suboptimal due to reduced GPU parallelism. n: Input array size. npad: Padded size, calculated as 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil}. 1. Preparation: Calculate npad = 1 << ilog2ceil(n). Determine numscans and arraysizes/gridsizes by iteratively dividing the length by blocksize until it fits in one block: python len = npad numscans = 0 while (len + blocksize - 1) / blocksize > 1: numscans += 1 len = (len + blocksize - 1) / blocksize Allocate device memory for devidata, devbuffer, devodata, arraysizes, and gridsizes. Copy input idata to devidata[0] for n elements. 2. Forward Pass (Inclusive Scan): Loop i from 0 to numscans - 1: Launch kernScanInclusive on devidata[i] into devbuffer[i]. Copy devbuffer[i] back to devidata[i]. If i < numscans - 1: Extract the last element of each block from devidata[i] into devidata[i+1] using kernExtractLastElementPerBlock to prepare the next level's input. 3. Backward Pass (Exclusive Scan/Shift): Loop i from numscans - 1 down to 0: Launch kernShiftToExclusive on devbuffer[i] to produce exclusive indices in devodata[i]. If i >= 1: Launch kernAddOffsetPerBlock to add the offset from devodata[i] to devbuffer[i-1] to produce the final exclusive indices for the next lower level. 4. Final Copy: Copy the final exclusive scan results from devodata[0] to host output odata for n elements. The core work-efficient scan within a single block (used in steps 2 and 3 above) follows these steps: 1. Upsweep Phase (Reduction): For each thread with global index id < n: Iterate d from 0 to log2n - 1: If (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: idata[id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1] += idata[id + (1 << d) - 1]. Synchronize threads after each d. 2. Reset Last Element: The last thread (tid == blockDim.x - 1) or the thread processing the last element (id == n - 1) stores the total reduction sum in a local variable reductionsum and sets idata[id] = 0. 3. Downsweep Phase (Scan): Iterate d from log2n - 1 down to 0: If (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: temp = idata[id + (1 << d) - 1] idata[id + (1 << d) - 1] = idata[id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1] idata[id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1] += temp. Synchronize threads after each d. 4. Convert Exclusive to Inclusive: If the thread is the last thread in the block or processes the last element: odata[id] = reductionsum. Otherwise: odata[id] = idata[id + 1]. Unverified code. Assumes idata is padded to power of two size internally if necessary. """ tid = 0 # Represents threadIdx.x id = tid npad = 1 << ilog2ceil(n) log2n = ilog2ceil(n) # Upsweep Phase for d in range(log2n): if (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: idxleft = id + (1 << d) - 1 idxright = id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1 if idxright < npad: idata[idxright] += idata[idxleft] syncthreads() # Reset Last Element reductionsum = 0 if tid == blocksize - 1 or id == n - 1: reductionsum = idata[id] idata[id] = 0 syncthreads() # Downsweep Phase for d in range(log2n - 1, -1, -1): if (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: idxleft = id + (1 << d) - 1 idxright = id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1 if idxright < npad: temp = idata[idxleft] idata[idxleft] = idata[idxright] idata[idxright] += temp syncthreads() # Convert Exclusive to Inclusive if tid == blocksize - 1 or id == n - 1: odata[id] = reductionsum else: odata[id] = idata[id + 1] Non-Power-of-Two Sizes: The algorithm works best with power-of-two length arrays. For non-power-of-two arrays, intermediate array sizes must be rounded up to the next power of two, requiring extra memory. Memory Access Patterns: High memory throughput indicates non-optimal memory access patterns. SM workload imbalance is a main bottleneck in the upsweep phase, where some Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) are underutilized by as much as 43.66%. Block Size: A block size of 1024 does not yield ideal results for any algorithm, likely due to excessive block size reducing GPU parallelism and leaving computational resources underutilized. Known Errors: The pseudocode in GPU Gems 3 Chapter 39 Example 39-2 contains known errors. Blelloch’s algorithm is an exclusive parallel in-place algorithm for computing the prefix sum of an array of size N. It solves the problem by decomposing the computation into two distinct phases: an up-sweep (reduce) phase that builds a binary tree of partial sums, and a down-sweep (scan) phase that distributes these sums to compute the final exclusive prefix values. Unlike Kogge-Stone, which is an inclusive algorithm, Blelloch’s method explicitly excludes the current element from its own sum, making it suitable for operations where the current value must not influence its own prefix result. It is a work-efficient alternative to naive parallel scan, building on the principles of Work-Efficient Scan. An optimized GPU scan implementation using shared memory and bank conflict avoidance, based on GPU Gems 3 Chapter 39 Examples 39.1 and 39.2. It optimizes memory access patterns to avoid shared memory bank conflicts. The size of shared memory is dynamic and related to the block size. Occupancy is affected by the amount of shared memory used per block relative to the SM's limit. Using maximum shared memory per block reduces occupancy (e.g., max 1 block per SM), which may not yield best performance. Time Complexity: O(\log n) parallel depth per block. Work Complexity: O(n) total work, compared to naive O(n \log n) work. Memory Complexity: In-place on a single device array for single-block execution. For multi-block execution, auxiliary arrays are required for each scan level. Measured Performance: Tested on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, Ryzen 3700X @ 2.22GHz, RTX 2060 Super. The upsweep phase consumes the majority of execution time (averaging 28.38 ms), while the downsweep phase is shorter (averaging 20.26 ms). Scaling: Performance improves with block size up to an optimal point (128 or 512 threads per block), after which it degrades due to reduced parallelism. Strengths: Work-efficient, suitable for arbitrary input sizes (with padding), in-place operation for single blocks. Limitations: SM workload imbalance in upsweep phase, non-optimal memory access patterns, requires extra memory for non-power-of-two sizes. The Work-Efficient Scan is based on the "Work-Efficient" algorithm described in GPU Gems 3, Section 39.2.2. It is a standard parallel primitive used in stream compaction and other GPU algorithms. name: Blelloch’s Prefix Sum Algorithm
head: Blelch's algorithm, Blelloch Scan, Blelloch's parallel prefix sum, Parallel Prefix Sum via Binary Tree, Tree Scan Algorithm, Up-sweep/Down-sweep Scan, up-sweep/down-sweep prefix sum
body: Blelloch’s algorithm is an exclusive parallel in-place algorithm for computing the prefix sum of an array of size N. It solves the problem by decomposing the computation into two distinct phases: an up-sweep (reduce) phase that builds a binary tree of partial sums, and a down-sweep (scan) phase that distributes these sums to compute the final exclusive prefix values. Unlike Kogge-Stone, which is an inclusive algorithm, Blelloch’s method explicitly excludes the current element from its own sum, making it suitable for operations where the current value must not influence its own prefix result. It is a work-efficient alternative to naive parallel scan, building on the principles of Work-Efficient Scan. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array Input of size N. Output: An array Output of size N such that Output[i] = \sum{t=0}^{i-1} Input[t] for 0 \le i < N. Constraint: The algorithm is in-place; Input and Output initially share the same values, and Output is overwritten during execution. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on a single array Output of size N. Threads are indexed by tid (thread ID). The implementation assumes a block size of N/2 threads, where each thread handles two elements in the initial step, or generally maps to the indices defined by the indicator variable. Parameters: stride: The distance between elements being summed. Starts at 1 in up-sweep, N/2 in down-sweep. indicator: The index of the element currently being processed by the thread. Steps: 1. Initialization: Let tid be the thread ID. Initialize stride = 1. Initialize indicator = 2 tid + 1. 2. Phase 1: Up-sweep (Reduce): Loop while stride < N: If indicator < N and indicator >= stride: Update Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride]. Synchronize all threads (syncthreads()). Update indicator = 2 indicator + 1. Update stride = 2 stride. Synchronize all threads (syncthreads()). Result: The last element Output[N-1] holds the total sum of all input values. 3. Phase 2: Down-sweep (Scan): Initialize indicator = N tid + N - 1. Initialize stride = N / 2. If indicator < N: Set Output[indicator] = 0. Loop while stride >= 1: If indicator < N and indicator >= stride: Store temporary = Output[indicator]. Update Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride]. Set Output[indicator - stride] = temporary. Synchronize all threads (syncthreads()). Update indicator = (indicator - 1) / 2. Update stride = stride / 2. Result: The array Output contains the exclusive prefix sums. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def barrier(): """Synchronizes all threads in the block (standard hardware primitive).""" pass def blellochscankernel(Output, N, tid): # Phase 1: Up-sweep (Reduce) indicator = 2 tid + 1 stride = 1 while stride < N: if indicator < N and indicator >= stride: Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride] barrier() indicator = 2 indicator + 1 stride = 2 stride barrier() # Barrier between phases # Phase 2: Down-sweep (Scan) indicator = N tid + N - 1 stride = N // 2 if indicator < N: Output[indicator] = 0 while stride >= 1: if indicator < N and indicator >= stride: temporary = Output[indicator] Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride] Output[indicator - stride] = temporary barrier() indicator = (indicator - 1) // 2 stride = stride // 2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Race Freedom: The algorithm requires careful permission management. In each iteration, some threads lose write permissions because their indicator exceeds the array bounds N. To maintain correctness, thread 0 collects these lost permissions in each iteration and redistributes them at the barrier. In-place Verification: Because the algorithm is in-place, elements change in every iteration. Verifying functional correctness requires tracking the history of values using ghost variables, as intermediate steps are non-trivial. Synchronization: Barriers are strictly required between iterations in both phases and between the up-sweep and down-sweep phases to ensure that partial sums from previous levels are available for the next level. Time complexity is O(\log N) parallel time, corresponding to the number of levels in the binary tree. Memory complexity is O(N) for the input/output array, as the algorithm is in-place and requires no additional auxiliary storage proportional to N beyond the input array itself. Strengths include work-efficiency with linear total work O(N), avoiding the high memory bandwidth usage of naive approaches, and widespread adoption in libraries such as the AMD APP SDK and NVIDIA CUDA SDK. Limitations include the requirement for synchronization barriers at every level, which can introduce latency on hardware with poor barrier performance, and the lack of explicit power-of-2 requirements in the sources, though boundary checks handle arbitrary N. Blelloch’s algorithm was introduced by Guy E. Blelloch. It is frequently cited alongside Kogge-Stone as one of the two primary parallel in-place prefix sum algorithms used in practice. The algorithm is implemented in major parallel computing SDKs, including the AMD Accelerated Parallel Processing (APP) SDK and the NVIDIA CUDA SDK. Formal verification of its correctness, particularly regarding data race freedom and in-place state management, has been studied in recent literature. name: Kogge-Stone Parallel Prefix Sum
head: Kogge-Stone's algorithm
body: The Kogge-Stone algorithm is a parallel prefix sum (scan) method that computes inclusive prefix sums in a single phase using an in-place update strategy. Unlike Blelloch’s algorithm, which employs a two-phase (up-sweep/down-sweep) approach, Kogge-Stone’s single-phase structure simplifies functional correctness verification while maintaining data race freedom through explicit synchronization. It serves as a foundational primitive for volume rendering pipelines requiring cumulative distribution functions or histogram binning, building on the general principles of Naive Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan). Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array Input of size N. Output: An array Output of size N, which initially holds the input values and is overwritten with the inclusive prefix sums. Parameters: N (array length), offset (distance between elements, starting at 1), tid (thread ID). Data Structures: Output: A global memory array of size N. The algorithm operates in-place, meaning the output overwrites the input. temp: A local register variable used to store the intermediate sum for a thread to prevent data races during in-place updates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize offset to 1. 2. Each thread i (where 0 \le i < N) executes the following loop: a. Read the current value at Output[i] into temp. b. If i \ge \text{offset}, add Output[i - offset] to temp. c. Execute a thread block barrier to ensure all threads have read their required values before any writes occur. d. If i \ge \text{offset}, write temp back to Output[i]. e. Execute a second thread block barrier to ensure all writes are complete before updating the offset. f. Double the offset: \text{offset} = 2 \times \text{offset}. 3. Repeat until \text{offset} \ge N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inclusiveprefixsumkernel(Output, N, tid): offset = 1 while offset < N: temp = Output[tid] if tid >= offset: temp = Output[tid - offset] + temp syncthreads() # Block barrier if tid >= offset: Output[tid] = temp syncthreads() # Block barrier offset = 2 offset Parameters: offset: The distance between elements to be summed. It starts at 1 and doubles each iteration (1, 2, 4, \dots) until it exceeds N. temp: An auxiliary variable used to store the intermediate sum for a thread to avoid data races during in-place updates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Races: Since the algorithm is in-place, threads must read current values before updating. This is handled by using the auxiliary variable temp and barriers to synchronize reads and writes. Without barriers, a thread might read a value that has already been updated by another thread in the same iteration, leading to incorrect results. Boundary Conditions: The condition tid >= offset ensures that threads do not access memory locations outside the array bounds (specifically, tid - offset would be negative). Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. A variant that reduces the number of operations per element by using a different tree structure, trading off some simplicity for better performance on large datasets. Choose when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. See Work-Efficient Scan. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output array. The algorithm is in-place, requiring no additional global memory beyond the input/output array. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Single-phase structure makes functional correctness verification easier compared to two-phase algorithms like Blelloch’s. Limitations: Requires explicit synchronization barriers, which can introduce latency. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The algorithm is analyzed in the context of formal verification of parallel prefix sums and stream processing. Its single-phase nature distinguishes it from later algorithms like Blelloch’s. The algorithm is frequently used in formal verification studies due to its straightforward structure. name: Global Accumulator + Compaction
head: FGatherVisibleCountsCS, FPrefixSumVisibleCountsCS, Global counting
body: A two-pass GPU compute system that gathers visible splat counts per proxy and computes prefix sums to generate indirect dispatch and draw arguments for global Phase-3 rendering passes. It aggregates per-proxy visibility data into a global array and prepares execution parameters for subsequent geometry generation and indexing stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: PerProxyVisibleCount (SRV StructuredBuffer<uint>), ProxyIndex (uint32), ProxyCount (uint32), MaxRenderBudget (uint32). Output: GlobalVisibleCountArray (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalBaseOffsets (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalCalcDistIndirectArgs (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalSortIndirectArgs (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalSortParams (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalDrawIndirectArgs (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>). Data Structures: 1. GlobalVisibleCountArray: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size ProxyCount. 2. GlobalBaseOffsets: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size ProxyCount. 3. GlobalCalcDistIndirectArgs: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for distance calculation dispatch arguments. 4. GlobalSortIndirectArgs: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for radix sort dispatch arguments. 5. GlobalSortParams: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for sort parameters. 6. GlobalDrawIndirectArgs: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for draw call arguments. Steps: 1. Gather Visible Counts: Dispatch FGatherVisibleCountsCS with 1 thread per proxy. Each thread copies GPUResources->VisibleSplatCountBuffer[0] into GlobalVisibleCountArray[ProxyIndex]. 2. Compute Prefix Sums & Indirect Arguments: Dispatch FPrefixSumVisibleCountsCS with 1 thread total. The thread iterates through GlobalVisibleCountArray to compute exclusive prefix sums, calculates the total visible splat count, applies the MaxRenderBudget clamp, and writes the results to the indirect argument buffers for the CalcDistances, RadixSort, and DrawSplats passes. Formulas: Let C[i] be the visible splat count for proxy i. The exclusive prefix sum offset is O[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} C[j] for i \in [0, ProxyCount), with O[0] = 0. The total visible splat count is T = \sum{j=0}^{ProxyCount-1} C[j]. The clamped total is T{clamped} = \min(T, MaxRenderBudget) if MaxRenderBudget > 0, otherwise T{clamped} = T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gathervisiblecounts(perproxyvisiblecount, globalvisiblecountarray, proxyindex): globalvisiblecountarray[proxyindex] = perproxyvisiblecount[proxyindex] def prefixsumandcompact(globalvisiblecountarray, globalbaseoffsets, globalcalcdistindirectargs, globalsortindirectargs, globalsortparams, globaldrawindirectargs, proxycount, maxrenderbudget): currentoffset = 0 if proxycount > 0: globalbaseoffsets[0] = 0 for i in range(1, proxycount): currentoffset += globalvisiblecountarray[i-1] globalbaseoffsets[i] = currentoffset totalsplats = currentoffset + globalvisiblecountarray[proxycount - 1] else: totalsplats = 0 if maxrenderbudget > 0 and totalsplats > maxrenderbudget: totalsplats = maxrenderbudget # Write indirect arguments for Phase-3 passes globalsortparams[0] = totalsplats # Indirect argument layouts (count, baseInstance, etc.) are not specified in the sources globalsortindirectargs[0] = 0 globalsortindirectargs[1] = 1 globalsortindirectargs[2] = 1 globalcalcdistindirectargs[0] = 1 globalcalcdistindirectargs[1] = 1 globalcalcdistindirectargs[2] = 1 globaldrawindirectargs[0] = totalsplats globaldrawindirectargs[1] = 1 globaldrawindirectargs[2] = 0 globaldrawindirectargs[3] = 0 globaldrawindirectargs[4] = 0 Parameters: MaxRenderBudget: uint32. Cap on total visible splats. 0 means no cap. Edge Cases: If ProxyCount is 0, the prefix sum loop is skipped and all totals are 0. MaxRenderBudget clamping may truncate the scene, requiring subsequent logic to handle partial rendering or culling. A GPU compute shader that prepares indirect dispatch and draw arguments from the visible splat count generated by the preceding Global Accumulator + Compaction pass. It serves as the orchestration layer that translates per-proxy visibility data into the specific argument structures required by the graphics API for subsequent Phase-3 rendering and sorting kernels. Unlike the compaction pass which gathers data, this method configures the execution parameters for the geometry generation and indexing stages. Choose it when explicit control over dispatch dimensions and sort parameters is required for the rendering pipeline. Time Complexity: O(P) for gathering counts and O(P) for the sequential prefix sum pass, where P is the proxy count. Memory Complexity: O(P) for GlobalVisibleCountArray and GlobalBaseOffsets. Strengths: Centralizes visibility data and directly generates batched rendering arguments for downstream passes. Limitations: The single-threaded prefix sum approach may become a bottleneck if P is extremely large. When to use: When transitioning from per-proxy visibility culling to global batched rendering passes for splat distance calculation, sorting, and drawing. Implemented in the OpenSplat4D project, this method is part of a Gaussian Splatting performance optimization suite. It addresses the need to efficiently transition from per-proxy visibility culling to global batched rendering passes for splat distance calculation, sorting, and drawing. The prefix sum computation leverages the fully optimized one-way prefix sum provided in the CUDPP library. name: Indirect Argument Preparation
head: FPrepareIndirectArgsCS
body: Indirect Argument Preparation is a GPU compute shader that prepares indirect dispatch and draw arguments from the visible splat count. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on argument buffer population rather than data compaction or scheduling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: VisibleSplatCount (StructuredBuffer<uint>). Output 1: IndirectDispatchArgs (RWStructuredBuffer<uint>, uint3 storing numGroupsX, numGroupsY, numGroupsZ). Output 2: IndirectDrawArgs (RWStructuredBuffer<uint>, 5 uints for DrawIndexedIndirect). Output 3: SortIndirectArgs (RWStructuredBuffer<uint>, uint3 storing NumTiles, 1, 1). Output 4: SortParamsBuffer (RWStructuredBuffer<uint>, uint2 storing SortCount, NumTiles). Data Structures: All buffers use 32-bit unsigned integers (uint) with standard row-major memory layout. IndirectDispatchArgs and SortIndirectArgs occupy 12 bytes each (3 × 4 bytes). IndirectDrawArgs occupies 20 bytes (5 × 4 bytes). SortParamsBuffer occupies 8 bytes (2 × 4 bytes). Numbered Steps: 1. Sum the VisibleSplatCount buffer to obtain the total visible splat count for the frame. 2. Compute the number of work groups by dividing the total splat count by ComputeThreadGroupSize, rounding up to the nearest integer. 3. Write the computed group counts into IndirectDispatchArgs as a uint3 (numGroupsX, numGroupsY, numGroupsZ). 4. Write the total splat count and standard API defaults into IndirectDrawArgs (5 uints for DrawIndexedIndirect). 5. Write NumTiles and fixed 1 values into SortIndirectArgs. 6. Write SortCount and NumTiles into SortParamsBuffer. Formulas: Total splats: N = \sum{i=0}^{M-1} \text{VisibleSplatCount}[i], where M is the buffer length. Work groups: G = \lceil N / S \rceil = (N + S - 1) // S, where S is ComputeThreadGroupSize. Parameters: ComputeThreadGroupSize (uint32): Thread group size for compute shaders. Typical values are powers of two (e.g., 64 or 128). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero splats: If N = 0, G = 0 and dispatches should be skipped to avoid invalid API calls. Buffer alignment: Structured buffers require 4-byte alignment; all argument structures naturally satisfy this. Derivation of NumTiles and SortCount: The sources do not specify how these values are computed; they are treated as precomputed inputs or derived from scene resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def PrepareIndirectArgs(visiblesplatcounts: list[int], computethreadgroupsize: int, numtiles: int, sortcount: int) -> dict: # Inputs: visiblesplatcounts (StructuredBuffer<uint>), computethreadgroupsize (uint32) # Parameters: numtiles (int), sortcount (int) [G: derivation not given in sources] # Outputs: IndirectDispatchArgs, IndirectDrawArgs, SortIndirectArgs, SortParamsBuffer # Step 1: Compute total visible splats totalsplats = sum(visiblesplatcounts) # Step 2: Calculate dispatch group counts (ceiling division) numgroups = (totalsplats + computethreadgroupsize - 1) // computethreadgroupsize # Step 3: IndirectDispatchArgs (uint3: numGroupsX, numGroupsY, numGroupsZ) # Sources do not specify axis distribution; defaulting to 1D dispatch indirectdispatchargs = [numgroups, 1, 1] # Step 4: IndirectDrawArgs (5 uints for DrawIndexedIndirect) # Standard layout: indexcount, startindexlocation, startvertexlocation, startinstancelocation, instancecount indirectdrawargs = [totalsplats, 0, 0, 0, 0] # Step 5: SortIndirectArgs (uint3: NumTiles, 1, 1) sortindirectargs = [numtiles, 1, 1] # Step 6: SortParamsBuffer (uint2: SortCount, NumTiles) sortparamsbuffer = [sortcount, numtiles] return { "IndirectDispatchArgs": indirectdispatchargs, "IndirectDrawArgs": indirectdrawargs, "SortIndirectArgs": sortindirectargs, "SortParamsBuffer": sortparamsbuffer } A GPU compute shader that finalizes the parallel volume building process by synchronizing atomic counters and configuring indirect dispatch parameters for subsequent rendering passes. name: Indirect Dispatch Orchestration
head: IsoMesh Compute Pipeline Dispatch
body: Indirect Dispatch Orchestration is a GPU compute shader that finalizes the parallel volume building process by synchronizing atomic counters and configuring indirect dispatch parameters for subsequent rendering passes. It acts as a single-thread compute shader that clamps counters to their allocated limits to prevent out-of-bounds execution, bridging the gap between parallel work generation and sequential GPU submission. It differs from Indirect Argument Preparation by focusing specifically on the data preparation and boundary clamping logic rather than the broader scheduling strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A buffer of atomic counters (vertex count, triangle count, intermediate vertex count) populated by previous kernels. Input: Compute shader instance parameters (thread group sizes). Output: Indirect dispatch arguments for vertex generation, triangle generation, index buffer building, and intermediate vertex indexing kernels. Data Structures: CounterBuffer: A structured buffer or compute buffer containing atomic counters. vertexCount: uint triangleCount: uint intermediateVertexCount: uint IndirectArgs: A structured buffer or compute buffer containing indirect dispatch arguments. vertexGenArgs: uint[4] (Thread counts X, Y, Z, Padding) triGenArgs: uint[4] indexBuildArgs: uint[4] intermediateIdxArgs: uint[4] Steps: 1. Reset Counters: Reset all append buffer counters to zero. This ensures a clean state for the current frame or volume update. 2. Map Kernel Dispatch: Dispatch the map kernel using thread group sizes derived from the compute shader instance. This kernel typically processes the volume data to identify active regions. 3. Vertex Generation Dispatch: Dispatch the vertex generation kernel. This kernel generates vertices based on the mapped data. 4. Vertex Counting Dispatch: Dispatch the vertex counting kernel using indirect dispatch with an offset pointing to the vertex count in the counter buffer. This kernel counts the number of vertices generated. 5. Triangle Generation Dispatch: Dispatch the triangle generation kernel using indirect dispatch with the same offset. This kernel generates triangles based on the counted vertices. 6. Index Buffer Building Dispatch: Dispatch the index buffer building kernel using indirect dispatch with an offset pointing to the triangle count. This kernel builds the index buffer for rendering. 7. Intermediate Vertex Indexing Dispatch: Dispatch the intermediate vertex indexing kernel using indirect dispatch with an offset pointing to the intermediate vertex count. This kernel handles intermediate vertex indexing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Build Setup & Indirect Dispatch Management
head: Build Setup Compute, Indirect Dispatch Setup
body: This method finalizes the parallel volume building process by synchronizing atomic counters and configuring indirect dispatch or draw parameters for subsequent rendering passes. It acts as a single-thread compute shader that clamps counters to their allocated limits to prevent out-of-bounds execution, bridging the gap between parallel work generation and sequential GPU submission. It differs from Indirect Dispatch Orchestration by focusing specifically on the data preparation and boundary clamping logic rather than the broader scheduling strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: push.setup (enum controlling operation type), build.maxRenderClusters (limit), BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP (constant). Input/Output: SceneBuilding buildRW (coherent SSBO), Readback (SSBO). Output: Configured indirect parameters in buildRW and readback values in Readback. Data Structures: 1. SceneBuilding buildRW (Coherent SSBO): traversalTaskCounter: uint traversalInfoWriteCounter: uint traversalGroupCounter: uint renderClusterCounter: uint indirectDrawClusters: Struct { count: uint, first: uint } indirectDispatchBlasInsertion: Struct { gridX: uint, gridY: uint, gridZ: uint } maxTraversalInfos: uint maxRenderClusters: uint 2. Readback (SSBO): numRenderClusters: uint numTraversalInfos: uint numRenderedClusters: uint Steps: The method executes as a single-thread compute shader. The logic branches based on push.setup. 1. Clamp and Configure Draw Parameters: If push.setup == BUILDSETUPDRAW: Calculate numRenderedClusters = min(renderClusterCounter, build.maxRenderClusters). Set buildRW.indirectDrawClusters.count = numRenderedClusters. Set buildRW.indirectDrawClusters.first = 0. 2. Record Traversal Info for Readback: Determine the effective traversal count. If USESEPARATEGROUPS is false, use buildRW.traversalInfoWriteCounter. Otherwise, use buildRW.traversalGroupCounter. Calculate effectiveTraversalCount = max(buildRW.traversalInfoWriteCounter, effectiveGroupCounter). Set Readback.numTraversalInfos = effectiveTraversalCount. 3. Clamp and Configure BLAS Insertion Dispatch: If push.setup == BUILDSETUPBLASINSERTION: Use the clamped numRenderedClusters from Step 1 (or re-calculate if not previously set). Calculate grid X dimension: gridX = (numRenderedClusters + BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP - 1) / BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP. Set buildRW.indirectDispatchBlasInsertion.gridX = gridX. Set gridY and gridZ to 1 (standard 1D dispatch assumption unless specified otherwise). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsetupcompute(pushsetup, build, readback, BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP, USESEPARATEGROUPS): # Step 1: Handle Draw Setup if pushsetup == BUILDSETUPDRAW: # Clamp atomic counter to allocated limit to prevent OOB numrenderedclusters = min(build.renderClusterCounter, build.maxRenderClusters) build.indirectDrawClusters.count = numrenderedclusters build.indirectDrawClusters.first = 0 # Step 2: Record Traversal Info # Determine which counter represents the active group count if not USESEPARATEGROUPS: groupcounter = build.traversalInfoWriteCounter else: groupcounter = build.traversalGroupCounter # Take max to ensure all info is captured effectivetraversalcount = max(build.traversalInfoWriteCounter, groupcounter) readback.numTraversalInfos = effectivetraversalcount # Step 3: Handle BLAS Insertion Setup if pushsetup == BUILDSETUPBLASINSERTION: # Re-calculate or use existing clamped count # Note: If BUILDSETUPDRAW was not run, renderClusterCounter might be unclamped. # Safe practice: clamp again here if count is needed for dispatch sizing. currentclustercount = build.renderClusterCounter if pushsetup != BUILDSETUPDRAW: currentclustercount = min(currentclustercount, build.maxRenderClusters) # Ceiling division for grid size gridx = (currentclustercount + BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP - 1) // BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP build.indirectDispatchBlasInsertion.gridX = gridx build.indirectDispatchBlasInsertion.gridY = 1 build.indirectDispatchBlasInsertion.gridZ = 1 # Optional: Update readback for clusters if not done in draw setup if pushsetup == BUILDSETUPDRAW: readback.numRenderedClusters = build.indirectDrawClusters.count readback.numRenderClusters = build.renderClusterCounter # Original unclamped or total generated Parameters: push.setup: Enum. Values: BUILDSETUPTRAVERSALRUN, BUILDSETUPDRAW, BUILDSETUPBLASINSERTION. BLASINSERTCLUSTERSWORKGROUP: Constant defining workgroup size for BLAS insertion dispatch. Typical value: Not given in the sources. USESEPARATEGROUPS: Boolean flag. If false, traversalInfoWriteCounter is used for readback logic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Counter Overshoot: Traversal and cluster counters are atomic and may overshoot their allocated limits during concurrent execution. The min() clamp is critical to prevent out-of-bounds indirect dispatches. Coherence: SceneBuilding must be a coherent SSBO to ensure visibility of atomic updates across different shader stages or invocations. Branching: The method is single-threaded but handles multiple setup types. Ensure the caller invokes the correct setup type corresponding to the required subsequent pass. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to scene size, as it performs a fixed number of atomic reads, comparisons, and writes. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, relying on existing SSBOs. Performance: Negligible overhead compared to the parallel build phases. The single-thread nature ensures no contention. Strengths: Prevents GPU hangs or crashes due to invalid dispatch sizes; centralizes parameter configuration. Limitations: Single-threaded bottleneck if the setup logic were more complex; relies on correct atomic counter management in prior stages. When to use: After any parallel volume building or traversal phase that produces atomic counters requiring clamping before submission. This method is part of the Proxy-GS rendering pipeline, specifically handling the transition from parallel compute to indirect drawing/dispatch. It addresses the common GPU programming challenge of synchronizing parallel atomic counters with sequential submission requirements. name: Parallel Vector Multiplication
head: CUDA Vector Multiplication, OpenCL Parallel Vector Multiplication, Vector Add/Multiply Kernel
body: Parallel Vector Multiplication is a fundamental GPU primitive where each thread independently multiplies corresponding elements from two input arrays to produce an output array. It solves the problem of element-wise vector scaling or Hadamard product computation at massive scale by mapping one thread per data element. It is distinct from sibling primitives like Parallel Prefix Sum (which requires inter-thread dependency) or Atomic Fragment List Insertion (which requires synchronization), as it involves no communication between threads. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two arrays of floating-point values, A and B, of size N. Output: One array C of size N, where C[i] = A[i] \times B[i]. Data Structures: Arrays are stored in global memory. Data types: global const float for inputs and global float for output. Vector types float2, float3, float4, float8, and float16 are supported to increase arithmetic throughput per instruction. In compressive rendering contexts, vectors may represent sampling matrices where S^T S x operations insert 0 in the location of missing pixels. Steps: 1. The GPU kernel is launched with a grid of threads sized to cover the entire vector length N. 2. Each thread calculates its unique global index id using getglobalid(0). 3. The thread reads A[id] and B[id] from global memory. 4. The thread computes the product P = A[id] \times B[id]. 5. The thread writes P to C[id] in global memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vectormultiplykernel(globalid, a, b, c, n): # 1. Retrieve global unique ID id = globalid # 2. Bounds check to prevent out-of-bounds access if id < n: # 3. Load inputs from global memory vala = a[id] valb = b[id] # 4. Multiply result = vala valb # 5. Store output to global memory c[id] = result Parameters: Vector Width: Vector types float2, float3, float4, float8, and float16 are supported, with arithmetic operations on these types being as fast or faster than scalar floats. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: If N is not a multiple of the grid size, a bounds check is required. Missing Pixels: In compressive rendering contexts, "multiplication" may involve sparse matrices where missing pixels are treated as zero. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of elements. Memory Complexity: O(N) for input and output arrays. Performance: Massive calculations (e.g., S^T S x in compressive rendering) complete in a few milliseconds using CUDA. Modern GPUs feature between 16 and 480 stream processors, with adding processors halving calculation time. Strengths: Extremely high throughput for independent element-wise operations with minimal synchronization overhead. Limitations: Does not handle dependencies between elements, and memory bandwidth becomes the primary bottleneck due to low arithmetic intensity. The method originates from early GPU computing frameworks like CUDA and OpenCL, leveraging the SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) architecture. It is used in compressive rendering for applying large sampling matrices. It also accelerates raycasting and raytracing by distributing independent pixel calculations across multiprocessors. Groups pixels into tiles to reduce memory latency and enable shared memory usage. It differs from global compositing by optimizing cache locality and is chosen for high-resolution volumes. Tiled Parallel Compositing Computes final pixel colors directly without intermediate buffers. It avoids the overhead of fragment lists and is chosen for simple transparency models. Parallel Direct Compositing Executes instructions across hardware subgroups to share data without global memory. It differs from thread-level primitives by enabling fast intra-group communication and is chosen for reductions or shuffles. name: Parallel Direct Compositing
head: Direct compositing method
body: Parallel Direct Compositing is a distributed memory volume rendering technique where image compositing is performed directly across processors following the subdivision of the data domain. Unlike tiled approaches that require complex synchronization or reduction trees, this method relies on a host processor to collect and combine subimages, accepting a serial bottleneck in display rates in exchange for simplified communication logic and decreasing relative communication costs as processor count increases. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset. A distributed memory environment with p processors. A bidirectional torus network topology. Outputs: A final 2D composite image of resolution n pixels. Data Structures: Subimages: Each processor i maintains a local buffer containing the rendered portion of the final image corresponding to its assigned data block. The layout is a standard 2D pixel array. Global State: Not explicitly maintained during compositing; the host processor manages the aggregation logic. Steps: 1. Domain Subdivision: The 3D data domain is subdivided into blocks. Each block is assigned to a specific processor in the distributed system. 2. Local Rendering: Each processor independently renders its assigned data block into a local subimage. This phase requires no inter-processor communication. 3. Subimage Transmission: Processors transmit their local subimages to a designated host processor. The transmission occurs over the network (e.g., bidirectional torus). 4. Aggregation: The host processor invokes a library function to collect all incoming subimages and combine them into the final image. 5. Display: The final image is displayed on a remote workstation or stored. Formulas: The communication cost C{comm} for the compositing phase on a bidirectional torus is modeled as: C{comm} = C1 \cdot p \cdot n \cdot t{trans} + C2 \cdot t{overhead} Where: p: Number of processors. n: Number of pixels in the image. t{trans}: Per-pixel transfer cost. t{overhead}: Per-message overhead. C1, C2: Positive constants smaller than 1, representing efficiency factors of the network and protocol. Parameters: Typical values for C1 and C2 are not specified, only that they are positive constants < 1. Network topology: Bidirectional torus. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Serial Bottleneck: The display rate is limited by the serial data stream resulting from the host processor collecting subimages. Network Latency: Performance is further degraded by network latency, particularly as the number of processors increases if the per-message overhead t{overhead} dominates. Mitigation: Image compression techniques can be applied to alleviate bandwidth and latency issues, though direct transfer is often used for large-scale scientific simulations where frame rates are not critical. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def paralleldirectcompositing(localvolume, imagew, imageh, rank, totalranks, ishost): # Step 1 & 2: Render local data block to a local subimage (RGBA pixels) subimage = [[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imagew) ] for in range(imageh)] for y in range(imageh): for x in range(imagew): # Standard volume rendering: cast ray, accumulate color/alpha subimage[y][x] = renderpixel(localvolume, x, y) if ishost: # Step 3 & 4: Host collects subimages and combines them finalimage = [[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imagew) ] for in range(imageh)] # Host inserts its own subimage first finalimage = assembletile(finalimage, subimage, rank, totalranks, imagew, imageh) # Receive and assemble subimages from all worker ranks for r in range(totalranks): if r == rank: continue workersubimage = receivesubimage(r, imagew, imageh) finalimage = assembletile(finalimage, workersubimage, r, totalranks, imagew, imageh) return finalimage else: # Step 3: Worker sends its subimage to the host sendsubimage(0, subimage) return None def renderpixel(volume, x, y): # Standard front-to-back or back-to-front compositing along a ray # Returns an RGBA tuple [r, g, b, a] return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def assembletile(target, source, srcrank, totalranks, w, h): # Maps a worker's subimage tile to its correct spatial position in the final image # Assumes a simple row-major tile decomposition of the image tilesperrow = max(1, totalranks // (h // max(1, w // totalranks))) if tilesperrow == 0: tilesperrow = 1 tileh = h // totalranks tilew = w // tilesperrow ty = (srcrank // tilesperrow) tileh tx = (srcrank % tilesperrow) tilew for dy in range(tileh): for dx in range(tilew): sy = ty + dy sx = tx + dx if sy < h and sx < w: target[sy][sx] = source[dy][dx] return target def receivesubimage(senderrank, w, h): # Blocks until a message of size wh4 floats arrives from senderrank # Returns a 2D list of RGBA pixels return [[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(w) ] for in range(h)] def sendsubimage(receiverrank, data): # Sends the 2D list of RGBA pixels to receiverrank pass Time and Memory Complexity: The rendering phase is scalable with no communication required. The compositing communication cost is given by C1 \cdot p \cdot n \cdot t{trans} + C2 \cdot t{overhead}. Analysis shows that communication cost decreases as the number of processors p increases, making the method acceptable for large p. Measured Performance: Tests on an Intel Paragon XP/S (NASA Langley Research Center) with a 256 \times 256 image and 60^3 data points: | Nodes | Raw Compositing (s) | Communication Compositing (s) | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 125 | 0.0455 | 0.0612 | | 216 | 0.0310 | 0.0583 | Scaling analysis for simulation and resampling on the same hardware (8 to 216 nodes): Simulation compute time: 10.665s (8 nodes) \rightarrow 0.4109s (216 nodes). Resampling time: 13.01s (8 nodes) \rightarrow 0.681s (216 nodes). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple communication pattern; communication overhead decreases relative to compute as processors increase; no synchronization barriers during rendering. Limitations: Display rates are limited by the serial collection of subimages on the host; performance degrades with high network latency. When to Use: Suitable for large-scale scientific simulations on massively parallel computers where interactive frame rates are not the primary constraint, and the simulation does not run multiple time steps per second. Best used when the network topology supports efficient bulk data transfer (e.g., torus) and a dedicated host processor is available for aggregation. Parallel Direct Compositing was developed and analyzed in the context of runtime volume visualization for parallel Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). The library was implemented in C/C++ using Intel's native communication library NX on a 72-node Intel Paragon XP/S operated at the NASA Langley Research Center. The analysis was consistent with Neumann's results regarding communication costs. The approach was designed for distributed memory message-passing environments, with suggestions for future portability using MPI or PVM.
