r) seg.color[0] alpha g = g + (1.0 - g) seg.color[1] alpha b = b + (1.0 - b) seg.color[2] alpha a = a + (1.0 - a) alpha return (r, g, b, a) def parallelcompositingoverlapping(rank, size, imagewidth, imageheight, volumedata): rowsperproc = imageheight // size startrow = rank rowsperproc endrow = (rank + 1) rowsperproc if rank < size - 1 else imageheight localraybuffer = RayBuffer(imagewidth, endrow - startrow) for y in range(startrow, endrow): for x in range(imagewidth): # Ray casting and segment generation step # In practice, traverse volume along ray for (x,y) and collect visible faces segments = castraylocal(x, y, startrow, volumedata) for seg in segments: destrank = seg.pixely // rowsperproc if destrank == rank: localraybuffer.addsegment(seg.pixelx, seg.pixely - startrow, seg) else: # sendsegmentto(destrank, seg) pass finalimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(endrow - startrow)] for in range(imagewidth)] for y in range(endrow - startrow): for x in range(imagewidth): segments = localraybuffer.getsegments(x, y) finalimage[x][y] = compositesegments(segments) return finalimage def castraylocal(x, y, startrow, volumedata): # Generate ray for pixel (x, y) and traverse volume to collect visible ray segments # Returns list of RaySegment objects with pixel coordinates return [] Parameters: Image Partitioning: Even horizontal strips are used for simplicity. Performance Gain: Overlapping improves performance by up to 40%. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Irregular Shapes: Irregular data shapes and partitioning cause rays to enter/exit multiple faces, creating varying numbers of local ray segments. Variable Buffer Sizes: This variability leads to variable ray buffer sizes and linked list lengths, affecting memory management and performance. Network Congestion: Non-overlapping approaches send large messages at once, causing congestion. Overlapping mitigates this but requires careful message grouping. A variant where ray segments migrate according to mesh-cell to processor assignment. Each processor traverses its local RayBuffer to packetize and gather ray-segment lists belonging to mesh-cells assigned to other processors into send-buffers, which are then sent via point-to-point communication. At the end, each processor gathers all ray-segments belonging to pixels of mesh-cells assigned to itself. The task-to-task cut-edge component of the cutsize of the current partition of the remapping graph constitutes an upper bound on the total number of ray-segments communicated in this step for all pixel-assignment schemes. Combines per-process rendered sub-images into a single image using a binary tree reduction over MPI ranks. A parallel execution strategy where compositing time is overlaid with rendering time by using two processes per node: one for rendering and one for compositing. Each node runs two processes: one renders octree leaves, the other waits for partial images from child nodes, composites them, and sends them to the octree root. A node renders an image, sends it off for compositing, then renders another image, etc.. Determine the compositing responsibility index by the node number. Traverse octree leaves in viewing order to allow true overlaying of rendering and compositing steps. Time Complexity: The overlapping approach reduces the peak network load, potentially improving overall throughput by up to 40% compared to non-overlapping methods. Memory Complexity: Requires a Ray Buffer (2D array of linked lists) per processor, the size of which depends on the viewing position, data shape, and partitioning. Strengths: Reduces network congestion by sending smaller messages throughout rendering. Suitable for unstructured grids where ray segment counts vary. Limitations: Irregular data shapes and partitioning lead to variable buffer sizes and linked list lengths, complicating memory management. Requires sorting of ray segments at each processor. When to Use: When network bandwidth is a bottleneck and data partitioning results in irregular ray segment distributions. When Not to Use: When data is regular and compositing cost is low compared to ray-tracing, or when simple batch processing is sufficient. This method was proposed for parallel volume ray-casting on distributed-memory architectures, particularly for unstructured-grid data. It addresses the inefficiency of separating local rendering from global compositing, which causes network congestion due to large, simultaneous message transfers. The approach leverages the fact that for regular data, compositing order can be determined a priori, but for unstructured domains, rays must be sorted by visibility order at the responsible processor. name: Hierarchical MPI Image Reduction
head: Binary Tree Image Composition, MPI Reduce for Volume Rendering, Tree-based Image Compositing
body: Hierarchical MPI Image Reduction is a parallel compositing strategy that combines per-process rendered sub-images into a single final image using a binary tree reduction over MPI ranks. It addresses the bottleneck of sending all partial images to a single root process for final assembly, which causes network congestion and memory pressure on the root. Unlike flat reductions, this method distributes the compositing load across the process hierarchy, reducing the communication depth and balancing the workload. Inputs and Outputs: Input: rgbaimage (accumulated color and opacity per pixel), maxtime (computation time metric), earlyrayterminations (ray termination count), and size (total MPI processes). Output: A single composite image held by rank 0. Data Structures: imagelist: A list containing the local rgbaimage. d: Tree depth, calculated as \lfloor \log2(\text{size}) \rfloor. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate tree depth d = \lfloor \log2(\text{size}) \rfloor. 2. Initialize imagelist with the local rgbaimage. 3. At the top level (i = d), odd-ranked processes send their rgbaimage, maxtime, and earlyrayterminations to rank - 1. Even-ranked processes receive this data, composite it with their local image, and update their metadata. 4. For each tree level i from d-1 down to 0: Compute destination rank: \text{dest\rank} = \text{rank} - \lceil 2^d / 2^i \rceil. If \text{dest\rank} \ge 0, the current rank sends its imagelist to destrank. Otherwise, the current rank receives imagelist from sender\rank = rank + \lceil 2^d / 2^i \rceil, composites the received image with its local image, and aggregates maxtime and earlyrayterminations. 5. Repeat until i == 0, where rank 0 holds the final composite image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def compositefronttoback(imgfront, imgback): """Standard front-to-back volume compositing. Expects (H, W, 4) arrays with channels [R, G, B, A].""" af = imgfront[:,:, 3] ab = imgback[:,:, 3] alphaout = af + (1.0 - af) ab rgbout = imgfront[:,:,:3] + (1.0 - af)[:,:, np.newaxis] imgback[:,:,:3] result = np.zeroslike(imgfront) result[:,:,:3] = rgbout result[:,:, 3] = alphaout return result def hierarchicalmpiimagereduction(comm, localrgbaimage, localmaxtime, localearlyrayterminations): rank = comm.Getrank() size = comm.Getsize() if size == 1: return localrgbaimage, localmaxtime, localearlyrayterminations d = math.floor(math.log2(size)) imagelist = [localrgbaimage] maxtime = localmaxtime earlyrayterminations = localearlyrayterminations # Level i = d: Initial odd/even pairing if rank % 2 == 1: partner = rank - 1 comm.Send(localrgbaimage, dest=partner) comm.Send(np.array([maxtime]), dest=partner) comm.Send(np.array([earlyrayterminations]), dest=partner) recvimg = np.emptylike(localrgbaimage) recvtime = np.empty(1) recvterm = np.empty(1) comm.Recv(recvimg, source=partner) comm.Recv(recvtime, source=partner) comm.Recv(recvterm, source=partner) imagelist[0] = compositefronttoback(recvimg, localrgbaimage) maxtime = max(maxtime, recvtime[0]) earlyrayterminations += recvterm[0] else: partner = rank + 1 recvimg = np.emptylike(localrgbaimage) recvtime = np.empty(1) recvterm = np.empty(1) comm.Recv(recvimg, source=partner) comm.Recv(recvtime, source=partner) comm.Recv(recvterm, source=partner) imagelist[0] = compositefronttoback(recvimg, localrgbaimage) maxtime = max(maxtime, recvtime[0]) earlyrayterminations += recvterm[0] # Tree reduction for levels i = d-1 down to 0 for i in range(d - 1, -1, -1): offset = math.ceil(2d / (2i)) destrank = rank - offset if destrank >= 0 and destrank < size: comm.Send(imagelist, dest=destrank) else: senderrank = rank + offset if senderrank < size: recvlist = [None] comm.Recv(recvlist, source=senderrank) imagelist[0] = compositefronttoback(recvlist[0], imagelist[0]) recvtime = np.empty(1) recvterm = np.empty(1) comm.Recv(recvtime, source=senderrank) comm.Recv(recvterm, source=senderrank) maxtime = max(maxtime, recvtime[0]) earlyrayterminations += recvterm[0] if rank == 0: return imagelist[0], maxtime, earlyrayterminations return None, None, None Parameters: size: Total number of MPI processes, determines tree height d. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point accumulation order affects final color. Front-to-back compositing is non-commutative. Boundaries: The tree depth d is based on \lfloor \log2(\text{size}) \rfloor. If size is not a power of 2, some ranks may be idle or the tree is unbalanced; the implementation handles this by having rank 0 send data to ranks \ge 2^d after the tree reduction. Degenerate Input: Empty images or zero opacity should be handled to avoid division by zero in compositing formulas if normalized. Communication Overhead: Two sub-images sent up the tree can only be combined if they cover the same area of the final image; if they do not, both are passed along, potentially resulting in more communication and synchronization costs than a sequential design. A parallel reduction algorithm that combines per-rank volumetric data into a single global grid on rank 0 using a tree-based approach with point-to-point MPI communication. It operates on 3D grid structures (dense or sparse) and uses a MERGEGRID operation instead of pixel-wise compositing. For dense grids, standard MPI reduction with addition across two ranks is used instead of explicit tree-based point-to-point communication. The reduction proceeds in \lceil \log2 P \rceil steps, with communication depth O(\log P), where P is the total number of MPI ranks. Time Complexity: The reduction proceeds in \lceil \log2 P \rceil steps, with communication depth O(\log P). Memory Complexity: Each rank holds its local grid/image. The root holds the final global grid/image. Performance: Reduces network congestion compared to flat reductions by distributing the compositing load. Best performance achieved with tree schemes was equivalent to the sequential scheme; some tree schemes had much worse performance. Strengths: Efficient for large-scale parallel rendering where final image assembly is a bottleneck. Limitations: Requires careful handling of compositing order to maintain physical accuracy. Unbalanced trees (non-power-of-2 ranks) can lead to idle processes or complex logic. The method originates from parallel volume rendering implementations using MPI, where hierarchical reduction is used to aggregate partial results. It is commonly used in scientific visualization and astrophysics simulations where large volumetric datasets are rendered in parallel. The tree-based reduction of volumetric grids is described in the context of visualizing cosmological simulations. name: Parallel Sphere Rendering with Global Z-Buffer Reduction
head: CM-5/T3D Sphere Renderer, Parallel Sphere Rendering
body: This method performs parallel volume rendering of atomic data by treating atoms as opaque spheres and resolving visibility through a global z-buffer reduction across distributed processors. It solves the problem of correct front-to-back compositing in a distributed memory environment without requiring a global sort of all primitives. Unlike hierarchical approaches that rely on spatial partitioning for load balancing, this method uses a trivial load-balancing strategy where each processor renders a disjoint subset of the atom list, relying on the global reduction to resolve occlusion. It is distinct from standard ray-casting volume rendering by explicitly rasterizing geometric primitives rather than sampling a scalar field. Inputs: A dataset of atoms, where each atom is defined by position and radius. Image dimensions W \times H (pixels). Number of processors P. Camera parameters (viewpoint, projection matrix). Outputs: A final W \times H RGB image buffer. Each processor maintains local buffers for the current chunk of atoms: 1. Local Z-Buffer: An array of size W \times H storing the depth (z) of the closest primitive rendered to each pixel by this processor. Initialized to \infty for new chunks, or retained from previous chunks if processing partial datasets. 2. Local Image Buffer: An array of size W \times H storing the RGB color of the closest primitive. Initialized to black (0,0,0) for new chunks. 3. Composite Z-Buffer: An array of size W \times H used to store the result of the global minimum reduction. 4. Composite Image Buffer: An array of size W \times H used to store the result of the global maximum reduction. T3D Specific Packing: On the T3D architecture, the z-buffer and RGB color are combined into a single 64-bit integer to optimize reduction operations. Bits 63–24 (40 bits): Depth value (z). Bits 23–0 (24 bits): RGB color value. This packing allows a single integer maximum reduction to simultaneously resolve depth occlusion and select the correct color. Tessellation Factor: For comparison benchmarks, an SGI sphere drawing routine uses a tessellation factor of 3 with an octahedral tessellation method. Projection: Orthogonal projection is used for bit-mapped sphere primitives on SGI hardware. 1. Data Distribution: If parallel disk I/O is unavailable (e.g., T3D Alpha processors), Processor 0 reads the atom data from disk and distributes it to other processors. Each processor p receives a subset of atoms Ap. 2. Local Rendering: Each processor renders its assigned atoms into its local z-buffer and image buffer. 3. Global Z-Buffer Reduction: Processors perform a global reduction on the z-buffer using a minimum operator to find the closest z-value for each pixel across all processors. 4. Visibility Masking: Processors loop over the composite z-buffer. If the value at a pixel matches the processor's original local z-buffer value, the pixel is kept; otherwise, it is obscured by a closer pixel on another processor and set to black (minimal value). 5. Global Image Reduction: Processors perform a second global reduction on the image buffer using a maximum operator. Only pixels that were not set to black contribute to the final image, resulting in each processor having an identical image for the current chunk. 6. Iteration: If the dataset does not fit in memory, the renderer reads the next portion of atoms and renders them into the existing (non-empty) z-buffer and image buffers, repeating the reduction and compositing steps until the entire dataset is processed. 7. Tiling: If the image is computed in tiles, the process repeats for the next tile until a full image is rendered. 8. Output: Processor 0 writes the final image to the image file. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelsphererendering(localatoms, width, height, numprocessors, myrank, isfirstchunk): # Initialize buffers if isfirstchunk: zbuffer = [float('inf')] (width height) imagebuffer = [0] (width height) else: zbuffer = previouszbuffer imagebuffer = previousimagebuffer # Local rendering for atom in localatoms: # Project sphere to screen space and rasterize pixels = projectspheretopixels(atom, width, height) for px in pixels: # Calculate depth and color for the pixel zval = calculatedepth(atom, px) colorval = atom.color if zval < zbuffer[px]: zbuffer[px] = zval imagebuffer[px] = colorval # Global Z-buffer reduction (MIN) compositezbuffer = allreducemin(zbuffer, numprocessors) # Visibility masking for px in range(width height): if zbuffer[px] != compositezbuffer[px]: imagebuffer[px] = 0 # Global Image reduction (MAX) compositeimagebuffer = allreducemax(imagebuffer, numprocessors) # Update buffers for next chunk previouszbuffer = compositezbuffer previousimagebuffer = compositeimagebuffer if hasmoredata: return parallelsphererendering(nextchunk, width, height, numprocessors, myrank, False) else: if myrank == 0: writeimage(compositeimagebuffer) return compositeimagebuffer def allreducemin(arr, numprocessors): # Standard parallel minimum reduction across processors return [min(arr[p][i] for p in range(numprocessors)) for i in range(len(arr))] def allreducemax(arr, numprocessors): # Standard parallel maximum reduction across processors return [max(arr[p][i] for p in range(numprocessors)) for i in range(len(arr))] I/O Bottleneck: On the T3D, parallel disk I/O is not available to Alpha processors. If all processors try to read the data file, the YMP host becomes overloaded. The solution is to have Processor 0 read the data and distribute it to other processors. Precision: On the T3D, the z-buffer and RGB color are combined into a single 64-bit integer. The depth value occupies the most significant 40 bits, and the RGB color occupies the remaining 24 bits. Depth values must fit within 40 bits to avoid overflow into the color channel. Compositing Time (CM-5): The compositing operation takes O(N \log P) time, where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of processors. Compositing Time (T3D): The Binary Swap compositing scheme runs in O(N/2 + N/4 + N/8 + \dots + N/P) time, which simplifies to O(N) as P \to \infty. This is optimal for a dense image distribution on P processors. Memory: Each processor stores O(N) for the z-buffer and image buffer, where N = W \times H. Rendering rates for 5 million spheres on a 1024 \times 1024 image: | Platform | With I/O (spheres/sec) | Computation Only (spheres/sec) | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | T3D | 660,000 | 1,689,000 | | CM-5 | 318,000 | 334,000 | | SGI Onyx (Tessellated) | 19,000 | 19,000 | | SGI Onyx (Bit-mapped) | 79,000 | 87,000 | Note: SGI times do not include data transfer time from SDA to local disk, which takes several minutes over Ethernet. Strengths: High performance on massively parallel supercomputers. Portable to other supercomputers or workstation clusters using basic message passing primitives. Does not rely on hardware-specific rendering engines, allowing integration with polygonal and volumetric renderers. The T3D optimization merges two global reductions and the comparison into one operation using 64-bit integer packing, reducing compositing overhead. Limitations: The algorithm uses trivial but efficient load balancing, which may not account for spheres of varying radii. Requires significant memory for z-buffers if image resolution is very high. The method was developed for the CM-5 and later ported to the T3D supercomputers. The CM-5 version used two separate global reductions (minimum for z-buffer, maximum for image). The T3D version improved upon this by merging the z-buffer comparison and color compositing into a single 64-bit integer maximum reduction operation, utilizing the Binary Swap compositing scheme. The algorithm is designed for rendering atomic data (spheres) in scientific visualization. It is particularly suited for environments where global sorting is too expensive and hardware-accelerated rasterization is not available or portable. It serves as a building block for hybrid renderers that combine polygon, sphere, and volume rendering. name: Hybrid-memory Compositing
head: Compositing Phase, Fragment exchange, Image assembly
body: Hybrid-memory compositing is a parallel image assembly strategy that reduces communication overhead by aggregating ray-casting fragments in shared memory before exchanging them across the network. It solves the bottleneck of high message counts in distributed-memory compositing by allowing threads within a node to merge data locally, thereby sending fewer, larger blocks to the compositing tasks. It differs from pure distributed-memory approaches by leveraging intra-node shared memory to reduce the number of MPI messages by approximately 6x. Inputs: Ray-casting fragments generated by rendering tasks. A subset of tasks designated as compositors. Image space partitioning scheme defining which compositor owns which region. Outputs: Final composited image components on the root task. Data Structures: Fragment Buffer: Stores ray-casting results aggregated in memory shared by six threads. MPI Buffers: Temporary structures for MPIAlltoallv and MPIReduce. Overallocation occurs if the compositing subset is too small relative to the image size. Steps: 1. Local Aggregation: Threads within a node (specifically, a group of six threads as observed in the reference implementation) aggregate fragments in shared memory. This reduces the volume of data sent over the network by performing partial compositing or merging before exchange. 2. Fragment Exchange: Use MPIAlltoallv to move fragments from the task where they originated during raycasting to the compositing task that owns their region of image space. The hybrid-memory implementation exchanges less fragment data because its larger data blocks allow for more compositing to take place during ray integration. 3. Image Reduction: Reduce the final image components to the root task using MPIReduce for assembly and output to a file or display. One-sixth as many hybrid-memory tasks participate in this reduction compared to distributed-memory tasks, improving performance. 4. Compositor Selection: Use a subset of tasks for compositing rather than all tasks. The ratio of compositors to renderers is tuned based on scaling behavior. Parameters: Compositor Subset Size: For strong and weak-dataset scaling: Optimal range is 2,000 to 8,000 tasks. For weak scaling: Optimal range is 2,000 to 30,000 tasks. Thread Grouping: Aggregation occurs in memory shared by six threads. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Weak Scaling Overallocation: In weak scaling, setting the compositing subset too small leads to overallocation from temporary data structures and MPI buffers because additional data is concentrated in fewer compositors. Inflection Points: Performance inflection points exist due to interconnect fabric characteristics. For hybrid memory, the inflection point is at 13,824-way concurrency (strong/weak-dataset) and higher for weak scaling. MPI-hybrid compositing is a parallel image compositing optimization that reduces communication overhead by aggregating fragments in memory shared by six threads before exchanging them between processing elements (PEs). It sets itself apart from pure MPI-only compositing by leveraging hybrid parallelism to perform more compositing during ray integration, thereby sending fewer and smaller messages. Time and Memory Complexity: Message Count: Hybrid-memory uses on average about 6x fewer messages than distributed-memory during fragment exchange. Data Volume: Exchanges less fragment data due to larger data blocks allowing more compositing during ray integration. Measured Performance: Strong Scaling (216,000-way concurrency): Best compositing time: 0.35s (4,500 compositors). Distributed memory compositing time: 1.06s (6,750 compositors). Hybrid memory is 3x faster in compositing. Total render time: 0.56s (hybrid) vs 1.25s (distributed), a 2.2x speedup. Rendering time was ~0.2s for both; compositing dominated total time. Weak Scaling: Optimal subset range: 2,000 to 30,000 compositing tasks. Inflection point arises at higher concurrency than in strong scaling. Small Scale (448-way concurrency, 4608^3 dataset): Minimum compositing time: 0.15s (median 0.19s). Raycasting time: 1.18s. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduced message count and data volume; superior compositing performance at high concurrency (216,000+ cores). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the compositor subset size; small subsets in weak scaling cause memory overallocation. Gains are less pronounced when raycasting dominates (e.g., weak scaling with large datasets). When to Use: High-concurrency environments (e.g., >13,824 cores) where communication overhead dominates. Systems with hybrid memory architectures (multi-core nodes with shared memory). When Not to Use: Low-concurrency scenarios where raycasting dominates and compositing overhead is negligible. Environments where the interconnect fabric does not benefit from fewer, larger messages. Hybrid-memory compositing was analyzed in the context of large-scale volume rendering on multi-core and many-core systems. The approach builds on observations by Peterka et al. that reducing the number of compositors at higher concurrencies increases overall performance. The specific implementation details and performance metrics (6x fewer messages, 2.2x total speedup at 216,000 cores) are derived from studies on systems like JaguarPF and Longhorn. name: MPI-hybrid Compositing
body: MPI-hybrid compositing is a parallel image compositing optimization that reduces communication overhead by aggregating fragments in memory shared by six threads before exchanging them between processing elements (PEs). It sets itself apart from pure MPI-only compositing by leveraging hybrid parallelism to perform more compositing during ray integration, thereby sending fewer and smaller messages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of fragments generated during the raycasting phase, each associated with a specific PE and image region. Output: Composite color and opacity values for the final image pixels. Data Structures: Fragment Buffer: Memory shared by six threads. The exact layout is not specified, but it holds fragments originating from the raycasting phase. Compositing PEs: A subset of the total processing elements dedicated to compositing tasks. Steps: 1. Fragment Aggregation: During or immediately after ray integration, fragments originating from the same group of six threads are aggregated into a shared memory buffer. 2. Local Compositing: Because fragments are grouped into larger data blocks, additional compositing operations can be performed locally during ray integration, reducing the amount of data that needs to be exchanged. 3. Fragment Exchange: The aggregated fragment data is exchanged between PEs using the MPI Alltoallv call. This step sends fewer messages compared to MPI-only approaches because the fragments are already partially composed and grouped. 4. Final Compositing: The received fragments are composited to produce the final pixel values. Parameters: Thread Group Size: Six threads share memory for aggregation. Time and Memory Complexity: Communication Overhead: MPI-hybrid uses on average about 6× fewer messages than MPI-only during compositing. Data Volume: MPI-hybrid exchanges less fragment data because its larger data blocks allow for more compositing to take place during ray integration. Measured Performance: Scale: 216,000 cores. Compositing Time: 0.35s for MPI-hybrid (4500 compositors) vs. 1.06s for MPI-only (6750 compositors), a 67% reduction. Raycasting Time: Roughly 0.2s for both implementations. Total Render Time: 0.56s for MPI-hybrid vs. 1.25s for MPI-only, a 55% improvement. Scaling: Performance gains improve at higher concurrency levels. The advantage of MPI-hybrid over MPI-only becomes greater as the number of cores increases. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduced memory footprint, reduced MPI overhead, and reduced communication traffic. Particularly effective at high concurrency where fragment exchange is the most expensive operation. Limitations: Relies on the implementation of the MPI Alltoallv call, which may vary across libraries. When to Use: Use MPI-hybrid compositing for large-scale distributed-memory supercomputers with multi-core CPUs, especially at high concurrency levels where communication overhead dominates. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Hybrid Parallelism for Volume Rendering on Large, Multi-core Systems". History and Development: The study demonstrated that hybrid parallelism offers performance improvements and better resource utilization for raycasting volume rendering on large, distributed-memory supercomputers. The findings align with previous work by Peterka et al. (2009b) on MPI implementations for IBM BG/P systems, suggesting similar optimizations in MPI libraries. The approach is compatible with other compositing algorithms like "Radix-k" introduced by Peterka et al. (2009a). Where it is Used: Large, distributed-memory supercomputers comprised of multi-core CPUs. name: Ray Compaction
body: Ray Compaction is a parallel primitive that filters a list of active rays by removing terminated ones and compacting the survivors into a dense, contiguous buffer. It solves the problem of sparse ray lists, ensuring subsequent processing stages operate only on valid rays. It sets itself apart from siblings like Ray Buffer Reordering by serving as a foundational atomic-indexing step, whereas In-Kernel Stream Compaction (InK-Compact) avoids separate prefix-sum launches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: raysaliveold (array of ray state/position data), raystold (array of ray termination flags or distances), N (number of input rays). Output: raysalive (compacted ray data), rayst (compacted flags), alivecount (total number of surviving rays). Data Structures: raysaliveold: Array of size N. raystold: Array of size N. Rays are considered terminated if raystold[n] < 0. raysalive: Array of size N (worst case). rayst: Array of size N. alivecounter: Global atomic integer, initialized to 0. Steps: 1. Initialize alivecounter to 0. 2. Launch a GPU kernel with one thread per input ray n (0 \le n < N). 3. Each thread n checks if its ray is alive: if raystold[n] >= 0. 4. If alive: a. Atomically increment alivecounter to obtain a unique new index: index = atomicAdd(&alivecounter, 1). b. Copy the ray data: raysalive[index] = raysaliveold[n]. c. Copy the termination flag: rayst[index] = raystold[n]. 5. After kernel completion, read alivecounter to determine the number of valid rays in the output buffers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atomicadd(counter, value): counter[0] += value return counter[0] - value def raycompactionkernel(raysaliveold, raystold, raysalive, rayst, alivecounter, threadid): if threadid < len(raystold): if raystold[threadid] >= 0: index = atomicadd(alivecounter, 1) raysalive[index] = raysaliveold[threadid] rayst[index] = raystold[threadid] def compactrays(raysaliveold, raystold, N): raysalive = [0] N rayst = [0] N alivecounter = [0] alivecount = 0 for tid in range(N): raycompactionkernel(raysaliveold, raystold, raysalive, rayst, alivecounter, tid) alivecount = alivecounter[0] return raysalive, rayst, alivecount Parameters: N: Number of input rays. Typical values depend on resolution (e.g., W \times H for primary rays). Termination Threshold: Defined by application logic; rays terminate when raystold[n] < 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Atomic operations on integers are precise. If rayst stores floating-point termination distances, ensure the comparison logic (>= 0) aligns with the termination definition. Boundaries: Output buffers must be sized to N to handle the case where all rays survive. Degenerate Input: If all rays terminate, alivecount is 0, and subsequent steps must handle empty buffers. Uses double-buffering and atomic counters to reorder rays without prior sorting. Choose when maintaining strict input-output order is required without global reductions. Computes output indices entirely within a single kernel using bit-decomposition scans. Choose when minimizing kernel launch overhead and synchronization is critical. Time Complexity: O(N) work, where N is the number of input rays. The atomic add operation is the bottleneck, potentially causing contention. Memory Complexity: O(N) for input and output buffers. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the ratio of alive rays. High contention on alivecounter can reduce throughput. Strengths: Simple to implement; low memory overhead compared to sorting-based methods. Limitations: Atomic contention can limit scalability on high-core-count GPUs. When to Use: When ray lists are moderately sparse and simplicity is preferred. When Not to Use: When strict input order preservation is required without additional sorting steps, or when extreme sparsity makes sorting-based approaches more efficient. Originating from parallel volume rendering implementations on GPUs, Ray Compaction is a standard technique for managing active ray lists. It is commonly found in CUDA-based volume renderers where efficient memory usage and processing of only active rays are critical. The method leverages atomic operations, a fundamental GPU primitive, to achieve thread-safe compaction. megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Buffer Reordering
body: Ray Buffer Reordering is a GPU kernel primitive that compacts a list of active rays by moving them from a current buffer to a next buffer, effectively removing terminated rays. It solves the problem of maintaining a dense, contiguous list of alive rays for subsequent volume rendering steps, such as ray marching or feature sampling. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a double-buffering strategy with atomic counters to assign new indices, ensuring thread-safe reordering without requiring a prior sort or global reduction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: aliveindices array of size 2 \times B, containing ray indices. Indices < 0 denote terminated rays. Input: B, the batch size or number of rays. Input: cindex, the index of the current buffer (0 or 1). Output: aliveindices array of size 2 \times B, with compacted alive rays in the next buffer. Output: counter, an atomic counter tracking the number of compacted rays. Data Structures: aliveindices: A flat array of integers. The layout is double-buffered: indices [0, B-1] correspond to buffer 0, and [B, 2B-1] correspond to buffer 1. counter: A single integer value, atomically incremented. Steps: 1. Reset the atomic counter to 0. 2. Determine the next buffer index: n\index = (c\index + 1) \pmod 2. 3. Update the global state to reflect the new current buffer index. 4. For each ray i in [0, B-1]: a. Read the ray index from the current buffer: src\idx = alive\indices[i \times 2 + c\index]. b. If src\idx \ge 0 (ray is alive): i. Atomically increment the counter to get a unique destination index dest\idx. ii. Write the source index to the next buffer at dest\idx: alive\indices[dest\idx \times 2 + n\index] = src\idx. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raybufferreorder(aliveindices, B, cindex, counter): # Step 1: Reset counter counter[None] = 0 # Step 2: Determine next index nindex = (cindex + 1) % 2 # Step 3: Update current index state # In a real kernel, this updates the global state variable tracking the active buffer # self.currentindex[None] = nindex # Handled by caller or separate kernel launch # Step 4: Iterate and reorder for i in range(B): # Read from current buffer srcidx = aliveindices[i 2 + cindex] if srcidx >= 0: # Atomically increment counter to get destination index destidx = atomicadd(counter, 1) # hardware atomic intrinsic # Write to next buffer aliveindices[destidx 2 + nindex] = srcidx Parameters: B: Batch size. Typical values depend on the scene and GPU memory, often in the range of thousands to millions. c\index: 0 or 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Atomic operations on integers are precise. No floating-point issues. Boundaries: Ensure B does not exceed half the size of aliveindices. Degenerate Input: If all rays are terminated (src\idx < 0), the counter remains 0, and the next buffer is empty. The Structure of Arrays (SoA) Ray Buffer is a memory layout strategy for ray data optimized for GPU coalesced access, storing ray properties in separate contiguous arrays per attribute. It solves the problem of inefficient memory bandwidth utilization in ray tracing by ensuring that threads in a warp access contiguous memory locations for the same attribute, rather than strided access across interleaved structures. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly managing the trade-off between memory footprint (via conditional graylization) and computational throughput, whereas variants like SSE Packet Architecture focus on SIMD register packing for CPU or hybrid execution. Choose it when memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and ray attributes are frequently accessed in parallel. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(B), where B is the number of rays. Each ray is processed once. Memory: O(B) for the double-buffered aliveindices array. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the GPU's atomic operation throughput and memory bandwidth. For large B, the atomic contention on counter can become a bottleneck. Scaling: Scales linearly with B. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple, thread-safe, no sorting required. Limitations: Atomic contention on the counter can reduce performance for very large B. Requires double the memory for the buffer. When to Use: Use when compacting rays is a frequent operation and the number of alive rays is significant. When Not to Use: Avoid if memory is extremely constrained or if the number of alive rays is very small, as the overhead of atomic operations may outweigh the benefits. Ray Buffer Reordering is a technique used in GPU-based volume rendering and ray tracing to manage the state of active rays. It is commonly found in implementations of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and other ray-marching algorithms where efficient management of alive rays is crucial for performance. The specific implementation described here is derived from unofficial sources related to Taichi-based NGP renderers. name: Structure of Arrays (SoA) Ray Buffer
body: The Structure of Arrays (SoA) Ray Buffer is a memory layout strategy for ray data optimized for GPU coalesced access, storing ray properties in separate contiguous arrays per attribute. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, direction, t-range bounds, and a mask indicating valid rays. Output: A set of device pointers to contiguous arrays containing ray state. Data Structures: The layout consists of base arrays allocated for totalRays elements. The exact fields and types are: 1. cameraCenterXDevice: float 2. cameraCenterYDevice: float 3. cameraCenterZDevice: float 4. directionXDevice: float 5. directionYDevice: float 6. directionZDevice: float 7. neartDevice: float 8. fartDevice: float 9. gtMaskDevice: uchar 10. accumulatedDensityDevice: float 11. accumulatedWeightsDevice: float Conditional Allocation: The layout adapts based on the graylized boolean flag: If graylized is true: Two additional arrays are allocated: 12. accumulatedGrayDevice: float 13. gtGrayDevice: uchar If graylized is false: Six additional arrays are allocated to store RGB channels separately: 14. accumulatedRedDevice: float 15. accumulatedGreenDevice: float 16. accumulatedBlueDevice: float 17. gtRedDevice: uchar 18. gtGreenDevice: uchar 19. gtBlueDevice: uchar Parameters: totalRays: The total number of rays to allocate. graylized: Boolean flag determining whether ground truth and accumulated color are stored as a single gray channel or split into RGB. whiteBKGD: Boolean flag affecting ground truth color computation; if true, adds white background fill. Algorithm Steps: 1. Allocate 11 base arrays (origin, direction, t-range, mask, density, weights) with size totalRays. 2. If graylized is true, allocate 2 gray arrays. 3. Else, allocate 6 color arrays (3 accumulated, 3 ground truth). 4. Initialize totalRays based on dataset size and mask filtering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocatesoaraybuffer(totalrays: int, graylized: bool, whitebkgd: bool): """ Allocates the SoA Ray Buffer according to the specified layout and parameters. """ # Step 1: Allocate 11 base arrays cameraCenterXDevice = [0.0] totalrays cameraCenterYDevice = [0.0] totalrays cameraCenterZDevice = [0.0] totalrays directionXDevice = [0.0] totalrays directionYDevice = [0.0] totalrays directionZDevice = [0.0] totalrays neartDevice = [0.0] totalrays fartDevice = [0.0] totalrays gtMaskDevice = [0] totalrays accumulatedDensityDevice = [0.0] totalrays accumulatedWeightsDevice = [0.0] totalrays # Step 2 & 3: Conditional allocation if graylized: accumulatedGrayDevice = [0.0] totalrays gtGrayDevice = [0] totalrays accumulatedRedDevice = accumulatedGreenDevice = accumulatedBlueDevice = None gtRedDevice = gtGreenDevice = gtBlueDevice = None else: accumulatedRedDevice = [0.0] totalrays accumulatedGreenDevice = [0.0] totalrays accumulatedBlueDevice = [0.0] totalrays gtRedDevice = [0] totalrays gtGreenDevice = [0] totalrays gtBlueDevice = [0] totalrays accumulatedGrayDevice = gtGrayDevice = None # Step 4: Initialize totalRays based on dataset size and mask filtering # (Handled by the calling routine; this function assumes totalrays is provided) return { "base": { "cameraCenterXDevice": cameraCenterXDevice, "cameraCenterYDevice": cameraCenterYDevice, "cameraCenterZDevice": cameraCenterZDevice, "directionXDevice": directionXDevice, "directionYDevice": directionYDevice, "directionZDevice": directionZDevice, "neartDevice": neartDevice, "fartDevice": fartDevice, "gtMaskDevice": gtMaskDevice, "accumulatedDensityDevice": accumulatedDensityDevice, "accumulatedWeightsDevice": accumulatedWeightsDevice }, "color": { "accumulatedGrayDevice": accumulatedGrayDevice, "gtGrayDevice": gtGrayDevice, "accumulatedRedDevice": accumulatedRedDevice, "accumulatedGreenDevice": accumulatedGreenDevice, "accumulatedBlueDevice": accumulatedBlueDevice, "gtRedDevice": gtRedDevice, "gtGreenDevice": gtGreenDevice, "gtBlueDevice": gtBlueDevice } } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A data layout strategy for coherent ray tracing where ray information is stored vertically within a packet to exploit SIMD (SSE) parallelism. It sets itself apart from its siblings by operating on groups of neighboring or similar rays in packets, performing computations on SIMD groups of four rays (packlets) and masking differing hit results. Choose this when targeting CPU or hybrid architectures with strong SIMD support and high spatial coherence. Ray directions are stored as separate arrays of X, Y, Z components (vertical), rather than a single horizontal array of 3-vectors, and arrays are 16-byte-aligned to permit access to a packlet of four rays in a single SSE register. Hit results (position, normals) are also stored in aligned SSE arrays within the packet structure. See parent: Ray Buffer Reordering. Not given in the sources. name: In-Kernel Stream Compaction (InK-Compact)
head: In-Kernel compaction, InK-Compact
body: In-Kernel Stream Compaction (InK-Compact) is a parallel primitive that compacts a stream of valid elements into a contiguous output array while preserving input order, executed entirely within a single GPU kernel as a device function. It solves the performance bottleneck of conventional stream compaction methods (like Thrust or Chag::PP) which require leaving the kernel to launch separate prefix-sum and scatter kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of N elements X[0 \dots N-1] with an associated predicate P[0 \dots N-1] indicating validity. Output: An array Y[0 \dots M-1] containing only elements where P[i] is true, preserving their relative order from X. Auxiliary: An intermediate buffer Y' of size sufficient to hold block-local outputs and global section management structures. Data Structures: Section Management: For a kernel divided into S sections, each section Si has: flag Si(f): Boolean, initially false, becomes true when section i is ready to write to final output. offset Si(u): Integer, the starting index in the final output array Y for section i. counter Si(c): Integer, atomic counter for the number of blocks in section i that have completed local compaction. Block Counts: A buffer B(c) to store the total write count k(c) for each block in the current section. Shared Memory: ww(c)[w(n)]: Stores the total number of valid elements written by each warp in the block. s(u)[w(n)]: Stores the warp offset for each warp. Parameters: w(s): Warp size, typically 32 threads in CUDA 4.0. w(n): Number of warps within a block. S(N): Section size, number of blocks per section. Chosen as 32 to fit bit-decomposition into a single warp. Algorithm Steps: 1. Thread Offset Computation (t(u)): Each thread t(i) computes its local offset within its warp. Compute warp index: w(i) = \lfloor t(i) / w(s) \rfloor. Compute warp lane: w(l) = t(i) \pmod{w(s)}. Compute thread mask: t(m) = \text{MAXINT} \gg (w(s) - w(l)). This mask has bits 0 to w(l)-1 set to 1. Compute ballot: b = \text{ballot}(P[t(i)]) \ \& \ t(m). Compute thread offset: t(u) = \text{popc}(b). Compute warp total: The last thread in the warp (w(l) = w(s)-1) computes w(c) = t(u) + P[t(i)]. Store w(c) into shared memory ww(c)[w(i)] by the last thread only. Perform memory fence and synchronization syncthreads() to ensure visibility. 2. Warp Offset Computation (wi(u)): Compute the offset of the current warp relative to the start of the block. Perform synchronization using syncthreadscount() with each thread's predicate to gather total writes in block and ensure visibility. Perform bit-decomposition scan over \log2(w(s)) bits. For each bit j from 0 to \log2(w(s))-1: b(j) = \text{ballot}(w(c) \ \& \ 2^j). Accumulate: wi(u) += \text{popc}(b(j) \ \& \ t(m)) \gg j. Synchronize syncthreads() to ensure all warps have computed their offsets. 3. Stage 1: Local Block Compaction: Each block computes its local write count k(c) = \sum w(c). Each thread stores its valid element into the intermediate buffer Y' at index: \text{index} = (\text{block\id} \times \text{threads\per\block}) + (w(i) \times w(s)) + t(u). A single thread atomically increments the section counter: atomicAdd(&Si(c), 1). All blocks within the section, except for the section controller block, are allowed to exit the compaction function. The section controller is designated as the block within the section that increments the section-counter Si(c) to the number of blocks within a section S(N). 4. Stage 2: Block Offset Computation: The section controller loads the block counts k(c) for all blocks in the section into shared memory. It performs a bit-wise prefix sum scan on these block counts to determine the starting offset for each block within the section. The scan is performed using bit-decomposition over \log2(w(s) \times w(n)) bits, fitting into a single warp if S(N)=32. The total number of valid elements in the section, t, is computed. The section offset is calculated: Si(u) = S{i-1}(u) + t (for i>0). For S0, S0(u) = 0. The section controller sets the flag Si(f) = \text{true} after a memory fence. 5. Stage 3: Section Synchronization: Blocks in section Si (where i>0) wait for the flag S{i-1}(f) to become true. Section S0 proceeds immediately. Once the flag is true, the section controller moves the compacted data from the intermediate buffer Y' to the final output array Y at the computed offset Si(u). All blocks in the section then use the block-specific offsets computed in Stage 2 to write their local outputs to the final array Y. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inkcompact(inputdata, predicates, outputbuffer, sectionflags, sectionoffsets, sectioncounters, intermediatebuffer, blockcountsglobal): tid = getthreadid() warpid = tid // warpsize laneid = tid % warpsize # 1. Thread offset t(u) mask = (1 << warpsize) - 1 >> (warpsize - laneid) # MAXINT shr (w(s) - w(l)) validmask = ballot(predicates[tid]) & mask threadoffset = popc(validmask) # Warp total w(c) by last thread if laneid == warpsize - 1: warptotal = threadoffset + int(predicates[tid]) sharedwarptotals[warpid] = warptotal syncthreads() # 2. Warp offset wi(u) via bit-decomposition scan warpoffset = 0 for j in range(int(log2(warpsize))): bj = ballot(sharedwarptotals[warpid] & (1 << j)) warpoffset += popc(bj & mask) >> j syncthreadscount(predicates[tid]) # Gather block total # 3. Stage 1: Local block compaction localidx = (getblockid() threadsperblock) + (warpid warpsize) + threadoffset if predicates[tid]: intermediatebuffer[localidx] = inputdata[tid] mysectionid = getblockid() // sectionsize oldcount = atomicadd(sectioncounters[mysectionid], 1) iscontroller = (oldcount == sectionsize - 1) if not iscontroller: return # 4. Stage 2: Block offset computation (Controller only) # Load block counts into shared memory for b in range(sectionsize): sharedblockcounts[b] = blockcountsglobal[mysectionid sectionsize + b] blockoffsets = prefixscan(sharedblockcounts, sectionsize) # Standard parallel scan totalvalid = blockoffsets[sectionsize - 1] + sharedblockcounts[sectionsize - 1] if mysectionid == 0: sectionoffsets[mysectionid] = 0 else: while not sectionflags[mysectionid - 1]: pass sectionoffsets[mysectionid] = sectionoffsets[mysectionid - 1] + totalvalid memoryfence() sectionflags[mysectionid] = True # 5. Stage 3/4: Scatter to final output blockoffset = blockoffsets[getblockid() % sectionsize] finalbase = sectionoffsets[mysectionid] + blockoffset # Controller block copies compacted data from intermediate to final buffer if iscontroller: for i in range(threadsperblock): srcidx = (getblockid() threadsperblock) + i if predicates[srcidx]: outputbuffer[finalbase + i] = intermediatebuffer[srcidx] Out-of-Kernel Compaction (OfK-Compact) is a stream compaction technique where the compaction logic is executed outside the primary rendering kernel, typically by invoking a host-side library function after the kernel completes. It solves the problem of removing invalid or empty rays from an output array generated by a parallel GPU kernel. Unlike InK-Compact, which performs compaction immediately within the operating kernel to avoid synchronization overhead, OfK-Compact relies on separate kernel launches or library calls, introducing potential bottlenecks but offering a simpler implementation pattern. In-Kernel Collation (InK-Collate) is a compromise compaction method that preserves local ordering within a block but not global ordering of kernel blocks, avoiding inter-block dependencies. It computes a kernel offset k(u) using an atomic add on a global counter by thread 0 in the block, then stores output at tf = k(u) + s(u){w(i)} + t(u). It shows little performance difference from InK-Compact in ray-tracing applications where global order is not strictly required, but avoids the complex section management and synchronization of InK-Compact. Chag::PP Compaction is a conventional out-of-kernel method where kernels output ray indices to an output array in the same location as read, setting non-valid elements to zero/null. After kernel completion, a host-side Chag::PP.compact method is called to compact the array. It is slower than InK-Compact. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method performs \log2(w(s)) operations per thread for warp offset and \log2(w(s) w(n)) for block offset. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires an intermediate buffer Y' of size N (or sufficient for block-local outputs) and small shared memory for warp/block counts. Performance: On an NVIDIA 480 GTX, InK-Compact is on average 99% faster than Thrust and 28% faster than Chag::PP in a ray-tracing pipeline. When used out-of-kernel, it runs on par with Chag::PP. Strengths: Eliminates kernel launch overhead, avoids writing invalid elements to global memory, and maintains high thread coherency in multi-kernel pipelines. Limitations: Register burden due to running as a device function, though mitigated by register reallocation on architectures like Fermi. Requires careful management of section synchronization. In-Kernel Stream Compaction was introduced by D. M. Hughes et al. in 2013. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of multi-kernel pipelines in GPU ray-tracing, where conventional compaction methods (Thrust, Chag::PP) required leaving the kernel to perform prefix-sum and scatter operations, causing synchronization bottlenecks. The method builds on previous work in warp-level primitives (Billeter, Harris) but introduces bit-decomposition and balloting for inter-warp scans and a novel section-based approach for block-level ordering. It is used in multi-kernel isosurface ray-tracing pipelines for stages such as Generation-Traversal, Traversal-Intersection, Intersection-Traversal, and Intersection-Shade. name: Out-of-Kernel Compaction (OfK-Compact)
head: OfK-Compact, Thrust, Thrust Compaction, copy-if, out-of-kernel implementation
body: Out-of-Kernel Compaction (OfK-Compact) is a stream compaction technique where the compaction logic is executed outside the primary rendering kernel, typically by invoking a host-side library function after the kernel completes. It solves the problem of removing invalid or empty rays from an output array generated by a parallel GPU kernel. Unlike its sibling In-Kernel Stream Compaction (InK-Compact), which performs compaction immediately within the operating kernel to avoid synchronization overhead, OfK-Compact relies on separate kernel launches or library calls, introducing potential bottlenecks but offering a simpler implementation pattern. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An output array generated by a preceding kernel (e.g., ray generation or traversal) containing valid ray indices and invalid elements marked as zero/null. Output: A compacted array containing only valid ray indices, with no gaps. Data Structures: The input array is a flat array of integers (ray indices). Invalid elements are explicitly set to zero or a null value by the preceding kernel. Steps: 1. The preceding GPU kernel (e.g., for ray generation or traversal) executes. For each ray, if the ray is valid, it writes its index to the output array at the same location it was read from the input array. If the ray is invalid, it writes zero or null to that location. 2. The kernel completes execution. 3. The host code invokes a compaction library function (such as Thrust's copy-if or removeif) on the output array. 4. The library function iterates through the array, removing elements that satisfy a predicate and compacting the remaining valid elements into a contiguous block. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def outofkernelcompact(outarray, numrays): # Step 1: Execute the rendering kernel # The kernel writes valid ray indices to outarray[i] if ray i is valid, # otherwise it writes 0 to outarray[i]. launchrenderingkernel(outarray, numrays) # Step 2: Call out-of-kernel compaction # The library function iterates through the array, removing elements # that satisfy a predicate (e.g., being zero/null) and compacting # the remaining valid elements into a contiguous block. validindices = [i for i, val in enumerate(outarray) if val != 0] outarray[:len(validindices)] = validindices validcount = len(validindices) # The valid rays are now in outarray[0...validcount-1] return validcount Parameters and Edge Cases: Predicate: The condition for removal is defined by the library's predicate. Precision: No specific precision issues noted, but standard floating-point or integer comparison applies. Pitfalls: Requires synchronization between the GPU kernel and the host call to the library. Uses the Thrust library function thrust::removeif to remove elements satisfying a predicate (zeros) from an array. It is a standard, high-level API approach for out-of-kernel compaction, relying on Thrust's optimized implementations. Time Complexity: Depends on the underlying library implementation (e.g., Thrust). Generally efficient but incurs host-device synchronization overhead. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: When InK-Compact is used in an out-of-kernel fashion (wrapped in a global kernel and called similarly to Thrust), it runs on par with Chag::PP. However, the main advantage of InK-Compact is avoiding the need to leave the kernel, which reduces bottlenecks associated with kernel synchronization and additional launches. Strengths: Simpler to implement using existing libraries; no need to write custom compaction kernels. Limitations: Higher overhead due to kernel launches and synchronization compared to in-kernel methods; register cost is minimal but present if wrapped in a kernel. When to use: When simplicity is prioritized over maximum performance, or when integrating with existing library-based pipelines. When not to use: When minimizing kernel launch overhead and synchronization is critical, favoring InK-Compact instead. Originated from the need to handle sparse data in volume rendering pipelines, specifically in stages like Generation, Traversal, and Shading. The method mimics the usage pattern of libraries like Thrust and Chag::PP. It was evaluated in the context of comparing in-kernel vs. out-of-kernel compaction strategies, highlighting the trade-offs between implementation complexity and performance. name: Manager/Workers Parallel Implementation
head: LSF-HPC Cluster Implementation, LSF-HPC worker model, Master/Slave Worker Architecture, Task-based parallelism
body: The Manager/Workers Parallel Implementation is a distributed task-scheduling architecture designed for load-balanced execution on clusters where processor availability varies over time. It solves the problem of coordinating independent computational tasks (such as isosurface extraction or volume rendering) across distant workers by centralizing state management in a single manager process. Unlike sibling methods that rely on static partitioning or hardware-specific synchronization primitives, this approach uses a dynamic task queue where workers request work and the manager assigns tasks based on global knowledge of data boundaries and worker status. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., a grid of voxels or AMR blocks) and a set of available worker processes. Output: A final aggregated surface mesh or rendered image. Data Structures: Task: A message object containing: type: Enum {EXTRACT, SEND, MERGE, FINISHED}. workerid: Unique identifier for the target worker. targetid: (Optional) Identifier for the destination worker in SEND tasks. blockid: (Optional) Identifier for the data sub-block in EXTRACT tasks. Worker State: Each worker maintains a local surface mesh (initially empty). Manager State: The manager maintains a global view of: Extracted blocks. Worker surface availability. Topological neighbors of workers/blocks. Parameters: Task Scheduler: Typically Platform LSF-HPC or similar HPC job schedulers to dispatch tasks on the distant grid. Worker Count: Can range from 1 (sequential fallback) to N (cluster size). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: The manager identifies all available workers and the full set of data blocks. Workers start in an infinite loop waiting for tasks. 2. Worker Loop: Each worker executes the following logic: Request a task from the manager. Execute the task based on its type: EXTRACT: Perform the core computation (e.g., tandem(E0)) on the assigned sub-block. Append the resulting local surface to the worker's current mesh. Note: For block borders, a "time lag" method may be used to prevent edge collapse by preserving vertices on boundaries before simplification. SEND: Send the current accumulated surface mesh to the specified targetid. Clear the local surface memory after sending. MERGE: Receive a surface mesh from another worker (or the manager) and merge it with the current local surface. Simplify the combined surface and dump finished components if applicable. FINISHED: Set a local finished flag to true and terminate the loop. 3. Manager Loop: The manager iterates until all data is processed and all workers are finished: Wait for a task request from a worker with ID id. Check conditions in priority order: 1. Has Surface: If the worker id currently holds a surface mesh that needs aggregation, send a MERGE task. This task likely includes the ID of the worker to merge with (determined by the manager's knowledge of topology). 2. Has Neighbor: If the worker has no surface but has topological neighbors that might hold relevant data, send a SEND task with a targetid to forward its current (empty or partial) state or request data. Note: Sources indicate SEND is used to send current mesh to target; the logic implies routing intermediate results. 3. Has Block: If there are un-extracted data blocks, send an EXTRACT task assigning a specific block to the worker. 4. Else: Send a FINISHED task to terminate the worker. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def workerprocess(workerid, taskqueue): finished = False localsurface = EmptyMesh() while not finished: # Block until a task is received from the manager task = taskqueue.receive() if task.type == "EXTRACT": # Extract surface from the assigned sub-block # E0 is the extraction algorithm (e.g., extended tandem) newmesh = extractsurface(task.blockid, algorithm=E0) localsurface.append(newmesh) elif task.type == "SEND": # Send current surface to target worker # The manager determines the targetid based on topology taskqueue.send(task.targetid, localsurface) localsurface = EmptyMesh() # Clear memory elif task.type == "MERGE": # Receive mesh from another worker and merge incomingmesh = taskqueue.receivemesh() localsurface.merge(incomingmesh) # Simplify and dump finished components if needed localsurface.simplify() elif task.type == "FINISHED": finished = True def managerprocess(workerids, datablocks, taskqueues): # Global state maintained by manager extractedblocks = set() workersurfaces = {wid: None for wid in workerids} # Topology map: which workers/blocks are neighbors topology = buildtopology(datablocks) finishedworkers = set() while len(finishedworkers) < len(workerids): # Wait for any worker to request a task requestingworkerid = taskqueue.waitforrequest() # Priority 1: Merge if worker has surface if workersurfaces[requestingworkerid] is not None: # Find a target to merge with (e.g., a neighbor or the manager) targetid = findmergetarget(requestingworkerid, topology) task = Task(type="MERGE", targetid=targetid) taskqueues[requestingworkerid].send(task) # Priority 2: Send if worker has neighbor but no surface to merge? # Note: Source logic says "If has neighbor(id) then send SEND". # This implies routing or handoff even if surface is empty or being prepared. elif hasneighbor(requestingworkerid, topology): targetid = findneighbor(requestingworkerid, topology) task = Task(type="SEND", targetid=targetid) taskqueues[requestingworkerid].send(task) # Priority 3: Extract if blocks remain elif len(extractedblocks) < len(datablocks): blockid = getnextunextractedblock(datablocks, extractedblocks) task = Task(type="EXTRACT", blockid=blockid) taskqueues[requestingworkerid].send(task) # Priority 4: Finish else: task = Task(type="FINISHED") taskqueues[requestingworkerid].send(task) finishedworkers.add(requestingworkerid) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision/Boundaries: When extracting from sub-blocks, borders must be handled carefully. The "time lag" method is used to preserve vertices on block boundaries to ensure mesh continuity and quality after simplification. Statelessness: Workers are stateless regarding global progress; they do not know which blocks are processed or who holds which data. All state is in the manager. Single Worker Mode: The algorithm degrades gracefully to a single worker, which processes blocks sequentially. A variant implementation using Python's multiprocessing module for dynamic load balancing. It employs a master process that dynamically sends work to available worker processes until rendering is complete. To optimize CPU usage, it starts more processes than available processors, relying on the OS task scheduler to map processes to idle cores. Data distribution uses a "sort last" strategy. Pitfalls include: OS-defined process limits (e.g., on 64-core machines), lack of shared memory for NumPy arrays (requiring separate arrays per process, complicating load balancing), and limitation to a single HPC node unless MPI is used, which restricts total RAM and caching capabilities compared to distributed clusters. Time Complexity: Depends on the task scheduler's efficiency and network latency. The manager's decision loop is O(1) per request, but global state updates are required. Memory Complexity: Distributed across workers. Each worker stores only its local surface mesh, reducing peak memory usage compared to brute-force approaches. The manager stores global metadata, which is minimal. Performance: Critical bottleneck is often I/O (reading large datasets) rather than computation. The architecture allows for efficient load balancing on clusters with varying processor availability. Strengths: Adaptable to dynamic cluster resources; simple worker implementation; no shared memory requirements between workers. Limitations: Manager becomes a bottleneck if task requests are frequent; network overhead for sending meshes; OS scheduler limitations in Python variant. The architecture was proposed for parallel isosurface extraction on very large geophysical datasets. It was designed to work with Platform LSF-HPC, a task scheduler for high-performance computing clusters, to handle time-varying processor allocations. The approach extends the "tandem algorithm" for isosurface extraction, incorporating simplification and merging steps. It has also been adapted for volume rendering of AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) simulations, where dynamic load balancing is crucial due to irregular data distribution. name: Master/Slave Parallel Rendering Architecture
head: MovieMaker Parallel Rendering Architecture
body: The Master/Slave Parallel Rendering Architecture is a shared-memory parallelization strategy designed to generate visualization movies from large-scale (TB-scale), three-dimensional, time-evolving simulation data within strict time limits (e.g., 12 hours). It distinguishes itself from other parallel rendering systems by utilizing standard non-parallel disk I/O combined with task overlapping to hide storage latency, whereas alternatives like Yu et al. require complex parallel disk I/O infrastructure. It builds on Manager/Workers Parallel Implementation by specifically addressing the I/O bottleneck inherent in shared-memory clusters through asynchronous data loading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Simulation data defined in Cartesian geometry with a rectilinear grid system (uniform and/or non-uniform in x, y, and z directions). Data is typically stored on disk in time steps (e.g., 1 GB per step). Output: A sequence of visualization images (movie) generated via volume rendering, isocontouring, or streamlines. Data Structures: Shared Memory Area: A contiguous memory region accessible by all processes (master and slaves) where simulation data is loaded. The maximum grid size is constrained only by the available shared memory size. Configuration File: Contains parameters for visualization methods and fine-tuning settings. Partial Images: Rendered sub-images returned by slave processes to the master via shared memory. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The master process reads the configuration file. 2. Data Loading: The master process reads the simulation data for the current time step from disk into the shared memory area. 3. Task Distribution: The master process controls slave processes, assigning rendering tasks while maintaining dynamic load balance through active monitoring. 4. Rendering Execution: Slave processes execute rendering commands (volume rendering, isocontouring, or streamlines) using the data in shared memory. They render partial images (sub-images) and return them to the master via shared memory. 5. Task Overlapping (I/O Hiding): While slave processes render the current time step, the master process simultaneously reads the data for the next time step from disk into shared memory. This overlaps disk I/O latency with computation time. 6. Image Composition: The master process assembles the partial images returned by the slaves into the final frame. 7. Iteration: Steps 2–6 repeat for each time step in the simulation dataset. Formulas and Parameters: Target Performance: Processing one GB of data within 40 seconds. I/O Latency Hiding: The system assumes reading 1 GB of data takes approximately 1 second. The total read time for a movie (e.g., 1,024 steps) could reach ~1 hour, which is hidden by the rendering time of the slaves. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def masterprocess(): config = readconfigurationfile() sharedmemory = allocatesharedmemory() # Pre-load first time step currentstepdata = readdisktosharedmemory(sharedmemory, step=0) for step in range(totalsteps): # Task Overlapping: Read next step while current step renders if step + 1 < totalsteps: nextstepdata = readdisktosharedmemory(sharedmemory, step=step+1) # Dispatch rendering tasks to slaves # Slaves render currentstepdata and return partial images partialimages = dispatchrenderingtasks(sharedmemory, step, config) # Compose final image from partial images finalimage = composeimage(partialimages) saveimage(finalimage, step) def slaveprocess(slaveid): while True: command = receivecommandfrommaster() if command.type == "RENDER": # Render using OpenGL off-screen subimage = renderoffscreen(command.datapointer, command.params) # Return sub-image to shared memory writetosharedmemory(command.returnaddress, subimage) elif command.type == "EXIT": break Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: The maximum grid number is constrained only by the shared memory size. Large grids may exceed available RAM. I/O Bottleneck: If disk read speed is significantly slower than assumed (1s/GB), the overlapping may not fully hide latency, leading to idle time. Load Imbalance: Dynamic load balancing is required; static assignment may lead to inefficient resource usage if rendering tasks vary in complexity. Active monitoring and control of slave processes to ensure efficient resource utilization. Asynchronous disk I/O to hide storage latency during rendering. Use of OpenGL for rendering without display output. Time Complexity: The system aims to process 1 GB of data within 40 seconds. Measured Performance: On an SGI Onyx 3800 (12 CPU, 24 GB memory, 11 MPI processes), average processing times for a 640x640x640 grid (4-byte float) were: Volume rendering 40 seconds, Isocontouring 33 seconds, Streamlines 10 seconds. Memory Complexity: Limited by shared memory size; supports TB-scale data through time-step processing. Strengths: Simple disk I/O implementation (no parallel file system required); effective hiding of I/O latency; supports multiple visualization methods (volume, isocontour, streamlines). Limitations: Requires shared-memory architecture; performance limited by single-disk I/O speed for large datasets; maximum grid size limited by RAM. When to Use: When generating movies from large-scale simulation data on shared-memory clusters where parallel disk I/O is unavailable or too complex to implement. When Not to Use: When data exceeds available shared memory; when disk I/O is significantly slower than 1s/GB; when parallel file system access is available and preferred. The Master/Slave Parallel Rendering Architecture was developed by Fumiaki Araki and Akira Kageyama at the Earth Simulator Center, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology. It was introduced in the paper "MovieMaker: A Parallel Movie-Making Software for Large Scale Simulations" (arXiv:physics/0601211) on January 30, 2006. The system was designed to address the growing output data size of high-performance computer simulations, specifically targeting the generation of movies from 1 TB-scale data within 12 hours. It contrasts with earlier parallel rendering systems that required parallel disk I/O solutions.
