name: Single-Event Upset (SEU) Fault Injection in 3DGS
head: Bit-flip injection, Single-bit upset injection
body: Single-Event Upset (SEU) fault injection in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) simulates transient bit flips in GPU memory to measure rendering corruption from hardware errors. It differs from neural network weight perturbation because 3DGS primitives are spatially localized and redundant, whereas network weights are shared globally; this method quantifies whether such redundancy provides robustness or concentrates risk into rare catastrophic failures. Inputs and Outputs Input: A trained 3DGS model with N primitives stored in GPU memory, a set of K held-out camera views, and a fault site tuple (field, primitive, component, bit). Output: Corruption metrics (peak pixel error, LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR, non-finite flag, corruption footprint) for the rendered views. Data Structures A trained 3DGS model consists of N primitives. Primitive i stores six fields in memory: 1. Mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 2. Logarithmic scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (renderer applies \exp) 3. Quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized at render time) 4. Opacity logit oi \in \mathbb{R} (renderer applies logistic \sigma) 5. DC color term c{0i} \in \mathbb{R}^3 6. Higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients c{Ni} \in \mathbb{R}^{((\ell+1)^2-1) \times 3} IEEE-754 Bit Layouts The bit positions determine the impact of a flip: fp32: Sign is bit 31, exponent is bits 23–30, mantissa is bits 0–22. fp16: 5-bit exponent, 10-bit mantissa. bf16: 8-bit exponent (from fp32), 7-bit mantissa. Algorithm Steps 1. Reinterpret: Cast the stored floating-point value at the fault site to an unsigned integer of the matching width. 2. Flip: XOR the integer with a mask having a single bit set at the target position. 3. Restore: Reinterpret the modified integer back to the original floating-point format. 4. Render: Render the K held-out views using the corrupted parameter. 5. Measure: Compute metrics on the GPU. 6. Cleanup: Restore the original value to the working copy. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import numpy as np def flipbit(value: float, bitindex: int, widthbits: int) -> float: # Reinterpret float as unsigned integer of matching width if widthbits == 32: bits = struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', value))[0] elif widthbits == 16: bits = struct.unpack('H', struct.pack('e', value))[0] else: raise ValueError("Unsupported width") # Flip the bit using XOR bits ^= (1 << bitindex) # Reinterpret back to float if widthbits == 32: return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', bits))[0] else: return struct.unpack('e', struct.pack('H', bits))[0] def injectseu(modelparams, faultsite, cameras, renderer, cleanimages): fieldname, primidx, compidx, bitidx = faultsite widthbits = 32 if modelparams.dtype == 'fp32' else 16 # 1. Get clean value cleanvalue = modelparams[fieldname][primidx][compidx] # 2. Inject fault corruptedvalue = flipbit(cleanvalue, bitidx, widthbits) # 3. Write to working copy modelparams[fieldname][primidx][compidx] = corruptedvalue # 4. Render K views in a single batched call corruptedimages = renderer(modelparams, cameras) # 5. Compute metrics on GPU diff = corruptedimages - cleanimages peakerror = np.max(np.abs(diff)) footprint = np.mean(np.abs(diff) > (1.0 / 255.0)) psnr = 10 np.log10(1.0 / np.mean(diff2)) isnonfinite = np.any(np.isnan(corruptedimages)) or np.any(np.isinf(corruptedimages)) # 6. Restore value modelparams[fieldname][primidx][compidx] = cleanvalue return { 'peakerror': peakerror, 'footprint': footprint, 'psnr': psnr, 'nonfinite': isnonfinite } Parameters and Typical Values Precision: fp32 is the baseline; fp16 and bf16 are tested by casting clean parameters to the target format before injection. Views (K): Multiple held-out views are averaged to compute the corruption footprint. Catastrophic Threshold: An upset is catastrophic if the corruption footprint exceeds 1% of the frame or produces non-finite values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Exponent Overflow: Flipping high exponent bits in fp32 can cause overflow to non-finite values. Scale Sign Flip: For the scale field, the activation is \phi = \exp. A sign flip on a typical log scale \theta \approx -3 changes it to +3, multiplying the primitive size by e^6 \approx 4 \times 10^2. Global Metrics: Full-frame PSNR is a poor discriminator for single upsets in large scenes because a single corrupted primitive among hundreds of thousands barely moves the global average. Analyzes the mathematical impact of bit flips on specific fields. For the scale field, the relative change is |\Delta s|/s = |\Delta \theta|, meaning a mantissa flip changes scale by a fixed relative amount 2^{b-p} independent of the exponent e. For a normal fp32 value \theta = (-1)^\epsilon 2^e (1+m), flipping mantissa bit b changes the value by |\Delta \theta| = 2^{e+b-p}. Flipping the sign bit gives \Delta \theta = -2\theta, and flipping exponent bit j multiplies magnitude by 2^{\pm 2^j}. Time and Memory Complexity Time: The parallel injection engine keeps the GPU busy with a stream of independent corrupted renders, saturating device throughput. Memory: Clean parameters remain resident on the GPU; only one working copy is modified at a time. Measured Performance Redundancy Scaling: For a converged model of N primitives, the typical (median) image error of one uniform-random single-bit upset scales as \sigma^2(N) = \Theta(N^{-\alpha}) for a scene-dependent exponent \alpha > 0. Dose Budget: Under k independent uniform single-bit upsets, the expected squared image error is E\|\Delta I\|^2 = k \sigma^2(N). The dose k\tau at which error exceeds threshold \tau scales as k\tau = \Theta(N^\alpha \tau). Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Directly measures hardware vulnerability; identifies critical bit positions (e.g., scale sign bit). Limitations: Full-frame PSNR is insensitive to local corruption; catastrophic upsets are rare but dominant in mean error. When to Use Use for evaluating robustness of 3DGS deployments against hardware errors. Originated from the paper "Single-Event Upsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering: Bit-Level Criticality, Spatial Extent, and a Parallel Support Guard". It addresses the gap in understanding whether the redundancy of 3DGS primitives provides robustness against transient faults, contrasting with extensive prior work on neural network weight perturbation. name: Hybrid MPI + OpenMP Parallelization
head: Hybrid Parallelization, MPI+OpenMP Volume Rendering, yt hybrid parallel volume rendering
body:
Hybrid MPI + OpenMP parallelization combines message-passing across distributed nodes with shared-memory threading on SMP nodes to leverage large supercomputing resources for volume rendering. It is distinguished from pure MPI approaches by its ability to reduce inter-node communication overhead for data-intensive tasks, and from pure OpenMP by its scalability to clusters with millions of cores. The method is primarily implemented in the yt framework, where it balances computational load against memory constraints inherent to the rendering pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Simulation dataset (e.g., AMRKDTree bricks), rendering parameters (image plane resolution, camera position), and hardware topology (N{node}, cores\per
ode). Outputs: Rendered image plane stored in memory. Data Structures: Image Plane: A 2D array of pixel values. In this specific implementation, each MPI task stores the entire image plane in its local memory. This is a critical constraint for memory management. Task Configuration: Defined by the tuple (N{mpi}, N{mp}), where N{mpi} is the number of MPI processes and N{mp} is the number of OpenMP threads per process. Parameters: N{mpi}: Number of MPI tasks. N{mp}: Number of OpenMP threads per MPI task. P: Total number of available CPU cores. N{node}: Number of SMP nodes. cores\per
ode: Number of cores per node. OMP\NUM\THREADS: Environment variable controlling default OpenMP thread count. numthreads: Keyword argument in the snapshot() function to override OMPNUMTHREADS. Numbered Steps: 1. Topology Analysis: Determine the total number of cores P and the node structure (N{node}, cores\per
ode) of the target hardware. 2. Configuration Selection: Choose N{mpi} and N{mp} such that N{mpi} 	imes N{mp} = P. If the simulation contains many grids or AMRKDTree bricks, increase N{mpi} to distribute the spatial data partitioning. If the image plane resolution is large (specifically > 2048^2), decrease N{mpi} and increase N{mp} to prevent memory exhaustion, as each MPI task holds the full image plane. 3. Environment Setup: Set the environment variable OMPNUMTHREADS to N{mp} or pass numthreads=N{mp} to the rendering function. 4. MPI Initialization: Launch N{mpi} MPI processes across the available nodes. 5. Thread Launch: Within each MPI process, spawn N{mp} OpenMP threads to execute the volume rendering kernel. 6. Execution: The threads collaboratively render the volume. Since each MPI task stores the entire image plane, no inter-process synchronization is required for image assembly, but memory usage scales linearly with N{mpi}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setuphybridparallelization(nnode, corespernode, imageres, numgrids): """ Determine optimal Nmpi and Nmp based on hardware and workload. """ # Total cores P P = nnode corespernode # Heuristic for Nmpi and Nmp # Constraint: Nmpi Nmp = P # If image plane is large, memory is the bottleneck. # Each MPI task stores the full image plane. # Large image planes (>2048^2) require fewer MPI tasks to fit in memory. if imageres > 2048: # Decrease Nmpi to reduce memory pressure per node # Increase Nmp to maintain core utilization # Example: Maximize Nmp such that Nmpi is small enough for memory # Not given in sources: exact memory limit formula. # We assume a conservative split favoring threads. nmp = corespernode nmpi = nnode else: # If many grids/bricks, communication/partitioning is the bottleneck. # Increase Nmpi to distribute data. # Not given in sources: exact grid count threshold. # We assume a balanced or MPI-heavy split. nmpi = nnode nmp = corespernode # Ensure product equals P assert nmpi nmp == P return nmpi, nmp def runvolumerender(nmpi, nmp, dataset): """ Execute hybrid parallel volume rendering. """ # 1. Set OpenMP threads # In Python, this is often handled by the underlying C++ library (yt) # or environment variables. import os os.environ['OMPNUMTHREADS'] = str(nmp) # 2. Launch MPI processes (handled by mpiexec outside this function) # 3. Inside each MPI rank: # 4. Initialize rendering with numthreads # The 'snapshot' function is specific to yt. # We assume a generic interface here. renderer = VolumeRenderer(dataset) renderer.setnumthreads(nmp) # 5. Render # Each MPI rank renders its portion of the data # but stores the FULL image plane in local memory. imageplane = renderer.render() return imageplane Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: If N{mpi} is too high for large image planes (>2048^2), the system may run out of memory because every MPI task duplicates the entire image plane. Desktop/Laptop Use: On single-node machines with limited cores, pure OpenMP is often preferable to MPI due to lower overhead. Topology Awareness: Incorrect mapping of MPI tasks to sockets/nodes can degrade performance. Users must understand the hardware topology. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and rays, parallelized by P cores. Speedup is limited by Amdahl's law and communication overhead between MPI tasks. Memory Complexity: O(N{mpi} 	imes W 	imes H) for the image plane storage, where W, H are image dimensions. This is a significant limitation compared to tiled approaches where memory scales with N{mpi} only for the tile. Scaling: Scales well on supercomputers with many nodes if the dataset is partitioned effectively (many grids). Scaling is constrained by memory bandwidth and capacity when image planes are large. Strengths: Leverages existing MPI infrastructure for distributed data; reduces inter-node traffic for image assembly by keeping images local to nodes. Limitations: High memory footprint for high-resolution images; not suitable for resource-constrained environments. This method is documented in the yt project's visualization documentation, specifically regarding volume rendering on supercomputing resources. It addresses the need to scale volume rendering to large datasets that exceed the memory of a single node while avoiding the communication bottlenecks of pure MPI image compositing. 3D Visualization and Volume Rendering, https://yt-project.org/doc/visualizing/volumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-28 https://yt-project.org/docs/dev/visualizing/volumerendering.html#volume-rendering-components, https://yt-project.org/docs/dev/visualizing/volumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Parallel Partitioning and Tiling
body: Parallel Partitioning and Tiling is a family of strategies that decompose volume rendering workloads—whether in object space (data) or image space (pixels/scanlines)—to enable efficient execution on multi-core CPUs or GPUs. It solves the problem of uneven computational load and memory bandwidth bottlenecks by distributing data or screen regions among processing units. It differs from sibling methods like Tiled Parallel Compositing by focusing on the initial decomposition and load-balancing mechanisms (such as Z-ordering or Y-buckets) rather than the final compositing stage, and from Multipass Partitioning (MPP) by often employing static or semi-static partitioning schemes rather than iterative redistribution. The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores). Common principles include: 1. Thread Mapping: Assigning one or more threads to process specific data elements (e.g., one thread per pixel or one thread per voxel sample). 2. Memory Hierarchy Utilization: Leveraging global memory for large datasets, shared/local memory for intermediate results (reductions), and registers for per-thread state. 3. Synchronization: Managing concurrency conflicts using atomic operations, barriers, or spatial partitioning (tiles) to ensure data consistency without excessive serialization. 4. Data Parallelism: Performing identical operations on different data elements simultaneously, often requiring coalesced memory access patterns to maximize bandwidth. A two-pass parallel algorithm for direct volume rendering that groups polygons representing isosurfaces or volume slices into scanline-based "y-buckets" to maximize coherence and avoid the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. It solves the problem of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently in software by parallelizing on a scanline basis to limit duplication compared to tile-based methods that break scanlines and lose coherence. Choose this when rendering polygonal representations of volume data (e.g., isosurfaces) where front-to-back visibility order is critical and data is irregular. A multi-core parallel rendering technique for isosurface visualization that decouples data structure traversal from ray casting to optimize cache performance and load balancing. It solves the problem of uneven computational load and poor spatial locality in parallel volume rendering by dividing the screen into contiguous regions for initial block list generation (Phase I) and then dynamically assigning Z-ordered, weight-balanced groups of image tiles to threads for ray casting (Phase II/III). It differs from standard static tiling approaches by using a space-filling curve (Z-order) to group tiles based on their estimated complexity (weight), ensuring that threads with heavier workloads are processed in spatially coherent batches, thereby reducing synchronization overhead and improving cache hit rates. Choose this for high-performance CPU-based ray casting of hierarchical volume data (BONO trees) where load imbalance is significant. A parallelization strategy for volume rendering that exploits parallelism in object space by dividing the volume dataset into subvolumes and assigning them to independent processors. Unlike image-space methods that decompose the screen, this approach distributes the data itself, making it suitable for large-scale datasets where loading the entire volume into every processor's memory is infeasible. It generates distributed subimages that must be merged via image compositing to form the final result. Choose this for distributed memory systems or large datasets that exceed single-node memory capacity. A simple CPU-based parallelization strategy that divides a 3D volume rendering task among multiple threads by splitting the X-axis range into contiguous sections. It is suitable for straightforward, uniform volume traversal where load balancing is not critical and the volume data is accessed sequentially along one axis. Divides a 3D volume rendering task among multiple CPU threads by splitting the X-axis range into contiguous sections. Calculate thread count from system processors: int threads = max(1, sysinfo.dwNumberOfProcessors - 1); Compute X-section width: float xsection = (2.0f vw.aspx) / threads; For each thread i, set start/end bounds: threadargs[i].start = -vw.aspx + i xsection; threadargs[i].end = threadargs[i].start + xsection; Launch threads with beginthreadex and wait with WaitForMultipleObjects. Each thread iterates X from start to end, Y from -vw.aspy to vw.aspy, Z from -vw.aspz to vw.aspz, stepping by voxelsize. Thread argument struct: iter3dthreadargs contains float start; float end; voxieframet vf; point3d voxelsize; int funcidx; The concept of parallel partitioning in volume rendering has evolved from early object-space parallelism to sophisticated image-space tiling and dynamic load balancing. Early methods focused on distributing data across distributed memory systems. Later, image-space methods like Y-Bucket parallelization addressed the inefficiencies of tile-based rendering for polygonal volume data. More recent approaches, such as dynamic tile grouping with Z-ordering, aim to optimize cache performance and load balancing on multi-core CPUs by decoupling traversal from ray casting. The simple X-axis split partitioning is demonstrated in hobbyist implementations for holographic fractal rendering on CPU platforms. jtomori/holographicfractals, https://github.com/jtomori/holographicfractals, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Y-Bucket Parallelization
head: Y-bucket grouping
body: Y-Bucket Parallelization is a two-pass parallel algorithm for direct volume rendering that groups polygons representing isosurfaces or volume slices into scanline-based "y-buckets" to maximize coherence and avoid the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. It solves the problem of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently in software by parallelizing on a scanline basis to limit duplication compared to tile-based methods that break scanlines and lose coherence. The method processes polygons representing volume data (stored in counter-clockwise order when viewed from outside the grid to recognize boundaries and visibility order). Inputs: A set of polygons representing volume slices or isosurfaces. A set of processing units (processors). Outputs: A rendered image where pixels are filled based on front-to-back visibility. Data Structures: 1. Y-Bucket Array: An array where each entry corresponds to a specific scanline (y-coordinate). It stores the count of polygons belonging to that scanline. 2. Output Array: A common array partitioned to store the final pixel data. 3. X-Bucket Structures: Linked lists associated with the leftmost pixel of a polygon's horizontal span. These lists maintain polygons in front-to-back visibility order. Steps: 1. First Pass (Polygon Distribution): Each processor distributes polygons into y-buckets based on their vertical extent. Polygons are assigned to the y-buckets corresponding to the scanlines they cover. Invalidated polygons are marked or excluded. 2. Second Pass (Bucket Allocation and Structure Creation): The number of polygons belonging to each y-bucket is determined by accessing the Y-Bucket Array. Space for each y-bucket is allocated by partitioning the common Output Array. The space for one y-bucket is further partitioned into space for each processor to fill within that y-bucket. Each processor creates appropriate y-bucket structures for all polygons it processed in the first pass, excluding those invalidated. This step is transitional; its work per processor is proportional to the number of scanlines, not the number of polygons. 3. Third Parallelizable Component (Scanline Processing): Scanlines are processed in order from bottom to top. For each active polygon, information is transferred to an x-bucket data structure associated with the leftmost pixel in which the polygon appears. A linked list of these x-bucket structures is maintained in front-to-back visibility order. This component involves the bulk of the computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ybucketparallelization(polygons, numprocessors, numscanlines): # Step 1: First Pass - Distribute polygons to y-buckets ybucketcounts = [0] numscanlines for polygon in polygons: ymin, ymax = polygon.verticalextent() for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): ybucketcounts[y] += 1 # Step 2: Second Pass - Allocate space and create structures # Partition common output array based on ybucketcounts outputoffsets = [0] (numscanlines + 1) currentoffset = 0 for y in range(numscanlines): outputoffsets[y] = currentoffset currentoffset += ybucketcounts[y] outputoffsets[numscanlines] = currentoffset # Partition space for each processor within each y-bucket # This is a transitional step; work is proportional to scanlines processoroffsets = [[0] numprocessors for in range(numscanlines)] for y in range(numscanlines): count = ybucketcounts[y] perproc = count // numprocessors remainder = count % numprocessors offset = outputoffsets[y] for p in range(numprocessors): processoroffsets[y][p] = offset offset += perproc + (1 if p < remainder else 0) # Each processor creates structures for its polygons # (Source does not specify exact distribution mechanism) for p in range(numprocessors): for polygon in polygons: if not polygon.isinvalidated(): y = polygon.primaryscanline() idx = processoroffsets[y][p] processoroffsets[y][p] += 1 # Store polygon reference in outputarray at idx # Step 3: Third Parallelizable Component - Process scanlines for y in range(numscanlines): # Bottom to top # Transfer active polygon info to x-buckets xbuckets = {} for polygon in polygons: xmin = polygon.leftmostpixel() if xmin not in xbuckets: xbuckets[xmin] = [] xbuckets[xmin].append(polygon) # Sort xbuckets[xmin] by front-to-back visibility order # Perform compositing for the scanline # (Source does not specify exact compositing algorithm) for xmin in sorted(xbuckets.keys()): for polygon in xbuckets[xmin]: # Composite polygon into scanline y at xmin pass Parameters: Number of processors: Determines the partitioning of space within y-buckets. Number of scanlines: Determines the size of the y-bucket array and the work in the second pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The second pass is a transitional step and can be parallelized by standard techniques, but its workload is small relative to the third pass. Polygons must be stored in counter-clockwise order to correctly identify boundaries and visibility order. This method extends Y-Bucket Parallelization by introducing "x-buckets" and "x-actives" lists to maintain front-to-back visibility order within a scanline. It is chosen when rendering irregular and multiple grids in software to maximize coherence and avoid ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. Time Complexity: The second pass work is proportional to the number of scanlines, not the number of polygons. The third parallelizable component involves the bulk of the computation, processing each scanline and managing linked lists of active polygons. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for y-bucket counts, the partitioned output array, and x-bucket linked lists. Strengths: Maximizes coherence by processing scanlines; avoids the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells; limits duplication compared to tile-based methods. Limitations: The second pass is a transitional step with limited parallelism benefit; relies on software processing of polygons. The method was introduced in the 1996 paper "Hierarchical and parallelizable direct volume rendering for irregular and multiple grids". It addresses the challenges of rendering complex volume data by leveraging scanline-based parallelization. name: Parallel Direct Volume Rendering with Y-Buckets and X-Buckets
head: Hierarchical Parallelizable Direct Volume Rendering for Irregular/Multiple Grids, Scanline-based direct volume rendering for irregular grids, Scanline-based parallel DVR, Y-bucket/X-bucket parallelization, k-d tree based volume rendering
body: This method is a parallel direct volume rendering algorithm that processes polygons representing isosurfaces or volume slices by grouping them into scanline-based 'y-buckets' and processing pixels within those buckets using 'x-buckets' and 'x-actives' lists to maintain front-to-back visibility order. It solves the problem of rendering irregular and multiple grids efficiently in software by maximizing coherence and avoiding the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. Inputs: A volume defined over irregular, curvilinear, or rectilinear grids, potentially multiple intersecting grids. Geometrical transformation parameters (world-to-screen). Clipping box defining the subvolume to be rendered. Polygon structures containing vertex indices. Outputs: A rendered image with color integration and element ordering. Polygon ID: A unique integer identifier for each polygon. Grid ID: Encoded in certain bits of the Polygon ID, specifying the associated grid or surface. Position/Index: The remaining bits comprise either an index into an array of polygon structures (for irregular grids) or a direct encoding of the polygon's position within the grid (for curvilinear and rectilinear grids). Vertex Information: For curvilinear/rectilinear grids, vertex information is encoded into the Polygon ID, bypassing the need for separate polygon structures, as every cell has the same facial structure of 12 triangles and cell vertices can be inferred from the cell ID. Polygon Structure: Consists of an array of vertex indices. Implementation permits only triangles. Y-Bucket: Associated with each horizontal scanline. Contains IDs for polygons that first appear on that scanline. Processed in bottom-to-top order. Polygons are excluded if outside the clipping box or do not cross any pixel center. X-Bucket: Associated with each pixel in a scanline. Contains polygons whose screen-space horizontal span covers this pixel. X-Actives List: Maintains the list of polygons currently intersecting the current pixel, sorted in front-to-back order. Updated from the previous pixel's x-actives and the current pixel's x-bucket. Y-Actives List: Maintains the list of polygons currently intersecting the current scanline. Updated from the previous line's y-bucket and this line's y-bucket. 1. If a new geometrical transformation is specified, convert locations from world space to screen space. 2. For each (horizontal) scanline, create its y-bucket in bottom-to-top order. 3. Initialize y-actives list as empty. 4. For each scanline, initialize its x-bucket and x-actives list as empty. 5. For each pixel in scanline, in left-to-right order: update x-actives list from previous pixel's x-actives and this pixel's x-bucket; composite polygons in x-actives in front-to-back order. Update y-actives list from previous line's y-bucket and this line's y-bucket. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def paralleldvryxbuckets(polygons, transformation, clippingbox): # Step 1: Transformation if transformation is not None: for poly in polygons: poly.screenvertices = [transformworldtoscreen(v, transformation) for v in poly.vertices] # Step 2: Y-Bucket Creation ybuckets = {} for poly in polygons: if isinsideclippingbox(poly.screenvertices, clippingbox): scanlines = getscanlinescrossed(poly.screenvertices) for sl in scanlines: ybuckets.setdefault(sl, []).append(poly.id) # Step 3: Initialize Y-Actives yactives = [] # Iterate scanlines bottom-to-top for scanline in sorted(ybuckets.keys()): # Step 4: Initialize X-Bucket and X-Actives for this scanline xbuckets = {} xactives = [] # Update Y-Actives from previous line's y-bucket and this line's y-bucket yactives = updateyactives(yactives, ybuckets.get(scanline, [])) # Determine pixel range for this scanline based on y-actives polygons pixelrange = getpixelrangeforscanline(yactives) # Step 5: Pixel Processing (left-to-right) for pixel in pixelrange: # Get polygons starting/ending at this pixel currentxbucket = getxbucketforpixel(pixel, yactives) # Update X-Actives from previous pixel's x-actives and this pixel's x-bucket xactives = updatexactives(xactives, currentxbucket) # Composite polygons in x-actives in front-to-back order compositepixels(xactives, pixel) def transformworldtoscreen(vertex, transformation): return transformation.apply(vertex) def isinsideclippingbox(vertices, clippingbox): return clippingbox.intersects(vertices) def getscanlinescrossed(vertices): minsl = int(min(v.y for v in vertices)) maxsl = int(max(v.y for v in vertices)) return range(minsl, maxsl + 1) def updateyactives(yactives, newybucket): # Add new polygons from y-bucket, remove those that ended return yactives + newybucket def getpixelrangeforscanline(yactives): minx = min(min(v.x for v in poly.screenvertices) for poly in yactives) maxx = max(max(v.x for v in poly.screenvertices) for poly in yactives) return range(int(minx), int(maxx) + 1) def getxbucketforpixel(pixel, yactives): return [poly for poly in yactives if poly.minx <= pixel <= poly.maxx] def updatexactives(xactives, xbucket): xactives.extend(xbucket) xactives.sort(key=lambda p: p.screenz) return xactives def compositepixels(xactives, pixel): color = (0, 0, 0, 0) for poly in xactives: alpha = poly.getalphaat(pixel) color = blendfronttoback(color, poly.getcolorat(pixel), alpha) return color def blendfronttoback(accumulated, new, alpha): return (accumulated[0] (1 - alpha) + new[0] alpha, accumulated[1] (1 - alpha) + new[1] alpha, accumulated[2] (1 - alpha) + new[2] alpha, accumulated[3] + alpha (1 - accumulated[3])) Performance: Images of volumes with about one million cells can be produced in one to several minutes on a workstation with a 150 MHz processor. Preview Speed: Previews show enough detail to navigate effectively in very large data sets, rendering useful images very quickly (about one second for one-million-cell grids) by displaying each region associated with a tree node as one cell. Numerical Accuracy: Standard techniques lose accuracy in screen-z, leading to significant errors in color integration and element order. A new perspective transformation is used to achieve greater numerical accuracy on geometrical elements spanning a great range of sizes. Clipping Box: Any group of polygons to be rendered includes the faces of a clipping box, which delimits the subvolume to be rendered. The six faces (12 triangles) of the clipping box are treated much like other polygons. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Images of volumes with about one million cells can be produced in one to several minutes on a workstation with a 150 MHz processor. Previews render useful images very quickly (about one second for one-million-cell grids). Scaling: The method is highly scalable, particularly the parallelizable component of grouping polygons by scanline into y-buckets. Strengths: Maximizes coherence, avoids difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells, generalizes polygon faces, easy to implement, fits naturally into scanline methods, processes multiple intersecting grids, handles wide range of cell sizes. Limitations: Not designed for massively parallel machines; ray-casting parallelizes better but is slower for irregular grids. When to Use: When rendering irregular or multiple grids, when maximizing coherence is important, when avoiding ray-casting complexities is desired. When Not to Use: When designing for massively parallel machines, as the algorithm prioritizes coherence over massive parallelism. The method is based on Watkin's scanline algorithm. Early approaches for direct volume rendering used ray-casting, cell projection, and splatting. Most research addressed only rectilinear grids. The algorithm was chosen because the designers were not designing for massively parallel machines, wanted to maximize coherence, and wanted to avoid the difficulties of ray-casting intersecting cells. It generalizes polygon faces and is easy to implement. name: Multi-core BONO Tree Traversal and Ray Casting with Dynamic Tile Grouping
head: Phase I/Phase II Multi-core Scheme, Z-ordered Dynamic Tile Allocation
body: This method is a multi-core parallel rendering technique for isosurface visualization that decouples data structure traversal from ray casting to optimize cache performance and load balancing. It solves the problem of uneven computational load and poor spatial locality in parallel volume rendering by dividing the screen into contiguous regions for initial block list generation (Phase I) and then dynamically assigning Z-ordered, weight-balanced groups of image tiles to threads for ray casting (Phase II/III). It differs from standard static tiling approaches by using a space-filling curve (Z-order) to group tiles based on their estimated complexity (weight), ensuring that threads with heavier workloads are processed in spatially coherent batches, thereby reducing synchronization overhead and improving cache hit rates. The method operates in three distinct phases: Phase I (Block List Generation), Phase II (Tile Grouping), and Phase III (Dynamic Ray Casting). Inputs: p: Number of available processor cores/threads. k: Maximum size of the block list for a pixel group (memory limit). T: The BONO tree data structure representing the volume. R: The set of rays corresponding to the screen pixels. S: Screen resolution (e.g., 1024 \times 1024). TileSize: Dimensions of small image tiles (e.g., 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16). Outputs: Rendered image. List LI: A sequence of groups, where each group is a pair of indices (first, last) defining a contiguous range of Z-ordered tiles. 1. Block List (Li): For each pixel (or small group of pixels), a list of 3D data blocks from the BONO tree that the ray intersects. Constraint: |Li| \le k. 2. Tile Grid: The screen is partitioned into N tiles of size TileSize \times TileSize. 3. Z-Order Map: An array mapping tile index i to its Z-order position. 4. Weight Array (W{tile}): An integer array where W{tile}[j] is the number of non-empty block lists within tile j. 5. Group List (LI): A list of tuples ((first\tile\idx, last\tile\idx), group\id). 1. Divide the screen into p almost equal contiguous horizontal (or vertical) regions, one per thread. 2. For each thread t responsible for region Rt: a. Initialize empty block lists for all pixels in Rt. b. Traverse the BONO tree T. c. Traversal Rule: For a node N, traverse its children in front-to-back order only if: i. The projection of N's minimum bounding box intersects Rt. ii. At least one pixel in Rt has a block list size < k. d. If the node is a leaf (data block), add the block to the lists of all intersecting pixels in Rt, provided the list size < k. e. Note: Due to the limit k, only a fraction (no more than 10%) of total BONO tree nodes are accessed. 1. Partitioning: Partition the entire screen into small tiles of size TileSize \times TileSize. 2. Z-Ordering: Order these tiles using a Z-order (Morton code) space-filling curve. 3. Weighting: a. For each tile j, compute weight wj = \sum{p \in Tilej} (1 \text{ if } Lp \neq \emptyset \text{ else } 0). b. Compute total weight W = \sum{all \ tiles} wj. 4. Grouping Algorithm: a. Initialize an empty list LI. b. Let remaining\weight = W. c. Let current\tile\index = 0 (in Z-order). d. While remaining\weight > 0: i. Target weight for this iteration: Target = remaining\weight / 2. ii. Divide Target into p equal sub-targets: SubTarget = Target / p. iii. For each group g from 0 to p-1: 1. Start with start\tile = current\tile\index. 2. Accumulate weights from Z-ordered tiles starting at start\tile until the sum reaches or exceeds SubTarget. 3. Let end\tile be the index of the last tile included. 4. Append (start\tile, end\tile) to LI. 5. Update current\tile\index = end\tile + 1. iv. Update remaining\weight = remaining\weight / 2. e. Termination: The process repeats logarithmically relative to screen size. The first iterations create large groups (coarse-grained), and subsequent iterations create smaller groups (fine-grained). 1. Initialize a shared queue/pointer to the list LI. 2. For each thread t: a. Loop: i. Atomically fetch the next available group (first, last) from LI. If none remain, terminate. ii. For each tile index j from first to last: 1. For each pixel p in tile j: 1. Retrieve block list Lp. 2. If Lp is empty, skip. 3. Shoot ray through blocks in Lp (front-to-back). 4. Shading: If ray intersects isosurface: Calculate intersection position by solving the trilinear interpolation equation. Compute normal using forward difference gradient. Apply diffuse shade model. Else if ray exits volume without intersection: Mark pixel as background. iii. If any pixels in the processed tiles have block lists of size k but no intersection was found (unfinished pixels), handle them in a separate pass (Step iv of the source description). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import threading def multicorebonorendering(p, k, bonotree, screenwidth, screenheight, tilesize): # Phase I: Block List Generation regionheight = math.ceil(screenheight / p) blocklists = {} for t in range(p): ystart = t regionheight yend = min((t + 1) regionheight, screenheight) locallists = {(x, y): [] for y in range(ystart, yend) for x in range(screenwidth)} traversebono(bonotree, locallists, ystart, yend, screenwidth, k) blocklists.update(locallists) # Phase II: Dynamic Tile Grouping tiles = [(x, y) for y in range(0, screenheight, tilesize) for x in range(0, screenwidth, tilesize)] bits = int(math.log2(max(screenwidth, screenheight))) + 1 zorderedtiles = sorted(tiles, key=lambda t: zorder(t[0], t[1], bits)) weights = [] for tile in zorderedtiles: tx, ty = tile w = sum(1 for dy in range(tilesize) for dx in range(tilesize) if (tx+dx, ty+dy) in blocklists and len(blocklists[(tx+dx, ty+dy)]) > 0) weights.append(w) totalweight = sum(weights) LI = [] currentidx = 0 remainingweight = totalweight while remainingweight > 0: targetweight = remainingweight / 2 subtarget = targetweight / p for g in range(p): if currentidx >= len(zorderedtiles): break startidx = currentidx currenttileweight = 0 while currentidx < len(zorderedtiles) and currenttileweight < subtarget: currenttileweight += weights[currentidx] currentidx += 1 endidx = currentidx - 1 if startidx <= endidx: LI.append((startidx, endidx)) remainingweight /= 2 # Phase III: Dynamic Ray Casting liqueue = list(LI) liptr = 0 lock = threading.Lock() def phaseiiithread(): nonlocal liptr while True: group = None with lock: if liptr < len(liqueue): group = liqueue[liptr] liptr += 1 if group is None: break startidx, endidx = group for idx in range(startidx, endidx + 1): tile = zorderedtiles[idx] tx, ty = tile for dy in range(tilesize): for dx in range(tilesize): px, py = tx + dx, ty + dy if (px, py) not in blocklists: continue raylist = blocklists[(px, py)] if not raylist: continue color = castray(raylist, px, py) writepixel(px, py, color) # Step (iv): Handle unfinished pixels (size k, no intersection) separately threads = [] for in range(p): t = threading.Thread(target=phaseiiithread) t.start() threads.append(t) for t in threads: t.join() def traversebono(node, lists, ystart, yend, screenwidth, k): if node.isleaf: for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(screenwidth): if len(lists[(x, y)]) < k: lists[(x, y)].append(node.block) return if not node.bboxintersectsregion(ystart, yend): return if not any(len(lists[(x, y)]) < k for y in range(ystart, yend) for x in range(screenwidth)): return for child in node.childrenfronttoback: traversebono(child, lists, ystart, yend, screenwidth, k) def zorder(x, y, bits=10): z = 0 for i in range(bits): z |= ((x & (1 << i)) << (2 i)) | ((y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1)) return z def rayintersectsblock(px, py, block): return True # def solvetrilinearintersection(px, py, block): return (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) # def computeforwarddifferencegradient(pos, block): return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # def applydiffuseshading(normal): return (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) # def writepixel(px, py, color): pass # def castray(raylist, px, py): pass # p: Number of cores/threads. Typical values tested: 1, 2, 4, 8. k: Upper bound on block list size. Limits memory usage and traversal depth. Exact value not specified, but it is critical for limiting BONO node access to <10%. TileSize: Small image tile dimensions. Typical values: 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16. Unfinished Pixels: Pixels whose block lists reach size k but contain no intersecting voxels must be handled separately. These pixels will not be processed in the main ray casting loop if the logic assumes intersection or empty lists. A post-processing step or specific flag is required. Boundary Conditions: The screen division in Phase I must handle non-divisible screen heights (e.g., 1024 / 8 = 128, but if p=3, regions must be "almost equal"). Time Complexity: Phase I: Proportional to the number of pixels in the region and the number of BONO nodes accessed. Node access is limited to <10% of total due to k. Phase II: Grouping overhead is small, approximately 2-3 milliseconds. The grouping process requires at most a logarithmic number of iterations relative to screen size. Phase III: Proportional to the total number of pixels and the average length of block lists. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of block lists. Each pixel stores up to k block references. BONO tree overhead varies by dataset (e.g., 10.53% to 25.05% of data size for tested datasets). Measured Performance: Hardware: Clovertown platform (2 Quad-Core Intel Xeon 5320, 1.86 GHz), 8GB RAM, 8MB L2 cache. Resolution: 1024 \times 1024. View Angles: Zenith \phi \in \{15^\circ, 45^\circ, 75^\circ\}, Azimuth \theta \in \{22.5^\circ, 45^\circ\}. Scalability: Tested on 1, 2, 4, 8 cores. Strengths: Better load balancing than static tiling due to weight-based grouping. High cache performance due to Z-order spatial locality. Minimal synchronization overhead due to coarse-to-fine grain task allocation. Limitations: Requires preprocessing (Phase II) which adds latency. Complexity of implementation compared to simple static tiling. The method was developed for interactive high-resolution isosurface ray tracing on multi-core processors. The work addresses the limitations of standard octree ray casting with static tile allocation, which suffers from load imbalance and poor cache utilization. The BONO tree is used as the underlying data structure for efficient spatial indexing. name: Object Parallel Rendering
head: Object-Space Parallel Rendering, Parallel Object-Order Rendering
body: Object Parallel Rendering is a parallelization strategy for volume rendering that exploits parallelism in object space by dividing the volume dataset into subvolumes and assigning them to independent processors. Unlike image-space methods that decompose the screen, this approach distributes the data itself, making it suitable for large-scale datasets where loading the entire volume into every processor's memory is infeasible. It generates distributed subimages that must be merged via image compositing to form the final result. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V, a set of p processors, and a camera viewpoint. Outputs: A final composite image. Data Structures: The volume V is partitioned into p disjoint subvolumes V1, V2, \dots, Vp. Each processor i stores Vi in its local memory. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the volume V into p subvolumes. 2. Assignment: Assign each subvolume Vi to a distinct processor Pi. 3. Parallel Rendering: Each processor Pi independently renders its subvolume Vi from the shared viewpoint to generate a local subimage Ii. Note: Because a single ray may traverse multiple subvolumes assigned to different processors, the accumulation of optical properties (color and opacity) is distributed. Global Early Ray Termination (ERT) is difficult to utilize in this scheme because a processor cannot know if a ray will terminate in a remote subvolume. Local ERT may be applied within a subvolume. 4. Compositing: Merge the p distributed subimages \{I1, \dots, Ip\} into the final image using image compositing. This step resolves the depth ordering of fragments generated from different subvolumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectparallelrender(volume, viewpoint, numprocessors): # Step 1: Partition volume subvolumes = partitionvolume(volume, numprocessors) # Step 2 & 3: Parallel rendering of subvolumes # In a real distributed system, this runs on separate nodes. # Here we simulate the local computation for each processor. subimages = [] for i in range(numprocessors): localvolume = subvolumes[i] # Render local subvolume. # Rays are cast from viewpoint. # If a ray exits localvolume, the contribution from remote subvolumes # is not available locally, so the subimage represents only the # visible portion from this subvolume's perspective. localimage = rendersubvolume(localvolume, viewpoint) subimages.append(localimage) # Step 4: Merge subimages finalimage = compositeimages(subimages) return finalimage A parallelization method for geometric ray tracing that divides 3D space (world space) into subregions and distributes objects within those subregions across independent computers. Rays are cast from the computer containing the eye, processed in subregions along their paths, and passed to neighboring subregions until termination. Workload is balanced via adaptive subdivision and message passing between neighbors. This contrasts with the more popular method of dividing the screen into subscreens. A parallel rendering architecture for distributed memory systems where the total memory is an aggregation of physically separated but interconnected systems, viewed as a logically contiguous big space. It uses object space partitioning for data decomposition to map naturally to the distribution scheme, reducing the amount of synchronization needed compared to image decomposition. Strengths: Scalability for Large Data: Suitable for large-scale datasets that do not fit into the memory of a single processor or shared memory system. Memory Efficiency: Each processor only needs to load its assigned subvolume, avoiding the need for every processor to load the entire volume. Limitations: Compositing Overhead: Requires a final image compositing step to merge distributed subimages. Communication Cost: In distributed memory systems, inter-node communication is expensive, and the compositing step may require significant data transfer. Algorithmic Complexity: It is not easy to utilize global Early Ray Termination (ERT) because accumulation tasks for a single ray can be assigned to more than one processor, making it difficult to determine if a ray can be terminated early across subvolume boundaries. Load Balancing: Requires careful partitioning to ensure equal workload among processors, potentially requiring adaptive subdivision. Complexity: Time: O(N/p) for rendering per processor, where N is the total number of voxels/ray steps, plus O(C) for compositing, where C is the cost of communication/compositing. Memory: O(V/p) per processor, where V is the total volume size. Object parallel rendering was developed as an alternative to screen parallel rendering (image-space) to address the memory limitations of parallel systems when handling large datasets. While screen parallel rendering is effective for small datasets, it fails for large-scale data because every processor would need to load the entire volume. The concept of dividing object space (volume) among processors for optimization was also applied to geometric ray tracing by Mark Dippe and John Swensen in 1984, who subdivided 3D space instead of the 2D image plane. This approach is particularly relevant for distributed memory architectures, where object space partitioning is frequently used to reduce synchronization needs. name: Image-Space vs Object-Space Parallelism
head: Forward vs Reverse Mapping Parallelism, Object-Space vs Image-Space Parallelism
body: This family distinguishes between two task organization schemes for volume rendering on multicomputers. It separates Object-Space Parallelism, which processes data regardless of its projection, from Image-Space Parallelism, which processes pixels by mapping them back into the data. The distinction is defined by the direction of the mapping between the data space and the image space. Data distribution may be static or dynamic, and of any granularity. In object-space parallelism, tasks are performed per macro at each node, regardless of that data’s projection onto the viewing plane. This is a forward mapping of the data toward the screen projection. In image-space parallelism, tasks are performed per screen element (pixel or ray). This is a reverse mapping of a pixel into the data at a node. The redistribution task generally performs an image-space sort of the data and usually forms the boundary between object-space and image-space tasks. The data is already partially sorted due to its organization into macros and distribution among nodes. The parent scheme that exploits parallelism in object space by dividing the volume into subvolumes. Strategies where parallelism is derived from the image plane, often requiring ray casting per pixel. Strategies where parallelism is derived from the data volume, often using forward projection or splatting. The specific definitions of forward mapping (data to screen) and reverse mapping (pixel to data) as the basis for task organization are attributed to Westover (1990) and elaborated upon in the taxonomy of algorithms for multicomputers.
